<meta>This page appears to be a flyleaf or a preliminary page following the title page of the 1559 edition of Erasmus's Adagia. It contains a handwritten definition of the word "adage" and the bookplate of a later owner, Dr. Georgius Leonhartus Huth.</meta>

# Adage

A brief saying, <gloss>most frequently</gloss> which, because it is so often used for its wit <note>The Latin "argutia" refers to a certain sharpness, cleverness, or pointed wit characteristic of a proverb.</note> (in various actions and social dealings), has now become famous.

A brief saying, to which very frequent use on account of its wit has now added fame.

Wit is present, moreover, through either an implied meaning <note>original: "connotationem"</note>, an authority to be respected, or a remarkable example.

Above the shield sits a helmet with elaborate scrolling decorative foliage (mantling), topped by a crest showing the upper body of a figure wearing a flat cap or beret. The entire coat of arms is enclosed within a rectangular frame. At the bottom, a decorative scroll contains the name of the owner: GEORGE LEONHART HUTH, Doctor of Medicine.</image-desc>

--- Page 5 ---
<meta>This page begins the preface to Erasmus’s expanded collection of proverbs, the *Adagia*. It serves as an introductory letter to his readers, explaining the history of the book’s publication and his reasons for continuing a project he once thought he had finished.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM SENDS GREETINGS TO ALL LOVERS OF PHILOLOGY.

<sig>aa 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: -thenes [completing Demosthenes]</meta>

<margin>
This preface is suited to the edition of the year 1533, in which almost a half-thousand [proverbs] were added. In the later edition, no additions were made, or rather, far fewer.
</margin>

IF, ACCORDING to the ancient proverb, moderation is best in every matter, it was only right to apply moderation to the collecting of proverbs as well; for even of the best things, if there is not a surfeit, there is certainly a limit. For many reasons, I had decided to take a holiday from this kind of study hereafter: either because the nature of the subject is infinite—so that one who attempts to omit nothing achieves nothing, especially as ancient authors who have remained hidden until now are emerging into the light; or because so much effort has been spent on this business that I feared the reader, weary of the abundance, would cry out "Enough, already!" <note>original: "Ohe iam satis est"; a quote from Horace</note> rather than desire any addition; or because my age and mind, no longer averse to this kind of literature but no longer the same, are now drawn more toward matters in which it is neither unseemly nor useless to spend one's dying days; or because I considered that these types of "little flowers" and gems, with which the learned are accustomed to adorn their writings, have a bit more grace if one plucks them for oneself from authors not entirely common, rather than taking them from trite collections of this sort. Although this reason did not deter the Greeks from having so many grave and learned men write "collections of proverbs" <note>original: *parœmiologias*</note>. With me, too, the calculation of utility won out, because I saw that this work was of great benefit, both for washing away errors from ancient authors and for removing the obstacles <note>original: *falebras*; literally "rough places" or "pitfalls" in a text</note> at which those moderately learned often stumbled. Therefore, that we have now added this no small finishing touch <note>original: *coronidẽ*; literally a "coronis," a curved mark at the end of a book or section</note> was granted, to speak without deceit, more to the urgent demands of the printers than to my own inclination.

For a certain "Pyladean" friendship <note>referring to Pylades, the legendary devoted friend of Orestes; an emblem of inseparable loyalty</note>, which I once had with that excellent man JOHANNES FROBEN, and now share with his son HIERONYMOUS FROBEN—who is very like his father—and the equally wonderful industry of both in promoting the best studies, means that while I sometimes wanted to deny them certain things, and perhaps ought to have, I could deny them nothing. I hope, however, that this portion of labor brings as much utility to students as it has brought pleasure to me. Furthermore, even if none of these things were true, it seemed somewhat uncivil and less than candid to leave nothing remaining for other learned men girt for the treatment of this same subject—men who, equipped either by vigor of intellect, youthful industry, or a more extensive reading of volumes, will bring a richer harvest to studies. So far is it from my intention to obstruct their efforts that I shall even rejoice greatly if someone should eclipse our work.

There is only one thing I would not wish the reader to forget, as I have advised long ago: let him not wonder if some things in this work occur that were written at different times. The cause is the frequent editions, not without new additions. For first we gave a taste of this subject at Paris <note>original: *Lutetiam*</note>, through the printer Jean Philippe, a German by nation, who then had his workshop in the street of Saint Marc at the sign of the Trinity in the year 1500. The printer did not specify the month, but the letter which Faustus Andrelinus prefixed to it holds the fifteenth day of June of that same year. Somewhat later, Josse Badius rivaled this edition, then Matthias Schürer at Strasbourg; after these, we published the work increased to the size of a proper volume at Venice, with Aldus Manutius in the year 1508. Without my knowledge, Johannes Froben rivaled the Aldine edition at Basel, by whom the same work has been printed more than seven times, but never without additions. Since, however, this kind of writing consists of the industry of plucking from here and there, he who was the first among the Latins to attempt <term>παροιμιολογεῖν (paroemiologein): to collect or write about proverbs</term> would not carry away much praise, unless his skill in judging and treating them earns something. If anyone produces an edition older than that which I have shown to be the first, I will gladly grant him the praise that this noble thought came to his mind before others. And indeed it is strange that while among the Greeks so many most famous writers treated this genre by profession, among the Latins there was not one, even from the crowd of grammarians, who undertook a similar task; since in my opinion the gardens of the Latins flourish with "little flowers" of this sort no less than those of the Greeks, but I know not by what means a more leaning admiration for the Greeks has caused the Latins to seem to have neglected their own.

<margin>
The Latins do not yield to the Greeks.
</margin>

Otherwise, I do not see why Virgil should be held inferior to Homer and Hesiod, or Seneca (whoever he was) to Euripides, or Plautus and Horace to Aristophanes. For Marcus Tullius [Cicero], as far as this matter is concerned, far surpasses Demosthe-

<summary>Erasmus introduces the 1533 edition of his Adagia, explaining his reluctant decision to expand the work due to his friendship with the Froben printers. He provides a brief publication history of the collection from its 1500 origins in Paris to its growth into a massive scholarly resource.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Proverbs, Johannes Froben, Aldus Manutius, Latin literature, Greek literature, Humanism, Printing history</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Erasmus is finishing a thought regarding the initial attempts at collecting proverbs and then begins a chronological defense of his own work's priority and scope compared to his contemporaries.</meta>

### TO THE READER

...one. Therefore, whoever first undertook this task among the Latins, undertook a task that was neither unrefined nor fruitless. Two years had already passed since I had first introduced a "taste" of this work in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiae"</note>, when by chance while living in Louvain, I obtained a small book from Jerome Busleyden <note>A prominent Dutch humanist, diplomat, and patron of learning who founded the Collegium Trilingue</note>, who had then recently returned from Italy, which promised a collection of proverbs. In it, I found nearly seventy proverbs, collected mostly from the commentaries of Filippo Beroaldo <note>An influential Italian humanist scholar known for his annotations on classical texts</note>. I compared the year and the day. The year was the same, but my edition had preceded his by three months; and the fact itself clearly showed that neither of us was known to the other then, but that the same thought had occurred to both our minds. Thus, if it matters who first attempted this subject, both of us were first—if he is "first" who has followed no one else. I am speaking of the Latins.

But if he "increased" the proverbs who published more of them, then I certainly increased them, for in my very first edition I gave more than eight hundred, a good portion of which I had drawn from the Greek fragments of Diogenianus <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian whose work survived in abridged collections</note>. But after I sent forth so many <term>Thousands</term> <note>original: "Chiliadas"; from the Greek "chilioi" (thousand), referring to the large volumes of proverbs Erasmus compiled</note>, it became easy for anyone to add some supplement to their own collections, claiming it was "plucked from good authors"—and they wouldn't even be lying. For we ourselves have plucked all these "Thousands" from the very best authors, indicating with a careful list of names, as is proper, what we owe to whom; so much so that we have not even cheated Apostolius <note>Michael Apostolius, a 15th-century Byzantine Greek scholar who compiled a vast collection of Greek proverbs</note> of his due portion of praise; so far was I from wanting to hawk myself in "borrowed feathers."

I would consider these things unworthy of mention, were I not to see some people acting seriously as if they were the ones who first introduced this example. Others act as if they have borrowed nothing from my "Thousands," but have finished the whole thing under their own auspices and by "their own Mars" <note>original: "suoq; Marte"; a Latin idiom meaning by one's own strength or effort</note>. Yet, if they are plucking what they produce from ancient authors—since there remains an infinite abundance of proverbs that we have passed over—why do they heap up so many that we have already produced, and bring so few that we have left untouched? Why do they so rarely cite authors not cited by us? And if they know some tiny new thing, do they believe the theft is immediately well-disguised if they "attach new handles to old pots"? <note>A metaphor for presenting old material in a new way to hide its origin</note> If they have not read our works, with what face do they claim to have nothing in common with me? If they have read them and think they should conceal it, they certainly should have achieved this through diligence and skill in handling the material, so that the trickery would not be detected.

For my part, although I seem to be so well-versed in good authors that there is no great need to steal from the miscellanies of more recent writers, yet there is no teacher today so trivial that, if he were to publish a little book promising proverbs, I would not deign to read it. As the saying goes: "there is no book so bad that you cannot pluck some good from it." <note>A sentiment famously attributed to Pliny the Elder</note> To be unwilling to read those who handle the same subject as you is a mark of shameful arrogance; to conceal it when you have read them is a mark of even more shameful ambition; to deny the benefit received is a mark of the most shameful ingratitude.

I have said these things for their sake rather than my own. For as far as my own mind is concerned, I want everyone to be "three and four times" free to forge and re-forge proverbs, whether they want our own or prefer the ancient ones. If they do it less successfully than I, they will not have harmed my name; rather, an inferior purple cloth placed next to it will only make my own purple shine more brightly. <note>Purple was the color of high status; Erasmus suggests poor imitations only highlight his superior quality</note> But if they do so more successfully, I shall congratulate our common studies, and myself among them. Nor do I doubt that this age has many young men who are able to outrun me in this racecourse. The palm of victory is in the middle; let him who can, seize it. But more on these things than I had intended. There is one thing in which I will perhaps need the reader's fairness: since this work has been published so many times at long intervals, I do not think I have everywhere avoided repeating the same things.

->Farewell, whoever you are, friend reader.<-

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s introductory material. On the previous page, he defended his work's originality against contemporary collectors; here, he explains the practical organization of the extensive indices he created to help readers navigate his thousands of collected proverbs.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
### To the reader, concerning the two Indices.

<sig>aa 3</sig>

I began the literary <note>alphabetical</note> index against all hope, finding it confused and mutilated, because more learned men hardly deign to stoop to these humble tasks. Since this state of affairs was also inconvenient for me—to the point that some items were shoved into the wrong places because of it—I have "swallowed this boredom" and ensured that the index is both fuller and accurately arranged according to alphabetical order. Not content with this alone, I have also added things that crop up incidentally while discussing a proverb, whether they are related to the proverb's type or are otherwise worth knowing. Sometimes the same adage is expressed in various ways; occasionally, I gather several under the same entry. This diligence serves that purpose as well. 

Furthermore, so that the word order (which is sometimes different in the titles of the work than in the Index) does not cause confusion, know that in the Index I begin the proverb's entry with the words that are most important and distinctive. Most prominent are the proper names of people, places, animals, or things; following that, I use whatever is least common in the context. An example of the first is: *Pasetes’s obolus* <note>original: "Obolus Pasetis"</note> or *Obolus of Pasetes*; of the second: *Do not go to Abydos rashly* <note>original: "Ne temere Abydum"</note> or *To Abydos do not rashly go*; and *It is not for everyone to reach Corinth* <note>original: "Non est cuiusuis Corinthum appellere"</note>; of the third: *Drink hellebore* <note>original: "Bibe elleborum"</note> or *Hellebore, drink*; of the fourth: *Often even a gardener has spoken very opportunely* <note>original: "Sepe etiam est olitor ualde opportuna loquutus"</note>, and *A gardener has spoken opportunely*. For some entries in which nothing stood out, I have listed them twice. 

By following this target, you cannot fail to find what you seek. Nor has the wording been changed so much that even a slightly educated person could not easily recognize the proverb; nonetheless, this was not done in very many cases, for there was no need. The second index, which follows the thematic grouping of meanings <note>original: "sententiarum congruentiam"</note>, was compiled by us in a hurry some time ago in Venice. We have left it as it was, except that we added many things that were missing. More headings could have been added, and there are not a few adages that fit under several headings—for instance, *The leaking jar* <note>original: "Dolium perfusum"</note> could be said of a greedy man, a spendthrift, or a forgetful one—but the index would have grown to an immense size. We have pointed out much; what remains, we leave to your wits. To gain more fruit from this index, the catalog of headings arranged by similarity and opposition of meaning should be read through carefully once or twice.

---

->GREETINGS TO THE READER.<-

Whatever is treated here and there in this work, dear reader, and which is not mentioned in the first Index, you will find noted here in such abundance that you might complain of an excess rather than a deficiency. Nothing has been omitted here unless it is already contained in the first list. Farewell.

<meta>This page contains two dedicatory letters by Erasmus of Rotterdam to Charles Blount (Carolus Montioius), son of William Blount, Lord Mountjoy. The first was written during Charles's childhood (1528) and the second following his father's death (1536).</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM SENDS GREETINGS TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS BOY, CHARLES MOUNTJOY

So that you may be a truly legitimate <note>original: "γνήσιος" (gnēsios) - meaning born in wedlock or authentic</note> son of your most distinguished father, and a true heir to his goodness, my dearest son Charles, it must be your chief care that you do not fall away from your father’s honors. You should prepare yourself to succeed him in his virtues even more than in his wealth. For although he is famous for the ancient portraits of his ancestors, and his noble lineage does not lack a just abundance of riches, yet if you judge him as a whole, he is much more illustrious and wealthy in the ornaments of literature and the riches of virtue than in pedigrees or possessions. Custom and law do not allow children to succeed parents in other possessions until they have departed this life; but of those things which are the chief goods, children ought to take up the inheritance from their earliest years <note>original: "à teneris unguiculis" - literally 'from tender little nails,' a Latin idiom for early childhood</note>. Your father’s most loving devotion hopes for this with most ardent prayers. Excellent foundations have already been laid for this, as you have tasted the first principles of both literatures <note>referring to Latin and Greek</note> as much as your age allows. You have everywhere incentives for progress and spurs that are by no means blunt: first, your father himself; then, that most noble girl and your near equal in age, Princess Mary <note>Mary I of England, daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon</note>, born of a learned King and a learned and no less pious Queen. She already writes letters that are well-composed in Latin and display a character worthy of such a lineage. Then there are all the girls of the More family <note>The daughters of Sir Thomas More, famous for their humanist education</note>, like a certain choir of the Muses, so that I think there is no need to urge one who is already running. It seemed right only to remind you of this: since the work of the *Adages* <note>Erasmus's famous collection of Greek and Latin proverbs</note> was long ago dedicated to your father’s name, you should enter yourself into the partnership of this possession. You will take nothing away from your father’s praise, but you will add no small splendor to the work; finally, unless my mind deceives me, you will gain a fruit that is by no means to be regretted. It is nothing new for the same monument to be inscribed to several people; and if it were new, I would answer that a father and a son most like his father should be considered as one rather than two. For what else is a son but a father growing young again in another? And perhaps your father does not have enough leisure to attend to such cares because of his business at court, and so, as if weary, he hands this torch to you. Read, therefore, my Charles, this work consecrated to your father, and while reading, imagine that Erasmus, once your father’s teacher, is speaking with you. May the Lord Jesus preserve and prosper your whole life, most distinguished boy. Given at Basel, in August, in the year of our Lord 1528.

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM TO CHARLES MOUNTJOY<-

After you lost a most loving parent through the death of the most illustrious man William Mountjoy, and I lost a most constant patron and friend, most distinguished young Charles, it is only right that you, who shared in the inheritance while he was alive, should now take up the entire succession of your father’s goodwill toward me. You alone should take up the guardianship of the work dedicated to you both together, in which your father is in a certain way still alive for you. It is fitting to bear his death with more moderation because he departed at a ripe age, with his reputation untarnished, and with all his affairs happily settled according to his heart's desire. Farewell. The ninth day of February, in the year from the Nativity 1536.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS WILLIAM MOUNTJOY,<-
->BARON OF ENGLAND, SENDING HEARTY GREETINGS.<-

Once in Paris, most honored WILLIAM MOUNTJOY, I gathered a small "forest" of proverbs, as it were, in a very few days and without much precision—largely because of a great scarcity of Greek volumes. I did this so that you might have a little private commentary for your own use, as I had noticed you take a particular delight in this kind of literature. Some people, acting with zeal for me but with misguided and excessive enthusiasm, saw to it that those notes were published and printed, but so corrupted by errors that the work seemed almost intentionally ruined. Nevertheless, even as it was gathered and edited, it received more favor than I expected—whether due to your influence or the inherent spirit of the work itself. Indeed, it seemed to bring so much help to students of refined literature <note>literally "candidates of more polished letters"</note> that they confessed they owed much to your greatness and something even to my industry.

Therefore, to repair the fault of that previous edition (which was not my own) and to earn the gratitude of all scholars with a more abundant gift—and specifically to aid the studies in your England, which are flourishing more and more every day—I have returned this same work to the anvil. Having now obtained a nearly adequate supply of Greek books, I have reduced more than three thousand and two hundred adages <note>original: "chiliadas adagiorum treis, & cēturias duas," referring to the 3,200 proverbs in this expanded edition</note> from many authors into this commentary. 

It was my intention, as they say, "with the same oil" <note>a Greek idiom meaning to do two things at once or with the same effort</note> to add notable metaphors, clever sayings, excellent maxims, charming allusions, and poetic allegories. All such material seemed related to the genre of proverbs and equally conducive to enriching and beautifying speech. I had even more carefully planned to attach allegories of sacred scripture from the ancient theologians; there, I felt I would be on my own ground <note>original: "in mea harena," literally "in my own arena"</note> and performing the duty of my own profession, as that part pertains not only to the cultivation of the mind but also to the piety of life. 

But when I saw this part of the work growing into such a massive volume, deterred by the nearly infinite magnitude of the labor, I recalculated. Content with this current course, I have "handed off the torch" <note>a metaphor for passing on a task</note> to whoever else wishes to take up the next stages of the work. I do not yet regret this labor, as it has in some part renewed my memory of childhood studies that were becoming obsolete. But it seemed permissible to travel abroad in such studies only so far. To grow old in someone else's business and spend a great part of one's life on it—that I judged neither becoming for me nor likely to escape criticism. 

Therefore, I shall treat theological allegories, since they are my proper duty, when there is a sufficient supply of Greek volumes in that genre. I will do this all the more gladly because I see that for many centuries now, theologians have neglected this primary part and spent all their effort on the subtleties of logical disputes—a thing not to be blamed in itself, unless it were the only thing being done. I omit the remaining parts more willingly because I have learned that Richard Pace <note>Erasmus refers here to the English humanist and diplomat</note> has for some time now been preparing himself for them of his own accord. He is a man who can illustrate Britain with his genius; he possesses such purity of character and modesty that he is most worthy of your favor and that of men like you. With such a fit successor, it will happen that I have escaped the remaining labor not only with no loss to scholars, but even with some gain, and this entire work, whatever it is worth, will be owed to your Britain. 

You have the reasons why I undertook this work and why I took on only this much. Now, hear briefly what I have followed. In place of a formal order—if there is any order at all in these things—I have substituted an index in which I have sorted the proverbs that seemed to be of "similar coinage" and related into their own tribes. In collecting them, I was not so superstitious as to fear writing something down unless it bore the <term>phatin</term> <note>Greek: "it is said," a common marker for a proverb</note> or some other manifest symbol of its kind. Nor, on the other hand, was I so reckless as to sweep up everything that approached the appearance of an adage in any way; otherwise, someone might rightly complain that, like Midas with gold, whatever I happened to touch turned immediately into a proverb. 

Almost all the Greek passages we cite, we have rendered into Latin <note>translated here as English</note>, not unaware that this is contrary to the custom of the ancients and unhelpful to the elegance of the speech; but I have taken the needs of our own time into account. And I wish...

<summary>Erasmus dedicates his expanded collection of over 3,000 proverbs (the Adagia) to Lord Mountjoy, explaining his process of revising the earlier, flawed edition and his decision to focus on classical adages rather than theological allegories.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface of Erasmus's Adagia, addressed to his patron. The catchword "DES." refers to the author's name, Desiderius Erasmus.</meta>

# THE LETTER OF ERASMUS

->EPISTOLA ERASMI<-

May the skill of Greek literature be so widely propagated everywhere that this labor of mine might be deservedly looked down upon as superfluous. But I do not know how it is that we are so hesitant toward such a fruitful matter, and although we embrace the shadow of erudition more quickly than that without which no true erudition exists, and upon which alone the integrity of all disciplines depends. The poems, of which an infinite number occur here, I have rendered each in its own kind of meter, with very few exceptions; namely some Pindaric and Choric verses, because I saw it would be a matter of a certain ridiculous anxiety if I had rendered them in the exact same number of syllables: and again, it would be inept if I had wished to stitch on a different genre from the nearest series. In the rest, however, as far as the law of meter is concerned, I have permitted myself the same liberty—rarely indeed, but still sometimes—which the authors from whom we borrow them permitted themselves: such as in the trimeters of Aristophanes, an anapest in the even-numbered places; in the hexameters of Homer, a <term>long syllable</term> <note>original: "μάκρον"</note>, and the lengthening of a final syllable in the first beat of any foot, and if there are any other things of this kind. I thought this should be mentioned so that no one might rashly misinterpret it as a mistake made through ignorance. Certainly, as far as was possible in such an infinite crowd of things, especially ancient ones; then in such a great corruption of manuscripts; and finally in such a narrow space of time, which it was necessary to measure by our leisure rather than by the requirements of the work, I have diligently given my effort so that nothing might be found wanting by the fair-minded reader. 

Yet some things remain which do not satisfy even me. Regarding these, if hereafter anything becomes more certain, either through later reflection—which according to the proverb is usually better—or if a more abundant supply of books provides it, I shall by no means be ashamed to <term>recant</term> <note>original: "παλινῳδεῖν", literally to sing again or take back one's words</note>, following the example of the ancients. In this, if anyone else gets ahead of me and corrects our work, I shall even be grateful to him: so far will I be from thinking an injury has been done to me. Indeed, just as I approve the diligence of those who attempt this, so I admire the good fortune of those who can also ensure in their writings that nothing is left for Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery and harsh criticism</note> to pluck at. Certainly, my own mediocrity cannot promise that, especially in this kind of subject matter. But if we have been able to unearth anything unknown to the common crowd, of which kind you will find not a few things in this volume, I share them freely and without boasting: on the other hand, if anything has deceived me, I will no less freely allow myself to be corrected: equally prepared either to kindly teach what I know, or to frankly learn what I am ignorant of. For it has never pleased me to follow the example of those who, if they find a single little word, rejoice, exult, and triumph as if they had captured Babylon, and throw their service in the faces of students as if it were a reproach. Again, if anyone disagrees with a word, they fight there just as if for their hearths and altars. 

There is hope, however, that our late-night labors will be most approved by the fair-minded reader if you indeed receive them with the countenance you usually show, my unique Maecenas <note>A reference to Gaius Maecenas, the famous Roman patron of the arts; Erasmus uses it here as a title for his own patron</note> of studies. For by what other word could I more briefly or fully encompass either that singular affection of yours toward me, or the sum of your praises: you who are indeed the only one worthy of that most beautiful eulogy of Apuleius: "The most noble among the learned, the most learned among the noble, the best among both": to which must be added, "the most modest among all." For just as you have decorated the ancient nobility of your family with erudition, and your erudition with a wonderful brightness of life: so to all these you have added the most beautiful peak and <term>finishing touch</term> <note>original: "colophonem", a Greek term for a finishing stroke</note>, as they say, an admirable modesty of soul. Indeed, it would be a mark of absolute praise for you, and like the longest encomium, to have pleased the King—not only those kings our age has seen, but those whom the annals of the ancients record—the most wise King, and (which is the chief virtue of kings) the most diligent in choosing those whom he loves. 

Although it is the custom for writers to occupy a good part of their preface with the praises of those to whom they dedicate their labors—and this seems a debt paid to true virtue, so that its memory may be consecrated for posterity, which is done by no monuments more rightly than by books—to me indeed there lay open a field for praising you, truly and without disguise, as great as for no one else: yet because my simplicity is by no means unknown to you, which shrinks vehemently not only from flattery but even from every appearance of smooth-talking; and your singular modesty is accustomed to endure nothing less than even the most modest praises; leaving these things aside, we shall proceed to the treatment of the adages, which indeed it seemed best to begin from a definition, according to the precept of the philosophers. Read, and fare-well, or rather in the meantime be with me as much as possible.

<summary>Erasmus concludes his preface by discussing his translation methods for Greek poetry, his openness to scholarly correction, and a glowing dedication to his patron, whom he praises for his modesty and royal favor.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the introductory matter of Erasmus's monumental collection of adages, following the title and dedicatory materials. It establishes the theoretical framework for what constitutes a proverb.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S FIRST THOUSAND PROVERBS.

#### WHAT A PROVERB IS.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a classical figure (possibly a scholar or saint) seated at a desk with a book, surrounded by ornate foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

A PROVERB <note>original: "Paroemia"</note>, according to the definition of Donatus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian</note>, is a saying adapted to specific things and times. Diomedes <note>A Latin grammarian of the late 4th century</note>, however, defines it in this manner: A proverb is the use of a common saying, adapted to things and times, when something other than what is said is signified. Among Greek writers, various definitions are circulated. By some it is described in this way: *a proverb is a discourse useful for life, possessing much utility within itself by means of a certain moderate concealment* <note>original: "παροιμία ἐστὶ λόγος ὠφέλιμος ἐν τῷ βίῳ, μετὰ μετρίας τινὸς ἐπικρύψεως"</note>. By others it is defined this way: *a proverb is a discourse covering a clear thing with obscurity* <note>original: "παροιμία ἐστὶ λόγος ἐπικαλύπτων τὸ σαφὲς ἀσαφείᾳ"</note>. Nor is it hidden from me that many other definitions of the proverb exist among both Latin and Greek authors, but I did not think it would be worth the effort to report them all here. This is partly because in this work I have primarily proposed to follow that brevity which Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet</note> requires of a teacher wherever possible; and partly because they sing almost the same old song and fall back to the same point. Most importantly, among so many definitions, none is found that so encompasses the force and nature of the proverb that it does not either have something redundant or something missing. 

Indeed, Donatus and Diomedes—not to examine others for the moment—seem to require some sort of "wrapping" <note>an allegorical or metaphorical layer</note> in every proverb, as they have made it a species of allegory. Furthermore, they expect something "sententious" <note>original: "γνωμικὸν", meaning a moral maxim</note> when they add "adapted to things and times." Likewise, all the Greek definitions involve either a sentiment conducive to the conduct of life, or a coating of metaphor, and some join one with the other. And yet you will find many things cited under the name of a proverb by authors who are "unmoved" <note>original: "ἀκινήτους", meaning authors of unshakeable authority</note> which are covered by no metaphor. Conversely, there are not a few which pertain nothing at all to the instruction of life, and are entirely "diametrically" <note>original: "ἐκ διαμέτρου"</note> opposed to the nature of a moral maxim, as they say. 

Two examples shall suffice for many. *Nothing in excess* <note>original: "μηδὲν ἄγαν"</note>—everyone places this among the adages, yet it has no "wrapping" or concealment. And *Who could miss the door?* <note>original: "τίς ἂν διὰ θύρας ἁμάρτοι;"</note> is recorded by Aristotle under the title of a proverb; yet I do not see how that contributes to the conduct of life. Now truly, that not every proverb is covered by some allegory is clear even from Fabius <note>Quintilian, the Roman rhetorician</note>, whose words in the fifth book of his *Institutes* are these: "To which is related that genus of proverbs which is like a shorter fable." Clearly, he indicates that there are other types of proverbs which are not related to allegory. Although I would not deny that the greatest part of adages are colored by some species of metaphor. Then, I confess those are the best which equally delight with the pigment of a figure of speech and profit by the utility of their sentiment. But it is one thing to commend a proverb and demonstrate which is the best; it is another to define what it is in a general sense. 

To me—if the grammarians will grant me peace—an absolute definition of the proverb, adapted to this project of ours, seems possible to be handed down in this way: **A proverb is a well-known saying, distinguished by some clever novelty.** In this, "saying" serves as the genus, "well-known" as the difference, and "distinguished by some clever novelty" takes the place of its specific property. For it is the consensus of logicians that a perfect definition consists of these three parts.

#### WHAT IS PROPER TO A PROVERB, AND TO WHAT EXTENT.

Therefore, two things pertain peculiarly to the nature of a proverb: "being common talk" and "novelty" <note>original: "τὸ θρυλλύμενον, καὶ καινότης"</note>; that is, that it be celebrated and commonly tossed about. For from this comes the Greek word for proverb <note>original: "παροιμία"</note>, namely "from the road" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ"</note>, as if it were something worn down or "by the wayside" <note>original: "παροδίου"</note>, because it walks about everywhere in the mouths of men. And the Latin word for adage <note>original: "adagium"</note> is as if you said "a thing driven around" <note>original: "circumagiū"</note>, according to Varro. Secondly, it must be "clever" <note>original: "scitum"</note>, so that it may be distinguished from common speech by some mark. For we do not immediately admit into this catalog whatever is worn out by popular speech or made new by a figure; but that which is commended by antiquity and erudition alike: for that is what we call "clever." From what things novelty is added to adages, we shall soon show; now we shall indicate in a few words in how many ways "celebrity" <note>fame or common usage</note> occurs. They come into the speech of the common people either from the oracles of the gods, of which kind...

<summary>Erasmus defines the "proverb" by critiquing classical grammarians and offering his own definition: a well-known saying marked by clever novelty. He emphasizes that while many proverbs use metaphor or offer moral advice, these are not strictly required for a saying to be classified as an adage.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, definition of proverb, philology, Donatus, Diomedes, Quintilian, metaphor, allegory, Greek etymology</keywords>

--- Page 110 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s introduction to his collection of adages, specifically discussing the origins and stylistic qualities of proverbs. Catchword from previous page: "dicta" (sayings).</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>4</page-num>

that one: *neither third nor fourth* <note>original: "οὔτε τρίτος, οὔτε τέταρτος" (oute tritos, oute tetartos). A Greek proverb referring to something of no account or value.</note>. Or they come from the sayings of wise men, which antiquity celebrated like oracles, such as: *Beautiful things are difficult* <note>original: "Δύσκολα τὰ καλὰ" (Dyskola ta kala).</note>. Or from some very ancient poet, like that line from Homer: *Even a fool knows a thing once it is done* <note>original: "ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω" (rechthen de te nēpios egnō).</note>. Likewise that from Pindar: *To kick against the goad* <note>original: "ποτὶ κέντρον λακτιζέμεν" (poti kentron laktizemen). Meaning to struggle uselessly against authority or fate.</note>. And that from Sappho: *Neither honey for me, nor the bee* <note>original: "μήτε μοὶ μέλι, μήτε μέλισσα" (mēte moi meli, mēte melissa).</note>.

Indeed, while languages remained uncorrupted, the verses of poets were even sung at banquets. Or they come from the stage—that is, from the fabled plays of tragic and comic writers—such as that type from Euripides: *Upward flow the rivers* <note>Meaning things are happening against the natural order.</note>. Again, that from Aristophanes: *Go to the crows!* <note>A Greek equivalent of "go to the dogs" or "go to hell."</note>. Comedy, in particular, through a kind of mutual exchange, both employs many things tossed about by the common people and gives birth to things to be tossed about by them in turn. Some are drawn from the plots of myths, like *The jar of the unfaithful* <note>original: "ἀπίστου πίθος" (apistou pithos). Referring to the Danaids, condemned to fill a leaking jar in Hades.</note>. Or *The helmet of Hades* <note>original: "ἄϊδος κυνῆ" (aidos kynē). From the myth of Perseus; it refers to something that makes the wearer invisible.</note>. Some are pulled from fables <term>apologues: moral fables, like Aesop's</term>, from which comes: *But we do not see the knapsack on our own back.* Some are born from events, such as this: *Leucon carries one thing, Leucon’s donkey another* <note>original: "ἄλλα μὲν λεύκων, ἄλλα δὲ λεύκωνος ὄνος φέρει". Refers to a master and servant having different goals or secrets.</note>. Some are borrowed from histories, such as: *He conquers the Romans by sitting still.* Some have proceeded from <term>apophthegms: pithy, clever remarks or retorts</term>, such as: *He who does not possess himself, seeks Samos* <note>original: "ὃς αὐτὸς αὑτὸν οὐκ ἔχει, σάμου θέλει". A pun on "Samos" and "Samos" (a type of vessel or place), implying a lack of self-control.</note>. There are those snatched from a word spoken rashly, like: *Hippoclides doesn't care* <note>original: "οὐ φροντὶς ἱπποκλείδη". A famous historical anecdote about a man who danced away his marriage prospects.</note>. Finally, the customs or character of a nation, a specific man, or even a living creature—and lastly, some remarkable and commonly known power of a thing—have made a place for an adage. Examples include: *Syrians against Phoenicians*; *To "akkizein"* <note>original: "ἀκκιζέιν". To pretend to refuse something you actually want.</note>; and *A fox is not taken by gifts*; and *Twice cabbage is death* <note>original: "δὶς κράμβη θάνατος". Referring to something tedious or repetitive.</note>; and *Egyptian Clematis*.

->HOW NOVELTY ADDS TO THE PROVERB.<-

Now, what we have said regarding novelty is by no means simple. For sometimes the subject matter itself brings this with it, such as *crocodile tears*. Sometimes a figure of speech procures it, since an adage may be varied through almost every species of rhetorical scheme, which it is not necessary to pursue one by one. I shall touch only upon those it most frequently receives. **Metaphor** is almost always present. It encompasses many parts. **Allegory** is no less frequent, although this is considered by some to be a species of metaphor. An example of the former: *The whole matter is in the shallows* <note>Meaning the danger is over.</note>; of the latter: *The wolf gapes* <note>original: "λύκος ἔχανεν" (lykos echanen). Meaning a missed opportunity.</note>. Nor is **hyperbole** infrequent, such as *more naked than a snake's slough* <note>original: "γυμνότερος λεκβηθροῦ".</note>. Sometimes it reaches the point of an **enigma**, which, according to Quintilian, is nothing other than a more obscure allegory, such as: *The half is more than the whole* <note>original: "πλέον ἥμισυ παντὸς" (pleon hēmisy pantos).</note>. Sometimes **allusion** adds charm to a proverb, such as: *Strike thus!*; and *When two go together*; and *Such things, both good and evil, are brought to pass in your halls.*

Sometimes the **dialect** and **idiom** itself—that is, the property of the word—adds the likeness of a proverb, such as *an Ogygian evil* <note>original: "ὠγύγιον κακόν". Meaning an ancient or immense evil.</note>. It happens sometimes that **ambiguity** <note>original: "ἀμφίβολον" (amphibolon).</note> lends grace to a proverb. Of this kind is: *An ox on the tongue*; and *As many as the mouse in the pitch* <note>original: "ὅσα μῦς ἐν πίσσῃ".</note>. For "ox" signifies both the animal and a coin. Likewise, "mouse" is the name of a creature and also the name of a certain athlete. And "Pisa" is the name of a city, but with the addition of a small letter, *pissa* signifies "pitch." Sometimes the very novelty of the expression creates the proverb, such as: *In wine there is truth*. For if you say, "drunken men speak the truth," it will not seem like an adage. Likewise, if you say, "Without food and drink, lust languishes," it will not have the face of an adage. On the contrary, when one says: *Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus freezes*, everyone recognizes the appearance of an adage. Yet this novelty, like all others, proceeds from a figure of speech. Meanwhile, antiquity also decorates them, such as: *Give a pledge, but mischief is at hand.* Finally, in all proverbs you will find forms of the **ridiculous**. But to pursue these minutely might perhaps seem a matter of troublesome diligence. Nevertheless, we shall speak a little more copiously about proverbial figures shortly.

->How the proverb differs from those things which seem related to it.<-

There are, however, certain things related to proverbs, for instance: **maxims** <note>original: "γνῶμαι" (gnōmai).</note>, which our people call "sententiae"; additionally **fables** <note>original: "αἶνοι" (ainoi).</note>, which are called "apologues" by us; then **apophthegms**, which in Latin are "brief and skillful [responses]..."

# ON THE PROPRIETY OF PROVERBS
<note>original: "DE PAROEMIARVM PROPRIETATE"</note>

...sayings, it will be permissible to translate. Furthermore, there are *scoffs* <note>original: "σκώμματα" (skōmmata)</note>, that is, witty or mocking sayings. Finally, there is whatever presents itself as an allegory or some other proverbial figure. Although it is not difficult to distinguish these from the genre of adages if one knows how to apply each to a definition as if to a carpenter’s square and rule, nevertheless, to satisfy even the less experienced, I will not be burdened to explain the matter more simply and with a "fatter Minerva" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "with plain common sense" or without excessive refinement.</note>, as they say, so that it may be clearly established what I have followed in this work.

First, the relationship between a **maxim** <note>original: "sententia"</note> and a **proverb** <note>original: "parœmia"</note> is such that each can be joined with the other, and each again can be separated from the other, no differently than "whiteness" from "a man." For just as what is white is not immediately a man, nor is a man immediately white, yet nothing forbids that which is a man from being white; so it often happens that a maxim encompasses a proverb. But it does not follow that what is a proverb will also be a maxim, nor vice versa. For example: *The miser lacks what he has as much as what he does not have.* And: *Envy feeds on the living; after death it rests.* These are adages just as they are maxims. On the other hand: *I am sailing in the harbor* <note>Meaning to be out of danger.</note>, while it is a proverb, is not a maxim. Again, *Not the sword to a child* <note>original: "μὴ παιδὶ τὴν μάχαιραν"</note>, that is, do not give a sword to a boy; this equally encompasses the nature of a proverb, a maxim, and finally, an allegory. 

Yet there have been those, especially among the Greeks, who were not burdened to take up labor in this genre, writing a *gnomology* <note>original: "γνωμολογίαν"</note>, that is, a collection of maxims, among whom the most prominent was Nicolaus Stobaeus. I would certainly sooner approve of their labor than wish to emulate it. 

But to the rest. Aphthonius, in his *Preliminary Exercises*, simply calls a **fable** <note>original: "αἶνον" (ainon)</note> a *myth* <note>original: "μῦθον"</note>. This has, as he says, various names from its inventors: Sybaritic, Libyan, Cyprian, Aesopic. Quintilian says the *ainos* was called a "mythic discourse" or "Aesopic" by the Greeks, and by some Latins "apologation," though that name is not sufficiently accepted in use. Nor does he deny that the *ainos* is close to the proverb, but distinguishes them such that the *ainos* is a complete moral tale, while the proverb is like a shorter little fable. As an example, he cited: *The pack-saddle is not our burden, ox.* <note>Meaning: that's not my problem.</note> Hesiod used it in this manner:

> Now I will tell a fable for kings, though they are wise themselves.
> Thus the hawk addressed the dappled-necked nightingale.

Archilochus and Callimachus use it in the same way. Although Theocritus, in his *Idylls*, seems to have used *ainos* for a proverb:

> There is a certain saying: even the bull went into the woods.

Now indeed, **apophthegms** <note>Terse, pointed sayings attributed to a specific person.</note> differ from proverbs by no other distinction than do maxims. For just as that saying:

> He does not have himself, the Samian goddess,

is at once an adage and an apophthegm; so too is that remark of Simonides to someone sitting silent at a banquet: *If you are a fool, you are doing a wise thing; but if you are wise, a foolish one.* Likewise that: *It is fitting for Caesar's wife to be free not only from crime, but even from the suspicion of crime,* is indeed an apophthegm, but not likewise a proverb. Also: *You are accustomed to sit on two chairs,* is at once a proverb and a *reproach* <note>original: "λοιδορίον" (loidoryon)</note>. Conversely: *Mother never, father often.* Also that saying of Turonius: *They are for the character,* is indeed a scoff, but not likewise an adage. Although there are some things in this genre said so aptly that they can easily be admitted into the rank of adages, such as: *I am a friend as far as the altars.* <note>Meaning: I will help you, but not to the point of offending the gods/breaking the law.</note> For there is present at once brevity, a maxim, and a figure of speech. 

We have pressed these points somewhat wordily lest anything be expected from us in this work except what falls under the name of a proverb; and lest anyone think that something was passed over through negligence which we, being prudent and deliberate, omitted as foreign to our subject.

-> THE COMMENDATION OF THE DIGNITY OF PROVERBS. <-

Furthermore, lest anyone despise and scorn this part of learning as if it were too humble, excessively easy, and almost childish, I will set forth in a few words how much dignity these seemingly tiny things held among the ancients; then how much utility they bring if one uses them skillfully in the proper place; and finally, that it is not within just anyone's power to use proverbs correctly. In the first place, I think it is sufficient argument that the knowledge of adages was held in no small regard among the greatest men, because authors of the first rank did not think them unworthy of being diligently written about in several volumes. The first of these is **Aristotle**, surely so great a philosopher that he alone would suffice in place of many. He left behind, according to the testimony of Laertius, [books] concerning...

one volume of proverbs. Likewise, Chrysippus wrote two books on proverbs addressed to Zenodotus. Cleanthes wrote on the same subject. If the labors of these men were still extant, it would not have been necessary for us to fish out certain items with such great sweat from these minor writers, who are as careless as they are utterly corrupt <note>Erasmus is complaining about the poor quality of surviving manuscript copies of ancient texts</note>. There are some collections of proverbs found under the name of Plutarch, but they are very few and almost bare. Among the proverb-writers <term>parœmiographos: writers of proverbs</term> there are cited from time to time, both by others and by Athenaeus in the *Banquet of the Learned* <note>original: "Dipnologia", referring to the Deipnosophistae</note>, Clearchus of Soli (a pupil of Aristotle) and Aristides; then Zenodotus, who reduced the proverbs of Didymus and Tarrhaeus into a compendium. The proverbs of Theophrastus are also cited in the short commentaries on Demosthenes. From this it is clear that they also left behind commentaries on these matters. Nor does it escape me that a work is circulated under the name of Zenobius. But since I find certain things in the commentator on Aristophanes attributed to that Zenodotus who condensed Didymus and Tarrhaeus—which are read word-for-word in these commentaries—I would like it to be without deception on my part if he is cited in this work under the title of Zenodotus, whatever his name actually was; for what does it matter? Here, among others, he alleges a certain Milo to be a proverb-writer. A certain Daemon is also cited, both by many others and by the one who interpreted several phrases from the orations of Demosthenes, who seems to have composed many books on proverbs. For "Book 40" is cited. The collections of Diogenianus are also extant. The preface of Hesychius testifies that proverbs were explained more copiously by him, which Diogenianus had recently reviewed, even if the work itself conflicts with its own prologue; for while he claims to provide a list of authors and the subjects of the proverbs, he is so bare here that nothing could be more so. Whence I am led to the conjecture that this work was described more copiously by the author and later contracted into a compendium by someone else. Suidas, who must himself be placed in this number, brings forward a certain Thaetetus who wrote about proverbs.

But why do I mention these, when those wise Hebrews did not hesitate to publish several books under this title, and to include the adorable mysteries of the secret divine power in proverbs <note>Referring to the Book of Proverbs in the Bible</note>, in the unearthing of which the talents of so many great theologians have sweated, and sweat today? Nor is it a light argument that among good authors, as each was most learned and eloquent, so he sprinkled the greatest number of adages <term>adagiorũ: proverbs or common sayings</term> into his books. And to begin with the Greeks, what is more "proverb-like" <note>original Greek: *παροιμιωδέσπερον*</note>, if I may say so, than that great, not to say divine, Plato? Aristotle, otherwise a serious philosopher, is by no means burdened by interweaving frequent proverbs like little gems into those disputations of his. In this part, as in others, Theophrastus emulated him. Plutarch, a grave and holy and almost stern author, how many adages does he overflow with on every side? He did not think it beneath him to both propose and examine certain proverbs among his *Problems*, following the example of Aristotle.

Now to come to the Latins, omitting the grammarians and poets of both kinds (unless someone thinks Marcus Varro should be numbered among them, who gave proverbial titles to those *Menippean Satires* of his, so that it is clearly consistent that he borrowed the themes of his plays from nowhere else but proverbs), the Roman Emperors did not think it beneath their imperial majesty to respond with a proverb when consulted on great matters, which even now stands in the *Digests* <note>A collection of Roman law</note>: *Neither all things, nor everywhere, nor from everyone* <note>original Greek: *ὅτε πάντα, ὅτε πάντη, ὅτε παρὰ πάντων*</note>. Finally, who would dare to disdain this genre when he sees that certain oracles of the holy prophets consist of proverbs? Among their number is that one: *Our fathers have eaten a sour grape, and our teeth are set on edge.* Who does not also see that the venerable Christ himself was peculiarly delighted by this kind of speech? Among the Greeks this adage is carried: *I know the tree by its fruit* <note>original Greek: *ἐκ τοῦ καρποῦ τὸ δένδρον γινώσκω*</note>. Likewise in Luke it is read: *For there is no good tree that brings forth rotten fruit, nor a rotten tree that brings forth good fruit* <note>original Greek: *οὐ γάρ ἐστι δένδρον καλὸν...*</note>. Among the Greeks, the philosopher Pittacus sends his consultant to children playing with a top, from whom he might be taught a proverb about choosing a wife, and hear: *Drive the one that is your own* <note>original Greek: *τὴν κατὰ σαυτὸν ἔλα* — meaning "stay in your own lane" or "marry your equal"</note>. Christ cites a proverb of children playing in the marketplace: *We have piped to you, and you have not danced; we have mourned to you, and you have not wept* <note>original Greek: *ηὐλήσαμεν ὑμῖν...*</note>. Very similar to this is that saying of Theognis, if it is permitted to compare sacred things with profane: *For not even Jupiter pleases everyone, whether sending rain or withholding rain* <note>original Greek: *οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ζεὺς...*</note>. But if the authority of antiquity moves anyone, no...

# ON ADAGES AND PROVERBS

No type of teaching seems to have been more ancient than that of the adage <note>original: "paroemiarum"</note>. In these, as if in symbolic emblems, almost the entire philosophy of the ancients was contained. What else were the oracles of those ancient wise men but proverbs? Such great honor was once paid to them that they seemed not to have originated from man, but to have fallen from heaven. "From heaven," says Juvenal, "descended 'Know Thyself'" <note>original: "$\gamma\nu\tilde{\omega}\theta\iota$ $\sigma\epsilon\alpha\nu\tau\grave{o}\nu$"</note>. Accordingly, they were inscribed before the doors of temples as things worthy of the gods; and they were seen engraved everywhere on columns and marbles as things worthy of immortal memory. If an adage seems like a very small thing, let us remember that such things should be valued not by their bulk, but by their price. For what sane person would not value tiny gemstones more than certain huge rocks? And, according to Pliny, in the smallest creatures, such as the little spider or the gnat, the miracle of nature is greater than in the elephant, if one only looks closely. Likewise, in the world of letters, those things which are smallest sometimes possess the most genius.

### TO HOW MANY THINGS THE KNOWLEDGE OF ADAGES IS USEFUL.

It remains for us to show in a few words that there is no less utility in proverbs than there was dignity in ancient times. The knowledge of adages is conducive to many other things, but especially to four: to philosophy, to persuasion, to the beauty and grace of speech, and to the understanding of all the best authors. First, lest it seem strange to anyone that I have said proverbs pertain to the science of philosophy, Aristotle (according to Synesius) considers adages to be nothing other than the remnants of that ancient philosophy which was extinguished by the greatest disasters of human affairs. He believes they were preserved partly for their brevity and conciseness, and partly for their wit and charm. Therefore, they should be inspected not lazily or listlessly, but more closely and deeply; for beneath them lie, as it were, certain sparks of ancient wisdom, which was much more clear-sighted in investigating the truth than later philosophers have been. Plutarch likewise, in the commentary he titled *How the Young Man Should Study Poetry*, thinks the adages of the ancients are very similar to sacred mysteries, in which the greatest and most divine matters are usually signified by tiny and seemingly almost ridiculous ceremonies. For by these brief sayings, through a kind of wrapping, the same things are hinted at which the princes of philosophy have handed down in so many volumes. For that adage of Hesiod, "The half is more than the whole" <note>original: "$\pi\lambda\acute{\epsilon}o\nu$ $\eta\mu\iota\sigma\upsilon$ $\pi\alpha\nu\tau\grave{o}\varsigma$"</note>, means nothing other than what Plato—both in the *Gorgias* and in his books on politics—tries to show with so many arguments: "It is better to suffer an injury than to inflict one" <note>original: "$\beta\acute{\epsilon}\lambda\tau\iota o\nu$ $\epsilon\tilde{i}\nu\alpha\iota$ $\alpha\delta\iota\kappa\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$ $\tilde{\eta}$ $\alpha\delta\iota\kappa\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$"</note>. What dogma has ever been produced by philosophers that is either more healthy for the right institution of life or closer to the Christian religion? Yet such a great matter is embraced by a tiny little proverb: "The half is more than the whole." For he who takes the whole cheats the other, as he leaves nothing for him. On the contrary, he who takes only half seems to be cheated in some part. But it is better to be cheated than to cheat. Furthermore, if anyone should discuss more diligently and deeply that Pythagorean saying, "Friends' goods are common property" <note>original: "$\kappa o\iota\nu\grave{\alpha}$ $\tau\grave{\alpha}$ $\tau\tilde{\omega}\nu$ $\phi\acute{\iota}\lambda\omega\nu$"</note>, he will surely find that the sum of human happiness is comprised in so brief a saying. For what else does Plato strive for in so many volumes but to persuade us of community and its author, friendship? If mortals could be persuaded of this, immediately war, envy, and fraud would vanish from our midst; in short, the entire army of evils would depart from life at once. What else did Christ, the prince of our religion, do? Surely he handed down to the world only one single precept of charity, warning that upon this one thing the sum of both the laws and the prophets depends. Or what else does charity urge, but that all things of all people should be common? That is, that being joined together with Christ in friendship—by the same glue, surely, with which he coheres with the Father—we might imitate that most perfect communion as far as we are able, through which he and the Father are one, and we likewise are one with him. And, as Paul says, we are made one spirit and one flesh with God, and now by the right of friendship all his things are common with us, and all our things common with him. Then, coupled with one another by equal bonds of friendship, like members of the same head, as if one and the same body, we may be animated by the same spirit, grieve at the same things, and rejoice at the same things. This is also what that mystical bread—made from many grains into the same flour—and the drink of wine—poured from many clusters into the same liquid—admonishes us. Finally, as the sum of created things is in God, and God in turn is in all things, the universality of all things is reduced as if into one. You see how great an ocean of philosophy, or rather of Theology, such a tiny adage has opened to us.

### THAT PROVERBS CONDUCE TO PERSUASION.

But if it is not enough for someone to be wise himself, but he also desires to persuade others, how not unuse- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "unuseful" to be continued on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s introductory argument regarding the utility of proverbs, moving from their general value to their specific use as legal and rhetorical evidence.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

That this storehouse of proverbs is not useless, Aristotle himself sufficiently declares; for more than once in his instructions on rhetoric, he counts proverbs among the forms of evidence <note>original: "testimonia"</note>. Just as, he says, if someone wishes to persuade another not to form a close relationship with an old man, he will use the evidence of this proverb: *Never do a kindness for an old man* <note>original Greek: μή ποτ' εὖ ἔρδειν γέροντα</note>. Again, if someone should persuade another to kill the children of a man whose parent he has killed, this proverb will be of use: *A fool is he who, having killed the father, leaves the children behind* <note>original Greek: νήπιος ὃς πατέρα κτείνας παῖδας καταλείποι</note>. Now, to whom is it not known how much weight evidence carries in the faculty of persuasion? Nor do aphorisms <note>original: "sententiæ"</note> contribute in a small way. Yet among these, he also places proverbs. Quintilian likewise, in his books of *Institutes*, makes mention of proverbs in several places, as if they contribute to speaking well in more than one way. For in the fifth book, he joins proverbs <note>original: "parœmias"</note> with examples, as possessing a power equal to them, which is of the highest importance. Again, in the same book, he places them in the category of arguments which the Greeks call *judgments* <note>original Greek: κρίσεις</note>. Of these, there is both very frequent use and no small utility for persuading and moving an audience. Indeed, I would rather write down the very words of Fabius <note>Quintilian’s full name was Marcus Fabius Quintilianus</note>. "Nor indeed," he says, "would these sayings, commonly spoken and received by popular belief, be evidence without use. For they are in a way even more powerful, because they are not adapted to specific court cases, but were said and done by minds free from hatred or favoritism, simply because they seemed either most honorable or most true." And a little lower: "Those things also which are commonly received become, by this very fact—that they have an uncertain author—as if they belong to everyone. Such as: *Where there are friends, there is wealth*. And: *Conscience is a thousand witnesses*. And in Cicero: *Like with like*, as it is in the old proverb, *most easily gather together*. For these would not have endured forever unless they seemed true to everyone." Thus far we have related the words of Fabius. The same author, a little later, connects the oracles of the gods to proverbs, as if they were related and kindred to them. Now, what of Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>? Does he not, in his speech for Lucius Flaccus, take away the credibility of witnesses with a proverb? It is of this kind: *In a Carian, the danger* <note>original Greek: ἐν Καρὶ κινδύνῳ; meaning to take a risk at someone else's expense</note>. Or did he not, in the same speech, diminish the credibility of the whole Greek nation in giving testimony with this proverb: *Give me a mutual testimony* <note>A reference to "scratching each other's backs" in court</note>? What of the fact that even the philosophers themselves everywhere support their reasonings with proverbs? It is therefore less surprising if historians frequently seek the credibility of their narrative from some adage. Indeed, that which has perished in literature, which could not be preserved in inscriptions, on colossal statues, or in marbles, is preserved unharmed in a proverb—so that I may mention this praise of adages in passing. Finally, Saint Jerome does not find it burdensome to confirm a Gospel sentiment with the evidence of a common adage: *A rich man is either a rogue or the heir of a rogue*. Not even Paul himself disdains to use the evidence of proverbs in several places, and not without justice. For if *probability* <note>original Greek: τὸ πιθανόν</note> holds the primary role in persuasion, what, I ask, is more probable than that which everyone says? What is more likely than that which the consensus of so many ages and so many nations has approved, as if by a single vote? There is surely, there is in these proverbs a certain native and genuine force of truth. Otherwise, how could it happen that we see the same sentiment spread among a hundred peoples, poured into a hundred languages, which has neither perished nor grown old through so many centuries, which even the pyramids could not withstand? So that the saying seems rightly stated: *Nothing is stronger than truth*. Furthermore, it happens, I know not how, that a sentiment, when launched like a proverb, strikes the mind of the listener more sharply and leaves certain stings of thought fixed within. For it will touch the mind far less if you say, "Human life is fleeting and short," than if you cite the proverb: *Man is a bubble*. Lastly, regarding what Fabius writes about laughter—that the greatest difficulties of cases, which can be dissolved by no arguments, are laughed away by a joke—the proverb performs this best of all.

-> THAT THE PROVERB CONTRIBUTES TO ORNAMENTATION. <-

Furthermore, how much dignity or charm <note>original: "Veneris," referring to Venus/beauty</note> the timely use of proverbs adds to speech, I do not think needs to be explained at length. For first, who does not see how much majesty they procure for a speech from their very antiquity? Then, if there is any figure of speech which adds grandeur and sublimity to discourse; again, if there is anything that makes for the grace of expression; finally, if there is any method of wit—since the proverb is usually varied through all types of figures and all forms of wit—surely it will bring whatever those things are accustomed to provide, and will add a certain genuine and peculiar grace of its own besides. Therefore, if adages are interwoven skillfully and in the right place, the result will be that the whole discourse shines as if with certain little stars of antiquity, and smiles with figures...

He emphasizes that their longevity and universal acceptance prove their inherent truth and their ability to strike the listener's mind more effectively than plain speech.</summary>

...should smile with colors, shine with the little gems of ideas, and entice with the delicacies of wit; finally, it should rouse through novelty, delight through brevity, and persuade through authority.

### THAT THE PROVERB CONDUCES TO THE UNDERSTANDING OF AUTHORS.

Even if there were no other use for proverbs <note>original: *paroemiarum*</note>, they are certainly not only useful but necessary for understanding all the best—that is, the most ancient—authors. In these authors, while many passages are corrupted, these proverbs are often the most corrupted of all, because they almost always possess an enigmatic quality that prevents them from being understood even by those with moderate learning. Furthermore, they are often thrust in abruptly, sometimes even in a mutilated form, such as "upward rivers" <note>original Greek: *ἄνω ποταμῶν*. A proverb meaning things are happening against the natural order.</note>. Occasionally they are indicated by a single word, as in Cicero’s *Letters to Atticus*: "Help me, I beg you, while it is the beginning" <note>original Greek: *ἀρχὴ*</note>. That proverb, however, indicates:
"To heal the beginning is much better than the end" <note>original Greek: *ἀρχὴν ἰᾶσθαι πολὺ λώϊον ἠὲ τελευτὴν*</note>, <gloss>that is,</gloss>
It is better to apply the remedy at the start than at the finish.
These things, therefore, pour forth much darkness if they are ignored. But on the other hand, they bring a great deal of light if they are understood. From this ignorance come those monstrous corruptions in both Greek and Latin manuscripts; from this come the foul slips of translators turning Greek into Latin; from this come the ridiculous dreams and sheer ravings of certain learned men in explaining authors. I would report some of these here, were it not that I judge it more agreeable and more suited to my purpose that, after reading our commentaries, each reader's own thoughts might suggest to him how greatly writers of big names have raved in certain places. Finally, it sometimes happens that a writer silently alludes to a proverb; if this escapes us, even if the meaning of the sentence seems understood, a great part of the pleasure will be missing because the proverb was unrecognized. Of this kind is that line of Horace:
"That a horse may carry me, a king feed me." <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.17.43.</note> And in Virgil:
"Camarina appears from afar, never permitted by the fates to be moved." <note>Virgil, *Aeneid* 3.700.</note> For in the former lies the proverb "a horse carries me, a king feeds me" <note>original Greek: *ἵππος με φέρει, βασιλεύς με τρέφει*</note>; and in the latter, "do not move Camarina" <note>original Greek: *μὴ κινέιν τὴν Καμάριναν*. Referring to a marsh that, when drained against an oracle's advice, allowed enemies to cross and capture the city.</note>.

### COMMENDATION FROM DIFFICULTY.

But if, according to the proverb, "beautiful things are difficult" <note>original Greek: *Δύσκολα τὰ καλὰ*</note>, and the common people loathe as cheap whatever seems easy—to say nothing for the moment of myself and how much sweat this work has cost me—let no one think it is so very easy either to understand or to weave a proverb into speech. Indeed, just as it takes no small skill to set a little gem cleverly in a ring and to interweave gold with purple fabric, so it is not, believe me, for just anyone to introduce a proverb fitly and becomingly into an oration. What Fabius <note>Quintilian, the Roman rhetorician.</note> writes about laughter—that nothing is more dangerous to affect—one might say with no less justice about the proverb. For in this sort of thing, just as in music, unless you show yourself a supreme craftsman, you may be ridiculous; you must carry away either exceptional praise or laughter.

### TO WHAT EXTENT ADAGES SHOULD BE USED.

Accordingly, we shall indicate to what extent and in what ways it is fitting to use adages. In the first place, it will be necessary to remember what Aristotle elegantly advised in his rhetorical commentaries regarding the use of epithets, and that we should observe it in the employment of adages: namely, that we should use them not as food, but as seasonings; that is, not to the point of satiety, but for the sake of grace. Furthermore, let us not introduce them in just any place; for just as it becomes ridiculous if you bind a gem in certain [unfitting] places, so it is absurd if you use an adage out of its proper place. Indeed, what Fabius taught in the eighth book of his *Institutes* regarding the use of "sentences" <note>Aphorisms or maxims.</note> could be taught in almost as many words regarding proverbs. First, as has been said, let us not use them too frequently. For their density gets in each other's way, preventing them from shining out. Just as in a painting where nothing is sketched around the edges, nothing stands out. Therefore, even when craftsmen bring several works together onto one panel, they distinguish them with spaces, lest shadows fall upon the bodies. For every proverb stands on its own, and therefore after it there is always a new beginning. Hence the speech becomes almost disjointed, and being composed not of limbs but of fragments, it lacks structure. Furthermore, just as a border of purple inserted in the right place brings light, certainly a garment interwoven with too many marks would suit no one. There is also this disadvantage: that for those who hunt for frequent proverbs, it is necessary to mix in some that are either cold or forced. For there can be no selection where one labors for quantity. Finally, whatever is either immoderate or untimely loses its grace. In familiar letters, however, it will be permitted to play with this kind a little more freely; in serious oratory, they should be used as sparingly as they are accurately.

<summary>Erasmus argues that proverbs are essential for decoding ancient literature and warns that their misuse in rhetoric can appear ridiculous or cluttered. He emphasizes that adages should be used like seasoning—sparingly and with great skill—rather than as the main substance of a text.</summary>
