# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### THE VARIOUS USES OF PROVERBS.

At this point, I believe it will not be out of place if I indicate in a few words the ways in which the use of proverbs <term>parœmiarum; from the Greek 'paroimia' meaning proverb</term> can be varied, so that you may be able to produce the same adage in one form or another. To begin with, nothing sometimes prevents you from adapting the same saying to several meanings. For example, that phrase *a leaking jar* <note>original: "τετρημένος πίθος", Latin: "pertusum dolium"</note> can be applied to a forgetful person, a spendthrift, a greedy person, a blabbermouth, or an ungrateful person. For whatever you pour into the mind of a forgetful man flows out; nothing lasts with a prodigal; the greed of the covetous is never filled; the blabbermouth and the chatterbox hold nothing back; and whatever you bestow upon an ungrateful man is wasted. Sometimes, through irony, a proverb is even turned toward opposite meanings: for instance, if you were speaking of a notorious liar, you might say, *Hear words from the tripod* <note>original: "ἄκουε τὰ ἐκ τρίποδος"; an allusion to the infallible oracles of Apollo at Delphi</note>, meaning "Listen to the absolute truth." It also happens that by changing a single small word, a proverb may fit different people, such as *the gifts of enemies are no gifts* <note>original: "ἐχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα"</note>; and so one can say *the gifts of the poor are no gifts*, *the gifts of flatterers are no gifts*, or *the gifts of poets are no gifts*, so that the same adage is turned toward enemies, the poor, flatterers, or poets. For the gifts of enemies are believed to bring destruction; and if the poor, or flatterers, or poets give anything, these are more truly "baits" than gifts. In short, you may adapt a proverb to everything in which this similarity fits in any way.

There is a method common to almost all proverbs whenever a shift is made from a person to a thing, or vice versa. Toward a person, it works like this: the proverb says, *Not even Hercules against two* <note>original: "οὐδ’ Ἡρακλῆς πρὸς δύο"</note>. But I am more like Thersites <note>A character from the Iliad known for being the ugliest and most cowardly of the Greeks</note> than Hercules—how could I respond to both? It can be twisted toward a "thing" in this way: The proverb says, *Not even Hercules against two*; how can I be equal to enduring both sickness and poverty at the same time? A proverb is also varied by inversion, as it is said, *Not even Hercules against two*, and yet you, a single man, go out to fight against two Hercules? Likewise in this way: contrary to the common Greek proverb, *I looked for treasure and found charcoal*. And we have changed the phrase, not *gold for bronze* <note>original: "χρύσεα χαλκείων"</note>, but clearly, *bronze for gold* <note>original: "χάλκεα χρυσείων"</note>. Furthermore, sometimes an adage is explained and compared, and sometimes it is related as a simple allegory. Occasionally it is even presented in a mutilated <insert>shortened</insert> form, as if when someone answers something that is irrelevant, you say, *to ask for scythes* <note>original: "ἄμας ἀπαιτεῖν"</note>. And in Cicero, *the things which are written* <note>original: "τὰ μὲν γεγραμμένα"</note>, meaning "the things given." Sometimes it is enough to have alluded to it with a single word, as in Aristotle, all such people are *potters* <note>original: "κεραμεῖς"</note> among themselves <note>An allusion to the proverb "potter envies potter," meaning professional rivalry</note>. There are also other methods of varying them, but if anyone desires to pursue them more precisely, he may seek them from our commentaries which we wrote *On the Twofold Abundance of Words and Things* <note>Erasmus refers to his famous textbook "De Utraque Verborum ac Rerum Copia"</note>.

### ON PROVERBIAL FIGURES.

It remains for us to prepare ourselves for the catalog of proverbs, but only after we have shown some proverbial figures. For some sayings do not look much like proverbs, while others are *proverb-like* <note>original: "παροιμιώδεα"</note>, that is, in a proverbial figure, so that they can easily be adopted into the rank of proverbs. Therefore, on the whole, every maxim is related to the genre of proverbs, as is the metaphor, and especially the allegory. This is particularly true of those taken from notable things celebrated by the common people, such as from navigation or war. Of this kind are: *to sail with favorable winds*, *to make shipwreck*, *to turn the sails*, *to hold the tiller*, *to drain the bilge-water*, *to give the sails to the wind*, and *to shorten sail*. Likewise those: *to sound the trumpet for war*, *to fight with turned swords*, *to sound the retreat*, *to fight at close quarters and from a distance*, *to join feet* <note>to engage in hand-to-hand combat</note>, *to join hands*, and six hundred other things of that kind. If these are carried a little further into a figurative sense, they pass into the form of a proverb. Likewise those which are drawn from well-known things familiar to everyday senses: such as whenever gestures of the body are transferred to a matter of the mind. Examples of this are: *to press the thumb* for "to favor"; *to wrinkle the forehead* for "to take it badly"; *to snarl* for "to be indignant"; *to smooth the forehead* for "to become cheerful." Furthermore, those which are drawn from the senses of the body, such as *to smell out* for "to find out," or *to taste* for "to experience." They take on the face of a proverb whenever words peculiar to the arts are twisted elsewhere, such as *through all [the notes]* <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν"; meaning "in total harmony"</note> from the musicians; *diametrically* <note>original: "ἐκ διαμέτρου"</note> from the mathematicians; likewise *words a foot and a half long*. *To return to the anvil* from the blacksmiths; *according to the ruler* from the stonemasons; *I have drawn no line* from the painters; *to add the final act* from the stage. Sometimes a silent allusion, without a figure, brings something proverbial. This will be best whenever it looks toward a very famous author or subject unknown to no one, such as Homer among the Greeks or Virgil among the Latins. Of this kind is that in Plutarch: *since indeed many and good witnesses will be present for Plato* <note>original: "ἐπεὶ μάρτυρές γε τῷ πλάτωνι πολλοί τ’ ἀγαθοί τε παρέσονται"</note>. For an allusion was made to the custom of sacred rites, in which sa-

# ON THE FIGURES OF PROVERBS

The priest was accustomed to say, "Who is here?" <note>original: τίς τῇδε</note>. Then those who were present would respond: "Many and good men are present" <note>original: πολλοί τ' ἀγαθοί τε παρέσῐν</note>. Likewise, that phrase in Cicero’s letters to Atticus: "When two go together" <note>original: σύν τε δύ' ἐρχομένω</note>. And in Lucian, "sons of physicians" <note>original: ἰατρῶν παῖδες</note>, used for physicians themselves. Added to the appearance of the proverb are those forms familiar to pastoral poetry: **impossibilities, necessities, absurdities, contraries, and similarities** <note>original: ἀδύνατα, ἀναγκαῖα, ἄτοπα, ἐναντία, ὅμοια</note>.

<margin>**Impossibilities** are of this sort:</margin>
"But the labor is equal to measuring the waves on the shore" <note>original: Ἀλλ' ἴος γὰρ ὁ μόχθος ἐπ' ἄονι κύματα μετρεῖν</note>. And in Virgil:
"Therefore the light-footed stags shall sooner feed in the sky,
And the seas leave the fish naked on the shore."

<margin>**Necessities** are of this kind:</margin>
"As long as the wild boar loves the mountain ridges, as long as the fish loves the rivers." And in Seneca:
"As long as the bright stars of the ancient universe shall run their course."

<margin>This will be an example of **Absurdities**:</margin>
"And let the same man yoke foxes and milk he-goats."

<margin>Of **Contraries**, this:</margin>
"Now even the thorn-bushes hide the green lizards,
Yet love burns me." Likewise in Theocritus:
"Behold, the wave of the sea is silent, and the blasts of the wind are silent:
Yet the cares within my breast are not silent" <note>original: Ἠνὶ δὲ σιγᾷ μὲν πόντος... Ἀδ' ἐμὰ οὐ σιγᾷ στέρνων ἔντοσθεν ἀνία</note>.

<margin>Of **Similarities**:</margin>
"The fierce lioness follows the wolf, the wolf himself follows the she-goat." And in Theocritus:
"The goat seeks the clover, the wolf himself pursues the goat" <note>original: Ἁ αἲξ τὸν κύτισον, ὁ λύκος τὰν αἶγα διώκει</note>. There are also two other figures very closely related to the genre of proverbs, which consist either of the repetition of the same or a similar word, or the joining of opposites. Of this kind are: "I shall destroy you, a bad man, badly" <note>original: ἀπ' οὗ ὅλῶ κακὸν κακῶς</note>. "From a bad crow, a bad egg" <note>original: κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν</note>. And, "The wise student of a wise man" <note>original: θρέμμα σοφῶ σοφόν</note>. This is almost a solemn custom among the Greek comic and tragic poets alike. And "worthy things happen to worthy people." "A friend to a friend." "A bad man to bad men." "A good man to good men." "Each is dear to each." "Her own king pleases the queen." And "hand rubs hand." "Jackdaw to jackdaw." The genre of **Contraries** is as follows: "To take up just and unjust things, well and foully" <note>original: ἰδ' ἄδικα λάζυσθαι, εὖ καὶ μιαρῶς</note>, in Aristophanes. "To those willing and unwilling" <note>original: ἑκόντί τε καὶ ἄκον</note>, in Plato. "Sacred and profane, a holy deed" <note>original: ἱερὸς καὶ ἐπὶ, ὅσι' ἔργον</note>, meaning no word or deed was left out. Likewise among our own authors: "But where right and wrong are overturned." "He sang of things done and undone." Valerius Maximus used this trope in such a way that it does not hold together according to the true sound, but only exaggerates: "He says that while he held the highest command, he was slaughtered by you, a Roman knight, despite his protesting against every right and wrong <note>original: phas & nephas</note>." For how does it make sense for a wicked crime to be said to have been committed "against every wrong"? "By right or by wrong." "To do and to suffer anything." "Worthy and unworthy things." "What did he say, or what did he keep silent?" "At home and at war, publicly and privately." "What you know, you do not know; secretly and openly; in jest and in earnest." "With hands and feet; by night and by day." "Whether you place them first or last; neither great nor small." "Both young and old." "With gods and men applauding." To this form also belong these phrases found everywhere among the poets: "A maiden not a maiden, a brideless bride, a marriage that is no marriage, a city that is no city, evil Paris of Paris, unhappy happiness, gifts that are no gifts, a fear not to be feared, a war that is no war, an unadorned adornment, a thankless grace, impoverished wealth" <note>The author provides a long list of Greek oxymorons followed by their Latin/English equivalents</note>. This **Opposition** <note>term: enantiosis (a rhetorical device of using opposites)</note> sometimes also occurs in a compound word, such as "foolishly wise" <note>original: μωρόσοφος</note> and "bittersweet" <note>original: γλυκύπικρος</note>. For thus, as Plutarch testifies, lovers call their affection a mixture of pleasure and pain, so that they gladly waste away. To this also belongs that **enigmatic opposition**, such as: "Carrying I do not carry, having I do not have; a man and not a man, a bird and not a bird, seeing and not seeing, upon wood and not wood, sitting, with a stone and not a stone, he strikes and does not strike" <note>This refers to a famous Greek riddle about a eunuch hitting a bat</note>.

<meta>catchword: and not</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...and not a bird, and you see it and do not see it, sitting on a wood and not a wood, and not sitting, he throws a stone and not a stone. This riddle is recounted both in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, c. 200 AD</note> citing Clearchus, and in Tryphon, whom Plato also mentions. Of this form are also these: <gloss>tongueless talker</gloss> <note>original: "ἄγλωσσος λάλος"</note>, that is, a wordy person without a tongue. <gloss>vulnerable invulnerable</gloss> <note>original: "τρωτὸς ἄτρωτος"</note>, that is, one who can be wounded yet cannot be wounded. <gloss>shaggy smooth</gloss> <note>original: "δασὺς λάσιος"</note>, that is, hairy yet sleek. <gloss>offspring non-offspring</gloss> <note>original: "ἄγονος γόνος"</note>, that is, a fetus that is not a fetus. Athenaeus proposes and solves many such riddles in his tenth book. Nor does the logic of adages reject enigmatic obscurity—though it is disapproved of elsewhere—indeed, it embraces it willingly as if it were a family member. This would be the case if someone were to tell a person of unsound mind to "sail to Anticyra" <note>A place famous for hellebore, used to treat madness</note>, or to "slaughter a pig," or to "pluck a squill from the tombs," the first of which is found in Horace, the second in Plautus, and the third in Theocritus. Furthermore, many oracles have passed into the law of proverbs, and the symbols of Pythagoras seem to belong to the nature of parables. Hyperbole is especially characteristic of the genre of adages, such as: "he terrifies the sky with arms," and "he bursts rocks with his shouting," and "I am dissolving with laughter"—especially if some species of metaphor is mixed in. It is expressed in various ways: either by naming, or by comparison, or by likeness, or by epithet. Examples are: "A second Aristarchus" <note>A famous harsh critic</note>. And: "This Phalaris of ours" <note>A reference to a cruel tyrant</note>. And: "Louder than Stentor." "Like a lioness on a sword." "A Stentorian voice," "Nestorian eloquence." Truly, it will not be a burden to point out some sources from which this kind of figure can be drawn.

->FROM THE THING ITSELF.<-

For it is sometimes taken from the thing itself, as when we call a wicked man "wickedness"; a disgraceful man "disgrace"; a pestilential man "the plague"; a glutton "the abyss"; a shady character "the darkness"; a contaminated man "the stain"; a filthy man "the mud"; a contemptible man "the dregs"; an impure man "the dunghill"; a portentous man "a portent"; a troublesome man "an ulcer"; one worthy of prison "the prison." Almost every one of these can also be expressed through comparison, such as <gloss>more golden than gold</gloss> <note>original: "χρυσοῦ χρυσότερα"</note>, that is, more golden than gold itself; and: "more wicked than wickedness itself," "blinder than blindness," "more talkative than talkativeness," "more deformed than deformity," "more thirsty than thirst itself," "poorer than poverty," "more unfortunate than misfortune," "more speechless than speechlessness itself." To this class also belong those like: "Father of hungers," and "The fountain of all eloquence." And: "more than most speechless." And: "more than lost."

->FROM SIMILAR THINGS.<-

Closest to this are those drawn from similar things, such as: Sweeter than honey. Blacker than pitch. Whiter than snow. Calmer than oil. Softer than the earlobe. Purer than gold. More stupid than lead. Slower than a log. Deader than the shore. More wrathful than the Adriatic. Deader than the sea. More soakable than a sponge. Thirstier than the sands. Drier than pumice. More talkative than the bronze of Dodona <note>A reference to the resonant bronze cauldrons at the oracle of Dodona</note>. More fragile than glass. More rolling than a ball. More unstable than a buskin <note>A high boot that could fit either foot</note>. Slenderer than an Egyptian vine. Taller than an alder tree. Harder than a whetstone. Clearer than the sun. Fairer than a star. Paler than boxwood. Bitterer than Sardinian herbs. Viler than seaweed. More seething than Etna. More tasteless than a beet. Juster than a scale. More distorted than a thorn. Vainer than a flask. Lighter than a feather. More unstable than the wind. More hateful than death. More capacious than the abyss. More tangled than a labyrinth. Viler than a Chorcho <note>A reference to a proverbially worthless person or place</note>. Lighter than cork. More incontinent than a leaking jar. More translucent than a lantern. More dripping than a water-clock. Purer than a spring. More changeable than the Euripus <note>A strait known for its violent currents</note>. Dearer than one's eyes. Sweeter than light. Older than life. More brittle than a dried bramble. More troublesome than twice-cooked cabbage. Purer than a nail. More licentious than the Floralia <note>A Roman festival known for its lewdness</note>.

->FROM LIVING CREATURES.<-

Likewise from living creatures, such as: More talkative than a woman. More deceptive than a sparrow. More lustful than a goat. More lively than a deer. Longer-lived than a crow. More clamorous than a jackdaw. More vocal than a nightingale. More harmful than a Dipsas <note>A venomous snake whose bite caused intense thirst</note>. More venomous than a viper. More fraudulent than a fox. Rougher than a sea-urchin. Gentler than an Acarnanian piglet. More slippery than an eel. More timid than a hare. Slower than a snail. Healthier than a fish. More mute than a fish. More playful than a dolphin. Rarer than a phoenix. More fertile than a white sow. Rarer than a black swan. More of a turncoat than a Hydra. Rarer than a white crow. More voracious than a vulture. More wicked than scorpions. Slower than a tortoise. Sleepier than a dormouse. More unlearned than a pig. More stolid than a little donkey. More cruel than water-snakes. More fearful than a doe. More thirsty than a leech. More quarrelsome than a dog. Shaggier than a bear. Lighter than a water-spider, of which kind Lucian also heaps up several: <gloss>being more wrathful than puppies, more timid than hares, more flattering than monkeys, more licentious than donkeys, more rapacious than cats, more contentious than roosters</gloss> <note>original: "ὀργιλώτεροι μὲν τῶν κωνιδίων ὄντες, δειλότεροι δὲ τῶν λαγῶων, κολακικώτεροι δὲ τῶν πιθήκων, ἀσελγέστεροι δὲ τῶν ὄνων, ἁρπακτικώτεροι δὲ τῶν γαλῶν, φιλονεικότεροι δὲ τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων"</note>. Likewise Plutarch against usury: <gloss>more untrustworthy than jackdaws, more voiceless than...</gloss> <note>original: "ἀπιθανώτεροι τῶν κολοιῶν, ἀφωνότεροι τῶν"</note>

->FROM THE PERSONS OF THE GODS<-

Proverbs are derived from the persons of the gods: More untouched than Diana. More kind than the Graces themselves. More lustful than Priapus. More beautiful than Venus. More eloquent than Mercury. ->FROM NATIONS<-

From various peoples: More treacherous than a Carthaginian. Harsher than a Scythian. More inhospitable than the Scythian-Taurians. More lying than a Cretan. Vainer than the Parthians. Shorter than a Pygmy. More stolid than an Arcadian.

->FROM OFFICES<-

From occupations or ranks: More perjured than a pimp. Softer than a catamite. More boastful than a soldier. Gloomier than an Areopagite <note>A judge of the high court in Athens</note>. More violent than a tyrant. More monstrous than an executioner.

->ON SOFTENING THE PROVERB<-

Now, although this point may seem small and humble, yet since we have undertaken the duty of teaching, we shall not be burdened to advise the less experienced: namely, that in using adages, we should remember what Fabius <note>The Roman rhetorician Quintilian</note> commands to be done with new words or harsh metaphors. He says it was most elegantly taught by the Greeks, namely "to rebuke the hyperbole in advance" <note>original Greek: προεπιπλήττειν τῇ ὑπερβολῇ</note>. So it will behoove us to "rebuke the proverb in advance" <note>original Greek: προεπιπλήττειν τῇ παροιμίᾳ</note>, that is, to pre-correct and, as it were, meet the proverb halfway if it ever seems too obscure or otherwise harsh. For this genre admits—as was shown a little above—metaphors however harsh, the licentious coining of words, shameless hyperboles, and allegories obscure even to the point of being riddles. The Greeks "rebuke in advance" in roughly these ways: "According to a certain proverb," "as they say," "they say," "the thing said," "as the saying goes," "as the ancient word says," "just as they say," "as it is said," "as we say in proverbs," "as they say in jest," "it is well said." The Latins use almost the same methods: "They say," "as they say," "as it is in the old proverb," "according to the common trite speech," "just as it is commonly said," "to use an old word," "as it is said in the adage," "they say this truly."

<summary>This page categorizes proverbs based on their origins in mythology, history, and national stereotypes, while providing rhetorical advice on how to introduce such sayings into polite conversation.</summary>
<keywords>proverbs, mythology, Greek history, Roman history, rhetoric, Erasmus, Quintilian, metaphors, national stereotypes, classical literature</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### All things are common among friends. Proverb 1

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a classical figure, possibly a scholar or deity, seated in a landscape with architectural elements in the background.</image-desc>

*Between friends, all things are shared.* <note>original Greek: Tὰ τῶν φίλων κοινά</note> Since there is no other proverb more wholesome or more celebrated than this, I have chosen to begin this review of adages with it, as if with a happy omen. Indeed, if this sentiment were as firmly fixed in the minds of men as it is constantly on their lips, our lives would surely be relieved of the greatest part of their evils. From this proverb, Socrates concluded that all things belong to good men, just as they belong to the gods. "All things," he said, "belong to the gods. Good men are friends of the gods, and among friends all things are common. Therefore, all things belong to good men." It is cited by Euripides in *Orestes*: *For among friends, all things are common.* <note>original Greek: Κοινὰ γὰρ τὰ τῶν φίλων</note> The same author in *The Phoenician Women* writes:

->*For the griefs of friends are shared.*<- <note>original Greek: Κοινὰ γὰρ φίλων ἄχη</note>
->The same in *Andromache*:<-
->*For those who are truly friends have nothing of their own,*<-
->*but their wealth is shared.*<- <note>original Greek: Φίλων γὰρ οὐδὲν ἴδιον... ἀλλὰ κοινὰ χρήματα</note>

Terence in *The Brothers* says: "For this is an old saying, that all things are common among friends." They testify that this was also in a play by Menander. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the first book of *On Duties* says: "As it is in the Greek proverb, all things are common among friends." It is also cited by Aristotle in the eighth book of *Ethics* and by Plato in the fifth book of *Laws*. In that passage, Plato attempts to show that the happiest state of a republic consists in the community of all things: *The first city, the best state and laws, are those where that old saying is observed as much as possible throughout the whole city. It is said, and truly so, that the things of friends are common.* <note>original Greek: πρώτη μὲν τοίνυν πόλις... κοινὰ τὰ φίλων</note> He also says that a city would be happy and blessed in which these words were not heard: "mine" and "not mine." But it is remarkable how much this "community" of Plato's displeases—or rather, is stoned by—Christians, even though nothing was ever said by a pagan philosopher more in accordance with the mind of Christ. Aristotle, in the second book of *Politics*, tempers Plato's opinion, wishing for possession and ownership to remain with individuals, but that for the sake of use, virtue, and civil society, all things should be common according to the proverb. Martial, in his second book, jokes about a certain Candidus, who always had this adage on his lips while sharing nothing with his friends:

->*Candidus, "friends share all," these are your words, Candidus,*<-
->*Which you loudly proclaim day and night.*<-
->And thus he concludes the epigram:<-
->*You give nothing, yet you say, Candidus, "friends share all."*<-

Theophrastus speaks elegantly in Plutarch’s short commentary titled *On Brotherly Love*: *If the things of friends are common, it is especially fitting that the friends of our friends should be common to us.* <note>original Greek: Εἰ κοινὰ τὰ φίλων... τοὺς φίλους</note> Marcus Tullius in the first book of *On Laws* seems to attribute this adage to Pythagoras when he says: "For whence comes that Pythagorean voice: *The things of friends are common, and friendship is equality*?" <note>original Greek: τὰ φίλων κοινὰ καὶ φιλίαν ἰσότητα</note> Furthermore, Timaeus, according to Diogenes Laertius, records that this saying first proceeded from Pythagoras. Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights* (Book 1, Chapter 9) testifies that Pythagoras was not only the father of this sentiment, but even introduced a kind of communion of life and resources such as Christ wishes to exist among all Christians. For whoever was received by him into that band of disciples would give whatever money or property they had into a common fund; which in Greek and by a Roman word is called <term>κοινόβιον</term> <note>koinobion: a communal life or monastery</note>, namely from the fellowship of life and fortunes.

### Friendship is equality. A friend is another self. 2

These sayings are also attributed to Pythagoras as the author, because they embrace the same sentiment: *that friendship is equality, and one soul, and a friend is another self.* <note>original Greek: τὴν φιλίαν ἰσότητα εἶναι... τὸν φίλον ἕτερον αὐτόν</note> For nothing is so common as where there is equality of fortune; nor is there dissension where there is the same mind; nor a divorce where there is a joining of two into one. Aristotle in the *Great Ethics*, book 2: *Whenever we wish [to describe] a very [dear] friend...*

<note>original: "CHILIADIS PRIMÆ CENTVRIA I"</note>

The same author says in the same book: <note>original: "ἔστι γὰρ, ὡς φαμὲν, ὁ φίλος ἕτερος ἐγώ"</note> that is, "For a friend is, as we are accustomed to say, another self." Plato, in the sixth book of *The Laws*, cites it as an ancient saying and tosses it about as a proverb: <note>original: "παλαιὸς γὰρ ὁ λόγος ἀληθὴς ὢν, ὡς ἰσότης φιλότητα ἀπεργάζεται, μάλα μὲν ὀρθῶς ἀρκτὴ, καὶ ἐμμελῶς"</note> that is, "For that old word is both truly and elegantly spoken: that equality is the author of friendship." Yet Plato does not mean by this that all things should be shown as equal to the young and the old, the learned and the unlearned, the foolish and the wise, or the strong and the weak; rather, things ought to be distributed to each according to their worth. Otherwise, as Plato says in that same place: <note>original: "τοῖς ἀνίσοις τὰ ἴσα ἄνισα γίγνοιντ' ἂν"</note> that is, "to those who are unequal, equal things will be unequal." And just as "extreme law is turned into extreme injustice," so extreme equality becomes extreme inequality. As Pliny wittily said, "nothing can be found more unequal than equality in the casting of votes." Although some think this was also taken from Homer, with whom this phrase appears several times: <note>original: "ἴση ἐμῇ κεφαλῇ"</note> that is, "Equal to my own head" <note>meaning "as dear as my own life"</note>. Nor does the Law of the Hebrews differ from this, commanding that we love our neighbor just as ourselves. And Aristotle cites all these under the title of a proverb in the ninth book of his *Ethics*.

### THE SYMBOLS OF PYTHAGORAS
<note>Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher; his "symbols" were cryptic maxims intended to teach moral lessons through metaphors.</note>

But since we have happened upon the mention of Pythagoras, I will not find it burdensome to add his remaining symbols—which were celebrated among the ancients like oracles—at least those which I have been able to find among the Greek writers for the present. For although these may seem at first glance <note>original: "prima fronte"</note> to be somewhat superstitious or even ridiculous, nevertheless, if one extracts the allegory, he will see they are nothing other than certain precepts for living rightly. For there is no need to imitate the superstition of the Tyrrhenians <note>Etruscans</note>, who observe these things even without any allegory, as Plutarch testifies in his *Table Talk*. The same author, in his *Life of Numa*, records that certain symbols of this kind belonged to Numa in common with the Pythagoreans.

->Do not taste those things which have a black tail.<-

<note>original: "μὴ γεύεσθαι τῶν μελανουρῶν"</note> that is, "Do not taste of those which have a black tail." Plutarch interprets this in his commentary *On the Education of Children* as: do not have dealings with the wicked, or those who are of black and infamous character. Tryphon the Grammarian, mentioning this among examples of enigmas, interprets it in this way: <note>original: "Ψευδῆ λόγον μὴ προΐεσθαι. τὸ γὰρ ψεῦδος ἐν τοῖς ἐσχάτοις μέρεσι μελαίνεται, ἢ ἀμαυροῦται"</note> that is, "Do not utter a lying speech. For a lie turns black or grows dark in its final parts." Some refer this to the cuttlefish, which hides itself with the ink it carries in its tail. Although Pliny, in book 32, the last chapter, lists the "Black-tail" <term>Melanurus: a type of sea bream</term> among the fishes, while he discussed cuttlefish extensively in earlier books, so it seems the Black-tail and the Cuttlefish are not the same fish. Theodorus Gaza translates *melanurus* as "Oculata" <note>the "eyed" fish</note>, which fish he names only in the place we just indicated.

->Do not step over the balance.<-

<note>original: "Μὴ ζυγὸν ὑπερβαίνειν"</note> that is, "Do not leap over the scales," which means: Do not do anything beyond what is just and fair. For that the scales were commonly held as a symbol of equity in the old days is indicated by that Doric proverb: <note>original: "σαχάνης δικαιότερος"</note> that is, "more just than a balance." Demetrius of Byzantium interprets it in this manner in Athenaeus, book 10 of the *Deipnosophistae*.

->Do not sit upon a choenix.<-
<note>A choenix was an ancient Greek dry measure, roughly a day's ration of grain.</note>

<note>original: "Χοίνικι μὴ ἐπικαθίσαι"</note> that is, "Do not sit upon a choenix." Saint Jerome interprets this as: do not be anxious about your food for the morrow. For a *choenix* is a measured portion and a daily food supply, as in Homer's *Odyssey*, book 19:
> For I will not endure an idle man, whoever touches my *choenix*.
> <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ἀεργὸν ἀνέξομαι, ὅσκην ἐμῆς γε Χοίνικος ἅπτηται"</note>

Laertius and Suidas explain it in the same way. Furthermore, a daily ration of food was formerly distributed to slaves by the *choenix*, so that they in turn might perform their weight of work; for which reason the Pythian Apollo called the Corinthians "choenix-measurers," because they possessed forty-six thousand slaves. The authority for this is Athenaeus, book 6. Plutarch, however, interprets it far differently: namely, that one should not indulge in idleness, but provide for a living through industry, lest it be lacking in the future. He mentions this symbol in his *Table Talk* in these very words: <note>original: "μετὰ δὲ πυθαγορικῆς χοίνικος, ἐφ' ἧς ἀπηγόρευε καθῆσθαι, διδάσκων ἡμᾶς, ἀεί τι τοῦ παρόντος εἰς τὸ μέλλον ἀπολείπειν, καὶ τὸ αὔριον ἐν τῇ σήμερον μνημονεύειν"</note> that is, "Together with the Pythagorean *choenix*, upon which he forbade us to sit, teaching us always to leave something of the present for the future, and to remember tomorrow while it is yet today." This means that from that which...

He also thinks the ancestors wished to signify the same thing by making it a religious habit to remove empty tables. Demetrius of Byzantium, in the writings of Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae' (Banquet of the Learned)</note>, interprets it to mean that one ought not to look only at what belongs to the present day, but that tomorrow must always be expected—agreeing almost entirely with Plutarch. For my part, since in symbols of this kind it is not only permitted but even necessary to divine the meaning, I believe this Pythagorean enigma was taken from the passage of Homer which we just cited: it signifies that one ought not, through laziness, to pursue leisure and the food of others, but that each person should provide for themselves by their own industry the means by which they may maintain a clean life. For it is parasitic and foul to live off another’s plate <note>original: "aliena vivere quadra"</note>, and to possess no skill by which you might live as a <term>house-guest (oikositos)</term> <note>original: οἰκόσιτος; one who provides their own food while living in another's house</note>. Homer notes this even in the character of Irus, when he says in the *Odyssey*, Book 18:

<gloss>that is,</gloss>
<term>But he was distinguished by a lazy belly,</term>
<term>To eat and drink incessantly. But in him there was no</term>
<term>Strength or force.</term>
<note>original Greek: μετὰ δ’ ἔπρεπε γαστέρι μάργῃ, Ἀζηχὲς φαγέμεν, καὶ πιέμεν. ὁ δέ οἱ λίς Οὐ δὲ βίη.</note>

But he was notable for an idle belly, continually drinking and eating; yet no industry and no strength was present. Nor does that saying of the Apostle Paul—not at all unknown to the common people—differ from this: "He who does not work, shall not eat." When the sixth edition of our *Chiliades* <note>Erasmus's "Thousands" of adages</note> was being prepared, if I am not mistaken, in the year 1517 after the redemption of the world, there opportunely came to light the work *Ancient Readings* by Ludovico Celio Rhodiginus. Regarding what I think of that work as a whole, I have no need to pass judgment now; although the mere taste of the work (for I have only sipped from it) immediately reveals a man flitting through every kind of author with an insatiable greed for reading, and delighting in weaving new garlands from the unraveled wreaths of others. However, as to why he nowhere included mention of Giorgio Valla, Volaterranus, or myself—though it is probable he was helped not a little by our commentaries—I know this was done by his judgment, not out of malice. Even when treating this very symbol, he denies that he wishes to bring forward anything that "bubbles up" <note>original: "rebulliat"</note> in the commentaries of others (for so he speaks), even though he brings forward not a few things which I find in my own *Chiliades*. For I do not think it concerns me that he even gives birth to proverbs, but of the sort that you could fill six hundred "thousands" if that task were to your heart. When a little more leisure falls to me, I shall not find it burdensome to observe more attentively if there is anything there pertaining to our present purpose, by no means intending to defraud the man of his praise if he has contributed anything. Furthermore, as to the explanation of this enigma, it does not escape me what he divined concerning the *choenix* and the rolled-up blankets; I neither approve nor refute his invention for the present. Certainly, it would not please me to divine in that manner if something were otherwise supplied by reliable authors; as soon as those defenses fail us, then perhaps we ourselves shall divine, but in such a way that we do not expend much serious effort on matters of this kind. For what is the point of anxiously inquiring what he meant, who took pains to ensure he could not be understood? While I was writing this, I learned from the letters of learned men that Rhodiginus has met his final day, not without heavy grief and loss to studies. For those who knew him intimately say he was a man of Christian integrity, untiring in the labor of study, even as he reached extreme old age. Therefore, I easily forgive so many virtues if he felt less than candidly toward us. For the public utility of studies carries more weight with me than the consideration of my own name.

->Do not join hands with everyone.<-

<term>Do not thrust out your right hand to everyone.</term> <note>original Greek: Μὴ παντὶ ἐμβάλλειν δεξιάν.</note> That is, do not extend your right hand to just anyone; which means: do not rashly admit anyone into your familiarity, but choose whom you would love. The same is cited and explained by Plutarch in his essay *On Having Many Friends*. It agrees with that apophthegm of Solon, which Diogenes Laertius records from Apollodorus: <term>Do not be quick to acquire friends, but those whom you have acquired, do not reject.</term> <note>original Greek: Φίλους μὴ ταχὺ κτῶ, οὓς δ’ ἂν κτήσῃ μὴ ἀποδοκίμαζε.</note>

->Do not wear a tight ring.<-

<term>Do not wear a narrow ring.</term> <note>original Greek: Μὴ φορεῖν στενὸν δακτύλιον.</note> That is, do not wear a tight ring. This means, according to the interpretation of Saint Jerome, do not live anxiously; and do not cast yourself into slavery, or into a way of life from which you cannot extricate yourself. Indeed, whoever wears a narrow ring in a way casts chains upon himself.

->Do not poke the fire with a sword.<-

<term>Do not stir the fire with iron.</term> <note>original Greek: πῦρ σιδήρῳ μὴ σκαλεύειν.</note> That is, do not poke the fire with a sword; which means, do not provoke one who is moved by anger. Rather, it is better to yield, and to soothe a swollen mind with gentle words. So says Saint Jerome.

Diogenes Laertius explains it thus: that the anger of the powerful and the fierce should not be provoked with insults, because the more a flame is stirred, the more and more it gains strength. Plutarch does not disagree with this interpretation. However, Plato in the sixth book of *The Laws* used it in such a way that it seems commonly said of those who labor in vain at what can by no means be accomplished, showing that it was a kind of game to try to cut fire with a sword. Saint Basil, in his *Letter to his Nephews*, related it to almost the same sense: that "To cut fire with a sword" and "To draw water with a sieve" mean the same thing. Lucian alluded to this excessively in the second book of his *True Histories* when he was departing from the Blessed Isles, pretending he was warned by Rhadamanthus that if he ever returned to this world of ours, he should observe three things: <note>original Greek: μὴ πῦρ μαχαίρᾳ σκαλεύειν, κτλ.</note> *not to stir the fire with a sword, not to eat lupines, and not to approach a boy over eighteen years of age.* Indeed, he remembered that he would eventually return to that island. Horace, by this saying, seems to indicate cruelty joined with insanity. For love is a madness in itself, which, if it breaks out into fights and slaughter, is "poking the fire with a sword." In the second book of his *Satires*, Satire III:

-> Do not eat your heart. <-

<note>original Greek: Μὴ ἐσθίειν τὴν καρδίαν</note> That is, *Do not eat your heart.* This means: do not torture your own soul with cares. Demetrius of Byzantium explains it in this manner in Athenaeus. Or: do not make your life shorter with anxieties. For Aristotle, in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, says that the heart is the fountain of all senses, life, and blood. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
*Yet biting my spirit, I was born so.* -> That is, <-
Biting my own mind, I speak thus. -> Likewise Theognis, <-

And in Book XXIV: *You eat your own heart.* -> Likewise in the Odyssey, Book IX: <-
*There for two nights and two days continuously*
*We lay together, eating our spirit with weariness and grief.* -> That is, <-
Here we sat for two suns and nights,
Gnawing the mind with cares and labor alike. -> Also in the Iliad, Book I: <-
*But you will gnaw the spirit within.* -> That is, <-
You shall gnaw your heartstrings within.

-> Abstain from beans. <-

<note>original Greek: Κυάμων ἀπέχεσθαι</note> That is, *Abstain from beans.* Various interpretations of this enigma are found. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Education of Children*, explains it in this way: that one must abstain from handling the duties of the republic, because anciently, in the election of magistrates, votes were cast by beans instead of pebbles <note>The "bean" was the ancient ballot; thus, "avoid beans" meant "stay out of politics."</note>. However, the same author in his *Problems* brings forward a different cause: namely, that all legumes bring wind and impure moisture to the body, and for this reason incite one to Lust <note>original: "Venerem," referring to Venus/sexual desire</note>. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] seems to have been of the same opinion, writing in the first book of *On Divination* in this manner: "Plato therefore bids us go to sleep with the body so affected that there is nothing to bring error or disturbance to the mind. For which reason it is thought the Pythagoreans were forbidden to eat beans, a food which causes great flatulence. This food is known to be contrary to those seeking tranquility of mind." Yet Aristoxenus, in Aulus Gellius, Book IV, Chapter XI, refutes this opinion, affirming that Pythagoras used no legume more often than beans, because that food would gently move and soothe the bowels. Furthermore, Gellius thinks the cause of the error regarding not eating the "cyamos" <note>bean</note> was that in the poem of Empedocles (who followed Pythagorean teachings), this verse is found:
*Wretches, utter wretches, keep your hands off beans.* -> That is, <-

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the Pythagorean symbols (Adagia), specifically focusing on the prohibition of beans and the symbolic warnings against returning to life at its end.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"Ah, you wretches, keep your hands away from beans!"
<note>original: "Ah miseri a cyamo, miseri subducite dextras." A line attributed to the philosopher Empedocles.</note>
For most people have thought that the word *kyamos* <note>Greek: κύαμον</note> refers to the common legume. But those who have examined the poems of Empedocles more diligently and skillfully (to use the words of Aulus Gellius) say that *kyamoi* in this passage signifies the testicles. They say they were called *kyamoi* by Pythagoras in a hidden and symbolic way, as if they were "terrible for conceiving" and "the causes of conceiving" <note>original: "εἰς τὸ κύειν δεινοὶ, & αἴτιοι τοῦ κύειν"</note>—that is, effective for carrying in the womb, the causes of pregnancy, and providing the power for human generation. Therefore, by that verse, Empedocles did not want to lead men away from eating beans, but from the discharge of sexual activity. Regarding the reasons for the forbidden bean, Laertius records these points from Aristotle: "Aristotle says in his book *On Beans* that Pythagoras commanded abstinence from beans either because they are similar to the private parts, or because they are like the gates of Hades (for this is the only legume without joints), or because it corrupts, or because it is similar to the nature of the universe, or because it is oligarchic, since they are used for casting lots." <note>original: "φησὶ δὲ Ἀριστοτέλης... κληροῦνται γοῦν αὐτοῖς."</note> That is, Aristotle says in the book *On Beans* that he ordered abstinence from beans either because they were similar to the shameful parts, or because of the gates of the underworld (for this one legume is devoid of generation), or because it corrupts, or because it is similar to the nature of the universe, or because it pertains to oligarchy, for they cast lots with beans. With what Aristotle touched upon in the last place, the opinion of certain people agrees, who think Pythagoras deterred men from taking up public office by this riddle. I am even more pleased by what is added by the one who collected the stories touched upon by Gregory Nazianzen: that to "eat beans" refers to those who, corrupted by profit, cast their votes. Plutarch, in the same Gellius, testifies that Aristotle left it written that Pythagoras abstained from "the womb, the heart, and the sea-nettle," <note>original: "μήτρας καὶ καρδίας, & ἀκαλυφῆς"</note> and certain others of that kind. Theon the grammarian, in Plutarch’s *Symposics*, relates that among the Egyptians there is such a great religious awe of beans that they neither sow nor eat them; indeed, it is not even lawful to look at them, according to Herodotus. Furthermore, among the Romans, beans were held among the funereal things, since it was not permitted for the Priest of Jupiter <term>Flamen Dialis: the high priest of Jupiter in Roman religion</term> to touch or name them, because they were thought to belong to the dead. For they were also thrown to the ghosts <note>original: "lemuribus... laruis"</note> and used in sacrifices for deceased parents, and in their flower, letters of mourning seem to appear, as Pompeius Festus testifies. Pliny thinks the bean was condemned by Pythagoras for the reason that it dulls the senses and causes insomnia, or because the souls of the dead are in it. For which reason they are also taken up in sacrifices for parents. Whence Plutarch also testifies that legumes are especially powerful for summoning the spirits of the dead. Varro records that the priest does not eat them for this reason: because in its flower, mournful letters are found. However, where Plutarch in his *Roman Questions* reports among other things that beans were condemned because they are "namesakes of Lethe and Erebus," <note>Lethe is the river of forgetfulness; Erebus is the darkness of the underworld.</note> I did not sufficiently understand what he meant—until, having consulted the Greek manuscripts, I finally discovered an error of either the scribe or the translator. For the Greek text reads: "Whether, as the Pythagoreans avoided beans for the reasons mentioned, or because the vetch and the chickpea are namesakes of Erebus and Lethe?" <note>original: "πότερον ὡς οἱ πυθαγορικοί... τῇ λήθῃ."</note> Thus far we have related Plutarch's words. Now, the *lathyros* and *erebinthos* are types of chickpeas. *Lethe* sounds like "oblivion" to the Greeks. *Erebus* takes its name from "darkness"—inauspicious words to those devoted to wisdom. This slip was useful in this regard: that we have shown the flaw in the Latin manuscript, lest anyone stumble over the same stone.

->Do not put food into a chamber pot.<-

"Do not throw food into a chamber pot." <note>original: "Σιτίον εἰς ἀμίδα μὴ ἐμβάλλειν."</note> Plutarch interprets this: do not put refined speech into the mind of a wicked man. For speech is the food of the mind; it is corrupted and rots if it falls into an insincere mind. This is what Epictetus warns in Gellius: one must look again and again at what kind of mind we are sending speech into. For if we put it into an impure vessel, it turns into vinegar or urine. Horace alluded to this: "Unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour in turns sour."

->When you have reached the end, do not wish to turn back.<-

"Do not turn back when you have come to the boundaries." <note>original: "Μὴ ἐπιστρέφεσθαι ἐπὶ τοὺς ὅρους ἐλθόντα."</note> This is, according to Plutarch's interpretation: When the fatal day is present, and you see the end of life is near, bear it with an even mind, and do not be disheartened by a shameful desire for life. In the *Life of Numa*, he reports it slightly differently: "Those who have entered upon a journey should not turn back." <note>original: "βαδίζοντας εἰς ἀποδημίας, μὴ μεταστρέφεσθαι."</note> Jerome puts it otherwise: "After this death, do not desire life." Just as we commonly hear some people saying that line of Virgil:
> "O, if only Jupiter would bring back my past years!"

<summary>Erasmus explores the symbolic meanings behind Pythagoras's prohibition of beans, linking them to sexual abstinence, politics, and death, while also explaining maxims regarding the proper audience for wisdom and the acceptance of mortality.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, beans, Empedocles, Aristotle, Plutarch, symbolism, death rituals, Lethe, Erebus, chamber pot, mortality, Virgil</keywords>

# THE FIRST CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

->Sacrifice an odd number to the gods above, and an even number to those below.<-

<note>original: "Τοῖς μὲν οὐρανίοις περιττὰ θύειν, ἄρτια δὲ τοῖς χθονίοις."</note> That is, one must sacrifice odd numbers to the heavenly gods, but even numbers to the gods of the underworld. Plutarch relates this only as a Pythagorean riddle and does not interpret it. However, in his *Roman Questions* <note>Plutarch’s "Roman Questions" explored the origins of Roman customs.</note>, he teaches that among the ancients, the first month was held sacred to the celestial gods, while the second was for the gods below, in which it was customary to perform certain purifications and offer sacrifices to deceased parents. Furthermore, they wished for three days to be the leaders and authors of the entire month: the Calends, Nones, and Ides <note>The three marker days of the Roman calendar month.</note>, which they held as festive and sacred, dedicated as it were to the gods above. The days that followed these—that is, the day after the Calends, Nones, and Ides—they attributed to the spirits of the dead, and consequently judged them to be ill-omened and religiously restricted. Similarly, among the Greeks, the third bowl of wine was attributed to Jupiter the Savior, while the second was given to demigods and spirits. 

The principle of all number is the "One" <note>original: "ἑνάς" (henad)</note>, which is opposed by the "Two" <note>original: "δυάς" (dyad)</note>, the first among even numbers, having neither end nor perfection, whereas the number three is absolute. You will find much regarding the mysteries of numbers in Plato and the Pythagoreans, and even some in the ancient theologians. As for explaining the sense of this symbol, I believe it signifies that because God is a most simple mind and perfect in Himself, He is delighted chiefly by the gifts of the soul. For things of the body are composite and multiply immensely through propagation, whereas the soul is simple, immortal, and content in itself.

->Do not walk on the public highway.<-

<note>original: "Λεωφόρῳ μὴ βαδίζειν."</note> That is, do not walk along the common road. Saint Jerome explains this as: "Do not follow the errors of the common people." For nowadays human affairs are in such a state that the "best" things are those which please the most people. Hence some express it thus: "Turn aside from the royal road; enter by the footpaths." This precept is certainly not foreign to Evangelical doctrine, which warns that, having turned away from the spacious road through which most people walk, we should enter through the narrow way, trodden by few, but leading to immortality.

->Help one lifting a burden, but by no means one laying it down.<-

<note>original: "Φορτίον συγκαθαιρεῖν, μὴ δὲ συναποτίθεσθαι."</note> Saint Jerome reports it thus: "A burden should be added to those already loaded; one should not struggle for those setting it down." He thinks the meaning is this: precepts should be increased for those proceeding toward virtue, while those surrendering themselves to idleness should be left alone. Hence it should be uttered in this way: <note>original: "φορτίον συγκαθαιρεῖν, μὴ δὲ συναποτίθεσθαι"</note>—that is, one must help the person lifting the burden, yet the one who lays it down is not to be assisted. I thought this should be noted because this symbol has been corrupted in certain printed books.

->Wipe out the trace of the pot in the disturbed ashes.<-

<note>original: "Χύτρας ἴχνος συγχέειν ἐν τῇ τέφρᾳ."</note> That is, the mark of the pot in the stirred ash. Plutarch, in his *Table Talk*, interprets this to mean that no evident trace of anger ought to be left behind; but as soon as the swelling of the mind has boiled over and subsided, every memory of past evils must be utterly removed.

->Do not urinate upon or stand on the clippings of nails and hair.<-

<note>original: "Ἀπονυχίσμασι καὶ κουραῖς μὴ ἐπουρεῖν, μηδ’ ἐφίστασθαι."</note> That is, do not urinate on the trimmings of nails or hair, nor stand upon them. I have not yet found any interpretation of this. But my conjecture is this: if we have any relatives or kin who are humble and useless, they are nevertheless not to be everywhere despised and pursued with insults.

->Do not turn aside from the public highway.<-

<note>original: "Ἐκτὸς λεωφόρου μὴ βαδίζειν."</note> That is, do not walk outside the public road. This is also recorded among the Pythagorean symbols by Diogenes Laertius, although it is the opposite of the one above. Nor is there reason to wonder at this contradiction: since it is rightly taught that one should "speak like the many, but think like the few," so there are certain matters in which it is skillful to agree with the common people, and others, conversely, in which a good man ought to differ as much as possible. As Horace <note>referred to as "Flaccus"</note> rightly says: "Sometimes even the common people see rightly; there are times when they wander."

->Do not nourish those things which have hooked claws.<-

<note>original: "Γαμψώνυχα μὴ τρέφειν."</note> That is, do not feed creatures with curved talons. "I flee from greed," according to the interpreter Tryphon. I myself think it agrees with that saying of Aeschylus, which we shall add in its proper place: "A lion's cub is not to be reared in the state"—that is, one should not admit "people-devouring kings" <note>original: "δημοβόρους... βασιλέας"</note> as Homer says, or factious and overly powerful men who concentrate the wealth of the citizens into the hands of a few, which is a common practice nowadays.

<summary>Erasmus interprets several Pythagorean "symbols" or maxims, offering moral and political commentary on topics ranging from religious numerology to the dangers of greed and political tyranny.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Plutarch, Jerome, Diogenes Laertius, Homer, Aeschylus, symbols, mystery of numbers, virtue, greed, Roman calendar, political philosophy</keywords>

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->Do not speak against the sun.<-

<note>original: "Πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον τετραμμένον μὴ λαλεῖν"</note> That is, do not speak facing the sun. This means you should not fight against obvious truths. For that which is most certain and most widely confessed, we say is "clearer than the sun." Therefore, he speaks against the sun who says:
> There is nothing hard inside the olive, nor anything hard on the outside of the nut. <note>A quote from Horace, Epistles 2.1.31, used to describe someone denying the obvious reality of things.</note>

->Turn away a sharp sword.<-

<note>original: "ὀξεῖαν μάχαιραν ἀποστρέφειν"</note> That is, you should turn aside a sharp blade. I believe this suggests that one must abstain from dangerous business. For there is another proverb carried about: <note>original: "μὴ παιδὶ μάχαιραν"</note> "Do not give a sword to a child"—it is understood that you should not entrust it.

->Do not urinate facing the sun.<-

<note>original: "Πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον τετραμμένον μὴ ὀμιχεῖν"</note> That is, do not urinate against the sun. I believe modesty is being commended here. However, Pliny gives a superstitious reason for this in Book 28, Chapter 6. I will transcribe his own words: "They hand down omens of health from the urine. If it is white in the morning and then turns red, it signifies digestion is beginning in the former case and is completed in the latter. Red urine is a bad sign, black is the worst. It is bad if it is bubbling and thick; if the sediment in it is white, it signifies that pain is imminent in the joints or internal organs. If it is green, it indicates a disease of the organs; if pale, bile; if reddish, blood. It is also bad if things like bran or little clouds appear in it. Thin white urine is also faulty. But thick urine with a heavy odor is deadly. In children, thin and watery urine is bad. The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests/magicians often cited by Pliny for folk beliefs.</note> forbid being naked against the sun or moon for this reason, or for one's shadow to be sprinkled by the urine. Hesiod advises that it be done against an obstacle, lest the nakedness offend some god." The passage which Pliny cites, and from which the Pythagorean symbol appears to be taken, is in the work titled *Works and Days*:
> Do not urinate standing upright facing the sun,
> But remember to do so from when it sets until it rises.
> Do not do it on the road, nor moving along off the road.
> Do not strip yourself bare; for the nights belong to the blessed gods.
> The godly man, who is wise and pious, does it sitting down,
> Or by drawing near to the wall of a well-fenced courtyard.

->Do not have swallows under the same roof.<-

<note>original: "ὁμωροφίους χελιδόνας μὴ ἔχειν"</note> That is, do not keep swallows under the same roof. Saint Jerome, following the authority of Aristotle, interprets this as meaning one must abstain from the company of talkative people and whisperers. But this interpretation is refuted in Plutarch’s *Table Talk*, Book 8. For it does not seem fair that we should drive away a domestic bird that loves human company without doing harm, just as if it were a bloodthirsty bird of prey. As for the excuse they give regarding its "chattering," that is trivial, since we do not bar roosters, jackdaws, partridges, magpies, and many other much noisier birds from our domestic company; indeed, almost nothing fits the swallow less than "chattering." Nor does it seem acceptable that some refer this Pythagorean symbol to the tragedy told about the swallow <note>The myth of Philomela and Procne, involving transformation into birds after a gruesome crime.</note>, as if it brings a grim omen with it. For by that logic, the nightingale ought to be cast out as well, since she belongs to the same tragedy. Therefore, it seems closer to the truth that the swallow is disapproved of because it seems guilty of the same evil for which birds with hooked talons are held infamous. Indeed, it lives on flesh and hunts cicadas—a most vocal animal sacred to the Muses. Furthermore, flying low to the ground, it ambushes tiny living creatures; then, alone among birds, it frequents our roofs while bringing no utility. For the stork, although it does not even use our roof, nevertheless returns no small favor for our shared company by clearing away toads and snakes, the enemies of men. In contrast, the swallow, after it has raised its chicks under our roof, departs without returning any gratitude for the hospitality shared. Finally, what is most serious of all, there are only two domestic animals which never [submit] to human company...

# THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

they become tame through living together, nor do they allow themselves to be touched, nor do they accept companionship, nor the sharing of any matter or instruction. The fly is always trembling lest it suffer some harm, and for this reason, it is unteachable and half-wild. Likewise, the swallow seems by nature to hold man in hatred; therefore, it is never tamed, as it is always distrustful and always suspecting some evil. Regarding these matters, Pythagoras rightly warned, through the symbol of the swallow, that an ungrateful and unstable house-guest should be sent away. Plutarch says much the same in the place I have indicated. To these, it seems one thing should be added: that Cicero—or whoever was the author of the *Rhetoric addressed to Herennius*—borrows a metaphor for unfaithful friendship from swallows, which are present at the beginning of spring but fly away when winter is imminent. <note>original: "Rhetoricis ad Herennium"</note>

->Always keep your bedding rolled up.<-

<note>original Greek: Τὰ στρώματα ἀεὶ συνδεδεμένα ἔχειν</note> That is, always keep your bedding rolled up. Even in these times, it is considered inelegant and rude if someone does not tidy the blankets of their bed. However, what this symbol truly means, I leave for others to divine. Nevertheless, I suspect it commends modesty, even in those matters where we are compelled to satisfy the necessities of nature.

->Do not wear the figure of God on a ring.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐν δακτυλίῳ θεοῦ εἰκόνα μὴ περιφέρειν</note> That is, do not carry the image of God around on a ring. Perhaps it warns that the mention of God should not be mixed in everywhere indiscriminately.

->Do not wipe a seat with oil.<-

<note>original Greek: Λαθὼν εἰς θᾶκον μὴ ὀμόργνυσθαι</note> That is, do not wipe a seat with oil. No interpretation of this occurs to me. I believe it is hinted that the best things should not be abused for those purposes for which they seem neither worthy nor useful.

->Do not pluck a crown.<-

<note>original Greek: Στέφανον μὴ δρέπεσθαι</note> That is, do not pluck a crown. Saint Jerome, in his writing against Rufinus, interprets this to mean that the laws of cities must be observed and not criticized, because the turreted walls of cities present the appearance of crowns. <note>Erasmus refers to the "corona muralis" or mural crown given to Roman soldiers.</note>

->Do not pick up what has fallen.<-

<note>original Greek: Τὰ πεσόντα μὴ ἀναιρεῖσθαι</note> That is, do not pick up what has fallen. It warns us to become accustomed to taking food more moderately. Aristophanes, in his *Heroes*, as witnessed by Laertius, offers a superstitious reason for this symbol: that what falls from the table belongs to the Heroes <note>In Greek mythology, "Heroes" were deified spirits of the dead.</note>, and therefore it is a sin to taste it. Others express it thus: <note>original Greek: μὴ δὲ γεύεσθαι ἅττ’ ἂν ἐντὸς τῆς τραπέζης καταπέσῃ</note>, that is, do not taste whatever falls within the table.

->Abstain from a white cock.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἀλεκτρυόνου μὴ ἅπτεσθαι λευκοῦ</note> That is, do not lay a hand on a white cock, because it is sacred to the Month <note>original: "Mensi"; likely referring to the lunar deity or the passage of time</note>, as it is the announcer of the hours.

->Do not break the bread.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἄρτον μὴ καταγνύειν</note> That is, do not break the bread. It warns that friendship must not be severed, because in ancient times friendship was established through bread. From this, Christ our Prince, having distributed bread, consecrated a perpetual friendship among his own. Therefore, it is not fitting to break that through which friends are joined together.

->Set out the salt.<-

<note>original Greek: Τὸν ἅλα παρατίθεσθαι</note> That is, set out the salt. It warns that justice and equity should be applied to every business. For salt preserves whatever it occupies, and it consists of the purest things: water and the sea.

->Do not split wood on the road.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐν ὁδῷ μὴ σχίζειν ξύλα</note> That is, do not split wood on the road. Some explain this as meaning that life should not be tortured and shortened by cares and anxious thoughts.

->Do not make a libation to the gods from unpruned vines.<-

<note>original Greek: Μὴ σπένδειν θεοῖς ἐξ ἀμπέλων ἀτμήτων</note> That is, do not make an offering to the gods from vines that have not been pruned. Nothing is pleasing to those above which is not pure and purged. Plutarch attributes this riddle to Numa in his *Life of Numa*, divining that gentleness is commended by it, which is a part of piety—just as Gospel doctrine rejects the gifts of a fierce man who refuses to be reconciled to his brother. For that which is not purged is wild, and flour is useful for softening things that are hard. For he adds what I shall subjoin shortly.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### Do not sacrifice without meal.
<note>original: "Ne sacrificato sine farina." / "Μὴ θύειν ἄτερ ἀλφίτων."</note>
This means: Do not offer a sacrifice without flour. This riddle commends a gentleness of character, as has been stated previously. <note>Barley meal or flour was a humble, bloodless addition to ancient sacrifices, symbolizing peace and agricultural labor.</note>

### Worship turning around.
<note>original: "Adorato circumactus." / "Προσκυνεῖν περιφερόμενον."</note>
That is: Worship by turning the body around. This is surely in imitation of the heavens, which are driven in a perpetual rotation. Indeed, antiquity believed the heavens to be God. Plutarch attributes this practice to Numa <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious rites</note> as something peculiar to him. While he mentions the rotation of the heavens, he also adds other interpretations: namely, since sacred rites face the rising sun, a worshiper who turns his body toward the east appears to turn himself toward God, making his vows while completing a circle through both parts of the world. He adds a third explanation, which he seems to approve of most: that the turning of the body signifies the "Egyptian wheels." I believe he refers to hieroglyphics, by which they signified that nothing in human affairs is stable or permanent; rather, in whatever way it pleases God to turn and roll our lives, it is right that we take it in good part.

### Those about to worship should sit.
<note>original: "Adoraturi sedeant." / "Καθίσας προσκυνήσοντας."</note>
That is: Let those about to worship sit down. This signifies that one ought to conceive certain vows and persevere in those things which are best. Plutarch also ascribes this to Numa, except that in the volume published by Aldus <note>The famous Venetian printer Aldus Manutius</note> we read "those who have worshiped" rather than "those about to worship," adding that this was a sort of omen that the vows would be ratified and firm. He adds that to some, this rest seems to be a distinction between actions; as if those who have finished a prior action, by sitting in the presence of the gods, might begin a second action under their auspices. Some think there is another meaning: that those who perform sacred rites should not do so in passing or as if doing something else, but should be free and entirely intent on the divine matter. Hence the same Plutarch relates that whenever the high priest approached auguries or sacrifices, the heralds would cry out: "Do this!" <note>Latin: "Hoc age." A ritual command to focus entirely on the task at hand.</note> That voice exhorted those attending the rites to do so reverently and attentively. He reports the same in his *Roman Questions*: those who had made vows to the gods were accustomed to remain in the temples and keep quiet, because the actions of this life frequently involve a person in troubles.

### Rising from bed, disturb the print of the body.
<note>original: "Ἀναστὰς ἐξ εὐνῆς συνταράσσειν τὰ στρώματα."</note>
That is: When you have risen, throw the bedclothes into confusion. This seems to be the same as the previous rule about folding up bed-covers. <note>A Pythagorean rule intended to erase the "trace" of the self, discouraging vanity or the lingering of the soul in the body's imprint.</note>

### Abstain from fish.
<note>original: "A piscibus abstineto." / "Ἰχθύων μὴ γεύεσθαι."</note>
That is: Do not taste fish. As to why Pythagoras ordered one to abstain from the sea-nettle, perhaps the reason was that this fish is sacred to Hecate, because of the mystery of the "triad" <note>The number three</note> which they say is dedicated to this goddess. But for what reason he forbade the eating of other fish as well is not so easy to explain. However, in Plutarch’s *Table Talk*, someone offers a reason of this kind: that fish seem to be, in a way, companions of the Pythagorean discipline because of their <term>silence <gloss>original: "ἐχεμυθίαν"</gloss></term>; so much so that it even passed into a proverb: "More mute than a fish." Theon the grammarian, in the same Plutarch, alleges a different reason: that the fish is a native and nursling of the sea—an element not only most foreign, but even most hostile to human nature. For the gods are not nourished by this, as the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy</note> believe regarding the stars; moreover, Osiris, the parent and savior of the Egyptian region, perished in this chosen element. Furthermore, the Egyptians do not use sea water for drinking, nor do they consider anything born or nourished in it to be pure or fit for human use, as we share neither common air nor a common region with them. On the contrary, this air, through which all other things live and are nourished, brings destruction to them, as if it were against their nature and useless for their birth and life. It is no wonder, he says, if they abstain from living creatures that are alienated from human nature by the element of the sea, and are therefore unfit to mix with our spirit and blood; for the Egyptians do not even deign to speak to sailors if they happen to meet them, because they make their living from the sea. Again, Sulla in the same passage brings forward another cause: namely, that Pythagoras usually ate only those things which had been sacrificed to the gods as first-fruits. But no fish is suitable for sacrifice. Plutarch himself refutes the above reasons, saying that for this very reason one ought to eat fish more, because they seem to be of a foreign race. For it would be clearly monstrous and "Cyclopean" if creatures of the same kind were to feed on each other by mutual slaughter. For as they tell the story, once Pythagoras, having bought the haul of a net...

# THE FIRST CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<note>original: "CHILIADIS PRIMÆ CENTVRIA I"</note>

having released the captured fish, he did not despise them as enemies or aliens, but spared them as if they had become friends and captives, paying the price of their ransom. He gives a twofold reason why the eating of fish was not approved by Pythagoras: partly because the matter seemed joined with injustice—to pursue, kill, and devour an animal that by its own nature in no way harms man, nor is able to harm him. Secondly, because the eating of fish pertains not to necessity, but to luxury and the superfluous pleasure of the gullet. Hence it is that Homer depicted not only the Greeks, while they were campaigning around the Hellespont, as abstaining from fish, but even the Phaeacians themselves, who were otherwise gluttons. He did not even serve seafood to the gluttonous suitors, though both were islanders. For among such people we generally see both greater ferocity and luxury. Nor did the companions of Ulysses ever use a hook or nets as long as flour was available. But when all provisions were consumed, shortly before they devoured the cattle sacred to the Sun, they began to fish: not for the sake of a side-dish, but to drive away hunger. Several other things are mentioned in this place by Plutarch <note>Greek biographer and essayist, c. 46–120 AD</note> regarding abstinence from fish, but these seemed sufficient for the interpretation of the symbol. To Pythagoras is also attributed that noble sentiment, witnessed by Plutarch in his commentary *On Exile*: **Choose the best way of life, and habit will make it pleasant.** <note>original Greek: ἑλοῦ βίον ὃν ἄριστον, ἡδὺν δὲ αὐτὸν ἡ συνήθεια ποιήσει</note> Saint Jerome also records this Pythagorean dogma, in which that man seems to have embraced the sum of all moral philosophy: **One must flee by every means and cut away disease from the body, ignorance from the soul, luxury from the belly, sedition from the city, discord from the family, and in short, excess from all affairs.** <note>original Greek: δεῖ φυγαδεύειν πάντα τρόπον... τὸ ἀκρατές</note>

->He does not command well, except he who has obeyed command.<-
<margin>III</margin>
**It is not possible to rule well without having been ruled.** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστιν εὖ ἄρξαι μὴ ἀρχθέντα</note> This adage remains widely celebrated today: that no one acts rightly as a master who has not previously acted as a servant. Aristotle cites this in the *Politics*, book 3: **Wherefore this also is rightly said, that it is not possible to rule well without having been ruled.** Again in the same book: **For they say that he who is to command well must first be commanded.** Plato expressed it more proverbially in the *Laws*, book 6: **Now every man ought to consider concerning all mortals, that he who has not served could never become a master worthy of praise.** Plutarch, writing on an unskilled leader: **For there is no uprightness in one who is falling, nor teaching from one who is ignorant, nor order from one who is disordered, nor arranging from one who is chaotic, nor commanding from one who has not endured command.** He specifically attributed this praise to Agesilaus: **That he came to power not uninstructed in how to obey.** Seneca, in *On Anger*, book 2: **No one can rule, except he who can also be ruled.** The adage was born from that noble apophthegm of Solon, which Diogenes Laertius records in his *Life*: **Exercise command, but only when you have first learned to endure command.** Thus it can be applied either to those who learn to command others by first obeying another's authority, or to those who command their own desires before they exercise power over others. For he is not fit to dominate others who is himself a slave to his passions; nor can one be a king to others unless reason has ruled him.

->The Gardens of Adonis.<-
<margin>IIII</margin>
**The Gardens of Adonis.** <note>original Greek: Ἀδώνιδος κῆποι</note> This was said of trivial things, yielding little fruit, and fit only for a brief and present pleasure. Pausanias testifies that the Gardens of Adonis were once among the delicacies, crowded mostly with lettuce and fennel, in which seeds were accustomed to be planted in pots; and so the matter passed into a proverb against futile and trifling men, born for silly pleasures: such as singers, sophists, lewd poets, confectioners, and others of that kind. These gardens were sacred to Venus because of Adonis her lover, snatched away in the first flower of his youth and turned into a flower. Plato makes mention of these in the *Phaedrus*: **A sensible farmer, concerning those seeds for which he cared and wished to be fruitful...** <column-break/>

<summary>This page discusses the Pythagorean rationale for abstaining from fish and introduces two classical adages: the necessity of learning to obey before commanding, and the "Gardens of Adonis" as a metaphor for superficial pleasures.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Plutarch, Aristotle, Plato, Seneca, Solon, leadership, obedience, Gardens of Adonis, temperance, classical proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on classical adages, specifically focusing on the fleeting nature of "Gardens of Adonis" and the metaphor of "striking and fleeing."</meta>

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>original: "νεθὶ, πότερα σπουδῇ..."</note> "Now then, would any farmer who has sense, if he had seeds he cared for and wished to bring to fruit, sow them with great zeal during the summer in the **Gardens of Adonis**, and rejoice to see them becoming beautiful within eight days? Or would he do such things only for the sake of play and the festival, if he ever did them at all?" <note>Erasmus is quoting Plato's *Phaedrus* (276b), where Socrates compares superficial writing to these short-lived gardens.</note>

Likewise, Plutarch in his commentary titled, <term>On those who are punished late by the deity</term> <note>original: "περὶ τοῦ βραδέως ὑπὸ θεῖου τιμωρουμένου"</note>, that is, *On the Delay of Divine Vengeance*: "But is God some small and trivial thing, so that—since we have nothing divine in ourselves, nor anything that approaches his likeness in any way, being made of flesh and unstable, but rather like leaves, as Homer said, withering away entirely and perishing in a short time—he takes such great account of us? Just as women tend to the **Gardens of Adonis**, placed in earthen pots and nurtured for a few days: souls that will last but a short time, sprouting in tender flesh and not receiving a solid root of life, and soon perishing at any chance occasion."

Theocritus also mentions this in Idyll 15:
> And there are tender gardens, kept in silver baskets.

The proverb is also expressed in this way: "More fruitless than the **Gardens of Adonis**." <note>original: "ἀκαρπότερος τῶν ἀδώνιδος κήπων"</note> With a similar figure of speech, Isaeus (as cited in Philostratus) calls youthful pleasures <term>Gardens of Tantalus</term>, because they are very much like shadows and dreams; they do not satisfy a person’s soul, but rather irritate it. Similarly, Pollux called the style of the sophist Athenodorus "Gardens of Tantalus," because it was youthful and light, putting on an appearance as if it were something, when it was actually nothing.

-> To flee after fixing the sting. <-

"Do you think you will flee after casting your spear?" <note>original: "Βαλὼν φεύξειν οἴει;"</note> This is a proverbial metaphor used when someone, after delivering a taunt or performing some mischief, immediately withdraws so that they are not forced to defend what they said, or to receive a blow in return. Eryximachus the physician, in Plato’s *Symposium*, says to Aristophanes—who was preparing to leave so he wouldn't be forced to praise Love himself, and was trying to escape with some poetic jokes: "Do you think, Aristophanes, that you will escape after casting your spear at us? Pay attention, and speak as one who must give an account. Though perhaps, if it seems right to me, I will let you go."

He uses it also in the *Phaedo*, and in the first book of the *Republic*, although in the latter place he changes the metaphor and refers it to a bath-attendant who leaves after pouring water: "Having said these things, Thrasymachus intended to depart, just like a bath-attendant who has drenched our ears with a sudden and heavy flood of words." And shortly after in the same place: "As if you had cast a word at us, do you intend to leave?"

Plutarch looked to this proverb in his commentary *On those who are punished late by the deity*: "But even if he departed after casting it," he said, "it was not well to leave the weapon sticking in."

Aristotle alluded to this proverb in the third book of the *Physics* <note>original: "Naturalium auditionum"</note>. For in refuting the opinion of Anaxagoras, who had said that the infinite is immobile and rests in itself, he denies that it is enough to simply say this and run away, since he ought to have also given the reason why the infinite could not be moved. "For it is not enough," he says, "to depart after having said everything"—if I may briefly correct the spelling, not of Aristotle, but of the printer.

It will therefore apply to those who pronounce certain things like oracles, providing others with material for guesswork, as they do not explain why they feel that way. It seems to be transferred from bees or wasps, which immediately fly away after fixing their sting. Indeed, Plato hints at this in the *Phaedo*. It can also be referred to the Parthians, who, having thrown a javelin at the enemy, immediately turn their horses and hurry away in flight, not daring to engage at close quarters. Very similar to this is what is found in Cicero...

<summary>Erasmus explains the "Gardens of Adonis" as a metaphor for things that are beautiful but fleeting and rootless, and the phrase "to flee after fixing the sting" for those who make bold claims or insults and then avoid defending them.</summary>
