# FIRST CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
->c<-

Cicero in the fourth book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "A pebble," he says, "for the one departing; but we shall see. For a pebble is usually troublesome to those walking." <note>original: "Scrupulum... abeunti." A 'scrupulus' was a small sharp stone; figuratively, a source of anxiety or a 'scruple.'</note> He says the same more clearly in the oration *For Lucius Flaccus*: "But what did it profit Flaccus, who prevailed for so long until he came forward here? He died with the sting already released, and his testimony spoken."

### To untie the knot.
->VI<-

*To untie the knot* <note>original Greek: "Κάθαμμα λύειν"</note> was a saying used for someone who easily finished a business matter that was otherwise hindered. They say this originated from the story that Midas used to be carried in a chariot bound with certain inextricable knots made from the bark of a cornel tree. Regarding this chariot, which was placed in a temple, a rumor spread among the Phrygians that whoever untied its bond would gain the empire of Asia. Alexander the Great unraveled it by removing the pin that connected the yoke to the pole; some say he cut it through with a sword. We shall mention this history in another place, under the proverb *The Herculean knot*. Marcus Tullius Cicero in the fifth book of *Letters to Atticus*: "Let no honor be held for Caesar by the Senate until this knot is unraveled." That is, while this business is being finished.

### Dodonaean bronze.
->VII<-

*Dodonaean bronze* <note>original Greek: "Δωδωναῖον χαλκεῖον"</note>, that is, a Dodonaean cymbal or bell. It is customarily said of a person of wicked and relentless talkativeness. Zenodotus cites this from Menander’s *Ariphorus*. He records that in Dodona there were two high columns; on one was placed a bronze basin, and on the other a hanging statue of a boy holding a bronze whip in his hand. Whenever the wind blew more violently, it happened that the lash, being driven, would strike the cauldron repeatedly, and the struck vessel would give off a ringing sound that resonated for a long time. Others refer this to Corinthian bronzes, which ring more clearly than others. Stephanus mentions this adage under the word *Dodone*. Juvenal seems to have alluded to the adage when he says:
> so that you would believe as many basins and bells were being struck at once,

taxing the talkativeness of women. Suidas brings a different interpretation of the adage from Daemon. For he says the oracle of Jupiter, which was once in Dodona, was surrounded on all sides by bronze cauldrons so that they touched one another in turn. Thus, it was necessary that if any one were struck, all would resonate in succession, the sound passing from one to another through contact. And that ringing lasts for a long time, with the sound evidently returning in a circle. He thinks the proverb was said of stingy people who complain about even the smallest matter. But Aristotle refutes this invention as fictitious, bringing the other interpretation which we just related, concerning the two columns and the statue of the boy. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Talkativeness* <note>original Greek: "περὶ τῆς ἀδολεσχίας"</note>, indicates that in Olympia there was a certain portico so constructed by mathematical principle that it returned many echoes for a single voice, and for that reason was called *seven-voiced* <note>original Greek: "ἑπτάφωνον"</note>. He compares this to excessively talkative men, whom if you touch with a single little word, they immediately produce such a mass of words that there is no end to the chattering. Julius Pollux also mentions this adage in his sixth book, in the chapter on talkative people, with these words: *the bronze from Dodona* <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἐκ Δωδώνης χαλκεῖον"</note>.

### Prow and stern.
->VIII<-

*Prow and stern* <note>original Greek: "Πρώρα καὶ πρύμνη"</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the last book of his *Letters to Friends*, writing to his dear Tiro, relates this proverb in these words: "To me, it was 'prow and stern'—as the Greek proverb goes—to let you go so that you might settle my accounts." By "prow and stern," therefore, we signify the sum total of our plan: because the whole ship depends on the prow and the stern, as if from the head and the heel. Among the Greeks, I find it pronounced in this way: *things perish from the prow and from the stern* <note>original Greek: "τὰ ἐκ πρώρας, καὶ τὰ ἐκ πρύμνης ἀπόλλυται"</note>, that is, they perish from the front and back alike; or the ship perishes from prow to stern, which is to say, to the point of total destruction. Philostratus in his *Heroics*: "But it is necessary to be bound to the ship like Odysseus; otherwise, as they say, both prow and stern are lost." <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλὰ προσδεδέσθαι... ἀρχεῖται"</note> A similar figure is used in the Apocalypse: "I am the Alpha and the Omega." I am the sum of all things. All things proceed from me as from a fountain, and all things are referred back to the same, as if to a harbor of happiness. For Alpha is the first letter among the Greeks, and the great Omega is the last. Nor does that line from Theocritus in his *Encomium of Ptolemy* differ from this: "Among men, let Ptolemy be celebrated among the first, and the last, and the middle." <note>original Greek: "Ἀνδρῶν αὖ πτολεμαῖος... μέσσος"</note> Likewise that line of Virgil: "From you is the beginning, in you it shall end."

To this belongs what Demosthenes said: that delivery is "the first, the second, and the third" thing in oratory.

<summary>This page explores three classical adages: "To untie the knot" (referencing Alexander the Great), "Dodonaean bronze" (referencing incessant talkativeness), and "Prow and stern" (referencing the entirety or essence of a matter).</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

he said, understanding it to mean the whole of eloquence. Plato in the fourth book of *The Laws*: <note>original: "ὁ μὲν δὴ θεὸς... ἔχων"</note> that is, "Now God himself, as is said in the ancient word, encompasses the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things." Plutarch in his essay *On Educating Children*: <note>original: "ὅτι γὴ πρῶτον... νόμιμός ἐστι"</note> that is, "One thing is the first, the middle, and the last point here: a serious upbringing and lawful education." Aristotle in the third book of *Rhetoric* mentions a certain Alcidamas, who called philosophy "the wall and trench of the laws," implying that the entire defense of the laws is situated in philosophy. But the Philosopher <note>Erasmus often refers to Aristotle simply as "the Philosopher."</note> condemns that metaphor as harsh and cold; as if that earlier one, **prow and stern**, were not even harsher. Truly, in a serious speech, these might perhaps be flawed; but in adages, harshness does not offend in the same way, as they are often very similar to riddles, and those that are twisted a bit further from the literal sense seem almost the most praiseworthy. Therefore, whenever we wish to signify the sum of an entire business, and all its momentum and defense, we shall say **prow and stern**, or **trench and wall**; for example: "Piety ought to be the **prow and stern** of our studies." For some, "money is the **prow and stern** of all their reasoning." Against the force of the Carthaginians, Scipio was equally "trench and wall," that is, the chief protection.

->**Shadows.**<-
->**IX**<-

**Shadows** <note>Greek: Σκιαὶ (Skiai)</note>, was a term used in a proverbial joke in olden times for those who came to a banquet, not having been invited themselves, but as companions of those who had been invited, following them just as a shadow naturally follows a body. Horace alluded to this proverb in the first book of his *Epistles*, writing to Torquatus:
>Brutus for you, and Septimius too,
>And unless a prior dinner or a more pleasing girl
>Detains Sabinus: in short, there is room for several **shadows**;
>But the smell of "goats" <note>A Roman slang term for armpit odor.</note> presses too closely on crowded feasts.

In this passage, even Acron <note>A famous 2nd-century commentator on Horace.</note> makes no mention of the proverb. I suppose he passed over it as a commonly known thing. Christopher Landino, a man otherwise learned, interprets "shadows" as places in the countryside covered by shade, where guests might comfortably recline. Furthermore, he interprets "goats" as biting jesters. Finally, on the phrase "Say how many you wish to be," he explains it this way: "Write back, of what fortune I should provide guests for you. For if you desire those more worthy than yourself, you will be last; if inferior, you will be first." I would not have added these remarks, had it not been useful to show into what delusions an educated man is sometimes driven by the ignorance of a single proverb. The sense of Horace’s poem, however, is this: He advises Torquatus to come to dinner accompanied by a few, namely Brutus, Septimius, and Sabinus; not that there will be a lack of room on the couches if he wishes to bring more **shadows** with him, but that it would be an inconvenience if the odor of armpits should offend the sweetness of the banquet if they are seated too tightly. Then, if he absolutely wants more **shadows**—that is, companions—he should give advance notice of the number, lest the preparation be insufficient. Thus he calls Brutus, Septimius, and Sabinus the "shadows" of Torquatus if they come, not being invited themselves, but brought along by Torquatus, whom Horace invited, as his companions. The same author says elsewhere:
>With Servilius Balatro
>Vibidius, whom Maecenas had brought as **shadows**.

That is, voluntary companions. Plutarch, in the seventh book of *Table Talk*, relates what "shadows" are in these words: <note>original: "τὸ δὲ τῶν ἐπικλήτων... ἔχοντος"</note> that is, "The custom of bringing companions, whom they now call **shadows**, who are not invited themselves but are brought to the dinner by those who were invited, was investigated as to where it originated. They thought it arose from Socrates, who persuaded Aristodemus to go with him, uninvited, to Agathon’s banquet. For something ridiculous had happened to Aristodemus. Since he did not notice Socrates being left behind on the way, he entered first, exactly like a shadow preceding a body when the light is behind it." Thus far Plutarch. This story about Socrates and Aristodemus is in Plato, in the dialogue titled *The Symposium*.

->**Nothing compared to Parmeno’s pig.**<-
->**X**<-

<note>Greek: Οὐδὲν πρὸς τὴν παρμένοντος ὗν</note> That is, **Nothing compared to Parmeno’s pig.** This was said regarding rivalry, which...

# FIRST CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY

which was a long distance from the thing it was imitating. Plutarch in his *Table Talk* <note>original: "Symp. v. Decad. ij. Prob."</note> tells the story of how the adage was born, roughly to this effect: There was a certain man named Parmeno, of that class of people who, even in our own times, imitate and represent the various voices of animals and men so skillfully that to those listening—but not seeing—the voices seem real rather than imitated. Nor are there lacking those who are greatly delighted by this craft. Parmeno, therefore, was said to be as popular as he was famous for this art. When others tried to rival him, everyone immediately said: *Well enough, but nothing compared to Parmeno’s pig* <note>original: "εὖ μὲν, ἀλλ' οὐδὲν πρὸς τὴν παρμένοντος ὑῦ"</note>. One man came forward carrying a real piglet hidden under his arm. When the people believed its voice was an imitation and immediately shouted out (as they are accustomed to do): *What is this compared to Parmeno’s?* <note>original: "τί ἂν εἴη πρὸς τὴν παρμένοντος;"</note>, the real pig was brought out and shown openly, refuting their judgment—since it proceeded not from truth, but from imagination. He mentions the same Parmeno and his sketched pig in his commentary *On Listening to Poets*. We shall use this adage not inopportunely whenever someone, deceived by opinion, judges a matter wrongly. For instance, if someone were to admire an unlearned and modern epigram beyond measure, persuaded that it was ancient. Conversely, if he were to condemn something ancient and learned as if it were recent. For this imagination is so powerful that it imposes itself even upon the most learned men in their judging.

### XI. Syncretism.

*Syncretism* <note>original: "Συγκρητισμὸς"</note> was called a Cretan proverb whenever it happened that those who just now seemed the bitterest enemies were suddenly reduced to the highest concord; something that frequently happens, especially if some evil should fall upon both in common. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Brotherly Love* <note>original: "περὶ Φιλαδελφίας"</note>, records and explains the proverb in these words: *Furthermore, one must remember this in differences with brothers, and observe that practice of the Cretans to associate and draw near especially then, and to flee enemies who do not accept them. One should imitate that very thing of the Cretans, who, often rioting and warring among themselves, when enemies attacked from outside, ended their strife and stood together; and this was what was called "syncretism" by them.* <note>original: "ἔτι τοίνυν ἐκεῖνο δεῖ μνημονεύειν... συγκρητισμός."</note> Thus far Plutarch. Quintus Curtius relates something similar about the Sudracae and Malli in book nine: those who were otherwise accustomed to war with each other were joined by a partnership of danger when Alexander was imminent. To this belongs what we shall record elsewhere from Aristotle: *Evils bring men together* <note>original: "συνάγει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τὰ κακά"</note>. The adage will be rightly applied to those who enter into friendship, not because they love each other from the heart, but because one needs the help of the other; or so that, with joined forces as it were, they may ruin a common enemy. This is something we see practiced many times in these days: that they join arms, though otherwise of the most hostile minds toward one another. Such a madness for revenge exists even among Christian men. It is also recorded by a certain Apostolius of Byzantium, a very recent compiler of Greek proverbs.

### XII. Those around salt and bean.

*Around salt and bean* <note>original: "περὶ ἅλα καὶ κύαμον"</note>. This was said against those who pretended to know what they did not know. For those about to give divine responses <note>diviners or oracles</note> would set out a bean and salt. From this, those who communicated with each other about secret matters were called *not even around salt and bean*. Indeed, it is found written in this manner in Diogenianus and other collectors of Greek proverbs. But Plutarch, in his *Table Talk* <note>original: "Symp. probl. Decad. iiii."</note>, writes not "bean" but "cumin," unless perhaps the manuscript is corrupted: *But perhaps that has escaped you which they say, those around salt and cumin, that the former is not a poem, but the latter is mild.* <note>original: "ἐκεῖνο δέ πως ὑμᾶς λέληθε... τὸ δὲ ἤπιον."</note> Again, in the fifth Decade of the same work: *Florus asked, while we were dining at his house, who those were who were said in the proverb to be "around salt and cumin."* <note>original: "Ἐζητεῖ φλώρος... λεγόμενοι."</note> Apollophanes the grammarian resolved the question thus, saying the adage signifies the highest familiarity. For those who are greatly familiar with each other eat even salt or cumin together, and do not require an elaborate preparation...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

any food. From this comes that joke of Octavian Caesar <note>The Emperor Augustus</note> to a certain man by whom he had been received at a very meager and frugal banquet: "I did not know I was such a close friend of yours." <note>Implying only the closest friends or family would be served such humble fare.</note> To this also pertains what we shall relate in its proper place: *not to transgress the salt and the table.* <note>original Greek: ἅλα & τράπεζαν μὴ παραβαίνειν</note> That is, one must not violate the law of friendship which is established by these things. Furthermore, that the name of salt implies a frugal way of life can be learned everywhere from the poets. Horace in his *Odes*:
> He lives well on little, for whom the paternal
> salt-cellar shines upon a slender table.
-> The same author in his *Satires*: <-
> Let me have only a three-legged table, and a shell of pure salt.

But in divinations, it seems salt was customarily applied more for the sake of religion. Why this honor was especially given to salt is asked in Plutarch, in the place I just cited. For even Homer calls salt "divine," and Plato wrote that salt is most dear and familiar to divine things. Accordingly, the Egyptians, for the sake of honor, abstain from salt entirely, so much so that they do not even eat bread seasoned with salt. Although Plutarch thinks the Egyptians abstained for this reason instead—whenever they wished to live purely—because he thinks it especially excites lust, and that because of its heat. Furthermore, it is not unlike the truth that they renounced salt for themselves as the sweetest seasoning of all, so that it might not undeservedly be called the "seasoning of seasonings." <note>term: *opsoniorū opsonium* — the ultimate condiment that makes all other food palatable.</note> For there are those who for this reason have called salt "grace," because without it all things seem tasteless and unpleasant. Yet salt seems to have this most divine quality in itself: that it keeps putrefaction and decay away from bodies deprived of life, and does not allow them to perish entirely, resisting death for a long time, as it were, and acting in the place of the soul as far as is permitted. And yet nothing is more divine than the soul. Just as it is the soul's duty to protect and hold together living things, and not allow the frame to fall apart; likewise salt, following the example of the soul, restrains the harmony of bodies tending toward decay, and preserves the friendship between the members. By this same reasoning, they consider the fire of lightning sacred and divine, because the bodies of those struck endure for a long time and do not rot. Salt also has this quasi-divine quality: it is believed to have a certain genuine power of procreation, even by this argument: that as was said a little above, it awakens and sharpens seminal vigor. Accordingly, those who take care in breeding dogs feed them salted meats and salt-fish, so that they may be rendered more eager for procreating. Added to this is the fact that an immense force of mice is said to be born from salt-ships. Nor are there wanting those who say that women even become pregnant without the work of a man if they lick salt. Furthermore, they think the poets alluded to this, who not without cause feigned that Venus, the mistress of procreation, was born from the salt sea, whom they also surname *haligene*, that is, "salt-born." <note>original Greek: ἁλιγενῆ</note> Indeed, they make all the sea gods fertile and the progenitors of many children. Finally, there is no animal, neither terrestrial nor winged, so fertile as are all marine creatures. These sorts of things are discussed concerning salt in Plutarch, which I was the more pleased to relate because even in Christian mysteries—especially baptism, by which we are reborn and born anew unto salvation—salt is mixed in among the first things, so that from these things which the ancients felt about salt, the theologian might also adapt something for his own use.

### Supported by two anchors.
### XIV

*He rides on two.* <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ δυοῖν ὁρμεῖ</note> That is, supported by two [anchors], he sits in the harbor. Used of firm and unmoved things, and of those who have properly established their affairs. Derived from ships remaining safely within a harbor with anchors cast from the prow and the stern at the same time. Aristides mentions this in his *Panathenaic Oration*. From the same metaphor is derived what Demosthenes said against Ctesiphon: *He does not ride at anchor on the same as the many*, <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς ὁρμεῖ τοῖς πολλοῖς</note> understanding "anchor"; that is, he is not supported by the same anchor as the common run of men.

### A story without a head.
### XIV

*A headless story.* <note>original Greek: Ἀκέφαλος μῦθος</note> That is, a speech without a head; it is said of something imperfect and mutilated. Plato in the sixth book of *The Laws*: "Certainly then, I say, I would not willingly leave a story without a head; for wandering about everywhere in such a state, it would appear shapeless." That is: "By no means indeed, after I have undertaken the parts of speaking, would I willingly leave a speech without a head. For if such a thing should meet someone while wandering, it would seem foul." Again in the *Gorgias*: "But they say it is not lawful to leave even stories in the middle, but rather to put a head on them, so that it does not walk about without a head." Perhaps he alluded to that which Plutarch relates in the dialogue *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. Among the Cretans, a certain festival was conducted with new and absurd ceremonies, where an image of a man without a head was shown. They said this was the father of Meriones, who, having raped by force a

# FIRST THOUSAND, FIRST CENTURY
<note>The header indicates this is the first hundred of the first thousand proverbs in Erasmus's collection.</note>

...Nymph, he would have been found without a head. This proverb is recorded by Zenodotus.

->Between the sacrifice and the stone.<-
<margin>XV</margin>

Tyndarus in the works of Plautus <note>A Roman comic playwright</note>, one of the captives, when his deceits had been discovered and he had no trick left by which he might escape, says: "Now I am utterly destroyed. Now I stand **between the sacrifice and the stone**, and I know not what to do." Apuleius in the eleventh book of his *Golden Ass* writes: "Since the hardship of poverty stood in the way, as the old proverb says, I was tortured, being placed **between the sacrifice and the stone**." Apuleius explains the allegory of the adage by alluding to the priesthood into which he was to be initiated, and to a poverty harder than stone, through which the necessary funds were not available. It appears to be derived from the ancient ceremonies of striking a treaty, in which a herald struck a pig with a stone, pronouncing these words: "Whichever people shall first break the treaty, may Jupiter strike them just as I strike this pig with this stone." But from wherever the adage flowed, it is clear enough that it was usually said of those who are reduced by confusion to the utmost danger.

->Between the hammer and the anvil.<-
<margin>XVI</margin>

<note>original Greek: μεταξὺ τοῦ ἄκμονος καὶ σφύρας</note> That is, **Between the anvil and the hammer**. A similar thing is recorded by the theologian Origen in a certain homily on Jeremiah, in these words (for we lack the Greek original): "There is a proverb among the nations, worn by common speech, so that they say of those who are pressed by anxieties and great evils: They are **between the hammer and the anvil**."

->Now my forces are driven into a narrow place.<-
<margin>XVII</margin>

A different allegory signifies the same thing in Terence's *The Self-Tormentor*, when he says: "Now my forces are driven entirely into a narrow place."
The metaphor is taken from an army that is struggling, shut up in an unfavorable location, and besieged on all sides by enemies so that escape is difficult.

->On the razor's edge.<-
<margin>XVIII</margin>

Not far removed from the previous ones is that which was taken from Homer, and having been celebrated by the greatest authors, passed into an adage: <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ ξυροῦ ἀκμῆς</note> that is, **on the point or edge of a razor**, used for that which is in the highest crisis. For thus Nestor speaks in the tenth book of the *Iliad*:
"For now indeed the matter for all stands **on the edge of a razor**,
Whether there be most dismal destruction for the Greeks, or life." That is,
"Now indeed for all the matter is placed on the point of the iron.
Whether they live, or are consumed by sad death."
<margin>Sophocles in *Antigone*:</margin>
"Reflect, having stepped once more now **upon the razor of fortune**."
These are the words of the prophet Tiresias, warning Creon that he should be wise, having been placed in such great danger. Again in the *Epigrams*:
"Kings of Europe and Asia, contending in war,
For both of you the matter stands **on the edge of a razor**." That is,
"Kings of Europe and Asia, powerful in Mars <note>The god of war</note>,
Now for both of you the matter is on the point of the razor."
Concerning Menelaus and Paris deciding in a single combat which of them should possess Helen. Theocritus in the *Dioscuri*:
"Saviors of men who are already **on the razor**." That is,
"Certain safety of men now standing on the point of the iron."
It seems to be taken from street-performers who walk on the points of swords, or from those who handle iron with their hands, as the published commentaries on this author suggest.

->The matter is on the hinge.<-
<margin>XIX</margin>

Not entirely different from this is: **The matter is on the hinge**, which Servius noted was a proverb when explaining that line of Maro <note>Virgil</note>: "He will not cease at so great a hinge of things."
And he changes it to mean the same as if you said, "The matter is at the turning point." Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> said: "The hinge of the matter turns on this," instead of, "The whole matter depends on this." Quintilian in book 12: "For I say nothing of those who deny it, for whom it matters not where the hinge of the lawsuits turns." Also in book 5: "For if he confesses, the garment could have been bloody for many reasons; if he denies it, he places the hinge of the case here, and if he is struck in this, he falls even in the following points." It is taken from doors which are supported and turned by hinges.

->A razor against a whetstone.<-
<margin>XX</margin>

<note>original Greek: ξυρὸς εἰς ἀκόνην</note> That is, **A razor against a whetstone**. Usually said of those who by chance have fallen into those matters...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...they fell into a situation they least desired. Nor can a razor fall more awkwardly than if it strikes a whetstone <note>original: "in cotem incurrat"</note>. Not far removed from this is that line from Horace:

> And seeking to fix his tooth in something fragile, he shall strike against the solid. <note>Horace, Satires 2.1.77. A metaphor for a critic attacking someone stronger than themselves.</note>

This will be rightly applied to one who, eager to do harm, has finally encountered a man by whom he is harmed in turn, since he is unable to hurt him. For indeed, a razor, if it falls upon something soft, cuts through it; if it strikes a whetstone, it is blunted. Tarquin had this in mind when he said he intended for the Augur Attus Navius to cut a whetstone with a razor—signifying that a razor can do nothing against a whetstone. However, Livy reports in his first book that the augur performed exactly what Tarquin believed could not be done.

### The Boot of Maximinus. XXI

"The Boot of Maximinus" <note>original: "Caliga Maximini"</note> was a common saying used against dull-witted men of immoderate height. Julius Capitolinus records this adage in his *Life of the Emperor Maximinus*. For since Maximinus was, as we have said, eight and a half feet tall, some people placed his shoe—that is, a royal military boot <note>term: campagium (a high-ranking Roman military boot)</note>—in a grove between Aquileia and Arzia; it is well known that it was larger than the footprint and measure of a normal man. From this, it became a common expression when speaking of tall and foolish men: "The Boot of Maximinus." Thus far Julius. Therefore, the proverb is more correctly used if spoken with hatred or contempt, because this Maximinus, from whom it originated, was equally hated by the Roman people and the Senate; for he was a Thracian by birth, of low-born stock, and finally, of barbaric and wild character. Furthermore, even now, men of remarkable height are commonly ill-spoken of, as if they were sluggish and lazy.

### Egyptian Clematis. XXII

Close to this is a saying reported by Demetrius of Phalerum: *Egyptian Clematis* <note>original Greek: κληματὶς ἀιγυπτία</note>. He says this was used as a joke against those who were excessively tall and of a dark complexion. It was likely born from the appearance of that herb, which Dioscorides mentions in his fourth book and Pliny in his twenty-fourth book, chapter fifteen. The Italians, he says, call it *centunculus* (patchwork-weed), with beaked leaves resembling the hood of a traveling cloak, lying in the fields. The Greeks call it *Clematis*. But since there are many species of Clematis, which Pliny lists there, only one seems to have given rise to the proverb: namely, that which is specifically called "Egyptian Clematis." It is so called because Egypt produces it most abundantly; it has a long, thin leaf like a laurel, and is effective against serpents—especially asps—when drunk with vinegar. The same plant is called *daphnoides* by some and *polygonoides* by others. Diogenes Laertius, in his *Life of Zeno*, writes on the authority of Apollonius that Zeno had a slender body, a tall stature, and dark skin. He then cites the author Chrysippus, who wrote in the second book of his *Proverbs* that for this reason, Zeno was called "Egyptian Clematis" by someone.

### The matter has come to the Triarii. XXIII

There exists a Roman adage, especially elegant and noteworthy: "The matter has come to the Triarii" <note>original: "Res ad triarios redijt"</note>. We may use it when we wish to indicate that a matter has been reduced to such danger that we must strive with a final effort and our greatest strength, fleeing to our last resorts; if these are of no use, it seems nothing remains from which you might hope for help. For example, if in some literary dispute where mediocre men are wavering, we were forced to refer the matter to a single man of the highest learning; or if in a precarious business we were compelled to implore the help of our most powerful friends, whom we usually do not disturb unless driven by some great necessity. Finally, if a matter cannot be unfolded by those common counsels, one flees to some new and exceptionally clever plan. Just as Terence’s Phormio says in the play of the same name, when indicating the old man's cruelty: "Phormio, the whole sum of the matter returns to you." The adage was born from the method and logic of arranging the Roman army. It is both reported and explained by Titus Livy in the eighth book of his first Decade, whose words I have chosen to provide below. "Finally, the battle line was distributed into several ranks. A rank held sixty—or as others read, six hundred—soldiers, two centurions, and one standard-bearer. The first line was the *Hastati* (spearmen), fifteen companies <note>term: manipuli (sub-units of a Roman legion)</note> separated by a small space. A company had twenty light-armed soldiers and another crowd of shield-bearers. The light-armed were those who carried only a spear and javelins. This first front in the battle line held the flower of the youths growing into military service. Next was the more robust age-group of the same number of companies, who are named *Principes*. All these shield-bearers followed, with especially distinguished arms. This line of thirty companies they called the *Antepilani*, because under the standards there were already fifteen others..."

# FIRST CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<sig>c 4</sig>

they would station ten rows, of which each row had three parts. Each of these parts they called a "first company" <note>original: *primū pilum*</note>. It consisted of three banners. A banner consisted of six men, or as others say, one hundred and eighty-two. The first banner led the **Triarii** <note>The veteran third-line soldiers of the Roman legion, used as a last resort</note>, veteran soldiers of proven valor. The second led the *rorarii* <note>skirmishers</note>, who were of lesser strength in age and deeds. The third led the *accensi* <note>supernumeraries</note>, a group of the least reliability. For that reason, they were cast back into the rear line. When the army was drawn up in these rows, the *hastati* <note>spearmen of the first line</note> were the first of all to enter the battle. If the *hastati* could not rout the enemy, they retreated step by step and were received by the *principes* <note>the second line of seasoned soldiers</note> into the intervals between their rows. Then the fight belonged to the *principes*, and the *hastati* followed them. The **Triarii** sat under their banners, with their left leg extended, shields leaning on their shoulders, and spears with points upright fixed in the ground, so that the battle line bristled as if protected by a rampart. If the battle also went poorly for the *principes*, they would gradually rise from the first line toward the **Triarii**; once they had received the *principes* and *hastati* into the intervals of their own rows, they immediately compressed their ranks and, as it were, closed the paths. Then, in one continuous column, with no hope left behind them, they fell upon the enemy. This was most terrifying to the enemy, when they saw a new battle line suddenly rising up, increased in number, just as they were pursuing those they thought defeated. Thus far Titus Livius <note>The Roman historian Livy</note>, from whose words I think the proverb is sufficiently clear, so that there is no longer a need for our interpretation. Likewise, Vegetius, in *On Military Matters*, Book II, declares that the **Triarii** used to be placed behind all the lines, equipped with every kind of weapon, who would sink down on one knee: so that if it happened that the first line was defeated, the victory might be restored by them with the battle renewed. Modestus, in his little book *On Military Terms*, says: "The sixth row, behind all the others, held the warriors who were the strongest, protected by shields and every kind of armor, whom the ancients called **Triarii**. These men, so that they might attack the enemy more fiercely while rested and fresh, were accustomed to sit behind the final lines; and if anything happened in the first rows, all hope of restoring their strength depended on them." Flavius Vopiscus, in the *Life of Emperor Firmus*, indicates that every most robust soldier was accustomed to be chosen for the **Triarii**, showing that he was of the strongest sinews by this argument: that he could even overcome a **Triarius**.

->To release the sacred anchor.<-
<margin>XXIIII</margin>
Close to this is that which is celebrated among the Greeks: *to let go the sacred anchor* <note>original Greek: ἱερὰν ἄγκυραν χαλάζειν</note>. That is, to release the sacred anchor whenever one flees to the final defenses. It is a metaphor from sailors, who call the largest and strongest anchor "sacred," and only cast it when they are struggling in extreme danger. Lucian in *The Tragic Jupiter*: *I hear by the sacred anchor, which no machine could break away.* That is: "Hear now the 'sacred anchor,' as they say, which you can break by no force." For thus he calls an insoluble argument. Again in *The Fugitives*: *It seemed best, having considered the matter, to let down the final anchor, which sailors call sacred.* Again in the *Apology*: *Perhaps that one anchor of mine is still dry.* That is: "Perhaps that one anchor still remains intact for me," meaning: "That is what remains to me, to which I can flee for refuge." Euripides in *Helen*: *The anchor is my only hope that does not carry away my fortunes.* That is:
>My anchor hangs from a single fortune.<-
>This means: Only one hope remains to me.<-
Aristides in *Themistocles*: *And as if hanging from his voice like a sacred anchor.* Saint Chrysostom, in his fourth sermon *On Lazarus*, calls the conscience a *sacred anchor*, because it never allows a man to be carried away by the force of desires, like a storm of winds, without resisting.

->I shall move the piece from the sacred line.<-
<margin>XXV</margin>
Diogenianus thinks the same thing is meant by: *I move from the sacred [line]* <note>original Greek: κινῶ τ' ἀφ' ἱερᾶς</note>. This is said of those who prepare to try extreme measures. Julius Pollux, explaining this in Book IX, says the adage was born from a certain game of dice <note>or counters/checkers</note>. The game was of such a kind that each of the players had five stones, placed on as many lines: whence Sophocles said, *the five-lined spring*, that is, the dice-game of five lines. Between these lines, five on each side, there was one in the middle which they called "sacred": hence, he who moved his piece from there was said to move the stone of the sacred line. This was not done except when the situation demanded that the player flee to his final resources. Plato uses this adage in Book V of *The Laws*: *just as a piece from the sacred line.* Plutarch, in the book titled *Whether an Old Man Should Engage in Public Affairs*: *They bring up old age to us at the last, as if from the sacred line.* That is: as if it were the most serious cause. The same author in his commentary *On Comparison*...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

of terrestrial and marine creatures: <note>original: φήσει κινήσαντες τὴν ἀφ’ ἱερᾶς, βραχέα ποδὶ θεότητος αὐτῶν καὶ μαντικῆς ἅπτωμεν</note> "Come now, having moved the piece from the sacred line, let us touch briefly upon their divinity and divination." Again, the same author against Colotes the Epicurean: <note>original: εὐθὺς οὖν τὸν ἀφ’ ἱερᾶς, κεκίνηκεν ὁ κολώτης</note> "Straightway, therefore, Colotes moved the piece from the sacred line." This means he immediately tackled the most serious point, namely, to attack Apollo’s judgment concerning Socrates. The same author, in the *Life of Marcius Coriolanus*, writing about the Roman state being disturbed by Coriolanus’s threats: <note>original: ἀπὸ τὴν ἀφ’ ἱερᾶς ἀφῆκεν</note> "He let go of the piece from the sacred line." For when things were desperate, he fled to the religion of the gods, sending priests, temple-wardens, initiators, and augurs to supplicate. Theocritus also alluded to this in the *Bucoliasts*: <note>original: καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ γραμμᾶς κινεῖ λίθον</note> "And he moves the stone from the line," a matter we have mentioned elsewhere. <note>The "sacred line" refers to a move in an ancient board game, similar to checkers, used as a last resort or a decisive opening move.</note>

### More naked than a leberis. XXVI

<note>original: Γυμνότερος λεβερίδος</note> "More naked than a *leberis*," said of those who are exceedingly thin or destitute. For *leberis* signifies the sloughed-off skin of a snake, than which nothing can be more empty. This happens to almost all creatures covered with a skin, though a softer one: such as the gecko, the lizard, and especially snakes; these shed their skins roughly twice a year, in spring and autumn, particularly the viper. In the snake, the skin first begins to peel away from the eyes, so that they appear blind to those who do not understand the matter; then, in one night and day, the entire "old age" <note>The Greeks used the word for "old age" to describe the discarded snakeskin.</note> is cast off from head to tail. Among insects, the *silpha* and the gnat are rejuvenated, as are those whose wings are covered by sheaths, like beetles, and likewise locusts and cicadas. Among marine creatures, the crab also sheds, and that more than once a year. This slough is also called *syphar* by the Greeks, which is noted for its wonderful lightness and dryness, all moisture having been consumed by the new offspring, according to Aristotle in Book 8 of *On the Nature of Animals*. Suidas says that Leberis was a man who was poor beyond measure, so that he gave rise to a common saying. Athenaeus in the *Deipnosophists*: <note>original: σαυτὸν ἀποφαίνεις λεγώτερον λεβερίδος</note> "You show yourself to be emptier than a *leberis*."

### He who says what he wants, will hear what he does not want. XXVII

If he says what you like, you will hear what you do not like. Saint Jerome, writing against Rufinus, cites this specifically as a proverb: "And you shall hear nothing more on this," he says, "except that common saying: When you have said what you want, you will hear what you do not want." Terence in the *Andria*: "If he persists in saying what he wants to me, he shall hear what he does not want." Again, in the prologue to *Phormio*: "If he had competed with kind words, he would have heard well of himself." He alluded to the same in the prologue of *Andria*: "Let them cease to speak ill, lest they learn of their own ill deeds." Even more obscurely in the prologue of *The Eunuch*: "Then if there is anyone who thinks a remark has been made too harshly against him, let him think thus: let him know it was a response, not a remark." For he calls a "response" an insult returned for an insult. 

But this passage reminds me to correct the error of certain people who had written in the margin that I read in the following lines "because he hurt first" <note>original: quia laesit prius</note>; indeed, it was read thus in the common copies. I was the first to restore the genuine reading from the faith of the ancients, namely this: "as it is, first <insert>he who by translating well, and by describing them badly, made not-good Latin plays out of good Greek ones, the same man has now recently given us Menander’s *Phasma*</insert>." Thus "as it is" <note>original: quale sit</note> has the same force as *hoion* among the Greeks and *velut* among the Latins, or "as for example," which we use when about to propose an illustration. For he had mentioned returning an insult, and immediately subjoins an example of it. Then "first" <note>original: prius</note> corresponds to the adverb that follows, "recently" <note>original: nuper</note>. He who *previously* had badly translated many plays which you do not remember, the *same* man *recently* gave an inept play, the *Phasma*, which you can remember. 

But to return to the matter, the first father of this adage seems to have been Homer, in whom this verse appears in the 20th book of the *Iliad*: <note>original: ὁπποῖον κ’ εἴπησθα ἔπος, τοῖον κ’ ἐπακούσαις</note> "Whatever word you speak, such a word you might hear in return." Likewise Hesiod in the book titled *Works and Days*: <note>original: Εἰ δὲ κακὸν τ’ εἴποις, τάχα κ’ αὐτὸς μεῖζον ἀκούσαις</note> "If you speak evil, perhaps you yourself will soon hear greater evil in turn." Again in the same: "If he spoke first, or if having spoken an unpleasant word, even if not lying, know that it will return to you with double interest." Euripides in *Alcestis*:

# CHILIAD I, CENTURY I

If you speak ill of us, you shall hear many things, and they will not be false evils. <note>original: "Εἰ δὲ ἡμᾶς κακῶς ἐρεῖς, ἀκούσῃ πολλὰ κ’ οὐ ψευδῆ κακά."</note> That is:
If you have spoken poorly to us,
In turn you shall hear many evils, and none of them false.

Sophocles expressed the same idea far more elegantly, as cited by Plutarch:
For he who loves to pour out empty talk,
Will hear the very words he chose to speak. <note>original: "φιλᾶ γὰρ γλῶσσαν ἐκχέας μάτην, Ἀκούῃ ἀκούειν οὓς ἑκὼν εἴπῃ λόγους."</note> That is:
Indeed, he who has rashly cast his words,
Is accustomed to hearing, against his will, the words he spoke willingly.

<margin>Cited from Sophocles,</margin>
He who loves to pour out much tongue in vain,
Will hear himself spoken of poorly for the things he chose to say. <note>original: "φιλᾶ δὲ πολλὴν γλῶσσαν ἐκχέας μάτην, Ἀκούῃ ἀκούειν οὓς ἑκὼν εἴπῃ κακῶς."</note> That is:
He who has poured out many words rashly, is accustomed
To hearing, against his will, the evil things he spoke willingly.

Furthermore, in our own times, a similar saying is commonly repeated: "As you greet, so shall you be greeted," which means: as your speech is, so shall you be answered. Plautus says: "If you speak an insult, you shall hear one." Caecilius in *The Chrysium*, as found in Gellius: "You shall hear ill, if you speak ill to me." To the same point belongs that line of Euripides found everywhere among authors: "The end of unbridled mouths and lawless folly is misfortune." <note>original: "Ἀχαλίνων στομάτων, ἀνόμου τ’ ἀφροσύνης τὸ τέλος δυστυχία."</note> That is: The end or the tax of an unbridled mouth and wicked senselessness is calamity. This is also celebrated among the aphorisms of Chilo: "Do not speak ill of your neighbors; otherwise you will hear things that will grieve you." <note>original: "Μὴ κακολογεῖν τοὺς πλησίον, εἰ δὲ μὴ ἀκούσεσθ’ ἐφ’ οἷς λυπήσεσθε."</note> That is: One must not speak ill of those with whom we deal; otherwise they will hear things that bring annoyance. To this, I believe, should be added the verse which Quintilian cites as a common saying: "Nor did he answer poorly, for that first man had asked poorly."

### The Phrygians learn wisdom too late. XXVIII

This proverb is borrowed from a very ancient tragedy by Livius Andronicus entitled *The Trojan Horse*: "The Phrygians learn wisdom too late." <note>The Phrygians here refers to the Trojans.</note> It is used by Cicero in his *Letters to Friends*: "In the Trojan Horse," he says, "you know it is said: The Phrygians learn wisdom too late." It applies to those who repent of their foolish deeds too late. Indeed, the Trojans, having already suffered so many slaughters, only began to deliberate about returning Helen in the tenth year; if they had returned her to Menelaus when he first demanded her at the beginning, they would have escaped innumerable calamities. Euripides in *Orestes*:
You are wise indeed, but too late, having then shamefully left your home. <note>original: "ὀψέ γε φρονεῖς εὖ τότε λιπὼν αἰσχρῶς δόμους."</note> That is:
But now truly you are wise too late,
Since you then basely abandoned your ancestral gods.

For these are the words of Electra to Helen. It is also recorded by Festus Pompeius under the title of a proverb. According to Plutarch, Demades used to say that the Athenians never decreed peace except when dressed in mourning clothes: implying they were more eager for war than was sufficient, and did not think of peace until warned by the slaughter of their own people. But how much more senseless are we than the Athenians, we who, not even taught by the evils of so many years, still do not hate war, nor do we finally begin to think about peace, which ought to be perpetual among Christians.

### The fisherman, once stung, will be wise. XXIX

The same sentiment is found in that most celebrated Greek saying: "The fisherman, once struck, will bring wisdom." <note>original: "ἁλιεὺς πληγεὶς νόον οἴσει."</note> And they say it arose from an event of this kind: When a certain fisherman reached his hand toward the fish he held within his net and was stung by a scorpion-fish, he said, "Once struck, I shall be wise." Thus, taught by his own misfortune, he was more cautious for the future. Pliny, in book 32, demonstrates that it is peculiar to the sea-dragon and the scorpion-fish to wound with their spines if they are picked up by hand. Zenodotus says the proverb appears in Sophocles.

### Even a fool recognizes the deed once done. XXX

The same is expressed differently by others: "Even a fool understands the matter once it is finished." <note>original: "ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω."</note> It is taken from Homer, who used this sentiment in several places, such as in the *Iliad*, books 17 and 20:
Do not stand against me yourself,
Before you suffer some evil. Even a fool knows the deed once done. <note>original: "μήτε αὐτὸς ἴσαο’ ἐμοῖο, πρίν τι κακὸν παθέειν. ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω."</note> That is:
Beware of coming to meet me, before
You receive some harm: for even the senseless man knows the deed.
Euripides alluded to this in the *Bacchae*:
For being near the evil, he learned. <note>original: "κακὸν γὰρ ἐγγὺς ὢν ἐμάνθανεν."</note>
For he learned by being close to the misfortune.

It draws on a wide array of classical sources including Homer, Sophocles, and Cicero to illustrate these moral lessons.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

Concerning Pentheus <note>A mythical King of Thebes who rejected the god Bacchus and was torn apart by his own mother in a divine frenzy.</note>, who, having learned too late and only to his own destruction, began to revere Bacchus. Not different from this is what that six-foot line <note>original: "senarius," a common meter in Greek and Latin verse.</note> warns, famous among Greek maxims:
*Repentance comes to men as a loss.* <note>original: "Ἡ δὲ μετάνοια γίγνετ’ ἀνθρώποις λείση."</note> That is,
Men judge only when they already regret. To the same point belongs that line of Virgil:
*Be warned, learn justice, and do not slight the gods.* <note>original: "Discite iustitiam moniti, & non temere diuos." From the Aeneid.</note>
Likewise that saying of Demosthenes: *I do not buy regret at such a price.* Whence very elegantly Fabius, in the works of Titus Livius, calls the outcome "the teacher of fools": *The outcome does not teach this,* he says, *which is the teacher of fools, but reason.* Pliny, in the Panegyric he delivered to Trajan, calls this kind of late and fruitless wisdom "wretched": *Terror,* he says, *and fear, and 그 wretched wisdom born of dangers, warned us to turn our eyes, ears, and minds away from the Republic (for there was no Republic at all).*

<margin>31</margin>
->The fool grows wise after the harm is received.<-

Hesiod expressed the same sentiment a little differently when he said in the book titled *Works and Days*:
*Justice prevails over insolence,
Coming to the end; the fool learns by suffering.* <note>original: "Δίκη ὑπὲρ ὕβριον ἴσχει... παθὼν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω."</note> That is,
At last his own punishment catches up
With the guilty man, and having suffered, the fool finally grows wise.
Homer also seems to allude to this sentiment in the *Iliad*: *So that you may know by your own loss.* <note>original: "Ἵνα γνόης ἀπίνων."</note> Plato in the *Symposium* says: *Which things I certainly say to you as well, Agathon, so that you are not deceived by this man, but may be on guard by knowing from these things that happened to us; and not, according to the proverb, grow wise like a fool after suffering harm.* To this should also be referred that line of Plautus in *The Merchant*: *He is happily wise who is wise at another's peril.* To the same effect, Tibullus in the third book of his elegies:
*Happy is whoever, through the pain of another, learns to be able to avoid his own.*
To this also allude those cries of the "late-wise": *Now I know what love is.* *Now I feel both that she is wicked and that I am wretched.* *Ah, I have barely realized it at last, blockhead that I am.* The adage seems to have flowed from that most ancient fable of the two brothers, Prometheus <note>Meaning "Forethought."</note> and Epimetheus <note>Meaning "Afterthought."</note>, which is indeed recounted in Hesiod to roughly this effect: Jupiter, angry at Prometheus because of the fire stolen from heaven and returned to mortals, and desiring to retaliate with a similar trick, gave Vulcan the task of molding a likeness of a girl from clay with the greatest possible skill. As soon as this was done, he warned the individual gods and goddesses to each add their own gifts to the likeness. Whence the name "Pandora" <note>Meaning "All-gifted."</note> was given to the maiden. Thus, heaped with almost every gift of beauty, dress, character, and tongue, Jupiter sends her to Prometheus with a box—beautiful indeed on the outside, but hiding every kind of calamity within. He, having refused the gift, warned his brother that if any gift were sent in his absence, he should not accept it. Pandora returns, and having persuaded Epimetheus, gives him the box. As soon as he had opened it and felt Jupiter's *gifts that are no gifts* <note>original: "ἄδωρα δῶρα," a Greek oxymoron for a gift that brings ruin.</note> as the diseases flew out, he surely began to be wise too late. Where Hesiod, openly alluding to the adage, says: *But he, having accepted it, realized when he already held the evil.* <note>original: "Αὐτὰρ ὁ δεξάμενος ὅτε δὴ κακὸν εἶχ’ ἐνόησεν."</note>
He signifies the same in the *Theogony*: *Iapetus,* he says, *bore Prometheus,
shifty and of various counsel, and the error-minded Epimetheus.*
He calls Prometheus "crafty" and equipped with various plans, but Epimetheus "wise after the mistake." Whence Pindar in the *Pythian Odes* calls him "late-minded," as if wise too late. This is even indicated by the names themselves. For *Prometheus* signifies to the Greeks one who has a plan before he approaches a matter; *Epimetheus*, one to whom a plan comes to mind only after the deed is done. *Prometheuesthai* is to meet imminent evils with a plan. Lucian, in a certain dialogue, cites from some comic poet this little verse said against Cleon, who was wise late and only after business was finished: *Cleon is a Prometheus after the facts.* <note>original: "Κλέων προμηθεύς ἐστι μετὰ τὰ πράγματα."</note> The same author at the end of the same dialogue says: *For indeed, to deliberate after the fact is the work of an Epimetheus, not a Prometheus.* The proverb is also expressed in this way: *Wiser after the wanderings.* <note>original: "Μετὰ τὰ πλανὰ φρονιμώτερος."</note> Again in this manner: *What I suffered, I learned.* That is, as the sentiment—

# FIRST CHILIAD: FIRST CENTURY

I shall render the meaning rather than the exact words: *What hurts, teaches.* <note>original: "Quæ nocēt, docent." A common Latin proverb similar to "experience is the best teacher."</note> Yet it is much more advisable to be made wiser by the misfortunes of others, according to the Greek sentiment:
*Looking upon the evils of others, I emerged instructed.* <note>original: βλέπων πεπαιδευμ’ εἰς τὰ τῶν ἄλλων κακά.</note>

There is also that saying tossed about by our own common folk: *Mortals emerge wiser through shame and loss.*

-> Some evil, on account of a neighboring evil. XXXII <-

Lysimachus in Plautus's play *The Merchant* says: "Now I experience the truth of that proverb, that there is some evil on account of a neighboring evil." From these words of Plautus, it is clear enough that this sentiment was celebrated in common speech. Hesiod expressed it elegantly in the work titled *Works and Days*:
*If any local matter arises at home, neighbors arrive immediately without their belts, while kinsmen gird themselves. A bad neighbor is as great a curse as a good one is a great blessing. He has a share of honor who has a share of a good neighbor; nor would an ox perish unless a bad neighbor were nearby.* <note>Erasmus translates Hesiod's Greek into Latin verse here, emphasizing that neighbors help instantly in an emergency, whereas relatives take time to dress and travel.</note>

Nor does this sentiment hold place only among private neighbors; it has also been observed through experience that entire peoples have been subverted by their neighbors. This happened to the Aetolians and Acarnanians, neighbors who destroyed one another with mutual slaughters. Likewise with the Carthaginians and the Byontines, histories mentioned by the commentators of Hesiod. Virgil seems to have alluded lightly to this in his *Eclogues* when he says:
*Neither shall the evil contagions of a neighboring flock harm them.* And,
*Mantua, alas, too near to wretched Cremona.* <note>Cremona's lands were confiscated after the Roman civil wars, and because Mantua was nearby, its lands were seized as well.</note>

The <term>proverb</term> <note>original: parœmia</note> warns us to seek the company and fellowship of the good, and to withdraw ourselves as much as possible from the wicked. Hence that clever story of Themistocles in Plutarch: when he was selling a certain estate, he ordered the crier to add this: *that it also has good neighbors.* It was as if the estate would be far more salable by the recommendation of the neighborhood. Not far removed from this is that verse of the same Hesiod:
*Often an entire city suffers for one bad man.* <note>original: πολλάκι δὴ ξύμπασα πόλις κακοῦ ἀνδρὸς ἐπαυρεῖ.</note>

-> Hand rubs hand. XXXIII <-

Socrates, in Plato's *Axiochus*, says that the comic poet Epicharmus always had this little verse on his lips: *Hand washes hand; give something and receive something.* <note>original: Ἡ δὲ χεὶρ τὴν χεῖρα νίζει, δός τι & λάβοις τι.</note> This was a witty jab at the man's greed, for he would teach no one for free; Socrates claimed he had learned what he was about to say from him, but not for free—rather, for a paid fee. It is a sentiment worthy of a Sicilian man and a crafty poet (as Cicero calls him). It warns that almost no mortal can be found who wishes to bestow a favor on someone from whom he does not hope some benefit will return to him in turn; rather, duty is invited by duty, and favor provoked by favor. The <term>adage</term> <note>original: adagium</note> is also expressed in this way: *Hand washes hand.* <note>original: χεὶρ χεῖρα νίζει.</note> Both metaphors carry the same weight. For it is a mutual convenience whenever a hand either rubs or washes a hand. Among Greek sentiments, a couplet of this sort is circulated:
*For man saves man, and city saves city; hand washes hand, and finger washes finger.*
Seneca also uses this in his playful book *On the Death of Claudius Caesar*.

-> Favor begets favor. XXXIIII <-

Sophocles expressed the same sentiment more simply in *Oedipus at Colonus*:
*Favor brings favor.* <note>original: χάρις χάριν φέρει.</note> Again, in the same author's *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*...

<summary>This page discusses proverbs regarding the profound influence of neighbors on one's well-being and the social principle of reciprocity, where favors and duties are exchanged like "hands washing each other."</summary>

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>36</page-num>

<margin>phoro: <note>original: "χάρις χάριν γάρ ἐστιν ἡ τίκτουσ’ ἀεί"</note></margin> For grace always begets grace. That is, a benefit always gives birth to a benefit. Hesiod, as if explaining this in the first book of his *Works and Days* <note>Erasmus refers to this as "Georgics" in the Latin, following a common humanist naming convention for agricultural poems</note>, says:
Love him who loves you, and be present to him who approaches you.
Give to him who gives, and give not to him who gives not.
To a giver, someone gives; but to a non-giver, no one gives. That is,
It is right that a lover be loved: join yourself to him who draws near.
Give to the one who gave to you: to the one who gave not, do not give.
Someone gave to the giver, but to the non-giver, no one gave.
By these words, it is signified that a benefit is invited by a benefit, and a duty is provoked by a duty. Euripides in *Helena*: <note>original: "χάρις γὰρ ἀντὶ χρέιτος ἐλθέτω"</note> That is,
Let benefit respond to benefit.

->To return like for like. <note>original: "ἴσῳ ἴσον ἀποδιδόναι"</note> XXXV<-

Terence in *The Eunuch* uses this proverb, which is not at all unlike the previous one: *Return like for like.* By this we are warned to be such toward others as we find them to be toward us. And according to the Medea of Euripides, let us be friends to friends, hostile to enemies, treacherous to the treacherous, stingy to the stingy, loud to the loud, and wicked to the impudent: in short, let us retaliate for any merit with a similar merit. The same author in the prologue of *Phormio* says: Let him think that what was brought by him has been returned to him. We might also use this not unsuitably whenever we weigh words with words, flatteries with flatteries, or promises with promises. To this belongs that rather witty story which Aristotle relates in the 9th book of his *Ethics*. Dionysius had summoned a cithara player <note>A professional performer on the kithara, a lyre-like instrument</note> to play for him at a wedding; and he struck a bargain with him on these terms: that the more skillfully and better he played, the more generous a reward he would receive. The player exerted all his artistry to play as expertly as possible, hoping for a very grand prize. But the next day, when the musician asked for the agreed-upon pay from the one who had hired him, Dionysius said he had already paid what he promised: namely, that he had returned like for like, and had repaid pleasure with pleasure—referring to the hope of gain, which had indeed been greater the more skillfully he had sung. However, in this passage, the philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> denies that like was returned for like, because one received what he wanted, while the other was frustrated in what he expected. Euripides seems to have had this in mind when he says in *Andromache*:
The modest man will find us modest in return,
But the angry man will meet with the anger of the provoked. That is,
The moderate man will feel us to be moderate likewise,
But the moved man will find us stirred up.
Furthermore, the proverb can be seen to have arisen from the drinking parties of the ancient Greeks, among whom it was the custom to drink from equal cups. Archippus in the second *Amphitryon*, quoted in Athenaeus, book 10: <note>original: "Τίς ἐκέρασε σφῷν ὦ κακοδαίμον ἴσον ἴσῳ;"</note> That is,
Who, you scoundrel, mixed for you like for like? Likewise Cratinus in *Pytine*:
I shall repay the one who brings like for like. That is, But to the one returning like for like, I shall respond.
Also in book 6: <note>original: "ὁ δ’ ὄξος ἦν τῇ ψάμμῳ ἴσῳ ἴσῳ τὸν ἰχθὺν πωλούντων"</note> That is, Not through those who sell fish at Rome, like for like: meaning they are sold valued individually by price. This phrase "like for like" <note>original: "ἴσῳ ἴσον"</note> was solemn among those offering a toast, as is easily clear from the same author. It signified either that the cups were equal, or that as much water had been added as there was wine. Of this form are those phrases: "to make things even," meaning to weigh equally, and "to place an equal pebble" <note>A metaphor for balancing an account</note>. Pliny to Flaccus: I received the most beautiful thrushes, with which I cannot place an equal pebble, neither from the resources of the city nor from the Laurentine estate, due to the storms of the now-turbid sea. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the book *On the Orator* to Brutus, referred "like for like" to a rhetorical figure, in which the members of a sentence correspond to each other with an equal number of syllables. For, he says, when either like is returned for like, or contrary is opposed to contrary, or words that fall similarly are compared with words, whatever is so concluded usually happens to fall rhythmically.

->The same measure. XXXVI<-

What we have just related seems to pertain equally to the return of a duty and an injury, but it should be referred more to the compensation of a benefit, as Hesiod says:
With the very same measure, and better if you are able. That is,
Either with the same measure, or even better, if there is any capacity.
This teaches that a favor ought to be measured back with the same measure, or even more abundantly, if the means are available; and in this part, we should entirely imitate fertile fields, which [return] the seed deposited...

# SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
### 37
<sig>d</sig>

...they are accustomed to return with much interest. Cited by Lucian as a proverb in *Images*: <term>αὐτῷ τῷ μέτρῳ φασὶ καὶ λώϊον</term> <note>original Greek: "autō tō metrō phasi kai lōion"</note>, that is: "With the same measure, as they say, or even better." Marcus Tullius Cicero in *Letters to Atticus*, Book 13: "But I was preparing myself for what he had sent me, so that I might return it 'with the same measure and better,' if only I were able." For even Hesiod adds this: <term>αἴ κε δύνηαι</term> <note>original Greek: "ai ke dynēai"</note>, "if you are able." Our teacher Christ was not burdened by using this adage in the Gospel, when he said it would come to pass that by the same measure we have measured out to others, others shall measure back to us. For thus he speaks in Matthew: <term>ἐν ᾧ γὰρ κρίματι κρίνετε, κριθήσεσθε. καὶ ἐν ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε, μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν</term> <note>original Greek: "en hō gar krimati krinete, krithēsesthe..."</note>, that is: "In the judgment you judge, you shall be judged: and with the measure you measure to others, it shall be measured back to you."

---

### 37
->Dull Minerva: Fat Minerva: A Coarser Muse.<-

Minerva, according to the fables of the poets, presides over the arts and intellects. From this also flowed the expression: "Against the grain of Minerva" <note>Latin: *Invita Minerva*, meaning against one's natural instinct or talent</note>. Furthermore: "With a fat, or dull, Minerva" <note>Latin: *Pingui, seu crassa Minerva*</note>, which has indeed long been celebrated as a proverb. Columella in *On Agriculture*, Book 12, Chapter 1: "In this discipline of the countryside," he says, "such scrupulosity is not considered, but as the saying goes, 'with a fat Minerva,' a forecast of future weather will happen to be useful enough for the bailiff." The same author in the preface of the first book: "For husbandry can be administered neither with the greatest subtlety, nor again (as they say) 'with a fat Minerva'." The same in Book 10: "Nor is the subtlety of Hipparchus necessary for the 'fatter letters' <note>i.e., simpler education</note> of rustics, as they say." It is said to be done "with a fatter Minerva" when something is done more roughly and simply, and as if more unlearnedly, not with exquisite art nor the most exact care. Whence also that Priapus <note>A minor fertility god, often associated with crude or direct speech</note>, when he could have sought an obscene thing more urbanely through a covering of words, asks in naked words: "My Minerva," he says, "is thick" <note>meaning: I am a plain-spoken fellow</note>.

And Horace, describing a philosopher not equipped with those exact reasons and arguments of the Stoics, but expressing philosophy through character without art, and not so much eloquent as simple and sincere, says:
> A rustic, abnormal, wise, and of a thick Minerva.

Aulus Gellius in Book 14, Chapter 1: "He did not think it could be comprehended and perceived by any human talent in so brief and small a space of life, but that a few things could be conjectured, and to use his own word, <term>παχυτέρῳ</term> <note>original Greek: "pachyterō"</note>, that is, more thickly, or with a fat Minerva."

---

### 38
->With a Coarser Muse.<-

<term>παχυτέρᾳ μούσῃ</term> <note>original Greek: "pachytera mousē"</note>, that is: With a coarser Muse. Quintilian expressed the same proverb thus in *Institutes of Oratory*, Book 1: "On account of certain more unskillful people, I am pleased to remove the doubt of this utility even with a 'coarser Muse,' as they call it." It is found several times among suitable writers as "with a fatter formula," for that which is plainer and more intelligible. It is also said "to speak in Latin" for that which is open and simple. Marcus Tullius Cicero in *Against Verres*: "Know that I speak in Latin, not in the manner of an accuser." The same in the *Philippics*: "But as those are accustomed who speak plainly and in Latin." In the *Priapeia*: "It is much simpler to say 'to sodomize'—that is speaking in Latin."

---

### 39
->More rudely and more plainly.<-

That expression among the Greeks is indeed less elegant, but it carries the same weight: <term>ἀμαθέστερον καὶ σαφέστερον</term> <note>original Greek: "amathesteron kai saphesteron"</note>, which is reported in the same Gellius: "For you know," he says, "I believe that old and common word: 'Speak more unlearnedly and more clearly'." It appears to be taken from the comedy of Aristophanes titled <term>Βάτραχοι</term> <note>original Greek: "Batrachoi"</note>, that is, *The Frogs*:
<term>ἀμαθέστερόν πως εἰπὲ καὶ σαφέστερον</term> <note>original Greek: "amathesteron pōs eipe..."</note>, that is: "Speak somewhat more unlearnedly and more clearly." In this verse, Bacchus taxes the obscurity of Euripides, who had proposed I know not what with too little lucidity. Suidas and the commentator advise that a proverb underlies this, which is carried in this manner: <term>Σαφέστερόν μοι κ’ ἀμαθέστερον φράσον</term> <note>original Greek: "Saphesteron moi k' amathesteron phrason"</note>, that is: "Tell it to me more clearly and more unlearnedly." I suspect it was taken from the fact that anciently those "wise men" <note>Greek: *sophoi*</note>, as they call them, used to cover the mysteries of wisdom with certain coverings of enigmas by design; namely, so that the profane crowd, not yet initiated into the sacred rites of philosophy, could not reach them. Indeed, even today some professors of philosophy and theology, when they sometimes pass on things that any little woman or cobbler might say, nevertheless, so that they may seem learned, they entangle and involve the matter in certain thorns and portents of words. Thus Plato obscured his philosophy with his numbers; thus Aristotle rendered many things more obscure with mathematical comparisons.

---

### 40
->A Sow teaching Minerva.<-

A most worn adage among Latin authors: <term>ὗς τὴν ἀθηνᾶν</term> <note>original Greek: "hys tēn athēnan"</note>, that is: A sow teaching Minerva, [suggesting...]

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to plain speaking and intellectual simplicity, contrasting "fat" or "thick" Minerva (common sense) with overly complex or obscure academic language. He cites various classical authors to show that speaking "unlearnedly" often means speaking more clearly and effectively.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin proverbs (Adages), specifically focusing on metaphors involving the goddess Minerva and the pig.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

It teaches or warns that one should listen. It is usually said whenever someone unlearned and dull attempts to teach the person from whom he himself ought rather to learn; or, to use the words of Pompeius Festus <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>, when someone teaches another that which he himself does not know. This is because, as we have said, the protection of arts and intellects is attributed by the poets to Minerva. Furthermore, there is no other animal more brutish or more filthy than the sow, as it takes immense pleasure in dung—either because of the size of its liver, which is the seat of concupiscence and lust, or because of the thickness of its nostrils and its dull sense of smell, which prevents it from being offended by stench. Moreover, it is so prone to the ground and devoted to food that if it happens to be forced to look upward, it immediately falls silent in a stupor due to the unfamiliarity of the sight, as Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A Greek commentator on Aristotle</note> relates. Nor is there any other creature more unteachable; hence it seems to have been given by nature not for any practical use, like some cattle, but solely for banquets. Pliny bears witness to this in Book 8, Chapter 51: "This animal," he says, "is the most brutish of all; it was thought, not without wit, that its soul was given to it instead of salt, just to keep the meat from rotting." Varro affirms the same in Book 2 of *On Agriculture*: "They say the swine was given by nature for feasting. Therefore, a soul was given to them in place of salt to preserve the flesh." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] explains the meaning of these words in Book 5 of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "For of all things," he says, "which nature creates and protects, those which are either without a mind or not much different from it, their highest good is in the body; so that the saying about the pig seems not unskillfully put: that a soul was given to that beast instead of salt, lest it should rot." There are, however, beasts in which there is something resembling virtue, such as in lions, dogs, and horses, in whom we see certain movements not only of the body (as in pigs) but also, to some extent, of the mind. Aristotle writes in his *Physiognomics* that men with small foreheads appear unteachable and unfit for disciplines, belonging to the "swine type," as being of all things the most alienated from docility and human arts. For almost all other creatures are capable of being taught. Hence, even now, we commonly call those who are senseless and born only for their bellies and guts "swine." Indeed, Suetonius, in his *Catalog of Illustrious Grammarians*, reports that Palaemon was so arrogant that he called Marcus Varro a "pig," claiming that letters were born and would die with himself. Furthermore, if we wish to signify something unlearned and illiterate, we say it came "from the sty." Just as Marcus Tullius says in *Against Piso*: "Brought forth from the sty, not the school." From this, therefore, the adage was born: **The Sow teaches Minerva.** <note>original: "Sus Mineruam"</note> Lucius Caesar, in Cicero’s *On the Orator*, Book 2, says: "Thus, while Crassus is listening, I shall first speak of wit and teach—as the saying goes—the 'sow' teaching that orator whom, when Catulus recently heard him, he said others ought to be eating hay." Cicero says the same in the first book of *Academic Questions*: "For even if it is not 'the sow teaching Minerva,' as they say, yet whoever teaches Minerva acts foolishly." Jerome, in his writing *Against Rufinus*, says: "I pass over the Greeks whose knowledge you boast of; while you chase foreign things, you have almost forgotten your own speech, lest by the old proverb, the Sow should seem to teach Minerva." He uses the same with changed words in a letter to Marcella, which begins: "Charity has no measure." Marcus Varro and Euhemerus traced the adage back to fables, as can be conjectured from the words of Pompeius. "Which matter," he says, "placed in the middle (as they say), they preferred to wrap in foolish myths <note>original: "μύθοις"</note> rather than relate simply." A phrase of Demosthenes is celebrated by many; when Demades was shouting at him: "Demosthenes wants to correct me—the sow teaching Athena" <note>original: "Δημοσθένης ἐμὲ βούλεται διορθοῦν ἡ ὗς τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν"</note>, he replied: "And yet, this Athena was recently caught in adultery" <note>original: "αὕτη μὲν οὖν ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ ἡ ἀθλινᾶ μοιχῶν οὖσα ἐλήφθη"</note>. The remark alluded to the virgin goddess Minerva.

-> The sow has undertaken a contest with Minerva. <-
-> XLI <-

This is either the same, or certainly very close to what is read in Theocritus’s *Wayfarers*:
"Once a sow dared to strive in a contest with the divine Athena." <note>original: "ὗς ποτ’ Ἀθαναίαν ἔριν ἤρισεν"</note>
This is used whenever the unlearned and stupid, ready to fight, do not fear to challenge the greatest men in all learning to a literary contest. A commentator on Theocritus writes that the proverb <note>original: "παροιμίαν"</note> is commonly expressed as: "Since you are a sow, you contend against Athena." <note>original: "ὗς ἂν πρὸς Ἀθηνᾶν ἐρίζεις"</note> Some scholiast adds that those who strive with words are said to "contend" <note>original: "ἐρίζειν"</note>, while those who strive with deeds are said to "assert" <note>original: "φάσκειν"</note>. Thus it is all the more ridiculous if an unteachable sow contends with Minerva, the presiding deity of disciplines.

-> Minerva being unwilling. <-
-> XLII <-

Among the Latins, this is also very famous: "Minerva being unwilling" <note>original: "Inuita Minerua"</note>, used for that which is done while the intellect resists, nature repugns, and heaven does not favor. Cicero in *On Duties*: "Minerva being unwilling, as they say." Likewise in the twelfth book of his *Letters to Friends*: "During the Quinquatria <note>A festival of Minerva</note>, in a crowded Senate, your cause..."
