# FIRST CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<sig>d 2</sig>

I have pleaded your case, **not against Minerva's will** <note>original: "non invita Minerva." A Roman proverb meaning to act against one's natural grain or without divine inspiration; Minerva was the goddess of wisdom and intellect.</note>. Again, in Book IV of the same work: "And since you wish it so, I think I shall do it **not against Minerva's will**." Horace says:
> You shall say or do nothing **against Minerva's will**.

Seneca alluded to this when he said, "Talents that are forced respond poorly."

### The bull has also gone into the woods. XLIII

"The bull has also gone into the woods" <note>original Greek: Ἔβα κἀι ταῦρος εἶν ὕλαν</note>. This is a pastoral proverb with a slightly scandalous allegory, signifying a divorce or the neglect of an old mistress. However, it is permitted to use it in a more modest way if it is applied jokingly to those who seem to neglect their old friends and grow unaccustomed to their flock of familiar companions. Or even against those who defect from their usual studies and follow a different way of life. Theocritus, in the Idyll titled *Theonycho*, specifically records it as a proverb:
"As the saying goes, even the bull has gone into the woods" <note>original Greek: Αἰνῶ θλὼ λέγεταί τις, ἔβα κἀι ταῦρος εἶν ὕλαν</note>. That is:
It is said of old, the bull withdraws into the forest.

A lover complains that he has long since been left by his mistress, and shows that much time has passed since Cynisca—that is, "Little Bitch," for that was the girl's name—has been amusing herself with a certain Lycus, and cares nothing for returning to her former habit. She is no more concerned than bulls, who themselves sometimes withdraw from the herds of cows and either join with the remaining bulls or wander solitary through the groves, touched by no desire for females. This withdrawal, this neglect of the cows, and a kind of "divorce," the shepherds call by a specific word, *apagelaō* <note>Greek: ἀπαγελάω</note>, a word composed of "away from" and "to herd" or "to despise," which means to look down upon, neglect, and consider as nothing; and from *agelē*, which means a herd. Bulls are said to *apagelaō* when, separated from the company of cows, they care so little for them that they not only do not seek mating, but do not even wish to use the same pastures. Aristotle demonstrates this animal behavior, and the term itself, in Book VI of *On the History of Animals* with these words: "But the bull, when the time for mating is near, then becomes a fellow-grazer and fights with the others; but in the time before that, they are with one another, which is called *apagelaō*. For often those in the province of Epirus do not appear for three months; and generally all wild animals, or at least most of them, do not graze with the females before the time for mating." <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ ταῦρος ὅταν ὥρα τῆ ὀχείας ᾖ... οὐ συννέμονται ταῖς θηλείαις πρὸ τῆς ὥρας τοῦ ὀχεύειν.</note> We shall weigh those words rather than merely count them, in this manner: But the bull, when the time for mating arrives, only then begins to use common pastures with the cows and fights with the other bulls. For before that time they graze among themselves, which some call *apagelaō*. Indeed, the bulls in the province of Epirus frequently do not appear for a space of three months. Furthermore, wild animals, either all or certainly most, do not join the common pastures with females before the time of mating.

It seemed to me worth noting that in the translation by Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar who translated Aristotle into Latin</note>, for the Greek word *apagelaō*—which the Roman tongue can in no way render—the word "to co-herd" <note>Latin: coarmentari</note> was written. This word cast no small fog over even learned men, so that they thought the passage in Aristotle was corrupted and, by changing the reading, they introduced a far different sense, thinking that Theodorus had hallucinated significantly in his translating. But I, having weighed the whole matter more diligently, seem to see that the meaning of Aristotle's words fits perfectly without the change of any word: namely, that the bull joins with the cows and stays in the same pastures when the time for mating approaches, and then he does not get along with the rest of the herds of bulls but wages war with the others; but at other times, the bulls socially use the same pastures with other bulls, nor do they seek the company of females, but live among themselves, which same thing happens in almost all wild animals. This society of bulls with bulls, neglecting the herds of cows, is called *apagelaō*. I ask, what difficulty is there here, why should we think the Aristotelian reading must be changed? Unless he [the translator] found something almost familiar. For the word "to co-herd" is undoubtedly not genuine but substituted, introduced either by the negligence of scribes or the rashness of someone poorly learned. For I suspect we should read either "to de-herd" <note>Latin: dearmentari</note> or "to ab-herd" <note>Latin: abarmentari</note>. For I cannot be led to believe that Theodorus, a man so perfect in every kind of learning, had slipped, especially on a word that is neither particularly monstrous nor unusual to Greek authors, since its etymology immediately indicates its force; moreover, it is read in Theocritus, an author so well known and common, "among shepherds or cowherds":
They grazed together and wandered among the leaves...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...nor again do they stray from the herd. <note>original: οὐδ’ αὖ ἀμαγελᾶντες</note> That is:
And these graze together, and among the leafy herbs
They wander, and seek no separation from the flock.

In addition to this, Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia</note> shows that a bull was called "straying from the herd" <note>original: ἀπιμάγελου</note> if he looked down upon the flock, that is, one who neglected the herd. Virgil seems to me to have alluded to this somewhat in his *Silenus*:
Ah, unhappy maiden, you now wander in the mountains:
While he, his snowy side cushioned by soft hyacinth,
Chews the pale grass under a dark oak,
Or follows some female in the great herd. Close off, O nymphs,
Nymphs of Dictae, close off the forest glades now.
If by chance any wandering tracks of the bull
Should present themselves to our eyes: perhaps him,
Either captivated by the green grass, or following the herds,
Some cows may lead to the Gortynian stalls.
<margin>For when he says,</margin>
His snowy side cushioned by soft hyacinth,
He chews the pale grass under a dark oak,
he implies a bull "straying from the herd." Likewise, when he says: "The wandering tracks of the bull." The poet signifies either the bull that Pasiphae <note>In Greek mythology, the Queen of Crete who fell in love with a white bull</note> loved, or one truly "straying from the herd," or straying to the extent that, having neglected his own herd, he followed other cows. Furthermore, the same Maro <note>Virgil's cognomen</note> mentions the battle of bulls among themselves at the time of mating in the third book of the *Georgics*:
Nor is it the custom to stable the warriors together, but the one
Defeated departs, and goes into exile far off on unknown shores,
Moaning much at his ignominy, and the blows of the proud
Victor, then the loves he lost unavenged.
And looking back at the stalls, he departs his ancestral realms.

Indeed, I think this very word, if it is applied to people, is proverbial, just as those terms "to be lustful as a boar" <note>original: καπρᾶν</note> and "to be mad for horses" <note>original: ἱππομανᾶν</note> are; and that Theocritus <note>Greek pastoral poet</note> chiefly looked to this when he said it is told as a proverb: "The bull too has gone to the woods." <note>original: Εβα καὶ ταῦρος ἀν’ ὕλαν</note>

The Scholia <note>Ancient grammatical or explanatory commentaries</note> which are circulated on Theocritus take "the bull too has gone" as using "and" as a connective conjunction, changed from an expletive; they add that it is a proverb accustomed to be said of those who were absent and not about to return. For if a bull has once fled into the woods, he cannot be caught. Whence one might not unsuitably say that a husband sleeping apart from his wife for a long time is "straying from the herd"; and he who has ceased to visit his friends, "strays from the herd"; and he who has for a long time abstained from the company of books, "strays from the herd." Likewise, one who shrinks from the banquet of men and lives by himself, it will be permitted to call "straying from the herd." And he who has wandered from legitimate companionship and withdrawn, will not inaptly be said to "stray from the herd." Nor is that which is found in Aristophanes’ *Lysistrata* entirely foreign to this form: "And at home I spend my life un-bulled." <note>original: οἴκοι δὲ ἀταυρώτη διάγω τὸν βίον</note> That is, I shall lead a celibate life at home without a bull. For in this way he signified the celibate life of a woman neglecting the bull, that is, the husband. So also Horace: "May she perish badly, that Lesbia who, when you were seeking a bull, showed you a sluggish one."

->The year produces the harvest, not the field.<-
<margin>44</margin>
The year brings the crop, not the soil. <note>original: Ἔτος φέρει οὐχὶ ἄρουρα</note> That is, the season produces the grain, not the field. This is a proverbial half-line of verse which is cited by Theophrastus <note>Successor to Aristotle and father of botany</note> in the eighth book of *On Plants*: "For growth and nourishment, the temperament of the air contributes the most, and generally the condition of the year. For when timely rains, fair weather, and winters occur, all things are fruitful and productive, even if they are in salty and thin-soiled places. Wherefore they say the proverb—not without reason—that the year produces the harvest, not the field. But the regions also differ greatly." That is: For growth or nourishment, the temperateness of the sky helps most of all, and the condition of the year as a whole. For if rains, clear skies, and winters happen opportunely, all things come forth more happily and abundantly, even in salty and insufficiently rich fields. Whence it is not out of place that they say as a proverb, "The year produces the fruit, not the field." Nevertheless, it matters not a little what the nature of the regions may be. Here I thought it should be mentioned in passing that in the printed copies one reads "not rightly" <note>original: οὐ καλῶς</note>; and this itself, as is my opinion at least, is "not right," partly because Theodore Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek humanist who translated Theophrastus into Latin</note> translated this passage not incorrectly, and partly because it does not fit the sentiment of Theophrastus. For he admits it is true that the climate has the greatest...

<sig>d 3</sig>

the condition of the sky <note>original: "caeli conditionem"</note>, a fact also attested by the proverb, in which the entire logic of the harvest is attributed to the weather not without cause; nevertheless, some distinction also lies in the character of the soil itself. Therefore, I suspect we should read *not simply* <note>original Greek: "οὐχ ἁπλῶς"</note> instead of *not well* <note>original Greek: "οὐ καλῶς"</note>. Although, for my part, I see that even the phrase *not well* can be defended in some way. Namely, that Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known as the father of botany.</note> might be rejecting the common saying which attributes all momentum to the sky, since a great part also depends on the quality of the soil. However, the former reading appeals to me more, and I believe learned men will add their vote to my opinion. He repeats the same adage in the third book of *On the Causes of Plants*, giving the reason why wheat grows equally in cold and hot regions; he does not deny that the nature of the field contributes something to fertility, but says the surrounding air has by far the greatest momentum, as does the temperament of the heavens and the seasons, and which winds the field is exposed to. Plutarch also mentions this in his *Table Talk* <note>original: "Symposiacis"</note>, the seventh decade, second problem. Furthermore, if one wishes to expand the use of the proverb, it may be applied quite seasonably to this sentiment: if one were to say that for virtue, education brings far more momentum than lineage. It matters very little from what ancestors you are born, but it matters most by what principles you are educated and in what morals you are instructed. For the sky, as it were, educates that which the earth brings forth. Euripides seems to have alluded to this adage in *Hecuba*, whom he makes speak thus:

> Is it not strange that even poor soil,
> if it receives a lucky season from the gods, bears a good ear of corn,
> while good soil, if deprived of what it needs,
> yields a bad crop? But among men,
> he who is wicked is nothing else but wicked,
> and the noble man is noble, nor does misfortune
> corrupt his nature, but he remains upright always.
> Is it the parents who make the difference, or the upbringing?
> To be raised well certainly holds

> It is no new thing, then, if bad
> Earth, with a favoring sky, bears a good crop:
> While good earth, destitute of what it needed, produces
> Bad fruit. But whoever of mortals is bad,
> Can be nothing else than always bad,
> The worthy man always worthy. Adverse fortune does not
> Corrupt the nature of the man, but he remains always honest.
> Is it the parents, or rather those who educate?
> To be rightly educated, certainly, involves
> -> The teaching of the honorable. <-

Hecuba seems to attribute a little more to birth than to instruction, and she wonders, therefore, why the same thing does not happen in the morals of mortals as happens in the yield of crops. Furthermore, Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> elegantly showed how much more power instruction has than lineage by presenting two dogs to the multitude: one of them, born of an ignoble mother, followed the wild beast vigorously because of his training; the other, sprung from noble parents, because he had not been trained, shamefully abandoned the beast and stopped at the smell of bread and food.

### In the shallows.
### XLV

A proverbial metaphor: *To be in the shallows* <note>original: "In uado esse"</note>, used for that which is in safety and out of danger, taken from those swimming or sailing. Terence: "The whole matter is in the shallows" <note>Meaning the danger is over and one can stand on firm ground.</note>. Plautus in *The Pot of Gold*: "This matter now seems to be almost in the shallows of safety." A shallow is a stretch of water where anyone who stands has already escaped the danger of drowning.

---

### To sail in harbor.
### XLVI

Related to this is the allegory, *to sail in harbor* <note>original Greek: "ἐν λιμένι πλεῖν"</note>, by which we signify that we are now away from danger. This is because those who are still sailing in the midst of the waves sail at the mercy of the winds and the tide. On the contrary, those who are already within the harbor have no business with waves and winds. Whence the very common metaphor: we call a man in whose protection we find rest a "harbor." And those who bring themselves to some tranquil and safe way of life are said to "betake themselves into the harbor." Terence in *The Woman of Andros*: "Now it happens at his risk; I am sailing in harbor." Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> uses it slightly differently in the seventh book of the *Aeneid*,

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Now rest is won for me, and every port is in sight. <note>original: "Nunc mihi parta quies, omnisq; in limine portus." A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, signifying the completion of a task.</note>

->The weary ox plants its foot more firmly.<-
->XLVII<-

Saint Jerome <note>Diuus Hieron.</note> used a very elegant adage when writing to the blessed Augustine, wishing to deter him so that a young man might not challenge an old one. For those who are already weary with age are indeed slower to be roused to a fight; but they rage and press more heavily if that elderly valor is ever provoked and warmed up again. "Remember," he says, "Dares and Entellus <note>Characters from the Aeneid; Entellus was the older boxer who defeated the younger Dares.</note>, and the common proverb, that **the weary ox plants its foot more firmly.**" It appears to be derived from the ancient custom of threshing, when wagons were driven by oxen over the sheaves to shake out the grain: partly by wheels equipped for this purpose, and partly by the hooves of the bulls. And that Mosaic law, which the Apostle Paul cites to Timothy, forbids "muzzling the ox while it treads out the grain." Therefore, the weary ox, because it plants its foot more heavily, is more suitable for threshing. But the same is not true for a horse in a race. It may also seem to allude to the fact that young men excel in agility of body, while old men are superior in stationary combat and strength. Virgil declares this in the encounter of Dares and Entellus. Nor is that which I find placed in the Greek collections very far from this: **A slow ox** <note>original: <greek>ἀρεμαῖος βοῦς</greek></greek></note>. That is, a slow ox—it is understood—moves its foot. For it moves gradually indeed, but it presses down more heavily.

->You wander from the whole path.<-
->XLVIII<-

**You miss by the whole road** <note>original: <greek>Τῇ πάσῃ ὁδῷ ἀφαμαρτάνεις</greek></note>. To wander from the whole path is a proverb against those who err greatly. Terence in *The Eunuch*: "You wander from the whole path." It is transferred from travelers, who sometimes are accustomed to wander from the road in such a way that, though not without some cost, they still arrive where they were heading; but sometimes they wander so much that they turn far aside and head in the opposite direction. Hence those who wander from the truth are also said to "exorbitate" <note><term>exorbitate</term>: literally to go out of the track or orbit.</note>. Aristotle in the *Ethics*: "They do not wander by the whole path." The same author writes in the first book of *Physics* that those ancient philosophers, the investigators of natural causes, "exorbitated," and as if driven from the road, wandered entirely from the truth. It is taken from Aristophanes’ *Plutus*:
**Or have we missed the way entirely?** <note>original: <greek>Ἢ τῇ ὁδῷ τὸ παράπαν ἡμαρτήκαμεν;</greek></note>
Have we wandered completely out of the way?
Furthermore, even today it is frequently said that those who undertake something with right counsel are "on the road"; those who approach a matter in an improper manner are "off the road." These metaphors are almost proverbial and very common among the learned: to drive from the road, to lead back to the road, to show the road, to make a road, to pave the road, to open the road, to block the road, to cut off the road. Cicero in the first *Philippic*: "But if you think so, you are ignorant of the whole road to glory." That famous apophthegm <note><term>apophthegm</term>: a concise, pithy saying.</note> is also well known: **They run well, but off the road** <note>original: <greek>Καλῶς μὲν τρέχουσι, ἀλλ’ ἐκτὸς τῆς ὁδοῦ</greek></note>.

->To err by the whole sky.<-
->XLIX<-

Bordering on this is what Macrobius uses in the third book of the *Saturnalia*: "Did it never," he says, "Praetextatus, come into your mind that Virgil had erred by the whole sky, as they say?" It seems to be taken from Aristophanes’ *The Frogs*:
**For immediately I had erred by as much as the heavens.** <note>original: <greek>Εὐθὺς γὰρ ἡμαρτήκειν οὐρανίου γ’ ὅσον.</greek></note>
It is said by Euripides against Aeschylus, who had erred greatly in what he had said. The metaphor is drawn either from the fable of Phaethon or Ceres; or from sailors, who regulate their course by observation of the sky and stars; therefore, when pilots wander greatly, they sometimes imagine the North Star <note><term>cynosura</term>: the constellation Ursa Minor, used for navigation.</note> to be in a far different part of the sky, and wander in their whole course. Unless we prefer to take "sky" for "region," as Horace does:
"They change their sky, not their soul, who run across the sea."

->To fetch trouble for oneself on one's own beast.<-
->L<-

He who is the author of his own evils is said to **fetch trouble for himself on his own beast**, as if at his own expense and by his own labor, he brings a bundle of evils to himself as if on his own wagon. Plautus in *Amphitryon*: "The man himself fetches trouble from me on his own beast." The metaphor is taken from freight wagons. For "beast of burden" <note>original: <insert>iumentum</insert></note> also signifies this, according to Gellius in book twenty, chapter one: or certainly from animals carrying loads on their backs.

->To cut this man's throat with his own sword, with his own weapon.<-
->LI<-

He is said to be "slaughtered by his own sword" or "his own weapon" who is refuted by his own words, or who is caught by his own invention or trick: finally, against whom is retorted, in whatever way, either a word or deed that proceeded from himself. Just as if someone, following the example of Protagoras, should retort a "turning" dilemma <note><term>antistrephon</term>: a rhetorical argument that can be turned back against the opponent.</note> against the one who proposed it; or if, like Phalaris, he should finish off Perillus, the inventor of the evil <note>Perillus invented the Brazen Bull for the tyrant Phalaris, who then made Perillus its first victim.</note>, with his own invention. Thus in Terence’s *The Brothers*, the old man Micio rebukes the cruelty of his brother Demea—

# FIRST CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<sig>d 4</sig>

...expanding, he uses a sentiment of this kind: "Old age brings this one fault; we are all more attentive to property than we ought to be." <note>original: "Hoc unū affert uitiū senecta, attētiores ad rem sumus oportet." From Terence's Adelphoe.</note> Demea, a little later, retorts this same thing against his brother: "Finally," he says, "I do not make that word my own, which you, Micio, said well and wisely a while ago: It is a fault common to all, that in old age we are too attentive to property. It is fitting that we escape this stain." By this reasoning, since he was binding Micio and driving him to give the field he was asking for, Demea then said: **"I cut this man's throat with his own sword."** <note>original: "Suo sibi hunc iugulo gladio."</note> The metaphor is transferred from those who, in a fight, are sometimes pierced by their own weapons. Plautus in *Amphitryon*: "And to drive this man from the doors with his own weapon, by his own malice." Cicero in *Pro Caecina*: "It is necessary that your defense be finished off either by your own sword, as the saying goes, or by ours." Ovid alluded to this in the *Heroides*:
> I gave the rowing-gear by which you, about to flee, might leave me:
> Alas, I suffer wounds made by my own weapons.

To the same point belong those words of Cicero: "It is necessary that you run onto your own blade." And again: "This is the blade of your defense; it is necessary that your speech run onto it." Nor does that phrase of Livy from Book 2 of the Second Punic War wander far from this: "Hannibal felt he was being attacked by his own arms." Lucian in *The Fishermen*: <gloss>Since, as you say, you took the arrows from us and shot them against us.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὡς πρ' ἡμῶν τὰ τοξεύματα...</note> That is: These very weapons, taken from us as you admit, you have hurled against us. Plutarch relates that the leader Brasidas, having pulled a spear from his own body, stabbed the one who had sent it with that same spear. Marius, one of the "Thirty Tyrants," is narrated by Trebellius Pollio to have been killed by a certain soldier who, while attacking, said: "This is the sword which you yourself made." For Marius, before his rule, had been a blacksmith, and had used the labor of that soldier in his smithy. You would say this man was truly "slaughtered by his own sword."

<margin>52</margin>
->**He fell into the pit which he made.**<-

The same thing is valid in that which is reported in the Odes of David, Psalm 7: <gloss>He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the ditch which he made.</gloss> <note>original Greek: λάκκον ὤρυξε...</note> This is transferred either from those who lie in wait for wild beasts with dug pits or other traps of that kind, or from wars, in which sometimes a foe catches a foe by digging tunnels.

<margin>53</margin>
->**He is caught in his own snare.**<-

Nor does it mean anything else, that which is read in the same author, Psalm 9: <gloss>In this snare which they hid, their foot was caught.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἐν παγίδι ταύτῃ...</note> A well-known metaphor, surely borrowed from those who set traps for birds or wild beasts with prepared nooses.

<margin>54</margin>
->**You have devised this trick against yourself.**<-

Lucian expressed the same sentiment differently: <gloss>Thus you have composed a sophism against yourself.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ὥσε σόφισμα κατὰ σαυτοῦ...</note> That is: And so you have found a device for your own destruction. This refers to a legacy-hunter who, when he had named a rich man as his sole heir and produced the will to provoke the rich man to do the same, was suddenly crushed by a falling roof and left his own property to the one whose wealth he had gaped at. It should be used when a trick devised against another falls back on the head of the author, as not infrequently happens.

<margin>55</margin>
->**The thrush excretes its own doom.**<-

Very similar to these is that Greek adage: <gloss>The thrush excretes its own evil.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Κίχλα χέζει αὑτῇ κακόν.</note> It is accustomed to be said against those who provide the cause of their own destruction. For indeed, birdlime <note>A sticky substance used to catch birds.</note>, according to Pliny, does not grow unless it is ripened in the belly and returned through the bird's droppings, especially those of wood-pigeons and thrushes. Servius also mentions this in his commentary on the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. Likewise, Aristotle in Book 9 of *The History of Animals* makes three kinds of thrushes, the first of which he says is called <term>ixoboron</term> (lime-eater) or, as Athenaeus says, <term>ixophagon</term>, because it feeds on the mistletoe berry. Since birds are caught by birdlime, they "excrete their own evil." Plautus expressed it a little differently: "The bird itself," he says, "creates its own death." Although I would not hesitate to affirm that "excretes" (*cacat*) was written by Plautus, not "creates" (*creat*); then the passage was corrupted by some half-learned person ignorant of the Greek proverb, who substituted the false word "creates." Sophocles in *Antigone*:
> <gloss>Whoever sows useless children,</gloss>
> <gloss>what else would you say he creates but troubles for himself</gloss>
> <gloss>and much laughter for his enemies?</gloss>

The proverb will therefore fit those who take powerful sons-in-law for themselves, by whom they are afterwards oppressed by force.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs (Adagia), focusing on metaphors for self-inflicted harm and the danger of provoking the powerful.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->He found the source of evil for himself.<-
<margin>56</margin>
There is also a six-foot verse celebrated as a proverb among the same authors: <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς γὰρ εὗρε πῆ κακῶ τὴν πηγήν</note> "For he himself found the source of the evil." Or <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς εὗρε τῷ κακῷ πηγήν</note> "He himself found the fountain for the misfortune." So says Aeschylus in *The Persians*:
"Now the fountain of evils seems to have been found for all my friends." <note>original Greek: Νῦν κακῶν ἔοικε πηγὴ πᾶσιν εὑρῆσθαι φίλοις</note>
The verse is Trochaic <term>Trochaic: a poetic meter often associated with a rapid, tripping rhythm</term>. For there are indeed destructive springs whose water, if tasted, brings death or madness, which it would have been better not to have discovered.

->The goat and the sword.<-
<margin>57</margin>
To almost the same purpose belongs: <note>original Greek: αἲξ μάχαιραν</note> "The goat [found] the sword." It is said of those who themselves discover the means by which they perish. The adage arose from an event of this kind: Once, when the Corinthians were preparing to perform a divine rite for Juno Acraea <note>Juno of the Heights</note>—for that is her surname; they say the statue of this Juno was placed there by Medea—those who were hired to provide the sacrificial victim buried a knife under the earth and pretended they had forgotten it. However, a goat, scratching with its feet, dug it up and revealed it, and so the goat was sacrificed. Some express the proverb this way: <note>original Greek: αἲξ δ’ ἔχει τὴν μάχαιραν</note> "The goat providing the knife." Others in this way: <note>original Greek: οἷς τὴν μάχαιραν</note> "The sheep [found] the knife."

->The crow and the scorpion.<-
<margin>58</margin>
Close to these is also that saying: <note>original Greek: Κορώνη τὸν σκορπίον</note> "The crow [seized] the scorpion." It applies to those who prepare to harm others, from whom they will receive just as much evil in return. Just as the crow, having snatched up a scorpion, received a fatal wound from its arched tail and died. There exists a Greek epigram by Archias on this matter, which I will not be burdened to include:
"Once a crow, dwelling in the shining air,
Snatched a leaping scorpion from the earth.
Quickly, the creature struck the bird's foot with its sting
And robbed it of life. See how what it intended for another,
The wretched bird received as its own death."
And this often happens in human affairs: that he who seems to have captured is himself captured. As Horace also says:
> "Captive Greece took captive her savage conqueror." <

->You have eaten a hot lunch.<-
<margin>59</margin>
That line of Plautus seems to allude to this: "You have eaten a hot lunch today," meaning, "You have done something that will be a great evil to you." This is taken from those who gorge themselves on harmful and deadly foods, only to feel the torments of the belly afterward.

->To irritate the hornets.<-
<margin>60</margin>
<note>original Greek: τὰς σφηκιὰς ἐρεθίζειν</note> "To provoke the wasps' nests." To this sentiment must also be referred what is found in Plautus’s *Amphitryon*: "You will irritate the hornets." This was said by the poet regarding the nature of women, whom if you oppose when they are angry, you provoke them more, and you will not depart without harm. The hornet is a type of insect related to wasps, most persistent and with a most pestilential sting. Indeed, Pliny reports in *Natural History*, Book 11, Chapter 21, that the stings of hornets are rarely without fever. He adds that it is handed down by some that a man can be killed by twenty-seven <note>literally "three times nine"</note> stings of this creature. Aristotle, in Book 9 of *On the Parts of Animals*, besides other things he records about hornets, also relates that while among the bee kind some lack stings (such as drones and kings), and some wasps are found without stings, no hornets are found not armed with a sting. Although, regarding the leader, he expresses some doubt as to whether it is stung. Saint Jerome uses this adage in a certain letter. Plautus expressed the same sentiment with a different allegory:
"If you wish to oppose a Bacchante <note>a female follower of Bacchus</note> in her revelry,
You will make a madwoman even madder; she will strike you more often."

<summary>Erasmus explores several ancient proverbs concerning self-destructive behavior and the danger of provoking those who can retaliate, citing classical authors like Aeschylus, Plautus, and Aristotle.</summary>

# FIRST CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY

If you do not obey, you shall be released by a single blow. <note>original: "Si nobsequaris, una te soluas plaga." This refers to the ritual strikes of the Bacchic worshippers.</note>

For it was the custom that those celebrating the Bacchanalia would strike those they met with their thyrsi <term>thyrsus: a staff topped with a pine cone, carried by followers of Dionysus</term>. Aristophanes in *Lysistrata*—for I found it inscribed under this title—says:
*Lest someone, like a wasp's nest, should strike and irritate me.* <note>original Greek: "Μὴ μῆτις, ὥσπερ σφηκιὰν βλήξῃ me κἀρεθίζῃ."</note>
Unless someone, as if it were a wasp's nest, should deceive and goad me.
I believe the one who wrote the epitaph of the abusive poet Archilochus alluded to this:
*Step lightly by the tomb, traveler, lest you ever*
*Stir the wasps sitting upon this mound.* <note>original Greek: "Ἠρέμα δὴ παρὰ τύμβον ὁδοιπόρε, μήποτε τοῦδε / Κινήσῃς τύμβῳ σφῆκας ἐφεζομένους."</note>
That is:
Lest by chance you irritate the hornets who sit upon this sepulcher,
Traveler, take your silent way.
Xenophon in his fourth book indicates where this originated: namely, from those who strive to remove wasps from their caves. *“And I see,” he said, “that as many as wish to take out wasps, if they try to hunt them while the wasps are flying out, are struck by many.”* <note>original Greek: "ὁρῶ δ’ ἔγω γ’ ἔφη, ὅτι ὁπόσοι σφῆκας ἐξαιρεῖν βούλοντ’, ἐὰν μὴ ἐκθέοντας τοὺς σφῆκας πειρῶντ’ θηρᾷν, ὑπὸ πολλῶν τυπτόμενος."</note> That is, "And I see," he says, "that whoever wishes to catch hornets, if indeed they attempt to hunt them as they fly out, are struck by many hornets."

->You provoke the lion.<-
->LXI<-
That which is reported by Diogenianus has a similar force: *Do not prick the lion*, <note>original Greek: "μὴ λέοντα νύσας"</note> that is, you prick or provoke the lion. This is said of those who provoke and stimulate a powerful and fierce person to their own destruction. The metaphor is too well known to require explanation.

->Do not move an evil well placed.<-
->LXII<-
This also has the same power: *Do not move an evil that is lying well.* <note>original Greek: "Μὴ κινείν κακὸν εὖ κείμενον"</note> That is, do not move an evil that is well settled, or resting. It is used against those who, by their own folly, stir up trouble for themselves, or those who resuscitate and renew evils already buried by time. Theognis seems to have recorded this proverb in this verse:
*For very often an evil lying at home is better.* <note>original Greek: "Πολλάκι γὰρ τὸ κακὸν κατακείμενον οἴκοι ἄμεινον."</note>
That is: For very often it is better to have an evil stored away at home. Very similar to this is that saying:
He stirs the slumbering fires.

->You wake the eight-footed creature.<-
->LXIII<-
Cratinus in *The Thracian Women*, quoted in Suidas: *You awaken the eight-footed one.* <note>original Greek: "ὀκτώπουν ἀνεγείρεις"</note> That is, you wake the eight-footed creature, namely the scorpion, which has eight feet and usually lies hidden under rocks; you should not wake it except at your own peril, because of the poison it carries in its tail.

->To move Camarina.<-
->LXIIII<-
*To move Camarina.* <note>original Greek: "Κινεῖν τὴν Καμαρίναν"</note> That is, to move Camarina is to bring evil upon oneself. Lucian in *The Ill-Omened Day*: *You see how much better it would have been for you to leave Camarina unmoved.* <note>original Greek: "ὁρᾷς ὡς ἄμεινον ἦν σοι ἀκίνητον τὴν Καμαρίναν ἐᾷν"</note> Servius the grammarian explains where the adage originated, commenting on that passage of Virgil in the third book of the *Aeneid*:
*And Camarina appears far off, never permitted by the fates to be moved.*
Camarina, he says, is a marsh next to the town of the same name; when it was once drained, it created a plague. They consulted the oracle as to whether it would be better to drain it completely. The god forbade Camarina to be moved. But they dried it out, not obeying the oracle, and while the plague indeed ceased, they paid the penalty for neglecting the oracle when enemies entered through the drained land. Suidas records almost the same things, adding further that to some, Camarina is a shrub whose branches, if one moves and shakes them, emit a certain foul odor. But the former opinion seems to me to come closer to the truth. Stephanus also mentions this adage in a heroic verse, and expresses it in this manner:
*Do not move Camarina, for it is better unmoved.* <note>original Greek: "Μὴ κινείν Καμαρίναν, ἀκίνητος γὰρ ἀμείνων."</note>
Do not move Camarina, for it is better not to touch it.
He says, moreover, that Camarina is a town and a marsh of the same name in Sicily. Silius [Italicus] also mentions it in his fourteenth book, imitating Virgil:
*And Camarina, which the fates did not allow to be moved.*

->You stir up the Anagyrus.<-
->LXV<-
That which is celebrated among the Greeks seems in no way dissimilar to the above: *You stir the anagyrus.* <note>original Greek: "ἀνάγυρον κινεῖς"</note> This is used against those who are the authors of their own misfortunes, and who provoke someone to their own destruction. How the proverb was derived is told variously by authors. Some refer it to the nature of a shrub, which Dioscorides mentions in his third book, which some call *magyrum* and others *anagyrum*; some call it *acopon*, effective indeed in medicines...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s encyclopedic collection of Greek and Latin adages, focusing on proverbs derived from natural history, mythology, and the theater.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<page-num>46</page-num>

<note>original: "Anagyrum commovere"</note> ...sharp, but with an exceedingly heavy smell, especially if rubbed by hand; its fruit, when tasted, induces violent vomiting. Hence, the adage seems to be derived either from the annoyance of the odor that follows one who plucks it—since the word *akopi* <note>Greek: ἀκοπὶ, meaning "without toil" or "painless," here used ironically</note> appears to have been found for the same thing—or from its effectiveness in inducing vomiting. Pliny also mentions this in Book 27, Chapter 4. There are those who say Anagyrus is a place in Attica belonging to the Erechtheid tribe, according to Stephanus, where this very foul-smelling shrub grows in abundance; thus we might accept "Anagyrus" for the shrub just as we accept "Anticyra" for hellebore. Again, others think Anagyrus was a certain divinity <note>original: "genium"</note> who, because his shrine was violated, utterly overthrew all his neighbors. Mention of this adage is made by Aristophanes in *Lysistrata*. Indeed, the passage in Aristophanes goes like this:

"From where does this stench come? From Anagyrus, by Zeus!"
"At any rate, it seems to me that Anagyrus has been disturbed."

Suidas records something much like this: that Anagyrus was a certain divinity, named after the place we mentioned, who took revenge on an old neighbor who had cut down his grove in the following manner. He instilled an insane love for the old man's son into the man's concubine; when she could not entice the young man's mind, she voluntarily denounced him to the father, claiming he would not stop soliciting her for debauchery. The father, persuaded by the woman, threw his son headlong from the roof and killed him. Later, repenting of the deed, he strangled himself with a noose. Finally, the woman threw herself into a well. The author cited for this story is Jerome—I know not which one—in a work *On the Writers of Tragedies*.

### The goat brings horns against herself. LXVI

<note>original: "Ἡ αἲξ καθ’ ἑαυτῆ τὰ κέρατα"</note> That is, *The goat brings horns against herself.* This belongs to the previous class of proverbs, born from a fable. A certain goat, having been wounded by a javelin, looked around to see where the evil had come from; seeing the bow, which was constructed from goat horns, she spoke in this manner: "I grew horns for my own destruction."

### Atlas the heavens. LXVII

<note>original: "Ἄτλας τὸν οὐρανόν"</note> That is, *Atlas [sustains] the heavens.* The word "undertook" or "supported" is understood. It is usually said of those who involve themselves in great and troublesome affairs and bring evil upon themselves. For this man received the Heavens as a guest. But having been caught because he had laid snares for him, he was cast headlong into the Atlantic sea. Furthermore, the fable of Atlas sustaining the heavens on his shoulders and neck is too well known to be recounted in this place.

### A God appearing from a machine. LXVIII

<note>original: "Θεὸς ἀπὸ μηχανῆς ἐπιφανείς"</note> That is, *A God appearing unexpectedly.* It is said of those who, in perplexed circumstances, find someone arising beyond hope to bring safety and unravel the difficulty of the business. It is taken from the custom of tragedies, in most of which some god was shown by certain machines: and this not on the stage itself, but from on high, who would suddenly change the circumstances and put an end to the play. This is attested by Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the first book *On the Nature of the Gods*, when he says: "Because you do not see how nature could produce this without some mind, you flee to a god, just as tragic poets do when you cannot explain the exit of a plot; whose help you certainly would not require if you saw the immense and boundless magnitude of regions in every direction." There is no doubt that Cicero here imitated that passage from Plato’s *Cratylus*: "Unless indeed, just as the tragedy writers, whenever they are at a loss, flee to machines by raising up gods." Because this proverb was unknown to him, the Latin translator of Plato rendered this passage incorrectly or certainly obscurely. Namely, in this manner: "Unless perhaps as the tragedians, as often as they are in doubt, flee to gods by means of certain fabricated mechanisms." The one who translated the *Life of Lysander* from Plutarch seems to have stumbled over the same stone. For when Lysander had decided to innovate the republic and weighed that the business was too difficult to be unraveled by common counsels, he did what poets are accustomed to do in tragedy: he strove to achieve what he had determined through fabricated oracles and the religion of the gods. The Greek text reads: "Just as in a tragedy, raising a machine before the citizens, he composed and prepared oracles as if given by the Pythian [Apollo]..."

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, FIRST CENTURY I.

...composed and prepared hidden things and oracles. Aristotle indicates the same somewhat obscurely, but certainly <gloss>is</gloss> elegantly, in 
<margin>Aristotle, Book 1 <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>original: "μετὰ τὰ φυσικά"</note></margin>
the first book of the <term>Metaphysics</term>: <term>For Anaxagoras, he says, uses Mind as a mechanical device for the creation of the world; whenever he is at a loss for the cause by which something is necessary, he drags it in. But in other matters, he assigns the cause of things happening to everything rather than to Mind.</term> <note>Anaxagoras was a pre-Socratic philosopher; Aristotle critiqued him for only using "Mind" as a last resort to explain the universe.</note> These words may be translated thus: For Anaxagoras uses Mind just like some tragic god who is accustomed to be suddenly revealed, in order to establish the world. For when he is stuck in explaining the cause of why it must be so, then he brings that in. Furthermore, in other matters, he makes anything else the cause of what happens, <gloss>rather than</gloss> Mind. Whence in Greek tragedies that phrase is almost a ritual: <term>Many are the forms of divine things.</term> <note>original: "πολλαὶ μορφαὶ τῶν δαιμονίων"</note> i.e., Many are the forms of the gods, etc. When they explain the plot by introducing a deity: as in the *Orestes* of Euripides, Apollo appearing in the midst of the tumults suddenly settles the most disturbed affairs. You see an example of this thing drawn from Homer, who, just as in the *Iliad* book 1 he introduces Pallas [Athena] to restrain the raging Achilles, so in many other places he summons some deity. Which indeed Horace in the *Art of Poetry* forbids to be done in comedies, unless the difficulty of the situation is greater <gloss>than</gloss> can be explained by human help:
*Let no god intervene, unless a knot worthy of such a deliverer*
*Should fall out.*
By which reasoning Plautus in *Amphitryon* introduced Jupiter, and for that reason calls it a tragic-comedy. Lucian in *Philopsendes*: <term>And as the saying goes, I thought fortune had brought a god from a machine to embrace me.</term> <note>original: "Καὶ τὸ τοῦ λόγου, θεὸν ἀπὸ μηχανῆς..."</note> that is, And according to the proverb, I thought this man had been brought to me by fortune just like some god suddenly appearing. He alluded to the same in the book *On Salaried Posts*: <term>For such people are peculiar to this kind of tragedy, so that another god from a machine sits upon the mast-head.</term> <note>original: "οἰκεῖοι γὰρ οἱ τοιοῦτος..."</note> that is, For these belong particularly to a tragedy of this sort. Or some other god suddenly arisen and sitting in the yardarms. Euripides looked to this in *Iphigenia at Aulis*: <term>I, a god, have appeared to you in my might.</term> <note>original: "θεὸς ἐγὼ πέφλωκά σοι μένος"</note> that is, Indeed I, a very great god, have appeared to you. Lucian in *The Sects*: <term>Standing by, just as in a tragedy, a god appearing from a machine.</term> <note>original: "Ἐπικὰς, ὥσπερ ἐν τραγῳδίᾳ τις..."</note> that is, Assisting according to the proverb of the tragedians: A god shown unexpectedly. In Athenaeus book 6, some poet or other makes a certain glutton complain that the fish-sellers would snatch away the fish as soon as they were shown,
<term>They sent away the buyers more quickly</term>
<term>than a seller from a machine, just like the gods.</term> <note>original: "ἀι θάττον ἀπἐπέμψασι..."</note> that is, And they soon remove the sold items from sight, and sell them as if from a machine in the manner of the gods.
Hence, as often as safety is shown unexpectedly, it is accustomed to be ascribed to a god. So Pliny in book 25: "For even among things discovered, sometimes chance finds them, sometimes—to speak truly—a god." The same in book 27: "This chance, therefore, this is that god who has discovered very many things in life."

---

->Man is a god to man.<-
<margin>69</margin>
Not very far from this is also that saying: <term>A human is a divinity to a human.</term> <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπου δαιμόνιον"</note> that is, Man is a god to man, <gloss>which</gloss> is accustomed to be said of him who has brought sudden and unhoped-for safety, or who has helped with some great benefit. For antiquity thought a god was nothing else <gloss>than</gloss> to be useful to mortals. Whence the authors of grain, wine, and laws, and whoever brought anything for the convenience of life, antiquity held them as gods: to such an extent that they even worshipped certain beasts as deities: as among the Egyptians the stork, because it is believed to go out to meet, ward off, and destroy the serpents that fly up from the Arabian marshes at a certain time of year; among the Romans the goose, <gloss>because</gloss> it saved the Capitoline citadel from the eruption of the Gauls by waking the guards with its honking. Which Marcus Tullius [Cicero] indicates when he writes in the first book *On the Nature of the Gods*: "I shall conclude that beasts were consecrated by the Barbarians <gloss>on account of</gloss> a benefit." Indeed, on the authority of Prodicus of Chios, even inanimate bodies were held as gods, such as the sun, moon, water, and earth, because they seemed to lead toward life, and because mortals were delighted in a greater way by their convenience. The Scythians, as Lucian testifies in *Toxaris*, swear by the wind and the sword as <gloss>if</gloss> by gods, because the former is the author of breathing, the latter of death. But since, as Cicero says, very many things, whether convenient or inconvenient, are accustomed to arise for man from man, and it is the property of a god either to save or to do good: therefore he who succors one in grave danger, or who bestows some huge benefit, since he performs as if the role of a god, is said to have emerged as a god to the one he helps. To this agrees that ritual closing in Homer and Hesiod,
<term>Gods, the givers of good things.</term> <note>original: "θεοὶ δωτῆρες ἐάων"</note> i.e., Gods, the bestowers of goods.
That which Strabo says in book 10: "It has been rightly said that mortals then most imitate the gods when they are beneficent." The same in book 17 relates that certain Egyptians make a double god: an immortal one, who is the author of all things, and a mortal one of unknown name: then from whom [be-] <note>The text cuts off mid-word "beneficio" (benefit), matching the catchword.</note>

<summary>This page explores the origins of the phrases "God from a machine" (Deus ex machina) and "Man is a god to man," tracing how classical authors used divine intervention as a literary device and how human benevolence was historically equated with divinity.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...those who have been affected by a great benefit almost worship their benefactors as gods. Furthermore, among the common people, those who are saved in tangled and desperate circumstances or from a double-edged danger say they were saved by some god. Horace says: -> So Apollo saved me. <- <note>original: "Sic me servavit Apollo." A quote from Horace's Satires 1.9.78.</note> Again, in his Odes, he writes that he was saved in war through Mercury, and again from the strike of a falling tree by the help of Faunus. Juvenal alluded to the same thing when he said:
> If some god, or someone like the gods
> and better than the fates, were to give forty thousand to you, poor little man.

Likewise Virgil in his *Tityrus*:
> O Meliboeus, a god has created this leisure for us.
> For he will always be a god to me: a tender lamb
> from our sheepfolds shall often stain his altar.

Then he gives the reason why he considers Caesar as a deity, subjoining the benefit:
> He permitted my cattle to roam, as you see, and myself
> to play what I wished on my rustic reed-pipe.

Pliny the Second, in the second book of his *Natural History*, indicated the Greek <term>homily</term> <note>original: οἰμιίαν (homilian) - here referring to a common saying or conversational topic</note> more clearly, but feeling as impiously about the gods as he did foolishly a little later regarding the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies. For when he had mocked the multitude of gods, and had utterly taken away the care for mortals from that one supreme being (whom he thinks is either this world or some unknown nature), he said: "For a mortal to help a mortal is God. And this is the path to eternal glory. By this path the Roman leaders went; by this path now goes with his children, with a heavenly stride, the greatest ruler of every age, Vespasian Augustus, coming to the aid of exhausted affairs. This is the most ancient custom of returning thanks to one who has deserved well: that such men are enrolled among the deities. Indeed, the names of all the other gods, and those which I mentioned above the stars, were born from the merits of men." Thus far Pliny. Ovid says:
> To save a man is a pleasure becoming to a man,
> and favor is sought better by no other art.

Plutarch, in the commentary which he titled *Against an Uneducated Prince*, denies that the gods are happy on the account that they live for a very long time, but because they are the leaders and authors of virtue. Furthermore, Paul refers the sum of virtues to charity; and charity is situated in this: that we deserve as well as possible from as many people as possible. Gregory Nazianzen looked toward this in his oration *On the Care for the Poor*: "Become," he says, "a god to the afflicted by imitating the mercy of God. For man has nothing so equally divine as beneficence." Although among Christians the title of "God" is not to be shared with any mortal even in jest, nor is such a notable and foul flattery to be received into our customs at all; nevertheless, it is possible that there is a use for this adage that is neither wicked nor unbecoming, if one were to speak in this way: "When I was pressed by such great evils that no mortal either wished or was able to help, you alone stood forth for me beyond hope, and by your benefit you not only saved me when I was otherwise about to perish, but even made me somewhat more distinguished than I was before. So that—either nowhere else at all, or certainly in us two—that old Greek adage has a place: <term>A man is a divine spirit to a man</term> <note>original: ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπου δαιμόνιον (anthrōpos anthrōpou daimoniōn)</note>." Or in this way: "I owe everything to literature, even my life; but I owe literature itself to you, who by your liberality supply my leisure and that of others. For what is it that the Greeks say, 'A man is a divine spirit to a man,' if this is not it?" Or in this fashion: "He who helps with a moderate benefit may indeed be a friend; but he who by his art and singular care and industry retains and restores a life already fleeing—which is exactly what a doctor does—what else is he than what the Greeks frequently say: 'A man is a divine spirit to a man'?" Or thus: "The matter had been brought to such a point that not even Safety herself could help. There you stood forth for me like a present deity, and having driven away my troubles with wonderful speed, you restored me to my former position, neither hoping nor expecting it, so that I understand that it was not said rashly by the Greeks: 'A man is a divine spirit to a man'." Or thus: "In other matters indeed you have always been most friendly to me; but in this cause, you were not only most friendly, but I might almost say what the Greeks say: 'A man is a divine spirit to a man'."

<sig>LXX</sig>
### Man is a wolf to man.
<term>A man is a wolf to a man</term> <note>original: Ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπῳ λύκος (Anthrōpos anthrōpō lykos)</note>. That is, "Man is a wolf to man." This is, as it were, the opposite of the previous one, and seems to have been fashioned from it, which Plautus uses in *The Ass-Dealer*: "Man is a wolf to man." By this we are warned not to trust an unknown man, but to beware of him just as we would a wolf. "A man," he says, "is a wolf to a man, not a man, when he does not know what sort of person he is."

# THE SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

->A quail saved the vigorous Hercules.<-

This is a six-foot verse <note>original: "Senarius"</note> among the Greeks, celebrated as a proverb. However, Zenodotus <note>An Alexandrian grammarian</note> denies that it is found in any of the ancient writers. It was commonly said of those who were saved in a moment of danger by those from whom they least expected help. They trace the origin of the adage to a fable of this sort: a certain quail was a favorite of Hercules; when it was being roasted, the smell of the bird restored him to life after he had died. Athenaeus also mentions this story in Book 9, writing that Hercules, the son of Jupiter and Asteria, was killed by Typhon while traveling in Libya, but was recalled to life by the smell of a quail held near him by Iolaus. For this reason, the Phoenicians sacrifice quails to Hercules.

<margin>An evil genius. 72</margin>

To the proverb we just mentioned, "A man is a god to a man," the "evil genius" seems to be the opposite. The Greeks call this an <term>alastor</term> <note>original: ἀλάστωρ; an avenging spirit or a person who brings bad luck</note>, a name we use for those to whom we attribute the greatest part of our misfortunes—a practice still common in everyday speech today. For there are some people so ill-omened for others that they may rightly seem like a kind of evil fate, born for their destruction. Furthermore, the proverb appears to have arisen from the opinion of the ancients, who assigned two "geniuses" to every individual, whom they call <term>daemons</term> <note>spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</note>. These were assigned not only to men, but even to places and buildings: one of them plots our ruin, while the other strives to help us. This was the opinion of Empedocles, cited by Plutarch in his essay *On Tranquillity of Mind*. This relates to the story of Brutus, which the same Plutarch records in his *Life of Brutus*. For when that fatal day loomed over Brutus, and he was keeping his usual late-night watch in his tent in Asia, the lamp already dying out, he seemed to see a tragic figure, larger than human size. Immediately, with an undaunted spirit, he asked who among men or gods it might be. The figure replied with a murmur: "I am your evil genius, Brutus; you shall see me at Philippi." And indeed, that same image appeared again to him as he fought at Philippi, which was his final battle.

Plutarch relates a similar story about Mark Antony and Augustus: namely, that while they lived together amicably in other matters, Octavian was always superior in the games they held in competition. This matter distressed Antony significantly. There was in Antony’s retinue a certain Egyptian magician. Whether he truly knew Antony's fate or was merely feigning to please Cleopatra, he warned Antony to separate himself as far as possible from Caesar <note>Augustus</note>, because Antony's genius, though otherwise bold, dreaded the genius of the other; the closer he approached, the more humble and dejected his spirit became. Plato also testifies that Socrates had a certain peculiar genius, about which Apuleius and Plutarch wrote. Terence seems to have felt the power of the genius when he says in *Phormio*: "It happened to me, I know this well. I remember being left behind by my angry god." Indeed, our own ancient theologians, following those ancients I believe, assign two geniuses—whom they call angels—to everyone from the very beginning of life: a friend who looks after our interests, and an evil one who threatens our destruction in every way. Naevius explains the "good genius" in *Stalagmonis* (quoted in Donatus): "My man is from my favorable god." Likewise Persius: "With the gods angry and a sinister genius." Finally, all those common phrases smack of this proverb: "The gods being angry," or "The gods being favorable." Terence: "I do not know, except I am sure enough the gods were angry at me for listening to him." Horace in his *Satires*:

> And he labors undeserving,
> Born with whatever Vertumni <note>gods of change</note> there are being unfavorable.

The same in his *Odes*:

> O best guardian of the Romulean race,
> Born of the good gods, you are absent.

Homer in the *Iliad*, Book 5: "Some god is angry, having noticed." <note>original: Θεὸς νύτις ἔσι νοήσας</note> And Virgil: "I believe indeed with the gods as guides and Juno being favorable." To the same point belong these: "Antipho is loved by the gods alone"; and, "The gods look back at us"; and, "Provided Jupiter is present"; and, "If any sinister powers permit"; and, "May Apollo be present on the right"; and six hundred other such phrases found everywhere among the poets. It will be more elegant, however, if you descend to specifics: such as, "He wrote poems with the Muses, however many there are, being angry." "He sings with Apollo angry." "He pleaded that cause most foolishly, clearly with Persuasion <note>Suadela</note> angry." "We fought with Mars on the left <note>unfavorable</note>." "We sailed with Neptune favorable." "I believe Mercury was angry when I made a pact with this old fox." "He works for children with Venus angry" (said of one who begets ugly children). "With Minerva unwilling" (of one who practices an art with little success).

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### 73. By a Favorable Hercules, or Hercules as a Friend

This is of the same kind, though more obscure, as what is read in Horace: *Wealthy by a friendly Hercules* <note>original: "Dives amico Hercule"</note>. And likewise in Persius: *O if a jar of silver would rattle under my rake, by a favorable Hercules* <note>original: "dextro Hercule"</note>. This indeed applies to those who are very fortunate in accumulating wealth. They believe this originated from the fact that Hercules, when about to die, said that those who consecrated a tenth part of their goods to him would be wealthy. Consequently, many rich men were accustomed to do so. However, Plutarch in his *Roman Questions* <note>original: "Probl." referring to Quaestiones Romanae</note> offers another reason for this custom: namely, that Hercules himself once sacrificed a tenth part of the oxen he had taken from Geryon on the Palatine Hill, or because he freed the Romans from the tithe usually paid to the Etruscans.

### 74. With Gods and Men Applauding

That hyperbole is also proverbial: *With gods and men applauding* <note>original: "Diis hominibusque plaudentibus"</note>; used for that which is done happily and auspiciously. Cicero, in a letter to his brother Quintus: *We crushed Vatinius, by whom he was openly attacked, according to our judgment, with gods and men applauding.* The same author in the first book of *Letters to Friends*: *I have not only said it, but I am also doing it, with gods and men approving.* Again, in the third book to his brother Quintus, he turns the proverb to the opposite meaning: *Unless our friend Pompey,* he says, *overturns the business against the will of gods and men.* Although this phrase itself—*gods and men*—is certainly proverbial due to its figure of speech, and is almost a standard expression among the poets. *The faith of gods and men!* <note>An exclamation of shock or appeal</note>; *hated by gods and men*; *he fears neither gods nor men.* Homer writes:
*Both the immortal gods and mortal men.* <note>original Greek: Ἀθάνατοί τε θεοὶ, θνητοί τ’ ἄνθρωποι</note>
And again:
*Father of both men and gods.* <note>original Greek: Πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε</note>

### 75. With Good Birds, With Evil Birds

To this class also belongs the expression: *With good, or evil birds* <note>original: "Bonis, aut malis avibus"</note>. We use this when we mean a matter turns out successfully or otherwise, taken from the observations of the augurs <note>term: augurs (priests in ancient Rome who interpreted the will of the gods by observing the flight of birds)</note>. Horace in his *Odes*:
*The ship sets out under an evil bird, carrying the stinking Mevius.*
And again:
*Under an evil bird you lead home a bride, whom Greece will reclaim with a great army.*
And yet again elsewhere:
*You shall be described by Varius, a brave man and a victor over enemies, as a bird of Maeonian song.*
Homer in the last book of the *Iliad*:
*Do not yourself become an unlucky bird for me in these halls.* <note>original Greek: Μὴ δέ μοι αὐτὴ ὄρνις ἐνὶ μεγάροισι κακὸς πέλευ</note>
These are the words of Priam to his wife, who was discouraging him from setting out alone to the camp of Achilles to ransom the body of Hector with gold, and who was prophesying many gloomy things, as women are accustomed to do. A certain Latin tragic writer used the phrase *Averted bird* <note>original: "Aversa avi"</note>, speaking of Agamemnon setting sail against the auspices: *He commands them to sail, with favorable rumor but an averted bird.* This is cited by Marcus Tullius Cicero in the first book of *On Divination*. To this form should also be referred: *by a lucky omen*, *well-omened*, *with good auspices*, *inauspiciously*, *with happy auguries*, and other things of that kind which, taken from the art of the augurs, have passed into common speech.

### 76. The Owl Flies

From the same superstition flowed that Greek saying, *The owl flies*, or *has flown* <note>original Greek: γλαὺξ ἵπταται</note>. For among the ancient Athenians, the flight of an owl was considered a symbol of victory, because this bird was believed to be sacred to Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, the patron goddess of Athens</note>, who was said to make even the ill-advised plans of the Athenians turn out well. Regarding this matter, we shall speak somewhat more fully in the proverb: *The ill-advised rashness of the Athenians.* From this, it became customary to say *The owl flies* when things were succeeding happily and according to one's desire. The authors are Zenodotus and Suidas. It will be said not unpleasantly that "the owl has flown" whenever a matter is believed to have been accomplished not by strength, but by the intervention of money, because the Athenian coinage had an owl engraved upon it. Whence also that saying: *Owls of Laurium*, which will be mentioned elsewhere. Plutarch, in the *Life of Pericles*, records that while he was haranguing the people from the upper deck of a ship, an owl flew to the right and perched on the mast; this omen caused everyone to come around to his opinion.

### 77. Born on the Fourth Moon

*To be born on the fourth moon* <note>original Greek: Ἐν τετράδι γεγεννηθῆναι</note> is said of those who are born with little luck...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

But later, Caesar was said to have "removed the hay from him," <note>original: "foenum detraxisse"</note> because while everyone else fled from him and dreaded him as they would a goring bull, Caesar was the first who dared to resist him. Saint Jerome also employs this adage in a certain letter, threatening those by whom he might happen to be provoked.

-> You seek a horned beast. LXXXII <-

That line of Plautus has almost the same meaning: *You seek a horned beast,* said of one who provokes a person prepared to retaliate for an injury, and whom you challenge only to your own misfortune. Horace alluded to this in his Odes: -> I raise my ready horns. <- <note>original: "Parata tollo cornua"</note>

-> Dionysius at Corinth. LXXXIII <-

*Dionysius at Corinth.* <note>original: "Διονύσιος ἐν Κορίνθῳ"</note> A proverbial allegory by which we signify someone who has been reduced from the highest dignity and power to a private and humble fortune; just as Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, having been expelled from power, taught children grammar and music for pay at Corinth. Cicero, in his *Letters to Atticus*, book nine: "Regarding the aristocrats, let it be as you wish. But you know that saying: *Dionysius at Corinth*." Quintilian, in his *Education of the Orator*, book eight: "There is allegory in historical examples, if they are not placed with the aforementioned reasoning. For just as 'Dionysius is at Corinth,' which all the Greeks use, so many similar things can be said." Here Cicero, when he says "You know that saying," and Quintilian, "Which all the Greeks use," both certainly signify that it was a commonly tossed-about phrase. Furthermore, Plutarch revealed where the adage originated in his little book titled *On Garrulity* <note>original: "περὶ τῆς ἀδολεσχίας"</note>—that is, on futile talkativeness. For praising sayings that are brief and weighty, he records that response given by the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> to King Philip when he was threatening war and acting fiercely: *Dionysius at Corinth.* When the king wrote back to them that if he ever led his army into Laconia, he would utterly destroy the Lacedaemonians, they responded with only a single word: *If.* <note>original: "Δίκα" (Dika/Ei)</note> Plato sailed to Sicily three times, not without a sprinkling of sinister rumors. Whence Molon, who bore a hostile mind toward Plato, used to say it was no wonder if Dionysius was at Corinth, but rather if Plato was in Sicily. For necessity pressed the King, but ambition solicited Plato.

-> This bean will be threshed on me. LXXXIIII <-

Terence in *The Eunuch*: "But indeed, this bean will be threshed on me." <note>original: "At enim isthæc in me cudetur faba"</note> That is, according to the commentator Donatus: this evil will fall back on me, this fault will be punished on me. It is a metaphor either from the bean, which is stripped of its pods and beaten or crushed with clubs (as is done on threshing floors in the rustic fashion), where the floor itself does not suffer, but rather that which is threshed upon it. Others prefer to refer it to a poorly cooked bean, which, if it has not softened but remained hard, was sometimes accustomed to be crushed with a stone over the cook's head by angry masters—as if they were taking vengeance on the bean, not the cook, though meanwhile the entire misfortune reaches the cook.

-> You stirred this mash yourself, you must eat it all. LXXXV <-

Donatus noted a similar sentiment to the one above, which is read in the same poet [Terence] in *Phormio*: "You stirred this yourself, you must eat it all." <note>original: "Tute hoc intristi, tibi omne est exedendum"</note> These are the words of Phormio the parasite, who, since he had been the author of the plan to marry the girl, thinks it fair that he should likewise settle the matter at his own risk. They think it is a metaphor from the garlic-mash of rustics. Indeed, this sentiment is still in the mouths of our own common people today. And another very similar to it: "The wool you have prepared for the distaff, you must spin yourself," that is, you stood forth as the author of the beginning, now you must unfold the same.

-> Let the smith wear the shackles he made himself. LXXXVI <-

Ausonius, in his Trochaic verses, subjoins a certain proverb closely related to the Terentian one, and interprets the poet's metaphor with another:
> You, a troublesome hunter of debts, read troublesome poems.
> What you have stirred, you must eat: so the old word commands,
> That the smith himself should wear the shackles he made.
It applies to those who are the authors of their own misfortunes. Moreover, it seems to be taken from the poet Theognis, who says: "No man, dear Cyrnus, forges fetters for himself." <note>original: "οὔτις ἀνὴρ φίλε Κύρνε πέδας χαλκεύεται αὐτῷ"</note> Something similar to this, humbler indeed but still apt, is commonly said: "He prepared the whip himself, with which he should be beaten." And that is taken from boys or slaves, who are sometimes forced to prepare the rods themselves with which they are to be flogged.

-> You who caught the tortoises, eat them yourselves. LXXXVII <-

A proverb related to these is recorded by Greek writers:

# FIRST THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED
<sig>e 3</sig>

<margin>Eat the turtles, or do not eat them.</margin> <note>original: "χελώνας ἐσθίειν ἢ οὐκ ἐσθίειν"</note> **Eat the turtles, or do not eat them.** That is: Either do not touch them at all, or if you do, eat them up. This is cast at those who, after rashly undertaking something, implore the help of others whom they previously refused to involve in the business. They believe the proverb was born from a fable of this sort: Some fishermen, having cast their net, hauled up some turtles. When they had divided them among themselves, they found there were not enough to feed everyone, yet by chance Mercury approached, and they invited him to the feast. But he, understanding that he was by no means being called out of kindness, but rather so that he might relieve them of food they found distasteful, refused. He added: that they themselves should eat the turtles they had caught. According to Pliny, there are people in Carmania who live on the flesh of turtles, from which the name "Turtle-eaters" <note>original: "χελωνοφάγοις"</note> was given to them. Strabo asserts that turtles are found there of such great size that their shells cover entire huts.

->**The spirit of Temessa will be present.**<-
->**LXXXVIII**<-

Strabo, in the sixth book of his *Geography*, reports that Temessa is the first city of Bruttium after Laos; it is also called Tempsa. It was founded by the Ausonians, then held by the Aetolian companions of Thoas, and after these were expelled, by the Bruttians; finally, Hannibal and the Romans utterly destroyed it. Near this city was a small shrine surrounded by wild olive trees, sacred to a certain Polites, one of the companions of Ulysses. It is said that because he was violated by the barbarians, he exercised a heavy wrath against them—so much so that it passed into a proverb that one must take care lest the "spirit of Temessa" loom over them. Later, as Aelian says, a famous boxer of remarkable strength named Euthymus came there from Italy to the Locrians. He was known to carry a stone of immense size, which is still shown at Locri. He fought with Polites and emerged victorious from the contest, thus freeing the neighboring people of Temessa from the tribute that the spirit had been accustomed to extort. Indeed, he compelled the spirit to return with interest what it had taken by force. From this, it is thought the proverb arose for those who make filthy and unjust gains: "The spirit of Temessa will be present." By this, they signified that things snatched away against the law, by fraud or force, must eventually be paid back with interest. Pausanias, in his *Eliaca*, tells the story slightly differently: namely, that a companion of Ulysses was killed for raping a maiden, and because of this, his ghost used to wander and bring destruction to every sex and age unless they appeased him by offering a maiden every year. It was commonly believed that the ghost was the local spirit, whom the boxer Euthymus suppressed upon returning to Temessa, freeing the maiden who had been devoted to death and taking her in marriage. In the Greek text of Suidas, the passage seems not to be free of errors. For so we read in the Aldine edition: <note>Erasmus here critiques a corrupted Greek passage regarding the hero of Temessa</note>. Perhaps the reading would be more tolerable if you remove the conjunction "and." However, since Strabo recounts the proverb before mentioning the hero was restrained, he indicates it was rather used against those who provoke a powerful man. Even so, nothing prevents a proverb from being adapted to various uses.

->**Termerian evils.**<-
->**LXXXIX**<-

<margin>Termerian evils.</margin> <note>original: "Τερμέρια κακά"</note> That is, **Termerian evils.** By an ancient proverb, these are said to be immense evils, especially those which someone has inflicted upon others and which eventually recoil upon their own head. Plutarch mentions this adage in his *Life of Theseus*; Theseus, following the example of Hercules, traveled the lands and was accustomed to punish every wicked person he found with the same penalty they had cruelly exercised upon others. For Hercules slew Damascus and finished off Cycnus in the manner of gladiators; finally, he crushed Termerus, who used to break human heads, with a similar blow. Hence, against those whose own misdeeds are turned back upon them, the proverb is said: "A Termerian evil." To this same sentiment belongs the story we read of the "Seller of Smoke" in Thurii, who was killed by smoke; and Phalaris, whom [Perillus] perished by his own invention when he was placed inside the bronze bull. There is also that very festive story related in the *Life of the Emperor Gallienus*. When a certain man had sold glass gems to the Empress as if they were real, and having been caught, she demanded he be punished, the Emperor ordered the seller to be seized as if to be thrown to the lions. Then he let out a capon <note>a rooster</note>. While everyone wondered at such a ridiculous thing, he ordered it to be announced by a herald: "He practiced an imposture, and he has suffered one." And so he dismissed the merchant. But regarding "Termerian evils," Suidas brings a much different interpretation: namely, that there is a place in Caria named Termerium, which tyrants sometimes used as a prison. It is located between Melos and Halicarnassus. From this place, when later robbers...

Although Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century grammarian</note> places the city of Termera in Lycia, which he says took its name from a man named Termerus. Finally, "Termerian evils" can be understood as "extreme evils." For *terma* in Greek signifies an end, and they call the final day of life the *termarian* day. Furthermore, the Latins call that which they wish to be seen as highest and greatest "extreme": such as "extreme madness" or "extreme insanity." The Greeks do the same, saying "extreme evil" <note>original: ἔσχατον κακόν</note> for the greatest evil.
