->90. Neoptolemic vengeance.<-

"Neoptolemic vengeance" <note>original: Νεοπτολέμειος τίσις</note>. This is very similar to the previous adage, used when someone suffers the same kind of treatment they have inflicted on others. Pausanias reports this in his *Messenian History* and explains it in these words: "Indeed, over time, what is called Neoptolemic vengeance overtook the Lacedaemonians themselves. For it happened to Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles—who had killed Priam at the very hearth of his courtyard—that he himself was slaughtered at Delphi at the altar of Apollo; and from this, they call it Neoptolemic vengeance when one suffers exactly what he has done to others." Euripides, in his *Orestes*, speaking through the character of Apollo regarding Neoptolemus, says: "For it is his fate to die by the Delphic sword."

->91. To serve the stage.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero used the phrase "to serve the stage" <note>original: seruire scenæ</note> to mean serving the time, and accommodating oneself to present circumstances. The metaphor is taken from stage actors who do not act according to their own judgment, but look only to this: to please the eyes of the people in whatever way they can, otherwise they are to be hissed and booed off. For he writes thus to Brutus: "You must now serve the people and the stage, as they say. For the eyes not only of your army, but of all citizens, and almost all nations, are fixed upon you." It will also apply to those who have undertaken some illustrious business, from which it is necessary to depart either with the highest praise or the highest infamy, because of the expectations of so many. Furthermore, Phocylides <note>A Greek gnomic poet</note> warned that a wise man must serve the time: "Worship the occasion, and do not blow against the winds." That is:
>Remember always to cautiously serve the times,
>Nor wish to blow back against the blasts of the wind.
Moreover, this metaphor is drawn from sailors, who, once they have entered the sea, must be carried by the will of the winds and the tide, and would struggle in vain if they wished to fight against them.

->92. To use the market.<-

Akin to this is "to use the market" <note>original: τῇ ἀγορᾷ χρῆσθαι</note>, which means to be content with the present state of affairs, and however fortune offers itself, to apply one's mind accordingly. Terence in the *Phormio* says: "You knew how to use the market." Donatus <note>A famous Roman grammarian</note> reminds us that this is a common proverb, and the metaphor is drawn from merchants, who do not prescribe the price of what they bring before reaching the place of commerce, but take counsel on whether or not to sell their goods according to the market price they find. Seneca says: "Let us use the market, and whatever chance brings, let us bear it with an equal mind." The same author in his 72nd Epistle used the phrase "born under the hand" for something done on the spur of the moment. "Therefore," he says, "counsel ought to be born on the day, and even this is too slow: let it be born 'under the hand,' as they say."

->93. Adopt the mind of a polypus.<-

There exists a Greek adage to be placed in this category: "Hold the mind of a polypus" <note>original: πολύποδος νόον ἴσχε; a polypus is an octopus</note>. By this we are commanded to assume different manners and different countenances according to the time. Homer seems to praise this in Ulysses, whom he calls "of many turns" <note>original: πολύτροπον</note>, that is, of versatile character. The adage is born from the nature of this fish, which Pliny mentions in Book 9, Chapter 29. Furthermore, Lucian, in the dialogue of Menelaus and Proteus, writes that it changes color especially in fear. For when fishermen are frequent, it attaches itself to rocks, and to whatever rock it adheres, it imitates its color with its body, evidently so that it cannot be caught. Indeed, as Basil the Great reports, fish are often deceived by the false image and swim toward it, offering themselves voluntarily to the predator. Furthermore, the proverb is taken from Theognis, whose couplet about the polypus survives today. It is also cited by Plutarch in his essay *On Having Many Friends*.

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY I
->e 4<-

**Keep the mind of the many-tangled octopus, which appears to be like the rock with which it associates.** <note>original: Πουλυπόδου νόον ἴσχε πολυπλόκου, ὃς ποτὶ πέτρῃ τῇ προσομιλήσῃ, τοῖος ἰδεῖν ἐφάνη.</note> That is: You should have the mind of the crafty octopus, which immediately reflects the color of the rocks to which it has moved. Clearchus, in his book on proverbs, as cited by Athenaeus, quotes this couplet without naming the author: **My son, have the mind of the octopus, O hero Amphilochus, adapting yourself to whatever city of the people you come to.** <note>original: Πουλυπόδου μοι τέκνον ἔχων νόον ἀμφίλοχ’ ἥρως, τοῖσιν ἐφαρμόζων ὧν κε πόλις δήμου ἵκηται.</note> That is: My son, hero Amphilochus, be like the octopus in nature to me, and fit yourself to the people, whomever you approach. Plutarch cites the same poem from Pindar. From this, that proverbial verse is also celebrated: **Now it is necessary for this man to become different, and to follow the place.** <note>original: Νῦν μὲν ὅδ’ ἀλλοῖος τελέθει, καὶ χώρου ἐπείδει.</note> That is: It is expedient for a man to become now this person, now that, according to the place.

This warns us to accommodate ourselves to every way of life, and acting as a sort of **Proteus** <note>A sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note>, to transform ourselves into any form as circumstances require. Plutarch likewise used the phrase **versatile rhythm** <note>original: πολύτροπον ῥυθμὸν</note> to mean moving into a different opinion. Aristophanes also notes this in *Plutus*, advising that one must live **according to local customs** <note>original: τρότοις ἐπιχωρίοις</note>, that is, by the manners of the region and the natives. To the same point belongs: **The law is the region itself** <note>original: νόμῳ τῇ χώρᾳ</note>. By this, it is signified that every region has certain peculiar institutions which guests should not condemn, but strive to imitate and express to the best of their ability.

Nor should anyone think this adage teaches foul flattery, by which some agree with everyone on everything, or the vice of inconsistency in character, which Horace elegantly censures in his *Satires*, and which historians note in Catiline and the Emperor Avidius Cassius. Finally, Holy Scripture <margin>Ezekiel 27.</margin> <note>The margin cites Ezekiel, though the "fool changing like the moon" is a common reference to Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 27:11.</note> mentions it regarding a certain wicked man, saying a fool changes just like the moon, while a wise man, following the example of the sun, is always like himself.

In the case of **Alcibiades** <note>A famous Athenian statesman known for his charisma and shifting loyalties.</note>, one might doubt whether his behavior deserves blame or praise; certainly, there was a most happy and admirable dexterity of character and wit in him, who played the octopus so well that in Athens he played with jokes and wit, bred horses, and lived charmingly and elegantly. Yet among the Spartans, he shaved his head, wore a coarse cloak, and washed in cold water. Among the Thracians, he fought and drank. But when he came to Tissaphernes, he adopted the customs of the royal people in luxury, softness, and pride.

However, there is a certain difficult, stubborn, and peevish simplicity of the unskillful, by which they demand that everyone everywhere live only according to their own customs, and they condemn whatever pleases others. Conversely, there is a certain honorable reasoning by which good men sometimes comply with the customs of others, lest they be either hateful or unable to be of use, or so that they may rescue themselves or their own from great dangers. Just as **Ulysses** did with Polyphemus by feigning many things, and acting the beggar among the suitors. Likewise **Brutus**, with his feigned stupidity and even feigned madness. Indeed, even the holy Apostle **Paul** boasts with a certain sacred vaunting that he used this pious craftiness, and became "all things to all men," so that he might win all for Christ.

Nevertheless, nothing prevents the use of the adage from being extended more widely to mark vices, namely in men born with a certain versatile wit who put on whatever persona belongs to those with whom they happen to deal. Plautus elegantly described this type in the *Bacchides*: "No man," he says, "can be useful unless he knows how to do both good and evil. Let him be wicked with the wicked, let him snatch, let him steal what he can from thieves. Confess that the man is a useful 'shifter' whose heart is wise: let him be good to the good, evil to the evil. However the matter is, so let him have his mind." Eupolis, in Athenaeus, says: **A citizen who is an octopus in character.** <note>original: Πολίτης πωλύπους ἐς τὸν τρόπον.</note> That is: A sophisticated man who is an octopus in his manners.

Clearchus, in his *Natural Causes*, cites these verses from Pindar: **Applying his mind most of all to the skin of the sea-beast, he associates with all cities.** <note>original: Πόντου θηρὸς χρωτὶ μάλιστα τὸν νόον προσφέρων, πάσαις πολίεσσιν ὁμιλεῖ.</note> That is: Adapting his mind greatly to the color of the sea-beast, he has familiarity with all states. And in the same place, he gives the reason why this happens to this fish. **Aristotle** drew a similar metaphor from the **chameleon** in the first book of his *Ethics*. For he says if things depend on fortune, since fortune changes repeatedly, it follows that a person will vary like a chameleon, now happy, now miserable; however luck looks back with one face or another, so he also changes his face and mind. **Pliny** mentions the chameleon in Book 28, Chapter 8, writing that this animal is almost equal in size to a crocodile; otherwise...

He says that no animal is considered more fearful, and for that reason, it undergoes a change into various colors. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Flattery*, writes that the chameleon imitates any color except white. The same author, in his *Symposiacs* <note>Table Talk</note>, tries to give a reason regarding the polyp <note>octopus</note>, why it does not merely change color—which also happens to humans in fear—but even adapts itself to the color of whatever rock it happens to be near. There are also certain birds that change both their color and their voice according to the seasons of the year, as the same Pliny testifies in Book 10, Chapter 29, and Aristotle in Book 9 of *On the Nature of Animals*. In the changing of the voice, the nightingale holds the first place. Hence, in Euripides, Hecuba commands Polyxena to imitate the nightingale and turn herself into every kind of voice, if in any way she might persuade Ulysses not to kill her.

### More versatile than a buskin. 94

*More versatile than a buskin* <note>original Greek: Εὐμεταβολώτερος κοθόρνου</note>. This was said of a man who is not very constant, of slippery faith, or who belongs to an uncertain and ambiguous faction. The comparison is drawn from a type of footwear which the Greeks call *kothornos* and the Latins, changing a letter, call the *cothurnus* <note>a high, thick-soled boot</note>, which it was the custom for tragic actors to use. It was, moreover, "square-shaped and fitting either side"—that is, quadrangular and able to be fitted to either the right or the left foot. Suidas adds that they were of such a kind that they suited men and women alike. The famous line of Maro <note>Virgil</note> testifies to this:
->To bind the calves high with the buskin.<-

The proverb is expressed in two ways: by comparison, "more changeable than a buskin," and by naming, as when we call a man himself a "buskin" <note>Greek: κόθορνον</note> if he attaches himself to different parties. For thus was Theramenes, the Athenian rhetorician and disciple of Prodicus of Chios, named: because he sat, as it were, on two chairs, favoring both the cause of the people and that of the Thirty Tyrants, appearing now to be of this faction, now of that—or rather, of both. Plutarch, in his *Political Precepts*, says: "But they thought that Theramenes especially ought to put on the buskin to associate with both sides and join neither." Lucian, in his *Affairs of the Heart*: "But I would pray, if it were possible, to become like that good Theramenes, the 'buskin,' so that both of you might depart as victors on equal terms." The same author in *The False Logician*: "And another gave him the name of 'buskin,' comparing the man's inconstant and ambiguous character to that type of footwear." Plutarch indicates that the general Nicias was also commonly given the nickname "buskin" because of the craftiness of his character. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> was also spoken ill of by this name. Homer, if I am not mistaken, calls Mars—who frequently changes sides—by the new word *alloprosallos* <note>shifting from one to another</note>. Nothing, however, prevents the adage from being taken in a good sense, as if one were to call a man of easy manners and a certain dexterity of wit, who gets along with every kind of person, a "buskin." For this reason, Homer called Ulysses *polytropos* <note>of many turns/ways</note>, because he aptly played every role: leader, beggar, or father of a family.

### More variegated than a hydra. 95

*More variegated than a hydra* <note>original Greek: Ποικιλώτερος ὕδρας</note>. This refers to the crafty and deceitful, because the water-snake is distinguished by its many-colored markings. It is aptly said of the sly and the "turncoats," or even those who are inconsistent with themselves. This six-foot verse is cited in Athenaeus, Book 3 of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The Learned Banqueters</note>:
"You have made him more variegated than a peacock."
Related to this is the fact that the poet Mnaseas of Colophon was given the nickname "Salpa" by a popular joke because he was "variegated" in his poetry. For that fish <note>the salpa or dreamfish</note> is wonderfully colored, with golden and reddish lines drawn at certain intervals from the neck to the tail across silvery sides, though otherwise it is of poor flavor.

### The Ring of Gyges. 96

*The Ring of Gyges* <note>original Greek: Γύγου δακτύλιος</note>. This applies either to men of inconstant character or to the fortunate, who, as if by a divine wand, obtain whatever they wish at their own will. Lucian mentions this adage in *The Wishes*, where someone wishes for several rings of the kind Gyges had: one to become rich, another to be made pleasing and lovable, and another through which he might be allowed to fly wherever he pleased. For the superstition of the ancients attributed much to the efficacy of rings, so that they were sold with various incantations...

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 1

...others against the bites of wild beasts, others against slander, others for various purposes, either to ward off troubles or to secure advantages for those who wore them. Hence, in Aristophanes' play *Plutus* <note>The god of Wealth</note>, the character Dicaeus says to a Sycophant <note>A professional informer or slanderer in ancient Athens</note> who is threatening him with a lawsuit:
> I care nothing for you, for I wear this ring
> which I bought from Eudamus for a drachma.
And again in the same play:
> But there is no [remedy] for the bite of a sycophant.
The word "remedy" is understood. He speaks in this way by alluding to the bites of wild beasts. This proverb arose from a story of this kind, which Plato did not hesitate to recount in the second book of *The Republic*. Nor will it trouble us to recount it here. 

Gyges, the father of a certain Lydian, was a hired shepherd for the king who ruled the Lydian people at that time. When a most violent storm once arose, a great force of rain fell, followed by lightning and an earthquake, so that in the region where Gyges happened to be pasturing his flocks, the earth opened up with a huge chasm. When he noticed this—being alone, for the other shepherds had fled in terror—he descended into it. There he saw many wonderful things, including a bronze horse, enormous and hollow. There was a window in the side of the horse, and looking through it into the belly, he saw the corpse of a man larger than human size. The body had no clothing or ornaments, except for a ring placed on its finger. When he had taken it and returned from the cave, he went back a few days later to the assembly of shepherds, where a representative was to be chosen to report to the king each month regarding the accounts of the flocks. 

As he sat among the others, he noticed that whenever he turned the stone set in the ring toward the inside of his hand, he suddenly became invisible to everyone, and they spoke of him as if he were not there. Marvelling at this, he turned the face of the ring outward again, and immediately became visible to the shepherds. Having tested this power more carefully and frequently, and having fully explored that the ring possessed this virtue—to make him invisible when the gem was turned toward himself, and visible when turned toward others—he arranged to be sent to the king as the representative of the shepherds. Having arrived, he seduced the king's wife and plotted with her to murder the king. Finally, having killed him, he took the kingdom and the queen in marriage; thus, from a shepherd, he suddenly became a king by the benefit of that fateful ring. 

Plato mentions this same story in the tenth book of *The Republic*. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] also relates it in the third book of *On Duties*. Furthermore, Herodotus in his first book tells the story quite differently and makes no mention of a ring. Very similar to this is the <term>Helmet of Hades</term> <note>original: "Ἄϊδος κυνῆ", a mythical cap of invisibility</note>, which we shall discuss in another place.

### 97. The Divine Wand.

The "divine wand" <note>original: "Virgula divina"</note> is not very different from this, used whenever we suggest that whatever we desire happens to us as if by divine intervention, without human effort. This is because antiquity, just as with rings, believed there was a certain fateful or even magical power in carrying wands. Marcus Cicero says in the first book of *On Duties*: "But if everything necessary for our living and refinement were supplied to us by a divine wand, as they say..." It is also cited several times in Nonius Marcellus. Varro wrote a work titled *On the Divine Wand*, which appears to have been one of his Menippean Satires, from which many wonderful and proverbial sayings are derived. 

The adage seems to have originated primarily from that wand of Homer's, which he attributes to Pallas [Athena]; it was so famous that Antisthenes, the founder of the Cynic sect, wrote a book about it, comparing it (as I conjecture) to his own staff. Homer mentions this wand in several places, such as when Athena suddenly turns Ulysses from a squalid old man into a youth, making him radiant and handsome, in the *Odyssey*, book 13:
> Having spoken thus, Athena touched him with her wand.
And again, turning him from a youth back into an old man, in *Odyssey* book 16:
> Having thus spoken, Athena touched him with her wand,
> and immediately made him an old man again.
And again in the same book, when she restores his youth and increases his strength...

<summary>This page explores the origins of proverbs related to magical objects, specifically the Ring of Gyges which grants invisibility and the "Divine Wand" used to describe effortless success.</summary>
<keywords>Ring of Gyges, invisibility, Divine Wand, Plato, Cicero, Homer, Athena, Ulysses, Greek mythology, ancient proverbs</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"Athena touched him with her golden wand." <note>original: ἡ καὶ χρυσείῃ ῥάβδῳ ἐπεμάσσατ’ ἀθήνη</note> That is,
"She spoke, and with a golden wand Athena stroked him."
In the same manner, a miraculous wand is attributed to Mercury as an enchanter, which they call the *caduceus* <note>The herald's staff carried by Hermes/Mercury, often entwined with snakes</note>. From the *Odyssey*, Book 24:
"He held the wand in his hands,
Beautiful and golden, with which he soothes the eyes of men
Whom he wills, and again awakens those who sleep." <note>original: ἔχε δὲ ῥάβδον... τοὺς δ’ αὖτε καὶ ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρει</note> That is,
"Then he takes in his hands the golden and beautiful wand:
With this he soothes the eyes of those he chooses with sleep,
And again releases the eyes of others from sleep."
He repeats almost the same things in *Odyssey*, Book 5, and *Iliad*, Book 24:
"Immediately then he bound the beautiful sandals under his feet,
Ambrosial and golden, which bore him over the moist sea
And over the boundless earth along with the blasts of the wind.
And he took the wand, with which he soothes the eyes of men
Whom he wills, and again awakens those who sleep." <note>original: Αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’... τοὺς δ’ αὖτε καὶ ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρει</note> That is,
"Soon, when he had placed the golden sandals beneath his feet,
Beautiful and breathing of ambrosia, which bore him
Through the liquid air and across the vast reaches of the wide
Earth, with the breath of the wind accompanying:
Then he takes the wand; with this he soothes the eyes with sleep
Of whomsoever he wishes, and with the same he drives sleep away."
Imitating him, Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note> thus describes the same *caduceus* in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:
"Then he takes the wand. With this he calls pale souls forth from
the underworld, others he sends down to gloomy Tartarus,
He gives sleep and takes it away, and unseals the eyes from death.
Relying on it, he drives the winds and swims through the turbulent clouds."
Nor was a wand lacking for Circe to perform her monstrous deeds in transforming the companions of Ulysses, in *Odyssey*, Book 10:
"Having struck them with her wand, she shut them in the sties.
And they had the heads of swine." <note>original: ῥάβδῳ πεπληγῦα... οἱ δὲ συῶν μὲν ἔχον κεφαλάς</note> That is,
"She drove them into the number of pigs by the stroke of her wand,
Having been struck, and behold, they had swinish heads."
Again, a little further down:
"Whenever she strikes you with her very long wand." <note>original: ὁπποτέκην λύρκησ’ ἐλάσῃ παδυμήκεϊ ῥάβδῳ</note> That is,
"When Circe shall strike you with the blow of her very long wand."
Somewhat later, Ulysses alone, having drunk Circe's cup, was not transformed into a beast:
"But when I had drunk it, she did not enchant me,
Though she struck me with her wand." <note>original: Αὐτὰρ ἐπὰν εἴκῃσι... ῥάβδῳ πεπληγῦα</note> That is,
"But when I had drunk the offered cup, the blow of the wand
Did not soothe <note>In this context, 'soothe' implies the casting of a spell</note> me."
Finally, when she restored his companions to their former shape for the sake of Ulysses, she employed the service of the wand. Indeed, even in the writings of the Hebrews, Moses uses a wand in performing miracles. This he turns into a snake, this he restores to its former shape; with this he turns the water of the river into blood, killing the fish; with this he summoned gnats; with this he divided the waves of the Red Sea; with this, having struck the flint, he drew forth a spring. Perhaps it pertains to this that a wand was also granted to kings, which they call a scepter. Whence in Homer several times: "Scepter-bearing kings." <note>original: Σκηπτοῦχοι βασιλῆες</note> That is, *Sceptrigeri reges*. To the same point looks what we have related elsewhere: "I carry a laurel staff."

---

->A fool speaks foolish things. XCVIII<-

Euripides in the *Bacchae*: "For a fool speaks foolish things." <note>original: Μωρὰ γὰρ μωρὸς λέγει</note> That is, for the speech of a fool is foolish. Our prophet Isaiah expressed that sentiment in just as many words. Seneca to Lucilius says: "Among the Greeks, it has passed into a proverb: Such was a man's speech, as was his life." It is not entirely clear what kind of thing this was, except that a certain poem exists, celebrated among the Greeks:
"A man's character is known from his speech." <note>original: Ἀνδρὸς χαρακτὴρ ἐκ λόγου γνωρίζεται</note> That is,
"The figure of a man is recognized by his oratory."
The philosopher Democritus, according to Laertius, used to say that speech was the "image of life" <note>original: εἴδωλον τοῦ βίου</note>, and as it were, a kind of shadow. Than which sentiment nothing could be said more truly. For in no mirror does the figure of the body shine back better or more expressively than the image of the innermost heart in speech...

# FIRST THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED
<meta>original: CHILIADIS PRIMAE CENTVRIA I.</meta>

...is revealed. Just as bronze vessels are known by their ring, so are men known by their speech. <note>Erasmus is comparing the "sound" of a person's words to the resonance of metal to judge quality.</note>

### To tear the traveling cloak.
->XCIX<-

In daily life, it is a very common expression "to tear the traveling cloak" <note>Latin: *scindere penulam*</note> when someone is being particularly insistent about holding a guest back and inviting them to stay longer. Those who do this grab the cloak by hand, as if trying to delay them by force. This adage flowed down from antiquity, like many others. Cicero, writing to Atticus in Book 13 regarding Varro, says: "He came to me, and at such a time that he ought to have stayed. But I acted in such a way as *not to tear his traveling cloak*. For I remembered your advice, and there were many things prepared." And a little later: "C. Capito was with T. Carinas. I barely *touched their cloaks*, yet they remained."

### Faith should be placed in the eyes more than the ears.
->C<-

<margin>Eyes are more trustworthy than ears <note>original Greek: ωτῶν πιϛότεροι ὀφθαλμοί</note></margin> That is, one should believe the eyes rather than the ears. Things that are seen are more certain than things heard.

<margin>Likewise Horace, in his Art of Poetry:</margin>
> Things dropped through the ear stir the mind more slowly
> Than those placed before the faithful eyes, which
> The spectator delivers to himself.

<margin>The ears are less trustworthy than the eyes <note>original Greek: τὰ ὦτα ἀπιϛότερα ὀφθαλμῶν</note></margin>
This next point is slightly different. More relevant is what Plautus says of a madam's hands: they have eyes, not ears, meaning they only believe what they see <note>A reference to "cold hard cash" or seeing payment before acting</note>. Again, those who wish history to be a record of deeds done say it is named <term>from the act of seeing <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ ἱϛορεῖν (para to historein)</note></term>. Finally, consider that famous passage in Virgil about the two gates in the underworld: The Ivory gate, through which they signify that things which are heard pass out, because of the ivory whiteness of teeth. And the Horn gate, through which things seen by the eyes are understood, because of the blackness of the pupils. In short, the ears contribute more to learning, but the eyes are more certain for establishing the truth. Hence, in common speech, if someone tells a story that seems unlikely, we usually ask if they saw it themselves. If they say no, the truth of what they heard is questioned. This proverb is cited in a letter from Julian to Leontius: <term>The word is a Thurian gate to the ears <note>original Greek: ὁ λόγος τοῖς ὦσι θύρειος</note></term> and <term>among men, ears are less trustworthy than eyes <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀνθρώποις ὀφθαλμῶν ἀπιϛότερα</note></term>. He called it "Thurian" to indicate Herodotus was the author of the saying—either because of his divine inspiration, or because that writer lived and died among the Thurians. It is taken from the book *Clio*: <term>For it happens that ears are less trustworthy to men than eyes <note>original Greek: ὦτα γὰρ τυγχάνει ἀνθρώποισιν ἐόντα ἀπιϛότερα ὀφθαλμῶν</note></term>.

# FIRST THOUSAND, SECOND HUNDRED
<meta>original: CHILIADIS PRIMAE CENTVRIA SECVNDA.</meta>

### The exchange of Diomedes and Glaucus.
->I<-

The exchange between Diomedes and Glaucus recorded in Homer has passed into a proverb whenever we signify an unequal trade—that is, giving back worse things for better ones: <term>gold for bronze <note>original Greek: χρύσεα χαλκείων</note></term>. For in the sixth book of the *Iliad*, the poet introduces a certain Glaucus, son of Hippolochus, a leader of the Lycians who was more of a boaster and a show-off than a fighter. Opposite him was Diomedes, a man of courage and cunning. These two met <term>to fight in single combat <note>original Greek: μονομαχησόμενοι</note></term>. But Glaucus, when asked by Diomedes who among men or gods he might be, set forth the lineage of his birth in a long speech, explaining his homeland of Lycia and the city of Ephyra. Soon Diomedes, being a Greek and perceiving the stupidity of the barbarian from the arrogance of his speech, thought he should be mocked rather than killed. He replied that an ancient hospitality and bond had existed between their ancestors, and that guest-gifts (which they call *xenia*) had been exchanged between them. Now, having fixed his spear in the ground, he began to urge that they set aside the fight and renew the friendship of their ancestors; that one should host the other in Lycia and the other in Argos once they returned safely home. Meanwhile, if they should happen to meet, they would refrain from using weapons against each other, observing the sanctity of hospitality, while still using the right of war against everyone else. "Lest we seem to do this out of treachery rather than respect for hospitality," he said, "let us exchange armor, so the rest of the army may understand that we are joined by the bond of our ancestors." Having said this, both leaped from their horses, shook hands, and pledged their faith, as if sanctioning a treaty of hospitality. They exchanged armor, but it was quite unequal: <term>"Then indeed," <note>original Greek: ἔνθ’ αὖτε</note></term> says Homer, <term>"Zeus the son of Cronus took away the wits of Glaucus, who exchanged armor with Diomedes the son of Tydeus..." <note>original Greek: Κρονίδης φρένας ἐξέλετο Ζεύς, ὃς πρὸς Τυδείδην Διομήδεα τεύχε’ ἄμειβε</note></term>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

*Gold for bronze, a hundred oxen’s worth for nine.* <note>original: "Χρύσεα χαλκείων, ἑκατόμβοι’ ἐννεαβοίων"</note> That is:
> Here Jupiter robbed foolish Glaucus of his wits,
> Who straightway traded armor with Tydeus’ son <note>Diomedes</note>,
> And gave away gold—worth a hundred oxen—
> For the bronze he received; the madman gave
> What was bought for a fortune for cheap goods,
> Which you would say were worth barely nine heifers.

This adage is used everywhere by the most praised authors. Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, depicts Socrates responding to Alcibiades in his usual manner, because Alcibiades, greedy for gain, wished to exchange the beauty of his body for the better beauty of a mind: *And in truth, you intend to exchange gold for bronze.* <note>original: "καὶ τῷ ὄντι χρύσεα, χαλκείων διαμείβεσθαι νοεῖς"</note> Although the translator, instead of "bronze," used "orichalcum" <note>a gold-colored alloy</note>. Likewise, Aristotle in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, in the section on justice: *But he who gives his own, just as Glaucus gave his armor to Diomedes, as Homer says, gold for bronze,* and so forth. Plutarch, writing against the Stoics, elegantly twists this to say that Glaucus’s exchange was not entirely unfair, because iron armor is no less useful to those about to fight than golden armor; but he who prefers bodily health to honor, or abandons virtue for the sake of physical health, truly exchanges *gold for bronze*. Cicero, in the *Letters to Atticus*, book six: *You have my response to everything—not "gold for bronze" as you requested, but like for like.* Cicero indicates that both are proverbs: "like for like" regarding equal compensation, and "gold for bronze" regarding an unequal exchange. The younger Pliny, in a letter to Flaccus: *You will receive sterile and simply ungrateful letters, not even imitating that cleverness of Diomedes in exchanging gifts.* Martial in his epigrams:
> I think even you, Glaucus, were never so stupid,
> Who gave *gold* <note>original: "χρύσεα"</note> to one giving *bronze* <note>original: "χάλκεα"</note>.

Aulus Gellius, in *Attic Nights*, book two, comparing and weighing the translation by Caecilius against Menander himself (whom he had translated), and showing how much it degenerates from the Greek elegance, says: *By Hercules, the armor of Diomedes and Glaucus were not valued at a more disparate price.* Mention of this adage is also made in the preface to the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note> of Imperial Law, in these very words: *In our times, such an exchange of laws has been found as Glaucus and Diomedes made between themselves in Homer, the father of all virtue, exchanging dissimilar things.* Thus far Justinian—a man, to speak frankly, who was excessively *self-loving* <note>original: "φίλαυτος"</note> and pleased with himself beyond what is right, who preferred those "patchworks" of his and unequal rhapsodies of laws to the complete volumes of so many most learned men. Now truly, I do not wonder at it, but I am greatly ashamed of the commentary of I know not what interpreter on that passage. For what wonder is it if this was unknown by those who once and for all despise all antiquity? Furthermore, the more than scurrilous impudence is shameful even to the legal profession itself, in him who professes to be an interpreter of the law, yet does not fear—in a matter utterly unknown to him—to bring forth a most tasteless fable, not from authors, but from dreams. But I am most ashamed and amazed that teachers are found who seriously teach such a piece of nonsense—I will not say so unlearned, but so absurd—in public schools as if it were a brilliant discovery, nor do they even notice that the fiction does not at all agree with the words of Justinian. For he means that in place of the abandoned, useless, and loathsome volumes, better and shorter ones were received—that is, a vastly unequal exchange was made. That fellow, whoever he was, made up a story about people exchanging equal things, namely each giving what he had in excess and receiving what he lacked. Therefore, it will be appropriate to use this whenever a service or gift is repaid with a far unequal gift, or vice versa. Or whenever someone has increased his wealth, but at the cost of his reputation; has attained a magistracy, but with the loss of a good mind; has found a fine fortune, but lost peace of soul. He has been admitted into the friendship of a prince, but has fallen from the friendship of Christ.

---

-> Kings have many ears and eyes. <-

<margin>II</margin>
*Many are the ears and eyes of kings.* <note>original: "Ὦτα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὶ βασιλέων πολλοί"</note> That is, the ears and eyes of kings are many because they observe through spies what everyone says or does. The same is reported by Lucian in the booklet titled *On Those Who Serve for Wages*, and again in *Against the Unlearned*. Aristotle also mentions it in the third book of the *Politics*. The Greeks call such men *ear-listeners* <note>original: "ὠτακουστὰς"</note>, whom Darius the Younger first employed, being distrustful of himself. Dionysius of Syracuse added *informers* <note>original: "προσαγωγίδας"</note>, that is, scouts, according to Plutarch. The allegory is drawn from the fact that kings have many scouts everywhere, and for that reason they are called the "eyes of kings," and many listeners, through whom as if...

# SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND ADAGES
f
<meta>catchword: bad we-</meta>

as if they use ears. Nor are they lacking in hands and feet in great numbers, and perhaps not even bellies. See what kind of monster a tyrant is, and how formidable, equipped with so many eyes—and those being spies—so many ears—and those as long as a donkey's—so many hands, so many feet, so many bellies, not to mention other less honorable parts. Aristophanes, in *The Acharnians*, calls Pseudartabas "the King's Eye" <note>original: "Pseudartabam regis oculum"</note> because through him the king learned what was happening. On the other hand, Andromache in Euripides calls her son the "eye of her life":
> This boy was the only eye of life remaining to me.
> <note>original Greek: Εἷς παῖς ὅδ' ἦν μοι λοιπὸς ὀφθαλμὸς βίου.</note>
This is because he was the sole delight in her life. For nothing is dearer than an eye. Hence, we call those we love "our eyes."

### The long hands of kings.
-> III <-
What was written by Ovid—"Do you not know that kings have long hands?"—is even a common saying: "One must beware of kings, because they have very long arms." This is surely because through their agents, whom they use in place of arms, they can strike even those far away. It can also refer to time: that kings, even if they hide their feelings for a long time, are usually accustomed to eventually take punishment from those with whom they are angry. This is witnessed by Homer in the first book of the *Iliad*, where Calchas speaks in this manner:
> For a king is too powerful when he is angry with an inferior man.
> For even if he swallows his anger for that same day,
> yet he keeps a grudge afterward, until he fulfills it.
> <note>original Greek: Κρείσσων γὰρ βασιλεύς, ὅτε χώσεται ἀνδρὶ χερῆϊ...</note>

### To drive out a nail with a nail.
-> IIII <-
To drive out a nail with a nail <note>original Greek: Ἥλῳ τὸν ἧλον ἐκκρούειν</note>. And: "You have driven out a peg with a peg," which means you have repelled one evil with another evil. Lucian in *The Lover of Lies*: "And with a nail, as they say, you knock out a nail." The same author in his *Apology*: "I fear lest, if I add a charge of flattery to the accusation of mats <note>referring to a specific legal or social context in Lucian's text</note>, I might seem, according to the proverb, to drive out a nail with a nail—the smaller with the larger." Aristotle, in the penultimate chapter of the fifth book of *Politics*, writes that wicked men and flatterers are friends to tyrants. For these are ultimately useful to them, as bad men are for bad deeds. "And wicked men are useful for wicked things; for nail [is driven by] nail, as the proverb goes." Synesius to Olympius: "Wicked outsiders vex the Church; attack them, for pegs drive out pegs." Saint Jerome to the monk Rusticus: "The philosophers of this world," he says, "are accustomed to drive out an old love with a new love, as if driving out a nail with a nail." Marcus Tullius Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*, book four: "Finally, like a sick man who does not recover, he must often be cured by a change of place." He also thinks an old love should be cast out by a certain new love, just like a nail by a nail. Julius Pollux in his ninth book writes that the adage was born from a game called *kyndalismos* <note>original: κυνδαλισμός</note>, in which they would knock out a peg fixed in clay soil with the forceful strike of another peg. He cites this proverbial six-foot line:
> A nail with a nail, and a pole with a pole.
> <note>original Greek: Ἥλῳ τὸν ἧλον, παττάλῳ τὸν πάτταλον.</note>
There is a place for this adage, therefore, not only when we blunt vice with vice, evil with evil, trickery with trickery, force with force, or even boldness and slander with the same; but also whenever we drive away a troublesome thing with a different trouble: as when we subdue the incitements of lust with labors, or master the care of love with other greater cares. Eusebius in *Against Hierocles*: "For he drives out demons, one with another, as they say, demon [with demon]"; it would be strange if he were not alluding to this proverb. Nor is the mime of Publilius Syrus far from this: "Danger is never overcome without danger."

### For a bad knot, a bad wedge must be sought.
-> V <-
That sentiment is also alluded to by this: "For a bad knot, a bad wedge must be sought." So says Saint Jerome to Oceanus: "In the meantime, according to the common proverb, for a bad knot in a tree, a bad we-"

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of ancient adages, specifically focusing on metaphors for compounding evils or using inappropriate remedies. It follows the previous discussion on "A hard wedge for a hard knot."</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...a [hard] wedge must be sought. <note>original: "malus cuneus" - referring to the proverb "A tough wedge for a tough log."</note> This may be used whenever we repel an evil with a similar malice. It is taken from wood-cutters who, if they happen upon a particularly hard knot in the timber, do not wish to risk their axe on it, but instead insert a wedge that is more "hard" than "good." <note>Erasmus plays on the word "good" (bonum) meaning both high quality and morally upright.</note> This agrees with that saying of Sophocles found in Plutarch’s essay *On Tranquility of Mind*:
"They wash away bitter bile with a bitter medicine." <note>original Greek: πικρὰν χολὴν κλύζουσι φαρμάκῳ πικρῷ</note>

->To heal evil with evil.<-
->VI<-

"To heal evil with evil." <note>original Greek: τὸ κακὸν κακῷ θεραπεύειν</note> That is, to cure one ill by means of another. Sophocles in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*:
"Speak words of good omen, lest by healing evil with evil, you add a greater plague to your ruin." <note>original Greek: Εὔφημα φώνει, μὴ κακὸν κακῷ διδούς / Ἄκος, πλέον τὸ πῆμα τ' ἄτης τίθει.</note>
Tecmessa is urging Ajax not to add a second, greater evil—suicide—to the evil of his madness. And Herodotus in *Thalia* <note>Book 3 of his Histories</note> says: "Do not heal evil with evil."

->To add disease to disease.<-
->VII<-

To add disease to disease; that is, to double the misfortune. Euripides in *Alcestis*:
"Do not add disease to me while I am already sick, for I am burdened enough by calamity." <note>original Greek: Μὴ νοσοῦντί μοι νόσον / Προσθῇς. ἅλις γὰρ συμφορᾷ βαρύνομαι.</note>
Of the same figure is that line from Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 14:
"Lest perhaps someone should receive a wound upon a wound." <note>original Greek: Μή πη τίς ἐφ' ἕλκεϊ ἕλκος ἄρηται.</note>
Likewise Sophocles:
"You have struck a second disease upon a disease."
Not far from this form is what appears in Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 7: "terrible upon terrible," <note>original Greek: ἀεινόθεν αἰνῶς</note> used when we indicate that more bitter things are added to the already bitter. For so Menelaus speaks there:
"This disgrace shall surely be a terror upon terror."

->Do not add fire to fire.<-
->VIII<-

"Do not add fire to fire." <note>original Greek: Μὴ πῦρ ἐπὶ πῦρ</note> This is used by Plato. The meaning is clear: Do not join calamity to calamity, or do not further provoke one who is already moved to anger. Diogenianus thinks it originated from a certain charcoal-burner who, as a fire grew out of control and consumed everything, cried out: "Do not add fire to fire!" Plato, in the second book of *The Laws*, forbids boys from drinking wine until their eighteenth year, lest the heat of the wine be added to the fervor of their youth, and they seem to "suggest fire to fire." Likewise Plutarch in his *Marriage Precepts*: "Lest fire be added to fire." He uses it in several other places, including his *Precepts on Health*: "So that fire is not added to fire, as the proverb says—fullness to fullness, and undiluted wine to undiluted wine."

->To add oil to the furnace.<-
->IX<-

A related sentiment is: To add oil to the furnace; used for providing fuel or nourishment to an evil so that it increases more and more. Horace in his *Satires*:
"Add poems now—that is, add oil to the furnace."
That is, add material for a greater madness. Saint Jerome uses this in his letter to Eustochium: "Wine and youth are a double fire for pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame?"

->To extinguish a fire with oil.<-
->X<-

"You are extinguishing a fire with oil." <note>original Greek: Ἐλαίῳ πῦρ σβεννύεις</note> This is usually said when someone applies remedies that only irritate the evil further. For instance, if one tries to overwhelm sadness of the soul with foul pleasures. Or if one wishes to appease an offended person with brawling and insults. If this is spoken ironically, it differs little from the previous adage. Lucian alluded to this in his *Timon* when he said: "If he saw someone burning in a conflagration, he would want to extinguish it with pitch and oil."

<summary>Erasmus explores various ancient proverbs regarding the compounding of problems, such as "adding fire to fire" or "healing evil with evil," drawing on classical Greek and Latin authors.</summary>
<keywords>proverbs, medicine, fire metaphors, Sophocles, Plato, Horace, Jerome, irony, remedies, classical literature</keywords>

# CHILIAD I, CENTURY II
<sig>f 2</sig>

### Owls to Athens.
### XI

<margin><note>original: "γλαῦκας εἰς Ἀθήνας"</note> Owls to Athens.</margin> That is, "Owls to Athens": one must understand the implied verb "you are carrying" or "you are sending." It is applicable to those merchants who transport goods to a place where they already abound in great quantity—for instance, if someone were to import grain into Egypt or saffron into Cilicia. It becomes more elegant if the metaphor is transferred to the mind: such as if someone were to teach a more learned man, send poems to a poet, or give advice to a man of great wisdom. Cicero, writing to Torquatus, says: "But again, 'Owls to Athens,' since I am saying these things to you." Likewise: "And the verses you ask for—that is, I shall send a night-owl to Athens." Aristophanes in *The Birds*: "What do you say? Who brought an owl to Athens?" <note>The owl was the symbol of Athens and its patron goddess, Athena.</note> Lucian uses and explains the same in his *Timon* and *Nigrinus*. Furthermore, the proverb arose because the owl is very common in Attica, being almost peculiar to that region. It is said to frequent Laurium in Attica, where the gold mines are; hence they are called "golden owls." This bird was once dear to the Athenian people, as it was held sacred to Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena.</note> because of its blue-gray eyes, with which it sees even in the darkness, unlike the common sort of birds. From this, it was also believed to be an auspicious sign for deliberations, as indicated by the proverb: "The owl flies." There was also a saying about Minerva: that she could turn even the Athenians' bad counsel into a good outcome. Daemon, however, in his interpretation of Aristophanes, thinks it is called "Owls to Athens" not only because of the great abundance of owls in Athens, but because an owl was engraved on the Athenian coins—both gold and silver—alongside the face of Minerva. Furthermore, that coin was called a <term>tetradrachm</term> <note>a silver coin worth four drachmae</note>, whereas previously they had been accustomed to using <term>didrachms</term> <note>two-drachma coins</note>, the stamp of which was an ox; from this also arose that proverb, "An ox on the tongue" <note>meaning someone has been bribed to stay silent</note>. There are those who record that the <term>triobol</term> <note>a three-obol coin</note> was not the same, which they also call a <term>hemidrachm</term> <note>half-drachma</note>. For a drachma contains six obols. The triobol coin had the image of Jupiter on one side and an owl on the other. Therefore, it seemed absurd to carry an owl to Athens, since everywhere there everything abounded with owls. Plutarch also testifies regarding Athenian coinage in his *Life of Lysander*, where he mentions a servant who, indicating his master's theft <gloss>riddlingly</gloss>, said: "Many owls are roosting under the roof-tiles," showing that money stamped with owls was hidden there.

### You warn the mindful, you teach the taught, and similar.
### XII

The same sentiment occurs in the comedies of Plautus and Terence: "You warn the mindful, and you teach the taught." That Greek saying has the same power: "You speak to one who possesses the knowledge," or "You tell one who knows." Plato in the *Greater Hippias*: "You will tell these things to one who knows them, Socrates." Euripides in *Hecuba*: "You have said nothing new, but to those who well know what you have reproached." Homer, both elsewhere and in the *Odyssey*, Book 17:
<margin>For I know and understand these things you command to one who is already wise.</margin> That is: "I both know and grasp it; you tell these things to one who already knows."
Hesiod in Book 2 <note>likely referring to the *Shield of Heracles* or a fragment</note> regarding Nestor advising his son:
<margin>As if to one thinking and understanding good things himself.</margin> That is: "With a friendly mind, though he is wise in these things by himself."
Cicero in the first book of his letters to Atticus, letter 9: "For our friend Gnaeus <note>Pompey the Great</note> has desired a likeness of Sulla's reign in a wonderful way; I speak to one who knows."

### If you do it often, you will throw differently at different times.
### XIII

Aristotle, in his short book *On Divination in Sleep*, records a proverbial verse of this kind: "If you do it often, you will throw differently at different times."
By this, it is signified that one ought to attempt a thing frequently, and not be immediately exhausted if at some time it falls out poorly according to one's wish. For it will happen that to one venturing again and again, it will eventually fall more happily. These are Aristotle's words: "For as it is said, if you throw many times, you will throw differently at different times." He is dealing with the dreams of melancholics, in which he does not think there is any divine vision, even if it happens sometimes that certain events correspond to their dreams. But he says this happens because, by a fault of nature, they dream many and varied things; sometimes a <term>coincidence</term> <note>original: "συμβεβηκός"</note> arises—that is, a chance event which by luck happens just as it was dreamed by them. Themistius in an oration, when they paraphrase it thus (translated by Barbaro, for the Greek manuscript was not at hand): "Those who throw the javelin all day long sometimes hit the mark and take the prize." There is an old adage: "If you toss often, you will eventually throw a Venus" <note>The highest throw in dice</note>. There are those who think—and in my opinion not absurdly—that the metaphor is drawn from archers, not from gamblers. For

<summary>Erasmus explains three proverbs: "Owls to Athens" (redundancy), "Teaching the taught" (superfluous advice), and "Throwing often" (persistence and probability). He provides historical context on Athenian coinage and Aristotelian theories on dreams.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Athens, Owls, Numismatics, Coinage, Aristotle, Cicero, Proverbial Wisdom, Probability, Greek Literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's commentary on common proverbs (Adagia), specifically focusing on the role of chance and the consequences of bad advice. It follows a discussion on the "Shot of the Archer."</meta>

And this is what "to throw" <note>original: Βάλλειν (ballein)</note> signifies. Indeed, there is a cleverness hidden in that word, which in its first sense means to release an arrow, and in the second to strike a target. It happens that those who shoot frequently will, even by chance, eventually hit the mark. Although Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book of *On Divination*, when dealing with chance occurrences <note>original: symptomatīs</note>—which we just mentioned—applies the metaphor to both cases. For who is there, he asks, who shoots all day long and does not eventually aim straight? We dream all night long, and there is hardly a night when we do not sleep, yet we are surprised if what we dream sometimes comes true? What is as uncertain as a throw of the dice? Yet there is no one who, by throwing often, does not eventually throw a "Venus" <note>The highest possible throw in ancient dice games, where four dice all showed different numbers.</note>, sometimes even a second or third time. Furthermore, that the Venus throw was once the most fortunate in this kind of game is clearly shown by Octavius Augustus in a certain letter to Tiberius found in Suetonius: "During dinner," he says, "we played like old men <note>original: γέροντικῶς (gerontikōs)</note> both yesterday and today. For at such a throw, whenever anyone threw a 'dog' <note>The lowest throw in dice.</note> or a 'six' <note>original: senionem</note>, he contributed one denarius to the middle for each die; all of these were taken by the one who had thrown a 'Venus'." Thus far Augustus. This will also apply to those who achieve something by luck rather than skill. Even today there is a common proverbial joke about a blind man who happened to strike a crow with his javelin.

### Bad Counsel. XIV

->Bad counsel is worst for the counselor.<-

This is a proverbial six-foot line <note>A senarius, a common meter in Latin verse.</note> directed at those upon whose heads falls the very thing they wrongly advised for others. Indeed, as the Greeks say, "Counsel is a sacred thing" <note>original: ἱερὸν ἡ βουλὴ (hieron hē boulē)</note>. And just as it should be gladly received when the situation demands it, so it must be given religiously and without deceit if someone is in need. Otherwise, some divine power will not fail to exact punishment from the one who has violated a sacred and divine thing through treachery. Aulus Gellius, in the *Attic Nights*, Book 4, Chapter 5, thinks this adage arose from a certain history, which he relates from the annals of Maximus and the narratives of Verrius Flaccus in this manner: A statue of the very brave man Horatius Cocles, placed in the Roman assembly-place <note>the comitium</note>, was struck by lightning from heaven. To expiate this lightning-bolt with sacrifices, soothsayers <note>haruspices</note> were summoned from Etruria. With a mind hostile and unfriendly toward the Roman people, they had planned to manage the matter with contrary religious rites; they urged that the statue be wrongly moved to a lower spot, which the shadow of surrounding buildings would never allow the sun to reach. When they had persuaded the people to do this, they were informed against and betrayed; having confessed their treachery, they were executed. It was then established that the statue should be moved to an elevated place, just as the true reasons discovered later advised; thus it was placed in a higher spot in the Area of Vulcan. This matter turned out well and prosperously for the Republic. Then, because the Etruscan soothsayers had been punished and avenged, this verse was skillfully composed and sung by boys throughout the whole city:
> Bad counsel is worst for the counselor.

Thus far Gellius. Furthermore, Valerius Maximus in Book 7 records a similar matter regarding Papirius Cursor: when he, as consul, was besieging Aquilonia and wished to engage in battle with the enemy unless the omens forbade it, the keeper of the sacred chickens <note>pullarius</note> urged him to engage. Although the omens had reported unfavorable signs to his ears, once the truth was known, Papirius placed the chicken-keeper in the front line. He was the first to be pierced by a weapon, thus expiating the violated religion. Titus Livius [Livy] mentions this in the tenth book of his first Decade. Not dissimilar is what Socrates relates in the *Tripartite History*: Eutropius the Eunuch, while striving to punish certain people who had fled to a temple for sanctuary, persuaded the Emperor to pass a law stating that the sanctity of the temple should benefit no guilty person. Once the law was passed, it happened that when Eutropius offended Caesar, he fled under the altar; dragged from there, he was beheaded, destroyed by his own counsel. Virgil silently noted the proverb in the twelfth book of the *Aeneid* when he says:
> The augur Tolumnius himself falls, he who was the first to hurl a weapon against the opposing enemy.

Marcus Varro, in the third book of *On Agriculture*, Chapter 1, openly cites the adage in these words: "I believe," he says, "not only what is said, that 'Bad counsel is worst for the counselor,' but also that good counsel should be considered good for both the one who gave it and the one who is consulted." Sophocles in *Electra*:
> For nothing is more hateful than bad counsel. <note>original: Βουλῆς γὰρ οὐδέν ἐστιν ἔχθιον κακῆς.</note>
referring the harm to the one to whom the counsel is given. It is apparent, however, that this Latin verse, as Gellius also noted, was expressed from those Greek verses of Hesiod found in the work titled *Works and Days*:
> A man fashions evil for himself while fashioning evil for another. <note>original: οἱ αὐτῷ κακὰ τεύχει ἀνὴρ ἄλλῳ κακὰ τεύχων.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores the proverb "Bad counsel is worst for the counselor," providing historical and literary examples where treacherous or ill-intended advice backfired on the giver. He cites Roman history, Greek poetry, and legal anecdotes to illustrate the "sacred" nature of giving advice.</summary>

# SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
<sig>f 3</sig>

<margin>Bad counsel is worst for the counselor.</margin> <note>original Greek: κακὴ βουλὴ τῷ βουλεύσαντι κακίστη.</note> That is:
He harms himself, who seeks to injure another.
A foolish thing is a very bad matter for a poor advisor.
Plutarch, in his commentary *On Listening to the Poets*, considers the meaning of this little verse to be the same as the dogma of Plato in the *Gorgias*: where Socrates says that it is worse to commit an injury than to suffer one, and more damaging to inflict evil than to receive it. And indeed, this sentiment is found in almost as many words in the Hebrew author of *Ecclesiasticus*, chapter 27: "To him who works a most wicked counsel, it shall fall back upon him." There is also a Greek Fable <note>An Aesopic fable</note> on this sentiment, not without charm, nor entirely unworthy of being added to these commentaries. A Lion, ailing due to old age and for that reason keeping himself in his den, was being visited by the rest of the animals out of duty to their king, with the exception of the Fox. Therefore, the Wolf, seizing the opportunity, accused the Fox before the Lion of treason—that she held him for nothing, who was the head of all things, nor had she come to visit him out of contempt. Meanwhile, the Fox arrived during the Wolf's story and heard the final part of the speech. Thus the Lion, having spotted the Fox, immediately roared against her. But she, having asked for a moment to clear herself, said: "Who among all who have gathered here has profited you as much as I, who have run about everywhere and found a remedy for your disease from the doctors?" When the Lion immediately told her to reveal the remedy, she said: "If you skin a living Wolf and wrap yourself in his hide, you will recover." The credulous Lion immediately attacked the Wolf and killed him. When he was dead, the Fox laughed that the slanderer's bad counsel had fallen back upon his own head.
The same is also reported by Plutarch in this manner:
<margin>He who prepares evils for another, prepares them for his own heart.</margin> <note>original Greek: ᾧ κακὰ τεύχει, ἑῷ κακῷ ἥπατι τεύχει.</note> That is:
He who prepares foreign harms for others, prepares losses for his own liver.

### To each his own is beautiful. XV

A proverbial sentiment: *To each his own is beautiful*, used against those whom their own things—of whatever quality they may be—please with a certain great zeal rather than by judgment. It arises from the common disposition of mortals, in whom that <term>Philautia</term> <note>Self-love or vanity</note> is so deeply ingrained that you will find no one so modest, so attentive, or so sharp-eyed, who is not corrupted by a certain inclination of the mind so as to be blind and deluded in estimating his own things. And whom have we ever seen born in so barbarous a region to whom his own fatherland does not seem the best? What nation is so wild, with so harsh a tongue, that it does not despise others in comparison to its own? What nation has so beastly a physical appearance that it does not appear most beautiful to itself? Therefore Aristotle truly wrote in the *Rhetoric*, book 2: <margin>Since all are self-lovers, it is necessary that their own things be sweet to all, such as their works and words. Therefore they are also for the most part lovers of flatterers.</margin>
Since all are lovers of themselves, it is necessary that their own things be pleasant to each, such as their deeds and their words; for that reason, they also generally delight in flatterers. Although this is true in all matters, just as Horace says, "Blind is the love of self," yet it seems to apply especially to craftsmen, and among these most particularly to poets, and furthermore to lovers. For Aristotle most rightly wrote in the *Ethics*, book 4: that every craftsman is intensely delighted by his own work, no differently than by things born from himself. Nor do poets love their own poems differently than parents love their children. For the work of a craftsman is like a certain offspring of the intellect, concerning which he says the midwife judges more correctly than the mother herself. Likewise, it is the custom of loving grooms to extol their own brides in competition. A great example of this exists concerning the youths of Plato. Whence even today the common folk cleverly say: "No deformed lover is ever found." This is because to a lover, even things not beautiful seem most beautiful. This sentiment Theocritus elegantly expressed in *Idyll* 6:
<margin>For indeed</margin>
<margin>things not beautiful, have appeared beautiful.</margin> <note>original Greek: τὰ μὴ καλὰ, καλὰ πέφανται.</note> That is:
For often, not rarely Polyphemus,
Those things which are least beautiful, seem beautiful to love.
The same proverb is expressed in the *Lysis*, but inversely: <margin>And there is a danger, yes a danger, according to the ancient proverb, that the beautiful is the friend.</margin> That is: There is a danger that, according to the old adage, that which is beautiful is the friend. As if something should not be held beautiful because it is a friend, but rather everyone loves to be a friend because it is beautiful. To this also pertains what Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> writes in *On Ends*, book 1: "For each is led most by his own study." And again in the first book of *Duties*—

<summary>This page explores two major proverbs: the idea that malicious advice backfires on the giver (illustrated by an Aesopic fable of a fox and wolf) and the concept of "Philautia" or self-love, which makes people biased toward their own works, country, and beloveds.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...of their own pursuits: each of them, delighted by his own study, looked down upon the other. Although this is worthy of pardon to the extent that that common *self-love* <note>original: "philautia" (φιλαυτία) — a Greek term for excessive self-love or conceit</note> prevails, so that each person favors his own children, his own arts, his own institution, his own inventions, and his own country a little too dearly—unless it carries us away to the point of blindness, so that we both slander the virtues of others and flatter our own vices, bestowing upon them the name of virtues. And thus each man is to himself what Suffenus was to himself in Catullus, or "Mine is mine to me," or finally, they deceive themselves. And at this point, Porphyrio <note>A 3rd-century commentator on Horace</note> indicates that Horace is referring to a common opinion: that men not only do not grieve over their own evils, but are even delighted by them. And on this matter, a Greek adage was celebrated, but that adage is missing from the text due to the fault of the scribes. To the same point belongs what Horace said elsewhere:
> Ugly defects escape the blind lover, or even these very things
> Give delight, just as Agna’s polyp delighted Balbinus.

For to Balbinus, the foolish lover, even the polyp <note>A growth or tumor in the nose</note> of his girlfriend Agna seemed to smell sweet. Now, a polyp is a foul-smelling disease of the nostrils, just as a "goat" is of the armpits. Whence we call people "polypous" or "goaty." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] to Atticus, book 14: "Accept from me," he says, "my dear Atticus, a *universal theorem* <note>original: "katholikon theorema" (καθολικὸν θεώρημα)</note> of those matters in which we are sufficiently practiced. No one was ever, neither poet nor orator, who thought anyone better than himself." This even happens to the wicked. "What do you think of the talented and learned Brutus, whom we have even tested? Recently I had written an edict at your request. Mine pleased me, his pleased him. Furthermore, when, led by his own prayers, I had almost written to him about the best style of speaking, he wrote not only to me, but also to you, that what pleased me did not meet his approval. Therefore, let us, I pray, allow each man to write for himself. To each his own bride, to me mine; to each his own love, to me mine." Not very skillfully put. For this was from Attilius, a very harsh poet. Thus far Cicero. From whose words it appears these two little verses, "To each his own," etc., were taken from some play by Attilius. The same Tullius [Cicero] in the *Tusculan Disputations*, book 5: "Indeed, we have heard of those very devoted to music; even the Tragic poet—what is good is nothing to the point. For in this genre, I know not how, more than in others, 'to each his own is beautiful.' Thus far I have known no poet—and I had a friendship with Aquinius—who did not seem the best to himself. So it is. Your things delight you, mine delight me." Plautus expressed the same sentiment in *Stichus* with different words, but quite elegantly. "His own king," he says, "pleases the queen; to each his own bride pleases the groom." To this should also be referred that line of Theocritus:
*For indeed, I do not have a bad form, as they say to me.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ γὰρ θὴν, ὅκ’ ἔοικ’ ἔχω κακὸν, ὥς με λέγοντι.</note>
-> Maro [Virgil] imitating this: <-
Nor am I so hideous; recently I saw myself on the shore,
When the sea stood calm with the winds.
Horace alluded more openly to the adage in a certain letter:
Those things for the ears of Jove
You keep. For you trust that poetic honey flows from
You alone, beautiful to yourself.
He said "beautiful to yourself" instead of "pleasing to yourself." Not different from this form is what Saint Augustine, in several other places and especially in Letter 47, brings forward from a certain Tychonius: "What we want, is holy." This is a half-line of heroic verse. Would that this saying did not find such a place in the character of those who today arrogantly claim piety for themselves more than the Pharisees ever did; who, though they are soaked in vices neither to be borne nor named, nevertheless with a strange arrogance rave against the lives of others.

<margin>XVI</margin>
-> The smoke of the fatherland is brighter than a foreign fire. <-
This has the appearance of a proverb, and pertains to the same sentiment which Lucian wrote elegantly in his *Praise of the Fatherland*: *For indeed, even the smoke of the fatherland will be seen to be brighter than the fire among others.* <note>original Greek: ἡ γὰρ τοι πατρίδος καὶ ὁ καπνὸς λαμπρότερος ὀφθήσεται τοῦ παρ’ ἄλλοις πυρός.</note> Philostratus in *Ariadne*: *Theseus indeed sees, but it is the smoke in Athens; of Ariadne he no longer knows, nor did he ever truly know.* <note>original Greek: ὁ Θησεὺς δὲ ὁρᾷ μὲν, ἀλλὰ τοῦ ἐν Ἀθήναις καπνοῦ. ἀριάδνης δ’ οὐκ οἶδεν ἔτι, οὐδ’ ἔγνω ποτέ.</note> In Homer, Ulysses longs to see the smoke rising from his native land, from which the proverb is derived. For so it is read in the *Odyssey*, book 1.

<header>THE SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND</header>

<margin>
<note>original: "ἐκ θ' καπνοῦ ἀρθρώσκοντα νοῆσαι, ἧς γαίας"</note> To see the smoke rising from his own native land. <note>A reference to Odysseus' longing for Ithaca in Homer's Odyssey.</note> That is: Longing to discern with his eyes the rising smoke of his birth-land.

### The living voice. XVII

In former times, the "living voice" <note>Latin: *viva vox*</note> referred to that which was not written, but perceived from the very mouth of the speaker, as if it were alive and effective. For things are sometimes called "living" when they are natural rather than artificial, such as "living marble" or "living <term>rock</term> <note>natural, unquarried stone</note>." There is, moreover, in natural things a certain genuine grace that no art can achieve through imitation. Furthermore, writing is indeed a kind of voice, but it is a manufactured one, and merely an imitator of the true voice. It lacks action and motion—that is to say, life. Indeed, as the author Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> suggests, delivery is, as it were, the life of a speech. The invention of subject matter is like the bones; the arrangement imitates the muscles; the style represents the flesh, skin, and color. Memory performs the role of the breath; but that which comes to all of these, the delivery, is like a vital motion. For there is no surer proof of life than motion. Hence rivers are called "living," and also "living silver" <note>quicksilver/mercury</note>. Conversely, those things are called dead which are sluggish and faint. Cicero, in the second book of *Tusculan Disputations*: "For although reading provides enough examples for imitation, nevertheless that 'living voice,' as they call it, provides fuller nourishment, especially that of a teacher." The same author to Atticus, book two: "Where are they now who say <note>original: "ζώσης φωνῆς"</note> 'the living voice' [is better]? I have seen so much more from your letters than from his conversation regarding what was happening." Furthermore, what Cicero produced in an abrupt and mutilated form, some have completed in this manner: <note>original: "ζώσης φωνῆς μᾶλλο ψόφημα εἶν"</note> "The living voice is more than a mere sound." Pliny the Younger, in a certain letter to Nepos: "Besides, as is commonly said, the living voice affects us. For although what you read may be sharper, those things sit deeper in the mind which the delivery, the expression, the bearing, and even the gestures of the speaker fix there." Seneca in his fifth letter: "Nevertheless, the living voice and intimacy will profit you more than a formal speech." Saint Jerome in his general preface: "The living voice has a certain hidden energy; poured from the teacher's mouth into the ears of the disciple, it sounds more strongly." Thus far his words. Whence that famous remark of Aeschines concerning Demosthenes: <note>original: "τί δὲ εἰ αὐτ’ θηρί’ ἀκηκόειτε;"</note> "What if you had heard the beast himself?" And this: "In the writings of Demosthenes, a great part of Demosthenes is missing."

### Silent teachers. XVIII

What we have just related was also used by Aulus Gellius, and he added another contrasting phrase: "Since," he said, "there was a scarcity of the 'living voice,' as they say, I should learn from 'silent teachers,' as the saying goes." By "silent teachers" he meant books, which indeed speak to us, but as Socrates says in Plato, they do not respond appropriately to one who has doubts. Nor are letters unpleasantly called "silent instructors," because it is the way of the mute to speak not with a voice, but with nods and signs. Likewise, books converse with us through certain marks and significant characters. For just as spoken words are, as it were, <note>original: "εἴδωλα"</note> images of the thoughts of the mind according to Aristotle, so the shapes of letters may rightly be called certain likenesses of voices. Nor is it surprising: since that <note>original: "ἀρχέτυπον"</note> archetypal model of the heart represents and pours out the emotions of the mind more effectively than that other, which does not imitate the thing itself, but an imitation of it. Nor is it without reason that many often ask whether it is more conducive to acquiring erudition <note>original: "ζώση φωνῆ χρῆσθαι, ἢ τοῖς ἀφώνοις διδασκάλοις"</note> "to use the living voice, or silent teachers"—that is: whether reading or listening profits more. Each has its own peculiar advantages. For from books, the things learned are generally more scholarly and more numerous. For one learns only as much as he can follow with the speed of his intellect and embrace with the fidelity of his memory. Add to this that these [silent] teachers are never burdened by bestowing their labor upon us. And the supply of them is as ready as it is abundant. To this is added leisure and the privacy of thought. One may inspect details more closely, revise them, and weigh them. But on the other hand, what we perceive from a teacher's discourse costs less effort of the mind, the eyes, and the health—especially if he is one whom we both admire and love. Then, they sink deeper into the soul, stick more tenaciously, and occur to the mind more promptly. Therefore, it will be wise to join one method of study with the other: and where there is an abundance of the living voice, to listen more willingly than to read—provided the one you hear is of at least moderate learning. Where there is none, you should fly to books (but only the best ones), as if you were going to perform a task of no less value. Finally, to add this as well, books are called "silent teachers" by the same figure of speech by which Marcus Tullius [Cicero] calls the law a "silent magistrate," and the magistrate a "speaking law"; and by which Plutarch calls poetry "speaking painting," and painting "silent poetry."

<summary>Erasmus explores the classical adages "The Living Voice" and "Silent Teachers," weighing the benefits of oral instruction against the study of written books. He concludes that while speech has more vitality and emotional impact, books offer a more abundant and accessible source of scholarly knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>living voice, silent teachers, pedagogy, Cicero, Pliny, Seneca, Jerome, Demosthenes, Aulus Gellius, Plato, Aristotle, Plutarch, education, rhetoric, books vs. speech</keywords>
