# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->The forehead is before the back of the head.<-
<note>Latin: "Frons occipitio prior." A metaphorical way of saying the front of the master is more effective than his back; i.e., his presence matters.</note>

This was a celebrated adage among the ancient farmers, tossed about like a riddle: *The forehead is before the back of the head.* By this, antiquity signified that business is conducted more rightly when the person whose business is at stake is present as a witness. "Before" is used here to mean "better" or "more effective." Otherwise, who was unaware that the forehead is the front part of the head and the back of the head is the rear? Nevertheless, this double-meaning adds no small grace to the saying, which on account of its antiquity was held as an oracle. It appears in Cato’s book *On Agriculture*, chapter 4: "If you build well," he says, "you will visit more willingly and more often; the farm will be better, and fewer mistakes will be made: you will gather more fruit: *the forehead is before the back of the head.*" Pliny says much the same thing in his *Natural History*, Book 18, chapter 5: "They falsely claim," he says, "that he who lives well visits his field more often, and that the master’s forehead profits the land more than the back of his head." Again, in chapter 6 of the same book: "And therefore the ancestors said that the master’s eye is the most fertile thing in the field." Aristotle, in the first book of his *Economics*, seems to attribute this sentiment to a certain Persian, subjoining another similar to it which came from a certain Libyan. But it is better to provide his own words, should anyone desire them: <gloss>that is, And that response of the Persian and the Libyan will be rightly preserved.</gloss> <note>original Greek: καὶ τὸ τοῦ Πέρσου καὶ Λίβυος ἀπόφθεγμα εὖ ἂν ἔχοι.</note> For when one was asked what fattens a horse most, he replied: "The master’s eye." The other, asked what manure was best, said: "The master’s footprints." Both signified that the master’s presence carries the most weight for conducting business well. Likewise, Columella thinks it a bad thing to frequently lease out a farm, but worse still is the "city-dwelling farmer" who prefers to cultivate the land through his household servants rather than by himself. To this pertains what is related by Gellius: when a certain stout and sleek man had a horse that was lean and scrawny, and was asked what the cause was, he replied that it should not seem strange if he were in better condition than his horse, since he fed himself, but a slave looked after the horse. Plutarch, in his essay *On the Education of Children*, <gloss>that is, Hence also that elegant saying by the groom, that nothing fattens a horse so much as the King’s eye.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Κἀνταῦθα διὰ ῥηθὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἱπποκόμου χάριεν, ὡς οὐδὲν οὕτω πιαίνει τὸν ἵππον, ὡς βασιλέως ὀφθαλμός.</note> It is of this same figure that Aeschylus, in the tragedy titled *The Persians*, calls the master’s presence the "eye of the house":
> For I consider the master’s presence to be the eye of the home.
> <gloss>that is, For I judge the master's presence to be the eye of the house.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ὄμμα γὰρ δόμων, νομίζω δεσπότου παρουσίαν.</note>

To the same point belongs what Titus Livius said quite charmingly: that things done through the eyes of others do not usually proceed successfully enough. Terence hints at something similar in *The Eunuch* when he says: "As it happens when masters are away," signifying that when the masters are absent, the servants do everything more indulgently and sin more licentiously. Truly, all these things tend toward this: that each person should care for his own business in person, and not trust too greatly in the industry of another. This is to be observed by no one more than a Prince—provided he bears the soul of a Prince and not a robber—that is, if he has the public good at heart. But today, bishops and kings do almost everything through the hands, ears, and eyes of others; they think nothing pertains to them less than the commonwealth, being distracted either by their private affairs or occupied by pleasures.

---

->Like delights in like.<-
<note>Latin: "Aequalis aequalem delectat."</note>

Similarity is the mother of goodwill, and the conciliator of habit and familiarity. Whence we see that young men meet together willingly, the old congregate with the old, the learned are captivated by a gathering of the learned, the wicked flock with the wicked, drunkards with drunkards, sailors love sailors, the wealthy have a bond with the wealthy, and in general, like rejoices in like. On this sentiment there exist several proverbs of the ancients, among which is this: <gloss>that is, Like delights in like.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἧλιξ ἥλικα τέρπει.</note> Which you use, Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in *Cato the Elder*: "Equals," he says, "as it is in the old proverb, most easily congregate with equals." For the first conciliation of familiarity proceeds from equality of age, which the Greeks call *homelikia* <term>homelikia: being of the same age</term>. Alluding to this, Homer says in the 17th book of the *Odyssey*:
> Moreover, we are of the same age.
> <gloss>that is, Indeed we are of equal age.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἀτὰρ καὶ ὁμήλικος ἐμοῦ.</note>

Plato looked to this in the first book of *The Republic*, where Cephalus, who testifies that he has already reached "the threshold of old age" <note>original Greek: ὅτι γήραος οὐδός</note>, says: "For many of us often come together in the same place, being of a similar age, preserving the ancient proverb." That is, many of us frequently meet...

<summary>Erasmus discusses two proverbs: the first emphasizes that a master's personal presence is essential for success, while the second explores the natural social bond between people of similar age, status, or character.</summary>
<keywords>oversight, management, agriculture, social circles, similarity, friendship, Cato, Pliny, Aristotle, Cicero, Plato</keywords>

# SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...we are born almost equal, observing that ancient proverb. Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, when reviewing what things are pleasant to whom, writes that in general those things which are joined by nature or are similar delight one another; for instance, a human delights in a human, a horse in a horse, and a youth in a youth. And the commonly tossed-about proverbs tend toward this: <note>original Greek: ἧλιξ ἥλικα τέρπει</note> *An equal delights an equal.* There are also others of that kind. His words are these: <note>original Greek: τὰ συγγενῆ καὶ ὁμοῖα φύσιν ἀλλήλοις ἐστὶν... (Aristotle, Rhetoric 1.11.25)</note> *Things related by kin and similar in nature are, for the most part, pleasant to one another, such as a human to a human, a horse to a horse, and a youth to a youth. Whence the proverbs are spoken, such as "an equal delights an equal," and "always like to like," and "beast knows beast," and "jackdaw to jackdaw," and all other such things.* Theognis says that friendship coheres between equals, neighbors, and the elderly:
<note>original Greek: Πάντες μὲν ὑμᾶσιν ὅμως...</note>
*All these indeed honor and love one another in turn,*
*Neighbors, those equal in strength, and the elderly.*
-> that is, <-
All these respect each other, and love in return,
Neighbors, equals in power, and the old.

Nor is it foreign to this proverb what Empedocles says in Aristotle’s first book *On the Soul*, that the soul is something fashioned out of all the elements—indeed, that it is itself a part of them—and that it knows each thing because it has something kindred with each individual element. Whence also Plato says in the *Timaeus* that the soul consists of the elements. The verses of Empedocles go like this:
<note>original Greek: Γαίῃ μὲν γὰρ γαῖαν ὀπώπαμεν... (Empedocles, Fragment 109)</note>
*For by earth we see earth, by water, water,*
*By air, divine air, but by fire, destructive fire,*
*By love, love, and by strife, mournful strife.*
Because at first we despaired of these verses being able to be translated more conveniently, we have subjoined the version by Argyropylus: <note>Johannes Argyropylus (1415–1487) was a Greek scholar central to the revival of Greek learning in Italy.</note>
> For by earth we know earth, by liquid, water,
> And air by air, surely fire is discerned by fire,
> So also by love, love, and by sad discord, strife.

Although in the first verse I suspect that "wave" was changed into "water" by the scribes. Later, at the request of friends, we added our own version, such as it is:
> Earth indeed is felt by earth, and liquid by liquid,
> Pure air by air, but by fire, harmful fire,
> Sweet love by love, and by hate, deadly feud.

Argyropylus, for the sake of filling out the meter, rendered the single word *opōpamen* <note>we have seen/perceived</note> with two, "we know" and "is discerned"; he omitted two epithets, "divine" and "destructive." Then, for the sake of a repeated word, he lost it twice, in "water and liquid" and in "discord and strife," not to mention the harshness of the composition in "For by earth." He also wove in the adverb "surely" of his own accord. We added an epithet to love, but one the poet would have added if the laws of meter had allowed, since he added his own to the contrary word, "mournful strife." These things are not said by me to carp at a man who has deserved the best from the best studies, but so that youths, for whom these things are chiefly written, may profit in judgment. One of the philosophers, Zeno if I am not mistaken, recorded in Augustine that the soul itself is a number moving itself, and for this reason it is captured and charmed by numerical things: just as even children are affected by musical modes through a certain kindred sense of nature, though they are entirely ignorant of what music is. Aristotle, in this very place we have cited, brings up this definition without naming the author.

<margin>XXI</margin>
-> Like rejoices in like. <-
<margin>Like is dear to like.</margin>
*Like is dear to like.* That is, Like rejoices in like. Aristotle in the eighth book of the *Ethics*: <note>original Greek: ὅμοιον ὁμοίῳ φίλον</note> *Like is dear to like.* That is, Like seeks like. Also in the ninth book: *Like is a friend to like.* Whence also is that saying: <note>original Greek: ὁμοιότης δὲ φιλότητος μήτηρ</note> *Similarity is the mother of friendship.* Therefore, where there is absolute similarity, there is the most vehement love, which the fable of Narcissus indicates. Agathon in Plato’s *Symposium*: <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ παλαιὸς λόγος εὖ ἔχει...</note> *For the ancient saying holds well, that like always draws near to like.* Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How a friend may be distinguished from a flatterer*, records these six-line verses:
<note>original Greek: Τέρπει γέροντα γλῶσσαν ἡδίστω ἔχων...</note>
*A boy delights a boy, a woman what is suitable to a woman,*
*A sick man a sick man, and to one caught in misfortune,*
*He who has tried it is a singer of charms.* That is,

->**DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES**<-

To the old man, the tongue of the old is most pleasant,
And to the boy, the boy; and the woman is suited to the woman,
Likewise the sick man to the sick, and he who is placed in misfortune,
Is pleasing to, and agrees with, one exercised in misfortunes.
<note>original: "Seni senilis lingua..." These lines are likely from a Greek tragic fragment translated into Latin by Erasmus.</note>

Diogenes Laertius, showing that Plato imitated certain things from the writings of Epicharmus, brings forward this also: That to a dog, a dog seems most beautiful; and to an ox, an ox; and to a female donkey, a donkey; and to a pig, a pig. We have said elsewhere, "To every queen, her own king is pleasing." <note>A variation of "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."</note> Plato in the eighth book of *The Laws* says: *We call that which is like to like "friend" according to virtue, and equal to equal.* <note>original: "Φίλον μὲν τὸ καλήμεθον..."</note> Although the adage is rightly transferred also to those whom a similarity of vices brings together. Against whom is that line of Catullus:
It suits beautiful, wicked lewdsters.
And that of Martial:
Worst wife, worst husband,
I wonder that you do not get along well.
And likewise that of Juvenal:
Great is the harmony among the soft. <note>original: "Magna inter molles concordia." Referring to the solidarity among those of similar "effeminate" vices.</note>

### God always leads like to like. XXII

This adage can seem to have been born from Homer, in whose *Odyssey* book 17, Melanthius the goatherd, having spotted Eumaeus the swineherd bringing Ulysses himself with him—but in the habit and appearance of a ragamuffin—makes a taunt against both, as if two similar people had well met: *Now indeed the wicked man leads the wicked; as always, God leads like to like.* <note>original: "Νῦν μὲν δὴ μάλα πάγχυ..."</note> That is:
Now behold, the evil man accompanies the evil, so that
God leads like to like, and equal to equal.
Aristotle in the eighth book of *Ethics* cites it as a proverb: *Whence they say, like to like.*

### A jackdaw always sits by a jackdaw. XXIII

*A jackdaw always sits near a jackdaw.* <note>original: "Ἀεὶ κολοιὸς πρὸς κολοιὸν ἱζάνει"</note>
A proverbial six-foot line is cited by Diogenianus: and it is noted by Aristotle in the book of *Rhetoric* which we just cited: where among many other proverbs of this sentiment, he mentions this one too. Likewise in the eighth book of *Ethics*: *And jackdaw to jackdaw.* To the Greeks, it is a trochaic dimeter, no doubt plucked from some poet. Gregory <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> elegantly used the adage in a certain letter to Eudoxius: *You hear also from the proverb that a jackdaw sits by a jackdaw.* Furthermore, Marcus Varro testifies in the third book of *On Agriculture* that gatherings of jackdaws were known of old. Whence Plutarch in the book *On Having Many Friends* says: *For it is not of the herd, nor of the jackdaw-kind.* <note>Meaning a friendship should be deeper than a mere flocking together.</note> Indeed, the name was given to this bird from the word *kolaō*, which is "to glue together." Marcus Varro wants "jackdaws" <term>graculos: the Latin name for the bird</term> to be so called in Latin because they fly in flocks <term>gregatim</term>. Quintilian does not approve, asserting the word was fashioned from the voice of the birds.

### Cricket is dear to cricket, ant to ant. XXIIII

Moreover, regarding what Aristotle added in that place we just cited—"And if there are any others of that kind"—there is no doubt that he meant those which are in the ninth Idyll of Theocritus: *Cricket is friend to cricket, and ant to ant, and hawks to hawks.* That is:
The ant is pleasing to the ant, the cricket to the cricket,
The hawk is pleasing to the hawk.
Furthermore, the "citizenship" of ants and the "singing in unison" of crickets are well known.

### Potter envies potter, smith envies smith. XXV

From this pattern, those who are engaged in the same craft are to be excepted, for the reason that among these, the similarity of the trade brings about emulation <note>rivalry or competition</note> more than goodwill. Hesiod indicated their mutual envy among themselves in the work titled *Works and Days* with several metaphors, yet not condemning that kind of contest of craftsmen, but rather approving and praising it. For the poet had proposed two kinds of emulation: one which is useful and beautiful for mortals, the other foul and ruinous. This latter one incites men to brawls and wars because of the struggles for wealth and honors; but by the former, as if by examples set before them, they are awakened to industry and honorable arts. He describes honorable emulation, therefore, in these words:

# CENTURY II OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

<margin>and neighbor [vies with] neighbor</margin>
<margin>and [he] strips for work. This strife is good for mortals,</margin>
<margin>and potter is angry with potter, and craftsman with craftsman.</margin>
<margin>and beggar envies beggar, and singer envies singer.</margin>
I have translated these most elegant verses <note>original: "Versus longe elegantissimos"</note> only so that they may be understood. For hardly anyone could match them, let alone I:
> Neighbor is rival to neighbor, as he
> Sees him hastening toward wealth with diligence; indeed
> This sort of reckoning benefits mortals.
> The craftsman is troublesome to the craftsman, and to the potter
> Is he: immediately one beggar envies another
> One, and the envious singer hates the singer.

This is cited frequently among various authors, notably in Aristotle’s *Moralia* <note>The Nicomachean Ethics</note>. Again, in Book VII of the same work, it is referenced as a proverb: <margin>they say all potters are [rivals] to one another.</margin> That is, they say all potters of that kind are among themselves. "Potters," he says, clearly alluding to the Hesiodic adage. Likewise, in Book III of the *Rhetoric*: <margin>whence it is said, potter against potter.</margin> He also cites this line there, I know not from which poet:
<margin>for even the potter knows how to envy his kin.</margin> That is,
Kinship itself has learned how to envy.

This is a similarity which Plutarch in his *Symposiacs* calls <term>machimon</term> <note>original: μάχιμον; meaning "warlike" or "combative"</note>: that is, bellicose and pugnacious, such as is found among roosters; and such as exists between sophists, beggars, and poets. For this reason, he forbids that kind of men from being joined together at banquets, lest some altercation arise, which he calls <term>epieike</term> <note>original: ἐπιεικῆ; here used ironically for a "fitting" or "customary" squabble</note>, of the sort found among jackdaws. To this category belong farmers, hunters, and trainers. And for that reason, they are rightly paired together at the table—unless it happens that they love the same woman.

### 26. A Cretan against a Cretan.

<margin>A Cretan against a Cretan.</margin> A Cretan against a Cretan; understand, as fits the sense, "is born to circumvent," or something of that sort. It is used whenever a rogue deals with a rogue, or a treacherous man with the treacherous. The adage is taken from the character of the Cretans, whom antiquity burdened with many reproaches.

### 27. A Cretan with an Aeginetan.

For the sentiment holds: <margin>A Cretan against an Aeginetan.</margin> That is, a Cretan deals with an Aeginetan. It applies to those who are equally wicked, who deal with one another through mutual deceits. For these people also formerly had a bad reputation, against whom some say that oracle was issued: <margin>neither third, nor fourth.</margin> <note>A reference to a famous oracle telling the people of Aegina they were of no account.</note>

### 28. To play the fox with a fox.

<margin>to play the fox against another fox.</margin> That is, you in turn play the fox with a fox. Always proverbial. Deal with the crafty using craftiness. Horace says:
> Let the intentions lurking beneath the fox-skin deceive you.

<margin>but as he says in *The Wasps*: it is not permitted to play the fox.</margin> That is, one must not act like a fox.
Indeed, I have translated <term>alopekizein</term> <note>original: ἀλωπεκίζειν</note> as "to play the fox" <note>original: "vulpinari"</note>, lest anyone reject the word as if it were my own invention; it is cited from Marcus Varro by Nonius Marcellus. For he dared to say "to fox" for the Greek term, just as Horace said "to youth" <note>original: "iuvenari"</note> for the Greek <term>neanieuesthai</term> <note>original: νεανιεύεσθαι</note> regarding the proverb "to play the king" <note>original: βασιλεύειν</note>.

### 29. Cretize with a Cretan.

<margin>to Cretize against a Cretan.</margin> That is, against a Cretan, "Cretize"—meaning, use lies against a liar. Plutarch used this in the *Life of Lysander*: <margin>against a Cretan, then, as the saying goes, Cretize.</margin> And again in the *Life of Paulus Aemilius*: <margin>It did not escape those who knew him accurately that he was Cretizing against the Cretans.</margin> That is, it was not hidden from those who knew the man thoroughly that he was using Cretan arts against the Cretans. This is because the vanity of the Cretans—concerning the burial of Jupiter among them and other lies of that sort—passed into a common fable. This is openly testified by that verse of Epimenides, which the Apostle Paul also cites:
<margin>Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies.</margin>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin proverbs (Adagia). The previous page likely discussed other regional stereotypes or common sayings.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

**Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies.** Saint Jerome, in the commentaries he wrote on this epistle <note>referring to Titus 1:12</note>, indicates that this verse is found in the work of Epimenides, which he titled *On Oracles*. For this reason, Paul calls him a prophet, whether in jest or because of the subject matter. Moreover, the beginning of this poem, <note>original Greek: Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσαι</note> "Cretans are always liars," was used by the poet Callimachus of Cyrene in a hymn written against the Cretans in praise of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, accusing them of vanity because they repeatedly boasted that his tomb was among them, even though he was immortal. Ovid, looking back on this, says: "Nor do the Cretans invent everything." From this, the Greeks use the <term>Cretanize (Krētizein)</term> <note>to act like a Cretan</note> to mean "to lie." Suidas indicates another cause for the adage, writing that Idomeneus the Cretan, when he was given the task of distributing the brass collected from spoils taken from enemies, chose by far the best part for himself. Hence, it seems to apply also to those who defraud others and everywhere study their own advantages too intensely. The same author thinks the adage fits even those who act with lies in vain against a master of lying. Just as they commonly say it is most difficult to steal among thieves, so it is most difficult to impose with lies upon liars.

->With a Carian, you play the Carian. XXX<-

Diogenianus records one very similar to this: <term>A Carian, you reproach a Carian (Karis kara kakizeis)</term>, that is, "When with a Carian, you act like a Carian." You act rustically with a rustic, you speak barbarously to a barbarian, coarsely with a coarse man. The Carians are a people of Asia, of whom we shall speak in another place, whose customs gave rise to several proverbs.

->The Cretan and the sea. XXXI<-

<term>The Cretan [does not know] the sea (Ho Krēs tēn thalassan)</term>. That is, "The Cretan and the sea"—it must be understood: "he does not know it," or "he fears it." Strabo the Geographer records and explains this proverb likewise in Book 10, writing that once the Cretans held the leadership in the skill of sailing and the practice of maritime affairs; and hence the proverb became frequent in antiquity: "The Cretan does not know the sea," used against those who pretend not to know what they are exceedingly skilled in. For how is it consistent that Cretans, since they are islanders, should be ignorant of the sea by which they are surrounded on all sides? Aristides used the same in *Pericles*: <term>The Cretan [does not know] the deep (ho Krēs ton ponton)</term>. Zenodotus writes that it appears in Alcaeus. Akin to these is what Horace has in the *Epistle to Octavius*: "I myself, who affirm that I write no verses, am found to be more of a liar than the Parthians," because the Parthians fight most especially when they feign flight.

->To bring it to the navel. XXXII<-

There exist among several authors proverbs for finishing a task, among the number of which is this: "To bring it to the navel," used for finishing and completing a book. For "navels" <note>umbilici</note>, according to the interpreter Porphyrio, are certain ornaments made of bone, wood, or horn, imitating the shape of our navels, which were added to volumes <note>scrolls</note> once they were finished; and from this the proverbial figure was born: "it has come to the navel," that is, to the end. Horace in the *Epodes*:
> God, God, for he forbids me
> To bring the promised poem, the swift iambics
> Begun, to the navel.

Martial in the fourth book of *Epigrams*:
> Ho there, now it is enough; ho, little book!
> We have already arrived even at the navels,
> Yet you seek to proceed and go further.

The same in the fifth book:
> The page which, decorated with cedar and purple,
> Has grown with black navels.

The same in the third:
> Now you may walk anointed with cedar oil,
> and decent with double honor on your fronts,
> you may revel in painted navels.

Again in the eleventh:
> You bring back to us a book unrolled even to its horns,
> And as if it were perfected, Septitianus.

But for my part, I do not know whether this proverb can be transferred to anything other than a book or a poem, unless the metaphor becomes too harsh.

->To place the highest roof-ridge. XXXIII<-

That one is more general: "To place the highest roof-ridge," used for completing a thing in all its parts. You will find examples in Cicero in the third book of *Offices*, and in Pliny in his *Epistles* several times. It is transferred from builders, who, when the building is finally perfected, are accustomed to place some roof-ridge <note>the "crowning achievement" or finishing touch</note>; to whom, just as the foundation is the first part of setting up the work...

# SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<margin>Signature: g</margin>
<margin>Page: 73</margin>

Just as the pediment is the final completion. Thus, just as they say "to lay the foundations" for the act of beginning something, they likewise use "to add the pediment" to signify perfection and the "final hand," as they call it. Closely related to this is the Greek saying: <note>original: κολοφῶνα ἐπέθηκεν</note> *He put the Colophon on it.* <note>Colophon was a city whose cavalry was so effective they were said to always end a battle; it now refers to the finishing stroke or a publisher's emblem at the end of a book.</note>

### 34. To add the finishing touch.
<note>original: Summam manum addere</note>

The phrase "To add the finishing touch" <note>literally: "to add the highest hand"</note> has the same force. It is likely a metaphor born from craftsmen, who first fashion a rough likeness of a work—which they call the "first hand"—then shape it more precisely, and finally polish it with the greatest care, calling this the "highest" or "final hand." **Ovid** says:
> Yet those works could scarcely be read with patience by anyone,
> If the finishing touch were missing from them.

Shortly after, he used "the final file" to mean the same thing:
> Since that work required the middle of the anvils,
> The final file was also lacking from my writings.

The same author <note>Erasmus likely means Seneca here, writing to Lucilius</note> says to Lucilius: "The final drink delights those devoted to wine—that which sinks them, which puts the finishing touch on their drunkenness." By the same figure of speech, we say "nothing is lacking except the final hand." Examples are too frequent among writers to be worth repeating here.

### 35. To add the final act of the play.
<note>original: Supremum fabulæ actum addere</note>

To the same pattern belongs the phrase: "To add the final act of the play," used instead of "to impose the final end." This is taken from the poets who write comedies or tragedies, who distribute their plays into certain acts. Hence that line of Horace:
> Let it not be longer than a fifth act.

He writes, moreover, that one should add the greatest skill to the final act, just as Marcus Tullius [Cicero] writes to his brother Quintus: "This I both pray and urge you to do at the last: that just as good poets and industrious actors do, so you should be most diligent in the final part and conclusion of your duty and business; so that this whole year of your command may seem, like a third act, to be most perfect and most ornate." The same author in his letters to Atticus, book 13: "For indeed this play had been sung to the end, but I wished to complete it a little more." Cicero, in his work *On Old Age*, transfers this to a life fully lived. Likewise, Apuleius in the third book of his *Florida*, speaking of the comic poet Philemon, says: "They announced that the poet Philemon, who was expected to finish his fictional plot in the theater, had already completed his own play at home." Indeed, he had already told human affairs to "farewell and applaud." <note>The traditional closing of a Roman comedy.</note> I believe the saying in Lucilius, cited by Nonius, belongs to this form: "The mender made the best patchwork quilt."

### 36. The catastrophe of the play.
<note>original: Catastrophe fabulæ</note>

By a proverbial figure, we call the outcome of any matter a "catastrophe." Furthermore, among proverbial figures, we have advised that every discipline and craft has its own peculiar vocabulary which—just as is customary in sacred ceremonies and magical prayers—they use with almost a certain superstition. Whenever these terms are drawn into another context, they almost take on the appearance of a proverb. For example, from military discipline: "to sound the retreat," "to desert one's post," "the line of the *triarii*," and "the matter has come down to the *triarii*." <note>The triarii were the veteran third line of the Roman army; the phrase means "it has come to the last resort."</note> From music: "prelude" for a preface or the beginning of a business; "the highest and lowest string" for a loud or deep voice; and "to stumble on the same string" for sinning repeatedly in the same matter. Furthermore, every play, as Donatus shows, is distributed into four parts: the *protasis*, *epitasis*, *catastasis*, and *catastrophe*. The *protasis* is that first stir, already as if smoldering. The *epitasis* is the most feverish disturbance. The *catastrophe* is the sudden change of affairs. Hence Lucian elegantly calls the exit and outcome of a business a "catastrophe," both elsewhere and in his commentary *On Those Who Serve for Hire*: "After all these things, finally, the catastrophe of the drama happened to them," that is, what the outcome was. And in *Alexander the False Prophet*: "Such was the end of the tragedy of Alexander." Likewise in the *Life of Peregrinus*: "Again I see you laughing, O good Cronius, at the catastrophe of the drama."

### 37. From head to heel.
<note>original: A capite usque ad calcem</note>

When we signify a whole thing, we say "from head to heel." The use of this adage can be threefold: it refers either to the body, the mind, or a situation. The latter two possess more elegance, surely because they contain more figurative meaning. Regarding the body, in Homer's *Iliad*, book 5: "From feet to head." Likewise Theocritus in his *Idylls*:

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<sig>k 2</sig>

"And observe me continually from my head to my feet." <note>original Greek: Καί μ' ἀπὸ τῆς κεφαλῆς ποτὶ τὼ πόδε συνεχὲς ἄθρει</note> That is:
*He surveyed me entirely with his light from head to foot.*
Plautus in *Epidicus*: "Look at me, Epidicus, from my little toenail to the top of my hair." Horace:
*Handsome from his head to his lowest ankles.*
Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in *Defense of Roscius the Comic Actor*: "Do not that very head and those shaved eyebrows seem to reek of malice and cry out of cunning? From the tips of his nails to the top of his head, if the silent figure of the body offers any conjecture to men, does he not seem to be composed entirely of fraud, fallacies, and lies?" To the point, as in Aristophanes’ *Plutus*:
"Listen then, for I shall tell you the whole business
From the feet to the head." <note>original Greek: Ἀκουε τοίνυν, ὡς ἐγὼ τὰ πράγματα / Ἐκ τῶν ποδῶν ἂν τὴν κεφαλὴν ὑμῖν' ἐρῶ</note> That is:
*Hear then, since I shall recount the whole affair
To you from the feet even unto the head.*
Although here the comic poet, for the sake of a joke, placed the feet and head in reverse order. Saint Jerome, in the preface to the book he titled *Hebrew Names*: "I compared it with him from the top, as they say, to the furthest nail." This can be transferred to the mind in this way: "I shall paint for you his character and talent briefly—the whole man as he is, from the highest hair, as they say, to the lowest heel." Although the example from Marcus Tullius, which we just cited, seems to pertain more to the mind than to the body. Furthermore, the adage is divided when we call the "head" of a business the principal author, just as we also say the "source." Terence: "That you are the head <note>meaning the source or leader</note> of this affair." Likewise among the Greeks, "the head of the matter." <note>original Greek: τὸ κεφάλαιον τοῦ πράγματος</note> Lucian in *The Tyrannicide*: "the head of the tyranny." <note>original Greek: τῆ τυραννίδι ἡ κεφαλαί ου</note> And Plato in the third book of *Laws* said "the source of seditions." <note>original Greek: τὴν τῶν στάσεων πηγὴν</note> Also: "To come to the heel" <note>the end</note>. "In the heel of the work." "In the very last heel of your letter." "To begin from the head itself." "To run back from the heel to the head." And other formulas of speaking of that kind, which are met with everywhere among authors. Plutarch against the Stoics: "from the feet from the beginning up to the head." <note>original Greek: ἐκ ποδῶν ἐπ' ἀρχῆς ἄχρι κεφαλῆς</note> That is: *From the entrance and the beginning even unto the finishing stroke.*

---

->I pass the torch in the race. XXXVIII<-

**To pass the torch in the race** <term>lampada tradere: a metaphor for passing on a responsibility or office</term> is a proverbial metaphor for transferring your role to another, and then another, as if in succession. Lucretius:
*And like runners they pass on the torch of life.*
He is discussing living creatures, which propagate by succession, life being poured from some into others by turns. Marcus Varro in the third book of *On Agriculture*, chapter 15: "But, O Merula, lest our friend Axius learn physics while hearing this—since I have said nothing of the profit—I now pass the torch to you in the race." By these words he signifies that he is handing over the next part of the discourse to Merula, and he succeeds him in the turn of speaking. Lucretius seems to have imitated Plato, who writes in the sixth book of *Laws* that citizens ought to devote effort to begetting and educating children, so that the life which they themselves received from their ancestors they may in turn pass on to posterity like a burning torch. To the same point belongs that line of Persius:
*Since you are ahead, why do you ask for the torch from me in the middle of the race?* Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
"And now no one is able to carry the little torches
Because of a lack of exercise." <note>original Greek: λαμπάδια δ' οὐδεὶς οἷός τε φέρειν / ὑπ' ἀγυμνασίας ἔτι νυνί</note> That is:
*Now no one can carry the torch,
Because they do not care to be exercised.*
He censures the laziness and sluggishness of the citizens. In this passage, the commentator adds that the ancients used to carry torches in three contests—or as they said, "to run the torch-race" <note>original Greek: λαμπαδηχεῖν</note>—in the festivals of Prometheus, Vulcan, and the Panathenaic games. Furthermore, Prometheus is believed to have been the first to institute this kind of game, in this manner: those running would carry a burning torch. When exhausted, he would give it into the hand of the next person. He, likewise tired, gave it to another, and one after another in succession they handed it over in turn, representing a sort of image of the Promethean story: how he brandished the stalk <note>the fennel stalk used to steal fire</note> in which he had caught the celestial fire with perpetual motion so it would not be extinguished again while flying down to earth. Plato mentions this in the first book of the *Republic*, signifying that torch-processions <note>original Greek: δαδουχίας</note> were also customarily celebrated in honor of Minerva. Pausanias, however, in his *Attica*, describes the ritual of these games more copiously. Herodotus also mentions it, though in passing, in *Urania*, showing that the custom was devised by the Persians, so that with horses and runners stationed, one would hand over commands to another like a torch, so they could be carried more swiftly. The author of the *Rhetoric to Herennius* says: "For it is not as in the wrestling-ground, where he who receives the burning torches is faster in the continuous race..."

# SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>g 2</sig>

...the one who hands it over: thus a new General who receives an army is better than the one who <unclear>leaves</unclear> it. For this reason, <unclear>because</unclear> one is exhausted by the race, the other receives the torch fresh; here the skilled General hands over the command <unclear>to another</unclear>. Therefore, he is said to "hand over the torch" who, being either worn out or having completed his service, transfers the duty to be performed from himself to another. And in turn, "to pass the torch" is said of those who, as Terence says, trade mutual services and bring help to one another in succession. <note>original: "lampadem tradere" — a metaphor derived from ancient Greek torch races (lampadedromia) where runners passed a light to successors.</note>

-> The beginning is half of the whole. XXXIX <-

<note>original Greek: ἥμισυ παντὸς ἀρχή</note>. That is, the Beginning is half of the whole. By this adage it is signified that the greatest part of the difficulty in undertaking a business lies in the beginning. It is a half-line of verse from Hesiod, cited by Lucian in *Hermotimus*. It is also recorded by Aristotle in the fifth book of the *Politics*: "The beginning is said to be half of the whole." Plato in the sixth book of *Laws* says: "For in proverbs it is rightly said that the beginning is half of the whole, and we all praise a thing well begun on every occasion. But to me it seems to be more than half, and no one has yet sufficiently praised a beginning that was well made." That is, in proverbs indeed <unclear>the start</unclear> of the whole is called half. And that surely, having begun rightly, we should all praise from every side. But that, as it seems to me at least, is more than half. Nor has anyone <unclear>truly</unclear> praised it enough according to its merit. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia/lexicon.</note> reports these things from a certain Marinus: "It is written that the beginning is not only the beginning, nor according to the proverb, half of the whole, but the entire thing itself." That is, however, to us that beginning is not just a beginning, nor according to the proverb a half, but the solid whole itself. Aristotle likewise in the first book of *Ethics*: "For the beginning seems to be already half of the whole." Horace in his *Epistles*:
> He who has begun has half the deed done. Dare to be wise.

Ausonius:
> Begin: to have begun is half the deed. Let the other
> Half remain: begin this again, and you will finish.

<unclear>Plutarch</unclear> in the booklet titled *How the Young Should Hear Poems*, cites this verse from Sophocles:
<note>original Greek: ἀρχὴ παντὸς λώϊστος ἀρχικῶς καλῶς...</note>
which means:
> If you begin any matter well,
> It is probable the end will be likewise good.

-> It is better to cure the beginnings than the end. XL <-

<note>original Greek: ἀρχῶν ἰᾶσθαι πολὺ λώϊον ἢ τελευτῶν</note>. That is, it is much better to treat the beginnings than the end. <unclear>Found</unclear> in Suidas as a proverb. To the same sentiment, Theognis:
<note>original Greek: ἀρχῇ πῆμ’ ἕλκει φάρμακα φυομένῳ</note>
which means:
> Medicines must be applied to a growing evil.

Similarly Persius in his third satire:
> Meet the disease as it approaches.
> And you see, you may see. Meet the disease as it approaches.

And likewise Ovid:
> Resist the beginnings: medicine is prepared too late,
> When evils have gained strength through long delays.

<unclear>This</unclear> pertains to the adage that an evil is removed with less trouble immediately at the start while it is still fresh, than after it has become chronic: that children should be kept from vices while their age is still tender and manageable; that offenses should be <unclear>settled</unclear> immediately, lest they grow into a grudge; that the smallest evils are to be avoided, from which greater ones sprout; that occasions should be avoided which seem likely to produce some evil.

-> Do not hesitate to sow. XLI <-

A <unclear>rustic</unclear> adage, but not unworthy of being recorded in this volume: "Do not hesitate to sow." By which we are warned never to be reluctant to undertake something of the sort from which no <unclear>loss</unclear> but much profit can proceed—if not for the present, certainly for the future; if not for us, at least for posterity. Columella in the twelfth book *On Agriculture*: "Wherefore that common saying about <unclear>planting</unclear>, used by farmers: 'Do not hesitate to sow.' For building sometimes depends on <unclear>harvests</unclear>, and commerce depends on fortune, and has turned out badly for many. In the same way, there is one trouble or danger after another, but from planting trees <unclear>much</unclear> benefit is taken, nor does it cost a great expense." Virgil expressed the same sentiment, adding a figure of speech, in the second book of the *Georgics*:
> Do we still hesitate to sow, and to bestow our care?

-> To put on the winged sandals. XLII <-

There is also in Marcus Tullius [Cicero] a proverbial allegory, "To put on the winged sandals," for that which is to prepare for flight, and as if wanting to fly away somewhere. For he writes thus to Atticus in the fourteenth book:

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

There is no one among them who does not fear leisure; therefore, let us put on our winged sandals. <note>original: "talaria induamus"</note> This is taken from Homer, who frequently equips Mercury with winged sandals when he is about to fly off somewhere:

> Immediately then he bound beneath his feet his beautiful sandals,
> Ambrosial, golden, which carried him both over the moist sea,
> And over the boundless earth, along with the blasts of the wind. <note>original Greek: Αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’ ὑπὸ ποσσὶν... Homer, Odyssey 5.44-46</note>
> *that is,*
> Soon as he placed the golden sandals beneath his feet,
> Beautiful and breathing of ambrosia: which at once bore him
> Through the liquid air, and across the wide expanses of the vast
> Earth, with the dominant blast of the wind. <note>Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation of the Greek above.</note>

Virgil, as if interpreting this passage of Homer, says in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:

> And first, he says, he binds the golden sandals to his feet,
> Which carry him aloft on wings, whether over the seas
> Or the land, equally with the rapid gale.

Therefore, we shall say "to put on winged sandals" <note>talaria induere</note> of those who prepare to flee. For this very use of "to fly away" <note>auolare</note> and "to fly back" <note>reuolare</note> is frequent in Marcus Tullius Cicero for fleeing and returning.

### Trifles and Gewgaws. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XLIII

The common people used to call futile and nonsensical things *Tricae* and *Apinae*. Martial says:

> Whatever I played at as a youth, and once as a boy,
> And our *Apinae* [trifles]. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The same author elsewhere:
> They are *Apinae* and *Tricae*, and if there is anything cheaper than those.

From this, by a similar figure of speech, they used to say *Tricari* [to dally/trick] for acting foolishly. Cicero uses it in various places, especially in the fifteenth book of his letters to Atticus: "Trifles <note>Tricae</note> of course, as such a man is." And again: "Balbus," he says, "is playing tricks" <note>tricatur</note>. The adage was born from an event. For Pliny, in the third book of his *Natural History*, chapter 11, shows that Trica and Apina were once towns in Apulia; describing the bays of Europe, he says: "Diomedes there destroyed the nations of the Monadi and Dardi, and two cities which have turned into a playful proverb, Apina and Trica." Stephanus shows that Trica was a city of Thessaly, perhaps taking its name from Trica, the daughter of Peneus. Nonius Marcellus interprets *tricae* as hindrances and entanglements, derived from the Greek <note>ἀπὸ τῶν τριχῶν</note> meaning "from hairs," in which young chicks become entangled; from this is said "to extricate" <note>extricare</note> and "to intricate" <note>intricare</note>. Lucilius, in the same author, calls those who delay men with nonsense *Tricones*. And "tricine gain" for that which is slow or dry; and Varro speaks of "Atellan trifles" <note>tricas Attellanas</note> as very complicated nonsense. Indeed, I would not deny that the word alludes to hairs. However, it is closer to the truth that the proverb was named after the town. Pliny, in book eight, chapter 48, shows that sheep used to be praised for the shortness of their legs and the covering of their bellies; those whose bellies were bare, he called *apicae*, as if they were rejected and condemned things.

### A Corycaean was listening. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XLIIII

"A Corycaean was listening." <note>original Greek: Κωρυκαῖος ἠκροάσατο</note> This is used when someone, attempting to conceal what they are doing, is nevertheless caught by the curious. I shall add from authors where the adage originated. Corycus is a very high mountain in Pamphylia with many harbors, and for that reason, it is convenient for the ambushes of pirates, whom they called Corycaeans after that mountain. These men had devised a new method of lying in wait. Indeed, dispersed through the harbors of Mount Corycus, they mixed themselves with merchants as each happened to land, eavesdropping on what goods they carried, where they intended to sail, and finally at what time they had decided to set out. As soon as they learned these things, they reported back to the pirates, with whom they practiced a partnership in maritime robbery. And so, attacking together when the opportunity arose, they plundered the voyagers. When this matter became known to the merchants, they concealed and disguised most things for fear of ambushes. But when they could not remain hidden even so, with the Corycaeans sniffing out everything, the matter passed into a proverb: "A Corycaean listened to this." It is said of a matter vehemently disguised, yet discovered. Suidas says that Corycus is a promontory of Pamphylia, below which is the city of Attalea. The citizens of that city, so that they themselves would not be harassed by the pirates who took refuge in the citadel of the promontory, scattered through other harbors and eavesdropped on who had landed and where they were heading, and reported these things to the pirates. The same author reports from Ephorus that the Corycaeans were certain strangers who founded a small town in Lydia under the peak of Corycus looking out over the sea, neighbors to Myonessus. These men were accustomed to mix with merchants landing in the harbor, as if they were merchants themselves about to buy some goods; then they reported what they had learned to the Myonessians. The Myonessians would attack the voyagers, carrying off the plunder, or the prices with which the merchants ransomed themselves...

# CHILIAD I, CENTURY II
### g 3

<unclear>...sharing</unclear> the spoils, which the Greeks call *lytra* <note>original: "λύτρα" - ransoms or spoils</note>, with the Corycaeans. But Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century grammarian</note> records that this is a very high mountain, neighboring the Ionian town of Teos, below which lies a harbor of the same name. In that place, he mentions both the ambushes of pirates and the proverb. Strabo also writes concerning the mainland of Lydia, whose words I will transcribe from Book 14: <note>original: "πρὶν δὲ ἐλθεῖν..." - Erasmus provides the Greek text of Strabo's Geography, which he then translates into Latin below. I have translated the sense into English here.</note> "Before reaching Erythrae, first there is the small town of Erae belonging to Teos, then Corycus, a high mountain, and under it the harbor of Casystas, and another harbor called the 'Beautiful Harbor,' and several others in succession. They say that the whole of Corycus was once a haunt of pirates called Corycaeans, who devised a new way of attacking voyagers. For, dispersing themselves among the harbors where merchants put in, they would approach and eavesdrop on what they were carrying and where they were headed; then, when the men had put out to sea, they would gather together, set upon them, and plunder them. Hence, we call anyone who is a busybody and tries to overhear things done in secret and spoken in confidence a 'Corycaean,' and we use the proverb: 'The Corycaean was listening,' whenever someone thinks they are acting in secret but is not actually hidden, because of those who eavesdrop and strive to inquire into things that do not concern them." Thus far <unclear>Strabo</unclear>. In his words, there seems to be some corruption: one is removed if you read "pirates" <note>original: "ληστὰς"</note> for "piracies," another if you read "of things done and spoken in secret," for so the translator reads it. Therefore, since there are two cities of the same name, authors refer the proverb to both. Stephanus shows there is also a city of Corycus in Cilicia, which has a harbor and sea-access, as Pomponius Mela says, joined to the mainland by a narrow neck of land, near which is that famous Corycian cave celebrated in literature. Now, we have heard that the Cilicians were pirates. I believe this is the same one that Zenodotus and Suidas place in Pamphylia, since Pamphylia is near Cilicia, and formerly a good part of Cilicia was reckoned as part of Pamphylia. The same Stephanus mentions an island of that name; again, that there is a Corycian promontory in Crete, and a harbor of the same name in Ethiopia. Comic poets also introduce a certain god called "Corycaeus," who overhears and eavesdrops on what is being done, as Menander does in *The Dagger* and Dexippus in *The Treasure* according to Suidas. Hesychius also touched on this in three words, indicating that "Corycus" meant to the Greeks a leather vessel, or a ship, or a spear. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> uses this adage in the last letter of Book 10 to Atticus: "Therefore, hereafter I shall not write to you what I am going to do, but what I have done; all the 'Corycaeans' <note>original: "κωρυκαῖοι"</note> seem to be eavesdropping on what I say."

-> Fortune favors the brave. <-
-> XLV <-

<margin>Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, Book 2.</margin> For not only does fortune favor the brave, as it says in the ancient proverb, but reason does so much more. It is cited elsewhere from Ennius. It is used in the *Aeneid* of Maro <note>Virgil</note>, whence it is used everywhere by everyone. Ovid, in the second book of the *Fasti*:
> Luck and God favor the daring.

The same author alluded to it:
> Venus herself helps the happy.

<margin>Livy</margin> In Marcus Livius, Book 4 of the Macedonian War: "They said that fortune favors the brave." The adage warns that fortune must be bravely tempted, for things usually turn out successfully for such people. On the other hand, it suggests that fortune, as it were, favors that kind of man, while being hostile to those who dare to attempt nothing, but like snails remain perpetually hidden within their shells.

-> To spur the running horse. <-
-> XLVI <-

<unclear>To urge on</unclear> one who is running <note>original: "τρέχοντα ἐποτρύνειν"</note>. That is, "To spur the running horse," is to exhort someone toward that which they are already tending of their own accord. And by this figure of speech, we mitigate or rather forestall the offense of giving advice. Cicero to Cassius: "That I might see Caesar in Italy—for so we thought—so that, with many most honorable men saved, I might 'spur him on as he runs' (as they say) toward peace." The same to his brother Quintus, Book 2: "Wherefore you act indeed like a brother in exhorting me. But by Hercules, you are spurring one who is already running." Again to Atticus: "As for your exhorting me that..."

<keywords>Corycaeus, eavesdropping, pirates, Strabo, Cicero, Fortune favors the brave, encouragement, classical adages, Latin proverbs, Greek etymology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on common Greek and Latin proverbs (Adages), focusing on metaphors for encouragement, hesitation, and repetition.</meta>

I will spend those days explaining philosophy: you are indeed "spurring one who is already running." <note>original: "currentem tu quidem"</note> Likewise in *The Orator*, Cicero says: "For it is easier to incite one who is running, as they say, than to move one who is sluggish." Pliny writes to Cannius: "I know you do not lack stings <note>stimuli</note>: yet my affection for you calls me out to urge on one who is already running." The metaphor is drawn from those who compete in a race, to whom the cheering of the crowd usually adds speed. Lucian, quoting Homer, writes to Nigrinus: "Take heart, good man, for as Homer says, you are exhorting and calling out to one who is already running." <note>original Greek: Θάρσει ὦ γαθέ... translated as "Bono es animo..."</note> This appears in the *Iliad*, Book 8:
"Most noble son of Atreus, why do you urge me on when I am already hastening of my own accord?" <note>original: "Ἀτρείδη κύδιστε..."</note> The same is alluded to in the *Odyssey*, Book 1:
"Having spoken thus, she urged on Pallas, who was already eager and desiring it." <note>original: "ὡς εἰπὼν, ὤτρυνε..."</note>
Therefore, we "incite the runner" when we call someone to a task toward which they are already carried by their own desire and inclination. As Dio mentions, the singer Timotheus used to incite the mind of Alexander the Great to a sudden desire for war by a certain song called the "Song of Pallas." He was indeed inciting him, but inciting one who was "running" of his own accord, as Alexander was by nature bloodthirsty and most thirsty for war. Otherwise, he would never have moved that Sardanapalus <note>A legendary king of Assyria known for effeminacy</note>, who was "un-Bacchic," that is, most soft. Terence, in the *Andria*, twisted this into a negative sense, omitting the metaphor: "Come now, if this man is not insane enough of his own accord, egg him on." To this belong those familiar phrases of Marcus Tullius Cicero: "To recall from the course." In the beginning of the *Topics*: "Your will recalled me from the very course." Also, "To be in the course," and "To interrupt the course."

### To add the spur to the runner. XLVII

Pliny the Younger expressed the same sentiment using a metaphor drawn from elsewhere in a certain letter to Pompeius Saturninus: "You were demanding that I send you something from my writings, when I had already intended that very thing. You have therefore added spurs to one running of his own accord." The metaphor is taken from horsemen, who sometimes add the spur even to horses running of their own will so that they may run faster. Thus, one adds the spur to us who goads the sluggish; he adds it to "runners" who increases and sharpens our desire and zeal. Ovid says:
->There is no need to apply the spur to a horse already at a gallop.<-
Furthermore, these metaphors are almost entirely proverbial: "To apply the spur," "To apply the goad," just as those: "To put on the bridle," "To restrain with the bridle," "To recall with the bridle." Cicero to Atticus: "He even adds and, as it were, applies the spur." Likewise to the same in Book 6: "But the one, as Isocrates said of Ephorus and Theopompus, needs bridles, the other needs spurs." Plato in *Laws*, Book 9: "Once again, O Cleinias, having been awakened, you have caught hold of me as if with a halter." <note>original Greek: αὖθις ὦ κλεανία...</note> That is: "Opportunely, Cleinias, you have checked me as I was running with momentum." And that phrase of Cicero: "He recalled him from the middle of the course."

### I am at the crossroads. XLVIII

"I am at a crossroads of calculations." <note>original Greek: Ἐν τριόδῳ εἰμὶ λογισμῶν</note> That is: I am at a crossroads of counsel. This is used for those who doubt, and who are of uncertain mind, hesitating over what they should preferably choose. It is a metaphor from those who are making a journey, and if ever a three-way road <note>a crossroads</note> occurs, they doubt which path they ought to enter. For you will frequently find "path" used for "plan of counsel" among Greek authors, as in Euripides' *Hecuba*: "I do not know where to look in vain," that is, "the path of your counsels." Theognis says: "I stand at the crossroads." Plato also alludes to this in *Laws*, Book 7, forbidding that if any wonderful and unusual thing occurs, we should immediately run to embrace it; rather, just as if we had come to some crossroads, ignorant of the way, we should stand still, and not proceed further until it has been investigated where each path leads, "just as," he says, "those who have arrived at a crossroads."

### Twice and thrice, that which is beautiful. XLIX

"Twice and thrice the beautiful thing." <note>original Greek: Δὶς καὶ τρὶς τὸ καλόν</note> That is: Again and a third time, that which is beautiful (one must understand: "should be said"). It is used by Plato in various places, especially in the *Philebus*: "Regarding those things we mentioned before. The proverb seems to hold well, that it is necessary to repeat in speech twice and thrice that which is well-put." Likewise in the *Gorgias*: "For they say it is a beautiful thing to both say and consider beautiful things twice and even thrice." Again in *Laws*, Book 6: "I say indeed just as I said even twice. For it does no harm to say twice that which is beautiful." Lucian in *The Dipsads*, quoting the same Plato, says: "For indeed, twice for the beautiful thing," meaning: there is no satiety in honorable things. Entirely such is the power inherent in excellent things,

# SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
g 4

The more often and the more closely they are inspected, the more and more they please, as Horace says:
> Which, if you stand closer,
> Will please you more, even if repeated ten times.
<note>original: "Quæ si propius stes, / Te magis, ac decies repetita placebit." From Horace's Ars Poetica.</note>

Things that are artificial or common sometimes delight at first by their very novelty, but soon become distasteful. In the same way, Pliny in Book 15, Chapter 14, mentions a type of wild fruit which they call the "strawberry tree" <note>Latin: unedo</note>, because only one can be eaten. It is a fruit of no honor, as he says, and hence the reason for its name <note>The name 'unedo' was traditionally derived from 'unum edo'—I eat one—implying it is so unpleasant you won't want a second.</note>.

### The anger of brothers is the most bitter.
### 50

Whenever a grudge arises between brothers, it is usually more atrocious than the common hatred of enemies. History provides many examples: Cain and Abel; Romulus and Remus; Jacob and Esau <note>implied by context</note>; and the hatred of the Emperor Antoninus Severus’s son toward Geta, which was so cruel and persistent that it could not be satisfied even by Geta's most atrocious death, but extended to all his friends. Regarding this matter, a proverb is cited and recorded by Aristotle in Book 7 of the *Politics*: <term>παρ' οἷς γὰρ διὰ τὴν δυσχέρειαν ὑπολαμβάνουσιν, πῶς τὸ βλάβος, καὶ ταύτης ἀπορρεῖν νομίζουσιν. ὅλιγῳ χαλεποὶ γὰρ πόλεμοι ἀδελφῶν. καὶ οἱ τὸ πέρα σόρξαντες οὐδὲ τὴ πόρα μισοῦν.</term> <note>original Greek translated below</note> That is, he says, those to whom they believe a benefit is owed, by those same people they think they are not only cheated of a benefit, but actually harmed. Whence the proverb says: "For the wars of brothers are harsh." And those who love beyond measure, likewise hate beyond measure. Thus far Aristotle.
Euripides wrote in *Iphigenia at Aulis*:
<term>αγνήτοισι γίγνεσθ' λόος ὅταν ποτ' ἐμπέσωσιν εἰς ἔριν.</term> <note>original Greek translated below</note> That is:
What words they use to wrangle with each other,
When brothers fight with mutual blows,
Whenever a lawsuit or contention arises.

### He will carry the bull, who carried the calf.
### 51

This proverb seems to have been born in the brothel, but it can be conveniently turned to a more modest use if we ever wish to signify that an adult will commit greater sins who, as a boy, became accustomed to smaller vices. It appears in the fragments of Petronius Arbiter in these words: "I was stunned, and I affirmed that a most modest boy was not sufficient for such impudence, nor a girl of her age able to accept the law of womanly endurance. Therefore, said Quartilla, I was smaller when I first endured a man: may I have my Juno angry at me if I ever remember being a virgin. For as an infant I was defiled with my peers, and as the years went on, I applied myself to older boys, until I reached this age." From this also arose that proverb, that he is said to be able to carry the bull who carried the calf. It seems absurd to refer the proverb to the feat of Milo of Croton, who, being accustomed to carrying a calf every day for several furlongs, carried the same animal when it had become a bull without any trouble. And so it will fit those who gradually become accustomed even to the greatest things.

### One ought to remember the living.
### 52

One ought to remember the living. An old proverb against those who talk a great deal about the deceased, which the common people think is ominous—to have the dead in one's mouth and to bring them forward as if summoned. Whence also Marcus Varro, in Book 3 of *On the Latin Language*, thinks that "death" <note>Latin: lethum</note> is named <term>ἀπὸ τῆς λήθης</term> <note>from 'lethe' or forgetfulness</note>, as if it were fitting for one who has departed life to go into oblivion. And at a funeral, the herald used to say: "That one has been given over to death." The proverb is cited by Cicero in Book 5 of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*. There, when Piso and then Quintus Cicero said they were vehemently moved by the memory of famous men from the contemplation of the places where they once lived, and each had withdrawn into memories that delighted them most, then Pomponius Atticus said, as if joking: "But I, whom you are accustomed to attack for following Epicurus, spend much time with Phaedrus, whom I love uniquely, in the gardens of Epicurus which we just passed; but, reminded of the old proverb, I remember the living. Yet I cannot forget Epicurus, even if I wished, whose image our associates have not only in pictures, but even on cups and rings." Thus far Cicero.
It is likewise read in the *Truculentus* <note>A play by Plautus</note>: "While he lives, you should know the man; when he is dead, let him rest."
Because the common people do not even remember the benefits of friends, the saying of Thales is rightly celebrated: "One ought to be no less mindful of absent friends than of those present."

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->To wrestle with ghosts. 53<-

"To wrestle with ghosts" <note>original Latin: *Cum laruis luctari*</note> is a saying applied to those who pursue the deceased with insults; nothing could be more unworthy of an honorable man. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> cites Aristophanes, who wrote:
"Stop, stop, O hundred-headed Hermes, for you were insulting Cleon when he was already a corpse." <note>original Greek: Παῦε παῦε ὦ ἑκατοβ’ ἑρμῆ...</note>
Lucian says in *The Sects*: "They fight a shadow-battle against you who are absent." <note>original Greek: Σκιαμαχῶσι πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἀπόντας</note> This refers to both the dead and the absent. Pliny mentions this in the preface of his *Natural History* in this manner: "Nor did Plancus lack wit when Asinius Pollio was said to be preparing orations against him, to be published by himself or his children after Plancus's death; Plancus remarked: 'Only ghosts wrestle with the dead.'" By this saying, he struck back at them so effectively that among the learned, nothing seemed more shameless than Pollio's plan. Aristotle, in his *Rhetoric*, cites Plato’s *Republic*, writing that those who bark at the dead are like little dogs who bite the stones thrown at them but do not touch the person who threw them.

->To cut the throats of the dead. 54<-

Similar to the above is "to cut the throats of the dead" <note>original Latin: *Iugulare mortuos*</note>, meaning to attack the deceased and fight with those who are already extinguished. The metaphor is taken from war, where it is cowardly and ridiculous to cut the throat of one already prostrate and killed; it is brave, rather, to clash with the living. Diogenes Laertius relates this in his life of Menedemus. He says that when Bion was zealously attacking divine matters, he was "cutting the throats of the dead"—meaning things already exploded and rejected by everyone's judgment. Aristophanes wrote in *The Birds*: "You are killing the dead." <note>original Greek: σὺ τεθνηκότας ἀποκτείνεις</note> The metaphor becomes more elegant if twisted a bit further: as if one were to say a man "cuts the throats of the dead" who attacks a book condemned by everyone, or disputes against an opinion long ago rejected by universal vote, or censures a thing already detested by all.

->The swan song. 55<-

"The swan song." <note>original Greek: Κύκνειον ᾆσμα; Latin: *Cygnea cantilena*</note> This is recorded among the Greek proverbs. It was also noted by Aelian in his work *On the Nature of Animals* as a proverb. It is suited to those who discourse eloquently at the very end of their lives, or who write with a sweeter voice in extreme old age. This often happens to writers: their final works are the least bitter and the most honeyed, as their eloquence matures with age. Furthermore, that swans produce certain wonderful songs when death is imminent is a fact as celebrated in all literature as it is unproven and uncredited by anyone. For Lucian denies that he ever saw singing swans even when sailing on the river Po. Aelian adds that swans do not sing unless the West Wind is blowing (which the Latins call *Favonius*). Martial wrote:
"With a failing tongue he modulates sweet songs,
The swan, the singer of his own funeral."
Nor are philosophers lacking who attempt to provide a cause for this, affirming it happens because the breath struggles to break out through a long and narrow neck. Saint Jerome, praising the eloquence of old age in a certain passage, mentions several writers and says: "All these, I know not how, sang something swan-like as death approached." The same Jerome, in his epitaph for Nepotian, asks: "Where is our *human-speaker* <note>original Greek: βροτόλαλος; a term for someone with a charming, human voice</note>, whose voice was sweeter than a swan's song?" We also used this in a certain Epigram, which we once composed extemporaneously for that never-sufficiently-praised patron of all studies, William, Archbishop of Canterbury:
> You shall see bright poets arise,
> Pouring a swan-like melody to the high stars,
> Which even the age of posterity shall hear.

Athenaeus mentions the adage in the fourteenth book of the *Deipnosophists*, citing the author Chrysippus: he tells of a certain man so immensely delighted by jokes that when he was about to be executed by the hangman, he said he wished to die only after singing his "swan song"—meaning, I suppose, some witty saying which, as soon as he had uttered it, he would not delay in dying. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the preface to his third book *On the Orator*, speaks of Lucius Crassus: "That divine voice and speech of the man was like a swan song; we came into the Senate after his death as if expecting to hear it, gazing at the very spot where he had last stood."

->Nestorean eloquence. 56<-

In a very similar way, the eloquence of Nestor, the leader of the Pylians, passed into a proverb, whenever an old man's...
<margin>the eloquence of an old man</margin>

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY

we signify the sweet-speaking nature of old age. For Homer attributes to this man <note>Nestor, the wise elder of the Greeks</note> not only a life spanning three generations, but also a certain eloquence sweeter than honey. For he says in the *Iliad*, Book 1:

<margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin>
> The sweet-worded Pylian orator rose up, 
> from whose tongue the voice flowed sweeter than honey. <note>original Greek: Ηδυεπὴς ἀνόρουσε...; Latin: Exorthus est Pylius...</note>

Imitating this passage, Theocritus—according to Plutarch—wrote in his *Bucolics*:
> And the Muse poured sweet nectar over his mouth. <note>original Greek: Καὶ οἱ γλυκὺ μοῦσα...; Latin: Praeterea quod in os...</note>

That line from Horace also looks toward this idea:
> For if you alone [think you] distill poetic honey. <note>original Latin: Si enim manare poetica mella Te solum.</note>

-> Attic Wit. Attic Eloquence. 57 <-

Among the other peoples of Greece, a certain wit and a kind of native, peculiar elegance belongs to the Athenians <note>the inhabitants of Attica</note>, so much so that it has even passed into a proverb: *Attic wit* or *Attic eloquence*, used to describe the highest excellence. Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "Didn't I say there was Attic eloquence in this?" when he was mocking a tasteless and uncharming soldier. Saint Jerome, writing to Pammachius and mocking Jovinian (as I believe), says: "This is Plautine eloquence; this is Attic wit, comparable even to the speech of the Muses, as they say." Although that remark about the "speech of the Muses" refers to Marcus Varro’s famous eulogy of the playwright Plautus, in which he said that if the Muses themselves wanted to speak Latin, they would have spoken with the voice of Plautus. Lucian also alluded to this in his booklet *On Salaried Posts*: "And if they hear someone speaking ungrammatically, they want it to seem purely Attic and as if it came from Mount Hymettus." <note>original Greek: κἂν ἔτι σολοικίσαντος...</note> Now, Hymettus is a mountain in Attica famous for its beekeeping; hence the terms "Attic honey" and "Hymettian honey." Martial also testifies that these were the finest in his *Xenia*:
> If the bee, the plunderer of Theseus’s Hymettus, 
> sent you this noble nectar from the woods of Pallas Athena.

-> The matter proceeds in the manner of Mandrabulus. 58 <-

<margin>The matter goes like Mandrabulus. <note>original Greek: Μανδραβούλου χωρεῖ τὸ πρᾶγμα.</note></margin>
The matter proceeds in the order of Mandrabulus; that is, it slips daily into a worse state. The proverb arose because a certain Mandrabulus, having found a treasure, dedicated a golden sheep to Juno of Samos in the first year, a silver one the next year, and a bronze one in the third. Lucian, in *On Salaried Posts*, says: "But you rejoice anyway, and you deceive yourself, always hoping that future things will be better. But the opposite of what you hoped happens, and as the proverb says, the matter proceeds according to Mandrabulus—diminishing, so to speak, every single day and moving backward." <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ χαίρεις γε...</note> Alciphron says in a certain letter: "And according to the proverb, things proceed according to Mandrabulus." <note>original Greek: Καὶ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν...</note> It is therefore used quite elegantly against those who decline for the worse. Just as Menedemus says in Plutarch: many people come to Athens for the sake of study; at the start they turn out to be wise men, then philosophers, later rhetoricians, and finally common ignoramuses. Nor would it be out of place to add here that noble sentiment of Plato from the first book of *Laws*: "For a man to conquer himself is the first and best of all victories. But to be defeated by oneself is the most shameful and worst of all things." <note>original Greek: Τὸ νικᾶν αὐτὸν αὑτὸν...</note> For he conquers himself who becomes better instead of good; but to turn out inferior to oneself is to be rendered worse.

-> Become an old man early. 59 <-

Become an old man early, if you wish to be an old man for a long time. This is a Latin proverb by which we are warned that, before old age, we should cease from youthful labors and begin to take care of our health, if we wish to have a vigorous and long-lasting old age. For the lot of old age is leisure and rest. It was used by Cato the Elder in Cicero’s writings: "For," he says, "I have never agreed with that old and praised proverb which warns one to become an old man early if you wish to be an old man long." Although this was not approved by Cato—a harsh man who would not grant himself a release from labor even in extreme old age—it should nevertheless be heard by us, especially if you apply it to the vices of youth, such as lust...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

excess, drunkenness, and a turbulent life: unless a person leaves these behind in good time, they will either never reach old age, or they will have a very short one.

->60. A teacher of the elderly<-

Γεροντοδιδάσκαλος <note>original: *Gerontodidaskalos*</note>, that is, a teacher of the elderly. This title is cited quite often by Nonius Marcellus among the titles of Varro’s plays; there is no doubt that it is proverbial, as are most of the others. It applies to someone who spends effort in vain on a matter that is late and ill-timed. For just as youth is teachable and follows any shape you give it, so old age is intractable, slow, and forgetful. Hence Theognis says:
> Do not teach me; I am at such an age that I am past learning. <note>original Greek: Μή με δίδασκ’, ἐπὶ τηλίκῳ εἰμὶ μαθεῖν.</note>
Euripides in the *Bacchae*:
> I, an old man, shall lead you, another old man, like a tutor. <note>original Greek: Γέρων γέροντα παιδαγωγήσω σ’ ἐγώ.</note>

And indeed, this verse is found in Sophocles’ *Philoctetes*, which Aulus Gellius testifies was famous and proverbial in the thirteenth book of his *Attic Nights*. Varro seems to have taken his title from Plato’s *Euthydemus*, where Socrates relates that his teacher Connus—from whom he learned to play the lyre as an old man—was called a "teacher of the elderly" by the boys as a joke. To this sentiment belongs what they say Diogenes once said: "To heal a corpse and to admonish an old man are the same thing." <note>original Greek: Νεκρὸν ἰατρεύειν, καὶ γέροντα νουθετεῖν, ταὐτόν ἐστι.</note> However, this is a useless sentiment if it discourages the elderly from learning those things which it is shameful not to know.

->61. To change an old man’s tongue<-

While old age is slower for every kind of instruction, it is especially so for learning a language, a faculty given by nature primarily to children. For this reason, it is common knowledge that children easily express themselves in any language; conversely, those older in years either do not achieve it or imitate it with little success. Hence the proverb, *to change an old man’s tongue*, used for those laboring in vain and out of season. Saint Jerome, in his preface to the four Gospels, says: "It is a pious labor, but a dangerous presumption, to judge others when one is to be judged by all—to change an old man’s tongue and to pull a graying world back to the beginnings of toddlers." By this, he means that the adult age is less manageable for all things than those raw and tender years. This was said with an elegant metaphor by Ovid <note>original: "Naso"</note>:
> The tree which provides broad shade for those walking,
> Was a mere twig at the time it was first planted.
> Then it could be plucked from the top of the earth by hands,
> Now it stands, increased in its own strength to an immense size.
Therefore, character should be formed while the age is still soft; one should become accustomed to the best things when the mind is like wax for anything. For after the mind has, as it were, hardened with the years, we can hardly unlearn what we learned wrongly, and what we do not know is hammered into us only with the greatest difficulty. I do not say this to deter the older ones from learning—since no age is too late to learn—but to sharpen the zeal of children for study. Nor should this be overlooked, though it is a common saying: *An old parrot ignores the rod.* Although the meaning of the adage is not obscure in itself, it will be clearer from the words of Apuleius in the second book of his *Florida* concerning the parrot: "When it is forced to emulate our rustic speech, its head is tapped with an iron key so that it may feel the master’s command. This is the 'rod' for the learner. But it learns immediately as a chick up to two years of age, while the mouth is easily shaped and the tongue is tender enough to be turned. But a parrot caught when old is both unteachable and forgetful." Thus far Apuleius. Pliny also indicates in Book 10, Chapter 42, that this bird has a wonderful teachability, but only in the first two years of life. Close to these is the common, though hardly elegant, saying: *It is too late to train old dogs to the leash.*

->62. An old man marries an old woman<-

Not far from this is what Varro reports in the third book of *On the Latin Language*: *An old man marries an old woman* <note>original: "Cascus cascam ducit"</note>, used whenever like delights in like: an old man with an old woman, a deformed person with a deformed one, a barbarian with a barbarian, a wicked man with a wicked one. For in ancient times, *cascus* was the word for what we call *vetus* (old); and this, as the same Varro is author, comes from the language of the Sabines, which pushed its roots into the Oscan language, in which an old man is called *Casnar*. Therefore Ennius, as one skilled in the Oscan tongue, wrote: "Which the ancient [*Casci*] Latin peoples first fathered."
