# THE SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> calls the ancient Latins "the early ones" in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations*. Thus, one thing was ingrained in those ancients, whom Ennius calls *casci* <note>An archaic Latin word for "old" or "ancient."</note>. Moreover, Varro cites a proverb originating from a certain Manilius, who said it was no wonder if a "cascus" (old man) had married a "casca" (old woman), because he was making a "harmonious" wedding. This appears to be a joke about an old woman married to an old man, playing on the word *cascus* as if it were derived from *canendo* (singing). In the same place, an epigram by a certain Pavius is cited, which he wrote against a youth named Casca:
> There is nothing [old] about you when your Casca calls you Casca.

Why should it seem absurd for a youth to have married an old woman, except when the *casca* (that is, the old woman) calls that young man "Casca" as if by his own name? Perhaps the humor of the proverb refers to a marriage ritual mentioned by Plutarch in his *Roman Questions*: those leading a bride into the groom's house commanded her to speak these words: "Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia."

-> Twice through all. <-
<margin>64</margin>
*Dis dia pason* <note>original Greek: Δὶς διὰ πασῶν</note>, that is, "Twice through all [the notes]." By this proverb, they signified a vast and very long distance between things. <margin>Twice through all</margin> Whence, things that seemed most in conflict with one another and differed in their whole kind were said to differ from one another by a *dia pason* <note>The Greek term for an octave; literally "through all."</note>. Lucian, in his book *How to Write History*, says: "And as the musicians say, this is 'twice through all' in relation to each other." The same author says in his *Apology*: "Consider also that there is a very great difference in their ways of life; as if someone who was a poor hireling in a house—one who even had to endure his book being treated lightly—were to pass into public life, managing common affairs and doing good to the best of his power, and receiving a salary from the Emperor. Come, weigh these things, and contemplate each by itself. You will surely find, according to that musical proverb, that there is a 'twice through all' <note>A double octave</note> difference between them. These two ways of life agree with each other only as much as silver with lead, bronze with gold, an anemone with a rose, or a monkey with a man. For while pay is received in both cases, and in both you may see one person serving another, the dissonance of the business itself is not small." Thus far Lucian. As he indicated, this is borrowed from the art of music. For Macrobius, in his second commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*, mentions five types of harmonies: the fourth (*dia tessaron*), the fifth (*dia pente*), the octave (*dia pason*), the octave-plus-fifth, and the double octave (*dis dia pason*). From the composite harmonies of the fourth and fifth, the octave is formed, which was given this name because it yields a full symphony. It seems to me that the proverb "All is eight," which we shall mention elsewhere, also refers to this. Similarly, Plutarch and whoever else wrote on the discipline of music among the Greeks or Latins, set the goal of harmonies at that which is called the double octave. Boethius also, in the first book of *On Music*, relates that in ancient times the harmonic system consisted only of a heptachord—that is, seven strings—of which the lowest was called the *hypate* and the highest the *nete*. Then, as others added more strings, the number of voices grew until it reached a doubled heptachord. There the limit of progress seemed to be, except that the very logic of symphonies seemed to lack the *mese* (middle) string, which in the heptachord had held a place consistent with its name; when related to either extreme string, it produced the harmony of a fourth. Therefore, when this was added and put in its proper place, they arrived at fifteen strings, of which they called one extreme the *proslambanomene* <note>The lowest note added to the scale</note> and the other the *nete hyperbolaeon* <note>The highest note</note>. Thus it happens that the *mese* yields the "twice through all" harmony in both directions; again, either of the extremes related to the *mese* constitutes the same harmony. Furthermore, the highest related to the lowest yields the symphony they call "twice through all," because in the manner I have described, it encompasses twice that harmony named the octave. Since the harmonic system stopped at this limit, and it was not permitted to go further, it was drawn into popular speech so that things separated by the longest distance were said to be a "twice through all" apart, just as if you were to say...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Very similar to that is the phrase *across the diameter* <note>original: "ἐκ διαμέτρου" (ek diametrou); a geometric metaphor for total opposition</note>. But since, as if acting without foresight and having almost forgotten our purpose, we have entered into the subject of music a little more deeply than the plan of the work required, I would like to add in passing something that I certainly think is neither commonly known nor unpleasant to learn. 

For while I was smearing these notes into my commentaries, by a stroke of luck there arrived **Ambrose Leo of Nola** <note>A physician and scholar from Nola (c. 1443–1525) known for his work on medicine and mathematics</note>, an outstanding philosopher of this age, endowed with an incredible diligence and skill in investigating the mysteries of the disciplines; nor is he moderately practiced in unrolling and examining the writers of both languages <note>Latin and Greek</note>. Therefore, after he had come upon us while we were writing, and after I had read out what I had already written, I said: "I fear, Ambrose, that the common crowd of musicians might cause trouble for this adage of ours, *twice through all* <note>original: "Δὶς διὰ πασῶν" (Dis dia pasōn); the Greek term for a double octave</note>, and might protest, claiming that *twice through all* differs entirely from my opinion. For they do not hesitate to extend the limit of harmonies even to the twentieth degree of the voice. Therefore, you, who are an author of 'Problems' and not only most knowledgeable in music but also most skilled, I wish you would explain this to me in a few words, if it is not a bother: for what reason did antiquity think it so unworthy to progress even a tiny bit beyond the fifteenth string <note>The two-octave range of the Ancient Greek 'Greater Perfect System'</note>, so that the matter was even tossed about as a proverb? Or how has it happened that these moderns <term>neoterici</term> <note>Modern scholars or musicians of the Renaissance period</note> do not fear to extend the boundaries of symphonies by such a space, overstepping the marks of the ancients and, as the saying goes, *leaping beyond the dug-up lines* <note>original: "ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα πηδῶντες" (hyper ta eskammena pēdōntes); a proverb for exceeding limits, originally from athletics</note>, not fearing to proceed even to the twentieth string?"

To this he replied with a friendly smile: "Truly, you are a man more than sufficiently diligent, since you are even anxious about what the *rabble* <note>original: "συρφετὸς" (syrphetos); a derogatory term for a messy heap or a vulgar crowd</note> of singers might think of your Adages. Although, to repel the slanders of musicians, that one shield was enough: that you are reporting an ancient adage. It was certainly fitting that it should square with the reasoning of the ancient musicians from whom it was derived. Nevertheless, so that I may satisfy you more than them, hear in a few words what I have either observed or feel on this matter. 

First, as to what moved the more recent musicians to overstep the limits of antiquity, let them see to it themselves. But for my part, I see a double reason why antiquity thought one should stop at the *double octave*. First, because nature itself seems to have set this as a goal-post for symphonies, since she granted this measure to the human voice, so that it stretches only to the fifteenth degree. If anyone tries to go beyond that, it is no longer a natural voice, but a forced and artificial one, appearing more like a *yelp* <note>original: "gannitus"; a sharp, barking or whimpering sound</note> than a voice. Conversely, if you strive to depress it lower, it immediately degenerates from the character of a voice into a sort of growl. Therefore, since it is everywhere fitting for art to respond to nature as far as possible, it seems to me not without reason that the ancients circumscribed the theory of art with the same barriers with which nature had circumscribed the human voice. 

This cause, I think, was enough to persuade. However, the other is more pressing. It is of this sort: You know it is written in **Boethius**, in the fourth book *On Music*, that musical harmony ought to be weighed not by reason alone, but also by sense. For this reason **Ptolemy**, in the book I mentioned, rejects the opinion of certain **Pythagoreans** who, in judging harmonies, gave the most to reason and the least to sense, saying that sense, like a woman, provides only certain beginnings of knowledge, but that perfect science consists in reason. Again, he refutes the opinion of **Aristoxenus**, who gave more than enough to the senses but very little to reason; whereas musical harmony ought to be so tempered that reason does not conflict with sense, nor sense cry out against reason. Nor did **Aristotle** disagree with Ptolemy in the second book of the *Physics*, denying that music is purely mathematical, but consists partly of reason and partly of senses. 

This can by no means happen if one proceeds beyond the fifteenth tension, that is, the *double octave*. Reason, however, forbids nothing from progressing even to the thousandth tone, with the same harmonies which the *octave* <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν" (dia pasōn)</note> embraces recurring repeatedly. Nor is it permitted to proceed here otherwise than happens in the numbers of arithmetic, where the *one-and-a-half ratio* <note>original: "ἡμιόλιον" (hēmiolion); the sesquialter ratio (3:2), which produces a musical fifth</note> is recognized no differently in twelve thousand and eight thousand than in four and six. But the sense of harmony vanishes, as it were, beyond the fifteenth voice, and now it does not matter much what the ratio of the harmony is, which the sense does not approve—and it does not approve it because it does not perceive it clearly. Furthermore, the cause of its failing to perceive it is an interval longer than is right. The power of reason extends itself into the infinite; but on the other hand, the sense of the body is confined within very narrow limits. For what happens in the sense of the eyes—that if those things toward which the power of seeing is directed are removed further than is right, the sight is blunted and fails, and fails more the greater the interval by which they are distant—that happens much more to the sense of the ears, which is certainly less agile than that of the eyes. Now indeed, because...

Leo explains that this limit is based on the natural range of the human voice and the physical limitations of human hearing, which cannot perceive harmonic ratios clearly beyond that point.</summary>

# CHILIADES, FIRST THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY
<sig>h</sig>

...just as the senses fail in perceiving those things placed before them, the same occurs to the mind through the sense of hearing. If you bring one color closer to another—or as the Greeks say, <term>parà tēn porphýran</term> <note>original: "παρὰ τὴν πορφύραν" - literally "beside the purple," a Greek idiom for comparing things by placing them side by side</note>—does not the sense immediately discern through comparison how much one differs from the other, or how much they agree? Likewise, if you place one voice near another to the ears, they judge without hesitation what the agreement or discord of one is with the other. But if they are separated by an interval greater than is right, the judgment soon begins to be uncertain. Furthermore, just as the sense of the ears is dulled more quickly than that of the eyes, so too is the judgment of the former blunted more quickly than the latter, because one thing depends upon the other. 

There is no reason why I should confirm this with more rules of art, since experience itself can immediately provide proof to anyone. Strike any string on an instrument: at the same time touch the one that is an octave <note>original: "octaua"</note> from it; immediately the sense, acting as a messenger to reason, will fully perceive the harmony and judge it to be most perfect by its own calculation. Again, having struck one, move another which is a fifteenth <note>two octaves</note> from it; the sense will both perceive and approve the symphony, recognizing that which it had just before in the <term>dià pasōn</term> <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν" - the Greek term for an octave</note>. 

But truly, if having touched the lowest, you move the nineteenth from it, although reason does not protest that it is a harmony—being a <term>dià pasōn</term> combined with a <term>dià pénte</term> <note>original: "διὰ πέντε" - a perfect fifth</note>—the ear, having received the sounds, does not perceive the logic of the harmony in the same way. Unless the sense had certain limits within which its judgment was certain and tested, nothing would forbid you, if you liked, from proceeding with a symphony even unto a <term>chiliákis dià pasōn</term> <note>original: "χιλιάκις διὰ πασῶν" - a thousand-fold octave</note>. For reason accepts whatever is encountered in number, provided it recognizes the same analogy. 

But nature has prescribed certain limits to the senses, beyond which, if they progress, they gradually begin to grow dim and hallucinate, as it were; they no longer judge certainly as they are accustomed, but as if through a mist, or as they say, through a dream. It was not fitting, however, that something whose judgment was uncertain should be drawn into the precepts of art. And since they understood that the judgment of the ears vanishes beyond the fifteenth degree of the voice, they decreed that the boundary of harmonies must be fixed there, lest anyone might deservedly cast your proverb in your teeth: <term>aphanès mousikēs oudèn óphelos</term> <note>original: "ἀφανὲς μουσικῆς οὐδὲν ὄφελος"</note>. **There is no use in hidden music.** 

Now therefore, the moderns, who against the authority of the ancients added the <term>hyperbolēn</term> <note>the highest note/string in the Greek system</note> beyond the highest string, and likewise added one to the lowest, would not have acted improperly if they had terminated the progress of harmonies at the nineteenth string; because this lowest string, when related to the highest, presents a perfect symphony—if not to the ears, certainly to reason. But in the twentieth, there is neither a sense of harmony, nor a harmony to be perceived. Thus there is no reason, Erasmus, for you to fear any reproach toward your proverb. Since these things seemed to me to be said both elegantly and quite probably by my friend Ambrosius <note>likely Ambrosius Leo of Nola, a friend of Erasmus</note>, and not at all foreign to the nature of a proverb, I wished to add them to these lucubrations of mine as a supplement, by no means unwelcome, I think, to a reader who is not altogether fastidious.

### Where there is fear, there is also shame. LXIIII

<margin><term>Aidōs, ēdè déos</term></margin>
<term>Aidōs, ēdè déos</term> <note>original: "Αἰδώς, ἠδὲ δέος"</note>, that is, **Where there is fear, there is also shame.** A proverbial sentiment which remains common today, similar to that line of Terence: *We are all made worse by license.* And the greater part of men refrains from evil deeds through fear of the cudgel. Plato in the fifth book *Of Laws*: <term>where you plant shame...</term> <note>original: "ποῦ αἰσχυντίαν φύτευσον"</note>. That is, "Boldness truly gives birth to impudence." But he calls it <term>áphobon</term> <note>fearless</note> when fear is absent. Likewise in the *Euthyphro* he quotes from some poet. For it is a hemistich <note>half-line</note> of heroic verse:
<term>Hína gàr déos, éntha kaì aidōs</term> <note>original: "Ἵνα γὰρ δέος, ἔνθα καὶ αἰδώς"</note>. That is,
**Where fear is, there also is shame.** Suidas indicates this is by Epicharmus.

### Out of doors, Carians, the Anthesteria is over. LXV

<margin><term>Thýraze kâres, ouk ét’ anthestēria</term></margin>
<term>Thýraze kâres, ouk ét’ anthestēria</term> <note>original: "Θύραζε κᾶρες, οὐκ ἔτ’ ἀνθεστήρια"</note>. That is,
**Get out, Carians, for the Anthesteria is finished.**
This is used when someone hopes for the same advantages forever, or thinks the same thing will always be permitted which was allowed once for a specific time. For example, if someone having once experienced the liberality of another, repeatedly returns seeking a gift; or when children, having been granted the opportunity for holiday and play for a time, prolong it beyond the limit. The origin of the proverb is explained in this way: The Athenians had a month called Anthesterion, because it produced many flowers. In this month certain feasts were held, and freer banquets, just as was customary during the Saturnalia among the Romans, in which even slaves were permitted to recline at table, being temporarily freed from labor. But when the holidays were finished, and they were called back to their usual labors...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

In this way, masters used to say yesterday: "Out with the Carians, the Anthesteria is over." <note>original: "Foras Cares, non iam amplius anthiſteria."</note> They called slaves "Carians" because that nation used to make a living through mercenary labor, acting as the slaves of whoever hired them. Some say the Carians once held part of the Attic region, and when the Athenians celebrated the solemnity of the Anthesteria <note>A three-day flower festival in Athens honoring Dionysus, where slaves were briefly allowed to join the festivities.</note>, they were accustomed to receiving the Carians into the city and their homes to share in the feast. Afterward, once the time of the solemnity had passed, if they found any Carians lingering in the city, they would say in jest:
*Out the door, Carians, the Anthesteria is no more.* <note>original Greek: θύραζε κᾶρες, οὐκ ἔτ’ ἀνθιστήρια.</note>
That is: "Go out, Carians, for the Anthesteria is finished."
The Greek word sounds much like what you would call the *Floralia* in Latin, the license of which is well known in the writings of many. This is not unlike what Seneca says in his playful work on Claudius: "It will not always be the Saturnalia." <note>The Saturnalia was a Roman festival where social norms were overturned and slaves were treated as equals for a day.</note> For during the Saturnalia, slaves also enjoyed freedom.

-> 66. Thieves [fear] the shouting. <-

*The thieves [fear] the cry.* <note>original Greek: οἱ φῶρες τὸν βοήν.</note> That is: "Thieves [fear] the shouting." One must understand the verb "fear" or "noticed." This will apply to those who, being conscious of their guilt, fear they will be caught, or who flee in terror after committing a crime. This is a quality of every guilty conscience, but especially of theft: it makes a man trembling and a "shunner of the light." Hence it is found among the sayings of the Hebrews: *The wicked flee though no one pursues.* <note>A reference to Proverbs 28:1.</note> Virgil alluded to this:
> And when I shouted, "Where is that fellow rushing off to?"
> "Tityrus, gather the flock!"—you were hiding behind the sedge-bushes.

-> 67. They flee the scarlet cord. <-

*They flee the cord smeared with red earth.* <note>original Greek: τὸ σχοινίον φεύγουσι τὸ μεμιλτωμένον.</note> That is:
"They avoid the rope smeared with red ochre."
This is aptly said when someone hastens to perform his duty, not from the heart, but lest he fall into a fine. The verse is taken from Aristophanes; his commentator and likewise Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> record something of this sort. The Athenian magistrates tried various ways to ensure the people came to the assembly in as great a crowd as possible. They blocked the other streets that did not lead to the forum with barriers; then they removed goods from the market so that no one would linger there for that reason. Finally, they prepared a rope smeared with a red color, which the Greeks call *miltos*—which Pliny interprets as *minium* <note>Cinnabar or red lead.</note> in Latin, and some call cinnabar. Two public servants, encircling the people with this rope, drove them toward the assembly. Everyone strove to escape the cord, because whoever appeared marked by the color from contact with the rope was forced to pay a fine. Hence, we may elegantly say of those who fear a mark of disgrace that they "flee the scarlet cord."

-> 68. More fortunate than Carcinus’s Strobilus. <-

*More fortunate than Carcinus’s Strobilus.* <note>original Greek: Εὐδαιμονέστερος καρκινοῦ στροβίλου.</note> A proverbial irony used against the unlucky and the wicked. Carcinus was a certain poet whose sons were called "Strobili" by Aristophanes; he also calls them *glykypikylous*, that is, "sweet-necks." The point is taken from a play on names. For in Greek, *Carcinus* means a crab, and *Strobili* means snails (or spinning tops). Both kinds are distorted and foul. The adage is reviewed in Suidas and Zenodotus; it appears in Aristophanes’ *Peace*.

-> 69. If you squander anything on a feast day. <-

Plautus in the *Aulularia*, speaking through the character of the old man Euclio: "If you squander anything on a feast day, you may well go hungry afterward, unless you have been thrifty." A proverbial pattern. It warns us not to be so profuse in ceremonial expenses that we lack the means to bear daily ones. For feast days were celebrated either for offering sacrifices, or for daily banqueting, or for games in honor of the gods, or for observing holidays; working days were granted for the administration of private and public business. It will be applied, not incorrectly, to those who waste their substance while young and will go hungry when old, or who pour out wealth unseasonably and will later regret it.

-> 70. A Tartessian cat. <-

*A Tartessian cat.* <note>original Greek: γαλή ταρτησσία.</note> They used to say this of things that were large and ridiculous. The Tartessians are a people in Iberia <note>Modern-day Spain.</note>, among whom the largest cats are said to be born. Perhaps it is also said, not ineptly, of the rapacious. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
*Just as they watch me, like a cat that stole the meat,*
*While I hold the spits.* That is—

# SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>h 2</sig>

<unclear>...like</unclear> a cat with stolen meat,
<unclear>...carrying</unclear> spits.
Lucian, when he says, <term>ἁρπακτικώτεροι τῶν γαλῶν</term> <note>original: "harpartikōteroi tōn galōn"</note>, that is, "more rapacious than cats," certainly indicates that their greed was a matter of common knowledge.

### To bear the yoke. LXXI

<unclear>Plautus</unclear> in *The Weevil*: "Does she bear the yoke yet?" Someone is asking about a girl, whether she was yet <unclear>mature enough</unclear> to receive a husband. That this is the meaning is sufficiently proven by what follows: "She is as <unclear>innocent</unclear> as if she were my own sister." Horace in his *Odes*, speaking of a girl not yet ripe for a husband:
<unclear>...not yet</unclear> strong enough to bear the yoke with a submissive neck.
<unclear>...indicating</unclear> from where the metaphor is drawn, namely from a young ox which does not yet have the <unclear>strength</unclear> to sustain an equal share of the work in pulling the plow. For the union of two people is an equal <unclear>partnership</unclear>, just as it is in a yoke. From this also comes the word "conjugium" <note>marriage; literally "joining together under a yoke"</note>.

### A saffron robe for a cat. LXXII

<unclear>Γαλῇ</unclear> <term>κροκωτόν</term> <note>original: "Galē krokōton"</note>. That is, "A saffron robe for a cat"—one must understand "you give" or "you add." It was usually said whenever <unclear>something is added</unclear> to the unworthy, or to those whom it does not suit at all. Or when something is given to those who <unclear>do not know</unclear> how to use the gift: as if someone were to give a beautiful book to a man totally estranged from the Muses. The <term>crocota</term> <note>a saffron-colored garment</note> is a type of rounded and fringed garment which wealthy matrons used to wear. In Nonius <unclear>under the word</unclear> "Richa," it is listed among delicate garments along with the saffron robe. For so I think it should be <unclear>read</unclear>: "a soft saffron robe, a richa with sleeves." And according to Plutarch, some used to <unclear>paint</unclear> Hercules <term>Κροκωτόφορον</term> <note>original: "Krokōtophoron" - wearing a saffron robe</note> while serving Omphale. The adage is taken from the fables <unclear>of Aesop</unclear>, which we have related in another place. Furthermore, whether this word <term>γαλῆ</term> <note>galē</note> signifies a cat, or <unclear>a marten</unclear>, or what is commonly called a "catus," since it is a matter of controversy among the learned, <unclear>I leave</unclear> it for others to judge.

### You have a weasel. LXXIII

<unclear>Γαλῆν</unclear> <term>ἔχεις</term> <note>original: "Galēn echeis"</note>, that is, "You have a weasel." It applies to one for whom everything is ill-omened, as if <unclear>the gods</unclear> were angry, as they say. It was once believed that this animal was ill-omened and unlucky for those <unclear>who encountered</unclear> it or kept it in the house; so it does not differ much from those sayings: "He has the horse of Sejanus," or <unclear>"He has</unclear> the gold of Toulouse" <note>both refer to possessions that bring ruin to their owners</unclear>. Hence even now among certain nations, specifically among the <unclear>British</unclear>, it is considered an unlucky omen if, when a hunt is being prepared, someone mentions a weasel, <unclear>since</unclear> an encounter with one is commonly held to be inauspicious. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

### Maximus the Boastful. LXXIIII

<unclear>Χαῦνος</term> <term>μάξιμος</term> <note>original: "Chaunos maximos"</note>, that is, "Maximus the Boastful." It was said against one who claimed more for himself than was proper <unclear>in wisdom</unclear>. It was taken from the character of a certain arrogant Maximus who was immoderately <unclear>pleased with himself</unclear>. In some copies I find <term>κομπᾶς μάξιμος</term> <note>original: "kompas maximos"</note>. To the Greeks, <term>κόμπος</term> <note>kompos</note> signifies arrogance <unclear>and insolence</unclear>, whence <term>κομπάζειν</term> <note>kompazein - to boast</note>. Accordingly, Euripides also uses <term>γλώσσης τε κόμπος</term> <note>original: "glōssēs te kompos"</note>, <unclear>that is</unclear>, "boasting of the tongue." This is also listed in the collections of Diogenianus.

### From much chaff I have gathered little fruit. LXXV

<unclear>Ἐκ πολλῶν</unclear> <term>ἀχύρων ὀλίγον καρπὸν συνήγαγον</term> <note>original: "Ek pollōn achyrōn oligon karpon synēgagon"</note>. That is, "from much chaff I have gathered little fruit." <unclear>That is</unclear>, with much labor I have obtained not much profit: or from a wordy speech <unclear>I have</unclear> perceived very little good sense: from a huge volume I have brought back the smallest amount of learning. <unclear>Taken</unclear> from the threshers of wheat.

### He who has learned should pull the oar. LXXVI

<unclear>Ἐρέσσειν</unclear> <term>μαθόντα</term> <note>original: "Eressein mathonta"</note>. That is, "It behooves him to pull the oar who has learned how." <unclear>It is fitting</unclear> for one to practice that art in which he was previously instructed. It is recorded by Plutarch in the commentary <unclear>whose</unclear> title is, <term>ὅτι διδακτὸν ἡ ἀρετή</term> <note>original: "hoti didakton hē aretē" - That virtue can be taught</note>. The same is advised by that famous passage of Horace in the *Art of Poetry*:
<unclear>He who</unclear> knows not how, abstains from the weapons of the field;
<unclear>He who is unskilled</unclear> in the ball, the quoit, or the hoop, remains still,
<unclear>Lest</unclear> the crowds raised in the stands laugh with impunity.
<unclear>He knows nothing</unclear>, yet he dares to fashion verses. Indeed, even in modern times this <unclear>common</unclear> adage is tossed about: "He who knows not the law of the game, let him stay away."

### To take the thongs from the ox itself. LXXVII

<unclear>Ἐκ τοῦ</unclear> <term>βοὸς τοὺς ἱμάντας λαμβάνειν</term> <note>original: "Ek tou boos tous himantas lambanein"</note>. That is, they are said "to take the thongs from the ox itself" who, in order to <unclear>harm someone</unclear>, take the means from the very person they are hurting. As if someone were to attack with verses the man from <unclear>whom</unclear> he had learned the method of composing poetry: or a tyrant should extort money from the citizens,

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...by which a bodyguard is maintained to oppress the city; or if someone were to attack the art of rhetoric using the tools of rhetoric. This is a metaphor taken from farmers, who cut thongs from the hides of oxen to bind those very oxen. Plutarch, in the commentary titled *That it is not possible to live pleasantly* <note>original: ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι ζῆν ἡδέως</note>, says: "What then would anyone say? For nature itself is sufficient, containing within itself the matter of diseases, and just as in the proverb, taking the thongs from the ox, it takes the pains from the body." That is: What then would anyone say? The very nature of the body is enough, containing the material of diseases within itself, and according to what is usually said in a joke, just as taking thongs from the ox itself, so it takes pains from the body itself.

->**Judge all from one.**<-
->LXXVIII<-

*Judge all things from one* <note>original: Ἐξ ἑνὸς τὰ πάντα ὅρα</note>, that is, *Judge all from one*. Virgil likewise says:
*And from one crime | Learn of them all.*
The adage warns that from the experience of a single event, one ought to make a conjecture about other similar things. It is cited by Suidas. However, he shows it was said against those who wrongly judge all things from any single instance. For he reads not "judge" <note>original: ὅρα</note>, but "he judges" <note>original: ὅρᾳ</note>. As if someone, having found one Frenchman <note>original: Gallum</note> to be treacherous, were to judge that all are such.

->**Love is born from the gaze.**<-
->LXXIX<-

*For from looking, love is born to mortals* <note>original: Ἐκ τοῦ εἰσορᾷν γὰρ γίγνεται ἀνθρώποις ἐρᾷν</note>. That is:
*Love is born from seeing for mortals.*
A proverbial six-foot verse <term>Senarius: a line of verse consisting of six metrical feet</term>, warning that the eyes are the primary reconcilers of love. For that which is unknown is not loved; mutual love is born from living together. And the eyes are especially the enticements to loving. For in them is the peculiar seat of the soul. And in these, the poets say, Cupid keeps watch and hurls his arrows. Maro <note>Virgil</note> indicated the adage, as it were, when he said:
*As I saw, how I perished, how a wicked error swept me away.*
Again in the *Georgics*:
*The woman | burns by being seen.*
Likewise in Terence, Chaerea had only to see the young woman to begin to burn uncontrollably. Juvenal reports as a portent the case of a blind lover:
*Who burned with love for a girl he never saw.*
We read that certain philosophers, and among them Democritus, removed their own eyes, as if they were the authors of all evil desires. Therefore, it is for pious men to remember that it is by no means safe to see what it is not permitted to desire. Diogenianus mentions the proverb.

->**You laugh at me from on high.**<-
->LXXX<-

*You laugh at me from on high* <note>original: Ἀφ’ ὑψηλοῦ με καταγελᾷς</note>. Said of one who laughs at someone with pride and contempt. Translated from those who speak from a high place. Whence also "to look down upon" <note>original: despicere</note> is said by the Latins for "to despise," because whoever is in an elevated place, being as it were safer, neglects him who stands in a lower place.

->**You have your foot out of the mud.**<-
->LXXXI<-

*You have your feet out of the mud* <note>original: Ἐκ τοῦ πηλοῦ πόδας ἔχεις</note>. That is, you have your feet out of the mud; this means you have emerged from danger, or you have been placed outside of danger. Taken from travelers. Similar to that other saying, *outside the reach of the missile* <note>original: ἔξω βέλους</note>. And they say those who are involved in troublesome business from which they cannot extricate themselves are "stuck in the mud."

->**Out of the shade into the sun.**<-
->LXXXII<-

To lead *out of the shade into the sun* is to bring a matter previously hidden and idle into public view and into the common use of life. Translated from athletes, whose custom it is to strengthen the body's vigor by enduring sun and dust. It is the mark of the delicate, however, to lurk in the shade. It becomes more elegant if twisted toward a matter of the mind; as if one were to say that philosophy was brought *out of the shade into the sun* by Socrates. Examples are found everywhere among writers.

->**To keep watch in Naupactus.**<-
->LXXXIII<-

*To keep watch in Naupactus* <note>original: Φρουρῆσαι ἐν ναυπάκτῳ</note>. The Achaeans, having captured Naupactus, killed Pausanias, who had been put in charge of the outposts and the guard, according to Theopompus. Whence the matter seems to have passed into a common joke against those who perish by their own laziness, or who administer a hateful office full of danger. Cited from Zenodotus. Suidas expresses it in this manner: *You will keep watch in Naupactus* <note>original: φρουρήσεις ἐν ναυπάκτῳ</note>. He also brings forward another origin of the adage. Since a very tiny salary was paid to those who protected Naupactus with a garrison, and they had to buy many things pertaining to their needs, it was tossed about as a military joke, as it appears, against those who sweat in vain, and whose hopes frustrate them. Naupactus is a city of Aetolia, which Philip held, named from the "fastening of ships," because the Heraclidae first built a ship there.

# On the Nature of Thought

The faculty of **thought** is not merely a passive reception of images, but an active movement of the soul toward understanding. When we consider the way a concept forms within the mind, we must recognize that it follows a specific order, much like a stream following its carved path.

->The Internal Word<-

As the ancients said, "The word conceived in the heart is the beginning of all action." <note>original: "Verbum in corde conceptum." This refers to the Scholastic idea that thoughts are 'internal words' before they are spoken.</note> This internal process remains hidden from the eyes of men, yet it is fully visible to the Creator. <margin>Thought is the mirror of the spirit.</margin>

We must distinguish between three types of mental activity:
1. **Simple Apprehension**: The basic grasping of an object without judgment.
2. **Judgment**: The affirmation or denial of a relationship between concepts.
3. **Reasoning**: The process of drawing new conclusions from known truths. <gloss>This is the highest labor of the intellect.</gloss>

It is through this third stage that we climb the ladder of knowledge, moving from the visible world to the invisible truths that govern our existence. <insert>Even the unlearned possess this spark of reason by nature.</insert>

<summary>This passage explores the mechanics of human thought, categorizing mental activity into apprehension, judgment, and reasoning as a path toward higher truth.</summary>
<keywords>philosophy of mind, logic, internal word, reasoning, intellect, scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Adages, following the numbering from the previous page. The text focuses on proverbs derived from Homeric epic and Plutarch’s essays.</meta>

->And my weapon also has a sharp point.<-
->LXXXVIII<-

This has the very appearance of a proverb, as written in Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 20, in the persona of Hector: <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ δὲ καὶ ἐμὸν βέλος ὀξὺ πάροιθεν</note> *“For my weapon also is sharp at the point.”* We shall use this correctly whenever we admit that we are indeed inferior, yet not so lacking that we cannot do harm. Similar to this is that line of Virgil: *“And from our wound, too, the blood follows.”* Likewise, that in Ovid: *“I too have strength, and my weapons can wound.”*

->The coward’s color changes.<-
->LXXXIX<-

<note>original Greek: Τῶ κακῶ ὤπεται χρώς</note> That is, *The coward’s color changes.* Plutarch, in his *Natural Questions*, in the problem "Why the octopus changes color," brings this forward as a common proverb: *“Wherefore it is said, the coward’s color changes.”* For it happens in fear that the face turns pale, especially in the timid, as the blood flees back to the vital organs. It gains a bit more charm if applied to the mind: as if you were to say a philosopher fears nothing at all of those things the common crowd dreads, *“For indeed the coward’s color turns.”* Furthermore, the proverb was born from Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 13. The verse goes thus:
*“For the coward’s color changes from one to another,*
*Nor does his spirit allow him to sit still,*
*But he shifts his weight and sits on both feet,*
*And his heart beats loudly within his chest*
*As he foresees his fate, and there is a chattering of teeth.*
*But for the brave man, the color does not change, nor is he greatly <margin>terrified.</margin>”*
That is: The coward’s color turns and varies constantly, nor does his mind remain certain, but wavers here and there; shifting from his heart, he settles on both feet. His heart throbs violently beneath his breast as his mind contemplates death, and his teeth begin to gnash. In contrast, for the brave man, the color does not vary, nor does he greatly shudder.

->Do not approach a council before you are called.<-
->XC<-

<note>original Greek: Μὴ πρότερον εἰς βουλὴν εἰσέλθης, πρὶν ἂν κληθῆς</note> That is, *Do not go to a council before you are summoned.* This sentiment, which is now celebrated under the name of Cato <note>referring to the Distichs of Cato, a popular medieval schoolbook</note>, seems to have been proverbial, even by the testimony of Plutarch, whose words in the first book of *Table Talk* are these: *“It would be a ridiculous and proverb-worthy reproach,”* he said, *“if a counselor came who was not invited.”* Unless one prefers to refer this to that other proverb: *“Unbidden friends go to the feasts of good men,”* which we shall discuss elsewhere.

->Sailing near land is most pleasant, as is walking near the sea.<-
->XCI<-

Plutarch, in the first book of *Table Talk*, cites this as a common saying: <note>original Greek: Πλοῦς μὲν ὁ παρὰ γῆν, περίπατος δὲ ὁ παρὰ θάλατταν ἡδύς</note> That is, *Sailing near the land, and again a walk which is made near the sea, is most pleasant.* It will be correctly twisted toward this meaning: that we say each thing is only truly pleasant if it is applied tempered by an admixture of a different kind. For instance, if you sprinkle a bit of erudition into games, or conversely, mix something playful into your studies. Very similar to this is what the same author cites from the poet Philoxenus in the commentary titled *How the Young Should Listen to Poets*: *“Of meats, those which are not meat are sweetest; likewise of fish, those which are not fish.”* In the same way, philosophy mixed with poetry delights more, and poetry mixed with philosophy captures the mind more effectively.

->The Cupids’ purse is tied with a leek leaf.<-
->XCII<-

<note>original Greek: Πράσου φύλλω τὸ τῶν ἐρώτων δέδεται βαλάντιον</note> That is, *The purse of loves is tied with a leek leaf.* It is mentioned in the same place we just cited, but it is better to record his own words: *“What one might wonder at most is a stingy and penny-pinching man falling into love; just as iron into fire, he is loosened and softened, becoming tender, fluid, and more pleasant. So that the proverbial saying does not seem entirely ridiculous: that the purse of loves is tied with a leek leaf.”* It was also said of the smiling Thrasy... <note>The text cuts off mid-word; likely "Thrasymachus" or "thrasys" (bold/daring).</note>

<meta>This page continues the second century of the first chiliad (thousand) of Erasmus’s Adages. The previous page likely discussed the transformative power of love or specific Greek proverbs regarding character.</meta>

# SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>h 4</sig>

<margin>He eats leeks. For it makes the spirit cheerful and expansive. <note>original: Πράσον ἐσθίει. ποιεῖ γὰρ ὁ θυμὸς ὢ ἱλαρὸς, καὶ διακεχυμένος.</note></margin> That is to say: even if someone is remarkably stingy and sordid, as soon as he falls in love, he becomes softer and more tender, flexible and more pleasant, not unlike something <gloss>than</gloss> placed upon a fire. Thus, that popular joke does not seem entirely ridiculous: that Cupid’s purses are tied with a leek leaf. The reason for this is <gloss>that</gloss> love is very similar to drunkenness. It makes the belly warm and relaxed. Plutarch, therefore, seems to feel that the proverb alludes to the nature of the leek, the power of which is to heat, to provoke urine, to stir up Venus <note>sexual desire</note>, to move the menses, and to loosen the bowels, as Dioscorides teaches in Book II. Suidas shows that this adage was said of those who, out of love, engage in immoderate expenses and indulge in luxury, as those who are in love with hired company are wont to do. Plutarch, in the booklet he titled <term>The Lamp-lit Banquet <note>original: Φωτικὸν; likely referring to a lost or misattributed work on love</note></term>, also mentions this among other praises of Cupid or love: that it renders a man splendid instead of sordid, generous instead of stingy, civil instead of gloomy, and bold instead of timid. Hence, Cupid’s little purses are said to be tied with a leek leaf <gloss>because</gloss> they are easily untied, or because a leek leaf is quite fragile; but the genuine force of this is the power to loosen the body and move it.

### He whom fortune has painted. XCIII
<margin>Fortune writes in black; let all time be unable to whiten it. <note>original: Τύχη μέλανα γράφει, ἔστω κ’ πᾶς χρόνος δυνάτης λουκάναι.</note></margin> That is: him whom fortune has painted black, not even an entire age can make white. This means that for him whom fortune resists, whatever he attempts will turn out unhappily. It is an allusion to the black and white pebbles used in voting <note>black for condemnation, white for acquittal</note>. It is recorded in the Collections of Apostolius.

### He who does not wish to die before his time. XCIIII
Athenaeus, in his *Table Talk*, records a proverb of this kind regarding the Sybarites <note>inhabitants of Sybaris, famous for luxury</note>: <margin>He who does not wish to die among the Sybarites before his fated day must see the sun neither setting nor rising. <note>original: Δεῖ τὸν μὴ συνάφ’ μὴ πρὸ μοίρας ἀποθανεῖν, μήτε δυόμενον, μήτε ἀνίσχοντα τὸν ἥλιον ὁρᾷν δεῖ.</note></margin> He who does not wish to die before his fatal day among the Sybarites, it is not fitting for him to see the sun, neither setting nor rising. He writes that this was commonly tossed about <gloss>because</gloss> the city of the Sybarites was situated in a low place, as if in a valley, so that in the summer time they felt immense cold in the morning and evening alike, but intolerable heat at noon. Cicero, in Book VII of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, teaches that the same was said against certain debauchees, to which people the name was given from their luxurious lifestyle. For they were drunk at sunset and snoring in the morning. Columella, in the preface to his work on husbandry, uses it against gluttons who consume their nights in lust and drunkenness, and their days in sleep or gaming. "Soon after," he says, "so that we may come fit for the cook-shops, we steam out yesterday's indigestion in Spartan baths, and having dried out the sweat we seek a thirst; by night we consume ourselves in lust and drunkenness, by day in gaming or sleep." And we perhaps say <gloss>that</gloss> we see neither the rising nor the setting sun.

### Wise as far as the beard. XCV
<margin>Beard-growers, and sophists by the beard, and philosophers by the beard. <note>original: Πωγωνοτροφοί, καὶ ἀπὸ πώγωνος σοφισταί, καὶ ἀπὸ πώγωνος φιλόσοφοι.</note></margin> That is: wise men, sophists, and philosophers as far as the beard. Thus were they called who had nothing of a philosopher except the beard and the cloak. It is used several times in Plutarch’s *Symposiacs*. Horace alludes to this when he says:
> To nourish a wise beard.

Lucianus likewise repeatedly jokes about the philosophers' <term>deep beard <note>original: τὸν βαθὺν πώγωνα</note></term>. In *The Eunuch*, Bagoas says: "If it were necessary to measure a philosopher by his beard, the goats would carry off the first prize." Similarly, Martial:
> If the beard on your chin delights you, and it is no smaller than yours.

The joke is twisted against those who establish the entire sanctity of life not in the soul, nor in morals, but in outward dress.

### They fought among stones, yet could not lift a stone. XCVI
Plutarch, in the fourth decade of the *Symposiacs*, in the first problem: <margin>For seeing the boy using food along with Philo, but also needing nothing else, "By Hercules," he said, "how true is the saying, that they fought among stones, but it was not possible to pick one up." <note>original: ἰδὼν γὰρ τὸ παιδίον ἅμα τῷ Φίλωνι σίτῳ χρωμένου, ἀλλὰ καὶ μηδενὸς δεόμενον, ὦ ἡράκλες, ἔφη, οἷον ἄρα ἐστὶ τὸ λεγόμενον, οἷς ἐμάχοντο, λίθου δ’ οὐκ ἦν ἀνελέσθαι.</note></margin> That is: when he saw the servant boy using bread along with Philo, and requiring nothing else besides: "Good heavens," he said, "that was truly marvelous which is commonly said, <gloss>that</gloss> they fought among rocks, yet could not lift a rock."
It is a saying against those who do not enjoy a present advantage, either through laziness or through a perverse opinion of things, like those who find it a burden to lift a stone from a heap with which to repel adversities—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

*They perished of thirst, though the water rose above the chin.* <note>original Greek: Δίψῃ δ’ ἐζόλλυτο, ὕδωρ δ’ ὑπερεῖχε γενείου.</note>

->In another world.<-
->XCVII<-

*As if in another world.* <note>original Greek: Ὡς ἐν ἄλλῳ κόσμῳ.</note> This is a proverbial figure of speech which even the common people use today: regarding those who differ far and wide from the customs of others, or to whom everything seems new, or who are situated far from their fatherland. Plutarch says in his *Table Talk*: *But the race of Greeks is entirely foreign and alien to us, as if they were born and living in some other world.* <note>original Greek: Τὸ δὲ τῶν Ἑλλήνων γένος ἔκφυλον ὅλως καὶ ἄποικον ἡμῶν, ὥσπερ ἐν ἄλλῳ τινὶ κόσμῳ γεγονότων καὶ ζώντων.</note> Horace used a similar figure in his *Odes*:
*Why do we change our lands for those warmed by another Sun?*
And Macrobius in the preface to the *Saturnalia*: *Unless perhaps, having been born under another sky, the vein of the Latin tongue will not admit us.* For since the soil is common to all, it must be a figure of speech to be "born under another sky." And regarding the Elysian Fields <note>The mythical dwelling place of the blessed after death.</note> in Virgil:
*They know their own sun and their own stars.*
He said "their own," as if distinct from ours. Likewise Claudian:
*There are other stars for us, there are other worlds, and you shall see a purer light.*
Again, Virgil in the *Eclogues*:
*And the Britons, utterly divided from the whole world.*
Moreover, this usually happens to most mortals: that if ever new guests arrive in a region far removed from their own nest, there is nothing they do not dread, nothing they do not stand amazed at, nothing they do not wonder at, just as if they had been carried off into another world.

->The stored fish.<-
->XCVIII<-

*A stored fish* <note>original Greek: Ἀποκείμενος ἰχθύς.</note> seems to have passed into a proverb against those who save nothing for the future. For in olden times, fish were considered delicacies. It is the mark of a prudent man to always have something set aside from his food with which to welcome a sudden guest, and not to imitate the Homeric Achilles, whom the ambassadors or Priam find in an empty and hungry house. It seems the adage should be expressed thus: *One ought not to always drag the stored fish into the middle.* Plutarch in his *Table Talk*: *But I, laughing, said: "That man, my friend, is the 'stored fish' of the proverb, not to be dragged into the middle along with the Pythagorean quart-measure."* <note>The "Pythagorean choenix" or quart-measure refers to a rule against sitting on one's rations, i.e., not living only for the day.</note> This can be applied to a speech or a story that is not very charming in itself, yet is repeated to the point of boredom. It is suitable for a person who is stingy or anxious about tomorrow.

->It is not for the same man to speak both much and to the point.<-
->XCIX<-

*To speak many things and to speak things seasonable are two different matters.* <note>original Greek: Χωρὶς τό τ’ εἰπεῖν πολλὰ καὶ τὰ καίρια.</note>
This six-foot verse <note>A "senarius," a common meter in ancient drama.</note>, celebrated as a proverb, warns that we must avoid loquacity <note>excessive talking</note>, for it is almost inevitable that anyone who attempts to speak much will slip into error. It also appears in the proverbs of the Hebrews: *In much speaking, sin is not absent.* <note>A reference to Proverbs 10:19.</note>

->The birds of Psaphon.<-
->C<-

*The birds of Psaphon.* <note>original Greek: Ψάφωνος ὄρνιθες.</note> This is used when someone hunts for fame by some new trick, such as when someone bribes people to praise him and dictates, as it were, the eulogies by which he wishes to be celebrated among the common folk. They say there was a certain man in Libya named Psaphon who, desiring a reputation for divinity, caught a great many vocal birds capable of mimicking human speech. He taught them to sound these words: *Psaphon is a great god.* <note>original Greek: Μέγας θεὸς Ψάφων.</note> Having taught them thus, he released them into the mountains. And those birds, having learned the lesson, sang it, and taught the other birds to sound it as well. Furthermore, the Libyans, being ignorant of the trick and believing it happened by divine power, resolved to perform divine rites for Psaphon and enrolled him among the number of the gods. I found this proverb in the collection of Apostolius.

### One ought to be born either a king or a fool.

Annaeus Seneca, a man of most delightful wit—as Tacitus says (which is indeed clear from that playful little book he wrote against Claudius Caesar <note>The *Apocolocyntosis* or "Pumpkinification" of Claudius</note>, for it was recently discovered in Germany and has come to light)—records a proverb of this kind in that same work we just mentioned: *One ought to be born either a king or a fool.* But it is better to set it down in his own words: "I know," he says, "that I have been made a free man since the day he died, who had made the proverb true: that one ought to be born either a king or a fool." Again, in the same book: "He killed in one house Crassus the Great, Scribonia, Bassa, and the Assarii—nobles, nonetheless. But Crassus was so foolish that he was even capable of reigning." In another place, he alludes to the same idea more obscurely in verse:
->He takes up the royal seasons of a stupid life.<-
What Hesiod truly wrote—that it is not entirely for nothing that a saying is celebrated in popular speech—perhaps it would not be out of place to investigate what circumstance gave rise to this proverb: which joins two things so dissimilar, namely a king and a fool, in such a way that it wishes each to seem most like the other. This is especially striking since the particular praise of kings, and the only truly royal quality, is to excel others in wisdom, prudence, and vigilance. It is likely, therefore, that those ancient kings were for the most part endowed with remarkable stupidity, a fact which can be learned partly from the books of the poets and partly from the records of historians. Indeed, Homer makes his Agamemnon—and the Tragedians who imitated him do the same—more ambitious than wise. For what is more foolish than to purchase the title of General at the cost of the most cruel slaughter of one's only daughter? What is more absurd than to bicker so childishly over a foreign girl: so much so that, unable to restrain his passions, he robbed Achilles of his little mistress—and certainly not without the greatest danger to the entire army. Then, how absurdly Achilles fumes when deprived of his love, and how childishly he laments to his mother! Yet the poet proposed him to us as the absolute model of an excellent prince. Furthermore, how unwisely Ajax rages; how fiercely Priam dotes, while embracing Helen—a woman of prostituted modesty—and calling her daughter, denying that he regrets the war in which he had received so many disasters, been robbed of so many children, and been made mournful by death, all so that Paris would not lose his girlfriend. Why say more? The whole *Iliad*, as Horace elegantly wrote, is at length nothing other than:
->Whatever folly the kings commit, the Greeks pay the price.<-
->The story contains the passions of foolish kings and peoples.<-
The *Iliad* and *Odyssey* also have their Suitors and Alcinouses, thick and stupid. Even Hercules himself is depicted as robust and spirited, but of a dull and thick mind. Now Hesiod, whom some wish to be older than Homer, calls princes <term>gift-eaters</term> <note>original: δωροφάγος (dorophagos)</note> and <term>simpletons</term> <note>original: νηπίος (nepios)</note>. I suppose because they had little wisdom in administering the state, being intent on heaping up wealth through right or wrong rather than on the common interests of the people. They imagine that Midas to be of this sort, marked with ass's ears on account of his stupidity of mind. And I do not know whether this also pertains here: that the ancient theologians—namely the poets—attribute wisdom to Apollo and Pallas [Athena], but to Jupiter, the monarch of gods and men, they leave only the three-forked lightning bolt and that nod and brow with which he makes all Olympus tremble. Otherwise, what spendthrift, what buffoon ever trifled more gaily, or what rascal was more wickedly a rascal, than this one to whom they gave the kingdom of the world? He deceives Juno with tricks, now becoming a swan, now a bull, now gold; he lays snares for girls, snatches Ganymede, and fills heaven with bastards. In the same way, they depict Neptune and Pluto as fierce and inexorable, but do not attribute wisdom to them. But to come to more recent histories and leave fables aside, what kind of heart do you believe Croesus, King of the Lydians, had—if indeed he was such as Herodotus depicted—who, relying on his piled-up gems and gold, was indignant at Solon because he did not grant him the title of "happy"? Or what can be imagined more foolish than Xerxes, when he sent legates to Mount Athos and terrified it with most insulting and threatening letters; or when he ordered a certain number of lashes to be inflicted upon the Hellespont sea? Nor did that Alexander the Great play the fool any less regally when, having disowned his father, he rejoiced to be hailed as the son of Jupiter; while he competed in wine-drinking; while he allowed himself to be worshiped as a god by flatterers at banquets; while he complained that this world was too narrow for his victories and, having crossed the Ocean, sought other worlds to conquer. I shall not mention meanwhile the Dionysiuses, Phalarises, Juliuses, Neros, Tiberiuses, Caligulas, Heliogabaluses, Commoduses, and Domitians, of whom one claimed for himself the name of a god, when he was unworthy of the name of a man;

<summary>Erasmus explores the proverb "One ought to be born either a king or a fool," arguing through classical examples that absolute power often coincides with a lack of wisdom. He cites Homeric heroes, Greek gods, and Roman emperors to illustrate that rulers frequently act with the impulsivity and folly of children.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion on the moral responsibilities of a ruler, contrasting true kingly wisdom with the superficial qualities often praised by the masses.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

One man has offered himself up entirely to be mocked by flatterers; another, headlong in his ambition, has shaken the entire world with the most insane upheavals of affairs. But I might seem foolish were I to enter into a full catalog here and, as they say, "seek water in the sea." <note>original: "aquam in mari." A proverbial expression for performing a redundant or endless task.</note> Rather, leaf through the annals of both the ancients and the moderns; there you will surely find that in several centuries there has scarcely existed one or two princes who did not bring the greatest ruin upon human affairs through notable folly. For a prince is either foolish to the great misfortune of the whole world, or wise to the great benefit of all; yet it is easier to do harm than to do good, and destruction creeps—or rather pervades—more quickly than utility. 

But now we see some princes seeking anything rather than that which alone renders them worthy of the title of "Prince"; and the foolish common people admire everything in kings rather than that which alone ought to be required. "He is a young man." In that way you might recommend a bridegroom to a bride, but not a prince to a republic. "He is handsome." A woman might rightly praise him on that account. "He has strong arms or a sturdy frame." You have spoken well if you are praising an athlete. "He is robust and tolerant of labor." Porters and camp-followers are recommended by that title. "He has amassed much gold." You are describing a diligent moneylender. "He is eloquent." Thus do I admire a sophist. "He sings beautifully, he dances beautifully." That is praise for actors and flute-players, not for kings. "He is invincible at drinking" (for ancient princes also delighted in this praise). Fitting, if you are praising a sponge to me. "He is tall and stands out among all from the shoulders up." Excellent, if something must be reached down from a high place. Then there are those: "He plays skillfully at dice, skillfully at checkers." This is a praise shared with the lowest scoundrels, and shameful for a prince. 

You may gather everything—finery, gold, gems, statues, a lineage traced back to Hercules, or if you prefer, to Codrus or Cecrops <note>Legendary early kings of Athens.</note>—unless you describe to me a heart far removed from the folly of the common folk, free from the sordid desires of humble things and from the most false opinions of the multitude, I do not hear praise worthy of a king. For it was not without reason that the divine Plato wrote that republics would only be happy if either the rule were entrusted to philosophers, or if philosophy should follow those to whom the rule had fallen. <note>A reference to the "Philosopher King" from Plato's *Republic*.</note> Furthermore, to "follow philosophy" is not to carry around a cloak or a beggar's pouch, or to grow a long beard. What is it then? It is to despise those things which the common people foolishly admire, and to feel far differently about things than the multitude of men feels. 

Nor do I see how it can happen that he who thinks whatever he pleases is permitted to him; who admires riches as something great; who thinks any oath whatsoever should be violated for the sake of power; who is snatched away by empty glory; who serves shameful lust; who vehemently dreads death—how such a man can act as a salutary prince. And first, indeed, it is necessary to judge rightly concerning individual things; because if opinions are infected—as if the springs from which all actions of life gush forth—all things must necessarily be carried out wrongly. The next step is that they should shrink from the base and be carried toward the honorable. For true wisdom <term>sapientia: the virtue of practical and moral wisdom</term> embraces not only the knowledge of the truth, but also the zeal for and love of the honorable. 

Indeed, one might perhaps find a man who perceives that war cannot be undertaken without the grave destruction of human affairs, and that some old and obsolete title of dominion is not worth so much; yet ambition impels him to throw everything into confusion with arms. And there is perhaps one who sees that the greatest plague of the republic arises from this: that those are admitted to hold magistracies not who can benefit the republic most through prudence, experience, and integrity of life, but those who bid the highest sum of money; yet avarice drags him here, so that, neglecting the public evil, he conducts the business of the treasury. And there is no lack of those who understand that it is the duty of a prince—just as he receives taxes from everyone—to consult the interests of everyone, to preside over judgments, to shut out crimes, to watch over magistrates, and to correct useless laws; yet pleasure calls him away from this zeal, through which there is no leisure to be vacant for cares worthy of a prince. There is one who feels he could be of the greatest benefit to the affairs of mortals, but truly not without risk to his life; this man will desert the republic, whoever shall think it the most unhappy thing to die. 

Therefore, first of all, the mind of the prince must be freed from all errors, so that he may perceive what is truly honorable, what is truly glorious, what is truly magnificent. Then, a hatred of baseness and a love of the honorable must be instilled, by which he may clearly see what becomes a prince, and desire nothing except what is worthy of a good and salutary prince. Let him see where the honorable lies, and let him measure all things by this one standard, nor ever wander from this mark. And this they call wisdom, which it is necessary that a prince should excel other mortals in as much as he precedes them in dignity, wealth, adornment, and power. And would that at least all Christian princes would imitate that wisest king <note>King Solomon.</note> who, when given the choice of whatever he wished from Him who could provide anything, opted for nothing other than wisdom—and that wisdom by which he might rightly govern the people committed to him. And I ask, what else does he instill in his...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ideal ruler, following the previous page's focus on the symbolic duties of a prince. The catchword "appellari" (to be called) from the previous page leads into the definition of the prince's character.</meta>

# CHILIADS, FIRST CENTURY, THIRD HUNDRED

love and the pursuit of wisdom? <note>original: "sapientiae"</note> The Egyptians aimed at the same thing when they represented the image of a prince by painting an eye with a scepter. Truly, what the eye is to the body, the prince is to the state. <note>original: "repub."</note> What the sun is in the heavens, the prince is among the people. The sun is the eye of the world; the prince is the eye of the multitude. What the mind is in a human being, the prince is in the city. The body obeys the mind. And indeed, the mind commands the body, but for the body's own good; nor will the kingdom be like a tyrant, but for the benefit of those over whom it presides. Finally, the prince reflects a living image of God, who moderates the universe with a salutary power. And a prince is more magnificent the closer he approaches the form of his archetype. God sees everything, feels everything, and is corrupted by no passions. He is so powerful that he is likewise the best. He does good to all, even the unworthy. He does not punish except rarely, and then only when forced. He administers this world for us, not for himself. It is his reward if he has been of service. On the contrary, a prince who is a pestilence seems to reflect the image of an evil demon. <note>original: "cacodaemonis"</note> Either he lacks wisdom, or if he has it, he uses it for public destruction. Whatever power he possesses, he abuses to the ruin of the state. And while he harms everyone greatly, he still wishes he could do more. Nothing is more noble than a good king, nothing better, nothing closer to God. Conversely, nothing is more foul than a bad prince, nothing worse, nothing more similar to an evil demon. A salutary prince is a kind of divinity. But no beast is more harmful than a tyrant. A tyrant is anyone who seizes power for himself, by whatever name he may be painted or sculpted. It is not our place to pronounce judgment on the highest powers, yet we are forced, not without sighs, to desire this wisdom I have mentioned in Christian princes. Otherwise, from where do so many revolutions come, so many broken and rescinded treaties, such frequent riots, so many slaughters, so many battles, so many threats, so many disagreements, if they do not proceed from folly? And I do not know if some part of this evil should not be blamed on ourselves. We do not entrust the tiller of a ship except to one skilled in that art, where the danger is only to four passengers or a few goods; and yet we entrust the state, in which so many thousands of people are at risk, to anyone. To become a charioteer, one learns the art, practices, and meditates; but to become a prince, we think it is enough to be born. Yet to rightly govern a principality, as it is by far the most beautiful duty, so it is also by far the most difficult of all. You choose to whom you entrust your ship; do you not choose to whom you trust so many cities, so many human lives? But let it be that the custom is too deeply rooted to be overturned. Princes are born, and whoever fortune favors—whether he be honest or dishonest, foolish or wise, sane or of a disturbed mind—provided he has the shape of a man, the highest affairs must be entrusted to him. By his judgment, the world will be shaken by wars and slaughters, and all things sacred and profane will be thrown into confusion. But if this matter can hardly be changed, it was at least proper to provide help through diligent education; <note>original: "institutione"</note> and if it is not permitted to choose one fit for empire, we must strive to make him fit for empire, whomever fortune has given us. With what solicitude, what care, what vigilance a father of a family educates a boy who will be the master of a single house. With how much greater care, then, must he be instructed who will be a great good if he is good, or a great destruction if he is evil, and on whose single nod the safety or ruin of the world will depend? With what decrees, with what precepts of philosophy must his heart be fortified: not only against such great storms of affairs as usually arise in states, but also against the indulgence of fortune, which arrogance and pride usually accompany; against the luxuries by which even the best nature can be corrupted; and most of all against the pestilential flatteries of sycophants, and that most poisonous song which they sing most loudly when the prince is most insane. Here, in my view, some extraordinary craftsman should be employed for the little infant. For a prince is not rightly formed unless he does not yet understand that he is a prince. Immediately, I say, a molder must be brought in; in choosing him, it is necessary to be even more diligent because we are not allowed to choose the prince, but we are allowed to choose his instructor. Let him instill into that still empty and yielding heart the opinions of a true prince, and fortify it with the best decrees concerning honor; let him show the difference between a true prince and a tyrant; let him place before his eyes how close a thing to God a salutary king is, and what a foul beast, how abominable a thing a tyrant is. Let him warn him that he who wields power for himself is a robber of the state, not a ruler; that there is no difference between pirates and princes with the souls of pirates, except that the more powerful they are, the greater the destruction they bring to human affairs. Let him impress upon him how many thousands of men, indeed how the whole world, he can benefit if he proves himself to be one wise and good man. Let him teach that among Christian men, empire is nothing other than the administration of the state, not dominion. Empire indeed...

<summary>Erasmus argues that since princes are born into power rather than chosen, their education is the only way to ensure they become "living images of God" rather than "evil demons." He emphasizes that ruling is the most difficult of all arts and requires rigorous moral training from infancy to resist the poisons of flattery and tyranny.</summary>

-> FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM <-

to be called [a prince], but he should remember that he is to rule over both free men and Christians—that is, those who are doubly free. To be a prince, it is not enough to have been born; ancient portraits <note>original: "uetustas imagines" - referring to the Roman custom of displaying wax masks of ancestors to prove nobility</note> are not enough, nor is a scepter or a crown. A mind excelling in wisdom, a mind always anxious for the public safety, and looking toward nothing except the common good: these make a prince. Let [the tutor] warn him not to measure himself by the applause of the foolish common people, nor by the praises of flatterers. Let him do nothing by the impulse of hatred, love, anger, or the instinct of any emotion. In appointing magistrates, in establishing laws, and in other duties, let him look to only one goal: namely, honor and public utility. It is not enough if he himself does no injury to anyone; a prince must also guarantee the integrity of his officials. A prince's praise is not found in this: if he extends the borders of his dominion, or if he drives back neighbors with arms; but rather if, in whatever dominion he happens to possess, he makes it more flourishing through justice, frugality, and the other arts of peace. Let [the tutor] teach that he should be most inclined to reward the good, easy to forgive, and should approach punishment no differently than a friendly doctor who is about to amputate or cauterize a hopeless limb; so that he avoids with all his zeal everything from which he perceives a great evil will come to the state. Above all, however, let him decline war by every possible means, because from other things, various evils are born; but war pours out the entire troop of evils all at once. These and similar decrees must be fixed in the boyish mind through the sayings of wise men <term>apophthegms: concise, pithy sayings or maxims</term> and the examples of praised princes.

But now we see that hardly any men are educated either more corruptly or more carelessly than those whom it concerns everyone should have been most excellently instructed. This infant, destined to rule the world, is committed to the most foolish little women, who instill nothing into his mind worthy of a prince; so much so that even if a teacher advises something correctly, or if he seems naturally more inclined toward gentleness, they discourage him and teach him to act the "prince"—that is, to act the tyrant. Finally, everyone fawns, everyone flatters. The nobles applaud, the servants comply, and even the teacher flatters—not acting to make the prince healthy for the fatherland, but to prepare a magnificent fortune for himself. The Theologian also flatters, whom they commonly call a "confessor," hunting for some bishopric. The magistrate fawns, those who play games together fawn, those who live together fawn; so that Carneades <note>A Greek skeptical philosopher</note> said most correctly: that no art is learned rightly by kings except the art of riding. This is because the horse alone, since it does not feel the distinction between a prince and a commoner, does not know how to flatter a king; instead, it throws off whoever it may be who does not know how to sit fitly on its back. Immediately [the prince] is taught pride, he is taught arrogance; he is reminded that whatever he pleases is permitted. He hears that all the possessions of all men belong to the prince, that the prince is superior to the laws; that in the breast of the prince, the entire world of laws and counsels is hidden. He hears "sacred majesties," "serenities," "divinities," "earthly deity," and magnificent titles of this sort. In short, while he is still a boy, he learns nothing else but to play at tyranny. Soon he is snatched away to girls; they all invite, praise, and serve him. Here is present a most effeminate crowd of peers; no laughter, no conversation, except about girls. Following this come dice, dances, banquets, lutes, and wandering about; in these, the best part of his life is wasted. But if ever he wishes to amuse his leisure with letters, old wives' tales are read, or histories more ruinous than these. From these, a mind fortified by no antidote drinks in admiration and "zeal" (as the Greeks call it) for some most pestilential leader: for instance, Julius Caesar, or Xerxes, or Alexander the Great. And in these very men, the things that are worst please the most. From these they take mad impulses; from these they take the worst example.

Consider now, if you please, a talent not chosen from many (as it ought to have been), but whatever happened to occur. Consider an education so corrupt that it could ruin even the talent of Aristides <note>An Athenian statesman known for his fairness and nicknamed "The Just"</note>. Consider so many poisons of flattery, consider the luxuries (which agree poorly with wisdom), consider the pleasures, consider the splendor of fortune, consider the power, consider the fierce age of youth, naturally prone to the worst things. Above all, consider a heart infected with the falsest opinions. And are you surprised if this man, having set out from these rudiments to manage the state, administers it with little wisdom? "But he is young," they say, "he will eventually become wise through the experience of affairs." But a prince ought not to be "young" even if he is young in years. And while all prudence gathered from experience is wretched, in a prince it is most wretched of all. It will cost the state too much if the prince does not understand that offices must be committed to upright men until after he has seen the republic undermined by the recklessness of the wicked. Nor should it be allowed that—just as those who learn to play the lute break and ruin several lutes before they master the art, as Xenophon wrote—so a prince should learn [at the cost of the state's destruction].
