# THIRD CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

administer the republic. It is no wonder, then, if we sometimes see things happen in a backwards manner: namely, that while the passions arising from the body ought to be restrained by the mind, disturbances instead proceed from the mind into the body. It is as if the eye saw less clearly than the rest of the body, or as if a ruler—who, acting in God's stead, ought to be a source of safety for all—became harmful and pestilential to everyone. Do we not see magnificent towns founded by the people but overturned by princes? The Republic enriched by industry, but despoiled by the greed of princes? Good laws passed by the hands of the commoners, but violated by princes? The people striving for peace, while princes stir up war? These things gave occasion to the adage we recorded <note>Erasmus refers to the proverb "One ought to be born either a king or a fool," discussed on the preceding page.</note>, from which I have somehow wandered; but now I return to it. It was said, therefore: *One ought to be either a fool or a king*, because the barbarian kings among the ancients were generally of this sort—would that the princes of our own time were most unlike them! For to fools, all things are permitted because of their lack of wit; and to kings, all things are even turned into praise because of their power. We might also interpret the saying regarding the "happiness" of kings and fools: for kings, whatever they wish for, fortune supplies; while fools are no less happy in their own *philautia* <note>original: "philautia" — Greek for self-love or conceit</note>, through which they believe they lack no good thing. Furthermore, the proverb seems to have arisen among the Romans, among whom the title of "King" was hated as something barbarian and tyrannical, and as being at odds with the public liberty which they especially pursued at that time.

### II. Small drops produce a shower.

<margin>Small drops begetting a rainstorm.</margin> That is, tiny droplets producing a heavy rain. Whenever a matter begins small, it grows into something greater. Just as in Plautus’s *The Menaechmi*:
> First the leaves fall, then the trees will fall.

One must be watchful in small matters, lest we fall by degrees into the greatest inconveniences, as warned by the proverbial six-foot verse:
<margin>If you do not guard the small, you will lose the great.</margin> That is,
> You will lose the great things, unless you save the small.

A *psecas* <note>original: "psecas" — Greek for a tiny drop or drizzle</note> is a thin bedewing, such as is produced by dense mists.

### III. Drunkenness without wine.

<margin>Wine-less intoxication.</margin> That is, drunkenness without wine. Theophrastus, as Plutarch testifies in his *Symposiacs*, <margin>called the barbershops "drunkenness without wine."</margin> That is, he called the barbershops "wine-less intoxication" because those sitting there became so intoxicated by gossip that they would blurt out whatever was in their minds, no differently than drunkards do over their cups—words which, as Pliny says, will return to haunt them through the throat. Horace calls insolence a form of drunkenness: *Drunk with sweet fortune.* Commonly, people call arrogance and the license of behavior that usually accompanies prosperity "bread-drunkenness." And this is indeed not a little more dangerous than the kind wine brings on. For the heat of wine is dispelled in a few hours or by sleep; this other kind usually lasts in many people for their entire lives.

### IV. To bear the palm.

To "bear the palm," to "award the palm," and to "snatch the palm," and other similar expressions: although they seem simple because of frequent use, they are nonetheless of a proverbial pattern. For the palm does not signify victory in itself, but rather a tree <term>with enduring leaves <note>original: "empyllon"</note></term>, which is perpetually green with foliage, and which the Greeks call <term>phoenix <note>the date palm</note></term>. As for why the metaphor was taken from this tree, I believe the cause was that, as Plutarch reports in his *Natural Questions*, this was the common crown for all sacred contests, even though individual games had certain specific trees or herbs with which victors were distinguished—such as laurel, olive, myrtle, or celery. There are those who think this tree was sacred to Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> before the laurel, and that the palm was the most ancient mark of a victor, not any other tree. Why this tree was specifically chosen for that use by the ancients, Aulus Gellius gives the reason in the *Attic Nights*, Book 3, Chapter 6, writing that there is something peculiar in the palm tree that suits the character of brave men. For if, he says, you place great weights upon its wood, and press and load it so heavily that the magnitude of the burden cannot be borne, the palm does not yield downward, nor is it bent low, but it rises up against the weight and curves upward. For this amazing fact he cites authors: Aristotle in the 7th book of *Problems*, and Plutarch in the 8th book of *Symposiacs*. And I have found Plutarch's words on this matter...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient adages, specifically focusing on the symbolism of the palm tree as a metaphor for resilience, followed by new entries on moderation and medical pretension.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
<page-num>98</page-num>

I found in that book which Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author</note> cites: "For the wood of the palm tree, if you place a weight upon it and press down heavily, does not yield downward or sink into the ground, but rather curves upward in the opposite direction, as if resisting the force." You might see the same thing in athletic contests; those who, through weakness and softness of spirit, yield to those pressing upon them are bent down. But those who stoutly endure the training are elevated and grow, not only in their bodies but also in their wisdom. <note>Erasmus provides a Greek quote from Plutarch followed by his own Latin translation; both are rendered here in English.</note> Pliny affirms the same in Book 16, Chapter 42: "The fir and the larch," he says, "are strong at sustaining weight, even when placed horizontally. Oak and olive trees warp and yield to a weight, but the former resist; nor do they break easily, failing from decay sooner than from loss of strength. The palm tree is also strong, for it curves in the opposite direction. While the poplar sags downward under weight, the palm, on the contrary, forms an arch." Theophrastus affirms the same in his fifth book *On Plants*. Virgil aptly described this strength of a manly soul, which matches the natural power of the palm, when he said:

> Yield not to misfortunes, but go forth more boldly against them,
> As far as your fortune permits you. <note>Virgil, Aeneid 6.95</note>

Nor is that passage from Horace inconsistent with this:

> Like an oak pruned by hard axes
> On Algidus, fertile with dark foliage,
> Through losses, through slaughter, from the very
> Steel it draws wealth and spirit.
> No Hydra, its body cut, grew firmer
> Against Hercules, who grieved to be conquered,
> Nor did the Colchians or Echionian Thebes
> Send forth a greater monster.
> Sink it in the deep, it comes out fairer;
> Wrestle it, and with much praise it will cast down
> A fresh victor, and wage
> Wars for wives to tell of. <note>Horace, Odes 4.4.57-68</note>

---

### Leave something for the Medes.
-> VI <-

<note>original: λάπει τι κὴ μήδοις</note> That is, leave something for the Medes. A proverbial joke against those who leave nothing behind at a banquet, or who squander their entire inheritance. Plutarch in his *Table Talk* says: "Among us Boeotians, the saying 'Leave something for the Medes' is on everyone's lips, from the time when the Medes <note>The Persians</note> were overrunning and plundering Phocis and the furthest borders of Boeotia." He adds that people today commonly say: "Leave something for the guests who might arrive." The adage can be applied in various ways, or through irony, as if you were to say to a rich man who intends to leave his wealth to unworthy and extravagant heirs: "Leave something for the Medes"—that is, "Prepare what those who wish you ill may scatter." Or it could apply to one who is excessively wasteful, or immoderately talkative, just as Terence says in *Phormio*: "Be sparing, please, so that you may have some left for her."

---

### The hands of the Gods.
-> VI <-

<note>original: Θεῶν χεῖρες</note> That is, the hands of the Gods. In the past, I believe, this was said ironically of those powerful medicines composed of many ingredients sought from far away, with which today both doctors and pharmacists commonly practice their deceptions. Plutarch, in the fourth decade of his *Table Talk*, both records the proverb and cites Erasistratus <note>A famous Greek anatomist and royal physician</note> as disapproving of these mixtures made by doctors: "But much more so when you mix those 'royal' and 'antidote' powers which they used to call 'the hands of the gods.' Erasistratus used to expose the absurdity and wordiness of those who mixed together minerals, herbs, animal parts, and things from the earth and sea into the same concoction. For it is fine that these things display their knowledge, art, and medical arrogance; but by heaven, the complexity merely fascinates and charms the appetite." That is: "Indeed, much more so when those royal and effective..."

<keywords>resilience, palm tree, Virgil, Horace, Plutarch, Medes, greed, medicine, Erasistratus, irony</keywords>

# THIRD CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<note>This header refers to the organization of Erasmus's *Adagia*, which grouped proverbs by the thousands and hundreds.</note>

...they prepare mixtures of remedies which they have called "the hands of the gods." <note>original: "deorum manus"</note> Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician</note> refutes the absurdity and the meddlesome curiosity of those who mixed together at once metallic substances, wild herbs, things produced by the earth, and things from the sea. It would have been well if, setting aside such things, they had limited the art of healing to barley-groats, pumpkin, and water-mixed oil. But in truth, the very variety of things deceives us and entices our appetite. Thus far Plutarch. Galen cites this adage from Herophilus in his sixth treatise. It is pleasing to transcribe here, in passing, the words of C. Pliny, in which he censures the mixtures of physicians. These are found in the preface of his twenty-fourth book: "From this," he says, "medicine was born. Nature had intended these alone to be remedies: prepared by her, easy to find, and without expense—the very things we live on. Later, the frauds of men and the ingenuity of profit-seeking invented those laboratories in which a private heaven is promised to every man for a price. Immediately, inexplicable compositions and mixtures are chanted. Arabia and India are valued in the midst of us. A medicine for a small ulcer is charged to the Red Sea, while the poorest man sups on remedies every day. For if a herb were sought from the garden, or a fruit looked for, no art would become cheaper." Thus far Pliny.

---

### As many men, so many opinions. VII
<note>original: "Quot homines, tot sententiae."</note>

Nothing even today is more common among the people than this sentiment from Terence: *As many men, so many opinions.* Similar to this is another from the same author: *Each has his own custom.* Persius likewise says:
*A thousand types of men, and a diverse use of things.*
*Each has his own will, nor is life lived by a single prayer.*
To this also belongs that epigrammatic saying which states: one can find those who do not refuse to yield their paternal inheritance, but no one can be found who is willing to yield in matters of intellect. Horace most fittingly added an allegory:
*--- to me, the guests seem almost to disagree,*
*demanding many different things with varying palates.*
He composed the very first of all his Odes on the argument of this sentiment: that different pursuits please different people, and different things are dear to different hearts. Terence alluded to this most wittily in *The Phormio*, when of three advocates, the first says "yes," the second says "no," and the third thinks the matter must be deliberated. The holy Apostle Paul also seems to have alluded to this when he warns that, to preclude rivalry, we should allow every man to abound in his own sense. <note>A reference to Romans 14:5</note> If the common crowd of theologians listened to this advice, there would not be such sword-fighting today over little questions of nothing: for there are certainly some things which can be ignored without injury to piety. Euripides explained this sentiment more broadly in *The Phoenician Women*:
*If the same thing were beautiful and wise to all,*
*there would be no uncertain strife among men.*
*But now nothing is similar or equal to mortals,*
*except in names. In reality, this is not so.* <note>original Greek: "Εἰ πᾶσι ταὐτὸ καλὸν ἔφυ..."</note>
The same author in *Hippolytus*:
*For one god or man is a care to one, and another to another.* <note>original Greek: "Ἄλλῳ γὰρ ἄλλῳ..."</note>
Homer looked to this in the *Odyssey*, Book 14:
*For different men take pleasure in different works.* <note>original Greek: "Ἄλλος γάρ τ' ἄλλοισιν..."</note>

---

### Listen to him who has four ears. VIII
<note>original: "Eum aufculta, cui quatuor sunt aures."</note>

Among the collections of Greek proverbs, he records: *Listen to him who has four ears.* <note>original Greek: "ἄκουε τοῦ τὰ τέσσαρα ὦτα ἔχοντος"</note> Zenodotus provides an interpretation of this adage of this sort: that an oracle once gave a response to Entimus the Cretan and Antiphemus the Rhodian, telling them to watch for the one who had four ears. This was a certain Phoenician man, whom the oracle warned should be guarded against. Furthermore, as to why he was said to have four ears, it is not sufficiently clear whether he truly had them, or if it should be taken as an allegory—perhaps because he had scouts stationed in four different places. But they, taking the god's response...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

lest they should neglect anything ridiculous, they fell upon a robber and were killed by him. And so, they believe this proverb arose commonly from this event. But it pleases me more what the same author reports from Aristophanes the Grammarian <note>Aristophanes of Byzantium, a Hellenistic scholar</note>, that the Spartans were accustomed to fashion the statue of Apollo in such a way that he had four ears and as many hands: or that, as Sosibius testifies, he used this figure when they were fighting at Amyclae: or signifying, as I myself conjecture, that a prudent man must both hear as many things as possible and test them through the experience of life. Furthermore, it was believed in antiquity that no oracles were more certain than those of Apollo. Whence also that celebrated saying: *From the tripod* <note>original: "τὰ ἐκ τρίποδος" - referring to the seat of the Delphic Pythia; meaning a definitive truth</note>. And so the proverb warns that those who are wiser than others due to long experience in many things ought to be listened to, just as the elderly usually are. Whence also in Homer, the speech of Nestor is praised as being most worthy of everyone's hearing: and in the second book of the *Odyssey*, he makes the Egyptian hero, an old man, speak in the first place:
*Who was already bent with age, but knew ten thousand things.* <note>original: "ὃς δὴ γήραϊ κυφὸς ἔην, καὶ μυρία ἤδη"</note>
Euripides aimed at the same point in the *Phoenician Women*, a passage to which Lucian alluded in *The Gallic Hercules*, which I thought should be mentioned in passing, because that dialogue among many others was translated into Latin by us: and the allusion has some obscurity, but I will repeat the poet's verse:
*O child, not all evils are attached to old age, Eteocles, but experience has something to say wiser than the young.* <note>original: "Ω τέκνον οὐκ ἅπαντα τῷ γήρᾳ κακὰ / Επόκλεες πρόσεστιν, ἀλλ’ ἡ ’μπειρία / Εχει τι λέξαι τῶν νέων σοφώτερον"</note>
These are the words of Jocasta, now an old woman, to her young son Eteocles. We have translated them thus:
*O son Eteocles, by no means are all things bad*
*That come with age, for through experience*
*And use of things, it can speak—not a little—*
*Better and more prudently than raw youth.*
<margin>||</margin> Our common people now express the same thing, using a somewhat coarse but nevertheless apt metaphor, when they say: *One must keep watch when the old dog barks.* That is: one should by no means neglect it whenever <margin>||</margin> the elderly warn that danger must be avoided. For old dogs do not bark rashly, as the young ones do.

---

->The dice of Jove always fall luckily.<-
->IX<-
*For the dice of Zeus always fall well.* <note>original: "Αεὶ γὰρ εὖ πίπτουσιν οἱ Διὸς κύβοι"</note> That is,
*The dice of Jove always fall luckily.*
This is a six-foot line <term>senarius: a line of verse with six feet</term> celebrated as a proverb, and usually said against those for whom all things turn out according to their heart's desire by a certain perpetual favor of fortune. It appears to be transferred from the throwing of dice, where perhaps it was observed in antiquity that the "dice of Jove" were luckier. For it was the custom in throwing dice, for the sake of an omen, to first speak the names of gods or men. Whence also the "throw of Venus" is numbered among the lucky ones, as even the proverb testifies: *If you throw often, eventually you will throw a Venus.* <note>The "Venus" was the highest possible throw in Roman dice games</note>. Unless we prefer to refer it to the story of Jove's victory and Juno's defeat. There are those who think it fits those who have paid worthy penalties for their deeds, as if Jove were not allowing guilt to go unpunished. To me, it seems it can be said not absurdly also of fortunate and very powerful men, whose even less-than-right deeds are applauded, as the proverbial verse attests:
*How easily the fortunes of the illustrious always fall.* <note>original: "Ως εὐκόλως πίπτουσιν οἱ λαμπρὰ τύχαι"</note> That is,
*How easily the affairs of the powerful always turn out.*
Not far from this sentiment is that of Euripides in the tragedy titled *The Phoenician Women*:
*All things are easy for the gods.* <note>original: "Πάντα δ’ εὐπετῆ θεοῖς"</note>
Then that frequent saying in Homer: *The gods are able to do all things.* <note>original: "Θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται"</note>

---

->A Thessalian trick.<-
->X<-
*A Thessalian trick.* <note>original: "Θεσσαλῶν σόφισμα"</note> That is, *A Thessalian invention*, Suidas writes that this is applied to various things: both to those who desert their post in the battle line; then to those who use a more delicate style of dress; then to those who circumvent someone with deceits. Moreover, they think it arose from some history of this kind: a response was given by an oracle to a certain Aratus of Thessaly, that he should beware lest he be secretly defeated by those who sought the oracle against him with a greater and more splendid vow. As soon as he heard this, he pronounced a vow that he would sacrifice a hundred heads of men to the god. Then afterwards, when he had finished the things for which he had come according to his heart's desire, he began to fulfill the vow and the sacrifice without end...

He begins an explanation of the "Thessalian trick" involving deceptive oracles.</summary>

# FIRST CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
<sig>i 3</sig>

he did not hesitate, as if it were neither pious enough nor worthy of Apollo. From this event, they say, the custom arose that they were thereafter accustomed to promise a hecatomb <note>A grand public sacrifice of 100 oxen</note> to that god every year, yet they never actually rendered what they had promised. Euripides also notes the deceitfulness of the Thessalians in *The Phoenician Women*:
"And how, sensing this, did Eteocles introduce the Thessalian trick into the dealings of the land?" <note>original: Καὶ πῶς νοήσας ἐπεκλῆς τὸ Θεσσαλῶν Εἰσήγαγε τὸ σόφισμ’ ὁμιλίᾳ χθονός.</note> That is:
But Eteocles, sensing this, soon employed the Thessalian art because of his dealings with that race. The same author says elsewhere:
"Many were present, but the Thessalians are untrustworthy." <note>original: Πολλαὶ πῆ ἄι, ἀλλ’ ἄπιστοι, Θεσσαλοί.</note> That is:
A great crowd of Thessalians was indeed present, yet of slippery faith.

Demosthenes declares the same in the *First Olynthiac*: "Then there are the affairs of the Thessalians; for these were surely untrustworthy by nature and always so to all men." <note>original: Εἶτα τὰ τῶν Θεσσαλῶν, ταῦτα γὰρ ἄπιστα μὲν ἦν δήπου φύσει καὶ ἀεὶ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις.</note> That is, he says: To these things are added the affairs of the Thessalians, which were indeed natured to be unfaithful to all mortals, and always so. By some, this adage is recorded thus: "For the affairs of the Thessalians are always untrustworthy." <note>original: ἀεὶ γὰρ τὰ τῶν Θεσσαλῶν ἄπιστα.</note> That is: For the affairs of the Thessalians are always unfaithful. A commentator on Aristophanes thinks the proverb originated from Jason, because he broke the faith promised to Medea—a thing she indeed reproaches him for in Ovid’s *Heroides*. The proverb is also mentioned by the one who transmitted the fragments of Athenaeus to us.

### XI. Thessalian wings

"Thessalian wings." <note>original: Θεσσαλικαὶ πτέρυγες.</note> This was once said as a proverbial joke regarding long-sleeved garments, which the Greeks call *cheiridotas* <note>sleeved tunics</note>, because the Thessalians used this style out of luxury and indulgence. In Virgil <note>referred to as Maro</note>, this kind of dress is reproached by enemies as being insufficiently manly for the Trojans:
"And tunics have sleeves, and mitres have ribbons."
And in Plautus, a certain man in Carthaginian dress is mocked like an exotic bird because of his sleeves, or the corners hanging down and standing out on both sides like wings.

### XII. A Thessalian woman

"A Thessalian woman." <note>original: Θεσσαλικὴ γυνή.</note> This was commonly said of sorceresses and those skilled in evil arts. This is because that nation, above others, was noted by this name, as is sufficiently clear from Apuleius’s *The Golden Ass* and many other writers. Hence Horace in the *Odes*:
"What witch, what magus will be able to free you with Thessalian poisons, what god?"
Plautus in the *Amphitryon* calls a sorcerer a "Thessalian." And Strepsiades in Aristophanes’ *Clouds* consults Socrates on whether a Thessalian enchantress should be employed to draw the moon down from heaven, so that he might not be forced to pay his debts on the New Moon. They believe that superstition spread to the Thessalians from Medea; for when she fled through that region, carried through the air, she dropped a small casket full of poisons and magic herbs, and these, being scattered, sprouted up. Furthermore, Pliny in Book 30, Chapter 1, teaches that magic, having propagated as far as the Thessalians, for a long time took its surname from that people; so much so that Menander, a man skilled in the subtleties of literature, also titled a play *The Thessalian Woman*, which encompassed the evasions of women who draw down the moon.

### XIII. To rejoice in one's bosom

To rejoice in one's bosom is to feel a silent pleasure within oneself, and not to bring forth outward signs of joy as the common people do. Tibullus:
"He who is wise, let him rejoice in his silent bosom." Propertius likewise:
"Keep your joys enclosed in a silent bosom." The same author:
"To weep in each other's mutual bosom."
This is said of lovers who pour out the secret cares of the soul to one another, which they nevertheless hide from others. Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 4: "Since these things are not praiseworthy, let them cease to speak boastfully, so that he may rejoice in his bosom." Pliny Caecilius <note>Pliny the Younger</note> in Book 2, Epistle 1: "For which reasons I must weep for his untimely death in your bosom." It appears several times in Seneca. For instance, in Epistle 106: "If you do not boast of your goods, if you know how to rejoice in your bosom." And indeed, that figure of speech seems to be borrowed from Homer, who in the 22nd book of the *Odyssey* says:
"Rejoice in your soul, old woman, and restrain yourself." <note>original: Ἐν θυμῷ γρηὺ χαῖρε, καὶ ἴσχεο.</note>
"Press down your joys in your silent bosom, aged nurse."
It is said "in the bosom" just as if you were to say "in your heart," not on your lips or forehead; with which parts the vul- <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "bus uul-" indicates the next page begins with "vulgus" (the common people).</note>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

the common people are accustomed to betray what they hide in the innermost chambers of the soul. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in a certain letter to his brother Quintus says: *Believe me, it is in my bosom, nor do I ungird myself.* <note>original Latin: "Mihi crede, in sinu est, neq; ego discingor."</note> With these words he promises the loyalty of silence. For if anyone "ungirds" themselves, that which was entrusted to the "bosom" <note>The 'sinus' or fold of the toga used as a pocket</note> flows out. Plutarch, in the *Life of Cato of Utica*, seems to have used the phrase "from the bosom" to mean intimate familiarity: *having persuaded certain men, Calpurnius, who was the father of Caesar’s wife, and Gabinius Paulus, from the bosoms of Pompey—men, as they say, who knew his character and life.* <note>original Greek: ὑπάτους πείσαντά τι καλπύρνιον... translated here from Erasmus's Latin version</note> That is, Calpurnius Piso, who was the father of Caesar's wife, and Gabinius Paulus from the intimate circles of Pompey, as they say, who knew the man's habits and life. Scaevola, in the *Pandects* <term>Pandects: a compendium of Roman law</term> book 22, title *On Proofs*, chapter 27, uses it slightly differently: *Because,* he says, *I held all the fortune and substance, if any she had received from her mother, in my bosom without any security.* He said "in my bosom" instead of "in my power": for what we commit to another's trust, we are said to "deposit in their bosom." So Terence says: *He gives this into my hand.*

->Bear, do not blame, what cannot be avoided. XIV<-

Aulus Gellius writes that several maxims of Publilius the Mime, most suited for common speech, were usually circulated among the public, of which this one is more wholesome than any dogma of the philosophers: *Bear, do not blame, what cannot be avoided.* By these words we are warned that fatal evils, which can by no means be declined or driven away, should at least be softened by equanimity of mind. Nor does Euripides teach anything else, though in different words, in the *Phoenician Women*, when he says: *The fortunes from the gods.* <note>original Greek: τὰς τύχας τὰς ἐκ θεῶν</note> That is, *The fates of the divinities must be endured.* The same author at the end of the same tragedy says: *For being a mortal, one must bear the necessities from the gods.* <note>original Greek: Τὰς γὰρ ἐκ θεῶν ἀνάγκας θνητὸν ὄντα δεῖ φέρειν</note> That is, *Indeed it is necessary for a mortal to bear the fates of the divinities.* Homer in the *Odyssey*, book 9: *There is no way to avoid a sickness sent from great Jove.* <note>original Greek: Νοῦσον γ' ὅπως ἔστι διὸς μεγάλου ἀλέασθαι</note> That is, *It is permitted to no one to avoid an evil proceeding from King Jove.* To this also pertains that wise saying of Varro: *A wife's fault is either to be taken away or to be endured.* Likewise the adage which we shall discuss in its own place: *Do not kick against the pricks.* <note>original Greek: μὴ πρὸς κέντρον λακτίζειν</note> That is, *Do not kick against the goad.*

->The sources of the sacred rivers flow upward. XV<-

A proverbial allegory, by which we signify that something is being done preposterously, and the legitimate turns of things are inverted: the sort of thing it would be if a boy should advise an old man, a disciple should try to teach a teacher, or a slave should command a master. The adage is taken from Euripides' *Medea*:
*Upward flow the sources of the sacred rivers,*
*And justice and all things are turned back.*
*For men have deceitful counsels, and the faith*
*Of the gods no longer stands firm.*
By these words the chorus indicates that the ancient order of things is inverted, that men now use womanly deceits and do not stand by their promises; conversely, women dare manly deeds. Lucian uses this proverb in *Terpsion*, where a disappointed legacy-hunter accuses Pluto because he himself, still a youth, had been snatched away by death while the old man he was hunting survived, and this contrary to the natural order. *For this,* he says, *is "upward of the rivers."* Again the same author in the *Apology for the Book on Those Who Live for Hire*: *How great indeed is the dissonance of your life compared to your writing; it is a "flowing upward of rivers," and everything is turned upside down, and you sing a recantation toward that which you once hated.* Far and wide, he says, your life now disagrees with your writings. And now that which they say would happen, that rivers should march upward, and all things likewise would be inverted and recanted for the worse. Diogenes Laertius also uses it in the *Life of Diogenes the Cynic*, recounting how Diogenes, just as if he were the master and not the slave, commanded his owner to do what he was ordered; and the other replied with the proverb, *Upward of the sacred rivers.* But Diogenes said, *If you had bought a doctor with your money because you were sick, would you obey him when he advised you, or would you respond in that fashion, "Upward of the rivers"?* Aristotle also uses it in the *Meteorology*. Virgil alluded to the same in the *Aeneid* when he said:
*And the river Aufidus flees backward from the Adriatic waves.*
Where Servius <note>A famous commentator on Virgil</note> warns that there is an underlying proverb about a thing that is neither likely nor consistent. Horace in the *Odes* expressed it thus: *Who would deny that steep*
*Rivers can glide back to the mountains,*
*And the Tiber be turned back:*
*When you, having bought up from everywhere the noble*
*Books of Panaetius and the Socratic school...*

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY III
<sig>i 4</sig>

<margin>Porphyrion <note>A 3rd-century scholar known for his commentaries on Horace.</note> noted this proverb here.</margin>

### To lean toward the lucky side of the ship. XVI
<note>Literally: "To turn toward the successful wall."</note>

Aristophanes, in the comedy titled *The Frogs*, employs a most beautiful adage. I wish it existed only in literature, and not also in the lives of nearly all mortals:
<unclear>to</unclear> turn oneself toward the 
<unclear>prosperous</unclear> wall,
<unclear>for</unclear> it is always the mark of a 
<unclear>clever</unclear> man, both by nature and 
<unclear>one</unclear> who has sailed much,
<unclear>to roll</unclear> himself always
<unclear>toward</unclear> the wall that is doing well. That is:
> It is the part of a prudent man,
> Wise and shrewd,
> To know the waters he has sailed, so that
> He may always shift himself
> To the more fortunate side.

The proverb is more conveniently expressed this way: *To lean toward the successful wall.* The commentator on Aristophanes believes this is a metaphor taken from those who travel by ship: when one side of the ship is pressed down by a wave, they immediately run across to the other side, which stands higher out of the water. 

It will also be said of those who, out of regard for their own advantage, always attach themselves to more powerful and fortunate friends. Just as flies fly toward the smell of a kitchen, so these people follow the better fortune in a friendship, rather than loyalty. Or those who, while the outcome of a war is uncertain, remain quiet; but as soon as fortune has inclined so that it appears which side will carry off the victory, they immediately join themselves to it. 

With this spirit we read of that Mettius <note>Mettius Fufetius, a legendary dictator of Alba Longa who betrayed the Romans in battle.</note> in Virgil, and Polymnestor, who followed the victorious arms rather than the faith of the conquered, murdered Polydorus, and took possession of the gold by force. Aristophanes lightly mocks this kind of person in his play *Plutus*. Indeed, here Chremylus, having now become rich, complains that he is being overwhelmed by the kind of greeters who had smelled the gold:
<unclear>Oh</unclear> crows! How troublesome friends are,
<unclear>coming</unclear> immediately whenever one is doing well. That is:
> To the gallows! How annoying it is, when
> Friends fly forth only at the first sign of prosperity.

To the same point belongs that line of Euripides from *Medea*:
<unclear>For</unclear> the saying goes, every friend flees out of the way. That is:
> How all friends desert a man in want.

Antiphanes in *The Ancestors*, cited by Athenaeus in Book 6:
<unclear>Whenever</unclear> you might come, let it be when I am doing poorly. That is:
> Be by my side then, when things go badly.

The commentator warns that a proverb underlies this, usually said of those who desert the company of friends when they are in danger. However, the poet alluded to the proverb by twisting the words into the opposite, for the proverb is rightly accustomed to be expressed thus:
<unclear>Whenever</unclear> you might come, let it be when I am doing well. That is:
> Be by my side then, when things are prosperous.

To this also belongs that passage in Euripides' *Orestes*: <margin>friends</margin>
<unclear>In</unclear> times of trouble, one must help one's friends;
<unclear>But</unclear> when the deity gives wealth, what need is there of friends?
<unclear>For</unclear> the god himself is enough when he wishes to help. That is:
> It is right to be friends in afflicted circumstances.
> What use is there for friends when kind fate favors?
> Since the Rhamnusian goddess <note>A title for Nemesis or Fortune, named after her sanctuary at Rhamnus.</note> herself is sufficient,
> To help with her own abundant favors.

<summary>This page explores the proverb "To lean toward the lucky side," examining the human tendency to seek out powerful or wealthy friends while abandoning those in distress. Erasmus draws on Greek comedy and tragedy to critique "fair-weather" loyalty and opportunistic behavior.</summary>
<keywords>opportunism, friendship, Aristophanes, Euripides, nautical metaphors, loyalty, fortune, greed</keywords>

--- Page 210 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin proverbs, specifically focusing on the nature of friendship and the power of gifts. It follows the previous discussion on how fortune tests the loyalty of companions.</meta>

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES<-

The same poet <note>Euripides</note> alluded more closely to the adage in the same tragedy, except that he applied the general sentiment specifically to heralds:
*For the race of heralds is somehow like this: they always honor the successful. But he, in turn, becomes an old friend to his friends, whoever is able to be a friend to the city.* <note>original Greek: Τὸ γὰρ γένος κηρύκων...; Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation which is here rendered into English</note> That is to say:
For that race of heralds is such that
They accommodate themselves to the side of the more fortunate,
And they love him who is among the leaders,
And him who holds the reins of public affairs.
The same author in *Hercules Furens*:
*And whoever wishes to enjoy good things, and to sail along with friends who are unfortunate, etc.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ τῶν μὲν καλῶν...</note> That is to say:
He whose affairs are favorable, anyone seeks to go
As a companion to him as he sails; not so for the unhappy.
To this pertains what Aristotle shows in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics* to be a spoken proverb: *Time reveals the loved one.* <note>original Greek: χρόνου δείκνυσαι τὸν φιλούμενον</note> That is: Time shows who truly loves. For a storm proves friendship and unmasks those false friends.

### A friend to a friend. XVII

Regarding what is found in Terence’s *Phormio*—*He is the only man who is a friend to a friend*—Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence</note> indicates this is a <term>paroemia (proverb)</term>, and that it is read as such in Apollodorus, whose Greek play was the source for *Phormio*: *He alone knows how to love his friends.* <note>original Greek: Μόνος ἐπίσταται φιλεῖν τοὺς φίλους</note> Aristophanes, quoted in Athenaeus:
*But I care nothing for taunts, for being a friend to my friends, I am useful in deeds, not just in words.* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐδὲν μέλει...</note> That is to say:
But I do not dwell on witty insults,
Since I am a friend to a friend in deeds; nor
Is it my purpose to be helpful in words alone,
But in reality and action at the same time.
The very figure of speech reveals it as a proverb, just as we demonstrated at the beginning. It will apply to those who shrink from no duty, provided they please their friends. To this, that line of Euripides in *Medea* seems related:
*Heavy to enemies and well-disposed to friends.* <note>original Greek: Βαρεῖαν ἐχθροῖς καὶ φίλοισιν εὐμενῆ</note> That is:
Benevolent to friends, but harsh to enemies.
Theocritus in *The Beloved*:
*But they loved each other with an equal yoke; surely then there were golden men of old, when the one loved returned the love of the lover.* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλήλους δ’ ἐφίλησαν...</note> That is:
Equal love to both; the golden mortals once
Lived then, when the loved one loved the lover back.
Aristotle, according to Laertius, was often accustomed to say: *O friends, there is no friend,* <note>original Greek: ὦ φίλοι, φίλος οὐδείς</note> signifying that true friendship had perished among mortals.

### Even gods are captured by gifts. XVIII

As Ovid wrote:
*Gifts (believe me) capture both men and gods:*
*Jupiter himself is appeased by the giving of presents.*
Euripides in *Medea* shows that this was celebrated in common speech when he says:
*The saying goes that gifts persuade even the gods. Gold is stronger than ten thousand words for mortals.* <note>original Greek: πείθειν δῶρα καὶ θεὺς λόγος...</note> That is:
They say that even the gods themselves are swayed by gifts.
Certainly among men, more than a thousand words,
Yellow gold prevails and truly outweighs all.
This little verse is also celebrated, which Plato also used in the third book of *The Republic*:
*Gifts persuade the gods and venerable kings.* <note>original Greek: Δῶρα θεὺς πείθει καὶ αἰδοίους βασιλῆας</note>
With gifts they sway the gods and venerable kings.
Hence Seneca, reporting the <term>apophthegm (pithy saying)</term> of a certain philosopher, says: *Of all things, it is most difficult to accept.*

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning the loyalty of friends during hardship and the cynical reality that both gods and men are easily swayed by bribery and gifts.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, loyalty, bribery, Euripides, Aristotle, Ovid, Plato, Seneca, Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the collection of Greek and Latin adages, following the previous entries in the third century of the first chiliad.</meta>

### XIX. Hand off the slate.

Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> says in a certain letter: "Hey you, hand off the slate! The master is here sooner than you think." <note>original: "Heus tu manum de tabula. Magister adest citius quam putas."</note> It appears that by this proverbial figure of speech, "hand off the slate," he was warning someone to stop writing satires. However, it clearly alludes to a saying by Apelles, the most noble painter. When he was admiring a work by Protogenes—a work of immense labor and excessively anxious care—he remarked that everything between them was equal, or even that Protogenes was better, except in one thing: Apelles surpassed him because Protogenes did not know when to "take his hand off the slate." This is a memorable precept: that excessive diligence often does harm. Pliny mentions this in Book 35, Chapter 10. Therefore, whenever we advise someone to step away from a tedious task they have in hand, we shall tell them to "lift their hand from the slate." This will apply aptly to certain writers who are more than sufficiently precise and possess a sort of morose diligence; they suppress their late-night labors without end, always adding or changing something, and they sin most in this very way: by trying to commit no sin at all.

<sig>XX</sig>

### I prefer to buy rather than to ask.

Tully, in his speeches against Verres, cites this as a proverb: "I prefer to buy rather than to ask." <note>original: "Emere malo quam rogare."</note> By this he means that what is bought with prayers is by no means received for free; indeed, nothing is bought more dearly than what is requested. For that word "I ask" <note>original: "Rogo"</note> is harsh to noble minds, and according to Seneca, it should never be expected even among friends. The phrase is derived from an old custom where a neighbor would ask to borrow furniture from a neighbor which he perhaps did not have at home. That this was the custom in ancient times can be learned from Plautus's *Aulularia* and *Rudens*. Apuleius also says in his *Florida*: "He who prays does not buy at a light price, nor does he who is asked receive a small price," so much so that you would rather buy all your utensils than ask for them. The same sentiment is found in a Greek proverb celebrated by Mercury, which he rendered elsewhere as: "Pray to have a neighbor, but more so to have a pot." <note>original: "εὐχοῦ τὸν πλησίον ἔχειν, ἀλλ’ πλέον δὲ τὴ χύτρα"</note> This means it is indeed desirable to have a wealthy neighbor from whom you can borrow what you lack at home, but it is much better to possess whatever the use of life requires in your own house.

<sig>XXI</sig>

### I wouldn't turn a hand. I wouldn't stretch out a finger.

This is a proverbial hyperbole: "I wouldn't turn a hand," <note>original: "Manum non uerterim"</note> used for when I do not labor at all, or it matters nothing to me. For nothing is easier than to turn a hand. It appears among others in Cicero's *Apology for Magic*: "What Mezentius thinks of me," he says, "I wouldn't turn a hand." Cicero also says in Book 5 of *On Ends*: "They would not even turn a hand." In Book 3 of the same work, he writes: "Chrysippus and Diogenes used to say that if utility were removed, one should not even stretch out a finger for the sake of it." I strongly agree with them. He is discussing glory or fame there, which should be entirely despised if it brings no utility, according to that line from the *Satires*: "Is your knowledge nothing, unless another knows that you know it?" And, "What will it be, however great, if it is only glory?" We have spoken of the "turned thumb" elsewhere. Furthermore, Quintilian writes in Book 11 that the gestures of the hands have so much weight in delivery that they seem to speak in a manner like a second language on behalf of all words. But that gesture is a source of wonder where the hand, slightly turned upwards, is unfolded and turned at the same time as the fingers are gathered one by one starting from the smallest. We turn the hand for a question, however it is composed. Even today, we flip an upright hand whenever we signify the smallest difference. In the passage I just cited from Quintilian, where it says "on behalf of all words," I think it is more correctly read as "on behalf of all members" <note>original: "pro omnibus membris"</note>; so that you signify that whatever can be expressed by the gesture of the other parts of the body, the hand alone can provide. In Plutarch's *Life of Timoleon*, a certain man sent to Andromachus, after many things said inhumanly and barbarically, finally stretched out his hand and showed it now palm up, now palm down, threatening by this gesture that he would overturn their city. But Andromachus, laughing, did nothing but turn his hand similarly from palm up to palm down, and ordered him to leave as soon as possible, unless he wanted his ship to be turned over in the same way.

<sig>XXII</sig>

### The Leontines are always near the bowls.

"The Leontines are always around the mixing bowls." <note>original: "Ἀεὶ Λεοντῖνοι περὶ κρατῆρας"</note> This was said against those devoted to pleasure, or those always addicted to the same pursuits. The Leontines were a people of Sicily. When Phalaris had conquered them, to prevent them from ever preparing a rebellion, he took away their arms and relegated them to drinking parties and pleasures; and from this was born the adage recorded by Zenobius.

<summary>This page explores four classical adages concerning the importance of knowing when to stop working, the social cost of borrowing, the insignificance of things without utility, and the reputation of the Leontines for decadence.</summary>
<keywords>Apelles, Protogenes, Cicero, Seneca, Quintilian, Timoleon, Phalaris, Leontines, Greek proverbs, Latin adages, artistic diligence, social etiquette, gestures</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### The Cestreus fasts.
->XXIII<-

*The Cestreus fasts* <note>original Greek: Κεστρεὺς νηστεύει</note>. This is appropriately said of the famished and the ravenous. From this, those who gape with hunger are called *cestreus*, and the act is called *cestreuein* <note>to act like a cestreus</note>, which Hesychius records was once a taunt directed at the Athenians. Others prefer to apply it to those who lead an innocent life, abstaining from harming others, yet gain no reward from their innocence. For the *cestreus* <note>likely a species of mullet</note> is a type of fish that, while others survive by devouring one another, is the only one to abstain from the flesh of others; for this reason, it is not caught with bait, but hides itself in the mud and remains there. As some believe, it feeds on mud. Indeed, even when captured, it does not feed on bait or any living creature, despite having sharp teeth. Furthermore, it is devoured by the wolf-fish with impunity, and because it is not a glutton itself, it is considered poor eating. In times of fear, it hides its head, believing its whole body is then safe. Hence Aristophanes says in Athenaeus:
*Is there a colony of Cestreus-men here?* <note>original Greek: Αρ’ ἐνθάδ’ εἰσὶν ἄνδρες κεστρέων ἀποικία;</note> ->This alludes to Cestrina, a part of Chaonia.<-
And Diphilus in the same author:
*I would be a Cestreus for the sake of this extreme fasting.* <note>original Greek: Κεστρεὺς ἂν εἴην ἕνεκα νηστείας ἄκρας.</note>
Again, in the seventh book, he cites from Anaxandrides:
*While eating many things like perch, he is a fasting mullet.* <note>original Greek: τὰ πολλά δ’ ἐσθίοντες ὥσπερ πέρκαι, κεστρινός ἐστι νῆστις.</note>
The adage is recorded by Zenodotus, Diogenianus, Suidas, and Athenaeus in the seventh book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The Banquet of the Learned</note>, who adds among many other things that the fish is called the "sailor" <note>original: ploten</note> by some, and is devoured by the conger eel, just as the conger is devoured by the moray. Theodorus Gaza translates it as *mugil* <note>the mullet</note>.

### Where there are friends, there is wealth.
->XXIIII<-

Plautus says in the *Truculentus*: "It is a true word that is remembered: where there are friends, there also is wealth." It is also cited as a proverb by Quintilian <note>referred to here as Fabio</note> in the fifth book of his *Institutes of Oratory*. The meaning is that friends are more powerful than money, and that for the protection of one's life, friends without money carry more weight than wealth without friends. Hence among the Scythians, according to Lucian, he was considered the wealthiest who possessed the most loyal and best friends. However, if one looks at the morals of this current age, one might think the adage should be inverted: *where there is wealth, there are friends.* Since:
> The common crowd judges friendships by their utility. And,
> That once venerable name of friendship
> Is for sale, and sits like a prostitute for gain.

### The earth flies.
->XXV<-

*The earth flies* <note>original Greek: Η γῆ ἵπταται</note>. Said of something violently absurd, which can in no way happen. Suidas brings this forward as an example of "the impossible." Julian, in a certain letter, cites it as a proverb with a changed verb: *The earth is a trifle, as the saying goes.* This adage belongs to the same family as those we have recorded elsewhere: *Jupiter is childless* and *There is nothing hard inside the olive, nor outside the nut.*

### An Iliad of woes.
->XXVI<-

*An Iliad of woes* <note>original Greek: Ἰλιὰς κακῶν</note>. Said of calamities that are both very great and very numerous. This is because in Homer’s *Iliad*, no kind of evil is left unmentioned. From this, learned men believe the plots of tragedies were taken, just as comedies were taken from the *Odyssey*. It is a wordy work, barely finished in twenty-four volumes. Hence Demosthenes says: *Having said these things, he handed the decree to the scribe to read; it was longer than the Iliad, but emptier than the speeches he usually gives.* Eustathius inverts the adage in this manner: *The proverb speaks of an Iliad of evils, but this is an Iliad of all things good.* Synesius in a letter to his brother: *In short, an Iliad of woes besieges our city.* Plutarch in his *Conjugal Precepts*: *But the marriage of those two created an Iliad of woes for the Greeks and barbarians.* For he is speaking of the marriage of Paris and Helen, which was the cause of inestimable evils.

<summary>Erasmus explains four adages: the "Cestreus" (a fish) as a symbol of fasting or innocence, the value of friendship over wealth, the impossibility of the "flying earth," and the "Iliad of woes" as a metaphor for immense suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Cestreus, mullet, friendship, wealth, impossibility, Iliad, Homer, Demosthenes, Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the collection of Greek and Latin adages (proverbs) compiled by Erasmus, focusing on metaphors for abundance, specifically regarding evils and misfortunes.</meta>

# FIRST THOUSAND, THIRD HUNDRED
<meta>catchword: Heap</meta>

<margin>A Lerna of evils.</margin>
### XXVII
<note>original: "Λέρνη κακῶν"</note> **A Lerna of evils.** That is, a "Lerna of evils," used likewise for many evils gathered and heaped together in one place at the same time. Strabo mentions this proverb in the eighth book of his *Geography*, writing that Lerna was a certain lake shared by the territories of Argos and Mycenae. Because refuse was brought there from all sides by everyone, the common proverb was born: <note>original: "Λέρνη κακῶν"</note> **A Lerna of evils.** In this lake, the poets imagine that the famous seven-headed Hydra lived, which Hercules destroyed with Greek fire <note>an incendiary weapon</note>. Hesiod writes that this Hydra was the offspring of Echidna and Typhaon, raised by Juno—doubtless out of her hatred for Hercules. Zenodotus says there was a certain place in the Argolid where, because they threw every kind of filth indiscriminately, foul and pestilential mists used to be exhaled from it. However, he also reports and suggests that the adage may refer to the fable of the Danaids. For they say that the fifty young sons of Aegyptus, to whom Danaus had married his fifty daughters, were all slaughtered in the same night, and their heads were piled up in that place. From this, the proverb arose. Nor does he deny it possible that, as an insult, he ordered refuse to be carried to the same place where the captives had been heaped. Therefore, whenever we mean a person who is remarkably infamous and contaminated by every kind of baseness, or a gathering of pestilential men—a virtual sinkhole and cesspool of criminals—we shall rightly say: <note>original: "Λέρνην κακῶν"</note> **A Lerna of evils.** In Hesychius, the comic poet Cratinus called a theater consisting of a varied and mixed dregs of humanity <note>original: "Λέρνην θεατῶν"</note> **A Lerna of spectators.**

<margin>A sea of evils.</margin>
### XXVIII
<note>original: "Κακῶν θάλασσα"</note> **A sea of evils.** That is, "A sea of evils," usually said of immense and oceanic calamities. It is taken from the fact that the sea is something infinite, or because infinite waves break upon those who are tossed within it. Euripides in *Hippolytus the Crown-Bearer*:
> Into what a sea of evils have I entered, wretched man,
> From which I shall never swim out again.

That is,
> I behold, miserable, so great a sea of evils,
> From which no hope of swimming out shines forth.

Plautus, in the *Asinaria*, calls a prostitute and a madam "the sea," as if they were the authors of all calamities. "The sea," he says, "is not the sea; you are the most bitter sea." Aeschylus in *The Suppliants*:
> A multitude of evils rushes in like a flooding river,
> An abyss, a sea of ruin, not easily crossed.

That is,
> A disaster of evils rushes in like a river,
> And this deep sea, as if it lacked a bottom,
> Cannot be sailed without the greatest danger.

Hence, even the Sacred Scriptures, when signifying the inexhaustible force of something, call it an "abyss." Thus Saint Chrysostom, in the sixth book of *On the Priesthood*, says: "Behold the abyss of cares." "Look," he says, "at the immense sea of labors."

<margin>A sea of goods.</margin>
### XXIX
It is also said in the opposite sense, <note>original: "ἀγαθῶν θάλασσα"</note> **A sea of goods.** That is, "A sea of blessings," regarding great and powerfully accumulated advantages. Either because the sea itself provides innumerable riches of things—fish and gems—or because it is so vast and deep that it cannot be exhausted, nor does it ever overflow, even though such a great force of rivers flows into it.

<margin>A treasury of evils.</margin>
### XXX
<note>original: "Κακῶν θησαυρός"</note> **A treasury of evils.** That is, "A storehouse of evils." It is found in the same manner elsewhere, as in Euripides' *Ion*:
> How the great treasury of evils is opened!

That is,
> How great a treasury—I might say a vast larder—of evils is spread open.

Hence, among the Greek maxims, there is this six-foot line:
> A bad woman is a treasury of evils to a bad man.

That is,
> A woman is a treasury of evils, if she is bad.

Plautus brought this adage here in the *Mercator*: "You have indeed brought a treasury of evil here." From this also comes that phrase in the Sacred and Secret <note>mystical or divine</note> Scriptures: "He treasures up evil for himself," that is, they collect, summon, and as it were, store it away. For we properly call a "treasury" a force of useful things stored up together.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs describing overwhelming abundance, using metaphors like the swamp of Lerna, the infinite sea, and the storehouse to characterize both extreme misfortune and great wealth.</summary>
<keywords>Lerna, Hercules, Danaids, sea metaphors, Euripides, Plautus, Chrysostom, abundance, Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<meta>catchword: Set before</meta>

### A heap of goods.
-> XXXI <-

*Agathōn sōros* <note>original: Ἀγαθῶν σωρὸς</note>. That is, a heap of good things. Used in reference to immense wealth. Hence we frequently read of "heaped-up feasts," "heaped-up riches," and "accumulated wealth" to describe abundance, as if they were piled up in a mound, measured neither by weight nor number, but poured out by the pile itself. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
> For a heap of good things has rushed into our house,
> though we have done no wrong. <note>original: ἡμῖν γὰρ ἀγαθῶν σωρὸς εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν / ἐπεισπέπαικεν, οὐδὲν ἠδικηκόσιν.</note>

The same author in the same play:
> How I bring you all good things in a mass. <note>original: ὡς ἀγαθὰ συλλήβδην ἅπαντά σοι φέρω.</note>

Again, in the same play, he turns the phrase jokingly toward a bad sense:
> For it is clear you have come bringing a heap of money. <note>original: δῆλος γὰρ εἶ σωρὸν ἥκειν χρημάτων ἔχοντα.</note>

These are the words of the chorus of old men, to whom the servant Carion jokingly replies:
> Rather, let him bring to you a heap of old men's miseries. <note>original: πρεσβυτικῶν μὲν οὖν κακῶν ἔγωγ’ ἔχοντα σωρόν.</note>

He alluded, however, to their old age, which was already near the grave. For *soros* <note>original: σορός</note> written with a short 'o' <term>omicron: the Greek letter for a short 'o'</term> signifies a funeral mound or coffin, while *sōros* <note>original: σωρὸς</note> with a long 'o' <term>omega: the Greek letter for a long 'o'</term> means a mound or heap. Therefore, it is likely that the servant intentionally mispronounced the syllable of that word. These and other similar phrases are more elegant, as we have often advised, if they are twisted slightly away from their simple meaning. For example, if one were to say that in other orators various virtues of speaking stand out, but in Marcus Tullius [Cicero] alone there is "a heap of all good things" <note>original: τῶν πάντων ἀγαθῶν σωρὸν εἶναι</note>. Those familiar phrases of Cicero reflect the nature of this adage: "to heap up with favors," "to satisfy most heapingly [abundantly]," and "a heap of merits."

### An anthill of goods.
-> XXXII <-

*Agathōn myrmēkia* <note>original: Ἀγαθῶν μυρμηκία</note>. That is, an anthill of goods, used for immense riches. For *Myrmecia* in Greek signifies a cavern or a column of ants. Although it may seem to be taken from those ants mentioned by Pliny in Book 11, Chapter 31, which he says are the color of cats and the size of Egyptian wolves. He says that in the northern region of the Indians, who are called the Dardae, these ants dig gold out of caverns. The Indians steal this gold, which is dug up in winter, during the summer heat, while the ants are hidden inside their burrows because of the warmth; yet the ants, sensing the scent, fly out with great speed and often tear the thieves to pieces, even though they flee on very swift camels. Saint Basil seems to have looked to this when he wrote to his nephews that whatever remained beyond the necessity of use—whether it be Lydian soil or the work of gold-bearing ants—should be despised all the more because there was less need for it. Yet nothing prevents this from being referred to our own common ants, not only because of the innumerable multitude of their columns, but also because of a certain natural industry of the creature in accumulating its store, dragging with its mouth whatever it can and adding it to the heap, as Horace <note>original: Flaccus</note> wrote. Indeed, I believe it happened because of this that in ancient times a gathering of ants portended wealth. As Cicero testifies in Book 1 of *On Divination*: when Midas the Phrygian was a boy, ants piled grains of wheat into his mouth while he slept. It was predicted he would be very rich, which came to pass. Theocritus alluded to this in his *Encomium of Ptolemy*:
> Just as a multitude of laboring ants is always poured out. <note>original: μυρμάκων ἅτε πλῆτος ἀεὶ κέχυται μογεόντων.</note>
> Wealth is piled up.

The same in the *Syracusans*:
> Ants without joints and without measure. <note>original: μύρμακος ἀνάρθμοι καὶ ἄμετροι.</note>

Signifying a frequent crowd of men. Akin to this type is what Plato said in Book 9 of the *Republic*: "a swarm of pleasures" <note>original: τὸ τῶν ἡδονῶν σμήνος</note>, and Socrates in Plutarch of Chaeronea: "a swarm of virtues" <note>original: ἀρετῶν σμήνος</note>, for an immense crowd and number. Furthermore, the passage Plutarch cites is in Plato's *Meno*. Close to these is what the same author cites in the *Cratylus*: "a swarm of wisdom" <note>original: σμήνος σοφίας</note>, that is, a swarm of learning. Likewise, what Alexis wrote in *Pamphila*, as recorded in Athenaeus, Book 8:
> I set the table, then bringing in wagons of good things... <note>original: παρέθηκα τὴν τράπεζαν, εἶτα παραφέρων Ἀγαθῶν ἁμάξας</note>

# FIRST CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
k
<meta>catchword: impious</meta>

...so the table was set, and thereafter he brought in wagons of Good Things.

### 33. A Dathus of good things.
<margin>A Dathus of good things. <note>original Greek: Δάθος ἀγαθῶν</note></margin> That is, a "Dathus of good things": it is customarily said with the same meaning as the previous entry. Now, Dathus is a colony of the Thasians near the Strymon river; while it is otherwise opulent and flourishing, it also possesses veins of gold, so that from this fact it passed into a proverb, "A Dathus of good things," referring to a dense abundance of resources. Among others, Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> mentions the proverb, though in his work we read *Datos*, not *Dathus*.

### 34. A Thassus of good things.
<margin>A Thassus of good things. <note>original Greek: Θάθος ἀγαθῶν</note></margin> That is, a "Thassus of good things." A similarly born adage, namely from the fertility of the place. For Thassus is an island near Thrace. Zenodotus relates a certain story of this kind: Callistratus the orator, departing from Athens, tried to persuade the Athenians to inhabit the region lying opposite, boasting many splendid things about its fruitfulness—both that it had veins of gold and the finest soil. Finally, in short, he said, "It is a Thassus of good things." From this it passed into common speech, "A Thassus of good things," used for those who make splendid promises.

### 35. Gifts of enemies are no gifts.
The superstition of the ancients believed that gifts should be observed most carefully—by whom and with what intent they were given—because those given by people who wished us ill were frequently a source of destruction. Such was that deceptive box sent to Prometheus by Jove through Pandora; just like the robe with which Medea gifted the new bride of Jason; and again that robe which Deianira sent to Hercules. Interpreters of proverbs think this maxim was born from the history related in Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 7. It tells how Hector and Ajax, having ended their combat in friendship, exchanged gifts between themselves: Hector gave Ajax a sword, and Ajax gave Hector a belt. Subsequently, the gift of each proved fatal to both. For Ajax, defeated by Ulysses and realizing what he had said and done during his madness, took his own life with that very sword. Likewise, Hector was killed and dragged through the valley by the walls of Troy by means of that belt. 

The adage is cited in Sophocles’ *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*, but it is cited in such a way that it seems not to have originated with Ajax, but rather to have been used by him as an already ancient saying. For after he had resolved to die, he cursed that sword which he had received as a gift from his greatest enemy, saying it had been most ill-omened for him, and never thereafter had anything succeeded happily for him among the Greeks. Then, confirming this suspicion with a common saying, he says:
> The gifts of enemies are no gifts, and bring no profit. <note>original Greek: Ἐχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα, κ’ οὐκ ὀνήσιμα</note>
> That is:
> Truly it is a proverb of mortals,
> Gifts of enemies are gifts that come to you
> Unlucky, truly ill-omened and harmful.

Regarding this matter, a Greek epigram is related as follows:
> Hector gave a sword to Ajax, and to Hector, Ajax
> Gave a belt. The favor of both led to death.
> <note>original Greek: Ἕκτωρ Αἴαντι ξίφος ὤπασεν, ἕκτορι δ’ Αἴας / Ζωστήρ’. ἀμφοτέρων ἡ χάρις εἰς θάνατον.</note>

Again, from another epigram:
> Gifts from enemies were sent as non-beneficial gifts,
> And under the guise of care, they hold a fate of death.
> <note>original Greek: Δῶρα παρ’ ἐχθρῶν οὐκ ὀνίμονα πέμπετο δῶρα / Καὶ μετὰ φειδοῦς πότμος μοῖραν ἔχοντα μόρον.</note>

There is also that line in Euripides where Medea, refusing the guest-gifts of Jason as if they would bring ruin, says:
> For the gift of a wicked man has no profit.
> <note>original Greek: Κακοῦ γὰρ ἀνδρὸς δῶρ’ ὄνησιν οὐκ ἔχει.</note>

By which he shows that Virgil also alluded to this when he says in the *Aeneid*, Book 4:
> ...he unsheathes
> The sword, a gift not sought for such a use.

He speaks of the sword left behind by Aeneas, with which Dido stabbed herself; whom [she considered] Aeneas an enemy, and...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

the same [scripture] calls him impious. To this section we should add what the proverbs of Holy Scripture warn: that we should never feel secure regarding a reconciled enemy. Likewise, there is that proverbial iambic verse:
*Never consider the words of an enemy to be those of a friend.* <note>original Greek: λόγου παρ' ἐχθροῦ μὴ πότ' ἡγήση φίλου</note> That is to say:
Never deem words spoken by a foe to be friendly.
And another similar to it:
*By distrusting enemies, you shall never suffer harm.* <note>original Greek: ἐχθροῖς ἀπίστω μὴ πότ' ἂν πάθοις βλάβην</note> That is:
Distrusting a foe, you will bear no evil.

The proverb can also be applied to those who, being poor, try to ensnare the wealthy with small gifts, as if drawing out their liberality in that manner. For this is not giving a gift, but demanding one. Hence Plutarch, in his short commentary *On the E at Delphi*, approves of what Dicaearchus thinks was said by Euripides to Archelaus:
*I, a poor man, do not wish to give gifts to a rich man, lest you judge me a fool, or lest in giving, I seem to be begging.* <note>original Greek: οὐ βούλομαι πλουτοῦνti δωρεῖσθαι πένης, μή μ' ἄφρονα κρίνης, ἢ διδούς, αἰτεῖν δοκῶ</note> That is:
I would wish to give nothing as a poor man to a rich one,
Lest I be held a fool, of course, if under the
Title and appearance of a gift, I seem to be asking for one.

It will also fit those who use the services of demons through the magical arts; for these ultimately result in the destruction of those who use them. It applies to legacy-hunters, and finally to those who try to win favor through any service, not from the heart, but looking toward something else. Therefore, by changing a small word, the proverb can be renewed: namely in this way, *The gifts of flatterers are no gifts*, and *The gifts of strangers are no gifts*, and finally *The gifts of poets are no gifts*, just as we advised at the beginning of this work.

->I am Davus, not Oedipus. XXXVI<-

The intellect of Oedipus was made famous by his skill in both proposing and solving the "cups" <note>A metaphor for difficult riddles</note> of enigmas, on account of his solving the problems of the Sphinx, so much so that the use of his name passed into a proverb. As in Terence’s *Andria*, the slave Davus, pretending not to understand what his master had said, says: "I am Davus, not Oedipus." This can be adapted to anyone by changing the name: "I am Paul, not Oedipus"; "I am Anthony, not Oedipus." Indeed, the figure itself is proverbial and can be fashioned in the same way from any person or thing made famous by common report. For example: "How could I remember all these things? I am Peter, not Lucullus." <note>Lucullus was famous for his wealth and luxury, but here perhaps implies a man of vast capacity or memory</note> "How could I be sufficient for such great labors? I am Nicholas, not Hercules." "How will I be able to persuade someone of such a hard matter? I am Richard, not Cicero." But similar to the Terentian saying is that of Euripides in *Hippolytus*:
*I am no prophet to know hidden things clearly.* <note>original Greek: οὐ μάντις εἰμὶ τἀφανῆ γνῶναι σαφῶς</note> That is:
I am no augur, that I might know hidden things openly.
Likewise in *Hecuba*:
*I was not born a prophet, so that without hearing I might investigate the path of your counsels.* <note>original Greek: οὔπω πέφυκα μάντις, ὥστε μὴ κλύων ἐξιστορῆσαι σῶν ὁδὸν βουλευμάτων</note> That is:
I am hardly divine, nor unless I have heard can I
Know the way of your thoughts.

Therefore, this can be twisted against those who intentionally speak obscurely and <term>enigmatically</term> <note>original: αἰνιγματικῶς; speaking in riddles</note>: or against those who, either through ignorance or a superstitious affection for unknown words, obscure their style and stand in more need of a prophet than a reader. Plato testifies in several places that Heraclitus was of this sort, as does Aristotle in the third book of his *Art of Rhetoric*, adding that the man's obscurity arose from an ambiguous composition of words, since it was uncertain whether a certain word should be referred to what preceded or what followed. Consequently, to understand his books, Socrates said there was need of some "Delian diver." <note>A reference to the difficulty of reaching the bottom of Heraclitus's thought</note> Alluding to this, Martial jokes thus against Sextus, an affecter of obscurity:
*Your books need no reader, but Apollo himself.*
*In your judgment, Cinna was greater than Maro [Virgil].*

The grim Jerome reproaches Jovinian with this same Heraclitus and his vice. Although Laertius writes that this philosopher, whenever he pleased, used the most lucid speech, so that it appears his obscurity was intentionally affected, so much so that he was even accustomed to instruct his disciples: *Darkness.* <note>original Greek: σκότος</note> That is, "be obscure."

# THE THIRD CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>k 2</sig>

Soon, he says, the eloquent Solon
Commanded us to speak of the final stages of the extreme end of life.
<note>original: "mox, inquit, facunda Solonis / Dicere extremæ iussit spatia ultima vitæ."</note>
Sophocles expressed this sentiment more copiously in *Oedipus the King*,
<margin>that is,</margin>
"Looking toward that final day, consider no one happy until he has passed the boundary of life without suffering any pain."
<note>original Greek: μηδέν' ὀντ' ἐκείνην τὴν τελευταίαν ἰδεῖν... This is a famous Greek tragic trope: "Call no man happy until he is dead."</note>
That final day of the fates must be awaited by a mortal, so that he judges no one blessed unless he has completed his entire span of time having suffered no evil.
The same author expressed the same idea somewhat differently in the *Women of Trachis*,
<margin>that is,</margin>
"There is an ancient saying among men, that you cannot fully know the life of mortals before someone dies—whether it was good or whether it was bad for them."
<note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ἔστ' ἀρχαῖος ἀνθρώπων φανείς...</note>
This proverb exists of old among men: that no one can truly know anyone, whether they be good or bad, before the fatal years are finished and they have met their final day.
<margin>Similarly Euripides in *Andromache*, that is,</margin>
"One must never call any of the mortals blessed until you see the final day of the one who has died."
<note>original Greek: χρὴ δ' οὔποτ' εἰπεῖν ὄλβιον βροτῶν...</note>
Do not pronounce any of the mortals to be blessed ever, until you have seen the final day of the deceased.
<margin>The same in *The Trojan Women*, that is,</margin>
"Consider none of those who are prosperous to be fortunate until they die."
<note>original Greek: τῶν δ' εὐδαιμόνων / μηδένα νομίζετ' εὐτυχεῖν πρὶν ἂν θάνῃ.</note>
Do not announce any of these, whom Fortune carries forward with favorable breezes, to be blessed until they have departed life happily.
<margin>"In the present fortune"</margin>
He repeats the same in other words in *The Children of Heracles*,
"For I proclaim to all, to everyone, that they should learn not to envy the one who seems to be fortunate until they see him dead, for fortunes last but a day."
<note>original Greek: πᾶσι γὰρ ἅπασι λαμπρὰ κηρύσσω μαθεῖν...</note>
<margin>that is,</margin>
In this very state of affairs, he openly warns mortals that no one should think a man blessed just because he is carried away by prosperous successes, until they have seen him depart from life. For the turns of events are so changeable.
<margin>Ovid expressed it thus in the *Metamorphoses*,</margin>
"Indeed, the final day must always be awaited for a man, and no one ought to be called blessed before his death and final funeral rites."
<note>original: "Scilicet ultima semper / Expectanda dies homini est..."</note>
Even today, it is on everyone's lips everywhere: "A matter must be judged by its outcome."

<margin>Cant. Lect. 96.</margin>
### XXXVIII
Second thoughts are better.
<note>original: "Posterioribus melioribus."</note>
Among the Greek proverbs, this is recorded: "Second things are better." By this they signified that those things which had succeeded poorly in the first attempt sometimes turn out better on the second, and the error of the prior plan is corrected by the later plan. Indeed, many think this originated from sacred rites, in which if the first victim had not been favorable, they would repeat the sacrifice hoping for better omens. This is sufficiently indicated by the pimp in Plautus, who, having slaughtered a victim to Venus, was often unable to obtain a favorable omen. Plato, in the fourth book of *The Laws*, seems to refer the advice to the throw of dice or a game. This is because it often happens that he for whom the game has fallen inconveniently wishes to play the game anew and asks for it to be repeated, hoping that he will now play more luckily. For he says: "Again in this, as those who play are accustomed to say, let us repeat with second things being better from the start."
<note>original Greek: πάλιν ἐν τούτῳ οἱ παίζοντες, ἀμεινόνων ἐξ ἀρχῆς δευτέρων ἐπαναπολήσωμεν.</note>
Although in this passage "those who play" could refer not to some game, but rather to a playful joke. But Cicero supports the first interpretation in the second book of *On Divination*—

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

In the first book <note>referring to Cicero's *De Divinatione*</note> he says: "What consistency is there in the gods, that they should threaten in the first entrails but promise well in the second?" The same author in the twelfth *Philippic*: "For second thoughts, as they say, are usually wiser." Also to his brother Quintus: "I can have no *second thoughts* <note>original Greek: δευτέρας φροντίδας</note> regarding Caesar’s affairs"; that is, I find no suitable plan by which I can remedy previous evils. Davus, that character from Terence, looked to this when he said:
"It didn't succeed this way; let us try another path."
Indeed, Aristotle seems to have alluded to the same in the first book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original Greek: τῶν μετὰ τὰ φυσικὰ</note> when he says: "For because of wondering, men both now and at the first began to philosophize." He speaks of those who, provoked by admiration of natural causes, approach philosophy. He wishes them, once the causes are known, to cease wondering and turn to better things. Furthermore, the proverb can be seen to have arisen from the tragedy of Euripides titled *Hippolytus*:
> *For somehow second thoughts are wiser.* <note>original Greek: Αἱ δευτεραί πως φροντίδες σοφώτεραι</note>
> That is: Since a later thought is usually
> more prudent for mortals.
These are the words of the nurse to Phaedra, as if recanting and singing a "palinode" <note>a poem retracting a previous sentiment</note> of her earlier speech, after she sees that Phaedra is thinking of dying. He also looked to this in *The Suppliants*:
> *But if anything is not well in the home,*
> *we correct it with later judgments,*
> *but for a lifetime, it is not possible.* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἐν δόμοις μὲν ἤν τι μὴ καλῶς ἔχῃ, γνώμαισιν ὑστέραισιν ἐξορθούμεθα, αἰῶνα δ’ οὐκ ἔξεστιν</note>
That is: In a house, if something is not quite right, it is permitted to correct it with later opinions, but not so with life. From this, the Greeks also use the term *metanoia* <note>repentance or change of mind</note>, because a later thought perceives that things should have been done differently.

### It is finished. XXXIX
Proverbially, even today we signify despair with these words: "It is finished" <note>Latin: Actum est</note>; the Greeks say *pepraktai* <note>πέπρακται</note>. Euripides in *Hippolytus*:
> *Alas, alas, it is finished; the queen is no more.* <note>original Greek: φεῦ φεῦ πέπρακται, βασιλὶς οὐκ ἔτ’ ἔστι δή</note>
Terence in *The Eunuch*: "It is finished, it is over, you have perished." Donatus <note>a 4th-century grammarian</note> thinks "it is finished" is taken from the law; "it is over" <note>ilicet</note> from the judgment; and "you have perished" from the punishment. For these three words together indicate despair by a certain progression. Since it was not right to rescind the sentence of the judges, or to obtain a judgment twice on the same matter (as Terence says), it became commonly accepted that one would say "it is finished" regarding hopeless business, even if it was later found that some were restored to their original state by a judge. Or certainly it was said because whatever is finished cannot now be undone, according to proverbial sentiments which testify that not even God is permitted to make what has been done undone. Plautus: "Unless you prepare some defense for the matter, this thing is finished. Death is certain." We say it either absolutely, "It is finished," or with some addition of this kind: "It is finished for the republic," "It is finished for all your people," "It is finished for human affairs," "It is finished for your safety, unless you stay awake."

### To have the thing done. XL
Almost the opposite of this is that which is read several times in Martial: "To have the thing done" <note>Latin: Rem factam habere</note>, used for that which is certain and indubitable. Indeed, promises are hardly certain. But you can finally trust those things which have already been performed and exhibited. As to Procillus:
"You thought the thing was done for you immediately." Again: "Now you believe you have the thing done, Bithynicus." He said "the thing done" as if it were not promised, but prepared and completed. From which we also call silver "wrought" <note>factum</note>—not raw, but worked and engraved. Or he looked to legal custom, according to which Terence said: "All things done and transacted." And Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the third invective against Catiline: "And that which had to be done first, has been done and transacted." This is used in contracts whenever everything pertaining to a legitimate agreement is applied.

### To sell smoke. XLI
An exceedingly elegant adage exists in Martial: "To sell smoke" <note>Latin: fumos uendere</note>, used for the practice of selling the goodwill of princes for a price, under the pretense of a recommendation and the opportunity of familiarity. For smoke at the beginning seems to be something great, but it vanishes instantly. This is Martial's poem:
> *Neither to sell empty smoke around the palaces,*
> *Nor to applaud Canus, nor to applaud Glaphyrus.*
