# CHILIAD I, CENTURY III
### k 3

...and we vomit out a deceptive hope and display of great things, which are nothing but smoke and mists. Saint Jerome <note>original: "Diuus Hieron."</note> in his work *Against Rufinus* says: "From such a forest of books, you cannot produce a single sprout or fruit. These are true smokes, these are mists." For Rufinus had reproached Jerome, claiming that Jerome cast the writings of poets like "smoke" before virgins who would not understand them. But Jerome retorts with the weapon of the proverb, which had been unskillfully thrown, and hurls it back at him more learnedly, indicating that by this word he does not mean obscurity, but rather a vain and false display. Plutarch, in *On the Daemon of Socrates*, writes: <term>ἡ δὲ τύφου ὥσπερ τινὰ καπνὸν φιλοσοφίας εἰς τοὺς ἰδιώτας ἀποσκεδάννυσι</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is: "But vanity scatters a kind of smoke of philosophy among the unlearned." <note>Erasmus translates the Greek 'idiotas' as 'sophistas' in his Latin text, but the Greek refers to common people or non-experts.</note> Furthermore, Helius Lampridius elegantly and clearly explains that this type of man is the greatest plague of royal courts in his *Life of the Emperor Heliogabalus*. I have chosen to include his words here: "Zoticus," he says, "had such influence under him that he was regarded by all the chief officials as if he were the master’s husband. Moreover, this same Zoticus, using this pretext of familiarity, sold all of Heliogabalus’s words and deeds, hunting for enormous riches by 'selling smoke' <note>The phrase 'selling smoke' (fumos vendere) refers to the practice of taking bribes in exchange for influencing a ruler, often when no such influence is actually exerted.</note>, promising various things to different people while deceiving them all. Leaving the Emperor’s presence, he would say to individuals: 'I spoke this about you,' 'I heard this about you,' 'This is going to happen to you.' Such are the men who, if admitted to excessive familiarity with princes, sell the reputation not only of bad princes but even of good ones; and they feed on the infamous rumors of emperors who, through foolishness or innocence, do not see through this." So far Lampridius. 

But he made the punishment of Thurinus Verconius even more notable, which Helius reports in the *Life of Alexander Severus* in this manner: "Alone," he says, "in the afternoon or morning hours, he never saw anyone except those he knew had lied about him, specifically Verconius Thurinus. Because he had been an intimate friend, Thurinus had sold everything—even through fabrications—in such a way that he brought infamy upon Alexander’s rule as if he were a foolish man whom Thurinus held in his power and could persuade of anything. He had convinced everyone that everything was done at his nod. Finally, Alexander caught him with this trick: he sent someone to ask for something publicly from himself, but to secretly ask Thurinus for protection, so that he might plead for him to Alexander in private. When this was done and Thurinus had promised his support, claiming he had said certain things to the Emperor when he had said nothing, but that it depended on further effort to obtain it, he waited for the outcome. When Alexander ordered the man to petition again, and Thurinus, as if busy with other things, merely nodded to him but said nothing in the meantime, the request was nonetheless granted. When Thurinus received huge rewards as a 'seller of smoke' from the man who had earned the favor, Alexander ordered him to be accused. After everything was proven by witnesses—those present when he took the money and those who heard what he promised—Alexander ordered him to be tied to a stake in the Transitional Forum. There, he killed him by setting a fire of wet straw and wood to create smoke, while a herald cried out: 'He is punished by smoke, who sold smoke.' Yet, lest he seem too cruel in only one case, he investigated most diligently before condemning him, and found that Thurinus had often taken money from both sides in legal cases when selling outcomes, and from all who had received commands or provinces." And a little later in the same work: "Nor did he give anyone the opportunity of selling smoke about him, or of speaking ill to him about others, especially after the execution of Thurinus, who had often sold him as a fool and a madman." 

What the "Transitional Forum" <note>The Forum Transitorium in Rome, also known as the Forum of Nerva.</note> was, he seems to explain in the same *Life*, when he says in another place: "He who sold smoke about him and had received a hundred gold pieces from a soldier, he ordered to be raised on a cross along that road where the path of his slaves to the Emperor’s suburban estates was most frequent." Furthermore, we read that the Emperor Avidius Cassius was the first to devise that kind of punishment: placing a very long stake of one hundred and eighty feet <note>The Latin 'materia' here refers to the timber/wood of the stake.</note>, and tying the condemned from top to bottom, he placed a fire at the bottom, so that as some were burned, others were killed by the torture of smoke and fear. So far that author. A truly monstrous punishment, yet worthy of such pestilential deeds. Would that today the courts, not only of princes but also of bishops, did not swarm with this most foul kind of men, and did not have many Thurini—or rather, worse than Thurini—who not only sell a falsely promised service but even sell silence itself, performing a sort of 'Demosthenic' feat <note>A reference to the orator Demosthenes, who was famously bribed to remain silent.</note>; or what is even more wicked, they harm with the poison of their tongues those from whom they have accepted payment for a promised service. Would that the princes of our time would care to imitate Alexander Severus, who, although a pagan, a Syrian by birth, and a very young man, nevertheless acted against...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>original: "DES. ERAS. ROT. ADAGIORVM"</note>

informers, denouncers, thieving judges, "sellers of smoke" <note>A Latin idiom for those who sell false promises of influence at court</note>, and that entire class of courtly plagues, that he was as hostile toward them as he was otherwise of the most gentle character; toward these alone he was implacable. Even in our own time, a proverb is circulated regarding the glittering promises of courtiers. For they speak of "Courtly Incense," meaning that fragrant vapor which is now scattered from a hanging censer during sacred rites. This is not at all far from our own theme. They also add "Courtly Holy Water," referring to that water placed before temples so that those entering or leaving may sprinkle themselves with it <note>implying courtly favors are as common, cheap, or fleeting as holy water at a door</note>.

### 42. The Pillar of the Family
### <note>original: "Columen familiæ. XLII"</note>

Terence used the phrase "Pillar of the Family" in his play *Phormio*, undoubtedly as a proverb. He was describing an elderly slave to whom an old man, about to travel abroad, had entrusted the behavior of the youths and the management of the household, as if to a tutor and guardian. Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century grammarian</note> thinks it is called *columen* just as you might say a "column" (*columna*) upon which the rest of the house rests; hence, in ancient times, senior slaves were called *columellae* ("little columns"). This is supported by that line from Virgil:
*Upon you the whole leaning house reclines.* <note>original: "Inte omnis domus inclinata recumbit."</note>
Likewise, that line of Euripides in *Iphigenia in Tauris*:
*For the male children are the pillars of the houses.* <note>original: "Στῦλοι γὰρ οἴκων εἰσὶ παῖδες ἄρσενες."</note>
Pindar, in his *Olympian Odes*, calls Hector the "Pillar of Troy": *He who overthrew Hector, the invincible, unshakable pillar of Troy.* <note>original: "ὃς ἔκβρ’ ἔσφαλε τροίας ἄμαχον, ἀστραβῆ κίονα."</note> He is speaking here of Achilles. Related to these is what Juvenal said:
*It is a wretched thing to lean upon another’s fame, lest the roof collapse and fall when the pillars are withdrawn.*

### 43. The Anchor of the House
### <note>original: "Ancora domus. XLIII"</note>

Using a similar figure of speech in the same Euripides, Hecuba calls Polydorus the "Anchor" of the family and the race:
*Who now alone remains as the anchor of our race.* <note>original: "ὃς μόνος οἴκων ἄγκυρ’ ἔτ’ ἐμῶν."</note>
Furthermore, we have noted elsewhere—when we explained the "Sacred Anchor"—that "Anchor" is commonly used proverbially by the Greeks to signify a refuge. In short, whatever it is that we lean upon, and in whose reliability we are supported, is called an "anchor." The metaphor is taken from ships which, when supported by anchors, rest as if defended from the waves. Hence also that passage in Aristides’ first *Panathenaic Oration*: *All the Greeks now seemed to be at moorings, as it were, resting upon two anchors.* <note>original: "πάντες ἤδη ὥσπερ ὁρμεῖν ἔδοξαν οἱ ἕλληνες."</note> This is as if they were supported by a double protection. I also cited this passage a little earlier.

### 44. I am Nothing
### <note>original: "Nullus fum. XLIIII"</note>

Those hyperboles found in the comic poets are also proverbial: "I am nothing," "I am slain," and "I am undone." By these, we signify despair and great misfortune. Euripides in *Iphigenia in Tauris*:
*They are clearly nothing at all.* <note>original: "Δῆλοί γ’ εἰσὶν οὐδὲν ὄν’ αμέ."</note>
Again, in *Iphigenia at Aulis*:
*You were nothing, but fortune had struck you down into ruin.* <note>original: "Οὐδὲν καθ’, ἀλλ’ ὀλέπλησο τῇ τύχῃ."</note>
I believe this is the very thing Athenaeus cites from Plato in his tenth book: *For you were not even "it," as the proverb says.* <note>original: "ὑμεῖς γὰρ οὐδ’ ἦν, καθάπερ ἡ παροιμία."</note> Although this refers not to death, but to contempt. It may seem to be taken from Homer, where in the ninth book of the *Odyssey*, Ulysses invents the name "Noman" (*Outis*) for himself—that is, "No one"—hinting that he had almost perished. The Cyclops was deceived by the invention of this name.

### 45. Willing or Unwilling
### <note>original: "Nolens uolens. XLV"</note>

Donatus reminded us that all figures of this kind are proverbial (as shown above), specifically those consisting of opposites, because they seem to possess something of an enigmatic quality. They are frequent among the Greek poets, as in Euripides’ *Hecuba*:
*And he, both unwilling and willing.* <note>original: "ὁ δ’ οὐ θέλων τε καὶ θέλων."</note>
The same in *Iphigenia in Tauris*:
*Indeed, I am an exile in a certain way, unwillingly-willing.* <note>original: "φεύγω τρόπον γε δήτιν’ οὐχ ἑκὼν ἑκών."</note>
To this form belongs what Terence says in the *Andria*: *You were compelled by your own will.*

<summary>Erasmus explores metaphors for stability (pillars and anchors) and expressions of total ruin or internal contradiction (being "nothing" or "unwillingly willing"). He draws on a wide range of classical sources including Terence, Euripides, Pindar, and Homer to explain these common idioms.</summary>

# THE FIRST CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

<meta>catchword: to join</meta>

### To kick against the goad.
->XLVI<-

<margin>To kick against the spikes.</margin> <note>original: "πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν"</note> That is, to strike with the heel against the goads. It means to struggle in vain against those whom you cannot defeat, or to provoke those who, when challenged, may cause you harm. It can also mean to resist fate and misfortune—which you cannot avoid—by bearing them with impatience, whereby you not only fail to escape them but actually double your trouble. For example, if someone who has a quarrelsome wife constantly argues with her, he achieves nothing except making her even more litigious. Terence in *Phormio*: "For it is folly to kick against the goad." Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century Roman grammarian</note> advises that the Greek phrase <term>to shepherd</term> <note>original: "ποιμαίνειν"</note> is used with an ellipsis: for the word "to strike" is missing, which the Greeks express with the verb <term>to kick</term> <note>original: "λακτίζειν"</note>. Plautus in *Truculentus*: "If you strike goads with your fists, it hurts all the more." This adage also appears in the <term>Acts of the Apostles</term> [9:5]: "It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks," which means it is hard to fight against God. Euripides in the *Bacchae*:
> I would rather offer sacrifice to him than, in anger,
> kick against the goads, being a mortal against a god.
Pindar in the *Pythian Odes*: "To kick against the goad is indeed [a slippery path]." The metaphor is drawn from oxen, which farmers prick from behind with sharpened sticks. From this, the term <term>ox-goads</term> <note>original: "βουκέντρα"</note> is used in the proverb:
> Many are the ox-goaders, but few are the plowmen of the earth.
If the oxen ever resist by kicking against the goad, they are injured even more severely, so far are they from harming the goad itself. Plutarch, in his essay <term>On the Control of Anger</term> <note>original: "περὶ τῆς ἀοργησίας"</note>, mentions a certain Ctesiphon, a pantomime performer, who in a fit of rage kicked back at a mule that had kicked him.

### To speak into the ear.
->XLVII<-

<margin>To speak into the ear.</margin> <note>original: "εἰς οὖς λέγειν"</note> That is, "to speak into the ear," a phrase people still commonly use today to mean entrusting something secretly and privately. It is a metaphor taken from those who move close and whisper into the ear so they cannot be overheard by others. Hence that expression found several times in Homer:
> Coming close to his head, so that the others might not learn of it.
Horace in his *Satires*: "I want to say something [in your ear]." Euripides in *Ion*:
> I wish to speak something into your ear, so they may tell you what I want.
Lucian in *The Cock*: "Communicating certain things into the ear with the Syracusans." To this also pertains that Gospel saying [Matthew 10:27]: "And what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops"; that is, what you have received in secret conversations, proclaim openly.

### He hasn't even a penny to buy a rope.
->XLVIII<-

A proverbial hyperbole used for those who suffer from the greatest domestic poverty. Lucian in *Timon*: "Those who yesterday did not have even an <term>obol</term> <note>A small ancient Greek coin</note> to buy a noose." Now, a man must be very poor indeed if, in his wretchedness, he wishes to strangle himself with a noose; but he seems more than the poorest of the poor if he lacks even the tiny coin required to buy the rope to hang himself.

### The fawn against the lion.
->XLIX<-

This is a proverbial allegory: <term>the fawn against the lion</term> <note>original: "ὁ νεβρὸς τὸν λέοντα"</note>. One must understand "attacks," "defeats," or "provokes," or something of that kind depending on the context, whenever the natural order of things is reversed and one who is much inferior in strength overcomes the more powerful. Lucian in *The Dependent Scholar*, speaking of a young man caught by an old man, or a legacy-hunter caught by his target: "Just like that thing in the proverb: the fawn against the lion." Whoever wrote *The Megara* (attributed to Hercules) had this in mind:
> Why, wretched woman, does your illustrious son suffer such boundless things,
> like a lion by a shameless [foe], as if a lion were urged on by a fawn?
This can be applied quite elegantly whenever a far inferior person challenges a more powerful one, or someone many times more ignorant competes with the most learned.

<summary>This page explores four classical proverbs concerning futile resistance to power, secret communication, extreme poverty, and the reversal of natural strength.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
L

->To yoke foxes.<-

Regarding a thing that is clearly absurd, the saying is used: <note>original Greek: ζεύγνυεν τὰς ἀλώπεκας</note> *To yoke foxes*. Virgil says in his *Palaemon*:
> Let him who hates not Bavius love your songs, Maevius,
> And let that same man yoke foxes and milk he-goats.
For the fox is an animal vehemently averse to the plow.

->To milk a he-goat.<-

<note>original Greek: τράγον ἀμέλγειν</note> That is, *To milk a he-goat*: it has the same meaning. Lucian, in his *Life of Demonax*, records among his witty sayings this one: When he observed two philosophers, both equally unlearned, arguing with one another—one proposing ridiculous questions and the other responding with irrelevant answers that had nothing to do with the matter—he said, "Friends, does it not seem that one of these is milking a he-goat, while the other holds a sieve underneath?" It is recorded by Diogenianus in these words: <note>original Greek: Πότερον ὁ τὸν τράγον ἀμέλγων, ἢ ὁ τὸ κόσκινον ὑποτιθείς, ἀφρονέστερος;</note> That is, *Which is the more foolish: the one who milks the he-goat, or the one who holds the sieve?* since both act with equal absurdity. Not far removed from this are the sayings: *The lips have similar lettuce* <note>A proverb meaning "like for like," often used for bad things matching bad things.</note> and *A worthy lid for the pot*.

->Concerning the shadow of an ass.<-

<note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ ὄνου σκιᾶς</note> That is, *Over the shadow of an ass*: used for a matter of no consequence. Sophocles in *Cedalio*, according to Suidas, says: <note>original Greek: τὰ πάντα ὄνου σκιά</note> that is, *all things are the shadow of an ass*: meaning trifles and things of no value. In the same author, Aristophanes says in *Daedalus*: <note>original Greek: περὶ ᾧ νῦν ὁ πόλεμος νῶιν ὑμῖν ἔστι; περὶ ὄνου σκιᾶς</note> that is, *What is this war between you now about? Surely about the shadow of an ass.* Aristotle also cites this in his *Didaskaliai*, saying a certain play existed with this title: <note>original Greek: ὄνου σκιά</note> that is, *The Shadow of an Ass*. I believe it was a comedy by Archippus, which Zenodotus mentions. Lucian in *The Sects* says: <note>original Greek: πάντες, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, περὶ ὄνου σκιᾶς μάχονται οἱ φιλοσοφοῦντες</note> that is, *All philosophers, so to speak, fight to the death over the shadow of an ass.* Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: <note>original Greek: περὶ τοῦ μάχη νῶιν; περὶ ὄνου σκιᾶς</note> that is, *What is our fight about? About the shadow of an ass.* Demosthenes in a certain *Philippic*: <note>original Greek: πρὸς ἅπαντας περὶ τῆς ἐν Δελφοῖς σκιᾶς νυνὶ πολεμῆσαι</note> that is, *To fight with everyone at present over the Delphic shadow.* Accordingly, there are those who believe this adage was first born from the author Demosthenes, recounting a story of this kind: When Demosthenes was once defending a man in a capital case and found the judges inattentive and shouting over his speech, he said, "Lend me your ears for a little while, for I shall tell you a new and charming story, pleasant to hear." When they had pricked up their ears at these words, he said, "A certain young man had hired an ass to carry some goods from Athens to Megara. On the way, when the midday heat grew heavy and he could find no shade to protect himself from the sun's burning, he took off the pack-saddle and, sitting under the ass, covered himself with its shadow. However, the driver would not allow it, pushing the man away and shouting that the ass had been rented, not the ass's shadow. The other man contended the opposite, asserting that the shadow of the ass was also rented to him." And so a most bitter quarrel broke out between them and lasted so long that they even came to blows: the one stubbornly affirming the shadow was not rented, the other responding with equal contention that the shadow was indeed rented. Finally, they went to court. Having spoken these things, when Demosthenes perceived the judges listening intently, he suddenly began to descend from the tribunal. Then, being called back by the judges and asked to finish telling the rest of the story, he said, "You are happy to hear about the shadow of an ass, but you are burdened by hearing the case of a man whose life is in danger?" Plutarch tells it slightly differently in his *Life of Demosthenes* in these words: <note>original Greek: λέγουσι δέ ποτε κωλυόμενον ὑπὸ ἀθηναίων ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ...</note> that is, When the Athenians shouted over him as he spoke in the assembly, he said he wished to tell them something briefly. When silence was made, he said, "A young man in the summer season hired an ass for a fee to use it while traveling from the city to Megara. Furthermore, at noon when the sun was burning fiercely, each of them wanted to get under the shadow of the ass. But they kept each other away, with the one saying he had rented out the ass, not the shadow. In turn, the one who had rented it responded that he had full right to it." And having spoken these things,

# THIRD CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

You are eager to hear about the shadow of an ass, but you do not wish to listen to a man speaking of serious matters?" Some say the ass was hired at Athens, not for Megara, but for Delphi, which is also apparent from the words of Demosthenes, who mentions the "Delphic shadow" at the end of his oration *On the Peace*: <note>original: "οὐκῶν ὄυνθες καὶ κομιδῆ σχέτλιον..."</note> that is, "Is it not therefore foolish and exceedingly wretched, having been so pitted one against another over private and most necessary matters, to now fight with everyone over a Delphic shadow?" Apuleius, in *The Golden Ass*, joked that he was born from this. Menander used this adage in his *Manual*, and Plato in the *Phaedrus*, when he says: "Unskilled orators act shamelessly and dangerously whenever they praise base things as honorable before an ignorant crowd—not concerning the shadow of an ass (a light matter of no importance), but," as he says, "praising a horse as if it were an ass, or evil as if it were good." <note>Erasmus here clarifies that the "shadow of an ass" represents a dispute over nothing.</note> Procopius in a certain letter says: <note>original: "καὶ αὐτὸς δὲ οἶμαι..."</note> that is, "I myself also think, most learned one, that while you feel the opposite regarding the art, you move a dispute over the 'shadow of an ass,' as they say, for the sake of mockery." Origen used the same in the preface to the third book he wrote *Against Celsus*. But it is long since time that we depart from the shadow of the ass, lest someone rightly laugh at us for being more curious than is proper about the shadow of an ass.

### Concerning goat’s wool.
-> LIII <-

Very similar to this is the Latin adage, "Concerning goat’s wool" <term>De lana caprina: a metaphor for a useless argument</term>, which appears to have been born from a similar event: two people fighting contentiously over whether a goat has wool or bristles. Or others who fight over goat hair—a useless thing of the smallest importance—just as the joke is told about "ass's wool." Horace says in his *Epistles* to Lollius:

> One man, prone to compliance more than is right,
> A mocker of the lowest couch, so dreads the rich man's nod
> That you would think a boy was repeating his lessons
> To a cruel master, or an actor playing a second part.
> The other often brawls over goat’s wool,
> Armed for a fight over trifles.

He speaks of those who are peevish in friendship, who take up a quarrel with a friend for however frivolous a cause.

### To dispute about smoke.
-> LIIII <-

Close to this is what is read in Aristophanes' *The Clouds*: <note>original: "Καὶ λεπτολογεῖν ἤδη ζητεῖ..."</note> This was said against philosophers who dispute too anxiously about smoke—that is, about things of nothing. There is no small amount of comic wit in those very words fashioned for the joke: <term>leptologein</term> (to speak subtly) and <term>scholobatein</term> (to walk on shadows/trifles), one of which means to dispute about thin and frivolous things, the other to be tormented, worried, and anxious over mere nonsense. For this reason, he even calls the school of Socrates a "thinking-shop" <note>Greek: phrontisterion</note>.

### Blinder than a mole.
-> LV <-

This is recorded by Suidas and Diogenianus: <note>original: "τυφλότερος ἀσπάλακος"</note> that is, "Blinder than a mole." It is said of those who are blind beyond measure, or who have very little judgment. For the metaphor becomes more pleasant if it is transferred to the mind. Pliny writes in his eleventh book that among the genus of quadrupeds, the mole lacks sight, yet the likeness of eyes is present if one pulls back the overlying membrane. And from this the adage arose.

### Blinder than a "leberis."
-> LVI <-

To the same sentiment belongs this: <note>original: "τυφλότερος λεβερίδος"</note> that is, "Blinder than a leberis." It is cited from Aristophanes. A *leberis* is, as we have shown elsewhere, that dry skin which snakes, cicadas, and other kinds of living creatures cast off whenever they renew their youth. In this skin, only the likeness of eyes appears, and a certain very thin membrane with which the eyes of snakes are covered. There are those who report that this—which is very well known regarding snakes and cicadas—also happens to certain fish. Lycophron, in an iambic poem, calls that skin a *Syphar*:
"The *Syphar* shall perish, having fled the cover of the sea."
Moreover, he calls an old man a *Syphar* symbolically, according to his custom, either because that age is blind, or because...

<note>original: "Τὶ μὰν ξύσιλθ, τί γὰρ σύφαρ ἀντ’ ἀνδρὸς;"</note>
"For what is Xysilus, what is a Syphar in place of a man?"
You call a dry and itchy old man "Xysilus" <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ ξύειν"</note> from the word "to scrape"; or "Syphar," as if he is no longer the man himself, but merely a juiceless and empty skin. This itself smacks of a proverb. They say that "leberis" properly signifies the outer membrane that covers the grape-skin, in which only the traces of eyes appear. The adage is expressed in three ways: "Blinder than a leberis" <note>original: "τυφλότερ@ λεβερίδ@"</note>; "Nakeder than a leberis" <note>original: "γυμνότερ@ λεβερίδ@"</note>; and "Emptier than a leberis" <note>original: "λεγώτερ@ λεβερίδ@"</note>.

### LVII. Blinder than Tiresias.

Taken from a very well-known fable: "Blinder than Tiresias" <note>original: "τυφλότερ@ τειρεσίε"</note>. Juvenal says:
> Nor that any of the gods are deaf, or a Tiresias.

He used "Tiresias" as a proverbial figure for a blind man, just as Horace used "Irus" for a poor man:
> It will matter much whether a rich man speaks, or an Irus.

### LVIII. Blinder than Hypsea.

Horace used a similar figure in his *Satires*:
> Lest while gazing at the best parts of a body with the eyes of a Lynceus <note>Lynceus was a mythological hero famed for keen sight.</note>, you become blinder than Hypsea toward those things which are defects.

It is clear enough that the proverb arose from a certain woman named Hypsea, who was infamous for her well-known blindness.

### LIX. An inheritance without sacred rites.

Whenever some convenience was presented unexpectedly and without expense, the ancients called it "an inheritance without sacred rites." Indeed, they proverbially called any profit that fell to them from elsewhere without their own effort an "inheritance," because those things which happen this way seem to be given by Fortune for free, as if to those who are sleeping. Ergasilus the parasite says in Plautus’s *The Two Captives*: "I have obtained a most stuffed inheritance without sacred rites." And elsewhere: "It is a harvest, an inheritance without sacred rites." For otherwise, it was the custom for heirs to perform certain sacred rites at their own expense, either for the health of a struggling relative or at the funerals of the deceased. The same Plautus says elsewhere: "Such inheritances do not often come my way." Cicero in the *Fifth Action against Verres*: "Here Verres thought an inheritance had come to him, because that man had come into his kingdom and hands." Andreas Alciatus, in the first book of his *Omissions*, prefers the origin of the adage to be referred to the custom of ancient law. For a law of the Twelve Tables held: "Let private sacred rites be perpetual." Cicero interprets these words in the second book of *On Laws*, stating that everyone to whom the money of a head of household passed was bound to celebrate the sacred rites. He records the interpretation of Scaevola the Pontiff, in which it is handed down that an inheritance is bound to sacred rites in five ways. Therefore, those to whom an inheritance returned by right of kinship were bound by the fellowship of common rites. However, a good thing that happens unexpectedly is usually sweeter, like "an inheritance without sacred rites." Our friend Alciatus discusses these and other matters most learnedly; I gladly add my vote to his opinion, as it differs very little from my own. Furthermore, in the saying of Plautus, I think there is an allusion to that Greek proverb: "To devour un-sacrificed holy things" <note>original: "ἄθυτα ἱερὰ κατεσθίειν"</note>. Also to that line of Hesiod:
> To take and eat food from the pots before the offerings are poured.
<note>original: "ἀπὸ χυτροπόδων ἀνεπιῤῥέκτων ἀνελόντα ἔσθιειν"</note>

### LX. Between the slaying and the offering.

A particularly elegant adage exists in Marcus Tullius [Cicero]’s letters to Atticus: "Those many things," he says, "indeed all of them, the sum <note>original: "κεφάλαιον"</note> of which is: let no burden of labor or time be added to me, as they say, *between the slaying and the offering*." It seems to signify delay and doubtful hesitation, and as it were that interval between abandoning what has been started and beginning what must be renewed. It is taken from the ancient ritual of auspices, in which the priest performed certain ceremonies between the slaying of the victim and the offering of the entrails, as Marcus Varro testifies in the second book of *On the Latin Language*. "For the Flamen Dialis," he says, "takes the auspices for the vintage, and when he has ordered the grapes to be gathered, he sacrifices a lamb to Jupiter; between the slaying and the offering of its entrails, the Flamen gathers the wine." Furthermore, that the "slain entrails" signified a prolongation of time among the ancients is declared by Cicero in book—

# FIRST CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

### To finish the task.
<note>original: "Pensum absoluere"</note>

To fully discharge <unclear>a task</unclear> is to fulfill your part and perform your required duty. The metaphor is drawn from <term>wool-working</term> <note>The Latin 'pensum' refers to the weight of wool weighed out to a slave to be spun in a day</note>, in which a specific weight of wool was distributed to women for their work. Plautus in the *Mercator*: "I have finished my **task** which was given to me." The same author in the *Bacchides*: "I shall take care of my **task**." And Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the third book of *On the Orator*: "Now I shall proceed to the rest, and recall myself to my duty and my **task**." Varro in *On Agriculture*: "That our **task** be finished." Jerome to Rusticus: "And you should discharge the **tasks** of your work." Truly, the further this metaphor is removed from its original context, the more elegant the adage will be—for instance, if it is applied to a speech, to study, or to other matters of the mind.

<margin>62</margin>
### Not even in a dream.
<note>original: "Ne per somnium quidem"</note>

<margin>Lucian in The Cock.</margin>
<unclear>Not even in a dream</unclear> <note>original Greek: "oud' onar"</note>. This was said proverbially by the Greeks for that which is never seen, never happens, and is at no time present. Otherwise, almost no one is so utterly destitute of all happiness that they do not at least dream of something more joyful while at rest. Lucian in *On Those Who Give Their Company for Hire*: "Never even in a dream filled with white bread," <note>original: "oud' onar leukou pote artou emphoretheis"</note> that is, never even in a dream satisfied with white bread. He used the same in *The Cock*, when he says that to kings, not even in a dream did anything pleasant happen: "from whom it was not possible to enjoy anything sweet even in a dream." <note>original: "hyph' hon oud' onar apolausai tinos hēdeos egineto"</note> Again in *On Amber*: "Furthermore, those singing sweetly, and in the way you describe, we have not heard even in a dream." <note>original: "oud' onar akēkoamen"</note> Theocritus alluded elegantly to this in his *Idylls*, where Eunica, a city girl, rejects a rustic man attempting to give her a kiss, saying she is so far from giving him a kiss that he should not even hope for it in a dream. The poem goes thus: "Get away from me! Do you wish to ruin me? I have not learned to kiss a rustic, but to press sophisticated lips. Do not kiss my beautiful mouth, not even in your dreams." <note>original Greek: "Errho ap' emoio... mē mou kysēs to kalon stoma, mēd' en oneirois"</note> That is:
->Away from here, to a bad end!<-
->Do you, a rustic man, wish to give a little kiss?<-
->But I have never learned to give kisses to peasants.<-
->I am accustomed to fix kisses on more urban lips.<-
->Lest you ever touch my bright mouth with your filthy lips,<-
->Not even through sleep.<-
<margin>Cicero to Atticus.</margin>
And Marcus Tullius in the *Letters to Atticus*: "A political man, not even in a dream, can any be found." <note>original: "politikos anēr, oud' onar"</note> Theocritus in *Megara, the Wife of Hercules*: "Which has happened to no other, not even in a dream." <note>original: "hō d' oud' onar ēlythen allō"</note> Galen in *On Natural Faculties*, book 2: "And these things were not unknown to Erasistratus, if only he had ever, even in his dreams, had some acquaintance with the Peripatetics in their schools." <note>original Greek: "tauta ouk echtha... kan kat' onar pote tois ek tēs paideias synetychen"</note> However, men of even the lowest lot are accustomed sometimes to see magnificent things in sleep, just as in Lucian, Micyllus, who was very wealthy in his dreams, was in reality a cobbler, someone almost poorer than Irus <note>Irus was the beggar in the Odyssey</note>. For to dream is a kind of hoping. Virgil in the *Eclogues* calls the empty hopes of lovers "dreams":
<margin>Horace in the Satires.</margin>
"Do lovers fashion dreams for themselves?" Horace looked to this in his *Satires* when he said:
->If he has relieved you from long servitude and care,<-
->Waking, you will hear: 'Ulysses, you are heir to a fourth part.'<-
"Not even in a dream" is just as valid as if you said: "that which you do not even dare to hope for."
<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
Plutarch, in the booklet he wrote against the Stoics, brought out the adage slightly differently: "Whose dreams it is not permitted to escape, even outside of common thoughts." <note>original Greek: "eirata lathein mallon oude para tas koinas ennoias"</note> Saint Chrysostom, in his third sermon against the Jews, expressed it thus: "Not even as a dream." <note>original: "oud' hōs onar"</note>

<margin>63</margin>
### Through a cloud, through a mist, through a dream.
<note>original: "Per nebulam, per caliginem, per somnium"</note>

When we possess a certain ambiguous and thin, almost vanishing memory or understanding of things, we say proverbially that we "record them through a cloud," "remember them through a dream," or "see them through a mist." Just as those things we saw as boys, we remember as old men "as if through a dream," with only certain thin images of things clinging to our minds, such as the fleeting memory of dreams. Furthermore, that which we look at through the middle of a cloud...

<summary>Erasmus explores metaphors for completion (the wool-worker's task) and the "not even in a dream" idiom used to describe impossible hopes or total absence, drawing heavily from Greek and Roman literature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on classical adages, specifically focusing on metaphors for partial perception and the origins of humorous proverbs regarding self-betrayal.</meta>

...we see only a confused image of it, like an uncertain shadow. These are the sorts of things seen through a mist in the darkness. From this, therefore, the metaphor is drawn. Forms of speech of this kind are frequently encountered among writers. Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus, Roman comic playwright</note> in *Pseudolus*: "There are things we wish to ask you, which we ourselves know and have heard as if through a cloud." The same author in *The Two Captives*: "I recall to memory that I heard it as if through a cloud." Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the fifth book of *On Moral Ends*: "In a weak age and a feeble mind, the force of nature is perceived through a mist." Plato in the seventh book of *Laws*: <gloss>original Greek: "ἃ δὴ λέγω... κατὰ τι σκότος"</gloss> that is, "Furthermore, regarding what I say, an effort must be made so that we may make it clear, as if by bringing examples into the light. For these things seem similar to those which are spoken through a certain mist." In the same book one reads <gloss>original Greek: "καθ’ ὕπνον"</gloss> that is, "through sleep," or "in dreams."

### Concerning the donkey’s look-in.
LXIIII

<gloss>original Greek: "Περὶ ὄνου παρακύψεως"</gloss> i.e., Concerning the donkey’s look-in. An old adage used to be said against those who, by a laughing pretext, bring a false accusation against someone, or summon someone to court over frivolous matters. The event which provided the occasion for the fable is narrated in various ways by authors. Some record something of this sort: a certain potter had fashioned various shapes of birds and had them arranged in his workshop. But a certain donkey, while the stable-boy following him was inattentive, thrust his head through the small window of the workshop and knocked down and shattered both the birds and the other vessels alike. The owner of the workshop summoned the stable-boy to court. And when he was asked by everyone for what reason he was bringing the lawsuit, he said, "Concerning the donkey’s look-in." Others maintain the birds were not earthenware but real ones, which, when the donkey (as has been said) thrust his head through the window, were disturbed, broke their perch, and overturned the other vessels. The rest of the fables agree in one way or another. Lucian <note>Greek satirist</note> in his *The Ass* invents this proverb from a story where, while the donkey tried to look through a window with his head turned sideways to see what was happening, he betrayed both himself and his masters. And that matter, received with great laughter by everyone, passed into an adage, <gloss>original Greek: "ἐξ ὄνου παρακύψεως"</gloss> that is, "from the donkey’s look-in." According to Lucian’s opinion, it will better fit those who, by their own stupidity, while they clumsily strive to hide, are ridiculously betrayed. Emulating this passage of Lucian, Apuleius <note>Author of the Roman novel The Golden Ass</note> in the ninth book of his *Metamorphoses* writes in this manner: "When this contention and clamorous noise was known, the donkey—otherwise curious and endowed with a restless impudence—while I yearned to look out with my neck turned sideways through a certain little window to see what that tumult meant, one of the fellow-soldiers, by chance having cast his eyes toward my shadow, testified to everyone in person. Finally, a great shout immediately arose. And ladders having been brought out at once, certain men, laying hands on me, dragged me down like a captive; and now, all hesitation removed, examining everything more scrupulously, even that chest having been lifted, the wretched gardener was found, produced, and presented to the magistrates to pay the penalty, and they led him away to the public prison; and with the greatest laughter they did not cease to mock me concerning my 'look-in.' Whence also 'Concerning the look-in and the shadow of a donkey' became a frequent proverb." Thus far Apuleius.

### The shrew-mouse perished by its own evidence.
LXV

Close to this is that line of Terence <note>Roman playwright</note> from *The Eunuch*: "Wretched me, I have perished today by my own evidence, just like a shrew-mouse." These are the words of Parmeno, who, having been deceived by Pythias, had betrayed himself to the old man. Donatus <note>A famous grammarian and commentator on Terence</note> advises that it is a proverb against those who are betrayed by their own voice. And from this he thinks the metaphor was drawn, because it is characteristic of shrew-mice <term>forex: a shrew or field mouse</term> either to squeak more loudly than mice, or to make more noise when they gnaw on trifles; many people, turning their attention to that sound, pierce them even through the darkness of night. Saint Aurelius Augustine uses this adage in the first book of *On Order* toward his friend Licentius, who, while he scared away a shrew-mouse with a noise by striking a tablet, betrayed to Augustine himself that he was awake. Origen alluded to the same in his third homily on Genesis: "But," he said, "I shall seem to be caught by my own evidence."

### You are dressing me in the lion’s skin.
LXVI

<gloss>original Greek: "Ἐνδύετά μοι τὴν λεοντῆν"</gloss> that is, You are dressing me in the lion’s skin. It is usually said against those who undertake a business greater than their ability, and who carry themselves more magnificently than suits their condition. Some think it was taken from Hercules, whose dress this was—to be covered by a lion’s skin, then in one hand to carry a club and in the other a bow; and in this dress he descended to the underworld to drag out Cerberus. Alluding to this, Aristophanes in *The Frogs* depicts Bacchus, in the likeness of Hercules, equipped with a lion’s skin and a club, preparing to descend to the underworld to hear Euripides competing with Aeschylus. He is mocked by Hercules, however, because that equipment was not—

# ADAGES: THIRD HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
### 121
<meta>catchword: Ears</meta>

...it would suit him, seeing as he was soft and effeminate. To this same point belongs the fact that Menippus, in the works of Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century Greek satirist</note>, pretends to have returned from the underworld in that same attire. Nothing, however, prevents the proverb from being traced back to that fable mentioned by Lucian in *The Fisherman*: A certain donkey, weary of servitude, broke his halter and fled into the woods. There, by chance, he found a lion’s skin and draped it over his body. And so he carried himself as a lion, terrifying both people and beasts with his voice and his tail. For the people of Cyme <note>An ancient Greek city in Aeolis</note> are unfamiliar with lions. In this manner, this masked donkey reigned for some time, regarded and feared as a monstrous lion. This lasted until a certain stranger traveling to Cyme (who had frequently seen both lions and donkeys, and for whom it was therefore not difficult to distinguish between them) recognized him as a donkey by the evidence of his protruding ears and several other clues. Having given him a sound beating, the stranger led him back and returned him to his owner. Meanwhile, he stirred up no small amount of laughter among all the Cymaeans once the truth was known—the very people who, believing him a lion, had recently been nearly frightened to death. 

Now, he calls them "donkeys" here, not those found in Italy, but those in Aeolis above Lesbos. The Lesbians and Cymaeans were noted for their stupidity, as Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer</note> indicates. Socrates uses this adage in Plato’s *Cratylus*, saying that one ought not to be deterred by the magnitude of the proposed dispute once one has put on the lion’s skin. Lucian says in *The False Critic*: <term>Πᾶν λινῷ...</term> <note>original Greek: "There is no need for anyone to strip off the skin to reveal you are a pack-ass..."</note>, that is: There is no need for anyone to strip the skin from you to make it clear you are a common pack-ass, unless some stranger has just arrived to us from the Hyperboreans themselves, or is so much a Cymaean that he does not understand what he sees—namely, that you are the most ferocious donkey of all donkeys—or is waiting to hear you braying like a wild beast. Eusebius of Caesarea, writing against Hierocles, says: <term>οἰχήσεται μὲν ἡμῖν...</term> <note>original Greek: "The foul donkey of philosophy, hidden in the lion's skin, will depart from us."</note>, that is: The foul donkey of philosophy, covered in a lion’s skin, shall depart from us. Lucian changed the proverb slightly in *The False Critic* when he said: <term>τοσοῦτον χρόνον ἐλελήθει με...</term> <note>original Greek: "For so long I did not notice a ridiculous ape was hidden under the lion's skin."</note>, that is: For so long a time I did not notice that a ridiculous ape was hidden under the lion’s skin.

---

->**The ears of Midas the donkey.**<-
->**LXVII**<-

<term>Μίδας ὄνου ὦτα</term> <note>Greek: Midas onou ota</note>, that is, **The ears of Midas the donkey.** This is recorded by Diogenianus. It arises from the very famous fable of Midas, King of Phrygia, to whom Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> attached donkey ears because he stupidly preferred the singing of Pan to his own. Although Midas hid them for a long time under a turban, they were finally discovered by his barber, turned into a joke, and spread among the common people. 

Furthermore, the adage may be rightly applied either to stupid, thick-headed men of dull judgment, or to tyrants who, because they have donkey-like ears that are very long, hear things even from a distance—as if they had sent out eavesdroppers to report back what they heard. Plutarch, in his book *On Curiosity*, calls these people <term>ὠτακουστὰς</term> <note>Greek: otakoustas - "ear-listeners"</note> and <term>πυλαγωγίδας</term> <note>Greek: pylagogidas - "gate-keepers/informants"</note>. For this reason, Lucian, in his little book titled *On Not Easily Believing Slanderers*, when painting a picture of Slander, gave the image the ears of Midas because of his zeal for eavesdropping and catching what everyone is doing in turn: <term>ἐν δεξιᾷ τις ἀνὴρ κάθηται...</term> <note>original Greek: "On the right sits a man with enormous ears, almost like those of Midas."</note>, that is: On the right sits a certain man with very large ears, almost like those Midas had. Aristophanes says in *Plutus*:
> <term>ἀλλ’ ἂν, ἢν πῦ ὦτ’ ὄνο λάβητε.</term> <note>original Greek: "But if you take the ears of a donkey..."</note> that is,
> If indeed, therefore, you take up the ears of a donkey.

The Greek commentator reminds us of the proverb about donkey ears and the various allegories of that story. Some authors say that this Midas was turned into a donkey because of his contempt and criticism of the god’s songs. Others relate that when he once passed some donkeys on the road and insulted them, an angry Bacchus added donkey ears to Midas. There are those who think his ears were naturally very long and protruding like a donkey's, and that the fable arose from this. However, most prefer the explanation that this allegory signified that Midas, as a tyrant, was accustomed to sending out "Corycaeans" <note>Informers named after the port of Corycus</note> and eavesdroppers, through whom he could learn whatever was done or said throughout the whole region, using them as his ears. When the common people marveled that he found out even things done secretly and far away, it gave rise to this fable—that Midas was said to have the ears of a donkey. This is either because no other animal hears more sharply than a donkey (except for the mouse) or because it has the longest ears of all. Persius...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Who does not have the ears of an ass?
Some say this was first written by the poet <note>The Roman satirist Persius</note> as:
*King Midas has the ears of an ass.*
Then, out of fear of Caesar <note>referring to the Emperor Nero</note>, he changed the writing to: *Who does not have them?*

->Hence those tears. LXVIII<-

This seems to have been used proverbially by Horace as an allusion to the *Andria* of Terence <note>A famous Roman comedy</note>; *Hence those tears.* Marcus Tullius Cicero used it in this manner in his speech *For Marcus Caelius*: *Hence those tears*; meaning, "and this is surely the cause of all these crimes and charges." It is said regarding the cause of a matter that has been hidden for some time, which is finally truly discovered. For example, if someone should say that barbarians condemn Greek literature simply so they themselves do not appear poorly educated, one might aptly add: *Hence those tears*, that is, this is what bothers them. Such allusions are frequently taken from famous authors and transferred into the place of a proverb, even if no proverbial figure was originally present. Of this kind is that phrase from Homer repeated often in Cicero’s *Letters to Atticus*, *I revere the Trojans* <note>original: "αἰδέομαι τρῶας"</note>, that is, I fear what people will say.

->This is Helen. LXIX<-

With a similar figure, Lucian said in *The Eunuch*, *This, my dear friend, was the Helen for whom you fought a duel* <note>original: "Αὕτη ὦ πάμφιλε ἑλένη, ὑπὲρ ἧς ἐμονομάχου"</note>. He speaks of two Peripatetic philosophers shamefully contending before judges out of greed for pay and profit. He alluded to a *monomachia*, that is, a single combat, which Homer describes between Menelaus and Paris in the third book of the *Iliad*.

->To whiten ivory with black ink. LXX<-

*To whiten ivory with black ink* means to apply external grooming and ornament to a genuine beauty, by which 그 native grace is obscured rather than highlighted. Thus, a madam in a play by Plautus says to a girl endowed with natural beauty who nevertheless asks for white lead <note>a common ancient cosmetic</note> to smear on her cheeks: "You might as well try to whiten ivory with black ink." This is because all such seduction brings dishonor to things naturally beautiful, not loveliness. It is as if someone tried to decorate Truth—than which nothing is more beautiful—with the pigments of rhetoricians. Furthermore, just as white lead was used to procure a fair complexion, so was purple dye used to tint the cheeks with red. He used a similar form in the play *Mostellaria*: "You wish to patch up a most charming work with new paint."

->To encrust a clean vessel. LXXI<-

The metaphor from Horace, found in the third Satire of his first book of *Sermons*, pertains to almost the same thing:
> But we turn virtues themselves upside down, and
> We desire to encrust a clean vessel.
That is, those things which are right in themselves, we deprave and cover up by imposing foreign names upon them. Although it can also be adapted to the previous sentiment: that is, when we apply a coating to things that are decent in themselves, which covers and obscures their native grace rather than increasing it.

->Of the beautiful, even the autumn is beautiful. LXXII<-

*Of the beautiful, even the autumn is beautiful* <note>original: "Τῶν καλῶν καὶ ὁπώρα καλή"</note>. A proverbial metaphor born from an aphorism of Archelaus, which Plutarch records him saying to Euripides, who was kissing the now-maturing and aging Agathon at a banquet. It is not unlike that Homeric phrase, which we shall render in another place, *to know from the stalk* <note>original: "ἐν τ' καλάμης γινώσκειν"</note>. For in the spring months, everything is tender and bright, while everything is still in flower or in the grass. But in the time of autumn, after they have grown into stalks or stems, they appear more rugged. It applies, therefore, to those things which, since they are excellent by nature, do not seem worthy of disdain even when they have ripened. Otherwise, there is almost nothing so foul that it does not occasionally shine with youth. It is also elegantly said of those who carry their age well.

->The sources of great rivers are navigable. LXXIII<-

It seems that same metaphor was used in the saying recorded and noted by Quintilian in the eighth book of his *Institutes*: *The sources of great rivers are navigable.* He says that sentence was chanted often when he was a young man. It signifies that even the smallest resources of the powerful prevail more than the entire wealth of the poor. However, Quintilian notes this class of maxims because they appear openly false.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to hidden motives, the corruption of natural beauty through over-ornamentation, and the enduring grace of the elderly. He draws on a wide range of classical authors including Horace, Cicero, and Homer.</summary>

# THIRD HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
->I 2<-

The plant of a noble tree is immediately with its fruit. <margin>74</margin>
<note>original: "Generosioris arboris statim planta cum fructu est"</note>
He <note>Erasmus refers to a previous author or source</note> adds this in the same place: "The plant of a noble tree is immediately with its fruit." This seems to suggest that excellent and well-born talents mature and arrive at their potential immediately. Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> also critiques this type of sentiment. However, it seemed right to me to include these among the proverbs, because he testifies that they were commonly celebrated; and even a somewhat more impudent hyperbole, as was said a little earlier, is not rejected from this genre.

### To pierce the eyes of crows. <margin>75</margin>
<note>original: "Cornicum oculos configere"</note>
Cicero, in his speech *In Defense of Murena*, writes in this manner: "Then also, if there was any admiration among our people for that study of yours, once your mysteries were published, it became entirely idle and cast aside. A few once knew whether a legal action could be taken or not, for they did not have the calendars. Those who were consulted were in great power, from whom even the days were sought as if from Chaldean astrologers. A certain clerk was found, Gnaeus Flavius, who **pierced the eyes of the crows** <note>meaning he outsmarted the experts at their own game</note>, and set forth the calendars for the people to learn day by day, and plundered the wisdom from the legal experts themselves. Therefore, those men were angry because they feared that once the system of days was understood, legal action could be taken without their help; so they composed certain shorthand notes so that they might be present at everything." He says the same in the speech *In Defense of Lucius Flaccus*: "Here, by Hercules, he pierced the eye of the crow, for he struck this Hermippus, a learned man and his own citizen, to whom he should have been known." Furthermore, whether the proverb arose from some fable, or from an event, or was taken from a metaphor, is not sufficiently clear. From wherever it flowed, it seems to have the same force: **To pierce the eyes of the crows** is as if you were to say, by some new invention to obscure the learning of the ancients, so that those who came before seem to have known nothing and seen nothing. It is, however, expressed through irony.

Saint Jerome used this sentiment in his second *Apology against Ruffinus*: "But since different copies are carried about according to the variety of regions, and that genuine ancient translation is corrupted and violated, you think it is our choice either to judge from many which is true, or to build a new work upon the old, and—while the Jews mock us—to **pierce the eyes of the crows**, as they say." Jerome felt this because, by putting forth his own correction, the Jews (from whom the truth of the Old Testament was sought at that time) would seem to know nothing. Macrobius used it not much differently in the seventh book of the *Saturnalia*: "And because," he says, "we confess ourselves unequal to the labyrinths of speaking, come, Vectius, let us urge Eustathius to communicate to us, with a contrary arrangement, whatever can be said for a variety of food, so that a violent tongue may succumb to its own weapons, and Greek may snatch this applause from Greek, as if **a crow should dig out the eyes of a crow**." Thus far Macrobius.

It would not be irrelevant to remind the reader to consider again and again whether the longevity and harmony of crows gave place to this proverb. Indeed, in antiquity, the crow was a symbol of concord. Its longevity was also celebrated in a Greek proverb. Thus, anyone who wishes to condemn and rescind those things which antiquity approved with great consensus might seem to want to **pierce the eyes of the crows**. Nor is it very absurd if one takes it in this way: that he is said to pierce the eyes of crows who takes away the sight of the most sharp-sighted and keen-eyed, and pours darkness over them; or that he touches the very thing itself with a needle, as they say—being such a great craftsman that he strikes not only the man or the bird, but the very eyes themselves with his dart.

### With a gladiatorial mind. <margin>76</margin>
<note>original: "Gladiatorio animo"</note>
That which we read in Terence’s *Phormio* has the appearance of a proverb: "Aha! They are approaching me **with a gladiatorial mind**." By this it is signified that one strives to harm another in such a way that he attempts it at his own peril, with a stubborn mind, prepared either to destroy or to perish. For to a gladiator committed to a contest, this is the proposed lot of the fight: either to kill if he has taken the lead, or to fall if he has hesitated. Aristotle calls this kind of boldness, joined with contempt for one's own safety, "Celtic."

### For a piece of bread. <margin>77</margin>
<note>original: "Frusto panis"</note>
**For a piece of bread** is commonly said even in our times for a thing however small and cheap. Marcus Cato, in a certain speech, reproaching Marcus Coelius for his cheapness—not only in speaking but also in keeping silent—says: "He can be hired **for a piece of bread**, either to keep silent or to speak." This passage is cited by Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights*. It seems to be a hyperbole taken either from dogs, whom we are accustomed to invite with a piece of bread, or from beggars.

<summary>Erasmus explores several Latin proverbs, most notably "piercing the eyes of crows," which refers to outsmarting experts or overturning established tradition, and "with a gladiatorial mind," describing a reckless, all-or-nothing attitude.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient Greek and Latin adages, focusing on metaphors for behavior, discernment, and social chaos.</meta>

### To guard the cloak one’s mother gave.
### 78

**To guard the cloak one’s mother gave** is a phrase used to describe living childishly according to someone else’s rules. It is found in Quintilian, Book 5: "For what," he asks, "is more wretched than that law, which follows the pre-formed letters given to infants, and as the Greeks are fond of saying, anxiously guarding the cloak one’s mother gave?" From these words of Fabius <note>Quintilian’s full name was Marcus Fabius Quintilianus</note>, it is clear that this was a proverb among the Greeks. Lucian also uses and explains the adage in *Nigrinus*: "And where did this peacock come from? Perhaps it is his mother’s garment." These jibes are directed at someone who arrives dressed in multi-colored, flashy clothing. Plutarch, in his essay *On the Fortune of Alexander*, writes: "Like a tiny child, guarding the cloak which his fatherland wrapped around him, just as if his mother had put it on him." This describes one who keeps to a cloak that the custom of his country, acting like a nurse, had provided. Indeed, even the expression "to live according to a prescription," which is now quite common, appears to be a proverbial metaphor drawn from children. As Plato says, "on the tablet," the teacher writes out a model on the writing-board <note>original: "en tē graphidi"</note>, which the children then get used to imitating as they form their letters. Horace mocks this kind of slavish imitation as a form of bondage:
> O imitators, a servile herd, how often your
> commotions have moved me to laughter and jest.

And Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> thinks nothing is more useless for speaking well than to be so enslaved to the rules of art that you do not dare to depart a finger’s breadth from them, even when the logic of the case demands it.

### To know the difference between bronze and lupins.
### 79

This has the appearance of a proverb, found in Horace’s *Epistles*:
> Yet he is not ignorant of the difference between bronze and lupins.

That is: he knows the distinction between cheap things and precious ones. Horace is discussing those who do not bestow favors on just anyone as if they were throwing them away, but place them carefully, weighing both the merit of the recipient and the value of the gift. Furthermore, Juvenal noted the usefulness of the lupin <note>Lupin seeds were used as stage money or cheap food</note> proverbially:
> I prefer a tunic of lupin,
> than if the whole village praised me.

Lucian also notes this in his booklet *On Salaried Posts*, when he asks whether there was such a lack of lupins and spring water that a man would throw himself into such slavery.

### When I am dead, let the earth be mixed with fire.
### 80

There is a Greek iambic line <note>original: "pythōmenos"</note> found in Suetonius Tranquillus’s *Life of Nero*:
"When I am dead, let the earth be mixed with fire." <note>original: "Emou thanontos gaia michthētō pyri"</note>
When this was said by someone in common conversation, Nero replied, "Nay, while I am alive!" <note>original: "emou zōntos"</note>—alluding to the burning of the city, which he carried out shortly thereafter. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> mentions this proverb in the third book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "Since that voice is called inhuman and wicked by those who say they do not care if, after they are dead, a conflagration of all the lands follows—a sentiment they usually pronounce in a common Greek verse." Likewise, Seneca in the second book of *On Clemency* says that many great but detestable sayings have entered human life and become famous among the common people, such as "Let them hate, so long as they fear." To this, he says, the Greek verse is similar, which bids the earth be mixed with fire once the speaker is dead. Indeed, the same sentiment persists today among mortals: "When I die," they say, "the whole world dies for me." By this they mean it matters nothing to them what good or evil happens to posterity once they are taken from life, as they will feel nothing.

### To mix the sea and sky.
### 81

**To mix the sea and sky** is a proverbial hyperbole for throwing everything into confusion or leaving no stone unturned. Titus Livy writes: "Why is it that they mix heaven and earth, and earth and heaven?" And elsewhere: "Why, pray, do they mix sky and lands?" Juvenal says:
> You may shout, and confound
> the sea with the sky: I am but a man.

Lucian, in the dialogue of *Prometheus and Hermes*: "Why then, by the gods, was it necessary to pour out such talk, and mix earth with sky, as the saying goes?"
Virgil, in the fifth book, says of Juno attempting everything:
> She mixed all the seas
> with the sky.

<summary>This page explores proverbs regarding slavish adherence to rules, the ability to discern value (bronze vs. lupins), and expressions of extreme chaos or nihilism, including Nero's infamous remark on the burning of Rome.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Quintilian, Horace, Nero, Cicero, Seneca, Livy, Virgil, Greek proverbs, Latin literature, social conduct, nihilism, metaphors</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Greek and Latin adages, specifically focusing on metaphors of movement and confusion. The previous page likely discussed the mixing of heaven and earth.</meta>

The same author says something slightly different in the twelfth book:
> If he should pour the earth into the waves,
> Mixing them with the storm, or dissolve the sky into hell.
<note>original: "Si tellurem effundat in undas, Iunio miscens, cœlúmue in tartara soluat." A reference to Virgil's Aeneid, describing total chaos.</note>

Xenophanes in the *Lysistrata* used a similar figure of speech:
<gloss>Zeus the high-thunderer.</gloss> <note>original: Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης</note> that is,
<gloss>Jupiter crashing on high.</gloss>
<margin>and things above, below</margin>
<margin>and things below, above</margin>
Archus <note>likely a reference to Arrian or Plutarch</note> in the *Life of Romulus* uses it this way: those who make gods out of men and men out of gods, and who tell fables about the gods as if they were human, "mix heaven and earth." <gloss>To completely deny the divinity of virtue is impious and ignoble, but to mix the earth with heaven is the height of stupidity.</gloss>

### You will mix the sacred with the profane. LXXXII

Horace used a similar figure:
*You will mix the sacred with the profane.*
It means you will do anything <note>i.e., you have no moral boundaries</note>. Likewise: *Confounding right and wrong.* Among the ancients, there was a great distinction between the affairs of men and those of the gods, to the extent that even Homer distinguishes the names which the gods are accustomed to use from human words. And Pythagoras commanded that one should abstain from certain things because they were consecrated to the deities. Hence, those who have no scruples and who dare anything are said to *mix the sacred with the profane.*

### Up and down (Topsy-turvy). LXXXIII

In Plautus and other authors, this is found used proverbially: *I bear it up and down* and *I hold it up and down.* This stands for: it makes no difference to me, I do not worry about it. Plautus in *Amphitryon*:
*Things were done [wrongly], yet I did not commit them; he accuses me, and I think I shall hold that as "up and down" (of no consequence).*
Gellius writes in the sixteenth book of *Attic Nights* that "to bear up and down" has the same value as being indifferent, not making much of what happens, and sometimes neglecting and despising it; it is what the Greeks call <gloss>indifference</gloss> <note>original: ἀδιαφορεῖν</note>. He cites Laberius in *The Compitalia*:
*Now you are sluggish, now you bear it up and down.*
And Marcus Varro in *Sisenna*: *But if the principles of all these were not similar, it would be "up and down."* Finally, he records these verses from Lucilius:
*This game where all things were "up and down":*
*Up and down, I say, all things were a game and a joke.*
This comes from that Greek figure, <gloss>up and down</gloss> <note>original: ἄνω καὶ κάτω</note>, by which we signify no order and no distinction between things.

### To and fro (Back and forth). LXXXIIII

*To and fro* is said as a proverbial figure, and it is valid just as if you were to say "from here and from there," or "on both sides." However, it becomes a more elegant metaphor whenever it refers to mutual altercation, debate, conversation, or a quarrel. This kind is found in Cicero's *On the Republic*:
*With many words held to and fro, that day was consumed by us.*
The same in his books *On Duties*:
*With benefits given and received to and fro.*
Seneca in *On Benefits*, book 5: *The return of a benefit and gratitude ought to go to and fro.* In a similar form we say: *The matter was agitated to and fro*, *With disasters given and received to and fro*, *Contended with insults to and fro.*

### Upwards and downwards. LXXXV

Very similar is that from Terence's *The Eunuch*: *I will make you so steady for these six whole months, Parmeno, that you won't be running upwards and downwards.* That is, hither and thither, or certainly running back and forth between the master and Thais, as the servants of lovers are accustomed to do. This will indeed have a bit more grace if it is transferred further, as if one were to say: *The lawyers, from volume to volume, from law to law, from interpreter to interpreter, constantly contradicting themselves, wander upwards and downwards.* That metaphor seems to be borrowed from the fable of Sisyphus rolling the stone in the underworld. To which that Greek phrase <gloss>up and down</gloss>, which we just mentioned, is so close that it seems to be the same. Demosthenes in the first oration *Against Philip*: <gloss>If it is reported that Philip is present anywhere else, you all jump together up and down.</gloss> That is, if it is announced that Philip is in some other place, you equally run accurately upwards and downwards.
Xenophanes <note>likely a misattribution or obscure fragment</note>:
<gloss>They chatter in the marketplace, both up and down.</gloss>

Erasmus traces these expressions through classical authors like Cicero, Plautus, and Demosthenes to explain their metaphorical nuances.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"They flee the red-stained rope." <note>original: "τὸ σχοινίον φεύγεσι τὸ μεμιλτωμένον." A reference to the Athenian practice of marking citizens with red dye to force them into the assembly.</note> That is:
But these men speak in the forum, and avoid
The little rope smeared up and down with red.
Euripides in *The Bacchae*:
"Mixing everything together, up and down." <note>original: "Ἄνω κάτω τὰ πάντα συγχέας ὁμῦ."</note> That is:
Confounding all things together, up and down.
Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "It is necessary for everyone to examine these arguments by turning them up and down," <note>original: "χρὴ πάντας τῸς λόγος ἄνω καὶ κάτω μεταστρέφοντα ἐπισκοπεῖν."</note> that is: We ought to turn all reasons up and down, and so consider them. The same author in the *Theaetetus*: "And it might happen, as the saying goes, that everything is up and down," <note>original: "καὶ γένοιτ’ ἂν τὸ λεγόμενον, ἄνω κάτω πάντα."</note> that is: Let it be as they say, all things up and down. He also used this in the *Parmenides*. The rhetorician Aristides uses the same in several other places, as well as in *Cimon*: "For I truly do not see how all things could be more mixed up and down," <note>original: "ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐχ ὁρῶ πῶς ἂν μᾶλλον πάντα ἄνω καὶ κάτω γένοιτο."</note> that is: I certainly do not see in what way the universe could be more mixed up and down. Menander, according to Plutarch:
"Nor to say 'Alas for me' while turning up and down." <note>original: "οὐ δὲ στρεφομένως ἄνω κάτω, οἴμοι λέγειν."</note>
Instead of "up and down," Euripides said "backward and forward," <note>original: "πάλιν τε καὶ πρόσω."</note> as if you were to say, "to the front and to the back."
"The gods mix these things backward and forward." <note>original: "φύρεσιν ταῦθ’ οἱ θεοὶ πάλιν τε καὶ πρόσω."</note>
The verse, corrupted by scribes, will be restored if you read:
"The gods mix these things backward and forward."
In Athenaeus, book six:
"But by metaphor
Each of them [transfers] these things up and down." <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ μεταφορᾷ ἕκαστος αὐτῶν ταῦτ’ ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω."</note>
He is speaking of poets who find nothing new themselves, but mix up the inventions of others, and by treating them differently, make them their own. Therefore, the proverb will be applied either to one who attempts everything, or to one who confuses everything, or to the intelligence of one who looks around a business from every side. Clearly very similar to this is what appears in Terence’s *The Mother-in-Law*: "To run backward and forward," instead of "hither and thither." For "backward" <term>rursum</term> properly sounds like "behind," and "forward" <term>prorsum</term> like "before." Donatus also noted this proverbial pattern. Of such a kind are also those: "up and down," "inside and out," "this way and that," and in Greek: "up and down," "forward and backward." The further it recedes from physical things, the more elegance the adage will have. Of this kind is that of Julian against Galen in the book where he refutes him: "They would by no means persuade us or themselves in truth that they know what nature is, which they chatter about up and down, everywhere magnificently proclaiming it." <note>original: "οὐδ’ ἂν πείσειεν ἡμᾶς... πανταχῆ."</note> Thus, one who weighs a matter in his mind in various ways can be said to have "reasoned it up and down."

### A man for all hours. LXXXVI

The ancients used to call a man "a man for all hours" <note>original: "Omnium horarum homo." This is the origin of the phrase "A Man for All Seasons."</note> if he were equally suited for both serious business and jokes, and with whom one would like to live constantly. Quintilian <note>referred to as "Fabius" in the text.</note> is the authority that Asinius Pollio was so called. In Suetonius, Tiberius was accustomed to declare—even in his notebooks—that two of his fellow drinkers were his most pleasant friends and "friends for all hours." Ennius depicted a friend of this sort both elegantly and vividly under the persona of Geminus Servilius. Although the poem appears in Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights*, book twelve, chapter four, I will not be burdened to write it down here:

> Having spoken this, he calls the one with whom he often gladly shared
> His table, his conversations, and his affairs
> Courteously, when the great day had already passed
> In large part; concerning small things and great ones to be done,
> In counsel, in the forum, and in the broad and sacred senate.
> To whom he might boldly speak matters great and small, and jokes;
> Who would pour out things tinged with evil, and things good to say,
> If he wished, and would place them in safety.
> With whom there was much pleasure and joy, both secretly and openly;
> A mind which no thought persuades toward evil...

<summary>Erasmus explores the proverbial use of "up and down" to describe both chaos and thorough investigation, and introduces the famous concept of the "man for all hours"—a versatile and loyal companion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of character and social adaptability before transitioning to a new proverb regarding the power of wealth.</meta>

...he might commit a slight offense, yet he was hardly a bad man; likewise, he was a refined, faithful, and pleasant person, eloquent and content with his own lot, shrewd and fortunate, speaking favorably at the right time, obliging, and a man of few words. He possessed much ancient and buried knowledge, understanding the things that antiquity often produces, as well as customs both old and new. He knew the laws of many ancients, and of both gods and men; a prudent man, who knew when to speak much and when to keep silent. <note>Erasmus is quoting the Roman poet Ennius's description of a dependable friend.</note>

And among the philosophers, it is handed down that Aristippus was such a man; by the command of Dionysius, he did not refuse to dance in feminine purple robes along with the others, while Plato refused, adding that even in the festivals of Bacchus <note>The Bacchanalia, festivals of the wine-god Dionysus known for wild revelry.</note> one ought to remain modest. Hence Horace says: *Every color of life suited Aristippus.* <note>original: "Omnis Aristippum decuit color." This refers to Aristippus's ability to adapt to any social circumstance or fortune.</note>

On the other hand, those who follow only certain personal whims and are not easy-going in the company of any man are called "Glaucocoran men" <note>original: "Glaucocorum hominum," likely referring to a specific type of social awkwardness or "owl-eyed" staring mentioned in Greek comedy.</note>, as seen in Terence. In Horace, however, we say such a person *plainly lacks common sense.*

### All things obey money. LXXXVII

There seems to be no sentiment more frequently on the lips of all nations than this one, which is even now in use by everyone: *All things obey money.* It is recorded among the Proverbs of the Hebrews, in Ecclesiastes, chapter 10 <note>Ecclesiastes 10:19: "but money answers all things."</note>; nor is it celebrated any less by Greek and Latin authors alike. Euripides in *The Phoenician Women* says:
*To mortals, nothing is dearer than money,*
*And it holds the greatest power among men.*

In Aristophanes' *Plutus*:
*So much so that you can find nothing healthy anywhere,*
*But all alike are servants, conquered by profit.*

The famous saying of Demosthenes in the *First Olynthiac* also alludes to this: *There is a need for money, and without it, none of the necessary things can be accomplished.* Again, Aristophanes in the same *Plutus* humorously pursues the idea that whatever deeds, whether good or bad, are carried out among mortals, they are done for the sake of money; indeed, even for the gods themselves, divine worship is performed for no other reason. And among many other things, he records this universal sentiment:
*Whatever is distinguished or splendid,*
*Whatever is charming, comes to men through you alone.*
*For all things together obey wealth.*

Hence Horace calls money a "queen":
*Birth and wife, along with dowry, faith and friends,*
*Both lineage and beauty, Queen Money bestows.*

No one has described the tyranny of money more wittily than Euripides, making Bellerophon speak in this manner. A few verses are recorded by Seneca in his thirty-ninth book of letters <note>Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, 115 (Erasmus cites it as the 39th book in his edition).</note>, for the play itself is no longer extant. Since these verses are especially elegant to know, I will not be burdened to write them down, though I have corrected them in several places, since they are found corrupted in Seneca:
*It is best to be called the worst, so long as I am called rich.*
*Whether a man is good or rich, we all ask.*
*Where, why, and from where—they only ask what you have.*
*Everywhere, a man has been worth as much as he possessed.*
*You ask if it is shameful for us to possess wealth? Nothing is.*
