# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

"Whether a man is wealthy, we all ask; no one asks if he is good."
"I pray to live wealthy, or else to die poor."
"He dies well, whoever dies while making a profit."
"Money, the immense blessing of the human race."
"To which neither the pleasure of a mother, nor of sweet children,
Nor a father hallowed by his merits, can be equal.
If something so sweet shines in the face of Venus,
Rightly does she stir the loves of gods and men alike."

When these last verses, he says, were pronounced in the tragedy, the entire audience rose up as one to drive out both the actor and the poem, until Euripides himself leaped into the midst of them, begging them to wait and see what end this admirer of gold would meet. In that play, Bellerophon <note>A hero of Greek mythology; here Erasmus refers to a lost play by Euripides where Bellerophon speaks as a miser.</note> paid the penalty, just as everyone pays in their own way. Now, of these verses which Seneca recites in Latin, several of the later ones are found in Greek in Athenaeus’s *The Deipnosophists* <note>Literally "The Banquet of the Learned," a 3rd-century Greek work.</note> Book 4, though without naming the author; I will transcribe them here:

"O gold, most beautiful welcome for mortals,
For neither a mother has such pleasures,
Nor children in the home, nor a dear father,
As you and those who possess you in their dwellings provide.
If Aphrodite <note>original: "κύπρις" (Cypris), a common epithet for Venus/Aphrodite.</note> looks with such eyes,
It is no wonder she has ten thousand loves."

->that is,<-

O gold, the most adorned prize for men,
So that neither mother, nor father, nor children
Bring such delights into the home
As you provide to those who possess you.
But if the eyes of Venus shine in this way,
It is no wonder if she excites innumerable loves.

Meanwhile, one cannot help but marvel at the perverse and backwards nature of mortals. They will not endure a sound sentiment in a fictional play, spoken by a wicked character and recited by an actor in a theater, and they drive it out with a riot; yet each man forgives himself for the same thing at home. For how many are there who do not say through their lifestyle and pursuits exactly what that actor was sounding off? They shudder at these voices in the theater, yet do not shudder at them in their whole lives? What is more infamous, what is more cursed among all people than the word "lie," yet what is more common in the actual behavior of men? What is more detestable than perjury? Examine the lives of men; everything is full of perjury. See what princes swear to the people, what bishops swear, what abbots—indeed, what all Christians swear in baptism. Compare their behavior, and you will find a veritable <term>myrmecia</term> <note>original: "μυρμηκίαν" (myrmekian), a Greek term for an "anthill" or a "swarm," used here to describe a teeming mass of broken oaths.</note> of perjuries. How we abominate the name of "thief"! Yet in life you will find nothing else. Unless, perhaps, it is not theft to take borrowed money with no intention of returning it, to deny a deposit when it is safe to do so, to seize another's inheritance or possession in bad faith, to cheat a buyer, to pilfer something from the materials you have received for a job, to foist off glass as gems, or to sell one kind of wine for another. In short, to pass up no opportunity for defrauding one's neighbor. But I return to the proverbs.

---

->The speech of truth is simple. LXXXVIII<-

This adage is recorded in the collections of Diogenianus. It also appears in the *Phoenician Women* of Euripides, in this manner:

"The tale of truth is simple in its nature,
And has no need of intricate interpretations,
For it has its own fitness. But the unjust argument,
Being diseased in itself, requires clever medicines."

->that is,<-

For the speech of truth is accustomed to be
Simple, nor does it need the crafty ambages <note>A Latinate term for "windings" or "verbal evasions."</note>
Of interpreters: since it agrees with itself.
But an unfair speech, because it is diseased in itself,
Demands exquisite medicines for itself.

It is cited by Seneca in Epistle 49. For, as that tragic poet says, the speech of truth is simple. The proverb may be used against rhetoricians and poets who attempt to disguise lies with the allurements of words...

# THE SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...or toward smooth-talkers, who, because they do not speak from the heart, are accustomed to decorate their words more elaborately. They imitate true feelings with words all the more diligently because they are devoid of actual emotion. Just as hired mourners at a funeral wail and say almost more than those who are grieving from the soul. On the other hand, that simple and rustic truth ignores the "makeup" of that kind of speech. <note>original: "σῦκα, τὴν σκάφην σκάφην" — "Figs are figs, a tub is a tub." A Greek expression for calling a spade a spade.</note> That is, you call figs "figs," and a hoe a "hoe." Or it refers to those who deliver their prophecies in ambiguous words so they cannot be caught in a lie, seeking a crack through which they might slip away. Finally, it applies to those who speak perplexingly while disguising the truth. Vanity is often detected by this sign, as in the *Eunuch* of Terence:
"You wicked woman, are you speaking to me in riddles?"
"I know, he went away, I heard, I was not present."
"Are you going to tell me plainly what this is all about?"

### LXXXIX
->The tunic is closer than the cloak.<-

In Plautus’s *Trinummus*, one reads this proverbial allegory: "The tunic is closer than the cloak." <note>The tunic was the undergarment, while the cloak (pallium) was the outer wrap.</note> It signifies that we are more bound to some friends than others, and that an equal consideration should not be given to everyone. Among the ancients, the first place in duty was held by parents; the second by orphans entrusted to our faith; the third by clients; the fourth by guests; and the fifth by blood relatives and in-laws, as Gellius indicates in Book 5, Chapter 13. Furthermore, certain matters pertain to us more than others. The *pallium* was the outermost garment among the Greeks, just as the *toga* was for the Romans. The tunic was covered by the toga, as frequently seen in Homer, where "cloaks" and "tunics" <note>original: "χλαῖνας χίτωνάς"</note> are named together.

### XC
->The knee is closer than the shin.<-

<margin>The knee is closer than the shin.</margin> <note>original: "γόνυ κνήμης ἔγγιον"</note> Those who collected Greek proverbs say that this adage was born from a specific event. When a certain man in battle saw two people equally in danger for their lives—his brother and his cousin—and could not bring help to both at once, he left the cousin and defended his brother. Meanwhile, he uttered this sentiment, which later passed into a proverb: *The knee is closer than the shin.* This is cited by Aristotle in the ninth book of *Ethics*: "All proverbs," he says, "agree on this, such as 'One soul,' 'Friends' things are all common,' 'Friendship is equality,' and 'The shin is closer than the knee.'" Theocritus, in the Idyll titled *The Graces*, attributes this adage to a stingy man who helps no one and wishes to share nothing with friends:
> Each man keeps his hand hidden in his cloak,
> watching only for the source
> from which his heaped-up money might grow,
> rather than giving to a friend even after wiping off the rust.
> Instead, he immediately says: "The shin is further than the knee;
> let something come to me first."

Gellius in Book 9 seems to have turned the meaning toward things that pertain more closely to the matter at hand. Therefore, Plautus seems to have fashioned his own version from this: "The tunic is closer than the cloak." This adage is confirmed by that sentiment of Hesiod:
<margin>Never make a companion equal to a brother.</margin> <note>original: "μηδὲ κασιγνήτῳ ἶσον ποιεῖσθαι ἑταῖρον"</note>
An order must be maintained among those whom we love. Nothing, however, prevents this from being applied to things: for example, if someone should say that greater care should be taken for life than for money, for the body than for clothing, or for the soul than for the body, he would rightly cite: *The knee is closer than the shin.*

### XCI
->Everyone prefers things to be better for themselves than for another.<-

Terence expressed almost the same sentiment simply in the *Andria*:
That is a word commonly said:
That they prefer it to be better for themselves than for another.
In the same play, he twisted the proverb to fit a character:
"I am my own closest neighbor."
Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, says: "For it seems that a man is most of all a friend to himself."

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning social priorities and self-interest, explaining that it is natural to prioritize those closest to us (family over friends) or our own well-being over others.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

A lover of self <note>original: "Φίλαυτος" (Philautos)</note>, that is, for it seems to some that everyone is their own best friend. Plato says the same in the fifth book of the *Laws*: <margin>Plato, Book 5 of the *Laws*.</margin> "That which they say is necessary, that every man is by nature a friend to himself, and that this is as it should be." <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἄρα τὸ δεῖν ὃ λέγουσιν..."</note> Indeed, even today a proverb is celebrated among theologians: "Charity begins with oneself," <note>Erasmus refers to the common medieval maxim *charitas bene ordinata a seipsa incipit*.</note> evidently born from these words of the mystical song: "He set in order charity within me." <note>A reference to the Song of Solomon 2:4 in the Vulgate: "Ordinate in me charitatem."</note> Truly, what I think of that, we shall treat more diligently elsewhere when the occasion arises. But Euripides expressed the sentiment of Terence in *Medea*:
<margin>Euripides in *Medea*.</margin>
> "As every man loves himself more than his neighbor." <note>original Greek: "ὡς πᾶς τις αὑτὸν τοῦ πέλας μᾶλλον φιλεῖ."</note>
> Which is to say:
> Because each person loves himself more than a friend. Or thus:
> Because each person loves himself more even than a friend.

Again, in the collections of Greek maxims:
"No one loves anyone more than himself." <note>original Greek: "φιλεῖ δ' ἑαυτοῦ πλεῖον οὐδεὶς οὐδένα."</note>

### Self-Lovers. XCII <note>original: "Φίλαυτοι" (Philautoi)</note>

Those who are vehemently pleased with themselves, and who zealously study their own advantages while the affairs of others are either neglected or even ruined, are elegantly called *Self-Lovers* by the Greeks. The vice itself is called *Self-Love* <term>Philautia: A Greek term for excessive or blind self-love, often used by Erasmus to describe intellectual arrogance.</term>. Horace describes this aptly with a circumlocution:
<margin>Horace.</margin>
"Blind," he says, "is the love of self."
Plato reckons this vice to be the fountain of all evils. Aristotle, in the ninth book of the *Ethics*, indicates sufficiently that this *Philautia* was a shameful name, tossed about commonly as a proverb, when he says that men who love themselves beyond measure are spoken ill of by the multitude, since they are called by the foul and infamous nickname of *Self-Lovers*. Conversely, those who are displeased with themselves are called "stinking": Martial says, "One is a bit rancid, the other a bit stinking."
Moreover, this vice is almost innate, so that one's own things are more approved of than those of others—a trait which seems to have been especially prominent in the Africans. Nowhere, however, is this plague more incurable than in the dogmas with which we have once been imbued by persuasion; a point which Galen elegantly notes in the first book of *On Natural Faculties*: "So then, self-love regarding sects is an evil hard to overthrow and difficult to move, which one might call more difficult to cure than any mange." <note>original Greek: "ὅτως ἄρα δυσκαταστρεπτόν τι κακόν..."</note>

### Beyond the range of darts. XCIII

"Beyond the darts," <note>original: "Ἔξω βελῶν" (Exo belon)</note> that is, *Beyond the range of missiles*, used for that which is in safety and outside of danger. It is a metaphor taken from wars, where those who do not wish to be struck by javelins remove themselves further than they can be reached by the throw of a weapon, or keep themselves in a place defended from missiles. Hence that frequent phrase among historians: "They had now come within a stone's throw." Quintus Curtius in Book 3: "Both armies were now in sight, but beyond the range of a dart." The same author in Book 4: "So that they might be beyond the range of a dart." And again: "They had not yet come within range of a dart." This the Greeks call "Within the darts" <note>original: "ἐντὸς βελῶν" (entos belon)</note>. Nor indeed is it only said of those who are too far away to be reached by a javelin, but also of those who are safe in any way. Seneca, in the seventh book of *On Benefits*, used a similar trope, "beyond the stroke": "A sacrilegious man cannot truly do injury to God, whom divinity has placed beyond his stroke." Lucianus in *The Wishes*: "To look on while standing beyond the range of darts." Someone wishes for wings so that he might watch the combatants from on high, himself safe from missiles. The same author: "And being now beyond the dart," that is, he was now beyond the cast of the weapon. Polyphemus, himself safe from missiles, had already fled so that the Cyclops could not reach him with a weapon, at the end of the *Odyssey*, Book 10. The same author again: "Why are the Muses not struck, and why are they beyond the range of darts?"—that is: Why do you not strike the Muses, and why are they safe from your weapons? He alluded to this in *Nigrinus*: "And just as Jupiter led Hector away, so I, withdrawing myself from the darts, as they say, 'from the darts, and from the slaughter of men, and from the blood, and from the tumult,' have chosen to stay at home for the rest of my time." This is found in Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 11:
"Out of the range of darts, lest someone perhaps add wound
To wound." <note>original Greek: "Ἔκ βελέων, μήπω τις..."</note> Conversely, when we wish someone to appear liable to danger, we can say he is "within the dart." Lucianus in *Bacchus*: "Observing what had happened within the range of the dart," that is, not even staying long enough to be within range. Virgil in Book 11...

The phrase "Behind the front lines" <note>Latin: *Post principia*</note> carries almost the same meaning. It is likewise taken from warfare, in which the safest

### Far from Jove and the lightning. XCVI

Just as in a wound the blood appears before the blow, and just as the

shun the man from afar.
This is also recorded by Diogenianus among the adages. It warns, however, that it is not very safe to have

pertains what Aristotle warned Callisthenes: that he should speak with Alexander either rarely, or pleasantly. Likewise what Plutarch relates in the *Life of Solon*: he was scorned by Croesus because

this manner: "By Jove, no; rather either as little as possible or as best as possible." <note>original Greek: μὰ Δία, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἥκιστα ἢ ὡς ἄριστα</note> Ovid alluded to the proverb, having been struck by this lightning:
> Live for yourself, and as much as you can, avoid a life of great luster.
> The lightning comes to strike the escape from the illustrious citadel.

<margin>"Often there are seven," he says, "and with more uninvited guests <note>Latin: *umbris*, literally 'shadows'</note>,</margin>

Pliny, in the twenty-eighth book, second chapter, writes that Servius Sulpicius provided a reason why it was considered an ill omen to leave the table, because in those times, banquets did not yet number more than five guests. Chaerephon, in Athenaeus's sixth book, seems to allow up to thirty guests, but only at weddings. Furthermore, those who were given the task of counting the guests are called "regulators of women" <note>Greek: *gynaikonomous*; these were Athenian officials who supervised public behavior and banquets</note>. He tells a rather witty story there: A parasite <note>In antiquity, a "parasite" was a professional guest who provided wit or flattery in exchange for a meal</note> had come uninvited to a wedding and was the last to sit down; the banquet-regulators, having counted the guests, ordered him to leave because, contrary to the law, he was the thirty-first person. But he said, "Count them again, starting with me." In this way, he would not be the supernumerary one. It is also mentioned by Julius Capitolinus in the life of the Emperor Lucius Verus: "Indeed, a very famous banquet of his is reported," he says, "in which it is said twelve people first reclined, although there is a very well-known saying about the number of guests: Seven is a banquet, nine is a brawl <note>original Latin: *Septem convivium, novem vero convicium*. Erasmus notes that *convicium* (brawl/reproach) sounds like *convocium* (a shouting together)</note>." He used "brawl" to mean a great noise, as if it were a "clashing of voices." This can be applied to "polyphilia" <note>an excess of friends</note>, or to a crowd of reasons in an argument, or a mass of examples in persuasion, or even to "polytechnia" <note>possessing too many different skills</note>. In any matter, a crowd produces confusion and annoyance.

### To knock someone off their step.
->XCVIII<-

"To knock someone off their step" is a proverbial allegory for being dismayed in spirit, as if being moved from a stable state of mind. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the first book of *On Duties* says: "It is the mark of a brave and constant soul not to be perturbed in difficult times, nor to be 'knocked off one's step,' as the saying goes, but to use the counsel of a present mind." A similar figure of speech is "To put back on the step," as if restoring someone to their original place. Quintilian in the fourth book of his *Institutes* says: "Or if they should falter in any way, a timely question from the one who brought them forward may, as it were, 'put them back on their step'." Belonging to the same form are: "To move from a place," "To dislodge from a step," and "To restore to a place."

### Wiser after the misfortune.
->XCIX<-

*Meta ta deina phronimoteros* <note>original Greek: Μετὰ τὰ δεινὰ φρονιμώτερος</note>, that is, "Wiser after bitter things." This is used when someone becomes more cautious through their own misfortune, not unlike those who, having tasted poison, do not realize it is poison until they begin to feel its harmful power. It is related to what is said elsewhere:
> Even a fool knows a thing once it is done. <note>original Greek: Ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω</note>
Likewise this:
> After the events, Cleon is Prometheus. <note>original Greek: Κλέων προμηθεύς ἐστι μετὰ τὰ πράγματα. Cleon was an Athenian politician known for rashness; Prometheus means 'Forethought', while his brother Epimetheus means 'Afterthought'</note>
This adage is listed in the collection of Apostolius, whom I would not bring forward as an authority unless a lack of more suitable authors forced me to.

### Hatched from an egg.
->C<-

*Ex oou exelthen* <note>original Greek: Ἐξ ὠοῦ ἐξῆλθεν</note>, that is, "He emerged from an egg." They say this is used only for those who are remarkably beautiful and radiant, as if you were denying they were born in the common manner of men, but from an egg, in the manner of Castor and Pollux. For it is in the fables of the poets that Leda, the daughter of Tyndareus, after a tryst with Jupiter, laid two eggs, from one of which came the twins Castor and Pollux, youths of extraordinary beauty; from the other was born Helen, whose beauty is made famous by the writings of everyone.

### FIRST CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY

### Not everyone can make port at Corinth.
->I<-

*Ou pantos andros es Korinthon esth' ho plous* <note>original Greek: Οὐ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ἐς κόρινθόν ἐσθ’ ὁ πλοῦς</note>, that is:
It is not granted to just anyone to reach Corinth.
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a classical figure or scholar in a landscape.</image-desc> This is an ancient and elegant adage concerning matters that are arduous and dangerous to approach, which not just any man should attempt. It arose because, as reported in the works of Suidas, the approach for sailors into the Corinthian port was neither easy nor safe enough. However, Strabo, in the eighth book of his *Geography*, attributes the origin of the proverb elsewhere, namely to the luxury and the prostitutes of the Corinthians. For he shows that Corinth, because it was on the Isthmus and had two ports—one facing Asia and the other opposite Italy—was extremely wealthy due to the frequency of merchants. In that same city, there was a temple sacred to Venus, so enriched that it had more than a thousand girls whom the Corinthians had consecrated to Venus, so that in her...

# FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
m
<meta>catchword: also</meta>

...they might stand in the way. And so, for the sake of these things, a frequent multitude flocked together from all sides into the city, so that the state was enriched in a greater measure; indeed, even merchants and guests, making immoderate expenditures beyond the luxury and delights of the city, were drained dry. There spreads a common proverb: **It is not for every man to sail to Corinth.** <note>original: "Cuiuslibet non est Corinthum appellere." A famous proverb warning that not everyone has the wealth or luck to survive the temptations of a high-priced city.</note> Horace and Gellius refer this adage to Lais, the noble prostitute. For the former writes in his *Epistles* to Scaeva:

> It does not happen to every man to reach Corinth:
> He sat still, who feared he might not succeed.

To which he clearly alludes, for it is well known that he was accustomed to Lais, and so accustomed that he boasted that he "possessed Lais, but was not possessed by Lais." <note>A reference to the philosopher Aristippus, who claimed he enjoyed the courtesan's company without becoming her slave.</note> Here, indeed, Gellius in Book 1, Chapter 8, relates a history of this kind from a Peripatetic philosopher: Lais, he says, the Corinthian, earned a great deal of money on account of the elegance of her beauty. Assemblies of the wealthier men from all over Greece were frequent at her house, nor was anyone admitted unless he gave what she had asked; and she asked for an excessive amount. From this they say that frequent <margin>adage:</margin> Greek proverb was born: **The voyage to Corinth is not for every man.** <note>original: "οὐ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ἐς κόρινθον ἔσθ’ ὁ πλοῦς"</note>

For he would go to Corinth to Lais, who was unable to give what was demanded. The famous Demosthenes <note>The great Athenian orator.</note> approached her secretly and asked that she grant him access to herself. But Lais demanded ten thousand drachmas <note>original: "μυρίας δράχμας" — an astronomical sum in ancient currency.</note>. Struck and terrified by such insolence from the woman and the magnitude of the money, Demosthenes turned away, and departing, said: "I do not buy regret at such a price." In Greek: **I do not buy repentance for ten thousand drachmas.** <note>original: "καὶ μυρίων δραχμῶν μεταμέλειαν"</note> Others prefer to refer this generally to all the prostitutes of the Corinthians, for which matter even the Old Comedy criticized the city. Aristophanes in *Plutus* says:

> And they say of the Corinthian mistresses,
> that whenever a poor man happens to try them,
> they do not even pay him any mind; but if he is rich,
> they immediately turn their attention toward him.

I would not be burdened to turn these little verses into Latin, if they were as decent as they are elegant. Strabo mentions a certain witty remark of a prostitute, from which one may gather the meaning. For when a certain matron reproached one of this profession, saying she did no work and practiced no wool-spinning, she replied: "On the contrary, although I am as I am, I have already woven three webs in a short space of time." <note>A double entendre referring to her "work" with clients.</note> However, it does not seem absurd to me if the proverb is referred to the dangerous navigation to Corinth, which Strabo mentions in the same book. So that from here it was afterwards derived for other uses. A friend elegantly twisted the proverb against a certain parasite:
**The voyage to the table is not for every man.** <note>original: "οὐ παντὸς ἀνδρὸς ἐπὶ τράπεζάν ἐσθ’ ὁ πλοῦς"</note>
It is recorded by Stobaeus, from a certain comic poet named Nicolaus. Eustathius also mentions and explains this proverb while describing the catalog of ships, and adds that it was imitated from that verse of Sophocles:
**The voyage is not for all prudent mortals.** <note>original: "οὐ πᾶσι πλοῖοί εἰσι σώφροσι βροτῶν"</note>
This verse, which Eustathius mentions, is in Sophocles' *Philoctetes*. Therefore, the application of this adage is harsher, either when we signify that a matter is greater than the strength of the one who attempts it—as if someone born with little talent and provided with little travel-money should try to attain learning—or one who has a weak little body should strive to emulate the hermits Paul and Anthony; or whenever someone prepares to undertake an unsafe business which does not usually turn out well, such as if someone institutes a lawsuit before "market-greedy" judges <note>original: "ἀγοράγους" — judges who are easily bribed or focused on profit.</note> that will never end, or devotes himself to the courts of princes, or undertakes a war. For almost none of these things is accustomed to happen without regret, so that one does not repent of the plan.

### Enough of the oak.

<margin>11</margin>
**Enough of the oak.** <note>original: "ἅλις δρυός"</note> An ancient adage against those who, having left behind a sordid way of life, depart toward a more elegant and refined one. It originated from the fact that those ancient mortals, being rude and living in the woods, ceased to live on acorns once Ceres showed them the use of grain. Although Strabo in Book 16 testifies that even in his age many nations lived on acorns; among the Spaniards...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

even held as a delicacy, so much so that it was served at the second course <note>The dessert course of a Roman banquet</note> in place of sweetmeats. Such "treats" were certainly suitable for those who used urine in place of toothpaste. This will apply quite neatly to those who, having abandoned that ancient virtue, transfer themselves to the manners and counsels of their own age and begin to use the customs of more recent times. Cicero used it in this manner, writing to Atticus in Book 2, in the letter beginning, *Many things trouble me*. "The contentions of Clodius, which are put before me, touch me only moderately: for I seem to be able either to undergo them with the greatest dignity, or to decline them with no trouble. You will say perhaps, *enough of the oak* <note>original Greek: ἅλις δρυός (halis dryos). A proverb meaning "enough of old ways" or "enough of the primitive life," referring to the time when men lived on acorns before discovering grain.</note>, take care of your safety, if you love me. Woe is me, why are you not here?" And so indeed it is read in all copies, but for my part—with the learned, I hope, approving—I would contend it should be read thus: *Enough of the oak of dignity*, take care of your safety, if you love me. This is so you understand that the consideration of dignity is to be discarded like the oak, and that ancient pursuit of virtue must be let go, and hereafter one must consult safety rather than reputation. Regarding this, he writes elsewhere that he has this in mind, namely to the same Atticus in Book 4: "The recantation seemed to me a bit shameful, but farewell to true, right, and honest counsels." He interprets the adage openly, as it were, in this same Book 2: "What then, you will say: shall we have these men as hired mercenaries? What shall we do, if we cannot do otherwise? Should we be slaves to freedmen and even to slaves? But as you say, *enough of the oak*." He is clearly explaining what he understood by "the oak," that is, integrity and virtue. However, nothing prevents us from using the proverb in a general sense whenever any former pursuit or institution is abandoned.

### To open a window, and similar metaphors. III

**To open a window**: used for providing an opportunity, or as it were, a handle. Terence in *The Self-Tormentor*: "Alas, how great a window for wickedness have you opened?" Truly this is used only in a bad sense, whereas this other is used even in a good sense: **To open the door**. Pliny to Suetonius Tranquillus: "And indeed that action opened the ears of men to me, and opened the door of fame." Plutarch in his book *On Osiris*: "Opening great floodgates to the godless common people." <note>original Greek: μεγάλας μὲν τῷ ἀθέῳ λεὼ κλισιάδας ἀνοίγοντας</note>. Of the same form is that of Cicero in *For Plancius*: "Although I have entered into the cause by a way you did not wish." Likewise these: **To open the way**, **to prepare the way**, **to block the way**, **to lay the foundations**; which we have mentioned elsewhere. In a different sense indeed, a certain Cynic philosopher was called a **door-opener** <note>original Greek: θυρεπανόικτης (thyrepanoiktes)</note>, because he would burst into everyone's houses to rebuke whatever displeased him: but nevertheless, that word can be twisted to refer to those who open the way for others.

### To seek a handle: and similar metaphors.

A **handle** <term>Ansa: literally the handle of a jug or tool, used metaphorically for a "starting point" or "pretext"</term> is that by which anything is grasped and held. From here the metaphor is drawn, providing various forms of adages. Plautus in *The Persian*: "Do you not see that he is seeking a handle?"—that is, looking for an opportunity to cancel or invalidate the agreement. This is also drawn from a figure of the Greeks, among whom it is frequent to say **to seek a grip** or **to provide a grip**. <note>original Greek: λαβὴν ζητεῖν (labēn zētein) and πέρδην λαβεῖν (perden labein)</note>. Aristophanes in *Lysistrata*:

> For if any of us gives even a tiny handle to the women,
> They themselves will immediately leave nothing undone of their troublesome handiwork.

Plato in the third book *Of the Laws*: "And the discourse itself gives us, as it were, a handle." Aristides in *Pericles*: "To seem to provide a handle for envy." The same man said with a similar figure in *Timon*: "Nor will he give a place for slander." Again, Plato in the seventh book *Of the Laws*: "So that they provided handles of contention to many." Again, in the eighth book of *The Republic*, he indicates the metaphor is taken from wrestlers, whose art it is to so compose the body that they cannot be gripped: "Again then, just like a wrestler, provide the same handle." To the same point belong: **To fall into the same handles**, and **To seize the handle**, **to pass by the handle**, **to neglect the handle**; and if there are any others. Epictetus wrote in his *Handbook* that every thing has two handles, one by which it can be held, the other by which it cannot. Therefore, each thing must be seized by that part where it can be held; the good is to be gathered from everywhere, the bad is to be endured. A certain philosopher refused to admit young men uninstructed in mathematical disciplines because he said they lacked a "handle for philosophy." Plutarch, moreover, in his booklet *On Listening to the Poets*, wrote elegantly that there are many parts of the body through which vices insinuate themselves, but for virtue...

# FIRST CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY
m 2
<meta>catchword: says,</meta>

...indeed, that there is only one handle <note>original: "ansam" — a metaphor for a point of entry or a way to influence someone</note>, namely the ears of young men, provided they are pure and not already occupied by the flattering talk of corrupt men.

### V. The Cyclops’s gift.

<margin>The Cyclops’s gift.</margin> <note>original Greek: Κύκλωπος δῶρον</note> That is, a gift from a Cyclops: used to describe a useless or harmful gift. Such are the favors of tyrants and bandits, who are accustomed to consider it a great favor that they harm someone less severely or later than others. Cicero expresses this sentiment in his *Second Philippic*: "What other favor do bandits have, Members of the Senate, except that they can boast they gave life to those from whom they did not take it?" Lucian, in *The Downward Journey*, says: "That promise of the Cyclops does not please me at all, namely that he promises: 'I will eat Nobody last.'" <note>original: "Vtin" — the Latinized version of "Outis," the name Odysseus used to trick the Cyclops</note> These are the words of Micyllus the cobbler; when he complained that he was not immediately received into Charon’s boat with the others, and the Fate Clotho reckoned it as a favor that he might gain a little time before descending to the underworld, he replied in this manner. There is no doubt that Lucian was referring to the passage in Homer, in the ninth book of the *Odyssey*, where the Cyclops Polyphemus, delighted by the sweet wine Odysseus had given him, promises a gift. After receiving it, he says he will be greatly pleased if Odysseus serves him again from his flask. Odysseus gave him the bowl of wine again and again. Furthermore, when Odysseus believed the Cyclops was softened by the wine and would answer more mildly, he asked for the promised gift. To which the Cyclops replied in this fashion:

> "Nobody <note>original: "Vtin"</note> I shall eat last among his companions,
> And the others before him. This shall be your guest-gift."

<margin>Nobody</margin> For <note>original Greek: οὖτις</note> *outis* in Greek means "nobody": a name Odysseus had invented for himself so that he could deceive Polyphemus.

### VI. I shall paint you in your own colors.

"I shall paint you in your own colors": that is, I shall describe you exactly as you are. This is a metaphor taken from the art of painters, who sometimes express and represent a person's face just as it is, but sometimes disguise it with pigments. Or perhaps it alludes to Aesop’s jackdaw, who tried to sell himself using the colors (feathers) of others. Saint Jerome, writing against Rufinus, says: "I too could paint you in your own colors, and play the madman against a madman." Again in the same work: "For you boast that you know crimes which I confessed to you when we were the closest of friends, and that you will bring these into the open, and that I must be depicted in my own colors." Pliny, in the preface to his *Natural History*: "And lest I seem to attack the Greeks entirely, I would wish to be understood by their example, and to be painted in the colors which you will find in these little books." And Cicero, in the last letter of the second book of *Letters to his brother Quintus*: "In your colors, and with my brush." Although this last one is used in a slightly different sense.

### VII. Decorated according to your virtues.

Not much different is that Terentian irony: "Decorated according to your virtues." In *The Brothers*: "If I held a kingdom, you would be decorated according to your virtues." That is, you would have rewards worthy of your deeds. For in the past, kings used to bestow honor on those who had performed some noble exploit.

### VIII. Milesian fashions at home.

<margin>Milesian fashions at home.</margin> <note>original Greek: Οἴκοι τὰ μιλήσια</note> This was usually said against those who celebrate domestic luxury in a place where it is least approved. For at home, everyone is free to live according to their own custom. It is the duty of a guest to both praise and imitate the dress and manners of those with whom he stays as much as possible; certainly, he should not boast of his own ways while condemning those of others. This is what certain insolent men tend to do: wherever in the world they go, they find fault with everything belonging to everyone else, and impertinently extol their own things with praise, even holding up their vices as the highest virtues. This adage is recorded by Angelo Poliziano in his *Miscellanies*, and he adds that it arose because once, when a certain Milesian guest was extolling the luxuries of his homeland among the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemonios"</note>, he was answered in this way: "Milesian fashions at home, for not here." <note>original Greek: οἴκοι τὰ μιλήσια, μὴ γὰρ ἐνθάδε</note> He cites as the author of this sentiment a certain Zenodotus, a collector of adages. Indeed, the collections of a certain Zenobius are circulated, but whether he calls him Zenodotus is not yet clear enough to me; however, in these collections, I find a story of this kind, which Suidas also relates: A certain Aristagoras, having traveled from Persia to Sparta, requested that they bring help to the Ionians who were being harassed in war by the Persians. But when he came forward into the assembly, dressed with a neatness of clothing unusual among the Spartans...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

affluence, and other Ionian luxuries, one of the Ephors <note>A high-ranking magistrate in Sparta</note> is said to have warned him with this saying: *Milesian things at home.* <note>original Greek: οἴκοι τὰ μιλήσια</note> Furthermore, an Ephor is a Spartan magistrate whose duty is to judge contracts, as Aristotle testifies in the third book of his *Politics*; otherwise, the word itself sounds as if you were saying "an inspector." However, Athenaeus, in his twelfth book, tells the cause of the adage differently: namely, that the Milesians, having imitated the luxury of the Colophonians, passed their own disease even to neighboring regions. Since they were ill-spoken of for this reason, they would remind themselves to enjoy their luxuries at home, and not to display them abroad. He puts the proverb in this manner: *Milesian and domestic things should be consumed at home, and not in public.* <note>original Greek: οἴκοι τὰ μιλήσια κάπτισχεία, καὶ μὴ ἐν μέσῳ</note> Just as the severity of the Spartans has been celebrated in the writings of many, so the luxury of the Milesians passed into common speech, to the point that whatever people want to be understood as soft and unmanly, they call "Milesian." Hence a certain Aristides gave the title *Milesian Tales* <note>original Greek: μιλησιακῶν</note> to his book, which was full of obscene stories. And Lucian, in his *Affairs of the Heart*, calls lewd love-talk "Milesian." Martianus Capella says: "For certainly the poetic myth also contains Milesian delights of diversity." Indeed, even Apuleius, in an iambic poem with which he wished to begin his work, calls his soothing and prurient narratives "Milesian speech." Julius Capitolinus, in the *Life of Clodius Albinus*, says: "Some say his *Milesian Tales* are not ignobly famous, although they are only moderately well written." And that these things were said of Apuleius's stories is evidenced by what he cites a little later from a letter of Severus: "The greater grief was that you thought him worthy of praise as a man of letters, when he, occupied with certain old wives' trifles, grew old among the Punic Milesian tales of his friend Apuleius and literary playthings." Thus far Capitolinus. As for why he said "his friend Apuleius," it pertains to the fact that Albinus himself, just like Apuleius, was an African. Furthermore, the chief softness of the Milesians was in their clothing, because among them were the softest textiles of all. Whence also Tyrius Maximus calls the Milesians "most slippery" <note>original Greek: ὀλισβοτάτους</note>, doubtless from the elegance of their dress. And Virgil, in the *Georgics*, calls the most delicate fleeces "Milesian." Likewise Horace:

->He will avoid a cloak woven at Miletus<-
->worse than a dog or a snake.<-

signifying a garment that is soft and lacking in severity. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*: *Wrapped in Milesian blankets.* <note>original Greek: Στρώμασι μιλησίοις ἀναπεπραμμένοις</note> Theocritus and many other writers also mention these. But for understanding the sense of the adage, more than enough has now been said.

Euripides alluded to the proverb in *Helen*:
*Perhaps you were grand there, but not here.* <note>original Greek: οὐκὴν ἐκεῖ γε σεμνὸς ἦσθ’, ἐκ ἐνθάδε</note>
Antiphanes also alluded to it in Athenaeus, book four, in these verses:
*Since you are in Sparta,*
*you must participate in those laws.*
*Go to dinner at the common mess,* <note>term: phiditia — the public mess halls of Sparta where simple meals were eaten to promote equality</note>
*enjoy the black broth served there,*
*and wear the rough cloaks.* <note>term: bystacas — a type of coarse Spartan garment</note>
*Do not despise them, nor seek other fineries.*

### Bad women marry in the month of May.
<margin>IX</margin>
A Roman adage is found in Ovid: *Bad women marry in the month of May.* <note>original Latin: Mense Maio nubunt malæ</note> It can be said against women of untimely lust, or against those who do anything at an improper time, or who undertake something under a poor omen. For formerly it was considered ill-omened for women to marry in the month of May; either because in that month the shade of Remus, killed by his brother's henchman Celer, is believed to have appeared to his foster-father Faustulus and to Acca Larentia, and to have commanded that funeral rites be paid to his spirit. Whence, by the authority of Romulus, the festival was called *Remuria*, which posterity, by changing a letter, began to call *Lemuria*, as if from the *lemures* <note>term: lemures — restless or malevolent ghosts of the dead</note>. And it was customary to offer sacrifices to the shades of ancestors on these days; and for that reason, those days were held among the funereal ones, and ill-suited for weddings. Ovid in the *Fasti*:

### FOURTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

The same times are unsuitable for the torches of the widow <note>original: "viduae taedis"</note> and the virgin; she who married then did not last long. For this reason, if proverbs move you, the common folk say that **bad women marry in the month of May.**

Plutarch, in his *Roman Questions* <note>original: "Problematis"</note>, reports several other reasons why people abstain from marriage in this month: either because it falls between April, which is sacred to Venus, and June, which is dedicated to Juno—both of whom are goddesses presiding over weddings. Therefore, out of respect for the goddesses, they would marry either a little earlier in April or postpone it slightly until June. Or perhaps it is because of certain funeral atonements <note>original: "piacula"</note> which the Romans performed at that time, casting effigies of men from the bridge into the Tiber, whereas previously they had been accustomed to casting actual Greeks. For this reason, the Flaminica <note>The wife of the high priest of Jupiter</note> acts as if in mourning during those days and does not wear her usual festive attire. Or it may be because May <note>Maius</note> seems to be named after the elders <note>maioribus</note>, and June <note>Iunius</note> after the younger men <note>iunioribus</note>. Furthermore, an advanced age is unseasonable for marriage, and thus ill-omened. Wherefore Euripides wrote:

*Old age bids Venus farewell,* <note>original Greek: τὸ γῆρας τὴν κύπριν χαίρειν ἐᾷ</note>
*And Venus is vexed by the elderly.* <note>original Greek: ἀφροδίτη τοῖς γέρουσιν ἀχθεται</note>

That is to say, when old age commands the Goddess of Love to be gone, Venus in turn is hostile to the old.

---

->**You have entrusted the sheep to the wolf.**<-
<margin>10</margin>
*The sheep to the wolf.* <note>original Greek: Οἶν λύκῳ τὴν ὄϊν</note> That is, the wolf gets the sheep. Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "You scoundrel, you have entrusted the sheep to the wolf." This was said of the youth Chaerea, to whom a maiden was entrusted alone as if he were a eunuch. Donatus <note>A famous Roman grammarian</note> remarks that this is a proverb containing a sense of feminine modesty and the cunning of a courtesan. We shall use this appropriately whenever something is committed to the care of someone from whom it ought to be guarded. Cicero says in his *Third Philippic*: "Indeed, he had said in the assembly that he would be the guardian of the city, and would keep an army at the city until the first of May. O what a 'splendid guardian,' as they say—the wolf! Was Antony a guardian of the city, or its plunderer and tormentor?" It seems to fit perfectly whenever a business is entrusted to an enemy, or to one who wishes us the worst; furthermore, because the wolf and the lamb disagree by a certain natural hatred. Homer shows this in the 22nd book of the *Iliad*:

*As there are no faithful oaths between men and lions,* <note>original Greek: ὡς λύκοι καὶ ἀνθρώποι ὅρκια πιστά</note>
*Nor do wolves and lambs possess a like-minded spirit,*
*But they think evil of one another continually.*

Likewise, Horace says in his *Odes*:

*As great a discord as falls by lot to wolves and lambs,*
*So is my discord with you.*

To this should be added what Suidas reports: *Before a wolf shall shepherd a sheep.* <note>original Greek: πρὶν ἂν λύκος ὄϊν ποιμανεύσει</note> This refers to a thing that is in no way likely. Close to this is that line of Plautus in *Casina*: "The larder is entrusted to a good sub-butler." But closer still is what appears in *Truculentus*: "Alas, his sheep are not far from the wolves."

---

->**Tallow for the weasel.**<-
<margin>11</margin>
*The weasel's fat.* <note>original Greek: Γαλῆ στέαρ</note> One must understand: "you give" or "you entrust." This is used when things are given to those who are, by nature, most greedy for them. For this animal delights especially in tallow. It is as if one were to praise a man most greedy for praise, or provoke a natural drunkard to drink, or invite someone to a game that is immensely pleasing to him. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

---

->**I have drawn no line today.**<-
<margin>12</margin>
*Today I have led no line.* <note>original Greek: Σήμερον οὐδεμίαν γραμμὴν ἤγαγον</note> This adage arose from the painter Apelles; it applies to those who have ceased from the exercise of their study or art. It is related by Pliny in Book 35, Chapter 10, whose words I shall not be burdened to transcribe into this commentary: "It is well known," he says, "what happened between Protogenes and him. The former lived at Rhodes, and when Apelles had sailed there, eager to know his works (having known him only by reputation), he immediately sought out his workshop. Protogenes was away, but a single old woman was guarding a large panel on a frame prepared for painting. She replied that Protogenes was out, and asked who she should say had sought him. 'By this man,' said Apelles; and snatching up a brush, he drew a line..."

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<page-num>238</page-num>

...drew a line of the greatest thinness through the first line using a different color. When Protogenes returned, the old woman showed him what had happened. They say the artist, immediately contemplating the subtlety of the work, said: "Apelles has been here," for such a perfect work could fall to no one else. He then drew an even thinner line in a third color within those two, and as he left, he instructed that if the other man returned, she should show him this and add that this was the man he was looking for. And so it happened. For Apelles returned, but blushing at being surpassed, he cut the lines with a third color, leaving no further room for subtlety <note>original: "subtilitati," referring to the extreme precision of the brushwork</note>. At this, Protogenes confessed himself defeated and rushed to the harbor to find his guest. It was decided that this tablet should be handed down to posterity as a marvel to all, but especially to artists. It is well known that it was consumed in the earlier fire of Caesar’s house on the Palatine Hill; we had previously viewed it with great eagerness. It was of considerable size, containing nothing else but lines that escaped the sight, appearing like a blank space among the excellent works of many others, and for that very reason it was alluring and more noble than any other work. Apelles had, moreover, a perpetual habit of never spending a day so busy that he did not practice his art by drawing a line, which from him has passed into a proverb <note>The famous phrase "Nulla dies sine linea" or "Not a day without a line."</note>. Thus far Pliny. Furthermore, Statius referred to this line, by which he was immediately recognized by Protogenes, in his *Hercules Vindex Epitrapezios*, when he says:
->A line which confesses the ancient Apelles from afar.<-

### Neither to swim, nor to read. XIII

<note>original Greek: μήτε νεῖν μήτε γράμματα</note> "Neither to swim nor to read" (the word "knows" is understood). This is said against those who are unlearned beyond measure, and who learned absolutely nothing of the liberal arts in their childhood. For these two things were learned immediately by boys in Athens. And indeed in Rome as well, a fact which Suetonius clearly declares in his life of Augustus: "He mostly taught his grandsons reading, swimming, and other rudiments himself." He recorded the same of Caligula: that although he was otherwise very teachable, he nevertheless did not know how to swim, as if this were something everyone should know. Plato in the third book of *Laws* says: "Those who are the opposite of these should be called fools, even if, as the saying goes, they know neither reading nor swimming." Likewise Aristides in the *Common Apology for the Four Orators*: "But as this saying goes, thinking him worthy of rebuke as one who knows neither reading nor swimming."

---

### To bite the bit. XIV

Decimus Brutus, in the eleventh book of his *Familiar Letters*, seems to have used "To bite the bit" <note>original: "Mordere frenum," similar to the English "champing at the bit," but here implying resistance to control.</note> to mean even slightly resisting servitude. "If you bite the bit, may I perish if everyone, as many as there are, will be able to bear you when you try to speak." That is, if you signify in any way that you bear your servitude with an indignant mind. Cicero’s response supports this meaning: "If I were timid," he says, "nevertheless that letter of yours would have wiped away all fear from me; but as you advise, I have bitten the bit." For since I had all my hope in you while you were shut in, what do you think now? However, Papinius [Statius] in the *Epithalamium of Stella and Violantilla* used it in a different sense, namely for accepting servitude and receiving the bit:
> ->Fame, be silent; he has submitted to laws, and bitten the bit.<-
That is, he has accepted the bonds of marriage. Although, whether Cicero's words can also be taken in this sense, I leave to the learned to examine. The proverb seems to be taken from a play by Aeschylus titled *Prometheus*, in which Hermes speaks thus:
> For you are not softened at all, nor moved by my
> prayers. But biting the bit like a newly-yoked
> colt, you use force and fight against the reins.
>
> ->You do not grow mild, unbent by my prayers.<-
> ->But biting the bit, like an unbroken colt,<-
> ->Becoming fierce, you fight to overcome the reins.<-

---

### With hands and feet. XV

When signifying extreme effort, we say: "With hands and feet." For by the hands, the industry of finishing a business is declared; by the feet, the speed of hurrying it. Davus in Terence’s *Andria*: "I owe it to you, Pamphilus, in exchange for my service, to try with hands and feet." Aeschines uses this adage once or twice in his oration against Demosthenes. Homer in the twentieth book of the *Iliad*:
> But as much as I am able with both hands and feet.
>
> ->Indeed, whatever I can do with hands and feet.<-

# FIRST CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY
m 4

### With every nerve.
### XVI

<margin>**With every nerve** <note>original: "Omnibus neruis"</note>, that is, with the greatest force and the greatest zeal. For according to the <unclear>philoso</unclear>phers, strength is situated in the nerves. From this comes the expressions "to strain the nerves" and "to exert the nerves"; and a <unclear>speech</unclear> is said to be "nervy" when it is vigorous and powerful, and not at all sluggish. Cicero to his brother Quintus: "So strive with all your <unclear>nerves</unclear> and faculties." The same author in Book 15 of the *Letters to Friends*: "You should strain every nerve in that matter." Likewise in the second speech against <unclear>Verres</unclear>: "In which I would strain every nerve of my age and industry."</margin>

### With sails and horses.
### XVII

<margin>A similar effort is signified by **With sails and horses** <note>original: "Velis equisq;"</note>, used more for fleeing or overtaking than <unclear>for</unclear> <unclear>persua</unclear>ding. Marcus Tullius to his brother Quintus in the second book: "So I, who have slept so long in honoring that man—though you, by Hercules, often woke me—will correct my slowness by running, now with horses, <unclear>now</unclear> with sails." In that passage, in the common editions, "men" is written instead of "sails." <unclear>The same author</unclear> in the third book of *On Duties*: "Epicurus flourishes with these worn-out ideas, being almost the author and <unclear>helper</unclear> of the same opinion. With these, 'with horses and sails' as they say, if one intends to protect and retain what is honorable, one must <unclear>fight</unclear> to the finish." In these examples, he used the same metaphor in a slightly different way: the former used it for speed, the latter for both types of battle, cavalry and naval.</margin>

### With oars and sails.
### XVIII

<margin>Very similar is **With oars and sails** <note>original: "Remis uelisq;"</note>. It is transferred from the fact that when a ship is <unclear>carried</unclear> by both rowing and sail at the same time, it is the greatest effort of the sailors. Cicero in the third book of *Tusculan Disputations*: "It is a foul thing, wretched, <unclear>detesta</unclear>ble, to be fled from with every struggle, with sails, so to speak, and oars." The same in the first *Philippic*: "<unclear>For</unclear> truly I am incensed with such a great desire for return, that to me neither oars nor winds will <unclear>suffice</unclear>." Plautus in *Asinaria*: "With oar and sail, as much as you are able, hurry and flee." <unclear>When</unclear> a ship is propelled by rowing, the Greeks call it "sailing with two oars" <note>original: "δικώπου πλεῖν"</note>, that is, a secondary course; <unclear>when</unclear> it is carried by sails, it is called "running by sail" <note>original: "ἱστιοδρομεῖν"</note>; when by favorable winds, "running with the breeze" <note>original: "οὐριοδρομεῖν"</note>. Aristophanes turns the metaphor to the opposite, <unclear>namely</unclear> to signify slowness, in *The Assemblywomen*: "neither when we run nor when we row" <note>original: "οὐδ’ ὅτε θεομὲν οὔτε ἐλαύνομεν"</note>, that is, <unclear>neither</unclear> do we run now, nor are we propelled at other times. <unclear>Lucian</unclear> explains: "We navigate neither by winds nor by oars." Although nothing prevents it from referring to the same course. Virgil expressed it simply in the third book of the *Aeneid*: "The whole crew makes all <unclear>sails</unclear> and sought [the land] with oars and winds." <unclear>To</unclear> this form belongs what Plato says in the ninth book of *Laws*: "Flee the company of the wicked without turning back" <note>original: "τὰς δὲ τῶν κακῶν ξυνοσίας ἀμεταστρεπτί"</note>, that is, do not <unclear>even look</unclear> behind you. He alluded to the fable of Eurydice, to whom the law was given that she should not look <unclear>back</unclear>. And in Genesis, Lot is ordered to flee from Sodom "without turning back" <note>original: "ἀμεταστρεπτί"</note>. And Virgil: "Throw the head away, do not look back."</margin>

### By ships and four-horse chariots.
### XIX

<margin>With the greatest zeal and the greatest haste, Horace <note>referred to as Flaccus</note> said, **By ships and four-horse chariots** <note>original: "Nauib. atq; quadrigis"</note>, in his *Epistles*: "A restless boredom exercises us; with ships and <unclear>chariots</unclear> we seek to live well. What you seek is here." <unclear>Theognis</unclear> against usury: "Do not care for horsemanship, nor yoked vehicles, nor the <unclear>assurance</unclear> of speed which they overtake and destroy. But on any old donkey you happen upon, or a pack-horse, flee the <unclear>enemy</unclear> and the tyrant moneylender."</margin>

### With swift chariots: With the chariots of Jove.
### XX

<margin>To flee **with swift chariots**, and **to flee with the chariots of Jove**, stands for fleeing as quickly as possible. Therefore in Plautus, it is borrowed from Homer, who assigns chariots to the gods, by which they may be snatched <unclear>wherever</unclear> they wish, suddenly, from Olympus to the earth, and back from the earth to heaven. To these Cicero <unclear>alludes</unclear>, writing to his brother Quintus: "Since you write that our poem is approved by him [Caesar] as if traveling in a <unclear>chariot</unclear>, just give me Britain, which I shall paint with your colors and my brush." <unclear>Plautus</unclear> in *Aulularia*: "Whatever he orders, let him hasten to perform with swift chariots." Livy, in the fifth <unclear>book</unclear> of the first decade, relates that Camillus, after Veii was captured, entered the city in such a triumph that he was carried in a <unclear>chariot</unclear> joined to white horses, and for that reason the triumph was more famous than it was popular. Because he was seen to be striving to equal the chariot of the Sun and of Jove.</margin>

<summary>This page explores various classical idioms for exerting maximum effort or speed, drawing on metaphors of physical anatomy (nerves), naval travel (sails and oars), and rapid transport (chariots and horses).</summary>
<keywords>metaphor, speed, effort, Cicero, Plautus, Horace, Virgil, classical idioms, sailing, chariots</keywords>

--- Page 246 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s monumental collection of "Adagia" (Adages), providing Greek and Latin origins for common metaphors and idioms. The previous page likely concluded a different set of proverbs.</meta>

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES<-

<margin>XXI</margin>
### To go before with white horses.
When they wished to signify that someone was far superior to others in some matter, and preceded them by a long interval, they said he "went before with white horses." This was either because in antiquity white horses were considered better, or because victors in a triumph were accustomed to be carried by white horses; or perhaps because white horses are believed to be luckier and more auspicious, if we refer the metaphor to equestrian competition. Indeed, Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman novelist</note> indicates this when he says: "After I emerged from the steep mountains, the dewy turf, and the cloddy plains, carrying myself on a native horse of pure white, though he was by then quite exhausted." For he does not add "native" (that is, Thessalian) or "white" without reason; both pertain to the emphasis of swiftness. Horace, in his *Satires*, says of a certain Persius:
> So confident and swollen, and of such bitter speech,
> That he outran the Sifennas and Barruses with white horses.
Now, Sifenna and Barrus were men of noted abusiveness—even if Acron <note>An ancient commentator on Horace</note> reads "barbarians" so that it serves as an epithet. Not dissimilar to this is that line of Plautus in *Asinaria*: "For if the opportunity of this moment withdraws itself, by Pollux, he will never catch it afterwards even with a four-horse chariot of white." The Greeks simply say *pappediazein* <note>original: παππηδιάσαι</note> for "to far excel," because the equestrian course is more unimpeded.

<margin>XXII</margin>
### To hold with the teeth.
"To hold with the teeth" <note>Latin: *Mordicus tenere*</note> is to defend something with the greatest tenacity, which the Greeks call *odax* <note>original: ὀδάξ, meaning "biting with the teeth"</note>. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the first book of *Academic Questions*: "For we shall say that clarity, which we ought to hold with our teeth, is absent from all such visions." Saint Aurelius Augustine, in a certain letter to Saint Jerome: "Those men move me more, who, when they interpreted later and held the way and rules of Hebrew words and locutions 'with their teeth' (as the saying goes), not only failed to agree among themselves, but even left many things behind." Seneca spoke in the same sense in the seventh book of *On Benefits*, using the phrase "With both hands": "These things," he says, "our Demetrius orders one who is setting out to hold with both hands; these things he must never let go."

<margin>XXIII</margin>
### With the whole body, with all the little nails.
These have a similar meaning of tenacity: "With the whole body," and "With all the little nails." The metaphor is taken from wild beasts, which are accustomed to hold on with teeth, claws, and the whole body because they do not want a thing to be wrenched away. Lucian in the dialogue of Diogenes and Crates: "For to guard it by every device" <note>original: τὸ γὰρ πάσῃ μηχανῇ ἐφυλάττεσθαι</note>, that is, "Moreover, they kept the gold with teeth and nails and every resource." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book of *Tusculan Disputations*: "With the whole body and with all the nails (as they say), they asserted themselves in the contention of the voice."

<margin>XXIIII</margin>
### Both nights and days.
Everywhere they signify constant and indefatigable diligence by this figure: "nights and days."
Horace in *The Art of Poetry*:
> Turn them with a nightly hand, turn them with a daily one.
Hesiod:
> Both nights and days <note>original: Νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα</note>.
Likewise elsewhere:
> Both when she seeks her bed, and when the holy light comes <note>original: ἡ μὲν ὅτ' εὐνάζῃ, ἡ δ' ὅταν φάος ἱερὸν ἔλθῃ</note>.
And repeatedly in Homer:
> All nights and all days <note>original: Νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα πάντα</note>.

<margin>XXV</margin>
### By land and by sea.
This also has a proverbial face: "By land and by sea," whenever we signify extreme effort and zeal. Theognis:
> For one must likewise over the land and the broad back of the sea
> Seek, O Cyrnus, some escape from harsh poverty <note>original: Χρὴ γὰρ ὁμῶς ἐπὶ γῆν τε, καὶ εὐρέα νῶτα θαλάσσης / Δίζησθαι χαλεπῆς κύρνε λύσιν πενίης</note>.
And Horace:
> Fleeing poverty through the sea, through rocks, through fires.

<margin>XXVI</margin>
### With the whole breast.
When we signify a sincere and absolute love, we say "with the whole breast" <note>meaning "with all one's heart"</note> and "with the whole soul": "with all strength and with all the spirit" <note>original: παντὶ σθένει καὶ παντὶ θυμῷ</note>. Cicero in the first book of *On Laws*: "Where is that sacred friendship, if the friend himself is not loved for his own sake 'with the whole breast,' as the saying goes?" It is also cited in Aristotle’s *Ethics*.

<summary>This page explores several classical adages related to superiority, tenacity, and diligence, providing etymological roots and literary examples from authors like Cicero, Horace, and Homer. Erasmus explains the transition from physical actions (like horses racing or beasts clawing) to metaphorical expressions of character and effort.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, white horses, tenacity, diligence, Cicero, Horace, Greek idioms, Latin metaphors, classical education</keywords>

# FIRST CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY

<margin>XXVII</margin>
In place of a single word, one may say **With the whole soul** <note>original: "Toto animo"</note>, or in Greek, **with all one's spirit** <note>original: "παντὶ θυμῷ"</note>. However, the phrase **With the whole breast** <note>original: "Toto pectore"</note> can also refer to zeal and application. As Marcus Tullius [Cicero] does in the thirteenth book of his *Letters to Friends*: "Let us think of the gardens of Scapula with our whole breast." Likewise in the twelfth book: "Embrace the thought with your whole breast." Seneca in his third letter: "Think for a long time whether someone should be received into your friendship; but when you have decided it should be done, admit him with your whole breast." Cornelius [Tacitus] in the *Dialogue on Orators*: "That sincerity and discipline tended toward this: so that each person's nature, pure, whole, and distorted by no depravities, might immediately seize honorable arts with the whole breast." Saint Augustine somewhere said **With all the guts** <note>original: "Totis uisceribus"</note>, as they say, softening the expression as if it were a common folk idiom. The Hebrews say **With the whole heart**.

### With a soft arm; With a light arm.

The meaning is nearly the opposite: **With a soft arm** <note>original: "Molli brachio"</note> and **With a light arm** <note>original: "Leui brachio"</note> signify negligent or half-hearted effort. Cicero in the second book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "As for your rebuking me in a way with a soft arm regarding my intimacy with Pompey, I would not wish you to think so." The same author to the same person in the fourth book: "The consuls, who had acted on that matter with a light arm, referred the business to the senate."

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
### To attack with every kind of weapon.

One finds in suitable writers the phrase **To attack with every kind of weapon** <note>original: "Omni telorum genere oppugnare"</note>, used for "to pursue or harass with everything." The metaphor seems to be taken from that line of Homer: *with arrows and with great hand-stones* <note>original: "τ' ἰοσί τε, μεγάλοισί τε χερμαδίοισιν"</note>, that is, they press on with both swords and huge rocks. Very close to this is **With the edge and with the point** <note>original: "Cæsim ac punctim"</note>. For in these two ways we strike the enemy.

<margin>XXIX</margin>
### At close quarters and from a distance.

To the same form belongs the Greek *from near and from far* <note>original: "ἐγγύθεν & πόῤῥωθεν"</note>, that is, **At close quarters and from a distance** <note>original: "Cominus atq; eminus"</note>. This is transferred from war, in which men fight now crowded together with swords, now twisting missiles from afar with machines. If this is transferred to matters of the mind, it becomes more elegant. While we must live with men, we must fight against vices at close quarters and from a distance. Those who fight at close quarters are said to fight **hand-to-hand** <note>original: "συσταδὸν"</note>; those with spears are said **to fight through spears** <note>original: "διὰ δορὰτων μάχεσθαι"</note>.

<margin>XXX</margin>
### To move every stone.

**Move every stone** <note>original: "πάντα λίθον κίνει"</note>, that is, move each and every stone. This means to try everything and leave nothing unattempted. Most say this adage was born in this way: Xerxes, having attacked the Greeks and been defeated at Salamis, moved away from there himself, but left Mardonius behind to prosecute the war in his name. But when Mardonius also fought unsuccessfully at Plataea and was put to flight, a rumor grew among the common people that he had left a huge treasure buried in the ground within the circuit of his tent. Enticed by this hope, Polycrates the Theban bought that field. But when he had sought the treasure for a long time and achieved nothing, he consulted the Delphic oracle on how he might find the money. Apollo replied with these words: **Move every stone**. When he had done so, he is said to have found a great force of gold. There are those who think the metaphor is taken from those who hunt for crabs on the shore. For these usually hide under rocks, which those seeking crabs must move. The adage is also expressed in this way: **I will move every rock** <note>original: "πάντα κινήσω πέτραν"</note>, that is, I will risk everything. Euripides in the *Heracleidae* says **to move every rock**, meaning that nothing is left undone. Pliny the Younger in a certain letter says: "I immediately see the jugular, and I press there. He certainly presses what he has chosen, but in choosing he often errs. I replied that it could happen that what he thought was the jugular was actually the knee, or the shin, or the ankle. But I, who cannot perceive the jugular, try everything, test everything, **I move every stone**." Saint Basil to his nephews: "To prepare for that life, every stone, as the saying goes, must be moved." Perhaps that critical line in the *Bucoliasts* <note>Theocritus, Idylls</note> alluded to this:
"And she moves the stone from the line."
This refers to Galatea acting playfully and trying everything to provoke Polyphemus toward her, a point we have discussed elsewhere. The Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> notes it is said as a proverb, signifying the same as **to move every rope** <note>original: "πάντα κινέειν"</note>. He adds a metaphor taken from some game: a player who cannot defeat his opponent by any other means moves the stone from the "sacred line." For what he suggests about a stone statue that Galatea could move by her beauty is, in my opinion, forced.

<summary>Erasmus explains various metaphors for total commitment and thoroughness, such as "moving every stone" and "with the whole breast," tracing their origins to Greek history, poetry, and Roman oratory.</summary>
<keywords>adages, Cicero, Seneca, Homer, Xerxes, Mardonius, Delphic oracle, metaphors, diligence, ancient warfare</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Adages, moving from nautical metaphors for effort to the famous imagery of gambling and risk. The previous page likely concluded a different set of Greek-derived proverbs.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### 31. To move every rope.
**Omnem rudentem mouere.**

*Panta kalon seiein* <note>original: Πάντα κάλων σείειν</note>, that is, to move every rope. Though the metaphor is drawn from a different source <note>likely seafaring</note>, it conveys the same meaning <note>as "leaving no stone unturned"</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:
> Now, because of you, it is necessary to let out every rope,
> And to carry a fierce prize, and an inescapable argument.

The sense of these verses is: Now you must deploy every cable, bring forth a powerful premise, and use unavoidable logic. Lucian in *The False Prophet* writes: "And wishing to avenge that man, I moved every rope" <note>original: Καὶ πάντα κάλων ἐκείνην ἀμυνάς βουλόμενος</note>. Apollonius in a letter to Euphrates says: "They say a merchant ought to move every rope" <note>original: πάντα φασὶ δεῖν τὸν ἔμπορον κάλων σείειν</note>. Plato also used it in the dialogue titled *Sisyphus*: "Let us consider then, by Jove, letting out every rope, as they say, and letting out every voice" <note>original: σκοπῶμεν νὴ Δία... πάντα κάλων ἐφιέντες</note>. Julius Pollux in the first book of his *Vocabulary of Things* writes: "We were sailing having shaken out every rope, and with all cables" <note>original: ἐπλέομεν πάντα ἀνασείσαντες κάλων</note>. In this manner, it signifies a difficult voyage in which everything must be attempted.

### 32. To cast every die.
**Omnem iacere aleam.**

To cast every die is to risk the whole business and commit it to the judgment of Fortune. Indeed, dice is a game of luck more than skill. Hence, by a proverbial figure of speech, whenever we indicate the outcome of a doubtful matter—as if it depends not on the will of the thrower but on Fortune—we say "the die is cast." Thus Terence in *The Brothers* said the life of men is just as when you play with dice: if that which you need does not fall by the throw, you must correct it by skill. Lucian, in the dialogue titled *The Loves* <unclear>or Images</unclear>, says: "I will dare to throw the die" <note>original: Τολμήσω ἀναρρίψαι τὸν κύβον</note>. Euripides in *Rhesus*:
> It is right to bear rewards worthy of the labor,
> Whoever bravely exposes his life to the dice of the deity.

Aristides says in *Pericles*: "And one die was cast for all things: lives, money, reputation, and leadership" <note>original: Καὶ εἰς ὑπὲρ πάντων κύβος ἀνερρίφθη</note>. Julius Caesar at the Rubicon—the river which divides Italy from Gaul—hesitated for a moment, reflecting on how arduous an undertaking he was attempting. After his mind was emboldened by an omen, he said: "Let us go where the omens of the gods and the iniquity of our enemies call us: let the die be cast." Plutarch in his *Apophthegms* <note>Sayings of Kings and Commanders</note> records him saying it this way: "Let every die be thrown" <note>original: πᾶς ἀνερρίφθω κύβος</note>. Alluding to this, Lucan writes:
> Let the die of fate fall,
> The measure of either leader.

Plutarch, in the *Life of Coriolanus*, seems to use "the furthest die" in the same sense: "As if throwing the final die" <note>original: ὥσπερ ἔσχατον κύβον ἀφιέναι</note>.

Likewise Petronius Arbiter:
> Let the die fall with Fortune as judge.

Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the second book *On Divination*: "Do you not perceive that a certain 'die' exists in choosing sacrificial victims, especially when the reality itself teaches us? For when the most dismal entrails are found without a 'head' <note>a part of the liver</note>, than which nothing seems more dire, the very next victim often provides a beautiful omen." Here, Cicero used "die" to mean "chance." The proverb seems to be taken from Menander, for Athenaeus in his thirteenth book cites these verses from the comedy titled *The Basket-Bearer* or *The Flute-Girl*:
> You will not marry if you have any sense, leaving this life behind.
> For I myself have married, therefore I advise you not to marry.

To this, the other responds:
> The matter is decided; let the die be cast.
> <note>original: Δεδογμένον τὸ πρᾶγμα, ἀνερρίφθω κύβος</note>

The Greek verses in Athenaeus are somewhat corrupted by the ignorance of scribes. But they can be restored with no trouble. For I think they were originally written thus:
> You will not marry if you have any sense, at least leaving this life,
> For I myself have married, therefore I advise not to marry.

<summary>Erasmus explores two proverbs regarding effort and risk: "moving every rope" (exerting all possible effort) and "casting the die" (committing to a risky, irreversible course of action), famously associated with Julius Caesar.</summary>
<keywords>nautical metaphors, gambling, Julius Caesar, Rubicon, risk, fate, Greek comedy, classical philology</keywords>
