<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s "Adagia," a collection of Greek and Latin proverbs with his scholarly commentary. This section falls within the first Chiliad (thousand), fourth Century.</meta>

# FIRST CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY

<margin>Plato. "All of life."</margin>
Plato, according to Plutarch, said that human life is like a game of dice: one must hope for a favorable toss, but must also know how to use whatever has actually fallen to one's advantage. What falls is a matter of luck, but to distribute and manage those chance falls correctly is within our own power. Terence seems to have imitated this comparison in his play *The Brothers*.

### 33. To commit the sails to the winds.

<margin>Quintilian</margin>
Quintilian used a similar figure of speech in the preface to his *Institutes of Oratory*: "Let us commit our sails to the winds, and pray for a good voyage as we loose the cables." This means: let us try the uncertain outcome of publication and see how it lands. Very similar is that line in Seneca’s *Agamemnon*:
<margin>Seneca</margin>
"Whatever the wind has given the ship," <note>original: "Quidquid uentus dedi ratem"</note> that is, I have committed the matter to the judgment of fortune. Theognis says:
<margin>Theognis</margin>
->“Setting our white sails, we are carried along.”<- <note>original: "τῷ φέρεσθαι καθ' ἰδία λευκὰ βαλόντες"</note>
->that is, now we are carried along, stretching our canvas to the winds.<-
<margin>Plutarch</margin>
Among the Greeks, the phrase "to sail" or "to be carried" is used for someone who is swept toward something with their whole heart and greatest effort. Thus Plutarch, in his life of *Cato the Elder*, writes regarding Scipio: Cato reproached him for corrupting the youth. Scipio replied that he had no need of an overly diligent treasurer, since he was being swept toward war <note>original: "πλεοῖς"</note> with "full sails." Ovid writes:
<margin>Ovid</margin>
->“Since I am carried on a great sea, and have given my full sails to the winds.”<-

***

### 34. Under every stone a scorpion sleeps.

->“Under every stone a scorpion sleeps.”<- <note>original: "ὑπὸ παντὶ λίθῳ σκορπίος εὕδει"</note>
->that is, Under every stone a scorpion sleeps, or (to preserve the meter, for it is an anapestic dimeter):<-
->Under every stone a scorpion, every one.<-
This adage teaches that one must be careful not to speak rashly in the presence of captious and slanderous people. For whatever one touches, there is a danger of being bitten. It is well known that scorpions usually lie under rocks; if someone lifts them incautiously, they are struck and wounded. This also applies to sycophants <note>professional slanderers or "yes-men"</note> who are prone to find fault with anything, or to lazy people who use trivial excuses to avoid work. Aristophanes in *The Women at the Thesmophoria*:
<margin>Aristophanes</margin>
->“Praise the lack of it...<-
->look out, for under every stone<-
->a scorpion, a herald, or a rhetorician lurks.”<-
An old commentator on the plays cites this line from the *Captives* of Sophocles:
<margin>Sophocles</margin>
->“For a scorpion keeps watch under the stone.”<-
It signifies that nothing is safe and everything must be guarded against.

***

### 35. An ass at the lyre.

<margin>Varro</margin>
"An ass at the lyre"—understand "as a listener"—that is, an ass listening to a lyre. This is said of those who, through ignorance, have no judgment and possess "thick ears." Marcus Varro gave this proverbial title to one of his satires. These words of his survive in Gellius, from the satire titled *The Will*:
<margin>Gellius</margin>
"If one or more sons are born to me within ten months: if they are 'asses at the lyre,' let them be disinherited." He calls those who are unteachable in the liberal arts and unmanageable "asses at the lyre." Saint Jerome, writing to Marcella:
<margin>Jerome</margin>
"Although I could rebuke them by my own right (for the lyre sings in vain to an ass), yet I do not, lest they accuse us of pride, as they are wont to do." And the same author against Vigilantius: "Although I act foolishly in teaching the teacher of all, and imposing a limit on him who knows not how to speak and cannot remain silent. That Greek proverb is true: 'An ass at the lyre.'" Lucian, concerning those who serve for hire:
<margin>Lucian</margin>
"For what does an ass have in common with a lyre?" <note>original: "Τί γὰρ κοινὸν ὄνῳ καὶ λύρᾳ;"</note> as the saying goes. The same author against an unlearned man: "But you, an ass hearing a lyre, were twitching your ears." From this, the adage is also expressed this way: "An ass twitching its ears." Again, in this manner: "Someone was telling a story to an ass, but it just twitched its ears." This is used against those who, although they understand nothing, nevertheless nod or smile at the speakers as if there were nothing they *didn't* understand. It is innate to an ass to twitch its ears from time to time, as if signaling that it now understands, even when it has heard nothing.

<summary>This page explores three classical adages regarding the unpredictability of life's "toss," the danger of hidden enemies (scorpions under stones), and the futility of presenting art or wisdom to the ignorant (the ass at the lyre).</summary>

--- Page 250 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs (Adagia), specifically focusing on metaphors for the unlearned or boorish person who cannot appreciate art or wisdom. It follows the previous page's discussion of similar metaphors involving animals.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...heard it. Sometimes they refer this to an ass not merely listening to a lyre, but attempting to play it himself. Lucian <note>A 2nd-century Greek satirist</note> says: *Especially whenever he sings, and wishes to appear elegant and charming, they say the ass is playing the lyre himself.* <note>original: "ὄνον αὐτολυρίζειν φασί"</note> The same author in *The False Logician*: *As the saying goes, it was an ass listening to a lyre, and I fart right back at it,* <note>original: "ὄνος δ’ ἦν τὸ τοῦ λόγου, ὄνου λύρας ἀκούειν καὶ πέρδομαι ὀρθῶς"</note> that is, according to the common proverb, you are seeing an ass trying to play the lute. This little verse is also cited: *The ass listened to the lyre, and the pig to the trumpet.* <note>original: "ὄνος λύρας ἤκουε, καὶ σάλπιγγος ὗς"</note>
This is rightly twisted against those who ungracefully attempt a skill in which they are unskilled, and for which they are naturally unsuited. Stratonicus, in the eighth book of Athenaeus’s *The Learned Banqueters*, wittily inverted the adage. There was a certain Cleon, nicknamed "The Ox"; when he sang skillfully with his voice but did not use the lyre as well, Stratonicus approached him while he was singing and said: "Once, they spoke of the 'ass at the lyre,' but now it is the 'ox at the lyre.'"

### XXXVI
->The pig heard the trumpet.<-

*The pig heard the trumpet.* <note>original: "Σάλπιγγος ὗς ἤκουε"</note> This will apply to those who hear truly excellent things, but neither understand nor admire them. Or to those who are neither delighted nor moved by what they hear. Horses are stirred to war by the blare of trumpets; it would sooner drive a pig away than inspire it to fight. A six-foot line of verse of this kind exists in Suidas:
*The ass listened to the lyre, and the dull pig to the trumpet.*

### XXXVII
->The jackdaw has nothing to do with the lute.<-

*The jackdaw has nothing to do with the lute,* that is, the dull and unskilled have nothing to do with fine literature. For the jackdaw is a bird of foolish and annoying chatter, and so noisy that Quintilian, in the first book of his *Institutes*, thinks its name was given from the sound of its voice. Furthermore, it loves gatherings of its own kind, where the noise becomes more hateful through mutual chattering. Moreover, the lute requires silence and attentive ears. Aulus Gellius, in the final study of his *Attic Nights*, quite elegantly twists this adage against certain men of duller wit, endowed with stupid loquacity—profane and "un-Mused" <note>original: "ἀμούσους", meaning lacking in culture or the arts</note>—that is, strangers to the sacred rites of the Muses. Such men can either mock or even despise more polished literature and more elegant learning, but they can by no means understand it. They are pleased only by those things which they themselves have learned: filthy, silent, and unlearned things. With equal persistence, they bark against the learning of others and everywhere claim and insist upon their own ignorance, despising everyone but themselves. Gellius, driving away this class of men from his commentaries (than which nothing can be more polished or more erudite) as if with a club, says: "It is an old adage: The jackdaw has nothing to do with the lute."

### XXXVIII
->The pig has nothing to do with marjoram ointment.<-

And he immediately connects a similar one to it: *The pig has nothing to do with marjoram ointment,* <note>original: "amaracino"</note> that is, the best things are displeasing to the stupid. Marjoram <note>Amaracus</note> is a type of herb, named in the Sicilian tongue after Amaracus, the son of the Cypriot king Cinyras, who is recorded in fables to have been turned into this herb. However, Servius, in his commentary on the first book of the *Aeneid*, writes that Amaracus was the king's perfumer boy, who accidentally tripped while carrying ointments and created a greater scent by the spill, from which the best marjoram ointments began to be named; he was later turned into the marjoram herb. It is also called *sansucum* and by various other names, as Dioscorides records in his third book, saying it has a most pleasing scent and is entirely fragrant. Pliny, in Book 13, Chapter 1, mentions marjoram among the noble ointments, reporting that it was once most highly praised in Cos; later, quince ointment was preferred in the same place; he then teaches that a most noble ointment is made from various ingredients. The same author in Book 21, Chapter 22, writes that the most praised and fragrant *sansucum* grows in Cyprus, and he shows its various remedies; and that an oil is also made from it, which is called *amaracinum* or *sansucinum*. Since marjoram ointment is of this nature, and on the other hand nothing is more filthy than a pig, nothing more fond of dregs (wherefore Virgil said: *The filthy pigs remembered.* Furthermore, Horace: *Or the pig, friend to the mud.* And, *The muddy pig rushes.*), nothing certainly is less suited to a swine's snout than the delights of the perfumer; for to the pig, only that which smells of filth smells sweet. Especially since among ointments, by a certain peculiar property of nature, marjoram is an enemy to the swine kind, so much so that it is like poison to them.

<summary>Erasmus explains several proverbs—the ass at the lyre, the pig hearing the trumpet, and the jackdaw with the lute—all of which satirize uncultured people who cannot appreciate fine art or learning. He concludes with the "pig and marjoram" adage, noting that fine things are often wasted on, or even repulsive to, the ignorant.</summary>

# THE FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<margin>Signature: n</margin>
<margin>Catchword: Thence</margin>

We do not believe Lucretius, whose verses in his sixth book are these:
> The sow flees the scent of marjoram, and fears every
> Ointment; for to bristly swine it is a sharp poison.
<note>original: "Amaracinum fugitat fus..." Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 6.973. Marjoram was a prized perfume in antiquity.</note>

There was once a time when the Egyptians considered the pig so filthy a beast that if anyone even touched one while passing by, they would immediately hurry to the river to wash both themselves and their clothing. Swineherds, even if native-born, are the only ones kept apart, so that they are neither received into temples nor admitted into marriage or family alliances; the authority for this is Herodotus in his second book. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> seems to have alluded to this adage when he says: *That man’s armpit stinks, full of ointment.* That is to say, the best things are displeasing to the worst people. Something similar is said of the beetle, for whom ointment is as dung, and dung is as ointment; Plutarch almost implies that this is a common saying in his commentary where he compares the dogmas of the Stoics with the sayings of the poets: *They say that beetles flee perfume and seek out foul-smelling things.* <note>original Greek: λέγουσι οἱ κάνθαροι τὸ μύρον ἀπολείπειν...</note>

### What has a dog to do with a bath? XXXIX

*What is there in common between a dog and a bathhouse?* <note>original Greek: Τί κοινὸν κυνὶ καὶ βαλανείω</note> I record this adage all the more gladly because it rubs and renews my memory as well as my longing for Rodolphus Agricola of Friesland. I hold this man in the highest public honor throughout both Germany and Italy: the former for giving him birth, the latter for instructing him in the best literature. For nothing more perfect in all literary gifts has ever been produced from the Alpine world—may there be no ill-will in the saying. There was no noble discipline in which that man could not compete with the greatest masters: among the Greeks he was the most Greek, among the Latins the most Latin. In poetry, you would have called him a second Maro <note>Virgil</note>; in his prose, he reflected the charm of a Politian, yet surpassed him in majesty. His speech, even when extemporaneous, was so pure and so authentic that you would swear he was no Frisian, but a native of the city of Rome. To such perfect eloquence he joined an equal erudition. He had penetrated the mysteries of philosophy. There was no part of music in which he was not most exactly skilled. At the end of his life, he had applied his whole mind to Hebrew literature and the Holy Scriptures. And while he was attempting these things, envy snatched the man from the earth, not yet forty years old, as I understand. Some monuments of his work exist: certain letters, poems of various kinds, the *Axiochus* <note>A pseudo-Platonic dialogue</note> rendered into better Latin, and Isocrates' *To Demonicus* translated. Then there are one or two orations delivered in the public assembly of the scholars of Ferrara; for there he both learned and publicly taught. His commentaries on dialectic lie hidden with I know not whom; they recently came into public view, but in a mutilated state. There were also several Dialogues of Lucian; but, as he himself was negligent of glory—and most mortals are accustomed to care for the affairs of others quite carelessly—they have not yet emerged into the light. Although these very things which do exist, even if not published by him, clearly display a certain divinity in the man. Lest I, as a German, seem to be blinded by an immoderate zeal for my fatherland, I shall transcribe the epitaph by Hermolaus Barbarus of Venice concerning him; it is truly most elegant, and you might doubt whether it is more worthy of the one who wrote it or the one he adorned with it. It is as follows:
> Truly the fates have enclosed in this marble Rodolphus
> Agricola, the hope and glory of the Frisian soil.
> Truly while he lived, Germany earned whatever praise
> Latium <note>Rome/Latin culture</note> possesses, or whatever Greece possesses.

For what could have happened to our Rodolphus that was greater or more magnificent than such a splendid and full testimony, and one rendered not while he was alive, but after he had departed this life? In such a case, the cause can hardly be attributed to affection rather than judgment. Furthermore, it was not from a German, lest the zeal for a common fatherland diminish the weight of the testimony; finally, it was from that man <note>Hermolaus Barbarus</note> who illustrated not only Italy, but this entire century of ours. His authority among all the learned is so great that it would be most impudent to disagree with him; his usefulness in restoring literature is so distinguished that anyone for whom the memory of Hermolaus is not sacrosanct must be considered either a complete stranger to all letters or certainly most ungrateful. To these so full and absolute praises of the man, I myself am moved to favor him even more particularly and intensely because it was my lot, while still a boy, to have as a teacher his disciple Alexander Hegius of Westphalia. Hegius then directed the once-celebrated school of the town of Deventer, in which we, as young boys, learned the first elements of both languages <note>Latin and Greek</note>. He was a man, to speak briefly, very like his own teacher: as much in the integrity of his life as in his uncommon learning. In him, even Momus <note>the god of mockery/criticism</note> himself could perhaps have found only one thing to carp at: that being more negligent of fame than was right, he took no account of posterity. For—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

thence, if he wrote anything, he wrote it in such a way that he seems to have been engaged in a playful matter rather than a serious one. Although even those writings are of such a kind that they deserve immortality by the judgment <note>original: "calculis," literally "pebbles" used for voting or counting</note> of the learned. Therefore, I have not wandered into this digression without reason: not to boastfully toss about the praises of Germany, but to fulfill the role of a grateful disciple and to pay the debt of duty to the memory of both men as best I could: because to the one I owe the piety of a son, and to the other the affection of a grandson. Now to the adage, which I remember learning when I was still a boy and unlearned in the Greek tongue, from a most learned letter of my dear Rodolphus <note>Rodolphus Agricola (1444–1485), a preeminent Dutch humanist</note>, in which he attempted to persuade the council of Antwerp, with great loyalty and eloquence, to appoint someone to head the school who had learned good literature, and not, as they usually do, entrust that duty to a speechless theologian or natural philosopher: who, while he trusts he can speak on any subject, is ignorant of what speaking itself is. For what will such a man do in a school of literature? Truly, to use a Greek proverb, the very same thing as **a dog in a bath**. Lucian, in his work *Against the Unlearned*, says: <term>τὸ πτωχότατον ἐκεῖνο ὑποφθέγξεται, τί κοινὸν κυνὶ καὶ βαλανείῳ;</term> <note>original Greek</note> that is, "And every one of the onlookers immediately applies that most common saying to you: **What has a dog to do with a bath?**" The same author in *The Parasite* says: <term>κἀμοὶ γὰρ δοκεῖ, ἢι συνησίῳ φιλόσοφόν τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν, οἷον ἐν βαλανείῳ κύων,</term> <note>original Greek</note> that is, "And in my opinion, such a thing is a philosopher at a banquet as a dog in a bath." It will apply to those who are utterly useless for a certain matter, just as there is no use at all for dogs in a bathhouse.

### You are teaching a donkey to run under the bit. XL

**You are teaching a donkey to run under the bit**, that is, you are teaching the unteachable. For a horse is fit for running, but a donkey is useless for equestrian racing. Horace says:
> You would lose your labor unhappily, as if someone should teach
> a little donkey to run in the field, obeying the bit.

Acron <note>A Roman commentator on Horace</note> advises that this was said proverbially of the donkey. It is the opposite of what we have recorded elsewhere, <term>τὸν ἵππον εἰς πεδίον</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is, **The horse to the field**.

### You reap another man’s harvest. XLI

<term>ἀλλότριον ἀμᾶς θέρος</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is, **You reap another man’s harvest**. The use of this adage is twofold, for it applies equally to those who enjoy the benefits produced by the labor of others, and to those who care for a business not their own with little diligence. The metaphor is drawn from an ancient custom where neighboring farmers lent their mutual labor to one another in reaping the grain. However, it happens by human nature that each man is far more attentive in his own business than in another’s. This is elegantly warned of in that Fable of the Lark, which I would not be reluctant to recount if it were not easy for anyone to read it in Aulus Gellius. It can also refer to what sometimes happens, that when those who did the sowing are cast out, others succeed in their place and enjoy the sweat of others without labor. Whence that line of Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>:
> Lo, for whom have we sown our fields?

Aristophanes in *The Knights* says: <term>τἀλλότριον ἀμᾶς θέρος</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is, **You reap another man’s harvest**. It was said against Cleon, who, coming into a situation already prepared and weakened by the many labors of Demosthenes, and Pylos having been captured, transferred all the glory of the victory to himself, leaving nothing to Demosthenes but envy. Close to this is that line of Homer from the first book of the *Odyssey*:
<term>Ἐπεὶ ἀλλότριον βίοτον νήποινον ἔδουσιν.</term> <note>original Greek</note> that is,
> Since they consume the livelihood of another without payment.

Aristophanes expressed the same sentiment in the same play thus:
<term>Ἐγὼ δὲ περιπατῶν γ' ἀπ' ἐργαστηρίου</term>
<term>Ἔψαντος ἑτέρου τὴν χύτραν ὑφηλόμην.</term> <note>original Greek</note> that is,
> While I was walking a bit further from the workshop,
> while another was cooking, I snatched away the prepared pot.

### To unweave Penelope’s web. XLII

**To unweave Penelope’s web** is to undertake vain labor, and to destroy again what you have accomplished. It arose from Homer, who in the second book of the *Odyssey* feigns that Penelope, the wife of Ulysses, deluded her pressing suitors with this condition: that she promised she would marry when she had finished the web she had in her hands. After they had accepted this condition, the clever woman began to unweave by night what she had woven during the day:
<term>Ἔνθα καὶ ἡματίη μὲν ὑφαίνεσκεν μέγαν ἱστόν,</term>
<term>Νύκτας δ' ἀλλύεσκεν ἐπεὶ δαΐδας παραθεῖτ'.</term> <note>original Greek</note> that is,
> There by day she would weave the great web,

# THE FIRST CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY
<sig>n 2</sig>

<margin>Plato in the Phaedo. Cicero in Academic Questions, book 2.</margin>
...he used to undo at night by the light of lamps.
What of that art <note>referring to Dialectic or Sophistry</note> which, he says, like **Penelope’s web**, unweaves itself and destroys the earlier parts at the very end? Dialectic feels this, for by the same reasoning with which it confirmed something, it utterly dissolves it again, so that it seems as if nothing has been achieved. Seneca says in *On Benefits*, book five: "For what good is it to laboriously untie knots which you yourself made just so you could untie them?" Aristides, in his defense of the four orators, says: <margin>Aristides</margin> <note>original Greek: οὐκ οἶδ' ὅτι ἂν ἴσον ἀναλύοντες...</note> "I know not what they gain by unweaving as much as they have cut away from wisdom; they say they are occupied with mutual cancellations," that is, unweaving some web or other. For as much as they gain in wisdom, they lose again by becoming arrogant. Since he connects this to other specific proverbs which we shall mention shortly, it indicates that this too is surely a proverb.

-> To transplant an old tree. XLIII <-

<margin><note>original Greek: Γέροντα μεταφυτεύειν</note></margin>
That is, to transplant an old tree. This is said of those who, late in life and at an advanced age, try to unlearn things they have been accustomed to since youth. Or, it refers to simple tasks that we attempt in vain. For a tree should not be moved from its place once it has fixed its roots deep, though it may be moved if it is still a sapling. For the ancients said a tree should not be moved if it was younger than two years or older than three, according to Pliny. However, the adage seems to pertain particularly to the oak, which drives its roots deepest of all, as in the phrase <note>original Greek: γεράνδρυον</note> "an old oak." Or perhaps because they believe the oak was the first of all trees. For this reason, the tree was sacred to Jupiter, and the grove of Dodona <note>A famous ancient oracle site</note> was of oak, from which the first of all oracles are believed to have been given. Seneca used the adage elegantly in his book of epistles, book 13, letter one: "If these things," he says, "seem too gloomy, you will blame the villa, in which I learned from Aegialus, a most diligent father of the household (for he is the owner of this land), that even an old plantation can be moved. This is necessary for us old men, every one of whom plants an olive grove for another."

-> You are measuring the sand. XLIIII <-

<margin><note>original Greek: Ψάμμον μετρεῖς</note></margin>
That is, you seek the measure of the sand, or you measure it. This means you are undertaking a task of infinite labor and no resolution; or, you are striving in vain for what you cannot achieve. Athenaeus in book 8 brings forward a certain Alexis, who spoke of countless things as <note>original Greek: Ψαμμακόσια</note> "sand-hundreds," as if equaling the number of sands. <note>original Greek: ὀνόμασι δ' χρώμενον...</note> "using the name 'sand-hundreds,'" if I may imitate the coinage of that word. Plato in the *Theaetetus* says: <note>original Greek: μᾶλλον αὐτὸν λέληθεν...</note> "It is more hidden from him than the 'measures' of the sea, as they say," that is, more than the sands of the sea.

-> You are counting the waves. XLV <-

<margin><note>original Greek: Κύματα μετρεῖς</note></margin>
That is, you are counting the waves. It has the same meaning as the previous one. Virgil elegantly touched upon this proverb in the second book of the *Georgics*:
> If one wished to know the number, he might as well
> Seek to learn how many grains of sand are stirred by the West wind on the Libyan plain,
> Or, when the violent East wind falls upon the ships,
> To know how many Ionian waves come to the shores.

<margin>Theocritus in The Graces:</margin>
> But the labor is equal to counting the waves upon the shore,
> As many as the wind pushes toward the land from the gray sea.

The adage could also have been born from a certain Aesopic fable, which Lucian relates in *The Sects*: A certain man sat on the seashore trying to count the individual waves; when the waves overwhelmed him unawares and he was vexed in spirit because he could not encompass them in number, a clever fox approached and relieved the man with timely advice, saying: "Why are you annoyed by the waves that have passed? You ought to begin counting from here, and let those others go."

-> To fart at a deaf man. XLVI <-

<margin><note>original Greek: Κωφῷ ἀποπέρδειν</note></margin>
That is, to let out a sound in the presence of a deaf man; it is said when something is done in vain. Or when a sin is committed in the presence of stupid people who cannot perceive it. Or when someone is attacked with insults who ignores them as if he does not hear. It is recorded by Diogenianus and Suidas.

-> To weave spiders' webs. XLVII <-

<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀράχνης ὑφαίνειν</note></margin>
That is, to weave the webs of spiders. This refers to inventions of frivolous things and of no fruit, and to undertaking anxious labor. The proverb is used in turn by Saint Basil at the beginning of his explanation of the *Hexameron* <note>A treatise on the six days of Creation</note>. Whence also in Diogenes Laertius, in the life of Zeno, the philoso—

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of "Adagia" (Adages), specifically focusing on metaphors for wasted effort and futility. It follows the previous discussions of Greek and Roman proverbial wisdom.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

A certain philosopher used to say that dialectical arguments <note>Logic-based reasoning</note> were like spider webs; although they appear to be something laborious and precise, they are nevertheless trifles and weak. And someone else compared laws to spider webs, which, while easily torn apart by large birds, entangle only the flies.

### XLVIII
->You are washing a brick.<-

Several related proverbs are found among the Greeks by which we signify useless labor. For example, *plinthos plyneis* <note>original: "πλίνθον πλύνεις"</note>, that is, "You are washing a brick." This is used by Terence in *Phormio*: "Shall I speak? I’ll inflame him. Shall I be silent? I’ll instigate him. Shall I clear myself? I would be washing a brick." <note>Meaning: trying to clean a clay brick only turns it into mud; a futile task.</note> Theocritus in *The Graces* says:
"And to wash a dark brick with violet-colored water," that is,
"And to have washed a black flint with flowing waves."

### XLIX
->You are boiling a stone.<-

Very similar to this is what is recorded by Aristophanes in the comedy titled *The Wasps*: *lithon hepseis* <note>original: "λίθον ἕψεις"</note>, that is, "You are boiling a stone." This stands for "you labor in vain." "But whenever someone entreated him, bowing his head thus, he would say, 'You are boiling a stone.'" For a stone never softens, no matter how long the boiling lasts. Generally, it applies to any useless labor, and specifically to a hard-hearted man who softens for no prayers.

### L
->You are washing an Ethiopian; You are whitening an Ethiopian.<-

The same meaning is held by *Aithiopa smēcheis* <note>original: "αἰθίοπα σμήχεις"</note>, that is, "You are washing an Ethiopian," and *Aithiopa leukaineis* <note>original: "αἰθίοπα λευκαίνεις"</note>, that is, "You are whitening an Ethiopian." Lucian in his book *Against the Ignorant*: "And according to the proverb, I attempt to wash an Ethiopian." For that native blackness of the Ethiopians, which Pliny thinks happens from the heat of the neighboring sun, cannot be washed away by any water, nor does it turn white by any means. This likewise will specifically fit when a dishonest matter is adorned with the false colors of words, or when an unpraiseworthy person is praised, or an unteachable person is taught. The adage seems to have arisen from an Aesopic fable. For a certain man, having bought an Ethiopian and thinking that color had happened not by nature but by the negligence of the previous master, applied everything used to whiten clothes; he so harassed the wretched man with perpetual washings that he drove him into sickness, while the color remained as it had been.

### LI
->To plow the shore.<-

*Aigialon aran* <note>original: "Αἰγιαλὸν ἀρᾷν"</note>, that is, "To plow the shore." It is to undertake a sterile labor. Ausonius to Theon:
"What are you doing, placed on the furthest edges of the earth,
O poet-cultivator of sands, for whom the shore must be plowed?"
You signify that he labors in vain. This will have a specific use when service is bestowed upon one from whom you will never receive any fruit: as if one were to teach "an ass the lyre" <note>A common adage for teaching the unteachable</note>, or bestow a benefit upon an ungrateful person. For saltiness ensures that coastal shores are almost always sterile; which is also testified by the proverb: *halmyron geitonēma* <note>original: "ἁλμυρὸν γειτόνημα"</note>, that is, "A salty neighborhood," meaning sterile. Moreover, sea-water is so sterile that it does not even bear trees. Plutarch brings forward various causes for this matter in his commentary *On Natural Causes*, in the very first problem.

### LII
->You entrust seeds to the sand.<-

*Eis psammon speireis* <note>original: "Εἰς ψάμμον σπείρεις"</note>, that is, "You entrust seeds to the sand." This is because sands are sterile, especially coastal ones, and not suitable for sowing. Oenone to Paris in Ovid:
"What are you doing, Oenone? Why do you entrust seeds to the sand?
You plow the shores with oxen that will not profit."
Yet in our Brabant <note>A region in the Low Countries, Erasmus's homeland</note> there are farmers so industrious that they compel even the thirstiest sands to bear wheat.

### LIII
->You are sowing in the water.<-

*Eis hydōr speireis* <note>original: "Εἰς ὕδωρ σπείρεις"</note>, that is, "You cast seeds into the water." Theognis:
"It is the same as sowing the sea of gray salt," that is,
"Like one who entrusts seeds to the waters of the ocean."
He speaks of those who confer a benefit upon ungrateful and wicked men; and he says it perishes just as if you were sowing in the waves of the sea. A commentator on Aristophanes also expresses the proverb in this way: *tēn thalattēs speireis* <note>original: "τὴν θαλάττης σπείρεις"</note>, that is, "You are sowing in the sea."

### LIV
->You sow among the rocks.<-

*Kata petrōn speireis* <note>original: "Κατὰ πετρῶν σπείρεις"</note>, that is, "You are sowing among the rocks." To which indeed the allegory <note>Likely referring to the Parable of the Sower</note> can be believed to have alluded...

the Gospel parable of the seed that fell upon the rocks. For this kind of soil is almost entirely sterile; it cannot be broken by the plow, or because that which is sown has no place to strike roots.

### 55. To cut the fire.
<term>pyr skainein</term> <note>original Greek: πῦρ σκαίνειν</note>, that is, to strike at the fire. This belongs to the same category, although we have previously referred to this among the Pythagorean symbols. Aristides, in his collective defense of the four Rhetoricians, says: <term>who, by being silent toward you in all those prefaces, was striking at the fire, boiling a stone, and every kind of impiety</term> <note>original Greek: ὃς ὑμᾶς σαυτῷ ἁπάσαις ταῖς προοιμίαις ἐνεχέμυντο, εἰς πῦρ σκαίνειν, καὶ λίθον ἕψειν, καὶ πᾶσα ἀσέβεια</note>; that is, did you not understand that you yourself were liable to all those proverbs: that you were striking at the fire, that you were boiling a stone, that you were sowing among rocks? He censures the man who, in the service of the tyrant Dionysius, achieved nothing of any value.

### 56. You write in water.
<term>eis hydōr grapheis</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς ὕδωρ γράφεις</note>, that is, you write in water. This means you are doing nothing. Lucian in *The Tyrant*: <term>Are you joking, Charon, or as they say, are you already writing on water, or do you expect some small coin from me?</term> <note>original Greek: παίζεις ὦ χάρων, ἢ καθ' ὕδατος φασὶν ἤδη γράφεις, ἢ καὶ μικύλον τινὰ ὀβολὸν παρ' ἐμοῦ προσδοκᾷς</note>; that is, are you playing, Charon, or are you now writing in water (as the saying goes), since you expect something from Micyllus? Plato in the *Phaedrus*: <term>Will he then seriously write these things in black water, sowing with a pen?</term> <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἄρα αὐτοῖς γ' ὕδατι γράψει μέλανι, σπείρων διὰ καλάμου</note>; <term>not with a pen?</term> <note>original Greek: μὴ καλάμῳ</note>; that is, will he studiously write these things in black water, sowing with a reed? From this sort of thing comes a six-foot line among the Greek maxims:

> <term>I write the oaths of wicked men in water.</term> <note>original Greek: φαύλων ὅρκων εἰς ὕδωρ γράφω.</note>

Xenarchus distorts this in *The Pentathlete* quoted in Athenaeus, book ten:

> <term>I write a woman's oath in water.</term> <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ γυναικὸς εἰς ὕδωρ γράφω.</note>
> Likewise Catullus, speaking of a desiring lover:
> "What a woman says to her eager lover,
> One ought to write on the wind and rapid water."

### 57. You build on sand.
<term>ep’ ammou oikodomeis</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπ' ἄμμου οἰκοδομεῖς</note>, that is, you build on sand. The Gospel parable seems to allude to this. That which you have built upon sand does not stand. Therefore, it will be rightly used whenever someone undertakes an expense that will be useless, because the foundations were not properly laid beforehand.

### 58. You farm the winds.
<term>anemous geōrgeis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνέμους γεωργεῖς</note>, that is, you farm the winds. I say "farm" for "practicing agriculture." It is cited by Zenodotus: it is said of those who bring back no fruit from their labors.

### 59. You teach iron to swim.
<term>sidēron pleein didaskeis</term> <note>original Greek: σίδηρον πλέειν διδάσκεις</note>, you teach iron to float. Said of those who attempt a thing which, because nature resists it, can by no means be done.

### 60. To draw water with a sieve.
<term>koskinon hydōr antlein</term> <note>original Greek: κόσκινον ὕδωρ ἀντλεῖν</note>, or <term>with a sieve</term>, that is, he draws water with a sieve. This is also not ineptly said of the forgetful. Plautus in the *Pseudolus*: "It matters no more than if you were to carry rain in a sieve." It was once held among the <term>impossibilities</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδυνάτων</note>, or it is proven by the fact that it is placed among miracles that Tuccia, a Vestal Virgin, carried water in a sieve in the six hundred and thirty-eighth year from the founding of the city: as Pliny witnesses in book 28, chapter 2. Dionysius of Halicarnassus mentions this in the second book of *Roman Antiquities*. It is taken from the fable of the daughters of Danaus, whom Plato imagines paying this kind of penalty in the underworld: that they continually carry water into a leaking jar using leaking vessels. Alciphron in a letter from Galen to Cyrtone: <term>And as the saying goes, like the women who pour jars into the leaking vat.</term> <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὸ λεγόμενον δὴ τὸ γυναικῶν τῶν ἀμφορέας ἐκχέουσι πίθους</note>. Lucian in *Timon*: <term>As if from a perforated basket.</term> <note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ ἐκ κοφίνου τετρυπημένου</note>. It is also expressed in this manner: <term>to draw water into a perforated jar</term> <note>original Greek: εἰς πίθον τετρυπημένον ὕδωρ ἀντλεῖν</note>. Plautus in the *Pseudolus*: "You are pouring words into a perforated jar; we are wasting our effort."

### 61. You scatter fragrant vapor upon dung.
<term>epi kopron thymiās</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ κόπρον θυμιᾷς</note>, that is: you scatter the scent of spices upon dung. For all fragrance perishes if it is overcome by a foul smell. It is found in Suidas. It will apply to those who apply an excellent thing to the unworthy: a similar type is "Perfume on lentils."

### 62. I have lost both oil and labor.
To this also belongs that which is in Plautus’s *Poenulus*: "Then by Pollux, I have lost both oil and labor." That is, whatever I spent, whether of resources or of work, has been spent in vain. The metaphor—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...the metaphor is drawn from the contests of gladiators and wrestlers; those about to compete were thoroughly anointed with certain oily unguents. Cicero says in his *Letters*: "For why should I think you miss the athletes, you who have looked down upon gladiators? In whose case Pompey himself admits that he **lost both his oil and his labor**." <note>original: "oleū & operam perdidisse." A common Roman expression for wasting time and money, similar to "throwing money down the drain."</note> However, it can also refer to the lamps of those working late into the night, as Cicero seems to have done when writing to Atticus in Book 13: "Before daybreak, while I was writing against the Epicureans, I scribbled something or other to you by the light of the same oil and labor, and sent it off before dawn." The same author says to the same man elsewhere: "Let us not grieve, lest both the oil and the labor of our scholarship be lost, but let us confer with a calm mind." In this passage, the phrase has more grace because it is transferred to the work of the mind. Therefore, "oil" here stands for "expense," for the adage is also expressed that way. Plautus says in *The Rope*: "They lose both their labor and their expense." To the same point belongs that phrase which a certain greeting-raven had learned to croak: "Labor and outlay have perished."

Macrobius mentions this story in Book 2 of the *Saturnalia*. Since it seems by no means unworthy of being remembered, I will not be burdened to write it down, and in his own words: "Octavius," he says, "was returning in majesty after the victory at Actium. Among those congratulating him, a man met him holding a raven, which he had trained to say: 'Hail, Caesar, Victorious Commander!' Caesar, marvelling at the dutiful bird, bought it for twenty thousand sesterces. A partner of the craftsman, to whom none of that liberality had reached, affirmed to Caesar that the man had another raven, and asked that he be compelled to bring it. When brought, it expressed the words it had learned: 'Hail, Victorious Commander Antony!' Not at all provoked, Caesar thought it enough to order the man to divide the gift with his comrade. Having been greeted similarly by a parrot, he ordered it to be bought. Marvelling at the same in a magpie, he bought this one too.

This example spurred a poor shoemaker to train a raven for a similar greeting; exhausted by the expense, he used to say often to the bird when it would not respond: 'Labor and outlay have perished.' Eventually, however, the raven began to say the dictated greeting. Hearing this as he passed by, Augustus responded: 'I have enough of such greeters at home.' The raven had enough memory to tack on the words it used to hear its complaining master say: 'Labor and outlay have perished.' At this Caesar laughed, and ordered the bird to be bought for more than he had bought any bird until then." Thus far we have rendered the words of Macrobius.

Saint Jerome, writing to Pammachius, seems to have tacked on another adage, as it were, to this one: "He loses oil and expenses who sends an ox to the *ceroma*." <note>The *ceroma* was a mixture of oil and wax used by wrestlers.</note> Indeed, this very phrase, **To send an ox to the ceroma**, smacks of a proverb: it stands for teaching the unteachable, or appointing someone to a duty for which they are least suited, as you can see the nature of the thing is repugnant to it. For *ceroma* is the name of the ointment with which athletes were once anointed; it was made from oil and certain types of earth. Furthermore, an ox is useless for such contests.

### You hunt the winds with a net.
->LXIII<-
<margin>You hunt the wind with a net.</margin> <note>original Greek: Δίκτυῳ ἀνεμον θηρᾶς.</note> That is, you catch the winds with a net. Concerning those who labor in vain: or those who foolishly pursue things for which there is no hope of attaining. Or those who pointlessly chase a pointless thing. For wind can be contained in a leather bottle, but by no means in a net.

### You row through a calm sky.
->LXIIII<-
<margin>You row in a windless sky.</margin> <note>original Greek: Αἰθέρα νηνεμον ἐρέσσεις.</note> That is: You row in calm air. It is cited in Zenodotus concerning those who labor to no effect; it is just as if you were to say, "You beat the air," in the manner of rowers.

### You lash a dead man.
->LXV<-
<margin>Lashing a corpse.</margin> <note>original Greek: Νεκρὸν μασίλας.</note> That is, you flog a dead man. Against those who rebuke people who are not moved at all by a reprimand, or those who pursue and tear apart those who have departed from life.

### You decorate the pot.
->LXVI<-
<margin>You embellish the jar.</margin> <note>original Greek: χύραν ποικίλλεις.</note> That is, you decorate or paint the cooking pot. Concerning those who try in vain at a profoundly absurd thing. For it is a foolish labor to apply the allure of painting to a common pot, a vessel held in low esteem and destined for kitchen uses. Very similar to this is a common saying: "To gild walnut shells with gold leaf."

### You glue an egg.
->LXVII<-
<margin>You glue an egg.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὠὸν κολλάεις.</note> That is, you join an egg together with glue. It is cited by Diogenianus. He labors ridiculously who tries to mend and cement a broken eggshell with glue.

### You beat a skin.
->LXVIII<-
<margin>You skin a wine-skin.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ασκόν δέρεις.</note> That is, you beat a skin, or you flay a wine-skin. It appears in Aristophanes’ *The Clouds*. Apuleius seems to have alluded to this in *The Golden Ass*, when he mentions three wine-skins beaten and wounded by him. Taken either from the rites of Bacchus, or from those who make an empty noise by striking skins.

### You are plucking a wineskin.
### LXIX

<term>ἀσκὸν τίλλεις</term> <note>original Greek: askon tilleis</note>. That is: You are plucking a wineskin. This is said either of someone who feels nothing, or of something that lacks hair <note>i.e., attempting the impossible or the redundant, like trying to pluck hair from a smooth leather bottle</note>.

### To do what has already been done.
### LXX

Terence says in *Phormio*: "Ho there! As they say, do not do what is already done," and <term>πεπραγμένον μὴ πράττειν</term> <note>original Greek: pepragmenon me prattein; "not to do what is finished"</note>. This is taken from legal judgment and custom, where it is not permitted to try a case a second time once a verdict has been pronounced. Plautus says: "You are doing a finished thing." That is, you are laboring in vain. Quintus Fabius says in Titus Livius, Book 23: "I know it seems to many of you, Conscript Fathers, that what is being done today has already been done, and that the speech is held in vain, as if one were giving an opinion on the province of Africa as a fresh matter." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in his book *On Friendship* indicates it is commonly said of a business that is handled perversely. "But when," he says, "we are punished for negligence in affairs, then it is most especially so in choosing and cultivating friends. For we use backwards counsels and 'do what is done,' which we are forbidden from by the proverb."

### You are feeding a whetstone.
### LXXI

<term>ἀκόνην σιτίζεις</term> <note>original Greek: akonen sitizeis</note>. That is: You are feeding a whetstone. It is said of gluttonous men who eat a great deal of food, yet are rendered no more stout for it. For even today a proverb is commonly tossed about regarding the thinness of a whetstone; they say, "As fat as a whetstone," meaning someone is very skinny. Nicolaus Barbarus, in a certain letter to Pico [della Mirandola], interprets this proverb as bestowing a benefit where no gratitude will return: so that it is related to what is said elsewhere, "Feeding wolf cubs," since bad gratitude returns from a benefit.

### You are calling for Hylas.
### LXXII

<term>Ὕλαν κραυγάζεις</term> <note>original Greek: Hylan kraugazeis</note>. That is: You are calling for Hylas. Said of those shouting in vain, or generally of those accomplishing nothing. The proverb arose from this event: Hylas, son of Theodamas, a beautiful youth among the Argonauts, was beloved by Hercules. While in Mysia, having gone out to get water, he perished in a spring; hence he is imagined to have been loved and snatched away by Nymphs. Polyphemus was sent to track him down, and called out the name of Hylas with a great shout, yet accomplished nothing. And from this the proverb arose. Virgil seems to have referred it to the shout of sailors when he says:
> So that the whole shore echoed "Hylas, Hylas!"

Theocritus mentions this in Idyll 13:
<term>τρὶς μὲν Ὕλαν ἄϋσεν, ὅσον βαθὺς ἄφυσε λαιμός,</term>
<term>τρὶς δ' ἄρ' ὁ παῖς ὑπάκουσευ, ἀραιὰ δὲ ἵκετο φωνή.</term> <note>original Greek</note> That is:
> Three times he called Hylas with as much a shout as he could,
> Three times, as he strained from the depths of his throat,
> The boy heard, and a thin voice struck his ears.

Nothing prevents this from being referred to the custom of sacred rites which were instituted in memory of the snatched Hylas, in which the name of Hylas was called out. It would be more charming and elegant when someone vainly desires an absent thing, either deploring it or wishing for it. As if someone reduced to poverty should wish for himself a hundred talents which he once had. Aristophanes seems to have looked toward this part in *Plutus*:
<term>τὸν ὄντα δ' οὐ ζητοῦντα, καὶ μάτην καλεῖς.</term> <note>original Greek</note> That is:
> You seek him who is not here, calling in vain.
Said of Mercury, deploring those cakes which he was once accustomed to eat in the sacrifices.

### You are wasting water in vain.
### LXXIII

<term>εἰς κενὸν ἀναλίσκεις ὕδωρ</term> <note>original Greek: eis kenon analiskeis hydor</note>. That is: You are wasting water in vain. This will fit those who give advice to no purpose. It is taken from the ancient custom of the law courts, in which speeches were timed by a <term>clepsydra</term> <note>a water-clock used to time orators</note>. Aeschines, against Demosthenes, shows that the first water was usually poured in for the accusers, the second for the advocates, and the third for the judges to determine the penalty, unless the defendant had been acquitted by the first votes. The same Demosthenes challenges Aeschines to speak, if he can, even "in his own water" <note>i.e., during Demosthenes' allotted time</note>, regarding what had been written by the same author. <term>ἀναβὰς ἐν τῷ ἐμῷ ὕδατι εἰπάτω</term> <note>original Greek: "let him come up and speak in my water"</note>. Alluding to this, Lucian in *The Dead Come to Life, or The Fisherman*, jokes about a certain rhetorician who, among barbarians at a banquet, speaks not by the measure of water, but by the measure of a wine jar. The same in *The Double Indictment*: <term>ἐκείνως γὰρ τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκχεῖ</term> <note>original Greek</note>. That is: For truly in his presence the water flows. Plato seems to hint at this in *Theaetetus*, saying that some can teach what has been done <term>πρὸς μικρὸν ὕδωρ</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is, "by a little water." And in the same: <term>Κατεπείγει γὰρ ὕδωρ ῥέον</term> <note>original Greek</note>. That is: "For the flowing water urges on," because it is the orator's duty to speak according to the prescribed water-clocks. Apuleius in *The Golden Ass*: "Again, with the herald's loud bellowing..."

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s encyclopedic collection of Greek and Latin adages, focusing on metaphors for time-keeping and the performance of impossible or futile tasks.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...the accuser, being summoned, a certain elder rises, and for the duration of his speaking time, after water has been poured in, he prays to the people <note>original: "populum sic adorat"</note> using a certain vessel with a neck shaped like a slender pipe, and because of this the water flows out drop by drop. Pliny the Younger to Falco: *And he who could order anyone to be silent, had silence imposed upon him by the water-clock.* <note>The clepsydra or water-clock was used in ancient courts to limit the length of speeches.</note> The same author to Arrian: *I spoke for nearly five hours. For to the twenty water-clocks, which I had received as the most generous allowance, four were added.* Quintilian in book 12: *And if you take any time for yourself, it must be approved; even a speech labored over and gathered by the study of days and nights runs out of water.* Marcus Tullius [Cicero] at the end of the second book of *Tusculan Disputations*: *Tomorrow, then, to the water-clock, for so we say.* The same author in *On the Orator*, book 3, speaking of Pericles: *But this man,* he says, *no mere ranter had taught to bark at the water-clock, but (as we have heard) that famous Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, a man supreme in the knowledge of the greatest things.* Philetas in Athenaeus, book 2: <note>original: "τὸ δ' αὐτὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ οἱ ῥήτορες πρὸς ὕδωρ εἶπον"</note> *that is, I have spoken only so much as the rhetoricians are accustomed to say by the water.* For the conversation had been about water. From this, the grace of an allusion was snatched. Demades joked about Demosthenes being a <note>original: "ὑδροπότω"</note> <term>water-drinker</term>, because while others spoke by the water, Demosthenes wrote by the water. Philostratus, in his life of Adrian the Sophist, calls those sophists who practiced by the water <note>original: "ἐπ' ἀξίᾳ κλεψύδρας"</note> *worthy of the water-clock.* Furthermore, the ancients distinguished the hours by lines and shadows. P. Scipio Nasica was the first to invent the water-clock, by which the hours could be distinguished even on a cloudy day and at night. Now, instead of water-clocks, they use sand-clocks <note>original: "clepsammis"</note> and <note>original: "ἀμμώδεσι"</note> <term>sand-timers</term>.

## ->To fish in the air, To hunt in the sea.<- LXXIII

Of the same kind are those phrases which Plautus uses in *The Ass-Dealer* <note>Asinaria</note>: *To fish in the air, and to hunt in the sea with a javelin.* These will apply simply to those who fruitlessly strive after <note>original: "ἀδίωκτα"</note> <term>unpursuable things</term>, or who perversely seek something in a place where it cannot even be hoped for. As if someone were to seek a tranquil life in magistracies, a blessed life in pleasures, or a happy life in riches. Thus Libanus the slave, ordered by his master Demanetus to swindle his own wife out of some silver, indicating that it could in no way be done—to take anything from such a stingy woman—says: *Order me at the same time to fish in the air, or to hunt with a javelin in the middle of the sea.*

## ->You are asking for water from a pumice stone.<- LXXV

Not very different from the above is what is read in the same poet: *To ask for water from a pumice stone*, used for when one asks in vain from another for that which the person being asked is himself most in need of. For nothing is drier than a pumice stone, nothing more parched. It is just as if someone were to ask to be taught by the most unlearned, to expect counsel from the most ill-advised, a gift from a beggar, protection from the helpless; or finally, money from the greedy and stingy. Plautus: *For you are now asking for water from a pumice stone, which is thirsty itself.* A pumice (he says in the same place) *is not as dry of water as this old man.* Moreover, the pumice is a porous stone with which books are usually polished; it is of such a dry nature that if you cast it into a boiling pot, it extinguishes the heat—not just for a time, but entirely. Theophrastus thinks there is no other cause for this than that, by its extreme dryness, it strives to draw all the froth to itself. He also mentions a certain Eudemus of Chios, who used to fortify himself with pumice sprinkled with sharp vinegar, so that after a seventh potion of hellebore, neither baths nor the drinking of wine would provoke him to vomit.

## ->To strip the clothes off a naked man.<- LXXVI

To this sentiment also belongs what is used by the same poet: *To strip the clothes off a naked man*, used for hoping for profit from one who has nothing that can be taken away. For so the same Libanus in Plautus’s *Asinaria*, being warned by his master to scrape some silver away from him by trickery to buy a mistress for his son, says: *You are talking great nonsense; you order me to strip the clothes off a naked man.* St. Chrysostom also cites a commonly tossed-about proverb, in which they said: *Not even a hundred men can rob one naked man.* Apuleius wrote in the first book of *The Golden Ass*: *A naked man cannot be robbed even by ten wrestlers.*

## ->To reap the asphodel.<- LXXVII

<note>original: "Τὸν ἀνθερίκον θερίζειν"</note> *That is, to reap the asphodel stalks*, was said of those who undertook vain and sterile labor. The *anthericus* is a kind of herb that cannot be mowed, but must be plucked by hand, just like flax. The very tips of the ears of grain are called *antherices*, or *atheres*. Herodotus calls the stalks of the asphodel *antherices*, according to Suidas; he says they are too tough to be broken. Pliny also mentions the *anthericus* in book 21, chapter 17. In the Greek commentaries, I find *Antherices* and *atherices* used interchangeably.

## ->You are weaving a rope out of sand.<- LXXVIII

<note>original: "Ἐκ τῆς ψάμμου σχοινίον πλέκειν"</note> *That is, to weave a rope out of sand.* This is to labor in vain, because...

# FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<column-break/>
...can be achieved by reason. For what is more foolish than to wish to weave a rope from sand, which in no way clings together? Both proverbs—namely this one and the one we just reported—are used by Aristides <note>Aelius Aristides, a 2nd-century Greek orator</note> in his collective defense of the four orators: "Sinking into a place where they are of no use, uttering wonders at a shadow, dragging out words, as you said, O Sophocles, or harvesting what was woven beneath, weaving a rope of sand, I know not what linen web they are unraveling." <note>original Greek: Καταδύοντες γ' εἰς οὐδὲ χρησιμὸς... ψάμμου σχοινίον πλέκοντες</note> That is to say, hiding themselves away, they devise that "admirable" wisdom of theirs, dragging out words like a shadow, so that they bring forth no fruit at all. Columella, in the preface to his poem *On the Cultivation of Gardens*, says: "and I know not what web they are unweaving." By these adages, he signifies that "shadowy" <note>term: umbraticum (shadowy/cloistered) - referring to philosophers who stay indoors and debate abstract theories rather than engaging with the real world</note> style of philosophers. For even if there are many parts of it, so to speak, about which we can say something, they are ultimately so meager that, as the Greeks say, nothing can be made from the incomprehensible smallness of sand. This proverb will be particularly suited to uses of this kind: if one tries to bring into harmony people who are utterly different in character and between whom nothing agrees; or if someone weaves a speech out of discordant arguments, fashioning a sort of Chimera or a monster of the kind Horace describes: a human head on a horse's neck, with the remaining limbs gathered from various kinds of creatures, so that:
->A lovely woman above ends in a fish below.<-

### 79. Wool from a donkey.
Close to this is that other saying: "You are looking for donkey's fleece." <note>original Greek: ὄνου πόκας ζητεῖς</note> This is said of those who foolishly seek things that exist nowhere. The adage is also expressed in this way: "Donkey's wool." Aristophanes says:
> "In the plain of Forgetfulness, who goes for donkey's wool?" <note>original Greek: ἐν λήθης πεδίον, τίς εἰς ὄνου πόκας;</note> That is,
> who goes for the wool? Who goes to the soil of Lethe? <note>Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note>

"Donkey's wool" signifies vain things that exist nowhere. The Greek meter consists of a trimeter if the second part is read as "tes."

### 80. You are shearing a donkey.
The same meaning is found in: "You are shearing a donkey." <note>original Greek: ὄνου κείρεις</note> This is said of those who undertake an absurd and futile task, because you can neither comb a donkey on account of its shaggy hair, nor shear it since it has no wool. Aristophanes mentions this in *The Frogs*.

### 81. You are looking for a wolf's wings.
"You are looking for a wolf's wings." <note>original Greek: λύκου πτερὰ ζητεῖς</note> This is said of those who seek things that do not exist. Or, it refers to one who merely terrifies with proud words, but will never actually do what he threatens. For it is impossible for a winged wolf to be found. The proverb is recorded by Suidas.

### 82. Things in the underworld.
In the same place, the commentator notes this adage as having the same meaning: "The things in Hades." <note>original Greek: τὰ ἐν ᾅδου</note> That is, things among the dead. He cites Aristarchus as the author and thinks it arose because Cratinus <note>An Athenian comic poet</note> imagined someone in the underworld twisting a rope, while a donkey gnawed away at what he had already twisted, so that the one twisting labored in vain. However, that phrase "things in Hades" generally pertains to all things handed down in the fables of the poets which cannot be believed; hence, when we wish to signify things that are empty and like dreams, we aptly say, "the things in Hades." Athenaeus, in the fourth book of the *Deipnosophistae* (The Learned Banqueters), reports that Democritus wrote a volume titled *On the Things in Hades*, which, as must be guessed, was filled with prodigious fables, and the proverb seems to be derived from this.

### 83. The lazy man twists the rope.
This is so similar to the previous one that it might seem the same; it refers to Ocnus <note>A mythological figure representing delay or sloth</note> (the "lazy donkey"), as Pausanias relates in his *Description of Phocis*. He says it was celebrated among the Ionians: "Ocnus gathers the cord." <note>original Greek: συνάγει ὄκνος τὴν θώμιγγα</note> I will transcribe his own words on this matter: "After him there is a man sitting, and the inscription says he is Ocnus. He is depicted in this manner: he twists a rope, while a female donkey stands by, which continually eats what has been twisted. They say this Ocnus was an industrious man, but had a wasteful wife, so that whatever he gathered by working was soon after consumed by her. And among the Ionians, whenever they saw someone laboring at something that brought no benefit, they would say of that person: 'Ocnus is gathering the cord.'" That is to say: After these there is a certain man sitting, the title is there, that he is Ocnus. He was made in this way, so that he himself twists the small rope, while a she-donkey stands by, which steadily gnaws away what was twisted. They say this Ocnus was a hard-working man...

<summary>This page catalogs several classical proverbs regarding futility and wasted effort, such as "weaving a rope of sand" or "shearing a donkey." It explains their origins in Greek comedy and mythology, specifically the myth of Ocnus and his ungrateful wife.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin proverbs (Adagia), specifically focusing on metaphors for wasted effort and futile speech.</meta>

striving and intent on his work, but having a wife so extravagant and wasteful that whatever he scrapes together by his labor is immediately consumed by her. I have also learned that it was a common saying among the Ionians, if they saw someone toiling at a task that brought no profit: "This man is twisting the rope of Ocnus." <note>Ocnus is a mythological figure in the underworld, condemned to forever weave a rope of straw which is eaten by a donkey as fast as he makes it.</note> It seems the subject of the painting was derived from the double meaning of a phrase. For the Greeks say "to gather a living" <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">συνάγειν τὸν βίον</foreign></note> to mean "to provide for one's sustenance." He who increases his wealth "gathers," while he who squanders it "scatters." This subject appears to have been celebrated in the works of many ancient artists. Indeed, Pliny, in his *Natural History*, mentions among the remarkable subjects of the painter Socrates one concerning a donkey gnawing on broom-grass. He says: "And the sluggish man, who is called Ocnus, twisting the broom-grass which a little donkey gnaws away." It is said the same kind of painting existed at Delphi, dedicated by Polygnotus of Thasos. Regarding this, they deny it signifies laziness or sloth, as Varro thought, but rather a man who is hardworking and industrious, yet burdened with a spendthrift wife. For this reason, Pausanias says it was not a male donkey, but a female one in the painting. Hermolaus Barbarus testifies that the same subject, carved in marble, can be seen in two places in Rome: namely, in the Capitol and in the Vatican gardens. Propertius also used this adage:
> More worthy is he to twist the rope like slanting Ocnus,
> And, little donkey, to eternally feed your hunger.

Yet it is a wonder why Pliny wrote that he who twisted the rope was called "Ocnus" (that is, "the Sluggish"), and not rather the donkey that gnaws it. Especially since Propertius does not call the one who twists it "Ocnus," but says the rope is twisted *for* him: so that you might understand the donkey to be Ocnus rather than the twister. Plutarch mentions this adage in his commentary *On the Power of Fortune*: "But just as the rope-weaver is depicted in Hades, near whom one of the grazing animals consumes what has been woven." <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">Ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ τὸν ᾄδου ζωγραφούμενον σχοινοπλόκον, ᾧ τινι πλήσιον τῶν βοσκομένων καταναλίσκει τὸ πεπλεγμένον</foreign></note>

### You are speaking to the shore. LXXXIIII

"You are speaking to the shore." <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">Αἰγιαλῷ λαλεῖς</foreign></note> This is recorded by the Greek collectors of adages. It is said against those who either persuade or pray in vain: just as if they were speaking to a deaf person. For the shores are called "deaf" because of the constant crashing of the waves. Ovid:
> He, deafer than the sea, dragged her by her unadorned hair 
> Into his house as she cried out the name of Orestes.

### You are speaking to the wind. LXXXV

Suidas adds this as well: "You are conversing with the wind." <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">Ἀνέμῳ διαλέγῃ</foreign></note> This stands for that which is done in vain. For the wind scatters all things and forces them to vanish. Hence Virgil spoke of "commands torn by the ears," which had passed into oblivion. Plautus in *The Haunted House*:
> This man knows nothing but how to talk of interest to the wind.

A similar figure is read in Athenaeus: "To speak to the earth and the sky." <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">γῇ καὶ οὐρανῷ λαλεῖν</foreign></note>

### He speaks words to a dead man. LXXXVI

"Telling a story into the ear of a dead man." <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">Νεκρῷ λέγειν μῦθον εἰς οὖς</foreign></note> Plautus: "I am now speaking words to a dead man." Terence: "Words are being made to a dead man." Again, Plautus: "It is of no more use than if one were to tell a joke to a dead man at his tomb." To this belongs what is found in Aeschylus’s *Agamemnon*:
> I, living, seem to lament in vain to a tomb. <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">Ἔοικα θρηνεῖν ζῶσα πρὸς τύμβον μάτην</foreign></note>

The adage arose from the ridiculous custom of the ancients, who called out to the deceased three times with their voices (hence they were called "the acclaimed"); furthermore, in funeral processions, they lamented much toward the dead. Lucian mocks this custom in his booklet *On Mourning*, which I have translated into Latin.

### You sing to the deaf. You tell a story to the deaf. LXXXVII

"You sing to the deaf" <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">κωφῷ ᾄδεις</foreign></note> has the same force. Virgil in the *Eclogues*:
> We do not sing to the deaf; the woods echo everything. 
Horace:
> He would think he were telling a little story to a deaf donkey. 
Terence in *The Self-Tormentor*:
> Truly, he does not know what a story he tells me, who am now deaf to it.

Likewise, Titus Livius in his tenth book on the Macedonian War: "Which I fear I have sung to empty ears."
Aeschylus in *Seven Against Thebes*:
> Did you hear, or did you not hear? Or am I speaking to the deaf? <note>original: <foreign language="Greek">Ἤκουσας ἢ οὐκ ἤκουσας; ἢ κωφῷ λέγω</foreign></note>

# FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

<margin>...did you hear, or did you not hear, or am I speaking to a deaf man? Ovid alluded to this in the third book of the *Loves*.</margin>
<margin>...what use</margin>
> What use is a painted tablet to wretched Thamyras?
<note>Thamyras was a mythical poet blinded for challenging the Muses; a painting is useless to a blind man.</note>

<margin>...it seems [to come] from</margin> from a ridiculous situation: as often happens, a guest encounters a deaf man whom he questions,
<margin>...many [things]</margin> while those who know the man is deaf laugh.

### You sing in vain. LXXXVIII

<margin>...you sing in vain.</margin> That is, You sing in vain. <note>original Greek: μάταιος ᾄδεις</note> You harp to a deaf man. <note>original Greek: πρὸς κωφὸν ψάλλεις</note> That is, You sing to no purpose. Regarding those who
<margin>...persuade in vain.</margin> Derived from singers who, when they are unpleasant to their listeners, sing fruitlessly,
<margin>...by no one</margin> since they are heard by no one: or those who sing at their own expense, carrying away no reward. For the Greeks
<margin>...for the Greeks</margin> frequently call a speech a "song" by a proverbial metaphor. Hence that line in [Euripides']
<margin>...ides' Hecuba:</margin> *Some song will come.* <note>original Greek: ἤξει τί μέλος</note> That is, Some refrain will come. And, *To sing the same song*,
<margin>...To sing to the ears</margin> and *sounding out of tune* <note>original Greek: πὰρ τὸ μέλος φθεγγόμενος</note>—that is, sounding beyond the melody. The poet Lycophron
<margin>...illustrated</margin> illustrated this adage and explained it at the same time:
> For you will stir the useless sounds of strings to the deaf sea,
> and I harp songs that are deaf and unrewarded.

That is,
> You will stir the vain sounds of the lute,
> striking songs that are at once unrewarded.

<margin>...The interpreter</margin> adds that the proverb is also expressed in this way: *Strings to a deaf horn.* <note>original Greek: Εἰς κωφὸν κέρας τὰς χορδὰς</note> That is,
<margin>...in vain</margin> you strike the strings. It is taken, moreover, from lyre-players who sing in such a way that they receive no
<margin>...gift,</margin> and eat their food at home: that is, at their own expense and <insert>their own</insert> livelihood, just as
<margin>...having been heard,</margin> they sing for others. Unless it seems to someone that it should be referred to Aesop's fable about the flute-player
<margin>...in vain</margin> inviting the fish with songs. For he had heard the story of Arion. <note>Arion was a musician saved by dolphins who were charmed by his music; the flute-player in the fable fails to replicate this with fish.</note>

### You are talking to a stone. LXXXIX

<margin>...You are talking to a stone.</margin> <note>original Greek: λίθῳ διαλέγῃ</note> *You are talking to a stone.* It has the same meaning. And in Terence, in *The Self-Tormentor*,
it is used several times for a stupid man. What Laertius relates is not unskillful:
To someone asking in what respect his son would turn out better if he were educated, Aristippus said: "If
nothing else, at least in the theater one stone will not sit upon another."

### You are talking to a wall. XC

<margin>...you are talking to the wall.</margin> <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὸν τοῖχον λαλεῖς</note> That is, *You are talking to a wall.* And this also is recorded by the Greek
collectors. It is also expressed in this way: *To speak through a wall.* <note>original Greek: διὰ τοίχου λαλεῖν</note> It is accustomed to be said
whenever someone does something exceedingly absurd. Perhaps it was taken from lovers
who speak to the doors and windows, or even the walls of their mistresses, just as
if some sense were present in them. Plautus in the *Truculentus* uses it for that which is to speak
silently: "I," he says, "will be the wall; you speak."

### To act the trifler. XCI

An adage as worn among the Latins as the Greeks: *To act the trifler* <note>Latin: Nugas agere</note>, for that which is to do a frivolous thing
of no value, or to labor in vain. *You are talking nonsense* <note>original Greek: λῆρον ληρεῖς</note>, familiar to the Attics, i.e., You trifle trifles. Aristophanes
in *The Clouds* calls Socrates the priest of subtle trifles, as if he were the author of frivolous
arts. *You are settled in the thinnest trifle.* <note>original Greek: Σύ γε λεπτοτάτῳ λήρῳ ἱδρύ</note> Galen called it *long nonsense* <note>original Greek: λῆρος μακρὸς</note> in the book *On Natural Faculties*: *The whole hypothesis of pores for natural psychology is a long piece of nonsense.*
That is, the whole supposition of pores for natural power is great nonsense. It becomes more pleasant
when it is referred to a person, as in Athenaeus, book VI: *But the poets, he says, are full of nonsense and silly talk.* <note>original Greek: λήρῳ εἶναι καὶ ὕθλοις</note> That is, you are doting and out of your senses, which is a metaphor taken from old women who, after they
have begun to lose their wits through age, are accustomed to babble certain futile trifles. Ausonius tells Paulus
to speak the truth in matters. <insert>furrow:</insert>
> He allows the Pierian sisters to talk nonsense <term>lirare</term>,
> while he himself turns the furrows <term>aulaka</term>.

In these verses the allusion is somewhat obscure, and I might almost say inept. For the man, being bilingual
in both languages, looked equally at both meanings of the name. For <term>leros</term> <note>original Greek: λῆρος</note>
signifies "trifles" to the Greeks, and <term>lirae</term> or <term>porcae</term> are what the ridges between furrows are called by the Latins. For farmers
first break the ground, then break the clods, and finally <term>lira</term> (make ridges). Hence he added,
"while he himself turns the <term>aulakas</term>" (furrows). For formerly farmers were said to "delirare" (deviate from the furrow) who turned aside from the straight
order of the furrows. From there it was transferred to those who lose their wits.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->You are shooting at the sky.<-
<margin>92</margin>
<note>Greek: Εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν τοξεύεις</note>, that is, you are aiming an arrow at the heavens. It is found in Zenodotus <note>A 3rd-century BCE Greek grammarian</note> and Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note>, used for those who labor in vain, or those who dare to provoke people they cannot harm. For one who shoots at the sky can hit nothing, unless he seems to be attacking the gods. Yet it often happens that the javelin falls back upon the one who threw it. A similar sentiment exists even among the proverbs of the Hebrews, namely in Ecclesiasticus chapter 27: "He who throws a stone on high, it will fall upon his own head; and a deceitful blow will divide the wounds of the deceitful. And he who digs a pit shall fall into it; and he who sets a stone for his neighbor shall stumble over it; and he who sets a snare for another shall perish in it."

->You are tying a dolphin by the tail.<-
<margin>93</margin>
<note>Greek: Δελφῖνα πρὸς τὴν οὐραῖον δεῖς</note>, that is, you bind a dolphin by its tail. Used for those who attempt something to no purpose. This is because a dolphin's tail is slippery and cannot be held by that part. Or because the tail is so powerful that by its movement it is carried along and sometimes even overturns ships, making it invincible in that area. It will also apply to those who attack someone in a way that they can by no means be overcome.

->You are holding an eel by the tail.<-
<margin>94</margin>
<note>Greek: Ἀπ’ οὐρᾶς τὴν ἔγχελυν ἔχεις</note>, that is, you hold an eel by the tail. This is aptly said of those who have dealings with men of slippery faith and the treacherous, or who possess some fleeting and uncertain thing which they cannot keep for long.

->You hold an eel with a fig leaf.<-
<margin>95</margin>
The opposite of the previous one is this: <note>Greek: Τῷ θρίῳ τὴν ἔγχελυν</note>, that is, an eel with a fig leaf (the word "you hold" is understood). This is used when someone who is otherwise flighty and slippery is held by a knot tighter than they can slip out of. For the leaf of a fig tree is rough—Plutarch wrote that its name was even derived from its roughness—and for that reason, it is most suitable for restraining an eel, which is slippery by nature.

->You are caught by the middle.<-
<margin>96</margin>
Close to this sentiment is that phrase in Aristophanes’ *The Frogs*: <note>Greek: νῦν ἔχῃ μέσος</note>, that is, "Now you are held by the middle." Said of one who is so held that he can extricate himself by no means. It is a metaphor taken from wrestlers and athletes, who, if they seize someone by the waist, easily win. These are the words of Aeacus to Bacchus: "But now you are held by the middle." To the same point belongs that line in Terence: "I would grab him up by the middle."

->You are teaching a dolphin to swim.<-
<margin>97</margin>
<note>Greek: Δελφῖνα νήχεσθαι διδάσκεις</note>, that is, you teach a dolphin to swim. This applies to those who try to advise someone in a matter in which that person is himself most expert and has no need of a teacher. For the dolphin is of such swift impulse in swimming that it not only surpasses every kind of aquatic creature in speed, but even land animals, as Aelian states in Book 12. Indeed, it even leaps over ships and, with a held breath, hurls itself like a missile.

->You are teaching an eagle to fly.<-
<margin>98</margin>
<note>Greek: Ἀετὸν ἵπτασθαι διδάσκεις</note>, that is, you teach an eagle to fly. A different metaphor declares the same meaning. For what the dolphin is among fish, the eagle is among birds. They also have this in common: that both are said to be <term>panderkes</term> <note>Greek: πανδερκής, meaning "all-seeing"</note>. Gregory seems to have alluded to this in a certain letter to Eudoxus the rhetorician: "Let the masses be happy, and let the jackdaws—as it were—test the flight of eagles," meaning let the common people be, or the jackdaws who judge the flight of eagles.

->You are stuck in the same mud.<-
<margin>99</margin>
Terence in *Phormio*: "You are stuck in the same mud." This applies to those who are so entangled in some business that they cannot extricate themselves. It is a metaphor from travelers who, as soon as they fall into the mud, while they try to pull out one foot, the other is submerged deeper. Again, to pull this one out, the other which they had pulled out must be fixed in again. Horace alludes to the same: "In vain," he says, "desiring to pull the foot out of the filth."
Similar to this is: "To be stuck in the same footprint." Quintus Curtius, Book 4: "For three days, bloodless with fear, now burdened by their own arms, they remained stuck in the same footprint."

->He is stuck in the water.<-
<margin>100</margin>
A proverb not unlike this is used by Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in Book 3 of *On Duties*: "He indeed says many things in many places, but the water sticks, as they say." He means that Epicurus is inconsistent with himself in his arguments and involves himself in contradictions, while the things he says in one place fight with what he said elsewhere; thus he wavers, as it were, and does not stand on solid ground. This is what usually happens to those who, when they wander from the truth, involve the matter in a torch-cloud of words. It appears to be a metaphor either from those floating, who...

Or certainly, this comes from the orators' water-clock <note>original: "clepsydra" — a water clock used in ancient courts to time speeches</note>, which we have mentioned elsewhere, so that we might say a man "sticks in the water" who, even though the water has already finished dripping, still cannot extricate himself from his legal case.
