->THE FIFTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND<-

### Many things fall between the cup and the upper lips.
1
Sulpitius Apollinaris, the grammarian, in Aulus Gellius's *Attic Nights*, book thirteen, chapter seventeen, notes two particular adages, one Greek and the other Latin: both of which carry the same meaning. The Greek is a hexameter verse, he says, of a proverbial nature:
"Many things happen between the cup and the edge of the lip," <note>original Greek: πολλὰ μεταξὺ πέλει κύλικος καὶ χείλεος ἄκρου</note> that is,
**Many things fall between the cup and the upper lips.**
By this we are warned that nothing should be hoped for as so certain, nor is anything so close at hand, that some chance event cannot intervene and snatch it away. Indeed, it is so unsafe to trust in things to come, that even those things we hold in our hands are scarcely certain. Some trace the origin of the adage to a story of this kind. Ancaeus, the son of Neptune and Astypalea of Phoenicia, while he was planting a vineyard and pressing his servants hard, was told by one servant, who was moved by the weariness of the work against his master, that it would never happen that he would taste wine from that vineyard. Later, when the vine had grown successfully and the grapes had ripened, Ancaeus, exulting and joyful, summoned that same servant and ordered him to pour him some wine. Then, just as he was about to move the cup to his mouth, he reminded the servant of what he had said, as if mocking a vain prophecy. But the servant replied to his master with this sentiment: "Between the cup and the top of the lips, many things can intervene." The event favored the servant's sentiment. For while he was speaking, before he could swallow the wine, another servant entered and announced that the vineyard was being laid waste by a certain wild boar. Hearing this, Ancaeus set down the cup and immediately rushed toward the boar, by which he was struck and killed during the hunt. Lycophron used this adage in his Iambics:
"Wretchedly learning many things through my own misfortune,
Before fate, which manages the affairs of mortals,
Sends its lot between the cup and the drinking lips." <note>original Greek: Πολλὰ τλήμων σὺν κακῷ μαθὼν ἔπω / Πρὶν καὶ χάλοὺς καὶ δεπασραίων ποτῶν / Χείλει κυλινδῇ μοῖρα πέμπτηται βροτῶν</note>
The authors cite Aristotle as an authority, who himself mentioned the story of Ancaeus, in which that prophecy was made to Ancaeus as he was establishing the vineyard; he had summoned a certain seer who predicted that it would never happen that he would taste wine from it, and when the wine was pressed into the cup, he mocked the seer as a "false prophet" <note>original Greek: ψευδόμαντιν</note>. The rest agrees with what we have reported from the commentaries of others. Festus Pompeius indicates it was said by an augur to a neighbor who happened to pass by. Lycophron, however, twisted it elsewhere, namely to Agapenor the father, and Ancaeus the son of Actor and Eurythemistis, and to the Calydonian boar. Dionysius, in Zenodotus, prefers to refer the proverb to Antinous, whom Homer mentions in the *Odyssey*, book 22. This Antinous was one of the suitors of Penelope, through whose throat Ulysses drove a weapon while he was holding a cup and already preparing to drink. And so, with the cup slipping from his hands, he fell and died. It would not be out of place to add the Homeric verse:
"He spoke, and aimed a bitter arrow at Antinous.
Indeed, he was about to lift a beautiful cup,
Golden, with two handles, and was already moving it in his hands,
That he might drink of the wine; and slaughter was not in his heart
Or mind. (For who would think that among men feasting,
One man among many, even if he were very strong,
Would bring upon him evil death and black fate?)" <note>original Greek: Ἦ, καὶ ἐπ' Ἀντινόῳ ἰθύνετο πικρὸν ὀϊστόν... etc.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explains the proverb "Many a slip 'twixt cup and lip," tracing its origins to the mythological figure Ancaeus and the death of the suitor Antinous in Homer's Odyssey.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>Erasmus begins by quoting Homer’s Odyssey, Book 22, describing the sudden death of the suitor Antinous.</note>

Odysseus aimed and struck him in the throat with an arrow, and the point passed clean through his soft neck. He slumped to one side, and the cup fell from his hand as he was struck; immediately, a thick jet of human blood gushed from his nostrils. ->that is,<-

> Having spoken these words, he aimed a bitter shaft at Antinous.
> He was just then raising a beautiful golden cup,
> Two-handled and gleaming with gold, and was even now
> Moving it toward his lips to drink; no thought of slaughter
> Stirred in his trembling heart (for who would ever believe

Nor do I think it irrelevant to remember here what was said to Julius Caesar as if mocking the vanity of a prophecy: that the Ides of March had come, but had not yet passed. <note>A reference to the famous warning Caesar received before his assassination.</note>

### II. Between the mouth and the morsel

The Latin version is of this sort: *Inter os et offam* (Between the mouth and the morsel). It is derived from the taking of food, just like that Greek expression <note>original: "ἀπὸ ποτου"</note> "from the drink." For the Romans of old used to live on *offae* <term>offa: a small ball of flour or a morsel of food</term>, as Valerius Maximus testifies. Therefore, "Between the mouth and the morsel" is the same as saying between the mouth and the food. Furthermore, the proverb is cited by Aulus Gellius from a certain speech by Cato regarding aediles <note>Roman officials</note> who were improperly elected, in these very words: "Now they say that there is good grain in the stalks and the grass. Do not have too much hope there. I have often heard that many things can intervene between the mouth and the morsel." Truly, between the morsel and the grass, there is a very long interval indeed. Festus records the adage as: "Between the hand and the chin."

### III. Flee so as not to pass the house

There exists in Terence’s play *Phormio* a particularly elegant adage: *Ita fugias ne præter casam* (Flee in such a way that you do not run past the house). By this we are warned not to flee one fault in such a way that we incautiously tumble into another, greater one. "We act by our own fault," he says, "so that it is profitable for men to be wicked, while we strive to be called too good and kind. Flee so as not to pass the house, as they say." These are the words of the old man Demipho accusing himself, because while he was eagerly striving to escape the reputation of being a miser, he had run into the reproach of being a fool. Donatus explains the metaphor of the adage in this way (if indeed this commentary is truly by Donatus): "Flee so that you do not pass by your own house, which should be your safest refuge." Or, "Flee so as not to pass the house where a thief can be better guarded, caught, and punished with lashes." Or, he says, it was the word of someone chasing a thief and meanwhile taking care that he does not pass the house, lest in passing he might even snatch something from there. Who could endure this sort of "divination" by those guessing uncertain and varied things, if we did not see that this same habit belongs to both the interpreters of law and the commentators of Greek adages? The first interpretation pleases me more. For some, in the heat of fleeing, even run past those places where they could have rested comfortably. The Greeks call this by a single word <note>original: "ἀποσφῆλαι"</note> *aposphēlai*, that is, to pass by or be carried past wrongly, wandering away from that which ought to have been embraced. I believe Lucian had this adage in mind in his work *Nigrinus* when he writes: <note>original: "ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν ταῖς τραγῳδίαις καὶ κωμῳδίαις λεγόμενοι, ἤδη καὶ παρὰ θύραν βιαζόμενοι"</note> "Just as they say in tragedies and comedies: Now even driven past the door."

### IV. Having avoided Charybdis, I fell into Scylla

<note>original: "τὴν χάρυβδιν ἐκφυγὼν, τῇ σκύλλῃ περιέπεσον"</note>
These are "headless" iambic dimeters; it is uncertain whether chance poured them out or art fashioned them. This is their meaning: Having avoided Charybdis, I fell into Scylla; that is, while I avoid a more serious evil, I fall into another different one. The adage is taken from the Homeric fable which tells that Ulysses, while he moved his ship closer to Scylla for fear of Charybdis, lost six of the number of his companions. Some say Scylla was the daughter of Nisus, King of the Megarians, who, because her father's golden hair was removed, was turned into this sea monster, as Pausanias mentions in his *Description of Greece*...

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning the unpredictability of fate and the danger of overcorrecting one's actions, using classical examples like the death of Antinous and the monsters Scylla and Charybdis.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of classical adages, specifically focusing on the mythological dangers of Scylla and Charybdis as metaphors for difficult choices.</meta>

# CHILIADS: FIRST CENTURY V.

Anthiacis. Virgil seems to agree with this in his *Bucolics* <note>original: "Eclogues"</note>, when he says:
> Why should I speak of Scylla, daughter of Nisus, of whom the story persists
> That she, her white waist girt with barking monsters,
> Harassed the Dulichian ships with sea-dogs?

Sallust indicates that Scylla was the daughter of Phorcus and the nymph Crateis. Since Glaucus loved her, Circe—who was herself possessed by love for him—became envious upon seeing his preference for Scylla. She infected the spring where the nymph was accustomed to bathe with magical poisons. When Scylla descended into it, she was transformed from the waist down into various forms. For it is a peculiarity of Circe to turn humans into the shapes of wild beasts. Shuddering at her own deformity, Scylla threw herself headlong into the sea, and her appearance provided the basis for the legend. Regarding the truth of the matter, the opinions of writers differ. Sallust thinks it is a rock jutting out into the sea which, to those viewing it from afar, mimics a female form; the waves dashing against the shallows seem to imitate the barking of wolves and dogs, and so they imagined her to be girt from the waist with such beasts. In the Greek commentaries, I find that Scylla was a woman of wonderful swiftness, to whom the name Scylla was given <term>from the word *skyllien* (to tear or despoil)</term>, because pirates roaming there used to infest the Tyrrhenian and Sicilian seas, plundering whatever ships passed by; and from this the fable was born. Concerning Charybdis, the poets' fables relate that she was a most voracious woman who, because she had stolen the oxen of Hercules, was struck by Jove's thunderbolt and cast into the sea. She was turned into a monster of this sort, which still preserves its former nature. For it swallows everything; and whatever it swallows, it casts up near the shore of Tauromenium, as Sallust is the authority. Hence, as if by a proverb, Horace calls a prostitute of insatiable greed a "Charybdis":
> Ah, unhappy youth,
> In what a Charybdis you are struggling,
> Boy worthy of a better flame!

Servius says Scylla is in Italy and Charybdis in Sicily. Virgil, in the third book of the *Aeneid*, elegantly describes this narrow passage between two dangers:
> These places, they say, once shattered by the force of a vast ruin
> (So much can the long passage of time change things)
> Leaped apart, though once both lands were one;
> The sea came with force between them, and with its waves
> Cut the Italian side from the Sicilian, and washed between
> The fields and cities separated by the shore with a narrow tide.
> Scylla occupies the right side, implacable Charybdis the left.

And the same author elsewhere:
> It is better to round the long goal of Pachynus
> And fetch a wide compass, than once to have seen
> The misshapen Scylla in her vast cavern. <note>The Latin text provided is a summary: "Better that both paths be passed with a small margin of death."</note>

Homer, in the <term>12th book (mu)</term> of the *Odyssey*, describes both dangers at great length, and depicts Circe warning Odysseus that he should turn his course toward Scylla rather than Charybdis, because it is better to lose six of his companions than for all to perish together. He declares there is far more danger in Charybdis than in Scylla:
<term>
> For if you should be there when she sucks down the water,
> Not even the Earth-shaker (Poseidon) could rescue you from destruction.
> But rather, hugging Scylla's rock, drive your ship
> Past her quickly; since it is much better
> To mourn six comrades than all of them at once.
</term>
That is:
> For if you are there when she swallows the waves
> In her throat: not even Neptune could snatch you
> From such great danger: but come, pass by the rock
> Of Scylla with a swift course,
> Since it is much better to lose six companions
> Than that destruction should take everyone at once.

This adage may be used in three ways: first, when we advise that if we ever fall into such straits that we cannot escape without some loss, we should choose the lesser of two evils—following the example of Odysseus—and lean toward that side where there is less damage. For instance, if someone were in danger regarding both his life and his money, he would prefer to be closer to [losing] his money...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

of money than with the danger of life, because the loss of resources can be repaired in some way, but life, once lost, is never restored. Or when we show a business to be doubtful and dangerous, in which there is need for the greatest moderation so that you do not err on either side. In this case, we will not take account of which danger is greater; rather, it is understood only that a huge crisis underlies both sides. An example of the former would be: "Remember it is far better to fall into the Scylla of expense than into the Charybdis of ill health." Or: "It is preferable to run into the loss of financial property, as if into Scylla, than to fall into the Charybdis of infamy." An example of the latter is this: "Take care that you favor the people in such a way that you do not offend the mind of the prince. Govern cautiously and circumspectly, remembering that your course lies between Scylla and Charybdis." <note>Scylla and Charybdis are two mythical sea monsters situated on opposite sides of a narrow strait; avoiding one often meant drifting too close to the other.</note> There is a third way, if you invert it, in this manner: "While you fear appearing poorly learned, you have run into the reputation of being arrogant; this is clearly what is said: while you avoid Scylla, you have fallen into Charybdis." This little verse is celebrated among the Latins, by whatever author it was created, for it does not occur to me at present:
*He falls into Scylla, desiring to avoid Charybdis.*

->Fleeing the smoke, I fell into the fire.<-
<margin>V</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κάπνον γε φεύγων εἰς τὸ πῦρ ἐνέπεσον</note> *Fleeing the smoke, I fell into the fire.* That is, while I avoid the smoke, I have fallen into the flame itself. This is a proverbial iambic verse close to the previous sentiment. Lucian says in *The Dialogue of the Dead*: <note>original Greek: ἐλελήθειν δ’ ἐμαυτὸν ἂν αὐτόφασι τὸ πῦρ ἐκ τοῦ κάπνου βιαζόμενος</note> "I did not realize that, as the proverb says, I was being forced out of the smoke into the fire itself." Plato also uses this in the eighth book of *The Republic*, when he says the people, while refusing to serve free men, run into the flame as if having avoided smoke—namely, so that they are forced to serve even slaves. Horace alluded to this when he said in his *Satires*:
> For in vain will you have avoided that vice,
> If you have twisted yourself perversely to another.

And in the *Art of Poetry*:
> The flight from a fault leads into vice, if it lacks skill.

Plutarch in *On Shyness*: <note>original Greek: τῇ δὲ δυσωπίᾳ συμβέβηκεν ἀτεχνῶς φεύγουσι κάπνον ἀσβέστῳ πῦρ ἐμβάλλειν ἑαυτούς</note> "It undoubtedly happens to those with foolish shame that, fleeing the smoke of infamy, they throw themselves into the fire." That is, into another greater evil.

->A broad fingernail, and similar proverbial hyperboles.<-
<margin>VI</margin>
To depart by "a finger’s breadth" or "a fingernail" is frequent in Cicero, meaning by the smallest space. However, the metaphor becomes more festive whenever we signify by these words a perfect imitation and full agreement in every respect, as in the second book of *Academic Questions*: "From this rule I am not allowed to depart by a transverse <note>crosswise</note> fingernail, as they say." In the same place: "For where does he either follow Xenocrates, whose books on the method of speaking are many and highly approved, or Aristotle himself, than whom surely nothing is more acute, nothing more polished? From Chrysippus, not a foot." He is speaking of Antiochus, who, having despised the rest, followed Chrysippus in all things. Again in the fourth book of *Academic Questions*: "Which things having been granted, they cannot move forward a finger." The same to Atticus: "It is most certain to me, never to depart a finger from the most honorable opinion." Again to the same in book thirteen: "Care must be taken, and this in all of life, that one ought not to depart a transverse fingernail from our conscience." The same in the *Letters to Friends*: "Press on then, as they say, not a transverse fingernail from the pen." Those things which Euclio says in Plautus's *Aulularia* are indeed less figurative, but still proverbial: "By Hercules, if you move from that spot a transverse finger or a broad nail." And Cicero in *Against Verres*: "They did not depart a finger." The same to Atticus, book thirteen, first letter: "We have not yet stepped a foot out of the villa, so great and constant were the rains we were having." The same in the second book of *Academic Questions*: "I do not ask from these men those things of the Mathematicians, which, if not granted, they cannot move forward a finger." And Saint Jerome imitates this: "And following the footsteps of the apostolic will, let us not recede from his opinions even by a point, as it is said, and a transverse nail." The metaphor seems partly taken from those who measure a board or a stone or something similar with the breadth of their fingers whenever the precise measure of a thing is looked at (for we are accustomed to measure other things by cubits; the smallest of measures is the finger). Partly it is from the measurers of acreage, who measure the space of the ground by furlongs, paces, and as the smallest measure, feet. Commonly even now they say, "A stalk's breadth," by a similar figure, for that which is "not even so much."

->He has no place to set his foot.<-
<margin>VII</margin>
From which that proverbial hyperbole also seems to be drawn, frequent in Cicero: "Where he might set his foot..."

# FIRST CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY 161

<margin>o 3</margin>
<note>The left margin of the original manuscript is damaged or shadowed, resulting in missing letters at the start of several lines. These have been reconstructed based on the known Latin sources Erasmus is quoting.</note>

He has nowhere to set his foot. This stands for: he does not possess even the smallest piece of land. In the *Letters to Atticus*, Book 13: "The son of Ariobarzanes has come to Rome; he wants, I think, to buy some kingdom from Caesar. For as things stand now, he has nowhere to set his foot on his own property." Likewise in the *Second Philippic*: *What place was there on earth where you could set your foot on your own land?* Again in *Book 7 to Atticus*: "See that there is no one in Italy who is not in that man's power." Also in the fourth book *On Moral Ends*: *For what of wisdom? She had nowhere to set her foot,* once all duties were removed. This will be appropriately used against a man who is remarkably thin and poor, who does not have even a footprint's worth of possession in the fields. In the same author <note>Cicero</note> there is a joke about a farm, which he says could be thrown from a sling <note>original: "mittere funda" - a pun on 'fundus' (farm) and 'funda' (sling)</note>.

---

->To stumble twice against the same stone. VIII<-

<note>original Greek: δὶς πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν αἰσχρὸν προσκρούειν λίθον</note> That is, it is a disgrace to strike against the same stone twice. This elegant and proverbial six-foot line is cited by Zenodotus in his collection of adages. Cicero in the *Letters to Friends, Book 10*: *For that fault, to stumble twice against the same stone, is rebuked by a common proverb.* Ovid in the second book of *Tristia*:
*And so madness is a companion to my sickness,*
*And I bring my foot back again to the very wounds I remember.*
It is used by Ausonius in a certain *Letter*: *For indeed,* he says, *you asked that you might stumble twice against the same stone in your letter; but I, whatever the fortune might be, would blush even once.* Now, *To stumble twice against the same stone* means to sin again in the same matter. For a first error, even by the Greek adage, deserves pardon; but pardon is not usually given to one who repeats a fault. Among Greek maxims, this one is also celebrated:
<note>original Greek: δὶς ἐξαμαρτάιν ταὐτὸν ἐπ' ἀνδρὸς σοφῷ</note> That is, it is not the mark of a wise man to slip twice in the same thing. There is also a Greek epigram, author uncertain:
<note>original Greek: νηπύτιος ὃς πρῶτα συνεὶς ἀπλήξ γήμας, πάλιν δ' ὑτέρα λέκτρα διώκει, / ὥσπερ τις ναυηγὸς πλὼς δὶς βυθὸν ἀργαλέον.</note> That is:
*He is a fool who, having experienced marriage once, seeks a second bed,*
*Just like a shipwrecked sailor who sails twice into the cruel deep.*
Publilius Syrus the Mime is also not foreign to this form:
*He wrongly accuses Neptune, who suffers shipwreck a second time.*
Though Scipio does not permit a wise man to err even once, so as to say, "I did not think" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ὤμην</note>.

---

->To go wrong on the same string. IX<-

Horace in the *Art of Poetry* expressed a similar sentiment with a different metaphor:
*The harp-player,* he says,
*Is laughed at, who always goes wrong on the same string.*
The metaphor is drawn from musicians, for whom it is exceedingly shameful to make a mistake often on the same strings. Therefore, it will be aptly said of those who either fail frequently in a similar matter, or commit the same fault again and again. For a first slip is attributed either to chance or to imprudence; a repeated one is attributed to stupidity or ignorance.

---

->Not so like as one egg to another. X<-

There are several adages of similarity among authors, among which is: *Not so like as one egg,* concerning things of indistinguishable likeness. Cicero in the *Academic Questions, Book 2*: *Do you see how the similarity of eggs to one another is a proverb?* Yet we have heard this, that there were many at Delos, when those affairs were flourishing, who used to raise hens for the sake of profit. When they had inspected an egg, they were accustomed to say which hen had laid it. Nor is that against us. For it is enough for us to distinguish them. The same proverb is cited by Fabius Quintilian. It is also used by Seneca in the little book he wrote as a satire against the Emperor Claudius.

---

->Not so like as milk to milk. XI<-

This has the same force, and is used by Plautus in *Amphitryon*: *Nor is milk more like to milk than that man is like me.* It is said by Sosia concerning Mercury, who had taken on his form. The same in *The Braggart Soldier*: *As similar as milk is to milk.*

---

->Not so like as water to water. XII<-

This holds the same power, which Plautus uses in the *Menaechmi*: *Neither water to water, nor milk to milk, believe me, is anywhere more similar than this man is to you, and you to him.* To this form also belongs that from...

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

the same scene: "It is as similar as your mirror can be." Again in *The Braggart Soldier*: "For water can never be taken from the top of a well more similar to other water." <note>original: "Tam cosimilis est, quàm potest speculum tuum... Nam esummo puteo similior nunquam potest aqua aquæ sumi." Erasmus is quoting the Roman playwright Plautus to show how the ancients expressed perfect similarity.</note>

->As similar as bees to bees.<-
<margin>XIII</margin>

To these, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> also adds this in his *Academic Questions*: "As similar as eggs are to eggs, and bees to bees." Here he jokes about the "worlds" of Democritus, which are supposedly identical to one another in every respect. They use a similar form when they say, "as similar as a sheep to a sheep."

->The Acanthian cicada.<-
<margin>XIV</margin>

*Acanthia tettix* <note>original Greek: Ἀκανθία τέττιξ</note>, that is, the Acanthian cicada. This proverb was usually directed at the unlearned and the speechless, or those ignorant of music. Stephanus of Byzantium is the authority for the story that near the town of Acanthos in Aetolia, the cicadas—which are vocal elsewhere—are mute; hence the proverb arose, the author of which he cites as Simonides. Pliny, in the eleventh book of his *Natural History*, chapter twenty-seven, writes that in the territory of Rhegium all the cicadas are silent, while across the river in Locris they sing. Pausanias testifies to the same in his second book on the affairs of Elis. Strabo, in his sixth book of *Geography*, reports that the territory of Rhegium is divided from that of Locris by a river named the Alex. He notes that the cicadas on the Locrian bank chirp loudly, while those in Rhegium are mute. He conjectures the cause is that the Rhegian region, being shady and dark, makes the membranes of the cicadas sluggish with moisture. In the Locrian territory, because it is sunny, the membranes are dried by the sun's heat and emit a sharper sound. 

The miracle of the Rhegian cicadas is increased by the legendary fame of their neighbors' singing. For the same Strabo cites Timaeus as his authority that once, in a Pythian competition, Eunomus the Locrian and Ariston of Rhegium entered a singing contest. Ariston invoked Delphic Apollo to aid his singing, because the people of Rhegium had once set out from Delphi. Eunomus replied that the Rhegians should not even compete in music, since among them the cicada—the most vocal of animals—lacked a voice. While both were competing, one of the strings on Eunomus’s lyre broke during the performance; a cicada flew down and perched there, supplying with its own song the note that would otherwise have been missing. Having been declared the victor, he dedicated a statue of a lyre-player with a cicada sitting on the lyre. Strabo relates roughly this account.

->To be weighed in the same balance.<-
<margin>XV</margin>

To be weighed in the same balance <note>original: "Eadem pensari trutina"</note>, that is, by the same law. Horace in his *Satires*:
> "By this law he shall be placed in the same balance."

The same author in his *Epistles*:
> "Roman writers are weighed in the same
> balance."

This agrees with that rule of the legal scholars: "Submit to the law which you yourself have brought forth." Or indeed: "Let it be dealt with you by the same agreement by which you have dealt with others."
<margin>Persius,</margin>
> "And you should correct the dishonest tongue
> in that balance."

Very similar to this is "To require by the same rule," or *iso stathmo* <note>original Greek: ἴσῳ σταθμῷ</note>, that is, with an equal balance or scale. Plutarch: "But malice, having been received in an equal balance, dragged everything down like a lead weight on a net." <note>original Greek: Αὐτ’ ἴσῳ σταθμῷ πᾶσαν ἡ κακία παραδεχθεῖσα μολυβδὶς ὥσε δίκτυον κατέσπασεν.</note>

->He has lost his belt.<-
<margin>XVI</margin>

He has lost his belt <note>original: "Zonam perdidit"</note>. A military proverb used for the "penniless" <note>original Greek: ἀχρημάτους</note>, that is, those who have no money. Acron suggests it is drawn from a certain Greek fable; Porphyrio says it comes from the custom of soldiers, who carry whatever they have with them in their belt. Lucilius, as cited by Nonius, describes such a man quite charmingly:
> "He who has no beast of burden, no slave, no companion,
> Carries his pouch and whatever money he has all with him:
> He eats, sleeps, and bathes with his pouch. All the man's
> hope is in one pouch; the rest of his life is bound to it."

For Lucilius calls a small bag or purse hanging from the arm a *Bulga*. Thus also Horace:
> "With tablets and money-boxes hanging from the left arm."

Although Festus asserts that *Bulga* is a Gallic word. In a similar way, Gracchus speaks in Gellius: "When I set out from Rome, I took out belts full of silver; I brought them back from the province empty." Horace in his *Epistles*: "He will go wherever you wish, who has lost his belt." Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian*: "You who have no belt, why have you come to this city? Or what do you seek?" In these words of Plautus there is a double allusion: both to the loose-fitting clothing of the Carthaginians, and to the money carried in a belt, without which one cannot live very comfortably in a sumptous city.

# FIFTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
<note>A "Chiliad" is a group of 1,000 proverbs; a "Hundred" is a sub-section of 100.</note>

Pescennius Niger <note>A Roman usurper, died 194 AD</note>, according to Spartianus, forbade soldiers from carrying a money-belt with them into war. His reasoning was that if they had any money, they should entrust it to public keeping, to be received back after the battle. By doing this, he simultaneously removed any distraction from the soldiers and deprived the enemy of plunder should any misfortune occur. There is a similar passage in Lampridius regarding Alexander <note>Emperor Alexander Severus</note>: "A soldier does not feel fear unless he is well-clothed, shod, armed, and has something in his money-belt."

-> XVII. We shall count the entrails once they are cooked. <-

Thus we shall count the entrails. Diomedes the Grammarian, where he defines what a proverb is, provided this example. He ascribes this meaning to it: we shall know the outcome from the event itself. Close to this is the phrase from the comic playwright: "The matter will reveal itself." For, as Ovid says:
*The result justifies the deeds.*
Among the Greeks, the phrase is *auto deixei* <note>original: αὐτὸ δείξει</note>, that is, "the thing itself will show it."

-> XVIII. The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing. <-
*The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog one great thing.* <note>original Greek: Πόλλ' οἶδ' ἀλώπηξ, ἀλλ' ἐχῖνος ἓν μέγα.</note>
That is:
Many things to the fox, but to the hedgehog one greatest thing.

Zenodotus cites this iambic line from Archilochus. It is said against those who are crafty and stitched together with various deceits, or rather, we use it when we wish to indicate that some people achieve more with a single clever trick than others do with diverse maneuvers. For the fox protects itself against hunters with many joined deceits, and yet is caught quite often. The hedgehog—which I believe to be the land-urchin <note>the common hedgehog</note> (for in this place mention is made of the land animal, not the sea-urchin fish)—is protected against the bites of dogs by one single art alone. Indeed, it rolls itself up into the appearance of a ball with its spines, so that it cannot be gripped by a bite from any side. In the same Zenodotus, certain verses of this kind are cited from Ion of Chios, the tragic poet; Athenaeus also cites these same lines in his *Deipnosophistae* <note>original: "Sermonibus conuiualibus" or "Banquet of the Learned"</note> from a tragedy titled *Phoenicia*:
*I truly hate the hedgehog's wretched tricks,*
*Who, as soon as he senses the scent of other beasts,*
*Crouches down and rolls his body around his spines,*
*Impossible to touch or to bite.*
<note>original Greek: Μισῶ γ' ἐχῖνον μᾶλλον ὀιζυρὰς τέχνας... etc.</note>

Plutarch cites the proverb and alludes to the poem in his commentary titled *Whether Land or Sea Animals are Cleverer* <note>original: Πότερα τῶν ζώων φρονιμώτερα, χερσαῖα ἢ θαλάσσια</note>. I will add his words below: "Among land animals, the hedgehog's defense of itself through its natural ingenuity has given rise to the proverb: *The fox has many arts, but the hedgehog one great one.* For when a dog attacks it, as they say:
*Rolling his body, he covers himself in his own spines,*
*He lies motionless, so that he cannot be touched by the mouth*
*In any way, nor can he be bitten.*"

Plutarch, or whoever is the author of that work, mixed some of his own words into the verses; let no one suspect this happened through my error. But Pliny describes the nature and cleverness of this animal most copiously in Book Eight, Chapter Thirty-Seven: "They prepare food for winter," he says, "and having rolled over fallen apples, they carry them fixed to their spines—holding one more in their mouth—to hollow trees. They also predict the change from the north wind to the south by hiding themselves in holes. When they sense a hunter, they draw in their mouth and feet and the entire lower part (where they have a thin and harmless down) and roll into the shape of a ball, so that nothing can be grasped except the prickles. In desperation, they discharge a urine that is corrosive to their own bodies and damaging to their spines." Whoever desires to know the rest may seek it from the place I have indicated.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>original: "petat"</note> ...seeks. These things pertained most especially to the understanding of children. Also famous is the cleverness of the sea urchin <note>Latin: *echinus*</note>, which, sensing a coming storm at sea, grips little stones to weigh itself down so that it might stabilize its mobility with weight, lest it wear down its spines by excessive rolling. Seeing this, sailors soon restrain their ships with several anchors. The author is Pliny, in book nine, chapter thirty-one. That the fox is a "shifter" <note>Latin: *versipellem*, literally "one who changes skin"</note>, equipped with various arts, is indicated by many other fables, and particularly by that one related by Plutarch in his *Moralia*: When a leopard once looked down upon a fox because he himself had a hide variegated with spots of every kind of color, the fox replied that she had that beauty in her mind which he had only on his skin. Indeed, it is not a little better to be endowed with a crafty wit than with a multicolored skin. The Greeks call one who is skillful and armed with various deceits *poikilophrona* <note>original: ποικιλόφρονα</note> and *poikilomēlin* <note>original: ποικιλόμηλιν</note>; the Latins call such a person "sly" and "skin-shifter." Another fable is told, not far removed from this proverb: When a fox was once boasting in a conversation with a cat that she had various tricks, so many that she even had a bag full of ruses; the cat replied that he had only a single art in which he trusted if any danger should arise. During their chatting, the noise of approaching dogs was suddenly heard. Thereupon the cat leapt up into a very high tree, while the fox, surrounded by the pack of dogs, was caught. The fable suggests that it is sometimes better to have a single plan, provided it is true and effective, than many deceits and frivolous plans. Just as if a poor man were to solicit the heart of a girl with many-layered arts, while a rich man had only this one thing, which is found in Ovid: "Take as much as you please." You would rightly say:
*The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.* <note>original: πολλ' οἶδ' ἀλώπηξ, ἀλλ' ἐχῖνος ἓν μέγα.</note>

### To imitate the cypress.
-> XIX <-

> Horace in *The Art of Poetry*: <column-break/> And perhaps you
> know how to imitate a cypress. But what use is this, if a sailor
> pays you to paint him escaping hopeless from a shipwreck?

Acron <note>A famous commentator on Horace</note> warns that this is a proverb, arising from a certain unskilled painter who knew how to paint nothing except a cypress tree. When a certain shipwrecked man asked him to represent his likeness and depict his shipwreck, the painter asked whether he wanted a cypress added to the scene. This matter first turned into a joke, and then even into a proverb. It will be neatly used against those who, whatever they have learned, insist on thrusting it in everywhere inappropriately, even when it has nothing to do with the matter at hand.

### Flame is very close to smoke.
-> XX <-

This appears in Plautus, in the *Curculio*: "Flame is very close to smoke." The adage warns that danger must be fled early; whoever desires to avoid an evil must first avoid the occasion of it. Just as he who does not wish to be corrupted should abstain from the company of the wicked; he who does not wish to lie with a girl should not give her a kiss. For the poet immediately adds: "Nothing can be burned by smoke, but it can by flame." For smoke is the sign of a flame soon to break out.

### The matter has come to the rope.
-> XXI <-

Terence in *Phormio*: "By your doing, the matter has come to the rope for me most clearly." By this adage, the utmost desperation of affairs is signified. For in such a state, certain madmen are accustomed to flee to the noose. Juvenal writes:
> Can you endure any female master while so many ropes are available?
To the same point belongs that saying: "A tree must be chosen for a hanging."

### Poverty has been allotted wisdom.
-> XXII <-

*Penia de tēn sophian elache* <note>original: πενία δὲ τὴν σοφίαν ἔλαχε</note>, that is, "Poverty has been allotted wisdom." Zenodotus cites this from Euripides. Others attribute it to Ariston. Wealth is lazy, but in truth, want is the discoverer of many arts; a fact which Poverty herself boasts of in Aristophanes' *Plutus*, claiming the invention of all arts for herself. Virgil says:
Labor conquered all things,
Relentless labor, and want pressing in hard circumstances.
Evils often stir the wit. -> Ovid <-
The belly is the master of art and the giver of wit. -> Persius <-
This little verse is also circulated among the Greeks:
*Hunger becomes the teacher of many.* <note>original: πολλῶν ὁ λιμὸς γίνεται διδάσκαλος.</note> That is,
Wicked hunger stands as the mistress of many.
Xenophon called poverty "self-taught wisdom." For while the former [wealth] persuades with words, the latter [poverty] by force toward...

> Poverty, Diophantus, alone awakens the arts,
> she herself is the teacher of labor. <note>original Greek: Ἁ πενία, Διόφαντε, μόνα τὰς τέχνας ἐγείρει, αὐτὰ τῶ μόχθοιο διδάσκαλος.</note> that is,
> Poverty rouses the arts, O Diophantus,
> the teacher of working, and the mistress of study.
<unclear>Rightly</unclear> also is that said, that Jupiter removed the ready abundance of things from the Golden Age: <unclear>so that</unclear> practice, by meditating, might forge the arts. Likewise that not inelegant Mime writer says:
<unclear>Whom</unclear> poverty bids to try many things.

<unclear>And</unclear> to that place is referred the proverb which we see happen, I know not how, that wealth is in the hands of <unclear>miserable</unclear> and wicked men, while the learned and the upright are almost always of slender fortune. On which subject <unclear>he treats</unclear> two problems under the title of Aristotle; in one of which he asks how it happens that poverty <unclear>upright</unclear> men are mostly occupied with. And he gives various causes for this: either because the wicked man prefers to acquire riches by divine lawlessness rather than have a long-lasting companionship with poverty—whence she flees from those for whom she sees she would be an occasion for the greatest crimes, and <unclear>comes</unclear> to those whom she thinks will use her rightly and modestly. Or, because being helpless in both strength and counsel, <unclear>as</unclear> (a woman), she hopes there will be more help for her among "men of many tears" <note>original Greek: πολυδάκρυας ἄνδρας — a poetic way of describing those who have suffered and are thus more compassionate.</note> (as the <unclear>proverb</unclear> has it). Or, because since she is herself an evil, she avoids the wicked, lest if "fire be added to fire," <note>original Greek: πῦρ ἐπὶ πῦρ — a common Greek idiom for making a bad situation worse.</note> that is, if evil is added, it should then become intolerable and incurable. In the other problem he asks what the cause is that the <unclear>reckless</unclear> possess wealth, and not likewise the good. Is it because they [Riches] are blind, he says, and for that reason they err in their <unclear>choice</unclear>? These things, since they savor of poetry and sophistry more than the philosopher, especially <unclear>since</unclear> it seems hardly likely to me that they proceeded from Aristotle. But what he said about blind <unclear>riches</unclear> is taken chiefly from the *Plutus* of Aristophanes. In which place Plutus, who is the god of <unclear>wealth</unclear>, being asked whence the evil of blindness had befallen him, answered in this manner:
> For when I was a youth, I threatened that
> I would go only to the just and wise and orderly;
> but he [Zeus] made me blind,
> so that I might recognize none of these.
> Thus does he envy the good. <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ γὰρ ὢν μειράκιον... τοῖσι χρηστοῖσι φθονεῖ.</note> that is,
> Jupiter himself punished me with this evil,
> Because, forsooth, envying mortals.
> When I was a boy, I threatened that it would be so, that to the upright,
> The wise, the modest, only would I go. But Jupiter
> Took away this light, so that it might not be permitted to me
> To distinguish anyone, now to distinguish.
> For to such a degree does he envy men of merit.

<unclear>Him</unclear> Lucian, having imitated in his *Timon*, tells certain similar things about Plutus, whom he <unclear>not only</unclear> makes blind, but also lame: blind indeed always, but then finally <unclear>limping</unclear> whenever he is sent to good men; at other times he is of the swiftest feet.

### Pot Friendship. XXIII
<margin>The pot boils, friendship lives. <note>original Greek: Ζεῖ χύτρα, ζῇ φιλία.</note></margin>
Pot friendship. This will fit those common friends whom the dish, not benefits, wins over. Of which kind Juvenal says:
> He has nothing who is not captured by the smell of his own kitchen:
> Thus he judges of you.
And Latin literature calls them "table friends." Plutarch also, in the booklet titled *How to tell a flatterer from a friend*, says that kind of men are "oil-flask carriers and table-sitters," <note>original Greek: αὐτοληκύθους καὶ τραπεζέας — terms for parasites who hang around for food.</note> commonly called parasites, because they love for the sake of the belly and food, not from the heart: and who are then present as often as they hear, "and pour water on the hands." For Aristophanes the grammarian, in Athenaeus, Book 10, relates that the washing of hands which preceded dinner is called "and of the hand" <note>original Greek: καὶ χερός</note>; after dinner, "the washing off" <note>original Greek: ἀπόνιμμα</note>. Of the same people, if I mistake not, that was said by Menander the comic poet, as cited by Athenaeus:
> For when they have taken the water, they are the dearest friends. <note>original Greek: Ἐπὰν γὰρ ὕδωρ λαβόντων ποθιμηθῶσι φίλτατοι.</note> that is,
> As soon as the water is given, then friends stick closest.
Whence the proverb in this manner: The pot boils, friendship lives. <note>original Greek: Ζεῖ χύτρα, ζῇ φιλία.</note>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### You speak of things older than the parchment.
-> XXIII <-

*Archaiotera diphtheras laleis* <note>original Greek: Ἀρχαιότερα διφθέρας λαλεῖς</note>, that is, **You speak of things older than the parchment.** This applies to those who tell silly stories, or speak of matters that are excessively ancient and long since obsolete. For the "diphthera" <note>A Greek term for a prepared animal skin or parchment used for writing</note> was something left over from those ancient fables. Indeed, they say the *diphthera* was the hide of that goat which nursed Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, also known as Zeus; the goat is often identified as Amalthea</note>, upon which it was believed in antiquity that he wrote down everything that happened. Hence, things that did not appear in the writings of historians, nor were preserved in the memory of men, were said to be sought, as it were, from "Jupiter’s parchment." Furthermore, in the works of Aristophanes, you will frequently read *archaia* or *palaia* <note>Greek: ἀρχαῖα, παλαιὰ</note>—that is, ancient and old things—to mean "nonsense," because antiquity is, I believe, generally very full of fables. Likewise, *archaikos* <note>Greek: ἀρχαϊκῶς</note> is used for that which is "raving" or "foolish." In a similar way, we call old, obsolete, and ceased things *kronika* <note>Greek: κρονικὰ; literally "pertaining to Cronus/Saturn," the old god deposed by Jupiter</note>. Thus in Athenaeus, Book 7, someone (Arrian, I believe) says: *tauta sitia kronika estin o hetaire* <note>Greek: ταῦτα σιτία κρονικά ἐστιν ὦ ἑταῖρε</note>, that is, "These foodstuffs are from the age of Saturn, my friend." The poets imagine that Saturn was driven from his kingdom, and Jupiter reigns in his place.

### I hold a wolf by the ears.
-> XXV <-

This appears in Terence’s play *Phormio*: the young man Antipho had a wife at home whom he could neither cast out—either because he did not wish to, as he was desperately in love with her, or because it was not legally possible since she had been assigned to him by a court verdict—nor, on the other hand, could he keep her because of his father’s violence. And when he was called "lucky" by his cousin for possessing at home the one he loved, he replied: "On the contrary, as the saying goes, **I hold a wolf by the ears.** For I find no way to let go of her, nor do I know how to keep her." Soon after, the pimp, as if repeating the proverb, says the same thing happens to him regarding Phaedria, whom he could neither keep (since he paid nothing) nor drive away (because he was shamelessly charming and promised mountains of gold). Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence</note> ascribes the Greek proverb to these Greek words: *ton oton echo ton lykon, hot' echein hot' apheinai dynamai* <note>Greek: τῶν ὤτων ἔχω τὸν λύκον, ὅτ' ἔχειν ὅτ' ἀφεῖναι δυνάμαι</note>, that is, **I hold the wolf by the ears; I can neither hold on nor let go.** Suetonius writes in his life of Tiberius: "The cause of his hesitation was the fear of dangers threatening from every side, so that he often said he was **holding a wolf by the ears.**" Plutarch, in his *Political Precepts*, says: *lykon d' phasin ton oton kratein* <note>Greek: λύκον δ' φασὶν τῶν ὤτων κρατεῖν</note>, that is, they say a wolf cannot be held by the ears; whereas men are led chiefly by this part—namely, by persuasion. It is said of those who are involved in the kind of business that is neither safe to abandon nor possible to endure. It seems to have arisen from an actual event, like many other sayings. Or certainly from this: that while a hare is most easily held by its very long ears, a wolf, because its ears are short in proportion to its body, cannot be held by them—nor, on the other hand, can such a biting beast be released from one's hands without the greatest danger. Caecilius, in Aulus Gellius Book 15, Chapter 9, expressed the same sentiment but without the metaphor. For he says: "These are the worst kind of friends, with a cheerful face but a sad heart, whom you know not how to grasp nor how to let go." Theognis alluded to this, though in a slightly different sense:
> My heart is in a difficult state regarding your friendship.
> For I can neither hate you, nor love you.
From which that famous line seems to have been fashioned:
> I can live neither with you, nor without you.
It is also cited by Marcus Varro as an example of a proverb: **I hold a wolf by the ears.**

### A necessary evil.
-> XXVI <-

Close to this is that saying, *anankaion kakon* <note>Greek: ἀναγκαῖον κακόν</note>, that is, **A necessary evil**: spoken of those whom you cannot reject because their labor is needed in certain matters, yet you cannot comfortably endure them because they are wicked men. It seems to have arisen from a witty remark by a certain Hybreas, mentioned by Strabo in Book 14. Since Euthydamus had something of the tyrant about him but was otherwise useful to the city in many ways—so that his virtues seemed to balance his vices—the orator Hybreas spoke of him in a speech thus: "You are," he said, "a **necessary evil** for the city. For we can live neither with you, nor without you." Likewise, the Emperor Alexander Severus used to call the tax collectors (whom he had decided to remove, but then realized could not be removed without damage to the Republic) a **necessary evil**. Of this sort also was Publius Cornelius Rufinus, a man who was indeed thievish and exceedingly greedy, but also an outstanding General; Fabricius Luscinus preferred to be "robbed" by him <note>i.e., taxed or exploited</note> than to be sold as a prisoner of war, as recorded by Gellius in Book 4 and Cicero in *On the Orator*, Book 2. It can also be twisted to refer to wives, with whom life is uncomfortable, but without whom the Republic cannot exist at all. It can also be applied to things. For example, if one were to say that a medicine...

### XXVII. Not without Theseus.

<margin>Not without Theseus. <note>original: "Οὐκ ἄνευ Θησέως"</note> When we signify that a matter was accomplished with another's help.</margin> It signifies a communion and fellowship in all things. For Zenodotus 
relates that Theseus was a help to very many brave men in their struggles; indeed, he 
was present in the field at the finishing of the Calydonian boar, and he aided Pirithous in fighting 
the Centaurs, and served with Hercules when he was waging war against the Amazons. The fable of the boar goes like this: Oeneus, 
the father, when offering the first fruits of the year's produce to the gods, had passed over Artemis; she, 
in a great rage, sent a monstrous boar into the Calydonian fields, devastating everything. To finish it off, 
Oeneus summoned every excellent man, proposing rewards for the deed. Among the many 
came Meleager, who indeed finished the beast, but only after Theseus was called to help. The rest 
of the story does not pertain to the sense of the proverb. Regarding Pirithous, it is told thus: Pirithous 
received the Centaurs at a banquet for his bride Hippodamia, as they were kinsmen of the bride. As soon as they 
grew warm with unmixed wine, they began to offer violence to the bride. A fight having broken out, Theseus, bringing aid to Pirithous, 
slaughtered the monstrous Centaurs. Regarding Hercules, they tell it thus: When Eurystheus enjoined upon Hercules 
to take away the belt of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, and he was about to make a pact, 
Juno, always hostile to him, took on the form of an Amazon and spread a rumor everywhere that 
a guest—or rather an enemy—had arrived, who, having violated the queen, was taking the belt she wore as an insignia 
by force. When this was heard, the Amazons took up arms against Hercules. 
Hercules, thinking this was done not by error but by deceit, killed Hippolyta and took the belt. Then, in order 
to take vengeance on the Amazons, he attacked them in war and overwhelmed them, but he is said to have been 
aided by the help of Theseus. This adage is also cited by Plutarch in his *Life of Theseus*, and it signifies that Theseus, as has been said, 
was a help to others, yet from most of these struggles he carried back no reward; and he cites 
Herodotus as the author of this. Aristides alluded to the proverb in his oration to the Thebans: 
<note>original: "Καὶ ὅτε γίνω ἡρακλεῖ Φίλε ἐδ’ ἔκεσε, θησεὺς αὐτὸν ἀθλιώαζε ἀγαγὼν ἀνακλαῖ"</note> that is, 
"And when Hercules himself had need of a friend, Theseus, having led him to Athens, restored him." 
Hence, whenever some deed is celebrated under another's name, which was nevertheless 
performed by the work of another—as if someone should publish a book in his own name in which there is the 
help of a more learned man—it will be aptly noted by this adage: <term>Not without Theseus</term>, that is, 
as if one were to say, no fortune could be pleasant to him <term>without Theseus</term>.

### XXVIII. A sphere down a precipice.

This proverb is referred to by Eustathius in his commentary on the second book of Homer's *Iliad*: 
<margin>The sphere headlong. <note>original: "ἡ σφαῖρα κατὰ πρανῶς"</note></margin> that is, a globe down a slope; "it rolls" or "it is sent" must be understood. It is just 
as if you were to say "to urge on one who is already running." For a sphere, even of its own accord, easily rolls down a sloping place. 
Nor will it poorly fit those who have found a kind of life toward which they seem 
naturally inclined, so that it agrees with that other saying: <term>A horse into the plain</term> <note>original: "ἐφ’ ἵππου εἰς πεδίον"</note>, that is, sending a horse onto flat ground.

Horace in his *Odes*: 
> [Who could give] even to fishes

<unclear>against</unclear> the unlearned: "Nay, you are more voiceless than the fishes." 
<unclear>Again</unclear> in *The Cock*: "I shall be much more mute than the fishes." 
<unclear>Whence</unclear> Plutarch in his *Symposiacs* thinks the Pythagoreans abstained from fishes 
<unclear>as if</unclear> recognizing them as members of their own discipline, on account of <term>silence</term> <note>original: "ἐχεμυθία"</note>, that is, the restraint of speech, 
<unclear>which</unclear> among the kinds of living creatures is peculiar to fishes. For of the others, each has its own voice. 
<unclear>Birds</unclear> are very many and tuneful; some even repeat human speech. And even of the terrestrial

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

the manticore among the Egyptians, if we believe Pliny. Fish alone have no voice. Aristotle provides the reason: they have neither lungs, nor windpipe, nor throat. Even so, there are some that emit a certain sound and squeak; among these are the dolphin, the lyre-fish, the chromis, the voga (which appears to be named from this, because it emits a voice: Athenaeus in book 7 records it was sacred to Mercury), and the scallop. But he thinks that sound is not emitted by natural vocal organs, but either by the rubbing of the gills or from internal parts around the belly. Plutarch thinks that the Greeks call a fish <term>ichthyn</term> <note>original: ἰχθὺν</note> for this reason: because it has its voice "compressed." And Lucian in *Halcyon* says, <term>for those things that live in the water are indeed voiceless</term> <note>original: ἄφωνος γὰρ δὴ τάγε καθ' ὕδατος διαιτώμενα</note>. Athenaeus, in the eighth book of the *Deipnosophists*, cites the author Mnaseas of Patrae, who recorded that in the river Clitor in Arcadia, the fish are vocal. Likewise Philostephanus, who wrote that in the river Aornus, which flows through the city of Pheneus, the fish called <term>poikilois</term> <note>original: ποικίλοις; meaning "spotted" or "variegated"</note> have a voice almost like that of thrushes. Although Aristotle denies a voice to all fish, except for the scaphros and the river-hog. The ancients, however, used to call any fish <term>ellopa</term> <note>original: ἔλλοπα</note> because it could not emit a voice; for <term>elleisthai</term> <note>original: ἐλλεῖσθαι</note> means to be restrained from <term>tes opos</term> <note>original: τῆς ὀπός</note>, that is, the voice <note>original: ὄψ</note>. Hence in Theocritus, <term>ellopieuein</term> <note>original: ἐλλοπιεύειν</note> is used for "to fish." Athenaeus adds that the Pythagoreans did not entirely abstain from other living creatures, but ate some of them and even sacrificed some; they only refused to taste fish, as if they were sacred on account of the <term>echemythia</term> <note>original: ἐχεμυθίαν; the vow of silence</note> which Pythagoras taught.

### More talkative than a turtle-dove.
-> XXX <-

<term>More talkative than a turtle-dove</term> <note>original: Τρυγόνος λαλίστερος</note>. This was usually said of talkative people and those who are excessively wordy. The metaphor is taken from the nature of the bird, which is said to cry out not only with its mouth but also with the rear part of its body—I suppose because when it emits its voice, it also seems to move that part. It is cited in Zenodotus from the *Plotium* of Menander. Aelian, in book 12, chapter 10, mentions this proverb and the bird that is talkative from both parts of its body. Theocritus, in the *Syracusans*, calls certain talkative women "turtle-doves":
> <term>The turtle-doves will wear us out, broad-voweled in everything they say.</term> <note>original: Τρυγόνες ἐκναισεῦντι πλατιάσδοισαι ἅπαντα.</note>

### A frog from Seriphos.
-> XXXI <-

<term>A frog from Seriphos</term> <note>original: Βάτραχος ἐκ σερίφου</note>. This was said of silent men, and those entirely unskilled in singing or speaking. It arose from the fact that frogs from Seriphos, when transported to Scyros, did not emit a voice. In this manner, the collections of Greek proverbs excerpted from the books of Didymus, Tarrhaeus, and others record it. Suidas says the same in so many words. And <term>A Seriphian frog</term> <note>original: Βάτραχος σερίφιος</note>: for it is recorded that on the island of Seriphos, the frogs are considered mute. Pliny mentions this in book 8, chapter 58: "At Cyrene," he says, "the frogs were mute; when vocal ones were brought in from the continent, their kind persisted. They are still mute on the island of Seriphos. These same frogs sing when moved elsewhere, which they say also happens in the lake Sicendus in Thessaly." Although in common copies there is mention of Seriphian cicadas, not frogs; but Hermolaus restored the genuine reading based on the authority of ancient manuscripts. Seriphos is one of the islands the Greeks call the <term>Sporades</term> <note>original: σποράδας; "the scattered ones"</note>. However, Pliny's words do not seem to agree entirely with the Greek commentaries. For he says they are mute in Seriphos, while the Greeks say they fail to emit a voice when transported to Scyros—as if they were vocal in Seriphos but became mute in Scyros. But to one looking more closely at the matter, there is nothing absurd. Seriphos had mute frogs. They transported them to Scyros as a marvelous thing; when the people of Scyros marveled that they were mute, contrary to the nature of their native frogs, they said: "A frog from Seriphos." That expression passed into a proverb.

### Others do the sowing, others will reap.
-> XXXII <-

<term>Some indeed sow, but others in turn will reap</term> <note>original: Ἄλλοι μὲν σπείρουσιν, ἄλλοι δ' αὖ ἀμήσονται</note>. Without the metaphor, they also express it this way: <term>Others labored, others received the profit</term> <note>original: ἄλλοι κάμον, ἄλλοι ὤναντο</note>. Very similar to these is that saying of Fabius in Livy, in the tenth book *From the Founding of the City*: "That it was unworthy to say that under the tree he had planted, another should gather the fruit." Hesiod alludes to this when he writes in the *Theogony* about drones:
> <term>They reap the toil of others into their own bellies.</term> <note>original: Ἀλλότριον κάματον σφετέρην ἐς γαστέρ' ἀμῶνται.</note>
> That is: And they reap into their own stomach the sweat of another.

Likewise Theognis,
> <term>Lest you hand over your exhausted labors to another.</term> <note>original: Οὔτε γὰρ ἂν πεκάμων, ἄλλω κάματον μεταδοίης.</note>

With a similar figure, it was said by Diocletian before he was Caesar: "I kill the boars, but another enjoys the feast."

# FIFTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>P</sig>

...the choice meat. This refers to a story from the life of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor, r. 284–305 AD</note> to roughly this effect: While he was still serving in minor posts among the Tungri in Gaul, he was staying at a certain inn and became well-acquainted with a certain Druidess. When she scolded him for being stingy, he is said to have replied in jest, not seriously, that he would be generous once he became Emperor. To this she replied: "Do not joke, Diocletian; you will indeed be Emperor when you have killed the Boar." <note>original: "si Aprum occideris." A pun on the name 'Aper' (Boar).</note> Taking this woman's word as an omen, he began to hunt boars with great zeal, clearly not understanding the riddle of the omen, which the outcome later revealed. For when the Emperor Numerianus had been killed by the faction of his father-in-law, Arrius Aper, and the crime was discovered, the soldiers appointed Diocletian as the avenger and hailed him as Augustus. Therefore, in an assembly, so that he might fulfill the Druidess's saying, he stabbed Aper with his own hand, adding that famous line:
**"You fall by the right hand of the great [Diocletian]."** <note>original: "magni dextra cadis." A parody of Aeneid 10.830.</note>
Meanwhile, because he had killed many boars while still a private citizen without the imperial light ever shining upon him, they say he used to say: "I kill the boars, but another enjoys the meat."

### You throw what belongs to another. XXXIII
<margin>"You throw what belongs to another" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλότρια βάλεις</note></margin> This is used whenever a matter does not turn out according to one's desire. It is a metaphor from those who play at dice, who, when throwing, sometimes have results fall that are not at all suited to their strategy. Therefore, if ever hope frustrates us, we are rightly said to "throw what belongs to another." The adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

### Shake another oak tree. XXXIIII
<margin>"Shake another oak tree" <note>original Greek: Ἄλλην δρῦν βαλάνιζε</note></margin> This applies to those who ask for something without success, or who continually ask for a loan from the same person. We may use this adage against them so that, leaving us alone, they might trouble the ears of others with their prayers. The proverb arose from the fact that mortals once lived on acorns before the use of Ceres' grain <note>i.e., bread/agriculture</note> was discovered. Those who gathered these acorns after they were shaken down, being hired for that purpose, were called *balanistae*, that is, acorn-gatherers. If they were ever looking around to see if any acorns remained in the tree, passers-by would shout in jest: "Shake another oak!" The common people seized upon this cry and turned it into a proverb. It is quite elegantly applied to a business that should be abandoned because no more profit can be taken from it; or to a friend who has ceased to be useful; or to a teacher who should be changed because there is nothing more to learn from him.

### To leave the nuts behind. XXXV
To leave the nuts behind means to set aside childish studies and trifles and turn toward more serious and grave matters. As in the verse:
<margin>"Whatever we do, having left our games, we play at being uncles." <note>A reference to Persius, Satire 1, meaning to act with the severity of an elder.</note></margin>
The metaphor comes either from the ancient ceremony of weddings, in which the groom, leading his wife home, would scatter nuts to signify he was now renouncing childhood. Thus Catullus in his wedding poem:
> Give the nuts quickly:
> Let him give the nuts.
> Husband, give the nuts.

->Virgil, Eclogue 8.<-

Furthermore, Pliny in Book 15, Chapter 22, offers other reasons why nuts were traditionally used in wedding ceremonies in antiquity. But it is better to quote his words: "Walnuts," he says, "although they too are part of the Fescennine wedding songs, are much smaller than pine nuts in total size, but larger in the proportion of their kernel. Nature has granted them a special honor, being protected by a double covering: first a cushioned husk and then a woody shell. This is the reason they were made sacred for weddings, being fruitful in so many ways—or, what is more likely, because when they fall they make a rattling or dancing sound." Festus likewise says that nuts were usually scattered by boys at weddings so that it might be a good omen for the new bride entering the house of her new husband. Servius adds that favorite boys, when they left their shameful service, would scatter nuts, signifying that they would henceforth despise all childish things. From this, therefore, the proverb can be seen as derived from the games of children which are played with nuts. That boys once played with pebbles and nuts is testified by Horace when he says:
<margin>"Aulus and his nuts."</margin>

<summary>Erasmus explains the origins of three adages: one concerning Diocletian's rise to power through a pun on "Boar," another on moving on from exhausted resources ("Shake another oak"), and a third on maturing into adulthood ("Leaving the nuts").</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Therefore, following this proverbial form, those other figures of speech will also belong here: *Never to leave the nuts.* *To return to the nuts.* *To throw away the nuts.* *To leave off the nuts.* *To indulge in nuts.* *To seek the nuts again,* and others of that kind. <note>original: "à nucibus recedere... Redire ad nuces." These phrases all refer to the transition between childhood and adulthood, as nuts were common toys for Roman children.</note>

<margin>36</margin>
## Old men are twice children.

*Old men are twice children* <note>original Greek: Δὶς παῖδες οἱ γέροντες</note>, that is, *Old men are twice boys.* This is one of those proverbial titles of the satires of Varro. It will apply to those who, although they are of advanced age, are nevertheless detained by certain boyish pursuits at an unseasonable time and in an unseemly manner. Or to old men who are losing their wits through the defect of age, as if they had rolled back into childhood a second time. Seneca says: "We are not," he says, "twice children, as is commonly said, but always; but the difference is this, that we play at greater things." Plato in the first book of *The Republic*: "It seems then that not only an old man might become a child twice, but also a drunken man." Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
> You will say that you think that deed belongs to a child,
> But I myself would answer back, that old men are twice children.

<margin>Sophocles in Peleus:</margin>
> I alone, the housekeeper, guide and re-educate
> Peleus, the son of Aeacus, an old man, in place of a boy;
> For a man growing old is turned back into a child once again.

Theopompus: "It is rightly said that old men are twice children." Plato: "It seems that an old man might become a child twice." Antiphon: "Nurturing an old man is just like nurses nurturing a child." Lucian in the dialogue titled *Things Relating to Saturn*: "For thus I might fulfill the proverb, as they say, that old men become children again." To this pertains what Varro writes in the third book *On the Latin Language*, that repeatedly in the Atellan farces <note>A type of early Roman masked comedy</note> there is a character called the "old boy," which the Oscans <note>An ancient people of Southern Italy</note> call *casnar* in their own language. For the ancients used to call a boy a *pupus*. Nor indeed was the proverb said only because old men lose their wits by the fault of age: but also because in two ways, when life is already as if spent, the beginning seems to return in old men, as Aristotle skillfully said in a certain *Problem*, in which he asks in what way those things which are called "prior" and "posterior" are to be understood. For first, both whiteness and thinness of the hair return, both of which are familiar to children; then stammering, like a second infancy. Furthermore, the gums are disarmed of teeth, or certainly furnished with very few, and those wobbling, which is itself common with infants. Moreover, the whole body of old men shrinks to a boyish measure: there is a similar weakness of strength. Now indeed, similar foods also suit both ages. Finally, the silliness of manners, the levity of mind, and this very thing—to know nothing—seems to represent a certain infancy in old men. For Aristotle is the authority in the *Politics* that after forty-eight years the vigor of the mind vanishes. Wherefore Euripides says in the *Bacchae*:
> I see your old age is lacking in mind.
Which is why it happens that old men are wonderfully delighted by children, as if those who are now similar are inclined toward the love of their likes.

<margin>37</margin>
## To throw sixty-year-olds off the bridge.

*To throw sixty-year-olds off the bridge* is to cast the elders into leisure and to banish them from every function of business, just as if they were delirious and useless for every duty of life. It arose from the fact that formerly sixty-year-olds did not have the right of casting votes, their age having been dismissed, as it were, from public duties. Or because formerly the Roman youth, so that they alone might cast votes, threw the weak old men headlong from the bridges. For votes had already begun to be cast from a bridge; and that opinion is more approved by Sisinnius Capito in Festus Pompeius than that common one by which they think that after the city was liberated from the Gauls, because of a lack of food, sixty-year-olds began to be thrown from the bridge into the Tiber. Varro, in the second book *On the Life of the Fathers*, reveals an honorable and religious cause: when they had reached the fifth stage of life, and were fifty years old,

...and they were free from public business, unencumbered, and at leisure. Therefore, they think it passed into a proverb: **That sixty-year-olds ought to be thrown from the bridge**; because the vote was cast while crossing a bridge <note>The *pons suffragiorum*, a narrow walkway used by voters in Roman elections</note>. Nonius Marcellus understood that "sending sixty-year-olds across the bridge" was a common way of speaking. Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*: "To those men, the right of voting in the assembly of words, and as if to throw the sixty-year-olds from the bridge." Ovid says in the *Fasti*:

"Depontani" <note>literally "off-the-bridgers"</note> is the name given to old men, now as if retired from service and sent from civil business into leisure. Plato, in the sixth book of *The Laws*, speaking of the magistracy of the <term>nomophylakes</term> <note>original: τῶν νομοφυλάκων — "guardians of the laws"</note>, does not admit anyone younger than fifty to hold that office, nor does he allow anyone older than seventy to remain in it: so that if one enters the office at fifty, he may administer it for twenty years; but if at sixty, for ten. It will be permitted to use the proverb either in hatred of old age, as if someone is no longer useful for anything and should be banished from the duties of life; or simply regarding those who, because of the frailty of age, have been granted a discharge and have received a vacation from their usual duties.

### XXXVIII
->Twice-served cabbage is death.<-

<margin>
"Twice cabbage is death," that is, **Cabbage served twice is death.**
<note>original: δὶς κράμβη θάνατος</note>
</margin>
Pliny, in his twentieth book, chapter nine, records cabbage in the third place among the species of <insert>medical</insert> plants. Dioscorides, in his second book, makes <unclear>three</unclear> species of cabbage. The first of these, besides being effective for many remedies, removes the discomforts of drunkenness and hangovers if you eat it raw with vinegar before dinner, as Marcus Cato suggests. Aristotle thinks the cause is that, since the plant itself is cold and has a sweet and dispersing juice, it causes the wine-soaked humors to be drawn down into the bowels, while the thin humors slip away, and the plant itself remaining in the stomach cools the body. And so, with the vapors drawn away from both sides and the body cooled, the hangover ceases. Indeed, there is a certain power in cabbage to resist wine, so much so that if it is planted in a vineyard, the wine produced is diluted. Consequently, among the Egyptians and the Sybarites, it was a solemn custom to take cabbage before all else; some even had the custom of taking cabbage seed in an amethyst vessel before a drinking party, so that they might indulge in wine without the danger of drunkenness. This is roughly what <unclear>Athenaeus</unclear> says in his first book, adding that the ancients held cabbage and radish to be the same. Theophrastus recorded that even a living vine flees the smell of a radish. But to return to the proverb, Suidas writes that it was anciently used at banquets, but when twice-cooked it brought such nausea that it passed into a proverb among the Greeks for loathing. Whenever they wished to signify something repeated again and again, not without annoyance, they would say, **"Twice cabbage is death"**; that is, "twice-boiled cabbage." Politian thinks Juvenal alluded to this adage when he writes in his seventh Satire:
> Why do you teach, O iron-hearted Vectius,
> While a crowded class kills cruel tyrants?
> Whatever they just read sitting down, these same things standing up
> He will endure, and sing the same things in the same verses,
> **Repeated cabbage kills the wretched teachers.**

He calls a declamation "repeated cabbage" when it is repeated again and again with the greatest boredom. Neighboring to this is what we mentioned in another place, **"Corinth, son of Zeus,"** <note>original: ὁ Διὸς κόρινθος — a proverb for annoying repetition</note>. The opposite of it is, **"Twice or thrice that which is beautiful,"** <note>original: δὶς ἢ τρὶς τὸ καλὸν</note>. For that which is excellent in itself, even if repeated ten times, as Horace says, will please; but that which is inept, though it may be tolerated at the first taste by the recommendation of novelty, once it is repeated, it brings an unbearable loathing. And yet this herb was quite <unclear>honored</unclear> by the ancients, so much so that it did not lack religious significance, and for this reason was called "the prophet" <note>original: μάντις</note>; it was the custom to swear by it, especially among the Ionians, **"No, by the cabbage!"** <note>original: νὰ μὰ τὴν κράμβην</note>, so that from this too the proverb of loathing might seem to have arisen. The author is Athenaeus in the ninth book of the *Deipnosophistae*.

The proverb can also be turned into a more elevated form, in this manner: "If they say that even Hercules is not a match against two, how shall I, who am so weak, stand against two Herculeses?" Although we briefly showed the use of this proverb in the entrance <note>original: "vestibulo"</note> of this work. Plato in the eleventh book of *The Laws*: <note>original Greek: ὀρθὸν μὲν δὴ... "It is a true saying, and one long ago celebrated as a proverb, that it is hard to fight against two things that are contrary, just as it is in diseases and many other matters."</note> It signifies to us that there is a double fight, both against riches and against poverty. He used the same in the *Phaedo*: where, to Socrates jokingly urging him to refute Cebes and Simmias with argument, Phaedo responds: <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ πρὸς δύο... "But indeed, against two, not even Hercules is said to have been sufficient."</note> Catullus alluded to the same in his *Marriage Poem*, when he said:

->Do not fight against two.<-

This sentiment, although not in the same words, is read several times in Homer, as in the *Odyssey*, book 13 <note>original: "ν"</note>:
<note>original Greek: Χαλεπὸν γὰρ... "For it is difficult for one to restrain many."</note>
Telemachus speaks thus of himself and the suitors. Likewise in the *Iliad*, book 5 <note>original: "Ε"</note>:
<note>original Greek: Αἰνείας δ’ οὐ λάθε... "Aeneas, otherwise a strenuous warrior, did not stand still as soon as he saw two men standing joined together."</note>

They tell the occasion of the adage in various ways. Some say the Molionidae once attacked Hercules from ambush; and he, terrified by the multitude of men, did not dare to resist, but consulted his safety by flight, and that this passed into common speech. But it is more likely what Suidas reports: that Hercules, having established the Olympic contest and relying on his strength, first dared to contend with two, and finished them both. These they say were Cteatus and Eurytus, born of Neptune as father and Molione as mother. Then, in the next Olympiad, he engaged in a similar way with two others, and was overcome by them. Although there are those who think these were Laeus and Pherandrus—but those who conquered Hercules, not those who departed conquered. But Plato in the *Euthydemus* brings forward a history far different from these: namely, that Hercules, having engaged with the Hydra and likewise with a certain huge crab that had emerged from the sea, came off inferior, and because of this implored the help of his nephew Iolaus. But I shall not be burdened to transcribe his very words. In that dialogue, therefore, which I mentioned, Socrates, disputing with two sophist brothers—and as they are, insulting ones—as if one man engaged with two monsters, when Dionysodorus reproached him for fleeing and not responding to questions, he answered in this way: <note>original Greek: Εἰκότως γὰρ εἶπεν... "Not without justice, I said, do I flee. For since I am unequal to either one of you, why should I not flee both? Indeed, I am much weaker than Hercules, who nevertheless was not able to fight equally against both the Hydra—a sophist who, because of her wisdom, if one head of the argument were cut off, many sprouted back in place of the one—and against a certain crab, another sophist come from the sea, and recently, as I think, arrived. By whom when Hercules was distressed on the left, and sharply bitten by words, he implored the help of his nephew Iolaus, who abundantly succored him. But if my Iolaus, Patrocles, should come, he would rather take up the other part of the contest."</note> With a biting allegory, clearly, Socrates calls one of the sophist brothers a Hydra, the other a crab, and himself Hercules; and Ctesippus, he calls Iolaus.
