# FIFTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
## P 3
<margin><note>original: "εἷς ἀνὴρ οὐ πάνθ' ὁρᾷ"</note> One man does not see all things.</margin>
**One man does not see all things.** <note>Erasmus begins with a Greek proverb about the limitations of individual perspective.</note> This proverb can be applied to various situations: to an unpleasant life if a companionable friend is not present; or to a business that should by no means be entrusted to a single person; or to the study of literature, which, without a rival of the same Muse (as they say), clearly grows cold; or finally to any difficult task that cannot be conveniently finished without the help of another. Zenodotus <note>An ancient Greek grammarian and literary critic.</note> makes mention of this.

---

<margin>An ass among apes.</margin>
<margin><note>original: "ὄνων ἐν πιθήκοις"</note> The saying: an ass among apes.</margin>
### An ass among apes. XLI

This is used when someone who is dull-witted falls among people who are sharp-nosed <note>meaning "sarcastic" or "mocking"</note> and fond of joking, by whom he is laughed at with impunity. It appears in Aulus Gellius, Book 2, Chapter 23, where the comic poet Menander, in the play titled *Plotius*, introduces a man complaining about an injury from his wife with these words: <unclear>mon</unclear>, that is, **"An ass among apes, as the common saying goes."** It is well known that the ape is a most impudent animal, so much so that it does not fear even the lion, playfully attaching itself to his back. Indeed, even today people commonly say something similar: **"An owl among the birds,"** when someone rather stupid falls among aggressive and witty people. However, nothing prevents it from being used more generally when someone falls into a violently troublesome business or into some misfortune from which he cannot extricate himself.

<margin><note>original: "ἀν' ὄνοι"</note> An ass among bees.</margin>
### An ass among bees. XLII

This has a similar meaning to the previous one; it is said when someone unluckily falls among wicked and troublesome people. It is a metaphor, although the adage seems to have been born from some specific event. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia/lexicon.</note> mentions it.

<margin><note>original: "ὄνων"</note> An ass in ointment.</margin>
### An ass in ointment. XLIII

This is used when luxuries are offered to those who are by no means suited to them, or who neither know how to use them nor take pleasure in them. For an ass prefers stalks and hay to ointment, by which it is even offended. There would be a place for this adage if ever an unlearned person falls upon the best authors, whom he either neglects or even corrupts out of ignorance; or if it happens that some servant lives with most learned men, whose conversation he neither knows how to enjoy nor takes any pleasure in at all. The proverb is recorded by Diogenianus.

<margin><note>original: "οὔτε οὐρανῷ ἅπτεται"</note> It touches neither heaven nor earth.</margin>
### It touches neither heaven nor earth. XLIIII

This is said of a violently absurd or vain thing, which has no proximity or relevance to the matter being discussed. Lucian in *The False Prophet*: "He sent me eight oracles which, as they say, **touched neither heaven nor earth.**" Aristides, in his work on Cimon, lightly alluding to the proverb, indicates the metaphor is taken from those who hang in mid-air, free from both sides.

<margin><note>original: "οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος"</note> Nothing to the song.</margin>
<margin>Nothing to the song.</margin>
<margin>Song/Verse</margin>
### Nothing to the verse. XLV

This is said of those things which differ widely from what was proposed. It seems to be transferred from the stage, where an actor represents the type of song through dancing and gesture. I do not know whether there was one person to recite the verses and another to perform the gestures. For it appears there was a specific reciter, whose voice is that at the end of the Comedies: "Calliopius recited." Otherwise, I see what Cicero's warning pertains to: that an actor should choose a play to which he is naturally suited. Also, in the prologue of a play by Terence, the prologue-speaker complains that "noisy" plays are brought to him, and less laborious ones to others. But if the dance did not correspond to the rhythms of the song, they would say: <note>original: "οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος"</note> **"Nothing to the song."** Lucian in *The Parasite*: "See how these things are 'nothing to the song,' as they say, for I was not asking about those things." Those who did not respond to the rhythm in dances were called "clumsy-footed." 

Andreas Alciatus <note>A famous Italian jurist and friend of Erasmus.</note>—the glory of Imperial Law in this century and indeed of all studies, no less to be looked up to for his incredible brilliance of mind than for his exact skill in all liberal disciplines—in the second book of his *Dispunctiones*, agrees with me on the meaning and use of the proverb. However, he differs somewhat on the origin; he prefers it to have been born from oracles, which were once delivered in verse, especially heroic verse, of which Pythian Apollo was the inventor. To the Greeks, a verse is called <term>epos</term> because "things follow" <note>original: "epontai"</note> the oracles. Eustathius brings this etymology in the beginning of Homer's *Iliad*. From this, our friend Alciatus argues that the phrase was used whenever things did not match what was promised or proposed.

<summary>Erasmus explains several Greek and Latin proverbs concerning social mismatching (the "ass among apes"), irrelevance ("neither heaven nor earth"), and artistic or logical inconsistency ("nothing to the song"). He cites various classical authorities and his contemporary, the jurist Andreas Alciatus.</summary>
<keywords>proverbs, adages, social satire, classical literature, Menander, Lucian, Alciatus, philology, metaphors</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...it was customary to say, **Nothing to the verse** <note>original: οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος</note>. Ulpian used this in the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, Book 11, Title on interrogatory actions, chapter 12. Regarding what the praetor says about "not having responded at all," later commentators took it to mean that he who does not respond to the specific questions asked is seen as not having responded at all—that is, **nothing to the verse**. Suidas indicates that **nothing to the verse** is sometimes used to mean "rashly" or "about nothing," or "beside the point." He cites these verses from some poet or other:

*I will not utter "nothing to the verse" so reasonably,*
*Until I have learned how the whole matter stands.*

The first Greek verse will be consistent if you read it as "so rashly" <note>original: προΰτως</note>. Aristophanes used the same in *The Assemblywomen*, a passage we referred to under the proverb "Outside the song."

->### Nothing to the strings. XLVI<-

**Nothing to the strings** <note>original: Οὐδὲν πρὸς τὴν χορδήν</note>. This is said of those whose lives are wildly inconsistent, or whose character is at odds with their speech. Lucian, in *On the Dance*: "And nothing, as they say, to the strings; for the foot says one thing, and the rhythm another." The same author in *Dialogues of the Courtesans*: "And because the foot responded properly to the cithara <note>A lyre-like stringed instrument</note>." Plutarch, in his essay *On Shyness*: "And yet, it is not because of a lack of harmony with the lyre—as Plato used to say—that great blame arises, and friends are divided against friends, doing and suffering the worst things; but rather because of a discord regarding laws and justice." The passage Plutarch cites is in the seventh book of *The Laws*: "rendering the voices in accord with the notes of the lyre. But the dissonance and variety of the lyre, when the strings emit certain melodies while the poet has composed a different melody, and so forth." Saint Augustine seems to have alluded to this proverb in a certain letter to Licentius: "Or if I sing," he says, "but you dance to another tune, I do not even then regret it. For the singing itself has its own joy in its melody, even when the one for whom it is sung with a modulation full of charity does not move his limbs to it."

->### The ant is a camel. XLVII<-

**The ant is a camel** <note>original: Μύρμηξ ἡ κάμηλος</note>. Said of things that are wildly unequal, or of someone who is now very small and now very great; as if a camel were suddenly turned into an ant. Lucian in the first letter of the *Saturnalia*: "For as we live now, the ant is a camel, as the proverb says." He is speaking of wealth being unequally distributed among mortals, so that one has a vast surplus while another lacks much. Nor will it be unseasonably said of those who are inconsistent with themselves, being immoderate in either direction. Euripides describes this kind of person in *The Trojan Women*:

*Why do you leap thus, now into these ways, now into those?*
*You hate too much, and you love whomever you happen upon.*

->### To smear the face. XLVIII<-

**To smear the face** <note>original: Os sublinere</note>, used for "to give words" <note>to deceive</note> and to mock with a certain art, is found several times among authors. Nonius Marcellus thinks it is derived from a ridiculous kind of game in which the faces of those sleeping are painted. Plautus in *The Pot of Gold*: "I thought Faith was of the greatest faith. She has smeared my face most foully" <note>meaning: she has cheated me</note>. The same author elsewhere: "My face has been properly smeared." Again in *Epidicus*: "If I had assigned someone to this business who was less a man than a scholar, and less clever at the matter, my face would have been smeared." Marcus Varro in *The Mysteries*, cited in Nonius: "That you defrauded the innkeeper, and smeared the good man with mud, when the toll-collectors brought in the brass." Sophocles in *Antigone*:

*These men also see it, but they smear their mouths for you.* <note>i.e., they keep silent or flatter you to your face while hiding the truth</note>

Virgil likewise, in a *Bucolic* poem, introduces boys playing a prank, smearing the face of Silenus with the juice of mulberries:

*And now, as he opens his eyes,*
*She paints his forehead and temples with blood-red mulberries.*

Erasmus draws on a wide array of classical sources, from Roman law and comedy to Greek tragedy and Patristic letters.</summary>

# FIFTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>P 4</sig>

<margin>Smiling at the ground, he says, "Where are you weaving these chains?" <note>original: "Solum ridens, Quò uincula nectitis? inquit." A poetic image of someone laughing at futile efforts to restrain them.</note></margin>

### To give words.
->XLIX<-

<margin>"To give words" is commonly found among all authors to mean "to deceive." Persius in his 5th Satire:</margin>
> As you prefer, give words <note>deceive</note>, and cheat your own nerves. &emsp; Terence:
<margin>It is difficult to give words.</margin>
> Ovid:
<margin>Every lover gives those <note>words</note>.</margin>
The same author elegantly applied this to deceiving the cares of the mind:
> So that I might cheat my mind with studies and labors:
> Rising above my cares and giving words to them.

Examples of this are so frequent and well-explained that it is hardly worth the effort to pursue them further. I would only advise that a certain charm is added to the proverb if it is twisted further away from simple speech—namely, toward a fraud or imposture that is carried out even without the deception of words. An example of this kind would be if someone said that this world "gives words" to its worshippers, or that the "alchemical art," as they call it, "gives words" to those devoted to it; or that he "gives words to himself" who promises himself things that are by no means to be hoped for.

### To add a hand.
->L<-

<margin>No less common is the expression found in Plautus’s *The Persian*: "To add a hand," meaning to make a fool of someone. I believe it is derived from those who laugh at someone by holding their hand up to their ear and moving it. Plautus’s words are these: "What do you say, you gallows-bird, you wearer-out of whips? How have you thrown me, the clever one, into such a mess today? How has a hand been added to me by the Persian?" Likewise in *The Little Carthaginian*: "In what a fine way I added a hand to greedy Venus." Again in the same scene: "I will see to it that the gods and other goddesses are more content and less greedy when they know the pimp added a hand to you, Venus." The same in *The Pot of Gold*: "Thus I added a hand to all those filthy men." Also in *Casina*: "Wasn't a hand added to us quite charmingly and deservedly?" Although I find it written variously, sometimes "I added" <note>original: "adj" or "addidi"</note> and sometimes "was added" <note>original: "addita"</note>. It seems more correct to me to read "I added," so that we take the metaphor from the gesture of those mocking, as I mentioned, which Persius recalls:</margin>
> Nor did the mobile hand imitate white ears. <note>A gesture mimicking donkey ears to mock someone's stupidity.</note>

### To shear the hair all around.
->LI<-

<margin>"To shear the locks all around" <note>original Greek: περικείρειν τοὺς πλοκάμους</note>, that is, to cut the hair in a circle, is a proverb among the Greeks for holding someone up to ridicule. For this is usually done as a joke to stupid people, so that their hair is shorn off without them noticing. Lucian in *The Misanthrope*: "You sat there while your locks were being shorn all around by them." He uses the same in *The False Prophet*.</margin>

### To make a dye.
->LII<-

<margin>"To make a dye" <note>original: "Fucum facere"</note>, meaning to commit an imposture and to delude with skillful dissimulation, is frequent among good authors. Terence in *The Eunuch*: "To have come secretly through someone else's roof-tiles, and a dye was made for the woman" <note>meaning she was deceived</note>. In this passage, "made" is a supine, not a participle. Indeed, another writer says to Cicero: "If you sense that he who promised you wishes to 'make a dye,' as they say, pretend as if you have heard and know nothing." For *fucus* is a type of seaweed, which the Greeks call *phykos*, useful for dyeing wool. Hence one may find *fucus* used simply for "color," and *fucare* for "to color." Horace in the *Odes*:</margin>
> Nor dyed with crocodile dung.
<margin>The same is true if we signify a color that is not natural or genuine, but artificial and, as it were, adulterated, as the same Horace says:</margin>
> Nor does the wool, treated with dye, recover its lost colors.
<margin>From this, they call that medicament "dye" <note>fucus</note> with which women, by applying it to their skin, hide the flaws of their beauty and, as it were, put on a mask. Plautus: "They hide the flaws of the body with dye." Just as dye is a color added by art, so a "Mask" <note>original: "Persona"</note> is a face that is not true, but applied. Whence it was elegantly said by Seneca: "That he prefers a mask to a face," that is, he prefers to seem rather than to be. Likewise Lucretius in his third book:</margin>
> For only then are true voices drawn from the bottom of the heart; the mask is ripped away, the reality remains.
<margin>Cornelius Tacitus in the *Dialogue on Orators*: "Thus a teacher was not lacking, indeed the best and most learned, who presented the face of eloquence, not a mere image." Therefore we call those "Masked" <note>original: "Personatos"</note> who project themselves as something other than what they are. Indeed, they also call them "Deceptions" <note>original: "Offucias"</note>, certain empty imitations of things—</margin>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...beautiful things, which as if by some trickery, deceive the eyes of those looking on. The Greeks call this kind of deception by the simple word *phenakizein* <note>original: φενακίζειν; to cheat or deceive</note>, and the deception itself *phenakismos*, and the craftsman of such dyes a *phenax*. The author of the Greek Etymological dictionary, an unreliable and impure source, thinks the word is derived from *plokamous* <note>original: πλοκάμους</note>, which is what the Greeks call false hair. The Latins call it a *galericulum* <note>a small wig or cap</note>. Furthermore, Julian used the word "color" to mean a deceptive dye, as cited by Ulpian in the fourteenth book of the *Pandects* <note>A compendium of Roman law</note>, Title on the Macedonian Decree of the Senate, chapter 9. But Julian, he says, adds: "if a 'color' [pretense] was sought," such as if a son of the family who was about to receive a loan of money should act as a guarantor. Moreover, rhetoricians call the plausible reasoning they devise for a defense a "color." Juvenal says: "Tell us some 'color,' tell us, Quintilian." And when a top rhetorician was stuck, a wife caught in the act defended herself with a most impudent "color": "It was once agreed 
> That you should do what you wanted, and that I too could 
> Indulge myself." <note>Juvenal, Satire 6</note>

## To add a white pebble, and similar figures.

"To place a white pebble" <note>original: Λευκὴν ψῆφον τιθέναι</note>, that is, *To add a white pebble*, we frequently read among the learned as a term for "to approve." It is taken from the fact that in ancient times, when pebbles were cast into an urn, the sentences of the judges were delivered such that they acquitted with white ones and condemned with black ones. If by some chance the numbers were equal, the accused was nevertheless set free; Aristotle gives the reason for this most copiously in his *Problems*. Ovid mentions the custom of pebbles in the 15th book of the *Metamorphoses*:
> It was the ancient custom, with snowy and black stones,
> To condemn the guilty with these, and clear them of fault with those.
> Then too, the grim sentence was passed in this way, and every
> Black pebble is dropped into the pitiless urn.
> But when the overturned urn poured out the pebbles to be counted,
> The color of them all was changed from black to white.

The younger Pliny says in a certain letter: "For the more I may apply your file <note>meaning: your critical polishing</note>, I will confess that both I myself and my companions do not shrink from publication: if only you perhaps *add a white pebble* to our error." That is, if you approve of this error of ours by your judgment. Lucian in his *Apology* says: "Not with a casual glance would the white pebble be carried from you and from me," that is, "I would value it no small amount if it should happen to me to carry away from you a white and full vote." Plato in the second book of *The Laws*: "I would hardly place this pebble," that is, "I would not grant this approval." To this should be added what Alcibiades said when he was unwilling to entrust himself to the opinions of the judges; he said he would not even trust his mother, but would hold even her suspect in such a danger, lest she should substitute a black pebble for a white one. Aristides, in his *Pericles*, used the simple word *anapsephizein* <note>original: ἀναψηφίζειν</note> for "to approve," and he uses that word as a Platonic term.

## To mark with chalk. To mark with charcoal.

To this same form belong those other sayings: *To mark with chalk*, for that which is to approve, and *To mark with charcoal*, which is to condemn. This is because Pythagoras used to say that whatever was of a bright color belonged to the nature of good, and what was black, to evil. Whence we also call happy things "white" and infamous people "black." Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in his speech for Caecina, says of the witness Sextus Clodius Phormio: "No less black," he says, "and no less confident than that Phormio of Terence." And Horace:
> This man is black; you, Roman, beware of him.

The same author in his *Satires*:
> Whether they are sane, or to be marked with chalk or charcoal.

Persius, imitating him, says in his fifth Satire:
> Those things which were to be followed, and those to be avoided in turn,
> You marked the former first with chalk, the latter soon with charcoal.

Again, Horace in his *Odes*:
> Let not the fair day lack a Cretan mark.

He calls a white pebble a "Cretan mark" <note>original: Cressa nota</note>, with which the ancients were accustomed to mark lucky days. Although there are some who read *Thressa* [Thracian] in this place instead of *Cressa*, because this custom is said to have belonged to the Thracians. To this form also belongs: *To mark with a pearl* <note>original: Unione signare</note>, which is frequent among authors for counting something among happy and prosperous things. It is drawn from the superstition of the ancients, who marked each day of the year by casting pebbles into an urn—or as among the Scythians, into a quiver. The day they thought had passed prosperously, they marked with a white pebble or chalk; one that was exceptionally happy, with a pearl. Conversely, the day they marked as unlucky with a black stone. Persius says:
> Count this day, Macrinus, with a better stone.

Pliny mentions this superstition in book 7, chapter 40: "Vain mortality," he says, "and ingenious at deceiving itself, calculates in the manner of the Thracian na-

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 5
<sig>T 3</sig>

distinctly colored pebbles, placing them in an urn to represent the experience of each day; at the end of the month, he counts the separated piles and thus pronounces judgment on each day. What of the fact that even that famous "praised day" had its origin in evil? Thus far Pliny. Plutarch, in the *Life of Pericles*, <note>original: "in uita Periclis"</note> relates a history not unlike this, which it might not be out of place to transcribe here: *Dividing the whole multitude into eight parts, he assigned them by lot; to the one who drew the white bean, he granted the privilege of feasting and resting while the others fought. Therefore, they say that those who experience a stroke of good fortune call that a "white day," from the white bean.* <note>original Greek: ὀκτὼ μοίρᾳ διελὼν... ἀπὸ τοῦ λευκοῦ κυάμου προσαγορεύειν</note> That is, having divided the entire mass into eight parts, he used lots: and to whomsoever the white bean fell, he permitted them to spend the time in banquets and leisure while the others remained in battle. Wherefore they also say that those for whom things succeed pleasantly call that day "white," surely from the white bean. To this same idea belongs our habit of saying that things of particular excellence are "of a better mark": as when Catullus bids someone be greeted "from a better mark." <note>A metaphor for high-quality wine or distinguished status.</note> Livy, in his first Decade, used "sad mark" <note>original: "triste nota"</note> to mean the opposite: *Posthumius was marked by no sad mark,* that is, he was sprinkled with no infamy of cruelty.

### To pull back the pebble. LV
<note>Calculum reducere</note>

To pull back the pebble is to change a deed of which you repent, or to alter a plan for a matter that was not conveniently established. Nonius cites Cicero in the *Hortensius*: "Therefore I concede to you, as if playing at twelve scripts <note>An ancient board game similar to backgammon</note> long ago, that you may pull back your pebble if you repent of any move made." This is a metaphor taken from those who calculate accounts, or, what is nearer the truth, from the game of "little soldiers" <note>term: ludus latruncularum; a Roman strategy game similar to chess or checkers</note>. In short, all metaphors fashioned from pebbles have a proverbial flavor. For example, "To call to the pebbles" <note>Ad calculos uocare</note> means to enter into an account and estimate value. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the dialogue *On Friendship*: "There are those who call friendship to the pebbles too precisely and meanly, so that the ratio of things given and received is equal." Valerius Maximus in his fourth book, in the chapter on liberty: "If you recall it to the pebbles <note>i.e., judge it by strict accounting</note>, it is small, being reduced to seven acres hidden in Pupinia; but if you judge it by the greatness of spirit, it is greater than all money." Also, "To return to the pebbles" is to return to reason and a consideration of things. Cicero to Atticus: "Wherefore let us now at least return to those pebbles which we once used, so that we may employ not only glorious plans, but also those a little more healthy." And in the letters of Pliny, "To move the pebbles" is used for proposing reasons. And "To place pebbles on both sides" means to weigh the reasons on both sides. And "Let this pebble be added" means let this weight of evidence be joined. Nor does anything prevent one from saying, by the same logic, "To withdraw a pebble" or "To take away a pebble."

### To prefix a Theta. LVI
<note>$\Theta$ præfigere</note>

To prefix a $\Theta$ <note>The Greek letter Theta</note> stands for "to condemn." Persius says:
> <margin>To prefix a Theta means to condemn.</margin>
> <margin>You are skilled at prefixing the black $\Theta$ to vice.</margin>
Ausonius, writing to a gluttonous teacher in Choliambic verse:
> <margin>O teacher, may the cut-out Theta mark your name</margin>
> <margin>with that obscene sign.</margin>
There are those who refer this to the shape of the Greek letter, because it seems to represent the appearance of a pierced human heart. For I do not know if we ought to believe Isidore, who writes in the first book of the *Etymologies* that it was a military custom to mark the slain with a $\Theta$ and the survivors with a $\tau$. Certainly, this sign $\tau$ <note>The letter Tau</note> is mentioned even in the Apocalypse, which is attributed to the name of the blessed John the Evangelist. But it is more likely, as Asconius Pedianus writes, that formerly the lots cast into the urn in trials used to have a triple mark: $\Theta$ as a symbol of condemnation <note>from the Greek 'thanatos', meaning death</note>, $\tau$ for absolution, and $\Lambda$ for "ampliation," <note>term: ampliatio; a legal delay when a verdict was unclear</note> that is, whenever they indicated that the matter was not sufficiently clear and the case ought to be argued anew.

### To mark with stars, to note with an obelus. LVII
<note>Stellis fignare, obelo notare</note>

*To mark with signs, or to judge by the stars.* <note>original Greek: ις σημειῶσαι, ἢ ἄστροις τεκμαίρεσθαι</note> Eustathius, in the fifth book of the *Odyssey*, reminds us that this was said of those who travel a long and deserted way, so that they must mark the position of regions by the observation of the stars. The metaphor is drawn from sailors, who, when they have been carried so far from land that there is "heaven on all sides and sea on all sides," are accustomed to steer their course by the evidence of the stars, especially the Cynosure and the Helice <note>The Little and Great Bear constellations</note>, as Aratus witnesses in the *Phaenomena*:
> *One they call by the name Cynosure,*
> *The other Helice. By Helice the Achaean men*
> *Judge where it is necessary to guide their ships.*

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->On this the Phoenicians rely when they cross the sea.
But while one is clear and easy to distinguish,
appearing large from the very start of the night,
the other is small, yet better for sailors,
for it revolves in a tighter circle;
by this the Sidonians <note>The people of Sidon, famous ancient navigators</note> steer most accurately.<-

I shall add the translation of these verses from the interpretation by Germanicus Caesar <note>original: "Germanici Caesaris interpretatione"; Germanicus was a Roman general and nephew of Tiberius who translated Aratus's astronomical poem.</note>:

->Here the nurses of Jove, Helice and Cynosura <note>The Great and Little Bear constellations</note>, shine.
Helice gives the Greeks their course with her larger stars,
but Cynosura guides the Phoenicians. Yet Helice is bright in her entirety,
and shines with a clear splendor, second to none,
when the sun has hidden its glowing face in the Ocean;
the star which the Cretans call the seven flames flickers in the sky.
Yet Cynosura is more certain for those who furrow the sea,
since, being small, she turns entirely around a faithful axis,
and has never failed the Sidonian ship that watches her.<-

And Ovid, imitating Aratus in the fourth book of his *Tristia* <note>Sorrows</note>:

->The Great and Lesser Beasts, of which you, the one, guide Greek ships,
the other, Sidonian; and both remain dry from the sea.<-

Virgil indicates the same in the fifth book <note>of the Aeneid</note>, speaking of Palinurus:

->Giving such words, he held fast to the tiller, clinging,
never letting go, and kept his eyes fixed beneath the stars.<-

The same author elsewhere:

->He notes all the stars gliding through the silent sky.<-

Similarly Homer, both elsewhere and in the fifth book of the *Odyssey*:

->But he steered the ship skillfully with the rudder,
sitting there, nor did sleep fall upon his eyelids,
as he gazed at the Pleiades and late-setting Bootes,
and the Bear, which they also call by the name of the Wagon,
which turns in its place and watches Orion,
and alone has no share in the baths of the Ocean.<-

That is:

->He indeed, guiding the ship with art, sits clinging to the tiller,
nor does he allow his eyes to grow numb with falling sleep,
watching the Pleiades and Bootes as he slowly hides his face,
and the Bear, known by the other name of the Wagon,
which, fixed in its place, turns itself around the same spot,
and is never splashed by the liquid waves of the Ocean.<-

From this, **to observe the way by the stars** <note>original: "ἀστεροις σκοπεῖσθαι τὴν ὁδὸν"</note> seems to be said of those who, by certain small notes and conjectures grasped through skill, investigate or achieve a matter otherwise difficult to track down; or those who gather from certain signs long in advance what is going to happen. Later the meaning was shifted, so that those who mark something as noteworthy are said to "pre-note" it with stars. The opposite of this is **to mark with an obelisk** <note>original: "ὀβελίζειν"</note>, which is to essentially slit the throat of and condemn a passage by pre-noting it. This was transferred from Aristarchus <note>A celebrated grammarian and librarian at Alexandria</note>, who reduced the poems of Homer into a single body and arranged them into books. He condemned the "bastard" verses—that is, the adulterated and substituted ones which did not seem to taste of that true Homeric vein—by marking them with **obelisks** <note>original: "ὀβελίσκοις"</note>, which are little spits or daggers. On the other hand, he illuminated those which seemed remarkable and genuine with **asterisks** <note>original: "ἀστερίσκοις"</note>, that is, little stars. This custom was followed by both Origen and Saint Jerome in the Holy Scriptures. Indeed, this very name of "Aristarchus" passed into a proverb, because he devised that custom of approving or condemning with marks. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> to Atticus: "This whole passage, which I usually paint in various ways in my speeches concerning the aristocracy—of which you are the **Aristarchus**—about flame and sword (you know those **oil-flasks** <note>original: "ληκύθους"; a metaphor for rhetorical ornament</note>), he wove together very seriously." He calls Atticus the "Aristarchus" of his orations, meaning his censor and corrector, because it was Atticus's habit, if he disapproved of anything in Cicero's writings, to mark them with red wax. Marcus Tullius declares this elsewhere, in the sixteenth book of his letters to Atticus: "Those things which seemed flourishing to me, by your judgment; for I was terrified of those **little red wax-marks** of yours." The same to Dolabella: "The other man brings forward, I think, a debt in two short lines; the other **Aristarchus** marks these with an **obelisk**. I, like a critic of old..."

<summary>Erasmus explains the transition of celestial navigation metaphors into literary criticism, specifically how the "star" and "obelisk" became symbols for approving or rejecting text, citing Aristarchus and Cicero.</summary>
<keywords>navigation, constellations, Aristarchus, literary criticism, asterisks, obelisks, Cicero, Homer, philology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of classical adages and metaphors for literary criticism and public opinion, following the previous page's focus on scholarly judgment.</meta>

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, FIFTH HUNDRED

I am about to speak. Likewise, Marcus Varro, in *On the Latin Language*, calls those "Aristarchuses" who are critics <note>original: "criticos"</note> and judge books. And Horace says: "He will become an Aristarchus," meaning a corrector and punisher of another's writing. Even Saint Jerome frequently calls someone of his own time an "Aristarchus" because, by his own whim, he would condemn some things and approve others.

### To be marked with a fingernail, and similar phrases. LVIII

To the same category belong these phrases: *To mark with a fingernail*, because a mark is usually made with a nail where something is displeasing. Horace said, "To place a mark with a turned pen," which means to condemn. In the same sense, the *Censorial rod* <note>original: "Censoria uirgula"</note> is read repeatedly in Jerome to represent the authority of correcting and marking. Likewise in Quintilian, in the first book of *Institutes*: "Which the ancient grammarians used so severely, that they would not only mark with a certain censorial rod." This is derived from the Roman Censors, whose duty it was to "mark" <note>The "Censorial Mark" (nota censoria) was a formal stigma placed on a citizen's record for perceived immorality.</note> matters if they judged anything in the city's morals worthy of correction, as I have already said. To this same category belong the *Sponge*, the *File*, and the *Chisel*, which have passed into proverbs for amendment. The sponge deletes what is not pleasing. The file removes and polishes what is redundant and unrefined. With the chisel, that which is rough is shaped and formed. Accordingly, Augustus said his *Ajax* <note>A tragedy Augustus began writing but destroyed.</note> had "fallen upon the sponge," meaning he had deleted it. Things that are polished are called "filed." And they call a refined style the "sculpture of an oration."

### To turn the stylus. LIX

*To turn the stylus* is to change what you have written. Horace in his *Satires*:
> You must often turn the stylus.
The ancients used to write on wax tablets with a pointed stylus; one part of it was sharp, with which they scratched letters into the wax surface, and the other part was wider, with which they smoothed over and erased what they had scratched. Jerome, writing against Rufinus: "As long as I did not refuse your praise, you followed me as a teacher, called me brother and colleague, and declared me a true believer. But after I did not acknowledge your praises and judged myself unworthy of such a great man, you *turned the stylus*, and you now vilify everything you previously praised, pouring out both sweet and bitter from the same mouth." Jerome imitated Cicero, who in the fourth book of the *Verrines* writes in this manner: "He was once afraid and moved; he turned the stylus in his records, and by doing so, he overturned his entire case." One also finds *To fix the stylus* and *To turn the stylus* used for attacking and inveighing against someone in writing.

### He has carried every point. By everyone's pebbles. LX

We read *He has carried every point* <note>original: "Omne tulit punctum"</note> and *By everyone's pebbles* <note>original: "cunctorum calculis"</note> to mean the approval of everyone's opinion. The first is transferred from the custom of the assemblies, where a tablet used to be carried, in which they signified by a "point" <note>A hole or mark on a ballot.</note> placed there for which candidate they were voting. The latter comes from the judicial lots, which we mentioned a little earlier. Horace:
> He has carried every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet.
Those who write only pleasant things please only those who seek pleasure. On the other hand, other things are approved only by those who seek utility. But he who joins pleasure with utility will be praised by the vote of all. The same author in his *Epistles*:
> But did not Alcaeus win by that man's point? Who is he by mine?
> A Callimachus?
The same appears in a Choliambic epigram cited by Porphyrio:
> Whom that Rufus, the founder,
> Is more elegant than the Planci by so many steps.
> But he did not carry seven points.
Plutarch in *Themistocles*: "The common pebble of the Greeks," <note>original: "η κοινη ψῆφος Ἑλληνων"</note> that is: the common consensus of the Greeks; he said this to mean the consensus of all Greece. Cicero in the second book of *Tusculan Disputations*: "What flame is there through which they did not run, who once collected these things point by point?" He is discussing magistrates who were created by the votes of individual citizens. Apuleius in the sixth book of his *Golden Ass*: "Certainly by the pebble of all, however the sentence was destined," that is, by the votes and opinions of everyone.

### The Cumaeans are wise too late. LXI

"The Cumaeans are born late," <note>original: "Οψιγονοι οἱ κυμαιοι"</note> that is: The Cumaeans are wise too late. This adage is recorded by Strabo in the thirteenth book of his *Geography*; he thinks they were commonly ill-reputed as being stupid and

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin adages, specifically focusing on the perceived stupidity of the inhabitants of Cuma and the meteorological metaphor of the Caecias wind.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...senseless, for this reason: that for two hundred years the harbor officials exacted taxes under the pretext of building the city, which the people nevertheless did not cease to pay even after the city had already been constructed. He added another story: that the Cumaeans, having borrowed public money, built porticoes; then, when they had not returned that money by the prescribed day, they were prohibited from walking there. Sometime later, when there was a heavy rain, the creditors, for the sake of mockery, sent a herald to publish an edict that the Cumaeans might go under the porticoes. And so, having been warned by the voice of the herald, they went under. From this the adage was born: **The Cumaeans are wise too late** <note>original: "Sero sapere Cumanos"</note>, since they did not realize until they were told that they should escape the rain. Stephanus also notes that Cuma and Lesbos were commonly ill-reputed for stupidity. However, the proverb does not refer to the Cuma in Italy, but to the one in Aeolis, which was also called Amazonium and Phriconitis, or, as Herodotus says in his first book, Phriconis. Very similar to it is: **The Phrygians are wise too late.** For nothing prevents it from being said also against those who, unless taught by their own misfortune, do not obey those who advise them rightly.

->Drawing evils to oneself, like the Caecias wind draws clouds. LXII<-

*Drawing evil to himself as the Caecias wind draws a cloud* <note>original Greek: Κακ’ ἐφ’ αὑτὸν ἕλκων ὥστε καικίας νέφος</note>, that is: Thus you draw evils to yourself, as the Caecias draws a cloud. It is a six-foot verse <term>senarius: a common meter in Latin and Greek drama</term>, celebrated as a proverb against those who produce and summon for themselves the material for litigation and business. The simile is drawn from the nature of that wind whose name is Caecias <note>The Northeast wind</note>, which Pliny writes blows in the region between the north wind and the sunrise; it is the only one, contrary to the nature of other northern winds, that does not drive clouds away but attracts them. Indeed, I shall add his own words: "Of the winds," he says, "the coldest are those which we have said blow from the north. Neighboring these is the Corus. These both restrain the others and drive away rains. The South and Southwest winds are humid, especially the South wind in Italy. They say also that in the Black Sea the Caecias draws clouds to itself." Thus far Pliny. Aristotle, in his book *On the World*, thinks the Caecias blows around the summer solstice; he adds that it is considered by some to be the same as that which others call *Thrascias*, and is a wind very close to the *Argetes*. Moreover, Aristotle in his *Meteorology* attempts to show the cause of why this wind does not propel clouds away from itself in the manner of the others, but calls them to itself. Either because, he says, another wind blows against it at the same time; or because this one, blowing from a high part of the sky—say, the east—is not carried across the land transversely, but in a curved line, and because of the reflection back to where it arose, it returns there. And so it happens that it gathers clouds to itself. Whence the same author, in the book *On the World*, numbers the Caecias among those winds which are called *anakampsipnoi* <note>original: ἀνακάμψιπνοι</note>, that is, "bent-back" or "receding" blasts. In the twenty-sixth section of his *Problems*, he gives two causes for this thing. He thinks one is this: that at the same time another wind blows contrary to the Caecias. The other is not different from what we have related: namely, that the Caecias blows from a higher region of the sky, certainly from that which turns toward the east; and he gathers that this is higher than the western region from the size and depth of the western sea. Thus it happens that the Caecias, invading against the western region, gathers clouds and draws them to itself in its own backward reflection. Plutarch also makes mention of this in the *Life of Sertorius*, writing that this general, having noticed the nature of the Caecias which happened to be blowing then, forced the Cacitani (or as the Greek manuscripts have it, the Characitani) enemies to surrender in this manner: Opposite the caves in which they were keeping themselves, he placed mounds of ash. When these were stirred up by the charging of horses, the Caecias carried so much dust into the mouths of the caves that, since they could not endure it, they gave themselves into Sertorius's hands. The adage is recorded by Aulus Gellius in Book 2, Chapter 22, and that from Aristotle. It is also recorded by Theophrastus in his book *On the Nature of Winds*. But by him, and likewise by Aristotle, it is recorded so that it seems it can also be said in a positive sense. For he says, *Drawing wealth to himself as the Caecias draws clouds* <note>original Greek: ἕλκων ἐφ’ αὑτὸν ὡς πλοῦτον ὥσπερ ὁ καικίας νέφη</note>. Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How one may be helped by enemies*, says: *For as the Caecias draws clouds, so also a wicked life draws reproaches upon itself* <note>original Greek: ὡς γὰρ ἡ καικίας τὰ νέφη, οὕτως καὶ ὁ φαῦλος βίος ἐφ’ αὑτὸν ἕλκει τὰς λοιδορίας</note>. He uses the same in a positive sense in his *Political Precepts*. Whence it seems it can be said of any matter in either direction. As in: "This man draws a flock of learned men to himself, just as the Caecias draws clouds." "This man draws money to himself from everywhere, just as the Caecias draws clouds." "All good fortunes follow this man no differently than clouds follow the Caecias." "Quarrels are never absent wherever this man is present; for he draws lawsuits to himself no differently than the Caecias draws clouds." Similarly, it can be applied to the matter: "Ambition is a tumultuous thing; for it draws envy, rivalry, extravagance, and other inconveniences of that kind to itself no differently than the Caecias draws clouds." "Modesty attracts the goodwill of all men to itself, just as the Caecias draws clouds."

<summary>Erasmus explains two adages: one regarding the legendary stupidity of the Cumaeans who only realized they should avoid rain when told, and another regarding the Caecias wind, which uniquely attracts clouds rather than dispersing them, serving as a metaphor for people who attract either trouble or fortune.</summary>
<keywords>Cumaeans, Caecias wind, Sertorius, Aristotle, Pliny the Elder, proverbs, meteorology, stupidity, attraction of evils</keywords>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 5
<sig>q</sig>

### 63. To carry oil in the ear.
<note>Latin: Oleum in auricula ferre.</note>

"To carry in the ear" is found in the works of Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note>. On this point, the commentator Calderinus—otherwise a very learned man—does not satisfy me. For the poet seems to be mocking a man with a "stiff ear," a trait also noted by the Greeks as *holding the ear up* <note>original Greek: ἀν' ὦς ἔχων, ἀντὶ τοῦ ἄνω τὸ ὦς ἔχων</note>, that is: having an upturned or attentive ear. Martial’s verse is as follows:
> You said something charming, Marullus:
> He said he carries oil in his ear.

In his *Problems*, Aristotle wrote that ears are bothered by poured-in water, but not by oil. Indeed, if water falls into the ear, we cure it by pouring in oil; once the ear is made slippery, the water flows out. Divers are also accustomed to drop oil into their ears so that water does not cause harm. Therefore, the adage seems to have arisen from the gesture of those who have some liquid in their ear and, to prevent it from flowing out, tilt the ear upward—acting as if they are turning away or loathing to hear. Nor can it truly be applied to flatterers who drop "oil" into the ear, as they provide pleasure rather than healthy advice. The opposite of this is that line from Persius:
> To scrape tender ears with the biting truth.

That Gospel passage concerning the "sellers of oil" <note>Matthew 25:9</note> might also pertain here. But whoever prefers a more serious interpretation here must read "into the ear" in the accusative case. Since this bears the appearance of a proverb and Martial indicates it was commonly tossed about, I did not think it should be passed over.

### 64. What if the sky should fall?
<note>Latin: Quid si coelum ruat?</note>

<margin>*What if the sky should fall?* <note>original Greek: τί εἰ οὐρανὸς ἐμπέσοι</note></margin>
*What if the sky should fall?* This is a proverbial irony used against those who are ridiculously afraid in the safest of circumstances. Aristotle indicates where this originated in his *Metaphysics*, writing that those ancient and unrefined mortals were persuaded that this sky we see was held up by the shoulders of Atlas. If he were to withdraw himself, the sky would fall from on high. This was not only handed down in the fictions of poets but also affirmed by natural philosophers. Plutarch, in his booklet *On the Face Which Appears in the Orb of the Moon*, cites Phenendas, who feared the moon might fall to earth and pitied those living beneath it—such as the Ethiopians or the people of Taprobane <note>Ancient name for Sri Lanka</note>—should such a weight fall. He feared for the earth and sky unless they were propped up by the pillars of Atlas. Theognis wrote:
<note>original Greek: ἐν μοι πεῖσοι μέγας οὐρανὸς εὐρὺς ὕπορθεν / χάλκεος, ἀνθρώπων δεῖμα παλαιγενέων.</note>
-> that is, <-
> May the vast Olympus fall upon my head,
> That which the men of old used to fear.

<margin>*What if the sky should fall now?* <note>original Greek: τί εἰ νῦν ὁ οὐρανὸς ἐμπέσοι</note></margin>
*What if the sky should fall now?* I return to those who say: "What if the sky falls now?" Thus Horace in his *Odes*:
> If the world should break and fall,
> The ruins will strike him unafraid.

### 65. To fear one's own shadow.
<note>Latin: Vmbram suam metuere.</note>

<margin>*To fear one's own shadow* <note>original Greek: τὴν αὑτοῦ σκιὰν φοβεῖσθαι</note></margin>
*To fear one's own shadow* is said of those who tremble like children where there is no danger at all. It is transferred either from those who, having caught sight of their body's shadow, are suddenly terrified; or from certain melancholics who (according to Aristotle), because of weak spirits in the nearby air, see a kind of image of themselves and believe they are seeing their own ghosts. Socrates says in Plato's *Phaedo*: "But you, as the saying goes, are afraid of your shadow," meaning you lack confidence in yourself. Cicero, in a letter to his brother regarding a petition for status: "But the other man, by the gods, with what splendor he shines! First, with the same great nobility. Is it greater? No, but by virtue." Wherefore, those who fear their own shadow like a ghost will certainly be negligent. However, this passage was corrupted in the manuscripts in more than one way. In the seventh decade of *Table Talk* <note>Plutarch's Symposiacs</note>, it says: *to be stirred by the name of a 'shadow' is simply to seem to fear a shadow.* He is discussing those called "shadows"—guests who do not come by the host's invitation, but follow someone who was invited to a banquet.

### 66. He even fears flies flying past.
<note>Latin: Vel muscas metuit praeteruolitantes.</note>

<margin>*He even fears the flies flying past* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰς παραπετομένας μυίας φοβεῖται</note></margin>
This seems to be a proverbial hyperbole, which Aristotle mentions in the seventh book of his *Politics*: *and even the flies flying past*, meaning for the most trivial reason. He mentions a similar one in his *Ethics*...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>original: "ralium septimo"</note> ...in the seventh book of his *Moralia*, speaking of those who are by nature so timid that even if a mouse makes a noise, they immediately tremble with fear.

### 67. To break the rope by stretching it too much.

<note>original: "Ἀποῤῥαγήσεται τεινόμενον τὸ καλώδιον"</note> *The stretched cord will snap.* This was commonly said of those who, while trying extreme measures, alienate those with whom they deal and cause the loss of the entire matter because they are too intent on profit. Lucian, in a certain dialogue, depicts a mother acting as a procuress, scolding her daughter for treating her lover with too much stubborn contempt at a banquet; she warns there is a danger that the young man, provoked and irritated beyond measure, might turn his love and his money elsewhere. "And see to it," she says, "lest we break the rope by stretching it too much." <note>original: "καὶ ὅρα, μὴ τῇ λίαν ἀποῤῥήξωμεν πάνυ τείνασαι τὸ καλώδιον"</note> Pindar, quoted in Plutarch, speaks of "releasing the rope of unbearable cares." <note>original: "τὸ τῆς δυσφόρου χω-νίου μεριμνῶν"</note> Although this is somewhat different from the adage, it agrees more with what Seneca says in his *Letters to Lucilius* about unraveling the chain of business, or even breaking it if it cannot be unraveled. The proverb can be applied generally to any immoderate effort that results in some harm. Close to this is a proverb of the Hebrews, said not unskillfully nor without charm: "He who blows his nose too hard draws blood." Nor is that line by the mime writer Publilius Syrus inconsistent with this:
> Patience, when often offended, becomes fury.

And another similar to it, by the same author I believe, though it is attributed to Seneca:
> A good mind, when wounded, is much more severely angered.

### 68. To urinate into a chamber pot.

<note>original: "Εἰς τὴν ἀμίδα ἐνουρεῖν"</note> *To piss in the pot.* This is used when people who seem worthy of nothing better are treated meanly or employed for some dishonorable task, being themselves base and dishonorable, and as if made to endure insults. Lucian, in *On Salaried Posts*, says: "They would suffer nothing strange or bitter, nor would those others seem to insult them, if, as the saying goes, they urinate into the chamber pot." <note>original: "οὐδὲν ἂν ὅτ᾽ αὐτοὶ δεινὸν πάσχοιεν ἂν, εἴτ᾽ ἐκεῖνοι ὑβρίσαι δοκεῖεν, εἰς τὴν ἀμίδα, φασὶν, οὐ-ροῦντες"</note> For a chamber pot is, as it were, born for this use. Conversely, Martial jokingly rebukes a certain Bassus who defecated into a gold vessel while drinking from glass:
> You receive the burden of your belly in wretched gold,
> Bassus (and you are not ashamed); you drink from glass, so you defecate more expensively.

### 69. Ionic laughter.

<note>original: "Γέλως ἰωνικός"</note> *Ionic laughter.* This is said of the soft and pleasure-seeking. For the softness of the Ionians, like the arrogance of the Sybarites, passed into a proverb, because the former were the most luxurious among the Greeks, and the latter among the barbarians. Athenaeus, in the twelfth book of the *Deipnosophists*, speaking of the luxury of the Ionians, says there exists a "golden proverb" which testifies to the character of that nation (as I understand it). The same author in the fourteenth book teaches that there was once a type of dance, lascivious and impudent, which was called "Ionic." Valerius Maximus, in his second book of *Memorable Deeds*, recorded that the Ionians were the first to invent the use of ointments and crowns to be given at banquets, and the custom of the second course—no small incitements to luxury. Maximus Tyrius, in the dissertation titled *What is the End of Philosophy?*, says: "The Crotonian loves the Olympic wild olive, the Spartan loves armor, the Cretan loves hunting, the Sybarite luxury, and the Ionian loves dances." Hence Horace in his *Odes*:
> The mature maiden joys to be taught
> Ionic movements.

meaning lascivious dances and unseemly gestures. Whence also in Aristophanes, "Ionically" <note>original: "ἰωνικῶς"</note> is used for "softly and delicately" <note>original: "ἀβρῶς"</note>.

### 70. Megarian laughter.

<note>original: "Γέλως μεγαρικός"</note> *Megarian laughter.* This should be said of those who joke at inappropriate times, and who, as Quintilian forbids, would rather lose a friend than a joke. Or those whose arts have now fallen into contempt, obscured by the succession of greater artists. It will also fit well for old men who shamefully pursue certain unseemly games and youthful pleasures at an age that does not suit them. For Ionic comedy flourished for a time; then it fell into contempt...

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 5
<sig>q 2</sig>

<margin>Laughter out of season is a terrible evil among mortals. <note>original: "γέλως ὁ μὴ ἐν καιρῷ ἐν βροτοῖς δεινὸν κακόν."</note></margin> ...it came, mocked by the Athenians. Regarding untimely laughter, this six-foot verse is also celebrated, which is:
To laugh out of place is a very heavy evil.

### Chian Laughter. 71.
<margin>Chian laughter. <note>original: "Χῖος γέλως."</note></margin> That is, Chian laughter, referring to soft and wanton playfulness. Indeed, the comedy of the Chians' manners is well-known. This adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

### Whatever comes into the cheek. 72.
Whatever comes into the cheek <note>A Latin idiom meaning "whatever comes to mind" or "speaking without a filter."</note>. We use this whenever we mean that someone is speaking freely and safely, without looking around, and saying whatever chance brings to mind. Just as we are accustomed to do among faithful friends, in whose presence we may trifle and babble anything without fear of punishment. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the 14th book of *Letters to Atticus*: "Or if there is nothing, you shall write whatever comes into the cheek." The same author in the 12th book: "What about when we are together, and we chatter whatever comes into the cheek?" This will be rightly twisted against those who speak rashly and inconsiderately, as if their speech were not born in their heart, but merely in their throat.

### Whatever comes onto the tongue. 73.
This is clearly a close relative to that which Lucian uses in his booklet *On the Way to Write History*: <margin>Recalling or inventing whatever word they say has come onto an untimely tongue. <note>original: "ἀνανοῦντες ἢ τὸ ἀναπλάττοντες ὅτιπερ ἐπ’ ἀκαιρίαν γλῶτταν φασιν ἐλθεῖν."</note></margin> That is: Reminiscing and making up whatever word has come rashly onto the tongue, as they say. Plato said this in the eighth book of *The Republic*, quoting from the tragic poet Aeschylus. Athenaeus also used it in the fifth book of the *Deipnosophists*: <margin>For as the poet said, whatever [comes] onto an untimely tongue. <note>original: "ὅτι γὰρ τὸν εἰπόντα ποιητὴν, ὅτιπερ ἐπ’ ἀκαιρίαν γλῶτταν."</note></margin> That is: According to the poet who said, "Whatever has come rashly onto the tongue." Isocrates, as if envying this, says in his *Panathenaic* oration: <margin>I would seem similar to those who speak randomly, vulgarly, and whatever occurs to them. <note>original: "ὅμοιος ἂν εἴη δόξαιμι τοῖς εἰκῆ καὶ φορτικῶς καὶ ὅτι ἂν ἐπέλθῃ λέγουσι."</note></margin> That is: I shall seem like those who speak rashly, arrogantly, and futilely whatever has come into their mind.

### To satisfy Momus, and similar phrases. 74.
<margin>To please Momus. <note>original: "Μώμῳ ἀρέσκειν."</note></margin> That is: To satisfy Momus. This is a proverbial hyperbole. Hesiod in his *Theogony* mentions a certain Momus, whom he says was born of Night as his mother and Sleep as his father. It is the custom of this god to produce no work of his own, but to curiously inspect the works of other gods, and if anything is omitted or done wrongly, to carp at it with the utmost freedom. For <margin>Momus <note>original: "μῶμος"</note></margin> in Greek signifies "reprehension" or "blame." Aristotle, in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, mentions this figure, who accused Nature because she added horns to the heads of oxen and not rather to their shoulders, presumably so they could strike more forcefully. Lucian seems to have alluded to this when, in the second book of *True Histories*, he writes that he saw oxen with horns in their ears, not on their foreheads like the rest, but under their eyes. And he denied that this was for Momus <note>Meaning it was beyond even Momus's criticism</note>. Lucian mentions him in many other places, especially in the *Dialogue of the Sects*, where he relates a story of this kind about him: Minerva, Neptune, and Vulcan contended among themselves for the prize of craftsmanship. So that each might produce a chief specimen of their art, Neptune fashioned a bull, Minerva built a house, and Vulcan composed a human being. Momus was chosen as the judge and spectator of the contest. Having inspected each one's work, besides other things he criticized in the works of the others, he noted this especially in the craftsmanship of the human: that the artisan had not added a window or little doors in the chest, so that it could be seen what lay hidden in the heart, because he had fashioned it otherwise with many winding recesses. Philostratus also mentions this fable in a certain letter to his wife, writing about Momus to this effect: That he found nothing else to criticize in Venus except that he found fault with her sandal, as being creaky, too talkative, and annoying with its noise. But if Venus had walked without a sandal, just as she emerged from the sea, entirely naked, Momus would have found no handle at all for carping. Indeed, although this god is not as welcome as the others—because few people willingly admit true criticism—nevertheless, I do not know if any other in that great crowd of poetic gods is more useful. Although now our "Jupiters" <note>A metaphor for powerful rulers or patrons</note> want Momus to listen only to Euterpe <note>The Muse of music/pleasure</note>, preferring flattering things to healthy ones. This Momus, therefore, provides various forms of adages. Either when Plato writes in the sixth book of *The Republic* that a philosopher should be of such a kind that he cannot be criticized even by Momus. Or when Lucian's Venus, even when about to go to judgment, says she would not hesitate even if Momus himself were to be the judge.

<summary>This page explores the origins of several adages related to speech and criticism, specifically the Greek god Momus, who personifies the spirit of fault-finding and the importance of constructive critique.</summary>
<keywords>Momus, Chian laughter, free speech, Cicero, Lucian, Plato, Aristotle, mythology, criticism, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Or when Cicero writes to Atticus in the fifth book: "Because you exhort me so greatly, and what is worth more than everything, in which you labor, so that I might even satisfy the Ligurian Momus <note>Momus was the Greek god of mockery and harsh criticism; to satisfy him means to be beyond reproach.</note>, I would die if anything could be done more elegantly." Therefore, all formulas of this kind will have the appearance of a proverb: *I would not hesitate to contend with you even with Momus as judge.* *The life of that man is more blameless than even Momus himself could pluck at.* *Not even Momus could find fault with this face.* *Nor would I refuse Momus as a judge.* *These things would satisfy even Momus himself.* And if any similar ones can be imagined. To this form belongs that line of Ovid concerning the beauty of Adonis:
*Even Envy would praise his face.*
Briefly, all hyperboles of this kind obtain the appearance of a proverb, such as that line of Terence:
> Even Salvation herself, if she desired, could not save this house.
Said of a family beyond hope. Likewise of a place vehemently fortified: *Not even Mars himself could storm this citadel.* Of a stubborn and persistent man: *Not even Vertumnus <note>The god of change and seasons.</note> himself could turn this man's mind.* Of a woman beyond measure lustful: *Not even Priapus himself could satisfy this woman's lust.* Of a thing in no way probable: *Not even Persuasion <note>original: "Pitho"</note> herself could persuade that.* Of a thing difficult to keep silent: *Neither Harpocrates <note>The god of silence.</note> himself nor Angerona could contain this.* In such a great noise of things: *Not even Sound itself could catch any sleep.* Of a man beyond measure suspicious and distrustful: *That man would not even have faith in Faith herself.* *This man would deceive even Argus <note>The hundred-eyed giant.</note>,* said of one who is vehemently crafty. *This man is more wretched than even Envy herself could envy.* But we gave warning about these formulas of speaking at the beginning of this work.

-> To speak to the sky and the earth. <-
<margin>75</margin>
Those who cry out in vain are said to speak to the sky and the earth. For those who distrust the help of men are accustomed to exclaim, "O sky! O earth!" Theognetus in Athenaeus, book three, and again in book fifteen:
<note>original Greek: Ἐφιλοσόφηκας, γῆ καὶ οὐρανῷ λαλῶν, Οἷς οὐδὲν ἔστιν ἐπιμελὲς τῶν σῶν λόγων.</note>
*You have philosophized, speaking to the earth and sky,*
*To whom there is no care for your words.*
It is close to that which we reported elsewhere: *You are speaking to the wind.*

-> To strike a reef in the harbor. <-
<margin>76</margin>
It is found in Quintilian’s *Institutes*: *To strike a reef in the harbor*, used for someone who blunders immediately at the very entrance of a work. It is also used by Saint Jerome in his second apology against Ruffinus: *Immediately upon exiting the harbor, I struck the ship.* The same to Pammachius: *Exiting from the harbor, we immediately struck.* It is taken from sailors who, with great disgrace, crash the ship before they have even left the port. Papyrius Fabianus turned it to a different sense, as Seneca reports in his *Controversies*: *You sink the ship in the harbor,* concerning an old man who began to live luxuriously at an inappropriate age. It will be aptly said of all who, when a business is now almost finished with praise, degenerate at the very end. The same is found among the Greeks, *to stumble in the harbor.* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ λιμένι προσκόψαι</note> A certain Greek author, Nilus, reports it thus: *Do not be carried away in spirit, lest perhaps your shipwreck happens in the harbor.* <note>original Greek: μὴ ἐπαίρου, μή πως τὸ ναυάγιον ἐν τῷ λιμένι γένηται</note>

-> To fail, or stumble, on the threshold. <-
<margin>77</margin>
Next to this is that saying: *To stumble, or fail, on the threshold.* Translated from those who, about to go out of the house, immediately strike their foot on the threshold before they have begun to do anything. Virgil:
*Why do we fail, dishonored, on the very first threshold?*
That is, immediately, and when the war has scarcely been entered. Quintus Curtius said it somewhat differently in book six: *We stand on the very threshold of victory,* meaning victory is very near. The opposite of this is what Seneca writes in his *Letters to Lucilius*: *He fails at the top of the slope.* A metaphor drawn from those who, having almost climbed the mountain, then become exhausted when they are closest to the summit.

-> The pack-horse in the gate. <-
<margin>78</margin>
Close to the above is: *The pack-horse <note>term: "cantherius" - specifically a gelded horse, often used as a beast of burden.</note> in the gate.* It arose from a certain Sulpicius Galba; when he was about to depart for his province, a pack-horse had fallen in the gate. He said, "I laugh at you, pack-horse in the gate, since you are about to go on such a long journey and are already tired when you have scarcely entered upon it." This saying passed into a proverb. The adage is reported by Pompeius Festus under the word *ridiculus*, and he indicates it is suitable when someone loses heart at the beginning of a thing scarcely started. He explains what a *cantherius* is: namely, a horse with its testicles cut out; so that a *cantherius* differs from a horse as a barrow <note>castrated pig</note> from a boar, a capon from a rooster, or a wether from a ram.

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 5

### 79. Without dust
<margin><unclear>Proverb</unclear>ial. That is, <unclear>he conquers</unclear> or obtains. <unclear>In a wrestling</unclear> match <unclear>according to Ho</unclear>mer, <unclear>Alci</unclear>biades <unclear>where it is writ</unclear>ten as a <unclear>bloodless</unclear> matter, <unclear>it is imitated</unclear> also</margin>
The Greeks say something happens "without dust" when someone obtains it easily and without trouble. The metaphor is taken either from *aphe* <note>original: "ἀφή" - the grip or the sand used by wrestlers</note>, that is, from the touch of the dust with which a wrestler would sprinkle himself when about to engage in a wrestling match; or certainly from the dust by which Homer wrote it is not unseemly to be soiled for those who compete at Olympia or those who wage war. Pliny in his thirty-fifth book says: Alcibiades [praised] Dioxippus, who conquered in the Olympic pancratium <note>A brutal ancient Greek sport combining boxing and wrestling</note> without the touch of dust, which they call <term>akoniti</term> <note>original: "ἀκονιτὶ" - literally "without dust," meaning without a struggle</note>. Aulus Gellius in his fifth book says: "The cause for an ovation," he says, "is when a victory occurs through a sudden surrender, without [effort], as is often said, and a bloodless victory." Horace in his Epistles:

->A fighter around the villages and around the crossroads<-
->would scorn to be crowned at the Olympics, who has hope,<-
->and the sweet condition, of a palm without dust.<-

<term>Anidroti</term> <note>original: "ἀνιδρωτὶ"</note>, that is: without sweat, and <term>anaimati</term> <note>original: "ἀναιματὶ"</note>, that is, without blood.

---

### 80. A deserted cause
<margin><unclear>As the proverb</unclear> says <unclear>where someone</unclear> yields, <unclear>and does not</unclear> fight <unclear>against</unclear> it, that is, <unclear>Again</unclear> and <unclear>without</unclear> accusers, <unclear>that is</unclear>, <unclear>to this</unclear> <unclear>deserted</unclear> <unclear>restitution</unclear> <unclear>judged</unclear> to be paid. <unclear>The defendant</unclear> would defend, <unclear>law is ad</unclear>mitted, <unclear>But</unclear> if, <unclear>as we</unclear> said, <unclear>eremo</unclear>dicium,</margin>
<unclear>... ...</unclear>, that is, a deserted cause, when no one fights back. The metaphor is taken from the courts, where one party yielding hands over the case to the adversary. Therefore, to win by a deserted cause is to win without a fight. Lucian in *Zeus Rants*: <term>What else will we seem to have done, than to have conquered by a deserted cause?</term> <note>original: "ὡς δὲ τί ἄλλο, ἢ ἐξ ἐρήμης κρατεῖν ἔστω"</note>. The same in *Toxaris*: <term>Likewise whole cities were taken by no one defending them</term> <note>original: "ὡσαύτως πόλις ἐρήμην ὑπ' οὐ ἁλῶναι"</note>. Socrates also uses it in his *Apology* in Plato: <term>Accusing in a deserted cause, with no one defending</term> <note>original: "ἐρήμην κατηγοροῦντες ἀπολογουμένου"</note>. Legal experts call this by the compound word <term>eremodicium</term> <note>A legal term for a judgment given in the absence of the opposing party</note>. Thus Paulus in the *Pandects*, book 4, Title on Minors, chapter "Even if without fraud." Likewise, he is helped by <term>eremodicium</term>. It is established, however, that restitution of the case ought to be granted to men of every age if they show they were absent for a just cause. Again in book 46, Title on "Judgment to be paid," chapter "When he complained." If, after a stipulation to pay the judgment was entered, someone should defend the defendant and later suffered a sentence from a deserted trial, whether he is admitted to the clause concerning the matter judged, etc. Again in the *Code*, book 3, Title on Judgments, chapter "It must be hastened." But if he was absent, and a similar search for him proceeded, just as for the person of the plaintiff, as we said, even in the absence of the defendant a deserted trial may be contracted. These are the words of Justinian. It is therefore <term>eremodicium</term> <note>original: "ἐρημοδικίον"</note> when a sentence is carried while one party is absent.

### 81. Without plowing and without sowing
<margin><unclear>Whence</unclear> without <unclear>happening</unclear> Lucian <unclear>but</unclear> Homer <unclear>uses</unclear> all things. To you <unclear>Horace</unclear> appears <unclear>yearly</unclear> where <unclear>the vine</unclear> unpruned <unclear>is accepted</unclear> it is <unclear>written</unclear> to this <unclear>Lucian</unclear> in <unclear>Homer</unclear> a plant, <unclear>nor as</unclear> usually <unclear>without</unclear> sowing, <unclear>produces</unclear> grain, <unclear>points</unclear>, and</margin>
Those things which happen to us by chance without our effort, they say happen <term>unsown and unplowed</term> <note>original: "ἄσπαρτα καὶ ἀνήροτα"</note>. Lucian in *The Parasite*: <term>Because he alone, according to the excellent Homer, neither plants with his hands nor plows, but all things unsown and unplowed are his to graze upon</term>. The same in *The Professor of Rhetoric*: <term>And for you let all things grow without the labor of sowing and plowing</term>, that is, without study. It appears the proverb is from the fable of the Fortunate Isles, about which Horace says in his Odes:

->Where the unplowed earth yields grain every year,<-
->And the unpruned vine flourishes continually.<-

It was taken, I believe, from Homer, who in the ninth book of the *Odyssey* describes the land of the Cyclopes in this manner:

> <term>They reach the land of the high-minded, lawless Cyclopes,</term>
> <term>Who, trusting in the immortal gods,</term>
> <term>Neither plant any plant with their hands, nor plow.</term>
> <term>But all things grow for them unsown and unplowed,</term>
> <term>Wheat, barley, and vines which bear</term>
> <term>Wine from fine clusters, and the rain of Zeus makes them grow.</term>

> <unclear>They come</unclear> into the land, which the great-hearted Cyclopes
> <unclear>Devoid of laws</unclear> inhabit; these, relying on divine power,
> <unclear>Neither</unclear> fix plantings in the earth with their hands,
> <unclear>Nor freely</unclear> break the soil for crops. Indeed all these,
> <unclear>Without</unclear> seed, and born from no plowing,
> <unclear>Vines</unclear>, grain, and burdened with full clusters
> <unclear>All things</unclear>, and Jupiter increases these with generous rains.

### The sleeping man’s net catches fish.
-> LXXXII <-

<note>original: "Εὕδοντι κύρτος αἱρεῖ"</note> That is, *The net catches for the sleeper.* This is used against those who obtain what they desire without any effort. It originated from an event that supposedly happened: while some fishermen were asleep, fish by chance became entangled in their nets and were caught. Some attribute this to Timotheus, the Athenian General <note>An Athenian statesman and general of the 4th century BC</note>, who, because many things turned out successfully for him more through the favor of fortune <gloss>than</gloss> by his own labor, was given the nickname "The Lucky." Out of envy for him, some people used to paint Fortune driving cities into his net while he lay nearby sleeping. According to Plutarch, he mocked these people by saying: "If I capture such cities while sleeping, what do you think I shall do when I am awake?" Terence alluded to this when he said in *The Brothers*: "What, did you believe the gods would finish these things for you while you slept? And that she <note>the bride</note> would be brought home to your bedroom without any effort of yours?" A similar expression is found in Titus Livy, Book 7 of *From the Founding of the City*: "A singular leader of war, who thinks victories fly down from heaven into his lap while he does nothing." Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the final speech against Verres: "But the same is not permitted to me as to those born of noble stock, to whom all the benefits of the Roman people are delivered while they sleep." Indeed, even today it is commonly said of that kind of man: "He is more fortunate than he is wise." And the comic poet Eupolis, quoted in Athenaeus, says:
"O city, city... how much more lucky you are than you are wise."
This agrees with what will be said in the proverb: *The unadvised rashness of the Athenians.*

### When a mule gives birth.
-> LXXXIII <-

An ancient adage: *When a mule gives birth*, used whenever we mean that something will never happen, or is so rare that it seems wicked or foolish to hope for it. It seems to have arisen from what Herodotus relates in *Thalia*: When the city of the Babylonians was being besieged by Darius, a certain Babylonian, insulting Darius and his army with taunts, said: "Why do you sit there idle, Persians? Why don't you rather depart? You will capture us <note>original: "ἐπεὰν ἡμίονοι τέκωσι"</note> when mules give birth." He said this because he believed it would never happen, since mules are sterile by nature. But a little later it happened that a certain mule belonging to Zopyrus gave birth; encouraged by this omen in the hope of capturing Babylon, he took the city. A similar story is told by Suetonius in the *Life of Galba Caesar*. When an eagle snatched the entrails from the hands of Galba's grandfather while he was performing a ritual for a lightning strike and carried them to a fruit-bearing oak, the response was given that the highest but late-coming power was portended for the family. But he, mocking the idea, said: "Certainly, when a mule gives birth." Galba seized upon this omen so strongly that later, when he was planning a revolution, nothing encouraged him as much as the birth of a mule; while others shuddered at it as a foul omen, he alone accepted it as most joyful, remembering the sacrifice and his grandfather's saying. Pliny, in Book 8, Chapter 44, writes about the sterility of mules in this way: "It has been observed that those born from two different species become a third kind, and are like neither parent. And those very ones which are so born do not reproduce in any kind of animal; therefore, mules do not give birth." Alexander of Aphrodisias gives the cause for this: because if females of different nature and habit are mixed, they produce a third thing different from both, and they lose the power of the simple elements entirely; just as if you mix white with black, both colors are abolished, and a dark color <note>original: "fufcus"</note> is returned, different from both, which the Greeks call <note>original: "λουκόφαιον"</note> "white-gray." But Aristotle discusses this much more exactly in the second book of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 6, refuting the theories of Democritus and Empedocles. Although it is recorded in the Roman annals that mules have often given birth, this was held to be a prodigy <note>a supernatural omen</note>, as Pliny testifies in the same place I just cited. Theophrastus says they commonly give birth in Cappadocia. Aristotle, in the first book of *On the Nature of Animals*, Chapter 6, records that mules mate and reproduce in Syria above Phoenicia; but that animal there is of its own kind, even if similar.

### At the Greek Calends.
-> LXXXIIII <-

A related meaning is *At the Greek Calends*, standing for "never." This is because the Greeks do not have "Calends" <note>the first day of the month in the Roman calendar</note> in the manner of the Romans, but rather <note>original: "νουμηνίας"</note> "New Moons." And the Greeks used to pay interest at the return of the moon. Hence Strepsiades, in Aristophanes' *Clouds*, wishes for some sorceress who might, by her charms, prevent the moon from ever rising: for thus it would be that he would not pay interest, since moneylenders give loans by the moons, and interest grows with the moons. Augustus, therefore, alluded to this when he said that those who he meant would never repay a loan would pay "at the Greek Calends." Regarding this, Tranquillus <note>Suetonius</note> writes in his *Life of Augustus* in this manner: "In daily conversation he used certain phrases quite frequently and notably..."
