<margin>85</margin>
### The moon of Acessaeus.
<margin>Ἀκεσσαίου σελήνη.</margin>
**The moon of Acessaeus.** <note>original: "Acessaei luna"</note> This is said against procrastinators who repeatedly invent new excuses to delay a business matter. It originated from the habits of a certain sailor of that name. Since he was lazy, he was accustomed to postpone his voyages in such a way that he always seemed to be waiting for a more favorable moon. For the Greeks, and especially the Spartans, were superstitious observers of the moon whenever they were about to undertake any business. Euripides <note>Ancient Greek playwright</note> alludes to this silently in *Iphigenia in Aulis* when Agamemnon responds that his daughter will marry only when the "lucky circle" has arrived—meaning, of course, the full moon. Lucian, in his booklet *On Astrology*, openly reports that Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> established a law for the Spartans that they should not enter battle until the full moon. Aristophanes jokes about this superstition: <margin>at the full moon.</margin> <note>original: "τῇ πανσελήνῳ"</note> that is, at the time of the full moon, signifying something that will happen late or never. Indeed, when Datis and Artaphernes, leading the Persian armies, rushed into Marathon, the Spartans were waiting for the full moon so they could then set out for battle. Therefore, before they could arrive, the Athenians had already engaged in the war. Herodotus mentions this history in Book VI. From this, it is used as a proverb for those who hesitate and put things off for any reason: <margin>at the full moon.</margin> <note>original: "ἐν τῇ πανσελήνῳ"</note> The adage is recorded by Diogenianus. We shall say more elsewhere regarding the "Laconian [Spartan] moons."

<margin>86</margin>
### When it has lightened through Harma.
<margin>Ἐπὶ δὲ ἅρματι ἀστράψῃ.</margin>
**When it lightens through Harma.** <note>original: "Vbi per Harma fulgurat"</note> This is said of things that happen too slowly, or too late, or very rarely; or when someone waits too anxiously and superstitiously for the right opportunity to act. Strabo, in the ninth book of his *Geography*, indicates the origin of the adage, writing that there is a certain deserted and sparsely populated village near Mycaletus in Boeotia, or Mycalessus, which they call *Harma*, that is, "the Chariot." There is another place distinct from this, but of the same name, in Attica. Because of this similarity of name, they shared a common tradition. The Boeotian *Harma* was so named because, after Amphiaraus <note>A hero of Greek myth</note> was swallowed by the earth, his empty chariot was carried to that spot where his monument now stands. Others say that while Adrastus was fleeing, his chariot was broken in that place, though he himself was saved by the intervention of a god. From this arose the proverb: <margin>whenever it lightens through Harma.</margin> <note>original: "ὁπότε δι’ ἅρματος ἀστράψῃ"</note> This refers to the Pythian priests who watched for a specific lightning bolt from that location; when it was seen, they would send sacred offerings to Delphi. They observed for three days and three nights each month from the hearth of "Jupiter of the Lightning," which is located between the Pythium and the Olympium. These are roughly the facts from Strabo. Plutarch clearly shows the use of the adage in his *Symposiacs*: <note>original: "οἱ γὰρ, ἰηφύεις..."</note> *For those who rarely, and "through Harma" as they say, offer a glimpse, are forced to describe whatever is convenient and known.* It seems to be said of things that are rare and uncertain. It can also be applied jokingly to things we believe will never happen, just as they say, "At the Greek Calends" <note>A famous proverb meaning 'never,' as the Greeks did not have 'Calends' in their calendar.</note>.

<margin>87</margin>
### The Lydian stone, or the Heraclian stone.
<margin>Ἡ Ἡρακλεία, ἢ λίθος λυδή.</margin>
**The Heraclian, or Lydian stone.** <note>original: "Heraclius, siue Lydius lapis"</note> This is said against those who possess a sharp and exact judgment. It is recorded by Theophrastus in his book *On the Nature of Stones*. He says there is a certain stone called Lydian or Heraclian which, by rubbing, tests gold and silver to prove what kind they are. Some think this is the Magnet, or "Herculean stone," which attracts iron—hence the name <margin>magnet.</margin> <note>original: "μαγνῆτις"</note> was added. But from the words of Theophrastus, it is clear enough that the <term>touchstone</term> <note>A small tablet of dark stone used for assaying precious metals</note> is meant, which the Latins call the *index* (indicator). This is the stone into which the shepherd Battus was transformed in Ovid, his desire to betray others remaining even in the stone. It was not called "Heraclian" after Hercules, but from Heraclea, a city in Lydia. Pliny mentions this in Book 33, Chapter 8, in these words: *Accompanying the mention of gold and silver is the stone they call the "little whetstone" (coticula). It used to be found only in the river Tmolus, as Theophrastus authorizes, but now it is found everywhere. Some call it Heracleum, others Lydian. They are small, not exceeding four inches in length and two in width. Experts, when they have taken a filing from the vein for a trial, can immediately say how much gold is in it, how much silver or copper, with a wonderful method that does not fail.* Theocritus alluded to this in his *Aites*:

<summary>Erasmus explains three proverbs related to procrastination, rare occurrences, and the testing of character or quality, drawing on classical sources like Strabo, Pliny, and Theophrastus.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

To have a mouth like a Lydian stone. <note>original: Λυδίῃ ἴσον ἔχειν πέτρῃ σόμα</note> That is,
->To have a mouth equal to a Lydian stone.<-
Doubtless this refers to one who, in various kisses, could best judge to whom they belonged; for this is how lovers play the fool. The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on a classical text</note> thinks these stones are found among the Lydians, and that the proverb arose from this. And lest you doubt that he speaks of a touchstone <note>A Lydian stone or "basanite" used to test the purity of gold</note>, there follows: "by which the money-changers rub gold to see if it is not a base imitation." <note>original: χρυσοῦ ὁποίῃ τείβονται μὴ φαῦλον ἐτήτυμον ἀργυραμοιβοί</note> That is,
->By whose touch the banker explores the gold,<-
->To see if it be upright.<-
The adage can be applied either to a person or to a thing. To a person in this way: "You are the best judge of my writings, and plainly, as the saying goes, a Herculean stone." <note>original: ἡρακλέα λίθος; another term for a magnet or touchstone</note> Also in this manner: "In weighing and estimating talents, he has a most refined nose <note>A metaphor for keen judgment</note>, and is altogether a Lydian stone, as they say." It is transferred to a thing in this way: "Liberty opens the talents of youths, just as the command entrusted to them is, as they say, the Lydian stone."

### A white mason’s line. LXXXVIII
A white line. <note>original: Λευκὴ στάθμη</note> That is, a white mason's line <term>amussis: a tool used by builders to ensure straightness, usually marked with red chalk</term>, which means without any selection, and without distinction. Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights*: "For all those, and especially the Greeks among them, reading many and various things, whatever matters they stumbled upon, they swept together into a mere heap with a 'white line,' as it is said, without any care for distinction." Plutarch in his commentary *On Garrulity*: "There is in reading a 'white line,' just as this talk is of blindness," etc. <note>original: ἔστι μὲν ἐν ἀναγνώσει λευκὴ στάθμη πῶς ὅδε λόος ἀβλεψίας</note> That is, a talkative person is plainly a white line toward speeches, because he babbles anything about any subject without any selection. The adage is also expressed more clearly by some as: A white line on a white stone. <note>original: Λευκῷ λίθῳ λευκὴ στάθμη</note> It is said either against those who have no judgment, or against the stupid, or against those who prove or signify uncertain things by uncertain means. Sophocles in *Cidalion*, quoted in Suidas:
->By your words I judge,<-
->No more than a white line on a white stone.<-
It is cited by Nonius Marcellus from Lucilius, book 30 (but corruptly, I think, as are most of his fragments): "And he loved everyone. For he makes no distinction, nor does a white line signify anything." It is also used by Plato in the dialogue titled *Charmides*, where Socrates says that toward handsome youths he is just like a white line on a white stone, because he could not distinguish enough between their beauties and loved them all equally. For that cord is usually smeared with red ochre <note>original: minio</note> so that it may make a distinction; hence Persius called it "the red mark" <note>original: rubrica</note>:
"As if he directs the red mark with one eye."

### The same by the same. LXXXIX
The same through themselves. <note>original: Αὐτὰ δῐ᾿ αὑτῶν</note> That is, the same by the same. It is recorded in the collections of Diogenianus concerning those who always hammer home the same things, or do the same things assiduously. It is not unlike that which we rendered in another place: "Corinthus, son of Zeus" <note>original: ὁ Διὸς Κόρινθος; a proverb for tiresome repetition</note>. It can also be twisted against those who treat trifling matters triflingly, as if someone were to write unlearned commentaries on an unlearned author, or obscene ones on an obscene author.

### To the level. XC
It is frequent among authors to say "To the level" <note>original: Ad amussim</note>, "perfectly leveled," or "exactly adjusted," for that which is done with exquisite diligence and most exact care. Gellius, book 1, chapter 4: "He looked at all these older writings so curiously, either weighing their virtues or searching out their faults, that you would say the judgment was made 'to the level'." And "leveled things" <note>original: Amussitata</note> for things examined, in Nonius. The metaphor is taken from stonemasons or carpenters, who explore the equality of the work with that measuring cord. Although Festus, in the entry *Examussim*, testifies that for some the *amussis* is not a line or a ruler, but an iron tool which builders use in polishing. Persius, concerning a poet composing perfect verses, whom we just cited:
> He knows how to stretch the verse,
> No differently, he says, than if he directs the red mark with one eye.

Likewise in the poem about a good man, which they attribute to Virgil:
> Lest anything gape, lest any corner protrude, so that they may
> Meet in equal parts, lest the level should stray.

Basil the Great uses the same in his *Address to Young Men*, when he commands that every discipline be referred to the end of happiness, just as if directing stones "to the level," according to the Doric proverb. Born
<meta>catchword: to seem</meta>

->CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 5<-

<note>The left edge of the text is partially cut off in the image.</note>

<unclear>P</unclear>ossibly in Homer, *Odyssey* book 5, when he speaks of Ulysses building a ship for himself:
<note>original Greek: ἐπὶ στάθμην, καὶ ἐπὶ στάθμην ἴθυνε</note>
"He guided it by the line, and by the line he made it straight." That is,
<unclear>A</unclear>nd with much skill, he brought it to the level of the carpenter's rule. Again, in *Iliad* book 15:
<note>original Greek: ὥστ’ ἐπὶ στάθμην δόρυ νήϊον ἐξιθύνῃ / τέκτονος ἐν παλάμῃσι δαήμονος, ὅς ῥά τε πάσης / εὖ εἰδῇ σοφίης ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν ἀθήνης</note>
"As the carpenter's line makes the ship's timber straight in the hands of a skilled craftsman, who knows all his craft well by the promptings of Athena." That is,
For just as the rule levels the ship-timber,
In the fingers of the learned builder, who knows the art
With strength, and holds it rightly, with Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena</note> as his advisor. It is found in the same author and in several other places.

### To the fingernail. XCI

<margin>To the fingernail</margin>
"To the fingernail" <note>Latin: *Ad unguem*</note> has the same meaning. The metaphor is taken from marble-workers, who, by running a fingernail over the surface, test the joints of the marbles. Horace says:
<margin>Horace: To the fingernail</margin>
"A man made to the fingernail." That is, perfect. The same author in his *Art of Poetry*:
<unclear>A</unclear> good and wise man finds fault with what
<unclear>H</unclear>as not lived through many days and many erasures, and
<unclear>H</unclear>as not been corrected ten times over "to the fingernail."
<unclear>V</unclear>irgil in the second book of the *Georgics*:
<unclear>I</unclear>ndulge in the rows, yet no less let every path
<unclear>S</unclear>quare with the trees planted "to the fingernail" in a cut boundary. Persius:
<unclear>A</unclear>s the joint lets the severe
<unclear>F</unclear>ingernails slide over its smooth surface. Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*, book 1: "Nor is anyone of such futile judgment that he would not approve of the order of the Roman year, thus amended 'to the fingernail,' as they say." In a similar way, the Greeks call that which is exact and exceedingly accurate "two-nailed" <note>original Greek: διόνυχον</note>. Plutarch in *Precepts of Good Health*: "Therefore a diet is called very strict and 'two-nailed'." That is: a very exact way of life, which is said to be observed "to the fingernail." "To two-nail" <note>original Greek: διωνυχίζειν</note> is used for "to examine accurately." Athenaeus also uses this word in book 3: "Furthermore, he explains 'to the fingernail' all the probabilities to those who dispute with thorns <note>i.e., subtle or prickly arguments</note>."

### To return to the anvil. XCII

<margin>To return to the anvil</margin>
Because of Horace, he said "to return to the anvil" <note>Latin: *Incudi reddere*</note> for that which is to be refashioned, changed, and corrected:
<unclear>A</unclear>nd to return poorly turned verses to the anvil.
<unclear>I</unclear>n a similar form they say "To cook again" <note>Latin: *Recoquere*</note>. Quintilian in book 12: "But especially to Apollonius Molon, whom he had also heard at Rome, he gave himself again at Rhodes to be reshaped and, as it were, 'cooked again'." Likewise Horace: "A scribe 'cooked again' from a member of the commission of five."

### A Lesbian rule. XCIII

<margin>A Lesbian rule</margin>
A "Lesbian rule" <note>Latin: *Lesbia regula*</note> is said whenever things are done backward—not the deed according to the principle, but the principle is accommodated to the deed. And when the law is applied to customs, rather than customs being corrected to the law; or when a prince accommodates himself to the customs of the people, when on the contrary it is fitting for the common people to establish their life according to the judgment of the prince, provided the prince himself looks toward the rule and goal of honesty. Aristotle makes mention of this rule in the 5th book of the *Ethics*: "For of an indefinite thing the rule is also indefinite, just as the leaden rule of Lesbian building: for it is moved according to the shape of the stone, and the rule does not remain fixed."

### Unworthy to hand him the chamber pot. XCIIII

<margin>Unworthy to hand him the chamber pot</margin>
This is a proverbial hyperbole concerning those who are vehemently unequal and cannot be compared in any part. Martial:
<unclear>S</unclear>o that if you are worthy to offer your chamber pot <note>Latin: *matella*</note> to Pylades,
<unclear>O</unclear>r to feed the pigs of Pirithous.
<unclear>F</unclear>or it is the most sordid service to offer a pot to one who needs to urinate; he who is unworthy of this is seen as nothing if not vastly inferior. Whence Saint Jerome in his letter to Nepotian, regarding the sordid services of legacy-hunters, also mentions this: "They themselves," he says, "place the chamber pot, and sit by the bed." Plutarch in his *Laconian Apophthegms* relates that a certain Spartan boy, captured and sold by Antigonus, obeyed his buyer in all things that were not unbecoming to a free-born person. But when ordered to bring the chamber pot, he refused the service, adding, "I will not serve."

[page 190]

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES<-

<note>original: "serviam: Surgente domino, puer, Senties, inquit, quem emeris."</note> ...I shall serve: As the master rose, the boy said, "You shall feel whom you have bought," and at once, having climbed to the roof, he threw himself headlong. Even today there is a very common saying among the people: **He is not worthy to pull off his shoes.** This adage was used in the Gospel writings by John the Baptist. Furthermore, they say that those whom they wish to appear completely unequal should not even be named on the same day.

### Loose brooms. To loosen the brooms.
<margin>95</margin>

Cicero calls men of no account and of no counsel at all "loose brooms" <note>original: "scopas dissolutas"</note>, writing to Atticus in the seventh book of his letters in these very words: *I saw Caesar at Minturnae on the eighth day before the Kalends of February in the morning, with the most absurd mandates, not addressed to men, but to loose brooms, so that he seems to me to have done that very thing for the sake of mockery.* The same author, in *The Complete Orator*, acting against those who despise the rhythms of oratory, said "to loosen the brooms" to mean making a thing entirely useless. For brooms tied together seem to have some form and are suited for sweeping the floor. Furthermore, if you loosen them, nothing is more useless, nothing more inelegant. These are the words of Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>: *But if loose things delight some more, let them follow them indeed: provided that if someone should dismantle the shield of Phidias, he would take away the entire beauty of the arrangement, not the charm of the individual works; as in Thucydides, I miss only the circuit of the speech, while the ornaments remain. Those men, when they loosen a speech in which there is neither substance nor any word that is not abject: they seem to me to loosen not a shield, but as it is in the proverb (though it is a humbler saying, yet it is similar), the brooms, so to speak.*

### With open pipes.
<margin>96</margin>

**With open pipes**, that is, with a clearer voice. Translated from flute-players, who play some things with the holes of the pipes stopped up, as if with a more suppressed sound, and some with open pipes, with a sharper sound. Quintilian in the eleventh book of the *Institutes*: *But those now almost with open pipes, as they say, who wherever they have fallen, seek the old custom of the forum and the ancient manner of the courts.* The metaphor will be more charming if someone is said to "attack someone with open pipes," that is, not to disparage secretly, but to pursue openly and tear apart with insults; or, "to celebrate someone's praises with open pipes," that is, openly and magnificently. Perhaps to this meaning belongs that Greek six-foot verse <note>iambic senarius</note> which Tully cites in the second book of the Letters to Atticus, from some poet or other: *Indeed our Gnaeus <note>Pompey the Great</note>,* he says, *I simply do not know now what he is thinking:*
<note>original Greek: φυσᾷ γὰρ οὐ σμικροῖσιν αὐλίσκοισιν ἐπί.</note> ->that is,<-
**For he no longer breathes through tiny pipes.**
He seems to hint that Pompey is promising great things through the agrarian law and is setting a massive thing in motion. Athenaeus in his fourth book mentions a type of pipe which Anacreon calls "half-holed" <note>original Greek: ἡμιόπους</note>, smaller than the others and with a less clear sound, which the name itself indicates.

### What need was there to play on long pipes?
<margin>97</margin>

Dio in his first book records an adage of this kind: <note>original Greek: τί γάρ με ἔδει μακροῖς αὐλοῖς αὐλεῖν;</note> that is, **To what purpose did it pertain for me to play on long pipes?** And they say this applies to those who have undertaken a vain labor or expense. It is drawn from Otho, who after the slaying of Galba had performed a sacrifice in which the entrails portended inauspicious outcomes. Therefore, repenting of the expense and the labor spent in vain, he is said to have spoken thus: *What need was there for me to play on long pipes?* which words then passed into a common story. Formerly in sacrifices, it was customary to play with long pipes: which custom was later abolished, according to Plutarch. Suetonius also mentions this in the *Life of Otho*: *Also on the following day,* he says, *while taking auspices and a storm having arisen, having slipped heavily, he repeatedly murmured: <note>original Greek: τί γάρ μοι καὶ μακροῖς αὐλοῖς;</note> that is, What have I to do with long pipes?* In which place I wonder what moved a certain translator of no obscure name to reject the words of Suetonius as if they were counterfeit and think that Dio's should be substituted: as if indeed it were a sin for authors to explain the same sentiment in different forms, or as if Suetonius did not speak even more elegantly than Dio.

### Would that those things might fall to me, which are between Corinth and Sicyon.
<margin>98</margin>

Eustathius, explaining the second book of the *Iliad*, says this verse was once celebrated as a proverb:
<note>original Greek: εἴη μοι τὰ μεταξὺ κορίνθου καὶ σικυῶνος.</note> ->that is,<-
**May I have what lies between Sicyon and Corinth.**
It came into an adage from the fact that both cities were most wealthy, and the far most fertile lands lay between them. Aristophanes in *The Birds* indicates it arose from an oracle:
*But when the gray wolves and the crows shall dwell...*

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient Greek and Latin adages, specifically focusing on the first Chiliad (thousand) of proverbs. It follows the previous page's exploration of geographical and superlative metaphors.</meta>

->CHILIAD ONE, FIFTH CENTURY<-

**The land between Corinth and Sicyon.** <note>original: "τὰ μεταξὺ κορίνθου καὶ σικυῶνος"</note> That is, between the dog and the wolf: where staying in the same seat, the space divides Sicyon and Corinth. The Interpreter <note>A reference to ancient commentators or scholiasts</note> ascribes this to Aesop, who, when consulting about how to acquire wealth, received this response: **"Would that I possessed the land between Corinth and Sicyon."** That is: *Would that you had the fields that lie between Sicyon and Corinth.* It is also mentioned by Zenodotus, and likewise by Athenaeus in the fifth book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned," a famous collection of ancient lore</note>. It is suitable for when people wish for immense things. It can also be twisted as a joke against someone who, though he cannot attain what he sees, nevertheless dreams of it as if he could. A similar figure of speech was used by Theocritus in the *Harvest-Home*: **"Would that I had all that they say Croesus once possessed."** That is: *They say Croesus held much; would that those things were mine.*

## To be a god, to make a god. XCIX

These are proverbial hyperboles used for those worthy of singular praise. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book of his *On the Orator* says: **"In this you seem to me to be a god."** That is: singular and supreme. Terence in *The Brothers*: **"I make you a god."** That is: I extol you with the highest praises. This arose because the mortals of old, if they looked up to someone for extraordinary and far from common virtues, they numbered him among the gods. This happened to Alexander the Great, Scipio Africanus, Octavian Augustus, and many others. Aristotle supports this in the seventh book of his *Ethics*, saying: **"This virtue they call heroic, as if greater than man, and closest to divinity."** Hence Homer also makes Priam speak of Hector in this manner in the 24th book of the *Iliad*: **"Nor did he seem to be the son of a mortal man, but of a god."** That is: *Indeed, he no longer seemed to be the son of a mortal man, but born of divine seed.* Among the Spartans, as the same author testifies, there was a peculiar custom that when they vehemently admired someone, they called him a "divine man." Socrates mentions the same in Plato’s *Meno*: **"And the Spartans, whenever they praise a good man, say: 'This is a divine man.'"** From this come those solemn phrases in Homer: **"like a god"** <note>original: "θεῷ ἰκελὸς"</note> and **"god-like in appearance"** <note>original: "θεοειδὴς"</note>, and **"equal to a god"** <note>original: "ἰσόθεος"</note> and **"very divine"** <note>original: "ζάθεος"</note>. Conversely, we call men of remarkable wickedness "beasts," and this is very common even among the populace. Saint Jerome, writing to Aurelius Augustine, twisted this with irony against certain people who were not content with the common judgment of men but desired new things, calling them "those gods." Quintilian, in the first book of his *Institutes*, indicates that a man perfected in every respect was commonly called a "mortal god." For the wise, he says, in forming one who is to be perfect in every way and, as they say, a kind of "mortal god," believe he must be instructed not only in the knowledge of celestial or mortal things, etc.

## To be in heaven. C

Bordering on this is "To be in heaven," used for being fortunate and glorious beyond measure. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] to Atticus, book 2: **"Bibulus is in heaven, and I know not why; but he is praised as if he were the one man who restored our state by delaying."** The same author elsewhere to the same: **"But if those things which were agreed upon are not kept, I am in heaven."** Again elsewhere: **"For nothing is more 'in heaven' for those being besieged."** Horace alluded to this when he said: **"They mix me with the gods above."** That is: *They make me great and famous.* And Theocritus in the *Wayfarers*: **"I shall leap to heaven for you."** On the other hand, those who suddenly fall from the height of happiness are said to have "fallen from the stars." Marcus Tullius to Atticus, book 2, speaking of Pompey: **"O spectacle joyful to Crassus alone, but not to the rest. For because he had fallen from the stars, he seemed to have slipped rather than to have been cast down."** But consider, reader, whether this saying pertains more to that which we recorded above: *A third Cato fell from heaven.* Related to this form is "To carry to heaven with praises," meaning to praise exceedingly. Titus Livius [Livy] in the second book of his first Decade: **"A great rumor throughout the city: they carry the Fabii to heaven with praises."**

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### THE SIXTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

->Often even a gardener has spoken very opportunely.<-

Aulus Gellius, in his *Attic Nights* <note>A 2nd-century collection of miscellany and lore</note>, Book 2, Chapter 6, testifies that this little verse was once a celebrated proverb:
*Pollaki kai keporos aner mala kairion eipen.* <note>original Greek: Πολλάκι καὶ κηπωρὸς ἀνὴρ μάλα καίριον εἶπεν.</note> that is,
Often even a gardener has spoken very opportunely.

By this we are reminded that a salutary opinion is not to be despised because of the humility of its author; for it happens sometimes that a man of the lowest lot and reputation, or one who is minimally learned, says something by no means to be scorned even by the greatest men. To this corresponds that line of Caecilius <note>A Roman comic poet</note> quoted by Cicero in the *Tusculan Disputations*: "Often there is wisdom even under a shabby cloak." Nor is that line in *The Two Captives* <note>A play by Plautus</note> discordant: "How the greatest talents often lie hidden in obscurity." Furthermore, as far as the Greek proverb is concerned, I thought the reader should be warned that it is found written in this manner in all the manuscripts of Gellius I have seen so far. 

However, as I recall, a doubt was once cast upon me, and a mistake suggested, by Paulus Bombasius of Bologna—among the professors of fine letters in that city, he is as much the most learned as he is by far the most famous. And rightly so, since he was the first there to begin teaching both Greek and Latin literature with equal skill, both publicly and privately; a man, moreover, of the keenest scent <term>naribus emunctis: a Latin idiom for someone with sharp, discerning judgment</term> and the sharpest judgment. To me, he is so closely joined—both because of his extraordinary and multifaceted erudition and because of an incredible sweetness of character—that I do not know if I have ever had a closer necessity or a more pleasant intimacy with any mortal. 

I remember him saying once in those literary conversations of ours that the word *keporos* (gardener) in the proverb from Gellius did not please him at all; it seemed clearly substituted and counterfeit. He suspected—as many things are corrupted in that author—that in place of *moros* (a fool), some "gardener" or other had slipped in that *keporos*. At that time, although it seemed very likely and the judgment of such a learned man carried great weight with me, I still did not dare to dissent alone against such a consensus of manuscripts. 

But while I was wandering up and down through the Greek authors, by a stroke of luck, in certain collections—bearing no author's title, but appearing to be either by Stobaeus or certainly excerpted from him—I found a verse of this kind cited from a tragedy of Aeschylus entitled *The Phrygians*:
*Pollaki toi kai moros aner katakairion eipe.* <note>original Greek: Πολλάκι τοι καὶ μωρὸς ἀνὴρ κατακαίριον εἶπε.</note> that is,
Often even a fool has spoken opportunely.

Therefore, I go over entirely to the side of my friend Bombasius <note>literally "I walk into his feet," a Roman voting metaphor</note>, and I advise all the learned that *moros* (fool) should be read instead of *keporos* (gardener), especially because the same sentiment is now commonly expressed in these very words: "A wise saying sometimes proceeds from a foolish man." It responds to that which we cited above from Euripides:
*Mora gar moros legei.* <note>original Greek: Μωρὰ γὰρ μωρὸς λέγει.</note> that is,
For a fool speaks foolish things.
For although this is truly said, it happens sometimes that a fool, either by chance or unawares, says something excellently and vehemently suited to the matter. This is something we see happening frequently. For what could have been said more fittingly, even by the most deceptive man, than what Suetonius records as being said by a certain man of unsound mind regarding Pompey and Julius Caesar: "Hail King, hail Queen." This was at a time when Pompey was suffering from the envy of affecting a kingdom, and there was a rumor that Caesar had served as a wife to King Nicomedes.

***

->The Horn of Plenty.<-

*Amaltheias keras.* <note>original Greek: Ἀμαλθείας κέρας.</note> i.e., The Horn of Plenty (Cornucopia). When we signify that all things exist in abundance, we say "the horn of plenty." It is translated from a very ancient fable which is told in various ways among authors. Some tell it in this manner: Rhea, having given birth to Jupiter, hid the infant in Crete for fear of his father <note>Saturn/Cronus, who ate his children</note>, to be nourished by two nymphs, Adrastea and Ida, the daughters of Melisseus. They nursed him with the milk of a certain goat whose name was Amalthea. Jupiter, when grown, placed this goat among the stars, and she is called by the Greeks *aix ourania*, that is, the heavenly goat. He gave one of her horns to the nurse-nymphs as a reward for their service, adding this power: that whatever they wished for would sprout forth in abundance from that horn. Ovid, in the fifth book of the *Fasti*, tells the story a little differently in this way:

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 6

->r<-
<meta>catchword: LIFE,</meta>

Amalthea, the noble one of Cretan Ida,
<unclear>Is said</unclear> to have hidden Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> in the woods.
<unclear>To her</unclear> belonged the beautiful mother of two kids <note>young goats</note>,
<unclear>Visible</unclear> among the Dictaean flocks,
<unclear>With horns</unclear> reaching for the air and curved back upon her shoulders,
<unclear>With an udder</unclear> such as the nurse of Jove ought to have.
<unclear>She fought</unclear> against the god, but broke her horn against a tree,
<unclear>And was</unclear> shorn of half her beauty.
<unclear>The nymph</unclear> took this up, wreathed it with lovely herbs,
<unclear>And full</unclear> of fruit, she brought it to the lips of Jove.
<unclear>He</unclear> attained the heights of heaven, and on his father's throne
<unclear>He sat</unclear>, and nothing was greater than the unconquered Jove,
<unclear>When</unclear> he made his nurse, and the nurse's fertile horn,
<unclear>Into that</unclear> which even now bears the name of its mistress.
<note>original Latin: "Amalthea, Cretaea nobilis Ida..." This poem recounts the myth of the goat Amalthea whose horn became the Cornucopia.</note>

<unclear>Achelous</unclear> is also said to have given the Horn of Plenty to Hercules and the people of Aetolia, because the horn of the river Achelous had been restrained <note>referring to the taming of the river's flow</note>: whereby he rendered that region, previously sterile, most fertile. The horn, for its part, signifies the hardness of the earth, and the fruits signify its fertility. Therefore, a certain Phocion, a Peripatetic philosopher, gave this title to his book, as Aulus Gellius testifies. Pliny likewise shows that the Greeks were accustomed to place this overly arrogant inscription upon their commentaries, as if nothing were not contained within them, and anything whatever could be sought and received from there. Lucian, in *On Those Who Serve for Wages*: "And you said it was a horn of Amalthea, and you shall milk the milk of birds." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ἔφης δ᾽ ἀμαλθείας κέρας, καὶ ἀμελξεας ὀρνίθων γάλα."</note> That is, you shall have a horn of plenty, and you shall milk "hen's milk." Philostratus calls the sophist Dion a "horn of Amalthea," as one polished in every kind of virtue. A certain slave in Plautus calls a particular letter a "horn of plenty," because the greatest advantages could be taken from it. Aulus Gellius, in Book 14, Chapter 6: "And at the same time he gives me a book of great volume, overflowing, as he himself said, with all kinds of learning. I receive it eagerly and gladly, as if I had obtained a horn of plenty." Athenaeus calls the second course of a meal, furnished with various delicacies, a "horn of plenty." A verse of this kind is cited by Suidas:
"The goat's horn of Amalthea provides me with all things for life." <note>original Greek: "Πάντα μοι βίῳ ὅδην ἀμαλθείας κέρας αἰγὸς."</note>
It is a heroic adage. This adage is also expressed in this way: "the heavenly goat." <note>original Greek: "αἲξ οὐρανία."</note> An old comedy notes a certain Polyagrus, who prostituted his wife for gain, whom he calls a "heavenly goat" on account of the immense profit, as Plutarch testifies in his commentaries *On Listening to the Poets*: "Fortunate Polyager (that is, the possessor of many fields), who nourishes a heavenly goat that brings him wealth." <note>original Greek: "Εὐδαίμων πολυαγρὸς οὐρανίαν αἶγα πλησφόρον τρέφων."</note> The same author says elsewhere against the Stoics: "But he who has obtained the Stoic Amalthea," <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ τὴν σωινίαν λαβὼν ἀμάλθειαν."</note> mocking the paradoxes of the Stoics, who attribute everything—wealth, freedom, health, and kingship—to their "wise man." Horace in his *Odes*:
"May Plenty bring her full horn."

### Hen's milk. III

"Milk of birds" <note>original Greek: "Ὄρνιθων γάλα."</note> has the same meaning. For it is said of the wealthy, for whom anything whatever is supplied. Or of things rare to find, and for that reason precious: so that it is a hyperbole signifying that nothing at all is lacking. Pliny, in the preface to his *Natural History*, mocking certain faulty and magnificent inscriptions of the Greeks, says: "They inscribed it *Cerion*, which they want to be understood as a honeycomb; others *the horn of Amalthea*, which is the horn of plenty, as if one could drink 'hen's milk' from the volume." Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
"By Hercules, I would drink hen's
milk, I would take it for my life, which you now take from me."
<note>original Greek: "Πίνων δ᾽ ἂν ὀρνίθων γάλα..."</note>
Eustathius, in his commentary on the fourth book of the *Odyssey*, cites this adage from a play by Anaxagoras titled *The Eggs*. Aristophanes the comic poet mentions it in the play titled *The Birds*:
"So that for all, for themselves, for their children, and their children's children,
Wealth-health, happiness..."

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Life, safety, youth, laughter,
Dances, feasts, and bird’s milk,
So that you all may be weary <gloss>from the abundance of good things.</gloss> that is,

We shall give to you yourselves, to your children, and to your children’s children, an opulence of good health, happiness, resources, peace, youth, laughter, dances, festivals, and bird’s milk, so that you will be burdened by the very plenty of these good things. Strabo, in the fourteenth book of his *Geography*, relates concerning the lands of the Samians <note>Inhabitants of the island of Samos</note> that because they were so abundantly fertile in all things, it was a common saying that they even produced "bird’s milk." He also testifies that this adage is found in the works of the comic poet Menander. Athenaeus, in the ninth book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned," a famous collection of ancient lore</note>, cites these iambic verses from a certain writer of Middle Comedy named Mnesimachus, <gloss>and as the saying goes,</gloss>
Bird’s milk is available, a rare thing,
And a pheasant well-plucked of its feathers. that is, And as the proverb says,
Milk is supplied—a rare thing—from a bird, and
A pheasant properly stripped of its plumage. Again, in book nine, he cites from Numenius,
Nor that which they call the milk of birds. that is,
And that which is called the milk of a hen.
The same author indicates in his third book that for some, "bird’s milk" refers to the white of an egg.

->I do not sleep for everyone.<- <sig>IIII</sig>

Those who do not serve everyone, nor accommodate themselves to everyone in all matters, are said "not to sleep for everyone." They think the metaphor is taken from certain overly compliant husbands who knowingly abandon their wives to adulterers, meanwhile feigning sleep over their cups so that the adulterer may do as he pleases. Juvenal, noting this kind of compliance, says:
> Skilled, he says, at staring at the ceiling,
> And skilled at snoring through his nose into his cup while wide awake.

Plutarch, in the book he titled <term>Erotikos</term> <note>A dialogue on Love</note>, tells a rather witty story on this matter. When a certain Galba had received Maecenas <note>The famous patron of the arts and friend of Augustus</note> at a banquet, and perceived from his nods that the man was inflamed with passion for his wife, he gradually lowered his head as if he were sleeping. But when, in the meantime, a certain servant approached the table and tried to steal the wine secretly, Galba—now wide awake and watchful—cried out: "You wretch, did you not know that I sleep for Maecenas alone?" Festus Pompeius mentions this adage and explains it in the manner I have described, citing Lucilius and showing it was drawn from a certain Cappius, who was nicknamed *Pararencho* because he used to feign sleep so that his wife might commit adultery with impunity. He indicates that Lucilius also mentions this. Marcus Tullius Cicero also uses it in the seventh book of his *Letters to Friends*: "Once it was 'I do not sleep for everyone,' but for me, my dear Gallus, it is 'I do not serve everyone.'" Cicero seems to indicate that the one—namely, "I do not sleep for everyone"—was old, while the other—"I do not serve everyone"—was new. Both are certainly proverbial, but the former pertains to a concession of rights, while the latter pertains to the rendering of service. The same Cicero says in the thirteenth book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "It is a fine thing to hate someone freely and, as the saying goes, not to serve everyone." This passage, if I may mention it in passing, does not seem to me to be free of error. Perhaps it was written: "And just as one does not sleep for everyone, so one does not serve everyone." Indeed, this very word "to serve" is not without metaphor when we say: to serve the stage, to serve the time, to serve vices, to serve a wife’s temperament, to serve the people, or to serve private interests—meaning to do everything possible to satisfy them.

->Sardinians for sale.<- <sig>V</sig>

<term>Sardanioi onioi.</term> <note>Greek: Σαρδάνιοι ὤνιοι</note> i.e., Sardinians for sale. In that little book titled *On Illustrious Men*, which some attribute to Pliny and others to Suetonius (though the style of both argues against it), a proverb of this sort is recorded: "Sardinians for sale," used for a business of infinite length and inextricable complexity. They say it arose from the fact that Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, when he had subdued Sardinia during his second consulship, brought back so many captives from there that the long-drawn-out sale passed into a proverb. Plutarch, in his *Roman Questions*, offers another reason: namely, that a solemn custom once grew up among the Romans that those who put on games in the Capitol would announce "Sardinians for sale," and a certain boy would come forward in mockery wearing a *bulla* <note>A protective amulet worn by Roman children</note>. He thinks this custom arose because the Veientes, a people of the Etruscans, had waged war with Romulus for a long time, and Romulus eventually captured their city. Even if Titus Livius relates in his first book that the Veientes were indeed conquered by Romulus,

# SIXTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

...but nevertheless, the victor refrained from attacking the fortified city. For this reason, he declared both the king himself and the very many captives led back to Rome to be "for sale." Furthermore, since the Etruscans were under the <unclear>jurisdiction</unclear> of the Lydians (as Herodotus also testifies in Book I), and the <unclear>capital</unclear> of the Lydians was Sardis, it happened from this that they declared the Etruscans for sale under the name of "Sardians." Plutarch <unclear>relates</unclear> the same in his *Life of Romulus*, though somewhat differently. He says that after the Veientes were defeated, their <unclear>captive</unclear> leader—who, being of advanced age, was seen to have conducted the matter more imprudently than his <unclear>age</unclear> warranted—was mocked. From this, the custom grew that whenever the Romans sacrificed a <unclear>victim</unclear> for a victory won, they would lead an old man dressed in purple through the forum to the Capitol, with a *bulla* <note>A protective amulet worn by Roman boys</note> hanging from his <unclear>neck</unclear> (which was then the badge of children), and the herald would proclaim "Sardians for sale!" Veii is the capital of Etruria, and the Etruscans are thought to be colonists of the Sardians. Marcus Tullius Cicero used this <unclear>adage</unclear> in the seventh book of his *Letters to Friends*, writing to Gallus: "You have," he says, "Sardians <unclear>for sale</unclear>, each one more wicked than the last." Cicero means this regarding despicable and dishonest people, and (unless I am mistaken) <unclear>also</unclear> regarding the actual Sardinians. For he writes a little before this passage: "I count that as profit, not <unclear>only</unclear> a man more pestilential than his own country."

->The shaggy-foot desires meat. VI<-

<term>Δασύπους κρεῶν ἐπιθυμεῖ</term> <note>Greek: Dasypous kreon epithymei</note>. That is, "The shaggy-foot <note>A poetic or technical name for a hare or rabbit</note> desires meat." It is said against those who seek <unclear>things</unclear> which they already have in abundance at home. For the *dasypus* is of the genus of hares. Now the hare, <unclear>according to</unclear> Pliny in Book VIII, chapter 55, is an innocent animal, good for eating, fertile, and born to be the prey of all. It is the only animal besides the *dasypus* that practices superfetation <note>Conceiving a second litter while already pregnant</note>, <unclear>having</unclear> one offspring ready, another in the womb covered with fur, another featherless <note>Erasmus/Pliny likely mean "hairless" here</note>, and another in the very beginning of birth. It is <unclear>called</unclear> a *dasypus* because of its hairy and shaggy feet.

->You are a hare yourself, yet you seek choice meat. VII<-

There are <unclear>those</unclear> who think this is the same as the previous one, which is read in Terence's *The Eunuch*: "You <unclear>yourself</unclear> are a hare, and yet you seek choice meat." It was said by a boastful soldier to an <unclear>effeminate</unclear> youth who was playing with his mistress, though he himself was of an age where he could have served as a mistress. Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence</note> explains the allegory in various ways, indicating that this proverb fits the "soft" <note>effeminate or weak</note> because the hare provides choice meat from its hind parts—that is, from the loins and buttocks—and is most delicious in that part of the body; or because dogs follow it like lovers; or because the hare is said by naturalists to be of uncertain sex, sometimes male, sometimes female. These <unclear>commentaries</unclear> seem rather cold to me, and I think it is truer and simpler to refer it to the Greek proverb, <term>Δασύπους κρεῶν ἐπιθυμεῖ</term> <note>The shaggy-foot desires meat</note>. Flavius Vopiscus, writing on the Emperor Numerian, says that this line in Terence actually belongs to Livius Andronicus, the oldest of the Roman comic poets.

->In an equal yoke. VIII<-

Pliny used the <term>term</term> "In an equal yoke" in his *Letters* to mean "with equal zeal and equal effort." It will apply <unclear>to those</unclear> who carry out a common business with shared rivalry and similar exertion. It is a metaphor taken from oxen <unclear>who</unclear> pull a wagon with an equal yoke. Pliny's words are these: "Glory indeed has, especially in <unclear>studies</unclear>, something <term>ἀκοινώνητον</term> <note>Greek: akoinoneton - unshared or solitary</note>; yet for us there was no contest, no struggle, and each of us strove in an equal yoke, not for himself, but for the cause." Theocritus says in *The Beloved*:
> <term>ἀλλήλους δ' ἐφίλησαν ἴσῳ ζυγῷ</term> <note>Greek: allelous d' ephilesan iso zygo</note>. That is,
> <term>They loved each other with an equal yoke</term>.
This refers to mutual and equal love, which the Greeks call <term>ἀντέρωτα</term> <note>Greek: anterota - reciprocal love</note>. Close to this are the things Saint Jerome writes to Augustine: "There are said to be very many in Rome who are able and dare to meet with you, and in the discussion of the <unclear>divine</unclear> scriptures, pull the yoke equally." There is also a Greek proverb:
> <term>ἐγὼ καὶ σὺ ταὐτὸν ἕλκομεν ζυγὸν</term> <note>Greek: ego kai sy tauton helkomen zygon</note>. That is,
> <term>Both I and you pull the same yoke together</term>. Which we shall discuss in its proper place.

->To embrace in one bundle. IX<-

The <term>term</term> "To embrace in one bundle" is read in the same Pliny, meaning to do something with the same labor and at the <unclear>same</unclear> time, not separately. "We feared," he says, "lest the day, the night, or our own strength should <unclear>fail</unclear> us, if we were to embrace so many crimes and so many defendants in one bundle, as it were." It is a metaphor taken from those <unclear>who</unclear> gather many things together at once so they can be carried more conveniently. The Greeks call this <term>συλλήβδην</term> <note>Greek: syllebdyn</note>, that is, "comprehensively."

->Do not pass by the salt and the table. X<-

<term>Ἅλα καὶ τράπεζαν μὴ παραβαίνειν</term> <note>Greek: Hala kai trapezan me parabainein</note>. That is, "Do not pass by the salt and the table." Do not neglect <unclear>friendship</unclear> and intimacy, or: Do not violate the laws of friendship. For by these things friends were once united...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM: ADAGES

friends: and in ancient times, close associates frequently held mutual banquets among themselves. This is also testified by Diogenes Laertius in his *Life of Pythagoras*. Theocritus also agrees in his poem *Hylas*,
<note>original: οἱ μίαν ἄμφω ἑταῖροι ἀεὶ δαίνυντο τράπεζαν</note>
"Both companions always feasted at a single table."
That is, they both used to dine at the same table, faithful as friends indeed. He is speaking here of Hercules and Telamon. Then, in Euripides' *Hecuba*, when she is exaggerating the crime of Polymnestor, she also makes mention of the table of hospitality:
<note>original: Κοινῆς τραπέζης πολλάκις τυχὼν ἐμοί</note>
"Having often shared a common table with me."
Indeed, in the first book of Ezra, chapter four, we read: "Now because we are mindful of the salt which we have eaten in the palace, and because we count it a crime to see the king’s dishonor," etc. <note>Erasmus refers to the ancient custom where eating a ruler's salt implied a bond of loyalty.</note> From this comes the fact that (as Alexander teaches in his *Pythagorean Commentaries* found in the same Laertius) Pythagoras forbade the breaking of bread, clearly so that what joined friends together should not be severed. He also judged that salt should especially be placed on the table, because it reminds us of equity and justice; for salt preserves and protects whatever it takes hold of, and it is created from the clearest of things: water and the sea. Origen, in his work *Against Celsus*, book two, brings forward a certain iambic poet <note>Archilochus</note> who attacked Lycambes because he had "transgressed the salt and the table." Origen twists this to refer to Judas, the betrayer of Christ. The same author, writing on Matthew, says this of Judas: "He was mindful of neither the same salt, nor the table, nor the shared bread." And I do not know whether Christ himself, the prince of our religion, alluded to this; for he seems to have intended to hide his deepest mysteries in the most common things, foreknowing that this symbol, though mocked by the Jews, would be embraced by the nations. Certainly, among the Macedonians, by ancestral rite, they entered into a covenant which they wished to be held most sacred by tasting bread divided by a sword. The authority for this is Quintus Curtius in his eighth book.

### XI. Like a Bacelus.

<note>original: Ἰκελῷ Βακήλῳ, καὶ Βάκηλος εἶ</note> "Like a Bacelus," and "You are a Bacelus." This was said against <term>catamites</term> <note>men who took a passive role in same-sex relations</note> and those who were insufficiently manly, or against those who were large in body but stupid in mind. It is drawn from the statues of a certain Bacelus. Suidas says that *Bacelus* properly signifies one who has been castrated, and therefore it is said of the "soft" <note>effeminate</note>, because that class of men suffers most from this defect. Antiphanes, in his play *The Carians*, censures a certain Bacelus in Athenaeus, book four:
<note>original: οὐχ ὁρᾷς ὀρχούμενον / Ταῖς χερσὶ τὸν Βάκηλον, οὐδ’ αἰσχύνεται;</note>
"Do you not see the Bacelus dancing thus with his hands, and he is not ashamed?"
Suetonius mentions this in his *Life of Augustus*, writing that he was accustomed to use this peculiar word, *Bacelus*, constantly to mean a "fool," although in common manuscripts it is written as *Baccolus*. Hermolaus thinks that in Quintilian, *Bacelus* can be rightly read instead of *Bagoas*. The words of Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> are these: "But truly, the most famous sculptors and painters, when they desired to depict or mold the most beautiful bodies, never fell into this error of taking some Bagoas or Megabyzus as a model for their work." <note>Bagoas and Megabyzus were famous Persian eunuchs.</note> Truly, I do not see why the writing of Fabius should be changed, since *Bagoas* in the barbarian tongue signifies a eunuch, by which name Lucian introduces a certain philosopher who displayed the face and body-shape of a eunuch. Indeed, Ovid in his *Loves* calls the slave guarding a girl "Bagous":
"Bagous, who has the care of guarding your mistress."

### XII. Batalus.

<note>original: Βάταλος</note> That is, "You are a Batalus." Formerly, this was said as an insult against the effeminate. Plutarch shows that this nickname was given to Demosthenes as a boy and was cast at him as a reproach by his enemies. Furthermore, he brings forward various reasons for this nickname: either because a certain Batalus was a flute-player, soft and effeminate, who was the first of all to come onto the stage in women's sandals and who, so to speak, "unmanned" music; or because a certain obscene poet had the name Batalus; or because among the Athenians, *Batalus* was the name for a part of the body that cannot be named with modesty. Libanius mentions this matter. Indeed, the same Demosthenes in his later years was called *Argas* with a similar insult: either because there was someone of this name who was the author of evil laws, or because, as Suidas thinks...

# SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

<note>original: "Argas"</note> Argas is a kind of serpent. The Greeks also use the term <note>original: "βαταλίζεσθαι" (batalizesthai)</note> "to live like Batalus" for those who live in a shameful and effeminate manner.

---

<margin>XIII</margin>
### He has struck the wagon well.

"He has struck the wagon well" is a rustic proverb. It appears to be commonly said of those who give a push to something that was already leaning of its own accord. It is a metaphor taken from loaded wagons which, by the very weight they carry, are prone to being overturned. This happens more easily in the direction toward which they are already inclining due to sloping ground. Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian and teacher of St. Jerome</note> pointed out this adage when explaining the words of Parmeno in the *Eunuch*: "Now you have struck me down." Not far from this sentiment is that line of Plautus in the *Curculio*: "He who advises is almost like one who helps." These are the words of a pimp who was already quite ready to keep his word, but was urged on by the banker—an act that was done as if the advisor wasn't even needed. Sophocles expressed the same idea elegantly, as cited by Plutarch in the *Life of Artaxerxes*:
<margin><note>original: "Τὰ φαῦλα δ’ ἐπ’ ἢ κακῶν ὁδοιπορεῖ"</note></margin> That is:
> Persuasion is easy for all evil things. Most people are inclined toward the worse.

---

<margin>XIV</margin>
### The danger is in the Carian.

<margin>"The danger is in the Carian." That is, "make the danger in the Carian": meaning, perform a dangerous experiment on a person or a thing of little value, so that if it turns out poorly, there is not much loss to be suffered. From this, the customs of the Carians gave rise to the adage. This people, according to Pomponius, is of uncertain origin; some consider them <note>original: "αὐτόχθονας"</note> "autochthons" (indigenous), while others think they are Pelasgian Curetes. They were a race so fond of arms and fighting that they were accustomed to serve even for foreign pay as mercenaries. Hence Theocritus in the *Encomium of Ptolemy*: "to the Carians greedy for battle."</margin>
From this, the customs of the Carians gave rise to the adage. This people, according to Pomponius, is of uncertain origin; some consider them indigenous, while others think they are Pelasgian Curetes. They were a race so fond of arms and fighting that they were accustomed to serve even for foreign pay as mercenaries. Hence Theocritus in the *Encomium of Ptolemy*:
> To the Carians greedy for battle.

<margin>"And if he is a slave and a Carian."</margin>
Herodotus in *Euterpe* shows that the Carians were of a barbarian and servile disposition, ready to endure anything if pay was offered. Aristophanes indicates the same in *The Birds*. Strabo, in the fourteenth book of his *Geography*, relates that the Carians once wandered throughout all Greece, earning wages everywhere as mercenaries. Furthermore, they so excelled in military matters that throughout the poets, weapons of war are called "Carian." For instance, Anacreon spoke of a "Carian breastplate" and Alcaeus of a "Carian crest," to which Aristophanes alludes in *The Birds*. Suidas writes that the Carians were the first of mortals to serve for pay, as they held their own lives cheap. Therefore, those who had hired them were accustomed to put the Carians first in danger, so that they might receive the first attacks of the enemy at their own peril; or wherever the war seemed most difficult, they were thrown into the fray. The Persians in their own language called them <note>original: "κάρδας" (kardas)</note> "Kardas," because they used them as low-value things. In these times, the Swiss <note>original: "Eluetij"</note> seem to emulate the reputation of the Carians; a people otherwise simple in war and by no means an evil sort of men. Indeed, I believe they would be worthy to be free of this reputation and to flourish excellently in other honorable studies, if they would leave wars behind and turn their minds to such things.

<margin>"But if you young men are afraid, let the danger be in me as if in a Carian. Since I am an old man, I am willing to risk it, and I hand myself over to this Dionysodorus as if to Medea the Colchian. Let him destroy me, if he wishes, or boil me; let him do whatever he wants, provided he turns me out a good man." That is: "But if you young men... let the danger be in me as in a Carian."</margin>
Socrates uses this adage in Plato’s *Euthydemus*, submitting that the danger of transformation should happen to him rather than others, as if he were a lowly Carian: for if you lose him, the loss is not very heavy. "For since I am an old man, I am ready to undergo the danger, and I hand myself over to this Dionysodorus, just as to Medea of Colchis. Let him destroy me: and, if he wishes, let him cook me in a cauldron. Otherwise, let him do whatever he wants, so long as he makes me virtuous." He alluded to this same thing in the *Laches*, when he says: those who first begin to teach and make a trial of their art at the great risk of others are to be tested; not some hired Carian, but the children of citizens are being brought into difficulty.

<margin>"But now, having neglected this, and not making the trials on their own bodies." That is: "In the Carian, truly, not in their own bodies making the danger."</margin>
Aristides imitated this in his *Panathenaic Oration*. Marcus Tullius Cicero used the same in his speech *For Lucius Flaccus*: "What," he says, "of all Caria? Is it not a common saying in your own voice: 'If anything must be tried with danger, it should be done in Caria'?" It appears this passage is corrupted, and I would not fear to swear that it should read "in the Carian" <note>original: "in Care"</note>, not "in Caria." Opposite to this is the saying: "to fish with a golden hook," which we shall discuss elsewhere.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

<margin>15</margin>
->To learn the potter’s art on a large jar.<-

Likewise that saying, <note>original: "ἐν πίθῳ τὴν κεραμείαν μανθάνειν"</note> "to learn the potter’s art on a large jar." This is said of those who immediately take on the greatest matters as experiments for their skill, when it is more proper to proceed gradually from small things to the highest. For a potter does not begin his craft immediately with a large jar—that is, a very large vessel—but with certain tiny vessels, in which there is no heavy loss if something goes wrong. Plato uses this sentiment in the *Laches*: <note>original: "Σκοπεῖν χρὴ μὴ ὃν τῷ περὶ ἡμῶν ὁ κίνδυνος κινδυνεύηται..."</note> "We ought to consider lest this danger be undertaken by us, not on a Carian <note>The Carians were considered cheap mercenaries; to "risk a Carian" meant to experiment on something of little value.</note>, but on our sons and the children of our friends; and that it plainly happens to us as the proverb says: the pottery-work on a large jar." 

Dicaearchus twists the proverb toward another meaning, to warn that every craftsman ought to be exercised in his own business: such as a charioteer in driving chariots, a pilot in steering a ship, a doctor in curing diseases. As if it were absurd for a potter to be occupied in chariot-driving—a matter clearly foreign to him—and not rather with the jar. And so that sentiment pertains here: 
"Let each man practice the art which he knows." 
And that passage from Horace in his *Epistles*: 
"He who is ignorant of a ship fears to sail it; 
None dares give southernwood <note>a medicinal herb</note> to the sick 
Unless he has learned how. What belongs to doctors, 
Doctors promise; smiths handle smiths' tools. 
But we, unlearned and learned alike, write poems everywhere." 

Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> uses it in a similar way in his *Apology for his Flight*: <note>original: "ὡς τόγε παιδεύειν ἄλλους ἐπιχειρεῖν..."</note> "Thus to wish to teach others before they themselves are sufficiently taught, and to practice piety in the souls of others—the 'pottery on a large jar' as they say—seems to me to be the mark of remarkably foolish men."

<margin>16</margin>
->Let the shoemaker not go beyond his sandal.<-

Bordering on this is the saying, "Let the shoemaker not go beyond his sandal." That is, let no one attempt to judge those things which are foreign to his own art and profession. This adage indeed arose from Apelles, the most noble painter. Concerning him, Pliny writes in Book 35, Chapter 10, in this manner: "He used to display his finished works on a porch to those passing by, and hiding behind the panel itself, he would listen to the faults that were noted, preferring the public as a more diligent judge than himself. They say he was rebuked by a shoemaker because he had made one fewer loop inside the sandals. The next day, when the same man, arrogant because of the correction of his previous warning, began to cavil about the leg, Apelles indignantly looked out and denounced him, saying that the shoemaker should not judge above the sandal." Which itself passed into a proverb. Thus far Pliny. 

Very similar to this is what Athenaeus relates. Stratonicus the cithara-player <note>a professional lyre player</note> said to a blacksmith contending with him about music: "Do you not feel that you are speaking beyond your hammer?" To the same point pertains what his grandson wrote in his letters: that no one judges rightly of a craft unless he is himself a craftsman. And what Aristotle said in the first book of the *Ethics*: "Each man is a fit judge of those things in which he is educated." And what he also wrote in the second book of the *Physics*: "A blind man disputing about colors." These words have now passed into a proverb among the scholars of our time, whenever someone disputes about unknown things. To the same sentiment must be referred what Fabius Pictor says in Quintilian: "Arts would be happy if only artists judged them."

<margin>17</margin>
->The gods help those who act.<-

Varro, in the first book of *On Agriculture*: "And since, as they say, the gods help those who act, I will first invoke the gods." It signifies that divine help is accustomed to be an aid not to the idle, but to the industrious and those striving to the best of their manly ability. To this I think should be referred that Homeric verse, which has now passed as if into a proverb: 
<note>original: "Τηλέμαχ’ ἄλλα μὲν αὐτὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶ σῇσι νοήσεις..."</note>
"Telemachus, some things you will perceive yourself in your own heart, 
And other things a divinity will suggest to you." 
Marcus Tullius [Cicero] used this in the ninth book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "Everything must be done by you while unprepared. But nevertheless, 'Some things you yourself, and other things a divinity will suggest.'" That is, 
Partly...

### With Minerva, move your hand as well.
<margin>XVIII</margin>
A neighboring proverb is, *With Athena, move your hand as well* <note>original: σὺν Ἀθηνᾷ καὶ χεῖρα κίνει</note>. That is, while Minerva helps, move your hand in the meantime. The adage warns us not to slacken our own industry through trust in divine aid. It is particularly suited to women who practice wool-working, who indeed favor and invoke Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and crafts</note>, but nonetheless apply themselves intensely to the work in the meantime. There are those who think it originated from a certain mule-driver whose cart was stuck fast in the mud; while he ought to have helped it, he idly implored Hercules. The god replied that he should move his hand to the laboring donkey in the meantime, and only then would he be of help. Others bring a different story to this: namely, that a certain man, when he was about to compete, consulted Minerva whether he would depart as the victor. The answer was that he would. When he entered the theater and stood with idle hands during the contest, he was struck by his opponent and defeated. To this adage belongs that most elegant verse which Aristotle cites from a tragedy of Agathon in the fifth book of the *Eudemian Ethics*: *Fortune loves art, and art loves fortune in turn* <note>original: ἡ τύχη ἐρᾷ τῇ, καὶ τύχη τέχνην</note>. In Suidas, this six-foot line <note>term: senarius — a common meter in Latin and Greek drama</note> carries the same meaning: *First do something yourself, then call upon the god* <note>original: πρῶτον δρῶν, εἶτα τὸν θεὸς κάλει</note>.

### By our own Mars.
<margin>XIX</margin>
When we are aided by no outside help, but accomplish a matter by our own wit and our own strengths, we are said to accomplish it by our own Mars <note>Mars was the god of war; here "Mars" represents one's own fighting spirit or effort</note>. Or even when a matter is conducted at our own risk. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the third book of *On Duties*: "Therefore we shall fill this remaining part with no supports, but, as they say, by our own Mars." Thus far he spoke. The same man in the second *Philippic*, speaking of Deiotarus: "For the King, of his own accord, with no notes from Caesar, as soon as he heard of his death, recovered his lands by his own Mars." In the Code, second book, title *That it be not permitted to the more powerful*, first chapter: "The Divine Claudius, a most learned prince and our parent, established a decree that those who had called upon the patronage of the more powerful should be punished by the loss of their case, so that by this proposal, judicial lawsuits should run their course by their own Mars rather than leaning on the protection of powerful houses." Again in book three, title *On Judgments*, chapter eleven: "That must undoubtedly be observed, that it should not be the fault of either litigating party, nor the judges, that a lawsuit does not run its course by its own Mars, but by the license of the advocates, it is given to the judge." It seems to be translated from generals who sustain a war by their own auspices and resources; indeed Plautus said "by my own resources" instead of "by my own Mars." These phrases also savor of the proverb: *By a varied Mars*, *By an equal Mars*, *By an unfavorable Mars*. Almost the opposite of this adage is that which we have recorded elsewhere: *Not without Theseus* <note>original: οὐκ ἄνευ Θησέως — meaning one had help from a great hero</note>.

### He is wise in vain, who is not wise for himself.
<margin>XX</margin>
Even today it is a most frequently tossed-about saying among the common people: "He is wise in vain, who is not wise for himself." Plato in the *Greater Hippias* says: "And it seems to many that it is not a wise man who is not especially wise for himself" <note>original: Καὶ πολλοῖς... σωθῆναι, ὅτι οὐ σοφὸν, ᾧ οὐ αὐτῷ μάλιστα δὲ σοφός</note>. Cicero also uses it in a certain letter to Trebatius, showing it was taken from a tragedy: "And when," he says, "I began to act Medea, always remember that: The wise man who cannot be of use to himself, is wise in vain." This is a trochaic verse. The same man in the thirteenth book of *Letters to Friends*, to Caesar the Emperor: "And so from the grandiloquence of Homer I betake myself to the true precepts of Euripides: I hate the wise man who is not wise for himself" <note>original: μισῶ, ὃς οὐ αὐτῷ σοφός</note>. The old man Praecilius praises this verse excellently. The same man in the first book *On Divination* cites from the poets: "Those who are not wise for their own selves, show the way to another. From those to whom they promise riches, they themselves seek drachmas." It is cited by Lucian in the *Apology*: "For I hate the man who is not wise for himself." Alexander twisted this against Callisthenes, who did not adapt himself to the customs of those with whom he lived, but made it known that nothing of what was done there pleased him. And that liberty brought ruin to a great man, while Anaxarchus the philosopher, the most absolute of all flatterers, was held in high esteem. The men of this present age follow this sentiment so perfectly to the nail <note>term: ad unguem — a sculptor's term meaning "to perfection"</note>,

Of this kind is that line in Suetonius: *Look upon Sulla, Romulus, who is lucky for himself, not for you.* <note>original: "Aspice felicem sibi, non tibi, Romule Syllam." A jab at the Roman dictator Sulla, suggesting his "good fortune" benefited only himself at the expense of the state.</note>

### 21. A gelding in the ditch.

*A gelding in the ditch*: a rustic proverb, but one born from military affairs. This may be used whenever someone is dragged into a task for which they are in no way suited. Or where a matter is violently hindered or dangerous. It is recorded by Titus Livius <note>Livy</note> in the third book of his third decade. He relates that when Fabius was besieging Capua during the Second Punic War, Jubellius Taurea, the most noble among the Campanian knights, challenged anyone from the Roman army to single combat, and Claudius Asellus dared to step forward. Then, when each had eluded the other for a long time in the open field, the Campanian ordered them to descend into a hollow road <note>a "sunken lane" or ditch</note>, saying that otherwise it would be a contest of horses, not of horsemen. When the Roman, more fierce in deed than in word, immediately descended there, Taurea again eluded him with a speech which afterwards turned into a rustic proverb: *You least know,* he said, *a gelding in the ditch.* Although the meaning of the adage is not entirely clear from Livy's words, it is easily grasped by conjecture. For it stands in opposition to that which we shall mention elsewhere: *the horse into the plain.* <note>original Greek: ὃν ἵππου εἰς πεδίον. A proverb for putting someone in their natural element.</note> For just as a horse is most powerful on the plain, so it is least powerful in a ditch.

### 22. The talents of Tantalus.

*The talents of Tantalus.* <note>original Greek: Τάλαντα ταντάλε.</note> Used of immense wealth. For Tantalus the Phrygian entered into the fables of men on account of his magnificent riches, so that it is even imagined that he suffers something similar in the underworld to what those tenacious rich men usually suffer amidst their heaped-up wealth. Horace says:
> *Thirsty Tantalus catches at the cups that flee from his lips—*
> *Why do you laugh? Change the name, and the story*
> *is told about you.*
He shows that the allegory of the fiction pertains to sordid rich men. The adage is used by Plato in the *Euthyphro*. Suidas says it is also found in Epicharmus and Anacreon. It is also expressed in this way, with a certain charming wordplay: *The talents of Tantalus he talent-weighs.* <note>original Greek: τάλαντα ταντάλε ταλανίζει. Erasmus is noting a pun on the name Tantalus and the verb for weighing/balancing money.</note> That is, he balances and accumulates. Furthermore, that Tantalus was exceedingly wealthy is testified even by that song from a tragedy in Plutarch’s book *On Exile*:
> *I sow fields a twelve-day journey long.* <note>original Greek: Σπείρω δ' ἀρούρας δώδεχ' ἡμέρων ὁδόν.</note>
The same author elsewhere calls huge riches *the wealth of Tantalus.* <note>original Greek: πλότου ταντάλου.</note> Antiphanes in Athenaeus, book six:
> *Such as Thribon once had, a man who was*
> *softly stripped of the very talents of Tantalus.*

### 23. The talents of Pelops.

With a similar figure, Theocritus in Idyll 9 spoke of the *talents of Pelops*:
> *May I have neither the lands of Pelops, nor golden talents,*
> *Nor may I outrun the blasts of the winds with my feet.*
Furthermore, among the Athenians, a <term>talent</term> <note>A massive unit of weight and currency.</note> was the largest sum of money. A small talent was worth sixty pounds; a great talent, eighty. Hence that line in the *Phormio*: *If someone were to give a great talent. Nay, a great evil.* And Aristophanes:
> *But I, an Opuntian,*
> *Would certainly not become one, even if someone gave me a talent of gold.*
That is, I would not wish to be one-eyed <note>The people of Opus were stereotyped as having eye ailments.</note> for any amount of money.

### 24. The riches of Midas.

*The wealth of Midas*, and *richer than Midas* <note>original Greek: Μίδ'ς πλοῦτος, καὶ μίδας πλουσιώτερος.</note> passed into a proverb because of the immense wealth of that king, which also gave rise to many fables. Statius in the *Surrentine Villa of Pollius*:

<meta>This page continues the first chiliad (thousand) of Erasmus's Adages, specifically the sixth century. It follows the discussion of wealth and transitions into the power of public reputation and the importance of finishing one's work.</meta>

# THE FIRST CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY

<margin>Richer than the treasures of Midas, and the gold of Lydia.</margin>
This Midas was a tyrant of Phrygia to whom, according to the fables of the poets, it was granted by the gods—after he had received Bacchus with hospitality—that he might choose whatever he wished, and would receive whatever he had chosen. He requested that whatever he touched with his body should immediately turn into gold. It is recorded by historians <note>original: "Historicorum liberoditum [liberatum] est"</note> that while he was a boy sleeping, ants piled grains of wheat into his mouth; the response of the oracles was that he would be the wealthiest of all mortals, and so it happened. Pliny gives him the first place among the remarkably wealthy in his thirty-third book.

->What the common people say is not entirely without reason. XXV<-

This is used as a proverb by Aristotle, and among the learned that noble sentiment of Hesiod long ago passed into a proverb: <note>original Greek: Φήμη δ' οὔτις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται... "No rumor is ever entirely lost which many people spread; she is herself a kind of goddess."</note> as Aristides says in his defense of Pericles, stating that whatever has been spread by the rumor of the people is not usually entirely in vain. This is found in the second volume of his work titled *Works and Days*:
<margin>Hesiod in *Works and Days*.</margin>
> No rumor is ever entirely lost which many people
> spread; she is herself a kind of goddess. That is:
> Take care to avoid the troublesome rumors of men.
> Fame is an evil; it arises and climbs most easily, but
> it is difficult to bear, and heavy to quiet once it has started.
> Indeed, no rumor that flies among the people
> perishes entirely in vain, because she herself is a deity.

This sentiment can be understood in two ways: either that what is widely publicized and approved by the consensus of the people does not seem to be entirely false; or that a rumor, even a false one, cannot be completely abolished once it has spread among the common folk. Therefore, he warns that we should take anxious care lest we happen to become a subject of common talk, even through false rashness. Moreover, when he called Fame a goddess, he felt the same as Homer, who in several places introduces his *Ossa* <note>The Greek personification of Rumor</note>; for so he calls the goddess herself. Virgil emulated this in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:
> And Fame goes through the cities,
> A foul goddess spread everywhere into the mouths of men.

->When you build a house, do not leave it unfinished. XXVI<-

Although no sentiment of this poet <note>Hesiod</note> has failed to pass into a proverb, I would more gladly review those which, because of their enigmatic wrapping, come closer to the appearance of a proverb; such is the kind from the same book I just cited:
<margin>Hesiod in *Works and Days*.</margin>
> When building a house, do not leave it unfinished,
> Lest the cawing, chattering crow sit upon it and croak. That is:
> And fabricating a house, do not leave it mutilated or raw,
> Lest the garrulous crowing crow sit upon it.

Proclus the interpreter warns that this passage is understood in two ways. To some, it seems the poet warns that everyone should take care to finish their dwelling before winter, lest they lack a place to ward off the discomfort of the cold. For winter is indicated by the symbol of the crow, which is a winter bird. Furthermore, while it is true at all other times, it is especially so in the winter months: <note>original Greek: οἶκός ἐστι φίλος, οἶκός ἐστι ἄριστος</note>
<margin>Proverb.</margin>
That is: *A home is dear, a home is best*, as the proverb goes. Others think it signifies that a building, once started, ought not to be left half-finished, lest you become a laughingstock to the public, and those passing by speak against you and criticize your fickleness for not completing what you began. Indeed, that this habit of speaking ill is peculiar to the common people is even testified by the parables of the Gospel <note>Likely referring to Luke 14:28-30 regarding the man who builds a tower without finishing it</note>. The poet wished to indicate that insolence of detractors through the crow, a garrulous and noisy bird; hence even the proverbial word
<margin>To croak.</margin>
*krozein* <note>Greek: κρώζειν</note> was derived. But Proclus himself prefers that we take it universally <note>original: "καθολικῶς"</note>: that a proper end must be imposed on every business we have once undertaken, so that nothing at all is lacking, and everything strives toward perfection. The further this is removed from simple speech, the more learned and proverbial it becomes. For instance, if someone were to exhort another not to grow idle in the study of letters, but to put the finishing touch on their laudable undertakings, lest they be a mockery to the public for ceasing what was well begun, they might cast this line of Hesiod at them:
> When building a house, do not leave it unfinished.
