# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Let not the croaking crow sit upon the fire-pot of meat. <note>original: "Μὴ πῦρ ἐφεζομένην κρεῶν λακέρυζα κορώνη." A line from Hesiod's Works and Days, warning against ill omens or perhaps greed.</note>

### XXVII. Do not snatch food from a chytropode before it is sacrificed.

There is also that enigmatic saying which follows immediately in that same passage:
"Nor from the unboiled chytropodes <note>original: "χυτροπόδων" - a three-legged cooking pot or tripod</note> should you take
Food to eat, nor should you wash." That is:
"Neither take food straight from the tripod
Before the sacrifice, nor eat after washing."
Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> also indicates that it was considered irreligious to eat food directly from the dish. For he writes in this manner in the second book of *On Ends*: "And yet we shall find that profligates are first of all so lacking in religion that they eat from the dish; secondly, they so little fear death that they have that line from the *Hymnis* <note>A lost play by Caecilius Statius</note> constantly in their mouths:
'Six months of life are enough for me, the seventh I pledge to the Underworld.'"
This is a trochaic verse. Suetonius, in his life of Vitellius, reveals that he was so profoundly and even unseasonably given to gluttony that even during a sacrifice, or on any journey, he never restrained himself from snatching the sacrificial entrails and grain almost directly from the altar fire, still dripping, or from the smoking victuals in the roadside taverns, whether they were from the day before or half-eaten. As far as the simple meaning is concerned, it teaches that we should not rush to take food like cattle, but should only eat if we have first offered the first-fruits to the gods. For in ancient times, as Plutarch records in his *Table Talk*, even the daily table was held among sacred things; therefore, when about to take food, they would consecrate the first-fruits <note>original: "τὰς ἀπαρχάς"</note> to the gods. And then, not indecorously or in a tumult, but with a certain religious feeling, they approached the banquet with washed hands, no differently than if attending a sacred feast. This custom lasts even today among well-mannered Christians. 

But it becomes more proverbial if we understand it to mean that our ministers or servants are not to be despoiled or inhumanly plundered, but rather a portion of money should be left for them to live on. Perhaps it might also apply to those who, with over-hasty greed, strive to carry off a benefit before it is proper: and in a sense to harvest the crop before the grain has ripened. For example, if someone should demand a legacy or a promise immediately and on the spot, when it would be more civil to remain silent for a few days; or if someone, having just obtained power, should immediately begin to despoil the people with taxes; or if someone should hasten to embrace a young bride before she is of age or before the wedding ceremonies have been observed. It is taken from the ritual of sacrifices, in which they used to feast in olden times. To this also pertains what we have related elsewhere from Athenaeus, book nine: "from the pan" <note>original: "ἀπ' τηγάνε"</note>—that is, from the frying pan. In book six he cites this six-foot verse from Pherecrates:
"He said he ate small fry from the frying pan."
Some used the word *teganon* for *lopas* <note>types of dishes or pans</note>, which the Ionians called *eganon*. From this comes the compound word *escharopeganon* <note>a pan for use on a brazier</note>. Thus Phrynichus in Athenaeus, book six: "It is sweet to take from the brazier-pan without a contribution" <note>original: "ἄνευ συμβολῶν" - i.e., a 'potluck' where you didn't pay your share</note>. That is, if nothing is to be paid, and if one is allowed to go free of charge. Again, elsewhere in the same author, from Archestratus: "Snatching from the spit." This is said of a woman who was reported to have devoured the sacred offerings before they were sacrificed. In the same book six, Anaxandrides says:
"The beautiful handiwork of painters,
Hanging in panels, is admired.
But this [food] is snatched solemnly from the dish,
And immediately vanishes from the frying pan."
In general, it can be applied to anyone who approaches a business irreverently and, as they say, with unwashed feet <note>a common adage meaning to start a task without proper preparation or respect</note>.

### XXVIII. This one is better.

Plutarch, in his *Greek Questions*, relates a certain proverb in this manner: "From what was the proverbial saying 'This one is mistress' <note>original: "αὕτη κυρία"</note> said? When Dinon the Tarentine was general, a man who was good in military affairs, while the citizens were voting on some opinion of his, as the herald announced the winning side, he himself, stretching out his right hand, said: 'This one is better' <note>original: "ἄδε κρείσσων"</note>. For so Theophrastus has recorded. How then did the herald there announce the..."

# SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

-> This one is the winner; this one is the majority, but this one is better. And the victory of the better over the lesser. <-

The sense of these words is roughly this, from which the following arose as a proverb: **This one is the winner.** Dinon of Tarentum <note>A general from the Greek colony of Tarentum in Italy</note>, a leader of the army and a man of first-rate courage as well as military skill, once gave his opinion in an assembly. When his view was rejected by the votes of the citizens, and the herald was announcing the opinion that had won by a show of hands, Dinon said: **"This one is better."** This is how Theophrastus recorded it. However, Apollodorus adds in his *Rhytinus* that when the herald replied, "But these opinions are more numerous," Dinon immediately countered, **"But these are better."** And so the opinion of the few was promulgated.

From these words, it is clear that this was a common saying used whenever people wanted to indicate that a particular counsel was superior or more useful, even if it seemed otherwise to the majority; or where those who were fewer in number outweighed the rest in influence. To demonstrate the matter with examples: the greatest part of the world measures happiness by pleasure and profit; very few embrace virtue. Beware lest the example of the multitude carry any weight, **for this [virtue] is superior.** <note>original Greek: ἄυτη γὰρ κρείσσων</note> Likewise: "There is almost no one in the prince's entire court who does not wish you well; but one man opposes you, who has such power everywhere that he acts as a tyrant over the prince himself. Therefore, if the matter depended on votes, you would have won; but **this one is sovereign.**" <note>original Greek: ἄυτη κυρία</note>

Furthermore, explaining that passage in Horace’s *Epodes* gently, as if pointing to the proverb with a finger:

> All the cursed city,
> Skill is better than the ignorant herd.

In many copies, it is read—corruptly, in my opinion—as "the victory of the stronger." <note>original: κρεσσόνων νικᾷ</note> If I am not mistaken, it should be corrected to "the victory of the better," <note>original: κρεσσόνων νικᾷ</note> that is, the victory of the more excellent. For the Ode is a public address which commands that a decision be made by the common votes of all. But if it cannot happen that what is best is approved by the multitude, at least let that opinion win which is superior, even if supported by the votes of the few.

To this end, Plato wrote in the first book of *Laws* that the most beautiful kind of wisdom is when the crowd yields to their superiors, and in deciding, the weight of the vote is considered more than the number. Plato's words from the book I mentioned are these: "In all cities where the judgments of the better overcome the multitude of the worse, that city may rightly be said to be superior to itself, because the cause of the most just wins in such a place; but the opposite happens where the opposite occurs." <note>original Greek: Ἐν ὁπόσαις μὲν αἱ κρίσεις νικῶσι τὸ πλῆθος τῶν αὑτῶν χεῖρον...</note>

Pliny had the same thing in mind when he complained in his letters that votes are counted, not weighed. The famous line from Livy also pertains to this: "The larger part defeated the better part." Homer indicates the same in his first book: "Since now the worse things win." <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ τὰ χέρονα νικᾷ</note>

Nor should we overlook what Diogenes Laertius records about the philosopher Zeno. When he saw Theophrastus being celebrated and praised because he had more listeners, Zeno replied: **"His choir is larger, but mine is more in harmony."** <note>original Greek: ἐκείνη μὲν χορὸς μείζων, ὁ ὑμὸς δὲ συμφωνότερος</note>

Thus, there will be a place for the adage either when we deny that we should look to how many people we please, but rather to how *good* they are; or when we urge that one ought to follow not what pleases the most, but what is best in itself, even if approved by very few. Or when we say that the zeal of one or two people—who excel in wealth, favor, or authority—is to be valued more than the goodwill of the multitude, which is superior only in number but inferior in everything else. Just as in Plautus, a character says he despises those "tiny gods," provided he has Jupiter alone on his side.

Nor will it be absurdly applied whenever a single force is more powerful than all the rest; as if one were to say: "This cause is approved by more people, supported by more reasons, relies on equity, and is stated in the laws, but the other is **sovereign**." <note>original Greek: κυρία</note> For "so I will it, so I command it." For all things must yield when someone issues an oracle of the kind Agamemnon utters in Homer:

> I shall not give her up; I myself will come and take her. <note>original Greek: μὴ δώσην, ἐγὼ δ’ ἕκεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι</note>

That is: "Which indeed I will snatch away, if they should happen to be reluctant to hand them over." Lucian uses a similar expression in *The Runaways*: "Those who place justice in their hands." <note>original Greek: τὸ δίκαιον ἐν τῇ χειρὶ τιθεμένων</note> When one of his sons asked Pyrrhus to whom he would leave his kingdom, he replied: **"To whichever of you has the sharper sword."** <note>original Greek: ὃς ἂν... ὑμῶν τὴν μάχαιραν ἔχῃ</note> Plutarch, in his *Life of Pyrrhus*, considers this saying not far removed from that tragic curse:

"It seems the brothers must decide the matter with iron." <note>original Greek: σιδὴρῳ ἔοικε διαδικάζειν τοὺς ἀδελφούς</note>

Erasmus draws on classical anecdotes from figures like Zeno, Plato, and Agamemnon to illustrate how authority or excellence often overrides the majority.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

"Brothers divide the house with sharp steel" —— Shares must be maintained.

In regard to those who conduct their affairs by force, and for whom—as Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC), often called the father of Roman poetry.</note> says—the matter is settled by the sword, for whom right lies in arms, and for whom laws are silent amidst weapons, the following may be rightly turned back upon them with irony: *She is your mistress, and Justice is mistress.* <note>original: "αὐτὴ κυρία σου, καὶ δίκη κυρία"</note> For in Greek, *kyria* <note>The Greek word for "mistress" or "authority."</note> signifies not only a mistress, but also one who prevails in authority. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> indicates that a "sovereign assembly" is called *kyria* by them: in which magistrates were usually created. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* calls it a "sovereign assembly," in which they "ratified the decrees," <note>original: "ἐκύρωσαν τὰ ψηφίσματα"</note> that is, the votes prevailed. Sometimes it refers to the matter at hand, as in Euripides’ *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
*My word, which is more authoritative than his, speaks.* <note>original: "οὐμός, ὃς ὁ τῶδε μῦθος κυριῶτερος λέγειν"</note> That is:
Our speech ought to have more weight than this man's oration here.
For the servant signifies that, although he was inferior in status to Menelaus, he was nevertheless superior in this: that he had the more just cause. Not far removed from this is what Marcus Tullius [Cicero] said in *Against Piso*: "But I pass over how each of us was made; let the lot truly be the mistress of the field."

->A Delian diver.<-
->XXIX<-

*A Delian diver.* <note>original: "Δήλιος κολυμβητής"</note> Formerly, this was commonly said of someone very skilled at swimming, and who could swim on the very surface of the water. The adage was born, or certainly made more illustrious, from an apophthegm <note>A concise, pithy saying.</note> of Socrates. For when Euripides had presented him with a book by Heraclitus—to whom the nickname "The Obscure" <note>original: "σκοτεινός"</note> was added because of his affected obscurity of writing—and asked what he thought of it, Socrates is reported to have answered in this way: *What I understood was noble; and I believe also what I did not understand; although it requires a certain Delian diver so as not to be suffocated in it.* <note>original: "Ἃ μὲν συνῆκα, γενναῖα. οἶμαι δὲ καὶ ἃ μὴ συνῆκα, πλὴν Δηλίου γέ τινος κολυμβητοῦ δεῖσθαι μὴ ἀποπνιγῆναι ἐν αὐτῷ"</note> Thus spoke Socrates, alluding both to the proverb and to the excessively abstract and deep meanings of Heraclitus: so that unless a remarkably skilled swimmer were found, there would be a danger that the reader might be suffocated and drowned in that book. Laertius, in his life of Heraclitus, attributes this saying to a certain Crates, who first brought Heraclitus’s book *On Nature* to the Greeks and commended it with this eulogy.

->By speaking, they learn to speak.<-
->XXX<-

*By speaking, the ability to speak is provided.* <note>original: "Ἐκ τοῦ λέγειν τὸ λέγειν πορίζεται"</note> That is, by speaking we achieve the ability to speak. Syrianus, the interpreter of Hermogenes, censures the sophist Evagoras, who thought the faculty of speaking did not consist in reason, but in practice alone, and that it happened that by speaking we attained the faculty of speech. *From himself,* he says, *he also produced the vulgar proverb: that speaking is provided from speaking,* <note>original: "Ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ δὲ, inquit, καὶ τὴν συρφετὼν παροιμίαν, τὸ λέγειν ἐκ τοῦ λέγειν πορίζεσθαι"</note> that is, thinking, according to the common proverb, that the faculty of speaking comes by speaking. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] also used this in the first book of *On the Orator*: "In which," he says, "they are deceived by what they have heard: that men usually bring it about that they can speak by speaking." But it is also said that men most easily achieve "speaking perversely" by "speaking perversely." Pliny, in the sixth book of his *Epistles*: "I see also many of small talent and no learning, who have achieved doing well by doing." The adage, however, applies more widely, namely to the skill of any matter whatsoever, which practice—the best teacher of all things—chiefly supplies. Hence, all of this kind will be proverbial: By building you will learn the craft of building; by singing, music; by soldiering, the military art; by writing, you will learn to write.

->Many and good.<-
->XXXI<-

*Many and good.* <note>original: "πολλοὶ κἀγαθοί"</note> This was said in ancient times as a proverbial figure. It was transferred from the ritual of sacred rites, in which the priest about to perform a divine ceremony would say: *Who is here?* <note>original: "τίς τῇδε;"</note> Then those who were present would respond: *Many and good.* <note>original: "πολλοὶ κἀγαθοί"</note> And they said this partly for the sake of a good omen; for it was necessary in sacred rites to "speak well," <note>original: "εὐφημεῖν" (euphemein)</note> that is, to say things of good omen; and partly so that if anyone were conscious of a committed sin, he might depart from the mysteries. Plutarch in his *Table Talk*: *Since many and good witnesses are present for Plato.* <note>original: "Ἐπεὶ μάρτυρές γε τῷ πλάτωνι πολλοί τ’ ἀγαθοί τε πάρεσιν"</note> But we have mentioned this before. Aristides also alluded to this in his *Pericles*: *But as one of the noble and good men, he gave him a testimony free from envy and pure.* <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὡς γ’ ἂν εἷς τῶν καλῶν κἀγαθῶν, ἀνεπίφθονόν αὐτῷ καὶ καθαρὰν τὴν μαρτυρίαν ἀπέδωκε"</note> Indeed, even that Homeric phrase is now received in place of a proverb: *both noble and great.* <note>original: "ἠύς τε μέγας τε"</note> It is also found frequently in Aristophanes. The proverb will therefore have a place whenever we signify witnesses, judges, or companions who are suitable and by no means to be rejected.

->The sons of heroes are a nuisance.<-
->XXXII<-

*The children of heroic men are a bane.* <note>original: "Ἀνδρῶν ἡρώων τέκνα πήματα"</note> This was observed by the ancients...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of classical adages and proverbs, specifically focusing on the themes of lineage, inheritance of character, and the relentless nature of misfortune.</meta>

->SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD<-

It has long been observed that the sons of outstanding men have often fallen far short of the character of their progenitors. Hence **Demosthenes** <note>The famous Athenian orator (384–322 BC)</note> said: *It is as if by some fate that the sons of good men turn out to be worthless.* <note>original: "Τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἀνδρῶν, ὥσπερ εἱμαρμένην εἶναι, φαύλους ἀποβαίνειν τοὺς υἱούς."</note> This sentiment of Demosthenes is cited by **Aristides** in his life of Cimon. The translator, whoever he was—a man neither careless nor unlearned—cites in this passage the proverb we just mentioned. Even today there remains a common joke: *From the wisest fathers, the most foolish sons are propagated.* **Euripides** in the *Heracleidae* applied this sentiment generally to all mortals:
> For perhaps among many, few
> Are the sons who are not worse than their father. <note>original: "παῦροι γὰρ πολλοῖς ἴσως / πατρὸς ὤν ὅς τις ἐστὶ μὴ χείρων πατρός."</note>

**Homer** agrees with this sentiment in several places, specifically in the *Odyssey*, Book 2:
> For few sons are like their father;
> Most are worse, and only a few are better than their father. <note>original: "παῦροι γάρ τοι παῖδες ὁμοῖοι πατρὶ πέλονται, / οἱ πλείους κακίους, παῦροι δέ τε πατρὸς ἀρείους."</note>

**Aelius Spartianus** <note>One of the purported authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies</note> elaborates on this theme in his life of Septimius Severus, demonstrating with many examples that it has almost always happened that men distinguished by virtue, letters, or the favor of fortune either had no children at all, or left such heirs that it would have been more beneficial for human affairs had they died childless.

### Never a good son from a bad father. XXXIII

**Euripides** testifies that this sentiment was a celebrated proverb: that good children are not born from a bad father:
> Coming to the point, as the old saying rightly goes,
> A good man cannot be born from a bad father. <note>original: "ἐλθὼν, παλαιὸς αἶνος ὡς καλῶς ἔχει, / οὐκ ἄν γένοιτο χρηστὸς ἐκ κακοῦ πατρός."</note>

This saying is supported by that proverb: *A bad egg from a bad crow.* <note>original: "κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠόν."</note> Likewise that of **Theognis**:
> For a rose does not grow from a sea-onion. <note>original: "οὐδὲ γὰρ ἐκ σκύλλης ῥόδα φύεται."</note> And others of that kind, which will be reported in their proper places.

### As one wave leaves, another catches him. XXXIIII

**Aristides** says of **Themistocles**: *Later events always overtook Themistocles that were greater than the former ones, and that which is said in the proverb happened to him: for as this wave left him, another caught him, until he emerged victorious through the triple-waves.* <note>original: "τρικυμίας" (trikymias) – referring to the "third wave," which the Greeks believed was the largest and most dangerous, similar to the Roman "tenth wave."</note> It seems to have been a proverbial verse, which Aristides slightly twisted for his own use. It should be read in its entirety as follows: *This wave left me, but that one caught me.* The metaphor is taken from the danger faced by sailors, who, after the impact of one wave, always expect another, as storms follow one another in succession. Sailors also count the assaults of the waves in their peril. For they especially dread every tenth wave, which they called the *decuman* wave. The Greeks call those most heavy storms "triple-waves" <term>tricymias: a Greek term for a giant or "third" wave</term>. This can be aptly applied to the onslaughts of evils when (as usually happens) calamity follows calamity, according to that proverbial verse:
> Fortune is never content to strike anyone just once.

### To flee with two feet. XXXV

*To take refuge with two feet.* <note>original: "Δυσὶν ποδοῖν καταφεύγειν."</note> **Aristides** in the *Panathenaic Oration*: *And indeed this is the first point: that all who had need of help fled to this city, truly as if with "two feet," and did not look toward any other of the cities; this is a great and evident argument, and a monument better than a pillar, that she excelled from the very beginning.* He who wrote the scho- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "scholiast" or commentator is intended.</note>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...he illustrated this author with certain others by no means to be despised. The proverb is taken from those who hasten in a race, so that it seems not unlike that other one, **with both hands** <note>original: ἀμφοτέροις χερσίν</note>. By this proverb we signify diligence and speed in completing a business. Or it is taken from sailors, as if you were to say, **with two rudders**. For they call the "foot" of the ship the steering-oar, because the ship seems to walk with it, as it were, when it is turned this way and that. Therefore, it is closely related to what we have said elsewhere, **to ride at two anchors** <note>original: ῦπ᾿ ἀμφοῖν ὁρμεῖν</note>. Thus we may take either sense: either that they were accustomed to flee to the city with the greatest zeal and speed, or that it was the safest refuge of all. However, Aristophanes in *The Birds* referred it to the meaning of speed when he said:

> We flew away from our fatherland **with both feet**. <note>original: Ἀνεπόμεσ᾿ ἐκ τῆ πατρίδος ἀμφοῖν ποδοῖν.</note>

The commentator <note>The ancient scholiast on Aristophanes</note> reminds us that this is taken from ships running with a favorable wind; the meaning, however, is this: with the greatest force and the greatest effort.

### Who could miss the door? XXXVI

**Who could miss the door?** <note>original: Τίς ἂν θύρας ἁμάρτοι</note> This is usually said when someone wanders far from the truth and is entirely deceived in their judgment. It is used by Aristotle in the second book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: τῶν μετὰ τὰ φυσικά</note>, right at the very beginning. In all the manuscripts that I have happened to see, I find **door** <note>original: θύρας</note> written with a *u* <note>The Greek letter upsilon (υ)</note>. Furthermore, Argyropylus <note>Johannes Argyropylus (1415–1487), a primary translator of Aristotle into Latin</note> translates it as "door," and he is neither a bad translator nor a philosopher to be looked down upon by anyone. To this we add Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were standard in European universities</note>, whose authority in the schools of philosophy is now paramount; in explaining this passage, he clearly declares that he understood it to mean a "door." Finally, in the commentaries of Alexander of Aphrodisias, I find **door** <note>original: θύρας</note> in the same way.

But if it were somehow permissible to disagree with so many manuscripts and such great authors, a more probable reading would seem to me to be if we read **the beast** <note>original: θήρας, written with an eta (η) instead of an upsilon (υ)</note>. That "door" crept in is not surprising. First, because the slip of a single small letter was very easy—I know not whether by chance—especially since there is almost no difference in sound <note>Erasmus refers to the "itacism" in Greek pronunciation where different vowels sounded similar</note>. Secondly, the logic of the metaphor is more obvious and more "at hand"; it is possible that it even deceived learned philosophers. For the story was perhaps not as well known to them as that common comparison regarding the entrance to a house and the first principles of knowledge. Lastly, the agreement of the manuscripts among themselves will seem by no means surprising to those who are even moderately practiced in weighing and comparing codices. For it often happens that a mistake in a single archetype, provided it bears some appearance of truth, is then propagated and prevails throughout the entire posterity of books.
**And to the children of children, even those born hereafter.** <note>A Greek poetic formula for perpetual legacy</note>

I do not say these things because I wish to fight with swords over this matter if someone happens to feel differently, or because this is foreign to our purpose, or because I am unaware of how slippery and full of danger it is to change anything in such great authors. I only bring forward the conjectures by which I am led. If these seem suitable to anyone, he will subscribe to our opinion; if not, he will hold the old view all the more willingly because it has prevailed even after being called into doubt.

First of all, a very ancient and most corrected manuscript of the orations of Aristides the Rhetorician cast a no small doubt in my mind; in it, I find not only **the beast** <note>original: θήρας</note> written, but also the very ancient story indicated, as well as the author from whom this Aristotelian proverb, if I am not mistaken, flowed. Therefore, in the oration of Aristides titled *Pericles*, these are the words: "So then, recently, in order to catch one of the beasts among your rivals, you overshot the mark, and the same thing happened to you as happened to Pindar’s Peleus, who **missed the beast** and how he destroyed Eurytion, who was most dear to him." Thus, before you captured any of your adversaries, you brought down one of your friends encountered in the hunt. And the same happened to you as to Peleus in Pindar, who, wandering from the wild beast he was seeking, killed Eurytion, whom he held most dear.

The scholia <note>ancient marginal notes</note> which exist for this author support this; they have no certain title, yet, as the matter shows, they are by a man neither careless nor unlearned. Therefore, I will not be burdened to add his words as well: "Pindar mentions," he says, "in his *Hymns*, that Peleus unintentionally killed Eurytion, the son of Irus (whose father was Actor), one of the Argonauts, while hunting with him. For he calls him 'friend' because he was a relative. For Peleus, before Thetis, had as his wife the daughter of Polymelus..."

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY VI
<sig>S 2</sig>

he had also had as a wife the daughter of Actor. Furthermore, Actor was the father of Irus, whose son was Eurytion. From this, it seems not unlike the truth that the adage originated from Pindar, which Aristotle used without naming the author: so that we may understand that man <term>to miss the door</term> <note>original: τὶ θύρας διαμαρτάιν</note> who not only fails to strike the beast in the specific part he intended, but misses the entire target, not even touching what he aimed for. Now truly, I would not ask anyone to approve of this interpretation unless it appeared to fit Aristotle’s sentiment "to a hair," as they say. For the philosopher discusses in that place the knowledge of natural things, how it is at once both easy and difficult. He brings forward as an argument for its ease the fact that no one fails to grasp some part of it; and for its difficulty, the fact that no one holds the whole. That there has been no one who has touched upon nothing of the truth in the knowledge of nature, he supports with a proverb, as if with a pillar: "Who," you will say, "could <term>miss the door</term>?" <note>original: τίς ἂν θύρας ἁμάρτοι</note>. It is as if holding exact knowledge of particulars is like striking whatever part you aimed for without error; conversely, to slip everywhere is like missing the whole body and having one's aim deflected into a far different sky. 

But so that it may be clear even to the curious and <term>attentive</term> <note>original: ἀνατάσῳ - likely meaning a diligent or intent reader</note> reader, I will transcribe the words of Aristotle himself from the book I mentioned: <term>The study of truth is in one sense difficult, in another easy. A sign of this is that no one is able to attain it adequately, nor does anyone fail entirely, but each says something about nature, and individually they contribute nothing or little to it, but from all of them gathered together a certain magnitude arises. So it seems to be, as we are accustomed to say in the proverb, "Who could miss the door?" In this respect it would be easy, but to be able to have the whole and not the part shows its difficulty.</term> <note>original Greek: ἡ περὶ τῆς ἀληθείας θεωρία... τὴν χαλεπότητα αὐτῆς. This is from Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book Alpha.</note> That is to say: The consideration of truth is partly difficult, partly easy. The argument for this is that neither has anyone attained it according to the dignity of the subject, nor again has anyone been entirely frustrated; but since each person discusses something of nature, it happens that each brings either nothing or a little of importance to it; yet from all collected into one, a certain magnitude is forged. Therefore, if the matter seems to be in the manner we say in the proverb, "Who would not touch the entrance?"—on this account it would be easy. But to have the whole, yet not be able to have the part, declares its difficulty. 

In these words of the philosopher, I do not see what place there is for a literal "door." But that similarity between "principles" and "entrances" provided, I believe, the handle for the error. Rather, Aristotle feels that <term>to miss the door</term> <note>original: ἁμαρτάνειν τὶ θύρας</note> refers to him who in no part attains what he seeks; that which he soon calls <term>to have the whole</term>, as if to have it confusedly and generally; to which he makes the opposite <term>to have the part</term>, as if to hold it exactly, and not only to touch the beast, but to touch this or that part of the beast which you most desired. Although the interpreters bring so many senses to this passage that none seem to have perceived a suitable one. The same person retains also another reading that pleases others. Whenever that happens, a suspicion immediately arises in me that some error lies beneath. Otherwise, <term>the account of truth is simple by nature</term> <note>original: ἁπλῶς ὁ μῦθος τῆς ἀληθείας ἔφυ</note>, as Euripides truly said. 

Now indeed, my strongest weapon remains: Alexander of Aphrodisias. Besides the fact that his entire discourse seems to support our opinion, he also specifically warns that the metaphor of the proverb is drawn from archers, none of whom are accustomed to miss a wide target—certainly such as the whole beast is—even though they sometimes miss the bullseye itself. But it would be better to transcribe his words as well, as far as they pertain to the explanation of the proverb: <term>It seems to me, he says, that the fact that many attempt to discuss it, and none of them seem to miss it entirely, shows that this is natural to us, namely truth. For because no one has spoken of it according to its worth, its very magnitude and difficulty are indicated, and that one ought not to pursue the search for it as a side-matter. It is as he says it must be, for the proverb is also with us because it is difficult. He exhorts us through what he has said, and pushes us neither to despise it as entirely easy, nor to despair of it as entirely difficult. So it seems to be as we say in the proverb, "Who could miss the door?" Because everyone has said something sound, even if they are not all at the mark, it would be a sign that it is easy, as he showed by using the proverb. "Who could miss the door?" which is said of easy things that have nothing difficult or unpleasant. It is said of archers who shoot at a wide target. For if the target set before them is wide, it is easy to hit it. If it is broad, it is not difficult to reach the end, wherefore all succeed since it is easy.</term> <note>original Greek: δοκεῖ δέ μοι... ῥᾳδίου ὄντος. Alexander of Aphrodisias was a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> That is: It seems to me that because very many attempt to discuss it, and none of them seem to fail you entirely, he demonstrates by this argument that this treatment is natural to us. But truly, because no one has spoken of it worthily and fully: from this both its amplitude and difficulty can be argued. At the same time, he warns that one ought not to carry out the treatment of it cursorily or carelessly; rather, it must be pursued, because by nature we are inclined toward it...

<meta>catchword: pensi (likely "pensi" or "pensitanda" - to be weighed/considered)</meta>

<summary>Erasmus analyzes Aristotle's use of the proverb "Who could miss the door?" arguing it is an archery metaphor for the accessibility of general truth versus the difficulty of specific knowledge. He cites Alexander of Aphrodisias to support the idea that while the "whole" (the broad target) is easy to hit, the "part" (the exact mark) is difficult.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>Erasmus is discussing a debate over a Greek proverb regarding whether one "hits the door" or "hits the target."</note>

...we may seem to have considered it; yet again, not carelessly, because it is difficult. And with these words he exhorts us that we should neither despise it as being entirely easy, nor again be deterred from it through despair as if it were exceedingly difficult. Therefore, if it seems to be just as we say in the proverb, **Who has not touched the door?** <note>original: "quis non attigerit ianuam?"</note> because everyone who has spoken about it has said something correctly, he demonstrates its ease by applying the proverb—namely that one: **Who would not hit the door?** This is certainly accustomed to be used for things that are easy to do, in which there is absolutely nothing difficult or arduous. It is taken, however, from archers shooting at a proposed target. For if the target is tiny, it is easy for them to miss and not hit it; but if it is large, they hit it without difficulty. Thus far we have reported the words of Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note>, from which I think it is clear enough that we should read *thyras* <note>original: "θύρας" - doors</note> and not *thyras* <note>Erasmus is debating a subtle Greek spelling/accentuation difference</note>. Although we leave this whole matter, whatever it may be, to the judgment of the learned. For if there is anyone whom that "door" pleases greatly, he will have a means by which he can defend his vote not entirely absurdly. For I do not know whether it was also customary in ancient times, as we see today in some places, that the mounds which support the target are protected on the sides and also from the back by walls, with a roof overhanging above, so that the opening which lies open seems to have the appearance of a door. Furthermore, a man must be exceedingly unskilled who not only fails to hit the target or the mound, but even wanders away from the very entrance, which it would not be difficult for anyone to hit. To me, however, it seems closer to the truth that it is traced back to a Pindaric fable. But upon this, as I have said, the learned shall pronounce. We, having performed the duty of a commentator, consider it sufficient to place before the public for weighing what we have found among authors and what seems right to us. Similar to this proverb seems to be what is read in Plato’s *Phaedrus*: **Lysias missed the mark entirely.** <note>original: "Λυσίας τοῦ παντὸς ἡμάρτηκε"</note> Lucian alluded to this lightly in *Timon* when he says: the thunderbolt of Jove, which he had hurled at the philosopher Anaxagoras, with his hand missing the mark, indeed wandered away from him, but was diverted into the temple of Castor and Pollux. Nor is it different from this form: **To miss by the whole sky**, and **To wander the whole way**, which we have recorded elsewhere.

### A Salty Neighborhood.
#### XXXVII
**A salty neighborhood.** <note>original: "Αλμυρὸν γειτόνημα"</note> This was said of a sterile, wild, and inhuman neighborhood. Aristides says in *Themistocles*: **Let it be a salty neighborhood, as they say.** The interpreter added a note that the adage was taken from the lyric poet Alcman. Plato in the 4th book of *Laws*: **Indeed, truly a salty and wicked neighborhood.** It can be transferred either to a business of much labor but little fruit, or to troublesome neighbors. It is derived from fields bordering the sea, which are usually unfit for cultivation. Hence Virgil also condemns "salty land" as being least fertile. To this we see that coastal people themselves are generally more inhuman than others, as if they contract something of wildness from that most wild element <note>the sea</note>.

### You sing to a broken string.
#### XXXVIII
**You sing to a broken [string].** <note>original: "Πρὸς ἐῤῥωγυῖαν ᾠδήν"</note> Understand: either string or lyre. Suidas shows this was usually said of those who labor in vain. It was the custom of the ancients to sing to the lyre; if any string in it were broken, you would adapt your voice to it in vain, since it would not respond. We have told the story of the cicada supplying the place of a broken string elsewhere. However, it will not be improperly applied when one's services are not reciprocated, or when one persuades the obstinate, or prays to the inexorable.

### You frighten with a wineskin.
#### XXXIX
**To frighten, or be frightened, by a wineskin.** <note>original: "Ασκῷ ἢ ἀσκίῳ μορμολύττεσθαι"</note> Usually said whenever someone either conceives or strikes an empty fear. Taken from those who terrify children or otherwise fearful people with the noise of empty vessels, or rather those who drive away birds with the sound of such vessels, as Aristophanes indicates in *The Birds*. It appears in Diogenianus, and he thinks **to mock with a wineskin** is related to this. Hesychius pronounces in a single word, *askophlauein*, for empty fear. He thinks it means the same as **to fight with a shadow**, that is, you are terrified by a shadow.

### You terrify a lion with a mask.
#### XL
**You terrify a lion with bugbears [masks].** <note>original: "Μορμολυκίοις ἐκφοβεῖς τὸν λέοντα"</note> Recorded in the same author. It will be suitable for empty threats and terrors to be laughed at. Although, as Pliny says, such a savage animal is even more terrified by the turning of wheels, empty chariots, and the combs and songs of roosters, but most of all by fires. Which, unless my memory fails me, I found in some author...

## 41. A Scyrian Sovereignty

<margin>Scyrian rule <note>original Greek: Σκυρία ἀρχή</note></margin>
<unclear>S</unclear>cyrian rule, that is, the Empire of Scyros. This refers to a cold and meager kingdom. Scyros is an island inhabited by the Pelasgians and Carians; it is stony, infertile, and produces nothing of value. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> <unclear>re</unclear>ports that some relate this proverb to Theseus. It is said that when he invaded the domain of Lycome<unclear>des</unclear> and solicited his wife for adultery, he was cast down from a height. From this, "Scyrian sovereignty" came to mean a cruel rule. We also read of "Scyrian rocks," though I do not know if that pertains specifically to this. According to the first interpretation, the adage is elegantly applied to any office where, besides an empty title and the burdensome <unclear>ca</unclear>re of administration, no profit is gained. The author of this is Zenodotus.

## 42. After the Lesbian singer

<margin>After the Lesbian singer <note>original Greek: μετὰ Λέσβιον ᾠδόν</note></margin>
<unclear>A</unclear>fter the Lesbian singer. By this adage, they used to signify someone who holds not the <unclear>f</unclear>irst, but the second place. Similar to this are: "Nothing to do with you and the Pythian" <note>referring to the Delphic Oracle</note> and <unclear>"a</unclear>t Parmeno’s pig." This is a Spartan proverb, born from an occasion <unclear>w</unclear>hich Suidas narrates: When the affairs of the Spartans were in turmoil due to seditions, the <unclear>o</unclear>racle commanded that they should summon a Lesbian singer. Thus Terpander, a <unclear>m</unclear>an of Lesbos from Antissa, was summoned and sent to the Spartans. By his singing, he so soothed their minds <unclear>t</unclear>hat he quelled all sedition and restored the citizens to harmony. From this event, it happened that the <unclear>S</unclear>partans granted the first place in the musical art to Lesbian singers; and if they heard any <unclear>o</unclear>ther person of talent, they would immediately say: "After the Lesbian singer." Zenodotus cites this proverb from a play by Cratinus titled *Chiron*. Plutarch mentions <unclear>t</unclear>his adage in the commentary he inscribed *On the Slowness of Divine Vengeance* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ βραδέως τιμωρουμένων</note>, although to me the style does not smell of Plutarch. However, nothing prevents <unclear>t</unclear>his proverb from being turned toward other matters: for instance, if someone, affirming that erudi<unclear>ti</unclear>on must be sought but only after money has been acquired, should say: "After the Lesbian singer."

<unclear>C</unclear>allippides was an old proverbial name for one who, in managing affairs, though he <unclear>m</unclear>ight boast of doing much, nevertheless accomplished nothing; or as Terence says, one who, by <unclear>a</unclear>cting busily, makes no progress. Marcus Tullius Cicero to Atticus, book 13: "Regarding what you write to me about Varro, <unclear>y</unclear>ou know that I previously used to write orations or something of that kind, so that I <unclear>al</unclear>so could weave Varro in. "Do you know me, O King, or have you heard who I am?" Agesilaus, having looked the man over, replied: "Are you not Callippides, the <term>deicelictas</term>?" <note>original: "dicelictas" / "δικηλικταὶ". This refers to a specific type of Spartan mimic or actor.</note> For that is what the Spartans call mimes. This is from Plutarch. The word <term>deikeliktai</term> among the Greeks signifies an image, a representation, or an imitation, as Eudemus testifies. From this, the Spartan mimes seem to have derived their name, which itself is also said by us to come <term>from imitation</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς μιμήσεως"</note>. One may therefore conjecture that this Callippides, or whoever he was, was so accustomed to using gestures that while he seemed to move with wonderful agility, he nevertheless did not move from his spot. Aristophanes also mentions this name in *The Clouds*, indicating that the word was derived <term>from horses</term> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῶν ἵππων"</note>.

### The Bath-keeper.
<margin>44</margin>

<term>Balaneus</term>. That is, a Bath-keeper, or the proprietor of a bath-house. This name was used as a common insult against a man who was more curious than is proper about other people's business. This is because this class of men, since they live in leisure and are not occupied by their own affairs, are accustomed to minding the business of others. Just like that Damasippus in Horace:
> Minding the business of others,
> Having been cast out of my own.

Barbers are of the same sort. Whence the same Horace says: ->I suppose<-
->It is known to all the blind and the barbers.<-
Plato, in the first book of *The Republic*, seems to use this for wordy people. Indeed, curiosity and talkativeness are twin vices, as Horace also witnesses:
> Flee the inquisitive man, for he is also a chatterbox.

Diogenianus mentions this adage.

### In the manner of a Bacchante.
<margin>45</margin>

<term>Bakches tropon</term>. That is, in the manner of a Bacchante. It was usually said of gloomy and silent people, because those Maenads, inspired by Bacchic fury, were of this sort. Diogenianus is the source. But Juvenal applied it to an intemperate life:
> Who pretend to be like Curius but live like the Bacchanalia. <note>Curius Dentatus was a Roman symbol of austerity; the Bacchanalia were wild, drunken festivals.</note>

### A quarrel is sought by the weary.
<margin>46</margin>

Seneca, in the third book of *On Anger*, records a proverb of this kind: *A quarrel is sought by the weary.* Or, *The weary man seeks a quarrel.* In what sense this was used in antiquity is not entirely clear. But if one may follow conjectures, it appears to have been said of certain people who are more peevish and prone to brawling: not because they are offended, but because they are otherwise in a bad state of mind, just as those to whom fortune is adverse are difficult and somewhat morose. But I will add Seneca’s own words, from which the sense of the proverb can, I think, be gathered: "Therefore, those who suspect their stomach, when about to proceed to conduct business of greater importance, should temper their bile with food, which fatigue moves most of all: either because fasting drives in the heat and harms the blood, stopping its course in the laboring veins; or because the body, thinned and weak, weighs upon the mind. Certainly for the same reason, those tired by illness or age are more prone to anger. Hunger and thirst must also be avoided for the same reasons. For they exasperate and inflame the mind. It is an old saying, *a quarrel is sought by the weary.* But equally so by the hungry, and by every man whom something burns. For just as ulcers ache at a light touch, and then even at the suspicion of a touch: so the affected mind is offended by the smallest things; so much so, that a greeting, a letter, a speech, or a question calls some out to a dispute. Sick things are never touched without a complaint." Thus far Seneca. To this pertains what Pliny writes in Book 22, Chapter 24: "So also in fatigue they are more prone to anger and to lawsuits."

### The gladiator takes counsel in the arena.
<margin>47</margin>

*The gladiator takes counsel in the arena.* This warns that a plan must sometimes be changed according to the circumstances, and one must, as they say, serve the time. This is also recorded by Lucius Annaeus Seneca in the third book of his letters to Lucilius. "Now you understand," he says, "that you must be withdrawn from those impressive but evil occupations. But you ask how you can achieve this. Certain things cannot be shown except by one who is present. A doctor cannot, through letters, choose the time for food or a bath. The vein must be felt. It is an old proverb: *The gladiator takes counsel in the arena.* Something in the adversary's face, something in the movement of the hand, something in the very inclination of the body, warns the observer. What is usually done, and what ought to be done, can be commanded and written in general. Such advice is given not only to those absent but even to posterity. But when that ought to happen, or in what manner, no one will advise from a distance. One must deliberate with the things themselves." Thus far he. Caesar, in the fifth book of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*: "Which usually happens to those who are forced to take counsel in the midst of the business itself." We also say, *To take counsel from the circumstances.*

# THE SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
S 4
<meta>catchword: where</meta>

### More uncultured than the Libethrians.
### XLVIII

<margin>More uncultured than the Libethrians.</margin> <note>original: "Ἀμουσότερος Λειβηθρίων"</note> That is, more unlearned than the Libethrians. A proverbial hyperbole, fitting for a man who is an utter ignoramus and entirely estranged from any commerce with the Muses. The proverb is taken from the rustic ignorance of this people. For they say the Libethrians were such dull-witted despisers of music, poetry, and in short, all the more elegant disciplines, that some believe Orpheus was killed among them; among these is Zeno, who writes that the Libethrians were a Persian race. Servius believed Libethrum was a fountain, from which Virgil in the poem *Meliboeus* named the Muses "Libethrides." Pliny makes mention of the Libethrian spring, which he locates in Magnesia, a region bordering Thessaly. Solinus calls Libethrum a masculine noun. Likewise, Strabo in his book of *Geography* mentions Libethrum: "In this place," he says, "a temple was consecrated to the Muses, along with the horse-spring <note>The Hippocrene</note> and the cave of the Libethrid nymphs." From this, one may suspect that those who consecrated Helicon, Pieria, Libethrum, and Pimplia to the same Muses were Thracians. For they were called Pieres, whose lands the Macedonians now possess since they were driven out.

### To disparage one's own domestic treasure.
### XLIX

<margin>You disparage the treasure at home.</margin> <note>original: "Τὸν οἴκοι θησαυρὸν διαβάλλεις"</note> That is, you calumniate or expose your own domestic treasure. It means you criticize and tear apart your own things. It is very similar to that phrase of Horace which we related elsewhere: "To hack at one's own vineyards." The rhetorician Aristides says in *Pericles*: "We would be disparaging the treasure at home if we were to find fault with these things." No one of sound mind exposes or rebukes what he has stored at home; rather, everyone protects his own and envies the things of others. It will also apply to those who do not conceal their own secrets.

### As the man is, so is his speech.
### L

Annaeus Seneca, in the letters he wrote to Lucilius (Book 20), says: "Among the Greeks, it has passed into a proverb: Such was men's speech, as was their life." That Greek proverb appears in Aristides, in the second *Defense of Rhetoric against Plato*: "The proverb is not ineffective which says: as the life is, so also is the speech; or again, the other way around." That is, the adage is not out of harmony with those who say: of what sort the character is, of that sort also is the speech. And again: of what sort the speech is, of such sort is the character. Toward the same sentiment is what Diogenes Laertius records among the sayings of Solon: "Speech is the image of deeds." Persius, in his fifth Satire, wove this sentiment into an allegory when he said:
> ...cautious to discern
> what rings solid, and what is the plaster of a painted tongue.

He suggests, marvelously, that a man's soul is seen through his speech no differently than vessels are judged by the ringing sound they return when struck by a finger. The same author in Satire 3:
> ...but the jar, when struck, responds
> with a flaw, being poorly baked from green clay.

This proverb has a place not only when speech convicts a wicked or an honest man, but also when we weigh the genius of anyone from their style, and conjecture the entire habit of the mind from the very method of their speaking. For the style of the pompous is turgid; of the dejected, humble and bloodless; of the harsh, rough; of the bitter, strained, gloomy, and abusive; of those overflowing with luxuries, ornate and loose. In short, the whole image of life and every force of the mind is represented in speech just as in a mirror, and even the innermost parts of the heart are detected by certain secret traces. Thus, Seneca writes that the delights and softness of Maecenas could be gathered from the man's own diction. To this pertains what Socrates in Plato commands Charmides to do—to speak so that he might "see" him—intending, of course, to judge the man by his speech. The same Socrates in the *Gorgias* denies that he knows Archelaus, son of Perdiccas, because he had never entered into conversation with him. Yet the common people proclaim they know a man whom they have only seen, even though the soul of a man is not perceived except through speech.

<margin>The stuttering woman was persuaded.</margin>
### LI

<margin>The stuttering woman was persuaded.</margin> <note>original: "Ψελλὴ δ' ἐπίσθη"</note> That is, the stuttering woman does not believe <note>The translator notes a pun on the Greek words for 'persuaded' and 'believed'</note>. A proverbial joke used when someone tries to hide their own faults, which they reveal even while trying to conceal them. For example, if someone were to deny they have a lisp, yet could not do so without lisping. For it is said *pisthe* for *peisthe*, because those who suffer from a defect of the tongue struggle most with two letters, sigma and rho. It is reported... <note>text cuts off</note> The <term>lambdacism</term> <note>speech defect involving the letter L</note> of Alcibiades was also noted, who used to pronounce the letter L instead of R, due to a defect of the tongue, as I believe, but more so out of affectation. In Aristophanes' *Wasps*...

## **We are caught by our own wings.**

*Tois auton pterois haliskometha.* <note>original: "Τοῖς αὐτῶν πτεροῖς ἁλισκόμεθα."</note> That is, we are caught by our own feathers. Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
"We have suffered these things, according to Aeschylus,"
-> "Not by others, but by our own feathers." <-
-> <note>original: "τάδ' οὐχ ὑπ' ἄλλων, ἀλλὰ τοῖς αὐτῶν πτεροῖς."</note> <-
Aeschylus, however, as the commentator reminds us, in the play titled *The Myrmidons*, calls this a Libyan proverb, because it is drawn from a Libyan fable. The fable is told as follows: an eagle, struck by an arrow, looked upon the shaft fashioned in the likeness of feathers, and is said to have remarked: "Not by others, but by our own feathers are we caught."
-> That is, <-
-> Not by others, but by our own feathers <-
-> are we caught. <-
Athenaeus used this in his eleventh book: "And these things not by others, but by your own wings you are caught," as that remarkable Aeschylus said. It applies to those who themselves provide the occasion for their own misfortune, like Chremes in Terence’s *The Self-Tormentor* <note>original: "ἑαυτὸν τιμωρεμένῳ"</note>, when he encourages a servant to direct some trick against Menedemus, by which he himself is soon after deceived by the same ruses.

<sig>LIII</sig>
## **Of good fortune. Or of the good spirit.**

*Agathou daimonos.* <note>original: "Ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος."</note> That is, of the Good Spirit, or of good fortune—understand the word "in the name of." It is a phrase used by those wishing for a good omen when embarking on some matter, much like that line in Persius: "May this go well." Thus, it will be more witty when applied as a joke to one who begins a task—a trivial one indeed—but labors as if it were of the greatest importance. As if some stingy fellow were finally to unseal a jar of wine, or at last set out a long-kept cheese "in the name of the good spirit." Zenodotus and likewise the commentator on Aristophanes show that the proverb arose from the fact that formerly, when the banquet was finished and the table removed, it was customary for unmixed wine to be brought in. And that cup is called the cup of the *Agathos Daimon* <term>Agathos Daimon: A "Good Spirit" or personal protective deity in Greek religion, often honored with a toast of unmixed wine at the end of a meal.</term>, that is, of the good spirit. The commentator on Aristophanes in *The Wasps* cites Theopompus as the author of this account. Nor is it different from what he brings from Apollodorus, an opinion which Aristophanes seems to support in *The Knights*:
-> "By Zeus, no! But unmixed wine of the good spirit." <-
-> <note>original: "Μὰ Δί', ἀλλ' ἀκρατου οἴνου ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος."</note> Likewise in *The Wasps*: <-
-> "May it never be given to me to drink unmixed wine as a reward of the good spirit." <-
-> <note>original: "Μηδὲ ποτε πίοιμ' ἀκράτου μισθὸν ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος."</note> The same in the same work: <-
-> "And pour a libation in the name of the good spirit." <-
-> <note>original: "Καὶ ἀπάρξου ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος."</note> Slightly differently in *Peace*: <-
-> "For now it is permitted for us to seize in the name of the good spirit." <-
-> <note>original: "Νῦν γὰρ ἡμῖν ἁρπάσαι πάρεστιν ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος."</note> <-
Although Athenaeus, in the eleventh book of the *Deipnosophists*, clearly demonstrates that after the washing which the diners used to perform, a cup was usually brought in which was called that of the "good spirit." Which custom indeed persists today among the Germans. He shows that this cup was called the *metaniptron* <term>metaniptron: Literally "after-washing"; a drink taken after washing the hands following a meal.</term>, because it was brought after the hands were washed, a custom which is even today religiously observed among the British. Antiphanes in *The Lamp*:
-> "To devour the metaniptron of the good spirit." Again the same: <-
-> "But truly, the metaniptron of the good spirit." <-
Whoever received this cup toasted another, as the same author indicates. For it was the custom among the ancients that those offering a toast, or about to drink, would first mention some god or man for the sake of an omen, and they brought him forth for the sake of honor. Just as in Lucian’s *The Lapiths*, Alcidamus the Cynic toasts in the name of the wife of Hercules. Likewise Horace:
-> "Give quickly to the new moon, <-
-> Give to the midnight, give, boy, to the augur." <-
Others prefer the idea that the adage is derived from the fact that in ancient times the first cup was called that of the "good spirit," and they were accustomed to use that phrase as a good omen because of Bacchus, as if he were a local and household god. Furthermore, they used to call the second day of every month the day of the "good spirit" in ancient times. It is also said that among the Thebans there was a shrine of the "good spirit." Finally, there is also an island...

# SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...of this name in the Indian Sea, as Stephanus shows. Plutarch, in the third decade of his *Various Small Questions* <note>original: "variarum quæstiuncularum," likely referring to his *Greek Questions*</note>, demonstrates that in ancient times there was a custom not to plow <note>or perhaps "not to taste," likely a typo for "ararent" vs "gustarent"</note> wine unless they had first offered a libation to some god, so that the drink, like a medicine <term>pharmakon (medicine/remedy)</term>, would be harmless and healthful to them. And indeed, at Athens, on the eleventh day of the month, they would sacrifice the first of the wine; they called that day the "Jar-Opening" <note>original: "pithoegia"</note>. But among the Boeotians, on the seventh day of the incoming month, after performing rites to the Good Spirit <note>original: "bono dæmoni"</note>, they would taste it when the West Wind <note>Zephyrus</note> arose, because that wind especially stirs and moves the wine—so much so, that whatever wine escapes its influence is seen as likely to last. The month was called <term>Pithoigios (The Month of Jar-Opening)</term>. Aristides, in his work on Themistocles, seems to have alluded to this proverb when he says: <term>But he stood before the Greeks in place of the Good Spirit</term> <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ καθέσει τοῖς Ἕλλησι ἀντ’ ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος"</note>. That is: "He truly stood for the Greeks in the role of a good guardian spirit." Although this should perhaps be referred more to what we have said elsewhere regarding the "Good Spirit and Evil Spirit."

### 54. Bad at the water.

<margin>Perhaps this relates to that passage in Cicero: <unclear>pertains</unclear> for "plainly." 273. <unclear>pue</unclear> I made wine from those who <unclear>came</unclear> to the waters indeed.</margin>
<term>Bad at the water</term> <note>original: "Ἐπ’ ὕδωρ κακός"</note>. This was once said of men of the lowest sort, and perhaps those addicted to the meanest profits, because in antiquity those who used to supply water to litigants were held in ill repute and were by far the most despised. For we know that in other contexts, the ancients were accustomed to speak in court according to the measure of water-clocks <term>clepsydras (water-clocks used to time speeches)</term>. They would pour water for the speakers through these water-clocks. Certain thin, useless men would pour and dispense this water. Furthermore, those who performed this service were considered outcasts in Athens, lacking both property and a good reputation, not unlike how Roman laws viewed stage-performers and certain ministers of other public contests. There is another similar to this: <term>Go to the water</term> <note>original: "Ἐπ’ ὕδωρ ἴθι"</note>, which means "get lost" or "go to a bad end."

### 55. The curse of the Phocaeans.

<term>The curse of the Phocaeans</term> <note>original: "Φωκέων ἀρά"</note>. This refers to an oath bound by many chains. For in treaties, to prevent them from being violated, they employed not only promises, handshakes, and sacrifice, but also curses upon the head of whoever did not stand by the agreements. This can be gathered from Euripides, whose verses in *Iphigenia in Aulis* are these:
> <term>They swore and gave their right hands</term>
> <term>To one another, and through the sacrificial fires</term>
> <term>They poured libations and invoked these curses.</term>

The meaning of these verses I once translated thus:
> The suitors went with an oath,
> They joined right hands among themselves, and further
> They placed sacred offerings on the altars of the gods:
> They bound themselves, and to that end
> Obliging themselves with dire curses.

But to return to the proverb, it arose from an incident of this kind. The Phocaeans, a people of Ionia, once left their ancestral soil by a common council of the people, driven by a devotion and certain curses, so that no one would ever think of seeking their homeland again. Following the oracle of Diana and with Aristarcha as their leader, they went to Narbonnese Gaul, and there founded the most flourishing city of Marseille <note>Massilia</note>. Herodotus mentions this history in his first book, and Strabo in his fourth. Horace also remembers it in his book of *Epodes*:
> ...what might be profitable for all, or at least the better part
> Who seek to be free from wretched labors.
> Let no opinion be stronger than this: as the cursed state
> Of the Phocaeans fled,
> Leaving their fields, ancestral hearths, and temples to be inhabited
> By wild boars and ravenous wolves.

Then he reveals what the ritual of the curse was:
> ...but let us swear to this: as soon as stones shall swim,
> Lifted from the bottom of the shallows, let it not be a sin to return.
> Nor let it grieve us to turn our sails homeward, until
> The Po river shall wash the Matinian peaks,
> Or the towering Apennines run out into the sea,
> And a new lust joins monsters together.

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"A wondrous love, so that tigers delight to lie down with stags,
And the dove is defiled by the kite:
Nor do the trusting herds fear the tawny lions,
And the smooth goat loves the deceptive seas.
These things, and whatever can cut off sweet returns,
Let us go, an entire city under a curse."
<note>original: "Mirus amor..." These Latin verses are from Horace’s Epodes (16.30-36), referring to the "Oath of the Phocaeans" who swore never to return home until iron floated on water.</note>

Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century grammarian</note> identifies Phocaea <note>original: *φωκαίαν*</note> as a city of Ionia, the derivative of which is Phocaean <note>original: *φωκαιεύς*</note>, according to Herodotus, and also Phocaean <note>original: *φωκαεύς*</note>; there is another of the same name in Mycale in Caria. However, there is also Phocis <note>original: *φωκίς*</note>, a region of Boeotia near Parnassus, from which the derivative is Phocian <note>original: *φωκεύς*</note> and Phocic <note>original: *φωκικοί*</note>. I thought it necessary to advise on this because some people seem to slip up due to the similarity of the names. Indeed, this proverb is derived from the Phocaeans of Ionia: whereas the one we shall report elsewhere—"The desperation of the Phocians"—was born from the Phocics of Boeotia. The proverb is recorded by Zenodotus.

<margin>56</margin>
->Sybaritic speech.<-

*Sybaritikoi logoi* <note>original: *Συβαριτικοὶ λόγοι*</note>. That is, Sybaritic discourses. Hesychius relates that a certain Acopon <note>original: *Ακωπον*</note>, a Sybarite I believe, applied himself with the greatest zeal so that he might possess a style of speech that was elegant and opulent; from this arose a proverbial joke, so that a more polished and carefully wrought speech was called "Sybaritic." Regarding the luxury of the Sybarites in preparing banquets, it is mentioned in the proverb "A Sybaritic table." Thus also the "Asiatic style" of speaking became a proverb. For it generally happens that as the life is, so is the speech. It is also suitable for arrogant and bombastic speech. For the Sybarites were also noted for their haughtiness while walking through the streets.

<margin>57</margin>
->To begin from the line.<-

*Apo grammēs archesthai* <note>original: *Ἀπὸ γραμμῆς ἀρχεσθαι*</note>. That is, "To begin from the line," is said of those who take their beginning from the very start of a matter. Aristides the Sophist says in his work on Themistocles: "This was the first examination and judgment of Themistocles, wherein he showed what kind of man he was, having begun from the line." <note>original: *Αὕτη πρώτη Θεμιστοκλέους...*</note> That is: This was the first specimen and proof of Themistocles. From here, look at the man, having started from the line. He who added the scholia <note>ancient explanatory notes</note> to this author thinks this proverb is closely related to that one: "Starting from the hearth" <note>original: *ἀφ’ ἑστίας ἀρξάμενον*</note>. To me, it seems more related to those which we have mentioned elsewhere: "From the head," or "From the starting gates." For so they called the place from which the horses were first released, which is itself called an *oppidum* <note>a barrier or town-gate</note>, according to Festus. The metaphor is taken from those who compete in races in the stadiums. For a certain line is drawn for them, at which they stand equally until they receive the signal to run: as the interpreter of Aristophanes shows in the passage we shall soon cite. Tertullian, in the first book *Against Marcion*, says: "Come then, back to the lines and to the step." He said "to the lines" in place of "from the beginning."

<margin>58</margin>
->From the starting gates.<-

*Apo balbidōn* <note>original: *Ἀπὸ βαλβίδων*</note>. That is, "From the barriers," or "From the starting gates." It has the same meaning as that which we just reported. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
"And indeed, straight from the starting gates I will demonstrate concerning the rule." <note>original: *Καὶ μὴν εὐθὺς γ’ ἀπὸ βαλβίδων...*</note> That is:
And immediately from the starting gates, I shall disclose from the source of the matter. <gloss>that is, "immediately from the beginning."</gloss>
The interpreter shows, as I just said, that the metaphor is borrowed from the stadiums, in which the "carceres" <note>starting gates</note> were certain barriers from which the race began, which the Greeks call *balbidas* or *aphetērias*. Next to these, a line was stretched upon which those about to run would stand. Hence those formulas frequent even among Latin writers: "From the starting gates to the goal," and "From the goal to the starting gates." We have cited these examples elsewhere.

<margin>59</margin>
->A new swallow.<-

*Nea chelidōn* <note>original: *Νέα χελιδών*</note>. That is, "A new swallow." Suidas cites this adage from Aristophanes' *The Birds*, his memory failing him, as I believe. For it appears in this poet’s *The Knights*, in these verses:
"For I deceived the cooks, speaking thus in silence:
Look, boys! Do you not see? It is time, a new swallow!
They looked, and in the meantime I stole the meat." <note>original: *Ἐξαπάτων γὰρ τοὺς μαγείρους...*</note>
The interpreter advises that this is said as a proverbial figure, and is just as valid as if you said "the beginning of spring," because that bird appears at that time. Just as Horace says:
"With the west winds and the first swallow." Suidas says it is usually said whenever they would deceive someone.
Taken...

# FIRST CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY

taken from a children's game. For they, acting with deliberate effort and pretending to see a new swallow, 
<margin>Theognis in Athenaeus</margin> 
point it out to others; then, while the others are gazing and intent, they meanwhile snatch away what they want. Theognis, in the eighth book of Athenaeus, declares that it was a custom for the Rhodians to invite the swallow every year with public vows around springtime—which they called *chelidonizein* <note>original: χελιδονίζειν; literally "to act like a swallow" or "to sing the swallow-song"</note>—crying out in this manner: "The swallow has come, has come, bringing beautiful seasons and beautiful years." <note>original: ἦλθε ἦλθε χελιδὼν καλὰς ὥρας ἄγουσα & καλοὺς ἐνιαυτούς</note> Therefore, it will apply to those who deceive and cause harm by casting out some false hope.

### The brain of Jupiter and of the King. LX

"The brain of Jupiter" <note>original: Διὸς ἐγκέφαλος</note> and "The brain of the King." <note>original: Βασιλέως ἐγκέφαλος</note> This is said of something exceedingly sumptuous and sweet, or of those who live softly and delicately. Clearchus writes in Athenaeus that sumptuous feasts among the Persians are called "the brain of Jupiter and of the king." Athenaeus, in book 12, teaches that Sardanapalus <note>An Assyrian king legendary for his decadence.</note> was accustomed to serve "the brain of Jupiter and of the king"—an exquisite food, I believe—to those who had invented some new pleasure. The same author in book 14 counts "the brain of Jupiter" among the delicacies of the second course <note>The dessert or "second tables."</note>. In Apuleius, in his first *Apologia*, Ennius is cited: "What wisdom have I passed by? The brain of almost-supreme Jupiter."
"Here is captured the great and good [fish] for Hector's fatherland."
Diphilus, in Athenaeus, commemorates "the brain of Jupiter" among the praises of the second course. The same man calls a very choice food "the flower of nectar" <note>original: νεκταρέον ἄνθος</note>. And elsewhere he teaches that "the milk of Venus" <note>original: ἢ ἀφροδίτης γάλα</note> was a name used by Aristophanes. Again, in another place, he indicates that sweet foods were called "the foods of Helen." <note>original: ἢ ἑλένης βρώματα</note>

### You move what should not be moved. LXI

<margin>You move the immovable.</margin>
"You move the immovable." <note>original: Ἀκίvητα κιvεῖς</note> This will apply either to those who attempt something impossible, or those who violate sacred things, or those who change treaties, or those who attack with insults those to whom reverence is owed because of their authority. Zenodotus thinks it arose from the fact that it is not lawful to move altars, tombs, or shrines, to which a certain reverence and religious awe is due. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Daemon of Socrates*, writes that this voice was uttered to a certain man who summoned his deceased friend Timanes: "Do not move the immovable." <note>original: τὰ ἀκίνητα μὴ κινείν</note> The same author uses it in his *Phocian* works against one who seemed to tear down the accepted opinion concerning the gods. Plato mentions this in the 8th book of *The Laws*, bringing forward a law which he calls the law of "Jupiter of the Boundaries," lest anyone move the boundary stones of a neighboring citizen or guest; likewise, lest anyone move the sacred boundaries of a city or region; and that each man should rather wish to move a massive rock than a tiny stone fixed by treaty and oath. He says: "He truly seems to think he is 'moving the immovable.'" <note>original: νομίζει... τὰ ἀκίvητα κιvεῖv ἀληθῶς ἔοικεν</note> 
<margin>Plato, Laws, book 8 and 11.</margin>
The same in book 11 of *The Laws*: "For that saying is rightly spoken by many: Do not move the immovable." <note>original: ὧδι πολλοῖς γὰρ δὴ λεγόμενον εὖ τὸ μὴ κινεῖν τὰ ἀκίνητα</note> He mentions it also in the third book of the same work. And in a certain epigram it is read thus:
<margin>Do not move the Camarina.</margin>
"For Hades is still unmoved." <note>original: ἔτ᾽ ἀκίvητοι γὰρ αἴδης</note> That is: 
<margin>Move the immovable.</margin>
Not even Libitina <note>The Roman goddess of funerals.</note> touches things that are not known. Sophocles in *Antigone*:
<margin>To speak through the mind things not to be moved.</margin>
That is: "That I should speak forth things not to be moved while I am of sound mind." The same in *Oedipus at Colonus*: "For who would speak words into the air which it is a sin to move?"
<margin>Plutarch in the booklet On Listening:</margin>
"Moving the strings of desire that should not be moved." <note>original: ἀνθυμία κινῆσα χορδὰς τὰς ἀκινήτας</note> The same in *On Garrulity*:
<margin>Upon the strings of the mind that are not to be moved.</margin>
That is: "Moving the mind toward things of the soul that are least to be moved."
The oracle which appears in Herodotus's *Erato* alluded to this more elegantly:
<margin>But I shall move even Delos, though it be immovable.</margin>
"And I shall move Delos, although it is still unmoved." <note>original: ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ καὶ Δῆλον, ἀκίvητόν περ ἐοῦσαν</note> For that referred to the fable—or if you prefer, the history—of Delos being previously floating, and afterwards fixed for the sake of Apollo. Whence Maro <note>The poet Virgil.</note> says: "He granted that it be inhabited unmoved and despise the winds."

<margin>Neither honey, nor bees.</margin>
"Neither honey, nor bees." <note>original: μήτε μέλι, μήτε μέλισσας</note> This is usually said against those who refuse to bear an inconvenience that is joined with some advantage. Just as if someone [refused] bees because they are

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin adages, focusing on the relationship between effort and reward, and the metaphorical use of animal longevity.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...thorny, and is unwilling to endure them, he shall not enjoy the honey which he desires. For the gods above have so tempered the affairs of mortals that inconvenience is always the companion of conveniences. Tryphon the grammarian <note>A Greek grammarian of the Augustan age</note> brings forward this example of a proverb in his work on figures, and quotes the Lesbian poetess Sappho: *Neither honey for me, nor the bee.* <note>original: "Μήτ’ ἐμοὶ μέλι, μήτε μέλισσα"</note> That is, I want neither the sweetness if it requires the sting.
A Mime <note>A form of popular Roman drama</note> is celebrated for a sentiment tending toward this:
*You must bear what hurts, so that you may endure what profits.*
That line of Plautus pertains to the same point: *He who bravely suffers evil, later possesses good.* Homer also hints at the same thing, somewhat more obscurely but nonetheless elegantly, I believe, through the herb *moly* <note>A magical herb in the Odyssey used to protect against Circe</note>, to which he attributes a black root and a milk-white flower: signifying by the symbol of the black root the trouble of labor, through which one arrives at tranquility of mind, the reward of perfect virtue.

->Coughing instead of a fart. LXIIII<-

*Coughing instead of a fart.* <note>original: "Βὴξ ἀντὶ πορδῆς"</note> This was commonly said whenever someone, being in a tight spot, pretends one thing for another. For example, if someone caught in the house of an adulteress should pretend he had come to buy something. It is transferred from those who disguise a fart with a loud cough; a type of person who, even in this day, is not infrequently caught to great laughter.

->Longer-lived than crows. LXIII<-

*Having lived beyond the crows.* <note>original: "Ὑπὲρ τὰς κορώνας βεβιωκώς"</note> A proverbial hyperbole concerning those who are exceedingly aged. It is taken from the prodigious longevity of that bird, about which Plutarch writes in the commentary entitled *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, quoting Hesiod, who, speaking in the person of a Naiad <note>A water nymph</note>, embraces the various ages of animals thus:
*The chattering crow lives nine generations*
*Of men in their prime, but the stag lives four times the crow.*
*The black raven grows old through three ages of stags; but the phoenix*
*Lives nine times the raven’s life, and we live nine times the phoenix,*
*We fair-haired Nymphs, daughters of Zeus the aegis-bearer.*
That is:
The chattering crow passes through thrice three ages of man,
But the stag completes four spans of the crow,
The dark raven passes three times the stag’s age.
The Indian Phoenix lives nine times the raven’s years.
But we nymphs, the fair-haired, nourishing offspring of thundering Jove,
Exceed ten times the phoenix’s centuries.
Someone or other—whoever it was—seems to have interpreted these verses of Hesiod. The poem exists among the remains of the appendices of Maro <note>Virgil</note>, and is of this sort:
> Six and ninety years he exceeds,
> Which the just life of aging men completes,
> These the chattering crow surpasses nine times in living,
> And the stag exceeds four ages of the crow,
> The raven conquers the swift-footed stag three times, but the phoenix,
> That bird capable of rebirth, multiplies that ninefold.
> Whom you, Hamadryad Nymphs, whose life is longest,
> Surpass by ten times in perpetual time.
> These boundaries restrain the long-lived fates of living things,
> God, the arbiter of the secret age, knows the rest.
I have chosen to write down these verses together for this reason: so that I may more often be granted indulgence when translating from time to time (which will be necessary), if ever I seem not to render everything exactly to the rule. For in these verses it appears how much liberty antiquity allowed itself in translating the poems of poets. Pliny renders this same sentiment of Hesiod quite conveniently and briefly, saying: *Hesiod attributes nine of our ages to the crow; four times that to stags; and three times that to ravens.* Even if to some authors these things seem fabulous. Among these, Aristotle thinks that no other animal is longer-lived than man, with the single exception of the elephant.
->Martial:<-
*And a survivor of all the crows.*
Concerning an excessively long-lived old woman. Likewise Horace in his Odes:
*Lyce, destined to be preserved for a long time, equal to the ages of an old crow.*

<summary>Erasmus discusses proverbs related to the necessity of enduring hardship to gain rewards and the hyperbolic use of animal lifespans (crows, stags, and phoenixes) to describe extreme old age.</summary>
