# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 6

To this pertains what that <term>philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle, often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in Renaissance texts</note> is read to have envied in the crows as he was dying: a longevity which nature had denied to man. Synesius says in a certain letter: *It is likely that we, the most just of princes, possess a spirit more vital than a crow's.* <note>original Greek: Εἰκὸς ἐστὶ κορώνης ψυχικώτερον πνεῦμ’ ἡμῖν, τὸν δικαιότατον.</note> That is to say, it is fitting that a most just ruler should command for as many years as a crow lives.

<margin>65</margin>
### The old age of Tithonus.
<margin>Lucian in the dialogue *On Long-Lived Men*.</margin>
**The old age of Tithonus.** Fables tell that Tithonus, being beloved by Aurora <note>The Goddess of the Dawn</note>, was carried up to heaven, and having been drenched in her nectar, reached such a great age that he even prayed to be turned into a cicada. Lucian says in a certain dialogue: *And he lived beyond Tithonus.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ὑπὲρ Τιθωνὸν ἐβίωσεν.</note> That is, the old man lived longer than Tithonus. Aristo of Chios took on the persona of this Tithonus in his book *On Old Age* because of the miracle of his vitality, as Marcus Cicero testifies in his work *Cato*. Suidas records the adage in this manner: *You have grown older than the depths of Tithonus.* <note>original Greek: κατεγηράσας Τιθωνοῦ βαθύτερον.</note> That is, may you grow older than Tithonus.

<margin>66</margin>
### The old age of Nestor.
<margin>Iliad, Book 1.</margin>
Certainly, among the Latins, the years of Nestor passed into a proverb; Homer attributes three lifetimes to him in the third book of the *Odyssey*:
> *The rumor is that he has already ruled over three generations of men.* <note>original Greek: τρὶς δ’ ἤδη φασὶν ἀνάξασθαί μιν ἀνδρῶν.</note>

<margin>He reached 90 years, as Jerome explained in his letter *On Long and Short Life*, chapter 1.</margin>
He affirms the same in the first book of the *Iliad*. And Juvenal writes:
> *And he who now counts his years on his right hand.* <note>A reference to ancient finger-counting; once a person reached 100, they switched from the left hand to the right.</note>

Indicating this by his age. Briefly, anything taken from those who possessed unusual vitality will take on the form of a proverb. For example: *Livelier than a Phoenix*, which Hesiod writes lives for nine generations of crows; *Livelier than a stag*; *Livelier than a crow*; and *Livelier than Tiresias*, whom tragedy feigns to have lived through six generations of men. Also, *Livelier than the Seres* <note>The Chinese</note>, whom Greek histories report to live for three hundred years. If anyone desires examples of this kind, let him read Lucian’s *On Long-Lived Men* and the forty-eighth chapter of Pliny’s seventh book.

<margin>67</margin>
### He lives beyond his allotted portion.
There is a proverb which Lucian says in *The Lover of Lies*: *For he now lives beyond the spindle.* <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ γὰρ τὸν ἄτρακτον ἤδη βιοῖ.</note> That is, he lives beyond his portion, beyond the spindle. This means he lives beyond his fated day. This is an allusion to the spindles of the Fates, by which the poets imagine the lifespan of mortals is wound. Indeed, even Theologians call the boundary of life "fate" and a "period" which no one is permitted to run past.

<margin>68</margin>
### When we are well, we easily give right counsel to the sick.
A sentiment from Terence, uttered by a young man who was not particularly wise, yet it is a most wise and elegant sentiment: *When we are well, we easily give right counsel to the sick. If you were in my place, you would feel differently.* It seems to have been born from an oracle of the philosopher Thales. For he, as Laertius is the author, when asked what was the most difficult thing, replied: *To know oneself.* <note>original Greek: γνῶναι σεαυτὸν.</note> When asked what was easiest, he replied: *To give counsel to another.* <note>original Greek: ἄλλῳ ὑποτίθεσθαι.</note> The comic poet added this grace of metaphor. Euripides in *Alcestis*:
> *We are all wise [when advising others], but you fear unreasonably.* <note>original Greek: πάντες σοφίζομεν, ἀλλ’ ἀναισίμως φοβεῖ.</note>

These are the words of Hercules consoling Admetus over the death of his wife. But he replies:
> *It is easier to advise than to endure when placed in evils.* <note>original Greek: ῥᾷον παραινεῖν, ἢ παθόντα καρτερεῖν.</note>

And similar to this is the proverbial sentiment:
> *For when we set out to admonish, we are wise; but when we ourselves err, we do not recognize it.* <note>original Greek: ὅταν γὰρ ὁρμῶμεν εἰς τὸ νουθετεῖν σοφοὶ, αὐτοὶ δ’ ἁμαρτάνοντες, οὐ γινώσκομεν.</note>

### To rule the mind.
This sentiment is taken from the common habits of men. For everyone prescribes correctly to the sick what should be avoided and what should be done, and they sometimes rebuke them because they do not obey those giving good advice for the sake of their health. Later, when they themselves fall into illness, those excellent warnings do not help them, but they likewise have need of other advisors and rebukers. Furthermore, every desire is a disease of the mind, by which, as if blinded, one either does not see clearly, or if he does see, he cannot follow those things which are necessary for health. For Phaedria in Terence, though prudent and knowing, puts his hand into the flame, and perishes while alive and seeing. Likewise, Horace [speaks of] following things that should be fled...

<summary>This page examines classical proverbs regarding extreme old age (citing Tithonus, Nestor, and the Phoenix) and the human tendency to give better advice to others than to oneself.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...follows, fleeing what it believes would be beneficial. The greedy man perceives at last how monstrous a thing ambition is. Conversely, the ambitious man clearly sees the disease of the greedy; each gives right counsel to the other regarding someone else’s misfortune, yet neither is wise in his own.

<margin>69</margin>
### What is above us is nothing to us.

<note>original: "τὰ ὑπὲρ ἡμᾶς, οὐδὲν πρὸς ἡμᾶς"</note> *What is above us is nothing to us.* This is a Socratic saying, deterring one from the curious investigation of celestial matters and the secrets of nature. The proverb is cited in turn by Lactantius in book three, chapter twenty: "From these," he says, "I shall choose one that is approved by all. Socrates held this famous proverb: *What is above us is nothing to us.*" It can also be twisted against those who speak rashly about the business of princes or the mysteries of theology. It is also permitted to turn it into the opposite: *What is below us is nothing to us,* when we mean things too trivial to be our concern.

<margin>70</margin>
### Known to the bleary-eyed and the barbers.

Things that have already passed into common talk are said to be "known to all barbers and the bleary-eyed," because in the past, all rumors used to be told in the gatherings at barbershops. Aristophanes indicates this in *Plutus*:
> And yet there was much talk, by Hercules,
> Among those sitting in the barbershops,
> How the man had suddenly become rich.

And in Terence, Antipho learns about a girl in a barbershop. Likewise, Horace says of the barbershop: "They rejoice when, with shaved heads, the talkative sailors tell of dangers safely passed." The same author says in his *Satires*: "I think it is known to all the bleary-eyed and the barbers."
Where he explained the proverb, he meant a matter tossed about by the common people. For the bleary-eyed <note>those with chronic eye inflammation</note> sit in the barbershops seeking a remedy for their eyes. Plutarch recounts many things worth reading about the talkativeness of barbers in the little book he wrote *On Garrulity*. It will not be tedious to relate one of them. Once, he says, when there was talk in a barbershop about Dionysius, and it was said that his tyranny was made of adamant and was impregnable, the barber, laughing, said: "Is it really us saying this about Dionysius, at whose throat I frequently hold a razor?" As soon as Dionysius found out about this saying, he had the barber crucified; and so, as Pliny says, the words returned through the throat to their author. As to why the race of barbers is so talkative, he thinks the cause is that the most talkative people gather and sit in their shops, and by constant association, the barbers themselves are infected with the disease of garrulity. For these reasons, Theophrastus—as the same Plutarch testifies—called them "wineless banquets" <note>original: "τὰ κωφὰ ἄοινα συμπόσια"</note>, because men are made as if drunk there by talkativeness. Indeed, bath-keepers also suffer from a bad reputation, because idle people sit there too, chattering about anything. Why, it even happened that the ancients called bronze-smiths' shops "lounges" <note>original: "λέσχας"</note>, as John the Grammarian indicated, because in the winter cold the crowd of poor people used to gather there for the sake of warmth, and sitting there, they would kill time with idle stories. Hesiod orders the farmer to avoid these places as fit for the lazy:
> Pass by the smithy’s seat and the warm lounge in the winter season.
<note>original: "πὰρ δ' ἴθι χάλκειον θῶκον καὶ ἐπαλέα λέσχην, ὥρῃ χειμερίῃ"</note>
That is: In the winter months, bid farewell to the iron seat and warm trifles.

<margin>71</margin>
### The lazy ox longs for the saddle, the horse longs to plow.

Horace expressed this quite elegantly:
> The lazy ox longs for the saddle, the horse longs to plow.

Signifying that vice implanted in human natures, that they always admire another’s lot more, while they despise and are disgusted by their own; they long for the untried and condemn the experienced. Indeed, they are called "ephippia" <note>saddles</note>, which are commonly called equestrian seats, added so that the rider may sit more comfortably. The ancients plowed with oxen, not horses. It seems to be an allegory taken from some fable. Without metaphor, Terence said: "We are dissatisfied with ourselves."

<margin>72</margin>
### The crop is more fertile in another’s field.

Ovid changed the metaphor, explaining the same sentiment:

> The crop is always more fertile in another's field;
> And the neighbor's herd has a larger udder.
<note>Ovid, Ars Amatoria 1.349-350. A classic expression of "the grass is always greener."</note>

->Persius, Satire 6:<-

> Other people's things please us more; ours please others more.

And Horace:

### Let him drink the dregs, who drinks the wine. 74

There is no doubt that Aristophanes spoke proverbially in *Plutus* when he said the dregs must be drained by the same man who previously drank the wine. That is, he who has enjoyed the best things ought to be equally content with the worse:

> <unclear>...Since</unclear> you thought yourself worthy to drink
> <unclear>...the wine</unclear>, you must now also drink the dregs.
<note>original: "...ἐπειδὴ καὶ τὸν οἶνον ἠξίους πίνειν, κἀποὺ δεῖν τὴν τρύγα."</note>

that is,

> Because if you were not burdened by drinking the wine, the dregs
> must now likewise be drained by you, of course.

These were the words of Chremylus concerning a woman who, once blooming and flourishing in her youth, had pleased him, but was now loathed by the young man.

### Richer than Croesus or Crassus. 74

Among the Greeks, the opulence of Croesus, King of the Lydians, passed into a proverb, especially made famous by the saying of Solon. Among the Romans, likewise, the wealth of Marcus Crassus, whose very surname was attached to his riches. He used to deny that anyone was rich unless they could maintain a legion on their annual income. In land alone, he possessed twenty thousand sesterces. Several others are mentioned by Pliny in Book 23, Chapter 10, and also Book 3, who possessed immoderate wealth. Though you may breathe of Croesuses, and <unclear>...as</unclear> Aristotle—that holy philosopher and almost a god to our own theologians—it is read that his heirs brought forth seventy plates for sale at auction. But these have not passed into common speech. Therefore, there is no need to record them here. The adage will be more festive if we even change the number, as Saint Jerome did: "Though you breathe of Croesuses and <unclear>...the</unclear> letters do not follow the purse." Horace also spoke of "the treasures of the Arabs" for heaped-up wealth, not without a proverbial appearance, just as he spoke of "Persian apparatus" for exquisite and sumptuous displays.

### The riches of Pactolus. 75

<unclear>...To be as rich as</unclear> Pactolus. That is, the riches of Pactolus, used for the greatest wealth; Philostratus said this somewhere. Now, the Pactolus is a river of Lydia, flowing from Mount Tmolus, abounding in golden sands, whence it was nicknamed "the gold-flowing" <note>original: "χρυσορρόας"</note> by the poets. Of this kind, they also tell of the Tagus in Iberia, the Ganges in India, and the Hebrus in Thrace. Pliny adds the Po in Italy, and denies that any <unclear>...gold</unclear> is more perfect than that found in rivers, as it is polished by the very flow and friction. Horace in the *Epodes*:

> <unclear>...Though you be</unclear> rich in cattle and much land,
> <unclear>...and</unclear> the Pactolus flows for you.

Juvenal:

> <unclear>...Let not</unclear> all the sand of the shaded
> Tagus, and the gold rolled into the sea, be worth so much to you.

One may adapt these hyperboles for various uses. For instance, if someone should say: "No one could sustain such great expenses, not even if the Pactolus itself flowed in his house." Or: "Not even the Tagus itself could satisfy this man's greed." Or: "He hoped for nothing mediocre, but conceived whole great Pactoluses in his mind." Or: "He was promising Pactoluses," that is, the most abundant riches.

### Poorer than Irus or Codrus. 76

Conversely, the poverty of Irus and Codrus gave rise to a proverb. Ovid:

> He who was just now a Croesus, shall go suddenly <insert>as an Irus</insert>.
<note>original: "Ibit subito, qui modo Croesus erat."</note>

Regarding Codrus, Juvenal says:

> Codrus had a bed <unclear>...shorter than</unclear> his Procula; his whole estate was packed in a single carriage.

Homer makes mention of Irus in *Odyssey* 18. He writes that he was a public beggar among the Ithacans, of massive body and appearance; called Arnaeus by his mother, he was named Irus by the young men because he would go as a messenger <note>A play on the Greek 'Iris', the messenger of the gods</note> whenever needed. When Ulysses was matched against him, though he himself was disguised as a beggar, he cast the man out. Furthermore, Hecale is famous for her poverty, whom Plautus mentions in the *Cistellaria*: "If indeed things go as I wish, you shall never become a Hecale."

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
a 2

Ovid also mentions this:
> Why is there no one to take Hecale, no woman to take Irus?
> <note>Hecale was a poor old woman who hosted Theseus; Irus was the beggar in the Odyssey.</note>
> Surely because the one was needy, and the other was a pauper.
<note>original: "Cur nemo est Hecalen, nulla est, quæ ceperit Irum? / Nempe quod alter egens, altera pauper erat."</note>
In the introduction of this work, we have sufficiently shown in how many ways these formulas may be used.

### The last of the Mysians.
-> 77 <-

*The last of the Mysians.* <note>original Greek: Μυσῶν ἔσχατος</note> That is, the furthest or least of the Mysians. Strabo, in the twelfth book of his *Geography*, reports that the Mysian people were so utterly despised that they gave rise to a proverb. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> employs this in his oration *For Lucius Flaccus*: "What," he says, "is so worn and celebrated in the Greek tongue as the saying, if someone is held in contempt, that he is called the last of the Mysians?" The same author writes to his brother Quintus: "Unless you think I am moved by the complaints of some Paconius—not even a Greek, but rather a Mysian or a Phrygian," clearly declaring the contempt held for that race. Therefore, we shall signify the highest contempt and the lowest humility by this adage.

### The last of the Mysians is sailing.
-> 78 <-

*The last of the Mysians is sailing.* <note>original Greek: Ἔσχατος μυσῶν πλέι</note> This was said as a proverbial joke about someone who labored in vain. The origin of the proverb, as is the case with most, is told in more than one way. Some relate that once, when the Greeks were suffering from a plague, the oracle responded that they should sail to the "last of the Mysians." At first, they were uncertain what the oracle meant. Finally, after wandering for a long time, they discovered that Aeolis was situated at the furthest reaches of the Mysians, and the divinity had advised them to migrate there. Others write that Telephus, after killing his maternal uncles, consulted the Pythian oracle as to where in the world he should migrate (for in ancient times it was the custom for murderers to change their soil <note>go into exile</note>). The response was that he should betake himself to the furthest region of the Mysians. He came to Teuthrania, which is the furthest part of Mysia, and obtained the sovereignty of that place. There are those who say he did not flee because of the murder of his uncles, but to seek his mother, whom he finally found in Teuthrania. However, the proverb was frequently said whenever harsh things were commanded that were difficult to do.

### To touch a sore.
-> 79 <-

*To move or touch a sore.* <note>original Greek: Κινεῖν ἢ θιγεῖν ἢ ἕλκος</note> That is: to move or touch an ulcer is to stir up pain, and to make mention of a matter that burns us greatly. Terence says: "What was less necessary than to touch this sore?" At which point Donatus <note>a famous Roman grammarian</note> advises that a proverb lies beneath the phrase. Octavius Augustus, as Suetonius Tranquillus records, bore the infamous lives of his daughters, the Julias, and his granddaughter more heavily than death itself; he was not accustomed to call them anything other than his "three abscesses" or "three cancers," surely because he could not remember them without great pain. Marcus Tullius expressed this metaphor quite elegantly against Clodius, who was driving the people—already exasperated by hunger—into a frenzy with seditious speeches: "So that you," he said, "might exist in this sore like a fingernail" <note>i.e., scratching it to make it worse</note>. Plutarch in *On Flattery*: "When he had moved the sore of a secret speech." <note>original Greek: Κενθίς ἡ λόγῳ κινησαυρος ἕλκος</note>

### To rub the scar.
-> 80 <-

When a pain is renewed by the passage of time, the scar is said to be "rubbed." It is well known from where the metaphor is drawn: namely, from a bodily wound that has already closed and been covered by a scar. If this is opened again by rubbing, the pain of the former wound becomes raw again. Cicero to Atticus: "I do not rub the wounds of Appius." The same author in his speech against Rullus: "Lest I should seem to rub the closed scar of the Republic." He also used the phrase "to rub the pain" in the second book of *On the Orator*. We also say "to rub the memory" and "to lightly rub the memory" <note>original: "Refricare memoriam" and "Suffricare memoriam"</note> for that which is a slight renewal, but almost always in a bad sense.

### To scent out, and several similar metaphors.
-> 81 <-

Metaphors which are drawn from the senses of the body, because they are as if "at hand" and taken from what is nearest to us, are almost all proverbial, as we advised at the beginning of this work. For instance, "To scent out" <note>Odorari</note> for finding out, or knowing something sagaciously caught and noticed. "Scent" <note>Odor</note> for suspicion or rumor. Cicero: "There is some scent of a dictatorship." "To smell out" <note>Olfacere</note> in Terence’s *The Brothers*, for detecting. "To get a whiff of" <note>Subolere</note> in the same author, for being suspected. "To smell of" <note>Obolere</note>, for being troublesome or being under suspicion. From this, people are called "Nosey," or "of a wiped nose" <note>sharp-witted</note>, or "of snotty noses" <note>ignorant</note>. Finally, the "nose" itself passes into a proverb for judgment. Horace: "Not because they had no nose" <note>meaning they didn't lack taste/discernment</note>.
And things which are displeasing "stink." To this also belong: "It smells of a lie," and "They reek of Attic style" <note>meaning they are overly refined in the Athenian manner</note>.

<unclear>light</unclear> a lamp. Likewise, we use the word "Taste" for a thing, as in that first experience and <unclear>tasting</unclear>, and as it were, a sample. He is a Briton by nation, whom I am pleased to mention often; a young man—to say nothing for now of his character—altogether worthy of such talent, being highly learned in both Greek and Latin literature, and no moderately practiced in turning over authors of <unclear>every</unclear> kind of profession. Furthermore, he is most sharp-eyed in noting those things which the common crowd of readers pass by with "unwashed feet," as they say. Finally, he possesses a judgment by no means youthful, but refined and <unclear>polished</unclear>. He, I say, under the happy auspices of the Muses, has conceived a work in his mind, and I believe <unclear>already</unclear> has it in hand, which will be of great use, unless I am mistaken, to students of more polished literature. In this work, he intends to gather into one volume whatever notable metaphors exist among the writers of both languages, whatever is wittily and skillfully said, and whatever gems and delights of speech of this kind there may be.

-> For me, there is neither sowing nor reaping in that matter. LXXXII <-

<unclear>Plautus</unclear> in the *Epidicus* used a truly elegant adage: "For me, you will say, there is neither sowing <note>original: "feritur," literally "struck" or "planted"</note> nor reaping in that matter." That is, that business does not pertain to me at all, as it is done neither at my risk nor for my profit. The metaphor is very well known. For he who does the sowing does it at his own expense and his own risk; he who reaps receives the profit and is in safety. The opposite of this is found in Plautus's *Mercator*: "For yourself you plow, for yourself you harrow, for yourself you sow, and for yourself you reap."

-> From the hearth itself. LXXXIII <-

<margin>Begin from the hearth.</margin> "Begin from the hearth" <note>original Greek: Ἑστίας ἄρχου</note>. That is, start from the home. This means one should take the beginning from domestic and familiar things. Whence it will be said against magistrates and censors of other people's lives, whose duty it is to first correct their own people and homes. For the Greeks call *Hestia* what we call the <margin>Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "No, but so that..."</margin> Lar and Vesta. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "No, but so that <margin>...beginning as if from the hearth."</margin> beginning as if from the hearth, I may wear someone down." It was born from an ancient rite of sacrifices, in which the firstfruits were sacrificed to the household gods <note>original: "laribus"</note>. Aristocritus, <margin>on the authority of the interpreter,</margin> on the authority of the interpreter, relates a fable of this sort: When Jupiter had gained power after the Titans were conquered, he allowed Vesta the option to choose whatever she wanted from the parts of the kingdom. She asked for perpetual virginity; then for the firstfruits of all the sacrifices which men should sacrifice to the gods. From this, it passed into custom that in every sacrifice the first parts were granted to the hearth. <margin>Plato used this adage: "I would wish it, O Socrates, but I fear lest the opposite..."</margin> Plato used this adage in the *Euthyphro*: "I would wish it, O Socrates, but I fear lest the opposite <margin>...should happen. Plutarch in his booklet on <margin>friendship: "First, therefore, as if beginning from the hearth."</margin> friendship: "First, therefore, as if beginning from the hearth." # THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...said of those who, from the very beginning, are either good or bad. As if you were to say, from the very cradle, because the Hearth-God <note>original: "Lar"; the Roman spirit of the household</note> receives them immediately at birth.

<margin>84</margin>
->To cut down one's own vineyards.<-

To this is related that line of Horace: **That I may cut down my own vineyards.** <note>Horace, *Epistles* 2.1.220</note> That is, that I may begin with myself, and as a poet myself, I may pluck and tear at poets. The metaphor seems to be taken either from those pruning a vineyard, or from those who through some injury damage young vines. Horace says in his Epistles:
> Indeed, we poets often do ourselves many evils,
> So that I may cut down my own vineyards.

<margin>85</margin>
->What things, bad or good, are being done in our own halls.<-

Aulus Gellius writes that this Homeric verse, which is from the *Odyssey*, book 4, was always on the lips of Diogenes as a proverb:
"Whatever of evil and of good has been wrought in your halls." <note>original Greek: ὅττι τοι ἐν μεγάροισι κακόν τ' ἀγαθόν τε τέτυκται</note>
What others attribute to Socrates, Diocles ascribes to Diogenes, as Laertius reports. Socrates, by this saying, was discouraging the study of natural and supernatural things, as well as mathematical disciplines, and calling people back to the care of moral philosophy, because the latter deals with those things which properly belong to us. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Preserving Good Health*, used it proverbially: "If he thinks it more his duty to be seen laying claim to geometry, or dialectics and music, than to seek and learn
**what things, bad or good, are being done in our own halls.**" <note>Erasmus translates Plutarch's Greek into Latin, here rendered as English. The Greek text emphasizes that self-knowledge is more vital than abstract arts.</note>
By this verse we are warned to care especially for those things which pertain to ourselves, and not to inquire into external matters or the affairs of others. Martial wittily notes this vice in a certain Ollus, who was a most curious observer and sharp critic of other people's misfortunes, even though he himself had an unfaithful wife, a daughter ready for a husband, and was still in debt for his basic toga. Diogenes the Cynic, since this poem (as I just said) was habitually on his lips, used to say that grammarians were acting quite ridiculously by inquiring into the misfortunes of Ulysses with such zeal while remaining ignorant of their own. To this can also be referred that almost solemn phrase in Homer (found in the *Iliad*, books 1, 2, and 21):
"But go into the house and attend to your own tasks." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σαυτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε</note>
Plutarch defines <term>meddlesomeness</term> <note>original: "polypragmosyne"</note> as "a love of learning the evils of others." And he says that kind of people are like the Lamiae <note>mythological monsters</note>, who keep their eyes stored away at home but put them back in when they are about to go out. And so it happens that they are blind at home, but most sharp-sighted abroad. Against those who are so perversely sighted, you might elegantly hurl that saying of Sophocles regarding old men:
"Seeing from afar, but up close, entirely blind." <note>original Greek: Γόῤῥωθε λεύσσων, ἐγγύθεν δὲ πᾶς τυφλός</note>
For it happens to the elderly that they do not perceive things moved closer, but see things further away; Plutarch gives the cause of this in the first decade of his *Table Talk*.

<margin>86</margin>
->To descend into oneself.<-

To descend into oneself is for someone to inspect his own vices. The metaphor is taken either from mines or from cellars; those who descend into them can know what is stored and hidden there. It is an allusion, moreover, to those caves and recesses of the human heart, for which Momus <note>the god of mockery and criticism</note> wished a window to be provided. Persius says:
> How is it that no one tries to descend into himself, no one:
> But the pack on the back of the person in front is watched. <note>Referring to the fable that we carry our own faults in a bag behind us, and others' faults in front.</note>

<margin>87</margin>
->Dwell with yourself.<-

Very close to the Homeric poem seems to be this other one by the same Persius:
"Dwell with yourself, so that you may know how short your furniture is."
That is, live in your own house, so that you may understand how meager your fortune is. A metaphor from those who live in the households of princes and, as commonly happens, swell with pride from another's wealth just as if it were their own, to whom...

<meta>catchword: to whom</meta>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 6
<sig>t 4</sig>

<unclear>whom</unclear> if they had to live at home, they would scarcely have a salt-cellar <note>original: "salinum"; a symbol of the barest necessities of a household</note> to set out. Dwell with yourself, then, and measure yourself by your own modest furniture, and weigh yourself by your own evils and goods. Nor is that which Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> writes in *Cato the Elder* irrelevant here: "To live with oneself," as the saying goes.

<margin>88</margin>
->Live within your own harvest.<-
<margin>that is,</margin>
Persius explained the same idea with a different metaphor in his sixth satire:
*Live within your own harvest.* <note>original: "Messe tenus propria uiue"</note>
Make your expenditures according to the measure of your means. This is drawn from farmers, who measure their expenses by the yield of their fields. For a situation cannot remain stable when expenses exceed income, as Plautus says. Alexander, in the sixth book of Athenaeus, used an elegant word for a boaster of wealth: *ptochalazona* <note>original: "πτωχαλαζονα"; a "beggar-braggart"</note>, expressing with that same word pride joined with poverty. Now the world is full of this kind of men, who combine a more than tyrannical pride with a profession of poverty.

<margin>89</margin>
->Measure yourself by your own foot.<-
That line of Horace pertains to the same sentiment:
*It is right for everyone to measure himself by his own module and foot.*
Lucian, in the booklet titled *In Defense of Images*, says: *But judge and measure both things by their own proper measure* <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ δακείνας τὴ συμμετρὴς τῷ οἰκείῳ μέτρῳ"</note>. This is surely what Horace said, "by his own module" <note>original: "suo modulo"</note>, or "by his own measure" <note>original: "οἰκείῳ μέτρῳ"</note>, and as if interpreting himself, he added, "foot." Pindar likewise says:
*Always to look for the measure of everything according to oneself.* <note>original: "κατ’ αὐτὸν αἰεὶ παντὸς ὁρᾷν μέτρον"</note> That is,
It is necessary for each person to look at the limit of every single thing according to his own condition. And Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
*Go away, you shall measure yourself elsewhere.* <note>original: "συμμετρήσεις σαυτὸν ἀπιὼν ἀλλαχῆ"</note> That is,
Depart, you will measure yourself again from this place, having gone elsewhere.
The adage applies so that no one expands himself beyond his condition, nor estimates himself by the praises of flatterers, or the opinion of the common people, or the favor of fortune, but by his own true gifts and virtues. It is transferred from those who estimate the measure of the human body by the number of feet. Furthermore, the just measure of any man consists of seven of his own feet, if we believe painters and sculptors. To this also pertains that line of Martial:
<unclear>What</unclear> weighs its own weights, can bear its own.

<margin>90</margin>
->We do not see the knapsack that is on our back.<-
Catullus in his Scazon: *But we do not see the knapsack that is on our back.* That is,
We do not see our own faults, while we look through those of others with curious eyes. The proverb was born from some Aesopic Fable, which is reported in this manner in Stobaeus: *Aesop says that each of us carries two pouches, one in front and the other behind. And into the one in front we put the sins of others, but into the one behind, our own.* <note>original: "Αἴσωπος δύο πήρας ἕκαστον ἡμῶν φορεῖν..."</note> This is roughly the meaning of those words. Aesop imagined that every mortal has two knapsacks, that is, pouches, one hanging before the chest, the other from the shoulder-blades and back. But into the former, he says, we drop the faults of others; into the latter, our own. Persius says:
*How no one tries to descend into himself, no one,*
*But the knapsack on the back of the one preceding is watched.*
Horace:
*When you look through your own evils with bleary, anointed eyes,*
*Why do you see so sharply in the faults of friends?*
Saint Jerome: "But that is true rebuke among friends, if our own works do not see those of others; according to Persius, let us consider the knapsack."

<margin>91</margin>
->To cast the speck out of another's eye.<-
Not only the writings of poets but also the Gospel (for they will not be burdened by being cited in this order) have noted the blind <term>self-love<gloss>philautia</gloss></term> of the human mind, when they say there are some who see a speck in a brother's eye, but do not see the beam in their own. That is, they are offended by even the smallest faults of others, but flatter themselves in their own greatest ones. For so Matthew has it: *And why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye? Or how will you say to your brother, "Let me cast out the speck from your eye," and behold, a beam is in your own eye?* <note>original: "τί δὲ βλέπεις τὸ κάρφος..."</note> That is, why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but the beam which is in your own eye, you do not understand? Or how do you say to your brother, "Allow me, I will cast the speck out of your eye," and behold, a beam is in your own eye? For so the Greek words rendered word-for-word sound. Saint Jerome: "He who..."

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Roman proverbs, focusing on self-reflection and staying within one’s social or natural limits.</meta>

<page-num>224</page-num>
-> DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES <-

while he, as the saying goes, tries to remove the speck from another’s eye through the beam in his own <note>A reference to Matthew 7:3-5</note>. Horace elegantly notes this class of men:

> When you look over your own faults, he says, with eyes as blurry as if smeared with ointment, why do you look so sharply at the vices of your friends, <margin>The same author elsewhere:</margin> as keenly as an eagle or a serpent of Epidaurus? He who demands that his friend not be offended by his own large tumors, it is only fair that he forgive that friend’s small warts.

This itself carries the clear appearance of a proverb. He used "tumors" to mean major vices and "warts" for minor ones, which elsewhere he called "freckles."

### Keep yourself within your own skin.
<margin>92</margin>

*Keep yourself within your own skin.* Porphyrio <note>A 3rd-century commentator on Horace</note> advises that this is a proverb by which we are forbidden from forgetting our lot in life and attempting things greater than our capacity. He thinks it is derived from the fact that formerly leaders slept in skins—that is, in tents made of hides. To me, it seems more correctly referred to that donkey of Cumae, whom the Fables <note>Aesop's Fables</note> tell of having fitted himself with a lion’s skin, and thus for a time behaved as a lion. But that matter turned out badly for him; when he was recognized, to the great laughter of all, he was stripped of the foreign and <gloss>added</gloss> skin and beaten to death with clubs. 

Nor would one absurdly refer this to Cleon of Athens, who, having been made a leader of the army from a "leather-seller"—that is, a tanner—brought back a victory by the favor of fortune at the capture of Pylos. He plundered his own city through theft and was raised to the highest wealth in that manner; finally, being cast out and treated badly by another, he paid the penalty because he did not rest "in his own skin." He is introduced in the comedy of Aristophanes titled *The Knights*, and is frequently bitten by the same poet in other places. Plautus certainly seems to have alluded to this when he portrays a boastful and bragging soldier covered in elephant hide, not his own—either because it signified stupidity, or because he spoke of things greater than his ability. Horace says:
> And rightly so, since I did not rest in my own skin.

Martial says of a certain cobbler who, following Cleon’s example, was first raised to the highest riches, and as the winds blew, so he raised his sail high; then he was reduced back to his former poverty by his own lavish spending, so that he was now nothing but a common laborer:
> You have played enough, he says; it is enough: but believe me, remember to
> Keep yourself, cobbler, within your own skin.

Likewise Seneca in his *Letters*: They remove the wise man from everything and force him "within his own skin." Ovid expressed this without the metaphor thus:
> Believe me, he who has remained well hidden has lived well; and each man
> ought to remain within his own fortune.

Lucian also alluded to this in *Images*: <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι μένομεν ἐπὶ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων"</note> *we no longer remain upon the things that are present*; this refers to those who, elated by the successes of fortune, do not sufficiently remember their own condition. Finally, it does not seem absurd to me if the proverb is referred to the story of the flayed Marsyas <note>A satyr who challenged the god Apollo to a music contest and was skinned alive as punishment</note>, who, because he was unmindful of his condition and dared to contend with Apollo, was stripped of his own skin.

### To stretch wings larger than the nest.
<margin>93</margin>

There is a phrase in the *Letters* of Horace which is undoubtedly a proverbial metaphor: *To stretch wings larger than the nest.* This is used for one who increases the estate and fortune, however modest or thin, which he received from his ancestors. Indeed, if this is done through virtue, it is the highest praise, so far is it from being something I think should be considered a vice.
> You say that I, he says, born of a freedman father and in thin circumstances,
> stretched wings larger than my nest,
> so that as much as you take away from my birth, you add to my virtues.

The metaphor is taken from the chicks of birds, which grow so large as their feathers sprout that they cannot be contained by the mother’s nest.

### Spit into your own bosom.
<margin>94</margin>

In our own time, this adage is circulated in many regions. For they bid a man who is criticizing the vices of another to *spit into his own bosom*, as if warning him that by the recollection of his own domestic evils he should cease to arrogantly attack the life of another. That the same was accustomed to be done by the ancients can be gathered somehow from the words of Pliny, who writes in Book 28, Chapter 4, that this...

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY

In the same manner, we seek forgiveness from the gods for any overly bold hope by spitting into our own bosom. In the same chapter, he writes on the authority of Salpa <note>A female physician or midwife mentioned by Pliny the Elder</note> that numbness in any affected limb is soothed if one spits into the bosom. Both of these points are not entirely foreign to our common proverb. For indeed, he who carps at the faults of others sins with a certain wicked hope, as if he hopes to be free from any possible reproach, when there is no one who is not held by some vice; or he lacks the sense of his own evil, as if of himself, held by a certain numbness. Seneca, in the seventh book of *On Benefits*: **"Perhaps the vice of which you complain, if you examine yourself diligently, you will find in your own bosom."** Lucianus in his *Apology for those serving for wages*: <margin>original: "ὅτι οὐκ εἰς τὸν κόλπον πτύεις πρὸς τούτους κατηγορεῖν."</margin> <margin>that is:</margin> **"And that you did not first spit into your own bosom before you began to accuse them."** The same author in *The Wishes*: <margin>original: "ὑπερμαζᾶς γε ὦ ἀδάμαντε, καὶ ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ οὐ πτύεις, οὐδὲ οἶδα ὅτις ὢν νουθετεῖς."</margin> Someone jokes with a friend because, as if forgetting himself, he imagines immense wealth, and would not spit into his bosom so that he might recognize who he actually was. Theocritus indicates the same in his sixth *Idyll*. For Polyphemus, when he had extolled his own beauty a bit too arrogantly, says:
<margin>original: "ὡς μὴ βασκανθῶ δὲ, τρὶς εἰς ἐμὸν ἔπτυσα κόλπον, ταῦτα γὰρ ἁ γραῖά με κοτυτταρὶς ἐξεδίδαξεν."</margin>
The sense of this verse is roughly this: **"Lest envy harm me, or the evil eye do me hurt, thrice into my bosom have I spit; for the old woman Cotyttaris taught me that."** The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on a text</note> adds that this custom of spitting in the bosom to ward off envy still endured among common women in his own age. He also cites a verse of Callimachus:
<margin>original: "τίς δέ σ᾽ ἐπὶ κόλποισιν ἐπιπτύουσι γυναῖκες;"</margin> that is,
**"Why does every woman spit into her bosom at you?"**
To this perhaps belongs what Lucianus says in the *Necyomantia*: <margin>original: "τρὶς ἄν μοι πρὸς τὸ πρόσωπον ἔπτυσε."</margin> that is, **"After he had spit three times in my face."** Nor is it foreign to this what Persius wrote in his second *Satire*:
**"Behold, a grandmother or a god-fearing aunt takes the boy from his cradle, and his forehead and wet lips with an infamous finger and purifying spit she first hallows."**
This superstition stems from what Athenaeus indicates in book one: that the ancients, to drive away the evil eye, were accustomed to be wiped three times. He cites this little verse of the Cyrenian:
<margin>original: "τρὶς ἐκμαξάμενοι θεοὶ διδόασιν ἀμύνον."</margin> that is,
**"If you wipe yourself three times, the good deities grant better protection."**

### Know thyself.
### XCV

To the same sentiment belong those three sayings, most celebrated among all the <term>apophthegms</term> <note>concise, pithy sayings</note> of the wise, so much so that—as Plato testifies in the *Charmides*—they were inscribed by the Amphictyons <note>A league of neighboring Greek tribes</note> before the doors of the Delphic temple, as if they seemed worthy of a god. The first of these is <margin>original: "γνῶθι σεαυτόν,"</margin> **Know thyself.** In this is a commendation of modesty and moderation, lest we pursue things either too great or even unworthy of us. For from this arises every plague of life: while each person flatters himself, and as much as he unfairly detracts from others, so much does he through the vice of <term>philautia</term> <note>self-love or narcissism</note> attribute to himself beyond his merit. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] to his brother Quintus in the third book: **"And that 'Know thyself,' do not think it was said only to diminish arrogance, but also so that we might know our own good qualities."**
There is also this six-foot verse among the proverbial sentences:
<margin>original: "τὸ γνῶθι σεαυτὸν πανταχοῦ 'στι χρήσιμον."</margin> that is,
**"It is useful everywhere to know yourself."** A certain *Satire* of Varro is cited by Nonius Marcellus with this title: **"Know thyself."** Ovid in *The Art of Love*:
**"That letter celebrated throughout the world, which bids each man to be known to himself."**
And **"Know thyself"** descended from heaven, says Juvenal.
Aristotle attributes this sentiment to Pythagoras as its author. The Platonic Socrates thinks it originated from Apollo. Plato in the *Phaedrus*: <margin>original: "οὐ δύναμαί πω, κατὰ τὸ Δελφικὸν ἐπίγραμμα, γνῶναι ἐμαυτόν."</margin> that is, **"I am not yet able, according to the Delphic inscription, to know myself."** There are those who think this was also borrowed from Homer, as if from the Ocean, in whose work Hector, though he made an attack against all the others, nevertheless avoided Ajax as his superior. For thus the poet says:
<margin>original: "Αἴαντος δ᾽ ἀλέεινε μάχην τελαμωνιάδαο."</margin> that is, [he avoided the battle of Ajax, son of Telamon].

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on famous ancient Greek proverbs, specifically focusing on the origins and variations of the maxims "Know Thyself" and "Nothing in Excess."</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

He fled the encounter with Ajax, son of Telamon. <note>original: "Congressum Aiacis fugit Telamone creati." A poetic reference to avoiding a superior opponent.</note>
Diogenes attributes this to Thales. In his work, Antisthenes ascribes it to Phemonoe, while others claim Chilon used it. Thales, however, when asked, "What is difficult?" said, "To know oneself." "What is easy?" "To advise another." <note>original: "τί εἴη δύσκολον; ἔφη, τὸ ἑαυτὸν γνῶναι. τί εὔκολον; ἑτέρῳ ὑποτίθεσθαι."</note> Macrobius, in his first commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*, records that to someone consulting the Delphic oracle on what path leads to happiness, the response was: "If you know yourself." This oracle was also given to Croesus, according to Xenophon in the *Education of Cyrus*. This six-foot line from Antiphanes is cited by Greek collectors of maxims:
If you are mortal, my good man, then think mortal thoughts. <note>original: "Εἰ θνητὸς εἶ βέλτιστε, θνητὰ καὶ φρόνει."</note>
->that is,<-
Excellent man, if you are mortal, see that you contemplate things that are mortal.
Pindar expressed the same sentiment thus: Mortal things befit mortals. <note>original: "θνατὰ θνατοῖς πρέπει."</note>
Demonax, when asked when he began to practice philosophy, said, "After I began to know myself." Socrates <term>φ</term> <note>The symbol φ likely stands for "Philosophus" (The Philosopher).</note> was judged the only wise man by the oracle of Apollo when all of Greece held wise men; he interpreted it thus: that he surpassed others who claimed to know what they did not know, because he knew that he knew nothing—and he professed this was the one thing he knew. However, Anaxarchus surpassed this modesty of Socrates, for he used to declare that he did not even know that he knew nothing. In the works of the comic poet Menander, someone corrects this most praised saying of all:
In many ways it seems sharply put, but not well said,
This "Know thyself"; for it would have been more useful
To "Know others." <note>original: "Κατὰ πόλλ’ ἂν ὀξὺ, οὐ καλῶς εἰρημένον / Τὸ γνῶθι σαυτὸν, χρησιμώτερον γὰρ ἦν / Τὸ γνῶθι τοὺς ἄλλους."</note> ->that is,<-
In many ways the saying seems mistaken,
"Know thyself," for it would have been more to the point to say, ->"Know others."<-

### Nothing in excess.
### XCVI

The second proverb embraces nearly the same sentiment in different words: "Nothing too much" <note>original: "μηδὲν ἄγαν" (muden agan).</note>—that is, "Nothing in excess." Indeed, as it was commonly celebrated, Terence in the *Andria* even attributes it to the character of Sosia, a freedman. Diogenes Laertius ascribes it to Pythagoras. Aristotle, in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, refers the authorship to Bias while discussing the immoderate passions of the young, whom he says err everywhere through excessive vehemence; for they love too much, and likewise hate too much. The elderly are not the same, but to use Aristotle's own words: "And according to the suggestion of Bias, they both love as if they will one day hate, and hate as if they will one day love." <note>original: "καὶ τὴν Βίαντος ὑποθήκην, καὶ φιλοῦσιν ὡς μισήσοντες, καὶ μισοῦσιν ὡς φιλήσοντες."</note> There are those who attribute it to Thales. Some to Solon, according to Laertius. Plato cites it from Euripides in a certain place. Nor are there lacking those who refer it to Homer as if to the source; these are his verses in the fifteenth book of the *Odyssey*:
I am also annoyed with any other
Host who is a host, who loves excessively,
Or hates excessively; all things are better in due measure. <note>original: "Νεμεσσῶμαι δὲ καὶ ἄλλῳ / Ἀνδρὶ ξενοδόκῳ, ὅς κ’ ἔξοχα μὲν φιλέῃσιν, / Ἔξοχα δ’ ἐχθαίρῃσιν, ἀμείνω δ’ αἴσιμα πάντα."</note> ->that is,<-
That host does not please me at all,
Who simultaneously hates and loves violently beyond measure.
But I think it is better that all things be moderate. ->The same in the tenth book of the Iliad:<-
Son of Tydeus, neither praise me too much, nor yet rebuke me. <note>original: "Τυδείδη, μήτ’ ἄρ με μάλ’ αἴνεε, μήτ’ ἔτι νείκει."</note> ->that is,<-
Do not excessively praise the son of Tydeus, nor disparage me.
For my part, I would prefer to refer it to Hesiod. His is that line in the work titled *Works and Days*:
Observe due measure; the right moment is best in all things. <note>original: "Μέτρα φυλάσσεσθαι, καιρὸς δ’ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος."</note> ->that is,<-
Keep to the measure; moderation is best in every matter.
Euripides uses it in several other places, as well as in the *Hippolytus*:
Thus I certainly approve less of whatever
Is vehement, than of what the common people say, ->"Nothing in excess."<- <note>original: "οὕτω τὸ λίαν γ’ ἧσσον ἐπαινῶ / τοῦ μηδὲν ἄγαν."</note>
Pindar, according to Plutarch: "The wise have praised beyond measure this word: Nothing in excess." <note>original: "σοφοὶ δὲ καὶ τὸ μηδὲν ἄγαν ἔπος, αἴνησαν περισσῶς."</note> ->Sophocles in the Electra:<-
Do not be overly distressed by those you hate, nor forget them. <note>original: "Μηθ’ οἷς ἐχθαίρεις ὑπεράχθεο, μή τ’ ἐπιλάθου."</note> ->that is,<-
Let not that man whom you hate torment you too much or beyond measure,
But neither should you, unmindful, neglect your enemy.

# THE SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...us in *The Little Carthaginian* <note>Plautus, *Poenulus*</note>, "Moderation in all things, sister, is best." To the same point belongs that passage of Homer in the *Iliad*, Book 13:
-> There is a satiety of all things: of sleep and of love, <-
-> of sweet song and of the faultless dance. <-
<note>original Greek: πάντων μὲν κόρος ἐστὶ καὶ ὕπνου καὶ φιλότητος, μολπῆς τε γλυκερῆς καὶ ἀμύμονος ὀρχηθμοῖο.</note>
that is,
-> A fullness of all things comes to pass: of love, <-
-> of sleep, of the charming lyre, and the graceful dance. <-

Pindar seems to have imitated this in the *Nemean Odes*:
"There is a satiety even of honey and the delightful flowers of Aphrodite." <note>original Greek: ἔστι δὲ καὶ μέλιτος καὶ τὰ τέρπν’ ἄνθ’ ἀφροδίσια.</note> That is: Even honey and the joyful flowers of love have their limit. Pliny, in Book 11, says: "The most destructive thing in all of life is 'too much'." Horace writes:
-> There is a measure in things; there are, finally, fixed boundaries, <-
-> beyond and short of which right cannot find a stand. <-
And again the same author:
-> Virtue is a mean between vices, drawn back from either side. <-
Phocylides says:
"A measure in everything is best." <note>original Greek: παντὸς μέτρου ἄριστον.</note> That is: The moderation of all things is best. And Alpheus in an Epigram:
"Nothing in excess; 'too much' pleases me not." <note>original Greek: μηδὲν ἄγαν, ἄγαν με τέρπει.</note> That is:
-> Let there be nothing in excess; too much is not pleasing to me. <-

Quintilian wrote that moderation reigns in pronunciation, just as it does in all other things. And in Plutarch’s *Life of Camillus*, he teaches that piety is the middle ground between contempt for the gods and superstition: "But caution—and that 'nothing in excess'—is best." <note>original Greek: ἤ δὲ εὐλάβεια, νὴ τὸ μηδὲν ἄγαν, ἄριστον.</note> That is: Piety and, as they say, nothing too much, is the best thing. There is nothing among all things in which one cannot sin through excess, except for the love of God: which Aristotle also admits in other words, substituting "wisdom" for God. To this belongs what Athenaeus relates from some poet in Book 1 regarding the praises of wine:
-> For it is in the heart to sweep away the sorrows of men, <-
-> if one drinks to measure; but beyond measure, it leads to dancing. <-
<note>original Greek: ἔνεστι γὰρ καρδίας, ἀνίας ἀνθρώπων ἀλαπάζει, ἐὰν δέ τις ἐπὶ μέτρον, ὑπὲρ μέτρον δὲ χορεύειν.</note>
that is,
-> Wine drives all cares from the human breast <-
-> if you drink moderately; but without measure, it will be harmful. <-

## Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand. XCVI.

"Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand." <note>original Greek: ἐγγύα, παρὰ δ’ ἄτη.</note> That is: Give a guarantee, but harm is nearby. Socrates, in Plato, thinks all these sayings pertain to the same sentiment. For he who acts as a surety <term>surety: a person who takes responsibility for another's debt or conduct</term> for another, promises that which is not in his own power to provide—namely, the good faith of another person. But he believes Apollo granted the first part, while the other two were added by mortals. Pliny, in Book 7, chapter 32, likewise ascribes the fame of this to Chilon, but in such a way that they were held as oracles: "Again," he says, "mortals gave a share of the oracles to Chilon the Lacedaemonian, consecrating three of his precepts at Delphi in golden letters, which are these: 'Know thyself,' 'Desire nothing too much,' and 'The misery of debt and litigation'." Pliny explained what it means to give a pledge: to be a guarantor for the money of the one who is trusted; and it often happens that the guarantor is forced to pay the money to the creditor. We also give pledges before judges for a defendant's appearance, and if he fails to show, the guarantors are punished. They trace this saying back to Homer as the author. This is his verse in the *Odyssey*, Book 8:
-> Pledges for the worthless are worthless to take. <-
<note>original Greek: δειλαί τοι δειλῶν γε καὶ ἐγγύαι ἐγγυάασθαι.</note>
Athenaeus, citing Plutarch in *Plato's Symposium*, refers this to the Homeric fable of Ate <note>the goddess of mischief/ruin</note>, who, having been present at Jove's pledge regarding the birth of Hercules, was cast down by him to the earth. Cicero... these three apophthegms are concluded by Plutarch in his booklet *On Garrulity*. XCVII.

## He knows what is white and what is black. XCVIII.

"He knows the white and the black." <note>original Greek: ἴσθι τὸ λευκὸν καὶ τὸ μέλαν.</note> That is: He knows what is white, what is black. This can be understood in two ways. Either he knows the difference between right and wrong, or he knows that which no one, even the unlearned, is ignorant of. For the difference between white and black is too evident for anyone not to see it. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
-> For I have known this man, as everyone knows him, <-
-> who knows white, or the upright law. <-
<note>original Greek: τοῦτον ἔγνωκα γὰρ οὐδὲ εἰς ὅστις οὐκ ἐπίσταται, τὸ μὲν λευκὸν οἶδεν, ἢ τὸν ὄρθιον νόμον.</note>
that is,
-> Because there is no one who does not know Arignotus the lyre-player, <-
-> who knows white, or knows the correct melodies. <-
The former sense shows and explains the proverb. It seems to be drawn from those ancient mortals who knew only two natural colors, white and black, according to Pompeius.

## Whether you are white or black, I know not. XCIX.

Regarding things... whether you are white or black, I know not. It is usually said of a person who is utterly unknown. Cicero, *Philippics*...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

secondly: "No one made me an heir except a friend, so that some grief of mind was joined with that benefit, if there was any. But you, Lucius Rubrius Cassinas, whom you never saw, made you his heir. And indeed, see how much he loved you, when you do not even know whether he was **white or black** <note>original: "albus, aterue"; a Roman idiom meaning to be completely indifferent to or ignorant of someone's character or existence</note>, yet he passed over his own brother's son." Quintilian, in the eleventh book of the *Institutes of Oratory*, says: "Some poet says he does not care much whether Caesar be a **white or a black man**." He is pointing his finger, I believe, at Catullus, whose poem against Caesar survives:
I do not strive too much, Caesar, to wish to please you,
->Nor to know whether you are a white or a black man.<-
Apuleius in his *Apology for Magic*: "Until recently, I was even gladly ignorant of whether you were **white or black**; by Hercules, I still do not know well enough." Saint Jerome against Helvidius: "Who, I pray, knew you before this blasphemy? Who valued you at two pence? You have achieved what you wanted. You have become famous through crime. I myself, who write against you, though I stay in the same city with you where you stammer and blush, know not whether you are **white**, as they say, **or black**." Horace at the end of an epistle: ->"Changeable in countenance, white and black."<-
In this place, Porphyrion <note>A 3rd-century commentator on Horace</note> advises that it was said as a proverbial figure, **white and black**, for that which is "good and bad"; and that Horace rendered "white" as either generous or joyful, and "black" as mean and wretched. Matron alluded to this more wittily in Athenaeus, book four, speaking of the cuttlefish:
"The only good fish, she knows both the white and the black." <note>original Greek: ἡ μόνη ἰχθὺς ἐσθλὴ, τὸ λευκὸν καὶ μέλαν οἶδε.</note>
For the cuttlefish is white in color, but has a black juice <note>ink</note> which it scatters in fear so it might not be caught.
->"He did not know he was born."<-
Very similar to this figure is "I did not know he was born," for that which I am utterly and in every way ignorant of. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the ninth book of his *Familiar Letters*, to Papirius: "For I know that letters have already been brought to me from the last kings, in which they thank me because by my vote I called them kings—men whom I did not only not know were called kings, but did not even know were born." Very similar to that is the phrase in Aristophanes' *Wasps*: "Who would not even have known I lived?" <note>original Greek: ὅς γε οὐδ’ οἷς ἔζης? ἤδη.</note> that is, he would have had no regard for me at all.
Likewise Theocritus in *The Sorceress*:
"Nor did he know whether we are dead or alive." <note>original Greek: οὐδ’ ἔγνω πότερον τεθνάκαμες ἢ ζωοὶ εἰμές.</note>
Plautus used the same sentiment in *Euclio*: "You should regard me no more than if I had never been born."

### THE SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

->I hate a drinking companion with a memory.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring a seated figure in a landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>
"I hate a drinking companion with a memory." <note>original Greek: Μισῶ μνάμονα συμπόταν.</note> This is directed against those who blabber outside the things said freely among friends and over drinks. Lucian, in *The Lapiths*, cites it from some poet. Martial says:
"I hate a drinking companion with a memory, Procillus."
For the poet jokes against a certain Procillus, who, having been told over drinks to come to dinner the next day, came in earnest: just as if things said over wine ought to have weight. Plutarch mentions this proverb in the very first problem of his *Table Talk*, where he asks whether it is fitting to philosophize at banquets. He thinks, however, it was said against those who insist and urge beyond measure at banquets, driving others to drink and demanding the prescribed measure of the cup. For some, not very eager to drink, usually escape by distracting their fellow guests into forgetfulness with intervening conversation. Then, if someone by chance remembers and demands it, they lie and say they have already drunk. The Dorians in Sicily call the overseers of banquets or measures *Mnamonas* <note>Remembrancers</note>, whom the Latins call *modiperatores* <note>controllers of the measure</note>, according to Nonius, because they command the measure of drinking. From this, the proverb will seem to fit those who require the prescribed measure at a banquet too exactly. To others it seems rather that the proverb advises *amnestia* <note>amnesty</note>, that is, the forgetting of all things that are either done or said at banquets. For this is attested by the fables of the Mafori <note>likely a reference to the Muses or Bacchic attendants</note>, who consecrated both Joy and Forgetfulness to Bacchus at the same time: surely hinting this, that one ought not to remember if anything...

> And so we too have withdrawn our hand from the cane. <note>original: "Et nos ergo manum ferulæ subduximus." A reference to finishing one's basic schooling.</note>

Plutarch relates elsewhere in the same work that the Spartans had a custom where, if they received a guest into the house, they would point to the doors and say, <gloss>No word goes out this way</gloss> <note>original: "ταύτῃ ἐκ θύρας ἔρχεται λόγος"</note>. I write a woman's oath in wine.

-> To this belongs that Greek six-foot verse: <-
-> that is, <-

That whatever is blurted out during drinking bouts is usually in vain. This alludes to a proverb which I have recorded elsewhere, <gloss>I write in water</gloss> <note>original: "εἰς ὕδωρ γράφω"</note>, meaning a vanishing thing. To this also pertains the fact that, as Plutarch testifies in his *Table Talk*, the ancients imagined Bacchus <note>The god of wine</note> to be the son of Oblivion; and someone in that work jokingly inverted this, saying that wine should rather be called the *mother* of oblivion than the son, because wine—especially in excess—takes away a man's memory even before old age.

### To sit on two chairs. II

**To sit on two chairs** is to be of uncertain parties and of wavering loyalty, trying to satisfy both sides. Using a newly coined word, Homer calls Mars <gloss>one who plays both sides</gloss> <note>original: "ἀμφοτερίζειν"</note>, that is, a friend now favoring this side, now that. Macrobius, in his *Saturnalia*, writes: When Laberius the mime-writer was elected to the Senate by Caesar, and was not received by Cicero into the seating area—Cicero saying, "I would receive you, were we not sitting so cramped"—Laberius replied quite bitingly, "And yet you used to sit on two chairs," mocking the slippery loyalty of so great a man. But what Cicero said—"were we not sitting so cramped"—was a jab at Caesar, who was admitting so many people into the Senate from all over that the fourteen rows of seats could not hold them. Thus far Macrobius. It is, however, a most shameful proverb by common consent: to play along with both sides. Yet Solon passed a law that those who, in a civil tumult, adhered to neither party should be punished.

### To whitewash two walls from the same bucket. III

Very close to this seems to be: **To whitewash two walls from the same bucket.** This is used for gaining double favor from a single thing, and by the same effort deserving thanks from two people at once. Marcus Curius to Cicero: "But, my great friend, do not show this letter to Atticus. Let him remain in error and think me a good man, and not one who is accustomed to whitewash two walls from the same bucket." For Marcus Curius wanted to seem excellent to both Atticus and Cicero equally, and to make two friends for himself with one single act. It seems to be drawn from those who spread plaster over walls. One also reads a Greek adage of this kind in Suidas: <gloss>To smear two walls</gloss> <note>original: "δύο τοίχους ἀλείφειν"</note>. It refers to those who, in political factions, flatter both sides. To this sentiment belongs that of the Hebrew prophet: **To limp on both feet.** Also that of the Gospel: **To serve two masters.** And again that from the Apocalypse, concerning those who are **neither hot nor cold.**

### With one daughter to provide two sons-in-law. IV

Something similar to this is still commonly said today, and it is certainly worthy of being counted among the authoritative adages: **With one daughter you wish to provide twin sons-in-law.** This is used when someone promises the same benefit to two people at once, or demands thanks from two people for the same service he performed for one.

### You know not what the late evening may bring. V

> You know not what the late evening may bring.

In the Menippean Satires of Varro, this title is cited both by Aulus Gellius and by Macrobius; nor is there any doubt that it is proverbial, as are most of the others. By this we are healthily warned not to cast aside care for the future, being carried away by the prosperity of present successes. Nor should we rejoice in any matter before we have seen the outcome. The common people say the same thing today: The day has not yet... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

> Finally, what the late evening may bring. <note>original: "Deniq; quid ferus uesper uehat."</note>

dealing with the signs of the sunset. It can also be referred to that sentiment of Solon: *Look to the end of a long life.* <note>original Greek: ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου.</note> Titus Livius, in Book 5 of the 5th Decade: "In prosperity, it is unbecoming to consult anyone with pride or violence, nor to yield to present fortune, since what the evening may bring is uncertain." King Philip alluded to this in the same author, Book 9 of the 4th Decade, when responding to the Thessalians he added a threatening conclusion: "The sun of all their days has set." <note>A metaphor for total destruction.</note>

<margin>6</margin>
### ->**Many carry the wand, but few are Bacchi.**<-
->Many indeed are the wand-bearers, but few are the true followers of Bacchus. <note>original Greek: Πολλοί τοι ναρθηκοφόροι, παῦροι δέ τε βάκχοι.</note><-
->One may see many wand-bearers, but few true Bacchi.<-

A hexameter verse celebrated as a proverb among the Greeks, by which it is signified that many mortals possess the insignia of virtue, or even the reputation, who nevertheless lack true virtue. Just as not all are true theologians who wear the theological cap, or who are gifted with this name. Not all are poets who carry themselves about by that title. Not all are monks who are burdened by the cowl. Not all are Christians who act out the Christian through ceremonies. Not all are noble who wear a gold chain. Not all are virgins who have loose hair. Not all are kings who are distinguished by a diadem. Not all are bishops who wear the two-horned mitre or the silver staff <term>pedum: a bishop's crosier</term>. Not all are Supreme Pontiffs who are called "Most Holy" and are distinguished by the triple crown. Not all are Emperors who display the eagle on their banners. Neither the "wearing of a beard" nor the "wearing of a philosopher's cloak," as Plutarch says, makes a philosopher—that is, a beard worn or a cloak worn. It is translated from the ceremonies of the Bacchanalia, in which they used to shake <term>thyrfos: thyrsi, wands wreathed in ivy and vine leaves</term>, which are certain vine-covered spears, when inspired by frenzy. It is used by Plato in the dialogue titled *Phaedo*. Plutarch alluded to this elegantly in the booklet he wrote against Colotes: *One of our companions, Aristodemus of Aegina, has been seized by a religious frenzy—for I know the man—not in appearance, nor as a wand-bearer, but as a most frantic initiate of Plato.* <note>original Greek: Εἷς τῶν ἑταίρων κεκορύβανται ὁ Αἰγενεὺς...</note> He calls him a "wand-bearer" who is an Academic <note>A follower of Plato's Academy</note> in name and dress only, not in reality. There is also that witty remark of Herodes Atticus to a man in a cloak, with long hair and a beard reaching down to his waist: "I see the beard and the cloak; the philosopher I do not yet see."

<margin>7</margin>
### ->**Not all who have a lyre are lyre-players.**<-

Marcus Varro, in the second book *On Agriculture*, expressed the same sentiment with a different metaphor: "But not all," he says, "who have a lyre are lyre-players." To this should be added what Seneca wittily wrote: that a certain person preferred the mask to the face. He calls it the "face" when someone appears as they truly are; the "mask" when someone puts forward what they are not. It can also be twisted against the greedy, if you deny that those are wealthy who possess riches, but rather those who know how to use them rightly. Just as he is not a lyre-player whoever holds a lyre, but he who knows how to use the lyre rightly. He is not a king to whom a wide empire has fallen, but he who knows how to administer it.

<margin>8</margin>
### ->**Many are the pebble-throwers, few are the prophets.**<-
->Many are the pebble-throwers, but few are the men who are prophets. <note>original Greek: πολλοὶ θριοβόλοι, παῦροι δέ τε μάντιες ἄνδρες.</note><-
->One may see many pebble-throwers, but few true prophets.<-

This verse is similar to the one above, celebrated in the same way by the Greeks. Philochorus, according to Zenodotus, is the authority that once three nymphs, the nurses of Apollo, inhabited Parnassus, who were called the *Thriae*; from which it was later accepted that the pebbles and lots of diviners were called *Thriae*. Hence *thrioboli* are those who throw the *thriae* into the divine urn. There are those who assert that the method of divining by lots was discovered by Minerva. When this method flourished more than the Delphic oracles, it was rendered lying and vain, and that by the work of Jupiter, wishing to do a favor for Apollo. Then, when mortals again frequented the Delphic oracles, the Pythia <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi</note> spoke in this manner: *Many are the pebble-throwers, but few are the men who are prophets.*

<margin>9</margin>
### ->**Many who goad the oxen, few plowmen.**<-

This verse also has a similar meaning:
->Many are the ox-goaders, but few are the plowmen of the earth. <note>original Greek: πολλοὶ βουκένται, παῦροι δέ τε γῆς ἀροτῆρες.</note><-
->Many who goad the bull, but the plowman is rare.<-

He emphasizes that true identity comes from action and character rather than titles or ceremonial objects.</summary>

# SEVENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>u 2</sig>

### 10. An ape in purple.

<margin>An ape in purple. <note>original Greek: Πίθηκος ἐν πορφύρᾳ</note></margin> That is, a purple-clad ape. This proverb can be applied to various uses: either to those who, although adorned with magnificent dress, are nevertheless recognized for what they truly are by their very face and actions; or to those upon whom an unseemly dignity is bestowed; or whenever artificial and foreign ornaments are inappropriately applied to a thing. For what is so ridiculous as an ape dressed in a purple garment? And yet we see this happen not infrequently among those who keep apes as pets; they adorn and dress them as much as possible in the human fashion, sometimes even in purple, in order to deceive the inattentive or the unskilled, so that they might venerate an ape as a man—or, if the trick is discovered, the matter becomes even more ridiculous. How many apes of that kind can one see in the courts of princes! If you were to strip away the purple, the collar, and the gems, you would find them to be mere <term>handicraftsmen<note>The Latin 'cerdones' refers to low-born laborers or cobblers; Erasmus uses it here to denote lack of nobility or true character.</note></term>. It will be more elegant if the metaphor is extended further, such as to those who simulate holiness with a beard and a cloak. Augustine somewhere calls such people "philosophers of the staff," not without wit. And Ammianus in Book 14 calls a certain Antigonus a philosopher more by his dress than his character. We have spoken previously regarding those who are "wise only as far as the beard."

### 11. An ape is an ape, even if it wears golden insignia.

<margin>An ape is an ape, even if it has golden symbols. <note>original Greek: Πίθηκος ὁ πίθηκος, κἂν χρύσεα ἔχῃ σύμβολα</note></margin> An ape will still be an ape, even if it wears golden insignia. This corresponds to the previous adage, warning that the ornaments of fortune do not change a man’s nature. The adage is cited by Lucian in his oration against the unlearned. It seems to have originated from apes which, among the Egyptians, imitated human dancing. Lucian relates a <term>fable<note>original: apologum</note></term> in this manner: A certain Egyptian king trained several apes to learn the method of dancing. For just as no animal approaches the human form more closely, so no other animal imitates human acts more easily or willingly. Therefore, having been taught the art of dancing, they immediately began to dance, dressed in headbands and purple robes, and wearing masks. For a long time the spectacle was greatly pleasing, until a certain witty fellow among the spectators threw some nuts, which he was carrying secretly in his lap, into the middle of them. Thereupon the apes, as soon as they saw the nuts, forgot the dance and began to be what they had been before; they suddenly turned back from dancers into apes. Having smashed their masks and torn their clothes, they fought among themselves for the nuts, to the great laughter of the spectators. A similar fable is told of a cat, which Venus had beautifully adorned <insert>into the rank of a girl</insert> and she acted the woman <note>original Greek: ἐγυναικίζε</note> quite aptly, until a mouse ran out from some hole into the middle, and she declared herself to be nothing other than a cat.

### 12. An ass among the Cumans.

<margin>An ass among the Cumans. <note>original Greek: Ὄνος παρὰ κυμαίους</note></margin> That is, an ass among the people of Cyme. This applies to those who, though they are inept and ridiculous, are nevertheless held in high value among strangers by the very novelty of their presence. Or to those upon whom some honor is added by fortune beyond their merit, which breeds pride and insolence, as usually happens. Demosthenes notes this elegantly in the first of the Olynthiac orations: <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ εὖ πράττειν παρὰ τὴν ἀξίαν, ἀφορμὴ τοῦ κακῶς φρονεῖν, τοῖς ἀνοήτοις γίνεται</note> i.e., "For success and the prosperity of affairs which happens to the undeserving is wont to provide a cause for madness to the foolish." To which that quote from Aeschylus agrees:
<margin>A foolish man experiencing good fortune is a heavy burden. <note>original Greek: Βαρὺ φέρημ’ ἄνθρωπος εὐτυχῶν ἄφρων</note></margin> that is,
> A mindless man is a heavy weight when using prosperous things.

We remember elsewhere the story of the runaway ass who, among the Cumans, behaved as if he were a lion.

### 13. Anger grows old most slowly of all.

<margin>Anger grows old last. <note>original Greek: Ὁ θυμὸς ἔσχατον γηράσκει</note></margin> i.e., Anger is the last thing to grow old. Opposite to this is that apophthegm of Aristotle, who (according to Laertius), when asked what thing grows old most quickly, replied: "A favor." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] embraced both: "He who is pleased," he says, "forgets; he who is pained, remembers." For commonly mortals are accustomed to remember injuries most tenaciously, and to forget benefits most quickly. The Greek adage seems to be taken from Sophocles, whose words in *Oedipus at Colonus* are these:
<margin>For there is no other old age for anger except for the dead; no pain touches them. <note>original Greek: Θυμοῦ γὰρ οὐδὲν γῆράς ἐστιν ἄλλο, πλὴν θανόντων· οὐδὲν ἄλγος ἅπτεται</note></margin> that is,
> For no old age happens to wrath
> After death; no pain touches those buried.
