# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Homer suggests this same idea through a truly charming fiction concerning the "Prayers" <note>original: *Litae*; personifications of prayer and repentance</note> and "Folly" <note>original: *Ate*; the goddess of mischief, delusion, and rash action</note>. He depicts this goddess as one who is accustomed to sending harm and turmoil into the affairs of mortals, and describes her as having sharp eyes and very swift feet. However, following a long distance behind her come the goddesses of Prayer, who strive to mend whatever Folly has disturbed. He imagines these goddesses with squinting eyes and lame feet, surely implying that offenses are quick, but reconciliations are slow, because men are accustomed to remembering injuries for a long time. I will transcribe the poem of Homer itself from the ninth book of the *Iliad*:

> For Prayers are the daughters of great Zeus,
> Lame and wrinkled, with eyes looking askance,
> Who take care to follow behind Folly as they go.
> But Folly is strong and fleet of foot, wherefore she
> Outruns them all by far, and arrives first across every land,
> Harming men; but these others heal the damage afterward.
> Whoever reveres the daughters of Zeus as they draw near,
> Him they greatly benefit, and they hear him when he prays.
> But whoever denies them and stubbornly refuses,
> They then go and beseech Zeus, the son of Cronus,
> That Folly may follow that man, so that being harmed, he may pay the penalty.

We shall render the meaning of these verses for Latin ears, though we cannot capture their innate character or grace:

> For the great son of Saturn also fathered Prayers,
> Wrinkled, with lame feet, and damaged sight,
> Who come from behind Folly, that they might heal her work.
> Folly herself, strong of foot and excelling in might,
> Therefore outstrips them far with a swift pace; she seizes
> And arrives first throughout all lands,
> Harming mortals: but these follow behind
> To mend whatever evils she has stirred up.
> But truly, he who reveres and listens to the daughters of Jove,
> As soon as they approach, they procure many benefits
> For this grateful man, and in turn receive his vows.
> But if anyone rejects them stubbornly and denies them,
> Then, having approached Father Jove, they pray that Folly
> May immediately attend him, and that he may finally pay the penalty through his own loss.

Mention is made of this same Folly in *Iliad* book 19, where Jupiter, blaming this goddess because he had been deceived by Juno, seized her by the hair and cast her headlong down to earth, forbidding her ever to return to the company of the heavenly gods. Some think this fiction of Homer is related to that which Christians believe concerning Lucifer being cast down from the heavens.

### If you are a vulture, wait for the corpse.

Legacy hunters <note>original: *captatores*</note> and those who chase after inheritances <note>original: *haeredipetae*</note> are called "vultures" by a common metaphor, because they gape after childless old men as if they were corpses. For it is characteristic of this bird to live only on carcasses. Whence nature has added such keenness of scent to it (according to Pliny) that it flies two or three days in advance to where corpses are going to be; and for that reason, as the great Basil reports, it is accustomed to accompany the camps of soldiers in a huge flock. In this, the bird is less harmful than those men who loom over the masters of great wealth, because it neither touches crops nor kills or pursues any animal, however defenseless; it feeds only on corpses, either of those that died naturally or were left behind by others. Among these, however, it abstains from the corpses of its own kind, that is, of birds. As Plutarch also teaches in his *Roman Questions* <note>original: *problematis rerum antiquarum*</note>—not to mention anything for the moment from the opinion of the Egyptians, who say that all vultures are female and conceive from the East wind, just as trees become pregnant from the West wind. Therefore, those who dare to either accuse wealthy men or remove them with poison are called "kites" <note>birds of prey known for stealing</note>; but those who merely hunt with services and flatteries so that they may be included in a will are called "vultures" by the proverb. Seneca in book 15, letter 96: *If you are a vulture, wait for the corpse.* Martial in book 6:

> Silanus has lost his only son.
> Do you cease to send gifts, Oppianus?
<note>Oppianus is the "vulture" waiting for the grieving father to die so he can inherit the estate.</note>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 7

## 15. He mocked the gaping raven.

<margin>Alas, cruel crime and evil Fates! Whose vulture shall this corpse be? <note>original: "Heu crudele nephas, malæq́; Parcæ, Cuius uulturis hoc erit cadauer?"</note></margin>
Diogenianus mentions this proverb in his collections, but in a different form: *like a vulture* <note>original: "ἀπὸ γυπὸς"</note>. It serves as a warning against those who lie in wait for someone, either in the hope of an inheritance or some other gain.

A similar figure of speech was used by Horace regarding a man who had skillfully frustrated one who was hunting for his inheritance: **He mocked the gaping raven.**

<margin>Often, he says, the old fox mocked the gaping raven. <note>original: "Plerunq́;, inquit, recoctus Coruum delusit hiantem." Horace, Satires 2.5.56.</note></margin>
For this bird also hovers over corpses. He is speaking of Coranus, who, after dangling the hope of a will before his father-in-law Nasica through trickery, died and left him nothing but a reason to weep. This adage seems to be modeled after and imitated from that of the Greeks: *The wolf gapes* <note>original: "λύκον ἔχανον"</note>. So one might likewise say: "he mocked the gaping wolf," or *the raven was gaping* <note>original: "κὄραξ ἔχανεν"</note>.

## 16. To caw like a crow.

Indeed, the Greeks use the proverb *to caw* <note>original: "κεκῴζειν"</note> to mean gaping after prey or chattering foolishly. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
<margin>You seek to take a share. That is: I know why you croak; surely if I have flown off with anything by theft, you want to carry off a portion for yourself. <note>original: "Ζητεῖς μεταλαβῶν..."</note></margin>
*I know what that cawing means: that you seek to share in whatever I might have stolen.*

The commentator notes that this is a proverb used against those who "crow" in vain, after the fashion of crows. These are the words of the old man Chremylus, who says he is well aware of what Blepsidemus intends by turning his speech up and down while striving to elicit a confession—namely, so that as an accomplice he might come into a share of the loot. Persius in Satire 5:
> I know not what weight you are foolishly cawing to yourself. <note>original: "Neſcio quid tecum graue cornicaris inepte."</note>

Saint Jerome also used this in his letter to the monk Rusticus.

## 17. In wine there is truth.

<margin>*In wine there is truth* <note>original: "Ἐν οἴνῳ ἀλήθεια"</note>. This adage is used everywhere among authors, signifying that drunkenness removes the disguise of the mind and brings whatever is hidden in the breast into the open. Hence, Holy Scripture forbids wine to be given to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns. Pliny, in Book 14, Chapter 22, wrote that wine betrays the secrets of the mind to such an extent that men speak even of deadly things over their cups, and cannot contain words that will not even return through their throats; and commonly, he says, truth is attributed to wine. The apothegm of a certain Persian is also celebrated, who denied that there was any need for tortures to seek out the truth, for the truth is drawn out by wine. Horace approves of this in his Odes:</margin>
> You apply a gentle torture to a character
> that is usually harsh; you reveal the anxieties
> of the wise and their secret
> counsel through the jesting Bacchus. <note>original: "Lyæo" - a name for Bacchus/Wine.</note>

The same author in *The Art of Poetry*:
> Kings are said to urge with many cups,
> and to torture with wine, the one they labor to see through,
> to know if he be worthy of friendship.

And again elsewhere:
> What does drunkenness not reveal? It discloses hidden things.

<margin>*Wine and truth* <note>original: "οἶνος καὶ ἀλήθεια"</note>. Because those who have drunk deeply not only blurt out their own secrets, but also speak more boldly against others. In Plutarch’s *Life of Artaxerxes*, when Parysatis spoke to Mithridates, who had said something rather insolent through wine:</margin>
This proverb is also related in this manner in Athenaeus, Book 2: *Wine and truth*. Because those who have drunk deeply not only blurt out their own secrets, but also speak more boldly against others. In Plutarch’s *Life of Artaxerxes*, when Parysatis spoke to Mithridates, who had said something rather insolent through wine: <margin>There is indeed no envy, Mithridates; but since the Greeks say, "wine and truth," etc. <note>original: "φθόνος μὲν οὐδεὶς..."</note> This proverbial sentiment is also celebrated by the Greeks:</margin> *For what is in the heart of the sober man is on the tongue of the drunkard.* <note>original: "τὸ γὰρ ἐν καρδίᾳ τοῦ νήφοντος..."</note> Theognis:
<margin>For what is in the heart of the sober man is on the tongue of the drunkard. Theognis,</margin>
<margin>Gold or silver is distinguished by craftsmen in the fire; wine, betraying the man, proves his character. <note>original: "γινώσκει δ' ἀνδρὸς..."</note></margin>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the proverb "In wine there is truth," exploring how intoxication, childhood, and madness are thought to reveal hidden realities, before transitioning to the proverb "An ox on the tongue."</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Athenaeus cites this six-foot line from Euripides:
*For bronze is the mirror of the form, but wine is the mirror of the mind.* <note>original: "Κάτοπτρον γὰρ εἶδος χαλκός ἐστ᾽, οἶνος δὲ νοῦ."</note>
That is to say:
*Beauty shines in bronze, but wines betray the heart.*
In the same author, Ephippus says:
*The abundance of wine forces you to speak much,
and they say those who are drunk speak the truth.* <note>original: "οἶνος σε πλήθει πολλ᾽ ἀναγκάζει λαλεῖν, οὐκὲν μεθυόντάς φασι τ᾽ ἀληθῆ λέγειν."</note>
That is to say:
*The great power of wine forces you to say much:
Therefore, they say the drunk speak true things.*
But in the same tenth book, he records a saying of Anacharsis <note>A Scythian philosopher famous for his blunt wisdom.</note>: *that false opinions occur to those who are drunk.* <note>original: "ὅτι ψευδεῖς δόξαι τοῖς μεθύουσι γίγνονται."</note> And shortly after he tells a rather witty story. One of the guests said to Anacharsis, "You have married a very ugly wife." But he replied, "Indeed, she seems the same to me. But hey, boy, hand me a cup of unmixed wine, so that I may make her beautiful." Therefore, not only to the lover, but also to the drunkard, *things that are not beautiful appear beautiful,* <note>original: "τὰ μὴ καλὰ καλὰ πέφανται"</note> as Theocritus says. Yet how can one speak the truth who fails in the judgment of things? But truth does not always correspond to a lie, but sometimes to pretense. It can happen that a man speaks from his heart, yet says what is false; and another speaks the truth who does not speak truly <note>i.e., he says a fact by accident while intending to deceive.</note>. Finally, the proverb does not refer to insane drunkenness, which makes fixed things seem to move and single things seem multiple, but to moderate drinking, which shakes off <term>dysopia</term> <note>A Greek term for "shamefacedness" or social awkwardness.</term> and makeup. Alcibiades says in Plato’s *Symposium*: *As for what follows, you would not seem to hear it from me, whether I speak or not, unless I first recounted that proverb: Wine, both with children and without children, was truthful.* <note>original: "τὸ δὲ ἐντεῦθεν οὐκ ἂν μοι δοκεῖτε λέγοντος ἢ μὴ πρῶτον μὲν, τὸ λεγόμενō, οἶνος ἄνευ τε παίδων, καὶ μετὰ παίδων, ἦν ἀληθής."</note> From these words it is clear that the same thing was tossed about in a proverb regarding childhood as was said of wine. Even today a common proverb persists, that the truth is not heard except from three kinds of men: children, the drunk, and the mad. To this I think should be added that proverbial little verse:
*The slipping tongue speaks the truth.* <note>original: "ἡ γλῶσσ᾽ ἁμαρτάνουσα τ᾽ ἀληθῆ λέγει."</note>
For it is believed to be true which falls from the unwary, since that alone is free from the suspicion of fiction. From such a slip, omens of more certain faith are gathered:
*Often the name of Orestes comes out instead of Neoptolemus,
And I love the error of the voice as an omen.*
Finally, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in his *Topics*, among those things which create certain belief, mentions childhood, sleep, imprudence, wine-drinking, and madness.

### 18. An ox on the tongue.

<margin>An ox on the tongue.</margin>
*An ox on the tongue.* <note>original: "Βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώττης."</note> This is used against those who do not dare to speak freely what they think. It is transferred either from the strength of the animal, as if it were weighing down the tongue and not allowing it to speak; or from the fact that the coinage of the Athenians once bore the figure of an ox. Likewise among the Romans, King Servius was the first to stamp bronze with the image of sheep and oxen, according to Pliny in book 18, chapter 3. Plutarch testifies to the same in his *Problems of Ancient Things*, because for the ancients almost all possession consisted of flocks and herds. Whence they wish for "money" <note>Latin: *pecunia*</note> to be named from "cattle" <note>Latin: *pecus*</note>. Therefore, those who kept silent for fear of paying a fine, or who did not dare to speak because they were corrupted by money, were said to have "an ox on the tongue." But Julius Pollux, in the ninth book of his *Vocabulary*, explaining this proverb, records things largely consistent with these, adding that the coin itself was commonly called "an ox." Furthermore, in the Delian spectacles, if a gift was to be given to someone, the herald was accustomed to announce: "So many oxen shall be given to him." An ox, however, was worth two Attic drachmas, whence there were those who believed this coinage was peculiar to the Delians, not the Athenians. He adds also that in the laws of Draco there exists mention of *fifty oxen*, <note>original: "πεντήκοντα βοῶν"</note> that is, of paying ten oxen—meaning ten coins. Nor were there lacking those who felt that Homer also spoke of coinage, not of the animal, when he said:
*Gold for bronze, a hundred-oxen value for nine-oxen value.* <note>original: "Χρύσεα χαλκείων ἑκατόμβοι᾽ ἐννεαβοίων."</note>
But Julius Pollux refutes this opinion in another place, showing that it was an exchange of things without coins. He who wrote the scholia <note>ancient commentaries</note> on Homer, book 2, relates that the ox was held in honor among the ancients for many reasons, but especially because it is an animal sacrificed to Apollo. Therefore, on one side of the coin they engraved an ox, and on the other a royal face. The adage, however, is expressed in this manner: *An ox has stepped upon the tongue,* <note>original: "βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώσσῃ βέβηκεν"</note> advising that it was usually said when someone was silent for the sake of money. Theognis...

# FIRST CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<sig>u 4</sig>

<margin>An ox on the tongue</margin> <note>original: "Βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώσσῃ"</note> that is, I have an ox on my tongue.
Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*: "He was the first of men to restrain his tongue, placing an ox upon it as a sign of silence." <note>original: "γλῶτταν δὲ ὡς πρῶτος ἀνθρώπων συνέσχε, βοῦν ἐπ' αὐτῇ σιωπῆς ἐπιθεὶς"</note> He is speaking of Pythagoras, the founder of the rule of silence. Likewise, regarding the scholar Scopelianus: "Nor should we be astonished if some, having their tongues bound, find an ox of silence occupying it." <note>original: "οὐδ' ἂν ἐκπλαγείημεν τὴν γλῶτταν ὑπὸ τῇ τῆς ἀφωνίας ἐπ' αὐτῇ βεβλημένοι"</note> It appears in Aeschylus’ *Agamemnon*:
<margin>As for the rest, I am silent; a great ox has stepped upon my tongue.</margin> <note>original: "Τὰ δ' ἄλλα σιγῶ, βοῦς ἐπὶ γλώσσης μέγας βέβηκεν"</note> that is,
> As for other matters, a certain huge ox has occupied my tongue.

### XIX
### He suffers from "Silver-Quinsy."
<margin>He suffers from silver-quinsy.</margin> <note>original: "Ἀργυράγχην πάσχει"</note> that is, He suffers from the silver-throat-ache. This is closely related to the previous entry, originating from an event recorded by Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights* and also by Plutarch in the *Life of Demosthenes*. It happened like this: When Demosthenes had spoken sharply in the assembly against the envoys of the Milesians <note>The Milesians were people from Miletus, an ancient Greek city</note> who had come to seek aid, and had successfully blocked their requests, the case was postponed to the following day. The envoys then went to Demosthenes and bribed him with a large sum of money not to speak against them. The next day, when the action was to be heard, Demosthenes came out into the assembly with a great deal of wool wrapped around his neck, pretending that he was suffering from *synanche* <note>a severe sore throat or quinsy</note>, and that this prevented him from speaking as usual. Then someone from the crowd, who suspected the trickery, cried out that he was suffering not from *synanche* (sore throat), but from *argyranche* (silver-throat). Now, *synanche* is a type of disease which the common people, through a corruption of medical terms, call "squinancy" <note>modern: quinsy</note>. Aretaeus of Cappadocia, in his first book on acute diseases, notes that it is called by two names: either *kynanche* (dog-throat), because the ailment is common in dogs, or *synanche*, because it constricts and suffocates the breath.

### XX
### The horse carries me, the king feeds me.
<margin>The horse carries me, the king feeds me.</margin> <note>original: "Ἵππος με φέρει, βασιλεύς με τρέφει"</note> that is,
> The horse carries me, the king feeds me.

This is counted among the Greek adages, and they add that it originated thus: A certain young man was serving as a soldier under King Philip. When he was advised to seek a discharge and retire from military service, he refused to do so, using these very words:
<margin>The horse carries me, the king feeds me.</margin> that is, The horse carries me, the King feeds me.
Meaning that he lived most comfortably, as one who traveled on someone else's feet and was fed by someone else's money. Horace alluded to this in his *Epistles*, speaking in the persona of Aristippus:
> <margin>Epistles, Book 1, Ep. 17</margin> This way of life is better and 
> much more worthy, that a horse should carry me and a king feed me.

In this same passage, Acron <note>an ancient commentator on Horace</note> reminds us of this proverb, which Diogenianus also mentions. It was adapted from some tragedy, for it is an anapestic dimeter verse.

### XXI
### Even corchorus among the herbs.
<margin>Even corchorus is among the herbs.</margin> <note>original: "Ἔνεστι καὶ κόρχορος ἐν λαχάνοις"</note> that is, Even corchorus is among the vegetables. This was usually said of men of no value who nevertheless strive to be counted among the important. For *corchorus* is a cheap kind of herb which Pliny, in his twenty-first book, lists in his catalog of vegetables. Elsewhere he mentions it among wild-growing plants. He writes that corchorus is a plant used for food in Alexandria, with rolled leaves similar to a mulberry, useful for many remedies. Theophrastus mentions the proverb in his seventh book *On Plants*, chapter seven, referring to corchorus among the vegetables that can be eaten either cooked or raw, but noting it is infamous in the proverb because of its bitterness. Suidas and Hesychius are the authorities for the idea that some consider the *corchorus* to be a very contemptible fish, of the same value as the *hippurus*. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "Nor did we touch the corchorus." <note>original: "μηδ' ἥψασθε τοῦ κορχόρου"</note> Nor was the commentator silent here regarding the proverb.

### XXII
### A jackdaw among the Muses.
<margin>A jackdaw among the Muses.</margin> <note>original: "Κολοιὸς ἐν ταῖς μούσαις"</note> that is, A jackdaw among the Muses. An unlearned man among the most learned; the most speechless among the most eloquent. It is rightly said of men who boast of false learning and impudently chatter against erudite men. For the jackdaw is a bird that is not at all musical, but is nonetheless hatefully talkative and noisy. Close to this is what Virgil says in his *Eclogues*:
> <margin>Eclogue 9</margin> A goose cackling among the tuneful swans.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s monumental collection of Adages (proverbs), transitioning from the discussion of swans and geese to the proverb regarding "Perfume on lentils."</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

That swans are tuneful is so frequently chanted in all the writings of the poets that nothing is more celebrated, even if it has happened to no one actually to hear this song. Nor are philosophers lacking who even attempt to provide a rational explanation for this matter. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author who wrote in Greek about natural history</note> adds that they do not sing unless the West Wind is blowing. From this is also derived the proverb, *a swan’s song* <note>original: "κύκνου ᾆσμα"</note>. Conversely, geese cackle with a certain annoying screech. Therefore, when an unlearned person prattles among the eloquent, the adage will be seasonably employed: **A goose among swans.**

### XXIII
## Perfume on lentils.

*A tale over lentils* <note>original: "τὸν ἐπὶ φακῇ μῦθον"</note>, that is, you are telling a story over a dish of lentils. This is used when someone introduces mention of some cheap and worthless man while others are speaking of distinguished men. It is read in this manner in all the common editions of Aulus Gellius, Book 13, Chapter 27. However, I prefer to subscribe to the correction of Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a Venetian scholar</note>, who restored this passage so that it reads, *Perfume in the lentils* <note>original: "τὸν ἐν φακῇ μύρον"</note>. It applies to a person or a thing that is applied entirely out of season to those whom it least suits. For instance, if you were to mix a philosopher into a banquet of wanton youths, or if you began to dispute grave and theological matters over drinks. Just as someone would foolishly mix precious perfume into the cheap legume of the lentil. Indeed, according to Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note>, the lentil both dims the eyesight, is heavy on the stomach, harmful to the intestines, hostile to the nerves, lungs, and head, and produces turbulent dreams. It will also be said where many dissimilar things are confused together. The words of Fronto in Gellius are these: "See to it, however, that you do not think that 'many mortals' must always and in every place be said instead of 'many men,' lest that Greek proverb from Varro’s satire plainly come to pass: *Perfume in the lentils*." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] employed the same in his first book of letters to Atticus: "They sent," he says, "ambassadors with authority to visit the Gallic states and take care that they did not join with the Helvetians. The ambassadors are Quintus Metellus Creticus and Lucius Flaccus, *perfume on the lentils*." <note>Cicero implies these distinguished men were wasted on a trivial or mismatched mission.</note> This passage also suffers from the same error as that of Gellius. Furthermore, the adage is cited by Aristotle in his book *On Sense and the Sensible*: "For these men are boasters; a certain common fellow said mockingly, when he was cooking lentils, 'not perfume.'" That is: For it is true what Strattis says when taxing Euripides, that when the lentil is being cooked, one ought not to pour in perfume. In which place, truly, it is not worth mentioning here what monstrosities our common manuscripts contain. Athenaeus also cites it in the fourth book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned"</note>:

> I wish to give you both a piece of wise advice,
> When you cook lentils, do not pour in perfume.

From the *Phoenissae* of the comic poet Strattis. He also cites from the *Necyia* of Sopater: "Ulysses of Ithaca is present as *perfume in the lentils*; take heart, my soul." He also brings forward Clearchus, the collector of proverbs, who also recorded this under the title of a proverb, *Perfume in the lentils*. Adding that it exists in Varro, and that many of the Latins used that proverb, to whom it was nevertheless unknown from where Varro took that iambic verse. Aristophanes seems to me to have alluded to this when he says in *The Peace*:
"Moreover, you shall plant thyme above, and pour on perfume."
Furthermore, by "perfume" I understand scented oil, such as that from a perfumer. Otherwise, to mix common oil with lentils is nothing extraordinary. Athenaeus in Book 2 cites this trimeter from Eupolis:

> A cheap and bad dish, sumptuously seasoned.

Moreover, this legume is especially celebrated among writers, just like the bulb, the onion, and garlic; some have even written an encomium <note>a speech of high praise</note> of the lentil. Certain things are beautiful in themselves, which nevertheless do not suit each other. It is the mark of an elegant man, therefore, to know what is fitting for what. The philosopher Diocles was considered a "dainty-eater" <note>original: "ὀψοφάγος"</note>. To someone asking him which fish was better, the conger eel or the *labrax* (which we call the sea-wolf), he replied: "One boiled, the other roasted." Thus Flaccus [Horace] says of the poet: "Bad in war, useful to the city." Whenever a task is delegated to someone poorly suited for it, you may aptly say: *Perfume on the lentils*. This shall also be added: I find this word written variously among authors, sometimes with an acute accent <note>original: "φακλῶ"</note>, sometimes with a circumflex <note>original: "φακλῶ"</note>; since this occurs so frequently, it can hardly seem to have happened through the ignorance of a scribe. From which I conjecture that *phaklo* was said by contraction for *phakelon*. For <unclear>phakelon</unclear>...

<margin>24</margin>
### A golden ring in a swine's snout.
This is closely related to a saying found in the proverbs of the Hebrews: *A golden ring in a swine's snout.* For so it is written in Proverbs, chapter 11: <note>Proverbs 11:22</note> *As a golden ring in a swine's snout, so is a beautiful woman who is foolish.* This applies whenever something excellent in itself is employed where it is least appropriate. For example, if wealth falls to the foolish, beauty to the lazy, noble birth to the cowardly, eloquence to a wicked man, or high office to the unworthy. By these things, they are not only not adorned, but they are actually made more ridiculous. In ancient times, certain barbarians especially believed they were adorned by inserting golden rings into their ears. A bronze ring is also used in the snouts of swine to prevent them from damaging fields by rooting with their snouts—a behavior peculiar to this animal, which is why it is believed to have "taught" the art of plowing. But if one were to insert a golden ring into a swine's snout, the matter would be utterly laughable. A verse by Menander is celebrated among the Greeks which does not differ much from this sentiment:
*A wicked man who speaks a golden word.* <note>original Greek: Χρηστὸς πονηρὸς, χρυσὸν ὅταν εἴπῃ λόγον.</note>

To this pertains what Aulus Gellius records in his *Attic Nights*: When someone of ill repute had given an opinion that was beneficial to the Republic, the authorities ordered that the same opinion be pronounced by another man of the highest integrity and decreed in his name; they considered it absurd for good counsel or a good sentiment to proceed from a bad man. To these should be added the saying of Antiphanes found in Athenaeus, book six:
*A mud-fish having a silver platter.* <note>original Greek: Σίλουρος ἀργυρᾶς πίνακ’ ἔχων.</note>

Some think the "Silurus" <note>the mud-fish or catfish</note> is what we now commonly call the Sturgeon, a fish highly praised above all others.

<margin>25</margin>
### A leaden sword in an ivory scabbard.
Bordering on this is the saying: *A leaden sword in an ivory scabbard.* <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐλεφαντίνῳ κολεῷ τὸ μολύβδινον ξίφος.</note> This arose from an <term>apophthegm</term> <note>a concise, pithy saying</note> of Diogenes the Cynic. For when a certain youth of remarkable beauty had said something foul and obscene, Diogenes remarked: "You draw a leaden sword from an ivory scabbard."

<margin>26</margin>
### All eights.
*All eights.* <note>original Greek: Πάντα ὀκτώ.</note> This is used when we mean that nothing is lacking, or when many things are similar to one another. They believe the proverb originated here: The poet Stesichorus is said to have been buried most splendidly in the town of Catania, with a monument constructed by a careful plan based entirely on eights: eight columns, eight steps, and eight corners. From this, the proverb *all eights* became common. Julius Pollux also mentions this in his ninth book when discussing the game of dice; he says there is a certain throw called the "Stesichorean," which is the number eight, named after his monument. There are those who say that the man who united the Corinthians into a single city distributed all the citizens into eight tribes, and the common saying arose from this. Nor are there those lacking who write—citing Evangelius as the author—that there are eight gods who rule the sum of things: fire, water, earth, heaven, the sun, the moon, Mithras, and night. The Persians, however, consider Mithras to be the same as the sun. Again, others say there are eight types of contests in the Olympic games, and the adage was derived from there: *All eights.* 

But if one is permitted to guess at a riddle, it might not absurdly seem to have arisen from the story related by Plutarch in his commentary *On the Daemon of Socrates*. An oracle replied to the Delians and other Greeks that there would only be an end to their troubles if they doubled the altar which was at Delos. When they did not understand what the oracle meant, they ridiculously doubled each side of the altar, and through ignorance of <term>geometric proportion</term> <note>doubling the sides of a cube increases its volume eightfold, not twofold</note>, they unwittingly made it eight times as large. Plato, being highly skilled in geometry, was consulted on the matter and replied that the god was reproaching the Greeks for their ignorance and warning them to apply themselves to geometry. Finally, it appears the Emperor Heliogabalus played upon this proverb; Aelius Lampridius records that it was his custom to invite to dinner at one time eight bald men, eight one-eyed men, eight men with gout, eight deaf men, eight black men, eight very tall men, and eight very fat and obese men.

<margin>27</margin>
### All is the same dust.
*All is one dust.* <note>original Greek: Πάντα μία κόνις.</note> Concerning indistinguishable similarity. Lucian says: *For they say all is one dust to us.* Alluding to the state of the dead...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

the ashes of the dead, among whom no distinction appears. Close to this is another which we shall demonstrate in another place: **Of the same flour** <note>original: "Eiusdem farinæ"</note>. For the ancients used to call fine flour "pollen."

### The cart draws the ox.
### XXVIII

**The wagon drives the ox** <note>original Greek: Ἡ ἅμαξα τὸν βοῦν ἐλαύνει</note>. That is, the cart leads the ox. This is said of a matter that is carried out backwards or perversely. For instance, if a wife should dictate to her husband, if a student should rebuke a teacher, if the people should command a prince, or if reason should obey emotion. Lucian in *Terpsides*: **And as the proverb goes, the wagon often carries away the ox.** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν, ἡ ἅμαξα τὸν βοῦν πολλάκις ἐκφέρει</note>. That is: Now that happens which is commonly said: the wagon frequently carries off the ox itself. The metaphor is drawn from wagons sliding backwards down a slope and taking the ox along with them.

### From horses to donkeys.
### XXIX

**From horses to donkeys** <note>original Greek: Ἀφ’ ἵππων ἐπ’ ὄνους</note>. This is used when someone turns from more honorable studies to those that are less honorable: as if a philosopher became a singer, a theologian a grammarian, a merchant an innkeeper, a steward a cook, or a blacksmith an actor. It will also apply when someone falls from a more elegant condition to more lowly circumstances. Procopius the Sophist says in a certain letter: **As the saying goes, we have passed from horses to donkeys.** <note>original Greek: τὸ δὴ λεγόμενον, ἀφ’ ἵππων ἐπ’ ὄνους μεταβεβήκαμεν</note>.

### To step across from donkeys to oxen.
### XXX

Different from this is that phrase of Plautus: **To step across from donkeys to oxen** <note>original: "Ab asinis ad boues transcedere"</note>. This stands for moving from a humble condition to the ranks of the wealthy. For thus in Plautus’s *Aulularia*, Euclio—a poor man whose family alliance a certain rich man was seeking—says: *It comes to my mind, Megadorus, that you are a wealthy man of great influence, and I likewise am a poor man, the poorest of the poor. Now if I should marry my daughter to you, it comes to mind that you are the ox and I am the little donkey. When I am joined with you, and I cannot carry the load equally, I, the donkey, would lie in the mud, and you, the ox, would regard me no more than if I had never been born. I would find you unjust, and my own rank would mock me; I would have no stable stable in either place if a divorce should occur. The donkeys would tear at me with their teeth, and the oxen would charge me with their horns. This is the great danger if I step across from donkeys to oxen.* Thus far Plautus. The allegory seems to be borrowed from some fable or other, which does not occur to me at present.

### Fallen from a donkey.

**Fallen from a donkey** <note>original Greek: Ἀπ’ ὄνου καταπεσών</note>. This is said against those who do something inconsiderately and unskillfully, or against those who lose present advantages which they do not know how to use due to ignorance. However, in the Greek words there is a witty allusion to a similar phrase, changed only by the accent: **fallen from the mind** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ νοῦ</note>, as if one were senseless and lacking control of their mind. Plato uses this adage in the third book of *The Laws*: **It seems to me that the discourse, like a horse, must be pulled back at every turn, and not, as if possessing an unbridled mouth, be carried away by the force of the argument to "fall from the donkey," as the proverb says.** <note>original Greek: Ἐμοὶ φαίνεται ὁ λόγος... ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄνου πεσεῖν</note>. Plutarch also uses it in *Gryllus*. Again, Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:

> For things were truly going badly for you, as it seems to me.
> By the gods, I fell out while driving horses!
> Why then do you talk nonsense, as if you had fallen from a donkey?

->that is,<-

> Something bad, it seems, has happened to you.
> So, by the gods, while driving horses, I wretchedly fell out.
> Why do you babble these things, as if you had slipped from a donkey?

The first verse is spoken by Strepsiades mocking the Moneylender, who is seeking back the money lent to his son. The second is the Moneylender’s, noting the young man with a silent allusion, who had wasted that money on the hobby of breeding horses. The third is again Strepsiades’, saying that the man is raving, just as if he had fallen not from horses, but from a donkey—that is, **from his mind** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ νοῦ</note>. Since even in Latin, those who have lost their wits are said to be **fallen from the mind** <note>original: "Mente delapsi"</note>. Suetonius in *Augustus*: *He was also accustomed to appoint a guardian for those of tender age or those fallen from their mind.* Some also attach a fable of this sort to this proverb: Two men, having by chance found a certain donkey in a deserted place, began to contend between themselves as to which of them should lead it home as his own; for it seemed to be offered by fortune to both equally. While they were arguing about this matter, the donkey slipped away, and neither gained possession of it. And from this they claim the proverb was born. To me, it is more pleasing that the allusion I mentioned was sought in the adage, especially because I notice that grammarians [study] it...

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 7

...that there was some fable, or history, or even a fictional story attached to every adage.
<margin>Ulpian</margin>
However, just as Suetonius spoke of those "fallen in mind" <note>original: *mente lapsos*, meaning mentally unstable</note>, so Ulpian, in the title *On Magistrates*, spoke of those "fallen in resources" <note>original: *facultatibus lapsos*</note> who had been reduced to poverty.

### 31. A burden of the earth.
<margin>$\alpha\chi\theta\omicron\varsigma$ $\alpha\rho\omicron\upsilon\rho\eta\varsigma$</margin>
*Achthos aroures*, that is, **A burden of the earth**. This is said of a profoundly useless man, who does nothing else but weigh down the earth with his mass. It is recorded among the Greek adages, originating from Homer, in whose work
<margin>Achilles in Iliad 18</margin>
Achilles speaks in this manner in the 18th book of the *Iliad*, resenting his idleness and the fact that he does not enter the battle with the rest of the troops:
<margin>$\epsilon\tau\omega\sigma\iota\omicron\nu$ $\alpha\chi\theta\omicron\varsigma$ $\alpha\rho\omicron\upsilon\rho\eta\varsigma$</margin>
*Etosion achthos aroures*. ->that is,<-
I sit idle, a useless weight upon the earth. ->Again in the Odyssey, book 20:<-
<margin>$\alpha\chi\theta\omicron\varsigma$ $\alpha\rho\omicron\upsilon\rho\eta\varsigma$</margin>
*echthos epimasson aleten, mete ti techneenta, mete ti alkimon, all' autos achthos aroures*; ->that is,<-
...at last you bring us a gluttonous wanderer,
Himself lacking in bread and wine, and hungry,
Entirely untaught in any skills, nor standing
With any strength, but only a useless weight of the earth?
From Plato in the *Theaetetus*: *oiontai gar akouein, hoti ge leroi eisin, ges allos achthe*. That is: They think they are not considered trifles and useless burdens of the earth. Nor is it ungraceful—and unless I am mistaken, it refers to "a burden of the earth"—what Athenaeus records in his eighth book: A certain Stratonicus <note>A famous Greek musician known for his wit</note> was traveling in Corinth. When an old woman had been staring at him fixedly for a long time, he finally said: "By the gods, mother, what do you want, or why do you stare at me so continually?" "I am marvelling," she replied, "if your mother's womb could bear you for ten months, when this city can barely carry you for a single day." On such people would fit the epitaph which Athenaeus, in book 10, indicates was inscribed on the tomb of Timocreon, a poet of hatred, but otherwise a glutton and a drunkard:
<margin>Timocreon of Rhodes</margin>
*polla phagon, kai polla pion, kai polla kak' eipon anthropous, keimai timokreon rhodios*. ->that is,<-
Having eaten much, and drunk much, and said many evil things against
such men, I, Timocreon of Rhodes, lie here.

### 32. An Arabian flute-player.
<margin>$\alpha\rho\alpha\beta\iota\omicron\varsigma$ $\alpha\upsilon\lambda\eta\tau\eta\varsigma$</margin>
*Arabios auletes*, that is, **An Arabian flute-player**, or *Arabios angelos*, that is, **An Arabian messenger**; a term used for those who, once they have begun, never stop. Horace wrote that this vice belonged to singers: if asked to sing, they can never be brought to begin; if they start unbidden, they
<margin>Menander</margin>
never stop. Cited from Menander: *arabion ara ego kekineka aulon*. By Hercules, I have set an Arabian flute-player in motion.
<margin>Julius Pollux, Cantharus, Alcibiades</margin>
Julius Pollux mentions the adage in the chapter *On Talkative People*, in this manner: *Arabios aulos*, an Arabian flute. It is also cited by Cantharus in *Medea*: *kitharodou exegagen arabion*. That is: He brought forth an Arabian from the lyre-player. This little verse about the Arabian flute-player is also celebrated among the Greeks:
*en men aulei, d' he drachmes de pauetai*. ->that is,<-
He plays for a drachma, but is silenced for four.
For he would be provoked to play for a very small price, but would not stop except for a great reward. They think the adage arose from the fact that formerly free-born men did not learn the art of playing the flute—though they did eventually—but only slaves practiced it, who were mostly brought from Arabia. Later, it began to please free men so much that anyone unskilled in it was considered uneducated. This lasted until Alcibiades threw away his flutes, having seen the deformity of his face in a mirror <note>Alcibiades famously rejected the flute because it distorted the player's facial features</note>. Consequently, it is used against those who suffer from the disease which the Greeks call *apaulogian* <note>original: $\alpha\pi\alpha\upsilon\lambda\omicron\gamma\iota\alpha\nu$, meaning incessant talking</note>, that is, those who do not know how to make an end of speaking. Against whom there is that saying of Sophocles:
<margin>Sophocles</margin>
*hostis adonta legei aei, auton tis estin o barys*. ->that is,<-
Whoever delights in speaking continually,
Does not see that he is a burden to all present.

### 33. Every land nourishes a craft.
<margin>$\chi\epsilon\iota\rho\omega\nu$</margin>
*cheiron pasa gaia trephei*. That is, **Every region nourishes a craft**. A proverbial sentiment by which it is taught that the most certain provision for a journey is education or some manual skill. For these are not snatched away by robbers, and wherever in the world you go, they accompany you, bringing no extra baggage.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### The cart draws the ox.
### XXVIII

**The wagon drives the ox** <note>original Greek: Ἡ ἅμαξα τὸν βοῦν ἐλαύνει</note>. That is, the cart leads the ox. This refers to a matter that is carried out backwards or perversely. For example, if a wife should dictate to her husband, if a student should rebuke a teacher, if the people should command a prince, or if reason should obey emotion. Lucian in *Terpsides*: **And that which is according to the proverb, the wagon often carries away the ox.** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν, ἡ ἅμαξα τὸν βοῦν πολλάκις ἐκφέρει</note>. That is: Now that happens which is commonly said: The wagon oftentimes carries off the ox itself. The metaphor is taken from wagons sliding backwards down a slope and carrying the ox away with them.

### From horses to donkeys.
### XXIX

**From horses to donkeys** <note>original Greek: Ἀφ’ ἵππων ἐπ’ ὄνους</note>. This is used when someone turns away from more honorable studies to those that are less honorable: as if a philosopher became a singer, a theologian a grammarian, a merchant an innkeeper, a steward a cook, or a blacksmith an actor. It will also apply when someone falls from a more refined condition to more lowly circumstances. Procopius the Sophist says in a certain letter: **As the saying goes, we have moved from horses to donkeys.** <note>original Greek: τὸ δὴ λεγόμενον, ἀφ’ ἵππων ἐπ’ ὄνους μεταβεβήκαμεν</note>.

### To rise from donkeys to oxen.
### XXX

Opposite to this is that line from Plautus: **To rise from donkeys to oxen.** This stands for passing from a humbler condition to the ranks of the wealthy. For so in Plautus’s *Aulularia*, Euclio—a very poor man whose alliance a certain wealthy man was seeking—says: "It comes to my mind, Megadorus, that you are a wealthy man of great influence, and I likewise am a poor man, the poorest of the poor. Now if I should betroth my daughter to you, it comes to mind that you are the ox and I am the little donkey. When I am joined with you, and I cannot carry the burden equally, I, the donkey, would lie in the mud, and you, the ox, would regard me no more than if I had never been born. I would find you unjust, and my own class would mock me; I would have no stable stable in either place if a divorce should occur. The donkeys would tear me with their teeth, and the oxen would run at me with their horns. This is a great danger, for me to rise from donkeys to oxen." Thus far Plautus. The allegory seems to be borrowed from some fable or other, which does not occur to me at present.

### Fallen from a donkey.

**Fallen from a donkey** <note>original Greek: Ἀπ’ ὄνου καταπεσών</note>. This is said of those who do something inconsiderately and unskillfully: or of those who lose present advantages which they do not know how to use due to ignorance. However, in the Greek words there is a witty allusion to a similar phrase, changed only by the accent: **fallen from the mind** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ νοῦ</note>, as if one were senseless and powerless of mind. Plato uses this adage in the third book of *The Laws*: **It seems to me that the discourse, like a horse, must be pulled back at every turn, and not, as if possessing an unbridled mouth, be carried away by the force of the argument and, according to the proverb, fall from the donkey.** <note>original Greek: Ἐμοὶ φαίνεται ὁ μῦθος... ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄνου πεσεῖν</note>. That is: To me indeed the speech seems like a horse that must be restrained on all sides, lest having no bridle and being swept away by its own momentum, it should—according to the proverb—fall from the donkey as if falling from the mind. Plutarch also uses it in *Gryllus*. Again, Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:

> For you were truly in a bad way, as it seems to me.
> Yes, by the gods, while driving horses I fell out miserably.
> Why then do you babble such nonsense, as if you had fallen from a donkey? <column-break/> 
> <note>The Greek verses above are translated here into English</note>

The first verse is spoken by Strepsiades mocking the Moneylender, because he is seeking back the money lent to his son. The second is the Moneylender’s, noting the young man with a silent allusion, who had wasted that money on the hobby of breeding horses. The third is again Strepsiades’, saying that the man is raving, just as if he had fallen not from horses, but from a donkey—that is, **from his mind** <note>original: "apo nou"</note>. Since even among the Latins, those who have lost their wits are said to be **fallen from the mind** <note>original: "Mente delapsi"</note>. Suetonius says in his *Life of Augustus*: "He was also accustomed to appoint a governor for those of tender age or those who had fallen from their minds." Some also attach a fable of this sort to this proverb: Two men, having by chance found a certain donkey in a deserted place, began to contend between themselves as to which of them should lead it home as his own; for it seemed to have been thrown in the path of both equally by fortune. While they were arguing about this matter, the donkey slipped away, and neither gained possession of it. And from this they think the proverb was born. To me, it is more pleasing that the allusion I mentioned was sought in the adage, especially since I notice that grammarians [study this].

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning social reversals and intellectual failure, notably the Greek pun between "falling from a donkey" and "losing one's mind." He cites classical authors like Plautus, Plato, and Aristophanes to illustrate these metaphors of status and folly.</summary>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 7

...that he was so diligent that he added some fable or history, even if fictitious, to every adage. Just as Suetonius spoke of those "fallen in mind" <note>original: "mente lapsos," meaning insane</note>, so Ulpian, in the chapter *On Consulting Magistrates*, spoke of those "fallen in resources" <note>original: "facultatibus lapsos"</note> who had been reduced to poverty.

-> 31. A burden to the earth. <-

<margin>A burden to the earth.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἄχθος ἀρούρης</note> That is, a weight upon the soil. This is said of a profoundly useless person, who does nothing else but weigh down the earth with his mass. It is counted among the Greek adages, originating from Homer, in whose *Iliad* (Book 18) Achilles speaks in this manner, being indignant at his own idleness and the fact that he was not entering battle with the rest of the troops:
<margin>But I sit by the ships, a useless burden to the earth.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ἧμαι παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης</note> That is:
"But I sit by the ships, a useless weight of the earth."
<margin>Nor do you eat the food of others upon the earth, like that man who is in need, nor sharpening any strength, because of his violence, but merely a burden to the earth.</margin> <note>original Greek: Οὐδ' ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἔδεις... Erasmus quotes a passage from the Odyssey (Book 20) regarding a beggar.</note> Again in the *Odyssey* (Book 20), that is:
"Who, then, brings us this wandering glutton,
himself needy of wine and bread,
utterly untaught in any skills, possessing no strength,
and only a useless weight of the earth?"
<margin>A burden to the earth.</margin> It is cited from Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "For they think they hear that they are not trifles, but otherwise burdens of the earth." <note>original Greek: οἴονται γὰρ ἀκούειν...</note> That is: They think they are not considered as mere nonsense and useless burdens to the earth. Nor is it unrefined, nor entirely "unrelated to Dionysus" <note>original: ἀπροσδιόνυσον, a Greek proverb meaning "irrelevant" or "off-topic"</note> if I am not mistaken, what Athenaeus records in his eighth book: A certain Stratonicus of Rhodes was traveling in Corinth. When an old woman stared at him fixedly for a long time, he finally said: "By the gods, mother, what do you want, or why do you stare at me so continuously?" "I am marveling," she replied, "if your mother's womb could carry you for ten months, when this city can barely carry you for a single day." For such people, the epitaph would be fitting which Athenaeus (Book 10) indicates was inscribed on the tomb of Timocreon of Rhodes, a poet who was otherwise a glutton and a drunkard:
<margin>Having eaten much, and drunk much, and said many evil things about men, I, Timocreon of Rhodes, lie here.</margin> <note>original Greek: Πολλὰ φαγὼν...</note> That is:
"I ate much, and I drank much, I said many bad things against
mortals; here I lie, Timocreon of Rhodes."

-> 32. An Arabian flute-player. <-

<margin>An Arabian flute-player.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀράβιος αὐλητής</note> That is, an Arabian piper, or, <margin>An Arabian messenger.</margin> <note>original Greek: ἀράβιος ἄγγελος</note> That is, an Arabian messenger; it is usually said of those who, once they have started something, never stop. Horace <note>referred to as "Flaccus"</note> wrote that this vice plagued singers: if asked to sing, they can never be brought to start; but if they start unbidden, they never stop. He cites from Menander: "By Hercules, I have stirred up an Arabian flute." <note>original Greek: ἀράβιον ἄρα ἐγὼ κεκίνηκα αὐλόν</note> Julius Pollux mentions the adage in the chapter *On Talkative People* in this way: "Arabian flute." <note>original Greek: ἀράβιος αὐλός</note> Cantharus also cites it in *Medea*: "He stirred up an Arabian lyre-player." <note>original Greek: Κιθαρωδὸν ἐξηγάραιο ἀράβιον</note> This little verse about the Arabian flute-player is also celebrated among the Greeks:
<margin>He plays the flute, but for silver he does not stop.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ὁ μὲν αὐλεῖ...</note> That is:
"The Arabian does not sing, but is restrained by four [coins]."
For he could be provoked to play for a very small price, but would not stop except for a great reward. They think the adage arose from this: that formerly free-born men did not learn the art of piping, regarding it as a sordid trade, but only slaves practiced it, who were mostly brought from Arabia. This practice began to please the free-born to such an extent that anyone ignorant of it was considered unlearned. This lasted until Alcibiades threw away the flutes, having seen the deformity of his face in a mirror <note>Piping was said to distort the facial features unpleasantly</note>. It also applies to those who suffer from the disease which the Greeks call "the inability to stop talking" <note>original Greek: ἀποπαυλογίαν</note>. Regarding them, there is that saying of Sophocles:
<margin>Whoever delights in speaking constantly, is a heavy companion to himself.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ὅστις ἡδεται λέγων ἀεὶ...</note> That is:
"Whoever rejoices in speaking continuously,
seems so to himself, but does not see those who are present."

-> 33. Every land nourishes a craft. <-

<margin>Every land nourishes a craft.</margin> <note>original Greek: Τέχνην πᾶσα γαῖα τρέφει</note> That is: Every region supports a skill. A proverbial sentiment by which it is taught that a craft—whether it be learning or some manual trade—is the most certain "traveling money" <note>term: viaticum (provisions or money for a journey)</note>. For these things can neither be snatched away by robbers, and wherever in the world you go, they accompany you, adding nothing to your luggage.

<summary>Erasmus explores three proverbs: "A burden to the earth" (referring to useless people), "An Arabian flute-player" (referring to those who don't know when to stop), and the value of having a portable skill or "craft." He draws on a wide range of classical sources including Homer, Plato, and Athenaeus.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<page-num>240</page-num>

...medicine. Suetonius writes that it was once predicted to Nero by mathematicians that he would be deprived of his empire; hence that most famous saying of Nero’s emerged: <note>original: "τὸ τέχνιον πᾶσα γαῖα τρέφει"</note> *Every land supports a little craft*, so that he might practice the art of the lute-player with greater excuse—an art pleasing to a prince, but necessary for a private citizen. And so, when he understood he was to perish, he repeatedly said: *What an artist dies in me!* <note>original: "Qualis artifex pereo"</note> as if it were an indignity that one who was so great a musician, and who could live anywhere in the world, should now be driven to death by hunger. For I do not agree in this instance with the opinion of the interpreters who explain this passage in Suetonius differently. Likewise, he was offended by no insult more than when someone called him a "bad lute-player." The same happened to Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, who, after being stripped of his power, opened a school in Corinth and taught boys letters and music. It appears, moreover, that the line Suetonius cites is a senarius <note>A line of verse consisting of six feet</note>, but corrupted by the change of a few syllables; perhaps it should be restored thus: *Every land indeed nourishes a little craft.*

Among the maxims of the Greeks, a senarius of this kind is circulated, not very different from this proverb:
->A craft is a harbor from misfortune for men. That is,<-
->Art itself is a port of poverty for mortals.<-

This means that a craft is the sole refuge in poverty. Whence those who are wise, even if their family estate is abundantly sufficient, nevertheless compel their children to learn some trade, so that if it happens that fortune takes away their wealth, or they are ordered into exile, they have the means to provide a living for themselves. But now many, who have nothing at home, grow old in the households of the wealthy; from which, if they are driven out, they must either beg or "take up what they did not lay down," <note>A proverbial expression for stealing</note> contrary to the law of Plato. The author who wrote the Latin *Cornucopia* <note>Likely Niccolò Perotti</note> cites a proverb very similar to this one, which I believe is commonly tossed about: *To each man, his own art is his travel-money.* A most honorable travel-money indeed, provided the art is honorable. Otherwise, there are those now wandering everywhere who have no art, but carry around "indulgences and dispensations," as they call them, bought and to be resold, as their travel-money.

### You were not on this white board.
<margin>XXXIII</margin>

*You were not on this white board* <note>original: "Non eras in hoc albo"</note>, that is, you were not in this number. It is a metaphor taken from the whitened tablet <term>album: a white tablet used in Rome for public notices or lists</term> on which the names of judges were formerly written. Pliny, in the preface to his *Natural History*: "When I was pledging this work, you were not on this white board," that is, you were not in the number of those whom I believed would read these things. There was also the *Pretor’s Album*, in which laws and legal formulas were described. In the first book of the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, under the title *On Discovery*, Labeo says that he also "discovers" who brings his adversary to the *album* and demonstrates what he is about to dictate. And in this place, he certainly does not mean by "Adversary" the person with whom the lawsuit is, but the notebooks <note>original: "adversaria"</note> marked at the time for the sake of memory. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] used it in this sense in his oration *For Roscius*, and not just once. Andreas Alciatus <note>A famous 16th-century legal scholar</note> thinks it should be read as *adversaria* [notebooks], not *adversarium* [adversary], in the third book of his *Dispunctiones*. Likewise, in the second book of the same work, under the first title, much mention is made of the *album*. Quintilian, in the eleventh book of his *Institutes*: "Some of whom have transferred themselves to the white board and the red headings" <note>original: "album & rubricas"</note>; clearly mocking the petty lawyers and formula-makers who learn the science of law not from the books of the Jurisprudents, but from the Pretor’s notice board. Titus Livy, in the ninth book of his first Decade: "He made public the civil law, which had been hidden in the secret archives of the pontiffs, and set up the calendar around the forum on a white board, so that it might be known when legal action could be taken." Apuleius mentions the *album* in the sixth book of the *Metamorphoses*. Indeed, when Jupiter is about to address the gods, he makes him begin thus: "Gods enrolled on the *album* of the Muses." In these words, it seems to me there is an obscure but witty allusion by the writer to the gods fashioned by poets: as if only those are in the number of the gods whom the Muses (by whose inspiration poets write) have placed there.

### Smoother than oil.
<margin>XXXV</margin>

*Smoother than oil* <note>original: "Oleo tranquillior"</note>, a proverbial hyperbole used for men who are not at all prone to anger and are endowed with a gentle nature, taken from the nature of the liquid, than which nothing is more silent or more smooth. Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian*: "I will make this dog smoother than oil for you." Moreover, the nature of oil is so tranquil that it even calms the sea, the most savage of all things; and for this reason, divers are said to spray oil from their mouths because it mitigates the rough nature of the element and brings down light. Pliny is the authority for this in his second book. Plutarch confirms the same, and gives the reason why this happens in his booklet *On Natural Causes*. Again, in the sixth decade of his *Table Talk*, giving the reason why Homer, among so many liquids, calls only oil <note>original: "ὑγρὸν"</note> *moist* or *liquid*, he shows that there is nothing rough in oil, but it is smooth on all sides, and for that reason especially reflects images like a mirror. Furthermore, it does not make a noise when moved or struck, as other fluids do, nor does it struggle with fire, but feeds it silently. Finally, there is no other...

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY
<note>original: "CHIL. PRIMÆ CENTVRIA .VII"</note>
x
<meta>catchword: Ear</meta>

which spreads so widely when it is rubbed onto the body, or dries more slowly, or softens equally well. Plato also uses this adage in the *Theaetetus* regarding knowledge, comparing calm minds—which approach learning and debate quietly and peacefully—to smoothly flowing oil. <margin>Theaetetus.</margin> <note>original Greek: "πᾶν δὲ τὸ τῆς μαθήσεως..."</note> That is: "But this man enters into studies and inquiries so gently, circumspectly, and at the same time with such ease, with great mildness, in the manner of oil flowing without a sound, that you might marvel that one so great acts in such a way."

### XXXVI
->Softer than the bottom of the ear.<-

Very similar to this is what Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> employs in the second book of his letters to his brother Quintus, <margin>M. Tullius.</margin> saying: "In what way do you think I ought to behave in the Republic and toward our enemies? Know that I shall be, if you wish, softer than the bottom of the ear." Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a Roman historian</note> says in his nineteenth book: <margin>Ammianus.</margin> "Stern at first, but in this matter, as they say, softer than the very bottom of the ear." The metaphor is drawn from that part of the ear <note>the lobe</note> than which there is nothing softer or more flexible in the human body, seeing as it is neither stiffened by bone, nor hardened by cartilage, nor stretched by sinews.

### XXXVII
->Softer, or milder, than celery.<-

<note>original Greek: "σελίνου πραΰτερος"</note> Milder than celery. A similar figure of speech was used by Theocritus: <margin>Theocritus.</margin> <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ πολὺ ἀπίοιο πεπαίτερος"</note> That is:
> But certainly more gentle than a pear.

However, among the Greeks, *apius* can mean a radish or a type of pear.

### XXXVIII
->Softer than a sponge.<-

Of the same kind is <note>original Greek: "σπογγιᾶς μαλακώτερος"</note> that is, "Softer than a sponge." For thus someone speaks in agreement in a certain comic poet, cited by Plutarch in his commentary <margin>Plutarch.</margin> on the difference between a flatterer and a friend:
<note>original Greek: "εἴ μοι βάκχε..."</note> That is:
> If you should wish, Bacchus, to set me against that soldier,
> I would make him as soft as a ripe fruit with lashes,
> And I would render that man’s face
> Softer than any sponge.

In the same way they used to say, "Softer than a melon." Theopompus, in the tenth book of Athenaeus, <margin>Athenaeus.</margin> says: <note>original Greek: "μαλακώτερος πέπονος..."</note> that is, "He seems to me softer than a melon or a cucumber." To this form belongs what the same author cites from Epicharmus: <note>original Greek: "πραΰτερος ἔγωγε μαλάχας"</note> that is, "I am indeed milder than mallow," because that herb has the power of soothing. Likewise, "Softer than a *cinaedus*" <note>a term for a submissive or effeminate dancer</note>. Plautus in the *Aulularia*: "Thus I am softer with clubs than any *cinaedus*." For <margin>Plautus.</margin> they called dancers and pantomimes *cinaedi* because they sang with gestures. Furthermore, Catullus says:
> And Thallus, softer than the fur of a rabbit.

### XXXIX
->To the fortunate, even three-month children are born.<-

<note>original Greek: "τοῖς εὐτυχοῦσι καὶ τρίμηνα παιδία"</note> That is:
> To the fortunate, even three-month children are born.

This is a proverbial jest against the "good fortune" of princes and the wealthy, to whom everything turns out favorably through flattery, and who think nothing is forbidden to them; so much so that what is condemned as a great crime in a common man is celebrated as a mark of virtue in them. Suetonius Tranquillus explains how this proverb arose, beginning his life of Claudius Caesar with these words: <margin>Suetonius.</margin> "Livia, having married Augustus while pregnant, gave birth to Drusus (the father of Claudius Caesar, first named Decimus and later Nero) within the third month; and there was a suspicion that he had been fathered by his stepfather <note>Augustus</note> through an adulterous relationship." Immediately, this verse became common:
<note>original Greek: "τοῖς εὐτυχοῦσι καὶ τρίμηνα παιδία"</note> That is:
> To the fortunate, births occur even in three months.

For births in the seventh, tenth, and eleventh months are considered legitimate; in the fourth and eighth, they cannot live and are very rare; but in the third month, no births are recorded to have survived. The authority for this is Pliny, Book 7, Chapter 5. <margin>Pliny.</margin>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### To pull the ear.
<margin>40</margin>

"To pull the ear" was a phrase used by the ancients to mean "to remind." The figure of speech is taken from an ancient ritual in which those about to summon someone to court would tweak the person's ear, calling upon him as a witness whom they wished to remember the event. Hence that line from Horace in his *Satires*: "And if it is permitted to call a witness, I indeed offer my ear." <note>original: "Oppono auriculam." In Roman law, touching the ear was a formal way of asking someone to be a witness to a legal summons.</note> For just as the forehead was anciently sacred to the Genius <note>A personal guardian spirit</note>—as Servius writes in his commentary on Virgil’s *Silenus*—and the fingers to Minerva, and the knees to Mercy, so the ear was sacred to the Goddess of Memory, whom the Greeks call <term>Mnemosyne</term> (Memory). Virgil says in his *Silenus*:
> When I was singing of kings and battles, Cynthius <note>Apollo</note> pulled
> my ear, and warned the shepherd: "Tityre, it is proper for a shepherd
> to feed fat sheep, but to sing a slender song."

Calpurnius imitated this in his *Bucolics*: <margin>For poverty often pulls the ear</margin> "Envious poverty pulls the ear more often, and says: 'Care for humble things.'"
Calpurnius added a good deal of elegance to the proverb by applying it to his specific situation, though Poverty can be taken here as a goddess. Seneca, in the fourth book of *On Benefits*: "I will not give it as a gift, but I will redeem my words, and I will pull my own ear; I will punish the rashness of the promiser with a loss." Again in the second book: "I will speak with myself and pull my own ear." That is: I will be my own monitor, lest I sin in a similar way. He uses it in this manner in several other places, such as in his fortieth letter: "Let there be someone, therefore, as a guardian, to pull the ears from time to time, to drive away rumors, and to protest against the praising crowds."

### Another Hercules.
<margin>41</margin>

A proverbial hyperbole, <term>outos allos Herakles</term> <note>original: οὗτος ἄλλος ἡρακλῆς</note>, that is, "This man is another Hercules." It is said of a man who is exceptionally vigorous and most enduring of labors. There exists a certain satire with this title among the *Menippean Satires* of Terentius Varro, which is surely based on the proverb. Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*: <term>The friend wishes to be, as the proverb says, another Hercules, another self.</term> <note>original: ὁ φίλος βούλεται εἶναι, ὥσπερ ἡ παροιμία φησίν, ἄλλος ἡρακλῆς ἄλλος οὗτος</note> Plutarch writes that this nickname was commonly attributed to Theseus, because he performed many brave deeds following the example of Hercules. Diogenes Laertius, in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, shows that the philosopher Cleanthes was also commonly called "another Hercules" because he was the most patient of all in his labors; so much so that by drawing water from a well at night he earned his daily living—whence he was called <term>Phreantles</term> (the Well-Drawer) instead of Cleanthes—and yet he nonetheless performed outstanding work in philosophy during the day.

Clearchus, cited in Zenodotus, brings forward another story from which this adage arose. For he says that Briareus, who was himself also called Hercules, set out for Delphi and, having carried off some treasures and monuments from those kept in that place according to an old custom, he betook himself to the columns which they call the "Pillars of Hercules," and likewise took possession of those things which were there. Then the Tyrian Hercules came to Delphi to consult the oracle, and the god replied: <term>Another Hercules</term> <note>original: ἄλλος ἡρακλῆς</note>. That is, "This is another Hercules." And so the oracle passed into a proverb.

There are also those who trace the origin of this saying to a certain cowherd named Titormus, who surpassed Milo of Croton in many feats of strength. Milo, confessing himself defeated, said with hands raised to heaven: <term>O Jupiter, have you fathered another Hercules for us here?</term> <note>original: ὦ ζεῦ, οὗτος δὴ ἡρακλῆς ἡμῖν ἕτερος ἔαν ἔφας</note> To this pertains that line of Theocritus in his *Idylls*:
<term>They say this man contends with the strength and might of Hercules.</term> <note>original: φαύτινιν ἡρακλῆα βίλω καὶ κάρτος ἐρίσδεν</note>
> They say this man competes with the strength and power of the son of Alcaeus <note>Hercules</note>.
> <term>And my mother said I was better than Pollux.</term> <margin>And the shepherd adds,</margin> <note>original: Κἤμ' ἔφαθ' ἁ μάτηρ πολυδεύκεος ἦμεν ἀλείνω</note>
> My mother also said I excelled Pollux.

For Pollux was excellent in the contest of boxers. And the little Greek flatterer in Juvenal equates a weak rich man to Hercules "holding Antaeus far from the earth." Macrobius, in the third book of the *Saturnalia*, writes in this manner: "He assigns the Salii <note>Priests of Mars</note> to Hercules because of the abundance of deeper learning, because among the Pontiffs that god is considered the same as Mars." And indeed, the Menippean satire of Varro affirms this, which is inscribed <term>This is another Hercules</term> <note>original: ἄλλος οὗτος ἡρακλῆς</note>, because when he spoke much about Hercules, he proved him to be the same as Mars. Among the Latins also, the name of Hercules was attributed to a certain Ruticellus of prodigious strength. He used to lift a wild mule, as Marcus Varro writes, cited by Pliny in his seventh book. But to Hippocrates the physician, because he had predicted a plague coming from the Illyrians and sent his disciples around the cities to help, Greece decreed by merit the same honors as to Hercules; for Hercules also was considered an <term>Alexikakos</term> (Averter of Evil). The author is the same Pliny in the same book.

<summary>Erasmus explains two proverbs: "Aurem uellere" (to pull the ear), used for reminding someone of a duty or fact, and "Alter Hercules" (another Hercules), used to describe someone of immense strength or endurance.</summary>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 7

<margin><note>Text lost in binding</note></margin> It seems that the name of Hercules was commonly transferred to all men of extraordinary strength, in the same way that the name of Cato was applied to the grave and wise. Indeed, Varro counts forty-three "Herculeses," and adds that all who performed some brave deed were honored with this name. Macrobius also testifies in his *Saturnalia* that this name was common to many before the stepson of Amphitryon <note>The famous Greek Hercules</note>. In the same way, leaders of remarkable bravery were called "Achilles"; among their number was Lucius Siccius Dentatus, called the "Roman Achilles" on account of his immense courage, because he had fought the enemy in one hundred and twenty battles and did not have a single scar on his back. The author is Aulus Gellius, book two, chapter eleven. Finally, they call an argument "Achillean" when it is insuperable and insoluble.

### 42. The most wicked of bipeds.

"The most wicked of bipeds" is said of a man who is vehemently disapproved of, and who surpasses even the beasts in wickedness. It was said against a certain orator named Regulus, whom Pliny portrays in his letters in his own colors <note>i.e., in his true, unflattering light</note>, where this adage is also recorded. But before him, Cicero twisted it against Clodius in the *Speech for His House*: "With this man as your proscribed, this man as your advisor, this man as your servant, you have destroyed the Republic—a man who is the most foul not only of all bipeds, but even of quadrupeds." The Emperor Alexander [Severus] used a similar figure in Aelius Lampridius: "Surely you remember, fathers, when that monster—the filthiest not only of bipeds but even of quadrupeds—bore the name of Antoninus"; he was referring to Heliogabalus, the most effeminate of all emperors, whom one might not unjustly call the "Roman Sardanapalus" <note>A legendary decadent Assyrian king</note>. Furthermore, in this expression, the general classification of "human" adds a certain pleasing and novel <term>emphasis</term> <note>original: ἔμφασιν</note>, just as we commonly say "no animal" to mean "no man."

### 43. Adamantine.

<margin>adamantine</margin>
<term>Adamantine</term> <note>original: ἀδαμάντινος</note>, that is, "made of adamant," used for one who is inexorable or indefatigable. The incredible hardness of this stone gave rise to the proverb; about which Pliny writes in book 37 in this manner: "Diamonds [adamants] are tested on anvils; they so reject the blow that the iron flies apart on both sides, and even the anvils themselves leap asunder. Indeed, its hardness is unspeakable, and at the same time it is a nature that conquers all things and never grows hot." Whence it received its name from the Greek interpretation for "unconquerable force." Thus far Pliny. Hence, whatever is unconquered and impregnable, we call "adamantine."

<margin>Hesiod.</margin>
<term>He held a strong-minded spirit of adamant.</term> <note>original: ἀδάμαντος ἔχ' κρατερόφρονα θυμόν.</note> That is:
*He sat with his mind created from solid adamant.*

<margin>Theocritus in Amaryllis,</margin>
<term>Lest perhaps she looks back, for she is not made of adamant.</term> <note>original: μή ἴσως ποτήσῃ, ἐπεὶ ἢ ἀδαμαντίνα ἐστί.</note> That is:
*She will never look back, for perhaps she is not made of adamant.*

To this pertains the fact that Homer depicts Vulcan ensnaring Venus and Mars with adamantine chains, and that Virgil [Maro] fashioned the gates and columns of the underworld out of adamant. Socrates, in Plato's *Gorgias*, calls arguments "adamantine," that is, impregnable. Again, in the tenth book of the *Republic*, he said <term>having an adamantine nature</term> <note>original: ἀδαμαντίνως ἔχοντα</note> regarding holding firmly to an idea: <term>One must surely go to the underworld holding this idea with an adamantine resolve.</term> <note>original: ἀδαμαντίνως δεῖ δὴ τὴν ἰδέαν τὴν τοιαύτην ἔχοντα, εἰς ᾅδου ἰέναι</note>. Plutarch, in the *Life of Dion*: "From this, a slackness proceeded and gradually crept around the youth, and those adamantine chains—with which the elder Dionysius said he would leave the monarchy bound—were loosened and destroyed." Horace in his *Odes*: "Mars covered in an adamantine tunic."

<margin>Also elsewhere:</margin>
*If cruel Necessity fixes*
*adamantine nails*
<margin>Nails.</margin>
*into the topmost heights [of heads] with hard death.*

St. Augustine against the Manichaeans: "But when I begin to show certain and necessary reasons, which follow those propositions linked by 'adamantine chains,' as they say." And the surname "Adamantine" was added to several writers on account of their indefatigable endurance in study, such as Didymus the Grammarian and Origen the Theologian. Pindar uses it in a similar sense in the fifth *Isthmian* ode, praising a certain Lampon as being among the strongest, just as the Naxian whetstone is among others:
<term>I would say this man is among athletes</term>
<term>as the Naxian stone is among others.</term>

A Naxian whetstone. -> that is, <-
<note>original: "Chalkedeman takenon" (Greek: Χαλκηδῆμαν τακένων)</note>
You might well say that such a man among athletes is like a Naxian whetstone among other stones and iron-tamers. Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 7, mentions Naxian marble, which was long held in high value; from this, whetstones were called "Naxian," even those produced on the island of Cyprus. Now, Naxos is one of the Cyclades islands not far from Paros, whose marbles are celebrated for their whiteness. -> To test the gold with a Naxian stone. <note>original: "Χαλκῷ λίμαν τάνόναν" (Greek). Erasmus interprets this as using a whetstone to test or sharpen.</note> <-

concerning a firm resolve of the mind that cannot be shaken. Homer in *Iliad* 10:

# SEVENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>X 3</sig>

<margin>The senseless laughed at the misfortunes of others.</margin>
...meanwhile the flesh wastes away with blood.
The eyes are filled with tears, the anxious mind mourns.
<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely describing the physical symptoms of madness.</note>
This is derived from the story of Ajax. He is said to have taken it so poorly when Ulysses was preferred over him in the succession of Achilles' armor, that out of grief he turned to insanity. Thus, with his sword drawn, he leaped into a flock of sheep, believing he was slaughtering the Greek forces. Then he beat two very large pigs, which were hanging from a beam, with whips, thinking they were Agamemnon and Ulysses—the former because he was the judge, and the latter because he was the victor, against whom he was most enraged. He insulted these animals with much laughter, adding whatever grand insults his bitter bile suggested. Then, after he had come to his senses, partly out of shame and partly out of fear, he brought death upon himself. This adage will be twisted quite effectively against those who break into laughter for no reason, which the common people say is a sign of either madness or stupidity. That proverbial six-foot verse also bears witness:
<margin>Unseasonable laughter is an evil, even if the cause be laughable.</margin>
<note>original: "Γέλως ἄκαιρος, κἄνλε υν γέλοιον ἦ."</note>
that is,
he is so foolish that there is no cause for the laughter.
