### XLVII
->The Dog’s Revenge.<-
<margin>The Dog’s Revenge.</margin>
That is, "The vengeance of a dog." A Macedonian adage used against those who, contrary to expectation, pay the penalty to those they once harmed. It was born from the death of the tragic poet Euripides. In Macedonia, there is a certain village called the "Village of the Thracians," because it was once inhabited by Thracians. Here, when a certain dog belonging to King Archelaus had wandered off, the Thracians slaughtered it, sacrificed it, and devoured it. When Archelaus found out, he imposed a heavy fine on them. But since they were unable to pay, they induced Euripides to plead with the king to remit the fine, which he did. Later, however, when Euripides was alone in a certain forest and Archelaus was returning from the hunt, dogs surrounded Euripides and tore him to pieces, devouring him. It was believed, moreover, that those dogs were the offspring of the dog that the Thracians had sacrificed. Hence the adage became common among the Macedonians: "The Dog’s Revenge." Either he suffered what he deserved, or some other fitting end. Valerius Maximus, in Book 9 in the chapter on common deaths, reports that when Euripides had been invited to dinner by Archelaus, King of the Macedonians, and was returning home from the banquet, he was torn apart by dogs. Aulus Gellius, in the *Attic Nights*, Book 15, chapter twenty, confirms that these dogs were set upon him by a certain rival. He adds that these rivals were Arrideus the Macedonian and Craterus the Thessalian, both poets who were burned by the glory of Euripides. They fabricated the story that he had been mangled by the king's dogs. There are those who tell that he was not torn apart by dogs, but by women, when he was seeking the young Craterus, the favorite of Archelaus, at an unseasonable time. For Gellius also testifies that Euripides was
<margin>A woman-hater,</margin>
<note>original: "Γυναικομύγην"</note>
that is, a hater of women. But regarding the former opinion, Plutarch tells a story not entirely dissimilar in his dialogue *On the Comparison of Land and Sea Animals*: Pyrrhus, he says, while on a journey, found a dog guarding the body of a murdered man. When he learned that the dog had remained there for three days without food and would not be pulled away from the corpse, he ordered the dead man to be buried and the dog to be brought with him. A few days later, a muster of the soldiers was held, and everyone passed by the king as he sat. The dog remained quiet until he caught sight of his master's killers passing by; immediately enraged, he rushed at them with a cry and barked repeatedly, looking back at Pyrrhus from time to time, so that a suspicion arose not only in Pyrrhus himself but in all who were present. Consequently, when some other conjectures were added from elsewhere, as often happens, two men were seized, and having easily confessed, they were punished. He adds that the killers of Hesiod were also betrayed by his dog, which gave evidence. To these he adds what he says happened in his own memory: A certain man broke into the temple of Aesculapius, and having taken several gold and silver monuments, he fled secretly and unknown, as he thought. But the dog guarding the temple, whose name was Capparus (for he was unworthy to perish 
<note>original: "ἀνώνυμος" — anonymous/unnamed</note>
unnamed), when he saw that none of the sacristans were moved by his voice, followed the fleeing sacrilegious thief. At first, he was pelted with stones, yet he did not leave. When day broke, he did not approach closely, but followed while keeping watch from a distance, and would not take the food offered to him. He slept near the man when he slept, and followed him in the same way when he departed. If travelers were met, he would fawn over them with his tail, but barked and lunged at that one man alone. When people learned these things from one another, and recognized the descriptions of both the dog and the man, they apprehended the sacrilegious thief and led him to punishment, with the dog now leading the way joyfully...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

and exulting, because a harmful creature had been hunted down. For this reason, a dog was decreed to be fed at public expense, and the care of that matter was entrusted to the priests. But to return to the proverb, it appears it can be aptly said in this sense whenever the author of an inflicted evil is concealed. For example, when an enemy is removed by poison, and a rumor is spread among the common people that he died of a fever; or when a prince sends guards into someone’s house to plunder everything, and the report is spread that it was despoiled by robbers; or when a tyrant overthrows one whom he wishes ill, and then the hatred for the deed is shifted onto the magistrates as if they had done it without his knowledge. It seems to have flowed from this that today the Germans commonly say, whenever some certain misfortune happens from an uncertain author which you can impute to no one, that "it happened by the bite of a dog."

->XLVIII<-
### In your own kingdom.

Whatever is one’s private property is called his kingdom. Hence the Virgilian character Meliboeus says:
*Seeing my kingdom after some harvests, I shall marvel.* <note>original: "Post aliquot mea regna videns mirabor aristas." from Virgil's Eclogues.</note>
Scaevola, in Cicero’s *The Orator*, says: *Unless we were in your kingdom, we would not have endured it.* That is, in your villa. For he is speaking to Crassus in the Tusculan villa, which was then the villa of Crassus. Furthermore, the proverb is commonly tossed about: *Every man is a king in his own home*; which, however, seems to have flowed down from antiquity itself. Since in Homer, in the first book of the *Odyssey*, this little verse exists:
*But I shall be the master of our own house.* <note>original Greek: "Αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν οἴκοιο ἄναξ ἔσομ’ ἡμετέροιο."</note> That is:
*In our own halls, I shall indeed act as king.*

->XLIX<-
### It is situated in your grove and shrine.

"In your grove and shrine" is read in Plautus, standing for that which is "in your power, at your discretion, under your protection, or in your hand." It is a metaphor taken from shrines and groves dedicated to deities. Somewhat different is what Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> says in his oration *For Aulus Caecina*: *You are moving within my camps and defenses.* That is, you are acting with me, and what you say fights for my side.

->L<-
### Within one's own stalls.

By a similar figure of speech, Plautus says in *Casina*: *He knows, if he should obtain it, that what he loves will be within his own stalls.* This stands for that which is "certain and ready." For what is enclosed within our own fences, we possess safely and surely. Moreover, it was said regarding an old man who was taking pains so that a maidservant whom he loved might marry his bailiff, with this plan: that without his wife knowing, he might enjoy her in the countryside whenever he pleased. Likewise in *The Rope*: *This man calls me to my master as arbiter within my own stalls.*

->LI<-
### He is in my debt.

When we signify that someone is bound to us by favors, so that he is now entirely and certainly ours, we say he is "in our copper." <note>original: "In aere meo est." A Latin idiom for being in one's debt or "on one's books."</note> For in ancient times, all money was copper, the use of gold not yet having been discovered for striking coins. I remember reading in Cicero, in the thirteenth book of the *Letters to Friends*: *And by Hercules, I have always held it so in my mind, that you were in my debt <note>original: "in aere meo"</note>, on account of our connection with our friend Lamia and our singular intimacy.* Likewise in the fifteenth book: *As for Marcus Fabius, whom you give to me as a friend by your recommendation, I make no profit in him. For there are many years since he has been in my debt and has been cherished by me.*

->LII<-
### From tender little nails.

*From tender nails* <note>original Greek: "Ἀπὸ τῶν ἁπαλῶν ὀνύχων"</note>, that is, *From tender little nails.* This stands for "from earliest childhood." It is a metaphor taken from puppies, whose little nails have not yet hardened. Marcus Tullius says: *From tender nails, as the Greeks say.* Flaccus <note>Horace</note> in the *Odes*:
*And she meditates on unchaste loves / From her tender nail.*
Plutarch in the booklet *On the Education of Children*: *So that they might love their children from the heart and, as the saying goes, from the nails.* <note>original Greek: "Ὡς ἂν ψύθ’ οθεν νὴ ϯὸ δὴ λεγόμενον ἐξ ὀνύχων ἀγαπῶσι τὰ τέκνα."</note> That is, from the very first infancy. He is speaking of mothers who nurse their own offspring at their own breasts.

->LIII<-
### From the cradle.

"From the cradle" <note>original: "Ab incunabulis"</note> has the same meaning, that is, from the first rudiments of life. Plautus in *Pseudolus*: *But this servant who came here from Carystus, what has he known ever since his cradle?* Likewise Titus Livy: *Imbued from the cradle with a hatred of the tribunes.* Marcus Tullius calls that first instruction from the foundations "the cradles of the orator." And Virgil:
*The cradles of our race.*
Aurelius, in the first book of the *Pandects*, under the title "On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect": *The authority of the prefects, initiated in these cradles, deserved to be increased so much that it is not possible to appeal from the Praetorian prefects.* Aristotle in the *Ethics*, book 2, says: *From infancy, among the young.* <note>original Greek: "ἐκ νηπίων, ἐν νέων."</note> The latter of which he cites from Plato.

<summary>Erasmus explores several proverbs related to personal domain ("In your own kingdom"), legal/financial obligation ("In my debt"), and the earliest stages of life ("From the cradle"), drawing heavily on classical authors like Cicero, Plautus, and Virgil.</summary>

# SEVENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

<margin>54</margin>
### With the nurse's milk.

This passage is found in Plato’s tenth book *On Laws*: <note>original: "νῦν δὴ πειθόμενοι τοῖς μύθοις, οὓς ἐκ νέων παίδων ἔτι ἐν γάλαξι τρεφόμενοι, τροφῶν τε ἤκουον καὶ μητέρων"</note> "Now indeed believing the fables which, as young children still being nourished on milk, we heard from our nurses and mothers," etc. In a similar way, "Rattles" <note>Latin: *Crepundia*</note> is used as a term for the earliest stage of life.

---

<margin>55</margin>
### Singing the praise before the victory.

<note>original: "Πρὸ νίκης τὸ ἐγκώμιον ᾄδῃς"</note> That is, you sing the encomium <note>a speech or song of high praise</note> before the victory. This is said against one who boasts prematurely, before a matter is finished. Among the Greeks, those who had acted strenuously in war were praised with a certain speech or song; this praise is properly called an *encomium*. There exists a poem by Theocritus in praise of Ptolemy titled *The Encomium*, and Lucian’s *Encomium of Demosthenes*. Among the Romans, there were orations, public thanksgivings, triumphs, and rewards for valor. From this, one might say: "Before you have conquered, you prepare a triumph." Plato says in the *Lysis*: <note>original: "πρὶν νικᾶν δ' ἐλπίδας τε καὶ ᾠδὰς εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἐγκώμιον"</note> "Before you conquer, you both create hopes and sing an encomium for yourself." Not far from this is what Plato says in the *Theaetetus*: <note>original: "φαινόμεθα ἀγεννὲς ἀλεκρυόνων δίκην, πρὶν νικῆσαι, ἀποπηδήσαντες ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ᾄδειν"</note> "We shall seem like ignoble roosters who, before they have conquered, leap away from the argument to crow." Indeed, it is the custom of this animal to declare the victor with song. To this belongs what we have related elsewhere on the authority of Solon: "Look to the end of a long life." And that line of Pindar in the *Isthmian Odes*: <note>original: "ὁδὸν δ' ἀφάνδα Τύχας οὐ μαρναμένων, πρὶν τέλος ἄκρον ἱκέσθαι"</note> "The path of Fortune is hidden even to those who fight, until the final end is reached." For the fortune of those still fighting is uncertain until the very end is achieved.

---

<margin>56</margin>
### Attracting all things like a magnet stone.

<note>original: "Πάντας γ' ὑφέλκων οἷα μαγνῆτις λίθος"</note> That is:
->Attracting all things just like a magnet stone.<-
Suidas cites this verse from Pisides. It appears to be proverbial. The metaphor is drawn from the nature of the stone, which draws iron to itself and holds what it has attracted. Some think this is the same as the stone called "Heraclean," which we mentioned elsewhere in the proverb "The Lydian Stone." Pliny extols this title in Book 36, Chapter 16, in this manner: "What is more sluggish than the stiffness of a stone? Behold, nature has granted it senses and hands. What is more pugnacious than the hardness of iron? But it yields, and allows itself to be ruled; it is dragged by the Magnet stone; and that material, the tamer of all things, runs toward some void, and as it comes nearer it stops, is held, and clings in an embrace." For this reason, they call it by another name, *Siderite* <note>from the Greek word for iron</note>; some call it *Heracleon*. It was named "Magnes" after its discoverer, as Nicander asserts, having been found in India. Thus far we have rendered Pliny's words. Among many species of magnet, he mentions the Ethiopian one, with an attraction so effective that it draws not only iron, but even another Magnet to itself. Consequently, the honor of this stone is so great that it is usually weighed against silver. He also mentions *Haematite* <note>Bloodstone</note>, which is not as violent in attracting iron, but is remarkable for another miracle. Since it is blood-red in color—from which it also takes its name—if it is ground down, it yields a blood-like fluid. Therefore, the prodigious power of this stone created the proverb. Suidas cites Euripides from the *Oeneus*:
<note>original: "Πάντας γ' ἐλκεῖ, καὶ μεθίστησιν πάλιν"</note> That is:
->The Magnet stone<-
Which draws, and turns back again, and moves away. Close to this is what we said elsewhere:
<note>original: "Ἕλκει ἕλκων, ὥς τε καικίας νέφω"</note> That is:
->Drawing in such a way as the Caecias wind draws the clouds.<-

---

<margin>57</margin>
### To carry logs into the forest.

To carry logs into the forest is to wish to increase someone in those things with which he himself most abounds.
Horace in his *Satires*:
> And I, though born this side of the sea, when I was making
> Greek verses, Quirinus <note>the deified Romulus</note> forbade me,
> Appearing after midnight when dreams are true:
> "You would no more insanely carry logs into a forest, than if..."

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

To fill great crowds with the evils of the Greeks. <note>original: "Græcorum malis magnas implere cateruas." A reference to bringing unnecessary or overwhelming trouble.</note>
By the same reasoning we say, "To carry water to the sea." We joined both of these in a certain epigram:
> To grant verses to you, Peter, is like
> Adding wood to the forest, or waves to the wandering sea.
Both agree with what we have related in another place: "Owls to Athens." <note>A famous ancient proverb meaning to bring something to a place where it already exists in abundance, as Athens was famous for its owls.</note>

### You lend light to the sun.
<margin>58</margin>
<note>original: "τὸ φῶς ἡλίῳ δανείζεις"</note> That is, you give a loan of light to the sun. We say this when we teach a most learned man, or give urgent advice to one who is already exceedingly prudent; or when we attempt to explain things that are perfectly clear in themselves, or to celebrate with speech things that are illustrious by their own nature. For the sun is thought to be the source of all light, which is accustomed to lend light, not to receive it as a loan. This is recorded in those collected works which circulate under the name of Plutarch. There is something similar in Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> concerning those who try to illuminate things that are clear of themselves: he says they act just as if someone were striving to bring a mortal light to the most brilliant sun.

### The fountains themselves are thirsty.
<margin>59</margin>
The fountains themselves are thirsty. A proverbial irony used against those who seek from others that which they themselves have in great abundance at home. Cicero wrote to his brother Quintus: "Regarding what you ask, since the fountains themselves are now thirsty, if I have any space, I will write." He means that his brother is more abundant in words, yet he seeks them from Cicero, just as if he were in need of poems. The same author wrote to Atticus in Book 12: That he had come not to <term>the gate of the courtyard</term> <note>original: "ἀνθύρω πυλών"</note> but to <term>I am hungry</term> <note>original: "πεινῶ"</note>, as you write, especially in such great straits.

### The pot itself gathers the vegetables.
<margin>60</margin>
The pot itself gathers the vegetables. This will apply to those who cast their own fault onto something else, or who are so fashioned for some crime that they cannot help but sin. Catullus wrote against Caesar:
> Mentula commits adultery, Mentula commits adultery certainly.
> This is what they say: the pot itself gathers the vegetables.
For a pot is born for cooking vegetables; or it would be most absurd if someone were to say the pot "gathers" the vegetables which it cannot cook unless someone puts them in. Therefore, the pot is not the cause, but rather the one who threw in the bad vegetables. Not very different from this is what Tertullian cites from Homer as a proverb: "The iron itself draws the man." This was discussed by us in another place, in the proverb "Take away the opportunity for evil." Likewise: "The pot itself touched the lentil."

### The curse of Oedipus.
<margin>61</margin>
<term>The curse of Oedipus</term> <note>original: "Οἰδίποδος ἀρά"</note>. That is, the imprecation of Oedipus. Used regarding tragic and immense evils. Those who collect Greek adages cite from Aeschylus a story of this kind: Eteocles and Polynices, according to the custom, used to send their father the front portion from every sacrifice. However, when they once—through carelessness and thoughtlessness—had sent the hip, that is, the hind part, he, thinking this was done not out of forgetfulness or imprudence but for the sake of insult, cursed them with dire imprecations. Others tell that Oedipus, as soon as he realized he was a parricide and had then had intimacy with his mother, tore out his eyes with his own hands. When this matter became known to the inhabitants of that place, they expelled Oedipus from the city. Going into exile, he devoted his sons to curses because they did not defend their father in his calamity. These were by no means in vain: for the young men were destroyed by mutual slaughter, the mother brought death upon herself, and Oedipus himself perished by a lightning bolt. What sort of imprecations these were, Diogenes the Cynic almost indicates in Laertius, who used to say jokingly that he had encountered <term>the tragic curses</term> <note>original: "τὰς τραγικὰς ἀρὰς"</note>. For he was without a home, without a city, deprived of a fatherland, poor, wandering, living life from day to day. Sophocles, in *Oedipus the King*, feigns that Oedipus, still ignorant of whom Apollo had spoken of for expulsion as one who polluted the city with his crimes, prayed many dire things against him—that is, against himself.
Euripides in *The Phoenician Women*:
<term>He prays the most unholy curses upon his children.</term> <note>original: "Ἀρὰς ἀρᾶται παισὶν ἀνοσιωτάτας."</note>
These are the words of Jocasta concerning Oedipus. The same author in *Oedipus at Colonus* makes Oedipus curse Polynices so that he might be killed by a brother's hand, and kill in turn:
<term>Taking up those curses</term>
<term>Which I call down upon you, that neither by the land of your kin...</term>
<note>The text breaks off here, following the Greek verse.</note>

<unclear>May you neither prosper nor ever be free from disease</unclear> <note>original Greek: αὐτῆσαι, μήτε νοσῆσαι ποτὲ</note>

### LXII
-> **We build our walls according to our means.** <-
We say "we build our walls according to our resources." This applies to those of slender fortune and small means who, nevertheless, live elegantly according to their own measure. Plautus says in *Stichus*: "Those who have gods at home <note>meaning wealth or luck</note> drink from bowls and frog-shaped goblets. We drink from our little Samian earthenware. Yet we do it; we build our walls according to our means." Thus far Plautus. Likewise, it is commonly said even today: "Tiny birds build tiny nests."

### LXIII
-> **There is a change in all things.** <-
Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "There is a change <term>vicissitudo: a regular change or succession, like the tides</term> in all things." This sentiment signifies that in the affairs of mortals nothing is perpetual, nothing is stable, but all things recede and approach like the ebb and flow of an estuary. And by these turns of fortune, empires, wealth, glory, pleasure, and learning are transferred from some to others; in short, whatever is either convenient or troublesome. Sophocles in *Oedipus at Colonus* elegantly describes these turns of human affairs:
<unclear>O dearest son of Aegeus, for the gods alone</unclear>
<unclear>old age does not exist, nor do they ever die.</unclear>
<unclear>All other things are confounded by all-powerful time.</unclear>
<unclear>The strength of the earth decays, the strength of the body decays,</unclear>
<unclear>faith dies, and faithlessness sprouts in its place.</unclear>
<unclear>The same spirit never remains among men</unclear>
<unclear>who are friends, nor between city and city.</unclear>
<unclear>For some now, and for others in later time,</unclear>
<unclear>pleasant things become bitter, and then dear again.</unclear>

We shall render the meaning of these verses as follows: <margin>Only for the gods</margin>
> Old age is never troublesome, nor does death occur.
> Because powerless time mixes all things together.
> For through this, force and strength perish,
> And the vigor of our body dies away.
> Faith dies, perfidy sprouts in its turn,
> Neither is the mind the same, nor does the same fragrance
> Ever endure for a friend toward a little friend,
> Nor does it remain for city against city.
> Since for these immediately, for those after a little time,
> Things which had been pleasant become bitter and sad, and

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

Things once ungrateful become grateful in their turn. <margin>Homer likewise in Iliad, Book 6</margin>
<note>original: "Νίκη δ' ἐπαμείβεται ἄνδρας"</note> Victory shifts between men.
->that is,<-
Victory happens now to these men, now to those. <margin>Likewise in Iliad, Book 18</margin>
<note>original: "ξυνὸς Ἐνυάλιος, καί τε κτανέοντα κατέκτα"</note> Mars is impartial, and kills the one who would kill.
The god of war is common to all, and in turn slays the slayer.

Indeed, one must not overlook in this place that most beautiful fiction of the same poet concerning the two jars, from which Jupiter mixes the affairs of mortals in varying ways. The poem appears in the last book of the Iliad, which it would not be out of place to transcribe here:
<note>original: "Δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακείαται ἐν Διὸς οὔδει..."</note>
Two jars sit on the floor of Jupiter's palace,
Filled with the gifts he gives: one of evils, the other of blessings.
To whom Jupiter, who delights in the thunderbolt, gives a mixture,
That man meets sometimes with evil, and sometimes with good.
->that is,<-
For two jars of Jove stand at the threshold, full
Of the gifts which he grants: in this one are evils, in that one goods.
From here, the one rejoicing in the sharp lightning-bolt dispenses a mixture,
Now distributing evils and sorrows, now goods again.

The adage seems to be drawn from a response of Aesop. For when he was asked, according to Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, biographer of Greek philosophers</note>, what Jupiter was doing, he replied: <note>original: "τὰ μὲν ὑψηλὰ ταπεινοῖ, τὰ δὲ ταπεινὰ ὑψοῖ"</note> He brings down the high things, and lifts up the humble.
<margin>Euripides in Ion,</margin>
<note>original: "τὰ θνητὰ τοιαῦτα οὐδὲν ἐν ταυτῷ μένει"</note>
->that is,<-
Such are the affairs of mortals,
That nothing remains in the same state.
<margin>Euripides in The Suppliants,</margin>
<note>original: "ὁ γὰρ θεὸς πάντ' ἀναστρέφει πάλιν"</note>
->that is,<-
Fortune turns all things into their opposite.
<margin>Theognis in his Maxims,</margin>
<note>original: "Ζεὺς γάρ τοι τὸ τάλαντον ἐπιρρέπει ἄλλοτε ἄλλῳ..."</note>
->that is,<-
For now Jupiter inclines the scale to this man, now to that,
So that at one moment you are rich, and at another you possess nothing.

In these verses Theognis—to point this out in passing—alluded to a passage in Homer’s Iliad, Book 8, where Jupiter weighs the fates of the Trojans and the Greeks in golden scales. A short verse of this kind is circulated with the same meaning:
<note>original: "τὰ θνητὰ πάντα μεταβολὰς πολλὰς ἔχει"</note>
->that is,<-
The affairs of mortals possess various turns of fortune.

This saying is also celebrated: <note>original: "κύκλος τὰ ἀνθρώπινα"</note> Human affairs are a circle. That is, they are a circle (you should understand) because they are driven around and return as if in an orbit, with Fortune turning the wheel. So
<margin>Pindar in Theron,</margin>
<note>original: "ῥοὰς δ' ἄλλοτ' ἄλλαι..."</note>
The sense of these verses is that pleasant and sad things, in the manner of tides, happen to mortals in turn. Homer in several places calls it <note>original: "ἐτεραλκέα νίκην"</note> an "alternating victory." That is, a victory falling by turns now to these, now to those.

<margin>64</margin>
### The pleasant change of things.

<note>original: "Μεταβολὴ πάντων γλυκύ"</note> Change in all things is sweet. That is, the pleasant vicissitude of all things. A proverbial sentiment, used commonly by other authors, but especially by Aristotle in the second book of his *Rhetoric*. <note>original: "Καὶ τὸ μεταβάλλειν ἡδύ..."</note> And to change is pleasant, for change is according to nature. Always doing the same thing creates a satiety of the established condition. Whence it is said: Change in all things is sweet. It is used by the same author in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*. It clearly was taken from Euripides’ *Orestes*: Change in all things is sweet. Virgil alluded to the same in his *Eclogues*:
You shall speak in turns; the Muses love alternating songs.
There is also a certain witty Mime <note>A short dramatic farce or its author</note> circulated to this effect:
Nothing is pleasant, unless variety commends it. Likewise another similar to this:

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, SEVENTH HUNDRED
<meta>catchword: The Eagle</meta>

...the habit of such things is the worst.
It is in the nature of human sensation to be so prone to boredom that nothing can be so sweet that it does not immediately cause nausea if used a little too long; nothing is so excellent that it can please for a long time.
Whence also that line from Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note>:
*Rare use commends pleasures.*
Novelty, moreover, has such great power in every matter that, through the recommendation of newness, even bad things sometimes please as if they were the best.

->To hunt with unwilling dogs.<-
->LXV<-
**To hunt with unwilling dogs.** By this adage it is signified that what is extorted from the unwilling does not succeed happily enough. Nor should we employ the service of those who do not lend us their efforts from the heart. In Plautus <note>Roman playwright</note>, in the play *Stichus*, Panegyris, threatening her father so that he might not marry her and her sister to men against their will, says: "It is folly, father, to lead unwilling dogs to the hunt." And she adds a sentiment by which she explains the metaphor: "The wife who is given to a husband against her will is an enemy."

->To lead unwilling oxen to the wagon.<-
->LXVI<-
A similar saying persists even today, celebrated among the common people: that it is inconvenient to make a wagon be pulled by unwilling oxen, or to drive a wagon with unwilling horses. It seems, however, to be taken from Theognis <note>Greek elegiac poet</note>:
<margin>Theognis</margin>
*Never drive [me] under the wagon by force with a goad.* <note>original Greek: Μήποτε βίῃ κεντρῷ ὑφ' ἅμαξαν ἔλαυνε.</note> That is:
Neither should you ever lead me, subdued by the whip and goads,
To be drawn by an unwilling wagon.

->The slow catches the swift.<-
->LXVII<-
<margin>Homer, Odyssey, Book 8</margin>
*Truly the slow overtakes the swift.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ κίχησί τοι βραδὺς ὠκύν.</note> That is: The slow man catches the fast one. This applies to him who, though weaker in strength, overcomes the more powerful through art and ingenuity. The adage arose from the eighth book of the *Odyssey*, where a most delightful fable is told: how Vulcan <note>The blacksmith god, known for his limp</note>, being lame, when he held his wife Venus in suspicion because she was meeting secretly with Mars, and since he lacked the strength to catch the adulterer, fled to arts and ingenuity. He bound his bed all around with adamantine and unbreakable little chains; when he had done this, he pretended to go away. Then, when they were in the tightest embraces, Mars and Venus were entangled in those bonds—the more they turned about, the more they were trapped—and behold, Vulcan suddenly returns, and with the sun betraying them, he summons all the gods as witnesses of the discovered adultery. In which place Homer says:
*Truly the slow overtakes the swift.*
*As even now Vulcan, being slow, has caught Mars,*
*Though he is the swiftest of the gods who hold Olympus,*
*Being lame, [he caught him] by his arts; wherefore the fine for adultery is owed.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ κίχησί τοι βραδὺς ὠκύν. / Ὡς καὶ νῦν ἥφαιστος ἐὼν βραδὺς εἷλεν ἄρηα, / Ἐόντα περ ὠκύτατον θεῶν, οἳ ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι, / Χωλὸς ἐὼν τέχνῃσι, τὸ καὶ μοιχάγρι' ὀφέλλει.</note> That is:
Never does the slow man fail to catch the swift and the quick,
As now Vulcan, though he is slow of foot,
Has captured Mars, who is the most nimble
Of all those gods who hold the stars above.
Though he is lame in his foot, he finished the deed by art.
Whence also the caught adulterer must pay the penalty.
To this also pertains the fable of the fox and the crow, seeking the same prey in a race, which the fox, unequal in speed, claimed for himself by ingenuity. Likewise of the crab racing with the fox. Likewise of the *parrydus* <note>likely a small bird, perhaps a wren</note>, a little bird competing in flight with the eagle. Something of this kind happens also among fish, which, though they are very slow, capture the swiftest by art. Among their number is the ray, which, hiding itself in sandy or muddy places, stretches out those filaments of its own to entice fish, and draws the enticed ones all the way to its tail. Likewise the torpedo <note>electric ray</note> hides itself in the sand or mud: and it affects fish that happen upon it with numbness, and so feeds upon them. By which art it even hunts man. The stingray, called *trigon* by the Greeks, also hides itself, but for a different reason. And so it happens that, although they are sluggish themselves, they are sometimes caught having a mullet in their belly. The authority is Aristotle in the ninth book of *On the History of Animals*. Pliny, moreover, in his ninth book, testifies that mullets have a primary speed, so that fearing the force of other fish, they leap over ships lying across their path.
Theognis recorded the adage in this manner:
*Truly the slow overtakes the swift.*
*As even now Vulcan, being slow, has caught Mars.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ κίχησί τοι βραδὺς ὠκύν. / Ὡς καὶ νῦν ἥφαιστος ἐὼν βραδὺς εἷλεν ἄρηα.</note> That is:
The slow and the sluggish, by pursuing, catches the swift.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs regarding the futility of forced labor and the superiority of cunning over physical speed, illustrated by the mythological tale of Vulcan trapping Mars and Venus.</summary>
<keywords>Adagia, Erasmus, Vulcan, Mars, Venus, Homer, Theognis, Plautus, Aristotle, Pliny, natural history, proverbs, ingenuity, adultery, hunting metaphors</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### The tortoise defeats the eagle.
-> LXVIII <-

Not differing from this is the story related by Diogenes Laertius in his *Life of Menedemus* the philosopher, taken from a satyr play by the poet Achaeus titled *Omphale*:
<margin>"Was the swift one then captured, and how? And how was the eagle overtaken by the tortoise in a short time?" <note>original Greek: Ἠλίσκετ’ ἄραγε καὶ πῶς ἀθηνῶν ταχὺς, Καὶ πῶς χελώνης ἀετὸς ἐν βραχεῖ χρόνῳ.</note></margin> that is,
> Truly the swift was captured by the weak,
> And the eagle in a brief time by the tortoise.

Menedemus is said to have been in the habit of using these iambic verses against those who contended with him for civic honors. It can be understood through irony, or simply applied when someone wins through a more powerful art, and accomplishes by persistence what he cannot do by brute strength.

### Ill-timed benevolence differs nothing from hostility.
-> LXIX <-

This is an iambic verse celebrated among the Greeks as a proverb:
<margin>"Untimely goodwill differs nothing from enmity." <note>original Greek: Ἄκαιρος εὔνοι’ οὐδὲν ἔχθρας διαφέρει.</note></margin> that is, **Inopportune kindness is equal to hatred.**
Suidas, under the entry *akairon* <note>meaning "untimely" or "inappropriate"</note>, relates that Hippolytus responded with this verse to Phaedra’s nurse when she said she was seized by love for him. It will apply to those who, while striving to be dutiful, do harm or become a nuisance through their zeal because they have no regard for the timing. For example, one who rebukes a friend at an unsuitable time, or those who bring envy upon a man through immoderate and ill-timed praise; or those who supply money to a youth, by which he is made worse. Another similar saying is also circulated:
<margin>"A friend who harms me differs nothing from an enemy." <note>original Greek: Φίλος με βλάπτων οὐδὲν ἐχθροῦ διαφέρει.</note></margin> that is,
> When a friend does harm, he is no different from a foe.

Horace alluded to this in his *Epistles*:
> I care nothing for a service that weighs me down.

And again elsewhere:
> But officiousness presses upon the one it foolishly loves.

Likewise, Seneca says in the second book of *On Benefits*: "Often there is no difference between the gifts of friends and the prayers of enemies. Whatever the latter hope will happen to a man, the ill-timed indulgence of the former drives him toward and prepares him for. What is more shameful than what happens so frequently: that there is no difference between hatred and a benefit?" In these words of Seneca, in place of *vota* <note>prayers/wishes</note>, which we have restored from ancient manuscripts, the common editions had *acta* <note>deeds</note>. This had to be noted lest someone, out of ignorance, try to "correct" it as a mistake, as has happened in many cases before. To this belongs that saying of Ennius, rightly praised by Cicero in the second book of *On Duties*: "Good deeds ill-placed, I reckon to be ill deeds." The proverb will gain some grace if it is deflected a little further: for instance, if you should say that none do as much harm to good literature as those who handle it zealously but with little success. Or, that no one obstructs a reputation more than an inept herald. Or, that favorable fortune is more harmful than adversity.

### Know the time.
-> LXX <-

*Gnothi kairon* <note>Greek: γνῶθι καιρόν</note>. That is, "Know the opportunity." It is celebrated especially among the maxims of the Seven Sages; and, like many other things, it is ascribed to several authors and used by everyone. Hesiod says:
<margin>"Observe due measure; the right time is best in all things." <note>original Greek: Μέτρα φυλάσσεσθαι, καιρὸς δ’ ἐπὶ πᾶσιν ἄριστος.</note></margin> that is,
> Observe the limit, for in all matters it will be
> Best if one has looked for the fit time.

Theocritus alluded to this in an *Idyll*:
<margin>"But some things happen in summer, others in winter." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν θέρεος, τὰ δ’ γίγνεται ἐν χειμῶι.</note></margin> that is,
> Truly some things occur in the summer, and others in the winter time.

Indeed, Isocrates writes to Demonicus that in every matter, whatever is ill-timed is unpleasant. So great is the importance of observing the time and the opportunity in all affairs. The same is advised by these Greek sentiments:
<margin>"How great is a tiny thing given at the right time." <note>original Greek: Ὡς μέγα τὸ μικρόν ἐστιν ἐν καιρῷ δοθέν.</note></margin> that is,
> Even a very small thing is greatest when given in its place.

And again another:
> It is a fine thing to know the measure of every occasion. <note>original Greek: Καλὸν τὸ καιροῦ παντὸς εἰδέναι μέτρον.</note>

Furthermore, Pindar in the *Pythian Odes*:
<margin>"Opportunity likewise holds the summit of every matter." <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ καιρὸς ὁμοίως παντὸς ἔχει κορυφάν.</note></margin> that is,
> Time/Opportunity holds the peak in every thing alike.

Also that saying of Horace:
> It is sweet to be foolish in the right place.

Opportunity <term>kairos: the ancient Greek concept of the "opportune moment" or "right time" as opposed to chronological time</term> has such power that it can turn the honorable into the dishonorable, loss into profit, pleasure into annoyance, and a benefit into a crime; and conversely, in short, it changes the nature of all things. This holds the chief importance in undertaking and finishing any business.

<summary>Erasmus explores three proverbs concerning the importance of timing (Kairos) and persistence, warning that even good intentions like benevolence can become harmful if they are poorly timed.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, persistence, timing, Kairos, benevolence, Seneca, Horace, Greek philosophy, Seven Sages</keywords>

# FIRST CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
y
<meta>catchword: Which</meta>

so that it seems the ancients did not without cause grant her divinity: although among the Greeks this is a god, and is called *Kairos* <note>original: καιρός; the Greek concept of the "opportune moment" or "right time."</note>. Antiquity used to fashion his image in this manner: standing with winged feet upon a rolling wheel, he whirls himself in a circle with the swiftest rotation; the front part of his head is shaggy with hair, while the back is smooth, so that the former may be easily grasped, but the latter by no means. From this comes the saying, "To seize the opportunity." To which whoever wrote this little verse alluded both learnedly and elegantly: *With forehead hairy, behind this Opportunity is bald.* I am also pleased to add the poem of Posidippus <note>A Greek epigrammatist of the 3rd century BCE.</note> on this matter, which I wonder why Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a renowned Italian humanist scholar.</note> thought should be translated. It is of this sort:

> "Who and from where was the sculptor?" "From Sicyon." "And what was his name?"
> "Lysippus." "And who are you?" "Time <note>original: καιρὸς; here personified as Opportunity</note> the all-subduer."
> "Why do you stand on tip-toe?" "I am always running." "And why do you have
> double wings on your feet?" "I fly with the wind."
> "And why do you carry a razor in your right hand?" "As a sign to men
> that I prove sharper than any edge."
> "And the hair, why is it over your face?" "For him who meets me to take hold of."
> "By Zeus! Why then is the back of the head bald?"
> "Because once I have rushed past someone on my winged feet,
> no one, however much they desire it, shall grab me from behind."
> "For your sake, then, the artist fashioned me,
> stranger, and placed me in the porch to be a lesson."

These verses I have translated thus, not that I might compete with the Greek archetype, but wishing to use a "coarser Minerva" <note>term: crassiore Minerva; a Latin idiom meaning a plain, unrefined, or common-sense approach.</note> and clearly off-hand: which, even if I were silent, the poem itself would indicate; namely, so that they might at least be understood by those who do not know Greek:

> "What is the artist's home?" "Sicyon." "By what name?" "The name
> given is Lysippus." "Who are you yourself? Speak."
> "I am Opportunity, the fame that tames all things." "Come, why on wings
> do you stand?" "I am turned and rotated continually."
> "Why do you wear twin winged sandals on your feet?" "I will tell you:
> the light breeze carries me, a fledgling, here and there."
> "What does the razor held in your right hand mean?" "This sign
> teaches that I am sharper than any blade."
> "Why the hair over the face? What does it warn?" "This:
> that each may seize me as I am offered."
> "But why is the back part of the head bald?"
> "He whom I have once passed by with winged feet,
> though he may wish to catch me then in swift pursuit,
> it would not be allowed, as soon as I have turned my back on the man."
> "And so for your sake the skillful hand of the sculptor
> fashioned me in this image, stranger,
> and placed me here to be seen at the very front of the house:
> clearly that I might both warn and teach everyone."

It would not be beside the point to also subscribe the epigram of Ausonius <note>A 4th-century Roman poet.</note>: which, as Poliziano reminds us, seems to be modeled on the Greek, although it differs in several other ways, and especially in that here "Repentance" is added as a companion. The poem goes like this:

> "Whose work?" "Phidias's—he who made the statue of Pallas, and he
> who made Jove; I am his third masterpiece."
> "I am a goddess, rare and known to few: Opportunity."
> "Why do you stand on a wheel?" "I cannot stay in one place."
> "Why do you have winged sandals?" "I am fleeting. The things Mercury
> usually makes prosper, I hand over when I wish."
> "Do you cover your face from me?" "I do not wish to be recognized." "But hey,
> are you bald at the back of the head?" "Lest I be held while fleeing."

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Who is this companion joined to you? Let her tell you, I ask, who are you?
->I am a goddess, to whom not even Cicero himself gave a name.<- <note>original: "nec Cicero ipse dedit." Erasmus refers to the Greek concept of *Metanoea* (Repentance/Afterthought), for which there was no direct Latin equivalent in Cicero's time.</note>
I am the goddess who exacts punishment for what is done and what is not done.
->Indeed, so that one may repent, I am called Metanoea.<-
Now tell me what she does with you: if ever I have flown away,
->She remains; those whom I have passed by hold onto her.<-
You too, while you ask, while you delay by questioning,
->You will say that I have slipped from your hands.<-

### It smells of the lamp. 71

*It smells of the lamp* <note>original Greek: Τὸν λύχνον ὄζει</note>. This refers to a matter that has been meditated upon and worked out with much late-night study. The saying arises because scholars, staying awake by the light of a lamp, are accustomed to laboring intensely if they wish to forge something with greater accuracy. It was once cast as a taunt against Demosthenes <note>The famous Athenian orator</note> that his *enthymemes* <term>Enthymeme: a type of logical argument or rhetorical syllogism</term> "smelled of the lamp," because he spoke everything from a written draft and was well-prepared at home. From this, that famous tribute to him is celebrated: that he consumed more oil than wine. For he was a sober man and a "water-drinker"; even in his extreme old age, he practiced by that little lamp of his.

### The lamp of Aristophanes and Cleanthes. 72

The lamp of Aristophanes and Cleanthes passed into a proverb because of their remarkable diligence in study. Thus, a person is said to "work by the lamp of Aristophanes or Cleanthes" if they weigh every single detail with the greatest zeal and exquisite care. Varro, in his book *On the Latin Language*, says: "Because I did not wish to overlook not only the lamp of Aristophanes, but also the late-night labor of Cleanthes, who explain the words of poets just as they signify." I believe, however, that the adage refers to Aristophanes the Grammarian <note>The librarian at Alexandria, not the playwright</note>. Nor was the little lamp of Epictetus <note>The Stoic philosopher</note> lacking in fame, which after his death was bought for a great sum of money. Furthermore, what Juvenal says—
*Shall I not believe these things worthy of the Venusian lamp?* <note>Referring to Horace, born in Venusia</note>
—pertains more to investigation than to late-night study.

### To speak from the wagon. 73

The freedom of Old Comedy progressed to such an extent that it criticized by name not only the leading citizens, but even the gods. This is apparent from Aristophanes, who in the *Plutus* treats Jupiter, Mercury, Aesculapius, and all the other gods insultingly. Likewise, he treats Bacchus in *The Frogs* not very honorably. Since among those ancients, plays of this kind were performed on wagons by youths whose faces were smeared with wine-lees so they could not be recognized, and who threw taunts with great license at anyone they met, the adage was born: *to speak as if from a wagon* <note>original Greek: ὡς ἐξ ἁμάξης λαλεῖν</note>. This refers to those who revile others openly and freely. Aristophanes notes this in *The Clouds*, saying: "You shall not mock me, nor do to me what those wine-lees-demons do." Unless we prefer to refer this to a custom that lasted even in later ages among the Athenians. For at the festival they call the *Lenaea*, it was the custom for poets to compete with one another with written songs suited to provoking laughter, which they pronounced while sitting in wagons, shouting insults at one another in turn. There are those who refer it to the Eleusinian mysteries, which they call "the Great," in which women were carried in a carriage and, while being carried, would provoke each other with mutual insults according to custom. Lucian, in *The Tragic Jupiter*, says: "How the tongue spares no one, but speaks freely from the wagon, seizing the innocent and the guilty alike." Demosthenes also charged Aeschines with having brought forth against him things "to be said and not said," as if from a wagon. Hence this very thing, the license of Old Comedy, has the flavor of a proverb. Saint Jerome, writing to the monk Rusticus, says: "For I shall name no one, nor shall I select and graze specific persons with the license of Old Comedy." Aristophanes alluded to this, I believe, in *The Knights*:
*Alas for me, you say nothing from the wagon-maker.*
Since *wagon-makers* <note>original Greek: ἁμαξουργοὶ</note> are what they call the builders of wagons.

### Wagons loaded with insults. 74

Lucian alluded to the same thing when he said in *The Eunuch*: "And they poured out whole wagons of slanders upon each other." He is speaking of two philosophers arguing insultingly with one another. It signifies hyperbolically so—

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 7
y 2
<meta>catchword: I eat (original: Κρέω)</meta>

...as many insults as a wagon could carry. This very figure of speech relates to a proverb when we say, "Wagons loaded with promises," or "Ships loaded with promises," to describe very grand and excessive pledges. For the Greeks also use the term *wagon-sized* <note>original: ἁμαξιαῖα</note> to describe things that are massive or boastful, a name derived from wagons. Alexis, quoted in Athenaeus, Book 9, twisted this into a positive sense: "The table was set, and then he brought around wagons of good things."

### Let him lift you up, who does not know you. LXXV

*Let him lift you up, who does not know you.* If we wish to indicate to someone that their tricks are no longer unknown to us, and that we cannot be deceived by them hereafter, we may aptly say: *Let him lift you up, who does not know you.* Quintilian mentions this in Book 6. He says it is similar to what is called a *planus* <note>A Greek-derived word for a wandering impostor or cheat.</note> and to proverbs applied opportunely, such as when a man fell into the water and asked to be helped out, the reply was: "Let him lift you up, who does not know you." These words of Fabius <note>Quintilian's first name</note>, which are otherwise somewhat obscure, are interpreted as it were by Horace in his *Epistles*, where he discusses a jester named Planus. This man would often fall down of his own accord as if his leg were broken, and with piteous cries would beg passers-by to lift him from the ground. However, if any stranger ignorant of the trick approached to help, he was made a laughingstock by the jester. But when his pretense became known to most people, and he eventually did break his leg for real and prayed to be lifted up, no one helped, as everyone thought he was playing his usual tricks as a *planus*. Indeed, what happened to the man is what they say Aristotle once said; when asked what gain liars receive, he replied: "This: that they are not believed even when they speak the truth." The verses of Horace are these:

> And the man once mocked in the crossroads cares not to lift
> The *Planus* with the broken leg, though many a tear
> May flow, and though he swears by holy Osiris,
> "Believe me, I do not play, cruel men, lift the lame!"
> "Seek a stranger," the hoarse neighborhood shouts back.

Regarding this word *planus*, Aulus Gellius in Book 16, Chapter 7, mentions it among unusual words used by the mime-writer Laberius, and says it signifies a "sycophant" or "trickster." Marcus Tullius Cicero uses it with the same meaning in the oration he delivered *For Cluentius*. It is a Greek word, *planos* <note>original: πλάνος</note>, and signifies both a wanderer and an impostor. The proverb can also be expressed this way: *Seek a guest*, or *Seek a stranger*, just as Horace put it. It is suitable against those by whom we have been deluded before, having been made more cautious and less credulous by that experience. Similar is that line of Juvenal:

> He is known, and finds no fools.

That is, only fools are easily deceived. Not far from this is the Greek saying: *The fox is not caught twice* <note>original: οὐκ αὖθις ἀλώπηξ</note>; understand: "is not deceived a second time."

### To fart at, and to fart against the thunder. LXXVI

We find "to fart at" <note>original: oppedere</note> used proverbially for "to cry out against" and "to despise." Horace in his *Satires*: "Do you wish to fart at the circumcised Jews?" Aristophanes in *Plutus*:

> To fart at the buttocks.

Also in the same work elsewhere:

> To fart down at the buttocks. That is,
> To fart at grim poverty.

Meaning that those who have now become rich can neglect their former poverty. The same author in *The Clouds*:

> And even to fart against the thunder of heaven.

Where Strepsiades is introduced worshipping the clouds and despising the thunder of Jupiter. A commentator adds that this was usually represented on stage by a certain device: pebbles were dropped from an amphora into a bronze vessel, thus imitating the sound of thunder, so that this was, as it were, "farting back" at the thunder. For my part, I think it alludes to the ancient custom of *poppysmus* <note>A smacking or clucking sound made with the lips, often used as a superstitious charm.</note>. In ancient times, when it lightened, they would make clucking sounds with their lips, believing it to be a remedy so that the lightning would not strike. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "And if I flash lightning, they make clucking sounds." From this, some people in jest, as if mockingly imitating the *poppysmus* of others, would emit a sound from the belly. The Cyclops in Euripides, in the tragedy of the same name, despising the thunder of Jupiter, speaks in this manner:

> Having drunk a jar of milk, [I strike] my cloak...

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to deception and social contempt, specifically the "Planus" (the trickster who cried wolf) and the vulgar metaphor of "farting at" something to show disdain.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adages, Planus, deception, Horace, Quintilian, Aristophanes, Greek proverbs, Latin idioms, superstition, thunder</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"I croak like a bird at the thunders of Zeus." <note>original: "Κρώζω, διὸς βρονταῖσιν ὡς ὄρνις κτυπῶ."</note> That is:
When I have drunk a jar of milk, I shake my 
cloak, making a noise equal to the thunders of Jove.

---

->**He has prophesied in the cave of Trophonius.**<- LXXVII

"Εἰς τροφωνίου μεμάντευται." That is: *He has prophesied in the cave of Trophonius.* This is said of a man who is exceedingly gloomy and grim, because it was once believed that anyone who descended into the cave of Trophonius would never laugh again afterward. Aristophanes says in *The Clouds*:

> How I dread
> Entering there, as if into the cave of Trophonius.

That is:

> How I shuddered, indeed,
> No differently than if entering the cavern of Trophonius.

Furthermore, the story of Trophonius is told in various ways by the Greeks. Some say this Trophonius was a master craftsman in stone-cutting and built a subterranean shrine in Lebadia, a region of Boeotia, which was commonly named after him—that is, after the craftsman. Then, those who wished to consult the oracle used to sit naked at the entrance of the cave; from there, they were swept underground by a certain blast of air. They would carry certain honey-cakes with them to throw to the ghosts and serpents they encountered. Then, having received the oracle, they were returned to the surface through another opening. Others tell the story this way: Agamedes was the king of Stymphalus, which is part of Arcadia; he married Epicaste, whose son was Trophonius. These men surpassed all mortals of that time in craftsmanship and had undertaken the building of the Delphic temple; they also built a certain treasury in Elis for Augeas, where he might store his gold. Afterward, having loosened a joint in a certain stone which they had left for this very purpose, they used to enter at night and steal the money, with Geryon—the brother of Agamedes and son of Epicaste—as their accomplice. When this matter left Augeas deeply perplexed, it happened by chance that Daedalus <note>The legendary inventor and architect of the Labyrinth.</note>, fleeing from Minos, turned aside to him. Augeas entreated him to find the thieves by some art. Daedalus set certain traps with great skill, in which Agamedes was caught. Seeing that there was no escape, Trophonius cut off Agamedes' head so that he could not be recognized, and fled with Geryon to Orchomenus. When Augeas pursued them there on the advice of Daedalus, they fled again: one, Geryon, to Athens (as Callimachus testifies in his *Arcadia*), and the other to Lebadia in Boeotia. There, having prepared a subterranean dwelling for himself, he remained for the rest of his life. When he died, it was commonly believed that certain oracles were given there, and they began to sacrifice to Trophonius just as to a god. Some say that Agamedes and Trophonius fled after stealing by the help of Daedalus, and that as Trophonius fled, the earth opened in a chasm and swallowed him alive near Lebadia. Some years later, when the Boeotians were suffering from a plague, the consulted oracle replied that honor must be paid to the spirit of Trophonius. But since they were ignorant of where on earth his monument was, they found it by the indication of bees. For where they saw them swarming out of a certain hole, they guessed that was the place. Therefore, it was decided to send someone down into that cave to explore the matter. A certain man entered and encountered two dragons; by throwing honey-cakes to them, he escaped unharmed. From this, the custom grew that those about to enter the cave of Trophonius carry several cakes with them. Before they enter, they spend certain days in ceremonies, carrying spears in their hands (as some say) to ward off the force of the serpents. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations* records that Trophonius and Agamedes, having finished building the temple to Delphic Apollo, prayed to the god for a reward for their labor—nothing specific, but whatever was best for a human. Apollo indicated he would give it to them after the third day. When that day dawned, they were found dead. More recent writers say that Trophonius was a man hungering for glory beyond measure, very much like Empedocles <note>A philosopher who allegedly jumped into Mt. Etna to prove his divinity.</note>, and having built himself a subterranean home, he gave oracles; then, when he died of hunger, a certain spirit moved in and continued to give oracles. Later, through human superstition, many lowered themselves into that cave and stayed for several days. Indeed, this fable of Trophonius seems so similar to the one told about the Cave of Saint Patrick, which is in Ireland, that one might believe one was born from the other. Although even today there are many who descend; but first they are exhausted by a three-day fast, lest they enter with a healthy head. Those who have descended say that the [desire] for laughing...

### Singing for the sake of the watch. LXXVIII

<margin>Aristophanes in The Clouds.</margin>
<term>φυλακῆς ἕνεκα ᾄδων</term> <note>original Greek: "phylakes heneka adon"</note>, that is, Singing for the sake of the watch. It was once said of a man who was watchful and diligent. It is derived from the fact that those who keep watch are accustomed to sing, as if to solace their shared weariness with song, or lest they fall asleep in the meantime. So says Strepsiades in the *Clouds* of Aristophanes, having been poorly received in the school of Socrates,
> <term>ἐκ τῶν χρωμάτων, φρεδῶν χροιά,</term>
> <term>ψυχή, φερεδ' ἂν ἔμβας,</term>
> <term>ὅτι γ' ἐγγὺς ἐπὶ κακοῖς,</term>
> <term>ᾄδων ὀλίγῳ φερεδ' ἂν γεγύνημαι.</term> <note>Erasmus provides a Latin translation of these Greek lines, which are rendered here into English.</note> that is,
> Out of money, and of a wasted color,
> My soul is gone, my shoes are worn out,
> Because to these evils is added this:
> That I, singing while awake, have almost perished.
The proverb is read in two ways, <term>φερεδᾶς ᾄδων</term> and <term>φερεδὸς ᾄδων</term>. It alludes to this word <term>φερεδὸς</term> which signifies "wasted" and "empty."

### A slave bought with salt. LXXIX

<margin>A slave bought with salt.</margin>
<term>ἁλώνητον ἀνδράποδον</term> <note>original Greek: "haloneton andrapodon"</note>, that is, A slave bought with salt. It was once said of any barbarian or worthless little man. For merchants in the past, importing salt into inland regions, would bring back slaves from the barbarians. And it was a peculiar custom of the Thracian people to exchange slaves for salt. Whence a certain comic poet says,
<margin>A certain comic poet.</margin>
> <term>ἔοικας εἶ πᾶς ἁλὸς ἠγορασμένος.</term> that is,
> You seem to be a Thracian entirely redeemed by salt.
Things of this sort are generally reported by Zenodotus.

### The load of salt went back to where it came from. LXXX

<margin>Whence the cargo came, it has returned to whence it comes.</margin>
<term>ὅθεν ὁ φόρτος ἦλθον ἦλθεν ὅθεν ἥκει</term>. that is,
It had come to that place, from whence it had flowed.
It is said proverbially of those who cannot protect what they have acquired. Or of those for whom ill-gotten gains have come to a bad end. The adage was born from an event. A certain merchant was carrying a ship laden with salt; while the sailors were sleeping, the bilge water greatly increased by the influx of seawater, and it dissolved and ruined all the salt, and sank the ship itself: and so, that which had been born from seawater—for salt crystallizes from it—was melted back into the same.

### You sleep while carrying salt. LXXXI

<margin>You sleep while carrying salt.</margin>
An adage is also born from these words, arising from the same event: <term>ἅλας ἄγων καθεύδεις</term>. that is, You sleep while carrying salt. It will apply to one who acts sluggishly and carelessly in a dangerous matter, because salt is easily ruined by the influx of bilge water.

### Ill-gotten gains come to a bad end. LXXXII

This corresponds to the previous sentiment, which is found in the second Philippic of Cicero: "But as it is," he says, "in I know not which author, Ill-gotten gains come to a bad end." As to why he doubts the author...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of ancient adages, focusing on themes of self-possession, the necessity of public display for talent, and metaphors for uselessness.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Tullius <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> doubts it, but it is found in Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian*: "Ill-gotten, ill-spent." <note>original: "Male partum, male disperit"</note> Festus Pompeius cites from Naevius: "Ill-gotten gains slip away badly."

### He who does not possess himself, asks to possess Samos. LXXXIII
"He who does not have his own self, wants Samos." <note>original Greek: ὃς αὐτὸς αὑτὸν οὐκ ἔχει, σάμον θέλει</note> That is, he who does not even own himself, desires Samos.

This applies to those who impudently demand something, or those who fret over minor things while neglecting the greater. It arose from a certain story mentioned by Plutarch in his *Sayings of the Spartans*. When the Athenians surrendered their city to the victor, they requested that he at least leave them Samos. He replied in this manner: "Since you do not belong to yourselves, you ask to possess others." And from this the proverb was derived: "He who does not have himself, seeks Samos." Dion the Sophist, in his booklet *On Untrustworthiness*, elegantly adapts this to another sense: "He who is not a friend to himself, how can he be a friend to another?" <note>original Greek: ὅς τις αὑτῷ οὐ φιλός, πῶς ἄλλῳ φιλός;</note> It will also fit those who affect power over others when they cannot govern themselves.

### Hidden music has no respect. LXXXIIII
"Hidden music has no respect." This was once a celebrated adage among the Greeks; its meaning is that no matter how remarkable your natural talents are, if you do not bring them forth, it is just as if you did not have them. Persius seems to have alluded to this when he says:
> Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know it.

There exists something similar in the proverbs of the Hebrews, namely in the twentieth chapter of Ecclesiasticus: "Hidden wisdom and a concealed treasure, what use is there in either?" This saying of ours is reported by Suetonius in his *Life of Nero*, where he writes that the Emperor, forgetting his imperial dignity, was so devoted to music that he not only omitted nothing of what artists of that kind usually do to preserve or strengthen the voice, but even yearned to appear on stage; repeatedly tossing out the Greek proverb among his friends: "Hidden music has no respect." Aulus Gellius uses the same in the last chapter of the 13th book of *Attic Nights*: "You know," he says, "that old word of the master: that excellent music which is hidden is worth nothing." It is used by Lucian in *Harmonides*: "For there is no use, as they say, for unuttered and invisible music." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ ὄφελος ἀρρήτου φασὶ καὶ ἀφανοῦς τῆς μουσικῆς</note> Ovid undoubtedly alluded to this when he said:
> Though you surpass Thamyras and Orpheus in song,
> There will be no great favor for an unknown lyre.

There are, however, some mortals who, either by a native flaw of character or even by deliberate effort, conceal what they know and are reluctant to share it with others. It often happens to these people that they are neglected as if they were unlearned. To these should be ascribed what the Greeks call "blind wealth" <note>original Greek: τυφλὸν πλοῦτον</note>, that is, hidden riches and concealed resources. Plutarch calls it this in several places, as does Lucian. Plutarch, in his *Life of Lycurgus*, testifies that this saying was commonly tossed about among the Spartans: that there, Wealth was kept unhonored, no differently than a painted image, lifeless and motionless. For Lycurgus had so established the state that riches could be of no use or ornament to anyone.

### Made of fig-wood. LXXXV
Fig-wood, being brittle and useless for almost everything, has given rise to several proverbs. For they call a soft and useless man a "fig-man" <note>original Greek: ἄνδρα σύκινον</note>, as Theocritus says in *The Reapers*:
> Lest someone passing by should say: they are men of fig-wood,
> And this wage has gone to waste.

The commentator notes the proverb is drawn from the wood of the fig tree, which is useless, brittle, and weak; hence the term "a fig-wood defense" is used for something useless. In Aristophanes' *The Wasps*, someone asks: "Of what wood are you?" He answers: "Of fig-wood." In that passage, the interpreters note that a very sharp and annoying smoke comes from fig-wood. In the same author's *Plutus*, a Sycophant <note>term: Sycophant - in ancient Athens, a professional informer or accuser</note> threatens that if he finds a "fig-man" of his own sort, he will avenge the injury.

# SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

"If I take a partner, let him be a fig-wood one." <note>original: εἰ σύζυγον λάβω τινὰ, καὶ σύκινον</note> That is,
To happen upon a yoke-mate of the same kind:
->A man of fig-wood.<-
The same author <note>Aristophanes</note> says in the same play,
"And yet I know he is a powerful god,
to pay the penalty for this gluttony." That is,
->But by Hercules, I know that very powerful god<-
->Shall pay the price this day upon my shoulders.<-
Calling a god "powerful" in spirit who is actually weak and has no strength. Horace alluded to this when he makes a <term>fig-wood</term> <note>ficulnus: referring to wood from a fig tree, which is notoriously weak, brittle, and prone to rotting; thus a metaphor for anything useless or unreliable</note> statue speak thus:
"Once I was a fig-wood trunk, a useless log." And a little later:
"The fig-tree split with a fearful crack."
Lucian spoke with the same intent in *The Ignorant Book-Collector*:
"Having a sycamore and fig-wood mind." <note>original: συκαμίνην ἔχων καὶ συκίνην γνώμην</note> That is,
->Possessing a certain fig-wood intellect.<-
Likewise, Alexander the False Prophet had this in mind when he burned the books of Epicurus with fig-wood logs, signifying that he was a philosopher of no value. And <term>fig-wood assistance</term> <note>original: συκινη ἐπικουρία</note>—that is, "ficulnum auxilium"—stands for something empty and useless. Aristophanes in *Lysistrata*:
"We had a fig-wood assistance." That is,
"There was for us a help that was no help."
And <term>fig-wood dagger</term> <note>original: συκίνη μάχαιρα</note>—that is, "ficulna machæra"—stands for a false accusation. And <term>fig-wood ship</term> <note>original: συκίνη ναῦς</note>—that is, "ficulna nauis"—stands for a cheap little boat of the smallest value. Indeed, among the people of Naxos, they fashion a statue of Bacchus (whom they call <term>Bakcheus</term>) out of fig-wood; and another whom they call <term>Meilichios</term> <note>The "Mild" or "Gracious" one</note> is also made of fig-wood. For they call figs <term>malicha</term>. They believe Bacchus is the author not only of wine, but also of figs. So says Athenaeus in Book 3. Theocritus used a different figure in *The Beloved*: "men were golden of old," that is, "aurei quondam uiri." Likewise, "Sacred protection," and "Sacred anchor," and "Adamantine strength."

<margin>86</margin>
## The wolves saw him first.

Used for those who were seen first by another. It is said of a hoarse person, or one whose voice has suddenly been taken away. It is thought to be wittily applied to those who fall silent out of fear of someone, though they are otherwise fierce. Virgil in the *Eclogues*:
->Voice itself has failed Moeris:<-
->The wolves saw Moeris first.<-
Theophrastus warns that natural philosophers are the authors of the idea that there is a power in wolves such that, if they see a human first, they take away his voice. Nor are there philosophers lacking who attempt to provide a cause for this phenomenon. Socrates, in Plato’s first book of the *Republic*, turns the matter into an allegory, saying that Thrasymachus would have taken away his voice if he had not, by chance, spotted him first. "And I," he said, "having heard him, was stunned, and looking at him I was afraid. And I think that if I had not seen him before he saw me, I would have become speechless." Theocritus in *Idyll* 14:
"Won't you speak? You've seen a wolf." That is,
->Can you not find your voice? A wolf has been seen by you.<-
It is worth noting meanwhile that Theocritus reversed the sentiment when he denies the man can speak not because he was seen *by* a wolf, but because he *saw* the wolf. But Theocritus was merely alluding to the proverb while signifying a rival who had been seen, whose name happened to be "Lycos" <note>Greek for Wolf</note>.

<margin>87</margin>
## Whatever is seen in a dream.

"Whatever you see in a dream." <note>original: τὰ ἐν ἐνυπνίῳ βλέπεις</note> This is said of immoderate wishes. Since whatever you desire, it happens that you dream of it at will: just like Micyllus in Lucian’s work dreams he is rich and powerful. In Theocritus, a fisherman dreams of a golden fish. And men of the lowest station sometimes dream of marriage to queens. A certain shepherd in Theocritus’s ninth *Idyll* says:
"Would that I had as many as in a dream,
many sheep and many goats." That is,
->I wish for whatever is accustomed to be seen under the night:<-
->A great force of sheep, and many goats.<-
Theophrastus notes it is uttered in this manner: "To bring forth whatever is seen in a dream." He also cites a verse of Homer,

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>260</page-num>

"Not even if he gave me as many things as there are grains of sand and dust." ->that is,<-
"Not to me, even if you gave as many as the vain dreams 
that bring sleep to the weary."
<note>Erasmus is quoting a variation of Homer, Iliad 9.385. The Latin verse here is a poetic translation of the Greek.</note>
However, in the first book of the *Iliad* by this same poet, it appears slightly differently:
"Not even if he gave me as many things as there are grains of sand and dust." ->that is,<-
"Not to me, even if you gave as much as there is of sand and dust."
Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> seems to have alluded to this against Sallust: "From where did you—who just now could not even buy back your paternal home—suddenly, as if blessed in a dream, acquire the most precious gardens, a villa at Tibur, and the remaining possessions of Caesar?"

### The Goods of Porsena.
LXXXVIII

"The goods of Porsena" was a saying used for things that, having been snatched from enemies, are sold for a small price. Livy writes in the second book of *From the Founding of the City* that this name endured until his own age. He thinks it originated because during war, the goods of Porsena used to be sold at Rome, and that custom arose from the king's departure. If that is less approved, he considers that the custom was born from a more gentle beginning. He thinks it closest to the truth that Porsena, departing from the Janiculum <note>A hill in Rome</note> according to the terms of a treaty, gave his wealthy camp—with supplies gathered from the nearby and fertile fields of Etruria—as a gift to the Romans, since the city was then impoverished from a long siege. Then, lest these goods be plundered by the common people being let in, they were sold as if they were enemy property, and called "the goods of Porsena," a title signifying the gratitude for the gift rather than an auction of a king's fortune. Perhaps it will not be inaptly said of things which fall to us by someone's gift, or by a convenience of fortune, without our own effort. For Livy does not indicate the specific use of the adage.

### A Leonine Society.
LXXXIX

A "Leonine Society" <note>A "Lion's Partnership"</note> is when all the profit goes to one person while the rest are cheated; it is the sort of thing that usually happens with kings, or with very powerful men of the common sort. It appears in the *Pandects* <note>A compendium of Roman Law</note>, in which Aristo relates from Ulpian that Cassius responded that such a partnership could not be entered into where one would feel only the gain and the other only the loss; and he was accustomed to call this a "leonine society." Furthermore, the "Cassian" name—undoubtedly proverbial—appears to have been born from a Greek fable of Aesop, which is circulated as follows: A lion, a donkey, and a fox had entered into a partnership so that whatever they took by hunting, they would share in common. When they had obtained prey, the lion ordered the donkey to divide it. He, being stupid, distributed it into three equal portions. Indignant at this, because he was made equal to the others, the lion attacked and tore the donkey apart. The fox remained; he ordered her to divide it anew. She assigned almost the entire prey to the lion, saving hardly a few scraps for herself. The lion, approving the distribution, asked who had taught her that art of dividing. And the fox said, "The calamity of the donkey."

### From the Tripod.
XC

"Things from the tripod." <note>Greek: Τὰ ἐκ τοῦ τρίποδος</note> That is, "Spoken from the tripod." It was accustomed to be said of those things which we wish to seem vehemently true and beyond doubt. The adage is uttered in various ways: "As if from the tripod" <note>Greek: ὡς ἐκ τρίποδος</note>; "Everything from the tripod" <note>Greek: πᾶν ἐκ τρίποδος</note>. That is, most certain, just as if they proceeded from the oracle of Apollo. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in a certain letter to Brutus says: "Consider these things as if they were issued from the oracle of the Pythian Apollo." It is transferred from the tripod of either the Delphic or Pythian oracle. For these two oracles once held the highest credit among mortals. Concerning the Pythian, Strabo testifies in the ninth book of his *Geography* that it was once most celebrated, and that this is clear from the huge treasuries built there in which sacred monies were collected, as well as from the works of the most excellent craftsmen; then from the Pythian games celebrated there, and finally from the innumerable oracles which existed committed to writing. He describes the tripod thus: "Reliable authors," he says, "record that the divine dwelling itself is a deep and curved cave, opening with a mouth that is not very wide. And from here a breeze is returned, as the sacred divinity breathes out. Moreover, a high tripod hangs over the opening, which as soon as the Pythian prophetess has climbed it, having inhaled the spirit of divination, she utters responses, partly in meter and partly in free speech." The comic poet says: "This response is no more true than that of Apollo." Plato in the twelfth book of *The Laws*: "Not even if the Pythian himself affirmed it." Indeed, those figures of speech also smack of the proverb: "Whatever he says, he wants to seem an oracle." "Whatever he says, he wants to be law." The "dogmas" <note>Greek: δόγματα</note> of the Stoics, that is, their decrees. And what Cato says in Pliny concerning doctors: "And..."
