<meta>This page continues the discussion of classical adages, specifically those relating to the certainty of oracles and the bonds of brotherhood. The text transitions from the previous page's discussion on "speaking from the tripod."</meta>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 7

...think that a prophet has spoken. That is, believe that what I have said will be true. Pliny himself says elsewhere: *And I wish that as many as possible would judge this as a fact, and not merely as something said by a prophet.* <note>original: "Vtinamq; hoc, & non à uate dictum, quàm plurimi iudicent."</note> And Plutarch, in his commentary *On how to tell a flatterer from a friend*, says: *When he hears whatever has been said and departs in such a way that he thinks he has received an oracle, not just an opinion.* <note>original Greek: "Ευτ’ ακαλεας οτι ευ επη, χρησμον ειληφεναι φησεις"</note> However, those things which Athenaeus records in the second book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned," a famous collection of ancient lore.</note> are somewhat different from these: namely, that in the contests of Bacchus the prize was a tripod, and because of this, those who spoke the truth were commonly said to "speak from the tripod." Moreover, the tripod was a cauldron supported by three feet. There were two kinds of these: one belonging to Apollo, on account of the truth of his oracles; the other to Bacchus, in which wine was mixed, because those who are drunk speak the truth. Just as it is said in the proverb: *In wine there is truth.* <note>original: "In uino ueritas."</note> Galen used a similar figure of speech in the first book of *On Natural Faculties*, as if from the inner shrine: *For that wolf babbled on, just as if he were uttering an oracle from some inner shrine, saying that urine is a surplus from the nourishment of the kidneys.* <note>original Greek: "Απεφλυαρησε γαρ ο λυκος ετος, ωσπερ εξ αδυτου τινος χρησμον αφθεγγομενος..."</note> That is, he pronounced it just as if he were returning an oracle from a sanctuary.

### A Leaf of the Sibyl. XCI

"A leaf of the Sibyl" <note>original: "Folium Sibyllæ"</note> carries the same weight among the Latins. Juvenal says: *Believe that I am reciting to you the words of the Sibyl:* <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; their words were considered absolute truth.</note> that is, an indubitable matter. Aristophanes in *The Peace*: *By Zeus, certainly not such things, for the Sibyl did not say these things.* <note>original Greek: "μα τον Δι’ ου τοιην, ου γαρ ταυτ’ ειπε σιβυλλα"</note> That is: I certainly do not recognize it, for the Sibyl does not sing such things.
<margin>The adage is derived from the Cumaean Sibyl, whose oracles are celebrated among the first. It was her custom, as Marcus Varro testifies, to write her oracles on palm leaves. Virgil followed this in the third book of the *Aeneid*:</margin>
> You will see the frenzied prophetess, who beneath the deep rock
> Sings the fates, and commits marks and names to leaves.
> Whatever songs the maiden has described on the leaves,
> She arranges in order, and leaves them shut away in the cave.
> They remain unmoved in their places, nor do they depart from their order.
Likewise in the sixth book:
> Do not commit your songs only to leaves,
> Lest they fly away, the disordered playthings of the rapid winds.

### Let a brother stand by a man. XCII

<margin>Let a brother stand by a man.</margin> <note>original Greek: "Αδελφος ανδρι παρειη"</note> This was usually said of faithful help, because in dangerous matters a brother is hardly ever accustomed to fail a brother. In Plato’s second book of *The Republic*, Adeimantus, taking the side of Glaucon who was disputing against Socrates, says: "Has not Socrates discussed this matter enough?" "Why so?" "Because that which most needed to be said has not yet been said." Then Socrates replies: *Therefore, as the saying goes, let a brother stand by the man;* <note>original Greek: "ουκουν το λεγομενον, αδελφος ανδρι παρειη"</note> so you, if I have overlooked anything here, help me. He testifies that the same adage is taken from Homer in the *Protagoras*, where Socrates calls upon Protagoras to protect Simonides (a man of the same city) from the calumny of Protagoras. "I seem to myself," he says, "to call upon you just as Homer says Scamander, when besieged by Achilles, called upon Simois:"
*Dear brother, let us both together strive to check the strength of this man.* <note>original Greek: "φιλε κασιγνητε, σθενος ανερος αμφοτεροι περ σχωμεν"</note>
This passage is in the 21st book of the *Iliad*. Again, in the 22nd book of the *Iliad*, Hector, now unequal to Achilles, calls upon his brother Deiphobus to bring him help. For Pallas Athena had appeared to him in the likeness of Deiphobus. Deceived, Hector cries out in vain:
*He called his brother Deiphobus with a loud shout to hurl his long-shadowed spear.* <note>original Greek: "Δηιφοβ’ η τ’ εκαλεω δολιχοσκιον εγχος αλασθαι"</note>
When he was abandoned by him, he understood that his fatal day was at hand. Plutarch, in the *Life of Caesar*, reports that when Casca was holding Caesar's sword, he implored his brother's help in this manner, with these Greek words: *Brother, help!* <note>original Greek: "αδελφε βοηθει"</note>

### Not rashly to Abydos. XCIII

<margin>Not rashly to Abydos.</margin> <note>original Greek: "μη εικη την αβυδον"</note> That is, do not sail rashly to Abydos (it must be understood). Lest some heavy danger...

<summary>This page explores adages related to the absolute truth of oracles (the Sibyl and the Tripod) and the necessity of fraternal support in times of danger, citing classical authors like Virgil, Plato, and Homer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient Greek and Latin adages, focusing on the dangers of rashness and the nature of mutual flattery.</meta>

<page-num>262</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

undertake a danger without a suitable cause. For instance, if someone should warn another not to throw themselves easily into a prince's court, because that path does not turn out happily for everyone; or not to join in with drunken drinking parties, because it rarely happens that one leaves without trouble; or not to touch the writings of poets, because they are accustomed to corrupting the minds of many. Athenaeus in his twelfth book relates that after Alcibiades had received his inheritance from his guardians, he sailed to Abydus on the Hellespont and was there corrupted by luxury and delights, so that it is not unlike that saying: **It does not happen to every man to go to Corinth.** <note>A proverb meaning not everyone can afford or survive a life of luxury.</note> The people of Abydus had a bad reputation for being slanderers, so you may understand that for that reason it was not safe to spend time there. Stephanus and Suidas mention the adage. Stephanus records the adage thus: <note>original Greek: ἀ μη δ' εἶπὴ ἄβυδον πατεῖν</note> *Do not even think of treading on Abydus.* That is, let no one enter it without careful consideration. He indicates it is used for the reckless, adding that this was commonly thrown at those who inhabited Abydus, an island of Miletus. A certain small town in Picardy was once pointed out to me, which they say no guest could pass through without being marked by some mocking jest.

<margin>94</margin>
## One swallow does not make a summer.

<note>original Greek: Μία χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ</note> That is, *A single swallow does not bring about the spring.* This means that one day is not enough for the preparation of virtue or learning. Or, a single good deed or a single kind word is not sufficient for you to earn the name of a good man or a good orator; for that matter consists of many virtues. Or, to know something for certain, a single conjecture is not enough. But if many should agree, then finally the conjecture will be probable. Indeed, it can happen that one particular swallow appears earlier by chance. It is taken from the nature of the swallow, which is the herald of spring, for it flies away in winter. Hence Horace says: **With the west winds and the first swallow.** <note>Horace, Epistles 1.7.13.</note>
You will feel it at the beginning of spring. Aristotle in the first book of his *Ethics*: <note>original Greek: Τὸ γὰρ ἔαρ μία χελιδὼν ποιεῖ, οὐ μία ἡμέρα</note> *For neither one swallow nor one day makes a spring.* And in the same way, neither one day nor a brief time makes a man blessed or happy. Aristophanes in *The Birds*: <note>original Greek: δεῖσθαι δὲ ἔοικεν οὐκ ὀλίγων χελιδόνων</note> *He seems to have need of many swallows.*
The commentator indicates an allusion to the proverb we just cited: *One swallow does not make a spring.*
To this, that line of Sophocles in *Antigone* seems related:
<note>original Greek: πόλις γὰρ ἔστ' οὐδ' ἥτις ἀνδρός ἐστ' ἑνός</note> That is,
*For that which belongs to one man is no city.*
For just as one swallow does not make a spring, so one man does not make a city, nor does one coin make a man rich.

<margin>95</margin>
## Lend me your testimony.

<note>original Greek: Δάνεισόν μοι μαρτυρίαν</note> That is, *Lend me your testimony.* This means: Give me your testimony now, and you will receive mine in return if you ever desire it. This is rightly applied to those who praise and extol each other in mutual retaliation; or who support each other with mutual zeal, or who testify to win favor, neglecting their religious oath. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in his speech *For Flaccus*, rejecting the reliability of Greek witnesses as fickle:
> Nevertheless, he says, I say this about the whole race of Greeks. I grant them their literature, I grant them the study of many arts; I do not take away the charm of their speech, the sharpness of their wits, or their flow of oratory. Then, if they claim anything else for themselves, I do not object. But that nation has never cultivated the sanctity and good faith of testimonies; they are ignorant of the power, the authority, and the weight of this entire matter.

From this comes the saying, *Lend me your testimony.* It is not thought to be of the Gauls or the Spaniards. This whole thing belongs to the Greeks, so that even those who do not know Greek know in what words the Greeks are accustomed to say this. From these words of Cicero, it is clear enough that this adage was very well-worn in that age.

<margin>96</margin>
## Mules scratch one another.

*Mules scratch one another.* Used where the wicked and the unpraised admire and extol each other in turn. It is transferred from mules, who, like other beasts of burden, are accustomed to scratch each other with their teeth. This title, *Mules scratch one another*, is cited by Nonius Marcellus among the other titles of the *Menippean Satires* of Marcus Varro; it is surely a proverb. Ausonius in his second preface to the *Monosyllables* says: *But so that we may end with a proverb what we began with an adage: Mules scratch one another.* Varro also mentions this in the fourth book of *On the Latin Language*. Although that passage is foully corrupted, not only by the fault of the times but also by those common printers, to whom this is uniquely...

# SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...it seems their sole purpose is to utterly destroy all good books. But it should be read thus: *Amica Philoptorus*; <note>original: "Amica Philoptorus" - likely a corruption in the source text Erasmus is correcting</note> of him who, as an old man, says a boy was struck, a girl was struck. So let "mutual effort" stand. I think it should be read as "mules scratch each other," <note>original: "mutuum muli," implying "muli mutuum scabunt"</note> so that "scratch" is understood. Symmachus <note>A 4th-century Roman statesman and orator</note> says in a certain letter: "Mules scratch each other," and lest I seem to border on this proverb, I restrain the proclamation of your virtues with a "pressed tooth" <note>i.e., with silence or restraint</note>. However, it does not seem this adage can be taken correctly except in a bad sense: as if the unlearned praised the unlearned, the deformed the deformed, or the wicked the wicked in turn. Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet</note> records a story of this kind about two brothers who "scratched each other" and, by mutual service, one extolled the other with praise in turn:
*There was at Rome a brother,* he says, *a lawyer, so that the rhetorician might hear nothing but honors in the other's speech; so that this one would be a Gracchus to him, and he a Mucius to the other.* <note>Horace, Epistles 2.2.87-89. Gracchus and Mucius were famous Roman orators/lawyers.</note>
The same author, noting unlearned poets who nevertheless listened to and praised each other as they recited:
*I depart an Alcaeus by his vote; who is he by mine? Who but Callimachus?* <note>Horace, Epistles 2.2.99-100. Alcaeus and Callimachus were esteemed Greek poets; here used as empty flattery between hacks.</note>

### They trade mutual services.
->XCVII<-
To this is related that line of Terence from the play *Phormio*: *They trade mutual services.* <note>original: "Tradunt operas mutuas"</note> It refers to young men who defend each other in their vices. It seems to be transferred from neighboring farmers who are accustomed to lend mutual labor to one another. Or from craftsmen who sometimes use mutual help, especially blacksmiths.

### Old men rub each other.
->XCVIII<-
To this belongs also that joke turned into a proverb about old men rubbing each other. Aelius Spartianus <note>One of the supposed authors of the Augustan History</note> tells the story in the *Life of the Emperor Hadrian*. This Hadrian, seeing a certain veteran in the bath rubbing himself against the marble walls due to a lack of slaves, gifted him both several slaves and the funds for their upkeep. When the rest of the veterans saw that this had turned out successfully, they too began to rub themselves against the marbles in the sight of the Emperor, so that in this way they might elicit the prince's generosity. But he, having called the old men forth, ordered that they should rub each other down in turn, and thus there would be no need for boys. This joke later passed into a common tale. The saying of Scipio Aemilianus is also celebrated: that beasts of burden, because they lack hands, require the rubbing of another. By this it is signified that those who cannot perform distinguished deeds need a herald to acquire fame for them.

### Scratch the one who scratches you.
->XCIX<-
*Scratch in turn the one who scratches.* <note>original Greek: Τὸν ξύοντα ἀντιξύειν</note> This is recorded in the collections of Diogenianus. It is only fair to deserve well of one who deserves well of you, and to repay service with service. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note> thinks the metaphor is transferred from donkeys biting each other in turn; and it can be said in both senses: of those who help each other with mutual services, or those who affect each other with mutual insults. Regarding this sentiment, that not-unpleasant mime is celebrated under the name of Seneca (though falsely):
*Expect from another what you have done to another.* <note>A maxim of Publilius Syrus, often attributed to Seneca in the Renaissance.</note>
Aristides, in the common defense of the four orators, says: *The proverb "scratch the one who scratches" is attributed even to donkeys. But the followers of Homer would say it is more fitting to compare Pericles to lions than to donkeys.* <note>original Greek: Τὸν ξύοντα δ’ ἀντιξύειν καὶ τοῖς ὄνοις ἡ παροιμία... Erasmus translates the Greek passage into the following Latin/English sense.</note> To this belongs the saying: *Hand washes hand.* <note>original Greek: χεὶρ χεῖρα νίζει</note> Which Plato cites in the *Axiochus*:
*It was always his habit to turn over in his mind that saying of Epicharmus:*
*Hand washes hand; give something, and receive something.*
Although the Aldine edition <note>The famous press of Aldus Manutius in Venice</note> has "to speak" instead of "to think"—that is, to have it in one's mouth—the Greek trochaic tetrameter will stand better if you read "take something" <note>Greek: λάμβανέ τι</note> instead of "receive something" <note>Greek: λάβε τι</note>. We cited this same thing in another place, but differently, having followed a faulty manuscript since the Greek Plato was not yet at hand for us to consult. It seemed right to remind the reader of this, lest anyone build a false accusation against me on this account, that I have rashly altered Plato's writing. As far as the meaning is concerned, it matters nothing at all whether you prefer to read "washes" or "scratches," since just as hand performs a mutual service to hand by washing, so it does by scratching.

He includes a humorous anecdote about the Emperor Hadrian and the origins of social cooperation metaphors.</summary>

->Iron sharpens iron.<-

It was not my intention to mix the proverbs of theologians into this collection—not because I look down upon them, but partly because I judged that this honor should be reserved for the Sacred Scriptures, and partly because they are already in everyone's hands. However, I will not be reluctant to include this one, since it fits so perfectly with the others. It is found in the Proverbs of Solomon, chapter twenty-seven: *Iron is sharpened by iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend.* <note>Proverbs 27:17</note> The Hebrews pronounce it in this manner (since there is some value in hearing an adage in its own native tongue): *Barzel be-barzel yaḥad.* <note>original: "ברזל בברזל יחד"</note>

---

->THE EIGHTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND<-

### Seek a wife who is your equal.

*Seek the one according to yourself* <note>original Greek: Τὴν κατὰ σαυτὸν ἔλα</note>, that is, marry a wife who is your equal. This adage warns that no one should be lured by greed or ambition to marry a woman of higher status than himself. For marriages of that kind almost always turn out unfavorably. Plutarch, in his short book on the education of children, warns parents to betroth their children to wives who are not much wealthier or more powerful. For it is wisely said in the proverb: *Marry a wife of your own lot.* This is also celebrated among the sayings of the Wise Men, and is attributed by some to Pittacus <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, c. 640–568 BC</note>: *Seek the one according to yourself*, meaning, marry from among your equals. For if you marry a woman born of those more powerful than you, you will acquire masters for yourself, not in-laws. Diogenes Laertius, in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, records something of this sort, which he asserts was also celebrated by Callimachus in a rather elegant epigram.

A certain young man from Atarneus consulted Pittacus as to which of two women he should marry. For two were offered: one equal in wealth and birth, the other superior in both. But Pittacus, raising the staff on which he leaned, advised him to go to the crossroads of the city where boys gathered for the sake of play; he should consult them and follow whatever advice they gave. The boys, from a proverbial song, replied: *A wife who is an equal should be married.* And so the young man, passing over the other, married his equal. Callimachus persuades Dion to do the same. This sentiment pleased Pittacus all the more because he himself had married a woman more noble than he—the sister of Draco—whose command and arrogance he had endured with great difficulty. Thus, he seems to have discovered this saying not just in time, but to his own misfortune. The epigram survives, although there one reads *going* <note>Greek: ἰὼν</note> instead of *seek* <note>Greek: ἔλα</note>, erroneously in my opinion; it is as follows:

> A stranger from Atarneus once asked Pittacus thus,
> The son of Hyrradius, the man of Mitylene:
> "Old father, a double marriage calls me; one bride indeed,
> In both wealth and lineage, is equal to me;
> The other excels. Which is better? Come now, you
> Advise me which of the two I should lead to the wedding."
> He spoke. And the old man, raising his staff, his elderly weapon,
> Said: "Look, those boys there will tell you the whole story."
> And there, under the lashes of whips, having swift spinning-tops,
> The boys were turning them at the wide crossroads.
> "Follow in their footsteps," he said. And the man stood
> Nearby, and they were saying: "Seek the one according to yourself."
> Hearing this, the stranger refrained from grasping at
> The greater house, having agreed with the omen of the children.
> And as he brought the humble bride to his home,
> So you too, Dion, seek the one according to yourself.

Because Ambrogio Traversari <note>Ambrosius Camaldulensis (1386–1439), a monk and translator of Greek works into Latin</note>, the translator of Diogenes, rendered these verses into Latin not altogether unsuccessfully, I will not find it burdensome to add them here:

> A guest from Atarneus once asked Pittacus,
> Born of Hyrradius, the Mitylenean:
> "Great elder, two women desire to marry me, of whom
> One matches me in both lineage and wealth;
> The other excels. Advise me which is better, and say
> Which of these two should rather be taken by me..."

# EIGHTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

*Lifting his staff, he spoke thus: "These weapons of old age*
*Will provide the counsel of the boy which you seek.*
*Like a top spun swiftly in a circle by the constant*
*Lash of a whip, it turns in the broad crossroads.*
*Follow their warnings." Thus he spoke, and as the man*
*Inquired, they replied: "Take for yourself a peer."*
*After he heard this, clinging to the boys' advice,*
*The stranger abstained from a grand marriage.*
*And happily he brought a peer into his small home:*
*Thus, Dion, if you are wise, take an equal for yourself.*
<note>original: "Tu tibi sume parem." This poem recounts a story where a man seeks advice on marriage and is told by children playing with tops to "choose your equal."</note>

It is either an allegory from the children's top, which is driven around by whips. For each boy, according to his strength, drove a top that was suitable for him. Deianira, in Ovid, applied this proverb to her own sex:
*Just as unequal bullocks come poorly to the plow,*
*So a young bride is overwhelmed by a great husband.*
*It is not an honor, but a burden; a beauty that will harm the bearer:*
*If you wish to marry fitly, marry an equal.*
<note>Ovid, Heroides 9. Deianira warns that marrying someone of much higher status or power (like Hercules) is more burdensome than honorable.</note>

Plutarch, in *On the Education of Children*, says: "Drive the one that is according to yourself," <note>original: "τὸν τὴν κατ’ σαυτὸν ἐλαύν"</note> that is: It is the part of a wise man to marry a wife who is his equal and suitable for him. I thought I should add here that verse from the play titled *Thesmophoriazusae* by Aristophanes:
"For a woman is a queen to an old bridegroom." <note>original: "δέσποινα γὰρ γέροντι νυμφίῳ γυνή." Suggesting an old man becomes a slave to a younger wife.</note>
The same is advised by that verse of Euripides in *Rhesus*:
"I would not wish to marry a woman greater than myself." <note>original: "οὐκ ἂν ἐμαυτῷ μείζοναν γαμεῖν θέλω."</note>
Truly, it will be appropriate to look not only at whether the wife is an equal in the nobility of her family or the measure of her household wealth, but also that her age does not differ too much, as well as her beauty and her way of life. It can also be extended further, namely to undertaking a business for which you are equal and fit to complete. Likewise, to a type of man who is suitable, and to a friend accommodated to your own character.

->He dares not even say 'mu'.<- **II**

Those who, out of fear, did not dare to gape, were formerly said "not to dare to make a *mu*." It is related more fully by Varro in the third book of *On the Latin Language*. For he thinks the verb *mussare* <term>to mutter or keep silent</term> is derived from the sound of the letter *mu* <note>the Greek letter Μ</note>, just like the Greek *myzein* <note>μύζειν</note>, because the mute can sound no more than *mu*. For that letter is the most mute of all, especially at the end, wonderfully constricting and closing the mouth. Varro's words are these: "From which he says the same thing which is the least; they do not mutter, nor do they dare to make a *mu*." It seems to be a poem by Ennius, for he had cited him a little earlier. He says, "that which is the least, they do not (as they say) dare to make a *mu*." Among the Greeks, *myzein* means both to mutter and to make a sound through the nostrils. Aristophanes, in *Thesmophoriazusae*:
"Mu, mu, everything has been done quite well." <note>original: "μὺ μὺ πάντ’ εὖ πεποίηται καλῶς."</note>
For when Mnesilochus had said, "mu mu," Euripides responds:
"Why do you mutter? Everything has been finished perfectly."
And among the Latins, *mutire* and *mussare* mean to bear something silently, and as if to swallow one's voice. Terence: "The injury of the young men must be borne in silence." <note>original: "Mussitanda iniuria adolescentium."</note> Virgil: "King Latinus himself mutters." <note>original: "Mussat rex ipse Latinus."</note>
In Aristophanes' *Knights*, two men about to complain privately to themselves about the vices of the city, chant this iambic line:
"Mu mu mu mu mu mu mu mu mu mu mu mu."
In which one may conjecture that this is the voice of those who are afraid to speak.

->Not even a 'gry'.<- **III**

"He does not even utter a *gry*." <note>original: "οὐδὲ γρὺ φθέγγεται."</note> This is likewise a proverbial hyperbole among the Greeks for that which is "not even the least bit." For *Gry* signifies something very small: either the dirt under the fingernails (a truly useless thing), or the grunting of a pig made by those who respond with a grunt instead of speech, or the smallest of coins. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
"...and he forces me along,"
"and that too, arriving, not even a whole *gry*."
that is,
"...and he compels me at the same time,"

<sig>z</sig>
<meta>catchword: And</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

And meanwhile, when asked what these things mean, he answers nothing at all, not even a "gry" <note>original: "ne gry quidem." A 'gry' was a tiny Greek measure, used to mean the smallest possible sound or thing.</note>. From this is also derived the verb "to mutter" <note>original: γρύζειν (gryzein)</note>. Likewise in the same play: "Do you even dare to mutter and talk nonsense, you cursed man?" <note>original: γρύζαν δὲ καὶ φλυᾶρον ὦ κατάρατε;</note>—that is, "Do you wretches even dare to grunt?" Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius* says: "He spoke not at all, nor could he be induced even to mutter" <note>original: οὐδαμῶς ἔφθεγξατο, οὐδ’ ἐπήχθη γρύξαι</note>—that is, he did not speak in any way, nor could he be led to even open his mouth. The use of this word is quite frequent in Aristophanes.

---

#### IV
->I do not value it at a hair.<-

This is a familiar hyperbole among the Latins: "I do not value it at a hair" <note>original: Non facio pili</note>, or "Not a hair better," when they mean something of the smallest importance. Catullus says: "They do not make a cohort worth a hair." Cicero wrote to his brother: "For I shall not love you even a hair's breadth less." The same author says: "Meanwhile, in Cappadocia, not even a hair" <note>original: ne pilum quidem</note>. Although in common copies "a felt cap" <note>original: pileum</note> is written in this place. Indeed, this adage is on everyone's lips even in these times. The usefulness of a hair was also a proverb among the Greeks, hence "worth a hair" <note>original: ἄξιος τριχός</note>, referring to a man of no worth. The harsher the metaphor, the more charming it is: for "I do not value it at a hair" has almost no figurative quality beyond hyperbole; but "Not a hair more learned," "Not a hair more unpleasant," "Not a hair more honored," and speeches of that kind, because they recede a little further from simple speech, receive a good deal more grace.

---

#### V
->I do not value it at a nutshell.<-

To be "of a nutshell" <note>original: Nauci esse</note> and to "make of a nutshell" <note>original: Nauci facere</note>, standing for that which is nothing and to value as nothing, is found quite often in Plautus. However, what "nauci" actually signifies, a certain servant in Plautus—though he used the word—denies that he knows. Plautus says: "The man who is fearful in uncertain matters will not be worth a nutshell." Certain grammarians, among them Pompeius Festus, say that *nauci* signifies the shell of a nut, or the pit of an olive, or that thin membrane seen dividing the middle of a walnut; in short, the husk of any thing, which the Greeks call *pyrina*, they think was called *nauci*. Some derive it from the Greek word *nake* <note>original: νάκη</note>, which indicates a goat skin. There are also other opinions about *nauci*, which whoever wishes to know may read Festus under the entry "Naccae." Ennius said "I do not hold at a nutshell" in Marcus Tullius [Cicero's] first book *On Divination*: "In short, he does not hold the Marsian augur at a nutshell."

---

#### VI
->I do not value it at a flock of wool, or I value it at a flock.<-

By the same reasoning it is said: "To value at a flock" <note>original: Flocci facere</note>, and "To not value even at a flock," for that which is to not value even the slightest bit. A "flock" <note>term: floccus - a scrap of wool</note> is a tiny piece of wool which, being useless, is plucked from the fleece and flies away, or certainly something similar of no importance. Examples are met with everywhere among authors, so that it does not seem worth the effort to insist on them in this place.

---

#### VII
->I do not value it at this.<-

To this form belongs that line of Terence from *The Brothers*: "I shall not value any of it at this" <note>original: Huius quicquam non faciam</note>. Donatus <note>A famous Roman grammarian</note> reminds us that this is "deictic" <note>term: deictic - pointing or gesturing</note>, indicating someone showing either a flock of wool, or a straw, or the tip of a finger, or something of this sort. Athenaeus in his twelfth book recorded that a statue of Sardanapalus was placed on his monument with this gesture of the fingers, to signify that all human affairs are utterly to be despised, and are not worth even the snap of a little finger.

---

#### VIII
->I would not buy it for a rotten nut.<-

In Plautus, in *The Braggart Soldier*, it is: "I would not buy your life for a rotten nut," meaning not for the smallest price. And we commonly say, "I wouldn't buy it for a hollow nut," and "I wouldn't buy it for a nutshell." Aristophanes in *The Peace*: "I would not buy it even for a single dried fig" <note>original: οὐκ ἂν πριαίμην οὐδ’ ἂν ἰσχάδος μιᾶς</note>—that is, I would not buy it even for a single nut. Similar to these is what is read in the same Plautus, as cited by Festus: "I wouldn't buy that word for a *titiuillitium*." For by this word the Latins were accustomed to signify a thing of nothing, just as the Greeks say *ppolo*; and again *Butubata*, a word used by Naevius for trifles, according to Festus.

---

#### IX
->He did not spend even a farthing.<-

The hyperbole of the "farthing" <note>term: teruncius - a tiny Roman coin worth three ounces of copper, or a quarter-penny</note> appears several times in Cicero, as it is clearly a type of the smallest coinage. To Atticus: "And I also hope that in the whole spirit of our command, not a farthing will be spent in the province." Plautus in *The Two Captives*: "They do not value jesters at a farthing anymore."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Greek and Roman adages concerning value and worth, specifically focusing on metaphors for things of little to no value versus things of great honor. It follows the previous page's exploration of small currency as a measure of character.</meta>

# EIGHTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
<note>Erasmus organized his thousands of proverbs into "Chiliads" (groups of 1,000) and "Centuries" (groups of 100).</note>

Just as the Greeks say "half an obol" <note>original: ἡμιωβόλιον</note> to refer to a most worthless thing. Varro thinks the *teruncius* <note>A tiny Roman coin worth three ounces of copper</note> was named from "three ounces."

### X. A man of three obols
Hence Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian* called a man "of three obols" <note>original: hominem trioboli</note> to mean a most wicked man, clearly of no value. A man of the smallest sort. Aristophanes used a very similar figure of speech in *The Wasps* to describe worthless verses as "verses of three obols" <note>original: τριωβόλου ἐπῶν</note>. Gregory, in a letter, said of a vile and despised man: "rather a slave worthy of a few obols" <note>original: μᾶλλον ἀνδράποδον ὀλίγων ὀβολῶν ἄξιον</note>. They are also called "three-obol men."

### XI. A man of three asses
In a similar way, Persius calls a most contemptible little man a "three-as groom" <note>original: tressis agaso; an 'as' was a low-value copper coin</note>. Likewise:
> He bids for a hundred Greeks at a clipped hundred-as piece.

That is, for the smallest price. He used "three-as" <note>original: tressis</note> in a novel way, as if the man were valued at only three *asses*. The *as* was a type of small copper coin. Persius's poem in the fifth satire goes like this:
> ...a scabby three-as groom
> rules you, and those whom a single whirl
> makes a Roman citizen. This man is Dama, not a three-as groom.
<note>Persius is discussing the ease of freeing a slave (Dama), noting that a simple turn by a magistrate makes a citizen, yet the man remains worthless in character.</note>

Finally, there is that saying of Jerome: "Who would value you at a two-penny piece?" <note>original: dupondio; a coin worth two asses</note>. Justinian, in the preface to the *Pandects* <note>A massive compilation of Roman Law</note>, did not want young law students to be called by the old nickname "two-pennies" <note>original: dupondios</note>—which was as ridiculous as it was frivolous—but rather by the new name, "the Justinians."

### XII. Worth a hair
"Worth a hair" <note>original: Ἄξιος τριχός</note> is said by the Greeks of those worthy of no good thing, because nothing is more contemptible than a single hair. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
> I am willing to die right here,
> if I have taken anything of yours worth even a hair.

This adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

### XIII. Not worth even a "one"
"Worth not even a one" and "Worth a one" <note>original: Ἄξιος οὐδὲ μονὸς, καὶ ἄξιος ἑνός</note> are said of the most worthless things. The metaphor is taken from the throwing of dice, in which the "one" <note>original: monas</note>—that is, the number of the single unit—was the lowest. For everywhere in the calculation of numbers, the unit is the smallest thing, and not even a number at all, as the philosophers maintain. Conversely, when they mean something of great price, the Greeks use the common figure "worthy of many honors" <note>original: πολλῶν τιμίων</note>, and "worth the whole world" <note>original: τοῦ παντὸς ἄξιον</note>. On the other hand, "worth a little" <note>original: ὀλίγου ἄξιον</note> is used for things they despise. It is common and vulgar to be counted as only one man; therefore Homer, in the eleventh book of the *Iliad*, wishing to explain the dignity of a physician, says:
> For a man who is a doctor is worth many others.

Plato looked to this in the fifth book of *The Laws*: "For this man is to be valued as one, but that man as worth many others." To this form also belong those figures of the rhetoricians, when they say that "one person is a whole theater to them," or that they "value the judgment of one man more than that of an infinite multitude."

### XIV. Worthy of an obelisk
"Worthy of an obelisk" <note>original: Ἄξιος ὀβελίσκου</note> means worthy of any honor whatsoever. For columns and pyramids of this sort were erected to the greatest men, inscribed with magnificent titles, or huge colossi, which stupid princes once took pleasure in having fashioned. However, the proverb has a double meaning, because the critic Aristarchus used to "slaughter" with obelisks <note>A horizontal line (—) used in ancient manuscripts to mark doubtful or spurious text</note> those passages he did not approve of. Suidas mentions this among others.

### XV. Let him stand in gold at Olympia
When the Greeks mean someone is worthy of the highest reward, they usually say: "Let him stand in gold at Olympia." Lucian in *The False Critic* says: "Let him stand in gold, as they say, at Olympia." This was because having a statue among illustrious men in such a famous place was considered the chief honor of that age. Virgil alluded to this when he said:
> ...if the breeding season fills up the flock, you shall be in gold.

Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "I promise to set up a golden statue of equal size to you at Delphi." And a little later in the same work: "beside the mute stone..." <note>original: λίθῳ; this matches the catchword for the next page</note>

<summary>Erasmus examines various ancient metaphors for value, ranging from worthless "three-obol" men and "three-as" grooms to the highest honors like golden statues at Olympia or being "worth many men."</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<note>original: "λιθίνω ἀνάθημα σφυρήλατον ἐν ὀλυμπία στάθη"</note> *Let a hammered offering be set up in stone at Olympia.* That is, let him stand as a wrought monument among the statues of the Cypselids at Olympia. The translator perhaps read <note>original: "χρυσήλατος"</note> *wrought gold*, or certainly dreamed it, as he rendered it "golden." Furthermore, the kings of Corinth are called Cypselids after Cypselus, who, having driven the Bacchiadae from Corinth, gained power there and amassed great wealth; as evidence of this, Strabo says: <note>original: "τὸ ὀλυμπίασιν ἀνάθημα κυψελιδῶν σφυρήλατος χρυσὸς ἀνδριάς συμμεγέθης"</note> *the offering of the Cypselids at Olympia was a life-sized statue of hammered gold.* Philostratus also alluded to this in the *Life of Apollonius*: <note>original: "καὶ στεφανώσουσί σε ὀλυμπία"</note> *and they shall crown you at Olympia.* Persius used a similar figure of speech in his second satire:

> Let them be the foremost, and let them have a golden beard.

For it was customary to add a golden beard to certain statues.

->**Worthy of anything.**<- XVI

<note>original: "Ἄξιος τοῦ παντός"</note> That is, *Worthy of anything* <note>literally: "worthy of the whole"</note>. This is recorded by all the collectors of Greek adages. Plato uses it in the *Sophist*: <note>original: "καὶ τοὺς μὲν δοκῶσιν εἶναι τῷ μηδʼ ἑνὸς τίμιοι, τοὺς δʼ ἀξίους τῷ παντός"</note> *to some they seem worthy of nothing, to others again, worthy of everything.* Similarly, Terence said: *A man of any price.* Although this adage was only just mentioned.

->**Worthy of an Argive shield.**<- XVII

<note>original: "Ἄξιος εἶ τῇ ἀργείᾳ ἀσπίδος"</note> That is, *You are worthy of an Argive shield.* Said of a noble person who is to be honored in a grand manner. It is derived from the fact that formerly among the Argives <note>people of Argos</note>, it was the custom for pure and chaste boys to carry certain shields in processions. This honor was granted to that age group by an ancient decree.

->**Worthy of forfeiting one's bail.**<- XVIII

When we wish to signify a matter of the greatest importance, which ought to be sought even at the greatest expense, we say it is "worthy of forfeiting one's bail." For those who have been summoned to court <term>vadati: those under a legal bond to appear</term> cannot be absent except at their own great peril. Pliny the Younger, in the preface to his *Natural History*, says: *Inscriptions for the sake of which bail might be forfeited.* This means things for which everything else should be set aside, even the most serious matters. Seneca, in the fourth book of *On Benefits*: *We promise bail, yet it is forfeited. An action is not granted against everyone. A greater force excuses the one who forfeits.* These words of Seneca declare that the reason excusing a deserter of promised bail must be extremely urgent. Horace writes: *And by chance he now had to answer to his bail.* He mocks a wicked chatterbox who preferred to risk his legal case rather than leave his trifles. A similar form is *To fight as if for altars and hearths*, used when there is a contest over a dear and serious matter. Celsus used a similar figure in the sixth book of the *Pandects*, under the title *On the Recovery of Property*: *To be deprived of the household gods and ancestral tombs.* Imagine, he says, a poor man who, if forced to return it, would have to do without his household gods and ancestral tombs; it is enough to permit you to take from these things what you can, provided the land is no worse than if the building had not been there in the beginning.

->**To sleep on either ear.**<- XIX

*To sleep on either ear* means to be at leisure, secure, and free from care. Terence in *The Self-Tormentor*: *Every fear has now been taken from you, so that you may sleep at leisure on either ear.* Basil also uses it in a certain letter, but in a negative sense, meaning a lazy or supine security. Menander in the *Plotius*, quoted in Gellius:
<note>original: "Ἐπʼ ἀμφοτέραν τὴν ἐπίκληρον ἣ μέλλει καθευδήσειν"</note>
*Let the heiress sleep on both ears, since she is well-endowed.* For so someone or other translated it.

->**On the right ear.**<- XX

Pliny used *On the right ear* in the same sense. For he writes thus to his friend Romanus: *It is not for nothing that you sleep on your right ear in confidence of me; idleness does not go unpunished.* That is, there is no reason for you to be so secure. For doctors advise that in our first sleep, which is usually the deepest, we should lie on the right ear; when we wake and wish to fall back asleep, we should lie on the left. Furthermore, he who wishes to have a light sleep lies on neither ear, so that he may wake more easily.

->**To sleep with feet stretched out.**<- XXI

Akin to this is the saying <note>original: "ἀρτάναντα τὰ πόδε καθεύδειν"</note>, that is, *To sleep with feet stretched out.* Lucian in *On Salaried Posts*: *And when at last fortune allows you to sleep with feet stretched out.* That is, now at last that which is usually desired has happened, so that you may sleep with feet extended. To the same figure belongs what Mercury said in Aristophanes’ *Plutus*: <note>original: "ἀναβάδην ἀναπαύομαι"</note>, that is, *I rest with my feet up, and flat on my back at leisure.* We also use this to signify "supineness," negligence, and thoughtlessness. And *To join hands* <note>to fold hands</note> in the proverbs of the Hebrews refers to the lazy man,

<meta>catchword: lazy man,</meta>
P.

# EIGHTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>Z 3</sig>

<margin>XXII</margin>
->To hang from the nose.<-

"To hang from the nose" <note>original: *Naso suspendere*</note> means to mock someone in a clever and subtle way. Pliny, in Book 11, Chapter 32, teaches that the nose was dedicated to subtle mockery by the ancients. Indeed, nothing of this sort is read among the oldest authors. I will subscribe the words of Pliny: "And the nose is higher only in man, which they have dedicated in new ways to subtle mockery." Horace in his *Satires*:
"You hang [them] from your hooked nose." | The same author elsewhere:
"Balatro, hanging everything from his nose." | Persius says of Horace, who mocks cleverly and covertly:
"Pale with a wiped nose, to hang the people." | The same author elsewhere:
From which they are called "Nosey" <note>original: *Nasuti*</note> who know how to mock others learnedly. | Martial:
"It is not given to everyone to have a nose." | The same:
"Even boys have the nose of a rhinoceros." | The same again:
"Be as nosey as you like, be a nose indeed." | Persius:
"You laugh," he says, "and indulge too much in hooked
nostrils."
The Greeks express this with a simple verb, <term>mykterizein</term> <note>original: μυκτηρίζειν</note>, <term>antimykterizein</term> <note>original: ἀντιμυκτηρίζειν</note>, that is, to mock, or to mock in turn, from <term>mykteros</term> <note>original: μυκτῆρος</note>, which means "from the nose." Cassius to Cicero, in the fifteenth book of the *Letters to Friends*: "And those whom you have hurt with a ridiculous or sarcastic remark, they want, in a rustic way, with a sword, to <term>mock in turn</term> <note>original: ἀντιμυκτηρίζειν</note>," that is, to hang from the nose in return.

<margin>XXIII</margin>
->Worthy of playing 'fingers' with in the dark.<-

When someone was of the most certain loyalty, they used to say he was worthy of "flashing fingers" <note>original: *micaretur*</note> with in the dark. Cicero in the third book of *On Duties*: "Is it not shameful for philosophers to doubt what even peasants do not doubt? From whom was born that proverb worn smooth by age. For when they praise someone's loyalty and goodness, they say he is worthy of flashing fingers with in the dark." The same in the second book of *On Ends*: "Why is justice praised? Is that proverb worn smooth by age true, 'one with whom you flash fingers in the dark'?" Now, "flashing" <note>original: *micare*</note> is a kind of game which still lasts among the Italians <note>The game of Morra, where players suddenly extend fingers and guess the total number</note>, where both contestants suddenly guess the number of extended fingers. Cicero makes mention of this in the second book *On Divination*: "For what is luck? Almost the same as flashing fingers, as throwing the knucklebones, or the dice." Marcus Varro: "I must flash fingers with the Greek, whether I follow his number first, or he mine." Nemesianus in a Bucolic poem: "Toss your flashing fingers." Saint Augustine mentions it in the eighth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter five: "For that," he says, "we have easily when we wish, to omit other things, even by flashing three fingers." Furthermore, he with whom you flash fingers in the dark is free to cheat if he wishes. Therefore, he is said to be "worthy of flashing fingers in the dark" who is of such certain faith that even if he could do so safely, he would not wish to deceive anyone with a lie. The Greeks have something similar: "This man is worthy of trust even if he has sworn an oath": <term>The omen is worthy of the vote and of faith</term> <note>original: ὁ δ' οἰωνὸς ψήφου καὶ πίσθεως ἄξιος</note>, that is, "This man is worthy of being believed even without an oath." The opposite of which is: "I would not believe him even if he had sworn."

<margin>XXIIII</margin>
->A witness from Jove's tablets.<-

<term>A witness from the tablets of Zeus</term> <note>original: Ἐκ Διὸς δέλτων ὁ μάρτυς</note>. This was said among the Greeks for a most certain and indubitable witness. Lucian in the booklet *On Those Serving for Hire*: "If anyone calls you an adulterer or a pederast, he is immediately, according to the common saying, a witness from Jove's tablets." Allusion is made, if I am not mistaken, to the <term>diphthera</term> <note>a goatskin or parchment</note> in which Jupiter is imagined by the poets to describe all the acts of mortals.

<margin>XXV</margin>
->An Attic witness.<-

<term>An Attic witness</term> <note>original: Ἀττικὸς μάρτυς</note> is read in the collections of Diogenianus for a most proven and incorruptible witness. But if someone were to twist this through irony toward a vain witness, he would not have spoken inelegantly.

<margin>XXVI</margin>
->Attic faith.<-

<term>Attic faith</term> <note>original: Ἀττικὴ πίστις</note> is read in the same author, concerning those who are least vain and least perjured. It was thought that among the Athenians there was a temple constructed to the goddess Faith. Plautus also mentions her in *The Pot of Gold*. Velleius Paterculus mentions it in these words: "If anyone imputes to the Athenians this time of rebellion in which Athens was captured by Sulla, he is surely ignorant of truth and antiquity. For the faith of the Athenians toward the Romans was so certain that always, and in every matter, what-"

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to character and credibility, including the origins of "hanging from the nose" as a metaphor for mockery and the game of Morra as a test of honesty.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of proverbs related to "faith" or national character, following the discussion of "Attic faith" from the previous page.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

whatever he did with sincere loyalty, the Romans would proclaim it was done with "Attic faith." <note>original: "Attica fide"</note> Quintilian, in Book 12, Chapter "On the Styles of Speaking," writes in this manner: "I think that if those people found a more abundant soil or a more fertile crop within these borders, they would deny it was 'Attic,' because it returns more than it received in seed; for Menander mocks this 'faith' of that land." From these sources, we gather that "Attic faith" was a term used because they neither subtracted from nor added to their agreements. Such was the "faith" of a soil that was not particularly fertile, whereas the "faith" of fields is usually praised if they return what was entrusted to them with interest.

->Greek faith.<-
<margin>27</margin>
*Hellenike pistis* <note>original Greek: Ελληνικὴ πίστις</note>, that is, **Greek faith**, is likewise found to mean a certain or reliable faith. Perhaps it is the same as the previous entry, unless we prefer to take it ironically. Ausonius writes to Paulus:
> With us you will find "shared celebrations" <note>original Greek: κατηγοπάλια (katēgopalia) - likely referring to a festival or shared sport</note>, if you please to use
> Not Punic, but **Greek faith**.

The same author says of his bailiff Philo:
> He borrows on **Greek faith**.

<margin>q. 302</margin>
Plautus used the term **Greek faith** for a situation where business is conducted not with words or formal stipulations, but with cash in hand. For thus the madam Clareta speaks in his play *Asinaria*: "Daylight, water, sun, moon, night—these I do not buy with silver; but everything else we wish to use, we purchase with **Greek faith**." That is, with ready money. Euripides says in *Iphigenia in Tauris*: "Greek faith is nowhere to be found" <note>original Greek: πίστις Ἑλλὰς οὐδαμοῦ</note>. Indeed, on this account, that nation had a very bad reputation in ancient times.

->Punic faith.<-
<margin>28</margin>
The treachery of the Carthaginians <note>The Romans called the Carthaginians "Poeni," hence "Punic."</note> passed into a proverb, because that race was particularly noted for perjury and vanity, as Titus Livius abundantly testifies. These are his words in the second book on the Punic War: "What faith was kept by Hannibal with Punic sanctity." Likewise in the first book of the Second Punic War: "Great vices equaled these great virtues of the man: inhuman cruelty, treachery more than **Punic**, nothing of truth, nothing of the sacred, no fear of God, no oath, no religion." With these colors he paints Hannibal. Quintus Curtius suggests the same regarding the Tyrians when they were abandoned by Punic aid. Again, Maximinus says in Julius Capitolinus: "The Africans," he says, "exhibited **Punic faith**." And there is what we just cited from Ausonius: "**Punic faith**." Sallust in the *Jugurthine War*: "I find that Bocchus, more with **Punic faith** than for the reasons he was professing, held both the Romans and the Numidian in suspense with the hope of peace." Plautus says: "No Carthaginian is more Punic than I," alluding to their treacherous character. The Carthaginians were always considered treaty-breakers. The same author says in *The Little Carthaginian*: "And he knows all languages, but he knowingly pretends he does not; he is clearly a Carthaginian, what more need be said?"

->In one hand he carries a stone, in the other he offers bread.<-
<margin>29</margin>
Those who flatter to one's face while slandering in secret, who act as friends openly but harm privately—or those who help in one place but hurt in another, showing a false hope of benefit so that they may utterly destroy when the opportunity arises—these are said to **carry a stone in one hand and offer bread in the other**. This is transferred from those who entice dogs by showing them bread, and then strike them with a stone when they approach. Euclio in Plautus’s *Aulularia* says:
> Now he seeks me out while he makes promises; he gapes for my gold to devour it.
> **In one hand he carries a stone, while the other shows bread.**

Saint Jerome writes to Rufinus: "I preferred to expostulate these things with you as a friend, rather than to rage publicly when provoked, so that you might realize I cultivate reconciled friendships purely, and not according to the Plautine sentiment of **holding a stone in one hand and offering bread with the other**." He elegantly alluded to the same thing when writing to the same Rufinus: "Do we not give you bread for the reason that we strike the brains of heretics with a stone?" Gregory the Theologian has something similar in a letter to Bishop Eusebius of Caesarea: "Just as if someone were to stroke a man's head with one hand, and strike his cheek with the other" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς τῇ μὲν χειρὶ καταψήχοι τὴν κεφαλὴν, τῇ δὲ παίοι τὴν παρειάν</note>.

->To blow hot and cold from the same mouth.<-
<margin>30</margin>
"To bring forth the hot and the cold from the same mouth" <note>original Greek: Ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ στόματος τὸ θερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρὸν ἐξάγειν</note>. Double-tongued people, and those who now praise and now vilify the same person, are said to **breathe hot and cold from the same mouth**. This was born from a certain fable by the storyteller Annianus <note>Erasmus refers to a version of Aesop's Fables</note>. A certain Satyr, when he was shivering violently in a winter frost that was raging beyond measure, was led into a house by a certain countryman. He marveled why the man blew into his hands held up to his mouth, and asked why he did so. The man replied that he did it so the warmth of his breath might heat his cold hands. Later, when the hearth was built and the table set, and the man blew again into his boiling porridge, the Satyr marveled even more and inquired what this meant. "So that," the man said, "my breath might [cool] the porridge which is too hot..."

<summary>Erasmus discusses proverbs concerning national stereotypes of honesty (Greek and Punic faith) and metaphors for hypocrisy, such as offering bread while hiding a stone or blowing hot and cold.</summary>
<keywords>Attic faith, Greek faith, Punic faith, Hannibal, hypocrisy, Aesop's Fables, Plautus, Saint Jerome, double-tongued</keywords>

# EIGHTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

<note>Erasmus is recounting a fable about a Satyr and a traveler.</note> Then the Satyr, rising from the table, said: "What is this I hear? Do you blow both hot and cold from the same mouth? Farewell, for I have no reason to share a lodging with a man of that sort." Aristotle provides the cause for this phenomenon, which the Satyr wondered at, in his *Problems*, Section 34, problem seven. He thinks it happens because when one blows more forcefully, he does not move the air as a whole, but exhales through a more contracted mouth, so that the heat coming from the mouth is immediately vanished by the rest of the air (which is moved greatly by the force of the breath) and turns into cold. This is different for one who exhales with open jaws. There is something close to this in the epistle of the apostle James, for there we read: <margin>James 3</margin> "Out of the same mouth proceedeth sweet and bitter." <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ στόματος βρύει τὸ γλυκὺ καὶ τὸ πικρόν</note> To this can be added what Pliny reports in his second book, something more than miraculous: that there is a certain spring in Dodona which, though it is extremely cold and extinguishes torches if one plunges them in while burning, will ignite them if they are brought near after being extinguished. All these things can be twisted to apply to rhetoricians, who know how to praise and blame, to diminish and to exalt the same thing. Likewise to lawyers, who now defend and now attack the same cause. Plutarch twists it to this sense: that Circe, with the same wand, takes away the mind and restores it; she makes beasts and she makes men. There exists among the Greeks this proverbial six-foot verse:
*To praise and blame the same man is the mark of a wicked person.* <note>original Greek: αὐτὸν αἰνεῖν καὶ ψέγειν, ἀνδρὸς κακοῦ</note>

<margin>Isaiah 5</margin>
The Hebrew prophet, namely Isaiah, bodes ill for those who call good evil and evil good, sweet bitter and bitter sweet. Athenaeus in his fourth book teaches that there is a type of flute called by the Greeks a *magadis* <term>magadis: an ancient stringed instrument or flute capable of playing in octaves</term>, or an "old magadis," which yields both a deep and a high-pitched voice at the same time. From this he brings a verse from Alexandrides:
*I shall speak with a great magadis, small and great at the same time.*
In Greek it is called *magadizing* <note>original: μαγαδίζειν</note> to sound two voices at once, the deep and the high, "through all" <note>original: διὰ πασῶν, referring to an octave</note> as the musicians say. <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle, in the nineteenth section, problem eighteen according to the Greek codices (seventeenth according to Theodore’s version), uses this word *magadizing*, asking why this harmony I mentioned sounds on the magadis. Again in problem 39, according to the Greek codices: *They magadize in the harmony of the octave.*

### Hands with eyes: XXXI

<margin>Plautus in the Asinaria</margin>
Plautus spoke of "hands with eyes" <note>Latin: oculatas manus</note> regarding those who want promised things to be shown, not just promised in speech; they have eyes with which to see what is produced, but no ears with which to hear promises. Thus a certain madam in the *Asinaria*, when a young man was promising mountains of gold and she was not moved by the promises, said: "Our hands always have eyes; they believe what they see." The Terentian pimp Sannio was of the same opinion: "I was never so foolish," he said, "that I would not rather take away whatever I could in the present." Chaerea alluded to this in the *Eunuch*: "Now make your promises appear."

### A blind day, and a day with eyes. XXXII

<margin>Plautus in the Pseudolus</margin>
Plautus likewise used "blind day" and "day with eyes" for a day on which ready money is not counted out, and one on which it is. For thus a certain pimp speaks in the *Pseudolus*: "By Hercules, buy oil on a blind day, and sell it on a day with eyes; now by Hercules, even ready minae <term>minae: ancient units of currency</term> can be made from the profit." That is, buy when money is not present but on a deferred date, and resell when the money is present. Legal experts also call a "blind day" and "blind testimonies" those which are offered in writing by those who are absent. For "blind" refers not only to those who do not see, but to those who are not seen and are absent.

### To chew mastic. XXXIII

"To chew or gnaw mastic" <note>original Greek: σχίνον τρώγειν</note> is a Greek proverb said of those who are excessively devoted to the care of the body. For a dentifrice is usually made from the mastic tree. It is a certain powder prepared for whitening the teeth. Toothpicks were also made from mastic; that is, certain points suited for cleaning the teeth. Martial in his *Apophoreta*: <margin>Martial</margin>
*Mastic is better, but if a leafy point is lacking to you, a quill can relieve your teeth.*
Indeed, Dioscorides in his first book indicates that <margin>Dioscorides</margin> the juice of mastic boiled in water fixes loose teeth if they are rinsed with it; and also that the points made from it are useful for wiping the teeth if rubbed against them. Therefore, those of this sort who always have a toothpick in their mouth are said to "gnaw mastic," and are called "mastic-gnawers." <note>original Greek: σχινοτρώγαι</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs regarding inconsistency (blowing hot and cold), the preference for immediate payment over promises (hands with eyes), and vanity or excessive grooming (chewing mastic).</summary>
<keywords>Satyr, Aristotle, James the Apostle, Plautus, magadis, debt, toothpicks, mastic, ancient hygiene, rhetoric</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

they are called "gnawers." For care of the teeth was once considered a mark of shame among the refined, and Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century Roman writer and philosopher</note> was charged, among other crimes, with having prepared a tooth-powder. The adage may be rightly transferred to the rest of one's bodily grooming.

### To scratch the head with a single finger. XXXIIII

The soft and effeminate are said to scratch their head with one finger, clearly anxious lest they disturb a carefully arranged hairstyle. They think this was first said by the poet Calvus against Pompey <note>Pompey the Great, the Roman general; Calvus mocked his vanity</note>, and from there it was transferred to all who are insufficiently manly. Juvenal in his ninth satire says:
*Those who scratch their head with one finger.*
You recognize the soft and unchaste from their gestures. Furthermore, Seneca testifies in his letters that this gesture was anciently considered a sign of impurity: "There are," he says, "indications of all things, if they are observed. And one may take evidence of character even from the smallest things. The unchaste man is revealed by his gait, the movement of his hand, sometimes a single answer, the finger brought to the head, and the shifting of the eyes. Likewise, laughter reveals the wicked, and the face and habit demonstrate the insane."

### To scratch the head with the tip of the finger. XXXV

*To scratch the head with the tip of the finger.* <note>original Greek: Τὸ ἄκρῳ δακτύλῳ τὴν κεφαλὴν κνᾶν</note> This is the same as the previous one. Lucian, in *The Professor of Rhetoric*, describes a man softened by luxuries in these words: "If you should happen upon a certain all-wise and all-beautiful man, with a wobbling gait, a bent neck, a womanly gaze, a honeyed voice, smelling of perfume, scratching his head with the tip of his finger." <note>original Greek: Εἰ τύχοις δὲ πάνσοφόν τινα... κνώμενον</note> That is: "Among these, however, a man remarkably wise and of distinguished form, with a slippery gait, a broken neck, a womanly appearance, a voice like honey, smelling of ointments, scratching his head with the tip of his finger."

### A Phrygian is improved by blows. XXXVI

*A Phrygian is improved by blows.* This is said of barbarians and men of a slavish disposition, who are made better not by shame or warnings, but by beatings. Whereas, on the contrary, a noble mind, as Seneca says, is more rightly led than dragged. Cicero, in his speech *For Lucius Flaccus* regarding Asiatic witnesses, says: "Your Asia consists of Phrygia, Mysia, Caria, and Lydia. Is it our proverb, then, or yours? That a Phrygian is usually made better by blows." The adage is recorded in Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> in a trochaic verse:
*A Phrygian man, when beaten, is better and more serviceable.* <note>original Greek: Φρὺξ ἀνὴρ πληγεὶς ἀμείνων καὶ διακονέστερος</note>
Athenaeus shows that the most highly praised slaves were usually sent from Phrygia:
*Slaves from Phrygia, but from Arcadia, auxiliaries.* <note>original Greek: Ἀνδράποδ’ ἐκ φρυγίας, ἀπ’ δὲ ἀρκαδίας ἐπικούρους</note>

### You are nothing sacred. XXXVII

*You are nothing sacred.* <note>original Greek: Οὐδὲν ἱερὸν ὑπάρχεις</note> This is the speech of one expressing contempt, used proverbially. Indeed, the Greeks called whatever they wished to seem excellent and powerfully conducive "sacred," such as "sacred counsel" <note>original Greek: ἱερὰ βουλή</note> for a holy matter of advice, and Aristides called a "sacred city" <note>original Greek: ἱερὰν πόλιν</note> one that was the protector of all; and as we have cited in another place, the "sacred anchor" <note>original Greek: ἱερὰν ἄγκυραν</note>. Plutarch, in the *Life of Pelopidas*, mentions a "sacred band." Theocritus in *The Wayfarers*:
*But if you wish to wager a kid, though it is nothing sacred.* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἄν ἄικα λῇς ἔριφον θέμεν, ὤιτι μὲν οὐδὲν ἱερόν</note>
These are the words of one scorning a pledge. Those who pass down the origin of the proverb say that Hercules, upon seeing an image of Adonis, looked down on it with these words: "You are nothing sacred." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν ἱερόν εἶ</note> Either because he thought the honor of divinity should be held only by those who had deserved well of the mortal race, or because thieves who fled into his temple were not safe due to the religious sanctity of the place, as they were in the shrines of other gods. Now it is applied to any matter held in contempt. The notes of the commentator on Theocritus do not differ from this interpretation, citing Cleandrus as the author of this meeting.

### Nothing healthy. XXXVIII

The Greeks signify the greatest corruption of morals and no respect for honesty with these words: *Nothing healthy.* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν ὑγιές</note> Examples are met with everywhere in the comedies and tragedies of the Greeks. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
*We shall know if he does not change his ways, that he is a rogue, unjust, and nothing healthy.* <note>original Greek: Γνωσόμεθα δ’ ἢν μὴ μεταβάλλοντα... ὑγιὲς μηδέν</note>

He uses classical anecdotes involving figures like Hercules and Pompey to illustrate how physical gestures and cultural origins were used to judge character.</summary>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 8

<margin>If I thought this very thing were advantageous. <note>original Greek: εἰ δέω τόδ' αὐτὸ νομίσας ξυμφέρειν</note></margin> That is, they think it would be expedient to act contrary to established institutions and ancient customs; since he was deceitful, there was **nothing healthy** <note>The phrase "nothing healthy" (nihil sani) is a common idiom for total moral corruption or lack of integrity.</note> in him that would lead to the advantages of his own life. Andromache, in the tragedy named after her by Euripides, describes the character of the Spartans thus:

<margin>O inhabitants of Sparta, most hated of mortals by all men, councils of deceit, masters of lies, weavers of evils, twisted and **nothing healthy**. <note>original Greek: Ὦ πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποισιν ἔχθιστοι βροτῶν...</note></margin> That is: O you, most hated of all mortals, dwelling in Sparta, of fraudulent counsel, princes of lies, and makers of evils, winding, **nothing healthy**.

Aristophanes, in *The Women at the Thesmophoria* (if the title does not deceive): concerning women,

<margin>Wine-bibbers, traitresses, chatterboxes, **nothing healthy**, a great evil to men. <note>original Greek: οἰνοπώτιδας, τὰς προδότιδας...</note></margin> That is: Wine-drinkers, traitresses, talkative women, nothing healthy, the greatest evil to husbands.

Where he clearly used "**nothing healthy**" proverbially for those who are utterly depraved. Marcus Tullius Cicero to Atticus in the fifteenth book: "What more do you ask? **Nothing healthy**." Interpreting this, as it were, in the letter which preceded it: "What more do you ask? Nothing sincere."

### 39. Dion’s "gry"

<margin>Dion’s gry. <note>original Greek: Δίωνος γρύ</note></margin> That is, Dion’s "gry" <note>A "gry" (γρύ) was a tiny Greek unit of measure, used idiomatically to mean "the slightest sound" or "a scrap."</note>. It is rightly said either when we despise someone with great spirit and do not even deem them worthy of a response, or when we signify a thing of no value. We have spoken of "gry" in another place. The adage arose from an event. Dion of Alexandria was a man of the highest praise in philosophy. He had a brother who was a wrestler named Tophius. Thus, when one of his brother's competitors attacked Dion with insults, vomiting out things speakable and unspeakable against him—while a great crowd, as usually happens, flocked to the shouting—Dion did not respond to the curses with even a word, clearly mindful of the dogmas of philosophy. However, when he was already within the vestibule of his own house (for the abuser had followed him that far), showing no sign of anger, he responded only this: "**Not even a gry**," that is, "Not even a grunt." The young man, unable to control his mind, strangled himself with a noose. That matter passed into a common story.

### 40. A blind leader to the blind

<margin>A blind man as a leader to a blind man. <note>original Greek: Τυφλὸς τυφλῷ ὁδηγός</note></margin> That is, a blind leader to the blind. An adage also celebrated in the Gospel writings, which I record here all the more gladly. It may be used whenever an unlearned man attempts to teach the unlearned, or an ill-advised man attempts to give counsel to the imprudent. Marcus Tullius Cicero alluded to the proverb in the last book of *On Ends*: "Moreover, we have heard that the house of Drusus used to be filled with consulters; when those whose business it was could not see for themselves, they applied to a blind leader." Thus Cicero. For Drusus, though completely deprived of his eyesight, looked out for others with his mind, though he perceived nothing with the eyes of his body. To this fits that line of Horace: "A blind man shows the way." Horace to Scaeva:

> As if a blind man should show the way; yet, look.

Indeed, Porphyrion <note>A 3rd-century scholar and commentator on Horace.</note> thinks this was said just as if you were to say: "A pig teaching Minerva" <note>A proverb for a fool trying to teach a wise person.</note>. For a matter is conducted preposterously when a blind man tries to point out the way to those who can see. In Aristophanes' *Plutus*, the slave Carion is annoyed with his master because he, though seeing, followed Plutus, who was blind:

<margin>He follows behind a blind man, doing the opposite of what he ought to do. For we who see lead the blind, but this man follows, and forces me to do the same. <note>original Greek: ἀκολουθεῖ κατόπιν ἀνθρώπῳ τυφλῷ...</note></margin> That is: He follows a little man who is captured and bereaved of sight, following from behind, acting preposterously. For we who see lead the blind: but this man follows us, and at the same time forces me to do the same.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### Blind speculation. XLI

*Alasskopia* <note>original: Αλασσκοπιὰ</note>, that is, **Blind speculation**, is a compound word among the Greeks, from *laein*, which is "to see," whence *alaos* "blind," and *skopein*, that is, "to look into." So Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note> notes, citing Homer. The *Etymologicum* <note>A Greek grammatical and etymological dictionary</note> adds other conjectures, citing the same saying from Methodius. Suidas warns that the word is proverbial whenever those to whom a business has been entrusted turn a blind eye, or those delegated to keep watch see nothing at all. It is a metaphor taken from those who, from high watchtowers, diligently look around in every direction and report what they have seen to others. Homer uses this several times: "He did not keep a blind watch" <note>original: οὐ δ' ἀλασσκοπιὴν εἶχε</note>, which the *Etymologicum* cites from Methodius. This stands for: "he watched by no means blindly." It will be appropriately used whenever we wish to indicate that someone has sagaciously scented out and caught onto a matter. For instance, if you were to say that bishops, who are otherwise supine and blind to everything else, "keep no blind watch" if something arises from which a bit of profit is hoped for. Or conversely, if someone was mistaken or hallucinating, you might say "he kept this blind watch."

### You will swim without corks. XLII

Those are said to **swim without corks** who, by reason of their age, no longer need a guardian of their morals, or who have advanced so far in learning that they no longer require the help of teachers. Horace says:
> As soon as age has strengthened
> Your limbs and mind, you will swim without corks.

That is: without a guardian or tutor, you will rule and moderate yourself. Acron <note>A 2nd-century commentator on Horace</note> notes this is a proverb; he thinks the metaphor is borrowed from youths who, when they first learn to swim, swim with bark or corks bound under their bellies; then, becoming more practiced, they begin to swim without such supports. Plautus in the *Aulularia*: "Like boys learning to swim, a wicker frame is put on them. So they labor less, swim more easily, and move their hands." Among the Greeks it is *phellos* <note>original: φελλὸς</note>, for it is written variously, which the Latins translate as *suber* (cork), for so Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza, a 15th-century Greek scholar</note> translates it. It is the bark of a tree that is always buoyant, and for that reason suitable for ships, especially for anchors (for it indicates the location of the anchor so that sailors may be careful) and for the drag-nets of fishermen: for it supports the top ropes of the nets. It is also useful for the stoppers of jars, and finally for the footwear of women in the winter months—whence, by a proverbial joke among the Greeks, they are called "tree-barks": now men are not ashamed to use such footwear in the summer months. Pliny mentions this in Book 27, Chapter 8. Lucian in his *True Histories* tells of the "Cork-feet" <note>original: φελλοπόδας</note>, whence the Greeks use the term *phelloneps* to mean "to float on top." And *phellos* refers to places where a little earth covers the rocks.

### As we can, since we may not as we would. XLIII

"For we live not as we wish, but as we can" <note>original: Ζῶμεν γὰρ οὐκ ὡς θέλομεν, ἀλλ' ὡς δυνάμεθα</note>. That is:
**We live not as we please, but as we are permitted.**
A proverbial six-foot verse <note>term: Senarius - a line of verse consisting of six feet, common in Latin comedy</note>, by which we are warned that we must serve time and necessity. Terence’s Mysis in the *Andria*, when asked what kind of life they led at Athens, modestly confessing the gain of a prostitute, says: "As we can, they say, since we may not as we would." Caecilius in the *Plotius*, according to Donatus: "Live as you can, since you cannot as you wish." Likewise Plato in the *Greater Hippias*: "Our affairs, Hippias, are not such as one would wish (as people say in the proverb every time), but such as they can be." He alluded to the same in the *Cratylus*: "As we are able, by laboring." For thus those who undertake some business speak for the sake of modesty. To this also belong those Greek sentiments:
> We would all be very rich, but we cannot. And,
> We all wish to live well, but we cannot.

No one is satisfied with his own fortune, and everyone destines something else in his prayers, which, however, I know not if anyone has ever attained. It will be used when we indicate that our own things please us too little, but that the ability is lacking, not the will: namely, that fortune is not very favorable, or life not sufficiently blameless, or a letter not sufficiently learned.

### The ill-advised rashness of the Athenians. XLIIII

*He ton Athenaion dysboulia* <note>original: Ἡ τῶν ἀθηναίων δυσβουλία</note>. That is, **The ill-advised rashness of the Athenians**. It applies to those for whom badly-counseled plans turn out well. For this was once commonly attributed to the Athenians: that they themselves indeed consulted sluggishly and looked forward too little, but Minerva, the presiding deity of the city, [corrected] that...

<meta>catchword: fes, illo (that...)</meta>
