# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 8

<margin>The customs of the Athenians:</margin>
The forum <note>The public marketplace and site of political assembly</note> has a habit of turning poorly planned initiatives into good outcomes. This is similar to what is commonly said today: "He is luckier than he is wise," referring to someone who succeeds not through their own industry, but through the convenience of fortune. Eupolis, quoted in Suidas and Athenaeus (Book 10), says regarding the customs of the Athenians:
<margin>O city, city, how much more fortunate you are than you are wise. <note>original Greek: Ὦ πόλις πόλις ὡς εὐτυχὴς εἶ μᾶλλον ἢ καλῶς φρονεῖς.</note></margin>
That is:
> Formerly we saw no one put in charge of a banquet
> until he had earned it; now, it seems, we see
> generals appointed so. O city, city,
> how much more blessed you are than you are wise.

Aristophanes also notes this Athenian thoughtlessness in this verse from *The Clouds*:
<margin>For they say that poor judgment is an inherent trait of this city. <note>original Greek: Φασὶ γὰρ δυσβουλίαν τῇδε τῇ πόλει προσεῖναι.</note></margin>
That is:
> They say and report that foolish counsels attend this city.

In the same passage, a commentator adds a fable of this sort: When Neptune <note>Poseidon</note> was defeated by Minerva <note>Athena</note> and could not gain control of the Attic region, in his anger he sent upon them "dysboulia" <term>dysboulia: ill-counsel or chronic bad decision-making</term>. However, this vice became "epichorion" <term>epichorion: a local or vernacular trait</term> among the Athenians. Minerva then modified it: whatever they had decided poorly, she would turn toward a good result. Aristophanes alluded to this same idea in *The Wasps*:
<margin>For our counsel had already flown through the army before the fight. <note>original Greek: Ὡς γὰρ ἡμῶν πρὶν μάχεσθαι καὶ στρατὸν διέπτατο.</note></margin>
That is:
> Our plans had already fluttered through the troops before the battle.

Demosthenes seems to allude to this in no small way when he says in the *First Olynthiac*, right at the very beginning: "But I also suppose that by your good fortune, many necessary things might occur to some of you on the spot." <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ τῆς ὑμετέρας τύχης ὑπολαμβάνω...</note> That is: "But I also think it is part of your luck that it occurs to some to say the right thing at the right moment." Truly, he reproaches them for this vice more clearly in a certain oration, saying that while other men are accustomed to deliberate first and then act, the Athenians, on the contrary, deliberate only after the deed is done. Theognis writes:
<margin>To him who possesses a wretched mind but a favorable deity, even his evil deeds turn out for the good. <note>original Greek: Ὧι τινι χρῶνται δειλαῖες φρεσί...</note></margin>
That is:
> To him whose mind is clumsy, but whose gods are favorable,
> even that which he undertakes rashly turns out well.
Aristophanes says in *The Assemblywomen*:
<margin>There is an old saying among us elders, that whatever foolish things we have planned, it all turns out for our better interest. <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ τὶς ἡμῖν γεραιτέρων λόγος...</note></margin>
That is:
> There is a certain speech handed down from our ancestors,
> That though we may decide with folly and madness,
> Nevertheless, the outcome of all things yields to our benefit.
The middle of the Greek verse will be free of error if the conjunction is removed, as the Aldine edition had it. And in Livy, the "Fortune of Rome" is frequently mentioned, which is not far removed from what we related elsewhere: "The net catches for the sleeper." <note>original Greek: εὕδοντι κύρτος αἱρεῖ. A proverb meaning success can come even to the idle if they are lucky.</note>

### 45. When you are no longer who you were, there is no reason to wish to live.

Cicero, in a certain letter in Book 7 of his *Letters to Friends*, used the sentiment of this old proverb. "It is an old saying," he remarks, "that when you are no longer who you were, there is no reason to wish to live." This is derived from the feelings of mortal men, who think nothing is less tolerable than to live neglected and marked for shame among those with whom they once lived with splendor and authority. They would rather choose exile anywhere, or even depart from life, than endure the shame of changed fortune. Euripides noted this in *Hecuba*, whom he depicts speaking in such a way as to say that her shame prevents her from looking at Polymnestor. For she is ashamed, in such a calamitous state of affairs, to be seen by him to whom she once appeared flourishing. Likewise in *Alcestis*:
<margin>O friends, O children, I am no longer; I am nothing. Farewell, friends, may you look upon the light. Even to those who have fared badly. <note>original Greek: Ὦ φίλαι, ὦ παῖδες...</note></margin>
That is:
> O friends, why should I live
> Hearing such ill reports, and so badly afflicted?

Ajax says something to the same effect in Sophocles:
<margin>For what man desires a long life... <note>original Greek: Τίς γὰρ ἄνδρα τὸν μακρῷ χρήζει βίῳ</note></margin>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

"He is the worst who changes nothing." <note>original: "Κακίστον ὅς τις μηδὲν ἐξαλλάσσεται"</note> ->that is,<-
It is a foul thing to prolong life further
If one cannot disentangle oneself from one's own evils.

Likewise, a little later in the same tragedy <note>Sophocles, *Ajax*</note>,
"The noble man must either live honorably or die honorably." <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἢ καλῶς ζῆν, ἢ καλῶς τεθνηκέναι, τὸν εὐγενῆ χρή"</note> ->that is,<-
Truly it becomes a high-born man either to live
With dignity, or with dignity to meet his death.

This six-foot line <note>iambic senarius</note> is also circulated,
"Life is a disgrace to those for whom Fortune has begrudged a living." <note>original: "ζῶσιν αἰσχρὸν οἷς ζωὴ φθονήσεν ἡ τύχη"</note> ->that is,<-
For those whom harsh Fortune has envied the means to live,
For them to wish to live is unseemly and foul.

But that passage in Euripides’ *Hecuba* comes closer to Cicero’s sentiment, where Polyxena reasons that she has no cause to wish to live, because she has already been stripped of all the ornaments of her former fortune.
"For why should I live? To whom my father was king
Of all the Phrygians; this was my first life.
Then I was nurtured under fair hopes
As a bride for kings." <note>original: "τί γάρ με δεῖ ζῆν; ᾧ πατὴρ μὲν ἦν ἄναξ..."</note> ->that is,<-
For what cause for living now remains for me?
As one whose father was king of all the Phrygians.
Indeed, this was the beginning of my life in the light,
Then I was raised for great hopes, betrothed
To kings.

And the rest which follows. For they are too long for me to think they should be recounted here.

### To press the thumb, To turn the thumb. XLVI

In ancient times, there was a significance of favor and zeal in the thumb. He who favored someone would press the thumb down; he who favored less would turn the thumb. These gestures passed into a proverb, so that now he is said "to press with the thumb" who favors in any way, and "to turn" who wishes ill. Pliny, in Book 18, Chapter 2, says: "We are even commanded by a proverb to press our thumbs when we show favor." Juvenal says,
"With the thumb turned by the mob,
They kill anyone to please the crowd."

Horace used the phrase "With both thumbs" to mean with the highest favor:
"He who believes you agree with his own interests,
As a supporter, will praise your play with both thumbs."

Porphyrio <note>a 3rd-century commentator on Horace</note> explains it in this manner: "With both thumbs," that is, with both hands, by way of <term>synecdoche</term> <note>a figure of speech where a part represents the whole</note>. Or does he who praises more vehemently, joining his hands, join the thumb with the next finger? Acro <note>another Horace commentator</note> puts it this way: "With both thumbs" by synecdoche, meaning with both hands, both raised and moved repeatedly. For this is the gesture of those praising strongly. Certainly, as can be gathered from these, the origin of the proverb escapes both of them.

### To rub the face, Of a rubbed-raw brow. XLVII

The brow was held in antiquity to be sacred to shame. And the face likewise, which is also testified by the proverb in which they say, "Shame is in the eyes." Hence, those who have unlearned all shame are said by a proverb "to have rubbed the brow or the face," as if the shame were wiped away from the countenance by the hand. The metaphor appears to come from the gesture of certain people who, when about to say or do something among strangers, rub their face with their hand; this is a sign of a certain rustic bashfulness which you are trying to overcome. Quintilian notes this gesture among the faults of delivery in his eleventh book: "For those things are faulty," he says, "to stare at the ceiling, to rub the face, and as it were, to make it shameless." Plutarch writes that this gesture was peculiar to Marcus Tullius [Cicero], that when about to speak, he would stroke his face with his left hand. Otherwise, Cicero himself does not deny that he was rather trembling at the start of a speech. Calvus, cited by Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> in his ninth book, says: "Rub your brow, and say that you are more worthy to be made praetor than Cato." It signifies that saying this is vehemently shameless. Pliny in the preface to his *Natural History*: "I have rubbed my face, yet I have not succeeded, since you encounter me in another way in your greatness." Marcus Tullius, in the third book of *Tusculan Disputations*, said in the same sense, "To rub the mouth": "Why does Epicurus hesitate? And why do we not admit that we speak of that pleasure, which you yourself are accustomed to speak of when you have rubbed your mouth?" Seneca, in Book 5, Epistle 40: "You ought to rub your brow, and not listen to yourself."

...also relevant is the fact that we call the shameless "Brazen-faced" <note>original: *Effrontes*</note>. And we say: "With what forehead <note>meaning: with what nerve</note> do you dare to do these things?" For as Horace said:

Persius imitated this:

<note>This refers to removing the mask of modesty or shame.</note>
And that common expression: "With what mouth will you rebuke your son?" Also, "Impudent mouth," "hard mouth," "iron mouth," when we indicate shamelessness. Ovid says:

<note>Meaning: You aren't braver or wiser, you just have less shame.</note>

Again in *The Orator*: "What a mouth that patron has, who dares to approach such cases without any knowledge of the law." > Hippocrates asks me for honey-wine with the mouth of a man.
Homer’s Achilles calls Agamemnon <term>dog-faced</term> <note>original: *κυνῶπ᾿* (kunōp’)</note>, that is, having the look of a dog. And in the same author:

That is, having the eyes of a dog and the heart of a deer: signifying shamelessness joined with cowardice. I am not sure if the following from Athenaeus in the *Deipnosophists* (quoting the poet Chaeremon) belongs here:

That is, the gods grant better things to those who have wiped themselves three times. It indicates, unless I am mistaken, that he demands rather impudently to be told what was done at the banquet.

<margin>48</margin>
**To smooth the forehead; To wrinkle the forehead.**
We are said to "unfold the forehead" when we become cheerful, and to "contract" it when we snarl—that is, when we are annoyed. Pliny writes in Book 11: "The forehead is present in others, but in man alone it is the index of sadness, cheerfulness, clemency, and severity." Terence says: "Smooth your forehead." Horace in the *Odes*:
> ...they smoothed the worried forehead.
The same author elsewhere:
> ...[remove] the cloud from your brow.
"With a smoothed forehead" means cheerfully. "You ought to speak with me with a more smoothed forehead," in Plautus. Conversely: "with a drawn-back forehead," "with a wrinkled forehead," "with a contracted forehead," "with a shriveled forehead." Plautus: "Shriveled with severity." They claim this metaphor is taken from goat horns <note>original: *caprinis cornibus*</note>. Also: "A cloudy forehead," "a serene forehead," "an unfolded forehead."

<margin>49</margin>
**To raise the eyebrow; To lower the eyebrow.**
Pliny says: "The eyebrows are movable for man both together and alternately. And in them is a part of the mind. With them we deny, with them we grant. These especially indicate pride. Pride has its receptacle elsewhere, but here it has its seat: it is born in the heart, it rises here, it hangs here. Nothing is higher or more abrupt in the body where it might be solitary." So far Pliny. From this, we use the proverb "The eyebrow is raised" to signify arrogance; "the eyebrow is drawn down" to indicate disdain. Suidas also cites:
> <term>All of them with contracted eyebrows and puffed-out cheeks.</term> <note>original: *πάντες τὰς ὀφρῦς, καὶ τὰς γνάθους φυσῶντες*</note>
Which the Greeks say in a single word: <term>to be down-browed</term> <note>original: *κατωφρυᾶσθαι* (katōphryasthai)</note>. Lucian transferred this from a person to a thing, calling arrogant and haughty speech <term>down-browed words</term>. The eyebrow is said to be "laid down" when one retreats from pride. And we call haughty men "supercilious" <note>literally: "eyebrow-ish"</note>. Finally, "Eyebrow" itself is used metaphorically for pride and arrogance: "Who could bear the 'eyebrow' of the philosophers?" Furthermore, regarding what Pliny says about us nodding 'yes' or 'no' with our eyebrows, Homer is the source, in whom this verse is read several times:
> <term>He spoke, and the son of Cronus nodded with his dark eyebrows.</term> <note>original: *ἦ, καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ᾿ ὄφρυσι νευσε κρονίων*</note>
That is: He spoke, and the father nodded with his dark brows, and made all of Olympus tremble with his nod. Maro [Virgil] emulated this:

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on common Latin and Greek idioms, specifically focusing on metaphors for "turning a blind eye" and the medicinal/proverbial use of hellebore for madness.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

people commonly say: As parents **wink** at certain lighter faults of their children. And, Nature as it were **winks** at certain faults of youth. And husbands must **wink** at certain errors of their wives; and corrupt judges **wink** in a legal case. We "hallucinate" when we are imprudent, we "are blind" against our will, but we **wink** <note>Latin: *connivere*, to close the eyes or overlook</note> by deliberate effort. Examples are frequent in the legal speeches of Cicero. To "wink" is, moreover, to close the eyes repeatedly, just as those do who, because of weakness of sight, cannot bear the light of the sun, and thus they are easily deceived. On the contrary, those who <term>look intently</term> <note>original Greek: *atenes ephoran*</note>, that is, look with fixed eyes, nothing can escape them. What we call "winking," the Greeks call sometimes <term>blinking</term> <note>original Greek: *skardamyktein*</note>, sometimes <term>peering</term> <note>original Greek: *illopain*</note>. Whence is that line in Aristophanes’ *Knights*: <term>look at me without blinking</term> <note>original Greek: *blepson d’ em’ askardamyktos*</note>, that is, look at me un-winkingly, or not winking at all. What we call "to hallucinate," they call <term>to look askance</term> <note>original Greek: *parablepein*</note>; what we call "to be blind," they call <term>to be dim-sighted</term> <note>original Greek: *amblyottein*</note>. All of these, if they are transferred to matters of the mind, will pertain to the nature of proverbs.

### Drink hellebore.

Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: <term>drink hellebore</term> <note>original Greek: *pith’ elleboron*</note>. By this saying he signifies that someone is insane. He said <italic>pithi</italic> <note>drink (a dose)</note> indeed, not <italic>pine</italic> <note>drink (regularly)</note>: because, as the commentator advises, grammarians refer the latter to a simple drink, but the former to a potion of drugs. The same shows that the word <term>to need hellebore</term> <note>original Greek: *elleborian* or *elleborizesthai*</note> was coined from this to mean "to be mad." And those who are mentally unstable are said <term>to need hellebore</term> <note>original Greek: *elleborou deisthai*</note>. And these same people, even among Latin authors, are ordered by the proverb to "eat hellebore" and "purge themselves with hellebore," because in ancient times there was great use of this herb for relieving defects of the mind and head. Pliny, in the twenty-fifth book of his *Natural History*, chapter five, makes two kinds of hellebore, as does Dioscorides in his fourth book: White, which Italy calls *veratrum album*; and black, which others call *entomon*, even if we read *atomon* in Dioscorides. Others call it *polyrrhizon*, many call it *Melampodion*, from its discoverer Melampus the seer (or a shepherd of the same name), because he noticed that goats were purged by it; then, by giving their milk, he cured the raving daughters of Proetus. But Aulus Gellius, following Pliny, says the distinction of color appears not in the seed, nor in the twigs, but in the root. By the white, vomiting is induced, and by it he purges the stomach and upper belly. By the black, the lower bowel is flushed; the taking of either is dangerous, but as the white is more effective, so it is more dangerous. Yet this very practice began to be so common that many, for the sake of their studies, in order to perceive more sharply what they were meditating upon, took it quite often. Specifically, the Academic philosopher Carneades, when about to write against the books of the Stoic Zeno, is read to have been accustomed to purge the upper parts of his body with white hellebore, lest any corrupt humors in the stomach should overflow to the very dwellings of the soul and weaken the persistence and vigor of the mind. Pliny testifies that there was even a religious use for the black variety. For with this they even fumigated and purified houses, sprinkling both themselves and their cattle. Then it was gathered with a solemn prayer and quite superstitiously, as Theophrastus also mentions. For first it was circumscribed with a sword; then he who was about to cut it looked toward the rising sun and prayed that he might be allowed to do this by the gods' permission. He also watched for the flight of an eagle: if it flew closer, it was an omen that he who had cut it would die that year. From Pliny, therefore, one may gather that both kinds, both white and black, have an effective remedy not only for many other evils but also against melancholy. Whence the proverb was born, which is expressed in so many ways. Plautus in *The Menaechmi*: "This matter cannot be settled by three acres of hellebore." Demosthenes warns Aeschines in a legal action to purge himself with hellebore. Lucian in the *Dialogue of Menippus and Tantalus*: <term>You are talking nonsense, Tantalus, and truly you need a drink, by Jove, you seem to need pure hellebore</term> <note>original Greek: *lereis o tantale...*</note>. And in the same author, Rhadamanthus, in the second book of *True Histories*, pronounces that Ajax should drink the hellebore handed down by Hippocrates before he is received into the company of heroes, alluding to his madness. In the same place, one reads that Chrysippus was not allowed to migrate to the Island of the Blessed unless he had already taken hellebore for the fourth time. Doubtless, this alludes to the fact that he is recorded to have drunk it three times in his life, as Petronius also testifies in a certain poem. Horace:
> He expelled the disease and bile with pure hellebore.
Ovid in the *Letters from the Black Sea*, book 4:
> Go drink, I would have said, the juices that purge the breast,
> And whatever grows in all of Anticyra. <note>Anticyra was a Greek city famous for its hellebore.</note>
Persius:
> Better to gulp down pure Anticyras.
Signifying a madman. Ausonius to Theon:
> And may you drink hellebore, the sharpness of the Samian Lucumo.

# EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
A 2
<meta>catchword: Let him eat</meta>

### 52. Let him sail to Anticyra.

<margin>"Let him sail to Anticyra" <note>original: Πλεύσειεν εἰς ἀντικύρας</note>. Horace elegantly updated the face of this adage when he said in his *Satires*: "If anyone goes to Anticyra."</margin>
By these words, he signifies a Stoic madman, or anyone suffering from a disease of the mind who might be worthy of the name of "wisdom," since no one is truly wise unless they are sane. This is spoken with the same figure of speech by which the Greeks say, "You should sail to Massalia" <note>original: πλεῦσαι εἰς μασσαλίαν</note>. Strabo, in the ninth book of his *Geography*, points out two places named Anticyra: in one, located after the town of Crissa, hellebore grows; in the other of the same name, located near the Malian Gulf and Mount Oeta, it is prepared most excellently. People sail there from many regions for the sake of their health. Pausanias wrote in his final book that above Anticyra there are mountains that are extremely rocky; in these, hellebore grows. He notes that the black variety purges the bowels, while the white variety induces vomiting and purges the upper parts of the body. Stephanus adds that there was a certain man of Anticyra who freed Hercules from his madness by giving him hellebore. Horace writes:
> A head incurable by even three Anticyras
> He would never entrust to Licinus.

He said "three Anticyras" to represent a total supply of hellebore, signifying a hopeless and incurable madness. By a similar figure of speech, today people still order those who are considered of unsound mind to be "deported to Anticyra." To this same form belongs the saying, "He needs a barber," or "He has need of a guardian." Horace says:
> If you think you are full of wind and do not need a guardian.

For <term>tutors</term> <note>legal guardians for minors</note> were given to orphans, but <term>curators</term> <note>legal guardians for the incapacitated</note> were given to those captured by madness. Thus Columella writes in book one, chapter seven, that Cato used to say that a man who lived on a farm with neither healthy air nor fertile soil should be handed over to his kinsmen and clansmen as if he were of disturbed mind. Varro, in book 1, chapter 2 of *On Agriculture*, says: "He who neglects a healthy place is captured in mind and must be led away to his kinsmen and clansmen." Cicero, in book 2 of *On Invention*: "If a madman emerges, let the power over his goods and money belong to his kinsmen and clansmen." For the <term>Twelve Tables</term> <note>The foundation of Roman law</note> take away the administration of affairs from the mad and transfer it to the clansmen and kinsmen, just as we read in the first book of the *Institutes*, under the title "On Curators," and in the twenty-seventh book of the *Pandects*, the final title "On the Curator of a Madman." Again, in the first book of the same work, title eighteen, "On the Office of the Prefect of the City," and in Cicero’s third book of *Tusculan Disputations*: "The Twelve Tables forbid one who is so affected from being the master of his own affairs." The words of the Twelve Tables are these: "Let the administration of his own goods be forbidden to the spendthrift and the madman, and let them be under the care of their kinsmen."

### 53. He has drunk Strychnine.

<margin>"He has drunk strychnine" <note>original: Στρύχνον ἔπιεν</note>. This likewise applies to the insane, from the nature of the herb strychnine <note>nightshade</note>, which, if even tasted, immediately produces madness. Dioscorides, in his fourth book, identifies four kinds of strychnine. The last of these he calls "manic" <note>original: μανικόν</note>, that is, "insane." Pliny, in book twenty-one, chapter twenty-one, after demonstrating two healthy kinds of strychnine, says: "The third kind, its flowers and clusters, should be described with the least possible care. For we are treating remedies, not poisons." Even a small amount of its juice leads to this madness. However, Greek authors turned this into a joke, saying that by the weight of a <term>drachma</term> <note>a small Greek unit of weight</note>, a playful loss of shame is produced, showing that various sights and conspicuous images flit before the eyes. A double dose produces legitimate madness; if more is added to the weight, death is presented. This is the poison which the most innocent authors simply called *Dorycnion*, from the fact that spear-points in battles are dipped in it, as it grows everywhere. Dioscorides writes that the root of strychnine drunk with wine, in the measure of a drachma, produces certain visions and not unpleasant delusions; taken in a double dose, it induces a certain stupor; drunk in a quadruple dose, it takes away life. The remedy is to drink much honey-wine and vomit it back up. Whence it seems to me more fitting to apply this to "Self-Lovers" <note>original: Φιλάντους</note>, and those who, as Horace says, are "beautiful to themselves." For Theophrastus relates that those who have tasted strychnine seem to themselves to be most beautiful. We see many such men who cannot help but be pleased with themselves in every matter, just as if they lived on strychnine. There is a different kind of madness by which men are displeased with themselves in all things, but the former is more common and more incurable. Nor would I have stepped aside in this work—lest someone suspect that adages are not being collected by me but invented—except that Pliny, by saying the Greeks turned it into a joke, sufficiently indicated that the nature of this herb had passed into a proverb.</margin>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>54</margin>
### Eat nasturtium.

*Eat nasturtium* <note>original: "Ἔσθιε κάρδαμον" (Esthie kardamon)</note>. This was once said to a sluggish, lazy, dull, or stupid person, because it was believed that this plant possesses an efficacy opposite to that of the rocket plant <note>Eruca sativa, often associated with stimulating lust</note>. For it rouses the force and vigor of the mind and restrains Venus <note>sexual desire</note>, whereas the rocket, on the contrary, sharpens lust and dulls the power of the mind. Hence, the name among the Greeks seems to be *kardamon*, as if it were "heart-taming" <note>original: "κάρδαμον, quasi cor domans"</note>. Pliny says in Book 19, Chapter 8: "The nasturtium took its name from the torment of the nostrils <note>Latin: "narium tormento," a pun on "nasus" (nose) and "torquere" (to twist)</note>." And from this, the proverb used the word to signify vigor, as if it were something that rouses one from torpor. Among the Greeks, it takes its name from the heart. Dioscorides relates that the nasturtium has a power similar to the rocket and mustard regarding the sharpness that bursts into the nostrils. However, in saying that the nasturtium stimulates Venus, he disagrees with Pliny. Aristophanes in *Thesmophoriazusae* says: "Yesterday I ate nasturtiums. Why are you acting like a nasturtium?" <note>original: "ἔχθες ἔφαγον κάρδαμα. τί κάρδωμα;"</note>. The same author in *The Wasps*: "Of the sharp-tempered and the just, and those whose eyes look like nasturtiums" <note>meaning sharp or keen-eyed</note>.

<margin>55</margin>
### Sacrifice a pig.

I also think it should not be overlooked that Plautus, in the *Menaechmi*, orders a man whom he means to be out of his mind to sacrifice a "pure and sacred pig." "Young man, for how much do they sell sacred, pure pigs here? Here, take a coin from me. Order yourself to be purified at my expense: for I certainly know that you are insane." I believe this is because, by the custom of the ancients, one who was driven by the fits of some angry deity was accustomed to purge himself with this sacrificial offering. The same author a little later in the same play says: "For by Hercules, you are certainly not sane enough, Menaechmus, you who now curse yourself. If you were wise, you would order a little pig to be brought to you." Horace in his *Satires*: "Let him sacrifice a pig to the fair Lares" <note>household gods</note>. He speaks of one who would now seem to have recovered his senses from insanity.

<margin>56</margin>
### Many Syrian vegetables.

*Many Syrian vegetables* <note>original: "πολλὰ σύρων λάχανα" (polla syron lachana)</note>. This will be said either of those skilled in the magic arts who practice it with harmful herbs, or of those who abound in cheap things. Perhaps it might also be rightly said of those who spend too much labor on things of little fruit; namely, those occupied not in tilling fields but in tending gardens, which bring more pleasure than profit. The proverb is cited by Pliny in Book 20, Chapter 5, where, having mentioned various remedies of the *staphylinus* herb (which they also call the wild parsnip), he adds: "Syria is most industrious in gardens. From this also comes the proverb among the Greeks: *Many Syrian vegetables*." He plants a herb very similar to the *staphylinus*, which others call *gigidion*. Thus far Pliny. However, as for my thinking that the proverb could fit sorcerers, I am moved by the conjecture that he had a little earlier cited Orpheus as an authority that there is a love-charm in the *staphylinus*. Nor were the customs of the Syrians unknown to the common people, as that adage testifies: *Syrians against Phoenicians*. And in this proverb, Caelius Rhodiginus pities us for being so remarkably tormented, yet he himself does not provide any relief.

<margin>57</margin>
### A sword smeared with honey.

*A sword smeared with honey.* This was usually said of ruinous flattery. Saint Jerome to Aurelius Augustine: "Some of my friends, and vessels of Christ—of whom there is a very great abundance in Jerusalem and the holy places—suggested that this was not done by you with a simple mind, but that you were seeking praise and rumors and the petty glory of the people, so that you might grow at our expense; so that many might know that you challenge me and I fear you; that you write as a learned man and I keep silent as an unlearned one, and that at last someone has been found to put a limit to my talkativeness. But I, to speak simply, did not wish to respond to your dignity at first because I did not clearly believe the letter was yours, and—as the common proverb says of certain people—it was a *sword smeared with honey*." If this passage is free of error, Jerome calls Augustine's letter a sword smeared with honey because it contained both a rebuke (like a sword with which he might be slain) and flatteries (with which he might disguise the bitterness of the rebuke). Furthermore, Augustine, in responding, openly explains the proverb, namely by praying against and loathing treacherous smooth-talk. Pliny in Book 21 relates that in Heraclea in Pontus, the same bees sometimes produce honey containing a most ruinous poison. Those who eat it throw themselves on the ground seeking coolness, for they melt away in sweat. The cause of this is the fodder. It is a white herb which they call *aegolethron* <note>goat-bane</note>. This is an allusion to the barbaric custom of those who are used to dipping their weapons in poisons.

<summary>Erasmus explores four proverbs concerning physical and mental health, sacrificial customs, and the dangers of deceptive flattery, drawing heavily on Pliny, Plautus, and the correspondence between Jerome and Augustine.</summary>
<keywords>nasturtium, insanity, sacrifice, Syrian gardens, flattery, Jerome, Augustine, Pliny, ancient medicine, herbal lore</keywords>

# EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
A 3

the wound would be incurable: the most immediate evil was "incendiary oil" <note>original: *oleum incendiarium*, likely referring to Greek Fire or a similar naphtha-based weapon</note>, which, if it clung to the body, would burn tenaciously; the fire was only provoked by throwing water on it, and could only be smothered by sprinkling dust alone. The author is Marcellinus, Book 23.

---

->**Deadly Mead.**<-
<margin>58</margin>

<margin>Deadly honey-wine.</margin> *Deadly honey-wine* <note>original Greek: θανάσιμον μελίϰρατον</note>. That is, "Deadly Mead." This has the same meaning as the previous entry. Dion was accustomed to calling beautiful courtesans "deadly mead." Indeed, nothing prevents one from twisting this to refer to flattery or foul pleasures: in short, anything that is so pleasant that it is equally destructive. We also read of "Honeyed poison" in Pliny. And Diogenes used to call a speech designed for favor and the "itching of the ears" a "honeyed noose" <note>original Greek: μελιτίνω ἀγχόνη</note>, because it delighted with flattery but strangled the mind of the one who accepted it. This is clearly very similar to that phrase of Jerome’s, so much so that there might be a mistake in the manuscripts, and "noose" <note>Latin: *laqueum*</note> should be read instead of "sword" <note>Latin: *gladium*</note>. For who would want to smear a sword with honey? To this same pattern belongs what Irenaeus reports in Book 3, Chapter 19, regarding the bad mixing of gypsum: for gypsum is a present poison, and when added to milk, it deceives.

---

->**You are knitting flax to flax.**<-
<margin>59</margin>

<margin>You are joining flax to flax.</margin> *You are joining flax to flax* <note>original Greek: λίνον λίνω συνάπτεις</note>. That is, you connect flax to flax. I find a double meaning for this adage among the Greek interpreters. One is: you join weak things to weak things, trifles to trifles; for you do or say the same things for the same reasons. Ctesippus in Plato’s *Euthydemus* says: "You are certainly not joining flax to flax, as the proverb says, if your father is the father of all." This is irony directed at a sophist who seemed to have gathered this conclusion through frivolous subtleties. Aristotle, in the <margin>third book of the *Physics*.</margin> third book of the *Physics* <note>original Greek: τῆς φυσικῆς ἀϰροάσεως</note>, discussing the infinite, prefers the opinion of Parmenides over that of Melissus. For Melissus said the infinite itself was the "whole." But Parmenides said the "whole" was finite, equidistant from the center. For, he says, it cannot be that the infinite is joined to the entire universe, just as flax is joined to flax. I will subscribe the philosopher's own words, if perhaps they are required: <note>Erasmus provides the Greek text of Aristotle's Physics 207a, arguing that the "whole" and the "infinite" are not the same thing and cannot be simply tied together like pieces of string.</note> Suidas cites this adage from the *Polity* of Strattis. Proclus also, in discussing questions arising from the sayings of Plato, uses it in a certain place so that it seems to apply to one who joins together conflicting things, showing how Plato spoke against and in conflict with Homer: "For is it not 'joining flax to flax' to weave these things together?" This is related to what is cited from Athenaeus, Book 6, from a Theban poet—Pindar, if I am not mistaken: "Gluing wood to wood." For the former had spoken of parasites, and the one who takes up the discourse says something about flatterers that matches the previous point.

---

->**I grow old always learning many things.**<-
<margin>60</margin>

<margin>I grow old always being taught many things.</margin> *I grow old always being taught many things* <note>original Greek: γηράσϰω δ’ αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασϰόμενος</note>. That is:
> To the one constantly learning many things, old age comes.

This pentameter from the elegies of Solon <note>An Athenian statesman and poet</note> passed into a proverb; it signifies that wisdom is prepared by the experience of life and many things. It agrees with the sentiment cited in Gellius: "Experience begot me, Memory my mother bore me." It is cited by Plato in the 7th book of the *Republic*. Again in the dialogue *On Philosophy*, asking whether philosophy is "much-learning." What else, he says, is philosophizing than doing what Solon said? For he said,
> To the one constantly learning many things, old age comes.

It certainly seems that something must always be learned by him who would turn out to be a philosopher, whether young or old, so that he learns as much as possible in life. It is also cited in the *Laches*, and by Seneca in a certain letter to Lucilius: "One must learn as long as one is ignorant, and, if we believe the proverb, as long as one lives." It is cited once and again in Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in *Cato the Elder*. Furthermore, the famous Demea in Terence recounted Solon’s sentiment when he said: "No one has ever had a life's account so well calculated that circumstances, age, and experience did not always bring something new." It warns that those things you believe you know, you do not; and what you thought primary, you reject upon experience. There is a little verse, neither unskilled nor inelegant, celebrated under the name of Seneca, which alludes to this. But I suspect it is one of Publilius Syrus's, led by the conjecture that I do not yet find it in the number of those specifically referred to by Aulus Gellius under Publilius's title.
The verse is this: "The later day is the disciple of the prior day."

<keywords>Solon, Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Cicero, mead, logic, philosophy, lifelong learning, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### A life in a jar.
<margin>61</margin>

*Life of a jar* <note>original Greek: Ζωὴ πίθου</note>, that is, *A life in a jar*, is a proverb used to describe a frugal, meager life, removed from all noise and ambition. In short, it refers to the kind of life that the famous Cynic philosopher Diogenes is read to have led in Athens. He was content with a single cloak and a staff to drive away dogs, and he lived by choice in a large ceramic jar <note>often translated as a "tub," though it was a large earthenware storage vessel</note> suspended from a pole as his dwelling. He survived on raw herbs and plain water, using a hollowed-out piece of bread as a dish and his cupped hand as a cup. He used to claim he learned this from a boy he once happened to see scooping up water in that manner. Furthermore, he said the idea of living in a jar came to him after observing snails; he judged no other dwelling to be quite so convenient, as he could crawl out into the sun or hide away from the winds and heat. The comic poet Eubulus depicts them thus in the second book of Athenaeus: *With unwashed feet, sleeping on the ground, having their dwelling in the air* <note>original Greek: Ἀνιπτόποδες, χαμαιεῦναι, ἀέρες, ἀελοίνοιο</note>. Likewise, in the fourth book, regarding the Pythagoreans, quoting Antiphanes:

| | |
|---|---|
| *Fasting, filth, and cold must be endured a little,* | |
| *Silence, gloom, and the rigor of the frost,* | that is, |
| *And likewise a body that knows no bath.* | |

The name of the *Hamaxobii* <note>literally "wagon-dwellers"</note>—a people of Sarmatia—could be twisted into this same form, so that those who live harshly and filthily are called *Hamaxobii*. The name was given to this tribe because they use wagons in place of houses.

### To live for the day; To live for the moment.
<margin>62</margin>

*To live for the day* is to live content with present circumstances and what is at hand, not at all anxious about the future. This life is called by the Greeks a *daily life* <note>original Greek: καθημέριος βίος</note>, and those who live in that manner are called *day-livers* <note>καθημερόβιος</note>. Theocritus in Idyll 14:
*We are but mortals, and we do not look toward tomorrow.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ θνατοὶ πελόμεσθα, τὸ δ’ αὔριον οὐκ ἐσορῶμεν</note>

Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
*I shall supply you with plenty of barley and a daily living.* <note>original Greek: Κριθὰς ποιεῖν σοι, καὶ βίον καθ’ ἡμέραν</note>

Homer in the *Odyssey*, book 18:
*Rustic fools, thinking only of the things of the day.* <note>original Greek: Νήπιοι, ἀγροιῶται, ἐφημέρια φρονέοντες</note>

Persius:
*And you live for the moment.*
That is, without anxiety for the future. From this we also get the phrase *to speak extemporaneously*, that is, without premeditation. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fifth *Philippic*, used a similar form: *To live for the hour*. Hannibal did not do this, for he reserved many things for future use; but those who "lived for the hour" thought not only nothing of the fortunes and goods of the citizens, but not even of their own advantage. Not far removed from this sense is what Horace writes in *The Art of Poetry*: *And it changes by the hour*, that is, repeatedly. Christ approved of this life as the happiest of all, as he both followed it himself and proposed it to be followed by the apostles. Yet it is a wonder to say how much it is disapproved of today, even by those who demand to be seen as more than Christian.

### A softened life.
<margin>63</margin>

*A macerated life* <note>original Greek: Βίος μεμαλαγμένος</note>, that is, a life soaked or thoroughly softened. This refers to those living luxuriously, for whom everything is easily supplied. It is recorded by Diogenianus, Zenodotus, and Suidas. I believe the metaphor is taken from legumes or salted fish that have been soaked and are now more suitable for eating, or from wheat already milled, ground, and kneaded. The opposite of this is a *thorny life* <note>original Greek: Βίος ἀπαυθάδης</note>.

### The day itself is sometimes a mother, sometimes a stepmother.
<margin>64</margin>

This is a verse from Hesiod in his book *On the Observation of Days* <note>The Works and Days</note>, regarding auspicious and inauspicious days. It later became a proverb, approved by the long age of man, as the philosopher Favorinus records in Gellius. It is as follows:
*The day itself is sometimes a stepmother, sometimes a mother.* <note>original Greek: Ἄλλοτε μητρυιὴ πέλει ἡμέρη, ἄλλοτε μήτηρ</note>
By this verse, it is signified that things cannot go well every day, but well on one and poorly on another. The metaphor is drawn from the fact that mothers wish their children well, while stepmothers hate their stepchildren. Accordingly, Pliny says he doubts whether Nature is more often a stepmother or a mother, since she produces so many poisons and just as many remedies.

<meta>catchword: Now</meta>

# EIGHTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

<margin>65</margin>
### Now it rains, and now Jupiter shines in the clear sky.

Theocritus <note>Greek pastoral poet, c. 3rd century BCE</note> explained this matter through an inverted metaphor in the character of Battus:
*Sometimes the sky is clear, and sometimes it rains.* That is,
Now it rains, and now Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, often used metonymically for the sky or weather</note> shines in the clear sky.
Sometimes circumstances are adverse, sometimes they are favorable; just as the sky is now serene and calm, now turbulent and stormy. Akin to this is an allegory by Pindar <note>Greek lyric poet</note> in the Pythian Odes: that the same winds do not always blow, but now these, now others:
*But for a short time the blasts of high-flying winds.* That is,
But other blasts of winds flying on high.
And in the Isthmian Odes, Hymn 4: *But at different times a different wind, rushing upon all men, drives them.* That is,
But at other times another wind, blowing upon all, drives them.

---

<margin>66</margin>
### It has more aloes than honey.

*It has more aloes than honey.* This is a proverbial metaphor; you declare it just as if you were to say, "more trouble than pleasure." For the aloe is a certain shrub with a heavy scent and a very bitter taste, which Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> mentions in Book 3. Plautus <note>Roman comic playwright</note> says in *Amphitryon*: "Thus it is arranged for each in the life of men, thus it has pleased the gods, that sorrow follows as a companion to pleasures; indeed, that more inconvenience and evil is present, if any good has fallen to one's lot." In the same author, it is read elsewhere that "the life of man has more aloes than honey." And Juvenal <note>Roman satirist</note> says of a wife: "She has more aloes than honey."
Lucilianus expressed this without the metaphor in his *Floridi*: "But it is a true word indeed, that nothing has ever been given to men by the gods so prosperously, but that some difficulty was nevertheless mixed in." These turns of human affairs, and the mixture of sad and happy things, Homer indicated very elegantly in the last book of the *Iliad* through the fiction of the two jars which sit on the threshold of Jupiter, one of which is full of sorrows, the other of joys. Tempering the fortunes of mortals from these,
*To whom he gives a mixed life, he meets now with sorrows.* That is,
To whom he mixes life, the same man mixes it now with sorrows.
As we have also indicated above. Truly, the Homeric Jupiter tempers things quite spitefully, mixing in far too much of evils than of goods, so that if everyone were to count their fortune with pebbles <note>term: pebbles (calculos); used by the ancients for counting or voting</note>, the ratio of those things which happened to us according to our heart's desire would be very small.
This was elegantly said by Pindar in the Pythian Odes: *For the immortals distribute two troubles to mortals alongside one good.* Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> in Book 27 inverts the sentiment when he says: "There is nothing in the nature of things so small that some good is not joined to it." Since it has been found that even in aconite <note>A highly poisonous plant, also known as monkshood</note>, than which no other poison is more harmful, there is a remedy, both for other things and for defects of the eyes. In the same manner, Euripides <note>Greek tragedian</note>, as cited by Plutarch:
*Good and evil things cannot exist separately, but there is a certain mixture.*

---

<margin>67</margin>
### Ships laden with insults.

In a similar figure, Homer said in *Iliad* Book 20, that the weight of insults was such that a ship of a hundred oars could not carry it; of which kind Lucian had said, "whole wagons of slanders," as was said before. For the passage in Homer goes like this:
*...to speak many insults to both, which not even a ship of a hundred benches could carry as a burden.* That is,
One of which a raft driven by a hundred oars would not carry.
And regarding himself, which will be said in another place: *As many as not even a hundred Egyptians could lift.*
Philippus, in Athenaeus <note>Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> Book 1, describing what is usually imported from each region, mixes in this danger as a joke:
*And again, from the land of the Lycians, many lies in very many ships.* That is,
And from Perdica <note>A port in Lycia</note> many lies in many rafts.
Unless I am mistaken, this refers to the customs of the Lycians. For Perdicia is a part and port of Lycia. The Lycians were held to be strong, and Virgil in the fourth book of the *Aeneid* speaks of them as if they were vain.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### To raise one's horns.
<margin>68</margin>

"To raise one's horns," used to describe someone being carried away by pride, is even now a very common folk saying. Horace says of Bacchus <note>The god of wine, often depicted with horns</note>: *And you grant horns to the poor man.* Ovid likewise says regarding drunkenness:
> Then laughter comes; then even the poor man takes up horns.

<margin>Horace in the Epodes:</margin>
The metaphor is drawn from cattle, which threaten with lowered horns.
> I raise my ready horns.
> For I am fiercest against the wicked.

### To raise one's crests.
<margin>69</margin>

"To raise one's crests." A different metaphor, but the same meaning. Juvenal writes:
> What could be more obvious? And yet his crests were rising. That is, he was pleasing himself.

The metaphor is drawn from crested birds, in whom upright crests are signs of alacrity and spirit; unless we prefer to refer it to the crests of soldiers' helmets—certainly no class of men is more insolent or more stupid. Regarding this sentiment, Aristophanes said in *The Peace*, "To pull down the crests," <term>πῦρ ἡμῶν οὖν λόφος ἀφέλει</term> <note>original Greek: "pyr hēmon oun lophos aphelei"</note>, that is, *which stripped us of our crests.* This refers, of course, to the return of peace. Conversely, those who yield their rights and voluntarily lower their legitimate power to a private, moderate station are said to "lower the fasces" <note>The fasces were bundles of rods and axes symbolizing Roman magisterial authority</note>. Pliny writes in Book 7, Chapter 30: "Gnaeus Pompey, having finished the Mithridatic War and being about to enter the house of Posidonius—a man famous for his profession of wisdom—forbade the lictor to strike the door according to custom, and he lowered the lictorial fasces before the doorway; he, to whom both the East and the West had submitted." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in *Brutus*: "For when you were engaged in the greatest causes, and when our age was already yielding to you and lowering its fasces." And in Titus Livy, in the second book from the founding of the city: "Publicola, having lowered the fasces, ascended into the assembly." This trope adds grace to a saying, as if you were to say, "Philosophy lowers its fasces to Theology."

### The heart falls into the feet.
<margin>70</margin>

Of those who are vehemently terrified and frightened, it is said that their "heart falls into their feet." Indeed, we commonly hear today: "My whole heart was in my knees," meaning "I was utterly breathless with fear." Homer in the *Iliad*, Book 15:
<term>Τάρβησαν, πᾶσιν δὲ παρὰ ποσὶ κάππεσε θυμός.</term> <note>original Greek: "Tarbēsan, pasin de para posi kappese thymos"</note> That is:
A great fear rushed upon them all, and soon the heart fell down to the lowest feet.

### A wasp buzzing against a cicada.
<margin>71</term>

<term>Σφὴξ βομβέων τέττιγι ἐναντίον.</term> <note>original Greek: "Sphēx bombēōn tettigi enantion"</note>
That is, a wasp buzzing against a shrill cicada.
It is found in Theocritus in the *Wayfarers*. For with these words a certain shepherd mocks another shepherd by whom he is challenged. It will apply to one who competes, being far unequal, with a superior. Or one who causes trouble for those far more excellent than himself. It is like that other saying: "A puppy barking at a lion."

### A magpie competes with a nightingale. A hoopoe with swans.
<margin>72</margin>

Those lines read in the same poet [Theocritus] in the same Eclogue have a similar meaning:
<term>οὐ θεμιτὸν λάκων ποτ’ ἀηδόνα κίσσας ἐρίσδεν, οὐδ’ ἔποπας κύκνοισι.</term> <note>original Greek: "ou themiton lakōn pot’ aēdona kissas erisden, oud’ epopas kyknoisi"</note> That is:
It is not right, Lacon, for a magpie ever to challenge a nightingale, nor for a wicked hoopoe to squawk against tuneful swans.

### Hairs for wool.
<margin>73</margin>

<term>Τρίχας ἀντ’ ἐρίων.</term> <note>original Greek: "Trichas ant’ eriōn"</note> That is, "Hairs instead of wool." These words also appear to be spoken proverbially by the same poet in the *Wayfarers*, concerning a thing that is vehemently unequal, or a business that is absurd beyond measure.
<term>Τίς τρίχας ἀντ’ ἐρίων ἐποκίξατο; τίς δὲ πηδύσας Αἰγὸς πρωτοτόκοιο κακὰν κύνα βόλετ’ ἀμέλγειν;</term> <note>original Greek: "Tis trichas ant’ eriōn epokixato; tis de pēdysas aigos prōtotokoio kakan kyna bolet’ amelgein?"</note> That is:
Who would ever shear bristles in place of wool? Who, being mad, would wish to milk a vile dog instead of a first-born goat?
A goat has hair rather than wool; a sheep is wool-bearing. These things are said against a shepherd who, about to compete, offered a kid against a lamb.

### You compare a pipe to a trumpet.
<margin>74</margin>

<term>Αὐλὸν σάλπιγγι συγκρίνεις</term>. <note>original Greek: "Aulon salpingi synkrineis"</note> That is, "You compare a pipe to a trumpet." It is recorded by Diogenianus. It is suitable for things that are unequal beyond measure, because the pipe emits a thin sound, while the trumpet a very great one.

### You compare a bee to a cicada.
<margin>75</margin>

<term>Τέττιγι τὴν μέλιτταν συγκρίνεις</term>. <note>original Greek: "Tettigi tēn melittan synkrineis"</note> That is, "You compare a bee to a cicada." For although the cicada is larger...

<summary>This page explores various proverbs regarding arrogance (raising horns or crests), cowardice (heart falling to the feet), and the absurdity of comparing unequal things (wasps vs. cicadas, or pipes vs. trumpets).</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adages, metaphors, pride, humility, classical literature, Horace, Ovid, Juvenal, Aristophanes, Pliny, Cicero, Livy, Homer, Theocritus, Diogenianus</keywords>

--- Page 395 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded the discussion of the proverb regarding the cicada and the bee, noting the disparity in their voices.</meta>

->EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND<-

so melodious, since a bee is not only of a tiny little body, but indeed almost mute. Lucian, in *The Professor of Rhetoric*, touches upon both proverbs: <note>original: "τοσούτῳ ὑποφωνοῦντα εὑρήσεις, ὁπόσῳ ἡ σάλπιξ τῶν αὐλῶν, καὶ οἱ τέττιγες τῶν μελιττῶν"</note> that is, "You will find him as much superior in voice as the trumpet surpasses the flutes, or as the cicadas surpass the bees."

### 76. You compare a tortoise to Pegasus.

<note>original: "Χελώνην πηγάσῳ συγκρίνεις"</note> That is, You compare a tortoise to Pegasus. This is said of things that should by no means be compared to one another. Pegasus was a winged horse, if we believe the fables, while nothing is slower than a tortoise. Virgil, in his poem *Tityrus* <note>The First Eclogue</note>, gathered several formulas for expressing dissimilarity:
> Thus I knew pups were like dogs, and kids like their mothers;
> Thus I was accustomed to compare great things to small.
> But this city has thrust her head as far above others,
> As cypresses are wont to do among the bending wayfaring-trees.

### 77. Puppies smell one way, pigs another.

In the plays of Plautus, specifically in *Epidicus*, one reads a somewhat cruder metaphor, yet one well-suited for signifying the matter: "Puppies smell one way, pigs another." By this saying, it is signified that it is not merely a wish to distinguish one man from another, but that there is something native, genuine, and specific within each person—shining out in the very face and eyes—by which you may easily discern a free man from a slave, a nobleman from a peasant, or an honest man from a rogue. And this is, as it were, a man's own peculiar "scent" by which he is detected, provided one has a keen nose. Martial alluded to this in his sixth book:
> When she thought herself quite safe through a thousand frauds,
> When she had done everything, Thais still smells of Thais.

To this also belongs that remark of someone in Fabius <note>Quintilian</note>: "He does not even have the face of a free man." When this had been said by someone regarding a man of ugly appearance, his adversary retorted, affirming it was rightly said: for he cannot be a free man who does not have a "liberal" <note>noble or gentlemanly</note> face.

### 78. As you have sown, so shall you reap.

Cicero spoke with a most elegant metaphor: "As you have sown, so shall you reap." That is, you will carry back a reward worthy of your deeds. Plautus in *Epidicus*: "But how bitter it is, when you reap a bad harvest for good deeds." That is, when you receive a wrong in return for a benefit. And in Plato: "What kind of harvest is he going to make here? Surely not a good one." This metaphor is also common in the Holy Scriptures: "They who sow in tears shall reap in joy." And Saint Paul: "He who sows in the flesh shall from the flesh reap corruption." <note>Erasmus notes the contrast here</note> But how bitter it is, [to reap] eternal life for good deeds. And: "If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?" Euripides refers to this in *Hecuba*:
<note>original: "ὑμᾶς δὲ ἐχρῆν ὅμοια τοῖς βουλεύμασιν"</note> That is,
"But may you have things consistent with your designs."
Finally, that phrase is almost a solemn ritual among the Greek poets: "badly to a bad man." Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
<note>original: "οὐδὲ μουσικὴν ἐπίσταμαι πλὴν γραμμάτων, καὶ ταῦτα μὲν κακῶς κακά"</note> That is,
"I know nothing of the arts of the Muses,
Except my letters, and those badly learned by a bad man."
Also frequent is: "I will destroy you, a bad man, in a bad way." The commentator warns of this proverbial figure, about which we spoke in the introduction to this work. Again, Euripides in *Hecuba*: <note>original: "τὸν μὲν κακόν κακόν τι πάσχειν, τὸν δὲ χρηστὸν εὐτυχεῖν"</note> That is,
"That the bad man should suffer something bad, but the good man should prosper." The same author in the same play:
<note>original: "ἐπεί τοι μὴ καλὰ πράσσειν ἐτόλμας, τλῆθι καὶ τὰ μὴ φίλα"</note> That is,
"Since you did not fear to commit deeds that are not honorable,
Endure also those things that are not pleasing."
It is quite witty what Laertius relates concerning Diogenes. During dinner, certain people threw bones to him as if to a dog, because he was a <term>Cynic</term> <note>The word 'Cynic' derives from the Greek word for 'dog-like'</note>. He repaid that insult thus: he approached, <unclear>pious</unclear>, and standing near them he urinated on them, playing the dog to them in turn. But more closely related to this is what the same author relates of Zeno, who was beating a slave caught in a theft. The slave meanwhile cried out that it was "in his fate" that he should steal. To which Zeno replied: "And also that you should be beaten." The slave, since...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>The previous page likely ended with an anecdote about a slave and a philosopher.</note> ...having heard his master disputing about the necessity of fate, he used that as a pretext for his own crime; but the philosopher wittily turned the argument back against him.

### 79. A Carian Muse

<term>Karikē mousa</term> <note>original: Καρίκη μοῦσα</note>, that is, a Carian muse. <term>Karika aulēmata</term> <note>original: καρικὰ αὐλήματα</note>, that is, Carian songs. This was commonly said of a mournful, rustic, unlearned, or annoying song. It will apply well to an unlearned poet or orator. In antiquity, it referred to a sad, shrill, and unpleasant song, because, as Athenaeus records in the fourth book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned," a famous Greek work on dining and culture</note>, the Carians, just like the Phoenicians, were accustomed to use flutes the size of a palm in mourning, which produced a mournful and shrill sound. These flutes are called <term>gingros</term> <note>original: γίγγρος</note> in the Phoenician tongue, because they are used in the mourning for Adonis. Furthermore, they call Adonis <term>Gingrōn</term>, that is, Gringen. From this comes their verb <term>gingrainō</term> <note>to pipe shrilly</note>. Julius Pollux records similar things in his fourth book, except that I find it written there as <term>gingran</term>. Aristophanes notes Carian music in *The Frogs*:

->The crooked songs of Melitus and Carian flute-tunes.<-
->that is,<-
->The winding songs of Melitus, and Carian<-
->measures of the flutes.<-

The ancients called these same <term>Carian flute-tunes</term> <term>skolia</term>, that is, "crooked" or "oblique," either from the appearance of the flutes or from the zigzag order of singing at banquets, which we mentioned in the proverb: *To sing to the myrtle*. Plato also mentions it in Athenaeus’s *The Laconians*:

->A certain young girl, holding a pipe, plays a Carian melody.<-
->that is,<-
->The girl, having the reeds, will play<-
->A Carian strain.<-

Plato the philosopher also, in the seventh book of *The Laws*, makes mention of the Carian muse, which he interprets as a <term>funeral dirge</term> <note>original: ἐπικηδειον ᾠδήν</note>, that is, a mournful song. Hesychius indicates the term is derived from the fact that women from Caria were usually hired for funeral processions to act the part of mourners. Therefore, you might rightly call an unlearned and unpleasant speech a <term>Carian muse</term>. To this fits that line of Sopater in the fourth book of Athenaeus:

->The barbarian Muse rejoicing in the pectis.<-
->that is,<-
->The barbarian Muse exulting with the pectis.<-

The <term>pectis</term> is a type of instrument equipped with two strings. The same Athenaeus doubts whether Caria was the same as what is called Phoenicia. For the Phoenicians call pipes or reeds <term>gingras</term>, a word formed, it seems, from the shrillness of the sound. With these agree the things Plato writes in the seventh book of *The Laws*, which I just cited: "It is not at all fitting for such a lamentation to occur where citizens are listening, whenever the days are not pure but are dedicated to Aphrodite; then, rather, it is most fitting for a chorus hired from outside to lead the deceased with songs, just as those who are hired for funerals lead out the dead with a certain Carian muse," and so forth. Homer censures the Carian barbarism in speaking in the second book of the *Iliad*:

->Nastes led the Carians, who have a barbarian voice.<-

From this, in popular Greek speech, those whose speech is barbarian and rustic are said to <term>karbazein</term>, <term>karbaizein</term>, or <term>karbanizein</term> <note>verbs meaning to speak like a foreigner or "gibber"</note>. And Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in Quintilian’s chapter on pronunciation, says that those orators from Lycia and Caria sing well in their epilogues, clearly rebuking their style of delivery. Strabo, in the fourteenth book of his *Geography*, shows that the Carians were frequently mixed with the Greeks, yet they sounded the Greek language in a barbarian and coarse way—the same thing that happens to Greeks in the Roman language, and to us in the British language. Strabo calls this vice <term>pachysomia</term> (thick-mouthedness), <term>kakosomia</term> (bad-mouthedness), and <term>barbarosomia</term> (barbarian-mouthedness). Marcus Tullius also mentions the songs of the Carians and Phrygians in his *Brutus*. There was also a type of tumultuous and military dance, from which they sometimes came away wounded, for it was performed by armed men; Julius Pollux in his fourth book calls this the <term>Carian</term> dance.

### 80. An Attic Muse

The opposite of this is <term>Attikē mousa</term>, that is, an Attic muse, used for charming and witty speech. For among the styles of speaking, the Attic is praised above all. Diogenes Laertius and Plutarch, in the *Life of Plato*, write that this nickname was commonly given to Xenophon—that he was called the "Attic Muse"—on account of the man's remarkable charm in speaking. From this also, Attic eloquence...

<summary>Erasmus discusses the proverb "Carian Muse," explaining it as a metaphor for unrefined, shrill, or mournful speech and music, contrasting it with the "Attic Muse" which represents refined elegance.</summary>

# FIRST THOUSAND, EIGHTH HUNDRED

<margin>81</margin>
...eloquence, and they call it "Attic wit," as we have indicated elsewhere. But when applied to a specific person, it will be more elegant, especially if irony is added: for instance, if you call someone who is inelegant and completely a stranger to all literature and the Graces an "Attic Muse." For that is what all such people are called.

->To drink from the same cup.<-

"To drink from the same cup" means to be affected by the same inconveniences and to be liable to common evils. Plautus says in *Casina*: "So that the old man might drink from this same cup from which I drank." <note>original: "Ut senex eodem hoc poculo quo bibi biberet."</note> This is metaphorically taken either from athletic games or from those who fear poisons. The same expression remains very common among our own people today. For if they ever threaten to return a favor in kind, they say they will "draw from the same cup." Martial censures a certain man who served his guests diluted and bitter wine while he himself drank from the finest vintage—a custom prevalent among many wealthy people today—and this proverb may seem to have originated there. It also happens sometimes that those who have imprudently tasted a drink strive to entice others to drink from the same. In Holy Scripture, there is also mention of the "cup of Babylon" when some calamity to be inflicted is signified. Finally, our Lord in the Gospel asks the sons of Zebedee whether they could drink from the same cup from which he himself was destined to drink, adding another similar proverbial phrase: "From the same baptism." For there is no doubt that both were celebrated in common speech. It is slightly different in what Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:

<margin>that is,</margin>
"He shall never willingly drink from the same cup with us." <note>original Greek: μηδ' ἑκὼν μεθ' ἡμῶν πιεῖται ποτηρίῳ.</note>
He never drinks from the same cup as the ignoble. ->He is censuring a lewd person.<-

<margin>82</margin>
->A horse to the plain.<-

"A horse to the plain." <note>original Greek: Εἰς πεδίον τὸν ἵππον.</note> This is used whenever someone is challenged to that in which he is most capable and in which he takes the greatest joy. A horse in a field is, as it were, in its own arena. In Lucian’s *The Captive*, when he himself demanded judges, Plato responds: "Just like that saying: a horse to the plain," <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἐκεῖνο εἰς πεδίον τὸν ἵππον.</note> clearly signifying a man who is rhetorical and practiced in pleading cases. Plato says in *Theaetetus*: "You challenge horsemen to the plain, as words against words," <note>original Greek: ἱππέας εἰς πεδίον προκαλεῖς, ὡς λόγους εἰς λόγους.</note> meaning he challenges Socrates to a contest. However, some manuscripts have "horse" <term>hippon</term> in this place, not "horseman" <term>hippea</term>. Synesius says in a certain letter: "I certainly challenge you to this very thing, a horse to the plain, just as the proverb exhorts us." <note>original Greek: Ἐπ' αὐτὸ δὴ τοῦτο προκαλῶ, ἵππον εἰς πεδίον...</note> It seems to be a metaphor from military service. For whenever an infantryman deals with cavalry, he flees the level fields and seeks out more obstructed places.

<margin>83</margin>
->The crow defeats the goldfinch.<-

"The crow surpasses the goldfinch." <note>The goldfinch (acanthis) was prized for its song, while the crow was known for harsh cawing.</note> Calpurnius the Bucolic poet says in Eclogue 6:
"It is scarcely believable, if the crow should defeat the goldfinch,
If the ugly owl should surpass the nightingale."
For the goldfinch is a vocal bird, and especially tuneful. The crow is indeed noisy, but not at all tuneful. Theodorus sometimes translates <term>acanthidem</term> as a "siskin," sometimes as a "greenfinch," and Horace even used it for a "nightingale." It should be pronounced so that the *ae* makes two syllables. For to the Greeks, <term>akanthyllis</term> signifies a nightingale. Pliny uses the Greek word *acanthidem*, as if you were to say "little thorn-bird," because it lives among thorns, and for that reason it hates donkeys, because that animal devours the flower of the thorn. It is among the smallest of birds, yet of such fertility that it gives birth to twelve at a time. The authority is Pliny, Book 10, chapters 63 and 74.

<margin>84</margin>
->The tortoise will have outrun the hare.<-

"The tortoise will have passed the hare in a race." <note>original Greek: Πρότερον χελώνη παραδραμεῖται δασύποδα.</note> This is said of something not at all likely. Nothing is slower than a tortoise. Whence Plautus speaks of a "tortoise-like gait"; and in Cicero’s books *On Divination*, someone calls the tortoise "slow-stepping" and "ground-bearer." The hare, however, excels in speed. Diogenianus mentions this adage. Of this kind are those lines in Theocritus’s *Thyrsis*:

"Now let brambles bear violets, let thorns bear them too,
And let the beautiful narcissus bloom on the juniper,
Let all things be changed, and let the pine tree bear pears,
Since Daphnis is dying; let the deer drag the hounds,
And let the owls from the mountains cry out to the nightingales."

<margin>that is,</margin>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

> Now let the brambles bear violets, let the thorns bring forth,
> And let the juniper be adorned with the lovely flower of the narcissus:
> Let all things be overturned, let the pine tree bear sweet pears,
> Since Daphnis has died, let the doe now hunt the hounds,
> And let the owl sing like the nightingale upon the highest mountains.
<note>original: Virgil, Eclogues 5. Erasmus quotes these lines to illustrate the "world turned upside down" theme, where the natural order is reversed.</note>

<margin>85</margin>
->You are comparing crabs to a hare.<-

"You compare a crab to a hare" <note>original: Καρκίνος δασύποδι συγκρίνεις</note>, that is, you compare things that are exceedingly different. For just as the speed of hares is well known, so too is the slowness of crabs. This is very similar to the adage we just related. This is also recorded by the same author. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> adds, "The crab will catch the hare" <note>original: καρκίνος λαγωὸν αἱρεῖ</note>: said of absurdities and things that can in no way happen.

<margin>86</margin>
->Son of the Earth.<-

In the past, men born of an obscure and unknown lineage were called "sons of the earth," because the earth is the common parent of all. Or perhaps because, according to the histories of some, the first mortals were born directly from the earth. Tertullian <note>An early Christian author</note> says in his *Apology against the Heathens*: "For the common people also call those 'sons of the earth' whose lineage is uncertain." In the tenth book of Athenaeus, one reads of the "earth-born man" <note>original: γηγενὴς ἄνθρωπος</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero writes to Atticus in his first book: "And I did not dare to entrust a letter concerning such great matters to this 'son of the earth,' whoever he may be." The same author writes to Trebatius in the seventh book of his *Letters to Friends*: "Your friend Gnaeus Octavius, born of the highest lineage, is a son of the earth." Persius writes:
> Manius is ready to be my heir,
> A progeny of the earth. Ask of me who my fourth
> Father was: I could not say readily, yet I will tell you: add one more,
> And one more again, and he is now a son of the earth.
Juvenal writes:
> Whence it happens, that I would rather be a little brother of the giants.
Clearly alluding to the proverb. For the poets tell fables of the giants being fathered by the earth. To this pertains what Ion asks of Xuthus in the play by Euripides:
"Was I then born from a mother earth?" <note>original: τῆς ἄρ’ ἐκπέφυκα μητρός;</note> To which the other responds:
"The soil does not give birth to children." <note>original: οὐ πέδον τίκτει τέκνα.</note>
In Pausanias, Strabo, and other authors of that kind, we read of certain peoples called "autochthons" <note>original: αὐτόχθονας, meaning 'sprung from the land itself'</note>, who do not trace their origin back [to migrants] as most do, but wish to be seen as born from the very soil itself; the Athenians are among their number. Those who had won nobility for themselves through virtue, though not distinguished by any ancestral wax masks <note>term: imagines - wax portraits of ancestors displayed by Roman nobility to prove their lineage</note>, were called "new men." Furthermore, those who were unknown and appeared suddenly, having set out from an uncertain region, were called "Sons of Heaven," as if sent down from the sky. In the Mosaic writings <note>The Bible</note>, Melchizedek is introduced as "without father, without mother" <note>original: ἀπάτορα ἀμήτορα</note>; and by a similar reasoning, things were said to be "fallen from heaven" <note>original: οὐρανοπετής</note>. Juvenal writes:
> A third Cato has fallen from the sky.
Although this is more suited to men of extraordinary virtue. Plutarch, in the invective he wrote against Herodotus, speaks of a certain ship from which a voice was suddenly heard by Adeimantus: "That ship, as it seems, was fallen from heaven" <note>original: ὡς πέλης ὅτος ἰὼ ὡς ἔοικεν οὐρανοπετής</note>. And this figure of speech is taken from the tragedies, in which characters were suddenly revealed to the people by certain machines, so that they wished to seem to have come from heaven. Among the Romans, those were called "New Men" who, born of obscure ancestors, had become known through their own virtues—a thing which Marcus Tullius Cicero turned into a point of glory for himself, though his enemies cast it at him as a reproach.

<margin>87</margin>
->Born from oaks and rocks.<-

Close to this is that Homeric saying: "Born from an oak, or from rocks." This will apply either to a man of obscure birth, or to one who is of a rustic and wild disposition and of savage manners. The adage is derived from the fact that in ancient times men lived in hollow oaks in place of houses, and hence were imagined to be born from oaks. Thence comes the line:
> And those born from the hard oak.
Furthermore, it was believed that after the human race was destroyed by the flood, it was restored from stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha. Homer in the *Odyssey*, book 19.

<header>EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND</header>

<margin><note>original Greek: "Οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ δρυός ἐσσι παλαιφάτου, οὐδ᾽ ἀπὸ πέτρης."</note></margin>
->that is,<-
For you are not sprung from the oak of ancient story, nor from a rock.
<note>A reference to Homer’s Odyssey; it implies one has human feelings or a known lineage rather than a mythical, stony origin.</note>
Imitating this, Pallas says in an epigram:
<margin><note>original Greek: "Οὐ γὰρ ἀπὸ δρυός εἶ, οὐδ᾽ ἀπ᾽ πέτρης φασίν."</note></margin>
->that is,<-
Surely, as they say, neither oak nor stone brought you forth.
Plato wittily applies this in the eighth book of the *Republic*: <margin>Politics</margin> "Or do you think that constitutions are born from an oak or a rock somewhere, and not from the characters of those living in the cities?" That is, do you believe republics are born from some tree or cliff, and not rather from the habits of those who dwell within the republic? This also suits the cruel and heartless, as in Theocritus’s poem about the Goatherd and Cupid:
<margin><note>original Greek: "Α. Λέαινας"</note></margin> He sucked the teat of a lioness, and his mother reared him in the thicket.
->that is,<-
Clearly he drew from the udders of a lioness, and in the grove a wild mother fed him.

---

<margin>Food of the Gods. i. LXXXVIII</margin>
## Food of the gods.
This was said of particularly exquisite banquets, because Homer imagines that the gods live on nectar and ambrosia, and for that reason never grow old. Suetonius <note>referred to here as Tranquillus</note> says in his life of Nero: "He began his parricides and murders with Claudius. Even if he was not the author of the death, he was aware of it; nor did he hide it, as he was accustomed to praise mushrooms—the type of food in which the poison had been administered—as the 'food of the gods,' using the Greek proverb." Horace says in his *Epistles*:
> and the nights, and the suppers of the gods.

Aristophanes in *The Frogs* speaks of "the festivities of the blessed gods," signifying the courtly banquets of kings.

---

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
## A third Cato.
"A third Cato" is a proverbial irony. It is used against gloomy, somber men and those who censor the lives of others. For the gravity and integrity of the two Catos—the elder, named the Censor, and the younger, named of Utica—was once so celebrated by the common people that they were said to have been sent down from heaven to wage war against vice. Juvenal writes:
> A third Cato has fallen from the sky.

---

<margin>XC</margin>
## The eighth wise man.
Very similar to this in every respect is that phrase of Horace in his *Satires*: "The eighth of the wise men." It refers to one who attributes much wisdom to himself. For among the Greeks, seven wise men are counted, and their sayings are celebrated like oracles, even if there is great variation among writers regarding their names. The number, certainly, is agreed upon by all; hence, through irony, they called someone "the eighth wise man" as if he were worthy to be added to those seven. Horace:
> From this, Stertinius is to me the eighth of the wise men.

Likewise Ausonius:
> Whoever has been added as an eighth sage
> Above the seven men of Greece.

---

<margin>XCI</margin>
## He gives twice, who gives quickly.
I remember reading somewhere in Seneca, if I am not mistaken: "He gives twice, who gives quickly." Likewise in the second book of *On Benefits*: "A benefit is ungrateful which has stuck long in the hands of the giver." This sentiment teaches that one should help friends without hesitation or grudge when there is need, but rather offer service voluntarily and before being asked. Among the Greek epigrams, this one is also circulated <margin>Anthology</margin> under the name and title of Lucian:
> <note>original Greek: "Ὠκυτέρης χάριτος γλυκερώτερος..."</note>
> A swift favor is sweeter, but if you are slow,
> every favor is empty, and should not even be called a favor.

The poem cannot be conveniently translated into Latin <note>or English</note> because the wit and point of the epigram lie in the word *charis* <term>charis: a Greek word meaning favor, grace, or gratitude</term>, which in Greek sometimes signifies a benefit, sometimes the grace by which something is commended, and sometimes the goddess herself. A similar Greek sentiment is cited in Ausonius:
> <margin><note>original Greek: "εἰς τὸ βραδύτης, ἄχαρις χάρις."</note></margin>
> Toward slowness, a graceless grace.

Likewise the beginning of a Heroic poem from some epigram: "A slow benefit is a hollow one." He translates it thus:
> The grace which is slow is ungrateful: for grace,
> While it hastens to be done, is a more pleasing grace.

Again, he translates it another way:
> If you are to do anything, do it quickly: for a thing done quickly
> Will be pleasing; a slow grace makes it ungrateful.
