# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<sig>N v</sig>

Hence also Hector, in Euripides’s *Rhesus*, despises and condemns help that is brought too late to friends:
*I hate to help friends when it is too late.* <note>original Greek: μισῶ φίλοισιν ὕστερον βοηδρομεῖν.</note>
There is also a rather charming Mime <note>A short, often humorous dramatic performance or poem</note> on this same sentiment:
*That which is needed is twice as pleasing if you offer it of your own accord.*
Likewise, another similar to this:
*He gives a benefit to the needy twice over, who gives quickly.*

### Honor nurtures the arts.
<margin>92</margin>

That which is found in Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>, "Honor nurtures the arts," seems to be taken from Aristophanes’s *Plutus*:
*For where there is no reward, the art itself no longer flourishes.* <note>original Greek: οὔτε γὰρ ὁ μισθὸς, οὐδὲν ἔτ’ ἔστ’ ἡ τέχνη.</note>
For he concludes that it is not logical for there to be any good doctors in Athens when there are no rewards for doctors. Diogenianus, however, records this among the adages. Martial alluded to this when he said:
*Let there be Maecenases <note>Wealthy patrons of the arts</note>, Flaccus, and Virgils will not be lacking; even your own fields will provide a Virgil for you.*
And Aristotle writes that honor is the reward of virtue. Furthermore, the laws of the ancients did not only threaten punishment for evildoers, but also invited people to act rightly with rewards and honors. Pindar, in the ninth hymn of the *Isthmian Odes*, cites a sentiment as if it were commonly celebrated: *There is a certain saying among men, that a good deed accomplished should not be buried in the ground in silence.* <note>original Greek: ἔστι δέ τις λόγος ἀνθρώπων, τετελεσμένον ἐσλὸν μὴ χαμαὶ σιγᾷ καλύψαι.</note> To this pertains the Gospel parable, that a lamp is not to be hidden under a bushel basket. In this way, the right actions of illustrious men are to be proclaimed so that they may shine before others as an incentive to take up virtue.

### It would be apparent even to a blind man.
<margin>93</margin>

A proverbial hyperbole frequent among authors, "It would be apparent even to a blind man," used for a matter that is exceedingly obvious. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
*How do you know it is so? Clearly even a blind man could see this.* <note>original Greek: Τῷ δ’ ἐκ κείναις; δῆλον ὅτι καὶ τυφλῷ</note>
Eusebius against Hierocles: *But indeed, they say it is clear even to a blind man.* <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τυφλῷ φασὶ δῆλον.</note>
Plato in the eighth book of *The Republic*: *It is surely clear even to a blind man that it has been transformed.* <note>original Greek: καὶ τυφλῷ γε δῆλον, ὡς μετεσκεύασται.</note>
The same in *The Sophist*: *For how can this not appear, as the saying goes, even to a blind man?* <note>original Greek: πῶς γὰρ οὐ φαίνεται, τὸ γε λεγόμενον δὴ τοῦτο, καὶ τυφλῷ.</note>
It can be seen to be taken from the eighth book of Homer’s *Odyssey*:
*Even a blind man, O guest, could distinguish this mark.* <note>original Greek: Καί κ’ ἀλαός τοι ξεῖνε διακρίνειε τὸ σῆμα.</note>
Quintilian in book 12: *For who is ignorant that it is by far the most honorable thing, and most worthy of liberal disciplines and that spirit which we require, not to sell one's labor, nor to diminish the authority of such a great benefit; since most things can seem cheap for the very reason that they have a price. This is clear enough, as they say, to the blind. Nor shall anyone who possesses sufficient means—and these are modest—make this profit without the reproach of sordidness.* In these words of Fabius <note>Quintilian</note>, a word seems to be missing, so that you should read: "This is, as they say, sufficiently *clear* to the blind." King Antigonus, who had only one eye, alluded to this adage when, upon being brought a document written in very large letters, he said: *These things are indeed clear even to a blind man.* <note>original Greek: τωυτὶ γὰρ καὶ τυφλῷ δῆλα.</note> Plutarch recounted this in the second decade of his *Table Talk*. In Titus Livius <note>Livy</note>, in the second book of the *Macedonian War*, when Phaneas interrupted Philip (who was speaking rather violently against the Aetolians) and said that the matter did not turn on words, but must be won by war or by obeying those who are better, Philip replied: "That indeed is apparent even to a blind man," joking about the poor health of Phaneas's eyes.

### The oak is felled by many strokes.
<margin>94</margin>

*The stiff oak is tamed by many strokes.* <note>original Greek: Πολλαῖσι πληγαῖς δρῦς σορὰ δαμάζεται.</note>
This six-foot verse <note>term: senarius; a line of verse consisting of six metrical feet</note> appears in the collections of Diogenianus, concerning a task that is indeed difficult, but which may nevertheless be overcome by steady industry. Not unlike this seems that saying of Hesiod:
*For if you add a little to a little, and do this often, soon even that may become great.* <note>original Greek: Εἰ γάρ κεν καὶ σμικρὸν ἐπὶ σμικρῷ καταθεῖο, Καὶ θαμὰ τοῦτ’ ἔρδοις, τάχα κεν μέγα καὶ τὸ γένοιτο.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores the origins of three proverbs: that honor encourages excellence, that obvious truths are visible even to the blind, and that persistence can overcome great obstacles.</summary>

# EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<note>The author, Erasmus, organizes his collection of thousands of proverbs into "Chiliads" (thousands) and "Centuries" (hundreds).</note>

...a great and immense profit will be fashioned for you.

This pertains not only to the nature of profit, which is often forged into something very large from the smallest bits, but also to constant industry. Even if that industry is not intense, if it is perpetual and untiring, it easily accomplishes even the most difficult things. Just as a single blow seems to bring no momentum toward felling the mass of an oak's strength, yet it is easily laid low by frequent strikes.

### To pluck the hairs of a horse's tail little by little. XCV
<note>Adage 95</note>

He "plucks the hairs of a horse's tail little by little" who accomplishes by time and persistence that which cannot be done by force and impulse. Horace says in his *Epistles*:

> I pluck little by little, I take away one, and then I take away another,
> Until he falls, deceived by the logic of the crumbling heap,
> He who looks back to the annals and judges virtue by years.
> <note>original: "Paulatim uello, demo unum..." Horace, Epistles 2.1.45-48. The "logic of the heap" refers to the Sorites paradox: how many grains make a heap?</note>

This originated from a certain deed of the general Sertorius, a matter which Plutarch mentions in his *Life*. <note>Quintus Sertorius (c. 123–72 BCE), a Roman general who led a rebellion in Spain.</note> Since he could not persuade his troops—who were gathered from a barbarian crowd—by logic that counsel has more weight in military affairs than rash strength, he proposed a demonstration after they had fought with little success. He set out two horses: one lean and weak, the other vigorous with a bushy tail. To the weak horse, he assigned a young man of massive body and admirable strength. Conversely, to the vigorous horse, he set a small and feeble little fellow. The latter, by plucking individual hairs little by little, denuded the entire tail in a short space of time. The youth, on the other hand, attempted to tear away the whole tail at once, grasping it with both hands with force and impulse. While he sweated in vain, it was a cause of laughter for the bystanders. At this, Sertorius rose—by whose counsel and command these things had been done—and said: "You see, fellow soldiers, how much more intellect can do than strength."

### Even a mouse might bite a wicked man. XCVI
<note>Adage 96</note>

*Even a mouse might bite a wicked man.* <note>original Greek: Κἂν μῦς δάκοι ἄνδρα πονηρόν</note>

This is a heroic hemistich <note>half-line of verse</note>. It signifies that by whatever means, vengeance is never lacking for the wicked, but that they pay their deserved penalties in some fashion. It also applies to those who stir up a quarrel over a matter however trivial, complaining that they have been harmed and pretending to be offended so that they do not have to give anything. 

This recently happened to a certain doctor in Britain, a man joined to me by a common homeland and by close friendship. I would like to insert this story in passing. When he had cured a certain Londoner—a man remarkably wealthy and considered exceptionally honest—by his art and care, and not without risk to his own health (for the man was held by a most pestilential fever). And, as happens in times of danger, the man had promised mountains of gold to the doctor if he would not find it burdensome to be present at his side in such a crisis of life, entreating him by the friendship that existed between them. To be brief: he persuaded him, and the doctor helped him as a fellow countryman. <note>original: "Germano" - Erasmus often uses this to refer to people from the Low Countries/Greater Germany.</note> He was there; he did everything. The man recovered. 

When the doctor modestly reminded him about the money, the trifler eluded him, denying that there was any doubt about the fee, but saying that the key to the money chest was in his wife's possession. "And you know," he said, "the nature of women. I don't want her to notice such a large sum of money being given by me." Then, after a few days, the doctor met the man—now looking sleek and showing no traces of illness—and addressed him, not yet reminding him of the fee. The man firmly asserted that the money had been paid by his wife on his orders. The doctor denied it had happened. 

Now see what a handle that "good man" snatched up! When the doctor happened to address him in Latin in the singular number <note>The doctor used "tu" (thou/you singular) instead of a more formal address, which the Londoner used as an excuse to take offense.</note>, the man, as if provoked by an atrocious injury, cried: "What? You, a German, 'thou' an Englishman?" and soon, as if out of his mind, shaking his head with rage and threatening dire things, he withdrew. And in that manner, that "honest citizen" cheated him—a rich man indeed, whom his plague ought to return to. We laughed at the story, yet not without pain on account of a friend so unworthily frustrated, nor without wonder at such remarkable ingratitude. Even lions, when helped in danger, remember the service; even dragons remember; yet a human to a human, a friend to a friend who so deserved it, returns mockery in place of a fee that no amount could sufficiently repay. 

And I have said these things in detestation of the deed, not out of hatred for the nation. For it is not fair that all Britons be judged by this one scoundrel. The adage is recorded among the Greek epigrams:

> They say in the manner of a warrior, even a mouse might bite a wicked man.
> <note>original: Φασὶ πτοιομαχῶς, κἂν μῦς δάκοι ἄνδρα πονηρόν</note>

Magis—whoever he is, for the author is uncertain—inverted the proverb, saying that good men are bitten even by a mouse, while against the wicked, not even a dragon dares to set its teeth. That is, the innocent are harmed everywhere...

<summary>This page discusses two proverbs: one regarding the power of persistence over brute force (illustrated by Sertorius and the horse's tail) and another regarding the inevitable downfall of the wicked, including a personal anecdote about a greedy Londoner cheating a doctor.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<page-num>292</page-num>

...to be harmed, because they seem able to be injured with impunity, as they are unlikely to return the injury.

### Even a goat might bite the wicked. XCVII.

<note>original: "Κἂν αἲξ δάκῃ ἄνδρα πονηρόν"</note> That is,
->Even a goat will bite the guilty.<-

This is found in the collections of Diogenianus. The meaning does not differ at all from the previous one. For a goat is otherwise not at all prone to biting, except that to the wicked, all things are hostile. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> indicates the orthography: for when the word refers to the body—that is, when it signifies a man who is afflicted and miserable—he wants the accent on the first syllable, *pónēros*, whence those in adverse circumstances are said to "fare poorly" (*ponērōs echein*). And Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
"You tell us of wretched (*ponēros*) allies indeed." That is,
"You truly announce miserable reinforcements to us."
When it refers to the soul, the accent is on the last syllable, *ponērós*, that is, "wicked," and *ponērōs* means "wickedly." For when we say a "wicked coin" or "wicked water," we are transferring a human quality to an inanimate thing, just as we speak of a "villainous cold" or "deceitful riches."

### He will start a lawsuit even if a donkey bites a dog. XCVIII.

This proverbial six-foot line is also celebrated among the Greeks:
<note>original: "Δίκην ὑφέξει κἂν ὄνος δάκῃ κύνα"</note> That is,
He will start a lawsuit even if a donkey bites a dog.
This will apply to those who stir up a legal dispute over the most trivial matter. It seems to have arisen from some specific event. Moreover, there exists among legal experts an action based on the law "If a quadruped should cause damage" <note>A reference to the Roman *Lex Aquilia* or similar statutes regarding property damage by animals</note>. It is cited by Zenodotus and Suidas, although in both it is written *makros* [long] instead of *mikros* [small], the latter of which seems to me to be required by the sense.

### Lawsuit births lawsuit, and injury births injury. XCIX.

<note>original: "Δίκη δίκην ἔτικτε, καὶ βλάβην βλάβη"</note> That is,
Lawsuit births lawsuit, and injury births injury.
A verse usually said against the quarrelsome and those greedy for litigation, for whom one suit is born from another, one after the other; business is sown from business, and injury propagates injury. It is found in Suidas.

### A good leader makes a good follower. C.

<note>original: "Ὁ καλῶς ἄγων, καὶ καλῶς ἕπεσθαι ποιεί"</note> That is, He who acts as a good leader makes a good companion. It rests with the prince to ensure the state is well-mannered, provided he himself is a good commander. It rests with the bishop to make the people pious, provided he himself leads a pious and upright life. A wise and uncorrupted magistrate makes the citizens both honest and upright. A good head of a household makes a well-ordered home. A learned and diligent teacher makes a scholarly pupil. A frugal husband draws his wife into his own habits. Whence whoever is in charge of a business ought, above all, to take care that he performs his own duty before he demands duty from others. But nowadays you may see some princes who demand the observation of laws from the people, while they themselves live entirely <term>lawlessly (anomōs)</term>, as if released from all laws. They require integrity from magistrates and officials, while they themselves openly sell offices or grant them as favors. You may see some bishops who demand religion and piety from their flock, while they themselves are far removed from all piety. The metaphor is taken from military service, in which the soldier is usually of the same sort as the leader. It is cited in the Greek collections, but is <term>anonymous (adespoton)</term>. However, it appears in Plutarch—an author of no small repute—in the *Life of Lycurgus*: "But obedience is a lesson learned from rulers; for he who leads well produces good following." That is, that the people be obedient to what is said, they learn this from the prince. For he who offers himself as a good leader makes it so that others follow well.

To certain learned men—among whom is the author of a work by no means to be despised entitled *The Horn of Plenty* <note>Niccolò Perotti's *Cornu Copiae*</note>—it is pleasing that this belongs to the order of proverbs, nor do we greatly differ from their opinion. For it is consistent that the matter was tossed about as a common jest. Virgil alludes to the adage in the tenth book of the *Aeneid* when he mentions "and tawny Camers,"

# THE NINTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
B 3

...born of the high-spirited Volscens; he was the wealthiest in land among the Ausonians and reigned over silent Amyclae.
<note>original: "magnanimo Volscente satum..." quoting Virgil's Aeneid 10.563-564</note>
Clearly, the poet indicates a well-known event by this epithet. Servius the commentator explains it in this manner: Since the arrival of enemies was repeatedly announced among the people of Amyclae, and falsely so, the city was frequently shaken by empty terror. Consequently, a law was passed providing that no one should ever announce the arrival of an enemy. Yet it later happened that the enemies were truly approaching. When no one announced it because of the legal prohibition, the city was captured by surprise. This misfortune, as it appears, gave rise to a popular joke used whenever someone’s own silence proved harmful: they would say that Amyclae perished through silence. The same author cites Lucilius: "I must speak; for I know that Amyclae perished by keeping silent." <note>Lucilius was an early Roman satirist.</note> However, in this passage, Amyclae should be understood not as one of those hundred cities of Laconia founded by the son of Lacedaemon, but as a certain town situated between Gaeta and Terracina. It was founded by those Laconians who were companions of Castor and Pollux, and they gave it that name to recall the Laconian Amyclae. Servius believes the Laconians were followers of the Pythagorean discipline. Since Pythagoras was believed to have forbidden <term>the eating of flesh</term> <note>original: σαρκοφαγίαν (sarkophagian)</note> based on the fiction that human souls migrate into the bodies of living creatures—and for that reason forbade the killing of any animal, as Juvenal also attests: "He abstained from all animals just as if from a human"—they thought it was a divine law to allow serpents, which were born from the neighboring marshes, to live. The multitude of these grew so great that they abandoned the city, as Pliny also testifies. Therefore, the common saying that Amyclae perished by silence might also seem to have originated here, because the observation of Pythagorean dogma brought destruction upon them. The first rule of this dogma is <term>restraint of speech</term> <note>original: ἐχεμυθία (echemythia)</note>, that is, silence, which he imposed for five years upon those who wished to be initiated into his philosophy, as Aulus Gellius declares. Furthermore, regarding Servius's claim that the Laconians belonged to the Pythagorean faction, I do not recall reading this in any other author, except for what Plutarch records in his *Table Talk*: that the Tyrrhenians were so addicted to this philosopher's decrees that they used to observe even those things he prescribed through symbols with a ridiculous superstition. Either the people of Amyclae were from these groups, or they were followers of the same institution. Silius Italicus mentions the silence of Amyclae:
> ...and Amyclae, which silence destroyed.

Catullus also mentions it, unless the title of the poem "On Spring" is misleading, which our friend Aldus Manutius recently showed us, having been found in a very ancient library in France:
> While they were silent, silence destroyed Amyclae.

One may adapt the proverb to various uses: for instance, if someone lost loaned money because they did not summon the debtor, or if they lost possession by the "right of prescription" (as they call it), one might call it the "silence of Amyclae." Or if someone, pleading their case too boldly and being ordered to answer quietly, says: <term>Silence destroyed Amyclae</term> <note>original: τὰς ἀμύκλας ἡ σιγὴ ἀπώλεσεν</note>. The Greeks call this useless silence <term>speechlessness</term> <note>original: ἀμυξίαν (amyxian)</note>, and the opposite vice <term>loquacity</term> <note>original: ἀδολεσχίαν (adoleschian)</note>. Plutarch’s precepts exist regarding both.

### You are more timid than the one looking out.
### II

<term>A hare looking out from the acanthus</term> <note>original: λαγὼς ὁ ἐπ’ ἀκάνθοντος</note>. That is: You are more fearful than one who peers out. It is said of a man who is excessively afraid. They say it arose from a story of this kind: A certain man, timid by nature, having heard of the fame of Hercules, had hidden himself out of fear in a certain cave. Later, when he happened to peer out and saw Hercules passing by chance, he was struck dead by immoderate fear and immediately stiffened, turning into a rock. This rock is still seen in the likeness of a man, as if in the aspect of one looking out. Whence they call that rock <term>the hare on the acanthus</term> <note>original: λαγὼ ἐπ’ ἀκάνθοντα</note>. Suidas is the authority. Zenodotus also mentions it, as he does the one following.

### More timid than Pisander.
### III

<term>Pisander the hare</term> <note>original: λαγὼς ὁ πίσανδρος</note>. That is: More timid than Pisander. This was also once said of those who were immoderately fearful. They say that Pisander was of such prodigious timidity that he was afraid he might see his own soul somewhere, having left him while he was still alive. This seems to be the same as that saying of Cicero: "To be afraid of one's own shadow."

### Diomedean necessity.
### IIII

<term>Diomedean necessity</term> <note>original: Διομήδεια ἀνάγκη</note>. This is said of those who do something driven by force, not of their own will. It is used by Plato in the sixth book of the *Republic*: <term>The so-called Diomedean necessity makes him do everything that is approved there</term>. That is: It is a Diomedean necessity, as they say, to do whatever they approve. Some trace the origin of the adage to that Thracian Diomedes, who...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

it is said that the shore compels its guests to have relations with his most hideous daughters; once this was done, he would kill them. From this the fable spread that the mares of Diomedes were accustomed to eating men in place of fodder—namely, that these daughters, driven by men, were called "mares." And indeed, the commentator on Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen* interprets it in this sense, where this verse is found:
<note>original Greek: Καὶ ταῦτ’ ἀνάγκη μ’ ἐστὶ διομήδ’ ἀγάγειν</note>
"And it is necessary for me to lead this Diomedean [necessity]."
A young man asks whether there is any necessity for him to pursue an old woman. She responds that there is, and a "Diomedean" one at that. Others refer it to Diomedes, the leader of the Greeks, bringing forward a story of this kind: When Diomedes and Ulysses were returning at night after having stolen the Palladium <note>A sacred statue of Athena that protected Troy</note> by their common effort, Ulysses, in order to transfer the glory of the deed to himself alone, intended to kill Diomedes who was walking ahead and carrying the Palladium with him. And so, when he had brandished his sword at the other's head from behind, Diomedes noticed the shadow of the sword by the light of the moon, dodged the blow, and having seized Ulysses, bound his hands and compelled him to walk in front, repeatedly striking his back with the flat of his sword. Hence, "Diomedean necessity." Suidas and Zenodotus record roughly this same account.

### To the old stalls.
<note>original Greek: Εἰς ἀρχαίας φάτνας</note> That is, *To the old stalls.* It was said against those who, having been shaken out of some more elegant life, are reduced to their former thinness. Or, on the contrary, concerning those who are restored to their former fortune from which they had fallen; or those who betake themselves to their accustomed companionship. It is a metaphor taken from animals, for whom familiar and well-known stalls are usually most pleasing. Plautus also used it in *The Weevil*: "He could not be held back by an iron catapult from returning here to eat at his own stall."

<margin>VI</margin>
### Another life, another diet.
<note>original Greek: Ἄλλος βίος, ἄλλη δίαιτα</note> That is, *Another life, another way of living.* This will apply to those who, having changed their fortune for the better, likewise change their way of life and character. It is a metaphor from those who begin to live more elegantly when a more elegant situation has fallen to them. Aristophanes alluded to this in *Plutus* <note>The god of Wealth</note> when he says:
"Then, having become rich, he no longer takes pleasure in lentils." ->that is,<-
"But before this, because of poverty, he devoured everything."
Concerning a young man now loathing an old female friend after he had ceased to be in want. Horace alluded to this:
"The age is not the same, nor is the mind."

<margin>VII</margin>
### You ought to be dragged through the middle of a ring.
<note>original Greek: Διὰ δακτυλίου δεῖ σε ἑλκυσθῆναι</note> That is, *You must be dragged through a ring.* This will apply to one who becomes exceedingly thinned and slender in body, whether by disease, or care, or study, or some other thing. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
"And so indeed you might drag me through a ring." ->that is,<-
These are the words of an old woman wishing to seem so wasted away and exhausted by grief that she could be dragged through a ring. For my part, I think the adage is taken from a game in which an egg, softened in vinegar, is dragged through a ring. Pliny mentions this in Book 10, Chapter 60. It was a matter of magic to pass something through a ring. For the brain of a goat, passed through a gold ring before milk was given to infants, was instilled as a drop against the "comitial" disease <note>Epilepsy</note> and other diseases of infants, as the same author testifies in Book 28, Chapter 10.

<margin>VIII</margin>
### The old woman acts the Bacchant.
<note>original Greek: Γραῦς βακχεύει</note> That is, *The old woman acts the Bacchant.* It was customary to say this of those who, contrary to their age, are indecorously playful. For while the license of the Bacchanalia is permitted to young women in some way, it is certainly most foul in old women. Since it is a species of madness for an old woman to love, or to drink, or to lead dances, or to indulge in other girlish games.

<margin>IX</margin>
### The goatish old woman.
<note>original Greek: Γραῦς καπριῶσα</note> That is, *The goatish old woman.* Concerning an old woman still itching with untimely lust, and as Plautus says, "acting like a bitch in heat." Aristophanes in *Plutus*: <margin>But when</margin>
"The old woman devours the provisions of goatish lust." ->that is,<-
"But he knew how to devour the provisions of the goat-like old woman."
Concerning a young man, to whom a lustful old woman supplied everything, so that in turn from him [he might receive] pleasure...

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
<page-num>295</page-num>

<note>The text begins mid-sentence discussing the lust and odor of goats.</note> will bring. The lust of goats is well known, as is their odor, which follows them even when they are in heat.

<margin>To weep at the stepmother’s grave.</margin>

## To weep at the stepmother’s tomb.
->X<-

That is, to cry at the stepmother’s grave is to feign a gesture of sorrow when in reality you are rejoicing. For it is not natural for a stepson to take the death of a stepmother badly; nevertheless, for the sake of duty, he sometimes weeps at the tomb. This can be aptly said of the heirs of a wealthy man, regarding whom that mime of Publilius <note>Publilius Syrus, a Roman writer of mimes famous for his moral maxims.</note> exists, which is especially elegant:
>The heir’s tears are a mask for laughter.<

## Elephants give birth more quickly.
->XI<-

There are some who think this should also be numbered among the adages, because it was written by Pliny the Elder in the preface to his *Natural History*: "For regarding the grammarians," he says, "I have always expected a birth against my little books which I published on grammar; and they have repeatedly suffered miscarriages for ten years now, when even elephants give birth more quickly." Thus far Pliny. Therefore, one may use these words to signify immoderate hesitation and the overly slow efforts of certain people. Furthermore, regarding the birth of elephants, Plautus says in *Stichus*: "I have often heard it commonly said that a pregnant elephant is accustomed to be so for ten continuous years." Pliny supports this in Book VIII: "The common people believe they carry in the womb for ten years." Although Aristotle thinks they give birth in two years, and not more often than once each. Theophrastus reports that a certain Indian tree does not bear fruit before a hundred years. In Latin, those who are laboring or intending something in their mind are said to be "in labor" <note>original: "parturire"</note>. Hence, it will be permitted to turn the adage into this form: "When at last will you give birth, I pray, to that which you have been in labor with for so many years now, so that even elephants do not take longer?"

<margin>To collect tribute from a dead man.</margin>

## To demand tribute from a dead man.
->XII<-

That is, those who amass riches from everywhere by right or wrong were said to demand tribute from a dead man. Aristotle cites this in Book II of the *Rhetoric*: "Even if he should carry it away from a dead man." Or "he takes tax from the deceased," showing it was commonly said against those who shamefully hunted for profit from everywhere, from minute and sordid things—like Vespasian from urine—or from shameful things, like from pimping and the gain of the body; or when it is extorted from anyone at all: from friends, from the poor, from doctors, and finally even from the dead. It was given as a reproach to the Roman emperors that they dug up the monuments of the Corinthians and took away the Corinthian bronzes, with the very name of the act reproaching the foulness of the thing. For things taken in that manner were called <term>nekrosylia</term> <note>original: "νεκροσυλία" — grave-robbing or despoiling the dead</note>. The Attics call <term>pheron</term> <note>original: "φέρον"</note> the profit or tax which is brought in from any matter, even of money. Those who collect spoils of this kind they call <term>phorologous</term> <note>original: "φορολόγους" — tax-gatherers</note>, a race of men hated by all, and hated with the best of rights. Moreover, <term>pheron</term> is derived from the verb <term>pherein</term> <note>original: "φέρειν"</note>, which is "to bear," from which the word <term>foenus</term> <note>interest/usury</note> was also said by the Latins, a word which the ancients did not use except for the produce of the earth, which, like a most grateful debtor, returned a hundredfold for individual grains. Indeed, it is against nature, as Aristotle wrote in the *Politics*, for money to give birth to money. But today the matter is so accepted among Christians that, while farmers are despised—than whom no other race of men is either more innocent or more necessary to the state—usurers are held almost among the pillars of the church; even though those ancient mortals also condemned usury, the laws of the pagans moderated and restrained it, those of the Hebrews forbade it entirely, and the decrees of the holy popes detested and attacked it in every way. Not that I am particularly hostile to usurers, whose craft I see could be properly defended if the authority of the Fathers had not long ago condemned it. Especially if you look at the morals of these times, I would sooner approve of a usurer than this sordid race of merchants who, with tricks, lies, impostures, and disguises, hunt for a little gain from everywhere, buying here so that they may sell for double there, or plundering the miserable common folk with monopolies: and yet we consider these men, doing nothing else in life, to be almost the only honorable ones. I think this proverb is either the same as, or certainly very closely related to, the one we recorded elsewhere:

<margin>For he asks for flour even from statues.</margin>
->that is,<-
->He demands flour even from the statues themselves.<-

For as a joke he put "flour" for "tax," because all things are referred to food, and they used to place statues for the deceased for the sake of memory. Therefore, he who scrapes together tax even from here seems to extort it from the dead. Among the ancients, however, there was great religious respect for burial and the immunity of tombs. Now the madness of possessing has proceeded so far that there is nothing anywhere in the nature of things, not even sacred...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->Page 296<-

...nor is anything so profane that some profit cannot be squeezed out of it. And this is done not only by princes, but even by priests. Once, under tyrants—though they were still unrefined and did not yet fully understand what tyranny was—these things were common to all: the seas, the rivers, the public roads, and wild animals. Now, certain nobles, as if they alone were men, or rather gods, claim everything for themselves. The wretched sailor is forced, even at great peril, to change his course and to do or suffer whatever a most insolent pirate <note>Erasmus likely refers here to toll-collectors or local lords acting like pirates.</note> decrees—as if it were not enough for the unlucky man to struggle with waves and winds, unless these human storms were added as well. A harbor appears, and something is extorted; a bridge must be crossed, and a fee must be paid. A river must be traversed, and you feel the "right" of the princes; if you have a small pack, it must be ransomed from those sacrilegious men. And what is much more cruel than this: the very spirit of the poorest commoners is cheated, and the nourishment of the poor is gnawed away so many times by tithes <note>original: "decimis"</note> and taxes. It is not permitted to carry grain from your own fields unless it has been tithed. You do not grind it, you do not bake it, unless it is gnawed at again. Wines are not imported unless they are tithed multiple times. You do not store them in your cellar unless you give half, or certainly a quarter of the total price, as dregs to those most wicked Harpies <note>In mythology, Harpies were bird-like monsters who snatched food; here, Erasmus uses them to represent greedy tax collectors.</note>. Among some people, more than half of the beer (as they call it) is set aside for the prince. You do not slaughter a beast unless you pay the tax-gatherers; you do not resell a horse, bought with your own money, unless you pay something. I saw, when I was living in the countryside of Bologna—after Julius <note>Pope Julius II, known as the "Warrior Pope."</note> had already taken possession of that city—farmers in extreme poverty whose entire wealth consisted of two oxen (for by their labor they supported the whole family) paying one ducat for each ox. There are places where it is not free to enter into a legitimate marriage unless a tax is paid. But why should I try to list every single thing? The greed of these men surpasses all eloquence. There is nothing in existence from which they do not wring some gain. There is no limit, no end; daily they devise new ways of flaying the people, and whatever they have once seized by taking advantage of the times, they hold onto with their teeth. These things are hateful enough in themselves, but when they are carried out even more hatefully by insolent officials, they bring no small amount of ill-will upon the princes. Yet the princes think nothing is beneath them if profit can be gathered from it—that is, if the hunger of the thin increases so that the luxury of the great (or rather, the plunderers) may be fed. Nor are there lacking those who make no small profit from the crimes of the guilty, using laws like nets. Now, what magistrate is there, what office, what governorship, that is not bought among many? Finally, since so many things cannot fill this truly "leaking jar"—that is, the treasury <note>original: "fiscum"</note> of the princes—war is used as a pretext; the leaders collude, and the unhappy people are sucked dry to the very marrow, just as if a princedom were nothing other than a massive business venture.

However, although it is foul that Christian princes appear more inhuman in these matters than any ethnic <note>i.e., Pagan</note> tyrants ever were, it is somewhat less cursed than the fact that among priests also—for whom all money ought to be held in contempt, and whose duty it was to share their gifts freely as they were freely received—nothing is not for sale, nothing is exempt. What tragedies they stir up for those tithes of theirs! How hatefully they harass the wretched common folk! Baptism is not given—that is, one is not allowed to become a Christian—unless you pay. And so, under these "distinguished" auspices, you enter the doors of the Church. They do not approve a marriage unless you pay; they do not hear the confessions of the penitent unless they hope for a reward. They perform sacrifices for hire. They do not sing psalms for free, they do not pray for free, they do not lay on hands for free. They hardly bless you with a distant wave of the hand unless you give. They do not consecrate a stone or a chalice without a fee being paid. Even that truly papal duty of teaching the people has been corrupted by profit. Finally, they do not impart the body of Christ unless you pay. I will not even mention in the meantime how great a harvest is gathered from lawsuits, from "dispensations" (as they call them), from "pardons" (which the common people call indulgences), from the conferring of priesthoods, and the confirming of bishops and abbots. But what is done for free among these men, when even burial is bought, even in someone else's soil? Among the Pagans, a common tomb stood for the wretched poor; there was a place where you could bury whomever you wished for free. Among Christians, the dead are not even allowed to be covered by earth unless you rent a small space from a priest; and according to the price, a large and magnificent place will be given. If you pay the most, you will be allowed to rot in the church right next to the high altar; but if you give sparingly, you will be rained upon among the commoners under the open sky. It would be shameful if they merely accepted a price offered to them; now they call it their "right," and it is a wonder to say with what wickedness they demand it. That barbarian and gentile, Ephron <note>original: "Hebron" (Erasmus likely means Ephron the Hittite from Genesis 23).</note>, offered Abraham, an unknown guest, the gift of a tomb for free, and could hardly be persuaded by prayers to accept the offered money—and we priests sell the right of burial in another's land? Or rather, we rent out for money what is public as if it were private. And no one reaps this kind of harvest more greedily than those who bring nothing...

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...people, but they live entirely for themselves or certainly for the prince. Others sing that old song to us: "The laborer is worthy of his hire" <note>original: "is est operarius mercede." A reference to Luke 10:7</note>. This is as if there were no difference between a bishop and a fellow-soldier, or a ditch-digger. Servile labors are compensated with a price; the duty of Princes and priests is too sublime to be valued by a wage.

### The gull is in labor. XIII

<margin>The gull is in labor. That is, the Cepphus is in labor. <note>original: "Λάρος ὤδινει. id est, Cepphus parturit."</note></margin> In ancient times, this was said against those who promised great things but exhibited nothing worthy of those promises. They say the *cepphus* (or *cemphus*) is a small bird of slow wit—whence it passed into a proverb for stupidity—which some call a gull. Among these is Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek humanist and translator of Aristotle</note>, though others translate it as "coot." They say it lives on sea foam, is light with many feathers but has a tiny body, and when it is in labor, it cries out loudly. From this the proverb was born: *The gull is in labor*, used when someone makes a great display of themselves but is about to deliver very little. The interpreter of Aristophanes writes much the same in the commentary on the comedy *Peace*. Hesychius records that it is a very light bird flying about, easily moved by the wind; therefore, an inconstant and light-headed man is called a "gull." Pliny, in Book 8, Chapter 19, mentions a four-legged *cephus* which was once brought from Egypt and shown to the Romans, whose hind feet were like human feet and front feet like hands. He says it was never seen in Rome after that. But that, indeed, has nothing to do with the proverb.

### The mountains are in labor, a ridiculous mouse will be born. XIV

<margin>The mountain was in labor, then it brought forth a mouse. <note>original: "Ὤδινεν ὄρος, εἶτα μῦν ἀπέτεκεν."</note></margin> A common proverb, usually said of boastful men and show-offs who, through magnificent promises and the authority of their expression and dress, stir up a wonderful expectation of themselves; but when it comes to the reality, they bring forth mere trifles. Lucian uses this adage in the booklet titled *How to Write History*; he says the common people shout this at someone assuming the persona of a desirable Hercules or a Titan: *The mountain was in labor*. Athenaeus, in the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The Banquet of the Learned</note>, Book 14, relates that Tachos, King of the Egyptians, touched upon Agesilaus, King of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, with a taunt of this kind when he had come to bring him reinforcements in war: *The mountain was in labor, and Jupiter was afraid, but it brought forth a mouse.* Now, Agesilaus had a tiny body. Furthermore, offended by the saying, he replied: *And yet, eventually I shall appear to you as a lion.* It happened later that when a sedition arose among the Egyptians and Agesilaus did not stand by the king, the king was forced to flee to the Persians. Moreover, the Greek seems to be an anapestic verse. Horace also uses it in the *Art of Poetry*:
> What will this promiser bring forth worthy of such a wide gap?
> The mountains will be in labor, a ridiculous mouse will be born.

Porphyrio <note>A 3rd-century commentator on Horace</note> thinks it arose from one of Aesop's fables. It is told in this way: When once rude and rustic men saw the earth on a mountain swelling and moving, they flocked from all sides to such a horrific spectacle, expecting the earth to bring forth some new and great portent—the mountain being in labor, no doubt—and that the Titans would break out again to renew the war with the gods. At last, when they had waited a long time with suspended and astonished minds, a mouse crept out of the earth, and immediately a huge laugh arose from everyone.

### To promise mountains of gold. XV

<margin>To promise mountains of gold. <note>original: "Χρυσᾶ ὄρη ὑπισχνεῖσθαι."</note></margin> A proverbial hyperbole concerning those who promise immense things and display the most ample hopes. It is derived from the arrogance of the Persians, who, because of their veins of gold, used to boast of golden mountains. Plautus in *Stichus*: "Nor would he earn for himself the mountains of the Persians, which are said to be of gold." And the same author in *The Braggart Soldier* said "mountains of silver" for the same meaning: "Then he has mountains of silver, not just lumps." Terence in *Phormio*: "He enticed the old man by letter, almost promising mountains of gold." In which place I think it should be noted in passing—which I suspect escapes the common run of interpreters—that "almost" <note>original: "Modo non"</note> is said for what is among the Greeks *mononouchi* <note>original: "μονονουχὶ"</note>, that is, "all but"; it has the same force as if you said "nearly." For you will find "all but" used in the Greek manner both in Livy and in Suetonius, and more than once in Valerius Maximus. Apuleius in the first action of the *Apology*: "Who, if he is needy through avarice and insatiable for every gain, is not satisfied even by mountains of gold." Saint Jerome against Rufinus: "So that when you have promised mountains of gold, you do not bring forth even a scorpion coin <note>A very small, low-value coin</note> from your treasures." Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of Greek and Latin adages, focusing on metaphors for abundance, consensus, and mismatched comparisons.</meta>

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES<-

"And he defecated for eight months on mountains of gold." <note>original: Κἄχεζεν ὀκτὼ μῆνας ἐπὶ χρυσῶν ὀρῶν</note> That is, he spent eight months sitting amidst mountains of gold. He used "defecated" instead of "sat down," following the lewdness of Old Comedy. Phoenix of Colophon <note>A 3rd-century BCE Greek iambic poet</note>, as cited in Athenaeus, Book 12, speaking of the immensely wealthy King Ninus, says he made a sea out of a mountain—that is, possessing a sea of gold. Sallust spoke somewhat differently in the *Catiline Conspiracy*: "He began to promise seas and mountains." In the same manner, Persius says: "To promise great mountains." Thus, the <term>hyperbole</term> <note>rhetorical exaggeration</note> of magnitude lies not in the gold itself, but simply in the scale of the mountains.

<margin>XVI</margin>
### To draw with both hands.

"To draw with both." <note>original: Ἀντλᾷν ἀμφοτέραις</note> That is, to draw with both, understanding "hands." It is customary to say this of those who do something with the greatest effort. Likewise, Aristophanes in *The Knights*: "And with both hands he gulps down the public funds." <note>original: Κἀμφοῖν χεροῖν μυστιλᾶται τῶν δημοσίων</note> That is, he flees while scattering public goods with each hand. Close to this is that Homeric line from *Iliad* 7: "I know how to shift my ox-hide shield to the right and to the left." <note>original: οἶδ’ ἐπὶ δεξιά, οἶδ’ ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ νωμῆσαι βῶν</note> One also finds "reaching out with both hands," <note>original: ἀμφοῖν ὠρεγμένοιν</note> meaning to give abundantly and prodigally, or even very kindly. Plato in *The Sophist*: "And as the saying goes, one must not grasp it with one hand, but with both." <note>original: καὶ τὸ λεγόμενον δ’ οὐ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ληπτέον, ἀλλ’ ἀμφοῖν χεῖν</note> It seems that what is written in Aristides' *Cimon* departs somewhat from this form; he cites this passage from the hymn of some poet: "Asia groaned heavily, for she was struck with both hands by the enemy's might." <note>original: μέγα δ’ ἔστυγε ἀσία τὸ ἀντλᾷν γὰρ ἀμφοτέραις χερσί, κράτει πολεμίῳ</note> Closer is what appears in the same author's *Panathenaic Oration*: "But he drove with both hands until he brought both Greeks and barbarians as far as Attica." <note>original: ὁ δὲ ἀμφοτέρᾳ τῇ χειρὶ ἤλαυ’ ἄχρι οὗ μέχρι τ’ ἀττικῆς ἔλπωας ὁμῶ καὶ βαρβάρους</note> Although in this passage it can be understood literally, referring either to land and sea forces together, or to barbarians and Greeks. Since we also call a large group a "hand," as in Virgil: "A glowing hand of youths flashes forth." <note>original: Iuuenum manus emicat ardens</note> Regarding "With a full hand," it has been discussed elsewhere; the Greeks call this "with a rich hand," <note>original: ὑμνίᾳ χειρί</note> from which they also give Ceres the epithet *Hymnia*, just as we call her "Nurturing" <note>Latin: Alma</note> because she feeds us abundantly, and "Hymnian water," because it nourishes copiously.

<margin>XVII</margin>
### With one mouth.

"With one mouth," meaning with the highest consensus, is encountered everywhere among authors. Terence: "All men with one mouth said all good things." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the discourse *On Friendship*: "For there is one thing in human affairs concerning the utility of which all agree with one mouth." Seneca in *Epistles*, Book 11, Letter 82: "In such a diversity of judgments, all will affirm to you with 'one mouth,' as they say, that gratitude must be returned to those who deserve well." Aristophanes in *The Knights*: "And they all cried out as if from a single body." <note>original: οἵ δὲ ἐξ ἑνὸς σώματος ἅπαντες ἀνεκραγον</note> That is, they all shout together with one mouth. Plato in *Laws*, Book 1: "To harmonize all with one voice and from one body." <note>original: μιᾷ δὲ φωνῇ, καὶ ἐξ ἑνὸς σώματος, πάντας συμφωνεῖν</note> The same in *Republic*, Book 2: "For all sing from one mouth how noble a thing are both temperance and justice." <note>original: πάντες γὰρ ἐξ ἑνὸς στόματος ὑμνοῦσιν, ὡς καλὸν μὲν ἡ σωφροσύνη τε καὶ δικαιοσύνη</note>

<margin>XVIII</margin>
### You compare an eagle to an owl.

"You compare an eagle to an owl." <note>original: Ἀετὸν γλαυκὶ συγκρίνεις</note> Martial in a Scazon poem: "And you seek to make eagles similar to owls." The eagle has the sharpest vision, so much so that it gazes toward the sun "without blinking." <note>original: ἀσκαρδαμυκτῶς</note> And there are those who relate that this bird tests its chicks by this experiment to see if they are degenerate or genuine. In contrast, the owl flees the light of the sun by every means. Pindar in a certain passage compares jackdaws with the eagle.

<margin>XIX</margin>
### To herd foxes with lions.

To herd foxes with lions is to mix unequal and dissimilar things. Martial: "Why herd foxes with lions?"

### NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

<margin>Pindar in the Isthmian Odes.</margin>The fox relies on tricks, the lion trusts in strength. Although Pindar joined both together, indicating that a brave lion ought to excel in exhausting the labors of contests, while the fox excels in counsel. For he writes thus in the Isthmian Odes: <note>original: "Τόλμα γὰρ ἐοικὼς θυμὸν ἐριβρεμετᾶν θηρᾶν λεόντων ἐν πόνῳ, μήτι δ' ἀλώπηξ"</note> that is, *In spirit like the roaring lions in enduring labors, but in counsel a fox.*

->XX. An eagle in the clouds.<-

<margin>Aristophanes in The Knights.</margin><note>original: "Ἀετὸς ἐν νεφέλαις"</note> That is, *An eagle in the clouds*. Most interpret this as referring to a great matter indeed, but one which you cannot easily attain; others apply it to those who far excel the rest. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
->How I rejoice<-
->at the prospect of becoming an eagle in the clouds.<- <note>original: "Ω'πόρ' ἥδομαι γενησόμενος ἀετὸς ἐν νεφέλαις"</note> That is,
->I rejoice in that name,<-
->because I shall clearly become an eagle in the clouds.<-
These are the words of the Athenian people, promising themselves that they will rule the entire world. And a little further down in the same comedy, it is pronounced like an oracle:
->An eagle in the clouds, and King of all the earth.<- <note>original: "Ἀετὸς ἐν νεφέλαις, καὶ πάσης γῆς Βασιλεύς"</note> That is,
->For you are an eagle, and you rule over the whole circle of the earth.<-
These things are said of the Athenian people, unless perhaps one prefers an allusion to the vain hopes of this prince. Again in *The Birds*: *You shall become an eagle in the clouds.* The commentators warn that the poet alludes to an oracle once given to the Athenians, which predicted that the Athenians would surpass other cities by as great a distance as the eagle in the clouds is higher than other birds. Pindar likewise in the Nemean Odes, a passage we just touched upon, calls himself an eagle and his rival Bacchylides a jackdaw, clearly because he surpassed him by an immense distance:
->The eagle is swift among winged creatures,<-
->who quickly seizes from afar, seeking out<-
->the blood-red prey with its feet,<-
->while the croaking jackdaws feed on low ground.<-
The meaning of these verses is this: The eagle is swift among birds, which, flying suddenly from a distance, has snatched the bloody prey; but the talkative jackdaws feed on the ground.

->XXI. To chase flying things.<-

Akin to this is what Aristotle uses in the third book of the *Metaphysics*: <note>original: "τὰ πετώμενα διώκειν"</note> that is, *To chase flying things.* He is speaking of things that are exceedingly obscure and which are most difficult to track down. Not unlike that is the saying:
->Where are you heading, and at what do you aim your bow?<-
->Or do you follow crows everywhere with a shard or mud?<-
This is used for those who propose no certain goal of life for themselves, but live for the moment, changeable at any occasion.

->XXII. The cranes of Ibycus.<-

<margin>The cranes of Ibycus.</margin><note>original: "Αἱ Ἰβύκου γέρανοι"</note> That is, *The cranes of Ibycus*. This passed into a proverb among the Greeks; it is customarily said whenever, through some new and unforeseen chance, crimes are revealed and the wicked pay the penalty to those they harmed. They record that it arose from an event of this kind: Ibycus, a certain poet, when he had fallen among bandits and was about to be killed, by chance called upon a flock of cranes flying overhead to witness. Some time later, when those same bandits were sitting in the marketplace and cranes again flew overhead, one of them whispered to another: "Look, the avengers of Ibycus!" Those sitting nearby caught the remark and became suspicious, especially since Ibycus had been missing for a long time. Asked what that speech meant, they answered hesitantly and inconsistently, and being subjected to tortures, they confessed the crime. And so, as if by the evidence of the cranes, they paid the penalty for Ibycus—or rather, they perished by their own evidence, as the saying goes. Plutarch relates something very similar in his commentary *On Garrulity*. Ausonius mentions this adage in his *Monosyllables*:
->When Ibycus perished, the high-flying crane was his avenger.<-
There exists a Greek epigram on this matter, under the title of Antipater, which we shall not be burdened to transcribe:
->Ibycus, robbers slew you, when from the island<-
->you came to a small, deserted, pathless shore,<-
->but you called upon a cloud of cranes, who came to you...<-

<summary>This page explores classical proverbs regarding animal metaphors for character and the "Cranes of Ibycus," a famous story about how hidden crimes are eventually brought to light by fate.</summary>
<keywords>Pindar, Aristophanes, Aristotle, Ibycus, Ausonius, Antipater, Eagle in the clouds, chasing flying things, Cranes of Ibycus, Athenians, justice, metaphors</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

"Witnesses to the most painful death of those being destroyed.
Not in vain did you cry out; the avenging Fury
Took payment for your murder through the noise of these birds
Upon the Sisyphian land <note>original: "Sisyphian land" refers to the territory of Corinth</note>. O profit-loving tribes
Of pirates, why do you fear the wrath of those who live?
For not even he who previously slew the singer Aegisthus
Escaped the eye of the black-robed Furies."

I would have translated these verses in my usual manner, had not my guest—or rather my Pylades <note>A reference to the mythological Pylades, the ultimate loyal friend of Orestes</note>, and if there is any term even more friendly than that—Peter Gilles of Antwerp, already rendered them into Latin, and in my opinion, quite successfully. I shall include his lines here, both to gladly avoid this bit of labor and to eagerly seize the opportunity to mention an incomparable friend.

> Once, as you came to the deserted shore, O Ibycus,
> Robbers snatched your life away from you,
> While you implored the cloud of cranes, who came
> As witnesses to your death as you were dying.
> Yet it was not in vain, since by the clangor of the birds
> The Fury avenged the slaughter on Sisyphian soil.
> Alas, tribe of thieves, greedy for gain and plunder,
> Why did the anger of the gods not terrify you?
> Since not even Aegisthus, who had once killed the bard,
> Escaped the encounter with the black Furies.

Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> mentions this poet in the fourth book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, where he testifies that his poetry was exceedingly playful.

### More true than the events at Sagra. <margin>23</margin>

"More true than the things at Sagra." This was once said against skeptics, and those who only believe when taught by a great misfortune. It is recorded by Strabo in the sixth book of his *Geography*. He says that after Locri, the river Sagra flows, on whose bank are the altars of Castor and Pollux. Near these, ten thousand Locrians, together with the Rhegians, joined battle against one hundred and thirty thousand Crotoniates and reported a victory. From this event, the adage was born against the incredulous: "More true than the things that happened at Sagra." Many add that on the day the battle began, the outcome of the war was announced to those at the Olympic Games; the truth of the battle was discovered with such speed. Justin mentions this fight in his twentieth book, although he differs from Strabo on the number of the slain. Eustathius also mentions it in his commentary on the *Boeotia* of Homer, adding that it is usually said of things that are indeed very true, but not believed. Finally, Marcus Tullius mentions it in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*. For he says, "Regarding Sagra, it is even a common proverb among the Greeks, who, when they affirm something, say it is more certain than the events at Sagra."

### To receive the wooden sword. To present the wooden sword. <margin>24</margin>

"To receive the wooden sword" <term>rudis: a wooden practice sword given to gladiators upon retirement</term> means to be dismissed from duty. "To present the wooden sword" means to discharge someone; these are frequently encountered in suitable authors. The metaphor is derived from the fact that in ancient times, gladiators who were permitted to cease their gladiatorial duties were said to be "presented with the wooden sword." That cessation was granted by a rod, which they called a *rudis*, whence those dismissed in this manner are called *rudiarii*. Therefore, whoever is restored to leisure from any duty, either due to age or weakness, will be said to have "received the wooden sword." Horace in his first epistle:
> Having been watched enough and already presented with the wooden sword,
> Maecenas, you seek to shut me in the old school again.
Likewise Juvenal:
> Therefore he will give himself the wooden sword, if our
> Advice moves him.
Ovid:
> Thus, while slow old age takes away my strength,
> It was time for me also to be presented with the wooden sword.

Marcus Tullius in the second *Philippic*: "So good a gladiator, did you receive the wooden sword so quickly?" The metaphor will be more elegant if it is extended a bit further: as if someone were to exhort another to abstain from the labors of study and grant himself the wooden sword; or we might call one who has left courtly life a "veteran" <note>original: "rudiarium"</note> of courtly life. The opposite of this seems to be what Quintilian <note>referred to here as "Fabius"</note> says: "A candidate for sharp eloquence," although I personally think it should be read as "ancestral" <note>Latin: "avitae"</note> instead of "sharp" <note>Latin: "acutae"</note> in this passage.

<summary>Erasmus discusses the origins of the proverbs "Ibycus's Cranes," "More true than Sagra," and the "Rudis" (wooden sword), explaining their roots in Greek history, myth, and Roman gladiatorial custom.</summary>
<keywords>Ibycus, Sagra, gladiators, retirement, Peter Gilles, Cicero, Horace, ancient proverbs, cranes of Ibycus</keywords>

# CHILIADS. FIRST CENTURY IX

...for students of good literature. For those who seek office are properly called "candidates" <note>original: "candidati," referring to the white togas (toga candida) worn by Roman office-seekers</note>. But if the term is transferred elsewhere, it passes into the form of a proverb.

->**From a bad crow, a bad egg. XXV**<-

*From a bad crow, a bad egg* <note>original Greek: Κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠόν</note>, that is, a bad egg comes from a bad crow. This will be aptly used whenever a bad disciple comes from a bad teacher; a wicked son from a wicked father; an unpraiseworthy man from an unpraiseworthy country; and finally, a criminal deed from a criminal man. Some refer the metaphor to the nature of the animal, which is neither fit for human food itself, nor produces an egg useful for anything. There are those who say it happens that crow chicks devour their own parents if they do not feed them to satiety, and the adage is derived from this. Others prefer to refer it to a story of this kind: A certain Corax <note>The name "Corax" means "Crow" in Greek</note> was the first in Syracuse, after the death of Hieron, who began to profess the art of rhetoric for a fee. A certain young man, Tisias, made a bargain with him on the condition that he would only pay the fee once he had thoroughly learned the art. Later, when the art was known but he hesitated to pay the reward, Corax called his disciple to court. There the youth proposed a dilemma of this sort. When he asked what the goal of the art was, and Corax replied, "to persuade by speaking," the youth said: "Come then, if I persuade the judges that I owe nothing, I shall not pay, because I won the case; but if I do not persuade them, I shall not pay, because I have not yet learned the art." But Corax turned the dilemma back upon his disciple as a flawed and <term>reciprocal argument</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντιστρέφον (antistrephon), an argument that can be turned against the person who made it</note> in this manner: "On the contrary," he said, "if you persuade them, you will pay, because you possess the art and owe it by our pact; but if you do not, you will pay, because you were condemned by the sentences of the judges." When the judges heard this device, so crafty and so shrewd, admiring the cunning of the youth, they shouted out: *From a bad crow, a bad egg.* There are those who say this was shouted by the circle of bystanders when one person brought a lawsuit against another. Things of this sort are generally read in the *Prolegomena to the Rhetoric of Hermogenes*. From this story, unless I am mistaken, was fashioned the one told by Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights*, Book 5, Chapter 10, concerning the sophist Protagoras and his disciple Euathlus; although it is somewhat long and easily found, yet because it seems the most charming of all, I will not be reluctant to write it down. Gellius, therefore, having shown the flawed dilemma <margin>Aulus Gellius, Book 5, Ch. 10</margin> which they call <term>Antistrephon</term> because it can be turned back against an adversary in the same words, says: "Such is that well-known one which they say Protagoras, the sharpest of sophists, used against his disciple Euathlus." For the lawsuit between them and the controversy over the agreed fee was this: Euathlus, a wealthy young man, was eager to learn eloquence and the pleading of cases; he gave himself as a disciple to Protagoras and promised to pay a fee—a large sum of money as much as Protagoras had asked. He gave half of it immediately before he began learning, and he agreed to give the remaining half on the first day he pleaded a case before judges and won. Afterward, when he had been a listener and follower of Protagoras for quite a while, and had indeed made abundant progress in the study of eloquence, he nevertheless would not take on any cases. As a long time passed, and Protagoras saw him doing this so as not to pay the rest of the fee, he formed a plan which he thought was clever: he decided to seek the fee based on the pact and contested the suit with Euathlus. And when they had come before the judges to present and establish the case, Protagoras began thus: "Learn, most foolish young man, that in either way it happens that you must pay what I seek, whether the judgment is pronounced against you or for you. For if the suit is given against you, the fee will be owed to me by the sentence, because I have won; but if the judgment is in your favor, the fee will be owed to me by our pact, because you have won." To this Euathlus replied: "I could have met such a double-edged trap by not speaking myself and using another advocate. But there is a greater prelude for me in this victory, when I defeat you not only in the case, but also in the argument. Learn therefore you also, most wise master, that in either way it happens that I shall not pay what you seek, whether the judgment is pronounced against me or for me. For if the judges find for me in the case, nothing will be owed to you by the sentence, because I have won; but if they pronounce against me, I owe you nothing by the pact, because I have not won." Then the judges, thinking this was doubtful and inexplicable because of what was said on both sides, lest their sentence in favor of either party should destroy itself, left the matter undecided and postponed the case to a very distant day. Thus far Gellius. But why should the judges not have rightfully pronounced at least this sentence: *From a bad crow, a bad egg*? Lucius Apuleius tells the same story in the books of the *Florida*—I will not say more copiously, for it cannot be told more copiously than it was related by Gellius—but yet more flowery and, so to speak, more pictorially. Aristophanes mentions Aeschylus in *The Frogs*, and likewise in *The Acharnians*.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<margin>XXVI</margin>
->Out of the wicked comes forth wickedness.<-

This harmonizes with that Hebrew saying from the first book of Kings, chapter 24 <note>original: "Ab impijs egredietur iniquitas." See 1 Samuel 24:13 in modern Bibles.</note>, which David specifically cites as an ancient proverb: *Out of the wicked comes forth wickedness.* It signifies that something evil always arises from the dishonest, while no evils proceed from the good. Therefore, there was no reason for Saul to fear being killed by David. Such an impious deed could only be perpetrated by the impious; David would not stain his hands with the murder of a king. Furthermore, if it pleases anyone to know, the proverb is pronounced in the Hebrew tongue in this manner: <note>original: מרשעים יצא רשע (Mersha'im yetze rasha)</note>. Indeed, many proverbs have this peculiar quality: they demand to be sounded in the language in which they were born; if they migrate into a foreign tongue, much of their grace departs. Just as there are certain wines that refuse to be exported and do not maintain the genuine grace of their flavor except in those places where they are produced. Nearly the same thing is said among the Greeks in a proverbial verse:
*For from a noble mind, good deeds are born.* <note>original: γνώμης γὰρ ἐσθλῆς ἔργα χρηστὰ γίγνεται</note>
That is:
From honest souls, honest acts flow forth.

<margin>XXVII</margin>
->A Lemnian evil.<-

<note>original: Λήμνιον κακόν (Lemnion kakon)</note>. That is, a Lemnian evil; used for evils that are immense and pitiable. The history from which the adage was born is told in various ways, and it is of no great importance to pursue it too anxiously. Herodotus, in his book *Erato*, mentions both the proverb and the history to roughly this effect: The Pelasgians, having been expelled by force from Attica, inhabited Lemnos. Wishing to take revenge on the Athenians for this injury, and being well-acquainted with their festival days and ceremonies, they set an ambush and carried off the wives of the Athenians while they were performing sacred rites to Minerva at Brauron. Having transported these women to Lemnos by ship, they used them as concubines. However, when the women bore many children, they raised them all in the Athenian customs and taught them to speak the Attic tongue. Thus it happened that the boys would not associate with the Pelasgian girls, and if ever a Pelasgian tried to strike one of them, all the "Athenians" would band together to bring him aid. In short, the Attic youth grew so strong that in most matters they seemed to hold the upper hand. Therefore, it seemed best to the Pelasgians to slaughter the sons born of the Attic women. This they carried out, even killing the mothers. Afterward, driven by sterility, childlessness, pestilence, and many other evils, they consulted the Delphic oracle on how they might be relieved of their calamities. From this, Herodotus says, the proverb spread throughout all Greece, so that huge and pitiable evils were called "Lemnian." Some think the adage was born from this, others from the fact that at one time the Lemnian women, offended by the foul smell of their husbands, destroyed them all with the help of Hypsipyle <note>Erasmus writes "Thoas," the father of Hypsipyle, whom she actually saved.</note>. Euripides mentions this in *Hecuba*:
*And the women utterly cleared the males out of Lemnos.* <note>original: Καὶ λῆμνον ἄρδην ἀρσένων ἐξῴκισαν</note>
Likewise Seneca in *Agamemnon*: *And Lemnos, noble for its crime.*

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
->You have caught a cicada by the wing.<-

<note>original: Τέττιγα πτερῶ συνείληφας (Tettiga ptero syneilephas)</note>. That is, *You have caught a cicada by the wing.* It is said against those who provoke someone to their own disadvantage. Lucian, in *The False Logician*, writes that the iambic poet Archilochus—who was exceptionally well-equipped for speaking ill—responded in this way to someone by whom he had been provoked with insults: *You have caught a cicada by the wing.* Now, there is a certain wonderful and prodigious talkativeness in this insect, especially when the sun is burning hot. Pliny denies that they have a voice, but rather a creaking sound made by friction; and it emits that sound not with its wings, as flies, bees, and gnats do (for in those the creaking stops as soon as they stop flying), but in the cicada, if you press its wings, it shrieks even more vehemently. He says there are two cavities in its chest, and by the rubbing of a moving membrane as air enters, the sound is produced from its vitals. Therefore, just as if you grasp a naturally talkative cicada by the wing it cries out more loudly, so if you give a poet an occasion for a quarrel, not only will he not be silent, but he will shriek more loudly and smear all his "black papers" with bile <note>A metaphor for writing bitter, satirical poetry.</note>. Hence they say Plato warned that no one should make an enemy of a poet. And Horace said: *The irritable race of bards.*

<margin>XXIX</margin>
->A Tenedian axe.<-

<note>original: Τενέδιος πέλεκυς (Tenedios pelekys)</note>. That is, a Tenedian axe. It will apply either to those who judge and punish too severely, or to those who quickly settle controversies and the ambiguities of lawsuits. It is derived from the fact that formerly the King of Tenedos, carrying an axe, was accustomed to hear lawsuits; and once the case was decided, pro-

<keywords>wickedness, David and Saul, Lemnian massacre, Pelasgians, cicadas, Archilochus, poets' anger, Tenedian axe, swift justice</keywords>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 9
<sig>C 2</sig>

immediately to strike with an axe the one who had committed the injury; or because a certain King of Tenedos <note>Tenedos is a small island in the Aegean Sea, near ancient Troy.</note> passed a law against adulterers, that the bodies of both should be cut down with an axe, and he even carried out the example of this law upon his own son. Furthermore, he ordered that an image be engraved on their coinage: an axe on one side, and two faces emerging from the same neck on the other. Stephanus also mentions this in his catalog of cities. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Pythian Oracles*, shows that the axe was a type and emblem of the Tenedians, and this was because of the crabs found among them in the place called Asterium. The words of Plutarch, if anyone should happen to require them, are these: <gloss>original: "Just as the people of Selinus are said to have once dedicated a golden celery plant, so the Tenedians dedicated the axe, because of the crabs produced among them near the place called Asterium. For they alone, it seems, have the shape of an axe on their shell."</gloss> Lucian in the *Philopseudes*: <gloss>original: "Then that happened; for you may consider that an axe has come to me, even for lies."</gloss> That is: For thinking according to that which is commonly said, that a certain axe has come to me to cut through lies. To me, it seems to be an allusion to the deed of Alexander the Great, who cut the insoluble knot on Midas's wagon with a sword, as we have shown elsewhere. Pausanias also mentions this in his *Description of Greece*, but he refers the origin of the adage to another story. He writes that the axe was among the votive offerings, a monument of Periclytus, whose father was Euthymachus of Tenedos, concerning which a hidden story is told: that Cycnus was the son of Neptune and reigned in Colonae. Furthermore, Colonae was in the Trojan land, opposite the island whose name was Leucophrys. Now when Cycnus had a daughter named Hemithea and a son named Tennes by Proclea (she was the daughter of Clytius and sister of Caletor, whom Homer in the 15th book of the *Iliad* records was killed by Ajax because he had thrown fire onto the ship of Protesilaus). When she had died, Philonome, daughter of Craugasus, succeeded her. When she fell in love with Tennes and was rejected, she lied to her husband, claiming that she had been solicited for debauchery by him against her will. Cycnus, persuaded by his wife's lie, shut Tennes together with his sister in a chest and cast them into the sea. However, they were washed up unharmed on the island of Leucophrys, whose name was later changed from Tennes to Tenedos. When Cycnus finally discovered he had been deceived, he sailed to his son, both to acknowledge his error and to beg for forgiveness. But when Cycnus had landed and tied his ship to some tree or rock, Tennes, out of anger, cut the ropes with an axe. From this, the proverb began to be said of those who obstinately deny something: "This is the man who could cut through this or that with a Tenedian axe." A different history is now related to this in the proverb: "A man of Tenedos."

### The treasure turned out to be coals.
-> XXX <-

<gloss>original: "The treasure has turned out to be coals."</gloss> That is, the treasure was nothing but charcoal. This applies to those who are frustrated in their hope, and who, having expected magnificent things, find mere trifles. It seems to have arisen from a certain event in which someone, digging in the hope of treasure, found buried coals. That matter turned into a joke and common talk. For in ancient times, coals were usually buried in the earth to mark the boundaries of fields, because, as Saint Augustine testifies in his work *The City of God*, no substance is more durable or more perpetual than coals buried under the earth. Lucian in *Zeuxis*: <gloss>original: "And according to the proverb, our treasure was coals."</gloss> Again in the *Philopseudes*: <gloss>original: "For in that speech, you who were believed to be a treasure turned out to be coals to us."</gloss> The same in *Timon* concerning found gold: <gloss>original: "But indeed, I fear lest I find coals upon waking."</gloss> Again in *The Wishes*: <gloss>original: "And your treasure shall be coals."</gloss> Alciphron in a certain letter: <gloss>original: "Will not all my treasures turn into ashes?"</gloss>

### Eight-foots.
-> XXXI <-

<gloss>original: "Eight-foots."</gloss> That is, in a Scythian proverb, those who possessed two oxen and one wagon were called "Eight-foots." Lucian in *The Scythian or The Guest-Friend*: <gloss>original: "Those who are called Eight-foots among them."</gloss> It can be said as a joke against a man who thinks himself wealthy, or against one whose riches are merely rustic. For among rustic riches, Hesiod especially counts <gloss>original: "the plowing ox."</gloss> The allusion to the scorpion, the polyp, the cuttlefish, and the squid—creatures with eight feet, and for that reason called *octapoda* by the Greeks—adds grace to the proverb. The scorpion also gave place to a proverb: "You are stirring up an eight-foot." Since this animal is said to sleep under every stone. Suidas writes *oktapoun* with an omega, not an omicron.

<keywords>Tenedian axe, Tennes, Cycnus, treasure to coals, Eight-foots, Scythian wealth, Plutarch, Lucian, Greek mythology, proverbs</keywords>
