# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<margin>XXXII</margin>
*Better to run back again than to run badly.* <note>original: "πάλιν δρομῆσαι μᾶλλον ἢ δραμεῖν κακῶς"</note> That is,
It is better to run back than to continue a bad course.
A six-foot line of verse <term>Senarius: a line of six iambic feet, common in Roman comedy</term> celebrated as a proverb, the meaning of which is this: It is better to change a plan for the better than to persist in badly established ways. Lucian’s "The Ass" <note>A satirical Greek novel formerly attributed to Lucian of Samosata</term> turned this thought over in his mind, in a way not at all like an ass: *For that saying is true: better to run back again than to run badly.* <note>original: "Ἐκεῖνα γάρ δὴ τὸ τοῦ λόγου, πάλιν δρομῆσαι μᾶλλον, ἢ δραμεῖν κακῶς"</note> That is,
It finally seemed best, according to the common proverb,
To run back rather than to run wrongly.
Indeed, even in this age, people commonly say that he does not go entirely astray who turns back in the middle of his course; they mean to praise those who recover their senses from folly in good time.

<margin>XXXIII</margin>
<margin>Running alone, he won.</margin>
### Running alone, he won.
*Running alone, he won.* <note>original: "Μόνος θέων ἐκράτη"</note> That is, he won while running alone. Said of those who win when no one is competing against them. A metaphor taken from the racecourses. However, it is no trouble to win if no one competes with you. It is neatly said against those who are pleased with themselves, as if they had proved their case beautifully, when there is no one present to argue against them. Lucian in *Images*: *I think this is easy, and like the proverb, to win while running alone.* <note>original: "ῥᾴδιον δὲ οἶμαι τό γε ὧδε, καὶ τὴν παροιμίαν, μόνον θέοντα κρατεῖν"</note> That is, it is not difficult, according to the proverb, to win when you run alone. Akin to this is what we have reviewed elsewhere: *to win a deserted cause* <note>original: "ὁρμῆμα νικᾶν"</note>. Nor is it far from that other: *to win without dust* <note>original: "ἀκονιτὶ νικᾶν"</note>, that is, to win without a struggle. And *to win without sweat* <note>original: "ἀνιδρωτὶ νικᾶν"</note>, which we have mentioned elsewhere.

<margin>XXXIV</margin>
<margin>To know the lion by its claws.</margin>
### To judge the lion by its claws.
*To know the lion by its claws.* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῶν ὀνύχων λέοντα γινώσκειν"</note> That is, to judge the lion by its claws is to weigh an entire matter from a single conjecture—to know many things from a few, and the greatest things from the smallest. The proverb seems to have been born from the sculptor Phidias, who, as Lucian tells in *The Sects*, having inspected only the claw of a lion, calculated how large the whole lion was, and fashioned the whole from the evidence of the claw. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*, seems to attribute it to Alcaeus. For he writes: *Not depicting the lion from the claw in the manner of Alcaeus.* <note>original: "οὐ κατ’ ἀλκαῖον ἐξ ὄνυχος τὸν λέοντα γράφοντας"</note> That is, gathering the greatest things from the smallest. Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*: *I see what sort he is already, as if from a claw.* <note>original: "οἷον ἐξ ὄνυχος ἤδη ὁρῶ"</note> Basil the Great to Maximus the philosopher: *Speech is truly the image of the soul. And we might learn of you not through a letter, but as they say, the lion from the claw.* <note>original: "εἰκόνες ὄντως τῶν ψυχῶν εἰσιν οἱ λόγοι. καὶ μάθοιμεν ἂν οὐ διὰ γράμματος, ὅν, φασιν, ἐξ ὄνυχος τὸν λέοντα"</note> This is done by mathematical reasoning, as Vitruvius teaches in Book 3: that from even the smallest member, the proportions of the whole body may be gathered. Just as Pythagoras calculated the measure of Hercules' body from the stadium at Pisa, which Hercules had measured with his own feet. So from the pulse of a single artery, doctors judge the health of the whole man; so from the hair, or the belt, or a nod of the eyes, one may guess a man's whole life; so from a single letter we estimate a man's entire learning; from a single answer, we weigh a man's whole wisdom.

<margin>XXXV</margin>
### The tail bears witness to the fox.
*The tail bears witness to the fox.* <note>original: "Ἡ κέρκος τῇ ἀλώπεκι μαρτυρεῖ"</note> Usually said against those who reveal what kind of people they are by some small detail. For the fox has a tail larger and hairier in proportion to its body, so that it is not easy to hide. Otherwise, it might be seen as a dog. Hence it will apply to an outcome that declares what the rest was like. Some are lambs at the first approach, but in the end are found to be foxes.

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
### I judge the cloth by the hem.
*I know the fabric from the hem.* <note>original: "Ἐκ τῆς κρασπέδου τὸ ὕφασμα γινώσκω"</note> That is, from one small thing I make a conjecture about the rest. A metaphor from merchants, who, having inspected the edge of the cloth, easily judge the quality of the whole.

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
### I know by the taste.
*I know from a taste.* <note>original: "Ἐκ γεύματος γινώσκω"</note> That is, from the slightest experience. Also a saying from merchants, who, having only tasted the wine or oil, immediately pronounce judgment on the rest. For every fruit of a tree has its own particular flavor and character, and also a peculiar shape; whenever these changed into something different, it was considered a portent, as Theophrastus elegantly writes in the *History of Plants*, Book 2, Chapter 4. Hence Pliny says: "By that taste, I promise you the rest." Seneca: "And I wanted to give you a taste." And we call such an experience a "tasting." It would not be out of place to add here what Irenaeus relates...

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
<sig>C 3</sig>

as a proverb, so that you may learn the sea is salt, there is no need to drink it all. Indeed, from a few drops one may discover the nature of the entire sea.

-> I judge the Ethiopian by his face. XXXVIII <-

<margin>I recognize the Ethiopian by his sight. <note>original: Ἐκ τοῦ αἰθίοπα ἐκ τῆς ὄψεως γινώσκω.</note></margin> That is, I recognize the Ethiopian from his very countenance. A person displays by some sign what kind of character they possess. For an Ethiopian reveals his homeland by the blackness of his face, his curled hair, his swollen lips, and the whiteness of his teeth. For an Ethiopian can change his garment, but he cannot change his face.

-> I know the tree by its fruit. XXXIX <-

<margin>I know the tree from the fruit. <note>original: Ἐκ τοῦ καρποῦ τὸ δένδρον γινώσκω.</note></margin> That is, I know the tree from its offspring: I judge the man from his deeds. This proverb <term>parœmia</term> also appears in the Gospel writings, as we showed at the beginning of this work. A dirty garment, a shaved head, fasting, prayer, and a gloomy brow are leaves that frequently lie, just as that fig tree lied to Christ. But to patiently endure infamy for the glory of Christ, to wish well to the malevolent, and not to repay injury—this is the fruit of a good tree. If anyone performs these things constantly and eagerly, they prove a sincere soul. For pretense can neither be long-lasting, nor can it happen that nature, yielding at some point, does not betray the sickness of the soul.

-> To dance in the dark. XL <-

<margin>To dance in the darkness. <note>original: Ἐν τῷ σκότῳ ὀρχεῖσθαι.</note></margin> That is, to dance in the dark. It means to conduct business secretly, with no witness and no judge. It is translated from those who lead dances, whom no one in the dark can judge whether they move their feet correctly or otherwise. Lucian in *The Sects* says: "They say we would be dancing in the dark." <note>original: ἐν σκότῳ φασὶν ὀρχεῖσθαι.</note> From these words, it seems the adage can also be said against those who act rashly, with no judgment and no certain reason. Just as Lucian says that we, destitute of philosophy, would be as if dancing in the dark, so that whatever comes into our hands, we believe it to be that which was sought. It appears that Plato alluded to this secretly in the eighth book of *The Republic*: "Lest we discuss things obscurely, let us first define them." <note>original: ἵνα μὴ σκοτεινῶς διαλεγώμεθα πρῶτον διορισώμεθα.</note> For he who disputes confusedly dances, as it were, in the dark.

-> An Areopagite. XLI <-

<margin>Areopagite. <note>original: Ἀρεοπαγίτης.</note></margin> That is, an Areopagite. This was said of a somber and severe man, or even of a judge who was intensely incorruptible. One also finds "more gloomy than an Areopagite." <note>original: σκυθρωπότερος ἀρεοπαγίτου.</note> At Athens, the authority of the Areopagites was supreme; these were the judges who pronounced on capital cases with such integrity that they heard cases at night and in the dark, rather than in the light, so that they might look not at the speakers, but only at what was said. Lucian testifies to this in *The Sects*. Cicero alluded to the proverb in the first book of *Letters to Atticus*: "The Senate is an Areopagus <note>original: ἄρειος πάγος</note>, nothing is more constant, nothing more severe, nothing more brave." Likewise in the fourth book of the same work: "From which it was understood that those three Areopagites <note>original: τοὺς ἀρεοπαγίτας</note> do not care a straw for bribery, the assemblies, the interregnum, majesty, or finally the whole Republic."

-> An Attic look. XLII <-

<margin>Attic look. <note>original: Ἀττικὸν βλέπος.</note></margin> That is, an Attic look: it is just as if you were to say an impudent face. It was said against those who displayed impudence and confidence in speaking by their very expression. For the manners of the Athenians were noted for this vice. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
> And in his very face is an Attic look. <note>original: καὶ τὸ πρόσωπόν τ’ ἐστὶν ἀττικὸν βλέπος.</note>

Where Strepsiades speaks of his son returning from the Socratic school, whom he could guess from his very brow could plead a bad case, because he displayed I know not what of Attic cunning combined with impudence. Indeed, Achilles in Homer calls Agamemnon "dog-eyed" <note>original: κυνώπης</note> on account of his impudence. Hesychius warns that such people are also called "dog-glancers" <note>original: κυνωβλέπας</note>.

-> They sacrifice to the Lar. XLIII <-

<margin>At the sacrifice. <note>original: Ἐπὶ τῇ θύσῃ.</note></margin> That is, they sacrifice to the Lar <note>The Lar was a Roman household deity; the proverb refers to keeping things within the home</note>. It will be said against the stingy, who impart nothing of their own to anyone; or against greedy guests, who send nothing from the set feast to their friends, nor leave anything behind. For among the ancients, it was a religious matter not to carry anything outside from those things sacrificed to the Lares. Aristophanes alluded to this in *Plutus*, where Carion says to Mercury, who is begging that something from the sacrifice being performed inside be shared with him: "But," he says, "carrying out is not allowed." <note>original: οὐκ ἐκφορά.</note> Likewise in the same play, to a woman wishing to scatter sweets before the doors: "Nothing," he says, "before the hearth, as is the law." <note>original: οὐδὲν πρὸ τῆς ἑστίας, ὥσπερ νόμος.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explains several classical adages regarding character judgment, secrecy, judicial severity, and stinginess, drawing on authors like Lucian, Plato, and Aristophanes.</summary>
<keywords>Ethiopian, character, Areopagus, Athens, impudence, Attic look, sacrifice, Lares, stinginess, Erasmus, Adagia</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
kk

It is not fitting to carry anything out, but rather to bring it in. ->that is,<-
*Indeed, inside, as is the custom at the hearth of the Household God,* <note>original: "Larem"</note>
*For it is a sin to carry anything out; rather, it is proper to bring it in.*

Among the Romans, according to Plutarch, it was considered a sin for a table to be cleared entirely empty: either because they believed something should always be reserved for the future; or to habituate themselves to tempering their desires by abstaining from things present; or to win the favor of their servants by this means, with whom they might seem to share the table in some way; or because it was held as a religious matter that nothing should be seen empty during sacred rites. Furthermore, the table is a certain sacred thing. Cato, in his book *On Agriculture*, advises that the mistress of the estate should sacrifice to the Household God <note>original: "Lari"</note> on certain days, according to her means, with a crown added to the hearth. A contrary adage could be fashioned from this: **To sacrifice to Hecate.** <note>original: "τῇ ἑκάτῃ θύειν"</note> For in the sacrifices to this goddess, those who brought in the supper tasted nothing of it themselves, nor did they carry anything away except for the commotion and the smoke, as Plutarch says in his *Symposiacs*. The same was accustomed to happen if anything was offered to the other gods whom they call the "Averters." <note>original: "ἀποπομπαίους" - gods who turn away evil</note> This will be twisted to apply to those who look out for others but not themselves: they prepare wealth for others, but do not enjoy it themselves.

### He has made a "Protervia."
XLIIII

It was a religious requirement among several other sacrifices that nothing should be left over from the sacred feast; or if anything remained, it was to be consumed by fire—just as Moses handed down concerning the Paschal Lamb. Furthermore, the Romans call that type of sacrifice a *Protervia*. <note>A Roman sacrificial feast where leftovers were burned; the name implies "pressing forward" or "wantonness."</note> From this comes that celebrated and witty saying of Cato against a certain Albidius, who had consumed his entire patrimony through luxury, with the exception of one house which burned down in a fire: "He has made a *Protervia*," Cato said, because he had burned up, as it were, those things which he had been unable to devour. The author is Macrobius in the second book of the *Saturnalia*. To this effect is what is found in Athenaeus, book 8: Theocritus of Chios said to Diocles "the Glutton," <note>original: "Gurgiti"</note> who, after devouring a hot fish, said he had "blown out the heavens": "Only one thing remains for you," he said, "to drink up the sea; and thus you will have finished off the three greatest things of all: earth, sea, and sky." But whenever expenses exceed income, and the disease does not depart but turns into a second nature, what remains except for one to turn to evil arts to supply money for ever-growing luxury? And this is one of the greatest plagues of our Germany, especially among those who glory in the title of nobility—though there are those among them who feign nobility so they may do these things with impunity. They suborn people to call them "Young Lords," <note>original: "Ionckeri" (Junkers)</note> they boast of their fathers' castles, they add a plume to their hat, and they paint a shield in which a right hand balancing a sword carves up an elephant. They sign their letters with three letters: *Equ.* <note>Abbreviation for "Eques" (Knight)</note> If someone is born in some tiny village, say, "Bird-Rich" <note>original: "Ornithoplutus"</note> in the district of "Village-Equal," <note>original: "Isocomo"</note> he does not write that he is from "Village-Equal," for that is common, but "Bird-Rich of Village-Equal." And then they think they have the right to declare war on whomever they please. If the severity of the laws restrained the intemperance of such youths, there would not be so many upon whom they were forced to either inflict punishments or grant pardons. For through dice, cards, whores, drinking bouts, and idleness, one comes to debt, and soon to robberies and deceptions. They run into military service and return with plunder not taken from the enemy. Exercised in these fundamentals, they shrink from no crime. Among the ancients there were sumptuary laws; even in Corinth, a city more corrupt than the rest, there was a law opposed to those living more sumptuously than their family means allowed. Diphilus records it in Athenaeus, book 6, in these verses:

> Such a law exists, my best friend, among the
> Corinthians: whenever we see a man always buying
> expensive delicacies, we inquire from where
> he lives, and what he does. And if he has property
> whose income covers his expenses,
> they let him enjoy his life as an exceptional man.
> But if he happens to be spending beyond his means,
> they forbid him from doing this any longer.
> And whoever does not obey, they impose a fine.
> But if he lives luxuriously while having nothing at all,
> they hand him over to the executioner. By Hercules!
> For it is not possible for such a man to live
> without some evil, you understand. But he must
> either be a clothes-stealer by night, or a house-breaker...

<summary>Erasmus discusses the Roman "Protervia" sacrifice and uses it to critique the reckless extravagance and "fake nobility" of his contemporary Germany. He contrasts modern decadence with ancient sumptuary laws that punished those living beyond their means.</summary>
<keywords>Protervia, Cato the Elder, luxury, German nobility, Junkers, sumptuary laws, Corinth, social critique, debt, military plunder</keywords>

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

<margin>
Do not ask these things while sharing a drink,
nor in the crowded marketplace, nor when testifying
according to the law; we purge the land by knowing.
<note>original: "μὴ πυνθάνου ταῦτα..." These Greek verses describe the strict surveillance of spending habits in ancient Corinth.</note>
</margin>

->that is,<-

This was provided for by law here among the Corinthians:
If we see someone always buying provisions sumptuously,
we ask him where he gets his means of living, and
what work he does. If he possesses the resources
so that his income can cover these expenses,
we allow him to continue enjoying his goods.
But if his spending happens to exceed what he possesses,
we forbid him from doing this in the future;
if he does not obey, he is then punished with a heavy fine.
But if he who has nothing lives luxuriously,
they hand him over to the torturers. By Hercules!
For you should know that such a man cannot lead a life
without any evil, but it is necessary that he either
drives off plunder by night, or digs through the walls of houses,
or joins in business with those committing such acts,
or acts as a slanderer <term>sycophantam: a professional informer or professional accuser in ancient Athens</term> in the forum, or provides
perfidious testimony. We cast out this race of mortals
from this city, like refuse.
But today in Germany, even in famous cities, the law tolerates this race of spendthrifts and gluttons, who not only have nothing, but even owe much to many; yet no one says to them, "Hey you, where do the resources for your luxury come from?" If that were done, perhaps one would find that what Diphilus <note>A Greek poet of the New Comedy</note> wrote is true.

->The rope pulled in nothing for him.<-
XLV
<note>original: "τούτῳ μὲν μηδὲν ὁ κάλως ἐπεσπάσατο"</note> that is, That rope indeed pulled in no fish. A proverb in iambic verse, by which was signified labor undertaken in vain, where what one attempted did not turn out according to one's wish. It is transferred from the hooked line used by those fishing, who often pull back the hook empty. It seems to have arisen from a play by Aristophanes titled *Thesmophoriazusae*, where this verse is read. The same author alluded to the adage in *The Wasps*: "But it did not pull in." That is, it did not draw. Said of one who had set a snare for his father so that he might not go out anywhere.

->Let your hook always hang.<-
XLVI
With a similar metaphor, Ovid said in the *Amours*:
"Chance is powerful everywhere; let your hook always hang:
In the pool where you least believe it, there will be a fish."
->that is,<-
Fortune must always be tried, and every opportunity attempted. Similar to that other saying: "To move every stone" <note>To leave no stone unturned.</note>.

->A rich man is either a rogue, or the heir of a rogue.<-
XLVII
Saint Jerome writes to Hedibia in this manner: "Whence also that common saying seems to me to be most true: A rich man is either a rogue, or the heir of a rogue." If that saying of Hesiod is true—that what mortals commonly say is not entirely without grounds—this proverb should be weighed not at all carelessly by those who foolishly boast of their wealth. For great riches are almost never acquired without fraud. Either the possessor himself gathered them through right or wrong, or an heir succeeded him who acquired them by that path. Plato in the fifth book of *The Laws* says: <note>original: "ὡς τε ὁ λόγος ἡμῖν ὀρθὸς..."</note> that is, "Thus it is true, as we commonly say, that the very wealthy are not good men." This little verse from the comedies of Menander is also circulated among the Greeks: "No one ever became rich quickly while being just." That is:
->No just man ever turned out rich quickly.<-
Nor did that man look back <note>i.e., he was blunt</note> who is read to have said to Sulla as he was boasting of himself: "How can you be a good man, you who possess such great wealth, when nothing was left to you by your father?" Plutarch relates this in the life of that man.

->The Herculean knot.<-
XLVIII
<note>original: "Ἡράκλειον ἅμμα"</note> That is, the Herculean knot; it is read among the learned to mean a very tight and indissoluble bond. Seneca to Lucilius: "One knot remains for you, but it is a Herculean one." For so he calls...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...calls a syllogism that can scarcely be dissolved. This will apply to those who are joined by the tightest necessity. Plutarch almost indicates the origin of this in his *Life of Alexander*. He writes that Alexander the Great, having subdued the town of Gordium (the royal seat of Midas), wished to see that famous wagon, fastened with a marvelous craftsmanship made of rowan bark. A rumor had spread among the barbarians regarding this: whoever untied its knots was destined by the fates to rule the entire world. Alexander cut it apart with his sword. Aristobulus writes that he dissolved it very easily: namely, by removing the pin by which the yoke is attached to the pole. Ausonius alluded to this when writing to his friend Paulinus: "Truly, you have surpassed the persistence of Alexander of Macedon, who, when he could not loosen the thongs of the fatal yoke, cut them, and penetrated the cave of the Pythia <note>The Delphic Oracle</note> which it was a sin to lay open." Again, to the same man in a poem:
*I believe the Pellaean leader <note>Alexander</note> could have more quickly*
*Loosened those fatal thongs of the yoke, hidden by obscured*
*Beginnings, and concealing the head of the knot at both ends.*

Furthermore, it is clear enough from the words of Pliny in his *Natural History* (Book 28, Chapter 6) that the knot shown by Hercules was considered religious and sacred among the ancients: "And to bind wounds with the **Knot of Hercules** <note>A square or reef knot</note> makes the healing wonderfully faster." And even the daily growth <note>of a bandage or garment</note> is said to have a certain useful power when tied with such a knot. Festus Pompeius shows that it was an ancient custom for a new bride to be girded with a woolen belt tied with the Knot of Hercules, which the husband would untie in bed for the sake of a good omen, so that he himself might be fortunate in raising children; for Hercules left behind seventy children. Athenaeus (Book 11) relates that the Heracleotans, a people of Boeotia, are distinguished from others by this mark: <term>that they wear above their ears the so-called Heraclean bond</term> <note>original: ὅτι ἐπὶσημ’ υἱὶ τῶν ὤτων αὐτοῖς ὁ λεγόμενος ἡράκλειος δεσμος</note>, that is, a headband called the Heraclean. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] used a similar sense in his speech against Verres (Book 7): **With a beam-nail** <note>Latin: *Trabali clauo*, meaning something fixed unmoveably</note>. "And so that he might fix this favor, as they say, with a beam-nail, he investigated the cause of the Mamertines with his council." Horace also mentions these "Beam-nails."

### There once were brave Milesians.
XLIX

<term>There once were brave Milesians.</term> <note>original: Πάλαι ποτ’ ἦσαν ἄλκιμοι μιλήσιοι</note>
With this iambic verse, they used to mark those who had fallen from their former fortune or had degenerated from the customs of their ancestors. Briefly, it will apply to all who have ceased to be what they were and have become worse: to an old man, to a rich man turned poor, to a private citizen who once ruled, or to an obscure man who once flourished. The origin of the proverb is told variously by the Greeks. Some say the Milesians once flourished in the glory of war above all others, so much so that they overcame whomever they challenged. Accordingly, Polycrates, the tyrant of the Samians, when about to wage a certain war and intending to summon the Milesians as allies for that purpose, consulted the oracle on the matter. The God replied: *There once were brave Milesians.* Others bring forward a different story. When the Carians were planning a war against certain people and had decided to use the help of that nation which was then most powerful among its neighbors, some thought the Milesians should be summoned, while others thought matters should be settled with the Persians. Thus, Apollo, consulted on this matter, replied with the verse just mentioned. When the oracle was spread through all Asia, almost all the Milesians were slain in a battle joined with the Persians. Thus, the oracle passed into a proverb with a laugh. Again, others write: the Carians, while warring with Darius, went to the Branchidae <note>The Oracle of Apollo at Didyma</note> according to an old oracle which warned them to call the strongest to their aid; they consulted the god of that place whether they should use the help of the Milesians. He replied: *The Milesians were once brave*, signifying, of course, that they were now unwarlike and effeminated by luxury. But Zenodotus refutes this fiction by the very calculation of time. For he says this verse is read in Anacreon, who flourished in the age of Cyrus, King of the Persians, of whom Darius was the third successor. Therefore, Angelo Poliziano preferred to refer it to the Milesian customs turning toward softness, as Athenaeus also does in the *Deipnosophistae* (Book 12). Aristophanes uses this adage once or twice in the *Plutus*:
<term>And how he interprets from fortune, that</term>
<term>There once were brave Milesians.</term>
That is:
*And besides these things, he reported this also,*
*That there once were brave Milesians.*

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 9

It is spoken in the persona of a young man who is called back by an old woman; he had once courted her for profit when he was a poor youth, but having since become wealthy, he now loathes her in her exhausted state. Aristophanes alluded to this same idea in *The Wasps*, joking about old men:
<margin>original: "Ἦ πάλαι ποτ’ ὄντες ὑμεῖς ἄλκιμοι μὲν ἐν χοροῖς, ἄλκιμοι δ’ ἐν μάχαισιν. οἴχετ’ αὐτὸ δὴ τοῦτο μόνον, ἄνδρασι μαχιμώτατοι. εἴη ποτ’ ὦν, πρὶν ταῦτα. νῦν δ’ οἴχεται γε, κύκνου πολιώτεροι δή." <note>Aristophanes, Wasps 1060-1063</note></margin>
->that is,<-
You who were once brave in the dances, brave in battles: and according to this, finally, only the most warlike; these things were once before, long ago: but now they have perished, and you are now whiter than a swan. Aristophanes in *The Frogs* notes <term>Milesian blankets</term> <note>original: "μιλήσια στρώματα" — famous luxury goods from Miletus</note>, as the delights of the effeminate. It is also used by Synesius in a certain letter to a female philosopher, signifying that he had been reduced from his former happiness to calamity.

### We were Trojans.
<note>Latin: "Fuimus Troes" — a famous expression for "our time has passed."</note>

<margin>original: "Ἦμεν πρῶτον." <note>We were first.</note></margin>
that is, We were Trojans. This figure of speech is so commonly found in Greek tragedies that it has passed into an adage used whenever they signify that someone has perished. Euripides in *Hecuba*: <term>And I also once was</term> <note>original: "Κἀγὼ γὰρ ἦν ποτέ"</note>. Sophocles in *Electra*:
<margin>original: "Ἀπολώλαμεν δυστυχῶς, οὐδὲν εἰμ’ ἔτι."</margin>
->that is,<-
Wretchedly I have perished, hereafter I am nothing.
Virgil imitated this in the second book of the *Aeneid*:
We were Trojans, Troy was, and the great
Glory of the Teucrians. And again elsewhere:
And the fields where Troy was. <note>signifying it is now extinct.</note>
Ovid expressed the same sentiment with a different metaphor in his book *On Sorrows*:
We also flourished, but that flower was fleeting.
And our flame was from straw, and it was brief.
To the same figure belongs that line from the play by Terence titled <term>The Self-Tormentor</term> <note>original: "ἑαυτὸν τιμωρούμενον"</note>: "I had not, Chremes," as if signifying he had perished. Likewise that from Plautus's *The Rope*: "That word is most wretched, and the worst: 'to have had'." Furthermore, there is that noble utterance of Marcus Tullius Cicero concerning the executed conspirators: "They have lived," when he meant they were killed. They think this figure of speech became frequent from that very ancient song of the Spartan choir. Plutarch mentions this choir in the booklet titled: *How one may praise oneself without envy*. Diogenianus also mentions it in his collection of Greek adages. This choir consisted of a triple series and circle: of old men, boys, and youths. This was the song of the old men:
<margin>original: "Ἁμές ποτ’ ἦμεν, ἄλκιμοι νεανίαι."</margin>
->that is,<-
We were once vigorous young men.
<margin>original: "Ἁμές δέ γ’ ἐσσόμεσθα πολλῷ κάῤῥονες."</margin>
->Then this was the song of the boys:<-
->that is,<-
We shall one day be far superior.
<margin>original: "Ἁμές δέ γ’ ἐμέν. αἰ δὲ λῇς αὐγάσδεο."</margin>
->Finally, this was the song of the youths,<-
->that is,<-
But we are so now; or try us, if you wish.
Tyrtaeus established this choir among the Spartans, which they call a <term>triple-dance</term> <note>original: "τριχορείαν"</note>, according to the three-fold distinction of ages. For childhood is the entrance of life, manhood the progress, and old age the exit.

### The death of a Pyrausta.

<margin>original: "Πυραύστου μόρος."</margin>
that is, The death of a Pyrausta <note>A "fire-fly" or "fire-moth" in ancient lore.</note>. It was said against those who bring destruction upon themselves. For Zenodotus says the Pyrausta is an insect that flies toward lamps, and thus, its wings being burnt, it falls and perishes. He cites this line from Aeschylus:
<margin>original: "Δέδοικα μωρὸν κάρτα πυραύστου μόρον."</margin>
->that is,<-
I greatly fear the very foolish death of the pyrausta.
Aelian reports the same things about the pyrausta in the twelfth book of *On the Nature of Animals*, citing that passage from Aeschylus. Pliny also mentions the pyrausta in the eleventh book, thirty-sixth chapter: "Nature," he says, "also produces an element contrary to itself: for in the copper furnaces of Cyprus, from the middle of the fire, a winged four-footed creature the size of a large fly flies out: it is called the pyralis, by some the pyrausta (or, as some manuscripts have it, the pyrotus). As long as it is in the fire, it lives; when it has escaped by a slightly longer flight, it then dies." Of which kind...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s monumental collection of Greek and Latin adages, providing philological commentary and historical context for common proverbs.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Aristotle almost certainly recorded in the third book of *On Animals* <note>original: "De animalibus"</note> that a worm is born from older snow, which cannot survive if removed from the snow. We ourselves have seen this in the Alps. If one chooses to apply this to the present adage, it will also suit those who are *short-lived* <note>original: "ὠκύμοροι" (okymoroi)</note>, that is, those who perish quickly. Nor would it be ungracefully turned against those who can live nowhere except in their own fatherland; if they happen to travel abroad, they are offended by everything.

<sig>LII</sig>
->You have come after the feast.<-

*You have come after the feast* <note>original: "Κατόπιν τῆς ἑορτῆς ἥκεις"</note>. This is recorded by Diogenianus. It is said of those who were not present for some remarkable business because they arrived too late, after the matter was already finished. Socrates says in Plato’s *Gorgias*: "Have we, as the saying goes, come after the feast and are we lagging behind?" <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἦ τὸ λεγόμενον κατόπιν ἑορτῆς ἥκομεν, καὶ ὑστεροῦμεν;"</note>. It is also read in this way: *After the Panathenaea* <note>original: "Παναθηναίων κατόπιν"</note>, referring to the great Athenian festival. Likewise: *You have come after the Pythian games* <note>original: "πυθίων ὕστερον ἥκεις"</note>.

<sig>LIII</sig>
->Offered goods stink.<-

Offered goods stink <note>original: "Merces ultroneæ putent"</note>. That is, things offered voluntarily to those who do not ask for them are unwelcome. It seems to be a metaphor taken from merchants, who are accustomed to view goods offered voluntarily by a seller with suspicion, as if the seller were eager to push them off. The adage is cited by Saint Jerome in his *Hebrew Questions*: "It is a worn-out proverb," he says, "that offered goods stink." Hence, we also intentionally remain silent about things that should be said, so that you might more greedily wish to hear what is kept quiet. He uses the same in his letter to the virgin Demetrias. That sentiment of Ovid’s does not differ from this:

> What comes easily, we hold easily and sluggishly.
> What torments us with hope and fear, we delight to possess.

Indeed, it is still commonly on everyone's lips that a favor offered voluntarily is often unwelcome. Yet that witty Mime <note>referring to Publilius Syrus</note> contradicts this:

> It is doubly pleasing when, if something is needed, you offer it voluntarily.

<sig>LIIII</sig>
->To enter with unwashed feet.<-

*To go up with unwashed feet* <note>original: "Ἀνίπτοις ποσὶν ἀναβαίνειν"</note>. This means to approach an excellent task overconfidently and unskillfully, as if profanely and irreverently. It is a metaphor taken from sacred ceremonies, in which they commanded all things to be presented pure and washed. Lucian in the *Life of Demonax*: "He certainly did not come to these things with unwashed feet, as they say" <note>original: "οὐ μὴν ἀνίπτοις γε ποσί"</note>; that is, by no means untrained or ignorant. The same author, in *The Professor of Rhetoric*, notes those who approach the duty of rhetoric with "unwashed feet," meaning they are equipped with no good disciplines. Aeneas the Sophist says in a certain letter: "Most people indeed burst into sacred matters with unwashed feet, as the saying goes." Aulus Gellius in *Attic Nights*: "With unwashed feet and words, as they say, he criticizes the speech of a most learned man." Macrobius in the first book of the *Saturnalia*: "They pass by with unwashed feet." He is speaking of schoolmasters who neglect that hidden learning in Virgil’s poetry. Galen, in the seventh book of *On the Power of Simple Remedies*, calls such people *uninitiated* and *profane* <note>original: "ἀμυήτος καὶ βεβήλους"</note>. "And perhaps," he says, "it is not at all surprising if some who are not initiated into the mysteries have dared to read the books of the mysteries. But neither did those who wrote them write for the profane, nor do I write these things for those who are not yet exercised in the first rudiments." In general, the proverb calls any speech that is insufficiently modest, and too bold or petulant, "unwashed."

<sig>LV</sig>
->With unwashed hands.<-

*With unwashed hands* <note>original: "Ἀνίπτοις χερσίν"</note>. This is recorded by Diogenianus for that which is done irreverently and without preparation. It is likewise a metaphor from the purity of sacred rites. Hesiod in *Works and Days* forbids anyone from pouring a libation of wine to Jove in the morning with "unwashed hands":

> Never pour sparkling wine to Zeus at dawn
> With unwashed hands, nor to any other of the immortals.

And the same author forbids anyone to even step into a river or a spring with "unwashed hands." Hence the frequent mention of *hand-washing water* <note>original: "χερνίβες" (chernibes)</note> in Homer. That word sounds as if it means the washing of hands, with which they used to begin a divine rite in ancient times, and even a banquet...

<meta>catchword: banquet,</meta>

He draws on a vast array of classical sources including Plato, Jerome, Ovid, and Homer to explain these metaphors.</summary>

# THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD

...as a sacred matter. Gregory, surnamed the Theologian <note>Gregory Nazianzus</note>, in his *Apology for his Flight to Pontus*, joins both together: "with unwashed hands, as the saying goes, and uninitiated feet <note>original Greek: ἀνίπτοις χερσὶν... καὶ ἀμυήτοις ποσὶ</note> he introduces himself to the most holy things." That is, with unwashed hands, as is commonly said, and profane feet, they thrust themselves into the most sacred matters. Gaius, in the first book of the *Pandects*, under the title *On the Origin of Law*, says: "If it seems a sin, so to speak, for those pleading cases in the forum to explain the matter to the judge without making any preface, how much more unseemly will it be for those promising an interpretation to overlook the beginnings and not seek out the origin, and with unwashed hands, so to speak, immediately handle the material of the interpretation?" 

Both proverbs will be rightly used against those who either too boldly, or poorly instructed in those things which were necessary, invade a business; for example, if someone should take up the office of a prince, endowed with neither virtue, nor wisdom, nor experience in affairs. Or if he attempts to interpret the Divine Scriptures while being raw and unskilled in the Greek, Latin, and Hebrew languages, and finally in all antiquity—without which it is not only foolish, but even impious, to undertake the handling of the mysteries of theology. Which nevertheless, alas, what a sin! many now do everywhere, who, equipped with a few cold syllogisms and childish sophistries, by the immortal God, what do they not dare? What do they not teach? What do they not decree? If these men could see what laughter, or rather what grief, they provoke in those skilled in languages and antiquity, what monsters they bring forth, into what shameful errors they repeatedly fall: surely they would be ashamed of such great rashness, and would return at least once to the first elements of letters. 

Many judge correctly without the precepts of logic, not to mention sophisticated quibbles. Mortals were wise even before their god, Aristotle, was born. No one ever understood the meaning of another while ignorant of the speech in which he explained his meaning. Hence the blessed Jerome, when he had decided to interpret the secret scriptures, lest he should approach so great a matter with "unwashed feet," as they say: I ask you, did he equip his mind with sophisticated trifles? With Aristotelian decrees? With these even more trifling trifles? Not at all. What then? With inestimable sweat, he acquired for himself a mastery of the three languages. He who is ignorant of these is not a theologian, but a violator of sacred theology. And truly, with both hands and feet unwashed, he does not handle, but profanes, defiles, and violates the most sacred thing of all.

### The old age of an eagle.
<margin>LVI</margin>
<margin>The old age of an eagle. <note>original Greek: Αἰτοῦ γῆρας</note></margin>
That is, *Aquilae senecta*. It was said of old men who were more fond of drinking than eating. For Pliny, in book 10, chapter 3, reports that eagles perish neither from old age nor from sickness, but from hunger; because the upper part of the beak grows so much that it cannot be opened. Therefore, the eagle in its old age only drinks, or sucks blood from prey, since almost no birds with hooked talons use drink, except the kestrel and the kite—although these also drink very rarely. The author is Aristotle in the eighth book of *On the Nature of Animals*. But the same author, in the ninth book, telling almost the same things about the eagle's beak as Pliny, adds a fable given to this matter, which signifies that this happens to the eagle because formerly, when it was a man, it did an injury to a guest. 

Terence in *The Self-Tormentor*: "It truly seemed, as the saying goes, an eagle's old age." These are the words of Syrus flattering his master because he had drunk vigorously at a banquet the day before. There is, moreover, a certain thirstiness peculiar to the elderly. Either because nature desires to compensate for the coldness of age with the heat of wine, or because the cheerfulness of wine diminishes the annoyance of old age. Whence Plato also, while he entirely forbade the use of wine to youths, permitted it in moderation to men, and granted more generous drinking bouts to the elderly. Then, as to why old age is more prone to wine, Alexander of Aphrodisias also gives the cause in the fourth problem from the last: because increasing age diminishes heat, while wine both moistens and warms at the same time. Whence it is also commonly called "the milk of old men." It is said that even "the virtue of ancient Cato often grew warm with pure wine," as Flaccus <note>Horace</note> says.

### The old age of an eagle is the youth of a lark.
<margin>LVII</margin>
<margin>The old age of an eagle, the youth of a lark. <note>original Greek: Αἰτοῦ γῆρας, κορυδοῦ νεότης</note></margin>
That is, *Aquilae senecta, corydi iuventa*. Concerning a vivid and green old age, which is more excellent than the youth of some others. For an old eagle is better than a lark, even in its prime. Euripides expressed this without allegory in *Andromache*:
<margin>For a high-spirited old man is better than many a youth. <note>original Greek: Πολλοῦ νέου γὰρ κἂν γέροντι εὔψυχος ᾖ κρείσσων</note></margin>
> ->that is,<-
> An old man stands before many youths:
> To whom a noble mind is present.

### A camel, even a mangy one, carries the burdens of many donkeys.
<margin>LVIII</margin>
<margin>A camel even if mangy, takes up the loads of many donkeys. <note>original Greek: Κάμηλος καὶ ψωριῶσα, πολλῶν ὄνων ἀνατίθεται φορτία</note></margin>
That is, *Camelus etiam scabiosa, complurium asinorum tollit onera*. Concerning those who so far excel certain others that even when old, or otherwise sick, they are still more excellent than those who are healthy. Or concerning those who [carry on] with matters little pro...

even in prosperous times, he still carries more weight due to the remnants of his former fortune than others do with their affairs intact. Synesius <note>A 4th-century Greek bishop and philosopher</note> made use of this.

### To sing a palinode. LIX

*Palinodein* <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\lambda\iota\nu\omega\delta\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$</note>, that is, **to sing a palinode**, is to say things different from what you said before and to turn your opinion to the contrary. It is a metaphor taken from a deed of the lyric poet Stesichorus, whom Plato mentions in the *Phaedrus*. When he had disparaged Helen in a poem, he was deprived of his sight; but understanding the cause of his blindness (Achilles having announced it by the command of Helen, as Pausanias writes in his *Laconica*), he immediately "sang a palinode" and praised Helen, whom he had previously disparaged, and thus recovered his sight. Socrates jokingly says here that he wishes to imitate him and sing a palinode for Love, whom he had previously disparaged, before he is deprived of his eyes. In Greek, *palinodia* <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\lambda\iota\nu\omega\delta\acute{\iota}\alpha$</note> sounds like what you would call a "recantation." Indeed, Flaccus <note>The poet Horace</note> used this word in his *Odes*, promising a palinode to a girlfriend whom he had provoked with an insulting poem:

> Provided that to me
> You become a friend, with your reproaches
> Recanted, and restore my peace of mind.

The Saintly Augustine to Jerome: "Wherefore seize, I beseech you, a noble and truly Christian severity with charity, for the sake of correcting and amending that work, and 'sing a palinode,' as they say." Then, alluding to the story of Stesichorus, he says: "For the truth of the Christians is incomparably more beautiful than the Helen of the Greeks. For our martyrs fought more bravely for the former against this Sodom than those heroes fought for the latter against Troy. Nor do I say this so that you may recover the eyes of your heart—far be it from you to have lost them—but so that you may pay attention; for though you have them healthy and vigilant, I know not by what feigning you have turned them away." Responding to these things, Jerome says: "But if you should rebuke my words to my face, and demand a reason for my writings, and compel me to amend what I have written, and challenge me to a palinode, and 'restore my eyes' to me, in this friendship is wounded." Truly, regarding this palinode, Augustine himself later almost "sang a palinode," writing to Jerome that he had added the bit about Stesichorus rather foolishly and too "literarily." To me, it also seems rather arrogant toward a man so much more learned. But this is worthy of pardon in a young African and a bishop. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> to Atticus: "Prepare a divine palinode." John Chrysostom used this adage specifically in place of a proverb. Likewise Plato in his third letter to Dionysius.

### To turn the sails. To pull back the rope. LX

**To turn the sails** is to change one's opinion or way of life to the opposite. Horace in his *Odes*:

> To spread the sails, and to repeat the courses
> I am forced to abandon.
> Now backward...

The metaphor is transferred from sailors, who correct an error in their course by turning the sails. Persius, in his fifth Satire, innovating this somewhat, said **to pull back the rope** instead of changing one's purpose to the opposite:

> Those things I had granted above, I take back, and pull back the rope.

### Forgiveness for the first-timer. LXI

*Syngnome protopiro* <note>original Greek: $\Sigma\upsilon\gamma\gamma\nu\acute{\omega}\mu\eta$ $\pi\rho\omega\tau\omicron\pi\epsilon\acute{\iota}\rho\omega$</note>, that is, **Forgiveness for the first-timer**. It is recorded by Diogenianus. Those who, being unskilled, begin to be occupied in some new business, are to be forgiven if they have erred through inexperience. Chrysostom expressed the sentiment in a certain homily: "And to him who has stumbled at the beginning, we all give pardon on account of inexperience." This is also circulated: "Pardon for the one sinning for the first time." Pindar in his *Hymns* said "bearing the labor of two faults," meaning that a repeated crime ought not to go unpunished. Elsewhere we have recorded "twice a child at the same stone" <note>A reference to the proverb "to trip twice over the same stone"</note>. Celsus in the first book of the *Pandects*, under the title *On Laws and Senate Decrees*: "For the law ought rather to be adapted to those things which happen frequently and easily, than to those which occur very rarely; because legislators disregard things that happen once or twice, as Theophrastus says." The Greek words of Theophrastus are as follows: "For [the law] does not legislate for the one who transgresses once or twice."

### A Euripus of a man. LXII

*Euripos anthropos* <note>original Greek: $\mathrm{E}\ddot{\cup}\rho\iota\pi\omicron\varsigma$ $\ddot{\alpha}\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi\omicron\varsigma$</note>, that is, **A Euripus of a man**. This is said against inconstant men with uneven characters. It will also fit the shifts of fortune, which tosses the affairs of mortals up and down as if by a certain tide; so that Plautus rightly said in *The Two Captives*: "The gods hold us men like balls." The metaphor is drawn from a certain prodigious speed of the ebbing and flowing of the Euripus sea. Now, the Euripus is a part of the sea between Aulis, a port of Boeotia, and the island of Euboea; of which...

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

Strabo mentions this in Book 9, as does Pliny in Book 2; the latter remarks that some waters have a private nature of their own. For instance, the tides at the Euripus of Tauromenium <note>The Strait of Messina</note> change frequently, and in Euboea the tide ebbs and flows seven times in a day and night with such rapid conversion that, according to Pomponius Mela, it carries along ships even against the wind or when fully laden. Nor has a sufficiently suitable cause for this stupendous phenomenon been fully investigated by writers. Even Titus Livius, in Book 8 of the Second Punic War, believes it is driven thus by certain winds standing there. Seneca says in *Hercules Oetaeus*:
> The unstable Euripus turns its wandering waves,
> Seven times it turns them back, and brings as many again,
> Until the Sun <note>original: "Titan"</note> sinks his weary light into the Ocean.
Boethius likewise says:
> As one is carried in the manner of the fluctuating Euripus.
Cicero in *Pro Plautio* writes: "What sea, what Euripus, do you say has so many motions, such great and varied agitations, changes, and waves, as the perturbations and tides found in the system of public elections?" Aeschines reproached Demosthenes, saying that by frequently changing factions, he had surpassed the Euripus itself in his inconstancy. Hence the Greeks call an inconstant man *Euripiston*. Gregory the Theologian, in a certain letter to Sophronius, the Master of the Horse, writes: <note>original Greek: "ὄψει οἷα τὰ ἡμέτερα..."</note> "You see what the condition of our affairs is, and how the course of human business revolves in a sort of wheel, now these people flourishing and now those withering; while neither prosperity nor adversity, as they say, stands firm for us, but changes and leaps to the opposite as quickly as possible, so that one might sooner trust the breezes or letters written upon water than human happiness." With these words, he beautifully depicts the "Euripus of the human condition." One also finds the phrase "Fortune of the Euripus," meaning a volatile fortune, for nothing is more unstable than this; and "Euripus of the mind," because thought is carried now here, now there.

---

<margin>LXIII</margin>
<margin>You sleep the sleep of Endymion.</margin>
-> You sleep the sleep of Endymion. <-

This will apply to those who either fatten themselves with immoderate sleep, or who live in long-lasting idleness, exerting themselves in no business but leading a soft and holiday-filled life. It arises from the very well-known fable of Endymion. He was a youth of surpassing beauty and was beloved by the Moon. She obtained for him from his father Jove, through her prayers, that he might have whatever he wished. Endymion wished that he might sleep a perpetual sleep, <margin>to sleep the ageless sleep.</margin> that is, continuing immortal and free from old age. Aristotle used this adage in the tenth book of the *Ethics*, concluding that neither leisure is suitable for the gods, nor does any other action seem worthy of them except contemplation. Furthermore, since it is agreed by all that they live, it is consistent that they also do something: "For," he says, "it is not fitting for them to sleep the sleep of Endymion, as the saying goes." Cicero, in the fifth book of *On Ends*, discussing how we are chiefly prompted by nature to do something, says: "Therefore, even if we thought we should enjoy the most pleasant dreams, we would not want the sleep of Endymion given to us; and if it should happen, we would consider it the likeness of death." The same author in the first book of *Tusculan Disputations* says: "Although some make death lighter, wanting it to be very like sleep. As if anyone would want to live ninety years in such a way that, when he had completed sixty, he slept the remainder! Not even the birds would want that, let alone the man himself." As for Endymion, if we wish to listen to the fable, he fell asleep at some time or other on Mount Latmos, which is a mountain in Caria; I believe he has not yet woken up.

---

<margin>LXIIII</margin>
<margin>You have slept beyond Epimenides.</margin>
-> You sleep beyond Epimenides. <-

That is, you have slept longer than the sleep of Epimenides. It was said against those who lead a life of perpetual idleness. The history of Epimenides the Cretan theologian is found in the *Attic Nights* of Gellius, and also in Diogenes Laertius. He, weary from walking, turned aside into a certain cave and there fell asleep; he did not wake from his sleep before forty-seven years had passed. Pliny mentions this in Book 7, Chapter 52, in these words: "With great fabulousness indeed—which I for my part do not accept in the same way regarding Epimenides of Knossos—that as a boy, weary from heat and travel, he slept in a cave for fifty-seven years; wondering at the appearance and change of things when he woke up, as if on the following day; hence, in an equal number of days, old age came on, though he nevertheless lasted until the hundred and fifty-seventh year of his life." Lucian in *Timon* says: "For you have slept beyond Epimenides himself." If there is any...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

If the transmigration of souls <note>original: "μετεμψύχωσις" (metempsychosis)</note> taught by the true Pythagoras is real, it is quite plausible that the soul of this theologian Epimenides has migrated into these sophisticated theologians of ours. They have introduced so many empty dreams into the world that sleep would scarcely suffice for many of them for two hundred continuous years.

<margin>65</margin>
->Early sowing often deceives; late sowing is always bad.<-

Columella, in his work *On Agriculture*, writes in this manner: "But while all things in farming must be done energetically, this is especially true of sowing. There is an old proverb among farmers: Early sowing is often accustomed to deceive, but late sowing never fails to be bad." Thus far Columella. The adage warns us that in every business one must hurry, and that it is slightly better to occupy the proper time too early than to approach it too late. For example, if someone were to advise that a boy should be entrusted to teachers for instruction while still at a tender age. For it is more prudent to anticipate the time than to finally begin in more advanced years.

<margin>66</margin>
->Melian famine.<-

<note>original: "Λιμὸς μηλιαῖος" (Limos meliaios)</note>, that is, a Melian famine. Used for extreme hunger and the most difficult circumstances. For Melos is a town in Thessaly <note>Erasmus likely means the island in the Aegean</note> which Nicias, the Athenian general, besieged and captured, not so much by siege engines as by starvation. This is generally what Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> says. He expresses it in this way: <note>original: "λιμῷ μηλίῳ"</note>, by a Melian famine. Thucydides mentions this history in his fifth book. The proverb appears in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*: "And again you will destroy the gods with a Melian famine."

<margin>67</margin>
->Saguntine famine.<-

The Saguntine famine entered into a proverb by a similar reasoning. The histories of Titus Livius, Valerius Maximus, and Marcus Tullius Cicero in the *Philippics* mention it. Saguntum is a town in Spain, near the river Ebro, joined in alliance and treaty with the Romans. It was reduced by a long Carthaginian siege and famine to such a point that the citizens, having built a fire in the forum, threw whatever precious things they had into it; and finally, they threw themselves and their children into the same fire, lest they fall into the hands of the enemy. Ausonius says: "Now, now, let it free Lucania, already consumed by a Saguntine famine." The Greeks call a violent and intolerable hunger, which induces a fainting fit <note>original: "λειποθυμίαν" (leipothymian)</note>, a "bull-hunger" <term>boulimos: an intense, ox-like hunger</term>. And those who faint, especially due to lack of food, are said to suffer from "boulimia." Aristotle, in the 4th problem of the 8th section, asks why men suffer more from "boulimia" in the cold and winter months (for he uses this word); and what Aristotle calls <note>original: "βωλιμίαν"</note>, Theodorus translates as "canine hunger." It was an old custom among the Greeks to drive famine out of the house with rods, saying: "Out with hunger, in with wealth and health!"

<margin>68</margin>
->The Field of Famine.<-

<note>original: "Λιμοῦ πεδίον" (Limou pedion)</note>, that is, the Field of Famine. It is said of cities pressed by great hunger. There is, moreover, a certain place by this name. They add that when the Athenians were once suffering there from the greatest hunger, an oracle warned them to appease the gods with certain sacrifices at a designated spot; they designated the field which is behind the treasury. And from this, they call that place the Field of Famine.

<margin>69</margin>
->You are making an elephant out of a fly.<-

<note>original: "Ἐλέφαντα ἐκ μυίας ποιεῖς"</note>, that is, you make an elephant out of a fly. That is, you exalt and amplify tiny matters with words. Lucian, in his *Encomium of the Fly*, says: "Though I have much more to say, I will stop my speech, lest I seem, according to the proverb, to be making an elephant out of a fly." It may seem to be taken from Homer, who describes the impudence of the fly during the battles of gods and heroes, comparing the invincible and fierce warrior Menelaus to one in the Iliad, book 17. Indeed, Saint Augustine, in his book *Against the Manichæans on the Two Souls*, does not hesitate to compare and prefer a fly to the sun, as a living creature over an inanimate one.

<margin>70</margin>
->An elephant does not catch a mouse.<-

<note>original: "Ἐλέφας μῦν οὐχ ἁλίσκει"</note>, that is, an elephant does not catch a mouse. A noble and lofty mind ignores cheap prey and tiny profits. An exceptionally learned man does not hunt down those tiny apes of the literati. A very powerful man is not offended by the small injuries of the weak. This adage is used quite ridiculously in this age by those "philosophasters" and "theologasters" <note>Erasmus's mocking terms for pseudo-philosophers and bad theologians</note> whenever they slip most foully through ignorance of the Latin and Greek languages—which they almost always do. "The eagle," they say, "does not catch flies" <note>original: "Aquila non capit muscas"</note>; as if they were truly eagles when they babble those sophisticated trifles, or as if the knowledge of languages were not the very greatest part of erudition.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to timing in agriculture, extreme historical famines (Melian and Saguntine), and the metaphorical use of animals to describe scale and intellectual arrogance.</summary>
<keywords>proverbs, Columella, agriculture, Saguntum, famine, Aristotle, Lucian, Augustine, scholasticism, Greek language, Latin language</keywords>

### The eagle looks at the woodworms.
->LXXI<-

<margin>The eagle sees the woodworms. <note>original: "Ἀετὸς θρίπας ὁρᾷ"</note></margin>The eagle looks at the woodworms. Said of great men who neglect very small things. There is a certain very tiny bird <note>The author likely refers to a wren or a small insect-eating bird</note> which the eagle, despite being very sharp-sighted, does not deign to pursue, as it is a prey unworthy of its talons. I find this explained in this manner in the Greek commentaries, though I suspect it may be a corruption. For I find that a *thrips* <term>thrips: a wood-boring worm or louse</term> is actually a type of small worm.

### It hangs by a hair; It hangs by a thread.
->LXXII<-

<margin>It hangs from a hair. <note>original: "Ἐκ τριχὸς κρεμᾶται"</note></margin>It hangs by a hair. Said of a matter that is exceedingly dangerous. It seems to have originated from the story of the tyrant Dionysius, regarding the sword hanging over a head by a single hair <note>The famous Sword of Damocles</note>. Persius alluded to this in his third Satire:
> And the sword hanging from the gilded ceiling
> Terrified the purple-clad neck beneath.

This verse is cited in Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, from the third book of Ennius’s *Annals*:
> This night all Etruria shall hang by a thread.

That is, it will be in the greatest crisis. No saying is more common among the people today than this. Synesius says in a certain letter: <margin>They say that life hangs by a thin thread. <note>original: "ἐπὶ λεπτῆς φασὶ μίτης τὸ ζῆν κρεμᾶσθαι"</note></margin> They say life hangs by a slender thread. To the same purpose belongs that Spartan saying mentioned by Plutarch in his *Spartan Apophthegms*. For when someone was praising Lampis of Aegina as being by far the wealthiest man because he possessed many ships, a certain Spartan said: <margin>I do not care, he said, for a happiness that is tied to a rope. <note>original: "οὐ προσέχω, ἔφη, τῇ εὐδαιμονίᾳ σχοινίῳ ἐξηρτημένῃ"</note></margin> "I care nothing," he said, "for a prosperity hanging from ropes." He was clearly implying that maritime wealth is uncertain and subject to the whims of fortune.

### There is nothing hard inside an olive, nor outside a nut.
->LXXIII<-

This is a proverbial verse in Horace’s *Epistles*, to be said against those who are so shamelessly insane that they do not fear to deny even confessed facts, and to affirm manifest falsehoods as certainties; in short, to say anything at all so as not to appear defeated in an argument. Such is the sophist Euthydemus whom Plato introduces, who claimed his dog was his father, and that the same father belonged to everyone, and that everyone knew everything—and he stubbornly asserted such monstrosities so as not to be refuted. Horace’s poem is as follows:
> There is nothing hard inside an olive, nor outside a nut.

Of course, it is agreed among sane people that a nut has a hard shell and an olive berry has a hard stone inside. Therefore, anyone wastes their labor who disputes with the kind of men who call light darkness and darkness light, as the divine prophet says. Similar is what Galen brings forward in the second book of *On the Power of Simple Remedies*, that someone cited Anaxagoras as an authority who had declared that snow is not white. Galen’s words are: <margin>And yet some of them even bring forward Anaxagoras as a witness, who declared concerning snow that it was not white. <note>original: "καίτοι γ᾽ ἐξ αὐτῶν, οἷς τὸν Ἀναξαγόραν ἐπικαλοῦνται μάρτυρα, πρὶν χιόνα ἀποφαινόμενον ὡς οὐκ εἴη λευκή."</note></margin> And some of those men even bring Anaxagoras as a witness, who pronounced about snow that it is not white.

### Jupiter childless.
->LXXIV<-

<margin>Jupiter childless. <note>original: "Ζεὺς ἄγονος"</note></margin> Jupiter childless. Used when someone asserts a blatant falsehood. For it is well known that Jupiter has very many children, being a god most fond of women and most prolific; one who did not give birth from only one part of his body, but produced Bacchus from his thigh and Pallas <note>Athena</note> from his brain.

### You seek water in the sea.
->LXXV<-

<margin>You seek water in the sea. <note>original: "Ἐν θαλάσσῃ ζητεῖς ὕδωρ"</note></margin> You seek water in the sea. You look for something there, as if it were difficult to find, where nothing else is encountered: as if one were to track down one or two crimes in the character of a most wicked man when his whole life is contaminated; or if one were to hunt for a few things to criticize in unlearned writers when there is nothing that does not deserve criticism. Martial, if I remember correctly, says: "You seek water in the middle of the sea." Likewise Propertius in the first book of his *Elegies*:
> Now you, insane, seek water in the middle of the river.

### A river, you contend with the sea.
->LXXVI<-

<margin>A river, you contend with the sea. <note>original: "Ποταμὸς θαλάττῃ ἐρίζεις"</note></margin> A river, you contend with the sea. Used when the smallest take up a contest with the greatest. There is, however, a certain place in the Leontine tribe, as Suidas testifies, named <margin>Rivers. <note>original: "ποταμοί"</note></margin> "Rivers." The inhabitants of this place are called <margin>Potamioi <note>River-people</note></margin> as if they were "river-dwellers." These people were noted for enrolling as many people as possible into their city, whom the city could not conveniently hold. And from this comes the joke of the proverb: that since it was a "river"—that is, a place not very large—it seemed to emulate the sea by receiving everyone from everywhere into itself.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s massive collection of Greek and Latin proverbs, focusing on metaphors for victory, defeat, and superficial learning.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>77</margin>
### One stutterer understands another better.

"One stutterer understands another better," <note>original: *Balbus balbum rectius intelligit*</note> that is, one barbarian understands the speech of another barbarian. For it is so arranged by nature that he who stutters—that is, one who speaks with little fluency—understands the speech of one who stutters in a similar way better than one who speaks purely and articulately. This is aptly said against those unlearned people to whom unlearned things are more familiar and pleasing. Saint Jerome touches upon the stupidity of a certain monk with this adage, I know not whether more wittily or more sharply. "And therefore," he says, "he thinks himself learned, because he alone understands Jovinian." <note>Jovinian was a 4th-century monk whose writings Jerome attacked for being stylistically dense and heretical.</note> For there is a proverb, "A stutterer knows the words of a stutterer better." So says Jerome. Furthermore, the same Jerome mocks the style of Jovinian as monstrous and exceedingly obscure with wonderful wit in the preface to the books in which he refutes his errors.

---

<margin>78</margin>
### To give the grass.

"To give the grass" <note>original: *Herbam dare*</note> is commonly found among the learned to mean recognizing the victor and confessing oneself defeated. It is taken from the fact that, as the author Festus Pompeius states, this was a sign of victory in pastoral life. In ancient times, those defeated in a race or some other contest would immediately pluck grass from that very spot and hand it to their adversary as a symbol of acknowledged victory. Pliny, in Book 22, Chapter 4, speaking of the "siege crown" made of grass, says: "It was given from the green grass, plucked from the place where someone had saved the besieged." For among the ancients, the highest sign of victory was for the defeated to offer grass—that is, to yield even the earth, their nursing soil, and their very burial ground. "Which custom," he says, "I know still endures among the Germans." The same author in Book 8, Chapter 5, says of the elephant: "For their shame is wonderful; when defeated, they flee the voice of the victor and offer up earth and vervain." <note>Vervain: a sacred plant used in ancient rituals.</note> This adage will be even more witty if it is transferred to a literary victory.

---

<margin>79</margin>
### To give the hands.

With a similar figure of speech, Horace said "To give the hands" <note>original: *Dare manus*</note> to mean recognizing oneself as defeated. For those who surrender to a victor so they are not killed voluntarily offer their hands for chains. Horace in the *Epodes*:
> Now, now I give my hands to your powerful knowledge.

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the dialogue *On Friendship*: "At the end let him give his hands and allow himself to be conquered." If one turns this toward matters of the mind, it becomes more graceful. However, there is a class of men who never acknowledge themselves defeated in a dispute, even when they have been most thoroughly cast down. Galen depicts such people in his book <note>original: *Against those who speak falsely concerning the faculties*</note>: "But when someone retreats, having been struck and falling, yet conceding that he has struck his opponent—just like those amateur wrestlers who, when thrown by the professionals and lying on their backs like infants, are so far from recognizing their fall that they even grab the necks of those who threw them, not letting them get away, and in this way they imagine they have won." Indeed, when someone has been refuted, he nevertheless clings on just the same; not acknowledging that he has fallen, he is like those common wrestlers who, thrown by athletes and lying flat on the ground, are so far from admitting the slip that they hold onto the necks of those who threw them, not allowing them to be pulled away, and thus they think they have won.

---

<margin>80</margin>
### Like a dog from the Nile.

Those who taste any art or author lightly and, as it were, in passing, will be said to taste "like a dog from the Nile." This adage was born from a certain witty saying mentioned by Macrobius in the second book of the *Saturnalia*, which is as follows: After the flight from Mutina, when people were asking what [Mark] Antony was doing, a certain friend of his replied: "What a dog does in Egypt: he drinks and runs." For it is well known in those regions that dogs, terrified by the snatching of crocodiles, drink and run. Solinus says they do not lap except while running, lest they be caught.

---

<margin>81</margin>
### To throw away the spear.

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] said "To throw away the spear" <note>original: *Hastam abjicere*</note> in his speech *For Murena* to mean despairing of a cause and abandoning a contest. It is translated from military service. For whoever throws away his weapons in war despairs: he either looks toward flight or expects death. The Greeks, with a single word, call the timid and those who flee in war "shield-throwers" <note>original: *rhipsaspis*</note>, namely from the casting away of the shield. Demosthenes earned this nickname in a certain battle: as cowardly in war as he was invincible in the assemblies. Cleonymus is called a "shield-dropper" <note>original: *aspidapobles*</note> by Aristophanes in *The Wasps*. Plato, in the twelfth book of *The Laws*, declares the name "shield-thrower" to be by far the most disgraceful.

---

<margin>82</margin>
### To leave the arena.

Close to these is "To leave the arena" <note>original: *Harena cedere*</note>, meaning to desist from a contest and voluntarily concede the victory. It is translated from gladiatorial combat. So also Horace,

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>D 3</sig>

<margin>Now the Scythians meditate on retreating from the fields with loosened bows. <note>original: "Iam Scythæ laxo meditantur arcu Cedere campis." A quote from Horace regarding the retreat of enemies.</note></margin>
->To descend into the arena. 83<-

**To descend into the arena** is used for entering into a contest. It is a metaphor taken from the gladiatorial arena, of which Horace <note>referred to here as Flaccus</note> says:
> Lest he should too often entreat the crowd at the edge of the arena.

If these words are transferred to matters of the mind, they possess a proverbial metaphor. In citing examples, since they are found everywhere, I did not think I should dwell on them or delay the reader. Pliny, in his letters, used the phrase "my arena" to mean his professional duty. For he writes to Fabatus, and likewise to Baebius Priscus: "I will provide as much as I possibly can, especially in my arena," that is, in the court of the hundred men <note>the *centumviri*, a Roman court dealing with property and inheritance</note>.

->I have struck the South Wind. 84<-

**I have struck the South Wind**, that is, I have wasted my labor. It is found in Plautus’s *Epidicus*. Paul did not hesitate to use this adage in his epistles <note>1 Corinthians 9:26, "beating the air"</note>. For the air eludes the stroke of the one hitting it by giving way. It can be seen as taken either from those who practice the art of gladiatorship by brandishing their swords through the air, or from the history mentioned by Aulus Gellius concerning a certain tribe that waged war against this wind.

->To know by face. 85<-

**To know by face** is to have a slight acquaintance, as with someone you have seen only once or twice, but with whom you have not lived familiarly. If this is transferred to matters of the mind, it becomes more elegant. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in *Against Piso*: "Virtue itself has this quality, which you do not even know by face," that is, you have only the slightest inkling of it.

->He does not even know its shadow. 86<-

Very similar to this is the phrase used by Cicero in his letters to Atticus, book 8: "O man, loving and miserable, who has not even seen the shadow of <term>the beautiful</term> <note>original: "τῆϚ καλῆϚ" (tēs kalēs)</note>." Plutarch, in his essay *On Having Many Friends*, cites Menander, who said that man is happy who has even the <term>shadow of a friend</term> <note>original: "σκιὰν φίλοϚ" (skian philos)</note>. And in Athenaeus, a certain parasite called the rancid and black loaves of bread brought into a banquet <term>shadows of bread</term> <note>original: "ἄρτων σκιὰϚ" (artōn skias)</note>, as if they were the ghosts of bread, not bread itself. However, the adage seems more likely derived from ancient painting, which represented things rudely with shadows alone. And the Platonic image is well known, in which those who sit idle are delighted by the shadows of things <note>a reference to Plato's Allegory of the Cave</note>.

->Known by name only. 87<-

Very similar to this is that line of Horace in his *Satires*:
> A certain man ran up, known to me by name only.

For the common people also use this proverb to signify a certain thin and vulgar acquaintance. And it will have even more charm if it is translated to matters of the mind, as if one were to say that philosophy is scarcely known to someone even by name.

->At first face; At first forehead. 88<-

These also savor of a proverb, especially when they refer to incorporeal things: **At first face** or **at first forehead**, used for that which is seen at first glance, and before you consider it more closely and diligently. For that first sight often deceives, and not infrequently the eyes are clouded by a certain shame; then, having looked again and again, we perceive things that had previously escaped us, and we, as it were, recant that first judgment of the eyes. The use of this adage is frequent among Latin writers, specifically in Quintilian, book 12. Papinian, in book 12 under the title *On claims made without cause*, says: "The claim seems to fail at first face." Likewise in book 16: "When at first face she undertakes another's obligation, but in truth her own." Celsus in book 22: "At first forehead it seems more equitable that the petitioner should prove what he intends," etc.

->Inwardly and under the skin. 89<-

<margin>Known inwardly and under the skin.</margin>
**Known inwardly and under the skin** means known in every way; just as if you were to say known outside and in. Persius says:
> Keep your trappings for the people; I know you inwardly and under the skin.

That is, deceive others, but to me you are clearly known, nor can you perform an imposture. We also call the "top of the skin" that first forehead or appearance of a thing. Ausonius in his preface to the summaries of Homer: "This appearance of his is apparent to one looking at the top skin of the first work." And Horace: "Foul within, though beautiful with a fair skin."

->Known domestically. 90<-

With a similar figure, Lucian said in *The False Logician*: <term>A man given up, and knowing you accurately from home</term> <note>original: "Ἄνθρωπον ἐκδοθέντα, καὶ οἴκοθεν σὲ ἀκριβῶϚ εἰδότα" (Anthrōpon ekdothenta, kai oikothen se akribōs eidota)</note>.
<meta>The text continues on the next page with the definition of "from home."</meta>
