<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Adages, focusing on metaphors for superficial knowledge or insincere actions, following the previous discussion of domestic familiarity.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

That is: "By a free man, and one who knows you from living in the same house." This will be more elegant if applied to matters of the mind, as if one were to say the art of rhetoric is known to someone <term>oikothen</term> <note>original: οἴκοθεν; meaning "from home" or "from one's own resources"</note>. Of the same kind is that passage of Pliny, in a Letter to Atticus: "I looked into this man Clemens thoroughly and 'at home' <note>meaning intimately</note> when I was serving as a young soldier in Syria."

<margin>91</margin>
->To greet from the threshold.<-

Almost the opposite of the previous one is: "To greet from the threshold." This too will possess a great deal of elegance if it is turned toward incorporeal things. For instance, if one were to say he has only "greeted theology from the threshold"—meaning someone who has bestowed neither a very long nor a principal effort upon it, but has only tasted the first principles. Seneca in his forty-ninth letter says: "Nor do I deny that those things should be looked into, but only looked into, and greeted from the threshold." He is discussing the subtleties of the logicians, which he thinks it is quite enough to have touched upon lightly. It is a metaphor taken from those common friends who are not admitted into the inner chambers, but greet from a distance and from the doorway, and then depart.

<margin>92</margin>
->To taste with the tip of the lips.<-

"To taste with the tip of the lips" is to touch upon something briefly. It is derived from those who taste food or drink lightly, passing nothing from there into the stomach. Cicero in *For Caelius*: "Indeed, I have both seen and heard of many in this city, not only those who had tasted this kind of life with the tip of their lips." Likewise in *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2: "When he said it would be eternal, do you think he had tasted natural philosophy—that is, the reason of nature—with only the 'first lips,' as they say?" Quintilian in book twelve: "But I pass over this, about which I think no one who has tasted literature even with the 'first lips,' as they say, will doubt." Procopius the Sophist in a certain letter: <term>I am persuaded that he too is filled with it, for as you say, they say he touched this matter with the tip of his finger, since he did not stand aloof from pleasures.</term> <note>original Greek: πείθομαι δὲ κἀκεῖνον...; Erasmus provides a Latin translation which is here rendered into English.</note> That is: "Again I was angry at her, if when she had offered such a great thing to be tasted with the 'top of the finger,' as they say, she then robbed it of pleasure." In these words, it is said in a novel way because he attributes taste to the finger—unless he meant that those who taste lightly move the thing to be tasted to the tongue with the tip of the finger.

<margin>93</margin>
->With the surface of the lips.<-

The Greeks use "With the surface of the lips" <note>Latin: Summis labijs</note> a little differently; namely, when someone merely pretends something with words, but does not do it from the heart. Lucian in his *Apology*: <term>to philosophize from the edge of the lips</term> <note>original: τὸ ἀπ’ ἄκρων χείλων φιλοσοφεῖν</note>, that is, acting the philosopher with the surface of the lips. Likewise in the *Dialogues of the Courtesans*: <term>they have their oaths on the edge of the lip</term> <note>original: ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ τῷ χείλει τοὺς ὅρκους ἔχουσι</note>. That is: "Having an oath on the surface of the lips." He speaks of lovers who swear a "Venereal oath" <note>an oath of love</note> not from the heart. Seneca in book 1, chapter 10: "Those things did not come from the surface of the lips; these words have a foundation." In the same way, Saint Jerome in a letter to the monk Rusticus: "So that we do not invite guests," he says, "with a light and hurried speech and, so to speak, with the surface of the lips." This is a habit of certain courtiers and city-folk: to promise everything, but with those solemn words by which no one is moved even a little bit, unless they are remarkably foolish.

<margin>94</margin>
->To touch with the tips of the fingers.<-

A close relative to this is: "To touch with the tips of the fingers," used for touching something lightly; this will only truly seem an adage if a metaphor is added. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in that passage I just cited: "Indeed, I have both seen and heard of many in this city, not only those who had tasted this kind of life with the tip of the lips and touched it with the 'tips of the fingers,' as they say, but who had given their whole youth to pleasures, yet eventually emerged and betook themselves to 'good fruit' <note>meaning a productive, virtuous life</note>, as they say." The Greeks express it thus: <term>to touch with the tip of the finger</term> <note>original: τοῦ ἄκρῳ ἅψασθαι δακτύλῳ</note>. So Basil in his letters: <term>I myself know that we enjoyed the rich and sweetest honey of your church last year, even if only with the tip of a finger.</term> <note>original: οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς...</note> It can be seen as a metaphor taken from wrestlers. For the Greeks call it <term>akrocheirizesthai</term> <note>original: ἀκροχειρίζεσθαι</note> to grapple with someone without the rest of the body coming together, but only with the tips of the fingers. Lucian in the *Life of Demonax*: <term>nor had he touched the rich woman with the tip of his finger, as they say.</term> <note>original: οὐ δὲ περὶ τὴν πλουσίαν...</note> Euripides used a hyperbole without a metaphor in *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
> <term>King Agamemnon shall not touch your daughter,</term>
> <term>not even with the tip of his hand.</term>
> <note>original Greek: οὐχ ἅψεται σῆς θυγατρὸς... followed by Erasmus's Latin verse translation.</note>

<margin>95</margin>
->The half is more than the whole.<-

<term>The half is more than the whole</term> <note>original: Πλέον ἥμισυ παντός</note>. That is: "The half is more than the whole," a proverbial riddle by which the "golden mean" <note>the middle way between extremes</note> is commended. It is cited and explained by Plato in the third book of *The Laws*: <term>Do you not know...</term> <note>original: ἆρ’ οὐκ ἀγνοεῖτε</note>

<summary>This page explores several related adages concerning superficiality and moderation, such as "greeting from the threshold" and "touching with the fingertips," drawing on classical authors to explain metaphors for shallow learning or insincerity.</summary>
<keywords>superficiality, moderation, golden mean, classical education, metaphors, Cicero, Seneca, Lucian, Greek proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on classical adages, specifically focusing on the concept of moderation and the famous Hesiodic proverb regarding the "half being more than the whole."</meta>

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

...quoting Hesiod most correctly, saying that the half is often more than the whole, whenever taking the whole would be harmful; then the half is greater, because the portion you receive in exchange is worth more, though not greater in size. <note>original Greek: ὡς ἥμισυ τοῦ παντὸς πολλακις ἐστὶ πλεῖον... This refers to Hesiod's *Works and Days*, line 40.</note> Does he not show that he knew Hesiod spoke most rightly in saying the half is frequently more than the whole? Namely, when taking the whole would be damaging, but the half is moderate; in that case, he considered the moderate to be more than the immoderate, insofar as it is better than the worse option. In the same way, the interpreters of Hesiod explain it: that in the "whole" is signified <term>greed</term> <note>Greek: πλεονεξία (pleonexia) — the desire to have more than one's share</note>, and in the "half" is signified <term>equality</term> <note>Greek: ἰσότητα (isotes)</note>. For he who is content with the half stands in the middle ground; conversely, he who proceeds all the way to the whole, having overstepped moderation, must necessarily reach an extreme. He mentions the same adage in the fifth book of the *Republic*. Again, in the sixth book of the *Laws*, he declares that it is of primary importance in a city that the magistracies be committed to distinguished men. For the <term>beginning</term> <note>Greek: Ἀρχὴ (Arche) — meaning both "beginning" and "rule/office"</note> is said in proverbs to be the half of every work, and everyone always praises a good beginning; but this, as it seems to me, is already more than the half. Plato alluded here to the ambiguity of the word, for *Arche* to the Greeks sounds like both the "beginning" of a thing and a "magistracy" or "office." Pittacus, according to Laertius, when he had voluntarily resigned from his magistracy, cut back by half the land left to him by the Mytilenaeans (according to Sosicrates), saying that the half was better than the whole. He also refused money sent by Croesus, responding that he already had twice as much as he wanted. The poem exists in Hesiod, in the first book of the work titled *Works and Days*. For he writes to his brother Perses in this manner:

> We had already divided our inheritance, and many other things
> You snatched and carried off, greatly honoring the kings
> Who devour gifts, who wish to judge this case.
> Fools! They do not even know how much more the half is than the whole,
> Nor how great a benefit lies in mallow and asphodel.

These verses we have translated as follows:

> And now our father’s estate was to be divided between us,
> But you snatched many things beyond your lot, winning over
> Gift-devouring kings, who are eager to settle this suit.
> But truly, fools they seem to be, not knowing
> How much more excellent the half is than the whole, and how
> Great is the utility of mallow and the green asphodel.

What exactly <term>asphodel</term> <note>A hardy Mediterranean plant associated with the underworld and simple, frugal living.</note> is, however, seems to have been little agreed upon among the learned in the past. Since Gellius in his 18th book records that this question was proposed at the banquets of scholars as a matter known to few. Theodorus in some places translates it as "white daffodil." As for what pertains to the explanation of this adage, one may gather from many passages in Lucian that asphodel is a common and cheap herb, and that the spirits of the dead live on this, among whom there is no luxury and no ambition. Furthermore, in the seventh Idyll of Theocritus, asphodel is mentioned among the rustic herbs: "And those things with asphodel and much-curved parsley."

Therefore, the poet censures the immoderate luxury of kings and the wealthy, preferring the moderation of the common people to their arrogance. Plutarch likewise, in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*, thinks this passage of Hesiod should be referred to as an admonition toward frugality. Suidas thinks the proverb arose from an event, bringing forward a story of this kind: There were two brothers, one of whom, while dying, entrusted to the other by will both the guardianship of the son he was leaving as a ward and the management of his resources. But he, being the kind of man people commonly are—namely, that profit had more weight with him than piety—tried to seize the boy's property; while he was striving for this, he lost even his own. Then, when he asked for an accounting so that he might be restored to a better position, he was answered in this manner: "Fools! They do not know how much more the half is than the whole."

->that is,<-

How much more excellent the half is than the whole,
The fool does not know.
It belongs to kings, therefore, to take the half of the whole; to take the whole is the mark of a tyrant. Thus, it will be permitted to use the proverb in three ways: first, when we extol that truly "golden moderation," without which there is nothing in human affairs that is honorable, pleasant, or praised. Moreover, we measure moderation by opportunity, just as Pindar, imitating Hesiod, says:

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"A measure follows in every thing, and the best time to understand it is the right moment." <note>original: Ἔπεται δ' ἐν ἑκάστῳ μέτρον, νοῆσαι δὲ καιρὸς ἄριστος.</note> That is to say: A limit exists for every single thing; the best opportunity is in recognizing it. For indeed, what is too much in one place will be too little in another. The same is found in the last hymn of the *Nemean Odes*:
"In gains one must hunt for a measure,
For the madness of desires for unattainable things is sharper." <note>original: Κέρδων δὲ χρὴ μέτρον θηρεύεμεν, Ἀφυσίκτου δ' ἐρώτων ὀξυτέραι μανίαι.</note>
That is: In matters of profit, it is necessary to follow a limit, for the cravings for immense things possess more violent insanities.

Another way of using this principle is when we prefer **equality**, which Pythagoras called both the parent and the nurse of friendship; conversely, he called inequality the mother of discords and wars. Euripides expressed this elegantly in *The Phoenician Women*:
"That is more beautiful, my child,
To honor Equality, which always binds friends to friends,
Cities to cities, and allies to allies.
For equality is by nature the law for men.
But the lesser is always set as an enemy to the greater,
And thus begins the day of hatred.
For Equality established for men the measures and parts of weights,
And defined number;
And the sightless eyelid of night, and the light of the sun,
Walk the yearly circle in equal turns,
And neither of them feels envy when defeated.
Thus both sun and night serve mortals." <note>original: Κεῖνο κάλλιον τέκνον... (Euripides, Phoenissae 535-554)</note>

A third way of using this is when we deter someone from inflicting an injury, persuading them that it is better—according to the opinion of Plato—to suffer an injury oneself than to inflict one on another. Plutarch demonstrates that this proverb intends this meaning in his commentary *On Listening to the Poets*. I believe what Plutarch relates about Darius pertains to this: When he had summoned the governors of the provinces and asked whether the taxes were heavy, and they replied they were moderate, he ordered that only half be paid from each, judging it better to receive half with the goodwill of the provincials than the whole with the hatred of his people.

Perhaps today some sin against this proverb. For while certain <term>Theologians</term> and prelates wish to concede nothing at all regarding their dogmas and rights, they run the risk of losing even those things which they held by good right. In my opinion, one should not always despise the advice of the comic writer Syrus: "Rather than coming into danger of whether you keep or lose the whole, make it a half"—or as others read—"make it a division."

<sig>XCVII</sig>

->**The eye of a serpent.**<-

"The eye of a serpent." <note>original: ὄφεως ὄμμα</note> This is customarily said of those who look with sharp and intent eyes. The metaphor is taken from the animal. For this creature has eyes that are quite hard and piercing. Whence Horace <note>original: Flaccus</note> says:
"Why do you see so sharply into the vices of friends,
As either an eagle, or an Epidaurian serpent?"

<meta>catchword: Nemo</meta>

### Do not move the line.
->XCVII<-

<margin>Do not move the line.</margin> <note>original: Μὴ κίνει γραμμήν</note> "Do not move the line." A commentator on the hymns of Pindar explains this passage: "And so there the Libyan, matching the bride to a husband, stood her at the line." He is speaking of Antaeus, who set his daughter as the prize at the finish line for young men, so that whoever reached her first in a race might lead her home as his wife. He records a proverb of this kind: "Do not move the line." He believes it was transferred from the custom of the ancients, who marked the goal with a drawn line where the proposed prize was placed for the victor to take. However, another line was also drawn for the starting gates, as we have mentioned elsewhere, from which the race began. Therefore, both lines provided the occasion for a proverb: "from the line" <note>original: ἀπὸ γραμμῆς</note>, meaning from the very beginning, and "Do not move the line," meaning do not move the goal. It signifies that laws must not be changed, nor should the prescribed boundaries of things be overstepped. To this more specifically pertains that line of Theocritus in the *Bucolics*:
<margin>And he moves the stone from the line.</margin> <note>original: Καὶ τὸν ἀπὸ γραμμᾶς κινεῖ λίθον</note> That is, "And he moves the stone from the line."
He alludes to the stream of Galatea, carrying away some rock from the edge of the bank. There is also a "Sacred Line" in the game of counters <note>a board game similar to backgammon or checkers</note>, about which has been discussed elsewhere.

### To beat the same anvil.
->XCVIII<-

To assiduously beat the same anvil is to persevere with indefatigable diligence in the pursuit of some work. The metaphor is drawn from smiths, striking the anvil with frequent blows, and thus finally overcoming the hardness of the iron through perpetual labor. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book *On the Orator*: "But if I wished to instruct someone now who was entirely unrefined in speaking, I would rather hand him over to those persistent men who, in a single task, beat the same anvil day and night." This will apply well to schoolmasters and teachers of literature, who must endlessly hammer the same things into boys so that they might eventually stick.

### Biting Memmius tears the arm of Largus.
->XCIX<-

"Biting Memmius tears the arm of Largus." The orator Crassus says this verse was so commonly tossed about that it could be seen inscribed everywhere on all the walls in Terracina. The story from which the adage was born goes like this: A certain Roman named Memmius, while staying in Terracina, was desperately in love with a certain woman, but not without a rival. When he fell into a quarrel with this rival, Memmius was carried away by such anger that he seized the arm of Largus (for that was the rival's name) with his teeth. This matter afterwards turned into a popular joke; some witty and <unclear>learned</unclear> person noted this verse on all the walls of that city using five letters, depicting three Ls and two Ms: LLLMM. This was done, of course, to provide an opportunity for strangers to ask questions. Thus, when Marcus Crassus once came to Terracina, wondering at the strange riddle of letters, he asked a certain townsman what such letters meant. The man, having explained the story, unfolded the little verse:
"Biting Memmius tears the arm of Largus." <note>Latin: Lacerat lacertum Largi mordax Memmius</note>
Marcus Tullius [Cicero] made mention of this in the second book *On the Orator*. However, Lucius Caesar, who speaks in Cicero's work, believes this entire narrative was deliberately fabricated against his adversary Memmius.

### More vocal than a cicada.
->C<-

<margin>More tuneful than a cicada.</margin> <note>original: Τέττιγος εὐφωνότερος</note> "More vocal than a cicada." This was said of a man who was exceedingly talkative or very musical, because this insect, living only on dew, is said to delight most justly in song. Socrates, in Plato's *Phaedrus*, tells that certain men were so devoted to music that, neglecting food, they were about to perish in the midst of it, and were changed by the gods into cicadas. And Theocritus in *Daphnis*:
<margin>Sing, for you sing even better than a cicada.</margin> <note>original: Ἄειδον ἔτι γὰρ φέρτερον ᾄδεις</note> That is, "For you sing better than any cicada."
In Diogenes Laertius, a poem of Timon is cited regarding the eloquence of Plato:
<margin>As he led all others, that broadest one, but a sweet-speaking orator, equal to the cicadas, which sitting upon the trees of Hecademus, send forth a lily-like voice.</margin> That is, "He surpassed all, that broadest one, a sweet orator, whose writings do not yield to the cicadas."

<summary>This page explores four proverbs: "Ne moueto lineam" (respecting boundaries), "Eandem tundere incudem" (persistence), a local Roman riddle about a biting rival, and "Cicada uocalior" (praising eloquence or talkativeness).</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Which sit upon the trees in shady groves,
And send forth a pleasant voice from a melodic throat.
<note>Erasmus is quoting a Latin translation of a Greek poem about cicadas.</note>
There is, moreover, an allusion—which the Latin translator cannot fully render—in the word <term>platys</term> <note>Greek: broad/wide</note> to the name of <term>Plato</term>, and in <term>ekademia</term> to his Academy. There is likewise an allusion to a poem in Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 3, concerning the old men who <term>send forth a lily-like voice</term> <note>original: ὄπα λειριόεσσαν ἱᾶσι</note>, that is, they emit a flourishing or delicate voice. And in the same author, Book 11, Theopompus says <term>the cicada rings out</term> <note>original: τέττιξ κελαδεῖ</note>, that is, the cicada chirps; which, however, seems to be said there for the sake of a good omen.

## THE TENTH HUNDRED OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

### To act like a stork.
<note>original: Αντιπελαργεῖν (Antipelargein)</note>

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
"To act like a stork" among the Greeks means to repay a mutual favor in kind, especially the duty of nourishing and caring for those by whom you were once nourished or instructed. For example, if children in turn support and cherish parents weary with age, or if a student in turn instructs his teacher. The term is taken from the nature of the stork, which in Greek is called <term>pelargos</term>. Among birds, this one alone holds the symbol of <term>piety</term> <note>In the Roman sense: "pietas" refers to duty and devotion to family and gods.</note>. There exists, moreover, a law that teaches piety, which decrees that children must nourish their parents or be imprisoned. Homer seems to have had this in mind in the *Iliad*, Book 4, when he says:
> <term>Nor to his dear parents</term> <note>original: Οὐδὲ θανῦσι</note>
> <term>Did he repay the cost of his upbringing, for his life was short.</term> <note>original: Θρέπτρα φίλοις ἀπέδωκε, μινυνθάδιο δέ οἱ αἰών.</note> ->that is,<-
> Nor did he ever pay back to his dear parents
> The duty of nurturing; but a brief life befell him.
-><term>Euripides</term> alluded to the same in his <term>Orestes</term>:<—
> <term>And indeed, he might repay the price of nourishment to her who is dead.</term> <note>original: Καὶ μὴν τίνοι γ' ἂν τῇ τεθνηκυῖᾳ τροφάς.</note> ->that is,<-
> And yet he shall repay the turn of nourishment to the dead woman.
This law, which most mortals neglect, the stork alone expresses among all kinds of living creatures. For other animals love and recognize their parents only so long as they need their help for nourishment. The stork alone nourishes its parents in turn when they are weakened by old age, and carries them on its shoulders when they are unable to fly. The latter of these deeds is praised in <term>Aeneas</term>, from which he received the surname <term>the Pious</term>; the former is told with wonderful praise regarding a girl who nourished her captive mother for many days with her own breasts. For this reason, as <term>Suidas</term> records, in ancient times the figure of a stork was placed at the very top of a king's scepter, and a hippopotamus at the bottom: so that by the very staff he carried, he might be reminded that it is necessary to value piety most highly and to restrain violence. For the hippopotamus is a wild and violent animal, and indeed impious; for it mates with its mother after killing its father, according to <term>Plutarch</term> in his commentary titled: <term>Which animals are more prudent, those of the land or those of the water</term>. Vipers also suffer the infamy of impiety, because they are born by bursting through the mother's belly. So too scorpions and spiders, which kill their parents after the duty of incubation. <term>Aristotle</term> is the witness in Book 5 of *On the Nature of Animals*. Concerning the piety of storks, <term>Pliny</term> in Book 10, Chapter 23, testifies in these words: "Storks return to the same nests. They nurture the old age of their parents in turn." Furthermore, Saint <term>Basil</term> proposes to us the example of the storks' piety toward their parents. <term>Crates</term> the Cynic alluded to the same when writing to his wife <term>Hipparchia</term> about their newborn son, promising that he would take care to return him to his mother in her old age as a "stork" instead of a "dog." For philosophers of the Cynic sect are called "dogs." He means, therefore, that the boy will be pious, cherishing his parent in turn when she is decrepit. <term>Aristophanes</term> also mentions the piety of storks in *The Birds*:
> <term>But there is a law for all of us birds</term> <note>original: Ἀλλ' ἔστιν ἡμῖν πᾶσι ὄρνισιν νόμος</note>
> <term>Ancient, in the tablets of the storks,</term> <note>original: Παλαῖος ἐν τοῖς τῶν πελαργῶν κύρβεσιν,</note>
> <term>When the father stork has made all the young storks</term> <note>original: Ἐπὴν ὁ πατὴρ ὁ πελαργὸς ἐκπετασίμους</note>
> <term>Able to fly by nourishing them,</term> <note>original: Πάντας ποιήσῃ τοὺς πελαργιδεῖς τρέφων,</note>
> <term>The chicks must in turn nourish the father.</term> <note>original: Δεῖ τοὺς νεοττοὺς τὸν πατέρα πάλιν τρέφειν.</note> ->that is,<-
> Indeed, a very ancient law flourishes for us birds,
> Inscribed on the tablets of the storks: that as soon as
> The parent stork has raised its own
> Young storks, and they have now emerged as fledglings,
> The chicks in turn must nourish their own father.

<summary>This page discusses the Greek adage "Antipelargein" (to act like a stork), explaining the ancient belief that storks care for their elderly parents as a model for human filial piety. Erasmus cites numerous classical and Christian authors to contrast the stork's devotion with the perceived cruelty of other animals like the hippopotamus and viper.</summary>
<keywords>filial piety, storks, Antipelargein, natural history, Aeneas, Aristotle, Pliny the Elder, Aristophanes, Greek proverbs, moral education</keywords>

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 10
<sig>X 2</sig>

Plato uses the same concept in the first *Alcibiades*. But truly no one has used it more charmingly or successfully than Angelo Poliziano <note>A famous Italian Renaissance humanist</note> in a certain epigram: <margin>And yet a wonder: wake the old woman, we are playing the stork.</margin> <note>original: "Κἄτι γε θαῦμα ἤγειραι τὴν γραῦν ἀντιπελαργέομεν."</note> That is to say, if we Latins, who were once educated by the literature of the Greeks, should now in turn teach our literature to Greece, as if to an old and exhausted woman. Furthermore, this kind of duty, which children bestow in turn upon their parents, the Greeks express with a single word: *geroboskein*, or *gerotrophein* and *gerokomein* <note>To feed, nourish, or care for the elderly</note>. There exists a six-foot verse <note>iambic senarius</note> to this effect:
<margin>You will pursue life badly if you do not nourish your elderly parents.</margin> <note>original: "κακῶς διώξεις γηροβοσκῶν τοὺς γονεῖς."</note> That is: You shall live long if you comfort your aged parents.

### II. With one tenor.
They call the progress of a matter a "tenor." From this, we say that things which are similar to themselves and follow one another in a kind of perpetual series have the "same tenor." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the book *On the Perfect Orator*: "And he flows, as they say, in one tenor in his speaking." He is speaking of an evenness of style that refreshes the ears of the listeners with no jarring variety. The same author in the book *On Famous Orators*: "For there is one tone of the oration and the same style." In which place, I do not know whether it would be better to read "tenor" instead of "tone."

### III. To bring into a square.
Marcus Tullius said "to bring into a square" in the same book, meaning to arrange something into order and a fitting structure. It is taken from those who level trees or stones with mathematical squares <note>gnomons</note> so that they agree with one another on all sides; hence, we say that what is fitting "squares up." Virgil in the third book of the *Georgics*:
> Give room to the rows, yet no less let every path
> Square up with the trees placed exactly to the mark,
> Along a cut boundary.

### IV. To drain from the dregs.
Marcus Tullius, in his catalog of illustrious orators, used a wonderfully proverbial figure: "to drain from the dregs," meaning to pursue certain sordid, plebeian, and overly humble things. Atticus uses this proverb against Cicero in the book I mentioned, because Cicero wasted time commemorating certain obscure orators of almost no name. It is borrowed from those wretches who drain the wine along with the dregs themselves, so as not to leave anything at all in the jar; hence we also speak of the "lowest dregs of the people."

### V. To lead into a snare.
"To lead into a snare" and "To lead into the nets" means to corner someone so skillfully that there is no longer any escape. This was the custom of the Platonic Socrates: to drive the Sophists with those little questions of his to the point where they denied what they had previously affirmed, affirmed what they had denied, and finally said nothing that made sense. Quintilian in the fifth book of the *Institutes*: "For they are confused, and are led into a snare by the advocates of the opposing side." The Greeks call those who are already held captive *embrochous*. Ovid:
> The sought-after prey has fallen into my nets.

Euripides in *Hippolytus*:
<margin>Entangled helplessly in snares.</margin> <note>original: "ἐμπεσὼν ἐν βρόχοις ἡττημένως."</note> That is: Ensnared by invisible nets. In the same work a little later:
<margin>As many as can free the queen from all the snares.</margin> <note>original: "ὅσαι τ’ ἄνασσαν ἐξ ἀπάσας βρόχων."</note> That is: To extricate the wild beast from the tenacious nets.

### VI. A Boeotian sow.
<margin>Boeotian sow.</margin> <note>original: "Βοιωτία ὗς."</note> A very ancient adage, once accustomed to be hurled at a dull and unlearned man. It is used by Pindar in the *Olympian Odes*:
<margin>By truthful words we flee the 'Boeotian sow,' that ancient reproach.</margin> <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἀρχαίου ὀνείδεος ἅλασι λογοις φεύγομεν Βοιωτίαν ὗν."</note>
He warns Aeneas the choir-master to take care in singing the hymn so that they might escape that old disgrace, which was usually said of the unmusical: "A Boeotian sow." The commentator relates the origin of the proverb in this way: Those who inhabited the region of Boeotia in ancient times were called *Hyantes*, a barbarian and rustic people. Consequently, some people, with a corrupted pronunciation, called the *Hyantes* "Huas," which means "swine." And that taunt turned into a proverb, so that it was first said against the Boeotians, and from them it was twisted to apply to any unlearned, unrefined men of rustic manners: "A Boeotian sow." The commentator cites the same Pindar from the *Dithyrambs*:
<margin>They used to call the Boeotian nation 'swine.'</margin> <note>original: "ἦν σύας τὸ Βοιώτιον ἔθνος ἔλεγον."</note> That is:

<summary>This page explores several classical adages, including the duty of children to parents (antipelargosis), metaphors for consistency in speech, and the "Boeotian sow" as a slur for the uncultured.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

There was a time when they called the Boeotian people "swine."
He also cites from Cratinus <note>An Athenian comic poet</note>: "These are the race of Syboeotian-swine men." <note>original: Αὗτοι δ' εἰσὶ συβοιωτῶν ὑῶν γένος ἀνδρῶν</note> That is, these are the Syboeotian pedestrian race of men—a ridiculous word composed of "swine" and "ox." In the Greek commentaries I found: "A Boeotian ear." <note>original: Βοιωτῶν οὖς</note> That is, a Boeotian mind, used for someone stupid and brutish. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Eating of Flesh*, indicates that the Athenians gave the nickname of "swine" to the Boeotians because they were stupid, dull, tasteless, and above all, because of their gluttony. This is supported by Athenaeus in his tenth book, where he records these verses from Eubulus:
"We are vigorous at drinking and devouring;
In these things we are strong. The Athenians are
Prompt to speak and eat little, but the Thebans eat much."
<note>original: Πονεῖν μὲν ἄμμοι καὶ φαγεῖν μὲν ἀνδρικοί... The Greek text here contains several corruptions or dialectal variations noted by Erasmus below.</note>
->that is,<-
We are strenuous at drinking and devouring,
In these we prevail. The Athenians are
Ready to speak, and eat little; the Thebans are accustomed to eat much.
In the Greek verses, it appears that "to drink" <note>original: πίνειν or πιεῖν</note> was written instead of "to labor," and other small grammatical variations occur.
The same Eubulus says in *Europa*: "He founded a city of Boeotians,
Of men best at eating through the whole day."
->that is,<-
He prepared a city for Boeotian men,
Strenuous at gorging themselves all day long.
Again from Eubulus in another play:
"So strongly is everything the Boeotian way."
->that is,<-
To such an extent do Boeotian manners prevail.
He confirms this with many testimonies from many authors. Moreover, the vices of gluttony <term>polyphagia: excessive eating</term> and stupidity are related to one another. And from this, they make the Theban Hercules a glutton, but also one most alienated from letters, so much so that he murdered his teacher. He too was a Boeotian, having been born in Thebes. Again, Plutarch in *On the Daemon of Socrates*: "To awaken that old reproach of 'creeping' and 'hatred of learning.'" <note>original: Ἀνεγείρειν τὸ ἑρπυστικὸν καὶ μισολογίαν ὄνειδος</note> That is, to rub salt in that old insult against the Boeotians regarding their hatred of literature. Although Plutarch himself was a Boeotian, he was a man who was anything but stupid. Finally, since it is certain—either because of the Roman Empire's wide expansion or the commerce of traders—that words from the Germanic, French, and British languages were mixed, I suspect it flowed down to us from the Greeks that we commonly call a stupid man with no sharpness of mind "bot" <note>Dutch/Germanic for "blunt" or "dull"</note> instead of "Boeotian." For it is characteristic of this language <note>Germanic/Dutch</note> to contract words of many syllables into a single syllable.

---

->You hunt the impossible.<-
"You hunt things that cannot happen." <note>original: Ἀδύνατα θηρᾷς</note> That is, you hunt for things that cannot be done. Used against one who attempts what he cannot achieve. Taken from fowling or the hunting of prey which one has no power to catch. I would not have included this among the adages if I had not found it in the Greek collections. For aside from the metaphor of "hunting," it has little of the flavor of a proverb. However, the precept is not useless. Indeed, if the Greeks teach rightly that one should not attempt that which you doubt, much less should you attempt what is certain you will not attain. For example, if someone tries to acquire peace of mind through wealth or those common pleasures, or true erudition without the knowledge of languages, he "hunts the impossible." Pindar in the *Nemean Odes*: "The empty end of vain hopes." <note>original: κενεᾶν δ' ἐλπίδων χαύνου τέλος</note> The same in the third *Pythian Ode*:
"One must always look for the measure of every thing within oneself."
->that is,<-
It is necessary for a man to always see
The limit of each matter within himself.
The interpreter indicates this is the meaning: let no one attempt things greater than his own strength. The aphorisms of Chilon <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> are recalled: that one should not attempt what you cannot achieve. For some plans are magnificent, but for that very reason useless, because they are "impossible."

---

->To divine by a sieve.<-
"To prophesy by a sieve." <note>original: Κοσκίνῳ μαντεύεσθαι</note> That is, to discover a matter by a shrewd guess, or to divine foolishly about hidden things. Lucian in *The False Prophet*: "Divining by a sieve, as the saying goes." Theocritus also mentions it in the third *Idyll*:
"The sieve-diviner spoke the truth to me, Agroeo."
Furthermore, this kind of divining by a suspended sieve lasts even to the present day among certain people...

<summary>Erasmus discusses the "Boeotian" stereotype of stupidity and gluttony, linking it to modern Germanic etymology, and explores proverbs regarding impossible ambitions and folk divination.</summary>

# FIRST CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

...certain superstitious people. Among the ancients, prophecies were performed by means of a sieve, laurel, and a tripod. <note>Erasmus refers to various forms of divination: coscinomancy (sieve), daphnomancy (laurel), and the Delphic tripod.</note>

---

<margin>IX</margin>
### You are cutting the Hydra.

**You are cutting the Hydra** <note>original Greek: Ὕδραν τέμνεις</note>. This appears in Plato’s *Republic*, Book IV: "They are unaware," he says, "that they are truly **cutting the Hydra**" <note>original Greek: ἀγνοῦντες... οἵ, ὅτι οὐκ ὡς ὕδραν τέμνουσι</note>. To "cut the Hydra" means to remove one single problem in such a way that you receive several others in its place. The adage arises from the fable of the Lernaean Hydra, which some say had a hundred heads, others eight, one of which was immortal. Hercules struggled with this monster for a long time because when one head was cut off, several more grew back. Plutarch, in his essay *On the Fortune of Alexander*, writes: "**cutting a Hydra that was always sprouting anew through various wars**" <note>original Greek: ὕδραν τέμνων ἀεί τισι πολέμοις ἀναβλασάνουσαν</note>. He is speaking of Alexander the Great, for whom, as soon as one war was finished, another and then another immediately arose. Cyneas, recognizing the vast number of Romans who kept restoring their forces even after suffering defeat, said it seemed to him that Pyrrhus was fighting against the Lernaean Hydra. Hence Horace says in his *Odes*:

> Not the Hydra, with its body lopped, grew stronger
> Against Hercules, who grieved to be conquered.

This can be applied to those involved in lawsuits that never end. For one lawsuit gives birth to another, and often, in place of one killed off, three more are born. Seneca writes in a certain place that "sordid affairs," which call us away from the study of wisdom, can be broken off but not untangled, because one business is born from another, and occupation follows occupation just as wave follows wave.

---

<margin>X</margin>
### Not even a scrap. Not even a straw.

**Not even a scrap richer** <note>original: Ne ramenta quidem ditior</note> is a proverbial hyperbole found several times in Plautus, notably in *The Rope*: "By Hercules, you won't be a **scrap** luckier for leaving here today." It is just as if you were to say "richer by a bit of oakum," as people commonly say. Aristophanes used a similar figure in *Lysistrata*: "**not even a scrap, not even a straw**" <note>original Greek: ἄντιξ μηδὲ ψαδαῦ, κινῶδα μηδὲ κάρφος</note>; that is, he will leave nothing here, he won't even move a straw.
The same author in *The Wasps*: "**he does not see even a speck of sleep all night**" <note>original Greek: υπνὸ δ᾽ ὁρᾷ δι νυκτὸς οὐδὲ πασπάλην</note>. The commentator says that *paspale* <note>original Greek: πασπάλην</note> signifies the smallest possible thing. To some, that word indicates a magnet stone. He adds a similar figure in the same place: "**not even if he bowed his head in sleep by a chaff's weight**" <note>original Greek: μηδ᾽ ἐν κατὰ μύοισι λίην ἄχνω</note>. Now, *achne* <note>original Greek: ἄχνω</note> signifies that tiny and very light thing that flies out from threshed ears of corn. Homer also used this word in the *Iliad*, Book 5: "**As the wind tosses the light chaff across the sacred threshing floors**" <note>original Greek: Ως δ᾽ ἄνεμον ἄχνας φορέει ἱερὰς κατ᾽ ἀλωὰς</note>. Those skilled in Hebrew letters affirm that the word *achne* <note>original Greek: ἄχνυ</note>—which Jerome translated as "dust," following the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> who translated it as *achne*—sounds the same to the Hebrews as it does to the Greeks.

---

<margin>XI</margin>
### A sacrifice without smoke.

**A sacrifice without smoke** <note>original Greek: Ἄκαπνοσ θυσία</note>. This refers to an excessively meager banquet where no cooked meat is served. It is metaphorically taken from the sacrifices of the very poor, who offer meal-cakes, a bit of incense, milk, or garlands, whereas the gods expect that "savor of burnt meat" flying upward with the smoke, according to Homer. Lucian says in *The Loves*: "**Truly the god is a glutton, Lucian, and takes very little pleasure in 'smokeless sacrifices,' as they say**" <note>original Greek: βαρᾶγ᾿ δὴ ὁ δαίμων ὦ λυκῖνε, καὶ ταῖς ἀκάπνοις, ὥς φασι, τῶν θυσιῶν ἥκιστα τερπόμενῶ</note>. Athenaeus used it in the same sense: "**For we poets always offer sacrifices without smoke**" <note>original Greek: ἄκαπνα γὰρ τὰ ἀοιδῶι θύομεν</note>.

---

<margin>XII</margin>
### Hippoclides doesn't care.

**Hippoclides doesn't care** <note>original Greek: οὐ φροντὶς Ἱπποκλείδῃ</note>. Or, to render it as a verse: **Hippoclides has no worries**. For it is an iambic dimeter catalectic verse. By this adage, people used to indicate that they were neglecting something and not working very hard at it. It arose from a history told at length by Herodotus in his book *Erato*. To put it briefly: this Hippoclides was the son of Tisander, who along with many other young men was courting the daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon. But when Cleisthenes had tested the suitors for a whole year, and Hippoclides performed a certain unseemly dance at a banquet, throwing his legs up in the air, the father, offended by the young man's dishonorable play, said...

<meta>The text cuts off as Cleisthenes is about to rebuke Hippoclides; the catchword "οὐ πᾶ" indicates the start of the next page's Greek text.</meta>

<summary>This page explores four classical adages concerning endless tasks (the Hydra), extreme insignificance (scraps and chaff), meager offerings (smokeless sacrifices), and nonchalance (Hippoclides). Erasmus draws on a wide range of Greek and Latin authorities, including Plato, Homer, and Herodotus, to explain their origins.</summary>
<keywords>Hydra, Hercules, Alexander the Great, Seneca, Aristophanes, Plautus, Homer, Septuagint, Lucian, Hippoclides, Herodotus, Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

--- Page 436 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Adages, focusing on Greek historical anecdotes and moral fables that have become common sayings.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

“O son of Tisander, you have danced away your marriage.” <note>original: "Ω παῖ Τισάνδρου ἀπερχήσαό γε μὴν τὸν γάμον"</note> That is, *Son of Tisander, by your dancing you have fallen out of your wedding.* But he immediately replied, “Hippoclides doesn’t care.” <note>original: "οὐ φροντὶς Ἱπποκλείδῃ"</note> This, as Herodotus testifies, passed into a proverb. Plutarch turns this saying back against Herodotus himself in the booklet he wrote against him: “It seems to me that just as Hippoclides, gesticulating with his legs on the table as if they were hands, might say while dancing away the truth: ‘Hippoclides doesn’t care.’” <note>original: "Δοκεῖ μοι καθάπερ Ἱπποκλείδης..."</note> Lucian, in his *Apology*, says: “It would be enough for me to say, ‘Hippoclides doesn’t care.’” The same author in *Hercules* says: “And Hippoclides will not worry.” Eustathius also mentions this adage when writing on the first book of Homer’s *Iliad*. Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Wasps*, frequently repeating the phrase: “It matters little to me.”

->The Dog in the Manger<-
<margin>XIII</margin>

“The dog in the manger.” <note>original: "Ἡ κύων ἐν τῇ φάτνῃ"</note> This is said against those who neither enjoy a thing themselves nor allow others to use it; for example, if someone were to carefully lock away excellent books <term>codices: manuscript volumes</term> which he never reads himself, nor gives others the opportunity to read. Just as the dog in the manger does not eat the barley himself, yet prevents the horse from eating it. Lucian, in *Against the Ignorant*, says: “But you act like the dog lying in the manger, who neither eats the barley herself nor permits the horse, who is able to eat, to do so.” He uses the same in *Timon*. It is cited in Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note> under the proverb “A stranger to Dionysus,” though the author's name is suppressed: “You lead the dog to the manger, and you lead the donkey to Dionysus.” That is, you bring things that are irrelevant to the matter, but of those things which pertain to the proposed case, you bring nothing. Athenaeus reports something similar in Book VI concerning a certain tribe of Gauls called the Cordistae: they loathe gold and do not import it into their region, yet they never cease plundering others. They say this tribe are the remnants of the Gauls who, under the leader Brennus, plundered the Delphic oracle, and whom the leader Bathanatus pursued and treated harshly. Hence their hatred of gold, for the sake of which they suffered so many evils, yet they still begrudge it to others.

->The Catchers are Caught<-
<margin>XIIII</margin>

“The catchers are caught.” <note>original: "Αἱροῦντες ᾑρήμεθα"</note> This is used when a matter turns out perversely, so that we ourselves are ensnared by those we were trying to deceive. This happens not infrequently—that we fall into the very traps we had set for others. It often happens that one who feigns love to entice a girl into a romance begins to love her truly. And he who works to make another drunk with little invitations to drink is made drunk himself; and he who plots to drive a neighbor from power loses his own empire. So also Horace:
> Captive Greece took captive her savage conqueror.

Plato seems to have alluded to the same when he writes in *Theaetetus*: “It seems to me, O Socrates, that the argument which was trying to catch is itself most caught.” Sophocles in *Oedipus at Colonus*:
> Know that as you hold, you are held, and fortune has caught you while you were hunting.

Plautus in *Epidicus*: “Now the trickster himself is caught.” Lucian in the *Dialogues of the Courtesans*: “And I, wretch that I am, was caught by the very one I caught.” It is a metaphor taken either from war, fishing, or hunting.

->Perished in the Hunt<-
<margin>XV</margin>

Lucian said it more wittily in *Toxaris*: “And she herself perished in the hunt.” That is, while she was hunting the youth and striving to ensnare him, she destroyed herself. Furthermore, those phrases “to hunt for praise” or “to go fowling for fame” are proverbial metaphors, just like “to fish out” for inquiring and searching.

->The Wolf into the Snares<-
<margin>XVI</margin>

“The wolf into the snares.” <note>original: "Εἰς πάγας ὁ λύκος"</note> Used when some wicked person is finally brought into extreme danger. For since the wolf is a most treacherous animal, everyone applauds if it ever happens to be ensnared, and immediately everyone shouts, “The wolf into the snares!” It is recorded by Zenodotus.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning unintended consequences and selfishness, including the famous 'Dog in the Manger' and the story of Hippoclides 'dancing away' his marriage. He draws on a wide range of classical sources to show how these metaphors apply to human behavior and irony.</summary>
<keywords>Hippoclides, Herodotus, Dog in the Manger, irony, greed, hunting metaphors, Greek proverbs, Lucian, Plutarch, Brennus the Gaul</keywords>

# TENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST CHILIAD
->E 2<-

### An old fox is not caught in a snare.
->XVII<-

<margin><note>original Greek: Γέρων ἀλώπηξ οὐχ ἁλίσκεται πάγῃ.</note></margin> That is, an old fox cannot be captured by any traps. This proverbial hexameter line should be spoken of one who, through long age and much experience of things, is too clever to be caught by artifice or guile.

### A fox is not corrupted by gifts.
->XVIII<-

<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀλώπηξ οὐ δωροδοκεῖται.</note></margin> That is, a fox is not bribed by gifts. Suidas cites the author Cratinus for this adage. It refers to the shrewd and versatile, whom it is not easy to deceive by tossing them a small gift, a bit of flattery, or promises. For the seagull and certain other birds are caught by bait, but the fox is not. Moreover, the word <term>to receive bribes</term> <note>original: δωροδοκεῖν</note> is taken from public assemblies or trials, in which some, corrupted by money, deliver their verdict.

### An Attic in the harbor.
->XIX<-

<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀττικὸς εἰς λιμένα.</note></margin> That is, an Athenian in the harbor. This used to be said against those who are accustomed to show off their courage where it is safe and where there is no need for it. It is taken from Attic sailors, who, when about to enter the harbor, would behave magnificently for the sake of showing off; yet in the actual event—that is, in a naval battle—they were not nearly so vigorous.

### A Scyrian goat.
->XX<-

<margin><note>original Greek: Αἲξ σκυρία.</note></margin> That is, a Scyrian goat. Zenodotus cites Chrysippus as both the author and interpreter of this proverb. It applies to those who spoil a kindness with a wrongful act, or who contaminate and obscure virtues by attaching vices to them, or who do not finish well what was well begun. Just as the Scyrian goat, because it is wild, kicks over the pail it had filled with milk, and in this way destroys the benefit it had given. Others think it is said of those from whom the most profit is taken, because the goats of that region are said to yield the greatest quantity of milk. This is also affirmed by Athenaeus in the first book of the *Deipnosophists*, citing this poem by Pindar: <margin><note>original Greek: Σκυρίας δ' ἐξ ἀμέλγειν γάλακτος αἶγας ἐξοχώτατας.</note></margin> That is: "Truly, the Scyrian goats are most excellent for milking."

### A tree must be chosen for hanging.
->XXI<-

In a matter exceedingly shameful and in no way to be tolerated, the ancients used to say a tree must be chosen for hanging. This arose because once a certain little prostitute named Leontium dared to write against the eminent philosopher Theophrastus. Pliny the Elder says in the preface to his *Natural History*: "As if I did not know that even a woman wrote against Theophrastus—a man so great in eloquence that he gained a divine name from it—and that the proverb was born from this: a tree must be chosen for hanging." Thus far Pliny. Close to this is that passage in Euripides' *Alcestis*:
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἄξια καὶ σφαγᾶς τάδε Καὶ πλέον, ἢ βρόχῳ δέρην οὐρανίῳ πελάσαι.</note></margin>
> That is,
> Ho there, these things are worthy of slaughter,
> Or rather, that someone should choke
> His throat in a hanging noose.

Plautus says in *The Weevil*: "That is my prey; therefore, put yourself in a noose." Juvenal asks: "Can you endure any mistress while so many ropes are safe?" <note>i.e., while there are still ropes available to hang yourself.</note> There was a character in Plautus who, gripped by a weariness of life, wished for a coin to buy a rope. When I was publishing these things in the year 1525, I happened upon the commentaries of Caelius Rhodiginus. He says that many are blind in this sort of explanation, and he boasts that he has explained every difficulty, when in fact there is no difficulty; and if there were, his remarks about the hanging of the cross explain nothing. For criminals do not choose a tree for themselves, but are driven to the cross. However, those who contemplate suicide are accustomed to choose one kind of hanging over another, so that it appears they do this not from a lack of mental control, but by a certain and deliberate plan.

### A cat to Minerva.
->XXII<-

<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀθηνᾷ τὴν γαλῆν.</note></margin> That is, you are comparing a cat to Minerva (to be understood). This is used when much inferior things are compared with more excellent ones because they agree in some very slight matter. For what does the goddess Minerva have in common with a cat, except for the brightness of the eyes? For that eye color is attributed to Minerva, which is also present in cats at night. Hence even in Homer her epithet is <term>bright-eyed Athena</term> <note>original: γλαυκῶπις ἀθήνη</note>. This is also common to cats and owls: they see at night and equally lie in wait for mice. It is recorded by Zenodotus and Suidas. The Etymologist indicates a distinction in spelling, whereby <term>wild</term> <note>original: ἔναγρος</note> for a people (for there is a people of Scythia, from...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>original: "ludibus dicta"</note> is written with an epsilon. For a living creature, it is written with a diphthong, *eilē*, as if you were to say "Tail-twister" or "Tail-dragger," though I see this is often neglected by authors.

->To pay by a turning.<-
XXIII

<note>original: "Vorfuram soluere"</note>
A person is said to "pay by a turning" who extricates himself from present evils in such a way that he becomes entangled in other, more serious ones. For according to Donatus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian</note>, "to make a turning" <note>original: "uorfurā facere"</note> is to pay off a debt with borrowed money, or to take up a larger sum of money at a lower interest rate to cover a debt. The word is derived, as Festus Pompeius testifies, from the fact that they "turn" <note>original: "uertāt"</note> the creditor. Terence says in *Phormio*: "You are stuck in the same mud; you are paying by a turning." The evil that was present has been deferred for a day, but the blows are increasing. Cicero to Atticus: "Your precepts have produced such admirable restraint in me that I fear I must pay for what I exchanged with you by a turning." In the oration *For L. Flaccus*: "He denied that he had made any turning at all in Rome." Seneca in *On Benefits*, book 5: "What they call a 'turning' happens at home, and like a gambler's debt, it passes on immediately." The same author in book 3, in the final letter: "However matters stand, a turning must be made from Epicurus." That is, a loan must be taken from Epicurus with which I may satisfy you. He used a similar trope in book 1, letter four: "But to put an end to the letter, receive what pleased me today; and this too was taken from someone else's gardens." Lactantius used this proverb in book 2 of the *Institutes*: "When, therefore," he says, "you attribute the origin of things to nature and take it away from God, sticking in the same mud, you pay by a turning." Demosthenes elegantly explained this metaphor in the *First Olynthiac*: <note>original Greek: Δέδοικα ὦ ἄνδρες ἀθηναῖοι...</note> "I fear, men of Athens, that just as those who borrow money easily at high interest are wealthy for a short time, but a little later are stripped even of their principal; so we too, if we appear negligent for too long and seek everything for pleasure, may a little later come into such necessity that we must do many bitter things which we by no means wished, and run risks concerning this very land."

->He owes his soul.<-
XXIIII

<note>original: "Τὴν ψυχὴν ὀφείλει" / "Animam debet"</note>
Donatus warns that this is a proverb concerning one who is held by such immoderate debt that he owes more than all his resources—and finally, owes his very self. Terence in *Phormio*: "What if he owes his soul?" For in ancient times there was a law that he who was not solvent should be delivered as a bondman <note>term: "nexus" - a person who has pledged their physical body as collateral for a loan</note> to the creditor, to pay with his body (that is, with labor) what he could not pay with money. There exists in Gellius a law of the Twelve Tables which commanded that the body of a man who owed many creditors and was insolvent should be cut into pieces.

->Extreme law, extreme injustice.<-
XXV

<note>original: "Summum ius, summa iniuria"</note>
"Extreme law is extreme injustice"; that is, one departs furthest from equity when one adheres most superstitiously to the letter of the laws. For they call it "extreme law" when the dispute is over the words of the law, and no regard is paid to what the writer intended. For the voices and letters are, as it were, the "outer skin" of the laws. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] mocks the ineptitude of certain superstitious interpreters of the law both copiously and elegantly in his speech *For Murena*. Terence: "That is a true saying, Chremes: extreme law is often extreme malice." Cicero in the first book of *On Duties*: "From which 'extreme law, extreme injustice' has now become a well-worn proverb in speech." Columella in the first book of *On Agriculture*: "Indeed, we should not claim everything that is permitted. For the ancients thought extreme law was an extreme cross <note>i.e., a supreme torture or burden</note>." The younger Celsus is also cited in the *Pandects* <note>A compendium of Roman law</note>, book 45, under the title "On Verbal Obligations," in the chapter "If the slave Stichus": who wrote that the question is one of "the good and the equitable," a category in which one often errs under the authority of legal science. Likewise, Paulus in book 50, under the title "On the Rules of Law": "In all things indeed, but especially in law, equity must be regarded." With a similar figure, Seneca said in the first book of *On Anger*: "on the surface of the mind" <note>original: "summo animo"</note>, "If you understand that wickedness does not come from deep within, but clings, as they say, to the surface of the mind."

->Not even the fire-bearer was left.<-
XXVI

<note>original: "Οὐδὲ πυρφόρος ἐλείφθη" / "Ne ignifer quidem superfuit"</note>
By this we signify that everyone perished to a man, so much so that not even he was spared who carries the fire before the army. For it was an ancient custom that a seer preceded the battle line, crowned with laurel and carrying a torch. From this man the violence of war was withheld by both sides, because they considered it a sin to draw the sword against a sacred man. Therefore, if cruel...

<summary>Erasmus discusses proverbs related to debt, the dangers of literalist legal interpretation (Summum Ius), and the total destruction of an army where not even the sacred fire-bearer survives.</summary>
<keywords>debt, usury, legal equity, Roman law, Twelve Tables, Cicero, Seneca, Terence, fire-bearer, ancient warfare</keywords>

# TENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<note>original: "CHIL. PRIMÆ CENTVRIA X"</note>
E 3
<meta>catchword: text,</meta>

when they wished to signify a cruel slaughter, they would say that not even the "fire-bearer" was spared. Eustathius mentions this adage in his commentary on Book 12 <note>original: "μ"</note> of the *Iliad*, explaining these verses of Homer:
> I do not think that even a messenger will return 
> Back to the city.
> <note>original: "κ’ ουκ’ ἔπετ’ οἰω’ γὰρ’ ἄγγελον ἀφνέεθαι / Αψορ’ῥον ποτὶ ἄστυ."</note>

He advises that this also has a proverbial form: *not even a messenger was left behind* <note>original: "μηδὲ ἄγγελον ὑπολείπεσθαι"</note>. We use this whenever we mean that everyone was killed to a man, so that not even one survived to report what happened. For a messenger is usually left behind by an enemy specifically for that purpose.

->Total destruction. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXVII<-
<note>original: "πανολεθρία"</note>

Akin to this is *panolethria*, a word by which they signified utter annihilation, and the kind of ruin where nothing at all remains. Thucydides in the seventh book of his *History* says: *Being defeated in every way in all things, and having suffered no small misery in any respect, they were destroyed with "total destruction," as the saying goes, both infantry and ships, and there was nothing that did not perish.* <note>original: "πᾶσι πάντως νικώμενοι... πανολεθρίᾳ δὴ τὸ λεγόμενον..."</note> It will be more elegant if this is turned away from war, shipwreck, fire, and similar disasters toward other things. For instance, if you were to say that lust is indeed a great plague to the Christian religion, but greed is the absolute *total destruction* <note>original: "πανολεθρίαν"</note> of piety. Or that the ignorance of Greek literature was the *total destruction* of all good disciplines. In a similar fashion, Cicero, in his speech *Against Piso*, calls the Temple of Castor the "tomb of all laws and religions," because the authority of the laws and the worship of religions were suppressed there.

->A Thracian trick. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXVIII<-

<margin>A Thracian invention.</margin> <note>original: "Θρᾴκιον ἐννόημα"</note> *A Thracian invention*, or device. In Zenodotus, we read that this should be hurled at those who evade agreements by some clever and crafty trick. Furthermore, Strabo indicates where this proverb originated in the ninth book of his *Geography*, citing Ephorus: the Thracians, having struck a truce of several days with the Boeotians, nevertheless conducted raids during the night with no less vigor. When the Boeotians repelled them and complained that they had violated the truce, the Thracians replied that they had done nothing against the agreement: for they had agreed about the *days*, but had not raided during the *nights*. Zenodotus relates nearly the same things: namely, that the Thracians, having established a ten-day truce, made an attack by night on the Boeotians (who were acting more carelessly out of trust in the truce) and slaughtered some of them and led others away alive. When the Boeotians complained about the violated pact, they replied that the agreement contained days, not nights. This event gave rise to the proverb, *A Thracian invention*. For *ennoema* <note>original: "ἐννόημα"</note> is properly a "thought-out" cavil or sophistry by which we evade a pact. Plautus calls these "sycophanties" <term>sycophantias: deceptive tricks or swindles</term>. And Terence says: *Lest any trick be woven against his own head.* For they add some invention outside the agreement by which they subvert the whole matter.

->The Roman wins by sitting. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXIX<-

*The Roman wins by sitting.* An old proverb against those who, though calm and idle, nevertheless achieve what they want, or those who manage an affair not by force but by skill. Marcus Varro in the first book of *On Agriculture*, chapter 2, says: *Do you wish, then, that we use the old proverb, "The Roman wins by sitting," while that man is coming?* I believe it arose from the history of Fabius the Delayer <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, known for his "Fabian strategy" of attrition against Hannibal</note>, who broke Hannibal (who was exulting with youthful energy) by his own patience. Regarding him, that famous verse of Ennius exists:
> One man who, by delaying, restored our state.

It is cited by Cicero in *On Old Age*. It was used divinely by Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> in Book 6. Likewise, Livy, in his first book on the Macedonian War, reports something similar about the consul Sulpicius. *To whom,* he says, *if he were surrounded on all sides by troops, it could be believed that the Roman would win the war by sitting still.*

->To hit the mark. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXX<-

<margin>To reach the goal.</margin> <note>original: "ἐπιτυχεῖν τοῦ σκοποῦ"</note> *To hit the mark.* This means to obtain one's wish, or to grasp the matter itself by conjecture. Lucian in *Icaromenippus* says: *Your conjecture would not be far from the mark.* <note>original: "οὐκ ἂν τοῦ σκοποῦ εἴκαζες"</note> Also *to miss the mark* <note>original: "ἀποτυγχάνειν τοῦ σκοποῦ"</note> and *to wander from the mark* <note>original: "ἁμαρτάνειν τοῦ σκοποῦ"</note>; all other figures of this kind savor of proverbs. Diogenes used this adage wittily against a boy throwing stones at a gallows: *Well done,* he said, *you will finally hit the mark someday.* Pindarus in the ninth *Nemean Ode*: *I hurl the Muse closest to the mark.* <note>original: "ἀφίημι τὸν σκοπὸν ἄγχιστα μοῖσαν"</note> Likewise in the sixth ode:

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

In the sixth book <note>original: "sexto"</note>, "I hope, having spoken great things, to hit the mark." <note>original: "ἐλπομαι μέγα εἰπὼν, ἄντα σκοπῶ τυχαῖν"</note>. That is, I hope that having promised great things, I shall reach the goal. It is also said, "to shoot outside the mark" <note>original: "ἔξω σκοπῶ βάλλειν"</note>, which is to say, to speak of things foreign to the matter at hand. Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence</note> used this in his *Monody*.

->An old monkey is not caught in a snare.<-
<margin>XXXI</margin>

"The monkey is not caught by the noose" <note>original: "ὁ πίθηκος ἐκ ἁλίσκεται βρόχῳ"</note>. This is usually said against crafty shufflers who cannot be proven wrong. It was once said regarding Heraclides, who had carelessly and wrongly cited a line from Dionysius that actually belonged to Sophocles. A copy was sent to him so that, seeing the poem there, he might recognize his error. When he continued to shuffle and would not admit his slip—claiming it could happen by chance that verses in different poets might agree—someone wrote that a monkey is hardly caught in a snare. The author is Diogenes Laertius. The Greek verse goes like this:
"Stop, for the monkey is not caught by the trap;
He is caught indeed, but he is caught only after a long time."
That is:
An old monkey is not caught by a snare:
He is captured indeed, but captured quite late.

->Bounty has no bottom.<-
<margin>XXXII</margin>

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book of *On Duties*: "Altogether," he says, "we ought to remember that which has been used very often by our people, and has now come into the custom of a proverb: that bounty has no bottom." By this saying they signified that by foolish liberality, any amount of wealth may be exhausted, or rather, flow away. It seems to be a metaphor taken from the leaking jar of the Danaids <note>In mythology, the daughters of Danaus were punished in the underworld by having to fill a leaking jar with water forever</note> in the underworld. Things which lack a bottom the Greeks call "bottomless" <note>original: "ἀπύθμενα"</note>. Hence Parthenius, in Athenaeus’s eleventh book, spoke of a "bottomless bowl."

->The unfillable jar.<-
<margin>XXXIII</margin>

"The unfillable jar" <note>original: "Ἄπληστος πίθος"</note>. The use of this adage is varied. For first, it fits "those who eat one another" <note>original: "εἰς τοὺς ἀλληλοφάγους"</note>, that is, gluttons and the greedy; but more fittingly it applies to those with an unquenchable thirst for drink, who the more they drink, the more they thirst, as was once said of the Parthians. For Festus seems to have felt this way, citing someone—for the passage is mutilated—who called the belly a "leaking jar," although by nature the belly is also unfillable, because whatever you pour in through the mouth is excreted by other ways. It will also fit a forgetful person: if you pour any learning into him, it immediately flows out, and he forgets it before he has fully learned it. Aristophanes makes Strepsiades this way in *The Clouds*:
"One who, learning certain small trivialities,
Has forgotten them before he learned them."
That is:
He who learns such tiny subtleties
Has forgotten them before he even mastered them.
Plautus used it almost this way in *Pseudolus*: "We are pouring into a leaking jar; we are wasting our labor." It also applies to men who are excessively extravagant, as Aristotle indicated in the first book of *Economics*: "For if it were possible to acquire but not to keep, there would be no use in acquiring. For this is to draw water with a sieve, or as the proverb says, a leaking jar." It likewise fits the covetous, whose desires nothing can satisfy; indeed, the more they are filled with riches, the more empty they seem to be. This is elegantly testified by that poem of Solon <note>An Athenian lawmaker and poet</note> in Plutarch’s book *On the Love of Wealth*:
"No visible limit of wealth is set for men."
Zenodotus thinks that even Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of the underworld</note> itself is rightly understood as the unfillable jar, because it is never filled by so many thousands of the dead. And that wise Hebrew <note>Likely referring to King Solomon in the Book of Proverbs</note> names this among the insatiable things. It will also fit those who wickedly snatch from some what they wickedly squander on others. It is also used for those laboring in vain, as is shown in another place, such as in Catullus: "That same man might as well fill jars with the urns of virgins" <note>A reference to the Danaids</note>.
The adage arose from the well-known story of the daughters of Danaus, who are said to suffer this punishment in the underworld for murdering their bridegrooms: they must draw water in leaky vessels and pour it into a jar that is likewise perforated—a heavy, but useless labor. Horace mentions this story in his *Odes*: "And the jar empty of water..."

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to futility and greed, specifically the "leaking jar" of the Danaids, applying it to gluttony, forgetfulness, and the endless pursuit of wealth.</summary>
<keywords>cunning, greed, futility, Danaids, Cicero, Aristophanes, underworld punishments, ancient Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

# FIRST THOUSAND, TENTH CENTURY

...a jar with a leaking bottom. <note>original: "Dolium fundo pereuntis imo"</note> Likewise Tibullus writes:
*And the offspring of Danaus, who offended the divinity of Venus, carries Lethean waters in hollow jars.* <note>The Danaides were cursed in the underworld to eternally fill a leaking jar for murdering their husbands.</note>
Lucian mentions this in *Timon*. And Aristotle in the sixth book of the *Politics*. Again, Lucian in *Hermotimus* says: <note>original Greek: ἐπιῤῥέει γὰρ τὴν παροιμίαν τὸ πρᾶγμα ἐξαντλοῦμεν, οὐ τὸ ἔμπαλιν, ἢ ὁ τῶν δαναΐδων πίθος</note> that is, "For the business and labor flows in while it is being drained, and it happens the opposite way as with the jar of the Danaides." Plato also used it, both in several other places and in the *Gorgias*.

---

->While the bear is present, you look for its tracks.<- XXXIIII

<margin>Greek: "While the bear is present, you seek the tracks."</margin> This is said of those who, out of fear, avoid the business at hand and slip away into other trifles. It is a metaphor taken from fearful hunters who pretend they haven't noticed the bear and feign to be following tracks so that they might stay away from danger. Plato, in the fifth book of the *Republic*, wrote that men of this sort are like <note>original Greek: τοῖς κυνιδίοις, ἃ τοὺς λίθους δάκνει, τῶν βαλόντων οὐκ ἀπτόμενα</note> "little dogs who bite the stones, not daring to touch those who threw them." Not far from this is what Plutarch writes in the *Life of Lucullus*. For when Archelaus urged him to leave the enemy and cross into Pontus (saying that in this way he would immediately gain control of everything), <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔφη θαλάττορος εἶναι κυνηγοῦ, ὥστε τὰ θηρία παρελθὼν ἐπὶ κενοὺς αὐτῶν φωλεοὺς βαδίζειν</note> "he said he was not so cowardly a hunter as to pass by the wild beasts and go to their empty dens."

---

->Good men go to the feasts of good men of their own accord.<- XXXV

<margin>Greek: "Good men go to the feasts of good men unbidden."</margin>
*It is the custom for a good man to go to the feasts of the good of his own will.*
A proverbial hexameter, to be used when a good man, trusting in his virtue and the friendship that generally exists between all honorable people, approaches one like himself without waiting for those common little invitations. Some think it originated with Hercules, who, when he visited the house of Ceyx of Trachis uninvited, was the first to say this little verse. An iambic trimeter is also cited to the same effect:
<margin>Greek: "Uninvited, friends go to the revels of friends."</margin>
*A friend comes even of his own accord to the feasts of a friend.*
Homer silently noted the adage in the second book of the *Iliad*:
<margin>Greek: "And Menelaus, good at the war-cry, came to him of his own accord."</margin>
The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on classical texts</note> indicates that Menelaus's bravery in war was signified by this word. For a thin voice indicates a fearful person, and "war-cry" <note>Greek: βοὴ (boē)</note> among the Greeks sometimes declares "war," just as it does today among the Germans. <note>Erasmus likely refers to the German word 'Geschrei' or similar terms linking shouting to battle.</note> Zenodotus, in his collections, cites this adage with a different meaning from a comedy by Eupolis titled *Chrysogenes*:
<margin>Greek: "The brave go of their own accord to the feasts of the cowardly."</margin>
Plato means almost the same thing in the *Symposium*: "So that we may even ruin the proverb by changing it, as if indeed good men go to the feasts of the good of their own accord." Plato seems to feel that Homer made Menelaus the inferior person approaching the feast of a superior, because Agamemnon was strong in war while Menelaus was weak. This passage is also cited by Athenaeus in book four. However, I do not think this was Homer's intention, since he adds the praise of virtue, <note>original Greek: βοὴν ἀγαθὸς μενέλαος</note> "Menelaus good at the war-cry," and since in several places he depicts him conducting himself most bravely, and elsewhere honors him with the epithet "dear to Ares." In Athenaeus, book one, from Cratinus, someone who had come to a feast uninvited speaks thus: <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθοὶ ἂν πρὸς ἀγαθοὺς ἄνδρας ἑστιασομένους ἥκω, κοινὰ γὰρ τὰ τῶν φίλων</note> "For I, a good man, have come to feast with good men. For the things of friends are common."

---

->To fight with dogs in a well.<- XXXVI

<margin>Greek: "To fight with dogs in a well."</margin> This was commonly said when someone happens upon business with a brawling and contentious man from whom he cannot extricate himself. It is also expressed in this way: "to dog-fight in a well," using a compound word.
