# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...sixth book, <note>original: "ἔλπομαι μέγα εἰπὼν, ἄντα σκοποῦ τυχεῖν"</note> "I hope, having spoken great things, to hit the mark." It is also said <note>original: "ἔξω σκοποῦ βάλλειν"</note> "to throw outside the mark," which is used when someone speaks of things foreign to the matter at hand. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence.</note> used this in his *Monody*.

<margin>XXXI</margin>
->An old monkey is not caught in a snare.<-

<note>original: "Ὁ πίθηκος οὐχ ἁλίσκεται βρόχῳ"</note> That is, "A monkey is not caught by a noose." This is usually said against clever evaders who cannot be proven wrong. It was once said against Heraclides, who had carelessly and incorrectly cited a line from Dionysius as if it were from Sophocles. A copy was sent to him so that, upon seeing the poem, he might recognize his error. When he continued to make excuses and refused to acknowledge his slip—claiming it was possible for verses by different poets to happen to agree—someone wrote to him that "a monkey is not caught in a snare." The authority for this is Diogenes Laertius. The Greek verse goes like this:
<note>original: "Γέρων πίθηκος οὐχ ἁλίσκεται πάγῃ, Ἁλίσκεται μὲν, μετὰ χρόνου δ' ἁλίσκεται"</note>
An old monkey is not caught by a snare:
He is caught indeed, but he is caught too late.

<margin>XXXII</margin>
->Bounty has no bottom.<-

Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the second book of *On Duties* says: "In all things, we ought to remember that which has been used so often by our people that it has now passed into the custom of a proverb: that bounty has no bottom." By this saying, they signified that through foolish liberality, any amount of wealth can be exhausted, or rather, flow away. It seems to be a metaphor taken from the leaking jar of the Danaids <note>In Greek myth, the fifty daughters of Danaus were punished in Hades by having to fill a perforated jar with water for eternity.</note> in the underworld. Things that lack a bottom are called <note>original: "ἀπύθμενα"</note> *apythmena* by the Greeks. Hence Parthenius, cited in Athenaeus, book 11, spoke of a "bottomless bowl."

<margin>XXXIII</margin>
->The unfillable jar.<-

<note>original: "Ἀπλήρωτος πίθος"</note> That is, "The unfillable jar." The use of this adage is varied. First, it fits <note>original: "εἰς τοὺς ἀδηφάγους"</note> gluttons and the voracious; but it applies even more appropriately to those with an unquenchable thirst for drink, who the more they drink, the more they thirst, as was once said of the Parthians. Indeed, Festus seems to have felt this way, citing someone (the passage is fragmented) who called the belly a "leaking jar," although by nature the belly is unfillable because whatever you pour in through the mouth is excreted through other channels. It also fits a forgetful person: if you pour any learning into him, it immediately flows out, and he forgets it before he has fully learned it. Aristophanes depicts Strepsiades this way in *The Clouds*:
<note>original: "ὃς τὰς σκαλαθυρμάτ' ἄττα μικρὰ μανθάνων, Ταῦτ' ἐπιλέλησται πρὶν μαθεῖν"</note>
The sort of man who, learning some tiny little subtleties,
Has forgotten them before he even learned them.
Plautus used it similarly in *Pseudolus*: "We are pouring into a leaking jar; we are wasting our labor." It also applies to men who are excessively extravagant, as Aristotle indicated in the first book of *Economics*: "For one must be able both to acquire and to keep; otherwise, there is no benefit in acquiring. For that is 'drawing water with a sieve,' or as the proverb says, 'the leaking jar.'" It likewise fits the greedy, whose desires are never satisfied; indeed, the more they are filled with riches, the more empty they seem to be. This is elegantly testified by that poem of Solon found in Plutarch’s essay *On the Love of Wealth*:
<note>original: "Πλούτου δ' οὐδὲν τέρμα πεφασμένον ἀνθρώποισι"</note>
No visible limit of wealth is fixed for mortals.
Zenodotus thinks the "unfillable jar" can rightly be understood as Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of the underworld.</note> itself, because it is never filled by so many thousands of the dead. And that Hebrew sage <note>Likely a reference to King Solomon in Proverbs 30:15-16.</note> names this among the insatiable things. It will also fit those who wickedly seize from some what they wickedly lavish upon others. It is also used for those laboring in vain, as has been shown in another place, such as in Catullus: "That same man would fill the jars with the maidens' urns."
The adage arises from the well-known fable of the daughters of Danaus, who are said to suffer this punishment in the underworld for murdering their bridegrooms: they must draw water in leaking buckets and pour it into a jar that is likewise perforated—a heavy, yet useless labor. Horace makes mention of this fable in his *Odes*: "And the jar empty of water..."

# FIRST CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY
<sig>E 4</sig>

> A jar with a leaking bottom. <note>original: "Dolium fundo pereuntis imo." A reference to the Danaïdes, daughters of Danaus, who were punished in Hades by having to fill a leaking jar with water for eternity.</note> Likewise Tibullus:
> And the offspring of Danaus, who offended the divinity of Venus,
> Carries the waters of Lethe in hollow jars.

Lucian mentions this in *Timon*. And Aristotle in the sixth book of the *Politics*. Again, Lucian in *Hermotimus*: <margin>For the matter flows in, as the proverb says, into a thing being drained; or on the contrary, if the bottom leaks out.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἐπιῤῥεῖ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν...</note> That is, the business and labor flow in while it is being exhausted, and the opposite happens, just as in the jar of the Danaïdes. Plato also used it, both in several other places and in the *Gorgias*.

### While the bear is present, you look for its tracks. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXXIIII

<margin>While the bear is present, you seek the tracks.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἄρκτου παρούσης τὰ ἴχνη ζητεῖς.</note> That is, you look for the tracks of a bear that is standing right there. This is said of those who, out of fear, avoid the business at hand and slip away into other trifles. It is a metaphor taken from fearful hunters who pretend they haven't noticed the bear and feign to be following tracks so that they might remain far from danger. Plato, in the fifth book of the *Republic*, wrote that men of this sort are like <margin>little dogs that bite stones, not touching those who threw them.</margin> <note>original Greek: τοῖς κυνιδίοις, ἃ τοὺς λίθους δάκνει...</note> Not foreign to this is what Plutarch writes in the *Life of Lucullus*. For when Archelaus urged him to leave the enemy and cross over into Pontus (for in this way he would immediately gain control of all things), <margin>he said he would not be like a hunter who, passing by the wild beasts, goes toward their empty dens.</margin> <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔφη θαλαττοπορεῖν ἂν κυνηγῶν...</note> That is, he denied he was more fearful than hunters, such that he would wish to go to their empty lairs while the beasts were passed by.

### Good men go to the feasts of good men of their own accord. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXXV

<margin>Good men go to the feasts of good men of their own accord.</margin> <note>original Greek: Αὐτόματοι δ’ ἀγαθοὶ ἀγαθῶν ἐπὶ δαῖτας ἴονται.</note> That is:
It is the custom for good men to go to the feasts of the good unbidden.

A proverbial hexameter, to be used when a good man, trusting in virtue and the friendship that exists generally among all upright people, approaches one like himself without waiting for those common little invitations. Some think it originated with Hercules, who, when he visited the house of Ceyx of Trachis uninvited, was the first to say this little verse. A trimeter iambic is also cited with the same meaning:
<margin>Friends who are good men join the revels of friends.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθοὶ κωμάζουσιν εἰς φίλους φίλοι.</note> That is:
A friend comes even of his own accord to a friend's feast.

Homer silently noted the adage in the second book of the *Iliad*:
<margin>And Menelaus, good at the war-cry, came to him of his own accord.</margin> <note>original Greek: Αὐτόματος δέ οἱ ἦλθε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος.</note> That is:
Unsummoned, Menelaus had come of his own accord.

The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on classical texts.</note> indicates that by this word, the bravery of Menelaus in war was signified. For a thin voice indicates a fearful man, and <term>Good at the war-cry</term> <note>original Greek: Βοὴ ἀγαθὸς</note> among the Greeks sometimes declares war, just as it does today among the Germans. Zenodotus, in his collections, cites this adage with a different meaning from a comedy of Eupolis titled *Chrysogenes*:
<margin>Brave men go of their own accord to the feasts of cowards.</margin> <note>original Greek: Αὐτόματοι δ’ ἀγαθοὶ δειλῶν ἐπὶ δαῖτας ἴασιν.</note> That is:
Strong men go of their own accord to the feasts of a fearful man.

Plato means nearly the same in the *Symposium*: <margin>so that we may even spoil the proverb by changing it, as if indeed good men go to the feasts of good men of their own accord.</margin> <note>original Greek: ἵνα καὶ τὴν παροιμίαν διαφθείρωμεν...</note> Plato seems to feel that Homer made Menelaus, the inferior, go to the feast of the superior, because Agamemnon was strong in war while Menelaus was weak. This passage is also cited by Athenaeus in book four. However, I do not think this was Homer's intention, since he adds the praise of virtue:
<margin>Menelaus, good at the shout.</margin> <note>original Greek: Βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος.</note> That is:
Menelaus, good of voice.

Since in several places he depicts him conducting himself most bravely, and in some places even honors him with the mention <term>dear to strength</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλκὶ φίλος</note>. In Athenaeus, book one, from Cilatinus, someone who had come to a feast uninvited speaks thus: <margin>Being a good man, I have come to feast with good men, for the things of friends are common.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθὸς ὢν πρὸς ἀγαθοὺς...</note> That is: For a good man, I have come to feast with good men. For the possessions of friends are shared.

### To fight with dogs in a well. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; XXXVI

<margin>To fight with dogs in a well.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἐν φρέατι κυσὶ μάχεσθαι.</note> This was commonly said when someone falls into business with a quarrelsome and contentious person from whom he cannot extricate himself. It is also expressed in this way, <margin>to dog-fight in a well</margin>, using a compound word.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
### I shall provide the bath for myself.

<note>original: "Mihipsi balneum ministrabo"</note>
*I shall be my own bath-attendant.* <note>original Greek: Ἐμαυτῷ βαλανεύσω</note> This is used when someone serves their own interests, or when someone does their own business without waiting for the service of another. Aristophanes in *The Peace*: "But if these things are pleasing, I shall be my own bath-attendant." That is:
->And I myself shall prepare the bath for me, if these things please you.<-
The commentator warns that this is a metaphor from the baths, where, if the bath-attendant is absent, those who are washing draw and pour the water for themselves. Zenodotus thinks it can also refer to those who cook acorns thrown into a fire. Perhaps it might not be absurdly applied to those who shake down acorns. For to the Greeks, a *balaneus* <note>βαλανεὺς</note> signifies a bath-keeper, but *balanos* <note>βάλανος</note> means an acorn. Hence the double interpretation of the proverb.

<margin>XXXVIII</margin>
### A man in flight does not heed the twang of a lyre.

<note>original: "Vir fugiens haud moratur lyræ strepitum"</note>
*A man who flees does not wait for the sound of the lyre.* <note>original Greek: Ἀνὴρ δὲ φεύγων οὐ μένει λύρας κτύπον</note> This is a proverbial verse directed at those who, in dangerous or serious matters, neglect trivial things in their haste. For he who flees in war does not think himself free or at leisure to listen to some singer. This can be applied to many things. For instance, if you were to say that one should not trifle with frivolous and pleasurable nonsense when this life is subject to so many dangers. Seneca writes elegantly on this sentiment in a certain letter to Lucilius: "Let us pass over," he says, "these most clever trifles, and hasten to those things which will bring us some help. No one who is anxiously fetching a midwife for a daughter in labor reads the public decree or the schedule of the games. No one who runs to his burning house looks at a gaming board to see how a trapped piece might move. But by Hercules, news reaches you from all sides of the burning of your house, the danger to your children, the siege of your fatherland, and the plundering of your goods. Add to these shipwreck, earthquakes, and whatever else can be feared. Distracted among such things, do you have leisure for matters that do nothing but delight the mind?" Plutarch, in the booklet he wrote about the <term>Delphic</term> <note>Referring to the "E at Delphi," a mystical treatise on the temple of Apollo</note> oracle: *The harp is not for wailing, nor is the lyre welcome.* <note>original Greek: οὐ νάβλα κωκυτοῖσιν, οὐ λύρα φίλη</note> That is:
->The harp is unwelcome, the lyre unwelcome to one in mourning.<-
The saying from Ecclesiasticus accords with this:
->Music in mourning is an untimely story.<-

<margin>XXXIX</margin>
### A dog’s dinner.

<note>original: "Caninum prandium"</note>
A "dog's dinner" was a proverbial name for a sober meal in which no wine was drunk, because by a peculiar property of their nature, dogs shrink from wine. This adage is recorded by Aulus Gellius in Book 13, the final chapter of *Attic Nights*, in these words—which are surely from a book of Marcus Varro’s *Satires* titled *Freezing Water* <note>original Greek: ὕδωρ κρύον</note>: "Do you not see it written in Mnesitheus that there are three kinds of wine: black, white, and the middle kind which they call *yellowish* <note>original Greek: κιῤῥὸν</note>; and new, old, and middle? And that black wine produces strength; white, urine; and the middle, *digestion* <note>original Greek: πέψιν</note>. New wine cools, old wine warms, but the middle kind is a dog's dinner." Gellius says: "What a 'dog's dinner' signifies, we sought for a long time and with great anxiety. A sober dinner, in which no wine is drunk, is called 'canine' because a dog lacks wine." Therefore, since he had named a "middle wine" which was neither new nor old—and since men usually speak such that they say all wine is either new or old—he meant that the "middle" wine had no power, neither of the new nor the old. Therefore it was not to be considered wine, because it neither cooled nor warmed. Thus far Gellius. Plutarch in his *Table Talk* writes that Theophrastus used to jokingly call meat-banquets "wineless," as we have noted elsewhere.

<margin>XL</margin>
### A man who flees will also fight again.

<note>original: "Vir fugiens, & denuo pugnabit"</note>
*The man who flees shall fight once more.* <note>original Greek: Ἀνὴρ ὁ φεύγων καὶ πάλιν μαχήσεται</note> A proverbial verse by which we are warned not to immediately cast down our spirits if something succeeds poorly. For the conquered can conquer. Hence Homer calls victory *alternating* <note>original Greek: ἐπαλλαξὰ</note>, that is, shifting, prevailing now with these, now with those. In the same author, in the *Iliad* Book 8, Alexander speaks thus to Hector: *Victory changes among men.* <note>original Greek: νίκη δ’ ἐπαμείβεται ἄνδρας</note> Likewise elsewhere in the *Iliad* Book 3:
->For now Menelaus has conquered with the help of Athena,<-

<meta>The text breaks off mid-sentence; the next page begins with the Greek word "nun" (now).</meta>

<summary>Erasmus explores four proverbs regarding self-reliance, prioritizing serious matters over trifles, the definition of a "dog's dinner" as a wineless meal, and the hope of future victory after a defeat.</summary>
<keywords>self-reliance, stoicism, Seneca, Aulus Gellius, wine types, canine dinner, military resilience, Homer, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# TENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<meta>catchword: Not other-</meta>

<margin>If you ask me about the world. That is,</margin>
> With Pallas’s help, Menelaus now departs as victor.
> But I shall overcome him in turn in a later battle.
<note>original: "Palladis auxilio..." quoting Homer, Iliad 3.439-440</note>

Demosthenes was reproached by his enemies because in that battle where Philip, King of the Macedonians, defeated the Athenians at Chaeronea, he had fled after throwing away his shield; for this reason, he was called by the ignominious nickname *shield-dropper*. <note>original: ῥίψασπις (rhipsaspis)</note> Truly, Demosthenes—a man not particularly modest—is read to have habitually evaded this reproach with a very well-known proverbial verse:
<margin>The man who flees shall also fight again.</margin>
<note>original: ἀνὴρ ὁ φεύγων καὶ πάλιν μαχήσεται</note>
Close to this is that saying of Davus in Terence: "It did not succeed here, it must be attempted by another way." <note>Terence, Andria 670</note> Tertullian employs the adage in his book *On Flight in Persecution*. But, he says, some people, ignoring divine exhortations, apply to themselves that Greek verse of worldly sentiment: "He who was fleeing, will battle again"—so that he might perhaps flee again. And when will he conquer, who, since he fled, is already conquered?

### To know from the stubble. XLI
<margin>To know from the stalk. That is, one is said to judge from the stubble whenever we make a conjecture from certain traces remaining in old age as to what kind of person someone was in youth; the metaphor is transferred from crops. Homer in the 14th book of the Odyssey:</margin>
<margin>But nevertheless, I think that you, looking upon the stubble, know it. That is,</margin>
> Yet, having inspected the stubble, I suspect you
> Conjecture that.
<note>original: ἀλλ’ ἔμπης καλάμην... Odyssey 14.214</note>

Lucian uses this adage in *The False Prophet*, which I once translated into Latin. Aristotle in his *Rhetoric* interprets "stubble" as old age. For when, he says, he called old age "stubble," he created learning and knowledge through the state of the old man. For both have lost their bloom. Aristophanes in *The Wasps* used a not dissimilar figure:
<margin>But from the remnants of strength, it is necessary to have a youthful spirit. That is,</margin>
> Truly from the remains, the youthful vigor of these
> Ought to be gathered.

We likewise say: "To conjecture from the fragments" or "from the ruin" what kind of thing it once was.

### By the same cubit. XLII
<margin>By the same forearm. That is, by the same cubit; which is to say, by the same rule, by the same measure. Lucian uses this several times, both elsewhere and in the pamphlet On the Way to Write History: "And in short, one cubit, and an exact measure." Aristophanes in The Frogs:</margin>
<margin>For poetry shall be weighed by the talent-scale, and they will bring out rulers and cubits for verses. That is,</margin>
> For in the scale-pan shall poetic art be weighed,
> And they shall bring forth rules and cubits of songs.

Cornelius Tacitus spoke with a not dissimilar figure in the preface to his book *On Orators*, saying that he wished to pursue the things he had received from the most excellent men "with the same numbers and the same accounts." Pliny in the 8th book of his *Epistles* said "With an equal balance." That is perhaps <gloss>to the point</gloss>, but it would not be useless to advise that many metaphors drawn from measures are proverbial, such as: "To weigh a matter," "to weigh a deed," "to repay a benefit," "to re-measure a favor," "to poise a business," "to spend a cause," "to re-count a benefit," "equilibrium of duty," "to retaliate a reproach," and others of that kind.

### To be pointed out with the finger. XLIII
<margin>To be shown by the finger. That is, to be pointed out with the finger; used for that which is remarkable or distinguished; they still say it today as a common proverb. Horace in the Odes:</margin>
> Because I am pointed out by the finger of those passing by.

Persius:
> But it is a fine thing to be pointed out with the finger, and for it to be said: "This is he."

Lucian in *Harmonides*: "And to be notable in crowds, and to be shown by the finger." It can be seen to have arisen from that which Laertius relates in the *Life of Diogenes*. When certain guests had arrived at Athens so that they might see Demosthenes at home, whose fame they had heard of, Diogenes, <insert>stretching out his middle finger</insert>, said: "This is for you that leader of the Athenians." Simultaneously signifying that Demosthenes was both greedy for glory and of contaminated character. <note>The middle finger was an obscene gesture in antiquity, used here by Diogenes to insult Demosthenes's masculinity and character.</note>

<summary>This page examines proverbs regarding resilience in defeat, judging past quality by present remains ("stubble"), and the nature of public fame or infamy ("pointed out with the finger"). It draws heavily on Greek poets and Roman satirists to explain how physical measures and gestures become metaphors for social standing.</summary>
<keywords>Demosthenes, Homer, Aristotle, Aristophanes, Tacitus, Pliny, Horace, Persius, Lucian, Diogenes Laertius, proverbs, adages, metaphors of measurement, middle finger, cowardice, old age</keywords>

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>44</margin>
### Not even with the other foot.

<note>original: Μηδὲ τὸν ἕτερον πόδα</note> That is, not to depart even by a single foot. Lucian mentions this in *Harmonides*. Also in *The Sects*: "Who never once moved even his other foot out of Ethiopia." <note>original: οὐδὲ πώποτε ἐξ αἰθιοπίας τὸν ἕτερον πόδα προελθών</note> This should be numbered among those expressions we have recorded elsewhere, such as "a finger’s breadth," "a foot’s breadth," or "a nail’s breadth"; these are used to signify either a total agreement of opinion or a constant diligence in study. It is similar to the phrase "night and day," which Titus Livius expressed differently in the first book of the *Macedonian War*: "Others in the camp, without sentries, made the day equal to the nights through sleep and wine."

<margin>45</margin>
### Diametrically opposed. They are a diameter apart.

<note>original: Ἐκ διαμέτρου</note> That is, "From the diameter." This was formerly said of things that are vehemently in conflict with one another, a metaphor taken from the Geometricians, among whom the most perfect opposition is across the diameter. Lucian says in *The Tyrant*: "For their lives, as they say, are diametrically opposed." <note>original: ἐκ διαμέτρου γὰρ οἱ βίοι φασίν</note> Athanasius, in a certain book on the Synod of Nicaea: "Those who, so to speak, are diametrically opposed to the opinion of Sabellius." <note>original: οἱ τῇ διαμέτρῳ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ ἁπᾶν ἀντικείνῃ τῇ Σαβελλίῳ γνώμῃ</note> Basil, in a certain letter to Athanasius, used the phrase "by the diameter." For a diameter is a straight line cutting an object equally where it is widest; for instance, the diameter of a sphere is that which is stretched from the top of the circle to the top in such a way that it passes through the center, according to the definition by Macrobius in the second book of *Scipio’s Dream*. Euclid’s definition does not disagree with this. Latin speakers call this line the "measurer-through" <note>term: dimetientem; the Latin equivalent of the Greek diameter</note>. For the Greeks call it *diametros* <margin>from "measuring through"</margin> <note>original: παρὰ τὸ διαμετρεῖν</note> because it measures across. Aristotle gives the reason for the name in his *Problems*, Section 15, Problem 2. It is related to the phrase we reviewed in another place, "twice through all" <note>original: δὶς διὰ πασῶν; a musical metaphor for a perfect octave/harmony</note>.

<margin>46</margin>
### Hear what is said from the heart.

<note>original: Ἀκουε τὰ ἀπὸ καρδίας</note> That is, listen to those things spoken from the soul. For things that are serious and spoken without dissimulation are said to be "from the soul," and the common people say such things "proceed from the heart." Lucian in *Jupiter the Tragedian*: "Will you not hear, O Gods, what they say 'from the heart'?" <note>original: οὐκἂν ἀκούετε ὦ θεοὶ, τὰ γε ἀπὸ καρδίας φασίν</note> That is, hear things that must surely be spoken sincerely, as the proverb says. For the speech of flatterers and pretenders is born in the throat, not in the heart. Plutarch, in the commentary he titled *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*, records these iambic verses:

> For I would have a beggar, or if he wishes,
> Someone even worse than a beggar, provided he is well-disposed to me,
> Who, having cast off fear, will speak from the heart.

That is:
> I wish I had a beggar, or if it pleases,
> One even lower, who wishing me well,
> Might speak from his soul, his fear set aside.

He adds that this is not easily said by the wealthy or by princes, to whom the truth is hateful in every way; nor do delicate ears endure anything unless it is seasoned with much fawning and tastes of adulation. To this figure of speech belongs that phrase of Plautus, "to love with the heart." Also: "to pursue with heart, soul, and strength." Both are found in *The Captives*. The opposite of this is "From the top of the lips," meaning not from the soul. Seneca in his *Letters to Lucilius*: "Those things do not come from the top of the lips."

<margin>47</margin>
### Either drink or depart.

Either drink or depart. By this adage we are warned that we should either accommodate ourselves to the time and place, or withdraw ourselves from the company of men. Just as Cato is read to have done, who, when he could not adopt a facial expression suitable to the license of the *Floralia* <note>note: A Roman festival known for its theatrical indecency</note>, left the theater. This originated from those ancient Greek *symposia*—that is, drinking parties—in which it was the custom to choose someone by lot to preside over the banquet and prescribe the rules of the feast, which they called *nomoi*, or laws. Valerius Valentinus wrote about these laws in a humorous poem titled *Tapulla*, according to Festus Pompeius. Furthermore, they called the leader the *basileus*, or king. Plutarch calls him the *symposiarch*. Varro, cited in Nonius, writes that he was called the *Modiperator* by the Latins, as if "commanding the measure," so that no one should drink more than enough, or too little. Athenaeus, in book 10, teaches on the authority of Eupolis that those in charge of this matter were called *oinoptai* <note>note: "wine-watchers"</note>, and by others "the eyes." Horace also mentions this custom in his *Odes*:
-> Nor shall you cast lots for the kingship of such wine. <-
Among these humorous laws, this one is reported: "Either drink or depart." It is mentioned by Cicero in the fifth book of his *Tusculan Disputations*: "To me indeed," he says, "it seems that law should be observed in life which prevails in the banquets of the Greeks: 'Either let him drink,' it says, 'or let him depart.' And rightly so. For either let him enjoy..."

<summary>Erasmus explores four adages concerning social conduct and sincerity, ranging from the geometric metaphor of "diametrical opposition" to the ancient drinking-party rule of "drink or depart." He emphasizes the importance of speaking from the heart rather than the "top of the lips" and adapting to social environments.</summary>

# THE FIRST CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

he should likewise join with the others in the pleasure of drinking, lest by remaining sober he fall victim to the violence of the drunks, and so depart. Thus you should leave behind the injuries of fortune, which you cannot bear, by fleeing from them. So much for that author.
<margin>Either drink or depart.</margin> <note>original: "Ἢ πῖθι, ἢ ἄπιθι"</note> Some express it this way: *Either drink or depart.* How much more civilized is this law than the one the master of the feast prescribed for Empedocles at a banquet: that he must either drink, or have the wine poured over his head. Empedocles took this so indignely that the next day, having called a council, he prosecuted both the host who had arranged it and the master of the feast, and saw to it that they were condemned. Diogenes Laertius records this. But our "Mnamones" <note>A reference to unforgetting or harsh enforcers of rules</note> prescribe these most Scythian <note>Scythian: used here to mean "barbaric" or "uncivilized"</note> laws: "Either drink," they say, "or I will smash this tankard, just as it is, against your head." And so it happens not infrequently that a drinking bout turns into a single combat.

### To make a guess at home. XLVIII
<margin>To guess from one's own home.</margin> <note>original: "Οἴκοθεν εἱκάζειν"</note> *To guess from one's own home.* That which is not sought from elsewhere is said, by a proverb, to be done "at home." Plautus in *The Casket Comedy*: "I make this conjecture about myself at home." That is, I discover it from my own experience. Seneca in the fifth book of *On Benefits*: "A conjecture is made at home, as they say, and like a gambler's debt, it passes away immediately."

### He has it at home; it is born at home. XLIX
To the same metaphor belongs: *To have it at home.* For we are said to have that "at home" which is not foreign to us, nor is it necessary to borrow it from others. It clearly translates from the custom of asking for household goods from outside which you lack at home. Terence in *The Brothers*: "Bah, he has it at home, from whence he may learn." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] to Varro: "But why do I say these things to you, for whom such things are born at home?" The same in the second book of *Academic Questions*: "Cease, I pray, with these commonplaces; such things are born at home for us," meaning, these things are the proper domain of orators. Accordingly, you might elegantly say: "Why do you hunt for happiness in those external things? You have at home that from which you can be blessed." It is the mark of kings to have counsel at home, and not to hang upon the opinion of another.

### To break the token. L
In Plautus’s *The Casket Comedy*, one is said to have "broken the token" <term>tessera: a small tablet or shard used as a token of identity or hospitality</term> who has barred his own return into someone's house. Indeed, when a lover said he was bound by an oath to marry the madam's daughter, praying that she would not allow him to become a perjurer, she replied: "Go seek where your oath has enough support. Here with us now, Alcesimarchus, you have broken the token." Now, the *tessera* was a symbol of hospitality, which, when produced, allowed guests to be recognized if they ever returned.

### To pour cold water on. LI
*To pour cold water on.* Plautus in *The Casket Comedy* seems to have used this for "to rebuke secretly." For in that play, a courtesan complains about matrons inciting their husbands to hate courtesans as much as they can: "Thus they openly flatter our rank, but secretly, if the opportunity arises anywhere, they pour cold water under the jar: they tell their husbands we are accustomed to being their mistresses." It appears to be translated from those who, in equestrian contests, sprinkled water on the horses so that, being refreshed, they might run more fiercely, and in this way they urged them to the race. The Imperial Pandects <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note> mention this service in the third book, second title, regarding those marked with infamy, quoting Ulpian in these words: "And generally all are so defined, and it seems useful, that neither the stage-performers, nor the athletes, nor the drivers, nor those who sprinkle water on their own [horses], nor the other ministries of those who serve the sacred games, should be held as ignominious." So far Ulpian. This was done, I believe, in the Olympic or similar contests, sometimes also for this reason: lest the wheels, growing hot from the movement, should catch fire. Unless someone prefers it to be thought translated from those who, for the sake of a joke or mockery, secretly pour water into a banquet hall; or from those who, for mockery, sprinkle someone with water, which is a joke of the bath-keepers. Whence also Julius Pollux in book seven teaches that "cold" is sometimes used for "to rail at." So Aristophanes in *Plutus*: "Making a wash-pot of me and pouring out cold [water]." Someone complains that he was sprinkled with water for the sake of insult in the presence of many. But it is more probably translated from the copper-smiths' shops, where the craftsmen repeatedly sprinkle cold water into the fire so that the fire may be more vehement.

### Do not bestow a benefit upon an old man. LII
<margin>Never, ever do any good thing.</margin> <note>original: "Μήποτέ ποτε μηδὲν χρηστὸν ποιῇς"</note> *Never, ever do any good thing.* That is, never bestow any benefit upon an old man. It is cited specifically as a proverb by Aristotle in the second book of *Rhetoric*: "And if anyone advises not to make a friend of an old man, the proverb bears witness to him: Never do a kindness to an old man." That is, and if he advises...

<keywords>hospitality, drinking laws, Plautus, Cicero, Ulpian, equestrian games, metaphors for self-reliance, ancient Greek proverbs</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

when you do a favor for an old man. Even today it is commonly said: "A benefit should be bestowed neither upon an old man nor a child," because the former does not return it, and the latter does not remember it. There is also a certain proverb of this kind in Diogenianus: <note>original: μή ποτ’ εὖ ἔρδ’ εὖ γέροντας... (mê pot’ eu erd’ eu gerontas...)</note> "Never do a kindness to old men, nor to a woman, nor to children, nor to anyone’s dog, nor to a talkative rower." This is because whatever is spent on that class of people seems to perish. Seneca says in the third book of *On Benefits*: "Thus it happens that teachers and their benefits fall away, because we leave our entire childhood behind; thus it happens that things bestowed upon our youth perish, because youth itself is never revisited."

### A fool is he who, having slain the father, spared the children.

Immediately following the previous one, he added this under the name of a proverb: <note>original: καὶ οἷς υἱὸς ἀναιρῇ... (kai hois huios anairê...)</note> "And he who would persuade one to kill the children whose father you have killed." This proverb bears witness to it: "A fool is he who, having killed the father, leaves the children behind." He records the same later among his maxims: "A simpleton is he who, having killed the father, spared the children." It is a proverbial verse: <note>original: Νήπι@ ὃς πατέρα κτείνας... (Nêpios hos patera kteinas...)</note> "A fool is he who, having slain the father, leaves the pledges <note>i.e., the children</note> behind." Herodotus also used it in *Clio*: "For I seem to have acted now just as if someone, having killed the father, should spare his children." Philip of Macedon is written to have used this adage when he was removing from the scene even the children of those whose parents he had killed. For either one ought first to abstain from killing the parents, or likewise remove the sons, who would one day be the avengers of their father's death. There is a memorable saying of the soldiers who slaughtered the Emperor Maximinus along with his son: "From the worst breed, not even a pup should be left behind." To this pertains that line of Homer from the third book of the *Odyssey*: <note>original: ὡς ἀγαθὸν καὶ παῖδα... (hôs agathon kai paida...)</note> "How good it is for a son to be left behind when a man has perished." The adage will be of use whenever we advise that either men should not be provoked, or they should be finished off in such a way that no remnants remain to trouble us in the future.

### A "Good-Talker" <note>Greek: Chrestologos</note>

They were called *Chrestologoi*, and even today they are commonly called so, who speak honestly but act wickedly. This was said specifically of the Emperor Pertinax, as Julius Capitolinus testifies in his life. Paul, in his Epistle to the Romans, calls this kind of smooth-talking *chrestologia*: <note>original: καὶ διὰ τῆς χρηστολογίας... (kai dia tês chrêstologias...)</note> "Who through smooth talk and flattery seduce the hearts of the innocent."

### Well said! A fine story!

To this seem to belong those proverbial ironies found everywhere in comedies: "You have spoken beautifully," "A fine story you tell," <note>original: καλῶς ἔλεξας (kalôs elexas)</note>—said of a thing that is utterly absurd. Plato in the *Euthydemus* specifically mentions it as a proverb. Plato's words are: "For as the saying goes, 'You say everything beautifully.'" Likewise in the *Gorgias*: "Listen now, as they say, to a very beautiful speech."

### Potter’s wealth.

<note>original: Κεράμεος πλοῦτ@ (Kerameos ploutos)</note> That is, "Earthenware riches." Said of things that are uncertain, fragile, and by no means lasting. Just as the vessels of potters are easily shattered by any accident. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

### A sleeping hare.

<note>original: λαγὼς καθεύδων (lagôs katheudôn)</note> That is, "A sleeping hare." This fits one who pretends to do what he is not doing, or hides the fact that he is doing what he is doing. Such, some believe, was the sleep of Ulysses when he was set down on the island of Ithaca by the Phaeacians, according to Plutarch. For many other authors record that the hare sleeps with its eyes open, including Pliny in book eleven, chapter thirty-seven; he says this even happens to some men, whom the Greeks call *korybantiân* <note>to sleep with eyes open, like a Corybantian priest</note>. Nor, I think, would it be wrongly said of the fearful. The adage is recorded by many authors.

# TENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND
<sig>F</sig>

### Jupiter looked into the leather skin too late.
<margin>LVIII</margin>
*Zeus looked into the leather skins after a long time.* <note>original Greek: Ὁ Ζεὺς κατεῖδε χρόνιος εἰς τὰς διφθέρας</note> That is, Jupiter inspected the skin, even if late. A proverbial iambic verse applied to those who, though late, eventually pay the penalty for their misdeeds. For antiquity believed that Jupiter wrote all things in his <term>diphthera</term> <note>A writing tablet or scroll made of goatskin</note>, that is, a goatskin, and while he might overlook many things for a time, he eventually exacts punishment from the wicked. It will also fit well for princes who finally punish crimes that have been ignored for a long time.

### He has either perished, or is surely teaching letters.
<margin>LIX</margin>
*He has either died, or he is teaching letters.* <note>original Greek: Ἢ τέθνηκεν, ἢ διδάσκει γράμματα</note> That is, He has either perished, or is surely teaching letters. A proverbial iambic verse by which they used to signify in the past that someone was in a completely miserable state, even if it was not clear what they were doing. This came into common speech on the authority of Zenodotus. The Athenians, under the leadership of Nicias, once fought unsuccessfully against the Sicilians; many were killed, and most were led away as captives into Sicily, where they were forced to teach the sons of the Sicilians their letters. Consequently, the few who escaped by flight and returned to Athens, when asked what this or that person was doing in Sicily, would answer with the aforementioned little verse: "He has either perished, or he is teaching letters."

### One must either eat the meat of the tortoise, or not eat it.
<margin>LX}
*To eat the meat of the tortoise, or not to eat it.* <note>original Greek: Χελώνης κρέα φαγεῖν, ἢ μὴ φαγεῖν</note> That is, You should either eat the tortoise meat, or not eat it. A proverbial trimeter applied to those who handle undertaken business coldly, neither finishing it nor abandoning it. There are those who think this saying originated from the author Terpsion: among whom is Athenaeus in his eighth book, declaring that this man was the first to give instructions on <term>gastrology</term> <note>The art or science of good eating</note>, publishing rules through which it was clear what should be avoided and what, conversely, should be eaten. Among these was this one about the tortoise: "either eat, or do not eat." They add that the meat of the tortoise, if eaten in small amounts, causes stomach pains; but if eaten in abundance, it soothes them. Pliny reports something similar regarding lettuce. It is just as if you were to say: "One must either wage war, or not wage war," or "One must either study, or not study." For there are many things which, if you do them vigorously, are very beneficial; but if done lazily, they are harmful. Such are things that do not admit a middle ground, like music and poetry. There are, conversely, certain things which it is enough to have tasted. The famous Neoptolemus of Ennius and the Platonic Callicles thought the study of philosophy was of this kind. It is not unlike what is in the Apocalypse: *I wish you were either hot or cold.* <note>A reference to Revelation 3:15</note>

### Good laws are produced from bad morals.
<margin>LXI</margin>
Macrobius, in the third book of the *Saturnalia*, says: "It is an old saying: Good laws are produced from bad morals." For just as there would be no need for the medicines of physicians if there were no laboring under diseases, so there would be no need for making laws if people did not live wrongly. Hence, among the people of Aegina, a person who provided the occasion for establishing a law was formerly punished with a fine. The authority is Aristotle in the second book of the *Rhetoric*. Cornelius Tacitus in book 15 says: "It has been proven by experience that excellent laws and honorable examples among the good are born from the crimes of others." To this pertains what <margin>Solon</margin> Solon said when asked why he had not established a law against parricides <note>Those who kill their parents</note>: "because he had not expected there would be a parricide."

### A strange ox frequently looks toward the door.
<margin>LXII</margin>
*A foreign ox looks outside most of the time.* <note>original Greek: Βοῦς ἀλλότριος τὰ πολλὰ ἔξω βλέπει</note> That is, A strange ox frequently looks toward the door. Concerning those who are not treated quite to their liking among strangers, and therefore more often long for their own people. For everyone, life is most pleasant at home and, as it were, in their own stalls; abroad there are many things that cause pain, and many things are lacking. Plutarch seems to have alluded to this proverb in the *Symposiacs*, eighth decade, second problem: *so that you do not despise yourselves, nor look outside entirely.* That is, so that you do not seek from elsewhere what can be obtained from the interpreters of Plato themselves. Therefore, it will be rightly said "to look outside" of one who, not content with his own things, depends on others. He also uses this in the booklet *On Virtue and Vice*.

### The seventh ox.
<margin>LXIII</margin>
*The seventh ox.* <note>original Greek: Ἕβδομος βοῦς</note> That is, The seventh ox. In the past, this was said of stupid and brutish people, whence the celebrated iambic verse: *The wise proverb tells of the seventh ox.* They say this arose because in ancient times, after the sixth moon, they were accustomed to paint an image of an ox out of flour, which would represent the seventh moon with its horns. There are those who prefer it to have originated from...

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...because, whereas among the ancients six kinds of animals were usually sacrificed to the gods—the sheep, the pig, the goat, the ox, the chicken, and the goose—the poor, having no living animal to sacrifice, became accustomed to fashioning the likeness of an ox out of flour. Since this lacked sense and life, it passed into a proverb for stupidity. <note>Erasmus is explaining the origin of the "Flour Ox" proverb.</note> Euripides in *Erechtheus* and Achaeus in *Iris* are cited by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> as having used this proverb, although he does not record their specific verses.

<margin>64</margin>

### To smell with the tip of the nose.

*To smell with the very tip of the nose* <note>original Greek: τῶ ἄκρῳ ῥινὶ ὀσφραίνεσθαι</note>, that is, to perceive something by a slight trial or by some sort of conjecture. It appears in Lucian’s *Zeus Refuted*.

<margin>65</margin>

### If that pen had been mine.

"If the pen had been mine," said Marcus Tullius Cicero in the *Second Philippic*, meaning: "if this business had been committed to my judgment and my skill." The metaphor is drawn from the authors of plays, by whose pen and reed-pen <note>term: *calamus* (a reed pen used for writing on papyrus or parchment)</note> the entire play is composed. Cicero’s words are these: *But I fear one thing, that you may not approve; for if I had been there, I would have removed from the Republic not only the king, but the kingship itself. And if that pen had been mine, as they say, believe me, I would have finished not just one act, but the whole play.* Furthermore, the *stilus* is that pointed writing instrument with which we write on wax tablets. It is transferred, however, to the character and "thread" of a speech, to which Cicero alluded.

<margin>66</margin>

### An Indian elephant cares nothing for a gnat.

In the letters circulated under the name of Phalaris, there is a proverb of this kind: *The Indian elephant takes no notice of a gnat* <note>original Greek: ἰνδὸς ἔλεφας κώνωπος οὐκ ἀλεγίζει</note>. This was said on account of the singular hardness of the elephant's hide, by which it is said even to shake off javelins; it is so far from being able to be harmed by the bite of a gnat. It can be applied whenever we wish to indicate that lofty minds should disregard slight and common insults.

<margin>67</margin>

### To clean mud with mud.

*To be cleansed of mud by mud* <note>original Greek: Πηλῷ πηλὸν καθαίρεσθαι</note>. This is said when a filthy thing is removed by filth; that is, when the filth is not removed, but is either changed or even increased. Apollonius said in a certain letter: *But not even that man said to the Ephesians that mud is not cleaned with mud.* He is speaking of priests who would pollute the altars of the gods with blood and consider that to be an expiation. To this belongs a saying of Diogenes, if I am not mistaken. Having entered a filthy bathhouse, he asked: "Where do those who wash here go to wash?"—indicating that bodies are defiled by such baths rather than cleaned. The same happens to the Alexandrians, who nourish a force of ibises in their cities for this purpose: that they may devour snakes and the filth of the butcher shops; but they defile everything again with their own uncleanness.

<margin>68</margin>

### Wherever your feet carry you.

*Wherever the feet may carry* <note>original Greek: Ἔνθ' ἂν οἱ πόδες φέρωσιν</note>. This stands for "anywhere at all." It will fit when no certain goal is seen toward which our efforts are directed. Lucian in *Hermotimus*: *For we do not make words, but according to the proverb, wherever our feet carry us, there we shall go.* Horace in the *Epodes*:
> To go wherever your feet carry you, wherever through the waves
> The South wind or the unruly African wind shall call.

<margin>Again in the Odes: So also Theocritus in Hylas:</margin>
Go, where your feet and the breezes snatch you.

<margin>Where the foot might lead, he went. <note>original Greek: πόδ᾽ ὅπη ἄγοι ἐχώρει</note></margin>
He went wherever his feet led him.

<margin>Again in the Thalysia:</margin>
Where, I ask, are you dragging your feet in the midday heat? <note>original Greek: πᾶ δὴ τὸ μεσαμέριον πόδας ἕλκεις</note>

<margin>And Virgil:</margin>
Where do your feet take you, Moeris? To where the road leads into the city?

In a similar form, Plato in the third book of the *Republic*: *But wherever the argument, like a wind, carries us, there we must go.*

<margin>69</margin>

### A Cyclopean life.

*A Cyclopean life* <note>original Greek: Κυκλώπειος βίος</note>, used for a life that is exceedingly wild and barbarous, which is established neither by laws nor by civil discipline, nor governed by religion of the gods. Such a life Homer describes in the ninth book of the *Odyssey* under the persona of Polyphemus:
> You are a fool, stranger, or you have come from afar,
> You who bid me either to fear or avoid the gods.
> For the Cyclopes care nothing for aegis-bearing Zeus,
> Nor for the blessed gods...

# CHILIAD 1, CENTURY 10
F 2
<meta>catchword: belly</meta>

You are a fool, or surely you arrive here as a stranger from distant shores, you who would command me to be moved by care or by the fear of the gods. For we the tribe of Cyclopes care nothing for supreme Jove <note>Jupiter</note> nor the blessed gods. <note>original Latin: "Desipis, aut certe... diuósue beatos." This is a translation of Polyphemus's defiant speech to Odysseus.</note>
I shall make trial of these men, to see who they are, whether they are violent, wild, and unjust, or whether they are kind to guests and possess a god-fearing mind. <note>original Greek: "Τῶν δ' ἀνθρώπων πειρήσομαι... νόος ἐστὶ θεουδής." From Homer's Odyssey.</note> That is to say:
I will now experience what race of men this is, whether they be fierce, rustic, and ignorant of what is right, or whether they observe the law of hospitality, revering the power of the gods in their souls.

Euripides, emulating Homer, makes the Cyclops speak in this manner:
I do not shudder at the thunderbolt of Zeus, stranger, nor do I know that Zeus is a god more powerful than I. <note>original Greek: "Ζηνὸς δ' ἐγὼ κεραυνὸν... κρείσσων θεός." From Euripides' satyr play, *Cyclops*.</note> That is to say:
But, stranger, I do not dread the lightning of Jove, nor do I hold Jove to be a god more excellent than myself.

<margin>Strabo, Book 10.</margin> Strabo writes in the twelfth book of his *Geography* that this was commonly said against the nation of the Albanians, because they led the life of Cyclopes, being neither fond of cultivation nor skilled in any of the refinements of life.

->Far and wide<-
->70<-
When a great difference is signified, they say things stand apart "far and wide." Aulus Gellius says: "Thus I believe that the love and veneration for that most famous writer, and for all ancient speech, which makes for a blind judgment, is far and wide more ample, more prolix, and more flowing, to have said 'mortals' rather than 'men' in signifying the multitude of the whole city." These words from Ulpian are cited in the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>: "If the use of a piece of land is left behind, no one doubts that it is certainly less than a usufruct, and that they differ far and wide." It seems to have been a metaphor taken from land-surveyors.

->Like lips have like lettuce.<-
->71<-
**Like lips have like lettuce.** <note>A proverb meaning "like to like," or that bad things suit bad people.</note> This is used where similar things happen to similar people: such as an unteachable student to a poorly learned teacher; a wicked magistrate to a wicked people; an abusive advocate to an abusive patron; a moody husband to a moody wife; in short, whenever evils happen to the evil, and the worthy to the worthy. The adage was born from an ass feeding on thistles. Now, lettuce is a soft and tender herb, which is nevertheless not entirely unlike a thistle, especially the wild variety. Therefore, just as a thistle is thorny and exceedingly rough in its leaves, stalk, and even its flower, so too nothing is harder or more stony than the lips of an ass, so that no other "lettuce" seems more suited to them. Furthermore, that thistles were even accustomed to be served at banquets in place of lettuce is testified by Julius Capitolinus in his *Life of the Emperor Pertinax*. Pliny likewise, in his nineteenth book, says of thistles in this manner: "All things that are in price might seem to have been said, were there not remaining matters of the greatest profit, not to be spoken of without shame. For it is certain that thistles at Carthage the Great, and especially at Corduba, return six thousand sesterces from these small plots, since we turn even the monstrosities of the earth into gluttony, even those things which four-footed beasts avoid by instinct." Saint Jerome employs and simultaneously interprets the proverb, writing to Chromatius in this manner: "According to that saying also, at which Lucilius says Crassus laughed once in his life: *Like lips have like lettuce*, as an ass eats thistles; namely, so that a weak pilot might steer a leaking ship, and the blind lead the blind into a pit, and the ruler be such as those who are ruled." Thus far Jerome. Now, this Crassus was the grandfather of that Crassus who perished fighting against the Parthians, whose standards Augustus later recovered. He is numbered among those who are said never to have laughed in their lives, and for that reason were surnamed <term>Agelastoi</term> <note>Greek: ἀγέλαστοι</note>, that is, "the laughterless." Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in his *Speeches* testifies that Licinius Crassus, according to Lucilius, laughed only once in his life. Pliny, in the seventh book of his *Natural History*, chapter nineteen, says: "They say that Crassus, the grandfather of the Crassus slain among the Parthians, never laughed, and for that reason was called Agelastus, just as many are said never to have wept." Saint Jerome against Rufinus says: "I certainly, to move a most serious man to laughter, so that you might at some time imitate Crassus, whom Lucilius writes laughed once in his life." Macrobius also mentions this in the second book of the *Saturnalia*.

->A worthy lid for the pot.<-
->72<-
Very similar to this is that which is related by the same Jerome in his letter to Chromatius: **A worthy lid for the pot.** For he says, "In my country, a native rusticity, God..."

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

the belly is their god, and they live for the day; and he is considered the holiest who is the wealthiest. To this dish, according to the well-worn proverb of the common people, **a worthy lid has been found.** <note>original: "dignum operculum." This refers to the proverb "a worthy lid for a worthy dish," meaning two things or people are perfectly matched in their badness.</note> This signifies a bishop who has adapted himself to the wicked morals of the people. Jerome says the same against Rufinus: "That you should sell the book of Eusebius as if it were by Pamphilus, so that you might place your own 'lid' upon a poisoned dish." Plato, in the *Greater Hippias*, while discussing the beautiful and the becoming, has something not far removed from this proverb: *“Whether,” he says, “when someone boils that beautiful pot we were just speaking of, full of beautiful beans, is it more fitting to use a golden ladle <term>toryne</term><note>A stirring spoon or ladle.</note> or one made of fig-wood?”* What is called *toryne* in Greek, the translator of Plato renders as a "stirrer." The *Etymologist* indicates that the word *toryne* is peculiar to the Attics, signifying a mixer. Suidas says it is the instrument with which a pot is stirred.

-> LXXIII <-
-> If you live next to a lame man, you will learn to limp. <-

Plutarch, in his booklet *On Educating Children*, says: *If you dwell near a lame man, you will learn to limp.* The commentator on Pindar expressed it in this manner:
*If you remain a neighbor to even one lame man,*
*You yourself will soon learn to limp.*
To this belongs that saying of Hesiod, mentioned by us elsewhere: *A bad neighbor is a calamity,* etc. Indeed, such is the unhappiness of human affairs that vices leap across to others more easily than virtues. And yet what Hesiod adds is also true: *Just as a good neighbor is a great blessing.* So Pindar in the seventh *Nemean Ode*: *If a man has a taste for man <note>original: "geuetai andros aner." Erasmus notes the difficulty of the Greek text here regarding the word "taste" or "need."</note>, what should we say a neighbor is to a neighbor, if he be a friend with a constant mind? A joy worthy of all things.* Although I see that neither the reading nor the interpretation of this passage is certain among the Greeks. For some read "neighbor" instead of "tastes," and refer it to the communication of advantages or disadvantages which a man receives from a man, especially from a neighbor. And it seems it should be read "to be a neighbor," to correspond with the participle "having been loved." The commentator also brings in that line from Hesiod:
*Neighbors came ungirded, but kinsmen came girded.* <note>Meaning neighbors came in a hurry (without dressing fully) to help, while relatives took their time to prepare.</note>

<margin>It is a well-known story of Themistocles, who, when putting a field up for sale, ordered the crier to add to the other merits that it had a good neighbor. The proverb warns against the perilous company of wicked men, because just as bodily diseases spread, so especially do the vices of the mind creep into a neighbor by contagion. Ovid says: *While eyes look at the wounded, they are wounded themselves; and many things harm bodies by transition.*</margin>

Aristotle thinks this happens most especially in diseases of the eyes, because that part of the body is the most mobile. Likewise in the itch <note>scabies</note>, because it is on the surface of the skin and consists of a sticky fluid, it remains on the neighbor. Finally, in all diseases born from corrupted air, such as the plague, because the breath is easily drawn from one person into another. Lastly, there is a certain hidden consensus of nature, by which it happens that he who sees another yawning begins to yawn himself, and he who sees another urinating feels the urge to do the same. Alexander of Aphrodisias is the authority for this. And one learns to stammer who lives constantly with a stammerer. A companion rubs off his character or his "itch" onto his fellow. Aristotle, in Section 6, Problem 4, asks why bleary eyes, consumption, and the itch migrate to others by contagion, yet the same does not happen in all diseases. Plutarch, in his commentary *How to tell a flatterer from a friend*, writes that constant habit has such power that people even unintentionally imitate the vices of those with whom they live. Just as Plato’s associates used to imitate his hunchback; Aristotle’s friends expressed his stammer; and the associates of Alexander, King of the Macedonians, copied the tilt of his neck and the harshness of his voice in speaking. Plato, in the second book of *Laws*, elegantly indicates how contagion deceives: *Is it likely, or rather is it not necessary, that when someone associates with the evil habits of wicked men, and does not hate them but rejoices in accepting them—even if he blames them as if in jest, dreaming of his own wickedness—then it is surely necessary that the one who rejoices becomes like those in whom he delights?*

<summary>Erasmus discusses the proverb "If you live next to a lame man, you will learn to limp," exploring how both physical ailments and moral vices are "contagious" through social proximity. He cites various classical authorities to illustrate how humans naturally imitate the habits, defects, and characters of their neighbors and companions.</summary>

# THE FIRST THOUSAND, TENTH HUNDRED

<margin>Menander. 1 Corinthians 15. Tertullian. Aristotle.</margin>
### Bad company corrupts good character. 74

To the same effect is that six-foot line <note>original: "senarius," a common meter in Greek drama</note> by Menander, which the divine Apostle Paul did not hesitate to quote in his first epistle to the Corinthians:
*Bad company corrupts good character.* <note>original Greek: "Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρήσθ’ ὁμιλíαι κακαí."</note> That is to say: Wicked social interaction infects good morals.
Tertullian translated this Greek poem for his wife, but with the freedom of Latin comedy: "Seek out," he says, "socializing and trade worthy of God, mindful of that little verse sanctified by the Apostle: Evil meetings corrupt good character."
Aristotle records a very similar sentiment in the ninth book of his *Ethics*. This six-foot line is also celebrated among the Greeks:
*If you associate with the wicked, you yourself will turn out wicked.* <note>original Greek: "Κακοῖς ὁμιλῶν κ’ αὐτὸς ἐκβήσῃ κακός."</note>

<margin>Seneca, On Anger, book 3.</margin>
Although it might seem somewhat outside the scope of this project to collect such things, I cannot restrain myself from adding this passage from Seneca’s *On Anger*, book three; if it does not strictly pertain to the explanation of the proverb, it is certainly most conducive to the conduct of life. "Character," he says, "is absorbed from those we live with. And just as certain physical diseases jump across through contact, so the mind passes its evils to those nearest. A drunkard drags his companions into a love of wine. A crowd of the lustful softens even a brave man, if such a thing were possible. Greed transfers its poison to those nearby. The same logic applies to virtues from the opposite side: they mitigate everything they have with them. A region is not so beneficial to health, nor a climate so wholesome, as it is for weak minds to live among a crowd of better people. You will understand how much power this has if you see that even wild beasts grow tame by living with us, and no monstrous beast retains its violence if it has long endured the companionship of man." Thus far we have rendered Seneca's words. Furthermore, while every clash of companionship has great weight in correcting or depraving the dispositions of mortals, speech is especially powerful. Drawn from those secret inner chambers of the mind, speech brings with it a certain natural and hidden force—or to put it better in Greek, *energy* <note>original: "ἐνέργειαν"</note>—and pours it into the mind of the listener into whom it flows: a ready poison if it be pestilential, an effective remedy if it be healthy. Accordingly, I do not remember reading any aphorism of the philosophers that seems comparable to the one my friend John Colet <note>A famous English humanist and Dean of St. Paul's, a close friend of Erasmus.</note>—a man equally learned and incorruptible—was accustomed to repeat: "We are such as our daily conversations are; we turn out to be such as the things we frequently hear." Now, what has been said of conversation must also be understood regarding studies. Those who wear out their whole lives in Pagan literature turn out to be heathens. Those who unroll nothing but obscene authors must necessarily be rendered obscene in their morals. For indeed, reading is seen to be a kind of conversation.

### Annus the oven. 75

*Annus the oven.* <note>original Greek: "Ἄννον κλίβανον."</note> This was once said against those who had discovered something new. For a certain Egyptian named Annus is said to have devised the use of ovens <note>term: "clibanus" — a portable earthenware oven or bell-shaped cover for baking bread.</note> in which to bake bread. Indeed, the ancients used to live on porridge and meal, being ignorant of the use of baked bread. <margin>Pliny. Plautus. Seneca.</margin> Pliny writes much regarding the method of baking bread in furnaces in book eighteen, chapter eleven, and the name of the thing was even bestowed from this. For Plautus in the *Aulularia* calls it "artoptesia" <note>bread baked in a special pan</note>. Seneca, in a certain letter to Lucilius, shows that in ancient times bread was kneaded by hand and cooked under hot ashes and a tile; then, gradually, furnaces and other types were invented whose heat could be controlled at will. <margin>Suidas. Aristophanes.</margin> This bread was called "klibanites" <note>oven-baked bread</note>. Both Suidas and the commentator on Aristophanes' *The Acharnians* mention this adage. Although most examples have the word "anthros" <note>man</note>, I found it written as "Anno" in only one place, which pleases me more, as it is a proper name.

### Office shows the man. 76

*Power reveals the man.* <note>original Greek: "Ἀρχὴ τὸν ἄνδρα δείκνυσιν."</note> This is a "dimeter iambic" <note>a poetic meter</note> celebrated as a proverb. Some think it is an aphorism of Pittacus of Mitylene. <margin>Aristotle, Ethics 5. Theophrastus.</margin> There are those who attribute it to Solon, among whom is Sophocles, as they say. Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *Ethics*, cited it under the name of Bias. Likewise, Theophrastus in his *Proverbs* (though that work does not survive) ascribes it to Bias. I thought this should be added lest anyone quibble that it is a mere sentiment and not a proverb. <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Although Plutarch also shows in his *Life of Cicero* that it was a saying celebrated as a proverb, speaking in this manner: "But it seems most of all, as the saying goes, to reveal and test the character of a man..."

<sig>F 3</sig>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...those to whom a small gift given at the right time returned with great interest. Herodotus mentions the history that gave occasion to the proverb in his *Thalia* <note>Book 3 of Herodotus's Histories</note>, although in his work one reads *chlanis* <note>original: χλανὶς</note> rather than *chlamys* <note>original: χλαμύς</note>. A *chlanis*, however, is a military cloak. Strabo also mentions it in the fourteenth book of his *Geography*. The history goes as follows: A certain Syloson, having perceived that Darius, son of Hystaspes (while he was still acting as a private citizen), was exceedingly delighted by a very beautiful cloak of his, sent it to him as a gift of his own accord. Darius, mindful of such timely generosity when he had been placed in charge of affairs <note>i.e., became King of Persia</note>, handed over the entire city and island of the Samians into the hands of Syloson, compensating the gift of a single garment with so wealthy a kingdom. Valerius Maximus also mentions this matter in the fifth book of his *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*, under the title of gratitude. Furthermore, what others call a *chlamys* or *chlanis*, he calls a little cloak—that is, a type of mantle.

### The works of Syloson are a wide region.
<margin>85</margin>

-> By the grace of Syloson there is wide space. <-
-> Through Syloson the region was made more spacious. <-

A verse in six-foot meter <note>original: Senarius</note> turned into a proverb, which Strabo records in the 14th book of his *Geography*. For Syloson, having obtained the tyranny of the Samians through the generosity of Darius after Polycrates died, exercised his command so harshly—as is usually the case with those who are suddenly promoted from humble fortune to great affairs—that for this reason the island was deserted by its inhabitants. Thus the proverb began to be said:

-> By the grace of Syloson there is wide space. <-
-> The region is spacious thanks to Syloson. <-

It is suitable for one who conducts a magistracy harshly, or for an evil prince by whose fault a region is deserted by its inhabitants. It can be applied more elegantly with a broader shift in meaning: for instance, if it is said of a greedy man <note>original: πλεονέκτην (pleonekten)</note> who has plundered a house, or of a lavish and prodigal man whose luxury has left the coffers empty.

### The empire of Phalaris.
<margin>86</margin>

The rule of Phalaris <note>original: Φαλάριδος ἀρχὴ</note>. This is recorded among the Greek proverbs. It is rightly said of those who exercise their command or the power delegated to them too cruelly. The adage arose from Phalaris, the tyrant of the Agrigentines, whom his own cruelty made famous. Among many examples of his cruelty, the most celebrated is that bronze bull of Perillus (or Perilaus, for so Lucian calls him), an invention in which, when fire was placed beneath it, living mortals were burned so that as they died they gave forth a lowing sound instead of a human wail. One reads that he sent this bull—after the inventor himself had first been burned up in it—to Delphi, so that, dedicated to Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, it might be placed in his temple as a future monument both of exquisite art and a most cruel invention, and of a punishment deservedly turned back upon its author. But the Delphians rejected the gift, as it was sent by a tyrant. These things are generally read in Lucian. By a similar figure of speech, we read the term "Phalarism" <note>original: φαλαρισμὸν</note> used for monstrous cruelty. Cicero says to Atticus in the seventh book: "For as for that man whose 'Phalarism' you fear, I think he will do everything most terrifyingly." The same author says in his speech against Piso: "Since," he says, "we have Phalaris as a grammarian"—that is, one who punishes even a slip in writing with the death penalty.

### Manlian commands.
<margin>87</margin>

Just as the previous one fits those who are savage toward those over whom they have gained legal rights, so "Manlian commands"—a proverb closely related to it—will be properly twisted toward those who, through an excessively rigid observation of the law, forget humanity and equity. The history which gave cause to the proverb is narrated by Titus Livy in the 8th book of the first decade. It is also found in Valerius Maximus and several other writers. It goes roughly like this: When T. Manlius as consul was waging war with the Latins, and an edict had been issued that no one should fight outside the ranks, T. Manlius, the consul's son and prefect of a troop, was challenged by Genutius (or as Valerius says, by Geminius Metius, prefect of the Tusculan cavalry). Forgetting the consular edict, he engaged in combat and ran the challenger through with his spear. Then, when he headed to his father accompanied by his troop and adorned with spoils as if in triumph, the father immediately, in the sight of all, ordered his son to be bound to a stake because he had fought outside the ranks, then to be beaten with rods according to custom, and finally to be struck with the axe. A healthy example for the future, indeed, as Livy says, but at the time one that brought too much hatred upon the consul. Indeed, as Valerius records in the ninth book of *Memorable Deeds*, in the chapter on anger, when the victor returned to Rome, none of the young men went out to meet him; he had fallen into such great hatred of all the youth. Hence the surname "The Imperious" was commonly added to him. Valerius records a similar example of severity—

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to tyranny and excessive legal rigor, using the historical figures Syloson, Phalaris, and Titus Manlius Torquatus to illustrate how power can lead to depopulation, cruelty, or the abandonment of mercy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient Roman discipline and transitions into a series of Greek adages from the first chiliad (thousand) of Erasmus's collection.</meta>

# ELEVENTH CENTURY OF THE FIRST THOUSAND

We discussed in the second book, in the chapter on military discipline, Posthumius Tiburtus, whose son—a most brave youth—was struck down by his father’s axe because he had engaged the enemy successfully, yet without his father's command. <note>original: "securi percussus est"</note> However, Titus Livius, in the fourth book of his first decade, preferred to believe this of Manlius Torquatus rather than Posthumius. In the face of varying opinions among writers, Livius testifies that he uses this particular argument: that in the common proverb they are called "Manlian orders," not "Posthumian," even though Posthumius preceded Manlius in age. If the former had been the first author of such a savage example, he surely would have seized the notable title of cruelty; furthermore, the surname "Imperious" was bestowed upon Manlius, not Posthumius. Seneca also mentions in the third book of *On Benefits* a certain Manlius (or Manilius) who, having been banished by his father, returned to free him from the trouble of a lawsuit brought against him. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> rightly alluded to the proverb in the second book of *On Ends*: "See that those are not our 'Manlian' orders, or even greater, if you should command what I am unable to do." Perhaps instead of "our" <note>Latin: "nostra"</note>, the word "orders" <note>Latin: "iussa"</note> was written.

->I have heard the noise of many fig leaves. 88<-
<note>original Greek: πολλῶν ἐγὼ θρίων ψόφον ἀκήκοα</note>
That is: I have heard the rattling of many fig leaves.
This is a proverbial iambic verse by which we signify that we despise threats and empty clamor. Just as Thais in Terence's play considers the fierce and boastful threats of Thraso as nothing, calling him a great scoundrel. Aristophanes says in *The Wasps*:
"Since I, having heard many, know the noise of fig leaves."
Furthermore, *thria* <term>thria: Greek for fig leaves</term> are called fig leaves by the Greeks; when they are burned, they give off a certain threatening crackle, formidable to those who have not heard it before, but otherwise empty and contemptible. Unless you prefer to read it as *thrion* <note>original: θριῶν</note>, for so the Greeks call the pebbles which female fortune-tellers cast into an urn when they divine, as we have noted elsewhere. Such diviners are sometimes accustomed to predict dire things from the lots to terrify the foolish and credulous, when quite often nothing of what they threaten comes to pass.

->They are not even among the parsley. 89<-
<note>original Greek: οὐδ’ ἐν σελίνοις ἐστίν</note>
That is: They are not even in the parsley. This is used for something that has not even reached the entrance or the beginning of a matter. The metaphor is taken from those who enter gardens. For in ancient times, the outermost border of gardens was planted with parsley; those who had not yet passed it were seen as still being on the very threshold of the garden. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
"Indeed, it is not yet even in the parsley, nor yet in the rue."
That is, it does not even have the beginning of those things which are to come. A commentator relates another meaning in this place, wishing the adage to pertain to gymnastic contests, for which those who prepared infants were accustomed to place them in parsley immediately after they were born. Thus, "Not even in the parsley" seems to be said as if you were to say, "not even in the first rudiments." The comic poet added "rue" for the sake of a laugh, because he had spoken of parsley before. Furthermore, they think the custom of crowning with parsley was introduced long ago by Hercules after the Nemean lion was killed, which Pindar also seems to indicate elsewhere. For in the fourth Nemean hymn he says: "Where in the loud-sounding contest he flourished with Corinthian parsley." He means that someone was crowned by the Corinthians in Neptune's Isthmian contest.

->The backside defeats the washing. 90<-
<note>original Greek: πρωκτὸς λουτρὸν πολὺ νικᾷ</note>
That is: The backside wins out over the bath. Callistratus, in the commentary on Aristophanes, referred this adage to those who drive themselves into some evil, because that part of the body, even if it is washed, defiles itself again, so that it is itself the cause of why it cannot be kept clean. It will also fit when we signify that something is done in vain; for instance, if someone ransoms a criminal from prison, and he soon throws himself back into the same place by a repeated crime. Or if you reconcile people who will soon lapse back into their former hostility, or if you chastise an incorrigible nature, such as the race of women <note>Erasmus is reflecting a common period prejudice here</note>. It will also apply to those who "win" by their own misfortune. For example, if someone, through the intractability of their character, ensures they are never scolded by a teacher again. He thinks the adage seems to be taken especially from those with a loose belly, whom Nonius calls "the leaky ones." Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "The backside greatly overcoming the washing."
