<page-num>846</page-num>
-> DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES <-

Likewise, a disease is said to "conquer art" or the care of a physician when it is incurable. From the monuments of the ancients, you will discover that it was a public custom that after the bowels were emptied, a washing of that part was applied, which nevertheless had to be repeated from time to time. Martial, among the praises of the lapdog Issa, mentions that after depositing the burden of her belly, she would ask to be washed. We also read of a certain barbarian, impatient of slavery, who committed suicide by driving into his throat the wood to which a sponge was attached for wiping the anus <note>original: "tergendo podici". Erasmus refers to a famous anecdote from Seneca regarding a gladiator's suicide using a communal latrine sponge.</note>.

<margin>XCI</margin>
### Conscience is a thousand witnesses.

Quintilian, in the fifth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*, cites this sentiment as proverbial: *Conscience is a thousand witnesses.* The meaning needs no interpreter. For who does not know that conscience is the single most effective thing of all? So much so that no tortures betray a crime better than conscience, and no executioner punishes more severely than she does. Whence also that saying: *Alas, how difficult it is not to betray a crime with one's face.* There also exists a Greek sentiment, <note>original: "συνείδησις πλήττει τὴν ψυχήν"</note> *conscience strikes the soul.* Likewise Juvenal: *And strikes with a silent lash.* The poets felt this when they fabled about the dire and avenging Furies.

<margin>XCII</margin>
### The prey of the Mysians.

<note>original: "μυσῶν λεία"</note> *The prey of the Mysians.* This was once said against those who are harmed and plundered with impunity by anyone at all. The adage arose from the Mysians, who they say were once badly harassed by the incursions of their neighbors during the time King Telephus was traveling abroad. Aristotle uses this adage in the first book of the *Rhetoric*, treating conjectural topics: <note>original: "καὶ οὗτος πολλῶν ἀδικηθέντας..."</note> *And those likewise,* he says, *who having been treated unjustly by many, do not care for revenge. For as it is said in the well-worn proverb, these are the prey of the Mysians.* That is, they are attacked on all sides by everyone because by enduring an old injury, they invite a new one. Demosthenes used it against Aeschines. In which place, indeed, certain "know-it-alls" <term>scioli: a derogatory term for those with superficial learning</term> corrupted "of the Mysians" to "of the miserable" in the translation by Leonardo Bruni <note>original: "Leonardi Aretini"</note>. It is also cited from the *Medea* of Strattis and the Iambics of Simonides.

<margin>XCIII</margin>
### To leap beyond the boundaries.

<note>original: "Ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα πηδᾶν"</note> *To leap beyond the boundaries* <note>literally: "beyond the dug-out lines" of a jumping pit</note>. This applies either to those who perform some new and incredible feat far above the capacity of common men, or to those who digress from the proposed subject, or to those who exceed the limits prescribed for them and the measure of their mandated power. The adage was born from a certain Phayllus, a pentathlete of Opus (or of Croton, as some prefer), who is read to have been wonderfully strong in both the jump and the discus. Suidas says roughly this. There also exists an inscription on his statue of this kind: *Phayllus jumped five and fifty feet; and he threw the discus one hundred, except for five* <note>i.e., 95 feet</note>. Plato mentions this adage in the *Cratylus*: *And you leap beyond the boundaries.* Julius Pollux also records it in the third book of *On Vocabulary*. Lucian in *The Dream*: *He has already leapt beyond the boundaries.* This refers to a dream whose end is such that the sleep would endure even for one who is awake. Chrysostom in the Homily on 2 Corinthians 3: *He went beyond the boundaries*; he speaks of Paul, who, since he taught the Gospel for free, performed more than was required of the Apostles. Cicero in the first book *On the Orator*: *And knowledge circumscribed, as it were, by the forensic barriers of certain arts.* The same in his legal actions: *I shall decline from these barriers by which I have circumscribed myself.* For the place in which the public games were celebrated was circumscribed by ditches, barriers, or other boundaries of that kind.

<margin>XCIV</margin>
### The deeds of Psyra.

Psyra is a certain island, not far from Chios, which Homer also mentions in the third book of the *Odyssey*, calling it Psyria: *Whether we should return above rugged Chios toward the island of Psyra, keeping Chios itself on the left.* Strabo pronounces "Psyra" in the plural and the neuter gender. Pliny also mentions this...

nius in the fifth book of his *World History*. Because that island was both tiny and insignificant, it passed into a proverb for contempt and uselessness, so that things done in a sordid or unmagnificent manner were said to be "Psyrian deeds." This is essentially what Stephanus says. He also cites Cratinus:
<margin>Leading Bacchus into Psyra.</margin> <note>original: "Ψύρα τὸν Διόνυσον ἀγοντῶν"</note> that is,
Leading Bacchus into Psyra. <note>Meaning to bring something grand or divine into a tiny, worthless place.</note>
And again in *Nemesa*:

### A Cyprian Ox. XCV
<margin>Cyprian ox.</margin> <note>original: "Κύπριος βοῦς"</note> that is, A Cyprian ox. This was usually cast at a person who is brutish and dull-witted, for the reason that Cyprian oxen are said to be more brutish than others, seeing as they feed on human dung. This is recorded by Suidas and Diogenianus. The commentator on Aristophanes' *Plutus* writes that Boeotian oxen were <term>dung-eaters<note>original: "σκατοφάγους"</note></term>, that is, eaters of excrement. Aristophanes calls doctors by this name because, in treating the sick, they handle filthy things, inspecting urine or the excrement of the bowels. But Pliny agrees regarding the Cyprian oxen in the twenty-eighth book, final chapter, stating that Cyprian oxen seek out human excrement, not for the sake of food, but so that they might cure their colic with this remedy.

### A snack for a Cyprian ox. XCVI
Festus Pompeius cites this Sotadic verse from Ennius:
A snack for a Cyprian ox.
He shows that this is appropriate whenever a filthy and tasteless guest is received at a filthy and tasteless banquet. He relates the origin of the adage to the same one we just mentioned. It will be more elegant if it is turned toward matters of the mind, as when someone speaks filthily among the filthy, or unlearnedly among the unlearned.

### He has the horse of Seius. XCVII
"To have the horse of Seius" was once a proverbial saying used for a calamitous person who had been reduced to extreme poverty. The allegory is taken from a certain ill-fated horse, which was given the name "Seian" from its master, Gnaeus Seius. It was believed to have been descended from the horses of Diomedes. It was indeed of remarkable appearance, but possessed by such a fate that whoever was the owner of that horse would perish along with his entire household to the point of total destruction. This was proven by Gnaeus Seius himself, who was condemned to death and suffered a piteous execution; then by Dolabella, who was killed in war; after him Cassius, slain by enemies; and finally Antony, who was destroyed by a detestable end. Gaius Bassus reports that he saw this horse at Argos, of incredible beauty, vigor, and a most surpassing color—namely, scarlet. Aulus Gellius records and explains this adage more fully in the third book of *Attic Nights*, chapter nine. It is possible that this superstition about the horse flowed from that wooden horse of which Homer mentions in the eighth book of the *Odyssey*, which brought fatal destruction to the Trojans. Alluding to this, Virgil says:
"The fatal machine," he says, "scales the walls."
On the other hand, the superstition of the ancients believed certain things to be fatefully lucky. For Trebellius Pollio, in his book on the *Thirty Tyrants*, is the authority that the common people were persuaded that things turned out successfully for those who wore an image of Alexander the Great struck in gold or silver. Even today, there are those who promise princes "lucky swords" in war and such trifles. But it is more to be wondered at that there are those who believe such impostors.

### He has Tolossan gold. XCVIII
Very similar to this is the saying: "He has Tolossan gold." It is used for one who is afflicted by great and fatal evils and perishes by a strange and piteous end. It is recorded by Aulus Gellius in the same place we just cited, in this manner: "The meaning of that old proverb is the same, which we understand was said thus: 'He has Tolossan gold.' For when the consul Quintus Caepio had plundered the town of Tolossa <note>Modern Toulouse</note> in the land of Gaul, and there had been much gold in the temples of that town, whoever touched the gold from that pillage perished by a miserable and agonizing death." In most manuscripts of Gellius, it was previously read as "in the land of Italy," but erroneously, since Strabo and Justin place Tolossa in Gaul. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> mentions the Tolossan gold in the third book *On the Nature of the Gods*: "Consider," he says, "other inquiries into the Tolossan gold and the Jugurthine conspiracy." Strabo in his book...

--- Page 458 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the proverb "Gold of Toulouse" from the previous page, detailing its historical origins and the curse associated with it, before moving on to new adages regarding mixed blessings and wasted resources.</meta>

In the fourth book of his *Geography* <note>original: "Geographiæ quarto"</note>, Strabo reminds us that this "Gold of Toulouse" was actually part of the Delphic treasure. For Brennus, a Prausian by nation, had raided Delphi with the help of the Tectosages. Then, as Justin reports in his thirty-second book, when the Tectosages returned to their ancient homeland of Toulouse, they began to suffer from a plague. They were not freed from this until, warned by the responses of soothsayers, they submerged the gold and silver acquired through sacrilege into the lake at Toulouse. All of this was taken much later by the Roman consul Caepio. This very sacrilege brought destruction both to Caepio himself and to his troops. There were, moreover, one hundred and ten thousand pounds of gold and one and a half million pounds of silver. Strabo writes that the people of Toulouse had added to this sacred money from their private fortunes to better reconcile the god to themselves. Other things are also told in this passage by Strabo concerning the gold of Toulouse, cited from Posidonius; but since they did not seem to pertain greatly to the explanation of the adage, I considered it enough to have pointed out the location. Even today, this opinion persists among the common people: they believe that all those who do not keep their violent hands off sacred things will perish miserably.

### The head of a polyp. XCIX

*Polypicaput* <note>original Greek: πολύποδος κεφαλὴ</note>. That is, the head of a polyp <note>A "polyp" here refers to an octopus or similar cephalopod</note>. This is used against a fickle man, or one in whom you find both vices and virtues in equal measure—the sort of man Sallust describes Catiline to be. It also applies to a thing from which you might derive no small advantage, but which simultaneously causes harm through certain inconveniences. The allegory is drawn from the head of that fish, which (as Plutarch testifies in the essay titled *How a Young Man Should Study Poetry*) is indeed very sweet and good to eat, but produces sad and monstrous dreams. For this reason, the eating of it was forbidden to those who desired to foreknow the future from dreams, just as beans were forbidden, as the same Plutarch witnesses in his *Table Talk*. Accordingly, in the manner of poets, he calls poetry "the head of a polyp," in which there are many things both pleasant and fruitful to know, yet there are some things that are pestilential unless you are careful. Furthermore, from such things it is fitting to pick out what is useful and avoid what is harmful; following the teaching of Simonides, one should imitate the little bees, which, passing over the rest, fly only to those things from which they can extract something suitable for making honey, and collect nothing else than what will be of use. The proverb is recorded in full by Plutarch in this way:

> In the head of the polyp there is both evil and good. <note>original Greek: πολύποδος κεφαλῇ ἔνι μὲν κακὸν, ἤδ’ ἐσθλόν</note>

Likewise, Theognis says of wine in his maxims:

> You are both good and evil. <note>original Greek: ἐσθλὸς καὶ κακός ἐστι</note>

One might also adapt to this form the story of Achilles' spear, which brought the cure for the wound just as it had inflicted the wound itself.

### You wear out your cloak in summer. C

*Aestate penulam deteris* <note>original Greek: ἐν θέρει τὴν χλαῖναν κατατρίβεις</note>. That is, you wear out your traveling cloak in summer. This is recorded by Zenodotus, Diogenianus, and Suidas. It is rightly said against one who squanders necessary things rashly and out of season—things that would have been useful later if they had been saved. This is what young men commonly do, foolishly wasting their father's wealth in their youth, which ought to have sustained the weakness of old age. Nor will it fit poorly those who waste the strength of their bodies in pleasures to no purpose, which they will later miss when performing serious business. For the *chlaina* <note>Greek: χλαῖνα</note> is an outer garment, taken up according to the weather to ward off wind, rain, or cold; you might call it a *penula* <note>a heavy hooded cloak</note> in Latin. Juvenal says:

> And the cloak dripped with much rain.

Although the Latins also use the word *laena* for what the Greeks call a *chlaina*. Nonius indicates it is a type of military garment that is worn over everything else, like a mantle, a cloak, or a *penula*. In Diogenes Laertius, the comic poet Philemon casts a similar reproach at Crates, because he wore a thick cloak in summer and a ragged tunic in winter—evidently because he was learning temperance and endurance.

<meta>This page begins the second thousand of Erasmus’s Adages (Chiliads), specifically the first hundred of the second thousand. It introduces one of his most famous essays on the proverb "Make haste slowly."</meta>

# THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND PROVERBS BY DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM.

## Make haste slowly. <note>original: Σπεῦδε βραδέως (Speude bradeōs)</note>

<margin>I</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial S featuring a figure in a garden landscape.</image-desc>
Make haste slowly. This proverb carries a rather charming air of a riddle, precisely because it consists of words that contradict one another. Therefore, it should be categorized under that form which we demonstrated at the beginning of this work—namely, those expressed through <term>enantiosis (opposition)</term>, that is, by contrariety. Of this kind is the phrase <term>unhappy happiness</term> <note>original: δυσδαίμων εὐδαιμονία (dysdaimōn eudaimonia)</note>. Nor would it seem to me an absurd conjecture if someone were to think it was
<margin>Aristophanes in The Knights</margin>
modeled after the line in Aristophanes’ *The Knights*, <term>make haste quickly</term> <note>original: σπεῦδε ταχέως (speude tacheōs)</note>, so that whoever the wit was, he changed the <term>anadiplosis (repetition)</term> into an <term>enantiosis (opposition)</term>. To this stylistic color and the cleverness of the allusion, a great deal of grace and convenience is added by its absolute brevity. This brevity, in my view, is a particular ornament in choice adages just as it is in gems, and it contributes to their miraculous value. Indeed, if you
" consider the depth of meaning which this clipped brevity of words enfolds within itself—
" how fertile it is, how weighty, how wholesome, and how widely applicable to every
" aspect of life—you will surely come to the conclusion that among such a vast number
" of proverbs, there is none other so worthy of being carved upon every column,
" inscribed before the doors of every temple (and in letters of gold at that!), painted
" upon the folding doors of princely halls, engraved upon the rings of nobles, or
" expressed upon royal scepters. In short, it should be represented, propagated, and
" celebrated on every monument everywhere. It is so vital that it should always be
" observed in everyone’s mind and meet the eye at every turn. While it is of the
" greatest use to every mortal, it is especially so for princes and those to whom, to
" speak in Homeric words,
> <term>the people are entrusted, and so many cares are a concern.</term> <note>original: πᾶσ’ ὑπὸ σφραγῖδι καὶ τόσα μέμυλε (pas’ hypo sphragidi kai tosa memyle)</note>

For if something is perhaps overlooked through sluggishness or committed through rashness by men of common lot, the loss is lighter and the resulting inconvenience is repaired with an easier remedy. But truly, a single instance of a prince’s idleness, or a single headlong decision—immortal God!—what storms does it sometimes stir up, and what ruins of human affairs does it drag down with it? On the other hand, if there is present a <term>hastening slowly</term> <note>original: σπουδὴ βραδέως (spoudē bradeōs)</note>—that is, a certain ripeness and moderation tempered simultaneously by vigilance and deliberation—so that he does nothing through rashness that must be repented, nor overlooks anything through sluggishness that seems to pertain to the advantage of the Commonwealth, I ask you: what could be more fortunate, more firm, or more stable than such a rule? Although this happiness is by no means confined within the borders of the empire itself; rather, it flows out far and wide to neighboring peoples. Nowhere does that saying of Hesiod hold more true:
> <term>A bad neighbor is a calamity, as much as a good one is a great blessing.</term> <note>original: πῆμα κακὸς γείτων, ὅσσον τ’ ἀγαθὸς μέγ’ ὄνειαρ (pēma kakos geitōn, hosson t’ agathos meg’ oneiar)</note>

Therefore, I am of the opinion that this proverb, if any other, deserves by the best right to be called <term>basilikon</term>, that is, "royal." This is not only for the reason I just mentioned, but also because the minds of princes seem to be almost uniquely prone to these two vices. For the favor of fortune, the abundance of things, and the readily available allurements of pleasure—furthermore, the immediate freedom to do
whatever one pleases, and finally that most pestilential "bravo!" of flatterers always
clinging to them—all these things, I say, and others of that kind, it is no wonder if they breed sluggishness in some. This is especially true if the age of youth happens upon all these encouragements, accompanied by inexperience. Yet, on the other hand, it sometimes happens that the vigor implanted in the minds of princes—a certain "leonine" impulse, so to speak—is increased by the magnitude of fortune, excited by the successes of great affairs, inflamed by anger, ambition, or other such desires, and stimulated by fierce counsels. This carries them headlong at times, dragging both themselves and the entire weight of the empire into the abyss. Nevertheless, if one must
" err on one side or the other, it is far better for a king to be excessively slow than
" more headlong than is right.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s extensive commentary on the proverb "Festina Lente" (Make haste slowly), moving from the philosophical definition to historical examples of leaders who embodied or lacked this balance.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Homer seems to have attributed to Agamemnon a certain faulty softness of mind, that is, *slowness* <note>original: τὸ βραδέως (*to bradeōs*)</note>: so that no distinguished or spirited deed of his is recorded, except when he is angry over the seizure of Chryseis and robs Achilles of his Briseis. On the other hand, he attributes to Achilles impulses that are hardly moderated, that is, *manliness* <note>original: τὸ ἀνδρῶδες (*to andrōdes*), here implying a raw, aggressive masculinity</note>: unless someone considers it "slowly" when, in the council, he is about to attack the king with a drawn sword but is restrained by Pallas Athena, warned to limit his indignation to mere insults. Yet this very act—to rave with such manifest insults against the man who held supreme power in a crowded assembly of princes—was the mark of an ungovernable mind. Alexander the Great seems to have imitated Achilles, and clearly surpassed him: for his mental impulse drove him so headlong that he even drew his blade against his closest friends. Sardanapalus <note>An Assyrian king legendary for decadence and sloth</note> emulated Agamemnon, but emulated him in such a way that he surpassed him by a long interval. Indeed, one may find innumerable examples of both types who reflect either the former's sluggishness or the latter's ferocity; but you will find very few who, following this proverb, have rightly mixed timely speed with prudent slowness. One man, however, suffices for many: the famous Fabius Maximus, to whom the surname "the Delayer" <note>Cunctator</note> was added. He not only won immortal praise for himself but restored the Roman state by delaying, when it had been reduced to the brink of ruin by the leadership of others through ill-omened haste.

Therefore, I see it was not without cause that this *Make haste slowly* <note>original: σπεῦδε βραδέως (*speude bradeōs*)</note> so greatly pleased two Roman emperors, easily the most praised of all: Octavian Augustus and Titus Vespasian. In both of them, a certain singular greatness of mind was joined with an incredible gentleness and approachability. Thus, while they had bound the hearts of all to themselves with an amiable and popular character, they nevertheless achieved the greatest things with equal diligence and speed whenever the situation demanded a man of action. Augustus, then, was so exceedingly delighted by this saying—as Aulus Gellius relates in *Attic Nights*, Book 10, Chapter 11, followed by Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*, Book 6—that he not only used it frequently in daily conversation but also often inserted it into his letters. He used these two words to advise that both the speed of industry and the slowness of diligence should be applied to the task at hand. Gellius thinks this is expressed in Latin by a single word: *matura* (ripen or hasten maturely). For to "mature" is to do something neither too hurriedly nor later than is proper, but at the very right time. He argues Virgil used it in this sense in the first book of the *Aeneid*: "Hasten <note>Maturate</note> your flight." Although among authors this word generally means the same as "to hurry," it means to hurry in such a way that you do not anticipate the legitimate time. For while you might rightly call hurried things "premature," you would not call them "matured." Nor do these things differ from what Suetonius records in his life of Augustus: "He thought," he says, "nothing was less becoming in a perfect leader than haste and rashness." Thus he frequently tossed out these words:

-> Make haste slowly; for a safe commander is better than a bold one. <-
<note>original: Σπεῦδε βραδέως, ἀσφαλὴς γάρ ἐστ’ ἀμείνων ἢ θρασὺς Στρατηγός.</note>

These are roughly the words of Suetonius. The verse is a trochaic tetrameter catalectic <note>A specific meter of Greek poetry</note> plucked from some poet, as I conjecture, to which Caesar [Augustus] added his own word, *commander* <note>stratēgos</note>. The meaning is this: *Hasten slowly*. For he who conducts business safely and without a slip is better than one who is bold and overconfident. For things provided for by slow counsels are safer than those prepared by hot-headed ones.

Now, that this same saying pleased Titus Vespasian is easily gathered from his very ancient coins. One of these, made of silver and of clearly ancient Roman carving, Aldus Manutius <note>The famous Venetian printer and friend of Erasmus</note> showed to me. He said it was sent to him as a gift by Pietro Bembo, a Venetian patrician, a young man who is both among the foremost scholars and a most diligent investigator of all literary antiquity. The character of the coin was as follows: on one side it shows the face of Titus Vespasian with an inscription; on the other, an anchor, the middle of which (like a tiller) is entwined by a dolphin. That this symbol means nothing other than that saying of Augustus Caesar, *Make haste slowly*, is indicated by the monuments of hieroglyphic letters. For that is what they call the enigmatic carvings which were in great use in ancient times, especially among the Egyptian priests and theologians. They considered it a sin to betray the mysteries of wisdom to the profane commoners in ordinary letters as we do; instead, if they judged something worthy of being known, they represented it with the expressed figures of animals and various things. Thus, it was not immediately easy for just anyone to guess the meaning. But if someone knew the properties of individual things and the power and nature of each animal, and had looked into them deeply, he at last grasped the enigma of the thought by comparing those symbols. For example, when the Egyptians wish to signify their Osiris, whom they believe to be the same as the Sun...

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
G 2
<meta>catchword: tur</meta>

<margin>They carve a scepter, and in it they express the appearance of an eye, undoubtedly intimating that this is God, and being sublime in royal power, he looks down upon all things, because antiquity calls the sun the eye of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. Macrobius relates things of this sort in the first book of the *Saturnalia*. Likewise, they demonstrated the year in this way: they fashioned a serpent so coiled that it held its tail inserted in its mouth, intimating that the year always returns into itself by the same alternating successions of time. Whence Servius thinks the word <term>eniauton</term> <note>original: ἐνιαυτὸν; a Greek word for "year," often etymologically linked to the idea of "in itself."</note> was attributed to the year among the Greeks, and that Maro <note>Virgil</note> had this in mind when he said:
> And the year rolls on itself through its own tracks.</margin>

Even if Horus the Egyptian <note>Horapollo, the supposed author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note>, whose two books on symbols of this kind are extant, teaches that the carving of a serpent represents not the year, but an age <note>eternity</note>; yet he says the year is represented by the image of Isis, and sometimes by the Phoenix. Plutarch wrote about these matters in his commentary on Osiris, as did Chaeremon among the Greeks, according to the testimony of Suidas; I suspect that the monuments of this kind which we have recently seen were excerpted from his books. In these, this picture was also present: in the first place a circle, then an anchor, which, as I said, a dolphin embraces with a twisted body around the middle. The circle, as the inscribed interpretation indicated, since it is finished by no boundary, intimates eternal time. The anchor, since it delays and binds the ship and makes it stay, indicates slowness. The dolphin, because no other animal is swifter than this, or of more destructive impetus, expresses speed. If you connect these skillfully, they will produce a sentiment of this kind: <term>Always hasten slowly</term> <note>original: ἀεὶ σπεῦδε βραδέως; the famous motto "Festina Lente."</note>. Furthermore, this kind of writing possesses not only a great deal of dignity, but also no small amount of pleasure, if only one has thoroughly looked into the properties of things, as I said; this happens partly through the skillful contemplation of things and natural causes, and partly through the knowledge of the liberal disciplines. 

For example, if someone held firmly from the books of Aristotle which he inscribed *On Natural Hearing* <note>The *Physics*</note> that there is a certain analogy and similarity between magnitude, motion, and time; for each one of these three exists equally in the same way. Indeed, just as time adheres to motion, so motion adheres to magnitude. What a point is in magnitude, this a "moment" is in time, and an "impetus" in motion (let it be allowed to call it so for now, being that which is smallest and indivisible in motion; for we should not labor over words if we agree on the thing). Now, therefore, if you consider magnitude in a straight line, you will find two points, one of which is only the beginning, the other only the end—that is, from which the length flows, as it were, and in which it finishes. If you establish motion in the same, you will likewise find two impetuses: one from which the motion arises, the other in which it finishes. The logic of these is such that where the beginning is, it is only the beginning of that motion; where the end is, it is only the end. Time necessarily accompanies motion. For it is, as it were, the rule of this, whose nature if you contemplate separately, you see two moments (if I may speak thus): one the beginning of that time, the other the end. 

But again, if you consider in the same line the points of magnitude, the impetuses of motion, and the moments of time which intervene between the beginning and the end, you see that the nature of each of these is, as it were, two-fold. For related to the beginning, they are ends; related to the end, they are beginnings. Accordingly, where magnitude is finite, there both motion and time must be finite at the same time. Moreover, that magnitude is finite into which such a beginning fits that the same cannot be the end; such an end, I say, that the logic of a beginning does not fall into the same—which happens in all figures, except the circular or spherical. For just as in this there is no certain point which can properly be called the beginning, nor any which is so an end that it receives only that name, so there is no moment of this kind, nor impetus. From which it follows that there magnitude is not finite, nor motion finite, nor time finite. 

Again, where any point of magnitude can be at once both a beginning and an end, there it is necessary that the magnitude be infinite. By the same reasoning, where any impetus can be either the principle of motion or the end, there the motion is seen to be infinite. Finally, where any moment can be at once either the beginning of time or the end, there time must be [in]finite. But infinite time we call eternal, which indeed corresponds to eternal motion. Eternal motion likewise requires an eternal magnitude. These things cannot fit except in a spherical or circular magnitude. Whence certain philosophers gathered the eternity of the world, because they observed that the figure of the entire heaven and the stars is spherical, and the motion is likewise spherical. Furthermore, not only does the logic of a circle fit into a magnitude of this kind, but even the motion adhering to this is a certain circle. Likewise, the time measuring that motion does not reject the name of a circle, just as...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Aristotle also discusses these matters in the fourth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "περὶ φυσικῆς ἀκροάσεως" (On Physical Lectures)</note>. Therefore, anyone who has thoroughly learned these and similar ideas from the teachings of the philosophers will easily guess why the Egyptians wished to express eternal time through the circle. Now, however, let us look briefly at the power and nature of the Dolphin. Authors report that this creature, with incredible speed and admirable force, leaves the rest of the animal kingdom far behind. Accordingly, Oppian, in his second book *On the Nature of Fishes*, compares dolphins not just with any birds, but with eagles:

<margin>that is,</margin>
->As much as the Eagle is king among the light birds,<-
->Or lions among the swift-footed beasts,<-
->As much as dragons are among the creeping serpents,<-
->So much does the dolphin lead among the fish.<-

<margin>He also compares it to a javelin,</margin>
->Indeed, as much as the eagle, distinguished by royal honor,<-
->Outstrips all other swift birds,<-
->And as the lion among raw-flesh-eating beasts, and fierce dragons<-
->Surpass the serpent kind, by so much the exceptional dolphin<-
->Conquers the fish ruling the sea with its rush.<-

<margin>that is,</margin>
->For they fly through the sea like a bolt.<-

->For they fly through the wide waters in the manner of an arrow.<-

Finally, he even compares it to the wind, or rather to a whirlwind and a storm of winds.

<margin>that is,</margin>
->At times it runs through the deep wave like a hurricane.<-

->Sometimes through the high waves<-
->It rushes about in the manner of a whirlwind.<-

Pliny, in the ninth book of his *Natural History* <note>original: "historiæ mundi" (History of the World)</note>, chapter eight, following the opinion of Aristotle, reports things in no way different from these: namely, that the dolphin is the swiftest of all animals. It is not only faster than those of the sea, but swifter than any bird and sharper than any missile. He concludes that its singular speed is best proven by this fact: although its mouth is located a long distance from its snout—nearly in the middle of its belly—(which must necessarily cause no small delay when catching fish, for it cannot seize them unless turned on its back), nevertheless there is hardly any fish that can escape its swiftness. Nor is the dolphin unaware of this gift of nature, but as if for the sake of praise or spirit, it sometimes competes with ships sailing under full canvas. For the dolphin is especially a "friend of man" <note>original: "φιλάνθρωπος" (philanthropos)</note>, and even "fond of children" <note>original: "παιδίοις"</note> as some say; for this reason, it is the mortal enemy of the crocodile, than which no other animal is more hostile to man. Thus, it does not fear man as a stranger, but comes to meet ships; it plays about, leaping, and even competes with and passes any sail, however full. Furthermore, in the hunting of mullet at the Laterna lagoon, it magnificently demonstrates how much it prevails in speed, how much it excels in intelligence, and finally how much it wishes well to man. Now, what shall I say of its almost incredible force? Indeed, when driven by hunger it has pursued a fleeing fish into the deepest shallows and held its breath for a long time, it shoots up to breathe like an arrow from a bow, leaping out with such force that it often flies over the wind-filled sails of ships in a single bound. What symbol, therefore, was more suitable to express that sharp and untamed impulse of the mind than the dolphin? Furthermore, to signify slowness and hesitation, the "sucker-fish" <note>original: "ἐχενηὶς" (echeneis), which the Latins call the remora</note> was not a bad fit; but since its shape seemed too little known (for besides being very small, it is distinguished by no remarkable mark), the symbol of the anchor was preferred. If ever a ship is driven into danger by too-favorable winds, the anchor fixes and restrains the ship's immoderate course. Thus, it appears that this saying, "Make haste slowly," proceeded from the very mysteries of ancient philosophy, from whence it was adopted by two of the most praised emperors of all, so that for one it served as an adage, and for the other as an emblem, wonderfully fitting the character and genius of both. Now, however, it has come down to Aldus Manutius the Roman, as if to a third heir,

Not indeed, I believe, without purpose, nor without the will of the gods. <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note>
For the same emblems that once pleased Titus Vespasian are celebrated by him—emblems not only very well known, but also very welcome to all people everywhere to whom good literature is either known or dear. Nor would I believe this symbol was more illustrious then, when being born of the imperial name it was carried about to be handled by merchants, than it is now, when everywhere among nations, even beyond the boundaries of the Christian Empire, together with all kinds of literature in both languages...

# THE SECOND THOUSAND: FIRST CENTURY
-> G 3 <-

which is propagated through volumes, is recognized, upheld, and celebrated by all who worship at the shrines of liberal studies: especially by those who, having loathed that crude and bloated "barbarian" teaching <note>A reference to the Scholastic Latin of the Middle Ages, which Renaissance humanists considered unrefined.</note>, aspire to true and ancient erudition. To restore this learning, this man seems almost born for the task—formed and carved, if I may say so, by the Fates themselves. With such burning vows he desires this one thing, with such indefatigable zeal he labors, and to such an extent does he shrink from no toil, that the "literary furniture" <note>A metaphor for a library or a scholar's collection of tools.</note> may be restored whole, sincere, and pure to men of good intellect. Indeed, the reality itself clearly indicates how much momentum he has already brought to this matter, even if (I might almost say) it was against the will of the reluctant.

But if some god friendly to good letters breathes upon the most beautiful and truly royal vows of our Aldus, and if no sinister powers prevent it, I promise students that within a few years it will come to pass that whatever good authors exist in the four languages—Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldaica"; usually referring to Aramaic in this period.</note>—as well as in every branch of discipline, they shall have it all full and corrected through the work of this one man, and no one shall find any part of their literary furniture lacking. As soon as that happens, it will then become clear how many good manuscripts are still hidden away, either pushed aside through negligence or suppressed by the ambition of certain people whose only heart's desire is to appear uniquely wise. Then, finally, it will be known with what monstrous errors even those authors swarm who are now thought to be sufficiently corrected. 

If anyone wishes to make a conjecture about this matter, as if by a "tasting," let him compare the letters of Pliny—which will shortly come to light from the Aldine workshop—with the common copies; and what he discovers there, let him expect the same in other authors. By Hercules, it is a Herculean deed, and worthy of a truly royal mind: to restore to the world a thing so divine that had almost utterly collapsed; to track down the hidden, to unearth the pushed-aside, to recall the extinct, to repair the mutilated, and to correct what has been corrupted in so many ways—especially by the fault of those common printers to whom the small profit of a single gold coin is more precious than the entirety of literature. 

Add to this that however much you may exaggerate the praise of those who, by their virtue, either protect or even enlarge republics, they are certainly occupied with profane matters and within narrow boundaries. But he who rescues collapsed letters (for that is almost more difficult than to have fathered them) first of all labors upon a thing sacred and immortal; secondly, he acts not for one single province, but for all nations everywhere and for all ages. Finally, since this was once the duty of princes—among whom the glory of Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus, associated with the Great Library of Alexandria.</note> was chief—yet his library was contained within domestic and narrow walls. Aldus is building a library whose boundaries are none other than those of the world itself. 

I do not think I have wandered into this little digression without purpose: namely, so that students may favor and delight in these emblems <note>Referring to the Aldine anchor and dolphin device.</note> all the more eagerly, once they have learned they flowed from such illustrious authors, and furthermore, once they have understood what they signify. Finally, when they remember how much of a "good thing" that Dolphin promises, if only some god is present to favor these most beautiful endeavors. 

The story will be resumed from the detour, if I first set forth a complaint about certain printers who deserve very poorly of literature. It is not a new complaint, yet never was it more just than in these times, in which this fourth edition (unless I am mistaken) was being prepared for me. That was in the year 1525. The city of the Venetians is indeed most famous for many names, yet it is more celebrated because of the Aldine workshop, so much so that whatever books are brought from there to foreign nations are immediately more saleable just because of the city's title. 

And yet, certain sordid printers so abuse the allure of that name that authors come to us from hardly any city more shamelessly corrupted—and not just any authors, but the very first of all, such as Aristotle, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>, and Quintilian, to say nothing of the sacred volumes. It is provided by laws that no one may sew a shoe, nor make a chest, unless he has been approved by his guild of craftsmen; yet these great authors, to whose monuments even royalty is indebted, are sent out to the public by men so ignorant of letters that they cannot even read, so lazy that they do not care to re-read what is being printed, and so sordid that they would sooner allow a good book to be filled with six thousand errors than spend a few gold coins to hire someone to oversee the correction. Nor do any promise more magnificently in their titles than those who most shamelessly corrupt everything. 

By the authority of the laws, a "return of goods" <term>redhibitio: a legal right to return defective goods for a refund</term> is granted if someone sells cloth as if dyed with scarlet, if it is discovered that no scarlet was added to the dye; indeed, anyone who has put a false face on such merchandise is punished with a fine. And shall he enjoy his profit—or rather his theft—who by the same labor imposes upon so many thousands of men? Formerly, no less religious care was applied to transcribing books than is now applied to public and sworn notaries; certainly, more was owed. Nor has such a monstrous confusion of books proceeded from any other source than that to any obscure persons and monks, however unlearned...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s famous essay "Festina Lente" (Make Haste Slowly) from his Adagia, specifically focusing on the corruption of the printing industry and its social consequences.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Soon, the handling of such a sacred matter was entrusted even to common women without any selection. Yet how small is the evil brought by a negligent or unlearned scribe compared to a printer? In this matter, public laws are caught napping. A man is punished if he sells cloth dyed in Britain as if it were dyed in Venice; yet he enjoys the fruits of his audacity who sells mere "crosses" <note>original: "cruces" - likely referring to typographical errors or "tortures" for the reader</note> and torments of the mind in place of good authors? You will say, "It is not the seller's duty to guarantee the buyer against every flaw." Certainly, it ought to be so if the title promises exact diligence and the book swarms with errors—errors which even the learned do not immediately detect. Now, an innumerable swarm of printers confuses everything, especially among the Germans. Not just anyone is allowed to be a painter, yet printing is a trade forbidden to no mortal. It is not safe to paint or say just anything, yet it is permitted to print any material whatsoever. Where on earth do these swarms of new booklets not fly? Even if each one brought something worth knowing, the sheer crowd would still vehemently hinder studies, either by that very satiety—which is most ruinous in good things—or by this: that the minds of men, by nature eager for new things, are called away by these allurements from reading the ancient writers. Nothing better than those ancients can be produced, even if I do not deny that something might be found by the moderns <note>original: "neotericis"</note> which escaped them. There may exist, for example, someone who teaches something that was hidden from Aristotle; yet I do not believe anyone will arise who delivers the body of philosophy more perfectly than he did. So perhaps there will be someone in Sacred Scripture who sees certain things that escaped Chrysostom or Jerome; but I do not think there will be anyone who, in the sum of it, provides what they provided. Now, with those authors almost antiquated, we waste our hours on the trifles of everyone; meanwhile, honorable disciplines are neglected, and along with their authors, the authority of senates, councils, schools, lawyers, and theologians collapses. If things continue as they have begun, the supreme power will be reduced to a few, and there will be a kind of barbaric tyranny among us, such as exists among the Turks. Everything will obey the lust of one or a few, and there will be no traces of civil government, but everything will be governed by military violence. All honorable disciplines will lie prostrate; one law alone will flourish: *So wills the World-Ruler* <note>original: "ὁ κοσμοκράτωρ" (ho kosmokrator) - a Greek term for a world-tyrant or the devil</note>. The prelates of religion will either be of no value, or if they have any wealth or dignity, it will entirely serve those by whose nod and refusal—rather than judgment—all things will be tempered. How much better human affairs would be consulted if, just as in the elements of the world some things are tempered by others so that all consist in an eternal covenant, so in the republic each person’s legitimate authority remained. To the people should be given what is fair; to the senate and magistrate as much should be granted as learning, laws, and equity allow; to bishops and priests their own honor should remain; nor should monks be denied what is owed to them. The "concordant discord" <note>A musical metaphor for social harmony through balance</note> of all these, and a variety tending toward the same end, would preserve the state of the Republic far more faithfully than now, while everyone tries to snatch everything for themselves. Not even a household can stand unless the husband yields part of the duties to the wife, unless there is a distinction between children and servants, and unless servants are regarded not as beasts of burden but as men—and finally, unless there is a distinction between servant and servant, so that those who serve liberally are treated more indulgently and expect liberty as a reward for their duties. Someone will say here: "Hey, you diviner, what has this to do with printers?" Because no small part of this evil is brought in by their unpunished license. They fill the world with booklets—I will not say trifles, such as I perhaps write—but with foolish, unlearned, slanderous, infamous, rabid, impious, and seditious things; and the crowd of these causes even fruitful books to lose their fruit. Some fly forth without titles, or what is more wicked, with forged titles. When caught, they answer: "Give me the means to feed my family, and I will stop printing such books." A thief, an impostor, or a pimp might respond with a somewhat better face: "Give me a way to live, and I will stop using these arts"—unless perhaps it is a lighter crime to secretly diminish another's property than to openly snatch away another's reputation, or to abuse your own or another's body for gain than to attack the life and reputation of another, which is dearer than life itself. But enough of complaints for a long time now. The remedy must be pointed out. This evil will be mitigated if it becomes a concern for princes and magistrates that, as much as possible, the idle be excluded (whom mercenary wars chiefly breed for us); next, if the laws show a ready club to the wicked whom neither reason nor shame restrains, unless they turn to better things; finally, if rewards succor those attempting things that serve the public utility, if they lack strength—whether from princes, bishops, and abbots, or from the public treasury. For from merchants, most of whom have dedicated themselves to Mammon <note>The biblical personification of wealth and greed</note>, it would perhaps be wicked to demand such a duty. Those who, having built an altar or a tomb, or having hung up a tablet or a polished statue, permit themselves...

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
->G 4<-
<meta>Catchword: loins</meta>

...name among posterity, how much more living a fame would he prepare for himself by this path? I shall bring forward one example out of many. Scarcely any other has been more skillfully engaged in explaining the sacred volumes than Saint John Chrysostom <note>original: "diuus Ioannes Chrysostomus"; a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquence</note>, nor is any other writer more suitable for those preparing themselves for the duty of preaching. And he wrote a great many things, a good part of which we possess, however poorly translated, but with most parts corrupted and some even mixed in which have nothing of Chrysostom in them. Truly, how much light would reach sacred studies if such a great teacher were available entirely in Greek and corrected; or certainly, if we had him speaking in Latin just as he speaks in Greek. I will not recount here in how many ways money perishes for the great lords—how much they consume on dice, whores, drinking parties, unnecessary travels, pomp, sought-after wars, ambition, flatterers, fools, and actors. Let them at least cut away some portion from these things which perish shamefully, for either the public utility or their own glory, or both. 

Who among the learned did not favor Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous Venetian printer</note> when he was undertaking these labors? Who did not suggest something to relieve him, unequal as he was to such great tasks? How often were ancient manuscripts sent to him voluntarily from the Hungarians and Poles, not without an honorary gift, so that they might be published to the world with his assisted care? What Aldus was undertaking among the Italians (for he himself has yielded to the fates, though the workshop is still commended by the title of his graceful name), this Johann Froben <note>Erasmus’s printer in Basel</note> undertakes among the Cisalpines <note>Those "on this side of the Alps," referring to Northern Europe/Germany</note> with no less zeal than Aldus, and not entirely unsuccessfully, but—what cannot be denied—with unequal profit. 

If you ask the cause, I think this is one out of many: that there is not the same candor of minds among us as there is among the Italians, at least regarding literary matters. For I do not fear to proclaim what I have experienced. When I, a Dutchman <note>original: "homo Batauus"</note>, was publishing the work of *Proverbs* <note>The *Adagia*</note> among the Italians, all the learned men who were there voluntarily supplied authors not yet published by printers, whom they suspected would be of use to me. Aldus had nothing in his treasure-house that he would not share. The same was done by Johannes Lascaris, Baptista Egnatius, Marcus Musurus, and Brother Urbanus. I felt the kindness of some whom I knew neither by face nor by name. I brought nothing with me to Venice except the confused and undigested material of a future work, and that only from authors already published. With great temerity, we both attacked the task at the same time: I to write, Aldus to print. The sum of the business was completed within more or less nine months, and meanwhile, I was dealing with a "bad stone" <note>Erasmus suffered from kidney stones</note> not yet known to me. 

Here, let me consider how great a part of the utility would have been missing unless learned men had supplied hand-written books. Among these were the Greek works of Plato, Plutarch’s *Lives*, his *Moralia* (which began to be printed near the end of my work), Athenaeus’s *Deipnosophistae*, Aphthonius, Hermogenes with commentaries, Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* with the notes of Gregory Nazianzen, the whole of Aristides with notes, short commentaries on Hesiod and Theocritus, Eustathius on the whole of Homer, Pausanias, Pindar with accurate commentaries, a collection of Proverbs under the title of Plutarch, and again another under the title of Apostolius, a copy of which book Hieronymus Aleander provided to us. There were other minor things which either do not occur to me or are not worth relating. None of these had yet been published in type. 

Now, in turn, hear the "candor" of a certain Cisalpine friend, whom I held among my chief friends, and have not ceased to hold so, since one ought to know a friend's manners, not hate them. When I was preparing the Venetian edition, I had by chance seen at his house a *Suidas* <note>A large 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note> whose margins had proverbs noted down. The work was huge, and many things had to be turned over. Desiring therefore to save this labor, I asked that he make a copy of that volume available for even a few hours, while a boy transcribed the little notes into my book. Though I asked again and again, he flatly refused. When I had applied every kind of entreaty and could not prevail, I asked whether he himself intended to publish proverbs, for I would gladly yield to one who would handle the work more successfully. He swore there was no such thing. "What then," I said, "moves you?" At last, as if driven by tortures, he confessed that these things were now being published through which the learned had hitherto been wondered at by the common crowd. "Hence those tears" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "so that's the real reason"</note>. 

Very ancient manuscripts lie hidden in the colleges and monasteries of the Germans, French, and English; with a few exceptions, they do not share them voluntarily, so much so that when asked, they either hide them, or flatly deny them, or sell the use of them at an unfair price, ten times the value of the books. At last, though "beautifully preserved," either decay and moths corrupt them, or thieves take them away. The great lords, moreover, so little help the literary cause with their kindness that they think no money is more ruinously lost than that which is consumed for such uses; nor does anything please them at all from which some tax is not raised. But if the Cisalpine princes followed honorable studies with a candor equal to the Italians, the Frobenian serpents <note>Referring to Froben's printer's mark: a pole with serpents and a dove</note> would not be so far from the wealth of the Aldine dolphins <note>Aldus's famous anchor and dolphin mark</note>. He, "making haste slowly," produced no less gold for himself than name, being worthy of both. Froben, while he always carries his pole upright, looking to nothing other than the public utility, while from a...

<summary>Erasmus contrasts the generous scholarly culture of Italy, where he received rare manuscripts for his Adagia, with the secretive and stingy nature of Northern European collectors. He praises the printers Aldus Manutius and Johann Froben for their dedication to the public good over mere profit.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s famous essay on the adage "Make Haste Slowly" (Festina Lente). He is currently exploring the symbolic meaning of the dolphin (speed) and the anchor (slowness/stability) as depicted on ancient coins and the printer Aldus Manutius's mark.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...does not depart from dove-like simplicity, while he expresses the wisdom of serpents more through his distinguished deeds; he is rich in reputation rather than wealth, etc. But let there now be a limit to these digressions; let our discourse now return to the explanation of the adage. It will be permitted to use the proverb in three ways: first, whenever we advise that one must deliberate for a long time before <gloss>than</gloss> undertaking a business; then, <gloss>that</gloss> which you have decided must be carried out swiftly, so that the anchor pertains to the delay for consulting, and the Dolphin to the speed of completion. To this belongs that saying of Sallust: "Before <gloss>than</gloss> you begin, consult; when you have consulted, there is need for timely action." <note>Sallust was a Roman historian; this quote is from his 'Bellum Catilinae'.</note> Aristotle reviews this sentiment in the sixth book of the *Ethics* as <gloss>than</gloss> if it were commonly bandied about: "They say," you will say, "that those things about which you have already deliberated should be carried out quickly, but one should consult lingeringly." Laertius testifies that Bias was the author of this, who was accustomed to advise: <term>βραδέως ἐγχείρει τοῖς πραττομένοις, ὃ δ’ ἂν ἕλῃ, βεβαίως τηρῶντα διαμένειν</term> <note>original Greek: "bradeōs encheirei..."</note>, that is, "One should approach a business lingeringly, but in what has been undertaken, one must persevere with constancy." Nor does that Mime—Publilius, I believe—differ much from this: "War must be prepared for a long time, so that you may conquer more quickly." Likewise that one: "Deliberate on useful things; delay is the safest course." Add to these that proverb: <term>ἐν νυκτὶ βουλή</term> <note>original Greek: "en nykti boulē"</note>, that is, "In the night is counsel." Furthermore, that line of Sophocles in *Oedipus the King*: <term>φρονεῖν γὰρ οἱ ταχεῖς, οὐκ ἀσφαλεῖς</term> <note>original Greek: "phronein gar hoi tacheis..."</note>, that is, "Hasty wisdom is dangerous."

To these should be added that saying of Plato, which we have cited elsewhere: "He who hastens more than enough at the beginning, arrives later at the end." It is a little different, but nevertheless to be referred to this form, what Quintilian says: "That precocious type of talent does not easily reach fruitfulness." And what they say commonly: "Those who are wise while still boys, and as if before their time, turn out to be fools in old age." Accius seems to approve of this, who says in Gellius that he likes bitterness in youthful talents just as in unripe fruits: for these finally ripen (furthermore, ripeness brings timely sweetness), while the rest rot before their time. 

The second way of using the adage will be when we advise that the passions of the mind must be restrained as if by the reins of reason. Since Plato divided the human soul into three parts—reason, anger, and desire—he thinks the sum of philosophy is situated in this: if the passions obey reason no differently than a king, to whom for this very reason he thinks a seat was given in the brain, as if in a citadel. The Peripatetics, whose standard-bearer is Aristotle, think that the passions are certain impulses of the mind, like certain spurs given by nature, by which we are excited to the practice of virtue; although the Stoics reclaim against this, and specifically Seneca in the books he wrote to Nero *On Anger*. For they think that passions of this sort not only contribute nothing to virtue, but even hinder it: although not even they deny that in the mind of that wise man whom they imagine, there are left "first impulses" which are accustomed to precede reason, which you cannot root out entirely. But these, lest assent follows, are immediately rejected by reason. Homer hints at this when, in the first book of the *Iliad*, Pallas Athena stands behind Achilles and restrains him as he is already moving his hand to his sword. Therefore, you might rightly call those violent movements of the mind the dolphin; and the anchor, moderating wisdom. Seneca wrote that delay is profitable for nothing except anger. Indeed, whatever we desire or hate with impulse, there delay is salutary. Plutarch relates in the *Roman Sayings* that the philosopher Athenodorus, when he had obtained permission from Augustus Octavius to return home because of old age, advised him not to say or do anything while angry before he had recited the twenty-four letters of the Greek alphabet to himself by name. To which the listener responded that he still had need of him, so that he might also learn the art of keeping silent, and under this pretext he kept the man with him for a whole year. To this also looks that line of Terence: "See that this is not too hot just now." There are, however, certain talents which need spurs; there are those which need a bridle. Accordingly, those ancients rightly wished the anchor to be embraced by the dolphin, because it is necessary for one to be tempered by the other, and both to be joined with the other, so that clearly a certain habit of mind might exist such as Plato thinks is forged from music and gymnastics, if they are practiced equally. 

The third reason for use will be when we advise that headlong speed must be avoided in every business, a vice which is peculiarly implanted in certain talents, so that to them any delay, however small, seems long in every matter. The companions of this sort of haste are usually error and repentance, according to that famous little verse among the Greeks: <term>προπέτεια πολλοῖς ἐστὶν αἰτία κακῶν</term> <note>original Greek: "propeteia pollois..."</note>, that is, "Precipitation is the cause of evils for many." 

Against these should be sung that noble saying of Cato: "Quickly enough, if well enough," of which mention was made...

<summary>Erasmus explains the three applications of the "Festina Lente" proverb: deliberate planning versus swift action, the restraint of passions by reason, and the avoidance of reckless haste in business. He draws on a wide array of classical authorities including Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, and Plutarch to support these interpretations.</summary>
<keywords>Festina Lente, deliberation, speed, reason vs passion, Plato, Aristotle, Seneca, Plutarch, Cato, ethics, self-control</keywords>

# THE SECOND THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED
<header>SECOND THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED</header>

<margin>Jerome. Soon enough, if well enough. Cato.</margin>Jerome, writing to Pammachius <note>A Roman senator and friend of St. Jerome</note>, uses these words: "That saying of Cato is well-known: **Soon enough, if well enough.** <note>original: "Sat cito, si sat bene."</note> We once laughed at this as young men when it was mentioned by a finished orator in a short preface. I think you remember our mutual error, when the whole Athenaeum <note>A school or academy in Rome</note> rang with the voices of the students: **Soon enough, if well enough.**" Thus far Jerome. It will apply to those who seek fame too hastily, preferring a ready-made and great reputation to one that is solid and eternal. For things that ripen too early usually wither suddenly. But that which grows bit by bit is durable. Horace says:
> The fame of Marcellus grows \
> like a tree in the hidden passage of time.

<margin>Pindar in Nemean Ode 8. "Virtue grows, as when a tree shoots up with green dews, raised up among wise and just men toward the liquid ether."</margin>In short, for those who err either through laziness or through immoderate haste, it will be necessary to recall to memory that motto of Octavius Caesar, <term>Make haste slowly</term> <note>original: "Σπεῦδε βραδέως" (Speude bradeōs)</note>, along with that symbol once belonging to Titus Vespasian and now to Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous printer whose logo was a dolphin wrapped around an anchor</note>, so that they may remember the dolphin and the anchor.

### II
->Step by step.<-

<margin>A step following the feet.</margin>This is said as a proverb by the Greeks, which the Latins rendered as **step by step** <note>original: "pedetentim"</note>: used when someone approaches a business not headlong and inconsiderately, but gradually and with hesitation, and manages it with skill rather than force. It is a metaphor taken from those who enter a slippery place or thin ice cautiously, testing the ground. Terence in *Phormio*: "May the gods prosper what you do, yet go **step by step**." Quintilian: "But if the advocate does not know what a polished witness has brought forward, he will test it little by little, and as they say, **step by step**." Alexis, a writer of comedies already in extreme old age, when asked by someone as he walked with a slow gait what he was doing, replied: <term>I am dying step by step</term> <note>original: "Κατὰ πόδας βάσιν ἀποθνήσκω"</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero in *On Duties*, book 1: "If not, it must be done gradually and **step by step**." The same in the speech *For Publius Quinctius*: "So that good men, when they are openly defrauded and have no power of trial, nevertheless descend to that point timidly and **step by step**, compelled by force and necessity." And in the *Verrine Orations*, action 2: "Which things, however, will be said by me **step by step** and cautiously."

### III
->The quiet ox.<-

<margin>The quiet ox. That is, the ox walks slowly, or something similar is understood.</margin>This fits those who finish a matter quietly and bit by bit, without a tumult, but nevertheless with persistence; those whose merit is not speed. Oxen do not prevail by swiftness, but by strength; they are powerful through persistence, not through sudden impulse. Hence, in a stationary fight, the ox is an animal to be feared even by lions, and is suited for exhausting immense labors. To the same point belongs the saying: "The tired ox plants its foot more firmly." In sacred prayers, Plutarch relates in his commentary *On Osiris and Isis* that the Elean women in public and solemn vows were accustomed to invoke Bacchus in this manner, that he should come <term>with the foot of an ox</term> <note>original: "ἄξιε ταῦρε" (worthy bull)</note>: either because this animal, though endowed with immense strength and such a mass of body, nevertheless seems to walk peculiarly softly, as if **step by step**, with no noise; or because the feet of the ox make the stony fields better, whereas the feet of other animals cause harm.

### IIII
->With a silent foot.<-

Very similar to this is what was pointed out by whoever he was—certainly a writer by no means negligent—who explains the *Rhetoric* of Aristotle: <term>with a quiet foot</term> <note>original: "ἡσύχῳ ποδί"</note>. That is, with a silent foot, or a slow foot, when we approach a matter cautiously and step by step. Among the Latins, **with a silent foot** is used somewhat differently, for "stealthily" and "secretly," as in Ovid:
> Time glides by, and we grow old with **silent years**.

And Columella imitated this in verse:
> For times flee with a **silent step**, \
> and the year turns with no sound.

### V
->A cumin-splitter.<-

<margin>Cumin-splitter</margin>One who is excessively stingy and sordid was formerly called by the proverb <term>cumin-splitter</term> <note>original: "κυμινοπρίστης" (kyminopristēs) - someone so cheap they would try to saw a tiny cumin seed in half</note>. Aristotle is a witness in the fourth book of *Ethics*: "Of this kind is the **cumin-splitter**, and everyone of that sort." Theocritus also mentions it in Idyll 10:
<term>"It is better, O stingy miser, to cook the lentils."</term> <note>original: "Κάλλιον ὦ πικιλικτὰ φιλάργυρε τὰς φακὰς ἕψεν"</note>

<summary>This page explores various classical adages emphasizing the importance of deliberate, steady progress over reckless haste, featuring the famous "Make haste slowly" and metaphors involving oxen and "cumin-splitters."</summary>
<keywords>proverbs, Erasmus, Make Haste Slowly, Aldus Manutius, diligence, stinginess, Aristotle, Cicero, Horace</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Adages, specifically focusing on ancient Greek and Latin proverbs regarding stinginess, physical traits, and impossible situations.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Do not split the cumin seed with your hand. <note>original: "Μὴ ’πὶ τἀμὲς τὴν χεῖρα καταπρίειν τὸ κύμινον"</note> That is:
> The shepherd shows himself greedy to you, cooking a small lentil,
> Lest you prick your fingers, desiring to have split the cumin.
The commentator <note>Scholiast</note> does not hide that this was commonly said of people who were frugal and stingy beyond measure. Likewise, Alexis in *The Lover of Beauty* <note>Philocalo</note>, quoted in Athenaeus, book eight:
But I know well... that your way has long been that of a **Cumin-splitter**. <note>original: "Κυμινοπρίστης" (Cyminopristes)</note> That is:
But I know well
That your habits have long been those of a Cumin-splitter.
Now, cumin is itself a slender herb, especially the Ethiopian kind, which Hippocrates (according to Pliny) calls "royal." Plutarch notes it was once planted by those uttering curses, as it was believed to grow more successfully that way. This makes the insult even more fitting for those who have a bad reputation for stinginess. The same Plutarch, in the second decade of his *Table Talk*, indicates that a vehemently stingy man is often called "cumin." Indeed, speaking of those jests that can be said without causing pain: "Just as," he says, "if one were to call a splendid and generous man a *cimbix* <note>a skinflint</note> or a *cumin*." According to the lexicographer Suidas, a *kimbix* is a "bee-man" or "parsimony." Hesychius reads it as *cimbion*, adding it was said of the stingy; he notes *kymbos* refers to the bottom of an earthenware pot. Aristotle, in the book I just cited, says that very stingy men were commonly called *kymbikes*. Julius Pollux calls them *bembikes*, I suppose because they go wandering through the house constantly murmuring. For a *bembix* is a spinning top that boys play with. In the same author, a sordidly cheap woman is called an *obolosatis*, and a man an *obolosates*, as if weighing every tiny thing on a scale <note>from *obol*, a small coin</note>, from which comes the verb "to act like an obol-weigher." Eustathius indicates they are also called "hunger-pots" <note>limokymbikas</note> and "cumin-skinflints" <note>kyminokimbikas</note>, and thinks the word is derived from debased gold. Hesychius adds they are called "cress-carvers" <note>kardamoglyphos</note>, because they carve something out of a watercress plant due to their stinginess. Nor are there lacking those who call them *kniphas* or *knipas* or *knipsas* (for I find both written); a *knips* is a tiny insect not unlike a gnat.

---

<margin>VI</margin>
### To divide figs.
Related to this is what Martial reports in the fifth book of his *Epigrams*: "to divide figs" <note>original: "σῦκα μερίζειν"</note>; from which one might even coin the nickname "Fig-divider." Martial’s poem is as follows:
> He cuts four hundred [thousand sesterces], who says "divide the figs."
Signifying a sordid and stingy man, even if he is very wealthy. The joke is captured from the ambiguity of the word for a "cutter."

---

<margin>VII</margin>
### A bald Myconian.
A Myconian is bald. <note>original: "Μυκώνιος φάλακρος"</note> Strabo, in the tenth book of his *Geography*, reports that the Myconians were commonly called bald because on that island this defect is, as it were, a national trait and common to almost everyone. Pliny affirms the same in book eleven, chapter thirty-seven. Stephanus also mentions it. Myconus is one of the Cyclades islands. Although Herodotus writes in his fourth book that in Scythia there is also a race that is bald from birth. The grammarian Donatus also notes, interpreting Terence’s *The Mother-in-Law*, that "a Myconian bald man" is used as a proverb, and he cites the testimony of Lucilius: "All the youth of Myconus are bald." He defends Terence, who was criticized by some for ignorance because, while Apollodorus called a character bald, Terence changed it to "curly-haired"; Donatus thinks the poet did this not out of ignorance, but more wittily through irony, as if he had said "bald." Indeed, the proverb itself has the flavor of things rarely found: as if one were to speak of a "learned Scythian," a "warlike Italian," an "honest merchant," a "pious soldier," or a "faithful Carthaginian." The adage will be more elegant if we simply call bald men, or those with thin hair, "Myconians," just as one might call a haughty man a "Sybarite" or a merchant a "Phoenician." The Myconians were noted in old times for another reason: that because of their poverty they would hunt for other people's dinners; hence, those who came to a banquet uninvited were said to come "in the Myconian fashion." For Archilochus, in the fragments of his first book quoted in Athenaeus, attacks Pericles: "as one who, uninvited, burst into banquets in the manner of the Myconians."

---

<margin>VIII</margin>
### When water chokes the throat.
Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Ethics*, cites a certain adage of this kind: "The momentary rubbing in the proverb, which we say when water chokes the throat: what need is there to pour more on top?" <note>original: "ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ τὴν φάρυγγα πνίγῃ, τί δεῖ ἐπὶ πνίγειν"</note> The intemperate...

<summary>This page explores ancient Greek and Latin proverbs regarding extreme stinginess (the "cumin-splitter") and regional stereotypes, such as the baldness of the inhabitants of Myconus. Erasmus uses these to illustrate how physical traits or specific behaviors became shorthand for character types in classical literature.</summary>

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<page-num>359</page-num>

<margin>When water chokes the throat, what need is there to drink?</margin> However, he is subject to the proverb by which we say: *When water chokes the throat, what need is there to drink?* <note>original: "Cum aqua fauces strangulat, quid iam opus est biberer?"</note> He relates the same for the same purpose in the sixth book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, discussing the man who, though prudent, follows harmful things through the vice of intemperance, being by no means ignorant of what is best; but that this man is far more incurable than the one who, deceived by a false opinion, seeks things that should not be sought. Galen also used this somewhere: *When the water chokes, what shall we drink on top of it?* <note>original: "ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγῃ, τί ἐπὶ ῥοφήσομεν;"</note> that is, *When water suffocates, what shall we sip besides?* Perhaps Galen had written, *what shall we fear?* It applies to those who persist stubbornly in a most absurd opinion, or deny the obvious, with whom you would argue in vain. For it is well known that water is the remedy for throats parched with thirst and releases suffocation. Close to this is what we have said elsewhere:
*There is nothing hard inside the olive, nor anything hard outside the nut.* <note>A reference to a situation where the natural order is reversed or nonsensical.</note>

### In half of life, the happy do not differ from the unhappy. IX

Aristotle in the first book of the *Ethics*: *The good and the bad are least distinguishable during sleep, whence they say that for half of life the happy differ nothing from the others.* <note>original: "ὁ δ' ἀγαθὸς καὶ κακὸς ἥκιστα διάδηλοι καθ' ὕπνον..."</note> Furthermore, the upright and the wicked are in no way distinguished in sleep. From this arose the saying: *the happy differ nothing from the rest for half of their lives.* He relates the same in the second book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, giving this reason: that those who sleep do nothing. Moreover, happiness or unhappiness for a man arises from actions. Therefore, Ariston said not unskillfully in Plutarch’s commentary *On the Contention of Fire and Water*: *Say that sleep is the tax-collector of life for men; it takes away half of it like a wandering.* <note>original: "λέγε φανὸν τοῦ βίου..."</note> i.e., since it gives a small time of life to men, sleep, like a tax-gatherer, carries off half of it. Plato in the seventh book of *The Laws*: *For no one sleeping is worth anything, no more than he who is not alive.* <note>original: "Καθεύδων γὰρ οὐδεὶς οὐδενὸς ἄξιος..."</note> This proverb consoles those who are less fortunate and blunts the insolence of the rich and powerful. For sleep takes away from us the sense of ourselves: whence it happens that neither is their calamity troublesome to the miserable, nor is happiness pleasant to the fortunate. Furthermore, according to the philosophers, happiness is situated in the act of reason through the habit of virtue; sleep, however, is the rest of the soul, common to the good and the bad alike.

### You are in the same boat. X

Marcus Tullius <insert>Cicero</insert> in the second book of his *Letters to Friends* to Curio: *And if wherever you are, as I wrote to you before, you are in the same boat, yet I congratulate you that you are away.* He said *You are in the same boat* <note>original: "In eadem es naui"</note> instead of: *in a common danger.* Since the danger of shipwreck pertains commonly to those who are carried in the same vessel; nor does it matter greatly whether they are in the prow, or in the stern, or in the waist, since they are no further from the peril. The same author elsewhere: *For I wonder at this and complain of it, that any man should wish to sink another so much that he would even bore a hole in the ship in which he himself is sailing,* that is, that he would overturn the Republic, with which he himself must also perish. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
*Since the hull is full of the whole.* i.e.,
*Think of the city as the whole ship.*
It is familiar to poets to borrow a likeness from ships for the Republic.

### He who plows the olive grove. XI

Columella, in the sixth book of *On Agriculture*, relates a proverb of this kind: *Furthermore,* he says, *after several years have passed, the olive grove must be pruned. For it is fitting to remember the old proverb: He who plows the olive grove, asks for fruit; he who manures it, begs for it; he who prunes it, compels it.* Virgil alluded to this in the first book of the *Georgics*:
*And he frequently works the earth, and commands the fields.*
There will be a place for this adage when we mean that it cannot happen but that he who has spent the utmost effort obtains his wish. For common diligence, as it were, asks; moderate diligence obtains; extreme diligence compels. An allusion is made to those who obtain things from princes with such persistent zeal and duty that they seem to have obtained them not by prayers, but by force. Even in the Gospel writings, the persistent asker <note>The "Importunate Neighbor" or "Persistent Widow" parables</note> is praised and set forth to be imitated.

### Beautiful things are difficult. XII

*Difficult are the beautiful things.* <note>original: "Χαλεπὰ τὰ καλά"</note> i.e., *Arduous are the beautiful.* It appears in Plato in the *Greater Hippias* at the end of the dialogue: *For as to the proverb, whatever it says, "beautiful things are difficult," I think I know it.* And in the *Cratylus* near the beginning: *It is an old proverb, that beautiful things are difficult.* It is cited somewhere by Lucian: likewise by Plutarch in the booklet *On Educating Children*, under the name of a proverb. Some have recorded that Pittacus, when he had abdicated his office...
