<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s encyclopedic collection of Greek and Roman proverbs, focusing on metaphors for extreme stinginess and regional stereotypes.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Do not cut your hand while sawing the cumin. <note>original: "Μὴ 'πιτάμῃς τὴν χᾶρα καταπρίων τὸ κύμινον"</note> That is:
> A shepherd offers you a lentil to cook, you greedy man,
> Lest you dig into your fingers, desiring to have sliced the cumin.

The commentator does not hide the fact that these words were commonly used for men who were frugal and sparing beyond measure. Likewise, Alexis in *The Lover of Beauty* <note>original: "Philocalo"</note>, quoted in Athenaeus, book eight:
But I know well that your way of life has long been that of a Cumin-splitter. <note>original: "Ἀλλ' εὖ οἶδ' ὅτι Κυμινοπρίστης ὁ τρόπος ἐστὶ σοι πάλαι"</note> That is:
> But I know well
> That the habits of a Cumin-splitter have long been yours.

Now, cumin is by its nature a slender herb, especially the Ethiopian kind, which Hippocrates (according to Pliny) calls "royal." It was once said that it should be sown by those uttering curses, as it was believed to grow more successfully that way. This makes the insult even more fitting for those who have a bad reputation for stinginess. Plutarch, in the second decade of his *Table Talk*, indicates that a vehemently thrifty man is usually called "cumin." Indeed, speaking of those jests that can be said without causing pain: "Just as," he says, "if one were to call a splendid and kind man a *cimbix* <note>a skinflint</note> or a *cumin*." Now, <term>κίμβιξ</term> <note>kimbix</note> is a "bee" or "thrift" among the Greeks, according to the interpreter Suidas. Hesychius reads it as *cimbion*, adding that it was commonly said of the parsimonious; however, <term>κύμβον</term> <note>kymbon</note> refers to the bottom of an earthenware pot. Aristotle, in the book I just cited, says that extremely stingy men were commonly called <term>κυμινοπρίστας</term> <note>cumin-splitters</note>. Julius Pollux calls them <term>βέμβικας</term> <note>whipping-tops</note>, I suppose because they walk through the house always murmuring. For a <term>βέμβιξ</term> is a top that boys play with. In the same author, a woman who is excessively filthy is called an <term>ὀβολοστάτης</term> <note>obol-weigher</note>, and a man is called an <term>ὀβολοστάτης</term>, as if weighing every tiny thing on a scale; from which also comes the verb "to weigh obols." Eustathius indicates that these same people are called both "hunger-cumins" and "cumin-cumins," and he thinks the word is derived from adulterated gold. Hesychius adds that they are called <term>καρδαμογλύφους</term> <note>cress-carvers</note>, because they carve something out of a watercress out of stinginess. Nor are there lacking those who call them <term>κνίφας</term> or <term>κνίπας</term> <note>kniphas/knipas</note> (for I find both spellings); now, a <term>κνίψ</term> is a tiny creature not unlike a gnat.

---

->VI<-
### To divide figs.

Akin to this is what Martial relates in the fifth book of his *Epigrams*: <term>σῦκα μερίζειν</term> <note>syka merizein</note>. That is, "To divide figs": from which one might also coin the nickname <term>συκομερίστην</term> <note>fig-divider</note>. Martial’s verse is as follows:
> He cuts four hundred, he who speaks of "dividing figs."

Signifying a filthy and stingy man, even if he is very rich. The joke is captured from the ambiguity of the word <term>μερίζειν</term> <note>which can mean to divide or to distribute shares</note>.

---

->VII<-
### A bald Myconian.

<term>Μυκώνιος φαλακρός</term> <note>Mykonios phalakros</note>. That is, "A bald Myconian." Strabo, in the tenth book of his *Geography*, relates that Myconians were commonly called bald because this defect was, as it were, a national trait on that island, and common to almost everyone. Pliny affirms the same in book eleven, chapter thirty-seven. Stephanus also mentions it. Now, Myconus is one of the Cyclades islands. Although Herodotus writes in his fourth book that there is also a race in Scythia that is bald from birth. The grammarian Donatus also notes, in interpreting Terence’s *The Mother-in-Law*, that "a bald Myconian" is said as a proverb, and he cites the testimony of Lucilius: "At Myconus, all the youth are bald." He defends Terence, who was criticized by some for ignorance because, while Apollodorus called the character bald, Terence changed it to "curly-haired"; he thinks the poet did this not out of ignorance, but even more wittily through irony, as if he had said "curly" when he meant "bald." This indeed smacks of the proverb about things rarely found: as if one were to call a Scythian "learned," an Italian "warlike," a merchant "honest," a soldier "pious," or a Carthaginian "faithful." The adage will be more elegant if we simply call bald men, or those with thin hair, "Myconians," just as one might call a haughty man a "Sybarite" or a merchant a "Phoenician." The Myconians were noted in the past by another name as well: because of their poverty, they would hunt for other people's dinners; therefore, those who came to a banquet uninvited were said to come "in the Myconian fashion." For Archilochus attacks Pericles in the fragments of the first book of Athenaeus, saying: "as one who, uninvited, burst into the symposia in the manner of the Myconians." <note>original: "ὡς ἄκλητος ἐπεισπεσώντα εἰς τὰ συμπόσια μυκονίων δίκην"</note>

->VIII<-
### When water chokes the throat.

Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Ethics*, cites a proverb of this kind: "The argument that is at a loss is like the proverb where they say: when water chokes the throat, what must one drink on top of it?" <note>original: "ὁ δ' ἀπορηθεὶς λόος... ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ τὴν φάρυγγα πνίγῃ, τί δεῖ ἐπιπίνειν"</note> The intemperate...

<meta>This page continues the second chiliad (thousand) of adages, specifically the first century of that thousand. The author, Erasmus, continues his scholarly exploration of ancient proverbs, drawing heavily from Greek and Roman philosophy and literature.</meta>

->CHILIAD TWO, CENTURY I<-

However, he is subject to the proverb we use: <note>original: "Cũ aqua fauces strãgulet, quid iam opus est biberer?"</note> **When water chokes the throat, what need is there to drink?** He refers to this same usage in the sixth book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, discussing the man who, though wise, follows harmful things through the vice of intemperance, being by no means ignorant of what is best. He argues that such a person is far more incurable than one who, deceived by a false opinion, seeks things that should not be sought. Galen also employed this somewhere: <note>original: "ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγῃ, τί ἐπὶ ῥοφήσομεν;"</note> **When the water suffocates, what shall we swallow besides?** Perhaps Galen had written, "what shall we swallow *further*?" It applies to those who persist stubbornly in a most absurd opinion, or who deny the obvious, with whom it is useless to argue. For it is well known that water is the remedy for throats parched with thirst and dissolves suffocation. It is close to what we have said elsewhere: **Nothing is hard inside the olive, nothing is hard outside the nut.** <note>A metaphor for something being entirely backwards or paradoxical.</note>

# In half of life, the happy do not differ from the wretched. IX

Aristotle in the first book of the *Ethics*: <note>original: "ὁ δ’ ἀγαθὸς καὶ κακὸς ἥκιστα διάδηλοι καθ’ υπνον..."</note> **Furthermore, the good and the bad are by no means distinguishable in sleep; whence they say that for half of life, the happy differ not at all from the wretched.** He reports the same in the second book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, giving this reason: that those who sleep do nothing. Now, the happiness or misery of a man arises from his actions. Therefore, Ariston said not unskillfully, as quoted in Plutarch’s commentary *On the Contention of Fire and Water*: <note>original: "λίγον χρόνον τοῦ βίου..."</note> **God gave a small time of life to men, and sleep, like a tax-collector, takes away half of it.** Plato in the seventh book of *The Laws*: <note>original: "Καθεύδων γὰρ οὐδεὶς οὐδενὸς ἄξιος..."</note> **For no one who sleeps is worth anything, no more than one who is not alive.** This proverb consoles those who are less fortunate and blunts the insolence of the rich and powerful. For sleep takes away from us the sense of ourselves; thus it happens that neither is calamity painful to the miserable, nor is happiness pleasant to the fortunate. Furthermore, according to the philosophers, happiness is situated in the act of reason through the habit of virtue; sleep, however, is a rest of the soul, common to the good and the bad alike.

# You are in the same boat. X

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book of his *Letters to Friends* to Curio: **And if, wherever you are, as I wrote to you before, you are in the same boat, nevertheless I congratulate you that you are away.** He said **"You are in the same boat"** instead of: **"in a common danger."** Since the danger of shipwreck pertains commonly to those who are carried in the same vessel; nor does it matter greatly whether they are in the prow, or the stern, or the bilge, since they are no further from the peril. The same author elsewhere: **For I wonder at this and complain, that any man should wish to sink another so much that he would even bore a hole in the ship in which he himself sails**—that is, that he would overturn the Republic, with which he himself must perish. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: <note>original: "πᾶς γε γὰρ ὅδι τὸ σκάφος ὅλον"</note> **For this whole thing is the entire hull**—meaning, think of the whole city as a ship. It is familiar to poets to borrow a metaphor from ships for the Republic.

# He who plows the olive grove. XI

Columella, in the sixth book of *On Agriculture*, reports a proverb of this kind: **Moreover,** he says, **after several years have passed, the olive grove must be pruned. For it is fitting to remember the old proverb: He who plows the olive grove, asks for fruit; he who manures it, begs for it; he who cuts it, compels it.** Virgil alluded to this in the first book of the *Georgics*:
> And he frequently works the earth, and commands the fields.
There will be a place for this adage when we wish to signify that it is impossible for one who has expended the utmost effort not to obtain his wish. For common diligence, as it were, asks; moderate diligence obtains; extreme diligence compels. An allusion is made to those who, by relentless zeal and duty, obtain things from princes in such a way that they seem to have obtained them not by prayers, but by force. Even in the Gospel writings, the "importunate asker" is praised and set forth to be imitated.

# Beautiful things are difficult. XII

<note>original: "Χαλεπὰ τὰ καλά"</note> **Arduous are the things that are beautiful.** It appears in Plato in the *Greater Hippias* at the end of the dialogue: **Except to know what is meant by the saying, "Beautiful things are difficult," I think I understand.** And in the *Cratylus* near the beginning: **It is an old proverb, that beautiful things are difficult.** It is cited somewhere by Lucian; likewise by Plutarch in the booklet *On Educating Children*, under the name of a proverb. Some have recorded that Pittacus, when he had abdicated his office...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<page-num>360</page-num>

when he resigned his power, he said: <note>original: "χαλεπὸν ἐσθλὸν ἔμμεναι"</note> "It is difficult to be good." Furthermore, Solon, rebuking the softness and laziness of Pittacus, said: <note>original: "χαλεπὰ τὰ καλά"</note> "Beautiful things are difficult." The sayings of both men passed into proverbs. Plato used this in the fourth book of *The Republic*: "For perhaps, O Socrates, the saying is true, that beautiful things are difficult." He used the same in the second book of the *Politics* <note>Erasmus likely refers to the *Republic* here as well</note>: "For everyone sings with one voice that temperance and justice are beautiful things, but truly difficult and laborious." He uses it again in the sixth and seventh books of the same work and in many other places. There are those who think the proverb originated here: Periander of Corinth at first governed his empire in a popular and moderate fashion, but later his character began to turn tyrannical. As soon as this was known to Pittacus of Mytilene, distrusting the constancy of his own mind, he resigned his magistracy and, leaving his power behind, went into exile. When some people later asked for what reason he had fled from power, he replied that it was exceedingly arduous to be upright, because of how Periander had changed. Hearing this, Solon added his own apophthegm: "Beautiful things are difficult." To this also looks that which Plutarch mentions in his commentary *On Shyness*, that Plato, when he had recommended a certain Helicon to Dionysius in a letter, writing that he was an upright and modest man, added at the end of the letter: "I write these things to you about a man, who is by nature a changeable animal." Nor would one absurdly refer this to that most famous sentiment of Hesiod:

> Vice, indeed, can be seized in heaps by anyone
> Easily; the path to it is short, and it dwells nearby.
> But the immortal gods have placed sweat before
> Virtue; the path to it is long and steep,
> And rough at first. But when you reach the summit,
> It then becomes easy, though it was difficult before.
> ->that is,<-
> It is easy for anyone to encounter vice.
> The way to it is short, and it stays in a neighboring seat.
> On the other hand, the gods have hedged virtue with sweat on all sides,
> And the path to it is long and through arduous tracks,
> And is rough at first: but when as a victor you reach
> The high peaks, it now becomes easy, though it was arduous just now.

Nor is anything more common than what Aristotle said in the second book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*: <note>original: "περὶ τὸ χαλεπώτερον ἀεὶ καὶ τέχνη καὶ ἀρετή"</note> "Both art and virtue are always concerned with that which is more difficult." To the same point belongs the "Letter of Pythagoras divided by a two-horned fork" <note>The letter Y, symbolizing the fork in the road between virtue and vice</note>. And that Gospel saying about the narrow way which leads to life. Likewise concerning the double path in the underworld, one of which leads to the Elysian fields, the other to a bad end. We have spoken elsewhere of the *Litae* and *Ate* <note>Prayers and Ruin/Folly in Homeric myth</note>, by which fable it is declared that it is much more difficult to do well than to do ill, and to repair harmony than to break it. Pindar expressed that sentiment in the fifth *Pythian Ode*: "It is easy to shake a city, even for the weaker sort; but to set it back in its place again suddenly becomes a difficult struggle, unless a god becomes a pilot to the leaders." Elsewhere we have recorded that in a sedition even Androclides, the most abject of men, acts as a leader of war. And we in this age have seen by what sort of men great tumults have been stirred up. There is a celebrated and elegant saying of a Spartan, to whom, when certain people were extolling Philip with praises because he had overturned a most wealthy city, he replied: "But he could not build such a one." Voices of this kind ought to be inscribed on the minds of princes, who, though they cannot build even the smallest little town, seem to themselves like gods because they destroy cities and fields.

### Colophonian ferocity.
<margin>XIII</margin>
<note>original: "Κολοφώνια ὕβρις"</note> Colophonian ferocity. Used against the insolent, who fiercely despise and afflict men of humbler fortune. Or against those to whom their own ferocity brought destruction. Taken from the arrogance and pride of that nation. It is recorded by Diogenianus in his collection of adages. Theognis says:
> A fierce mind destroyed both Colophon and the Magnesians.
> ->that is,<-
> A fierce mind destroyed both Colophon and the Magnesians.

<summary>Erasmus discusses the proverb "Beautiful things are difficult," illustrating the struggle for virtue versus the ease of vice and destruction, concluding with a critique of rulers who find it easier to destroy than to build.</summary>

Something has already been said by us regarding the ferocity of this person in the proverb, *The Colophonian vote.* <note>original: "Colophoniũ suffragiũ." This refers to a deciding vote or a final blow, named after the Colophonian cavalry who were said to always end a battle.</note>

### 14. Trust no one, unless you have first consumed a bushel of salt with them.

This adage is commonly circulated among our own people: that one should not trust anyone unless they have first consumed a bushel of salt with them. They mean, of course, that a person’s character cannot be fully understood except through long-term living together and lengthy social interaction. It appears that this proverb originated in antiquity. Indeed, Aristotle, in the eighth book of his *Ethics*, relates something similar in these very words: <margin>original Greek: "ἐν ἡ πόσῳ δὴ χρόνῳ ἡ συνήθειας..."</margin> that is, "Furthermore, there is a need for a span of time and familiarity. For according to the proverb, it is not possible for us to know one another thoroughly before we have together consumed the so-called bushel of salt." He says the same in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*: <margin>original Greek: "Διὸ εἰς παροιμίαν ἐλήλυθεν ὁ μέδιμνος τῶν ἁλῶν."</margin> that is, "Wherefore the bushel of salt has passed into a proverb." In the same book, he also cites that half-line from some poet, if I am not mistaken:
"Not a friend without the passage of time." <note>original Greek: "οὐδ’ ἄνευ χρόνου φίλος."</note>

He adds from Theognis:
<margin>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ ἂν εἰδείης ἀνθρὸς νόον..."</margin> that is,
"You cannot know the mind of a man or a woman,
Just as with a beast of burden, unless you test them first."

Plutarch also notes this proverb in his commentary *On Brotherly Love*, in these words: "For strangers, as Theophrastus used to say, one ought not to judge while loving, but to love after judging. Where nature provides the lead toward goodwill, it does not wait for that celebrated bushel of salt, because it has planted the seed of friendship from the start; there, one ought not to be bitter or precise examiners of faults." <note>original Greek: "τοὺς μὲν ἀλλοτρίους..."</note> Marcus Tullius <insert>Cicero</insert> also mentions this proverb in his discourse *On Friendship*: "That is a true saying which is commonly stated: many bushels of salt must be eaten together so that the duty of friendship may be fulfilled." To this also belongs that line of Sophocles in *Oedipus*:
<margin>original Greek: "Χρόνος δἰκαιον ἄνδρα δείκνυσιν μόνον..."</margin> that is,
"The delay of time alone reveals the upright man,
But you might recognize a wicked one in a single day."

To this also belongs that proverbial six-foot line:
<margin>original Greek: "ἦθος δὲ βέβαιός ἐστιν ἀνθρώποις χρόνος."</margin> that is,
"Time is the mark and indicator of character for mortals."

The same is advised by that saying of Epicharmus:
<margin>original Greek: "Νᾶφε καὶ μέμνασ’ ἀπιστεῖν."</margin> that is,
"Be sober, and remember to trust no one."

The complete verse is cited in Cicero’s first book of *Letters to Atticus*. And yet, he is so entangled in new friendships that the crafty Sicilian <note>Epicharmus, a comic poet from Sicily.</note> frequently whispers to me that song of his: "Be sober, and remember to trust no one; these are the sinews of the mind." <note>original Greek: "Νᾶφε καὶ μέμνασ’ ἀπιστεῖν, ταῦτα νᾶυρα τῶν φρενῶν."</note> For we have restored the trochaic poem from the traces in the manuscripts, lest anyone rashly corrupt it. For the fact that he said *naphe* for *nephe*, and *memnas* for *memneso*, is a property of the <term>dialect<note>The Doric dialect of Greek used by Epicharmus.</note></term>. Cicero, in the short book *On Petitioning for the Consulship*, says: "Therefore, hold fast to that saying of Epicharmus, that the sinews and joints of wisdom are not to believe rashly."

Likewise, that line of Euripides in *Helen*:
<margin>original Greek: "Σωφρόνων δ’ ἀπιστίας..."</margin> that is,
"Than prudent distrust,
Nothing else is more useful to mortals."

I find it cited in fragments in this manner:
<margin>original Greek: "ἁλῶν μέδιμνον ἐκφαγών."</margin> that is,
"After you have eaten a bushel of salt."
Which one may certainly use, if you should say: "See what you are doing, trusting your secrets to that man, not yet having eaten a bushel of salt." Or thus: "Only then trust him, after eating a bushel of salt." It is, however, an iambic dimeter, taken from some poet, as I conjecture.

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<sig>I i</sig>

### He does not eat hare.
<margin>15</margin>
In ancient times, there was a superstitious belief that eating the flesh of a hare <note>Latin: lepus</note> would grant physical beauty. From this comes a joke by Martial in his fifth book addressed to Gellia, who, having sent a hare as a gift, added the common opinion to recommend the present: "You will be beautiful for seven days, Marcus." The poet turned this back on her, as she was quite ugly:

> If you do not deceive me, he said, if you speak the truth, my light,
> Then you, Gellia, have never eaten a hare.

Pliny, in book 28, chapter 9, writes that a hare taken as food preserves the grace of the body for seven days. Lampridius writes that a certain poet joked in this way about Alexander Severus <note>Roman Emperor, 222–235 AD</note> because he ate hare daily:

> That you see our king is beautiful,
> Whom his Syrian lineage brought forth,
> Hunting and the eaten hare make him so,
> From which he gains continuous charm <note>original: "leporem" — a pun on "lepus" (hare) and "lepos" (charm/wit)</note>.

The first poem is corrupted. When one of his friends brought these verses to Alexander, he is said to have replied to this sentiment in a sufficiently Christian manner (for it was a charge laid against him by his enemies that he kept images of Moses and a certain Christ in his private chapel):

> That you think your king is beautiful
> From a common, wretched little fable,
> If you think it true, I am not angry,
> I only wish you would eat little hares:
> So that you might become beautiful in soul, with evils driven out,
> Lest you envy with a spiteful mind.

If you see, reader, that the laws of meter are poorly observed, remember that an Emperor wrote it, whose role it is to prescribe laws, not to obey them. There is also a fish called the "sea-hare," which contains an incurable poison if anyone should eat it unawares. In the Indian Ocean, it kills a man even by touch, according to Pliny: it consumes him with a slow wasting away. The evil is detected by this sign: that those who have eaten it smell of fish. To this creature, man is in turn a pestilence, for it dies immediately upon contact with him. Domitian did away with many people by mixing this into their food; it is believed he removed his brother Titus by the same means, as Philostratus records in the *Life of Apollonius*. Therefore, of those who waste away and cannot be restored by any help of physicians, it can be said: **He ate a sea-hare.**

### With a full hand.
<margin>16</margin>
"With a full hand" <note>Latin: Plena manu</note> stands for that which is done amply, copiously, at length, and not at all stingily. It is a metaphor taken from those who do not give bit by bit and sparingly, but bestow with a full hand. Cicero to Atticus, book 2: "But by Hercules, your other friend Horace, with how full a hand, how ornately he raised our praises to the stars." Seneca in his *Declamations*: "Today I shall act liberally and with a full hand." The same author in the satire he wrote on Claudius Caesar: "But Lachesis, who herself favored the most handsome man, did that with a full hand, and grants many years to Nero." It becomes more elegant the more it is applied to matters of the mind.

### To love without a rival.
<margin>17</margin>
Those are said "to love without a rival" <note>Latin: Sine rivale diligere</note> who foolishly admire what no one else desires. Just as a monkey admires and embraces its own offspring, and unlearned poets love their own trifles alone. The allegory is taken from lovers who have an ugly girlfriend whom no one else wants. The adage appears in the *Letters of Ausonius*. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] to Atticus, book 6: "If Brutus can be moved by the speech of this scoundrel, you may love him alone; you shall have no rival in me." Likewise in book 3 to his brother Quintus: "O gods, how inept he is, how much he loves himself, without a rival!" Horace in *The Art of Poetry*:

> He would spend no further word or useless labor,
> To stop you from loving yourself and your works alone, without a rival.

### To drag by the feet.
<margin>18</margin>
"To drag by the feet" <note>Latin: Pedibus trahere</note> is to handle a matter according to one's own will. Marcus Tullius to Atticus, book 4: "I do not remember from where I fell, but from where I have risen. If I have my brother and you, those matters are dragged by the feet as far as I am concerned." The same in book 7 of the *Familiar Letters*: "For as to what you complain about the trials, I labor much less. All the defendants are dragged by the feet by me." In Titus Livius [Livy] three times...

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<sig>H 2</sig>

<margin>Livy, History of Rome, Book 4 <note>original: "Tite. Li. deca. lib. iiij."</note></margin> When Andronodorus was preparing to resign his position of power, his wife Demarata reminded him of a saying that Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Elder, Tyrant of Syracuse</note> used to employ: "One should not leave a tyranny sitting on a horse, but rather being dragged by the feet." Her point was that while it is easy to give up a great fortune on any day one wishes, building and securing such power is difficult and arduous. From these words, it is clear that those who are "dragged by the feet" are those who have been utterly defeated and are in the power of the victor. The metaphor seems to be derived either from the Homeric Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>, whom Jupiter, being far superior in strength, seized by the feet and cast down from heaven, as the poet testifies:
> He caught him by the foot and threw him from the celestial threshold. <note>original Greek: "Ῥῖψε ποδὸς τεταγὼν ἀπὸ βηλοῦ θεσπεσίοιο."</note>
> That is: Dragged by the feet, he cast him down from high Olympus.

<margin>Iliad, Book 22 <note>original: "Iliad. χ."</note></margin> It is also seen in the case of Hector, whom the victorious Achilles, in the twenty-second book of the *Iliad*, treated thus:
> He pierced the tendons of both feet behind, from heel to ankle, and threaded ox-hide thongs through them; he bound him to the chariot, but left the head to be dragged. <note>original Greek: "Ἀμφοτέρων μετόπισθε ποδῶν τέτρηνε τένοντε..."</note>
> That is: Where the lowest heel joins the ankle at the back of both feet, he bored through the nerves, inserted ox-hide straps, bound the body to the high chariot, while the head hung down and was dragged along.

Cacus is dragged in the same manner by the victorious Hercules in the eighth book of Maro <note>Virgil</note>:
> And the shapeless corpse is dragged out by the feet.

Juvenal, in his fifth Satire:
> You will be dragged by the sole of your foot like Cacus struck by Hercules, and put outside if you ever attempt to mutter anything.

### To lead by the nose. ->XIX<-

<term>To be pulled by the nose</term> <note>original Greek: "Ῥινὸς ἕλκεσθαι"</note>. That is, to be led by the nose, means to be led anywhere at another's whim, without one's own judgment. The metaphor is borrowed from buffaloes and similar animals, which are led around by a ring inserted into the tip of the nose, not unlike a horse with a bit. Although, for horses, a wooden or iron "bit-clamp" <note>original: "dentami"</note> is sometimes inserted into the nostrils, or even used during illness to restrain their ferocity. Nonius indicates that this instrument was called a *Postomis*. Lucian, in a certain dialogue between Juno and Jupiter, says:
> He who is now entirely your master leads you and carries you about, as they say, pulling you by the nose. <note>original Greek: "ὃς μὲν δὴ πάνυ ὑπὸς γε δεσπότης ἐστὶ..."</note>
The same author in *The Sects*:
> Nothing will prevent you from being led by the nose by anyone. <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν κωλύσει σε τῆς ῥινὸς ἕλκεσθαι..."</note>
Those who are driven to something whether they like it or not are said to be "dragged by a twisted neck." Philostratus, in his life of Heliodorus, seems to have used "dragged by the chin" for the same meaning:
> But they led him to the courts, both unwilling and dragging him by the chin. <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἤγαγον αὐτὸν εἰς τὰ δικαστήρια..."</note>
This is transferred from horses, which riders pull by the lower lip until they put on the bridle.

### A barbarian from the crossroads. ->XX<-

<term>A barbarian from the crossroads</term> <note>original Greek: "Βάρβαρος ἐκ τριόδου"</note>. This was said of a man of extreme humility and absolutely no value, just as if you were to say a lowly and cheap slave bought from some crossroads, not given as a gift or born in the house. Lucian, against the man who had called him Prometheus:
> What sort of barbarian is he, almost as if from the crossroads. <note>original Greek: "οἷος ἐκ τριόδου βάρβαρος ὡς παρὰ μικρόν"</note>
However, some read in this passage not "barbarian" but <term>filth from the crossroads</term> <note>original Greek: "βόρβορος ἐκ τριόδου"</note>, which reading alone is to be approved, in my opinion, because in that place mention is made not of some barbarian. Likewise Plato in the *Republic*:
> And those who are truly in a sort of barbaric filth. <note>original Greek: "καὶ τοὺς ἐν τῷ βορβόρῳ βαρβαρικῷ ὄντας"</note>
He is speaking of the soul submerged in the darkness of ignorance.

### A rare bird. ->XXI<-

"A rare bird" was a proverbial way of describing anything new and very difficult to find. Persius:
> If by chance something more fitting comes out, since this is a rare bird.
Juvenal:
> A rare bird on earth, and very much like a black swan.
The same author:
> Rarer even than a white crow.

The rarity of the swan and the phoenix passed into a proverb. The allegory is drawn from foreign and unusual birds, which sometimes fly into our region by chance, or are brought here as a marvel—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

carried. Hence that phrase so often repeated in Aristophanes:
*What bird is this?* <note>original: "Τίς ἔστιν ὄρνις οὗτοσί;"</note> That is, "Who is this guest and stranger?"

<margin>XXII</margin>
->Leisurely works.<-
<note>original: "Succisiua opera"</note>

Something is said to be done with "leisurely works" when it is performed during certain stolen hours, as it were, after we have already discharged our ordinary and lawful duties. The metaphor is drawn from hired laborers or slaves who, beyond the agreed-upon labor they owe, work a little something for themselves outside those fixed hours, which goes toward their personal savings <term>peculium: the private property a slave was allowed to hold</term>. Marcus Tullius Cicero in *On the Orator*, book 2: "The things I bring, which I snatched up in haste, which I did with 'leisurely works,' as they say—that man has pursued from boyhood with the greatest zeal and the best teachers." The same author in the second *Philippic*: "And yet, I have accomplished enough in every genre of my monuments through 'leisurely works' that my late-night vigils and my letters might bring some utility to youth and some praise to the Roman name." The same in *On the Laws*, book 1: "Certain 'leisurely times' occur which I do not allow to go to waste; for instance, if days are given for staying in the country, they are adapted to the number of things we are writing." Pliny in the preface to his *Natural History*: "Even while occupied with duties, we attend to these matters in 'leisurely times'—that is, during the night." Therefore, whatever we attend to in passing or while doing something else is attributed to "leisurely work." The Greeks call this by a nearly similar figure a *parergon* <note>original: "πάρεργον" — a side-project or secondary task</note>. Agathon in Athenaeus says:
*The side-task we treat as our main work,*
*And the main work we labor over as a side-task.*
Since these verses cannot be translated conveniently <note>Erasmus refers to the wordplay between 'ergon' (work) and 'parergon' (side-work)</note>, the meaning is this: we bestow our principal effort on what should have been done in passing, and what is of principal importance, we attend to in passing. We also read "not even as a side-task" <note>original: "τί οὐδ’ ἐν παρέργῳ"</note>, referring to something slightly foreign to the purpose, and "incidentally" <note>original: "παρέργως"</note>, which we usually translate as "in passing" or "negligently." Saint Jerome in a certain letter: "While the swift hand of the secretary marked this down at my dictation by the small lamp with 'stolen works,' as they say." He calls them "stolen" where others call them "leisurely."

<margin>XXIII</margin>
->With folded hands.<-
<note>original: "Compressis manibus"</note>

To sit "with folded hands" is said of those who are idle and doing nothing other than deploring their own fate. Titus Livy in *From the Founding of the City*, book 7: "Why do you, a veteran leader most brave in war, sit with 'folded hands,' as they say?" It also appears in the proverbs of the Hebrews: "You fold your hands a little," <note>Proverbs 6:10 / 24:33</note> regarding the lazy man; a figure taken from the gesture of those who are indeed worried, but nonetheless inactive.

<margin>XXIIII</margin>
->Jests and serious matters.<-
<note>original: "Ioca seriaq;"</note>

Whenever we share all our affairs with someone, we are said to join "jests and serious matters" with them. Marcus Tullius Cicero in *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, book 2: "But with whom can one share 'jests and serious matters,' as the saying goes—with whom all secrets, all hidden things? With you, most excellent man, and then even with an ordinary friend." Donatus, in his commentary on the *Adelphoe*, considers almost all figures of this kind that consist of opposites to be proverbial. Such types are: *spoken and unspoken*; *by what right or what wrong*; *done and undone*; *worthy and unworthy*; *divine law and human law*; *secretly and openly*; *by land and by sea*; *nights and days*; *young and old*; *neither in the smallest nor the greatest*; *fearing neither gods nor men*; *invited and uninvited*; *in safety and in ruin*; and innumerable others of this kind, which we mentioned at the beginning of this work.

<margin>XXV</margin>
->That web is being woven.<-
<note>original: "Ea tela texitur"</note>

A proverbial allegory: "That web is being woven," used for when a business of that sort is in hand, and such matters are being undertaken. A metaphor taken from weavers setting up a loom. Marcus Tullius at the end of *On the Orator*: "Although 'that web is being woven,' and that manner of living is being encouraged in the state and shown to posterity, so that we desire to have citizens similar to those our fathers did not endure." Plautus said "to begin the web" for starting a business: "This web has been begun by me not altogether badly." This is related to what we shall say elsewhere: "To begin the web."

<margin>XXVI</margin>
->Silence destroys many friendships.<-

"Silence destroys many friendships." <note>original: "Πολλὰς φιλίας ἀπροσηγορία διέλυσεν."</note> The adage warns that close relationships are nourished by constant living together and frequent conversation, but are dissolved by interruption and absence. Aristotle mentions this in the *Ethics*, book 8: "But if the absence becomes long-lasting, the absence seems also to bring about a forgetting of the friendship; hence it is said: 'Silence indeed destroys many friendships.'" The verse, as it is recorded in the collections...

# THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND

<note>original: "CHIL. SECUNDÆ CENTURIA I"</note>

is diminished by one syllable. A complete Heroic verse is cited by Aristotle:
*Silence often dissolves broken friendships.* <note>original: "Plurimum amicitiæ soluere silentia ruptas."</note>
In the fifth book of Athenaeus, these verses from an anonymous poet are cited:
> For among companions at a banquet, a friend who remains silent
> too long is cast out; yet the memory of such a meeting is a graceful thing.

->that is,<-

> It is not fitting to have stayed away from the tables of friends for long,
> For this renewal is a beautiful thing for a mindful soul.

More figurative, and for that very reason more elegant, is that saying of Alphius the moneylender in Columella: *Good debts sometimes become bad ones, if you never call them in.* He calls the debtors "Names," in the manner of legal experts, and "to call in" <note>original: "interpellare"</note> means to repeatedly demand the return of a loan. However, the word <term>aposiopesis<note>A rhetorical term for becoming silent or breaking off speech; here used for the "silence" between friends.</note></term> cannot be so conveniently rendered in Latin; for it does not simply signify silence, but that specific silence when one does not call upon or greet a friend.

<margin>XXVII</margin>
## To call to the cap.
<note>original: "Ad pileum uocare."</note>

"To call to the cap" is a proverbial figure used to mean inviting someone to liberty, or stirring up a sedition with huge promises. Macrobius used it in the first book of the *Saturnalia*: "Someone will say that I am now casting masters down from their summit, and in a way calling slaves to the cap." He also plucked these words from Seneca, who writes in his forty-seventh epistle in this manner: "Let him say now that I call slaves to the cap, and cast masters down from their summit." Livy, in book 24: "The next day the slaves were called to the cap, and those bound in prison were released, and the whole confused multitude created Hippocrates and Epicydes as praetors." The metaphor is drawn from the custom of the ancients, by which slaves, when they changed their status and were legally freed, received a <term>pileus<note>A felt cap worn by emancipated Roman slaves as a symbol of their new freedom.</note></term> after their heads were shaved. Hence in Plautus's *Amphitryon*, the slave Sosia, wishing for liberty, says: "May Jupiter bring it to pass that I, bald with a shaved head, might take the cap today." To this pertains what Plutarch relates in the *Sayings of Scipio*, who would not endure to treat with the Carthaginians for peace until they returned L. Terentius, whom they held captive. Terentius then followed Scipio in his triumph wearing the cap, just like a freedman. Likewise, what is related in the same place concerning T. Quintius, whom all the Romans followed in triumph wearing caps—those who had been captured in war and were serving as slaves among the Greeks, whom he had redeemed for five hundred drachmas and given as a gift. T. Livy mentions this in book 4 of the *Macedonian War*. Martial, in the second book of *Epigrams* to Olus:
> I redeemed my caps by losing all my baggage.
That is, by leaving behind and despising all possessions, I gained my liberty. For he who can possess nothing is forced to serve no one, and is free to live according to his own custom. And therefore he adds:
> If you can manage to have nothing, Olus,
> Then you can manage to have no king, Olus. <margin>Persius:</margin>
> The caps grant us this.
Suetonius in his life of Tiberius: "And having called the slaves to the cap in vain, he fled into Sicily." The same author in his life of Nero: "He died in the thirty-second year of his age, on the day he had once killed Octavia; and he provided such great public joy that the common people ran through the whole city wearing caps," signifying by this sign, of course, that liberty had been restored to them. Servius, in his commentary on the eighth book of the *Aeneid*, reports that Feronia is considered the goddess of slaves, in whose temple they were accustomed to receive the cap after their heads were shaved. It seems, moreover, that the cap was a mark of respected virtue among the ancients, from which the custom flowed that those decorated with the title of Master or Doctor receive a cap. Aulus Gellius, in *Attic Nights* book 7, chapter 4, writes that those slaves used to be sold wearing caps for whom the seller would provide no guarantee. Caesius Sabinus, the legal expert, writes that the reason for this was that slaves of that condition ought to be marked during the sale so that buyers could not be mistaken or deceived, nor would they have to wait for the terms of sale, but could perceive with their eyes what kind of "chattel" they were.

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
## A rival of the same Muse.

Those devoted to the same art or discipline are called "rivals of the same Muse." It is used in Aulus Gellius as a proverb. The Greeks call craftsmen of the same trade <term>homotechnous<note>original: ὁμότεχνους; meaning "of the same craft."</note></term>.

<margin>XXIX</margin>
## They live on darnel.
<note>original: "Lolio uictitant."</note>

By a proverbial enigma, those who are dim-sighted or going blind are said to "live on darnel" <note>Darnel (lolium) is a weed often found in wheat; eating it was thought to cause blurred vision or dizziness.</note>, whom the Greeks (according to Nonius) call Myopes. Plautus in *The Braggart Soldier*: "It is a wonder that you live on darnel when wheat is so cheap." "Why so?" "Because you are dim-sighted." "You scoundrel, by Pollux, you are indeed blind, not just dim-sighted." Moreover, darnel...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Pliny mentions darnel <note>original: "lolium"</note> among the pests of crops, along with thistles and caltrops. Virgil says in the *Bucolics*:
> Unlucky darnel and sterile oats hold sway.

Likewise in the first book of the *Georgics*:
> Soon too was labor added to the grain, that foul blight
> Should eat the stalks, and the lazy thistle
> Bristle in the fields; the crops perish, a rough forest rises up,
> Both burs and caltrops, and amid the shining tilth
> Unlucky darnel and sterile oats hold sway.

There is, moreover, a certain peculiar evil in darnel, in that it brings a fog over the eyes, a fact which Ovid indicates in the first book of the *Fasti* when he says:
> And let the fields be free of eye-spoiling darnel.

From this, naturally, comes a proverbial joke.

<margin>30</margin>
->To sing within. The Aspendian harper.<-

Those who are studiously devoted to their own private advantage, and who refer almost everything they do to domestic utility, were said by the proverb "to sing within"; the same were called among the Greeks <term>ἐνδὸν κιθαρίζειν</term> <note>to play the lyre inside</note>, that is, Aspendian harpers. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the third speech against Verres: "And he even carried off the Aspendian harper, of whom you have often heard—the one who is a proverb among the Greeks, of whom they said that he 'sang everything within'—and he placed him in the innermost part of his house, so that he might seem to have surpassed even that man himself in his own artifice." Most wittily did Cicero tax the greed of Verres, who placed the one "singing within" in his "innermost" rooms; that is, he himself "sang within" even more than the harper. The same author in *Against Rullus* regarding the agrarian law: "And this song this tribune of the plebs sings not for you, but for himself, within." For Cicero shows in that oration that the law, although it seemed popular, was nevertheless devised not for the people's utility, but for that of the Decemvirs <note>A commission of ten men</note>. Furthermore, concerning the Aspendian harper, Asconius Pedianus explains the meaning of the phrase in this way: When common harpers play, they use the service of both hands, so that with the right they hold the plectrum <note>a pick used to pluck strings</note>, which they call "singing outside"; with the fingers of the left hand they pluck the strings, which they call "singing within." But it seemed a difficult thing which the Aspendian harper used to do, who by no means used both hands, but performed everything—that is, the whole song—"within," and with the left hand alone; and thus with a silent and light modulation, the strings being touched by the left hand, the song was completed so that the sound reached only the harper himself, or the person standing closest. From this the proverb flowed, so that thieving men were commonly called "Aspendian harpers" by the Greeks, because just as the latter were concealers of their song, so the former were concealers of their thefts. Asconius admits the adage is also aptly said of those who consult much for their own internal advantages beyond what is honorable. Nor does the interpretation differ which Zenodotus brings from Zeno of Myndus in his collection of adages. Furthermore, Aspendus is a city of Pamphylia, according to Stephanus; hence they were called Aspendians, among whom harpers seem to have excelled in this artifice. Pliny appears to have alluded to this proverb in his twenty-eighth book, chapter five, when he says: "But he sang this for remedies, not for banquets."

<margin>31</margin>
->To the stone quarries.<-

<term>Εἰς λατομίας</term> <note>To the quarries</note>. That is, "To the stone quarries." This is very similar to those phrases, "to the crows" or "to blessedness" <note>euphemisms for 'go to hell' or 'get lost'</note>, when we signify that someone should be removed from our midst and taken away to some evil place. It was born from the dithyrambic poet Philoxenus, who, because he did not approve of the poems of the tyrant Dionysius—viewing them as unlearned—was thrust into the stone quarries by him. Later, recalled from there by the prayers of friends, when he had again heard Dionysius reciting his own poems, he stood up; and being asked by Dionysius what the matter was, he replied that it was better and preferable to spend his life in the stone quarries than to listen to those poems. Marcus Tullius, in his *Letters to Atticus*, book four, approves the spirit of Philoxenus, who preferred to be led back to prison than to flatter the tyrant. Lucian, in the booklet titled *On Those Who Serve for Pay*: <term>Σὺ δ’ ἂν μὴ ἐπαινῇς, ὃν τὰς λιθοτομίας διονυσίς εὐθὺς ἀφίξη</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is: "But if you do not praise it, you will immediately be banished to the stone quarries of Dionysius." Plautus in *The Two Captives*: "From there you shall go further into the stone-quarrying quarries." By this name a prison was famous which Dionysius had built. Plutarch, in the second book *On the Fortune and Virtue of Alexander*: <term>οἷος ἦν ἀνάπαλιν Διονύσιο... μέχρι τῆς κορωνίδ’ περιέγραψεν</term> <note>original Greek</note>, that is: "Such a man, on the other hand, was that Dionysius who cast the poet Philoxenus into the quarries because, having been ordered to correct his tragedy, he crossed it out from the very beginning all the way to the end." Marcus Tullius in the seventh speech against Verres: "You have all heard of the Syracusan quarries; most of you know them. It is a huge work, magnificent, belonging to kings and tyrants, entirely made of stone, depressed to a wonderful depth, and the work of many..."

<summary>Erasmus explains two major adages: "To sing within," referring to secretive self-interest based on a unique style of lyre playing, and "To the stone quarries," a phrase for punishment or rejection of bad art based on the poet Philoxenus's defiance of the tyrant Dionysius.</summary>
<keywords>darnel, Aspendian harper, self-interest, Cicero, Verres, Philoxenus, Dionysius of Syracuse, stone quarries, prisons, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<note>The title indicates this is the 1,100th-1,200th proverb in the collection.</note>

...utterly cut off. Likewise in the same work: "That prison which was built at Syracuse by the most cruel tyrant Dionysius, which is called the *Latumiae* <note>original: "latumiæ"; stone-quarries used as dungeons</note>, was the home of Roman citizens during his command. So that whoever had offended his mind or his eyes, he immediately cast into the *Latumiae*." The same author in the third action against the same man: "L. Suetius, a man endowed with every honor, who testified under oath before you, said that many Roman citizens in those *Latumiae* were most cruelly punished with death by force," etc. Titus Livius also mentions this prison in the sixth book of the Second Punic War.

->The old age of a horse.<-
->XXXII<-

<margin>The old age of a horse. <note>original Greek: Ἵππου γῆρας</note></margin> *The old age of a horse.* A proverb usually said against those who, after performing noble deeds in their youth, cast themselves down to sordid cares after they have grown old. The allegory is taken from noble horses which, having become sluggish with age, are thrust into a mill, or a cart, or some other work of that kind; though they were once held in high value while their strength was intact. Plutarch in the booklet titled *Whether an Old Man Should Govern the Republic*: "It will not seem entirely right to everyone; see that you do not at all force the so-called 'old age of a horse' to be laughed at." That is: Will it not clearly seem to summon the old age of a horse, as they commonly call it, when no one is compelling it? With this agrees that line of Ennius, which is cited by Cicero in *Cato the Elder*:
> Just as the brave horse who at the final lap
> Won the Olympics, now rests worn out by age.

->If it is a friend to you, it is no enemy to me.<-
->XXXIII<-

Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "But let it be, O Theodorus, a friend, and not an enemy to me, as the proverb-makers say." That is: If that thing is a friend to you, Theodorus, it is not an enemy to me; just as they say in the proverb. This means: If the thing pleases you, it does not displease me. It is captured, however, in a figure of speech using similar-sounding words, and then in the ambiguity of "friend" and "enemy," both of which he twists from persons to things; though both are more commonly referred to persons. It will be used whenever we comply with the will of another.

->Wiser than a tadpole.<-
->XXXIIII<-

Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "Did we not admire him like a god for his wisdom? Yet he happened to be no better in prudence than a tadpole <note>original: "rana gyrina"; literally a 'frog-tadpole'</note>." The adage is taken from the unformed offspring of frogs, which the Greeks call *gyrinos* <note>original: γυρῖνον</note>, from the shape of the body being rounded into a circle <note>original: "gyrum"</note>, by which it happens that they turn themselves wherever they wish with wonderful speed; as is testified by whoever it was who wrote the *Etymologicon* of Greek words. Hesychius also mentions tadpoles. Suidas even brings forward the testimony of Aristophanes:
<margin>As the fathers of tadpoles cry out. <note>original Greek: Ὡς πατέρων βοῶσι γυρίνων</note></margin> *As the fathers of tadpoles cry out.* That is: Just as the fathers of tadpoles shout. Nor are the things related by Pliny in Book 9, Chapter 51, inconsistent with these. "Frogs," he says, "come together, the male grasping the forelegs of the female and the hindquarters. They give birth to tiny black bits of flesh, which they call tadpoles, distinguished only by eyes and a tail; soon the feet are formed, the tail splitting into the hind legs. It is a wonder that, after a six-month life, they dissolve into mud with no one seeing it, and are born again from the spring waters, those which had been born before, by some hidden reason, since it happens every year." Thus far we have reviewed Pliny's words. Aratus also mentions them: "And then from the water the parents of tadpoles cry out." Furthermore, since talkativeness is attributed to the frog, which is usually the companion of stupidity, there must be very little mind in tadpoles, whom you would hardly perceive to be animals unless they moved. However, Jerome Aleander—a man not only famous for letters but joined to me by an old friendship—was the reason I weighed this passage more diligently; he, in turn, credits what he pointed out to Celio Calcagnini. I wished neither of them to be cheated of his praise. For I have never been so youthfully affected that I took pleasure in being Aesop's little crow <note>A reference to the fable of the crow wearing borrowed feathers; Erasmus is saying he does not want to take credit for others' research.</note>.

->Constrained in a well.<-
->XXXV<-

Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "For why would you use an inescapable question, being, as they say, constrained in a well?" It will fit those who are reduced to such straits that they can in no way extricate themselves. It is not very different from that other saying: "To fight with a dog in a well." Also that one: "A pack-horse in a ditch."

->You have come into the same handles.<-
->XXXVI<-

Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "As far as this matter pertains, my friend, you have come into the same handles." That is: you are nonetheless held fast, and you cannot escape.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...without you saying so. Likewise, Aristides in his *General Defense of the Four Orators* says: <note>original: ὡς ἄγχυ αὐτῶν λυει ὁ καλλικλῆς εἰς αὐτὰς λαβὰς ἐπανελθεῖν</note> "So it was necessary for Callicles to fall back into the same handles." <note>Aristides was a 2nd-century Greek orator; Callicles is a character in Plato's Gorgias.</note> This applies to one who is so entangled that, whichever way he turns, he is held fast and cannot extricate himself. Very similar to this is what Lucian writes in *Hermotimus*: <note>original: οἷόν τι ου ιν ἐκπεφευγῆναι, εἰς τὸν αὐτὸν κύρτον ἐμπέπτωκας</note> "For thinking you had escaped, you have fallen into the same fish-trap." Likewise that which will be discussed elsewhere: "To weep in a circle of feet." <note>A metaphor for being trapped in a recurring cycle of trouble.</note>

<margin>37</margin>
### How could I be absent from this feast?

Plato in the *Phaedrus*: <note>original: πῶς γὰρ οἷός τε εἴω τοιαύτης θοίνης ἀπέχεσθαι;</note> "For how could I abstain from such a banquet?" This refers to something exceedingly pleasant and desirable, such as a festive banquet. It alludes, I believe, to the fable in which they say Diana took it poorly that, while the other gods were invited by Oeneus to a sacred feast, she alone was passed over and sat at home alone, fuming because she smelled nothing of that sacrificial steam. Lucian mentions this in *The Lapiths* and also in his booklet *On Sacrifices*.

<margin>38</margin>
### Sweet elbow.

<note>original: γλυκὺς ἀγκών</note> *Sweet elbow.* This is the speech of one who feels aversion, or when we say one thing but mean another <note>i.e., irony or sarcasm</note>. Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "Has it escaped you, Phaedrus, that the 'sweet elbow' was named after that long bend <term>Ancon|The Greek word 'Ancon' means elbow, but also refers to a sharp bend in a river or coastline</term> in the Nile? And how does it escape you, regarding the 'elbow,' that those who are most proud among politicians are most in love with speech-writing and leaving behind compositions?" Thus far Plato. Now, the *Ancon* is a part of the Nile where sailors sweat and are in great danger. Hence, by a proverb of <unclear>averting evil</unclear>, they called it a "sweet elbow," as if praying against the dangers of that place. It has the same force as if you were to say: "Speak fair words," or "Speak only of good omens." 

There are those who think it originated from the comic poet Plato. In his play titled *Phaon*, he depicts an old man in love with a flute-girl, saying: "O golden headband! O sweet elbow to my delicate ways!" Suidas writes that *Ancon* was the name given by the Carthaginians to a dark and deep dungeon into which those who angered the tyrant were usually thrown. Furthermore, the highest ridges of mountains are called *Ancones*. Finally, among other things, the whirlpool and swelling of a river around the banks, due to the winding and the rebuffing of the current, is called an *Ancon*, taking its likeness (if I am not mistaken) from the shape of an elbow, because in certain places the bank runs out and projects in an elbow-like appearance. From this, the name *Ancon* was given to several towns and places, such as Ancona, a city of the Picentines, according to Stephanus. Likewise Ovid in the last book of the *Metamorphoses*:

<margin>As some read.</margin>
<margin>Valerius, Argonautica, Book 4.</margin>
> And the Ancon of the thick shore.
> Why should I mention what waters the Iris, what waters the Ancon twists?

Hence, one might not absurdly take it by <term>antiphrasis|The rhetorical device of using a word to mean its opposite, like calling a dangerous place 'sweet'</term>, as Zenodotus prefers. For others think it was spoken as an exclamation. Athenaeus, in the twelfth book of the *Deipnosophists*, shows that *Ancon* was a certain place in Sardis prepared for the service of pleasures, in which there were cook-shops, prostitutes, and other luxuries of that kind. It was called "Sweet Ancon" because of the allurements of pleasure, but in it many suffered shipwreck <note>Metaphorical shipwreck, meaning moral or financial ruin</note>. He also indicates that Polycrates among the Samians established many "architects of pleasure" after the example of the "sweet Ancon" of the Sardians, and that place was called *Laura*, or "The Flowers of the Samians." He adds that Omphale, the queen of that nation, forcibly shut up the virgins of the masters with their slaves for debauchery; the chaste called this the "sweet elbow." The Lydians, however, called the place where women were violated "sweet elbow," softening the atrocity of the crime with the word. He thinks the term was named from what was done there. The *Etymologist* indicates that an *Ancon* is called a place hard with bones, from "drawing back the hand," or from "breaking," or from "strangling." Hesychius adds that the bends in walls are called *Ancones*. Briefly, whatever is bent into the appearance of an elbow is called an *Ancon*, just as there are "elbows" on a lyre.

<margin>39</margin>
### An ox at the manger.

<note>original: Βοῦς ἐπὶ φάτνη</note> *An ox at the manger.* This is customarily said of those who have served their time, and who now, because of age, indulge in leisure and a softer life. It is also expressed this way: "An ox in the stall." It also fits those who engage in no honorable business, but in foul leisure and...

# SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY

<margin>40</margin>
...they serve me. Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus, a Greek sophist of the Roman Empire</note> says in *Cassandra*: "But he was among the youths and women, like an ox at the manger." That is, truly among young men and women, he is an ox at the stall. He is speaking of Agamemnon, who was leading a life of luxury. It is also expressed in this manner: "An old ox in the stable-yard." And again in this way: "An ox sitting idle in the stable." This refers to those who live softly and in leisure. Athenaeus <note>Author of the 'Deipnosophistae' or 'Banquet of the Learned'</note> in Book 8 relates a story that is not without wit, nor foreign to this proverb. A certain unskilled singer, having received Stratonicus at a banquet, was showing off his art to him amidst the cups. Since the banquet was splendid and magnificent, and Stratonicus was being frustrated by the performance and had no one else to talk to, he broke his cup and called for a larger one. When he had received many measures of wine and had shown the cup to be empty, drinking his fill, he fell asleep, committing the rest to fortune. But when by chance some revelers came upon the singer—men he knew—Stratonicus immediately became sober. When they heard that he, who always drank much wine, had become intoxicated, he replied concisely: "That treacherous and wicked singer killed me like an ox at the manger, once the dinner was served." Where we read the word *psalomython* <note>original: ψαλόμυθον, perhaps meaning 'harping talk'</note> in the text of Athenaeus, I think it should be read as *sphalomython* <note>original: σφαλόμυθον, meaning 'stumbling or deceptive talk'</note>. This will also apply to those who are nourished for their own destruction, just as those who fill themselves with the pleasures of the world are nourished as nothing other than victims for the underworld, like an ox at the manger.

### Not even with a bent knee.
<margin>40</margin>
"Not even having bent a knee." That is, not even with a flexed knee. Philostratus says in *Antaeus*: "And he does not appear to have even bent a knee without a struggle against Antaeus." The same author says in *Herodes*: "Here, he said, let us bend the knee." This is said hyperbolically <note>as an exaggeration</note> for that which is "not even the slightest bit." For he who already begins to compose himself for rest first bends his knee. Therefore, "not even having bent a knee" is as if you were to say: without taking a breath, or without any intermission. It appears to be taken from Aeschylus' *Prometheus*, where Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> speaks thus:
> Upon this joyless rock you shall keep watch,
> Standing upright, sleepless, never bending a knee.
Unless you prefer it to be borrowed from Homer's *Iliad*, Book 10, where Menelaus speaks thus of Hector:
> I think he will gladly bend his knees, if only he
> Escapes from the grim war.

### Where are you hurrying, surely not to the youth?
<margin>41</margin>
Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*: "When there was a Cilician saying: 'Where are you running? Surely not to the youth?' for it was said of him for whom he was about to have a characterization." That is, a saying celebrated among the Cilicians: "Where do you run? Surely to the youth?" It was commonly said of him and obtained the force of an adage. It is not entirely clear what that Cilician adage meant, unless perhaps it was taken from the oracle of Apollo, to which people hurried from all sides; for Apollo was depicted as beardless, just as Bacchus was.

### It is clear even to a child.
<margin>42</margin>
"Clear even to a child." That is, evident even to a boy. Used for a matter that is beyond measure clear and confessed. Plato uses it in a certain place which we have pointed out before, as does Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*. It is in the letters of Basil: "So that it is known even to a child." This is related to that which we have reported elsewhere: "Clear even to a blind man."

### Lest you fall in with Black-buttocks.
<margin>43</margin>
"Lest you happen upon the one with the black buttocks." This fits lewd and injurious men. It is the word of one threatening, lest they ever fall in with him who may exact punishment from them for their misdeeds. Philostratus uses this adage in the *Life of Apollonius*, Book 2: "And see, perhaps it was a case of falling in with Black-buttocks." Aristophanes in *Lysistrata*:
> For Myronides was rough in that place,
> And 'Black-buttocks' to all his enemies.
He called him "Black-buttocks" as if he were a punisher and avenger. Furthermore, *Melampygus* <note>Black-buttocks</note> signifies to the Greeks one who has a dark backside; which nickname was noted of Hercules, because he had that part of the body not plucked in the manner of water-leaches, nor white, as effeminate men are accustomed, but hairy and overgrown with black bristles. For just as the Greeks call those who are soft, unwarlike, and broken by luxuries...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...delights, they call them "bright-rumped" or "white-rumped," so likewise, on the other hand, they were accustomed to call the brave and vigorous "black-rumped" <note>original: μελαμπύγους (melampygous)</note>, as the interpreter of Lycophron asserts. The same author shows that the proverb is also expressed in this way: *You have not yet encountered a Black-rumped one* <note>original: οὔπω μελαμπύγῳ τετύχηκας</note>. They believe the proverb was born from a story of this kind, which we shall record partly from Suidas and partly from the narrations of Gregory of Nazianzus. Once there were two brothers who raged everywhere against everyone with every kind of mischief, from which, due to the atrocity of their character, they earned their names. For one was called Passalus and the other Achemon (or, as it is read elsewhere, Achmon). Their mother, named Senonis, when she saw them committing atrocious deeds everywhere, ordered them to beware lest they should ever encounter a "Black-rumped one." It happened then that Hercules was once sleeping under a certain tree, with his weapons leaning against it. The Cercopes (or Perperi) brothers approached <note>Erasmus notes both names are found in manuscripts</note> and attempted to attack the sleeping Hercules with his own weapons. He immediately sensed the ambush, and having seized and bound them, he suspended them from his club behind his back in the manner of hares, and carried them in that fashion. As they hung with their heads dangling downward, they saw Hercules’s backside, rough and bristly with black hair; remembering their mother’s warning, they chatted among themselves about this matter. As soon as Hercules heard this, being delighted by the nickname and breaking into laughter, he released them from their bonds and let them go. Plutarch notes this story in his booklet *On the Difference Between a Friend and a Flatterer*, when he says Hercules was delighted by the Cercopes. Herodotus also mentions it in his seventh book regarding a place called the "Black-rumped Rock" and the seat of the Cercopes. In this matter, Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous 15th-century humanist scholar</note> slipped up significantly, because he either did not know this fable or certainly did not remember it. Plutarch, in his booklet *On the Education of Children*, also relates this among the Pythagorean enigmas: *Do not taste things that have a black tail* <note>original: τὰν γένεσιν τῶν μελαμπύγων</note>. And he interprets it in this way: one must abstain from the company of dark and wicked mortals—though this is different from the proverb.

### The Owl’s Egg.
<margin>44</margin>

*The Owl’s Egg* <note>original: Γλαυκαῖον ὤον (Glaukaion oon)</note>. This is cited by Niccolò Perotti in his *Cornucopia* as a proverb, yet it is not explained. Perhaps in antiquity they signified by this adage a person who was abstemious and shrank from wine. For Philostratus, in the third book of the *Life of Apollonius*, relates a truly prodigious thing about the egg of an owl. Therefore, it is better to relate his own words: "One must," he says, "watch for where an owl nests, then it will be necessary to steal the eggs and give them to an infant to eat after being lightly cooked. For if the child eats any of these before tasting wine, a hatred of wine will be implanted in him, so that for his whole life he will be most sober." Aelian, in the first book of *On the Nature of Animals*, relates a fable that is a bit more like an old wives' tale. It would be better to review this also in the author's own words: "Storks," he says, "fend off bats that try to ruin their eggs with wonderful cleverness. For the bats, by touch, render the eggs wind-eggs and sterile. Therefore, they apply this remedy against them: they carry plane-tree leaves into the nest, which the bats, after touching them, become numb so that they can no longer do harm." Thus far Aelian. There are those who deny that an owl's egg can even be found. Therefore, the proverb will apply either to a man of no worth and no fruit (following Aelian's fable), or to a thing rare to find (following the opinion of the latter group).

### The Song of the Amazons.
<margin>45</margin>

*The Song of the Amazons* <note>original: Ἀμαζόνων ᾆσμα (Amazonon asma)</note>: applied to the delicate, the lewd, and those who are hardly men. Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*, book 3: "A youth from the number of the soft ones was considered so licentious that he was sometimes called the 'Song of the Amazons'." What "Song of the Amazons" actually means, I confess I have not yet sufficiently discovered among suitable authors. Unless someone prefers that we take it to mean that the Amazons used to celebrate songs in mockery of soft men. But if it were permitted to change the text, it would not displease me at all if we read "mazonymon" <note>large dish</note> instead of "Amazonon." For thus they call a very large type of dish on which food is brought into a banquet. It was the custom in antiquity that the more sumptuous feasts were brought in with a flute-player leading the way, such as the sturgeon. Horace, in his last Satire...

# SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY I

...the Mizonomo boys carrying the severed limbs of a great crane. <note>original: "Mizonomo pueri magno discerpta ferentes Membra gruis." This refers to a fragment of ancient poetry Erasmus is analyzing.</note> But for now, let this be my own dream, until something more certain is brought forward by the learned. Indeed, one should not despair of this, as new authors emerge into the light every day. When these [adages] were already in their fourth edition, the work of Caelius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), a contemporary scholar whose "Antique Lectiones" Erasmus often critiqued.</note> appeared; he relates that this proverb seems to him to be said not of Amazonian women, but generally of thin people. Since this commentary is remarkably dull, I was much more modest in professing that I did not know what I truly did not know.

### 46. The Gardens of Tantalus

<margin>Tantali horti. That is, the gardens of Tantalus.</margin> Said of goods which one is nevertheless not permitted to enjoy, or of those things which seem to be something when they are actually nothing. Philostratus in the *Life of Apollonius*, book 4: "You see the gardens of Tantalus," he said, "how they exist while not existing." <note>original: "Τὰς ταντάλω ἔφη κήπες εἴδετε, ὡς ὄντες ἐκ εἰσί."</note> The story is well known regarding Tantalus standing in water in the underworld, with fruits hanging over his head; while thirsty and hungry, he can touch neither. We have previously reported some things about these in the proverb "The Gardens of Adonis."

### 47. A Counselor is a Sacred Thing

<margin>Σύμβολον ἱερὸν χρῆμα. That is, a Counselor is a sacred thing.</margin> Zenodotus reports this from Epicharmus. The sense of the adage is that a wise counselor brings the greatest utility; or, that counsel must be given religiously and purely to those who need it. Plato in the *Theages*: "But indeed, O Demodocus, it is even said that a counselor is a sacred thing." <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ μὲν δὴ ὦ Δημόδοκε καὶ λέγεταί γε σύμβολον ἱερὸν χρῆμα εἶναι."</note> The same in the letter to Perdiccas: "It is just that I impart counsel that is both hospitable and sacred, as the saying goes." Suidas indicates the saying is used when deliberating on dangerous matters, so that it seems similar to that other proverb, "to cast the sacred anchor." <note>A metaphor for a final, desperate resource.</note> It is also expressed in this manner: "Counsel is a sacred thing." This six-foot line <term>senarius: a line of verse consisting of six metrical feet</term> exists among the Greek maxims: "Consultation is truly a sacred thing."

### 48. To Leave Before the Mysteries

<margin>Ἀπιέναι πρὸ τῶν μυςηρίων. That is, to leave before the mysteries.</margin> This is to withdraw oneself before a matter is finished. The metaphor is taken from sacred rites, in which the uninitiated <term>profane: those not initiated into the secret religious rites</term> were ordered to depart when the mysteries were about to be performed; the initiated remained, and it was not lawful to leave until the rituals were completed. Plato in the *Meno*: "Unless, as you were saying yesterday, it were necessary for you to depart before the mysteries; but if you would stay and be initiated..." and the rest which follows.

### 49. To Make Many Out of One

<margin>Ἐξ ἑνὸς πολλὰ ποιεῖν. That is, to make many out of one.</margin> They used to say this proverb of those who cut a thing into tiny pieces. It will apply to those who vary the same thing in different ways, so that it no longer seems like one thing, but many. Plato in the *Meno*: "And stop making many out of one, as the mockers say of those who shatter something every time." <note>original: "Καὶ παῦε πολλὰ ποιῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἑνός..."</note> A rather witty story is told in Titus Livy, in the fifth book of the *Macedonian War*, concerning a certain innkeeper who served the meat of a single pig prepared with such various equipment that the Roman general, marvelling, asked where such a great abundance of game could be found in the middle of winter. Then the innkeeper, smiling, confessed that all those types of food had been made from one domestic sow. "And those people do no differently," he said, "who terrify you by recounting various and horrific names, when all these are but one nation."

### 50. Corinthus, Son of Jove

<margin>ὁ Διὸς κόρινθος. That is, Corinthus, son of Jupiter.</margin> This was usually said against those who always say or do the same things. Pindar in the seventh *Nemean Ode*: "To repeat these things three or four times is a source of poverty for children, like 'Corinthus son of Jove' barking in vain." <note>original: "μαψυλάκας" (maphylakas) - one who babbles nonsense.</note> He says he does not want to repeat the same things over and over, as if he were telling trifles to children. For "barking in vain" signifies one who blathers nonsense to no purpose. A commentator brings a story to this place regarding this proverb which, in my mind at least, is not very relevant; nevertheless, I will add it. Aletes, he says, consulted the Oracle of Dodona (which then belonged to Jupiter) as to whether he could gain power over the Corinthians. The response was that he would gain it when someone gave him a clod of earth, or rubble, and that on the "day of many crowns." Therefore, having set out for Corinth, he asked a certain rustic for bread; the man [gave him] a clod...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the adage "Corinthus, Son of Jupiter," exploring its mythological origins and its application to tedious repetition.</meta>

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...he offered a piece of bread. Aletes realized the oracle was now fulfilled <note>The oracle had predicted he would gain the kingdom when someone offered him "earth," and the bread contained soil</note>, and he set his mind toward seizing power. On that day, sacrifices were being made to the Spirits of the Dead, and for that reason, since most of the citizens were away at the tombs, he approached and found the daughters of Creon already discussing the succession of the empire. He persuaded the youngest of them that if she were willing to help, he would take her as his wife as soon as he had obtained the princedom. Out of a desire for power, she betrayed the city and admitted Aletes through the open gates. Thus, as victor, he named the city "Corinth, Son of Jupiter," because it had fallen to him by the oracle of Jupiter. 

Then he adds another story, which agrees closely with the interpretation of others. It is of this sort: Once the Megarians were tributaries to the Corinthians. However, when they began to find the Corinthians' rule too insolent and were preparing a revolt, an ambassador was sent in the name of the Corinthians. Among many other fierce things he said to the Megarian commoners, he thundered out this phrase in indignation and shouting: <note>original: οὐκ ἀνέξεται ὁ Διὸς κόρινθος</note> "Corinth, son of Jupiter, will not endure it." When he repeated this quite often, the incensed people began to shout back, "Strike, strike the 'Corinth of Jupiter'!" and they drove the ambassador out. Now, this Corinth was a king of the Corinthians, descended from Jupiter—although Pausanias in his *Description of Corinth* denies that he found in serious authors that Corinth was the son of Jupiter, but says only that the Corinthian commoners claim so. 

Plutarch uses the adage in the commentary he wrote *Against the Stoics*: <note>original: πολὺς ἐν ᾧ Διὸς κόρινθος ἤδη λόγου αὐτῶν ἀνθιστᾷ, τὴν γὰρ ὑπερβολὴν ὑποκρούων ἵνα μὴ σκώπτειν δοκῇς, ἔαγε</note> "In many places now, their 'Corinth of Jupiter' stands against their own argument. For omit the circling of the pestle <note>A metaphor for repetitive or circular reasoning</note>, lest you seem to be mocking." 

Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
> Why, what is this matter?
> Is it anything but "Corinth of Jupiter" among the blankets?

These are the words of a servant, noting the <term>tautology</term> <note>The unnecessary repetition of the same idea in different words</note> of Bacchus, who had said:
> You might pick up the blankets again, once more, again.

The same author in *The Assemblywomen*:
> When it appeared to those looking again,
> The "Corinth of Jupiter."

Philostratus in *Antipater the Sophist*: "When his kinsmen were pushing him toward marriage, and thinking Antipater a 'Corinth of Jupiter'." Although here he seems to have used "Corinth of Jupiter" for a man who is greatly fortunate. 

Socrates also uses this adage in Plato’s *Euthydemus*: "But simply, as the saying goes, it becomes a 'Corinth of Jupiter'." It matches that which we have recorded elsewhere: <note>original: Δὶς κράμβη</note> "Cabbage twice served" <note>A proverb meaning that repetition is tedious or "death"</note>. And it may be used not only when the same things are said again and again, but also when one persists too constantly in the same business. For instance, if someone always serves the same food, or if someone always broods over literary studies, or hunts constantly, so that a loathing arises from the persistence, we shall rightly say: "The Corinth of Jupiter." For whatever is perpetual is troublesome. 

As Pindar witnesses in the *Nemean Odes*: "But indeed, a rest in every business is sweet. Even honey and the pleasant flowers of Aphrodite bring satiety." In some copies, instead of "honey" <note>original: μέλι</note>, it was written "it is a care" <note>original: μέλει</note>. So in an epigram:
> Anything in excess, anything ill-timed, is unpleasant; for there is an old saying
> That even honey, if the supply is immoderate, will become bile.

I should think it not useless to advise that the proverb can be understood in two ways. For the interpreter of Pindar also shows this: either when the same things are repeated too often, or when those who at the beginning speak magnificently and threaten fiercely, afterwards flee timidly. This is what happened to the ambassadors of the Corinthians, who, after they had thundered that phrase often in the assembly: "Rightly shall Corinth, son of Jupiter, groan, unless he takes punishment from you," later, when it came to blows, they fled like cowards. Nor should it be overlooked that the adage is...

-> accommo- <-
