# CHILIAD II. CENTURY I.

can be applied both to things and to persons. To things in this manner: "I have heard it a thousand times already; I can no longer bear **the Corinth of Zeus**." <note>original: "τὸν Διὸς κόρινθον" (ton Dios korinthon). A proverb for tedious repetition, referring to the Corinthians' boastful claim of being descended from Zeus.</note> To persons: as if one were to call a man who constantly repeats the same things **the Corinth of Zeus**. The commentator on Pindar also points this out.

### The turning of the shell.
<margin>51</margin>
**The turning of the shell**, <note>original: "ὀστράκου περιστροφή" (ostrakou peristrophe)</note> that is, the reversal of the tile. This refers to things suddenly changed into their opposite. Lucian in his *Apology for those in Dependent Posts*: "Then, forgetting everything, as they say, **the shell having turned**, he willingly surrendered himself out of fear into a servitude so manifest and conspicuous." <note>original: "testula... transmutata"</note> It is uncertain whether the metaphor is taken from a type of game which the Greeks call *ostrakinda*. (Plato alludes to this in his writings on love, namely in the *Phaedrus*: "Finally he becomes a fugitive from these things; and while he who was previously the lover is now necessarily deprived of his status, the shell having turned, he changes his course in headlong flight. But the other is forced to pursue, indignant and calling upon the gods.") Or perhaps it comes from **Ostracism**, a type of voting which was conducted using pebbles and beans. In this process, it was discovered that citizens who had provoked the envy of the masses—whether by excessive wealth, nobility, glory, or any other distinguished virtue—could be relegated to a ten-year exile. In this way, even **Aristides** was cast out, for no other reason than that it was annoying to the people that the nickname "the Just" was commonly given to him. Ostracism was conducted in this manner: shells, that is, small tiles, were given to each man in the assembly. On these, each man would write the name of the person he wished to leave the city. Then they carried all of these to a certain place in the forum surrounded by railings. Furthermore, the magistrates to whom this task was assigned first counted the total number; unless there were more than six thousand, nothing was enacted. Then, having separated the pebbles of each individual, he who was condemned by the most pebbles was ordered to go into exile for ten years—yet in such a way that it was meanwhile free for him to receive the fruits of his property. Thus, ostracism was not a punishment for wickedness, but a pacification of the envy inherent in common minds. However, this ostracism became obsolete after a certain **Hyperbolus** was ejected by it, a man who was contemptible and of low birth. These matters are related by Plutarch in the *Life of Aristides*. Therefore, since this ostracism was carried out with great license and rashness by the common people, and suddenly changed the fortune of every most excellent citizen, it does not seem absurd that the adage was derived from it. Regarding the game of shells, Julius Pollux records it roughly in this way: Boys, having drawn a line in the middle, distribute themselves into two parties, one of which was called "within the shell," the other "outside." Then, someone throwing a tile at the line, whichever side's top surface turned up, that side would pursue those who belonged to the other, while the rest turned to flight. Moreover, whoever among the fugitives was caught sat down and was called "the donkey." The one who threw the tile would say "night or day." For the inner part of the shell was smeared with pitch, which corresponded to night. This kind of game was called **the turning of the shell**. Plato, in the seventh book of the *Republic*, seems to refer to the game when he speaks thus: "This, as it seems, would not be the turning of a shell, but the leading of a soul from a kind of nocturnal day up to the true vision of reality." He is discussing philosophy, which leads the mind away from false images of good things to the knowledge of true goods.

### To have one foot in Charon’s boat.
<margin>52</margin>
Men of extreme and decrepit old age are even today commonly said to have **one foot in the grave**. Not far from this is what Lucian writes in his *Apology*: "Being now at the very threshold, and almost having **one foot in the ferry-boat**." <note>original: "τὸν ἕτερον πόδα ἐν τῷ πορθμείῳ" (ton heteron poda en to porthmeio). Referring to the boat of Charon, the ferryman of the dead.</note> The same author in *The Wishes*: "And having, as they say, **one foot in the tomb**." <note>original: "ἐν τῇ σορῷ" (en te soro)</note> Pomponius, in the fortieth book of the *Pandects* <note>A compendium of Roman law.</note> under the title *On the manumission of slaves by trust*, in the chapter *According to Julian*, said in these words: "I, led by a desire for learning—which I have considered the only best reason for living even into my seventy-eighth year—am mindful of this sentiment which Julian is reported to have said: 'Even if I had **one foot in the grave**, I would still wish to learn something more.'" I do not know whether what Lucian writes in *The Wishes* pertains to this: "As one who indeed already has **one foot in the ship**." Plutarch in his short commentary...

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

In his short treatise *On the Education of Children*, <note>original: "De puerorū institutione"</note> he notes that old men are commonly insulted by being called *cronoleros* <note>original: "κρονολήρους" — old fools from the age of Cronus</note> and *sorodaimones*, <note>original: "σοροδαίμονας" — spirits of the coffin</note> because they have lost their wits due to age and are near the grave, being more like ghosts of the tomb than men. Plautus used the term "an old man of Acheron" <note>Acheron was a river in the underworld; the term implies he has one foot in the grave.</note>. Terence used *Silicernium* <note>A funeral feast or a dry old man.</note>. And someone else used the term "one at the coffin's edge" <note>original: "capularem"</note>. The Greeks call them "tomb-elders" <note>original: "τυμβογέροντας"</note> according to the authors Hesychius and Suidas, as well as "near the tomb" <note>original: "τύμβον πέλας"</note> for those of extreme age: the former because they are close to the burial mound, the latter because they must soon be sent to the lower world—derived from *pempin* <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ πέμπειν"</note> which means to send, and *helos* <note>original: "ἔλος"</note> meaning marsh, because those who die were believed to be sent across the Stygian marsh to the underworld. <sig>L l l l</sig>

# To sow Hollow Arabia.

*Ten koilen arabian speirein* <note>original: "τὴν κοίλην ἀραβίαν σπείρειν"</note>, that is, To sow Hollow Arabia. This is used for sweating in vain, or bestowing labor on a very difficult and not at all fruitful matter. Lucian in his *Apology*: "As if he were attempting to sow Hollow Arabia." It signifies a marshy part of Arabia, by no means suitable for sowing. Plutarch in *On Talkativeness*: "For they say that because of its downward-sloping nature, the seed is entirely barren. But the speech of talkative people is altogether uncollected and fruitless." <sig>L l l l l</sig>

# More clear-sighted than Lynceus.

The keen-sightedness of Lynceus <note>An Argonaut famous for his supernatural vision.</note> passed into a proverb. Pliny in the second book of his *Natural History*, chapter 17, says: "The last and first moon are seen on the same day or night, with no other sign than when it is in Aries; a thing which has happened to few mortals. And from this comes the fable of Lynceus’s vision." There are those who hand down the tradition that Lynceus was the first to discover mines of metals—copper, silver, and gold. And from this arose the commonly known fable that he could also see things that were under the earth. The commentator on Lycophron is a witness to this. Plato also mentions this in a certain letter. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:

That is: "But you are indeed more clear-sighted than Lynceus himself to us: who, as it seems, having looked through the man himself, discern what is within." The same author in *Icaromenippus*: "How have you now suddenly become like a Lynceus, so that you discern all things?" Horace in his first epistle to Maecenas:
> Though you cannot contend in eyesight as far as Lynceus,

Apollonius in the *Argonautica* writes that this Lynceus was so clear-sighted that he even penetrated the earth itself with the sharpness of his eyes, and saw what was happening among those in the underworld.

# What is in the mind of the sober man, is on the tongue of the drunkard.

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
I 2
<meta>catchword: Aristoteles</meta>

<margin>Bold is the voice before the mixing bowl. <note>original: Θρασεῖα δὲ πρὸ κρητῆρος φωνὰ γίνεται.</note></margin> Often, those who wish to speak cannot restrain the voices that are about to pass through the throat. Pindar in the *Nemean Odes* says: "Bold is the voice near the mixing bowl." This is either because wine brings confidence, or because it is safe to speak grandly at a banquet, or because, as he says, one is praised deservedly and without danger in such a setting.

### To cross the Aegean in a little wicker boat. LVI

<margin>To sail across the Aegean on a wicker mat. <note>original: Ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς τὸν Αἰγαῖον διαπλεῦσαι.</note></margin> That is, to cross the Aegean in a boat made of twigs. This is said of those who attempt to accomplish an exceedingly difficult task with trivial effort. Lucian in *The Sects* says: "Wanting to sail across the Aegean or Ionian sea on a wicker mat, as the proverb says." This six-foot line is cited by Suidas. It also appears in Aristophanes' *Peace*:
<margin>He could sail in a little bundle or on a wicker mat. <note>original: Ἐν ῥιπὶ κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέοι.</note></margin> That is:
Let him sail in a small bundle and in wicker-work.
He cites Simonides as being rather fond of profit, because he wrote poems for gain.
<margin>Wicker <note>original: Ῥὶψ</note></margin> is a flexible vine or a willow branch, derived from the word "to bend" <note>original: ῥέπω</note>, evidently because it is bent due to its pliancy. This is also cited here:
<margin>If one sails with a favorable god, one might sail even on a wicker mat. <note>original: Ἐν ῥιπὶ πλέῃ, κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέοι.</note></margin> That is:
If anyone should sail with a favoring deity,
He might sail even in a willow wicker-boat.
This also appears among proverbial maxims, likewise cited by the commentator on Aristophanes:
<margin>If God wills, you may sail even on a wicker mat. <note>original: Θέλοντος κἂν ἐπὶ ῥιπὸς πλέοις.</note></margin> That is:
With God favoring, you may sail even in wicker.

### More long-lived than a Phoenix. LVII

Lucian in *The Sects*: "Unless you live the years of a phoenix." We have spoken elsewhere of the longevity of the phoenix. Its rarity also gave rise to a proverb, "Rarer than a phoenix," which is like that saying, "Rarer even than a white crow." For they say there is only one phoenix, if the writers are to be believed.

### When we have labored most, we are in the same state. LVIII

Lucian in *The Sects*: "Striving for the thing in the proverb, after much toil we are just the same." That is: The proverb is enacted when, though we have labored much, we are just as we were before. This refers to those who labor in vain. This happens to those who, after long study, are found to be no more learned, or after long business, no wealthier.

### To pound water in a mortar. LIX

<margin>To strike water in a mortar. <note>original: Ὕδωρ ἐν ὅλμῳ πλήττειν.</note></margin> That is, to beat water with a pestle. Lucian in *The Sects*: "Just as if someone, having poured water into a mortar, should strike it with an iron pestle." It applies to those who labor fruitlessly; for even if someone beats water until their shoulders ache, it will be nothing other than water. Lucian in the same work: "Not knowing that even if you strike the mortar until your shoulders drop off, as they say, the water remains water just the same." Suidas expresses it in this way: "Beating the water in the mortar many times, the water remains equally water." No matter how much you teach <term>a donkey the lyre</term> <note>A proverb for teaching someone who lacks the capacity to learn.</note>, no matter how much you advise a stupid person, he continues to be like himself.

### The Gnomon and the Rule. LX

That which is the most important part of any matter, and to which alone all other things are compared, they used to call the "rule" and the "gnomon" <note>A gnomon is a carpenter's square or the pin of a sundial; here it means a standard of judgment.</note> by a proverb. Lucian in *Harmonides*: "Is he not the most choice head of the matter, whom they call the gnomon and the upright rule of such things?" The same author in *The Scythian*: "This is your Greek rule." Likewise in *The Sects*: "A technical rule and an accurate plumb-line for such things." Furthermore, builders level their structures by the rule. They also use gnomons. Now, a gnomon consists of two straight lines which, by intersecting one another, form a divided square.

### The Head. LXI

It is of the same form when we call the chief part of a business or the author of a deed the "head." Terence in *The Brothers*: "That you are the head <note>The source or instigator.</note> of this affair." Examples are found everywhere among both Greek and Latin writers. In the same way, we also call the "Citadel" of some matter. Ari-

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Aristotle, in the preface of his *Rhetoric to Alexander*, says: <note>original: ὡς ἀκρόπολις ἐστὶ σωτηρίας</note> "Since it is the citadel of safety." The poet Poneros <note>Erasmus likely refers to a fragment found in Athenaeus</note> in the tenth book of Athenaeus said: <note>original: πάντων δ' οἰνῶν μητρόπολιν ἔιν' ἢ οἴνην</note> "Wine is the metropolis <note>The 'mother-city' or source</note> of all evils." From this arises drunkenness, from this madness, from this revelry. Plato, in the first book of the *Laws*: <note>original: Κεφάλαιον δὴ παιδείας λέγομεν τὴν ὀρθὴν τροφὴν</note> "We consider the head <note>The chief part</note> of education to be right upbringing." Plautus in the *Asinaria*: "I was the **head** for finding this money today, I was the **foot**." Indeed, we say "neither head nor foot" of a speech is visible <note>Meaning it makes no sense from beginning to end</note>. The same author in the *Captives*: "Because neither foot nor head appears anywhere." He uses the word "head" differently when he indicates that a matter is not explained point by point, but proposed in summary. Thus Aeschines against Timarchus: <note>original: ὡς ἠ' ἐν κεφαλαίῳ εἰρῆσθαι</note> "To speak as if in a summary." The same man in the oration *On the False Embassy* said in the same sense: <note>original: διὰ κεφαλαίων</note> "Through the main points." Likewise Demosthenes in the oration *On the Chersonese*: <note>original: ἐν κεφαλαίῳ δ' ἃ λέγω φράσας καταβήσομαι</note> "When I have stated what I am saying in summary, I wish to step down." Again in the oration *Against Zenothemis*: <note>original: τὸ δ' ἐν πρᾶγμα ὑπὲρ ὧ τὴν ψῆφον οἴσετε, ὡς εἰπεῖν ἐν κεφαλαίῳ, τοῦτόν ἐστι</note> "Therefore the business upon which you will cast your votes, to speak in summary, is this."

### A Dream.
-> LXII <-

We call a futile, empty, and worthless thing a "dream" by way of a proverb. Terence in *The Brothers*: "A dream of money." Lucian in *Harmonides*: <note>original: πάντα ἐκεῖνα ὑπώκνημα ὀνείρατα φασὶ, καὶ τῶν σκιαί</note> "All those things are 'wind-egg' dreams, as they say, and shadows of words." The same in the dialogue of *Nireus, Thersites, and Menippus*: <note>original: ὀνείρατά μοι λέγεις</note> "You are telling me dreams." Plato in the seventh book of the *Republic*: "And so the city will be inhabited by us and by you in reality, and not in a dream." The same in the *Theaetetus*: <note>original: Ἄκουε δὴ ὄναρ ἀντὶ ὀνείρατος</note> "Hear now a dream for a dream," that is, a frivolous argument for a frivolous one. And Syrus the slave in *The Brothers* calls his master a "dream" compared to Demea: "As great as you are, you are nothing but wisdom; he is futile, a dream." Plautus in *The Two Captives*: "This man dreams while awake." Plato in the third book of the *Laws* used "dreams" to mean faint traces. For when he had related that Darius was not the son of a king, but had come to the kingdom through right training and institution so that he obtained only a seventh portion in the division of the realm, he says: <note>original: ὃ νὺ νῦν ἔτι... σμικρὰ ὀνείρατα λέλειπται</note> "Of which thing even now some small dreams remain."

### Not even in the barbershops.
-> LXIII <-

Lucian in the booklet titled *How History Should Be Written*: <note>original: οὔτε ἃ λεγόμεν' ἐστὶ τοῖς, ὧδι κερσέων τὰ τοιαῦτα μυθολογέντων ἀκούσας</note> "Who has not even heard such things being told as stories in the barbershops, as the saying goes." This is because idle men usually lounge in the shops of barbers, and each brings his own story into the open. Whence Horace:
> They rejoice, when the head is shaved,
> To tell of the talkative sailors' dangers in safety.

Likewise elsewhere:
> I suppose
> It is known to all the bleary-eyed and the barbers.

Which we have mentioned elsewhere.

### Is Saul also among the prophets?
<margin>Is Saul also among the prophets? <note>original Hebrew: הגם שאול בנביאים</note></margin>
-> LXIIII <-

In the first book of Kings, the tenth chapter, a proverb of this kind is recorded: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" It arose from Saul, who, when he had happened upon a company of prophets, suddenly was himself seized by a divine frenzy and began to prophesy. Those who had known Saul before, marvelling at this, said among themselves, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" That voice was thereafter turned into a proverb among the Hebrews concerning a new, unexpected, and sudden occurrence. Among them, it is an iambic dimeter. Gregory Nazianzen in his *Apology for his Flight to Pontus* uses it thus, as if in these times everyone treats sacred literature and usurps some function: <note>original: αἰτιῶ τὸ... εἶν' Ἀλακῶν θεῶ, καὶ πάντων προφητευόντων, ὥστε εἶν' καὶ ἐν πρφηταις</note> "While instead of being taught by God, everyone prophesies, so that even Saul is among the prophets, according to the ancient history and proverb." Very similar to that are: "Corchorus <note>A bitter herb or poor man's vegetable</note> among the potherbs," and "Perfume in the lentils," or perfume mixed with lentils.

### The pitcher at the doors.
-> LXV <-

<note>original: Ἐπὶ θύραις τὴν ὑδρίαν</note> That is, "The water-pot at the doors." For Plautus used this word. Aristotle in the first book of the *Rhetoric*: "The end is a good, whence these things are said, and 'the pitcher is near the doors.'" <note>Refers to failing or stopping just at the finish line</note>

# CHILIAD II. CENTURY I. 377
<sig>I 3</sig>

...a good end for Priam <note>original: "τέλος πριάμῳ" (telos priamo). A reference to the tragic but ultimately dignified end of King Priam of Troy, suggesting that a long life must be judged by its conclusion.</note>. And, "It is a shameful thing to remain a long time" <note>original: "αἰσχρόν τοι δηρόν τε μένειν" (aischron toi deron te menein). A quote from Homer's Iliad regarding the Greek stay at Troy.</note>. And the proverb, "The water-jar at the doors."
That is, the end is good: from which those sayings arose, "And praise for Priam." Furthermore, "It is shameful to have stayed a long time."

<margin>The water-jar near the doors.</margin>
Now indeed, regarding that proverb, a certain interpreter—for our most learned friend Battista Egnazio <note>A Venetian humanist scholar and friend of Erasmus.</note> provided an anonymous book—says it signifies a thing that is despised and cheap. For people neglect those things which are met with everywhere, and which easily fall to anyone. Therefore, no one is eager to pick up a water-jar placed in the doorway, for it is easy to reach. But they seek more after pearls hidden away in chests. Plutarch, in his essay *On Having Many Friends*, says that a bramble-bush, which clings of its own accord, is neglected and passed by, while the vineyard and olive trees are sought after; citing this sentiment: "For one should not choose that which is easily caught" <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ αἱρετέον πάντων τὸ ῥᾳδίως ἁλισκόμενον" (ou gar haireteon panton to rhadios haliskomenon).</note>. That is, one should not take up what is allowed to be obtained very easily. Likewise, Seneca says in his *Letters*: "Many pass by open things, but pry into what is hidden and concealed. Sealed things invite the thief. Whatever lies open seems cheap. The burglar passes by open doors. The public has these habits, and every ignorant person likewise: they desire to break into secrets." Furthermore, the proverb seems incomplete and mutilated. Since Aristotle refers to many things in this manner, as if they were otherwise well enough known by themselves. It appears to be a half-line of iambic trimeter <note>A common meter in Greek drama.</note> borrowed from some comic poet.

---

### It is by no means difficult to praise an Athenian in Athens.

<margin>LXVI</margin>
<margin>Aristotle in the first book of the *Rhetoric*: "For as Socrates used to say, it is not difficult to praise Athenians in Athens."</margin>
Aristotle in the first book of the *Rhetoric*, that is: "For just as Socrates said, it is hardly difficult to praise Athenians in Athens." He cites the same thing in the same work when dealing with introductions: "It is by no means difficult to praise Athenians among Athenians, but among the Spartans it would be difficult." This is found in Plato's *Menexenus*, and it has passed into the status of an adage. It was said, however, because of the encomiums <term>encomium: a speech of high praise</term> and panegyric <term>panegyric: a public speech delivered in praise of a person or thing</term> orations which were customarily delivered in Athens for those who had died bravely in war. In these speeches, since many things were said in praise of the Athenian people, they were heard with favorable ears, because everyone favors their own praises.

---

### Justice itself is a small thing.

<margin>LXVII</margin>
Aristotle in the first book of the *Rhetoric*: "Wherefore they also say that justice is a small thing" <note>original: "διὸ καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην φασὶ, μικρὸν εἶναι" (dio kai ten dikaiosynen phasi, mikron einai).</note>. By this proverb they signified that it does not carry much weight if you are honest, unless you are also considered to be so; and that reputation is worth far more than the thing itself. But how much better is Aeschylus in the tragedy titled 
<margin>*Seven Against Thebes*, concerning Amphiaraus: "For he does not wish to seem the best, but to be so, reaping the deep furrow through his mind."</margin>
That is: "For he desires not to seem, but to be the best of men, enjoying the good harvest of a profound mind." Socrates spoke more rightly, advising that each person should be such as he wishes to be considered. Euripides is more modest in *Orestes*, approving of reputation when the reality is not present, as if it were the next best thing:
<margin>"Reputation is the strongest thing, even if it be far from the truth."</margin>
That is: "Though the reality be absent, reputation is best." Likewise Terence in *The Brothers*: "If that does not grieve you in reality, yet to pretend it is certainly the mark of a man."

---

### Wickedness needs only an opportunity.

<margin>LXVIII</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, *Rhetoric* book 2: "And against those for whom they have a pretext, whether on account of ancestors, or themselves, or friends, or those who have been treated well, or will be, either themselves, or their ancestors, or those for whom they care. For as the proverb says, wickedness needs only a pretext."</margin>
Aristotle, *Rhetoric* book 2, that is: "Or against those for whom they have an opportunity, whether in the name of their ancestors, or their own, or of friends, or of those by whom they have been treated with kindness, or when they are about to be, either themselves, or their elders, or those for whom they are concerned. For as it is said in the proverb, malice needs only an opportunity." This will apply to those eager to do harm, who, lest they seem to have hurt someone without cause, weave together pretexts. A line from a mime of Publilius <note>Publilius Syrus, a writer of sententious maxims.</note> is celebrated here, if I am not mistaken, to this effect: "He who wishes to do harm never fails to find a reason." And today a proverb is commonly circulated among our own people that is not entirely to be despised: "He will easily find a stick who desires to beat a dog." That line of Terence looks to the same point: "He invents excuses, so that he may not give diligently." Also that of Martial: "Not because I have so deserved, but it is a pleasure to do this."

<summary>This page examines several classical adages regarding the ease of praising people to their faces, the social value of reputation versus actual justice, and the tendency of the wicked to find excuses for their actions.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adages, Aristotle, Socrates, reputation vs reality, justice, pretexts for malice, classical rhetoric, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
<note>Page 378</note>

Perhaps Euripides also alluded to this when he spoke thus in *Iphigenia at Aulis*:

> Only a slight pretext was needed,
> Upon which I and your children, who have been left behind,
> Shall receive you with the reception you deserve to receive. <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ βραχείαις προφάσεως...; Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation which is here rendered into English.</note>

They also cite this line from Menander:
> A small pretext is enough for doing evil. <note>original Greek: Μικρὰ πρόφασίς ἐστι τοῦ πρᾶξαι κακῶς.</note>

### Or to take tribute even from a dead man. LXIX

To take even from the dead. <note>original Greek: Κἂν ἀπὸ νεκροῦ φέρειν.</note> This is said of a man who hunts for profit from any source, by fair means or foul. Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, when discussing things that are considered shameful, says: "such as [taking from] the poor or the dead. Whence also the proverb: 'to take even from a dead man.' For this comes from a base greed for gain." <note>original Greek: οἷον... πενήτων, ἢ τεθνεώτων...</note> Close to this is that other saying:
> He asks for flour even from statues. <note>original Greek: Αἰτεῖ γε καὶ τοὺς ἀνδριάντας ἄλφιτα.</note>

This originated from tyrants who collected taxes even from graves or the statues of the deceased. It is read in a certain letter to Crates by Diogenes: "Go also to the statues that are in the forum and ask them for food." <note>original Greek: Καὶ τοὺς ἀνδριάντας οὐκ ἂν τῇ ἀγορᾷ περιιὼν αἰτοῖς τὰ ἄλφιτα.</note>

### Shame is in the eyes. LXX

Shame is in the eyes. <note>original Greek: Ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς ἡ αἰδώς.</note> We are ashamed of those things which are out in the open. For the sight of others either strikes us with shame or renews it. Hence it happens that children, when they feel shame, cover their eyes. And in Plato, Socrates, when about to speak of love, covers his eyes out of shame, doubtless alluding to this. For this reason also the poets depict Cupid as blind, because he is most shameless. To the same point belongs that saying of Cicero: "A letter does not blush." We also see that those who are blind are very often lacking in modesty. Ovid had this in view when he said that night, being blind, is free from shame:
> Night, love, and wine, he says, persuade nothing moderate.
> The first lacks shame; Bacchus and Love lack fear.

Aristotle records the adage in the second book of his *Rhetoric*: "And those things which are before the eyes and in the open. Whence they also say proverbially, that shame is in the eyes." <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὰ ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ καὶ τὰ ἐν φανερῷ...</note> It is also cited in Athenaeus, book 13. The same author, inquiring in his *Problems* into the reason why the ears of those feeling shame turn red, while the eyes of those who are angry do so, cites this testimony. "Or is it," he says, "that shame in the eyes is a certain chilling accompanied by fear? So that it reasonably leaves the eyes: for when the heat is driven to the outside, it goes especially to these parts: or to the tips of the ears. For in others, just as in those who are angry, the heat leaps up, and it becomes most apparent in the eyes because of their white color." <note>original Greek: ἢ ὅτι... ἡ αἰδὼς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς κατάψυξίς τις...</note> This verse is cited from Euripides:
> My child, shame is born in the eyes of men. <note>original Greek: Αἰδὼς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς γίνεται τέκνον.</note>

Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
> But in these there is no shame,
> Not even in the eyes of these old shoes. <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ τούτοις γε οὐκ ἔνι...</note>

To this may also be referred what Aristotle cites from Sappho in the first book of his *Rhetoric*:
> Shame would not have held your eyes. <note>original Greek: Αἰδὼς κήν σε οὐκ εἶχεν ὄμματα.</note>

Hence also those figures of speech: "With what face, with what brow will you dare to rebuke your son?" And that in Cicero’s letters to Atticus: "For the candidates do not even dare to show their faces." <note>original Greek: φαινοπροσωπεῖν (to show a bold face).</note> Indeed, even today people commonly say: "You won't dare to show your face." In Euripides' *Iphigenia at Aulis*, Menelaus commands Agamemnon to look at him, clearly so that he might be ashamed of his deed.

# SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
-> I 4 <-

<note>original: "βλέψον πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ἵν’ ἀρχὰς τῶν λόγων ταύτας λάβω."</note> **Look toward us, so that I may take these as the beginnings of my speech.** That is: **Look straight at us, so that I may take this as the starting point for speaking.** Isocrates <note>A famous Greek orator</note> responds: <note>original: "πῶς γὰρ ἂν, ὃς οὐκ ἀνακαλύψω βλέφαρον ἀτρέμας γέγως;"</note> **For how could I, who will not uncover my eyelid, having become calm?** That is: **Shall I truly fear to lift my eyes to you, son of Atreus?** Perhaps there should have been added here what Achilles calls Agamemnon in Homer: <term>dog-faced</term> <note>original: "κυνῶπα"</note>, on account of his impudence, as if he had the eyes of a dog and was shameless.

### Misfortunes bring men together. LXXI

<note>original: "Συνάγει τοὺς ἀνθρώπους κακά."</note> That is: **Misfortunes bring men together.** A proverbial sentiment which declares that which commonly happens: that enemies sometimes become friends because of some misfortune falling upon both in common. Aristotle, in the first book of his *Rhetoric*, says: <note>original: "οὐδὲν γὰρ κωλύει γίνεσθαι ταὐτὰ συμφέροντα τοῖς ἐναντίοις..."</note> **For nothing prevents the same things from being advantageous to opponents. Whence it is said, that misfortunes bring men together, whenever the same thing is harmful to both.** That is: For nothing forbids the same thing from being conducive to both adversaries. Whence that saying arises, that men are reconciled by evils, as often as the same thing is injurious to both. We have spoken elsewhere of <term>syncretism</term> <note>The union of two opposing parties against a common third enemy</note>. Indeed, the proverb can also be turned this way: to say that the unlearned favors the unlearned, the infant the infant, the spendthrift the spendthrift. For it is not only a similarity in good things that glues a relationship together, but also from common evils a mutual benevolence is frequently born. Generally, those who have suffered shipwreck together love one another, as do those who have served in the military together, or those who were captured by an enemy at the same time; finally, those who labor under the same diseases of body or mind.

### Love as if you will one day hate, hate as if you will one day love. LXXII

<note>original: "Δεῖ φιλεῖν ὥσπερ μισήσοντα, μισεῖν δ’ ὥσπερ φιλήσοντα."</note> That is: **One must love as if one is to hate, and one ought to hate as if one is to love.** Aristotle, in his books on *Rhetoric*, sufficiently indicates that this sentiment of Bias <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> has passed into a proverb when he writes: **That saying of Bias, as they say, to love as if one will hate, but rather to hate as if one will love.** That is: One should not love as if one is to hate, as they say, but rather exercise hatred as if one is to be a friend someday. And a little further down: **But to love, as they say, but as if one will always love.** That is: One ought to love not as they say, but as if one will love forever. For the philosopher demonstrates there in what way commonly received and repeated sentiments are to be refuted and corrected.

Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in his discourse *On Friendship*, writes that this saying celebrated in the name of Bias was so displeasing to Scipio that he denied any voice more hostile to friendship could be found than his who said one ought to love as if he might someday hate. Nor indeed could he be led to believe that this was said by Bias (as was thought), who was considered one of the Seven Sages; rather, it was the sentiment of some impure or ambitious man, or one reducing everything to his own power. For in what way, he says, can anyone be a friend to him whose enemy he thinks he could be? Nay, it will even be necessary to desire and hope that the friend sins as often as possible, so that he may give him, as it were, more handles for reproof. On the other hand, it will be necessary to be vexed, to grieve, and to envy the right actions and advantages of friends. Therefore this precept, whoever's it is, has the power to destroy friendship. This instead should have been the precept: that we should apply such diligence in forming friendships that we never begin to love someone whom we could someday hate. Thus far Cicero.

The same Aristotle, a little earlier, refers to—and repeats in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*—this six-foot line: <note>original: "οὐδ’ ὡς φασιν, ὃς τις οὐκ ἀεὶ φιλεῖ."</note> That is: **He is not a friend, who ceases to love.** He who loves for the sake of profit, having obtained what he desired, ceases to love. But the friendship of the good, since it rests upon virtue, is immortal. This verse is found in Euripides' *Trojan Women*. Diogenes Laertius records the adage in a mutilated form: **He used to say to love as if they would hate, for most men are evil.** To this should be added that mime of Publilius, which is found in Aulus Gellius: **Hold a friend in such a way that you think it possible he could become an enemy.** And another by the same author, I believe, though under the title of Seneca: **So trust a friend, that there be no room for an enemy.** Sophocles likewise in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*: **For I have recently learned that our enemy is to be hated only so far as one who will love again. And toward a friend, I will wish to be of service and help...**

<summary>Erasmus explores two proverbs: one regarding how shared misfortunes create bonds between people, and the famous maxim of Bias on the limits of friendship and the dangers of total trust.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, Bias of Priene, Aristotle, Cicero, shared suffering, syncretism, social ethics, classical proverbs</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

> For I have recently learned that if I should ever be
> An enemy to any man, I should hate him only so far as
> One who might later be a friend: likewise toward a friend
> I should perform my duties as one who will not
> Always remain a friend: for to very many
> The harbor of fellowship is not safe enough.
<note>original: "Ὡς αἰεὶ τ’ οὐ μενοῦντα..." Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation of these lines from Sophocles' Ajax, which advise moderation in love and hate because circumstances change.</note>

---

->**The Attic Neighbor.**<- LXXIII

**Atticus aduena.** <note>original: "Ἀττικὸς πάροικος"</note> This was said of violent and fierce neighbors. Duris, according to Zenodotus, says it arose from the character of the Athenians, because they were once accustomed to drive their neighbors out of their own dwellings. Craterus thinks it originated because the Athenians who were sent to Samos expelled the native inhabitants. The adage is noted by Aristotle in the third book of his *Rhetoric*: "Furthermore," he says, "some proverbs are also maxims, serving as testimonies, such as: *The Attic neighbor*." Therefore, it will properly apply to those who have been recently admitted into some office in such a way that they eject those who were there before them.

---

->**Purple must be judged next to purple.**<- LXXIIII

**Ἡ πορφύρα παρὰ τὴν πορφύραν διακρίνεται.** That is, *Purple is to be judged by purple.* The most certain judgment arises from comparison. Hence, buyers about to purchase purple cloth, lest they be deceived, bring another piece of purple to compare it with. We may use this whenever we say that the insignificance or ignorance of the unlearned cannot be fully detected unless they are compared with the writings of the eloquent and the erudite. For indeed, if you compare even Sallust <note>A Roman historian known for his brief, punchy style.</note> with Cicero, the former—otherwise most eloquent in his own right—seems to fall silent. The adage is cited by the sophist Phoebammon in his commentary *On Rhetorical Figures*. Isocrates also mentions it in his *Panathenaic* oration: "But just as we consider and test purple and gold by showing them alongside another sample." I do not think it will be entirely irrelevant <note>original: "ἀπροσδιόνυσον" (literally 'nothing to do with Dionysus')</note> if I add a passage here about comparing purple from Flavius Vopiscus’s *Life of Aurelian*. "You remember," he says, "that there was in the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest on the Capitoline a short purple cloak made of wool; when the matrons and Aurelian himself held their own purple garments next to it, the others seemed to turn pale, like the color of ash, in the presence of that divine brilliance." This gift is said to have been given to Aurelian by the King of the Persians, who obtained it from the inner Indians, writing: "Accept a purple such as we have." For afterward, both Aurelian and Probus, and most recently Diocletian, having sent out most diligent searchers, sought that kind of purple but were unable to find it. For it is said that Indian *sandix* <note>A bright red or orange pigment.</note> produces such purple if it is properly treated. Quintilian alluded to this in his twelfth book, in the chapter *On the Kinds of Speaking*, dealing with a style of speech which, because it is mediocre, commands admiration on its own, but when compared to things that are excellent, ceases to be admired. "It holds admiration," he says, "and not undeservedly; for even that level is not easy to reach: but these things vanish and die by comparison with better things; just as wool dyed with seaweed <note>original: "fuco" - a cheaper red dye often used to imitate true murex purple.</note> pleases when away from true purples; but if you compare them, it is overwhelmed even by the sight of a better cloak, as Ovid says."

---

->**Saturnian blear-eyedness.**<- LXXV

**Κρονικαὶ λῆμαι.** That is, *Saturnian rheum.* It is said of those who are dim-sighted and stupid: especially those who lose their wits through the fault of old age. For *lema* is a thickened humor in the eyes from which "blear-eyedness" <note>lippitudo</note> arises. It is derived from *lyo* (I see) and the negative particle *me* (not): because thick tears of this kind occupying the eyes obstruct the sight. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
> But O you two, truly blear-eyed in your minds with Saturnian thoughts.
<note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὦ κρονικαῖς γνώμαις..."</note>
He said "thoughts" (*gnomis*) instead of "rheum" (*lemis*), from which the Greek *lemo* means to be blear-eyed or dim-sighted. Furthermore, they are called "Saturnian" as if to say "senile and ancient": because *Chronos* (Time), that is, Saturn, is depicted by the poets as gouty and old, and the god of time. Indeed, the Greeks sometimes call "ancient things" (*archaia*) "stupid things." Plato in the *Euthydemus*: "You are talking nonsense, and are more ancient than is fitting." That is, you are more foolish than is proper. And "more Saturnian" means "more foolish": that is, nonsense and ravings. Timotheus in Athenaeus, book 3: "Young Jupiter reigns, but of old Saturn was the ruler." Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:

<summary>Erasmus explains three proverbs: "The Attic Neighbor" (referring to aggressive displacement), "Purple next to Purple" (the necessity of comparison for true judgment), and "Saturnian Blear-eyedness" (the mental decline associated with old age).</summary>

# FOURTH CENTURY OF ADAGES

<margin>And the tragic poet says he is an ancient Saturn</margin> ->The mind, that is,<-
He says he will soon return the tragic actors 
to the mind of Saturn.
<note>original: "Seſe tragœdos mente Saturnos ait / Mox redditurum." Referring to becoming senile or "old-fashioned" like the god Saturn.</note>
->The same in *The Clouds*,<-
<margin>And how, O fool, do you both smell of Saturn and the moon-struck?</margin> ->that is,<-
And how, O fool, do you both smell of the Saturnalia and the moon? <note>original: "Saturnalia olens, & lunaris" - implying someone is ancient, out of date, or senile.</note> Dionysodorus, in Plato’s *Euthydemus*, calls Socrates a "Saturn," meaning he is slow-witted and stupid; "Thus," he says, "you are a Saturn," that is, "You are so very old-fashioned." Lucian alluded to this in *Timon*: "You have bleary eyes and are dim-sighted toward what is happening." And a little further down in the same work: "And little by little they reveal you, O noblest of gods, to be a Saturn, first by your bleary eyes." That is, little by little they turn you into a Saturn, most excellent of gods, by driving you from honor. Plutarch shows that those who were foolish in their old age were commonly called *kronolerous* <note>original: "κρονολήρους"</note>: that is, "Saturn-ravings," clearly on account of the old wives' tales told about this god. The same Plutarch relates these in his commentary *On the Face in the Moon*: that Saturn sleeps in a deep cave on a certain fortunate island, embracing golden rocks. Furthermore, this sleep happens to him because of chains skillfully fashioned for that purpose by Jupiter. Moreover, birds that frequent the summit of the cliff bring him ambrosia, and the whole island is filled with a wonderful fragrance, as if from a bubbling spring in the rock; demons are present to watch over and serve Saturn. These were once joined to him in friendship when he ruled over gods and men, and they predict many things about future events from him. But they report the greatest things and concerning the greatest matters in such a way that they seem to be the dreams of Saturn. For whatever Jupiter has turned over in his mind, Saturn dreams it. Certain trifles of this sort about Saturn are recorded in this book I mentioned. Now I leave it to the judgment of the learned reader whether this adage pertains to what the Pythagoreans call the sea <term>symbolically</term>—the "tear of Saturn"—as the same author testifies in his commentary *On Isis and Osiris*. Indeed, seawater is not only salty and bitter, but also thicker and more impure than the rest.

### To have bleary eyes like gourds.
->LXXVI<-
<margin>To be bleary-eyed with gourds.</margin> That is, "To have eyes as bleary as gourds." This belongs to the same form as the previous adage. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
<margin>And surely now you see them, unless you have bleary eyes like gourds.</margin> ->that is,<-
But now you clearly see them, unless perhaps you have bleary eyes like gourds.
<margin>gourds</margin> The Greeks call *kolokyntas* <note>original: "κολοκύντας"</note> what we call gourds. These are the words of Socrates pointing out the clouds. That is: unless you see absolutely nothing, and have such large rheum <note>eye discharge</note> in your eyes as big as gourds.

### To have bleary eyes like pots.
->LXXVII<-
<margin>To be bleary-eyed with pots.</margin> To have bleary eyes like pots. A proverbial hyperbole, very similar to the last one. Lucian, against an unlearned man who was buying many books, says: "bleary-eyed with pots," indicating tears equal in size to pots. Both of these adages are more elegant and pleasant whenever they are applied to the mind: as if one were to say of a man of dull judgment, who is profoundly blind and errs shamefully, that he is bleary-eyed not with rheum, but with pots.

### Rustic hatred.
->LXXVIII<-
<margin>A rustic hatred,</margin> that is, "Rustic hatred." The ancients called a fierce hatred by this name, because country folk are for the most part <term>misanthropes</term> <note>haters of mankind</note>, and they hate more bitterly and implacably. Lucian against the unlearned: "You suffer from a rustic hatred, as they say, from everyone on account of your foulness." From this we also call courtesy "civility" of manners and "humanity." And among legal experts, a "civil" action is distinguished from a "criminal" one. Finally, whatever the Greeks want to be understood as barbarian, monstrous, or cruel, they call *agrion* <note>wild/savage</note>.

### The Megarians are neither third nor fourth.
->LXXIX<-
<margin>The Megarians are neither third nor fourth.</margin> That is, "The Megarians are neither third nor fourth." This was once said of men who were excessively lazy and contemptible, and worthy of no honor. The adage arose from a certain oracle. Some, including Stephanus, Mneas, and Ion, think it was given to the Aeginetans; others to the Megarians. Thus Mneas relates that when the Aeginetans had defeated the Aetolians in Achaia and captured a tenth of the *pentecontors* (that is a ship of fifty oarsmen), they dedicated this to Pythian Apollo as a monument of victory. And they asked the god who were the most excellent of the Greeks, thinking that on account of that victory, the first praise would be granted to them by Apollo. The oracle responded in this manner:

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

A Thessalian mare, a Lacedaemonian woman,
And men who drink the water of fair Arethusa <note>The fountain of Arethusa in Syracuse, Sicily.</note>.
But even better than these are those who dwell between
Tiryns and Arcadia of the many sheep,
The linen-corsleted Argives, the spurs of war.
But you, people of Aegium, are neither third, nor fourth,
Nor twelfth, nor in the reckoning, nor in the number. -> that is, <-
The Thessalian mare excels the rest, and the Spartan woman.
Furthermore, the men who drink the beautiful streams of Arethusa.
Beyond these also, the race inhabiting the middle
Of Tiryns and Arcadia, famous for white sheep, wins out,
The Argives, the prods of wars, and powerful in arms.
But you, people of Aegium, no third rank receives you,
Nor fourth, nor twelfth, nor finally of you
Is there any reckoning anywhere, nor number, nor place.

The author who wrote the short commentaries on Theocritus <note>The Scholiast on Theocritus.</note> relates this epigram slightly differently, certainly in this manner:
Of all the earth, Pelasgian Argos is best,
Thracian horses, and Lacedaemonian women,
And men who drink the water of fair Arethusa.
But even better than these are those who dwell between
Tiryns and Arcadia of the many sheep,
The linen-corsleted Argives, the spurs of war.
But you, O Megarians, are neither third, nor fourth,
Nor twelfth, nor in the reckoning, nor in the number.

Callimachus likewise in his epigrams referred the proverb to the Megarians:
But of the wretched
Bride, as of the Megarians, there is no reckoning, nor number. -> that is, <-
But just as it once happened to the Megarians,
Of the unhappy Nymph, there is no place, or reckoning.

Likewise Theocritus in *The Love of Cynisca*:
But for us, we are worthy of no reckoning nor are we counted,
Wretched Megarians, in the most dishonored lot. -> that is, <-
There is no reckoning of us, nor are we placed in any number,
Like the Megarians once were, of the lowest lot.

There is also a rank among lovers, when this one is first with a mistress, that one second, another third or fourth. Just as in wills there is a first, second, and third heir. The proverb is also uttered in this form: *You are worthy of the Megarians' portion*, that is, worthy of the Megarians' part or place. To this also looks that famous line from Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 2:
Never counted in war, nor in counsel. -> that is, <-
Nowhere in deliberations, nowhere is he numbered in arms.

It is cited from Euripides:
For cowardly men have no
Number in battle, but are absent even if they are present. -> that is, <-
The fearful have no
Number in battle, but are away, though they be there most especially.

The Latins also seem to express this figure of speech. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>: *I think there is no one, who is at least in some number.* That is, who is of some importance, of some value. The same in *Philippics* 3: *A certain father, Bombalio, a man of no number, nothing is more contemptible than him.* Plutarch in his *Table Talk*: *But of my citizens, just as of the Megarians, there is no reckoning.* That is: *And yet of my citizens, as if of the Megarians, there is no account.* The same elsewhere in the same work: *But of the Democritean images, he said, just as of the Aegians or Megarians, there is no number nor reckoning.* That is: *And yet of the Democritean images, he said, just as of the Megarians or Aegians, there is no number, nor respect.* Indeed, I think that Aristophanes also lightly alluded to this when he writes in *The Acharnians*:

<summary>Erasmus explores the proverb "Not in the reckoning," tracing its origins to an oracle given to the Megarians (or Aegians) who were told they held no rank among the great powers of Greece. He provides numerous classical citations from poetry, drama, and oratory to show how "being in the number" became a metaphor for social or political importance.</summary>

# THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND

<margin>May the Megarians be washed away neither on land, nor in the market, nor in the sea, nor on the continent. <note>original: "Αἱ μὴ Μεγαρέας μήτ’ ἐν γῇ μήτ’ ἐν ἀγορᾷ, μήτ’ ἐν θαλάσσῃ, μή τ’ ἐν ἠπείρῳ κλύζῃ." This refers to a famous oracle that ranked the Megarians as "fourth" or last in importance.</note></margin>
-> that is, <-

-> It would be a sin for the Megarians to remain anywhere <-
-> In the land, nor the forum, nor in the sea, <-
-> Nor on the continent. <-

Indeed, by excluding the Megarians from four places, it surely looked toward that saying, *that they are fourth* <note>original: "ὅτι τέταρτοι." A reference to being ranked last or of no account.</note>. Although I suspect there is a flaw in the verses, namely in the phrase *neither on land*, unless perhaps in the fourth foot he allows himself a spondee, just as he allows an anapæst. It occurs to me that Marcus Tullius [Cicero] also alluded to this when he speaks thus in his *Brutus*: "To the two greatest, therefore, Crassus and Antonius, Lucius Philippus approached most closely, but at a long interval, yet he was the next. Thus, even if no one intervened who might prefer himself to him, I would still not call him second or third. For I would not count him second or third in a chariot race who has scarcely left the starting gates when the first has already received the palm; nor among orators, one who is so far from the first that he scarcely seems to be in the same race." In a similar form, Marcus Tullius in the second book of the *Academics* spoke of Democritus as being of the *fifth class*. "Who," he says, "would not prefer this philosopher to Cleanthes, Chrysippus, and the rest of a lower age, who, compared to him, seem to me to be of the *fifth class*?" That is, of the lowest order. Conversely, those are said to be of the *first class* who are preferred to others; and of *no class* who are utterly despised. This is a metaphor taken from the classes into which King Servius Tullius divided the Roman people according to their wealth. Florus, in his *Epitome* (book 49), called a man of the *lowest lot* one who was exceedingly obscure. "Andriscus," he says, "a man of the lowest lot, claiming to be the son of King Perseus, etc." Likewise, in *Epitome* 19, he called Gaius Glaucia a man of the *lowest lot*. This will be more elegant if it is transferred to matters of the mind: as if you were to say, a "genius of the lowest lot," or a speech scarcely to be compared with the writings of others, a "speech of the extreme class." To this form belongs when they call a man "of the first mark" or "of the last mark." And Marcus Tullius calls a greeting "from a better mark," meaning a careful salutation. Catullus adapted this to a person: "And whoever is of a better mark."

This is seen to be transferred from merchants, who attach a "mark" to wine or cloth indicating the price of the goods.

### A hare for its meat. LXXX

<term>A hare for its meat</term> <note>original: "Λαγὼς περὶ τῶν κρεῶν." A proverb describing someone fighting for their very existence or survival.</note>—that is, the hare is in danger regarding its meat, it is understood. It is said against those who are called into danger on account of some usefulness of their own. For we do not hunt the hare because it does harm, but because it has choice meat. For it is an animal both edible and timid, and defenseless, so that it seems nature produced the hare for the food of men. Moreover, the people of Rhegium were commonly called "hares," inasmuch as they were fearful and full of dread. The adage is also uttered in this manner: *the hare runs for its meat* <note>original: "ὁ λαγὼς περὶ τῶν κρεῶν τρέχει."</note>. That is, the hare runs for its life. It is said of those who contend fiercely because of great danger to themselves, or even the risk of their head [life]. The metaphor is transferred from hunting, in which the hare, because it understands it is being sought for death, flees with a most swift course, so much so that not infrequently it fails and dies in the middle of the run. Regarding this matter, Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Cleverness of Land and Sea Animals*, relates something by no means unworthy of being inserted in this place: <note>original Greek omitted for brevity; translation follows</note> "Furthermore, when dogs pursue a hare, if they kill it themselves, they rejoice to tear it apart and eagerly smear and stain themselves with blood. But if the hare, despairing of itself—as often happens—consumes whatever breath it has in the most intense running and so fails, the dogs, finding it dead, do not touch it at all, but stand still wagging their tails, just as if they had not contended for the sake of the meat, but rather had struggled for the victory." Charon, in Aristophanes' *Frogs*:
<margin>I do not carry a slave</margin> Unless he has fought the naval battle for the meat. -> that is, <-
I do not carry a slave, unless he has completed the naval
Battle, and fought for his meat.
The interpreter of Aristophanes adds at this place that at Arginusae, slaves were accustomed to fight not for money or any other reward, but for their lives. The same in *The Wasps*:
<margin>I will bite your heart with my tongue</margin> And run the race for the soul. -> that is, <-
I will make it so that you bite your heart, and run the race for your head and life. The same in the same play,

<meta>catchword: the hare</meta>

# FROM THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"Did I run for the flank or for the torch?" <note>original: Η λαγὼν ἢ λαμπάδα ἔδραμον;</note> that is,
Did you run for the hare, or the torch? Plutarch uses this more effectively in the Dialogue he wrote against Epicurus: "Aha!" he said laughing, "you seem to have been consumed for the sake of men's bellies, and are well worth the meat." <note>original: παπαὶ εἶπεν ἔγωγε γελάσας...</note> That is: "Good heavens," he says laughing, "you seem ready to make an assault upon the belly itself, and to be driven to that race which is said to be for the sake of meat." It signifies that he would bring the Epicureans into the greatest danger, because he had proposed, against the defenders of pleasure, that one cannot live pleasantly according to Epicurus. I suspect an allusion to ancient histories, which report that war sometimes broke out between peoples over meat snatched from sacrifices. Thus Pindar in the Nemean Odes: "Where he waged battles over meat." <note>original: ἵνα κρεῶν νὶν ὑπὲρ μάχας ἔλασεν.</note>

->The Carpathius and the hare.<-
LXXXI

"The Carpathius and the hare." <note>original: Ὁ καρπάθιος τὸν λαγών.</note> This was said against those who bring a harmful thing upon themselves. The adage is derived from this: since there were no hares on the island of the Carpathians, they took care to import them from elsewhere. But when the number of these animals had increased greatly—as they have a miraculous fertility—they began to devastate the crops of the island. Julius Pollux relates and interprets this proverb in the fifth book of *On Vocabulary* <term>On Vocabulary: referring to the 'Onomasticon', an ancient Greek thesaurus</term>. He adds that hares are not born on the island of Ithaca, nor were they in Sicily, until Anaxilas of Rhegium imported them; for which reason, as a victor in the Olympic games, he struck a coin for the people of Rhegium featuring a chariot and a hare. Aristotle also relates and interprets this in the third book of the *Rhetoric*.

->To grunt.<-
LXXXII

"To grunt" <note>original: γρύζειν</note>; they use this proverbially for "to open the mouth" or "to mutter." There are those who think "to grunt" is to emit a swine-like voice, derived from the sound "gry," which we have mentioned elsewhere. From this also the name "Gryllus" <note>meaning 'Piggy'</note> was fashioned in Plutarch, and "Grunnius Corocotta the piglet," whom Saint Jerome mentions. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
"Do you two dare even to mutter, you scum?" <note>original: γρύζειν δὲ καὶ τολμᾶτον ὦ καθάρματε;</note>
And again in the same play: "Nay, go to ruin and do not mutter a word." <note>original: Ἀλλὰ φθάρε καὶ μὴ γρύξης.</note>
With a similar figure of speech, Terence said in *The Brothers*: "Why are you snarling?" <note>original: Quid gannis?</note> And in *Phormio*: "That he might snarl back at those things."

->No animal, that is an animal.<-
LXXXIII

That figure also seems proverbial: "No animal, and what an animal." Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
"For Poverty, oh wretched one, is such that
nowhere is there any animal more deadly." <note>original: Πενία γάρ ἐστιν ὦ πίννη...</note>
The same author in *The Clouds*:
"But tell me, what kind of beast is Interest-upon-Interest?" <note>original: Τόκοι δ’ ἐπ’ ὀ τόκῳ τί θηκύου;</note>
Marcus Tullius [Cicero] to Atticus: "I recognized no trace of Terence; Metagenes has certainly perished. He made a journey through a property in which no animal remains." Nor does that phrase of Pliny’s wander far from this figure: "Regulus, the most wicked of two-legged animals."

->Not even a fly.<-
LXXXIIII

Akin to this is that proverbial hyperbole, "Not even a fly," by which we signify the greatest solitude of men. Plautus in *The Brutal Fellow*: "What women are you telling me about? Where there is not a single female fly in the house." Vibius Crispus, an orator born for delight (as Fabius [Quintilian] says), alluded to this:
"Whose character was as his eloquence,"
as Juvenal wrote, when asked if anyone was with Caesar in his private chamber, he replied: "Not even a fly is inside." He was marking with a double-edged joke the habit of Domitian, whose custom it was to seek a private hour for himself every day, during which he did almost nothing else but stab captured flies with a stylus.

->A common Mercury.<-
LXXXV

"A common Mercury." <note>original: Κοινὸς ὁ ἑρμῆς.</note> Lucian in *The Wishes*: "Therefore, as the common saying goes, 'Mercury is common,' put the wealth you have brought into the middle for all." <note>note: Mercury was the god of gain and luck; this phrase was shouted when someone found a treasure, claiming a share of the 'find'.</note> Plutarch in the booklet...

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
## K
<meta>catchword: they were</meta>

In the short book titled, *That the Philosopher ought especially to converse with Princes*, <note>original: "ὅτι μάλιστα τοῖς ἡγεμόσι δεῖ τὸν Φιλόσοφον διαλέγεσθαι"</note> Plutarch notes that through lack of culture and poor taste, the "Common Mercury" has become a "merchant and a hireling." <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἀμουσία καὶ ἀπειροκαλία τὸν κοινὸν ἑρμῆν ἐμπολαῖον καὶ ἐμμίσθον γίνεσθαι"</note> That is: *But through ignorance and lack of elegance, the common Mercury has been made a huckster and a seeker of gain.* Some believe this proverb arose because Mercury, as the author and inventor of thefts, first showed that things acquired by theft ought to be placed in a common pile. Others prefer to relate it to the fact that Mercury is the author of speech, through which every kind of commerce between men is established; hence he is also imagined by the poets to be a mediator between those above and those below, equally pleasing to the gods on high and those in the depths, because speech—the interpreter of the mind—reconciles the highest with the lowest, and kings with the common people.

There exists on this matter a rather charming fable by Aristides in the second book of his work written against Plato in defense of Rhetoric. I have chosen to include it here all the more because this author is by no means commonly known to the public.

<note>The following is a translation of the Greek passage provided in the source, which recounts a myth of human origins.</note>

When humans and other animals had recently been born, there was much tumult and confusion upon the earth. For they had no one to rule them, nor did they know how to manage themselves. There was no gathering together; rather, the stronger drove the weaker. They were not even fit to resist the other animals. In all things they were inferior to all others in one way or another; they were quickly overtaken by the flight of all birds—what Homer said happened to the Pygmies at the hands of the cranes then happened to all humans at the hands of all strong birds. In strength, they were far behind lions, boars, and many others, so that they perished in silence. Indeed, regarding the equipment of the body, they fell short not only of crows but even of snails, none of them being self-sufficient. As the race was thus perishing and slowly slipping away, Prometheus—who was always a lover of humanity—having no ambassadors to send on behalf of men (for they did not yet know how to send an elder), went himself of his own accord. Zeus, then listening to Prometheus speaking good and just things, and at the same time considering the truth of the matter himself, ordered his son Mercury to go to men carrying Rhetoric. Now, Prometheus had provided everyone with senses and the other members of the body like a hearth for all; but Zeus did not order the distribution of Rhetoric to be like a public handout <note>term: "theoric distribution" — a reference to the "theorika," money given to poor Athenian citizens to attend the theater</note> so that everyone should share in Rhetoric in succession, like eyes, ears, or feet. Instead, he ordered him to select the best, the most noble, and those with the strongest natures, and to entrust the gift to them, so that they might be able to save both themselves and others together. When Rhetoric came to men from the gods in this way, men were able to escape the harsh life among the wild beasts, and they ceased being enemies to one another in a cycle. They found common principles; descending from the mountains, they approached one another in various parts of the inhabited world. At first they lived in the open air, but later, as if already conquered by Reason, they established cities and built walls—not haphazardly as before, but so as to live in silent fellowship; and with the leaders of cities, they established laws, and came to know magistrates and civil government. And they brought offerings of thanks to the gods, making the first fruits of their speech, since even now the gods are most pleased when won over by speech, because it was first granted to them to know God as a gift. Thus, a great speaker is truly something clear and significant for a man from the beginning. And before those who are despised as being of no account, he who was truly someone on earth could use his will as he wished, making that will a safeguard of speech. And let our myth have its end.

If anyone prefers these things in Latin, we shall render the sense and flavor:

*In the beginning, when humans were recently born, there was a great tumult among them and the rest of the living creatures, and a disturbance upon the earth, because they could not interact with one another. For there was no thing coming between them to reconcile them; rather, those who were more powerful oppressed the inferior. Nor were they sufficiently fit to resist the other animals. For they were inferior to all of them in every respect, and were surpassed by some in one thing and others in another. For instance, they were surpassed by the whole race of birds in speed. Whence it happened that what Homer says happens to the Pygmies from the cranes, was then suffered everywhere from the stronger birds. Again, as far as strength is concerned, they were far surpassed by both lions and boars, and many others likewise. And in this manner they perished in silence. Furthermore, as to the protection and adornment of the body, they yielded not only to crows, but even to snails, nor did anyone have from himself what was necessary to protect life. Therefore, when the human race was perishing in that way and gradually slipping away, Prometheus, as he is always devoted to men, ascended into heaven as an orator on behalf of mortals: not indeed sent by them, for at that time no ambassadors were to be seen, but he went of his own accord. But Jupiter, partly out of favor for Prometheus, especially since he seemed to demand just things, and partly having considered the business with himself, orders his son Mercury to descend to men, bringing Rhetoric with him. He commanded, however, that he should impart it to mortals, not as Prometheus had given senses and the other members of the body to all equally—just as if distributing theater-money—so that all equally [might share] in Rhetoric...*

<summary>This page explores the mythological and proverbial origins of "Common Mercury," using a fable by Aristides to explain how Rhetoric was given to select humans to establish civilization and law.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, Prometheus, Aristides, Plato, Rhetoric, Pygmies, Homer, origins of civilization, Greek mythology, proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the origins of rhetoric and civilization, citing the Greek orator Aelius Aristides, before transitioning into a series of numbered proverbs (Adagia) with historical and literary commentary.</meta>

...they should be participants, no differently than they are of their eyes, hands, and feet: but rather that he <note>The god or nature</note> should select those most outstanding in talent, of the most noble character, and endowed with the most powerful natural ability, and finally bestow this gift upon them, so that they might be able to protect both their own safety and that of others. Furthermore, after Rhetoric had finally reached mortals, they were able to escape that most troublesome business they had with wild beasts; then indeed they ceased to practice hostilities against one another everywhere, once the beginnings of commerce were discovered. Departing from the mountains, some were joined to others in different parts of the world, living at first under the open sky: but later, when they had communicated with one another through words, they both founded a city and were distributed into ranks—not, as before, at random, but into the orders of the common people and leaders of war—and they established both princes and the state of the Republic with holy laws. They began to offer gifts to the Gods, consecrating the first fruits starting with speech. It is consistent that the gods even now rejoice in these things most of all. Since by this means it happened that we first came to know that there are gods. From this point onward man grew in such a way that he who had been weak and powerless at the beginning was afterwards raised on high: and he who before was held as nothing and despised, thereafter became the master of all things that are on the earth, having the right to use them as he pleased, prepared with no other bulwark for himself than speech. And here let the end of the story be for us. Thus far Aristides. There exists, if I remember correctly, a not dissimilar fable in Plato’s *Protagoras*.

## Feed wolf cubs. LXXXVI

Theocritus in *The Wayfarers* <note>original: "Hodœporis"</note> says:
*Feed even wolf cubs, feed them like dogs so they may eat you.* <note>original Greek: Θρέψαι καὶ λυκιδέας, θρέψαι κύνας ὥς τὺ φάγοντι.</note>
This is a proverb, according to the commentator, against those who are harmed by those for whom they have done well, or against the ungrateful. He adds a saying of Socrates: *By doing well to the wicked, you feed wolves.* <note>original Greek: κακῶς ποιῶν εὖ, θρέψαι λύκους.</note> For that is what usually happens to those who nurse the cubs of wolves. There exists on this matter a quite elegant Epigram, though by an uncertain author, concerning a sheep nourishing a wolf cub from her own udders:
*I nourish the wolf from my own breasts, not by choice,*
*But the shepherd’s folly forces me to do it.*
*Once grown by me, the beast will turn against me again.*
*Kindness is unable to change nature.*
<note>Erasmus provides the Greek text followed by his Latin translation, here rendered into English.</note>
Regarding the dogs, however, it is taken from the fable of Actaeon, who was torn to pieces by his own dogs. For the commentators on Theocritus also point this out. From these it is easily clear what that ancient proverb is which Marcus Varro mentions in his books *On Agriculture*, when treating the feeding of dogs. *Care must be taken,* he says, *to ensure they have food. For hunger leads them to seek food if it is not given; and it will lead them away from the flock if it is not provided. Unless, as some think, they even reach the point of fulfilling the ancient proverb, or even as they reveal concerning Actaeon, and bring their teeth against their master.* The same author in *Phoebus*, cited by Nonius, says: *Believe me, more slaves eat their masters than do dogs.* As if Actaeon had anticipated that, and had himself eaten his own dogs first, etc. Thus far the reports of Varro. Moreover, we read that even lions and dragons have returned gratitude to those who nursed them. Truly, there is no wild beast so ungrateful that it can be compared with the ingratitude found among men.

---

## You draw from the jar. LXXXVII

*To draw from the jar.* <note>original Greek: Ἐκ πίθω ἀντλεῖν.</note> This was said in olden times of one who abounded in desired things. For the jar <term>dolium: a very large earthenware vessel</term> is a huge wine vessel from which one may draw bountifully; nor is the loss easily noticed, evidently in such great abundance. Theocritus in *The Syracusans*:
*You draw more from the jar, but I have barely enough vinegar.*
The Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator</note> advises that the proverb was usually said of those who had a kind abundance of things at hand. It belongs to the rich to have jars; the poor drink flat wine from flasks. For the greater the volume of wine, the sweeter it is accustomed to be; where there is little liquid, it turns to vinegar more quickly. Hesiod also warns that one should be sparing when the jar is half-full, because thrift comes too late at the bottom. Very similar to this—

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<sig>K 2</sig>

is what frequently occurs in Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Christian Church Father known for his eloquence</note>, "from the springs," that is, from the sources, whenever he signifies a rich and ready abundance of material. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in his *Brutus* says that those who drink wine while it is still fermenting "drink from the vat": because the pressed wine is first received into vats; when it has cooled down a little, it is stored in vessels. It is worthwhile to provide his own words: "As if someone," he says, "should delight in Falernian wine, but neither so new that he wants it born under the most recent consuls, nor again so old that he seeks the consulship of Opimius or Anicius. <note>Opimius and Anicius represent famous vintage years from the Roman Republic</note> And yet those vintages are the best. I believe it, but excessive age does not have that sweetness we seek, nor is it indeed tolerable. Would someone who feels this way, if he wanted to drink, think he should draw for himself from the vat? Not at all, but he would follow a certain maturity. Thus I would judge for those men: both a new speech, as if fermenting from the must and the wine-press, should be avoided, nor should that famous, overly ancient style of Thucydides be pursued like an Anician vintage." Thus far Marcus Tullius. Nor do I think it foreign to this form what Athenaeus cites from Hipponax in Book 11, "to drink from a milk-pail." The Hipponactean Scazons <note>A type of "limping" poetic meter</note> go like this:
> Drinking from a milk-pail, for they had no
> cup; for the servant, falling, had smashed it.
that is,
> Drinking from a pail, for the chalice was missing,
> Since the attendant by chance had broken it in a fall.

-> Together with the basket itself. <-
-> LXXXVIII <-

"With the basket itself." This fits those who pour out, devour, and squander wealth immoderately. For it was the custom among the ancients, as Didymus testifies, for dinners to be brought in baskets. Plato is cited in Zenodotus:
> You snatched everything away at once, together with the basket itself.
that is,
> You grabbed all things together with the basket itself.

-> A locust will give birth to an ox first. <-
-> LXXXIX <-

"A locust will give birth to an ox first," a phrase for the impossible. Marcus Varro, in the third book of *On the Latin Language*, reports this verse from Ennius:
> And a locust shall sooner give birth to a Lucanian ox.
For the ancients called elephants "Lucanian oxen," because they were first seen by the Romans in Lucania <note>During the war with Pyrrhus</note>.

-> Through the darkness at the oak. <-
-> XC <-

"The things through the darkness at the oak": this was said of a huge and fatal calamity. Zenodotus cites Aristotle as the author, in his *Constitution of the Samians*. He says many of the Prienians were killed near a place named "The Oak." From this it became a custom that the women of Priene, mindful of that calamity, would swear "by the darkness that was around the oak." Plutarch also mentions this history and adage in his *Greek Questions* to roughly this effect: When there was war between the Prienians and the Samians, at first they inflicted moderate losses on each other; then, after a regular battle was joined, a thousand Samians were killed by the Prienians. Seven years later, having clashed with the Milesians, they lost all their leading and most noble citizens in a single battle. At which time Bion the Wise, sent as an envoy to Samos by the Prienians, achieved great praise. Therefore, after that atrocious and pitiable calamity, the women of Priene began to entreat and swear by the darkness that was around the oak, because they had lost their children, parents, husbands, and all their dearest pledges in that place.

-> He craved roasted flour. <-
-> XCI <-

"He desired roasted flour." This was said of one who, weary of domestic poverty, sought a more luxurious life among others. It was said against Plato, who, having left Athens, sailed three times to Sicily to visit Dionysius to make his fortune more splendid, as his rivals interpret it. For that journey was given to him as a reproach, as Aristides also testifies in the oration where he defends the four orators against Plato's calumny. And Diogenes, according to Laertius, when he noticed Plato at a certain sumptuous banquet abstaining from the other foods and using only olives, taxed the man's ambitious abstinence: "Why, O wise man, having sailed to Sicily for the sake of these tables, do you not now enjoy what is set before you?" To which they say Plato responded: "By the gods, Diogenes, even there I mostly made my meals of olives and such things." To which Diogenes replied: "Why then was there a need to sail..."
