# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

To Syracuse: at that time Attica did not bear olives <note>original: "εἰς συρακούσας: ἡ τότε ἀττικὴ οὐκ ἔφερεν ἐλαίας"</note>: that is, what point was there then in sailing to Syracuse? Did Attica not produce olives at that time? Theocritus says in the *Cyniscae*:
<margin>For he was seized by a love for what we like, roasted flour. <note>original: "Ηρατο μὲν τῶν θ' ἑμὶν δοκεῖ, ὀπτῶ ἀλεύρω."</note></margin>
->that is,<-
For I think he too was seized by a love for roasted flour.
Furthermore, he calls "roasted flour" a new and more elegant way of living, because we read that those ancient people lived only on porridge, evidently before the use of baking bread in an oven was discovered. Hence that Egyptian, Annus, who first devised the bread-oven, became a subject of a proverbial joke, as one who had invented something new, as I have related elsewhere. Pliny recounts many things concerning the delicacies of baking bread in Book 18, Chapter 11.

### Battology, Laconism.
XCII

*Battologia* is what the Greeks call "much-speaking" <note>excessive wordiness or babbling</note>, named after a certain Battus, a foolish poet who wrote long hymns in which the same things were frequently repeated. From this, the word *battologein* <note>to speak like Battus</note> was coined, which was so commonly used that the Apostle Matthew employed it. For Christ speaks thus in his gospel: "When you pray, do not use vain repetitions <note>original: "προσευχόμενοι δὲ μὴ βαττολογήσητε"</note> as the heathens do." Conversely, *Laconismus* <note>Laconism</note> came to signify "brief-speaking" <note>after the Spartans of Laconia, known for being concise</note>; it is used several times by Marcus Tullius Cicero in his *Letters*.

### The Silphium of Battus.
XCIII

The Silphium of Battus <note>original: "Βάττου σίλφιον"</note>. By this proverb, the Greeks refer to some new and rare honor. Aristophanes says in *Plutus*:
<margin>Not even if you gave me Wealth himself, and the Silphium of Battus. <note>original: "Οὐδ' ἂν εἰ δοίης γέμοι τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτὸν, καὶ τὸ Βάττου σίλφιον."</note></margin>
->that is,<-
Not if you were to give to me,
Plutus himself, and the very Silphium of Battus.
The sycophant denies he will rest, even if a reward however great is given. The same author says in *The Knights*:
<margin>Do you know that stalk of silphium, what it became worth? I certainly know it. <note>original: "Τὸν καυλὸν οἶσθ' ἐκείνου τοῦ σιλφίου τὸν ἄξιον γενομένου; οἶδα μέντοι."</note></margin>
->that is,<-
Do you know that stem
Which was considered worthy of silphium? Indeed, it is known to me.
The commentator ascribes a different origin to the adage. Battus set out from Thera, an island near Crete, warned by the oracle of Apollo—or, as others tell it, driven out by domestic sedition—and founded Cyrene. When the Africans, mindful of his benefit, desired to hold him in the highest honor, they presented him with the silphium plant, which was the most beautiful of all among them. At the same time, they struck a coin, on one side of which the king's face was engraved, and on the other the silphium with which he had been gifted by the city. Aristotle also mentions this in his *Republic of the Cyrenians*. But Herodotus tells it more extensively in *Melpomene*, adding that among the Libyans a king is called "Battus," and he was addressed by this name by the oracle, signifying he would be king. There are those who say an image was given; others again say a ring, in which the city was depicted, offering silphium to the king. Furthermore, Silphium holds the first glory among herbs, as its leaves, fruit, stalk, and juice are most precious. Hence the Ampeliotae (a certain people of Africa) hung a consecrated stalk of silphium at Delphi, as Alexandrides is the author. These things are generally brought up regarding *Plutus*; nor do the things Suidas records disagree. But the same man writes on *The Knights* that silphium is a shrub of unpleasant odor—or again, according to others, pleasant—and useful for medicines, the use of which Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, is believed to have first discovered, who is also said to have discovered honey. What this means, I do not know: the commentator on Aristophanes says that on the other side of the coin was engraved "The Kingdom" <note>original: "Βασιλείαν"</note> or "The Palace," if you shift the accent; instead of this, Zenodotus reads "Ammon." For he has it thus: "On the coin, they struck on one side Father Ammon, and on the other the silphium of Battus." <note>original: "ἐν τῷ νομίσματι, ὧδε μὲν πατρὸς ἄμμωνα, ὧδε δὲ θαττοῦ σίλφιον ἐτύπωσαν."</note> By "Ammon," I think, he means Jupiter, the giver of kingdoms, if indeed we believe Homer. Pindar also mentions this Battus in the *Pythian Odes*: "He prophesied to Battus as the founder of fruitful Libya." <note>original: "Χρῆσεν οἰκιστῆρα Βάττου καρποφόρῳ λιβύας."</note> Certain learned men think silphium is a type of laserwort <note>a medicinal resin-producing plant, now possibly extinct</note>.

### Do not remember evils.
XCIIII

Do not bear a grudge <note>original: "Μὴ μνησικακήσης"</note>: that is, do not refresh the memory of past wrongs. Thrasybulus, when he had freed the city of the Athenians from the cruelty of the Thirty Tyrants, introduced a decree that no past...

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY

<page-num>389</page-num>

...that a measurement of past affairs should be made. This "forgetting of evils" the Athenians call *amnesty* <note>original: ἀμνηστίαν (amnestian)</note>. The author Valerius Maximus mentions this in the fourth book of *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*, under the title "On Moderation of Mind." Marcus Tullius Cicero also recalls it in his first *Philippic* with these words: "In which temple, as far as was in my power, I laid the foundations of peace and recalled the ancient example of the Athenians. I even used the Greek word <note>original: Græcum etiam uerbum uſurpaui</note> which that city had used in settling discords, and I judged that every memory of discord should be blotted out by eternal oblivion." Aristophanes says in *Plutus*:

*Do not remember past wrongs, even if I captured Phyla.* <note>original: μὴ μνησικακήσης εἰ σὺ φυλὼ κατέλαβον</note>
->that is,<-
*Do not rub the sore of evil deeds, even if Phyla has been captured by you.*

The commentator, among other things, adds a certain story like this: Thrasybulus <note>An Athenian general who led the democratic resistance against the Thirty Tyrants in 404 BCE.</note>, having occupied a certain place named Phyla, overthrew the thirty tyrants; later, when he had said something rather arrogant, he heard the phrase "not to remember past wrongs" <note>original: μὴ μνησικακῆσαι (me mnesikakesai)</note>. That is, "Do not recall the memory of evils." And that saying passed into a proverb. Probus Aemilius reports that after the tyrants were driven out, Thrasybulus passed this law: that no one should be accused or punished for past acts. That law was called the "Law of Oblivion." He likewise publicly restrained his allies when they wished to rage against the law toward those with whom they had returned to favor, and he confirmed the law that had been passed. To him, in place of a reward for such great merits, a crown made of two olive twigs was given; and with this civil honor that wise man was content. The adage warns that the memory of past evils should not be rubbed raw by recollection. These are the words of Mercury to the slave Carion in Aristophanes. Plato in the 4th book of *Laws*: "For I say that we wish to remember past wrongs against you" <note>original: φάσκω γὰρ, ὅτι μνησικακεῖν βουλόμεθα ὑμῖν</note>. That is: "I shall certainly speak, but not because I wish to rub the memory of past evils into you." It seems to be taken from Homer, in whom this verse appears several times, namely in the *Iliad* (Book 19):

*But let us allow these things to have happened, though we are grieved.* <note>original: ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι ἐάσομεν ἀχνύμενοί περ</note>
->that is,<-
*Truly, though we are sad, let us permit these deeds to pass.*

Cicero uses this as if it were a proverb from time to time when writing to Atticus. To the same point belongs that line from the *Odyssey* (Book 1):

*Since it has been spoken.* <note>original: Ἐπεὶ δ' ἀπότι βέβακται</note>
*Dreadful, let the storm winds snatch it away with fears.* <note>original: Δεινὴ, ἀφὰρ τὸ φόβοισιν ἀναρπάξασαι ἄελλαι</note>
->that is,<-
*If any harsher word has been spoken,*
*Let the storm winds carry it far away through the empty air.*

Plutarch in *On Brotherly Love*: "It is necessary to consign that day to amnesty" <note>original: Δεῖ δὲ τὴν ἀμνησίαν τὴν ἡμέραν ἐκείνην τίθεσθαι</note>. That is: "It is proper to hand that day over to oblivion." This will be the use of the proverb if, according to that "vulpine" <note>fox-like or clever</note> counsel, we advise someone not to afflict themselves with the memory of past evils, since what is done cannot be undone. Lucian in *Caucasus*: "But to store up hatred for the next day and to remember past wrongs and preserve a certain memory of yesterday—away with it! It is neither fitting for gods nor otherwise kingly."

## Neither plant nor eat mint in time of war. XCV

*In war, neither eat nor plant mint.* <note>original: μίνθω ἐν πολέμῳ, μήτ' ἔσθιε μήτε φύτευε</note>
->that is,<-
*You should neither eat nor plant mint in the time of war.*

Aristotle, in the twentieth section of his *Problems*, reports this adage right at the beginning, seeking the reason why this saying has come into common use. He thinks the reason is that mint brings coldness to the body; the argument for this is that it diminishes the genital seed. Coldness, however, is contrary to fortitude and boldness, just as he shows in the last problem of the fourteenth section, when he says that those who are cold by nature are more fearful; on the contrary, those who are warm are bold. The proverb <note><term>paroemia</term>: a Greek term for a proverb or short, wise saying.</note> can also be turned to this sense: to warn that nothing should be done at an unsuitable time that might cause harm, just as mint is useless to those about to enter war.

## To the crows. XCVI

*Go to the crows.* <note>original: Βάλλ' ἐς κόρακας (Ball' es korakas)</note> That is, "go to the crows," which has the same force as if you said, "go to a bad end" or "to your destruction." Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:

*Go to the crows! Who is it that knocked on the door?* <note>original: Βάλλ' ἐκ κόρακας. τίς ἔσθ' ὁ κόψας τὴν θύραν;</note>
->that is,<-
*Away to the crows, who is it that struck the door?* Again in *Plutus*:
*Not to the crows?* <note>original: οὐκ ἐς κόρακας;</note> ->that is,<- *Won't you go to the crows?* Again in the same play:
*Go to the crows more quickly from us.* <note>original: Ἔρρ' ἐς κόρακας θᾶττον ἀφ' ἡμῶν</note>
->that is,<-
*May you depart from here to the crows more swiftly.*

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

This is found in this poet <note>likely referring to Aristophanes</note> and in many other places. Plutarch, in the commentary he wrote against Herodotus, censures him because he banished Isagoras to the Carians, as if "to the crows"—that is, he turned him into a Carian. It was elegantly said by Diogenes the Cynic: "It is better to go to the crows than to the flatterers" <note>original Greek: Κρεῖττον εἶναι ἐς κόρακας ἀπελθεῖν ἢ ἐς κόλακας</note>, because the latter devour even living and good men. Zenodotus writes that in Thessaly there is a certain place given the name "The Crows," into which criminals were thrown headlong; he notes that Menander also mentions this adage. Some, however, trace the origin of the saying to a story of this kind: The Boeotians, who once inhabited Arne, were told by an oracle that they would be expelled from their borders as soon as white crows appeared. It then happened that some young men, out of playfulness and drunkenness, took some crows they had caught, smeared them with gypsum <note>plaster or chalk</note>, and let them go again. When the Boeotians saw them flying, remembering the oracle and thinking the time had come to be ejected from their homes, they were greatly disturbed. Furthermore, the young men, terrified themselves by the commotion, fled and bought a place for themselves called *Coracon*, which means "of the crows." It happened some time later that the Aeolians, having ejected the Boeotians, occupied Arne. Among them, this custom was then accepted: that they would banish evildoers to that place named "The Crows."

The commentator on Aristophanes relates this story a bit differently: namely, that when the Boeotians were once overthrown and routed by the Thracians, the god responded that they should establish their home where they saw white crows. They saw certain crows sacred to the sun flying around in Thessaly near the Pagasetic Gulf, which boys had released covered in gypsum as a joke. The Boeotians, thinking the sign of the oracle was now fulfilled, established their seat there. There are those who refer the proverb to the flight of crows, because they are accustomed to fly in mostly deserted places. Thus the proverb would agree with that one: "To be deported by public decree into the furthest solitudes." Euripides in *Hecuba*:
> Will you not, as quickly as possible,
> Cast him out somewhere to the deserted islands?
> <note>original Greek: οὐκ ὅσον τάχιστα / Νήσων ἐρήμων αὐτὸν ἐκβαλεῖτέ ποι;</note>

Stratonicus the cithara-player <note>a professional lyre player</note> in the eighth book of Athenaeus, twists this against a certain singer. When the man was being annoying to him in some way, he said: "Go to the crows!" <note>original Greek: Βάλλ’ ἐς κόρακας</note>, playfully distorting the word to "Strum!" <note>original Greek: Ψάλλε</note> instead of "Go!" <note>original Greek: βάλλε</note>.

***

->Throw it into the water.<-
<margin>97</margin>
"Throw it into the water" <note>original Greek: Βάλλ’ ἐς ὕδωρ</note>, that is, take it out of our midst. It is said either against a person or a thing worthy of destruction. It is drawn from the punishment of certain people who were thrown headlong into a river or the sea. This was a punishment peculiar to parricides <note>those who kill parents or near relatives</note> among the Romans. Hence, in *Timon*, the philosopher orders gold to be cast into the sea, which the famous Crates of Thebes is read to have done at one time. Horace says:
> Or let us into the nearest sea
> Cast our gems and stones and useless gold,
> The substance of the greatest evil,
> If we truly repent of our crimes.

It does not seem absurd to me if this is referred to the water dispensed in water-clocks <note>clepsydras used to time legal speeches</note>, so that you understand it as "to be dragged into court"; and to the proverb which we mentioned in another place, "The wicked man under the water" <note>original Greek: ὑφ’ ὕδωρ ὁ πονηρός</note>. The adage is also uttered in this way: "Go to destruction" <note>original Greek: Βάλλ’ εἰς ὄλεθρον</note>, that is, go to your ruin.

***

->To the blessed place.<-
<margin>98</margin>
"Go to the blessed place" <note>original Greek: Βάλλ’ εἰς μακαρίαν</note>, that is, take yourself off to the blessed one. Some like this said by way of euphemism <note>using a mild word for a harsh reality</note> for that which is "to a bad end." For they imagine there is a certain place among the dead named *Macaria* <note>Blessedness</note>. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
> Take yourself hence, far from our feet, to Macaria.
> <note>original Greek: Ἄπαγ’ ἐς μακαρίαν ἐκ ποδῶν</note>

In a nearly similar manner, Athenaeus in the first book of the *Deipnosophists*: "To the blessed bath" <note>original Greek: εἰς μακαρίαν λουτρού</note>. For he curses a bath from which he had been badly affected. Plato in the *Greater Hippias*: "Take the man to the blessed place" <note>original Greek: Βάλλε εἰς μακαρίαν τὸν ἄνθρωπον</note>. Others allege a story of this kind: they tell that Macaria was the daughter of Hercules, of whom it had been predicted by an oracle that she should voluntarily offer herself to death; for thus Athens would be free from the incursion of...

# SECOND THOUSAND, FIRST CENTURY
<sig>K 4</sig>

Eurystheus <note>The king of Tiryns who imposed the labors on Hercules</note> demanded that one of the children of Hercules offer themselves voluntarily for slaughter. Thus, after Hercules had passed away, when Eurystheus was pursuing his children and they had fled to the Altar of Mercy, the Athenians—refusing to hand them over into the hands of their enemies—undertook a war against Eurystheus. Furthermore, an oracle was issued stating that the Athenians would be freed from Eurystheus’s incursion if one of the children of Hercules would devote themselves to the underworld. Macaria offered herself to a voluntary death. Once this was done, the Athenians engaged with the enemy and brought back a victory; many others were killed, including Eurystheus himself, who was slain by Hyllus (or Iolaus, the son of Hercules), who brought his severed head to Alcmene. She gouged out the eyes of the deceased. Moreover, the Athenians, decorating Macaria’s tomb with flowers and crowns, used to say: <term>Go to Macaria</term> <note>original: βάλλ’ εἰς μακαρίαν</note>. That is, "Send to Macaria." From this, therefore, the adage arose. At first, it was said of those who voluntarily cast themselves into danger for the sake of virtue; later, it began to be said of any sacrificial victim. Pausanias reports that Macaria is a marsh in Marathon in which a great force of Persians perished because, being ignorant of the paths, they fell into it; from which event the proverb might also seem to have been born. Stratonicus the cithara-player alluded to this in Athenaeus, book eight; being angry at a Macedonian disciple because he did nothing right, he said, <term>"To Macedonia,"</term> <note>original: εἰς Μακεδονίαν</note> making "Macedonia" out of "Macaria," while simultaneously alluding to that other proverb, "At home, not here, Milesian."

### Alabanda is most fortunate. XCIX

<term>Alabanda is the most fortunate of the Carians</term> <note>original: Ἀλάβανδα Καρῶν εὐτυχεστάτη</note>. That is, Alabanda is the most fortunate of Caria. Stephanus, in his commentary on cities, records that Alabanda is a city of Caria, founded by Car, from whose son it received its name. Indeed, after that son had served strenuously in a cavalry battle, he was called Alabandus. For the Carians in their own language call a horse *Ala* and victory *Banda*. He says that this word was also in use among the Romans, so that they called victory *banda*. I personally think that this word survives among the Germans, by which they call a powerful prince of ancient nobility a *Banner* <note>Bannerherr</note>, as one who once won this honor for himself through martial virtue. He adds from Philoxenus’s commentaries on Homer’s *Odyssey* that it is a type of solecism <note>a grammatical error</note> because it is called *Alabandía*: just as if someone were to put <term>not</term> <note>original: μὴ</note> for <term>not</term> <note>original: οὐ</note>, or among us *non* for *ne*, or *quod* for *ut*. Since Homer also calls the Carians <term>barbarous-speaking</term> <note>original: βαρβαροφώνους</note>. Juvenal, in his third Satire, lists Alabanda among the cities ruined by foreign delicacies and luxury:

> Here, high Sicyon is left behind, there Amydon,
> Here Andros, there Samos, here Tralles or Alabanda.

Stephanus reminds us that Alabanda was once the most opulent and flourishing among the cities of Caria, so that it even gave rise to the proverb we just cited. It will be applicable, therefore, when we wish to imply ample fortune and a voluptuous way of life, albeit one alienated from letters and the study of virtue. For instance, if some courtier or businessman should say: "Let others waste away in literature, let others philosophize in poverty, <term>Alabanda is the most fortunate of the Carians</term>." Thus, it is related to what was said in another place, <term>Happy Corinth</term> <note>original: εὐδαίμων ὁ Κόρινθος</note>. It can also be used in mockery, as if you were joking about someone of little distinction who nevertheless seems to excel among a fiercely barbarous and thick-headed people: "Alabanda of the Carians," etc.

### More unbending than a dried bramble. C

<term>More unbending than a parched bramble</term> <note>original: Ἀγναμπτότερος βάτου αὔου</note>. That is, a most rigid dry bramble. Or <term>More unbending than a bramble</term> <note>original: ἀγναμπτότερος βάτου</note>. That is, stiffer than a dry bramble-bush. It is a proverbial comparison for a difficult, inexorable, and stubborn man, or one "set in his ways," as they commonly say. The Greeks call this kind of men <term>self-willed</term> <note>original: αὐθεκάστους</note>, that is, living by their own particular institute and devoid of common sense. The adage is recorded by Suidas and Zenodotus alike. He notes it is drawn from the bramble, which as soon as it has dried out can be broken, but by no means bent. Whence it is more fittingly said of the elderly, who are more difficult by the vice of their age.

->SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY<-

### A grim message-staff. I

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a figure and foliage.</image-desc> <term>A grim scytale</term> <note>original: Σκυμάλη σκυτάλη; a scytale was a tool used by Spartans for sending encrypted messages</note>. That is, a sad message-staff. It was said of a sad or serious holiday, or of a messenger who brought grief. Aristophanes mentions this in *Lysistrata*. It is recorded by Diogenianus. Indeed, Aristophanes the Grammarian wrote a book <term>concerning the grieving scytale</term> <note>original: περὶ τῆς σκυτάλης ἀχνυμένης</note>, and he is cited by Athenaeus in the third book of the *Deipnosophistae*. Plutarch, in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*, calls it <term>the command to the wretched</term> <note>original: τὴν τῷ ἀθλίῳ ἐπίταξιν</note>

<summary>This page discusses the origins of several Greek proverbs, including the sacrifice of Macaria, the wealth and luxury of the Carian city Alabanda, and metaphors for stubbornness and grim news.</summary>
<keywords>Macaria, Hercules, Eurystheus, Alabanda, Caria, bramble metaphor, stubbornness, scytale, Spartan messages, Greek proverbs</keywords>

--- Page 504 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s encyclopedic collection of Greek and Roman adages, focusing on metaphors involving communication tools and the songs of birds.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"To another, in turn, something else, except for the grieving *scytale* <note>original: *skytale* — a staff used for ancient Spartan cryptography</note> on the back." That is to say: what else would you call that command of the Ethiopian than a "sad *scytale*"? Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his letters to Atticus, says: "You have a Laconian <note>Spartan</note> *scytale*." This expression seems quite fittingly applied to a very brief letter, or one written about obscure and secret matters, or even to a message conveying anxiety and sad news. 

What a Laconian *scytale* actually is, however, is explained by Aulus Gellius in the seventeenth book of *Attic Nights*, chapter nine. It is better to include his own words here: "The ancient Spartans," he says, "when they wished to conceal and hide official letters sent to their generals, so that their plans would not be discovered if intercepted by the enemy, sent letters of this kind. There were two smooth, oblong wooden rollers of equal thickness and length, polished and prepared identically. One was given to the general departing for war. The magistrates kept the other at home, along with the legal authority and the seal. When the need arose for more secret correspondence, they would wrap a strap of modest thinness, but as long as necessary, around that roller in a simple, rounded coil, so that the edges of the strap met and joined perfectly all along the cylinder. They then wrote the letters on that strap across the joints of the edges, with the lines running from bottom to top. Once the letters were written, the strap was unwound from the roller and sent to the general, who was aware of the trick. The unwinding of the strap rendered the letters truncated and mutilated, scattering their parts and tips into entirely different sections. Therefore, if the strap fell into the hands of the enemy, nothing could be guessed from it. But when the recipient took it, he would wrap it around the matching roller he possessed, starting from the end as he knew it should be done; the letters, coming together through the same circumference of the roller, would join up again, presenting a complete and uncorrupted letter that was easy to read." The Spartans call this type of letter a *scytale*, which means a "shielded staff." Thus far Aulus Gellius. Plutarch mentions this matter in his life of Lysander, whom King Pharnabazus deceived with a counterfeit *scytale*. Suidas relates almost the same things as Gellius regarding the *scytale*. Strabo, in the first book of his *Geography*, also records this hyperbole: "The field is narrower than a Laconian *scytale*."

->Museums of Swallows.<-

*Chelidonon mouseia* <note>original: Χελιδόνων μουσεῖα</note>. That is, "Museums of Swallows." Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
"These are mere scraps and foolish chatterings,
Museums of swallows, disgraces to the art."
->that is:<-
"Those things are leaves, and foolish babblings,
Museums of swallows, and the subversion of art."
The commentator warns that this is a proverb used against those who are excessively talkative and noisy. For swallows, with their senseless twittering, bring more weariness to listeners than pleasure. Indeed, this bird is not at all melodic, but possesses a certain annoying screech. Hence, among the Pythagoreans, it earned the status of a symbol for talkativeness, as they forbid anyone from having a swallow under the same roof. It is aptly said of unlearned poets, orators who are more talkative than eloquent, or any gathering of foolishly chatty people.

->Nightingales sitting in trifles.<-

*Aedonon leschais egkathemenai* <note>original: Ἀηδόνων λέσχαις ἐγκαθήμεναι</note>. That is, "Nightingales sitting in trifles." The previous proverb fits the ignorant yet talkative; this one fits the learned who take excessive delight in their own studies. Poets, most of all, are of this kind. Plautus, in the *Bacchides*, applied this to a girl: "I fear," he says, "that the little nightingale's song has failed." Although in the Greek proverb there seems to be a humorous corruption, so that *leschais* <note>places of talk/trifles</note> is said instead of *lochmais* <note>thickets/bushes</note>. It is derived from the incredible zeal for singing, as well as the skill, attributed to this little bird. Indeed, as Pliny relates in Book 10, Chapter 29, it sings for fifteen continuous days and nights without intermission when the budding of the leaves thickens. The bird is worthy of admiration on many accounts. First, such a great voice in such a tiny body, such persistent breath; then, in one bird, a perfect knowledge of music. The sound is emitted with modulation: now it is drawn out long with continuous breath, now varied with a turn, now distinguished by a break, joined with a twist, sent forward, called back, muffled unexpectedly (sometimes it even murmurs to itself)—full, deep, sharp, rapid, extended, vibrating when it sees fit, high, middle, low. In short, everything is in that tiny throat which human skill has devised through so many exquisite instruments. And lest anyone doubt it is an art, there are several songs for each individual, and not the same for all, but each has its own. They compete among themselves, and the spirited contention is plain to see.

# SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY

<margin>4</margin>
<unclear>In</unclear> death, life often ends, with the spirit failing before the song. Younger birds practice and receive songs from those they might imitate. The student listens with great focus and repeats it, and they take turns being silent. One can perceive the correction of a mistake and a certain kind of reprimand from the teacher. Pliny reports these and several other things concerning the song of nightingales in the place we mentioned. <note>original: "Plinius... quo diximus loco" referring to Pliny the Elder's Natural History.</note>

->An ass carrying mysteries.<-

<note>original Greek: Ὄνος ἄγων μυςήρια</note> That is, *An ass carrying mysteries.* It was said against someone who was involved in a duty beyond his worth or dignity. For example, if someone ignorant of letters were appointed head of a library. Aristophanes says in *The Frogs*:
<note>original Greek: Ὄνος ἄγων γ’ ἐγὼ γ’ ὂν ἄγων μυςήρια</note>
that is,
*By Jove, I am an ass carrying mysteries.*
*But I shall not endure these things any longer.*
The commentator asserts the adage was born from the fact that formerly, those things needed for performing the Eleusinian sacred rites <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret religious rites of ancient Greece.</note> were loaded onto and carried by an ass. It will also apply to those whose labor is of use only to others, while nothing returns to them in the meantime except hardship. Just as if someone were to carry food for others which he himself is not permitted to eat. Apuleius seems to have alluded to this when he imagines himself as an ass carrying around the goddess Ceres. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> ascribes that Demon refers this to a millstone, which they call an "ass" <note>original Greek: ὄνον</note>, because in sacred rites, they were accustomed to place crowns upon the grain mills. Therefore, it will be elegantly twisted against those upon whom honor is bestowed undeservedly. For instance, when the title of doctor, the cap and ring, and other insignia of that kind are granted to the unlearned.

<margin>5</margin>
->Again I see tranquility.<-

<note>original Greek: Αὖθις αὖ γαλην’ ὁρῶ</note> That is, *Once again I behold calm.* The commentator on Aristophanes writes that this is a proverb by which we signify emerging from evils, with fortune changed for the better. The metaphor is drawn from sailors, for whom tranquility is usually welcome when a storm subsides. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
<note>original Greek: καὶ μὴν ὅ γ’ ἐχθρὸς ἤγγελθεν ἡμῖν λέγειν, κυμάτων γὰρ αὖθις αὖ γαλην’ ὁρῶ</note>
that is,
*And Hegelochus likewise had the right to say to us,*
*from the waves, once again I see a calm path.*
Hegelochus was a certain actor of tragedies—lest any unknown word delay the reader. Moreover, Aristophanes notes in passing the tautology <note>The redundant use of words.</note> of Euripides, in whose work this verse appears in *Orestes*: "I see a calm." This same line was also mocked by Strattis. Although there also seems to be an underlying pun in the tragic words *galen' horo*, that is, "I see a cat," and *galen' horo*, that is, "I see calm things." <note>A famous ancient linguistic blunder where the actor Hegelochus mispronounced a word, making "calm" sound like "weasel" or "cat."</note> But most of all, Euripides, in that comic poet's work, censures Aeschylus for saying the same thing twice in these verses:
<note>original Greek: ἥκω γὰρ ἡμῖν εἶπον ὁ Σφὸς αἰσχύλος...</note>
that is,
*The wise Aeschylus spoke the same thing twice to us.*
*For he says, "I come to the land" and "I descend."*
*But "I come" is just as if someone said to his neighbor:*
*"Lend me a kneading-trough, or if you prefer, a bread-basket."*
<margin>Pindar in the Isthmian Odes</margin>
<note>original Greek: νῦν δὲ νῦν μοι γαιάοχος εὐδίαν ὄππασεν ἐκ χειμῶν@</note>
that is,
*But now Neptune has granted me tranquility after the storm.*

<margin>6</margin>
->It is in tranquility.<-

To this form belongs that line of Terence from *The Eunuch*: "Then moreover, I rejoice that my father Phaedria's love is in tranquility." Likewise: "Who might carry you away from tranquility onto a rock." And what we have said elsewhere: "I am sailing in the harbor." Also: "They are on land." Moreover, we use "In tranquility" with the same type of expression as when we say "In safety" or "In a favorable state."

<margin>7</margin>
->Though he is seven years old, he has not yet put forth teeth.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἑπταετὴς ὢν ὀδόντας οὐκ ἔφυσεν</note> That is, *Although he is seven years old, he has not yet brought forth teeth.* The commentator on Aristophanes advises that this is commonly said as a proverb. It seems to me to apply to one who, though great in age, still acts like a boy. Or one who, having stayed somewhere for a long time, has not yet attained any authority or honor. The metaphor seems to be borrowed from nature.

->THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-

from infants, in whom all teeth usually begin to grow around the seventh year of age. Aristophanes in *The Frogs* <note>original: "Ranis"</note> says:
*Let us mock Archidemus,*
*Who, being seven years old, has not grown his clansmen,* <note>original: "φράτερας" (phrateras). A pun on "teeth" (odontas).</note> that is,
*Let us tax Archidemus,*
*At seven years he has not yet produced his tribesmen.*
Where the poet, seizing an opportunity for a joke, changed "teeth" to "clansmen." For he incidentally censures a certain Archidemus who had neglected the Athenian custom, by which a foreigner living in that city for seven years, having been enrolled in the number of citizens, was then adopted as if into their kinship and legal rights.

<margin>VIII</margin>
### From a beautiful tree even to be strangled.
<note>original: "Ἀπὸ καλοῦ ξύλου κἂν ἀπάγξασθαι"</note> That is, it is fitting to be strangled even from a beautiful tree. The proverb advises that a calamity is more tolerable if it is joined with honor and is free from disgrace. For example, if a maiden should be seduced by a noble and very wealthy lover. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*, alluding to the proverb, says:
*For if from a worthy tree*
*You suffer anything, you will seem to wise men to suffer well.*
As if hanging were less miserable if one hangs from a distinguished tree. A very similar proverb is circulated even today among our own people: *If I must be drowned, let me be drowned in pure water*: that is, if one must perish, it is better to perish by an honorable death. Or if one must sin, to sin under a more honorable title. It can also be applied to those who are indeed conquered, but by a victor so distinguished that it seems more honorable and desirable to be conquered thus than to have conquered certain others. Whence comes that line of Virgil: *You fall by the right hand of great Aeneas.* <note>Aeneid, Book 10.</note>
And in Ovid, Ajax thinks it shameful for him even to have contended with Ulysses, even if he should depart as the victor. *It will be said,* he says, *that he fought with me.*
Likewise in Homer’s *Iliad*, book 21 <note>original: "φ"</note>, Achilles speaks in this manner:
*Would that Hector had killed me, who was bred here as the best,*
*Then a brave man would have been slain by a brave man, and a brave man would have despoiled him;*
*But now it is my fate to be caught in a wretched death.*
Pindar in the third *Pythian Ode* said in a not dissimilar sense, *a beautiful harm* <note>original: "καλὸν πῆμα"</note>: he speaks of Ixion, who, deceived by the image of Juno, prepared his own destruction.

<margin>IX</margin>
### Not a Chian, but a Cean.
Didymus thinks a proverb lies beneath these words of Aristophanes: *Not a Chian, but a Cean.* <note>original: "οὐ χῖος ἀλλὰ κῖος"</note> On account of a common taunt noting the inconstancy and fickleness of the race, changing their principles according to the requirements of the time, and adapting the same to the convenience of fortune. The verses of Aristophanes from *The Frogs* regarding Theramenes are these:
*He has fallen outside of evils, not a Chian, but a Cean.*
Although in this place Aristarchus reads *Coan*, not *Cean*. For Theramenes is said to have been a Coan. Perhaps it is an allusion to the fact that this Theramenes was a disciple of Prodicus the Coan. Lucian also mentions him in *The Loves*: *And so I myself also, if it were possible, would wish to become that "buskin" Theramenes.* <note>Theramenes was nicknamed "The Buskin" (Cothurnus) because that type of boot fit either foot, symbolizing his political shifting.</note> Unless perhaps it is an allusion to the similarity of the words, though the reality is far different. For the Chians were ill-reputed for effeminate manners, while the Ceans <note>People of Ceos</note> admitted neither flute-girls nor harlots into their city, as Athenaeus indicates in book 13. Therefore, he who a little before was a trifler, and soon takes on a stern face as if he were another person, is rightly described by this: *Not a Chian, but a Cean.* Aristarchus, who reads *Coan*, seems to have looked to the game of dice, in which the throw called the *Coan* had six points, while the *Chian* had only one. Thus the Coan was the luckier throw. By this saying, he indicates that Theramenes never consulted his interests unsuccessfully. Eupolis, who reads *Cean*, thinks Theramenes was adopted into the citizenship of the Ceans, though he was born a Coan. Didymus, however, puts forth the proverb: *Not a Chian, but a Cean.*

<summary>Erasmus discusses two proverbs from Aristophanes: the first suggests that a noble death or misfortune is preferable to a base one, and the second mocks the political flexibility of Theramenes using a pun on Greek islanders and dice throws.</summary>

# SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY

<margin><note>original: εἶχε τι</note> <unclear>he had something</unclear></margin> so that the change of name might indicate the man's versatile character, serving the needs of the time and always accommodating himself to the more powerful side. Stories of this kind are generally recorded in the commentaries about him. Furthermore, we have spoken of the "buskin" <note>a high-soled boot worn by tragic actors, used here as a metaphor for a fickle person who can fit either foot</note> elsewhere.

---

<margin>X</margin>
## Beyond the olive trees.

<margin>Beyond the olive trees he is carried.</margin> That is, "He is carried beyond the olive trees." This is said when someone transcends prescribed limits, or does things that are foreign to and irrelevant to the matter at hand. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
<margin>Lest your anger, seizing you, carry you beyond the olive trees.</margin> That is,
Lest it snatch you up and carry you beyond the olives.
The commentator says the adage was born from this: the stadiums in which running contests were held were hedged on both sides by olive trees planted in a row, which it was not permitted to pass. Therefore, he who passed the olives was seen to be running outside the stadium.

---

<margin>XI</margin>
## Wearing a crown, yet dying of thirst.

<margin>Having a crown, but perishing from thirst.</margin> That is, "Wearing a crown, but dying of thirst." This will be aptly twisted against a drunkard and a glutton, and one who has been reduced to poverty by squandering his wealth on delicacies. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
<margin>Just like Connas, having a dry crown, but perishing from thirst.</margin> That is, "Just like Connas, wearing a withered crown, but dying of thirst." He is censuring the comic poet Cratinus as if he were a little drunk and raving. The adage is also expressed in this way in Diogenianus:
<margin>A man of Delphi, though he wears garlands, is breathless with thirst.</margin> That is,
A Delphian man, while he carries wreaths, is exhausted by thirst.
It arose from the habits of a certain Connas. He was first a wine-loving flute player, and at banquets he would drink continually while crowned. For it was the custom of the ancients to wear crowns during drinking parties. Then, from a flute player he became an Olympic victor, and often carried away the crown as a winner in the Olympics, whence Cratinus calls him <term>polystephanon</term> <note>original: πολυστέφανον; "many-crowned"</note>. Otherwise he was very poor, not becoming a bit richer from his victories. For he is said to have possessed nothing except the wild olive wreath.

---

<margin>XII</margin>
## Small fry into the fire.

<margin>Small fry into the fire.</margin> That is, "Small fry to the fire." A proverb used for those things which perish or are consumed quickly, or which are finished easily and immediately. For the *Aphya* <note>a type of small fish, often translated as "anchovy" or "small fry"</note> is a type of fish that is white, soft, and tender, which is cooked through immediately when moved near the fire. Hence Athenaeus in Book 13 indicates that some prostitutes were called "aphyas" because they were pale, slender, and had very large eyes. For such is the small fry. It is fried in boiling oil; whence that saying is also common among the Greeks: <term>the honor of small fry is oil</term> <note>original: ἀφυῶν τιμὴ ἔλαιον</note>. And as soon as they touch the boiling oil, they are already cooked, so much so that they sizzle instantly with the oil and are immediately taken out of the pan as fully cooked. Suidas writes that this fish is also called <term>aphron</term> <note>original: ἄφρον</term>, that is, "foam," because of its whiteness, and
<margin>white foam</margin> recording many types of it. Athenaeus in the seventh book says it is called by some <term>aphrogenes</term>
<margin>foam-born</margin> <term>aphrogenes</term> <note>original: ἀφρογενὲς</note>, surely from foam, and for that reason sacred to Venus, because the fables of the poets say she was born from the foam of the sea. The same author cites Clearchus for what we said above, adding that the proverb is also expressed in this way: <term>the small fry saw the fire</term> <note>original: ἴδε πῦρ ἀφύα</note>. As if merely having seen it were enough for the cooking. Therefore, if a girl of marriageable age immediately grows hot upon seeing a suitor, "the small fry saw the fire" will be appropriate. It is not unlike what we reviewed elsewhere: <term>the horse into the plain</term> <note>original: χὺ ἵππον εἰς πεδίον</note>.

---

<margin>XIII</margin>
## The penalty of a dung-ball.

<margin>The penalty of a dung-ball.</margin> That is, "The penalty of a dung-ball," they say, when someone is punished for a frivolous and worthless thing. For <term>Bolitus</term> among the Greeks signifies any kind of dung, but specifically that of cattle. Furthermore, Solon passed a law which threatened punishment even to those who had stolen cattle dung. Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Knights*:
<margin>so that we are defeated by dung-balls</margin> that is,
As if conquered by cattle dung.
Hesychius thinks that <term>bolbiton</term> and <term>boliton</term> are the same to the Greeks, except that the former is peculiar to the Ionians. The Etymologist indicates the same. He says the excrements of the ox are so called because they are more liquid than those of other animals; he also cites Hipponax, who used the phrase <term>sister of a dung-ball</term> <note>original: βολίτα κασιγνήτην</note>, referring, I believe, to a woman held in extreme contempt. And <term>Bolippus</term>, as if fashioned from cattle dung. Cynulcus in Athenaeus, Book 13: <term>but having the other leg made of cattle dung</term> <note>original: ἀλλὰ Βολίτινον ἔχων θάτερον σκέλος</note>. In the fields of the Phrygians one can see houses...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>14</margin>
->The door never keeps anyone out.<-
The Greek phrase <note>original: οὐδέ ποτ’ ἴσχει ἡ θύρα</note> means exactly this: "The door never keeps anyone out." A commentator on Aristophanes <note>The famous Greek comic playwright</note> notes that this proverb refers to those who are exceedingly hospitable, whose doors are always open and exclude no one. He says it is taken from a comedy by Eupolis titled *The Friends*. It can be elegantly applied either to a gullible person who lets any lie enter his ears, or to a woman who denies no man.

<margin>15</margin>
->Always someone in Cydon’s house.<-
The Greek <note>original: Ἀεί τις ἐν κύδωνος</note> means: "There is always someone in the house of Cydon." Cydon was a certain Corinthian man so famous for his hospitality that he even gave rise to a proverb. It is recorded by Suidas as well as by Zenodotus, and also by the commentator on Aristophanes. While these sayings are not without charm when applied simply to "lovers of guests" <note>original: Φιλοξένους (philoxenous)</note>, they will have a bit more "Venus" <note>grace or beauty</note> if they are turned toward the mind: for instance, if one were to warn a pious man not to allow his mind to lie open to any and all thoughts.

<margin>16</margin>
->To walk on the tips of the nails.<-
The Greek <note>original: Ἐπ’ ἄκρων ὀνύχων</note> means: "On the tips of the nails." This is a proverbial metaphor for those who listen greedily, for such people are accustomed to raise themselves up on the tips of their feet. To "walk on the tips of the nails" <note>original: Καὶ ἐπ’ ἄκρων ὀνύχων βαδίζειν</note> is also used for the haughty. The adage is cited by the commentator on Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*, who thinks the poet alluded to this when he said:
"For immediately the crown sat upon the tips of your little buttocks." That is:
"Soon you sit back on the tips of your buttocks, with the crown adding spirit." This means:
"You are carried away and pleased with yourselves."

<margin>17</margin>
->You shall not gather the vintage unpunished.<-
The Greek <note>original: οὐκ ἐρήμας τρυγήσεις</note> means: "You shall not gather the vintage in a deserted place." This applies to those who, with no one watching, pluck grapes with impunity. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*: "But you shall not gather the vintage thus easily and in a deserted place anymore." That is: "Do not think you will carry out your harvest so easily and without punishment." For the Greeks say a thing is done "in a deserted way" <note>original: ἐρήμας (eremas)</note> when there is no one to forbid it and no one to stand in the way. Similar to this is the saying we shall mention in another place:
"Sweet is the fruit when the guardian is absent."
For it is customary to set guards over vines and orchards, especially in autumn, when the now-ripe fruit invites the thief. Likewise, they say "to accuse in a deserted court," "to write a deserted lawsuit," "to win in a deserted court," and "to judge or condemn in a deserted court," as we have indicated elsewhere.

<margin>18</margin>
->The mind is in the hides.<-
The Greek <note>original: ὁ νοῦς ἐστὶν ἐν ταῖς σκύτεσιν</note> means: "The mind is in the hides" <note>or "leathers"</note>. This was commonly said of those who are anxious and who seem to fear some imminent evil. Aristophanes in the comedy titled *Peace*:
"We committed those errors, but have forgiveness,
For our mind was then in the hides."
The metaphor is taken either from the thongs with which slaves are beaten (for these are made from ox hides; hence the riddle in Plautus: "Where dead oxen attack living men") or from shields, which are usually covered with ox hide. Therefore, it fits either those who fear the lash or those whom the fear of impending war keeps anxious. Not unlike this is that line from Terence’s *The Eunuch*: "For a long time now my mind has been in the dishes." Also that line of Aristophanes in *The Wasps* about a man greedy for lawsuits:
"His mind flies by night around the water-clock" <note>The *clepsydra* used to time speeches in court</note>.
In short, in whatever matter we are intent upon, we are said to "be" in that thing.

<margin>19</margin>
->He looks at the hides.<-
The Greek <note>original: Σκύτη βλέπει</note> means, to render it word for word, "He watches the hides." It is close to the previous one, by which they signified someone showing by his face that he suspected some evil was pressing upon him, and gathered this by certain conjectures: as if someone, having seen ox hides, should conclude there would be a war—

# SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
<column-break/>
because they are covered by shields. He cites an Adage from a play by Eupolis <note>An Athenian poet of Old Comedy</note> titled *Chrysogenes*:
*And no one looks at the leather, as the saying goes.* <note>original: "κοὐχὶς μὲν ἐν τὸ λεγόμθρον σκύτη βλέπει."</note> That is,
He stares plainly at the hides.
Perhaps it would not be absurd to say the proverb arose from the fact that on barbarian shields, certain horrific faces are usually painted or carved—faces of barbarians, or Cyclopes, or even beasts—so that for this reason, those with a fierce expression were said to "look at hides" (*skytē blepein*). Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> in book 13: *He made you no more temperate, but only taught you to look at hides.* That is, he taught you only to look grim. For he means the student learned nothing from the philosopher except a furrowed brow and a fierce countenance. However, this adage can only truly have its charm in its own language. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
*Make me look at hides today.* That is,
I will certainly see to it this day, that you stare at the leather.

### The spoon will grow.
-> XX <-
*The spoon will grow.* <note>original: "διὰθυς αὔξει."</note> Chrysippus, according to Zenodotus and the commentator on Aristophanes, says this proverb is usually said ironically of tiny little men. For a spoon is both small and curved. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
*Two useful vessels, a spoon and a ladle.* That is,
Two useful tools, a spoon and a *toryna*. Now, a *Toryna* is the tool with which a pot is stirred.

### Conna’s pebble.
-> XXI <-
*Conna’s pebble.* <note>original: "Κόννου ψῆφος."</note> This refers to a man or a thing of no value and no importance. The proverb flowed from a certain Conna, a cithara player, or, as some prefer, a lyre player from among those who played the instrument without singing. There are those who say Conna was a man of the lowest fortune, who became utterly impoverished after devouring his inheritance. Callistratus, in the commentary on Aristophanes, brings forth the proverb in this way: *Conna’s fig leaf*, because he was accustomed to play with it. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
*Unless they consider it Conna’s pebble.* That is,
They certainly think you are Conna’s vote; which is to say, they consider you worth nothing.

### A single thicket does not nourish two robins.
-> XXII <-
*The same thicket does not nourish two robins.* <note>original: "Μία λόχμη πρέφει δύο ἐριθάκους."</note> Zenodotus is the authority that this adage marks those who hurry to get rich from small matters. To me, it seems it can be said quite timely of those who do not get along well, and cannot live harmoniously in the same office. Now, the *Erithacus* <note>The European Robin</note> is a certain solitary bird, such that you will not easily find more than one in the same glade. Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek humanist</note> translates this sometimes as a *Sylvia* <note>warbler</note>, sometimes as a *rubecula* <note>redbreast</note>. Thomas Magister says it is called *erithila* by some, *erithakos* by others, and *erithakos* by most. Aristophanes elegantly alluded to this adage in *The Wasps*:
*For it could never be*
*That one thicket could ever nourish two thieves.* That is,
For it cannot happen
That one glade ever nourishes two thieves.
This is not entirely unlike what Alexander the Great is reported to have said: That the world does not hold two suns.

### I travel on foot, for I have not learned to swim.
-> XXIII <-
*I walk on foot, for I do not know how to swim.* <note>original: "πεζῆ βαδίζω, νήχειν γὰρ οὐκ ἐπίσταμαι."</note> A proverbial six-foot line <term>senarius: a line of verse consisting of six feet</term>, used against one who, being unskilled in greater matters, busies himself with smaller affairs. Or one who, because of lack of skill, lives a private and humble life; or one who of necessity betakes himself to another kind of work, since he is by no means fit for this or that: just as if someone should become a merchant because he is unteachable in letters. A similar verse is cited:
*I walk on foot, I do not know how to dig.* That is,
Unskilled at digging, I walk on my own feet.
In Aristophanes' *The Birds*, a sycophant <note>In ancient Greece, a professional informer or accuser</note> similarly excuses his profession: *For what should I do, since I do not know how to dig.* That is, what I ask would I do, when I do not know how to dig. To this should also be referred that Gospel saying: *I am not able to dig* (*skaptein ou dynamai*). <note>A reference to the Unjust Steward in Luke 16:3</note> For he used "digging" for any kind of hired labor. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
*In this place, for he does not know how to play the lyre.* That is,

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, focusing here on metaphors involving animals and nature drawn primarily from Greek comedy.</meta>

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES<-

Forgive me, for he has not been taught to play the lyre. <note>original: "canere doctus est chely." The 'chelys' was a lyre made from a tortoise shell.</note>
Doubtless alluding to the common adage, as if to say: Unskilled in the other arts, he provides for himself only through theft. Likewise in *The Knights*:
I do not even understand music. <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ μουσικὴν ἐπίσταμαι.</note>

### One house does not nourish two dogs. XXIV

One house cannot feed two dogs. <note>original Greek: Εἷς οἶκος οὐ δύναται τρέφειν δύο κύνας.</note> That is, the same house does not well nourish two dogs. This six-foot verse <term>senarius: a line of verse consisting of six metrical feet</term> is tossed about as a proverb against those between whom there is little agreement because of the same profit, which they both seek in common. Thus, the same kingdom does not bear two tyrants. The same republic does not bear two plunderers. The same office does not bear two ambitious men, each of whom tries to hold the first place. It is recorded by the commentator on Aristophanes.

### The stake deceived the vine. XXV

The stake deceived the vine. <note>original Greek: Ἡ χάραξ τὴν ἄμπελον ἐξηπάτησεν.</note> Used when someone is deceived or harmed by the person on whom they depended and on whose loyalty they relied. It is a metaphor taken from the stakes to which vines are tied for support. It happens sometimes, however, that once these stakes have taken root, they smother the vine with their own branches and foliage, or they fall over and drag the vine shoot down with them. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
So now, has the stake itself deceived the vine? <note>original Greek: Εἶτα νῦν ἐξηπάτησεν ἡ χάραξ τὴν ἄμπελον;</note> That is, has the very prop circumvented its own vineyard?

### He trembles in the manner of a certain cock. XXVI

He cowers like a cock. <note>original Greek: πτήσσει ὥς τις ἀλέκτωρ.</note> This will be aptly said of one who is in a bad state and agitated, or even trembling with fear. For among the Greeks, "to cower" <note>original: πτήσσειν (ptēssein)</note> means to shrink down and be terrified; it is used specifically of birds. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
Phrynichus cowers just like a cock. <note>original Greek: πτήσσει φρύνιχός ὥσπερ ἀλέκτωρ.</note>
This Phrynichus was the son of Melanthas, an Athenian writer of tragedies, whom the Athenians fined a thousand drachmas because he had composed a tragedy on the destruction of the Milesians. <note>Phrynichus's play "The Fall of Miletus" so upset the Athenians by reminding them of their loss that they banned the play and fined him.</note> Indeed, I would not have included this among the adages if the commentator on Aristophanes had not specifically recorded it as a proverb. Plutarch also mentions this in his *Life of Alcibiades*, who, though he had previously been fierce and insolent, began to be gentle and modest through his intimacy with Socrates, whose singular integrity he admired. He cites this verse from some poet:
He fixed himself like a cock, drooping his wing. <note>original Greek: Ἔπηξ’ ἀλέκτωρ ὥς, κλίνας πτερόν.</note> That is:
Fearful he retreats, in the manner of a cock,
When, defeated, he lowers his wings.
He mentions this also in the *Life of Pelopidas*. Cockfighting was solemnly and publicly exhibited among the ancients. Furthermore, although it is a pugnacious animal, nevertheless the cock, when it feels itself unequal in the conflict, retreats in a wonderfully dejected and suppliant manner, providing laughter for the spectators.

### We shall no more spare them than wolves. XXVII

We shall not spare them more than wolves. <note>original Greek: οὐ φεισόμεθα μᾶλλον ἢ λύκων.</note> The commentator on Aristophanes advises that this is a proverbial figure, born from the fact that in ancient times among the people of Attica, the law even invited the killing of wolves with a reward. For he who killed a wolf cub was given a talent; he who killed an adult was given two talents. <note>A 'talent' was a very large sum of money in antiquity.</note> From this they also gave Apollo the surnames *Lyceus* and *Lykoktonos* (Wolf-slayer). Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
For shall we spare these any more than wolves? <note>original Greek: φεισόμεθα γὰρ τι τῶνδε μᾶλλον ἢ λύκων;</note>

### Unless some bird saw it. XXVIII

Unless perhaps some bird saw it. <note>original Greek: πλὴν εἴτις ἆρ’ ὄρνις.</note> A proverbial hyperbole concerning a matter that is profoundly hidden. Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
No one then saw my treasure, unless perhaps some bird. <note>original Greek: οὐδεὶς ἆρ’ οὐ θησαυρὸν τὸν ἐμὸν, πλὴν εἴτις ἂν ὄρνις.</note>
Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> also cites this little verse from Aristophanes:
No one beholds me, except a bird flying past. <note>original Greek: οὐδείς με θεωρεῖ πλὴν ὁ περιιπτάμενος ὄρνις.</note>

# SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY II.
<sig>L 2</sig>

### 29. The legs of a Partridge.
<margin>Πέρδικος σκέλος <note>Greek: Perdikos skelos</note></margin> That is, the shin of a Partridge. "Partridge" was the name of a certain limping innkeeper, noted by Aristotle in several places, from which it passed into a proverb. Aristophanes the grammarian <note>A 3rd-century BC scholar from Byzantium, not the playwright.</note> mentioned it in his collection of proverbs in prose. It was said of thin and distorted legs. It appears in Athenaeus in the fragments of the first book:
<margin>Πέρδικός μοι κὴ τὸ πέρδικος σκέλος. <note>Greek: Perdikos moi kai to perdikos skelos</note></margin>
<margin>Πιέτω τις, ἢ πλακῶντα τὶς δότω. <note>Greek: Pietō tis, ē plakōnta tis dotō</note></margin> That is:
> Give me a drink, and the legs of a Partridge.
> Or let someone give them now, or offer a cake.

The same author does not seem to apply this very much to the proverb.

### 30. Raise the spur.
<margin>Πλῆκτρον ἀμυντήριον <note>Greek: Plēktron amyntērion</note></margin> That is, raise the avenging spur. The adage appears in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*:
<margin>Αἶρε πλῆκτρον, εἰ μάχῃ. <note>Greek: Aire plēktron, ei machē</note></margin> That is, raise the spur, if you are fighting.
It was commonly said of one who is already preparing for revenge. The metaphor is borrowed from fighting cocks, to which certain iron spurs are usually tied so that they may defend themselves during the contest; although Aristotle, in the second book of *On the History of Animals*, chapter 12, states that nature added the spur to those types of birds which, due to their body mass, are less suited for flight. Roosters are of this kind. Pliny confirms this in book 10: "And they exercise kingship," he says, "in whatever house they are: this too is produced by fighting among themselves, as if they understood that weapons were born on their legs; nor is there an end to it, often dying together."

### 31. You have less sense than the Dithyrambic poets.
<margin>Διθυραμβοποιῶν νοῦν ἔχεις ἐλάττονα. <note>Greek: Dithyrambopoiōn noun echeis elattona</note></margin> That is:
> You have less wisdom than the Dithyrambic writers.

This is hurled at the stupid and the frenzied. The adage is noted by the commentator on Aristophanes’ *The Birds*, taken from the Dithyrambic poets who, inspired by Bacchus, used to rave; whence also Horace says:
> If the man is mad, or making verses.

The same poet, extolling the grandiloquence of Pindar, says: "Whether he rolls down new words through daring dithyrambs, and is carried along in rhythms free from law." Philostratus, in *Lives of the Sophists*, occasionally calls immoderate vehemence and grandeur in speaking "the dithyrambic style" <note>original: τὸ διθυραμβῶδες</note>, and says such speakers "rave like Bacchants" <note>original: ἐκβακχεύειν καὶ ὑποβακχεύειν</note>.

### 32. A Corcyraean whip.
<margin>Κερκυραῖα μάστιξ <note>Greek: Kerkyraia mastix</note></margin> That is, a whip from Corcyra <note>Modern Corfu</note>. Said of a thing adorned with superfluous luxury. It will fit those things to which an ornament is added that is by no means becoming or congruent. Since the Corcyraeans were frequently agitated by seditions, it was their custom to carry huge whips adorned with ivory handles. Some say they were double-lashed. Thus they passed into a proverb. The author is the commentator on Aristophanes’ *The Birds*. When the orator Lycurgus was being attacked with insults because of his immoderate freedom of speech, he exclaimed: "O Corcyraean whip, how many talents you are worth!" <note>original: ὦ κερκυραῖα μάστιξ, ὡς πολλῶν ταλάντων ἀξία εἶ</note>. He was noting a useless people, yet bought at a great price. Plutarch records this in the *Lives of the Ten Orators*.

### 33. The Gull.
<margin>Λάρος <note>Greek: Laros</note></margin> That is, the gull or sea-mew. It was said of a talkative and senseless person, especially one who is captured having been deceived by a vain desire for something; derived from the nature of the bird, which delights in and approaches sea foam. It is caught in this manner: foam is first thrown at a longer distance, then closer and closer. Finally, those carrying it in their hands show it. Thus the gull, greedy for food and caught, is seized. Aristophanes uses this in *Plutus*; the commentator warns that the nickname is proverbial. Again, in *The Clouds*, he calls Cleon a "gull" because he gapes for thefts and plunder. Lucian, in the booklet *On Salaried Posts*, says: "Taking confidence, trusting the vein, if it is seen, in the manner of a gull, devouring the whole bait with an open mouth." <note>original: σαυρὸν ἢ πρακκαλέας θαῤῥῶν... καθάπερ ὁ λάρος ὅλον ποδιχανὼν τὸ δέλεαρ</note>. Athenaeus, in the tenth book of the *Deipnosophists*, indicates that this bird was attributed to Hercules by the ancients because he too was "gluttonous" <note>original: ἀδηφάγος</note>, that is, he was called a "voracious eater" <note>original: βορφάγον</note>. Formerly, the chief luxury of gluttons was in fish, as many books testify, whoever wrote on this subject among either the Greeks or the Latins.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...of its kind <note>original: "genere"</note> (making it all the more strange that today, for the sake of religion, the common people eat fish). Therefore, it is also fitting to apply this to gluttons, because the gull is a bird that craves fish.

<margin>XXXIV</margin>
->The seagull is in labor.<-

<note>original: "Κεπφος ωδινει" (Kepphos ōdinei)</note>, that is, the seagull is in labor. This was said of those who would promise enormous things, but then provide nothing worthy of their promises. For the gull <note>The *kepphos* is a light, frantic sea-bird, often identified as a petrel or gull.</note> is a bird covered in a great abundance of feathers, yet with very little meat; and when it gives birth, it makes a great noise. This adage is recorded by the commentator on Aristophanes in the comedy titled *Peace*. It is similar to that other saying:
> The mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born. <note>A famous line from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* regarding bathos or anticlimax.</note>

<margin>XXXV</margin>
->The hurrying bitch brings forth blind pups.<-

<note>original: "Η κυων σπευδουσα τυφλα τικτει" (Hē kyōn speudousa typhla tiktei)</note>, that is, the hurrying dog brings forth blind puppies. This was directed at those who, out of an excessive desire for haste, produce a thing that is poorly finished; for instance, if someone rushes the publication of a work that has not been properly refined. The saying arises from the fact that because the dog gives birth quickly, she produces pups that are blind, as if they were still immature. Aristotle, in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, demonstrates that this happens especially in animals that have many-cleft feet <note>Animals with paws or multiple toes, rather than hooves.</note> and nourish a large litter, such as the fox, the bear, the lioness, the dog, and the wolf. For all these give birth to blind young, and some even produce offspring that are not yet fully formed. He believes the cause is that since the body's moisture is not sufficient to nourish such a large litter, nature brings forth the offspring in an imperfect state instead. Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note> likewise, in the book he wrote *On Semen*, says: "Indeed, the proverb already says that dogs give birth to blind young because of their haste." However, Galen prefers to say that puppies are imperfect rather than blind, since it is moles that are properly called blind. Animals that produce blind offspring are called *alaotoka* by the Greeks, as if you were to say "blind-bearing" in English. Aristophanes alludes to this proverb in *Peace*:
> The tinkling goldfinch <note>original: "acalanthis"</note> in her hurried labor brings forth blind young.

And meanwhile, the Greek grammarians are uncertain what an *Acalanthis* is: some think it is the name of a famous dog, derived from "running gently" <note>original: "παρα το ακαλαν θειν" (para to akalan thein)</note>. There are others who suspect it is a bird. A *codon* <note>original: "κωδων"</note>, however, is a bell, which in the houses of the great, and today in colleges, is used to call the household to their duties. Others suspect the name comes from "flattering" <note>original: "παρα το ακαλανθειν" (para to akalanthein)</note>, because a dog, flattering those it knows, barks at strangers. This is the guesswork of the commentator on Aristophanes, the *Etymologist*, and Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>.

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
->To look into a dog’s backside.<-

Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen*:
> I would have told him to look at a dog's anus.

The commentator warns that this is commonly said of those who are dim-sighted, adding also this trochaic verse:
> To look down into a dog’s backside, and that of three foxes.

He alludes to the same thing in *The Acharnians*:
> Blow into the dog’s anus with your coals.
This is too obscene to be worth translating. Truly, I would be loath to record such trifles, were it not my intention to satisfy every part of the work I have undertaken, "and to furnish it even to the smallest detail." <note>original: "και τω ελαχιστω απαρτιω κοσμειν" (kai tō elachistō apartiō kosmein)</note>

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
->By trying, the Greeks reached Troy.<-

Theocritus <note>A Greek poet from Sicily, the creator of pastoral poetry.</note> in the *Syracusan Women* shows that by trying and experimenting, even the most difficult things can be accomplished, signifying this through a proverbial figure:
> By trying, he says, the Greeks came to Troy.
> Use <note>or "practice"</note> accomplishes all things, O fairest of children.

<margin>XXXVIII</margin>
->Follow God.<-

Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and essayist.</note>, in his short book *On Hearing*, records this adage, which is also celebrated among the seven oracles of the Sages of Greece: <note>original: "επου θεω" (hepou theō)</note>, that is, "Follow God." He thinks the meaning is this: "Obey reason." It is as if whatever reason dictates in the heart ought to be an oracle to everyone. Hence Virgil also said:
> Or is each man’s god his own fierce desire?
To which that verse celebrated by the Greeks bears witness:
> For the mind is a god within each of us.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of adages, transitioning from physical observations to philosophical proverbs about following divine reason, the power of speech, and the value of satirical writing.</meta>

For each man’s own mind is his god. And Menander, as quoted in Plutarch, says:
The mind is our god. <note>original: "ὁ νοῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός"</note> that is,
For our mind is a divine power. Cato of Utica says something very similar in the works of Lucan. It seems to have been taken from the first book of Homer's *Iliad*, where Achilles, obeying Pallas Athena, says:
Whoever obeys the gods, they listen to him very much. <note>original: "ὅςκε θεοῖς ἐπιπείθηται, μάλα τ’ ἔκλυον αὐτοῦ"</note> that is:
The gods are inclined to accept the prayers of one who obeys them.
This half-line of verse is found in more than one place in the same author: For some god was the leader. <note>original: "κὶ γάρ τις θεὸς ἡγεμόνυε"</note> that is, indeed, some divinity was the author. Plato says in the *Crito*: Let it be then, O Crito, and let us act in this way, since god leads the way. <note>original: "ἔα τοίνυν, ὦ κρίτων, κὶ πράττωμεν ταύτη, ἐπειδὴ ταύτη ὁ θεὸς ὑφηγεῖται"</note> Cicero, in the third book of *On Ends*, records among the precepts of the ancient wise men those things which were celebrated as proverbs. "There are," he says, "the old precepts of the wise, who command us to obey the time, to follow god, to know oneself, and to do nothing in excess."

### Tongue, where are you going? XXXIX

Tongue, where are you going? To set a city upright and then to overturn it again. <note>original: "γλῶσσα ποῖ πορεύη; πόλιν ὀρθώσουσα κὶ πάλιν ἀνατρέψουσα"</note> that is, Tongue, where are you going? To restore a city and then to subvert it once more. This is recorded by Suidas, Zenodotus, and Diogenianus. It teaches that the tongue brings the greatest utility to mortals, and yet brings the greatest destruction, even though it is an extremely small member of the body. Likewise, the holy Apostle James compares it to the rudder <note>Erasmus uses the term "clauo," the handle of the rudder.</note> of a ship, which, though it is the smallest part, either saves or destroys the whole vessel. Bias—as reported by Plutarch in his essay *On Listening*, and again in *On Talkativeness*—when Amasis, the tyrant of the Egyptians, ordered him to send the best and worst part of the meat from a sacrificial animal he had sent, Bias sent the tongue cut out. He was hinting that the use of this organ is paramount, whether you desire to do good or to do harm. Nor was it unskillfully said by Solomon in the eighteenth chapter: Death and life are in the power of the tongue.

### Showing off pots. XL

Showing off pots <note>original: "χύτρας ἐπιδείκνυσθαι"</note>—that is, to display cooking pots—means to extol something that is inherently ridiculous and mean as if it were something great. Plutarch, in his essay *On Listening*, rebukes the sophists whose custom it was to adorn flowery <note>original: "ἀνθηρὰς"</note>—that is, infamous—subjects with the varnishes of words, as when they praise vomiting, fever, the tyrant Busiris, and other things of that kind. "By Zeus," he says, "showing off their pots," that is, speaking at length to display their common vessels. Not that it should be entirely disapproved if someone, for the sake of exercising or relaxing their wit, plays occasionally with arguments of this kind, provided the joke is learned and mixes a bit of utility with pleasure. Since "what forbids one from telling the truth while laughing?" <note>A famous quote from Horace’s *Satires*.</note> Indeed, it happens that truth, recommended by such allurements, creeps more gracefully and without offense into the minds of mortals; so much so that Aulus Gellius does not hesitate to prefer the ridiculous fables of Aesop to those gloomy dogmas of the Stoics that supposedly fell from heaven. Plutarch himself played in the *Gryllus*—quite festively, yet in such a way that you can recognize a philosopher joking, not a buffoon. 

I myself, several years ago, played with the *Praise of Folly* <note>original: "μωρίας ἐγκώμιον" (Moriae Encomium)</note>, upon which I spent no more than seven days of labor, and that without the help of any books. For my baggage <note>Erasmus often used "farcina" to refer to his library or research materials while traveling.</note> had not yet been brought to me. Whatever kind of little book this is, I see it is greatly approved by fair-minded wits and those initiated into good letters; they affirm that, besides the festivity of the joking, there are not a few things there which contribute more to correcting the morals of men than the *Ethics* or *Politics* of Aristotle—who, being a pagan, taught about these matters in a more than pagan way. And yet I hear that some are offended—but only a few—and they are of such a sort that they approve of nothing unless it is barbaric, tasteless, and completely foreign to the Muses. These same men read Juvenal, though otherwise they are the fiercest enemies of poets, so that they might attack the vices of princes, priests, merchants, and especially women in their sermons; they often depict these vices in such a way that they actually teach obscenity. 

For my part, since the subject I undertook was not inconsistent with this, and such a wide field lay open everywhere, I did not bite anyone by name (except perhaps myself), and nowhere stirring up that hateful Camarina <note>A proverbial marsh in Sicily that was dangerously foul; the adage "do not move the Camarina" means "do not stir up a mess."</note> of crimes and vices, I touch upon certain ridiculous things rather than foul ones in a few words. "But you rebuke bishops," they say, "you rebuke theologians, you rebuke princes." First, they do not notice how moderately and least of all hatefully I do this. Second, they do not remember that rule which Saint Jerome so often hammers home: where there is a general discussion of vices, there is no injury to any specific person, nor is anyone "marked with charcoal" <note>A Roman expression for being singled out for blame or infamy.</note> as if they were evil. Rather, everyone is warned not to be evil—unless, perhaps, they contend that all princes are wise, and all theologians are perfect...

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning the divinity of the human mind and the dual nature of speech, concluding with a spirited defense of his "Praise of Folly" against critics who prefer dull or crude moralizing over learned satire.</summary>
<keywords>Menander, Plutarch, Cato, power of the tongue, Bias of Priene, Praise of Folly, satire vs. obscenity, St. Jerome, Aristotle's Ethics, moral education</keywords>
