<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s defense of his work, The Praise of Folly, specifically addressing critics who mistake the words of his character, Folly, for his own personal opinions. He then transitions back into his collection of adages, moving from "the pots" to proverbs about fleeting pleasures, exactness, and the wisdom found in overnight reflection.</meta>

...[fools: they think] that all bishops and popes should be such as Paul and Martin were; or likewise that monk-philosophers and priests should be like Anthony and Jerome. In short, they do not weigh that which is of most importance in dialogues: the decorum of the character. They imagine Erasmus is speaking, rather than Folly <note>Moria, the personification of Folly and narrator of Erasmus's famous satire.</note>. As if, indeed, if someone were to depict a Pagan speaking with a Christian, it were a sin for the Pagan to say anything that shrinks from Christian doctrine. Finally, while tyrants listen to anything from fools and laugh, thinking it beneath a citizen to be offended by any of their words, these people—I know not who—can hear nothing at all from Folly herself, as if whatever was said regarding vices, in whatever manner, pertained directly to them. But enough on this matter. It is better to return to the "pots." Therefore, this proverb would be related to that which was said elsewhere, <term>you paint the pot</term> <note>original: χύτραν ποικίλλεις; refers to wasting effort on trivial or decorative matters rather than substance.</note>, that is, "You variegate the pot."

->A boy and the ice.<-

<gloss>The boy with the ice.</gloss> <note>original: ὁ παῖς κρύσταλλον</note> This was said against those who, although they cannot hold onto something, still do not want to lose it. For instance, if someone refuses to step down from a magistracy for which he is unfit, or refuses to be released from a duty he can no longer maintain. It also applies to those who will not willingly part with what is bound to slip away soon anyway. As when we lose wealth and cling to it, even though it will leave us regardless. Or when we persist in a harmful matter and do not wish to lose what hurts us. It is recorded by Zenodotus, Suidas, and Diogenianus. Plutarch also mentions and explains it in his book *On Talkativeness*. It seems to be taken from Sophocles, who compares the behavior to boys who, seeing ice, grab it in their hands and delight in it; but as it soon melts, they can neither easily cast off the slippery mass nor hold it any longer. Likewise, love can neither be shaken off because of the attached pleasure, nor retained because of the troubles mixed with those pleasures, which are greater.

->One to one.<-

<gloss>One to one, they say</gloss> <note>original: Ἓν πρὸς ἓν φαδιν</note>, says Lucian, signifying that this is certainly a proverbial figure of speech when individual things are matched exactly with individual things. Theocritus in *The Sorceress*: <gloss>To me you said you would herd the cattle one to one.</gloss> <note>original: Ἐμὶν δ’ ὁ τυ βουκολιάσδεν <unclear>φῇ</unclear> πόθ’ ἓν</note> That is, if I may translate it literally: "But to me, you feed the oxen one to one." For that is how some learned men read it. Plato in the fifth book of *Laws*: <gloss>Every man must, as one to one, hasten to this.</gloss> <note>original: δεῖ δὴ πάντα ἄνδρα, ᾧ πᾶς ᾧ ἄν ἀνθρώπῳ</note> This also translates literally as: "It is necessary for everyone, one to one, to hurry toward this." That is, each for himself. The same in book six: <gloss>where he was woven one to one.</gloss> <note>original: ᾧ ἐφ’ ἑνὶ πλέχθη</note> He also uses the clearly proverbial figure in book one: <gloss>one to one.</gloss> <note>original: ᾧ πρὸς ἓν</note> Again in book four: <gloss>one for one.</gloss> <note>original: ἀνθ’ ἑνὸς ἕν</note> It can be seen as transferred from battle, whenever a matter is conducted fiercely, man against man in combat. Unless we prefer to refer it to that Spartan <term>apophthegm</term> <note>A concise, pointed saying.</note>. For Plutarch tells in his little book *On Talkativeness* that the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> sent a certain single ambassador to King Demetrius. When the tyrant was angry that they had come thus, saying, "The Lacedaemonians [sent] one to me?", the ambassador, not at all dismayed, replied, "One to one." Nor would you be wrong to say it was borrowed from the mathematicians, whose peculiar figure of speech this is: <gloss>one to one.</gloss> <note>original: ᾧ πρὸς ἓν</note> For thus they say proportions consist, which they call parity or equality.

->In the night is counsel.<-

<gloss>In the night is counsel.</gloss> <note>original: Ἐν νυκτὶ βουλή</note> The adage warns that one should not be headstrong in counsel, nor should anything be done immediately upon the first impulses of the mind. For the night is a friend to anxiety and silence, and is especially suitable for considering and consulting on serious matters. Furthermore, it often happens that sleep, having calmed desire, turns toward prudence. Whence it is even commonly said by our own common folk: "I will sleep on this matter," by which they mean they will deliberate at leisure. Furthermore, that headstrong counsel is usually avoided in the night is both said in common speech and elegantly warned by Sophocles in Plutarch’s book *On Talkativeness*:
> <gloss>For the end of counsel and of a race is not the same.</gloss> <note>original: οὐ γάρ τι βουλῆς ταυτὸ καὶ δρόμου τέλος</note> that is,
> For the race and counsel do not share the same goal.

Since in a race, the one who is fastest wins; in consulting, hesitation is safer, and speed is dangerous. Plutarch, in the *Table Talk*, the seventh decade, the ninth problem, mentions one who wrote that among the Lacedaemonians—if I am not mistaken—there was a <term>nocturnal assembly</term> <note>original: νυκτέρινον σύλλογον; a governing body that met at night.</note>, that is, a nightly meeting of the most serious men, to which the most difficult cases were referred. From this, among the ancients, the night was called <term>Euphrone</term> <note>A poetic Greek name for night, often personified as "the kindly one."</note>, <gloss>from thinking well</gloss> <note>original: παρὰ τὸ εὖ φρονεῖν</note>, that is, from being wise.

<summary>Erasmus concludes a defense of his satirical persona, Folly, before cataloging proverbs about the slipperiness of desire, the necessity of individual accountability, and the value of nighttime reflection over hasty action.</summary>
<keywords>Praise of Folly, literary decorum, fleeting pleasures, Spartans, King Demetrius, sleep on it, nighttime counsel, Euphrone, Sophocles, Plato</keywords>

### SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
L 4
<meta>catchword: mus</meta>

->Where one feels pain, there he also keeps his hand.<-
<margin>XLIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: ὅπου τις ἀλγεῖ, κεῖσε καὶ τὴν χεῖρ’ ἔχει</note> That is:
Where anyone hurts, there he frequently keeps his hand.

This is a proverbial six-foot line of verse <note>An iambic senarius, a common meter in Greek and Latin drama.</note> cited by Plutarch in his book *On Talkativeness*. The saying arises from a natural human habit: we frequently move our hand to whichever part of the body is causing us pain. We may use this proverb quite opportunely when we wish to indicate that someone is dwelling on or speaking willingly about things that trouble their mind. Stobaeus reports the same idea in this way: <note>original Greek: ὅπου τις ἀλγεῖ, κεῖσε καὶ τὸν νοῦν ἔχει</note> That is:
Where anyone hurts, there he also keeps his mind.

Cicero seems to have alluded to this proverb in the third book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "But I will not act in such a way as to either distress your mind with complaints, or too often bring my hand to my own wounds." Likewise, Plautus says in *The Persian*: "My master treats me like a bleary eye; he simply cannot keep his hand away." Plutarch twists the meaning slightly: wherever there is something that either causes pain or brings delight, that is where everyone keeps their tongue. Thus, the "wine-loving" Homer is convicted by his own praises of wine. And Pindar is criticized as a "lover of money" <term>philargyros</term> <note>From the Greek 'philos' (loving) and 'argyros' (silver/money).</note> because he spends so much effort in praising gold. For in this manner, he immediately begins his *Olympian Odes*: <note>original Greek: ἄριστον μὲν ὕδωρ, ὁ δὲ χρυσὸς, αἰθόμενον πῦρ ἅτε, διαπρέπει νυκτὶ μεγάνορος ἔξοχα πλούτου</note> That is: "Water is indeed best, but gold, like a blazing fire, stands out at night above all magnificent wealth." Again, in his third *Isthmian Ode*: <note>original Greek: καὶ μεγαλαυχίαν νομίζειν χρυσὸν ἀνθρώπων ποθεινότατον ἄλλων</note> That is: "And they judged gold, the most greatly-boasted thing, to be more desirable than all other things to men."

->There is more perfume among the Campanians than there is oil among others.<-
<margin>XLV</margin>
Pliny writes in the eighteenth book, eleventh chapter of his *Natural History*: "In Campania, however," he says, "is the most celebrated plain. It lies beneath rainy mountains, spanning forty miles of level ground. Such is the favor of its soil—to speak of its nature at once—that the top layer is like dust, while the lower layer is thirsty and porous like pumice. Even the fault of the mountains turns to its advantage, for it filters and passes through the frequent rains. It does not wash away the soil or turn to mud because of how easy it is to cultivate. This same earth returns the moisture it receives to no springs, but tempers it, and 'digesting' it, holds it within itself like sap. It is sown all year round: once with millet, twice with emmer wheat. And in the spring, the fields that have rested produce roses, more fragrant than those that are planted. Thus the earth never ceases to give birth. Whence the common saying: There is more perfume among the Campanians than there is oil among others." However, just as the Campanian plain surpasses all other lands, so it is itself surpassed by that part called Laboriae, which the Greeks call the Phlegraean plain <note>The "Phlegraean Fields" near Naples, famous for volcanic activity and incredible fertility.</note>. Thus far Pliny. If anyone wishes to pull this adage toward an allegory, it can be applied to either a region or a person who so excels others that they possess a greater abundance of exquisite things than others have of mediocre or common things.

->He does not even wish to walk the same road as him.<-
<margin>XLVI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Μηδὲ τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν βαδίζειν</note> That is: They are said "not even to walk the same road" who are separated by such extreme hatred that they not only cannot bear to share a table or a roof, but do not even wish to walk on a common path. From this comes the common irony: "He loves him so much that if they happened to meet by chance, he would turn off onto another road." Plutarch, in his commentary *On Brotherly Love*, says: <note>original Greek: τῷ δ’ ἀδελφῷ μηδὲ τὴν αὐτὴν ὁδὸν οἰόμενος δεῖν βαδίζειν</note> That is: "Thinking that he ought not even walk the same road as his brother." Matching this is that proverbial verse:
>Never be a fellow-traveler with a wicked man.
>That is:
>Do not be a companion on the road to a scoundrel.

->Outside the song.<-
<margin>XLVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Παρὰ τὸ μέλος</note> That is: To be done or said "outside the song" is said of that which is irrelevant to the matter at hand. Even if the genuine grace of the proverb perishes when translated into a foreign language, nonetheless <term>para melos</term> sounds exactly as if you were to say: "with little modulation," "with little harmony," "inappropriately," or "unbecomingly." For what melody <note>original: melos</note> is in music, decorum <note>propriety or fitness of behavior</note> is in life. Lucian says in *The Eunuch*: <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐφ’ ὧν ἄλλως λέγεται παρὰ μέλος τι φθεγξάμενος</note> That is: "And among those where one would fear to say anything 'beside the song,'" meaning, anything irrelevant to the matter. He imitated this figure of speech from Plato, who in the third book of *The Laws* writes in this manner: <note>original Greek: παρὰ μέλος ἐμοί γε ἂν δοκῇς φθέγξασθαι</note> That is: "You seem to me to have been about to speak 'beside the song' <note>meaning: out of tune or off-topic</note>." And in the *Critias*: "But if, on the other hand, we unintentionally fulfill the expectation of the spectators 'outside the song' concerning them—" <note>The text breaks off here as the sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page records several ancient adages regarding human nature, including the tendency to focus on what hurts, the extreme fertility and luxury of the Campania region, the avoidance of enemies, and the concept of "decorum" or social harmony as a musical metaphor.</summary>
<keywords>Plutarch, Cicero, Plautus, Pindar, Pliny the Elder, Campania, Laboria, Phlegraean Fields, social harmony, decorum, hatred, metaphors</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion on proverbs regarding speech that is either obsessive or irrelevant to the topic at hand. It concludes an entry from the previous page about how our speech reveals our hidden pains or desires (like Pindar's supposed love for money), and then moves into two new adages concerning the dangers of life and the frustration of non-sequitur answers.</meta>

->ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES<-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on Pindar.</note> ...we have spoken, he will demand a fitting punishment. Aristophanes, in his play *The Assemblywomen*, elegantly used a single word, *apartan* <note>original Greek: ἀπαρτᾷν</note>, to mean speaking things that are discordant or irrelevant to the matter. He says: 
> Paying close attention 
> So that you say nothing foreign or discordant 
> From those things which you must prove.

Aristotle, in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, notes that certain poets used the phrase "to sing a lyreless song" <note>original Greek: ᾄδεσθαι ὡς ἄλυρον μέλος</note>, referring to a dissonant song that does not harmonize with the strings. This can be aptly turned against those who live differently than they teach. Closely related to this is what we have recorded elsewhere: "nothing to the word," or "nothing to the verse" <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος</note>. Aristophanes uses this in a novel way in *The Assemblywomen* to mean "rashly":
> For I certainly will not, through my own sweat and thrift, 
> Pour out my resources rashly and to no 
> Purpose. 

The scholarly notes <term>scholia</term> explain "nothing to the verse" as meaning "at random" or "for no cause" <note>original Greek: ὡς ἔτυχε, ἕνεκα μηδενός</note>. The latter Greek verse does not maintain its proper poetic feet. It can be restored if we read it as: "I will not pour it out at all rashly or foolishly" <note>original Greek: οὐδέν τι πρὸς ἔπος κ’ ἀνοήτως ἐκβαλῶ</note>. I thought it better to cite this verse, even if slightly out of place, than to deprive the studious reader of it. 

It seems to have originated from an anecdote <term>apophthegm</term> about Themistocles. When the poet Simonides made an unfair request of him, Themistocles replied: "You would not be a good poet if you sang out of tune, nor would I be a good leader if I judged against the laws." This imagery was taken from ancient singers who matched their voice to the lyre. Or perhaps it comes from the harmony of vocalists, where if anyone is out of tune with the harmony, it greatly offends the ears. Lucian uses the term "singing out of tune" <note>original Greek: ἀπᾴδοντα</note> for things that do not pertain to the legal case. Marcus Tullius Cicero uses the phrase "side-trips from the road" <note>original Greek: ὁδῷ πάρεργα</note> for things foreign to the proposed subject.

<margin>XLVIII</margin>
### Fire, sea, woman: three evils.
This proverbial three-foot line of verse <term>trimeter</term> is circulated among the Greeks: "Fire and sea and woman: three evils" <note>original Greek: πῦρ καὶ θάλασσα καὶ γυνή, κακὰ τρία</note>. For nothing is more formidable than a conflagration, and the sea is likewise most dangerous. Hence Aeschylus says in *The Persians*:
<margin>(The Persians)</margin>
> The wave of the sea is invincible. <note>original Greek: ἄμαχον κῦμα θαλάσσης</note>

The proverb suggests that a woman is something very similar to these. Furthermore, a certain Spartan <term>Lacon</term> very wittily indicated that every woman is an evil; when he had married a very tiny wife, he said that "of evils, the smallest should be chosen." Even in Euripides, Medea confesses that the race of women is an evil:
> We are what we are—I will not say "evil"—we women. <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ φαμέν οἷον ἐσμέν, οὐκ ἐρῶ κακόν, γυναῖκες</note>

Euripides, as cited by Planudes in the *Life of Aesop*, grants the "principality" among all evils to a woman:
> Many are the rages of the sea's waves, 
> Many are the rivers, and the hot blasts of fire; 
> Bitter is poverty, and a thousand other things are bitter, 
> But nothing is so bitter and harmful as a bad woman.

<margin>XLIX</margin>
### I was asking for scythes.
"I was asking for scythes" <note>original Greek: ἄμας ἀπῄτουν</note>. This is said against those who respond with something that has nothing to do with the matter. Plutarch, in his essay *On Talkativeness*, warns that anyone who wishes to answer accurately must carefully learn the mind of the questioner, lest that which is commonly said in the proverb happens: "I was asking for scythes." There is a proverbial six-foot line <term>senarius</term> in the works of Suidas and Zenodotus:
> I asked for scythes, but they denied me the tubs. <note>original Greek: ἄμας ἀπῄτουν, οἱ δ’ ἀπηρνοῦντο σκάφας</note>

<meta>This page continues the second Chiliad of Erasmus’s collection of adages. The opening paragraph concludes a discussion from the previous page regarding linguistic confusion or excuses involving agricultural tools, specifically centered on the Greek word for a hoe or shovel.</meta>

SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
<meta>catchword: For it is</meta>

It seems to have arisen from this: a certain farmer, when a neighbor asked to borrow his scythe, denied him, saying he had a "two-tongued hoe" <note>The Latin here plays on *ligo* (hoe) and *bilinguis* (double-tongued or deceitful). Original: *bilingon esse domi*.</note> at home. The scholarly commentator <term>scholiast</term> on Theocritus’s *The Idylls* noted that the Athenians use the word *amlin* <note>original Greek: ἄμλιν</note> for what the common Greek language calls a *dikella* <note>original Greek: δίκελλαν</note> or *skapane* <note>original Greek: σκαπάνην</note>, which is to say, a hoe. But if *skaphe* <note>original Greek: σκάφη</note> means the same as *skapane*, the response would be as ridiculous as someone asking for a sword and the owner denying he has one by saying he only possesses a blade. There are those who believe a *skaphe* is actually a type of cup or a hollow vessel.

->A white bird.<-
<margin>50</margin>
*Leukos ornis* <note>original Greek: Λευκὸς ὄρνις</note>. That is, "A white bird." Marcus Tullius Cicero used this phrase to describe something new and auspicious in the seventh book of his *Letters to Friends*. He writes: "Since I have devoted myself to greeting friends—which happens even more frequently than it used to, because they seem to see a well-disposed citizen as if they were seeing a white bird—I hide myself away in my library." It can also be applied to a very rare and unusual thing, since very few birds are actually this color. Thus Juvenal says: 
> Rarer even than a white crow.

The saying "the son of a white hen" is discussed elsewhere in this work.

->To set foot in someone else's dance.<-
<margin>51</margin>
*En allotrio choro poda tithesthai* <note>original Greek: Ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ χορῷ πόδα τίθεσθαι</note>. That is, "To set foot in someone else's dance." This means to involve oneself in others' business or to claim roles for oneself that belong to others. Plutarch, in the essay titled *How a man may praise himself without envy*, writes: "For the proverb declares that he who sets his foot in another’s dance is meddlesome and ridiculous." <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ χορῷ πόδα τίθησι περιέργον ἡ παροιμία τὸ γελοῖον ἐπιδείκνυσι</note>. He says the same in his *Table Talk*: "But I, although setting my foot in someone else's dance, would say..." <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ δ’ καίπερ ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ χορῷ πόδα τιθεὶς εἴποιμι</note>. He was responding to a matter that did not belong to the profession of a philosopher. 

Related to this adage is a very elegant metaphor, not unlike a proverb, used by Aristides in his work on Miltiades: "Furthermore, in which part of the dance shall we place Miltiades, who fought at Marathon?" <note>original Greek: μιλτιάδην δ’ ἐν ᾧ χορῷ τάξομεν, ἢ πῶς λεγόμενον;</note>. The commentator adds that this metaphor is taken from the Dionysian dances. Certainly, it is borrowed from choral dances and performances. If a stranger were to mix himself into them, he would be mocked and hissed at immediately. Plato, in the *Euthydemus*, asks: "In what dance and choir shall we place this wisdom—among the good things, or how do you say?" <note>original Greek: τίν’ δὲ θίασον καὶ χορὸν τάξομεν, ἐν οἷς ἀγαθοῖς, ἢ πῶς λέγεις;</note>.

->Speak no great things.<-
<margin>52</margin>
*Me megala lege* <note>original Greek: Μὴ μεγάλα λέγε</note>. That is, "Do not speak grand words." This is recorded by Diogenianus and warns that one must refrain from boastful or arrogant speech, which is the most intolerable of all things. It was said because of the goddess Nemesis <note>The personification of divine retribution against hubris (pride).</note>, who does not allow such grandstanding to go unpunished. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fourth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, writes: 
> Never boast until you see the end. <note>original Greek: Μήπω μέγ’ εἴπῃς πρὶν τέλος αὐτὸν ἴδῃς</note>.

Aristophanes, in *The Frogs*, says: 
> O wondrous man, do not speak too grandly. <note>original Greek: Ὦ δαιμόνι’ ἀνθρώπων, μὴ μεγάλα λίαν λέγε</note>.

With these words, Bacchus restrains Euripides, who was arrogantly placing himself above Aeschylus. Sophocles, in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*, says: 
> Speak no great thing; do you not see the evil you are in? <note>original Greek: Μηδὲν μέγ’ εἴπῃς, οὐχ ὁρᾷς ἵν’ εἶ κακοῦ;</note>.

Theocritus, in *The Cyclops*, writes: 
> Speak nothing sublime. <note>original Greek: Μηδὲν μέγα μυθοῦ</note>.

Theognis says: 
> Never, Cyrnus, utter a great word in the marketplace, for no one 
> knows what a night or a day will bring to a man. <note>original Greek: Μή ποτε Κύρν’ ἀγορᾶσθ’ ἔπος μέγα, οὐδεὶς γὰρ οἶδεν ἀνθρώπων ὅτι νὺξ χ’ ἡμέρα ἀνδρὶ τελεῖ</note>.

Plato says in the *Phaedo*: "Do not speak grandly, lest some envy <term>bakania</term> <note>original Greek: βακανία; a reference to the 'evil eye' or malevolent envy.</note> overturn the argument we are about to speak." For antiquity invented the goddess Nemesis as the avenger of boasting. Thus Pindar, in his fourth *Isthmian Ode*, says: "But nonetheless, obscure your boasting with silence. Jupiter distributes these things and those." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ὅμως καύχημα κατάβρεχε σιγᾷ. Ζεὺς τάδε καὶ τὰ νέμει</note>. Indeed, the only way to appease envy is to attribute whatever good happens to God as its author. The same poet says in his tenth *Nemean Ode*: "It is a heavy thing to fall into the envy of men." <note>original Greek: ἔστι δ’ ἐν κέρδει ἀνθρώπων βαρὺς ἀντιλάξαι</note>.

<summary>This page explores three proverbs concerning rarity, social boundaries, and humility. It discusses "A white bird" as a metaphor for rare luck, "Setting foot in another's dance" as meddling, and warns against boastful speech to avoid the wrath of the goddess Nemesis.</summary>
<keywords>white bird, meddling, hubris, Nemesis, Cicero, Plutarch, Plato, Pindar, boastfulness, Greek proverbs</keywords>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES
Lllll
<meta>catchword: begin</meta>

For the nature of mortals is envious, and nothing is more quickly sated than hearing the praises of others. The same author, in the fifth hymn of the same work, says: "I am ashamed to speak great things" <note>original Greek: αἰδέομαι μέγα εἰπῆν</note>. Virgil seems to have alluded to this in his tenth book:
> He had said something great.

One also frequently finds the phrase "to think big" <note>original Greek: μέγα φρονεῖν</note>, used for someone who is insolent and haughty. Sophocles says in *Oedipus the King*:
> For she thinks as big as a woman. <note>original Greek: φρονεῖν γὰρ ὡς γυνὴ μέγα</note> That is: To have high thoughts, as a woman does.

There is also a proverbial six-foot verse <term>senarius</term>:
> When you are most fortunate, do not think big. That is: Do not be puffed up when things are going your best.

And "to breathe big" <note>original Greek: μέγα πνεῖν</note>, which means to breathe grandly. Euripides in *The Bacchae*:
> Even if he comes breathing big.

Horace elegantly calls this kind of grandiloquence "Bubbles and foot-and-a-half-long words" in his *Art of Poetry*:
> He casts aside bubbles and foot-and-a-half-long words. <note>original: *ampullas et sesquipedalia uerba*</note>

Terence also uses "magnificent words" to describe a boastful soldier. We also read "to speak tragically" <note>original Greek: τραγικῶς λέγειν</note> and "to act out a tragedy" <note>original Greek: ἐκτραγῳδῆσαι</note>, which means to extol something with magnificent words. Horace in his *Epistles* says:
> He breathes enough of the tragic spirit, and dares successfully.

Though it does not escape me that the poet in this passage simply said "he breathes the tragic."

### Practice can achieve anything.
*Meletē panta dynatai* <note>original Greek: Μελέτη πάντα δύναται</note>. That is: "Care achieves all things." Diogenes Laertius attributes this sentiment to Periander <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>, who even attempted to dig through the Isthmus of Corinth. It signifies that nothing is so arduous that it cannot be accomplished through diligence and care. Virgil says in the *Georgics*:
> Stubborn labor conquers all, and poverty pressing in hard times.

There is a proverbial saying among the Greeks: "The gods sell good things for labor" <note>original Greek: θεοὶ τὰγαθὰ τοῖς πόνοις πωλοῦσιν</note>. Horace alluded to this:
> The labor of Hercules broke through Acheron.

Sophocles in *Electra*:
> Nothing succeeds well without labor. <note>original Greek: πόνῳ τοι χωρὶς οὐδὲν εὐτυχεῖ</note>

A verse of Menander is also cited: "The wiser men say that all things sought after require care." Simply put, Antiphanes says:
> All things become slaves to diligence. <note>original Greek: τῆς ἐπιμελείας πάντα δοῦλα γίγνεται</note>

Now, although it is not my present purpose or the goal of this work to collect every single saying of this kind into one place, I will not find it burdensome—since the occasion has presented itself—to add the words of Seneca from the second book of *On Anger*. He says: "There is nothing so difficult and arduous that the human mind cannot conquer it, and that constant meditation does not bring into familiarity. No passions are so fierce or self-governed that they cannot be subdued by discipline. Whatever the mind has commanded, it has obtained. Some have made it a habit never to laugh. Some have cut off wine, others sex, and others all fluids from their bodies. Another, content with a brief sleep, extends an untiring watchfulness. People have learned to run on the thinnest and most treacherous ropes, to carry enormous burdens barely tolerable by human strength, to dive to immense depths, and to endure the seas without any turn to breathe. There are a thousand other things in which persistence transcends every obstacle, showing that nothing is difficult for a mind that has imposed endurance upon itself."

### What first, or what last?
*Ti proton ē ti hystaton?* <note>original Greek: Τί πρῶτον ἢ τί ὕστατον;</note>. That is: "What first, or what last?" A proverbial figure of speech which we use whenever we mean to signify such a great abundance of things that we hesitate as to where we should especially begin.

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on the Greek and Latin idioms for arrogance ("speaking big") and introduces two new adages: one emphasizing that persistence and practice (meletē) can overcome any obstacle, and another used to describe an overwhelming abundance of choices.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, arrogance, Periander, diligence, labor, Seneca, human endurance, practice, Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

407
SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
<meta>catchword: Lucilius</meta>

...let us begin: or when we hesitate in perplexity as to what we ought to do first. Lucian, in the booklet titled *On Those Who Serve for Pay*, writes: "And what should I say to you first, O Philotes, or what last, of all the things those who serve for pay are forced to suffer and do?" <note>original Greek: καὶ τί σε πρῶτον, ὦ Φιλότης, ἢ τί ὕστατον φῶσι κατά λέγειν ὅσαπερ ἂ παθεῖν ἢ ποιεῖν ἀνάγκη τοὺς ἐπὶ μισθῷ συνόντας;</note> That is: What indeed shall I recount to you first, my friend, or what last—as the saying goes—of those things which they are compelled to suffer and do who serve for wages? Furthermore, Lucian took this from the ninth book of the *Odyssey*, in which Ulysses speaks in this manner:
What first, what next, and what finally shall I recount? <note>original Greek: τί πρῶτον, τί δ' ἔπειτα, τί δ' ὕστατον καταλέξω;</note> That is: 
What first, what soon, and what at last as the final thing shall I say? **Juvenal** also writes:
Where do you turn yourself? What do you put first or last?
Of the same character is that line of Euripides in *The Mad Hercules*: 
Alas, which of you first, or which last shall I bring to my breast? <note>original Greek: οἴμοι τίν' ἡμῶν πρῶτον, ἢ τίν' ὕστατον πρὸς σέρνα θώμαι;</note> That is:
Which of you, oh which, shall I first or last move to my heart?

## To be gnawed by a Theonine tooth. LV

Those who are torn apart by insults are said to be "gnawed by a Theonine tooth" <note>original: *Dente Theonino rodi*</note>. The phrase is taken from a certain poet named Theon, known for a rabid loquacity and the most petulant foul-mouthedness. Hence, Ausonius, in a hendecasyllabic poem, calls a certain unlearned and biting poet "Theon," saying:
Nor hereafter shall you fear what is said everywhere:
"This is that false poet Theon,
The Laverna <term>the goddess of thieves and cheats</term> of good-bad poems." **Horace in his Epistles** writes:
He who is gnawed all around by a Theonine tooth.
He used a similar figure in an epistle to Julius Florus:
This one is delighted by iambic verses,
That one by Bionian discourses.
Acron <note>a famous commentator on Horace</note> reminds us that Bion was a philosopher who tore into poets with the most biting dialogues, such that he did not even spare Homer. Porphyrion <note>another ancient commentator</note> maintains he was the father of the comic poet Aristophanes. The "bitingness" of Zoilus is also nearly proverbial, though you should understand him as more of an envious critic than a mere barker. Horace calls this vice in some places "cuttlefish juice" <note>original: *succum loliginis*</note> and "black salt," because the bite adds a stain to one's reputation.

## An Hipponactean proclamation. LVI

Marcus Tullius Cicero used "an Hipponactean proclamation" <note>original: *Hipponacteum præconium*</note> to signify an infamous mark of disgrace; he used it proverbially in his *Letters to Friends* when writing of a certain Tigellius: "And I think he was already then condemned by the Hipponactean proclamation of Calvus Licinius." For Hipponax was an iambic poet <term>a writer of satirical verse</term>, bitter and of noted sharp-tonguedness. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, he intentionally broke the Archilochian trimeter into the "scazon" <term>the 'limping' meter, where the rhythm stumbles at the end</term> when he wanted to tear into his enemies, so that he might strike more forcefully. It is read that he pursued Bupalus and Anthermus with iambic verses because he had been painted by them with a deformed appearance. There was, however, a notable ugliness in the face of Hipponax, which is why some people displayed his image in circles of mockers; it is believed he drove some of them to the noose with his poems. Pliny denies this is true in his thirty-sixth book, chapter five.

## Archilochean edicts. LVII

That which Cicero writes to Atticus in his second book also has the appearance of an adage: "Therefore the Archilochean edicts of Bibulus against him are so pleasing to the people that we cannot pass the place where they are posted because of the multitude of those reading them." He calls "Archilochean edicts" those that are insulting and virulent. The bitingness of the poet Archilochus was celebrated everywhere. He pursued his father-in-law Lycambes, by whom he had been rejected, and Lycambes' daughter with such virulent verses that both of them choked themselves with a noose.

## The homeland of Archilochus. LVIII

The homeland of Archilochus <note>original Greek: Ἀρχιλόχου πατρίς</note>. Diogenianus testifies that this is commonly said of biting and slanderous people. For you may see some nations that are naturally witty and sharp-tongued, of which kind the Sicilians are said to have been.

## To bite with the back tooth. LIX

Those who secretly disparage and tear someone apart are said to "bite with the back tooth" <note>original: *genuino mordere*</note>. Persius says:
And he broke a molar <note>original: *genuinum*</note> on them.

THE ADAGES OF ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<meta>catchword: But</meta>

...you will perceive Lucilius to be a satiric poet <note>original: *Lucilium senties poetam Satyricum*</note>. Likewise, Saint Jerome says: "I could respond, I could even—if I wished—inflict a back tooth when provoked." Now, "back teeth" <note>original: *dentes genuini*, literally 'cheek teeth' or wisdom teeth</note> are the most hidden of all and are almost entirely covered by the gums. They emerge late in humans: namely around the twentieth year, and for many even in their eightieth year, as Pliny records in Book 11, chapter 37. For this reason, they are—not without cause—dedicated to the disease of envy and detraction. This may also be applied quite reasonably to those small teeth of a viper, through which people believe it injects its venom. Pliny says in the same chapter just cited: "For these too are the hollowed teeth of the viper beneath the jaw." It can also refer to dogs, which gnaw on harder bones with their back teeth. Every act of detraction is called a "bite." Hence Aristophanes jokes that there is no remedy in a ring against the "bite of a sycophant." Diogenes, when asked (as recorded in Laertius) which animal’s bite was the most deadly, replied: "Among wild animals, the slanderer’s; among the tame, the flatterer’s." Horace calls this poison "the juice of the cuttlefish" <note>original: *loliginis succum*, referring to dark, ink-like malice</note>.

->To fish with a golden hook.<-
<margin>LX</margin>

Those are said to "fish with a golden hook" who, out of a desire for a modest advantage, approach a danger that might cause them to lose things of the greatest value. This is recounted among the witty sayings of Augustus Caesar by Suetonius. For it sometimes happens that a fish carries the hook itself away with it. Furthermore, many metaphors drawn from fishing have been adopted as proverbs. Just as *expiscari* ("to fish out") is used in Terence for the act of diligently eliciting and searching something out. To "swallow the hook" is found in Plautus.

->May your hook always be hanging, as in Ovid.<-

Even if someone were to argue that this saying of Augustus is not strictly a proverb, it is certainly "proverbial," and not unworthy of being added to this collection. It may be that some even took pleasure in literally fishing with a golden hook. Indeed, according to Suetonius, Nero Caesar was accustomed to fish with a gilded net, with ropes woven of purple and scarlet. Therefore, whenever we pursue something in such a way that the benefit is mediocre if we succeed, but the loss is immense if our hope fails us, we shall aptly be said to "fish with a golden hook." This frequently happens to those who search the hidden veins of the earth, but more frequently to those commonly called Alchemists <note>original: *Alcumistae*</note>, about whom Demetrius of Phalerum spoke charmingly in the sixth book of Athenaeus: <term>ὅτι πολλάκις καταναλώσαντες τὰ φανερὰ τὰ ἀδήλων ἕνεκα, ἃ μὲν ἔμελλον οὐκ ἔλαβον, ἃ δ’ εἶχον ἀπέβαλον</term>. That is: Because frequently, having consumed certainties for the sake of uncertainties, they did not receive what they hoped to catch, but threw away what they already had.

->Wisdom is clouded by wine.<-
<margin>LXI</margin>

Pliny, in Book 23, Chapter 1 of his *Natural History*: "For those who have not eaten, drinking wine is a most useless modern invention. It hinders the cares and focus of the mind; it is suited for sleep and security for those heading into battle; and this was long ago the case with that Helen of Homer's, who served it before the meal." Thus it also passed into a proverb: "Wisdom is clouded by wine." So far Pliny. Furthermore, what Pliny cites is from the fourth book of the *Odyssey*. Likewise, in the ecclesiastical proverbs <note>referring to the Book of Ecclesiasticus or Sirach 19:2</note>, two things are mentioned that make even a wise man go mad: wine and women.

->Frugal men do all things rightly.<-
<margin>LXII</margin>

Marcus Tullius Cicero in the fourth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "We wish to refer the name of 'frugality' as if to the head of the matter; for unless all virtues were contained under that name, it would never have been so common that it now holds the place of a proverb: 'Frugal men do all things rightly.'" So far Cicero. The adage teaches that certain wicked men are sometimes useful in specific matters and conduct themselves excellently; but to be an upright and blameless man everywhere and perpetually—that, finally, seems to belong only to the man who is truly honorable by nature. Euripides alludes to this sentiment in *Hecuba* when he says:
> <term>Ἀνθρώποις δ’ ἀεὶ,</term>
> <term>ὁ μὲν πονηρὸς οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν κακὸς,</term>
> <term>ὁ δ’ ἐσθλὸς, ἐσθλὸς, οὐδὲ συμφορᾶς ὕπο</term>
> <term>φύσιν διέφθειρ’ ἀλλὰ χρηστός ἐστ’ ἀεί.</term>
> ->that is,<-
> But among mortals
> Whoever is bad is nothing else but bad,
> The frugal man <note>referring to the man of integrity</note> is always frugal: for heavy
> Fortune does not corrupt his nature, but he always remains honorable.

Likewise in *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
> <term>ὁ δ’ ὀρθὸς, ἐσθλὸν σαφὲς ἀεί.</term>
> ->that is,<-
> He who is upright is clearly always noble.

He uses examples from Roman emperors and Greek playwrights to illustrate how character and prudence dictate success and morality.</summary>

SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY

<margin>But he who is upright,</margin> He is always openly upright.
<margin>Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Ethics*: <note>original: "Τὸ, μέν γὰρ ἀγαθὸν ἁπλοῦν, τὸ δ' κακὸν πολύμορφον. καὶ ἀγαθὸς μέν ὅμοιος ἀεί, οὐ δ' μεταβάλλει τὸ ἦθος, ὁ δ' φαῦλος καὶ ἄφρων οὐδέν ἔοικεν ἑωυτῷ ἐν ἑσπέρας."</note></margin> that is: "For indeed, that which is good is simple, whereas that which is evil is many-formed. And he who is good is always like himself, nor does he ever change his character. But whoever is wicked and foolish in no way seems the same in the morning as he does in the evening." To this, that passage of the Sacred Scriptures <note>original: *literarum arcanarum*, literally 'secret letters,' a common Erasmian term for the Bible</note> harmonizes wonderfully: "A fool changes like the moon, but a wise man remains constant like the sun." <note>A reference to Ecclesiasticus 27:11.</note>

---

->One deception pushes out another. LXIIII<-

<margin>Terence in the *Andria*:</margin> "One deception pushes out another." Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence.</note> notes that this is spoken as a proverbial figure. It is taken from the habit of those who try to deceive, patching together trick upon trick so they might not be caught. Hence Plautus spoke of "sewn-up tricks" <note>original: *consutis dolis*</note>. And he calls these kinds of schemes <term>sutelas</term> <note>Literally "stitchings," used here to mean clever deceptions or "staged" tricks.</note>. <margin>Homer says: "To weave wiles," <note>original: "Ἐξ δόλος ὑφαίνειν"</note> that is, to weave deceptions.</margin>

---

->Thrift comes too late at the bottom of the jar. LXIII<-

This is a proverbial sentiment found in Seneca’s first letter: "Thrift comes too late at the bottom of the jar." It is truly worthy of being inscribed on every chest, every wine-jar, and every pantry. It warns that one must be sparing with necessary things in due time, rather than imitating the common crowd of spendthrifts, who only begin to save once they see that very little remains. The sentiment is even more elegant if applied to the matters of the soul—for instance, if one were to warn young people not to let those best years flow away in vain, lest what happens to most people happens to them: that they only apply their minds to honorable pursuits when they are already advanced in age. Then, when only a tiny fraction of life remains, they begin to be sparing with their time. For "thrift is too late at the bottom." This proverb appears to be taken from Hesiod, whose verses in the work titled *Works and Days* are as follows:

<margin>Hesiod: <note>original: "Ἀρχομένου δὲ πίθε καὶ λήγοντος κορέσασθαι, μεσσόθι φείδεσθαι, δειλὴ δ' ἐνὶ πυθμένι φειδώ."</note></margin> That is:

> When the jars are full, or now nearly empty of wine,
> Then take your fill; but in the middle, be more sparing.
> For it is absurd and wretched to be thrifty at the very bottom.

<margin>Persius alluded to this in his second Satire: "Until, deceived and hopeless, the last coin sighs in vain at the very bottom."</margin> Plutarch, in the third problem of the seventh decade of his *Table Talk* <note>original: *Symposiacis*</note>, indicates that the poet warned to drink the wine when it is at its best. However, wine is most wholesome and best to drink in the middle—just as the top part of oil is most praised, and the bottom part of honey. First, because the power of wine is heat, and this seems to collect mostly around the middle; therefore, that is the best part to keep. Second, the lower part of the wine is corrupted by being near the dregs, while the top part is damaged by the proximity of the air. For that air is an enemy to wine is sufficiently proven by the fact that wine in a full jar spoils less quickly than in one half-full. Furthermore, when jars are buried in the earth so that the air cannot reach them, they preserve their vigor for a very long time. Theocritus also says in the *Graces*:

<margin>A chest empty at the bottom. <note>original: "Κενεᾶς ἐπὶ πυθμένι χηλός."</note></margin> that is,
<margin>A box with an empty bottom,</margin> signifying an empty chest.

->A Sybaritic table. LXV<-

<margin>A Sybaritic table. <note>original: "Συβαριτικὴ τράπεζα"</note></margin> This was said of a banquet prepared with excessive luxury. The saying arose from the customs of that people. Sybaris is a town near Croton, as Herodotus testifies in his fifth book. Stephanus indicates it was later called Thurii. From this, they were called Sybarites, a people most industrious in the "architecture of pleasures." According to Suidas, they were so notable for luxury and delicacies that whatever was effeminate, whatever was soft, whatever was prepared with meticulous and ambitious luxury, was commonly called "Sybaritic." Hence Ovid, in the second book of his *Tristia*, writing to Augustus:

> Nor did he escape, who recently composed the *Sybaritida*.

He calls the *Sybaritida* a work by a certain Hemitheon, a lewd man of Sybaris, concerning the types of pleasures and obscene delicacies. Likewise, Martial in his twelfth book:

> Those who compete, he says, with "Sybaritic booklets."

Philo the Hebrew, in his *Life of Moses*, calls lascivious poems "Sybaritic wickednesses." Maximus Tyrius, in his third dissertation on pleasures, mentions "Sybaritic dances." Aristotle, in the first book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, also compares Smindyrides the Sybarite to Sar-

408
THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<meta>catchword: Atqui (But indeed)</meta>

You will feel the bite of Lucilius <note>A Roman satirist known for his sharp wit.</note>, the satiric poet. Likewise, Saint Jerome says: "I could answer, if I wished; though injured, I could sink in my molar." Now, molar teeth are the most hidden of all and almost covered by the gums. They emerge late in humans: namely, around the twentieth year, and for many even in the eightieth, as Pliny records in Book 11, chapter 37. For this reason, they are quite appropriately dedicated to the disease of envy and detraction <note>Erasmus suggests the molar represents hidden, deep-seated resentment that strikes late or unexpectedly.</note>. It can also be applied, not without reason, to those small teeth of the viper through which they are thought to pour their venom. Pliny says in the same chapter we just cited: "For these too are the hollowed teeth under the viper's jaw." It can also refer to dogs, who gnaw on harder bones with their back teeth. Furthermore, all detraction is called a "bite." Hence Aristophanes jokes that there is no remedy in a ring against the bite of a sycophant. Diogenes, according to Laertius, when asked which animal's bite was most pernicious, replied: "Among wild animals, that of the slanderer; among the tame, that of the flatterer." Horace calls this poison "the juice of the cuttlefish" <note>original: *loliginis succum*. This refers to black ink or metaphorical "black" malice.</note>.

### To fish with a golden hook.
<margin>LX</margin>
Those who, out of a desire for moderate profit, approach a danger that might cause the loss of the greatest things, are said to "fish with a golden hook." This is recorded by Suetonius among the witty sayings of Octavius Caesar <note>The Emperor Augustus.</note>. For it happens sometimes that the fish carries away even the hook itself. Many metaphors drawn from fishing are used in place of proverbs. For example, "To fish out" <note>original: *Expiscari*</note> in Terence, used for diligently eliciting and searching out information. "To swallow the hook" <note>original: *Vorare hamū*</note> in Plautus.

### Let your hook always hang, as in Ovid.
If anyone should argue that this saying of Augustus is not a proverb, it is certainly proverbial in nature, and not unworthy of being added to this collection. It may be that some have even enjoyed literally fishing with a golden hook. Indeed, according to Suetonius, Nero Caesar was accustomed to fish with a gilded net, with ropes woven from purple and scarlet. Thus, whenever we pursue a goal in such a way that if we obtain our wishes, the reward is mediocre, but if our hope fails, the loss is immense, we shall aptly be said to "fish with a golden hook." This frequently happens to those who search the hidden veins of the earth, and even more frequently to those commonly called Alchemists. Regarding them, Demetrius of Phalerum spoke gracefully in Athenaeus, Book 6: <note>original: "ὅτι πολλάκις καταναλώσαντες τὰ φανερὰ τ᾽ ἄδηλα θηρεύειν, ἃ μὲν ἔμελλον ἐκ ἔλαβον, ἃ δ᾽ ἄχρι ἀπέβαλον"</note> that is, "Because frequently, having consumed certain assets for the sake of uncertain ones, they did not catch what they hoped to take, and threw away what they actually possessed."

### Wisdom is clouded by wine.
<margin>LXI</margin>
Pliny, in the *Natural History*, Book 23, Chapter 1: "For those who are fasting, to drink wine is a most useless modern invention. It hinders cares and the vigor of the mind; for those preparing for battle it is suited for sleep and security; and it has been a long time since Homeric Helen served it before food." Thus it has also passed into a proverb: "Wisdom is clouded by wine." So far Pliny. Furthermore, what Pliny cites is from the fourth book of the *Odyssey*. Likewise, in the ecclesiastical proverbs <note>The Book of Proverbs or Ecclesiastes.</note>, two things are mentioned that drive even a wise man mad: wine and women.

### Frugal men do all things rightly.
<margin>LXII</margin>
Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in Book 4 of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "We wish to refer the name of frugality back to the source, as it were; for unless the virtues were contained under that name, it would never have been so commonplace as to now hold the place of a proverb: *Frugal men do all things rightly*." Thus far Cicero. The adage teaches that certain wicked men may sometimes be of use in specific matters and conduct themselves excellently; but to provide an upright and blameless life everywhere and perpetually, that seems to belong only to him who is truly honorable by nature. Euripides alludes to this sentiment in *Hecuba* when he says:
> <note>original Greek: "Ἀνθρώποις δ᾽ ἀεί, ὁ μὲν πονηρὸς οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν κακός, ὁ δ᾽ ἐσθλός, ἐσθλός, οὐδὲ συμφορᾶς ὕπο φύσιν διέφθειρ᾽ ἀλλὰ χρηστός ἐσ᾽ ἀεί."</note>
> ->that is:<-
> But among mortals,
> Whoever is bad, is nothing else but bad;
> The frugal man is ever frugal: for heavy
> Fortune does not corrupt his nature, but he remains always good.

Likewise in *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
> <note>original Greek: "ὁ δ᾽ ὀρθός, ἐσθλὸν σαφὲς ἀεί."</note>
> ->that is:<-

SECOND CHILIAD, SECOND HUNDRED
<meta>The "M" at the bottom is a signature mark for the printer to keep the pages in order.</meta>

But he who is honest is always honest openly.
Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Ethics*: <margin>For the good is simple, but the evil is many-formed. And the good man is always the same, and his character does not change, but the wicked and the foolish man is not at all the same in the morning and the evening.</margin> <note>original: "Τό, τε γὰρ ἀγαθοῦ ἁπλοῦν..."</note> that is: since that which is good is likewise simple, while on the contrary, that which is evil is varied. And he who is good is always consistent with himself, and never changes his character. But whoever is wicked and foolish seems by no means to be the same person in the morning and the evening. With this, that passage of sacred scripture <note>Erasmus refers to Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 27:11.</note> accords wonderfully: "A fool changes like the moon, but a wise man remains as the sun."

### One deception thrusts forward another. LXIII

Terence in *The Girl from Andros*: One deception thrusts forward another. Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Terence.</note> remarks that this was said as a proverbial figure. It is taken from the habit of those who attempt to deceive, who stuff tricks upon tricks so that they are not caught. Hence Plautus spoke of "stitched-together deceits." And he calls such schemes "sutures" <note>term: *Sutelas* (from *suere*, to sew), meaning crafty inventions or "sewn-up" tricks.</note>. <margin>To weave a deceit,</margin> <note>original: "Ἐξ δόλος ὑφαίνειν"</note> as found in Homer, that is, to weave tricks.

### Thrift at the bottom is too late. LXIIII

A proverbial sentiment found in Seneca’s first epistle: Thrift at the bottom is too late. It is a saying truly worthy of being inscribed on every chest, every wine-jar, and every pantry. It warns that one should be sparing with necessary things in due time, and not imitate the common crowd of spendthrifts, who only then begin to be frugal once they see that the very least remains. The sentiment will be even more elegant if it is applied to the matters of the soul—for instance, if one should warn young people not to let those best years flow away in vain, lest that which usually happens to most people happens to them: that when they are already great in age, they apply their minds to honorable pursuits, and when only a tiny fraction of life remains, they finally begin to be sparing of their time. For thrift at the bottom is too late. The proverb appears to be taken from Hesiod, whose verses in the work titled *Works and Days* are these:
<margin>When the jar is first opened and when it is failing, take your fill; be sparing in the middle. For thrift at the very bottom is a wretched thing.</margin> <note>original: "Ἀρχομένου δὲ πίθου..."</note>
> That is:
> When the jars are full, or when the wine is nearly gone,
> Then take your fill; but in the middle, be more sparing.
> For it is absurd and a heavy thing to be frugal at the very bottom.

Persius alludes to this in his second Satire:
> Until, deceived and hopeless,
> The last coin sighs in vain at the very bottom of the chest.

Plutarch, in the third problem of the seventh decade of his *Table Talk*, indicates that the poet warned that wine should be drunk when it is at its best. He argues that wine is healthiest and best to drink in the middle, just as the top part of oil is most highly praised, and the bottom of honey. First, because the power of wine is heat, and this heat seems to gather most around the middle; therefore, it is best to preserve it there. Furthermore, the lower part of the wine is spoiled by its proximity to the dregs, and the top part is damaged by the nearby air. For that air is an enemy to wine is sufficiently proven by the fact that wine in a full jar goes flat less quickly than in one half-full. Then there is the fact that jars buried in the earth, so that air cannot touch them, preserve their vigor for as long as possible. Theocritus says likewise in *The Graces*:
<margin>A chest empty at the bottom.</margin> <note>original: "Κενεᾶς ἀπὸ πυθμένι χηλός."</note>
> That is:
> A chest with an empty bottom, signifying a useless storage box.

### A Sybarite table. LXV

<margin>A Sybarite table.</margin> <note>original: "Συβαριτικὴ τράπεζα."</note> That is, a Sybaritic table. This was said of a banquet prepared with excessive luxury. It arose from the customs of that people. For Sybaris is a town near Croton, as Herodotus testifies in his fifth book. Stephanus indicates it was later called Thurion. From this, they were called Sybarites, a people most industrious in the architecture of pleasures. According to Suidas, they were so notable for luxury and delicacies that whatever was effeminate, whatever was soft, whatever was prepared with painstaking and ambitious luxury, was commonly called "Sybaritic." Hence Ovid, in the second book of his *Tristia*, writing to Augustus:
> Nor did he who recently composed the *Sybaritid* escape [exile].

He calls the *Sybaritid* a work by a certain Hemitheon, a Sybarite profligate, concerning kinds of pleasures and obscene delicacies. Likewise Martial in his twelfth book says:
> Those who compete, he says, with Sybaritic books.

Philo the Hebrew, in his *Life of Moses*, calls wanton poems "Sybaritic wickednesses." Maximus Tyrius, in his third dissertation on pleasures, mentions "Sybaritic dances." Aristotle, in the first book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, compares Smindyrides the Sybarite to Sardanapalus <note>A king of Assyria legendary for his self-indulgence and decadence.</note>...

It concludes by defining "Sybaritic luxury" through numerous classical references to the decadent city of Sybaris.</summary>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
<meta>The catchword "naus" at the bottom of the previous page suggests the continuation of the word "Sardanapalus," here appearing as "danapalo."</meta>

[Sar]danapalus <note>A legendary Assyrian king who became a proverb for indulgence.</note> among the pleasure-seekers. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia.</note> writes that "old wives' tales," or those lacking in modesty, were called "Sybaritic stories." He also reports that the Sybarites established a custom of training their horses to dance to the sound of the flute, and that the word "Sybarite" became a name for the luxurious, while "to Sybarize" meant to indulge in delights after the fashion of the Sybarites. Quintilian agrees in his third book: "Frugality," you might say, "would perhaps be an object of hatred among the Sybarites." Plutarch, in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*, records that it was a custom among the Sybarites for women to be invited to a banquet as much as a year in advance, so that they might have leisure to adorn themselves with gold and fine clothing. These and similar things are recorded by Angelo Poliziano in the fifteenth chapter of his *Miscellanea*. Furthermore, Aelius Lampridius <note>A biographer in the *Augustan History*.</note> depicts a Sybaritic banquet and mentions a "Sybaritic course" in his *Life of Heliogabalus*, an Emperor so lost to luxury that he earned a nickname and was commonly called "Apicius" <note>Named after the famous Roman gourmet.</note>. I will transcribe Lampridius’s words: "He always," he says, "either sat among flowers or among precious perfumes. He loved to have higher prices quoted to him for the things prepared for his table, asserting that this provided a 'stimulus' <note>term: *orexin* (from Greek *orexis*), meaning an appetite or longing</note> for the banquet. In a single dinner, he served the heads of six hundred ostriches just so that the brains might be eaten. He also once provided a banquet of such a sort that he had twenty-two courses of enormous feasts; between each one, they would bathe and enjoy the company of women, both he and his friends, with an oath that this truly produced pleasure. He also held a banquet in which single courses were prepared at the homes of individual friends; and while one lived on the Capitoline, another on the Palatine, another on the Caelian Hill, and another across the Tiber, and wherever each lived, the individual courses were nonetheless eaten in order at their houses, and they traveled to the homes of everyone. Thus, a single banquet was barely finished in a whole day, as they bathed and enjoyed women between every course. He always had a 'Sybaritic course' made of oil and fish sauce <note>term: *garum*, a fermented fish sauce highly prized in antiquity</note>, which the Sybarites invented in the same year they perished." Athenaeus also records many things concerning both the luxury and the destruction of the Sybarites in his *Deipnosophists* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned."</note>, both elsewhere and in the twelfth book, including this: that the Sybarites would not admit any craft into their city that could not be practiced without noise—such as blacksmiths, carpenters, and the like—so that there would be nothing to make a noise for those sleeping. For the same reason, it was forbidden by law for a rooster to be kept in the city. He records other evidence of their delights there, if anyone has the time to read it. Aristophanes, in *The Acharnians*, used "to Sybarize" to mean to live sumptuously and genially:
> And what will then be yours,
> to sail, to stay, to move, to sleep,
> to watch at the festivals,
> to feast, and to Sybarize.

-> that is, <-

> Now indeed it will be permitted for you to sail, to stay, to move, to sleep, to watch at the festivals, to be received at a banquet, to play at cottabus <note>A Greek drinking game involving throwing wine at a target.</note>, and to Sybarize. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> to Basil used a similar figure to describe a table overflowing with luxury as "the table of Alcinous" <note>The king of the Phaeacians in the *Odyssey*, famed for his hospitality and garden.</note>: "Not to the poverty of the lotus-eaters, but to the table of Alcinous." <note>original: "ὄψ ὡς λωτοφάγε πενίαν, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἀλκινόου τράπεζαν."</note>

### LXVI
-> A Sybaritic calamity. <-

<note>original: "Συβαριτικὴ συμφορά."</note> that is, a Sybaritic disaster. Stephanus noted this as a proverb. Furthermore, he tells how the Sybarites perished in this manner. They had received an oracle of this kind:
> Happy, entirely happy you shall be, O Sybarite,
> While you honor the race of the ever-living gods with joyful things.
> But as soon as a mortal man shall be preferred to them,
> Then war and domestic strife shall come upon you.

-> that is, <-

> Happy, altogether happy shall the Sybarite be,
> While you worship the power of the gods in prosperous times.
> But as soon as a mortal man is preferred before them,
> Then both war and civil turmoil shall come to you.

It happened then that a certain Sybarite was beating a slave with thongs in the field; when the slave fled to the altar of the gods, the master nonetheless continued to beat him as he pursued. When the slave saw that the reverence for the deity had been of no use to him, he immediately fled to the tomb of his master's father; then, finally, moved by religious awe for his parent, the master ceased the beating. Thus, according to the response of the oracle, the Sybarites were overthrown by the people of Croton. Aelius Lampridius, in the *Life of Heliogabalus*, writes that they perished in the same year they invented the dish made of oil and fish sauce, which for that reason he calls "Sybaritic," as we just said. Moreover, Athenaeus has recorded many things concerning the luxury and the calamity of the Sybarites.

<margin>Sybarites through the broad streets. That is,</margin>

### Sybarites through the broad streets. LXVII

Used against those who walk through the street with pride, as if showing themselves off. The adage is taken from the pride and luxury of the Sybarites. Africanus, in the speech titled *Cesti*, says: "But look," he says, "the Sybarites are swollen with pride." It is more elegant if it is twisted a little further: for instance, if you speak of a man behaving too insolently, or speaking too arrogantly about himself, or about an overly decorated style of writing, you might say: "A Sybarite through the broad streets" <note>original: "Συβαρίτην διὰ πλατείας"</note>. This is related to what is said in another place as "ophthalmias" <note>meaning "eye-disease" or "conspicuousness," original: "ὀφθαλμίας"</note>. The adage is recorded by Suidas and Zenodotus.

---

<margin>Syracusan table. That is,</margin>

### Syracusan table. LXVIII

A "Syracusan table" <note>original: "Syracusana mensa"</note> was a term used for a table that was extremely lavish and sumptuous. For just as the Syracusans were once very flourishing in wealth, so they were most addicted to pleasures and delicacies. Lucian, in the dialogue of *Similis and Polystratus*, says: "To prepare meals," he says, "surpassing those in Sicily" <note>original: "ἐξαρτύεσθαι... ὑπὲρ τὰς ἐν σικελίᾳ"</note>. That is, tables more elegant than the Sicilians'. Athenaeus in his twelfth book says: "There are banqueters whose luxury surpasses even that of the Sicilian table" <note>original: "δαιταλοί εἰσιν ὧν τρυφῇ νικᾷ τὰ ἐν τῇ σικελίᾳ τραπέζᾳ"</note>. That is, the tables of the Sicilians are famous for their delicacies. He adds, on the authority of Clearchus, that the Sicilians say even the sea is sweet among them, because they delight in the foods the sea provides. Diogenes mentions the "Sicilian table" in a certain letter to Aristippus. Likewise Aristides in his work on Pericles. Finally, Strabo in his sixth book mentions these and many other things. 

Plutarch, in the *Life of Nicias*, records from Diphilus: "Fat, and manured with a Sicilian belly, or fattened" <note>original: "παχὺς, ἀνθυλλωμένος τε καὶ σκελετινός"</note>. I wonder why the Latin translator thought it should be rendered as "anointed," since *anthulle* <note>original: "ἀνθύλλη"</note> signifies cow dung, a most useful fertilizer for fields. Plato, in a letter to the relatives of Dion, denies that that happy life situated in Sicilian and Italian tables and other pleasures ever pleased him. Aristotle also mentions the luxury of the Syracusans in his *Politics* of that nation, adding that Dionysius the Younger <note>A tyrant of Syracuse known for his excesses.</note> sometimes remained drunk for up to ninety days, and for that reason his eyes were dim and diseased. 

Theophrastus relates in Athenaeus that his friends and drinking companions used to pretend in banquets that they could not see the food or the cups placed before them, clearly flattering the dim-sighted king in that manner; hence they were called "Dionysian flatterers" <note>original: "Διονυσιοκόλακες"</note>. In the same author, Aristophanes in *The Banqueters* says:

<margin>But send me those things you have learned,</margin>
> "But rather drink much, then sing badly, a Syracusan table and Sybaritic banquets." <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ μάλαν πινῦν... συρακοσίων τράπεζαν συβαρίτιδάς τ᾽ εὐωχίας"</note>

That is: "But you did not learn these things under my leadership, but rather to drink, and then to sing poorly, and to enjoy the Syracusan table and Sybaritic feasts." Likewise Plato in the third book of the *Republic*:

<margin>O friend, you do not seem to approve of the Syracusan table and the Sicilian variety of appetizers.</margin>
> "O friend, you do not seem to approve of the Syracusan table and the Sicilian variety of appetizers." <note>original: "Συρακόσιον ὦ φίλε... οὐκ αἰνεῖς"</note>

Athenaeus in his fourteenth book cites Cratinus, who, describing an extremely elegant kitchen, well-steaming and sweet-smelling, speaks thus:

> "It seems to me someone lives in this hollow,
> An incense-seller, or a Sicilian cook."

In the same place, Antiphanes also praises Sicilian cooks as being outstanding in the art of seasoning. 

But in these times, the Sicilians imitate Spanish and Italian frugality so much that they almost surpass it, and they have clearly lost the glory of this proverb. Although Athenaeus, in the *Deipnosophists*, also counts Italian tables among the sumptuous ones. Yet in these times, they have certainly claimed for themselves that ancient praise of frugality; just as the Greeks have returned to their ancient glory of drunkenness after a long absence. 

From this, Faustus Andrelinus of Forlì—a poet not only laureate but also royal, and, if it please the gods, even the Queen's poet, an old boon companion of mine who has now taught poetry in the most celebrated Academy of Paris for more than thirty years—in a poem he wrote about the "Pavement of Paris," turned the adage against the English. "The British table," he says, "is pleasing." 

And I do not know from where this most common proverb among the French arose, so that when they want a man to be understood as being violently distended with food, they say: "He is as full as an Englishman." But just as they attribute "polyphagia" <note>term: polyphagia — excessive eating</note> to them, so they ascribe "polyposia" <note>term: polyposia — excessive drinking</note> to us <note>Erasmus refers here to his own people, the Dutch/Germans.</note>.

M 2 <meta>catchword: Spithama</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of adages, moving from the excesses of the Sybarites to metaphors for the shortness of life, the nature of time, and the corruption of the legal system.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>LXIX</margin>
->A span of life.<-

"A span of life" <note>original: "Σπιθαμὴ τοῦ βίου"</note>. That is, a very tiny measure of life. This is a proverbial figure of speech borrowed from land-surveyors, among whom a "span" <note>term: spithama (a measurement from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger)</note> or "palm" contains twelve digits, which is roughly the distance one can cover with the longest reach of the fingers. Even today, the unlearned people of our own country call a tiny little man "a palm" or "a handful of a man." The term is transferred from craftsmen, who measure material with four fingers joined together and call that measure a "wrestler's square" <note>term: palaesta (the width of the four fingers of the hand)</note>; or sometimes with the hand stretched out from the top of the thumb to the tip of the middle finger, which they call a "span" <note>original: "σπιθαμήν"</note>. In Psalm 38 <note>Psalm 39:5 in modern Bibles</note>, it says: "Behold, you have made my days as a handbreadth" <note>original: "ἰδοὺ παλαιστὰς ἔθου τὰς ἡμέρας μου"</note>, indicating the very brief span of life. This adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

<margin>LXX</margin>
->A point of time.<-

"A point of time" <note>original: "Στιγμὴ χρόνου"</note>. Terence used a similar figure when he said: "Then at that point of time I had this." That is, a very brief space. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the second *Philippic*: "Attend for a little while, and look up at a point of time with the thought of a sober man." Also in the eighth *Philippic*: "He showed the work and the fortification to the ambassadors; not even for a point of time while the ambassadors were present did the siege catch its breath." Among mathematicians, a point is an indivisible part of a line, which, as Euclid says, has no parts. Plutarch in *On the Education of Children* says: "All of life is a point of time" <note>original: "Στιγμὴ χρόνου πᾶς ἐστὶν ὁ βίος"</note>.

<margin>LXXI</margin>
->New Hymettian, old Falernian.<-

Macrobius, in the seventh book of the *Saturnalia*, asks: "Why are honey and wine considered best at different ages?" Honey when it is newest, and wine when it is oldest. From this comes that proverb used by gluttons: "A honey-wine that you temper correctly must be mixed with new Hymettian honey and old Falernian wine." I do not see where this adage could be of use to us, but nevertheless we have included it so that we do not seem to have borrowed nothing at all from the taverns. Unless, perhaps, one chooses to twist it so that we say certain things are best composed from diverse elements. <note>Hymettus was a mountain in Greece famous for honey; Falernian was a prestigious Roman wine.</note>

<margin>LXXII</margin>
->He who steals much and gives a little to his supporters will be safe.<-

Aelius Lampridius says in the *Life of Alexander Severus*: "He also added a well-known sentence about thieves, and in Greek indeed, which in Latin means this: He who steals much and gives a little to his supporters will be safe." In Greek it is:
"He who steals many things, by giving a few, shall escape" <note>original: "Ὁ πολλὰ κλέψας, ὀλίγα δούς, ἐκφεύξεται"</note>. That is:
"He who takes much, and gives a little, will be saved."
The adage warns (a thing which even in our own times thieves who are not entirely stupid commonly do) that one should only lay hands on great spoils, so that enough remains to corrupt and blind the judge, if by chance there is need. However, those who take small things are hanged when caught, since they have nothing to share with the officials.

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
->In a ladle.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero in the third book of *On the Laws*, discussing the "ballot law"—that is, the law regarding the right to cast votes by tablet—says: "And our grandfather, a man of singular virtue in this municipality as long as he lived, resisted Marcus Gratidius (whose sister, our grandmother, he had in marriage) when he was proposing the ballot law. For Gratidius was 'raising waves in a ladle' <note>term: simpulum (a small sacrificial ladle or cup)</note>, as the saying goes, waves which his son Marius later raised in the Aegean Sea." So much for Cicero. As far as one can gather by conjecture, they used to say something was happening "in a ladle" when it happened either secretly, or in a minute and lowly matter. For a *simpulum*, according to Festus, is a small vessel, not unlike a cup, from which women dedicated to divine matters are called *simpulatrices*. Marcus Varro writes that it is a tiny pouring vessel, which was later replaced by the *epichysis* <note>a Greek style of jug</note>. Hence the ancients called small things of no price "ladle-matters" <note>original: "fimpularias"</note>. Pliny, in book 35, chapter 12, says: "In sacred rites, even amidst such wealth, he approves of earthenware ladles as more innocent than those made of fluorspar or crystal." Marcus Varro also attests to this when he says in Nonius Marcellus that "the gods themselves are invited with a cheap ladle." Likewise Apuleius says: "To this day, the Roman people sacrifice to the immortal gods with a ladle and an earthenware dish." There are some who read *sympuuium* for *sympulum*, which Juvenal mentions in the sixth Satire:
"Or who would have dared to laugh at the ladle of Numa, or the black dish, or the brittle plates from the Vatican hill?"
Marcus Tullius in the *Paradoxes* says: "What about Numa Pompilius? Do we think the small cups and earthenware jars were less pleasing to the immortal gods than the bowls of Delos?" Polemon, cited in the eleventh book of Athenaeus, relates that even to his own age, certain Greeks drink from such vessels.

<summary>Erasmus explores several metaphors for smallness—the "span" of a life and the "point" of time—before discussing proverbs on corrupt legal systems and the humble sacrificial "ladle" used to describe a "storm in a teacup."</summary>
<keywords>span of life, point of time, Hymettian honey, Falernian wine, corruption, bribery, simpulum, sacrificial vessels, Cicero, Macrobius, Numa Pompilius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of proverbial expressions, moving from a discussion of clay vessels and children's games to metaphors for extreme changeability and the vital importance of friendship.</meta>

->CHILIADS SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY<-
413
M 3
<meta>catchword: Likewise</meta>

...customary [vessels] of clay, like the Argives at public banquets, and the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemonios"</note> at festivals, or after victories, or at the weddings of maidens. Therefore, it does not seem absurd to me if one thinks the allegory was taken from the play of children, who are accustomed to blow through a narrow pipe into a small ladle <note>term: simpulum (a small vessel used in sacrifices)</note>, creating as it were certain waves and a sound of water.

### More changeable than Proteus. LXXIIII

"More variegated than Proteus" <note>original: "Πρωτέως ποικιλώτερος"</note>. That is, more changeable than Proteus; this applies to a crafty and shifty person. Lucian, in *On Sacrifices*, calls Jove "more variegated than Proteus himself," because he frequently transformed himself into various other forms. Plato says in *Ion*: "But you are simply like Proteus, becoming all sorts of things, twisting up and down." <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἀτεχνῶς ὥσπερ ὁ πρωτεὺς παντοδαπὸς γίγνῃ, στρεφόμενος ἄνω καὶ κάτω"</note>. Horace says of those who easily change their opinion:

> With what knot can I hold this Proteus who changes his face?

Likewise elsewhere:

> Yet the wicked Proteus will escape these chains.

He calls someone "Proteus" who is evasive, and whom the Greeks call "hard to catch" <note>original: "δυσφώρατον"</note>. Furthermore, I think the story of Proteus <note>note: Proteus was a sea god in Greek mythology who could change his shape to avoid prophesying.</note> is too well known to be recounted here. It appears in the fourth book of Homer’s *Odyssey*, and likewise in the fourth book of Virgil’s *Georgics*. By a similar figure, one might also say, "more inconsistent than Vertumnus." For this god <note>note: Vertumnus was the Roman god of seasons and change.</note> changes himself into every kind of appearance, from which he also found his name among the Latins. Horace says:

> Born when all the Vertumni, however many there are, were unfavorable.

Ovid mentions him, describing how, while loving the goddess Pomona, he frequently assumed other forms. "More changeable than Empusa" <note>original: "Ἐμπευσοβολώτερος ἢ ἐμπύσης"</note>. Lucian mentioned her in his commentary *On the Dance*: "You might see them suddenly transformed into another species according to the occasion, and imitating Proteus himself. Indeed, one must also compare the example of Empusa, who turns herself into innumerable forms." <note>original: "ἴδοις τ’ ἂν ἐν αὐτῷ πρὸς τὸν καιρὸν ὠκέως μεταλλαττομένους..."</note> Aristophanes mentions her in *The Frogs*:

> **Dionysus:** And indeed, by Zeus, I see a huge beast.
> **Xanthias:** What kind? 
> **Dionysus:** A terrible one. At any rate, it becomes all sorts of things.
> At one moment a cow, now a mule, then again a woman
> of great beauty. 
> **Xanthias:** Where is she? Let me go to her.
> **Dionysus:** But she is no longer a woman, but already a dog.
> **Xanthias:** Then she is Empusa.

The commentator adds that Empusa is a certain specter <note>note: In Greek folklore, the Empusa was a shape-shifting monster often associated with the underworld.</note> that is usually sent by Hecate to be seen by the wretched and calamitous. She is accustomed to show herself in one form after another. Some think she used to appear at the midday hours to those who were performing sacrifices to the dead. I do not know if this can rightly be referred to what appears in the Psalms of the Hebrews: "From the occurrence and the noonday demon." <note>original: "ἀπὸ συμπτώματος καὶ δαιμονίου μεσημβρινοῦ" (Psalm 91:6)</note> There are those who assert that this is Hecate herself. They say, however, that she is seen with one foot, from which they think the name "Empusa" was given, as if "one-footed" <note>original: "ἑνόποδα"</note>. Demosthenes says that the mother of Aeschines (to whom Aeschines had changed the name to Leucothea) was called "Empusa," because for the sake of profit she would do and endure anything.

### A friend is more necessary than fire and water. LXXV

"A friend is more necessary than fire and water" <note>original: "Ἀναγκαιότερον πυρὸς καὶ ὕδατος ὁ φίλος"</note>. A proverbial hyperbole, warning that no one is so rich or powerful that they do not have need of the services of friends. For just as human life does not stand without fire and water, so it cannot exist without the companionship and help of intimates—whom the Latins for this very reason call "necessaries" <note>note: "Necessarius" in Latin can mean both "necessary" and "a close relative or friend."</note>, and friendship "necessitude." The adage implies that two very great benefits are gathered from friendship: pleasure and utility. For nothing is more pleasant than fire, nor more useful than water. For this reason Horace wrote:

> While I am sane, I would compare nothing to a pleasant friend.

<vocab>Proteus, Vertumnus, Empusa, Hecate, friendship, Horace, Lucian, Plato, Aristophanes</vocab>
