414

Likewise, Euripides says in Plutarch: 
"To look into the eyes of a friendly man is sweet" <note>original: "Εἰς ὄμματ' εὔνου φωτὸς ἐμβλέψαι γλυκύ"</note>. 
The adage is recorded by Plutarch in the commentary he titled *How to Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend*: "For which reason it is also said, a friend is more necessary than fire and water" <note>original: "Καθ' ὃ δὴ καὶ λέγεται, πυρὸς καὶ ὕδατος ὁ φίλος ἀναγκαιότερος"</note>. It is also found in Aristotle’s *Ethics* and in Cicero’s *On Friendship*. Even today, the unlearned common folk have a saying in their mouths which is most true: "It is more bearable to live without money than without friends."

---

## The wolf dances around the well. LXXVI

"The wolf dances around the well" <note>original: "Λύκος περὶ τὸ φρέαρ χορεύει"</note>. This is said against those who, having undertaken a useless task, are frustrated in their hopes. For they say it is the habit of a wolf that if it is ever thirsty and cannot safely lower itself down, it wanders around the well, gaping in vain for the water it cannot reach. There are some who think the proverb is derived from the fact that it sometimes happens that a wolf pursues some sheep or a man; when the prey has lowered itself into some deep well out of fear, the wolf paces around it, circling in the manner of a dancer out of a desire for the prey, which it nevertheless cannot seize. 

Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How to Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend*, says: "Those who use it have suffered the same thing, truly dancing that dance around the well" <note>original: "ὧι χρώμενοι πεπονθόσιν αὐτὸ, τῶν περὶ τὸ φρέαρ ὀρχηστικῶν ἀτεχνῶς ὀρχούμενοι"</note>. He is speaking, however, of immoderate and poisonous wit <note>term: dicacitate (biting or satirical wit)</note>, by which it happens that we bring no utility to those against whom we speak, and we procure the greatest evil for ourselves. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus, Suidas, and Diogenianus.

---

## The Lydian chariot. LXXVII

"The Lydian chariot" <note>original: "Λύδιον ἅρμα"</note>. Those who were far inferior to others in some contest were marked by this taunt: "You run beside a Lydian chariot" <note>original: "παρὰ Λύδιον ἅρμα θέεις"</note>. Plutarch, in the booklet he titled *On Distinguishing a Flatterer from a Friend*, writes: "Furthermore, he fears and respects the superior man; not, by Jove, like a pedestrian walking beside a Lydian chariot, but beside pure gold" <note>original: "του γ' κρείττονα τρόπον; καὶ Μηδικὸν, ὃ μὰ Δία παρὰ Λύδιον ἅρμα πεζὸς οἰχνεύων, ἀλλὰ παρὰ χρυσῖῳ ἐφθοψ"</note>. 

The adage is recorded by Diogenianus. Some refer it to Pelops the Lydian <note>note: Pelops was a mythical hero who won a chariot race against King Oenomaus to win the hand of Hippodamia</note>, who defeated his father-in-law Oenomaus with his chariot. Among these is Gregory of Nazianzus, who used it to say that he was as much inferior to the exceptional virtues of Basil as a man on foot is from a Lydian chariot. The proverb is also expressed in this way, as I said: "To run beyond the Lydian chariot" or "beside the Lydian chariot," so that a pedestrian is understood to be competing with a very fast Lydian chariot—a contest that would indeed seem quite unfairly matched. Achilles, in Euripides' *Iphigenia at Aulis*, competes in a footrace with a four-horse chariot and wins. Plutarch, in the *Life of Nicias*, quotes from Pindar: "For not, by Jove, as Pindar says, walking on foot beside a Lydian chariot" <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ μὰ Δία... παρὰ λύδιον ἅρμα πεζὸς οἰχνεύων, ὡς φησι πίνδαρος"</note>. Herodotus, in his first book, relates that the Lydians once excelled others in cavalry and hardly fought in any other way than from horses.

---

## The Cinclus. LXXVIII

"The Cinclus" <note>note: Likely referring to the Wagtail or the Water Ouzel, birds known for their constant movement</note>. By a rustic proverb, those who were exceedingly poor—having neither a home nor anything they could call their own—were called *Cincli*. Catullus describes such a man in Furius, who had neither a small villa, nor a house, nor a money-chest. For the Cinclus is a certain weak and feeble bird, so much so that it cannot prepare its own nest, and therefore it places its eggs in the nests of others. From this, country folk turned it into an adage, calling doctors and wanderers *Cincli*. The author is Aelian in the twelfth book of *On the Nature of Animals*. The Greeks call this class of men "hearthless" <note>original: "ἀνέσιος"</note>, that is, those without household gods. 

Suidas records that the Cinclus is a sea bird, slender, with almost no body, whose peculiarity is to frequently move its tail feathers; hence it was given the name "tail-shaker" <note>original: "σεισοπυγὶς"</note>, naturally from the agitation of the tail. He says it gave rise to the proverb used by Menander in *Thaïs*: "You are poorer than a snake's slough and a wagtail" <note>original: "πτωχότερος εἶ λευκίδος καὶ κιγκλοῦ"</note>. From this, "to wagtail" <note>original: "κιγκλίζειν"</note> is said of that which is moved about or makes a noise.

CHILIAD II. CENTURY II

### Things done under the armpits. LXXIX

"Actions under the armpit" <note>original: "Αἱ ὑπὸ μάλης πράξεις"</note>. That is, "under-the-arm deeds." Plutarch seems to have used this proverbial figure in the essay titled *How to Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend*: "A sorcerer and a manly man," he says, "is the beginning of every daring act, and in those things done under the armpit, he shows himself." <note>original: "γόης καὶ ἀνδρώδης ἁπάσης ἀρχὴ τόλμης, ἐν ταῖς ὑπὸ μάλης πράξεσιν ἀποφάνσις ἐστιν"</note>. That is: slow to labor and honest deeds, but in those things done under the arm, he refuses nothing. He is speaking of a flatterer, who is both lazy and useless for honorable duties, yet prompt for the services of pleasure: specifically, for bringing a mistress with discretion, for procuring delicacies, or for preparing a banquet. 

For my part, I believe the seat of flattery is placed under the armpits because these parts of the body are particularly sensitive to tickling, either due to the thinness of the skin or because we are unaccustomed to being touched there; or perhaps because that spot has small veins which, when warmed by rubbing, produce a certain kind of delight. Aristotle, in Section 35, Problem 2, indicates that tickling occurs most strongly under the arms and under the soles of the feet, suggesting the cause is either the softer skin or the unusualness of the contact, which also happens in the ears. And what else is flattery but a certain itching and "gargling" of the ears? 

Hence Lucian, in a certain dialogue between Charon, Menippus, and Mercury, strips a certain philosopher of all his vices: "Come now, do you also have something very heavy under your arm, Menippus? Flattery, Mercury, which was very useful to me in life." <note>original: "φέρε δὲ καὶ βαρύτατον ὑπὸ μάλης ἔχεις τι; ὦ μένιππε; κολακίαν ὦ Ἑρμῆ, πολλὰ ἐν τῷ βίῳ χρησιμεύσασάν μοι"</note>. That is: he still carries one thing under his arms, which is the heaviest of all. What is it, Menippus? Flattery, Mercury, which brought him much profit in life. Unless one prefers "under the arm" to be interpreted as Lucian says elsewhere, "under the fold" <note>original: "ὑπὸ κόλπῳ"</note>, meaning that use of Venus <note>a classical euphemism for sexual acts</note> which is not free from shame. For kisses and things done above the fold of the garment can somehow be consistent with honor, but below the fold, "it is no longer healthy" <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι ὑγιές"</note>.

### To sip and blow at the same time is difficult. LXXX

Tranio, a slave in Plautus’s play *The Haunted House*, was rebuked by his master for not returning sooner; when he claimed he had been elsewhere and could not be with his master and finish what he had been ordered to do at the same time, he said: "If you wish to ponder this word: to blow and sip at once is not at all easy." <note>original: "simul flare sorbereq̄, haud facile est"</note>. We shall aptly use this adage whenever we mean that certain affairs are of such a kind that they cannot be handled by the same person at the same time. For example, if someone tries to find time for both literature and pleasures; to indulge in both love affairs and thriftiness; to satisfy both a wife and one's studies; to give effort to both poetic and theological pursuits; to serve both the world and Christ. Just as it is impossible for someone to sip at the same time they are drawing a breath, and blow while the breath is being sent out. 

This saying seems akin to that Gospel phrase: "No one can serve two masters," and "No one can serve God and Mammon." Likewise, that saying of Phocion to Antipater: "You cannot use me as both a friend and a flatterer" <note>original: "οὐ δύνασαί μοι καὶ φίλῳ χρῆσθαι, καὶ κόλακι"</note>. To these we may add that six-foot verse which is falsely attributed to Seneca:
> To love and to be wise is scarcely granted to a god.

And as Horace says, imitating Terence:
"He would explain it no better than if 
he prepared to be insane with a certain reason and method." 
Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the *Eleventh Philippic*: "No one can handle two great things at once, especially not only by doing them, but even by thinking them through."

### One must implore Fortune while moving the hand. LXXXI

"One must call upon Fortune while putting a hand to the work" <note>original: "τὰν χεῖρα ποτιφέροντα δεῖ τὰν τύχαν ἐπικαλεῖν"</note>. This adage warns that we must trust in divine help in such a way that we do not strive any less with our own industry, as far as lies within us; otherwise, the gods will not hear the prayers of the sluggish and the lazy. As Alexander Hegius, the first teacher of my childhood—and one by no means to be regretted—elegantly wrote:
> God rightly turns away from the prayers 
> of the idle; He, than whom no one is 
> more diligent or more 
> hostile to leisure.

Plutarch, in his *Laconian Apothegms*, relates that among those people, all the gods and goddesses were usually depicted holding spears—even Venus herself was dressed in armor—as if not even they should lead a life of leisure, but should exercise themselves in warlike pursuits. They add, he says, also the proverb:
"Invoke Fortune while putting your hand to it."

<summary>Erasmus discusses three proverbs: the first relates armpits to the secret and "ticklish" nature of flattery; the second explains the impossibility of performing contradictory tasks simultaneously; and the third emphasizes that divine favor requires personal effort.</summary>

### One must call upon the gods while setting one's hand to the work. <note>Adage I.x.81</note>
<margin>Aeschylus in Stobaeus, that is,</margin>
"God loves to help the man who labors." <note>original Greek: "φιλεῖ δὲ τῷ κάμνοντι συσπεύδειν θεός"</note>
The deity is accustomed to be present for the one who works. Pindar is of the same opinion in his *Nemean Odes*: "They have reached the pinnacle of excellence who have tasted labors, not indeed without the favor of God." <note>original: "πρὸς ἄκρον ἀρετᾶς ἦλθον οἵτε πόνων ἐγεύσαντο, σὺν θεῷ δ’ τύχη"</note>. Therefore, we should not trust in our own industry so much that we neglect divine help; nor, on the other hand, should we hang so heavily upon that help that we abandon our own duty. Aeschylus seems to have alluded to this in *The Persians*:
<margin>"For I have not yet,"</margin>
"After a long time, the gods have washed these things clean in the light. But when a man himself is striving, God also joins in." <note>original: "Αλλ’ ὅταν σπεύδῃ τις αὐτὸς, χ’ ὡ θεὸς συνάπτεται"</note>
<margin>that is,</margin>
For a very long time now from the gods
I have wished that they would finish these things favorably for me. But
Where you yourself are watchful, the gods also set their hand to the work.
<margin>It is reported from the same source:</margin>
"God loves to help the man who labors." <note>original: "φιλεῖ δὲ τῷ κάμνοντι συσπεύδειν θεός"</note>
<margin>that is,</margin>
God rejoices to be present, but for the one who works.
Some, including Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note>, trace the origin of the proverb to a fable. A certain countryman, when his wagon was stuck in the mud, was calling upon Hercules while doing nothing. But Hercules, standing there, said: "Apply your hand to the wheel, and prick the oxen, and *then* call upon the god."
"One should call upon God while applying the hand." <note>original: "τὴν χεῖρα προσφέροντα τὸν θεὸν καλεῖν"</note>

### Let each man practice the art which he knows. LXXXII

Marcus Tullius Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "But even if this man is learned, as indeed he is, let him grant these matters to his teacher Aristotle; let him teach singing himself. For it is well commanded in that proverb of the Greeks: Let each man practice the art which he knows." <note>original: "Quam quisq; norit artem, in hac se exerceat"</note>
So far Cicero. It is an iambic senarius verse, warning us that we should involve ourselves only in discussing and handling those things in which we are skilled. As for those things of which we are ignorant, we should leave them to the more learned; we should not claim a profession that is not ours, nor "put our sickle into another's harvest" <note>a common idiom for interfering in another's business</note>, nor "let the shoemaker judge beyond his last." <note>a reference to the famous anecdote about the painter Apelles</note> In Aulus Gellius, Plato cites a passage from Euripides, though in a sense somewhat different from Cicero's—namely, that everyone is exceedingly delighted by his own way of life and pursuit because he trusts he will achieve some praise in it. He adds, Gellius says, that line of Euripides: "In whatever matter each man is distinguished, toward that he hastens, and to that he imparts the greatest part of his day, in which he may surpass himself; conversely, from that in which he is more stupid or is nothing, he flees and despises it." Furthermore, the verse which Marcus Tullius renders in Latin is found in Aristophanes' play titled *The Wasps*; it is of this sort:
<margin>that is,</margin>
"Let each man do the trade he knows." <note>original: "ἔρδοι τις ἣν ἕκαστος εἰδείη τέχνην"</note>
Let each man practice the art he knows.
In which place the commentator notes that this is a celebrated proverb. Stratonicus the cithara-player <note>a professional musician playing the lyre-like cithara</note> used it, as recorded in Athenaeus, book 8. To a certain musician who had previously been a gardener and was arguing with him about harmony, he replied: "Let each man do the trade he knows." Although in the Aldine edition <note>the famous Venetian press of Aldus Manutius</note> the word for "sing" is read instead of "do." Horace alluded to this proverb when he wrote:
"One who is ignorant of a ship fears to steer a ship; no one dares to give southernwood <note>a medicinal herb</note> to the sick unless he has learned how. What belongs to doctors, doctors promise; smiths handle smith's tools. But we, unlearned and learned alike, write poems everywhere."
The same author in his *Epistle to the Bailiff*:
"I shall vote that each of us willingly practices the art he knows."
To this pertains that Pindaric saying which Plutarch records in the commentary he wrote *On Contentment*: "The horse for the chariot, the ox for the plow; the dolphin speeds most quickly past the ship. For the boar planning slaughter, one must find a dog that can endure labor." <note>original: "ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ἵππον, ἔν δ’ ἀρότρῳ βοῦν, παρὰ ναῦν δ’ ἰθύειν τάχιστα δελφῖς. κάπρῳ δὲ βουλεύοντι φόνον, κώια δ’ ἐῖ τάλθυμον ἐξευρεῖν"</note> Clearly, this signifies that each individual should be employed in what he is strong at. Athenaeus in his eighth book relates that when Ptolemy was arguing somewhat contentiously with Stratonicus the cithara-player about the art of the cithara, the latter said: "A scepter is one thing, O King, and a plectrum <note>a tool for plucking strings</note> is another." <note>original: "ἕτερόν ἔφη ἐστὶν ὦ βασιλεῦ σκῆπτρον, ἕτερον δὲ πλῆκτρον"</note> And in Pliny, book 35, chapter 10, Apelles said to Alexander the Great...

<summary>This page discusses two major adages: the necessity of personal labor alongside divine prayer (God helps those who help themselves) and the importance of individuals sticking to their own areas of expertise.</summary>

SECOND THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY

When a man was talking a great deal of nonsense about painting in a great workshop, the owner politely urged him to be silent, reminding him that he was being laughed at even by the boys who were grinding the colors together.

<margin>83</margin>
### I gave an evil and I received one.

**I gave an evil and I received one.** <note>original: "Dedi malum & accepi"</note> This is an adage from Baetica <note>a Roman province in southern Spain</note>, which can be used whenever a similar exchange seems to have occurred—where an evil is returned for an evil and like is paid for like. It is as if someone had given away a wicked son-in-law and received an equally wicked daughter-in-law in return. This is reviewed and explained by Pliny the Younger in his *Letters*. He writes that Caecilius Classicus, a foul and openly wicked man, had conducted his proconsulship in that region <note>Baetica</note> with as much violence as greed, in the same year that Marius Priscus governed Africa. Now, Priscus was originally from Baetica, and Classicus was from Africa. From this, the Baeticians (as grief often makes people witty) coined a clever saying: **I gave an evil and I received one.** This also applies to those who entrust their children to bad teachers and receive them back even worse than they were when they handed them over. It applies further to those who provoke people from whom they then receive a more serious injury—which they say happens to those who hunt wild asses in Egypt. For when that animal is provoked, it frequently kicks back stones with such force that they strike the hunters, penetrating their chests or shattering their skulls. From this, a certain engine of war <note>the onager, a type of catapult</note> was also given its name, according to Ammianus in his twenty-third book.

<margin>84</margin>
### Someone will find fault sooner than they will imitate.

"Someone will blame more easily than they will imitate." <note>original Greek: "Μωμήσεταί τις μᾶλλον ἢ μιμήσεται"</note> That is, **Someone will find fault sooner than they will imitate.** Zeuxis <note>a famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE</note> was accustomed to write this on the works of the painter Apollodorus, who first discovered the imitation of shadows. It is recorded in this way: "Someone will find fault more quickly than they will imitate." <note>original Greek: "μωμήσεταί τις θᾶσσον ἢ μιμήσεται"</note> It seems appropriately said of any work of perfect and inimitable art. Furthermore, it is much easier to criticize excellent things than to rival them. Moreover, there is an elegant wordplay <term>paronomasia: a play on words that sound similar</term> in these two Greek words, *momēsetai* <note>will find fault</note> and *mimēsetai* <note>will imitate</note>; though they differ very little in sound, they describe vastly different things. Pliny alluded to this in his thirty-seventh book, chapter eleven: "Many imitated, no one equaled." Theognis <note>a Greek poet</note> wrote on the same sentiment:

Many find fault with me, both the wicked and the good,
But none of the unskilled are able to imitate me.
<note>Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation, here rendered as English: "Many carp at me, the learned and unlearned alike, / But no one from the flock of the unlearned has the power to imitate us."</note>

<margin>85</margin>
### To be at the doors.

"At the doors." <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις"</note> That is, **To be at the doors**, is said as a proverbial allegory for something that is pressing and already very near. Plutarch says, "When a fever is at the doors." So also the Creator of the world says in the Sacred Scriptures <note>Genesis 4:7</note> to the fratricide Cain: "If thou doest ill, thy sin shall immediately be at the doors."

<margin>86</margin>
### The Laconian says one thing, his donkey carries another.

"The Laconian says one thing, but the Laconian's donkey carries another." <note>original Greek: "Ἄλλα μὲν λάκων λέγει, ἄλλα δ' λάκωνος ὁ ὄνος φέρει"</note> That is, **The Laconian indeed says certain things, but the Laconian’s donkey carries others.** Among some, the proverb is also expressed this way: "Leucon says one thing, but Leucon's donkey carries another." <note>original Greek: "ἄλλα μὲν λεύκων, α' δ' λεύκωνος ὄνος φέρει"</note> This was said against those whose speech disagreed with their deeds. They say it originated from an event like this: A certain farmer named Leucon used to wrap skins full of honey in straw mats. When asked by the tax collectors what he was carrying, he would answer that he was carrying barley—clearly so that he would pay less money. But when it happened once that the donkey stumbled and spilled the load, the collectors ran up to help put the bundles back. But when they discovered in the meantime that there was honey in the skins, not barley, they dragged Leucon away by the neck as one who had defrauded them of the tax due. And laughing, they added this: **Leucon says one thing, but the donkey carries another.** In some manuscripts, the word "says" is not added; but even so, in my opinion, the saying is rendered more festive. That phrase was later turned into an adage. It is recorded by Zenodotus and by Diogenianus <note>Greek compilers of proverbs</note>.

<margin>87</margin>
### To escape with the body.

**To escape with the body** <note>original: "Corpore effugere"</note> is to decline a danger already imminent and almost pressing upon one by a certain skill. It is a metaphor taken from gladiators, who deceive a blow by a slight bend of the body. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his first speech against Catiline: "How many of your thrusts, aimed so that they did not seem possible to be avoided, have I escaped by a slight swerve and, as they say, with the body?" Thus far Cicero. And so, as often as someone...

<meta>catchword: someone</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Latin and Greek adages collected by Erasmus, transitioning from metaphors of narrow escapes to proverbs regarding personal risk, premature expectations, and being out of one's element.</meta>

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...we indicate that someone has escaped danger by the narrowest of margins; we shall say they "dodged the evil with their body." For those who are protected by walls or some other barrier are in less peril; but those who are exposed naked to missiles and have nothing to protect them but a timely twist of the body—these are seen to be in the most extreme danger. Catullus used an almost opposite figure of speech: *We avoid those weapons of yours with a cloak* <note>original: "Contra nos tela ista tua evitamus amictu"</note>, meaning: "We drive them off easily," no differently than one brushes away the attacks of flies.

<margin>88</margin>
->Playing with another's hide.<-

**To play with another’s hide** <note>original: "De alieno corio ludere"</note> is a proverb used for those who act carelessly because the risk belongs to someone else. The allegory is taken either from tanners, or from some Aesopic fable, or from slaves, who pay the penalty with their backs if any mistake is made. Apuleius writes in the seventh book of *The Golden Ass*: *But if the other bandits find out in any way, you won't run back to the donkey again and prepare destruction for me once more. In truth, you are playing with another’s hide.* These are the words of the donkey <note>the protagonist Lucius, transformed into a donkey</note>, accusing a girl because she had previously brought him into danger during an escape through her own fault, and was now acting in such a way that they would have to flee again—and primarily at his peril. It is also an allusion to a donkey’s hide, which is stripped off after death. There is something similar in Plautus: *The hide is being stripped from my back* <note>original: "De meo tergo degitur corium"</note>, meaning, "the matter is at my own risk." Nor is it unlike what Festus records: *For the shoulder-blades* <note>original: "Pro scapulis"</note>, meaning, "at the risk of a beating." A joke made by Seneca in his *Declamations* does not differ much from this form: *Cicero satisfied the father from the hide of Cestius.* For this Cestius was one of those who used to belittle Cicero’s genius. When he happened to be reclining at the same banquet as Marcus Tullius Cicero's son (who was then governor of Asia), and it was learned from a servant’s whisper that this was the Cestius who judged that Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero the elder</note> knew nothing, the son immediately had him removed from the banquet and ordered him to be thrashed with whips. A proverb not unlike this one is circulated among our own common people: **Cutting wide straps from another’s hide.** By this, they mean that everyone is less frugal with another's property than with their own. Tertullian used it somewhat differently in his book *On the Mantle*: *This alone was given to the chameleon, which is commonly said: to play with its own hide.* He means that the chameleon changes the color of its skin at its own will.

<margin>89</margin>
->To be in the blade.<-

When we indicate an immature hope, or that the goal is still a long way off, we say it is **in the blade** <note>original: "In herba esse," literally "to be in the grass/stalk"</note>. The metaphor is taken from crops that are still tender and sprouting, about which the farmer can promise himself nothing certain yet, because many accidents usually occur that prevent the cultivator from obtaining the desired result. But when he has finally carried the harvested grain into the barn, only then is it safe to hope for the best. Ovid says in Helen’s letter to Paris: *But you hurry too much, and your harvest is still in the blade.*

> *Perhaps this delay may be friendly to your wish.*

Persius says in his sixth satire:

> *Grind it up, what do you fear? Harrow, and the next crop is already in the blade.*

Cornelius Tacitus, in his *Dialogue on Orators*, used the phrase **in the blade** to mean something momentary and soon to perish, because it was plucked before its time. He is discussing the applause given to poets reciting their poems. *All that praise,* he says, *within a day or two, plucked like a crop in the blade or a flower, reaches no certain or solid fruit; it brings neither friendship nor a circle of clients, nor a lasting favor in anyone’s mind, but only a wandering shout, empty voices, and a fleeting joy.*

<margin>90</margin>
->To litigate in another's forum.<-

This proverb also tastes of the same figure: **To litigate in another’s forum**, meaning to be engaged in a new matter to which you are not yet accustomed. For different forums have different legal formulas and various methods of handling cases; someone ignorant of these, like a stranger in a foreign land, must necessarily find many things lacking. Martial says in the preface to his twelfth book: *Accept therefore the reason, in which this is the first and greatest point: that I miss the ears of the city to which I was accustomed, and I seem to myself to be litigating in another’s forum.*

<margin>91</margin>
->In times of strife, even Androclides acts as general.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐν δὲ διχοστασίῃ καὶ Ἀνδροκλείδης πολεμαρχεῖ</note> That is: **When sedition arises, even Androclides is a leader.** 
This heroic verse is a celebrated proverb against contemptible and humble men who, through some occurring opportunity, are granted dignity. Just as in a period of public tumult, sometimes the lowest people rule for a time. This can be turned against bad princes, who...

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "qui" (who), which will begin the next page.</meta>

<header>CHILIAD II. CENTURY II.</header>
<meta>catchword: dia</meta>

...by those who, once peace is restored, have less power in the State; for this reason, they sometimes deliberately stir up civil unrest through tyrannical skill, so they might more conveniently fleece the people at their own whim. Or it is directed against certain theologians, unworthy of the name, who stir up discord and riots among the Christian commoners, clearly so they might become famous on this occasion; they prefer to be notorious through a public evil than to live without glory. This is reported by Suidas, Diogenianus, and also by Plutarch in his *Life of Nicias*, and in his essay <term>On Brotherly Love</term> <note>original: *peri philadelphias*</note>. It is also expressed in this way:
<term>In times of discord, even the worst man attains honor.</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν δὲ διχοστασίῃ καὶ πάγκακος ἔμμορε τιμῆς.</note>
The same author cites this in his comparison of Lysander and Sulla, except that the Aldine edition there erroneously has "the most beautiful" <note>original: *pankalos*</note> instead of "the worst" <note>original: *pangkakos*</note>. Again, it is phrased this way:
<term>In desperate times, even a crab attains honor.</term> <note>original: ἐν γὰρ ἀμηχανίῃ καὶ καρκίνῳ ἔμμορε τιμῆς.</note>
To this sentiment also belongs that saying celebrated among the Greeks as a proverb:
<term>To a lucky Carian, even a poor fish is a great prize.</term> <note>original: Καρὶ τυχαίῳ γὰρ πτωχὸς ἰχθύϊ μέγα.</note>
That is: even a beggar has great power in the right place.

### Among the unlearned, even the crested lark has a voice. XCII

<term>Among the unlearned, even the crested lark has a voice.</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀμούσοις καὶ κόρυδος φθέγγεται.</note> This will apply to certain people who dare to sell themselves as scholars among the uneducated, though they are otherwise entirely speechless among the learned. Euripides expressed this elegantly without a metaphor in his *Hippolytus*:
<term>For those who are worthless among the wise,</term>
<term>are more musical in their speech before the crowd.</term>
That is: those who have no influence among the erudite stand out for their eloquence among the unskilled masses.
The <term>corydus</term> <note>the crested lark</note> is a very common type of bird, and not at all musical, yet it makes a noise of some kind among silent birds; however, singing near a nightingale, it could by no means be endured. I think we should add here what the parasite Philoxenus (nicknamed "The Ham-Cutter") wittily said to another parasite named Corydus, as recorded by Athenaeus in his sixth book. When a conversation arose about how thrushes were being bought at a high price, and Corydus—who was rumored to perform obscene services—was present, Philoxenus said, "But I remember when a 'Corydus' was valued at only a penny." It is common for parasites to be given names of contempt, although this Corydus is said to have been quite charming in his speech. A Greek epigram, though by an unknown author <note>original: *adēlou*</note>, also testifies that the lark is a very unmusical bird:
<term>If the lark could equal the swan in singing,</term>
<term>And the owl dared to compete with the nightingale,</term>
<term>If the cuckoo should claim to sing more clearly than the cicada,</term>
<term>Then I too could be an equal to my Palladius.</term>

### Every land is a fatherland. XCIII

<term>Every land is a fatherland.</term> <note>original Greek: πᾶσα γῆ πατρίς.</note>
This is a half-line from an oracle once given to Meleus the Pelasgian when he consulted it regarding a victory; Mnaseas also mentions it, as do Zenodotus and Dionysius of Chalcis. The adage advises that a wise and good man is happy in whatever nation he may live. Hence, when Socrates was asked where he was from, he replied that he was a <term>cosmopolitan</term> <note>original: *kosmikos*</note>, that is, a citizen of the world. Aristophanes suggests the same in his *Plutus* when he says:
<term>For home is wherever a man may fare well.</term>
These words are spoken by Mercury, who desires to be admitted into the family of the now-wealthy Chremyllus, even if it means leaving heaven; he believed that a man's fatherland was only where he lived happily, and that exile was wherever he lived uncomfortably. This proverbial verse is also circulated:
<term>To those who fare well, every land is a fatherland.</term>
Cicero, in the fifth book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, indicates that this was a saying of Teucer from a tragedy...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of proverbs regarding how people adapt to their circumstances, specifically finishing a thought on the cosmopolitan view that one's home is wherever one thrives, before moving into expressions of intense hatred and the metaphor of diluting wine.</meta>

...by some logic. Thus, the words of Teucer <note>A hero of the Trojan War who, when exiled by his father, declared he would find a new home elsewhere.</note> can be applied to every situation: **One’s fatherland is wherever one is well off.** <note>original: *Patria est, ubicunque est bene.*</note>

### Vatinian Hate. XCIIII

**Vatinian hate** <note>original: *Odium Vatinianum*</note> is a term used for a deadly and vehemently bitter hatred. Vatinius was a man whom Marcus Tullius Cicero attacked most fiercely; he had incurred such intense hatred from the Roman people once his disgraceful crimes were exposed that "Vatinian hate" passed into a proverb. Catullus writes:
*For that gift of yours, I would hate you with Vatinian hate.*

### A stepmother’s hate. XCV

In a similar figure of speech, we read of **a stepmother’s hate** <note>original: *odium nouercale*</note>, because a certain fatal and irreconcilable hatred toward stepchildren is innate in all stepmothers. This is elegantly indicated by a Greek epigram, which I shall not find it burdensome to include here. It is attributed to Callimachus, and is certainly not unworthy of that author:

<note>original Greek: Στήλην μητρυιῆς μικρὰν λίθον ἔστεφε κοῦρος, ὡς βίου ἠλλάχθαι, καὶ τρόπον οἰόμενος. ἡ δὲ τάφῳ κλινθεῖσα κατέκτανε παῖδα πεσοῦσα. φεύγετε μητρυιῆς καὶ τάφον οἱ πρόσγονοι.</note>

Since I knew I could not match the elegance of these verses, I have nevertheless translated them as best I could so they might be understood:

->A boy placed garlands on his stepmother’s small gravestone,<-
->Thinking that as her life had changed, so had her nature.<-
->But the stone, falling from the tomb, crushed the boy to death.<-
->Even from a stepmother’s grave, you stepchildren, flee!<-

Euripides says in the *Alcestis*:
*For a stepmother is an enemy to the children born*
*Before her, no gentler than a viper.* <note>original Greek: Ἐχθρὰ γὰρ αὐτὰ μητρυιὰ τέκνοις τοῖς πρόσθ᾽, ἐχίδνης οὐδὲν ἠπιωτέρα.</note>

### You have spoiled the wine by pouring in water. XCVI

<term>You have spoiled the wine by pouring in water.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀπώλεσας τὸν οἶνον ἐγχέας ὕδωρ.</note> That is, you have ruined the liquid of the wine by the infusion of water.

These are the words of Polyphemus <note>The Cyclops from Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note> from a tragedy by Aristias entitled *The Cyclops*, as testified by Chamaeleon in his book *On Satyrs*. In this way, he rebukes Odysseus for diluting the wine with water. In ancient times, people drank wine pure <note>original: *merum*</note>, not without harm, until Staphylus, the son of Silenus, showed how to dilute wine with water. For this was his invention, according to Pliny in his seventh book. This will be said against those who do certain things correctly at the beginning, but then, for however slight a reason, overturn their good deeds with bad ones. Ulpian, in the works of Athenaeus, says this against a man who had used the word <term>ballizein</term> instead of <term>komazein</term> <note>Both terms refer to dancing or revelry, but Ulpian is criticizing a "barbaric" or incorrect usage of the term.</note>, and did so barbarously: *But you, having bought a name for us from a prosperous land, have spoiled the wine by pouring in water.*

For the Cyclops, being a barbarian and a drunkard (as Homer also depicts him), thinks that wine is corrupted by water, whereas in the judgment of wise men, it is rendered better and more wholesome. Hence Plato also advises us to temper Bacchus, the "drunken god," with the Nymphs, the "sober goddesses" <note>This is a poetic way of saying wine (Bacchus) should be mixed with water (Nymphs).</note>. A Greek epigram by Meleager teaches the same thing, which is as follows:

<note>original Greek: Αἱ νύμφαι τὸν Βάκχον, ὅτ᾽ ἐκ πυρὸς ἥλαθ᾽ ὁ κοῦρος, Νίψαν, ὑπὲρ τέφρης ἄρτι κυλιόμενον. Τούνεκα σὺν νύμφαις Βρόμιος φίλος, ἢν δ᾽ ἀγὶν εἴργῃς Μίσγεσθαι, δέξῃ πῦρ ἔτι καιόμενον.</note>

->When Bacchus as a boy had leaped from the flames, in the waves<-
->The Nymphs washed him, while he was still soiled with ash;<-
->Hence Bacchus is a friend when joined with Nymphs. But<-
->You will receive a burning fire, unless you mix him.<-

Nevertheless, wine that is too heavily diluted has this disadvantage: the head of the person who drank it aches more severely the following day than if he had drunk it pure. Aristotle thinks the reason is that wine, which is naturally thicker, is made thinner by the addition of water; it thus penetrates the narrow passages of the head more quickly, carrying with it the harmful effects of the pure wine, of which it still retains much power. Furthermore, it is more difficult to digest.

### He threw away the spear. Shield-thrower.
->XCVII<-

**To throw away the spear** <note>original: *Abiecit hastam*</note> is certainly used as a proverbial figure for someone who, distrusting his own cause, loses heart and ceases to strive against opposition. Cicero says in his speech *For Lucius Murena*: "Do you see how gloomy and dejected he is? He lies low, he despairs, **he has thrown away the spear.**" Similarly, among the Greeks, the proverbial insult **shield-throwers** <note>original Greek: ῥίψασπιδες (*rhipsaspides*)</note> is applied to those who, being cowardly and fearful, abandon their post in the battle line and throw away their shields. This was a disgrace famously noted in Demosthenes <note>The great Athenian orator, who was accused of fleeing the Battle of Chaeronea.</note>. Lucian, in *Jupiter the Tragedian*, writes: "And it is clear he is about to **throw away his shield.**" Indeed, in ancient times, throwing away one's shield was considered so shameful that the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans, famous for their "with your shield or on it" military culture.</note> ordered Archilochus to depart from their borders because he had written that it was better to throw away a shield than to perish, as Plutarch testifies in his *Laconian Apophthegms*. That couplet by Archilochus is cited by Aristophanes in the play titled *Peace*, and it goes like this:

*Some Saian now boasts of the shield which, by a bush,*
*I left—a flawless piece of armor—against my will.*

The commentator reminds us that the Saians are a people of Thrace against whom Archilochus was fighting when he fled and threw away his shield. His example was later followed by Demosthenes, who was better equipped for speaking than for fighting. Cleonymus is also mocked by Aristophanes on this account, as in *The Wasps*: "**He threw away his shield.**"

Furthermore, Isocrates, in the oration he wrote *On the Peace*, declares that those who had either deserted their rank or thrown away their shield were once held in infamy. Aeschines indicates the same against Timarchus: that anyone who had not been in the war, or who had **thrown away his spear**, was not permitted to conduct any business in the public assembly. Finally, Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *Ethics*, commemorates among those things which the law forbids: "**not to desert one's rank, nor to flee, nor to throw away one's weapons.**" And a little later, dealing with those who are unjust but cannot be called "greedy" (since they gain no profit from it), he uses as an example: "**those who throw away their shields out of cowardice.**" I believe Horace suggests something of this sort in his *Odes* when he says:

> With you I experienced Philippi and the swift flight,
> my little shield being left behind, not well.
> <note>original: *relicta non bene parmula*</note>

Quintus Curtius, in his third book, writes: "Then the rest were scattered by fear, and wherever a path to flight lay open for each, they broke out, **throwing away the weapons** which they had taken up a little while before for the protection of their bodies; so much did their terror even fear their own defenses." It is found several times in Julius Caesar: "**having thrown down their arms.**" But the further it recedes from simple speech, the greater is the grace of the adage; for instance, if someone were to call a person a **shield-thrower** <note>original: *rhipsaspides*</note> who does not resist a demon suggesting shameful things, but immediately complies. We have made mention of this proverb before.

### Singers tell many lies.
->XCVIII<-

**Singers tell many lies.** <note>original Greek: Πολλὰ ψεύδονται ἀοιδοί (*Polla pseuodntai aoidoi*)</note> This will fit those who speak to gain favor and who flatter the ears. It is derived from the fact that singers, looking to delight and please, sing many false things in praise of their listeners. For nothing is more burdensome than the truth, and nothing is sweeter than flattery. Aristotle, in the first book of his *Metaphysics*, says: "But according to the proverb, **poets tell many lies.**" It is, if my memory does not fail me, a Homeric half-line regarding the cithara-players who were accustomed to sing at banquets. But this saying moves some people to such an extent that they entirely abstain from all the writings of all poets, losing no small portion of erudition.

### To feign refusal.
->XCIX<-

**To feign refusal** <note>original: *Accissare* / Greek: Ἀκκίζεσθαι (*Akkizesthai*)</note>. By this Greek proverb, those were described who, although they greatly desired to receive something, nevertheless falsely refused it; a custom which persists among many today. They write that **Acco** was a certain woman of noted foolishness, who was accustomed to talk with her own image in a mirror just as if with another woman; hence, those who did anything foolish or inept were commonly said to "accissate" and were addressed by the name of Acco. It appears it was also part of this woman's character to refuse what she nevertheless desired; whence **Accismus** is the name given to a feigned refusal of this kind. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his *Letters to Atticus*, says: "Of this, I think, we are certain: all is lost. Why then do we **feign refusal** for so long?" <note>original Greek: Ἀκκιζόμεθα (*Akkizometha*)</note> that is, why do we dissemble? Lucian, in his booklet *On Those Who Serve for Hire*: "But he, **feigning refusal**, says: 'Away with it! Shall I take from you?'" The same author in *The Loves*: "All sorts of elaborate **feigned refusals**." <note>original: *akkismōn*</note> That is: Every...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of proverbs, concluding a series on the concept of "feigned refusal" before beginning the Third Century of the Second Thousand (Chiliad). The focus shifts from social pretension to the rules of drinking and mixing wine in the ancient world.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S PROVERBS

...with all **feigned refusal** <note>original: *accismo*. From the Greek *akkismos*, a rhetorical term for pretending to be uninterested in something one actually desires.</note> removed, that is, without hesitation. Again in the same discourse: **There is much feigned refusal among men** <note>original Greek: πολὺς δὲ ἐν μετὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν ἀκκισμὸς (*polys de en meta tōn andrōn akkismos*)</note>. Likewise Philemon, in Athenaeus, Book 13: **There is not a single feigned refusal, nor any nonsense** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστ’ οὐδὲ εἷς ἀκκισμὸς, οὐδὲ λῆρος (*ouk est’ oude eis akkismos, oude lēros*)</note>. Plutarch indicates that Acco and Alphito were women used by mothers to frighten children away from sinning <note>Acco was a mythical "bogeywoman" who supposedly feigned madness or refusal, giving her name to the concept of *accismus*.</note>. Plato also employs this word in *Gorgias*: **But you are feigning refusal, Callicles** <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἀκκίζῃ ὦ Καλλικλῆς (*all’ akkizē ō Kalliklēs*)</note>.

### A Scythian feigning refusal of an ass.

**A Scythian feigning refusal of an ass** <note>original Greek: Ἀκκιζόμενος Σκύθης τὸν ὄνον (*Akkizomenos Skythēs ton onon*)</note>. This is used against those who reject in words what they desire in fact. They trace it back to a fable of this sort: Someone, seeing the carcass of an ass, said to a Scythian who happened to be nearby: "Look, here is something for you to dine on." He at first rejected and loathed it, but later prepared it and ate it. This is roughly what Suidas and Zenodotus say. Hesychius records it differently: **The Scythian asks for a feast of ass-dung** <note>original Greek: Σκύθης ὄνθου δ’ αἴτει (*Skythēs onthou d' aitei*)</note>, that is, "A Scythian's feast," implying he found it—if indeed this passage in Hesychius is free from error. For it is clearly mutilated, and perhaps the word for **dung** <note>original: *onthou*</note> was used in place of "useful," yet in such a way as to allude to the "ass" <note>original: *onou*</note>.

---

->THE THIRD HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND<-

### Drink either five, or three, or not four.

Athenaeus, in his tenth book, discussing heavy drinking, writes that a proverb of this kind was commonly celebrated: **Either drink five, or three, or not four** <note>original Greek: ἢ πέντε πίνε, ἢ τρία, ἢ μὴ τέτταρα (*ē pente pine, ē tria, ē mē tettara*)</note>. This prescribes the method for diluting wine. This proportion was most pleasing to the ancients: that to five measures of wine, two of water should be added, or one measure of water to two of wine <note>Ancient wine was much stronger and more syrupy than modern wine, and drinking it undiluted was considered a mark of barbarism.</note>. As a witness to this, he cites the poet Ion, who wrote that a certain seer foretold to Palamedes that the Greeks would sail away who "drank three cups to one." Likewise Nicochares in *Amymone*: **Greetings to the five and two** <note>original Greek: χαῖρε πέντε καὶ δύο (*chaire pente kai dyo*)</note>. Furthermore Amphias: **I, Bacchus, am a "five and two" to you all** <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ Διόνυσος πᾶσιν ὑμῖν εἰμὶ πέντε καὶ δύο (*Egō de Dionysos pasin hymin eimi pente kai dyo*)</note>. Plutarch discusses this matter somewhat more copiously in the third decade of his *Symposiacs* <note>Plutarch's "Table Talk," a collection of dinner-party discussions.</note>, testifying that it was celebrated in convivial songs: **Either drink five or three, but not four**, lest anyone should rashly change the words of Plautus, for they are recorded in his work as well.

Ariston jokes about this matter: just as in music the **one-and-a-half** <note>original: *hemiolium*</note> proportion produces the harmony of a **fifth** <note>original: *diapente*</note>, the double proportion produces the harmony called a **fourth** <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>. But he says that the one called the fourth is a dull and obscure harmony compared to the others, consisting of a **four-to-three ratio** <note>original: *epitrito*</note>. Likewise, in the harmonies of drinking, there are three harmonies of wine to water: the **fifth** <note>original: *diapente*</note>, the **three-fold** <note>original: *oia triōn*</note>, and the **fourth** <note>original: *diatessaron*</note>. For the harmony of the fifth is constituted from the one-and-a-half ratio, if three cups of water are mixed with two cups of wine. But if you mix two with two, a double proportion exists; the harmony of the fourth will occur if you add three cups of water to one cup of wine. And this is the **four-to-three ratio** <note>original: *epitritum*</note>, a proportion that belongs to the three magistrates in the Prytaneum <note>The seat of government in ancient Greek cities, where officials ate at public expense.</note> who are wise and sober, or to the logicians when, with furrowed brows, they dispute their anxious subtleties. Now, if you mix two of water to one of wine, a most turbulent **tone** <note>musical interval</note> is born, and as he calls it, **slightly tipsy** <note>original Greek: ἀκροθώρακα (*akrothōraka*)</note>, moving strings of the mind that ought not be moved. For by this ratio, one is neither entirely sober, nor is foolishness quite drowned in unmixed wine. But if you add two measures of wine to three of water, the most musical harmony of all exists, as it invites sleep and brings on tranquility and supreme peace.

When these things had been said in the gathering, Plutarch’s father added that the ancients gave two nurses to Jupiter, and likewise to Adrasteia; to Juno they gave one, namely Euboea; to Apollo two, Aletheia and Corythala. But to Bacchus they gave many, because it is necessary that this god be tamed and subdued by many measures of **nymphs** <note>A poetic way of referring to water, as nymphs were spirits of springs and streams.</note>, to make him more moderate and mild. This signifies that wine must be diluted with much water. Plautus mentions this proverb in *Stichus*, introducing drinking slaves: "But meanwhile, our general, why does the jug stop here? See how many cups of these we have drunk. As many as there are fingers on your hand." It is a Greek song:
> **Both drink five, and drink three, or not four.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ πέντε πίνε, καὶ τρία πίνε, ἢ μὴ τέτταρα (*Kai pente pine, kai tria pine, ē mē tettara*)</note>

Although this joke in Plautus is not free from the suspicion of a textual error. As for why the Greek song forbids drinking "four," it pertains to the ancient superstition in which it was believed that odd numbers were more effective for everything—something Pliny thinks is understood in the observation of days during fevers. Furthermore, regarding the avoidance of the number four in drinking cups, the same author writes in Book 28, Chapter 6, in this manner:

# THE SECOND THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY
## N 2
<meta>catchword: rum</meta>

...number: Democritus also discussed the number four in a dedicated volume, explaining why one should not drink in groups of four small cups or pints <note>original: *cyathi, sextarij*—ancient units of liquid measure; a *cyathus* was roughly 0.04 liters, a *sextarius* roughly 0.5 liters</note>. Horace certainly alluded to this in the third book of his *Odes*:
> Give quickly to the new moon,
> Give to the midnight, give, boy, to the augur
> Murena. With three or nine
> Fitting cups are the drinks mixed.
> He who loves the uneven Muses,
> The inspired poet will seek the cups thrice three times.
> The Grace, joined with her naked sisters,
> Fearing quarrels, forbids us
> To touch more than three.

Likewise, Ausonius says:
> Drink three, or three times three; such is the mystic law.

That is,
Either three cups, for the number of the Graces; or nine, for the number of the Muses.

### The Sicilian and the sea.
<margin>I</margin>
<margin>II</margin>
**The Sicilian watches the sea** <note>original Greek: Σικελὸς θάλασσαν (*Sikelos thalassan*)</note>. That is, the Sicilian gazes out at the sea—the verb is understood. This is said of those who are tempted once again to undergo a danger they have already experienced. They say it originated from a certain Sicilian who, while carrying a cargo of figs by ship, suffered a shipwreck. Afterward, as he sat on the shore and saw the sea calm and tranquil, as if inviting him to repeat the voyage, he is said to have remarked: **I know what you're looking for; you want figs** <note>original Greek: οἷον ὃ βλέπεις, οἷον ὃ βλέπεις (*hoion ho blepeis*)—literally "such as you look," implying "I see what you're after."</note>. This is recorded by almost all the collectors of Greek proverbs.

### He wants a fig.
<margin>III</margin>
**He asks for a fig** <note>original Greek: Σῦκον αἰτεῖ (*Sykon aitei*)</note>. This was said of someone who used flattery for the sake of some personal advantage. They say it originated from the fact that the Athenians used to flatter farmers so that they might receive early-ripening figs from them, offering good omens and prayers that the figs might grow successfully in the following year. However, after the peasants realized that the citizens' smooth talk was aimed at getting figs, they turned it into a proverb; thus, they said that anyone flattering out of hope for profit was "asking for figs." Aristophanes says in *The Wasps*: **But now you ask me for figs** <note>original Greek: Σὺ δὲ νῦν σῦκά μ’ αἰτεῖς (*Sy de nyn syka m' aiteis*)</note>.

### He bid a long farewell.
<margin>IIII</margin>
**Having bid a long farewell to the honors here** <note>original Greek: Μακρὰν χαίρειν φράσας ταῖς ἐνταῦθα τιμαῖς (*Makran chairein phrasas tais entautha timais*)</note>. This figure of speech is undoubtedly proverbial whenever it refers to a thing rather than a person. Whatever we renounce, we are said to "bid it goodbye" or "bid it a long farewell." The metaphor is taken from those who depart intending to be away for a long time, or never to return. It appears frequently in the works of Lucian and others. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the eighth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, says: **But he, bidding a long farewell to "The Good"** <note>original Greek: πολλὰ χαίρειν τῷ καλῷ (*polla chairein tō kalō*). "The Good" refers to the philosophical concept of moral virtue.</note>, **betook himself to Brundisium.** It is uncertain whether he is speaking of some philosopher who, though accustomed to saying many fine things about moral honor (which resides within oneself), later consulted his own safety as if renouncing philosophy; or whether he speaks of Pompey, who fled from Caesar into Greece, prioritizing his safety over his dignity. Likewise, Hippolytus in Euripides says: **I bid your Venus a long farewell** <note>original Greek: τὴν σὴν δὲ Κύπριν πόλλ’ ἐγὼ χαίρειν λέγω (*tēn sēn de Kyprin poll’ egō chairein legō*). Here, Hippolytus renounces Aphrodite/sexual desire.</note>.

Lucian uses this in *The Tragic Zeus*. The same author, in his *Apology for a Slip of the Tongue in Greeting*, interprets the proverb with these words: **For to "bid a long farewell" signifies no longer caring** <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ μακρὰν χαίρειν, τὸ μηκέτι φροντίζειν δηλοῖ (*to gar makran chairein, to mēketi phrontizein dēloi*)</note>. Marcus Tullius, in the fifteenth book of his *Letters to Friends*, used the phrase **to send a notice** instead of "bidding a long farewell": **You have sent a notice to Virtue** <note>original Latin: *nuncium remisisti*</note>, he says, **seduced by the allurements of pleasure.** By this same form of speech, we are said to "Repudiate," or "Renounce," or "Send a notice" to those things which we leave behind in scorn; the metaphor is taken from the formal custom of divorce. He who was seeking a separation used to say: **Keep your things for yourself** <note>original Latin: *Tua tibi habe*</note>. For so says Gaius <note>A famous Roman jurist</note> in the twenty-fourth book [of the *Digest*], under the second title concerning divorces and repudiations, in the chapter "Divorce." In <term>repudiations</term> <note>a one-sided ending of a betrothal or marriage</note>, that is, in renunciations, these words are approved: **Have your things for yourself**; likewise these words: **Manage your own affairs.** By these words, a divorce in marriage was carried out. However, in breaking off <term>betrothals</term> <note>the formal agreement to marry</note>, it was decided that a renunciation ought to occur, in which case these words are approved: **I will not make use of your condition.** Thus Alcmena in Plautus says: **Farewell, keep your things for yourself, and give me back mine.** Alluding to this, Cicero says against Antony: **He has become frugal; he ordered her to have her own things for herself.** Among legal experts, the phrase **to send a notice** <note>original Latin: *nuncium mittere*</note> is frequent, which occurs equally in marriages and betrothals, although the wording differs...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

With all **accismus** <term>accismus: a rhetorical term for a form of irony where someone feigns a lack of interest in something they actually desire</term> removed—that is, all evasion. Again in the same discourse: "Much indeed is the affectation among men" <note>original Greek: πολὺς δ’ ὁ μετὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀκκισμός</note>. Likewise, Philemon in Athenaeus, book 13: "There is no affectation, nor any nonsense" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστ’ οὐδὲ εἷς ἀκκισμὸς, οὐδὲ λῆρος</note>. Plutarch indicates that Acco and Alphito were women used by mothers to scare children away from misbehaving <note>these were nursery bogies or "bogeywomen" in Greek folklore</note>. Plato also uses this word in the *Gorgias*: "You are playing the coy one, Callicles" <note>original Greek: ἀκκίζῃ ὦ Καλλίκλεις</note>.

->**The Scythian pretending to refuse the donkey.**<-

"The Scythian pretending to refuse the donkey" <note>original Greek: Ἀκκιζόμενος Σκύθης τὸν ὄνον</note>. This is used against those who reject with words what they desire in fact. They trace it to a story like this: Someone, seeing a donkey's carcass, said to a Scythian who happened to be nearby, "Look, here is something for you to dine on." At first, he turned away with disgust and loathing; however, he later prepared and ate it. This is roughly how Suidas and Zenodotus tell it. Hesychius records it differently: "The Scythian asks for a donkey-feast" <note>original Greek: Σκύθης ὄνζον δ’ αἴτει</note>. That is, he implies "he found it"—provided the text in Hesychius is free of errors. It is clearly mutilated; perhaps *onzon* was said for "useful," yet in a way that alludes to the donkey.

---

->**THE THIRD HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND**<-

->**Drink either five, or three, but not four.**<-

Athenaeus, in his tenth book, while discussing heavy drinking, writes that a proverb of this kind was commonly celebrated: "Drink either five, or three, but not four" <note>original Greek: ἢ πέντε πίνειν, ἢ τρία, ἢ μὴ τέσσαρα</note>. This prescribes the method for diluting wine. This mixture was most pleasing to the ancients: either adding two parts water to five parts wine, or one part water to two parts wine. As a witness to this, he cites the poet Ion, who wrote that a certain seer predicted to Palamedes that the Greeks would sail away—those who drank three cups of water to one of wine. Also, Nicochares in *Amymone*: "Hail, drink five and two" <note>original Greek: χαῖρε πίνετε καὶ δύο</note>. Furthermore, Amphysias: "I, Bacchus, am a unique voice for you all: five and two" <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ δὲ Διόνυσος πᾶσιν ὑμῖν εἰμὶ φωνῆ ἰδίον</note>. Plutarch speaks on this matter more copiously in the third decade of his *Table Talk*, testifying that in convivial rules it was famously said: "Drink either five, or three, but not four." One should not rashly change the words of Plautus, for they are referenced in his work as well. 

Ariston jokes about this matter: just as in music the *hemiolic* proportion <term>hemiolic: a 3:2 ratio</term> produces the "perfect fifth" harmony <term>diapente</term>, and the double proportion creates the harmony called the "perfect fourth" <term>diatessaron</term>—though he says the *diatessaron* is a duller and dimmer harmony than the others, consisting of an *epitrite* ratio <term>epitrite: a 4:3 ratio</term>—so too in the harmonies of drinking there are three harmonies of wine to water: the perfect fifth, the "five-part" ratio, and the perfect fourth. For the "perfect fifth" harmony is created from the *hemiolic* ratio if three cups of water are mixed with two cups of wine. But if you mix two parts water with two parts wine, a double proportion exists. The "perfect fourth" harmony <term>diatessaron</term> occurs if you add three cups of water to one cup of wine. This is the *epitrite* ratio, a proportion that belongs to the three wise and sober magistrates in the Prytaneum <note>the seat of government in ancient Greek cities</note>, or to the dialecticians when they dispute their anxieties with furrowed brows. 

Now, if you mix two parts wine to one part water, a most turbulent tone is born—what he calls **tipsy** <note>original Greek: ἀκροθώρακα (*akrothorax*), literally "armored at the top," meaning slightly drunk</note>—moving the strings of minds that ought not to be moved. For through this ratio, one is neither entirely sober nor able to drown folly in unmixed wine. But if you add two parts wine to three parts water, the most musical harmony of all is created, as it invites sleep and brings about tranquility and the highest peace. 

After these things were said, Plutarch’s father added that the ancients gave Jupiter two nurses, and also Adrastia; to Juno they gave one, namely Euboea; to Apollo two, Alethia and Corythala; but to Bacchus they gave many, because it is necessary to render this god more moderate and mild, tamed and subdued by many measures of nymphs <note>the "nymphs" here represent water, which dilutes the "god" Bacchus, who represents wine</note>. This signifies that wine should be diluted with much water. Plautus mentions this proverb in *Stichus*, portraying slaves drinking together: "But meanwhile, our general, why does the jug stop here? See how many cups we have drunk. As many as there are fingers on your hand." There is a Greek song:
"Drink five, and drink three, but not four" <note>original Greek: Καὶ πέντε πίνε, καὶ τρία πίνε, ἢ μὴ τέσσαρα</note>.
Although this joke in Plautus is not free from the suspicion of being a textual error. As for why the Greek song forbids drinking four, it pertains to ancient superstition, in which it was believed that odd numbers are more effective for all things—something Pliny thinks is understood in the observation of days in fevers. Furthermore, regarding the avoidance of the number four in drinking, the same author writes in book 28, chapter 6, in this manner:

# THE SECOND THOUSAND, FOURTH CENTURY
<sig>N 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: rum</meta>

I
...also the number four: Democritus even wrote a volume on why one should not drink in groups of four cups or measures <term>sextarius: a Roman liquid measure, roughly a pint</term>. Horace surely alludes to this in the third book of his *Odes*:

> Give a cup to the new moon,
> Give one for midnight, boy, and one for the augur
> Murena: the cups are mixed with three
> Or nine measures, as is fitting.
> He who loves the uneven Muses,
> The inspired poet, will seek three times three cups:
> But the Grace, joined with her naked sisters,
> Fearing quarrels, forbids us
> To touch more than three.

Likewise Ausonius says,
> Drink three times, or thrice three times; such is the mystic law.

That is, either three cups, matching the number of the Graces; or nine, matching the number of the Muses.

II
### A Sicilian at sea.
<margin>A Sicilian at sea. <note>original Greek: Σικελὸς θάλασσαν</note></margin> That is, "a Sicilian gazes at the sea" is understood. This is said of those who are enticed once again to undergo a danger they have already experienced. They say it originated from a certain Sicilian who, while carrying a cargo of figs by ship, suffered a shipwreck. Later, sitting on the shore and seeing the sea calm and tranquil—as if inviting him to travel again—he is reported to have said: "I know what you want; you want figs" <note>original: οἶδ’ ὁ θέλεις, σῦκα θέλεις. The OCR "θεαὸς" appears to be a corruption of "θέλεις"</note>. This is recorded by almost all collectors of Greek proverbs.

III
### He wants a fig.
<margin>He asks for a fig. <note>original Greek: Σῦκον αἰτεῖ</note></margin> That is, he seeks a fig. This was said against one who used flattery for the sake of some personal advantage. They say it originated because the Athenians used to flatter farmers in order to receive early-ripening figs from them, offering good omens and prayers that the next year’s crop would be successful. However, after the peasants realized that the citizens' smooth talk was aimed only at getting figs, they turned it into a proverb; thus, they said anyone flattering in hope of profit was "seeking figs." Aristophanes in *The Wasps* says: "But now you ask me for figs" <note>original Greek: Σὺ δὲ νῦν σῦκά μ’ αἰτεῖς</note>.

IIII
### He bade a long farewell.
<margin>Bidding a long farewell to the honors found here. <note>original Greek: Μακρὰν χαίρειν φράσας ταῖς ἐνταῦθα τιμαῖς</note></margin> This figure of speech, whenever applied to a person, is undoubtedly proverbial. Therefore, when we renounce a thing or give it up, we are said to "say goodbye" to it or to "bid it a long farewell." The metaphor is taken from those who depart intending to be away for a long time, or perhaps never to return. It appears quite often in Lucian and others. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Letters to Atticus*, book 8, writes: "But he, bidding a long farewell to the 'honorable,' betook himself to Brundisium" <note>original Greek: πολλὰ χαίρειν τῷ καλῷ</note>. It is uncertain whether he speaks of some philosopher who, though accustomed to saying many fine things about honor (as if it were his own natural state), later consulted his own safety as if renouncing philosophy; or if he speaks of Pompey, who fled from Caesar to Greece, taking more account of his safety than his dignity. Likewise, Hippolytus in Euripides says: "To your Cypris <note>referring to Aphrodite, goddess of love</note> I bid a long farewell" <note>original Greek: τὴν σὴν δὲ Κύπριν πόλλ’ ἐγὼ χαίρειν λέγω</note>.

Lucian uses this in *Zeus Rants*. The same author, in his *Apology for a Slip of the Tongue in Greeting*, interprets the proverb with these words: "For the phrase 'to bid a long farewell' indicates that something will no longer be a concern" <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ μακρὰν χαίρειν, τὸ μηκέτι φροντίζειν φησί</note>. Marcus Tullius, in the fifteenth book of his *Letters to Friends*, used "to send a notice" <note>original: nuncium remittere</note> instead of "to bid a long farewell." He says: "You have sent a notice to Virtue, enticed by the allurements of pleasure." In the same manner, we are said to "repudiate," "renounce," or "send a notice" to those things we leave behind in scorn—a metaphor taken from the formal custom of divorce. For the one who was seeking a divorce used to say: "Keep your things to yourself" <note>original Latin: Tua tibi habe</note>. So Gaius says in his twenty-fourth book, under the second title *On Divorces and Repudiations*, in the chapter *Divortium*. In cases of repudiation—that is, in formal renunciations—these words are approved: "Have your things for yourself" <note>original Latin: Tuas res tibi habeto</note>; and also: "Manage your own affairs" <note>original Latin: Tuas res tibi agito</note>. Thus, by these words, a divorce in marriage was carried out. In the breaking off of betrothals <note>original Latin: sponsalia</note>, he says it was decided that a formal renunciation ought to occur, in which these words are approved: "I shall not make use of your condition" <note>original Latin: Conditione tua non utar</note>. Thus Alcmena in Plautus says: "Farewell, keep your things for yourself, and return mine." Alluding to this, Cicero says against Antony: "He has become frugal; he ordered that woman to keep her things to herself." Among legal experts, the phrase "to send a notice" <note>original: nuncium mittere</note> is frequent, which occurs equally in marriages and betrothals, though the wording differs...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal formulas for divorce and renunciation, specifically the Roman phrase "take your things with you," before transitioning into three distinct proverbs: the call for plain speaking ("calling a fig a fig"), the concept of a "witness from home" (self-testimony or conscience), and the stereotype of "Boeotian wit" (dullness).</meta>

...formula, as we have said. Regarding matters of the mind, it can be used more pleasantly; for instance, if someone says they are withdrawing from court life or some other pursuit, we might speak of them thus: "The Court has been told to keep its own things," or "Philology has been told to keep its own things." <note>This refers to the Roman legal formula for divorce: *tuas res tibi habeto* ("keep your things to yourself"), here applied metaphorically to leaving a career.</note>

### V. Calling a fig a fig, and a spade a spade.
<margin>V</margin>
*Calling a fig a fig, and a tub a tub.* <note>original Greek: τὰ σῦκα σῦκα, τὴν σκάφην σκάφην λέγων. Erasmus notes that the Greek word for a tub or trough (*skaphe*) was often rendered in Latin as a spade (*ligo*), which is the origin of the English idiom "to call a spade a spade."</note> That is: 
"Naming a fig a fig, and a spade a spade."
A six-foot iambic verse <term>senarius: a common meter in Roman comedy</term> from the comedies of Aristophanes that has been turned into a proverb. It applies to one who, using simple and rustic truth, describes a matter exactly as it is, without wrapping it in verbal ambushes or finery. For there are certain figures among the rhetoricians by which shameful things are spoken of honorably, harsh things softly, proud things modestly, and biting things flatteringly. But those of a "coarser Minerva" <note>An idiom meaning "plain common sense" or "unrefined intellect."</note> speak more roughly and plainly, marking each thing by its own name. Lucian in *Jupiter the Tragedian* says: "For I, as the comic poet said, am a rustic, calling a tub a tub." Again, in his instructions on writing history, he wants the writer to be free and incorruptible, one who narrates the event as it happened, calling a fig a fig and a spade a spade. It is also found in this manner: "I call a fig a fig, and a bread-trough a bread-trough." Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
"I would not pay a single obol <term>obol: a small Greek coin</term> to anyone 
Who would call a bread-trough a 'trough-ess'."
<note>original Greek: κάρδοπον... καρδόπην. This is a joke about gendered grammar; Socrates tries to force a feminine ending on a masculine noun.</note>
A *cardopus* is a bread-box. However, the poet makes Socrates a trifler, who contends that one should not say *kardopos* as Cleonymus used to, but *kardope*, "just as one rightly says Sostrata."

### VI. A witness from home.
<margin>VI</margin>
*The witness is from home.* <note>original Greek: οἴκοθεν ὁ μάρτυς</note> This is said when someone praises themselves, as if they have a witness at home and did not bring one from elsewhere. However, very little credit is usually given to this kind of witness, and they are rejected by the laws as suspect. Paul, in the second book of the *Pandects* <term>Pandects: also known as the Digest, a massive compendium of Roman law</term>, under the title "On Witnesses," in the penultimate chapter says: "It was not pleasing to interrogate witnesses whom the accuser brought from his own house." Again, in the *Code*, book 4, under the same title: "Even in civil law, the reliability of a domestic testimony is disapproved." Lucian in *Jupiter the Tragedian* says: "Well done! The witness is brought from home, as the saying goes." Seneca seems to have alluded to this when writing to Lucilius: "Wait for me a little, and the repayment will be made from home"—unless one prefers to read "from a gift" <note>original: *dono*</note> there. There are Greek writers who say this proverb fits those who, having lied before, later confess the truth—as if driven by conscience, which is the witness of the heart. Thus Plutarch calls the "judgment from home" the judgment of the mind, which is not corrupted. Not far removed from this is what Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the second book of *On the Orator*: "But that third thing—shouting against what is fitting and what is possible—is the mark of a man who, as you, Catulus, said of a certain shouter, 'is gathering many witnesses of his own stupidity by a domestic proclamation'." He called it a "domestic proclamation" because the man himself was broadcasting his own stupidity. The same author in the beginning of that book says: "Whom we, as boys, were able to refute by domestic witnesses: our father, our kinsman Gaius Aculeo, and Lucius Cicero." Here he simply calls "domestic witnesses" those joined by close kinship. Moreover, nothing can be more "domestic" than one's own conscience. The same Cicero, in the second book of his *Letters to Friends*, in a letter to Caelius beginning "Your rare letters": "You are a witness that my services were not lacking to him; since, I believe, 'the witness from home' happened to Phanias." For I suspect it should be read thus, although some had filled the gap with the words "a comic witness," unless perhaps "a household witness" <note>original Greek: οἰκιακός</note> is more pleasing than "comic" <note>original Greek: κωμικός</note>. The same Cicero, in his speech *For Flaccus*: "Nor in the whole testimony of the Aemonensians—whether it was fabricated here, as it appears, or sent from home, as he says—will I be moved." Terence says: "I make this conjecture at home" <note>meaning "in my own mind."</note>.

### VII. Boeotian wit.
<margin>VII</margin>
The Boeotians <note>People from Boeotia, a region in central Greece.</note> had a bad reputation among the ancients for stupidity, as was shown above. Hence, whatever was dull or foolish was called "Boeotian." Lucian in *Jupiter the Tragedian* says: "That which you have said is utterly rustic, harsh, and Boeotian." One also finds "a Boeotian pig," that is, a Boeotian...

<meta>catchword: pig (cum)</meta>

<summary>This page explores proverbs regarding plain speaking, self-testimony, and the regional stereotype of Boeotian dullness, drawing heavily on classical literature and Roman law.</summary>
<keywords>Aristophanes, Lucian, Cicero, Roman law, Pandects, plain speaking, conscience, Boeotia, proverbs, philology</keywords>

--- Page 541 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Boeotian stereotypes, specifically the regional reputation for dullness of mind, before transitioning into proverbs regarding their music, riddles, and legendary feats of gluttony.</meta>

...wit, for one that is stupid and dull. <margin>Horace in the Epistles:</margin>
"You would swear he was born in the thick air of Boeotia." <note>original: *Bœotum in crasso iurares aere natum.* Horace (Epistles 2.1.244) uses the "thick air" of the marshy Boeotian region as a metaphor for a lack of intellectual refinement.</note>

Plutarch, himself a Boeotian, writes in several places—including his essay *On the Eating of Flesh*—that the Athenians branded the Boeotians as "brutes," "stupid," and "fat." This was due to their gluttony, as we have mentioned elsewhere; the people of that nation were more devoted to exercising their bodies than to cultivating their minds. For this reason, according to the testimony of Stephanus <term>Stephanus of Byzantium: a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary</term>, some believed the name was given to the region for this character. He also cites Ephorus, who wrote that while the Athenians were devoted to seafaring, the Thessalians to horsemanship, and the Cyrenaeans to chariots, the Boeotians excelled in physical training, and the Spartans were diligent regarding the laws.

### VIII
### A Boeotian song.
*A Boeotian melody.* <note>original Greek: Βοιώτιον νόμος.</note> This was a common saying for things that had a peaceful and prosperous beginning, but a turbulent and sorrowful ending. This is why Sophocles wrote:
"Whenever anyone sings the Boeotian melody." <note>original: στ' αὖλις ᾄδῃ τὸν Βοιώτιον νόμον.</note>
The proverb arises from history: for the Boeotians at first lived a free and peaceful life, but after the death of Laius <note>The King of Thebes and father of Oedipus.</note> they fell into various calamities, so that their story seemed to decline from a happy start into mourning. It is cited by Zenodotus. Aristophanes, in his play *The Acharnians*, seems to use the term to describe a song that is uncouth and unlearned:
"Dexitheus enters, intending to sing a Boeotian tune." <note>original: δεξίθεος εἰσῆλθ' ᾀσόμενος Βοιώτιον.</note>

### IX
### Boeotian riddles.
*Boeotian riddles.* <note>original Greek: Βοιώτια αἰνίγματα.</note> This was said of indirect and obscure speech that was very difficult to understand. It is taken from the fable of the Sphinx, the monster of Thebes. She proposed a riddle of this kind to Oedipus: "A four-footed, two-footed, and then a three-footed thing." Oedipus interpreted this as being a human: who as an infant crawls on hands and feet; then, with a steady step, supports themselves on two feet; until a decrepit old age adds a staff, as if it were a third foot. There exists an epigram encompassing the riddle of the Sphinx in this manner:
"There is a thing on earth that is two-footed and four-footed, with a single voice,
And three-footed. It alone changes its nature among all things
That creep upon the earth, move through the air, or across the sea.
But when it walks urged by the most feet,
Then the speed in its limbs is at its weakest." <note>This poetic version emphasizes that the more feet a human uses (four as a baby or three as an elder), the slower they actually move.</note>
Hesiod <note>OCR reads "Heliodus," likely a typo for Hesiod.</note> therefore, in his second book of *Works and Days* <note>OCR reads "Georgics," likely confusing the title with Virgil's work.</note>, calls an old man bowed with age a "three-footed human":
"Then indeed they are like a three-footed mortal." <note>original: τότε δὴ τρίποδι βροτῷ ἴσοι.</note>

### X
### He carries an ox in his jaws.
*He carries an ox in his jaws.* <note>original Greek: Βοῦν ἐπὶ γνάθοις φέρει.</note>
This was formerly said of a glutton, as Zenodotus and Suidas indicate. It originated, as I conjecture, either from the athlete Theagenes of Thasos or from Milo of Croton. One of them ate a whole ox by himself, as attested by a Greek epigram and by the author Posidippus in the works of Athenaeus; the other (as Theodorus of Hieropolis relates in the same author) lifted a four-year-old bull onto his shoulders at the Olympic games, carried it the length of the stadium, and ate the whole thing by himself on that same day. Aulus Gellius also mentions this feat in his *Attic Nights*.

### XI
### Prophesy for the Boeotians.
*Prophesy for the Boeotians.* <note>original Greek: Βοιωτοῖς μαντεύεσαιο.</note> This is a phrase used by someone expressing abhorrence, just as we say, "Go prophesy those things to our enemies."
