--- Page 542 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of proverbs used to deflect bad luck or curses onto others, specifically enemies or the speaker themselves if they have spoken out of turn.</meta>

->Sing such things, madman, to the Dardanian <note>The Trojans, descendants of Dardanus.</note> head.<- 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; And, 
->May the wives and children of our enemies feel the blind 
movements of the rising South Wind, and the black sea.<- 
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; And, 
->May such banquets befall our enemies.<-

It will be said more aptly against someone who prophesies grim things, whenever we pray that those things might fall back upon his own head. Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic (3rd century BC).</note> writes that this arose from an actual event, citing Heraclides as his authority. Once, he says, when the Thebans consulted the oracle about the outcome of a war, the prophetess who was then delivering responses at Dodona <note>The oldest Hellenic oracle, where the rustling of oak leaves was interpreted.</note> said they would be victorious if they committed some impious act. Therefore, one of those consulting her seized Myrtila—for that was the name of the woman who foretold the fates—and threw her into a cauldron of boiling water that happened to be nearby. There are some who tell the story that a certain diviner named Bombus responded to the Thebans, when they inquired about the success of a war, that they would conquer as many as possible if they first sacrificed one of their leaders. But they instead killed and sacrificed Bombus himself; and from this the proverb arose.

<margin>XII</margin>
### He puts forward a ram.

*He puts forward a lamb.* <note>original Greek: Ἄρνα προβάλλει.</note> That is, he throws a ram in the way. This was said of someone eager for a quarrel or a fight. For in ancient times, those about to undertake a war would send a *fetial* <term>fetial: a type of Roman priest responsible for maintaining the religious laws of international relations, including the declaration of war</term>, who would lead a ram to the borders of the enemies and release it there: signifying by this act that their city and fields would soon be common pasture for the enemy. The authority for this is Diogenianus.

<margin>XIII</margin>
### Springs of silver.

*Springs of silver are speaking.* <note>original Greek: Ἀργύρου κρῆναί λαλοῦσιν.</note> By this adage, those were marked out who spoke foolishly and ignorantly, yet nevertheless with arrogance and confidence, because they relied upon their wealth. For the common crowd of the rich, "drunk on sweet fortune" as Horace says, also thinks it is owed to their riches that whatever they say should be immediately looked up to and approved by everyone as if it were learned. Noting this, Flaccus <note>The Roman poet Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus).</note> says, 
> My wealth—do not try to compete—
> allows for my foolishness. 

And likewise elsewhere,
> And whatever he wishes, he hoped would be to his great praise, 
> as if it were obtained through virtue.

To this also belongs that comic verse, by no means lacking in wit,
> Fortune makes a fool of the one whom she favors too much.

Likewise that from Antiphanes <note>A comic poet of Athens.</note> found in Stobaeus:
> Wealth, just like a bad doctor, 
> makes everyone blind whom it has received while they could see. <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ πλοῦτος ἡμᾶς, καθάπερ ἰατρὸς κακός, τυφλοὺς βλέποντας παραλαβὼν πάντας ποιεῖ.</note>

On the same sentiment, Menander <note>The most famous writer of Greek New Comedy.</note> writes in his *The Mourner for Himself*:
> Wealth is blind, and it shows those who look upon it to be blind. <note>original Greek: τυφλός ὁ πλοῦτος, ᾧ τυφλὸς ἐμβλέποντας εἰς αὑτὸν δείκνυσιν.</note>

Again, from the same author:
> Luxury becomes something far too insolent 
> whenever wealth drives the one who possesses it 
> into a different character, not the one he had before. <note>original Greek: ὑπερήφανόν τι γίγνεται λίαν τρυφή, ὅτε πλοῦτος, ἐξώκηλε τὸν κεκτημένον. Εἰς ἑτέρου ἦθος, οὐκ ἐν ᾧ τὸ πρόσθεν ἦν.</note>

We have said elsewhere, *He has hay on his horn* <note>A Roman proverb for a dangerous or bad-tempered man.</note>. Ferocity is usually the companion of success. Pindar, in his third *Isthmian Ode*, says:
"If any man has been fortunate, either in glorious contests or in the power of wealth, they say he maintains a magnificent satiety, and is worthy to be mixed with the praises of the citizens." <note>original Greek: ἔστιν ἀνθρώπων εὐτυχíαις... The word 'satiety' here implies a sense of fullness that can lead to insolence.</note>
This will also apply to those whose speech seems more than usually free and bold because of their confidence in their wealth. For just as poverty brings about timidity, so wealth is accustomed to bring about *parrhesia*, that is, confidence in speaking.

<margin>XIIII</margin>
### Land before land.

*To drive land before land.* <note>original Greek: τὴν πρὸ γῆς ἐλαύνειν.</note> This is a proverbial figure of speech for an exile, a wanderer, or one roaming about with no fixed home. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*:

<meta>catchword: and if-</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of proverbs (Adagia), moving from expressions of bad luck to metaphors for restlessness, extreme busyness, abundance, and intemperate drinking habits.</meta>

<page-num>427</page-num>
<header>THIRD HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND</header>

<margin>
And pursue land before land. <note>original Greek: Καὶ δίωκον γῆν πρὸ γῆς.</note>
</margin>
That is, to pursue one land after another. Likewise, elsewhere:
<margin>
But I flee, fearing land before land. <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ φεύγω γῆν πρὸ γῆς φοβούμενος.</note>
</margin>
That is, "But I, fleeing in terror, move from one soil to the next." Lucian writes in *The False Prophet*: "But it was necessary to be driven land before land," meaning to be carried from one country to another. Among the Latins, a person who moves elsewhere for the sake of exile is said to "change his soil" <note>Latin: *Solum vertere*.</note>. Alciphron says in his letters: "Rising up, I shall flee land before land to wherever it may be," which is to say, "By migrating, I would rather flee, exchanging one land for another." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] says in the fourteenth book of his letters to Atticus: "These and other things I cannot bear, and so I am thinking of 'land before land.'" He means that he is contemplating flight.

---

->There is no leisure even to scratch one's ears.<- XV

This is a proverbial hyperbole. When we mean that not even the slightest bit of leisure remains, we say there is not even enough free time to scratch one's ears. Lucian, in *The Double Indictment*, says: "Not even as much leisure, as they say, as to scratch an ear." That is, not even being so idle for a moment as to have time for such a trivial thing.

---

->Sooner would someone falling in a ship miss the wood.<- XVI

<margin>
Sooner would one falling in a ship miss the wood. <note>original Greek: θᾶττον ἄν τις ἐν πλοίῳ πεσών ἁμάρτοι ξύλου.</note>
</margin>
This means: "Sooner would wood be missing for someone falling in a boat." This is a proverbial hyperbole by which we signify such a great abundance of something everywhere that, wherever you turn, what you seek meets you. For since a ship is made of wood on all sides, anyone who falls in it cannot help but land on wood. Lucian uses this in *The Double Indictment*: "So that, according to the proverb, it would sooner happen that one slipping in a ship does not land on wood, than that the eye, wherever it looks, would fail to find a philosopher." Lucian is mocking such a great crowd of philosophers that everything everywhere seems full of them, and it is impossible to escape them.

---

->To Scythianize.<- XVII

<margin>
To Scythianize. <note>original Greek: Ἐπισκυθίσαι (*Episcythisai*).</note>
</margin>
This is a Spartan <note>Lacedaemonian</note> adage used for drinking unmixed wine too immoderately. Achaeus, in the satyr play *Aethon*, used the word "to Scythianize" <note>Greek: *skythisai* or *skythisei*</note> to mean drinking wine "neat" or unmixed with water. Athenaeus, in the tenth book of the *Philosophers at Dinner*, relates from the authors Herodotus and Chamaeleon that Cleomenes, the King of Sparta, went mad after imitating the Scythians’ habit of drinking unmixed wine, according to the Spartans' interpretation. There is a passage in Herodotus, Book 6 (titled *Erato*), adding that from this event a common saying arose among those same Spartans: whenever they wished to drink more intemperately <note>original Greek: *zoroteron pinein*</note>, they would say "to Scythianize." This meant "pour in the least amount of water," instead of the usual "pour in" <note>Greek: *epichyson*</note>, which implied adding water. In the eleventh book of the same work, Hieronymus of Rhodes teaches that "to Scythianize" was said instead of "to be drunk," and Athenaeus wonders whether the *skyphos* (a type of drinking cup) gets its name from the Scythians, as if it were called a *skythos*. He shows that the word appears changed in this way among various authors. Furthermore, he adds that the Spartans, perceiving that the Asiatic barbarians did everything with trickery, sent Dercyllidas there instead of Thimbron, because Dercyllidas lacked Spartan sincerity and possessed a crafty and fierce nature, believing he could not be deceived. For this reason, the Spartans called him "the Scythian" <note>skython</note>, as if he were a *skyphos* cup. The Scythians and Thracians are called "drinkers of unmixed wine," and for the most part their banquets are bloody and tumultuous. In the same author, Anacreon (if I am not mistaken) calls the drinking of unmixed wine a "Scythian draft," which Callimachus described with a compound word meaning "drinking unmixed wine." 

And I wish that this custom, which is more than barbaric, had stayed within the borders of the Scythians and Thracians and had not flowed down even to us. For we not only drink immoderately, but we even force others to drink, and we attack with a blade anyone who refuses—though it is almost more inhumane to force a man who is not thirsty to drink than it is to keep a thirsty man from drinking. As Sophocles elegantly says in the tenth book of Athenaeus:
> To be forced to drink
> Is an evil equal to being forced to thirst.
> <note>original: τὸ πρὸς βίαν πίνειν / ἴσον κακόν πέφυκε τῷ διψᾶν βίᾳ.</note>
You may conveniently apply this to the intemperate and immoderate use of any thing.

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

### Wine lacks a rudder.
<margin>XVIII</margin>

Athenaeus, in the same book discussing drinking parties, writes that a proverb of this kind is elegantly and commonly used: <term>wine has no rudder</term> <note>original Greek: ἄν οἶνον οὐκ ἔχεν πηδάλια</note>. This is because drunkenness says and does nothing with deliberation or moderation. Indeed, it overwhelms reason, which, like a rudder, moderates and governs those who are sober. To this point belongs that line of Ovid:
> Night, love, and wine persuade nothing moderate:
> The first lacks shame, while Bacchus and Love lack fear.

It is quite charming what Xenophon relates in the eleventh book of Athenaeus: that among the Persians, it was forbidden to bring <term>serving vessels</term> <note>original Greek: προχοΐδας (prochoidas), a type of jug or pitcher</note> into a banquet. This appears to have been a type of small vessel from which the servants would pour wine from the mixing bowl into the drinking cup. This rule was made so that those drinking beyond measure would not be deprived of the strength of both mind and body. He adds that the custom is still preserved among them; for although the serving vessels are not brought in, they nonetheless drink so much <term>that instead of being carried out safely, they are carried out when they can no longer leave while dancing</term> <note>original Greek: ὥστε ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀσφαλῶς αὐτὸν ἐκφέρεσθαι, ἐπειδὰν μηκέτι δύνωνται ὀρχούμενοι ἐξίεναι</note>. Thus, their drunkenness is less excusable than that of those who handle the "rudder of the Republic"—that is, kings and magistrates. Even the Divine Scriptures forbid giving wine to kings. Neither wine nor sleep is suitable for those sitting at the rudder, yet sometimes none indulge more in wine and sleep than they do.

### Wine compels even the unwilling to dance.
<margin>XIX</margin>

And again, in the same place, he writes that this verse is tossed about as a proverb:
<term>Wine commands even an old man to dance, even if he is unwilling</term> <note>original Greek: οἶνος ἀνώγει γέροντα καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα χορεύειν</note>.
It warns that nothing is so foolish or so out of character that drunkenness cannot incite it. He also adds another verse of similar sentiment:
<term>An abundance of wine throws even the wise into folly</term> <note>original Greek: οἶνος καὶ φρονέοντας ἀν’ ἀφροσύνην ἀνέβαλλε</note>.
The same author, in the fourth book of the *Sophists at Dinner*, cites a proverb from Eriphus, a certain writer of comedies:
<term>For it is an ancient proverb, and not a bad one,</term>
<term>They say that wine, O father, persuades old men</term>
<term>To lead the dance, even when they are unwilling.</term> <note>original Greek: λόγος γάρ ἐστ’ ἀρχαῖος... πείθειν χορεύειν οὐ θέλοντας</note>
To this belongs that saying of Plato in the first book of *The Laws*: <term>It seems that not only may an old man become a child for a second time, but so too may a drunkard</term> <note>original Greek: οὐ μόνον ἆρ’ ὡς ἔοικε ὁ γέρων δὶς παῖς γίγνοιτ’ ἄν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ μεθυσθείς</note>. Therefore, as it appears, not only is the old man a "child twice over," but also the one who is intoxicated. Likewise, Horace writes:
> Which might recommend me, a youth, to a Lucanian mistress.

### You are serving wine to frogs.
<margin>XX</margin>

<term>You pour wine for frogs</term> <note>original Greek: Βατράχοις οἰνοχοεῖς</note>. This was said against someone who provides something that is not needed by the recipient; for example, if someone were to discuss many points of philosophy among the unlearned. For frogs have no need of wine, as they take more pleasure in marsh water. This adage is explained by Zenodotus, Suidas, and Diogenianus. Pherecrates, quoted in Athenaeus's *Corianno*, says: <term>Go to the crows! You ought to be a cupbearer for frogs</term> <note>original Greek: ἔρρ’ ἐς κόρακας, βατράχοις οἰνοχοεῖν σε δεῖ</note>. For he is scolding a cupbearer who poured two parts of water for every four measures of wine. From this, one may conjecture that the proverb also applies to those who dilute wine with excessive water, so that they seem to be drinking water rather than wine, in the manner of frogs.

### Born from the same egg.
<margin>XXI</margin>

Perhaps this was simply said by Horace:
> Born from the same egg.
Inasmuch as it refers to the fable of Leda, who, having been made pregnant by Jove [Jupiter] when he was turned into a swan, gave birth to an egg from which the twins Castor and Pollux were born. Pausanias, in his *Description of Greece*, reports that this egg was shown among the Spartans, hanging by ribbons from the roof of a temple. However, if anyone should twist this saying to refer to those born of the same parents, or educated by the same teacher, or possessed of such similar temperaments that they might seem born from the same egg, nothing could be more proverbial; as in...

# SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

...countenance, character, habits, deeds, and indeed everything matches so closely that they are like birds <term>hatched from the same egg</term> <note>original Latin: "eodem prognatos ouo"</note>. Aristotle, in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, shows that it happens naturally for two chicks to be born from the same egg—and indeed perfect ones, if the yolk membranes are separated. If they are joined and fused, the offspring is born a monster.

---

<margin>He fell from the carriage <note>original Greek: Ἐξαμαξωλίσθη</note>. That is, "Fallen from the chariot." Aristophanes in *The Frogs*: "his mind fell from the carriage."</margin>
->Fallen from the chariot. XXII<-

This means, "He fell from the chariot." Even today, this proverb persists in common speech for someone who, having forgotten his purpose, turns elsewhere; or for one who wavers in his opinion, so that he is said to have "fallen from the chariot," much like the saying "Fallen from the donkey." Aristophanes in *The Frogs* writes:
->that is,<-
A mind falling from a chariot. That is, wandering from its purpose. It clearly originates from the myth of Phaethon, who they say was thrown from his chariot <note>Phaethon was the son of Helios who lost control of the sun-chariot and was struck down by Zeus</note>. Indeed, the mind is like the charioteer of the body, and the body like the vehicle. There is also a passage in Plato about souls falling from heaven because they were thrown from their chariots.

---

<margin>A number, merely sheep, huddled together like jars <note>original Greek: ἀριθμός, πρόβατ’ ἄλλως, νηνασμένοι ἀμφορᾶς</note>.</margin>
->Number. XXIII<-

Men of no good quality are called "a number" by the proverb, even by the common folk of these times. Aristophanes in *The Clouds* calls them "**worthless stones**" <note>original Greek: οντες λίθοι</note>.
->Horace:<-
We are but a number, born only to consume the fruits of the earth.
It seems the metaphor may be taken from counting stones (<term>calculi</term>), which are useful for nothing else but counting. Anacharsis, according to Plutarch, criticized the Athenians for using coins only for calculation. However, I prefer the idea that "number" is used in the same sense as the phrases "**a useless burden of the earth**" <note>original Greek: ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης</note> and "**one of many**" <note>original Greek: εἷς τῶν πολλῶν</note>—that is, one of the common crowd. Thus Horace, in his first book of *Satires*: "I am a little weaker, one of the many," even imitating the Greek idiom. And Seneca in his first book, Letter 10: "That man is not just one of the people." Notable people are named; those who have nothing notable about them are a crowd, and are merely counted. Hence Horace: "We are but a number." And Virgil: "The nameless crowd falls."

---

<margin>Using the very tops of the sails <note>original Greek: Ἄκροισι χρωμένους τοῖς ἱστίοις</note>.</margin>
->Using all sails. XXIIII<-

**Using the tops of the sails.** That is, to use the highest part of the sails. This proverbial metaphor is used for those who strive and apply themselves with the greatest effort, or who seize every opportunity. It is borrowed from sailors, who customarily raise the sail high so they may run faster. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
->that is,<-
Using the topmost canvas.
Pindar in the fifth *Nemean Ode*: "**Utter a voice, and stretch the sails to the highest yard-arm**" <note>original Greek: Δί’ ὃν φωνὰν, ἀνὰ δ’ ἱστία τεῖνον πρὸς ζυγὸν ἀκροτάτοις</note>. That is, give voice, and stretch the sails upward to the highest point of the yard. Just as things go well or poorly for someone, so the sail is raised high.

---

<margin>Take the top, and you will have the middle <note>original Greek: Ἄκρον λάβε, καὶ μέσον ἕξεις</note>.</margin>
->Take the top, and you will have the middle. XXV<-
->that is,<-
Seize the highest things, and you will gain the middle.
This is a half-line from a heroic poem. When people wanted to signal that something was said somewhat obscurely or perplexingly, advising that the matter should be weighed more carefully, they were accustomed to use this proverb. Zenodotus records that it originated thus: when the inhabitants of Aegina were driven from their homeland and consulted the oracle about seeking a place to live, the response was this riddle: "**Take the top, and you will have the middle.**" It is said they occupied a certain mountain peak and then lived around the middle of it. It can also be adapted to this meaning: that we should be advised to strive for the highest and most excellent things; for in this way it will happen that we reach at least a moderate level. We should set the highest things as our goal in the mind, so that we may at least obtain something modest. For it often happens, I know not how, that outcomes fall short of our hope and the target we set. But today, certain Aristotelian theologians <note>Erasmus often criticized Scholastic theologians for using Aristotelian logic to justify worldly behaviors</note> teach to what extent it is permitted to accept riches, to what extent to play dice, to what extent to wage war, and to what extent to seek revenge. It would be far better to loathe the pursuit of wealth, war, and pleasures in every way. In that case, we might follow these things more moderately. Now, while we are content with moderate things, we slip far below moderation.

---

->Ask for the unfair, so you may get what is fair. XXVI<-

Akin to this is what Quintilian records in the fourth book of his *Institutes of Oratory*: "Nor is it entirely without reason, as the common saying goes: One must ask for the unfair, so that you may receive what is fair." It seems to be derived from merchants, who cunningly bid far less for goods, and much more...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on proverbs, moving from the use of hyperbole in negotiation to metaphors for unrefined character, feigned madness for self-preservation, and the vanity of public speakers. It maintains the sequence of the "Second Chiliad, Third Century."</meta>

...they indicate [a higher value] rather than what is deserved, so that they might at least receive a fair price. This sentiment did not escape that Syrian character in Terence’s *The Brothers*, who, when dealing cunningly with the pimp Sannio, demands that he hand over a girl to Aeschinus for half the price; by this trick, he ensures that the pimp—now eager and even pleading—receives his full principal <note>Erasmus refers to a scene in Terence's play *Adelphoe* where psychological manipulation is used to make a hard bargain seem like a relief.</note>. There is also a common saying: "He who strives to acquire a golden chariot for himself will certainly obtain at least one wheel." Indeed, I believe Seneca alluded to this in the seventh book of *On Benefits*: "These things," he says, "we seek beyond measure so that they may return to their proper proportion." When we say, "He ought not remember it," we want it understood as: "He ought not preach about it, nor boast, nor be overbearing." Seneca has beautifully depicted the nature of <term>hyperbole</term> <note>A rhetorical device involving intentional exaggeration for emphasis, not to be taken literally</note>.

### Ad ambas usq; aures.

<margin>XXVII</margin>
->Up to both ears.<-

<note>original Greek: Μέχρι τῶν ἀμφωτίδων</note>. That is, one is said to be filled "up to both ears" when they gorge themselves beyond measure. The metaphor is taken from small vessels filled right up to the handles. This appears in the *Suda* <note>The Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>.

### Seruilis capillus.

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
->A slave’s hair.<-

<note>original Greek: Ανδραποδώδη τρίχα ἀνακινύειν</note>. That is, they are said to "display a slave’s hair" who possess rustic and unrefined manners. The saying is derived from the fact that at Athens, slaves about to be manumitted <note>The formal process of releasing a slave from bondage</note> would have the hair on their heads shaved off. Plato writes in the *Alcibiades* that some carry "slave-like hairs" in their soul, signifying those who are unlearned and stupid. These words are cited in the *Suda* from some unknown author: "many men gathered together, their passions not yet subdued, but still displaying, as they say, the slave’s hair of those who are agitated." Pliny, in the eleventh book, thirty-seventh chapter, records a prodigious thing: that certain men are born with a "shaggy heart." Pliny’s words are these: "They report that certain men are born with a hairy heart, and that none are more brave in industry, such as Aristomenes the Messenian." Aristomenes killed three hundred Spartans; though he was wounded and captured, he once escaped through a cavern of the stone quarries by following the narrow entryways of foxes. Captured a second time while his guards were weighed down by sleep, he rolled toward a fire and burned through his leather thongs along with his own flesh. Upon his third capture, the Spartans dissected his body to see the cause, and a hairy heart was found.

### Amyris insanit.

<margin>XXIX</margin>
->Amyris is mad.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἄμυρις μαίνεται</note>. That is, "Amyris is raving." This is a proverbial allegory which we may rightly use when someone looks after their own interests under the pretext of madness. Or when someone, alone in foreseeing danger, takes precautions in time while meanwhile believed by the common people to be out of his mind; then, the outcome of events proves that he alone was wise. Thus, this may be a voice as if reproaching the sluggishness of those who did not look out for themselves in time, nor began to be wise until they received a wound. Zenodotus says this arose from history: when the Sybarites <note>Inhabitants of Sybaris, a Greek colony in Italy famous for its extreme luxury and wealth</note> were flourishing in riches, they sent someone to Delphi to ask the oracle about the success of their affairs. The response was that the fortune of the Sybarites would be overturned when they began to hold men in higher honor than the gods. It happened afterward that a slave, fleeing from his master's beating, took refuge at the altars of the gods to no avail; but when he later fled to his master’s tomb, he was spared from the blows, as has been told elsewhere. As soon as Amyris saw this, he gathered his things and moved to the Peloponnese, while the rest of the Sybarites laughed at the man as if he were mad. Afterward, this same man became a marvel because of his feigned madness and gave rise to the proverb. It is cited by Eustathius in the second book of the *Iliad*, and also from the dictionary of Pausanias the rhetorician. He adds that some call this man Thamyris, and others Amyris, dropping the 'th'. It is customary in the manner of men that a prophet is only then believed and praised after we are already weighed down by the evils themselves. Hence Cassandra speaks in a certain tragedy in this manner, as cited by Plutarch:

> "And how is it that when people have suffered and lie in evils,
> I am called wise; but before they suffer, I am called mad?"

Those who spoke or recited for the sake of ostentation were called "Sophocles" and "Laudiceni" by a common insult. The adage was born, as it appears, in the age of Pliny the Younger, whose words we shall repeat from a little further back so that the meaning of the proverb may be more clearly understood. For in a certain letter, taxing the ridiculous arrogance and ambition of certain young men in pleading cases, he says: "But by Hercules, before my memory (as the elders are moved to say), not even the most noble—

# SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

Indeed, for the most modest young men, there was no place unless introduced by someone of consular rank. Such was the great veneration with which they cultivated that most beautiful office. Now, the barriers of shame and reverence have been broken down, and all things are open to all; they are not introduced, but they burst in. They are followed by listeners who are similar to the actors: hired and bought agents. These hired and bought men gather in the middle of the basilica, where they are given <term>doles</term> <note>Small gifts or payments, known as "sportulae" in Latin</note> as openly as if they were in a dining room. They move from one trial to another for the same fee. From this, they are now called—not without wit—*Sophocleis* <note>original Greek: σοφοκλεῖς. A pun combining "sophos" (wise) and "kaleisthai" (to be called), implying they are "called wise" only because they are paid to cheer.</note>. To these same people, a Latin name has been given: *Laudiceni* <note>A pun on "laudare" (to praise) and "cena" (dinner), meaning those who praise in exchange for a meal.</note>. Thus far Pliny. By both words, those are marked who preferred to be called and seen as eloquent rather than actually being so. For "Sophocles" in Greek is said to come from "wise" and "glory" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ σοφὸς καὶ κλέος</note>. But those men, by deliberate effort, interpreted it wrongly as being from "wisely" and "to be called" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ σοφῶς καὶ καλεῖσθαι</note>, that is, from the fact that they were called wise. In this, therefore, is a festive allusion to the name of the tragic poet; in the word *Laudiceni*, an allusion is made to the name of a people <note>The Laodiceans</note>.

### As many servants as we have, so many enemies we have. XXXI

Macrobius, in the *Saturnalia*, says: "From where do you think that most arrogant proverb <margin>Plautus in *Casina*.</margin> arose which is tossed about: 'We have as many enemies as we have servants'? We do not have them as enemies, but we make them so." Seneca also mentions this in his forty-seventh letter, whose words Macrobius seems to have secretly gathered, as he is truly a "drone" of all authors <note>Erasmus accuses Macrobius of being a literary thief or "drone" who lives off the work of others, specifically Seneca.</note>. The adage warns us not to trust them in any way, nor to consider those as friends in our hearts who cultivate us out of fear. Plato likewise warns in the sixth book of *The Laws* that the soul of servants is by no means whole, for Jupiter took away half of their mind—as Homer testifies—from those whom he made subject to servitude. True love, however, is the foster-child of liberty. Truly, whoever fears, hates. From this, a certain genuine hatred seems implanted in servants toward their masters. This will also apply to princes who exercise tyranny over their subjects. These are the words of Plato: "For there is nothing healthy in a slave's soul. For the mind does not possess its full strength in them. And the wisest of poets says:
> For far-seeing Zeus takes away half of the mind
> Of men, whomsoever the day of slavery seizes."

-> that is, <-
> For the servile soul holds nothing whole nor healthy. For one
> who is wise should believe nothing of these men.
> Since the most learned poet says,
> Jupiter deprives those of half their mind,
> Whomever the lot of a servant has ever captured.

They are reported in this manner by Plato. But they are found differently in Homer’s *Odyssey*, book 17, certainly in this manner:
> For far-seeing Zeus takes away half of the virtue
> Of a man, whenever the day of slavery seizes him.

Asinius Capito, in Pompeius Festus (for he also makes mention of the proverb), thinks that by a human error it was pronounced wrongly, because it is more likely that it was said this way in the beginning: "As many enemies, so many servants." This is because those who were captured and conquered were brought into servitude; hence they were also called <term>mancipia</term> <note>A Latin term for slaves, literally "taken by hand" as spoils of war.</note>.

### Called and not called, God will be present. XXXII

<margin>Thucydides, Book 1.</margin> An oracle once given to the Lacedaemonians passed into a proverb: "Called and uncalled, God will be present" <note>original Greek: Καλούμενός τε κἄκλητος θεὸς πάρεσται</note>. The use will be when we signify that something, even if not summoned nor cared for, will nevertheless happen whether we want it or not—think of old age, death, or the punishment of evildoers. Horace alluded to this in his *Odes*:
> Nor did the guard of the Underworld
> Bring back the clever Prometheus,
> Though bribed with gold. He restrains
> Proud Tantalus and the race
> Of Tantalus; he, called and not called,
> Listens to relieve the poor man
> Finished with his labors.

Perhaps Terence also looked to this in *The Eunuch*: "That there may always be a place for me, whether called or uncalled."

### What is drained out flows back in. XXXIII

"What is exhausted flows back" <note>original Greek: Ἐπιῤῥεῖ τὸ ἐξαντλούμενον</note>. This is used when someone spends labor in vain on some matter. Lucian in *The Sects* says: "The business flows back, according to the proverb, while it is being drained, just like the infinite multitude of the Danaids with their jar" <note>In Greek mythology, the Danaids were cursed in the underworld to eternally fill a perforated jar with water.</note>. It flows in, according to the proverb, the business while it drains, and so—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...and something different happened than in the case of the jar of the Danaids <note>In Greek myth, the Danaids were fifty daughters condemned in the underworld to eternally carry water in jars with holes as punishment for killing their husbands.</note>. He speaks of the study of philosophy, in which however much effort you have spent, there is never a lack of something to keep you busy with labors, and labor breeds labor; and according to Sophocles:
Labor brings labor upon labor. <note>original Greek: Πόνῳ πόνον φέρει</note> ->that is,<-
Labor brings forth labor by labor.
Zenodotus records a proverbial verse of this kind:
We have indeed pumped it out, but another wave flows in. <note>original Greek: Ἄντλῳ μὲν ἐξηντλήσαμεν, ἡ δ’ ἐπεισρέει</note> ->that is,<-
We have exhausted that one, but another flows in.
This is taken from sailors who, when a ship is pierced, exhaust the bilge water in vain, because just as much liquid is taken in through the cracks as is drawn out by them. Plato seems to have alluded to this proverb in the seventh book of *The Laws*: "What then is a great increase when it flows in?" <note>original Greek: Τί δὴ πολλὴ αὔξη, ὅτ’ ἂν ἐπιῤῥέῃ;</note> ->that is,<- "What then is much increase, when it flows toward us?" Athenaeus certainly cites this passage in the fifth book of the *Deipnosophists*: "For indeed, according to Plato himself, a crowd of such Gorgons flows in upon me." <note>original Greek: Κατὰ γὰρ αὐτὸν δὴ τὸν Πλάτωνα ἐπιῤῥέει δὴ ὄχλος μοι τοιούτων Γοργόνων.</note> ->that is,<- "Since indeed, according to Plato himself, a crowd of such Gorgons now flows toward me." Seneca, in the second book of *On Anger*: "Does he whose ship draws much water from all sides through loosened joints get angry with the sailors or the ship itself? Rather, he runs to meet it; he shuts out one force and pumps out another; he plugs the visible holes and, with continuous labor, resists those that are hidden and drawing in bilge water from a secret place; nor does he stop because as much as is pumped out is born again." In Athenaeus, in the fourth book, when at a banquet a dish of lentils was served again, cooked differently after a previous dish of lentils, someone alluding to the proverb said:
And we have indeed pumped out the lentil-soup, but another flows in. <note>original Greek: Καὶ τὴν μὲν ἐξηντλήσαμεν φακῆν, ἡ δ’ ἐπεισρέει</note> ->that is,<-
We had exhausted the lentils, but another flows in.
This is not different from that other saying: "The many things arising from the first."

### XXXIIII
->You live the life of a flute-player.<-

You live the life of a flute-player. <note>original Greek: Αὐλητοῦ βίον ζῇς</note> ->that is,<- You live the life of a flute-player. This was cast at a man who lived sumptuously, but at another's expense. For since flute-players were once employed in sacred rites, they were also accustomed to be present at those <term>pontifical dinners</term> <note>Grand, expensive banquets held by Roman priests (pontifices)</note>, and they did so for free. Regarding this class of men, if I am not mistaken, Aristotle reflects in his *Problems*, asking why <term>Dionysian artists</term> <note>original Greek: τεχνῖται Διονυσιακοί; performers, musicians, and actors who participated in festivals for the god Dionysus</note> were hardly ever men of good character. He gives a threefold reason: either because, being occupied for a great part of their lives in necessary arts, they do not give attention to the precepts of philosophy; or because they lead their lives continually in luxury and pleasure; or because poverty itself drives them to vice. Aulus Gellius records this problem in the 20th book of *Attic Nights*. Concerning the flute-players who had withdrawn from Rome to Tibur, Titus Livius tells the story in the ninth book of the first decade: "After they could not be persuaded to return," he says, "they were approached with a plan not at all foreign to the character of such men. On a feast day, different people invited different flute-players to banquets under the guise of celebrating the feast with song. They then put them to sleep, burdened with wine—a breed of men usually greedy for it—and threw them into wagons while they were overcome by sleep, and carried them back to Rome. They did not notice until, with the wagons left in the forum, the light of day found them full of the effects of their heavy drinking." Plautus used the phrase "to live musically" for leading a luxurious and idle life. Terence had this in mind: "See what idleness and another man's food can do." Likewise, Alexis in Athenaeus, in *The People Dying Together*:
How sweet it is to eat what belongs to another. <note>original Greek: Οὕτω τί τ’ ἀλλότρι’ ἐσθίειν, ἐστὶ γλυκύ.</note> ->that is,<-
It is so sweet to devour things that are not yours.
And that saying of Theopompus in the same author:
Euripides said this quite elegantly,
That man is happy who always dines on another's food. <note>original Greek: Εὐριπίδης τ’ ἄριστον ὃ κακῶς ἔχον, / Τἀλλότρια δείπνειν ὃν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα.</note> ->that is,<-
Euripides indeed spoke this elegantly,
That he is happy, who continually dines on another's property.

### XXXV
->Scythian speech.<-

The ferocity of the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people known to the Greeks as fierce and unrefined warriors from the regions north of the Black Sea.</note> passed into a proverb among the Greeks, so that whatever they wanted to be understood as rustic, barbarian, or savage, they called "Scythian." It is found in Lucian in several other places, and specifically in the dialogue of the courtesans Chelidonium and Drosa: "The rest indeed was Scythian speech." <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν ἄλλα ἡ δέη σκιυθῶν φωνή</note> ->that is,<- The rest was indeed the speech of Scythians. He means that at the end of a letter something milder had been said, but the rest showed no trace of humanity. Some think the proverb arose because the Scythians gave no other answer to King Darius than "to weep" <note>original Greek: κλαίειν; a Greek idiom meaning 'go to hell' or 'suffer the consequences'</note>, which very

# SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

Soon it passed into a proverb, that we bid those we despise to weep. Aelian in his *Epistles* mentions a response called "the Scythian answer": 
"I am both mad and sane, and I loathe the life of mortals." <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ μαίνομαι νὴ φρονῶ, καὶ μισῶ τὸν ἄνθρωπων βίον</note> ->that is,<- 
"So let this be your Scythian response, as they call it: I am insane and I am wise, and I hate the race of mortals." Diogenes Laertius, in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, believes this proverb arose from the harshness of Anacharsis <note>Anacharsis was a Scythian philosopher who traveled to Athens in the 6th century BCE and was famed for his blunt, "barbaric" wisdom.</note>. For he, though born a Scythian, was considered among the famous philosophers in Athens. But indeed, it is closest to what Athenaeus relates in Book 12: that the Scythians, once flourishing in wealth and luxury, fell into such ferocity that wherever they went, they would cut off the tips of the men's noses, and their women would prick the bodies of the Thracian wives with needles. Finally, since servitude under their rule was tearful for all, the proverb was passed down to posterity as "a Scythian saying" or "Scythian prescription." <note>original Greek: ἡ ἀπὸ Σκυθῶν ρῆσις</note> Furthermore, to "play the Scythian" <note>original: σκυθίζειν (skythizein)</note> is said to mean cutting off one's hair with a blade, which Stephanus indicates as well as Athenaeus. Finally, the words for "grim-faced" or "gloomy" <note>original: σκύθρωψ (skythrops) and σκυθρωπός (skythropos)</note>, used for the fierce, the sad, the austere, and the cruel, seem to be derived from the character of that nation; as is the word "to be angry" <note>original: σκύζεσθαι (skyzesthai)</note>, because that nation is beyond measure prone to wrath.

### 36. Even a wanderer accepts a clod of earth.

->The wanderer accepts even a clod of earth. <note>original Greek: Δέχομαι καὶ βῶλον ἀλήτης</note> <-

**Even a wanderer accepts a clod of earth.** This half-line of heroic verse is customarily said of those who find nothing burdensome and despise nothing, but consider whatever is given to them, however small or paltry, as a benefit. It can also be said, not unseasonably, of those who, struggling with a lack of resources, gladly accept anything from anywhere until they emerge into a more comfortable fortune. They trace the origin of the adage to an event of this kind: a certain Aletes, driven from Corinth, attempted to return to his homeland at the urging of an oracle. Meeting a certain rustic man on the way, he begged for food. That man, I suppose for the sake of a joke, picked up a clod of earth from the field and held it out. Aletes, accepting it as a lucky omen, declared: "The wanderer accepts even a clod of earth."

Pausanias also mentions this Aletes in his *Description of Corinth*. Plutarch, in his *Greek Questions*, recounts a history not at all dissimilar, from which the proverb might seem to have arisen. The Enianes, he says, after having moved their seats many times from one place to another, finally came down into the territory neighboring the Inachus, which at that time the Inachienses and Achaeans held. An oracle had been given out that if the inhabitants received them into the territory, the old inhabitants would be expelled; but the newcomers would retain the land if they accepted something from those who gave it willingly. Therefore, a certain Temo among the Enianes, a clever and cautious man, took up a pouch and approached the Inachienses in the habit of a beggar. There, when the king, amid laughter and insult, gave a piece of turf to the beggar, Temo threw it into his pouch and, as if content with it, immediately withdrew from sight; nor did he ask for anything else. The elders, moved both by the novelty of the event and the memory of the oracle, approached the king and judged that the man should by no means be neglected nor allowed to slip through their hands. When he realized this, he looked to his safety by flight, and having immediately offered a sacrifice of a hundred oxen and invoked Apollo, he stole away. Later, having joined in battle, the Enianes drove out the Achaeans and Inachienses and occupied their lands. This is roughly what Plutarch says. Thus, the proverb will also apply to those who, attempting something great, both endure and do anything so that they may eventually become masters of their wish.

### 37. Louder than Stentor.

A proverbial hyperbole: **Louder than Stentor.** Juvenal says:

> So that he might surpass Stentor.

This is taken from the story of Stentor, whom Homer mentions in the fifth book of the *Iliad*; he attributes to him an "iron voice," that is, an invincible one:

->Like great-hearted Stentor of the brazen voice. <note>original Greek: Στέντορι εἰσαμένῳ μεγαλήτορι χαλκεοφώνῳ</note> <-
->In the likeness of mighty Stentor, who has an iron voice, who<-
->was accustomed to shout as loud as fifty others. <note>original Greek: ὃς τόσον αὐδήσασχ' ὅσον ἄλλοι πεντήκοντα</note> <-

Equaling fifty others in shout and sound. The Greeks call such people "great-voiced." <note>original: μεγαλοφώνους (megalophonous)</note>

### 38. Going around in a circle.

Lucian in his *Hermotimus* said, "Going around everyone in a circle," <note>original Greek: Ἅπαντας ἐν κύκλῳ περιελθών</note> which is surely a proverbial figure (which still lasts today even among the unlettered common folk) for that which is "every single one, to a man, with no one passed over." From this, the Latin phrase "to canvas" <note>original: Ambire</note> is derived, because they would approach individuals; and "to go over a province" <note>original: Obire provinciam</note>, because those who undertake administration ought to be present everywhere. It will be more elegant if applied to matters of the mind, as if you were to say: "In deliberating, all advantages and disadvantages must be surveyed in a circle."

# THE ADAGES OF ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>XXXIX</margin>
->It is best to profit from the madness of others.<-

**It is best to profit from the madness of others.** Pliny the Elder, in his *Natural History*, Book 18, Chapter 5, specifically cites this as a proverb. He says: "To the same point belongs his statement that a farmer ought to be more prone to selling than buying; that land should be acquired in youth without hesitation, but one should not build upon it until the field is fully planted—and even then, only with hesitation. It is best, as the common saying goes, to profit from the madness of others <note>original: "aliena insania frui"</note>; but only so long as the upkeep of the farmhouses does not become a burden." Thus far Pliny. The same is recorded in almost the same words by Pliny the Younger in his letters, when speaking of the stupidity of Regulus <note>Marcus Aquilius Regulus was a notorious lawyer and "legacy hunter" in ancient Rome, known for his unscrupulousness and eccentricities.</note>, a man who was ridiculously ambitious, yet not entirely useless for stimulating legal studies. This adage warns us that we should become more cautious through the errors of others, and rendered more prudent by the dangers others face—that the foolishness of others should provide us an opportunity to be wise. There is a common verse tossed about to the same effect:
"Happy is he whom the dangers of others make cautious."
Cicero, in a certain letter, wrote that it is a fine thing to shape one's own life for the better based on the mistakes of others. Likewise, Plautus says: "He is happily wise who is wise at another's risk." There also exists a line from a mime of this sort, by Publilius <note>Erasmus writes "Publianus," referring to Publilius Syrus, a Syrian slave who became famous in Rome for his witty "Sententiae" or moral maxims.</note>, as I conjecture:
"From the vice of another, the wise man corrects his own."
And Demea in Terence’s play <note>Demea is the strict father in the comedy *Adelphoe* ("The Brothers").</note> commands one to take examples from others. This can also be taken in another sense: that a person is said to "profit from another’s madness" when they enjoy the misfortunes of others while remaining in safety themselves. For no pleasure costs less, nor is any usually more delightful. This proverb seems to be taken from the tragedy by Sophocles titled *Ajax the Whip-Bearer* <note>Known today simply as *Ajax*.</note>. In that play, while Ajax boasts in his madness that he has beaten his enemies (having actually vented his rage on cattle), the goddess Pallas Athena invites Ulysses to witness this spectacle with these words:
"Is it not, then, the sweetest laughter to laugh at your enemies?" <note>original Greek: οὐκοῦν γέλως ἥδιστος εἰς ἐχθροὺς γελᾶν</note>

<margin>XL</margin>
->Necessity is a powerful weapon.<-

**Necessity is a powerful weapon.** This refers to an inevitable circumstance. Livy, in the fourth book of his first decade, says: "You are superior because of necessity, which is the last and greatest weapon." <note>original: "Necessitate quæ ultimum ac maximum telum est"</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his book *On Friendship*, says: "Indeed, reputation is not to be neglected, nor should one think the goodwill of citizens is a mediocre weapon for conducting affairs." Pliny the Elder <note>Erasmus calls him "Plinius auunculus" (Pliny the uncle), as he was the uncle of Pliny the Younger.</note> uses the same adage in a certain place. It appears several times in Livy: "Another weapon was found for this matter," and "They were preparing that matter especially with this weapon." In these cases, "weapon" seems to be used to mean a plan or a sharp strategy for conducting business, perhaps a metaphor taken from hunters, who pursue with a weapon what they wish to capture. Hence, certain plans that never fail are called "sure weapons."

<margin>XLI</margin>
->Against necessity, not even the gods resist.<-

**Against necessity, not even the gods fight.** <note>original Greek: Ἀνάγκῃ οὐδὲ θεοὶ μάχονται</note> This sentiment is attributed to Simonides and is taken from Homer. It is recorded in two places by Plato: in the seventh and fifth books of the *Laws*: "But it seems that he who first mixed a god into the proverb said this with these things in view: that not even a god is ever seen fighting against fate." <note>original: "quod ne deus quidem unquam uisus est cũ fato pugnare"</note> The same author in the *Symposium* says: "Many and harsh things happened to the gods, as it is said, because of the reign of Necessity." <note>original: "ob necessitatis regnum"</note> Likewise, in the fifth book of the *Laws*, he writes: "Not even a god can force necessity." Titus Livy says: "Let necessity be obeyed, which not even the gods overcome." Palladius writes: "Necessity knows no holidays." Euripides in *Helen*:
"For that is a saying of the wise, not mine:
Nothing is stronger than dire necessity."
There exists a proverbial verse among the Greeks:
"For necessity soon drives all things into slavery."
Euripides in *Hecuba*:
"For necessity is rigid." <note>original: "Rigida nanque necessitas"</note>
Horace says:
"If dire Necessity fixes her adamantine
nails into the topmost heights..." <note>original: "Si figit adamantinos / Summis uerticibus dira necessitas / Clauos"</note>
The poets make Necessity a goddess, the mother of the Fates, who are themselves inescapable and inex... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it transitions to the next page.</note>

<summary>This page explores three adages concerning the wisdom of learning from others' mistakes and the irresistible, god-defying power of necessity, citing a wide range of classical authors including Pliny, Cicero, Plato, and Euripides.</summary>
<keywords>madness, caution, necessity, weapon, fate, gods, ancient proverbs, Pliny the Elder, Cicero, Plato, Euripides</keywords>

### SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
O 2
<meta>catchword: Aulœdus</meta>

...are called inexorable. This necessity is what philosophers call "Fate," which is an eternal series of things necessarily linked together. Yielding to this, Jupiter says in the works of Virgil <note>original: "Maronem," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro</note>:
"The Fates will find a way."
And a certain tragic character in Seneca's works says:
"The Fates lead the willing, but drag the unwilling along."

### Plucking squills from a tomb. XLII
<note>Greek: Σκίλλας ἀπὸ σήματος τίλλειν</note>, that is, "To pluck squills from a tomb," was an instruction given to those who seemed to be of unsound mind. For in ancient times, this herb was used to purify or expiate this particular ailment. Theocritus <note>A Greek poet from Sicily, known for inventing pastoral poetry</note> says in his *Idylls*:
"Go at once and pluck squills from the tomb of an old woman." <note>Greek original: Σκίλλας ἰὼν γραίας ἀπὸ σήματος αὐτίκα τίλλοις.</note>
This implies that the person is taking his defeat in a singing contest so irritably that there is a danger he might lapse into insanity. Another author records something similar:
"Go away from here and bury the cyclamen in the river Halens." <note>Greek original: Ἐλθὼν τὴν κυκλάμινον ὀρύσσειν εἰς τὸν Ἁλέντα.</note>
Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> in his second book demonstrates that the <term>Cyclamen</term> <note>A flowering plant often used in herbal medicine</note> is called *rapum* <note>turnip</note> by the Romans, and it is effective at drawing phlegm out of the head. Among its other remedies, he also mentions that its juice, mixed with honey, can be dripped into the nostrils, or a wool cloth soaked in it can be applied with a finger to clear the discharge from the head. He notes that its root can be sliced and stored just like a <term>squill</term> <note>Also known as a sea onion, used as a medicinal herb</note>. Finally, when crushed and made into lozenges, it is effective against those sorceries which the Greeks call <term>philtra</term> <note>love charms or potions</note>.

### Labors past are pleasant. XLIII
**Labors past are pleasant.** Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, writes: "What if the memory of past evils is actually pleasant? To the point that some proverbs are truer than your philosophical dogmas: for it is commonly said, 'Labors past are pleasant.'" This adage is taken from human nature itself; for it is innate in everyone that the secure recollection and recounting of past evils or dangers is delightful to each person—especially those significant or fatal events that were not joined with shame, such as wars, shipwrecks, and crises of that sort. Hence the saying by Horace:
"The sailors, now safe, delight in telling of their babbling dangers while their heads are shaved." <note>It was a custom for sailors saved from shipwreck to shave their heads as a votive offering.</note>
This proverb arose from Homer as if from a fountainhead, and was subsequently used in various ways by different writers. It appears in the fifteenth book of the *Odyssey*:
"But we two, eating and drinking in the hut, let us take delight in each other’s grievous sorrows as we remember them; for a man takes delight even in his pains after the fact, if he has suffered much and wandered much." <note>Greek original: νῶϊ δ’ ἐνὶ κλισίῃ πίνοντέ τε δαινυμένω τε, κήδεσιν ἀλλήλων τερπώμεθα λευγαλέοισιν· μνασμένω· μετὰ γάρ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι τέρπεται ἀνήρ, ὅστις δὴ μάλα πολλὰ πάθῃ καὶ πόλλ’ ἐπαληθῇ.</note>
This passage and the proverb are also cited by Aristotle in the first book of his *Rhetoric*, where he records what things are naturally pleasant or troublesome to people. Virgil, emulating Homer, wrote:
"Perhaps one day it will be a joy to remember even these things." <note>original: "Forsan & hæc olim meminisse iuuabit."</note>
Likewise in the tragedies of Seneca:
"What was hard to suffer is sweet to remember."
A proverbial Greek line of this kind also circulates:
"How sweet it is for those saved to remember their toils." <note>Greek original: Ὡς ἡδύ τοι σωθεῖσι μεμνῆσθαι πόνων.</note>
Cicero seems to indicate that this was taken from Euripides. He says, "And Euripides says it well; I will conclude it in Latin if I can. For you all know this Greek verse:
'Sweet is the memory of past labors.'"
The verse stands up [metrically] if you read "sweet thing" <note>original: "suaue"</note> instead of "sweet" <note>original: "suauis"</note>, unless you prefer to elide the "s" in the manner of the ancients; or, what is most convenient, omit the word "is," unless you prefer to place it after "labors."

### He becomes a flute-player who cannot be a lyre-player.

<margin>44</margin>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *Pro Murena*, makes a comparison between legal experts and orators. He says: "And so it seems to me that most people originally preferred the former [oratory]; later, when they could not achieve it, they slipped down into the latter [law]. Just as they say among the Greek artists that those become flute-players <note>original: "aulœdos"</note> who could not become lyre-players <note>original: "citharœdi"</note>: so we see some who could not turn out to be orators, and thus they descend to the study of law." This is the extent of Cicero’s comment. This saying is rightly applied to those who prefer to be considered of some importance in a much inferior rank, rather than be overlooked among the truly excellent. Nor will it fit poorly for those who, out of despair for better things, betake themselves to humbler pursuits. The same adage is cited in the *Decretals* <note>A collection of papal decrees forming part of canon law</note> from Augustine, directed against bad monks who fall away into the ranks of the ordinary clergy.

### He added the Colophon.

<margin>45</margin>
"He put on the Colophon" <note>Greek: Τὴν κολοφῶνα ἐπέθηκεν</note>. This is commonly said when the finishing touch is put on a matter, or when that thing is added without which a business cannot be settled. Strabo indicates the origin of the adage in the thirteenth book of his *Geography*, writing that the people of Colophon <note>An ancient Greek city in Ionia</note> formerly abounded in naval forces and excelled so greatly in cavalry that, wherever a war was being waged among nations that could not be ended, it was brought to a decisive conclusion by the help of the Colophonian horsemen. And from this arose the common proverb, "He added the Colophon." The proverb is also mentioned by Diogenianus. Festus Pompeius also pointed it out, writing that "colophon" was traditionally said when something was signified as finished, although I suspect that passage is not free from error. Plato used it in this sense in the second book of *The Laws*: "Therefore, concerning the use of intoxication, let us first impose the Colophon" <note>original Greek: Επί πίνων δὲ μύθους χρεὰ τὸν κολοφῶνα πρῶτον ἐπιθέμθυ</note>—meaning let us put a finish to it—even if we read "needs" <note>Greek: χρείας</note> in Plato, for a mention of the dance preceded it. And shortly after: "Here for us, guests, if it seems good to you, let the Colophon be placed upon the speech delivered about wine." He says the same in his third letter to Dionysius: "You have imposed a Colophon in a most splendid and youthful way upon all your promises." Again, in the *Theaetetus*: "And to these I am forced to add a Colophon, compelling that golden chain" <note>Greek: τὴν χρυσῆν σειράν</note>. For Socrates feels that Homer, by the "golden chain," signified the sun, by whose motion all things are preserved, and which would immediately perish if it stood still. Therefore, the principal argument by which he proves that the universe is corrupted by stillness and preserved by motion, he calls the Colophon. Likewise, Aristides says in his *Themistocles*: "And here is the Colophon of the speech," that is, the sum of the oration. Plutarch says in his booklet *On Music*, although the style almost shouts that it is not his: "I have made these verses, good teacher, the Colophon of those things discussed concerning music." He said the same in the booklet *On the Cleverness of Animals*: "So that the reasoning, imposing a peak <note>Greek: κορυφῶ</note> upon itself, may make an end." Gregory the Theologian in his booklet on his own flight says: "For now I come to the very Colophon of the speech." There are some who suggest the proverb is used for the absolute worst of evils. John Chrysostom seems to have used it in that way in his letter to Innocent, the Bishop of Rome. Hesychius notes that "Colophon" is sometimes used to mean a jackdaw <note>original: "graculum"</note>; because, as I think, that bird is usually placed on the highest peaks of buildings, as if warning—according to Hesiod’s crow—that men should build their nests, for it will not always be summer. In Latin, it is also said "to put on the apex." Cicero says in *Cato the Elder*: "Moreover, the apex of old age is authority." Seek the rest from the proverb which we have related elsewhere, "The Colophonian vote." We have spoken elsewhere of "Adding the Coronis" <note>A curved mark in Greek manuscripts signifying the end of a section</note>.

### No leisure for slaves.

<margin>46</margin>
"There is no leisure for slaves" <note>Greek: οὐ σχολὴ δόλοις</note>. This is cited by Aristotle in the seventh book of his *Politics*. It is taken from the condition of slaves, to whom their masters grant no leisure; indeed, they impose a little more work than they are able to perform, so that as they are stingy in their rations, they are liberal in the allotment of labor. It will be said against those who, because of the debased condition of their subservient position, do not have time to devote effort to honorable disciplines. For the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>Arts worthy of a free person (liber), as opposed to manual or servile labor</note> are so called because free-born men applied themselves to them, being those who had both leisure and resources. It will be adapted not at all unskillfully against the wicked, whose minds are occupied by vices so that they cannot learn the noble arts. For nothing is more occupied than servitude.

<summary>Erasmus explains three proverbs: the first concerns those who take up a lesser profession when they fail at a greater one; the second discusses "adding the Colophon" as a finishing stroke; and the third addresses how a lack of leisure prevents slaves and the vice-ridden from pursuing higher learning.</summary>
<keywords>career failure, finishing touches, Colophon, slavery, leisure, liberal arts, Cicero, Plato, Aristotle, social status, education</keywords>

SECOND MILLENNIUM, THIRD CENTURY.
O 3
<meta>catchword: Zaphlegees (Burning fiercely)</meta>

No slavery is more burdensome, however, than if one serves their own vices. Especially since such a person has many masters, and those most at odds with each other—and for that reason, by no means commanding the same things. For if at one time Sloth commands one to sleep until midday, Greed, on the other hand, commands one to be at the harbor at first light; when Stinginess dictates thrift, Love commands one to squander. Therefore, only the wise man is both free and lives in true leisure.

### You implore the Titans.
->XLVII<-

<note>original: "Τιτᾶνας καλεῖς"</note> That is: "You call upon the Titans." This is used when someone, distrusting their own strength, begs for outside help. It is taken from the myth of the giants, in which Jupiter, fearing for his own Olympus, summoned the Titans to his aid. According to the author Nonius Marcellus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian</note>, the ancient Latins used the word *Quiritari* <term>Quiritari: to cry out for the help of the Quirites (Roman citizens)</term> as a proverbial metaphor for this. It was drawn from the custom of the Romans who, when oppressed by force, would invoke the "Quirites." For that is what they called Roman citizens. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus. This allegory becomes more elegant if it moves further away from the simple literal figure—for example, if a theologian, unable to defend himself with Holy Scripture, turns to the arguments of the philosophers. "I call upon the Titans."

### Man is a bubble.
->XLVIII<-

<note>original: "Πομφόλυξ ὁ ἄνθρωπος"</note> That is: "Man is a bubble." This proverb warns that nothing is more fragile, more fleeting, or more empty than human life. For a bubble is that empty swelling seen on the water, born and vanishing in the same moment of time. Marcus Terentius Varro <note>An ancient Roman scholar</note> says in the preface he wrote for his books *On Agriculture*: "Thinking," he says, "that I must hurry; because if, as they say, man is a bubble, even more so is an old man. For my eightieth year warns me to pack my bags before I depart from this life." Lucian, likewise, in his work *Charon*, makes the lives of men similar to bubbles of this kind: some of which, as soon as they are born, immediately vanish; others last a little longer; all follow one after another at the briefest intervals. Indeed, nothing could be devised that better represents how this life of ours is nothing. First, with what great peril we come into the light! Then, how abandoned and subject to what great dangers is infancy! How fleeting is adolescence, how headlong is youth! Aristotle, in his books on *Politics* and likewise in the third book of the *Rhetoric*, teaches that the vigor of the human body already begins to vanish around the thirty-fifth year, and that of the mind in the forty-ninth. Hippocrates limits the final age of man to forty-nine. Now, if you subtract childhood and old age from the calculation of a lifetime, I ask you, how little is it that remains? And this very span, confined by such narrow limits, is infested daily by six hundred kinds of diseases; no fewer accidents, collapses, poisons, shipwrecks, wars, earthquakes, falls, lightning strikes, and what not, attack us. One man was choked by swallowing a grape seed <note>A reference to the poet Anacreon's legendary death</note>. There is one whom a hair in a drink of milk strangled. Nor was there lacking a man for whom a seed of frozen hail, falling from a roof, brought sudden destruction. And this is that animal which stirs up such great turmoils, and for whose desires this world is too narrow! I cannot restrain myself from adding here the words of Pliny from his seventh book, skillfully depicting the fragile brevity of life: "This gift of nature, whatever is given to us, is indeed uncertain and fragile; it is truly spiteful and brief, even for those to whom it falls most generously, if one looks at the entire span of time. What of the fact that, by the estimation of nightly rest, everyone lives only half the space of their life? An equal part is spent in a state similar to death, or in pain, unless rest occurs. Nor are the years of infancy counted, which lack sense; nor those of old age, living on for punishment. So many kinds of dangers, so many diseases, so many fears, so many cares, death so often invoked, so that no prayer is more frequent. Nature, indeed, has granted nothing better to men than the brevity of life. The senses grow dull, limbs are twisted, sight, hearing, and the ability to walk die prematurely; even the teeth and the instruments for food. And yet this time is counted as life." To the likeness of bubbles is added that noble comparison of Homer concerning the falling leaves of trees. For thus Glaucus speaks in the sixth book of the *Iliad*:
> <note>original: "Οἵη περ φύλλων γενεὴ, τοίη δὲ καὶ ἀνδρῶν, / φύλλα τὰ μέν τ’ ἄνεμος χαμάδις χέει, ἄλλα δέ θ’ ὕλη / τηλεθόωσα φύει, ἔαρος δ’ ἐπιγίγνεται ὥρη."</note>
> Just as the generation of leaves is, so is that of men:
> The wind pours some of these leaves on the ground, but again the
> Flourishing forest brings others forth, as soon as the breeze of spring breathes upon them.
Diogenes Laertius testifies that Pyrrho the Academic was particularly delighted by this poem. Again, Homer in the twenty-first book of the *Iliad*:
> <note>original: "Οἳ φύλοισιν ἐοικότες, ἄλλοτε μέν τε"</note>
> They who, being like leaves, at one time...

<summary>Erasmus discusses the adage "Titanas imploras" regarding seeking external aid and "Homo bulla," a reflection on the extreme brevity and fragility of human life using classical sources like Pliny and Homer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the adage "Man is a bubble," illustrating the fragility and transience of human life through a series of classical Greek and Latin poetic citations.</meta>

They become full of fire, eating the fruit of the field,
But at other times they perish, lifeless. <note>original: "Ζαφλεγέες τελέθουσιν, ἀρέρης καρπὸν ἔδοντες, Ἄλλοτε δ' αὖ φθινύθουσιν ἀκήριοι." From Homer's Iliad, 21.464-466, comparing men to leaves.</note>
That is:
Like the leaves of trees, now they overflow
With rich offspring, and happily feed on the crops of the fields;
Now again they perish, and being transitory, they vanish.
<margin>The same author in some other place:</margin>
Earth, the nourisher, feeds nothing more feeble than man. <note>original: "Οὐδὲν ἀκιδνότερον γαῖα τρέφει ἀνθρώποιο." From Homer's Odyssey, 18.130.</note>

Menander, in Plutarch’s small book of consolation to Apollonius:
The sum and substance of the matter is this: you are a man,
An animal than which none other more quickly
Rises to heights and falls again to lowliness.
And quite rightly too; for although it is by nature the weakest,
It manages the greatest affairs. <note>original: "Τὸ δὲ κεφάλαιον τῶν λόγων, ἄνθρωπος εἶ..."</note>
That is:
The head and sum of this speech: You are a man;
Than whom there is no other animal anywhere that
Now rises, now falls, more quickly and more frequently.
And rightly so indeed, since although it is the weakest,
It administers the greatest business.
<margin>Euripides in the same author:</margin>
Happiness is not stable, but lasts only for a day;
And in a single day it brings down things from on high,
And raises these things up. <note>original: "Ὁ δ' ὄλβος οὐ βέβαιος, ἀλλ' ἐφήμερος..." From Euripides, Ino.</note>
That is:
Prosperity is not stable,
But lasts for a day; and a single day
Has both dragged these things from on high, and raised
These others from the bottom to the top.

In this passage, Demetrius Phalereus <note>A 4th-century BC Athenian orator and statesman</note> is read to have criticized the poet—otherwise praised for his elegance—who should have said not a <term>νυχθήμερον</term> <note>original: "νυχθήμερον" — a period of twenty-four hours (night and day)</note>, that is, one day, but a <term>στιγμὴν χρόνου</term> <note>original: "στιγμὴν χρόνου" — a point of time</note>, that is, a mere instant of time. Pindar even surpassed the Homeric simile: for he called man not "leaves," but "the dream of a shadow." The passage is in the *Pythian Odes*, hymn 8: <term>Ἐπάμεροι. τί δέ τις; τί δ' οὔ τις; σκιᾶς ὄναρ ἄνθρωπος</term>. That is: Creatures of a day. What is "someone"? What is "no one"? Man is the dream of a shadow. Nothing is emptier than a shadow. For it seems to exist, when it is nothing. But even by this standard, something emptier perishes—namely, the dream of a shadow. So that no one can say, "this is someone"; nor again, "this is no one," because the change in human affairs is so sudden that he who seems to be something is soon nothing; and he who is seen to have perished is soon someone. Aeschylus, in Stobaeus, makes the life of man like the shadow of smoke:
For the race of mortals strives for transitory things,
And nothing is more certain than the shadow of smoke. <note>original: "Τὸ γὰρ βρότειον σπέρμ' ἐφήμερα φρονεῖ..." From Aeschylus, fragment 399.</note>
That is:
The mortal race pursues transitory things,
Nor is any matter certain, nor is it more safe
Than the shadow of smoke.
<margin>Sophocles likewise in Ajax:</margin>
Man is nothing but a breath and a shadow. <note>original: "Ἄνθρωπός ἐστι πνεῦμα καὶ σκιὰ μόνον." From Sophocles, Ajax, 125-126.</note>
That is:
Man is nothing other than a shadow and a gust of air.

Pindar in the *Nemean Odes*, hymn 11: <term>εἰ δέ τις ὄλβον ἔχων, μορφᾷ παραμείσεται ἄλλους, ἔν τ' ἀέθλοισιν ἀριστεύων ἐπέδειξεν βίαν, θνατὰ μεμνάσθω περιστέλλων μέλη, καὶ τελευτὰν ἁπάντων γᾶν ἐπιεσσόμενος</term>. That is: But if anyone possessing wealth surpasses others in beauty, and showing his strength, excels in the games, let him remember that he wears mortal limbs, and that he will eventually put on a shroud of earth as the end of all things. It would be fitting for this sentiment to be inscribed in halls, on drinking cups, on tapestries, and on the insignia of princes, rather than those boastful mottos such as "He who will," and "Yet further," <note>Erasmus likely refers to the mottos of contemporary nobility, such as Charles V's *Plus Ultra* (Still further).</note> and others of this kind. Nothing is more charming than that comparison of roses—suddenly budding, aging, and perishing—with the life of men. A poem exists under the title of Maro <note>Virgil</note>, which, even if it does not quite taste of the Vergilian vein, yet so overflows with graces and wit that it appears to have come from an author not only most learned but also most delightful, whoever he was. To this belongs what the poets imagine: that all mortals hang by the threads of the Fates <note>The Parcae</note>, and if these are hostile, they immediately fall. Some are suspended by white threads, others by black. Again, some hang lifted up on high, others near the earth. Yet the lot of all is this: as soon as the inexorable Atropos <note>The Fate who cuts the thread of life</note> has cut the thread with her thumb, he who was hanging immediately falls.

<meta>Catchword: falls.</meta>

<summary>Erasmus compiles numerous classical quotes from Homer, Pindar, and the Greek tragedians to emphasize the fragility of human life, famously describing man as "the dream of a shadow." He suggests these somber reflections are more appropriate for royal displays than the boastful mottos common in his own time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the adage "Man is a bubble," transitioning from classical poetic examples to contemporary 16th-century tragedies to illustrate the fragility of even the most powerful and gifted individuals.</meta>

### CHILIAD TWO, CENTURY THREE

...[continued from previous page]. Nor is there any difference, except that he who hung higher falls with a greater crash. 
Do you laugh, and think these are merely the games and jokes of poets? They are games indeed, but that game of the fates is too cruel and too insolent. If only they exercised it solely upon the common and useless men (to whom that Homeric line applies:
<margin>They crouched, mere burdens <note>original: "Ἔπτηξαν ἄχθ’ ἀείρεις." A reference to the Homeric expression "burdens upon the earth," used for men who contribute nothing to society.</note></margin>
and did not also snatch away before their time men endowed with heavenly genius, and the very best of princes. From these, the fates not only do not withhold this license to play, but they even seem to lie in wait for them with deliberate effort, out of a kind of ambitious envy. Thus, to our great literary loss, an untimely death recently snatched from the earth **Paulus Canalis**, a Venetian patrician <note>Paolo Canale (1481–1508) was a brilliant young Venetian scholar and friend of Erasmus who died at age 26.</note>. He was a young man scarcely twenty-five years old, but—immortal God!—endowed with such a happy genius, such sharp judgment, such rich eloquence, and such knowledge of languages and all disciplines! Inexorable fate thought it of no concern that it brought such a great loss to good literature, which he had already begun to support with vigor; that it stirred such heavy longing in the cultivators of letters; and that it suddenly cut down such great fruits and hopes of students.

Indeed, concerning the untimely death of **Philip**, my prince <note>Philip I of Castile, known as "Philip the Handsome" (1478–1506). He was the ruler of the Burgundian Netherlands and King of Castile, and a patron to Erasmus.</note>, I cannot even speak of it because of the bitter grief I feel for him, yet it would be wrong to pass over it since this occasion reminds me of his singular kindness toward me. Of all the princes the sun has ever seen, fortune showed him to the earth as the best, the greatest, and most distinguished—but, alas, what a crime! She only showed him, and immediately withdrew him. For what gifts of nature, what ornaments of fortune, what divine gift can be given to mortals by those above that was not both exceptional and most abundant in him? 

First, what heroic height of body, what dignity and grace of form! What vigor in his eyes! What a happy disposition, what firmness of limbs, what strength, what posture, what bearing! As for the splendor of his birth, what need is there to speak? Among his ancestors you will find so many kings, so many emperors, and so many heroes that nothing more illustrious, grand, or magnificent could even be imagined. To these was added a certain secret power, divinely implanted, by which it happened that, like a magnet, he drew the hearts of kings, nations, his own people, and foreigners—in short, of all mortals—to love him. So much so that not only the sight and meeting of him, but even the mere mention of Philip's name, somehow excited a wonderful goodwill. 

What can happen more happily for a supreme prince than this? A certain singular courtesy and dexterity of manners increased this fatal lovability. Thus, there was such a miraculous consensus among all kings and nations in loving him that even those who had been struggling in war a little before, having now laid down their arms, applied themselves with equal zeal to honoring Philip. Everything was so full of peace, harmony, grace, and joy wherever in the world he went. What ancient leader, what triumph would not be held in contempt by one who witnessed how much true goodwill, how much zeal, and how many honors were eagerly bestowed by so many kings, nobles, and nations—Gaul, Savoy, Spain, Germany, Britain—during those two journeys of his into Spain? Anyone who had contributed any ornament to Philip thought a great ornament had been added to himself. Concerning these matters, our *Panegyric* exists <note>Erasmus refers to his *Panegyricus ad Philippum*, a formal speech of praise he delivered to Philip in 1504.</note>. 

Add to these things the fertility of his wife, all his children being safe, and his father **Maximilian** <note>Maximilian I, the Holy Roman Emperor.</note> (to embrace infinite glories in one word). Add so many kings joined by the bonds of kinship. Add the greatness of the Empire in which he was born; add the splendor of the kingdom into which he was adopted; add the succession to his father’s majesty; add the hopes of such great things, which were certain for such a character, such fates, and such morals, if the gods had willed anything at all to be certain in human affairs. The things that had already happened were very great, and even greater because they had not grown, as they do for most, through violence, blood, and the calamities of others. For great empires are scarcely possessed otherwise. There was nothing bloody in so many tokens of our Philip's happiness, nothing joined with anyone's pain or loss. Indeed, the things that were imminent were so imminent that it seemed he would not invade them, but rather that he would not be allowed to refuse them. 

So many gifts, I say, so many ornaments, so much zeal of nations, so many just desires of kings, such holy and pious vows of a most loving father, such joys of the fatherland, such ample hopes, and such great expectation of the world were suddenly cut short by a hurried death. With a too-cruel example, it taught that no mortal is so close to the inhabitants of heaven as to not be a bubble. 

But it is high time that, having left these things behind, I return to the business I have undertaken.
