Let my discourse return to its path, lest anyone should justly be able to claim that I am delivering a funeral oration in the middle of a collection of adages. Although I see that Pliny frequently digresses into such topics for the sake of providing pleasure to the reader, in my case, it was grief that drove me somewhat off-course from my purpose; it was not the allure of the subject that enticed me.

<margin>49</margin>
->Best not to be born.<-

Pliny the Elder <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of the *Natural History*.</note> employs this most elegant sentiment, celebrated in the literature of all nations, in the preface to his seventh book. There, after collecting the innumerable dangers of our birth and the inconveniences of our life, he concludes: "And so there have been many who judged it best not to be born, or to be abolished as quickly as possible." Marcus Tullius Cicero writes that this saying originated from Silenus <note>In Greek mythology, Silenus was a wise satyr and companion to Dionysus. When captured by King Midas, he reportedly offered this pessimistic wisdom as his secret.</note>; Cicero expressed it thus in his book *On Consolation*, as witnessed by Lactantius <note>Lactantius was an early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) often called the "Christian Cicero."</note>: "Not to be born is by far the best, and not to fall upon these rocks of life; the next best, however, if you are born, is to die as soon as possible, and to escape the violence of fortune as if from a fire." The same Lactantius cites these two Greek six-foot verses, which Athenaeus shows in the third book of the *Deipnosophists* to belong to the comic poet Alexis:

Not to be born is always best for man,
But if one is born, to pass the gates of death as quickly as possible.
<note>original Greek: "Τὸ μὴ γενέσθαι μὲν κράτιστόν ἐστ’ ἀεὶ, / Ἐπὰν γένηται δ’, ὡς τάχιστ’ εἶν πύλας."</note>
That is:
It is best never to have come forth into the breezes;
The next best is to be abolished immediately once you are born.

<margin>He also brings forward Theognis.</margin>
For mortals, it is best of all not to be born,
Nor ever to see the rays of the piercing sun,
But once born, to pass through the gates of Hades as quickly as possible.
<note>original Greek: "Ἀρχὴν μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον, / Μηδ’ ἐσιδεῖν αὐγὰς ὀξέος ἠελίου, / Φύντα δ’ ὅπως ὤκιστα πύλας ἀίδαο περῆσαι." Theognis was a 6th-century BC Greek elegiac poet known for his gnomic (proverbial) wisdom.</note>
That is:
Not to be born at all is the primary thing for mortals, and
Never to behold the sun's grim light;
But when you are born, to visit the spirits of the dead as soon as possible.

<margin>It is also cited from Euripides.</margin>
I say that which is whispered everywhere 
Is best for a mortal: never to be born.
<note>original Greek: "Ἐγὼ τὸ μὲν δὴ πανταχῆ θρυλλουμένον / Κράτιστον εἶναί φημι, μὴ φῦναι βροτῶ."</note>
That is:
I think that what is celebrated everywhere is a true saying:
For a man, the absolute best is not to be born.

Menander harmonizes with this:
He whom the gods love dies young.
<note>original Greek: "ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλοῦσιν ἀποθνήσκει νέος." This famous line suggests that a short life is a divine favor to spare one from the miseries of aging and misfortune.</note>
That is:
He whom the gods cherish is taken away as a youth.

There exists an epigram on this sentiment by Posidippus—or, as others prefer, by Crates the Cynic <note>Crates of Thebes (c. 365 – c. 285 BC) was a famous Cynic philosopher who gave away his wealth to live in poverty.</note>—and responding to this from the opposite perspective is one by Metrodorus. Since these are most elegant, I will not be burdened to write them down here. The one by Crates is of this sort:

What path of life should a person cut through? In the forum are
Lawsuits and difficult business. In the home are 
Anxieties. In the fields, toil enough. In the sea, 
Terror. In a foreign land, if you have something, there is fear;
If you are in want, it is distressing. Do you have a marriage? You will not 
Be free from care. Do you not marry? You live even more lonely.
Children are labors. A childless life is a crippling. Youth is 
Senseless. Gray hairs, in turn, are feeble.
There was then a choice of one of two things: either 
Never to be born, or to die immediately upon being born.
<note>original Greek: "Ποίην τις βιότοιο τάμοι τρίβον;.." This poem systematically lists the hardships of every possible social status or stage of life to argue that life itself is undesirable.</note>

I have translated this off-hand, after a fashion, as follows:
What path of human life would you desire to enter upon?
Whichever way you turn, all things are full of evils.
The forum rings constantly with troublesome lawsuits and cases.
Perpetual anxiety tortures you at home.
The grim countryside kills with unceasing labors; if you plow 
The waves and the straits, a thousand dangers press upon you.
Living abroad, if you have ample resources,
You will fear everything, wretched, nor will you live safely.
On the other hand, if your purses hang empty of money,
How hard and miserable it is for a man to be an impoverished guest.
Do you seek marriage? How much care will follow you here?

You will be lonely if you are without a spouse.
If you raise children, they must be brought up with great labor.
Will you not raise them? A life without children lacks light.
If you are young, youth is wandering and ill-advised.
Gray old age is exhausted of its own strength.
Therefore, what remains, I ask, except to wish for one of two things:
Either never to have emerged from the sorrowful bounds
Of the mother's womb, or as soon as you have
Departed from there, to be hidden away in the depths of the Styx? <note>original: "Stygias abdier in latebras". The Styx was the river of the underworld in Greek mythology, here used as a metaphor for death.</note>

<margin>Metrodorus has a different view on this matter:</margin>
Traverse every path of life. In the marketplace there are 
Honors and wise dealings, and at home there is
Rest. In the fields is the grace of nature, and on the sea is
Profit. In a foreign land, if you have something, there is fame.
If you are in need, you alone know it. If you have a wife, the home will be
Best. If you do not marry, you live more lightly.
Children are a longing. A childless life is free from care. Youth is
Strong, but white hair is conversely pious.
Therefore, there is no choice between two evils: either never to be 
Born, or to die. For all things in life are good.
<note>original: "Παντοίην βιότοιο τάμοις τρίβον..." This is a famous Greek epigram by Metrodorus, written as a direct rebuttal to a pessimistic poem by Posidippus which argued life was nothing but suffering.</note>

If the assembly and the forum please you, from here most fertile

Well; conversely, there is a quiet life at home.

That a father's offspring usually brings to him.
Just as strength and vigor are constant in the bloom of youth,

Therefore, I see no reason why you should wish for one of two things:
Either never to be born, or to have perished immediately.
Since, indeed, what portion of human life is there
That is not to be wished for and loved for its own goods?

There also exists a poem by Ausonius <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 AD), a Roman poet and statesman.</note> on this sentiment that is not inelegant, in which, after collecting all the evils of this life, he concludes in this manner:

In this opinion, the Thracians also seem to have been, whose custom it was to follow those born into the light with tears, but the dead with banquets and dances. # THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

then he must endure it, having entered into life. On the other hand, they carry out the deceased man with play and joy, recounting from how many evils he has been rescued. Plutarch, in his essay *On Listening to the Poets*, cites these six-line verses from some tragic poet, which Aristides, in his work *Themistocles*, teaches are by Euripides:

Mourn the man for all the evils into which he enters,
But him who has died and ceased from labors,
Escort from the house with joy and good words. <note>original: "τὸν φῶτα θρηνεῖν..." / "Plorare natum..."</note> -> that is, <-

The ancients felt that human life is inherently miserable and calamitous. Hence Homer everywhere calls them "wretched mortals." <note>original: "ὀϊζυρὸς βροτοὺς"</note> And Virgil, emulating him, wrote:
<margin>The first flies.</margin>
The best day of life is the first to flee for wretched mortals. <note>original: "Optima quaeque dies miseris mortalibus aevi / Prima fugit." from Virgil's Georgics.</note>

Menander speaks elegantly in Plutarch’s little book *On Tranquility of Mind*:

Because the life of man is, by its very nature, liable to many troubles. Nor is Plautus without wit in his play *The Bacchides*:
To have lived is much better than to live.

### As if in a mirror. As if in a picture.

These are also proverbial hyperboles: "just as in a mirror" and "just as in a painting." <note>original: "καθάπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ, καὶ ὥσπερ ἐν γραφῇ"</note> They are used for something that is exceedingly evident and clear. Terence says in *The Brothers*: "Finally, I bid you look into the lives of all as if into a mirror." Plato, in the tenth book of *The Laws*, says: "as if in mirrors." <note>original: "ὡς ἐν κατόπτροις"</note> This is because among many things that reflect the images of objects—such as water, polished bronze, or certain gems—nothing renders a likeness as clearly as glass coated with lead. For glass, which among many substances is most capable of receiving images, does not actually hold them because of its transparency; therefore, the lead spread underneath, because of its blackness and natural density, halts the impressed image and does not allow it to slip away. Indeed, images vanish just like a candle's light in the sun whenever they are received in a body that is too thin and transparent, such as air, pure water, crystal, or glass that has not been darkened by placing some object behind it. Conversely, they do not stick in things that are too dense and dark, such as flint or wood. 

Therefore, Nature, the most skillful architect of all things, seems to have fashioned the eye of living creatures after the image of mirrors; for she joined a certain blackness to the back of the transparent part, which, if removed, immediately takes away the faculty of sight. From this it was wisely said: "As the eye is the mirror of art, so is the eye the mirror of nature." This is worthy of wonder: that a mirror not only most clearly represents the images of all things placed before it, but also their distances, colors, and motions—briefly, I might almost say the things themselves more clearly than they are, with this one difference: that it reflects them in reverse. The cause of this is that the appearance <term>species<gloss>The visual 'form' or 'image' believed by ancient scientists to flow from an object to the eye or a mirror.</gloss></term> which flows from a solid body through the air to the surface of the mirror is simple and pure, whence it happens that the back is no different from the front. Our friend Ambrosius Leo of Nola discussed many of these matters very acutely in his *Questions*. Now, the art of painting, having started from humble beginnings, grew to such a level of subtlety that it deceived not only the eyes of men but even birds, making them believe that things were real which were merely painted with colors. <note>Erasmus refers to the famous story of the painter Zeuxis, whose painted grapes were so realistic that birds flew down to peck at them.</note>

# SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
Ll
<meta>catchword: He alone</meta>

<margin>
There is no brine in him. <note>original Greek: Ἅλμη οὐκ ἔνεστιν αὐτῷ</note>
</margin>

### No saltiness is in him.
-> LI <-

There is no saltiness in him. This is said of the unrefined, the foolish, and the stupid. Salt is seen as the first and most common seasoning of all. Pliny, in his thirty-first book, indicates that this metaphor is taken from the use of salt, which serves as a seasoning in all foods and invites an appetite. "Therefore, by Hercules," he says, "human life cannot endure without salt; it is such a necessary element that the term has even passed over to the pleasures of the mind." For indeed, all the charm of life, the highest cheerfulness, and rest from labor are called "salts" <note>Latin: *sales*</note>; there is no word that captures this better. From this we get "unsalted" <note>Latin: *insulsa*</note> speech, which has no charm, and an "unsalted" man, whose manners are inelegant. Conversely, a "salty" <note>Latin: *salsum*</note> remark is one that bites with a certain sharpness. They also call festive and clever sayings "salts," which possess a certain seductive sting. Seneca does not want our "salts" to be "toothed" <note>meaning overly aggressive or biting</note>. Quintilian, in the sixth book of his *Institutes*, in the chapter on laughter, says: "In common usage, we take 'salty' to mean only 'funny.' Nature, however, does not necessarily intend this, although funny things ought to be salty. For Cicero says that everything salty belongs to the Athenians, not because they are the most inclined to laughter." And Catullus, when he says,
> There is not a grain of salt in so large a body,
does not mean there is nothing funny in her body. "Salty" will therefore be that which is not "unsalted"—like a simple seasoning of speech that is perceived by a hidden judgment and, as it were, excites the palate, defending the speech from boredom. Indeed, just as salt sprinkled a bit more liberally on food (if not excessive) brings its own pleasure, so too these "salts" in speaking have something that makes us thirsty to listen. Thus far Quintilian. Furthermore, the poem by Catullus that Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> cites goes like this:
> Quintia is beautiful to many; to me she is fair, tall, 
> And straight: these individual points I too admit.
> But that she is "beautiful" as a whole, I deny; for there is no charm, 
> No grain of salt in so large a body. <note>original: "Quintia formosa est multis..."</note>
In this place, a commentator on Catullus most foolishly criticizes Quintilian, as if he had not weighed the poet's words carefully, when the commentator himself was dozing and failed to weigh Quintilian's words. For Quintilian denies that everything called "salty" is necessarily "funny," even if the unlearned use the word that way in common speech. Terence alluded to this adage in *The Eunuch*: "A man who had the salt that is in you," wishing to imply the soldier was foolish and tasteless; later, with similar irony, he attributes "Athenian eloquence" to him. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Second Philippic*: "But you even wanted to be witty in a certain place. How little, good gods, did that suit you! In which there is no fault of yours: for you could have drawn some salt from your actress-wife." By "salt," he meant festivity. This is recorded by Diogenianus and Zenodotus.

---

<margin>
He is pungent. <note>original Greek: δριμὺς ἐστὶν</note>
</margin>

### He has vinegar in his breast.
-> LII <-

To this, the line from Plautus’s *Bacchides* is a twin: "Now I shall test whether you have sharp vinegar in your heart." It is also read elsewhere in the same author: "Does he have any vinegar in his breast?" meaning: "Does he have any sense? Does he have any cunning?" For just as salty things do, so also acidic things please the palate, sharpen it, and stimulate the stomach. Horace, in his *Satires*, used "vinegar" to mean biting wit: "But after the Greek was drenched in Italian vinegar," Persius exclaims. And this very phrase, "to drench in vinegar," has the appearance of a proverb, just like that other one from Horace’s *Satires*:
> Likewise because with much salt
> He rubbed the city down, he is praised on the same page.

---

### He alone is wise.
-> LIII <-

Diogenes Laertius relates that the philosopher Chrysippus was so pleased with himself that, when consulted by someone as to whom he should entrust his son to be instructed in the precepts of philosophy, he replied that the boy should be committed to him. "For if," he said, "I thought anyone else was better than me, I would be studying philosophy with him myself." Hence that Homeric line was commonly tossed about regarding him: that "he alone was wise, while the rest flit about as shadows." This is found in Homer’s *Odyssey*, book 10, concerning the prophet Tiresias, to whom alone Proserpina granted that even after departing this life he should be wise, while the other shades flit about, and they are indeed nothing but shadows:
<margin>
To him even in death Persephone granted a mind, to him alone to be wise; the others flit as shadows. <note>original Greek: Τῷ καὶ τεθνεῶτι νόον πόρε Περσεφόνεια...</note>
</margin>
-> that is, <-
To him, even when extinguished, Proserpina had given a mind,
He alone...

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

LIIII

"That he alone might be wise, while the rest flit about like shadows."
<note>original Latin: *Solus uti saperet, reliquis uolitantibus umbris*</note>
This is also used by Plato as if it were a proverb. From this, we can gather that this line of Homer was one of those many which Macrobius writes were commonly celebrated as adages. Thus, Cato the Elder also pronounced this about Scipio the Younger, as Plutarch relates in his *Precepts of Statecraft*, and again in his *Sayings of the Romans*:
"He alone has understanding, but the others flit about as shadows."
<note>original Greek: οἶος πέπνυται, τοὶ δὲ σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσι</note>
This will be aptly said of those who leave all others behind by such a great distance that the rest seem to be nothing but shadows compared to them—plainly what the Greeks call "nonsense and trifles."
<note>original Greek: λῆρος καὶ φλυαρία</note>

->To skin a skinned dog.<-
"You are skinning a skinned dog."
<note>original Greek: Κύνα δαρδὴν δέρεις</note>
Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> says this is usually said of those who suffer the same things again that once afflicted them. Aristophanes says in *Lysistrata* (for I find this work inscribed with that name):
"According to Pherecrates, to pull the skin from a dog that has already been skinned."
<note>original Greek: Τὸ τοῦ Φερεκράτους κύνα δαρδὴν δέρειν</note>
Diogenianus says it applies to those who take up a task in vain. There are some who think it applies better when someone afflicts one who is already afflicted. It is close to what we have said elsewhere, "to card charcoal,"
<note>original Greek: ἄνθρακα ξαίνειν</note>
that is, "You are skinning a leather bottle," which Aristophanes uses in *The Clouds*.

LV
->One must break through swords and fire.<-
"It is necessary to cast oneself through both swords and fire."
<note>original Greek: Διὰ καὶ μαχαιρῶν, καὶ πυρὸς ῥιπτεῖν δέει</note>
This is used when we indicate that any danger whatsoever must be undergone. Aristophanes in the comedy titled *Lysistrata* says:
"Even if it is necessary, I am willing to walk through the fire."
<note>original Greek: Κἄν με χρὴ διὰ τοῦ πυρὸς ἐθέλω βαδίζειν</note>
And Terence says that a parasite <note>a social climber who trades wit for meals</note> would not be reluctant even to snatch food from the flame. A comedy mocked the flatterers of Callias, saying: "That neither fire, nor iron, nor bronze could stop them from frequenting a dinner." <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐ πῦρ, οὐ σίδηρος, οὐδὲ χαλκὸς ἀργὸς μὴ φοιτᾶν ἐπὶ δεῖπνον</note> Plutarch cites these lines from Eupolis. He reports the same in his essay *On the Difference Between a Flatterer and a Friend*. Horace likewise says:
"Fleeing poverty through the sea, through rocks, through fires, the tireless merchant runs to the farthest Indies."
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, asks: "What flame is there through which those would not have run who once collected these things point by point?" That is, what did they not either do or endure?

LVI
->I will not attack with the tongue.<-
"I will not attack with the tongue."
<note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἐπιγλωττήσομαι</note>
The novelty of the figure of speech seems to have passed into a proverb, according to Diogenianus. Aristophanes in *Lysistrata* writes:
"But I shall by no means attack the Athenians with my tongue."
<note>original Greek: πόθεν οὖν Ἀθηναίων γ’ ἂν οὐκ ἐπιγλωττήσομαι</note>
Hesychius cites Aeschylus in *The Children of Heracles*. To the Greeks, "to tongue-attack" <note>original Greek: ἐπιγλωττᾶσθαι</note> is to set upon someone with verbal insults—as if you were to say "to in-tongue," just as we say "to invade" from the word for "palm" <note>referring to the Latin *vola*</note>. More properly, however, it pertains to those who give bad omens. For words are snatched up as omens, as if they were a prophecy of future evil or good. Hence, one must always refrain from curses. Pindar, in the fourth *Pythian Ode*, praises among other virtues a tongue that refrains from curses: "Depriving an evil tongue of its bright voice."
<note>original Greek: ὀρφανίζειν κακὰν γλῶσσαν φαεινᾶς ὀπὸς</note>
A commentator cites a poem of Hesiod on this sentiment:
"Do not be used to contending with companions, whether good or bad."
<note>original Greek: Μηδὲ κακῷ ἑτάρῳ, μὴ δ’ ἐσθλῷ νικητῆρα</note>
It will be useful when we wish to indicate that we do not want to speak about some dangerous matter, such as the affairs of princes or powerful men: "I will not attack with the tongue." The word is derived from the fact that those who speak recklessly are said to speak "whatever comes to the tongue," as we have shown elsewhere.

LVII
->Sand without lime.<-
As Suetonius is the authority, the Emperor Caligula was so pleased by a certain heat and force in speaking that he [said] Seneca...
<meta>The text cuts off here, with the catchword "ut Seneca" indicating the next page continues Caligula's critique of Seneca's disjointed writing style.</meta>

<summary>This page covers proverbs regarding intellectual superiority, redundant suffering, the bravery required to face extreme danger, and the cautious use of speech to avoid bad omens or political trouble.</summary>
<keywords>Homer, Plato, Scipio, skinning a dog, fire and swords, omens, Pindar, Caligula, Seneca, ancient rhetoric, Greek idioms</keywords>

--- Page 561 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of Greek and Latin adages. It concludes a critique of Seneca's literary style by the emperor Caligula before moving into several adages concerning frustration, soft-natured people, political deceit, and social hierarchy.</meta>

...as Seneca’s oratory was often called "sand without lime" <note>original Latin: *sine calce arenam*</note> by Caligula, as if it were disjointed, lacking in vigor and that structural order which acts as the binding for an entire speech, arranging every detail in its proper place. Although Caligula gave many proofs of an unsound mind, in this particular judgment he did not miss the mark by much. Seneca is said to be carried away by a certain impulse, paying very little attention to structure. This is a flaw he possesses among his otherwise excellent virtues. For sand sticks together poorly unless you mix in lime. Close to this is what was said in another place: "a disjointed broom." <note>original Latin: *scopae dissolutae*</note>

### The wolf gapes.
->LVIII<-

<term>The wolf gapes</term> <note>original Greek: Λύκος ἔχανον</note>. That is, "the wolf stands with its mouth open." This was said whenever someone left a situation frustrated after having hoped for much and desired much. For they say that a wolf, gaping for its prey, runs with its mouth wide open; if it is frustrated in its catch, it wanders about still gaping. Aristophanes says in *Lysistrata*:
<term>Nothing is as untrustworthy and safe as a gaping wolf.</term> <note>original Greek: οὐκ πίσον ὅδε, ἀτὰρ λύκῳ κεχηνότι</note>

As Lucian says in *The Cock*: <term>I was entering, and I had almost come away like a gaping wolf.</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ἔλαθον ἔν, μάτην λύκῳ κεχανὼν παρὰ μικρὸν</note> Dionysius the Sophist says in a certain letter: <term>Have I perhaps unwittingly fallen into the proverb and become like a wolf gaping in vain before a deaf man?</term> <note>original Greek: ἆρα μὴ λέληθα ἐμαυτὸν εἰς παροιμίαν ἐλθὼν, καὶ γέγονα λύκῳ χανὼν παρὰ κωφῷ</note> In the fourteenth book of Athenaeus, these lines are cited from Eubulus:
<term>Hurry, hurry, lest like a gaping wolf,</term>
<term>Frustrated by these things, you run for a long time hereafter.</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπῇ' ὑπῇχ', μηποθ' ὡς λύκων χανὼν / Καὶ τῷ δ' ἁμαρτὼν, ὑστέρου συχνὸν βοαμῆς</note>

### An Acarnanian piglet.
->LIX<-

<term>An Acarnanian piglet</term> <note>original Greek: Χοιρίσκος Ἀκαρνανίος</note>. This was said of someone soft, lovable, and kept as a darling. Lucian says in his *Dialogues of the Courtesans*: <term>For they tell me Chaereas is gentle, like an Acarnanian piglet.</term> <note>original Greek: λέγειν γάρ μοί φασι Χαιρέας, καὶ χοιρίσκος Ἀκαρνανίος</note> I believe this is an allusion to the piglet introduced by Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*, which serves as a symbol for those body parts used in obscene pleasures. <note>In Greek, the word for "piglet" was a common slang term for female genitalia.</note>

### A Megarian trick.
->LX<-

<term>A Megarian trick</term> <note>original Greek: Μεγαρικὰ μηχανὴ</note>. It is called a "Megarian device" or "artifice" when a matter is handled with deceit and craftiness rather than sincere faith. For long ago, the Megarians had a bad reputation among the common people as being fraudulent and fake, because they were accustomed to thinking one thing while saying another, as the commentator on Aristophanes indicates. This six-foot line is cited in the *Suda* <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>:
<term>But I have a certain Megarian trick.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ἔστι γάρ μοι Megarica τις μηχανή</note>

This is found in the play by Aristophanes titled *The Acharnians*. The pottery vessels of the Megarians are also celebrated; see whether the proverb might look toward this. Furthermore, it is well known that Euclid the Socratic was a Megarian, and he founded the Megarian school. He was a famous designer of machines. It is possible that the adage arose from this. Additionally, there is a city of the same name in Pontic Thessaly, and "Thessalian figments" have been discussed elsewhere. We will mention "Megarian Sphinxes" later.

### One servant excels another, one master another.
->LXI<-

<term>One servant excels another, one master another</term> <note>original Greek: Δοῦλος πρὸ δούλου, δεσπότης πρὸ δεσπότου</note>. 
> One servant is better than another, and one master better than another.

This is a proverbial verse, advising us that within the same class of men, not everyone is immediately equal; rather, one must take account of the individuals themselves, not just their social status. Just as a nobleman surpasses a commoner by his very birth, there is also no small difference between one nobleman and another, or between one commoner and another, so much so that you might prefer certain commoners to some of noble birth. Aristotle says in the first book of his *Politics*: <term>Some tasks are more necessary, others more honorable, and as the proverb says:</term>
<term>One servant excels another, one master another.</term>

### Daedalian works.
->LXII<-

<term>Daedalian works</term> <note>original Greek: Δαιδάλεια ποιήματα</note>. These are said to be works manufactured with a new and marvelous artistry. This arose because when those ancient sculptors were fashioning the "blind" <note>stiff or expressionless</note> forms of animals and—

<keywords>Seneca, Caligula, literary style, frustration, wolves, Acarnania, Megarian tricks, deceit, Euclid of Megara, Aristotle, social hierarchy, Daedalus, Greek proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of classical proverbs, specifically focusing on the legendary craftsmanship of the inventor Dædalus and the social observation that similar people—especially those with shared vices—recognize and associate with one another.</meta>

# ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...and immobile, Dædalus, with unusual skill, was the first to both introduce eyes and, by adding certain sinews, caused them to move here and there; he did this so skillfully that they seemed to the spectators to be alive and walking. Hence, they say that certain statues of Dædalus must be bound by the feet lest they flee. Plato mentions this in the *Meno* with these very words: <note>original Greek: ὅτι τοῖς Δαιδάλου ἀγάλμασιν οὐ προσέσχηκας...</note> "Because you have not paid attention to the statues of Dædalus; or perhaps they are not found among you. But why do you say this? Because even these, if they are not bound, run away and escape, but if they are bound, they stay put. What then? To possess one of his works that is unbound is not worth much more than possessing a runaway slave, for it does not stay with you. But if it is bound, it is worth a great deal."

He records the same in the *Greater Hippias*, speaking as if of things ancient and obsolete: <note>original Greek: εἰ ἄρα νῦν ὦ Ἱππία ὁ Βίας ἀναβιώη...</note> "If indeed Bias <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, known for his wisdom.</note> were to return to life now, O Hippias, he would be a laughingstock among you; just as the sculptors now say of Dædalus: if he were born now and produced such works as those for which he gained his name, he would be ridiculous."

Aristotle also mentions this in the first book of the *Politics* while speaking of slaves, whom he says are nothing other than living instruments. <note>original Greek: Εἰ γὰρ, inquit, ἠδύνατο ἕκαστον τῶν ὀργάνων...</note> "For if," he says, "it were possible for every instrument, either at a command or by sensing it in advance, to perform its own work—just as they say the statues of Dædalus do, or the tripods of Hephaestus, which the poet <note>Homer</note> says entered the divine contest of their own accord—so that combs <note>Weaving tools.</note> might weave by themselves and picks might play the lyre, then architects would have no need for assistants, nor masters for slaves." The passage Aristotle cites is in the eighteenth book <note>The text says "sixth," but the tripods of Hephaestus appear in Book 18.</note> of Homer’s *Iliad*.

He mentions the same in the first book of *On the Soul*, refuting the opinion of Democritus, who believed the soul moves the body because it is moved itself first. He says that Democritus offers something similar to what is found in the works of Philippus the comic poet. For he wrote that a wooden Venus was manufactured by Dædalus which was moved by pouring in quicksilver <note>original Latin: argēto uiuo (mercury)</note>. <note>original Greek: οἷον, inquit, Δημόκριτος, παραπλησίως λέγων...</note> "Just as," he says, "Democritus says, speaking similarly to Philippus the comic teacher: for he says Dædalus made a wooden Aphrodite that moved by pouring in molten silver."

Therefore, the proverb can be adapted to various uses. Either when we wish to signify things finished with extraordinary skill—for Homer calls skillful things "daedala":
> Who knew how to fashion all "daedala" <note>skillful works</note> with his hands.

Likewise, Pindar in the *Olympian Odes*:
> And stories "daedal-ed" <note>crafted/embellished</note> with various lies deceive.

And Virgil calls Circe "daedala" because she turned men into beasts with new and wonderful arts. Moreover, the Greeks call those skilled in polishing a speech <term>logodaedali</term> <note>word-crafters</note>, and those expert in opinions <term>ophiodaedali</term> <note>literally "snake-crafters," likely meaning cunning or devious thinkers</note>. Alternatively, it can be used when we wish to signify the inconstancy and instability of someone. Thus, in Plato’s *Euthyphro*, Socrates says that arguments that do not stand firm seem similar to the works of Dædalus. Euthyphro responds that Socrates is like Dædalus to him, since he does not allow his reasons to stand firm, but constantly refutes and overturns what he seemed to approve just a moment before.

<margin>LXIII</margin>
-> A thief knows a thief, and a wolf knows a wolf. <-
> <note>original Greek: Ἔγνω δὲ φῶρ τε φῶρα καὶ λύκος λύκον.</note>
> A thief recognized a thief, and a wolf a wolf.

Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, also cites this verse among the adages of similarity. For common people who suffer from similar vices love one another, especially thieves. And wolves, gathered like bandits, go on the prowl. We see in some people that love is born immediately because of a secret kinship of dispositions; conversely, hatred arises toward others because of a dissimilarity of nature. Democritus traced all causes of all things to this similarity and dissimilarity—so much so that when asked about a dog always lying on the same side, why it did...

<summary>This page discusses the legend of Dædalus’s moving statues as a metaphor for both technical mastery and unstable logic, then introduces the proverb that like-minded people—particularly those with shared vices—naturally recognize one another.</summary>
<keywords>Dædalus, Plato, Aristotle, Democritus, Homer, craftsmanship, robotics, slavery, ethics, similarity, thieves, wolves, Greek philosophy</keywords>

### SECOND THOUSAND, THIRD HUNDRED
P 2
<meta>catchword: Or thrice</meta>

...when he did this, he replied, <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἔχει τι κεραμεὺς ὅμοιον ἡ κύων</note> "because a dog has something in common with a brick." <note>Erasmus notes Aristotle's mockery of Democritus here; the Greek term *kerameus* usually means 'potter,' but Erasmus's Latin commentary treats it as 'later' or 'brick.'</note> Aristotle narrates this in passing in the second book of the *Magna Moralia*, among the proverbs of similarity, while mocking Democritus. For what does a brick have in common with a dog? Yet, certain doctors are not far removed from Democritus, for at every examination they throw at us I know not what "occult property" of things.

->Earth loves the rain.<-
<margin>LXIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἐρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖα</note> That is: For the earth rejoices in the rain.
This is used whenever someone desires those things which they know to be suitable and beneficial to themselves. Aristotle cites this half-line as a proverb in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, showing that not only is similarity a reconciler of friendship—as among thieves, jackdaws, and wolves—but also that dissimilarity sometimes exists as a cause of goodwill; conversely, similarity can cause hatred. For since the earth is dry by its own nature, it loves the rain; and "potter hates potter," <note>A reference to a famous Hesiodic proverb about professional competition.</note> but the unlearned loves the learned, and the woman loves the man. In the same place, he records that the poet was rebuked by Heraclitus for writing this verse:
<note>original Greek: Ὡς ἔρις ἔκ τε θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἀπόλοιτο</note> That is:
"Would that strife were taken away and left gods and men."
Athenaeus, in his thirteenth book, cites a verse from Euripides:
<note>original Greek: Ἐρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖ’ ὅταν ξηρὸν πέδον</note> That is:
"The earth indeed loves the rain when the ground is arid."
Aristotle, in the eighth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, cites the same sentiment from Euripides, but with the meter disturbed: <note>original Greek: Εὐριπίδης μὲν φάσκων, Ἐρᾷ μὲν ὄμβρου γαῖαν ξηρανθεῖσαν, Ἐρᾷ δὲ σεμνὸς οὐρανὸς πληρούμενος ὄμβρου, πεσεῖν εἰς γαῖαν</note> That is: When Euripides says:
"The earth seeks the rain when it has become parched with thirst,
And the majestic heaven in turn, when it is now filled 
With rain, longs to fall down upon the ground."
He brings this forward to confirm the opinion of those who said—contrary to common proverbs—that dissimilars are sought by dissimilars, and opposites by opposites. For the cold and dry earth seeks the rain, which (according to the nature of the air from which it comes) is hot and moist; and the rain, in turn, seeks the earth.

->Herculean baths.<-
<margin>LXV</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἡράκλεια λουτρά</note> That is: Herculean baths. This was said of excessively hot baths, such as we read the Neronian baths were. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
<note>original Greek: Ποῦ ψυχρὰ δῆτ’ εἶδες ἡράκλεια λουτρά;</note> That is:
"Where indeed have you ever seen cold Herculean baths?"
A commentator adds that the author Ibycus says Vulcan sent up hot baths for Hercules as a gift. And from that, all hot baths began to be called "Herculean," as the same Athenaeus testifies in his twelfth book. Furthermore, Aristotle in the last problem of the twenty-third section of the *Problems*, shows that baths of this kind were held sacred among the ancients, because they arise from sulfur and lightning—things of a fierce nature. Pisander, however, records that Minerva provided a hot bath for the exhausted Hercules. Whence it seems likely to me that the proverb can be rightly used whenever a service is applied a little more carefully to refresh the strength of those fatigued by age or any labor. For Plato, in the sixth book *Of Laws*, calls hot baths <note>original Greek: γεροντικὰ λουτρά</note> "old men's baths," and orders them to be provided for the elderly. Indeed, the ancients used to wash in cold water; hot baths were provided only to the sickly. But in these times, even wagon-drivers and sailors wash in hot baths. And the Germans pass the greatest part of their lives in stove-heated rooms, like fire-bugs. <note>Erasmus uses the term *pyraustae*, insects believed to live in fire.</note> Pindar also mentions these baths in his twelfth *Olympic*: <note>original Greek: θερμὰ νυμφᾶν λουτρὰ βαστάζεις</note> That is: "You frequent the warm baths of the nymphs." This is either because there was a place in that city named "Hot Baths," or because he himself, after many struggles were exhausted in the manner of Hercules, was now refreshed by hot baths, which the nymphs are said to have sent up for Hercules when he was fatigued by his labors. Furthermore, he declares that the human body is greatly restored by hot baths in the fourth *Nemean Ode*: <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ θερμὸν ὕδωρ τόσον γε μαλθακὰ τεύχει γυῖα, ὅσον εὐλογία φόρμιγγι συνάορος</note> That is: "Not even hot water softens and refreshes the limbs as much as praise joined to the lyre."

<margin>LXVI</margin>
### Either thrice six, or three dice.

<margin><note>original Greek: ἢ τρὶς ἕξ, ἢ τρεῖς κύβοι</note></margin> That is: "Either thrice six, or three dice." Whenever we wish to signify that we are risking the ultimate stakes, and intend to either win completely or be utterly defeated, we shall use this adage quite seasonably. It is taken from the ancient game of dice <note>original: *tesserae*</note>, in which the person who threw three sixes (totaling eighteen) surpassed everyone in every way; the one who threw three aces (totaling three) was the furthest from victory. For the ancients were accustomed to using three dice, not two as we do now. Furthermore, they call the throw itself a "die" <note>original: *tessera*</note>, which is sometimes a "full" throw and sometimes "empty." Thus, a throw of three sixes was the luckiest, while a throw of three aces was empty. Julius Pollux mentions this adage in the ninth book of his *On Vocabulary*. Furthermore, that these dice are the same as those the Greeks call *kyboi* <note>original Greek: κύβους</note> is attested by Aulus Gellius in book 1, chapter 20. For a *kybos*, you will say, is a shape squared on every side. Marcus Varro says: "Dice <note>original: *tesserae*</note> are square-shaped things with which one plays on a board, from which they themselves are called *kyboi*." Zenodotus cites this proverb from a play by Pherecrates titled *The Ant-Men*: for it is the closing line of a trochaic poem. Suidas also brings forward Aeschylus from the *Agamemnon*:
> For I shall count my master's fortunes as well fallen,
> Since my beacon-watch has thrown "thrice six" for me.
<note>original Greek: τὰ δεσποτῶν γὰρ εὖ πεσόντα θήσομαι, τρὶς ἕξ βαλοῦσα τῇ ἐμῆς φρυκτωρίας.</note>
It is used by Plato in the last book of the *Laws*: "What then must be done when these things are so? As the saying goes, friends, the matter seems to lie in our midst and in common, and we are willing to risk the whole state for the sake of the whole, either throwing 'thrice six' or 'three dice,' as they say—we must do everything." <note>original Greek: Τί ἐν δὴ ποιητέον... κῂ ὑποκινδυνεύειν πᾶσαν τὴν πολιτείαν... ἢ τρὶς ἕξ, φασὶν, ἢ τρεῖς κύβους βάλλοντας</note> That is: Therefore, when things have reached this point, what do you think should be done, stranger? According to what is commonly said, friends, it has seemed right to us to bring the matter into the public and common interest, and to be willing to undergo the supreme risk for the entire republic, leaving nothing undone, so that we throw either thrice six or three dice.

---

<margin>LXVII</margin>
### What a mouse at Pisa.

<margin><note>original Greek: Ὅσα μῦς ἐν πίσῃ</note></margin> That is: "How much the mouse at Pisa [suffered]," understanding "endured" or something similar. This is said of those who win and obtain their desires, but not without the greatest trouble, nor without great personal disadvantage. Suidas says it arose from a certain athlete, or boxer from Tarentum, who in the Olympic games at Pisa departed as victor only once, and that after receiving many blows. Plutarch, in the fifth commentary of his *Table Talk*, teaches that single combats <note>original Greek: μονομαχίας</note> were customary at Pisa, in which even those who had yielded were afflicted even unto death.

---

<margin>LXVIII</margin>
### A mouse tasting pitch.

<margin><note>original Greek: Μῦς ἄρτι πίσσης γευόμενος</note></margin> That is: "A mouse just now tasting pitch." Some say this is usually said of those who, having previously been somewhat bold and confident, appear plainly timid after getting a "taste" of danger. It is not yet sufficiently clear whether the allegory was transferred from a mouse caught in pitch, as Diogenianus prefers; or from that man whom Herodotus mentions in his first book as being caught in pitch and thus paying the penalty; or from that Tarentine boxer mentioned just now, so that in "Pisa" there is a pun <note>Erasmus notes the similarity between *Pisa*, the city, and *pissa*, the Greek word for pitch.</note> on the name of the city where the contests are celebrated. Theocritus says in his *Idylls*:
> But now at last, like a mouse, they say, Theonyche, we have tasted pitch.
<note>original Greek: Νῦν δὲ πόθ' ὡς μῦς, φαντὶ, θεώνυχε, γεύμεθα πίσσης.</note>
Furthermore, whether you refer it to the animal or to the boxer named "Mouse," the meaning of the adage remains roughly the same: namely, that an experiment has turned out badly. For if an inexperienced mouse ever falls into pitch, it either dies or struggles out with difficulty, and thereafter, mindful of the danger, it fears to touch it. Likewise, a boxer, previously fierce and boastful, as soon as he has experienced the Olympic contest and felt how much the victory cost him, thereafter abstains. Horace’s line looks toward this:
> Service to a powerful friend is sweet to the inexperienced; 
> He who has tried it fears it.
<note>original: *Dulcis inexpertis cultura potentis amici, / Expertus metuit.*</note>
In the same way, young men inexperienced in wars easily undertake war. Old men, having experienced how great a train of evils war drags with it, dread it. Therefore, it will be said not unseasonably of one who regrets an experiment, or who shrinks from attempting again a matter that was tried with little success. It is related to those things said elsewhere: "The Phrygians learn wisdom too late," and "The Cumaeans learn wisdom too late," and "The fisherman, once stung, will be wise." However, this is one particular plague of mortal life: that we do not learn to beware of evil as much as we learn to cure it once it has been admitted. Plato complains of this in the tenth book of the *Laws*: "Would that we, O children, did not turn toward unjust things as wanderers, but rather were disciplined before we suffered." <note>original Greek: ὡς αἴθ' ὑμᾶ ὦ παῖ τὰ ἄδικα βρεπόμεθα οἱ πλάνοι, φθάσαντες ἢ ἐξ ἀκαθεῖ πεζώμεθα.</note> That is: We do not apply ourselves to this...

<summary>This page explores proverbs regarding high-stakes risks (using the metaphor of ancient dice games) and the caution learned through painful experience (using the "mouse in pitch" metaphor). Erasmus draws connections between Greek athletics, classical literature, and the universal human tendency to only value wisdom after suffering.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on proverbs related to prudence and human behavior. The previous page ended with a discussion on the importance of avoiding wrongdoing rather than seeking remedies after the fact, citing a sentiment common in ancient comedy.</meta>

...most of us take care not to commit injustices, but rather seek to apply a remedy after we have done them. And yet, according to Plautus, it is much better by far not to commit an evil than to heal it once it has been admitted.

### The Delphic sword.
->LXIX<-

<note>original Greek: Δελφικὸν ξίφος</note>, that is, the **Delphic sword**. This was said of a thing that could be adapted to various uses. Just as the same vessels might be used in place of cups at banquets and in place of shields in wars. For the Delphic sword was manufactured in such a way that they might simultaneously slaughter sacred victims with it and inflict punishment upon criminals. Mention of this sword is made both by Euripides in his tragedies and by Aristotle in the first book of the *Politics*. Aristotle argues that nature does not produce individual things for multiple uses, but each for its own peculiar and proper end: <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ τοιοῦτον, οἷον χαλκοτύποι μάχαιραν Δελφικὴν πενιχρῶς, ἀλλ’ ἓν πρὸς ἕν</note>, that is, "For nature makes nothing of such a kind as coppersmiths make the Delphic sword, as if out of poverty, but rather one thing for one purpose." He mentions the same thing in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, discussing the tongues of insects which perform several functions, serving at once for tasting food, drawing it in, and defending against injuries like a sting. He denies that nature does this unless compelled by necessity <note>term: *inopia*—poverty or lack of resources</note>, so as to adapt the same instrument to dissimilar uses, since a very sharp tool seems more fit for defense, and a spongy one for tasting. "For where," he says, "it is possible to use two things for two tasks, and nothing else stands in the way, nature is not accustomed to doing anything such as the craft of the brazier does out of necessity, when it composes a **spit-lamp** <note>term: *obeliscoflychnium*—a combined roasting spit and lamp-stand</note> from a spit and a lamp. Nevertheless, if that cannot be done, she employs the same thing for multiple tasks." From this, it seems to me that the **spit-lamp** would fit the proverb more delightfully than the **Delphic sword**, unless perhaps this very item is the Delphic sword. Likewise, Euripides says in the *Orestes*: <note>original Greek: Θανεῖν γὰρ αὐτῷ μοῖρα Δελφικῷ ξίφει</note>, that is:
> For it is his fate to die by a Delphic blade.

The proverb will therefore apply either to the poor, who due to their need adapt the same garment or any other thing to various uses; or to a faulty prologue <note>gloss: a literary introduction</note> that is applicable to diverse cases. It will also be possible to adapt the proverb to a serious sense, as if someone were to call **erudition** a "Delphic sword," because it is of use in every age and every condition of life. For letters <note>gloss: literature and learning</note> are necessary for the young and pleasant for the old; they provide wealth to the poor and add ornament to the rich; they are a solace in adversity and a glory in prosperity; they increase the splendor of those born to a noble line, and they win the beginning of fame for those born to an obscure family.

### Before you begin, deliberate.
->LXX<-

**Before you begin, deliberate; but when you have deliberated, there is need for timely action.** Aristotle refers to this Sallustian sentiment <note>note: referring to the Roman historian Sallust</note> as a proverb in the fifth book of the *Eudemian Ethics* and the sixth of the *Nicomachean Ethics*: <note>original Greek: καὶ φασὶν πράττειν μὲν δεῖν ταχὺ τὰ δόξαντα, βουλεύεσθαι δὲ βραδέως</note>, that is, "And they say indeed that what has been decided must be done promptly, but one should deliberate slowly and hesitantly." Diogenes Laertius makes Bias the author of this saying. We have spoken more copiously on this sentiment under the proverb **make haste slowly** <note>original: *festina lente*</note>. Datames is praised by this name in the writings of Aemilius Probus <note>note: Erasmus refers to Cornelius Nepos</note>, because once he had thought a thing through, he dared to perform what he had conceived, being accustomed to think before he made an attempt.

### Margites.
->LXXI<-

Lucian used the name **Margites** to mean a stupid person in his *Hermotimus*: <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οἴει μαργίτῃ τινὶ διαλέγεσθαι</note>, that is, "But do you think you are talking to some Margites?" Homer describes him thus, as cited by Aristotle in the sixth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*:
> The gods of the divine ones willed him to be neither a digger,
> Nor a plowman, nor in any other thing
> Skilled or distinguished.

Suidas teaches that Margites was a certain man famous for his signal stupidity, who was unable to count above five; he did not dare to touch his own bride, fearing she would accuse him to his mother. When he had already become a young man, he asked his mother whether he had been born of the same father. Although some attribute these stories to Melitides and others to Coroebus (about whom we shall speak in their proper place), it appears clearly enough that the word is fashioned from "not" and "work" <note>original: *me* and *ergon*</note>, because he was useful for no action. Moreover, *Margites* was the title of a work that was attributed by some to Homer; that work, as it seems, has been lost <note>meta: catchword *intercidit*</note>.

<keywords>Delphic sword, Aristotle, Euripides, deliberation vs. action, Sallust, Margites, Homer, stupidity, versatility, education</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs, moving from the concept of utility and "unlucky numbers" to the irreversibility of time, the comprehensive nature of justice, and the practical difficulties of maintaining a lie.</meta>

...fell away. The commentator on Aristophanes’s play *The Birds* points this out. It agrees with that saying of Hesiod: **Useful in no way**, referring to one who neither has wisdom themselves nor obeys others; and also: **Of no account**.

<margin>LXXII</margin>
->What has been done cannot be undone.<-

Nothing is more common than this sentiment: **What has been done cannot be undone**. It appears in Terence’s play *Phormio*. Aristotle, in the fifth book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, writes: <note>original Greek: ἡ γυνὴ οὐκ ἐνδέχεται μὴ γεγονέναι</note>, that is, "It is impossible for that which has happened not to have happened." Soon after, he quotes a verse from a tragedy by Agathon:
<note>original Greek: μόνου γὰρ αὐτοῦ καὶ θεὸς στερίσκεται, ἀγένητα ποιεῖν, ὅσσ’ ἂν ᾖ πεπραγμένα</note>
Which means:
"For of this alone is even God deprived:
To make undone the things that once were done."
In Cicero’s *Letters to Atticus*, that Homeric verse from the *Iliad* (Book 18) is used more than once:
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν προτετύχθαι ἐάσομεν, ἀχνύμενοί περ</note>
Which means:
"But these things, though they grieve us, we shall let pass as done."
Nor is the poem of Phocylides <note>An ancient Greek gnomic poet known for his maxims</note> without wisdom:
<note>original Greek: Μηδὲ πρὸς χρομένοισι κακοῖς τρύχου σὸν ἦτορ. οὐκ ἔτι γὰρ δύναται τὸ πετυγμένον εἶν’ ἀτυχον</note>
Which means:
"Do not wear out your heart over evils already passed,
For what is once done can never be made undone."
Pindar holds the same view in his second *Olympian Ode*:
<note>original Greek: τῶν δὲ πεπραγμένων ἐν δίκᾳ τε καὶ παρὰ δίκαν, ἀποίητον οὐδ’ ἂν χρόνος ὁ πάντων πατὴρ δύναιο θέμεν ἔργων τέλος</note>
Which means:
"Of things that have been performed, whether justly or unjustly, not even Time, the father of all things, could make them undone once the deed has reached its end."

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
->Justice contains every virtue within itself.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πᾶσ’ ἀρετ’ ἔστιν</note>, that is:
**Justice contains every virtue within itself.**
Aristotle records this verse as a proverb in several places, including the fifth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*. It actually appears in the elegies of Theognis. Chaeremon <note>A minor Greek tragic poet</note> attributes the sum of all goods to **prudence** <note>term: *prudentia*—here meaning practical wisdom or "good sense"</note>. This little verse of his is cited by the Greeks:
<note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ φρονῶν εὖ, πάντα συλλαβὼν ἔχει</note>, that is:
"He who thinks rightly possesses all things gathered together."
Socrates also believed that all virtues were a form of knowledge. Aristotle discusses this in such a way as to admit it is true that no virtue exists without prudence, yet he denies that every virtue *is* prudence, since they are distinct habits of character. But **Justice** is frequently understood not as a specific type of virtue, but as the general category; just as in the Sacred Scriptures, a man is called "Just" who is free from every vice.

<margin>LXXIIII</margin>
->A liar ought to have a good memory.<-

Quintilian, in the fourth book of his *Institutes of Oratory*, cites this sentiment as a proverb: **A liar ought to have a good memory**. Likewise, Apuleius in his *Second Apology for Magic* says: "I have often heard it said, and not for nothing: a liar must be mindful." Saint Jerome also writes: "Forgetting the old proverb: liars must be mindful." The meaning of the adage is clear enough: namely, that it is extremely difficult for someone who lies to remain consistent unless they possess a supreme memory. Moreover, the memory of fabricated things is not a little more difficult than the memory of true ones. Consequently, the **architects of lies** are usually caught in this way: forgetting what they said previously, they say things that contradict their earlier statements. This is how Davus is caught in Terence’s plays, and how the deception of Psyche is discovered by her sisters in Apuleius's story.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
->A bad man melts with pleasure alongside a bad man.<-

<note>original Greek: Κακὸς κακῷ γὰρ συντέτηκεν ἡδονῇ</note>, that is:
**For indeed, a wicked man is a pleasure to a wicked man.**
This is cited by Aristotle among the proverbs concerning similarity in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*:
A bad [man...]

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient proverbs regarding human character and social relations. # SECOND THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY
<margin>P 4</margin>
<meta>catchword: only</meta>

A bad man is pleasing to another bad man because of their shared vices and fellowship. Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> likewise says:
**Great is the harmony among the effeminate.**
The same sentiment is brought forward from Euripides <note>A famous Greek playwright</note> by Aristotle in his *Great Ethics*. Aeschines, in his speech against Timarchus, also cites this same opinion from the *Phoenissae* of Euripides:
<note>original Greek: ὅστις δ' ὁμιλῶν ἤδεται κακοῖς ἀνὴρ, οὐ πώποτ' ἐρωτῶ, γινώσκων ὅτι τοιοῦτός ἐστιν οἷσπερ ἥδεται ξυνών.</note>
That is:
> Whatever man delights in living with the wicked,
> I never asked about: I know he is of the same sort
> As those with whom he loves to spend his time.

### Friendship is for the stable; happiness for the self-sufficient. LXXVI

Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, relates this sentence as if it were a common saying: that **Friendship belongs to the stable, and happiness to those who are content with their lot.** <note>original Greek: ὀρθῶς λέγεται ὅτι ἡ φιλία τῶν βεβαίων, ὥσπερ ἡ εὐδαιμονία τῶν αὐτάρκων.</note> Friendship is to be won through virtue, not through money or physical beauty. Indeed, if it is won through fleeting things, it must necessarily be fleeting itself. Nothing in human affairs is stable except for virtue alone, which is the only thing not subject to the mockery of fortune. Furthermore, the happiness of a man is not situated in his resources—which do not satisfy the soul's desire, but rather provoke it—but in this: that each man should be satisfied with his own fortune. Aristotle, in the second book of the *Rhetoric*, provides this little verse as an example of a simple and clear sentiment, if one looks closely:
<note>original Greek: οὐδείς φασιν, ὅστις οὐκ ἀεὶ φιλεῖ.</note>
That is:
> No one is a lover, unless he loves forever.
This is supported by that saying of Seneca <note>Roman Stoic philosopher</note>: **A friendship that was able to end was never a true one.**

### Do not rear a lion’s cub. LXXVII

A proverbial sentiment of Aeschylus <note>The "father of Greek tragedy"</note> is recounted by Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
<note>original Greek: οὐ χρὴ λέοντος σκύμνον ἐν πόλει τρέφειν, μάλιστα δὲ λέοντα μὴ 'ν πόλει τρέφειν, ἦν δ' ἐκτραφῇ τις, τοῖς τρόποις ὑπηρετεῖν.</note>
That is:
> One should not rear a lion's cub in the state,
> And especially one should not rear a lion itself there:
> But if one has been reared, one must submit to its ways.
Valerius Maximus <note>A Roman historian known for his collection of anecdotes</note> records this passage in the seventh book, in the chapter "On Wise Sayings." This riddle warns that one should not foster a power that is capable of overwhelming the laws; but if by chance such a person has emerged, it is not in the interest of the Republic to fight him, whom you could not defeat without great harm to the state. **A tyrant must either be endured or not received at all.**

### The one who conjectures well, call him a prophet. LXXVIII

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his work *On Divination*, book two, writes that there is a Greek verse commonly tossed about to this effect: **Call him the best prophet who conjectures well.** Plutarch, however, cites that verse in his booklet *On the Oracles of the Pythia*: <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν εἰκάζων καλῶς, ὃν αὖθ' ὁ τῶν μαντικῶν ἀνηγόρευσεν ἡ προοψία.</note> That is: "The one guessing well, whom the proverb called the best prophet." Although this passage in Plutarch was mutilated and mangled, it can nevertheless be gathered that the poem was of this sort:
<note>original Greek: Μάντις γ' ἄριστος, ὅστις εἰκάζει καλῶς.</note>
And he cites it thus from Euripides in the book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. Cicero also cites it in the seventh book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "I expect the future from you," he says, "**the best prophet.**" Theocritus <note>A Greek pastoral poet</note> alluded to this in *The Fishermen* (if those poems are indeed by Theocritus):
<note>original Greek: ἔστι γ' ἄριστος ἐστὶν ὀνειροκρίτας, ὁ διδάσκαλός ἐστι πῃ ὁ νοῦς.</note>
That is:
> No one
> Interprets dreams better than he who is guided
> By his own mind as his teacher.
The adage warns that foreknowledge of the future is not to be sought from lots or omens, but from **prudence**. For if someone is endowed with prudence, they will easily foresee what is going to happen from conjectures based on the past and the present. Therefore, Aristotle did not write without cause in the seventh book of the *Eudemian Ethics*: <note>original Greek: φρονίμων καὶ σοφῶν τυγχάνειν εἶναι τὴν μαντικὴν, καὶ μάλα.</note> That is: **Prophecy belongs to prudent and wise men, and to them only.**

[only] ... <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on true prophecy as rational foresight.</note> if only. I wish that princes would embrace this method of divination, since today a good part of them depend on prognosticators and astrologers—a race of men, as most are now, equally vain and seditious, and a plague to the Commonwealth.

<margin>LXXIX</margin>
### A tattered rag.

The Greeks call a man who is already an object of disgust and rejection a <note>original Greek: ῥάκος πολυχιδὲς (*rhakos polychides*)</note> **tattered rag**, that is, a cloth torn in every direction. The metaphor is taken from a garment worn out by long use and therefore cast aside, even though it was once highly valued when new. In this same way, some treat their friends as if they were clothes: while they are useful and in their prime, they embrace, care for, and show them off; but as soon as they are either worn down by age or have otherwise ceased to be useful, they neglect and reject them. Lucian <note>A 2nd-century Greek satirist</note> says: "Until, according to the proverb, it has rendered you a **rag torn everywhere** and driven you out." He uses a similar comparison in the same dialogue, namely *On those who serve for hire*, concerning new shoes, which are valued as long as they shine with newness; but once they are fouled with mud, they are tossed away into some corner, where, with no one caring for them, they become filled with decay and bedbugs. Solon <note>An Athenian lawmaker and poet</note> used to say that those who trained for the Olympic games were first expensive and therefore a burden to the Commonwealth; once they had won, they became a detriment to the city because of their pride; and finally, when they grew old, they were at last useless. To express this, Diogenes Laertius cites a line of Euripides:
> With threads loosened, tattered cloaks perish.

<margin>LXXX</margin>
### You have feared an empty fear.

<note>original Greek: Ἀδεὲς δέδιας (*Adees dedias*)</note> That is: **You fear a fear that is not to be feared.** This is used when someone is afraid in a safe situation. Virgil <note>The Roman epic poet</note> writes:
**Fearing all things, even when safe.**
There is also a certain proverbial quality in the very figure of the Greek saying because of its <term>antithesis</term> <note>a contrast or opposition between two things</note>. Just as in these other examples: **giftless gifts**, **an unbound bond**, **a bottomless bottom**, **a brideless bride**, **a gardenless garden**, and others of that kind, about which we have already remarked more than once. The Greeks also say <note>original Greek: μορμολύθη (*mormolythe*)</note> **bogeyman**, for a <term>mormolyceion</term> <note>a mask or "Mormo"</note> is a mask among the Greeks, resembling a ghost or an evil spirit, with which people terrify children. Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great</note> wrote to Athanasius: "Indeed, I would be quite a child if I were terrified by such **bugbears**." This adage is recorded in the collections of Plutarch, if indeed that title is to be trusted.

<margin>LXXXI</margin>
### Sycophant.

<note>original Greek: Συκοφάντης (*Sykophantēs*)</note> **Sycophant**: This title was commonly used as a term of reproach. Aristophanes <note>The Greek comic playwright</note> says in *Plutus*:
> With what a grim face he has entered, O good gods,
> This **sycophant**.
It is a proverbial insult against calumniators <note>those who make false and malicious accusations</note> and those who stir up a lawsuit for even the slightest reason. They believe it originated because, in ancient times among the Athenians, figs were highly valued, and those who stole them were punished. Those who watched for these thieves or reported them began to be called "Sycophants" <note>literally "fig-showers" from the Greek *sykon* (fig) and *phaino* (to show)</note> as a joke. These same people were called <note>original Greek: φιλεγκλήμονας, συκοπίς, συκεράς, συκολόγους, φιλοσύκους, συκώδεις, καὶ συκόπαιδας</note>—to give the sense rather than a word-for-word translation: **those who bring false charges about figs, those who live off figs, fig-wardens, fig-counters, fig-lovers, fig-like, and those who delight in figs like children.** Plutarch, in his essay *On Curiosity*, shows that this name arose because, when a law was passed forbidding anyone to export figs from Athens, certain people reported those they observed secretly exporting them. Hence they were called sycophants in popular jest, because they **revealed the figs**. He mentions this also in his *Life of Solon*. Festus Pompeius points out that among the Athenians, the death penalty was established for those who stole figs. Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician</note> affirms the same in the third book of the *Deipnosophistae*, adding that the place where the fig was first discovered was called the **Sacred Fig** by the Athenians. There is, however, a type of sycophant that reports not only the words and deeds of men, but even their dreams. Constantius <note>The Roman Emperor</note> gave a wide-open ear to such informers, as Ammianus <note>Ammianus Marcellinus, a Roman historian</note> records in his fourteenth book. He was particularly indulgent toward a certain Mercury, who was commonly called "Mercury of the Banquets" because he would mix into feasts under the guise of friendship; if anyone blurted out a dream from the night before, he would report it to the emperor with a twisted narration. Things reached such a point that people almost wished they had been born among the Atlantians, where they say dreams are never seen—a claim also made by Stephanus in his entry...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient Greek and Latin adages. The previous page discussed metaphors for social rejection (the "tattered rag") and the tendency of people to discard friends who are no longer useful.</meta>

...diction <note>original: "dictione"</note> regarding the Atlantes. The Greeks call observers of dreams <note>original: "oneiroscopos"</note>, interpreters of dreams <note>original: "oneiropolos"</note> or <note>original: "oneirocritas"</note>, and those who are terrified by dreams <note>original: "oneiroplectos"</note>.

<margin>LXXXII</margin>
### To outrun by many parasangs.

<note>original Greek: πολλοῖς παρασάγγαις ὑπερδραμεῖν (*pollois parasangais hyperdramein*)</note> This means **To outrun by many <term>parasangs</term>** <note>A Persian unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles or 30 Greek stades.</note>. It is said of someone who precedes another by a long distance or is superior in many respects. It is found in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, c. 200 AD</note> in the third book of the *Philosophers at Dinner*: "Surpassing that Sicilian Dionysius by many parasangs." This is even more charming when applied to matters of the mind. The Persians call a space of thirty stades a parasang, as Herodotus indicates in several places. This word was also used by Lucian in his *Icaromenippus*, a dialogue which I long ago translated into Latin.

<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
### Rotten salt-fish loves oregano.

Clearchus, in the third book of Athenaeus, says:
<note>original Greek: σαπρὸς τάριχος τὴν ὀρίγανον φιλεῖ (*sapros tarichos ten oreganon philei*)</note> That is,
**Rotten salted meats love oregano.**
Oregano is an herb with a sharp juice, similar to savory. Even today, thrifty heads of households add vinegar in place of oregano to meat that is already starting to smell, so that the rotten odor is not noticed. This will be aptly said of a matter that is inherently lacking in honor or pleasantness, and for that reason requires "exotic seasonings" and artificial ornaments. This custom still exists today among the stingy: they mix acids with fish that is beginning to rot, so that the stench does not offend the diners. Truth is pleasing in itself; honorable things are becoming on their own. Lies need makeup; shameful things need finery. That is to say, rotten salt-fish needs oregano.

<margin>LXXXIIII</margin>
### Gredier than the purple murex.

Athenaeus, in the third book of the *Philosophers at Dinner*, records a proverb of this kind from Apollodorus: <note>original Greek: λιχνότερα τῶν πορφυρῶν (*lichnotera ton porphyron*)</note> that is, **More gluttonous than the purple-fish.** He thinks this is derived either from the purple dye, which seems to snatch up everything it is applied to, staining nearby objects with its color and adding brilliance; or from the animal itself, which retains and devours whatever it finds. Both ideas can almost be gathered from the words of Pliny. Indeed, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-six, he writes about the color in this way: "But that flower of the purple, sought after for dyeing clothes, is held in the middle of their throats. Here, in a white vein, is a tiny amount of liquid. From this, the precious dye is 'drunk,' glowing with the color of a dark rose; the rest of the body is useless." And a little later: "For this—or as others read, for him—the Roman bundles and axes <note>The *fasces*, symbols of Roman magisterial power.</note> make a way. This same color signifies majesty in childhood; it distinguishes the Senate from the knights; it is called upon to appease the gods, and it illuminates every garment, mixed with gold in a triumphal robe. Therefore, let even the madness for purple be excused." Regarding its gluttony, he soon adds: "The tongue of the purple-fish is a finger's length, with which it feeds by devouring other shellfish; its sting is of such great hardness." This will suit gluttons, or those who turn everything to their own profit. Perhaps more harshly, but not inelegantly, it will be applied to kings who are <note>original Greek: δημοβόρους (*demoborous*)</note> **devourers of the people**, or to lawyers who, dressed in purple, turn everything into their own coffers and scrape something away wherever they go. The poets seem to have intended something similar when they imagined Midas turning everything to gold by the touch of his body.

<margin>LXXXV</margin>
### The salted small-fry as soon as it has seen the fire.

<note>original Greek: Τάριχος ἄπυος εὐθὺς ἂν ἴδῃ τὸ πῦρ (*Tarichos apyos euthys an ide to pyr*)</note> That is,
**The salted small-fry as soon as it has seen the fire.**
Athenaeus, in his third book, cites this as a proverb. *Tarichos* is salted fish, about which there are several proverbs, such as "If meat is not present." I believe this is the same as that other one: <note>original Greek: ἀφύα εἰς τὸ πῦρ (*aphya eis to pyr*)</note> "The small-fry into the fire," which we have already explained. In the same place, he also records this verse as a proverbial one:
<note>original Greek: οὐκ ἂν πύθοι τάριχος, ᾧ πῦρ ἄξιος (*ouk an pythoi tarichos, ho pyr axios*)</note> That is,
**The salted fish will not endure the heat it deserves.**

<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
### Those who dwell far away are not friends.

<note>original Greek: Τηλοῦ φίλοι ναίοντες οὐκ εἰσὶν φίλοι (*Telou philoi naiontes ouk eisin philoi*)</note> That is,
**He is not a friend, if the friend is far away.**
Athenaeus reviews this proverb in the fourth book of the *Philosophers at Dinner*. He calls it the most <note>original Greek: μισανθρωποτάτην (*misanthropotaten*)</note> **inhuman** or misanthropic of all, because it seems to blot out the memory of absent friends. Certainly, there is a richer fruit of friendship from those who are present, because of mutual services and daily companionship. Furthermore, it commonly happens that as soon as someone is out of sight...

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning vast superiority (measured in Persian parasangs), the use of "seasoning" to hide defects in character or goods, and the voracious greed of the powerful, likened to the purple murex snail. He concludes with a cynical proverb suggesting that distance inevitably ends friendship.</summary>
<keywords>parasang, oregano, purple dye, murex, greed, salt-fish, friendship, Athenaeus, Pliny the Elder, gluttony</keywords>

--- Page 570 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient adages. The top portion concludes a discussion on how physical distance leads to emotional distance, transitioning into three new adages concerning greed, self-inflicted harm, and terms of endearment.</meta>

...from the sight <note>original: "aspectu," partially obscured by page break</note> of those close to us, I know not how a certain forgetfulness of our familiars creeps in, so that it is now on everyone’s lips: **He who is removed from the eyes is also removed from the heart.** Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, admits that separation by location does not actually destroy friendship, but it does interrupt its duties. And since the common people judge friendships by their utility, once the duties—which are like the foster-children of friendship—are removed, friendship itself dies out. Accordingly, Hesiod warns that neighbors especially should be invited to a feast, 

->saying, "Call him who dwells near you." <note>original Greek: Καλεῖν ὃς τις σέθεν ἐγγύθι ναίει (*Kalein hos tis sethen engythi naiei*)</note><-

Even the proverbs of the Hebrews <note>Likely referring to Proverbs 27:10: "Better is a neighbor that is near than a brother far off."</note> admit that it is better to have a friend as a neighbor than a brother who is far away. Likewise, Chremes in Terence <note>A Roman playwright, c. 190–159 BC</note> places neighborliness in a category close to friendship. 

And Propertius <note>A Roman elegiac poet, c. 50–15 BC</note>, in his third book, does not differ from this:

->**As far as he shall go from the eyes, so far will love go from the heart.**<-

However, I personally do not see why it seemed to Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician, author of *The Deipnosophists*</note> that this adage was so utterly devoid of humanity. For, in my opinion, it does not so much teach us what we *should* do, as it warns us what the common crowd *usually* does. How many friends can you find so steadfast that, if you are absent, they do not begin to grow unlike themselves? Therefore, you may use this proverb like a **Delphic sword** <note>original: "Delphico gladio"; a term for a tool that serves two different purposes</note> in whichever way you please: either to understand that one must not trust friends who are separated by a long distance, or that one should not cultivate friends living far away from whom you cannot feel much benefit, but rather those whose presence you can enjoy.

---

<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
### Often he devours the sacred offerings before they are sacrificed.
<note>original Greek: Ἄθυτα δ᾽ ἱερὰ πολλάκις κατεσθίει (*Athyta d' hiera pollakis katesthiei*)</note> That is, 
**Very often he devours the sacred rites before they are immolated.**
This is a six-beat line <note>original: "Senarius"</note> found in the fourth book of Athenaeus, written by Simonides <note>A Greek lyric poet, c. 556–468 BC</note> against a certain ill-mannered and greedy woman at banquets. It will be neatly said of those who, driven by their bellies, immediately burst in to devour the feast without waiting for the ceremonies and "little refinements" <note>original: "elegantiolis"</note> which civilized people use when beginning a banquet—for instance, that the food be consecrated with certain prayers; then, that a certain urbanity and hesitation be used regarding the order of reclining; and further, that we do not thrust our nails into the food as soon as it is served. It is also aptly said of those who seize an inheritance without waiting for the legal process, and occupy another's property by force. The metaphor is drawn from sacrificial victims, which it was not lawful to touch until the mysteries were completed. Even Plato wishes for a libation to be offered to the gods at banquets; and antiquity considered the table a sacred thing, as Plutarch witnesses. Hence it is that even in these times people think it a sin to approach with **unwashed hands.** <note>original Greek: ἀνίπτοις χερσὶν (*aniptois chersin*)</note> However, Christ disregarded ceremonies of this kind in favor of those things which uniquely pertain to our spiritual welfare.

---

<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
### The Chian bought himself a master.
<note>original Greek: Χῖος δεσπότην ὠνήσατο (*Chios despotēn onēsato*)</note> That is, **The Chian purchased a master.** This will apply to those who bring trouble upon themselves. Eupolis <note>An Athenian poet of Old Comedy</note> used this adage in his play *The Friends*, according to Athenaeus in the sixth book of *The Philosophers at Dinner*. He says it arose because the Chians <note>Inhabitants of the island of Chios</note> were the first to establish the use of purchased slaves; later, having been conquered by Mithridates of Cappadocia, they were handed over in chains to their own slaves to be deported to the region of the Colchians. An oracle had once predicted that this would happen to them. As authors of this history, he cites Nicolaus the Peripatetic and Posidonius the Stoic. Nor was Stephanus silent on this: that this nation first used "bought servants" <note>original Greek: ὠνητοῖσι (*onētoisi*)</note>, just as the Spartans used those they called **Helots** <note>original Greek: εἵλωτας (*heilōtas*)</note>, meaning captives; the Sicyonians used those they called **club-bearers** <note>original Greek: κορυνηφόρους (*korynēphorous*)</note> from the club; the Italians used the Pelasgians; and the Cretans used those they call **domestic slaves** <note>original Greek: δμωΐτας (*dmōitas*)</note>. Chios is a very famous Ionian island, having a city of the same name. The possessive form is written with a circumflex: Chian.

---

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
### Soul and life.
<note>original Greek: Ζωὴ καὶ ψυχή (*Zoe kai psyche*)</note> That is, **Soul and life**, said of a matter that is exceedingly sweet. The proverb was born in the bedroom <note>original: "in cubilibus"</note> and from there was brought into common speech. It seems, moreover, to have been peculiar to women. Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist, 1st–2nd century AD</note> says:
> **"Life and soul!"** <note>original: "Ζωὴ καὶ ψυχή"</note> You use these words in public,
> though they were just left under the covers.

Likewise, Martial, in the tenth book of his *Epigrams*, says to Laelia:
> You constantly pile up **"Life and soul"** <note>original: "Ζωὴ καὶ ψυχή"</note> lasciviously,
> For shame! You who are a citizen of Hersilia and Egeria <note>Figures representing traditional Roman virtue</note>.

Juvenal had this in mind when he said:
**They couple in Greek.** <note>original: "Concubunt Graece." Referring to the Roman habit of using Greek for erotic talk.</note>
