# SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

Hesiod says that money is the soul of mortals, <note>original Greek: χρήματα γὰρ ψυχὴ πέλεται δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι (*chrēmata gar psychē peletai deiloisi brotoisi*)</note>
<margin>90</margin>
which means: "For money is the soul for wretched mortals." And Aristotle wrote that money is like a second soul to a man. Moreover, nothing in life is more pleasant or more precious.

### Those who love, fashion dreams for themselves.
Virgil, in his poem *The Sorceress* <note>The *Pharmaceutria*, or Eclogue 8</note>, says:
"Do we believe it, or do those who love fashion dreams for themselves?"
Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> notes that this was spoken proverbially by the poet. For whatever someone hopes for, he easily believes. Conversely, "We are slow to believe what hurts us when believed," as Ovid says. Fear and hope, as Lucian wrote both elegantly and truly in *The False Prophet*, were the inventors of divination and augury. Those who desire something intensely flatter themselves with their own wishes from every side, and twist anything into an omen of their desired outcome. On the other hand, those who are miserably afraid hunt for a remedy for their dread in every little thing. Not entirely different from this is that line from Terence: "It does not seem likely to me; and yet they are pleased with their own fiction." Nor does that line from Theocritus seem foreign to this theme:
<note>original Greek: πᾶσα κύων ἄρτως μαντεύεται, ἰχθύα κἀγώ (*pāsa kyōn artōs manteuetai, ichthya kagō*)</note>
which is: "Every dog dreams of bread, and I dream of fish."
Those who flatter themselves with their own wishes are said by the Greeks "to dream for themselves" <note>original Greek: ἑαυτοῖς ὀνειροπολεῖν (*eautois oneiropolein*)</note>; that is, to interpret their own dreams for themselves, because they seize upon everything to feed their own hope.

### Polyps.
<margin>91</margin>
The word **Polyps** <note>Referring to the octopus</note> was once used proverbially to describe people who were either stupid and dull, or greedy and "hook-fingered." Indeed, they attribute stupidity to the polyp for this reason: because it moves toward the hand of the person trying to catch it, and it is caught only because it does not retreat, according to Athenaeus. However, greed and tenacity are also attributed to it, because whatever it reaches with the lashes of its arms, it draws in and retains by suction. Plautus says in *The Pot of Gold*: "I know those polyps of yours, who hold onto whatever they touch." Nothing, however, prevents us from calling those people "polyps" who turn themselves into every kind of behavior, flattering everyone. Phocylides notes them elegantly:
"Do not hide one thought in your heart while speaking another.
Nor be like the polyp that clings to the rocks, changing according to the place." <note>original Greek: μηδ’ ἑτέρου κεύθῃς κραδίῃ νόον, ἄλλ’ ἀγορεύων. μηδ’ ὥς πετροφυὴς πολύπυς κατὰ χώραν ἀμαξός. (*mēd’ heterou keuthēs kradiē noon, all’ agoreuōn. mēd’ hōs petrophyēs polypus kata chōran amaxos.*)</note>
Ion says in the seventh book of Athenaeus:
"I hate the polyp for its constantly changing color." <note>original Greek: Στυγῶ μεταλλακτῆρα πολύπου χροός (*Stygō metallaktēra polypou chroos*)</note>
To this belongs what Plautus advises: that a wise man should be good to the good, and bad to the bad. On this account, Pindar, in the fourth Nemean hymn, praises a certain man as "soft-hearted toward the good, but a rough adversary to the spiteful." <note>original Greek: μαλθακὰ μὲν φρονέων ἐσλοῖς, τραχὺς δ’ παλιγκότοις ἔφεδρος (*malthaka men phroneōn eslois, trachys d’ paligkotois ephedros*)</note> Not far from this is what he says in the third hymn: "A child among young children, a man among men, and a third part among the elders—whatever our mortal race possesses." Pindar praises a man who tempers himself to all customs and ages. With the same title, he praises someone in the eighth Pythian hymn: "For you know how to act and feel softly alike, at the right time and with virtue." And again in the fourth hymn: "For he was a youth among the young, but an elder in counsel." Likewise, in the second hymn of the same work: "May it be mine to love a friend; but against an enemy, being an enemy, I will run like a wolf, or lie in wait."

### No bad big fish.
<margin>92</margin>
<note>original Greek: οὐδεὶς κακὸς μέγας ἰχθύς (*oudeis kakos megas ichthys*)</note>
That is: **No bad big fish.** This is a proverbial riddle, usually said of people with a very large body but no intelligence. Clearchus, in his commentary on proverbs cited in Athenaeus (book 8), wrote that it originated from this: Stratonicus the cithara-player <note>A musician and wit known for his sharp tongue</note>, when he had seen Porpin the Rhodian cithara-player—a man of huge physical bulk but not equally great in his art—responded to those asking who he was in this manner: "No. Bad. Big. Fish." <note>A pun on the idea that big fish are usually good to eat; here, "bad" implies lack of skill despite the large size.</note>
ancipiti <note>catchword: "ambiguous" or "on both sides"</note>

<summary>This page discusses proverbs related to human psychology and character, specifically how desire fuels self-deception, how the "polyp" symbolizes both grasping greed and social adaptability, and how physical size does not equate to talent.</summary>
<keywords>Hesiod, wealth, self-deception, Virgil, polyps, adaptability, Pindar, Stratonicus, physical bulk vs intelligence</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

...with a double-edged saying, signifying that he was a "nobody"—that is, someone of no value—wicked and dishonest, large of body, and finally a "fish," because he was mute, inarticulate, and a poor singer. Theophrastus, in his work *On Laughter*, admits that this was indeed said by Stratonicus, but not about Porpin; rather, it was aimed at the actor Simylas: *μέγας, ὠδὸς, ἄπυος, ἰχθύς* <note>original Greek: "mégas, ōdós, ápyos, ichthýs"</note>, which means: "A nobody, big, voiceless, a fish." <note>The humor lies in calling a singer "voiceless" and comparing a human to a mute fish.</note> But the version reported by Clearchus is more elegant due to a rather charming ambiguity. In the same passage in Athenaeus, Aristotle recounts a story concerning this adage in his *Constitution of the Naxians*. Among the Naxians, most of the wealthy lived in the city, while the rest were scattered through the villages. In a certain village named Lestadae lived Telegoras, a man of great wealth and nobility who held much authority among the common people. Not only did he receive many honors, but he was especially honored with daily gifts from the citizens; so much so that those selling goods, if a buyer offered less than they wanted, were accustomed to say they would rather give it as a gift to Telegoras than sell it for such a price. Accordingly, some young men were once haggling over a huge fish, and when the fisherman said (as was the custom) that he would rather send it to Telegoras as a gift than sell it for that much, the youths took offense at hearing the same old phrase. With a pretense of goodwill, they bought the fish and brought it to Telegoras. When he had gladly accepted it, they then attacked him and violated his daughters, who were of marriageable age. The Naxians, outraged by this deed, took up arms and attempted to attack the young men. From this, such a great sedition arose that Lygdamis, who was the leader of this tumult, seized the tyranny and oppressed his own country. This is Aristotle’s account. However, I do not see how this relates to the proverb, unless we make two separate proverbs, the second of which would be: "I would sooner give it to Telegoras than sell it for so much." For Athenaeus indicates that Aristotle was indeed discussing a proverb. The line seems to be a senarius <note>A line of six poetic "feet," common in Roman comedy.</note>, though the word order has been disrupted. It will be metrically sound if you read it as: *ὠδὸς μέγας ἰχθὺς κακός* <note>original Greek: "ōdós mégas ichthýs kakós"; "A singer, a great fish, a bad one."</note>.

<margin>93</margin>
->From a sea-onion, no rose is born.<-

Theognis used this proverbial figure when he wrote:
*οὔτε γὰρ ἐκ σκίλλης ῥόδα φύεται, οὐδ’ ὑάκινθος,*
*οὐ δέ ποτ’ ἐκ δούλης τέκνον ἐλευθέριον.* <note>original Greek: "oute gar ek skillēs rhoda phyetai, oud' hyakinthos, / ou de pot' ek doulēs teknon eleutherion"</note>
which is to say:
"For truly from a sea-onion no rose is born, nor a hyacinth;
Nor is a noble son ever born from a slave-woman."
This adage warns us that upright children are born from upright parents, and wicked ones from the wicked. Horace spoke in a similar vein in his *Odes*:
"Nor do fierce eagles
Procreate a timid dove."
It will be even more charming if applied to the unlearned pupil of an unlearned teacher, or the wicked foster-child of a wicked nurse. This adage belongs to the same class as "From a bad crow, a bad egg" <note>original Greek: κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ὠὸν (*kakou korakos kakon oon*)</note>. And also:
"An upright father would not produce a wicked offspring" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἂν γένοιτο χρηστὸς ἐκ κακοῦ πατρός (*ouk an genoito chrēstos ek kakou patros*)</note>, meaning:
"A wicked father will hardly beget an honest child."
The *Scilla* <term>Squill</term> is a type of herb not unlike aloe, about which Pliny writes much in various places. <note>The squill or "sea-onion" was often associated with bitterness or medicinal harshness, contrasting with the beauty of the rose.</note>

<margin>94</margin>
->We cannot all do all things.<-

"We cannot all do all things," from Virgil in his *Pharmaceutria* <note>Eclogue 8</note>. This is a proverbial sentiment; you will hardly find another more common. It seems to be taken from Homer, where, in the thirteenth book of the *Iliad*, Polydamas addresses Hector in this way:
"But you will by no means be able to choose everything for yourself at once.
For to one man God has given the works of war,
To another the dance, to another the lyre and song;
But in the breast of another, wide-seeing Zeus places
A good understanding, from which many men reap the benefit."
Which is to say:
"You will by no means be able to do all things bravely alone.
For the gods have given to some to be powerful in war,
To this one the art of dancing, to that one singing with the voice and lyre.
Again, in the heart of another, wise and great
Jupiter has sowed talent, and that man is useful to many."
Likewise in the eighth book of the *Odyssey*:
"Thus the gods do not give graceful gifts to all
Men—neither physical stature, nor even wit, nor eloquence."

<summary>Erasmus explores the origins of proverbs concerning the impossibility of excellence in all fields and the biological/moral necessity of like producing like, illustrated through the "sea-onion" and various classical anecdotes.</summary>
<keywords>Stratonicus, Naxos, Telegoras, heredity, education, squill, Virgil, Homer, human diversity, Lygdamis</keywords>

# SECOND CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
Q
<meta>catchword: One man</meta>

For to one man God gave a more meager appearance, but God crowns his form with words. <note>original Greek: Ἄλλῳ μὲν γάρ τ' ἔδωκ' ἀκιδνότερον θεὸς ἀνὴρ, ἀλλὰ θεὸς μορφὴν ἔπεσιν στέφει</note>
->that is,<-
The heavenly ones do not grant their gifts to everyone alike, whether it be beauty, or character, or the power of speech. For there is one who happens to have an unattractive appearance, yet God compensates for the lack of beauty with the gift of a tongue. <note>original Latin: Non ita coelestes tribuunt sua dona quibusuis...</note>
Euripides in *Rhesus*:
For he himself understands everything among mortals in one way, but let a different prize be assigned to another. <note>original Greek: Ἄλλως γὰρ αὐτὸς πάντ' ἐπίσταται βροτῶν πέφυκεν, ἄλλῳ δ' ἄλλο προσκείσθω γέρας</note>
->that is,<-
It is not given to any mortal to know all things, but one gift is present to one man, and another to another.
Theognis writes to the same effect:
Virtue and beauty follow few men, and I have received a smaller portion of both. <note>original Greek: Παύροις ἀνθρώπων ἀρετὴ καὶ κάλλος ὀπηδεῖ, ὀλείζω δὲ τούτων ἀμφοτέρων ἔλαχον</note>
->that is,<-
There are few who possess both virtue and wealth. Happy is he to whom these are given together by the lot of the gods.
Titus Livy in Book 22: "The gods did not give all things to the same man. You know how to conquer, Hannibal, but you do not know how to make use of the victory." <note>original Latin: Non omnia eidem dij dederunt. Vincere scis Hannibal, uictoria uti nescis. This famous rebuke was reportedly given to Hannibal by his general Maharbal after the Battle of Cannae.</note> Livy seems to have drawn this from the twenty-third book of the *Iliad*:
Nor was it possible, in any way, for the same man to be skilled in all deeds. <note>original Greek: οὐδ' ἄρα πῶς ἦν, Ἐν πάντεσσ' ἔργοισi δαήμονα φῶτα γενέσθαι</note>
->that is,<-
It never happened that the same man appeared skillful in every action.
To this also pertains that line of Pindar from the *Nemean Odes*:
Different arts to different men. <note>original Greek: Τέχναι δ' ἑτέρων ἕτεραι</note>
->that is,<-
Arts belong to some, and other arts to others.
The commentator shows that this was used among the residents of Attica as a proverb:
Different inventions of different people. <note>original Greek: ἄλλαι δ' ἄλλων ἐπινενοήσεων</note>
->that is,<-
The discoveries of some are different from those of others.
Likewise elsewhere:
We differ by nature, having been allotted a life—this man this kind, and others another. Furthermore, it is impossible for every happiness to happen to one person. <note>original Greek: φυᾷ δὲ ἕκαστος διαφέρομεν, βιοτὰν λαχόντες, ὁ μὲν τὰν, τὰν δὲ ἄλλοι. τυχεῖν δ' ἔν' ἀδύνατον εὐδαιμονίαν ἅπασαν</note>
->that is,<-
We differ by nature as we take up our lot in life; one man takes this, others that. Moreover, it cannot happen that all happiness falls to one man. The same author says in the first *Olympian Ode*:
In different things, different men are great. <note>original Greek: ἐπ' ἄλλοισι δ' ἄλλοι μεγάλοι</note>
->that is,<-
Some are great in some things, others in others.
He says it even more expressly in the eighth *Encomium*:
Different goods have come to different people, but by the favor of the gods, there are many paths to prosperity. <note>original Greek: Ἄλλα δὲ ἐπ' ἄλλου ἔβαν ἀγαθῶν, πολλαὶ δ' ὁδοὶ σὺν θεοῖς εὐπραγίας</note>
->that is,<-
Different blessings come to different men, but with the gods' help, the ways to happiness are many. Again, in the ninth hymn of the same title:
For some ways are more effective than others, but one single pursuit will not nourish us all. <note>original Greek: φυᾷ γὰρ ἄλλαι ὁδῶν ὁδοὶ περαιτέραι, μία δ' ἅπαντας ἄμμε θρέψει μελέτα</note>
->that is,<-
For some paths are more effective than others, but one study will not sustain us all.

### Many hands make a burden lighter.
<margin>95</margin>
A proverb is commonly circulated: "A burden is made lighter by many hands." By this, they mean that even difficult tasks are easily accomplished if one does not attempt the business alone but divides it among many helpers and assistants. It is derived from the lifting of heavy weights. It seems this sentiment has flowed down from antiquity even to our own age. For we read in Hesiod, in the work titled *Works and Days*:
The care of more and more people [accomplishes more]. <note>original Greek: πλειόνων καὶ πλεόνων μελέτη</note>
->that is,<-
The industry of more people is more powerful.
Likewise Homer in the twelfth book of the *Iliad*:
But help me! For the work of many is better. <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ἐπαμύνετεω. πλεόνων δέ τι ἔργον ἄμεινον</note>
->that is,<-
Be present as companions, for the industry of many is more powerful than that of a few.
Euripides alluded to this in *The Phoenician Women*:
One man who sees all... <note>original Greek: εἷς δ' ἀνὴρ ὃ πάνθ' ὁρᾷ</note>
->that is,<-

But no one man sees everything. Again, in the *Heraclidae* <note>A play by Euripides.</note>:
The battle of a single hand is weak. <note>original Greek: μιάς γὰρ χεῖρὸς ἀσθενὴς μάχη</note>
->that is,<-
A fight is ineffective when fought with only one hand.

<margin>XCV</margin>
### To forget one’s own name.
This is a proverbial hyperbole, **to forget one's own name**, used for a person who is forgetful beyond measure. Lucian writes in *Toxaris*: "Therefore, each of them would more quickly forget the name of his father." <note>original Greek: θᾶττον γοῦν τοὔνομα ἕκαστος αὐτῶν ἐπιλάθοιτο τοῦ πατρός</note> Ovid says:
"Forgetfulness of my own name shall come upon me first." <note>From Ovid's *Tristia* 4.9.27.</note>
It is also used by Saint Jerome in a certain letter. Pliny, in the seventh book of his *Natural History*, among the examples of lost memory, records Corvinus Messala the orator, who even forgot his own name. This was a condition believed to last for some time even after death. Hence the custom among the ancients of calling out the proper name before placing the corpses upon the funeral pyre.

<margin>XCVI</margin>
### Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus is cold.
Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "By Hercules, this saying is true: **Without Ceres and Liber <note>Liber is another name for Bacchus, the god of wine.</note>, Venus grows cold.**" These words are spoken in the persona of Chremes, a rustic youth who, when sober, hated prostitutes, but after drinking, does not shrink from them. For food and drink are the "irritants" <note>stimulants</note> of lust. He elegantly used **Ceres** to represent food, **Bacchus** for wine, and **Venus** for lust, maintaining the figure of speech consistently. For that very word, **is cold**, contains a metaphor which Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence.</note> claims is borrowed from the pitching of vessels, because cold pitch does not stick. Truly, that is a cold and overly labored interpretation—if I may say so with all due respect to such a great man—if indeed the interpretation is his. Lovers "burn," and those things which languish are "cold." Horace says:
"For hereafter I shall not burn for another woman."
And husbands who do not love very much are "cold" toward their wives. Saint Jerome, explaining Terence’s sentiment with a "rougher Minerva" <term>crassiore Minerva: a Latin idiom meaning a plain, blunt, or common-sense explanation</term>, says: "When the belly is stretched [full], those parts that cling to the belly are stretched." <note>Jerome is bluntly suggesting that a full stomach leads to sexual arousal.</note> He means that lust is the companion of <term>gastrimargia</term> <note>gluttony or "stomach-madness."</note>. Wine particularly incites lust, and for that reason, the letters of Paul forbid us from being drunk with wine, because in it is located lust.
Euripides says:
"Where wine is not present, there is no Cypris." <note>Cypris is a title for Venus, the goddess of love; original Greek: Οἶνος δὲ μὴ παρόντος οὐκ ἔστιν Κύπρις</note>
->that is,<-
In the absence of wine, no Venus is then present.
In the Greek collections, I read it this way:
"Venus is a dead thing without Bacchus and Ceres." <note>original Greek: Νεκροῦ Ἀφροδίτη Διονύσου δίχα καὶ Δήμητρος</note>
A Cynic philosopher in the sixth book of Athenaeus’ *The Deipnosophists* <note>Literally "The Banquet of the Learned," a 3rd-century collection of table talk.</note> relates the same sentiment in almost these words:
"For in an empty stomach there is no love for beautiful forms. Venus is bitter to those whom dire hunger oppresses." <note>original Greek: Ἐν τῇ κενῇ γὰρ γαστρὶ τῶν καλῶν ἔρως Οὐκ ἔστι...</note>
And soon after he adds a verse of Euripides, which the latter borrowed from Achaeus the Satyrist:
"Venus is present in fullness, but in the hungry man she is not at all." <note>original Greek: Ἐν πλησμονῇ τοι Κύπρις, ἐν πεινῶντι δ' οὔ</note>
Athenaeus, in the first book of *The Deipnosophists*, brings forward a couplet containing the same idea:
"For Venus is present to the full; but for the mortals who fare badly and are miserable, no Venus is present." <note>original Greek: Ἐν πλησμονῇ γὰρ Κύπρις...</note>
In this same author, in book ten, Aristophanes calls wine "the milk of Venus," because it nourishes lust:
"Wine is sweet for the drinker, the milk of the Cyprian goddess." <note>original Greek: Ἡδύς γε πίνειν οἶνος, ἀφροδίτης γάλα</note>
To this belongs an epigram attributed to an uncertain author:
"Hunger stops love; if not hunger, then time. But if neither of these extinguish the flame..." <note>original Greek: Ἔρωτα παύει λιμός. εἰ δὲ μὴ, χρόνος. Ἐὰν δὲ μηδὲ ταῦτα τὴν φλόγα σβέσῃ...</note>

<meta>This page concludes the previous discussion on how hunger and sobriety dampen lust, then moves through several adages regarding the reputations of specific cities—Marseille, Troezen, and Athens—before beginning a new "century" (a group of one hundred adages) with a story about gratitude from Plutarch.</meta>

...as the Greek says: "For the rest, hunger is the cure; if not, a noose for the neck." <note>original Greek: φθειρῶν δὲ τὸ λοιπὸν ἀρτηδὼν βρόχον. Note: The Greek text here likely contains a scribal error; "λιμὸς" (hunger) is expected where "φθειρῶν" (lice) appears.</note> That is to say:
Hunger calms love; if that is not enough, 
Time provides the cure. But if these cannot 
Extinguish the flame, then it remains for you to prepare a rope.

Apuleius intended the same meaning when he describes a drunken feast for Venus, while in the meantime Psyche goes hungry. <note>A reference to the myth of Cupid and Psyche in Apuleius’s *The Golden Ass*.</note> However, Aristotle indicates that immoderate drinking of wine renders one useless for sexual intercourse. He argues that the "seminal power" is diluted, and for that reason, Alexander the Great was less than vigorous in the service of Venus <note>Meaning: less sexually active.</note> because he was fond of wine. Athenaeus relates that Theophrastus said the same.

### Sail to Marseille.
### XCVIII

<margin>Athenaeus, Book 12.</margin> "May you sail to Marseille." <note>original Greek: πλεύσειας εἰς τὴν Μασσαλίαν</note> Athenaeus writes in his twelfth book that the people of Marseille were once so weakened by luxury that it became common to say as a proverb: **Sail to Marseille.** He does not specifically explain the meaning of the proverb, but it is easily guessed that it should be directed at those who are soft and whose manners and dress are insufficiently manly. Plautus says in his play *Cassina*: "Where are you, you who demand to live according to the customs of Marseille?" 

And yet, what Plautus says seems to me to refer rather to a severity of life. This is similar to how Plutarch, in his *Life of Agesilaus*, teaches that "Spartan discipline" was a name for a life that was severe and not at all indulgent in luxuries. Indeed, no nation was more praised than the people of Marseille, if we believe Cicero. Valerius Maximus records the same truth in his second book, in the chapter on Institutions, recounting many things about the discipline of that city: they admitted no mimes <note>Actors of low-brow or suggestive comedy.</note> onto the stage, lest the citizens’ morals be infected by the immodest plots of the plays; nor did they receive within their gates those who sought an idle and lazy life under the pretext of religion. 

Other authors report similar things about the severity of the people of Marseille, so that it appears Athenaeus was not speaking of the Gallic Marseille <note>Modern Marseille, France.</note> but of the Libyan one, which Virgil mentions in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*: 
"Here the priestess of the Massylian race was shown to me." <note>original Latin: "Hic mihi Massylæ gentis monstrata sacerdos."</note>
From this passage, one might conjecture that the Massylians were once infamous for sorcery, just as the Thessalians were. 

Furthermore, since the name in Athenaeus is *Massalia* and not *Massylia*, it is possible that it is neither the Marseille of Gaul nor the Massylia of the Moors, but some third place. Greek writers sometimes confuse these different names. Stephanus indicates there was a city of this name in Liguria, a colony of the Phocaeans, citing Hecataeus as his authority. He adds that Timaeus says when a ship's captain had sailed there and saw a fisherman, he threw a rope to the land and said, "Bind the cable." From this, the place was given the name *Massalia*. For in the Aeolic dialect, *masai* means what others call *desai* (to bind), and *halieus* means "fisherman"; thus, from *masai* and *halieus*, it was called Marseille.

### Sail to Troezen.
### XCIX

<margin>Eustathius.</margin> "May you sail to Troezen." <note>original Greek: πλεύσειας Τροιζῆνα</note> Eustathius, in his commentary on the second book of Homer’s *Iliad*, says this used to be said against those who had hairless chins but nonetheless faked a manly beard with attached hairs. He adds that the saying arose because there was a certain port in Troezen widely known by the name "The Beard." There is also another Troezen in Marseille.

### Attic sweets.
### C

<margin>Plato, Republic, Book 3.</margin> "Attic delicacies." <note>original Greek: γέμματα ἀττικά. Note: Likely a typo for πέμματα (sweets).</note> This refers to luxuries and dainties. It can be transferred to anything that is exceptionally sweet and pleasant. Plato, in the third book of his *Republic*, says: "You criticize the Attic sweets and what are thought to be the enjoyments of a good life."

### No one sacrificed an ox to a benefactor, except Pyrrhias.
### I

<margin>Plutarch in Greek Questions.</margin> "No one sacrificed an ox to a benefactor except Pyrrhias." <note>original Greek: οὐδεὶς εὐεργέτῃ βοῦν ἔθυσεν ἀλλ’ ἢ πυῤῥίας</note> This proverb was once used if ever there appeared a man of remarkable gratitude who repaid a received benefit 
amply. Plutarch, in his *Greek Questions*, explains the origin of the 
adage in this manner: A certain pirate ship landed at the island 
of Ithaca, on which by chance there was an old man along with 
earthenware jars full of pitch. A certain Pyrrhias, a merchant of 
Ithaca, I believe, ransomed the old man from the pirates for a price, 
not because he...

<summary>This page discusses proverbs related to the influence of wine and hunger on lust, the reputations of Marseille and Troezen, and begins the story of Pyrrhias's extraordinary gratitude.</summary>
<keywords>Athenaeus, Marseille, Plautus, Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Virgil, Troezen, Plato, Attic sweets, Pyrrhias, Plutarch, Ithaca, gratitude, luxury, temperance</keywords>

--- Page 576 ---
<meta>This page continues the story of Pyrrhias, a merchant of Ithaca mentioned at the end of the previous page. Having purchased an elderly captive from pirates out of compassion, Pyrrhias is now rewarded for his kindness.</meta>

...it was necessary, but partly because he felt pity for the old man’s fate, and partly because he was persuaded by the man’s speech. On the old man’s advice, he bought those jars of pitch from the pirates. Then, after the pirates had departed, the old man—wishing to return Pyrrhias’s favor because he had set him free not out of a desire for profit, but out of goodwill—revealed that a great quantity of money was hidden inside the jars, mixed in with the pitch. When the money was found and Pyrrhias had suddenly become wealthy, he praised the old man’s gratitude most magnificently and sacrificed an ox to him as a reward for his service. From this event, once the story became widely known, the proverb was born concerning a favor returned most generously. For the ancients used to call a royal sacrifice, a magnificent and sumptuous banquet, an **ox-sacrifice**. <term>Bouthysia</term> <note>original Greek: βουθυσία. A compound of "bous" (ox) and "thyo" (to sacrifice), used to describe a grand ritual or feast.</note> This proverb is also rightly applied to the common ingratitude of mortals, which is so prevalent that you can scarcely find one person who remembers a favor. This is not unlike the Gospel example, in which, out of ten lepers cleansed by Christ’s blessing, only one returned to give thanks.

## II. Smoke’s shadow

<term>Smoke's shadow</term> <note>original Greek: Καπνοῦ σκιά</note>. That is, the shadow of smoke. Antiquity used this as a proverbial hyperbole for anything utterly worthless. Sophocles says in *Antigone*:
<term>The rest I would not buy for the shadow of smoke.</term> <note>original Greek: Τά δ᾿ ἄλλα καπνοῦ σκιᾶς οὐκ ἂν πριαίμην.</note>
Since every shadow is an empty thing, you might almost call the shadow of smoke the "shadow of a shadow." This also appears in the works of Aristophanes. We have touched upon this elsewhere.

## III. A living corpse. A living tomb.

<term>A living corpse</term> <note>original Greek: Ἔμψυχος νεκρός.</note>. As a proverbial figure of speech, Sophocles says in *Antigone*:
> I do not consider
> This man to be alive, but judge him a living corpse.

This is cited in the twelfth book of Athenaeus. Euripides, in his *Aeolus* as quoted by Stobaeus, says:
> Alas, alas, how well the ancient proverb holds:
> We old men are nothing but a crowd,
> And shadows, truly we crawl along as imitations
> Of dreams; there is no mind within us,
> Though we think ourselves to be quite wise.

This is said against those who live in such a way that they do nothing worthy of life. Lucian calls a decrepit old man <term>a certain living tomb</term> <note>original Greek: ψυχόν τινα τάφον</note>. The words of a certain mime writer, Laberius—if I am not mistaken—recorded in Gellius, also relate to this:
> Like a tomb, I retain nothing but a name.

## IIII. To see from the forehead.

We say "to see from the forehead" when we perceive something immediately and, as it were, at the very first encounter. This is taken from the Physiognomists, who profess to be able to detect a person's character from the lines of their face and the general appearance of their body. Marcus Tullius Cicero wrote to Antony: "For you could have perceived my love for you not only from my speech, but also from my expression, my eyes, and my **forehead**, as they say." This adage is still very common today. Cicero, writing to his brother Quintus about the campaign for the consulship, calls the forehead the "door to the soul." He says: "Take care that access to you is open day and night; let it be open not only by the doors of your house, but also by your expression and your forehead, which is the door to the soul. If the face indicates that the will is hidden and shut away, it matters little that the house door is open." Thus Cicero. From this, things are said to be done with a "true forehead" when they are done sincerely. For sometimes the forehead says one thing, while the mind hides another. Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Knights*:
> That they might make it plain to us by their foreheads
> Whether they take joy in our words and deeds.

CHILIADS SECOND CENTURY IV
Q 3
<meta>catchword: If false</meta>

### Buying hope at a cost.
->V<-

This refers to the act of pursuing an uncertain gain, dependent on future events, by incurring a certain loss. Terence writes in his play *The Brothers*, "I do not buy hope for a price." A pimp in the play delivers this sentiment, noting that "to neglect money at the right time is sometimes the greatest profit." 

This proverb applies most aptly to those who, led by the hope of great rewards, seek to capture the favor of princes through gifts and servitude. They certainly do so at the expense of their time and life, which are the most precious costs of all. For what else are they doing but buying hope at a price? 

The metaphor seems to be drawn from a specific type of purchase where it is common to buy the "roll of the dice" rather than a physical object. For example, if someone buys a "cast of the net" while fishing, or the "spoils of the missiles" in hunting, or anything else of that kind. There is much discussion of this in the Pandects <note>original: Pandectis. This refers to the Digest, a massive collection of Roman legal writings compiled under Emperor Justinian.</note> Book 18, under the title "On contracting a sale." It occurs when someone buys the next year’s harvest from a field, or the offspring of an animal, or when a "catch" of fish, birds, or items thrown to a crowd is purchased—what they call "the die" <note>original: aleam, referring to a game of chance or risk.</note>. 

In the case of animal offspring, the buyer is not held to the contract if nothing is born (unless he did something to prevent the birth). However, in a "sale of the die" <note>original: in alea</note>, the buyer is held to the contract even if nothing is caught, because it was the *hope* that was purchased. Only in the case of items thrown to a crowd does the loss of the item caught void the legal action of the sale.

### He terrifies the heavens.
->VI<-

A proverbial hyperbole found in Virgil’s *Aeneid*:
> And he terrifies the heavens with his weapons.

This is suitable for the threatening and fierce, or for those "Thrasos" <note>Thraso was a famous braggart soldier in ancient comedy.</note> who speak with great arrogance. It seems to be derived from the "War of the Giants" against the gods, a fable too well-known to repeat here. Close to this is a phrase from Synesius in a letter against Andronicus: <term>trying to break through heaven with his head</term> <note>original Greek: τῇ κεφαλῇ τὸν οὐρανὸν διαφαυλίζειν</note>.

### Lighter than cork.
->VII<-

<term>Lighter than cork</term> <note>original Greek: φελλῶ κουφότερος</note>. A proverbial hyperbole for people who are inconstant and of slippery faith. The wood of the cork tree is porous and does not sink in water; indeed, it is tied to nets and swimming gear to keep them from sinking. Horace writes in his *Odes*:
> Though he is more beautiful than a star, 
> you are lighter than cork, and more 
> irascible than the cruel Adriatic sea.

Strabo, in his first book, mentions this among other proverbial hyperboles: <term>a shadow lighter than cork</term>. However, this passage in Strabo is not free from the suspicion of being a corrupted text. The Greek reads: <term>And just as there are some hyperboles, such as "a shadow being lighter than cork," "more irrational than a fleeing hare," and "a field having less land than a Laconian letter."</term> <note>original Greek: Καὶ καθάπερ εἰσί τινες ὑπερβολαὶ, ὡς τὸ κουφότερον εἶναι φελλοῦ σκιὰν, ἀλογότερον δὲ λαγὼς φευγὸς, ἐλάττω δ’ ἔχειν γλῶτταν ἀγροῦ ἐπιστολῆς λακωνικῆς</note>. 

Gregorius Tifernas (or perhaps Guarino) translated it this way: "And just as some things are excesses of excesses, like 'a shadow lighter than cork,' and 'a Phrygian more fearful than a hare,' and 'a field having less earth than a Laconian letter.'" 

First, for a shadow to be lighter than cork is not a remarkable hyperbole; in fact, it is no hyperbole at all. Even if we grant that in Greek "lighter than a shadow" is a common phrase, I think we should read <term>of a shadow</term> <note>original: σκιᾶς</note> instead of <term>shadow</term> <note>original: σκιὰν</note>, so that it refers to the "shadow of cork," just as we speak of the "dream of a shadow." Likewise, "more irrational than a fleeing hare"—or "a Phrygian more timid than a hare," as the translator seems to have read it. It is not absurd if we understand the "Phrygian hare" to be more fearful than others, as that nation was considered un-warlike and weakened by luxury. 

Pindar, in his second Pythian hymn, turned this metaphor to the praise of a man who, though weighed down by the slanders of the wicked, does not lose heart but remains buoyant by his own nature; for this reason, he calls him <term>an unsinkable cork</term> <note>original Greek: φελλὸν ἀβάπτισον</note>. Horace alluded to this in the first book of his *Epistles* when speaking of Ulysses:
> While he prepared a return for himself and his comrades, 
> he endured many hardships, remaining unsinkable in the adverse waves of events.

### To wipe the nose with the elbow.
->VIII<-

<term>Wiping with the elbow</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγκῶνι ἀπομυσσόμενος</note>. A proverbial irony for a man of filthy profit and abject condition. It is derived from the fish-salters, whose custom it is to wipe the mucus from their nostrils with their elbows, because their hands are covered in brine and salt-slime. The philosopher Bion, quoted in Suidas from Laertius, said: "My father was a freedman, <gloss>one associated with the census</gloss> <note>original: Censualis</note> who wiped his nose with his elbow." 

A witty remark of Marcus Tullius Cicero is celebrated, which he threw at the son of a fish-salter; the author of the *Rhetoric to Herennius* mentions it without naming the source, using it as an example of a figure of speech called "signification by consequence." As he says...

...if you should say to the son of a salt-fish seller: "Be quiet, you, whose father used to wipe his nose with his elbow" <note>This implies a person of such low social standing that they could not afford a handkerchief, using their sleeve or arm instead.</note>.

<margin>IX</margin>
->Iberian trifles.<-

Saint Jerome calls "Iberian trifles" <note>original: Hiberæ neniæ</note> mere nonsense in the preface he wrote for the Pentateuch of Moses: "Because many people in their ignorance," he says, "follow the ravings of the apocrypha and prefer Iberian trifles to authentic books." He says the same in his *Twelve Questions*: "And to follow Iberian trifles and Egyptian portents." I believe they are called "Iberian trifles" because of the legendary stories of sorcery commonly spread about that region. For Horace, in his *Odes*, bears witness that the Iberians <note>People of the Iberian Peninsula, roughly modern Spain and Portugal.</note> suffered from an ill reputation for sorcery. Unless, of course, one prefers to refer this to the gold-bearing river Tagus. However, Saint Jerome himself, in his letter against Vigilantius, indicates clearly enough that this should be understood as referring to portents and monsters, writing in this manner: "And because you live at the foot of the Pyrenees, and are a neighbor to Iberia, you pursue the incredible portents of Basilides, that most ancient heretic, and his ignorant 'knowledge'." Athenaeus, in his second book, records that although the Iberians were very wealthy, they were always accustomed to being <term>water-drinkers</term> <note>original: ὑδροποτᾶν (hydropotan)</note> and <term>solitary eaters</term> <note>original: μονοσιτεῖν (monositein)</note>—that is, drinking water and taking their food alone—due to their extreme parsimony; otherwise, they were most lavish in their dress. Stephanus cites this from Athenaeus. However, in place of <term>frugality</term> <note>original: μικρολογία (mikrologia)</note>, the word has been corrupted into <term>long-windedness</term> <note>original: μακρολογία (makrologia)</note>.

<margin>X</margin>
->Sicilian trifles, Wicker-work, Persian trifles.<-

"Sicilian trifles" <note>original: Siculæ nugæ</note> is a proverb used for trivial matters. Ausonius says in a letter to Symmachus: "Thinking not of that line of Catullus,
> To whom do I give this charming, new little book?
> To whom do I give this uncharming, rough little book?

but something <term>more bitter</term> <note>original: amargoteron</note> and more true, I did not search for long. You occurred to me, whom I would always choose above all others, if I had the power. And so I sent you these frivolities, vainer than Sicilian <term>wicker-work</term> <note>original: gerris Siculis</note>." Furthermore, the wit of the Sicilians is well-known in ancient literature. For Epicharmus was Sicilian, on whose model Horace said Plautus hastened to write. Plautus, however, is immoderate in his trifles and jokes, and not infrequently absurd. Furthermore, the Greeks call wicker baskets or shields <term>gerrhae</term> <note>original: γέρρα</note>. According to Festus Pompeius, that word was later commonly used for nonsense and frivolous things for this reason: when the Athenians were besieging Syracuse and frequently demanding <term>wicker-works</term> <note>barriers or shields for the siege</note>, the Sicilians mockingly shouted back "Gerrhae!" <note>implying "Nonsense!" or "Empty stuff!"</note>. From this it passed into a proverb. This is also why close friends who share all their silly jokes with one another are called <term>cogerrones</term> <note>companions in nonsense</note>. Suidas records <term>gerrha</term> in the neuter gender as a Persian word, which signifies both weapons and any kind of defense. The Greek *Etymologicon* adds that among the Sicilians, the female nature is called *gerron*, for *gerrha* is said by a change of letters to be like *psara*. Among the Greeks, *doras* signifies a skin or hide, and *gerra* are properly hide-covered defenses. Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian*: "This word is now well-timed, if it is an old word. For your flatteries are to me what is commonly said: genuine <term>gerrhae</term> <note>nonsense</note>. By Pollux, they are trifles, trifles." He said "genuine" <note>germanæ</note>, not "Germanic," meaning pure and true nonsense. What Plautus calls "trifles" <note>liræ</note>, the Greeks call <term>nonsense</term> <note>original: λῆρον (leron) or ληρήματα (leremata)</note>. They think the word is derived from <term>to escape notice</term> <note>original: λάθω (latho)</note> and <term>to flow</term> <note>original: ῥέω (rheo)</note>, because a thing spoken by a failing memory slips away. Just as <term>idle talk</term> <note>original: φλύαρον (phlyaron)</note> and <term>frivolity</term> <note>original: φλυαρείαν (phlyareian)</note> are said to be derived from <term>to bubble over</term> <note>original: φλύω (phlyo)</note> and <term>to flow</term>, because babblers overflow with a surplus of words. In this same Plautus we also read of "Persian trifles" <note>original: Persolas nugas</note>, I believe on account of the mountains of gold that are said to be in Persia.

<margin>XI</margin>
->He who is once a buffoon, is never a head of a household.<-

"He who is once a buffoon, is never a head of a household" <note>original: Qui semel scurra, nunquam paterfamilias</note>. Porphyrion, explaining Horace, notes that this was a proverb. The meaning is that one who has once cast off shame and, despising his reputation, has begun to act the buffoon, hardly ever returns to a productive life. The buffoon delights in the food of others; the head of a household prepares the means to live at home. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech for Publius Quintius, says: "I remember, it is an old saying, that it is much easier for a buffoon to become a rich man than a head of a household." Fortune frequently lavishes wealth on the unworthy, but she gives a sound mind to no one.

<margin>XII</margin>
->While there is breath in the sick man, there is hope.<-

"While there is breath in the sick man, there is hope" <note>original: Ægroto dum anima est, spes est</note>. This is a proverbial sentiment advising that hope should not be cast aside even in the most afflicted circumstances. Marcus Tullius Cicero to Atticus: "As it is said that while there is breath in the sick man, there is hope, so as long as Pompey was in Italy, I did not cease to hope." The adage seems to be taken from Theocritus’s character Battus:
"One must be bold, dear Battus; perhaps tomorrow will be better.
There is hope among the living, but the dead are beyond hope.
And Zeus is sometimes clear, and sometimes he rains."

<vocab>Erasmus, Adagia, Iberian trifles, Sicilian trifles, wicker-work, buffoon, head of household, hope, Jerome, Plautus, Cicero, Theocritus</vocab>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of hope, specifically moving from the idea that hope sustains the living to several adages regarding precision, reciprocity in services, the unpredictability of fortune, and the etiquette of receiving gifts.</meta>

463
SECOND CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY
Q 4
<meta>catchword: Time-</meta>

Since Philelphus <note>Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), a leading Italian Renaissance humanist who translated many Greek works into Latin.</note> translated these verses quite elegantly, I will not hesitate to include them:
“It is right to trust, Battus; perhaps you will have better things tomorrow.
There is hope for the living; there is no hope at all for the buried.
Now it rains, and now Jupiter shines from the clear sky.”
<margin>Also Euripides in *The Trojan Women*,</margin>
“To see the light is not the same as to die, my child.
For the latter is nothingness, but in the former there are hopes.”
<margin>which is to say,</margin>
“It is not the same thing, my dear son, to live and to die,
Since the latter is nothing, while in the former there are surely hopes.”
The story of Pandora's box pertains to this same idea; when all other diseases flew out of it, hope alone remained caught on the very rim of the jar.

### To cut to the quick. XIII
Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in his book *On Friendship*, used the phrase "to cut to the quick" <note>original: ad vivum resecare</note> for when a matter is examined more precisely than is necessary, or too peevishly. “But this,” he says, “is my first feeling: that friendship cannot exist except among the good. Nor do I cut this to the quick, as do those who discuss these matters more subtly.” The metaphor is borrowed from barbers who cut hair or nails. For they are often annoying when they strive to be overly diligent <note>i.e., cutting so close that they hit the living tissue.</note>. The same author, in his books *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, used the phrase "to act more pressingly" <note>original: pressius agere</note> for acting more exactly and accurately. Plautus, in *The Bacchides*, speaking through the character Chrysalus, says: “I will shear him of his gold right down to the quick.” This very word "to shear" <note>original: tondere</note> used for "to trick" or "to delude" is a common proverb among the Greeks.

### A service is the compensation for money. XIV
"A service is the compensation for money" <note>original: Hostimentum est opera pro pecunia</note>. This adage warns that nothing ought to be free, but that a duty should be balanced by a benefit. According to Pompeius Festus <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note>, a *hostimentum* is the compensation for a benefit, derived from the ancient verb *hostire* and *redhostire*, which means to return an equal amount. Nonius thinks the word *hostis* [enemy] comes from the same root, because a battle is undertaken from an equal cause. Thus, a madam in Plautus’s *Asinaria* responds to a young man who is reproaching her for his previous favors: “A service is the compensation for money.” That is to say: neither has anything to charge against the other. You loved the woman, and she was sent to you; I wanted money, and you gave it. Titus Livy says: “Never is service without reward, nor reward for servants without the expense of service.” But in the duties of friends, there is a different reckoning; for he who has returned a favor is not released from the debt of gratitude, nor does it happen through an exchange of duties that neither owes anything to the other. Closely related to these are: "Hand rubs hand," and "Scratch the one who scratches you."

### She fills both pages. XV
Pliny, in the second book of his *Natural History*, chapter seven, says when speaking of Fortune: “To her all expenses are charged, to her all receipts are credited; and in the whole account of mortals, she alone fills both pages.” This has the appearance of a proverb: "She fills both pages" <note>original: utranque paginam facit</note>. The metaphor is taken from account books which have two pages, one indicating what has been given, and the other showing what has been received. Thus, in human affairs, Fortune fills both pages: that is, if something good happens, she is praised as if she had given it; if something bad happens, she is attacked as the author of evils.

### Not everything, nor everywhere, nor from everyone. XVI
“Not everything, nor everywhere, nor from everyone.” <note>original Greek: οὐκ πάντα, οὔτε πάντη, οὔτε παρὰ πάντων (ouk panta, oute pantē, oute para pantōn)</note>.
This adage warns that in accepting gifts, one must employ not only modesty but also selection. For there are certain things which it is by no means becoming to receive. There is also a place and a time when it is beautiful to refuse a gift offered. There are some from whom it is dishonest to admit a gift. Horace praises the Homeric Telemachus, who refused the horses offered by Menelaus. This adage is cited by Ulpian <note>A famous Roman jurist (c. 170–223 AD).</note> in the *Pandects* [Digest], Book I, under the title "On the Office of a Proconsul," from a letter of the divine Emperors Severus and Antoninus. I will write down the words themselves: “As far as guest-gifts are concerned,” he says, “hear what we think. There is a Greek proverb: ‘Not everything, nor everywhere, nor from everyone.’ For it is inhumane to receive from no one; but to receive everywhere is very cheap, and to receive everything is very greedy.” Thus far their words. The Greek words were missing in all the manuscripts. Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), an Italian scholar who helped reconstruct classical texts.</note> restored them from the original sources, lest we meanwhile defraud him of his due praise. Theocritus alluded to this in *Thionychus*:
“He does not know how to refuse a request
Worthy of a prince, nor should one ask for just anything.”
<margin>which is to say,</margin>
“He is not accustomed to refuse when asked for
Things worthy of a prince, nor is he to be asked regarding just any matter.”

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
XVII
<meta>Catchword: ludo</meta>

->Time reveals all things.<-

Tertullian, whom Saint Cyprian was accustomed to call his "master," says in his *Apology against the Pagans*: "It is well that time reveals all things, as even your own proverbs and sayings testify." Aulus Gellius, in the *Attic Nights*, Book 12, Chapter 12, cites these verses of Sophocles on this sentiment:
<note>original Greek: Πρὸς ταῦτα κρύπτε μηδὲν, ὡς ἅπανθ' ὁρῶν Καὶ πάντ' ἀκούων, πάντ' ἀναπτύσσει χρόνος.</note>
"Therefore hide nothing, since time, seeing all and hearing all, brings everything to light."
The same author says in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*:
<note>original Greek: Ἅπανθ' ὁ μακρὸς κ' ἀναρίθμητος χρόνος Φύει τ' ἄδηλα, καὶ φανέντα κρύπτεται.</note>
"Vast and uncounted time brings forth all hidden things and likewise hides what has been revealed."
In the same passage, Gellius reminds us that one of the ancient poets called Truth the daughter of Time, because although she may sometimes lie hidden, she emerges into the light through the progress of time.
This proverbial six-foot verse is also cited to the same effect:
<note>original Greek: Ἄγει δὲ πρὸς φῶς τὴν ἀλήθειαν χρόνος.</note>
"Time brings the truth into the light."
And another similar to it:
<note>original Greek: Πάντ' ἀνακαλύπτων ὁ χρόνος πρὸς φῶς φέρει.</note>
"Time, uncovering all things, brings them into the air."
I believe Thales felt the same when he said that time is the wisest of all things, for it finds out everything. Nor did Pindar mean anything else in the *Olympian Odes* when he said:
<note>original Greek: Ἁμέραι δ' ἐπίλοιποι μάρτυρες σοφώτατοι.</note>
"The days to come are the wisest witnesses."
Elsewhere he calls time the father of all things, because there is nothing that does not happen in the course of time:
<note>original Greek: ἀφίκτου τ' ἂν χρόνος ὁ πάντων πατὴρ δύναιτο θέμεν ἔργων τέλος.</note>
"Not even Time, the father of all things, could make undone what has been done."
Pindar holds this same view in several places, and specifically in *Olympian 10*:
<note>original Greek: ὅτ' ἐξελέγχων μόνος ἀλήθειαν ἐτήτυμον χρόνος, τὸ δ' ἀφανὲς ἰὼν πόρσω κατέφρασεν.</note>
"Only time, which proves the certain truth, and moving forward, tells the story of what was hidden in the dark."
<margin>And compels it to be confessed</margin>
Virgil seems to have alluded to this in the sixth book [of the *Aeneid*]:
"Those who, having rejoiced in some empty theft among those above, have deferred their committed atonements until late death." <note>This refers to the idea that sins hidden in life are revealed and punished after death.</note>
Nor does the Gospel saying in Matthew chapter 10 differ: "There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, and hidden that shall not be known." Plutarch, in his *Roman Questions*, inquires why in ancient times divine rites were performed to Saturn with the head covered. He thinks it signifies that truth is often covered and unknown, but is opened by time. For Saturn is imagined as the author and god of time—since *Kronos* is Saturn, and *chronos* is time <note>Erasmus highlights the common ancient etymological pun between the god Kronos and the word for time, chronos.</note>. Livy felt no differently when he said in Book 22: "They say justice often suffers from truth, but is never extinguished." Seneca, in *On Anger*, Book 2: "Time must always be given, for the day opens the truth."

XVIII
->The Alpha of the cloaked ones.<-

Martial, in the second book of his *Epigrams*:
"Whom does my Publius not surpass in cloaks? Not even Codrus himself, the Alpha of the cloaked ones."
He used "Alpha" to mean the foremost or chief, surely as a proverbial figure. Elsewhere the same author jokes about someone who was offended because Martial had called him "Alpha"; he advises him to take his revenge by calling Martial "Beta" in turn, if he likes. This is transferred from the Greek practice of using letters as numerals <note>Alpha being 1 (the first), Beta being 2 (the second).</note>. He also calls such leaders "standard-bearers" and "front-rankers," using a metaphor from the military. As to why "Alpha" holds the first place among letters, Plutarch provides the reasons in a sophisticated manner in the ninth decade of his *Table Talk*. Protogenes the grammarian, from his...

It also introduces the adage "Alpha of the cloaked ones," explaining the use of the letter Alpha to signify the best or first of a class.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the primacy of the letter "Alpha" as a symbol for the "first" or "best," then moves into proverbs regarding the power of early habits and the difficulty of changing what one has first "tasted" or learned.</meta>

469
FOURTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND THOUSAND

<note>original: "ludo"</note> In the discussion, he brings forward the reason why vowels are rightfully preferred over consonants: because they can be sounded without the help of the others. Furthermore, he argues that the "double-natured" <note>vowels that can be either long or short, like alpha, iota, and upsilon</note> are deservedly preferred over those that are strictly long or short, because they encompass the power of both types. Among these double-natured vowels, the first place is correctly granted to *alpha*, because in the formation of syllables, *iota* and *upsilon* follow *alpha*, as in <term>aieion</term> <note>original: αἰείον</note> and <term>aas</term> <note>original: ἄας</note>. *Alpha* never follows those two to form a single syllable; instead, it recoils and maintains its own leadership. But Ammonius soon alleges a different reason: that Cadmus gave *alpha* the leading place among letters because in the Phoenician language an "ox" is called *alpha*. He thought the first place should be given to the ox, not the second or third, as Hesiod did when he wrote: <term>A house first of all, then a woman, then a plowing ox</term> <note>original: οἶκον μὲν πρώτιστα, γυναῖκά τε, βοῦντ’ ἀροτῆρα</note>. That is,
> First a home, then a wife, then an ox for the plow.
For he thinks these are the defenses needed if one wishes to escape hunger and poverty. Again, Plutarch adds this reason, which he says he learned from his grandfather Lamprias: that the first natural and articulated sound is made through the *alpha*, because the breath in the mouth is primarily formed and shaped by the movement of the lips. When these are pulled apart, this sound first comes out, wonderfully simple and requiring no effort, needing no help even from the tongue, but being carried through the space while the tongue lies still. This is why newborn children first utter this sound. These and similar points are recorded in the place I have indicated. There is also a dispute in Plato regarding the primacy of *alpha* among the letters. Indeed, those phrases also savor of a proverb: "to hold the first place," "to grant or assign the first place," and "I will not bear the later (lower) place." These are metaphors taken from the parts played by actors in plays; and among the Greeks, <term>to be first</term> <note>original: πρωτεύειν</note>, <term>to hold the first place</term> <note>original: τὰ πρῶτα ξέναι</note>, and <term>to carry off the first prizes</term> <note>original: τὰ πρῶτα φέρεσθαι</note>. It is clear this was taken from the actors of plays, among whom those who sustain the largest part of the play act the "first parts"; those who are inferior to them act the second and third parts. However, in the pleading of legal cases, there are also <term>first speeches, second speeches, and third speeches</term> <note>original: πρωτολογίαι, δευτερολογίαι & τριτολογίαι</note>, just as there are <term>protagonists, deuteragonists, and tritagonists</term> <note>actors of the first, second, and third parts</note>. If these are aptly transferred to other contexts, they take on the appearance of a proverb.

---

### To drink in the saliva.
-> XIX <-

Saint Jerome, in his preface to the Gospels, says: "For who, whether equally learned or unlearned, when he has taken a volume into his hands and sees that what he reads differs from the **saliva he once drank in**, will not immediately break out into shouting?" Truly, he spoke elegantly and with a proverbial figure: "which he once drank in," meaning from that first taste with which a child is imbued. The metaphor is taken from infants, into whose mouths nurses insert food they have already chewed, not without their own saliva. Once they have grown accustomed to this, nothing tastes good to them that differs from the flavor of that first saliva. Therefore, we must take care in every way to become accustomed to the best things. The same thing happens to most of us: whatever disagrees with what we "drank in" during those first years immediately displeases us. They also say that dogs love those whose saliva they have tasted. But I would prefer this to be referred to the previous metaphor. This also seems to be the point of that line from Persius:
> And you could step over a coin fixed in the mud, 
> nor swallow the **mercurial saliva** with greed.
Although I think it more likely refers to "mercurial figs," which we have mentioned elsewhere, which some people smeared with saliva or grease as a joke, so that those who tried to pick them up would be mocked, just as he previously mentioned the joke about a coin stuck in the mud. Certainly, this relates to our proverb, which is found in the same author's sixth Satire:
> Nor skilled in knowing the **thin saliva of thrushes**.
He used "saliva" to mean "taste" or "flavor."

---

### With which it is once seasoned.
-> XX <-

Not unlike this is that famous line from Horace:
> The jar will long preserve the odor
> **with which it was once seasoned** when new.
Therefore, Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> rightly advises that children should learn the best things immediately, because nothing sticks more tenaciously than what we perceived in our unformed years. And Aristotle, in the second book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*: <term>It makes no small difference, then, whether one is habituated this way or that right from youth; rather, it makes a very great difference, or rather, it is everything</term> <note>original: οὐ μικρὸν οὖν διαφέρει τὸ οὕτως ἢ οὕτως εὐθὺς ἐκ νέων ἐθίζεσθαι, ἀλλὰ παμπολὺ, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ πᾶν</note>. Thus, it is of no small importance whether we are accustomed to this or that way straight from childhood; rather, it matters most of all, or rather, every momentum is situated in that. And that <term>exclamation</term> <note>original: ἐπιφώνημα</note> of Virgil in the *Georgics*:
> So great is the power of habit in the tender years.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of Greek and Latin adages. Having previously discussed the symbolic primacy of the letter "Alpha," he now transitions into proverbs regarding difficult tasks, persistent habits, and the nature of servitude.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### To cleanse the Augean stable.
<margin>XXI</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Αὐγέου βουστάσιον"</note> Augeas’s cattle-shed. This is a proverbial allegory used for a man, or for a matter that is excessively filthy. Lucian writes in *The False Prophet*: "so that I would try to cleanse, if not the whole of Augeas's cattle-shed, at least as much as is within my power." <note>original: "ὥστε τὴν Αὐγέου βουστάσιον, οὐκ ἂν πᾶσαν, ἀλλ’ εἰς δύναμίν γε τὴν ἐμαυτὸ ἀνεκαθηράμην προθυμήσομαι"</note> This story shows that the place had gathered so much dung as three thousand oxen could produce over many years. Pausanias also mentions this in his description of Elis, noting something of the cattle and the dung. In the Greek epigrams, the cleansing of the Augean stable is counted among the labors of Hercules. Furthermore, Seneca uses this proverb in his satirical book on the death of the Emperor Claudius: "If you had fallen in with these people," he says, "brave as you may seem to yourself, you would have preferred to scour the sewers of Augeas; I have exhausted far more filth." <note>This refers to Seneca's *Apocolocyntosis*, a "pumpkinification" or satire of the late Emperor Claudius.</note> 

Even if this proverb was omitted in the copy first followed by Froben <note>Johann Froben, Erasmus's primary printer in Basel</note>, we have restored it from a copy made available to us from the library of the College that professes the liberal arts in the most flourishing University of Louvain <note>This refers to the Busleyden College, or the Trilingual College, which Erasmus helped establish for the study of Greek, Latin, and Hebrew</note>. For I do not think it fair to blame the University because, through a conspiracy of a few hayseeds <note>original: "feniculorum," literally "little stalks of fennel," used here as a derogatory term for unrefined opponents of humanism</note>, there was such a hateful resistance here against good literature and languages. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> says to Basil the Great: "How was it that first that garden was uncultivated and without vegetables, because of those who were clearing out the dung through the holes?" <note>original Greek: "πῶς, πρῶτον μὲν ἄκηπος κῆπος ἐκεῖνος ἦν ἀλαχανώτος, τῷ διὰ τὰς χίας κόπρον ἐκκαθαρομένων;"</note> That is to say, how were those gardens uncultivated and empty of greens, and the Augean filth cleared from the house? He means that a life ruined by luxury has been corrected for the better.

### It is dangerous for a dog to have tasted intestines.
<margin>XXII</margin>
-> <note>original Greek: "χαλεπὸν χορίου κύνα γεῦσαι"</note> that is, <-
-> It is dangerous for a dog to have once tasted the innards. <-
This was said as a proverbial allegory by Theocritus in his tenth *Idyll*. The adage warns that it is not easy for someone to refrain from sinning who has once tasted that lure, which acts as a sort of down-payment for vice. For example: someone who has once touched a prostitute, or who has once increased his wealth through perjury or theft, or who has once experienced the life of the court. It is also expressed this way in Lucian: "A dog will not stop once it has learned to gnaw leather." <note>original: "οὐδὲ κύων παύσαιτ’ ἂν ἅπαξ σκυτοτραγεῖν μαθών"</note> The commentator on Theocritus indicates that the proverb is also expressed in this way: "It is a dangerous thing for a dog that has learned to gnaw on leather." <note>original: "χαλεπὸν μαθεῖν κύνα σκυτοτραγεῖν"</note> Horace used a similar figure in his *Satires*:
> Which, if it has once tasted
> From one old man, sharing the little profit with you,
> Like a dog, it will never be scared away from the oily hide.

### A doubtful dinner.
<margin>XXIII</margin>
He called a "doubtful dinner" one that was sumptuous and furnished with various dishes, and it appears this proverb was invented by parasites <note>In Roman comedy, a "parasite" was a stock character who traded wit or flattery for a free meal</note>. Phormio says in the play by Terence: "A doubtful dinner is served." What is the meaning of that word? "Where you would doubt what to take first." The parasite explains the word which is otherwise ambiguous. For "Doubtful" <term>dubia</term> can also mean dangerous; and a "doubtful dinner" could be understood as one that is not free from the suspicion of poison. Horace says in his *Satires*:
> You see how everyone rises pale
> from a doubtful dinner.
And we call matters that are not very safe "doubtful."

### A dog around the intestines.
<margin>XXIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Κύων περὶ ἐντόσθοις"</note> That is, a dog near the intestines. This was said when someone saw those things he most desired set before him, yet which he was not permitted to enjoy. For dogs wander around the intestines, ready to devour them if they did not fear the club. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> thinks it can be applied to things that are useless and unpleasant: for intestines are not easily swallowed by dogs, and once devoured, they are often vomited back up.

### Golden shackles.
<margin>XXV</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Χρυσαῖ πέδαι"</note> That is, golden shackles. This is said as a proverbial metaphor for a servitude that is splendid and lovely, such as the life of courtiers generally is. Diogenes left it written in a certain letter that Aristippus was held in the royal court by golden shackles so that he could not fly away. Seneca says in a certain dialogue on the emotions of reason: "It is the mark of a fool to love his shackles, however golden they may be." He is speaking of a beautiful wife. Horace likewise says of a beautiful mistress:
> And she holds him bound
> by a pleasing shackle.

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Century of the Second Chiliad of Erasmus’s collection. Having just discussed the labors of Hercules (specifically the cleaning of the Augean stables), the text moves into further "Herculean" expressions and ancient exclamations of victory.</meta>

467
FOURTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD

### Herculean itch.
<margin>XXVI</margin>
<margin>Herculean itch.</margin> <note>original Greek: "Ἡράκλεια ψώρα"</note> This refers to a "Herculean itch." According to the lexicographer Suidas, this refers to an itch that is pleasant and easily cured, or perhaps one that requires "Herculean baths"—that is, hot springs. For they say that when Hercules was exhausted by those massive labors of his, Pallas and the nymphs frequently provided him with steaming baths. Neither Zenodotus nor Suidas indicates the specific use of this adage. I personally suspect it could be applied either to those who have damaged their health through great zeal or other labor and thus need some form of relaxation, or to those who, soothed by flattering adulations, "itch" as if with a certain pleasant scabies.

### The Herculean disease.
<margin>XXVII</margin>
<margin>Herculean disease.</margin> <note>original Greek: "Ἡράκλειος νόσος"</note> This is the Herculean disease. Dicaearchus, as cited by Zenodotus, believes this is the ailment which others call the "sacred disease" or the "comitial disease" <note>This refers to epilepsy. It was called "comitial" because if someone had a seizure during a Roman assembly (comitia), the meeting was immediately cancelled as a bad omen.</note>. It is among those conditions that cannot be helped by any medical skill, primarily because it is believed to be sent by a divinity; for this reason, the epithet "sacred" was added. Apuleius, in his first defense speech, thinks it is called "divine" because it violates the divine—that is, the rational—part of the soul. He says it arises whenever the flesh melts into a thick and frothy humor under the influence of a hostile "fire" <note>An ancient medical theory regarding the imbalance of humors.</note>. The signs are a heavy head, a twisting neck, throbbing temples, and especially a ringing in the right ear. He notes it is detected most effectively by the smell of a burning <term>jet stone</term> <note>gagate: a type of lignite coal believed to trigger seizures in epileptics when burned</note> or by the spinning of a potter’s wheel. They say Hercules fell into this condition either because of his immense labors or because Juno inflicted it upon him. 

Heraclitus called arrogance a "sacred disease," either because this evil usually follows the greatest of men, or because death alone brings a remedy. Herodotus, in his book *Thalia*, records that Cambyses was subject to this disease and killed some of his closest friends in fits of madness. Likewise, the tragic poets depict Hercules killing his own children. It seems to be called "Herculean" because, just as he was unconquerable, so this disease cannot be overcome by any physician's help. However, Aristotle, in the thirtieth section of his *Problems* (specifically the first problem according to Theodorus's division), believes that Hercules really was subject to this disease, and that all those who have excelled in genius, the study of philosophy, the administration of the state, or other arts, were prone to <term>black bile</term> <note>melancholy; ancient medicine linked genius and madness through the excess of this humor</note>. For my part, I do not see why this should be counted among adages, unless we use "sacred" or "Herculean disease" to describe a swelling of the soul or some other incurable vice—the sort of thing one finds in the avarice of old men or the talkativeness of women. Yet, I see it listed under the title of a proverb in almost all the Greek collections.

### Hail Paean!
<margin>XXVIII</margin>
**Hail Paean!** <note>Io Pæan</note> This is a proverbial exclamation which we are accustomed to use when a matter has been vigorously and successfully completed. It seems not unlike that Homeric phrase, <term>shoot thus</term> <note>original Greek: "βάλλ’ οὕτως"</note>, or the Latin expression, "Success to your courage!" <note>Macte virtute</note>. Athenaeus, quoting from the first book of Clearchus’s work on proverbs, cites <term>Hail Paeon, Hail Paean</term> <note>original: "ἰὴ παιῶν, ἰὴ παιάν"</note>; I find it written both ways. They think it originated thus: when Latona was bringing Diana and Apollo from Chalcis (a city in Euboea) to Delphi, she happened by chance to pass near the cave where the Python was said to be hiding. When the Python rushed at them with a <term>hissing</term> <note>original Greek: "ψιλίης"</note> sound, Latona, terrified in the manner of women, cried out for her son’s help with these words: <term>Shoot, boy!</term> <note>original: "ἵε παῖ"</note>. Thereupon Apollo, who happened to be carrying a bow, sent an arrow and slew the Python. From this, the cry was modified into <term>Hail Paean!</term> <note>original: "ἰὴ παιάν"</note>. 

Because this was traditionally repeated three times in sacrifices made to Apollo, some believe it was the original source of the <term>Heroic hexameter</term> <note>the meter of epic poetry</note> and the <term>Iambic trimeter</term>. For if you pronounce it with the first syllables long—
> <term>Hail Paean, Hail Paean, Hail Paean</term>

it will be a hexameter consisting of pure spondees. But if the first syllables are short, it will be an iambic trimeter of pure iambs. The grammarian Terentianus also mentions this. Likewise, Julius Pollux in his fourth book demonstrates that in the Pythian games there were five types of songs: the <term>trial</term> <note>peira</note>, representing Apollo scouting the location; the <term>summons</term> <note>katakeleusmos</note>, challenging the Python; the <term>iambic</term>, fighting; the <term>spondaic</term>, winning; and the <term>triumphal dance</term> <note>katachoreusis</note>, celebrating. From this, it was commonly accepted as a proverb that, when a thing is finished happily, we shout <term>Hail Paean!</term>. The Latins seem to have changed the Greek "e" into a long "o". Ovid, in his work *The Art of Love*:
> Cry Hail Paean! and twice cry Hail Paean!
> The sought-after prey has fallen into my nets.

And in triumphs it was shouted, "Hail Triumph!" <margin>Horace in the Odes:</margin>
> Not once only shall we say, "Hail Triumph!"

<keywords>Hercules, epilepsy, Apollo, Python, medical history, ancient music, Greek mythology, Ovid, Horace, black bile</keywords>

ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->No mortal is wise at all hours.<-
<margin>XXIX</margin>

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the massive Roman *Natural History*.</note> in book seven, in the chapter "On the excellence of nations," writes: "If we wish to make a true judgment and decide by casting aside all the ambition of fortune, no mortal is happy. Fortune has therefore dealt abundantly and indulgently with him who can rightly be called not unhappy. Indeed, even if other things are lacking, there is certainly the fear that fortune might strike. Once that fear is admitted, solid happiness is gone. What of the fact that no mortal is wise at all hours?" I wish that many would judge this to be false and not spoken by a prophet. From these words of Pliny, one may gather that this expression—that no one is wise at all hours—having been delivered like an oracle, has passed into common speech. The meaning is clear even without an interpreter: namely, that there is no one who does not act foolishly or sin in some part of their life. Furthermore, unhappiness is the companion of folly. Or certainly, if some misfortune occurs, it is usually imputed to folly. To the same point belongs what he adds a little later in the same place: "One day judges another, but the last day judges all." There exists in Aristophanes’ *The Frogs* a six-foot line of this kind, which he indicates belongs to Euripides:
<note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις πάντ’ ἀνὴρ εὐδαιμονεῖ"</note> There is no man who is happy in all ways.
That is,
Hardly anyone lives happy in every respect.
Likewise, Euripides in *The Suppliants*:
<note>original Greek: "πᾶν γὰρ ἐν βροτοῖς οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲν διὰ τέλους εὐδαιμονοῦν"</note> For among mortals,
There is nothing that is prosperous continually and to the end.
That is,
Indeed, in the universal affairs of mortals,
Nothing is constantly and entirely prosperous.
In the same manner, Horace writes:
"Nothing is blessed in every respect."
And Simonides in Stobaeus:
<note>original Greek: "πάμπαν δ’ ἄμωμος οὔτις ἔστ’ ἀκήριος"</note> No one is altogether without fault or free from harm.
That is,
No one is entirely free from evil or from crime.

->Each man's character shapes his fortune.<-
<margin>XXX</margin>

Cornelius Nepos in the *Life of Pomponius Atticus* says: "And so he brought it about that it seems truly said: Each man's character shapes his fortune." And a little later in the same work: "We have indicated above that his own character usually wins a man his fortune." This sentiment seems taken from common life. For we usually see bad things happen to bad people, and worthy things to the worthy; and so the common people say, "A bad man finds a bad end," and <note>original Greek: "κακοῖς τρὶς κακά"</note> "to the bad, triple evils." That is, three times evil for the evil. The proverbial verse also bears witness:
<note>original Greek: "ἐσθλῷ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ τ’ ἐσθλὰ καὶ διδοῖ θεός"</note> For to a good man, God also gives good things.
That is,
To a good man, fortune supplies good things.
Likewise Menander, as cited by Plutarch:
<note>original Greek: "ὁ νοῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ὁ θεός"</note> For our mind is our god.
That is,
To us, the mind is a god.
And in the same author, Heraclitus says: <note>original Greek: "ἦθος ἀνθρώπῳ δαίμων"</note> A man’s character is his divinity or fortune. To the same point belongs what Alcman wrote, that fortune is the sister of <note>original Greek: "εὐνομίας, πειθοῦς καὶ προμηθείας"</note> Good Order, Persuasion, and Foresight, as Plutarch reports in his commentary *On the Fortune of the Romans*. Plautus in the *Trinummus* says: "The wise man himself shapes his fortune." Titus Livius, in the first book of his fourth decade, says this of Marcus Portius Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman famous for his rigid morality.</note>: "In this man there was such force of mind and talent that, in whatever place he had been born, he seemed likely to make his own fortune." Pacatus in his *Panegyric* says: "To each man, his own prudence is his god." Fulgentius, in his commentaries on Virgil, cites from Telesiacus of Carneades: "All fortune dwells in the perception of the wise man." I believe it is the same thing that Marcus Tullius Cicero brings forward in his fifth *Paradox* from some poet or other. Although that passage is considered corrupted, I think it should be amended in this way: "To whom indeed even fortune herself, who has the greatest power, yields; and as the wise poet said, she is shaped by each man’s own character." For he feels that fortune is shaped for each person by their own character.

->The mad laurel is at hand.<-
<margin>XXXI</margin>

Pliny in book sixteen, chapter forty-five (or four, according to some divisions), says: "In the same region is the port of Amycus, famous for the killing of King Bebryce. His tomb, from his final day, has been covered by a laurel which they call 'mad,' because if any part of it is taken and brought onto ships, quarrels arise until it is thrown away." Thus far Pliny. It did not seem absurd to me to include this among the adages, since the matter was so well-known that from here the tree...

<summary>Erasmus discusses the relationship between wisdom, character, and fate, arguing that everyone is prone to folly and that one's internal character determines their external success. He also introduces a curious legend about a "mad laurel" that causes strife among sailors.</summary>
