### Alcinous’s Tale. XXXII

<margin>Alcinous’s Tale. 1.</margin>
<margin>I will not, however, tell an Alcinous tale, but that of a brave man, Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by race. <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ᾿ ὀυ μέντοι γε ἴω δ᾿ ἐγὼ Ἀλκινός γε ἀπόλογον ἐρῶ, ἀλλὰ ἀλκίμου μὲν ἀνδρὸς ἠρὸς τοῦ ἀρμενίου τὸ γένος παμφύλου.</note></margin>
"Alcinous’s Tale" refers to long-winded stories and old wives' fables. It is cited by Diogenianus <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD who compiled a collection of proverbs.</note> and Julius Pollux in his sixth book. The expression is taken from Homer’s *Odyssey*, where Ulysses, at a banquet hosted by Alcinous, King of the Phaeacians, recounts prodigious and ridiculous stories and monstrous lies—at least as they seemed to later critics—about the Lotus-eaters, the Laestrygonians, Circe, the Cyclopes, and many other such miracles, relying, it seems, on the ignorance and rusticity of the Phaeacians. Plato, in the tenth book of his *Republic*, writes: "I am not going to tell you an Alcinous tale," meaning a fiction, "but that of an excellent man, Er, the son of Armenius, of the Pamphylian people." Yet, in that very place, Plato tells a story that could easily compete with the fictions of the Laestrygonians and Cyclopes. For he writes that when this man had fallen among many others in battle, and his body was recovered ten days later while the other corpses were already rotting, his alone appeared whole and uncorrupted. Carried home to be buried with the proper ceremonies, on the twelfth day, just as he was to be placed upon the funeral pyre, he revived and told of the wondrous things he had seen during those ten days while he was living among the inhabitants of the underworld and then returning.

### Andabatae. XXXIII

This term is cited by Nonius Marcellus <note>A Roman grammarian who preserved many fragments of earlier Latin literature.</note> in several places, including under the word "Lusciosi" (the dim-sighted). Varro mentions it in his *Andabatae*, a title I suspect was a proverbial name for one of his satires, similar to many others he wrote, such as <margin>An ass at the lyre, Teaching an old man</margin> <note>original Greek: ὄνος λύρας, γέροντος διδάσκαλος</note> or *You Know Not What the Late Evening May Bring*. Marcus Tullius Cicero used it like a proverb in a certain letter to Trebatius in the seventh book of his *Letters to Friends*: "Whom before," he says, "we could not even cheat as an *Andabata*." Following this example, the divine Jerome wrote against Helvidius: "To prove this, he heaps up many examples from the scriptures, waving his sword in the dark after the manner of the *Andabatae*." The same author, writing against Jovinian, says: "We are endangered by the modesty of our response; it is as if we are between two rocks, a sort of Symplegades <note>In Greek mythology, the "Clashing Rocks" that crushed ships attempting to pass between them.</note> of necessity and prudence; on one side or the other, we suffer the shipwreck of either our shame or our cause. If we respond to the points proposed, we are flooded with shame; if shame demands silence, we seem to yield the field and give the adversary an opportunity to strike. It is better, however—as they say—to fight with closed eyes in the manner of the *Andabatae* than not to repel the direct arrows of truth with the shield of truth."

Again, in his second apology against Rufinus: "It is another matter if they wish to curse me with closed eyes, as the saying goes." And again in the same work: "There is a dialogue among the Greeks between Origen and Candidus, a defender of the Valentinian heresy, in which I confess I watched two *Andabatae* dueling with one another." I believe he alluded to this in his preface to Ezra: "It is another matter if they wish to curse me with closed eyes, as the saying goes." Jerome seems to have borrowed this from Tertullian, who in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* says: "If so abruptly, as some wish, they have—as they say—with closed eyes and without distinction cast out all flesh and blood from the kingdom of God." Thus far Tertullian. He said "with closed eyes" to mean "without selection" or "indiscriminately." Similarly, Augustine in his book against the letter of Parmenianus writes: "What force, if not blindness and vanity of mind, compels a man to throw something at another with closed eyes, as they say, which, once thrown, immediately returns and strikes him with a reciprocal blow, leaving untouched the one he wished to wound?" 

Whether there was actually a people who were accustomed to fighting in this way, or a type of gladiator who charged their opponent with closed eyes, or rather a type of game (as one might guess from Seneca), I must frankly admit I have not yet fully determined. Certainly, the word itself <margin>Andabatae</margin> indicates there were certain people who attacked the enemy in this fashion. Moreover, in the seventeenth book of the *Iliad*, Homer depicts Ajax entering the fight like a lion fighting for its cubs, leaping into the line of hunters with eyes covered:

<margin>Ajax stood covering the son of Menoetius with his broad shield,</margin>
<margin>standing like a lion over its young,</margin>
<margin>who, leading its cubs, is met in the woods</margin>
<margin>by hunting men. The lion, exulting in its strength,</margin>
<margin>draws down its whole brow, covering its eyes;</margin>
<margin>so did Ajax stand over the hero Patroclus.</margin>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

> But Ajax, defending on all sides with his broad shield
> The noble youth born of father Menoetius <note>Patroclus, the companion of Achilles.</note>,
> Stood like a lion fighting for his own offspring,
> Who, while leading his cubs, meets a band
> Of hunters in the woods, with pressing spears; he, 
> With his brow drawn down, covers his eyes.
> Thus surrounding the hero Patroclus, Ajax protects him.

Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> in a certain letter said, not without elegance, "night-fighting" <note>original Greek: νυκτομαχίαν</note>. He used it so that "for the future we may recognize those who are of the same mind as us, and not, as if in a night-battle, have no distinction between friends and enemies." <note>original Greek: ὥστε τὸ λοιπὸν γινώσκειν ἡμᾶς, τοὺς ὁμόφρονας, καὶ μή, ὡς ἐν νυκτομαχίᾳ μηδεμίαν φίλων καὶ πολεμίων ἔχειν διάκρισιν.</note> That is, "So that in the future we may know those who feel as we do, and not, as in a nighttime fight, lack any discernment between friends and foes." This will apply to those who, recklessly and without judgment, attack something or oppose someone. Nor would it be a bad fit for those described in the joke of Demonax, recorded by Lucian <note>A 2nd-century satirist known for his wit.</note>: "This one milks a he-goat, the other holds a sieve underneath," when one person makes an absurd proposal and the other responds to what was proposed with things that accomplish nothing.

<margin>XXXIIII</margin>
->Dog-like eloquence.<-

Sallust, quoted by Nonius Marcellus in the entry for "Rabula" <note>A "rabula" was a petty or brawling lawyer.</note>, says: "Dog-like eloquence, as Appius says, was practiced." This saying of Appius has passed into a proverb among learned writers against those who practice their study of eloquence only for the sake of slandering; the epithet is taken from the brawling and barking of dogs. Indeed, the letter "R," which is the first letter in "brawling" <note>original Latin: rixando</note>, is called the "dog’s letter" <note>because of its growling sound.</note>. Saint Jerome, in his letter to the monk Rusticus, writes: "They go out in public with processions of displays, so that they may practice dog-like eloquence." The same author frequently calls his detractors "dogs." This is taken from the school of philosophers whom they call "Cynics" <note>from the Greek word 'kyon', meaning dog</note>, either because of their filthy lifestyle or because they "bite" everyone they meet, since they live by begging, in the manner of dogs.

<margin>XXXV</margin>
->A Trojan hired tragic actors.<-

"A Trojan hired tragic actors." <note>original Greek: ὁ ἰλιεὺς τραγῳδὸς ἐμίσθωσε</note> This is used when someone voluntarily provokes another person, from whom he then hears of his own shames—as if the Trojans <note>referred to here as Ilienses, from Ilium, another name for Troy</note> were to summon an actor who would once again, as it were, renew the calamities they once suffered. Lucian in *The False Logician* writes: "For since, according to the proverb, you are a Trojan, you have hired tragic actors." <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ γὰρ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν ἰλιεὺς ὢν τραγῳδὸς ἐμισθώσω</note> He says the same elsewhere: "For we have truly suffered what happened to the Trojans: we have stirred up against ourselves one who has tragedies for sale, to sing of the disasters of the Phrygians" <note>Phrygian is often used as a synonym for Trojan.</note>. <note>original Greek: τὰ γὰρ τῶν ἰλιέων ἀτεχνῶς πεπόνθαμεν, τραγῳδὸν ὤνια ἔχον, ἐφ' ἡμᾶς κεκινήκαμεν, ἀσόμενον τὰς φρυγῶν συμφοράς.</note>

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
->Spending three minas, he bills twelve.<-

A proverbial irony found in Aristophanes’s *Plutus*:
"And yet you seem to me, by the gods, to be a friend indeed,
If for three minas spent you charge twelve." <note>A 'mina' was an ancient unit of currency; charging twelve for three is a massive overcharge.</note>
<note>original Greek: Καὶ μὴν φίλος γ' ἄν μοι δοκεῖς νὴ τοὺς θεὸς, / Τρεῖς μνᾶς ἀναλώσας γε λογίσασθαι δώδεκα.</note>
This will apply to those who cultivate friends only for the sake of their own profit, and expect a great many benefits in return for even a tiny service. In common speech they also say: "He gives a cap to receive a cloak."

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
->My right eye is twitching.<-

"My right eye is twitching." <note>original Greek: Ἄλλεται ὀφθαλμός με ὁ δεξιός.</note>
This is said when there is hope that we are about to see something joyful and greatly desired. It is derived from the superstition of common women, who are accustomed to divine what is about to happen from the itching of a limb. Hence those phrases often met with in Plautus: "My back is itching," "my teeth are itching," "my fists are itching," and, "Is it your teeth that itch, or your jaws?" Theocritus in his *Amaryllis* says:
"Look, my right eye twitches: shall I see her?"
<note>original Greek: Ἄλλεται ὀφθαλμός μου ὁ δεξιός. ἆρά γ' ἰδησῶ αὐτάν.</note>
It is also found in Plautus: "My eyebrow twitches." And today, people say in jest that their "right ear is ringing," signifying that a conversation is being held about them in their absence with praise. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist.</note> testifies that it was once a common belief that if a person was being praised while absent, his right ear would ring; if he was being slandered, the left. Lucian, in his *Dialogues of the Courtesans*: "So that, O Gargylion, your ears were ringing, for because..."

<meta>catchword: because for (διὰ γὰρ)</meta>

THE FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND
R 2
<meta>catchword: then phi-</meta>

<margin>“But indeed, the mistress remembered you with tears.” <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐμέμνητο ἡ κεκτημένη μετὰ δακρύων.</note> That is: Didn’t your ears ring, Parmeno? For the mistress was constantly remembering you with tears.</margin>

### Clouds on a wall. XXXVIII
Ausonius, in a certain letter to his son Gregory, spoke of "clouds on a wall" to describe something of no value, very much like a dream. "Did you never see," he says, "a cloud painted on a wall?" The title of the poem added to that letter signifies something frivolous and vain. For a cloud is a thing too empty to be expressed with colors.

### Do not be an uncle to me. To taste of uncles. XXXIX
The peculiar and natural severity of uncles toward their nephews gave rise to this proverb. Horace says in his *Odes*:
> Those who fear the lashes of an uncle’s tongue.

He calls an "uncle’s tongue" one that is severe and rebuking. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>, in the speech *Against Herennius* <note>Erasmus likely refers to *Pro Caelio* here, where Cicero discusses a stern uncle figure</note>, says: "There was in this case a certain uncle, a censor, a master." He rebuked Marcus Caelius in such a way as no parent ever did. Horace writes:
> Whether I wanted this wrongly
> Or rightly, do not be an uncle to me.

<margin>That is, do not punish me.</margin>
The phrase from Persius belongs to this same form:
> When we taste of uncles.

That is: after we have cast aside childish trifles and put on serious manners. The same poet, emulating Horace as he usually does, said: "Do not be a tutor to me," meaning, do not dictate to me or command me.

### To roll a stone. XL
<margin>“To roll a stone.” <note>original Greek: λίθον κυλινδεῖν.</note> That is: those who are exhausted by some inexhaustible and useless labor are said to roll a stone.</margin>
Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "I have been rolling this stone long enough now." Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence.</note> remarks that this was a proverb used against those who were afflicted by inescapable and useless toil, and he thinks it was drawn from the well-known myth of Sisyphus, who rolls a stone up and down in the underworld. Indeed, Terence aptly calls the stupid soldier a "stone," for whom the slave himself was a Sisyphus—crafty and clever.

### To take up a province. To hand over a province. XLI
In a proverbial figure of speech, those who entrust a business to be cared for are said to "hand over a province." Those who take the burden of caring for a matter upon themselves "take up" or "undertake a province." The metaphor is taken from the custom of the Romans, among whom those who held office were assigned different provinces by lot. Examples are found everywhere in authors. Terence in *The Self-Tormentor* says: "Clearly that servant of Clinia is a bit slow; therefore this province has been handed over to our man." Again in *Phormio*: "O Geta, you have taken up a difficult province." Plautus in *The Casket Comedy*: "Go to the country, go straight into your province." He calls the duty delegated to him a "province."

### Corinth both rises in hills and sinks in valleys. XLII
Strabo writes in the eighth book of his *Geography* that the Corinthians excelled in wealth and extraordinary arts, but their region was not very fertile because it was uneven, rough, and rocky. For that reason, this six-foot verse was tossed about as a proverb:
<margin>“Corinth is both beetling and hollowed.” <note>original Greek: Κόρινθος ὀφρυόετά τε καὶ κοιλαίνεται.</note> That is: in one place Corinth swells up, in another it is hollow.</margin>
Eustathius <note>A 12th-century archbishop and scholar.</note> also mentions this in his commentary on Homer’s "Boeotia." This kind of land is not as suitable for sowing as a plain is. I do not quite see where this adage might be useful, unless someone should twist it to describe an intractable man of a rough nature, who is inconsistent and little in harmony with himself. Caelius Rhodiginus <note>An Italian humanist scholar.</note> contends again and again that the proverb should be applied when we want to indicate a happiness spoiled by some inconvenience, as is generally the condition of human affairs. We would more willingly follow him as an authority if he had proven what he contends and asserts by the authority of even a single author.

### Healthier than Croton. XLIII
<margin>“Healthier than Croton.” <note>original Greek: Κρότωνος ὑγιέστερον.</note> Concerning a thing that is in no way harmful, but beneficial in every respect.</margin>
Zenodotus thinks the proverb is taken from a living creature. For there is a type of musical insect [called a *Croton*]; Theodorus translates it as a "tick," while Hermolaus prefers it to be called *ricinus* in Latin, a peaceful and harmless creature, troublesome neither by its bite nor by any other thing. Strabo, in the sixth book of his *Geography*, records that it originated because the site of the Crotoniates was once judged to be by far the healthiest—using this as evidence: that in a short space of time it produced as many as possible, both athletes and then phi- <note>The text cuts off here at the start of the word "philosophers."</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores several Roman and Greek adages related to social discipline (the "uncle"), useless labor (Sisyphus's stone), and the geographical reputations of cities like Corinth and Croton.</summary>
<keywords>Ausonius, Horace, Sisyphus, Roman provinces, Corinth, Croton, Sisyphus, educational discipline, Greek geography, health</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...then philosophers: that is, men outstanding in both body and mind. Among athletes, the most famous was Milo; among philosophers, Pythagoras. In the same book, he <note>Referring to the historian Strabo</note> relates that Myscellus and Archytas went to Delphi together to consult the oracle about founding a city. When the god offered a choice, Archytas chose wealth, while Myscellus chose a healthy location. Thus, the former founded Syracuse and the latter founded Croton. Consequently, one of these cities became a proverb for its opulence, and the other for its healthfulness. Palladas alluded to this proverb in an epigram:

> It was not without reason that I said there was a certain divine 
> and admirable power in *dizythum* <note>original: δίζυθος, likely a strong or "double" beer</note>. 
> For yesterday, when a man was suffering miserably, 
> exhausted by a long-lasting quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where the fever recurs every fourth day</note>, 
> I provided him with *dizythum*. Without much delay, 
> once I had done this, he became as healthy as a Crotonian.

->that is,<-

> A certain divine thing and a wonderful power
> In *dizythum* surely we spoke of, not rashly.
> For yesterday, a man whom a long quartan fever held,
> Now worn out and suffering miserably,
> I brought him *dizythum*: nor was there a long delay;
> Like one from Croton, once I had done this, he was healthier.

Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> prefers to refer the origin to the similarity of an animal <note>the tick</note>, because it is uniform on all sides and has no segments or incisions. For *healthy* <note>original: ὑγιὴς</note> is sometimes used to mean "whole" or "sound," just as we say "sound of life" <note>original: Integer vitae</note> or "sound of mind," for which the Greeks use the same word. It is, however, a type of insect <term>the tick; original: croton</term> that plagues dogs and cattle. This is the creature which Pliny mentions without a name in Book 11, Chapter 34: "It always has its head fixed in the blood; since it has no exit for its food, it eventually bursts from excessive fullness. It is never born on draft animals, but is frequent on cattle, sometimes on dogs (where it infests all parts), and on sheep and goats it is found only in the ears." 

However, Stephanus indicates that for the insect, the last syllable should be accented: *krotōn*. Hesychius adds that *Croton* is the name for a type of Egyptian gum, the various medicinal uses of which Pliny describes in Book 24, Chapter 11. Some say that *Sesamis* is also called *Croton*, perhaps the same plant Pliny calls *Sesamoides* in Book 25, Chapter 5, which he says was often mixed with hellebore so it could be taken more safely. That is, if I am not mistaken, a type of hellebore that Italy calls *veratrum*. Since this herb not only frees the body from otherwise incurable diseases but also purges the mind of madness, it seems quite probable that the proverb "Healthier than Croton" was derived from this. Dioscorides mentions *Sesame*, and Pliny mentions *Sesamē*. In Book 15, Chapter 7, Pliny mentions *Sesame* as a type of tree from which oil is usually made; some call it *Cyci* (an Egyptian word, it seems), others call it *Croton* <note>This is the Castor Oil plant, *Ricinus communis*</note>, others *rhibis*, and others wild *sisamum*. In the same place, he indicates that a similar type of oil is made from chestnuts and rice. Again, in Book 22, Chapter 25, he mentions *sesama*, the various uses of which in remedies he points out. 

Furthermore, I have not yet fully determined what *dizythum* is in the epigram, except that Pliny, near the end of the same book, shows that *zythum* is a drink discovered by the Egyptians made from grain; hence *dizythum* seems to be named as if you were to say "double beer." Even today, certain heavy drinkers treat their ailments with this.

<margin>XLIIII</margin>
### The last of the Crotonians is the first of the rest.

The last of the Crotonians is the first of the rest of the Greeks. <note>original Greek: Κροτωνιατῶν ὁ ἔχατος, πρῶτος τῶν ἄλλων ἑλλήνων.</note> Strabo, in the sixth book of his *Geography*, says this proverb arose because of the remarkable excellence of the Crotonians in the Greek games. For that city produced so many outstanding athletes that in one Olympic competition, the seven men who surpassed the others in courage and strength were all Crotonians. 

The chief glory of this people was Milo, celebrated in the writings of all, who won at the Olympics seven times in a row. If he took a stand, no one could move him from his spot. No one could straighten a single finger of his while he held an apple. Gellius mentions his wondrous death, which was not unworthy of his life <note>Milo reportedly died when he tried to split a tree with his hands; it snapped shut, trapping him until he was eaten by wolves</note>. 

There will be a place for this adage whenever we say that one group of people precedes another by such a great distance that the lowest member of the first group could appear as the leader of the second. For example, if someone were to say that the most cowardly of the Greeks in military matters is superior to the bravest of the Trojans. Or that one who is the most "wordless" <note>least eloquent</note> among Italians might appear the most eloquent among the Gauls. Or that the worst lyre-player could be considered the prince of flute-players.

He also introduces a related proverb about the extreme athletic superiority of Crotonians compared to other Greeks.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of proverbs derived from Greek geography and history. Having just discussed the health of Croton and the wealth of Syracuse, he now elaborates on specific Syracusan idioms before moving to the dangers of Cape Malea and the myths of Mykonos.</meta>

### Not even a tenth part of the Syracusans.
<margin>XLV</margin>
<note>original: οὐδὲ τὴν δεκάτην τῶν συρακουσίων ἔχεις</note> That is: *He does not possess even a tenth part of the wealth of the Syracusans.* Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian active around the time of Christ</note> writes in the sixth book of his *Geography*: "The phrase 'Syracusan' was applied to those who had fallen so far from their former wealth that they did not even measure up to the proverb, which says of those who do not live very sumptuously, that they do not have 'even a tenth of the Syracusans.'" This means that Syracuse reached such a peak of prosperity that it passed into a proverb. Indeed, regarding the rich and the splendid, people used to say that they could not achieve even a tenth part of the Syracusans' resources. They meant that the wealth of others, however great, was nothing compared to the riches of Syracuse. A bit of "Venus" <note>An ancient way of saying "wit" or "charm"</note> might be added to the proverb if it is twisted a little further; for instance, if someone, having first stated that Cicero leaves all others far behind him, should say that while the style of Quintilian is indeed wealthy and rich, it is hardly <note>original: τὴν συρακουσίων δεκάτην</note> "a tenth part of the Syracusan wealth" compared to Cicero.

### Rounding Malea, forget the things at home.
<margin>XLVI</margin>
Strabo, in the eighth book of his *Geography*, records that the city of the Corinthians, situated on the Isthmus, had two ports: one facing towards Asia, the other towards Italy. However, because the passage was like a narrow strait, it was not sailed without danger, just as in the Sicilian sea of old, especially when passing Malea <note>Cape Malea, the southernmost tip of the Peloponnese, notorious for shipwrecks</note>, due to the opposing winds found there. Hence, a proverb became famous:
<note>original: μαλέας δὲ κάμψας, ἐπιλάθου τῶν οἴκαδε</note> That is, 
*Rounding Malea, forget the things at home.* 
Malea is a promontory of Laconia, named after Maleus, a king of the Argives; it extends five miles into the sea, according to Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> in his notes on the fifth book of the *Aeneid*. In that same book, Virgil seems to have alluded to this proverb when he says:
> And the following waves of Malea.

Likewise, Statius in the seventh book of the *Thebaid*:
> And the wave sounds hoarsely around Malea.

Also in the *Tibur* of Manlius Vopiscus:
> If the ship must be trusted to Malea.

Homer also indicates in the ninth book of the *Odyssey* that navigation around Malea was dangerous, depicting Odysseus speaking thus:
<note>original: καί νύ κεν ἀσκηθὴς ἱκόμην ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν, ἀλλά με κῦμα ῥόος τε περιγνάμπτοντα μαλείαν καὶ βορέης ἀπέωσε, παρέπλαγξεν δὲ κυθήρων.</note>
->that is,<-
> And perhaps I would have returned safely to my fatherland’s shores,
> But as I was being carried past Malea, the wave and the current
> and the North Wind drove me away from there, and pushed me past Cythera.

Ovid alluded to this in his *Heroides*:
> You dared, O too much, and too much forgetting your own people,
> To touch the Thracian camp with a nocturnal deception.

For those who rashly throw themselves into danger seem to have forgotten their own people. Indeed, this is the one primary reason that deters the common people from undergoing the dangers of life: that they remember there are those for whom their safety is necessary (as Horace <note>original: Flaccus</note> says), and those whom they ought to and can benefit while unharmed, but to whom they would bring heavy grief if they perished. We shall seem to use this proverb not inopportunely whenever we wish to show the danger of an undertaking we are about to begin—either that it should not be undertaken at all, or that one’s life must be disregarded.

### Everything under one Mykonos.
<margin>XLVII</margin>
<note>original: πάνθ’ ὑπὸ μίαν μύκωνον</note> That is: *Everything under one Mykonos.* Strabo, in the tenth book of his *Geography*, says: "Mykonos is the island upon which they mythologize that the last of the giants lie, having been destroyed by Hercules. From this comes the proverb, 'Everything under one Mykonos,' used of those who bring things that are distinct by nature under a single heading." From these words, the usage of the adage is gathered more than the underlying reason for it. However, one may guess that since the greatest part and the remains of the giants were buried under Mykonos, it was commonly said that *all* the giants lay under it, even though others were situated under different mountains. Therefore, if someone in the same book teaches grammar alongside theology, and likewise logic and the writings of lawyers, it will be said of him quite aptly: "Everything under the same Mykonos." Or it may be used where diverse deeds are judged solely by what was done last. Mykonos is one of the Cyclades islands, according to Stephanus, who also mentions the proverb.

<summary>Erasmus explains three proverbs: one regarding the incomparable wealth of Syracuse, one warning of the life-threatening dangers of sailing past Cape Malea, and one criticizing the illogical grouping of unrelated topics under a single category, based on the myth of giants buried under the island of Mykonos.</summary>

<page-num>474</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

at the entry for Mykonos. However, Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and librarian at Alexandria</note> provides a very different legend that gave rise to the proverb. He says that Heleus commanded his sons, Hegetor and Hippocles, to conquer those islands scattered in the sea. Later, when Hegetor had attacked many and Hippocles only one—Mykonos—the latter nevertheless wished to be an equal partner in all the others. They consulted the oracle on this matter to see which islands should fall to Hippocles. The god replied: <note>original: μία μύκωνος</note> "One Mykonos." Plutarch used this elegantly in the first book of his *Table Talk*: <note>original: μίαν μύκωνον ἀκρούας τὸ συμπόσιον</note> "You are making the banquet one Mykonos," meaning that the guests were as yet indistinguishable from one another. From this, it is clear the saying was used for things that are mixed together or indistinct.

->XLVIII<-

->The Lerians are wicked.<-

<note>original: Λέριοι κακοί</note> *The Lerians are wicked.* This is rightly said against those who are all equally shameful due to a national vice. For the people of Leros became a proverb because of their notable wickedness of character, according to Strabo in the tenth book of his *Geography*. He cites the words of a certain Phocylides <note>A Greek gnomic poet known for his moral maxims</note>: "The Lerians are wicked; not this one while that one is not, but all of them, except Patrocles—and Patrocles is a Lerian." <note>original: Λέριοι κακοί, οὐχ ὁ μὲν ὃς δ' οὔ, πάντες, πλὴν Πατροκλέους, καὶ παροκλέης Λέριος</note> That is to say: the Lerians are bad, not in the sense that one is bad and another is not, but truly all of them, with the exception of Patrocles; and yet Patrocles himself is a Lerian. Leros is an island, one of the Sporades <note>A group of islands in the Aegean Sea</note> near the coast of Caria, which Pliny calls Lerion in several places, including the fifth book, chapter twenty-one. What is said here of the Lerians, Greek epigrams twist to apply to the Chians. The epigram goes:
*This also is by Demodocus: The Chians are wicked; not one is while another is not.*
*All except Procles—and Procles is a Chian.*
<note>original: Καὶ τόδε Δημοδόκου, Χῖοι κακοί, οὐχ ὁ μὲν, ὃς δ' οὔ. Πάντες πλὴν Προκλέους, καὶ Προκλέης δὲ Χῖος.</note>
In the Greek text of Strabo, the writing is faulty, as one should read *Parocles* rather than *Patrocles*. The translator must have used a more corrected manuscript, since the meter of the poem itself rejects "Patrocles." If you add "This also is by Demodocus," the couplet is complete. The saying is rendered more charming if you turn it from a person to a thing: for instance, if you say, "All fortune-tellers are liars, with the exception of Venantius, and yet Venantius is a fortune-teller." Or, "All soldiers are impious, with the exception of Langius, and yet Langius is a soldier." Ausonius <note>A Roman poet of the 4th century</note> imitated this Greek proverb regarding a certain Silvius, surnamed "the Good," who was a Briton by birth—a nation which even today commonly has a bad reputation among the French.

->XLIX<-

->He has sailed even to the Phasis.<-

According to Strabo in the eleventh book of his *Geography*, the Phasis <note>The modern Rioni River in Georgia, which flows into the Black Sea</note> is a gulf of the Euxine Sea and the goal of the furthest navigation, as the proverb testifies:
<note>original: Εἰς φᾶσιν, ἔνθα ναυσὶν ἔσχατος δρόμος</note> *To the Phasis, where the final course for ships lies.*
By "Phasis," he meant the region of Colchis, not just the Phasis river nor the city of the same name situated on the river. Theocritus says in his second *Idyll*:
<note>original: Πεζὸς δ' ἂν Κολχώς τε καὶ ἄξενον ἵκετο φᾶσιν</note> *On foot he reached both the Colchians and the inhospitable Phasis.*
Pindar uses a similar figure in his second *Isthmian Ode*: "But he used to cross to the Phasis indeed in the summer months, but in winter sailing to the banks of the Nile," <note>original: ἀλλ' ἐπ' ἄρα ποτὶ μὲν φᾶσιν ἔπλευσας, ἐν δὲ χειμῶνι πλευρὰ νείλοιο πρὸς ἀκτάς</note> that is, from Colchis to Egypt. For Strabo thinks the Phasians originated from the Egyptians, taking as proof their use of linen, which is so abundant among the Phasians that it is exported from there even to other regions. This is said of those who have traveled to the most distant regions of the world. Indeed, the figure itself is a kind of proverbial hyperbole, in the same way Juvenal said:
*In all the lands that exist from Gades even to*
*the Dawn and the Ganges.* <note>Gades is modern Cadiz; Ganges is the river in India—representing the West and East ends of the world</note>
And Horace in his *Odes*:
*If you were to drink from the remote Tanais, Lyce.* <note>The Tanais is the Don River, seen as the northern boundary of the world</note>
And Virgil in his *Eclogues*:
*But some of us will go hence to the thirsty Africans;*
*some will reach Scythia and the swift Oaxes of Crete.*
The expression seems to be taken from the story of Jason. It would be a similar figure if someone were said to have sailed "as far as the Pillars of Hercules," or "as far as the Britons," whom authors place outside the boundaries of the world because they are separated by the Ocean. Horace says in the third book of his *Odes*:
*I shall visit the quiver-bearing Gelonians,*
*and the Scythian river, unharmed.*
The same author in the same ode:

<page-num>475</page-num>
<header>SECOND CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

*I shall visit the Britons, fierce to strangers.* <note>Erasmus is quoting the Roman poet Horace, Odes 3.4.33.</note> The same poet says elsewhere: *And the Britons at the ends of the earth.* <note>Horace, Odes 1.35.29-30.</note>

<margin>L</margin>
### The boundaries of the Mysians and Phrygians are separate.

Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian</note> in the twelfth book of his *Geography* records certain neighboring regions, such as those of the Phrygians, Bithynians, Mysians, and Dolones. Also those of the Mygdones and Trojans, who live near Cyzicus. No one denies that each of these is circumscribed by its own borders. However, to judge those boundaries precisely is by no means easy. Furthermore, there was a proverb commonly tossed about regarding the Phrygians and Mysians in trimeter verse:
<margin>Separate are the boundaries of the Mysians and Phrygians.</margin>
*Separate are the boundaries of the Mysians and Phrygians, but to distinguish them is difficult.* That is:
The boundaries of the Mysians are separate,
and those of the Phrygians, but to define them is quite hard.
He provides the reason for this: these peoples did not defend their seats with enough stability, but were repeatedly driven from one place to another, rendering their boundaries uncertain. Pliny <note>A Roman naturalist and author</note> in his fifth book places Mysia within Phrygia. Plutarch, in his *Precepts of Health*, says: *For he said the professions of philosophers and doctors are separate, just like the boundaries of the Mysians and Phrygians.* <note>original: Χωρίς γὰρ ἔφη τὰ Φιλοσόφων, καὶ ἰατρῶν ὥσπερ ἰονίῳ μυστῶν καὶ φρυγῶν ὁρίσματα</note> That is, he claimed the profession of philosophers and doctors was distinct, no differently than the borders of the Mysians and Phrygians. To this day, such disputes over the borders of nations persist everywhere, with the long passage of time confounding everything. We may use this adage for things that differ entirely in their nature: for example, if someone, noticing that a philosopher and an orator aim at very different things, should say: *The Mysians and Phrygians are separate.* Or regarding men between whom there is no agreement and nothing in common, as Achilles says in Euripides:
*My affairs and those of Agamemnon are separate.* <note>original: Χωρίς τ' ἐμὰ καὶ τὰγἀμέμνονος</note> That is:
My affairs are separate from the goods of Agamemnon.

<margin>LI</margin>
### What the touchstone is to gold, gold is to man.

Among the many maxims of Chilon <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>, this one especially pleased the learned, according to Diogenes Laertius: *By which gold is tested on stone touchstones, giving a clear proof; but in gold, the mind of both good and bad men provides the test.* <note>original: ᾧ πλινθίναις ἀκὸναις ὁ χρυσὸς ἐξετάζεται... νόος ἔδωκεν ἔλεγχον</note> That is: Gold is explored on stone touchstones, providing a clear sample; but in gold, the character of both the upright and the wicked is detected. Stobaeus <note>A compiler of Greek excerpts</note> cites this poem from Antiphanes:
*Wealth is the touchstone of a man's character.* <note>original: πλοῦτος δὲ βάσανος ἐστὶν ἀνθρωπῶ τρόπων</note> That is:
Riches, like a pointer, prove a man's natural disposition.
Aristides alluded to this in his *Themistocles*: *Look at the man in this, starting from the line; and I do not mean the gold, but consider the touchstone itself.* <note>original: Ἐν τούτῳ ὅσα ἦν ἄνδρα... ἀλλὰ τὴν βάσανον σκοπῇ</note> That is: Behold the man from this point; I begin from the starting line. Do not consider the gold, as the saying goes, but the very indicator applied to it.

<margin>LII</margin>
### Beware of Thorax.

*Beware of Thorax.* <note>original: Φύλαξαι τὸν Θώρακα</note> That is: Beware of the Chest <note>A pun on the name of a mountain and the human anatomy</note>. Strabo in the fourteenth book of his *Geography* writes that there is a river named Letheus near the Hesperian Libyans; overhanging this is a mountain named Thorax, on which fame says Daphitas the grammarian was nailed to a cross because he had attacked kings with abusive poetry. From this, the saying spread among the common people, so that they would say: *Beware of Thorax.* That is: Beware of the Chest. By this proverbial riddle, we elegantly warn that the tongue must be reined in, lest voices petulantly emitted should one day return through the throat. Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a geographical lexicographer</note> only indicates that Thorax is a city of Aetolia, and also of Magnesia, but remains silent about the proverb.

<margin>LIII</margin>
### Abdera, the beautiful colony of the Teians.

Strabo in the fourteenth book of his *Geography* relates that when the Teians could not bear the insults of the Persians, they abandoned their city and migrated to Abdera, a city of the Thracians. And from this, that common saying arose:
*Abdera, the beautiful colony of the Teians.* <note>original: Ἄβδηρα καλὴ Τηΐων ἀποικία</note>
By this proverbial riddle, we signify that we do not lack a place to flee if someone continues to be troublesome beyond measure. Marcus Tullius Cicero perhaps alluded to this in the seventh book of his *Letters to Atticus*: *As for the power I hold, it is Abderite* <note>original: Ἀβδηριτικόν; likely implying a foolish or useless command, as Abderites were stereotyped as stupid</note>. And in the fourth book: *Here Abdera is not silent through me.* You will say: *Yet you do not keep quiet.* Forgive me, I hardly can. The Teians are also praised by Herodotus in his first book, because they preserved their liberty by leaving their homeland. Strabo mentions this too in his fourteenth book, not remaining silent in passing about the proverb, although the Aldine edition <note>The famous printing house of Aldus Manutius in Venice</note> is corrupted there...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's exploration of geographical and historical proverbs, specifically focusing on those derived from the Greek landscape and the early history of the theater. The previous page discussed the difficulty of defining boundaries between the Mysians and Phrygians.</meta>

<page-num>476</page-num>
<header>ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...it was preserved, as in many other places. My friend Joachim Vadianus <note>A Swiss humanist and scholar (1484–1551)</note>, a man equally sincere and learned, thinks the proverb fits when someone prefers a modest fortune, but one joined with freedom, over great wealth that is subject to servitude. I do not disagree with his opinion. For the air of the Abderites <note>The people of Abdera were proverbially known for their stupidity</note> was condemned, and likewise their pastures.

->A great city is a great solitude.<-
<margin>LIIII</margin>

Strabo <note>A Greek geographer</note> in the sixteenth book of his *Geography* says that Seleucia on the Tigris was larger than Babylon, but mostly deserted, and it could be said of it with the best right what some comic poet said of Megalopolis, a city of Arcadia: *A great city is a great desert.* <note>original: Ἐρημία μεγάλη ἐστὶν ἡ μεγάλη πόλις</note> That is, "A great city is a great solitude." This is a pun on the name of the city <note>Megalopolis literally means "Great City" in Greek</note>, which Pliny also mentions in his fourth book. It will apply to cities, houses, fields, or gardens, or anything of that kind that is large and spacious indeed, but poorly cultivated. It can also apply to a massive book that is unpolished and unrefined.

->To Scolon you shall neither go yourself, nor accompany another.<-
<margin>LV</margin>

Strabo, in his ninth book of *Geography*, writes that Scolon is a certain village of Atopia below Mount Cithaeron—a place unpleasant, uncultivated, fruitless, and harsh. And from here the proverb commonly spread: *To Scolon neither go yourself, nor follow another.* <note>original: Εἰς Σκῶλον μήτ’ αὐτὸς ἰμέν, μήτ’ ἄλλῳ ἕπεσθαι</note> That is: "Go not to Scolon yourself, nor as a companion to any other." Eustathius relates the same in the same words regarding Homeric Boeotia. For Stephanus also places Scolon in Boeotia. The name seems to have been given from the reality of the place, for *skolos* <note>original: σκῶλος</note> is a type of thorn among the Greeks. It will be appropriate to use this proverb if we ever mean that one should by all means abstain from the company of someone, or from a place where nothing is to be hoped for, whether for pleasure or for profit.

->Oenoe [invites] the ravine.<-
<margin>LVI</margin>

*Oenoe the ravine.* <note>original: Οἰνόη τὴν χαράδραν</note> That is, "Oenoe the bed of a torrent." For *charadra* among the Greeks signifies that fissure in the earth which rainwater, or a torrent, and sometimes an earthquake produces. Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and collector of proverbs</note>, in his collection of adages, says it was usually said against those who bring evil upon themselves. The proverb arose from this: Oenoe is a village in Attica whose inhabitants enclosed a nearby torrent bed within their borders. Then, with an excessive force of water rushing in and the fields being ruined because of it, they lost their farming. Strabo, in the eighth book of his *Geography*, mentions two places named Oenoe: one neighboring Eleutherae, the other at Marathon, about which the proverb is commonly tossed: *Oenoe the ravine.* He also records the adage in this way: *The Oeneans [and] the ravine,* <note>original: οἰναῖοι τὴν χαράδραν</note> where something is sought for convenience, but brings destruction instead. Hesychius records and explains this proverb from Demon, the author of proverbs. Stephanus indicates that Oenoe is one of the two cities belonging to Icaria. From which they are called Oeneans.

->Nothing to do with Bacchus.<-
<margin>LVII</margin>

*Nothing to do with Dionysus.* <note>original: Οὐδὲν πρὸς Διόνυσον</note> That is, "Nothing to do with Bacchus." This is said when someone prattles about things that have no relevance to the matter at hand. Various origins of the adage are handed down. Zenodotus says that in ancient times Dithyrambs <note>hymns to the god Bacchus</note> used to be sung to Bacchus in the choruses. Later, after the custom changed, they began to describe Ajax, Centaurs, and that kind of story. Therefore, the spectators shouted in mockery: "Nothing to do with Bacchus!" Warned by this insult, they thereafter began to introduce satyrs <note>the half-man, half-goat companions of Bacchus</note>, so that they might not seem to have forgotten the god entirely. Strabo, in the eighth book of his *Geography*, writes that when the city of the Corinthians was utterly destroyed by the Romans because of the violation of ambassadors, the soldiers insulted even the noble works of art with which that city abounded more than others. And he cites Polybius <note>A Greek historian</note> as a witness, who declares that he himself saw paintings thrown on the ground, on which the soldiers played dice. One of these was a painting of Bacchus by Aristides. Suidas reports that a certain Epigenes of Sicyon wrote a tragedy about Bacchus which seemed unworthy of the god, causing some of the spectators to shout: "Nothing to do with Bacchus!" And that phrase passed into a proverb. But he more approves the opinion of those who say that formerly poets used to handle subjects related to Bacchus, and those were eventually performed. Then gradually turning to writing tragedies, they wrote other stories and histories, leaving out...
<meta>catchword: of Bacchus</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's discussion of proverbs related to the theater and the god Bacchus (Dionysus). The previous page ended with geographical proverbs; here, he explores the expression "Nothing to do with Bacchus," which signifies irrelevance or poor comparison.</meta>

<page-num>477</page-num>
<header>SECOND THOUSAND, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

...mention of Bacchus. He says that the spectators therefore shouted, **Nothing to do with Bacchus.** <note>original: "Nihil ad Bacchum"</note> Chamaeleon <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note> is cited as a supporter of this opinion. Plutarch adds to this view in the first book of his *Symposiacs*, showing that the proverb arose from Aeschylus and Phrynichus <note>Famous Greek tragic playwrights</note>, who diverted their plot arguments toward historical stories and calamities. However, Theaetetus, according to the same Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> in his work on proverbs, writes that the painter Parrhasius <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BC</note> depicted Bacchus with the highest skill. Consequently, when a contest of skill was held among the painters at Corinth, and several produced paintings of Bacchus—none of which came close to Parrhasius’s Bacchus—the people shouted, **Nothing to do with Bacchus.** According to the same source, when someone called Coroebus <note>Proverbially known as a fool</note> by the name of Ulysses <note>Odysseus, known for his cunning</note>, the reply was: "You are bringing a dog to the manger, and you bring nothing to Bacchus." By both proverbs, it is signified that the comparison between Coroebus and Ulysses is far too unequal. Lucian, in his *Bacchus*, writes: *But what has this Dionysus to do with Dionysus? someone might say.* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ τί πρὸς τὸν Διόνυσον ἔτ’ ὁ Διόνυσος, εἴποι τις ἄν"</note> That is, what does this story about Bacchus have to do with the matter at hand? Thus, the adage seems to fit either a matter alien to the purpose, or something much inferior, or something contemptible. Plutarch, in the first of his *Symposiac Questions*, dealing with those who like to propose anxious syllogisms over their drinks—such as the one they call the "Master Argument" <note>original: "κυριεύοντα"</note>—says: *What has this to do with Bacchus?* <note>original: "τί ταῦτα πρὸς τὸν Διόνυσον"</note> In the same place, he says: *And I will send the rest shortly, if these do not seem entirely unskilled or irrelevant to Bacchus.* <note>original: "πέμψω δὲ καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ταχέως, ἂν ταῦτα δόξῃ μὴ παντελῶς ἀμῶα μηδὲ ἀπροσδιόνυσα εἶναι"</note> He used the word "irrelevant to Bacchus" <note>original: "ἀπροσδιόνυσα"</note> in a novel but quite elegant way, secretly alluding to the proverb. It signifies "not to be rejected" and "relevant to the matter." The same author, in the fourth book of the same work, says: *I think that the festival of the Sabbath is not entirely irrelevant to Bacchus.* <note>original: "οἶμαι δὲ καὶ τὴν τῶν σαββάτων ἑορτὴν μὴ παντάπασιν ἀπροσδιόνυσον εἶναι"</note> Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note>, in his eleventh book, writes: *attempting irrelevant solutions* <note>original: "ἀπροσδιονύσους λύσεις πραγματευόμενος"</note>; and in the third book, he mentions *unresponsive tunes* <note>original: "πάραυλα μέλη"</note>, meaning melodies that do not match the flute. Shortly after, he mentions *clashing cymbals* <note>original: "ἀκρότητα κύμβαλα"</note>, that is, cymbals not harmonizing with the rhythm of the dance. For he calls ill-timed speeches or things irrelevant to the matter "mythless stories" <note>original: "ἀμυθολογίας"</note>. We have spoken elsewhere of proverbs of this form: *Nothing to do with the verse.* Pindar, in the *Nemean Odes*, said *nor sing out of tune* <note>original: "μηδὲ μέλπ’ ἄχεθι"</note> instead of speaking otherwise than is fitting. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the sixteenth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, wrote: *But nothing seemed so irrelevant to Bacchus <note>original: "ἀπροσδιόνυσον"</note> to me at first as your writing those things back to me in response to the letters in which I had sought your advice.* Although some read *unexpected* <note>original: "ἀπροσδόκητον"</note> in this passage instead of "irrelevant to Bacchus." A similar kind of proverb is found in the same Cicero’s *Brutus*: *But let us return home.* As if interpreting this, he adds: *that is, let us return to our own people.* We still use this figure of speech today whenever we indicate that we are returning from a digression to what we had originally intended.

### To stuff patchwork quilts. LVIII
<margin>LVIII</margin>

Periphanes, in Plautus’s *Epidicus* <note>A Roman comedy</note>, says to a soldier who is preparing to narrate his battles in the usual military fashion: *Why don't you find someone else to stuff your patchwork quilts for?* <note>original: "Quin tu alium quæras, cui centones farcias"</note> That is, someone whom you can fill up with boastful lies and patched-together fables. For boastful men are accustomed to connect one lie to another, making no end or limit. "Centones" <note>Patchwork quilts</note> are garments stitched together from various scraps and sometimes even different colors. Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist</note> says:
> She entered the warm brothel with an old patchwork quilt. <note>original: "Intrauit calidum ueteri centone lupanar"</note>

By likeness to these, they call a type of poem a "cento"—one woven and, as it were, sewn together from different poems and fragments of poems summoned from here and there. The Greeks call them *kentrones* <note>original: "κέντρωνας"</note>, adding a letter which the Latins omit. There still exist "Homer-centos" <note>Poems made of lines from Homer</note>, which Saint Jerome also mentions, and the "Virgil-centos" of the woman Proba <note>A 4th-century Christian poet</note>, and the "Wedding Cento" of Ausonius <note>A Roman poet of the 4th century</note>, who even passes down the law of that type of verse.

### What I gave, I wish I hadn't given. LIX
<margin>LIX</margin>

The madam Melaenis in Plautus’s *Cistellaria* <note>The Casket Comedy</note> says: *In the midst of a new situation, I will use an old word: What I gave, I wish I hadn't given; what is left, I will not give.* <note>original: "Quod dedi, non datum uellem: quod reliquū est, non dabo"</note> She means she regrets having given the girl access, and will not do so in the future. The use of the adage will become more elegant if it is turned slightly away from its simple form—for instance, if someone, judging that they regret the previous effort they spent on the study of poetry and deciding not to waste more time on it, should say: *What I gave, I wish I hadn't given; what is left, I will not give.*

### Crocodile's tears.
<margin>60</margin>
**Crocodile's tears** <note>original Greek: Κροκοδείλου δάκρυα; original Latin: Crocodili lachrymæ</note>. This is said of those who pretend to be deeply distressed by the misfortune of someone to whom they themselves have brought ruin, or for whom they are currently plotting some great evil. There are those who write that the crocodile, upon seeing a human from a distance, sheds tears and then immediately devours them. The tears of the Emperor Bassianus <note>Known to history as Caracalla, reigned 198–217 AD</note> were very much of this kind, according to Aelius Spartianus <note>A historian in the *Historia Augusta*</note>. He would weep whenever mention was made of his brother Geta, whom he had murdered, or whenever he saw images of him. Others tell that this is the nature of the crocodile: when it is driven by hunger and is devising an ambush, it fills its mouth with a gulp of water and pours it out on the path where it knows other animals or humans will come to get water. This makes the descent slippery, so that they fall and are unable to flee, allowing the crocodile to seize and devour them. Then, after the rest of the body has been eaten, it soaks the head with shed tears and devours that as well.

### Even scraps are good after bread.
<margin>61</margin>
**Even barley cake is good after bread** <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθὴ καὶ μάζα μετ’ ἄρτον; the Latin heading "Bona etiam ossa" refers to "bones" or "scraps," but the text focuses on "maza," a coarse meal cake</note>. 
This is a half-line of heroic verse. Zenodotus <note>An ancient Greek grammarian</note> says it is usually said of those who, out of necessity, embrace worse things when better ones are gone. For **maza** <term>maza: a basic meal or barley cake, often considered the food of the poor compared to fine wheat bread</term> is something inferior to baked bread; it is a mixture of milk and flour which peasants are accustomed to using in place of bread. Indeed, we have shown elsewhere from Theocritus that wheat flour was once considered a luxury. A phrase found in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of *The Deipnosophistae*</note> (Book 6) has the appearance of a proverb, though it is slightly different: **Barley cake—or scraps—is dearer to a hungry man than gold and ivory.** This can be used when we want to say that a thing should be valued by its utility, not by common opinion. From the details Athenaeus provides regarding the preparation of banquets, it is clear that the barley cake was usually served first, and then the bread. But once the bread is consumed, even the barley cake is appreciated. We do as we can, when we cannot do as we wish. Xenophon, in the sixth book of his *Education of Cyrus*, depicts someone consoling soldiers who, having run out of bread, were forced to eat barley cakes. Those who live on this food are called **meal-eaters** <note>original: "ἀλφιτοσάγοι" (alphitophagi)</note>, just as those who live on bread are called **bread-eaters** <note>original: "ἀρτοφάγοι" (artophagi)</note>.

### If meat is absent, one must be content with salt fish.
<margin>62</margin>
**Salted meats must be approved by one lacking fresh meat** <note>original Greek: Ἄν μὴ παρῇ κρέα, σάρκτειον τῷ ταρίχῳ</note>. 
There are those who say that **tarichos** <term>tarichos: a general term for preserved, salted, or smoked meat or fish</term> is understood here as a fish, but a cheap and rotting one, the same as the **aphya** <note>a term for small, low-value fish like anchovies or fry</note>; perhaps here *tarichus* should be understood as a broth or sauce. For those who lack a main dish are accustomed to eating bread dipped in broth. There are frequent jokes about *aphyas* and *tarichos* in comedies. The meaning here is: when there is no abundance of better things, one must be satisfied with whatever comes along. This is recorded by Diogenianus.

### An Agathonian song.
<margin>63</margin>
**An Agathonian song** <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθώνεον αὔλημα</note>. This is rightly said of a speech that is charming rather than productive. Agathon was a certain flute player who soothed ears greatly with the sweetness of his songs. It is said that his character was not unlike his music, for he suffered from a reputation for "softness" <note>original: "molliciei," implying effeminacy or lack of moral rigor</note>. Both Suidas and Zenodotus are authorities for this. I am not sure if this is the same Agathon who was the victor in the tragic contest, at whose victory banquet Plato sets that famous dialogue, the *Symposium*. Aristophanes, in his play *Thesmophoriazusae*, mocks the softness of this man's poems in many ways.

### A gluttonous chariot.
<margin>64</margin>
**A gluttonous chariot** <note>original Greek: Ἀδηφάγου ἅρμα</note> was a saying used for gluttons and big eaters, because a chariot consumes a great deal of grease or axle-wax; or perhaps because keeping horses and chariots is an expensive matter. Hence the comic poet Aristophanes, in *The Clouds*, jokes about Strepsiades, whom his son had reduced to poverty by raising horses, contracting much debt. Flavius Vopiscus indicates that a certain **Phago** <note>A name derived from the Greek word for "eater"</note> was a favorite of Emperor Aurelian; this man allegedly ate a whole boar, a hundred loaves of bread, a wether <note>a castrated ram</note>, and a piglet in a single day at the emperor's table, and drank more than a large jar <note>original: "orca"</note> through a funnel. But more about this class of men can be found in Athenaeus's *The Banquet of the Learned*, where in Book 5, Socrates, seeing someone at a banquet gorging himself too immoderately on the side dishes, said: "O you who are present, one of you is using bread as a side dish, and the side dish as bread." It will be rendered more elegantly if you turn it toward a vice of the mind; for instance, if you say that the friendship of this or that prince is acquired and retained by an immoderate amount of money; or that desires are insatiable, even though the needs of nature require very little.

### To weep blood.
<margin>65</margin>
**To weep blood** <note>original Greek: Αἵματι κλαίειν</note>. This is a proverbial hyperbole signifying that there is nothing left to be done,

<meta>catchword: by which [quo]</meta>

<header>THE SECOND CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

...by which someone might be moved. For thus they used to speak in antiquity: "You will not move him, not even if you wept blood." Likewise, "to weep with blood" <note>original Greek: αἵματι κλαίειν</note>, that is, to groan with blood. This adage lasts even to this day. It seems to be transferred from portents, in which statues are sometimes seen to weep with bloody drops.

->### He feigns the death of a leopard.<-
->LXVI<-

**He feigns the death of a leopard** <note>original Greek: Θανάτου πάρδαλεως ὑποκρίνεται; original Latin: Pardi mortem simulat</note>. This was said when someone was plotting another’s destruction through cunning, just as when Brutus <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, who feigned idiocy to survive the tyranny of Tarquin the Proud</note> acted stupid and senseless so that he might later seize power. They trace this adage to a certain fable. In Mauretania <note>Erasmus uses the term "Maurusia"</note>, there is a huge abundance of monkeys. Now, the leopard <term>Pardalis; often used for leopards or panthers in ancient texts</term> is an animal by nature most hostile to monkeys, whom it cannot reach by strength because they fly up into the highest trees. Therefore, it uses these tricks against them: it stretches itself out on its back under the branches and, with legs extended, feigns death. The monkeys, trusting in their tree, rejoice at the sight. Then, when they think it is already dead, they send one down to explore whether the enemy is truly dead. She approaches cautiously and step by step; when she sees no sign of life—the leopard, of course, imitating a corpse in every way—she finally dares even to climb on it. As soon as the other monkeys see this, they cast aside all fear and descend, surrounding the leopard who bears it all. Finally, they trample it, insulting it for the sake of mockery, until the leopard, sensing they are now exhausted from dancing, suddenly revives. It seizes one with its teeth, another with its claws, tears them apart, and devours them. Truly, I have not found this story—lest I play the cheat with the reader—in any suitable author, but in the Greek collections of one Apostolius of Byzantium <note>Michael Apostolius (c. 1422–1478), a Greek scholar and refugee who compiled proverbs</note>, whose testimony Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Italian humanist scholar</note> also cites in a certain place, though he is otherwise not a very weighty author.

->### To bid one find a noose.<-
->LXVII<-

**To bid one find a noose** <note>original Latin: Mandare laqueum</note>. We use this expression for those whom we mean to neglect so much that even if they hang themselves, it is of no concern to us. Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> says of Democritus <note>The "Laughing Philosopher" known for his cheerful detachment</note>:
> When he himself bade a noose to threatening Fortune,
> And showed his middle finger.

Related to this is when we bid someone "to wail" <note>original Greek: οἰμώζειν</note>, that is, to weep; and "to wail loudly" <note>original Greek: μακρὰ οἰμώζειν</note>, that is, to weep clearly; and "to weep and bid a long farewell" <note>original Greek: καὶ κλαίειν καὶ μακρὰ χαίρειν</note>, that is, to weep and be well for a long time <note>A dismissive way of saying "go to the devil"</note>.

->### To show the middle finger.<-
->LXVIII<-

**To show the middle finger** <note>original Latin: Medium ostendere digitum</note>. Likewise, by extending the middle finger, they signified supreme contempt. Martial <note>A Roman epigrammatist</note> in Book 2:
> And hold out the middle finger.
For Martial calls this finger the "unchaste one" <note>Latin: impudicum</note>:
> He shows his finger, but the unchaste one.
Persius <note>A Roman satirist</note> calls it "infamous":
> With the infamous finger and purifying spittle beforehand.

I believe it pertains to this that in Laertius <note>Diogenes Laertius, author of "Lives of the Eminent Philosophers"</note>, Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic</note>—as we have said elsewhere—when some guests desired to see Demosthenes <note>The famous Athenian orator</note>, pointed him out not with his index finger but with his middle finger extended, hinting that he was hardly a man and effeminate. And a little later in the same place, he sufficiently indicates that something obscene is signified by the extension of the middle finger, when he says that those who extend the middle finger are considered insane, but not so those who extend the index finger. Thus, in the same verse, the Satirist <note>Juvenal</note> indicated extreme contempt with two adages:
> He bade a noose, and showed the middle nail.
Both will become more elegant if twisted further: as if you "bid a noose" to philosophical precepts and live according to your own custom. And merchants "show the middle nail" to the decrees of theologians; that is, they plainly despise and laugh at them.

->### To pluck the beard.<-
->LXIX<-

**To pluck the beard** <note>original Greek: Τὸν πώγωνα τίλλειν; original Latin: Barbam uellere</note>. This is also taken from a gesture—plucking the beard—by which we signify the highest contempt and mockery. Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet</note> in the *Satires*, Book 1:
> Playful boys pluck your beard.
Persius:
> For that reason Jupiter offers his stupid beard to you to pluck.
The same elsewhere:
> If a petulant harlot <note>original Latin: Nonaria, literally a "nine-o'clocker," a woman of the night</note> plucks the Cynic's beard.
And Dionysius the Sicilian <note>The tyrant Dionysius I of Syracuse</note> did not hesitate to pull the golden beard off Aesculapius <note>The god of healing; Dionysius famously looted temples</note>. Lucian <note>A Greek satirist</note> in his *Timon*, concerning Olympian Jove:
> You sat there while your locks were being braided <note>original Greek: ἐκάθου οὕτω πλοκάμους ἐπιπεπλεγμένος</note>,
that is, "You were sitting idle while your hair was being trimmed all around." And "he plucks the beard of a dead lion," said of one who is fierce toward the fallen—a matter we have touched upon elsewhere.

LXX

->### To strike with apples.<-

**To pelt with apples** <note>original Greek: Μήλοις βάλλειν</note>, that is, to seek with apples, is a phrase used for those who strive to achieve what they desire through gifts, or those who provoke mutual love with presents. The allegory is drawn from the fable of Atalanta, whom Hippomenes surpassed in a race, but did so by trickery; he threw down golden apples while running, and while the girl delayed from time to time to pick them up, the young man pulled ahead and won. Diogenianus records this adage. Plutarch, in his *Symposiacs*, indicates it was once a custom for people to throw apples, roses, and sometimes even pomegranates at those who were constantly victorious. From this, the adage seems to have arisen and was frequently said of those who greatly admire and approve of someone, or even those who flatter. Plutarch also relates in his ninth decade that when Anaxarchus was pelted with apples by Alexander after dinner, he stood up and recited this six-foot line from Euripides’s *Orestes*:
**Someone will soon be struck by a god’s mortal hand.** <note>original Greek: Βεβλήσεταί τις θεῶν βροτησία χερί</note>
It can also be understood more simply: to seek with apples when someone is provoked and challenged to love. Indeed, Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> interprets it this way. Hence that line in Virgil:
**Galatea, a mischievous girl, pelts me with an apple.**
And:
**I have sent ten golden apples, tomorrow I shall send others.**
And:
**I myself shall gather white apples with tender down.**
Even Acontius, in Ovid’s work, throws an apple inscribed with a message into Cydippe’s lap <note>Acontius tricked Cydippe into reading an oath of marriage aloud by writing it on an apple</note>. Aristophanes in *The Clouds* says, **Struck by an apple from a little harlot.** The commentator adds that the apple is a symbol of love because it is sacred to Venus. This is why, in the contest of beauties <note>The Judgment of Paris</note>, the prize was a golden apple, and it fell to Venus. Theocritus in his *Cyclops* says:
**He loved not with roses, nor apples, nor curls, but with destructive madness.**
The same author says in the *Hodoepori*:
**Clearista also pelts the goatherd with apples.**
In ancient times, small gifts consisted of apples, which is why Horace says in his *Epistles*:
**Let them hunt greedy widows with scraps and fruit, and catch old men to put in their preserves.**

LXXI

->### The sea will sooner bear the vine.<-

**The sea will sooner bear the vine** <note>original Greek: Τὸ πέλαγος πρότερον οἴσει ἄμπελον</note>. This is said of things that can in no way happen. For saltiness is most hostile to vines. Hence, I believe, Homer and Hesiod repeatedly call the sea **unharvested** <term>atrygeton; meaning literally "where no vintage is gathered"</term>, because no grape-harvest is gathered there. Salty earth is generally sterile for crops, but most hostile to vines. This is recorded in Diogenianus.

LXXII

->### To act like a beet, to act like a vegetable.<-

They commonly used the term **to act like a vegetable** <term>lachanizare; from the Greek lachanon, meaning garden herbs or vegetables</term> for being sluggish or languid, according to Suetonius in his *Life of Augustus Caesar*. In its place, Augustus innovated the word **to act like a beet** <term>betizare; from the Latin beta, meaning beet</term>. This will also apply to the dull and tasteless. Catullus says:
**More limp than a tender, hanging Sicilian beet.**
Likewise Martial:
**So that the bland beets of the craftsmen's lunches may have flavor, oh how often the cook will seek wine and pepper.**
The saying of Diogenes the Cynic, recorded in Laertius, pertains to the same thing: when certain youths called him a dog and said they would be careful not to be bitten by him, he told them to be of good cheer, for "a dog by no means eats beets," noting their softness <note>meaning he does not bother with "soft" or weak-willed people</note>. They call stupid people **bliteous** <note>original: Bliteos</note>. **Blite** <note>original: βλίτου</note> is a type of herb, and they think its name was given because of its dull flavor, almost like **stupid** <note>original Greek: βλάξ</note>, a word that signifies someone slow-witted and senseless. Aristophanes in *The Birds* says: **How stupidly you serve.** Plautus in *The Truculentus* says: **A courtesan is like blite and mud, unless she is wise in wine, for her own profit.** Laberius the mime-writer, in Nonius Marcellus, calls a tasteless and senseless person a **two-footed and bliteous beast.** In Menander’s work, husbands also insult their wives using the term for blite, calling them **bliteous.** Aristophanes in *The Clouds* says: **And they call you a dullard and a fool** <note>original Greek: βλίτημαν</note>. It is possible that the French word also flowed from here, by which they now commonly call the most contemptible and low-class men **Blitéros** <note>perhaps related to "blithering" or "blistre," suggesting a worthless person</note>, with a letter added.

LXXIII

->### More of a dispenser than a storer.<-

A truly elegant and proverbial iambic dimeter of Ausonius: **Both a dispenser and more than a storer...** <note>Erasmus is playing on the roles of the *promus* (who brings goods out) and the *condus* (who stores them away); someone who spends more than they save</note>

<summary>This page explores adages regarding symbolic gestures of affection (throwing apples), the impossibility of vines growing in the sea, and various metaphors for stupidity or lethargy derived from bland vegetables like beets.</summary>
<keywords>Atalanta, apples, Venus, Augustus, beets, stupidity, Diogenes the Cynic, botanical metaphors, Greek etymology</keywords>

--- Page 597 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on proverbs related to domestic management (the difference between a dispenser and a hoarder) before transitioning into adages concerning self-indulgence, unnecessary labor, and mismatched abilities or environments.</meta>

<page-num>481</page-num>
<header>FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND</header>

...rather a "steward" <note>original Latin: condus</note>, more lavish toward someone who knew how to squander what was acquired, but did not know how to seek or preserve what was sought. The metaphor is taken from household managers, especially those in charge of the larder, whom the Greeks call <term>stewards</term> <note>original Greek: ταμίας (tamias)</note>: whose role is to bring out [promere] certain things for the family's use, that is, to produce them, and to store [condere] others, that is, to set them aside. Now, he who only brings out [promit] hastens toward poverty and swift ruin. Plautus in the *Truculentus* calls those who are "sparing dispensers" [parce promos] filthy and stingy, as they gladly avoid expenditure.

### Indulging one's spirit. LXXIIII
Those figures of speech are also proverbial: **To defraud one's spirit**, meaning to deny nature what it craves; and **To indulge one's spirit**, meaning to follow one's inclinations. Terence in *Phormio*: "Defrauding his own spirit." Plautus in *Truculentus*: "But those who wage war with their own spirits, the sparing dispensers"—signifying the filthy and stingy. The same in *Aulularia*: "I myself have defrauded my spirit." Conversely, Persius in his fifth Satire:
> Indulge your spirit, let us pluck the sweets.
From this they also call a day "Genial" when it is joyful and pleasurable. And "To live genially" means to live softly and sumptuously. <note>The 'Genius' was considered a personal protective spirit in Roman religion, representing one's capacity for enjoyment and life force.</note>

### Tending to the skin. LXXV
Closely related is that figure frequent among poets: **Tending to the skin**. For those who care more for pleasure than reputation attend to this one thing: that the surface of their skin shines, and for that reason they employ washings, feasts, baths, ointments, sleep, banquets, and other luxuries of that kind. Horace in the *Satires*: 
> Order him to go home and
> take care of his skin. <note>original Latin: pelliculam curare</note>
->The same in the *Epistles*:<-
> You will see me fat, and sleek, and with well-tended skin,
> when you wish to laugh—a pig from Epicurus's herd. <space/> Persius,
> And the skin tended by the constant sun. <note>original Latin: curata cuticula</note>

<margin>See Cas. f. 256.</margin>
### You are looking for a knot in a bulrush. LXXVI
**You are looking for a knot in a bulrush** was said of an anxious, over-diligent, or fearful person who raises a doubt where nothing should be doubted. This adage is found in Plautus's *Menaechmi*, and in the very same words in Terence's *Andria*. Festus quotes from Ennius:
> You seek even in a bulrush, as they are wont to say, a knot,
explicitly citing the proverb by its title. According to Donatus, the bulrush [scyrpus] is a species of rush, smooth and knotless. However, in Gellius, "scyrpi" are called quibbles and subtleties. Unless perhaps one prefers to read "in the sea" <note>original Latin: in syrti</note>, where these little stones are smooth and round.

### He paints a dolphin in the woods, a boar in the waves. LXXVII
Horace in the *Art of Poetry* used a proverbial pattern when he said:
> He paints a dolphin in the woods, a boar in the waves.
This censures the folly of an unlearned poet who describes many things out of place and out of season, just as if a painter depicted a dolphin (a fish), following the saying of Callimachus, in the groves, or again a boar in the waves. Close to this is: <term>perfume on lentils</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν φακῆ μύρον (en phake myron)</note>, that is, perfume on a dish of beans.

### A crab catches a hare. LXXVIII
**A crab catches a hare** <note>original Greek: Καρκῖνος λαγωὸν αἱρεῖ (Karkinos lagon hairei)</note>. Said of a matter by no means likely, and absurd to speak of. Just as if someone were to say that a learned man is surpassed by the most unlearned.

### No roe-deer against a lion. LXXIX
**No roe-deer against a lion** <note>original Greek: Μὴ πρὸς λέοντα δορκάς (Me pros leonta dorkas)</note>. This means: do not contend, being far inferior, with someone more powerful. For the *dorcas* is a wild roe-deer. It is recorded by Diogenianus. Suidas records the full six-foot line:
**May I, a roe-deer, not join battle against a lion** <note>original Greek: Μὴ πρὸς λέοντα δορκὰς ἅψωμαι μάχης</note>. <space/> That is,
May I not take up a fight with a lion, being but a deer.
**I would not wish to enter a contest with a stronger man.** <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἂν ἢ ποτέροισιν ἐρίζεμεν οὐκ ἐθελήσω</note>. <space/> Homer, *Odyssey* 15 <unclear>ο</unclear> <space/> That is,
I would not wish to enter into strife with a more powerful man.

### To gnaw a dog's skin. LXXX
**To gnaw a dog's skin**, Martial seems to have used as a proverbial metaphor for an abusive and wicked man pursuing someone with insults. For he writes thus against a certain detractor and barker:
Perhaps there will not be lacking in this city,
