<page-num>482</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>Hh 2</sig>

One or two, three or four
Who wish to gnaw on a dog’s skin.

->Rougher than a sea urchin.<-
<margin>LXXXI</margin>
**Rougher than a sea urchin** <note>original Greek: Ἐχίνου τραχύτερος (Echinou trachyteros)</note>. This is said of a person who is intractable and has unpleasant manners. The metaphor is taken from the animal of which there are two kinds: the land variety, covered in spines <note>the hedgehog</note>, and the sea variety, which has a shell covered in fins and spines all over, which it uses to roll along like feet, according to Pliny. Martial writes:
> Once the shell is removed, the sea urchin will be soft.
Aristotle, in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, records that the urchin itself is quite small, but possesses spines that are both long and sharp. Athenaeus, in the third book of *The Deipnosophists*, recounts a rather witty little story from Demetrius of Scepsis: a certain Spartan, having been invited to dinner and served sea urchins, did not know how they were meant to be eaten. Not noticing how the other guests were consuming them, he grabbed one and threw it into his mouth, shell and all. Then, as the urchin crunched between his teeth and painfully tormented the man’s mouth, he said: "O wicked food! I will not let you go now to be easy on you, nor will I ever take you up again after this."

->The sea urchin delays birth.<-
<margin>LXXXII</margin>
**The sea urchin delays birth** <note>original Greek: Ἐχῖνος τὸν τόκον ἀναβάλλεται (Echinos ton tokon anaballētai)</note>. It is customary to say this of those who postpone something to their own detriment, such as those who delay paying back borrowed money, only to have to return it later with even greater interest. They say that the land urchin, when its belly is stimulated, holds back the birth; then, once the fetus has become rougher and harder due to the passage of time, it gives birth with even greater agony. The author is Suidas. Pliny, in book nine, chapter twenty-five, records that a fish called the <term>echineis</term> <note>the remora or suckerfish</note> can stop the flow of pregnant women and keep the fetus in the womb until the time of labor. However, this is **off-topic** <note>original Greek: ἀπροσδιόνυσον (aprosdionyson); literally "nothing to do with Dionysus," a proverb for something irrelevant</note>.

->First let two urchins enter into friendship.<-
<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
**Before two urchins should enter into friendship, one from the sea, the other from the land** <note>original Greek: Πρὶν ἢ δύο ἐχῖνοι ἐς φιλίαν ἔλθοιεν, ὁ μὲν ἐκ πελάγους, ὁ δ' ἐκ χέρσου</note>. This is said of those whose characters and interests are too different for there to be any hope of a close relationship ever forming between them. It would be quite elegant to adapt this to a specific situation: the "thorns" of the theologians do not sit well with polite literature; a sea urchin would sooner get along with a land urchin. For there is the sea urchin, about which Pliny and Aristotle say much, and there is the land urchin, which others call a <term>hedgehog</term> <note>original Latin: erinaceum</note>. What they have in common is that both are prickly, which is why they share a name. This is recorded by Suidas.

->The leech will not let go of the skin unless it is full of blood.<-
<margin>LXXXIIII</margin>
That line of Horace from the *Art of Poetry* also has the quality of a proverb:
> The leech will not let go of the skin unless it is full of blood.
It fits men who are excessively industrious or immoderate in any matter. You might see some of this sort who, once they have started, make no end of it until they stop from exhaustion. They have no consideration for the boredom of others, but measure the extent of the business only by their own inclination, not at all mindful of the ancient saying that warns us to stop playing while it is still pleasant, lest the annoyance of hatred follows and contaminates the pleasure. Everyone knows that once a leech has attached itself to the body, it cannot be pulled off by any means until it falls away, satisfied by the sucking of blood. Some call it a <term>bloodsucker</term> <note>original Latin: sanguisuga</note>, the Greeks call it a **bdella** or **bdellion** <note>original Greek: βδέλλαν/βδέλλιον</note>. It has a forked and hollow tongue, which it fixes deep into the skin. Pliny mentions it in book eleven, chapter thirty-four, and in the same place speaks of another animal, which has no name, that lives with its head always fixed in the blood until it bursts from excessive satiation, dying upon its own food because there is no exit for the meal.

->The ball is mine.<-
<margin>LXXXV</margin>
**The ball is mine.** That is, "I have won," or "I have obtained my wish," or "the matter is in my hand." This is found in Plautus’s *Truculentus*. It is taken from the well-known game of ball, where many chase it but one superior player captures it. He used a similar figure in the *Cassina*: "But if the mistress wishes to do her duty now, the whole lawsuit is ours"—meaning, "we have won." The metaphor is transferred from legal judgments.

->From the egg all the way to the apples.<-
<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
**From the egg all the way to the apples.** Horace used this proverbial figure in the third Satire of his *Sermones* to mean "from the beginning of the banquet to the end." 
> If he felt like it, he would shout "Hail Bacchus!" from the egg
> All the way to the apples, now in the highest [key]...

<summary>This page explores several animal-based and social metaphors, including the prickly nature of urchins (comparing them to theologians), the persistence of leeches, and common phrases for the beginning and end of activities.</summary>
<keywords>urchin, hedgehog, leech, Horace, Pliny, Aristotle, social manners, proverbs, banquet customs, Plautus</keywords>

<page-num>483</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD II. CENTURY IV.</header>
<sig>S 2</sig>

...with that voice, which now resonates from the lowest of the four strings <note>original: "Voce, modo hac resonat quæ chordis quatuor ima." This refers to Horace, *Satires* 1.3.6-7</note>. 
For in ancient times, they began a banquet with eggs and ended with apples. It will be more elegant if the expression is drawn out further, **From the egg all the way to the apples** <note>original: "Ab ouo usq; ad mala"</note>: that is, through the whole conversation, the whole voyage, or the whole work. Those who trace a matter back further than is necessary are noted by that Horatian verse:
> Nor does he begin the Trojan war from the twin egg <note>original: "Nec gemino bellum Troiano orditur ab ouo." A reference to the birth of Helen of Troy</note>.
Those who seek things from the very first beginnings are said to start **from the roots** <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν ῥιζῶν (ek tōn rhizōn)</note>, that is, from the roots and the lowest stems; they omit nothing and narrate in order. Also **From the head to the heel**, which we have mentioned elsewhere, is called by the Greeks **from above** <note>original Greek: ἄνωθεν (anōthen)</note> and **from the beginning** <note>original Greek: ἀρχῆθεν (archēthen)</note>.

---

->Virtue and wisdom are conquered by tortoises.<-
<margin>LXXXVII</margin>

Julius Pollux, in the ninth book of his *On Vocabulary*, writes that this verse was once a celebrated proverb:
> Virtue and wisdom are conquered by tortoises. <note>original Greek: τὰν ἀρετὰν, καὶ τὰν σοφίαν νικᾶντι χελῶναι (tan aretan, kai tan sophian nikanti chelōnai)</note>
That is, both virtue and wisdom yield to tortoises. It is, however, like a riddle, hinting that money has far more power than either virtue or wisdom. For in ancient times, the coinage of the Peloponnesians was called a **tortoise** <note>original: "testudo"; Greek: χελώνη (chelōnē)</note>, because of the figure of a tortoise engraved upon it. As a witness to this matter, he cites Eupolis, who in the play titled *The Captives*, called an obol <note>a small coin</note> **of the beautiful tortoise** <note>original Greek: καμιλελάνου (kamilelanou), likely a corruption of "of the beautiful tortoise"</note>. By a similar figure of speech, it was also said: **Many owls lurk under the roof-tiles** <note>referring to Athenian coins stamped with an owl</note>, and **An ox on the tongue** <note>referring to coins stamped with an ox</note>; both of which we have discussed in their own places.

---

->These sacred rites do not consist otherwise.<-
<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>

**These sacred rites do not consist otherwise.** This adage may be used whenever we admit a fault, but one that is appropriate to the circumstance or place: for example, if one acts somewhat shamelessly in the baths, or more rustically on a ship, or more intemperately in the drinking-bouts of drunkards, or more foolishly among silly women, or more deceitfully among courtiers, or more talkatively among the sophists <note>rhetoricians or philosophers</note>, or more flatteringly before the common people. Ausonius, excusing the license of his *Nuptial Cento*, says: "For it is a story about a wedding, and whether one likes it or not, **these sacred rites do not consist otherwise**." The metaphor is taken from religious rites, which are performed with certain specific ceremonies; if you change anything in them, it is considered an admitted sin. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Listening to the Poets*, writes: 
> For we know of sacrifices without choruses and flutes, but we do not know of poetry without myth and falsehood. <note>original Greek: θυσίας μὲν γὰρ ἀχόρους καὶ ἀναύλους ἴσμεν, οὐκ ἴσμεν δὲ ἀμύθου οὐδ’ ἀψευδοῦς ποιήσεως</note>

---

->Spring follows winter.<-
<margin>LXXXIX</margin>

**Spring follows winter.** By this adage, we signify the cycles of things which necessarily follow one another: as if someone, persuading another that the mind should be bolstered by the hope of better things in times of affliction, should say: "Spring follows winter," meaning that more joyful things will follow the sad. Thus Pindar, in his fourth *Isthmian Ode*:
> But now again, after the wintry gloom of changing months, the earth blossoms as if with crimson roses. <note>original Greek: νῦν δ’ αὖ μετὰ χειμέριον ποικίλου μηνῶν ζόφον, χθὼν ἅτε φοινικίοις ἄνθος ῥόδοις</note>
Ausonius, in his preface to the *Monosyllables*, made some use of this proverb. As the old saying goes: "Spring follows winter." I now weave in the naughtiness of similar trifles.

---

->A lover's oath.<-
<margin>XC</margin>

**A lover’s oath is not punished.** <note>original Greek: Ἀφροδίσιος ὅρκος οὐκ ἐμποίνιμος (Aphrodisios horkos ouk empoinimos)</note> The sense is that the oaths of lovers are void, and they do not concern the gods at all, being treated as a joke. As Ovid <note>referred to as "Naso"</note> writes:
> Jupiter from on high laughs at the perjuries of lovers, and bids the winds carry them into the sea.
And Horace:
> I say, Venus herself laughs at this; the simple nymphs laugh too.
And Tibullus:
> Jupiter laughs at the perjuries of lovers, and bids the winds carry them away as void.
This adage is cited by Plato in the *Symposium*: 
> And what is most extraordinary of all, as common folk say, is that to one who is in love, and to him alone, the gods grant pardon for breaking an oath. For they say a lover’s oath does not exist; so much do both gods and men permit everything to a lover. <note>original Greek: ὃ δ’ αἰνότατον... Ἀφροδίσιον γὰρ ὅρκον, οὔ φασιν εἶναι</note> 
In Plato’s words, the little word **punishable** <note>original Greek: ἐμποίνιμον (empoinimon)</note> seems to be missing. Procopius also mentions this in his last letter to Epiphanius: 
> Beautifully, therefore, does he who understands the sufferings of lovers, even if they wish to commit perjury, promise them pardon from the gods. <note>original Greek: καλῶς ἄρα καὶ ὁ τὰ τῶν ἐρώντων πειθόμενος πήματα...</note> That is: He beautifully understands the affe- <note>the text breaks off here to the next page</note>

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

...a proverb concerning the affection of lovers promises them forgiveness from the gods, even if they should choose to swear falsely. Plato in the *Philebus*, as cited by Athenaeus in Book 12: <note>original Greek: ὡς ὁ λόγος, καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἡδοναῖς ταῖς περὶ ἀφροδίτην... (hōs ho logos, kai en tais hēdonais tais peri aphroditēn...)</note> "As the saying goes, even in the pleasures of Aphrodite—which truly seem to be the greatest—swearing falsely has received forgiveness from the gods, just as if they were children, because they no longer possess a mind capable of reasoning." That is, as it is said, even in the pleasures concerning sexual matters, which certainly seem to be the most intense, perjury is granted pardon by the gods, exactly as if these pleasures were like children who are not yet masters of their reason.

There is also a reference from Callimachus:
-> He swore, but they say the gods do not let the oaths of <-
-> lovers enter the ears of the immortals. <-
<note>Erasmus provides the Greek text: ὤμοσεν, ἀλλὰ λέγουσι θεοὺς οὐ δ’ ὤμοτ’ / Ὅρκους μὴ δύνειν ὤατ’ ἐν ἀθανάτων.</note>
Which means:
He swore; but the common people say that in love,
The things you swear do not reach the ears of the gods.
The first verse is not without a textual error. This proverb can be applied to any promise where it seems that one's word need not be kept.

<margin>91</margin>
## Like my own name; Like my fingers.

These are proverbial exaggerations: **I hold it like my own name** and **I hold it like my fingers**, used whenever we wish to indicate a prompt and certain memory. Martial says:
> You tell me these things every day, Afer:
> And I remember them better than my own name.
<note>original: "Teneo melius ista, quàm meum nomen."</note>
Juvenal says:
> As well as his own nails and fingers.
<note>original: "Tanquam ungues digitosq́; suos."</note>
We remember nothing better than our own name; hence, in ancient times, they used to call out to the deceased by their own names. Furthermore, we call a person of monstrous forgetfulness "one who has forgotten his own name." In ancient times, counting was performed on the fingers; a booklet by Bede <note>The Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk</note> exists on that subject. Indeed, even today, people are jokingly accustomed to ask an unskilled or forgetful person how many fingers he has on his hands. Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How a Man May Become Aware of His Progress*, writes that it was once a custom to learn the names of the fingers by heart, and to use these as remedies when in fear. I will add his own words: <note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἐκμεμαθηκότες τὰ τῶν ἰδίων ὀνόματα δακτύλων... (hoi men gar ekmemathēkotes ta tōn idiōn onomata daktylōn...)</note> "For some learn the names of their own fingers and use them against fears, as if they had a remedy to drive away evils, reciting each one by one." What the Greek names for the fingers are, Gellius indicated in his *Attic Nights*. Caelius Calcagninus, as Aleander indicates, prefers this to be understood as the names of the "Idaean Dactyls" <note>Ancient mythical beings associated with the fingers</note>, whom we shall touch upon in the proverb: **Celmis in iron**, although in Plutarch the word used is "strength" <note>Greek: ἄλκη (alkē)</note> and not "Idaean" <note>Greek: ἰδαίων (idaiōn)</note>.

---

<margin>92</margin>
## Balls of good things.

**Balls of good things** <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθίδες (Agathōn agathides)</note>. That is, a ball of "goods": used for wealth that has been built up and abundantly accumulated. The metaphor is taken from a weaver's ball of yarn, around which threads are wound, or perhaps from that weaver's spool around which a great quantity of thread is wound, which they also call a *pēnion* <note>a bobbin or pirn</note>. Julius Pollux mentions this proverb in Book 7, Chapter 10, indicating it is very frequent among comic poets. It seems, however, to be a pun on the names *Agathide* and *Agathis*; just as Thucydides, in an epigram of Euripides, calls Athens "the Greece of Greece" <note>original Greek: ἑλλάδος ἑλλάδα (hellados hellada)</note>. In Book 5, he attributes this sentiment to Pindar. And just as the Greeks say "the extremes of extremes" <note>original Greek: ἔσχατα ἐσχάτων (eschata eschatōn)</note> or "the evils of evils" <note>original Greek: κακὰ κακῶν (kaka kakōn)</note>, a figure of speech which the Latins do not use.

---

<margin>93</margin>
## You have touched the matter with a needle.

This is found in Plautus’s *The Rope*: **You have touched the matter with a needle** <note>original: "Rem acu tetigisti"</note>, meaning "you have guessed the thing itself," erring in nothing. The metaphor can be seen as taken from some game in which the guesser touched with the very tip of a needle the thing another had marked: either a line, a pebble, or something similar. Therefore, "to touch with a needle" is just as if you were to say, "to touch the very point itself." For the smallest points are marked by a needle.

---

<margin>94</margin>
## With cleansed ears.

**With cleansed ears** <note>original: "Purgatis auribus"</note>, meaning attentive and free from distraction, has a proverbial flavor. Plautus in *The Braggart Soldier*:
> We both give you our attention with thoroughly cleansed ears.
<note>original: "Perpurgatis ambo damus tibi operam auribus."</note>
Horace in his *Epistles*:
> I have one who frequently rings in my cleansed ear.
<note>original: "Est mihi purgatam crebro qui personet aurem."</note>
Persius in his fifth Satire:
> This Stoic, his ear washed with biting vinegar.
<note>original: "Stoicus hic aurem mordaci lotus aceto."</note>
For the filth collected in the ears dulls the hearing; when it is removed, it makes it sharper.

<page-num>485</page-num>
<header>FIFTH HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND</header>
<sig>S 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Proverb</meta>

->Cleaner than a tiller.<-
<margin>XCV</margin>
<term>Cleaner than a tiller</term> <note>original Greek: Ἁγνότερος πηδαλίου (Hagnoteros pēdaliou)</note>. That is, purer than a rudder. This is a proverbial comparison for something that is vehemently blameless, or for a character that is in every respect upright and untainted. For a nautical tiller is washed by the continuous flow of waves, so that no filth can cling to it. This adage is recorded by Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>.

->From the lime-kiln to the coal-shed.<-
<margin>XCVI</margin>
Whenever it happens that we wander from the matter at hand to something else entirely different, we are said to "run down from the lime-kiln into the coal-shed"; or likewise, when we fall from one evil into a different one. Tertullian says in his book *On the Flesh of Christ*: "Therefore, as the saying goes, from the lime-kiln to the coal-shed—from Marcion to Apelles" <note>referring to jumping from one heretic to another</note>. Not unlike this is that passage from Cicero in his speech *For Murena*: "I will therefore respond first to Posthumius, who, I know not how, seems to me like a candidate for the praetorship running into the race for the consulship—like a trick-rider leaping into a four-horse chariot race."

->Datylus's day.<-
<margin>XCVII</margin>
<term>Datylus's day</term> <note>original Greek: Δατύλου ἡμέρα (Datylou hēmera)</note>. That is, the day of Datylus. Used when things have succeeded happily. It is taken from a certain Datylus who achieved the highest honors among the Athenians.

->To nourish a monster.<-
<margin>XCVIII</margin>
A monster is nourished when we signify that some hidden vice is lurking. I suspect the metaphor is taken from the fact that "monsters" (shameful secrets) are nourished and hidden away in private out of a sense of shame. Indeed, Pamphilus in Terence's play *Andria*, because he—having been previously rejected as a son-in-law—was being sought after again for a marriage alliance, suspected there was some flaw in the girl that was being concealed. He says: "Having been rejected, I am sought again. Why? Unless it is what I suspect: they are nourishing some monster. Since she can be pushed onto no one else, they come to me."

->The wolf does not care for the number.<-
<margin>XCIX</margin>
This proverb tastes of that Virgilian line in the *Eclogues*:
> Here we care for the cold of the North Wind as much as
> The wolf cares for the number [of sheep], or the flooding rivers for their banks.
It is rightly said of a person who is shamelessly thievish. There exists even today a commonly tossed-about adage: "The wolf does not fear to devour even the sheep that have been counted." Furthermore, thieves who are a little more timid are accustomed to keep their hands off of things that have been counted, for fear, clearly, that they might be caught by this evidence. Akin to this is that witty joke about a thievish slave, for whom nothing in the house was left unclosed or unsealed.

->It pleases them.<-
<margin>C</margin>
<term>It pleases them</term> <note>original Greek: Αὐτοῖς ἀρέσκει (Autois areskei)</note>. This is used when we signify that a matter is little approved by us, or that the cause does not concern us at all. Terence in the *Andria*: "It does not seem likely to me. And yet, the invention pleases them." It is not very far removed from that other saying, "To each his own is beautiful," or that everyone is flattered by their own plans and their own opinion. To this belongs that frequent phrase in Homer: <term>since it pleased his heart</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ ἄδεν θυμῷ (epei aden thymō)</note>. Also that phrase in the comic poets: "So it has pleased my mind." And in Virgil: "It seemed otherwise to the gods." Plato, in the third book of *The Laws*, recorded this proverb.

---

### THE FIFTH HUNDRED OF THE SECOND THOUSAND

->You have obtained Sparta, adorn it.<-
<margin>I</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a classical figure or deity amidst foliage.</image-desc>
**S**<term>parta is your lot, adorn it</term> <note>original Greek: Σπάρταν ἔλαχες, ταύταν κόσμει (Spartan elaches, tautan kosmei)</note>. That is: Adorn, or rather administer, the Sparta you have obtained. The adage warns that whatever province or station we have obtained by lot, we should accommodate ourselves to it and conduct ourselves according to its dignity. Marcus Tullius Cicero to Atticus, Book 4, Epistle 6: "What remains is: 'Sparta is my lot, I must adorn it.' By Hercules, I cannot. And I forgive Philoxenus, who preferred to be led back to prison." Also to the same man in Book 1: "That cause which you say has fallen to me as my 'Sparta,' I will not only never abandon, but even if I am abandoned by it, I will remain in my former opinion." What is cited by Cicero is an anapestic verse from some tragedy: "You have obtained Sparta, adorn this." The commentator on Theocritus indicates an allusion to this proverb in the *Idylls*:
<term>Contend with me there, and there together pasturing the bulls.</term>
<term>Treading your own land, keep to your own oaks.</term> That is,
> Compete with me here, and at the same time feed the bulls here.
> And treading your own land, do not desert the oaks.

<vocab>Erasmus, Adagia, Suidas, Tertullian, Cicero, Terence, Virgil, Plato, Homer, Theocritus, Sparta</vocab>

<keywords>cleanliness, digression, luck, hidden vices, thieves, self-satisfaction, duty, Sparta, classical literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient adages, specifically transitioning into a lengthy and famous moral and political reflection on the proverb "Sparta is yours; adorn it." It follows the previous page's discussion of short, pithy nautical and day-to-day comparisons.</meta>

<page-num>486</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

This proverb can therefore be adapted to various uses: for instance, when we advise that each person should maintain the decorum of the role they have undertaken. You are a Bishop: do not act like a satrap <note>a provincial governor in the ancient Persian empire, often associated with luxury and tyranny</note>, but like a bishop. You are a husband: care for the duties that belong to a husband. You are a courtier: act the part of a courtier. You are a judge: do not act as a friend or an enemy, but as a judge. Leadership has fallen to you: perform the office of a leader. You are a private citizen: conduct yourself as a private person. Aristophanes used it in much the same way. (For the comedy titled *Thesmophoriazousae* <note>original: θεσμοφοριάζουσαι; a play about women celebrating a festival</note> is attributed to him):

*It is right for a man who is a poet, regarding the dramas*
*Which he must compose, to have a character suited to them.*
<note>original Greek: Χρὴ γὰρ ποιητὴν ἄνδρα πρὸς τὰ δράμματα / Ἃ δεῖ ποιεῖν, πρὸς ταῦτα τοὺς τρόπους ἔχειν.</note>

Or it can be used when we command that everyone ought to be content with their own lot, whatever has befallen them. For just as a skilled pilot proves himself a good captain in every storm, so a wise man conducts himself wisely in every fortune. You have an ample family estate: manage it wisely. You do not: then utilize the advantages of poverty. Learning has fallen to your lot: use it to live well. It has not: do not let it waste you away; piety is enough to achieve salvation. Plutarch, in his essay *On Contentment* <note>original: περὶ τῆς εὐθυμίας (Peri tēs euthymias)</note>, advising that everyone should be satisfied with their own lot, says: **Sparta fell to you; adorn her.**
<note>original Greek: σπάρταν ἔλαχες, ταύτην κόσμει (Spartan elaches, tautēn kosmei).</note>

In the same book, he notes that this saying was handed down by Solon <note>an Athenian statesman and poet, one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>. It is also cited from Euripides:

*Sparta fell to you; adorn her,*
*But Mycenae is ours alone.*
<note>original Greek: Σπάρτην ἔλαχες, κείνην κόσμει, / Τὰς δὲ Μυκήνας ἡμεῖς ἰδίᾳ.</note>

These seem to be the words of Agamemnon to Menelaus. This is close to that Platonic saying: **Dispose of the present well.** <note>original: τὸ παρὸν εὖ τίθεσθαι (to paron eu tithesthai)</note>. That is: arrange what is at hand well, or be satisfied with it. Nowadays, the common crowd of men is more intent on increasing their property than on managing it well—contrary to what Socrates rightly advises in Plato’s *Theaetetus*: **For it is better, I suppose, to finish a little well than much insufficiently.** <note>original Greek: κρεῖττον γάρ που σμικρὸν εὖ, ἢ πολὺ μὴ ἱκανῶς περᾶναι.</note>

Therefore, this sentiment ought to have been inscribed everywhere in the courts of princes: **Sparta fell to you; adorn her.** You will hardly find any of them who truly considers what it means to play the role of a prince, or who, content with his own jurisdiction, does not try to add something to the borders of his empire. A prince’s duty is to provide for the interests of the commonwealth in every way; to protect public liberty; to nourish peace; to shut out crimes with as little destruction to his people as possible; and to see to it that he has holy and upright magistrates. When, therefore, he is indifferent to these things and plays at dice, dances, womanizes, plays music, hunts, trades, and in short is entirely focused elsewhere, then this adage must be shouted: **Sparta fell to you; adorn her.**

Again, when he neglects the jurisdiction that fell to him and acts abroad, gaping after other empires, bringing his own people into the greatest danger, exhausting them utterly, and subjecting himself and his entire fortune to the dice of war—all to add one or two little towns to his borders—then the adage should be suggested: **You have obtained Sparta.** Nothing is more beautiful for a prince than to make this kingdom, whatever it is that fortune gave him, more adorned by his own wisdom, virtue, and diligence. A small town fell to you? Imitate Epaminondas <note>a Theban general and statesman</note>: see to it that by your efforts you make that cold little town much more famous and wealthy. A wild and unmanageable nation fell to you? Work to make it gradually tame and obedient to the laws. A kingdom of little splendor fell to you? Do not harass your neighbors, but adorn what you have without harm to others.

An appetite for foreign rule has hardly ever ended happily. Certain nations are separated by temperament and the sound of their language, such as Germans and Spaniards; some nature itself has divided, such as islanders by the sea, or Italians by both the sea and the mass of the Alps; to others, chance has given their own boundaries. If everyone strove to adorn what they had obtained, surely everything would flourish everywhere. And among friends—Christian friends, of course—all things would be shared by all. Now it often happens that while we strive to undermine the things of others, we utterly subvert our own. And even if the matter turns out "successfully," at the cost of so much blood of our citizens, so much expense, so many dangers, so much sweat, so many bereavements, and finally so many evils that can never be counted, we buy some empty title or other, and the smoke of a great name. Xerxes, Cyrus, and Alexander the Great would have lived longer and achieved truer glory if they had preferred to govern their own states rightly rather than harass those of others with arms. Charles, Duke of the Burgundians, the great-grandfather of this man <note>referring to Charles V, the Holy Roman Emperor at the time Erasmus was writing</note>, if the force of intellect with which he was endowed, if the greatness of spirit...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
## CHILIAD II, CENTURY V

<page-num>487</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD II, CENTURY V</header>

If he had turned his mind to enriching his own lands rather than conquering those of others, and had not met an unhappy death in war, he might have been counted among the most praised princes. A great part of our own territory <note>Erasmus refers here to the Burgundian Netherlands</note> was at that time held by a certain fatal plague—a most foolish but, of all things, the most destructive internal strife. Everyone was divided into two factions: one was named after the Hook, the other after the Cod-fish. <note>original: "abhamo... piſce aſſello"; referring to the Hook and Cod wars (Hoekse en Kabeljauwse twisten), a series of civil wars in the County of Holland</note> City fought against city, village against village, house against house. Often, those whom the same bed joined were separated by opposing factions, and brother was pulled away from brother, the bonds of nature being broken. Everywhere, things were boiling over with robberies, quarrels, murders, and plundering. And meanwhile, that good prince, as if these matters were of no concern, was far away attacking the walls of others.

Charles VIII, King of the Franks, having traversed Italy, returned to his people—but with such great evil and danger to himself and his own that he regretted that success. Finally, there are those who claim he could have reached old age if he had left Italy to the Italians. What shall I say of Philip, <note>Philip I of Castile, known as Philip the Handsome</note> the father of this Charles? <note>Erasmus likely means Philip's son, the future Emperor Charles V, or is referring back to the lineage of the Burgundian house</note> He went to the Spains, not to test the luck of war, but having been summoned to take up his share of the kingdom, with all things peaceful on every side. And yet, how much did his fatherland weep for this "happy" journey, plundered as it was by unbearable taxes? He himself labored more than once in great danger to his life. He lost François de Busleyden, the Archbishop of Besançon <note>original: "Byzantīnum"; Erasmus frequently uses this term for Besançon (Vesontio)</note>, a man incomparable in every way. But even after he returned, it was not permitted to be free of those evils. Once more he left his people; tossed by a most savage storm, he was carried to England—at that time not very favorable to our countrymen. What happened there, what he suffered, what he promised, and by what agreement he was dismissed, I do not wish to recount. He served necessity, I confess and I forgive him, but what was the necessity to fall into such a situation? Even after being warned by these evils, he did not think of returning to his fatherland. The Spains had to be revisited, where this young man, born for the greatest things, perished—unless he himself had envied his own happiness. And so, the death of one man deprived the fatherland of its best prince and Maximilian of his only son.

What shall I say of the Most Christian King of the Franks, Louis, the twelfth of that name? He attacked the Venetians—who were at that time, so it seemed, invincible—and in a single conflict he restored so many towns to the Roman Pontiff Julius II, so many to the Emperor Maximilian, and recovered so many for himself. He returned, as it seemed, with matters most happily concluded. But what a sea of evils flooded over the French from this! Those who had produced so many notable triumphs for Julius with their own blood were, by the work of that same Pope, ejected from the borders of Italy with an even greater loss of blood. This was not all: with what mark of ignominy were they finally branded? Had the death of Julius not intervened, we would have seen that kingdom, the most flourishing in the whole world, utterly overturned.

And what shall I mention of the Most Serene King of the Scots, James? <note>James IV of Scotland</note> That man would have added absolute praise to absolute happiness if he had perpetually contained himself within his own borders. He was of such physical appearance that you could recognize him as a king even from a distance. He possessed a wonderful force of intellect, an incredible knowledge of all things, an unconquered greatness of soul, a truly royal loftiness of heart, the greatest courtesy, and the most effortless generosity. In short, there was no virtue that would befit a great prince in which he did not so excel that he was praised even by the vote of his enemies. He had been joined to his wife Margaret, sister of the most serene King of the English, Henry VIII—a woman of such beauty, such prudence, and such love for her husband, that he could not have wished for another from the gods. The Kingdom of Scotland, which is said to yield to many in both wealth, the fame of its inhabitants, and splendor, he had so illuminated by his virtues, so increased, and so adorned, that he would have earned the true praise of an excellent prince if he had stayed within this limit of his glory.

But oh!—the departure of a king is never happy for a kingdom, and rarely for the prince. While he was too friendly in spirit toward the King of the Franks—intending to turn away the King of Britain, who was attacking France with great threats, and recall him to the defense of his own island—he stepped outside the borders of his kingdom and provoked the English in war. To be brief? He died bravely indeed, but unhappily, not so much for himself as for his kingdom. He perished while still in the vigor of his age. For a long time Scotland might have enjoyed such a prince, for a long time Margaret such a husband, for a long time his son (for he had raised a son by her) such a father, and he in turn might have enjoyed all of them and his own glory, if he had not begrudged himself his own life.

Along with his most brave father, his son was also slain—a son most worthy of such a father, Alexander, Archbishop <note>of St Andrews</note>, a young man indeed about twenty years of age, in whom you would miss no praise belonging to a perfect man. There was a wonderful grace in his beauty, a wonderful dignity, a heroic stature, and a most placid disposition of mind, yet one most sharp for the learning of all disciplines. For I once had a domestic familiarity with him in the city of Siena, at which time he was being trained by us in the precepts of rhetoric and in Greek literature. Immortal God! how swift, how happy, how adaptable to anything his intellect was; how many things he could embrace at once! At the same time he was learning...

<sig>S 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: law- <note>original Latin: "iurecon-", likely for "iureconsultorum" (legal scholars)</note></meta>

<summary>Erasmus critiques several European monarchs (Charles VIII, Philip the Handsome, Louis XII, and James IV of Scotland) for abandoning their domestic duties for foreign wars, specifically lamenting the death of James IV and his son Alexander Stewart at the Battle of Flodden.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the adage "Sparta is yours; adorn it." Erasmus has been arguing that a ruler’s duty is to focus on the welfare of his own kingdom rather than seeking expansion through war. He now illustrates this through a poignant personal memoir of his former pupil, Alexander Stewart, who died alongside his father, King James IV of Scotland, at the Battle of Flodden in 1513.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
## CHILIAD II, CENTURY V

<page-num>488</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...the writings of legal scholars, though these were not particularly pleasing to him because of their mixed-in "barbarism" <note>Humanists like Erasmus used the term "barbarism" to describe the non-classical, Medieval Latin used by medieval lawyers and theologians.</note> and the irritating wordiness of the commentators. He listened to the rules of rhetoric and declaimed on prescribed themes, exercising his pen and tongue in equal measure. He learned Greek, and every day at a fixed time, he would recite what had been taught. In the afternoon hours, he devoted himself to music, playing the monochord, the flutes, and the lute. <note>original: "teſtudini," literally "the tortoise," a common term for a lute because of its shape.</note> Sometimes he even practiced singing. Not even the time spent at meals was without the fruit of study. A priest would continuously read some beneficial book—for instance, the decrees of the Popes, or the works of Saint Jerome or Ambrose. The reader’s voice was never interrupted, unless one of the learned men between whom he sat at the table offered an observation, or if he himself, not quite following what was being read, asked a question. After the meal, there were stories, but short ones, and these too were seasoned with learning. Consequently, no part of his life at all was free from study, except for what was given to divine service and sleep. For even if any time remained—which was rare given such a varied cycle of studies—whatever was left over he gave to the reading of historians, for he was especially captivated by that branch of knowledge.

Thus it happened that this young man, having barely passed his eighteenth year, achieved such mastery in every kind of literature that you would marvel at it in any grown man. Nor did it happen in his case, as it often does with others, that while he was gifted in letters, he was less inclined toward good character. His manners were modest, yet such that you could recognize a wonderful wisdom in them. His mind was sublime and far removed from those sordid passions—but in such a way that there was no trace of ferocity, no arrogance. He noticed everything, but hid much; he could never be provoked to anger, such was the gentleness of his nature and the moderation of his soul. He delighted immensely in wit, but it was learned and without a "bite"—that is, tinted not with the black salt of Momus, but with the bright salt of Mercury. <note>Momus was the Greek god of mockery and harsh criticism; Mercury was the god of eloquence and cleverness. Erasmus means his wit was sharp but kind.</note> If any trouble arose among the servants at home, it was marvelous with what dexterity and kindness he was accustomed to settle it. Finally, he possessed a great deal of religion and piety, but no superstition. In short, no one was more worthy to be born of a king, and of *that* king <note>James IV of Scotland.</note>.

Would that the piety in his father, which was so admirable, had been equally fortunate. The son accompanied him to war, so as not to fail his father in any way. I ask you: what business had you with Mars, the most stupid of all the poetic gods—you who were initiated into the Muses, or rather, into Christ? What had that beauty, that age, that mild nature, that bright talent to do with trumpet-blasts, <note>original: "tarantantaris," an onomatopoeic word for the sound of a war trumpet.</note> cannons, and iron? Finally, what has a scholar to do with the battle-line? What has a bishop to do with arms? To be sure, an immoderate piety toward your father deceived you; while you loved your father too bravely, you fell unhappily, slain alongside him. So many gifts of nature, so many virtues, so many exceptional hopes—a single storm of battle swallowed them all. Something of our own property perished there too: namely, the labor we spent in educating you, and that portion of industry which I claim as mine in you. 

But how great would his heap of happiness have been, had not some evil genius driven the king to this: that, having left the borders of his own kingdom, he wished to try the luck of Mars in foreign fields against a most fierce people. Would that he had preferred to perfect what he had so brilliantly begun. <gloss>that is, he obtained the first-fruits of governance.</gloss> <note>original: "ἀπαρχὴν ἔλαχε κοσμᾶν" (aparchēn elache kosman).</note> The proper and most beautiful field of praise for kings lies within the boundaries of their own realm. Among the race of bees, the others indeed wander here and there in flight; the king <note>In antiquity, the "queen bee" was thought to be a king.</note> alone lacks a sting, and his wings are much smaller in proportion to his body, making him unsuited for flight. The ancients used to depict Venus pressing a tortoise with her feet, implying that the mistress of a house should never depart from her home, since her entire duty is contained within the domestic walls. Yet it was much more to the point that a prince be reminded by this symbol; for if a prince errs, he errs to the misfortune not of one family, but of the entire world. 

Is there too little business at home that one must seek it abroad? Everywhere there is such a sink of crimes, so many sacrileges, so many robberies, so many oppressions, so many injuries, so many insults, so many corruptions of magistrates, so many laws either instituted by tyrants or twisted to serve tyranny—to say nothing of those smaller matters: the neglected town roads, the collapsing sacred buildings, the untended riverbanks. To heal these things in such a way that you spend the minimum of your people's blood as a remedy, so that the commonwealth feels the benefit but not the cost—is that not an outstanding duty for a prince, and one worthy of immortal praise? But if you absolutely desire to extend the borders of your glory beyond the limits of your jurisdiction, act so that your neighbors experience your greatness through your benefits, not your injuries. You burn villages, trample crops, demolish cities, drive off cattle, slaughter men, and thus at last declare yourself "great"? It is the kind of battle you would have undertaken with a robber. Hesiod wrote that a bad neighbor is a great harm, while a good one is a huge advantage. Let your neighbors prove this in you: act so that they admire you as great, while loving you as kind. But enough now for my grief...

<meta>catchword: fatis</meta>

<meta>This page concludes Erasmus’s moving tribute to his late pupil, Alexander Stewart, the Archbishop of St. Andrews, who died at the Battle of Flodden. Erasmus transitions from this personal eulogy back to his scholarly catalog of ancient Greek and Latin proverbs, beginning the fifth "Century" (a block of 100 adages) within his second "Chiliad" (a block of 1,000 adages).</meta>

...enough has been given to the memory of the pupil. It remains for us to return to the review of the proverbs.

->**Hunting luck happens even to the bad.**<-
<margin>II</margin>
<note>original Greek: Δίδοται καὶ κακίστη ἄγρα</note> "A catch is given even to the worst [hunter]." That is, even the lazy happen upon prey from the hunt. This is used when something fortunate happens to someone undeserving, and when the success should be credited to luck rather than to that person's hard work. The allegory is taken from hunting, a pursuit in which luck reigns supreme. Skill and virtue contribute very little. In contrast, education happens to no one unless it is won through labor. A kingdom may fall to those who sleep; wealth sometimes flows to the idle; honors may even happen to those who try to avoid them; but those things which are truly good must be prepared by our own industry. I suspect the proverb arose from an old custom where whatever was caught in a hunt was shared with everyone, even those who did not participate. Thus Theocritus says in *The Fishermen*:
<note>original Greek: Ὡς καὶ τὰν ἄγραν τ’ ὠνείρατα πάντα μερίζειν</note> "So that, like a hunt, dreams share out everything." <note>Theocritus was a Greek poet known for his pastoral idylls.</note>
Just as we do not entrust secrets to anyone but selected friends, we tell all sorts of things to anyone at all. The proverb is recorded by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> from Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic</note>. If you read "Give" instead of "Is given," it would be the start of a trochaic poem. For it is probable that this was plucked from some poet or another.

->**To walk on a stretched rope.**<-
<margin>III</margin>
Horace used a proverbial figure when he said:
"To walk on a stretched rope." <note>The Roman poet Horace used this to describe the difficulty of writing great drama.</note>
This stands for performing a task that is extremely difficult to do, where one cannot stray even a tiny bit. It is taken from tightrope-walkers, as Acron <note>An ancient commentator on Horace</note> suggests, who walk across a tensioned rope not without the highest art and the greatest practice. This feat, as one might guess, was a source of great wonder to the ancients. Today, nothing is more common. This is Horace’s poem:
"That poet seems to me to be able to walk a stretched rope, who wrings my heart with empty grief."

->**It has been a year.**<-
<margin>IIII</margin>
I believe no one will doubt that these expressions ought to be counted among the proverbial hyperboles: "It’s been a year," "It’s been an age," and others of that kind. Terence says in *The Self-Tormentor*: "And you know the ways of women: while they are getting ready, while they are starting, it's been a year." The same author says elsewhere, "For a long lifetime now," meaning "for a very long time." Plautus says in *The Asses*: "I would be willing to serve for a lifetime, if only I could meet Libanus." And: "It has been an age since any letters were returned by you." Therefore, we shall signify a very long time with figures of this sort.

->**Daylight takes away sorrow.**<-
<margin>V</margin>
Menedemus, in the Terentian play *The Self-Tormentor*, specifically cites this as a proverb: "Either I," he says, "was born with a nature remarkably suited for misery, or that saying is false which I commonly hear said: that daylight takes away the sorrow of men." Sophocles seems to have aimed at the same point in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*:
<note>original Greek: Χρόνος γὰρ εὐμαρὴς θεός</note> "For time is a gentle god."
Namely, because time eases and softens all things. Ovid says:
"What you endure poorly, get used to; you will endure it well; long passage of time softens many things."
Euripides says in *Alcestis*: <note>original Greek: χρόνος μαλάξει σε</note> "Time will soften you." Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in the fourth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "That this is so, the passing day declares, which as it proceeds so mitigates things that, even while the same evils remain, sorrow is not only eased, but in most people removed." The same author in the fifth book of his *Letters*: "For that which the passage of time is going to bring, we ought to anticipate through counsel and wisdom." It is also quoted from Iphiclus:
<note>original Greek: λύπης δὲ πάσης ἐστὶν ἰατρὸς χρόνος</note> "Time is the doctor for every pain." Euripides says:
<note>original Greek: Μέλλων τ’ ἰατρὸς τῇ νόσῳ διδοὺς χρόνον, ἰᾶται’ ἤδη μᾶλλον, ἢ τεμὼν χρόα.</note>
"The doctor who gives a delay of time to a disease heals it more than the one who cuts the skin."

->**You are bringing a lamp at midday.**<-
<margin>VI</margin>
<note>original Greek: λύχνον ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ ἅπτεις</note> "You light a lamp at noon." That is, you do something at an inappropriate time. Or you explain things that are perfectly clear by themselves. For what need is there for lamps when the lamps of the [sun] are brightest...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

It may seem to originate from a ridiculous deed of Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, a Greek philosopher known for his eccentric behavior intended to expose social hypocrisy.</note>, who carried a lamp during the day; when asked what he wanted, he replied: "I am looking for a man," <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπον ζητῶ</note> as Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of the Greek philosophers.</note> testifies. Seneca, in his book *On the Happy Life*, indicates that this sort of thing used to happen out of superstition whenever the wrath of a deity was announced: "When," he says, "someone shaking a sistrum <note>A percussion instrument used in ancient Egyptian religious rites.</note> tells lies by command; when someone skilled in cutting his own muscles stains his arms and shoulders with blood while keeping his hand steady; when some woman howls while crawling on her knees through the street, and an old man dressed in linen, carrying a laurel branch and a lamp in the middle of the day, cries out that one of the gods is angry, you all run together and listen."

<margin>VII</margin>
->**Bringing light to the sun.**<-

Quintilian, in the fifth book of his *Institutes of Oratory*, under the title "On the Use of Arguments," used a figure very similar to this one: he said that someone who tried to prove a thing that was already perfectly self-evident through long arguments was "bringing light to the sun." It seems to be the same as that which we related in another place: "Lending light to the sun." <note>original Greek: ἡλίῳ τὸ φῶς δανείζειν</note>

<margin>VIII</margin>
->**The Zoiluses.**<-

The bold but unfortunate biting wit of Zoilus gave rise to a proverb, such that people who disparage the praises of others and critics of others' labors are commonly called "Zoiluses." Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams.</note> writes: "I want to see Zoilus hanging."

This Zoilus was a certain sophist, most famous for the outrageous act of daring to attack Homer, the prince of all poets, in several books written against him; from this, he earned the nickname "Homeromastix" <note>Greek for "The Scourge of Homer."</note>, which itself passed into a proverb. For critics of noble authors began to be called by this name, as Pliny testifies in the preface to his *Natural History*. There were also "Vergiliomastiges" <note>"The Scourges of Virgil."</note>, among whose number was Perus. Zoilus therefore presented his commentaries composed against Homer to Ptolemy, the king of the Egyptians, clearly hoping for a huge reward from the king. But when nothing was sent, driven by poverty, he sent someone to ask for it. Then Ptolemy said he marveled that, while Homer had been dead for so many years and yet fed so many thousands of men, Zoilus—who was supposedly more learned than Homer—should be in want. Finally, when the opportunity arose, he was put to death. However, authors record different accounts regarding the manner of his death.

<margin>IX</margin>
->**Cillicon’s goods.**<-

"Cillicon’s goods." <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθὰ Κιλλικῶν</note> One should understand the meaning as "he makes" or "he has" these goods. It is appropriate when someone has prepared wealth for themselves through evil deeds and shameful arts. A certain Cillicon, a Milesian by birth, gave rise to this adage; he betrayed his homeland, Miletus, to the people of Priene and was enriched amply, but foully. When he was planning the betrayal and was asked what he was going to do, he replied: "All good things." <note>original Greek: πάντ' ἀγαθά</note> Hence the proverb is also uttered in this way: "All good things, as Cillicon said." <note>original Greek: πάντ' ἀγαθά ὡς ἔφη Κιλλικῶν</note> The authors are Suidas and Zenodotus. Aristophanes also alludes to this in *The Peace*:
"Nothing bad, but rather what Cillicon says." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν πονηρόν, ἀλλ' ὅπερ καὶ Κιλλικῶν</note>
The commentator adds the story of Cillicon's death. After the island was betrayed by Cillicon, a certain Syrian named Theagenes moved to Samos and was selling meat there. When Cillicon wanted to buy meat from him, Theagenes handed him a piece so that he might cut off what was extra. But instead, drawing his knife, he cut off the man's hand, saying: "With that hand, you shall not betray another city."

<margin>X</margin>
->**To cut the throat with a leaden sword.**<-

"To cut the throat with a leaden sword" means to defeat someone with a futile and weak argument. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his letters to Atticus: "When he said that he would nevertheless be 'slaughtered with a leaden sword.'" The same author, in his books *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, calls a cold argument a "leaden dagger." Likewise, Aurelius Augustine in his third book against Julian says: "And yet, you step into the contest weighed down by the sharp spears of the dialecticians, as it were, and you brandish leaden daggers." Demosthenes, in his first oration against Aristogiton: "For a knife is of no use to a cook if it does not cut." <note>original Greek: ὅτε γὰρ μαγείρῳ μαχαίρας οὐδέν ἐστ' ὄφελος ἢ ὡς ἀνύεται</note>

<margin>XI</margin>
->**To shave a lion.**<-

"To shave a lion" <note>original Greek: Λέοντα ξυρεῖν</note> is said of those who handle and mock fierce and powerful men to their own great peril. Socrates used this adage in the first book of Plato's *Republic*, saying he was not so insane as to dare to "shave a lion" and mock Thrasymachus, a very fierce man: "For I would not be so mad as to attempt to shave a lion and play the informer against Thrasymachus." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν με οὕτω μανίαι, ὥστε ξυρεῖν ἐπιχειρεῖν λέοντα, καὶ συκοφαντεῖν θρασύμαχον</note> For lambs are shorn and plucked without danger, but a lion in no 
<meta>way (catchword for next page: modo)</meta>

# CHILIAD II. CENTURY V.

...wishes to be treated in this way. Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his witty and biting epigrams.</note> seems to have alluded to this adage in the tenth book of his *Epigrams*, when he says:
> So if you have any shame, Ligella, do not
> Pluck the beard of a dead lion. <note>original Latin: "Quare si pudor est, Ligella, noli / Barbam uellere mortuo leoni."</note>

For the poet turns this into a joke, as if it were a safe and cowardly thing to want to mock <margin>re.</margin> a lion that can no longer feel anything. By "lion," however, he hints at a woman's private parts, now deadened by old age. Aristides, in his *Panathenaics*, relates this to Pericles <note>A prominent Greek statesman and general during the Golden Age of Athens.</note> when he was criticized by Plato: "So see that we do not attempt to shave the lion, <note>original Greek: ὡς θ’ ὅρα μὴ λέοντα ξυρεῖν ἐπιχειρῶμεν</note> we who attempt to slander Thrasymachus, but rather to mock Pericles, and that for his cowardice." That is to say: "See then that we do not try to shave the lion, not wishing to calumniate Thrasymachus, but to tax Pericles, especially for his timidity."

### Lest I be a Suffenus to myself.
-> XII <-

**Lest I be a Suffenus to myself,** that is, lest I flatter myself and foolishly admire myself. Suffenus was a poet of the most inept kind, sharp-tongued regarding the faults of others but blind to his own. Thus, it became a common proverb that those who were vainly pleased with themselves were called "Suffeni." Catullus <note>An influential Latin poet of the late Roman Republic.</note> says in an epigram:
> He is more boorish than the boorish countryside,
> As soon as he touches poetry; yet never is he
> So happy as when he writes a poem,
> So much does he rejoice in himself, and so much does he admire himself. <margin>In the same place.</margin>
> You could see <margin>You could.</margin> a Suffenus in everyone in some matter.

Horace <note>The leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> makes Mevius very similar to Suffenus—forgiving his own vices while most bitingly attacking those of others:
> "I myself forgive my own faults," says Mevius.

### The Sicilian eats unripe grapes.
-> XIII <-

**The Sicilian eats unripe grapes.** <note>original Greek: Σικελὸς ὀμφακίζει</note> The Greeks call a bitter and immature grape <term>omphaca</term> <note>From the Greek "omos" (raw) and "phagein" (to eat), meaning "to eat raw things."</note>. From this, the saying was used against those who, through a lust for stealing, would carry off anything, no matter how cheap. It is derived from the reputation of the Sicilians for theft. It is also not wrongly said of those who, because of an immoderate and premature greed, cause a huge loss to others just to make a tiny bit of profit for themselves. There are those who believe it can fit those who pluck the most beautiful things for themselves, like that Syrus in Terence <note>A Roman playwright; Syrus is a clever slave character in his comedies.</note>. Zenodotus says it was taken from Epicharmus. It is also mentioned by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note>.

### An old monkey is indeed caught.
-> XIIII <-

**An old monkey is indeed caught, but it is caught eventually.** <note>original Greek: Γέρων πίθηκος ἁλίσκεται μὲν, μετὰ χρόνον δ’ ἁλίσκεται.</note> This applies to a crafty person who has long eluded capture but at last pays the penalty. It will be useful for exhorting that everyone should act with true reason if they wish to be safe, rather than trusting in clever but dishonest plans. For no one is so well-equipped with tricks that they can deceive forever; eventually, some chance event brings hidden malice out into the open.

### With a following tide.
-> XV <-

**To proceed with the tide.** <note>original Greek: Κατὰ ῥοῦν προχωρεῖν</note> This is a proverbial and frequent metaphor among authors. It is taken from sailors, for whom the course is easier when the river or even the sea’s tide is following them. Lucian <note>A Hellenistic satirist and rhetorician.</note> says in *Zeus Rants*: "These things now go with the tide for Damis." Likewise elsewhere: "The rest is carried with the tide." Although here the use is slightly different: for Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery and blame.</note> accuses the gods of neglecting the affairs of mortals, allowing them to be carried anywhere, as if by a rushing river. Therefore, "to be carried with the tide" meant to be carried along haphazardly, with no one in control. Aeschylus <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Tragedy."</note> says in *The Persians*:
> When the deity flows well, trust <margin>that is,</margin>
> That the same deity will always favor fortune.
That is: "When fortune has been favorable, believe that it will likewise always be favorable and in the same way."

### With favorable winds.
-> XVI <-

**To be carried by favorable winds.** <note>original Greek: Ἐξ οὐρίων φέρεσθαι</note> This is recorded by Suidas. One is said to sail with favorable winds when things succeed according to one's wishes. The Greeks put it more elegantly: "from the stern," <note>original Greek: ἐξ οὐρίας</note> as if from behind. Libanius the Sophist <note>A 4th-century teacher of rhetoric.</note> says in a certain declamation: "Those who are so minded usually have things succeed according to their wishes." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "What if even Caesar, whose winds are now very favorable..."

<summary>This page examines proverbs regarding self-flattery, petty theft, and the eventual downfall of the cunning, while also defining nautical metaphors for success and favorable circumstances.</summary>
<keywords>Suffenus, Catullus, Sicilian theft, unripe grapes, old monkey, nautical metaphors, Lucian, Aeschylus, Cicero, favorable winds</keywords>

--- Page 608 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of proverbs related to favorable circumstances and shifts toward cautionary adages regarding the misuse of power and petty grievances. It concludes with an anecdote regarding the origin of a specific sacrificial custom in Rhodes.</meta>

I make things better: Plautus in *The Bacchides*: <note>A comedy by the Roman playwright Titus Maccius Plautus.</note> "This reasoning is beautifully applied," <note>original Latin: "Pulchre hæc cōfertur ratio."</note> perceiving that the matter is proceeding conveniently. In the same author, Tranio—who, while his master was away for three years, had lived quite festively and even "musically" <note>meaning a life of luxury and refinement</note> with the master's son—finally says upon the master's return, when he expected nothing but the cross: "Now the wind deserts the ship." <note>original Latin: "Nunc... uentus nauim deserit."</note> Horace in his *Satires*:
> We are not driven by swelling sails with a following north wind,
> Yet we do not spend our lives against adverse south winds. <note>original Latin: "Non agimur tumidis uelis... Non tamen aduersis ætatem ducimus austris."</note>
Indeed, this very "Shipwreck" is used as a proverb for misfortune, just as "Fire" is. Since many of Homer’s phrases are used in place of proverbs, what prevents that phrase, which is so frequent in that poet, from being included among the adages?
"Both wind and water carrying it along." <note>original Greek: φόρων ἄνεμός τε καὶ ὕδωρ.</note>
This is used whenever a matter proceeds happily in every respect. Likewise, that frequent phrase in the same poet:
"But the wind and the helmsman guided it." <note>original Greek: τὴν d' ἄνεμός τε κυβερνήτης τ' ἴθυνεν.</note>
This is used when industry or hard work is added to the favor of fortune.

<margin>Pindar in the *Pythian Odes*, first hymn,</margin>
"For seafaring men beginning their voyage, the first grace is for a favorable breeze to come." <note>original Greek: ναυσιφορήτοις, Ἐς πλόου ἀρχομένοις δ' ἀνθράσι πρῶτα χάρις πομπᾶιον ἐλθεῖν ὄυρον.</note>
<margin>For nautical men preparing for a voyage,</margin>
the primary thanks is given if a prosperous and favorable wind arrives.

### Parnus's little skiff.
<margin>XVII</margin>
**Parnus's little skiff.** <note>original Greek: Τὸ Πάρνης σκάφιδιον.</note> This is applicable to those who stir up a great deal of litigation and complaints over trivial matters. It is taken from a certain Parnus, who is read to have been most bothersome to the people on account of a small boat that had been taken from him. The author is Diogenianus. <note>A Greek grammarian known for collecting proverbs.</note> Since his case was frequently brought before the people, it eventually turned into a popular joke, much like that saying "Corinth, son of Zeus." <note>A proverb used for someone who repeats the same tiresome thing over and over.</note>

### Do not give a sword to a child.
<margin>XVIII</margin>
**Do not give a sword to a child.** <note>original Greek: Μὴ παιδὶ τὴν μάχαιραν.</note> One must understand "entrust" or "give." It is a proverbial allegory, warning that power should not be committed to either the young or the inexperienced and foolish, who are likely to abuse it to the ruin of both themselves and others. Do not entrust the administration of money to a youth: *do not give a sword to a child.* Do not entrust a kingdom to a minor: *do not give a sword to a child.* Do not delegate the role of preaching before the people to a fool: *do not give a sword to a child.* Do not entrust the magistracy to fools: *do not give a sword to a child.* Do not entrust the office of a bishop to one who is unlearned and has little heart: *do not give a sword to a child.* Plutarch, in the booklet titled *That bad women make their sons bad*, as cited by Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a compiler of extracts from Greek authors; the specific Plutarch work mentioned here is largely lost to us today.</note> (for that book has not yet come to light), says: "The proverb says: *Do not give a sword to a child.* But I would say: *Do not give wealth to a child, nor power to an uneducated man.*" He means that money is pestilential to youths, and power is dangerous to the ignorant man. The same author in his *Table Talk*, says: "Otherwise, one ought to give—as if to children who are unable to keep still—not a spear or a sword, but a rattle or a ball." <note>original Greek: πλαταγλὴν ἢ σφαῖραν.</note> Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> also used this in the fifth book of the *Deipnosophists* regarding a philosopher who had been entrusted with imperial power. Not entirely different from this form is what was elegantly and gravely said by Henry VII, King of Britain <note>Henry VII (1457–1509), the first Tudor king of England, known for his prudence and wit.</note>—a man of sharp judgment and remarkably strong in "Laconic" <note>Short, pithy, or concise speech.</note> sayings—when he had heard a certain theologian of the kind they call "mendicants" <note>Friars who lived by begging, such as Franciscans or Dominicans.</note> preaching. The man had raved with an unbridled tongue against the lives of princes, not with great liberty but with insanity (for there are those who seek fame in this way too). The King said: "It seemed like a sword committed to the hands of a madman."

### A Lindian sacrifice.
<margin>XIX</margin>
**The Lindians perform the sacrifice.** <note>original Greek: Λίνδιοι τὴν θυσίαν.</note> This was said against those who performed divine rites under an ill omen. It is taken from a story mentioned also by Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) who often critiqued pagan myths.</note> in the first book of the *Divine Institutes*. Hercules once forcibly took two oxen from a certain Lindian farmer and, having slaughtered them, prepared a feast for himself. The old farmer, however, as Hercules was eating, heaped many curses upon him, which provided Hercules with both pleasure and laughter; so much so that they say Hercules declared no feast had ever happened more pleasantly for him. But it would not be out of place to record Lactantius's words. "At Lindus," he says, "which is a town in Rhodes, the rites of Hercules..."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Lindian sacrifice to Hercules, where cursing replaces the usual holy silence, then moves into proverbs about false grief, impossible dilemmas, and learning from mistakes.</meta>

[page 493]

->CENTURY V OF THE SECOND CHILIAD<-

These rites are sacred, but their ritual is far different from others: for they celebrate them not with **holy silence** <note>original Greek: εὐφημίᾳ</note>, as the Greeks call it, but with curses and execrations. Indeed, they consider the rites violated if a "good word" <note>an auspicious or holy word</note> should happen to slip out from anyone, even by accident, during the solemnities. The reason given for this—if indeed any reason can be found in such vain superstitions—is as follows: When Hercules had arrived there and was suffering from hunger, he saw a certain plowman at work and began to ask him to sell him one of his oxen. But the man refused, saying it was impossible because all his hope for cultivating the land rested on those two bullocks. Hercules, using his habitual violence, since he could not receive just one, took both. But that unhappy man, seeing his oxen being slaughtered, avenged his injury with curses, which was most pleasing to that elegant and sophisticated man <note>ironic description of Hercules</note>. For while he prepared a feast for his companions and devoured the oxen of another, he listened with laughter and guffaws to the man reviling him most bitterly. But after it pleased the citizens to grant divine honors to Hercules out of admiration for his virtue, an altar was established for him, which they named from the event the **Ox-yoke** <term>βούθυον (bouthyon), meaning an ox-yoke or ox-sacrifice</term>: at which two joined oxen would be sacrificed, just like those he had taken from the plowman. Hercules himself appointed the man as his priest and commanded that he should always use those same curses in celebrating the sacrifices, because he claimed he had never feasted more pleasantly. Thus far we have rendered the words of Lactantius <note>an early Christian author, c. 250–325 AD</note>. Zenodotus adds that this custom became established among the people of Lindos because an oracle also commanded that certain insults be hurled during the performance of the rites. Gregory Nazianzenus also mentions this in his *Invective Orations*. The adage can be adapted to many uses: either to a quarrelsome banquet or dispute, or to any matter undertaken with ill omens.

---

<margin>Tears of the Megarians.</margin>
### Tears of the Megarians. XX

**Tears of the Megarians** <note>original Greek: Μεγαρέων δάκρυα</note> was a phrase used for tears that were either fake and not proceeding from true grief, or tears that were forced. Diogenianus relates a history of this sort: A certain Bacchius of Corinth had married the daughter of Clytius, the king of the Megarians. When she died, Clytius sent many maidens and youths to Corinth to bewail the girl in the funeral processions, specifically using fake tears. As they say of those who are hired to mourn at a funeral:
> They say and do almost more than those who grieve from the soul.
->On the other hand, Juvenal says:<-
> Lost money is mourned with true tears.

Suidas brings forward another cause: that among the Megarians there is a great abundance of garlic, and the sharpness of this vegetable forces tears from many even against their will. Hence, in Aristophanes, someone who is crying is jokingly said to have "smelled garlic." Therefore, if you apply it to feigned grief, the proverb would be related to that other one: "To weep at a stepmother’s tomb."

---

<margin>The wind lets you neither stay nor sail.</margin>
### The wind lets you neither stay nor sail. XXI

**The wind neither allows one to stay nor to sail** <note>original Greek: Ἄνεμος οὔτε μένειν ἐᾷ, οὔτε πλεῖν ἐᾷ</note>. Philoctetes says in Aeschylus:
> **The wind neither allows one to stay nor to sail.** <note>original Greek: Ἄνεμος οὔτε μένειν ἐᾷ, οὔτε πλεῖν ἐᾷ</note>
That is:
> Where the wind permits one neither to stay nor to go.

This is very similar to the saying: "I am holding a wolf by the ears." It will be useful whenever someone falls into such difficulties of circumstance that it is neither possible to abandon the business nor is there the ability to complete it. The metaphor is borrowed from a most savage storm of winds, when sailing is very dangerous for sailors, yet it is not safe to cast anchor. Quintus Curtius in Book 8 expressed this without the figurative language in this way: "And the army, stunned with terrified ears, dared neither to advance nor to halt." It is recorded by Diogenianus.

---

<margin>A fox is not caught twice in a snare.</margin>
### A fox is not caught twice in a snare. XXII

**But a fox is not caught twice in the snares** <note>original Greek: Ἁλ' οὐκ αὖθις ἀλώπηξ πάγαις</note>—the word "caught" is understood. He who is wise **does not strike the same stone once and twice** <note>original Greek: ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς πῶς τὸν αὐτὸν προσκρούει λίθον</note>. It is the mark of a stupid man to fall into a tasted evil a second time. In the collections of Plutarch it is expressed in this way: **A fox that has once escaped the snares is not caught again** <note>original Greek: ἀλώπηξ διαφυγοῦσα πάγας αὖθις οὐχ ἁλίσκεται</note>. Cunning is inherent by nature in this animal, just as boldness is in lions. Thus Pindar, in the fourth hymn of the *Isthmian Odes*, compares a brave man to a lion for his strength and to a fox for his prudence: **For he has the courage of the loud-roaring lion in his labor, but in craft he is a fox.** <note>original Greek: Τολμᾷν γὰρ εἰκὼν θυμοῦ φθεγξαμέναν θηρᾶν λεόντων ἐν πόνῳ, μῆτιν δ’ ἀλώπηξ</note>. It is related to what we have mentioned elsewhere: "To stumble twice against the same stone," which Gregory the Theologian used in a certain letter to Bosporius: **For the proverb grants only to the foolish to stumble twice against the same stone.** <note>original Greek: δὶς γὰρ πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν λίθον πταίειν τοῖς ἀνοήτοις μόνοις ἡ παροιμία δίδωσιν</note>.

<summary>Erasmus explores the origins of cultural rituals and various Greek and Latin proverbs concerning deceptive behavior, inescapable dilemmas, and the wisdom of not repeating mistakes.</summary>
