<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

<margin>XXIII</margin>
### An Abydenian dessert.
<note>original Greek: Ἀβυδηνὴ ἐπιφόρημα (Abydenē epiphorēma)</note>, that is, an Abydenian dessert, or an intrusion. It was a common saying used when someone makes a nuisance of themselves, either by shouting over people at a banquet or by causing a troublesome disturbance during any other activity. Zenodotus says this proverb appears in a play by Eudoxus titled *The Supposititious Son*. The saying arose because it was once a custom among the people of Abydos that when they hosted a citizen or a guest at a banquet—specifically during sacred and solemn feasts—children would be brought in by their nurses after the perfumes and garlands had been distributed. These children were then carried around to be kissed. However, because the children would wail and cry, and the nurses would chatter and make a racket, the banquet became chaotic and unpleasant. Therefore, when some friends are conversing pleasantly and some loud-mouthed brawler interrupts, whose talkativeness is going to make the conversation disagreeable, we may rightly say: **An Abydenian dessert.** 

Although in some manuscripts the word is read as <note>original Greek: ἐπιφώνημα (epiphōnēma)</note>, meaning an "acclamation," I believe this is a mistake. Athenaeus, in the fourteenth book of the *Dinner-Table Philosophers*, mentions this adage and demonstrates through the testimony of several authors that the word <note>original Greek: ἐπιφορήματα (epiphorēmata)</note> refers to sweets or the second course of a meal (the "dessert"), derived from the act of "bringing in" rather than "shouting out." Furthermore, Stephanus reads it as "dessert," not "acclamation," as do Zenodotus and Suidas. Only Hesychius reads it as "acclamation," suggesting it was said of those who slandered their guests. However, the fact that some manuscripts read "of the Abydenians" <note>plural</note> instead of "Abydenian" <note>singular</note> makes very little difference to the meaning.

<margin>XXIV</margin>
### A beggar's pouch is never filled.
<note>original Greek: Πτωχοῦ πήρα οὐ πίμπλαται (Ptōchou pēra ou pimplatai)</note>, that is, **A beggar's bag is never full.** Zenodotus says this is taken from the poet Callimachus. The meaning is clear enough: that beggary is insatiable. For the more you give to those who have the soul of a beggar, the more they demand. This can be applied to wicked people who are always demanding something from their friends, to the rich for whom nothing is enough, or to "people-devouring" princes <term>δημοβόρους (demoborous), a Homeric term for rulers who consume the wealth of their subjects</term>, whose greed no amount of plundering the commoners can satisfy. It fits most aptly those who are addicted to lust, greed, ambition, and other passions of that kind. For it happens to them that the more immoderately they fill themselves, the more they recognize their own thirst and hunger—just as is hinted at in the Gospel parable of the Prodigal Son, who could not even fill his belly with the pods the pigs ate.

<margin>XXV</margin>
### Laconian moons.
<note>original Greek: Λακωνικὰς σελήνας (Lakōnikas selēnas)</note>, that is, **Laconian moons**; one must understand "excuses" or something similar. This was said of uncertain and weak promises or pacts. For they say that the Laconians <note>Spartans</note>, whenever they were asked for promised military aid, would make excuses about the moon. They escaped their obligations under the pretext that—as Lucian testifies—Lycurgus had passed a law forbidding them from entering battle except during a full moon. In other matters as well, they observed the phases of the moon with great superstition when starting any business, and this gave rise to the proverb. 

In my opinion, Marcus Tullius Cicero alluded to this in a certain letter to Atticus (Book 7), which begins: "Dionysius, that excellent man." He writes: "Since the 4th of the Nones of January is the feast of Compitalia, I do not want to come to the Alban estate on that day, lest I be a burden to the household. I will come on the 3rd of the Nones. Therefore, I will head to the city on the day before the Nones. On what day your **moon** <note>original Greek: σελήνη (selēnē)</note> falls, I do not know; but I certainly do not want you to be inconvenienced by your ill health." Although I am well aware that in the common manuscripts of Cicero, the word is written as <note>original Greek: λήνης (lēnēs), meaning 'eye-mucus' or 'nonsense'</note> rather than "moon," and some have changed it to "assumptions," the sense leads us to read it as "little moon." For after Cicero had indicated which days he himself had observed or chosen (perhaps being a bit superstitious himself), he added regarding Atticus: "I don't know on which day your little moon falls," joking about Atticus’s own superstition, while still wanting him to take care of his health. This agrees with another proverb we have reviewed elsewhere: "The moon of Accesseus" <note>referring to someone who always waits for a 'better' moon and thus procrastinates</note>.

<margin>XXVI</margin>
### Greasier than a lamp, or Greasier than an oil jar.
<note>original Greek: Λιπαρώτερος λύχνου, λιπαρώτερος ληκυθίου (Liparōteros lychnou, liparōteros lēkythiou)</note>, that is, **Greasier than a lamp, greasier than an oil flask.** This seems to be a proverbial irony directed at those who, despite being great gluttons, do not become any more fit or robust—just as a lamp consumes a vast amount of oil but never becomes "fattened." It might also be aptly applied to men of "thick" (slow) judgment, or those devoted to luxury and pleasure. This is recorded by Diogenianus.

<margin>XXVII</margin>
### They drink water by measure, but eat bread without measure.
<note>original Greek: Μέτρῳ μὲν ὕδωρ πίνοντες, ἀμετρίᾳ δ’ μάζαν ἔδοντες (Metrō men hydōr pinontes, ametria d' mazan edontes)</note>, that is, **Drinking water by the measure, but eating barley-cake without measure.** Zenodotus writes that this verse was delivered as an oracle regarding the Sybarites <note>citizens of Sybaris, famous for their extreme luxury</note> and passed into common speech. The Sybarites were eventually destroyed by the inhabitants of Croton due to their immoderate luxury, as we have related elsewhere. Thus, the proverb can be applied to those who...

<summary>Erasmus explores several Greek adages concerning social nuisances (the noisy Abydenians), the insatiable nature of greed (the beggar's pouch), and the use of superstitious excuses for procrastination (the Laconian moons). He also touches on the irony of gluttons who remain thin and the hypocrisy of the luxurious Sybarites.</summary>
<keywords>Abydos, greed, Spartan superstition, Cicero, gluttony, Sybarites, insatiability, ancient customs, textual criticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion on social behavior and moral character, specifically focusing on the dangers of inconsistency—being wasteful yet stingy—before moving into a series of adages regarding decorum, the testing of character, and the hidden "sting" of the weak.</meta>

...luxuries and wealth, they are reduced to extreme poverty; or it refers to those who are preposterously stingy, being very parsimonious in the smallest matters but negligent in great ones—the sort of people you see most mortals are. It is a heroic verse, which, however, in all the manuscripts I have seen so far, is read in a corrupted state. It should be restored in this way: 

<note>original Greek: Κάι φειδῷ φιλἐοντα, καὶ ᾧ φιλἐοντα διώκῃ (Kai pheidō phileonta, kai hō phileonta diōkēi)</note> 

which means, "One loves with thrift, and pursues with the same." A similar thought is found in Theocritus in his *Bucoliastae*: 

"He pursues the one who turns away, and in turn turns away from the one who loves him."

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
### To bring on the character of a dancer in a toga.

To bring on the persona of a dancer while wearing a toga is to do something entirely unbecoming: for instance, if an old man or a theologian should act foolishly, or if someone should mix trifles with serious business. Martial writes in the preface to his second book: "Do not then, if it please you, do a ridiculous thing and **bring on the character of a dancer in a toga.**" The toga was the garment of Roman citizens, and it was taken up as a mark of honor by those who had already passed out of childhood, laying aside the <term>praetexta</term> <note>The purple-bordered toga worn by boys</note> and professing a manly spirit and behavior through their very dress; for this reason, it was called the "manly toga" <note>original: toga virilis</note>. Hence that line of Cicero in the *Philippics*: "You took up the manly toga, which you immediately turned into a woman’s robe." Furthermore, it was worn in times of peace, just as the <term>sagum</term> <note>A coarse wool cloak</note> was worn in war. This is why Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Philippics*, repeatedly orders that the <term>togae</term> be laid aside to take up the <term>sagum</term>. And the same author wrote: 

->**Let arms yield to the toga.**<- 

Likewise, Lucan says of Pompey: 

"He preferred arms to the toga, but even while armed, he loved peace."

<margin>XXIX</margin>
### An unexamined man.

<note>original Greek: Ἀβασάνιστος ἄνθρωπος (Abasanistos anthrōpos)</note>. That is, an unexamined man; one who is uninvestigated, untrained, or unproven. Suidas cites Aelian as the author in his book *On Providence*, who used the word <note>original: ἀβασάνιστον (abasaniston)</note> to mean "free from pain," because for the Greeks, the word <note>original: βασανίζεσθαι (basanizesthai)</note> also means to be tortured. However, there is a metaphor underlying "unexamined." The <term>basanos</term> <note>Greek: βάσανος</note> is a touchstone used to test the purity of gold, which the Latins call an <term>index</term>. There is a saying by Chilo: "What the touchstone is to gold, that gold is to a man." This means that a man's character is tested by gold in the same way that gold is tested by the touchstone.

<margin>XXX</margin>
### An Abronian life.

<note>original Greek: Ἀβρώνιος βίος (Abronios bios)</note>. That is, an Abronian life. This is said of those who live softly and luxuriously. It is taken from the habits of a certain Abron, noted for his luxury, just as among us Apicius and Aesopus are made famous by their excess. The Greeks call anything delicate and soft <note>original: ἀβρὸν (abron)</note> and <note>original: ἀβροδίαιτον (abrodiaiton)</note>; hence the latter term refers to one who is of elegant habits and lives sumptuously. This is recorded by Zenodotus.

<margin>XXXI</margin>
### Even the ant and the gnat have their bile.

<note>original Greek: Ἔνεσι κἂν μύρμηκι κἂν σἐρφῳ χολή (Enesti kan myrmēki kan serphō cholē)</note>. That is: 

"The ant has its own bile, and the gnat has its own." 

This adage warns us that no enemy should be despised, nor should anyone be rashly provoked; for there is no animal so small or weak that, when irritated, does not burn with anger. It also applies well to small, insignificant men who possess no real power, yet who plot revenge while their anger, as is typical, provides them with spirit. The "serphus" <note>original: σἐρφος</note> is a tiny animal not unlike an ant <note>often identified as a gnat or winged ant</note>. According to Plutarch, when Brasidas had rashly put his hand into a jar of dried figs and happened to be bitten by a mouse hiding there, he said: "Good heavens, how true it is that there is no animal so tiny or so weak that, when provoked, does not desire to avenge itself."

<margin>XXXII</margin>
### To fashion by hand.

To fashion by hand <note>original: manu fingere</note> is to shape something with art and care. The metaphor is taken from those who mold images out of wax or clay. Lucius Annaeus Seneca says in his letters: "Some talents are easy and ready; some must be fashioned, as they say, by hand." The same author says in the sixth book of *On Benefits*: "Let us learn to owe benefits securely and to watch for opportunities to return them, not to 'make them by hand.'" He used "to make by hand" to mean "to manufacture by our own efforts." Likewise, Pliny says in book 18: "Let us therefore confess our fault, for we are not even content with those things that grow naturally, since many types of them are 'made by hand'" <note>referring to artificial cultivation</note>. Juvenal also says in his seventh Satire: 

"Demand that he mold the boy's morals as if with his thumb, just as one makes a face from wax." 

->**Tibullus, Book One:**<- 

"And to wish to fashion grey hair with the hands." 

He is speaking of someone dyeing their hair with artifice. Persius, in his fifth Satire, writes: 

"And the artist brings out a face under your thumb."

<summary>Erasmus examines proverbs regarding personal conduct, focusing on the importance of decorum (the dancer in a toga), the testing of character (the touchstone), and the warning that even the smallest creatures or people can strike back when provoked.</summary>

--- Page 612 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of ancient adages, shifting from social decorum and the "toga" to metaphors of craftsmanship and the integrity of treaties and character. It maintains the theme of internal consistency versus outward appearance.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his work *Brutus*, calls a style that is highly polished "wrought" <note>original Latin: "factum"</note>. He writes: "But as it was understood, how much power an accurate and, in a sense, **wrought** speech would have." The metaphor is taken from sculptors and craftsmen who impose a form upon raw material. This is why silver that has been worked is called "wrought silver" <note>original Latin: "factum argentum"</note>, as opposed to that which is raw or unrefined.

<margin>XXXIII</margin>
### A Locrian treaty.

A Locrian treaty <note>original Greek: Λοκρῶν σύνθημα (Lokrōn synthēma)</note>. This was said of treaty-breakers, such as the Locrians were once considered to be. It is said they betrayed the treaty they had entered into with the Peloponnesians and defected to the side of the Heraclidae <note>The descendants of Hercules</note>. Or, as some prefer, it refers to how they mocked the Sicilians by failing to keep their word. Zenodotus provides roughly this account. It is recorded in almost the same words by Eustathius in his commentary on the "Catalogue of Ships" <note>original: "Boeotia"</note> in Homer.

<margin>XXXIIII</margin>
### A Cassiotic knot.

A Cassiotic knot <note>original Greek: Κασσιωτικὸν ἄμμα (Kassiōtikon amma)</note>. This is commonly said of sly and versatile manners. Cassius is a mountain and a city of the same name in Egypt, near Pelusium. Akin to this is what we have mentioned in another place: the Herculean knot <note>original Greek: Ἡράκλειον ἄμμα (Hērakleion amma)</note>, by which we signify a very close and indissoluble friendship. On the <term>caduceus</term> <note>The herald’s staff carried by the messenger god Mercury</note> of Mercury, there are two snakes, a male and a female, who form the Herculean knot by the intertwining of their bodies in the middle. From there, their upper parts come together for a kiss so that they form a circle with their bend; below, they are brought back to the head of the staff with a similar bend, where their tails also meet. This image of the caduceus can still be seen in the most famous antiquities. It is from these, I believe, that **Johann Froben** <note>Erasmus's primary printer in Basel</note>—the most diligent of the printers of this age, and to whom students of sacred literature owe the most—borrowed his personal emblem. However, outside the circle formed by the snakes' heads meeting, a dove was added sitting upon a scepter. The Egyptians consecrated this knot to Mercury, implying that treaties should never be dissolved, but ought to remain most powerful; hence the name "Herculean" was added. Although the Gauls, and I suspect even the Egyptians, consider Hercules to be none other than Mercury. This adage about the Cassiotic knot is mentioned by Diogenianus and Suidas. Stephanus expresses it differently, in this way: "Cassiotic cloaks" <note>original Greek: κασσιώτικα ἱμάτια (kassiōtika himatia)</note>, unless perhaps "straps" <note>original Greek: ἱμάντια (himantia)</note> was written instead of "cloaks."

<margin>XXXV</margin>
### A good singer is a good chef.

A good singer is a good chef <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθὸς ψάλτης, ἀγαθὸς ζωμοποιὸς (Agathos psaltēs, agathos zōmopoios)</note>. This was said in disparagement of the art of music, as if it belongs to the same type of man to delight the ears with song and the palate with delicacies <note>original Latin: "cupediis," referring to gourmet sweets or fine foods</note>. Archidamus, the son of Zeuxippus, when someone was recommended to him on the grounds that he was a "good singer," replied: 
> "But here among us, he is a good **chef**."

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
### Apply the stone to the rule, not the rule to the stone.

Plutarch, in his short commentary titled *How a Man May Become Aware of His Progress in Virtue*, records this trochaic proverb: 
"You are applying the stone to the rule, not the rule to the stone" <note>original Greek: πρὸς σάθμην πέτρον τιθεῖς, μὴ τι πῶς πέτρῳ στάθμην (pros stathmēn petron titheis, mē ti pōs petrō stathmēn)</note>. 
It warns that life must be corrected according to the laws, not that laws should be dragged toward our own customs. We should do that which is honorable, rather than thinking that whatever we do is right. I have discussed the "Lesbian rule" <note>A flexible leaden rule that could be bent to the shape of a stone, used as a metaphor for flexible or biased judgment</note> elsewhere.

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
### To seek oneself outside oneself.

Said in a proverbial style by Persius in his first Satire: 
> "Correct the faulty scale on that balance, and **do not seek yourself outside yourself**" <note>original Latin: "nec te quæsiueris extra"</note>. 

That is, you should measure yourself by your own qualities, not by public opinion. This corresponds to what he said elsewhere: "Live with yourself." For we have within our own homes those things which are properly ours, and they are not to be sought from elsewhere. He who is not content with a clear conscience but looks for fame is said to "look outward" <note>original Greek: ἔξω βλέπειν (exō blepein)</note>. Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How a Man May Become Aware of His Progress in Virtue*, says: "It is clear he is still looking outward and being pulled toward reputation." To this also pertains what we have noted elsewhere: 
"A foreign ox often looks outward" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλότριος βοῦς πολλάκις ἔξω βλέπει (Allotrios bous pollakis exō blepei)</note>.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of personal character and wisdom, moving from the self-sufficiency of the wise man to the hypocrisy of those who criticize others while ignoring their own faults. It then explores linguistic metaphors derived from the Greek theater.</meta>

...surely you lack much at home. Furthermore, the wise man carries all his goods with him in himself, "whole like the world, smooth and round" <note>This refers to the Stoic ideal of the self-contained sage, described by Horace in his *Satires* (2.7.86) as "teres atque rotundus."</note>.

<margin>XXXVIII</margin>
### A doctor to others, while you yourself are covered in sores.

Plutarch, in his essay titled *How One May Profit by His Enemies*, cites this verse from some tragedy:
"A doctor to others, while he himself is bursting with sores" <note>original Greek: Ἄλλων ἰατρὸς, αὐτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων (Allōn iatros, autos helkesi bryōn)</note>.
This is to be hurled at those who correct and attack the errors of others while they themselves are saturated with hidden vices. It is similar to that most common proverb: "Physician, heal thyself." Gregory [of Nazianzus], in his *Apology for His Flight*, says: "Let us flee far from the proverb, lest while attempting to heal others, we ourselves are bursting with sores" <note>original Greek: ἡ φὶ παροιμίας πόῤῥω θεώμεθα, ἄλλοις ἰατρεύειν ἐπιχειροῦντες, αὐτοὶ βρύοντες ἕλκεσι</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero reports a similar sentiment in his twelfth *Philippic*: "For he who professes to be the guardian of many, it behooves him, in the opinion of wise men, to first be the guardian of his own head." Xenophon, in his *Symposium*, indicates something similar is commonly thrown at diviners: "They say that diviners indeed predict the future for others, but do not foresee what stands before them for themselves" <note>original Greek: οἱ μάντεσιν λέγοντες οἵ ἥπερ, ἄλλοις μὲν προαγορεύειν τὸ μέλλον, ἑαυτοῖς δὲ μὴ προορᾷν τὸ ἀπόν</note>.

<margin>XXXIX</margin>
### To speak tragically.

"To speak tragically" <note>original Greek: Τραγικώτερον λαλεῖν (Tragikōteron lalein)</note>. This means to use grander words. For the character of tragic writers is sublime; tragedy loves <term>ampullae</term> <note>Literally "bottles," used here to mean bombastic or inflated speech.</note> and "foot-and-a-half-long words." Menander, quoted by Plutarch in his *Letter of Consolation to Apollonius*, says: "But if you have breathed the common air under the same laws as we have, let me **speak more tragically** to you" <note>original Greek: Εἰ δ’ ἦν τοῖς αὐτοῖς νόμοις, ἐφ’ οἷσπερ ἡμεῖς ἔπαθες τὸ ἀέρα τὸν κοινὸν, ἵνα σοι τραγικώτερον λαλῶ</note>. Plato also uses this in the third book of *The Republic*. Gregory the Theologian says in one of his letters: "It was not right, I think, when you were acting tragically, to celebrate in a comic fashion" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἦν οἶμαι προήκοντα τραγικῶς, πανηγυρίζειν κωμικῶς</note>. The same author, in a letter to Basil, writes: "O earth and sun, air and virtue! For I shall perform a little tragedy" <note>original Greek: ὦ γῆ καὶ ἥλιε, ἀὴρ καὶ ἀρετὴ, τραγῳδήσω γάρ τι μικρόν</note>. However, I suspect that "chaff" <note>original Greek: ἀθήρ (athēr)</note> was written instead of "virtue" <note>original Greek: ἀρετὴ (aretē)</note>, just as he had made "praiseworthy man" <note>original Greek: αἰνήρ (ainēr)</note> out of "man" <note>original Greek: ἀνήρ (anēr)</note>. For the one who first published these letters seems to have known Greek so well that he could barely read it! In Lucian, one frequently finds "to act out tragically" <note>original Greek: ἐκτραγῳδίζειν (ektragōdizein)</note> used for speaking magnificently and making a matter seem grander with words; and "to speak weightily" <note>original Greek: φορικῶς λαλεῖν (phorikōs lalein)</note> for speaking more grandly and loftily.

<margin>XL</margin>
### To have a tragic gaze.

"To have a tragic gaze" <note>original Greek: Τραγικὸν βλέπειν (Tragikon blepein)</note>. Aristophanes used a similar figure in *Plutus* when describing Poverty:
"She gazes with something of a mad and **tragic** look" <note>original Greek: Βλέπῃ γέ τι μανικὸν τι καὶ τραγῳδικόν</note>.
This will apply either to the haughty or to those who are sad and mournful.

<margin>XLI</margin>
### The tongue has sworn.

This phrase passed from tragedy into a proverb: "The tongue has sworn" <note>original Greek: ἡ γλῶσσ’ ὀμώμοχ’ (hē glōss' omōmoch)</note>. It is used when someone does not keep the faith of a promise, or when they do not promise from the heart. It is found in Euripides' *Hippolytus*:
"The tongue has sworn, but the mind remains unsworn" <note>original Greek: Ἡ γλῶσσ’ ὀμώμοχ’, ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀνώμοτος</note>.
The insults of Comic poets attacked this little verse. Aristophanes in his *Women at the Thesmophoria* <note>Erasmus writes "Bacchis," likely referring to a scene involving the character Mania or a confusion of titles, but the quote is famously parodied in *Thesmophoriazusae* and *The Frogs*.</note>:
"Or the mind which would not wish to swear by the sacred rites, / But the tongue having sworn, separately from the mind."
Likewise, in *The Frogs*, mocking Euripides:
"The tongue has sworn, but I will choose Aeschylus."
Similarly, Pindar in his fifth *Isthmian* ode, praising someone of a wise and truthful tongue, says:
"The tongue is not outside the mind" <note>original Greek: γλῶσσα δ’ οὐκ ἔξω φρενῶν</note>.

<summary>This page explores several adages related to hypocrisy and theatrical metaphors, contrasting outward speech or appearance with internal reality. Key entries include the irony of a "sick doctor" and the famous Euripidean line about a tongue swearing while the heart remains uncommitted.</summary>
<keywords>hypocrisy, tragedy, Greek drama, Euripides, Aristophanes, Plutarch, bombast, oaths, integrity, ancient medicine</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Greek and Latin proverbs, focusing on idiomatic expressions for time, the predictability of nature, the futility of resisting fate, and satirical puns regarding political corruption.</meta>

### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES

A saying of Euripides is cited by Plato in his *Theaetetus*: "If you answer that it is so, something of Euripides will happen to us: our tongue will be unrefuted, but our mind will not be unrefuted" <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ἀποκρίνῃ ὅτι ἔστιν, Εὐριπίδου τι ξυμβήσεται, ἡ μὲν γλῶττα ἀνέλεγκτος ἡμῖν ἔσται, ἡ δὲ φρὴν οὐκ ἀνέλεγκτος. This is a famous reference to Euripides' play *Hippolytus*, where a character says, "My tongue swore, but my mind remains unsworn."</note>. That is: if you respond in the affirmative, a "Euripidean" situation will occur where our words might technically stand, but our inner conviction does not.

<margin>XLII</margin>
->Yesterday and the day before yesterday.<-

"Yesterday and the day before" <note>original Greek: χθὲς καὶ πρώϊν (chthes kai prōin)</note>. This is a proverbial hyperbole, signifying a time that passed very recently. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Rivalry Between Fire and Water*, writes: "But the use of fire, as they say, was 'yesterday and just now' under Prometheus; the life of fire was not without the life of water." <note>original: ἡ δὲ πυρὸς χρῆσις, ἐχθὲς, φασὶ, καὶ πρώϊν, ὑπὸ προμηθέως... (hē de pyros chrēsis, echthes, phasi, kai prōin, hypo promētheōs...)</note>. It appears frequently in Lucian, specifically in the booklet *On Those Who Serve for Hire*. Likewise, Plato in the third book of *Laws*: "And many other things happened to others, so to speak, 'yesterday and the day before'" <note>original: τὰ δ' ἄλλα ἄλλοις πάμπολλα... χθὲς καὶ πρώϊν γεγονότα (ta d' alla allois pampolla... chthes kai prōin gegonota)</note>. I have read elsewhere, though the specific passage does not come to mind: "He who established gods for himself yesterday and the day before." Plato also says in the *Second Alcibiades*: "I think you are not unaware of things born yesterday and the day before" <note>original: οἶμαι δέ σε οὐκ ἀνήκοον εἶναι ψιλά γε χθιζά τε καὶ πρωϊζὰ γεγεννημένα</note>.

<margin>XLIII</margin>
->It will not rain after the night on which a wild sow has given birth.<-

Plutarch, in his commentary *On Natural Causes*, cites this verse as a commonly tossed-about proverb:
> No longer will it rain on the night when the wild sow brings forth her young. <note>original Greek: Μηκέτι νυκτὸς ὕσῃ, ᾗ κεν τέκῃ ἀγροτέρα σῦς</note>

Tame sows give birth often and at various times, but wild ones give birth only once, and almost always on the same days—namely, at the beginning of summer. For this reason, people say there will be no more rain once the wild sow has farrowed, because the rainy months have already passed. It could be used jokingly if we were to say that things will be more peaceful after some ill-tempered or quarrelsome person has finally had their way.

<margin>XLIIII</margin>
->To fight with the gods.<-

"To fight against God" <note>original Greek: θεομαχεῖν (theomachein)</note>. Those who either struggle against nature or resist fatal necessity are said to fight with the gods. The expression is taken from the myth of the Giants <note>In Greek mythology, the Giants attempted to overthrow the Olympian gods by piling mountains on top of each other.</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his dialogue *On Old Age*, says: "For what else is warring with the gods in the manner of the Giants, if not resisting nature?"
Euripides in the *Bacchae*:
> I will not fight against God, being persuaded by your words. <note>original: Κ' οὐ θεομαχήσω, σῶν λόγων πειθὰς ὑπο</note>

A six-foot verse of this kind is also counted among proverbial maxims:
> To fight with God and Fortune is a dire thing. <note>original: θεῷ μάχεσθαι δεινόν ἐστι καὶ τύχῃ</note>

That famous line from Homer is also well-known:
> It is not possible for any man to fight with a divinity. <note>original: οὐκ ἔστιν πῶς δαίμονι φωτὶ μάχεσθαι</note>

Pindar imitated this:
> One ought not to strive against God. <note>original: χρὴ δὲ πρὸς θεὸν οὐκ ἐρίζειν</note>

<margin>XLV</margin>
->The Doric Muse.<-

"The Doric Muse" <note>original Greek: Δωρικὴ μοῦσα (Dōrikē mousa)</note>. Used of those who are greedy for gifts. Aristophanes, in the *Knights*, jokes at the expense of Cleon <note>A prominent Athenian politician and general during the Peloponnesian War, often portrayed as a corrupt demagogue.</note>, saying that he could learn no other music except the "Doric" style—clearly playing on the well-known types of musical modes: Doric, Lydian, Phrygian, and Boeotian. However, he plays with the word by mockingly distorting it: he uses "Gift-taking style" <note>original: Δωροδοκηστί (Dōrodokēsti)</note> instead of "Doric style" <note>original: Δωριστί (Dōristi)</note>, saying: "That fellow can learn nothing unless it is in the 'Gift-taking' mode." In Greek, "to receive gifts" <note>original: Δωροδοκεῖσθαι (Dōrodokeisthai)</note> means to be corrupted by bribes so that you give a judgment in someone's favor. This is what Pythagoras calls "eating beans" <note>original: κυάμους ἐσθίειν</note>. For in ancient times, votes were cast using beans; therefore, "symbolically," those who made a profit from the voting process were said to "eat the beans." This is the interpretation given by the author, whoever he was, who collected the stories mentioned by Gregory of Nazianzus. Although someone has recently emerged who interprets Pythagoras's "beans" as "testicles," because the beginning of life is in them (arguing that *kyamos* [bean] was said as if it were *kyēma* [embryo/fetus]), I would only think him worth listening to if he had cited even one minor ancient author or a more serious argument. Hesiod also calls corrupt judges "gift-eaters" <note>original: Δωροφάγους (dōrophagous)</note>, that is, devourers of bribes.

### SECOND CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY
T 4

<margin>XLVI</margin>
### The shoe should not be larger than the foot.

"The shoe should not be larger than the foot" <note>original Greek: Μὴ ὑπὲρ τὸν πόδα τὸ ὑπόδημα (Mē hyper ton poda to hypodēma)</note>. That is, do not take on tasks beyond your strength, or do not behave more magnificently than your social condition allows. Lucian, in his *Images*, says: "Neither let the shoe be larger than the foot" <note>original Greek: μηδὲ ὑπὲρ τὸν πόδα ἔσω τὸ ὑπόδημα (mēde hyper ton poda esō to hypodēma)</note>. Again, in the dialogue immediately following: "These things seemed to you immoderate, and larger than the measure of the foot" <note>original Greek: ταῦτά σοι ἐκ μέτρων ἔδοξε, καὶ ὑπὲρ τὸν πόδα (tauta soi ek metrōn edoxe, kai hyper ton poda)</note>. And again in *The Cock*: "And by no means according to the proportion of the foot" <note>original Greek: καὶ οὐχὶ κατὰ λόγον τοῦ ποδός (kai ouchi kata logon tou podos)</note>.

<margin>XLVII</margin>
### A Mercury is not fashioned from just any wood.

"A Mercury cannot be made from just any wood" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐκ παντὸς ξύλου Ἑρμῆς ἂν γένοιτο (ouk ek pantos xylou Hermēs an genoito)</note>. This means that not everyone's intellect is suited for the disciplines of learning. For some, as Quintilian <note>Erasmus refers to him as "Fabius"</note> says, "should be sent away to the countryside." This allegory is taken from craftsmen who carefully select their materials. Indeed, Theophrastus demonstrates extensively in the fifth book of his *On Plants* that different materials are suitable for different things. Pliny also notes this in his sixteenth book. Some seek out materials with great superstition when carving a deity. And although that god Priapus <note>A god of fertility often represented by crude, simple wooden statues</note>, being easy-going and coarse, does not mind being made of fig-wood, the same would not be permitted for the god Mercury, who is so ingenious and endowed with all the arts. 

However, it pleases me more to refer this to the magical statues of Mercury, which they used to carve not from just any material, but from a specific wood; otherwise, it would not be fit for the use of the magical art. This was also one of the arguments of "magical crime" leveled against Apuleius <note>A Roman writer and philosopher famously accused of using magic to win a wealthy widow</note>: that he had commissioned a small seal of Mercury to be carved from boxwood, as he himself shows in his first *Apology for Magic*. Perhaps boxwood was chosen for this above all because it reflects the paleness of a human, or because its material is the most eternal of all. For it also holds its own against the heat of fire, according to Pliny. Apuleius, in his first *Apology*, attributes the proverb to Pythagoras: "For," he says, "Mercury ought not to be carved from every wood, as Pythagoras used to say." 

A similar saying is found in Athenaeus, book 5—though it is uncertain whether it was said by Demochares or Crates: "No one could fashion a spear point from savory <note>a type of herb</note>, nor an irreproachable soldier from Socrates" <note>original Greek: Ἐκ θύμβρας δόρυ ἂν δύναιτο κατασκευάσαι λόγχην, οὐδὲ ἐκ σωκράτους στρατιώτην ἀμέμπτον (Ek thymbras dory an dynaito kataskeuasai lonchēn, oude ek sōkratous stratiōtēn amempton)</note>. "Savory" <note>Latin: thymbra</note> is a kind of herb or shrub not unlike thyme or savory. Pliny mentions it in book 19, chapter 8, as being fit for seasoning; hence those who delight in sharp things are called "savory-eaters" <note>original Greek: θυμβροφάγοι (thymbrophagoi)</note> by the Greeks, a term which is also applied to those whose circumstances are harsh. Again, Athenaeus says in the same book: "But neither can a spear be made from savory, as Demochares says, nor a good man from such speeches" <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ οὔτ’ ἐκ θύμβρας... λόγχη, οὔτ’ ἐκ τούτων λόγων ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς γίνεται (all’ out’ ek thymbras... lonchē, out’ ek toutōn logōn anēr agathos ginetai)</note>.

<margin>XLVIII</margin>
### I am not one of those heroes.

"I am not of the number of those heroes" <note>original Greek: οὐκ εἰμὶ τούτων τῶν ἡρώων (ouk eimi toutōn tōn hērōōn)</note>. That is, I am not of the number of those who are more inclined to cause harm than to do good. This is taken from the concept of "genies" <note>minor spirits or protective deities</note>, who, when provoked, often bring destruction but very rarely help. Therefore, those who promised they would be helpful and bring no harm used this adage. Zenodotus cites Menander's *The Youths* as a source.

<margin>XLIX</margin>
### I know Simon, and Simon knows me.

"I know Simon, and Simon knows me" <note>original Greek: οἶδ’ α Σίμονα κὰὶ σίμων ἐμέ (oid' a Simona kai simōn eme)</note>. This was said of those who were equals <note>usually in wickedness</note>. Zenodotus and Suidas write that there were two leaders, Simon and Nikon, both of notorious wickedness. Simon, however, because he excelled in vices, obscured the reputation of the other. Hence, in the proverb, they name Simon alone. They say these two were Telchines <note>mythical sorcerers or spiteful spirits</note>, who, having brought the waters of the Styx onto the land, built Arnon. Among the Greeks, the Telchines are called evil spirits, or men who are sorcerers and evildoers. Strabo, in book 10, mentions the Telchines, saying there were nine who accompanied Rhea from Rhodes to Crete. They want the name "Telchines" to come from "to charm" <note>original Greek: θέλγειν (thelgein)</note>, which means to darken or to soothe, because they surround and deceive men who have been enticed. From this, they also call whatever is remarkably wicked "Telchinian" <note>original Greek: τελχινώδεις (telchinōdeis)</note>; and "to act like a Telchin" <note>original Greek: τελχινίζειν (telchinizein)</note> means to act contentiously and stubbornly. The Etymologist adds that all Cretans are called Telchines, and Crete itself was called "Telchinia." Chrysostom uses the adage in *Against Babylas*: "O the right hand of a Telchin!" <note>original Greek: διὰ δεξιᾶς τελχῖνος (dia dexias telchinos)</note>. For that is how he refers to a harmful right hand.

<margin>L</margin>
### Let this not be too "hot" just now.

Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "See that this is not too hot <note>or "clever"</note> just now" <note>original: Vide ne nimium callidum hoc sit modo</note>. Donatus shows this to be a proverb, although the reading is ambiguous. For it can be read as both *calidum* (hot/rash) and *callidum* (shrewd/crafty).

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning the limits of human ability, the necessity of natural talent for education, and the reputation of notoriously wicked or dangerous individuals and spirits.</summary>
<keywords>suitability, education, Mercury, magic, Apuleius, heroes, spirits, Telchines, Simon and Nikon, puns</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Latin proverbs, focusing on the distinction between rashness and cleverness, the dangers of overreaching one’s abilities, and the definition of a truly useless person. It picks up mid-sentence from a discussion on whether a plan should be called "calidum" (hot/rash) or "callidum" (clever/cunning).</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...hot <note>original: "calidum"</note>: so that the former refers to a hurried plan, and the latter to one that is too cunning. Indeed, both usually turn out poorly—either those things that are too "hot," which are established precipitously, or those that are conducted with overly bold deceits. And just as Fabius Maximus says in the writings of Titus Livy, "Rashness is not only foolish, but also usually unlucky," so too does craftiness sometimes lead to the greatest danger. Those who read the word as "clever" <note>original: "callidum"</note> seem to look back to what Chærea had said a little earlier: "I never saw a better plan given." Those who read "hot" <note>original: "calidum"</note> with a single 'l'—and in my opinion, more correctly—recognize a Greek figure of speech. For they call a deed "hot" <note>original: "thermón"</note> when it is either wicked, or headlong and daring. For instance, Penia in Aristophanes’s *Plutus*, speaking of the old men who are attempting a new thing by restoring sight to the blind Pluto, says:

->O hot deed, and unholy, and lawless!<-
<note>original Greek: Ω θερμὸν ἔργον, κἀνόσιον, καὶ παράνομον (O thermon ergon, kanosion, kai paranomon)</note>

The interpreter explains "hot" <note>original Greek: θερμόν (thermon)</note> as "unheard of, daring and headlong, and rash" <note>original Greek: πρὸ ὁδοῦ, τολμηρὸν, ἀκίνητον (pro hodou, tolmēron, akinēton)</note>. Likewise, Sophocles in *Antigone*:

->You have a hot heart for cold things.<-
<note>original Greek: Θερμὴν ἐπὶ ψυχροῖσι καρδίαν ἔχεις (Thermēn epi psychroisi kardian echeis)</note>

Antigone is being rebuked because she too eagerly desired to bury her brother. And Plutarch, in the fifth decade of his *Table Talk*, indicates that "stronger" <note>original Greek: ζωρότερον (zōroteron)</note> signifies "hot" to some; for instance, when Achilles in Homer orders Patroclus to "mix it stronger," he was demanding speed in the service. Just as we too, he says, frequently order servants "to pour or serve more hotly" <note>original Greek: θερμότερον ἐπιχέειν ἢ διακονεῖν (thermotheron epicheein ē diakonein)</note>, meaning to attend to the service more hotly and quickly.

<margin>51</margin>
->Woman, do not lift the sword.<-
<note>original Greek: Μὴ μάχαιραν αἶρε θῆλυ (Mē machairan aire thēly)</note>

This is a half-line of trochaic verse. Do not take on a massive task when you are unable to help. For it is the part of men "to fight for the fatherland," <note>original Greek: Ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης (Amynesthai peri patrēs)</note> as Homer says. It can also be drawn toward this meaning: do not show a hope that you cannot fulfill. Do not threaten or provoke an enemy when you cannot crush them once they are provoked. Brutus notes this of Cicero: that he irritated Antony with his speeches, but once Antony was irritated, Cicero could not suppress him; that is, "the woman was lifting the sword."

<margin>52</margin>
->Useful neither to himself nor to others.<-

Those who are entirely useless, and "born only to consume the fruits of the earth," are called, in a proverbial phrasing, "useful neither to themselves nor to others." Marcus Tullius Cicero in his books *On Duties*: "Wherefore, as I said before, those who are of use neither to themselves nor to others—in whom there is no labor, no care, and no industry—are despised." This is taken from that noble poem of Hesiod, from the work entitled *Works and Days*, which Aristotle frequently cites:

->That man is altogether best who considers all things for himself,<-
->Pondering what will be better hereafter and in the end.<-
->And he too is good who obeys one who speaks well,<-
->But he who neither understands for himself, nor, listening to another,<-
->Lays it to heart—that man, again, is a useless man.<-
<note>original Greek: Οὗτος μὲν πανάριστος, ὃς αὐτῷ πάντα νοήσῃ... ὅδ’ αὖτ’ ἀχρήϊος ἀνήρ</note>

Titus Livy rendered the sentiment of these verses quite elegantly and aptly: "I have often heard," he says, "that he is the first man who himself provides counsel on what is needed. Second is he who obeys one who advises well. He who knows neither how to provide counsel himself, nor how to obey another, is of the lowest intellect." You may see not a few mortals of this kind, who, since they cannot discern what needs to be done due to a poverty of mind, are yet—wonderful to say—so stubborn that they do not admit the advice of others. They clearly resemble that ass of Horace, who, since he neither knew the way nor would obey his leader, was driven headlong over a cliff. Zeno, according to Diogenes, inverted Hesiod’s poem in this way...

<summary>This page discusses proverbs regarding "hot" (rash) actions versus "clever" ones, using examples from classical drama and philosophy. It also introduces the proverb against women "lifting the sword" (taking on unsuitable burdens) and the definition of a useless person as one who neither thinks for himself nor listens to advice.</summary>
<keywords>rashness, cunning, hot deeds, Antigone, Cicero, Brutus, uselessness, Hesiod, social roles, ancient wisdom</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the fifth century of the second chiliad (thousand) of Erasmus’s collection of adages. # SECOND CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY

<margin>LII</margin>
*That man is best of all who would obey one who speaks well.*
*Yet that man is also good who understands all things by himself.* <note>Erasmus is quoting Hesiod’s *Works and Days* (293–295), a passage also famously cited by Aristotle. The Greek original is: Κεῖνος μὲν πανάριστος, ὃς εὖ εἰπόντι πίθοιτο. ἐσθλὸς δ' αὖ κἀκεῖνος, ὃς αὐτὸς πάντα νοήσῃ.</note> that is,
> Best indeed is he who obeys one who advises rightly.
> But again, he is good who knows all things through himself.

Namely, preferring the one who obeys well over the one who understands well. For to the latter, only intelligence is present, but to the former, even use and experience. <note>Erasmus offers a slightly unusual interpretation here, emphasizing the practical application of the one who follows good advice over the purely theoretical wisdom of the independent thinker.</note>

<margin>LIII</margin>
-> Neither rained upon, nor scorched by the sun. <-
*Neither does it rain, nor is it in the sun.* <note>original Greek: οὔθ' ὕεται, ὅτ' ἐπ' ἠλίστῳ (outh' hyetai, hot' ep' hēlistō). The Latin translation is: Neq; compluitur, neq; sole aduritur.</note> It was customary to say this of someone who lived a life far removed from all discomfort. To this, that line of Horace is the opposite: "He sweated and shivered." <note>original Latin: *Sudavit et alsit* from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, describing the rigorous training of an athlete.</note>
And "a side capable of enduring dust, sun, and rain." <note>original Latin: Et pulveris & solis, & coelestis aquę patiēs latus.</note> Merchants, soldiers, athletes, and sailors—men of that sort—must become accustomed to enduring the sun and tolerating rainstorms. He who lives softly at home is away from these evils. Therefore, it will fit a delicate person who is unfit for enduring labors. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*, noting the softness of Bacchus <note>The god Dionysus, who is portrayed as effeminate and cowardly in the play.</note>:
*And tell me of a place neither too hot nor too cold.* <note>original Greek: Καὶ μήτε θερμήν, μήτ' ἄγαν ψυχρὰν φράσης (Kai mēte thermēn, mēt' agan psychran phrasēs).</note> that is,
Give me a place neither sweltering nor too chilly.
This proverb is recorded by Zenodotus.

<margin>LIIII</margin>
-> The most beautiful of monkeys is deformed. <-
*Of monkeys, the most shapely is misshapen.* <note>original Greek: τῶν πιθήκων ὁ μορφότατος δύσμορφός ἐστι (tōn pithēkōn ho morphōtatos dysmorphos esti).</note> That is, the most beautiful of monkeys is ugly. This will be rightly said of those things which are inherently flawed by their very nature, and are not at all to be compared even with the lowest of those things which are in the order of the honorable. For example, if someone were to say that the most "upright" pimp is a perjurer, or the most "honorable" actor is infamous, or the "best" poem by Mevius <note>Mevius was a famously bad poet frequently mocked by Virgil and Horace; he serves here as the standard for poor quality.</note> is actually bad. It is cited by Plato and attributed to Heraclitus as the author.

<margin>LV</margin>
-> Seeking a side-dish, I lost my garment. <-
*For while seeking relish, I lost my cloak.* <note>original Greek: ζητῶν γὰρ ὄψον θοἰμάτιον ἀπώλεσα (zētōn gar opson thoimation apōlesa).</note> That is, while I was looking for a side-dish, I lost my clothes. This is used when a matter turns out very poorly, or when we lose greater things while chasing after some small ones. It is recorded by Suidas and others, though they do not indicate where it originated. However, it is not obscure that it arose from an event in which some thief, while he was striving to steal food, was caught and barely escaped after throwing away his cloak. Aristophanes alludes to this proverb:
*For these reasons, indeed, the garment was also lost besides.* <note>original Greek: Διὰ ταῦτα δὴ καὶ θοἰμάτιον ἀπώλεσα.</note> that is,
On account of these things, your clothing also perished in addition.

<margin>LVI</margin>
-> You could sooner hide an elephant under your arm. <-
Lucian in *Against the Ignorant Book-Collector*: *You could hide five elephants under your arm sooner than one lewd man.* <note>original Greek: θᾶττον ἂν πέντε ἐλέφαντας ὑπὸ μάλης κρύψας ἢ ἕνα κίναιδον (thātton an pente elephantas hypo malēs krypsas ē hena kinaidon). Erasmus’s Latin text here has "five" (pente) in the Greek but "one" in the initial heading.</note> This is said of those who cannot be concealed by any means from betraying the sickness of their mind by certain signs. It is, moreover, a proverbial figure of hyperbole, to which that saying in Marcus Tullius [Cicero] from Ennius is related (in the second book *On the Orator*): "A flame is more easily suppressed in the burning mouth of a wise man than he can hold back good [witty] words."

<margin>LVII</margin>
-> Fortunate Corinth, but I would rather be a Tenean. <-
*Corinth is indeed happy, but may I be a Tenean.* <note>original Greek: Εὐδαίμων γε Κόρινθος, ἐγὼ δ' εἴην Τενεάτης (Eudaimōn ge Korinthos, egō d' eiēn Teneatēs).</note> that is,
Fortunate Corinth, but let me become a Tenean.
Tenea is a certain wooded and pleasant village not far from Corinth. Furthermore, the wealth of the Corinthians was legendary. Strabo writes in his eighth book that this verse was delivered as an oracle to a certain Asian who was consulting whether it would be better to move to Corinth. From this, it seems to have passed into common speech like many other things; and thus it is included in the catalog of Greek adages. It would be timely to use this whenever, in a comparison between two things, we do not deny that one is more excellent in itself, but the other is more pleasing and agreeable to our mind. For example, if someone were to say: "I indeed confess that the knowledge of the law is more suitable for acquiring both wealth and fame than poetry is, but...
*Corinth is indeed happy, but may I be a Tenean.*"
Let that other thing be better or more useful, but this one is more pleasing to my soul. Strabo warns that "Tegean" <note>original: "Tegeates"</note> is wrongly read by some instead of "Tenean" <note>original: "Teneates"</note>. For Tegea is a city of Arcadia.

<margin>LVIII</margin>
-> An ass into the chaff. <-
*An ass into the husks.* <note>original Greek: ὄνος εἰς ἄχυρα (onos eis achyra).</note> That is, an ass into the chaff—one should understand, "has fallen." This was usually said when a more elegant fortune has happened to someone beyond expectation, or someone has by chance obtained that in which he especially rejoi— <note>Erasmus uses the catchword "gau-" to lead into "gauderet" or "gaudeat" (rejoices) on the following page.</note>

<meta>catchword: gau-</meta>

<summary>This page explores several proverbs regarding the value of following good advice, the nature of comfort versus hardship, and the inherent flaws in certain classes of people or things. It also discusses how one might prefer a simple, pleasant life (Tenea) over a wealthy, prestigious one (Corinth).</summary>
<keywords>Hesiod, Horace, Aristophanes, Plato, Heraclitus, Lucian, Cicero, Strabo, Corinth, Tenea, wealth vs. comfort, inherent nature, proverbs, Greek literature, Latin literature</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

...enjoys: just as if you were to see someone greedy for oysters eating his fill of them, you might not wrongly say, **A donkey into the straw.** <note>original Greek: ὄνος εἰς ἄχυρα (onos eis achyra)</note> That is, a donkey into the chaff. In the fragments of the second book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned" by Athenaeus</note>, this six-foot verse is cited from the comedies of Philemon:
<margin>that is,</margin>
*Now the donkey goes into the straw of the dainties.* <note>original Greek: ὄνος βαδίζει εἰς ἄχυρα τραγημάτων (onos badizei eis achyra tragēmatōn)</note>
It will be more pleasant if you transfer the meaning further—for example, if someone eagerly reads a poet by whom he is particularly delighted. It will also be suitable for this use: when someone contaminates a matter through ignorance, just as if a barbarian or an illiterate man were to defile a good author with bad commentaries. In the same way, Thomas and Nicolaus with their glosses, and Passavantius with equally tasteless additions, defiled his work *The City of God*. <note>Erasmus refers to Thomas Aquinas, Nicolaus of Lyra, and Jacopo Passavanti, medieval commentators whose "Gothic" or scholastic interpretations he often found lacking in classical elegance or accuracy.</note> For the donkey delights in rolling about, and destroys everything with this playfulness. Apuleius also indicates this when he writes that all the small plots of the garden were thrown into disorder by the rollings of his body. <note>A reference to *The Golden Ass*, where the protagonist is transformed into a donkey.</note> No one will fail to see that this adage was born from an actual event.

### A parrot speaks with one voice, a quail with another.

Martial used this proverbial pattern against a certain secret poet who, recounting Aesop’s fables, intended to spread his own inept little verses among the common people under Martial's name, so that readers, deceived by the title, would believe them to be Martial's:
> Do you believe this, Priscus,
> That a parrot speaks with the voice of a quail?
It will be suitable for musicians or poets of a vastly different style and a vastly dissimilar faculty. Among birds, the parrot expresses human voices most closely. Quails are more combative than talkative. Hence Ovid says in his *Epitaph of a Parrot*:
> Behold, the quails live amidst their battles.

### A bald man with hair.

"A bald man with hair" appears in the same Martial, undoubtedly as a proverbial figure:
<margin>Again, the same author:</margin>
> Nothing is more shameful than a bald man with hair.
> When you are bald, you shall be haired. <note>original Latin: Calvo turpius est nihil comato / Calvus cum fueris, eris comatus. Erasmus is referring to the use of wigs or hairpieces to hide baldness.</note>
This is aptly said of one who, destitute of true goods, sells himself using borrowed ones. For instance, if someone were to put forward the things of others as his own; or if someone were to pretend to be what they are not—just as if an old man with a fitted hairpiece or dyed hair were to affect to seem young, or if an ugly woman, having applied makeup, wished to be considered beautiful.

### First, Aegina nourishes the best boys.

<margin>Aegina has always first nourished the best boys.</margin> <margin>that is,</margin>
<note>original Greek: τὰ πρῶτ' ἀεὶ παῖδας Αἰγιν' ἐκτρέφει (ta prōt' aei paidas Aigin' ektrephei)</note>
This is said of any matter that, having begun with better beginnings, gradually slides down toward the worse, as the affairs of mortals do. The adage arose because of Achilles, Patroclus, Ajax, and Neoptolemus, because these men excelled in virtue while they were Aeginetans. Strabo agrees with these in his eighth book, stating that for this reason Aeacus set out from this island with his descendants. For Stephanus thinks the name of the island was given after Aegina, the mother of Aeacus. This same island once held the empire of the sea, and did not even yield to the Athenians in the naval battle at Salamis when competing for the leadership while the Persians were invading Greece. Homer also mentions this island. It is the most noble of the Cyclades, which was for a long time called Oenone, as the same Strabo and Stephanus indicate. On account of their endurance of labors, industry, and frugality, the Aeginetans were called **Myrmidones** <note>literally "Ant-people"</note>; for since they had land that was stony on the surface but suitable for grain underneath, they were seen living in excavated caverns in the manner of ants, and in the carrying away of stones, they represented the industry of that creature. Later, as the integrity of their morals slipped, the Aeginetans began to be heard of in this way: a fact testified by several proverbs, among which is this: *The Aeginetans are neither third nor fourth*, as was said in the proverb about the Megarians. Not dissimilar to that is: *Once the Milesians were brave.* <note>These proverbs imply that a group once famous for greatness has become irrelevant or fallen into decline.</note>

### The Unlaughing Stone.

**The Unlaughing Rock.** <note>original Greek: Ἀγέλαστος πέτρα (Agelastos petra). Latin: Irrisibile saxum.</note> This refers to a thing that is vehemently bitter and sad. Long ago, there was a certain rock in Attica on which they say Ceres sat down, when, having left behind her lit torches, she was searching for Proserpina, who had been snatched away by Pluto. Furthermore, when she had come to Eleusis, she sat there sadly on a certain rock, which for that very reason was called "the unlaughing." The author is Zenodotus. It will fit those who are severe and gloomy, whom they call *agelastoi*...

<meta>This page continues the fifth century of the second chiliad of Erasmus’s Adages. The previous page discussed the proverb "A donkey into the straw," used for someone indulging in their favorite thing or someone out of their depth. This page transitions from a brief mention of Socrates and Pericles into a series of proverbs related to sacrifice, moral effort, and regional reputations.</meta>

Pliny places Socrates in this number <note>Referring to those who are a source of great annoyance or difficulty to others</note>, while Aristides places Pericles there. Nor will it be inappropriately applied to a matter that is exceedingly troublesome.

### 63. Agamemnon’s victim. ###

<margin>Agamemnon’s victim. <note>original Greek: Ἀγαμέμνονος θυσία (Agamemnonos thysia)</note></margin> That is, the sacrificial animal of Agamemnon. This used to be said against those who are harsh and difficult to persuade. It arose from the story that when Agamemnon was about to perform a religious rite at Troy, an ox escaped, and it was only caught and brought back with great difficulty. This much is from Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic</note>. It will also apply to those who do something unwillingly and under compulsion. In ancient times, it was observed in sacrifices that the victim should stand calmly and willingly. If it broke its rope and fled, it was considered an ill omen. It seems to me that this could also refer to Agamemnon sacrificing his daughter Iphigenia at Aulis, though he did so very unwillingly. This is recorded by Zenodotus.

### 64. Gentler once the victim is slain. ###

"Gentler once the victim is slain"—Horace used this in a proverbial figure in his *Odes*:
*The victim, once slain, will come more gently.* <note>original Latin: Mactata veniet lenior hostia</note>
This refers to things that are spontaneous and tame. The metaphor is taken from sacrifices, in which the victim was tested by drawing a knife across its forehead; this act they called *mactare* <note>to slaughter or honor</note>. From this, those who are esteemed for their courage are called *macti virtute* <note>honored for their virtue; "well done"</note>.

### 65. A small evil, a great good. ###

<margin>A small evil, a great good. <note>original Greek: Μικρὸν κακὸν μέγ’ ἀγαθόν (Mikron kakon meg’ agathon)</note></margin> This adage advises that from a very small inconvenience and a little labor, the highest and greatest advantages may be gathered. It is reported by Diogenianus. The sentiment of Musonius <note>A Stoic philosopher</note>, which Aulus Gellius records in Book 16, does not differ from this: <margin>If you do something honorable with labor, the labor departs, but the honor remains. If you do something shameful with pleasure, the pleasure departs, but the shame remains. <note>original Greek: Ἄντι πράξης καλὸν μετὰ πόνε, ὁ μὲν πόνος οἴχεται, τὸ δὲ καλὸν μένει. ἄντι ποιήσης αἰσχρὸν μεθ’ ἡδονῆς, τὸ μὲν ἡδὺ οἴχεται, τὸ δὲ αἰσχρὸν μένει.</note></margin> That is, if you have done anything honorable with toil, the toil passes away, but the honor remains. If you have done anything disgraceful with pleasure, the pleasure passes away, but the disgrace remains. Cato <note>Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman</note> expressed the same sentiment, though perhaps with less rhythm and polish, yet faithfully, in this manner: "Consider in your minds: if you have done anything rightly through labor, that labor will quickly leave you; but the good deed will not depart from you as long as you live. But if you have done anything wickedly for the sake of pleasure, the pleasure will quickly pass away; but that wicked deed will remain with you forever."

### 66. The Eleusinian mysteries of the Athenians. ###

<margin>The Eleusinian mysteries of the Athenians <note>original Greek: Ἀττικοὶ ἐλευσίνια (Attikoi eleusinia)</note></margin>—that is, the Athenians' Eleusinian rites—with the phrase <margin>among themselves <note>original Greek: παρ’ ἑαυτοῖς (par’ heautois)</note></margin> being understood. Duris, according to Zenodotus, says the proverb was commonly used whenever certain people met among themselves in secret to discuss some hidden matter. The metaphor is drawn from the mysteries of the Eleusinian rites, which were conducted in honor of Ceres at Eleusis with the greatest reverence and mystic ceremonies, from which the uninitiated were barred. It was a capital offense to reveal anything from these mysteries to the public. The Roman sacrifices to the "Good Goddess" <note>Bona Dea</note> seem to have been of a similar kind; C. Bassus, according to Lactantius, reported she was called *Fatua*. For these were performed both at night and in secret, with men excluded.

### 67. In the place of Hermione. ###

<margin>In the place of Hermione. <note>original Greek: Ἀνθ’ ἑρμιόνος (Anth’ hermionos)</note></margin> To complete the sense of this phrase, a verb should be added according to the context, such as: "I will be to you," or "my house," or "this city will be to you," or something similar. It is equivalent to saying, "I will be like a sanctuary to you," or "like an altar that renders you safe." Hermione is a temple in the Peloponnese, sacred to Ceres and Proserpina, where those who flee for refuge are safe because of the sanctity of the place. Zenodotus cites Aristophanes in his *Babylonians* as having mentioned this adage. The word is pronounced in two ways, <margin>Hermionos</margin> or <margin>Hermiona</margin>, just as <margin>from a bed [klinē] comes "clinical" [klinikos]</margin>. The authority for this is Stephanus.

### 68. An Antronian donkey. ###

<margin>An Antronian donkey. <note>original Greek: Ἀντρώνιος ὄνος (Antrōnios onos)</note></margin> This was once said of someone who possessed a deformed and massive body but a stupid and dull mind. Antron was a city in Thessaly, which got its name from the fact that it abounded in caverns and caves. They say that donkeys of remarkable size were once found there, which gave rise to the proverb. The authorities are Stephanus and Suidas. The commentator on Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 2, also touches upon the proverb. Even today, there is a common joke about men with large bodies, as if they possess little wisdom; as if nature delights in balancing things such that whatever she adds to the mass of the body, she takes away from the mind. It is handed down by some that among the Antronians, massive millstones are found, which, because they are placed underneath, on account of their sluggishness and...

<summary>This page explores several classical proverbs, including the "Agamemnon’s victim" for stubbornness, the moral philosophy of enduring labor for lasting honor, and the "Antronian donkey" for those who are physically large but intellectually dull.</summary>
<keywords>Agamemnon, sacrifice, moral labor, Cato the Elder, Eleusinian mysteries, sanctuary, Hermione, Antronian donkey, Thessaly, physical size vs intelligence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the collection of adages from the previous page. The fragment at the top concludes a discussion on terms for stupidity or sluggishness, likely referencing the proverb "A donkey’s rest" or similar, before moving into meteorologically themed proverbs.</meta>

...rest, the Greeks call "donkeys" <note>original Greek: ὄνους (onous)</note>. We, on the other hand, call a stone "stupid and mindless."

<margin>69</margin>
->Stations of the winds.<-

"Stations of the winds" <note>original Greek: Ἀνέμων στάσις (Anemōn stasis)</note>. This refers to matters that are understood through long use and observation. It appears the proverb should be stated in full as: "The locals know the stations of the winds" <note>original Greek: ἀνέμων στάσις γινώσκουσιν οἱ ἐγχώριοι</note>. That is, the inhabitants of a region know the patterns of the winds to which they are subject. For example, the "Scyron" is known to the Athenians (a wind slightly deflected from the "Argestes"), yet it is unknown to the rest of Greece. In Narbonnese Gaul, there is the "Circius"—so named from its whirling and dizzying nature <note>from the Latin 'turbo' (whirlwind) and 'vertigo'</note>—or "Certius," as Cato calls it. It is their most famous wind, second to none in violence; yet it is not only unknown in other parts of the world, but it does not even reach Vienne, a city in that same province. Similarly, the South Wind <note>Auster</note> does not penetrate into Egypt, as Fabianus records in Pliny’s works. The "Iapyx" is familiar to the people of Apulia, and the "Atabulus" is a well-known and destructive wind in certain mountains of Apulia, from which its name is derived. There are many other such winds native to specific regions, as Favorinus testifies in the works of Aulus Gellius. 

Furthermore, the force and nature of these winds vary by region. As Aristotle testifies in his *Problems*, the "Hellespontias"—which some call the "Scyron"—brings rain to the land of Attica and the neighboring islands; the North Wind <note>Aquilo</note> does the same for the Hellespont and Cyrene, and the South Wind <note>Auster</note> for Lesbos. And while the South Wind is warm and rainy for others, it is cold and clear in Africa, where conversely the North Wind brings rain, according to Pliny. The "Etesian" winds <note>periodical Mediterranean winds</note>, which arise during the summer and blow or cease at certain hours of the day, come from the East in Spain and Asia, from the North in the Black Sea <note>Pontus</note>, and from the South in other parts of the world. Suidas records these words (though their source is uncertain): "For the locals not only know the 'stations of the winds' according to the proverb, but they also know the characters of the local people most perfectly" <note>original Greek: ἐγχώριοι γὰρ οὐ μόνον τὰς τῶν ἀνέμων στάσις... ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ τῶν ἐγχωρίων ἀνθρώπων ἤθη κάλλιστα γινώσκουσιν</note>. This may be applied to say that every nation's temperament is known to its own, every man's family is best known to him, every man's wife is best known to him, and every man knows his own craft in which he has spent the most time.

<margin>70</margin>
->Field of the wind.<-

"Field of the wind" <note>original Greek: Ἀνέμου πεδίον (Anemou pedion)</note>. This was said of a man who is unstable, light, and inconstant. It is recorded by Diogenianus. For in a flat plain, the winds wander here and there more freely, restrained by no obstacle. Homer also frequently calls empty things "windy" <note>original Greek: ἀνεμώλια (anemōlia)</note>. And those things which are not solid, but filled with air <note>like "wind-eggs"</note>, are called "under-the-wind" <note>original Greek: ὑπηνέμια (hypenēmia)</note>. Finally, we call unstable people "windy." Horace says:
*At Rome I love Tibur, being windy; at Tibur, I love Rome.* <note>original Latin: Romæ Tibur amo uentosus, Tibure Romam</note>
And elsewhere:
*I do not hunt for the votes of the windy public.* <note>original Latin: Non ego uentofæ uenor suffragia plebis</note>
Lastly, you might quite wittily call a house that is drafty on all sides a "field of the wind." Pindar, in his second *Olympian Ode*, elegantly expressed the various shifts in human affairs:
> But flows of tides at different times
> with both joys
> and labors come to men.
<note>original Greek: ῥοαὶ δ’ ἄλλοτ’ ἄλλαι εὐθυμιῶν τε μετὰ καὶ πόνων ἐς ἄνδρας ἔβαν</note>
This seems to be a metaphor taken from the ebb and flow of the sea. However, in his seventh *Encomium*, he expressed the same thought using a metaphor taken from the winds, which do not always blow the same way:
> In a single portion of time,
> now these, now those breezes rush through.
<note>original Greek: Ἐν δὲ μιᾷ μοίρᾳ χρόνου ἄλλοτ’ ἄλλαι διαθύνοισιν αὖραι</note>
Again, in his twelfth hymn, he expresses the same thing with a metaphor taken from dice:
> Many things fall to men contrary to their judgment,
> sometimes the opposite of pleasure; others,
> having encountered painful storms,
> find a deep hardship in time.
<note>original Greek: πολλὰ δ’ ἀνθρώποις παρὰ γνώμαν ἔπεσαν... (Erasmus quotes Pindar to show how human fortune shifts like the wind or the roll of dice)</note>

<margin>71</margin>
->Where stags shed their horns.<-

"Where stags shed their horns" <note>original Greek: Ὅπου οἱ ἔλαφοι τὰ κέρατα ἀποβάλλουσιν (Hopou hoi elaphoi ta kerata apoballousin)</note>. By this adage, they signified, as if in a riddle, that someone was involved in a difficult business. This is because stags, when about to shed their horns, withdraw into rough and inaccessible places. It will also suit those who withdraw themselves from common human society, imitating that Timon of Athens who was called the "misanthrope" <note>human-hater</note> for that very reason. It will likewise apply to a place that is extremely hidden and secluded.

<keywords>Stations of the winds, Field of the wind, Pindar, Horace, regional winds, inconstancy, Timon the Misanthrope, stags, meteorology</keywords>

# CHILIAD TWO, CENTURY FIVE

...we will signify. Finally, if we wish to suggest that something is found nowhere, we will say it is there, "where the deer cast off their horns" <note>original Latin: ubi cervi cornua abijciunt</note>; so that just as "On the Greek Kalends" <note>a phrase meaning "never," as the Greek calendar had no Kalends</note> is said regarding time, so this is said regarding place. For example, if someone were to speak in this manner: "Where was that famous deed done that you are boasting about?" I would answer: "In that place, I suppose, where the deer cast off their horns" <note>original Greek: ὅπου οἱ ἔλαφοι τὰ κέρατα ἀποβάλλουσι (hopou hoi elaphoi ta kerata apoballousi)</note>. Pliny, in Book 8, chapter 32, writes about deer changing their horns in this way: "The males have horns, and they are the only animals to lose them every year at a fixed time in spring. Therefore, right around that day, they seek out the most trackless places. Once the horns are lost, they hide as if they were unarmed, yet they also begrudge others their own bounty. They say the right horn is never found, as if it were endowed with some medicinal power. And it must be admitted this is more marvelous because they change them every year even in fenced preserves; it is thought they are buried by them." Thus far Pliny. Aristotle also mentions this proverb in Book 9 of *On the Nature of Animals*, whose words I shall not be reluctant to transcribe: <note>original Greek omitted for brevity; the following is Erasmus's translation</note> "Furthermore, once the male has grown fat—and he becomes quite fat in autumn—he by no means allows himself to be seen. Instead, he withdraws from public view, since because of his heaviness he might then be easily captured. In addition to this, they cast off their horns in rough places that are very difficult to find. From this, the proverb also arose: 'Where the deer cast off their horns.' For as if they have been stripped of their weapons, they take care not to be seen. They say that the left horn <note>Note: Pliny says right, Aristotle says left</note> has been seen by no one yet. For the deer hide it as if it possessed some magical remedy." However, Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Pythian Oracles delivered in prose*, shows that this oracle was issued concerning the tyrant Procles: that he should be allowed to flee and migrate to the place "where the deer cast off his horn," the god signifying that he should be buried and utterly removed from the world. He also mentions the adage in the seventh decade of his *Symposiacs*, in the second problem.

->To beat a stone.<-
LXXII

The courtesan Planesium in the plays of Plautus, warning her lover not to strike a slave who had already become hardened and calloused to lashings, says: "Do not, I pray you, beat a stone <note>original Latin: verberare lapidem</note>, lest you hurt your hand." It will be aptly said when someone rebukes an uncorrectable person, or teaches an unteachable one, or undertakes useless labor in any matter whatsoever.

->To bait men.<-
LXXIII

Terence used a proverbial metaphor in the *Adelphoe*: "Go, you will never make a fortune. You do not know how to bait men" <note>original Latin: inescare homines</note>. This is derived from those who entice fish by fixing food to a hook. It was quite appropriately said to a pimp, whose trade it is to first entice young men with "baits" of this sort so that he may later devour them whole. By a further translation, they call that enticement which draws one into a trap a "bait." Hence Plato, as Cicero testifies in *Cato the Elder*, calls pleasure the "bait of evils" <note>original Greek: τὴν ἡδονὴν δέλεαρ κακῶν (tēn hēdonēn delear kakōn)</note>, because men are caught by it just as fish are by a hook. The Greeks express the metaphor with a single word, "to bait" <note>original Greek: δελεάζειν (deleazein)</note>, meaning to catch with a lure. Aristophanes in *The Knights*: to Cleon, who was boasting that he had easily won over the people with flatteries, the Sausage-seller responds: "For you yourself caught them with much smaller baits than these," recriminating him for having "baited" the people with more base flattery. No small amount of grace will be added if this is turned toward a good purpose, such as toward matters of the mind: for instance, if one should say that the minds of children are to be "baited" toward a love of studies by certain lures or flatteries of glory, or the dispositions of princes "baited" toward a love of virtue by praises.

->To swallow the hook.<-
LXXIIII

No less elegant is that phrase in the *Curculio*: "He is mine, he is swallowing the hook" <note>original Latin: hamum vorat</note>. This refers to a pimp for whom a trap was being set, just as he was about to read a letter by which he was to be deceived. Lucian says: "to swallow the hook" <note>original Greek: καταπιεῖν τὸ ἄγκιστρον (katapiein to ankistron)</note>. Likewise in the *Epistles* of Horace:
"The fish is seen to scurry to the hidden hook."
Likewise, Plautus in the *Bacchides* expressed the same sentiment with a similar metaphor: "Now this thrush is seeking the worm from the trap." One is drawn from fishing, the other from fowling. 
We likewise alluded to this proverb in a certain epigram:
> We shall not be so foolish as to
> swallow a hook we have tasted so many times.
