<margin>LXXV</margin>
### Vulcan has prophesied to you.
<note>original Greek: Ἀφάις ϛι λελάληκεν (Aphais sti lelaleuken)</note>. That is, "Vulcan has prophesied to you." This is reported from Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>. I suspect this was said when someone believed they possessed a certain truth, as if they had heard it from an oracle. Among the people of Memphis <note>an ancient capital of Egypt</note>, Vulcan is called "Phais," from which the word *Aphais* is formed by adding a letter, much like the Greek words for "ear of corn" <note>original Greek: ϛάχυς ἄϛαχυς (stachys astachys)</note>.

<margin>LXXVI</margin>
### You sing the same old song.
<note>original Greek: Τὸ αὐτὸ ᾄδεις ᾄσμα (To auto aideis aisma)</note>. That is, "You sing the same song." This is said of someone who is annoying by repeatedly insisting on the same thing. For nothing is more hateful than that which is always the same. Dorio the pimp, in Terence's play *Phormio*, says: "You sing the same old song; I would be amazed if you brought anything new." It is common for poets to call a message or a report a "song." Euripides in the *Ion* says:
<note>original Greek: Τίς ἥδε μολπὴ, ὧ φόβῳ πινῶν πέρὶ; (Tis hēde molpē, hō phobō pinōn peri?)</note>
Which means: "What is this song, and for what fear is it sung?"
The same author in *Hecuba* says:
<note>original Greek: ἥξει τὶ μέλος γοερὸν γοεραῖς (hēxei ti melos goeron goerais)</note>
Which means: "Some mournful song will come to mournful women."
The proverb is taken from singers who, if they ever sing the same song for too long, bring weariness to the ears. Therefore, skilled singers frequently vary the type of song to avoid causing satiety.

<margin>LXXVII</margin>
### To be blind in the sun.
In the writings of Quintilian, one finds this expression, which is as elegant as it is proverbial: "To be blind in the sun" <note>original Latin: Caligare in sole</note>. It is used for someone who is blind in a matter that is perfectly clear. This tends to happen to those with faulty eyes, who see nothing in the most transparent light because the force of the brightness overwhelms their weak senses. The same thing happens to owls and small night-birds; for them, light acts as darkness. This is not unpleasantly turned against those who claim that whatever is learned or scholarly is "obscure." To such people, even the orations of Cicero are full of shadows, for they carry the night around in their own eyes. 

Similarly, in the works of Seneca, Portius used to say that a certain man "had thorns in his feet" when he complained that he was walking through thorns—essentially attributing a defect of his own nature to the ground. "But," he said, "it is your feet that have the thorns, not the place." In the same way, those people who claim to be offended by "night" or darkness in the works of good authors carry that night with them in their own eyes; they do not find it in the books.

<margin>LXXVIII</margin>
### The ox stirs up dust against itself.
<note>original Greek: Βοῦς ἐφ’ ἑαυτὸν κονίην (Bous eph’ heauton konien)</note>. That is, "The ox stirs up dust against itself," or "the ox hastens to its own ruin." This is used when someone is led, willing and ready, toward their own misfortune. For oxen, being tame animals, easily allow themselves to be bound and do not resist the yoke. Among the Greeks, the word for "dust" <note>original Greek: κονίην (konien)</note> signifies the act of stirring up dust through an eagerness to hasten. Some apply this to those who, being prudent and knowing, throw themselves into present danger, in the manner of an ox that allows the chains to be thrown around it by which it is led to the slaughter. This is recorded by Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and literary critic</note>.

<margin>LXXIX</margin>
### A tragic king.
<note>original Greek: Τραγικὸς βασιλεὺς (Tragikos basileus)</note>. That is, a "tragic king." He can be called this either because he is haughty and puffed up, or because he is a king in name only, while possessing very little actual power. In a similar way, a French proverb calls such a person a "paper king" <note>original Greek: χαρτοκαίσαρα (chartokaisara)</note>, meaning a king more by title than by wealth or dominion. Dionysius said this of Pheraeus, who, having gained power for only ten months, soon departed from life: he called him a "tragic king." For in tragedies, the reign lasts only as long as the play is being performed. Then, the mask having been laid aside, he who a moment ago was Agamemnon, or even Jupiter himself, goes home as a "three-penny little man" <note>original Latin: tressis homuntio, a term for someone of very low value or status</note>.

<margin>LXXX</margin>
### Against a net-fighter, a rod.
Martial, in a certain epistolary preface, says: "Finally you may see, before it delights you, a rod against a net-fighter" <note>original Latin: Contra retiarium, ferula. A 'retiarius' was a gladiator who fought with a net and trident</note>. This means: whether you think you should do that which everyone else condemns and hisses at. Domitius Calderinus, the interpreter, advises that a proverb lies beneath this, usually said against those who fight with a weak defense against someone who is extremely well-equipped. 

Yet shortly after, the same author slides into another explanation: namely, that in the past, if gladiators had failed to please the crowd, they were usually driven out, beaten with a rod. Close to this is a saying found in Aulus Gellius, in the first book of *Attic Nights*, chapter 2: "Would you not move a staff against that man? Hey, fellow, what have I to do with you?" Therefore, "to move a rod or a staff" against someone is to resist them or to repel an arrogant opinion. The "rod" <note>term: ferula; a giant fennel stalk used as a cane</note> is a type of wood with which children were once beaten, and likewise soldiers, if they were seen to do anything against discipline.
I believe...

I think the overseers of such contests in gladiatorial games are accustomed to doing the same thing.

### LXXXI. A woman as commander, and a woman as soldier.
<note>original Greek: Γυνὴ στρατηγεῖ, καὶ γυνὴ στρατεύεται (Gynē stratēgei, kai gynē strateuetai)</note>. That is, "A woman is the leader, and a woman is likewise the soldier." 

This is a proverbial six-foot line <note>an iambic senarius</note> used whenever an entire business is entrusted to the cowardly—when both those in command and those who obey are equally fearful. In the third book of Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note>, the playwright Alexis is cited in a play titled *Gynaecocratia* <note>The Rule of Women</note>. Nature formed woman for this purpose: not to command, but to obey, as witnessed by this Greek verse:
<note>original Greek: γυναικὶ δ' ἄρχειν οὐ δίδωσιν ἡ φύσις (gynaiki d' archein ou didōsin hē physis)</note>. That is, "Nature did not grant women the power to rule." 

Indeed, what reason and emotion are in a human being, man and woman are in life; and according to Moses, the <term>Demiurge</term> <note>the Creator or "craftsman" of the universe</note> subjected the woman to the man. Nevertheless, Plato does not entirely bar the female sex from administering the Republic, provided one is found who is fit for the task. Aeschines <note>an Athenian orator</note> seems to have alluded to this silently in his speech *Against Timarchus*, when he saw a wealthy house that was poorly governed, "whose leader was a woman, proud and senseless." 

The meaning is more humorous when it is deflected further—for instance, if someone were to call Tartaretus <note>Peter Tartaretus, a medieval scholastic philosopher often mocked by Renaissance humanists for his "barbaric" Latin</note> the author and chief leader of Peripatetic philosophy. Thus Virgil says: "A woman was the leader of the deed" <note>original Latin: Dux fœmina facti</note>. And in the Acts of the Apostles, Paul is called the "leader of the word." Similarly, Galen <note>the famous Roman physician</note> somewhere calls Aristotle "the father of the word," because the opinion had originated from him.

### LXXXII. More just than a balance.
<note>original Greek: Δικαιότερον σταθμοῦ (Dikaioteron stathmou)</note>. That is, "More just than a scale." This is a Doric <note>a dialect of ancient Greek</note> proverb concerning those of distinguished and incorruptible equity. For the Dorians call the <term>trutina</term> <note>a balance or pair of scales</note> a *stathma*. It refers to that kind of scale by which even the smallest moment of weight is felt and discerned. The Latins also call exact equality "Equilibrium." Hence, something is said to be done "with an equal lance" <note>original Latin: Æqua lance</note> when it is done with equal right and without respect for persons. Thus Modestinus <note>a Roman jurist</note> says in the *Pandects* <note>a compendium of Roman law</note>, Book 42, under the title *On Judged Matters*: "Reason of equity suggests that this should be observed with an equal lance even in the person of a woman." Likewise, the Emperor Justinian says in the *Code*, Book 5, under the title *On Natural Children*: "Wherefore we decree that in cases of this kind, all children—whether born before the marriage documents were issued or after—be weighed in one and the same balance." Using a similar figure, Nicarchus says in an Epigram:
"He has become straighter than any ruler."
<note>original Greek: Γέγονεν δ' ὀρθότερος κανόνος (Gegonen d' orthoteros kanonos)</note>.

### LXXXIII. More sterile than an agrippus.
<note>original Greek: Ἀκαρπότερος ἀγρίππου (Akarpoteros agrippou)</note>. That is, "More fruitless than an agrippus." This is a Laconic <note>Spartan</note> adage concerning those who are in extreme poverty and possess no resources. It also applies to the lazy and men of no industry. The Spartans call the wild olive tree an *agrippus*. This is found only in Zenodotus and Suidas <note>ancient Greek lexicographers</note>.

### LXXXIV. The vote of Jupiter.
<note>original Greek: Διὸς ψῆφος (Dios psēphos)</note>. That is, "The vote of Jupiter" was said of a sacred and inviolable judgment. Thus, you might rightly call the opinion of someone whose authority is, as it were, irrefutable, "The vote of Jupiter." Or, it may be used ironically when someone pronounces too arrogantly on a matter and demands their opinion be accepted as law or an oracle. They say that the place where Neptune and Minerva held their trial—to decide in whose name and under whose auspices the city of the Athenians should be established—was called "The Vote of Jupiter." Suidas cites Cratinus from the *Archilochoi*:
"Where the dice and the seats of the Great Thunderer are called."
<note>original Greek: Ἔνθα Διὸς μεγάλο θῶκος πεσσοὶ τε καλεῦντ' (Entha Dios megalo thōkos pessoi te kaleunt')</note>. For in ancient times, votes were cast like dice, certainly by those drawing lots.

### LXXXV. To go into the nerve.
<note>original Latin: In neruum ire</note>. Donatus, or whoever was the interpreter of Terence’s *Phormio*, demonstrates that this is a proverb for "to deceive." The metaphor is taken from archers, to whom it sometimes happens that while they stretch the bow too much, they break it or strain some "nerve" <note>in Latin, *neruus* refers to both a sinew/muscle and a bowstring</note>. This is close to the saying mentioned elsewhere: "We have snapped the cable where we stretched it too much." However, "He will go into the nerve" <note>In neruum ibit</note> was also used to mean "he will go into chains." For in antiquity, those who could not pay their debts were handed over bound to their creditors until they compensated the loan through labor...

For the young man in love fears, when Phormio draws him into that situation, that he might be forced by the agreement to either take the girl home as his wife, or certainly to repay the money he received; should he fail to do so, he would be bound and, according to the laws, suffer the penalty in his own body since he could not pay in coin. He thinks it would be better for him if Phormio either reveals the whole trick or truly carries the woman away. Furthermore, "To cast into the nerve" and "To take out of the nerve" are phrases used for leading away those bound because of debt. <note>The "nerve" (Latin: *nervus*) refers to a type of shackle or wooden stock used to imprison debtors.</note> But I will transcribe the words of Terence: "But he will not marry her, I know. However, when they demand the money back, for our sake he will surely go into the nerve instead." <note>From Terence's *Phormio*, Act 4.</note>

->LXXXVI<-

### He himself pipes for himself.

Αὐτὸς αὑτὸν αὐλεῖ. <note>original Greek: Autos hauton aulei</note> That is, "He is his own flute-player." This means that he declares by his own deeds what kind of person he is. For in ancient times, flute-players used to sing the praises of brave men. Therefore, for one who gains enough glory for himself through rightly performed deeds, why is it necessary for him to hire a trumpeter for his own praises? This <term>adage</term> <note>a traditional saying or proverb</note> can be applied in either direction, good or bad: "There is no need for a flute-player for this man, who is sufficiently famous through his own excellent deeds." Or, "There is no need to attack this man's life; it is foul and infamous enough on its own." It will also apply to those who praise themselves, which is the habit of roosters, even when they have just fled from a fight. Plato says in the *Theaetetus*: "We seem to me, like ignoble roosters, to be singing before we have won, having leapt away from the argument." <note>original Greek: φαινομεθά μοι ἀλεκτρυόνων ἀγεννῶν δίκην, πρὶν νενικηκέναι, ἀποπηδήσαντες ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ᾄδειν</note>

->LXXXVII<-

### He himself said it.

Αὐτὸς ἔφα <note>original Greek: Autos epha</note>, that is, "He himself said it." This is used whenever we signify that someone’s authority is so great that it suffices for believing something even without a logical reason. For example: In sacred literature, "He himself said it" is enough; in other matters, it is not so. This <term>adage</term> was born from Pythagoras, who, in order to procure more veneration and authority for himself and his followers, was accustomed to say in discussions, "He himself said it." This was as if he were not reporting his own ideas, but things received from some oracle. That phrase then passed into common speech. Suidas and Diogenes Laertius indicate that this saying originated from Pythagoras of Zacynthus. However, Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the first book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, tells the matter differently. For he says, "In disputing, one should not seek authors so much as the weight of reason. Indeed, the authority of those who profess to teach often stands in the way of those who wish to learn. For they cease to apply their own judgment; they take as certain what they see was judged by the person they approve of. Nor, indeed, am I accustomed to approve of that which we have heard concerning the Pythagoreans, whom they say, if they affirmed anything in a discussion and were asked why it was so, were accustomed to answer: 'He himself said it.' And 'He himself' was Pythagoras." So much could a prejudiced opinion do, that authority prevailed even without reason. Quintilian says in his *Institutes*: "For even unwilling judges," he says, "listen to one who presumes his own side is already proven; but that which happened to Pythagoras among his disciples cannot happen to an orator among his adversaries: 'He himself said it.'" But that phrase is more or less a vice, depending on the person speaking. Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Clouds*:

> Tell me, who is that man sitting in the hanging basket?
> It is Himself. Who is "Himself"? Socrates. Who is Socrates?
> Go then, and call out to "Himself" loudly for me.
> Nay, you call him yourself, for I have no leisure.

<note>original Greek: φέρε, τίς γὰρ οὗτος, οὑπὶ τῇ κρεμάθρᾳ ἀνήρ; / Αὐτός. τίς αὐτός; σωκράτης. τίς σωκράτης; / ἴθ’ αὐτὸς ἀναβόησον αὐτὸν μοι μέγα. / Αὐτὸς μὲν οὖν σὺ κάλεσον, οὐ γάρ μοι χολή.</note>

As for what he said, "the one in the hanging basket" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐπὶ κρεμάθρας</note>, to indicate this in passing, it was a novelty introduced for the sake of a laugh, as he wanted Socrates to be understood as looking up at the clouds with a suspended mind. For a *cremathra* is a hanging vessel in which the remains of food were usually stored. The phrase "He himself said it" is used in two ways: sometimes simply, but more frequently through irony, as if someone were to say to a person citing Aristotle like an oracle, "He himself said it," while demanding a reason for the statement and not being content with the simple authority of the writer. It will also be appropriate whenever we cast the resentment or the defense of an opinion away from ourselves and onto the author himself. Juvenal says:

> So I will, so I command, let my will stand for reason.

->Better yet, Horace:<-

> Not bound to swear by the words of any master.

# SECOND CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY
V 3

It seems necessary to point out that the phrase "He himself said" <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς ἔφη (autos ephe)</note> carries the same weight in this proverb as if you were to say, "The Lord has spoken." It appears that Pythagoras learned this figure of speech—familiar to the prophets—from the priests of the Egyptians. Aristophanes says in *The Frogs*: 
<margin>A boy might strike it rightly, for I am entering myself.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὀρθὸν παῖς ἐκκρούσειεν, ὅτι αὐτὸς εἰσέρχομαι</note> 
That is to say: 
"Tell the dancing girls that I myself am arriving." 
This implies "the master," because he is seen to arrive in person rather than just sending his servants. Likewise, in the secret writings of the prophets, we find: "Behold, I am here," meaning the Lord and Author. The proverb we mentioned previously, "With the sting fixed," pertains to this as well. Similarly, Augustine, in some passage reviewing the opinion of Manichaeus—if I am not mistaken—says: "Manichaeus said these things, and then he departed." He was noting that Manichaeus was satisfied with merely having spoken, even though what he said required further explanation. Galen likewise, in the first book of *On Natural Faculties*, says: 
"Having said these and similar things, he suddenly departed, leaving us as if he were traveling a smooth path without hesitation, so that we were unable to find even a plausible counter-argument." <note>original Greek: ταῦτα καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα εἰπὼν, ἐξαίφνης ἀπῄειν...</note> 
That is: having spoken these and similar words, he finished his speech with clear words, his mouth never wavering as if he could not slip, and then he hurried away, leaving us in such a state that we could find nothing at all to say in even probable contradiction.

->**Not feeding yourself, you feed dogs.**<-
->LXXXVIII<-

"While you do not feed yourself, you feed dogs." <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸν οὐ τρέφων κύνας τρέφεις (Auton ou trephon kynas trepheis)</note> This was said of a man who, although he could not provide the necessities of life for himself due to poverty, nonetheless tried to keep horses or servants at home. It is aptly said against those who, despite a narrow family budget that barely sustains life, nevertheless try to imitate the powerful and wealthy through an ambitious display of dress and other noisy status symbols. Briefly, it applies to all who care for things pertaining to pleasure or splendor while neglecting those things that are more necessary. Furthermore, primary care is owed to necessities, and secondary care to status—just as if someone were to labor in acquiring learning while remaining careless about the life that is being put at risk.

->**The earth's intestines.**<-
->LXXXIX<-

"The earth's intestines." <note>original Greek: Γῆς ἔντερα (Ges entera)</note> This was a saying for cheap things of no value. However, rocks are called the "viscera" of the earth. This is recorded by Diogenianus. For rocks are the "intestines" of the earth, and we call useless men "stones." There is a similar phrase: 
<margin>A useless burden of the earth.</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης (etosian achthos aroures)</note> 
That is: a useless weight upon the soil.

->**The Tenedian flute-player.**<-
->XC<-

"The Tenedian flute-player" <note>original Greek: Τενέδιος αὐλητής (Tenedios auletes)</note> was a name for a false witness and a slanderer. This arose because Philonome suborned her flute-player to testify before Cygnus that she had been solicited for adultery by Tenne, and even attempted by force. This is generally what Stephanus records in his catalog of cities. I have already spoken of Tenedos often elsewhere.

->**A *cyrbes* of evils.**<-
->XCI<-

"A *cyrbes* of evils." <note>original Greek: Κύρβεις κακῶν (Kyrbeis kakon)</note> This refers to those who are exceedingly wicked and contaminated by every kind of crime. Among the Athenians, there were certain four-sided tablets <note>term: <term>cyrbes</term> were triangular or square pillars of wood or stone used to display public laws</note> on which the laws were described and displayed, including various penalties for offenders. These they called *cyrbes*; in Lucian, they are called *axones*. This is not unlike what I recorded elsewhere: "An Iliad of woes." With a similar figure of speech in the ninth book of Athenaeus, Antiphanes (I believe) said: 
"And this was to me a side-dish of evils." <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῦτο μὲν μοι τῶν κακῶν παροψίς ἦν</note> 
For different kinds of food are usually served on the same platter, but things that bring pleasure; thus, the <term>trope</term> <note>a figurative use of a word</note> is more pleasing because it turns to the opposite, as if you were to say, "An Iliad of good things."

->**The ram repaid the price of his nursing.**<-
->XCII<-

"The ram repaid his rearing." <note>original Greek: Κριὸς τροφεῖα ἀπέτισεν (Krios tropheia apetisen)</note> This is cited from Menander. It fits when someone repays good deeds with a malicious act. The <term>allegory</term> <note>a symbolic story or image</note> is taken from the fact that a ram strikes with its horns the very vessel in which its fodder is placed, or attacks with its horns the very people by whose labor it was or is being fed. The proverb is also expressed in this way: "The service of a ram," <note>original Greek: κριὸς ἐλαυνόια (krios elaunoia)</note> for a service bestowed upon an ungrateful person who weighs a benefit against an injury. To this is related what is found in Aristophanes' *The Wasps*: "The stake [supporting] the vine." <note>original Greek: ἡ χάραξ τὴν ἄμπελον (he charax ten ampelon)</note>

->**From Dorian to Phrygian.**<-
->XCIII<-

To be said to come "from Dorian to Phrygian" <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ δωρίου ἐπὶ φρύγιον (Apo doriou epi phrygion)</note> was used for someone who had turned from a more temperate life to luxury, or who had moved from a modest fortune to a more boisterous way of life. The metaphor is taken from those very well-known types of ancient musical harmonies, in which the Do—

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the cultural and metaphorical meanings of musical modes, specifically focusing on the "Dorian" mode and its reputation for moderation, solemnity, and its use as a contrast to other styles like the Phrygian or Ionian.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES

...the Dorian is more moderate, just as Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> indicates, citing these words from an unknown author: "He chose a diet that was moderate and simple, as if prepared by poverty, and yet possessed a wealth that was not sluggish, but truly harmonized by fortune in a middle, musical, and Dorian fashion." <note>original Greek: τὴν ἡ τροφὴν ἐκληρώσατο μετρίαν... Δωρίῳ τρόπῳ</note> That is, he had obtained a moderate way of living, free from luxuries, neither squalid and troublesome due to poverty, nor dissolute due to riches, but a certain middle and moderate path, truly tempered to the Dorian measure of fortune. 

Suidas also reports another passage, suppressing the author's name, if I am not mistaken: "To speak in rounded little words, and having set out only the positions of the thoughts themselves in the middle, and having rearranged the tone of the tongue from the dialect into a turn, they say one should flee the Dorian." <note>original Greek: τὸ φάναι καὶ στρογγύλῳ λογάρια... ἀπὸ Δωρίας φασὶν τὴν φεύγειν</note> Although it is difficult to translate these words aptly if you do not know what precedes or follows them, I will nevertheless offer my "divination" <note>Erasmus's term for an educated guess or scholarly conjecture.</note> until the full passage is found. I will not seem to be one of those men who speak in rounded little phrases, but bringing the meanings themselves into the open, I shall have adapted the tone of the tongue from disputation to attention. (However, in Suidas, it reads *monon a.*). 

From these words, it appears that the Dorian mode was more refined, while the Phrygian was more severe. Apuleius, in the first book of the *Florida*, clearly indicates that Dorian music was far different from the Phrygian, since the latter inflamed minds toward religion, while the former inflamed them toward war. Apuleius’s words are as follows: "There was a certain flute-player named Antigenidas, a honey-sweet performer of every sound, and likewise a skilled master of every style, whether you wanted the simple Aeolian, the Iastian, the plaintive Lydian, the religious Phrygian, or the warlike Dorian." Thus far Apuleius: if we believe him, the Dorian mode cannot be "temperate" if it incites one to war—unless perhaps the flutes played more moderately for those about to enter battle, because a mind that is self-possessed is more effective there than one struck by madness. 

However, whether in Apuleius’s words "Aetolic" or "Aetolian" should be read instead of "Aeolian," and "Iassian" or "Iastian" <note>Referring to the Ionian mode.</note> instead of "Asian," I leave for the learned to weigh. Nevertheless, these do not entirely agree with what Lucian reports in *Harmonides*: "and to preserve the property of each harmony: the divine inspiration of the Phrygian, the Bacchic frenzy of the Lydian, the solemnity of the Dorian, the elegance of the Ionian." <note>original Greek: καὶ ἑκάστης ἁρμονίας διαφυλάττειν τὸ ἴδιον...</note> That is: to keep the character of each harmony: the divine impulse of the Phrygian (which Apuleius translates as "religious"), the Bacchic madness or license of the Lydian, the severity of the Dorian, and the pleasantness of the Ionian (which Apuleius seems to have translated as "varied"). 

On the other hand, Dio <note>Dio Chrysostom, a Greek philosopher and orator.</note> in his commentaries *On Kingship* reports that Alexander the Great used to be incited to war by the musician Timotheus playing in the Dorian mode. Athenaeus, in book fourteen, attributes to the Dorian harmony "the manly, the magnificent, and the intense." <note>original Greek: τὸ ἀνδρῶδες, καὶ τὸ μεγαλοπρεπὲς, καὶ τὸ σφοδρόν</note> That is: severity, majesty, and vehemence, as it is neither dissolute nor cheerful, but somber and not at all varied. 

Now Boethius, <note>An early 6th-century philosopher whose work on music was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> who is more recent than these, shows in the preface of his book *On Music* that this art has a primary power to move the <term>affects</term> <note>Emotions or mental states.</note> and, according to the logic of the modes, to either excite or calm various motions of the soul. He adds that Pythagoras, by the playing of a Phrygian mode, restored to a sober mind a young man (a barbarian by birth, specifically from Tauromenium) who was drunk with wine and raging with anger, and who was already attempting to set fire to the house of his mistress because she had admitted a rival. Pythagoras ordered a flute-girl to play <term>spondees</term> <note>A slow, solemn poetic and musical meter consisting of two long syllables.</note> instead. Boethius reports that the youth had been incited by the Phrygian mode and returned to himself when the mode was changed, but he does not specify into which mode the Phrygian was changed. Marcus Tullius [Cicero], whom Boethius cites there, mentions neither mode, only saying that the youth was calmed by the playing of spondees. 

If Timotheus incited Alexander to war with the Dorian mode, and this youth was incited to attack a house by the Phrygian, it appears these modes do not differ much from each other. Lucian attributes to the Phrygian "divine inspiration," that is, a frenzy, but specifically a sacred one. Of this frenzy, Plato makes three kinds: one which the Muses send to poets, another which Apollo sends to prophets, and a third which Cupid sends to lovers. However, both Bacchus and Mars have their own frenzy as well. Thus, that young man was raging, seized by a triple frenzy: that of Bacchus, Cupid, and Mars. 

We have taught elsewhere that the <term>Pyrrhic</term> <note>A fast, rhythmic dance or meter associated with war.</note> rhythms sharpen one for battle, hence the phrase "to look Pyrrhic," regarding those who are grim and agitated. The spondee, however, is the opposite of the Pyrrhic. Now, if Boethius had said the *mode* was changed, it could be probable that the same Phrygian mode can both incite with Pyrrhics and calm with spondees. And I do not know whether Boethius, when he says the mode was "changed," means that the harmonies were changed, or simply the speed of the notes. 

The proverb seems to have a place when one transitions to different subjects: for example, if someone who began a discourse on the precepts of Rhetoricians should digress into Theological matter. For my part, I think the ancients handed down different views on the types of harmonies because the harmonies themselves were changed along with the changing customs of the nations. For the severity of the ancient Asians was praised before it was [corrupted] by luxury...

### CHILIAD TWO, CENTURY FIVE 511

...lest it be made effeminate by luxury. The same happened to the Laconians, among whom are the Dorians. From this come those names of "mixed" modes: <term>Hypodorian</term> <note>original Greek: ὑποδώριον; a lower-pitched version of the Dorian mode</note>, <term>Mixolydian</term> <note>original Greek: μιξολύδιον</note>, and <term>Hypomixolydian</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπομιξολύδιον</note>. Athenaeus thinks the Hypodorian mode is the same as the Aeolian, to which he attributes a certain swelling pride and arrogance, yet also a touch of softness. Some students of music assert that the transition from the Dorian to the Phrygian mode is extremely difficult. We have shown elsewhere that the Phrygian melody was called <term>crooked</term> <note>original Greek: σκολιόν (skolion); implying it was complex or indirect</note> and was typically used in funeral dirges. But if the Dorian song is distinct from the Phrygian—insofar as the Dorian inflames the desire for war—it is logical that it consisted of pyrrhic rhythms, since the pyrrhic foot <note>a metrical foot of two short syllables</note> is the opposite of the spondee. 

Plato writes many things about these types of harmonies in his books on the *Republic*. Again, in the *Laches*, he teaches that the truly Dorian song and the truly Greek harmony is not the Phrygian, nor the Ionian, nor the Lydian, but rather that which occurs when one’s life is in harmony with good speech. Plutarch also discusses this in his book *On Music*. We have touched upon these matters just enough to perceive the sense of the adage.

### From the starting gates. XCIIII

<term>From the threshold</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ βαλβίδος (Apo balbidos)</note>. That is, "From the starting gate," or from the barrier; in other words, from the very beginning of a matter. The metaphor is taken from equestrian competitions, where the start of the race is at the "prisons" <note>original: carceribus; the stalls or gates where horses were held</note> and the end is at the goal-post. Therefore, when we signify that a business has just begun, we say: *From the very starting gates*; when it is finished, we say: *All the way to the goal*. For example, one might say it is a foul thing if an artist makes a mistake right from the starting gate, or that no one is so lazy that they do not seem energetic <term>from the starting line</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ βαλβίδος</note>. This appears in the works of Aristophanes. A similar expression found elsewhere is <term>from the line</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ γραμμῆς (ek grammēs)</note>, meaning from the very start.

### From heaven to earth. XCV

<term>From heaven all the way to earth</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ οὐρανοῦ μέχρι γῆς</note>. This is a proverbial figure of speech, essentially meaning the same as if you were to say: "concerning everything, from the furthest beginning to the ultimate end." Thus, in Plautus's play *The Persian*, when a bidder asks if he might question a certain girl, the seller, allowing him to ask as much as he wants, says: "From heaven to earth, whatever pleases you."

### Know a friend's habits, do not hate them. XCVI

Porphyrion, in his commentary on Horace, notes that this line was a proverb:
> Know a friend's habits, do not hate them.

We have restored this among the Greek maxims where it was found. It runs like this:
<term>Know what his character is like, but do not hate it</term> <note>original Greek: οἷος τρόπος γίνωσκε, μισήσῃς δὲ μή</note>.
This warns us that certain vices in the character of friends ought to be overlooked; they should be understood, certainly, but tolerated nonetheless, lest by being too severe and sharp-eyed in observing a friend's faults, you overset the friendship. This precept applies to lighter "illnesses" of character, not to those which involve the reputation or great danger of friends. To not know a friend's faults is the mark of a man who is not careful enough about whom he loves; to hate them is the mark of one who is unsociable. Faults must be known so that you may either correct them or at least lessen them; but not in such a way that you seem to hate your friend because of them. Indeed, no one will ever be a friend to anyone if he cannot bear any vices in a friend.

### Bithus against Bacchius. XCVII

Bithus and Bacchius were a famous pair of gladiators, mentioned also by Suetonius; they were equals in skill and equals in audacity. Hence, whenever two equally wicked people contend with one another so that neither wishes to yield to the other, we may aptly say: "Bacchius is matched with Bithus." Horace says in his *Satires*: "Is not 
> Bacchius better matched with Bithus?"

This signifies the equal wickedness and abusiveness between Rupilius and Persius. Whatever is remarkably wicked and ready for any conflict, we call "gladiatorial": *gladiatorial strength of body*, *gladiatorial audacity*, or *they approach me with gladiatorial minds*. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Philippics*, several times calls the brother of Mark Antony a "Mirmillo" <note>a specific type of heavily armed gladiator</note>, as in the sixth *Philippic*: "Will the mandates of the Senate and the words of the ambassadors even be heard by this Asiatic Mirmillo?"

### Efernius with Pacidiano. XCVIII

Similar to the above is that phrase from Lucilius: "Efernius matched with Pacidiano." These were also gladiators, equal in every respect and by far the most famous of all. Marcus Tullius Cicero writes in his book *On the Best Kind of Orators*: "As for me, to compare the greatest things with the smallest, a most noble pair of gladiators is brought forward. Aeschines, just like Efernius—as Lucilius says—not a filthy man but learned and sharp, is matched with this Pacidiano, by far the best man born." A spectacle of this kind was recently shown to us, to the great pleasure of everyone, by these...

### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES 512

...In those days in London among the British, there were two theologians: one was the great Standish <note>Henry Standish (c. 1460–1535), a conservative Franciscan friar and later Bishop of St Asaph, who frequently clashed with Erasmus and John Colet.</note>, the <term>leader</term> <note>original Greek: κορυφαῖος (koryphaios); the head or chief of a group</note> of those whom they call the Conventual Franciscans on that island. He was a man of wonderfully loud voice, a vigorous <term>Scotist</term> <note>a follower of the medieval philosopher Duns Scotus, whose complex logic Erasmus often mocked</note>, and of an intrepid spirit; he possessed such broad shoulders and bodily strength that he could have been a veteran soldier or a gladiator, had he not been a theologian. The other was an Italian from the fellowship of those whom the common people call the "Servite Brothers"—so named, as I understand it, because although they are blacker than beetles, they serve the Virgin Mary alone, having no dealings with Christ nor with any other among the saints. Truly, while this man was perhaps not inferior in learning, he was far unequal in those gladiatorial gifts, or so I believe. 

When this Italian had retired to Britain, as is the custom, toward the start of Lent, he wished to show that he had not entirely wasted the effort he had spent on theological studies for several years at <term>Paris</term> <note>original Latin: Lutetia</note>. He began to propose several "conclusions," as they call them, to be debated among the learned. Most of these concerned merchants, except for the first, which seemed to pertain to the insult of Saint Francis. That thesis held roughly this sentiment: that the Friars Minor <note>The Franciscans</note> sin if they receive money, whether themselves or through others, and consequently, those who give them money also sin, because whoever gives a Friar Minor the occasion for sinning, sins himself as well. 

The occasion that drove this foreigner to such audacity was this: the Servite was staying with the Augustinians, who call themselves "Hermits"—<term>ironically</term> <note>original Greek: κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν (kat’ antiphrasin); meaning "by the opposite," implying they are anything but solitary hermits</note>, I think. These men in London make a considerable profit from merchants, especially Italians, and for that reason they are hated by the Minorites <note>Franciscans</note>. Standish, therefore, in order to turn that profit toward his own people, warned the public in a sermon to be very careful about to whom they confessed. For he claimed that only two orders had been given the right by the Pope to hear the confessions of anyone at all: namely, the Minorites and the <term>Jacobins</term> <note>The Dominicans, so called after their house in the Rue St. Jacques in Paris</note>. 

Since this seemed to threaten the remaining orders with starvation, they took counsel and suborned the Servite to avenge such a capital injury with these "themes," since he could not speak to the people because he was ignorant of the British tongue. They therefore posted the conclusions I mentioned on all the church doors and corners. The rumor of this spread little by little, as usually happens, and when it reached the ears of Standish, that pious man of excellent spirit conceived a rage worthy of himself. He threatened dire consequences; the whole matter seemed to be heading toward some great tragedy, unless some god had intervened <term>from a machine</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ μηχανῆς (apo mechanes); a reference to a "deus ex machina," an unexpected plot device that resolves a conflict</note>. For that wise man understood that the matter looked toward "Saguntine hunger" <note>An adage referring to extreme starvation or desperation, based on the Roman siege of Saguntum</note> if such a proposition were even heard publicly. Among them, he is considered the most holy who possesses the most coins. 

Why say more? The Servite was forced to go to the man to clear himself and appease his spirit. The man went reluctantly. Many people were terrifying the guest, saying that Standish was a virulent, noisy man of immoderate bile; a man who was someone of importance among the common crowd—sailors, wagoners, shoemakers, cobblers, laundrymen, and others of that sort—and also a man of such strength of mind that he alone had most bravely sustained the cause of immunity against the entire Church of the British. For this reason, he was hated by all the priests and bishops, and by that part of the good commoners who wish the clergy well. 

When they came face to face, the Servite—since he had touched upon not only theology but also rhetoric—attempted to win the man over with this opening: "Excellent father," he said, "I truly come here unwillingly, because I hear from many that you are uncontrollably angry, and if some are to be believed, even a madman." Having thus far sought goodwill <term>very skillfully</term> <note>original Greek: μάλα ἐντέχνως (mala entechnos)</note>, he laid out the matter in a few words. "However," he said, "since these fathers have so strongly urged me, I am here to hear if you want anything." 

At this, the other man immediately began to rave at him with loud insults, saying the conclusion was scandalous, offensive to pious ears, savoring of heresy, and irreverent toward the Seraphic Order of Saint Francis, and that the Servite would soon pay the penalty unless he recanted. The Servite, as became a brave man, replied that he had proposed it for debate, not for recantation. 

Moved beyond measure by such an impious voice, Standish ordered the man to wait a little while and rushed inside. The Servite, not obeying even such a great man, had already begun to leave. But Standish soon returned with several of his hooded satellites (for he has very many, no less robust and no less daring than the King's own), caught the man as he was leaving, and, seizing him by the feet, dragged him inside like some <term>Cacus</term> <note>A fire-breathing giant and thief from Roman myth who was killed by Hercules; he famously dragged stolen cattle backward into his cave by their tails</note>. 

There the Servite, abandoned and fearing the worst (as usually happens in desperate situations), implored Jesus: "Jesus, Jesus!" he cried out again and again with as loud a voice as he could. Jesus was nowhere to be found among the Franciscans, but the poor wretch was being dragged in the meantime. However, some stone-masons nearby, roused by the name of Jesus, came running with their stones and tools and snatched the man from the hands of those satellites. And this was the first act of that play. The next, however, with great...

<meta>The previous page introduced a conflict in London between Henry Standish, a leader of the Conventual Franciscans, and an Italian friar of the Servite Order. It ended describing how the dispute was driven by "great..." [magnis]. This page begins with the conclusion of that word.</meta>

### CHILIAD TWO, CENTURY FIVE

XCIX

...[great] insults were hurled by both sides, with the leaders of each faction complaining loudly to their respective supporters. The Servite is even said to have hung a votive tablet to Jesus the Savior, featuring a painted scene and an accompanying inscription. Soon the story spread quickly among the people and even reached the ears of the Cardinal <note>Thomas Wolsey (c. 1473–1530), Archbishop of York and Lord Chancellor, who held supreme judicial power in England.</note>, who serves as the presiding judge of that realm. Since he possesses a witty nature, he thought this would be a rather amusing spectacle and ordered both men to appear before him. 

Standish accused him boldly; the Servite defended himself diligently. The Cardinal pronounced that, since it was a debatable <term>scholastic proposition</term> <note>a formal theological thesis intended for academic debate</note>, they should debate it publicly at St. Paul’s Cathedral—the most famous church on that island—shortly after Easter Thursday. Neither side refused the fight. The leaders adorned themselves; the soldiers prepared; the "conclusions" <note>the formal points of the argument</note> were posted on doors, at crossroads, and on every post. People flocked even from far away to see this spectacle. The people held various allegiances, but everyone’s expectations were equal. 

To make a long story short: the day destined for the battle arrived, and every corner was packed with the learned and the unlearned alike. But behold! Through the efforts of certain people, an edict was issued by the King via the Cardinal, forbidding the proceedings. At this, Standish—in order to claim the glory for himself—sent out some of his followers to spread word among the people that the Servite had fallen to his knees before him, begging that the debate not proceed. Most people were convinced of this, especially since the foreign guest did not know English—until some "god" <note>an inspiration or stroke of luck</note> put an idea into the Servite's mind. He climbed into the pulpit and addressed the multitude thus: "Most learned doctors, and you other most excellent men: there was to be a debate today, but the most reverend Cardinal, for just reasons, has ordered us to desist, so that you do not wait here in vain." 

When the <term>Minorites</term> <note>The "Lesser Brothers" or Franciscans; Erasmus uses the term "Minorites" to set up a logic pun later in the text.</note> saw such a prize of glory snatched from their hands, they attacked the man, nearly tearing him apart in the middle of the temple, had the provident Cardinal not assigned him several well-known guards from his own household. The Minorites, therefore, doing the only thing they could, shook their heads and made many threats from a distance. They went back to the Cardinal, loudly accusing the Servite of daring to testify to the people, against the royal prohibition, that he was ready to defend such an impious conclusion. Both parties were ordered to appear. 

Standish brought along not only his attendants but also a cowled boy, who was already a budding <term>Scotist</term> <note>A follower of the philosophy of Duns Scotus, often associated with complex, hair-splitting logic.</note>. It is of such great importance to be trained correctly from a tender age! As he made his way through the various courtyards to the Cardinal's inner chamber, Standish showed the boy off to the court nobles. Indeed, that boy was better known to many than a pet cat. Standish affirmed that the boy would finish off and trample the Servite. When they arrived, Standish pushed for the boy to be matched against him. But the Cardinal said it was not decorous for a boy to be matched against a "graduate," as they call them. For the Servite was a Bachelor of Theology—though whether he was "running" or "sitting," "formed" or "to be formed," is uncertain <note>Erasmus is mocking the overly technical grades of medieval theological degrees: "Baccalaureus Cursor," "Baccalaureus Formatus," etc.</note>. 

Instead, a certain Minorite was put forward—an Italian against an Italian—so that "crow might peck out the eyes of crow" <note>An adage meaning two of a kind fighting each other.</note>. Several learned men and nobles stood around with ears pricked. There, the Minorite, with arm extended, said: "Do you say that the Minorites sin if they handle money?" 
"I do," said the Servite. 
"Do you deny that the Pope can grant an indulgence so that it is allowed?" 
"I do not deny it." 
"But he has granted it to us." 
"I believe you." 
"Therefore, it is allowed." 
"I do not argue against that." 
"Then your conclusion is a lie!" 

The Servite eluded this spear-thrust thus: "My conclusion," he said, "pronounces judgment on *Minorites*. It is not allowed for *them*. For you, who are not Minorites, it is allowed." 
"On the contrary," said the other, "the Papal bull calls us Minorites." 
"It calls you that," said the Servite, "but it adds 'Conventual.' For 'Conventual Minorites' are 'Minorites' in the same way that a 'dead man' is a 'man'." <note>A classic logic trap: adding a qualifying adjective (like "dead") can negate the essential properties of the noun (a "man" is a living being; therefore a "dead man" is not a "man" in the true sense).</note> 

When the Minorite was struck dumb by this—for he had not expected such a solution—the Cardinal, admiring his dialectic sharpness, smiled quite pleasantly. When Standish saw that the first encounter had not gone well, he himself entered the arena. With a menacing face and an outstretched arm, he said: "I declare you excommunicated!" 
And when the Servite immediately denied it, Standish said: "We have a Papal bull that excommunicates all those who dare to say that the Conventual Minorite friars in England sin if they receive money. You have seen the bull, and yet you affirm this; therefore, you are excommunicated." 

At this, the Servite would have been completely <term>thunderstruck</term> <note>original Greek: εμβροντητος (embrontētos)</note> had he not slipped away by saying that the bull speaks of "Conventual Minorites" (who were not truly "Minor"), whereas his own conclusion spoke of "Minorites" in the absolute sense. The Cardinal, who was doing all this more for entertainment than in seriousness, dismissed them both, such that it was not yet clear which man was the stronger. The Servite returned to Paris <note>original Latin: Lutetia</note> to celebrate a triumph there. The followers of Standish, conversely, bragged among their own that he had been defeated by a boy, so much so that he had nothing to say for himself. The "conclusion" remains to be debated in the theological schools of Oxford and Cambridge. Since this spectacle was exceedingly delightful to us, I wanted to share that pleasure with you, best of readers, so that you might relieve the boredom of reading with this pleasant story.

<meta>The previous page concluded a contemporary anecdote regarding a legal and theological dispute in London involving Henry Standish and a Servite friar. This page, numbered 514, continues the collection of "Adages" (proverbial sayings) with entry 99 of the fifth "century" of the second "chiliad" (thousand), before transitioning into the sixth century. The catchword "Aquam" at the bottom of the page indicates the first word of the next page.</meta>

# A polypus driven by blows
<note>original: "Plagis adactus polypus"</note>

It is customary to say this when someone is finally improved by much misfortune. This occurs with unruly youths who are eventually tamed <note>original: "cicurantur" (to tame or domesticate)</note> by the experience of many evils. It is also suitable for those endowed with a more stubborn nature who cannot be corrected except by heavy punishments. They say that the **polypus** <note>In antiquity, "polypus" referred to an octopus or cuttlefish.</note>, once caught, is usually struck and beaten for a long time so that it becomes softer and more suitable for eating. The author of this is Zenodotus.

# Nisa is given to Mopsus
<note>original: "Mopso Nisa datur"</note>

This also appears to be a proverbial pattern, found in Virgil's *The Sorceress*:
->**Nisa is given to Mopsus.**<-
This is used when, against all hope, something remarkable happens to someone entirely unworthy, so that it appears that nothing is now impossible for anyone to hope for:
> Nisa is given to Mopsus: what may we lovers not hope for?
The emphasis is on the names. For by saying **Mopsus**, he understands the lowest and most dejected shepherd; by **Nisa**, a girl of extraordinary beauty. Not unlike this is the line from Sophocles in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*: "Nothing is unexpected" <note>original: "οὐκ ἔστ' ἀέλπτον οὐδέν"</note>, that is:
->**There is nothing that one may not hope for.**<-
On the same sentiment, Linus says in the works of Stobaeus:
> One should hope for all things, since nothing is unexpected.
> All things are easy for God to accomplish, and nothing is impossible.
That is:
> "Hope for all things, for there is nothing that cannot happen,
> All things are easy for the great gods to perform."

### THE SIXTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD

# What else but pain for the conquered?
<note>original: "Quid nisi uictis dolor?"</note>

"What else but pain for the conquered?" <note>original Greek: "Τὶ ἄλλο ἢ τοῖς νενικημένοις ὀδύναι;"</note> This is to be used when something is done openly as an insult. It is taken from a saying of Brennus <note>A chieftain of the Senones, a Gallic tribe that famously sacked Rome in 390 BC.</note>, who was openly mocking the Romans while weighing the gold he had demanded from them—at a time when they despaired of help—to lead the Gallic army away from Roman territory. I have chosen to transcribe the words of Plutarch himself:

"Then, it seeming best to the leaders, they met for a discussion, Brennus and Sulpicius, the Roman military tribune. It was agreed that the Romans would pay down a thousand pounds of gold, and the Gauls, having received it, would immediately depart from the city and the land. When the oaths had been sworn and the gold was brought, the Gauls initially cheated in secret, but then openly pulled back and tilted the scale. The Romans were indignant. But Brennus, as if in mockery and for the sake of ridicule, unbuckled his sword together with his belt and added it to the weights. When Sulpicius asked what this meant, he replied: 'What else but pain for the conquered?' From this, the saying became proverbial."

Thus, when the agreement had been made and the gold brought, the Gauls—unmindful of the pledged faith—began at first secretly, then openly, to weigh down and twist the scale. The indignation of the Romans rose against them. But Brennus, as if in jest and for the sake of mocking them, placed his sword, taken off with its belt, upon the scales. Furthermore, to Sulpicius asking what this was, he said: "What else, indeed, but pain for the conquered?" And that saying has now passed into a proverb.

Festus Pompeius <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> mentions this, adding the following: when Camillus <note>Marcus Furius Camillus, the Roman general who supposedly defeated Brennus after the gold was weighed.</note> cut down Brennus after he had been caught in an ambush, and Brennus complained that this was done against the treaty, Camillus turned Brennus's own words back on him: **"Woe to the conquered"** <note>original: "Væ uictis"</note>. For that is how Festus records the proverb. From this, it is clear that in Plutarch, the word should have been translated as "pain," not "reproach." The translator either slipped up or used a manuscript in which "reproach" <note>original Greek: "ὄνειδος"</note> was written instead of "pains" <note>original Greek: "ὀδύναι"</note>. 

Ballio in the works of Plautus seems to have alluded to this: "Woe to the conquered," when a defeated person is forced to obey even unfair conditions. And, unless I am mistaken, Virgil says in *Moeris*:
> Now, defeated and sad, since chance turns all things,
> we send these kids to him—and may it not turn out well for him.
Nonius Marcellus, in his entry on "Cestus," cites the title of a Varronian Satire: *Woe to the conquered*.

# SECOND THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY

### II. Drinking water, you produce nothing good.
<note>original: "Aquam bibens nihil boni parias."</note>
**Drinking water, you would produce nothing good and useful.** <note>original: "Ὕδωρ δὲ πίνων, χρηστὸν οὐδὲν ἂν τέκοις"</note>
They say the author of this is **Demetrius of Halicarnassus** <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric active in Rome in the 1st century BCE.</note>. The sense of it is that nothing excellent, worthy of posterity, or beautiful comes from poets if they drink water—that is, if they are poor and live on a meager diet. **Horace** <note>The Roman lyric poet.</note> says:
->**No poems can please for long, nor can they live,**<-
->**which are written by water-drinkers.**<-
Likewise, **Juvenal** <note>A Roman satirist.</note> writes:
->**But if Virgil had lacked a boy, or a tolerable**<-
->**lodging, all the snakes would have fallen from the Furies' hair,**<-
->**and the silent trumpet would have groaned nothing grave.**<-
The same author says:
->**Horace is sated when he cries out, "Enough!"**<-
A couplet of this kind by Demetrius of Halicarnassus is cited by Zenodotus, although in the collection of epigrams it is recorded under the name of **Niceratus**:
->**Wine is a swift horse for the gifted singer,**<-
->**But drinking water, you would produce nothing good.**<-
Although in the works of **Athenaeus** <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae' or 'Philosophers at Dinner'.</note> the first line is recorded differently:
->**Truly, wine is a great horse for a charming poet.**<-
The same verses are cited by Athenaeus in the second book of the *Philosophers at Dinner*, from a certain epigram that someone had written against **Cratinus** <note>An Athenian comic poet known for his heavy drinking, which he even mocked in his own plays.</note>, who is frequently criticized in comedies for being a drunkard. Indeed, even Horace attributes eloquence to wine:
->**Whom have the flowing cups not made eloquent?**<-
**Martial** <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams.</note> writes:
->**I can do nothing sober; when I drink,**<-
->**fifteen poets come to my aid.**<-
**Aristotle**, in the eighth book of his *On the History of Animals*, thinks that a parrot becomes more talkative if it drinks wine.

### III. The dog is worthy of its food.
<note>original: "Digna canis pabulo."</note>
**The dog is worthy of its food.** <note>original: "Ἀξία ἡ κύων τοῦ βρώματος."</note> This means almost the same as if you were to say: "The laborer is worthy of his hire." It suggests that hardly any servant is so useless that he does not seem worthy, if not of a large salary, then certainly of his sustenance. It is recorded by **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia and dictionary.</note>. It will apply to a man who is not entirely to be rejected or useless; or to a flatterer, and for that reason someone fit to frequent the courts of princes, where those who do not know how to fawn are held in no value.

### IV. The dog is worthy of a seat.
<note>original: "Canis digna sede."</note>
**The dog is worthy of a seat.** <note>original: "Ἀξία ἡ κύων θρόνου."</note> This is said when a new honor falls to someone undeserving. It seems to be taken from **Maltese dogs**, which some women hold in higher honor than their own husbands. Unless you prefer to refer it to **Anubis**, the Egyptian god <note>Depicted with the head of a jackal or dog.</note>. Furthermore, it is well known that such honor was given to dogs by their masters that they even erected monuments to them when they died. This is recorded by **Diogenianus** <note>A Greek grammarian and collector of proverbs.</note>.

### V. If he asks for wine, give him fists.
<note>original: "Si uinum postulet, pugnos illi dato."</note>
**If he should ask for wines, offer him fists.** <note>original: "Ἂν οἶνον αἰτῇ, κονδύλους αὐτῷ δίδου."</note>
This is used when people receive the opposite of the good things they expected. This six-foot verse is taken from some tragedy about the **Cyclops** and **Ulysses**. The story is very well known: how, in **Homer**, Ulysses repeatedly offers wine to the Cyclops **Polyphemus** when he asks for it, so that as soon as he lay down drunk and asleep, Ulysses could bore out his eye with a charred stake. Some think the metaphor is drawn from children who, when asking for things they should not have, sometimes receive a slap. **Terence** <note>A Roman playwright.</note> says in *Phormio*: "Plant your fists in his belly." He calls the blows themselves "fists" <note>original: "pugnos"</note>, just as the Greeks use the word *kondylous*. The adage is recorded by Suidas.

### VI. A scorpion instead of a perch.
<note>original: "Pro perca scorpium."</note>
**Instead of a perch, a scorpion.** <note>original: "Ἀντὶ πέρκης σκορπίον."</note> This is used when someone, trying to catch the best, catches the worst. For the **perch** is a highly praised fish, of which Athenaeus frequently makes mention when listing the delicacies of gluttons. The **scorpion** <note>Either the land arachnid or the venomous "scorpion fish."</note> is lethal; although there is also a fish of this name, of a contemptible flavor, which the adage seems more likely to refer to. **Lycophron** <note>A Greek poet and scholar.</note> spoke with a similar figure of speech:

<meta>This page concludes the final entries of the Fifth Century and begins the Sixth Century of the Second Thousand of Erasmus's Adages. The text continues from the previous discussion of proverbs regarding discipline and unexpected fortune, moving into the famous historical anecdote of Brennus and the Romans.</meta>

**The octopus driven by fourteen blows.** <note>original: "Plagis adactus polypus quatuor decem."</note>
This was a common saying used when someone finally becomes more corrected or improved after enduring much misfortune. It applies to headstrong youths who are eventually tamed by the experience of many hardships. It is also suitable for those endowed with a harder nature who cannot be corrected except through heavy punishments. They say that when an octopus is caught, it is customary to beat and strike it long and hard so that it becomes more tender and suitable for eating. The author of this is Zenodotus <note>An ancient Greek grammarian and literary critic.</note>.

### Nisa is given to Mopsus.
<note>original: "Mopso Nisa datur."</note>

This appears to be a proverbial pattern, also found in **Virgil** <note>The Roman epic poet.</note> in his *Pharmaceutria* <note>Eclogue 8.</note>:
**Nisa is given to Mopsus.**
This is used when an excellent thing happens to someone utterly unworthy, contrary to everyone's expectations, so that it seems nothing is impossible for anyone to hope for:
**Nisa is given to Mopsus: what may we lovers not expect?**
The emphasis, however, is in the names. For by saying "Mopsus," he understands the lowest and most abject shepherd; by "Nisa," a girl of extraordinary beauty. Not unlike this is the line of **Sophocles** <note>The Greek tragedian.</note> in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*: <greek>οὐκ ἔστ᾽ ἄελπτον οὐδέν</greek> <note>original: "ouk est' aelpton ouden"</note>, which is to say:
**There is nothing that one may not hope for.**
On the same sentiment, **Linus** <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology, often cited as a poet.</note> says in **Stobaeus** <note>A 5th-century compiler of Greek extracts.</note>:
<greek>ἔλπεσθαι χρὴ πάντ᾽, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἔστ᾽ οὐδὲν ἄελπτον.
ῥᾴδια πάντα θεῷ τελέσαι, καὶ ἀνήνυτον οὐδέν.</greek> <note>original: "elpesthai chrē pant'..."</note> which is:
"One should hope for all things, since nothing is beyond hope,
All things are easy for the great gods to accomplish, and nothing is impossible."

### SECOND THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY

### What else but pain to the conquered?
<note>original: "Quid nisi uictis dolor?"</note>

<margin><greek>Τί ἄλλο ἢ τοῖς νενικημένοις ὀδύνη</greek></margin> <note>original: "Ti allo ē tois nenikēmenois odynē"</note>
**What else but pain to the conquered?** To be used when something is done openly as an insult. It is taken from a saying of **Brennus** <note>A chieftain of the Senones, a Gallic tribe, who famously sacked Rome in 390 BCE.</note>, who was openly mocking the Romans while weighing the gold he had demanded from them—the price for leading the Gallic army out of Roman territory while they despaired of help. But I have chosen to include the words of **Plutarch** <note>A Greek historian and biographer.</note> himself: <greek>Εἶτα δόξαν τοῖς λογισμοῖς, συνελθεῖν εἰς λόγους Βρέννῳ καὶ Σουλπικίῳ τῷ χιλιάρχῳ ῥωμαίων, ὡμολογήθη, τῶν μὲ χιλίων λιτρῶν χρυσίου καταβαλλομένων, ἀνθ᾽ ὧν λαβόντας ἐκ τ᾽ πόλεως καὶ τ᾽ χώρας αὐτίκα ἀπελθεῖν. τῶν τεθέντων γὰρ μέτρων ὅρκων, καὶ τ᾽ χρυσίου κομισθέντος, τ᾽ μὲ Κέλτων ποδὶ τ᾽ σταθμὸν ἀγνωμονόντων, κρύφα τὸ πρῶτον, εἶτα φανερῶς ἀφελκόντων καὶ διαστρεφόντων τὴν ῥοπήν, ἠγανάκτει ῥωμαῖοι· πῶς οὐδ᾽, ὁ δ᾽ Βρέννος οἷον ἐφυβρίζων, καὶ καταγελῶν ἀπολυσάμενος τὴν μάχαιραν ἅμα καὶ τῷ ζωστῆρα προσέθηκε τοῖς σταθμοῖς. πυνθανομένου δ᾽ τ᾽ Σουλπικίου τί τοῦτο; τί γὰρ ἄλλο εἶπεν, ἢ τοῖς νενικημένοις ὀδύνη; ὅπερ μὲν οὖν καὶ παροιμιώδης λόγος γέγονε.</greek> <note>original: "Eita doxan tois logismois..."</note> that is: "Therefore, when it had been decided that the leaders should meet, Brennus and **Sulpicius** <note>The Roman military tribune.</note>, the leader of the Romans, agreed that the Romans should pay a thousand pounds of gold; as soon as they received the gold, the Gauls would depart from the city and the fields. When the oaths had been exchanged regarding these terms and the gold had been brought, the Gauls—forgetful of their pledged faith—began at first secretly, then openly, to weigh down and distort the scale. The Romans were filled with indignation against them. But Brennus, as if in mockery and for the sake of ridiculing them, unbuckled his sword together with its belt and placed them on the scales. Furthermore, when Sulpicius asked what this meant, he said, 'What else, indeed, but pain for the conquered?' And that saying has now passed into a proverb." **Festus Pompeius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> mentions this, adding that when **Camillus** <note>The Roman general who eventually defeated Brennus.</note> cut down Brennus after catching him in an ambush, and Brennus complained that it was being done against the treaty, Camillus turned his own words back on him: **Woe to the conquered.** <note>original: "Væ uictis."</note> For that is how Festus records the proverb. From this it is clear that "pain" <note>original: "dolorem"</note>, not "disgrace" <note>original: "opprobriũ"</note>, should have been translated in Plutarch. The translator either slipped or used a manuscript in which <greek>ὄνειδος</greek> <note>original: "oneidos" - shame/disgrace</note> was written instead of <greek>ὀδύνη</greek> <note>original: "odynē" - pain</note>. **Ballio** <note>A character in Plautus's play 'Pseudolus'.</note> in **Plautus** seems to have alluded to this: **Woe to the conquered**, used when the defeated person is forced to obey even unfair conditions. And, if I am not mistaken, **Virgil** in *Moeris*:
**Now, conquered and sad, since fortune turns everything upside down,**
**we send these kids to him—and may it not turn out well for him.**
**Nonius Marcellus** <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note>, under the word *Cestus*, cites the title of a **Varronian** <note>Referring to Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar.</note> Satire: **Woe to the conquered.**

### II. Drinking water, you would produce nothing good.

*Drinking water, you would produce nothing good* <note>original Greek: Ὕδωρ ὃ πίνων, χρησὸν οὐδὲν ἂν τέκοις</note>, which is to say:
**Drinking water, you will give birth to nothing honest or useful.**
They say the author of this was **Demetrius of Halicarnassus** <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note>. The meaning is that nothing excellent, worthy of posterity, or beautiful comes from poets if they drink only water—that is, if they are impoverished and live on a meager diet. **Horace** <note>The leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> writes:
> No poems can please for long, nor can they live,
> Which are written by water-drinkers.

Likewise **Juvenal** <note>A Roman poet known for his Satires.</note>:
> But if Virgil lacked a slave-boy or a tolerable 
> Lodging, all the snakes would fall from his hair,
> And the silent trumpet would groan nothing grand.
<note>Juvenal argues that great art requires material comfort; without it, Virgil could not have described the terrifying Furies or the grandeur of war.</note>

The same author says:
**Horace is full when he cries out, "Enough!"** <note>Meaning Horace only wrote his best poetry when his belly was full and his needs met.</note>
A couplet of this kind by Demetrius of Halicarnassus is cited by **Zenodotus**, even though in the collection of epigrams it is attributed to **Niceratus**:
*Wine is a dear and swift horse to the graceful singer,*
*But drinking water, you would produce nothing good.*
However, in **Athenaeus** <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae' (The Learned Banqueters).</note>, the first verse is recorded differently:
*Truly, wine is a great horse for the charming poet.*
These same verses are cited by Athenaeus in the second book of the *Deipnosophistae*, from a certain epigram written against **Cratinus** <note>A celebrated comic poet of Athens known for his heavy drinking.</note>, who was frequently mocked in comedies as a drunkard. Indeed, even Horace attributes eloquence to wine:
> Whom have the flowing cups not made eloquent?

**Martial** <note>A Roman poet famous for his short, witty epigrams.</note> writes:
> I can do nothing sober; when I drink,
> Fifteen poets come to my aid.

**Aristotle**, in the eighth book of his *History of Animals*, believes that a parrot becomes more talkative if it drinks wine.

### III. A dog worthy of its food.

*The dog is worthy of its food.* <note>original Greek: Ἀξία ἡ κύων τῷ βρώματι.</note> This means roughly the same as if you were to say: "The laborer is worthy of his hire." Scarcely any servant is so useless that he does not seem worthy of his keep, even if he does not deserve a large salary. It is recorded by **Suidas** <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note>. It can be applied to a man who is not entirely to be rejected or useless, or to a flatterer who is, for that very reason, fit to be employed in the courts of princes—where those who do not know how to flatter are held in no esteem.

### IV. A dog worthy of a throne.

*The dog is worthy of a seat of honor.* <note>original Greek: Ἀξία ἡ κύων θρόνου.</note> This is used when a new honor falls upon someone unworthy. It seems to be taken from the **Melitean dogs** <note>A breed of small lapdogs, ancestors of the modern Maltese, which were highly prized pets in antiquity.</note>, upon whom some foolish women bestow more honor than they do upon their own husbands. Unless you prefer to relate it to **Anubis**, the god of the Egyptians <note>The jackal-headed god often associated with the afterlife</note>. Furthermore, it is well known that such great honor was shown to dogs by their masters that they even erected monuments to them when they died. This is recorded by **Diogenianus** <note>A Greek grammarian and proverb collector.</note>.

### V. If he asks for wine, give him fists.

*If he asks for wine, give him fists.* <note>original Greek: Ἂν οἶνον αἰτῇ, κονδύλους αὐτῷ δίδου.</note> That is:
**If he demands wine, offer him your knuckles.**
This is used when people receive the opposite of the good things they expected. This iambic verse is taken from some tragedy concerning the **Cyclops** and **Odysseus**. It is a very well-known story how, in **Homer**, Odysseus repeatedly offers wine to the Cyclops **Polyphemus** when he asks for it, so that as soon as he lay down drunk and asleep, Odysseus could bore out his eye with a charred stake. Some think the metaphor is drawn from children, who sometimes receive a box on the ears when they ask for things they should not have. **Terence** <note>A Roman playwright.</note> says in *Phormio*: "Drive your fists into his belly." He calls the blows themselves "fists," just as the Greeks use the word for knuckles <note>original: "kondylous"</note>. The adage is recorded by Suidas.

### VI. A scorpion for a perch.

*A scorpion instead of a perch.* <note>original Greek: Ἀντὶ πέρκης σκορπίον.</note> This is used when someone, trying to catch the best thing, catches the worst. For the **perch** is a highly praised fish, which Athenaeus mentions repeatedly when listing the delicacies of gourmands. The **scorpion** <note>Likely the 'Scorpaena' or scorpionfish, known for its venomous spines.</note> is deadly; although there is also a fish of this name that has a contemptible flavor, which the adage seems to refer to more directly. **Lycophron** <note>A Greek tragic poet and scholar.</note> used a similar figure when he said:

<meta>catchword: but he instead</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>VII</margin>
*Like a pipus swallowing a scorpion in its throat.* <note>original Greek: Οἷ’ ἀντὶ πίπῶς σκορπίου λαιμῶ ἀνάλες</note>
That is:
**But that bird, in the manner of a pipus, swallowing a scorpion.**
For the *pipus* is a species of bird.

->**In return for his kindness, the Achaians took vengeance on Agamemnon.**<-

*In return for his good deeds, the Achaians paid back Agamemnon.* <note>original Greek: Ἀντ’ εὐεργεσίας ἀγαμέμνονα τῖσαν ἀχαιοί</note>
That is:
**For his merits, the Greeks treated Agamemnon poorly.**
Some record it in this manner:
*In return for his good deeds, the Achaians bound Agamemnon.* <note>original Greek: Ἀντ’ εὐεργεσίας ἀγαμέμνονα θῆκαν ἀχαιοί</note>
That is:
**For his benefactions, the Greeks threw Agamemnon into chains.**
This was said against the ungrateful, who repay a supreme benefit with a supreme injury. For **Agamemnon** <note>The legendary leader of the Greeks during the Trojan War.</note>, after enduring so many labors in the conquest of Troy for the honor of Greece, returned home only to be entangled in an inescapable robe and murdered by his wife **Clytemnestra**, with the help of her lover **Aegisthus**. It has been noted that this frequently happens to men who have served the state well: they receive the worst thanks from the people in exchange for their good deeds. **Pindar** <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet known for his odes.</note> writes in his fourth *Pythian Ode*: "This is said to be the most painful thing: for one who knows what is right to be forced by necessity to keep his foot outside," <note>original Greek: φανὴ δ’ ὕμιν ἐπ’ ἀνιαροτάτῳ, καλὰ γινώσκοντ’ ἀνάγκα ἐκτὸς ἔχειν πόδα</note> which is to say: they say it is most distressing when someone who knows the honorable path is forced to keep his foot away from it—meaning he does not enjoy the fruits of his goodness despite his merits toward others, but instead hears ill words in return for his good deeds.

<margin>VIII</margin>
->**Sing the songs of Tellen.**<-

*Sing the things of Tellen.* <note>original Greek: Ἄειδε τὰ τέλλωνος</note> That is: **Sing the songs of Tellen.** Some think this is said of those who are abusive and biting in their speech; others, of those who chatter foolishly. For this **Tellen** was reportedly a certain flute player and a poet of very foolish songs. Others record that he described jokes in very charming verses, flavored with much "comma-like" wit <note>meaning short, punchy, or sharp phrasing</note>. **Dicaearchus of Messana** <note>A Greek philosopher and geographer.</note> mentions this Tellen, as cited by **Zenodotus** <note>A scholar and grammarian of Alexandria.</note>, as does **Plutarch** in his *Sayings*.

<margin>IX</margin>
->**Azanean evils.**<-

*Azanean evils.* <note>original Greek: Ἀζαναῖα κακά</note> This was habitually said when someone spent a great deal of labor on a very difficult and fruitless matter. Or when a person had to deal with someone difficult, peevish, intractable, or stingy. They say **Azania** is a certain region of **Arcadia** <note>A mountainous region in the Peloponnese of Greece, often associated with rustic simplicity or, in this case, harsh terrain.</note>, sterile and unfit for cultivation, where the farmers reap little fruit for much sweat. These details are mostly gathered by the collectors of Greek proverbs. However, **Stephanus** <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, author of a geographical dictionary of the ancient world.</note>, in his work *On the Names of Cities*, opens the source of this adage for us. Indeed, he mentions several Azanias: one which is a part of Arcadia, where there is a certain spring whose water, if tasted, causes one to abhor wine so much that he cannot even bear the smell of it. A second is in **Marseille**, and a third in **Phrygia** <note>An ancient kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia (modern Turkey).</note>, which **Strabo** <note>A famous Greek geographer and historian.</note> also mentions in the twelfth book of his *Geography*. Concerning this Phrygian Azania, **Hermogenes**—as cited by Stephanus—tells a story of this sort: Since there were many rustic villas there, and a famine arose due to the sterility of the fields, the local shepherds gathered and performed a divine rite, seeking fertility from the gods. But when the gods did not hear their prayers and the sterility of the fields persisted, a certain shepherd named **Euphorbos** devised a new kind of sacrifice. He sacrificed an *echinus* to the earth <note>original Greek: ἐχῖνον τῇ γῇ</note>, which in the Phrygian tongue means a "fox and a hedgehog." Once the gods were appeased by this victim, the fields began to be fertile. When the neighboring shepherds learned of this, they granted Euphorbos the priesthood and the command. Afterward, the name of the place was changed, and instead of Azania it was called *Echinagyros*, which sounds in the Phrygian language just as if you said in Greek *echinalopeka*, or in Latin *echinouulpem* (**Hedgehog-fox**). Stephanus relates matters of this sort, from which one may guess that the proverb was born from that story.

<margin>X</margin>
->**The goat hasn't yet given birth, but the kid is playing on the roof.**<-

*The goat has not yet brought forth, but the kid plays on the house.* <note>original Greek: Αἲξ οὔπω τέκεν, ἔριφος δὲ ἐπὶ δώματα παίζει</note>
That is:
**The goat has not yet labored, yet already the kid plays in the house.**
This is said of those who attempt the final and completed stages of a task while skipping over the necessary preceding steps. Or of those who boast that they have already achieved something for which the foundations have not even been laid. Or those who act in a backward manner. For a birth must happen before a kid can play on the roof. This is recorded by **Zenodotus**.

<margin>XI</margin>
->**God finds the guilty.**<-

*God found the sinner.* <note>original Greek: Εὗρε θεὸς τὸν ἀλιτρόν</note> That is: **God finds the guilty.** This is said when vengeance finally catches up with the wicked, as if sent by divine power. **Theocritus** <note>A Greek poet from Sicily, known for his pastoral poetry.</note> says in his tenth *Idyll*:
*God found the sinner; you have now what you long desired.* <note>original Greek: Εὗρε θεὸς τὸν ἀλιτρόν, ἔχεις πάλαι ὧν ἐπεθύμεις</note>
That is:
**God found the ungodly man; you have what you wanted for a long time.**
The commentator on Theocritus indicates that the proverb was also commonly expressed in another form: *God found a sinner.*

<summary>This page catalogs proverbs concerning ingratitude (the murder of Agamemnon), fruitless labor (the sterile lands of Azania), and the folly of premature boasting. It also emphasizes that divine justice eventually catches up with the wicked.</summary>
