<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion on divine justice and moral character. On the previous page, he began citing poets to illustrate that although God’s punishment may be slow, it is inevitable. Here, he concludes that theme and moves into two new adages: one regarding the excuses of the lazy, and another on how subordinates tend to imitate the vices of their superiors.</meta>

A similar sentiment is found in Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 4:
> If the Olympian does not bring it to pass immediately, 
> he will bring it to pass in the end, and they will pay a great price.
<note>original Greek: Εἴπερ γάρ τε καὶ αὐτίκ’ ὀλύμπιος οὐκ ἐτέλεσσεν, ἔκ τε καὶ ὀψὲ τελεῖ, σύν τε μεγάλῳ ἀπέτισαν.</note>
-> that is, <-
For although Jupiter does not punish the guilty at once,
He will do so eventually, and they shall pay for their crimes at a heavy cost.

<margin>To this belongs that passage of Sophocles:</margin>
> If you have harmed the gods,
> no one, however powerful, could escape their pursuit.
<note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἂν δὲ τοῖς θεοῖς βλάπτης, δύναιτ’ ἂν οὐδὲν ἰχνύων φυγεῖν.</note>
-> that is, <-
Whenever someone has offended the gods,
No one can flee, no matter how mighty.

Furthermore, that proverbial six-foot line of verse agrees:
> No mortal man leaps over the blow of a God.
<note>original Greek: Θεοῦ δὲ πληγὴν οὐχ ὑπερπηδᾷ βροτός.</note>
-> that is, <-
No man escapes the strike of the gods.

<margin>Pindar likewise in the *Pythian Odes*:</margin>
> God catches the winged eagle, and overtakes the dolphin of the sea,
> and he humbles even the most high-minded of mortals.
<note>original Greek: Θεὸς ὃ καὶ πτερόεντ’ αἰετὸν κίχε, καὶ θαλασσαῖον παραμείβεται δελφῖνα, καὶ ὑψιφρόνων τιν’ ἔκαμψε βροτῶν.</note>
-> that is, <-
God both reaches the winged eagle and overtakes the sea-dolphin, and he casts down the most arrogant of men.

This sentiment is also supported in the *Olympian Odes*:
> If any man hopes that he will escape the notice of God while he acts, he is mistaken.
<note>original Greek: Εἰ δὲ θεὸν ἀνήρ τις ἔλπεταί τι λαθέμεν ἔρδων, ἁμαρτάνει.</note>
-> that is, <-
But if anyone expects to deceive God when he does something, he is in error.

### For the idle, it is always a holiday. XII

Those who are free from work are said to be "on holiday," and the idle are called "holiday-keepers," and idleness itself is called a "holiday"—metaphors that have been accepted as a proverb. Theocritus says in his *Idylls*:
> To the lazy, it is always a feast day.
<note>original Greek: Ἀεργοῖς αἰὲν ἑορτά.</note>
-> that is, <-
It is always a holiday for the sluggish. For on holidays, even the pagans abstained from secular business. Those who flee from labor wish for feast days, so they may be permitted to be idle and indulge their bellies and pleasures. Indeed, in ancient times, several holiday days were given to farmers for this purpose: so that they might refresh themselves from their weariness through play. However, they mixed this with religion so that their games might be more moderate. 

But today, the common crowd of Christians misuses holidays—which were once established for the practice of piety—for heavy drinking, for prostitutes, for gambling, for brawling, and for fighting. At no time are more crimes committed than when it is most appropriate to be free from crime. We never imitate the pagans more than when we ought to be acting most like Christians. Since it is clear that a practice invented to help religion is turning into the destruction of religion, I do not know what plan the popes have in mind by daily adding holiday upon holiday. It would be more fitting for them to imitate prudent physicians, who change remedies according to the nature of diseases, looking only to the goal of preserving good health. 

Therefore, when they see that a thing which was once healthily established according to the conditions of those times is now, due to the changed morals of Christians, a plague upon piety, what kind of religious duty is it to refuse to change the regulation with the same wisdom as those ancients who established it? What I say about feast days should be understood regarding many other things: not because I think the holidays of Christians should be condemned, but because I do not want them to grow to an immense number; and those few which the authority of the ancients established, I wish to see turned back to the purpose for which they were invented. For to true Christians, every day is a feast day; but for the wicked—who are the greatest multitude—feast days are less "festive" than secular ones. 

But to return to the proverb: it will be aptly applied to those who are always making some excuse to remain in idleness. For example, to those for whom literature is unpleasant, they excuse themselves now on account of health, now because of domestic chores; sometimes the harshness of winter stands in the way, other times the heat of summer, and occasionally the dangerous weather of autumn. Finally, they are called away from their books by the beauty of spring, which will soon vanish. After lunch, they say one should have nothing to do with books until the stomach has finished digesting. Before lunch, hunger makes a noise, making them less inclined. In the daylight, they say it is a lazy thing to sit indoors; yet to stay awake by the lamp is harmful to the eyes. If their household wealth is sufficient, they ask: "What is the need for letters?" If it is lacking, they say a poor man cannot practice philosophy. The young man says the flower of his age should not be consumed by the cares of the old. The older man says he must spare his health.

<note>original Greek: Τὰς δεσποίνας αἱ κύνες μιμέμεναι.</note>
That is, little dogs imitating their ladies. This is used when servants represent the ferocity of their masters, or disciples take on the arrogance of their teacher, or the ministers of princes adopt their haughtiness. Briefly, it applies whenever those who are subordinate express the character of those under whose command they live. Hence that saying of Juvenal:

<margin>14</margin>
### The punishments of Tantalus.

<note>original Greek: Ταντάλου τιμωρίαι.</note>
-> that is, The torments of Tantalus. <-
This should be said of those who possess good things but are denied the enjoyment of them. It is taken from the myth of Tantalus, whom the poets imagine standing in a river in the underworld, parched with thirst; but whenever he reaches down to drink, the water suddenly retreats from his lips. Furthermore, a tree laden with fruit hangs over his head, but when he stretches out his hand, it suddenly pulls away. Thus, the poor man is tortured by want in the presence of plenty. Horace testifies in his *Satires* that this was commonly said of stingy and sordid rich men:
> Thirsty Tantalus catches at the cups that fly from his lips.
> Why do you laugh? Change the name, and the story is told of you.
> You sleep with your mouth open over bags of money piled from every side,
> and you are forced to spare them as if they were sacred,
> or to take pleasure in them as if they were merely painted pictures.
The same author says in his *Odes*:
> Needy amidst great wealth.

Gregory of Nazianzus, in a letter to Basil, elegantly twists this to apply to the delights of this world, which never satisfy the soul: "And those people," he says, "like Tantalus, thirsting in the midst of waters, suffer that wretched feast which provides no nourishment."
<note>original Greek: πανδαισίαν (pandaisian)</note>
The Greeks use the term *pandaisia* for a banquet prepared with every kind of delicacy.

<margin>15</margin>
### For an old man, his jaws are his staff.

<note>original Greek: Ἀνδρὸς γέροντος αἱ γνάθοι βακτηρία.</note>
-> that is, <-
->The jaw serves as a walking stick for the elderly.<-
This was commonly said of those who, because their strength has failed due to age, are forced to adopt a finer and more abundant diet, so that they might replenish with food whatever old age wears away. Even today, an old man’s saying remains: "I support myself with my teeth." It is somewhat of a riddle: others walk with their feet, but the elderly walk with their teeth. For whatever has departed of the body's natural moisture must be restored with the support of food and drink. We commonly see that once an old man's appetite fails him, the end of his life is near.

<margin>16</margin>
### Not words instead of flour.

<note>original Greek: Μὴ λόγος ἀντ' ἀλφίτων.</note>
-> that is, <-
->No words in place of meal.<-
This was directed against those who gave a benefit in words rather than in reality. It is generally the habit of great men to feed their followers with splendid promises. Pomponius the jurist rightly advises in the *Pandects* <note>The Pandects, or Digest, is a massive compilation of Roman law.</note> that wealth should be increased by facts, not by words. It will also apply to those who repay a favor with promises, or those who offer comfort in speech when actual help is needed. The ancients called whatever pertained to sustenance *alphita* (barley-meal). It appears to be taken from some comedy, as it is a half-line of iambic trimeter verse. Concerning the Aristophanic proverb, "by no means the barley-meal," it has been discussed elsewhere.

<margin>17</margin>
### To weigh anchor.

This has some appearance of a proverb, as found in Marcus Varro’s work *On Agriculture*, in the final chapter: "To weigh anchor," used for preparing to depart. It is the same kind of expression as "to bind on one's winged sandals." These are his words: "Meanwhile the Peacock returns to us. And if you wish," he said, "to weigh anchor, the lot-casting for the tribes is being done sufficiently with the tablets." That is, if you wish to leave here, setting aside the dispute. However, there is a pun here on the ambiguous meaning of "tablets" (*tabulae*), which refers both to nautical planks and the legal tablets used for casting votes. Similar to this is Quintilian’s phrase, "To cast off the cable," for that is how many read it.

### Unrefined.

The Greeks call the inelegant and unlearned *amousoi*, <note>literally "without the Muses."</note> that is, "strangers to the Muses." In ancient times, nothing

...nothing was considered learned without music. Hence, in the comic poets, when someone denies they have learned their letters, they say they have not learned music. Quintilian, in his first book, in the chapter on the praises of music, says: "Indeed, it has become a celebrated proverb among the Greeks that the unlearned are far from the Muses and the Graces." Plato, in the eighth book of *The Republic*, used the term <term>more unmusical</term> <note>original Greek: ἀμουσότερον</note> to describe someone who is more wicked, rude, and shameless. And Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, writes: "As the poets say, the unlearned speak more 'musically' <note>original Greek: μουσικώτερον; meaning more persuasively or elegantly</note> before a crowd." This means that, as the poets say, those without formal education speak more charmingly to the masses. We call a remarkably elegant man "most musical"; indeed, whatever is moderate and well-composed, the Greeks call "in measure" <note>original Greek: ἔμμετρον</note>. Furthermore, Athenaeus calls unlearned and poorly timed stories "unmusical chatter" <note>original Greek: ἀμουσολογίαν</note>. Aeschines, in his speech against Timarchus, says: "For besides his other evils, this man is someone alien to the Muses and uneducated." 

Aristophanes, in *The Knights*, says:
"But, my good man, I do not even understand music."
-> that is <-
"Indeed, I do not even know music itself, my good friend."

He used to command men who were strangers to humanity and more refined letters to "sacrifice to the Graces and the Muses," just as Plato was frequently accustomed to warn Xenocrates <note>A student of Plato known for his severe and somber personality; Plato urged him to "sacrifice to the Graces" to soften his temperament.</note> to make an offering to the Graces. In the fourth book of Athenaeus, someone reproaching a Cynic for his lack of refinement says: "Not like you, who are unmusical, and never sacrifice to the Graces, nor even to the Muses." In the thirteenth book of the same author, a line is cited from some comedy:
"Whose Muses taught them left-handed letters." <note>original Greek: οὓς ἐδίδαξαν ἀριστερὰ γράμματα μοῦσαι.</note>
This seems to apply to someone who is perversely learned or malicious. Indeed, in the same work, Ephippus said of a certain person: "You carry your tongue in your mouth on the left side," unless perhaps you think it should be read "toward the left" <note>original Greek: ἐπ’ ἀριστερά</note>. He who interprets everything in a "left-handed" way <note>meaning unfavorably or sinisterly</note>, ignoring the good points, carries his tongue on the left side. From this we also get the expressions "sinister suspicions" and "sinister interpretations." There is also a famous saying by a certain philosopher, that he himself delivered the precepts of philosophy with his right hand, but his listeners received them with their left. Plutarch, in the *Life of Romulus*, wanting to show that a man was neither unlearned nor unrefined, says he lacked neither the Muses nor the Graces: "Sextius Sylla of Carthage, a man lacking neither the Muses nor the Graces."

### 19. The Vile-Litigator.

Marcus Cato used to call those who were eager for lawsuits and carpers of other people’s works <term>Vitilitigatores</term> <note>A portmanteau of *vitium* (vice/fault) and *litigator*. Erasmus translates this as "vile-litigators."</note>. Because of its novelty, this word passed into an adage among the learned, much like "Homer-floggers" <note>original: *Homeromastiges*, those who unfairly criticize Homer.</note> and "Virgil-floggers." Pliny, in the preface to his *Natural History*, writes: "Therefore we are secure, even against 'vile-litigators,' a word which Cato elegantly composed from 'vices' and 'litigators.' For what else do they do but litigate, or go looking for a lawsuit?" Let us follow through with the rest of our purpose.

### 20. Good wine needs no ivy hung over it.

"Good wine needs no ivy hung over it" means that true virtue does not require the praise of others. Or, that excellent things are pleasing in themselves and do not require external advertisement. It clearly arises from the custom of innkeepers, who used to hang an ivy sign <note>Ivy was associated with Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> in front of wine shops. Thus Plautus says in *The Carthaginian*: "One must actively lead a buyer to unsellable goods; good merchandise easily finds a buyer."
Horace writes:
"When he praises his wares beyond what is fair,
He who wishes to push off his sellable goods."

### 21. To sing to the myrtle.

"To sing to the myrtle" <note>original Greek: Ἀείδειν πρὸς μυῤῥίνην.</note> was a proverb applied to someone unskilled in letters and lacking eloquence, who could not speak among the learned. The metaphor is taken from an ancient custom where, at banquets, individuals would each sing their own song in turn. If someone refused to take up the lyre, being ignorant of music, he was jokingly given a branch of laurel or myrtle and compelled to sing to it. Furthermore, Quintilian testifies in his first book of *Institutes* that this was the ancient custom of singing: "Hence," he says, "also that custom that after dinner at banquets, the lyre would be passed around; when Themistocles confessed he was unskilled in it, he was—to use Cicero's words—considered quite unlearned." But it was also the custom of the ancient Romans to employ strings and flutes at feasts. Plutarch writes in the first book of his *Table Talk* that it was once the custom that in...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion on the cultural role of music in antiquity. ...at a banquet, they would first sing to the god with a common voice, **singing the paean** <note>original Greek: παιανίζοντες; a song of praise or thanksgiving, usually to Apollo</note>, as he says. Then, a myrtle branch was usually handed to each person, which he thinks is called an <term>aisakos</term> <note>original Greek: ἄισακον; a branch of laurel or myrtle held by singers</note>, because the one who received it would sing. After that, the lyre was passed around; whoever was skilled in the art took it and sang, tuning the sound of the strings to their voice. For those who refused or were unskilled in music, it was called a <term>skolion</term> <note>original Greek: σκολιὸν; literally "crooked" or "oblique"</note> song, because it was not common, nor easy for just anyone. Others say the myrtle was not passed in order, but transferred from couch to couch; for instance, after the person sitting first on the first couch had finished singing, he would hand it to the person reclining first on the second couch, and he in turn to the first of the third couch. Then, the second person of the first couch would hand it to the one reclining in the second place on the second couch, and in this manner, it would go through everyone. This is roughly what Plutarch says.

### The Lament of Admetus.
<margin>XXII</margin>

**The song of Admetus** <note>original Greek: Ἀδμήτου μέλος</note>, that is, the **Lament of Admetus**. This refers to a sad and mournful song. It can be applied to a complaining and miserable speech. It is understood as a type of song called a <term>skolion</term> <note>a "crooked" song sung at dinner parties</note>, about which Julius Pollux wrote much. It was called "oblique" either because of the shapes of the flutes, or because in banquets, as we just said, the turn of singing moved in an oblique order from couch to couch. Some understand these songs to be easy and effortless: certainly the kind that ought to be sung over drinks and on the spur of the moment. But regarding these, as was mentioned in the previous proverb, anyone who wishes to be more thoroughly taught should read the commentator on Aristophanes, in the place we will soon indicate.

They relate this adage to the following fable: **Admetus** was the king of the Pheraeans, whose herds **Apollo** is imagined to have pastured, hired for wages, when he was expelled from Olympus and lived as an exile among mortals in human form. They give this reason for his exile: **Aesculapius**, the son of Apollo, had thoroughly learned the medical art from his teacher Chiron. Then, having received from Pallas Athena the blood that had flowed from the veins of the **Gorgon**, he restored many to health through it. Furthermore, the blood that flowed from the left veins he used for the destruction of men, but that from the right, for their salvation. Indeed, it is common in fables that he even recalled some who had died back to life. Therefore, lest he be held as a god among mortals—since he seemed to provide what is proper to the gods—**Jupiter** struck him with a lightning bolt. Indignant at this, Apollo killed the **Cyclopes** who had manufactured that lightning for Jove. Taking this matter poorly, Jupiter intended to cast Apollo headlong from heaven to the underworld, but the intervention and prayers of **Latona** <note>Apollo's mother</note> obtained a milder punishment. Thus, he was forbidden from heaven and ordered to "turn his soil" <note>go into exile</note>, condemned to serve a mortal man for a year for wages.

Therefore, having set out to Admetus, Apollo pastured the king's herds, as has been said; and as he was a craftsman, he brought it about that all the cows gave birth to twins. And since he was treated very humanely by Admetus, to return the favor of duty to his patron, he obtained from the **Fates** <note>the Parcae</note> that when the fatal days of Admetus were wound on their spindles, he might escape death on this condition: if he could find someone else who was willing to die in his place, and redeem his life at the cost of their own head. Therefore, when that fatal day arrived, and no one was found who wanted to be a substitute for death—even his father and mother refusing—only **Alcestis**, his wife, held her husband's life dearer than her own. When she died, certain shrill and mournful laments were sung continuously at Admetus's house, until **Proserpina**, being moved by pity, sent Alcestis back. Or, as some say, until **Hercules**, having conquered the Underworld, brought her back to the world above. Euripides also mentions the "song of the child" in *Alcestis*:

-> "And it was possible to hear double songs." <- 
<note>original Greek: Διοσά δ' ἐπ' ἰῶ μέλει κλύαν</note>

<margin>Aristophanes also notes this in The Wasps,</margin>
"Taking Cleon by the right hand, he sings the word of Admetus: 'Learn, my friend, to love the good.' What 'crooked song' will you say to this?"
<note>original Greek: Ἄιδει Κλέωνος λαβόμενος τῆς δεξιᾶς / Ἀδμήτου λόγον, ὦ 'ταῖρε μαθὼν, τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς φίλει. / Τούτῳ τί λέξεις σκολιόν;</note>

<margin>He mixes anapests with iambics.</margin>
The commentator cites these verses from the play *The Storks*:
"And he indeed sang the strains of Admetus to the myrtle, but the other forced him to sing the song of Harmodius."
<note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν ᾖδεν Ἀδμήτου λόγον πρὸς μυρρίνην, / ὁ δ' αὐτὸν ἠνάγκαζεν Ἁρμοδίου μέλος.</note>
He gathers certain other things not unworthy of knowing, which may be sought from that source.

# SECOND CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY

### A war by no means tearful.
<margin>XXIII</margin>
**A tearless war** <note>original Greek: Ἄδακρυς πόλεμος</note>, that is, a war lacking tears, where victory is achieved without slaughter and blood. Alternatively, it is used when someone extricates themselves from a dangerous business in such a way that they depart without any harm to themselves; or when quarrelsome people fight with words, and there is no danger of coming to blows. It can also apply where a contest is conducted in such a way that no inconvenience happens to either party, such as in a literary dispute, in which the defeated departs more learned, and the victor more friendly. They say this arose from a certain ancient oracle of Dodona, in which a response was given to the Spartans when they were about to fight against the Arcadians: **there will be a tearless war** <note>original Greek: ἄδακρυν πόλεμον ἔσεσθαι</note>. Afterward, victory fell to them with absolutely no one killed. We likewise call it a **bloodless victory** <note>original Latin: incruentam victoriam</note>, when victory is achieved with no slaughter; and among the Greeks, **to conquer without blood** <note>original Greek: ἀναιμωτὶ νικᾶν</note>. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Fortune of the Romans*, calls the victory that Paulus Aemilius won over Perses a **tearless victory** <note>original Greek: ἄδακρυν νικὴν</note>. The proverb is also uttered in this manner: **he set up a bloodless trophy** <note>original Greek: ἀναίματον ἔστησε τρόπαιον</note>. Among the oracles of Pittacus <note>one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>, this one is also celebrated: **victories ought to be made without blood** <note>original Greek: δεῖν τὰς νίκας ἄνευ αἵματος ποιεῖσθαι</note>. The author is Laertius. Nor is that which I find in the Greek commentaries inconsistent with this: **a war has been stirred up in Greece truly without iron** <note>original Greek: πόλεμος ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀνὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κεκίνηται</note>, that is, a certain war moved without the sword. This signifies a war that is carried out with speech, not arms. For that alone is worthy of wise men. Otherwise, to clash with iron belongs to wild beasts and gladiators, whom I place below the category of wild beasts. And yet, no one would believe it, if we did not see it with our own eyes, how much this method of warring pleases Christian princes. They fight with machines <note>referring to early artillery and cannons</note>, such as no ferocity of the pagans or any barbarity ever devised. Indeed, there is a people among the Germans <note>likely a reference to the Landsknecht mercenaries</note> whose chief glory is this: that they have butchered the most mortals with the sword. While this is monstrous in itself, it is even more foul that they do this as hired mercenaries, like some butcher bought for the slaughterhouse. These sayings will be all the more proverbial if they are applied further: for example, to a legal lawsuit, a contention, or any other contest of that kind.

### The defeated weeps, the victor has perished.
<margin>XXIIII</margin>
->**The one who was conquered weeps; the one who conquered has perished.** <note>original Greek: κλαίει ὁ νικηθείς, ὁ δὲ νικήσας ἀπόλωλεν.</note><-
->**He who won, died; they who succumbed, lament.**<-
This is used whenever both sides depart with great harm to themselves, as usually happens in wars. It is the same in legal lawsuits and in contentions. For Hesiod makes two types of <term>Eris</term> <note>the goddess of Strife</note>, one of which is pestilential to mortals, and the other fruitful. In the former kind of contest, the one who wins departs more wicked, and the defeated is more unhappy. In the latter, the one who emerges superior departs more illustrious, and the one who is defeated departs better than he was. They record that this adage was born from a prophecy of the Erythraean Sibyl, which she gave concerning the battle fought at Chaeronea. For there the Athenians and Thebans were defeated and perished; Philip, the victor, was immediately taken off by Pausanias <note>Philip II of Macedon was assassinated shortly after his victory</note>. Georgius Gemistus mentions this in his *Hellenica*. Yet the same thing once happened to the Trojans and Greeks, after that most insane war waged for so many years over a poor little woman <note>Helen of Troy</note>. For Troy was utterly overturned, and the Greek victors either perished on the way back or found destruction at home.

### Faint-hearted men never set up a trophy.
<margin>XXV</margin>
->**For faint-hearted men have never**<-
->**Set up a trophy.** <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐ γὰρ ἀθυμοῦντες ἄνδρες, πώποτε Τρόπαιον ἐστήσαντο.</note><-
Suidas cites this from Eupolis. It is used by Plato in the *Critias*: **But indeed, faint-hearted men have never yet set up a trophy.** It will be aptly said against those who, through sluggishness and inertia of mind, dare to attempt nothing remarkable, nothing difficult; or who, through fear of danger, abstain from great affairs, since distinguished glory only falls to those in great dangers. Nor has anyone celebrated a triumph who did not dare to test the outcome of Mars <note>a metaphor for the risks of war</note>. There is something similar in that Hebrew Preacher <note>the author of Ecclesiastes</note>: he who observes the wind too superstitiously does not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap. **He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who looks at the clouds will not reap.** He also brings forward that saying against the timid from Sophocles: **For everything makes a noise to the fearful man.**

### Together with the bundles themselves.
<margin>XXVI</margin>
**Together with the bundles themselves** <note>original Greek: Αὐταῖς ἀμάλλαις</note>, that is, with the sheaves themselves. When everything perishes fundamentally, that is, when...

<margin>XXVII</margin>
->You have not even thumbed through Aesop.<-
<note>original Greek: Οὐδὲ τὸν Αἴσωπον πεπάτηκας</note>. That is, "You have not even worn out Aesop." This is said of those who are exceedingly stupid and unlearned. It is recorded by Suidas. It also appears in Aristophanes' play *The Birds*:
"For you said you were unlearned, and not at all a meddler,
Nor have you even thumbed through Aesop."
<note>Erasmus translates the Greek verse into Latin; here rendered into English</note>.
For in ancient times, even the common crowd of uneducated people knew the fables of Aesop. Therefore, anyone who had not read them was seen as knowing nothing at all. Aesop was Phrygian by birth and a slave to Xanthus, but was set free by Idmon the Blind. Plato the comic playwright imagines him coming back to life. From him, all fables in which brute animals are introduced are called "Aesopic" <note>original: αἰσωπικοὶ</note>; just as those in which humans are the characters are called "Sybaritic" or, in the diminutive, "Sybaritide."

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
->The fox drives the ox.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀλώπηξ τὸν βοῦν ἐλαύνει</note>. That is, "The fox leads the ox." Used when a matter is handled absurdly (for a fox has nothing to do with farming), such as if a poet were to preach on sacred matters, or a pimp were to manage the republic. It may also be twisted to apply to one who, not from the heart but looking elsewhere, pretends he wants to do something. This also appears in Suidas.

<margin>XXIX</margin>
->There is no remedy against the bite of a slanderer.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἔνεστι συκοφάντου δήγματος</note>. That is, "Against the strike of a slanderer, there is no [remedy]." One must understand the word "medicine" or "remedy" <note>original Greek: φαρμάκου</note>. This was said regarding calumny <note>slander</note>, the bite of which is not only most destructive but even unavoidable, because it is usually done in secret. In ancient times, it was believed that certain remedies existed in rings, such as against the bites of serpents, or some disease, or the "evil eye" <note>fascinationem</note>. It is found in Aristophanes' *Plutus*, where someone boasts of a magic ring that contains a remedy against every kind of evil, and the reply is: "But there is no remedy for the bite of a slanderer." Aristophanes <note>referring to another work or a contemporary</note> seems to have imitated this in Athenaeus, Book 3:
"But if indeed / my belly or navel should twist me, / I have a ring [bought] for a drachma / from Phertatus."
<note>Phertatus was likely a well-known maker of cheap charms</note>.

<margin>XXX</margin>
->More ignorant than Philonides.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀπαιδευτότερος Φιλωνίδου</note>. That is, "More unlearned than Philonides." This man was from Melite and had a very large body, but was otherwise dull and unlearned. He is noted several times in Aristophanes as being obsessed with women and wasteful on parasites <note>hangers-on who traded flattery for food</note>.

<margin>XXXI</margin>
->Away with a guest during a storm.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἄπαγε ξένον ἐν χειμῶνι</note>. That is, "Drive away a guest in a storm." This was usually said when someone arrived at an inconvenient time. For guests bring trouble if they arrive while one is in the midst of adversity and affliction; at such times, it is more fitting for family members to be present, as they are the soothers of grief. If strangers arrive, shame is added to the distress of the calamity—and shame is sometimes the greatest part of one's troubles. This will be rightly applied whenever something is requested from a prince who is occupied with unhappy business. The same adage warns that no outsider should mix themselves into the domestic troubles of others. Euripides said something similar in *Alcestis*:
"Did I not then rightly feel / A hateful guest, who arrives in the midst of misfortunes?"
<note>original Greek: Ἄρα γὰρ ἔγνωμ' Στυγνῶς δικαίως, ἐν κακοῖς ἀφιγμένος;</note>.
These are the words of a servant to Hercules when he arrives while the house of Admetus is already occupied by mourning. Again, in the same play:
"A guest is a burden to those in sorrow if he should arrive."

<margin>XXXII</margin>
->To gnaw tooth with tooth.<-
One is said to "gnaw tooth with tooth" who carps at someone who can neither be hurt nor even feel it; or who bites... <meta>catchword: bites</meta>

...bites, being himself endowed with an equal bitingness. Martial, in his thirteenth book of epigrams, writes against a certain detractor:
"What will it profit you to gnaw tooth with tooth?
You have need of meat, if you wish to be full."
<note>original Latin: "Quid dente dente iuuabit / Rodere? carne opus est, si satur esse uelis."</note>
This is similar to the saying: "Do not beat a stone."

### To swear by Jove the stone. XXXIII

Those who swear an oath most holily and religiously are said to **swear by Jove the stone**. Marcus Tullius Cicero writes in the seventh book of his *Letters to Friends* to Trebatius: "How will it please you to swear by Jove the stone, when you know that Jove cannot be angry with anyone?" This expression is taken from the ancient ritual of striking a treaty, which was performed by the *pater patratus* <term>pater patratus: the chief official of the Fetial priests, responsible for the ritual declarations of treaties or war</term> holding a stone in his hand and speaking prescribed words. This is described by Titus Livius and Macrobius. The Arabs also used a stone when striking treaties, as Herodotus reports in his third book. 

The adage can be used in various ways: "I would not hesitate to swear to you concerning this matter, even by **Jove the stone**"—that is, as sacredly as possible. Or: "I would rather have faith in this man unsworn than in you swearing by **Jove the stone**, as they say." Or: "He swore by **Jove the stone** that nothing of the sort had been intended"—that is, he asserted it with great emphasis. 

Aulus Gellius, in his *Attic Nights*, used it in this manner: "I am ready to swear," he said, "by Jove the stone—which is considered the most sacred oath—that Virgil never wrote this." Apuleius, in his discourse *On the God of Socrates*, says: "What then shall I swear by? By Jove the stone, according to the most ancient Roman rite?" 

I certainly think it relevant to mention what is cited from Augustine in the *Decrees* <note>The Decretum Gratiani, a collection of canon law</note>: that those are held guilty of perjury who have sworn by a stone and then failed to perform what they swore. Even if it is written there as "Upon the stone" <note>original Latin: "Super lapidem"</note>, this is, if I am not mistaken, a corruption by a scribe. However, it indicates there that this oath is sacred to the one to whom the oath is made; that is, if a Christian swears to a pagan, for whom this oath was most sacred. 

What is the point of repeating here what the glossary-writers and the theologians who followed them have invented about this stone? Their ideas are so absurd that stones themselves would scarcely say such things. It is enough for me to have pointed this out; let him who wishes read them. 

The ancients used to swear by the head of someone they held most dear; the Romans swore by the *genius* <term>genius: the guardian spirit or divine spark of an individual</term> of the emperor; Socrates swore by the dog and the goose; Zeno of Citium swore by the caper-bush; and many swore by the cabbage—"by the cabbages!" <note>original Greek: νὰ μὰ τὰς κράμβας</note> (as Athenaeus teaches in his ninth book, citing many examples from ancient poems), because a certain divining power was said to reside in the cabbage, and for that reason it was held sacred.

### Cimmerian darkness. XXXIIII

People call a state of great obscurity or a fog of the mind **Cimmerian darkness**. Lactantius, in the fourth book of his *Divine Institutes*, writes: "O blind heart! O mind blacker than the (as they say) Cimmerian darkness!" And Saint Jerome, as if emulating him—for he was an admirer of Lactantius's eloquence—says: "I ask, what is this great blindness, enveloped in Cimmerian darkness, as the saying goes?" 

The adage arises from the prodigious gloom of the Cimmerian region. Regarding this, Strabo writes in the first book of his *Geography* in this manner: "And indeed the Cimmerian Bosporus knows them, knowing the Cimmerians, knowing the whole region by the proper name of the Cimmerians, though being ignorant of those who, at that time or shortly before, overran the whole land from the Bosporus as far as Ionia. For the climate of their country is gloomy, as he says: 'The shining sun never beams upon them, but deadly night is spread over them.'" <note>Erasmus provides a Latin translation of Strabo's Greek, which includes a quote from Homer</note>. 

That is to say: He indeed knew the Cimmerian Bosporus, since he was not ignorant of the Cimmerians. For clearly, since he knew the name of the Cimmerians, he was not ignorant of the people themselves who, in his time or a little before his age, ran through the whole land from the Bosporus to Ionia. Therefore, he implies in what climate their region is situated when he makes it dark and—to use his own words—covered in shadows and mists, since the fiery Phoebus <note>The sun</note> never shines upon them, but black night falls upon them continually. 

Furthermore, the passage that Strabo cited (though differing by a few words from the poet) is found in the eleventh book of Homer's *Odyssey*:
"And he reached the boundaries of the deep-flowing Ocean.
There is the land and city of the Cimmerian men,
Covered in mist and cloud; nor does the
Shining sun ever look upon them with his rays,
Neither when he climbs toward the starry heaven,
Nor when he turns back from heaven toward the earth,
But deadly night is spread over wretched mortals."
<note>original Greek: Ἠδ’ ἐς πείραθ’ ἵκανε βαθυῤῥόου ὠκεανοῖο... etc.</note>
Which is to say:

> But he reached the furthest bounds of the deep Ocean.
> There are the people and the walled cities of the Cimmerians,
> Constantly covered by clouds and blind darkness.
> The burning sun never looks upon them with its rays,
> Not when it seeks the high, star-bearing pole in its chariot,
> Nor when it sinks back toward the lands from the great sky,
> But a black night hangs over these miserable mortals.
<note>original Latin: "Ast ille Oceani peruenit summa profundi... Sed nox incumbit miseris mortalibus atra." This is a translation of Homer’s *Odyssey* (Book 11) into Latin hexameters, describing the legendary land of darkness.</note>

Marcus Tullius Cicero also mentions the Cimmerians in the fourth book of his *Academic Questions*. He writes: "And to the Cimmerians indeed—to whom either some god, or nature, or the location of the place they inhabited, had denied the sight of the sun—fires were nevertheless available, the light of which they were permitted to use. But those people whom you approve of..." and so on. In this same region, the poet Ovid <note>referred to here as "Naso"</note> built the palace for the god of Sleep in the eleventh book of his *Metamorphoses*:

> Near the Cimmerians is a cave with a long recess,
> A hollow mountain, the home and inner shrine of sluggish Sleep,
> Where the rising, mid-day, or setting sun
> Can never reach with its rays: mists mixed with darkness
> Are exhaled from the ground, and twilights of uncertain light.

Among the Greeks, I find it constantly written with a diphthong: although the etymology offered by Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and commentator on Homer</note> disagrees, as he claims they were called <term>κιμμερίους</term> <note>Kimmerious</note> as if they were those "remaining in the mist" <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ ἀέρι μεμένους</note>. But it is actually more likely they were called <term>κιμμερίους</term> as if they were "wintery" <note>original Greek: χειμερίους</note>, even though in this case the "m" would be single.

### In vain against Hercules.
### XXXV

<term>Εἰκῇ τῷ ἡρακλεῖ</term> <note>Eikē tō hēraklei</note>. **In vain against Hercules**; one should understand: "you would attempt to build a slander." This was commonly said of those who conduct all their business in such a way that no one is able or dares to slander them. For it was the custom of Hercules to take away the property of others by force, not by deceit. It will be suitable to use this either for someone who is intensely praised and proven, or for someone very powerful whom it is not safe to accuse. Marcus Cato the Censor is remembered to have been called to court more than forty times, and was always acquitted by the judges' votes. Regarding this, Julius Caesar, in his *Anticatones* <note>a lost polemic written by Caesar against the character of Cato the Younger</note>, accused him of greed. Plutarch writes that this is exactly as if someone were to accuse Hercules of cowardice. For nothing fits Hercules less than this specific crime. There are some who think it applies when someone does everything with impunity and is never accused by anyone—just as Hercules was accustomed to driving off others' property without punishment.

---

### Lest it break out into the bowstring.
### XXXVI

Terence says in his play *Phormio*: "But I often fear this, Phormio, lest that bravery of yours finally **break out into the bowstring**." This applies to rash and inconsiderate audacity, which is often unfortunate and sometimes leads to a very great evil. The commentator Donatus thinks the metaphor is taken from archers, who, while they pull the bowstring excessively, sometimes break it, and not without danger to themselves.

---

### Old age itself is a disease.
### XXXVII

Terence says in *Phormio*: **Old age itself is a disease**. This seems to be spoken as a proverbial figure. For in the elderly, even if a specific sickness is absent, old age itself is a state of ill health. Hence that frequent phrase in Homer, <term>χαλεπὸν γῆρας</term> <note>chalepon gēras</note>, that is, "Troublesome old age." In the eighth book of the *Iliad*:
"Your strength is dissolved, and bitter old age pursues you." <note>original Greek: Σὴ δὲ βίη λέλυται, χαλεπὸν δέ τε γῆρας ὀπάζει</note>
And in Virgil:
"Diseases and sad old age come upon us."
Horace writes in the *Art of Poetry*:
"The coming years bring many advantages with them,
The receding years take many away."
Juvenal says:
"A whole troop of every kind of disease
Leaps around him."
I have also written in my poem *On the Disadvantages of Old Age*:
"Furthermore, foul Old Age is a massive disease
Which can be hindered by no help, nor driven off by medicines,
But rather, having suddenly arisen,
It drinks up the juices of the body, <margin>Dulls.</margin> and the vigor of the mind."
That proverbial six-foot line <note>an iambic senarius</note> testifies to the same:
"Fear old age, for it does not come alone." <note>original Greek: φόβου τὸ γῆρας, οὐ γὰρ ἔρχεται μόνον</note>
Likewise,

CHILIAD II. CENTURY VI.

Old age is a heavy burden for mankind. -> that is, <-
Old age is an exceedingly heavy load for mortals. -> Cited from Antiphanes, <-
Our life is very much like wine: -> that is, <-
When only a little remains, it turns to vinegar.
Our life is most similar to wine:
Where but a little stays, it turns to vinegar. -> Also from the same author, <-
Old age is like an altar of evils, -> that is, <-
One can see everything having fled to this for refuge.
Old age is a kind of altar for all evils,
So much so that one can see all things running back to it. -> Again from the same author, <-
For toward old age, as if to a workshop, -> that is, <-
All human evils come frequently.
To wretched old age, as if to some workshop,
The universal evils of mortals flow together.

The old woman in Plautus alluded to this when, excusing her slow pace, she says she carries a heavy weight. "So great," she says, "is this burden which I carry." "What burden?" "Seventy-four years." <note>This is a reference to the play *Mercator* by Plautus, where an old slave woman complains of her age.</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero says in *On Old Age* <note>original Latin: *Cato Maior de Senectute*</note>: "Which to most old men is so hateful that they say they are sustaining a burden heavier than Mount Etna." Aristotle, in the fifth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, calls old age a <term>natural disease</term> <note>original Greek: νόσον φυσικήν (noson physikēn)</note>, just as a disease is an "accidental old age," because some diseases produce the same effects in a person as old age, and old age generates things similar to diseases. Seneca calls it an "incurable disease." Donatus ascribes the words of Apollodorus from a Greek comedy: "Old age is itself a disease."

### Adrastia Nemesis. Rhamnusia Nemesis. XXXVIII

<margin>Adrastia the avenger.</margin> Adrastia Nemesis. This means: Adrastia Nemesis is present, or will be present, or something of that sort. It may be used against those whom we threaten with a change of fortune because of their insolence and arrogance, or those who have been reduced from a flourishing state to a calamitous fortune. They believe this Nemesis to be a goddess, the punisher of insolence and arrogance, who both forbids and punishes immoderate hopes. <term>Adrastia</term> <note>A name for Nemesis</note> is said to be derived <term>from the fact that no one runs away</term> <note>original Greek: apo tou apodidraskein mēdena</note>, because no guilty person ever escapes deserved punishment, even if it sometimes catches up later. Lucian says in the *Dialogues of the Courtesans*: "There is a certain goddess Adrastia, and she sees such things." Euripides in *Rhesus*:
> Adrastia, who is the daughter of Zeus,
> [Ward off] the envy of deeds of the body. -> that is, <-

Adrastia, daughter of Jove, may you ward off the envy of my words. **The same author in the same play writes:**
> I say this to you with Adrastia's [favor]. -> that is, <-

Truly, I would say this with Adrastia willing. **The Epigrams also testify to the same thing:**
> Nemesis [measures] with the cubit and the bridle, -> that is, <-
> Neither to do anything beyond measure, nor to speak unbridled words.
Nemesis hints at this by the cubit and the bridle she carries:
Let there be a limit in all things, and let words have a bridle. -> Also another: <-
> I announce to all: nothing beyond the measure. -> that is, <-
I, Nemesis, hold the cubit. You ask the cause?
For I command that a limit be present in all things.
<note>The "cubit" refers to a measuring rod, symbolizing proportion and the limits humans must not exceed.</note>

Strabo, in the thirteenth book of his *Geography*, records that she was called Adrastia not from "escaping," but from King Adrastus, who first established a temple for her; he confirms this with the verses of the poet Antimachus:
> There is a certain great goddess Nemesis, who all these things
> Has obtained by the lot of the blessed ones. But for her first an altar
> Adrastus raised, near the flow of the river Aesepus.
> And there she is both honored and called Adrastia. -> that is, <-
There is a certain great goddess Nemesis, to whom all these things
Are given by the lot of the gods. But to her Adrastus first built an altar
Near the sacred streams of the Aesepus.
And there she is both worshipped and holds the name Adrastia.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

Pliny mentions this town <note>The town of Parion, associated with the cult of Adrastia.</note> in book five, chapter thirty-two, with these words: "The colony of Parion, which Homer called Adrastia." Plato also mentions the goddess Adrastia in the *Phaedrus*. Ammianus, in book fourteen, says: "These and countless things of this kind are sometimes worked by Adrastia—the avenger of wicked deeds and the rewarder of good ones <note>original Latin: *ultrix facinorum impiorum, bonorumque praemiatrix*</note>—and would that she always were: whom by a double name we also call Nemesis. They say, according to the opinion of the ancient theologians, that she is placed above the moon and presides over the fates with general power, looking down on all earthly things as the queen and judge of all matters. She is especially hostile to pride; at one moment she crushes and weakens the haughty necks of the mind, and at another, raising the good from the depths, she exalts them to live well. Antiquity added wings to her as a symbol of speed; it gave her a rudder and a wheel, signifying that she runs through all things and governs each one." The same author says in book twenty-two: "Therefore Adrastia, the observer of human affairs, pulling his ear—as the saying goes <note>original Latin: *aurem, quod dicitur, uellens*</note>—and warning him to live more moderately," etc. Zenodotus traces the origin of the adage to a myth of this kind, which I will record, though not very willingly, lest I seem to cheat the eager reader. 

Eteocles and Polynices, after the death of their father Oedipus, agreed to a law regarding the kingdom of the Thebans: that they should manage the empire in alternate years. But Eteocles—for by chance the first year had fallen to him—refused to hand over the turns of the kingdom to his brother when the time had expired. Therefore, Polynices, having been rejected, fled to the territory of Adrastus at Argos, and arrived by night. Here, when he happened to have met Tydeus, who had fled from Calydon on account of a murder committed, he joined battle with him. A clamor and tumult having arisen between them, Adrastus intervened and separated the combatants. And there, remembering at once a certain oracle by which he had been warned to join his daughters in marriage to a boar and a lion, he took both as his sons-in-law. For one had the figure of a boar on his shield, the other a lion. And he promised to restore both to their homeland. And as soon as he had attacked Thebes in the name of Polynices, with the best of the Argives slain, Adrastus alone escaped. When the Thebans threw away the corpses of the slain unburied and did not deem them worthy of burial, the children of the slain, fleeing to the altar of Mercy, demanded the corpses of their parents. When the Athenians moved their army, the Thebans returned the bodies. At which time Evadne, the wife of Capaneus, throwing herself onto the pyre, was burned along with her husband's corpse. After that time, the sons of the Argives who had perished at Thebes never won any victory achieved under their own auspices, but served as mercenaries for foreigners. 

Diogenianus records the proverb in this manner: <term>Nemesis comes at the feet</term> <note>original Greek: ἡ νέμεσις παρὰ πόδας βαίνει (hē nemesis para podas bainei)</note>. That is, Nemesis is present at one's feet. Finally, Galen in the sixth book of *On the Use of the Parts of the Human Body*: <term>to remember and declare that the law of Adrastia is something no one escapes</term> <note>original Greek: μνημονεύσαι ὡς ἄξιας τὴν ἀδραστίας ὡς ὀδῶς ἐκφεύξαται ἔδυνμόν</note>. That is, to remember and declare that no one will escape the law of Adrastia. And a little further down: <term>I think you do not know the decree of Adrastia</term> <note>original Greek: οὐκ γινώσκας οἶμαι τὴν τὴ ἀδραστίας θεσμόν</note>. That is, not thinking, I suppose, of the law of Adrastia. He threatens physicians who teach false things as true. She is also called Rhamnusia, named after Rhamnus, a place in Attica, where, as Zenodotus shows, a statue was established for this goddess made of a single stone, ten cubits in size, the work of Phidias. She was formerly fashioned in the likeness of Venus, for which reason she also held an apple tree in her right hand, as Eudemus is the author. Although Zenodotus separated this adage, it seemed to me best to join it with the previous one, since there is no difference except for the change in the name. Pliny in book twenty-eight, chapter two: "Why do we also meet fascinations with a peculiar adoration? Some invoking the Greek Nemesis, whose statue for that reason is in the Capitol at Rome, although there is no Latin name for it."

<margin>XXXIX</margin>
-> Shaking laughter. <-

<term>Shaking laughter</term> <note>original Greek: Γέλως συγκρούσιος (Gelōs synkrousios)</note>. The Greeks call a more unrestrained laughter "shaking," because it shakes the person; some think this is the same as the "Sardonic" laugh. They think, and think rightly, that this laughter is greatly unbecoming to a grave man, because it seems to proceed from an unrestrained mind. Indeed, just as it is shameful for a grave man to wail in the manner of a woman if he suffers anything, so it is little becoming to be poured out into a loud laugh by immoderate joy. With a similar figure, Philostratus in the *Sophists* several times said, <term>to laugh broadly</term> <note>original Greek: πλατὺ γελᾶν (platy gelān)</note>, that is, to laugh with the mouth wide and gaping.

<margin>XL</margin>
-> Do not seek again the rose that has passed. <-

<term>Do not seek again the rose once it has passed</term> <note>original Greek: Ῥόδον παρελθὼν μηκέτι ζητεῖ πάλιν (Rhodon parelthōn mēketi zētei palin)</note>. That is,
> Do not seek again the rose once it has passed.

Do not torture yourself with the desire for things which cannot be recalled and restored, such as past youth, for...

# THE SECOND THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY

...of beauty, of strength, and of fortune. For just as nothing is more pleasing than a rose, so nothing is less lasting. In the same vein, Horace said in his *Odes*:

> Cease to seek out the place where the late rose
> lingers. <note>Horace, Odes 1.38.3–4. The poet suggests that simple decorations are better than chasing out-of-season luxuries.</note>

For roses have their season, but it is very brief. Yet those who are exquisitely refined seek the rose even at an unseasonable time. Hence, the saying will also apply to those who seek <term>ἔξωροι</term> <note>Greek: *exōroi*, meaning "out of season" or "past their prime."</note> pleasures: as if an old man were to play at ropes <note>A reference to youthful or acrobatic games.</note>, or an old man were to fall in love or act the lecher.

### You are comparing a rose to an anemone. XLI

<margin>You compare a rose to an anemone. <note>original Greek: Ῥόδον ἀνεμώνῃ συγκρίνεις.</note></margin>
That is, "You compare a rose to an anemone," used when someone compares things that are vastly unequal. The rose was held in high price by the ancients. The anemone is a type of poppy, the flower of which indeed imitates the rose in appearance, but has no grace of scent. It grows everywhere in the fields, whereas of old the highest honor was accorded to the rose.

### To speak roses. XLII

<margin>You have spoken roses to me. <note>original Greek: Ῥόδα μ’ εἴρηκας.</note></margin>
That is, "You have spoken roses to me," meaning words that are most welcome and as lovely as roses. Suidas cites this from Aristophanes, in whose work it appears in *The Clouds*. So too Plautus in the *Poenulus*: "By Hercules, I pray, how many things he speaks!" Akin to this is that line from Persius:

> Now from that tomb, now from those blessed remains, 
> shall violets not spring? <note>Persius, Satire 1.39–40. A metaphor for a poet's legacy.</note>

And again:

> Whatever he treads upon, let it become a rose.

The opposite of this is that phrase from Plautus’s *Aulularia*: "You are speaking stones," <note>original Latin: *Lapides loqueris*.</note> because those words were spoken as if to knock out one's brains.

### A Rhodian sacrifice. XLIII

<margin>The sacrifice of the Rhodians. <note>original Greek: Ῥοδίων τὴν θυσίαν.</note></margin>
That is, "The sacrifice of the Rhodians," used when a matter is carried out with quarreling and ill-omened words. It is recorded by Diogenianus. It is the same as what we related a little earlier: "The sacrifice of the Lindians." For Lindus is a city in Rhodes, according to Stephanus, from which it might seem that London among the Britons was derived, a city which Stephanus calls *Lindonium*, citing Martianus as the author. Indeed, both are islands, Rhodes and Britain. Furthermore, the ancient language of that nation, which is now called Welsh <note>original Latin: *Vualica*. Erasmus is reflecting a common 16th-century belief that the Welsh language had Greek origins.</note>, indicates clearly enough that it either originated from the Greeks or was certainly mixed with them. Not even their customs differ very much from the Greek ones.

### The oracle of the Rhodians. XLIIII

<margin>The oracle of the Rhodians. <note>original Greek: Ῥοδίων χρησμός.</note></margin>
That is, "The oracle of the Rhodians." Used when someone inquires too frequently and too diligently about a trivial matter. For the Rhodians, when sacrificing to Lindian Minerva, would prolong their banquets at the altar of the goddess for several days and remain there continually. Since it was not their custom to bring a chamber pot <note>original Latin: *matula*.</note> into the sacrifice, and they had consulted the god on this matter, and he had answered that they should bring one in, they began to doubt again whether they should bring a bronze one or one made of clay. When they approached the oracle yet again about this, the god, being indignant, replied: "Neither." It is recorded by Diogenianus.

### Do not despise a rustic orator. XLV

<margin>Do not despise a rustic orator. <note>original Greek: Ἀγροίκου μὴ καταφρόνει ῥήτορος.</note></margin>
That is, "Do not despise a rustic rhetorician." The adage warns us not to loathe anyone on account of their lack of skill or poor speech; nor should we look at who is speaking, or in what manner, but rather what is said. Regarding those who are powerful in eloquence, we should not care so much about what they threaten or promise. But as for those who possess rustic truth, if they say anything even in an unpolished way, it will by no means be right to ignore it. For people of this sort usually achieve more than they say. The author is Diogenianus.

### The city is the countryside. XLVI

<margin>The city is the countryside. <note>original Greek: Ἀγρὸς ἡ πόλις.</note></margin>
That is, "The city is the countryside." Used when someone in the city, having ignored the laws, conducts business by force and according to their own whim. For in cities, people live equally under laws, while in the countryside, life is conducted more licentiously. Epicharmus in Diogenianus says: "You are making the city into the countryside." It will also apply to a city in which not much respect is held for the laws. Seneca alluded to this in the satirical book he wrote against the Emperor Claudius: "You have made the place into mere huts; I want the discipline of the old Senate-house." <note>A reference to Seneca's *Apocolocyntosis*, a satire on the deification of Claudius. "Mapalia" refers to nomadic huts.</note>

### Chickpea Bacchus. XLVII

<margin>Chickpea Bacchus. <note>original Greek: Ἐρεβίνθιος Διόνυσος.</note></margin>
That is, "Chickpea Bacchus." Said of a thing that is vehemently despised. The adage is taken from a drink made from legumes, which imitates wine. Moreover, the ancients fashioned wine by various methods, some of which Pliny records in his fourteenth book.

# ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...in the sixteenth chapter. Likewise, in book twenty-two, chapter twenty-five, he mentions the **Zythos** <note>original: "Zytho." An ancient Egyptian beer.</note> of the Egyptians, the **Celia** of the Spaniards, and the **Ceruisia** <note>original: "Ceruisia." The root of the Spanish word "cerveza"; Gallic beer.</note> of the Gauls. This was a type of drink brewed from grain, invented out of a lack of wine in those regions which do not produce grapes. From this, it seems that another adage originated, which I have recorded elsewhere: *nothing to do with Bacchus* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν πρὸς Διόνυσον (*ouden pros Dionysos*). A phrase used when something is off-topic or irrelevant, as Bacchus/Dionysus is the god of wine, not beer.</note>, as someone might say upon tasting beer. Furthermore, an epigram attributed to the Emperor Julian testifies that beer was held in contempt and loathing by those accustomed to wine:

> Who are you? Where do you come from, Dionysus? For by the true Bacchus
> I do not recognize you; I know only the son of Jupiter.
> He smells of nectar, but you of a goat. Did the Celts, 
> in their poverty of grapes, fashion you from stalks of grain?
> Therefore one should call you "Demetrius" <note>A pun on Demeter, goddess of grain, rather than Dionysus, god of wine.</note>, not Dionysus,
> "Wheat-born" rather, and "Bromos" <note>A type of wild oat.</note>, not "Bromius" <note>An epithet for Bacchus, meaning "the noisy one."</note>.

->that is,<-
> Who are you, Bacchus? From where do you come? I swear to you by the true Bacchus,
> I do not know you at all; only the son of Jove is known to me.
> He gives off the scent of nectar, you of a goat. Tell me, 
> did Gaul, lacking vines, fashion you from ears of corn?
> Therefore, I shall not call you Bacchus, but of Ceres,
> And grain-born; nor Bromius, but rather "bromos."

Now, *bromos* is a certain type of barley; but Theophrastus, in the eighth book of *On Plants*, places it among those things which are almost wild and bitter. Pliny considers the greatest use of this kind of drink to be its foam, which nourishes the skin on women's faces. For as far as the drink itself is concerned, he says it is better to move on to the mention of wine. Nor would I object if anyone preferred to refer the proverb to the ritual of Bacchus's mysteries, in which they used to bind imitations of the obscene male member to their heads and thighs, and dance thus in honor of the god. The Greeks call these figures **Phalloi**, from which comes the name "Phallic song" in the works of the grammarian Terentianus. Those who carried them were called *phallophoroi* and *ithyphalloi*. Although Athenaeus indicates in his fourteenth book that the *Ithyphalloi* and *Phallophoroi* were different: the former took on the persona of a drunken man, while the latter performed without a mask, though they differed in other ways as well. Truly, these details have nothing to do with the proverb. Aristophanes alludes to this in *The Acharnians*:

> But you two must hold the phallus upright
> behind the basket-bearer,
> while I, following behind, will sing the phallic song.

->that is,<-
> Indeed, you must hold the phallus straight,
> Following her who carries the basket:
> Behind you, I shall sing the phallic song.

Long ago, this member was fashioned out of fig-wood, which antiquity dedicated to softness; hence Horace also carved his Priapus out of the same wood. Servius thinks that Virgil, in the second book of the *Georgics*, was also thinking of these phalloi when, describing the rites of Bacchus, he mentions hanging "oscilla":
> He hangs soft masks <note>original: "oscilla." Small figures or masks, often of Bacchus, hung from trees to swing in the wind for fertility.</note> from the tall pine.

He writes that these were usually fashioned from flowers in the image of the obscene male member and suspended between columns, so that those who stumbled upon them would be moved to laughter. Hence the epithet of Bacchus "Erebinthos" <note>Literally "chickpea," but used here as a slang reference to anatomy.</note>, whom they also call "Morychus" for a similar reason—namely, because the accessibility of the deity invited contempt.

<margin>XLVIII</margin>
->Do not seek soft things, lest hard things befall you.<-
*Do not seek soft things, lest you have hard things.* <note>original Greek: Μὴ τὰ μαλακὰ μώεο, μὴ τὰ σκληρὰ ἔχῃς (*Me ta malaka moeo, me ta sklera echeis*).</note> That is, do not seek luxuries, lest you endure hardships. It is cited by Phurnutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher.</note> in his work *On the Nature of the Gods*, in the chapter on the Muses, and it is reported as a commonly tossed-about saying. It applies to those who, while they seek what they want too shamelessly or stubbornly, offend those from whom they ask and receive what they do not want. Or to those who, while they chase pleasure beyond measure, fall into trouble.

<margin>XLIX</margin>
->Not even Execestides could find the way.<-
*Not even Execestides would find the straight path.* <note>original Greek: Οὐδ’ Ἐξηκεστίδης ἂν εὕροι τὴν εὐθεῖαν ὁδόν (*Oud' Execestides an euroi ten eutheian hodon*).</note> That is, not even Execestides could find the right way. Said of a perplexed and inexplicable business. A certain Execestides had a bad reputation among the people because...

SECOND THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY
Y
<meta>catchword: then</meta>

...because he was excessive in his travels, so that he might have all roads as well-known as possible. The same man is satirized by Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
"But if he is a slave and a Carian, just like Execestides." <note>original Greek: Εἰ δὲ δοῦλός ἐστι καὶ Κὰρ, ὥσπερ Ἐξηκεστίδης. The Carians were often stereotyped as slaves in Greek comedy.</note> that is,
"But if he is a slave and a Carian, just like Execestides." <note>original Latin: Quod si seruus est & Car, quemadmodum Execestides.</note> Again, at the beginning of the same play:
"By Zeus, not even Execestides himself could find a way out of here," <note>original Greek: Οὐδ’ ἂν μὰ Δία γ’ ἐντεῦθεν Ἐξηκεστίδης.</note> that is,
"Not by Jove would even Execestides find his way from here," <note>original Latin: Non per Iouem hinc uel ipse uiam Execestides.</note>
the word "find" being understood. From this, it began to be said of those who had completely lost their way, or who were distracted by a difficult and inextricable business.

### A Hermonian service.
<margin>50</margin>
*Hermonios charis*. <note>original Greek: Ἑρμώνιος χάρις.</note> That is, "A Hermonian benefit." This is used whenever someone strives to appear to be doing a favor out of a sense of duty, when in fact they are doing it because they are forced to, and not to accommodate anyone else, but because they are not allowed to do otherwise. They trace this proverb back to a story of this kind: A certain Pelasgian people, who inhabited Lemnos, crossed over in ships to Brauron <note>original: Bæbronē, uel... Brauronē.</note>, a region of Attica, and kidnapped women from there and carried them off. Later, when they were suffering from a plague, they were commanded by an oracle to satisfy the Athenians, and so they lived there. Thus, according to Herodotus, the Athenians, when asked how they wished to be appeased, announced that the Pelasgians should depart from Lemnos. When the Pelasgians heard this condition, they jokingly replied that they would do so if someone, setting out from home, crossed over to Lemnos in a single day’s voyage with a North wind. It later happened that while Darius was acting in Thrace and subduing everything on all sides, Miltiades, the general of the Athenians, setting sail from the Chersonese, attacked Lemnos, announcing to the Pelasgians that he was present after a single day's run from home with a North wind—for he held the Chersonese and was living there. Thus, Hermon, the prince of the Pelasgians, yielded Lemnos. And although he did this compelled by fear of Darius, he nevertheless pretended he was yielding willingly to do the Athenians a favor. I found a remark of this kind in the Greek collections. Aemilius Probus <note>Now known as Cornelius Nepos, a Roman biographer.</note>, in his life of Miltiades, tells the story somewhat differently. When the Athenians had decided to send a colony to the Chersonese, which was then held by the Thracians, they consulted Apollo on whom they should take as a leader to expel the Thracians, and he commanded them to enlist Miltiades. He, having attacked Lemnos, demanded that they surrender themselves voluntarily to the Athenians. The Lemnians jokingly replied that they would do so when he, having set out from home by ship, arrived at Lemnos with the North wind. For this wind is adverse to those setting out from Athens for Lemnos. Miltiades, so as not to waste time there, set out for the Chersonese. Once it was captured and things were organized there to his satisfaction, he returned to Lemnos and demanded the island according to the pact. For he had arrived from home with the North wind, since he now had a home in the Chersonese, where he had decided to remain. Thus, those who held Lemnos yielded out of fear. Certainly, Pamphilus, that character of Terence’s <note>A reference to the play *Andria* by the Roman playwright Terence.</note>, says it is not the duty of a free man to demand that a favor be credited to him when he has earned nothing. Yet in the courts of princes, and indeed everywhere in any gathering of mortals, everything is full of these "Hermonian" types, who precisely when they seem to be giving a benefit, are then most of all serving their own interests. Both Suidas and Hesychius mention the proverb.

### You are weaving a rope out of sand.
<margin>51</margin>
*Ex ammou schoinion plekeis*. <note>original Greek: Ἐξ ἄμμου σχοινίον πλέκεις.</note> That is, "You are weaving a rope out of sand." This was said against someone attempting something foolishly and in vain, or when someone labors to connect things that do not hold together at all. It will be aptly said of a speech or a syllogism that is poorly connected. It is related to those sayings: "Sand without lime," <note>A famous criticism of Seneca's style attributed to the Emperor Caligula.</note> and "Loose brooms." Irenaeus used this sentiment in his first book, saying that they do this who collect "Homerocentones." <note>Poems composed of fragments from Homer's works.</note> In short, it will fit any "impossible thing" <term>adynaton</term>, so that it also pertains to that form: "You are washing a brick," and "You are whitening an Ethiopian."

### There are halcyon days at the forum.
<margin>52</margin>
What Plautus said in the *Casina*: "There are halcyons around the forum," bears the appearance of a proverb. By this word, he signifies tranquility and silence. The same author in the *Poenulus*: "Unless you make that matter as tranquil for me as the sea once was, when the halcyon brings forth her young there." This proverb also exists in the Greek commentaries: "You are spending halcyon days." <note>original Greek: ἀλκυονίδας ἡμέρας ἄγει.</note> That is, "You are leading halcyon days," said of those leading a tranquil and idle life. Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
"And he led halcyon days continually." <note>original Greek: ἀλκυονίδας τ’ ἤγεθ’ ἡμέρας ἀεί.</note>
The adage is derived from a certain sea bird, which is called *Halcyon* by the Greeks and *halcedo* by the Latins, as Marcus Varro is the authority in the third book of *On the Latin Language*, lest anyone should corrupt the word used by Plautus...

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to forced favors (the "Hermonian service"), futile endeavors like weaving sand, and the "halcyon days" of peace, using historical anecdotes about Miltiades and classical literature.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of natural history and folklore as the basis for proverbs, specifically concluding the entry on "Halcyon Days" before moving into "Empedocles's Enmity" and the legal and philosophical weight of eyewitness testimony.</meta>

...might think it to be. The story of Ceyx and Halcyone is found in Ovid. <note>The myth tells of a couple turned into kingfishers (Halcyons) by the gods, who then calmed the seas so they could nest.</note> Regarding the bird itself, Pliny reports in book ten, chapter thirty-two: "The Halcyon is slightly larger than a sparrow, its color mostly sea-blue, with some purple and white feathers mixed in, and a slender, long neck. It breeds during the winter solstice, which are called the 'Halcyon days.' They do not appear except when the sea is calm, especially around Sicily. They build their nests seven days before the solstice and lay their eggs in the following seven days. These days are well known to sailors, for they do not fear storms during this time. The bird nests in the middle of the sea; the nests are shaped like a ball, with a slightly protruding and very narrow mouth, resembling large sponges, and are constructed from prickly thorns. They are so hard that they cannot be cut with iron, though they break if struck with force, like dried sea foam." Thus far Pliny. Lucian also testifies to the tranquility of the Halcyon days in the dialogue titled *The Halcyon* <note>original Greek: ἀλκυών</note>. Virgil, among his signs of a coming storm, also mentions this:

> "The Halcyons, beloved by Thetis, do not spread their wings 
> To the warm sun upon the shore." <note>Thetis is a sea goddess; Virgil suggests that when these birds stay on the shore, the calm weather is ending.</note>

Theocritus also mentions them in his seventh *Idyll*:

"And the Halcyons shall smooth the waves, and the sea, 
And the South wind, and the East wind, which stirs the furthest seaweed. 
The Halcyons, whom of all birds that hunt their prey from the sea, 
The green-eyed Nereids <note>Sea nymphs</note> love the most." 

->that is,<-

"And the Halcyons shall level the waves and the deep, and the South wind, 
And the East wind that moves the distant algae with its gusts. 
The Halcyons, the birds that, above all others, the gray-eyed 
Nereids love—those who hunt for their food 
->upon the ocean."<-

<margin>53</margin>
### Empedocles's enmity.

*Empedokleous echthra*. <note>original Greek: Ἐμπεδοκλέους ἔχθρα</note> That is, "Empedocles's enmity." It was said of a persistent and irreconcilable grudge. For they say Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who believed the universe was governed by 'Love' and 'Strife.'</note> was of such a character that he was constantly involved in feuds with various people, and he pursued them most stubbornly. It is also applicable when someone becomes an enemy to a friend over a trivial cause. This is recorded by Diogenianus. Suidas cites these words from Lysias: "I for my part love a friendship so small that even the enmity of Empedocles would not become permanent for us." <note>original Greek: φιλῶ δ’ ἔγωγε τὴν αὐτὴν φιλίαν σμικρὰν, ὥστε μηδ’ ἂν τὴν Ἐμπεδοκλέους ἔχθραν ἔμπεδον ἡμῖν γενέσθαι.</note> That is: "Indeed, I thought we were joined by such a bond of necessity that not even the enmity of Empedocles could stand in our way." This should be compared to what is said elsewhere as "Vatinian hatred" <note>An intense hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius</note> and "Step-motherly hatred."

<margin>54</margin>
### One eyewitness is worth more than ten ear-witnesses.

Plautus says in *The Truculentus*: "One eyewitness is worth more than ten who have only heard." <note>original Latin: Pluris est oculatus testis unus, quàm auriti decem.</note> This means that far greater trust should be placed in those reporting what they have seen with their own eyes than in those who relate what they have heard from others. The poets suggest the same thing when they imagine two gates for dreams in the underworld: one of ivory, through which false dreams come to those above; and the other of horn, through which true dreams pass. Virgil, in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, imitating Homer’s nineteenth book of the *Odyssey*:

> "There are two gates of Sleep, one of which is said to be 
> Of horn, by which an easy exit is given to true shades. 
> The other is finished with the gleaming shine of white ivory, 
> But through this the spirits send false dreams to the heavens. 
> Anchises, having followed his son and the Sibyl there, 
> Sends them out through the ivory gate."

Servius <note>An ancient commentator on Virgil</note> interprets this to mean that the eyes are understood by the gate of horn, because they are of a horn-like color; the teeth are understood by the ivory gate, being bony and white. True shadows exit through the horn gate because those things we perceive with our eyes are certain. False dreams exit through the ivory gate because things perceived through rumor (represented by the mouth and teeth) are often empty. Thus, Aeneas being sent out through the ivory gate signifies that whatever the poet narrated about the underworld should be considered fictional. Apuleius also mentions this adage in the first book of the *Florida*, telling how Socrates inverted the proverb: "One ear-witness is worth more than ten eyewitnesses." For when he had looked upon a handsome youth who had remained silent for a long time, he said: "Speak, so that I may see you." Socrates thus felt that the judgment of the ears was more certain than that of the eyes; for with the eyes we behold nothing but the form of the body, but from speech we discover the character of the mind. Justinian, in the third book of the *Institutes* concerning the degrees of kinship, calls it "Eyewitness faith" <note>original Latin: oculata fides</note> when a matter is subjected to the eyes. From this, they call it a "Blind day" when a contract is not immediately fulfilled, and an "Eyewitness day" when the business is transacted with cash in hand.

<summary>Erasmus concludes the natural history of the 'Halcyon days' before discussing the proverb of 'Empedocles's enmity' and the superiority of direct observation over hearsay.</summary>
<keywords>Halcyon days, Pliny the Elder, Empedocles, eyewitness testimony, Plautus, Gates of Sleep, Socrates, legal terminology</keywords>
