# SECOND THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY
<sig>Y 2</sig>

->Sleep creeps over a hungry fox.<-
<margin>55</margin>
*Peinōsi alōpeki hypnos eperchetai* <note>original Greek: Πεινῶσι ἀλώπεκι ὕπνος ἐπέρχεται</note>, that is: **Sleep creeps over a hungry fox.** This is used when someone sleeps because they have no food. For some of the poor, sleep takes the place of a meal, as evidenced by that verse celebrated as a proverb:
*Hypnos de pauei tēn kakēs achou dama* <note>original Greek: ὕπνος δὲ παύει τὴν κακὴς αχου δαμᾶ; Erasmus interprets this as "Sleep tames hunger, the worst of evils."</note>, which means:
**Sleep conquers hunger, the worst of all evils.**
Moreover, he calls the poor person a "fox" because poverty is clever and the inventor of many arts, according to the saying we mentioned elsewhere: *Penia tēn sophian elache* <note>original Greek: πενία τὴν σοφίαν ἔλαχε</note>, meaning: **Poverty has been allotted wisdom.** Nor would it be wrongly applied to those who feign indifference or "shut their eyes" to certain things so that they might seize an advantage when the occasion arises. Indeed, when pressed by hunger, the fox feigns sleep in order to catch and devour birds that are lured in. This happens by a certain natural logic, as sleep can extinguish hunger and thirst. The adage was recorded by Diogenianus.

->It has reached the ears of the gods.<-
<margin>56</margin>
*Eis theōn ōta ēlthen* <note>original Greek: Εἰς θεῶν ὦτα ἦλθεν</note>, that is: **It has reached the ears of the gods.** This is used when a deed committed in secret is found out by those who have the power to either reward a good act or punish a crime. For the poets imagine that whatever is done on earth, whether right or wrong, is scouted out by Mercury and reported to Jupiter. He then, having called a council of the gods, decides on the punishment. This phrase is still solemnized today in the letters of princes and popes: "It has reached our ears." That Vergilian shepherd uses it somewhat differently:
"And as often as Galatea spoke to us, 
Carry some part of it, O winds, to the ears of the gods." <note>Virgil, *Eclogues*</note>
This refers to remarkable things that you judge worthy of the ears of the gods. Likewise Horace:
"And you keep those things for the ears of Jupiter."

->Egyptians are marvelous at weaving machines.<-
<margin>57</margin>
*Deinoi plekein tas mēchanas Aigyptioi* <note>original Greek: Δεινοὶ πλέκειν τὰς μηχανὰς Αἰγύπτιοι</note>, that is:
**Egyptians weave stupendous machines.**
This was a common saying regarding the crafty and, as Plautus says, those who "stitch together" deceits. It can also be twisted to refer to the tangled subtleties of sophists and the inescapable labyrinths of their syllogisms. Or it can apply to sycophants and informers who weave slanders by mixing truth with falsehoods. Ammianus, in his 14th book, reports that a certain Paulus, who informed against many people using marvelous tricks under Emperor Constantius, was commonly given the nickname "The Chain" <note>original Latin: *cathena*</note> because he wove insoluble knots while complicating his denunciations. In ancient times, the works of the Egyptians were celebrated—items joined together from various pieces of wood with a certain miraculous skill, among which is the "Herculanean knot." This adage is related to the one we mentioned elsewhere, the *Kassiotikon hamma* <note>original Greek: Κασσιωτικὸν ἅμμα</note>, that is: **The Cassiotic knot.** For Cassium is in Egypt, as we showed a little earlier.

->The works of Aceseus and Helicon.<-
<margin>58</margin>
*Akeseōs kai Helikōnos erga* <note>original Greek: Ἀκεσέως καὶ Ἑλικῶνος ἔργα</note>, that is: **The works of Aceseus and Helicon.** In antiquity, things that appeared to be made with singular craftsmanship were called by this name. Two craftsmen of celebrated skill gave rise to the proverb: Aceseus, a Patarean by nation, and Helicon of Carystus. These two are said to have been the first to weave the *peplum* <note>a ceremonial robe</note> of Athena Polias. "Polias" was the title of Minerva who was worshipped on the acropolis of the Athenians.

->Acesias has treated it.<-
<margin>59</margin>
*Akesias iasato* <note>original Greek: Ἀκεσίας ἰάσατο</note>, that is: **Acesias has treated it.** This was usually said of a matter that was always trending toward the worse; the more it was cared for, the worse it became. The adage was prompted by a certain Acesias, an unskilled and stupid physician, who increased the pain while trying to heal someone suffering from foot pain. Hence Aristophanes says:
**Acesias, he says, treated the anus.** <note>original Greek: Ἀκεσίας τὸν πρωκτὸν ἰάσατο</note>
Because that part, no matter how much you care for it, is always becoming soiled by its very nature. The author is Diogenianus.

->The wells of Agamemnon.<-
<margin>60</margin>
*Agamemnoneia phreata* <note>original Greek: Ἀγαμεμνόνεια φρέατα</note>, that is: **Agamemnon’s wells.** This was said of new and marvelous works. For they say that Agamemnon dug wells both around Aulis and everywhere throughout Greece, so that during the heat of summer they would not suffer from a lack of water. The author is Zenodotus.

->You have eaten of the wild beast.<-
<margin>61</margin>
*Agriou bebrōkas* <note>original Greek: Ἀγρίου βέβρωκας</note>, that is: **You have eaten of the wild beast.** This was once said to someone yawning. For it was commonly believed...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on adages, transitioning from natural history metaphors to historical anecdotes and educational idioms. It follows a discussion on how certain foods or habits manifest in physical reactions like yawning.</meta>

...eating wild animal meat causes frequent yawning. It will be more elegant if it is aptly transferred to the sluggish, the yawning, and the negligent.

<margin>62.</margin>
### A spring of the countryside.
**A spring of the countryside.** <note>original Greek: Αγρῶ πηγὴ</note>. This is said of those who are excessively hardworking and sit at perpetual labor. Of the kind Terence portrays in Menedemus <note>Menedemus is the protagonist of Terence's play *The Self-Tormentor*, who works his land relentlessly as penance</note>. It will also fit a laborious business that never seems to be sufficiently exhausted. For this very word "spring" carries a hyperbole of abundance, not only among the Greeks but also among the Latins.

<margin>63.</margin>
### Aesopic blood.
**Aesopic blood.** <note>original Greek: Αἰσώπειον αἷμα</note>. The Delphians killed a certain Aesop who had done nothing to deserve it, and for that reason an angry deity prophesied dire things for them. There are those who think this is the same Aesop under whose name the fables <note>original: apologues</note> are circulated. They pass down stories of this kind regarding his death, although they are <unclear>closer to fables than the truth</unclear>. When he set out for Delphi and incited the anger of that people against him with insults and insulting fables, the Delphians secretly placed a sacred bowl in his pouch. They followed him to Phocis, seized him, and condemned him for sacrilege. Despite his pleas and dire curses, they threw him from a cliff. Soon a pestilence arose, and the consulted oracle advised that Aesop's ghost <note>manes</note> be appeased. Thus the Delphians established a monument to Aesop. Furthermore, the leaders and learned men of Greece, as soon as they learned of Aesop's unworthy death, avenged the "Aesopic blood" by removing those who had been the authors of his death. From this, it became a common saying either when someone suffered bitter things beyond their merit, or when the angry gods seemed to send punishment because of injured innocence. Plutarch mentions this history in his commentary titled *On those who are slowly punished by the deity* <term>original: περὶ τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ βραδέως τιμωρουμένων; a treatise on divine justice</term>. Namely, that Aesop had received a large amount of gold from Croesus to perform a splendid sacrifice at Delphi and to distribute four minae to each of the Delphians. But when some kind of disagreement occurred between him and the Delphians, he performed the sacrifice indeed, but sent the money he had received for distribution back to Sardis, judging the Delphians unworthy of such a benefit. Therefore, being angry, they condemned him for sacrilege and threw him from the rock they call Hyampea. By this act, the god indicated that a barrenness of the earth and a force of monstrous diseases were imminent. Consequently, the terrified Delphians continuously cried out through a herald in the public assemblies of Greece, asking if there was anyone who wished to take satisfaction in Aesop's name from them. At last, in the third generation, Idmon of Samos arrived—not related to Aesop, but a grandson of those who had bought Aesop in Samos. When they had given him certain penalties, they were relieved of their evils. Plutarch indicates in the same place that this is usually said whenever a punishment is given late.

<margin>64.</margin>
### We have withdrawn the hand from the rod.
**We have withdrawn the hand from the rod.** That is, we too have learned our letters and used the labor of teachers. For in ancient times, schoolmasters <note>original: literatores</note> used to strike the hands of students with a rod. The rod <note>ferula</note> is a type of shrub, nothing is lighter than it, as Pliny indicates in book thirteen, chapter 22. It is called *narthex* <term>original: νάρθηξ; Giant Fennel</term> by the Greeks, useful for supporting old men who stumble with age. Whence it is also sacred to Bacchus and Silenus, so that it may support those stumbling from wine, yet not weigh them down. For it is of the hardest wood on the outside, although it does not have wood inside. The poets imagine that Prometheus carried the celestial fire down to earth caught in this. Finally, the scepters of pedagogues are made from this, as Martial calls them, with which they might terrify more than hurt. Columella noted this elegantly in his poem:
> Nor the mild rods for the hands.

And in the same place:
> And the threatening rods are planted.

Whence those are said to have "withdrawn the hand from the rod" who have ceased to be involved in the grammar school, and are no longer boys to be taught, but are in some way learned. Juvenal in his first Satire:
> And we therefore have withdrawn the hand from the rod, and we
> Have given advice to Sulla. <note>Referring to student rhetoric exercises where they would advise historical figures on courses of action</note>

Jerome seems to take "withdrawn" to mean "subjected" or "placed under." For he writes thus to Domnio: "And we have learned our letters, and we have often withdrawn the hand from the rod." Unless perhaps boys are said to "withdraw the hand from the rod" when they pull back the hand for fear of a blow. There is a similar color of speech among the Greeks. Timocles is cited in Athenaeus, book thirteen:
<column-break/>
<term>original Greek: Δεῖν δ' ἔτι ἀγωνιᾶσαι, καὶ ῥαπισθῆναί γε, καὶ πληγὰς λαβεῖν ἁπαλαῖσι χερσὶν ἡδύ γε.</term>
that is,
> There is a need still
> To tremble, and to be struck with slaps, and on tender hands
> To receive blows; it is indeed a sweet thing.

<page-num>533</page-num>
->CHILIAD TWO, CENTURY VI<-
Y 3
<meta>catchword: from the noise-</meta>

<margin>65</margin>
### An Etnaean beetle.

**An Etnaean beetle.** <note>original Greek: Αἰτναῖος κάνθαρος</note>. That is, a beetle from Mount Etna. This refers to things that are large and foul. Aristophanes says in *The Peace*: "I do not know how he brought in this enormous Etnaean beetle." <note>original Greek: οὐκ εἶδ’ ὅπως εἰσήγαγ’ ἀετναῖον μέγιστον κάνθαρον</note>. He called it "Etnaean" as if to say it was weighed down with great size, either because there are various very large beetles on Mount Etna, or he said Etnaean because it was as large as Mount Etna itself. Furthermore, the beetle is a type of insect that is born from dung and feeds upon it. It has also been handed down in fables that Etna <note>the mountain</note> once covered and preserved one of the principal <term>Giants</term> <note>often identified as Enceladus or Typhon, buried under the volcano by Zeus</note> so that he would not perish by a thunderbolt along with the others. From this comes the saying: "Neither did the celestial fire reach him, when Etna pressed upon him." <note>original Greek: οὔτε πῦρ οὐράνιον ἐπ’ αὐτῆ ἦλθεν, ὅτε Αἴτνην πιέζ’ αὐτόν</note>. That is, the fire of heaven did not touch him, nor does Etna crush him. The author is Diogenianus.

---

<margin>66</margin>
### From your own workshop.

By now, nothing is more common than this figure of speech: **From your own workshop**, or **From someone else's workshop**. We say things are "brought forth from our own workshop" when they are invented by us and perfected by our own natural talent. We say they are "from someone else’s" when we use things borrowed from another as if they were our own. For a "workshop" <note>original: officina</note> is a place where craftsmen exercise their arts. The metaphor is taken from those who sell the work of others in their own shops. The further this is applied to matters of the mind, the more elegant it becomes; for example: "Who would not understand that this counsel proceeded from your workshop?" or "This whole business was a product of your workshop."

---

<margin>67</margin>
### To dance outside the chorus.

**To dance outside the chorus.** <note>original Greek: Ἐκτὸς χοροῦ ὀρχεῖσθαι</note>. One is said to "dance outside the chorus" when they say or do something foreign to the matter at hand. For those who lead choruses move while bound by certain limits and certain rhythms, so that they are not free to wander wherever they please. If anyone deviates from the law of the chorus, they are considered ridiculous.

---

<margin>68</margin>
### To begin the web.

Many metaphors drawn from weaving <note>original: textrina</note> take on the appearance of a proverb. Plautus says in *The Bacchis Sisters*: "This web was begun not at all badly by me." <note>original: Exorsa hæc tela est non male omnino mihi</note>. The same author in *Pseudolus*: "Neither do I know what I should do now, nor where to begin the weaving, nor do I have certain boundaries for finishing the web." Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>, in the book *On the Orator*, used "to weave through" <note>original: pertexere</note> for "to finish." He says, "Finish weaving now, Antony, what you have begun." For when we establish a matter with skill and counsel, we are said "to begin the web" <note>original: Exordiri</note>. And we "unweave" <note>original: Reteximus</note> those things which we reshape anew. Likewise, there is that phrase from the *Rhetoric to Herennius*: "I will now unweave you from the beginning," that is, I will explain what sort of person you are from the very start of your life. Related to this is what we mentioned in another place: "That web is being woven." Pollux cites "to set the warp" <note>original Greek: σήμονά στήσαι</note> from Greek authors.

---

<margin>69</margin>
### To lean against a falling wall.

By a proverbial figure, we are said **To lean against a falling wall** when we rely on and trust in a thing that is not firm enough; the metaphor is drawn from buildings. The Emperor Hadrian, concerning Commodus who had been adopted and destined for the succession of the empire, used to say frequently: "We are leaning against a falling wall, and we have lost four thousand million sesterces which we gave to the people and the soldiers for the adoption of Commodus." Moreover, he called it a "falling wall" because the man was sickly and seemed to be unfit for managing affairs. Likewise, one who relies on the protection of an old man, one who takes pride in beauty, or one who places the protections of life in the fleeting goods of fortune, will rightly be said to lean against a falling wall. Closest to this is that line of Maro <note>the poet Virgil</note>: 
> Upon you the whole leaning house reclines.

---

<margin>70</margin>
### To lean on a staff of reed.

To the same form belongs what seems to have been a proverb among the Hebrews: **To lean on a staff of reed**, said of one who fixes their hopes on those who not only cannot be a protection, but may even harm the one left destitute. Indeed, a reed staff <note>original: scipio</note> not only fails to support the one leaning on it, but even pierces and wounds the hand. In the eighteenth chapter of the Fourth Book of Kings <note>modern 2 Kings</note>, and likewise in the thirty-sixth chapter of the prophet Isaiah, and again in the twenty-ninth chapter of Ezekiel, Egypt and the King of Egypt are called a "staff of reed," in whose confidence war was undertaken; it is predicted that when it is broken, it will not only fail to support the one leaning, but will even bore through his hand. This is not very different from what we recorded elsewhere: "Fig-wood help."

---

<margin>71</margin>
### A bombylius man.

**A bombylius man.** <note>original Greek: Βομβύλιος ἄνθρωπος</note>. That is, a "bumblebee man" is said of one who is wordy and makes much noise, but is otherwise useless. The *bombylius* to the Greeks is a type of bee or wasp, named, so it seems, from its sound <note>the buzzing "bombus"</note>; it is large, but useless for making honey, and it knits its combs for itself out of mud. There is also a huge bee and fly, which from the noise... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword suggests "from the noise" (a strepitu)</note>

<summary>This page discusses various adages related to size, craftsmanship, and reliability, including the "Etnaean beetle" (symbolizing something large and foul) and the "falling wall" or "reed staff" (symbolizing misplaced trust). It highlights Erasmus's habit of blending classical Greek and Roman sources with Biblical Hebrew proverbs.</summary>
<keywords>Etnaean beetle, workshop metaphor, chorus, weaving metaphors, falling wall, staff of reed, bumblebee man, Hadrian, Commodus, Aristophanes, Biblical proverbs</keywords>

--- Page 652 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Latin adages, moving from phonetic-based insults (stuttering) to proverbs about gluttony, legal procrastination, and the metaphorical "veins" or "threads" of literary style.</meta>

<page-num>334</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...from the noise, they spoke thus. Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> adds that the Greeks use the word *boubyliai* <note>original: βουβυλίας</note> for bubbles, which we see formed from water and which quickly vanish. Likewise, a type of cup is called a *bombylion* <note>original: βομβύλιον</note> because it makes a sound like a living creature as the drink drips out little by little; although some think this word also comes from the sound "bo-bo." In the works of Suidas, someone used the word *bombylion* for a flute-player, adding the letter *alpha*, saying "everyone booms with flutes" <note>original: πᾶς δὲ αὐλοῖς βομβᾶν</note>. Furthermore, Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his third *Philippic*, mentions a certain Bambalio, a man of no worth and a stutterer. "A certain father," he says, "named Bambalio, a man of no account. Nothing is more contemptible than he, who, because of his hesitant tongue and the dullness of his heart, took his surname from a term of mockery." Hesychius says that for the Greeks, *bombalan* <note>original: βομβαλᾶν</note> means for the lips to tremble. For this usually happens to those suffering from this defect of the tongue, just as it does to those shivering from the cold. Although this word is written in various ways, the origin is the same: namely, from the sound made by those who speak hesitatingly or who are shivering violently. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus.

<margin>LXXII</margin>
->Buthus wanders about.<-

**Buthus wanders about.** <note>original: Βούθης περιφοιτᾷ</note>. That is, Buthus roams aimlessly. This was said of flighty and stupid people. It comes from the habits of a certain athlete named Buthus, who had been a victor in the Pythian Games. Cratinus <note>an Athenian comic poet</note> mentions him in his play *The Inferiors*, as Zenodotus testifies. Hesychius also mentions him, indicating that Aristotle mentions this man's victory somewhere as well. It is possible that this name was given to him because of his gluttony, as if he were someone who used to devour whole oxen. For Hercules was also nicknamed *Bouthoinas* <note>original: Βουθοίνας, meaning "Ox-eater"</note>, because once when he was hungry, he led away, killed, and devoured one of the oxen belonging to Theodamas, which the man was using to plow the earth. From this, it seems the term could be applied to gluttons—that is, an "ox-eater" <note>original: βωφάγος</note>.

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
->Bunas is the judge.<-

**Bunas is the judge.** <note>original: Βούνας δικάζει</note>. (In some manuscripts it is written as *Bylias*, not *Bunas*, but incorrectly, if I am not mistaken.) This refers to when a lawsuit is drawn out for a long time and never resolved. This is the custom now among the most corrupt advocates of our time, who repeatedly find a new reason to prolong a case so they can extort more money from the litigants. The proverb was born from a certain Athenian named Bunas. When there was a controversy between the Calydonians and the Eleans, both parties referred the matter to the judgment of Bunas. It was agreed that they would restrain themselves from violence until he had pronounced a decision on the matter. When Bunas realized this, he intentionally listened to both sides, but using fabricated excuses, he delayed the matter for a long time and never wished to pronounce a verdict on the lawsuit. The author of this story is Mnaseas, as cited in Zenodotus.

<margin>LXXIV</margin>
->The ox under the yoke.<-

**The ox under the yoke.** <note>original: Βοῦς ὑπὸ ζυγόν</note>. This is used when someone works tirelessly, or when someone involves themselves in a laborious business. It is derived from farming oxen. Furthermore, this will be a place to use the proverb when we deny that someone should be dragged into a business for which they are poorly suited, but rather it should be given to one who is fit for it: because an ox seems born for the yoke, but not a dog or a stag. Therefore, it is closely related to what is placed in another entry: "The ox bearing pack-saddles" <note>original: Bos clitellas</note>. Zenodotus records this.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
->With a thin thread.<-

**With a thin thread.** <note>original: Tenui filo</note>. This stands for a more subtle style and a speech that is less grandiloquent. For rhetoricians establish three <term>characters</term> <note>meaning "styles" or "modes"</note> of speech: the grand, the thin (or plain), and the middle; the metaphor is taken from spinners, or certainly from weavers. Horace says:
> "Poems spun with a fine thread." <note>original: Tenui deducta poemata filo</note>.

Ausonius, in the speech in which he gives thanks to the Emperor Gratian for his consulship, says: "I would have offered a taste, as they say, spun with a thin thread." The opposite of this would be "with a thick thread" <note>original: Crasso filo</note> or "a coarser thread." For example, if you were to say that the Barbarians <note>Erasmus often used this to refer to Scholastic theologians of the Middle Ages</note> treat theological matters with a "thick thread." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of *On the Orator*, said "with a richer thread" <note>original: Uberiore filo</note> to mean more copiously; and in his work *On Old Age*, he used "another thread of speech" for another style of speaking.

<margin>LXXVI</margin>
->A thin vein, A rich vein, A thin channel.<-

They express the same idea with another metaphor when they say: "A poor vein," "a kindly vein," or "a rich vein." They call one's natural talent and the genuine power of the mind a "vein" <note>original: vena</note>. The metaphor is drawn either from springs—some of which flow with a narrow vein, while others are so great they create a massive river—or from mines, where veins of metal differ not only in type but also in abundance. Very similar to these is what Quintilian says in his eleventh book: "Yet these flow with a fuller channel: 'O you Alban hills and groves!'" <note>original: Pleniore tamen hęc canali fluunt</note>.

<margin>LXXVII</margin>
->To eat barley-cakes.<-

*Hypomazan* <note>original: ὑπομαζᾶν</note>. Among the Greeks, *maza* <note>original: Μᾶζα</note> is a type of food made from wheat flour, which, it appears, was a delicacy; from which the common...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Greek and Latin proverbs, specifically focusing on adages related to luxurious living, missing the mark, great calamities, finality, and performing tasks with the wrong tools.</meta>

<page-num>535</page-num>
<header>SECOND CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Y 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: accommodated-</meta>

<margin>isomazan</margin>
...they used to say in the old style, *isomazan* <note>original: ἰσομαζᾶν</note>, for living sumptuously and splendidly, either because of excellent barley-cakes <note>known as *mazas*</note> or because one ate something even more refined than these. Julius Pollux <note>a Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD</note> indicates in Book 7 that this was an ancient term, for which more recent writers used *keithian* <note>original: κειθιᾶν</note>, a word derived from "swelling," referring to those for whom barley-cakes are their primary food. It is strange that while he cites this word from Aeschylus and Sophocles, he claims it belongs to "more recent" authors—unless perhaps it became more common in later times than *isomazan*. Euplous says to Thalasseros: "Either you live in luxury or you are mad; for I hear you are captivated by the love of a bold, foul-mouthed woman" <note>original: ἰσομαζᾶς ἢ μέμψας, ἀκούω γάρ σε λοιδορᾶ γυναικός θρασ.</note>. In a similar form, they spoke of *mathetian* <note>original: μαθητιᾶν</note>, from *mattya*, a type of food which Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> lists in Book 14 among the delicacies of the second course <note>dessert</note>.

### Not even hitting close. LXXVIII

<margin>oud’ iktar ballei</margin>
"He does not even hit close" <note>original: οὐδ’ ἴκταρ βάλλει</note>. This is said of those who are far from the goal and stray by a wide margin from the matter at hand. It is taken from unskilled archers. When Diogenes the Cynic <note>the famous philosopher who lived in a tub and sought an honest man</note> saw such an archer, he sat down right next to the target. When asked what he meant by this, he replied, "So that he doesn't hit me," implying the archer would hit anything rather than the target. Thus, for those who stray too far from the mark, they said "he doesn't even hit close." It is the same as saying, "not even close to similar" <note>original: οὐδ’ ἐγγὺς ὅμοιον</note>, that is, "nothing like it." Homer used the phrase "away from the mark" <note>original: ἀπὸ σκοποῦ</note>. Plato used this adage in the ninth book of the *Republic*: "And all these things, when compared to a tyrant's wickedness and the misery of the city, do not even, as the proverb says, hit close to the mark" <note>original: οὐδ’ ἴκταρ βάλλει</note>. Suidas <note>the author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> notes that the proverb arises from a linguistic idiom, like the one following. Lucian seems to have alluded to this in his dialogue *On Images*: "Not worthy of such great praise, not even close" <note>original: Μὴ οὖν τῆς τηλικαύτης ἀξίαν, μηδ’ ἐγγύς</note>. Likewise Aristides in his work on Miltiades: "These things are not so, not even close" <note>original: οὐκ ἔστι ταῦτα, οὐδ’ ἐγγύς</note>. This adage belongs to the group of those we have mentioned elsewhere: "Not missing the door," "To err by the whole sky," and "To err by the whole road."

### A Diolygian evil. LXXIX

<margin>diolygion kakon</margin>
"A Diolygian evil" <note>original: διωλύγιον κακόν</note>, meaning a massive evil; the very figure of speech is proverbial. Plato uses this adage in the *Theaetetus*: "Not a long and Diolygian piece of nonsense" <note>original: οὐ μακρὰ μὲν καὶ διωλύγιος φλυαρία</note>. In the works of Suidas, they relate this from some author, I believe Damascius: "And would these things not seem to be the greatest nonsense? Indeed they would, and rightly so. Not like the so-called old wives' tales, but beyond the greatest trifles." Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquence</note>, in his first oration against the Jews, says: "Shouting out a great Diolygian cry" <note>original: μέγα διωλύγιον ὀλολύξαντες</note>, meaning shouting clearly so the voice can be heard from afar. He is speaking of shepherds shouting to one another upon seeing a wolf. They indicate a twofold origin for the word. *Diolygion* <note>original: διωλύγιον</note>, as if it were "through the shouting" (*di' ololyzon*), because a cry never fails to penetrate; and *diolygion*, as if "through destroying" (*di' olyon*), meaning something that ruins and brings destruction. The proverb is used for someone held by some great and long-lasting evil.

### The same for you, both Pythian and Delian. LXXX

<margin>tauta soi kai pythia kai delia</margin>
"This is for you both Pythian and Delian" <note>original: ταὐτά σοι καὶ πύθια καὶ δήλια</note>. This is used whenever we signify some final work. It is as if you were to say, "This is the sum of all things you will do in life." The adage is cited from Menander <note>the famous Greek dramatist of New Comedy</note>. They say it arose from an oracle given to Polycrates, the tyrant of the Samians. For after he had captured the island of Rhenea and consecrated it to Apollo, he established magnificent games at Delos and sent to Delphi to ask whether these games should be called "Delian" or "Pythian" <note>referring to the two main centers of Apollo's worship</note>. The oracle replied: "The same for you, both Pythian and Delian," hinting that he would soon depart from this life—and so it happened. Thus the matter turned into a proverb. Furthermore, if you write it as *tauta* <note>original: ταυτὰ</note>, you translate it as "the same things"; if *tauta* <note>original: ταῦτα</note> [with different accentuation], you translate it as "these things." It makes little difference to the sense.

### Splitting wood with a key, and trying to open doors with an axe. LXXXI

<margin>to kleidi ta xyla schizein...</margin>
"You are trying to split wood with a key, but to open doors with an axe" <note>original: τῷ κλειδὶ τὰ ξύλα σχίζειν, τῇ δ’ ἀξίνῃ τὴν θύραν ἀνοίγειν πειρᾶς</note>. This is said when something is done backward or perversely: as if someone were to try to correct free men through fear, or win over slaves through kindness. Or if someone were to use philosophical arguments among the unlearned, but try to win among the learned through shouting and impudence. This is recorded by Plutarch in his essay titled *On Listening*.

### Bellerophontic letters. LXXXII

<margin>Bellerophontes ta grammata</margin>
"Bellerophontic letters" <note>original: Βελλεροφόντης τὰ γράμματα</note>. Some verb must be understood...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...it adds to the meaning, "He brings it," or some such phrase. There will be a place for this proverb whenever someone delivers letters, such as letters of recommendation, which have actually been written against himself. In common speech, these are called "Uriah's letters" <note>original: "literas Vrig," referring to the biblical story of King David sending Uriah the Hittite to the front lines with a letter ensuring his death</note>. A similar story is found among the Hebrews. Regarding "Bellerophontic letters," the Greeks recount a myth of this kind: Bellerophon, having gone into exile for the killing of Bellerus <note>a Corinthian hero</note>, came to Tiryns and was received as a guest by King Proetus. In the meantime, Antea, the king's wife, was seized by a passion for the young man and began to solicit his mind toward debauchery, offering herself to him. When he refused the shameful act, clearly moved by the sacred duty of hospitality, she took the initiative; her womanly love turning to hatred, she secretly denounced Bellerophon to her husband, claiming he had propositioned her for sex. Once she had persuaded the king, she incited his mind to the youth's destruction as much as she could, constantly singing that line of Homer into his ear:

->“Either die, Proetus, or kill Bellerophon,” that is,<-
->“Aut morere Prœte, aut interfice Bellerophontem.”<- <note>original Greek: Τεθναίης ὦ Προῖτ’ ἢ κάκτανε Βελλεροφόντην</note>

Proetus, therefore, possessing a truly royal disposition—and to use Homer’s word, <term>wily-minded</term> <note>original: ἀγκυλομήτης, meaning "crooked-counselor"</note>—sent Bellerophon to his host Iobates as if on official business, providing letters written as if in his recommendation. In these, he commanded Iobates to remove the youth from the world by any means possible. Bellerophon, being entirely unsuspecting due to his innocence, delivered the letters he had received just as they had been sealed. When Iobates had read them through, in order to comply with Proetus’s wish, he attempted to destroy the young man under an honorable pretext. For this is almost always the habit of evil princes. He inflamed the youth’s naturally fierce spirit to test his strength and acquire glory. First, he persuaded him to fight the Chimera. That was a three-formed monster, 

->“a lion in front, a dragon behind, and a goat in the middle.” That is,<-
->With the appearance of a goat.<- <note>original Greek: πρόσθε λέων, ἔπιθεν δὲ δράκων, μέσση δὲ χίμαιρα</note>

Lion-like at the front, dragon-like at the rear, and in the middle the Chimera itself. Bellerophon, sitting upon his winged horse <note>Pegasus</note>, pierced and finished this beast with his spear. Afterward, the king exposed the youth to various other dangers; when he returned victorious from all of them, the king, admiring his strength and guessing his innocence from the outcome, showed him Proetus’s letters, accepted him as a son-in-law, and at his death handed over the succession of the empire to him. Therefore, whoever unknowingly either reports or does something by which he rightly betrays himself, it shall be rightly said of him, <term>Bellerophon’s letters</term> <note>original: Βελλεροφόντης τὰ γράμματα</note>, or whoever is harmed under the pretext of duty. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian</note>. Plautus says in *The Bacchides*: "Silence, no man says it, these tablets convict you: those which you brought, these command that you be bound. Ah, your son has now made me a Bellerophon. I myself delivered the tablets so that I might be bound; so be it." The adage is also expressed in this manner: <term>Bellerophon against himself</term> <note>original: Βελλεροφόντης κατ’ ἑαυτοῦ</note>. Lucian says in his *Apology*: <term>in saying nothing to yourself</term> <note>original: ἐν τῷ μηδὲν σιωπᾶν σαυτῷ</note>, that is, <term>the Bellerophon who has written the book</term> <note>original: ὁ Βελλεροφόντης γεγραφὼς τὸ βιβλίον</note>, meaning: You who have written a book against yourself like Bellerophon. King Pharnabazus deceived Lysander with a similar trick, as Plutarch relates in his *Life of Lysander*.

<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
->Staining pure water with mud, you will never find a drink.<-
<term>By defiling bright water with filth, you will never find a drink.</term> <note>original Greek: Βορβόρῳ ὕδωρ λαμπρὸν μιαίνων, οὔποθ’ εὑρήσεις πότον</note> that is,
If you persist in clear water
With mud to defile, you will never find what you may drink.
This is a trochaic verse, which we have expressed in a half-line and a poem of the same kind. It was accustomed to be said whenever someone contaminates those things which are beautiful in themselves by mixing in those things which are most foul. For instance, if someone should mix obscenity into poetry, it is surely by their own fault; for the art in itself is pure. Or if someone should corrupt theological learning with heretical opinions, or defile it with impurity of speech, or contaminate it with profane letters; or provoke the friendship of a prince with frequent offenses. It will also apply to those for whom this life is heavy, and that through their own fault, because through a vice of the mind they seem to bring trouble upon things which are not troublesome in themselves. But if a mind approaches that is free from foolish affections, whatever happens will be a source of pleasure.

<margin>LXXXIIII</margin>
->The promises of Chares.<-
<term>The promises of Chares.</term> <note>original Greek: Αἱ Χάρητος ὑποσχέσεις</note>. This was accustomed to be said whenever someone promises easily and kindly, following that line of Naso <note>Ovid</note>:
"Make sure you promise; for what does it hurt to promise? 
Anyone can be rich in promises."
The adage arose from a certain Chares, an Athenian general, who used to promise anything to anyone, but did not perform what he had undertaken. Now, kings and popes <note>original: pontifices</note> almost always imitate this Chares, while they promise everything to everyone and refuse nothing, so that at least they may dismiss people happy with hope—

### SECOND THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY

...dismiss them: and they even voluntarily invite people to ask them for favors, clearly luring them with hope. He also tells of Vespasian's son <note>Titus, known for his generosity</note>, that when he was warned not to be so ready to make promises—since he promised far more than he could provide—he replied that it was not right for anyone to leave the Emperor’s presence feeling sad. The adage is recorded by Suidas, and I do not doubt it was taken from Aristophanes.

->You live in Cescus. LXXXV<-

<margin>You live in Cescus.</margin><note>original Greek: Κέσϰον οἰϰεῖς</note> **You live in Cescus.** This used to be said of a stupid person or a dullard. Cescus was a city in Pamphylia, whose citizens were commonly ill-reputed for their madness and folly. Near the city of Cescus was a river named *Akes* <note>original: ἄκης</note>, which means "witless." Although Suidas, who also mentions the proverb, places Cescus in Cilicia rather than Pamphylia. From this, it was bandied about in common speech: <margin>The city of Cescus, lacking a mind.</margin><note>original Greek: πόλις κέσϰος νοῦν οὐϰ ἔχουσα</note>—that is, "The city of Cescus is void of sense." This will also apply to a gathering or assembly of foolish men. It agrees with what we have shown elsewhere: "A Boeotian sow." Zenodotus records the adage. It should be noted in passing that this passage in Suidas is corrupted in the entry for *Cescos*, and instead of *Cescon on ekein*, one should read *Cescon oikein* <note>meaning "to live in Cescus" rather than a nonsensical phrase</note>.

->To complete the circle. LXXXVI<-

<margin>To complete the circle.</margin><note>original Greek: Τὸν ϰύϰλον ἀποτελεῖν</note> **To complete the circle** is to render a thing perfect in all its measures and all its parts. From this comes the word **encyclopedia** <term>original: ϰυϰλοπαιδεία, meaning a circle of disciplines</term>, which completes, as it were, a circle of all teachings; and also "general education." The metaphor seems to be taken from the mathematicians, among whom the circular figure is judged the most perfect and complete. Hence that deservedly praised poem about the wise man:
>Being like the world, smooth and round,
>So that no external blemish may settle on its polished surface.

A similar expression is *in every rhythm* <note>original: παντὶ ῥυθμῷ</note>, that is, **In every number** <note>meaning "perfect in every detail"</note>. Thus Quintilian <note>referred to here as "Fabius"</note> says in the preface to his eighth book: "Just as it is necessary for the highest knowledge to understand a thing through all its numbers and deep within, so it is more fitting for it to be handed down more simply and briefly to beginners." This seems to be derived from musicians.

->The hot part of the spit. LXXXVII<-

<margin>The hot part of the spit.</margin><note>original Greek: τὸ θερμὸν τοῦ ὀβελίσϰου</note> **The hot part of the spit.** One should understand "he grabbed," or something similar: used when someone, through ignorance of the business, approaches a matter from that side where it was least safe to approach. Or when someone, out of lack of skill, chooses the worse things instead of the better. Zenodotus says that Sophocles mentions this adage. The metaphor is taken from those who, through imprudence, grab that part of the roasting spit which is hot with their hand, then, having been burnt, throw it back and grab the other end. This is not entirely unlike: **The fisherman, once struck, will be wise** <note>original Greek: ἁλιεὺς πληγεὶς νόον οἴσει</note>, which we have recounted in another place.

->A Titanic gaze. LXXXVIII<-

<margin>To look like a Titan.</margin><note>original Greek: τιτανῶδες βλέπειν</note> That is, **to look like a Titan**, which means to stare with a Titanic expression. Moreover, they call a "Titanic" look one that is grim and gloomy, such as those ancient Titans are said to have possessed. Lucian in *Timon*: "For having spread out his beard, and raised his eyebrows, and muttering something to himself, he approaches looking with a Titanic gaze." The same author in *Icaromenippus*: "But Jupiter, looking at me very terrifyingly, most sharply and with a Titanic look..."

->Thracians know no treaties. LXXXIX<-

<margin>Thracians do not understand oaths.</margin><note>original Greek: Θρᾷϰῶν ὅρϰια οὐϰ ἐπίστανται</note> That is, **Thracians do not know treaties.** It happened among the Thracians that a certain eldest man died by a javelin driven through his chest. From this, it began to be said among the Ionians and Aeolians as a kind of riddle: *Thracians do not understand oaths*, because honor is more due to the elderly among those who live by laws <note>implying Thracians are lawless and disregard the elderly</note>. Furthermore, the murder of Polydorus by Polymnestor <note>a Thracian king</note>, violating the law of hospitality, sufficiently proves the barbarity, cruelty, and perfidy of the Thracians. And Euripides in *Hecuba*:
<margin>Perhaps among you it is easy to kill a guest, but to us Greeks this is a disgrace.</margin>
>That is:
>To slaughter a guest is perhaps a light thing to you,
>But to us Achaeans, that is a heavy matter indeed.

->To tuna-fish. XC<-

<margin>To harpoon like a tuna.</margin><note>original Greek: θυννάζειν</note> The Greeks use this metaphor for **to goad and sting**; either because this fish, for which the palate is plea—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of adages from the previous page, moving from the metaphor of the "tuna" fish to proverbs about speed (Heraclitus and Butes) and the proverbial reputation of the Lydians for theft and decadence.</meta>

...is more pleasing to the touch, or because the fish itself burns or stings when handled. Pliny, in his ninth book, chapter fifteen, records a marvel regarding the tuna <note>Latin: *thynnus*</note> that is quite new to hear. He says there is a very tiny creature in the sea, about the size of a spider and shaped like a scorpion. It attaches its sting under the fin of the dolphin and the so-called swordfish (which is often larger than a dolphin), causing such intense pain that these fish frequently leap right onto ships. Athenaeus, in the seventh book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned"</note>, related that a certain kind of tuna, which the Athenians call *thynnides*, has a fin attached under the belly called an *athera* <note>original Greek: ἀθέρα, meaning a spine or spike</note>. He adds that the fish is named <term>from the gadfly</term> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴστρου (*apo tou oistrou*)</note>, because it is driven by a sudden impulse, especially when it is agitated by the "sting" <note>the *oestrus* or gadfly's frenzy</note>, which happens to it around the summer solstice. This creature is a little animal on its head that looks like a scorpion and is the size of a drachma coin. The fish is so tormented by this affliction that they leap out of the water no less high than dolphins. He brings forward Aristotle as a witness to this fact. Lucian, in his *Tragic Jupiter*, says: <term>Away with it! A tuna-like conceit, O Poseidon, and altogether gross.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄπαγε, θυννῶδές γε τὸ ἐνθύμημα ὦ Πόσειδον, καὶ κομιδῆ παχύ. Erasmus uses "pingue" (fat/thick) to translate the Greek "pachy," implying stupidity or lack of refinement.</note> Again, in the same dialogue, Lucian alludes to the same word: <term>If my affairs have been thus shorn away by you.</term> <note>original Greek: Εἰ τ’ ἀμὰ οὕτως ὑμῖν ἀπεθρίσθη. Erasmus interprets this as "expuncta" (erased/canceled).</note> The adage is also listed by Diogenianus.

->Interest runs faster than Heraclitus.<-
<margin>XCI</margin>

<term>Interest runs faster than the swift-footed Heraclitus.</term> <note>original Greek: Θᾶττον ὁ τόκος ἡρακλείτου ποδινέω τρέχει</note> That is to say: interest runs more quickly than the fastest Heraclitus. This adage warns that one should abstain from borrowing money at interest, for the day the interest is due returns faster than one expects. The proverb is taken from a certain Heraclitus who was exceptionally gifted and outstanding in running speed. It is phrased according to the Doric dialect, using <term>Heracleito and podineo</term> <note>original: ἡρακλείτω & ποδινέω</note> instead of the standard Greek forms. It appears to have been a trochaic tetrameter catalectic verse, though a few syllables have become corrupted.

->Faster than Butes.<-
<margin>XCII</margin>

<term>Faster than Butes.</term> <note>original Greek: Θᾶττον ἢ βούτης</note> With this adage, people used to signify that something was completed as quickly as possible or explained by a shortcut. This is similar to those who signify a long meaning with a few, briefly pronounced words. They say the saying was born from this: In Athens, among the paintings of the Painted Porch <note>the Stoa Poikile</note>, a certain Butes was depicted, but painted in such a way that only the top part of his head and his eyes were visible. This was so the spectator would imagine the rest of his body was hidden by the mountain he was walking behind. Therefore, since the painter had not spent much labor on this image, the proverb came to be tossed about regarding things that are easily finished. Zenodotus is the authority for this.

->The Lydian closed the door.<-
<margin>XCIII</margin>

<term>The Lydian closed the door.</term> <note>original Greek: Λυδὸς τὴν θύραν ἔκλεισε</note> This used to be said of thieves, because the Lydians rarely departed without having stolen something. But if we are permitted to guess (and why shouldn't we be permitted in such an ancient matter, where neither the original author nor an interpreter survives?), I would prefer to take it as referring to those who, about to commit some shameful act, flee witnesses and hide themselves, since the Lydians were notorious for their soft and decadent lifestyle. This is why Plautus calls a Lydian "plucked" <note>referring to hair removal, a sign of effeminacy to the Romans</note>. Plutarch alludes to this—and I wish he had opened it up further—in the commentary he wrote against Colotes: <term>But it seems to me, just as the Lydian opens one door against himself, he instead involves Epicurus in many and great difficulties.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐμοὶ δ’ δοκεῖ, καθάπερ ὁ λυδὸς ἐφ’ αὑτὸν ἀνοίγειν τὴν θύραν μίαν... Erasmus notes that Lydus here seems to be making things worse for himself.</note> Unless one prefers that this passage in Plutarch refers to what is said elsewhere: "The Lydian man had no business." Hesychius mentions the proverb but adds nothing except these words: <term>Regarding foolish thieves</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ τῶν μωροκλεπτῶν</note>. However, he has provided us here with a corrupted reading in other books; it should be read not as "closed" <note>Greek: ἔκλεισε (*ekleise*)</note> but as <term>rattled</term> <note>Greek: ἐκίγκλισε (*ekingklise*)</note>, meaning he moved or tested it. For unskilled thieves often betray themselves while moving a door with a noise. According to Suidas, the Greek word *kinklidzein* has many meanings: it signifies <term>to shake, to lever, to make a sound, or to move.</term> <note>original Greek: σαλεύειν, μοχλεύειν, ἦχον ποιεῖν, κινεῖν</note> It is the primary art of thieves to move a door without sound, whether entering or exiting. I believe it is clear what Plutarch intends.

->A Lydian at midday.<-
<margin>XCIIII</margin>

<term>A Lydian at midday.</term> <note>original Greek: Λυδὸς ἐν μεσημβρίᾳ</note> This was said against a person of insatiable or even ill-timed lust. They say the Lydians were so lost to lust that they did not only devote themselves to sexual pleasure at night, but even at midday they would behave wantonly, performing foul deeds with their hands. From this, the Greeks use the verb <term>to live like a Lydian</term> <note>original Greek: λυδιάζειν (*lydiadzein*)</note> to mean living in the Lydian manner. Of a people... <meta>The catchword "Degentis hu-" connects to the next page's opening word.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Roman proverbs, specifically focusing on those derived from the reputations of the Lydians for decadence and the legal culture of Athens. # SECOND CHILIAD, SIXTH HUNDRED

Athenaeus, in the twelfth book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned"</note>, commemorates much regarding the luxury and delicacies of this city [Sybaris]. We remember elsewhere, specifically in the proverb **A Sybaritic table**, the nature of a Sybaritic banquet, in which Venus <note>Meaning sexual intercourse</note> was also mixed in. Furthermore, no time is more ill-suited for intercourse than either midday, because of the burning sun, or during a banquet, because the vital spirits are occupied around the stomach and digestion.

### XCV. A goatherd in the heat

**A goatherd in the heat** <note>original Greek: Αἰπόλος ἐν καύματι (*Aipolos en kaumati*)</note>. This has a similar meaning, namely, of ill-timed lust. For during these hours, goatherds—while their herds are led away to hide in the shade—are written to be accustomed to behaving wantonly. Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic</note> records both versions of the adage, as does the *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note>. It can be applied to any pleasure indulged in at an improper time.

### XCVI. The Lydian keeps a shop

**The Lydian keeps a shop** <note>original Greek: Λυδὸς καπηλεύει (*Lydos kapeleuei*)</note>. This was cast at those who were effeminate and addicted to pleasures. History records that this arose from a specific event: King Cyrus, having conquered the Lydians, commanded them—on the advice of Croesus—to practice shopkeeping and not to handle arms. Instead, they were to wear garments trailing down to the ground (which in ancient times indicated softness), so that in this manner they might be transformed into women, as it were, and become useless for rebellion. Herodotus, in his first book, records that the Lydians were the first of all people to become shopkeepers and peddlers. Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian</note> records that public spectacles were invented by them, and from this, the Romans derived their word *ludi* <note>Meaning "games" or "plays"</note>. Among the Greeks, the term <term>to keep a shop</term> <note>original Greek: καπηλεύειν (*kapeleuein*)</note> properly refers to those who sell food. Those things recorded by the *Suda* also taste of this proverb: **I live like a Lydian**, used for those who live according to Lydian customs.

### XCVII. Lydian sauces

**Lydian sauces** <note>original Greek: Λυδῶν καρύκαι (*Lydon karykai*)</note>. In ancient times, they called anything sumptuously prepared and seasoned with various delicacies "Lydian sauces." For the *caryca* was a Lydian type of food, prepared from many kinds of luxuries and blood. Athenaeus, in the twelfth book of the *Deipnosophistae*, records that the preparation of *carycae* was first invented by the Lydians. The adage is expressed in full in this manner: **Neither Lydian sauces, nor the sound of whips** <note>original Greek: Μήτε λυδῶν καρύκας, μήτε μασίγων ψόφους (*Mete lydon karykas, mete masigon psophous*)</note>. One must understand "I want" or something similar; that is, "I want neither flatteries nor insults," or "neither things too sweet nor, on the other hand, things too harsh." More will be said of this elsewhere.

### XCVIII. The Wolf-God’s drink

**The Wolf-God’s drink** <note>original Greek: Λυκείου πόμα (*Lykeiou poma*)</note>. They used to say this when someone purchased a pleasure at the risk of their own head. They tell of two sacred springs belonging to Apollo, one of which flowed with wine and the other with honey; when birds flew toward them, they were struck down by his bow. Furthermore, Apollo was called **Lyceius** <note>The Wolf-God</note> among other surnames, either from the "light" (*lux*) which he reveals, or from the wolves he killed. The authors for this are Zenodotus and the *Suda*, who advise that the second-to-last syllable should be circumflexed <note>A technical note on Greek pronunciation to distinguish meanings</note>. For **Lyceum** <note>original Greek: λύκειον (*lykeion*)</note> with the first syllable accented is a gymnasium in Athens, which some think was built by Pisistratus and others by Pericles. And from this arose the proverb, closely related to that other one: **Like a dog from the Nile** <note>Referring to drinking quickly to avoid the crocodile</note>.

### XCIX. The Wolf’s ten

**The Wolf’s ten** <note>original Greek: Λύκου δεκὰς (*Lykou dekas*)</note>. It appears this was said against those to whom some part of dishonest gain returned, however small. Or against those who had been corrupted by bribes, or who corrupted others. For in the forum at Athens, where legal cases were argued, there stood a carved figure of a certain spirit named Lycus, in the form of a wolf. Near this statue, "sycophants" <note>Professional informers or legal meddlers</note> corrupted by money were accustomed to linger, as if before some god presiding over their profit; a three-obol coin was set aside for him daily. This is according to Zenodotus, though Hesychius also touches upon it. The *Suda* adds that these sycophants were ten in number, acting like a "board of ten." Aristophanes mentions this in *The Wasps*:
->If you are able to carry away the image of Lycus.<-
This kind of profit was most hated among the ancients—those who summoned people to court so that they might carry off some portion of the penalty as a reward from the condemned. For this reason, they were called <term>Sectores</term> <note>Asset-strippers or "cutters" of goods</note> and <term>Quadruplatores</term> <note>Informers who received a quarter of the penalty</note>.

### C. Hermodorus imports words

**Hermodorus’s words are his merchandise** <note>original Greek: λόγος γὰρ ἑρμοδώρῳ ἐμπορεύεται (*logos gar hermodoro emporeuetai*)</note>.
->Hermodorus’s words are a matter of trade.<-
This was said against a man who brought nothing but words. Just as Laches, in Terence’s play *The Mother-in-Law*, asks his son Pamphilus whether he had brought back "nothing but a single sentence" with him from Lemnos. Or it is used against those who sell words for money: which applies to poets, advocates, and <term>sellers of smoke</term> <note>Those who sell false promises or influence</note>...

<summary>This page catalogs various Greek adages concerning the Lydian reputation for soft living and the Athenian legal system's corruption, specifically detailing the "Wolf's ten" in relation to professional informers.</summary>
<keywords>Sybaris, Lydians, Cyrus, Croesus, Apollo Lyceius, Athens, Lycus, sycophants, legal corruption, Hermodorus, Terence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding those who profit from the wisdom of others, specifically focusing on Hermodorus, a student of Plato. It then begins the Seventh Hundred of the Second Chiliad.</meta>

->THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-

and it could be rightly said against men of that kind. They say the proverb arose from a certain Hermodorus, a student of Plato, who used to carry off the commentaries written by Plato to Sicily and sell them there. From this, the Sicilians, who are known for their wit, turned the matter into a proverb, saying: **Hermodorus imports words as his merchandise.** <note>original Latin: "Hermodorum pro mercibus importare uerba."</note> Furthermore, sophists and philosophers call their scholarly works "words" <note>original Greek: λόγους (*logous*)</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero undoubtedly alluded to this in the thirteenth book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "Tell me, does it please you to publish first without my order? Not even Hermodorus did that, he who was accustomed to making Plato’s books public, from which comes the saying 'Hermodorus [deals] in words.'" <note>original Greek: λόγοισιν Ἑρμόδωρος (*logoisin Hermodoros*)</note> Furthermore, although Cicero cited the proverb in a truncated form, if you add the word "trades" <note>original Greek: ἐμπορεύεται (*emporeuetai*)</note>, it will form a complete Greek six-foot verse. From this, the term "word-merchant" <note>original Greek: λογέμπορος (*logemporos*)</note> was coined for someone who brings nothing but talk.

### SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH HUNDRED

#### I. Apple-bearing Hercules.
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring two figures, possibly classical or mythological, in a landscape setting.</image-desc>**Apple-bearing Hercules** <note>original Greek: Μήλιος ἡρακλῆς (*Mēlios Hēraklēs*)</note>. This was said in contempt against someone who carries a magnificent name but possesses no wealth and is powerful in no capacity. It arose from an event. The *Suda* <note>A Byzantine encyclopedia</note> records that when certain peasants were about to sacrifice an ox to Hercules, and the ox escaped after breaking its rope, they had nothing to sacrifice. They grabbed an apple <note>In Greek, the word *mēlon* can mean both "apple" and "sheep," a pun that likely fueled this legend.</note>, stuck four branches into it to serve as legs, then added two others in place of horns; thus they imitated an ox as best they could and sacrificed that ridiculous likeness to Hercules as a victim. 

Julius Pollux, in the first book of his *Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary of terms</note>, tells the story somewhat differently, in this manner. It is the custom, he says, among the Boeotians to perform divine rites to Hercules with apples. When the festival of the god was at hand and the time for sacrificing the victim pressed (furthermore, the victim was a ram), the animal was brought too late because the river Asopus had swollen so suddenly that it could not be crossed. The boys who were playing near the altar nevertheless performed the ritual of sacrifice. They added four straws to a particularly beautiful apple in place of feet, and again two others in place of horns, imagining that they were sacrificing a ram in that fashion. It was believed that Hercules was greatly delighted by this victim, and consequently, the custom remained among the Thebans to sacrifice apples to Hercules. From this, a surname was added to the god, so that he was called **Apple-bearing Hercules** <note>original Greek: ἡρακλῆς μήλιος (*Hēraklēs mēlios*)</note>.

#### II. Modesty is useless to a man in need.
> Modesty is not a good companion for a man in need.
<note>original Greek: Αἰδὼς δ' οὐκ ἀγαθὴ κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι (*Aidos d' ouk agathe kechremenoi andri pareinai*)</note>

So it is read in Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 17. It is also cited by Plato in his *Laches*. and shortly after:
> You say modesty is good for a poor man?
> Modesty does not bring good to a man in need.
<note>original Greek: Αἰδὼς δ' ὅτ' ἀγαθὴ φὴς ἔμμεναι ἀνδρὶ πένῃτι. Αἰδὼς δ' οὐκ ἀγαθὴ κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ κομίζει.</note>

<margin>Also in Hesiod, that is:</margin>
Truly, shame by no means benefits a needy man.
This verse passed into a proverb. It warns that shame must be cast aside whenever necessity presses. For modesty is not only vehemently useless for many things, but especially when the situation demands that we must do everything ourselves: for instance, modesty is useless when it deters one from learning what is shameful not to know. And, as Horace <note>referred to as "Flaccus"</note> says: "False modesty hides untreated sores." The same author says elsewhere: "A bad modesty presses upon you." Euripides alluded to the same in *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
> Nevertheless, as far as is possible, one ought to be modest.
<note>original Greek: ὅμως δ' ὅσου γε δυνατόν, αἰδεῖσθαι χρεών.</note>
Homer writes in the *Iliad*, Book 24, that modesty or reverence profits a man very much, and yet hinders him very much:
> Nor does he have modesty, which both greatly harms men and helps them.
<note>original Greek: οὐ δέ οἱ αἰδώς γίνεται, ἥτ' ἄνδρας μέγα σίνεται ἠδ' ὀνίνησιν.</note>
And one may see some endowed with this useless modesty who prefer to hide the defects of their body rather than have them removed by the help of friends. The painter Apelles is recorded to have been of such a nature; when he was hiding both his illness and his poverty, a kind friend secretly slipped a weight of gold under his pillow. But by far the greatest crowd consists of those who hide the diseases of the soul and their poverty with a useless modesty. Yet it usually happens to these people that after the evil bursts into the open, they then blush more miserably and in vain.

#### III. You reproach me for my belly.
These verses are also mentioned in the collections of Greek adages,

### SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH HUNDRED
<page-num>541</page-num>

You cast my belly in my teeth as the most beautiful reproach of all.
Full it is lighter, but empty it is heavy. That is:
> You object to my belly, than which no reproach is more beautiful.
> Full it is lighter; it hangs heavy when empty.

Indeed, I do not see where the proverb lies here, unless it is in the phrase, "a beautiful reproach," <note>original Greek: κάλλιστον ὄνειδος (*kalliston oneidos*)</note> which seems to have been used as a proverb among the Greeks. Euripides in *Iphigenia at Aulis* writes:
You have reproached me with a truly beautiful reproach. That is:
> You have surely reproached me with an honorable shame.

Alternatively, the proverb may lie in that somewhat <term>enigmatic</term> part: "Light when it is full, heavy when it is empty." For other small vessels are heavier the fuller they are, and lighter the more they are empty. On the contrary, the belly is lighter the more it is distended with food, because of the "spirits" <note>In ancient medicine, "spirits" (pneumata) were subtle substances that fueled bodily functions; food was thought to stir these up, making the body feel more active and "buoyant."</note> increased and aroused by nourishment.

-> It is shameful to be silent. <-

It is shameful to be silent. <note>original Greek: Αἰσχρὸν σιωπᾶν (*Aischron siōpān*)</note> This may be used whenever someone is spurred on to study or to undertake some business by the example of another. It was either born from, or certainly used by, Aristotle. When Isocrates was teaching <term>rhetoric</term> <note>the art of persuasive speaking</note>, Aristotle was moved by a sense of rivalry and began to teach the art of speaking during his afternoon "walks" <note>Aristotle's followers were called "Peripatetics" because he taught while walking.</note>, saying: It is shameful to be silent and to let Isocrates speak. <note>original Greek: Αἰσχρὸν σιωπᾶν λαλῆσαι δ’ Ἰσοκράτην (*Aischron siōpān lalēsai d’ Isokratēn*)</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his work *On the Orator*, shows that Aristotle borrowed this from a certain tragedy, changing only a few words. For he writes as follows: "When Aristotle was in his prime and saw Isocrates flourishing with the fame of his students—because Isocrates had transferred his own discussions from legal and civil cases to a vain elegance of speech—Aristotle suddenly changed almost the entire form of his own teaching and spoke a certain verse about Philoctetes <note>A Greek hero in the Trojan War</note> slightly differently. For Philoctetes said it was shameful for him to be silent 'with barbarians' <note>referring to non-Greeks</note>; but Aristotle said it when he 'allowed Isocrates to speak.'" In the sixth book of *Letters to Atticus*, Cicero writes: "Unless Bibulus were wondering about a <term>triumph</term>—he who, while he was the sole guest in Syria, did not set foot out of the gate any more than he did from his own house—I would be of a calm mind. But now, 'it is shameful to be silent.'" Today, some people misuse this, thinking nothing is more shameful than silence, lest among unlettered men they should seem insufficiently learned or eloquent. Hence that precept found in Lucian's *The Uneducated Orator*: Never be silent. <note>original Greek: μηδέποτε σιωπᾶν (*mēdepote siōpān*)</note> This is because, among the ignorant, a man is considered unskilled and speechless unless he chatters perpetually.

-> The spirit of the gifts is best. <-

In gifts, the spirit is best. <note>original Greek: Ξενίων δέ τε θυμὸς ἄριστος (*Xeniōn de te thymos aristos*)</note> That is:
> Truly, in gifts, the most excellent thing is the mind of the giver.

This is a Greek <term>hemistich</term> <note>half a line of verse</note> in <term>Heroic meter</term> that has become proverbial. It signifies that in the gifts of friends, one should not look at the price of the thing sent, but rather the spirit of the sender. Just as the famous Xerxes <note>King of Persia</note> gladly accepted water scooped up in the hands of a peasant. And Christ preferred the widow's small coins to all the gifts of the rich. And someone else advises us to take in good part a tiny gift sent by a poor friend, just as if it were the greatest. Pliny, in his preface, uses a different metaphor: "But even to the gods, peasants offer milk, and many nations offer supplications; and those who do not have incense make a sacrificial offering with only salted meal." Indeed, it is most common today that those who offer a gift ask that the intention be looked at, not the thing itself. The adage is cited by Phurnutus <note>Also known as Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> in his work *On the Nature of the Gods*.

-> He knows not the difference between head and groin. <-

Those who have arrived at such a point of impudence, or rather blindness, that they make no distinction at all between what is honorable and what is shameful, are said "not to know what is the difference between the head and the groin." Among the honorable members of the body, the head holds the first place, and therefore it is rightly left uncovered; but those parts which are below the belly are covered as being "dishonorable." Juvenal says of a drunken woman:
> For what does a drunken Venus care?
> She knows not the difference between the groin and the head.

It seems to be spoken as a proverbial figure.

-> A multitude of commanders lost Caria. <-

Many generals lost Caria. <note>original Greek: Πολλοὶ στρατηγοὶ Καρίαν ἀπώλεσαν (*Polloi stratēgoi Karian apōlesan*)</note> That is:
> Many leaders destroyed Caria.

This <term>senarius</term> <note>a verse of six feet</note> warns that nothing is more destructive than the license of a multitude when no one is obeyed, but each person carries out the business according to his own whim. The Greeks call this <term>anarchy</term>, an evil almost worse than <term>tyranny</term>, than which nothing can be worse. However, <term>polyarchy</term> <note>rule by many</note> is an equal evil to that which is called anarchy.

<summary>This page discusses proverbs related to human nature and social conduct, including the paradox of the hungry belly, the ethics of speaking out vs. silence, the value of a giver's intent over the gift's price, and the dangers of disordered leadership.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Isocrates, generosity, intent, honor vs. shame, anarchy, polyarchy, Caria, Cicero, Juvenal, belly metaphor</keywords>

### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES
<page-num>542</page-num>

The same lesson is taught by that Homeric line from the second book of the *Iliad*, which itself has passed into a proverb: "The rule of many is not good; let there be one ruler" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη, εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω (*ouk agathon polykoiraniē, heis koiranos estō*)</note>. That is:

-> To have many commanders is an evil: let there be one single king. <-

For with these words Ulysses restrained the rioting soldiers, among whom was Thersites <note>Thersites was a soldier in the Greek army at Troy, often depicted as ugly and foul-mouthed, who challenged the leadership of Agamemnon</note>. Dion also used this verse of Homer when he saw Heraclides stirring up a faction. The source for this is Cornelius Nepos <note>Erasmus uses the name Æmilius Probus, who was formerly believed to be the author of Nepos's *Lives of Illustrious Men*</note>. This adage arose from the Carians, who were once very prosperous but were later reduced to such a state by civil sedition that they even became a proverb for "utility" <note>referring to "risking a Carian," an earlier adage about using cheap mercenaries for dangerous tasks</note>, as we have shown in another place.

<margin>VIII</margin>
-> A white mouse. <-

"A white mouse" <note>original Greek: μυς λευκός (*mys leukos*)</note> is found in the works of Suidas; "a bad mouse" <note>original Greek: μυς κακός (*mys kakos*)</note> is found in Diogenianus. This was said of a person who is playful or of immoderate lust. For domestic mice are most <term>salacious</term> <note>lustful or lecherous</note>, especially white ones. Aelian, in Book 12, Chapter 10, teaches the remarkable lustfulness of mice based on the testimony of various authors. Among many things, he adds that Epicrates, in some play or other, when he wanted to indicate a woman of monstrous lust, called her a "mouse-den" <note>original Greek: μυωνίαν (*myōnian*)</note>, and he cites the proverb "a white mouse" from a comedy by Philemon. From this, it seems to have become an accepted custom that among lovers' endearments—just as one uses "little sparrow," "little dove," and that sort of thing—the nickname "mouse" is also used. Martial writes:
> For when you call me "mouse," when you call me "your eyes."

<margin>IX</margin>
-> Your face counts the years. <-

This was certainly said in a proverbial style by Juvenal regarding an old woman, already <unclear>past her prime</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἔξωρῳ (*exōrō*)</note> and entirely ill-timed for the games of Venus <note>meaning she is too old for romantic or sexual pursuits</note>, but who still tried to act like a young girl through the wickedness of her words: "Your face counts the years."
That is to say, the wrinkles on your brow display the number of your years, even though lust has not yet grown old within you. This fits the fable of the crocodile who was boasting of the fame of his ancestors and his leading roles in contests; the fox replied to him in this manner: "But even if you do not say so, it appears from your eyes [or appearance] that you have been seasoned by many years." <note>Erasmus provides the Greek: ἀλλὰ κἂν μὴ σὺ λέγῃς, ἀλλ’ ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν γε φαίνῃ, ὡς ἐκ παλαιῶν ἐτῶν εἶ γεγυμνασμένος.</note> For this animal has a skin armed as if with the hardest plates against all blows. Martial says to someone who still affected to appear as a boy:
> But in your case (he says), your beard cries out against you: you are a man.

<margin>X</margin>
-> Rarer than a phoenix. <-

"Rarer than a phoenix" <note>original Greek: φοίνικος σπανιώτερος (*phoinikos spaniōteros*)</note>. This is said of things or even people who are extremely rare to find. The adage arose from the legendary phoenix bird, about which Pliny writes in Book 10, Chapter 2. He says the noble phoenix of Arabia—though I do not know if it is a fable—is the only one in the whole world, and is not often seen. It is said to be the size of an eagle, with a golden luster around its neck, while the rest of its body is purple; it has a blue tail distinguished by rose-colored feathers, and its face is adorned with crests and its head with a feathery tuft. At this point, other miraculous things are mentioned about the phoenix, but since they have no bearing on the meaning of the proverb, I leave them to be read by whoever wishes. Ovid, in the fifteenth book of the *Metamorphoses*, speaking through the persona of Pythagoras, says:

> There is one bird that restores and seeds itself;
> The Assyrians call it the phoenix. It lives not on grain or herbs,
> But on the tears of frankincense and the juice of balsam.
> When this bird has completed the ages of its life,
> Upon the branches of an oak or the top of a trembling palm,
> It builds a nest for itself with its talons and hard beak.
> As soon as it has spread cassia and spikes of smooth nard,
> And crushed cinnamon with yellow myrrh beneath it,
> It lays itself on top, and ends its life amid the fragrances.
> Then they say that a little phoenix is reborn from the father's body,
> Destined to live for just as many years.
> When age has given it strength and it can carry a burden,
> It relieves the branches of the tall tree of the weight of the nest,
> And dutifully carries its own cradle and its father’s tomb.
> Through the light air it reaches the temple of Hyperion <note>Hyperion is a name for the Sun</note>,
> And places it before the sacred doors in Hyperion's temple.

<keywords>Ulysses, Homer, Mouse, Lust, Aging, Juvenal, Martial, Phoenix, Ovid, Pliny, Leadership, Rareness</keywords>
