### SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<page-num>543</page-num>
<sig>Z 2</sig>

There exists a poem regarding the Phoenix by Firmianus Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author known as the "Christian Cicero" for his polished Latin style</note> which is not without elegance, by the Muses, nor should it be looked down upon.

-> Not even to be praised at a dinner. <-
<margin>XI</margin>
Not even to be praised at banquets <note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἐπαινετέος οὐδ' ἐν τοῖς δείπνοις (*Ouk epaineteos oud' en tois deipnois*)</note>. You could not be praised, not even at funeral feasts. This was said of a man who was utterly beyond praise. It was the custom of the ancients, especially the people of Attica, to praise the deceased with encomiums, dirges, and epitaphs at funeral banquets—which the Greeks call <term>perideipna</term>—even if the person had deserved little in life. For as Ovid says: "Envy feeds on the living; after death it rests" <note>original Latin: *Pascitur in uiuis liuor, post fata quiescit*</note>.

From this it happens that we sometimes cheat the living of the praise they deserve, while we grant even unmerited praise to the dead. Festus Pompeius teaches that in ancient times it was customary to hire women to wail at funerals, not without praises for the deceased, and to lead the way for others in their mourning; hence they were called <term>praeficae</term> <note>professional mourners</note>, as if they were "placed in charge" <note>original Latin: *praefectae*</note>. He cites the testimony of Naevius: "By my faith, I think this woman is a professional mourner, who praises the dead man so." Perhaps it was derived from this that it seems to have been an ancient custom to speak the praises of others, even the living, during comparisons. Just as in Plato, Alcibiades delivers a praise of Socrates, and in Plutarch, Callisthenes praises Alexander the Great. However, praises of that kind did not seem very distinguished when sung over wine. Nor do I think it absurd if someone refers this proverb to the custom of the ancients, whereby it was common at banquets for a lyre-player to sing of the deeds of either the gods or of famous men. This is seen in Homer at almost every banquet. Likewise in Virgil:
> Long-haired Iopas makes the hall resound
> with his golden lyre.

Nevertheless, these praises too were mostly fashioned for the favor of the listeners. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

-> To walk over into an opinion. <-
<margin>XII</margin>
What it means "to walk over into an opinion" <note>original Latin: *pedibus in sententiam discedere*</note> and what a "foot-vote" <note>original Latin: *pedaria sententia*</note> is, Aulus Gellius explained sufficiently in Book 3, Chapter 18. If one transfers this to any kind of approval of another person’s opinion, it will take the form of a proverb. For example, if someone were to say: "It is not the mark of a prudent man to walk over into his wife's opinion the moment she wishes something." Or: "It is right that the emotions walk over into the opinion of reason, not the reverse." Indeed, I walk over into your opinion "with hands and feet and my whole body." It is translated from an old custom that used to be observed whenever there was a huge crowd of voters. Livy writes in the seventh book of his first decade: "When I have finished stating my opinion to you, then those of you who are pleased by the same will pass over silently to the right side. Whichever part is larger, by that counsel we shall stand." And a little later: "Those who see these things as beneficial, come now, pass over to the right side on foot." All passed over, and followed Decius as he went through the gaps in the guard posts. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the eleventh *Philippic*: "He said, however, that if any of those who were asked after him stated a weightier opinion, he would go over to it." The same author in a letter to Lentulus: "For they perceived that many more would go over to the opinion of Hortensius than would openly agree with Volcatius." In the same place: "They went in a crowd to 'all other things' <note>meaning they voted against the motion</note>." Likewise to Plancus: "The Senate left him in a crowd and walked over to 'all other things'." This method of casting votes was called a "division" <note>original Latin: *discessio*</note>. Pliny the Younger in his letters to Hadrian says: "But when the division took place, those who had sat in the curule chairs began to go over to the opinion of Cornutus. Then those who allowed themselves to be numbered with their colleague passed over to the opposite side." He who interrupted the opinions was said to "intercede" <note>or veto</note>. Titus Livius, in Book 9 of his history *From the Founding of the City*: "When everyone, following the man with nothing but praise, walked over to his opinion on foot, an intervention was attempted for a short time." The same author in Book 5: "When they walked over into that opinion on foot, the other military tribunes said nothing to the contrary." Pliny the Elder in Book 2, Chapter 7, changed the form of the speech somewhat: "This opinion," you will say, "began to sit <note>to be settled</note>, and the learned and the unlearned crowd alike go toward it at a run." By "going to an opinion at a run," he meant to agree vehemently and precipitously; and he used "to sit" for "to be pleasing." For Flavius Vopiscus, in his life of the Emperor Aurelian, indicates that another person's opinion was also usually approved by the stretching out of hands. For he writes: "Then, with some stretching out their hands, others walking over to the opinion on foot, and most consenting by word, the decree of the Senate was established." Sallust felt something of the same in the *Catilinarian War*, when he says that Silanus, being moved afterward by the speech of Gaius Caesar, said he would walk over to the opinion of Tiberius Nero—

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
<page-num>544</page-num>

...[voted] with a word, while others assented to Caesar in various ways. Quintilian said, "To go over to an opinion with hands and feet." <note>original Latin: *Manibus pedibusque in sententiam discedere*. This refers to a full-bodied endorsement of an idea.</note> Furthermore, those who signify their agreement through their expression and gestures are said to "go over to an opinion with the whole body." The kind of voting that is carried out by stretching out the hands is called <term>cheirotonia</term> <note>original Greek: χειροτονία</note> and "to vote by hand" <note>original Greek: χειροτονεῖν (*cheirotonein*)</note> by the Greeks, a term which the Sacred Scriptures also employ. As in 2 Corinthians 8: "having been chosen by vote" <note>original Greek: χειροτονηθείς (*cheirotonētheis*)</note>. Moreover, "to subscribe to an opinion," "to subscribe to a judgment," "to subscribe to a will," "to vote for," "to vote against," and other metaphors of that kind, whenever they are drawn somewhat far from simple speech, gradually pass into the form of a proverb.

<margin>XIII</margin>
->Endure and abstain.<-

Epictetus, a philosopher of the Cynic sect <note>Though Erasmus calls him a Cynic here, Epictetus is more famously known as one of the great Stoic philosophers. The two schools shared many rigorous moral principles.</note>, embraced the universal dogmas of philosophers pertaining to the happiness of human life—which others can hardly explain in so many volumes—within two words. These have long been celebrated as proverbs by the learned, and are truly worthy of being inscribed on every wall, on every column, and engraved on every ring. They are as follows: <term>anechou kai apechou</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνέχου καὶ ἀπέχου</note>, that is, "Endure and abstain." By the first, we are warned to bear adversity bravely; by the second, to restrain ourselves from illicit pleasures. They are recounted in Aulus Gellius's *Attic Nights*, Book 17, Chapter 19. In Athenaeus, this poem is cited without the author’s name:

"A man would be called good who brings good things,
But he would also be good who bears evils well."

<margin>XIIII</margin>
->You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will ever hurry back.<-

Since I see certain things being dragged into the heap of proverbs by the Greeks with a "twisted neck," as the saying goes <note>i.e., forced or strained into the category</note>, why should I hesitate to recount those things which, besides the form of an adage, are said so gracefully that they could not be spoken more beautifully? Such is that line of Horace in his *Epistles*:

"You may drive out nature with a pitchfork, yet she will ever hurry back."

The sense is that what nature has deeply implanted and sown within us is not easily unlearned. If it ever happens by force, whether through fear, shame, or any other cause, that we take on a foreign persona, we easily return to our natural habits when the opportunity arises. Just as those who fear to sin, not out of a love for virtue but for fear of the rod; as soon as the rod is lifted, they return to their former ways. And Terence says: "If he hopes it will be secret, he returns to his natural character." The metaphor is drawn from branches which, when a pitchfork is applied, are twisted in a direction other <unclear>than</unclear> nature had placed them; when the fork is removed, they lean back toward the same spot as before. Pindar, in the eleventh *Olympian Ode*, expressed the same sentiment differently: "For neither the tawny fox nor the loudly-roaring lions could change their inborn character." <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ ἐμφυὲς, οὔτ' αἴθων ἀλώπηξ, οὔτ' ἐρίβρομοι λέοντες ἀλλάξαιντο ἦθος</note>. For no matter how much you tame a lion, it always returns to its natural ferocity; nor does a fox ever forget its native trickery, no matter how much it is domesticated. The same author says in his thirteenth *Olympian*: "It is difficult to hide one's inborn character." Likewise, Horace elsewhere:

"Take away the danger,
And wandering nature will leap forth once the reins are removed."

<margin>XV</margin>
->An aged ship will by no means sail the sea.<-

"An old ship will not sail the deep." <note>original Greek: Ναῦς παλαιὰ πόντον οὐχὶ πλώσεται (*Naus palaia ponton ouchi plōsetai*)</note>. This applies to those who, because of the weakness of age, are ill-suited for undertaking arduous tasks and sustaining dangers; they are the first to perish, overwhelmed by the magnitude of the business, and they bring into peril those whose affairs are being managed. The allegory is well-known. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus.

<margin>XVI</margin>
->If you were not my father.<-

"If you were not my father." <note>original Greek: Εἰ μὴ πατὴρ ἦσθα (*Ei mē patēr hēstha*)</note>. This was commonly said whenever people withheld a reproach out of respect or fear, leaving the rest to be inferred. It is expressed in full thus:

"If you were not my father, I would say you were not wise."

This verse is found in Sophocles' *Antigone*. For these are the words of Haemon rebuking his father Creon because he was preparing to kill his son's betrothed. Thus, whenever we wish to indicate that the opinion of an elder, a powerful person, or someone otherwise venerable does not meet our approval, yet we do not wish to oppose them directly out of respect—as if someone wished to quietly condemn an Aristotelian opinion among the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>—he would speak in this manner: "This opinion has a most serious author." # THE SECOND THOUSAND, SEVENTH HUNDRED
<sig>Z 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: dissent</meta>

<margin>Reference.</margin> For perhaps it is not right to dissent from Aristotle. Otherwise, <note>original Greek: Εἰ μὴ πατὴρ ἦσθα</note> "If you were not my father," that is, unless I were deferring to authority, I have the means to refute you. If you utter this in a shortened form, it will have even more grace. It is recorded by Diogenianus.

### XVII. The great mouth of the year

<margin>The great mouth of the year.</margin> <note>original Greek: μέγα στόμα τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ</note>. This was said whenever an especially abundant harvest of goods, or a cheaper price of grain, added spirit and freedom of speech to people who were otherwise quite timid. For peasants are accustomed to speak more magnificently and promise more generously when they have hopes of a bountiful crop. This is recorded by Suidas. It does not differ much from that other saying, "He has hay on his horns" <note>An idiom for a dangerous or temperamental person, like a bull marked with hay to warn others.</note>, or the one that says, "Sources of silver are speaking."

### XVIII. Megarian sphinxes

<margin>Megarian sphinxes.</margin> <note>original Greek: Μεγαρικαὶ σφίγγες</note>. This is what the common people used to call certain prostitutes, either because among the Greeks the effeminate are commonly called <term>sphictae</term> <note>original Greek: σφίκται, from σφίγγω (*sphingo*), meaning "to bind tight" or "to compress."</note>, or because among the Megarians a nurse is called a "sphinx," or because the manners of the Megarians were once noted for being wicked, deceitful, and a subject of popular mockery. Hence Aristophanes in *The Wasps* censures "Megarian laughter" (which has been discussed elsewhere):
<margin>"But do not expect again a joke broken in the Megarian style."</margin> <note>original Greek: πῦρ δ’ αὖ γέλωτα μεγαρόθεν κεκλασμένον</note>.
Suidas also records this little verse, though, as is his habit, he keeps the author’s name silent:
<margin>"But we have a certain Megarian machine."</margin> <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἔστιν ἡμῖν μεγαρική τις μηχανή</note>.
By "Megarian laughter" or "joke," he understands the effeminacy of the Megarians. It is recorded in the collections of Diogenianus.

### XIX. The marrow of honey

<margin>The marrow of honey.</margin> <note>original Greek: Μέλιτος μυελός</note>. This was said of a thing that was exceedingly sweet. For this reason, Ennius (as quoted by Marcus Tullius Cicero) calls Marcus Cornelius Cethegus "the marrow of Persuasion" <note>Erasmus uses the Latin *Suada*, the goddess of persuasion.</note> because of his singular sweetness of speech. For nature seems to have hidden away that which is best in the innermost parts. Thus the common expressions "In the marrows" and "To love from the marrow" <note>meaning to love from the core of one's being</note> do not differ from this proverbial image. It follows the form of "what is mine is also yours." <note>original Greek: τὶ ἐμοὶ καὶ ἐμός</note>.

### XX. To obtain better birds

<margin>To obtain better birds.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀμείνονας οἰωνῶν τυχεῖν</note>. This is said of those for whom prosperity follows after adversity. For just as among the Latins the words "bird" <note>avis</note> and "winged-one" <note>ales</note> sometimes signify not an animal, but the omen and augury itself, it is the same among the Greeks with <term>oionos</term> and <term>ornis</term>, since "sign" <note>original Greek: σημεῖος (*semeios*)</note> is not understood in the same way, as Eustathius indicates in his commentary on the first book of the *Odyssey*. Horace says in his *Odes*:
"You lead her home with an evil bird." <note>meaning an evil omen</note>
And elsewhere:
"By the bird of Maeonian song."
Homer writes in the *Iliad*, book 24:
<margin>"Do not yourself become an evil bird for me in my halls."</margin> <note>original Greek: μηδέ μοι αὐτὸς ὄρνις ἐνὶ μεγάροισι κακὸς πέλου</note>.
Again, in book 12 of the same work:
<margin>"The one best omen is to defend the fatherland with courage."</margin> <note>original Greek: Εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης</note>.
Ancient times labored under this superstition, observing the flight and meeting of birds when undertaking great tasks; nor were there lacking those who professed this as an art. Hence the college of augurs among the Romans. Today, the superstition of this profession has been almost entirely driven out among Christians, but in such a way that an almost more pestilent and complicated evil has succeeded it: namely, those who pronounce future events from the stars, and others who, feigning the inspiration of the divine, wish to be regarded as prophets by the gullible and unlearned common folk. But what is truly strange is that both types find people to deceive. For they impose themselves not only on the commoners, but even on kings and the rulers of the world.

### XXI. Another kind of oar

<margin>Another kind of oar.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἄλλο γένος κώπης</note>. This was said in the past whenever someone introduced new things never seen before; or when someone, having turned away from former habits, established a new and unusual way of life. They say this originated from the story that when Hercules sailed to the Erythean cattle, he used a lion’s skin in place of a sail, a club instead of a mast, the straps of his quiver for ropes, his bow for an oar, and finally, a large cauldron for a ship. Since this was indeed an unusual way of sailing, whenever you see...

...if the neighbors disagreed, they would shout, <note>original Greek: ἄλλω γῆν κώπης</note> "To another land with the oar!" <note>Meaning one should row away to a different shore if they cannot get along.</note> This is mentioned in Plutarch's collections.

### Noisier than burning laurel.
->XXII<-

<note>original Greek: Μείζονα βοᾷ δάφνης χλωρᾶς καιομένης</note>. That is: He shouts louder than burning green laurel. This is because laurel, when thrown into the fire while still green, produces very loud crackling sounds. For this reason, it was traditionally burned in love-spells, as if representing the complaints of a lover. As Virgil says: "Daphnis burns me, the wicked man; I burn this laurel for Daphnis."
This is recorded by Diogenianus.

### Now is the harvest of legumes.
->XXIII<-

<note>original Greek: Νῦν ὀσπρίων ἀμητός</note>. That is: Now is the harvest of legumes <note>such as beans or peas</note>. It means: "Now is the seasonable time to do this or that." For example, if someone were to advise a young man that now is the time to acquire glory, to seek out learning, or to gather wealth, they might say, "Now is the harvest of legumes." The metaphor is taken from farmers, who are most vigilant during harvest and do not let that time waste away in idleness. It is listed by Diogenianus and the Suidas.

### Now the gods are blessed.
->XXIIII<-

<note>original Greek: Νῦν θεοὶ μάκαρες</note>. That is: Now the gods are blessed. This was a phrase used by someone rejoicing or offering congratulations whenever a criminal met with a punishment worthy of their deeds. It suggests that it is both pleasing and honorable for the gods when the wicked pay the penalty. Conversely, it is considered a reproach if wicked men enjoy prosperity, according to that proverbial sentiment:
<note>original Greek: Θεῦ δ’ ὀνείδος ὦσι κακῶς εὐδαιμονεῖν</note>. That is:
It is a disgrace to God if the wicked are prosperous.
Indeed, it is from this very observation that some have concluded there are no gods at all.

### To desert one's rank.
->XXV<-

<note>original Greek: Λιπεῖν τὴν τάξιν</note>. That is: To desert one's rank or station. This is said of one who fails in his duty in any undertaking. The allegory is drawn from those who stand in a battle line, for it was a capital offense for anyone to desert the position assigned to them by the commander. Hence, the term "Deserter" is the most shameful name among military men. Plato, in his book *On Laws*, orders that <note>original Greek: τὸν καταλελοιπότα τὴν φρουράν</note>, that is, "the one who has deserted his guard-post," should be publicly shamed in the forum as a mark of infamy, as if he had betrayed the entire republic by leaving his post. Aristophanes in *The Wasps* says: <note>original Greek: φυλακὴν καταλύειν νυκτερινὴν διδάσκομαι</note>, which means:
"I am taught to desert the nightly guard."
Lucian, in his booklet *On Salaried Posts*, writes: "It is necessary that you are always seen by him, and never fail to appear, but rising at dawn you should be the first seen in his service, and you must not 'desert your rank'." Isocrates used the phrase simply in his oration *On the Peace*: "They become more infamous than those who desert their ranks and throw away their shields." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Letters to Atticus*, phrased it as "To depart from the garrison." In *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, he said, "To desert the garrison." In *On Old Age*, he said, "To depart from one's station." He was clearly translating in various ways what the Greeks call <note>original Greek: λιπεῖν τὴν τάξιν</note>. In the first book of Athenaeus, the comic poet Eubulus cites this little verse from Archilochus:
"Whoever is absent from a shared meal through idleness,
Know that such a one will also easily desert his rank in battle."
Aeschines, in his legal defense, objects to Demosthenes <note>original Greek: ὡς γεγράφη λιποταξίου</note>, meaning that he had been indicted for deserting his rank—a man we have elsewhere noted was called a <term>rhipsaspis</term> <note>original Greek: ῥίψασπιδα; one who throws away his shield in flight</note>. But Demosthenes eventually drove the man who had indicted him to his death, as Aeschines charges in the same passage. Finally, in Latin, those who do not abandon their chosen way of life are said "To remain in their own class," and those who change it are said "To desert their class."

### No use for sheep.
->XXVI<-

<note>original Greek: Προβάτων οὐδὲν ὄφελος, ἐὰν ὁ ποιμὴν ἀπῇ</note>. That is: There is no use for sheep if the shepherd is absent. The adage warns that <term>anarchy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναρχίαν; lack of leadership</note> is the most ruinous thing of all. Servants do nothing correctly unless the master is present. Students are useless whenever the teacher is away. A people is useless unless governed by the authority of a prince. ### SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
547
Z 4

<note>original Greek: προϐάτων γὰρ οὐδὲν ὄφελος, ἂν ποιμὴν ἀπῇ</note>. That is:
**For sheep are of no use when the shepherd is missing.**
Regarding the foolishness of this animal, and how useless it is to itself unless the care of a shepherd intervenes, read what we have cited elsewhere from Aristotle under the proverb, *The habits of sheep*.

->Danger in the prow seat. XXVII<-

<note>original Greek: Κίνδυνος ἐν τῇ πρώρᾳ σελίς</note>. That is: **Danger in the seat of the prow.** This is used whenever we indicate that the primary danger or the "head of the business" is in a certain place. For enemies about to capture a ship make their first assault on the prow. The *selis* is the seat or bench that was usually located in the prows, if we believe Zenodotus <note>An ancient Greek grammarian and literary critic</note>.

->Attack the one skilled in the art. XXVIII<-

<note>original Greek: Βάλ’ ἐς ἔχοντα τὴν ἐπιστήμην</note>. That is: **Throw at the one who knows the art.** This is said when someone hurls an insult at a person who knows how to hurl one back, or when someone criticizes an expert as if they were unskilled, though the critic is not superior in knowledge of the craft. The metaphor seems taken from those who throw a javelin or a stone at someone who is skilled at either dodging the blow or throwing it back at the attacker.

->Philip's rooster. XXIX<-

<note>original Greek: Φίλιππος ἀλεκτρυών</note>. That is: **Philip's rooster.** This was commonly said when someone boasted of a trivial deed as if it were a great achievement. For Alectryon <note>whose name means "Rooster"</note> was a certain general under King Philip whom Chares the Athenian defeated. It appears that Chares used to speak of this deed far too often and too insolently before the Athenian people, so that it became a common vulgar expression. It is recorded in the works of Zenodotus.

->A girl gives birth, even if the man is poorly present. XXX<-

<note>original Greek: Τίκτει κόρη ὅταν κακῶς ἀνδρὶ πῇ</note>. That is: **A girl gives birth, even when she has been poorly attended by a man.** This will be appropriate to say whenever a matter is easily accomplished according to one's wish, even if it was handled negligently or lazily. Just as a girl, because of the vitality of her age, easily carries a womb, even if she had dealings with a man who was not much of a man. It is not the same for an old woman; indeed, a woman of advanced age requires "twice the man." This fact did not escape the theologian Augustine. For he explains the question of why Abraham (according to Paul) was considered "worn out" with Sarah, yet is read to have fathered offspring with Keturah, by saying that he was worn out for the elderly Sarah, but was a man for the young Keturah. An excellent talent attains good literature even under a bad and lacking teacher. On the contrary, if the student is <term>an ass at the lyre<note>original Greek: ὄνος λύρας; a metaphor for someone completely unsuited for a specific task or art</note></term>, even the best teacher wastes his oil and labor.

->Pasetes' half-obol. XXXI<-

<note>original Greek: Τὸ πάσητος ἡμιωϐόλιον</note>. That is: **Pasetes' half-obol.** Said of something new and amazing, and very similar to stage-magic. Just as when an orator makes the same cause seem first excellent and then terrible, or when the same matter appears massive and immediately tiny. And when sophists demonstrate that the same being is both a donkey and a man. Or where someone asserts that something was done which could not have happened without magic, one may cry out: "Pasetes' half-obol!" You might also use it opportunely when certain people give a gift in such a way that they soon pull it back to themselves by some trick. They say that a certain Pasetes, a magician, earned a great reputation for his skill in magic. He used certain incantations to make it seem as if a banquet, prepared in all its parts, suddenly appeared; then, whenever he wished, everything immediately vanished. He also used to buy things frequently and pay the price, but soon the coin would be found not with the seller, but with Pasetes. Suidas relates things of this sort.

->Your chick is always small. XXXII<-

<note>original Greek: Μικρός καὶ ὁ σὸς πῶλ@</note>. That is: **Your chick is always small.** Said when someone, because of their short stature, desires to be seen as a boy for a long time. It will also suit those who, although older in age, affect to be seen as youths through the delicacies of their words. Or when, out of love, an old man calls an old woman a "little doll," and he in turn is called a "little boy," as we have noted elsewhere. A commentator on Aristophanes warns that among the Greeks, whatever was exceedingly dear to someone was usually called their "chick." We use flattering diminutive words, and thus in *The Knights*, a certain man flattering the people called them <note>original Greek: δημίδιον</note> "little-people," and therefore soon hears: "How you have become well-disposed to him from a tiny little bit of flattery!" That is, you have become benevolent toward him from such small flatteries. He calls the flatteries "small," and he in turn hears that he himself had seduced the people with much more demeaning baits than those.

->The sacrifice of the Phaselitans. XXXIII<-

<note>original Greek: Φασηλιτῶν θῦμα</note>. That is: **The sacrifice of the Phaselitans.** As if it were something cheap and without blood. Sordid...

The author is Zenodotus. Eudemus likewise writes that they perform divine rites to the god Caprus with salted meats, and he cites Callimachus as a witness of this matter. Bordering on this is the saying: *A sacrifice without smoke.*

<margin>XXXIII</margin>
### Babys plays the flute worse.

<term>Babys plays worse</term> <note>original Greek: Κάκιον Βάβυς αὐλεῖ</note>. That is, Babys sings worse. This adage is usually cast at those whose practice always trends toward the worse. Of this sort are certain orators who, the longer they speak, the more ignorantly they speak. It refers to a story of this kind: They say Babys was the brother of Marsyas <note>a satyr who challenged the god Apollo to a musical contest</note>, who did not fear to challenge Apollo himself to a singing contest. Having been defeated by the god, Marsyas was hung upside down from a pine tree and flayed alive. Then, when Apollo was preparing to destroy Babys as well, Pallas <note>the goddess Athena</note> intervened, warning that he played the flutes so unluckily and unlearnedly that he seemed entirely worthy of being ignored, saying, <term>Babys plays worse</term> <note>original Greek: κάκιον Βάβυς αὐλεῖ</note>. Moved by these words, Apollo so despised Babys that he did not even judge him worthy of punishment, but rather judged that he should be left to his own ignorance. 

The adage is also used by comparison; for example, if a mention is made of an unlearned teacher, and someone responds to a person asking about the student: <term>Babys plays worse</term>. Indeed, I would not object if someone takes "worse" <note>original Greek: κάκιον</note> here as "more miserably," so that the meaning is that Babys is more unhappy while playing unlearnedly and being a laughingstock to all than if he were removed from the scene. Athenaeus mentions this adage in book 14, showing it was usually said of those who played worse day by day. Though this passage in this author is corrupted in the common printed copies, if I am not mistaken. For we read it thus: <note>original Greek: κὶ πίων ἢ Βάβυς αὐλεῖ</note>, that is, *And Cion or Babys plays*. The occasion for the error was that a little before, when commemorating inept flute-players whom the iambic poet Hipponax had torn apart, he named Cione, Codulus, and Babys. 

In the collections which our Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous Venetian printer</note> printed, I find: <term>Babys's chorus</term> <note>original Greek: τοῦ Βάβυος χορόν</note>, used for an unorganized and poorly modulated song, and a story is added of this kind: There were two sons of the river Meander, of whom Babys was accustomed to play with a single flute, and Marsyas with two in the Phrygian fashion. Since each had his own chorus, and Babys handled the flute unskillfully, the brother [Marsyas] was so lifted up in insolence that he also despised Apollo compared to himself; after he was flayed and a similar punishment was being prepared for Babys, he was exempted from punishment by Pallas's intervention. But I truly suspect the writing is corrupted, and should read <term>Babys's hand</term> <note>original Greek: τοῦ Βάβυος χεῖρα</note>, so that it is the same as what we just related.

---

<margin>XXXIV</margin>
### A meeting of Cercopes.

<term>A meeting of Cercopes</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀγορὰ κερκώπων</note>, that is, a gathering of Cercopes, was said of a meeting-place or assembly of crafty and wicked men. For they say there were certain Cercopes in Ephesus, men born to fraudulence, who tried to deceive Jove [Jupiter] himself with sewn-up tricks. Their mother had warned them not to fall in with the "Black-buttock" <note>Melampygus</note>, which is exactly what happened. For they were later bound by Hercules <note>who was known as the 'Black-buttock' because his backside was tanned and hairy</note> near the territory of Omphale. 

Some say that certain people were called <term>Cercopes</term> <note>original Greek: κερκώπας</note>—as if "tailed ones" or monkeys—among the Ephesians and Athenians because of their impostures and evil arts, so that the meaning of this adage is the same as that which we mentioned elsewhere: *A decade of wolves* <note>original Greek: λύκου δεκάς</note>. The orator Aeschines twists this insult against Demosthenes: <note>original Greek: ὅτι μὴ ἐν τῶ ποθ᾿ ὁ κέρκωψ, ἢ τὸ καλούμενον παιπάλημα, ἢ τὸ παλιμβόλον, ἢ τὰ τοιαῦτα ῥήματα, ἂν ὐδίλῳ πρότερον. νυνὶ δ᾿ ἐξηγητὴν ἔχων λαβὼν δι᾿ πάσης κακοηθείας μεμάθηκας</note>. That is: *That he was once a Cercops, or what is called a "fine-sifting" [scoundrel], or a "back-turner," or such words—before this I did not know. But now, having found this expositor of all malice, I have learned.* 

Those two words "fine-sifting" <note>pæpalema</note> and "back-turner" <note>palimbolon</note> also seem to have been commonly tossed about as insults. Hesychius indicates that <term>fine-sifting</term> <note>original Greek: παιπάλημα</note> was said of a man <term>variegated in malice</term> <note>original Greek: ποικίλον ἐν κακίᾳ</note>. It clearly comes from the word <term>to shake</term> <note>original Greek: πάλλω</note>, and the syllable *pai* is added by duplication. And *paipallein* is to look around and scrutinize, and to leave nothing untried. Again, *paipale* is the finest part of grain shaken out from a sieve. Both the casting of lots and the cleaning of grain happen by shaking. From this, *pale* means both "lot" and "flour." Therefore, those who turn themselves into everything seem to be marked by the scoff of "fine-sifting." At the same time, I suspect a pun on the words. For *pais* sounds like "boy," and *palisuia* means "I hunt" or "I lead into nets." 

The same author explains at length what <term>back-turner</term> <note>original Greek: παλίμβολον</note> is, namely a man who is least consistent with himself but easily rolls back in the opposite direction. I suspect the insult was taken from instruments so artfully constructed that they easily snap back in the opposite direction, and from there it was twisted to apply to a man of slippery faith.

# SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<meta>catchword: you pro-</meta>

### XXXVI
### A deer-like man.

<term>A deer-like man</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐλάφου ἀνήρ; original Latin: Ceruinus uir</note>. This was once a saying used to describe a man who was full of fear and trusted more in flight than in his own strength. For the deer is a creature most swift in its course, and in the hunt, it seeks its safety through its feet. Thus, in the first book of Homer’s *Iliad*, Achilles—acting as a brave man—hurls an insult at Agamemnon as if he were a weak and cowardly man, in this manner:
"You wine-heavy sot, with the eyes of a dog but the heart of a deer." <note>original Greek: οἰνοβαρές, κυνὸς ὄμματ’ ἔχων, κραδίην δ’ ἐλάφοιο</note>
He reproaches him for his drunkenness, his impudence in seizing the rewards of others, and his "deer-like heart," because he was timid when it came to a confrontation. Aristotle, in the ninth book of his *History of Animals*, records that the deer possesses a certain natural prudence; because it cannot protect itself with strength, it accomplishes its ends through cleverness. For example, it gives birth near paths so that it might be safer from wild beasts due to the frequent presence of humans. Furthermore, after it has given birth, it immediately eats the afterbirth so that it is not discovered. Moreover, when leading the fawn to its lair, it shows and accustoms it to where it should flee if any danger threatens—Aristotle says this is usually a steep rock.

### XXXVII
### To play the Cercops.

<term>To play the Cercops</term> <note>original Greek: Κερκωπίζειν; original Latin: Cercopissare</note>. People are said "to play the Cercops" when they either act wantonly or when they flatter. The metaphor is drawn from animals that wag their tails to fawn upon someone, as Chrysippus suggests (according to the testimony of Suidas). Alternatively, it refers to those who are troublesome, who disturb and make a racket, so that the word is derived from those Lydian <term>Cercopes</term> <note>mischievous forest creatures or gnomes in Greek myth</note> whom Hercules—because they quite petulantly disturbed him while he was lying with Omphale—bound and hung from his club by his mistress's order, as we related in the adage, *Lest you fall in with Black-Bottom* <note>referring to an encounter between Hercules and the Cercopes</note>.

### XXXVIII
### Farewell, dear light.

<term>Farewell, dear light</term> <note>original Greek: Χαῖρε φίλον φῶς; original Latin: Vale charum lumen</note>. It appears this was a common saying whenever a lamp was extinguished. However, they trace it back to a story—not a particularly chaste one, yet one that must be told for the sake of instruction. They say that a certain old woman, when she was preparing to indulge her lust while naked, extinguished the lamp so that the wrinkles and filth of her body would not cause offense; as she extinguished it, she said, "Farewell, dear light." I suspect these words passed into common jest all the more because they are used in tragedies by those about to depart from life, such as Polyxena in Euripides' *Hecuba*, Iphigenia in the play of her name, Alcestis and Electra, and many others. 

Nonetheless, Plutarch, in the seventh decade of his *Table Talk*, fifth problem, indicates it was said by someone who, upon seeing his mistress coming into view (when he himself was, I believe, blinded by wine), said, "Greetings, dear light." The proverb can be adapted to various uses: either when we mean we wish to act more licentiously (for the night covers every disgrace, and since, according to Hippo, it lacks shame, it seems suited to dishonest and shameful actions, which Lucian for that reason calls "nocturnal" things. Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Assemblywomen*, when he makes a woman who wants to relieve her bowels speak thus:
"Is this not honorable everywhere at night?" <note>original Greek: Η πανταχόθι νυκτὸς ὅδ’ιν ἦν καλῶς;</note>); 
or when we leave a friend or a thing we deeply love; or when we hint at a woman whose beauty is already withered and who can only be loved in the dark: "Farewell, dear light." Or when we mean that a thing most dear to us has perished. 

Indeed, Saint Ambrose, in the homilies he wrote on the Gospel of Luke, relates a story of this kind: to a certain Theotimus, when he was suffering from a grave disease of the eyes, the doctors had forbidden him from having sexual relations with his wife; if he did so, total blindness was imminent. But he, unable to restrain his lust, could not keep himself from embracing his wife. And so, when he was already burning in the midst of the heat of Venus, and the doctors' prohibition came to mind, he said, "Farewell, dear light," meaning, of course, that he had bought that very brief pleasure at the cost of his eyes. There is a similar story in Martial about a certain Phryx, a one-eyed heavy drinker, who, when he was forbidden by doctors from drinking wine (otherwise he would see nothing at all), immediately brought the cups to his lips and said, "Farewell, eye!" You ask the outcome? 
"Phryx drank the wine; the eye drank the poison."

<term>Let the guest come who will be of use</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐξίθ’ ἐλθοὶ ὅστις ὀνήσιμ</note>. 
Theopompus, as cited by Zenodotus, writes that this adage comes from an apophthegm of King Philip...

...that you have set out. For he [Philip of Macedon], when he had overturned the city of the Thessalians and sold off the guests he found there as slaves, used to say jokingly:
"Let any guest come who will be of use." <note>original Greek: Ξενῶν ἔλθοι ὅστις ὀνήσῃ</note>
This seems to be taken from an oracle or some poet, for it is a half-line of heroic verse. The adage warns that the arrival of those who bring some benefit is finally welcome. Ovid writes:
> Though you come yourself, Homer, accompanied by the Muses,

<margin>XL</margin>
->**Parnœtes found an obol.**<-
<term>Parnœtes found an obol</term> <note>original Greek: Ὀβολοῦ εὗρε Παρνοίτης; original Latin: Obolum reperit Parnœtes</note>. This can be applied to those who have devised some new reward to entice people. They say it originated from Callistratus, a leader of the Athenian republic, who was given the nickname Parnœtes. For he established the practice that certain small coins <note>An "obol" was a small silver coin in ancient Greece.</note> should be distributed to those attending the courts and public assemblies. The mockery of the Comic poets turned this administrative change into a proverb.

<margin>XLI</margin>
->**The doors of the Muses are open.**<-
<term>The doors of the Muses are open</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀνεῳγμέναι μουσῶν θύραι; original Latin: Apertæ musarum ianuæ</note>. It will be appropriate to use this adage whenever we indicate someone of easy and ready talent, who is quick to learn the best disciplines—as if the Muses were favoring them and supplying knowledge without grudge. Conversely, those who are slower to learn could be said to study "with the doors of the Muses closed." It can also be used to say that we should not hide the gift of learning, but impart it candidly and without envy, as if "supplying light from light." This is recorded by the scholar Zenodotus.

<margin>XLII</margin>
->**The field of Mars.**<-
<term>The field of Mars</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄρεως πεδίον; original Latin: Martis campus</note>. Suidas cites this from the *Pisander* of Alexandrides. It was hurled at those who seemed endowed with military overconfidence, and who conducted business by force rather than judgment; those who used fists instead of learned words, and who settled disputes not by law but by wicked shouting. These are people for whom "justice lies in arms," whom Hesiod elegantly calls by the compound word <term>Hand-justicers</term> <note>original Greek: Χειροδίκας—those who define right and wrong by their own physical power.</note>. Furthermore, whatever a person is strong in, the Greeks call that person's "field."

<margin>XLIII</margin>
->**To fight with silver spears.**<-
<term>To fight with silver spears</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀργυρέαις λόγχαις μάχεσθαι; original Latin: Argenteis hastis pugnare</note>. Those are said to "fight with silver spears" who, when a matter cannot be settled in any other way, accomplish it through gifts and bribery. Nothing is so difficult that it cannot be unraveled by money. As was elegantly said by Marcus Tullius Cicero in his second speech against Verres: "Nothing is so sacred that it cannot be violated, nothing so fortified that it cannot be taken by storm with money." They say the proverb arose from an oracle of the Pythian Apollo, who responded to King Philip when he asked how he could achieve victory:
"Fight with silver weapons, and you will conquer all."
<note>original Greek: Ἀργυρέαις λόγχαισι μάχου, καὶ πάντα νικήσεις</note>
Clearly, the oracle was hinting that Philip should solicit certain people toward treason through bribes, and in that way, he would obtain whatever he wanted.

<margin>XLIIII</margin>
->**Archytas’s rattle.**<-
<term>Archytas’s rattle</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀρχύτου πλαταγή; original Latin: Archytæ crepitaculum</note>. This was a jab used against a person who was vehemently talkative and noisy. Archytas devised a kind of bronze rattle to give to children to play with, so that in the meantime they would not touch or break any household vessels. This is taught by Aristotle in the eighth book of his *Politics*. Suidas indicates that Archytas was a Pythagorean and the teacher of Empedocles. Although several men of this name are recorded, it is agreed that this philosopher from Tarentum was the maker of that instrument, as he is said to have wonderfully excelled in mechanics. His wooden dove is also famous, which was so balanced by mathematical reasoning that it could fly. However, Diogenes Laertius testifies in his *Lives of the Philosophers* that there was also a certain architect of this name who wrote a book on machines. Aulus Gellius also mentions the dove in his tenth book, attributing the invention to Archytas the philosopher on the authority of Favorinus. But regardless of who invented it, it is consistent that it was some kind of instrument that sounded of its own accord. From this, the term is not absurdly turned against those who, by a flaw of nature, chatter about anything, in any place, and to anyone. The Greeks call such people "talkative," "infinite-worded," "inconsequent," and "story-filled" <note>original Greek: λάλος, ἀπειροεπέας, ἀκολουθους, & πολυμύθους</note>, while the Latins call them "garrulous," "chatterers," "brawlers," "babblers," and "tonguey." Against such people, Eupolis skillfully...

...“Excellent at babbling, but most incapable of speaking.” <note>original Greek: λαλεῖν ἄριστος, ἀδυνατώτατος λέγειν</note> That is:
Outstanding and best at chattering,
But for speaking, no one is less fit.
Nor was Epicharmus <note>A Greek comic playwright and philosopher known for his pithy sayings.</note> unskillful when he said:
“Not clever at speaking, but incapable of silence.” <note>original Greek: οὐ λέγειν δεινός, ἀλλὰ σιγᾶν ἀδύνατος</note> That is:
He had no strength in the powers of eloquence,
But he suffered from an inability to keep silent.
Something similar was held among the Romans; they called it a *Citeria*. This was a certain sharp-tongued and talkative effigy <note>A puppet or automaton moved by strings.</note> which used to be carried in processions for the sake of amusement. Whence Marcus Cato, in his speech against Marcus Caecilius, says: “What more should I say then? I believe he will eventually be carried in a procession, at the games instead of a *Citeria*, and will chatter to the spectators.” Therefore, phrases of this kind will have the appearance of a proverb: “More talkative than a *Citeria*,” and “You would call a *Citeria* mute compared to this man,” and “One man could compete with many *Citerias*.”

### You throw with a plow. XLV

“You throw with a plow” <note>original Greek: Ἀρότρῳ ἀκοντίζεις</note>. That is, those who do something recklessly, not looking ahead to what the outcome will be, are said to “throw with a plow”; or those who try to harm another to their own great disadvantage. For whoever seeks to hit another by throwing a plow, so that he may indulge his anger, deprives himself of a necessary tool, the use of which he will shortly miss. This is recorded by Diogenianus <note>A Greek grammarian and collector of proverbs from the 2nd century AD.</note>. It can be seen as a metaphor taken from times of war, in which plowshares, hoes, and rakes, and other tools of farming, are refashioned into the weapons of Mars <note>i.e., weapons of war.</note>. Plutarch, in his commentary *How one should listen* <note>Erasmus likely refers to Plutarch's essay "How the Young Man Should Study Poetry." The transcription shows <unclear>σ</unclear> in the Greek title.</note>, uses it as if regarding a thing exceedingly absurd: “For neither is he who wants to throw with a plow, since he does not wish to hunt a hare with an ox, unfortunate.” <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ θέλων ἀρότρῳ βαλόμενος, οὐ γὰρ βούλεται λαγὼ κυναγεῖν, ἀτυχὴς ἐστίν</note>. That is: For he who wishes to throw with a plow and hunt a hare with an ox is not simply unlucky [but foolish].

### An Athenian reaches out his hand even while dying. XLVI

“An Athenian reaching out his hand even while dying.” <note>original Greek: Ἀττικὸς ἀπεχὴ τὴν χεῖρα κἀποθνήσκων</note>. The insatiable greed of the Athenians for seizing gifts and chasing profits gave rise to this little adage. Hence, in Aristophanes, there is a frequent joke regarding “those who expect a snack” <note>original Greek: τοὺς ὀψοδόκοντας; a term for people waiting for handouts or bribes.</note>. The author is Diogenianus.

### The Hill of Argos. XLVII

“The Hill of Argos.” <note>original Greek: Ἀργὸς λόφος</note>. This is used where someone is entangled in immense evils. It can be applied either to a place or to a business subject to various calamities. They say it originated from a certain hill named Argos, infamous for frequent homicides and robberies.

### A hungry donkey ignores the club. XLVIII

“A hungry donkey ignores the club.” <note>original Greek: ὄνος πεινῶν ῥοπάλου ἀμελεῖ</note>. This applies to those who endure any insult for the sake of their belly or profit. Aristotle records this in the third book of the *Ethics*: “Since in this way even donkeys would be brave, for when they are beaten they do not leave their food.” <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ οὕτω γε κὴ οἱ ὄνοι ἂν εἶεν ἀνδρεῖοι, τυπτύμενοι γὰρ ἐκ ἀφίσανται τῆ τροφῆς</note>. That is: For in that way, even donkeys would be brave when they are hungry, because although they are beaten, they nevertheless do not depart from their fodder. He denies that one should be considered brave who tolerates hardships for any reason whatsoever. Otherwise, donkeys would be by far the bravest, since while they are hungry, they cannot be moved from their fodder by any blows. It appears to be taken from Homer, who describes “asinine patience” quite elegantly in the eleventh book [Lambda] of the *Iliad*:
> As when a sluggish donkey, passing by a field, overpowers the boys,
> upon whose back many clubs have already been broken,
> and entering, he crops the deep standing corn; while the boys
> beat him with clubs, but their strength is childish,
> and they drive him out with difficulty only after he has had his fill of fodder.
<note>original Greek: ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ὄνος παρ’ ἄρουραν ἰὼν ἐβιάσατο παῖδας / Νωθὴς, ᾧ δὴ πολλὰ περὶ ῥόπαλ’ ἀμφὶς ἐάγη, / Κείρει δ’ εἰσελθὼν βαθὺ λήϊον, οἱ δέ τε παῖδες / Τύπτουσιν ῥοπάλοισι, βίη δέ τε νηπίη αὐτῶν, / Σπουδῇ τ’ ἐξήλασσαν ἐπεί τ’ ἐκορέσσατο φορβῆς.</note> That is:
> Just as when a lazy little donkey passes through the crops
> despite the boys, around whose back many a club
> has already rattled, and no less slowly he enters
> the deep crop; but the boys with clubs,
> believing in their effort, at last with their childish
> strength drive him from the field, when he has filled his belly with pasture.

### Either the flower of the gourd, or the gourd itself. XLIX

“Either that [the flower], or the gourd.” <note>original Greek: ἢ κείνου, ἢ κολοκύντην</note>. This is worth just as much as if you said: either death or life, or profit or loss, or victory or the opposite. The Greeks [call it] the gourd's

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES<-

...they call the flower <note>original Greek: κολυον (koluon)</note>. It is uncertain whether it will soon wither away or whether it is about to produce a gourd. Therefore, they used the flower to signify death or frustrated hope, and the gourd to signify life. Diphilus, as cited in Zenodotus, says: <margin>50</margin> <note>original Greek: ἐν ἡμέραις αὐτὸς ἑπτά σε γόρου βελω πραχᾶν κολοκύντω ἢ κρίνον (en hēmerais autos hepta se gorou belō prachan kolokyntō ē krinon)</note>. That is: "I myself, old man, wish to show you within seven days either a gourd or a lily." This means: I can bring it about that you are either restored to health or that you die. Not unlike this is the passage in Homer's *Odyssey*, book 1, where a phantom appearing to the sleeping Penelope says:
<note>original Greek: ζώει ὅγ’ ἢ τέθνηκε, κακῶν δ’ ἀνεμώλια βάζει (zōei hog’ ē tethnēke, kakōn d’ anemōlia bazei)</note>. That is:
"He still survives, or he has perished: for the truth must be spoken."
And following this imitation, Horace’s Tiresias <note>A character in Horace's Satires, based on the blind prophet of Thebes.</note> said:
"O son of Laertes, whatever I say will either happen or it will not."

### The Naked Graces.
<margin>50</margin>
<note>original Greek: Αἱ χάριτες γυμναί (Hai charites gymnai)</note>. That is, "The Graces are naked." This adage advises that we should share with our friends with candor and kindness. Or, that nothing among friends should be faked or disguised, but rather everything should be naked and simple. For the poets imagine three *Charites*, that is, Graces, as the overseers of humanity and benevolence. Horace in his *Odes* says:
"The Grace, with the nymphs and her twin sisters, dares
to lead the dances naked." The same author elsewhere says:
"And the Graces with loosened belts."
There are some who apply this proverb to the ungrateful, because the "graces" (favors) are, as it were, stripped by them, since they are always taking away some benefit and repaying nothing. Thus, it will apply to those who, by their own kindness, are reduced to poverty, giving away to friends whatever they have obtained.

### The yoke of Crobylus.
<margin>51</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κρωβύλου ζεῦγος (Krobylou zeugos)</note>. That is, "The yoke of Crobylus." It is customary to say this of a partnership between two people of equal wickedness, such as those mentioned in Martial’s *Epigrams*, book eight:
"The worst wife, the worst husband,
I wonder that you do not get along well."
The proverb is derived from a certain Crobylus, a pimp of the most villainous sort. He kept two prostitutes at home, by whose charms he lured many young men to their ruin; nor was he content with luring them, for he also robbed them by stealth. Hence, it was called "the yoke of Crobylus," either because they seemed worthy to be coupled with him as equals in wickedness, or because he kept a "yoke"—that is, a pair—of prostitutes at his house.

### Mylus hearing everything.
<margin>52</margin>
<note>original Greek: Μύλος πάντ’ ἀκούων (Mylos pant’ akouōn)</note>. That is, "Mylus listening to everything." This was usually said when someone pretended not to hear and feigned deafness, while in fact catching and listening to everything with curious ears. It seems to be drawn from a mill <note>original: mola</note>, from which spies were accustomed to observe what was happening (for <note>original Greek: μύλη (mylē)</note> means a mill to the Greeks), or from the habits of some curious man named Mylus. Zenodotus testifies that Cratinus used this adage in his *Cleobulinas*. Hesychius indicates that Mylus was a certain comic poet, and furthermore that it is the name of a fish—I believe he means the mullet <note>original: mullum</note>. Additionally, the Greeks use <note>original Greek: μύλλον (myllon)</note> to mean curved, slanted, or distorted; for he writes it with a double "l". I have spoken elsewhere of the "Carcinistrobili" <note>An adage referring to something twisted or complicated like a crab or a top.</note>. Some princes also have this breed of sycophants <note>Professional informants or flatterers.</note>, who pretend to be deaf and mute so that they may more effectively report what they have overheard.

### We ten Rhodians, ten ships.
<margin>53</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἡμεῖς δέκα Ῥόδιοι δέκα νῆες (Hēmeis deka Rhodioi deka nēes)</note>. That is, "We ten Rhodians, ten ships." This is to be hurled at those who attribute too much to their own strength. It seems to have arisen from a saying of some "Thraso" <note>A stock character name for a braggart soldier.</note> who pitted ten men against ten ships. Unless we prefer to refer it to that passage in Homer:
"And Tlepolemus, son of Hercules, both brave and great,
Led nine ships of the haughty Rhodians out of Rhodes." That is:
"Tlepolemus the Heraclide, both great and good,
Brought from Rhodes thrice three ships suited to the excellent Rhodians."

### A crooked course.
<margin>54</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κάμπιος δρόμος (Kampios dromos)</note>. That is, "A crooked course." Used whenever a matter is conducted with artifice and dissimulation. Or whenever we tend toward one goal while pretending another, and proceed by certain "burrows" <note>Metaphorical tunnels or hidden paths.</note> and circuitous routes to that which we are trying to achieve. The adage is taken from a type of race which was called "crooked" because it was performed with specific bends and turns. As...

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES<-

...for others, force and speed were most effective, but in this, skill and method carried more weight. Virgil describes a race of this kind in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*:

> They rode out in equal ranks, and in groups of three
> They broke their columns into separate bands, and again, when called,
> They reversed their course and bore hostile weapons:
> Then they entered into other runs and other retreats.
<note>original Latin: "Olli discurrere pares, atq; agmina terni / Diductis soluere choris, rursusq; uocati / Conuertere uias, infestaq; tela tulere: / Inde alios ineunt cursus aliosq; recursus."</note>

And a little later:

> As once in high Crete the Labyrinth is said to have had 
> A path woven with blind walls, and a deceptive trap 
> With a thousand ways, where the signs of following
> Were deceived by an undetected and irreversible error.
<note>original Latin: "Vt quondam Creta fertur Labyrinthus in alta / Parietibus textum cæcis iter, ancipitemq; / Mille uijs habuisse dolum, qua signa sequendi / Falleret indeprehensus & irremeabilis error."</note>

This may seem to be borrowed from sailors who, when the winds blow against them, sail crosswise.

### Not even Jupiter pleases everyone. LV
Theognis in his *Sentences*: "For not even Zeus pleases everyone, whether he brings rain or holds it back."
<note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ Ζεὺς οὔθ' ὕων πάντας ἁνδάνει οὔτ' ἀπέχων.</note>
That is:
> Not even Jupiter himself,
> Whether it rains or not, pleases every single person.
<note>original Latin: "Neq; Iupiter ipse, / Siue pluat, seu non, unicuique placet."</note>

Even today, the common people say that no one can be found who satisfies everyone. For different things please different people. And as Horace says:
> Three guests seem to me almost to disagree,
> Demanding very different things with their varying palates.
<note>original Latin: "Tres mihi conuiuæ, propè dissentire uidentur, / Poscentes uario multum diuersa palato."</note>

Pindarus in his eighth *Olympian Ode*: "Nothing will be equally pleasant among men." 
<note>original Greek: τερπνὸν δ' ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἴσον ἔσσεται οὐδέν.</note>
Namely, because different things delight different people, and "to each his own is beautiful." Similar to this is that Gospel saying which we mentioned at the beginning of this work when we spoke of the dignity of proverbs: "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed for you, and you did not mourn." 
<note>original Greek: ηὐλήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ὠρχήσασθε. ἐθρηνήσαμεν ὑμῖν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκλαύσατε. Reference to Matthew 11:17 and Luke 7:32.</note>

### You will not persuade me, even if you do persuade me. LVI
"For you will not persuade, even if you should persuade."
<note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ πείσεις, οὐδ' ἂν πείσῃς.</note>
That is:
> Indeed, you would never persuade me,
> Not even if you actually did persuade me of that.
<note>original Latin: "Haud etenim persuaseris unquam, / Nec si etiā persuaseris istud."</note>

This was spoken in a proverbial pattern by Aristophanes. It is a type of hyperbole by which we signify something that is most impossible <term>adynaton</term>. It is just as if you were to say, "I will not believe it even if I see it."

### Pylaea and Tyttygias know these things. LVII
"Both Pylaea and Tyttygias know these things."
<note>original Greek: οἶδέ τε πυλαία ταῦτα καὶ τυττυγίας.</note>
By this riddle, the ancients used to attack wealth acquired through evil arts. Tyttygias was a certain kidnapper who used to sell slaves and the property of others, which he had carried off by theft, in Pylaea (which is a place in Arcadia), and through this profit he emerged wealthy. The author is Zenodotus.

### Polycrates feeds his mother. LVIII
"Polycrates feeds his mother."
<note>original Greek: Πολυκράτης μητέρα νέμει.</note>
They draw this adage from history, telling how Polycrates, the tyrant of the Samians, took a census of the mothers of soldiers who had died in war and handed them over to the wealthier citizens to be supported, commending each one with these words: "I give this woman to you as a mother." 
<note>original Greek: Ci ταύτην μητέρα δίδωμι.</note>
Zenodotus does not assign a specific use for the proverb; therefore, anyone is free to guess to which sentiment it might most rightly be applied. I think it can be used not inconveniently whenever someone is overly generous or dutiful in recommending friends—or when someone seeks to do good for another at someone else’s expense, so that while others are spending the money, he himself contributes nothing besides a few dutiful words. This custom remains common today among princes; for they command that their servants, who are now useless for courtly service due to age, be fed by monasteries or by the wealthier citizens.

### You praise yourself. LIX
"You praise yourself."
<note>original Greek: Σαυτὴν ἐπαινεῖς.</note>
An iambic half-line which is chanted when someone praises themselves and acts as their own trumpeter. In full, it is expressed thus:
"You praise yourself, woman, just like Astydamas."
<note>original Greek: Σαυτὴν ἐπαινεῖς ὥσπερ Ἀστυδάμας γύναι.</note>
Astydamas was a certain actor, the son of Morsimus. A statue was decreed to be placed in the theater for him...

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES<-

...had happened because, in performing the *Parthenaeus*, he had conducted himself both diligently and skillfully. Therefore, he wrote an inscription himself in which he included his own praises and brought it to the public assembly so that, once approved, it might be added to his statue. However, by the votes of the people, it was decreed that such an annoying inscription should not be carved. This matter was first stirred up by the jokes of comedians and later turned into a proverb, so that even now the common people say, not without wit, that the neighbors of a man who praises himself are malicious. This is recorded by Zenodotus. The inscription that Astydamas wrote for his own statue still exists in the works of Suidas:

> Would that I had lived in their time, or they in mine,
> Those who are thought to bear the first prize for a pleasing tongue.
> Truly, I would have been judged as a rival without restraint.
> But now they excel through time, which is not followed by envy.
<note>original Greek: "Εἴθ' ἐγὼ ἐν κἀνοις γενόμην, ἢ κἀνοι ἂμ' ἡμῖν..."</note>

Since Conrad Goclenius—a public professor of the Latin language at the Academy of Leuven, a young man learned to the fingertips in both languages, and a marvelous craftsman in both types of writing, whether you prefer prose or poetry, who will one day hold a chief place among the foremost leaders of erudition—has elegantly rendered these verses into Latin, there is no reason why I should attempt to translate them otherwise. Goclenius’s Latin verses are these:

> Would that they had lived with me, or I among them,
> To whom belongs the honor of a sweet-speaking tongue:
> I would indeed have held the first prizes without a contest,
> But now those things take them away, against which envy has no power.
<note>original Latin: "Vixissent utinam mecum illi, aut inter ego illos..."</note>

Julian also used this in a certain letter to Basil: "For I have praised myself just like Astydamas."
<note>original Greek: ἐπήνεσα γὰρ ἐμαυτὸν ὥσπερ ὁ Ἀστυδάμας.</note>

->A chorus of Syrbene.<-

<margin>LX</margin>
A "chorus of Syrbene" <note>original Greek: Συρβηνῆς χορός</note>. This was once a common saying regarding disorganized and tumultuous dances. For some think *syrbe* is a word that swineherds use toward pigs, from which *syrba* is also used for a tumult. Furthermore, Hesychius interprets *syrba* as "with noise." The same author soon adds that *syrbe* sounds to the Greeks like a flute-case, from which a flute-player is called a *syrbineus*, or one who is tumultuous. Athenaeus uses it in his 15th book: "When the banquet was full of noise, he asked, 'Who was that chorus of Syrbenians?'" For so Athenaeus consistently reports this word. He uses it again on the very next page of the same book; and a little later, quoting Clearchus, he teaches what a "chorus of Syrbenians" is: namely, one in which everyone sings whatever they please, and no one listens to what the leader of the chorus prescribes, nor to the one who teaches how it is necessary to sing. We once saw a playful little comedy performed at Paris <note>Lutetia</note> in which many people sang together, but with the harmonies so tempered that everything sounded dissonant. This was carefully arranged by a master of music; for an unskillful person could not have done the same. The metaphor seems to be drawn from that discordant grunting of pigs. It can be applied appropriately to men who are discordant and quarrelsome among themselves, or where a discordant symphony of unskilled singers offends the ears.

---

->The old age of Hesiod.<-

<margin>LXI</margin>
"The old age of Hesiod" <note>original Greek: Ἡσιοδίου γῆρας</note>. A long-lived and vigorous age was so called. For there is a certain epigram of Pindar concerning the longevity of Hesiod of this sort:

> Hail, you who reached youth twice, and twice encountered the grave,
> Hesiod, holding the measure of wisdom for men.
<note>original Greek: χαῖρε δὶς ἡβήσας, καὶ δὶς τάφου ἀντιβολήσας...</note>

Now, when he says that he "reached youth twice," I believe he signifies extreme old age, as if returning to childhood, according to the proverb we have mentioned elsewhere: "Old men are twice children." Furthermore, in saying he was "buried twice," he alludes, if I am not mistaken, to the history mentioned by Plutarch in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*. When he had been killed in Locris due to a suspicion, and his corpse cast into the sea, a school of dolphins took it up and brought it to Rhium. When the Locrians were performing a sacrifice there according to custom and recognized the fresh corpse of Hesiod, they set all else aside and searched for the authors of the murder; having caught them, they threw them alive into the sea and burned their houses. They buried Hesiod in Nemeum. But they hid the tomb because of the Orchomenians, who, warned by an oracle, were trying to carry the man's remains away to their own land. From this it is likely that, just as many cities claim the birth of Homer, so both the Nemeans and the Orchomenians claim the tomb of Hesiod for themselves. Unless we prefer to interpret "buried once" as when he was cast into the sea. Therefore, reader, see whether instead of *antibolesas* ("encountered") one should read *antipolesas*, which admits the genitive case when it means to obtain or acquire.

->SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY<-

### He has tasted the lotus.
<margin>LXII</margin>
<margin>λωτὸν ἔφαγον.</margin> <note>original Greek: "I ate the lotus."</note> That is: *You have tasted the lotus.* This was said of those who remained too long in foreign lands, as if they had forgotten their way home. You might also aptly use this against those who, once they have tasted a single dishonorable pleasure, cannot be called back to their former pursuits. The expression is taken from the story of the Lotus-eaters <term>Lotophagi; a legendary people in the Odyssey</term> mentioned by Homer in the ninth book of the *Odyssey*. He tells how the companions of Ulysses, having tasted the lotus herb among those people, refused to return to the ship unless driven back by blows.

<margin>But they gave them the lotus to taste.</margin>
<margin>And whoever of them ate the honey-sweet fruit of the lotus,</margin>
<margin>No longer wished to bring back word, nor to return.</margin>
<margin>But they wished to stay there with the Lotus-eaters,</margin>
<margin>Feeding on the lotus, and to forget their homecoming.</margin>
<note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ σφι δόσαν λωτοῖο πάσασθαι..."</note>

->that is,<-

> Indeed, they offered them the lotus to be tasted.
> But whichever of them had tasted the friend
> and sweet fruit of the lotus, no longer cared
> to send back any news, nor did he strive to return.
> Rather, they wished to remain there with the Lotus-eaters,
> forgetting their return, intent on picking the shoots of the lotus.

As for what the lotus is: Dioscorides, in his first book, teaches that it is the same as the "celtis" tree. Pliny also writes of it in his thirteenth book: "So sweet is the food there that it gave its name to both the people and the land; it is a land too hospitable, causing strangers to forget their own country." There is also a herb of the same name, which is itself very pleasing to the palate, about which Theophrastus writes extensively in the fourth book of *On Plants*, chapter nine. We also find this proverb in the collections of a certain more recent author; because it seemed not without charm, I did not mind adding it here.

### From the mouth of the wolf.
<margin>LXIII</margin>
<margin>Ἐκ λύκου στόματος.</margin> <note>original Greek: "From the wolf's mouth."</note> That is: *From the wolf's jaws.* This is used when something is recovered contrary to all hope, which seemed plainly to have perished—much like when money is snatched from robbers or a greedy tyrant and is recovered by some unexpected chance. For things recovered in such a way are usually more pleasing. So Horace says in his *Odes*: "Or the kid snatched from the wolf." It is a well-known metaphor. Diogenianus records the adage. It seems to have originated from a fable of Aesop, which tells of a crane who, having agreed on a fee, inserted her head into a wolf's throat to pull out a bone that was stuck there. When she demanded her reward, she was mocked by the wolf, who said it was reward enough that she had withdrawn her head from a wolf's mouth unharmed.

### Good men are prone to tears.
<margin>LXIIII</margin>
<margin>Ἀγαθοὶ δ' ἀριδάκρυες ἄνδρες.</margin> <note>original Greek: "Good men are very tearful."</note>
->that is,<-

> But whoever is upright, he is a man much prone to weeping.

This was said of those who were easily moved to mercy and could be swayed by prayers. For those who feel pity are said to "weep over" a situation.
<margin>Ovid writes,</margin>
> Things at which even wild beasts might have wept.

Similarly, Horace calls Pluto "un-weeping" <term>illachrymabilem; meaning cold or pitiless</term> because he is swayed by no prayers:
> Not even if you try to appease the un-weeping 
> Pluto with three hundred bulls for every day 
> that passes, my friend.

And Virgil’s Dido, accusing Aeneas of hardness of heart, says:
> Did he groan at my weeping? Did he turn his eyes?
> Did he, overcome, shed tears, or pity the one who loved him?

It can also be applied to Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was known as the "Weeping Philosopher" because of his melancholy view of human life.</note>, who was accustomed to follow human affairs with perpetual weeping. In contrast, we call hard and inexorable people "adamantine," "iron-hearted," or "having hearts of horn." One might also twist this to mean that good men almost always deal with poverty and are forced to endure much. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus.

### Bocchoris.
<margin>LXV</margin>
Bocchyris or Bocchoris—for I find both spellings. Plutarch, in the *Life of Demetrius*, calls him Bocchoris, noting that a precise judgment is commonly called "the judgment of Bocchoris." He was a king of the Egyptians, of such noted and incorruptible justice in deciding lawsuits that if people wanted to signify someone was remarkably just and upright, they would call him a "Bocchoris"—just as you might call a man a Rhadamanthus or a Minos <note>Rhadamanthus and Minos were legendary Greek kings who became judges of the dead in the Underworld.</note>. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Garrulity*, testifies that they tell...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of King Bocchoris of Egypt from the previous page, specifically regarding his reputation for wisdom and a famous legal judgment attributed to him.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
<margin>A a</margin>

...a story was frequently told about this man, that since he was by nature grave and stern, the goddess Isis was accustomed to send an asp to him. This snake would coil around his head and provide shade from above, so that, awed by this omen, he might judge rightly. This adage is recorded by Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>. It can also be said of those who do not pronounce judgment on any matter rashly. For they say this king was not accustomed to pass sentence unless the case was already fully understood and grasped through certain arguments. And yet, a certain judgment of this Bocchoris was criticized by the courtesan Lamia. A certain young man in Egypt was wasting away with love for a little prostitute named Thyonis. But she demanded a huge payment for a single night. Meanwhile, it happened that the young man dreamed at night that he was having an affair with Thyonis. Having seen this in his sleep, he was freed from his love and ceased to be a nuisance to the harlot. When she found out what had happened, she summoned the young man and demanded the promised fee. When they could not agree, they went before the judge Bocchoris. Having heard the case, he ordered that the young man should bring as much money in a small vessel as she had demanded, and while Thyonis was present and looking on, he should wave it back and forth with his hand, so that she might grasp at the shadow—since a dream is rightly compensated by a shadow. But the courtesan Lamia criticized this judgment as unfair: "By a dream," she said, "the young man was freed from the desire for sex, but the shadow did not free Thyonis from the love of money." This is found in Plutarch’s *Life of Demetrius*.

### The camel dances.
<margin>LXVI</margin>
Whenever someone attempts to do something unbecomingly and, as they say, "against the grain" <term>invita Minerva; literally "with Minerva unwilling," meaning against one's natural talent or inclination</term>, it was said that "the camel is dancing." For instance, if someone who is naturally severe and gloomy should affect to seem elegant and festive, they are doing violence to their own nature and character. Saint Jerome cites this under a child’s name and hurls it at Helvidius <note>an author Jerome considered unlearned</note>: "We laughed," he says, "at the proverb; we saw the camel dancing." Jerome is mocking the man's foolishness, who, although he was a total stranger to the Muses, nevertheless wanted to be considered eloquent.

### A dog to its chains.
<margin>LXVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Κύων ἐπὶ δεσμά"</note> That is: *A dog to its chains.* This was said whenever someone threw themselves into servitude or into some misfortune. It is taken from the behavior of dogs who, in their ignorance, offer themselves up to be bound. The author is Zenodotus. Hesychius indicates that "An ox to its chains" <note>original Greek: "Βοῦς ἐπὶ δεσμά"</note> is said with the same meaning.

### A Chian compared to a Coan.
<margin>LXVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Χῖος πρὸς Κῶον"</note> That is: *A Chian compared to a Coan.* This was said of a wildly unequal comparison. For in the game of dice <term>tali; ancient dice made of knucklebones</term>, the throw called the "Chian" corresponded to the "one" (the lowest), while the "Coan" corresponded to the "six" (the highest). What the Greeks call the Chian, we call the "dog" <note>the *canis* or lowest throw</note>; and what they call the Coan or the "sixer," we call the "six." Furthermore, just as the Coan was among the lucky throws, so the Chian was among the unlucky. Hence Persius writes: "His wish was to know what the lucky six would bring, and how much the ruinous 'little dog' <margin>would scrape away.</margin>"
However, the "six" seems to be lucky in itself, but is usually considered unlucky if a "dog" (a one) is added to it. For so Martial says: "Nor does the 'six' shake our ivory box when the 'dog' is with it."
If this is true, the adage will apply not only to a comparison of unequal things, but even to opposing things. For example, if someone compares a commoner to a king, it is "a Chian to a Coan." If one compares a youth to an old man, it is a matter of contrariety, not just inequality. Zenodotus, Hesychius, and Suidas mention this adage, except that Suidas has "a saying of blame" <note>original Greek: "ῥητὸν ψόγου"</note> instead of "for blame" <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ ψόγου"</note>. Whether that was committed by a scribe's error, or whether an inner and outer part of the die is to be understood, I leave to the learned to investigate. Meanwhile, there is an allusion to these peoples, as the morals of both were not without a bad reputation, but especially those of the Chians. Thus it would be similar to that other proverb: "A Cretan against a Cretan."

### Hunger is the best seasoning.
<margin>LXIX</margin>
*Hunger is the best seasoning.* This is celebrated among the sayings of Socrates. With this quote, he mocked the luxury of the Athenians, who tried to make food taste good to the palate with various delicacies and laborious sauces, when hunger provides that best of all, being both the finest and the cheapest seasoning. For nothing is eaten with more pleasure than that which is eaten by a hungry man. Even today, the common proverb remains in use: "Hunger makes even raw beans taste like sugar." Antiphanes, in the works of Stobaeus, says:
<note>original Greek: "Ἀγαθὸν ὁ λιμὸς γλυκέα πλὴν αὑτοῦ ποιεῖ"</note> That is:
> Hunger makes all things sweet, except itself.

What hunger does for food, thirst does for drink. For Darius, in his flight, although he had drunk turbid water fouled by corpses, said he had never drunk anything more pleasant. Naturally, he had never before drunk while so thirsty. Xenophon expresses the same sentiment in the fourth book of Athenaeus.

<summary>This page explores several ancient proverbs regarding justice, natural aptitude, and the relative value of things, featuring a famous legal anecdote about King Bocchoris and the origins of the "hunger is the best sauce" idiom.</summary>
