<meta>This page continues the discussion of proverbs related to appetite and the necessity of hunger as a seasoning, concluding a section likely started on the previous page before moving into new adages concerning vanity, imitation, and seeking unnecessary trouble.</meta>

# SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY 557

<note>original: "Xenophon"</note> Xenophon says, "It is sweet for the hungry man to eat barley-cake and cress, and sweet for the thirsty man to drink water drawn from a river after he has parched his throat." <note>original: "ἡδὺ μὴ μᾶζαν καὶ κἀρδαμα φαγεῖν πεινῶντι, ἡδὺ δ' ὕδωρ αὐασαμένῳ ἐκ ποταμοῦ δίψαντα πάυ"</note> In the same place, he relates a rather witty story about Socrates, who was frequently accustomed to walk before his house until late in the evening. When people asked him what he was doing there, he replied, "I am preparing my relish <term>obsōnium: a side-dish or seasoning, here used metaphorically for appetite</term> for dinner." Regarding Dionysius—who expressed distaste for the "black broth" they served at the Spartan communal meals—the cook replied that it was no wonder he disliked it, since the "seasonings" were missing: namely, the exercise of the wrestling ground and the race performed before dinner. I have mentioned this elsewhere. This proverb either originated with Socrates or was a common saying used by him. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, says: "I would say that which I hear Socrates saying—who places pleasure in no category of goods—that for you, hunger is the seasoning, and thirst is the seasoning for your drink." We may add some grace to this proverb if it is applied more broadly: for instance, to the study of letters, which is all the sweeter the more vehemently the letters are "thirsted" for. Also, rare usage commends pleasures.

---

### LXX. The door of Phanus.

<margin>ἡ Φάνη θύρα. i. Phani ostium.</margin>
This was sung as a refrain whenever someone had guarded something in vain: for example, if it happened that a man's wife was corrupted by adultery even though he had guarded her with great jealousy. They say it originated from a certain usurer named Phanus; or as others say, a blind man, who had obstructed the door of his pantry in such a way that it could not be opened without a noise, yet it was opened by a servant and the provisions were carried off. Others relate that this Phanus had a wife of questionable loyalty; because he suspected her of adultery, he closed the courtyard doors so that they could not be opened without a creaking sound. However, since she received her lover through the roof-tiles, the neighbors said jokingly, "The door of Phanus." This phrase later passed into common speech. I do not know if this is the same as what Eustathius <note>a 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop</note> mentions in the last book of the *Odyssey*: "The door of Phanias," named after a certain Phanias who pretended to have a great force of wealth hidden at home.

---

### LXXI. Either Philo "Philonizes," or Philo "Platonizes."

Saint Jerome, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers*, also records Philo the Jew, who attained such eloquence and all manner of Greek erudition, and so expressed the Platonic majesty and abundance in his speaking, that Jerome calls him a "second Plato." He testifies, moreover, that among the Greeks, it was commonly said of them: "Either Plato Philonizes, or Philo Platonizes." <note>original: "ἢ πλάτων Φιλωνίζει, ἢ Φίλων πλατωνίζει"</note> That is: Either Plato imitates Philo, or Philo imitates Plato. A work of his survives in which he treats the lives of several illustrious Hebrews, beginning from Abraham. However, he treats them not so much for historical knowledge as for the instruction and rule of living: namely, drawing everything into moral allegories, for which reason he should be read especially by theologians. His style is both clear and sublime, manifesting something divine, just as Plato’s does. He delights in symbols and the mysteries of numbers, which is itself a familiar trait of Pythagoras and Plato. He adapts everything to the instruction of character, not differing from Plato in this regard. This proverb can be applied through allegory to any two people who are exceedingly similar to one another. For this very saying was meant figuratively rather than literally, since it is well established that Philo lived long after Plato. Otherwise, it may be used proverbially in a negative sense: as if someone were to say, "Either Africa 'Cretizes' <note>implying both are liars</note>, or Crete 'Africizes'"; or "Galba was 'Neronizing,' or Nero was 'Galbanizing'." Similar to this figure of speech is that saying of Plato's (as Aristides says) in the *Polymnestus*: "Republics will be happy only if either kings philosophize, or philosophers rule." <note>original: "Εἰ μὲν, ἢ οἱ βασιλεῖς φιλοσοφήσουσιν, ἢ βασιλεύσουσιν οἱ Φιλόσοφοι"</note>

---

### LXXII. The Lydian man had no business.

<margin>Ἀνδρὶ λυδῷ πράγματα οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλ' αὐτὸς ἐξελθὼν ἐπρίατο. i. The Lydian man had no business, but he went out and bought some for himself.</margin>
This was commonly said when someone, impatient with leisure, brings trouble and turmoil upon himself. Plutarch seems to have alluded to this in his work *Against Colotes*: "But it seems to me that just as that Lydian, Epicurus opens up against himself not just one door, but hedges himself in with the greatest and most numerous difficulties." <note>original: "Ἐμοὶ δὲ δοκεῖ καθάπερ ὁ λυδὸς ἐφ' αὑτῷ ἀνοίγειν οὐ θύραν μίαν, ἀλλὰ ταῖς πλάσαις ἢ ἀρχείαν καὶ μεγίςαις ἐπεμβάλλειν τὸν Ἐπίκουρον"</note> It is taken from Croesus, King of the Lydians, who was previously happy and enjoyed most flourishing circumstances, but provoked Cyrus against himself; defeated by him, he fell into the greatest calamities. The author of this is Zenodotus.

---

### LXXIII. Never look at an old man's...

<margin>Ἀνδρὸς γέροντος μή ποτ' εἰς πυγὴν ὁρᾷν. That is,</margin>
Do not ever, I say, look into the backside of an old man.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES
<page-num>558</page-num>

That is: Do not demand from anyone that which they are unable to provide. It is like someone asking a philosopher for eloquence, an orator for a precise method of logical deduction, or an old man for the flexibility and cheerful spirit of a youth. The metaphor <note>Erasmus is likely finishing a discussion of an adage involving "milking a he-goat" or a similarly crude anatomical impossibility mentioned in earlier collections</note> is too crude for me to wish to interpret it; yet it is also too obvious for there to be any need. This is recorded by Zenodotus.

->Amaea has found Azesia.<-
<margin>LXXIIII</margin>

*Amaea sought out Azesia.* <note>original: "Ἀμαῖα τὴν Ἀζησίαν μετῆλθεν"</note> That is: Amaea has come to Azesia. This was commonly said of a thing that has been sought and desired for a long and long-continued time. The scholar Didymus is our authority that among the people of Troezen, Ceres <note>Demeter</note> is called Amaea, and Proserpina <note>Persephone</note> is called Azesia. The story is well known regarding Proserpina being abducted by Pluto to the Elysian fields, and Ceres searching the whole world for her daughter. This is recorded by Plutarch in his collection of Alexandrian proverbs.

->To receive someone like a hero on a shield.<-
<margin>LXXV</margin>

*Rather, like a hero on a shield I wish to welcome you.* <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ἥρως ἐν ἀσπίδι ξενíσαí σε βούλομαι"</note> That is: Indeed, I wish to receive you as a guest just as a hero does upon his shield. This was a common saying used when someone, relying on their own skills or good deeds, tried to deserve well of their friends. It is derived from the fact that in ancient times, heroes, living constantly in arms, spent their lives as if upon a shield; and if their friends needed anything that could be provided by arms, they provided it promptly, being rich in virtue alone. In Homer, heroes are received upon ox-hides, and in Virgil,
King Evander receives Aeneas on the skin of a shaggy lion.
Furthermore, shields in the past were covered with such hides.

->Jupiter's sandal.<-
<margin>LXXVI</margin>

*The sandal of Zeus.* <note>original: "Τὸ Διὸς σάνδαλον"</note> That is: Jupiter’s slipper. This was said ironically of someone who wanted to seem like a great personage because of their familiarity with some prince; for example, if someone is arrogant and fierce because he is the royal cook, or the Emperor's bodyguard, or the Pope's barber, it will be aptly called "the sandal of Jupiter." However, nothing prevents it from being adapted to things as well: such as if someone admires a royal horse or garment, as the common people are accustomed to do, for no other reason than that it belongs to the king. Suidas cites this from the playwright Eupolis.

->Light has dawned.<-
<margin>LXXVII</margin>

When a better hope for affairs begins to be shown, people say that "light has dawned." Euripides in his play *Orestes*:
*And a light for my troubles and yours.* <note>original: "Καὶ φῶς ἐμοῖς καὶ σοῖς κακοῖς"</note>
This was said regarding Menelaus, from whose arrival they hoped for some remedy for their misfortunes. Marcus Tullius Cicero in his first *Philippic* says: "A certain light seemed to be offered, with not only the kingdom we had endured but even the fear of a kingdom removed." Furthermore, Marcus Varro testifies in the second book of *On the Latin Language* that "light" was a sign of a favorable omen among the ancients. For he thinks that the "morning" <term>mane: the morning or early day</term> was named from the fact that in ancient times they called "good" *manum*. Following this sort of religious custom, the Greeks also, when a lamp is brought in, are accustomed to say, "Good light." <note>original: "φῶς ἀγαθόν"</note> We likewise exchange favorable greetings when a lamp is brought. For they interpret "light" as "life." Hence the phrases, "To break off the hated light" <note>meaning to die</note> and "It wearies me to look upon the vaults of heaven."
Euripides in *Iphigenia in Aulis*:
*To look upon this light is sweetest for men.* <note>original: "Τὸ φῶς τόδ’ ἀνθρώποισιν ἥδιστον βλέπειν"</note>
And among the Greeks, those who are alive are said simply "to see the light." <note>original: "βλέπειν φῶς"</note> The Egyptians represented life by the symbol of a lamp: because they believed life was nothing other than a fire nourished by moisture, like the liquid of oil.

->The wolf flees the eagle.<-
<margin>LXXVIII</margin>

*The wolf flees the eagle.* <note>original: "Λύκος ἀετὸν φεύγει"</note> This is used when an imminent danger cannot be avoided. For since the eagle is winged, the wolf flees in vain. It is recorded by Diogenianus, and Zenodotus also mentions it. Neither of them indicates the origin of the proverb. Indeed, I have never heard that eagles are a nuisance to wolves.

->The wolf hurries before the shout.<-
<margin>LXXIX</margin>

*The wolf hastens before the cry.* <note>original: "Λύκος πρὸ τῆς βοῆς σπεύδει"</note> This is used when someone conscious of a crime is afraid on his own accord before he is accused. Just as a wolf, as soon as it has snatched its prey, immediately hastens to flee, lest it come into danger when the shout of the country folk is raised. The author is Diogenianus.

# SECOND THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY
### SEVENTH HUNDRED
<page-num>559</page-num>
<header>SECOND THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Aa 4</sig>

->They ask to snatch a lamb from a wolf.<-
->LXXX<-

A certain pimp in Plautus's *Poenulus* says: "They ask to snatch a lamb from a wolf; they are talking nonsense." <note>original: "Lupo agnum eripere postulant"</note> This is said whenever someone tries in vain to recover prey once a rapacious person has laid hands on it. For it seems wicked to hope that a wolf would let go of a lamb once it has been seized. This is similar to what we have said elsewhere: "From the wolf's mouth." <note>original: "ἐκ λύκου στόματος" (ek lykou stomatos)</note>

->He who knows not the way to the sea, etc.<-
->LXXXI<-

Plautus in the *Poenulus* says: "He who knows not the way by which he may reach the sea, ought to seek out a river as a companion for himself." <note>original: "Viam qui nescit, qua deueniat ad mare, eũ oportet amnẽ quærere comitem sibi"</note> That is, he who cannot finish a matter conveniently must finish it by whatever means necessary. It can also be adapted to this sense: he who is not wise by his own wit should obey others who seem to have more wisdom. It can likewise be used thus: He who is ignorant of the proper way of living should set before himself those whose lives have been praised. For a river, even if it leads through long, winding paths, nevertheless eventually leads to the sea, since it flows into it. Similar to this is: "He who is ignorant of the way employs a staff-bearer." <note>original: "Qui uię ignarus est, uirgiferũ adhibet"</note> Cato the Censor, speaking against those who were constantly canvassing for magistracies, used to say quite skillfully that they were "just like those who always seek to travel the road with lictors, lest they wander." <note>original: "καθάπερ οἱ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀεὶ μετὰ ῥαβδούχων ζητεῖν πορεύεσθαι, μὴ πλανηθῶσι"</note> In other words, they were no different from people ignorant of the path who always wanted to walk with staff-bearers so they wouldn't get lost. For, according to custom, a lictor or someone carrying a rod <note>A "virga" or rod was a symbol of authority carried by the attendants of Roman magistrates</note> would precede a magistrate.

->Willing, yet with an unwilling mind.<-
->LXXXII<-

"Willing, yet with an unwilling heart." <note>original: "Ἑκὼν ἀέκοντί γε θυμῷ" (Hekon aekonti ge thymo)</note> That is, willing, but only with a reluctant spirit. This is a Homeric half-line from the fourth book of the *Iliad*. It should be said when someone feigns that they do not want what they actually desire, or vice versa. Terence used a similar figure of speech in the *Andria*: "You were compelled by your own will." <note>original: "Tu uoluntate coactus es tua"</note> Sometimes it is said of someone who is wavering and uncertain in mind, as in Euripides' *Hecuba*:
"Both willing and not willing." <note>original: "ὁ δ' ἤθελον τε καὶ οὐκ ἤθελον"</note>
It is also among the secret proverbs of the Hebrews: "The sluggard's 'I want' and 'I don't want'."

->The shadow of a vulture.<-
->LXXXIII<-

"A vulture's shadow." <note>original: "γυπὸς σκιά" (gypos skia)</note> This was said of a man of no value. It is recorded by Diogenianus. To me, it seems to fit better when applied to "legacy-hunters" <note>haeredipetae: people who flatter the wealthy in hopes of being mentioned in their wills</note> or otherwise rapacious people who gape after prey. It corresponds to that other saying: "If you are a vulture, wait for the corpse."

->Present, he is absent.<-
->LXXXIV<-

<margin>Present, he was absent</margin> "Present, he is traveling abroad." <note>original: "παρὼν ἀπῆν" (paron apen)</note> This should be said of one who does not notice the things being said because his thoughts are occupied with other matters. Hence, when we order people to be attentive, we usually speak to them thus: "Be here," and "Do this," and "Attend with your minds." Even today, people commonly say of someone traveling in thought that they are "not at home, but out." Terence says in the *Eunuchus*: "So that you become absent while present with that soldier." <note>original: "Cum isto milite præsens, ablens ut fies"</note> That is, present in body, but removed in mind. On the other hand, those who love are present even when absent; as Virgil says of Dido in the fourth book:
"Absent, she hears and sees him who is absent."
<margin>Theodoretus</margin> Theodoret of Cyrus, in the first book of his *Cure for Greek Maladies*, quotes from Heraclitus of Ephesus: "Stupid people, when they have heard, are like the deaf; the proverb bears witness to them that though present, they are absent." <note>original: "Ἀξύνετοι ἀκούσαντες κώφοις ἐοίκασι, φάτις αὐτοῖσιν μαρτυρεῖ, πάρεοντας ἀπεῖναι"</note> Likewise, Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
<margin>You always gape at the speaker, but your mind, though present, is traveling abroad.</margin> That is:
"You always gape at those speaking, but
Your spirit is abroad, and your mind, though present, is absent."

->I shall be washed together.<-
->LXXXV<-

<margin>I shall wash alongside</margin> "I shall be washed together." <note>original: "παραλοῦμαι" (paraloumai)</note> This was commonly said when someone worms their way into the company of another, or when someone admits another into their company—such as when a poorer person wishes to avoid expense. Suidas says it was once the custom for the rich to bathe together with the poor; because the poor did not have their own equipment like strigils, sponges, oil-flasks, and such things, they would use the equipment of the rich. The same author cites Aristophanes from the *Anagyrus*: "But it is necessary for everyone to wash together and to let the poor be." <note>original: "ἀλλὰ πάντας χρὴ παραλοῦσθαι, καὶ τοὺς ἀπόρους ἐᾶν"</note> That is: it is right for everyone to wash together and omit the sponges. It suggests that the poor would gain this advantage by entering the bath with the rich: they could save their own sponges. From this, it seems to me it could be neatly said when someone treats some trivial convenience—which they provide without any personal disadvantage—as if it were a huge favor.

<vocab>Plautus, Poenulus, Homer, Iliad, Terence, Andria, Euripides, Hecuba, Diogenianus, Virgil, Theodoret of Cyrus, Heraclitus of Ephesus, Aristophanes, Suidas, proverbs, adages</vocab>

<summary>This page explores adages concerning the futility of reclaiming lost items from the greedy, the necessity of following guidance when lost, and various expressions for distraction and social maneuvering in ancient contexts like the public baths.</summary>
<keywords>futility, guidance, Cato the Censor, lictors, ambivalence, legacy-hunting, distraction, public baths, social etiquette, ancient authors</keywords>

--- Page 678 ---
<meta>This page continues the seventh century of the second thousand (Chiliad) of Erasmus's *Adagia*. The opening sentence concludes a discussion from the previous page regarding empty honors or trivial favors.</meta>

Just as if a Cardinal grants an empty title of familiarity to someone—which does no harm to the one who grants it, but is of some benefit to the one who receives it—it will be rightly said, "he is clipping" <note>original: "ψαλίζει" (psalizei). This refers to cutting or trimming, perhaps implying a small "snip" of favor.</note>. One manuscript has "I am submerged together" <note>original: "ψαλύνομαι" (psalynomai)</note>, as if to say "I am drowning with you."

<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
->In the manner of a pine tree.<-
In the manner of a pine <note>original: "πεύκης τρόπον" (peukes tropon)</note>, that is, in the fashion of a pitch-pine. When someone is utterly destroyed, root and branch, so that they cannot be restored by any means, they are said to be ruined "in the manner of a pitch-pine." For they say that a pitch-pine, once cut down, does not sprout again. Staphylus <note>A Greek historian of the 3rd century BCE.</note> mentions this proverb, as cited by Diogeniano; Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> also mentions it.

<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
->The spear of Procris.<-
The javelins of Procris <note>original: "Πρόκριδος ἀκόντια" (Prokridos akontia)</note>. This is said of those who, as if with unerring weapons, achieve whatever they set their minds to. It is taken from a very famous fable told by Ovid in the seventh book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>Erasmus uses the Latin title *Transformationum*.</note> concerning Cephalus, who, having thrown an unerring javelin, killed his wife Procris, thinking she was a wild beast. The opposite of this is that line from Horace:
> The bow will not always strike whatever it threatens.
That is, you will not always achieve what you desire.

<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
->The dogs of Promerus.<-
The dogs of Promerus <note>original: "προμερὸς κύων" (promeros kyōn)</note>. This was commonly said when someone, by a strange turn of fate, suffered punishment at the hands of those they had once harmed. Promerus was a certain royal official. He held the tragic poet Euripides in extreme hatred, having been reported by him to the king at some point for I know not what reason. Consequently, he later set some fierce dogs upon the poet, by which he was devoured and died. Therefore, whenever a powerful person who has been offended suborns and sends subordinates to cause you trouble, you might seasonably say: "The dogs of Promerus." it is consistent with what is said in another place, "the dog's justice" <note>original: "κυνὸς δίκη" (kynos dike)</note>. It is recorded by Diogeniano.

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
->While holding office, listen to both the just and the unjust.<-
A ruler should listen to both the just and the unjust <note>original: "Ἄρχων ἄκουε καὶ δικαίως κἀδίκως" (Archon akoue kai dikaios kadikos)</note>. That is:
->O Prince, listen equally to things unfair and fair.<-
They say this adage is taken from the elegies of Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker and poet.</note>, even though this line is an iambic trimeter. It advises that one who is engaged in handling the duties of the Republic should be most patient with his ears, and should be accustomed to hearing both good and bad with an even mind; nor should he be easily moved from the right path by either the praise or the insults of the people. This agrees with that line of Sophocles in *Antigone*:
> But whomsoever the city has appointed, him it is necessary to hear,
> Both in small things and just things, and their opposites.
It can also be adapted to what a certain Roman Emperor is read to have said: "In a free state, tongues likewise ought to be free." <note>This sentiment is often attributed to Tiberius or Augustus.</note> Indeed, it is neither strange nor a great thing if princes permit the people to say what they wish, since they themselves are free to do what they wish. Furthermore, the common people are accustomed to judge the deeds of princes in various ways: what one approves, another condemns. A prince, however, ought to be of a greater mind than to think such voices should be seized upon or monitored; let him look only to what is of use to the republic. To this pertains the saying of Alexander, to whom, when someone reported that there were those who spoke ill of him, replied: "It is kingly to hear ill when you have done well."

<margin>XC</margin>
->Lightning from a basin.<-
Lightning from a basin <note>original: "Ἀστραπὴ ἐκ πυέλης" (Astrapē ek pyelēs)</note>. This refers to the empty threats of those who are unable to cause harm. For the flash which is produced in a kind of imitation of lightning by the vibration of shining vessels, or reflected from water, has no power to hurt and only terrifies children. Even today they have certain darts which, when vibrated in the sun, imitate lightning; but that is not the lightning "which strikes mountains and seas," as Pliny says. Diogeniano records the proverb. Augustine alluded to it (or whoever the author is) in the book *On the Five Heresies*: "Let not the crowd of enemies, nor the appearance of those at war, nor weapons shining like glass terrify us"—though I think it should read "Glassy things" <note>original: "Vitra"</note>.

<margin>XCI</margin>
->From empty husks.<-
But you make a threshing of grain from pure husks <note>original: "Ἀτὰρ ἐκ καθαρῶν ἀχύρων πεπνίκας σιτίον" (Atar ek katharon achyron pepnikas sition)</note>. That is, you have undertaken a sterile and fruitless labor. The adage arose from farmers, when poorly grown crops bring nothing into the granaries except stalks and husks. It is recorded by Diogeniano.

<meta>The catchword at the bottom is "Atre," likely beginning the next adage.</meta>

# SECOND CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<note>page 561</note>

### The eyes of Atreus.
<margin>XCII</margin>
*Atreou ommata* <note>original: "Ἀτρεὼς ὄμματα"</note>, that is, the eyes of Atreus. This was said of a grim and savage expression. For Atreus was depicted with such eyes in tragedies—he was the man who, because his wife had been defiled by adultery, served his brother Thyestes his own children to eat at a banquet.

### More silent than Hipparchion.
<margin>XCIII</margin>
*Aphonoteros Hipparchion* <note>original: "Ἀφωνότ. Ἱππαρχίων"</note>, that is, more silent than Hipparchion. This is used when someone suddenly falls silent just when their voice is most expected. This not infrequently happens to certain people who are about to speak in a public assembly: their voice sticks in their throat as if they were suddenly struck dumb. They say this happened to Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, famous for his eloquence</note>, a man who was otherwise extremely eloquent in public circles. This adage would therefore apply to such a situation. It is said that there were once two preeminent lyre-players among the Greeks, Hipparchion and Rufinus. When they were about to compete against each other in the solemn games, which were held every ten years among the people of Iuliopolis, it happened that Hipparchion, disturbed by the noise of the theater, fell silent. This incident passed into a common proverb. The authority for this is Zenodotus.

### Love of money will capture Sparta, and nothing else.
<margin>XCIIII</margin>
*Ha philochrematia spartan heloi, allo de ouden* <note>original: "Ἁ φιλοχρηματία σπάρταν ἑλοῖ, ἄλλο δὲ οὐδέν"</note>. That is:
One hunger for gold shall capture and subdue Sparta,
->And nothing else besides.<-
This refers to those who can be conquered by money alone, though they are otherwise invincible. The adage arose from an oracle given to Alcamenes and Theopompus, the kings of Sparta: that the Spartans would only be defeated when they began to hold gold and silver in high esteem. This corresponds to the famous saying of Philip, King of the Macedonians, who thought that no fortress was so well fortified that it could not be captured, provided an entrance could be found for a donkey laden with gold. It also matches the myth of Danaë, whom no guard could protect from the assault of gold <note>Referring to Zeus visiting her as a shower of gold</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions this in the second book of *On Duties*, and Plutarch mentions it in his *Laconic Sayings*.

### It does not befit a leader to sleep through the whole night.
<margin>XCV</margin>
Among the many verses of Homer which were once celebrated as proverbs, Macrobius <note>A Roman provincial of the early 5th century, author of the Saturnalia</note> testifies that we should especially include the one found in the second book of the *Iliad*:
*Ou chre pannychion heudein boulaephoron andra* <note>original: "Οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα"</note>. That is:
It is not worthy of a leader to sleep throughout the entire night.
The proverb advises that vigilance and care are most suitable for princes, as they carry such a great burden of business on their shoulders. Hence Virgil also depicts his Aeneas as either staying awake while others are sleeping or indulging in pleasure, or at least he wakes him up and portrays him as thoughtful, sober, and weighing future events in his mind:
> But pious Aeneas, turning many things over through the night.
And again:
> Aeneas, can you prolong your sleep in such a crisis?
And yet again:
> Are you awake, Aeneas, scion of the gods?
> Be awake.
A famous example of this was provided by Epaminondas, that great Theban general. Indeed, when the Theban citizens were indulging rather freely in drinking and enjoying pleasures on certain festival days, he alone remained awake and sober, inspecting the weapons and walking the city walls. When asked why he did this, he replied that he stayed "sober and wakeful so that the others might be allowed to be drunk and sleep" <note>original: "νήφειν καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖν, ὅπως ἐξῇ τοῖς ἄλλοις μεθύειν καὶ καθεύδειν"</note>, as Plutarch records in his essay *To an Uneducated Ruler*. Furthermore, the lines we just cited from Homer are spoken to Agamemnon by a dream-figure taking the form of Nestor. The full verse goes like this:
> Are you sleeping, son of the battle-wise Atreus, tamer of horses?
> It is not worthy of a leader to sleep throughout the entire night,
> To whom the people are entrusted, and who has so many cares.
In the tenth book of the *Iliad*, Homer again depicts Agamemnon alone as awake while the others sleep:
> The other leaders of the Achaeans by the ships
> Slept all night long, overcome by soft sleep,
> But not Agamemnon, son of Atreus, shepherd of the people.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES

"Sweet sleep held him, though many things were stirring in his mind." <note>original Greek: Ὕπνος ἔχε γλυκερὸς, πολλὰ φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντα.</note> ->that is,<-
But the rest of the leaders of the Greeks throughout the whole night
Slept, their limbs overcome by peaceful slumber.
But sweet sleep did not hold the son of Atreus, Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
As he turned many things over in his heart.
<note>Erasmus is quoting from Homer's *Iliad*, Book 10, lines 1-4. The "shepherd of the people" is a common Homeric epithet for a king.</note>

In a very similar way, Homer depicts Jupiter as wakeful in the second book of the *Iliad*:
"The other gods and horse-crested men
Slept all night long, but sweet sleep did not hold Zeus,
For he was pondering in his mind." <note>original Greek: Ἄλλοι μέν ῥα θεοί τε... Ἀλλ' ὅγε μερμήριζε κατὰ φρένας.</note> ->that is,<-
Then sleep held all the others, both gods and men,
Throughout the night. But the son of Saturn alone was sleepless,
Turning things over in his worried heart.

Plutarch relates in the same commentary <note>Plutarch's essay *On the Necessity of Not Borrowing*</note> that we just cited, something neither foreign to this proverb nor unworthy of mention: namely, that it was the custom of the Persian kings to always have a certain chamberlain whose duty it was to enter the royal bedchamber in the morning and wake the king with these words: "Arise, O King, and care for the matters which Mesoromasdes <note>The Greek form of Ahura Mazda, the supreme deity in Zoroastrianism</note> wished you to care for." <note>original Greek: Ἀνάστα ὦ Βασιλεῦ, καὶ φρόντιζε πραγμάτων, ὧν σὲ φροντίζειν ὁ Μεσορομάσδης ἠθέλησε.</note> That is: "Rise, king, and attend to the business which Mesoromasdes commanded you to attend to." But if a prince is learned and prudent, he has no need for such a chamberlain to remind him; rather, reason itself will always sound something like this in his heart: "Be careful," and "He must not sleep all night." <note>Erasmus refers back to the earlier adage about a leader's duty.</note> Plato, in the seventh book of the *Laws*, commends vigilance in many ways, especially in a ruler. I will transcribe his words: "When a ruler is awake in cities at night, they are fearsome to the wicked, to enemies, and to citizens alike." <note>original Greek: Ἐγρηγορότος δ' ἄρχοντος... i. Principes qui noctu uigilant...</note> And a little earlier in the same passage: "For no one who is sleeping is worth anything." <note>original Greek: Καθεύδων γὰρ οὐδεὶς, οὐδενὸς ἄξιος.</note> Those who act lazily are as if they were sleeping; sometimes they succeed, but rarely. Hence Pindar says correctly in the tenth *Olympian Ode*: "Few have attained joy without labor." <note>original Greek: Ἄπονον δ' ἔλαβον χάρμα παῦροι τινές.</note>

<margin>XCVII</margin>
->I cannot carry a goat, and you impose an ox upon me.<-
Plutarch in the commentary titled *On the Necessity of Not Borrowing*: "In the proverb it would be ridiculous: 'I cannot carry the goat, yet you put an ox on me.'" <note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς παροιμίας ἔσαι γελοῖον, οὐ δύναμαι τὴν αἶγα φέρειν, ἐπιτίθετέ μοι βοῦν.</note> ->that is,<-
You burden me with a bull, when I cannot even carry a kid.
This is used when someone refuses a lighter burden, only to have something much more intolerable imposed upon them. For example, if someone, out of impatience with poverty (for this is how Plutarch applies it), entangles themselves in <term>usury</term> <note>The practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates</note>, a burden that even the wealthy can scarcely tolerate.

<margin>XCVIII</margin>
->For they never drove off my oxen, nor my horses.<-
"For never yet have they driven off my oxen, nor indeed my horses." <note>original Greek: Οὐ γὰρ πώποτ' ἐμὰς βοῦς ἤλασαν, οὐδὲ μὲν ἵππους.</note> ->that is,<-
For they never stole my horses and oxen from me.
This seems to be used as a proverbial figure of speech for: "They never harmed me, or did me any injury." It is used when we deny that we have any reason to hate this or that person. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Avoiding Usury*: "And do not think I say these things to declare war against the moneylenders; for they never drove off my oxen, nor indeed my horses." That is: "For they never took anything of mine." The further this is removed from simple speech, the more proverbial it becomes. It is taken, however, from the first book of Homer's *Iliad*, where Achilles, arguing with Agamemnon, denies that he has any reason to wage war against the Trojans, except to do Agamemnon a favor:
"For I did not come here on account of the Trojan spearmen
To fight them, since they are not at fault toward me.
For never yet have they driven off my oxen, nor my horses,
Nor ever in fertile Phthia, the nourisher of men,
Did they ravage the harvest." <note>original Greek: Οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ Τρώων ἕνεκ' ἤλυθον... Καρπὸν ἐδηλήσαντο.</note> ->that is,<-
I did not come here for the sake of the Trojans, to
Wage war with them; for I have not been harmed by them.

<header>THE SECOND THOUSAND, SEVENTH HUNDRED</header>

For they never drove off my horses or my oxen;
Nor did they ever ravage the fields of Phthia, fertile in crops and men.
<note>original Latin: "Nunquam etenim uel equos mihi subduxere bouésue: / Nec Phthies unquam segetumq; uirumq; feracis / Sunt populati agros." These lines are from Homer's *Iliad*, Book 1, where Achilles argues he has no personal quarrel with the Trojans.</note>
This expression is derived from the custom of the ancient age, in which, since the life of mortals was still pastoral, the primary cause of war was the driving away of livestock. Homer indicates this elegantly in the eighteenth book of the *Iliad* <note>Erasmus marks it as sigma (σ), the 18th letter/book</note> when depicting the shield of Achilles:
> And apart from the people sat two scouts,
> Waiting for when they might see the sheep and the curved-horned cattle.
> These soon appeared, and two shepherds followed with them,
> Delighting in their pipes, and they foresaw no guile.
> But the scouts, seeing them beforehand, ran upon them, and quickly then
> They cut off the herds of cattle and the beautiful flocks
> Of white sheep, and they killed the shepherds as well.
<note>original Greek: τὴν δ' ἐπ' ἀπάνευθε δύω σκοποὶ εἴατο λαῶν... κτείνον δ' ἐπὶ μηλοβοτῆρας.</note>
And the rest that follows. Lest anyone complain that these verses have been neglected, we have translated them thus:
> Then, far from these, two scouts of the people
> Keep watch, if by chance they might see flocks of sheep or cattle.
> But these are immediately present, and behind them follow
> Two shepherds, soothing their hearts with reed pipes,
> Ignorant of the snare; against them, those others by arrangement soon
> Run forth, and the herds of oxen and the snow-white flocks
> They strike down, having slain the shepherds themselves.
<note>Erasmus provides his own Latin verse translation of the Homeric Greek, which is here rendered into English.</note>

->**XCVIII**<-
->**Happy is he who owes nothing.**<-
<note>original Greek: εὐδαίμων ὁ μηδὲν ὀφείλων. Latin: Felix qui nihil debet.</note>
A sentiment celebrated among the Greeks; anyone who has made the dangerous trial of what it is to be bound by debt will easily say it is twice true. He who has not experienced it should unroll Plutarch’s commentary *On Avoiding Usury* <note>original Latin: De uitandis usuris. A treatise by Plutarch on the miseries of borrowing money at interest.</note>, and he will easily recognize how wretched it is to be in debt. For what is more calamitous than to blush so often, to "rub the face" <note>A Roman idiom (perfricare faciem) meaning to cast off shame or harden oneself to embarrassment</note> so often, to flee, to hide, to lie, to dissemble? Now to act the suppliant, now to be demanded of; to be publicly called out, avoided, pointed at with a finger; in short, never to be your own master? For debt brings these and many other inconveniences with it. There exists a Greek epigram on this sentiment under the name of Automedon, of this sort:
> Happy first is he who owes nothing to anyone,
> Then he who is unmarried. Third, he who is childless.
> But if some madman marries, let him be grateful if he buries
> His wife immediately, after receiving a large dowry.
> Knowing these things, be wise. Leave it to Epicurus to seek in vain
> For the "void," and what the "monads" <note>A term for fundamental units or "ones"; Erasmus is mocking abstract philosophical pursuits in the face of practical misery.</note> are always doing.
<note>original Greek: Εὐδαίμων πρῶτον μὲν... καὶ τίν' ἀεὶ μονάδων.</note>

->that is,<-

> He who owes to no one is the most fortunate.
> Next to him is the bachelor: the third will be the childless man.
> But if anyone is so insane as to take a wife, to him
> This matter will finally bring welcome rewards:
> If by chance it happens that, having received a grand dowry,
> He immediately carries his wife to the tomb.
> Having learned these things, you will be wise; let Epicurus search in vain
> For where the void may be, and what the units shall become.

Plutarch, in the little book titled *On the Necessity of Not Borrowing* <note>original Greek: πῶς δεῖ τὸν μὴ δεῖν δανείζεσι</note>, writes that among the Persians there were two primary sins: first to be in debt, and next to lie. For they judged that these two were linked, because those who are burdened by debt are more often forced to lie. What Plutarch relates is also found in the first book of Herodotus.

->**XCIX**<-
->**At the snap of a finger.**<-
Those who command something rather arrogantly and haughtily are said to signal "at the snap of a finger." St. Jerome, in his epistle to the monk Rusticus, used this against a certain supercilious and disdainful man, who, when about to speak, would command silence with a snap of his little finger; then, with similar haughtiness, he would bring forth individual words at intervals, so that you would think he was sobbing rather than speaking. This gesture seems to have belonged to masters nodding to their servants for some humble service. Martial, in his third book, writes against Zoilus:

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages. The previous page concluded a discussion on the burdens of leadership and pastoral causes of war in Homeric times. This page begins with metaphors for subtle signals and transitions into a series of sayings regarding "the third to the Savior," drawing heavily on Greek ritual and political history.</meta>

The Eunuch knows the signals of the snapping finger. <note>original: "Digiti crepantis signa nouit Eunuchus." This refers to the practice of masters summoning slaves with a snap of the fingers.</note> Likewise in the *Distichs*:
> When I am called by the snap of fingers, and the servant delays,
> O, how often has the pillow become my mistress!
<note>original: "Cum poscor crepitu digitorum, & uerna moratur, / O quoties pellex culcitra facta mea est." From the *Distichs of Cato*, a collection of moral advice popular in the Renaissance.</note>

Marcus Tullius Cicero in the third book of *On Duties*: "Therefore, if a good man possessed such power that, by snapping his fingers, his name could creep into the wills of the wealthy, he would not use this power—not even if he were absolutely certain that no one would ever suspect him." There is a similar idea regarding the "nod and refusal of Jupiter," which Pliny cites in his *Epistles* from Homer. <note>Refers to the irresistible power of a divine command.</note> And those who finish a business with the slightest effort are said "to achieve it by a nod." Likewise, those who are promptly obedient are said "to comply with every nod."

<margin>C</margin>
### He provokes the sow.

He provokes the sow. <note>original: "συ δεινᾷ" (sy deina); this is likely a corruption of the Greek for "You provoke the sow."</note> This was said of one who is greedy for brawls. For a wild sow, when provoked, charges directly at the one who provoked it. For those skilled in hunting tell us that if anyone provokes a sow with a leveled spear, even if it was already chasing someone else, it will immediately turn its course and lunge at the provoker, not even flinching at the spear point.

-> THE EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND THOUSAND <-

<margin>I</margin>
### The third for the Savior.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, in a classical architectural setting.</image-desc>
The third for the savior. <note>original Greek: "Τὸ τρίτον τῷ σωτῆρι."</note> Proclus Diadochus, in his commentary on the three parts of the soul—following Plato's division—and on the four kinds of virtues, made use of this adage in these very words: "But these having been released, and the part of the soul distinguished according to its essence, one must say, as they say, the third to the savior." <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλὰ τούτων ἀπολυθέντων... τὸ τρίτον τῷ σωτῆρι φατέον." Proclus was a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> Proclus means that after two parts are completed, a third remains: namely, the manner in which the four virtues can be related to those three parts of the soul. Proclus seems to have imitated Plato in the *Charmides*: "Again then, I said, let us consider the third to the savior as if from the beginning." <note>original Greek: "πάλιν τοίνυν... τὸ τρίτον τῷ σωτῆρι ὥσπερ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐπισκεψώμεθα."</note> He seems to have alluded to the same thing, though more covertly, in the third book of the *Laws*: "But the third savior, seeing your government still fuming and spirited, cast the power of the Ephors upon it like a curb." <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ τρίτος σωτὴρ ὑμῖν... τὴν τῶν ἐφόρων δύναμιν."</note> He explains that the Republic of the Spartans was tempered in three ways to prevent it from breaking out into tyranny. First, a second family was added from which kings could be chosen; for in the beginning, it was only permitted from one. Second, the authority of the twenty-eight elders was set against the power of the nobles and princes, which held equal weight with the king in the most serious matters. Finally, the magistracy of the five Ephors was established, whom the king was forced to obey. He believes all these things were provided by divine providence for the safety of the state, and therefore he calls it the "third savior." 

The adage is taken from the sixth Isthmian hymn of Pindar, in whose work we read about the third cup of Jupiter the Preserver in this manner: 
<margin>For the third</margin> 
"To the Olympian Savior, to pour a libation for Aegina with honey-voiced songs." <note>original Greek: "Σωτῆρι περσαíνοντας... κατασπένδεν μελιφθόγγοις ἀοιδαῖς."</note> One must understand the word "mixing-bowl" <term>crater</term> <note>a large vessel used to mix wine and water.</note>. The sense of these verses is roughly this: Pindar hopes that at some point an Aeginetan may win the Olympic games, so that it may happen that they mix a third cup to Jupiter the Savior, not without praise for the victor and for Olympian Jupiter. By "mixing-bowl," he means either simply the one used at victory banquets, or "a mixing-bowl of songs," <note>original Greek: "κρατῆρα τῶν ὠδῶν"</note> just as elsewhere he says, "the sweet mixing-bowl of clear-sounding songs." <note>original Greek: "γλυκὺς κρατὴρ ἀγαφθέγκτων ἀοιδᾶν."</note> In that place, the commentator on Pindar shows that in ancient times it was the custom that in banquets the first cup was mixed for Olympian Jupiter, the second for the heroes, and the third for Jupiter the Savior. As a witness of this matter, he cites Sophocles in the *Nauplius*:
> Zeus, taker-away of sorrow, and the libation 
> Of the third cup to Zeus the Savior.
<note>original Greek: "Ζεῦ παυσίλυπέ τε καὶ Διὸς σωτηρίῳ / σπονδὴ τρίτου κρατῆρος."</note>
<margin>He also cites Aeschylus in the *Epigoni*:</margin>
> Libations first indeed to Zeus of timely marriage 
> and to Hera; then the second mixture 
> I distribute to the heroes; then the third, a libation to 
> the Savior Zeus of Dicte.
<note>original Greek: "λοιβὰς Διὸς μὲν πρῶτον... εἶτα τρίτον Διὸς τοῦ σωτῆρος δικταίαν λίβα."</note>
That is, the libations of Zeus of timely marriages first, and of Hera; then the second cup... 
<meta>Catchword: pocu (beginning of the word "poculum," meaning cup or drink).</meta>

<summary>Erasmus explores metaphors for subtle communication and then details the "Third to the Savior" adage, explaining its roots in Greek ritual libations and its application by Plato to describe the stabilizing "third" element in the Spartan government.</summary>
<keywords>finger-snapping, Cicero, Spartan constitution, Ephors, Plato, Pindar, Zeus the Savior, libations, mixing-bowl, Sophocles, Aeschylus, Proclus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek ritual customs as metaphors for life. The previous page ended with a discussion of the proverb "He provokes the sow," describing those who seek out conflict. This page transitions into a detailed explanation of the ritual of "the third cup to Jupiter the Savior," used as an adage for reaching the most important or final part of a task.</meta>

### [The third cup to Jupiter the Savior] <note>This is a continuation of the adage from the previous page, regarding the ritual of three libations.</note>

I grant a cup to the heroes. Then, in the third place, the desirable drop of Jupiter the Savior. He adds to this that the cup is called "of the Savior" <note>original: σωτῆρος (sōtēros)</note> because, up to this point, drinking remains within the bounds of sobriety and does not harm the mind. If anyone should progress beyond this, the matter would seem to turn toward lust and intemperance. This is according to the saying of Asclepiades found in Apuleius: "You consider that the first bowl belongs to thirst, the second to pleasure, the third to drunkenness, and the fourth to madness." This same cup "of Jupiter the Savior" is called "complete" <note>original: τέλειον (teleion)</note>, either because the limit of drinking ends here, or because this number is thought to be the most absolute among all, as it possesses a beginning, a middle, and an end. For this reason, it is most fittingly adapted to divine matters; Plato refers it to the soul as being divine and, for that reason, consisting of a triad.

Even the fact that they dedicated the first and last bowl to Jupiter, and the middle one to the heroes, is not without theological reasoning. First, the middle place was appropriate for heroes, either because, according to Plato’s opinion, they were of a middle condition between those highest gods "who inhabit Olympus," <note>original: οἳ ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι (hoi olympōn echousi)</note> as Homer says—whom Plato considers to be minds subject to no bodies—and us, who are burdened with bodies and therefore subject to passions and death. For the Platonists attribute bodies to daemons <note>In the ancient sense, "daemons" were intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil.</note>, though not of the same kind as ours, but rather aerial. St. Augustine testifies that he was of this opinion in his book *On the Nature of Daemons*, and in several other places. Or it is because, according to the fables of the poets, demigods are of a composite and middle origin, from one divine parent and one human parent—such as Hercules from Alcmene and Jupiter, or Castor and Pollux from Leda and Jupiter. Furthermore, they understand Jupiter to be that supreme mind embracing all things at once, so that he is the beginning and the end of all; for that reason, they began their drinking with him and ended with the same. Aristophanes mentions "Jupiter the Savior" more than once in *Plutus*, as in this passage:

> It seems to me that I should let Jupiter the Savior
> Be well, and remain here in this place hereafter.
<note>original Greek: τοῦ δὴ Διὸς τοῦ σωτῆρος κἀυτός μοι δοκῶ / χαίρειν ἐάσας ἐνθάδ' αὐτοῦ καταμένειν.</note>

The commentator notes that there was a temple in Athens dedicated to "Jupiter the Savior," <note>original: τοῦ Διὸς σωτῆρος (tou Dios sōtēros)</note> whom some also call "the Liberator" <note>original: ἐλευθέριον (eleutherion)</note>. Athenaeus also mentions Jupiter the Savior in the second book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>A famous ancient work titled *The Scholars at Dinner*.</note>, adding that it was once the custom that as soon as the food was set out, unmixed wine was poured, by which they declared how great the power of the "good god" was. Then, when each person had diluted the wine according to his own judgment, they would first speak the name of "Jupiter the Preserver," implying that wine thus tempered could be drunk safely and without harm. Likewise, in the eleventh book, he teaches that after dinner, once hands were washed, the cup of "Jupiter the Preserver" was usually brought in—which was the same as the one called "of the good daemon." He cites Diphilus as the authority, who wrote in his *Sappho*:

> Archilochus, receive this washing-cup
> Full of Jupiter the Savior, the best god.
<note>original Greek: Ἀρχίλοχε δέξαι τήνδε τὴν μετανιπτρίδα / μεστὴν Διὸς σωτῆρος ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος. The term "metaniptris" refers to a cup drunk after washing hands.</note>

It will be permitted to use this adage when we wish to signify that we are approaching that which is the last and most important part of a business. Before I make an end, it is worth noting from the words of Pindar that "Olympic Jupiter" and "the Savior" seem to be the same. Plutarch, in the fifth decade of his *Convivial Questions* <note>Also known as *Table Talk*.</note>, speaks of these three cups, if I am not mistaken: "For not even when we sacrifice to all the other gods do we pray most at the altars of the Saviors; but when three mixing bowls are blended, we make libations to some from the first along with the gods, to others from the second, and to others from the last. For envy stands outside the divine choir." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ θύοντες... φθόνον γὰρ ἔξω θείας χορῷ ἑστάναι.</note> He mentions this matter again in the seventh decade, demonstrating that when a sacrifice was made to one god, vows were made to all at once, but not by name.

### The rotation of the pestle.
-> II <-
<note>original: Ὑπέρου περιτροπή (Hyperou peritropē)</note> This means the turning around of a pestle. It is used when someone is always agitating the same thing, yet explains nothing. Plato the Comician <note>An Athenian poet of the Old Comedy.</note>, I believe, says in *Adonis* (cited in Zenodotus):

> For it seems to me that a rotation of the pestle is happening to you.
<note>original Greek: ἔοικε γὰρ ὑπέρου μοι περιτροπὴ γίγνεσθαί σου.</note>

Plutarch, in his work *Against the Stoics*, uses this to signify that their arguments always revolve back to the same point: "Since 'Jupiter's Corinth' <note>An ancient proverb for tiresome repetition.</note> is so abundant in their discourses, you will surely think to leave aside the 'rotation of the pestle' so that he does not mock you." That is:

<summary>This page discusses the Greek ritual of three libations—to the gods, the heroes, and finally to Jupiter the Savior—as a metaphor for completing a task. It also introduces the adage "the rotation of the pestle" to describe repetitive, fruitless arguments.</summary>
<keywords>Jupiter the Savior, Zeus Soter, libation rituals, three cups, Plato, Aristophanes, Plutarch, Pindar, Athenaeus, Stoic logic, Greek adages, pestle metaphor</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on adages derived from Greek literature and daily life. The previous page concluded a discussion on the ritual of the "third cup to Jupiter," and this page begins by connecting that theme of repetition and finality to the proverb "Much Corinthian Jupiter," before moving into a series of shorter adages regarding luck, similarity, and transactional honesty.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Thus, "Much Corinthian Jupiter" <note>original: "Multus igitur Iovis Corinthus"</note> is applied to those who repeat themselves. For you may omit "the circling of the pestle" <note>original: "pistilli circuituotionem"</note>, lest you seem ridiculous. This is why the phrase is usually said when people repeat the same things over and over, not without causing boredom. Logicians say that "the point is being begged" <term>begging the question: petitio principii</term> whenever an argument revolves back to the same starting point. Hesychius interprets this as being about those who always say the same things and yet make no progress in the meantime. To this, another phrase is so closely related that it might seem to be the same, which Plato recounts in the *Theaetetus*: "the rolling-pin, or the rotation, as it is sometimes called" <note>original: ἡ σκυτάλη, ἢ ὑπ’ ὅτε δὴ λέγεται περιτροπή</note>. That is, the rotation of the rolling-pin, or the pestle, or whatever else it may be called: when speech revolves back to the same point, just as in that dialogue Theaetetus is told to agree that the person who has a "right opinion" is the one who holds a "right opinion." The translator renders *scytala* as "a lash," though Plato is speaking of the leather strap that is wound around a stick.

<margin>III</margin>
### A sow under the club.
"A sow under the club" <note>original: ὑς ὑπὸ ῥόπαλον</note>. This is said when someone rushes headlong into immediate danger and ruin. For among certain people, it is the custom for sows to be slaughtered with a club. This is recorded by Suidas. Zenodotus indicates that it appears in the works of Dinolochus.

<margin>IIII</margin>
### If you cannot drive an ox, drive a donkey.
"If you cannot drive an ox, drive a donkey" <note>original: Εἰ μὴ δύναιο βοῦν, ἔλαυνε ὄνον</note>. That is, if you cannot do as you wish, do as you are able. If a more splendid fortune does not fall to you, perhaps you should be content with the one that does: if what you desire is not permitted, embrace that which is nearest to it. According to Suidas.

<margin>V</margin>
### A siren announces a friend, a bee a guest.
"A bee announces a guest, but a siren predicts a friend" <note>original: σειρήν μὲν φίλον ἀγγέλλει, ξένου δὲ μέλισσα</note>.
This is used whenever several people give good omens about the same matter; or when someone, flattering their own hope, divines that what they wish for will happen based on even the slightest evidence. For "Siren" in this context does not signify one of those Homeric maidens <note>Erasmus refers here to the mythical Sirens who lured sailors with song</note>, but a type of insect, not unlike a bee. According to Suidas. However, in Hesychius, it is read as *seirēn* <note>original: σειρήν</note> and not *seirin* <note>original: σείρῖν</note>.

<margin>VI</margin>
### Even if you had mentioned the wolf.
"Even if you had mentioned the wolf" <note>original: Εἰ καὶ λύκου ἐμνήσθης</note>. One must understand "he would have arrived." It is used whenever the person who was being discussed arrives unexpectedly. It is related to what we have recounted elsewhere: "The wolf in the story" <note>original: Lupus in fabula; the Latin equivalent of 'speak of the devil'</note>. This happens frequently in comedies and tragedies through the art and care of the writer, so that the person discussed enters immediately. It can be adapted to any situation, as when something being discussed happens to occur immediately or by chance in an author's text. Zenodotus records this adage. Plato says in the *Phaedrus*: "For they say, O Phaedrus, since it is just, that even what is said of the wolf should be told" <note>original: λέγεις γὰρ ὦ φαῖδρε δίκαιον ὤν, καὶ τὸ λύκου εἴπῃ</note>.

<margin>VII</margin>
### More like than a fig.
"More like than a fig" <note>original: ὁμοιότερος σύκῳ</note>. This was said jokingly of things that are extremely similar to one another. The metaphor is drawn from the similarity of figs to each other. Plutarch, in his work *Against the Stoics*, says: "It would be a marvelous and unexpected thing if a wood-pigeon were not like a wood-pigeon, nor a bee like a bee, nor a grain of wheat like wheat, or a fig, as the proverb goes, always identical to a fig" <note>original: σύκῳ... σύκῳ</note>. It is close to those we have mentioned elsewhere: "Not even one egg is so like another," and "Milk is not more like milk."

<margin>VIII</margin>
### Give and take at the same time.
"Give and take at the same time" <note>original: Ἅμα δίδου καὶ λάμβανε</note>. This is used when dealing with a person of uncertain loyalty, whom it is not safe to trust with anything unless you immediately receive what you bargained for. It can be twisted to refer to someone who will not perform a service or give a gift unless they are already certain of a return; they do not "buy hope with a price," as the pimp in Terence’s play says. Aristotle expressed this proverb more elegantly in the seventh book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, criticizing friends who are joined only by mutual utility: just as in marketplace commerce, they do not give a benefit, but sell it. He describes two types: "One is a completely vulgar and shopkeeper-like exchange from hand to hand; the other is more gentlemanly, involving a period of time" <note>original: ἡ μὴ πάμπαν ἀγοραία ἐκ χρερός εἰς χεῖρα, ἢ ἡ ἐλευθεριωτέρα εἰς χρόνον</note>. The philosopher alluded to that line from a comic poet, which is cited by a commentator on Pindar:
"For I immediately become a Phoenician <note>The Phoenicians were stereotyped in antiquity as shrewd, untrustworthy merchants</note>:
For with one hand I give, and with the other I receive."

<summary>This page explores several adages regarding repetitive speech, adapting to one's circumstances, and the nature of similarity and immediate exchange in social and business dealings. Erasmus draws on a wide range of classical sources, including Plato, Aristotle, and Plutarch, to explain how these common phrases originated and should be applied.</summary>
<keywords>repetition, Corinthian Jupiter, Scytala, luck, Siren, omens, Wolf in the story, similarity, figs, immediate exchange, Phoenicians, commerce, Aristotle, Plato</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Thousand, Eighth Century" of Erasmus’s collection. Having just discussed proverbs regarding repetition and social behavior, Erasmus moves into a sequence of adages characterizing the stereotypes of certain peoples (like the Phoenicians) and the indignities of aging, frequently drawing on classical poets like Horace and Pindar.</meta>

### VIII
The Phoenicians are noted for their excessive zeal for trade. Hence Pindar says in the *Pythian Odes*, hymn 2: <term>the Phoenician way is to care for trade</term> <note>original: "τὸ δὲ φοινίκιον ἐμπολαὶ μέλεθ’"</note>.
He calls it the "exchange of the Phoenicians" when something is given and received in turn. Furthermore, this class of merchants holds nothing sacred except for the singular profit of money, to which they have consecrated themselves entirely as if to a god. By this they measure piety, friendship, honor, reputation, and all things divine and human alike. Everything else is a mere trifle.

### IX
->May such enemies always pursue me.<-
<term>May such wars always pursue me</term> <note>original: "Ἀεὶ τοῖοί με πόλεμοι διώκοιεν"</note>. That is:
May such battles always follow me.
This is used when we gladly hate certain people and despise their hostility. For there is a type of person whom it is more dangerous to have served, as Seneca says, than to have offended; and whom it is more advantageous to have as enemies than as friends. To have displeased certain people is even praiseworthy. There are those with whom being joined in friendship is a disgrace, while being at odds in a feud is honorable. It can also be applied to those who defect from a friendship, but as enemies are unable to do any harm. It is also read in this manner:
<term>May such enemies always pursue me</term> <note>original: "Ἀεὶ τοῖοί με πολέμιοι διώκοιεν"</note>. That is:
May enemies of this kind always follow me.

### X
->An old woman kid.<-
<term>An old woman kid</term> <note>original: "γραῦς ἔριφος"</note>. That is, an old woman who is a young goat. Apollodorus, cited in Zenodotus, says there was a certain old woman named Eripha <note>from "eriphos," meaning kid or young goat</note>, because she had grown old in her virginity; it was as if she were simultaneously an old woman by age and a girl because she was still unmarried. There are some who record that a wild locust, called by some a *mantis*, is called a <term>old woman kid</term> in Sicily. They say that whatever animal it looked upon, some evil would happen to it. Therefore, the phrase seems to fit a sorceress or one who casts the "evil eye." Canidia in the works of Horace is of this kind.

### XI
->The old woman dances.<-
<term>The old woman dances</term> <note>original: "γραῦς χορεύει"</note>. This applies to one who does something indecorous: for instance, if an old man should play with nuts <note>a child's game</note>, or a theologian should frolic with the flowery ornaments of rhetoric, or a prince should play music after the example of Nero. It is similar to what we related above: "The camel dances." Horace, writing against an old woman of untimely lust, says:
> Near the famous Luceria of the shorn Teana,
> The lutes do not become you,
> Nor the purple flower of the rose,
> Nor, old woman, the dregs of the wine jar drained to the bottom.

In Plutarch’s *Life of Pericles*, we read that when a certain Elpinice attacked him publicly with unseemly insults, he answered nothing else but that little verse from Archilochus:
<term>Being an old woman, you should not be anointed with perfumes</term> <note>original: "οὐκ ἂν μύροισι γραῦς ἐοῦσ’ ἠλείφετο"</note>.
Why Lapsus translated this as "Being an old woman, you have not forgotten the ointment," I cannot quite guess, unless perhaps he read <term>forgot</term> <note>original: "ἐλάθετο"</note> instead of <term>anointed</term> <note>original: "ἠλείφετο"</note>.

### XII
->A leaping old woman raises much dust.<-
<term>An old woman, by leaping, raises much dust</term> <note>original: "γραῦς ἀνακροτήσασα πολὺν κονιορτὸν ἐγείρει"</note>.
This was usually said of those who, on account of their experience in affairs, would take on a great deal of business. The verse appears to be a heroic poem corrupted by only a single syllable.

### XIII
->Old woman, like a horse you will have a deep ditch.<-
<term>Old woman, like a horse, you shall have the deep-cleft ditch</term> <note>original: "γραῦς ὥσπερ ἵππος τὴν χαραδραίαν τάφον ἕξεις"</note>. That is: Old woman, like a horse, you shall be buried in a high-gaping and black cavern. This is said of those whom people cast aside completely as being utterly useless. After horses have grown old, they are sometimes thrown headlong into deep pits in the earth. So a woman once loved, as soon as her beauty has faded, is loathed by everyone. Such is Lyce in the works of Horace. Similar to that is: "The old age of a horse."

### XIV
->The honor of small fry.<-
<term>The honor of small fry</term> <note>original: "Ἀφυῶν τιμή"</note>. This is used whenever a tiny bit of honor falls to the humble. For the *Aphya* <note>a small, cheap fish like an anchovy or sprat</note> is a cheap little fish, for the cooking of which nothing is used except the oil in which it is fried. Hence the common saying: <term>The honor of the small fry is the oil</term> <note>original: "ἀφύας τιμὴ τ’ ἔλαιον"</note>.

<summary>Erasmus examines a series of classical adages regarding the stereotypes of greedy merchants, the dangers of false friends, and the social stigmas associated with aging and loss of utility. He uses examples ranging from Nero’s musical performances to the low culinary status of small fish to illustrate concepts of decorum and value.</summary>

<keywords>Phoenicians, trade and profit, enemies vs friends, Eripha, witchcraft, evil eye, Nero, indecorum, aging and beauty, small fry (aphya), Horace, Pindar</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Second Thousand, Eighth Century" of Erasmus’s *Adagia*. The previous page discussed proverbs regarding social behavior and the stereotypes of certain peoples like the Phoenicians. The catchword "Quod" indicates the beginning of the next page's first full sentence.</meta>

->Why don’t you hang yourself?<-
<margin>XV</margin>
<term>Why don’t you hang yourself, so that you might become a hero among the Thebans?</term> <note>original Greek: "Τί οὐκ ἀπήγξω, ἵνα θήβησιν ἥρως γένῃ?"</note>; that is, why don’t you hang yourself so that you may become a hero among the Thebans? Among other peoples, the highest honor was given to those who brought about their own death, especially for the safety of their country: for instance, among the Athenians, Codrus, who did not fear to die for his fatherland; among the Romans, the Decii, Quintus Curtius, Marcus Cato of Utica, Brutus, and many others. Among the Thebans, however, no honor was given to those who had committed violence against themselves. Therefore, people think this was said through irony, meaning "so that you might become a demi-god at Thebes." It seems this can be said against those who, led by a desire for fame, throw themselves into grave dangers. This is recorded by Zenodotus.

->What did Apollo sing to you?<-
<margin>XVI</margin>
<term>What has Apollo played for you on the lyre?</term> <note>original Greek: "Τί σοι Ἀπόλλων κεκιθάρεικεν?"</note>; that is, what did Apollo sing to you with his lyre? In other words, what did he answer you? This is an allusion to Apollo’s lyre, which the poets attribute to him. Aeschylus used this adage in his *Ajax the Locrian*. It is recorded by Zenodotus. It will be appropriate when someone asks a person returning from a prince what sort of answer they received: <term>What has Apollo played for you on the lyre?</term>

->What will you not become, having gone to Arbela?<-
<margin>XVII</margin>
<term>What might you not become, if you went to Arbela?</term> <note>original Greek: "Τί οὐ γένοιο, ἂν εἰς ἄρβελα ἐλθών;"</note>; that is, what will you not become having set out for Arbela? This was usually said of someone who, setting out abroad, promises themselves great things, relying on the ignorance and barbarity of the nation to which they are migrating. Indeed, Arbela was a city in Sicily, according to Stephanus, whose citizens once had a bad reputation for being stupid and easily deceived. Therefore, among such people, even someone who is held in contempt elsewhere could be something great. However, there is a city of this name in Persia, which Strabo mentions in Book 16. And to Quintus Curtius, it is a town of Mesopotamia famous for the slaughter of Darius’s forces.

->A good day from the quiver.<-
<margin>XVIII</margin>
<term>A good day from the quiver</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἀγαθὴ ἐκ τῆς φαρέτρας ἡμέρα"</note>. That is, a good day from the quiver. He used to say this about a fortunate day. It is transferred from a custom of the Scythians, for whom, as Phylarchus relates, it was the habit that in the evening, before they slept, they would cast a pebble into a quiver: a white one if by chance that day had passed without trouble; a black one if otherwise. Finally, when someone departed from life, they brought out his quiver; if they found more white pebbles in it, they pronounced him happy; on the other hand, if there were more black ones. And from this they estimated the sum of a life. Hence it was accepted as a proverb, so that they would say "it is a good day from the quiver" if something had happened according to one’s heart’s desire.

->The affairs of Cannacas.<-
<margin>XIX</margin>
<term>The things of Cannacas</term> <note>original Greek: "Τὰ καννάκου"</note>. That is, the affairs or the evils of Cannacas. They used this proverb in two ways: either concerning things to be admired for their antiquity, or concerning wretched and tearful lamentations and wailing. Cannacas was a certain king of the Phrygians, just as Hermogenes relates in his *Phrygian History*, who, when he had foreseen that a flood was coming, called everyone together to the temples of the gods and with many tears entreated the gods to turn away that evil. Hence the iambic writer Herodes says: <term>so that I may weep in the manner of Cannacas</term> <note>original Greek: "ἵνα τὰ καννάκου κλαύσω"</note>. These things are recorded by Zenodotus. Pliny, in his thirty-sixth book, reckons Cannacus among the noble sculptors. Stephanus, in his entry for "Iconium," mentions the adage, except that he calls him Annacus, not Cannacus or Cannacas; and he varies the story somewhat. For he says that a certain Annacus lived over three hundred years. Being anxious, he consulted the oracles as to how long he was destined to live. The response was that when Annacus died, all things would perish; when he died, the flood of Deucalion followed. Furthermore, having heard the response, the Phrygians mourned greatly, and from this arose the proverb concerning heavy grief: <term>to weep for Annacus</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ Ἀννακοῦ κλαύσεσθαι"</note>.

->What manner of horses.<-
<margin>XX</margin>
<term>What is the manner of the horses?</term> <note>original Greek: "Τίς τρόπος ἵππων;"</note>; that is, what is the style of the horses? This was used when someone introduced a new or foreign custom; for instance, if an Italian were to use Gallic clothing. It seems to have been said of guests arriving in a new kind of chariot. Metagenes in the *Thuriopersians*, quoted in the Suda: <term>What is the manner of the horses? How they no longer dance in barbarian places</term> <note>original Greek: "Τίς τρόπος ἵππων; ὡς οὐκ ὀρχοῦντ’ ἐν βαρβαρικοῖσι τόποις ἔτι"</note>. It has an affinity with that proverb which we reviewed a little earlier: <term>another kind of oar</term> <note>original Greek: "ἄλλο γένος κώπης"</note>.

->A Chironian wound.<-
<margin>XXI</margin>
<term>A Chironian wound</term> <note>original Greek: "Χειρώνιον ἕλκος"</note>. That is, they called an incurable evil a "Chironian wound." Chiron, in the war against the Centaurs, was struck by Hercules and received an incurable wound in his foot, from which he died. The author Zenodotus says the proverb was born from this. Our Virgil, however (for the poem is attributed to him), calls the "Chironian hand" a healing one:
> The wound lives on beneath the grieving breast, <note>Erasmus notes the paradox where Chiron is both a symbol of an incurable wound and a legendary healer.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores a series of adages derived from Greek history and mythology, covering themes of ironic honor in suicide, the interpretation of authority's responses, the vanity of seeking fame among the ignorant, and the Scythian method of measuring a happy life.</summary>
<keywords>Thebes, Apollo, Arbela, Scythian customs, Cannacas, Annacus, Deucalion's flood, Chiron, incurable wounds, Greek proverbs, ancient irony</keywords>

<header>SECOND THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY</header>

### VIII
->That not even a Chironian hand would lift.<-

Achilles is said to have been raised by this centaur, Chiron <note>In Greek mythology, Chiron was a wise centaur who tutored many heroes</note>. From this, the comic poet Plato—in his verses—censures Damon, who was thought to have trained Pericles for tyranny under the pretense of teaching him music:

> First, then, I beg you to tell me, for <gloss>that is,</gloss>
> as they say, you, the Chiron, raised Pericles. <note>original Greek: "πρῶτον μὲν οὖν μοι λέξον ἀντιβολῶ, σὺ γὰρ / ὥς φασιν ὁ χείρων ἐξέθρεψας περικλέα."</note>
> First, indeed, I pray you tell me this,
> You, since you are said to be the Chiron who educated Pericles. <note>original Latin: "Primum quidem illud obsecro dicas mihi, / Tu quippe qui Chiron educasse diceris Periclem."</note>

Lapus rendered this passage as: "For you, as they say, most wickedly educated Pericles." Furthermore, in the Aldine edition <note>A famous Venetian printing press</note>, there is a double error. First, the verse is incorrectly divided; second, the logic of the meter requires that we read "the Chiron" <note>original Greek: "ὁ χείρων"</note> instead of "O Chiron" <note>original Greek: "ὦ χείρων"</note>, meaning "you, that famous Chiron." Indeed, he calls Damon "Chiron" through a figure of speech, because he was to Pericles what Chiron was to Achilles: he certainly taught him to play the lyre, but he raised him to a "centaur-like" ferocity. Although this is mentioned in a somewhat tangential place, it seemed worth pointing out to scholars so that no one might unknowingly stumble over this stone.

### XXII
->Charon’s door.<-

<term>Charoneios thyra</term> <note>original Greek: "Χαρώνειος θύρα"</note>, that is, Charon’s door. This refers to someone in immediate danger of death, or to a matter of great sorrow. For in ancient times, this was the name given to one of the prison doors through which those condemned by the judges' sentences were led to execution. This is recorded by Zenodotus, Hesychius, and Suidas. For the poets imagine that souls are carried down to the underworld in Charon’s boat <note>Charon was the ferryman of the dead in Greek myth</note>. Hence Aristophanes says in the *Plutus*: "He gives the token of Charon" <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ χάρωνος τὸ ξύμβολον δίδωσι"</note>, meaning that death is imminent for him.

### XXIII
->He urinated on his father's ashes.<-

A person who acted with unrestrained madness, or for whom everything turned out poorly, was said to have "urinated on his father's ashes." In ancient times, there was the highest religious reverence for a father's tomb. This is clear from the story of Thamyris, which I have related elsewhere. Accordingly, the Furies—the avenging spirits of madness—were sent after anyone who violated his father's monument, just as they were for parricides <note>those who kill their own parents</note>, and nothing would ever go well for them. Horace says in his *Art of Poetry*:

> It is not quite clear why he keeps making verses; whether
> he urinated on his father’s ashes, or disturbed a mournful
> <term>bidental</term> <note>A sacred place struck by lightning, which was forbidden to be disturbed</note> as an unholy man; certainly, he is mad. <note>original Latin: "Nec satis apparet, cum uersus factitet, utrum / Minxerit in patrios cineres, an triste bidental / Mouerit incestus, certè furit."</note>

### XXIIII
->To lift the armpit.<-

<term>Maschalen airein</term> <note>original Greek: "μασχάλην αἴρειν"</note>, that is, to "lift the armpit," was a saying used for someone who drank greedily. It is taken from the gesture of heavy drinkers who, while draining their cups, stretch out their throat and chin and raise their elbows high so that no liquid remains in the cup. This same act they call <term>kothonizein</term>, from <term>kothon</term> <note>original Greek: "κώθων"</note>, which is a type of drinking vessel. Hesychius indicates that <term>maschala</term> is also a part of a ship's prow which contains the yardarm or the forestay. Some believe the <term>antemon</term> <note>the forestay or sail</note> is a type of sail. There are those who say the <term>maschala</term> is a basket woven from palm, because a palm branch is called a <term>maschale</term>, and sometimes the word is used for a rope. Others contend that the <term>maschala</term> is a machine by which loads are placed into or removed from ships. From this comes the joke against those who lift their cup high. Hesychius also cites this trochaic tetrameter without naming the author:

> So that we may lift the armpit high, having fallen into it. <gloss>that is,</gloss>
> Let us raise the armpit upwards as we rush in. <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἄνω τὴν μασχάλην αἴρωμεν ἐμπεπτωκότες."</note>

Perhaps Stratonicus the cithara-player <note>a professional musician</note> alluded to this in Athenaeus, Book 8, who, when characterizing the individual cities of Greece, called Byzantium the "armpit of Greece." <note>original Greek: "βυζαντίου ἀπὸν μασχάλην τῆ ἑλλάδος"</note> He said this, I believe, because they drank heavily there, or because it was the great marketplace <term>emporium</term> of Greece. It is a city of Thrace, the same one called Constantinople. The allusion adds charm to the proverb because there are drinking cups in the shape of ships, such as the <term>cymbia</term>, <term>scaphia</term>, and <term>triremes</term> <note>all names for both types of ships and types of bowls</note>. This is recorded from Zenodotus. Julius Pollux also mentions it in Book 6, Chapter 3, with these words: "Regarding those who were drunk, they used to say 'to lift the armpit,' as if that were the custom of those in their cups." <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μεθυόντων ἔλεγον τὸ μασχάλην αἴρειν, ὡς ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῷ μέθει."</note> He also brings forward evidence from a poem of Homer:

> Raising their hands, they died of laughter. <gloss>that is,</gloss>
> To die of laughter with hands raised. <note>original Greek: "Χεῖρας ἀνίσχονtes γέλῳ ἔκθανον"</note>

From these examples, it seems the saying comes not just from lifting the cup, but from the gesture of those rejoicing. Certainly, the custom remains among German soldiers today to indicate joy of spirit by raising the right hand.
