# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM: ADAGES

<page-num>570</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM: ADAGES</header>

->**Even more the Phrygian himself.**<-

<margin>XXV</margin>
More the Phrygian <note>original Greek: "μᾶλλον ὁ φρύξ"</note>, that is, *Even more the Phrygian himself*. I personally suspect this was a common saying used whenever things were approved not because they were truer, but because they were said more flatteringly. They tell a story that Croesus, the king of the Lydians <note>A king famous for his immense wealth</note>, once asked the **Seven Sages** <note>The most respected philosophers of early Greece</note> to whom they would award the highest title of happiness. When they gave various answers—some saying that untamed wild beasts seemed happiest to them because they would face death to protect their liberty, others pointing to storks because they maintain justice and duty by their own nature without needing laws—Solon, however, denied that anyone should be called happy until they had departed from life. Standing nearby was that Phrygian writer of fables, **Aesop**. He said, "O King, you excel the others as much as the sea surpasses the rivers." When the king heard this, he is reported to have replied, "More the Phrygian." This phrase then passed into a proverb. Indeed, I wonder if it should be read as "More, O Phrygian" <note>original Greek: "μᾶλλον ὦ φρύξ"</note>, so that it means you would gladly accept such praise, and even though it was the greatest, you still desire something more to be added. Thus, when someone openly flatters us, it would be appropriate to chime in with, "More, O Phrygian." This is recorded by Suidas and Zenodotus.

->**He is more pleased with himself than Peleus with his sword.**<-

<margin>XXVI</margin>
He is more proud than Peleus was of his sword <note>original Greek: "μέγα φρονεῖ μᾶλλον ἢ πηλεὺς ἐπὶ τῇ μαχαίρᾳ"</note>. This applies to someone who is insolent beyond measure and puffed up with pride over some matter. They say that this sword was forged by **Vulcan** <note>The god of fire and blacksmithing</note> and given by the gods to **Peleus** <note>The father of Achilles</note> as a symbol of his courage and wisdom. By using it in both battles and hunts, he achieved whatever he desired. Zenodotus says this is mentioned in the works of both Anacreon and Pindar.

->**You are noble from your purse.**<-

<margin>XXVII</margin>
You are noble from your purse <note>original Greek: "γενναῖος εἶ ἐκ βαλαντίου"</note>. This was tossed at someone who wished to be considered noble because of their wealth, though they were otherwise obscure and of humble birth. For wealth creates nobility—not only ancient wealth, according to **Aristotle**, but wealth acquired from anywhere and by any means. Moreover, this class of people tends to become more fiercely insolent than those who are famous for the ancestral portraits of their forefathers.

->**More fond of children than Gello.**<-

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
Gello, who is fonder of children <note>original Greek: "γελλῶ παιδοφιλωτέρα"</note>, that is, *The child-loving Gello*. This was usually said either of those who had died an untimely death, or of those who pursued their children with a strange kind of affection, yet corrupted them through that same indulgence and pampering. They say Gello was a certain maiden who died while still a young girl. The people of Lesbos believed her ghost wandered about and snatched away children. Thus, they blamed the deaths of children who died an untimely fate on this Gello. **Sappho** is cited as having mentioned this story.

->**A clod to the field.**<-

<margin>XXIX</margin>
A clod to the field <note>original Greek: "βῶλος ἄρουρα"</note>. This is used when someone adds a tiny thing to a massive one, believing that they are helping, though in fact they contribute nothing. Therefore, I suspect it should be read as "a clod to the field" <note>original Greek: "βῶλος ἄρουραν" or "ἀρούρᾳ"</note>, so that you understand the verb "he joined" or "he threw upon" <note>original: "προσῆψεν" or "ἐπέβαλεν"</note>. For it adds no weight if a clod is added to a field; it is just as if someone were to pour water drawn from a lake into the sea.

->**The art of Glaucus.**<-

<margin>XXX</margin>
The art of Glaucus <note>original Greek: "γλαύκου τέχνη"</note>. There is a double use for this proverb. For it is suitable either for a work completed quickly, or for something that has been fashioned with the highest skill and the greatest care. Some think the origin comes from a certain **Glaucus of Samos**, who was the first to invent the soldering of iron. Others say it comes from a certain Libyan, who is said to have manufactured four cymbals that corresponded to each other in such fixed proportions that the thickness of the first had a ratio of an **Epitrite** <note>A 4:3 ratio</note> to the second, an **Hemiolion** <note>A 3:2 ratio</note> to the third, and a double ratio <note>A 2:1 ratio</note> to the fourth. When struck, they produced a certain musical harmony. The author is Zenodotus.

->**Lauriotic Owls.**<-

<margin>XXXI</margin>
Lauriotic owls <note>original Greek: "γλαῦκες λαυριωτικαί"</note>. By this riddle-like phrase, they signified a great quantity of money. For **Laurium** is a region of Attica rich in veins of gold <note>Erasmus likely means silver, as Laurium was famous for silver mines</note>. Furthermore, the figure of an owl was engraved on gold coins, as we have mentioned in another place. A commentator adds that an owl was also commonly engraved on **tetradrachms** <note>A large silver coin of ancient Greece</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Birds*:
> Lauriotic owls shall never fail you,
> but they will dwell within, and in your purses
> they will build their nests. <note>original Greek: "γλαῦκες ὑμᾶς ὔποτ’ ἐλλείψουσι λαυριωτικαί, / ἀλλ’ ἐνοικήσουσι γλ’ ἔνδον, ἐν τοῖς βαλαντίοις / ἐννεοττεύσουσι."</note>

<vocab>Erasmus, Adagia, Phryx, Peleus, Gello, Glaucus, Laurium, Aristophanes, Zenodotus, Suidas</vocab>

# SECOND THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY

<page-num>571</page-num>
<header>SECOND THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Bb 4</sig>

The owls of Laurium <note>Laurium was a district in Attica famous for its silver mines; Athenian coins were stamped with the image of an owl.</note> will not leave you, but these will be present in your very houses, and they will prepare little nests for themselves in your purses.

->**Glaucus revived after drinking honey.**<-
->XXXII<-

Γλαῦκος πίνων μέλι ἀνέστη <note>original Greek: "Glaukos pinon meli anestē"</note>, that is, *Glaucus revived after drinking honey*. This was a common saying whenever someone who was reported dead by public rumor suddenly appeared in public again, seeming to return to life for those who were convinced he had passed away. It is quite clear that the proverb arose from an actual event. Specifically, a certain Glaucus, against everyone's expectation, recovered his health after tasting a honeyed medicine. This event was then turned into a popular joke. Some tell the story this way: a man named Glaucus was nearly killed by an excess of bile after drinking honey. As many doctors rushed to help him, the herb *polyidos*—which they call "dragon-herb"—restored him to health.

->**More noble than Codrus.**<-
->XXXIII<-

Εὐγενέστερος Κόδρου <note>original Greek: "Eugenesteros Kodrou"</note>, that is, *More noble than Codrus*. This can be used quite correctly as irony against those who boast of the smoky portraits of their ancestors and the antiquity of their birth. Codrus was the son of Melanthus. Melanthus was the sixth in descent from Neleus, from whom Nestor was also descended. This Melanthus, driven from his homeland of Messene, came to Athens; there, he engaged in single combat with Xanthus the Boeotian, who was then ruling Athens, and emerged victorious, seizing the rule of the Athenians. He was succeeded by his son Codrus, who was especially famous for his extraordinary devotion to his country. For when the people of Attica were at war with the Dorians, and an oracle had declared that victory would belong to the Athenian people if their king were killed by the enemy, Codrus—holding the glory of his country dearer than his own safety—provoked the enemy while disguised in a commoner's clothing and was slain. He left behind two sons: Mentor, who succeeded his deceased father in power, and Neleus, under whose leadership a colony migrated to Asia. This is essentially the account given by Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic from the 3rd century BCE</note>.

->**A Cadmean victory.**<-
->XXXIIII<-

Καδμεία νίκη <note>original Greek: "Kadmeia nikē"</note>, that is, *A Cadmean victory*. They cite various origins and meanings for this adage. Some think a "Cadmean victory" refers to a useless victory, because the Thebans Eteocles and Polynices, while disputing the turns of their reign, met in single combat and both perished. Herodotus mentions a victory of this kind in his first book when discussing the Phocaeans. Or it is so called because the Cadmeans <note>The ancient inhabitants of Thebes, named after their founder, Cadmus</note> indeed defeated the Argives who were fighting under Adrastus, but to their own misfortune; for they later paid a heavy price to the descendants of those Argives. Or because Oedipus, having solved the riddle of the Sphinx, won a magnificent victory over the monster, but afterward unknowingly married his own mother. As soon as he discovered this, he tore out his own eyes. Thus, that victory also had an unhappy ending. There are some who relate it to this: when Cadmus wished to hand over the alphabet he had received from the Phoenicians to the Greeks, he killed Linus because Linus was also putting forward his own letters. Afterward, the citizens drove Cadmus out, so that it did him no good to have surpassed Linus. Plutarch agrees with the first opinion; for he writes as follows in his commentary *Greek Questions*: <note>original Greek: "πόθεν τὰ Ἑλληνικά"</note> "The ancients did not call any other victory 'Cadmean' except the one between the brothers at Thebes, which they named as the most shameful and wretched." The same author, in his work *The Education of Children*, shows that a victory is called Cadmean whenever it is better to be defeated than to win. Plato used this adage in the first book of the *Laws*: "Education brings victory, but victory sometimes brings a lack of education; for many, having become more arrogant due to victories won in war, are filled with countless other evils because of their insolence. But education has never been Cadmean, whereas many such victories have been for men, and will be in the future." Aristides says in his *Pericles*: "So he thought he would win a Cadmean victory." In that passage, a scholar’s note suggests another origin slightly different from those I have related: that the Thebans, having slaughtered the Argives who fought with Polynices, refused them burial. The Athenians, enraged by this inhumanity, attacked and defeated the Thebans, and in a similar fashion forbade the bodies of the slain to be given burial. The writings of Pausanias in his *Description of Greece (Boeotia)* are not entirely at odds with this, nor do they entirely agree. He writes essentially to this effect: that after a battle was joined at the Ismenus river, those defeated in the encounter...
<meta>The catchword "sunt" at the bottom of the page suggests the sentence continues with "sunt uicti" (were defeated) or a similar construction on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page explores the origins of three Greek proverbs: one regarding unexpected recovery (Glaucus), one on true nobility and self-sacrifice (Codrus), and the famous "Cadmean victory," which refers to a win achieved at such a high cost that it is equivalent to a defeat.</summary>
<keywords>Glaucus, Codrus, Cadmean victory, Thebes, Athenian wealth, nobility, self-sacrifice, military history, irony, Greek mythology, Erasmus</keywords>

--- Page 690 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Cadmean Victory" (Adage XXXIV) from the previous page, which described the tragic war between the sons of Oedipus, and moves into reflections on wealth, social status, and futility.</meta>

...they were the Thebans, who, having been forced into flight, retreated within their walls as if the Peloponnesians were unaware of the siege. Furthermore, when the Peloponnesians rushed in with more rage than skill, quite a few were killed by the Thebans with javelins from the wall. Finally, they defeated the others as well by making an impression on the wandering and confused crowd, so that the entire army perished except for Adrastus. Nor did that victory cost the Thebans little, <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ ἐκείνους... τὴν σὺν ὄλεθρῳ κρατησάντων, καδμείαν ὀνομάζεσι νίκην"</note> for as he says, *They call a victory joined with the destruction of those who conquered a Cadmean victory.* But wherever the adage originated, they called a "Cadmean victory" one that was unhappy even for the victors themselves. Such was the victory of the Greeks at Troy, which cost every single one of them dearly. Doctors also call it a "Cadmean victory" when a disease is driven out in such a way that the patient dies from the remedy while nature itself succumbs.

<margin>XXXV</margin>
### Money makes the man.
<note>original: "χρήματα ἀνὴρ"</note>, that is, *Money is the man.* This means that a person is valued exactly as much as what they possess. Horace says: *Nothing is enough, because you are worth as much as you have.* <note>Horace, Satires 1.1.62</note> Zenodotus cites this from Pindar. It appears in the second *Isthmian Ode* in these very words: <note>original: "Νῦν δ' ἐφεῖκεν... χρήματα, χρήματ' ἀνήρ..."</note> *Now it falls to us to observe that saying of the Argive, which comes closest to the truth: Money, money makes the man.* He says this of someone who is deprived of possessions and friends at the same time. A commentator on Pindar testifies that Chrysippus was the author of this in his collection of proverbs, though he wrote that it belonged to Aristodemus the Spartan. The same commentator relates the verse we just reviewed from Alcaeus in this manner: *Money is the man; no poor man is ever noble or honored.* Laertius also mentions this aphorism in the *Life of Thales*, adding that it is very famous among the Lacedæmonians <note>The Spartans.</note>. These words of Alcaeus, testifying to the same thing, are cited in Suidas: <note>original: "Ὡς γὰρ δήποτ' ἀριστόδαμόν φασιν... χρήματ' ἀνήρ, πενιχρὸς δ' οὐδέποτ' ἐσθλὸς"</note> *For they say that once Aristodemus spoke no unskillful word in Sparta: Money is the man, and a poor man is never good.* Some prefer to attribute this to the Seven Sages. To this sentiment belong those verses from some comedy:
<note>original: "Τ' ἀργύριόν ἐστιν αἷμα καὶ ψυχὴ βροτοῖς..."</note>
*Money is both the blood and the soul for mortals,*
*He who does not have it, nor has worked hard to get it,*
*Walks about as a dead man among the living.*
The second Greek verse will be correct if you remove the "d" or read "mēd" instead of "mēde." The third will be correct if you read "tethneōs" instead of "tethnekōs." This six-foot line <note>A senarius.</note> is also celebrated and is not foreign to this sentiment:
<note>original: "Βίος Βίου δεόμενος οὐκ ἔστιν βίος"</note>
*A life in need of a livelihood is not a life.*
Furthermore, just as the word *bios* functions among the Greeks, so too among the Latins the word *uita* <note>life</note> signifies both the life that is the opposite of death, and the resources <note>means or faculties</note> by which we sustain life.

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
### Having become rich, he has now ceased to enjoy lentils.
<note>original: "ἔπειτα πλουτῶν οὐκ ἔθ' ἥδεται φακῷ"</note>, that is,
*The lentil has ceased to please the rich man.*
The lentil is a legume used for the food of the poor and the weak. It is loathed as soon as a more elegant fortune arrives. Hence the proverb is used against those who, having been raised to a more prosperous condition, feel disgust for those things which they previously, in their poverty, were satisfied with. The adage is taken from Aristophanes' *Plutus*. For it is said there regarding a young man who, while poor, had a relationship with an old woman, but having obtained riches, began to loathe her. It is not unlike that which we reviewed elsewhere: *Another life, another diet.*

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
### You are plucking a bald man.
<note>original: "φαλακρὸν τίλλεις"</note>, that is, *You are plucking a bald man.* This is used when someone undertakes a useless labor, or when one tries to take away something that the person from whom it is sought lacks. For instance, if one tries to squeeze money out of a poor man, or learning from the uneducated. It is very similar to that line in Plautus: *You are asking for water from a pumice stone.* <note>The pumice is a porous, dry volcanic rock.</note> Again, to that...

# SECOND CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY

...it is like "stripping the clothes from a naked man." Indeed, even today the common folk, when they want to signify that there is nothing left to be taken away, show the palm of the hand and bid someone to pluck hair from there, because that part of the body is bald on everyone.

->Sleep be absent from the eyes.<-
->XXXVIII<-

<margin>Sweet sleep be absent from the eyes <note>original Greek: ὕπνος ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν γλυκύθυμος</note></margin> that is, 
*Let mind-soothing slumber be away from the eyes.*
This is used when someone undertakes a matter that requires the highest level of diligence and care. For example, if someone were to take up the study of philosophy. This six-foot line of verse is taken from Aristophanes' *The Clouds*, where it is spoken by the character of Socrates, who is exhorting Strepsiades <note>Strepsiades is the elderly student in the play who seeks philosophy to escape his debts.</note> that, as he is about to devote himself to philosophy, he must both do and endure all things.

->Phocus's banquet.<-
->XXXIX<-

<margin>Phocus's contribution-feast <note>original Greek: Φώκου ἔρανος</note></margin> i.e., Phocus's reward, or banquet. It was customary to say this when someone received guests to their own misfortune. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent it from being applied even further: namely, to those people who are harmed by the very individuals they have benefited. They say that Phocus had a daughter who was of marriageable age. Since there were many suitors, he would call them together and establish rewards, but then he would constantly postpone the marriage by proposing new conditions. For this reason, the indignant young men murdered Phocus during a banquet. The source for this is Zenodotus. However, Plutarch tells this story differently in his *Amorous Narrations*. 

Eustathius, in his commentary on the first book of the *Odyssey*, identifies three types of banquets: <term>eilapine</term> <note>original: εἰλαπίνη</note>, which is prepared for splendor and magnificence; <term>gamos</term> <note>original: γάμον</note>, the wedding feast, which also tends to be quite expensive; and the <term>eranos</term> <note>original: ἔρανον</note>, at which many people gather, but each person brings their own food and pays their own share. This last method of banqueting is especially praised by Hesiod because, while it offers the most pleasure, it costs the least. For people eat and drink more moderately when each person consumes from their own supply. Hesiod's poem on the matter is as follows:
<margin>When the feast is shared, the pleasure is greatest and the expense is least. <note>original Greek: Αἵ κοινὴ πλείστη τε χάρις δ’απάνη τ’ ὀλιγίστη.</note></margin>
Furthermore, those who wished to appear more splendid would provide an *eranos* from their own resources and in a more lavish style. Homer encompasses these three forms of banquets at once:
<margin>What feast is this? What is the need for it? Is it a banquet or a wedding? Since it is certainly not a contribution-feast. <note>original Greek: τίς δαίς; τίς δὲ χρεώ; Εἰλαπίν’ ἠὲ γάμος; ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἔρανος τάδε γ’ ἐστίν.</note></margin>

->Older than chaos and the times of Saturn.<-
->XL<-

<margin>Older than chaos <note>original Greek: Χάους ἀρχαιότερος</note></margin> i.e., Older than chaos. Said of a thing that is excessively ancient and obsolete. Ibycus says: <margin>He flies in another's chaos. <note>original Greek: πόντων δ’ ὑπ’ ἀλλοτρίω χάει</note></margin> And again: <margin>But he talks nonsense, and by our follies he echoes things older than chaos and smelling of the times of Saturn. <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ φλυαρεῖ, καὶ μὰ τῶν ἡμῶν λήρων κατηχεῖ τὸ χάους ἀρχαιότερον, καὶ κρονίων ἀπόζοντα.</note></margin> The adage alludes to "Chaos," to which the poets trace the origin of the gods and all things. Ovid begins his work on the creation of the world from this point, just as the Hebrews do <note>A reference to the Book of Genesis.</note>.

->He boasts as if he had carried off the Argive shield.<-
->XLI<-

<margin>He prides himself as if he had taken down the shield from Argos. <note>original Greek: Ὡς τὴν ἐξ ἄργους ἀσπίδα καθελὼν σεμνύνεται.</note></margin> i.e., He is as proud as if he had stripped away the Argive shield. This was said against the haughty and those who carry themselves too magnificently. They say that among the Argives there was a certain sacred shield fixed with nails so that it could not easily be taken down. Others say that among them, the rank and selection of young men who excelled in strength was called the "Shield" (*aspida*). The source for this is Zenodotus.

->Like tearing apart a shellfish.<-
->XLII<-

<margin>As if to divide by a shellfish <note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ κογχυλίῳ διελεῖν</note></margin> i.e., Like tearing a shell apart. This was said of the weak and those far inferior in strength. For shells are broken against the ground so that the food may be taken out, or they are opened by cutting the nerve by which they contract and pull themselves apart. This is recorded in Suidas.

->More silent than a skiff.<-
->XLIII<-

<margin>More mouth-bound than a skiff. <note>original Greek: Συσομώτερος σκάφης</note></margin> i.e., More tongue-tied than a small boat. This was customarily said of those who, because of the humility of their social condition, do not dare to open their mouths in the presence of more prominent people. They say this originated because in the past, resident aliens and guests of a foreign state walked in the processions of the public games carrying a boat; hence, whenever they wanted to signify a guest rather than a citizen, they used to call them a *skaphe* <note>boat</note> or a *skaphephoros* <note>boat-bearer</note>. Consequently, there was a common threat: *I will make your mouth more closed than a skiff.* For those who live in a state that is not their own must keep many things to themselves. Just as it is not proper to be meddlesome in a foreign city, so it is not safe to be too free with one's tongue. For this interpretation, Suidas cites Theophrastus as the author in his work *On Laws*. Indeed, in most cases...

<meta>This page continues the Eighth Century of the Second Chiliad of Erasmus's *Adages*. ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...in most manuscripts, I find "more cringing" <note>original Greek: συσμώτερος</note> written, not "more humble" <note>original Greek: συσομώτερος</note>. Since this reading is more appealing, I shall not argue against it—namely, so that you may understand the term to mean someone humbled and contracted by fear.

<margin>44</margin>
->Naked as if from his mother.<-
Naked as if from his mother <note>original Greek: Γυμνὸς ὡς ἐκ μητρὸς</note>. That is, naked just as he came from his mother. This is a proverbial exaggeration <term>hyperbole: an intentional exaggeration for emphasis</term> regarding an extremely poor person. For we are born most naked of all, not even covered by hair, let alone clothes—a covering that is granted to all other animals. This saying is still in common use among our own people today: "As naked as the day he was born." Similar to this is another saying that will be mentioned elsewhere: "As if from a shipwreck."

<margin>45</margin>
->There is a Pylos before Pylos.<-
Plutarch, in the little book titled *On the Necessity of Not Borrowing*, testifies that this verse was celebrated as a proverb among the Messenians: 
"There is a Pylos before Pylos, and indeed there is yet another Pylos" <note>original Greek: Ἔστι Πύλος πρὸ Πύλοιο, Πύλος γε μὲν ἔστι καὶ ἄλλος</note>. 
The saying clearly applies when something is preferred over another as being more ancient or superior. Or, it is used when someone boasts of themselves as if they were the only one, or the highest, when others can be found who could compete with them. For Pylos was a city of the Messenians, famous for the hero Nestor <note>Nestor was the oldest and wisest of the Greek kings at the siege of Troy; several cities claimed to be his birthplace</note>, as some affirm. Plutarch, however, adapted this poem in the following way: 
"There is interest before interest, and indeed there is yet another interest" <note>original Greek: Ἔστι τόκος πρὸ τόκοιο, τόκος γε μὲν ἔστι καὶ ἄλλος</note>. 
This can be applied to those for whom one debt of interest is born from another. Eustathius, in his commentary on Homer's *Catalogue of Ships*, indicated where the adage originated. For he writes, following those who wrote about various peoples, that there were three cities named Pylos: one in Messenia, another in Triphylia, and a third in Arcadia. He claims Nestor held the Triphylian one. He also cites the geographer Strabo as a witness, who likewise established three Pyloses in the Peloponnese. Strabo treats this matter in the eighth book of his *Geography*, demonstrating that there were many cities of this name, each of which claimed Nestor for itself because of the man’s fame. However, he later concludes that Nestor's homeland was on both sides of the Alpheus river. Aristophanes alluded to the adage in *The Knights*: 
"But consider this, Pylos before Pylos, which I mentioned to you, / There is a Pylos before Pylos. For what does he mean by 'before Pylos'?" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ τόδε φράζου, πρὸ Πύλου Πύλον... τί γὰρ λέγει πρὸ Πύλοιο;</note>
A commentator adds that the short verse we cited a moment ago from Plutarch was delivered by an oracle.

<margin>45</margin>
->Achilles threw two dice and four.<-
"Achilles threw two dice and a four" <note>original Greek: Βέβληκ’ Ἀχιλλεὺς δύο κύβω καὶ τέσσαρα</note>. 
The lexicographer Suidas cites this verse from Euripides. No one explains exactly what the adage means, except that one may guess it was said of those who were victorious in everything, because that particular throw of the dice was lucky. A commentator on Aristophanes' *The Frogs* cites Aristarchus, who wrote that this six-foot line <term>senarius: a line of verse consisting of six feet</term> used to circulate under Euripides’ name, but falsely, as it belongs to <unclear>Aeschylus</unclear>. In Aristophanes, Bacchus uses it against Aeschylus, the victor over Euripides, from which it appears that the use of this proverb was common in auspicious acclamations.

<margin>46</margin>
->From slow-paced donkeys a horse came forth.<-
"From slow-paced donkeys horses sprang forth" <note>original Greek: Ἐκ βραδυσκελέων ὄνων ἵπποι ὤροντο</note>. That is, from slow donkeys a horse emerged. This is used when someone born of an obscure family turns out to be famous, or whenever a learned student proceeds from an unlearned teacher. It can also be spoken through irony, or through negation, as in: "A horse will never be born from a donkey." And: "Behold, a horse from donkeys for you!"—meaning, an arrogant and fierce person from the lowliest parents. The opposite of this is what we have recorded elsewhere: "The sons of heroes are a nuisance" <note>A common Greek sentiment that great men often produce disappointing children</note>, when those born from distinguished men do not live up to the virtues of their ancestors. For example, Socrates, in Plato's *First Alcibiades*, teaches that both of Pericles' sons, Paralus and Xanthippus, were stupid, and that Clinias turned out to be a madman. In short, no one was made wise by Pericles' efforts, whereas many wise men emerged from the company of Zeno. He treats the same subject in the *Meno*, mentioning also Aristides, who had a son named Lysimachus who was a "nobody"; and furthermore Thucydides, who had two sons, Melesias and Stephanus. Neither lived up to the father's virtue. To these may be added Marcus Tullius Cicero, who left behind a son who was unpraised and who degenerated greatly from his father's virtues.

<summary>Erasmus examines various adages concerning extreme poverty, the existence of rivals ("Pylos before Pylos"), and the frequent failure of great men to produce virtuous heirs.</summary>
<keywords>Poverty, Pylos, Nestor, Achilles, Luck, Pedigree, Pericles, Cicero, Parenting, Greek Proverbs, Ancient Gambling</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Eighth Century of the Second Chiliad of Erasmus’s *Adages*. The previous page concluded with a discussion of the hero Nestor and Pylos. This page begins with entry 48.</meta>

SECOND THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY

<margin>More timid than Epeus. <note>original Greek: Ἐπεοῦ δειλότερος</note></margin>
### More timid than Epeus. ->XLVIII<-

"More timid than Epeus" was a saying used for a person who was exceptionally fearful. It is derived from a certain Epeus <note>Epeus was the mythological Greek engineer who built the Trojan Horse; despite his skill, he was often depicted in later tradition as lacking courage in battle</note>, a man noted for his cowardice. This nickname was given to the comic poet Cratinus, perhaps as an allusion to the fact that while he was a leader of the Oeneid tribe, he behaved rather timidly in that office.

<margin>Ephesian letters. <note>original Greek: Ἐφέσια γράμματα</note></margin>
### Ephesian letters. ->XLIX<-

"Ephesian letters." This seems to be said of those who, with miraculous success—as if by a divine wand—attain whatever they desire. For they say the Ephesians possessed certain symbols and magic words which, when used, allowed them to emerge victorious in every business. The author is Diogenianus. Eustathius, in his commentary on the *Odyssey* (Book 21), relates that Croesus used these letters while on the funeral pyre. These were certain obscure words, very much like riddles and not at all coherent, which were inscribed on the feet, the belt, and the crown of the statue of Diana <note>The Temple of Artemis (Diana) at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>. Suidas adds a story of this kind: at the Olympic Games, a certain man from Miletus was wrestling with an Ephesian and could do nothing in the struggle because the Ephesian had Ephesian letters on his ankle. As soon as this was noticed and the letters were taken away, the Ephesian, who had already exhausted thirty opponents, collapsed in defeat. Hesychius indicates that these were certain ancient words held as sacred, to which impostors later added many more. He thinks the ancient ones were: *aski* <note>original Greek: ἄσκι</note>, which is interpreted as darkness; *kataski* <note>original Greek: κατάσκι</note>, light; *lix* <note>original Greek: λὶξ</note>, the thing itself; *damnameneus* <note>original Greek: δαμναμενεύς</note>, the sun; and *aision* <note>original Greek: αἴσιον</note>, the truth. Anaxilas also mentions these in Athenaeus (Book 12). For, recounting the luxuries of a certain philosopher, he says: "Besides these, wearing beautiful Ephesian letters in little sewn-up pouches." <note>original Greek: ἡ πρὸς τοῖς γ᾽ ὑπὸ σκυταλίοις ῥαπτοῖσι φορέων ἐφέσια γράμματα καλά</note>. Even today, there are those who deceive fools with these kinds of fabricated words. It is quite apparent that through the negligence of copyists, although Hesychius lists *eiphas* <note>original Greek: εἶφας</note> among the magic words, he nevertheless fails to mention it when interpreting each one.

### Taught in the same school. ->L<-

Those laboring under similar vices and equal in wickedness were said to be "taught in the same school." This saying remains so common in the vernacular that nothing is more well-worn. Terence says in *The Mother-in-Law*: "They all seem to me to be taught in the same school for mischief." <note>original Latin: In eodem omnes mihi videntur ludo doctę, ad malitiam</note>. For it usually happens that those who have had the same teachers agree in character and habits. Moreover, what Terence said regarding women—that they all share similar characters—is attested to by the Greek six-foot verse:
<margin>A woman never differs from a woman. <note>original Greek: τῶν γυναικὸς πινῶν οὐδὲν διαφέρει</note></margin>
->that is,<-
->A woman never differs at all from a woman.<-
The proverb implies that no good woman is to be found. <note>Erasmus is reflecting a common misogynistic trope of ancient and Renaissance literature here</note>

<margin>As if at the Spartan mess. <note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ ἐν φιδιτίοις</note></margin>
### As if at the Spartan mess. ->LI<-

"As if at the *phiditia*" <term>phiditia: the public mess halls in ancient Sparta where citizens ate simple communal meals</term> is a phrase we shall use when something is done rather sparingly or with excessive frugality. The Lacedaemonians (Spartans) had public places in which they took their food. In these, they received their guests and ambassadors, but with very meager preparation. From this, the Greek word seems to be derived from *pheido* <note>original Greek: φειδὼ</note>, which means "sparing." However, there are those who prefer them to be called *philitia* <note>original Greek: φιλίτια</note>, as if they were *philitia* <note>original Greek: φιλιτία</note>, because fellowship was joined at such banquets. Plutarch reviews both etymologies in his *Life of Lycurgus*. In the former, the "s" is dropped from the diphthong; in the latter, the "l" is turned into a "d." He also adds a third etymology: that they were called *phiditia* as if they were *editta* <note>original Greek: ἔδιττα</note>, from "taking food," which the Greeks (especially the Athenians) call *syssitia* <note>original Greek: συσσίτια</note>, and the Cretans call *andria* <note>original Greek: ἄνδρια</note>, as Plutarch indicates in the same place. Lycurgus instituted this kind of banquet to exclude luxury and drunkenness. Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions the *phiditia* in the fifth book of his *Tusculan Disputations*. "What," he says, "do we not see the diet of the Lacedaemonians in their *phiditia*?" There, when the tyrant Dionysius had dined, he said he was not at all delighted by that "black broth" which was the main course of the dinner. Then the man who had cooked it said: "It is not at all surprising, for the seasonings were missing." "Which ones?" asked the tyrant. The cook replied: "Labor in the hunt, sweat, a run from the Eurotas River, hunger, and thirst. For with these things are the feasts of the Lacedaemonians seasoned." However, this story is told differently in Plutarch in the *Coronis* <note>The "Coronis" or "Finishing Touch" refers to the end of a collection of Laconian apophthegms</note> which we see added to the Laconian sayings regarding the institutions of Lycurgus. There were also other types of banquets among the Lacedaemonians, one of which was the *aklon* <note>original Greek: ἄκλον</note>, which was prepared with certain kinds of food, and another *aklon* which was somewhat more splendid. The most frugal of all was that which was held in the *phiditia*. Athenaeus writes much about these in his fourth book, if anyone should wish to know. It can also be applied to speech; for instance, if someone says they are not content with simple language—as if they were being received at a Spartan *phiditia*—but instead desire something of splendor and a charm that stimulates the appetite.

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to cowardice (Epeus), magic and luck (Ephesian letters), shared moral failings (the same school), and Spartan frugality (the phiditia). Erasmus provides etymological roots and historical anecdotes, such as the famous Spartan "black broth," to explain the origins and applications of these sayings.</summary>
<keywords>Epeus, Ephesian letters, magic charms, Cratinus, Terence, Sparta, Lycurgus, frugality, black broth, phiditia, etymology</keywords>

ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<sig>LII</sig>

->Apply lighter bits to an aging horse.<-

"Apply lighter bits to an aging horse" <note>original Greek: Ἱππῳ γηράσκοντι τὰ μείονα κύκελα ἐπίβαλλε; original Latin: Equo senescenti minora cicela admoue</note>. This proverb advises that when strength begins to fail due to age, one must grant a certain amount of breathing room and refreshment from labor; as one’s vigor decreases, the workload should be lessened and relaxation increased. They say the saying is derived from cavalry horses, which, as they grew old, were fitted with a lighter *trisippion* <note>a "three-horse" mark or bit</note>. This *trisippion* is a kind of small wheel, a public brand, which was typically heated in a fire and pressed onto the jaws of horses. Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and literary critic</note> points out that the proverb appeared in the works of the comic poet Cratetes in his play *The Samians*. It appears to be a line of heroic verse if you simply read "apply the bits" <note>original: κύκλ’ ἐπίβαλλε</note>. For I have not yet found the word *kykela* <note>referring to bits or brands</note> in any author except Zenodotus. Hesychius mentions the *trilippion*. It seems, however, that a *kykelon* is something not unlike a *trisippion*.

<sig>LIII</sig>

->The Eretrians' letter R.<-

"The Eretrians' letter R" <note>original Greek: Ἐρετριέων ῥῶ; original Latin: Eretriensium Rho</note>. This refers to someone who pronounces that letter too frequently or too harshly. In this regard, the people of Picardy currently have a bad reputation among the French. It is also used to mark those who were excessively fond of the "lambdacism" <note>substituting 'l' for 'r'</note> of Alcibiades. Catullus mocks Arrius for this kind of speech, because he:
*Would say "Chommoda" when he meant "commoda" <note>advantages</note>,*
*And "hinsidias" for "insidias" <note>ambush</note>.*
*And then he believed he had spoken wonderfully,*
*When he had shouted "hinsidias" as loud as he could.*
Diogenianus records this proverb. Plato mentions it in the *Cratylus*: "You know that what we call *sklerotes* <note>hardness</note>, the Eretrians call *skleroter*." From this, it is clear that the Eretrians were fond of the letter Rho, which they substituted in place of Sigma; conversely, the Athenians changed Rho into Sigma, such as saying *tharsein* instead of *tharrein* <note>meaning "to be bold"</note>. Since that letter is said to signify impulse and violence, the proverb seems to apply well to headstrong and violent men.

<sig>LIIII</sig>

->Stung by the gadfly.<-

"Stung by the gadfly" <note>original Greek: Οἴστρῳ πεπληγώς; original Latin: Oestro percitus</note>. This means being moved by a great desire of the mind, and as if thunderstruck. For the *oestrus* is a type of insect with a terrifying buzz, from which its name was given by the Greeks; the Latins call it an *asilus* <note>a horse-fly or gadfly</note>. Juno used this insect to drive the cow Io into a madness. From this, poets seized by a divine frenzy are said to be "stirred by the gadfly." It is found in Plato, although the specific passage does not occur to me at the moment—I believe it is in the *Phaedrus*. From this also comes the compound word *oistroplex* <note>gadfly-struck</note> for an insane person, and *oistrelatein* for "to act insanely."

<sig>LV</sig>

->In great things, even the will is enough.<-

"In great things, even the will is enough."
Nothing is more celebrated than this sentiment from Tibullus. Angelo Poliziano <note>a famous Italian humanist scholar</note> translated it into Greek quite skillfully: <margin>(ce)</margin> "In great matters, even the intent alone suffices" <note>original Greek: Ἀρκεῖ δ’ ἐν μεγάλοις καὶ τὸ θέλημα μόνον</note>.
Apuleius writes in the fourth book of his *Florida*: "With greater will, naturally, than ability. He is to be praised all the more readily because in all good things, the attempt is a matter of praise, while the outcome is a matter of chance." Likewise, Marcus Varro, in Gellius (Book 1, Chapter 18), says: "In which I not only do not find fault with Laelius's talent, but I praise his industry. For fortune follows success, but praise follows the attempt." This is appropriate when someone has attempted things greater than their strength; even if they do not satisfy the magnitude of the undertaking, they deserve praise for the very reason that they attempted a most beautiful thing.

<sig>LVI</sig>

->I shall sleep in the mortar.<-

"I shall sleep in the mortar" <note>original Greek: Ἐν ὅλμῳ εὐνάσω; original Latin: In holmo cubabo</note>. This was said by those who threatened to go and learn something through divination. For some interpret *holmos* <note>a mortar</note> as a prophet. Others say that the tripods of Apollo were called *holmoi*. Aristophanes the Grammarian relates, as cited by Zenodotus, that those who fell asleep in these mortars suddenly conceived the spirit of divination. He adds that Apollo was nicknamed *Holmios* by Sophocles for this reason. However, in Hesychius, *holmos* is used for a mortar. In Athenaeus (Book 11), it is a type of cup shaped like a horn, so that it might also be jokingly directed at heavy drinkers.

<sig>LVII</sig>

->Of the same wax.<-

"In the honeycomb" <note>original Greek: Ἐν κηρίῳ; original Latin: Idem fauus</note>. They used to say "of the same honeycomb" of those who affirmed the same thing with one voice, or who had conspired together. It is derived from the cells of the honeycombs being connected to one another. Or perhaps because wax is tenacious and clings to itself. Or because they used to write on waxed tablets in the old days, hence Horace says: "He is praised on the same wax" <note>meaning he is mentioned in the same will or document</note>.

<summary>This page catalogs proverbs regarding the moderation of labor in old age, linguistic regionalisms (the rhoticism of the Eretrians), the frenzy of divine or romantic passion, the virtue of noble effort regardless of success, and the origins of prophetic and conspiratorial metaphors.</summary>
<keywords>old age, Eretria, linguistics, Rho, gadfly, passion, effort and success, Apollo, divination, honeycomb, wax tablets</keywords>

# SECOND THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY
Cc
<meta>catchword: quen-</meta>

...as if because images were once molded from wax in various forms—now of gods, now of kings, now of commoners—yet all of these were ultimately wax. Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and the first librarian of Alexandria</note> records this. It is not unlike what we have said in another place: *The same dust* and *The same flour*.

->It is situated on the knees of five judges.<-
<margin>LVIII</margin>
*It lies on the knees of five judges* <note>original Greek: Ἐν πέντε κριτῶν γόνασι κεῖται; original Latin: In quinque situm genibus iudicum</note>. This means that a matter has been placed in the judgment of another. For in ancient times, the task was given to five judges to pass sentence on the plays of comic poets, as Epicharmus <note>an ancient Greek dramatist and philosopher</note> testifies in the works of Zenodotus. Although mention of five judges is also made in Plato, both elsewhere and in the eleventh book of his *Laws*: *Let the judgment be in the hands of the five youngest of the guardians of the laws* <note>original Greek: Ἐν πέντε δὲ τῶν νομοφυλάκων τοῖς νεωτάτοις εἶναι τὴν κρίσιν</note>. However, this is an allusion to a frequent phrase in Homer:
*These things lie on the knees of the gods* <note>original Greek: Και ταῦτα θεῶν ἐν γόνασι κεῖται</note>.
We use this when we mean it is not within our own power to guarantee the outcome of a matter, but that it lies in the hands of the gods above and of fortune. Pindar in his *Olympian Odes* says:
*Now I have hope, but the end lies indeed with God* <note>original Greek: νῦν δ' ἔλπομαι μὲν, ἐν θεῷ γε μὰν τέλος</note>.

->Of a wiped nose. Of snotty nostrils.<-
<margin>LIX</margin>
A person is said to be *of a wiped nose* <note>original Latin: emunctae naris</note> if they possess a sharp and exact judgment, as if their nostrils were cleared and wiped of snot.
Horace says of Lucilius:
*Of a wiped nose, though harsh in composing verses.* <note>meaning he was shrewd and witty, even if his poetry was unpolished</note>
Conversely, those who are somewhat stupid are said to be *of a thick nose* <note>original Latin: obesae naris</note>. The same Horace in his *Odes* writes:
*Neither for a steady youth, nor one of a thick nose.*
Lucian in his *Alexander the False Prophet* says: *But to the unlearned and those whose noses are full of snot, it seemed a marvel* <note>original Greek: τοῖς δὲ ἰδιώτοις καὶ κορύζης μεστοῖς τὴν ῥῖνα τεράστιον</note>. The same author in *The Lover of Lies*: *Certainly to me, I say, unless I were completely full of snot in the nose* <note>original Greek: ἐμοί γε, λῶ δ' ἐγὼ, εἰ μὴ πάνυ τὴν ῥῖνα κορύζης μεστὸς εἴην</note>. Plato alluded to this in the first book of the *Republic*, where Thrasymachus, mocking Socrates for his dullness, wishes a nurse for him to squeeze the snot from his nose: *Since she overlooks you while you are still snotty-nosed, and does not wipe you, though you have need of it* <note>original Greek: ὅτι σοι ἔτι κορυζῶντα περιορᾷ, καὶ οὐκ ἀπομύττει, δεόμενον αὐτῆς</note>.

->Hunger and delay stir up bile in the nose.<-
<margin>LX</margin>
Sosia, a character in Plautus’s *Amphitryon*, says: "It is an old proverb: *Hunger and delay stir up bile in the nose*." That is to say, when the stomach is growling, every delay stirs up anger. As for his saying that they stir "bile into the nose," this agrees with what Theocritus says in his *Thyrsis*:
*For he is bitter,*
*And sharp bile always sits upon his nose.* <note>original Greek: ἔν τί γε πικρὸς, καί οἱ ἀεὶ δριμεῖα χολὰ ποτὶ ῥινὶ κάθηται</note>
The metaphor is drawn from animals that signal their anger by snorting through their nostrils. From this comes the fable of the fire-breathing bulls. Indeed, even in some humans, the nose provides evidence of a hot temper. Hence people are said to *wrinkle their noses* <note>original Latin: corrugare nares</note> at things that offend them. Horace writes:
<margin>Lest a dirty napkin</margin>
*Lest a dirty napkin wrinkle your nose.* Likewise, Persius in his fifth *Satire*:
*But let the anger fall from your nose, and that wrinkled sneer.*
This can be applied more broadly, namely to anyone who desires something vehemently, to whom every delay, no matter how tiny, seems very long; as the Mime <note>likely Publilius Syrus</note> attests:
*Even speed is delay to one who desires.*
The following from Horace looks toward this same idea:
*As the night seems long to those whose mistress has lied to them, and the day*
*Seems long to those who owe labor; as the year is sluggish*
*To wards, whom the harsh guardianship of their mothers oppresses.*

->More noble than Sparta.<-
<margin>LXI</margin>
*More noble than Sparta* <note>original Greek: ἐλευθερώτερον σπάρτης</note>. This was said of a person of excellent spirit, who was in no way fearful or humble. For in olden times, the Spartan character was noble and their disposition was impatient of all servitude, as if born for command. For this reason, they did not even encircle their city with walls, thinking it was abundantly fortified by laws and by a youth of brave men. They considered it most foul...

<summary>This page explores several proverbs regarding judgment and temperament, comparing "wiped" (sharp) versus "snotty" (dull) noses, and explaining the ancient Greek roots of judicial and emotional metaphors.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, proverbs, Sparta, judgment, Horace, Plato, Socrates, anger, nostrils, ancient law</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...anyone to return from battle unless as a victor: a fact also attested in an epigram. Nor did they admit tyranny into their Republic, but obeyed the laws with equal liberty. Finally, they practiced no humble labor, but carried out agriculture and sedentary arts through the Helots <note>a subjugated population in Sparta who functioned as serfs</note>, who were a class of slaves.

### A Locrian ox.

<margin>LXI</margin>
*A Locrian ox* <note>original Greek: Λοκρικὸς βοῦς</note>. This can be said of a worthless thing, or of a very trivial gift. It stems from a time when the Locrians, wanting to perform a public sacrifice but lacking an ox, made a likeness of an ox out of small sticks of wood and performed the divine rite for the gods with that. From this, the common people snatched up the adage.

### A sword of fig-wood.

<margin>LXII</margin>
*A sword of fig-wood* <note>original Greek: Συκίνη μάχαιρα</note>. This can be said of a frivolous cause, or one that can be refuted with the slightest effort. Furthermore, a "fig-wood sword" was a name for a sycophant <note>the word "sycophant" originally meant "one who shows figs," often referring to a petty informer</note>, because such a person is both soft and a slanderer. Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian</note> also mentions this.

### A fig for Mercury.

<margin>LXIII</margin>
*A fig for Mercury* <note>original Greek: Σῦκον ἐφ' ἑρμῇ</note>. This was said of a benefit that was ready and available to anyone. For in ancient times, the custom was that if a fig were found anywhere, it would be hung up as if sacred to Mercury. It was permitted for anyone who wished to take this "Mercurial fig," either because that god was believed to favor thieves, or according to that proverb, **Common Mercury** <note>original Greek: κοινὸς ἑρμῆς</note>, meaning "share and share alike." I believe Persius <note>a Roman satirist</note> alluded to this when he said:
> You might pass by a coin fixed in the mud, 
> Without swallowing the "Mercurial spit" of greed. <note>original Latin: Inq; luto fixum possis transcendere nummum, / Nec gluto sorbere saliuam Mercurialem.</note>
as has been indicated elsewhere.

### Like figs growing on the eyes.

<margin>LXIIII</margin>
*Like figs grown on the eyes* <note>original Greek: Ὡσπερ τὰ σῦκ’ ἐπὶ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς ἔφυ</note>. This was said of those who would persistently urge or press some business. The comparison is taken from "figs," which refers to a medical defect <note>likely styes or tumors</note> that grows on the eyes and cannot easily be plucked away without harming the eye itself. Aristophanes in *The Frogs* says:
*Like figs grown on the eyes*—that is,
*As a fig hanging over the eyes, so was he.*
This will be applied not inaptly to those who, since they are burdensome and intolerable, nevertheless cannot be plucked away except with great evil. I wish there were no such class of people, or that there never existed princes and high-ranking nobles who—being insatiable in their greed, utterly corrupt in their lust, most destructive in their cruelty, monstrous in their tyranny, and the truest enemies and plunderers of the state—are equipped for public destruction not only with arms and wealth but even with new arts of oppression which neither Dionysius nor Phalaris <note>notorious Greek tyrants</note> ever discovered. Yet they so adhere, so hang over, and are so fixed upon the people that they can neither be endured nor removed. To such an extent there is no senate, no magistrate, no religion, no part of the republic into which they have not penetrated by driving in their roots, like a plague spread through all the veins of the body. Indeed, these men—who are only sharp-eyed and clever when it comes to doing harm—have noticed that only one anchor of public safety remains: if the honorable concord of citizens and cities restrains the tyranny of the powerful. Therefore, their first care is to shatter this harmony. They feel that in peace they have the least power, since affairs are conducted by laws and counsel, not by deceits or arms. Consequently, they act in every way to ensure the people do not enjoy public peace. They perceive that the chief happiness of a state lies in having a prince who is upright, wise, and vigilant—that is, a true prince. Thus, with marvelous zeal, these "guardians" take care that the prince never becomes a man. These nobles, who grow fat on public evils, strive to ensure he is as effeminate as possible in his pleasures, so that he knows nothing of those things a prince most needs to know. Villages are plundered, fields are wasted, temples are robbed, innocent citizens are slaughtered, and sacred and profane things are mingled together, while the prince meanwhile idly plays at dice, dances, amuses himself with buffoons, hunts, loves, and drinks. O race of Brutus <note>the Roman who overthrew the kings</note>, long since extinct! Meanwhile, the eye of Jove is either blind or dull. There is no doubt that these corrupters of princes will pay the penalty to God, but it will be too late for us. In the meantime, they must be endured, lest anarchy—an even more destructive evil—should follow tyranny. This has been proven by the experiences of many republics, and recently the uprising of the peasants throughout Germany <note>the German Peasants' War of 1524–1525</note> taught us how much more tolerable the inhumanity of princes is than an *anarchy* <note>original Greek: ἀναρχίαν</note> that throws everything into confusion. While lightning strikes terrify everyone, they do not hit many. But a flooding sea spares no one, mixing and overturning everything. But because the impious nobles...
<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the final word "impious" transitions to the next page where Erasmus likely continues his critique of the ruling class.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s biting critique of the mendicant orders (friars), comparing their pervasive influence in society to a physical malady, before transitioning into shorter adages regarding military readiness and the frailty of old age.</meta>

...publicly, these are perhaps the scourge of the church: certain of those orders which the common people call "mendicants" <note>Members of religious orders like the Franciscans or Dominicans who originally committed to a life of poverty and begging.</note>. I do not accuse the pious, nor do I attack the order itself; I mark the wicked, who are everywhere a vast crowd. These men have so scattered themselves through the whole body of the state that nothing anywhere is done without them. They reign in the pulpits, which is the specific duty of bishops. They have seized tyranny in the schools, which is the next closest duty. Through them the ecclesiastical sacraments are administered; through them we are priests. They pronounce judgment on the profession of faith with more than censorial severity: "This man is a Christian, this one is a half-Christian, this one is a heretic, this one is a one-and-a-half-times heretic" <note>original: "sesquihæreticus"—a humorous term coined by Erasmus to mock over-zealous inquisitors</note>. Into their laps the people pour out the hidden acts of their lives and the most secret thoughts of the soul. Nor are they content with this; no treaties of princes are struck in which these men do not play a part. Without them, no marriage is contracted. In theatrical contests and public lotteries, they act as the judges <note>original: "agonothetas," the Greek term for officials who presided over games</note>, so little do they feel any shame. Finally, one is hardly allowed to die without them! There is no court of princes into which they have not crawled. If the princes have destined some impudent crime, they execute it through these men. If the Roman pontiffs plot anything that is somewhat foreign to that apostolic and ancient holiness, they use the ministry of these men most of all. Just as if there is some war, some riot, some tax collection, or some shameful indulgence, these men play the leading roles in such dramas. Meanwhile, the simple common folk are deceived by an appearance of holiness. Priests, when compared to these men, are not considered priests. Bishops, trusting in these men, sleep soundly on either ear <note>A Latin idiom meaning to be completely unconcerned or complacent.</note>. The common people, abandoned, are torn apart by a double kind of wolf instead of unique shepherds; for while the prelates exercise tyranny, these men are not shepherds either, but in another way are plunderers. Again, I warn that neither the pious nor the order itself is being marked by me. For those among them who are most incorrupt are accustomed to deplore the very things I deplore. And though bees are allowed to drive away their own drones <note>original: "fucos"</note>—since they lack stings, even if they are thievish—neither kings nor supreme pontiffs are able to drive these drones, more stinging than any hornets, from the state without a great ruin of the Christian religion. To such an extent have they fortified their factions; to such an extent have they occupied the whole world with their citadels and peoples; and daily they build new nests, surely under this pretext: that the religious devotion of the older monasteries (by whose recommendation they first arose) has perished—as if, indeed, the sincerity of these men will not also perish a little while later, if indeed there is any sincerity now. So it happens that the world is burdened with impious and idle flocks of monks, and princes are defrauded of their people, bishops of their flock, and the people of their shepherd; the purity and liberty of the Christian religion gradually slide down toward Jewish ceremonies. And just as it is difficult to say whether a concord between evil princes is more grave for the state or a disagreement—since if they wage war, they do so to the great misfortune of the people, and if they are reconciled, they conspire for public destruction—so you would not know whether it is more to be wished for, or rather, to put it better, whether the consensus among these men or their sedition is more to be detested, because either thing results in public evil. I believe, however, that "figs" <note>original: "ficos"</note> are mentioned here as a rigid tumor growing on the eyelids. Since this thing is most troublesome, it is nevertheless not removed without danger, because it hangs over the eye, a part most impatient of irritation and handling. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note> mentions this adage.

->With spear, with shield.<-
### LXVI
*With spear, with shield* <note>original Greek: Σὺν δορὶ, σὺν ἀσπίδι</note>. That is, "with spear, with shield." Used when someone approaches a matter with every effort.
Aristophanes in *Peace*:
*With spear and with shield.* That is,
"With spear, and with shield." Likewise in *The Wasps*:
*Running out with sword and shield.* That is,
"With a ready excursion, with shield and spear."
The metaphor is taken from a soldier equipped with all his weapons. That line from Homer will be correctly twisted to a similar use:
*With the spear itself, and with great hand-stones.* That is,
"They press on with spear and sword, and with huge stones."
Whenever a matter is carried out with all one's might.

->The skull of an old man is like a raisin.<-
### LXVII
*The skull of an old man is like a raisin* <note>original Greek: Ἀνδρὸς γέροντος ἀσταφὶς τὸ κρανίον</note>. That is,
"The skull of an old man is like a dried grape."
The adage warns that the elderly body is weak and flaccid, its juice exhausted and its flesh withered. Lucian in *The Tyrant* says of the elderly: "Since indeed they are all already raisins" <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ ἀσταφίδι γε πάντες ἤδη εἰσί</note>. For raisins are wrinkled and flaccid because their juice...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...boiled down with the sun <note>original: "cum sole decoctum"</note>. This is why the ancients called both raisins and shriveled old men "passos" <note>In Latin, "passus" can mean both "dried" (like fruit) and "having suffered/endured."</note> because of their wrinkled skin. Lucilius, as cited by Nonius, says:
*Wrinkled and shriveled old men all seek the same things.*

<margin>LXVIII</margin>
->After the leaves, the trees fall.<-

**After the leaves, the trees will fall on you.** We use this whenever we want to warn that if someone endures minor injuries now, more atrocious ones will follow. Just as the fallen leaves of trees are ignored at first, eventually it happens that the rotting trees themselves fall upon the head of the person standing beneath them. Plautus says in *The Brothers Menaechmus*: *Now the leaves are falling; now, if we stay here for three days, then the trees will fall on you.*

<margin>LXIX</margin>
->You tremble before the trumpet.<-

**You tremble before the trumpet**, that is, you are dismayed in spirit before the danger even appears. This is taken from cowardly soldiers who shake with fear before the war-trumpet is even sounded. For once the trumpet is heard, a strange sort of dread usually invades the minds of the soldiers. **Virgil** <note>The great Roman epic poet</note> asks: *Why does a tremor seize the limbs before the trumpet?* If this saying is twisted just a little further, it passes into the form of a proverb.

<margin>LXX</margin>
->A neglected corner.<-

**A neglected corner** <note>original: "Ameles angulus," from the Greek "Ameles gonia"</note>. This was a saying used for a person who is indolent and yawning, desiring nothing and attempting no good works. They say there is a place in Libya which was commonly called the "carefree corner" <note>original: "securus angulus"</note>, perhaps because it lay neglected and uncultivated. I find it written also as the "corner of the negligent man." This is recorded by Zenodotus and Hesychius <note>Ancient Greek grammarians and collectors of proverbs</note>.

<margin>LXXI</margin>
->Beyond the wealth of Callicrates.<-

**Beyond the fortunes of Callicrates** <note>original: "Hyper ta Kallikratous"</note>. This was said of immense wealth. Some say there was a man from Carystus named Callicrates who far surpassed the rest of the citizens in riches. Hence, if they wanted someone to be understood as exceedingly wealthy, they said he surpassed even the resources of Callicrates of Carystus. However, Aristotle, in his *Constitution of the Athenians* (as cited by the Suda <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world</note>), relates that a certain Callicrates was of the order of judges, and that he increased judicial fines beyond all measure; thus the proverb arose concerning immoderate exactions.

<margin>LXXII</margin>
->The chain of Vulcan.<-

**The chain of Vulcan** <note>original: "Hephaistoio desmos"</note>. Whenever someone was bound in inextricable knots, they were said to be held by the chains of Vulcan. The name is taken from those adamantine chains with which, in Homer, Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the god of fire and smithing</note> ensnared Venus and Mars, so that the more they tried to extricate themselves, the more they became entangled. Homer says in the eighth book of the *Odyssey*:

*He went to the forge, brooding on evils in his heart. 
He placed a great anvil on the block and hammered out chains 
Unbreakable and inescapable, so they might stay fixed where they were. 
But after he had crafted the snare, being enraged at Mars, 
He went to the chamber where his dear bed lay, 
And all around the bedposts he poured the chains in a circle. 
And many were also draped from the ceiling above, 
Fine as spiderwebs, so that no one could see them, 
Not even the blessed gods.* ->that is,<-

> He sought his home, where the blacksmith’s forge stands,
> Meanwhile turning over evils in the depths of his heart.
> But having placed a massive anvil on the block, he cut
> Chains that none could break or escape,
> In which they would remain both entangled and bound.
> But after he, indignant at Mars, had finished his snares and arts,
> He approached the chamber where the sweet bed 
> Stood, and here and there he fastened the deceptive chains to the supports,
> And suspended many from the highest part of the roof,
> Wonderfully thin, like the webs of spiders,
> So that they could not be caught by any eyes,
> Not even those of the gods.

This adage is recorded by the Suda.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs, shifting from metaphors of physical decline and impending danger to expressions regarding excess, wishful thinking, and moral character—specifically gluttony and ill-gotten gains.</meta>

# SECOND THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY

->Until one is full<- LXXIII

<margin>Until satiety <note>original: "Ἄχρι κόρου"</note>. That is, until one is satisfied, as much as one likes, or in great abundance.</margin>
This will truly be a proverb only if it is applied metaphorically, such as: "I have been occupied in poetic literature *until I was full*." Or, "He is famous among us *to the point of satiety*." And, "Quintilian delights in metaphors *until one is full*." They use the same meaning in a single compound word, *katakorōs* <note>original: "κατακόρως"</note>, which means "abundantly." Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist</note> adds *hyper koron* <note>original: "ὑπὲρ κόρον"</note>, meaning "beyond satiety." He notes that a person who eats in such a manner is commonly called a "glutton" <note>original: "ἀδδηφάγον"</note> or a "nabaros" <note>original: "νάβαρος"</note>—from *anabaros*, which is a measure of wheat—just as the Latins call a heavy drinker a "three-gallon-man" <note>original: "tricongium"</note>. Likewise, they say "up to the hair" <note>original: "ἄχρι χαίτας"</note>, meaning "up to the lip," a metaphor taken from vessels filled to the brim. Also, "Up to both ears," which I have mentioned elsewhere. Julius Pollux calls a full vessel "even-lipped" <note>original: "ἰσοχελὲς"</note> or "overflowing" <note>original: "ὑπερχελὲς"</note>, terms taken from the rim of a jar. This is also recorded by Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and the first librarian of Alexandria</note>.

---

->A generous vow<- LXXIIII

<margin>A magnificent vow <note>original: "Εὐχὴ μεγαλοδώρος"</note>. Said when someone conceives royal hopes in their mind and is already wealthy in their wishes.</margin>
The Greeks use the word *megalodōros* <note>original: "Μεγαλοδώρος"</note> for one who gives great gifts. Now, nothing is more liberal than a human wish; for it bestows on anyone as much as they ask for. Lucian mentions this in *The Navigium*. Ovid says, "Anyone can be rich in promises," but it is much easier to be generous and wealthy in one’s wishes.

---

->Would that I were home<- LXXV

<margin>Would that I were home <note>original: "οἴκοι γενοίμην"</note>.</margin>
This was usually said when someone desires to emerge from the evils in which they are entangled. It seems to be a metaphor taken from those who are in danger during a storm. For even now, those who sail in peril commonly say, "Would that I were home." It is recorded by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>.

---

->May you lose it as badly as you found it<- LXXVI

<margin>Would that you might cast out your nature as poorly as you found it <note>original: "Εἴθ’ φαύλως ὥσπερ εὗρες ἐκβάλοις τὴν φύσεσιν"</note>. That is, "I wish that just as you wrongly obtained your right, you might also wrongly lose it."</margin>
This means: I wish that just as you have wickedly acquired your reputation or your wealth, so you may lose them wickedly. This is similar to that line in Plautus: "Ill-gotten, ill-spent." Suidas cites this trochaic verse as a proverb from Aristophanes; it appears in *The Knights* and is spoken there against Cleon <note>A powerful and controversial Athenian politician</note>, the plunderer of the state.

---

->God provides good things spontaneously<- LXXVII

<margin>God sends forth good things of his own accord <note>original: "Αὐτόματος ὁ θεὸς ἀνίησι τὰ ἀγαθά"</note>. Said whenever things turn out happily without our effort, as if some god were taking care of it. Stobaeus brings forward this six-foot verse from the *Pluti* of Cratinus:</margin>
> God himself spontaneously sends forth all good things to all. <note>original: "Αὐτόματα πᾶσι θεὸς ἀνίει τὰ ἀγαθά"</note>
> God himself supplies these gifts of his own accord.
I have spoken elsewhere of the proverb "The sleeper’s net." <note>Refers to catching fish even while sleeping; i.e., effortless success.</note>

---

->Bellies<- LXXVIII

<margin>Bellies <note>original: "Γαστέρες"</note>. Used for gluttonous men who serve their stomach and abdomen.</margin>
Epimenides the Cretan, as cited by Saint Paul in the epistle he wrote to Titus:
> Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies. <note>original: "Κρῆtes ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργοί"</note>
So also Lucilius:
> Live on, you gluttons, you gormandizers, you bellies.
Terence in *Phormio* says: "Heap your fists into his belly." Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian</note> shows that this can also refer to the whole parasite. Plutarch, in his essay *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*, thinks these iambic verses fit a flatterer and a parasite better than a crab:
> The belly is the whole body; an eye looking
> everywhere; a beast hunting with every deceit. <note>original: "Γαστὴρ ὅλον τὸ σῶμα, πανταχῆ βλέπων / ὀφθαλμὸς, ἑρπετὸν πᾶσι δόλοισι θηρεύον"</note>
Aristotle, in the third book of his *Ethics*, shows that men devoted to the belly and gluttony are usually called *gastrimargoi* <note>original: "γαστριμάργους"</note> because they fill the belly with food and drink beyond measure. It is certain that the word is composed of *gastēr* (belly) and *margos* (insane). I would like to mention in passing a ridiculous thing I discovered on this occasion. The one who compiled the Greek *Etymologicum* for us denies that any grammarian or rhetorician explained where the word *gastrimargus* came from, but claims it was done by Aristotle in his work *On Animals*. For my part, I was gaping like a seagull, expecting some hidden secret. He says "Margos" is an animal which from pu-

<sig>Cc 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: trefa- (likely continuing "putrefaction" or "putrid")</meta>

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to excess, effortless fortune, and moral corruption, famously including the "Cretan Liar" paradox and the etymology of gluttony. Erasmus uses these classical fragments to illustrate human tendencies toward greed and wishful thinking.</summary>
<keywords>satiety, gluttony, Erasmus, Epimenides, Cretans, gastrimargos, Cleon, Aristophanes, Aristotle, St. Paul, ill-gotten gains</keywords>

--- Page 700 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of bizarre allegorical interpretations of nature and transitions into adages regarding cunning and the survival tactics of social parasites.</meta>

...[pu]trefaction, it is born between the earth and the water. Just as it is born from the earth, it does not cease to feed upon the earth until it has bored through it and emerges into the open air. As soon as it emerges, it remains dead for three days, until a moist mist arrives; soaked by this mist, the animal revives, and thereafter it no longer feeds upon the earth. And from this, those who followed the ancient philosophers called excessively voracious men *gluttons* <note>original: "γαστριμάργους" (gastrimargous), literally "belly-mad"</note>.

Now, what could be more foolish than this "dream"? But the author adds dream upon dream. "Nevertheless," he says, "these things can be understood in a pious sense. For all desire is born from corruption. After it is born, it does not cease to eat the heart in which it dwells, until through the habit of knowledge it comes out into the open. Once it has emerged, it dies to the three powers of the soul. And thus the grace of the Holy Spirit, appearing through the 'mist' of erudition, provides the droplets of cognition and brings life—not according to the former life subject to desires, but according to that life which, on account of virtue, holds familiarity with the gods." 

It seemed worthwhile to review these more-than-frivolous claims so that the reader might understand how much credit should be given to those "rhapsodies" <note>Erasmus refers here to collections of miscellaneous or poorly synthesized excerpts</note>. It is a mistake to think it a sacrilege to call into question whatever one finds smeared upon parchment, regardless of the occasion. It was once the hobby of certain people not only to drag the fables of the poets into Christian allegory, but even to devise new fables themselves to explain to us allegorically, as if the truth could not be learned without the application of a lie. Moreover, although this author was a Christian, he wishes to appear as if Aristotle were the author of his "dream"; he thinks he has beautifully "wiped our noses" <note>An idiom meaning to deceive or mock someone</note> because he says "gods" instead of "God." To be sure, Aristotle is not accustomed to accommodating the natures of living creatures to a moral sense, nor did he know what the Holy Spirit was.

Julius Pollux, in the sixth book of his *On Vocabulary*, reminds us that a heavy drinker was once called a *pithos* <note>original: "πίθον"</note>, that is, a "jar," and a glutton a *kados* <note>original: "κάδον"</note>, because *kados* signified a measure of grain, as if you were to call someone a "cask." Antiphanes, in Athenaeus's twelfth book, says of an obese and heavy-drinking man:

> This man, therefore, on account of
> His wine-bibbing and the fatness of his body,
> All the locals call a "wineskin" <note>original: "ἀσκόν" (askon)</note>.

In the same author, those devoted to food and drink are elsewhere called *thylakoi* <note>original: "θύλακοι"</note>, meaning "sacks." Nor is that saying obscure: "The jar hangs, not the man" <note>A joke implying the person is nothing more than the vessel they drink from</note>.

### A Ulyssean scheme.
<margin>LXXIX</margin>

*Oinuseōs mēchanē* <note>original: "Οἰνυσέως μηχανή"</note>, that is, a "Ulyssean invention," was said of something clever, astute, and crafty. Homer everywhere makes Ulysses versatile and a master of simulation and dissimulation. Whence, right at the beginning of the *Odyssey*, he calls him *polythropon* <note>original: "πολύτροπον"</note>, meaning "of many ways" or "versatile." Virgil likewise calls him:
"Ulysses, the inventor of crimes." 

This is recorded in Suidas. Plutarch, in the *Life of Lysander*, declares what a "Ulyssean scheme" is. The Spartans had recalled Lysander <note>A Spartan admiral</note> home by sending a *scytale* <note>A tool used for sending encrypted messages</note>. Fearing the accusations of Pharnabazus the satrap <note>A Persian governor</note>, who was in favor with the Spartans, Lysander arranged to have a meeting with him. He obtained from him, through many entreaties, a letter to the magistrates stating that he had been harmed by no injuries from Lysander. Pharnabazus, "playing the Cretan with a Cretan" <note>A proverb meaning to lie to a liar</note> as the saying goes, wrote a letter according to Lysander’s wishes and handed it to him to read; but secretly he had written another letter expressing his true mind, with a seal and inscription so similar that one could not be distinguished from the other, and he handed that one to Lysander. Lysander, suspecting nothing, delivered it. When the Ephors <note>Spartan magistrates</note> showed him the letter after reading it, Lysander understood that Ulysses was not the only crafty one.

### They live off their own juice.
<margin>LXXX</margin>

This is a proverbial figure of speech applied to parasites. Those who "live off their own juice" are those who, if a more elegant dinner happens to come along, gorge themselves; but on the other hand, when no hope of a dinner smiles upon them, they are forced to live on their own resources, bravely enduring hunger and lasting until the hope of a banquet returns. The metaphor is taken from snails, which, having retracted into their shells during a heatwave, nourish themselves however they can on their own moisture until rain falls. Plautus says in *The Captives*:

> When business is deferred, he says, when men go to the country,
> Business is likewise deferred for our teeth.
> Just as when it is hot, snails hide in the shadows,
> And live off their own juice if no dew falls.
> In the same way, parasites hide when business is deferred.
> In their misery, they live off their own juice in secret.
