# SECOND CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY
### Cc 4

->Friends stay far from unfortunate men.<-
->LXXXI<-

<note>original Greek: "Ἀνδρὸς κακῶς πράσσοντος, ἐκποδὼν φίλοι"</note> That is: 
**When a man is situated in misfortunes, his friends are far away.**
This proverb notes the habits of common friends who, in the manner of swallows, fly toward us or away from us according to the seasons: they fly toward us when things are prosperous, but fly away when the storm of circumstances rushes in. Aristides, in his *Panathenaic Oration*, specifically used the title of this adage, saying: <note>original: "Καὶ τὴν παροιμίαν ἐναλλάξας..."</note> "And by inverting the proverb—for it says friends are far away when one fares badly—he instead showed that many who were previously at odds became friends in the midst of calamities." <note>Aristides was praising how certain people find solidarity in shared disaster.</note> In this same vein, there exists a six-foot verse <term>senarius</term> of this sort:
**No happy man is a friend to those who are unfortunate.**
<note>original Greek: "Τῶν δυστυχέντων εὐτυχὴς οὐδεὶς φίλος"</note>
Likewise, another similar to it:
**Time proves a friend, just as fire proves gold.**
<note>original Greek: "Κρίνει φίλους ὁ καιρὸς, ὡς χρυσὸν τὸ πῦρ"</note>
Cicero openly alluded to this sentiment in the ninth book of his *Letters to Friends* <note>Epistulae ad Familiares</note>. For although true and false love are not easily distinguished unless some such time occurs, so that a faithful benevolence can be seen through some danger, just as gold is tested by fire. Other signs are common to both. Horace says:
**The price of friends is cheap when the good lack something.**
<note>Erasmus implies that true friends are hard to find when you have nothing to offer.</note>
Everywhere one finds friends who seek to get; those who give are very few. Pindar likewise writes on the same sentiment:
**The honor of friends vanishes when they are few and faithful; few among mortals are faithful in toil.**
<note>original Greek: "Οἴχεται τιμὰ φίλων..."</note> That is: Honor perishes for a man deprived of friends. There are few mortals faithful in afflicted circumstances.

->He knows the ways by which Eucrates escaped.<-
->LXXXII<-

<note>original Greek: "Οἶδε τὰς ὁδοὺς ὥσπερ ἔφυγεν Εὐκράτης"</note> That is: **He knows the roads by which Eucrates fled.** This fits a man who always finds some "crack," as Plautus says, through which he may slip away to dodge his duty. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:
**Beware lest he escape you, for he knows the ways**
**By which Eucrates escaped through the bran.**
<note>Eucrates was a miller who became a democratic leader in Athens; the "bran" or "husks" is a joke about his trade.</note>
He also touches in passing on the character of Eucrates, who, although he was a miller, nevertheless administered the republic. Furthermore, in *The Birds*, he censures a certain Execectides, a foreigner and a wanderer, to whom all the roads were known. It is suitable for a man who escapes under some pretext whenever faith must be shown or a promise kept.

->It lives, light the fire.<-
->LXXXIII<-

<note>original Greek: "Ζῇ, καῖε πῦρ"</note> That is: **It lives, kindle the fire.** We use this when we advise haste at the critical point of a dangerous business, and that an opportunity must be seized; just as when a tiny spark is found, one hurries so that even that does not perish. Similar to that is: *Now your iron is in the fire.* This is recorded in the *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world</note>.

->The belly has no ears.<-
->LXXXIIII<-

<note>original Greek: "Γαστὴρ ὦτα οὐκ ἔχει"</note> That is: **The stomach does not have ears.** When it is a matter of eating, honorable reasons are not admitted. This is attested by that six-foot verse celebrated among the Greeks in place of a proverb:
**For there is no word that can stand against hunger.**
<note>original Greek: "Λιμῷ γὰρ οὐδέν ἐστιν ἀντιστῆναι ἔπος"</note>
A saying of Cato is celebrated by Plutarch and Gellius, from a certain speech in which he discouraged an agrarian law. He began it by saying that it is difficult to speak to a belly that lacks ears. It may be applied not inaptly to those who, being addicted to the pleasures of the belly, admit nothing that is not "friendly" to the stomach. Seneca says in the 21st letter of his third book: "The belly does not hear precepts; it demands, it calls out. It is not, however, a troublesome creditor; it dismisses you for a small amount, provided you give it what you owe, not what you can."

->With even the little dust.<-
->LXXXV<-

We say "even with the little dust" <term>cum puluisculo</term> whenever all things are so taken away that nothing is left behind, not even the dust. The metaphor seems to be borrowed from those who sweep the grain from the threshing floor, not with...

<summary>This page explores several classical adages concerning the fickleness of fair-weather friends, the craftiness of those dodging responsibility, and the undeniable, irrational demands of physical hunger.</summary>
<keywords>Adagia, Erasmus, friendship, Eucrates, Aristophanes, hunger, Cato the Elder, Seneca, Greek proverbs, fair-weather friends</keywords>

--- Page 702 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Roman and Greek proverbs, moving from metaphors of "dust" and physical health to idioms concerning wasted effort, trickery, and social status.</meta>

...with fine dust. Plautus writes in *The Rope* [Rudentibus]: "He will now sweep me away entirely, including the dust." The same author says in *The Truculentus*: "So they might more quickly take the property from him, including the dust." <note>The phrase "with the dust" (cum puluisculo) implies taking every single thing, down to the smallest speck.</note> Juvenal used a similar figure, "With rust," to mean "entirely and with no part missing":
> Now if a friend does not deny a deposit,
> If he returns the old bag with all its rust.
<note>Juvenal, Satires 13.60-61. Rust implies that the money has sat untouched for so long that the container has corroded; returning it "with the rust" proves it was never opened or tampered with.</note>
The Gospel saying pertains to this same point, where the apostles are commanded to shake off even the dust from their feet: that is, to take not even the slightest thing away with them from those who reject them.

<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
### To be well in a pancratic way.

Plautus, in the *Bacchides*, used the phrase "To be well in a pancratic way" [Valere pancratice] to mean being in firm, robust health. This is because in the *Pancratiasts*, physical strength was the primary quality sought. <note>The Pancratium was an ancient Greek martial art combining wrestling and boxing; its practitioners were the ultimate symbols of physical toughness.</note> For the same idea, he used "To be well like an athlete," "To be well like a boxer," and "To be well royally" [basilice]. Terence likewise says: "They say she is a boxer," referring to a girl who is quite robust and well-built. The Greeks use the word "royally" [basilikos] as a proverbial figure for "magnificently." This manner of speaking is still common even in our own times.

<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
### It is shameful to have stayed long and returned empty.

This Homeric verse from the second book of the *Iliad* is undoubtedly among those that Macrobius writes have passed into common proverbs:
> <note>original Greek: Αἰσχρόν τοί δηρόν τε μένειν, κενεόν τε νέεσθαι</note>
which is to say:
> It is shameful to have stayed long and returned empty.
This will be appropriate when someone has raised a long-standing expectation about themselves, which they later fail to fulfill. For example, if someone travels abroad for a long time for the sake of study but returns home no more learned. Or if a merchant returns after a long absence no richer. Or if a very talkative person has performed nothing distinguished in life to testify that they have lived. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] employs this as a proverb in the sixth book of his *Letters to Atticus*.

<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
### To throw a javelin.

Plautus says in the *Epidicus*: "He is preparing to throw a javelin [*tragula*] at you," meaning he is preparing some trick against you. In the same passage: "He is building some structure." The verse is a trochaic tetrameter: "He is preparing to throw a javelin at you; he is building some structure or other."
Both figures appear to be proverbial. The same author in the *Casina*: "By Pollux, I will now cut down that javelin of theirs." Again in the *Pseudolus*: "But you threw a javelin at me." A *pilum* is a very similar type of spear, of which he said in the *Mostellaria*: "You threw a javelin [*pilum*] at me." <note>In these contexts, the spears represent a sudden, aggressive verbal or psychological attack or a "stinging" trick.</note>

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
### A man of three letters.

"A man of three letters" can be said ironically regarding someone who wishes to appear noble and well-born. This arises from the fact that in ancient times, people used to denote their status—their first name, family name, and surname—on their letters or insignia using three letters. For example, "Q.V.M." for Quintus Valerius Maximus. Hence the common joke about a "man of three letters." Plautus, in the *Aulularia*, twisted the joke in a different direction—namely, toward a thievish slave. For he adds: "Even a thief [FUR], a triple-thief." <note>The Latin word for "thief" is 'FUR', which contains exactly three letters. Erasmus explains that while three letters usually stood for a Roman citizen's honorable initials, here they stand for a criminal label.</note>

<margin>XC</margin>
### Three days' provisions.

"Three days' provisions" [Trium dierum commeatus] is used when extreme poverty is imminent. The metaphor is drawn from military rations. This is found in Aristophanes, notably in *The Acharnians*:
> <note>original Greek: Καί μοι ἐπισιτισμὸν σιτί’ ἡμερῶν τριῶν</note>
which means:
> And let me cook up three days' provisions.
The commentator adds that in ancient times, it was customary to order those going to war to prepare no less than three days' provisions for themselves. He mentions it in *The Knights* as well:
> <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ ποριῶ καὶ σῖτ’ ἡμερῶν τριῶν</note>
which is:
> I provide even that which is enough for three days. Accordingly, we shall call "three days' provisions" the smallest resources, which barely suffice for three days of life. Terence used a similar figure in *The Self-Tormentor* when he said, "A household of ten days."

<margin>XCI</margin>
### To perform tragedies over trifles.

He "performs tragedies over trifles" who raises a great commotion over a trivial matter and, as Terence says, "says great nonsense with great effort." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] says in *On the Orator*, book 2: "Lest we be thought worthy of either ridicule or hatred if we perform tragedies over trifles." Fabius [Quintilian] likewise uses it in his sixth book, in the chapter "On the Conclusion": "For to raise these tragedies in small lawsuits," he says, "is like wanting to fit the mask and buskins of Hercules onto infants." Indeed, this very phrase "To rouse a tragedy"...
<meta>catchword: fiali</meta>

He highlights how mundane terms—like a "man of three letters"—could be used as puns to mock a person's character or status.</summary>

# SECOND CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY

...if it deflects to somewhere else, it smacks of a proverb. Hence the Greeks also use the terms <term>to act out a tragedy</term> <note>original: "ἐκτραγῳδεῖν"</note> and <term>to speak tragically</term> <note>original: "τραγικῶς λέγειν"</note> to mean speaking solemnly or bitterly.

### To be driven sideways.
->XCII<-

One is said to be **driven sideways** when they are deflected from their intended purpose by some force or impulse. Thus Laberius the Mime, according to Macrobius in the second book of the *Saturnalia*, calls the course of fortune "athwart" or "sideways." For the kindness of Gaius Caesar invited this man—who was a Roman knight and an old man—to appear on the stage. In his prologue, therefore, he complains that he was compelled there by Caesar's authority against the judgment of his own mind.
> Necessity, he says, whose sideways impulse
> Many have wished to escape, and few were able,
> Which has thrust me down almost at the end of my senses, etc.
<note>Actors were considered "infamous" in Rome, so Caesar forcing a knight like Laberius to act was a public humiliation and a "sideways" diversion of his social status.</note>
So too, one who is carried away by headlong anger is said to be "snatched sideways." It appears to be a metaphor drawn from sailors: those who are carried on a straight course by a favorable wind are driven "sideways" by an adverse blast.

### You say Dionysius is like Thrasybulus.
->XCIII<-

<margin><term>You say Dionysius is like Thrasybulus.</term> <note>original: "Θρασυβούλῳ Διονύσιον φάτ’ εἶν’ ὅμοιον."</note> That is, you say Dionysius is the same as Thrasybulus.</margin> This is a dissonant comparison, used when someone compares things that differ by too great an interval. For Dionysius is remembered among the most pestilential of tyrants, while Thrasybulus is praised for being most devoted to the republic. <note>Thrasybulus was the Athenian general who overthrew the "Thirty Tyrants."</note> The phrase is taken from the *Plutus* of Aristophanes.

### Better than taxes.
->XCIIII<-

<margin><term>Better than taxes.</term> <note>original: "τὰ τῶν φόρων κρείττω."</note></margin> This was said when someone reaped a huge profit from misdeeds and injustice. It is recorded by Suidas and Zenodotus under the name of a proverb, but not explained by many. Harpocration, in his rhetorical dictionary, writes that it appeared in a speech by Hyperides against Athenogenes. I believe it arose from the fact that those who demand tribute in the name of princes almost always extort more than is fair. And princes demand in such a way that they snatch from the unwilling unless they give what is asked. To this agrees that line of Pindar from the eighth *Pythian Hymn*: <term>Profit is most welcome if one carries it from the house of a willing man.</term> <note>original: "κέρδος δὲ φίλτατον, γ’ ἑκόντος εἴ τις ἐκ δόμων φέροι."</note>

### A tragic ape.
->XCV<-

<margin><term>A tragic ape.</term> <note>original: "τραγικὸς πίθηκος."</note></margin> This was said as a proverbial insult toward one who performed honors and flourished in wealth, but was otherwise unworthy. They call a "little man" an ape—scarcely a human being, but rather a likeness of one. They add "tragic" because of the noise of fortune and the added theatrical mask. Demosthenes, in his speech *On the Crown* [Pro Ctesiphonte], calls Aeschines a "tragic ape" because, while he was a most wicked man, he acted the part of an upright citizen with splendid words. Philostratus mentions this proverb in his life of Aristides. Saint Jerome, in his *Epistles*, shows that this slur used to be commonly cast at Christians, but by the impious and heathens—as if they put on a display of holiness in their face and dress when they were actually wicked. However, this passage is not found in the same way in all copies, as we have pointed out in our *Scholia* (commentaries), in which we have clarified the works of that truly divine man through great labor, so that they might be read without hindrance by pious men of moderate learning. It also applies to those who profess themselves philosophers by their beard and cloak, when the rest of them does not match their attire. For so says Plutarch: <term>Neither growing a beard nor wearing a cheap cloak makes a philosopher, nor does wearing linen always make one a priest of Isis.</term> <note>original: "οὐτὲ γὰρ φιλόσοφος πωγωνοτροφίαι καὶ τριβωνοφορίαι ποιοῦσιν, ἔτι ἰσιακὸς ἀεὶ λινοστολίαι."</note>

### To feed the moths.
->XCVI<-

Things that perish from neglect and decay are said to **feed the moths**. The metaphor is drawn from clothes or books hidden away and untouched for a long time. Horace writes in his *Epistles*:
> When, handled by the hands of the common crowd, you begin
> To grow filthy, you will either silently feed the sluggish moths,
> Or you will flee to Utica, or be sent, bundled up, to Ilerda.
<note>Horace is addressing his book, warning it that if it seeks public fame, it will either end up neglected and moth-eaten or be exported to the provincial fringes of the empire like Africa (Utica) or Spain (Ilerda) as waste paper.</note>

### A firebrand to the fire.
->XCVII<-

<margin><term>A firebrand to the fire.</term> <note>original: "δαλὸς ἐπὶ πῦρ."</note></margin> This is used when someone is applied to those things toward which they are naturally inclined. For example, if a womanizer is placed in the company of girls, one greedy for blood is sent to war, or one thirsting for profit is sent into trade. For the Greeks call a piece of half-burnt wood a <term>dalos</term>. This is not very different from the saying: <term>to urinate in a chamber pot</term> <note>original: "ὡς ἀμὶς εἰς χύτραν"</note>—that is, putting something where it naturally goes. It is recorded by Suidas and Zenodotus.

<summary>This page catalogs proverbs concerning being forced off course, the irony of comparing polar opposites, the corruption of tax collection, and the hypocrisy of those who look the part of a philosopher or saint but lack the character.</summary>
<keywords>Laberius, taxes, tragic ape, hypocrisy, Saint Jerome, Horace, social status, corruption</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, THE ADAGES

### Laconian Spurge. XCVIII

<term>Laconian Spurge</term> <note>original: "Τιθύμαλλοϛ λακωνικόϛ"</note>. This was said of those who were bleary-eyed or whose sight was failing. Spurge—a type of herb found among the Spartans—gives off a milky sap when plucked, which is why some have called it "milk-herb" <note>original: "lactariam"</note>. It is of singular sharpness, and they used to smear it on their eyes toward nightfall to sharpen their vision. Dioscorides, in his fourth book, identifies several species of this plant and carefully records its use as a remedy for the eyes. The adage is recorded in the works of Suidas, who cites Aristophanes regarding the bleary-eyed Neoclides: <term>He crushed garlic together with spurge</term> <note>original: "σκόροδ’ ὁμοῦ τρίψαντα τιθυμάλλῳ"</note>.

Indeed, the verse survives in the play *The Assemblywomen*:
> What then was I to do?
> You should have crushed garlic together with the juice of Laconian spurge,
> Mixed it in, and smeared your own eyelids toward evening.
<note>Erasmus is quoting Aristophanes' *Ecclesiazusae*. The "Laconian" variety was famously potent. The joke in the play is that this "remedy" would actually be incredibly painful, a mock-prescription for a corrupt politician.</note>

The word <term>tithymallus</term> seems to be derived from a nurse's breast <note>from the Greek 'titthos' for breast, referring to the milky sap</note>. However, I find it written by others with a single "l," though Suidas writes it with a double "l," and yet he does not indicate the use of the proverb. If it is applied to the bleary-eyed, one should say, "He has need of spurge," or, "He is grinding spurge." For they say its sharpness is so effective that when its sap is collected, one must take care that it does not touch the eyes; and whenever it is taken into the stomach, it must be swallowed wrapped in something so that it does not scrape the throat. The sap of this plant is used to treat discharges of the eyes. Pliny writes much about these in his twenty-sixth book, chapter eight. Cornelius Celsus, in his fifth book, indicates that this herb is called "Sea Lettuce" <note>original: "Lactucam marinam"</note> by the Latins, and says it has the power to corrode.

### Sardinian Dye. XCIX

<term>Sardinian Dye</term> <note>original: "Βάμμα Σαρδωνικόν"</note>. This was said of an excellent color, especially purple. In a joking sense, however, it is transferred to someone who is blushing with shame, or one who is stained with blood because of a beating. Sardinia—or, as Hesychius writes, Sardon—is a large island opposite Italy, in which various and highly praised dyes for purple were made. Similarly, we read among the Latin authors of "Tyrian shellfish" and "Sarran purple" <note>Sarran refers to the ancient city of Tyre</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Peace*:
> When he says it is of a Sardinian dye.
And likewise in *The Acharnians*:
> Lest I stain you with a Sardinian dye.
<note>In the context of the plays, "staining someone with Sardinian dye" was a comedic euphemism for beating someone until they were covered in blood.</note>

### As much as a tortoise cares for a fly. C

<term>The tortoise cares nothing for flies</term> <note>original: "Οὐ μέλει τῇ χελώνῃ μυῶν"</note>. Suidas, quoting from some author or other, relates these words: "Agamemnon cared as little for Thersites' insolence as a tortoise does for flies (or for a flock of sheep), as the proverb says." Flies can do no harm to a tortoise because of the shell with which it is protected. This is close to what we have mentioned elsewhere: <term>The elephant does not care for the gnat</term>. It will be even more charming if twisted to apply to matters of the mind. A mind fortified by virtue and philosophy fears the onslaught of fortune no more than a tortoise fears flies.

-> THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD <-

### More foolish than Morychus. I

**M**ore foolish are you than Morychus <note>original: "Μωρότεροϛ ὦ μορύχου"</note>. A Sicilian proverb used against those who did something in a ridiculous or foolish manner. To me, it seems those especially liable to this adage are people who, while negligent of their own domestic affairs, spend their time abroad tending to the business of others. The character Ollus in Martial is of this kind, as are the "Lamiae" <note>mythical monsters who could remove their eyes</note> in Plutarch. Zenodotus records that among the Sicilians, "Morychus" was a nickname, given because during the grape harvest, the face of this god <note>Bacchus/Dionysius</note> used to be smeared with new wine and fresh figs. The ancients attributed the praise for the discovery of both trees to Bacchus, as Athenaeus testifies in the second book of the *Dinner-Sophists*. It comes from <term>moryxe</term>, which means to stain or defile; hence Homer also uses <term>memorygmena</term> for things that are defiled.

<summary>Erasmus explains proverbs involving the medicinal (and painful) Laconian spurge, the prestigious yet pun-filled "Sardinian dye," and the stoic indifference of a tortoise toward flies, before introducing a Sicilian proverb about the foolish Morychus.</summary>
<keywords>Laconian Spurge, Tithymallus, eye remedies, Aristophanes, Sardinian dye, Sardinia, purple, tortoise, indifference, Agamemnon, Morychus, Bacchus, Sicilian proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Ninth Century of the Second Chiliad. Erasmus transitions from discussing specific herbal remedies and their associated metaphors to a more literary and philological critique focused on the figure of Morychus and a defense of the scholar Angelo Poliziano against a nameless rival.</meta>

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD

<margin>Morych-like</margin> <note>original: "μωρυχώδ." (morychōdēs)</note> Bacchus is everywhere depicted by the poets as ridiculous and of little sense, as he is a drunken god—just as he appears in Aristophanes’ *The Frogs*. Consequently, in his sacred rites, certain playful acts were performed as if to mock him. Indeed, even a nickname was added for the sake of insult: <margin>Morychus.</margin> Among the Sicilians, a statue of this god was placed not inside a temple, but outside the shrine in the open air, near the entrance or vestibule. It was crafted from a stone called Psella by a certain Simmias, son of Eupalamus. Hence, a common joke was tossed around about him: <margin>You are more foolish than Morychus, who, leaving the things inside, sits outside the house.</margin> <note>original: "μωρότερος ει μορύχου, ὃς τὰ ἔνδον ἀφείς, ἔξω τῆς οἰκίας κάθηται."</note> Zenodotus cites this adage from a certain letter of Polemon to Diophilus.

Although it is quite foreign to my nature and character to waste effort tracking down or attacking the errors of others, I cannot restrain myself in this instance. I bring forward the ignorance—not to say the sluggishness—of a certain Italian of no small reputation, more for the sake of laughter than for a personal attack. This is especially necessary since he, <margin>wearing the lion's skin,</margin> <note>An allusion to Aesop’s fable of the donkey in a lion’s skin; someone pretending to be more important or learned than they are.</note> takes so much upon himself in literature that, snatching up the censor’s rod as it were, he not only passes judgment on other writers with great authority, but even lashes out at and "corrects" Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant Italian humanist scholar whom Erasmus deeply admired.</note> as if he were a mere schoolboy—a man who was in every way incomparable and inimitable. 

While this "honest man" concedes quite a lot to Poliziano, nevertheless his own delicate ears, accustomed to pure Attic style, find Poliziano lacking in the sense of the "Transmarine Venus" <note>A metaphor for a refined, foreign, or particularly elegant Greek charm.</note> because Poliziano translated "not at all" <note>original: "τὴν ἀρχὴν" (tēn archēn)</note> as "not even in the beginning." Let us, then, hear from this "Aristarchus" <note>A reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, the rigorous ancient critic; here used sarcastically.</note> about his own Transmarine Venus and his "genuine" Greek. 

First, you narrate this proverb from the very common collections of Zenobius, yet you cite Polemon as if you had read the passage yourself. This is something he does in his usual manner: namely, to appear as if he spends his time among obscure and non-vulgar authors. Next, the Greek words which I just recorded from that same source—<margin>who, leaving the things inside, sits outside the house</margin>—he translated in this way: "Who, leaving the inner habitation, sought that which was placed outside." 

Furthermore, regarding what is found in those same collections—<margin>Morychus, by which name Dionysus is called because he is stained by wine-lees on his face, or rather, because they smear him with the must of grapes and green figs</margin> <note>original: "μόρυχος οὗ ὁ διόνυσος ἐπεὶ τριγὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ μολύνεται, ἐπὶ πλέον τρυγῶσαι, τῷ ἀπὸ τῶν βοτρύων γλύκει, καὶ τοῖς χλωροῖς σύκοις."</note>—he expressed it this way: "Morychus is indeed an epithet of Bacchus <margin>from the staining of his face,</margin> <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ μολύνεσθαι."</note> that is, from the obvious defiling of his own face." For Bacchus is accustomed to defiling it with clusters of grapes and green figs. Then, where that same compiler, giving the etymology of the name, wrote: <margin>to smear is the same as to defile,</margin> <note>original: "μορύξαι γὰρ τὸ μολύναι" (moryxai gar to molynai)</note> our modern "Attic wit" interpreted it thus: <margin>"To smear,"</margin> he says, "is further the same as <margin>'to defile,'</margin> that is, to act foolishly, that is, to be out of one’s mind." 

Now, how great is this: <margin>"more foolish than any Morychus,"</margin> which he rendered regarding the placement of Bacchus! The Greek says: <margin>His statue stands more outside the temple than inside, in the open air.</margin> <note>original: "πλείω ἔξω τοῦ νεῶ τὸ ἄγαλμα αὐτοῦ ἔστι πλεῖον ἢ ἔνδον ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ."</note> Our "Transmarine Venus" brought it forth like this: "Moreover, he is named for the simplicity of Bacchus, whose statue is set in the open in the works of Hesiod." 

See how many "Venuses" <note>Erasmus is being sarcastic, calling the rival's errors "beauties."</note> this charming man has produced in one very short chapter. First, Bacchus, having loathed the inner chambers of his own buildings, seeks out foreign homes. Then, although he is made of stone (for a statue is mentioned), he nevertheless smears his own face with grape clusters and figs to delight the harvesters. To this, although <margin>to smear and to defile</margin> mean the same thing, he declares both mean "to act foolishly" and "to be out of one's mind"—but only to those who have thoroughly mastered that Transmarine Venus! 

Finally—and this is the most charming of all—out of the vestibule (since according to Pollux he calls the <margin>inner sanctuary</margin> of the temple that which is also called the <margin>gateway</margin>), he created "Hesiod." That is, he turned silent stones into the most eloquent of poets! And yet, such a craftsman as this has those who admire him. As the saying goes: "The lips have found their matching lettuce." <note>A proverb meaning "like finds like," usually used for two things that are equally bad or poorly matched.</note> Since there are innumerable things in this man’s commentaries rendered from the Greek with equal "bloom"—such as <margin>neither from heaven nor from earth,</margin> <note>original: "ὔτε ὀρανῶ, ὔτε γῆς ἀπομένοια."</note>—even the stone Morychus himself would laugh. 

By Hercules, the man is happy by his own strength, and even by the favor of Folly <note>original: "Moria," a pun on the Greek *moria* (folly) and perhaps his friend Thomas More, though here referring to his own work, *The Praise of Folly*.</note>—he who requires a sense of "Transmarine Venus" in others while he himself lacks common sense, being, as it seems, more familiar with the "Sea-born Venus" <note>Venus Anadyomene, born from the sea foam; Erasmus implies the rival's learning is as empty as bubbles.</note> than the transmarine one. But it is better, I think, for my pen to return to the business at hand, leaving the jokes aside. 

Aristophanes also jokes about Morychus in *The Wasps*: <margin>I live a noble life, just like Morychus.</margin> <note>original: "ζῶ βίου γενναῖον ὥσπερ μορύχου."</note> However, Suidas indicates that there was a certain tragic poet of this name whose life was not without a reputation for luxury and softness. He cites this line from Aristophanes against him. It also appears in *The Acharnians*:

> O dearest one, and long desired,
> You have come, longed for by the comic choruses,
> Dear to Morychus.

->that is,<-

Dearest and now for a long time craved

<meta>catchword: Optata (Desired)</meta>

### Laconian Spurge. XCVIII

<term>Laconian Spurge</term> <note>original: "Tithymallus Laconicus"</note>. This was said of people with bleary eyes or those whose sight was failing. Spurge is a type of herb, discovered among the Laconians <note>The people of Sparta.</note>, which drips with a milky sap when plucked—hence some have called it "milk-wort." It is of singular sharpness, and people used to smear it on their eyes toward nightfall to sharpen their vision. Dioscorides, in his fourth book, identifies several species of this herb and diligently records its use as a remedy for the eyes. The adage is recorded by Suidas, who cites Aristophanes regarding the bleary-eyed Neoclides: <note>original: "σκόροδ’ ὁμῶ τριψαντα πινυμάλλῳ" (skorod’ homō tripsanta tithymallō)</note>, "Who rubbed garlic together with spurge."

The verse appears in the *Assemblywomen*:
"What then ought I to have done?
You should have rubbed garlic together with the juice of Laconian spurge,
And smeared your eyelids for yourself in the evening."

The word for the plant <note>Tithymallus</note> seems to be derived from a nurse’s breast <note>from the Greek 'titthos' for breast, referring to the milky sap</note>. However, I find it written with a single 'l' in some authors, though Suidas writes it with a double 'l', yet he does not explain the use of the proverb. If it is applied to the bleary-eyed, one should say, "He has need of spurge," or, "He is rubbing spurge." For they say its sharp potency is so effective that when its juice is collected, one must take care it does not touch the eyes; and whenever it is taken internally for the stomach, it must be swallowed wrapped in something so that it does not scrape the throat. The juice of this herb is used to treat rheum in the eyes. Pliny writes much about these matters in his twenty-sixth book, chapter eight. Cornelius Celsus, in his fifth book, indicates that this herb is called "Sea Lettuce" in Latin and says it has the power to eat away flesh.

### Sardinian Dye. XCIX

<term>Sardinian Dye</term> <note>original: "Βάμμα σαρδωνικόν" (Bamma sardonikon)</note>. This was said of an excellent color, especially purple. It is transferred jokingly, however, to one who is blushing with shame, or one who is stained with blood from a beating. Sardinia (or, as Hesychius writes, Sardon) is a massive island opposite Italy, in which various and highly praised purple dyes were once made. Similarly, we read of "Tyrian murex" and "Sarran grain" <note>Sarran refers to the city of Tyre</note> among the Latin writers. Aristophanes says in *The Peace*:
"Which that man claims to be Sardinian dye."
And in *The Acharnians*:
"Lest I smear you with Sardinian dye."

### As much as a tortoise cares for a fly. C

"The tortoise cares nothing for flies" <note>original: "Οὐ μέλει τῇ χελώνῃ μυῶν" (Ou melei tē chelōnē myōn)</note>. Suidas, citing some unknown author, records these words: "Agamemnon cared as little for Thersites' outspokenness as a tortoise does for flies." Flies can do no harm to a tortoise because of the shell with which it is fortified. This is similar to what we mentioned elsewhere: "The elephant does not care for the gnat." It is even more delightful when applied to matters of the soul. A mind fortified by virtue and philosophy fears the onslaught of fortune no more than a tortoise fears flies.

-> THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD <-

### More foolish than Morychus. I

**M**ore foolish than Morychus <note>original: "Μωρότερος ὦ μορύχου" (Mōroteros ō morychou)</note>. A Sicilian proverb used against those who did something ridiculous or stupid. To me, those who are particularly liable to this adage are people who, while negligent of their own domestic business, spend their time abroad tending to the affairs of others. This is the kind of character Martial introduces in the person of Ollus, and such are the *Lamiae* <note>In folklore, these were creatures who removed their eyes at home and only put them in when going out.</note> in Plutarch. Zenodotus records that among the Sicilians, "Morychus" was a nickname for Bacchus, given because during the vintage, the face of this god's statue was traditionally smeared with <term>must</term> <note>Freshly pressed grape juice</note> and green figs. This was done because the ancients credited Bacchus with the discovery of both trees <note>The vine and the fig</note>, as Athenaeus testifies in the second book of the *Deipnosophists*. The name comes from <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ μορύξαι τὸ μολύναι" (para to moryxai to molynai)</note> the verb *moryxe*, which means "to stain" or "to contaminate." Hence Homer also used the word <note>original: "μεμορυγμένα" (memorygmena)</note> for things that are "sullied."

# SECOND CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY

<margin>Morychus the fool.</margin> <note>original: "μωρομύριχος" (mōromyrichos)</note> Bacchus is everywhere depicted by the poets as ridiculous and lacking in good sense, being a drunken god, as seen in Aristophanes' *The Frogs*. For this reason, certain playful acts were performed in his sacred rites, almost as if to insult him. Indeed, a nickname was even added for the sake of mockery: <margin>Psella.</margin> <term>Psella</term>. Among the Sicilians, his image was placed not inside the temple, but outside the sanctuary in the open air near the entrance or vestibule. It was made of a stone called Psella by the skill of a certain Simmias, son of Eupalamus. Consequently, a common joke was tossed about concerning him: <margin>You are more foolish than Morychus, who, leaving what is inside, sits outside the house.</margin> <note>original: "μωρότερος εἶ μορύχου, ὃς τἄνδον ἀφείς, ἔξω τῆς οἰκίας κάθηται" (mōroteros ei morychou...)</note> That is: "You are more foolish than Morychus, who, having neglected those things which are within, sits outside the house." Zenodotus cites this adage from a certain letter of Polemon to Diophilus.

Although it is entirely foreign to my nature and character to waste effort in tracking down or attacking the errors of others, I cannot restrain myself in this place. Not so much for the sake of attacking as for the sake of laughter, I must bring forward the ignorance—or should I say the sluggishness—of a certain man among the Italians of no small reputation. This is especially true since he considers himself among <term>those who wear the lion's skin</term> <note>original: "τῶν λεοντῆν φερόντων" (tōn leontēn pherontōn) — a reference to Aesop’s fable of the donkey in a lion’s skin, meaning those who pretend to be more important than they are.</note> and takes so much upon himself in literature that, having seized the censor’s rod, he not only pronounces with great authority on other writers but even lashes and corrects Angelo Poliziano—a man incomparable and inimitable in every way—as if he were some schoolmaster. 

While this "honest man" concedes quite a few things to Poliziano, those delicate ears of his, accustomed to pure Attic style, still find the sense of a "Transmarine Venus" <note>A term for a sophisticated or foreign grace, here used sarcastically to mock the critic's over-refinement.</note> lacking in him, because he did not translate <term>the ancient</term> <note>original: "τὸν ἀρχαῖον" (ton archaion)</note> correctly from the start. Let us hear, then, this "Transmarine Venus" and "genuine Greek style" from this Aristarchus <note>A name used for a severe or harsh critic, after the librarian of Alexandria.</note>. First, when explaining this proverb from the very common collections of Zenobius, he cites Polemon as if he had read the passage himself. He does this in his usual manner, evidently to appear well-versed in obscure and uncommon authors. 

Next, the Greek passage we just cited—<term>who, leaving the things inside, sits outside the house</term>—he rendered in this way: "Who, leaving the inner habitation, sought that which was placed outside." Furthermore, regarding what is in those same collections—<term>Morychus: a name for Bacchus; for at the door of the temple they smear his face, applying the dregs of the grapes from the new wine, or with green figs</term>—he expressed it this way: "Morychus is surely an epithet of Bacchus <term>from the smearing of his face</term>." That is, from defiling his own face. For Bacchus is accustomed to defiling it with clusters of grapes and green figs. 

Then, when the same compiler, giving the etymology of the name, wrote <term>for 'moryxai' means 'to smear'</term>, our modern "Attic wit" interpreted it thus: <term>moryxai</term>, he says, is the same as <term>molynai</term>, which means "to be foolish" or "to be witless." Now consider this: <term>more foolish than any Morychus</term>, which he rendered regarding Bacchus's stature. The Greek says: <term>outside the gate of the temple is his statue, entirely in the open or under the sky</term>. This "Transmarine Venus" expressed it thus: "Furthermore, it is said of the simplicity of Bacchus, whose statue is placed in the open in the works of Hesiod." 

See how many "Venuses" <note>Erasmus sarcastically uses "Venuses" to mean "beauties" or "graces" of style.</note> this charming fellow has produced in one very short chapter! First, Bacchus, having grown tired of the inner rooms of his own house, seeks out foreign homes. Then, although he is made of stone (for the mention is of a statue), he nevertheless smears his own face with grape clusters and figs to delight the grape-harvesters. Additionally, although <term>moryxai</term> and <term>molynai</term> mean the same thing, he declares both to mean "to be foolish" and "to be witless"—but only to those who have thoroughly mastered that "Transmarine Venus" of his. 

Finally—and this is the most "charming" part of all—from the vestibule (since, according to Pollux, he calls the <term>innermost sanctuary</term> of the temple that which is also called <term>the main gate</term>), he created "Hesiod." That is, he turned silent stones into a most eloquent poet! And yet, such a craftsman has those who admire him; that is, <note>A proverb meaning "like attracts like" or "a bad person finds a bad match."</note> "The lips have matching lettuce." For there are countless things in his commentaries, with Greek rendered in similar "bloom," so that he sees <term>even clearly</term>, as they say, <term>when he enjoys the earth</term>—things at which even the stone Morychus himself would laugh. 

The man is, by Hercules, happy by his own strength, or rather by the blessing of Folly <note>A nod to Erasmus’s "The Praise of Folly" (*Moriae Encomium*).</note>, since he seeks the sense of a "Transmarine Venus" in others while he himself lacks common sense and seems more familiar with a "Marine Venus" <note>Perhaps implying he is "all at sea" or "washed up."</note> than a "Transmarine" one. But I think it is better to leave these jests aside and let my pen return to the business at hand. Aristophanes also jokes about Morychus in *The Wasps*: <term>I live a noble life like Morychus</term>. That is: "To live a generous life, just like Morychus." But Suidas indicates that there was a certain tragic poet of this name whose life was not free from the mark of luxury and soft living. And he cites this verse of Aristophanes against him, which appears in *The Acharnians*:

> <term>O dearest one, so long desired,</term>
> <term>You have come, longed for by the comic choruses,</term>
> <term>Dear to Morychus.</term>
-> that is <-
> O most dear and long-desired

It explores the dual identity of Morychus as both a nickname for the god Bacchus and a historical tragic poet known for his luxurious lifestyle.</summary>

THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

You arrive as desired, with choirs smeared with dregs,
Pleasing even to Morychus. <note>These lines conclude the previous adage concerning Morychus, a figure associated with folly and the rites of Bacchus.</note>

<margin>II</margin>
### I do not value it at four obols.

"You think you are worth four obols." <note>original: "Τεττάρων ὀβολῶν εἶν’ οἴει" (Tettarōn obolōn ein’ oiei)</note> That is: he thinks he is worth four <term>obols</term> <note>An obol was a small silver coin of low value in ancient Greece; four obols would be a paltry sum.</note>. This is similar to those expressions we have recorded elsewhere: "I do not value you at an *as*," "I do not value you at two cents," and "I do not value you at a farthing." Suidas also records this, though he follows his frequent habit of concealing the author’s name: "The insolence of these servants is said to be worth four obols." <note>original: "τὴν παῤῥησίαν τῶν οἰκετῶν εἶν' ὀβολῶν τὸ λεγόμενον" (tēn parrēsian tōn oiketōn ein' obolōn to legomenon)</note> That is: consider your slander to be worth four obols, as the saying goes. The Latins also use the term <term>diobolare</term> <note>literally "worth two obols"</note> for things they wish to appear most cheap and worthless.

<margin>III</margin>
### You weave a thin thread.

"You weave a thin one." <note>original: "Λεπτήν πλέκεις" (Leptēn plekeis)</note> This is said of the poor, who usually labor over meager things. One also says "thin hope" <note>original: "λεπτή ἐλπίς" (leptē elpis)</note> for a small hope; and "thin care" <note>original: "λεπτή φροντίς" (leptē phrontis)</note> for a subtle or curious concern; and "you spread it thinly" <note>original: "λεπτή φαίνεις" (leptē phaineis)</note> for those who are stingy and take account of even the smallest trifles. This metaphor is drawn from weavers.

<margin>IIII</margin>
### Earthly baths.

"Earthly baths," or the "baths of the underworld." <note>original: "Χθόνια λουτρά" (Chthonia loutra)</note> This seems to be said (for we must conjecture) when something is applied too late, so that it will be of no use to the person to whom it is offered. For example, if someone were to advocate for a defendant after the irrevocable sentence of the judges had already been pronounced. It was an ancient custom to bring certain baths to the deceased at the tomb. Likewise, bodies about to be buried were washed beforehand. Hence Ennius writes:

> A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin.

This happens even in our own time, perhaps left over from ancient custom, when they sprinkle consecrated water on the monuments of the dead—especially among the Germans, who are more devoted to this practice than others.

<margin>V</margin>
### Thrice.

Not even that common proverbial figure is lacking, by which the Greeks amplify a matter by the addition of a number, especially the number three. This is perhaps because among the ancients three was considered the most complete and sacred number, so that whatever was said or done three times was held to be valid and effective; hence it was frequently used in the mysteries of the magi. Virgil writes in his *Sorceress*:

> First I tie these three threads of three different colors around you, 
> and three times I lead this image around these altars. 
> The god delights in an uneven number.

And in Theocritus, in a poem of the same title:

<margin>that is,</margin>
> Thrice I pour a libation, and thrice I pronounce these sacred words.
> <note>original: "Ἐς τρὶς ἀποσπένδω, καὶ τρὶς τάδε πότνια φωνῶ" (Es tris apospendō, kai tris tade potnia phōnō)</note>

Likewise in funeral ceremonies:

> And we call the final cry three times with our voice.

In the *Hecuba* of Euripides, the herald calls for silence by repeating the word three times:

<margin>that is,</margin>
> Be silent, Achaeans! Let all the people be silent!
> Be silent, hold your peace.
> <note>original: "Σιγᾶτ' ἀχαιοí, σíγα πᾶς λαός, Σíγα σιώπα" (Sigat' achaioi, siga pas laos, Siga siōpa)</note>

In stillness and silence.

<margin>that is,</margin>
Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
> I forbid these men, and again I forbid them, and yet again I strongly forbid them.
> <note>original: "Τούτοισιν ἀπαυδῶ, κἀὖθις ἀπαυδῶ, κἀὖθις μάλ' ἀπαυδῶ" (Toutoisin apaudō, kauthis apaudō, kauthis mal' apaudō)</note>

And it is read everywhere, not only among poets but also among orators: "thrice-wicked," "thrice-cursed," "thrice-blessed," "thrice-greatest," and "thrice-unhappy." <note>Erasmus lists the Greek terms: τρὶς μιαρὸς (tris miaros), τρὶς περίσημος (tris perisēmos), τρὶς μακάριος (tris makarios), τρὶς μέγιστος (tris megistos), τρὶς ἄθλιος (tris athlios).</note> The Latins imitated this primarily in poetry. Virgil:

<margin>Ovid:</margin>
> O thrice and four times blessed.
> You will say that all my things were twice true.

It is even now a familiar habit among the common people that if they wish to assert something more vehemently, they repeat it three times. The adage might seem to have arisen from this. In the first book of his *Geography*, Strabo mentions that Homer writes how Charybdis vomits up what she has swallowed three times a day and sucks it back three times; though it is well known this happens only twice a day, Strabo excuses him by this hyperbole, as if "thrice" here does not signify a literal number, but vehemence. To this form of speech belongs what is found in Plato in the tenth book of the *Republic*: "Seeing their works, they perceive them to be three degrees removed from reality." That is, when they see their works...

# SECOND CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY
Dd
<meta>catchword: Deafer</meta>

...works, they do not understand that these things are "three degrees removed from the truth." <note>A reference to Plato’s *Republic*, where he argues that art is an imitation of an imitation, and thus three steps away from reality.</note> He speaks of those who take their rules for living from poets, since poets present phantasms as if they were truths. A trace of this speech remains even in our day in the French language, which creates the superlative by adding this syllable, except that with the letters reversed, they sound *très* for *ter* <note>original: "tres sonant pro ter". Erasmus is noting that the French "très" (very) derives from the Latin "ter" (thrice).</note>.

### VI
->Theagenes’ money.<-

<margin>Theagenes’ money, and that of Aeschines.</margin> <note>original: "Θεαγένους χρήματα, τά τ' Αἰσχίνου" (Theagenous chrēmata, ta t' Aischinou)</note> That is, the wealth of Theagenes, just like that of Aeschines. A proverbial site for those who, though they were poor, nevertheless wished to be considered rich. Both men, Theagenes and Aeschines, were marked by this disease. Hence a nickname was added to them, a <term>kimbix</term> <note>a Greek term for a miser or a "cheapskate"</note>, after a certain Sellus who was foolishly ambitious; though he was of very meager means, he nevertheless affected the appearance of being wealthy. Because of this, those who suffered from this "disease" were said to <term>sellizein</term> <note>literally "to act like Sellus"</note>. It is neighbor to what is said in another place, "Phanias’s door" <note>original: "φανίας θύρα" (Phanias thyra)</note>. Aristophanes mentions the proverb in *The Birds*:

> Where all Theagenes’ vast wealth is,
> And all of Aeschines’ too.

### VII
->The stone of Tantalus.<-

<margin>The stone of Tantalus.</margin> <note>original: "Ταντάλου λίθου" (Tantalou lithou)</note> That is, "The stone of Tantalus"; they call a danger hanging over one’s head by this name. In Suidas, these words are recorded: "Since we have shaken off the stone of Tantalus from our heads." <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ τὸν ταντάλου λίθου τῇ κεφαλῆς ἀπετιναξάμεθα" (epeidē ton tantalou lithou tē kephalēs apetinaxametha)</note> Plato, as quoted in Stobaeus, says: "If someone should have the so-called stone of Tantalus hanging over them." <note>original: "ἐὰν ὁ τὸν λεγόμενον ταντάλου λίθον ἐπικρεμάμενον τις ἔχοι" (ean ho ton legomenon tantalou lithon epikremamenon tis echoi)</note> It is taken from the myth of Tantalus, whom some imagine suffers this kind of punishment in the underworld: a huge rock hangs over his head in such a way that it seems it will fall at any moment. Athenaeus, in the sixth book of the *Banquet of the Sophists*, relates the origin of the story in this way: Tantalus, greedy for pleasures, was admitted into the company of the gods. When he was granted the option to ask for whatever he wished, he demanded of Jove that he might live in that same fleeing manner amidst banquets, considering nothing happier than this. But Jove, being indignant, granted the permission and satisfied the man’s wishes. However, so that he could not enjoy what was set before him, he suspended a huge rock above his head, appearing as if about to fall; out of fear of this, Tantalus did not dare touch anything. Virgil, in the sixth book of his *Aeneid*, attributes this invention to the Lapiths, Ixion, and Pirithous:

> Why should I mention the Lapiths, Ixion, and Pirithous,
> Over whom a black flint, already, already about to slip,
> Hangs like one falling? Golden supports gleam 
> On high festive couches, and banquets are prepared before their faces
> In royal luxury. The greatest of the Furies 
> Reclines nearby, and prevents them from touching the tables with her hands,
> And she springs up lifting her torch, and thunders with her voice.

Pindar also uses it in the seventh *Isthmian* hymn: "Since some god turned aside the stone hanging over our heads for us." <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ τὸν ὑπὲρ κεφαλᾶς γε ταντάλου λίθον παρά τις ἔτρεψεν ἄμμι θεός" (epeidē ton hyper kephalas ge tantalou lithon para tis etrepsen ammi theos)</note> He refers to the fear of an imminent war. A commentator cites from Euripides:
<margin>Fearing the rock overhanging his head
which flies through the air.</margin>
<note>original: "Κορυφῆς ὑπερτέλλοντα δ' ἐμαίνων πέτρον ἀέρι ποτᾶται" (Koryphēs hypertellonta d' emainōn petron aeri potatai)</note>
> That is,
> Shuddering at the rock that hangs over his crown,
> It flies through the air.

Gregory Nazianzen, in a certain letter to his brother Basil, calls an anxious life exposed to dangers a "Tantalus life" <note>original: "ταντάλου ζωήν" (tantalou zōēn)</note>.

### VIII
->Deafer than the port of Torone.<-

<margin>Deafer than the port of Torone.</margin> <note>original: "Κωφότερος τορωναίου λιμένος" (Kōphoteros torōnaiou limenos)</note> That is, "Deafer than the port of Torone." They say there is a certain port of Torone, a city in Thrace, which stretches into the sea with two long and narrow arms, so that in the inner retreat of the port, no crash of the waves is heard. Hence the proverb is used against those who do not hear. Although others place Torone in Macedonia. Stephanus also mentions a gulf with the name "Toronean," from which the proverb might seem to be derived. Except that a "deaf sea" or a "deaf shore" is also called such when it resounds with a great crash, so that because of the noise of the waves, nothing else can be heard.

<summary>This page explores several Greek proverbs concerning the pretense of wealth (Theagenes and Aeschines), the psychological torment of impending danger (the Stone of Tantalus), and the literal or metaphorical silence of the port of Torone.</summary>
<keywords>Theagenes, Aeschines, Tantalus, Pindar, Euripides, Torone, Greek mythology, ancient proverbs, poverty, anxiety, Thrace</keywords>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

->Deafer than a thrush.<-
<margin>IX</margin>
<note>original: "Κωφότερος κίχλης" (Kōphōteros kichlēs)</note> That is, "Deafer than a thrush." Zenodotus cites this from Eubulus' *Dionysius*. He attributes a peculiar deafness to this bird, even though it is extremely talkative, as the proverb itself testifies. Thus, it can be neatly applied to those who, by constantly babbling themselves, do not listen to what is said by others in turn—a vice that one can observe in many people.

->The speech of the effeminate is also effeminate.<-
<margin>X</margin>
<note>original: "Ἔνεσιν ἐν τ’ ἄλοισιν ἄνανδροι λόγοι" (Enesin en t’ aloissin anandroi logoi)</note> That is, "In unmanly men there is unmanly speech."
As a person is, so they speak. He relates this from Zenodotus. It is close to what we mentioned elsewhere: "The fool speaks foolish things." Also: "As the man, so the speech." Although Virgil depicted Drances quite differently: a warrior strong in tongue but a coward in action.

->Stupider than Praxilla’s Adonis.<-
<margin>XI</margin>
<note>original: "Ἠλιθιώτερος πραξίλλης ἀδώνιδος" (Ēlithioteros Praxillēs Adōnidos)</note> That is, "Stultier than Praxilla’s Adonis." Used for those who are exceedingly stupid. Polemon, according to Zenodotus, records that Praxilla was a certain poetess from Sicyon <note>an ancient Greek city-state</note> who, in her songs, introduced Adonis being asked by those in the underworld what most beautiful things he had left behind among the living; he replied: the sun, cucumbers, and apples. Since it seemed extremely foolish to rank cucumbers and apples alongside the sun, the proverb began to be used for men of no judgment.

->Simonides’ songs.<-
<margin>XII</margin>
<note>original: "Σιμωνίδου μέλη" (Simōnidou melē)</note> That is, "Simonides’ melodies." This was said of the crafty and the deceitful. They say that he was the first to turn cunning and profit-seeking into an art. He reportedly kept two boxes: one for gratitude and one for rewards. When he opened them after some time, he always found the chest of gratitude empty and the chest of rewards full. By this invention, he signaled that he was unwilling to give his poems away for free. Plutarch mentions this in his little book *On Meddlesomeness*. Hence Aristophanes, as quoted in the Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, says: <note>original: "ᾄσαι σιμωνίδου μέλη"</note> "To sing Simonides’ songs." Aristophanes also mentions it in *The Birds*:
"First, I commanded him to take the lyre and
sing a song of Simonides."
Theocritus alluded to the two boxes in *The Graces*:
"But back they come, sluggish, to the bottom of the empty chest."

->If you have a sword, we have a spear at home.<-
<margin>XIII</margin>
Plautus says in *The Bacchides*: "If you have a sword, we have a spear at home." This is used whenever one evil is opposed by another. For both a sword and a <term>urbina</term> <note>a type of weapon, likely a pike or spear</note> are types of weapons. In Plautus, these are the words of Chrysalus, who is returning threats and blunting a soldier's ferocity with equally fierce words. Placidus Fulgentius reads *eruina* instead of *urbina* and interprets it as a long type of weapon. It is very similar to the sayings: "Like for like," and "For a tough knot, one must seek a tough wedge."

->The farmer is always rich for the next year.<-
<margin>XIIII</margin>
<note>original: "Ἀεὶ γεωργὸς εἰς νέωτα πλούσιος" (Aei geōrgos eis neōta plousios)</note> That is,
"The farmer is always rich for the next year."
This is often said of those who are "wealthy" only in the hope of future profit, and who flatter themselves with the expectation of grand things. It is derived from farmers, who always promise themselves a more abundant harvest the following summer, and in that hope, they already dare to make certain expenditures.

->The Furies are always virgins.<-
<margin>XV</margin>
<note>original: "Ἀεὶ παρθένοι ἐριννύς" (Aei parthenoi Erinnyes)</note> That is, "The Furies are always virgins." This somewhat obscure proverb serves as a deterrent against sinning. For the Furies, the avengers of wrongdoers, cannot be "defiled" or corrupted so as to prevent them from taking punishment from those who deserve it; for this reason, they are called virgins. Suidas cites this from Sophocles.

->An old ox is not mourned.<-
<margin>XVI</margin>
<note>original: "Γέρων βοῦς ἀπώλετο" (Gerōn bous apōleto)</note> That is, "An old ox is free from the grief of the household." This means that the death of the elderly is not mourned by friends because it is seen as timely. Indeed, even today, if the death of an aged person is announced, people say: "Nothing bitter about it," or "He did not die in the cradle." Even those to whom it does not pertain weep for the death of the young. Solon prays against such a death in...

Erasmus uses these proverbs to comment on human behaviors such as talkativeness without listening, groundless optimism, and the perception of death in old age.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Ninth Century of the Second Thousand (Chiliad) of Erasmus's *Adagia*. The previous page concluded a series of adages about stupidity and sensory dullness. This page transitions from a discussion on the proper way to view death into a series of adages concerning social status, geography, and suitability.</meta>

->NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND THOUSAND<-

...in Cicero’s book *On Old Age*. The elegy of Solon <note>Solon was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet</note> which Cicero mentions, goes like this:
<note>original Greek: "μηδέ μοι ἄκλαυτος θάνατος μόλοι, ἀλλὰ φίλοισι ποιήσαιμι θανὼν ἄλγεα καὶ στοναχάς."</note>
"Let not my death come unwept, but let me, having died, leave behind grief and sighs for my friends."
That is:
> Let no unmourned death come, but rather let it 
> Bring sorrow and groans to those dear to me.

Ennius <note>an early Roman poet</note>, on the other hand, says:
> Let no one honor me with tears, nor 
> perform a funeral with weeping.

But both felt correctly. Solon wishes to die beloved and missed by his people; Ennius does not think a death should be mourned when immortality follows it.
This verse is also attributed to Menander <note>a Greek dramatist</note>:
<note>original Greek: "πικρόν ἐστι χρῆμα γήρως ἐν οἰκίᾳ μένων."</note>
That is:
> An old man remaining in the house is a bitter thing.

## XVII. You arrived late, but go to Colonus.

<note>original Greek: "ὄψ’ ἦλθες, ἀλλὰ γ’ εἰς κολωνὸν ἵεσο."</note> That is:
> You arrive late; well then, take yourself from here to Colonus.
This is a proverbial phrase used against those who arrive after the proper time, or those who do anything for hire. Furthermore, a "Colonus" is a higher piece of land, appearing as a mound or a hill. There were two such places in Athens: one next to the temple of Neptune, where the knights would assemble; the other next to the temple of Vulcan, which was called <note>original: "ἀγοραῖος" (agoraios)</note> "of the marketplace." From this, they were called "Colonetae" who were hired for pay, because those who were looking for an employer would stand there. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> records something similar.

## XVIII. To the foot.

<note>original Greek: "Περὶ πόδα."</note> That is: "Next to the foot" or "Fitting." Whatever was suitable and perfectly adapted was said to be "at the foot." The metaphor is taken from shoes that fit the measure of the foot exactly. From this, the famous saying of Paulus Aemilius is celebrated, regarding him showing off a new shoe. "You all see," he said, "that the shoe is fine and new, but where it pinches my foot, only I can feel." He was implying that his wife, Papyria, was not suited to his character. Suidas cites Plato—the poet, I believe:
<note>original Greek: "ὡς ἔστι μοι τὸ χρῆμα πρὸς πόδα."</note> That is:
> How well this business fits my foot.

## XIX. Sarpedonian shore.

<note>original Greek: "Σαρπηδονία ἀκτή."</note> That is: "Sarpedonian shore." You would rightly use this for a turbulent matter, or for people who are exceedingly loud and noisy. For there is a certain shore of this name in Thrace, sacred to Neptune, which is constantly pounded by waves. There is also another of the same name in Cilicia. Again, another near the Ocean, where they say the Gorgons have their home.

## XX. More enslaved than Messene.

<note>original Greek: "Δουλοτέρᾱ μεσσήνης."</note> That is: "More enslaved than Messene." This was said of those who were least free and lived by the will of another. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> reduced the Messenians to slavery because they had revolted again and again, and they treated them even more harshly than their other slaves, so that they could not attempt a revolution anew. The history is recorded by Pausanias in his *Messenica* and by Justin in the fourth book of his *Epitomes*.

## XXI. Since you are a slave, you wear your hair long.

<note>original Greek: "Δοῦλος ὢν κόμην ἔχεις."</note> That is: "Since you are a slave, you have long hair." Used for someone who did something beyond what was proper—for example, if someone of low status were to imitate the dress of the patricians. For among the Lacedaemonians, they let the free-born grow their hair long. The adage is indeed recorded by Suidas, but it appears in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*:
<note>original Greek: "ἔπειτα δῆτα δοῦλος ὢν κόμην ἔχεις;"</note> That is:
> And then, since you are a slave, do you wear your hair long?

## XXII. City of slaves.

<note>original Greek: "Δούλων πόλις."</note> That is: "City of slaves." This can be said of a gathering or community of wicked, thieving, or ignoble men. There is a city by this name in Libya, according to Ephorus cited in Suidas and Hecataeus in Stephanus. If any slave brought a stone into this city, he immediately became free, even if he were a foreigner. There is also another, the name of which is <term>Hierapolis</term> <note>meaning "Sacred City"</note>, because it was dedicated to slaves; they say only one free man lived in it. There is again another in Crete, "Doulopolis of a thousand men," that is, inhabited by a thousand men, as Sosicrates records in the first book of his *Cretan Affairs*. There is likewise another near Thrace, <term>Poneropolis</term> <note>meaning "City of Villains"</note>; that is, un-

...city of the honest. <note>Erasmus is likely using "city of the honest" ironically here or completing a thought from the previous page regarding the "City of the Wicked."</note> In this place, Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great</note> is said to have gathered, as if into a bilge-tank, the infamous and those of discredited character—such as sycophants, false witnesses, legal prevaricators, and others of that sort—to the number of two thousand, according to Theopompus in the thirteenth book of his *Philippic History*. Plutarch also bears witness to this in his essay *On Curiosity*. There is also a region in Egypt called <margin>Slave-City</margin> <note>original Greek: Δουλόπολις (Doulopolis)</note>, according to Olympianicus. Plutarch, in his *Collection of Proverbs*, shows that it was customary to say of things rare to find—expressing it in this way—"It is not a Slave-City," <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι Δούλων πόλις</note> meaning "There is no such thing as a city of slaves." Not dissimilar is what Pliny tells of the Essene people in Syria, to whom the guilty flee from everywhere. This nation alone in the whole world lives without any women, having renounced all sexual desire; living among palm trees, their crowd is reborn daily from the equal throngs of newcomers, as many people, tired of life, are driven by the waves of fortune to adopt their customs.

->Flowers of the Samians.<-
->XXIII<-

<note>original Greek: Σαμίων ἄνθη (Samiōn anthē)</note> That is: **Flowers of the Samians.** This was said when someone might pluck the height of pleasure. This name was given to a certain place where women held banquets with men and filled themselves to satiety with every kind of pleasure. Having been made effeminate by these luxuries, they were later conquered by the Persians and driven into slavery. Stephanus <note>a Greek grammarian</note> reminds us that the island of Samos was once called <note>original Greek: Ἀνθεμοῦσαν (Anthemousan)</note> **Anthemusa**, certainly from its flowers. He says it was also called **Anthemutia**, evidently from its maidens. The adage is recorded in the *Collections* attributed to Plutarch. Athenaeus also mentions it in his twelfth book, citing Clearchus, showing that the place was so named because of the various beauties of the girls, who, like smiling flowers, invited one to lust. It will fit aptly for a city, a house, or even a man desperately addicted to pleasures.

->A bulk purchase.<-
->XXIIII<-

<note>original Greek: Ρωπικὴν ὤνησιν (Rhōpikēn ōnēsin)</note> That is: **A bulk purchase.** Used for cheap things bought at a high price. This happens sometimes in auctions, when the price of each item is not weighed individually, but many things piled together are valued as one. For among the Greeks, *rhopos* <note>original Greek: ῥῶπος</note> refers to brushwood, and they call a small bundle or a pack tied together from various things—or various colors mixed together—a *rhopon*. It often happens that an inattentive buyer is cheated in this kind of purchase. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus. Suidas also mentions it.

->The Royal little cow.<-
->XXV<-

<note>original Greek: Βασιλικὴ Βοΐδιον (Basilikē Boidion)</note> That is: **The Royal heifer.** This was said of prodigious fertility, arising from a miraculous event. In the time of Ptolemy the Younger, a certain cow produced six calves in the same birth. The author is Diogenianus. Similar to that line in Juvenal: 
> A sow more fertile than the white one. <note>A reference to the legendary white sow found by Aeneas, which had thirty piglets and marked the site of Alba Longa.</note>

->Pure from marriage.<-
->XXVI<-

<note>original Greek: Ἁγνὴ γάμων (Hagnē gamōn)</note> That is: **Ignorant of marriage.** This was said ironically of an unchaste woman, because she made herself available in a manner contrary to marriage. Horace says:
> Unacquainted with marriage, and as yet 
> unripe for a headstrong husband.

->More cowardly than the Rhegians.<-
->XXVII<-

<note>original Greek: Ρηγίνων δειλότερος (Rhēginōn deiloteros)</note> That is: **More fearful than the Rhegians.** Xenarchus, the son of Sophron (who wrote about the months), in the work of Zenodotus, criticized the people of Rhegium <note>a city in southern Italy</note> to win favor with the tyrant Dionysius, portraying them as lazy in military matters and fearful in spirit, as the collections of Greek adages testify.

->A chorus of the idle.<-
->XXVIII<-

<note>original Greek: Ἀργούντων χορός (Argountōn choros)</note> That is: **A chorus of vacationers.** It was said of a gathering of people behaving wantonly. For idleness drives one toward every kind of wickedness, especially the youth. This is related to what has been said elsewhere: "To the idle, it is always a holiday."

->The looting of Cinnarus's goods.<-
->XXIX<-

<note>original Greek: Ἁρπαγὴ τῶν κιννάρου (Harpathē tōn kinnarou)</note> That is: **The plundering of Cinnarus's property.** Said of wealth snatched away during a riot. Or when princes lay hands on the fortunes of others against the law. Timaeus left it written that a certain Cinnarus, a native of Selinus and a pimp by trade, reached the height of wealth through this business. While he lived, he promised he would consecrate all his resources to Venus; however, as he was dying, he left them to be plundered by the people. Not unlike this is what we mentioned elsewhere: "The goods of Porsena."

->The judgment of Rhadamanthus.<-
->XXX<-

<note>original Greek: Ραδαμάνθυος κρίσις (Radamanthyos krisis)</note> That is: **The judgment of Rhadamanthus.** Said of those who judge without corruption. Rhadaman-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Rhadamanthus, the legendary judge of the underworld, from the previous page. The text begins mid-sentence, completing his name.</meta>

...Rhadamanthus; for the judge of the spirits of the dead is swayed neither by gifts nor by favor from judging with severity. This can be applied to the necessity of death, which is equally common to the greatest and the least. This follows the line of Aeschylus found in Aristophanes’s *The Frogs*:
<margin>For Death alone of the gods does not love gifts.</margin> <note>original Greek: Μόνος θεῶν γὰρ θάνατος οὐ δώρων ἐρᾷ</note> that is,
Of all the gods, Death alone seeks no bribes.
Likewise Horace:
Pale death knocks with an impartial foot at the cottages of the poor
And the palaces of kings.
And elsewhere:
Not even if you appease with three hundred bulls
every passing day, my friend,
the tearless Pluto. <note>Pluto is another name for Hades, the ruler of the underworld.</note>
Likewise Pindar in the *Nemean Odes*:
<margin>But the common wave of Hades comes to all, and falls upon the unsuspecting and the expecting alike.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ κοινὸν γὰρ ἔρχεται Κῦμ’ Ἀΐδα, πέσε δ’ ἀδόκητον Καὶ δοκέοντα</note> that is,
The flood of the underworld happens to all in common, and it overwhelms both the one who expects it and the one who does not; that is, both the young and the old, or likewise the noble and the obscure. For they interpret <unclear>the unexpected</unclear> and <unclear>the expecting</unclear> in two ways.
Likewise in the *Olympian Odes*:
<margin>By the upright decrees of Rhadamanthus.</margin> <note>original Greek: Βουλαῖς ἐν ὀρθαῖς Ῥαδαμάνθυος</note>
And elsewhere, demonstrating that Rhadamanthus alone neither flatters anyone nor does anything for the sake of favor: <margin>But Rhadamanthus has fared well because he obtained the blameless fruit of the mind, and he does not delight his soul with deceptions within.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ Ῥαδάμανθυς εὖ πέπραγεν, ὅτι φρενῶν ἔλαχε καρπὸν ἀμώμητον, οὐδ’ ἀπάταισι θυμὸν τέρπεται ἔνδοθεν</note> that is, Fortunate is Rhadamanthus, who was allotted a blameless power of judgment, and is not inwardly delighted by deceptions in his soul. Plato also uses this in the twelfth book of *The Laws*.

### Rhadamanthus’s Oath. XXXI

<margin>The oath of Rhadamanthus.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ῥαδαμάνθυος ὅρκος</note> That is, "the oath of Rhadamanthus" was a term used for an oath that was indeed most true, yet did not call upon any god. Socrates was accustomed to swear by the dog and the goose so as not to summon any of the gods—either because he did not believe there were any gods, or because he did not think it the mark of a good man to call the gods as witnesses to his business. However, they attributed this type of swearing to Rhadamanthus. The rhetorician Aristides noted the adage in his work on Pericles when he said: <margin>Just as if you were to say that Rhadamanthus accustomed men to commit perjury—he who so excelled in piety and justice that even after he had departed this life, he is believed to be the judge for those who arrive there.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἂν εἰ λέγης τὸν Ῥαδάμανθυν ἐθίζειν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐπιορκεῖν...</note> that is, Just as if you were to say Rhadamanthus brought mortals into the habit of swearing falsely, he who so excelled in piety and justice that even having died, he is believed to be the judge for those who travel to that place. The Pythagoreans were accustomed to swear by the "quaternion," <note>The number four, which Pythagoreans considered sacred as the source of the number ten (1+2+3+4).</note> which they call the <unclear>tetraktys</unclear>.
<margin>No, by him who gave to our soul the quaternion.</margin> <note>original Greek: οὐ μὰ τὸν ἁμετέρᾳ ψυχᾷ παραδόντα τετρακτύν</note>
For they think this number pertains so much to the perfection of the soul that they venerate it among their secrets. The author is Macrobius in the first commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*. Pythagoras, in his *Golden Verses*, calls the quaternion the sacred fountain of the soul. The Greeks were accustomed to swear by the head of another. Juvenal says:
When the Greeks were not yet prepared to swear
By the head of another.
Virgil says:
I swear by this head.

### More loquacious than the shore. XXXII

<margin>More talkative than the surf.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ῥαχίας λαλεστερος</note> That is: "More loquacious than the shore." This was said of a loudmouth or a noisy brawler. For the Greeks call the shore *rhachia*, especially one rough with reefs and rocks, which is pounded by constant waves with a great crash; from which the Greek word <unclear>rhachia</unclear> seems to be derived, as if it were <unclear>trachia</unclear> (rough), for that word is applied to everything that is harsh and thorny.

### Make the best of your present fortune. XXXIII

<margin>To do well with what is present.</margin> <note>original Greek: Τὸ παρὸν εὖ ποιεῖν</note> That is: "Be content with what is at hand," and <margin>to arrange the present well.</margin> <note>original Greek: τὸ παρὸν εὖ τίθεσθαι</note> That is: "It is necessary to take what is present with equanimity." The adage warns us not to waste away with longing for the things of others, but whatever lot has befallen us, let us embrace it as the best. For a great part of happiness is that each person be pleased with their own fortune. Plato in the *Gorgias* says: <margin>As it seems, it is necessary for me, according to the old saying, to do well with what is present, and to act just as the proverb has it.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὡς ἔοικεν ἀνάγκη μοι καὶ τὸ παλαιὸν λόγον τὸ παρὸν εὖ ποιεῖν...</note> that is: It is necessary for me, as it seems, according to the ancient adage, to be content with what is at hand, and to accept this which is given by you.
