<meta>This page continues from the discussion of the judge Rhadamanthus. Erasmus is now moving into a series of shorter adages regarding wisdom, effort, and character, drawing on both Greek tragedy and Roman grammatical scholarship.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

Wise men ought to arrange the present situation as well as possible according to their power. <note>original Greek: Ἄνδρας σοφοὺς χρὴ τὸ γε παρὸν πρᾶγμ᾿ ὡς καλὸν Εἰς δύναμιν εὖ τίθεσθαι.</note> That is:

->It is the part of wise men to manage what good is at hand,<-
->As if it were good, according to their strength.<-

This is related to what we have reported elsewhere: *You have obtained Sparta, adorn it.* <note>original Greek: σπάρταν ἔλαχες, ταύταν κόσμει</note> That is, you have found yourself in Sparta, now arrange it well. Stobaeus <note>A 5th-century compiler of Greek extracts.</note> cites this verse from a tragedy by Euripides titled *Telephus*, which we thought should be mentioned in passing, for the adage was discussed in its own place.

<margin>XXXIIII</margin>
### He who in every matter, and at every time.

Aulus Gellius, <note>A 2nd-century Roman author interested in grammar and history.</note> explaining the force of the word *mormolukeion* <note>Greek for a "bugbear" or "hobgoblin" used to frighten children.</note>, says that this very ancient six-foot verse was celebrated as a proverb:

> But indeed, he who in every matter and at every time
> Lacks all praise, he is "unpraised,"
> And he is the worst and most despicable of all.

The proverb warns that there is almost no one of such a hopeless nature that they do not occasionally say or do something deserving of praise. This is reported in almost the same words by Macrobius in the sixth book of the *Saturnalia*, from which I seem to have detected a manifest error in the text of Gellius admitted by some scholar. For that scholar, not understanding that these were verses—*But indeed, he who in every matter and at every time*, etc.—suspected that a Greek verse had been omitted by the scribes, and in its place substituted this line:

Often even a gardener speaks very much to the point. <note>original Greek: Πολλάκι καὶ κήπουρος ἀνὴρ μάλα καίριον εἶπεν.</note>

However, the verse Gellius is actually considering is the Latin one which he subjoins immediately: *But indeed, he who in every matter*, etc. This is clear from Macrobius, who pilfered this passage almost word-for-word into his own commentaries. Furthermore, the Greek verse does nothing to explain the force of this word *illaudatus* <term>unpraised/blameworthy</term>; it was merely mixed in in passing, as if to prove what he had said: that no one is of such "fashioned" <note>original: *effictis*</note> morals that they do not sometimes do or say something that can be praised. In that passage, the word "fashioned" (*effictis*) is corrupted into "wild" (*efferis*); for a person can be "unpraised" even if they do not have wild morals. But he called "fashioned" morals those that are ruined and corrupt. There are, however, three <term>senarii</term> <note>A common meter in Roman comedy consisting of six iambic feet.</note> completing the thought, except that in some places they seem corrupted by scribes:

> But indeed, he who in every matter and at every time.
> This first one stands beautifully. The second will also stand if it is read:
> Who lacks all praise, he is an "unpraised" man.
> For the sense of the ears seems to require the small word "man" [*Vir*] in this verse. The third will stand if you read:
> And he is of all the most despicable and the worst.

The passage is in Gellius, Book 2, Chapter 6, if anyone wishes to compare.

<margin>XXX</margin>
### He who wants the kernel from the nut, breaks the nut.

He who seeks a benefit should not flee from labor. He who seeks pleasure must first experience sweat, without which true pleasure is not obtained. Plautus expressed this sentiment with a truly proverbial figure of speech: *He who*, he says, *wants to eat the kernel from the nut, breaks the nut.* He who seeks the food of the soul in the secret writings <note>Referring to the Bible and sacred texts.</note> should scrutinize the mystery hidden under the wrapper of allegory. For Saint Jerome uses it thus in several places. A nut is both hard and bitter on the outside, but inside it hides the sweetest food. To this we should refer that Homeric fiction concerning the herb *Moly*, which he says has a black root but a milk-white flower. He describes it thus in the tenth book of the *Odyssey*:

Its root was indeed black, but the flower was like milk;
The gods call it Moly, and it is difficult to dig up
For mortal men; but the gods can do all things. <note>original Greek: ῥίζῃ μὲν μέλαν ἔσκε, γάλακτι δὲ εἴκελον ἄνθος, μῶλυ δέ μιν καλέουσι θεοί, χαλεπὸν δέ τ᾿ ὀρύσσειν ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι. θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται.</note>

->The root was indeed black beneath, but the flower was milky,<-
->The gods call it Moly; it is a difficult thing for mortal<-
->Men to uproot: the heavenly ones can do all things.<-

This can be applied both to every field of study and particularly to grammar, which, while it is bitter to boys, is pleasant to the old. It would also fit the pursuit of virtue, the beginning of which is harsh, the progress easy, and the end delightful.

<margin>XXXI</margin>
### Who will praise a parent, except unhappy children?

Who would praise a father, except for ill-fated children? <note>original Greek: Τίς πατέρ᾿ αἰνήσει᾿ εἰ μὴ κακοδαίμονα τέκνα;</note> That is,

He uses classical examples from Euripides, Homer, and Aulus Gellius to illustrate how wisdom and virtue often require navigating difficult or "bitter" beginnings.</summary>

### THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND THOUSAND
Dd 4
<meta>catchword: Neither</meta>

**Who would praise a father, unless the offspring is void of praise?**
A common poem bandied about concerning those who boast of the deeds of their ancestors, clearly having nothing they can truly say of themselves. In this way, Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet (c. 55–138 AD) known for his critiques of Roman society.</note> mocks a certain Ponticus in his eighth Satire:
> But I would not wish you, Ponticus, to be valued for the praise of your ancestors, in such a way that you yourself do nothing for future praise. It is a wretched thing to lean upon the fame of another.

This could also be twisted to this meaning: Wicked sons praise their parents in such a way that the people long for them as good men, because they cannot endure these sons who are far worse. This is something that often happens with princes: namely, that they approve of and long for a dead man whom they hated while he was alive, because he seems good by comparison to his son. Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–119 AD).</note> reports and explains this adage in his *Life of Aratus*: "You speak of a certain old proverb, O Polycrates; it seems to me that the philosopher Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher (c. 279–206 BC) who was known for his prolific writing and occasional misquotations.</note> set it forth—fearing its ill-repute, as it seems to me—not as it actually is, but as he thought it would be better: 
*Who would praise a father, except fortunate sons?* <note>original Greek: Τίς πατέρ’ αἰνήσει εἰ μὴ δυσδαίμονες υἱοί;</note>
But Dionysodorus of Troezen, <note>A Greek grammarian.</note> refuting him, sets out the true version as it stands: 
*Who would praise a father, except wretched sons?* <note>original Greek: Τίς πατέρ’ αἰνήσει εἰ μὴ κακοδαίμονες υἱοί;</note>
And he says that those who are worth nothing on their own, but hide under the virtues of certain ancestors and indulge excessively in their praises, are silenced by this proverb." This is what Plutarch says. Marcus Tullius Cicero used it in the same sense in his *Letters to Atticus*.

---

-> For those men are no longer: but those who are, are wicked. <- -> XXXVII <-
*For some indeed no longer exist, and those who remain are bad.* <note>original Greek: Οἱ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ ἔτ’ εἰσίν, οἱ δ’ ὄντες κακοί.</note> That is:
Partly they are no longer here at all: but those who are, are evil.
This was commonly said when someone longs for things that once existed but have perished through the fault of the times. For example, if someone were to long for men like Codrus, Camillus, Fabricius, or Epaminondas <note>These are archetypal heroes of Greek and Roman history, celebrated for their patriotism and virtue.</note> among the princes of this age, or for Paul, Anthony, or Jerome <note>Famous early Christian hermits and scholars (the "Desert Fathers").</note> among the monks, you might not inappropriately sing this verse. It is from Aristophanes in *The Frogs*, a play in which Bacchus <note>Also known as Dionysus, the god of theater and wine.</note> is brought down to the underworld to find Euripides or some other good poet, because among those above, no one can be found who is not wicked.

---

-> Means must be sought first, then virtue. <- -> XXXVIII <-
*Seek a livelihood, and virtue when there is a livelihood.* <note>original Greek: Δίζεσθαι βιοτὴν, ἀρετὴν δὲ ὅταν ᾖ βίος.</note> That is, a living must be sought; but virtue, when a living is present. It is reported by Diogenianus. <note>A Greek proverb collector of the 2nd century.</note>
Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet (65–8 BC).</note> expresses this proverb in his *Epistles* as follows:
> O citizens, citizens, money is to be sought first,
> virtue after coins.

However, this is said through irony. For Horace does not mean that one should take account of wealth before character, but rather he mocks the common opinion chanted by the masses, which many parents in these times also seriously instill in their children.

---

-> The "threes" who are among the dead. <- -> XXXIX <-
*The groups of thirty in the underworld.* <note>original Greek: Τὰς ἐν ᾅδου τριακάδας.</note> That is, those who are "threes" <note>term: terniones. Here Erasmus is playing with the Greek word 'triakadas' (thirtieths or groups of thirty) and 'terniones' (sets of three) to discuss the number three.</note> among the dead. By this adage, those were mocked who tracked down hidden and abstruse matters with a certain curious diligence. It is not absurdly twisted against one who explores the mysteries of sacred literature too anxiously or even superstitiously, or who tries to interpret all the Homeric fables with empty allegories, or labors to explain the numbers of the Platonists and Pythagoreans. They say that "threes" are honored among the dead, as being sacred to Hecate <note>The goddess of magic, crossroads, and the underworld, often depicted with three faces.</note>; for this very reason, the *trigla* <note>The red mullet fish.</note> is sacrificed to her, and it was the custom to set up her statue at crossroads <note>A place where three ways meet.</note>. Looking toward this, Virgil says:
> And triple-formed Hecate, the three faces of the maiden Diana.

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
Page 596
<meta>catchword: turn</meta>

<margin>XL</margin>
->Not even as much as nightingales sleep.<-
<note>original Greek: οὐδ' ὅσῳ ἀηδόνων ὑπνώσιν</note>. That is, not as much as nightingales sleep. This applies to those who are very sparing with sleep. Nightingales are said to sleep very little, either because of the myth of Itys <note>In Greek mythology, Philomela was turned into a nightingale after the tragic death of her nephew/son Itys; her constant singing was seen as a lament that kept her awake.</note> who was killed, or out of fear. Personally, I think the saying arose because nightingales in the spring months chatter with a continuous song almost the entire night through.

<margin>XLI</margin>
->Into what kind of monster has fortune entangled me.<-
<note>original Greek: Οἵῳ μ' ὁ δαίμων τῷ αἰνι συγκάθαεξεν</note>. That is, "Into what a monster has fortune trapped me." *This is a Catalectic Trimeter verse.* It is appropriate to say this when business falls to you involving a person who is morose and difficult—someone you can neither live with nor extricate yourself from. The verse is taken from a tragedy by the poet Philoxenus, in which Ulysses, trapped in the cave of the Cyclops, speaks in this manner. It is recorded by Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic (c. 325–260 BC).</note>.

<margin>XLII</margin>
->To gaze with fixed eyes.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀτενὲς ὁρᾶν</note>. That is, to look with eyes fixed. If used metaphorically, it becomes a proverbial figure, namely for considering something more attentively and accurately. To look more fixedly, to inspect more closely. It is taken from lovers, who look at that which delights them with stunned eyes that are never moved away. The adage is listed by Diogenianus. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Listening*, says: "For the listener is heavy and tiresome who is utterly stunned and has fixed eyes, as the saying goes." Marcus Tullius Cicero says in *Pro Lucio Flacco*: "So that you may contemplate the whole cause with eyes as intent, as they say, as possible."

<margin>XLIII</margin>
->To cast dust in the eyes.<-
One is said to cast dust in the eyes who deliberately obscures a matter and robs an opponent of their judgment. It seems to be derived from military practice, for it often happens that an enemy intentionally stirs up dust against their foe. By this art, the Roman general Sertorius conquered certain people called the Cacitani (or as the Greek has it, the Characitani), according to Plutarch; I made mention of this in the adage regarding "Caecias attracting clouds." This proverb is used by, among others, Saint Jerome in his *Letters*. Cicero boasts that in a certain legal action he "cast darkness" over the judges. There is something similar in Plautus’s *The Braggart Soldier* regarding a "cataract" <note>original: glaucomate</note> arising in the eyes.

<margin>XLIIII</margin>
->A drop or dew.<-
<note>original Greek: Ψεκὰς ἢ δρόσος</note>. That is, "a drop or dew." This was a common saying for those who spit frequently. For a *psekas* <note>Greek for a small drop or drizzle.</note> is that sprinkling or "dewing" that occurs whenever we are moistened by the tiniest droplets, like a misty rain. Originally, however, it was said as a joke against Antimachus, the lyric poet, because he would constantly spit on those with whom he was speaking, splattering them. The same nickname was given to a certain Olympic man, whom some think proposed a law that poets should not mock anyone by name; thus it happened that far fewer came to the contest than before, and those who did come forward would praise rather than criticize. Hence, these kinds of flatteries seem to have been called *Psekas*. For the maidservants who sprinkle the hair of refined matrons with medicated dyes are also called *Pfecades*. The adage is recorded by Diogenianus. Cicero, in his letters to Atticus, used the word "to bespatter" <note>original: Confputare</note> for "to sprinkle with light insults," undoubtedly alluding to this adage.

<margin>XLV</margin>
->A singer’s cough is a sign of hesitation.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀπορία ψάλτου βήξ</note>. That is, "A singer’s hesitation is a cough." Suidas warns that this is a more modern adage. It is said whenever we do not have what we need to say ready, and we hide it by pretending to do something else—just as in Plato, Aristophanes fakes a hiccup at the banquet so as not to speak. It clearly comes from singers who, when they get stuck in a song, feign a cough so that the chant seems interrupted by that, rather than by ignorance. I think it is close to what is said elsewhere: "A cough for a fart" <note>A phrase used to cover up an embarrassing noise or mistake.</note>.

<margin>XLVI</margin>
->An exhausted mind.<-
<note>original Greek: Παρεξυλκωμένον νοῦν ἔχων</note>. That is, having a mind that has vanished. The word *parexylkomenon* sounds almost as if you were to say "worn away." The metaphor is drawn from the tongues (reeds) of flutes, which, after they have fallen out or worn down, make the flute useless.

<margin>XLVII</margin>
->All-Holy Diana.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἡ παναγαία ἄρτεμις</note>. That is, "The All-Holy Diana." This was once said of a person who loved traveling too much, a wanderer, unstable, and settling in no certain home. For Diana is said to wander.

<summary>This page catalogs several adages regarding human behavior, including the habits of light sleepers, the use of deception ("dust in the eyes"), and the social excuses people use when they forget their place or their words.</summary>
<keywords>nightingales, Philoxenus, Ulysses, fixed gaze, Sertorius, deception, Antimachus, social etiquette, coughing, Diana the wanderer</keywords>

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD
Page 597

...as the poets say, and to wander through the groves and mountains. Indeed, she even changes her home frequently, now living among those above, now among those below. Nor is her appearance always the same, but now in full orb, now diminished, now gone. <note>original Latin: "pleno orbe, nunc mutila, nunc nulla." This likely refers to the moon or the goddess Diana/Hecate, illustrating a fickle or changing nature.</note>

<margin>XLVIII</margin>
**Rufillus smells of lozenges, Gorgonius of a goat.**
This line from Horace’s *Satires* <note>original Latin: "Sermonibus"</note> carries the appearance of a proverb:
> **Rufillus smells of lozenges, Gorgonius of a goat.**
It should be said either against two people struggling with different vices, or against a single person who is inconsistent with himself—now more talkative than is proper, now excessively silent; sometimes childishly foolish, sometimes more severe than Cato; at times extravagant, at times stingy. For just as it is a fault to smell like a goat <note>A common Roman metaphor for bad body odor or lack of hygiene.</note>, it is equally to be criticized if one smells of perfumes. For *pastilli* <note>pastils or lozenges</note> are little pellets of ointment. One habit belongs to a filthy man, the other to an effeminate one.

<margin>XLIX</margin>
**The lame man performs the act of a man best.** <note>original Greek: Ἄριστα χωλὸς οἰφεῖ. Erasmus notes an alternative reading "οἰχέε," meaning "goes" or "acts."</note> This was commonly said when someone prefers their own lot—even if it is not particularly grand—above that of another, even if the other's is superior. They say it was born from a pithy saying of the Amazons. Tradition tells that it was once the custom of the Amazons to make male children lame by twisting the shin or hip. Furthermore, when they were at war against the Scythians, and the Scythians tried to entice them to defect to their side—saying that in the future they would have dealings not with lame and mutilated men, but with whole men—Antianira, the leader of the Amazons, replied in this way: **"The lame man does it best."** Athenaeus used this in book thirteen: "For truly the lame man performs the act of a man best." Theocritus calls a man eager for intercourse *Oliphos*, and Hesychius says *Oliphon*. It has also been observed in our own times that often those who have mutilated shins, or are missing some limb, are more fit than others for the use of Venus <note>That is, for sexual activity.</note>, nature surely making things equal. Aristotle gives the reason why a lame man is more lustful than others in his *Problems*, section ten, problem twenty-six: because in such a man, little nourishment flows downward due to the defect of the legs, but instead seeks the upper parts and is turned into seed.

<margin>L</margin>
->**Ogygian evils.**<-
**Ogygian evils.** <note>original Greek: Ὀγύγια κακά</note>. This will be rightly said of things that are either immense or ancient, for "Ogygian" signifies both in Greek. Others prefer to refer it to Ogygus, the first ruler of the city of Thebes. His descendant Cadmus fell into various calamities because of his daughters. Those who interpret "Ogygian evils" as the most atrocious misfortunes are looking to this history. Suidas says much the same, except that he prefers to say Ogygian evils are "ancient" ones. However, those who say Ogygian means "ancient" follow the idea that the region of the Boeotians and Thebans was once called Ogygia. Indeed, all of Attica once held this name, as Stephanus testifies. There is also a very ancient island called Ogygia, on which Homer feigns that the shipwrecked Ulysses emerged. From this, the word—now obsolete—passed into a sort of proverbial usage. The reason for this proverb lies not in a metaphor, but in the antiquity and strangeness of the word itself, as we pointed out at the beginning of this work. By a similar reasoning, and not without the appearance of a proverb, the Greeks call the primeval and very ancient "Ogygidas" and "Ogygians," after some ancient god who has been forgotten for many centuries. Suidas and Stephanus say roughly this about Ogygian matters.

<margin>LI</margin>
->**All crumbs.**<-
**All crumbs.** <note>original Greek: πάντα χναύματα</note>. They used to say "all *chnaumata*" whenever they meant "the whole business." For the Greeks call the fragments of cakes and that kind of food *chnaumata*. The Latins also say "the relics of war" and "the relics of the Greeks" <note>original Latin: "Reliquias Danaum," a famous phrase from Virgil's Aeneid.</note> by a similar figure of speech. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus.

<margin>LII</margin>
->**So one must come when the parts of the battle are finished.**<-
Plato says in the *Gorgias*: "They say, Socrates, that one ought to share in the duties of war and battle in this way." It was a proverbial joke for when someone arrived only after a business was finished. Just as cowardly soldiers are accustomed to do, who, once the conflict is over and the fear removed, finally show up—either to collect the plunder or for the *epinicia*, that is, to celebrate the victory feast. For that word "to share" <note>original Greek: μεταλαγχάνειν</note> signifies slowness and a late performance of duty. Socrates, responding, explains the proverb with a similar proverb: "Have we come, as they say, after the feast, and are we late?" It seems to be taken from Rhesus, the leader of the Thracians, whom Hector rebukes in Euripides because he had come too late to the alliance of war—namely, in the tenth year.

<summary>Erasmus explores several proverbs related to human behavior and historical myths, including the "lame man" proverb of the Amazons and the "Ogygian" metaphor for ancient or massive misfortune.</summary>
<keywords>Horace, Amazons, Ogyges, Thebes, Plato, Socrates, Rhesus, Greek mythology, ancient hygiene, compensatory nature, antiquity</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
Page 598

"You are an ally indeed, but a stranger to the table." <note>original Greek: Σύμμαχος μὲν εἶ, ξένος δὲ πρὸς τράπεζαν. This implies someone who is a partner in work or war but is excluded from the rewards or the intimacy of dining.</note> And the response to this is: "But I arrived later, yet nonetheless in time. For you have already been fighting for ten years, and you achieve nothing." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ὕστερον μὲν ἦλθον... These lines are from an ancient play, likely mocking a latecomer who points out the inefficiency of those already there.</note>

Diogenes, if I am not mistaken, alluded to this. For when someone had inscribed upon his house the title: "Hercules the Victor <note>original Greek: Callinicus</note>, son of Jove, lives here; let no evil enter," Diogenes added to the inscription: "The alliance after the war." <note>original Greek: μετὰ πόλεμον ἡ συμμαχία.</note> This signifies that it is pointless to call upon Hercules as a "driver away of evils" <note>term: depulsor malorum - a traditional epithet for Hercules as a protector</note> once a "bad guest" <note>a metaphor for a vice or a disaster</note> has already moved in.

->**Compliance wins friends, truth breeds hatred.**<-

"Compliance wins friends, truth breeds hatred." <note>original Latin: Obsequium amicos, ueritas odium parit.</note> This is a proverbial six-foot line <note>term: Senarius - a line of verse consisting of six iambic feet, common in Roman comedy</note> from Terence’s play *Andria*. It does not advise us on what *should* be done, but rather shows what commonly happens in the world. For common friendship is sustained by compliance—that is, by being agreeable or flattering. Indeed, "to wink at the vices of one's associates" is the thing that "both joins friends together and keeps them joined." <note>Erasmus is quoting Horace here, suggesting that overlooking a friend's faults is the glue of social bonds.</note>

But among true friends, nothing is more pleasant than the truth, provided it lacks a rustic, unpolished, or heavy harshness. Furthermore, he who desires to be a friend to the masses must comply with the manners of others and take care, as Persius says, "not to scrape tender ears with the biting truth." <note>Persius was a Roman satirist known for his difficult but sharp moral critiques.</note> That the poet Terence does not actually approve of this behavior is indicated when he says, "For in these times," meaning in these corrupt morals.

The same author expressed the same sentiment differently in his play *The Brothers* <note>original Latin: Adelphis</note>, saying: "As the man is, so you must treat him." Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Terence</note> reminds us that this was a proverbial saying. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Essay on Friendship*, says: "I do not know how it is, but that line which my friend Terence said in *Andria* is true: 'Compliance wins friends, truth breeds hatred.' Truth is troublesome, if indeed hatred—which is the poison of friendship—is born from it. But compliance is much more troublesome, because by indulging sins, it allows a friend to be carried toward a fall. However, the greatest fault lies with him who both scorns the truth and is driven by the very compliance offered to him." 

Pindar, in his *Fifth Nemean Ode*, says: "Simple and exact truth is not always the most profitable thing to show on one's face; and silence is often the wisest thing for a man to conceive." <note>Erasmus provides the Greek for this Pindaric quote.</note> He means that the plain truth should not always be brought forth exactly as it is, because it might be damaging; but it is the part of a wise man never to hide his opinion forever, but to bring it forth at the right time when there is hope of some benefit. In the fifth book of Athenaeus, this three-measure line <note>term: trimeter</note> is cited from Agathon:
"If I tell the truth, I will not please you; 
If I please you, I will not tell the truth."

->**With open arms.**<-

"With open arms" <note>original Latin: Obuijs ulnis</note> is found in Quintilian, used to mean "greedily" or "thirstily." It is a metaphor taken from those who, with arms outstretched, hurry to embrace those for whom they have felt a great longing and whom they most eagerly see. We also read "With open hands." Saint Jerome, writing to Pammachius—his former fellow student, companion, and friend—says: "I receive you, as they say, with open hands." Basil, in the preface to his dialogue, wrote "with both hands" <note>original Greek: ἀμφοτέραις χερσὶν</note> in the same sense. If these phrases are turned toward matters of the mind, they will have a proverbial character, as in: "I shall receive your letter with open arms."

->**The Field of Oblivion.**<-

"The Field of Oblivion." <note>original Greek: Λήθης πεδίον (Lethes pedion).</note> This is said either of those who are extremely forgetful, or of imaginary and frivolous things that exist nowhere. Aristophanes writes: "Who is for the Field of Oblivion?" The common people believe that the stories told about the underworld are mere trifles. And as Juvenal says:
"Not even boys believe in the black frogs in the Stygian whirlpool." <note>Juvenal was a Roman satirist; he is noting that by his time, the old myths of the afterlife were seen as fairy tales for children.</note>

->**All things are easy for the wise.**<-

"All things are easy for the wise." <note>original Greek: Ἅπαντα τοῖς σοφοῖσιν εὔκολα.</note> 
There is nothing so arduous that it cannot be easily accomplished through prudent counsel. Or, "Nothing is so..."

<summary>This page explores adages regarding social conduct, focusing on the tension between being agreeable (flattery) and being truthful, as well as metaphors for eagerness and forgetfulness. Erasmus synthesizes classical sources like Terence, Cicero, and Pindar to discuss how truth-telling affects friendship.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, truth vs flattery, Terence, Cicero, Hercules, Diogenes, Lethe, wisdom, open arms, Agathon</keywords>

# NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND THOUSAND
Page 599

## Everything is edible to the besieged.
<margin>LVII</margin> For indeed everything is edible to those under siege. <note>original Greek: Ἅπαντα γάρ τοι βρωτὰ πολιορκουμένοις.</note> That is:
To those besieged by the enemy, all things are food, whatever they may be.
A proverbial six-foot verse <note>term: Senarius - a line of verse with six feet, typical of ancient drama</note> meaning that when necessity presses, there is nothing we will not do. To the intensely hungry, there is no food that is not sweet. The saying originates from the sieges of cities, in which, for lack of food, people sometimes devour dogs, cats, roots of herbs, and even human waste.

---

## All things are alike.
<margin>LVIII</margin> All things are alike, and even the beautiful Rhodopis. <note>original Greek: Ἅπανθ’ ὁμοία καὶ ῥοδώπις ἡ καλή.</note> That is:
All things are the same, even the decent Rhodopis herself.
The condition of mortals is the same: the beautiful and the deformed alike grow old and die. Rhodopis is the name of a certain girl of celebrated beauty, whose name seems to have been given to her because of her "rosy appearance." Herodotus writes much about the courtesan Rhodope in his second book, and Pliny mentions her in his thirty-sixth book, chapter twelve. Since the Greek verse has "Rhodopis" <note>original: ῥοδώπις</note>, it is surprising why Juvenal shortened the syllable:
> While a damp beard rubs the loins of Rhodope. <note>original Latin: Dum Rhodopes uda terit inguina barba.</note>
This is recorded as a proverb by Suidas.

---

## The whole sea urchin is rough.
<margin>LIX</margin> The whole sea urchin is rough. <note>original Greek: Ἅπας ἐχῖνος τραχύς.</note> This applies to those with morose and unpleasant characters. The sea urchin—and likewise the hedgehog—is covered everywhere with spines, so that you cannot touch it anywhere without being hurt. <note>term: Echinus - Erasmus notes this word refers to both the marine sea urchin and the land-dwelling hedgehog, both known for their prickliness.</note> There is also a kind of person like this, with whom you can have no dealings without an argument. Aristophanes says in *The Peace*:
> You could never make a rough sea urchin smooth. <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ ποτ’ ἂν θείης λεῖον τὸν τραχὺν ἐχῖνον.</note> That is,
> From rough to smooth a hedgehog will never turn.

---

## Everything suits good men.
<margin>LX</margin> Everything is becoming to good men. <note>original Greek: Ἅπαντα τοῖς καλοῖσιν ἀνδράσιν πρέπει.</note> That is:
All things are thoroughly fitting for good and honest men.
Wickedness has this quality: even if a person of ill-repute does something right, somehow a sense of grace is missing. Conversely, a certain dignity accompanies true virtue, so that whatever a good man does appears becoming. However, this sense can also be taken to mean: "All things suit beautiful men," because physical grace commends a person whether they are speaking, singing, or doing anything else. It is even more elegant if you apply it this way: that whatever influential people say or do among princes is taken in a good light and praised; so much so, that what would be a capital offense for another person brings praise to them. This is recorded by Diogenianus.

---

## Pass over the prophet.
<margin>LXI</margin> Pass over the prophet. <note>original Greek: Πάρελθε τὸν μάντιν.</note> This will be appropriate to use whenever we advise that someone should be spared because they are exceptional and should be considered immune from common fate. For example, if one were to say that a poet, a theologian, or a priest ought to be spared. In ancient times, it was the custom for a crowned seer <note>term: vates - a prophet or divinely inspired poet</note> to walk before the battle line; it was not considered lawful to attack him with weapons, as he was a sacred man. The adage can also be used ironically.

---

## Let them hate, so long as they fear.
<margin>LXII</margin> Let them hate, so long as they fear. <note>original Latin: Oderint dum metuant.</note> This is a tyrannical saying, taken from tragedy and used by almost every writer. It was particularly familiar to Marcus Tullius Cicero. Seneca, in the second book of *On Clemency*, indicates that it even passed into common speech, writing that many great but detestable sayings have entered human life and become famous among the common people, such as: "Let them hate, so long as they fear." He says there is a similar Greek verse which commands one "to mix the earth with fires" once they are dead. He says the same in the first book of *On Anger*: for some words are uttered by angry men which seem to show a great spirit, but only to those who do not know what true greatness is—such as that dire and abominable "Let them hate, so long as they fear," which you should know was written in the age of Sulla. One may also use the adage jokingly: for instance, if someone superior in learning says it regarding secret enemies who nevertheless do not dare to open their mouths because of fear. It will also suit the wealthy, who say that line from Horace:
> The people hiss at me, but I applaud myself at home as soon as I look at the coins in my money-chest.
And likewise that line from Juvenal,

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Greek and Roman adages, specifically concluding a section on late-coming allies before moving into famous observations on friendship, social etiquette, and the intellectual ease of the wise.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<margin>LIII</margin> You come not as an ally, but as a guest to the table. ->that is,<-
<note>original Greek: Σύμμαχοϛ μὲν ὀυ, ξένοϛ δὲ πῶϛ τράπεζαν. Latin: Socius haud quidem aduenis, sed hospes ad mensam.</note>
To which the reply is:
Yet I come late, but nonetheless in time.
For you have already been fighting for ten years,
And you have accomplished nothing. ->that is,<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ὕστερον μὲν ἦλθον, ἐν καιρῷ δ’ ὅμωϛ. Σὺ μὲν γὰρ ἤδη δέκατον αἰχμάζειϛ ἔτοϛ, Κ’ὀυδὲν περαίνειϛ. Latin: Sero quidem, ast in tempore aduenio tamen. Nam tu quidem iam prælians decennium, Nihil explicas.</note>
Diogenes, if I am not mistaken, alluded to this. For when someone had inscribed this title upon his house: 
"The son of Jupiter, Hercules the Victorious <note>Greek: Callinicus</note>, dwells here; let no evil enter": Diogenes added another inscription, "An alliance after the war." <note>original Greek: μετὰ πόλεμον ἡ συμμαχία</note> that is, help after the battle. He was signaling that it was pointless to call upon Hercules as a "driver-away of evils" <note>term: depulsorem malorum</note> when an evil guest had already moved into that house.

### Compliance breeds friends, truth breeds hatred.

"Compliance breeds friends, truth breeds hatred." This is a proverbial six-foot verse <note>term: Senarius - a common meter in Latin comedy</note> from Terence’s play *The Girl from Andros* <note>original: Andria</note>, not advising what ought to be done, but showing what commonly happens. For common friendship consists of compliances. For looking the other way at the vices of one's associates:
"This thing both joins friends and keeps them joined." <note>A reference to Horace’s Satires</note>
But among true friends, nothing is more pleasant than the truth, provided that a rustic, clumsy, and heavy harshness is absent. Furthermore, he who desires to be a friend to as many people as possible in the common way must comply with the habits of others, and must take care, according to Persius: "To scratch tender ears with biting truth." <note>original Latin: Auriculas teneras mordaci radere uero</note> That the poet does not actually approve of this sentiment is sufficiently indicated when he says: "For in this time," that is, in these corrupt times.
The same author expressed the same sentiment differently in *The Brothers* <note>original: Adelphis</note>, saying: "As the man is, so you must behave." Donatus <note>a famous Roman grammarian</note> remarks that this was said proverbially. Marcus Tullius Cicero in his discourse *On Friendship*: "But I know not how it is true, what my friend Terence said in *The Girl from Andros*: 'Compliance breeds friends, truth breeds hatred.' Truth is troublesome, if indeed hatred is born from it, which is the poison of friendship. But compliance is much more troublesome, because by indulging sins, it allows a friend to be carried headlong into ruin. Moreover, the greatest fault lies in him who both scorns the truth and is driven into deception by compliance." Pindar, in the fifth Nemean hymn: "Because entire truth does not always appear with a profitable face. And silence is often the wisest thing for a man to perceive." <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἅπαντα κερδίων φαίνει λα πρόσωπον ἀλαθεῖ’ ἀτρεκήϛ. καὶ τὸ σιγᾶν πολλάκιϛ ἐστὶ σοφώτατον ἀνθρώπῳ νοῆσαι.</note> He feels that simple truth should not always be brought forth as it is, because it might be damaging; rather, it is the part of a wise man sometimes to hide his opinion, to be brought forth in due time when the hope of fruit is shown. In Athenaeus, book five, this three-measure verse <note>term: trimeter</note> is cited from Agathon:
"If I tell the truth, I will not please you,
If I please you, I will not tell the truth." ->that is,<-
<note>original Greek: Εἰ μὲν φράσω τἀληθέϛ, ὀυχί σ’ εὐφρανῶ, Εἰ δ’ εὐφρανῶ σ’, ὀυχὶ τἀληθὲϛ φράσω.</note>
If I speak true things, I shall not be a pleasure to you.
If I am a pleasure, I shall not have spoken true things to you.

<margin>LIIII</margin>

### With open arms.

"With open arms" <note>original Latin: Obuijs ulnis</note> is found in Quintilian, used for that which is done eagerly and thirstily. It is a metaphor taken from those who, with arms stretched out, hasten to the embrace of those for whom they were held by great longing, and whom they see most desirously. We also read "With open hands." Saint Jerome to Pammachius, a former fellow student, comrade, and friend: "I receive you with open, as they say, hands." Basil, in the preface of a dialogue, wrote "With both hands" <note>original Greek: ἀμφοτέραιϛ χερσὶν</note> in the same sense. If these are applied to matters of the mind, they will have a proverbial figure: as in, "I shall receive your letter with open arms."

<margin>LV</margin>

### The plain of oblivion.

"The plain of oblivion." <note>original Greek: Λήθηϛ πεδίον. Latin: Lethes campus.</note> This will be said either of those who are intensely forgetful, or of invented and frivolous things which exist nowhere. Aristophanes: "Who is for the plain of oblivion?" <note>original Greek: τίϛ εἰϛ τὸ λήθηϛ πεδίον;</note> For the common people believe that the things the poets hand down concerning the underworld are trifles. And, as Juvenal says: 
"Black frogs in the Stygian whirlpool, | Not even boys believe in them."

<margin>LVI</margin>

### All things are easy for the wise.

"All things are easy for the wise men." ->that is,<-
<note>original Greek: Ἅπαντα τοῖϛ σοφοῖσιν εὔκολα.</note>
All things are easy for wise men.
Nothing is so arduous that it may not be easily accomplished by prudent counsel. Or, nothing is so bit- <meta>The text cuts off here at the end of the page. The catchword "bum" indicates the next word is "bitter" (acerbum).</meta>

...word, which a wise man would not easily bear with a calm mind, since reason softens all things. If you add a word, it will form a six-foot verse <note>term: senarius; a common meter in Greek and Latin drama</note>: "All things are thus." It is cited by Zenodotus.

->Everything is edible to the besieged.<-
<margin>LVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἅπαντα γάρ τοι βρωτὰ πολιορκουμένοις</note> that is,
To those besieged by the enemy, anything and everything is food.

A proverbial six-foot verse: when necessity presses, there is nothing we will not do. To the truly famished, no food is unpleasant. It originates from the sieges of cities, in which people, through lack of food, sometimes devour dogs and cats, the roots of plants, and occasionally even human excrement.

->All things are alike.<-
<margin>LVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἁπανθ’ ὅμοια καὶ Ῥοδῶπις ἡ καλή</note> that is,
All things are the same, even the lovely Rhodopis herself.

The condition of mortals is the same; the beautiful and the deformed alike grow old and die. Rhodopis is the name of a girl celebrated for her striking beauty; her name seems to have been given because of her "rosy appearance." Herodotus writes much about the courtesan Rhodope in his second book, and Pliny mentions her in his thirty-sixth book, chapter twelve. Since the Greek poem uses the name *Rhodopis* (with a long 'o'), it is strange why Juvenal shortened it:
> While the damp beard rubs Rhodope's groin.

It is cited by Suidas as a proverb.

->The whole sea-urchin is prickly.<-
<margin>LIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ὅλος ἐχῖνος τραχύς</note> That is: The whole sea-urchin is rough. This applies to those with surly and unpleasant manners. The sea-urchin <note>The Latin *echinus* refers to both the sea-urchin and the land-dwelling hedgehog</note>, and likewise the hedgehog, is covered on all sides with spines, so that you cannot touch it anywhere without harm. There is also a type of person with whom you cannot deal in any way without a quarrel. Aristophanes says in *The Peace*:
<note>original Greek: οὐ δέ ποτ’ ἂν θείης λεῖον τὸν τραχὺν ἐχῖνον</note> that is,
You will never turn a rough hedgehog into a smooth one.

->Everything is becoming to good men.<-
<margin>LX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἅπαντα τοῖς καλοῖσιν ἀνδράσιν πρέπει</note> that is,
All things are perfectly fitting for good and honest men.

Wickedness has this quality: even if someone praised performs or speaks rightly, somehow that proper grace <note>term: decorum</note> is absent. In contrast, a certain grace accompanies true virtue, so that whatever a good man does appears to be becoming. Although this sense could also be taken as: "All things become handsome men," because beauty recommends one who speaks, or sings, or does anything at all. It will be more elegant if you turn it this way: to say that whatever those in favor with princes say or do is taken in good part and praised, so much so that what would be a capital offense for one person might even bring praise to another. It is cited by Diogenianus.

->Pass over the seer.<-
<margin>LXI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Πάρελθε τὸν μάντιν</note> that is: Omit the prophet. This will be appropriate whenever we advise that someone should be spared because they are exceptional and should be held exempt from the common lot. For example, if one were to say that a poet, a theologian, or a priest ought to be spared. In ancient times, it was the custom for a crowned augur to walk before the battle line; it was not lawful to attack him with weapons, as he was a sacred man. The adage can also be used ironically.

->Let them hate, so long as they fear.<-
<margin>LXII</margin>
Let them hate, so long as they fear. A tyrannical saying, taken from tragedy <note>Attributed to the poet Accius</note> and used by almost every writer. It was particularly familiar to Marcus Tullius Cicero. Seneca, in the second book of *On Clemency*, indicates that it even passed into common speech, writing that many grand but detestable sayings have entered human life and become famous among the public, such as: "Let them hate, so long as they fear." To this, he says, a Greek verse is similar, which bids one to "mix the earth with fire" once one is dead. He says the same in the first book of *On Anger*: for some words are uttered by angry men that seem to indicate a great spirit—though only to those ignorant of true greatness—such as that dire and abominable "Let them hate, so long as they fear," which you may know was written in the age of Sulla. One may also use the adage jokingly: for instance, if someone superior in learning says it of secret enemies who, however, do not dare to open their mouths out of fear: "Let them hate, so long as they fear." It will also fit the wealthy, who quote that line of Horace:
> The people hiss at me, but I applaud myself at home as soon as I contemplate the coins in my chest.

Likewise that line of Juvenal...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s catalog of ancient proverbs, moving from metaphors for surly behavior to expressions describing extreme aversion, legendary foolishness, and the physical decline of old age. It maintains the structure of citing a Greek or Latin phrase followed by literary examples from poets like Horace and Aristophanes.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

I would rather have a tunic of lupine seeds,
Than if the whole neighborhood in the entire village praised me. 
<note>original: "Tunicam mihi malo lupini, / Quàm si me toto laudet uicinia pago." These lines from Juvenal’s Satires suggest that the speaker prefers something worthless but real—like a tunic made of cheap lupine plants—over the empty vanity of public praise.</note>

<margin>LXII</margin>
->He hates it worse than a dog and a snake.<-
<note>original: "Odit cane peius & angue."</note>

This was also spoken by Horace using a proverbial figure:
"One man will avoid a cloak woven at Miletus <note>Miletus was famous for its luxury wool</note> more than a dog and a snake."
He refers, I believe, to a rabid dog. If this is applied more broadly, it becomes even more proverbial; for example: "This man is entirely devoted to profit; the literature he once loved, he now—as they say—avoids more than a dog or a snake." Or: "This man gives himself entirely to flatterers; he avoids friends from whom he might hear the truth more than a dog or a snake." The same Horace says in his *Odes*:
"Why does he avoid the olive oil <note>Used by athletes in the gymnasium</note> more cautiously than viper's blood?"
Similarly, Plautus says in *The Merchant*:
"Indeed, your wife is in the country, whom you said just now you hated as much as snakes."

<margin>LXIII</margin>
->More foolish than Coroebus.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἠλιθιώτερος Κορoίβου.</note>

"More foolish than Coroebus." This is a proverbial hyperbole used for those who are stupid and senseless. The foolishness of Coroebus was a celebrated story among the common people; he was said to have tried to count the waves of the sea, though he could not count past five. Eustathius mentions this in his commentary on the tenth book of the *Odyssey*, as does Lucian in his *Affairs of the Heart*. Although in other authors I read "Noreus" with an "n." Some add that this Coroebus was the son of Mygdon the Phrygian during the time of the Trojan War. Virgil also mentions a certain Coroebus:
"And young Coroebus had come,
Seized by an insane love for Cassandra,
And as a son-in-law, he brought aid to Priam and the Phrygians."
In that passage, Servius <note>A famous ancient commentator on Virgil</note> indicates that the material was taken from Euphorion. He says, "Euphorion introduces this Coroebus as a fool, and Virgil follows him," giving him the line:
"Whether it be trickery or courage, who would ask in an enemy?"
This is considered foolish because a victory sought through trickery is most shameful.

<margin>LXIV</margin>
->A fennel stalk of tow.<-
<note>original Greek: Στυππῖον γερόντιον.</note>

That is, "Tow or a straw-like fennel stalk." This refers to an old man whose strength is exhausted. It is very similar to what we have said in another place: "Man is a bubble." The metaphor is taken from wood that has dried out, lost all its sap, and become withered like straw. "Tow" <note>term: stupa; the coarse, dry fibers left over after processing flax or hemp</note> is what is shaken out from flax; it is dry and useless.

<margin>LXV</margin>
->The mats of Phormio.<-
<note>original Greek: Στιβάδες Φορμίωνος.</note>

That is, "The couches of Phormio." This refers to beds that are filthy, frugal, and not at all luxurious, such as military sleeping quarters, or the kind Ulysses makes for himself in Homer out of heaps of leaves and branches spread on the ground. It is recorded by Suidas <note>An ancient Greek encyclopedia</note> that Phormio was a certain military commander famous for his endurance in bearing the hardships of military service. This could also be applied more broadly to any somewhat harsh treatment. It appears in Aristophanes’ *Peace*:
"For if only I could see that day!
For I have endured many
Troubles and the mats which fell to Phormio’s lot."
These are choral verses, and therefore we have translated them into prose.

<margin>LXVI</margin>
->It is folly to think Jupiter exists.<-
<note>original Greek: Τῆς μωρίας, τὸν Δία νομίζειν ὄντα τηλικοῦτον.</note>

That is, "It is ignorance to believe he is Jupiter, having been born so many years ago." This can be applied to someone of great age who says or feels something absurd, since because of their age they should no longer be ignorant of anything. For childish superstition does not suit an old man. This is recorded by Suidas. It is a verse by Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
"Look, look! Olympian Jupiter! What folly
To believe any Jupiter exists at such an age!"

<header>THE SECOND CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY 601</header>

### I am telling you your own dream. LXVIII

->I am telling you your own dream.<-
<note>original Greek: Τὸ σὸν ὄναρ σοὶ διηγοῦμαι. Latin: Tuum somniū tibi narro.</note>

That is, I am telling you what you yourself know better than I do. In Suidas, <note>Suidas, or the Suda, is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> these words are cited from some author: "For if I were to try to make you known to yourself, as the saying goes, I would be telling you your own dream." 

Plato says in the eighth book of *The Republic*: "You are telling me my own dream." It seems to be derived from those who consult dream-interpreters. Some people even demand that these interpreters divine what they actually dreamed, as if it were not enough for them to merely explain the meaning. In the same way, certain ignorant sick people expect doctors to divine their gender, age, the whole nature of their disease, where and how it happened, and how they feel, merely by looking at a urine sample—and they almost expect the doctor to tell them what they dreamed while they had a fever.

### A bridegroom’s life. LXIX

->A bridegroom’s life.<-
<note>original Greek: Νυμφίου βίος. Latin: Sponsi uita.</note>

This is used to describe a soft and delicate life. It is related to an expression I mentioned elsewhere, "A musical life." Suidas cites this six-foot line, which appears in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*:
->Indeed, you truly live the life of a bridegroom.<-
-><note>original Greek: ὑμᾶς μὲν ἄγαν γε ζῆτε νυμφίου βίον.</note><-

This is because suitors were accustomed to being crowned with leaves and garlands, and to be cared for more delicately and elegantly, or because those longing for marriage seem soft. In the eighth book of Athenaeus, <note>Athenaeus was a Greek rhetorician and grammarian, famous for his 'Deipnosophistae' or 'Banket of the Learned.'</note> Stratonicus the lyre-player calls the Rhodians "White Cyreneans" and "a city of suitors." Unless we prefer to relate this to those suitors of Penelope in Homer, who cared for nothing except banquets, the lyre, dancing, dice, the discus, parasites, and other pleasures of that kind. Hence Horace calls men devoted to luxury "Penelope's suitors."

### It was both the report, and you were so. LXX

->It was both the report, and you were so.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἡ μὲν κλέος, ἠδ' καὶ ἦσθα. Latin: Et dicebaris erasq;.</note>

A proverbial half-line of verse, used whenever deeds match a person's reputation. Suidas mentions it from some poet. It is a fragment of Heroic poetry.

### Unharmed, I shall watch another suffering my own misfortune. LXXI

->Unharmed, I shall watch another suffering my own misfortune.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἐξάντης λάθω τοὺμὸν κακὸν ἄλλου ἔχοντα. Latin: Indemnis spectabo alium mala nostra ferentem.</note>

That is, I shall look to my own affairs based on the misfortunes of others. The word "unharmed" <note>original Greek: ἐξάντης (exantēs)</note> means placed outside of harm and unhurt. It is very similar to that line in Plautus: 
"He is happily wise, who is wise at another's peril."

### No sooner said than done. LXXII

->No sooner said than done.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἅμ' ἔπος, ἅμ' ἔργον. Latin: Simul & dictum & factum.</note>

This is used when someone performs what he promised in words without delay. The Latins say "with the word" to mean "immediately after you have spoken." And Virgil writes:
"And faster than the word, he calms the swollen seas."
It clearly is taken from Homer, in whose work this line appears:
->Immediately then, as the word was spoken, the deed was finished.<-
-><note>original Greek: αὐτίκ' ἔπειθ' ἅμα μῦθο' ἔην, τετέλεστο δὲ ἔργον.</note><-

The same thing is expressed by the Greeks in a single word, *autoboëi*, <note>original: "αὐτοβοεί" - literally "at the shout itself."</note> which seems to be transferred from a military shout, by which an enemy is sometimes routed before they even come to blows. Thucydides used it this way. Theopompus used it to mean "by main force"—that is, by strength and courage, not by ambush. For whoever devises an ambush for an enemy remains silent; but he who trusts in his own strength rushes upon the enemy with a shout. 

Some think the word comes from "oxen," <note>Erasmus notes a theory that the word derives from "bous" (ox).</note> as if derived from plowmen who, when they promise to finish a piece of work on the same day, are accustomed to say *autoboëi*, meaning "before I unyoke the oxen." It is transferred to the speed of any action, so that it carries the same weight as "on the spot" or "immediately."

### To throw lambs to the dogs. LXXIII

->To throw lambs to the dogs.<-
<note>original Greek: προβάλλειν τοῖς κυσὶν ἄρνας. Latin: Objicere canibus agnos.</note>

This was said of someone who exposed a person who was peaceful and unskilled in litigation to slanderers and experienced attackers, because that animal (the lamb) is the most peaceful of all. It is recorded by Diogenianus. It is a Heroic half-line, excerpted, as I conjecture, from some oracle.

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

->God in need of nothing.<-
<margin>LXXIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀνενδεὴς ὁ θεὸς. Latin: Nullius egens deus.</note>
God is in need of nothing. This proverb reminds us that no mortal is so absolute that nothing is found wanting in him; only God is perfect in every respect. It can also be said of the wealthy, or those endowed with many gifts of nature and fortune, as if they were like some god, since they have everything at hand that seems to belong to perfect happiness.

->I have lost the kernel, he left the shells as security.<-
<margin>LXXV</margin>
<note>original Latin: Nucleum amisi, reliquit pignori putamina.</note>
Plautus says in his play *The Captives*: "I have lost the kernel, he left the shells as security." These are the words of Hegio <note>Hegio is a character in Plautus's comedy who is tricked into releasing a high-value prisoner while keeping a slave.</note> when he realized he had been deceived, and that the master had been lost while the slave was kept in his place—the servant remained instead of the lord. For the one from whom profit was expected had fled, leaving behind the one from whom no advantage could be taken. The allegory is clear in itself.

->You entrust the watch to a naked man.<-
<margin>LXXVI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Γυμνῷ φυλακὴν ἐπιτάττεις. Latin: Nudo custodia mandas.</note>
You entrust the guard to a naked man. This is said whenever a task is assigned to someone who lacks the ability to perform it, and who is by no means fit to undertake the duty because of their poverty. For a naked man cannot conveniently keep watch because of the stinging night cold, nor is he fit for a fight while unarmed. This is recorded by Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic (c. 325–260 BC).</note>. The further it is turned into a metaphor, the more proverbial it becomes. For instance: "You enjoin me to write something against this poet, but, as the old proverb goes, you entrust the watch to a naked man. For I have nothing with which to sustain my leisure in the meantime." Hesychius differs somewhat from the accounts given by Suidas and Zenodotus, although that passage in the Aldine edition of Hesychius is corrupted. However, I conjecture the sense to be this: the proverb is usually said when something is commanded of those who have no need for it. Because they are forced to do it by command, unless I am mistaken, because a naked man has nothing that requires a guardian.

->May I happen to be saved now.<-
<margin>LXXVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Νῦν γένοιτο σωθῆναι. Latin: Nunc contingat seruari.</note>
May I happen to be saved now. This is used when we mean that we will be sufficiently cautious in the future, if only we are allowed to escape the present danger. This is the way Davus speaks in Terence's *The Lady of Andros*: "After this, I know well enough I shall be safe, if I can just avoid this evil now." They say it arose from a certain fable. An eagle had snatched a tortoise in its talons; it prepared to drop it from a great height so that, once broken, the eagle could feed on the meat. In this crisis, the tortoise prayed that it might be safe for the present, and for the rest, it would be its own concern never to fall into such danger again. <note>original Greek: Νῦν γένοιτο σωθῆναι, τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ αὐτῇ μελήσει.</note> That is: "Let me be safe now; the rest will be my own care." 

Some tell the fable this way: The tortoise once had a desire to fly and begged the eagle to teach it. When the eagle denied it was possible because nature was against it, the tortoise persisted nonetheless. So the eagle complied, and having carried the tortoise on high, let it go so it might try to fly. The tortoise, fearing a disastrous outcome, prayed that it might happen to be safe at that time: <note>original Greek: νῦν σωθῆναι.</note> "To be saved now." So says Diogenianus. Suidas records it this way: <note>original Greek: νῦν σωθῆναι, ἵν’ ἐμοὶ δίδαγμα ᾖ τῷ χρόνῳ λοιπῷ.</note> that is, "Would that I might now escape unharmed, so that this might be a lesson to me for the time remaining." 

Pliny identifies a third kind of eagle, which some call the *morphnos*, others the *plancus* or *anataria* (the "duck-eagle"), and Homer called the *percnos*. It lacks a tongue and is therefore mute, but it is armed with teeth, very black, and has a rather prominent tail. It has the instinct to break captured tortoises by throwing them from a height. And by such a chance, the poet Aeschylus is said to have perished, since it had been predicted that he would die by a falling object. To be careful, he stayed out in the open air that day. But an eagle, deceived by the shine of his head (which was bald and gleaming in the sun) and thinking it was a rock, dashed a tortoise against it so that it might eat the broken meat. The author is Valerius Maximus, in book nine, chapter twelve.

->I have sailed well now that I have been shipwrecked.<-
<margin>LXXVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Νῦν εὖ πεπλόηκα ὅτε νεναυάγηκα. Latin: Nunc bene nauigaui, posteaq; naufragiū feci.</note>
I have sailed well now that I have been shipwrecked. This is used whenever fortune, beyond expectation, turns what seems like an inconvenience into a benefit. Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoic philosophy (c. 334–262 BC).</note>, who left his previous teachers to become a student of Crates, is read to have said after being cast ashore in a shipwreck: "Fortune does well when she drives us toward philosophy." <note>original Greek: εὖγε ποιεῖ ἡ τύχη προσελαύνουσα ἡμᾶς φιλοσοφίᾳ.</note> The author is Suidas. Plutarch mentions this proverb in his essay *How to Profit by One's Enemies*.

->Now I have come into the territory.<-
<margin>LXXIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Νῦν εἰς χώραν ἦλθον. Latin: Nunc in regionem ueni.</note>
Now I have come into the territory. This was habitually said by those who finally reach the place where they ought to be of their own accord, after they have long been unable to do so. For it often happens that things—

<header>THE SECOND CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Ee 2</sig>

...that which was sought does not occur, until finally it comes to mind as if of its own accord. Some express it thus: *Now indeed you have come to the region* <note>original Greek: νῦν δὴ χώραν ἦλθες</note>. This is said when someone arrives at a place they previously said they would not go.

->LXXX<-
->Now comes that song of Datis.<-
*Now that famous song of Datis has come,* <note>original Greek: Νῦν τοῦτ’ ἐκεῖν’ ἥκει τὸ Δάτιδος μέλος. Latin: Nunc id quod aiunt, Datidis adest cantio.</note>
This was said when something joyful and festive had occurred. Datis was a certain Persian satrap <note>A provincial governor in the Persian Empire</note>, outstanding in military glory. When he attempted to speak Greek, he used to say: *I am delighted, and I am pleased, and I am glad.* <note>original Greek: ἥδομαι, καὶ τέρπομαι, καὶ χαίρομαι</note>. Since he pronounced these often and with poor Greek grammar <note>Datis used the middle-voice ending "-omai" for the word "glad" (chairo), which is grammatically incorrect in Greek</note>, the matter became a popular joke. The author is Suidas. It also appears in Aristophanes' play *Peace*:
*Now that famous song of Datis has come,*
*Which he, wearing his sheepskin, once sang at midday:*
*“How I am glad, and I am delighted, and I am pleased.”*
The commentator adds that a "Datism" is used to mean a barbarism <note>A grammatical error or unpolished speech</note>, because he said *chairomai* instead of *chairo*, following the sound of the other words—just as among us, someone is laughed at who says "my body" or "your house" using the wrong gender <note>original Latin: "corpus meus" and "domus tuus"</note>. For *chairomai* is not a word used by the Greeks. I wonder why the commentator joined this with a seemingly related phrase: *They asked for a bucket, but others brought a shovel.* <note>original Greek: ἅμας ἀπήτου, οἱ δ’ ἀπεκνένου σκάφας</note>. From this, one can guess that this proverb arose from ignorance of a language, which often provides material for laughter, as when Germans are eager to speak French, or the French to speak German. The same thing happens with those who are hard of hearing.

->LXXXI<-
->For not thorns.<-
*For not thorns.* <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἄκανθαι</note>. This was said regarding a condition changed for the better. The metaphor is taken from fallow lands which, once the thorns have been cleared away, begin to be fruitful. It applies well to a business that was previously fruitless and troublesome, from which profit is later obtained. Some think it originated because in ancient times, before the discovery of farming, fields were occupied by fruitless thorns, and mortals lived a harsh and rustic life. Then, once the method of cultivating the earth was shown, a milder way of life followed. And from this it began to be said: "For not thorns." This matches the interpretation we mentioned elsewhere of a boy carrying thorny branches and bread at weddings and saying: *I fled the evil, I found the better.* <note>original Greek: ἔφυγον κακόν, εὗρον ἄμεινον</note>. One also reads: *A thorny life,* <note>original Greek: βίος ἀκανθώδης</note> meaning a life that is inconvenient and fruitless.

->LXXXII<-
->I shall not be set as a lioness on a cheese-grater.<-
*I shall not be set as a lioness on a cheese-grater.* <note>original Greek: οὐ στήσομαι λέαινα ἐπὶ τυροκνήστιδος. Latin: Non ego leæna statuar in tyrocnestide.</note>
A proverb used by courtesans <note>Prostitutes or high-class companions in antiquity</note>, when a woman denies she will grant her favors. For on the hilts of military swords, elephants and lions are often placed. But these are carved lying down, either so they do not hurt the hand of the person using the sword, or so they are not easily broken off, as they might be if they were fashioned standing on their feet. "Cheese-grater" <note>tyrocnestis</note> seems to be a military word signifying a sword. The adage can also be twisted to a more modest use, as if someone, denying they will comply in all things or serve according to another's whim, should say: *I shall not be set as a lioness on a cheese-grater.* Suidas records the adage. It appears in Aristophanes' *Lysistrata*.

->LXXXIII<-
->Do not pray against the ox.<-
*Do not pray against the ox.* <note>original Greek: Μὴ τῷ βοὸς εὔχου</note>. The adage warns that one's life should not be established according to the mere wish of the mind, nor should anything be hoped for from the gods, except those things which each person can achieve through their own industry. It is mentioned in the *Collections* of Diogenianus. Where the metaphor is taken from is not entirely clear, except that it appears to be drawn from a farmer who, neglecting to use the labor of the ox in cultivating the fields, prays that a crop might come forth without his own work.

->LXXXIIII<-
->Not our burden; the ox carries the packsaddle.<-
Quintilian, in the fifth book of his *Institutes of Oratory*, brings forward this example of a proverb (which he says is like a short fable): *Not our burden; the ox carries the packsaddle.* It is well established that this is taken from a fable, but which fable it is, I have not yet found. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Letters*...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of Latin proverbs, specifically focusing on the humorous and illustrative use of metaphors in Cicero's letters and the challenges of textual corruption in early printed editions.</meta>

<page-num>604</page-num>
<header>ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

to Atticus, in the fifth book, in the letter beginning, *I arrived at Laodicea on the day before the Kalends of August* <note>original: "Laodiceam veni pridie Calendas sextiles." The Kalends of August refers to July 31st or August 1st.</note>: he seems to allude to this adage, and provides us, as it were, a handle for conjecture. Then, he says, *I was thinking of going to Taurus, so that by joining battle with Maphragones, if I could, I might settle the matter of your slave. Pack-saddles have been placed on the ox. Is it that one? It is not our burden, but we shall bear it; provided, if you love me, it is only for a year. But if you arrive in time, so as to rouse the whole senate. I am wonderfully anxious, because for a long time now everything has been unknown to me.* Likewise in the same letter a little earlier: *But it is incredible how much I am tired of the business; lest that course of my mind and industry, not unknown to you, should not have a large enough field, my excellent work sits idle. Since I am to dispense justice in Laodicea, while at Rome A. Plotius does so? And since our friend has so great an army, while I have only the name of two thin legions? Finally, I do not miss these things. The light, the forum, the city, home, and you all I miss. But I will bear it as I can, provided it be only for a year. If it is extended, it is all over.* Thus far Tully <note>A common nickname for Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note>. From these words indeed, although somewhat obscure, and I know not whether even faulty, one can catch the scent that *Not our burden, the ox [carries] pack-saddles* was a proverb for one refusing some duty as being poorly suited to himself. For it is not the nature of oxen to carry burdens with pack-saddles placed on their backs, but rather of donkeys and mules. Nor is it to be doubted that Fabius <note>Referring to the Roman rhetorician Quintilian.</note> borrowed that example from this passage of Cicero. Raphael Regius, who attempted to correct Fabius by adding scholia <note>Explanatory notes or comments.</note>, changes the writing in this way: *To us our burden, to you the pack-saddles,* interpreting this to mean that neither side would depart without a burden. To me, if it is permissible to change anything, it seems it should rather be read thus: *Is it not our burden, the ox [carrying] pack-saddles?* So that it is as if one were abominating an absurd thing, and one unworthy of itself: if someone should wish to place pack-saddles on an ox. Nor does this disagree with the sense of Tully's words, which we have just related. For he says that province is not suitable enough, or worthy of his talent, yet he will bear it however he can, provided it is not longer than a year. Hence the proverb can be uttered in a double form: *Pack-saddles have been placed on the ox,* when a business has been entrusted to someone poorly suited for it. And, *the ox [carrying] pack-saddles:* so that you may understand, *let him bear it.* Where someone prays to be excused from a province for which he is not suitable enough, or which he considers unbecoming to himself. In passing, I would wish to warn the reader not to immediately erase or strike through if he sees something in these things which we cite from authors that does not correspond to the emendation of certain people. Not that we profess everything we bring here to be purged of errors, but because even those who correct books often slip: as in this passage, which we just related from the *Letters*, in the Aldine edition <note>The famous printing press of Aldus Manutius in Venice.</note>, I know not by whose work—I will not say fault—so many words are changed? For it ought not be imputed to Aldus, both because he is learned, and because he is a friend. For first, who does not see it is more correct to say *opera cesset* <note>let work cease (singular)</note> than *opera cessent* <note>let works cease (plural)</note>? Then in what follows, to whom is it not clear that it is corrupted, both by the punctuation and by the word *exilium* <note>thin/meager</note> being changed into *exulum* <note>of exiles</note>? For thus he reads: *And why our friend has an army, while I have only the name of two legions of exiles?* When Tully placed *tantum* <note>only/so much</note> for "great," to which he opposed *exiles* legions, that is, tiny ones. And a little after: *So that with Maphragones, with signs joined, if I could, I might decree concerning your slave.* What was the reason that instead of *deciderem* <note>to settle/decide</note> it was changed to *decernerem* <note>to decree/fight</note>? As if that were not a much more elegant word. For if you read *decidere*, the word *certare* <note>to struggle</note> or *congredi* <note>to meet/clash</note> must be understood (of which kind of eclipses <note>Omissions of words in a sentence.</note> Cicero is most fond, especially in this work) so that you read: *So that with Maphragones, with signs joined:* and you understand, *I might clash.* Again, that which follows: *Pack-saddles are placed on the ox. Is it that one? Not our burden.* Some consensus, I know not by what silence <note>aposiopesis: a rhetorical device where a sentence is left unfinished.</note>, changed it to: *Those, it is not our burden.* Which again happened in what is added below: *But if you in time,* understand, *should be present.* For he changed it to: *But may you be present in time,* with the Latinity also corrupted, not to mention the sharpness of the meaning. I have warned of these things unwillingly and under compulsion, lest some, as there are a few, headlong as they are, should immediately condemn or erase because of the celebrity of the Aldine name if they catch something disagreeing with that edition, nor should they immediately throw away earlier manuscripts relying on emendations of this kind. Ammianus also used the proverb in his sixteenth book.

->LXXXI<-

---

->A known evil is best.<-

That line of Plautus in the *Trinummus* seems spoken in a proverbial pattern: *A known evil is best.* <note>original: "Nota res mala, optima est."</note> It was spoken, moreover, in the persona of an old man, attempting to persuade a friend not to divorce a wife, even though she was bad, in order to marry another: for the reason that it often happens that he who makes a change receives a worse one for the bad one, then an unknown for a known, and finally an unfamiliar for a familiar. For habit has so much power that the evils to which we have become accustomed seem best. Against which...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of proverbs concerning habit, change, and the necessity of hard work, drawing from classical comedy, philosophy, and mythology.</meta>

<page-num>605</page-num>
<header>THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE SECOND CHILIAD</header>
<sig>Ee 3</sig>

...the best, though because of its novelty it might seem the worst. Therefore, the adage deters us from rashly desiring to revolutionize things, and warns us to avoid that vice—which I suspect is the greatest of all—which the Greeks call <term>philokainon</term> <note>original: "φιλοκαινὸν", meaning a love of novelty or change</note>, that is, a craving for new things. This is accompanied by its twin, as if born from the same womb, which they call <term>apsikoron</term> <note>original: "ἀψίκορον", meaning "quickly sated" or fastidious</note>, because things loved just a moment ago are soon loathed. This agrees with a sentiment from Plautus, which Pacuvius Calavius used in Titus Livy’s history when persuading the Campanians not to change their senators; he compelled the people, once they had learned the truth, to say: "The most familiar evil is the most tolerable." To this also pertains that line from Ovid:

> Accustom yourself to what you bear poorly, and you will bear it well: <margin>Softens.</margin> long duration softens many things.

To the same effect is that mime-writer’s verse—I know not whose it is:

> A woman is only good when she is openly bad.

For once an evil is known, we either avoid it or we endure it by adapting ourselves to it. Likewise: "We endure customary vices; we do not rebuke them." Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, says: <term>for a living creature is always in labor, just as the natural philosophers testify, claiming that seeing and hearing are painful, but we have already become accustomed to them, as they say.</term> <note>original: "ἀεὶ γὰρ πονεῖ τὸ ζῶον... ὥσπερ καὶ οἱ φυσικοὶ λόγοι μαρτυρῶσι..."</note> That is: A living being is always exerting effort to hear and see, as the natural discourses testify when they admit it is indeed troublesome, but we have grown used to it, as the saying goes.

### I found it, but not what boys find in a bean. LXXXVI

Strophylus, the slave in Plautus’s comedy *Aulularia*, had stolen a pot full of gold that had been buried by an old man. Eager to signal this to his master, he says: "I found it!" When asked what he had found, he replies: "Not what boys keep shouting they have found in a bean." He uses this proverbial figure to signify that he has found something truly great. For there is a certain little worm called a "midas" that is born in beans; whenever boys catch one, they get excited and shout as if they had found something of great value.

### Midas is the best advisor at the dice. LXXXVII

<term>Midas who is most lucky at the throw in dice.</term> <note>original: "Μίδας ὁ ἐν κύβοισιν εὐβολώτατος."</note> That is:
Midas, who at the dice-table, is the best counselor.
The proverb arose from the game of dice. For "Midas" was the name of a specific throw. It is recorded by Suidas as a proverb. Let the diligent and learned reader consider whether it should be read as <term>eubolotatos</term> <note>meaning "lucky at throwing"</note> so that the verse becomes an iambic trimeter:
<term>For Midas is the most lucky at the throw in dice.</term> <note>original: "Μίδας γὰρ ἐν κύβοισιν εὐβολώτατος."</note> That is:
In dice, the Midas-throw is the most prosperous.
The adage can be applied to a matter that, by a stroke of luck, turns out well.

### Unless you clean and grind, you shall not eat. LXXXVIII

<term>If you do not clean and grind, you shall not eat.</term> <note>original: "Ἂν μὴ καθαρῇς καὶ ἀλέσῃς, οὐ μὴ φάγῃς."</note> That is:
Unless you both clean it and grind it, you will never eat.
That is, you will not obtain a living unless you apply your own industry to the task. When Ceres was showing the use of grain to Triptolemus <note>Triptolemus was the mythical figure who spread the knowledge of agriculture to humanity.</note>, she is said to have spoken thus. It appears to be a six-foot verse borrowed from some poet, but corrupted; it will be restored if you read <term>kalēsēs</term> <note>a contraction meaning "and grind"</note>. It can be applied more broadly: "Natural talent will not benefit you unless you exercise it." "The favor of princes will be useless unless you conduct yourself as you ought." "It will do you no good to have found a learned teacher unless you stay awake and study." It is recorded by Diogenianus.

### You differ in nothing from Chaerephon. LXXXIX

<term>In your nature, you will differ in nothing from Chaerephon.</term> <note>original: "Οὐδὲν διοίσεις χαιρεφῶντος τὴν φύσιν."</note> That is:
In your appearance, you do not differ at all from Chaerephon.
This used to be said of someone who was emaciated and pale. For Chaerephon was a writer of tragedies <note>Chaerephon is more famous as the pale, thin friend of Socrates; Erasmus here identifies him as a tragedian.</note>. He wrote about the history of the Heraclidae. Because he was excessively thinned and worn out by working late into the night, he was mocked with this common joke. Indeed, the nickname "the Owl" was even given to him. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
<term>In your nature, you will differ in nothing from Chaerephon.</term> <note>original: "οὐδὲν διοίσεις χαιρεφῶντος τὴν φύσιν."</note> That is:
In your shape, you will be no different from Chaerephon. He alluded to the same in *Plutus*:
<term>Differing not at all</term>
<term>From the Heraclidae whom Pamphilus painted.</term> <note>original: "οὐδὲν διοίσοντ’ ἀντικρὺς τῶν ἡρακλειδῶν, οὓς ἔπηξε τῶν παμφίλου."</note> That is:
Not even by a little bit
Differing from the Heraclidae of Pamphilus.
For Pamphilus had painted in the Stoa <note>The Painted Stoa in Athens.</note> the Heraclidae as suppliants to the Athenians, to whom they had fled for fear of Eurystheus. He calls them, therefore, the "Heraclidae of Pamphilus."
