<page-num>606</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM: ADAGES</header>

### You differ in no way from an elephant.
<margin>XC</margin>

<note>original: "Ἐλέφαντος διαφέρεις οὐδέν"</note>, that is, *You differ in nothing from an elephant.* This was said of those who were large and stupid. Even though Pliny attributes the highest intelligence to elephants, he does so only among the "brute" beasts. Truly, it was the massive bulk of the body and the ugliness of its form that gave rise to the adage. It is recorded by Diogenianus. Palaestrio, a character in the plays of Plautus, seems to allude to this when he says his master is "wrapped in the hide of an elephant" and possesses no more wisdom than a stone.

### Not even within the entrance-hall.
<margin>XCI</margin>

<note>original: "Οὐδ' ἐντὸς ἰωρᾶ"</note>, that is, *Not even within the vestibule.* This was commonly said of the haughty, the fierce, and the insolent, who keep everyone at a distance from themselves. There was a law in Athens that those polluted by the crime of homicide should stand outside the sacred boundaries. Since the front halls of the great are usually open to anyone, the adage seems to allude to this custom of exclusion.

### Neither with evils, nor without evils.
<margin>XCII</margin>

Aristophanes, as quoted in Suidas’s entry on the play *Lysistrata*:
<note>original: "Κἄστ' ἐκεῖνο τ' ἔπος ὀρθῶς καὶ κακῶς εἰρημένον, / Οὔτε σὺν πανωλέθροισιν, οὔτ' ἄνευ πανωλέθρων."</note> 
Which means: 
*That proverb was delivered not badly, but indeed correctly:*
*Neither with these pests, nor again without these pests.*
This was said regarding wives, with whom life is certainly lived uncomfortably; yet without them, a household cannot be maintained. It is similar to that line in the *Epigrams*:
*I can neither live with you, nor without you.*
And to the phrase we have recorded elsewhere, <term>necessary evils</term> <note>original: "ἀναγκαῖα κακά"</note>. In the same place, these verses are also cited:
<note>original: "Κακὸν γυναῖκας, ἀλλ' ὅμως ὦ δημότῃ / Οὐκ ἔστιν εὑρᾶιν οἰκίαν ἄνευ κακῶ."</note>
Which means:
*A wife is indeed an evil, yet, fellow citizens, without this*
*Evil, no man is permitted to produce a family.*
That saying of Cato is well known: that life with wives is lived uncomfortably, but without them, life cannot be lived at all.

### Not even in the skin.
<margin>XCIII</margin>

<note>original: "Οὐδ' ἐν δέρματι"</note>, that is, *Not even in the skin.* A proverbial hyperbole used for those who are excessively thin, as if they were so bare that they are not even covered by their own skin. It is mentioned by Suidas.

### You don’t even know the three of Stesichorus.
<margin>XCIIII</margin>

<note>original: "Οὔτε τὰ τρία στησιχόρῳ γινώσκεις"</note>, that is, *You don’t even know the three things of Stesichorus.* This was traditionally said of someone who was profoundly unlearned and ignorant. They believe the adage is taken from the fact that most of the poems of Stesichorus are <term>epodic</term> <note>original: "Epodica"</note>, consisting of three parts: the <term>strophe</term>, the <term>antistrophe</term>, and the <term>epode</term>. The *strophe* is the first sequence, proceeding through various types of meters. The *antistrophe* is the return, repeated through roughly the same types. The *epode* is the concluding strain in a different meter. Other tragic poets also use these occasionally, especially in their choruses.

### Sober wood.
<margin>XCV</margin>

<note>original: "Νηφάλια ξύλα"</note>, that is, *Nephalia* or *Sober wood.* It seems this could be said of those who abstain from wine and are far removed from all pleasure. Among the Athenians, "sober woods" were those that came from neither the vine, nor the fig tree, nor the myrtle. *Nephalia* sounds just as if you were to say "sober."

### A sober sacrifice.
<margin>XCVI</margin>

<note>original: "Νηφάλιος θυσία"</note>, that is, *A sober sacrifice.* This might be aptly said of an abstemious banquet, or one that is intensely frugal and sober. Among the Athenians, this type of sacrifice was offered to Memory, the Dawn, the Sun, the Moon, the Nymphs, Venus, and Urania. For in these rites, wine was not offered as a libation, but rather water diluted with honey. This is generally what Suidas says. Julius Pollux also mentions it in book six, chapter three, adding that "to perform sober rites" is the same as "to sacrifice soberly." They called this type of sacrifice <term>wineless</term> <note>original: "ἄοινον"</note>, just as they called the others in which wine was used <term>wine-poured</term> <note>original: "οἰνόσπονδα"</note>. Seleucus, in the second book of Athenaeus, denies that it was the custom among the ancients to bring a mountain of wine or any other luxury into sacrifices. For since sacrifices were carried out for the sake of the gods (which is why they called them <term>feasts</term>, <term>festivities</term>, and <term>drinking-bouts</term>—"feasts" because they used wine for the sake of the gods, "festivities" because they ate for the sake of the gods, and "revelries" because, as Aristotle indicated, they used wine *after the sacrifice*), it was not fitting—

<meta>Catchword: [conue]niebat (it was fitting)</meta>

<header>SECOND CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY</header>

it was fitting to conduct your business there. In that same place, Epicharmus notes the collapse of morals with these words: <note>original: "ἐκ μὲν θυσίας θοίνη, ἐκ δὲ θοίνης πόσις ἐγένετο, ἐκ δὲ πόσεως κῶμος, ἐκ κώμου δ’ ἐγγένετο θυανία, ἐκ θυανίας δίκη, ἐκ δὲ καταδίκης πέδαι, καὶ σφάκελος καὶ ζημία"</note>, that is: from sacrifice comes a feast; from a feast comes drinking; from drinking comes revelry; from revelry comes wantonness or sport; from wantonness or sport comes a lawsuit; from a lawsuit comes condemnation; from condemnation come shackles, gangrene, and a fine. However, this passage seems suspicious to me of an error. For the small phrase "from a lawsuit comes condemnation" seems to be missing in the sequence. It does not differ much from what we have placed in another location: *A dog's dinner.*

## In neglected fields, the fern grows, only fit for burning. XCVII

Horace in his third Satire:
> In neglected fields, the fern grows, only fit for burning.
<note>original: "Neglectis urenda filix innascitur agris."</note>

He provides a wonderful allegory: the mind must be cultivated with honorable disciplines; otherwise, it will happen that it is occupied by a useless forest of vices. For the fern is a plant hated by farmers, which tends to take over entire fields and is not easily cleared away once it has taken root.

## To look like a fleet. XCVIII

<note>original: "Ναύφρακτον βλέπεις"</note>. *Nauphracton* in Greek is a fleet equipped for war. Moreover, in triremes there are usually certain large openings like eyes, through which they insert the oars. Hence it was said somewhat enigmatically, "You look in the manner of a fleet," regarding those who look at someone with wide and very large, or grim and threatening eyes. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*:
<note>original: "πρὸς τῶν θεῶν ἄνθρωπε ναύφρακτον βλέπεις"</note>, that is,
"By the gods, man, you have a certain look of a fleet."
Perhaps the humor of the proverb was born from the fact that the Athenians several times conducted themselves successfully in naval combat, such as at Artemisium and Salamis, which lifted their spirits. Thus it seems to be said of the swollen and arrogant.

## Business out of leisure. XCIX

<note>original: "πράγματ’ ἐξ ἀπραξίας"</note>, that is,
*Business out of leisure.*
This iambic half-line is to be used when a matter turns out contrary to expectation, and a tumult arises from where we hoped for tranquility and leisure. For it happens to many that while they seek leisure and flee from honest industry, they fall into inextricable disturbances. The author is Suidas, though he does not indicate where it originated.

## A ship or a cap. C

<note>original: "πλοῖον ἢ κυνῆ"</note>, that is, *A ship or a cap.* Concerning an ambiguous matter. This is the kind of thing someone might say about an unknown word: "It signifies either a fish or a pumpkin." Nor would it be inappropriately said against those who present a persona different in their dress and behavior. For example, if someone were to add a military belt to a philosopher's cloak, or act like a monk in dress but a pimp in behavior and speech. It is a fragment of a six-foot line from Aristophanes' *Birds*: <note>original: "πλοῖον ἢ κυνῆ"</note>, that is, *Either a cap or a raft.* It is taken from this type of trireme, which today they commonly call *galeas* <note>galleys</note>, as if you were to say "capped ships." These were equipped so that they extended and moved oars in the place of wings. Furthermore, at the top of the mast they displayed a cap, or a traveling hat like that of Mercury. For the Peloponnesians call a traveling hat <note>original: "πέτασον"</note> a *kyne* <note>original: "κυνῆν"</note>, from "dog" <note>original: "ἀπὸ κυνός"</note>, because this type of hat was first accustomed to be made from the skins of dogs. From this, a military joke seems to have been born against the elated and haughty, and those with an arrogant brow. Likewise, Festus Pompeius indicates that certain merchant ships were called *Corbitae* because they had a basket <note>original: "Corbem"</note> at the top of the mast as a sign. Those which were prepared for war had "helmets" <note>galeas</note>; those built for speed carried the sign of Mercury’s hat.

# SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

## He kneaded the barley-cake that I had mixed. I

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'A' containing a small woodcut illustration of two figures in a domestic or outdoor setting.</image-desc>

<note>original: "Ἄλλων γε μεμαχὼς τὴν ὑπ᾿ ἐμοῦ μεμαγμένην"</note>, that is,
*That man kneaded the barley-cake previously mixed by me.*
This was commonly said of those who claim for themselves the praise of another's industry, and who, as Terence's Gnatho says, transfer to themselves through words the great glory earned by another's labor. *Maza* is a type of food made from milk and flour, prepared much like bread. The proverb is also cited in this way: <note>original: "Μάζαν ὑφερπάσας τὴν ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ μεμαγμένην"</note>, that is, *Having snatched away*

<margin>Ee 4</margin>
<meta>The catchword "pta" completes the word "subrepta" (snatched away) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Erasmus discusses proverbs regarding the necessity of mental cultivation to avoid vice, the origins of naval metaphors for arrogance, and the frustration of having one's work or credit stolen by others.</summary>
<keywords>Horace, Aristophanes, naval metaphors, arrogance, leisure and trouble, plagiarism, maza, Epicharmus, moral decline</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of adages derived from Greek comedy, specifically concluding an entry on taking credit for another's work before moving into puns on names, social indifference, and insults involving insects.</meta>

...the barley cake which I had kneaded. <note>original: "pinfueram... maza". The text is completing the adage "To snatch the maza I kneaded," referring to someone stealing the fruits of another's labor.</note> This is said when someone enjoys the labors of others. It is taken from Aristophanes’ *The Knights*, in a passage where the verse is as follows:

> And just recently, when I 
> Had kneaded a Laconian barley cake at Pylos, 
> This most meddlesome fellow, somehow running around and snatching it away, 
> Served it up himself—the very one I had kneaded— 
> And now he drives us away. 

That is: 

> Since I myself had long ago kneaded the barley cake in Pylos,
> That fellow ran up most craftily,
> And having snatched it, he soon served what I had kneaded, 
> While he pushes us aside.

Demosthenes was the general of the Athenians during the Peloponnesian War; he, along with his colleague Nicias, brought the city of Pylos to the brink of despair in all things through a long siege. He was succeeded by Cleon, a general who was a leather-tanner by trade, who transferred the glory won by another's labor to himself when Pylos was captured a few days later. Therefore, in this play, Nicias and Demosthenes complain about the praise snatched from them by Cleon. The history of Aristophanes is told not only in various ways but also so at length that I do not care to repeat it. I have indicated where it may be sought.

### Shipson to Shipmaster.

<note>original: "Ναύσων ναυκράτῃ" (Nauson Naukrate)</note>. That is, Shipson to Shipmaster. This is used whenever people respond to each other with similar terms. For example, if a master, being greeted, should greet a master in return; or if a rogue, being addressed, should address a rogue in turn. For both "Shipson" and "Shipmaster" are derived from "ship" <note>original: "navis"</note>. It is just as if you were to say "Sailor to Sailor." Hesychius indicates that this expression was fashioned by Cratinus: "Shipson" <note>original: "Nauson"</note> from "saving ships" <note>original: "feruandis nauibus"</note>, and "Shipmaster" <note>original: "Naukrates"</note> from "ship" <note>original: "naus"</note> and "to rule" <note>original: "kratein"</note>. The tone of the speech is taken from letters, as Suidas indicates, just as if you were to say, "Popeius sends greetings to Popilius," or "A youth calls upon a youth." Of this same form are those phrases, "little balls of thread" <note>original: "ἀγαθίδες"</note>, and "a wolf more wolfish than a wolf" <note>original: "λύκων@ λυκώτερ@"</note>. Aristophanes hints at something similar, if I am not mistaken, in *The Knights*: "Neither Ship-shiner nor Shipson," so that the word "man" is understood. However, I believe that in the proverb "Shipson" is not the name of a man, but of a city, just as "Naukratis" is a city in Egypt.

### Bring, bring the barley cake as quickly as possible for the beetle.

> Bring, bring the barley cake as quickly as possible for the beetle. 
> That is: 
> Serve, serve the barley cake without delay to the dung beetle.

With this little verse, Aristophanes begins his play <term>Peace</term> <note>original: "εἰρήνην" (Eirēnēn)</note>, which scholars record as a proverb. It may be used whenever foul food is served to a filthy dinner guest. Some people serve bran-bread to their servants, and bran is the refuse of wheat. Hence, he implies a "thoroughly-bran" <term>maza</term> <note>barley cake</note>—food returned from the belly. For from this source, beetles—which the Latins call *scarabaei*—are born and nourished. He makes this clear when he adds: "Give another barley cake, and on top of it one molded from the dung of an ass." Furthermore, the *maza* was a certain preparation made of flour and milk, imitating bread. It is very similar to what we have placed in another location: "A snack for a Cypriot ox" <note>A reference to another adage about feeding something low-quality to an animal that eats filth.</note>.

### It is not my business; let it be gone.

> It is not my business; let it bid many a farewell. 
> That is: 
> Let it be gone; it is not my concern.

We use this whenever we deny that we are troubled by a matter that does not pertain to us. He takes this from Diogenianus. It is not unlike that saying: "Whatever is done in our house, whether wrong or right." Also that which is found in Aristophanes’ *The Knights*: "Reaping another's harvest." Some adapt it to the same meaning, even if the comic poet meant it for one who enjoys the fruits of another’s labor. More closely related to this is what Pindar writes in the first *Nemean Ode*: "For that which is one's own presses upon everyone alike, but the heart is immediately free from pain regarding the trouble of another." That is: For what is one's own weighs upon each person equally. However, the heart is instantly free from distress concerning the grief of another.

### A loathsome beetle.

<note>original: "μύση κανθαρίς" (myse kantharis)</note>. That is: A loathsome beetle. This was said of a most contemptible and vile little man. *Cantharides* are little worms with a lethal poison. Although in this place it is spoken more of...

<keywords>Aristophanes, Cleon, Pylos, Maza, Barley cake, Puns, Pindar, Social indifference, Beetles, Greek Comedy, Peloponnesian War</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Roman adages, specifically those dealing with metaphors of insignificance (insects), the frustration of speaking to fools, and the irony of experts feigning ignorance.</meta>

...it comes from the word for a beetle, serving as a diminutive form: as if you were to say "little beetle." <note>original: "scarabeolus"</note> In the Sacred Scriptures as well, the "worm" has become a proverb for something held in contempt. This is the case in the mystical Psalms: *But I am a worm and no man.* <note>original: "Ego autem sum uermis & no homo" (Psalm 22:6)</note> For this, some translate the word as "beetle." <note>original: "scarabeum"</note> There is also that passage in Isaiah: *Fear not, thou worm Jacob,* according to the translation of Jerome. In the works of Suidas, <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia, often cited by Erasmus.</note> one reads the phrase *mice beetles*. <note>original: "μυσὶ κανθαρίς" (mysi kantharis)</note> I do not know what this is intended to mean; I suspect there is a mistake in the manuscript. If we read it as *abominable*, <note>original: "μυσὴ" (mysē)</note> it sounds like "hateful things"; if we read it as *Mysian*, <note>original: "μυσὸν" (myson)</note> it sounds like a "Mysian beetle." We have explained elsewhere that the Mysians were once a people held in great contempt. This interpretation is the one I find most convincing.

### VI
->It is troublesome for a wise man to speak among fools.<-
*To speak much among the foolish is a heavy burden for the wise.* <note>original: "Ἀργαλέον φρονέοντα παρ’ ἄφροσι πόλλ’ ἀγορεύειν"</note>
Nothing is more difficult to deal with than a foolish person, who twists whatever is said correctly into a different meaning. Therefore, among such people, a man of sense must either remain silent or adapt his speech to their manners. This is recorded by Diogenianus, but the same sentiment appears among the maxims of the poet Theognis.

### VII
->I shall measure it out by the bushel.<-
*I measure by the medimnos.* <note>original: "Μεδίμνῳ ἀμετρῶ". The medimnos was a Greek dry measure, roughly equivalent to a Roman modius or a large bushel.</note> This is a proverbial hyperbole, used by someone hoping for a massive and heaped-up profit. Indeed, in a great abundance of things, we do not measure by half-pints or quarts, but by the bushel. Suidas renders the full phrase as:
*I shall measure my father's money by the bushel.* <note>original: "Μεδίμνῳ ἀμετρῶ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀργύριον"</note>
However, there are some who deny that the Latin *modius* and the Greek *medimnos* are the same size.

### VIII
->There is no mind in Centaurs.<-
*Mind is not in Centaurs.* <note>original: "νοῦς οὐκ ἔνι κενταύροισιν"</note> This was said of the senseless and the stupid, and of those who attempt what cannot be achieved. The myth of the Centaurs <note>Mythical creatures with the upper body of a human and the lower body of a horse, often portrayed as wild and lawless.</note> is well known. The adage is cited by Diogenianus, who thinks it applies to contentious people and those who crave what belongs to others, because it was a greed for others' property that brought destruction upon the Centaurs. I wonder if the poet Plato <note>A writer of Old Comedy, not the famous philosopher.</note> had this in mind in the tenth book of Athenaeus:
> For it does not seem to me, as the proverb goes,
> That there is any mind in you,
> Just as there is no mind in an innkeeper.
<note>original: "Ὑμῖν γὰρ οὐδ’ ὡς καθάπερ ἡ παροιμία, / Ἐν ταῖς καπήλων νοῦς ἐνεῖναί μοι δοκεῖ"</note>
He is speaking about women who are fond of wine. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*: *There is no mind in the manes.* <note>original: "νοῦς οὐκ ἔνι ταῖς κόμαις"</note> He used "manes" <note>hair or manes of a horse</note> instead of "Centaurs," while punning on the hobby of breeding horses, which have manes.

### IX
->You anoint yourself with honey.<-
*You roll and smear yourself in honey.* <note>original: "Ἐν μέλιτι σαυτὸν καταπάττεις"</note> That is, you lead a soft and sweet life, as if it were not enough to eat honey unless you were entirely covered in it. It is found in Diogenianus.

### X
->An infant Mercury.<-
*An unspeaking Mercury.* <note>original: "Ἑρμῆς ἀμύθητος" (Hermēs amythētos)</note> This means a speechless or unlearned Mercury. It is a proverbial irony used when someone pretends to be ignorant of an art in which they are actually most skilled. For Mercury is the god of eloquence and learning. I should not hide the fact that in common copies the reading is *An uninitiated Mercury.* <note>original: "Ἑρμῆς ἀμύητος" (Hermēs amyētos)</note> If that reading pleases anyone more, it does not greatly displease me either. For who is more skilled in mysteries than Mercury, the interpreter of the gods, who is equally shared by those above and those below? He is, after all, the *mystagogue* <note>original: "μυσταγωγὸς"</note> himself—that is, the one in charge of the mysteries. It corresponds to the phrase found in Aristides’ speech on Pericles: *A Cretan at sea.* <note>A proverb for someone in their natural element but acting as if they are not.</note>

### XI
->Beggars' purses are always empty.<-
*The pouches of beggars are always empty.* <note>original: "Πτωχῶν ὄλαι ἀεὶ κεναί"</note> Said of the greedy and the insatiable. It is related to another adage: *A beggar's bag is never filled.* <note>original: "πτωχῶ πήρα οὐ πίμπλαται"</note> Suidas records both, although I do not find the word *olai* used for bags; I do find *oladas* used for flour vessels, though sometimes bellies are signified by that word because of their softness.

### XII
->A Melian ship.<-
*The Melian vessel.* <note>original: "Τὸ Μηλιακὸν πλοῖον"</note> Said of something futile and, as Terence says, full of holes—

<meta>catchword: full,</meta>

<summary>This page catalogs adages related to social conduct and irony, including the folly of speaking to the ignorant, metaphors for extreme wealth and luxury, and the ironic "Infant Mercury" used for experts feigning ignorance.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Centaurs, Mercury, metaphors for wealth, greed, irony, Greek comedy, ancient measures, Suidas, Diogenianus</keywords>

--- Page 732 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of adages derived from geography and mythology, specifically focusing on the city of Melia and the figure of Melanion. It transitions from the previous discussion on "Meliacus" (from Melos or Melia) into adages about chastity, illegitimacy, and seniority.</meta>

...full, and because it leaks this way and that, the saying seems to be frequently used. They refer the proverb to a certain history. It goes like this: a certain Aristotle of Melia, who was appointed as the leader for leading a colony, when many were refusing the voyage and making various excuses—some saying their wives were held back by ill health, others that their ships were leaking—and remained at home under these pretexts, he was indignant and called down a curse upon them: that they should never have sound ships and should always live under the rule of their wives. From this, it seems applicable whenever someone invents excuses to flee from their duty. Moreover, Melia is a city of Caria, according to Stephanus. Suidas indicates that *Melia* is also a type of ash tree, offering an example from the *Birds* of Aristophanes:
> Sitting upon the leafy ash tree. <note>original: "Ἐζόμενος μελίας ἐπὶ φυλλακόμος" (Ezomenos melias epi phyllakomos)</note>
-> that is, <-
> Residing in the leafy ash.

And perhaps the wood of this tree is useless for the construction of ships. Truly, even if the story about the people of Melia is true, there is certainly an allusion to the tree.

<margin>XIII</margin>
### More chaste than Melanion.
*More chaste than Melanion.* <note>original: "Μελανίωνος σωφρονέστερος" (Melaniōnos sōphronesteros)</note> It used to be said of one who greatly abhorred the company of women. They say that a certain Melanion, out of a hatred for women, departed into solitude: and through the pathless tracks of mountains and groves, he was accustomed to hunt wild beasts with a dog, who was his only companion, and he could never be called back home. Aristophanes mentions the adage in *Lysistrata*. Although this is not yet held among the published versions, we have read it in manuscript. It is said with a similar figure of speech, *More chaste than Hippolytus*: for he had a similar passion for hunting and a similar hatred of women.

<margin>XIIII</margin>
### Called his mother’s, like a goat.
*Called his mother’s, like a goat.* <note>original: "Τῆς μητρὸς ὡς αἴξ καλεῖται" (Tēs mētros hōs aix kaleitai)</note> It seems to have been said of illegitimate children whose father is uncertain, and for that reason, they are named after the mother. It is drawn from kids, who are distinguished among goats by their mother; for you could not possibly do so by the fathers. The proverb can also be turned into a joke, as if someone should playfully deny that he recognizes his father, but knows his mother: *I am called my mother’s, just like a goat.* <note>original: "ᾗ μητρὸς ὡς αἴξ καλεῖται" (hē mētros hōs aix kaleitai)</note> Even today a common joke remains, by which they say, "He is a wise son who knows his own father." This seems to have flowed from Homer, in whom, in the first book of the *Odyssey*, Telemachus, being asked whether he was the son of Ulysses, responds in this manner:
> My mother indeed says that I am his, but as for me,
> I do not know; for no one yet has known his own parentage. <note>original: "Μήτηρ μέν τ' ἐμέ φησι τοῦ ἔμμεναι, αὐτὰρ ἔγωγε / οὐκ οἶδ', οὐ γάρ πω τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω" (Mētēr men t' eme phēsi tou emmenai, autar egōge / ouk oid', ou gar pō tis heon gonon autos anegnō)</note>
-> that is, <-
> My mother says I am his, but truly
> I do not know; no man ever knew his own father.

<margin>X</margin>
### Like a place in the baths.
This has the appearance of a proverb, which is found in Tertullian’s third book *Against Marcion*. "But because he came to them first, and first marked out the proofs of virtues, therefore, just like a place in the baths, he occupied the faith and forestalled all those who came after." It will be suitable to use when a place is given not out of merit, but out of seniority. Indeed, this order is preserved even today among monks and Canons, and likewise among Theologians, doubtless to exclude contention regarding dignity. Among the ancients, everyone was estimated by the number of their years. Juvenal says:
> And he yields to Homer alone
> On account of a thousand years.

And Horace is annoyed with those who return to the annals and estimate virtue by years. Nor is it far removed from what is commonly tossed about today among our own people, taken from the law of the mill: *He who comes first, mills first.* <note>original: "Qui primus uenerit, primus molet"</note>

<margin>XI</margin>
### To carve millet on a lathe.
*To carve millet grains on a lathe.* <note>original: "τὰς κέγχρους ἀποτορεύειν" (tas kenchrous apotoreuein)</note> They were said to do this who attempt an absurd thing. For millet is too small for anything to be carved out of it. Suidas sets forth the proverb in this way: *You are acting more ridiculously than those who attempt to polish millet grains on a lathe.* <note>original: "γελοιότερον ἀπεργάζῃ, τῶν τὰς κέγχρους ἀποτορεύειν ἐπιχειρούντων" (geloioteron apergazē, tōn tas kenchrous apotoreuein epicheirountōn)</note>

<margin>XV</margin>
### Evils of the Magnesians.
*Evils of the Magnesians.* <note>original: "μαγνήτων κακά" (magnētōn kaka)</note> It seems to have been said of immense evils, or those which recoil upon their own authors. For the "Evils of the Magnesians" are joined with "Termerian evils" in these words, which are cited without the author’s name in Suidas: *Not even if I speak of the evils of the Magnesians, nor the Termerian evil, nor simply the whole tragedy.* <note>original: "κἄν τὰ μαγνήτων κακὰ, κἄν τὸ τερμέριον, κἄν πᾶσαν ἁπλῶς ἐκφθέγξωμαι τὴν τραγῳδίαν" (kan ta magnētōn kaka, kan to termerion, kan pasan haplōs ekphthengxōmai tēn tragōdian)</note> Although in Suidas one should read...

# SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

<margin>Riddles, or the evils of the Termerians.</margin> <note>original: "Γρίποι, τὰ Τερμερίων" (Gripoi, ta Termeriōn)</note> That is, the "evils of the Termerians," which we have discussed elsewhere. It appears to be taken from a history that mentions the afflicted people of Magnesia, who were said to have fallen into these troubles because they had violated some deity. Strabo, in the fourteenth book of his *Geography*, records that the people of Magnesia, once flourishing in wealth, were utterly destroyed by the Treres, a Cimmerian tribe. In the following year, the site was occupied by the Milesians. He hints that the proverb was taken from the poet Archilochus, who made mention of the "evils of the Magnetes." <note>The "evils of the Magnetes" refers to the total destruction of the city of Magnesia on the Maeander, used to describe sudden and complete ruin.</note>

->Many are the beds of a male dog.<-
->XVIII<-

<margin>Many are the beds of a male dog.</margin> <note>original: "Πολλαὶ κυνὸς ἀρσενοῦ εὐναί" (Pollai kynos arsenou eunai)</note> That is:
The beds of a male dog are infinite in number.
This is a proverbial hexameter line. It is rightly said of a man who is a womanizer, specifically one who is not content with a fixed marriage bed but takes pleasure in wallowing in the beds of others everywhere. For husbands in this day and age allow themselves this license. Furthermore, if anything of human frailty <note>A euphemism for death or an extramarital slip.</note> should happen to the wife, they throw heaven and earth into confusion—being as unfairly severe toward their wives as they are shamefully indulgent toward themselves.

->Many things in war are empty.<-
->XIX<-

<margin>Many empty things of war.</margin> <note>original: "Πολλὰ κενὰ τοῦ πολέμου" (Polla kena tou polemou)</note> That is, many things in war are hollow. This refers to groundless suspicion or a fear arising without cause, which the Greeks call <term>panic</term> <note>original: "πανικὸν" (panikon); referring to the god Pan, who was thought to cause sudden, irrational fear in crowds or armies.</note>. They believe this proverb arose because these types of "panic" terrors are usually accustomed to happen in wars. Or, it may be because the Spartans used to use certain slings and rattling strings to strike terror into the enemy. Polybius, as cited in Suidas, notes that when the moon suffered an eclipse during the time of Perseus, King of the Macedonians, a rumor spread among the common people that it signified the king’s downfall. This event simultaneously encouraged the Romans and terrified the Macedonians. Then, adding the adage, Polybius says, "Thus, the proverb is true: <term>many things in war are empty</term>." <note>original: "οὕτως ἀληθές ἐστι τὸ παροιμιῶδες, ὅτι πολλὰ κενὰ τοῦ πολέμου" (houtos alēthes esti to paroimiōdes, hoti polla kena tou polemou)</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fifth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, says: "In the meantime, you know there are certain <term>panic</term> things, also said to be <term>certain empty things of war</term>." <note>original: "πανικὰ ... τινὰ κενὰ τοῦ πολέμου"</note> It is a proverb regarding our arrival. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Listening*, says: "For just as in war, so also in listening, there are many empty things." <note>original: "περὶ τοῦ ἀκούειν, ὡς γὰρ τοῦ πολέμου καὶ ἀκροάσεως πολλὰ τὰ κενά ἐστιν" (peri tou akouein, hōs gar tou polemou kai akroaseōs polla ta kena estin)</note> Quintus Curtius Rufus alluded to this in his third book: "War stands on reputation, and he who retreats is believed to be fleeing." And again in the fifth book: "Reputation has the greatest momentum in war." Likewise in the eighth book: "For wars consist of reputation, and often even that which is falsely believed has taken the place of truth." But he says it more clearly in the seventh book: "That matter, like most vain and empty things in war, drew the Barbarians toward surrender."

->He served as general with Erasinades.<-
->XX<-

<margin>He served as general with Erasinades.</margin> <note>original: "Ἐστρατήγησε μετ’ Ἐρασινάδου" (Estratēgēse met’ Erasinadou)</note> That is, he campaigned with Erasinades. It was commonly said as a joke about those whose affairs were proceeding poorly in every way. Erasinades was a certain general who had besieged Arginusae. The battle was fought unsuccessfully, and he was killed to the point of extermination along with others who were resisting, among whom were Thrasyllus and Pericles <note>This refers to Pericles the Younger, son of the famous statesman.</note>, as well as the general himself. To the misfortunes of this Erasinades was added the fact that he was accused of stealing money from the Hellespont. Such accounts are found in Suidas.

->Do not trust a woman, not even a dead one.<-
->XXI<-

<margin>Do not trust a woman, even if she should die.</margin> <note>original: "Γυναικὶ μὴ πίστευε μηδ’ ἂν ἀποθανῇ" (Gynaiki mē pisteue mēd’ an apothanē)</note> That is:
Do not place your trust even in a dying woman.
A proverbial hyperbole. A woman is so little to be trusted that even if you see her dying, you should think she is faking it. We have mentioned elsewhere the story of the stepmother who, even when buried, killed her stepson when a statue fell upon the boy’s head. This is recorded by Diogenianus.

->The destruction of women.<-
->XXII<-

<margin>The destruction of women.</margin> <note>original: "Γυναικῶν ὄλεθρος" (Gynaikōn olethros)</note> That is, the ruin caused by women. Used for those who perish utterly and miserably. For women are said to have been the authors of almost all calamities for men. Witness Hesiod’s Pandora; witness the Trojan War; witness Hercules, destroyed by Deianira; witness the fable of the Danaids; witness the history of the Lemnian women; witness Cleopatra; and witness Eve, who is thoroughly infamous among all Christians. Although, it would be more fitting to attribute these things to the foolishness of men, who indulge their little women so much that, like those out of their minds with love, they follow them into any evil whatsoever. It would have been more proper for men to be the moderators, so that woman—by nature more foolish and likewise weaker—might be less senseless. For what the soul is to the body, the man ought to be to the woman. But just as the common people blame their vices on the body, though they proceed from the soul, and foolish princes blame the most insane turmoils of wars on the people, of which they themselves are the authors: so men cast the blame back upon women whenever they themselves have acted deliriously.

<summary>Erasmus explores several adages concerning human folly, the psychological terrors of war ("Panic"), and the historical tendency of men to blame women for their own failures and misfortunes.</summary>
<keywords>infidelity, panic, reputation in war, Erasinades, Arginusae, misogyny in proverbs, Pandora, Eve, male responsibility</keywords>

### ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>XXIII</margin>
->You must know many things to deceive God.<-
<note>original: "πολλὰ κεν εἰδείης οἷς τὸν θεὸν ἐξαπατήσαις" (Polla ken eideiēs hois ton theon exapatēsais)</note> That is,
> You would need to know many tricks to impose upon God himself.

Used whenever someone attempts to pull the wool over the eyes of a person who is exceptionally difficult to deceive because of their singular cunning. The adage originated from an oracle. Pindar expressed the sentiment differently in his *Pythian Odes*, in the third hymn, speaking of Apollo: <note>original: "Ψευδέων δ' οὐχ ἅπτεται, κλέπτει τέ μιν οὐ θεὸς, οὐ βροτὸς, ἔργοις οὔτε βουλαῖς" (Pseudōn d' ouch haptetai, kleptei te min ou theos, ou brotos, ergois oute boulais)</note> "He does not touch lies. Neither god nor man deceives him, neither by deeds nor by designs."

<margin>XXIIII</margin>
->Many Manniuses at Aricia.<-
In the works of Festus Pompeius <note>A Roman grammarian whose work is a vital source for archaic Latin.</note>, one reads that a certain Mannius consecrated a grove to Diana of Aricia, and he himself was called "The Arician." From this Mannius of Aricia—a most praised man—there arose very many famous men of the same name, so that the proverb was born: "There are many Manniuses at Aricia." However, Asinius Capito strongly disagrees, thinking the proverb is suited to the deformed; but this passage in Festus is so corrupted by errors that nothing certain can be elicited beyond what I have reported.

<margin>XXV</margin>
->A bronze wall.<-
A bronze wall is used by Horace in his *Epistles* to signify a certain and unchangeable decree of the mind, surely a proverbial figure of speech:
> Let this be your wall of bronze, 
> To be conscious of no guilt, to turn pale at no crime.

Vegetius <note>A late Roman author of a treatise on military matters.</note> calls the heavy armor of an army an "iron wall," as if it were a solid and impregnable defense. Using a similar figure in his second *Olympian Ode*, Pindar calls Hector an "invincible, unshakeable column." <note>original: "ἄμαχον, ἀστραβῆ κίονα" (amachon, astrabē kiona)</note>

<margin>XXVI</margin>
->Many will hate you, if you love yourself.<-
<note>original: "Πολλοί σε γοι μισήσουσιν ἂν σαυτὸν φιλῇς" (Polloi se μisēsousin an sauton philēs)</note> That is,
> Many will hate you, if you cherish yourself.

The proverb deters one from arrogance and <term>philautia</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "self-love" or "narcissism."</note>. For he who pleases himself too much must necessarily displease many. On the other hand, modesty is the chief conciliator of favor and goodwill. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> says that the nymphs who were scorned by Narcissus said what we have just reported. This six-foot verse harmonizes with it:
<note>original: "Λίαν φιλῶν ἑαυτὸν οὐχ ἕξεις φίλον" (Lian philōn heauton ouch hexeis philon)</note> That is,
> No one will be a friend to you, if you love yourself too much.

None are less suited to mutual love and goodwill than those who love themselves excessively.

<margin>XXVII</margin>
->A festival of evils.<-
<note>original: "Κακῶν πανήγυρις" (Kakōn panēgyris)</note> That is, a general assembly of evils. Said of evils attacking in crowds and following one after another. For among the Greeks, a <term>panegyris</term> <note>A grand assembly or national festival.</note> was the name for that solemn gathering of people to celebrate festive games, the word being composed from the fact that everyone came together on feast days. Pisides, quoted in Suidas:
> All at once, as if in a festival of evils,
> One misfortune after another held them in misery.

<margin>Homer, *Iliad* book 19.</margin>
<note>original: "Ὡς μοι δέχεται κακὸν ἐκ κακοῦ αἰεί" (Hōs moi dechetai kakon ek kakou aiei)</note> That is,
> How sad things are perpetually followed by sad things for me.

Hipponax, in the 15th book of Athenaeus:
"Now for a man to recite a rhapsody of evils upon evils."
The verse limps, but it will walk straight if you remove "and" or "now," and read "sit" instead of "kithi." Ausonius, in a poem, not inelegantly calls them "Chained Labors," because trouble follows trouble in the life of mortals.

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
->More wicked than Hippomenes.<-
<note>original: "Ἀσεβέστερος ἱππομένους" (Asebesteros Hippomenous)</note> That is, more impious than Hippomenes. This prince of the Athenians shut up his daughter (who had been defiled by some citizen) in a house together with a fierce horse, providing food for neither. The horse, driven to madness by hunger, attacked and killed the girl, and then died itself for lack of fodder. After this, the father demolished the house, and the place was given a name derived from the horse and the girl. Diogenianus records this adage.

<summary>This page explores several adages regarding the futility of trying to deceive the divine, the origins of local Roman proverbs like those from Aricia, and the psychological dangers of self-love. It also examines metaphors for cumulative misfortune and extreme cruelty through the myth of Hippomenes.</summary>

<header>SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>

### XXIX. A hand-eating bond

<margin><unclear>Isen de ...</unclear></margin> **A hand-eating bond** <note>original: "χείροβρωτι δεσμῷ" (cheirobrōti desmō)</note>, that is, a hand-devouring shackle. Someone once used this phrase to describe the long sleeves of garments from the Black Sea region <note>original: "Ponticarum"</note>, because they chafe and wear away the hands. The same charge is leveled against the Trojans in Virgil’s works: *And your tunics have sleeves, and your hoods have ribbons.* <note>original: "Et tunicæ manicas, & habent redimicula mitræ," Aeneid 9.616. Virgil used this to imply the Trojans were effeminate.</note> This is recorded by Zenodotus.

---

### XXX. Hercules’s Apple

<margin>Hercules's apple</margin> <note>original: "μᾶλον ἡρακλῆς" (malon hēraklēs)</note>, that is, **Hercules’s Apple**. This is appropriate to say when someone is grateful for even the smallest of gifts. Apollodorus, cited by Zenodotus in his books *On the Gods*, relates that among the Athenians, a peculiar type of sacrifice was offered to Hercules *Alexicacos*—that is, the "Averter of Evils." It once happened that a bull intended for sacrifice escaped; the people grabbed an apple, stuck four branches into it to serve as legs, and added two more as horns, creating a crude likeness of a bull. They then sacrificed this ridiculous substitute to Hercules in place of the animal. This event passed into a popular folk tale. This is the same as what we mentioned previously regarding the **Apple-like Hercules** <note>original: "μήλιος ἡρακλῆς" (mēlios hēraklēs)</note>, except that by the change of a single word, the usage of the proverb is slightly altered: for the former refers to something held in contempt, while this one refers to someone taking a small gift in good part.

---

### XXXI. To have the hand under the cloak

Those who are languishing in idleness are said to **have the hand under the cloak**. Quintilian, in his twelfth book, condemns those who never move while delivering a speech, and always keep their hand, as the saying goes, "under the cloak." For this reason, he says, "those who believe that the 'Attic' style consists only of being lean, clear, and expressive, but are content with a certain frugality of eloquence, and always keep their hand within their cloak, seem to me to be greatly mistaken." <note>Quintilian is arguing against the idea that a "pure" or "Attic" orator should be physically stiff or boring.</note> Thus far Fabius <note>Quintilian's full name was Marcus Fabius Quintilianus.</note>. The phrase is taken from the gestures of public speakers. Those who are sluggish hide their hand under their cloak; those who are moved by passion bring it out, for the movement of the hand and arm helps to express those matters that require a bit more intensity. Aeschines also hints at this in his speech *Against Timarchus*, speaking of the sobriety of the ancient orators: *So that what we all do now by custom—speaking with the hand held outside the cloak—was then considered a mark of boldness, and they were careful not to do it.* <note>original: "ὥστε ὃ νυνὶ πάντες ἐν ἔθει πράττομεν..."</note> He adds that in Salamis, a statue of Solon can be seen with his hand tucked inside his cloak.

---

### XXXII. To have the hand in the bosom

Theocritus used the phrase **to have the hand in the bosom** to describe people who are stingy and slow to give. For he says in *The Graces*:
<margin>They are conquered by greed,</margin>
> Everyone has his hands in his bosom, watching
> from where his silver might grow and increase. <note>original: "πᾶς δ᾽ ὑπὸ κόλπῳ χεῖρας ἔχων..." Theocritus, Idyll 16.16-17.</note>
> 
> Overcome by the desire for profit,
> each man keeps his hands in his cloak, and 
> looks only for how his money might grow for him.

Furthermore, when Scaevola says in the twenty-third book of the *Pandects* <note>The Pandects, or Digest, is a massive compendium of Roman law.</note>, under the title *On Proofs*, "I have had it in my bosom," he means "I have held it secretly in my power." This relates more to what we have said elsewhere: **To rejoice in one's bosom** <note>To celebrate or be happy in secret.</note>. These are the words of Gaius: "I give and bequeath a hundred to Titius, which he brought to me, for which I did not provide a legal receipt, because I held his entire fortune and substance—if he had received any from his mother—in my bosom without any formal security."

---

### XXXIII. To put pre-chewed food into the mouth

Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in his book *The Orator*, uses **To put pre-chewed food into the mouth** as a proverb. It stands for explaining a matter too minutely and in too many small fragments when teaching. Some people tend to do this as if they distrust the intelligence of their listeners, omitting nothing and hammering in even the most insignificant trifles. The figure of speech is taken from nurses, who put pre-chewed food into the mouths of infants who do not yet have teeth. Cicero’s words are these: "But if I now wished to train someone who was completely unpolished in speaking, I would rather hand him over to those who constantly hammer at the same anvil day and night—those who put all the tiniest particles and all the smallest 'chewed bits,' as nurses say, into the mouths of infant boys." Aulus Gellius, in his *Attic Nights* (book 4, chapter 1), also mentions this (even if the passage is corrupted in the common editions, which say: "For this indeed is well known, that every definition consists of genus and difference."): "But if you demand that I 'pre-chew' it, as they say, I shall certainly do that too for the sake of your honor." I believe it should be read...

<sig>Ff</sig> <meta>catchword: ...as (from "arbitror," I believe)</meta>

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to physical gestures, such as hiding hands or pre-chewing food, to describe character traits like greed, laziness, and pedantry. Erasmus draws on classical sources like Cicero, Quintilian, and Theocritus to explain the cultural origins of these metaphors.</summary>
<keywords>greed, laziness, oratory, Hercules, Roman law, education, metaphors, Quintilian, Cicero, Theocritus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs, moving through the tenth century of the second chiliad. The previous page concluded with a discussion of "Hercules’s Apple" and the idea of being grateful for small or crude substitutes. This page begins mid-explanation of an adage regarding "pre-chewing" information, then proceeds to catalog sayings about betrayal, choosing between two evils, the inevitable consequences of wickedness, and ethnic stereotypes of the ancient world.</meta>

...I think. But if you demand that I **chew it for you beforehand**, as they say, you ask too much. He used the word "to chew beforehand" <note>original: "praemandere"</note> to mean explaining a matter too crudely that is otherwise not difficult, unless someone is a complete child. This adage remains in use even today, when people say: "Is it not enough that the opportunity was given to you? Do you now demand that it be chewed for you as well?" It is not unlike what Cicero wrote to Atticus: "But enough of this, lest I seem to **occupy myself with trifles**." <note>original: "περὶ μικρὰ ἀσχολάζειν" (peri mikra ascholazein)</note>; even if, for me at this moment, these things are of the greatest importance. The Greeks use the term "to speak minutely" <note>original: "μικρολογεῖν" (mikrologein)</note> to describe someone who is overly anxious about tiny details.

### Bad betrayal.
<margin>XXXIII</margin>

**Bad betrayal** <note>original: "Κακὴ προδοσίς" (Kakē prodosis)</note>. This refers to a situation where someone performs a shameful deed or condition but does not receive the agreed-upon reward. It originated from some historical event, though the commentators do not specify which. There is a well-known saying: "I praise the betrayal, but I do not praise the betrayer." <note>This sentiment is often attributed to Augustus Caesar regarding a Thracian king.</note> Since betrayal is inherently a dishonorable act, it is nonetheless sometimes useful—both to the person for whose benefit it is done and to the one who commits it. However, when it does not succeed, or when the traitor is cheated of his prize, it is called a "bad betrayal." This is recorded by Diogenianus.

### Bad woodworms, bad vine-grubs.
<margin>XXXIV</margin>

**Bad indeed are the woodworms, and bad again are the vine-grubs** <note>original: "Κακὰ μὲν θρῖπες, κακὰ δ' ἴπες" (Kaka men thripes, kaka d' ipes)</note>. This was customarily said of a double evil, where it does not matter much which one you choose. For the Greeks, the *thrips* is a tiny worm born in wood that spoils timber, while the *ips* is a creature similarly harmful to horns and grapevines. This appears in the works of the same Diogenianus.

### The wicked drink the dregs of wickedness.
<margin>XXXV</margin>

**The wicked drink the murkiness of iniquity** <note>original: "Κακοὶ πίνουσι πονηρίας τὴν ὁμίχλην" (Kakoi pinousi ponērias tēn omichlēn)</note>.
The Greek verse seems to have been corrupted by an inversion of words, a problem we have detected more than once. It would be more consistent in this form:
**The wicked drink the mist of wickedness** <note>original: "πίνουσ' ὁμίχλην τῆς πονηρίας κακοí" (pinous' omichlēn tēs ponērias kakoi)</note>.
This was commonly said when a punishment worthy of their crimes befell evildoers. The metaphor appears to be drawn from those who, having drunk all the clear wine, finally reach the dregs at the bottom. Thus, the pain of punishment follows the pleasure initially gained from evil deeds.

### In the Lydian manner.
<margin>XXXVI</margin>

**By the Lydian law**, or **By the Lydian song** <note>original: "Λυδίῳ νόμῳ" (Lydiō nomō)</note>. This is applicable whenever someone relies on soothsaying or is a slave to omens and divinations. For the Lydians are said to have been plagued by this particular superstition. It also alludes to the type of musical harmony called "Lydian," for the prayers, incantations, and chants of the magi were performed in this style. Diogenianus mentions it, as does Hesychius, who thinks that "by the Lydian law" is the same as saying "by the Mysian law" <note>original: "μυσῷ νόμῳ" (mysō nomō)</note>, because the Lydians originated from the Mysians and were themselves highly devoted to divination. He adds another reason: that Lydians used to decorate their heads with feminine headbands, which makes the phrase fit for those who are effeminate. However, if we may be permitted our own "divining," we read that the Lydians were powerful in chariots and cavalry; thus, "by the Lydian law" might be the same as what Suidas calls the **chariot law** <note>original: "ἁρμάτειος νόμος" (harmateios nomos)</note> or **chariot song**, so named because it was first invented for Hector when he was dragged by a chariot, as Homer relates.

### The Lydians are bad, after them the Egyptians, etc.
<margin>XXXVII</margin>

**The Lydians are wicked; second after them are the Egyptians; and third of all, the Carians are the most wretched.**
<note>original: "Λυδοὶ πονηροί, δεύτεροι δ' Αἰγύπτιοι. Τρίτοι δὲ πάντων κᾶρες ἐξωλέστατοι"</note>
We may use this appropriately whenever bad people are compared with other bad people; when compared with the truly criminal, someone else may finally seem less blameworthy. For instance, in the writings of Athenaeus, Antiphanes had described fishmongers <note>original: "ἰχθυοπώλας" (ichthyopōlas)</note> as the most criminal of all men, yet he made an exception for the money-changers <note>term: bankers or usurers</note>, who were even more harmful than the fishmongers. Recorded by Diogenianus.

### Mud soaked in blood.
<margin>XXXVIII</margin>

Theodorus of Gadara, who was the teacher of Tiberius Caesar in the art of rhetoric, perceived in Tiberius—even while he was a youth—a certain cruelty joined with a sluggishness of mind. During his rebukes, Theodorus used to call him: **Mud soaked in blood** <note>original: "πηλὸν αἵματι συμπεφυρμένον" (pēlon haimati sympephyrmenon)</note>. By "mud" he hinted at the boy's slowness and stupidity, and by "blood" his innate cruelty. The source for this is Suetonius. It is not entirely unlike the insult a certain jester in Athens hurled at the Roman general Sulla: **Sulla is a mulberry, sprinkled with flour** <note>original: "συκάμινόν ἐσθ' ὁ σύλλας, ἀλφίτῳ πεπασμένον" (sykaminon esth' ho syllas, alphitō pepasmenon)</note>. This was because Plutarch said that Sulla...

### SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY
<sig>Ff 2</sig>

<unclear>moros</unclear> <note>original Greek: μωρος (mōros), meaning "foolish"</note>, the translator renders as "of the customs." He noted the appearance of Sulla, whose face, otherwise pale, had a reddish glow shining through—not constant, but as if sprinkled with spots. <note>This likely refers to the historian Plutarch's description of Sulla’s complexion, which was famously compared to a "mulberry sprinkled with flour."</note>

---

->**Goats free from the plow.**<-
<margin>XL</margin>
**Goats free from the plow** <note>original Greek: Ἐλεύθεραι αἶγες ἀρότρου (Eleutherai aiges arotrou)</note>. This means:
"Goats are exempt from the labor of plowing."
This is a proverbial half-line of heroic verse, once used by those who boasted they were liberated from some burden or annoyance. For example, if a "parasite" <note>In antiquity, a "parasite" was a social hanger-on who traded wit for meals.</note> were to brag about his good fortune because he is never called to perform public duties—ignoring the fact that he is simply unfit for any honorable work. Zenodotus is the source for this.

---

->**Strife breeds strife.**<-
<margin>XLI</margin>
**Strife breeds strife** <note>original Greek: Ἔρις δ' ἔριν ἀμφυτεύει (Eris d' erin amphyteuei)</note>. That is:
"But strife is sown by strife in turn."
This is a heroic half-line. It suggests that an injury should be cut short rather than retaliated. Otherwise, what end will there be to the cycle of evil if insults are returned for insults? The verse appears among the moral precepts of Phocylides:
<margin>Phocylides</margin>
"Not even in a dream; for strife breeds strife" <note>original Greek: μηδὲ μὲν ὄναρ, ἔρις δ' ἔριν ἀμφυτεύει</note>.
There is a close relative to this saying, which we mentioned in another place:
"Justice begat justice, and harm begat harm" <note>original Greek: Δίκη δίκην ἔτικτε, καὶ βλάβην βλάβη</note>.

---

->**Crooked wood is never straight.**<-
<margin>XLII</margin>
**Crooked wood is never straight** <note>original Greek: Ξύλον ἀγκύλον, οὐδέποτ' ὀρθόν (Xylon ankylon, oudepot' orthon)</note>. That is:
"Twisted wood is never straight."
This is also a heroic half-line. It refers to distorted and wicked natures that can hardly ever be brought back to a fruitful state. He who has grown old in vice rarely returns to a sound mind. It is also expressed this way: **wicked wood is never straight** <note>original: "τὸ ξύλον σκαμβὸν, οὐδέποτ' ὀρθόν" (to xylon skambon, oudepot' orthon)</note>. Galen used it in the fourth book of *On the Differences of Pulses*:
"I respond nothing to those men; but among ourselves, we quote the comic poet: just as crooked wood does not become straight, neither does an old tree produce shoots if it is moved" <note>original: "ἐκείνοις μὲν οὐδὲν ἀποκρίνομαι... ὡς οὔτε στρεβλὸν ὀρθὸν ξύλον, οὔτε γεράνδρυον μετατεθὲν μοχθύει?"</note>.
In this passage, "you" <note>original: "hymas"</note> was printed instead of "us" <note>original: "hemas"</note>, and "old tree" <note>original: "gerandrou"</note> instead of "aged wood" <note>original: "gerandryon"</note>. I mention this so that no one corrupts the writing further. We have reviewed this latter proverb previously. Horace shows where this metaphor comes from:
> "You may drive out Nature with a pitchfork," he says, "yet she will always rush back" <note>original: "Naturam expellas furca, tamen usque recurrit"</note>.
He indicates the metaphor is drawn from those who try to fix the flaw of a distorted tree by applying a pitchfork as a prop. This is also confirmed by the proverbial sentiment:
"It is not easy to change a wicked nature" <note>original: "Φύσιν πονηρὰν μεταβαλεῖν οὐ ῥᾴδιον" (Physin ponēran metabalein ou rhadion)</note>.

---

->**Worthy of Lesbians.**<-
<margin>XLIII</margin>
**Worthy of Lesbians** <note>original: "Λεσβίων ἄξια" (Lesbiōn axia)</note>. This was said of useless or vain things, because—as I conjecture—the people of Lesbos had a bad reputation for vanity. Perhaps it might also apply to the sordid and impure, for this mark was also once burned into them. From this came the word "to act like a Lesbian" <note>original: "λεσβιάζειν" (lesbiazein)</note>, meaning to pollute or defile. Aristophanes writes:
"He is already about to defile the fellow-guests" <note>original: "Μέλλει γε ἤδη λεσβιάζειν τοὺς συμπότας"</note>.

---

->**By a Lemnian hand.**<-
<margin>XLIIII</margin>
**By a Lemnian hand** <note>original: "Λημνία χείρ" (Lēmnia cheir)</note>. This was said for something nefarious, impious, or cruel. The proverb was born from the history we recounted elsewhere regarding the "Lemnian evil" <note>referring to the mythological massacre where the women of Lemnos killed their husbands</note>.

---

->**A hare appearing makes the journey unlucky.**<-
<margin>XLV</margin>
**A hare appearing makes the journey unlucky** <note>original: "Φανεὶς ὁ λαγὼς δυστυχῶς ποιεῖ τρίβος" (Phaneis ho lagōs dystychōs poiei tribos)</note>. That is:
"An encounter with a hare makes for an ill-omened path."
It is commonly believed even in these times that meeting a hare is an unlucky omen for those starting a journey. It can be applied to the interference of anyone who seems likely to bring some inconvenience. Suidas mentions this.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES
<page-num>616</page-num>

<margin>XLVI</margin>
### The threshold of old age.

**The threshold of old age** <note>original Greek: γῆραος οὐδός (gēraos oudos)</note>. In ancient times, they called the "threshold of old age" the very end of the autumn of human life, just as the winter of decrepit old age begins to set in. The phrase is taken from Homer, with whom it is a very frequent expression. For instance, in the *Iliad*, Book 22:
> For Father Zeus, the son of Cronus, will destroy me on the threshold of old age with a painful fate. <note>original: "ου γὰρ πατὴρ κρονίδης ἐπὶ γῆραος οὐδῷ / Αἰσῇ ἐν ἀργαλέῃ φθίσῃ"</note>

Similarly, in the *Iliad*, Book 24:
> A man of such an age as I am, on the wretched threshold of old age. <note>original: "Τηλίκου ὥσπερ ἐγὼν ὀλοῷ ἐπὶ γῆραος οὐδῷ"</note>

And in the *Odyssey*:
> Whom departing he left on the threshold of old age. <note>original: "ου κατέλειπεν ἰὼν ἐπὶ γῆραος οὐδῷ"</note>

Again, in the *Odyssey*, Book 23:
> And to reach the threshold of old age. <note>original: "Καὶ γῆραος οὐδὸν ἱκέσθαι"</note>

Plato employs this phrase as if it were a poetic proverb. It is found again in Hesiod’s *Works and Days*:
> Whoever provokes an aging parent, worn out by time, on the threshold of old age. <note>original: "ουκε γονῆα γέροντα κακῷ ἐπὶ γῆραος οὐδῷ Νεικῇ"</note>

<margin>XLVII</margin>
### Waging war with the tongue.

**To wage war with the tongue** <note>original Greek: γλώττῃ πολεμίζειν (glōttē polemizein)</note>. They say those "war with the tongue" who hurl magnificent insults and threaten the enemy, but only when it is safe to do so. In this manner, Menelaus <note>A central figure in the Trojan War, husband of Helen</note> accuses the Greeks of cowardice in the *Iliad*, Book 7:
> Alas, you boasters, Greek women and no longer Greek men, you are nothing but threats! <note>original: "ὤμοι ἀπειλητῆρες ἀχαιίδες ουκέτ᾽ ἀχαιοí"</note>

Virgil alludes to this in the *Aeneid*:
> Will your Mars <note>The Roman god of war, here meaning "military prowess"</note> always reside in that windy tongue and those flighty feet of yours?

For Turnus <note>The primary antagonist of Aeneas</note> says these things to Drances, a man who was powerful in counsel and speech but otherwise unfit for war. Virgil also depicts the Rutulians as abusive:
> O you true Phrygian women, for you are not Phrygian men! Your tunics have sleeves and your hats have ribbons. <note>A Roman insult suggesting the Trojans/Phrygians were effeminate due to their ornate clothing.</note>

Hector speaks in this same way in Homer's *Iliad*, Book 20:
> Indeed, I could contend even with the gods in speech, but with the spear it is difficult, because they are much stronger in power. <note>original: "Καί κεν ἐγὼν ἐπέσσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι μαχοíμην / ἔγχει δ᾽ ἀργαλέον"</note>

Furthermore, true bravery is neither abusive nor prone to threats. Homer hints at this in the *Iliad*, Book 13:
> Hector of the flashing helm answered him not at all, but leaped forward eagerly. <note>original: "Τὸν δ᾽ οὐ τι προσέφη κορυθαίολος ἕκτωρ / Ἀλλὰ πῆιξεν λελιημένος"</note>

And in Book 3 of the same work, he describes the Greeks going into battle in silence:
> But the Greeks went on in silence, breathing courage, eager in their hearts to bring aid to one another. <note>original: "οι δ᾽ ἀρ᾽ ἴσαν σιγῇ μένεα πνείοντες ἀχαιοί"</note>

And Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
> Pleading, deliberating, and waging war with the tongue. <note>original: "φράζων, βουλεύων, καὶ τῇ γλώττῃ πολεμίζων"</note>

Regarding such people, it is elegantly said in Livy's *History of Rome*, Book 7: "Fierce in the camp, fearful in the line of battle." Apuleius, using a playfully invented word, said **verbigerari** <note>A combination of "verba" (words) and "gerere" (to wage), similar to "to bandy words"</note> instead of "fencing with words." And Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian</note> indicates that those who use their tongue instead of a shield were called **tongue-shields** <note>original Greek: γλωσσάσπιδας (glōssaspidas)</note>. By this name, the ignorant could be known, as well as those who carry the venom of an asp <note>The "asp" (aspis) here is a pun on the Greek word for "shield" (aspis)</note> on their tongues. Heraclitus said to Hermodorus: "You have weapons in your tongues now that you have stolen the money." This expression is particularly suited to lawyers and rhetoricians: "Fighting and battling by waging war with their tongues."

<summary>Erasmus explores two adages: "The threshold of old age," a poetic metaphor for the onset of decline, and "Waging war with the tongue," which mocks those who substitute verbal bravado for physical courage.</summary>
<keywords>threshold of old age, verbal warfare, Homeric values, courage vs. rhetoric, Latin metaphors, Greek poetry, ancient insults</keywords>

# SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

Ff 3

### The gaping gull.
<margin>XLVIII</margin>
**The gaping gull** <note>original Greek: Λάρος κεχηνώς (Laros kechēnōs)</note>. This means a wide-mouthed or gaping gull. It was said whenever someone gaped too greedily for prey. For the gull is a greedy and voracious bird, which the Greeks also call a *kepphos* <note>a light, erratic sea-bird often used to symbolize a simpleton or a flighty person</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:
<margin>A gaping gull on the rocks making a public speech. <note>original: Λάρος κεχηνώς ἐπὶ πέτρας δημηγορῶν</note></margin>
These words cannot be conveniently rendered into Latin <note>and by extension, English</note> with the same force. For he calls Cleon a "gull" because of his rapacity; just as that bird watches from the cliffs to see if it can hunt any fish, so Cleon busied himself in administering the affairs of the Republic while, in the meantime, looking out for his own profit. Plutarch, cited in the third book of Athenaeus’s *The Banquet of the Learned*:
<margin>And standing there upon the threshold as he came, he was close to all, Chaerephon, looking like a hungry gull. <note>original: Στὰς δ' ἄρ' ἐπ' οὐδοῦ ἰὼν, σχεδὸν δέ οἱ ἰῶ πᾶσιτο Χαιρεφόων, πεινῶντι λάρωι ὄρνιθι ἐοικώς</note></margin>
that is:
> But indeed, arriving, there stood upon the threshold
> Chaerephon the parasite, a neighbor to him,
> Not unlike the bird commonly called the Gull, when it is hungry.

In the seventh book of the same author, this trimeter verse is cited:
<margin>Gormandizers like the gulls among the Syrians. <note>original: ὀψοφάγος ὥστε τοὺς λάρος ἐν σύροις</note></margin>
that is:
> To be like gulls, those Syrians greedy for delicacies.

Theodore Gaza translates the "Gull" as *Gavia* <note>a sea-mew or gull</note>, which Pliny mentions among the maritime birds along with the Kingfisher and the Diver, in book 10, chapter 32.

### Laconicism.
<margin>XLIX</margin>
**Laconicism** <note>original Greek: Λακωνισμὸν (Lakōnismon)</note>. They use this as a proverb for brevity of speech, either because the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> excelled more in deeds than in eloquence, or because they were particularly powerful in apophthegms <note>pithy sayings</note>. The chief grace of these is that they embrace a great deal of meaning in very few words. Such as that one: "**If**" <note>original: ἄικα (aika)</note>, which was the response to a long speech by an envoy. Or "**No**" <note>original: οὐ (ou)</note>, which occupied an entire letter. Or "**Either this, or on this**" <note>original: ἢ τὰν, ἢ ἐπὶ τᾶς (ē tan, ē epi tas)</note>, that is, "either [bring back] this [shield], or [be carried back] upon it." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] occasionally jokes about the laconic style of Brutus. And "to speak Laconically" <note>original: λακωνικῶς λέγειν</note> is used among the Greeks for saying something briefly and concisely. Also "to Laconize" <note>original: λακωνίζειν</note> means to affect brevity of speech. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> says in a letter: "To Laconize is not what you think—writing a few syllables—but writing few things about many matters." Likewise, Homer attributes a clear brevity to Menelaus, as if he were a Lacedaemonian:
<margin>Few words indeed, but very clearly spoken. <note>original: Παῦρα μὲν, ἀλλὰ μάλα λιγέως</note></margin>
that is:
> Few things indeed, but plainly the most eloquent.

Furthermore, the frugality and integrity of the Lacedaemonians was so much greater than in other parts of Greece that to live temperately and chastely was called "living Laconically." Whenever Cimon reproached something in the habits of his fellow Athenians, he used to say: "But the Lacedaemonians are not like that." In the same way, the honesty of the people of Marseilles passed into a proverb, which we have mentioned elsewhere. Indeed, these things are related: to speak little and to be an honest man. Charillus had this in mind when someone asked why Lycurgus had produced so few laws: "Because," he said, "those who speak little have no need for many laws." He was noting, in passing, the Athenians, for whose loquacity no amount of laws was sufficient. This saying is also celebrated among the maxims of Thales in Laertius. Pindar, in the fifth Isthmian Hymn: "It shall be told after the manner of the Argives, even in the briefest way." The commentator notes that talkativeness belongs to the Ionians. However, brevity of speech was familiar not only to the Laconians but also to the Argives, citing this from the *Mad Ajax* of Sophocles:
<margin>For a story in the Argive manner is short in its cutting. <note>original: μῦθος γὰρ ἀργολιστὶ συντέμνειν βραχύς</note></margin>
that is:
> An Argive speech brings much in few words.

Laertius, on the authority of Aristagoras of Miletus, reports that brevity was also peculiar to Chilon, whence he calls this kind of speaking "Chilonian." To this pertains that little verse, used almost proverbially, found in Athenaeus:
<margin>You will soon persuade a man of sense, if you speak well and quickly. <note>original: τῆς συνέσεως ἂν ἄυλως πάσχε τάχιστα λέγων εὖ</note></margin>
that is:
> You will soon persuade the wise, if you speak well.

### Living hidden.
<margin>L</margin>
**Live hidden** <note>original Greek: Λάθε βιώσας (Lathe biōsas)</note>. This adage advises that life is happier in humble fortune for those who live obscurely and are so removed from public affairs that when they depart from life, no one...

### The threshold of old age.
<margin>XLVI</margin>

**The threshold of old age** <note>original Greek: γήραος οὐδός (gēraos oudos)</note>. In ancient times, they used this expression to refer to the "threshold of old age," as if it were the very end of the autumn of human life, just as the winter of decrepit old age begins to set in. It is taken from Homer, with whom the phrase is quite frequent, as in the twenty-second book of the *Iliad*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> For father Zeus <note>Erasmus uses "Cronides," the son of Cronos</note> has assigned me to be destroyed by a bitter fate upon the threshold of old age. <note>original: οὐ γὰρ πατὴρ κρονίδης ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ, / Αἶσεν ἐν ἀργαλέῳ φθίσθαι.</note>

And again in the twenty-fourth book of the *Iliad*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> One of such an age as I am, upon the dismal threshold of old age. <note>original: Τηλίκου ὥσπερ ἐγὼν ὀλοῷ ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ.</note>

Likewise in the *Odyssey*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> Whom he left behind when departing, on the threshold of old age. <note>original: οὐ κατέλειπεν ἰὼν ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ.</note>

Again in the twenty-third book of the *Odyssey*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> And to reach the threshold of old age. <note>original: Καὶ γήραος οὐδὸν ἱκέσθαι.</note>

Plato also employs it in the place of a poetic proverb. Furthermore, in Hesiod’s *Works and Days*:
<margin>that is, to provoke <note>original Greek: νικέειν (nikeein)</note></margin>
> And he who provokes an aged parent, worn out by years, upon the threshold of old age. <note>original: ὅς κε γονῆα γέροντα κακῷ ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ</note>

### To wage war with the tongue.
<margin>XLVII</margin>

**To wage war with the tongue** <note>original Greek: γλώττῃ πολεμίζειν (glōttē polemizein)</note>. They say someone "wars with the tongue" when they magnificently hurl insults and threaten an enemy, but only when they are in a safe position. Thus Menelaus reproaches the cowardice of the Greeks in the seventh book of the *Iliad*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> Alas, women of Achaia, no longer men! You who are only threatening. <note>original: ὦμοι ἀπειλητῆρες ἀχαιΐδες οὐκ ἔτ’ ἀχαιοί.</note>

Virgil alluded to this in the *Aeneid*:
> Will your Mars <note>referring to the god of war, here meaning courage</note> always be in that windy tongue, and in those fleet feet of yours?

For Turnus said these things to Drances, a man powerful in speech during councils, but otherwise a coward in war. The same author depicts the Rutulians as abusive:
> O truly Phrygian women, for you are not even Phrygian men! You whose tunics have sleeves and whose caps have ribbons. <note>A Roman insult suggesting the Trojans were effeminate and over-dressed</note>

In the same way, Hector speaks in Homer's *Iliad*, book twenty:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> Indeed, I could contend with words even against the gods, but with the spear it is hard, because they are much stronger in power. <note>original: Καὶ κεν ἐγὼν ἐπέεσσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι μαχοίμην, / Ἔγχει δ’ ἀργαλέον. ἐπεὶ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰσιν.</note>

Certainly, true fortitude is neither abusive nor threatening. This is what Homer hints at in the seventh book of the *Iliad*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> To this man, Hector of the flashing helmet replied nothing at all, but rather leaped in close. <note>original: τὸν δ’ ὅτι προσέφη κορυθαίολος ἕκτωρ, / Ἀλλὰ πολεμίζειν λελιημένον.</note>

And in the third book of the same work, he imagines the Greeks going into battle in silence:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> But the Greeks <note>referred to as Danaans</note> marched in silence, breathing strength, and eager in their hearts to bring aid to one another. <note>original: Οἱ δ’ ἄρ’ ἴσαν σιγῇ μένεα πνείοντες ἀχαιοί, / Ἐν θυμῷ μεμαῶτες ἀλεξέμεν ἀλλήλοισιν.</note>

And Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
> Requesting, deliberating, and mixing up battles with the tongue. <note>original: φράζων, βουλεύων, καὶ τῇ γλώττῃ πολεμίζων.</note>

Concerning such people, it was elegantly said by Livy in the seventh book of his *History of Rome*: "Ferocious in the camp, but fearful in the line of battle." Apuleius, using a festively invented word, said <term>verbigerari</term> <note>literally "to word-clash"</note> instead of "to fight with words." And Hesychius indicates that some were called <term>glossakidas</term> <note>tongue-fighters</note> because they used their tongues instead of weapons. By this name, the ignorant might be known, as well as those who carry the poison of an asp upon their tongues. Heraclitus said to Hermodorus: "You have your weapons in your tongues, after you have taken away the money." It is the characteristic of lawyers and rhetoricians "to wage war and fight with their tongues."

### The gaping gull. XLVIII

**The gaping gull** <note>original Greek: Λάρος κεχηνώς (laros kechēnōs)</note>. That is, a gull with its mouth wide open. This was said whenever someone hungrily gaped after some prey. For the gull is a greedy and voracious bird, which the Greeks also call a *kepphos* <note>a type of light seabird often associated with silliness or greed</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*: "A gaping gull upon the rocks, making a public speech."

These lines cannot be easily rendered in Latin <note>Erasmus means the poetic meter and the specific pun on Cleon’s name are hard to translate directly</note>. For he calls Cleon <note>a notorious Athenian politician known for his aggressive populism</note> a "gull" because of his rapacity; just as that bird hangs around the cliffs to see if it can hunt any fish, so Cleon busied himself in the administration of the Republic’s affairs while, in the meantime, looking out for his own profit. Plutarch, in the third book of Athenaeus’s *The Banquet of the Learned*, writes:
> But indeed, arriving at the threshold stood
> Chaerephon the parasite, his neighbor, a man not
> Unlike the bird commonly called the Gull, hungry.

In the eighth book of the same work, this trimeter <note>a line of verse</note> is cited:
> To be as greedy for delicacies as the Syrian gulls.
> <note>original Greek: ὀψοφάγος ὥστ᾽ οὐκ λάρος εἶν σύροις</note>

Theodorus Gaza <note>a 15th-century Greek scholar who translated Aristotle into Latin</note> translates "Larus" as "Gavia" <note>a sea-mew or loon</note>, which Pliny mentions among the sea birds along with the Halcyon and the Diver in Book 10, Chapter 32.

### Laconism. XLIX

**Laconism** <note>original Greek: λακωνισμός (lakōnismos)</note>. They use this as a proverb for brevity of speech, either because the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> excelled more in deeds than in eloquence, or because they were particularly skilled in *Apophthegms* <note>pithy, concise sayings</note>. The chief grace of these is that they embrace a great deal of meaning in very few words. Such is that famous "If" <note>original Greek: ἄκα (aika)</note>—the response given to a long-winded speech from an envoy. Or: "Either this, or on this" <note>original: ἢ τὰν, ἢ ἐπὶ τᾶς. This refers to the Spartan mother's command to her son regarding his shield: come home with it, or be carried back dead upon it</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero sometimes jokes about the "Laconism" of Brutus. And among the Greeks, "to speak in the Laconian way" <note>original Greek: λακωνίζειν λέγειν</note> means to speak briefly and concisely. Also, "to Laconize" <note>original Greek: λακωνίζειν</note> means to affect brevity of speech. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> says in a letter: "To Laconize is not, as you think, to write few syllables, but to write few things about many matters." Accordingly, Homer attributes a clear brevity to Menelaus as a Lacedaemonian:
> Few words indeed, but very clearly spoken.
> <note>original Greek: παῦρα μὲν, ἀλλὰ μάλα λιγέως</note>

Furthermore, the frugality and integrity of the Lacedaemonians was so much greater than in other parts of Greece that those who lived a disciplined and chaste life were said to "live in the Laconian fashion." Cimon <note>an Athenian statesman</note>, whenever he found fault with the habits of his fellow Athenians, used to say: "But the Lacedaemonians are not like that." Likewise, the honesty of the people of Marseille passed into a proverb, which we have noted elsewhere. For these things are related: to speak little and to be an upright man. Charillus <note>a Spartan king</note> had this in mind; when asked why Lycurgus <note>the Spartan lawgiver</note> had produced so few laws, he replied: "Because those who speak little have no need for many laws." He was noting in passing the Athenians, whose talkativeness no amount of laws could satisfy. This saying is also celebrated among the maxims of Thales in the works of Laërtius. Pindar, in the fifth *Isthmian Ode*, says: "It shall be told in the manner of the Argives, even in the shortest words." A commentator notes that talkativeness belongs to the Ionians. However, brevity of speech was familiar not only to the Laconians but also to the Argives, as he cites from the *Mad Ajax* of Sophocles:
> For an Argive speech is short, cutting many things into few.
> <note>original Greek: μῦθος γὰρ ἀργολιστὶ συντέμνειν βραχύς</note>

Laërtius, on the authority of Aristagoras of Miletus, reports that brevity of speech was also peculiar to Chilon <note>one of the Seven Sages</note>, which is why he calls this style of speaking "Chilonian." This proverbial line in Athenaeus pertains to this:
> You will soon persuade a wise man, if you speak well.
> <note>original Greek: τοῖς συνετοῖς δ᾽ ἂν ἂλλ᾽ εἴποις γε τάχιστα λέγων εὖ</note>

### Living unnoticed. L

**Living unnoticed** <note>original Greek: Λάθε βιώσας (Lathe biōsas)</note>. That is: "Escape notice while living." The adage advises that life is happier in humble fortune for those who live obscurely and are so removed from public affairs that, when they depart from life, no one...
