It concludes the entry on the Epicurean motto "Live Unnoticed" and moves into architectural and natural metaphors for confusion and toil.</meta>

<page-num>618</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

...realize they had lived. For **live unnoticed** <note>original Greek: λάθε βιώσας (láthe biōsas)</note> cannot be aptly rendered word-for-word, but it carries this meaning: as if you were to say, "Let no one perceive that you have been alive." Plutarch wrote a commentary on whether this adage was rightly spoken or not, provided the title is not misleading. For when we were reading it, the phrasing itself seemed to clash somewhat with the title. Horace alluded to this:
> He has not lived ill who, from birth to death, has passed unnoticed.
> <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.17.10</note>

That is, a man whom no one noticed, neither entering this life nor departing from it. Ovid, if I am not mistaken, alluded to this in his books of the *Tristia*:
> Believe me, he who has hidden well, has lived well; and
> Each man ought to remain within his own fortune.
> <note>Ovid, *Tristia* 3.4.25</note>

This is recorded in Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> under the name of a proverb.

### Labyrinth.

**Labyrinth** <note>original Greek: Λαβύρινθον (Labyrinthon)</note> was the name once given to a speech, or to any matter that was vehemently hindered and inextricable. For example, if someone calls the study of philosophy a "Labyrinth" because once they have entered, there is never any exit. Or if one calls the pursuit of pleasure a "Labyrinth," because the entrance to it is a downward slope, but the exit is most difficult. It is taken from the Labyrinth of Daedalus, which fables place in a cave in Crete—winding, inextricable with its inexplicable twists—in which the Minotaur was kept. Suidas thinks it is named **because it has no door** <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ μὴ θύραν λαβεῖν (para to mē thyran labein)</note>, indicating that it also applies to talkative and triflers who find no end to their speech once they begin to chatter. Gregory the Theologian, in a letter to Eusebius of Caesarea, twists this against a shifty person:
> Since I am speaking with a man who not only does not love a lie, but is also most sharp at detecting it in another as quickly as possible, even if he involves himself in the most clever and varied labyrinths.
> <note>Erasmus translates Gregory’s Greek into Latin prose here; the Greek implies that truth-loving men can see through complex deceptions.</note>

Not unlike this was the **Meander**. This was a type of pattern originating from the example of Labyrinths, the kind of which we still see today in several floor pavements. Prudentius uses it in a poem that begins, "Worshiper of God":
> O tortuous serpent,
> Who through a thousand Meanders,
> And flexuous frauds,
> Disturbs quiet hearts.

From this also comes the name of the Meander, a river in Lydia, because it wanders in a winding course.

### Laborious with labor.

**Laborious with labor** <note>original Greek: Πόνῳ πονηρός (Ponō ponēros)</note>. That is, one who is burdened by toil. The figure itself contains a hyperbole of immoderate labor. It is recorded by Suidas under the title of a proverb. Theophilus, in the tenth book of Athenaeus, used this form when speaking of a remarkably beautiful and tall woman: **Beautiful in beauty, great in greatness, skillful in skill**, or **wise in wisdom** <note>original Greek: κάλλει καλῶς, μεγέθει μεγάλης, τέχνῃ σοφῶς</note>. A similar trope exists among the Hebrews whenever they either exaggerate or assert: **Pitying I will pity**, or **Laboring I have labored**. It appears, however, in Aristophanes' *Lysistrata*. There is also a joke underlying this due to the ambiguity of the word: for among the Greeks, **ponēros** <note>πονηρός</note> signifies not only one who is laborious and wretched, but also one who is wicked and cunning.

### The Laciadae.

**O Laciadae** <note>original Greek: Ω λακιάδαι (O lakiadai)</note>. This is a common insult against adulterers. The Laciadae were a people of Attica, of the Oeneid tribe, among whom there was a huge abundance of radishes. These radishes were used to mock those caught in adultery <note>Erasmus refers to "rhaphanidosis," a punishment where a radish was inserted into the rectum of an adulterer</note>. It is recorded in Suidas.

### To carry off the labor.

**To carry off the labor** <note>original Greek: Πόνον ἀναιρεῖν (Ponon anairein)</note>. This was commonly said of those who labored in vain, as if they were to bring back no fruit from their toil except the labor itself. The author is Diogenianus.

### The Milesian Sea Bass.

**The Milesian Sea Bass** <note>original Greek: Λάβραξ μιλήσιος (Labrax milēsios)</note>. This was said of the stupid and the greedy. For the **Labrax** <note>the European sea bass</note> is a type of fish with a wide gape of the mouth, from which it seizes the bait entirely along with the hook in its jaws, and because of this, it is easily caught. Hence, in Plautus, a pimp is given the name **Labrax**. Aristotle numbers this fish among those that live by prey and tearing flesh. Its tongue is bony and fixed, and its heart is triangular. Aristophanes, in the seventh book of Athenaeus, calls the sea bass the wisest of fish:
> The sea bass, the wisest of all fish.
> <note>original Greek: λάβραξ ὁ πάντων ἰχθύων σοφώτατος. This is likely ironic, given the fish's reputation for being easily hooked.</note>

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to complexity (the Labyrinth and Meander), futile or excessive toil (Laborious Labor), and social insults involving greed or infidelity (the Laciadae and the Milesian Sea Bass).</summary>

<page-num>619</page-num>
<header>SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>

It is said that in Miletus, a city in Asia, there are exceptionally large and numerous sea bass <note>original: *labraces*</note> because of a pool that flows into the sea, for this fish delights in fresh water. Aristophanes writes in *The Knights*:

> *But you, having devoured the Milesian sea bass,*
> *Will suffer punishment.* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ὁ λάβραξ ας καταφαγὼν μιλησίους / Κολάσησειας</note> 
> That is: You will not cause a disturbance once you have devoured the Milesian "wolves." For some believe this fish is the one called a "Wolf" <note>original: *Lupus*</note> in Latin.

-> You wash Pelias. <-
-> LVI <-

*You wash Pelias.* <note>original Greek: Λούης τὸν πελίαν (Louēs ton pelian)</note> This was clearly said when someone, having promised safety, instead brings destruction. Or when someone, attempting to be helpful, adds a great evil. It is drawn from the very famous story of Pelias: while his daughters, persuaded by Medea, were eager to restore him to youth, they placed him in a boiling cauldron and killed him. Perhaps it might not be inappropriately said of someone who, led by a false hope, takes up a useless task. For example, if someone relying on the art they call "Alchemical" <note>original: *Alcimicam*</note> promises himself that tin will become silver, or bronze will become gold. This is recorded in the *Collection of Adages* attributed to Plutarch.

-> Again and again the road to Pytho. <-
-> LVII <-

*Again and again the road to Pytho.* <note>original Greek: Αὖθις αὖ πύθωδ' ὁδός (Authis au pythōd' hodos)</note> That is:
The road toward Pytho again and again.
This is said of those who are annoying by asking the same thing about a matter over and over. Just as those ignorant of the way are accustomed to ask anyone they meet about the road. Furthermore, Pytho is a city sacred to Apollo <note>Pytho is the ancient name for Delphi</note> which was visited by many. It appears to be taken from a comedy, for it is an iambic half-line; however, Diogenianus does not indicate from which play, and it does not occur to me. Akin to this is *the Corinth of Zeus* <note>original Greek: ὁ Διὸς κόρινθος; a proverb for tedious repetition</note>.

-> When he sacrifices at Delphi, he eats the meat himself. <-
-> LVIII <-

Plutarch, in the seventh book of his *Symposiacs*, cites this iambic line as a proverb:
*Having sacrificed at Delphi, he buys the meat himself.* <note>original Greek: Δελφοῖσι θύσας αὐτὸς ὠψωνεῖ κρέας</note> That is:
He himself feeds on the meat sacrificed at Delphi.
It shows this was usually said of those who, having invited guests, devour the food set out themselves, so that the guests are only allowed to watch, not to eat. For in the Delphic sacrifices, the one who had sacrificed the victim also ate it. The opposite happened in those sacrifices offered to Hecate <note>goddess of the underworld and crossroads</note>, from which nothing returned to the one who offered it except smoke and noise. Although it can also be taken in a different sense, so that we understand the Delphic priest shares nothing of the victim with the one who gave the victim. Thus it happens sometimes that a greedy guest, or one who has brought several greedy <term>shadows</term> <note>original: *umbrae*; uninvited guests brought along by an invited guest</note> who are like Harpies, devours the entire dinner while the one who invited them goes hungry. The adage can also be twisted to apply to those who themselves enjoy a benefit that they seem to have given to others. As some bishops occasionally grant magnificent priesthoods to their nephews, but only the title goes to the boys, while the revenue goes to the bishops.

-> *To live like an Isthmian*. <-
-> LIX <-

*To live like an Isthmian* <note>original Greek: Ἰσθμιάζειν (Isthmiatzein)</note>. In the past, those who lived somewhat uncomfortably or unhealthily were said to "play the Isthmian," because the time of the Isthmian Games was prone to diseases due to the massive gathering of people. Suidas and Hesychius mention this. Perhaps it might not be absurdly said of those who struggle in vain, on account of the digging through of the Isthmus <note>referring to various failed ancient attempts to build a canal at the Isthmus of Corinth</note> which was unsuccessfully attempted by many. We have spoken of this matter more extensively elsewhere.

-> He must care for it himself. <-
-> LX <-

*He must care for it himself, but in the house.* <note>original Greek: Αὐτῷ μελητέον, ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῷ οἴκῳ</note> Zenodotus says mention of this adage is made in Aristophanes' *The Farmers*, and also in the writings of Plato the Grammarian. It arose from certain very large houses that were put up for rent to those wishing to lease them. From this, it seems appropriate (if indeed it is permitted to follow conjectures where Greek writers offer nothing to follow) to apply it to those who use the property of others too freely, as those who live in rented quarters are accustomed to do.

-> Hyperberetaea. <-
-> LXI <-

*Hyperberetaea* <note>original Greek: Ὑπερβερεταῖα</note>. These were once called things that were quite late, and which only arrived at last with difficulty. Among the Macedonians, the final month of the year was called *Hyperberetaios*. Hence, things that were deferred for a long time were called *Hyperberetaea*, just as among the Latins—

Erasmus uses these to critique social behaviors, including the greed of bishops and the futility of certain labors like alchemy.</summary>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...you might call them "December-like." And <note>original Greek: ἰσοϐέραιτοι (isoberaitoi)</note>, meaning "those who postpone until the day after tomorrow." Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> believes this was a month among the Macedonians which we call October, because summer is then late, and the things that grow then seem to come forth after the legitimate time.

<margin>LXI</margin>
## Ulysses’ crew.

In his *Epistles*, Horace called men who are worthless and addicted to pleasures "Ulysses’ crew," <note>original Latin: *Vlyffis remigium*</note> using it as a proverbial figure of speech. These are men who, like the sailors of Ulysses, could not restrain themselves from Circe’s magic cups, could not be torn away from the Lotus-eaters, and did not abstain from eating the forbidden cattle of the Sun. Hence Homer says in the first book of the *Odyssey*:

By their own follies they perished <gloss>that is, the senseless ones.</gloss> Fools. <note>original Greek: Νήπιοι (Nepioi)</note>

By a similar figure of speech, Horace spoke of the "suitors of Penelope" and the "Alcinous-types" as those who are luxury-loving and negligent of virtue. Likewise, in another place, he calls a man a "Phaeacian," meaning one who is sleek and has well-cared-for skin:

> That I may return a fat Phaeacian.

Regarding the Phaeacians, Homer writes in the eighth book of the *Odyssey*:

> For we always love the feast, the lyre, and the dance,
> And changes of raiment, and warm baths, and the bed. <gloss>that is,</gloss>
> Indeed, the lyre and the dance always captivate us,
> Along with various garments, warm baths, and couches.

The same is said of Penelope’s suitors in the first book of the *Odyssey*:

> These things are their concern: the lyre and song,
> Easy for them, since they devour the livelihood of others without penalty. <gloss>that is,</gloss>
> These things worry them: harmonies and lyres;
> And it is easy for those who devour another's goods with impunity.

<margin>LXII</margin>
## Zaleucus’s law.

<note>original Greek: Ζαλύκου νόμοϚ (Zalykou nomos)</note> i.e., Zaleucus’s law. This was said of an edict or command that was excessively rigid and lacking in human feeling. A certain Zaleucus gave rather harsh laws to the Locrians (those called the Epizephyrians), just as the laws of Draco among the Athenians are said to have been—laws "of a dragon" <note>a pun on Draco's name, which means dragon/serpent</note>, as was said, not of a man. Not unlike these are "Manlian orders" and "the rule of Phalaris." Valerius Maximus records the history in book six, chapter five. For when the son of Zaleucus, according to a law established by his father, was to lose both eyes for the crime of adultery, and the whole city wished to remit the punishment in honor of the father, Zaleucus resisted for some time. Finally, overcome by the prayers of the people, he had one of his own eyes plucked out first, and then one of his son's, thus tempering the measure of the punishment while keeping the law intact.

<margin>LXIII</margin>
## Zopyrus’s talents.

<note>original Greek: Ζωπύρου τάλαντα (Zopyrou talanta)</note> i.e., Zopyrus’s talents. Said of illustrious deeds that should be valued highly. This Zopyrus was a friend of King Darius; he cut off his own nose and ears and bloodied his whole body with whips so that, by these proofs, he might make the Babylonians believe he was an enemy of Darius, by whom he claimed to have been so cruelly treated. Thus, having entered the city of the Babylonians, he betrayed it to Darius. Hence they say Darius said he would rather have one "whole" Zopyrus than capture a hundred Babylons. And when offered a pomegranate, he wished for as many Zopyruses for himself as there were seeds in the fruit, as Herodotus relates in book four. Plutarch mentions this in his *Apophthegms* (Sayings of Kings). Zenodotus also lists the adage.

<margin>LXIV</margin>
## One whip drives all.

<note>original Greek: Μία μάστιξ πάντας ἐλαύνει (Mia mastix pantas elaunei)</note> <gloss>that is,</gloss>
One whip incites everyone.
A heroic half-line of verse used for a business or task that is easily accomplished, specifically by those who are ready and running of their own accord. Perhaps it is also aptly said of those who are driven by the same cause—for instance, the same hope of profit, a common pursuit, or the same love or hatred. It is taken from charioteers. The author is Suidas. Plutarch uses it in his *Life of Lycurgus*, writing that the city of the Lacedaemonians [Spartans] ruled over a willing and consenting Greece <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ σκυτάλης μιᾶς καὶ τρίϐωνοϚ (apo skytales mias kai tribonos)</note>—that is, by a single staff <note>A "scytale" was a staff used by Spartans to decode encrypted messages</note> and a coarse cloak.

<margin>LXV</margin>
## As if a Chalcidian wife bore for us.

<note>original Greek: Ὥσπερ χαλκιδικὴ τέτοκεν ἡμῖν γυνή (Hosper chalkidike tetoken hemin gyne)</note> i.e., As if a Chalcidian wife bore for us. This was said of a woman who had given birth to a great many children. They say there was a certain heroine...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of regional origins for proverbs, specifically focusing on Chalcis and its association with metalworking and abundance, before transitioning into various Greek and Roman adages regarding warfare, fate, and social customs.</meta>

<page-num>621</page-num>
<header>THE SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>

...named Combe, whose surname was Chalcis, because she was the first to fashion bronze weapons. She is said to have borne a hundred children when joined with a man. This is reported in the Euboean annals and is attested by Aristus of Salamis <note>A historian from Cyprus who wrote about Alexander the Great</note>. Some refer this to the city of Chalcis in Euboea, because a huge quantity of bronze weapons and chariots came from the workshops of the Chalcidians. For Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century geographer</note> thinks the city’s name was given because of the bronze workshops <note>In Greek, *chalkos* means bronze</note>. It will be permitted to use this expression when we wish to signify that much litigation, many wars, or many cares have arisen from a certain source.

### The Mede shall not lie in wait for these.
#### LXVII
<term>Τάδε μηδ' ὁ Μῆδος φυλάξει</term> <gloss>that is, The Mede shall not keep watch over these.</gloss> When Xerxes <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE</note> was preparing to lead his army into Greece, as Dicaearchus reports in the works of Zenodotus, the Greeks—desperate in their situation—consumed their resources so that not much would remain for the enemy to take, saying: "The Mede shall not keep watch over these." And so the saying passed into a proverb, used whenever someone spends their own property more lavishly so that it does not fall into the hands of others. For example, if someone were to distribute their money to friends to withdraw it from children who would waste it disgracefully, they might rightly say, <term>ταῦτα μηδ' ὁ Μῆδος φυλάξει</term> <gloss>The Mede shall not keep these.</gloss> Or if a wealthy citizen spends money on constructing buildings so that a greedy prince, threatening the fortunes of all, does not lie in wait for it.

### May you fall into Orcus’s backside.
#### LXVIII
<term>Αἰδὸς πρωκτὸν εἰσπέσοις</term> <gloss>that is, May you fall into the anus of Orcus <note>Orcus is a Roman name for the god of the underworld or the underworld itself</note>.</gloss> This is the speech of one calling down destruction and extreme ruin. it is recorded by Diogenianus. It is kin to those other sayings: <term>βάλλ' ἐς κόρακας</term> <gloss>go to the crows</gloss> and <term>βάλλ' ἐς μακαρίαν</term> <gloss>go to the place of the blessed</gloss> <note>often used ironically to mean "go to your death"</note>.

### Jupiter knows, though unwilling.
#### LXIX
<term>Ἄκων Ζεὺς οἶδεν</term> <gloss>that is, Unwillingly indeed Jupiter knows.</gloss> Used when someone promises something, but does so unwillingly. In some manuscripts I read, <term>ἄκων μὲν, ὡς Ζεὺς οἶδεν</term> <gloss>that is, Unwilling, as Jupiter knows.</gloss> It seems to me it would also be rightly applied when the guilty pay the penalty too late, so that it is similar to what we report elsewhere: <term>Ζεὺς κατὰ δὲ χρόνον εἰς τὰς διαφθοράς</term> <gloss>Jupiter eventually brings about destruction.</gloss> For he who gives or punishes late seems to do so reluctantly.

### Keep watch, or be enriched.
#### LXX
<term>Φρουρεῖν, ἢ πλουτεῖν</term> <gloss>that is, One must keep watch, or be wealthy.</gloss> This used to be said of those who spent lavishly from the property of others. For just as the wealthy, who have ample resources at home, pour them out largely, so soldiers do not spare the wealth of others but squander it vigorously, and what was gained through crime they lose even more wickedly. The Athenians used to hire islanders for high pay to keep watch. Not unlike that other saying:
<term>Ἵππος μὲ φέρει, βασιλεὺς με τρέφει</term> <gloss>that is, The horse carries me, the king feeds me.</gloss>

### Within the seventh.
#### LXXI
<term>Ἐντὸς ἑβδόμης</term> <gloss>that is, Within the seventh.</gloss> Understand "the moon." There was an edict in Athens that they should not lead out the army before the seventh day of the month. Perhaps we shall use this adage correctly whenever we advise that a business must be undertaken early and at its proper time. Zenodotus, Suidas, and Hesychius mention it, but they add nothing further. See whether it might be an allusion to what we have mentioned in another place, <term>ἑβδόμης βοῦς</term> <gloss>the seventh ox</gloss>, and:
<term>Τὴν ἑβδόμην βοῦν ἡ σοφὴ παροιμία</term> <gloss>and the elegant proverb of the seventh ox.</gloss>
This refers to the practice of shaping a flour-paste ox for children who had passed their sixth month, representing the horns of the first appearing moon.

### You are carried in a "cotyle."
#### LXXII
<term>Ἐν κοτύλῃ φορεῖσαι</term> <gloss>that is, You are carried in a cup.</gloss> I suspect this was said of those who were led here and there according to the will of another, wherever they pleased. Or where someone was fostered quite indulgently. The adage is drawn from a type of children's game called <term>ἐν κοτύλῃ</term> <gloss>in the hollow</gloss>. Julius Pollux mentions this in his ninth book *On Vocabulary*. It was of this sort: one person would join and clasp their hands behind their back. Another person, with knees placed upon those hands, would be lifted up, meanwhile covering the eyes of the carrier with their own hands. Being carried in this manner was called being carried <term>ἐν κοτύλῃ</term>, because one was carried by the embrace of the hands. For <term>κοτύλη</term> <note>original: "cotyla"</note> signifies many things to the Greeks, but among them it means the hollow part of the hand. Julius Pollux says this game is also called by other names, such as <term>ἱππάδαν</term> <gloss>the horseman</gloss> and <term>κυβησίνδαν</term> <gloss>the tumbler</gloss>.

### You have rushed into the bees.
#### LXXIII
<term>Εἰς μελίττας ἐκώμασας</term> <gloss>that is, You have leaped into the bees.</gloss> When someone unexpectedly runs into a huge troop...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of proverbs derived from literature and mythology. The preceding text concluded a section on the "swarm of evils," comparing a sudden onset of trouble to disturbing a nest of bees, and mentioned the social practice of young men bursting into banquets, citing Plato's *Symposium* and Terence's *Adelphi*.</meta>

...as if immersed in a swarm of evils, just as usually happens to those who unwittingly fall into a bees' nest. With the bees flying around and attacking from all sides, and pursuing even the one fleeing, whoever falls in hardly gets away without a wound. Moreover, young revelers are accustomed to burst into a banquet of their peers, just as Alcibiades in Plato's works <note>The *Symposium*</note> bursts into Agathon's banquet. And Syrus in the *Adelphi* <note>A comedy by the Roman playwright Terence</note> says of Demea, who rushes into his son's banquet: "He's gone, a dinner-guest not at all convenient, especially for Ctesipho."

### The Helmet of Pluto.

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
<term>Αϊδος κυνῆ</term> <gloss>that is, The Helmet of Pluto</gloss> <note>original: *Orci galea*; the Greek literally means "the dog-skin cap of Hades," referring to a helmet of invisibility</note>. This was habitually said of those who used some artifice to hide themselves. They trace the proverb back to a myth of this kind: When Acrisius <note>The King of Argos</note> consulted an oracle about having male children, he was told that a son would be born from his daughter Danae who would eventually kill him. Terrified by this, he prepared a bronze subterranean chamber in which he kept his daughter shut away, so that she could have no contact with any man. However, Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, seized with love for the maiden, transformed himself into gold and thus, slipping through the opening in the roof into Danae's lap, he made her pregnant. Perseus was born. As soon as the father discovered this, he placed both the mother and the infant in a chest and cast them into the sea. 

Later, as the chest happened by chance to be carried to the island of Seriphos, Dictys took up Perseus and raised him. But Polydectes, Dictys' brother and ruler of the Seriphians, began to love Danae; yet because Perseus was now grown, Polydectes could not possess her. Therefore, having summoned his friends—including Perseus—he said he wished to announce a contest for the hand of Hippodamia, daughter of Oenomaus. Perseus, believing that if he fought with the head of a Gorgon no one could resist him, requested horses among other things. Under the guidance of Mercury <note>Hermes</note> and Pallas <note>Athena</note>, he came to the daughters of Phorcys: Memphes, Ennyo, and Dino <note>The Graeae</note>. They say these sisters were old from the moment they were born, and that the three of them had only one eye and one tooth between them, which they used in turns. 

When Perseus had stolen these, he told the sisters—who were demanding them back—that he would return them if they showed him the way to the Nymphs. These Nymphs possessed winged sandals and a certain <term>cibisis</term> <note>original Greek: *κίβισις*, a leather pouch or wallet</note>. They also had the Helmet of Pluto <note>Hades</note>; whoever wore it saw whomever they wished, yet remained visible to no one. Thus equipped, Perseus—now capable of flight because of the sandals, as we have said—flew down to the Gorgons. There were three sisters: Euryale, Stheno, and Medusa. Their heads were covered with dragon scales, and they had massive tusks like boars, as well as hands and wings with which they traveled through the air. Furthermore, they possessed a power such that those who looked upon them were turned to stone. 

Only Medusa among the three was mortal. Perseus therefore attacked her; fixing his eyes upon his bronze shield—through which he could see the image of the Gorgon—and stretching out his hand, which Pallas guided toward Medusa, he cut off Medusa's head. The other two sisters flew up and pursued Perseus, but because they could not see him due to Pluto's helmet, they turned back. Thus Perseus, returning to Seriphos, attacked Polydectes as he was imploring his friends for help. When they rushed to the king's aid, Perseus showed the Gorgon’s head, and as many as looked upon it were turned to stone. With Polydectes thus removed and Dictys installed in his brother’s place, Perseus gave the Gorgon’s head to Pallas and the helmet to Mercury, along with the pouch and sandals; Mercury, in turn, restored them to the Nymphs. 

I omit the rest of the myth, which Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and collector of proverbs</note> pursues at greater length, since it pertains nothing to the explanation of the adage. Plato uses this in the tenth book of the *Republic*, saying that one ought always to follow honorable things for their own sake, even if one possessed the Ring of Gyges or the Helmet of Pluto. From these words, it is gathered that the meaning of this proverb is the same as that one: <term>γύγης δακτύλιος</term> <gloss>that is, the Ring of Gyges</gloss>. For both were born from a similar myth. Consequently, it will be rightly applied to those who, by some rare good fortune, achieve whatever they wish. Of this kind is also the saying, "The Divine Wand." Origen also used it in his first book against the heretic Celsus, declaring that it was more fitting for Christ, fleeing into Egypt, to withdraw himself from the infancy of Herod than if he had deceived him by hiding under Pluto’s helmet. The adage seems to have flowed from Homer, in whose works, in the fifth book of the *Iliad*, Pallas covers herself with the helmet of Pluto so she might not be seen by Mars <note>Ares</note>:

> <note>original: "τὸν μὲν ἄρης ἐνάριζε μιαιφόνος, αὐτὰρ ἀθήνη / δῦν’ ἄϊδος κυνέην, μή μιν ἴδοι ὄβριμος ἄρης."</note>
> Blood-stained Mars was indeed slaying him; but Pallas
> Put on the helmet of Pluto, lest mighty Mars see her.

The commentator notes that the proverb is said as: <term>δύσασθαι ἄϊδος κυνέην</term> <gloss>that is, To put on the helmet of Pluto.</gloss>

# SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

...concerning a man who strives to do harm through hidden snares. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* says: 
<margin><gloss>For my sake, take these things appropriately named from Hieronymus: the dog-skin helmet of Hades, shaggy with thick hair, then unfold the tricks and arts of Sisyphus.</gloss></margin> <note>original Greek: λαβὲ δ' ἐμοῦ γ' ἕνεκα...; original Latin: Meo causa sumito ab Hieronymo...</note> 
> For my sake, take from Hieronymus,
> The helmet of Pluto, shaggy with black hairs,
> Then unfold the deceits and arts of Sisyphus. <note>Hieronymus was a tragic poet known for dark, "shaggy" imagery; Sisyphus was the mythological archetype of the master trickster.</note>

---

->The beginning of war.<-
<margin>LXXV</margin>
<margin><term>Ἀρχὴ πολέμου</term> <gloss>The beginning of war.</gloss></margin> That is, the origin of a war, where someone is the first to provoke with an injury or an insult. It seems to be taken from the historians, whose custom it is to first set out the causes for which a war was begun. Lucian alluded to this when he said in *The False Prophet*: <margin><gloss>And from this point let him be plunged in, for the war has now begun.</gloss></margin> That is: And as Thucydides says, from here the war now arises. From this, a "non-warrior" <note>original: ἀπόλεμος</note> is said to do harm when he pursues a grudge without having been provoked by any injury.

---

->To lie in leaven.<-
<margin>LXXVI</margin>
<margin><term>Ἐν ζύμῃ κάθηται</term> <gloss>He sits in leaven.</gloss></margin> That is, those who were in a sour mood and swelling with anger were said "to lie in leaven." Plautus says in *The Merchant*: "Your wife lies in leaven," <note>original: Vxor tua in fermento iacet</note> meaning she is swelling with rage. The same author in *Casina*: "Now she is all in leaven: so she swells up at me." This is a well-known metaphor. For leaven <note>yeast or sourdough starter</note> possesses both sourness and the ability to swell. This is why in the Holy Scriptures, "leaven" carries the meaning of malice and rancor.

---

->You are standing on the very stone from which the herald makes his announcement.<-
<margin>LXXVII</margin>
Chrysalus, the slave in Plautus’s *Bacchides*, mocking the old man whom he was defrauding of money, says: "O fool, you do not know you are being sold right now. Indeed, you are standing on that very stone where the herald makes his announcement." This applies when someone is being deceived while present, seeing, and hearing everything. For even today, it is common to say those who are being tricked are being "sold." As for the mention of the "stone," this is drawn from a certain elevated stone that stood in Rome, as established by the testimony of many authors, from which heralds would announce items for sale at auctions. Because of this, in the legal writings of Justinian, the most worthless of men are called "bought from the stone." <note>original: de lapide emptos</note> I have spoken of the "Stone of Colonus" elsewhere.

---

->The sorrows of Ino.<-
<margin>LXXVIII</margin>
<margin><term>Ἰνοῦς ἄχη</term> <gloss>The sorrows of Ino.</gloss></margin> Ino, the daughter of Cadmus, bore two sons to Athamas: Learchus and Melicerta, as well as a daughter, Euryclea. Athamas, however, falling into madness, struck his remaining children with arrows and killed them. Ino threw herself into the sea along with Melicerta. The people of Megara received her with great honor when she was washed up by the waves, performing the proper funeral rites and changing her name to Leucothea <note>the "White Goddess" of the sea</note>. Melicerta was carried to Corinth and buried there by the Corinthians, who established the Isthmian Games in his honor, likewise changing his name to Palaemon. From this arose the proverb, used to signify an intolerable and—so to speak—soul-crushing grief: "The sorrows of Ino." For <term>Achos</term> is the specific word used by the Greeks for a pain that completely stupefies and takes away a person’s senses. Melicrates of Tyre, in the works of the same Zenodotus from whom I retrieved this, tells the myth that gave rise to the proverb in this way: Athamas first had a wife named Nephele, with whom he had two children, Helle and Phrixus. After she died, he married his second wife, Ino. She, acting as a stepmother plotting against Nephele’s children, persuaded the local women to "parch" the seeds before they were sown in the earth—that is, to burn them in a frying pan. When the crop failed and the year produced nothing, Athamas, in this distress, sent to Delphi to consult the oracle. But Ino corrupted the messengers with bribes to say, upon their return, that the god had replied the famine would only be ended if they killed Helle and Phrixus. Thus persuaded, Athamas brought Phrixus and Helle to the altar to be sacrificed. But the gods took pity on them and carried them away through the air on a ram with a golden fleece. Helle, because she did not hold on tight enough to the ram's back, fell into the sea, which is named the Hellespont after her. Phrixus, however, was carried safely to the region of Colchis. Athamas, turned to madness by the anger of the gods, attacked Ino's children, just as we have shown.

---

->In every story, there is also the curse of Daedalus.<-
<margin>LXXIX</margin>
<margin><term>Ἐν παντὶ μύθῳ καὶ Δαιδάλου μύσος</term> <gloss>In every story, there is also the curse of Daedalus.</gloss></margin> This applies to the authors of atrocious crimes or enormous calamities, such that they are frequently mentioned, but never without detestation. They say it arose from this story: Pasiphae, the Queen of Crete...

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to the 'The Helmet of Pluto' (concealment), the origins of war, anger likened to leaven, and the extreme grief of the mythological Ino. It also introduces the proverb regarding the 'curse of Daedalus' in the context of notorious crimes.</summary>

<keywords>Aristophanes, Lucian, Thucydides, Plautus, Ino, Athamas, Phrixus, Helle, Hellespont, Isthmian Games, Roman auctions, leaven of malice, Greek mythology, adages</keywords>

--- Page 748 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Daedalian Curses" begun on the previous page, detailing how the inventor’s ingenuity led to the creation of the Minotaur and the subsequent tragedy of the Athenian tributes. It transitions into a series of proverbs regarding the sharing of resources, the bliss of ignorance, and the experience of immediate danger.</meta>

...seized by love for a bull, she begged Daedalus to fashion a wooden cow for her, imitating a real cow as closely as possible. Enclosed within this, the woman conceived by the bull and gave birth to the Minotaur, an abominable monster. Minos, however, being angry for specific reasons, ordered the Athenians to send seven young women and as many young men every year to be thrown to the Minotaur. Since Daedalus seemed to have provided the cause for all these things, the people commonly called down terrible curses upon him, which is how the matter turned into a proverb.

---

->In turn, let someone also plunder the fire.<-
<margin>LXXX</margin>
<margin><gloss>In the fire, let strength also plunder the fire.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἐν τῷ πυρὶ ἴς καὶ τὸ πῦρ σκυλδυνάτω</note></margin> That is: 
Let someone also plunder the fire in their turn. 
The *Suda* <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world, often cited by Erasmus as "Suidas."</note> warns that this is said of those who do not return a fair share to the community. For when a common resource is entrusted to the hands of one or a few, the largest part remains with those who do the dividing. For what will he not plunder, who plunders even fire? Fire is by its nature so common that you possess it no less after you have shared it with others. Friendship makes all things common, but when it comes to the division, everyone strives to snatch what they can. I am not sure if, through a scribe's error, *skyldynato* <note>original: σκυλδυνάτω</note> was corrupted from *skyldyneto*, which would relate it to an enigma of Pythagoras.

---

->The most pleasant life is in knowing nothing.<-
<margin>LXXXI</margin>
Sophocles, in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*, speaking through the character of Ajax, who had now recovered his senses after a fit of madness, says:
<margin><gloss>For in understanding nothing, life is sweetest. For to not understand is a truly painless evil.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἐν τῷ φρονεῖν γὰρ μηδὲν, ἥδιστος βίος. Τὸ μὴ φρονεῖν γὰρ, κάρτ’ ἀνώδυνον κακόν.</note></margin> That is: 
The life here is most delightful if you know nothing. 
For to know nothing is an evil free from pain. 
Learned men cite this sentiment as a proverb. It is likely, however, that it was a common saying even from the plot of that story which Horace tells concerning a certain man of Argos, who thought himself happier being insane than being sane and full of anxiety: 
"By Hercules, you have killed me, friends, 
not saved me," he said, "since my pleasure has been snatched away, 
and this most welcome error of the mind has been removed by force." 
This harmonizes with the saying from Ecclesiastes: "In much wisdom, there is much indignation," and, "He who adds knowledge, adds labor." Heraclides Ponticus, in the writings of Athenaeus, is the authority for the story that Thrasylaus of Axon, son of Pythodorus, was seized by this kind of madness: he believed all the ships that docked in Piraeus <note>The primary port of Athens.</note> were his own. He would welcome them as they docked with the greatest pleasure. He would see them off as they set sail and follow them with his eyes; in short, he was happy, just as if he were the master of such great wealth. If anything was lost, he did not miss it; if anything was safe, he rejoiced greatly, boasting of his fortune to others, until his brother Crito returned from Sicily and handed the seized man over to a doctor. However, once he had returned to his senses, he claimed he had never lived more pleasantly than when he was held by that mental error. Indeed, while such great pleasures were present, he had never felt any trouble.

---

->Fire in the palm.<-
<margin>LXXXII</margin>
<margin><gloss>Fire in the palm.</gloss> <note>original Greek: πῦρ παλάμῃ</note></margin> That is: Fire in the palm. This was usually said whenever something was understood immediately by someone: as when a joke is told, someone instantly feels it was directed at them. It seems to be taken from those who, in a game, bring fire close to someone else's hands; they, roused by the sudden sensation, would jump back and cause laughter for the spectators.

---

->Left under the knife.<-
<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
One is said to be "left under the knife" who is deserted in immediate danger. The metaphor is taken from a sacrificial victim which is said to be "under the knife" when it is just about to be struck. It is related to those sayings: "Between the altar and the stone," or "Between the hammer and the anvil." Horace says in his *Satires*: 
"The rogue fled, and 
left me under the knife." 
That phrase of Aristophanes' does not differ much from this: "on the chopping block," <note>original Greek: ἐν ἐπιξήνῳ</note>
"I am willing to speak with my head held over the block." 
An *epixenon* <note>term: ἐπίξηνον</note> is a block on which cooks cut meat. In the same play, there is much joking afterward regarding the "chopping block." It is applicable to those who are ready to affirm something even at the risk of their lives.

# SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY
<margin>Signature: Gg</margin>
<meta>catchword: Fictilis (Earthenware)</meta>

### He has worn doors, like the huts of shepherds.
<margin>LXXXIV</margin>
<note>original Greek: τὴν θύραν ἔχει πετριμμένην ὥσπερ αἱ ποίμναι</note> That is: He has a worn-out door, just like the dwellings of shepherds. This is a proverbial irony directed at inhospitable men who are difficult to approach and live only for themselves, always keeping their doors shut; it refers to shepherds because they are removed so far from human commerce that hardly anyone ever visits them. Diogenianus mentions this. <note>Diogenianus was a 2nd-century Greek grammarian whose collection of proverbs was a primary source for Erasmus.</note>

### There is need of celery.
<margin>LXXXV</margin>
<note>original Greek: τὸ σελίνου δεῖται</note> That is: There is a need for celery. <note>The Greek term *selinon* can refer to celery or wild parsley.</note> They used to speak this way whenever they hinted at a fatal disease or when the danger of death was imminent. This is because, in ancient times, the tombs of the deceased were crowned with celery. Plutarch says in his *Table Talk*: "And of those who are completely failing in health, we say they have 'need of celery.'" The same author mentions the proverb and adds the reason in his *Life of Timoleon*. However, there is a joke beneath the adage, alluding to the crowns given to victors, which were also made of celery, especially in the Isthmian Games, as Diphilus testifies in Athenaeus, Book 6:
"We fight over celery as if at the Isthmian Games."

### Colder than Ialemus.
<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἰαλέμου ψυχρότερος</note> That is: Colder than Ialemus. This is rightly said of a song, a speech, an argument, a joke, or any such thing that is excessively "cold" <note>In classical rhetoric, "cold" meant dull, uninspired, or lacking wit.</note>. Some say Ialemus was the name of a mourner’s voice, for the Greeks use the word *ialemizein* to mean "to lament." Euripides, in *The Trojan Women*, uses "Ialemus" for wailing and grief: "What wailing, what grief, and tears upon tears are distilled in our halls." And Aristophanes—the grammarian, I believe—in his *Attic Words* quoted by Athenaeus, says: "At weddings, there is the Hymenæus; in mourning, the Ialemus." Others report that Ialemus was a son of the Muse Calliope, but an unfortunate man of no value, especially in singing where he was excessively "cold"; hence they call a dull and miserable song an "Ialemus-ditty." Martial, likewise joking about a certain dull orator, says that he is the only one fit to cool the hot Baths of Nero. Hesychius indicates that the proverb is also uttered this way: "More piteous than Ialemus." He also notes that "Ialemus" is said of anything that is of no value, just as the Latins use the word *Naeniae* <note>Nursery rhymes or trifles</note>, although that word properly refers to funeral dirges.

### You are drawing from the ground.
<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: χαμαὶ ἀντλεῖς</note> That is: You draw from the ground. This was said of labor spent in vain. For there is nothing you can draw from the soil—that is, from the very bottom of a well—if it is dry. It appears this can be said whenever, once a supply is exhausted, not much remains to be drawn out. Zenodotus mentions it.

### To creep on the ground.
<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
A speech "creeps on the ground" when it is more cramped and lowly than it ought to be, always as if lying down and never rising up. Horace says:
> I would not prefer my "conversations"
> That creep along the ground, over the recording of great deeds.

The same author says in *The Art of Poetry*:
> He creeps on the ground, being too safe and fearful of the storm.

This metaphor is either taken from sailors or from those who, prostrating themselves on the earth, crawl so that the whirlwind does not sweep them away while standing. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration against the Eunomians, turned this toward men, showing that it is not for just anyone to discuss divine matters: "The matter is not so cheap nor for everyone, especially those who walk upon the ground." Although nothing prevents one from understanding "common and humble things or actions" here as well. Very similar to this, or perhaps the same, is what Pindar says in the *Olympian Odes*: "That you might touch upon words that fall to the ground." Also in the *Pythian Odes*: "He did not cast forth a word that falls to the ground." He seems to have taken the metaphor from birds flying not far from the earth, which Pindar also attributes to jackdaws: "Jackdaws feed on lowly things." To this, the eagle in the clouds would be the opposite.

### Additions of vegetables.
<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: δι' τῶν λαχάνων προσθήκας</note> That is: Add-ons of vegetables. Used for a matter of no importance. It seems to be taken either from the vegetables placed on the table as a surely cheap food, or from the "extra portions" of vegetables that stingy or poor buyers sometimes demand. The author is Diogenianus.

<summary>This page explores several Greek and Latin proverbs concerning antisocial behavior, the symbolism of death (celery), and literary styles that lack elevation ("creeping on the ground"). It also clarifies the mythological and cultural origins of terms like Ialemus and the Isthmian crowns.</summary>
<keywords>celery, death omens, Ialemus, cold humor, Horace, Pindar, literary style, jackdaws, cheapness, Erasmian adages</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES

### A man of clay.

<margin>XC</margin>
**A man of clay.** <note>original Greek: Κεράμειος ἄνθρωπος</note> That is, a man made of earthenware: soft, weak, and fragile. The metaphor is drawn from ceramic vessels, which are easily shattered. It is closely related to the saying, **A man is a bubble.** In certain manuscripts, I read "a potter man" <note>original: κεραμεὺς ἄνθρωπος</note>; in others, "pottery man" <note>original: κέραμος ἄνθρωπος</note>. This last version pleases me more. For "Cerameus" sounds like a potter, whereas "ceramos" refers to the clay vessel itself. Similarly, we speak of a "man of fig-wood" <note>meaning cheap or useless</note>, or of iron, wax, oak, or adamant. Conversely, when we want something to appear extraordinary, we call it **golden.** Hence that frequent phrase among poets, **Golden Venus** <note>original Greek: χρυσῆ ἀφροδίτη</note>, and **the golden face of Justice**, and **the golden eye of Justice.** That is, the golden countenance and the golden eye of justice, which Athenaeus relates from Pindar (if I am not mistaken) in his twelfth book. Likewise, even today, we speak of **Golden words** or **Gem-like character.** Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his *Academic Questions*, speaking of the booklet Crantor wrote on grief, says: "For it is not large, but it is **golden** <note>original Latin: aureolus</note>, and as Panaetius instructed Tubero, it should be learned word-for-word." Whatever is cheap, the Greeks call **clay-like** <note>original Greek: κεραμεῖον or κεράμενον</note>. Thus, Saint Paul calls men **earthen vessels**: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels" <note>original Greek: ἔχομεν τὸν θησαυρὸν τοῦτον ἐν σκεύεσιν ὀστρακίνοις; see 2 Corinthians 4:7</note>. Marcus Tullius, in his sixth speech against Verres, says: "Then they said to the praetor that they had taken them because they thought the cups they had heard about were of some value, belonging to Pamphilus. But they found it to be a **muddy business** <note>original: luteum negocium</note>, not worthy of being among Verres's silver." And elsewhere, he calls a man **muddy** <note>original: Luteum hominem</note> to describe someone contemptible and of no value; sometimes he calls the person simply **Mud**.

### The tablet of the Hipparchs.

<margin>XCI</margin>
**The tablet of the Hipparchs.** <note>original Greek: Ἱππάρχων πίναξ</note> It is appropriate to use this whenever we signify that a mistake will not go unpunished. The adage originated with the Syracusans. Among them, it was the custom for the **Hipparchs**—that is, the commanders of the cavalry—to write the names of soldiers who had deserted their rank upon tablets. Zenodotus mentions this. Hesychius indicates that among the Spartans, the Hipparch was the one put in charge of the youth. He would note down on a tablet those who had done anything unseemly.

### A one-sided case.

<margin>XCII</margin>
**A one-sided case.** <note>original Greek: Ἑτερομολία δίκη</note> Among the Greeks, a "Heteromolia" case is one argued by only one party, with no one present to contradict them; it is derived from "the other party's coming" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου μολεῖν</note>, because only one side arrives. It is very similar to the **deserted case** <note>original: ἔρημη δίκη</note>. It may be used quite elegantly whenever someone condemns an absent person; for instance, when we criticize the books of the dead, one might rightly call it a "one-sided case." In Hesychius, it is expressed as a "single-sided case" <note>original: ἑτερόμοννον δίκη</note>, though whether that is the correct spelling, I do not know.

### The song of Harmodius.

<margin>XCIII</margin>
**The song of Harmodius.** <note>original Greek: Ἁρμοδίου μέλος</note> This was said of mournful and sad things. It is very similar to **The song of Admetus** <note>original: Ἀδμήτου μέλος</note>. Aristophanes uses it in several places, including the play titled *The Acharnians*:
"Never shall he sing the Harmodius song at my house." <note>original: οὐ γ’ παρ’ ἐμοὶ ποτε τὸν ἁρμόδιον ἄσεται</note>
The commentator indicates it was a type of song usually sung at crossroads in honor of Harmodius and Aristogiton, because they had overthrown the tyranny of the Pisistratids. The beginning of the song was: "Dearest Harmodius, you are not yet dead." <note>original: Φίλτατε ἁρμόδι’ οὔ πω τέθνηκας</note> It is recorded by Suidas and Diogenianus.

### He does not sing his father's songs.

<margin>XCIV</margin>
**He does not sing his father’s songs.** <note>original Greek: οὐ πατρῳϊκὰ αὐλεῖ μέλη</note> This was cast at someone who degenerated from the character of his ancestors. Children are usually delighted by the little songs of their elders, which they learned as small boys. Terence says in *The Brothers*: "By Pollux, Aeschinus, that was not a fatherly thing you did." <note>original: haud paternum istuc dedisti</note>

### This is no contest for a wild olive branch.

<margin>XCV</margin>
**This is no contest for a wild olive branch.** <note>original Greek: οὐ φυλίας ὁ ἀγών</note> This is used whenever the matter at hand is not about trifles, nor about glory or crowns, but about a serious matter and money. Indeed, in many contests, the prize of victory was a crown of olive, oak, or some other foliage. Diogenianus mentions this.

### Spear and herald’s staff.

<margin>XCVI</margin>
**Spear and herald’s staff.** <note>original Greek: Δόρυ κηρύκιον</note> This was commonly said whenever someone was simultaneously threatening and inviting reconciliation. It arose from an oracle, which is reported as follows:
"To a man of the bridge, a lover of the house..." <note>The text ends here mid-sentence.</note>

# THE SECOND CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY

<note>original Latin: CHIL. SECVNDÆ CENTVRIA X</note>

**Gg 2** <note>Signature mark for the printer</note>

### To a Gephyraean man, a house is pleasing.
<note>original Latin: Viro Gephyræo grata est domus</note>

The Gephyraeans <note>An ancient clan that migrated to Athens, famous for the "tyrannicides" Harmodius and Aristogeiton</note> were warned that they should follow the Athenian army and stay wherever they saw the troops become exhausted. Thus, when the Athenians were being attacked by Eumolpus, the Gephyraeans began a march toward Tanagra. They maintained an appearance of being prepared for both outcomes: their leader carried a herald’s staff <note>original Latin: caduceum; a wand signifying peace and diplomacy</note> in front, while the armed youth followed behind. In this way, they seemed to be seeking peace while simultaneously being prepared for war if anyone should provoke them. This is recorded by Suidas <note>The Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> and mentioned by Polybius in the fourth book of his *Histories*. He writes: "They sent Aridices as an ambassador to the Byzantines, and with him Polemocles with three triremes, wishing—as the proverb says—to send the spear and the herald's staff to the Byzantines at the same time." This is very similar to an elegant phrase used by Saint Jerome: **To seek peace with a shield.**

->**To blame the bellies of roosters.**<-
->XCVII<-

**To blame the bellies of roosters.** <note>original Greek: Ἀλεκτρυόνων μέμφεσθαι κοιλίαν</note> This is said of gluttons and those who consume a great deal of their wealth through luxury. This animal is said to have a remarkably hot stomach, so that it digests everything immediately. Aristophanes writes in *The Wasps*:
"He said I had the stomach of a rooster,
For it quickly swallows down the silver."
People of this kind are called by the Greeks "devourers of substance" <note>original Greek: καταφαγᾶς τῶν οὐσιῶν</note>; the verb implies a more aggressive "devouring" than the standard word. Furthermore, they indicate the greatest and most rapid wastefulness with the word **to vanish** <note>original Greek: ἀφανίζειν</note>, which means to consume something so thoroughly that no trace remains. Aeschines uses all these terms, but most frequently the last, in his speech *Against Timarchus*: "He made everything vanish."

->**A burning garment.**<-
->XCVIII<-

**A burning garment.** <note>original Greek: Αἰθὼς πέπλος</note> Or, as it is read in other copies, **Incense in a garment** <note>original Greek: ἐξ ὧν πέπλος</note>. Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian and literary critic</note> records that this was commonly said of those who stir up sedition and sow slanders. He believes the proverb arose from the robe stained with the blood of Nessus the Centaur. When Hercules put on this robe, which had been sent by his wife Deianira, he was consumed by a "sacred fire" <note>An ancient term for a burning, spreading skin disease or intense inflammation</note> and perished. He recounts the myth as follows: After Hercules had defeated and slaughtered the rest of the Centaurs, Nessus alone escaped. He came to the river Euenus, where he lived on the bank and made a living ferrying travelers across. 

It then happened that Hercules was traveling to Trachis to visit Ceyx, accompanied by Deianira. After Hercules had already crossed the river himself, he entrusted Nessus to carry Deianira across. But while ferrying her, the Centaur began to offer violence to the woman. As soon as Hercules realized this—likely because she cried out—he pierced Nessus’s chest with an arrow. Feeling the wound was fatal and that he could not escape death, Nessus called the woman to him. "If you wish," he said, "to prepare a most effective love charm to keep Hercules inflamed with love for you—or to bring him back to you if he ever falls for another—make sure you rub him with my blood." 

Persuaded by this, she saved the blood flowing from Nessus’s wound. Later, after Hercules had arrived at Trachis and then set out again to capture the city of Oechalia, he took the girl Iole as a captive. Planning to sacrifice victims to his father Jupiter for his success, he sent a message to Deianira, asking her to send him a magnificent robe. She, having learned of the capture of Iole and fearing that Hercules might value the girl more than herself—as is the way of jealous women—sent him the robe dipped and soaked in Nessus’s blood, believing she was sending a love potion. 

Dressed in this, Hercules performed the sacred rite. However, when the robe grew warm, the poison was activated and began to burn his body severely. He tried to tear it off, but it had already adhered so deeply that it could not be removed without tearing away his very flesh. Distracted by these agonies, Hercules was brought to Trachis. Meanwhile, Deianira, realizing what had happened, committed suicide by hanging. Hercules then commanded Hyllus—his grown son by Deianira—to take Iole as his wife. This done, he built a pyre on Mount Oeta and climbed upon it. Furthermore, when he gave the command, none of Hercules’s companions dared to set the fire, clearly fearing the contagion. A certain shepherd happened to be found who set the fire, and to him, Hercules gave his weapons as a reward for this service. They say that while the pyre was burning, a cloud surrounded Hercules with thunder, and he was thus taken up into the company of the gods. 

The proverb could also be applied, not unreasonably, to that robe which Medea sent as a gift to Jason's new bride, which was imbued with poisons. Some believe it was infected with naphtha <note>A flammable liquid hydrocarbon</note>. Thus, when the torches were brought near according to the marriage rite, the flame leaped across, equally...
<note>catchword: riter (meaning "equally" / "pariter")</note>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...it cruelly burned both the girl and the father who wished to help her. <note>original Latin: *exussit*; Erasmus is referring to the myth of Medea, who sent a poisoned, burning robe to Creusa, the new bride of her ex-husband Jason.</note> Mention of this event is made by Euripides in the tragedy titled *Medea*. As I have testified many times, had I not feared that I might seem to have passed over these sorts of fables through negligence—since they are found in common collections—I would by no means have included them here.

<margin>XCIX</margin>
->**The old age of a lion is more excellent than the youth of fawns.**<-
<note>original Greek: Γῆρας λέοντος κρεῖσσον ἀκμαίων νεβρῶν</note> That is: An old lion is more powerful than a vigorous fawn. It is cited in Stobaeus from the poet Hippothöon. The old age of a brave and energetic man is more excellent than the youth of certain idle and weak young men. It becomes more elegant if applied metaphorically: for instance, if one prefers the intellect of a learned and experienced old man to the intellect of an uneducated youth. It may also be said, not unsuitably, regarding a "raw and green" <note>An idiom for a healthy, vigorous old age</note> old age that still prevails in mental strength; to this applies that line of Euripides from his play *Ion*:
**Slow indeed of foot, but swift of mind.**
<note>original Greek: τὸ τοῦ ποδὸς μὲν βραδὺ, τὸ δὲ νόου ταχύ</note>
To the same point belongs this line from his *Andromache*:
**For even an old man, if he be stout-hearted, is better than many young men.**
<note>original Greek: πολλῶν νέων γὰρ, κἂν γέρων εὔψυχος ᾖ κρείσσων</note>
And Aristophanes says somewhere:
**I consider my own old age to be better than many long-haired youths.**
<note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ τὸ μὸν νομίζω γῆρας εἶναι κρεῖττον ἢ πολλῶν κικίνων νεανιῶν</note>

<margin>C</margin>
->**Nakeder than a peg.**<-
<note>original Greek: γυμνότερος πασσάλου</note> This hyperbole was said of a man in extreme poverty. For we even strip the bark from wooden pegs <note>original Latin: *paxillis*; small wooden pins or stakes</note>.

# THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND OF THE PROVERBS OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>I</margin>
### Herculean labors.
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'H' depicting a classical scene, possibly Hercules or a mythological figure, within an ornate square frame.</image-desc>
**Herculean labors.** <note>original Greek: Hρακλέιοι πόνοι</note> This is understood in two ways. Firstly, as many and vast tasks that require the strength of a Hercules, just as Catullus used it: "But to seek you now," he says, "would be a labor for Hercules." Likewise Propertius: "Then when you have endured those labors which fame says were Hercules'." And again elsewhere: "Not a labor for Alcides" <note>Alcides is another name for Hercules, referring to his grandfather Alcaeus</note>. 

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the second book of *On Ends*: "But when you were deserving of the highest praise from all nations, when you were bringing help and safety to the needy, I would have required of you to endure even the 'afflictions' of Hercules." (For our ancestors called even the labors of a god by that most somber word "afflictions" <note>original Latin: *erumnas*; a term suggesting toil mixed with sorrow or hardship</note>, as they were not to be shunned.)

Secondly, "Herculean labors" are said to be those which are of such a kind that they bring the greatest benefits to others, but bring almost no fruit to their author, except for a little bit of fame and a great deal of envy. And they think this happened by a certain fate, because Hercules was believed to have been **born on the fourth day of the moon** <note>original Greek: ἐν τετράδι γεννηθῆναι</note>, as has been said in another place. Homer, in the poetic manner, casts the blame on the goddess Ate <note>Goddess of mischief and ruin</note> and on Juno, who, being hostile to Hercules as the son of a mistress, exposed him to all dangers. 

Therefore, the Herculean labors are celebrated and even enumerated by the poets. By far the most difficult and greatest of all these was the Lernaean Hydra, a persistent and almost invincible evil even for him who had already conquered everything else. Horace indicates clearly enough in his *Epistles* that the ancients wished to express **envy** through this symbol, when he says:
"He who crushed the dire Hydra,
And subdued the well-known monsters with fatal labor,
Found that envy is only mastered at the very end of life."
For this most foul plague is accustomed to be the companion of the most beautiful deeds; and extraordinary virtue follows envy no differently than a shadow follows a body, as Josephus aptly said in his work *On the Capture of Judea*: **It is impossible for success to escape envy.** For who can escape the shadow of envy, unless they also [escape] vir...
<meta>The catchword "tis" at the bottom suggests the next page continues the word "virtutis" (of virtue).</meta>

<summary>Erasmus concludes his second thousand adages and begins the third, opening with a lengthy exploration of "Herculean labors." He interprets the myth as a metaphor for great works that benefit society but bring the author nothing but exhaustion and the "Hydra" of envy.</summary>

THIRD CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY 629

...escaped the light: these two are connected to each other, and the worst thing accompanies the best of all things. <note>Erasmus is arguing that great glory and great envy are inseparable companions.</note> Consequently, Pindar seems to have written with good reason:

> To be distressed by envy when good deeds are celebrated.
<note>original Greek: Τό δ᾽ ἄχνυσθαι φθόνῳ ἀμφιβοημένον τὰ καλὰ ἔργα. From Pindar’s *Pythian Odes*.</note>

He took it heavily and with indignation, for it is indeed a most unworthy thing that noble deeds should be repaid with the "reward" of envy. Nor indeed do those ancient writers seem to have assigned the symbol of the Water-snake <note>original Latin: *Excetrae*; referring to the Hydra of Lerna</note> to envy without a certain fitness. Firstly, it is a swamp-dwelling evil, because—as even the investigators of natural causes record—those endowed with a low and abject mind are more subject to this disease; these are the people in whom the blood is colder. For that reason, in the works of Naso <note>The poet Ovid</note> as well:

<margin>The House of Envy.</margin>
> The house of Envy is hidden in deep valleys,
> Lacking sun, accessible to no wind,
> Gloomy, and full of sluggish cold, and one which
> Always lacks fire, and always abounds in darkness.
<note>original Latin: *Inuidiae domus est in uallibus imis...* from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note>

Nor indeed is the struggle against a simple portent, but one armed with a hundred heads; if someone cuts off any one of them, two immediately sprout up in its place. Such is the nature of envy: if you struggle against it, you irritate it more and more; if you ever try to suppress it with the splendor of virtue, it rises up more fiercely and swells. If you cut it down here, it springs up larger there. It cannot be extinguished bit by bit; it is barely overwhelmed at last. Truly, that success falls to very few, and hardly even to Hercules himself. For although spite, like fire, seeks high places, there is nonetheless something so perfect and illustrious that envy cannot reach it. Horace boasts that he had reached such a place when he says:

> And greater than envy.
<note>original Latin: *Inuidiaque maior*. From Horace's *Odes*.</note>

->And again elsewhere,<-

> I am bitten even less by the tooth of envy.
<note>original Latin: *Etiam dente minus mordeor inuido*.</note>

Now truly, what else is it that those secret detractors are accustomed to vomit out against those who, striving to benefit the world through most beautiful labors, undertake something noble, if not pure venom and a poison more than lethal? For to generous and exalted minds, their own reputation—which these detractors attack—is usually much dearer and more ancient than life itself. Furthermore, what the fables of the pagans signified under the riddle of Hercules, the history of the Hebrews hints to us under the veil of Joseph. For what Lerna was to the former, the envy of his brothers was to the latter. This is how Philo interprets it in his book titled *The Life of a Politician*. <note>original Greek: πολιτικός βίος (*Politikos Bios*). Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher who harmonized scripture with Greek philosophy.</note> He considers Joseph to represent the person who handles the rudders of the state. He uses this argument: that while Joseph was still a shepherd, he had already earned his father’s favor through right actions and, at the same time, stirred up the rivalry of his brothers against him. For what else is administering a Republic than acting as a shepherd? Indeed, even Homer, whom Philo also cites there, repeatedly calls a king the:

**Shepherd of the people.**
<note>original Greek: ποιμένα λαῶν (*poimena laon*).</note>

In fact, gratitude responds more spitefully to the good deeds of no one than those who deserve well of the common people. But whereas Hercules was consumed by Greek fire, <note>original Latin: *igni Graecanico*; a reference to the poisoned Shirt of Nessus which eventually led to Hercules' death/apotheosis.</note> Joseph attained his goal through the greatness of his benefactions and the favor of the divine power, so that he overwhelmed envy and eventually had those very men as suppliants whom he had previously endured as rivals. They confessed that they now owed their lives to him, against whose life they had previously laid snares. Therefore, princes who handle public business ought to be endowed with such a mind that they look only to the common utility according to this example. They should not conduct their magistracy for themselves as if it were a shopkeeper's trade, nor should they wish to trap people in the snares of laws from wherever they perceive some profit can be snatched. Rather, they should deserve well of the good without charge; they should wage constant war with monsters—that is, with vices—content with the conscience of right-doing alone, as if it were a sufficiently great reward for noble deeds.

If fame responds spitefully to your merits, if spite hisses in secret, if the Lernean beast breathes its poison from all three hundred heads at once, then at last it will be proof of a truly sublime and unconquered mind: to strive no less lazily toward immortal praise, to consult the interests of others even at the cost of one's own greatest inconveniences, and to consider this the most beautiful and greatest fruit of virtue: if one is permitted to benefit as many as possible as much as possible. In this part, so far as is permitted to a mortal, one imitates the immortal Divinity. Since no thanks and no service can return from us to Him, He imparts His munificence to all—the grateful and the ungrateful, the worthy and the unworthy alike—with a goodness so native and genuine, like the sun, looking to this one fruit: that He might make as many as possible participants in Himself. But just as no profit from good deeds can flow back to God, so the annoyance of ingratitude cannot reach Him. For mortals, it often happens that for the highest merits they receive the highest...

<sig>Gg 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: ...highest [blame/injury] (mam / malorum)</meta>

<summary>Erasmus discusses the symbolic link between the Hydra and Envy, comparing the labors of Hercules to the biblical trials of Joseph. He argues that true leaders must persevere in virtue and public service despite the inevitable "poison" of detractors, following the selfless example of God.</summary>
<keywords>Envy (Invidia), Hercules, Hydra of Lerna, Joseph (biblical), Philo of Alexandria, Public Service, Virtue, Ovid, Horace, Pindar, Leadership, Selflessness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s reflection on the adage "Herculean Labors." Having established Hercules as a symbol of the struggle against envy, Erasmus now shifts to a personal defense of the scholar’s life. He argues that the grueling work of restoring ancient texts is a modern Herculean task, often met with more scorn than gratitude.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...the greatest envy, and bring back the greatest inconvenience. But if this title "Herculean" is owed to the labors of men, it certainly seems most owed to those who labor in restoring the monuments of ancient and true literature. Indeed, they undertake incomparable things despite the incredible difficulty of the task, yet they stir up the greatest envy of the common people against themselves. While noble things have always been subject to envy, this is especially true of novelty—not only among the unlearned, but even among the scholarly. Nowhere are we more ungrateful, more envious, more peevish, and nowhere less candid than in weighing the labors of those to whom, in my mind at least, no sufficiently worthy thanks can ever be returned. The unlearned ignore them; the semi-learned laugh at them; the learned—if you except a few, the foremost indeed, but still only a few—partly envy them and partly carp at them with more moroseness. And while many things correctly stated are overlooked, if by some chance the author should slip once or twice (for who does not slip eventually?), that is the only thing they note, the only thing they remember. 

Go on then, and redeem this magnificent prize with so many long nights of wakefulness, so much sweat, and so many hardships! Renounce the common pleasures of human life, neglect your family estate, spare neither your appearance, nor sleep, nor health. Accept the loss of your eyesight, summon premature old age, and despise the toll on your life, so that you may stir up the hatred of many against you and the envy of more, and so that in exchange for so many sleepless nights, you may carry away a few jeers. Who, I ask, would not be deterred from undertaking such labors, unless he were of a truly Herculean mind, able to do and suffer anything out of a desire to help others? 

To tell the truth, this thought moved my mind somewhat, and in the midst of exhausting these labors <note>original Latin: *exantlandis laboribus*; a term often used for draining a swamp or enduring trials</note>, a certain weariness arose. I thought of how maliciously fame responds to the great men our age has seen—even those who have been dead for some time—and how irreverently they are despised by those whom you might truly call "dwarfs," <note>original Latin: *ningos*, likely a variant or error for *nanos* (dwarfs)</note> who "offer them the chamber pot," <note>An idiom meaning to treat someone with utter contempt or as a lowly servant</note> as the saying goes. I thought of how ungratefully they are criticized by the semi-learned, and how few there are even among the scholarly who praise them candidly and with a full mouth. One finds something missing, another finds something he does not approve of, another attacks their life, and another praises so fastidiously that it would have been better to have criticized. 

Furthermore, none judge more unfairly than either the semi-learned, who measure another's learning by their own and think whatever they themselves have not learned must be condemned; or the learned, who have not yet tasted this kind of labor. For these people are clearly, according to the Greek proverb, <margin>To shear the Achaean from the tail. <note>original Greek: ἀπ᾿ οὐρᾶς κείρεσθαι ἀχαιός. A proverb for starting at the wrong end or judging without understanding the whole.</note></margin> standing themselves on the shore, watching the skill and danger of the sailor at their leisure. If they had made the trial themselves, they would read the late-night works of others with less disdain and more forgiveness. 

Since I see this happening to such giants in the literary world, or rather heroes, what should I predict for myself? I am not unaware that everything of mine is mediocre compared to theirs, or to speak more truly, nothing at all—especially in this genre of writing, in which there is much more labor than anyone could easily guess who has never made the attempt himself. Secondly, for many reasons, slipping is very easy. Finally, nowhere will a critic more quickly find something to miss. Therefore, I do not think it will be out of place if, since the topic itself seems to have prompted me, I discuss a few things regarding these matters—not to boast of my own talent or show off my industry, but to make the reader more fair toward me. And certainly, anyone will be much less unfair who considers with what immense sweat and what infinite difficulties this "forest of adages," however rough it may be, has stood for me.

For here is the first calculation: the antiquity of the things themselves, sought out not just from Evander or the Aborigines <note>The earliest legendary inhabitants of Italy</note>, but <margin>From the oars. <note>original Greek: ἐκ κωπῶν. Meaning from the very beginning or the foundations.</note></margin> as the Greeks say, even from the very Age of Saturn <note>The mythical Golden Age, signifying the deepest antiquity</note>, and if there is anything even older than this. From this it happens that most things are far removed from the customs of our times, <margin>Twice through all. <note>original Greek: δὶς διὰ πασῶν. Referring to the full musical scale; meaning a complete or vast distance.</note></margin> <margin>Twice from the hearth. <note>original Greek: δὶς ἀφ᾿ ἑστίας. Meaning to start over from the very beginning.</note></margin> as they say. Consequently, to understand what an adage means, you must either divine it and seek out some "swimmer god" <note>Erasmus refers to a "Delian diver," someone capable of reaching the deep and hidden meanings of obscure texts</note> or seek the explanation from ancient authors. And from which authors, exactly? Not from one or two, or a certain few, as happens in other subjects. For example, if someone sets out to write about the art of speaking, he has certain suitable authors, and not very many of them, whom it is sufficient to imitate. But here, it was necessary to—I will not say unroll—but to curiously and deeply shake out and search every writer, ancient and recent, good and bad alike, in both languages, in every branch of discipline, and briefly, in every kind of writing. Indeed, adages, like tiny gems, sometimes escape the eyes of the hunter because they are small, unless you look very sharply. Moreover, they are not out in the open, but most are hidden, so that they must be dug out before they can be collected. Who can sufficiently estimate how much infinite labor it is to search for such tiny things through every sea and land? Scarcely a human lifetime...
