### THE THIRD THOUSAND, FIRST CENTURY

...it would hardly suffice for you to examine and turn over so many poets of both languages, so many grammarians, orators, dialecticians, sophists, historians, mathematicians, philosophers, and theologians—someone might grow weary just listing their titles—and to do so not once, but up and down, as the matter required, rolling the **stone of Sisyphus** <note>A mythological figure condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity; a metaphor for endless, fruitless labor.</note>. Now this, I think, everyone sees and admits is a massive task. But how small a portion of our sweat is that? Look, there remains an even larger army of interpreters, in whose work the laziness and negligence of others, and even the ignorance of some, have added no small burden to our labors. For even these authors must be turned over, surely so that you may sometimes pick **gold from the dung** <note>original: "aurum è stercore"; a phrase attributed to Virgil, meaning to find something valuable in a poor quality source.</note>.

Come now, why should I mention the prodigious corruption of books, which has so overtaken all manuscripts, Latin and Greek alike, that whatever you touch to cite, it hardly ever happens that you don't strike a manifest error or suspect a hidden one? There a new sweat begins: copies must be explored and collected—and not just a few—so that from many, one more corrected version might emerge, or you might guess what is true and genuine by comparing many. This too would be bearable, if it didn't happen almost every time you cite something. And one must cite everywhere. 

To these many things, add this factor—one I think should by no means be scorned—that the works of the ancients, from which proverbs were drawn like from springs, are for the most part lost. Indeed, both types of Greek Comedy <note>Old and New Comedy.</note> have utterly perished, except for **Aristophanes** alone. Likewise, Latin tragedy is lost, except for **Seneca** alone. Perhaps even this could be tolerated if only the works of those who interpreted the proverbs they collected with commentaries were still extant. Among their number are **Aristotle, Chrysippus, Clearchus, Didymus, and Tarrhaeus**, and several others with them, of whose work not even the smallest fragment has reached us. 

There remain for us, therefore, certain more recent authors who are as negligent and lacking in selection as they are meager and mutilated, such as **Zenobius, Diogenianus, and Suidas**. I haven't yet decided whether we owe them ill-will, because they handed down to us so few and naked snippets from such perfect and copious authors, or gratitude, because through their zeal fragments of antiquity reached us at all—unless one thinks the loss of the originals is due to these epitomes <note>Summaries or abridgments.</note>. Just as some Latinists usually blame **Florus** for the loss of **Livy**, **Justin** for **Trogus Pompeius**, **Justinian** for Imperial Law, and the author of the *Sentences* <note>Peter Lombard, whose "Sentences" became the standard medieval theology textbook.</note> for the loss of ancient theology; and in my opinion, they do so not entirely without reason.

What about the fact that these authors disagree so much that they often write conflicting things? This adds yet another weight to your labors: you must not only turn over various interpreters on the same subject but inspect, compare, weigh, and judge them again and again. Now consider this also: in other books, there is often room for genius, so that the pleasure of discovery or "giving birth" to ideas is present; you can complete some portion of the work in any place or time by mental effort, and the faster your genius, the quicker you finish what you started. Here, as if tied to a **mill** <note>A metaphor for monotonous, grinding labor.</note>, you are not allowed to depart even a "breadth of a foot," as they say, from the manuscripts. 

For almost the entire business depends on the supply of manuscripts, especially Greek ones, the scarcity of which everyone knows. Thus, you partly wear out your eyes on decaying volumes, covered in mold, torn, mutilated, and gnawed everywhere by moths and beetles; then, not infrequently, they are extremely difficult to read—briefly, the kind of work where someone who spends much time on them easily contracts a certain decay and old age himself—and partly you depend on others' books. How much this matters, those who have tried it will recognize immediately, even if I am silent. 

Not to mention that if there is any pleasure in commentaries of this kind, it belongs entirely to the reader; it doesn't touch the writer at all, except for that hateful and ever-repetitive labor of collecting, sweeping together, explaining, and translating. Yet pleasure is the one thing, as **Aristotle** truly said, that allows us to persevere in labor for a long time. Elsewhere one may play with genius; one may occasionally frolic with the flowers of eloquence. There are pleasant excursions where you may rest when weary and refresh the strength of your mind. In every business, but especially in literature, variety wards off satiety and prevents boredom from arising. 

But here, I had to repeat—not <term>dis-</term><term>re-</term><term>pula-</term><term>re</term> <note>original: "disrepulare"; a rare term for repetitive pruning or cleaning.</note>, as it says in the Greek proverbs—but three thousand times those same things: what the adage meant, where it was born, and for what use it was suitable. Nowhere did that common Greek adage have more place than here: <term>twice and thrice the good things</term> <note>original: "δὶς καὶ τρὶς τὰ καλὰ" (dis kai tris ta kala); a proverb suggesting that good things bear repeating, though here used ironically regarding the repetition of work.</note>. Finally, there is some part of pleasure in handling matters that shine by being handled, and which of their own accord supply the author with splendor and abundance of speech. Here, everything handled is such that it shines through use, not through the handling itself, and only then shows its genuine...

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES<-

...grace, when they are seen appropriately inserted into speech like gems. Set apart, they grow cold, and seem to be some tiny, trivial things. Add to this that in other works, the value is judged by the main subject, and the reader labors no differently than the writer. But with this kind of work, because people read it in snatches, the reader brings to any single proverb a mind that is fresh, at leisure, and perhaps even eager—or, on the other hand, a mind that is fastidious and easily bored. How unfair, meanwhile, is my condition! I am the one required to satisfy the person at leisure, fill the one who is eager, and please the one who is bored in every single adage. Added to all this is the labor of translating Greek, which certainly no one will judge anything but extremely difficult, unless they have never attempted to turn good Greek into good Latin. 

Consider again the immense variety of authors whose vast crowd falls into this work; I believe there are no fewer than ten thousand. If someone, in the space of these months in which we finished this labor, had translated only so many poems into Latin, and did so in verse, they would not be accused of laziness in any way. Furthermore, I do not know what others will think. I myself believe it is no small thing, in such an immense number of proverbs, to remember what you said in which place, and not to be confused by the crowd of material. Therefore, when someone deals with such great difficulties—all of which would be difficult even to list—is it any wonder if a slip happens occasionally, especially when hurrying? Why I had to hurry will soon be explained. But if **Horace** <note>The Roman poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus.</note>—even in other subjects where these inconveniences are absent—forgives "the spots which either carelessness has shed, or human nature has too little guarded against," if he thinks it should be conceded that "sleep creeps in during a long work," if he is not indignant "when **Homer** <note>The legendary Greek epic poet.</note> occasionally nods," why on earth should we cause an uproar <note>original: "mare cœlo miſceamus"; literally "mix the sea with the sky."</note> if a very few errors are perhaps caught in a work of this kind? In such a task, besides those common causes for slipping, one is not free to finish the business under one's own auspices, and one has guides of the sort who constantly provide an opportunity for error. 

I say nothing, meanwhile, of the faults in the manuscripts, which sometimes deceive even the most learned men; I am silent about the boredom, which is especially prone to dulling the vigor of the mind; I say nothing of such a varied <term>farrago</term> <note>A confused mixture or medley; originally a mix of grains for animal feed.</note> of all sorts of things, which causes the mind, distracted here and there by so many topics, to be unable to always be present to itself. It remains for me to briefly address those who I predict will find a little lack of care and diligence in this <term>forest</term> <note>original: "sylua"; Erasmus uses "forest" as a metaphor for his vast collection of raw material.</note> of ours. For I see that some people are of such a mind that they measure books by their weight, not their learning, and consider a thing finished only when nothing more can be added. They are never satisfied unless something is excessively overdone, and they only judge there to be "abundance" when they mean "satiety" everywhere. 

One of these people will say that certain things could have been treated more copiously and fully by me. Then, while leafing through authors, someone will come across a passage that relates to a proverb—or does not relate to it, but seems to relate to it in their eyes—and they will immediately mock this as something omitted by us. First, I ask, who is so arrogant as to dare to profess such a thing? Who is so unfair as to demand, in this genre of writing, that no passage whatsoever be passed over? Even if you had read everything, noted everything, and prepared everything, does exactly what was needed occur to you immediately in such an immense crowd of things, and in exactly the place it was needed? 

Furthermore, what kind of bothersome diligence would it have been to search everywhere and adapt every possible way to enrich a proverb? What would have been the limit or end of the volumes if, for example, while explaining **Sardonic laughter** <note>original: "Sardoniū rifum"; a bitter or scornful laugh. Legends said it came from a Sardinian herb that caused facial contortions.</note>, I had wanted to repeat the description of that entire island from the books of all the geographers, reviewing the site's location, the antiquity of the people, and their origin "from head to heel" <note>original: "à capite... uſq; ad calcem"; meaning thoroughly or completely.</note>? Then, what the appearance of that herb is, what its power is, and to gather into one place whatever I might find recorded among any of the physicians regarding this? To this, I could add a commemoration of how that laughter is produced and for what reasons it appears in a dying person, according to the opinion of the natural philosophers. Then, I could search through all the monuments of history to find for whom this kind of laughter was familiar, and when. Then, how much this laughter misbecomes an honest man. In short, whatever is read about praised or unpraised laughter among the moral philosophers and poets, I could heap all of that into the same pile. Finally, if there were any <term>apophthegm</term> <note>A concise, pithy saying or maxim.</note>, any witty remark, any memorable deed, any fable, any story, any maxim—if there were anything at all, either related or contrary, which could be pulled into the explanation of the adage—should I accumulate all of it? If this had been my purpose, who does not see that single volumes could have been produced from single adages? What would be less absurd than this: if I were about to explain the proverb **An Iliad of woes** <note>original: "ιλιάς κακῶν" (Ilias kakōn); a metaphor for a vast number of troubles.</note>, I should have to narrate the entire Trojan War...

# THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND #

Should I begin from the very beginning—"from the twin egg," <note>original: "à gemino... ouo"; a reference to the Roman poet Horace, meaning starting a story from the absolute beginning, like the birth of Helen of Troy from an egg.</note> as **Horace** says? Or, as if I were about to explain "the schemes of Odysseus," <note>original: "ὀδυσσέου μηχάνημα" (odysseou mēchanēma)</note> should I reweave the entire plot of the *Odyssey*? Then, how frequently do commonplaces regarding death, life, friendship, enmity, and the just and unjust occur here? But I act foolishly by continuing to list them, since they are nearly as numerous as the proverbs themselves. It would have been no great task to enrich these with declamatory arguments, so that each one might have grown into the size of a whole volume. But such diligence, besides being utterly foolish, could neither be provided by the one who writes these *Thousands* <note>Erasmus refers to his work, the *Adagia*, which was organized into "Chiliads" or groups of a thousand proverbs.</note> nor endured by the one who reads them. Therefore, I have judged that in this work I must seek a middle ground rather than abundance, and a conclusion rather than endless progress. Although, if something came to mind in passing as we were hurrying—something that seemed worth knowing and not foreign to the proverb—we have not been burdened to add it as a "supplement." Finally, there are some places (for why should I not frankly admit it?)—though these are not very many—where we ourselves feel something is missing. We did not think these should be passed over in complete silence, even if what we had found in authors so far did not entirely satisfy us. Rather, it seemed best to record them so that we might provide an opportunity for more diligent investigation by others who have either more leisure, a greater supply of books, a luckier memory, or more abundant learning. Meanwhile, we ourselves make use of that line from the **Comic Poet**: "Not as we wish, but as we are able." <note>original: "ἐχ ὡς θελόμεθα, ἀλλ' ὡς δυνάμεθα" (ech hōs thelometha, all' hōs dynametha). A common Greek sentiment regarding doing one's best with limited resources.</note>

I saw also that a certain order could be introduced if, following the logic of similarities, dissimilarities, contraries, and related things, I had proposed numerous headings and assigned each proverb to its own class. But I deliberately omitted this, partly because in a miscellany of this kind, it seemed to me to be more fitting, in some way, if no order were present. Partly it was because I saw that if I had stuffed everything of the same sentiment into the same class, the equality would result in boredom for the reader, and they would soon cry out in disgust: "Twice-served cabbage is death" <note>original: "δὶς κράμβη θάνατος" (dis krambē thanatos); a Greek proverb meaning that repetition is unbearable.</note> and "the road in the book is Corinth." <note>original: "ἡ δ' ὁδὸς κόρινθος ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ βιβλίῳ" (hē d' hodos korinthos estin en tō bibliō). This likely refers to the proverb "Not everyone can go to Corinth," implying that a monotonous path is tiresome.</note> Partly, also, the magnitude of the labor deterred me. For why should I lie? I perceived that this could not be done unless I rewove the entire work from head to heel, and I could not think of publication until I had added that final "finishing touch," <note>original: "Colophonē"</note> so that the work would truly have required **Horace’s** nine-year rule. <note>Horace advised poets to keep their work hidden for nine years before publishing to ensure it was sufficiently polished.</note> But as it is, I was permitted to add things even while it was being published, if anything occurred to me that was too worthy to be omitted.

Furthermore, I can hardly be persuaded that any will be so unfair (though I think even these will exist) as to demand eloquence from a man who is a **Dutchman**—that is, something more than a **Boeotian** <note>Boeotians were proverbially considered dull and uncultured by other Greeks. Erasmus is using a self-deprecating joke, suggesting that as a northern European (Dutchman), he shouldn't be expected to have the refined eloquence of the Italians or ancient Greeks.</note>—but jokes aside, in a work that is entirely and properly suited for teaching. And it is for teaching things that are indeed not unworthy of being known, but are so minute and humble that they not only do not demand the ornaments and abundance of speech, but even reject and repudiate them. In such a varied collection of things, in such constant naming of even humble writers (which I had to use somewhat plainly and bluntly for the sake of teaching), in such frequent insertion of Greek speech, and in such constant translation, what place was there for splendor? What shine, what consistency, what flow of speech could there be? **Marcus Tullius Cicero** does not require eloquence from a philosopher; should anyone require it from a collector of proverbs? <note>term: parœmiographo (proverb-writer/collector)</note> **Seneca** never desires it, except when it costs little—when it is present of its own accord—to pursue great matters magnificently. But to affect the equipment of rhetoricians here, I ask you, what else would it be than what they say: "Perfume in the lentil soup," <note>original: "ἐν τῇ φακῇ μύρον" (en tē phakē myron); a proverb for mixing high luxury with humble necessity.</note> and "to fit a giant’s noose to a pygmy," <note>original: "τῷ πυγμαίῳ ἀγχονίαν κολόσσω ἐφαρμόζειν" (tō pygmaiō anchonian kolossō ephormozein)</note> not to mention "to decorate the earthenware pot." <note>original: "τὴν χύτραν ποικίλλειν" (tēn chytran poikillein)</note>

As for me, although I do not despise it in others, a passion for eloquence never greatly moved me. Rather, I know not how, a sensible speech has always pleased me more than one painted with cosmetics, provided that filth is absent and it represents the meaning of my mind without inconvenience. But if any virtue of speaking had ever been acquired by us, it would necessarily have perished in such a long, varied, and tumultuous examination of Greek and Latin authors. For this richness of style, even by **Cicero's** testimony, tends to become sterile with even a brief interruption. Then, even if the subject itself greatly invited the ornaments of speaking, there was no time for it. Indeed, all the time was too narrow for turning over so many books, noting so many passages, and embracing so many things in memory. Although, to express these very things in words that are not entirely bad will be considered, I think, a part of eloquence by one who truly knows what eloquence is. For I care nothing for those "apes of eloquence," as I might call them, who measure the virtues of speaking by a certain empty and childish tinkling of words. When they have finally interwoven one or two little flowers into their writings after many days of burning the midnight oil, and have sprinkled in four little words from **Cicero** and as many from **Sallust**, they immediately think they have reached the peak of

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES #

They believe they have attained Roman eloquence. They are so displeased by the style of Saint Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was a priest and scholar known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate). Erasmus admired his scholarship but noted that some of his contemporaries found Jerome's style lacking compared to classical Roman authors.</note> that he seems to them tedious, or even tongue-tied, mute, and infantile whenever they do not see those four little words of Marcus Tullius [Cicero]. If these people were ever put to the test—to see what it is like to pursue trifles of this kind in books—they might perhaps recognize their own lack of skill and less shamelessly despise another's eloquence. But someone might say to me, an advisor not to be ignored: "But this very thing was elegant: to add some measure of greatness to small matters through the art of speaking, to add some dignity to humble things, and, as Virgil says,
*To add this honor to small things.*" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Georgics* (Book 4, line 6), suggesting that even small subjects, like the life of bees, deserve poetic dignity.</note>

Nor indeed would there have been a lack of time, if only you had separated the work of collecting and polishing, and had given a proper amount of time to the material. What necessity was there, according to the saying of Plautus, *to sip and blow at the same time?* <note>original: "simul & sorberes & flares"; a proverb from the Roman playwright Plautus, meaning it is impossible to do two contradictory things at once.</note> Who forced you to rush the publication? And to finish such a vast, such a laborious work (if I may say so) in a year and a half, and to publish it as soon as it was finished? If you had followed the precept of Flaccus [Horace] and kept your late-night labors pressed away until the ninth year, it could not have happened otherwise than that you would have added not only the grace of eloquence, but also that the work would have come into the light more fully and more correctly; there would be nothing for you to regret, nor anything anyone would wish to add. Otherwise, you either should not have undertaken the task, or once undertaken, you should have satisfied its requirements in every way.

Here I indeed—for it is not my habit to fight against the truth—must acknowledge some part of the fault. For it was not hidden from me that this work required not a theologian, a man who had tasted ancient literature only lightly and as if running past, but someone who had worn out his whole life in unrolling, interpreting, and examining authors of that kind, and who was permitted not only to linger on, but even to die in studies of this sort. I clearly saw that this labor belonged neither to one man, nor to one library, nor to a few years; yet we alone, by our own "Mars," <note>original: "noſtroque... Marte"; an idiom meaning "by our own efforts" or "by our own strength."</note> as they say, finished it in less than a year and a half, aided by only one library—namely the Aldine <note>The library and printing house of Aldus Manutius in Venice, where Erasmus stayed while preparing the 1808 edition of the *Adagia*. Aldus was the most famous printer of the Renaissance, known for his high-quality editions of Greek and Latin classics.</note>, which is indeed most abundant, and better equipped with good books (especially Greek ones) than any other. From it, as from a spring, all good libraries throughout the whole world are born and propagated. Therefore, it was indeed most wealthy, I do not deny, but still only one.

It is true that I can, if not clear this fault, at least diminish it. First, because in the past it was not so much reason that incited me to take up this duty as it was chance, and the prayers of friends drove me. I can never greatly resist them at other times, but especially my "Maecenas" <note>A "Maecenas" is a term for a generous patron of the arts, named after Gaius Maecenas, the advisor to the Roman Emperor Augustus.</note> William Mountjoy <note>William Blount, 4th Baron Mountjoy, was a former pupil and one of Erasmus's most significant English patrons.</note>, a man of distinction among the nobles of the British court, urged me toward this. He is so deserving and so dear that I consider all things must take second place whenever his will must be obeyed. If even the dogmas of philosophers concede that for the sake of friends we may sometimes turn a little aside from the right path, I think pardon should be given to me, who, while I strive to please such a friend, took up a province that is indeed very beautiful, but perhaps not quite suited to me—especially when I saw no more learned man taking up this business. This was not because they judged themselves unequal to it, as I indeed believe, but because they saw those immense late-night labors and fled from them, especially since they understood how much less glory would come from such labors.

Furthermore, when we saw that this was the nature of the work undertaken—that it had no limit in itself—we necessarily had to measure the limit for it, not by the nature of the work, but by our own occupations. We spent as much on the work as we saw we could spare from our other studies without harm. Therefore, we finished it a little more hastily, partly because in this work we seemed to ourselves to be traveling abroad, as it were; and partly so that, once these were finished, we might return with our whole heart to those things which belong to our own profession, which we interrupted for some months, following the will of a friend more than our own judgment. Although I am not so greatly moved by the precept of Horace. For he gave that command to those who wrote for the sake of intellectual praise. We have looked at nothing except the utility of the reader. He gave it to those who would compose a poem, in which, according to Plato, the highest eloquence is required; we are collecting commentaries on adages. Finally, even if he perhaps provided that care in his poem—though he did not even maintain it himself—he might have done so for a few hundred lines. But to require the same in the *Thousands* [the *Adagia*], would seem both extremely arduous and perhaps not very humane, since this itself is abundantly laborious—even writing *Iliads*—so that you need not add the labor of changing things so many times, which seems not a little more difficult than the first task. Although I indeed think that the care which Horace requires should be measured not by a span of time, but by the intensity of purpose. Regarding this matter, I can truly affirm that I...

# THIRD THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED #

...strengths, so that what might seem to have been taken away from time, I might compensate for with vigilance and the assiduousness of my study. Thus, I hope that fair-minded readers will not find this part entirely lacking. For if you consider the amount of time, we have rushed the work; but if you estimate the nights and days spent in infatigable study, we have brought it to maturity. Even if my care does not correspond to the work in every way, this much will certainly be established: I have surpassed, with no small margin of diligence, whoever has ever written about proverbs, whether among the Greeks or the Latins (I speak of those whose commentaries still survive). Finally, since the work is both infinite and prepared for the common good, come now, what forbids us from sharing the task and perfecting it through collective effort? I have provided the "forest" <note>original: "syluam"; a metaphor for a raw collection of materials that others can build from.</note>, which is not, I think, entirely meager; let those who can carve, polish, and decorate it come forward. I have finished that part in which there was the most labor and the least glory; let it not bother others to add what will be both easiest and most magnificent. It matters nothing to me under whose name it is read; I will not struggle over who shall possess the greatest glory, provided that we have given the opportunity for such great utility to flow to students. Nor indeed will I be offended in the least if someone more learned corrects our work, someone more diligent enriches it, someone more precise arranges it, someone more eloquent illustrates it, someone with more leisure polishes it, or someone more fortunate defends it—so long as it is done for the public convenience of students, which we have looked to so exclusively in this work that we have taken no account of ourselves. 

Otherwise, I could have chosen for myself, as most people do, the kind of labor that would have cost me far less sweat and yet brought a far greater harvest of glory. For who would not have judged it a remarkable and magnificent feat if I had delivered all of Demosthenes or Plato, or some other such author, to Latin ears? <note>Erasmus suggests that translating a single famous classical author would have been easier and more prestigious than the grueling task of collecting thousands of proverbs from obscure sources.</note> And yet, it would be difficult to say how much less expenditure of time, sleepless nights, and "midnight oil" <note>original: "oleiq; impẽdio"; referring to the oil in a scholar's lamp.</note> it would have taken to complete that task than to collect these—as they seem—trifles. I could have chosen two or three "hundreds" <note>original: "centurias"; Erasmus organized his proverbs into groups of 100.</note> from so great a number, and in polishing, enriching, and refining them, I could have strained every nerve of my talent, preparing for myself a much richer harvest of fame with a not much smaller sowing of labor. But this would have been to act for my own private business, not the public business of students. 

Yet, as I indeed believe, in restoring the world of letters, one must display a Herculean spirit; that is, one's concern for the common utility should not be deterred or exhausted by any personal inconvenience. But enough of these matters, and I have long feared lest those to whom this seems like a Herculean task might find this long discourse—into which the adage of "Herculean labor" led us—tedious to read through. Therefore, I shall make an end, but only after I add this: when these were first being published, I surpassed all the labors of Hercules. <note>Erasmus is comparing his editorial work to the Twelve Labors of the mythological hero Hercules.</note> For Hercules, though otherwise always undefeated, could not be a match for two monsters at once. Thus, fleeing, he preferred to leave us a proverb <note>A reference to the proverb "Not even Hercules against two."</note> rather than test the god of war, thinking it better to be laughed at while safe than to be praised while dead. 

We, however, had to engage at the same time with two immense monsters, either of which involved so much business that it would require many Herculeses—far be it from a single little man to be a match for two. For at the same time in Basel, the *Thousands of Adages* <note>original: "adagiorum Chiliades"; the title of this work.</note> were being printed, so corrected and enriched that the restoration cost me no less effort than the first edition which we completed in Venice at the shop of Aldus Manutius. <note>Aldus Manutius (c. 1449–1515) was a famous Venetian printer and publisher who produced the first major edition of Erasmus's Adages.</note> And at the same time, the entire works of Saint Jerome <note>Erasmus's landmark nine-volume edition of the works of St. Jerome was published in 1516.</note> were being printed, from which I took upon myself the largest and most difficult part—namely, the books of his letters—a task by no means light, by the Muses, if anyone were merely to unroll such a volume of books. Now, by the immortal God, what a heavy struggle I had with the "monsters" of errors with which everything there was swarming. With how much sweat the Greek phrases had to be restored, which that man [Jerome] mixes in everywhere! For they were mostly either missing or incorrectly added. 

Nor indeed did those commentaries—whatever their quality—which we added with their arguments cost me a moderate amount of effort, not only because I was attempting something for the first time where there was no one to follow or whose discoveries could help me, but also because, as they say of Romulus, he was no less a magnificent boaster of his deeds than a performer of great things. So too Saint Jerome: just as he had in his heart a certain rich storehouse built from every kind of discipline and author, so no one shows off the riches of his learning in his writings more ambitiously, if I may put it that way. With a certain holy glory, he throws out, stuffs in, and presses upon the reader whatever is hidden in the Old or New Testament, whatever is found in fables or histories, and whatever is exquisite in Greek or Hebrew literature. Then, in arranging the order, which had been confused in various ways by different people—even if there is no praise for talent in this, nevertheless...

<summary>Erasmus describes the immense physical and intellectual toll of his work, comparing his simultaneous editing of the Adages and the works of Saint Jerome to "Herculean labors" performed for the public good.</summary>
<keywords>Herculean labor, Saint Jerome, Aldus Manutius, Basel edition, scholarly diligence, printing history, Greek and Hebrew literature, literary restoration</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Erasmus continues to describe the immense personal burden of his scholarly labor, specifically mentioning his work on the edition of Saint Jerome alongside his collection of Adages.</meta>

...was no small trouble. Such a mass of things had to be sustained by this little man <note>Erasmus often refers to himself as 'homuncio' (little man or manikin) to emphasize the weight of his intellectual tasks.</note>, and indeed by him alone. Except that in some Hebrew words—since I had only tasted those letters lightly and with the "tips of my lips" <note>original: "primoribus labris degustassem"; a common idiom for a superficial or basic knowledge.</note> as the saying goes—we were helped somewhat by the effort of Bruno Amerbach, a young man as learned as he is modest. To him, in turn, I lent a hand in the remaining portion of this work, assisting in restoring several Greek and Latin passages, weighing labor for labor. I should not fail to mention that it was no small task to identify, through certain conjectures and tracks, those works which had been falsely mixed into the scholarly labors of Jerome under a fake title—some being learned, others equally unlearned and childish, and several even showing signs of madness—so that they might be removed and returned to their proper places. Furthermore, I had to compile the life of that most holy man from all his own monuments, since it had been presented by others not only with the greatest vanity but even with the utmost lack of wit. Add to this that the nature of such labors is that the fruit and utility reach everyone, but the hardship is felt by no one except the one who sustains it. For the reader, who runs through entire books without hindrance, does not notice that we sometimes had to pause for several days over a single little word. Nor does he understand, or if he does, he certainly does not remember, at what great difficulties that ease which he reads and enjoys was won for us, and by how many troubles that trouble was taken away from everyone else. Consequently, I often seem to myself to have been **born on the fourth moon** <note>original: "quarta luna natus"; a proverb referring to Hercules, who was said to be born on the fourth day of the month and was destined for a life of endless labor.</note>, a man who by some fate happened to fall into more than Herculean labors of this kind.

->**I escaped the evil, I found the good.**<-
*I escaped the evil, I found the better.* That is,
I have evaded evils and obtained better things.
This is a proverbial half-line of verse, usually said whenever a more elegant fortune befell someone. They say it comes from wedding ceremonies. For in Athens, it was the custom that at weddings a certain boy would be brought in, covered all over with thorny branches and oak-tree acorns and crowned with them, carrying a basket filled with bread. He would say these words:
*I escaped the evil, I found the better.*
That voice was a good omen for the groom and bride, as if they were reaching toward a continually better fortune. For he called the thorns and acorns "evil," and the bread "good," because thorns are sterile (according to a proverb we placed elsewhere, "where there are thorns"), and those ancient rustics lived on acorns, according to the saying, "Enough of the oak, enough of the feast" <note>original: "ἅλις δρυός" (halis dryos); a Greek proverb meaning one has had enough of primitive ways and is moving to something better.</note>. Once the use of grain was discovered, acorns began to be loathed. Demosthenes, in his oration *On the Crown* (for Ctesiphon), indicates that this was usually said by those who were being initiated, when, after the hardships they suffered before the mysteries were completed, they were finally admitted to the honor of initiation. For he reproaches Aeschines, saying that while assisting in the sacred rites by night, after the mud was wiped off, he ordered them to say:
*I escaped the evil, I found the better.* Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
*Now that he is rich, he no longer delights in lentils.* That is,
Where one is wealthy, he no longer rejoices in the lentil-bean.
This refers to a young man who, having found Wealth (Plutus), loathed the old woman to whom he had been subservient when poor. The opposite of this is what Julius Pollux (Book 6) relates from Eupolis:
*While drinking wine, he preferred to drink vinegar.* This adage is recorded by Zenodotus.

->**An Egyptian wedding.**<-
*An Egyptian wedding.* That is, Egyptian weddings were said to be ill-omened and unhappy. This is taken from the well-known story of Aegyptus, who gave his fifty sons as husbands to the same number of his brother's daughters. But all of them, except one, were slaughtered by their brides. This can be applied to a feigned friendship, or to a gift given in the appearance of honor, when in reality the destruction of the recipient is sought. Thus, sometimes atrocious slaughters arise from the affinities or treaties of princes.

->**He acts as aedile without the people's vote.**<-
Plautus in *Stichus*: *Without the people's vote, yet this man here acts as aedile.* This is used when someone is too domineering in someone else's business or in another person's house. For Plautus refers it to a parasite who is in a house not his own, ordering and commanding no differently than if it were his. Close to this is what Cicero has in the third book of *On the Laws*: *But I ask what is more shameful than this thing: a senator without an appeal, an ambassador without mandates.* Likewise in the 13th *Philippic*: *A substitute for the senators, chosen by himself.*

### THIRD CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<note>Erasmus organized his thousands of proverbs into "Chiliads" (groups of 1,000) and then into "Centuries" (groups of 100).</note>

->Peace to be purchased.<-
->V<-

Saint Augustine, in his tenth Homily, relates that a certain ancient proverb of this kind was famous among the Carthaginians: <note>original: "Pœnos"</note> *To have a quiet time, lose something.* Those who can never bear to yield anything of their own rights rarely lack for lawsuits. It is sometimes a great profit to have shut out the annoyance and restlessness of a dispute by the sacrifice of a small thing.

->From two you see three.<-
->VI<-

<note>original Greek: "Ἐκ δυοῖν τρία βλέπεις"</note> *From two you see three.* This is a proverbial phrase used against those who are going blind, whether from old age, drunkenness, or some other defect of the eyes. This relates to that line of Virgil: <note>original: "Maronis"</note> *And the sun seems double, and double Thebes shows itself.* Likewise that line of Juvenal: *And the table rises up with double lamps.* In some ancient copies, I find it written in this way: <note>original Greek: "ᾧ δυοῖν τρία βλέπεις"</note> *In two you see three.* This was commonly said when someone sees one thing for another because their eyes are deceiving them. It becomes more elegant if it is turned toward a judgment of the mind.

->The toothless man envies the teeth of those who eat.<-
->VII<-

Saint Jerome closed that most learned letter of his, which he titled *To the Great Orator*, with a proverb of this kind: *Persuade him, I beg you, that as a toothless man he should not envy the teeth of those who eat, nor as a mole should he despise the eyes of the goats.* That is to say, let him not envy in others what has not happened for himself. For such is the character of certain men, that each one praises as much as he hopes he can achieve himself; but if they perceive something to be beyond their own powers, they deny that it is worth learning. In short, you will find few who approve in others what they despair of in themselves; and this is more true in the study of literature than in any other matter. Jerome seems to have rendered that Greek sentiment: <note>original Greek: "Αὐτὸς πτωχὸς τοῖς ἔχουσι μὴ φθονεῖ"</note> *Do not, as a beggar yourself, envy those who possess.*

->Eating the same onions.<-
->VIII<-

<note>original Greek: "τὰὐτὰ θύμου φαγόντες"</note> *Those who have eaten the same savory herb.* <note>The Greek "thymon" can mean thyme or a type of pungent wild onion.</note> This was said as a proverbial figure by Aristophanes in his play *Plutus*. It applies to poor and good men who are friends among themselves. For "thymon" is a very cheap kind of herb, by which the thin and the rustic sustain their lives however they can. Some think it is a wild onion, even if Pliny and Dioscorides disagree. Suidas advises that it is a type of wild and cheap herb, by whose eating the comic poet wished the poverty of the diners to be understood. Just as Hesiod signaled poverty through mallow and asphodel. To this is related what is written in Juvenal: *What shoemaker eats sliced leeks and the lips of a boiled ram with you?*

->Whole oxen from the oven.<-
->IX<-

Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*: *Then he set before us whole oxen from the oven. And who has ever seen oxen cooked in an oven?* Antiphanes, in the fourth book of Athenaeus, makes someone complain about the frugality of the Greeks, who serve only a little meat, while the ancestors used to serve whole oxen, deer, and rams roasted. Indeed, he says the cook of the Persian King served a whole camel, roasted and still hot. But for myself, I would rather be served a small partridge, roasted and hot. The same author in the same book related from Herodotus that among the Persians there was a custom on birthdays for the wealthy to serve an ox, an ass, a horse, and a camel cooked whole in an oven or furnace. This is a proverbial <term>hyperbole</term> <note>rhetorical exaggeration</note> concerning a barbaric abundance of things, or about luxuries supplied in great plenty. For in ancient times, foods cooked in an oven <note>original: "clibano"</note> were considered delicacies. First, bread began to be baked in an oven, which they called "clibanitis" <note>oven-bread</note>, and that thing seemed so new that it even gave rise to a proverb. Then meats and fish began to be cooked in the same way. Whence even tunny-fish and other things of that kind, cooked in the oven, were sent to friends as a small guest-gift.

->A hail of drachmas.<-
->X<-

<note>original Greek: "δραχμὴ χαλαζῶσα"</note> *A hailing drachma.* Said of profit which, as if sent from heaven, falls... <note>The sentence continues on the next page.</note>

<summary>This page contains the start of the third thousand of Erasmus's adages, covering proverbs five through ten. The entries focus on themes of social conduct, physical versus mental perception, envy in scholarship, the shared diet of the poor, and the excessive luxury of barbaric feasts.</summary>
<keywords>Augustine, Jerome, Aristophanes, Herodotus, envy, poverty, Persian luxury, proverbs, ancient diet, Greek literature, Latin literature</keywords>

--- Page 762 ---
<meta>This page continues the sequence of adages from the previous section. The opening paragraph concludes a discussion on "missiles" or prizes thrown to crowds in antiquity, before moving into adages regarding cunning, duplicity, and the comforts of home.</meta>

...fell to his lot. For in ancient times, the prize in the theater was a drachma, which was scattered among the people like a shower of hail. They say this custom was established by Diophantus. Hence, whenever a real storm of hail occurred, they would say jokingly, "a small hail-prize." <note>original Greek: βραχὺν χάλαζάν</note> This custom of throwing "missiles" <note>prizes or coins thrown to a crowd</note> has not entirely died out even today. The authority for this is Zenodotus; Hesychius also mentions it.

### Of Twelve Arts.

*Twelve-skilled.* <note>original Greek: Δωδεκαμήχανον</note> That is, "Of twelve arts." They used to call a man "twelve-skilled" if he was cunning, shifty, versatile, a master of many trades, and equipped with various deceits. They tell of a certain prostitute named Cyrene, who was given the nickname "Twelve-skilled" because she was said to have employed twelve different "figures" <note>positions or techniques</note> in the act of love. However, the term was imitated from the tragedy *Hypsipyle* by Euripides, in which he wrote of the "twelve-skilled star," as quoted by Suidas. Aristophanes also mentions this in *The Frogs*, although the commentator seems to have read "cave" <note>original Greek: ἄντρον</note> instead of "star" <note>original Greek: ἄςρον</note>, so that we might understand it as referring to the female private parts. Aristophanes puts it this way: "Do you dare to find fault with my songs, you who compose poems according to the twelve arts of Cyrene?"

### Double Men.

*Double men.* <note>original Greek: Διπλοῦς ἄνδρας</note> By a proverbial jest, they used to call those "double men" who were slippery and of insincere faith; nowadays people commonly call such types "double-tongued," and Virgil calls the Tyrians "double-tongued." <note>original: "Tyrios bilingues"</note> This was said as an allusion, however, because most names of men are two syllables long <note>In Latin, *bis-syllaba*, sounding like "double"</note>, especially those of slaves, whose class is considered crafty and fraudulent. Thus the meaning is ambiguous: it can be taken either as referring to one who "sits on two stools" <note>an old proverb for indecisive or treacherous people</note> or to one whose name has two syllables. Zenodotus cites an epigram of this kind:

> Indeed, I hate the man of double nature,
> A friend in words, but a foe in his ways.

This appears several times in Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 14: <note>original: "Odysseæ ξ"</note>

> Those who speak well, but cherish evil thoughts behind one's back.

And again in *Odyssey* Book 17: <note>original: "Odysseæ ρ"</note>

> While they spoke well, they were building up atrocities in their minds.

Again in the same work, Book 18: <note>original: "Σ"</note>

> He soothed their hearts with charming words, but his mind intended otherwise.

In Plato’s *Lesser Hippias*, someone cites these verses of Homer, which Achilles is said to have spoken to Ulysses:

> For it is right to speak out frankly what you feel,
> Just as I think and as I believe it will be done.
> For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades
> Who hides one thing in his heart and says another with his tongue.

### The well-to-do ought to stay at home.

*The one who is happily blessed must stay at home.* <note>original Greek: Οἴκοι μένειν δεῖ τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα</note> That is:
> He for whom all things are prosperous must remain at home.

The man who has an abundance of resources, if he wishes to lead a happy life, should live at home. Nowhere is life more comfortable, nowhere more free. He who is in need may seek his fortune by traveling and try his luck abroad. So says Menander:

> One must stay at home to remain free,
> Or he who is wealthy must cease to be "happily blessed."

This can also be twisted to this meaning: He who has a clear conscience should not hunt for glory through external praise, but should be content with the awareness of his own virtues.

<summary>Erasmus explains adages concerning the "twelve arts" of cunning (linked to the courtesan Cyrene), the "double man" (referring to duplicity and insincerity), and the wisdom of the wealthy staying at home to enjoy their freedom.</summary>
<keywords>cunning, duplicity, double-tongued, Cyrene, Aristophanes, Homer, domestic life, wealth, freedom, theater prizes</keywords>

<header>CHILIAD THREE, FIRST CENTURY.</header>
<sig>Hh 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: buster-</meta>

### To run through the point of a spear.
-> XIV <-

"To run through sharp things" <note>original Greek: Δι' ὀξέας δραμεῖν</note>. This was said of those who were involved in a highly dangerous matter. For they call a spear, or the point of a spear, "sharp" <note>original Greek: ὀξέαν</note>. The metaphor seems to be taken either from traveling acrobats, who walk along the very tips of spears and sword points, or from a military custom. In the latter, it was common for one who was deemed to have deserved death to be forced to walk naked through the middle of the troops' spears, which were pointed at him from both sides. It would also not be absurd to understand this as referring to the Thracian dance, which we have discussed elsewhere.

### Menecles says one thing, the piglet says another.
-> XV <-

"Menecles says one thing, the little pig another" <note>original Greek: Ἄλλα λέγει μενεκλῆς, ἄλλα τὸ χοιρίδιον</note>. That is:
The sow does not speak the same things as Menecles.
This is used when someone blathers a great many words that have nothing to do with the matter at hand. It seems to me that a proverb lies beneath this, even if it is not yet clear where it originated. Lucillius alludes to it in an epigram, which, since it is witty and elegant, I shall not be reluctant to include here:

> A little pig, an ox, and one goat I have lost,
> For which you, Menecles, have received a small fee.
> But I have nothing in common with Othryades,
> Nor am I bringing here thieves from Thermopylae.
> Our lawsuit is against Eutychides; so what is
> Xerxes doing here for me, or the Spartans?
> But remember me, for the sake of the law, or I shall cry out loudly:
> Menecles says one thing, the piglet says another.

The theme of this epigram also agrees with that found in Martial, Book VI:
> My case is not about violence, or murder, or poison,
> But I have a dispute concerning three she-goats.
> I complain that these were lost to a neighbor’s theft;
> The judge demands that this be proven to him.
> You, with a loud voice and your whole hand,
> Thundering about Cannae, the Mithridatic war,
> The perjuries of Punic fury,
> And the Sullas, the Mariuses, and the Muciuses.
> Now, Posthumus, speak about the three she-goats.

In this epigram by Martial, the phrase "With the whole hand" <note>original Latin: Tota manu</note> itself has the appearance of a proverb. Orators are accustomed to gesticulate with a sweeping hand in their arguments. Therefore, either phrase may be rightly said against someone who speaks "outside the corner" <note>original Greek: ἔξω γώνια; meaning out of bounds</note> and "nothing to do with Dionysus" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ διονύσου; an ancient phrase for irrelevant digressions</note>—that is, things that are outside the case and have no bearing on the matter. You might say: "The pig says one thing, Menecles another," or, "Speak about the three she-goats."

### You are not announcing war.
-> XVI <-

"You are not announcing war" <note>original Greek: Οὐ πόλεμον ἀγγέλλεις</note>. This was usually said when someone announced a very joyful thing, because war is the most calamitous of all things. And yet, today, many mortals cheer at the rumor of it—namely, that most wicked race of men <note>likely referring to mercenaries or war-profiteers</note> who are nourished by the evils of the human race. Julian, in a letter to Basil, says: "The proverb says, 'You are not announcing war,' but I would add from the comedy: 'O messenger of golden words!'" Julian doubled the proverb, since this too is proverbial: "Messenger of golden words" <note>original Greek: χρυσὸν ἀγγείλας ἐπῶν</note>. This is taken from Aristophanes' *Plutus*. They are the words of the old men in the chorus to Cario, who had announced the arrival of Plutus <note>the god of wealth</note>. Plato also used it in the *Phaedrus*: "You certainly do not announce war." And again in the third book of *The Laws*—

<summary>Erasmus explains three adages: "running through the spear-point" regarding danger, "Menecles and the piglet" regarding legal digressions, and "not announcing war" as a metaphor for good news.</summary>
<keywords>spear-point, Menecles, piglet, legal irrelevance, Martial, Lucillius, Julian the Apostate, war, golden words, Aristophanes</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...third. Pindar, in his fourth *Pythian* hymn, says: "And even according to the words of Homer, he added this: he said a good messenger <note>original Greek: ἄγγελον ἐσλὸν</note> brings the greatest honor to every business." <note>original: *Nuncium bonum ait honorem maximum in omni negocio ferre.*</note> Indeed, decorate your speech by comparing it with Homer's words. The verse that Pindar cites is brought forward here by the commentator:

"It is also a fine thing when a messenger knows the right things." <note>original Greek: Ἐσλὸν καὶ τὸ τέτυκται ὅτ' ἄγγελος αἴσιμα εἰδῇ.</note> 

This is found in the fifteenth book of the *Iliad*. It means: This also is excellent, when a messenger knows the best course of action.

---

->To bring the siege engines after the war.<-
<margin>XV</margin>

"To bring the machines after the war" <note>original Greek: Τὰς μηχανὰς μετὰ τὸν πόλεμον κομίζειν</note>. They used to say this about those who, once a business was finished, brought in their equipment too late. Brutus, in a certain letter to the Lycians, says: "Your machines <note>original Greek: ἀμηχανὰς</note> were brought after the war, as the proverb goes." He alludes to that passage in Plato, which we have rendered in another place: "In what way one ought to take up the war" <note>original Greek: ὅπως χρὴ τὸν πόλεμον μεταλαγχάνειν</note>. That is, this is the manner in which one should approach a conflict. We shall speak of Melitides in his own place; they say he came to Troy to bring reinforcements <term>suppetias: military aid or reinforcements</term> to Priam only after the city had already been captured.

---

->A word is the lightest of things.<-
<margin>XVI</margin>

"A word is the lightest thing" <note>original Greek: Κουφότατον πρᾶγμα λόος</note>. Synesius, in a letter to Theophilus, says: "Whenever a man of reckless tongue encounters a man of even more reckless hand, according to the common saying, he pays the heaviest penalty for that lightest of things—namely, speech." Furthermore, what Synesius cites seems to be found in Plato's fourth book *On Laws*: "For a light and winged word, there is a most heavy penalty." <note>original Greek: Λόγου κούφου καὶ πτηνοῦ λόγου βαρυτάτη ζημία.</note> This is because the punishment for light and fleeting words is often the most severe. This is also recorded in Plutarch’s essay *On Talkativeness*, citing Plato as the author. In Homer, this phrase is encountered everywhere:

"He spoke winged words." <note>original Greek: Ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα.</note>

He calls them "winged" because they fly out easily and do not know how to fly back. Likewise, Horace says: "And a word once sent forth flies irrevocably." <note>original: *Et semel emissum volat irrevocabile verbum.*</note> 
He cites this sentiment from Menander:

"It is not easier to restrain a heavy stone thrown by a drunkard from a crowd than to restrain a word once it has left the tongue." <note>original Greek: Οὔτ' ἐκ χορὸς μεθύοντα καρτερὸν λίθον / Ῥᾷον κατασχεῖν, ὅτ' ἀπὸ γλώσσης λόγον.</note>

Elsewhere we have indicated that "wingless words" <note>original Greek: ἄπτερος λόγος</note> is a Greek expression for words without feathers; these are words that the listener keeps to himself and does not allow to fly away to others.

---

->Not everything happens as you have determined in your mind.<-

Homer, in the eighteenth book of the *Iliad*: "But Jupiter does not fulfill all the thoughts of men." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' οὐ ζεὺς ἀνθρώποισι νοήματα πάντα τελευτᾷ.</note> That is: Jupiter does not immediately perfect whatever you have conceived in your mind. I thought this verse should certainly be listed among the adages because the same sentiment is commonly expressed even today. And Pindar, in his *Olympian Odes*: "Many things fall out for mortals contrary to their expectation." <note>original Greek: Πολλά δὲ ἀνθρώποις παρὰ γνώμαν ἔπεσον.</note> We have cited this same line elsewhere. We use it rightly whenever we wish to indicate that things do not turn out exactly as we had conceived in our hopes and prayers.

---

->He showed a mouse instead of a lion.<-

"He showed a mouse instead of a lion" <note>original Greek: Μῦν ἀντὶ λέοντος ἀπέδειξε</note>. This is said in a proverbial pattern for someone who, having promised great and mighty things, produced something entirely different. Synesius, in a letter to Anastasius, says: "For after ranting at him two or three times and insulting him 'from the wagon' <note>original Greek: τοῖς ἐξ ἁμάξης λοιδορησάμενος</note>—threatening him with all the things I might have said myself—he then displayed his 'gain' as a mouse instead of a lion." <note>The phrase "from the wagon" refers to the rowdy, coarse insults traded during ancient Greek festivals.</note> It seems the metaphor is taken from those who exhibit wild beasts; for the sake of a joke, they promise much—as if they were about to release a savage lion of unusual size—but then they release a tiny mouse into the cage.

<meta>catchword: Pu</meta>

<summary>This page covers four main adages: the folly of being late (siege engines after the war), the dangerous consequences of "light" words, the unpredictability of human plans, and the disappointment of grand promises that result in trivial outcomes (a mouse instead of a lion).</summary>
<keywords>Pindar, Homer, Brutus, Plato, Synesius, Horace, Menander, winged words, timing, broken promises, Greek proverbs, ancient humor</keywords>

# THE THIRD THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED
<margin>Hh 3</margin>

### With fists and heels.
<margin>XXI</margin>
**With fists and heels** <note>original Greek: πὺξ καὶ λὰξ</note>, that is, with punches and kicks. This is found as a proverbial figure of speech used to describe every kind of insult or an effort made with one's total strength. Synesius says in a certain letter to his brother: "He will neither strike with his fists, nor attack with his heels anyone who is better than him" <note>original: *Neq; pugnos impinget, neq; calcibus impetet quempiam meliorem*</note>. Aristophanes also uses it in his play *Peace*:
"To strike, to dig, with the fist and likewise with the leg." <note>original Greek: παίειν, ὀρύττειν, πὺξ ὁμοῦ καὶ τῷ σκέλει.</note>
In this passage, the commentator notes the proverb: **With the fist and the leg together** <note>original Greek: πὺξ ὁμοῦ καὶ τῷ σκέλει</note>. However, the comic poet, for the sake of a laugh, substituted "penis" <note>original: *mentula*</note> for "shin" <note>original: *tibia*</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his oration *In Defense of Sulla*, says that a certain man was accustomed to using not only the most wicked words, but also "fists and heels."

### The neighbor’s eye is hostile and envious.
<margin>XXII</margin>
**The eye of neighbors is hostile and envious, as the proverb says** <note>original Greek: δυσμενὴς καὶ βάσκανοσ ὁ τῶν γειτόνωψ ὀφθαλμός, φησὶν ἡ παροιμία</note>. This appears in the second book of Aristotle’s *Rhetoric*: "A neighbor envies a neighbor," following the sentiment of Hesiod. We do not envy those from whom we are separated by a long distance, but rather those whom we hope to almost equal. Hence Horace <note>referred to here as Flaccus</note> writes: "Because envy is greater." And elsewhere: "I am bitten even less by the envious tooth."

### To overturn the whole.
<margin>XXIII</margin>
**To overturn the whole** <note>original Greek: ὅλου ἀνατρέψην</note> is said of one who utterly ruins someone, as if from the very roots and foundations. Aeschines <note>OCR: Acinctus</note>, in a letter to Phoebiana, says: "Thus you, having overturned me entirely—as the proverb goes—have reduced me to such a state that I must be your slave." Cicero, in his first book on *Rhetoric*, says: "In the end, he turns everything upside down." This is derived from buildings that are subverted from their very foundations.

### The goods of the earth.
<margin>XXIIII</margin>
**The goods of the earth** <note>original Greek: τὰ τῆς γῆς ἀγαθά</note>. This refers to goods that are immense and of every kind—as if you were to say whatever the earth, the parent of all things, brings forth. Menander, in a letter to Glycera, says: "Promising royally, according to the common saying, the goods of the earth." A similar expression is "Promising mountains of gold."

### A wood-pigeon for a dove.
<margin>XXV</margin>
**A wood-pigeon for a dove** <note>original Greek: φάτταυ ἀντὶ περιστερᾶς</note>; one must understand a verb suited to the meaning of the sentence. In a letter from Mormis to Chremes: "Having redeemed a flute-girl whom he happened to love, and having dressed her in the robes of a bride, he brought her to me: a wood-pigeon instead of a dove, as they say—a courtesan instead of a bride." Plato used this in the *Theaetetus*: "As if he should receive a wood-pigeon instead of a dove." This refers to an error in the thing itself, not in the knowledge of it. Wood-pigeons are very similar to doves. This will be appropriate whenever something inferior and adulterated is substituted for that which is superior and legitimate.

### A Cilician does not easily speak the truth.
<margin>XXVI</margin>
**A Cilician does not easily tell the truth** <note>original Greek: Κίλιξ οὐ ρᾳδίως ἀληθεύει</note>. Dionysius says in a letter to Rufus the scholar: "It is an old saying that Cilicians do not easily speak the truth." Although the word **to speak the truth** <note>original Greek: ἀληθεύειν</note> sometimes means to make good on what you have said in practice. It fits a man greedy for gain, who for that reason frequently says not what is true, but what is profitable. The adage arose from the character of that nation, a name by which people now commonly label the inhabitants of Utrecht <note>Erasmus here makes a contemporary comparison between the ancient Cilicians and the people of the northern Netherlands</note>.

### To compare a gnat to an elephant.
<margin>XXVII</margin>
**To compare a gnat to an elephant** <note>original Greek: κώνωπα ἐλέφαντι παραβάλειν</note>. They are said to do this who compare the smallest things to the greatest. Libanius says to Casilus: "My situation is such as if one were to compare a gnat to an elephant." Of this kind is that famous line of Virgil:
"So I knew whelps were like dogs, and kids like their mothers; so I was used to comparing great things to small." And: "If it is permitted to compare small things to great."

<summary>This page lists several Greek and Latin adages concerning physical conflict, the nature of envy among neighbors, deception through substitution, and the absurdity of comparing vastly unequal things.</summary>
<keywords>fists and heels, envy, neighbors, substitution, Cilicians, truth-telling, gnats and elephants, Erasmus, proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, moving from general social observations to specific metaphors regarding professional duty, mental fortitude, and the finality of certain life choices like war and marriage.</meta>

# ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->As long as I hold the tiller straight.<-
->XXVII<-

**As long as I hold the tiller straight** <note>original: *Dum clauum rectum teneam*</note>, that is, as long as I perform my duty. It signifies that a poor outcome should not be blamed on the craftsman, provided he has performed what his art requires. Quintilian, in the second book of his *Institutes*, demonstrates that this was a proverbial saying. For a pilot, he says, also wishes to reach the port with his ship safe; yet if he is swept away by a storm, he will not be any less a pilot for it, and he will say that well-known line:
> As long as I hold the tiller straight.

It appears to be a half-line of verse taken from some poet. Some cite it from Ennius:
> As long as I hold the tiller straight and steer the ship.

Marcus Tullius Cicero alluded to this in the twelfth book of his *Letters to Friends*: "There is now one ship for all good men, which we are indeed doing our best to hold straight; would that the course were prosperous. But whatever the winds may be, our skill will certainly not be lacking." Likewise, Pindar in his first Pythian hymn says: <term>Steer the army with a just tiller</term> <note>original Greek: νώμα δικαίῳ πηδαλίῳ στρατὸν</note>.

->The largest anvil does not fear the noise.<-
->XXVIII<-

<term>The largest anvil does not fear the noises</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄκμων μέγιστος οὐ φοβεῖται τοὺς ψόφους</note>. That is:
> The greatest anvil fears no tumult.

A lofty mind is not moved by threats or by the storms of raging fortune. The metaphor is taken from the anvils of blacksmiths, which, although they are struck on all sides by frequent blows of the hammers, are nonetheless not moved from their place at all. Virgil makes a steadfast mind of this sort similar to the strength of an oak tree. Likewise, concerning an inexorable mind, he writes:
> Than if he stood as hard flint or a Marpesian crag.

There exists among the Greeks a complete two-line poem of this sort:
<term>The greatest anvil does not fear the noises,</term>
<term>And a prudent mind will withstand every force.</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄκμων μέγιστος οὐ φοβεῖται τοὺς ψόφους, Καὶ νῶς ἐχέφρων πᾶσαν ἑλκύσει βίαν.</note> That is:
> The greatest anvil fears neither noise nor tumult,
> Nor does a steadfast mind fear any violence.

->He sacrificed a pig to Venus.<-
->XXIX<-

<term>He sacrificed a pig to Venus</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀφροδίτῃ σῦν τέθυκεν</note>. This was usually said when someone brings a gift that is not at all pleasing. For the pig was hated by Venus because of her lover Adonis, who was killed by a boar. Or, on the other hand, it is used when someone harms one person to please another. In the same way, a goat is sacrificed to Liber <note>Bacchus</note>, not because it is pleasing, but because it caused harm <note>by eating the vines</note>.

->One is not allowed to err twice in war.<-
->XXX<-

<term>It is not possible to err twice in war</term> <note>original Greek: Ἁμαρτάνειν οὐκ ἔνεστι δὶς ἐν πολέμῳ</note>. In dangerous matters, it is not safe to slip. For if one errs once, it is all over for one's life, and there is no room for a second error. As in war, because everything is carried out in a tumult, there is no space given for recalling or restoring things if something has been instituted wrongly. Hence Homer, both elsewhere and in the nineteenth book of the *Iliad*, says:
<term>But truly, the breathing space of war is small.</term> <note>original Greek: ὀλίγη δέ τ’ ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο</note>

Therefore, in those matters in which, if an error is made once, there is nothing you can do in the future, one must act cautiously and circumspectly—as that not-unwitty mime actor warns:
> One must deliberate for a long time on what must be decided once.

Think of the priesthood, of marriage, and of other things of that kind: which, if they are entered into rashly, there is no way to amend your first thoughts with later "better" ones, as they say. What Vegetius cites from Cato pertains to this: "In other matters, if an error is made, it can be corrected afterward; but faults in battles do not admit of amendment, since punishment follows the error immediately." For either those who have fought lazily or unskillfully perish instantly, or, having been turned to flight, they do not dare to face the victors again. The adage seems to have been born from an apothegm: when Lamachus had rebuked a certain leader of a company because he had done something wrongly, and he replied that he would not do again what he had done: "In war," said Lamachus, "it is not even permitted to err twice," because the first error often takes away one's life.

->The vote of Panides.<-
->XXXI<-

<term>The vote of Panides</term> <note>original Greek: Πανίδος ψῆφος</note>. This was hurled at those who judged foolishly and without learning. They say this Panides was a king of Chalcis who preferred Hesiod to Homer; it is just as if you were to say "The judgment of Midas," because he too preferred the rustic song of Pan.

<vocab>Erasmus, Adagia, Quintilian, Pindar, Virgil, Homer, Vegetius, Lamachus, Panides, Hesiod, Midas</vocab>

<summary>This page explores proverbs regarding the necessity of performing one's duty regardless of the outcome, the resilience of a strong mind against hardship, and the finality of errors in war and life. It also includes a jab at poor artistic judgment through the story of King Panides preferring Hesiod over Homer.</summary>
<keywords>duty, pilot metaphor, mental fortitude, anvil, sacrifice, Venus, military strategy, irreversible decisions, marriage, literary judgment, Panides, Homer</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the reliability of popular judgment, noting how the masses often favor mediocrity over true excellence, before moving into several specific proverbial metaphors regarding character, effort, and fate.</meta>

# CHILIAD THREE, FIRST CENTURY

<note>original: "tepofuerit," likely continuing a sentence about preferring something else</note> preferred to the music of Apollo. In general, this adage applies to the judgments of the common people, who almost always prefer the worst things to the best. By the votes of such people, Philemon occasionally defeated the great comic poet Menander. Although Euripides wrote seventy-five tragedies, he was victorious in only five. Nor is the public's judgment of sacred preachers today any different from what Pliny wrote about public reciters in his own time: "If you ever pass through the basilica," he says, "and want to know how well someone is speaking, there is no need to climb the tribunal or lend an ear; it is an easy guess—know that the one being praised the most is speaking the worst."

For this reason, Socrates in Plato’s *Crito* wishes above all for it to be a fixed and settled decree for the wise man not to be moved by the opinion of the common crowd, but rather to hold in suspicion whatever is found to be vehemently pleasing to the masses. There is a clever saying of Antisthenes recorded in Diogenes Laertius; when someone said to him, "Many people are praising you," he replied, "Why, what have I done wrong?" Very similar to this is what Plutarch relates in his *Apophthegms* regarding Phocion: when the Athenian people, contrary to their habit, agreed with him with enthusiastic zeal while he was speaking, he turned to his friends and said, "What is this? Have I accidentally said something foolish?"

->More slanderous than Pattaecion. XXXIII<-

**More slanderous than Pattaecion** <note>original Greek: Πατταικίωνος συκοφαντικώτερος</note>. This arose from an actual event. For a certain Pattaecion was an infamous slanderer <term>slanderer: an informer or malicious accuser</term> who made it his habit to devise false accusations against good men, and by this foul trade he amassed wealth; at last, he was caught, convicted, and paid the penalty with his life. His chief obsession was to cause trouble for young men of good reputation. He was also pelted with stones by the townspeople for being a thief and a house-breaker. Hyperbolus was a similar character among the Athenians. Suidas records this.

->To stand on the whole foot. XXXIIII<-

**On the whole foot** <note>original Greek: ὀλῳ ποδί</note>, that is, with the whole foot or the entire foot. It is used for doing something with one's greatest strength and utmost effort. It is recorded by Suidas. Quintilian, in the twelfth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*, says: "Therefore, in these legal actions, one must **stand on the whole foot**, as the farmers say." It might seem to be a metaphor taken from those who stand firm in the battle line to defend their position and do not desert their post, or from wrestlers, whose art involves planting the foot skillfully—unless Quintilian himself did not testify that it originated with farmers.

->To grow a callus. XXXV<-

**To grow a callus** and **To become hard-skinned** <note>original: *Callum ducere* and *Occallescere*</note> are proverbial metaphors if they are applied to the mind. Quintilian, in book twelve, says: "And while the intellect is still being nourished, **to grow a callus**." We read quite often in Marcus Tullius Cicero that the "ears have become calloused" <note>original: *occalluisse aures*</note> when habituation takes away the sense of a grievance.

->Outside the instrument. XXXVI<-

Quintilian, in book eleven, says: "And their voice is different, almost **outside the instrument** <note>original: *extra organum*</note>; to which the Greeks gave the name 'bitterness,' being sharp beyond measure and almost beyond the nature of the human voice." Anything that is immoderate and beyond the common measure is said to be **outside the instrument**. It is like someone proposing the laws of Plato to the citizens of this current age. The metaphor is taken from a musical instrument, which remains within the twenty-note range. It also applies to someone who is extremely noisy.

->To stroke the head. XXXVII<-

**To stroke the head** <note>original: *Demulcere caput*</note> is an allegory accepted as a proverb for "to flatter," taken from the gestures of flatterers. However, Quintilian <note>referred to as "Fabius"</note> mentions this among "delays" in book eleven. In this hesitation, he says, "there are certain pauses that are not unseemly, as the actors call them: stroking the head, looking at the hand, or cracking the knuckles." Chremes, in the play *The Self-Tormentor*, says he cannot restrain himself from **stroking the head** of Syrus. It appears occasionally in Plautus as well. Saint Jerome wrote to Augustine: "I pass over the duties of salutation with which you **stroke my head**." Lucilius used the phrase "To scratch the head" in the same sense, according to Nonius: "This man, when he sees me, begins to flatter, to pet me, and to **scratch my head**."

->With the whole instrument. XXXVIII<-

Quintilian, in book eleven, says: "For there is a certain quality adapted to the ear, not by its size, but by its own character, which is, as it were, manageable for this purpose; certainly having in itself all the sounds and pitches that are required, and equipped, as they say, **with the whole instrument** <note>original: *toto organo*</note>." Thus far Quintilian. Therefore, you may rightly call things **equipped with the whole instrument** which consist of all their parts and fit together on every side. This is also taken from musical instruments.

->Beyond the thread. XXXIX<-

**Beyond the thread** <note>original Greek: Ὑπὲρ τὸ λίνον</note>. Lucian, in his *Jupiter Confuted*, says: "For nothing can happen outside the decrees of Fate, nor **beyond the thread**." He said **beyond the thread** to mean something outside the decree of the Fates. <note>The "thread" refers to the life-thread spun by the Parcae or Fates in mythology.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning the unreliability of public opinion and various metaphors for effort, flattery, and fate, drawing heavily on Roman orators and Greek dramatists.</summary>
