<page-num>644</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

...le. This is an allusion, however, to the threads of the three Fates <note>The Parcae, the personifications of destiny who spin the thread of life</note>. Similar to this is what we have recorded elsewhere: "Beyond the spindle" <note>original Greek: ὑπερκέρδη</note>.

<margin>X</margin>
## Everything is favorable; the old man dances.

**Everything is favorable; the old man dances.** This is a proverbial phrase that is appropriate to use whenever a private matter that was brought into danger turns out happily beyond expectation. Servius <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note>, explaining that verse of Maro <note>Virgil</note> from the third book of the *Aeneid*:

> We are purified for Jove, and we kindle the altars with vows:

refers to this adage and explains it in these words: "It should be known, of course, that it was the custom that when a ritual error had been committed, games were celebrated. For when the Romans were suffering from the anger of the Mother of the Gods <note>Cybele</note>, and could appease her neither with sacrifices nor games, a certain old man danced during the fixed Circensian Games <note>The Ludi Circenses, held in the Circus Maximus</note>, and this event was the cause of her appeasement. From this the proverb was born: **Everything is favorable; the old man dances.**" The same Servius, explaining a passage by the same poet in the eighth book of the *Aeneid*:

> When they saw the tall ships, and saw them glide
> Through the dark grove, and lean on silent oars,
> They are terrified by the sudden sight, and all, leaving
> Their tables, rise up—but bold Pallas 
> Forbids them to interrupt the sacred rites.

Servius says: "When the Circensian Games were once being celebrated at Rome for Apollo, and it was announced that Hannibal was attacking near the Colline Gate, everyone seized their arms and ran together. When they returned later, fearing a ritual pollution <note>piaculum: a transgression requiring atonement</note> because the games were interrupted, they found a certain old man dancing in the circus; when he was asked, he said he had not interrupted his dancing. Thus this proverb was spoken: **Things are safe while the old man is dancing.**" Verrius, in the works of Festus Pompeius, relates a story of this kind: "In the consulship of C. Sulpitius and C. Fulvius, while the praetor M. Calpurnius Piso was holding games, a sudden announcement of the enemy's arrival caused a rush to arms from the forum. But after they returned as victors to the theater, fearing that the interrupted games would bring a religious curse and that they would need to be restarted from the beginning, it was found that C. Pomponius, a freedman of advanced age, had been dancing to the flute-player. This cry, uttered out of joy that the religious rite had not been interrupted, is still celebrated today." There are those who think it was C. Volumnius who danced to the flute. Titus Livy <note>Livy, the Roman historian</note> also mentions this somewhere, unless my memory fails me. Close to this is what we have said in another place: "The owl has flown" <note>original Greek: γλαῦξ ἵπταται</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Wasps*:

> For our owl flew through the ranks before the battle.

This signifies that victory happened not by the courage of the soldiers, but by the favor of Minerva <note>Athena, whose symbol was the owl</note>.

<margin>XI</margin>
## You gave a sword to one who would kill himself.

**You gave a sword to one who would kill himself.** This has the form of an adage, which Plautus wrote in *Trinummus*: "You have given a sword for him to kill himself." That is, you provided the material and the help for his own destruction. Just as if someone were to put money into the hands of a young man in love, or entrust a high office to a rash youth, or allow a woman the freedom to go wherever she pleases. Aeneas also gave Dido the sword with which she killed herself. Servius says much about this passage, which we have discussed elsewhere under the proverb: "The gifts of enemies are no gifts" <note>original Greek: ἐχθρῶν ἄδωρα δῶρα</note>.

<margin>XII</margin>
## To plow another's field.

**To plow another's field.** <note>original Greek: Αλλοτρίαν ἄρουραν ἀρῷν</note>. This is said as a proverbial metaphor for someone who handles another's business, or who has an affair with another man's wife. Theognis says in his maxims:

> I hate a wandering woman and a foolish man,
> Whoever desires to plow the field of another.

Plautus likewise says of an adulterous husband: "He plows another's field, and leaves his own uncultivated." There is a similar rhetorical color used by the legal experts: "To irrigate another's fields while your own are thirsty." This is found in the Code <note>The Codex Justinianus</note> under *Services and Water*, the chapter *Praeses*. It is harsh and close to cruelty for a stream of water rising from your own estates to be passed on to the use of other neighbors to their injury, while your own fields are parched.

<margin>XIII</margin>
## The river waters what is far off.

**The river waters what is far off, but leaves behind what is closer.** <note>original Greek: Ποταμὸς τὰ πόῤῥω ποτίζων, τὰ δ᾽ ἔγγιον καταλείπει</note>. This is appropriately said of those who do good for outsiders who have no connection to them, while neglecting their own people. Diogenianus records this. It appears to be derived from...

<summary>Erasmus explores several proverbs related to unexpected good fortune (the dancing old man), self-destructive gifts (the sword), and the neglect of one's own responsibilities in favor of others' (plowing another's field or distant irrigation).</summary>

<page-num>645</page-num>
<header>THIRD THOUSAND, FIRST CENTURY</header>
<meta>catchword: Torqueri (To be twisted)</meta>

where a river rises, it is usually smaller and carries less clay with it; and the further it recedes from its source, the more abundant and rich it becomes.

### You lead a small stream into a great river.
->XLIIII<-

<note>original Greek: ποταμῷ μεγάλῳ ὀχετὸν ἐπάγεις</note>. That is, you lead a channel to a great river; meaning, you add a tiny and useless impulse to the greatest of matters. This is mentioned by Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia</note>. It is closely related to those other sayings: "Adding logs to the forest," "Water to the sea," or "A lamp to the sun."

### He cannot even say his father’s name.
->XLV<-

Synesius says in a certain letter against Andronicus: <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπος οὐκ ἔχων εἰπεῖν ὄνομα πατρὸς, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ πατρός φασι</note>. That is: "A man who cannot say his name, or rather, as they say, not even his father's." This applies to those who are extremely obscure, or of illegitimate birth, born of an uncertain father. This is the same kind of sentiment found in Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note>:

> Of whom none could point out the fatherland of the father.

From this, Plutarch <note>A Greek biographer and essayist</note> believes that illegitimate children were called *nothoi* because they were usually marked with these two letters, **S. P.**, which signified *sine patre* <note>Latin for "without a father"</note>.

### Not even if an ox should speak.
->XLVI<-

Alciphron, in a letter from Glycera to Menander: <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ ἐὰν μὲν οὐδενὶ τρόπῳ μὰ τὰς θεὰς, μηδὲ εἰ βοῦς μοι, τὸ λεγόμενον, φθέγξαιτο, πειθείην ἄν</note>. That is: "I would believe this by no means—by the goddesses!—not even if, as the saying goes, an ox had spoken to me." This is where the saying comes from, as it is frequently recorded in historical annals that an ox uttered a human voice <note>In Roman history, a speaking ox was considered a 'prodigy' or supernatural omen</note>. I remember reading, if I am not mistaken, a similar figure of speech in Plato: "Even if an oak tree should speak." For in ancient times, oracles were given from the oaks of Dodona <note>The oldest Hellenic oracle, where priests interpreted the rustling of oak leaves</note>.

### He sails the Aegean.
->XLVII<-

<note>original Greek: Τὸν αἰγαῖον πλεῖ</note>. That is, "He sails the Aegean," with the word "gulf" being understood. Aelian says in a certain letter: "The old man Laches, having abandoned farming and the practice of agriculture, boarded a ship and, as they say, 'sails the Aegean,' measuring the remaining seas; living among the waves, he lives the life of a gull, and struggles against various winds." Persius likewise says in his fifth Satire:

> Quickly to the ship! Nothing stops you from rushing 
> Across the Aegean in a vast vessel.

I believe this sea is more dangerous than others because of the frequent reefs. This is the source of that metaphor used by Marcus Tullius Cicero in his *Divinatio*: "I understand in what a rocky and difficult place I am moving." Nor is it infrequent in Jerome <note>The church father and translator of the Vulgate</note>: "The speech sailed out from rocky places," whenever he feels the difficulty of a question has been cleared. It will therefore apply to a man who, out of a desire for profit, refuses no danger whatsoever.

### Poets and painters are free.
->XLVIII<-

Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist</note>, in the dialogue he titled *On Images*: <note>original Greek: Καί τι παλαιὸς ἔτος ὁ λόος, ἀνεύθυνους εἶναι ποιητὰς καὶ γραφέας</note>. That is: "And yet, this is an old saying, that poets and painters are not held to account." The same author in his *Encomium of Demosthenes*: "The poetic race is free because of its variety." He means that it is permitted for poets and painters to imagine whatever they wish with impunity. Among the Greeks, *euthyne* refers to a legal case or accusation. Therefore, a magistrate who was compelled to give an account of his conduct was called *hypeuthynos* (accountable), while one who was free and from whom no account was required was called *aneuthynos* (unaccountable). This is indicated by Aeschines' oration against Ctesiphon. Diphilus, as quoted in Athenaeus's sixth book, says of poets:

| To whom alone belongs the power |
| :--- |
| To say and to do all things. |

That is:
> To whom it is permitted, and to them alone, to do and say whatever they please.

Horace alluded to this when he said:
> To painters and to poets 
> An equal power of daring anything has always been granted.

For poets are driven by a divine spirit, and therefore you would prescribe rules to them in vain. Seneca, in his book *On the Blessed Life*, says: "Whether we believe Plato, that he who is sane of mind knocks in vain at the doors of poetry; or Aristotle, that no great genius has existed without a mixture of madness." Furthermore, there is a great deal of kinship between poetry and painting. This is why Simonides, according to Plutarch, "called painting silent poetry, and poetry speaking painting." Hence Horace:
> As is painting, so is poetry.

<meta>catchword: Torqueri (To be twisted/applied)</meta>

This can be applied to those who are of a stubborn and obstinate disposition, whom it is necessary to leave to their own ways. Or it may apply to women, to whom everything is permitted, or to princes, for whom all actions are granted as a source of praise.

<margin>XLII</margin>
->To look through a lattice.<-

"To look through a lattice" <note>Latin: *Per transennam inspicere*</note> is spoken as a proverbial figure of speech for looking at something from a distance and summarily, rather than closely or in detail. The metaphor is taken from merchants who place lattices or screens <note>A *transenna* was a wicker-work screen or lattice-window</note> before goods they do not want to be handled; some even place transparent glass in the way, so that passers-by may only contemplate the items from a distance. They do not unpack or display them fully except to a suitable bidder. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the first book of *On the Orator*, says:

> If you had come into some house full of ornaments, or into a villa—if those things were set aside, as you say, and you were very eager to see them—you would not hesitate to ask the master to order them to be brought out, especially if he were a friend. Similarly, you should now ask Crassus to bring out that abundance of his ornaments, which we have glimpsed briefly in passing as if through a lattice, having been piled up in one place, and to set each thing in its proper place.

->Do not pronounce on a dispute.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the seventh book of his *Letters to Atticus*, writes: "I beseech you, <note>original Greek: μήτε δίκην</note>—'do not judge'—especially regarding yourself, from whom I have never seen anything done rashly." Cicero noted a proverbial poem which is cited by many others, including Lucian in his booklet *On Slander*:
<note>original Greek: μήτε δίκην δικάσῃς, πρὶν ἀμφοῖν μῦθον ἀκούσῃς</note>
That is:
> Do not be a judge until you have heard both sides.

Some attribute this to Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet</note>, but falsely. Thus Cicero calls it a "false Hesiod" <note>original Greek: ψευδοησίοδον</note>, since it belongs to Phocylides <note>A gnomic poet of Ionia</note>. It warns that one should not rashly pronounce judgment on anyone unless the matter has been diligently examined from both sides. It is also cited by Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
> Truly he was wise, whoever said: "Until you have heard the story of both, you should not judge."

Euripides expressed the same sentiment in *The Heraclidae*:
> What judges could decide a case, or who could understand a word, until they have clearly learned the story from both sides?

Seneca alluded to this in his play *Medea*:
> He who has decided something with one side unheard, even if he has decided justly, was not himself just.

This six-foot verse is also found among the Greek maxims:
<note>original Greek: Ἀνεξέταστον μὴ κόλαζε μηδένα</note>
That is:
> Do not punish anyone without having weighed the matter.

->When two go together.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the ninth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, writes: "If we had been together, counsel certainly would not have been lacking, for <note>original Greek: σύν τε δύ’ ἐρχομένω</note>—'when two go together.'" The same appears in the ninth book of his *Letters to Friends* addressed to Marcus Varro: "If you were somewhere near us, if there were any hope of safety, 'when two go together.'" It is aptly cited in Plato's *Protagoras*, teaching that an opinion is rendered firmer if it is confirmed by another. The source is in Homer's *Iliad*, Book 10, where Diomedes, about to go out to scout what the Trojans are doing, asks for a companion. For that, he says, would be both more pleasant and safer. The poem goes like this:

> But if some other man would follow with me, there would be more comfort, and there would be greater confidence. When two go together, one perceives before the other how there might be an advantage. But even if one should perceive it alone, his mind is nonetheless slower and his <margin>Counsel is thin.</margin> judgment is slight.

<summary>Erasmus discusses three proverbs: looking through a lattice (meaning a superficial glance), the legal necessity of hearing both sides of a dispute before judging, and the practical and intellectual benefits of having a companion when undertaking a task.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues a discussion on Homeric allegories and transitions into a series of adages regarding moderation, foresight, redundancy, and comparative merit.</meta>

<page-num>647</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY</header>
<meta>catchword: "tōn d'" (of those)</meta>

Apuleius, in his small book *On the God of Socrates* <note>Latin: *De dæmonio Socratis*</note>, claims that a fruitful allegory lies beneath this Homeric fiction: namely, that in dangerous matters, two things must be applied—counsel and help. Because Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note> is depicted as the most prudent, he serves as a symbol of counsel; Diomedes, as a youth excelling in strength, carries the image of help. Apuleius's words from that passage are: "Likewise, when spies must be chosen for perilous and afflicted circumstances to penetrate the enemy's camp in the dead of night, are not Ulysses and Diomedes chosen? Just like counsel and help, mind and hand, spirit and sword?"

---

## Sow with the hand, not the whole sack. LII

"One must sow with the hand, and not with the whole sack" <note>Greek: τῇ χειρὶ δεῖ σπείρειν, ἀλλὰ μὴ ὅλῳ τῷ θυλάκῳ</note>. That is, one should perform the sowing by hand, and not with the entire basket. This was a saying of Corinna to the poet Pindar, as Plutarch records in the commentary he titled *Whether the Athenians are more famous for war or for wisdom* <note>Greek: πότερον ἀθηναῖοι τῇ πολέμου, ἢ τῇ σοφίᾳ ἐνδοξότεροι</note>. Moderation must be maintained in every matter, and one should move step by step from one thing to another. It is derived from farmers, who, when they sow, do not pour everything out at once from the vessel itself, but scatter the seeds sparingly by hand, so that it suffices to cover the entire field. In the same way, kindness should be distributed so that you can provide for many. So too must labor in literature be moderated, so that the vigor of the mind remains sufficient for the other duties of life.

---

## From the front and from the back. LIII

"Before and behind" <note>Greek: πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω</note>. This is accepted as a proverb for looking into something diligently and comparing past events with present and future ones. It is taken from the first book of the *Iliad*, where Achilles, accusing Agamemnon of thoughtlessness, says:
> Nor does he know how to look both before and behind at the same time. <note>Greek: οὐδέ τι οἶδε νοῆσαι ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω</note>
Again, in the third book of the same work:
> He will see both before and behind at the same time. <note>Greek: ἅμα πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω λεύσσει</note>
Again in the eighteenth book <note>noted as 'sigma' in the Greek counting system</note> of the *Iliad*:
> For he alone looks both before and behind. <note>Greek: ὁ γὰρ οἶος ὅρᾷ πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω</note>
Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> used it as a proverb in the thirteenth book of his *Letters to Friends*, a verse which the elder Praecilius praises excellently, saying that the same man is able to see "both before and behind." Akin to this seems to be that line of Hesiod:
> Observing all things well on every side, lest you bring joy to your neighbors. <note>Greek: πάντα μάλ' ἀμφὶς ἰδὼν μὴ γείτοσι χάρματα γένη</note>
Plato in the *Cratylus*, advising that things which have been said should be examined again and again for what they are, uses this Homeric saying, "to look both before and behind." Marcus Tullius uses it in the *Third Philippic* to mean "from every side": "He is held from the back, from the front, and from the sides." He uses this figure of speech more than once elsewhere. Antiquity, in imagining the two-faced Janus, indicated the wisdom of kings, whose role it is both to remember and weigh the past and to foresee the future. For this reason, they also added two companions to divinity, Antevorta <note>She who looks forward</note> and Postvorta <note>She who looks backward</note>, whom the Romans once worshipped religiously, as Macrobius indicates in his commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*, book 1.

---

## Why do you castrate the Galli? LIIII

"Wretch, why do you cut?" <note>Greek: τάλας τί τέμνεις;</note>, that is, "Why do you castrate the Galli?" Why do you do what is already done? For the Galli <note>the eunuch priests of the goddess Cybele</note> are already castrated of their own accord. Why do you rob a naked person? Why do you afflict the afflicted? Why do you weaken an elderly body with fasts? Although this will be suitable for signifying any useless labor, just like the sayings "You are washing a brick" or "You are doing what is already done."

---

## How much better mules are than asses. LV

That line from Theognis has the very appearance of a proverb:
> You would know how much better mules are than asses. <note>Greek: γνώῃς δ' ὅσον ὄνων κρείσσονες ἡμίονοι</note>
This should be said when someone surpasses another by a long distance. It is mentioned in Athenaeus, in the seventh book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>The Banquet of the Learned</note>. It seems to be taken from Homer, whose verses are these from the tenth book of the *Iliad*:
> But when he was as far away as is the range of mules—for they are far better than oxen at dragging the jointed plow through deep fallow land. <note>original: ἀλλ' ὅτε δή ῥ' ἀπέην ὅσσον τ' ἐπίουρα πέλονται / ἡμιόνων, αἱ γάρ τε βοῶν προφερέστεραί εἰσιν, / ἑλκέμεναι νειοῖο βαθείης πηκτὸν ἄροτρον</note>
Again in the eighth book of the *Odyssey*...

<page-num>648</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<meta>catchword: οὐκ (not)</meta>

Of these, Clytoneus was by far the best at running, a blameless man of noble reputation; as far as the furrow of mules in a fallow field extends, so far did he outrun the people and reached the goal, leaving them behind. <note>Greek: Τῶν δὲ θέειν ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἔην κλυτόνωτος ἀμύμων, Ὅσσον τ’ ἐν νειῷ οὖρον πέλει ἡμιόνοιϊν, Τόσσον ὑπεκπροθέων λαὸς ἵκεθ’ οἷδ’ ἐλίποντο.</note> That is:
He surpassed all these in the race, the splendid Clytoneus:
As much as the furrow of mules precedes in the field,
So much did he, running ahead of the people, reach the goal,
Leaving them behind his back.
In ancient times, people plowed their fields with oxen, asses, and mules. This is the origin of that Mosaic law in Deuteronomy 22 which forbids putting an ox and an ass under the same yoke for the sake of plowing. Therefore, a plow drawn by mules reached the end of the furrow much faster—allowing the plowman to turn back—than one drawn by oxen. Hesiod likewise calls mules "hard-working" <note>Greek: ταλαέργους</note>.

### A difficult man.
A formidable man; quickly might he blame even the blameless. <note>Greek: Δεινὸς ἀνὴρ τάχα κεν καὶ ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳτο.</note> That is:
Perhaps the fierce and sharp man might blame even the innocent.
It is well-established by the testimony of many authors that this Homeric verse was once commonly tossed about as a barb against Demosthenes <note>The famous Greek orator</note>, because after taking money, he would sometimes defend the wicked and attack the good. Marcus Tullius Cicero twisted the same verse against Varro in the thirteenth book of his *Letters to Atticus*. In Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 11 <note>Greek: λ</note>, it is spoken by Patroclus:
You know well yourself, O elder nurtured by Zeus, how that man is
A formidable man; quickly might he blame even the blameless.
That is:
You yourself know well, old man, how fierce he is;
He would easily blame the innocent, and one free from fault.

<margin>Again in Iliad 13 <note>Greek: ν</note></margin>
Hector, since it pleases you to blame the blameless. <note>Greek: Ἕκτορ ἐπεί τοι θυμὸς ἀναίτιον αἰτιάασθαι.</note> That is:
Hector, when it pleases you to blame one who is free of fault.

### One omen is best: to defend the fatherland.
This Homeric verse also passed into a proverb:
One omen is best: to fight for the sake of the fatherland. <note>Greek: Εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης.</note> That is:
The one best bird is to fight to protect the country.
It is used by Marcus Tullius Cicero in his *Letters to Atticus*. Likewise by Pliny the Younger in his *Letters*. It is cited by Aristotle in the second book of his *Rhetoric* among his list of maxims. It is taken from the *Iliad*, Book 12 <note>Greek: μ</note>, where Hector, disregarding all other auguries <note>Omens interpreted from the flight of birds</note>, speaks in this manner:
You bid me obey the long-winged birds,
Of which I have no care nor regard, whether
They go to the right toward the dawn and the sun,
Or to the left toward the misty gloom.
But let us obey the counsel of great Zeus,
Who rules over all mortals and immortals.
One omen is best: to fight for the sake of the fatherland.
That is:
You now command me to obey the winged birds,
For which I have no care or regard, whether
They come to my right at the rising of the eastern sun,
Or to the left, toward the setting sun and the shadows of night.
But it is necessary for us to obey the judgment of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>,
The high-thunderer: he alone holds command over all,
As many as are mortal, as many as are free from death.
The one best bird is to fight to protect the country.
Quintus Fabius Maximus <note>The Roman general known as "The Delayer"</note> seems to have expressed this sentiment of Homer's in Cicero’s *On Old Age*. For although he was an augur himself, he dared to say that those things which were done for the safety of the Republic were carried out under the best auspices, while those things brought forward against the Republic were brought forward against the auspices. In Athenaeus, Heniochus twists this toward a parasite, citing a verse from the comic poet Metagenes:
One omen is best: to fight for the sake of the dinner. <note>Greek: Εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ δάπνης — a pun on "patris" (fatherland) and "depnis/dapnis" (dinner/feast)</note> That is:
The one best bird is to fight to protect the meal.

### Lest anything happen to his own head.
Terence in the *Phormio* used a proverbial figure of speech: "Lest anything happen to his own head" <note>Latin: *Ne quid suo fuat capiti*</note>, meaning so that he does not bring any trouble upon himself. This is modeled after that Homeric phrase in *Iliad* 18 <note>Greek: σ</note>.

<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY</header>

"Should I not have woven evils for the Trojans in my anger?" <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, 13.125. Erasmus uses the term "weaving" (Greek: *rhaptein*) to describe plotting or concocting a plan.</note>
-> The same in the *Odyssey*, Book 19: <-
"For nine years we wove evils for them, handling them with all sorts of tricks." <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, 3.118. The Greek *rhaptomen* means "we were sewing" or "weaving" mischief.</note>

### LIX
### May the earth gape open for me first.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the ninth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, says: "It won’t be long before he wants me to decide this: and let him not be content with Galba, Scaevola, Cassius, or Antonius."
"Then may the wide earth gape for me." <note>Greek: Τότε μοι χάνοι εὐρεῖα χθών. A traditional expression of extreme shame or a desire to die rather than face a certain situation.</note> -> That is, <-
May the wide earth itself then gape open for me.
This is a Homeric half-verse from the *Iliad*, Book 4. Lucian, in *The Lapiths*, says: "And as the saying goes, I prayed that the earth would swallow me up." <note>Greek: καὶ ὅσα δὴ τὸ λόγο, χανεῖν μοι τὴν γῆν ηὐχόμην.</note> Meaning: Now, according to the common proverb, I was wishing the ground would open for me. Aristides, in his life of *Themistocles*, writes: "He was neither at a loss, nor struck with consternation, nor did he pray for the earth to gape for him, nor did he count those happy who had long since died." <note>Greek: οὐδ’ ἀπορῆ, οὐδ’ ἐξεπλάγη, οὐδ’ ηὔξατο αὐτῷ χανεῖν τὴν γῆν, οὐδ’ ηὐτομόνησε πᾶν πάλαι κρμυνός.</note> And Vergil, in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:
"But I would pray that the earth first gape open to its depths for me,
Or that the Almighty Father strike me to the shades with his bolt—
To the pale shades of Erebus and the bottomless night—
Before, O Modesty, I violate you or break your laws."

### LX
### Clothes make the man.

"Garments [make] the man." <note>Greek: Εἵματα ἀνήρ.</note> That is, clothing makes the man. This is still a very common saying today. For they say it this way: "Dress reflects the man; let him who has it, wear it."
Quintilian affirms the same in the eighth book of his *Institutes*: "And a refined and magnificent dress," he says, "gives men authority, as is testified by a Greek verse." I believe this verse cited by Fabius <note>Quintilian's full name was Marcus Fabius Quintilianus.</note> is the one found in Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 6:
"From these things a good reputation and honor arise among men." <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, 6.29.</note> -> That is, <-
Truly, from these things a man's good name and glory arise.
A little further down in the same book, Homer sufficiently indicates how much weight the style of dress carries in winning over beauty and dignity for a person, when he portrays the maiden Nausicaa speaking of Odysseus in this way:
"For before he seemed to me to be quite unsightly,
But now he is like the gods, who possess the wide heaven." <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, 6.242–243.</note> -> That is, <-
Before he seemed most foul in his appearance,
Now he is like the gods, whom great Olympus nourishes.
For previously Odysseus had been naked, but now he had put on shining clothes, and immediately he seemed like a different person.
"Then he went and sat apart on the shore of the sea,
Gleaming with beauty and grace." <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, 6.236–237.</note> -> That is, <-
Then, coming to the sea shore, he sat down at a distance,
Shining with beauty and charm.

### LXI
### Softened by warm baths.

"Tender from warm baths." <note>Greek: Ἁπαλοὶ θερμολουσίαις.</note> This was said of people who were soft and overflowing with luxury. For even Homer is a witness that in ancient times warm baths were criticized as a mark of luxury, mentioning them among the delights of a pleasure-seeking life in the *Odyssey*, Book 8:
"Always dear to us are the feast, the lyre, and the dances,
Changes of clothing, warm baths, and the bed." <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, 8.248–249.</note> -> That is, <-
But feasts and dances are always dear to our hearts,
And songs, and various garments, and warm baths,
And sleep.
The adage is recorded by Eudemus in these very words: "Softened by warm baths," referring to those who live delicately in the softness of their beds. Persius alluded to this when he said... <note>Persius, *Satires*, 3. Erasmus's commentary on this quote continues on the following page.</note>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...And he shakes the boiled buttocks with hooked forceps. <note>original Latin: *Elixasq; nates labefactat forcipe adunca.* This line likely concludes a previous adage regarding medical or culinary practices.</note>

->Right foot in the shoe, left in the basin.<-
<margin>LX</margin>
"The right foot into the shoe, the left into the foot-wash." <note>original Greek: Δεξιὸν εἰς ὑπόδημα, ἀριστερὸν εἰς ποδόνιπτρον.</note> That is: The right foot in the shoe, the left in the basin. One must understand a verb appropriate to the sense, such as "he puts" or "he places." Suidas, citing Aristophanes, says this is commonly said of those who know how to adapt themselves appropriately to the condition of the current situation, and who assume different characters according to the place, time, and business. It is a heroic hexameter verse:
*The right in a little shoe, but the left in a foot-wash.*
A *podoniptrum* <term>podoniptrum: a vessel for washing feet, from the Greek *pous* (foot) and *niptron* (wash-basin)</term> is the vessel in which feet are washed; the name was bestowed by the Greeks.

->The Goddess Impudence.<-
<margin>LX</margin>
"Shamelessness is a goddess." <note>original Greek: Θεὸς ἡ ἀναίδεια.</note> That is: The Goddess Impudence. This was commonly said when someone gained profit or benefit from their own shameless audacity. For, as Homer says, "modesty is useless to a needy man," and you may see many mortals for whom it was a great benefit to have had no shame at all. Indeed, no one has ever dared a thing so foolish or absurd that it did not find someone to promote and admire it; and by far the greatest part of mortals, being quite foolish, admire the silliest things most. This is recorded by Zenodotus and Diogenianus. Theophrastus, in his book *On Laws*, recorded that there were altars to Contumely <note>Contumely: insulting treatment or contemptuous speech.</note> and Impudence among the Athenians. Istrus attests to the same in his 14th book. Likewise, Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the second book of *On Laws*: "For that was a flaw in Athens, that after the crime of Cylon was expiated, they built a shrine to Contumely and Impudence at the suggestion of Epimenides the Cretan; for it is fitting to consecrate virtues, not vices." Menander, in his collection of maxims, calls her the greatest of all goddesses:
"O greatest of the gods,
now you are Shamelessness, if it is right to call you a goddess.
It is right, for now to prevail is considered a god." <note>original Greek: Ω μεγίστη τῶν θεῶν / Νῦν ἔσ’ ἀναίδει’, εἰ θεὸν καλεῖν σε δεῖ. / Δεῖ, τὸ κρατεῖν γὰρ νῦν νομίζεται θεός.</note> **That is,**
>O greatest of goddesses,
>In this age, if it is lawful to call you a goddess,
>It is lawful, since now to have conquered is held as a god.

->To cast out of possession.<-
<margin>LXI</margin>
"To cast out of possession" passed from the language of legal experts into common speech, used for taking away someone's reputation which they have already obtained by general consensus, or for stripping someone of what they seem to hold by their own right. For the law always favors the possessor, and an interdict <term>interdict: a Roman legal decree often used to restore possession of property</term> was issued to prevent anyone from casting another out by force. This edict exists in the *Pandects* <note>The *Pandects* (or *Digest*) is a massive compendium of Roman law compiled by order of Emperor Justinian I.</note>, book 43, under the title "On Force and Armed Force," and Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions it in his speech *For Aulus Caecina*. Plato, in the book titled *Gorgias*, says: "Trying to expel me from my property and from the truth through enmity." <note>original Greek: ὑπ’ ἐχθρᾶς ἐκβαλὼν μὲ τῆς οὐσίας καὶ ἀληθῆς.</note> That is: You are trying to eject me from true possession. It appears several times in the works of Cicero. And in the same author there is also: "As if he had come into his own possession," used when someone acts too imperiously or lingers longer than is fair. Quintilian, in his book on rhetoric, says: "Which, while it yields in workmanship, is now almost driven out of possession." For the saying becomes more pleasant whenever it is transferred to matters of the mind.

->The wings of Daedalus.<-
<margin>L</margin>
"Daedalus’s wings." <note>original Greek: Δαιδάλου πτερά.</note> That is: Daedalus's wings. It is usually said when someone, otherwise not sufficiently fit to complete a duty, adds the assistance of some art or help. Or when someone, under pressing necessity, flees to new plans. The story is well known, which provided the occasion for the proverb: namely, about Daedalus, who escaped from the hands of King Minos by means of a new invention, with wings sewn on.

->Then I woke up.<-
<margin>LX</margin>
"Then I was awakened." <note>original Greek: Εἶτα ἐξηγρόμην.</note> That is: Then I woke up. With this saying, they signified that what was being said was vain or false. Aristophanes says: "And then I woke up." <note>original Greek: κᾆτ’ ἔγωγ’ ἐξηγρόμην.</note> Bacchus, in *The Frogs*, boasts to Hercules that he took part in a naval battle and sank twelve or thirteen enemy ships. Since this seemed not at all likely to Hercules—that Bacchus, an idle and effeminate god, had behaved himself so bravely in war—he jokes: "And then I woke up." Although the commentator warns that this speech is attributed by some not to Hercules but to Xanthias, and by some to Bacchus himself, to signify that he had lied about everything else he had related. I will add the verse of Aristophanes. Hercules:
"And having fought at sea..." Bacchus: "And we even sank ships
of the enemy, either twelve or thirteen." Hercules:

Ooo iii
<meta>catchword: Sphō (the beginning of Hercules' next line in Greek: Σφὼ)</meta>

<summary>This page discusses five classical adages: adapting to circumstances (the shoe and the basin), the social power of shamelessness (Goddess Impudence), legal metaphors for reputation (casting out of possession), resorting to ingenuity in desperation (Daedalus's wings), and a sarcastic expression for dismissing tall tales (then I woke up).</summary>

# THIRD THOUSAND, FIRST CENTURY
<meta>Catchword: tato. Signature: li 2.</meta>

<margin>Bacchus: "By Apollo!" Hercules: "Even I was asking."</margin>
->that is,<-

> And did you fight a naval battle, I pray?
> Indeed, we sank twelve or thirteen
> of the enemy’s ships. You, I ask? Us, of course.
> And afterwards, truly, my sleep left me.
<note>original Greek: Σφᾶς ... νὴ τ’ ἀπόλλω ... κατ’ ἔγωγ’ ἐξῃρόμην. This dialogue is from Aristophanes’ "The Frogs."</note>

This proverbial joke is still familiar to the common people today, whenever things people recount seem empty and very much like dreams. For we call frivolous things "dreams" <note>original Greek: ὀνείρατα (*oneirata*)</note>. "For I speak to you in every way as if recounting dreams" <note>original Greek: πάντη γάρ σοι οἷον ὀνείρατα λέγω (*pante gar soi hoion oneirata lego*)</note>; that is, you tell stories almost everywhere as if they were dreams. From this, the Greeks also call those who observe frivolous things "dream-watchers" <term>oneiroscopos: a person who interprets dreams, here used by Erasmus to mean someone focused on trifles</term>. Marcus Tullius Cicero seems to have alluded to this wittily when he concluded *Scipio's Dream*—in which he recounts many fables about the harmony of the spheres and about souls—with: "He departed, and I was released from sleep."

### Bought from the stone.
->LXVII<-

"Bought from the stone" <note>original Latin: *De lapide emptus*</note>. This was said of a most contemptible and exceedingly obscure man. For among the kinds of slaves, according to the proverb "Even an Azorian is preferred to a slave," <note>original Greek: καὶ Ἄζωρος πρὸ δούλου</note> those bought at auction were considered of the lowest stamp, especially those who had been sold publicly in the forum. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his speech against Piso: "When all the magistrates had issued a proclamation concerning me, except for one praetor from whom I should not have asked it—the brother of my enemy—and except for two who were *bought from the stone*." It is very similar to that Greek expression which we have rendered in another place, "A fox or a slave," or "A slave bought with salt" <note>original Latin/Greek: *Sale emptum mancipium* / ἀλώπηξ ἢ ἀνδράποδον</note>. Columella uses a very similar expression to signify a cheap slave of the smallest price: "Whom the common people indeed think," he says, "can be acquired for a small amount of bronze, or as a harmful person *from the stone*. But I, dissenting from the opinion of many, judge a vine-dresser to be especially valuable." In that passage, I think one should read either *noxium* (harmful/guilty), meaning one surrendered for a crime and ordered to be sold for that reason, or *nexum* (bound). For those were called *Nexi* <term>nexi: in early Roman law, citizens who had pledged their own person as collateral for a debt and were "bound" to their creditor</term> who, because they were unable to pay, were delivered to their creditors. However, the *nexi* are not properly contained under the name of slaves, nor are they sold. Julius Pollux, in the third book of his *Onomasticon* <note>original Latin: *de rerum vocabulis*</note>, calls the stone from which slaves were once sold a "stone platform" <note>original Greek: πρατῆρα λίθου (*pratera lithou*)</note> or a "selling place" <note>original Greek: πωλητήριον (*poleterion*)</note>.

### Give me a basin.
->LXVIII<-

<margin>"Give me a basin." <note>original Greek: δότε μοι λεκάνην.</note></margin>
Whenever something was so vehemently annoying that it could no longer be endured, they would order a basin to be handed to them, as if they were about to vomit from bile, nausea, and loathing of the situation. For example, if someone could not endure a speech that was beyond measure unlearned, or if someone offended by sophisticated trifles should say: "Give me a basin." It is recorded by Suidas. Moreover, it appears in Aristophanes' *The Clouds*. And Plutarch, in his *Political Precepts*, cites it from Plato the comic poet.

### You challenge Entellus as Dares did.
->LXIX<-

"You challenge Entellus as Dares did" <note>original Latin: *Dares Entellum provocas*</note> both has the appearance of a proverb and seems to have gained the status of a proverb among the learned. For Jerome says to Augustine: "Remember Dares and Entellus." It will be suitable to use whenever someone with youthful rashness provokes someone else who is not quite so ready to take up a contest, but who will be intolerable if he once enters into it. This is the character of old men: that while they gladly avoid trouble, they carry out what they have undertaken with persistence. The phrase is taken from the fifth book of the *Aeneid*, where a certain Dares, relying on his strength and fierce with youth, leaps forward into the middle and challenges anyone to a contest. When no one rises and the rest are deterred, he demands the prize from Aeneas as if he were already the victor. But Entellus, an old man who had long since retired from this kind of contest, finally rises to fight with boxing-gloves—partly at the instigation of Acestes, and partly from the memory of his old victories. For a long time, standing his ground, he endured the youth jumping insolently around him, until having fallen from a missed blow, he was so rekindled by shame that he would have plainly finished off Dares (who was by then far unequal to him), had not Aeneas intervened and snatched him away. I would have added the poem of Virgil itself, for it is by far the most delightful, were it not both a bit long and easily available.

### To Cynosarges.
->LXX<-

<margin>"To Cynosarges." <note>original Greek: Ἐς κυνόσαργες.</note></margin>
This was said as a proverbial insult, just like "To the place of the blessed" <note>original Greek: ἐς μακαρίαν (used ironically)</note> or "To the crows" <note>original Greek: ἐς κόρακας (meaning "go to hell")</note>. Moreover, Cynosarges was a certain place in Attica where illegitimate sons and bastards used to exercise. Its name was bestowed from "the white dog" or "the swift dog" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ κυνὸς ἀργοῦ (*apo kynos argou*)</note>. For to the Greeks, that word *argos* signifies both. He who collected histories from the polemical orations of Gregory of Nazianzus relates that Cynosarges was named from the dog's... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom catchword.</note>

<summary>Erasmus explains four proverbs regarding empty stories (dreams), low-status slaves (bought from the stone), extreme disgust (give me a basin), and rashly challenging a formidable veteran (Dares and Entellus).</summary>
<keywords>Aristophanes, Cicero, slavery, Roman law, Virgil, Aeneid, Entellus, Dares, Cynosarges, Greek etymology, boxing, rhetoric</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Roman adages, specifically focusing on those derived from place names and mythological associations. The previous page ended with the proverb "Bought from the stone," and this page begins mid-discussion on the origins of the "Cynosarges" gymnasium in Athens.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>Relating to the "White Dog." <note>original Greek: τατὸ κ ἐν γ., likely shorthand for *ta kata Kynosarges*</note></margin>They ascribe the cause of this name to the following story: when a certain Diomus of Athens (according to Stephanus, though Suidas names him Didymus) was once sacrificing to Hercules, a white dog—or as others say, a swift eagle—seized a portion of the victim and dropped it in a certain place. Terrified by this omen, Diomus consulted the god and received an oracle: he was to build a shrine to Hercules in the exact spot where the meat had been carried, for that place was pleasing to Hercules. Furthermore, since Hercules was of illegitimate birth—being born of an adulterous union—yet equal to the gods in honor due to his own virtue, it was decided that those who were illegitimate <note>original Latin: *spurii*, referring to children whose parents were not legally married citizens</note>, and who were not citizens under either their father’s or mother’s name, should exercise there. This is not inconsistent with what Plutarch writes in his small book titled *The Dialogue on Love*: "If, therefore, one must also call this affliction 'female love' and 'illegitimate,' as if it were consigning us to the Cynosarges or the women’s quarters; or rather, as they call a certain eagle *gnesion* <note>meaning 'genuine' or 'legitimately born'</note>, that is, noble, pure-bred, and a mountain-dweller, which Homer calls the 'black one' and the 'hunter.'" <note>original Greek: Εἰ δ' ἐν τῷ πάθει δὴ καὶ τὰς θήλεας ἔρωτα θήλειαν καὶ νόθον ὥσπερ ἂς κυνόσαργες συντελοῦντα, τὴν γυναικωνῖτιν, μᾶλλον δ' ὥσπερ αἰτύπ τινα λέγουσι γνήσιον καὶ ὀρθὸν, ὃν ἀμφὶ μέλανα καὶ θηρευτὰν προσαγορ</note> From this, the phrase "To the Cynosarges" <note>original Greek: εἰς κυνόσαργες</note> was used either as a taunt, as if calling someone a bastard, or as a curse, as if you were saying, "Go to the gallows!" Later, it is consistent that philosophers and sophists began to chatter in this place as well. For Suidas testifies that there were three gymnasia in Athens: the Lyceum, the Cynosarges, and the Academy. Plutarch also mentions this in his *Life of Themistocles*, who they say was illegitimate. There was a gymnasium of Hercules outside the gates of Athens where illegitimate youths would gather for the sake of exercise, because the god himself was of illegitimate birth, born of a mortal mother. Themistocles, while still a youth, skillfully enticed some noble-born youths to go there as well, so that he might gradually abolish the distinction between the illegitimate and the legitimate.

<margin>LX</margin>
->Cythnic calamities.<-

"Cythnic calamities" <note>original Greek: Κυθνώδης συμφορά</note>. Zenodotus cites Aristotle as his source for this. He says the people of Cythnus were so thoroughly harassed and afflicted by Amphitryon that "Cythnic calamity" became a proverb for the greatest disasters and immense misfortunes. Cythnus is one of the Cyclades islands, situated opposite Dryopis, according to Stephanus.

<margin>LX</margin>
->Cythonymus's disgrace.<-

"Cythonymus’s disgrace" <note>original Greek: Κυθωνύμου αἶσχος</note>. This was said against a man who was vehemently infamous, or one whose name ought to be suppressed—either because of his evil deeds or because of some calamity. Hence the Greek expression "the name of the un-heralded" <note>original Greek: ἀκελάδῳ nomine</note>. Even today, people commonly say a name should be covered up whenever they imply a crime is too foul for the perpetrator's name to be mentioned. The source is Zenodotus.

<margin>LXX</margin>
->Cyzicene staters.<-

"Cyzicene staters" <note>original Greek: Κυζικινοὶ στατῆρες</note>. Used of something skillfully engraved. For this is what the <margin>haters of logic <note>original Greek: μισολόγοι</note></margin> imply. These coins were once famous because they appeared elegantly carved. They represented on one side Cybele, the mother of the gods, with a woman’s face, and on the other the image of a lion. It seems to me that the proverb would be more applicable when we signify a man who is inconsistent and unlike himself, or one who acts far differently than he presents himself. Just as the Cyzicene coin showed the effeminate Cybele on one side and a lion on the other. A stater was worth 28 Attic drachmas, from which it seems the phrase could also be used for something of great price. Cyzicus was a city of the Propontis. Some place a city of the same name in Sicily. Besides others, Suidas mentions this expression.

<margin>LXX</margin>
->Cyrnian land.<-

"Cyrnian land" <note>original Greek: Κυρνία γῆ</note>. This was said of a region infamous for robberies, as they say Cyrnus once was. Cyrnus is an island to the north, opposite the noble fortress of Iapygia, according to Stephanus; however, due to the robberies there, it was inaccessible to sailors. Pliny asserts that this is Corsica: "In the Ligurian Sea," he says, "is Corsica, which the Greeks called Cyrnus." This nation still has a bad reputation among the Italians today. The proverb can be aptly twisted to refer to a man who is violent and greedy for the property of others. In the collections of Zenobius (in the flawed editions), I find "Cyrnian ruin" <note>original Greek: κυρνία ἄτη</note>, that is, Cyrnian harm.

<margin>LX</margin>
->Cinyras's wealth.<-

"Cinyras’s wealth" <note>original Greek: Κινύρου πλοῦτος</note>. This was said of immense riches. It is very similar to "The wealth of Midas." Ovid sufficiently indicates that his region was most opulent in the 10th book of the *Metamorphoses*: "I congratulate this land, because it is far from those regions." <note>Ovid is referring to the land of Cinyras and the incestuous Myrrha.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of King Cinyras of Cyprus, legendary for his immense wealth and the tragic story of his daughter Myrrha. It transitions into adages regarding indifference, physical health, and the fickleness of human fortune.</meta>

...which brought forth such great wickedness. Let the Panchaian land be rich in balsam, cinnamon, and its own costum, and let it bear frankincense sweated from the wood, and other flowers: as long as it also bears myrrh. <note>original: Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 10.307-310. The poet suggests that all the exotic perfumes of Arabia/Panchaia are not worth the "wickedness" of the story of Myrrha.</note>

Pindar, in his *Nemean Odes*, mentions the very wealthy Cinyras: "For wealth planted with God’s help is more stable for men, just as it made Cinyras abound with wealth in sea-girt Cyprus." <note>original: Pindar, *Nemean Odes* 8.17-18</note> Plato also mentions him in the second book of *The Laws*: "For if a man were even richer than Cinyras or Midas, but were unjust, he is both wretched and lives a miserable life." <note>original: Plato, *Laws* 660e</note> Suidas, under the entry for "growing old," records it in this way: "May you grow older than Tithonus <note>A mythological figure who was granted eternal life but not eternal youth</note>, wealthier than Cinyras, and more luxurious than Sardanapalus <note>An Assyrian king legendary for his decadence</note>, so that the proverb may be fulfilled in you: old men are twice children."

### LXXVI
## I care less for those things than for marsh frogs.

"I have no more care for such things than for the frogs in the pools." <note>original: Μέλει μοι τῶν τοιούτων οὐδ' ἦν... (Greek)</note> This is a proverbial hyperbole by which we signify that a matter does not concern us at all. It may also be rightly said against detractors whose insults we claim to stoutly despise. For even if frogs croak and bark incessantly at those passing by, repeating that hateful song without end—*brekekekex, koax koax*—nevertheless, no one is moved by it. To this point, Origen (as cited in the papal decrees) interprets "Egyptian frogs" as the empty chatter of logicians <term>dialecticians: students of formal logic and debate</term> and sophists.

### LXXVII
## Healthier than a gourd.

"Healthier than a pumpkin." <note>original: Κολοκύντης ὑγιέστερος (Greek)</note> Suidas and Zenodotus record this as an adage. Athenaeus, in Book 3, quotes this verse from Epicharmus:
> And it was far healthier than a gourd.

The Greek verse will be consistent if you read it as *en ei*. For as we have cited it, it is found in the edition of Athenaeus printed by Aldus. He does not indicate where the saying originated. Therefore, one must guess that it is derived either from the fact that a gourd is not easily damaged by bad air because of the hard shell that covers it, or because it is said to be effective for various remedies, as Dioscorides indicates in Book 2, and likewise Pliny in Book 20, chapter... <note>Erasmus leaves the chapter number blank</note>. Nor is there only one species used for medicine: the cultivated kind which the Greeks call *kolokynthe* is useful; the wild kind, empty inside, which the Greeks call *somphos* (as Pliny says), is also useful; and the smaller cultivated kind, *kolokynthis*, which you might call a "little gourd," is also effective. It seems to me the proverb is not absurdly derived from the fact that a gourd is plump and whole on all sides, not gaping with cracks, nor prone to worms. Indeed, the wholeness and plumpness of the body is an argument for health. This is related to the one we reviewed elsewhere: "Healthier than a tick" <note>original: *crotonis sanior*. This refers both to the well-fed insect and the city of Croton, famous for its healthy athletes</note>.

### LXXVIII
## With God’s will, everyone rejoices and weeps.

"With God's help, every man both laughs and laments." <note>original: σὺν τῷ θεῷ πᾶς καὶ γελᾷ κ' ὀδύρεται (Greek)</note> This adage warns that the change in human affairs is swift, and it does not lie within our power for things to be perpetually prosperous; rather, however it pleases Fortune, we are either lifted up by success or afflicted by adversity. This verse is found in Sophocles’ *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*. The same sentiment is expressed by Euripides in *Iphigenia at Aulis*:
> Atreus did not beget you, Agamemnon,
> For a life of only good things.
> It is necessary for you to rejoice and to grieve.
> For you were born mortal. Even if you are unwilling,
> The things the gods wish will come to pass.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of adages from the previous section, moving from expressions of indifference and health to those concerning divine favor, fortune, and historical anecdotes from Greek literature and mythology.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

**With God** <note>original: "Cum deo"</note> is used by the Greeks for that which happens by the favor of a divine power. Conversely, **Without God** <note>original: "Sine deo"</note> refers to what happens without the favor of the gods. Pindar in the fifth *Pythian Ode* says, "With god, or without." <note>original: σὺν θεῷ ἄτερ</note> That is, not without the gods. The same author in the ninth ode of that same work writes:
> The action of the gods is swift when they are hurrying, and the paths are short.
> <note>original: Ὠκεῖα δ’ ἐπειγομένων ἤδη θεῶν πρᾶξις, ὁδοί τε βραχεῖαι</note>

Again, in the tenth ode:
> When the gods have completed a task, 
> nothing ever seems to be unbelievable.
> <note>original: Θεῶν τελεſάντων, οὐδέν ποτε φαίνεται ἔμμεν ἄπιϛον</note>

And Virgil says:
> I truly believe [he came] not without a purpose, nor without the divine will of the gods.
> <note>original: Haud equidem, ſine mente reor, ſine numine diuūm. *Aeneid* 5.56</note>

Thus, that which happens beyond hope and of its own accord is said to happen **by divine providence.** Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
> But he himself comes forward into the assembly
> just as if by god's will.
> <note>original: Ἀλλ’ ὁ δὶ προσέρχεται, ὥσπερ κατὰ θεὸν εἰς ἀγοράν</note>

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the fifth speech against Verres: "How did this come into the mind of Metellus by divine inspiration?" And Horace in his third book of *Odes*, Ode 4: "Not without the gods was I a spirited infant." <note>original: Non ſine dijs animoſus infans</note> Also **With the Muses**, <note>original: σὺν ταῖς μούσαις</note> that is, with the Muses favoring the work. **With the gods**, <note>original: σὺν τοῖς θεοῖς</note> meaning with the gods' good help. 

There is a witty story about Stratonicus <note>A famous Athenian musician known for his sharp wit</note> recorded by Athenaeus in book 8. Although he was a mediocre lyre-player, he had in his school nine statues of the Muses and one of Apollo, but only two actual students. When someone asked him how many disciples he had, he replied: "**With the gods, twelve,**" playing on an ambiguity. For "with the gods" can be understood as either "including the gods in the count" or "with the favor of the gods." 

Furthermore, the ancients attributed the chief divine power to **Fortune**, to whom is credited whatever turns out well or poorly. Concerning this, Demosthenes says in his speech on Philip’s letter: "For Fortune is a great weight—rather, she is everything—in all the affairs of men." <note>original: μεγάλη γὰρ ῥοπὴ, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ ὅλον ἡ τύχη παρὰ πάντων τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πράγματα</note> Likewise Aeschines in his *Apology regarding the False Embassy*: "Everything is in the hand of Fortune." <note>original: ἡ τύχη πάντων ἐϛὶ κυρία</note>

<margin>LXXIX</margin>
->To wrestle with the Corycus.<-
<note>original: Πρὸς κώρυκον γυμνάζεσθαι</note> That is, **To wrestle against the Corycus** was said of one who took up a useless task. I suspect Corycus was some invincible wrestler—unless we prefer the "corycus" to be a leather bag <note>A punching bag or sandbag used by ancient athletes for training</note>, making the adage similar to "You are skinning a wineskin." However, in this sense, Hesychius writes the word with an *omega* and *upsilon* <note>κώρυκος</note>, while Suidas writes it with an *omicron* and *iota* <note>κόρικος</note>. Furthermore, Apuleius describes such a "battle" fought in Thessaly. <note>Refers to a scene in *The Golden Ass* where the protagonist "battles" inflated wineskins thinking they are thieves</note>

<margin>LXXX</margin>
->The mouth of the Curetes.<-
<note>original: Κρητῶν ϛόμα</note> This was a common saying when someone appeared to speak while inspired by a divine power. This is because the **Curetes**, the companions of Cybele, were thought to prophesy when seized by a certain sacred frenzy. This is recorded by Zenodotus and mentioned by Hesychius.

<margin>LXXXI</margin>
->It is better for us than yesterday.<-
This phrase from Aristophanes' *Plutus* seems to have a proverbial form:
> O Blepsidemus, things are going better for me than yesterday.
> <note>original: Ὦ Βλεψίδημε’ ἄμεινον ἢ χθὲς πράττομεν</note>

We use this when we signify that our fortune has changed for the better. There is also that line from Theocritus, which we cited elsewhere:
> Perhaps tomorrow will be better.
> <note>original: Τάχ’ αὔριον ἔσσετ’ ἄμεινον</note>

For "**Yesterday**" and "**tomorrow**" are used to represent the past and the future.

<margin>LXXXII</margin>
->A Cretan sacrifice.<-
<note>original: Οἱ κρῆτες τὴν θυσίαν</note> That is, "**The Cretans [perform] the sacrifice,**" with the verb "perform" or something similar understood. Zenodotus traces the adage to this story: Agamemnon, tossed by a storm, was driven to Crete. He entered Polyrrhenia (which is a town on the island of Crete, named for its abundance of sheep, according to Stephanus) and began a religious rite. In the meantime, however, his captives boarded the ships and fled. When this was reported to him, he is said to have left the sacrifice halved and unfinished—even though the victim was already burning—and hurried at a run to the seashore, greatly disturbed and dismayed in spirit. There he found barely one ship remaining in which he was carried away, having called down many curses upon the inhabitants of that island. From this, whenever a matter was handled in a tumult and with confusion, they called it a "**Cretan sacrifice.**"

# THIRD CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
Ii 4
<meta>catchword: and each</meta>

...[they] were doing. It seems to me that it will apply when someone does not enjoy the things they have prepared. Just as happened to Agamemnon, whose sacrificial victims the Cretans devoured. <note>This fragment at the top of the page concludes an adage from the previous leaf regarding wasted efforts or stolen rewards.</note>

### As soon as pity is felt, gratitude dies. LXXXIII

**As soon as pity is felt, gratitude dies.** <note>original: Αμ' ηλεηται και τεθνηκεν η χαρις; Latin: Simul & mifertum eft interiitq; gratia.</note>
This is a <term>senarius</term> <note>A line of verse consisting of six feet, common in ancient drama.</note> used as a proverb found in the works of Zenodotus. It is usually said against an ungrateful person who, as soon as they are relieved of their troubles, stops remembering the kindness of the one who helped restore them. This is similar to the saying: "While it hurts, he remembers; when it is pleasant, he forgets." On the contrary, the proverb advises: 
**Remember what you have received; forget what you have given.** <note>original: Χαριν λαβων μεμνησο, δος επιλαθου.</note>
Seneca teaches the same in his *Moral Essays*:
> One ought to remember a benefit received and forget a benefit given.

But such is the nature of the common people today that the memory of kindnesses is fragile, while the memory of injuries is tenacious. As Plautus says: "If you help someone, gratitude is lighter than a feather; if you offend someone, they carry a resentment as heavy as lead." <note>original: Si quid iuues, pluma leuior gratia: fi quid offendas, plumbeas iras gerūt.</note> These verses are also celebrated for the same sentiment:
**The one who is saved is by nature ungrateful and forgetful.** <note>original: Αμα δ' ο σωθεις εστιν αχαριστος φυσει.</note>
And:
**Gratitude grows old very quickly after the gift is given.** <note>original: Μετα την δοσιν ταχιστα γηρασκει χαρις.</note>

### He runs in vain. LXXXIIII

**He runs into the void.** <note>original: Εις κενον τρεχει.</note> That is, he runs in vain, used for someone who labors to no purpose. St. Paul the Apostle used this expression in several places. It is taken from those who compete in a race in a stadium. This line of verse is famous:
**A wretched man labors, running in vain.** <note>original: Αθλιος ανηρ εις κενον μοχθει τρεχων.</note>
The <term>apophthegm</term> <note>A concise, pointed saying.</note> of a certain author is also well-known: **They run off the road.** <note>original: τρεχουσι εξω της οδου.</note> This is said when someone works very diligently but without any certain plan to show what should be followed or to what extent.

### The bite of an asp. LXXXV

**The bite of an asp.** <note>original: Δηγμα ασπιδος.</note> This refers to an incurable evil or a particularly venomous tongue. The adage is recorded by Michael Apostolius of Byzantium, an author not particularly memorable except when a lack of better sources compels us. However, even Angelo Poliziano <note>A renowned 15th-century Italian humanist.</note> did not hesitate to cite him as a witness in a certain passage. A line of verse is circulated that matches the adage:
**A wicked woman is truly the venom of an asp.** <note>original: Ιος πεφυκεν ασπιδος κακη γυνη.</note>
Aelian, in the first book of *On the Nature of Animals*, reports that a remedy can be found for the bites of vipers and all other serpents, with the single exception of the asp—especially if it has tasted a frog, as he says in the next book. The strike of this creature alone is more powerful than any care and is conquered by nothing, except by a woman, who might kill it by her sight or touch alone <note>Erasmus is referencing ancient folklore regarding the perceived biological or "magical" power of women, often associated with menstruation or the "evil eye" in classical natural history.</note>—one of these traits it shares with the basilisk, the other with aconite. Similarly, Nicander in his *Theriaca* writes:
**The cruel asp, whose bite is incurable above all others.** <note>original: Ασπιδα φοινικεσσαν αμυδροτατον δακος αλλων.</note>
Pliny recorded that an asp never wanders without its mate; if it happens that one is killed, the other immediately pursues the killer, recognizing them even in the midst of a crowd in the marketplace. Some add that a person bitten by this serpent dies within four hours. However, nothing prevents the adage from being applied to a secret enemy—one who is all the more pestilential because this serpent infuses its poison secretly and without pain, so that no wound appears on the body after the bite; instead, a lethal sleep creeps over the victim, as Nicander describes. For this reason, some think the bite is called "very faint" <note>original: αμυδροτατον</note> by the same poet.

### When the tree has fallen, anyone gathers wood. LXXXVI

**When the oak has fallen, every man gathers wood.** <note>original: Δρυος πεσουσης πας ανηρ ξυλευεται.</note>
The commentator on Theocritus mentions this proverb, but "eating" <note>original: εδουσης</note> is written instead of "falling" <note>original: πεσουσης</note>, erroneously, if I am not mistaken. If fortune should cast someone headlong into ruin, everyone from all sides rushes in against them,

& and everyone plunders what he can. For they now believe they will escape punishment. An example of this situation is found in Juvenal, writing about Sejanus. <note>Sejanus was the powerful prefect of the Praetorian Guard under Emperor Tiberius; after his fall, the Roman populace turned on him and his memory with savage intensity.</note>

## Nothing is happy in every respect. LXXX

What Horace wrote in his *Odes*:
->**Nothing is blessed in every part,**<-
is a proverbial sentiment, which the Greeks express as:
**There is no man who is happy in all things.** <note>original: οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις πάντ’ ἀνὴρ εὐδαιμονεῖ.</note> That is to say,
**No mortal is lucky in all respects.**
Aristotle cites this <term>senarius</term> <note>A line of verse consisting of six poetic feet.</note> in the second book of his *Rhetoric* among his examples of maxims. There is a similar sentiment in Theognis. Clearchus, in the works of Athenaeus, cites this verse:
**Nothing blameless has ever grown for mortals.** <note>original: ἀμώμητον δ’ οὐδὲν ἔβλαστε βροτοῖς.</note> Which is to say,
**There is nothing among men that you cannot find fault with.**
Menander, quoted in Plutarch’s essay *On Tranquility of Mind*:
<margin>Is there some kinship between grief and life?</margin> **Is there some kinship between grief and life?** <note>original: ᎏρ’ ἔστι συγγενές τι λύπῃ καὶ βίῳ;</note> That is,
**Does some relationship exist between life and pain?**
To this sentiment belongs what we have said elsewhere: **All crested larks are born with crests.** <note>Erasmus implies that certain burdens or traits are inherent and unavoidable from birth.</note> Before Theseus came to Attica, he established certain sacred rites: some were to be performed with games and joy, others, conversely, with sorrow and mourning. However, when he landed in Attica, he found many people neglected and grieving because of the death of King Aegeus—who, despairing of his son’s return, had thrown himself headlong from a rock out of grief. Yet Theseus also found many others leaping for joy at the son’s return. Thus, it was established that in the **Oschophoria** <note>A festival of "carrying branches" (oschoi).</note>—the name of a festival involving the carrying of branches—not the messenger himself but his <term>caduceus</term> <note>A herald's staff, usually associated with Hermes.</note> should be crowned. Then, those participating in the rites would let out these cries: **Eleleu, iou, iou.** <note>original: ἐλελεῦ ἰοὺ ἰοὺ.</note> That is, "Alas!" The first of these is a cry of congratulation and is usually sung in war hymns <note>original: paeanib.</note> (as is clear from Aristophanes' *Peace*, where they frequently repeat those words, *iou iou*); the second is a cry of grief. From this, the Greeks called Ajax *Iou Iou Aias*, and used the word *aiazein* to mean "to wail." This, evidently, is the image of the life of mortals. This history is recounted by Plutarch in the *Life of Theseus*. Pindar, in his third *Isthmian Ode*, twists the sentiment to fit the occasion: **As the days roll on, life changes, now for some, now for others; but the children of the gods remain beyond the reach of arrows.** <note>original: αἰὼν δὲ κυλινδομέναις ἁμέραις ἄλλ’ ἄλλοισ’ ἐξάλλαξεν, ἀτρεσί γε μὲν παίδεσσι βίων.</note> Meaning: As the days roll forward, life turns now this way, now that. But the gods are beyond the reach of weapons.
For the commentator reminds us here that "children of the gods" is said instead of "gods." He has something similar in the seventh *Pythian Ode*: **For they say that stable happiness flourishes for a man if he bears this and that.** <note>original: φανῇ γάρ κεν ἀνδρὶ παρ’ μονίμαν θάλλοισαν εὐδαιμονίαν, τὰ δ’ ἦ τὰ φερει.</note> That is: they say a man's happiness truly blooms steadily if he bears both "this and that"—meaning if he bears both prosperity and adversity. Continuous happiness threatens a sudden end; that which is tempered tends to last longer. The commentator cited a Homeric verse for this sentiment: **The Muse loved him exceedingly, and gave him both good and evil.** <note>original: τὸν πέρι μοῦσ’ ἐφίλησε, δίδου δ’ ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε.</note> This song appears in the eighth book of the *Odyssey* concerning Demodocus. Again, Pindar in his fifth ode: **Whoever is free from labors does not exist, nor will he.** <note>original: πύθια ὅστις ἀποκλαρός ἐστιν, οὔτ’ ἔσσεται.</note> And shortly after: **Bearing both this and that.** <note>original: τὰ καὶ τὰ φέρων.</note> That is, being allotted these and those things, namely good things with bad. The commentator also cites another passage from Pindar in the third *Pythian Ode*: **The immortals deal out two evils to mortals alongside one good.** <note>original: παρ’ οὔλου πήματα σὺν δύο δαίνονται βροτοῖς ἀθάνατοι.</note> They also bring forward that Homeric passage which we recounted elsewhere from the twenty-fourth book of the *Odyssey*: <note>Erasmus likely means the *Iliad*, Book 24, which contains the famous image of the two jars.</note>
**For two jars lie on the floor of Zeus's palace.** <note>original: Δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακείαται ἐν Διὸς οὔδει.</note>
To this also belong those sayings of which we have spoken elsewhere: **Where there is honey, there is gall; where there is a teat, there is a bump.** <note>original: Vbi mel, ibi fel, ubi uber, ubi tuber.</note> There are others of this kind. Nor do I think it far from this sentiment that the ancient Romans worshipped two statues, **Angeronia** and **Volupia**: one named from *angores* (anguish), the other from *voluptate* (pleasure). Indeed, the priests perform sacrifices to Angeronia in the chapel of Volupia, signifying that pains and pleasures are mixed together in the life of men. They add that Angeronia was placed on the altar of Volupia with her mouth closed, because grief is a companion to pleasure, and pleasure to grief. She is depicted with this appearance, having her mouth bound and sealed. By this riddle they signify that those who hide their griefs and anxieties of mind reach the greatest pleasure through the benefit of patience. Macrobius writes something to this effect in the first book of his commentary on *The Dream of Scipio*. I shall finish if I add the verse of Aeschylus, which Julius Pollux (Book 6, Chapter 11) testifies is found in Aristophanes:
**...to be mixed into a bittersweet stream.** <note>original: ὀξυγλυκεῖαν τ’ ἄρα κεκρᾶσθαι ῥοάν.</note>

***

### THIRD THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED

And you will temper the sweet-tart pomegranate. <note>original: "punicum"</note> For the seeds of this fruit have a certain pleasant sharpness. In the same way, the life of mortals is tempered.

---

->**The fortunate have many kinsmen.**<-
LXXXVIII
**All those who are successful have relatives.** <note>original: τῶν εὐτυχούντων πάντων εἰσὶ συγγενεῖς</note> That is to say, 
**Every single person is a kinsman to the lucky.**
This is commonly said today: that the wealthy have the most relatives. Terence alluded to this in his play *Phormio*: "But if he had left a ten-talent estate, you would be the first to step forward; you would recite your lineage from memory, right back to your grandfather and great-grandfather." Pindar, in the tenth *Nemean Ode*, expressed this sentiment thus: **Honor perishes for a man stripped of friends, and few mortals are faithful in times of trouble.** <note>original: οἰκεῖται τιμὰ, φίλων τατωμλῶν φωτὶ, παῦροι δ’ ἐν πόνῳ πισοὶ βροτῶν.</note> Plato, in an epigram, wrote: **Or did you hardly learn that old saying: that no one is a friend to a man who has nothing?** <note>original: ἢ μόλις ἔγνως τὸτ’ ἔπθ, ὡς οὐδὲς οὐδὲν ἔχοντι φίλο.</note> Which is to say:
**At last, through experience, you know that ancient word:
To him who has nothing, no friend is present.**

---

->**Lovers’ quarrels.**<-
LXXXIX
**The angers of those who love.** <note>original: τῶν φιλούντων ὀργαί</note> This refers to those who are not truly angry with one another in their hearts, or to a fit of temper that will by no means last. Terence says in the *Andria*: "Lovers’ quarrels are the renewal of love." And according to a Greek sentiment:
**The anger of lovers lasts but a little time.** <note>original: ὀργὰ φιλούντων μικρὸν ἰσχύει χρόνον.</note>
Indeed, these types of little disagreements <note>original: "dissidiola"</note> which sometimes occur between friends—provided bitterness is absent—actually refresh the friendship, shaking off the boredom of long-standing habit. This is elegantly indicated by that writer of mimes, if I am not mistaken, Publilius: "Discord makes concord more precious."

---

->**First to be healthy, second beauty, third wealth.**<-
XC
Plato, in the second book of the *Laws*, says: **For they say that to be healthy is best, second is beauty, and third is wealth.** <note>original: λέγεται γὰρ, ὡς ἄρισον ὑγιαίνειν, δεύτερον δὲ κάλλος, τρίτον δὲ πλοῦτος.</note> He mentions this adage in other places as well. Stobaeus cites these lines from a certain Sclereus: <note>This likely refers to a popular Athenian "drinking song" or *scolion* often attributed to Simonides or Ariphron.</note> **To be healthy is best for a mortal man; second, to be born with a handsome form; third, to be wealthy without fraud; and fourth, to be in the flower of youth with one's friends.** <note>original: ὑγιαίνειν μὲν ἄρισον ἀνδρὶ θνατῷ, δεύτερον δὲ φυὰν καλὸν γενέσθαι, τρίτον δὲ πλουτεῖν ἀδόλως, εἶτα τέταρτον ἡβᾶν μετὰ τῶν φίλων.</note> Plato, however, in the first book of the *Laws*, sets it out this way: **Health leads the way, beauty is second, the third is strength, and the fourth is wealth—not blind wealth, but wealth that is sharp-sighted.** <note>original: ἡγᾶται μὲν ὑγίεια, κάλλος δὲ δεύτερον, τὸ δὲ τρίτον ἰσχὺς, τέταρτον δὲ πλοῦτος, οὐ τυφλὸς ἀλλ’ ὀξὺ βλέπων.</note> This ranking of wishes was even celebrated in popular songs of old, as Plato testifies in the *Gorgias*. Among Greek maxims, a <term>senarius</term> <note>A line of six poetic feet.</note> of this kind is recorded:
**In life, nothing is better than health.** <note>original: οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὑγείας κρεῖσσον οὐδὲν, ἐν βίῳ.</note>
And another similar to it:
**Health and wisdom are two blessings for life.** <note>original: ὑγίεια καὶ νοῦς ἐσθλὰ τῷ βίῳ δύω.</note>
To this also looks that famous line of Juvenal:
**That there may be a sound mind in a sound body.**
And Horace: "The owner must be healthy."
Aristo of Sicyon wrote a <term>paean</term> <note>A song of praise or triumph.</note> in praise of health, as Athenaeus records in his fifteenth book:
**Health, oldest of the blessed ones, may I live with you for the remainder of my life, and may you be a gracious housemate to me.** <note>original: ὑγίεια πρεσβίσα μακάρων, μετὰ σεν ναίοιμι τὸ λειπόμενον βιοτᾶς, σὺ δέ μοι πρόφρων συνόικος εἴης.</note>
And shortly after: **With you, blessed Health, all things flourish, and the springtime of the Graces shines; but without you, no one is happy.** <note>original: μετὰ σέιο μάκαιρα ὑγίεια, τέθηλε πάντα, καὶ λάμπει χαρίτων ἔαρ, σέθεν δὲ χωρὶς οὔτις εὐδαίμων.</note> Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, brings this up as an example of a maxim that does not require an "epilogue"—that is, an added explanation—because everyone is already so convinced of it: **For a man to be healthy is best, as it seems to me.** <note>original: ἀνδρὶ δ’ ὑγιαίνειν ἄρισον ὡς γέ μοι δοκεῖ.</note> This appears to be a *senarius*, though a corrupted one. Aristotle, in the first book of the *Eudemian Ethics*, recounts that someone wrote this sentiment on the vestibule of the temple of Apollo at Delos: that goodness, beauty, and pleasure do not all belong to the same person; and that which is most just...
