# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...it would be most honorable to have acted [justly], but the best is to be in good health, and the most pleasant of all is to obtain what one loves. <note>Erasmus is concluding a commentary on an ancient inscription from the temple of Leto at Delos which ranked justice, health, and love.</note> However, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, since happiness is the best and most beautiful thing, judges it to also be the most pleasant. The common people divide these qualities, even though in truth they are most closely joined. This proverb will have its place whenever we wish to indicate that one thing takes precedence over another, and that greater care is owed to those things which are superior.

->**To be hay. To be fed on ambrosia.**<-
<margin>XC</margin>
**To be hay**, and, **To be fed on ambrosia**. <note>original: "Fœnum esse, & Ambrofia alendus"</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero used both as proverbial figures; the first against unlearned and brutish men, the second for distinguished men, so that you might understand the former are to be equated with cattle and the latter with gods. For cattle live on hay. Ambrosia is the food of the "ever-living gods" in Homer. Cicero, in the second book of *On the Orator*: "Thus I, while Crassus is listening, will first speak of wit, and I—a pig, as they say <note>A reference to the proverb 'a pig teaching Minerva,' meaning an amateur teaching an expert.</note>—will teach that orator whom Catulus recently heard and then remarked that others 'ought to be hay.'" Again, the same author in the same book: "Catulus was joking," he says, "especially since he himself speaks in such a way that he seems 'worthy of being fed on ambrosia.'" Horace calls very elegant and sumptuous banquets "suppers of the gods," saying: *O nights and suppers of the gods!* <note>original: "O noctes cœnæq; deũm"</note> indicating nectar and ambrosia. For these things are attributed to the gods by poets only when they take their meals at home; otherwise, if they happen to be invited somewhere for a rich sacrifice, they take more delight in the steam of the roasting meat.

->**Hopes feed the exiles.**<-
<margin>XCI</margin>
**Hopes feed the exiles.** <note>original: Αἱ ἐλπίδες βόσκουσι φυγάδας</note> This is used when someone, cast down from their former fortune, always acts with the aim of being restored. It is drawn from human nature, by which we see that no one is so much an exile that he does not both wish and hope that he might eventually return to his fatherland by "right of postliminy" <note>A legal term referring to the restoration of rights to a person returning from exile or captivity.</note>. That this is so, we have also learned from the examples of many exiles, specifically Leo Bentivoglio of Bologna, whom the French expelled to please Pope Julius II while we were there. Ovid testifies that he was of the same mind while languishing in exile among the people of Tomis. Even the Jews today are not abandoned by hope. Euripides indicates that this was a proverbial sentiment. It is cited by Plutarch in the small book he wrote *On Exile*:
**Hopes feed the exiles, so the saying goes,
They look with charming eyes, yet they delay.** <note>original: Αἱ δ' ἐλπίδες βόσκουσι φυγάδας, ὡς λόγος, Καλῶς βλέπουσι γ' ὄμμασιν, μέλλουσι δέ.</note>

->**And children’s children.**<-
<margin>XCII</margin>
**Children’s children.** <note>original: Παῖδες παίδων</note> A proverbial figure by which we signify the long-lasting propagation of any matter. That it was used as an adage is sufficiently indicated by Plato in several places, especially in the third book of *The Laws*: **and children’s children, as the saying goes.** <note>original: καὶ παίδων παῖδας ὃ λεγόμενον</note> It is taken from that Homeric verse in the twentieth book of the *Iliad*, spoken by Neptune concerning Aeneas to Juno:
**And children’s children, and those who shall be born hereafter.** <note>original: Καὶ παίδων παῖδες, καὶ τοί μετόπισθε γένωνται.</note>
Which Virgil rendered thus:
**Both the children of children, and those who will be born from them.** <note>original: Et nati natorum, & qui nafcentur ab illis.</note>
Aristophanes alluded to the Homeric figure in *The Birds*:
**We shall give to ourselves, to our children, and to our children’s children.** <note>original: Δώσομεν ἡμῖν αὐτοῖς, παισί, παίδων παισίν.</note>
In *The Clouds*, he twisted the same figure as a joke toward usury, where one interest payment is born from another:
**Themselves and the principal and the interest of interest.** <note>original: Αὐτοί τε καὶ τ' ἀρχαῖα καὶ τόκοι τόκων.</note>
He was certainly alluding to what we have mentioned elsewhere:
**Interest upon interest, and yet more interest upon the rest.** <note>original: Ἐπὶ τόκῳ πρὸ τόκιο, τόκος δ' γε ἐπὶ τῷ ἄλλῳ.</note>

->**To be horse-mad.**<-
<margin>XCIII</margin>
**To be horse-mad** <note>original: Ἱππομανεῖν</note> was a proverbial insult used for women who were excessively lecherous and itching for men beyond measure. Aristotle says in the sixth book of *On Animals*: "Therefore, mares are said to be 'horse-mad,' from which name people also apply a slur, derived from this animal alone, toward women who are intemperate regarding sexual desire."

->**The character of sheep.**<-
<margin>XCIV</margin>
**The character of sheep.** <note>original: Προβάτων ἦθος</note> This was commonly hurled at the stupid and the dull-witted. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
**But you speak of the life of a little sheep.** <note>original: Ἀλλὰ προβατίου βίον λέγεις.</note>

<summary>This page explores several adages regarding human character and social status, including metaphors for intelligence (ambrosia vs. hay), the persistent hope of exiles, the concept of enduring lineage, and animal-based insults for stupidity or lust.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Cicero, Homer, exile, lineage, usury, animal metaphors, ancient Greek comedy, social status, Leo Bentivoglio</keywords>

--- Page 783 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of human nature and character through animal metaphors—specifically the sheep—and moves into adages regarding fragility, premature expectation, and the dangers of luxury versus simplicity.</meta>

...Indeed, you are preaching to me the life of a little sheep. <note>original: "Mihi imò uitam prædicas ouiculæ." This sentence concludes a point from the previous page regarding the perceived helplessness or simple-mindedness of certain characters.</note>

Aristotle, in the ninth book of his *History of Animals*, indicates why this became a common proverb, noting that <note>original Greek: διαφέρῃ κατὰ τὴν δειλίαν καὶ πραότητα... "They differ in cowardice and gentleness, and in courage and mildness, and now especially in witlessness..."</note> the character of a sheep is, as they say, simple and foolish. Indeed, it is the most helpless of all quadrupeds; it wanders off into the wilderness for no reason, and often in the winter months it wanders out of the folds. When they are caught in the snow, unless the shepherd drives them, they refuse to leave, but remain behind and perish, unless the shepherds bring in the rams. For only then do they follow. 

Accordingly, Aristophanes, mocking the witlessness of the Athenian people, calls them sheep in *The Wasps*:

<gloss>that is,</gloss>
->The sheep sit together in the assembly.<-
<note>original Greek: Εκκλησιάζῃ πρόβατα συγκαθήμενα. Aristophanes was a comic playwright who often lampooned the gullibility of the voting public.</note>

Nor should we pass over the fact that Diogenes the Cynic <note>A philosopher known for his biting wit and rejection of luxury.</note> called a certain wealthy but unlearned man a "golden-fleeced sheep" <note>original: "πρόβατον χρυσόμαλλον"</note>. And Plautus in his play *Bacchides* says:
> Who drove these sheep here? 
He says this in reference to foolish old men. Looking to this same idea, Origen, in explaining the book of Leviticus, interprets the sacrifice of a sheep as the correction of foolish and irrational emotions.

### The death of a mouse. <margin>XCVI</margin>
<note>original: "Muris interitus."</note>
<note>original Greek: Κατὰ μυὸς ὄλεθρον.</note> <gloss>that is, Like the death of a mouse.</gloss> Aelian, in the twelfth book of *On the Nature of Animals*, chapter 10, records that the mouse is a very short-lived creature, dying quickly as its own intestines waste away; from this arose the proverb "Like the death of a mouse." He adds that Menander used this in his work *Ithade*. It seems to apply to men of weak health, or those who are "short-lived" <note>original Greek: μικροβίους</note>, whom Homer calls "brief-lived" <note>original: "μινυνθαδίους"</note>. Or it applies to those who waste away bit by bit. For it is probable that mice die in the same way they are born in Egypt: where one part of them is a living mouse, and the other is nothing but mud. <note>This refers to the ancient theory of "spontaneous generation," where people believed animals could arise directly from inanimate matter like Nile mud.</note>

### To enlarge the pot before the lentils. <margin>XCVII</margin>
<note>original: "Ante lentem augere ollam."</note>
<note>original Greek: Πρὸ τῆς φακῆς αὐξάνειν τὴν λοπάδα.</note> <gloss>that is, To enlarge the cooking-pan before the lentils.</gloss> This is a proverbial figure of speech used for someone who conceives great hopes in his mind before the thing itself is actually in hand. Or for one who promises what he does not yet possess, or is prematurely pleased with himself, as if he already owned things that are still far from being attained. For instance, if someone, in the hope of a priesthood, begins to incur expenses for what he has not yet received. Or if someone increases the noise and display of his life in the hope of an office which it is uncertain he will obtain. 

The adage is cited from Crates in the works of Athenaeus: "Do not enlarge the pot before the lentils, lest you throw sand into the gears of civil strife." <note>The sense is: do not start living luxuriously before you have even basic food, or you will cause social unrest.</note> It is also cited by Plutarch in his commentary *On the Precepts of Good Health*, under the name of the same Crates, in these words: "Crates, therefore, thinking that seditions and tyrannies arise in cities chiefly from luxury and extravagance, warned playfully not to always enlarge the pan before the lentils, nor to throw sand into civil strife. But let each person exhort himself not to always enlarge the pan before the lentils, nor by all means passing over the watercress and the olive, and turning to delicacies and fish, provoke the body into rebellion through overindulgence, causing disturbances and diarrhea." 

<gloss>that is,</gloss> Crates, since he believed that in cities rebellions and tyrannies were born primarily from luxury and excess, warned in a jesting manner not to always enlarge the serving dish before the lentils, lest you throw us into civil strife. Rather, each man should urge himself not to always enlarge the dish before the lentils, nor in every way—having passed over the simple watercress and olive—to defect to sausages and fish, stirring up the body into "sedition" from over-fullness, as well as tumult and diarrhea. Crates twisted this saying, as it appears, from some poet, so that it might apply to people who are excessively spendthrift. He alluded, moreover, to the habit of the common people, who are accustomed to stir up rebellion if they see the elites preferred over them. For the "pan" <note>term: lopas (λοπάδα)</note> was used for more sumptuous foods, as can be gathered from Lucian’s *Saturnalia*. The lentil is the cheapest and most common legume of the people.

### They were ashamed to refuse, and did not dare to undertake. <margin>XCVIII</margin>
<note>original: "Pudebat recusare, & non audebant fufcipere."</note>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Letters to Atticus*, used this Homeric verse as if it were proverbial more than once:

<meta>The catchword Αἰδεόμην (I was ashamed) indicates the start of the next page's Homeric quote.</meta>

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to human character and social behavior, using the helplessness of sheep, the fragility of mice, and the dangers of premature luxury as metaphors for folly, weakness, and political instability.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Aristophanes, Diogenes the Cynic, Plautus, Origen, Aelian, Menander, Homer, Crates, Plutarch, Athenaeus, sheep metaphors, spontaneous generation, lentils vs luxury, social unrest, Cicero</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

<note>original: "Αἰδέομαι μὲν ἀνῄνασθαι, δεῖδω δ' ὑποδέχθαι."</note>
**I am ashamed to refuse, yet I fear to accept.** 
<gloss>that is,</gloss>
**Shame forbade me to decline, yet fear forbade me to approach.**

This may be used whenever a situation arises where honor suggests one course and utility another; where it would be disgraceful not to take up a task, but dangerous to actually undertake it. It can also be applied to those who, when asked for a favor, do not dare to say no out of shame, yet do not actually wish to perform what is requested due to a different flaw of character. This verse is found in the seventh book of Homer’s *Iliad*, where Hector challenges any of the Greek leaders to single combat; while all the others hesitate, Menelaus stands up:
<note>original Greek: "Ὣς ἔφαθ', οἱ δ' ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ, Αἰδέσθεν μὲν ἀνήνασθαι, δεῖσαν δ' ὑποδέχθαι."</note>
**So he spoke, and they all remained hushed in silence;**
**They were ashamed to refuse, yet they feared to accept.**
<gloss>that is,</gloss>
**Thus he spoke, and meanwhile all held their silence,**
**Shame forbade them to decline, yet fear forbade them to approach.**

### To pass the ball among themselves.

Plutarch, in his essay *On Progress in Virtue*, writes: <note>original Greek: "μάλιστα δ' εἰ τὸ φιλονεικεῖν καὶ δυσχεραίνειν..."</note> "Especially if the ambition and contentiousness of inquiries is diminished, and we cease treating arguments like leather straps or balls <note>The Greek *sphæra* refers to a ball or sphere used in play.</note> which we toss at one another, taking more joy in striking or knocking someone down than in learning or teaching." <gloss>that is,</gloss> Especially if the ambition and strife of questioning is relaxed, and we thus stop tossing arguments back and forth like straps and balls among ourselves in such a way that we enjoy hitting or casting down more than learning or teaching. It appears in Plato’s *Euthydemus*: <note>original Greek: "ὁ δ' Διονυσόδωρος ὥσπερ σφαῖραν ἐκδεξάμενος τὸν λόγον..."</note> "Dionysodorus, catching the argument like a ball, aimed it back at the young man." <gloss>that is,</gloss> Dionysodorus, as if having caught a ball, hurled the discourse back at the youth. Julius Pollux mentions this type of game in the ninth book of his *On Vocabulary*. 

Seneca refers what the Greeks record about the "sphere" to a game of ball (*pila*), showing that the same coordination required between the one giving a benefit and the one receiving it is like that between the thrower and the catcher of a ball. He says: "I wish to use our friend Chrysippus's comparison of the ball game; it is certain that the ball falls either through the fault of the thrower or the catcher. It only maintains its course when it is skillfully tossed and caught between the hands of both. However, a player must necessarily throw the ball differently to a tall companion than to a short one. The same principle applies to a benefit: unless it is adapted to both persons—the giver and the receiver—it will neither leave the former nor reach the latter as it should. If we are dealing with a practiced and skilled player, we will throw the ball more boldly; for however it comes, a quick and agile hand will knock it back. If playing with a novice or an unskilled person, we will not throw it so hard or with such force, but more gently, and we will meet them by directing it submissively right into their hand. This must be done with benefits, etc." In the same book a little later: "Just as in a game there is some credit in catching a ball skillfully and carefully, a man is not called a 'good player' unless he aptly and quickly returns what he received." 

It is not unlike the game they call *pila* today among the Italians, which Horace mentions:
**For playing ball is bad for those with sore eyes or weak stomachs.**
<note>original: "Namq; pila lippis inimicum & ludere crudis." Horace means that physical exercise is taxing for the unwell.</note>

Athenaeus in Book 1 teaches that the ball game was once called *phaininda*, "from the release of the ball-players." <note>original Greek: "φαίνινδα ἀπὸ ἀφέσεως τῶν σφαιριζόντων."</note> I do not fully understand what these words mean; I think it is more likely named from "to appear" (*phainesthai*), because the thrown ball flashes forth. In the same place, a poem by Antiphanes is cited: "Having taken the ball..."
**He delighted in giving it to one, while fleeing another;**
**He knocked one out, while setting another up again,**
**With voices sounding like trumpets.** 
<gloss>that is,</gloss> 
**Having taken the ball,**
**He rejoiced to have given it to this one, but at the same time fled that one.**
**He struck this one out, but raised up another,**
**With his voice sounding in the manner of a trumpet.**

This adage will fit those who attack each other in turn with witty insults. It is close, I believe, to that line of Persius: "We strike, and in turn offer our own legs to the arrows."
According to Seneca’s opinion, it will also apply to those who mutually flatter each other and play along in a dispute, as when a Scotist <note>A follower of the scholastic philosopher Duns Scotus.</note> responds to a fellow Scotist, or a Nominalist <note>A follower of the medieval school of Nominalism, such as William of Ockham.</note> according to the decrees of the Nominalists, so that truth is not sought, but a kind of theatrical play seems to be performed.

### Words are the physician for a sick mind.

This verse is celebrated among the Greeks as a proverb, and is cited by Plutarch in his letter to Apollonius:
<note>original Greek: "ψυχῆς νοσούσης εἰσὶν ἰατροὶ λόγοι."</note>
**Words are the doctors for a soul that is ill.**
<gloss>that is,</gloss>
**For a sick mind, speech is the physician.**
It appears to be taken from Aeschylus’s *Prometheus Bound*...
<meta>catchword: οὐκ (not)</meta>

<summary>This page explores adages related to the tension between shame and fear, the metaphorical use of ball games to describe intellectual and social exchanges, and the therapeutic power of language.</summary>
<keywords>Homer, Plutarch, Seneca, ball games, Scholasticism, Scotists, Nominalists, Aeschylus, social etiquette, intellectual debate</keywords>

--- Page 785 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of adages, specifically focusing on the philosophical idea that speech and reason act as medicine for the soul, particularly in tempering anger and desire, before transitioning to a new adage regarding the redirection of misfortune.</meta>

...surely you are convinced, once you realize that
**words are the doctors for a sick anger.**
<note>original: "ὀργῆς νοσύσης εἰσὶν ἰατροὶ λόγοι." From Aeschylus’s *Prometheus Bound*.</note>
<gloss>that is,</gloss>
**Indeed, Prometheus, this does not escape you: that speech is the physician for the disease of wrath.**

Indeed, as that wise Hebrew says, "A soft word breaks anger." <note>A reference to Proverbs 15:1: "A soft answer turneth away wrath."</note> And according to the Stoics, anger is nothing other than a "brief madness." Horace alluded to this in his *Epistles*:
> There are words and utterances by which you may soothe this pain,
> and cast off a great part of the disease.

Following the opinion of the Stoics, he calls the desires of the mind "diseases." These are healed by the "pharmacies of words" found in philosophy—that is, through wholesome warnings. In the works of Terence, Menedemus reproaches himself for not having treated the "sick mind" of the youth as he should have. For just as different medicines are applied to the diseases of the body according to the nature of the illness, so too the same kind of speech should not be applied to every ailment of the mind. Instead, one must sometimes warn gently, sometimes scold sharply, sometimes pretend not to notice, and sometimes apply a remedy to the unaware. This is in accordance with Paul’s advice: "Reprove, entreat, rebuke." <note>2 Timothy 4:2.</note> Several six-foot verses <term>senarii: a common meter in Latin and Greek drama</term> are also cited to this same effect:
**For speech is the only medicine for grief.**
<note>original: "λόγῳ γὰρ ἐστὶ φάρμακον λύπης μόνον."</note>
<gloss>and,</gloss>
**You have swayed me with speech, the wisest medicine.**
<note>original: "λόγῳ μ’ ἔπεισας φαρμάκῳ σοφωτάτῳ."</note>
<gloss>and,</gloss>
**Speech is a doctor for the suffering in the soul.**
<note>original: "ὁ λόγος ἰατρός τῶ κατὰ ψυχὴν πάθει."</note>

Isocrates, in his oration *On the Peace*, elegantly employed this sentiment: "But you ought first to know this: that while many and various cures have been found by doctors for the diseases of the body, for souls that are sick and filled with evil desires there is no other medicine except speech that dares to rebuke those who err. Furthermore, it is ridiculous to endure the cauterizing <note>burning</note> and cutting of doctors so that we may be freed from greater pains, yet to reject speech before knowing clearly whether it has such power as to benefit those who hear it." 

<gloss>that is,</gloss> But it is especially necessary for you to know that while doctors have discovered many diverse remedies for the diseases of the body, for minds that are ailing and choked with perverse desires, there is no remedy other than a discourse that is not afraid to scold those who go astray. Furthermore, it is a mockery that we endure the burnings and incisions of doctors to be delivered from more serious torments, yet we reject a speech before it is clear whether it possesses such force as to bring utility to the listeners. Truly, just as a friendly, wholesome, and timely speech is an effective and immediate remedy, so a speech that is hostile, or pestilential, or spoken out of season, is a deadly poison.

### THE THIRD THOUSAND, SECOND HUNDRED

#### If anything bad happens, let it be on Pyrrha.

<margin>1</margin> **If anything bad happens, let it be on Pyrrha.** <note>original: "εἴ τι κακὸν, εἰς πύῤῥαν." Pyrrha was the wife of Deucalion in Greek mythology, but here the name likely serves as a generic target for a curse.</note> One should understand "let it fall back upon," or "let it go to," or something of that kind. In this manner, they used to pray against an evil that was feared, detesting it and imprecating it upon the heads of their enemies. From this comes that figure of speech familiar to both Greek and Latin writers: "May this happen to our enemies." 

Ovid writes:
> May such feasts happen to our enemies.
> Also in the third book of *The Art of Love*:
> May the cause of such foul shame happen to our enemies.
> Also in the third book of the *Fasti*:
> May that color happen to our enemies.
> Also in the second book of the *Elegies*:
> May it happen to my enemies to sleep in an empty bed.
> May a severe life happen to my enemies.
> Also in the third book of the *Elegies*:
> May that shame happen to our enemies.
> Again, Virgil in the third book of the *Georgics*...

<summary>Erasmus discusses the classical and biblical idea that reasoned speech acts as a medicinal cure for anger and emotional distress, before introducing an adage used to redirect misfortune toward enemies.</summary>
<keywords>medicine of the soul, anger, Stoicism, Isocrates, Ovid, Pyrrha, healing speech, redirection of evil</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of proverbs used to deflect misfortune or describe self-inflicted harm. It transitions from the idea of "words as medicine" on the previous page to the ritualistic or proverbial ways the ancients spoke of turning evil away from themselves and toward their enemies.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

"May the gods grant better things to the pious, and that error to our enemies." <note>A quote from Virgil's *Georgics* (3.513), where he discusses a plague affecting cattle and prays that such madness only affects Rome's enemies.</note> 
The same author says in the eighth book of the *Aeneid* concerning the tyrant Mezentius: 
"May the gods bring such a fate back upon his own head and his race." 
<margin>Propertius</margin> 
"May my enemies end up with an unresponsive mistress." <note>The poet Propertius wishes the frustration of a cold or indifferent lover upon his rivals.</note> 
And Horace in his *Odes*: 
"May the wives and children of our enemies feel the blind movements of the rising South wind." 
And Terence in *The Self-Tormentor*, regarding an old man torturing himself with regret: "Oh, I beseech you, let that happen to my enemies." 
The same author says in *The Eunuch*: "Would that those who wish me ill were in such a state." 

The origin of this expression is reported by authors as follows: Once, the Pyrrhaeans were pursued with heavy hatred by all their neighbors. Because of this, if any evil seemed to be looming, people would pray to avert it by wishing it upon the Pyrrhaeans, saying: **To the land of the Pyrrhaeans.** <note>original: "εἰς τὴν πυῤῥαίων"</note> 
Pyrrha is a city on the island of Lesbos, according to Stephanus. There is also another city of the same name between Priene and Miletus. I do not know if it should be blamed on the scribes that Plutarch, in *The Banquet of the Seven Sages*, records "Priene" instead of "Pyrrha." 

The words of Plutarch are as follows: "And Thales, laughing, said: 'If there is any evil, let it go back to Priene,' just as Bias did when he first drew the lot." <note>original: "ἢ ὁ θάλης γελάσας... εἰς πριενίω."</note> <gloss>that is, And Thales laughing said: if there is any evil, back to Priene. For Bias will pay, just as he drew the lot first.</gloss> 
It seems to me the name of the place was changed on purpose because Bias was from Priene <term>Bias of Priene: one of the Seven Sages of Greece</term>, and thus as a joke, "Pyrrha" was changed to "Priene."

---

->**You draw down the moon to your own ruin.**<-

**Against yourself you will pull down the moon.** <note>original: "Ἐπὶ σαυτῷ τὴν σελήνην καθελεῖς."</note> <gloss>that is, You will drag down the moon against your own self.</gloss> 
In ancient times, it was believed that sorceresses could drag the moon down to earth with certain incantations. 
Hence Virgil says: 
"Incantations can even draw down the moon from heaven." 
<margin>And Horace in his Odes,</margin> 
"And through books of charms that have the power to call down the stars plucked from the sky." 
<margin>And again in his Satires,</margin> 
"And the moon blushing red, lest she be a witness to these things, hiding behind the large tombs." 
<margin>Likewise Juvenal,</margin> 
"She alone could assist the laboring moon." <note>Referring to the practice of making noise with brass pots during an eclipse to "help" the moon, which was thought to be under a witch's spell.</note> 

It was once believed that witches of this kind usually lost their eyes and feet as a result. There was a woman named Aglaonice who, since she could predict eclipses through her knowledge of astronomy, used to boast that she was dragging the moon down from the sky to the earth. She paid the penalty for this boasting, which will be discussed in the proverb "to drag down the moon." Therefore, this proverb was used for those who, by their own efforts, brought evil upon themselves. This is the kind of situation where someone uses clever schemes to bring about another's arrival, only to end up being overthrown by the very person they summoned.

---

->**The raven fetches water.**<-

**The raven fetches water.** <note>original: "Κόραξ ὑδρεύει."</note> <gloss>that is, The raven draws water.</gloss> 
This was usually said when someone achieved what they desired, but not without great trouble and through their own ingenuity. Or when someone tried to accomplish a task using new or unusual methods. 
It is derived from the fable of the thirsty raven who, by piling up small pebbles, raised the water from the bottom of a jar to the very top rim. Pliny records this as a real event in his tenth book, chapter forty-three. However, it seems more probable that the adage refers to that story which Ovid tells in the second book of his *Fasti* in this manner:
> It happened that Apollo was preparing a solemn festival for Jove,
> My story will not cause any long delays.
> "Go, my bird," he said, "lest the holy rites be delayed,
> and bring a little water from the living springs."
> The raven takes the gilded bowl in its hooked feet,
> and flies high through the airy path.
> There stood a fig tree, still thick with hard fruit;
> he tries it with his beak, but it was not fit to be picked.
> Forgetful of his orders, he is said to have sat under the tree,
> until the slow delay made the fruit sweet.
> And now full, he seizes a long water-snake with his black talons,
> and returns to his master, and brings back a made-up story:

<summary>Erasmus discusses proverbs related to redirecting bad luck toward enemies and the dangers of self-inflicted harm through cleverness, using the myths of Aglaonice and the fable of the thirsty raven as examples.</summary>
<keywords>Pyrrhaeans, Virgil, Horace, Aglaonice, moon magic, eclipses, ravens, Bias of Priene, Ovid, ancient superstition</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of ancient proverbs, moving from mythological origins of phrases regarding delay and punishment to metaphors involving character, size, and social standing. It highlights his characteristic blending of classical poetry, drama, and philosophy to explain common Greek and Latin idioms.</meta>

# THE THIRD THOUSAND, SECOND HUNDRED OF ADAGES
## Kk 2

> This for me was the cause of delay, the guardian of the living waters;
> This one held the springs, and hindered my duty.
> You add lies to your fault, says Phoebus, and you dare
> To try to deceive a prophetic god with words?
> But for you, while the milky fig still clings to the tree,
> No cold waters shall be drunk from any spring.
<note>Erasmus is quoting Ovid’s *Fasti* (2.247-252), which tells the story of the raven sent by Apollo (Phoebus) to fetch water. The raven delayed because he was waiting for figs to ripen, then lied about a snake guarding the spring. As punishment, the raven is cursed with thirst when figs are ripe.</note>

Hyginus and Aelian (in the first book of *On the Nature of Animals*) also mention this. Consequently, this proverb seems to me most suitable when applied to a slacker.

### 4. Attabas and Numenius have met.
"Attabas and Numenius have come together." <note>original Greek: "Συνῆλθον ἀτταβᾶς τε καὶ νουμήνιος"</note> That is, Attabas has been joined with his Numenius. Some read "Attagas" <note>Attagas refers to a type of partridge or heath-cock, often used metaphorically for a chatterbox or a rogue</note>.
This was a common saying whenever one wicked person associated with another. Diogenianus records that these two were a notorious pair of thieves. Diogenes Laertius mentions this in his life of Timon of Phlius <note>Timon was a Skeptic philosopher known for his sharp wit</note>. For Timon used this proverb to mock those who thought one should trust the senses when supported by the intellect, since he himself believed one should trust neither reason nor the senses. It is very similar to the saying used elsewhere: "Bacchius with Bithus." <note>Bacchius and Bithus were two gladiators so equally matched in skill and cruelty that they eventually killed each other.</note>

### 5. Of colossal size.
"A certain colossal magnitude." <note>original Greek: "Κολοσσιαῖόν τι μέγεθος"</note> This is a proverbial hyperbole used by Lucian for men of enormous physical bulk, named after the massive statues called Colossi. Among these, the Colossus of the Sun at Rhodes is the most celebrated, standing seventy cubits high—which, according to Pompeius Festus, is one hundred and five feet—and few people could wrap their arms around its thumb. Pliny also mentions others of prodigious size. In those days, the Roman emperors took immense delight in such things; it seems they were more concerned with being the "greatest" <term>maximos</term> rather than the "best" <term>optimos</term>. We also read of things being called "Aetnean" <note>Referring to Mount Etna</note> when they are very large. Regarding things that are large and violently troublesome, they were called "Athonian" <note>Referring to Mount Athos</note>, as we have mentioned elsewhere, just as they were called "Hamaxaean" <note>meaning "large enough to fill a wagon"</note>.

### 6. Of a bad stamp.
"Of a wicked stamp." <note>original Greek: "Πονηροῦ κόμματος"</note> This was said of a wicked, contemptible, or rejected person. The metaphor is taken from rejected coins. Aristophanes says in *Plutus*:
"He seems to be of the wicked stamp."
That is, he seems to be of unapproved coinage. This was said of a sycophant who had been reduced to poverty and hunger after Plutus (the god of wealth) regained his sight. The commentator explains that <term>comma</term> refers to a type of very cheap currency. It sounds exactly as if you were to say "of bad money." Again, in the same play: "He will know that he is of that wicked stamp." 
In the same author's *Frogs*: "and with the worst stamp." Also in the *Assemblywomen*: 
"And that stamp indeed turned out badly for me." 
He gives the reason: when he had gone into the marketplace to buy flour and had already put his bag down, the herald cried out that no one should accept copper coins, but that everything should be sold for silver. To this pattern also belong those proverbial metaphors: "a counterfeit man" <note>original Greek: "κιβδηλὸς ἄνθρωπος"</note> and "to play the counterfeit" <note>original Greek: "κιβδηλεύειν"</note> for committing a fraud, and "counterfeiting" <note>original Greek: "κιβδηλεία"</note> for an imposition. These words are found frequently elsewhere, particularly in the eleventh book of Plato's *Laws*, if anyone desires more certain evidence. Therefore, those whose character is disapproved are called "counterfeits," as if you were to say they are made of adulterated money. 
However, this is more aptly applied to the appearance of the face as an index of character and nature. For just as a coin is recognized at once by looking at its image—whether it is genuine or adulterated—so too the character is immediately detected from a person's very form, as Euripides testifies in these lines from *Ion*:
"For the most part, the appearance itself, as soon as one looks, / proves whether a man is noble-born or otherwise."

### 7. A benevolent killer.
"A well-wishing slayer." <note>original Greek: "Εὐνοῦς σφάκτης"</note> This applies to those who, while they bring the greatest [harm...]

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
## Kk 2

...destruction, yet he mixes it with a show of goodwill. They say it is drawn from the story of Orestes who, having slaughtered his mother Clytemnestra, held a funeral banquet as if in her honor. Some refer it to King Antigonus, who, after he had removed Semele from his path, took care of her bones with the highest honor to be carried back to her mother. There are those who prefer that the adage be referred to Ptolemy, the son of Philopator: he handed over his mother Berenice to be kept in chains in the palace by Sosibius; when she could not bear this insult from her son, she died by taking poison. But he, troubled by dreams, built a monument in the middle of the city, which is now called "the tomb." In this, he placed his ancestors along with his mother, and among them Alexander the Great. Not content with this service, the man established a temple to her in Aegialis, to which the name was given, "Berenice the Savior." This is according to Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian of the 3rd century BCE, known for his work on Homer and proverbs</note>. Close to this is what we have reviewed elsewhere: "Untimely goodwill differs not at all from hostility." Thus Horace <note>original: Flaccus</note> says:

> I care not for a service that weighs me down.

And Ennius spoke with no little skill, as cited by Cicero in the second book of *On Duties*:

> Good deeds ill-placed, I deem ill deeds.
<note>Latin: "Benefacta male locata, malefacta arbitror." Erasmus is warning that a "favor" done with bad intentions or at the wrong time is actually a harm.</note>

### Uglier than Corytheus.

"Uglier than Corytheus" <note>original Greek: Κορύθου ἀειδέστερος</note>. They say a certain Corytheus was a man remarkably foolish and senseless, and in addition to this, of a most unhappy and foul appearance; they say his children were all the same, taking after their father. From this, a common joke was told against a dull-witted man who was equally deformed. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus.

### To strive against the torrent.

Those who struggle in vain against those whom they cannot overcome are said "to strive against the torrent." The metaphor is taken from swimmers, who usually swim with the current of the river, especially if it is a torrent; for if they strive against it, they will make no progress. Aurelius Augustine uses this adage in a certain letter to Saint Jerome. And the prudence of Crispus is praised by Juvenal, because he yielded to the violence of Domitian and complied with a nature that was otherwise incurable:

> He, therefore, never directed his arms against
> The torrent. 

Similarly, Ovid says:

> A fool is the swimmer who, when he might depart diagonally,
> Battles to go into the opposing waters.

Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, one of the Church Fathers</note> says to Eudoxius the rhetorician: "The proverb also teaches that the force of a river is not to be forced." <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ μὴ βιάζεσθαι ῥεῦμα ποταμοῦ καὶ ἡ παροιμία φησί</note>.

### A friend as far as the altar.

"I am a friend as far as the altar" <note>original Greek: Μέχρι τοῦ βωμοῦ φίλος εἰμί</note>. Although it is not the purpose of this work to collect every kind of apophthegm <note>a concise, pointed saying</note>, yet this was said so aptly, and with such a proverbial appearance, and moreover so celebrated by great authors, that it seems deservedly to be adopted into this class. It was a response given by Pericles <note>The famous Athenian statesman</note> when a certain friend asked him to swear a false oath in a case for his sake: "I ought to help my friends, but only as far as the altar." So reports Aulus Gellius. Plutarch reports it in his booklet *On Shyness* <note>original title: περὶ δυσωπίας</note>: "I am a friend as far as the altar." The proverb warns that, although we should sometimes look out for the advantage of our friends and comply with their wishes, it seems permissible to deflect a little from the right path, but only so far as we do not violate the reverence of the Divine for the sake of a human friend. In ancient times, those taking an oath would touch the altar. Furthermore, to what extent and how far one should deflect from honesty for the sake of a friend is discussed copiously and learnedly by Aulus Gellius in the first book of *Attic Nights*, chapter three.

### Codalus's choenix.

"Codalus's *choenix*" <note>A choenix was a Greek dry measure, roughly a quart</note>, or "daily ration" <note>original Greek: Κοδάλου χοῖνιξ</note>. According to Suidas, this is said of large measures. Nothing else has been found by me on this matter among authors so far. One may guess it arose from some greedy servant for whom the *choenix* was made deeper and more capacious, so that he might defraud his master by artifice. In the collections circulated under the name of Hesychius, a fish "Codalus" is found, either the same as or certainly related to the *Cestreus* <note>A type of mullet</note>, which Gaza translates as "mugil." He mentions this proverb "Codalus's *choenix*" elsewhere, indicating there was someone who was accustomed to use larger measures.

### Worthy of a shell.

"Worthy of a shell" <note>original Greek: Κόγχης ἄξιος</note>. The Greeks call a "shell" a thing of no value, because...

...much like the Latin expressions "not worth a nutshell" <note>Latin: *nauci*</note> or "a tuft of wool" <note>Latin: *floccum*</note>. Hence, for whatever was most contemptible and of no value, they would say it was **worth a shell**. <note>original Greek: *κόγχης ἄξιον* (konches axion)</note>

## XIII. Sail with a pole.

**Sail with a pole** <note>original Greek: *Κοντῷ πλέιν* (Konto plein)</note> was a saying used for those who handled matters as was appropriate, or who followed a way of life suited to their own natural talents. For a pole <note>A *contus* is a long punting pole used to push a boat through shallow water.</note> is suited for no other use than for navigation. Likewise, not every person is fit for every kind of life. You may use this when you wish to advise someone to use a thing for the purpose for which it was invented. For example: "Why are you hoarding your coins? They weren't created to be stared at, but to support your life; you must sail with the pole." This is recorded by Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note>.

## XIV. He owes the penalty to Cydas.

**He owes the penalty to Cydas** <note>original Greek: *Κύδη δίκην ὀφείλει* (Kyde diken opheilei)</note>. When the first syllable of the word *kydos* is long, it signifies glory; when it is shortened, it signifies **slander and abuse**. <note>original Greek: *τὴν κυδοιδόρειαν καὶ κακηγορίαν*</note> From this, they derived the verb "to insult" <note>original Greek: *κυδοιάζειν* (kydoiazein)</note>. Therefore, when someone was brought to court or harassed over a trivial matter—such as a few words spoken rashly—they would say the proverb: **to pay the penalty of Cydas** or **to owe the penalty of Cydas**. <note>original Greek: *κυδὸς δίκην ἐκτίνειν, καὶ κύδὸς δίκην ὀφείλειν*</note> This means to have paid the price for an insult, or to owe the penalty for slander. For in ancient times, a heavy fine was imposed on those who spoke too insolently against anyone.

## XV. A woodworm in its place.

**A woodworm in its place** <note>original Greek: *ὁ κνὶψ ἐν χώρᾳ* (ho knips en chora)</note>. This was said of those who were constantly changing their residence and moving from one place to another. The poet Horace confesses that he himself was prone to this vice. The *knips* (or *knips*, for I find it written both ways) is a small worm born in timber. After it eats away at the wood, it is always striving to change its location. Some state the proverb this way: **A woodworm out of its place**, <note>original Greek: *κνὶψ ἐκ χώρας* (knips ek choras)</note> with the implied meaning that it is "moving away." 

Pliny, in book sixteen, chapter forty-one, mentions the "borer" <note>Latin: *teredo*</note> among the pests of timber; it is a worm with a very heavy head in proportion to its body, so named because it gnaws with its teeth, though properly the name *teredo* belongs to the kind that infests wood in the sea. He adds that one of this kind is called a *Cerastes*, which, as soon as it has gnawed enough to turn itself around, generates another. I doubt whether these details fit this proverb, for the Greeks record that the *knips* is a tiny winged, wood-eating insect <note>original Greek: *ξυλοφάγον* (xylophagon)</note> not unlike a gnat. If that is true, I do not see how it tallies with the report from Aristotle that the bird called the "wood-pecker" <note>original Greek: *ξυλοτήψ* (xyloteps); Latin: *picus Martius*</note> pecks at trees with its beak specifically to draw out the *knips* insects lurking in the wood. Suidas says that *knipos* (the genitive case of *knips*) can be treated as a nominative, and that the word signifies a **miserly person** or one living on a meager diet, presumably after the example of the woodworm, which feeds on the gnawings of wood—hardly a refined meal. Therefore, it seems plausible that the adage could be applied to stingy people who live on a harsh and frugal diet.

## XVI. The voice of Cycloborus.

**The voice of Cycloborus** <note>original Greek: *Κυκλοβόρου φωνή* (Kykloborou phone)</note>. This was said of noisy people and those who are violently clamorous, or those who had a defective and hoarse voice. The Cycloborus is a certain river in Attica; it is not a perennial stream but a torrent that flows down with a mighty roar, from which the proverb is derived. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:

> Greedy, a screamer, having the voice of the Cycloborus.
> <gloss>id est,</gloss>
> **Loud-mouthed, greedy, brawling with the voice of the Cycloborus.**

## XVII. You are pouring Thasian wine.

**You are pouring Thasian wine** <note>original Greek: *Θάσιον ἐνχέις* (Thasion encheis)</note>. This seems to have been a common saying whenever someone diluted wine not with water, but with some other more potent wine. For Thasian wines were once highly praised, as Apuleius testifies in his first *Apology*, saying: "It is rightly granted to the gardener and the innkeeper to commend their greens and wine based on the nobility of the soil—Thasian wine, Phliasian greens." And Pliny, in chapter seven of the fourteenth book of his *Natural History*, writes that among overseas wines, Thasian and Chian were held in the highest glory. Thasos is an island near Thrace; hence the proverb, **A Thasos of good things**. They say that Staphylus <note>Whose name means "Grape Cluster."</note> lived on that island, and Bacchus fell deeply in love with him. This is taken from Aristophanes' *Plutus*, where this verse appears:

> You pour Thasian wine, and rightly so, by Jove!
> <gloss>id est,</gloss>
> **You had poured in Thasian wine, quite rightly indeed.**

Chremylus, responding in a joking manner, denies that it is a surprise if it seemed so to the youth, since she was accustomed to set before him the most fragrant Thasian wine. <margin>XV</margin>
**To play the klapsiazon** <note>original Greek: *κλαψιάζειν* (klapsiazein)</note> was a common insult used against three types: those who took pleasure in the love of boys, or, as Diogenianus says, immoderately lustful women. It is clear enough where the proverb originates, except that Hesychius teaches that *klapsas* sounded to the Greeks like the womb or the female genitalia, from which it was accepted that they called lustful fondling *klapsiazein*, as Suidas also notes.

### Claudiana tonitrua.
<margin>X</margin>
**Claudian thunder.** Festus Pompeius seems to suggest that "Claudian thunder" passed into common speech, so called because Claudius Pulcher instituted a practice where, during theatrical games, stones were thrown in such a way as to imitate the sound of real thunder. For previously, only very light and small sounds were made when nails and stones were thrown into a bronze basin. This adage will apply—if it is deemed fit to be received into the flock of proverbs—to men who are immoderately loud and annoyingly noisy. It is very similar to what we have reported elsewhere: **Dodonæan bronze** <note>original Greek: *Δωδωναῖον χαλκεῖον* (Dodonaion chalkeion)</note>.

### Claudi more tenere pilam.
**To hold the ball like Claudius.** Marcus Tullius [Cicero] writes against Piso in this manner: "The Greek first began to distinguish and divide how things were said: that man, as they say, holds the ball like Claudius, because he had received testimony." So far Cicero. The proverb fits those who, whatever they have received from their teachers, whether learned or unlearned, are accustomed to hold and follow it with no selection and no judgment. The metaphor is taken from a lame man <note>Erasmus notes the wordplay on "Claudius" (a proper name) and *claudus* (the Latin word for lame).</note> who, distrusting his own feet, leans persistently on columns. Unless one prefers to refer it to a game of ball, which a lame man can only catch if you throw it conveniently to him. Otherwise, being slow of foot, he cannot catch it wherever it is thrown. Seneca says in book 7 of *On Benefits*: "What if you should forbid me to return the ball?"—that is, to give a benefit to one who is not fit to receive it. Plautus in *The Pot of Gold*: "But then during the day, he sits at home all day like a lame shoemaker." Generally, it will apply to all who depend on the judgment of another and lean on another’s authority, just like those for whom it is enough to have said, **"He himself said so."** <note>original Greek: *αὐτὸς ἔφα* (autos epha). This famously refers to the disciples of Pythagoras, who accepted his word as absolute truth.</note>

### Loripedem rectus derideat.
**Let the straight-legged man mock the crook-footed.** And indeed, how elegant and full of proverbial character is that line in Juvenal:
> Let the straight-legged man mock the crook-footed, and the white man the Ethiopian.

This will be suitable to use whenever someone reproaches others for an evil to which they themselves are liable, or chastises others for vices from which they are not immune—just as if a lame man were to insultingly object to another's lameness. It is necessary for him who is ready to speak against others to be as free from fault as possible; and it is most foolish to throw at another what can be turned back against oneself.
> For who would endure the Gracchi complaining about sedition?
> If a thief should displease Verres, or a murderer Milo?
<note>Erasmus quotes Juvenal here. The Gracchi were famous for political upheaval; Verres was a notoriously corrupt governor; Milo was a famous murderer. It is the height of hypocrisy for such people to complain about the very crimes they commit.</note>

That saying of Leo of Byzantium is celebrated: when a certain slanderer had reproached him for a defect in his eyes, while he himself was deformed by a hump, Leo said: "You have thrown a human insult at me, while you yourself carry Nemesis <note>The goddess of divine retribution, here implying his deformity is a punishment from the gods.</note> on your back."

### Clisthenem uideo.
<margin>X</margin>
**I see Cleisthenes.** <note>original Greek: *Κλισθένην ὁρῶ* (Klisthenen horo)</note>. This Cleisthenes had a bad reputation and was torn apart by the insults of comic poets because he was considered insufficiently manly, shaping himself into a womanly appearance with unseemly grooming, imitating that Sardanapalus of Assyria. Aristophanes in *The Women at the Thesmophoria*:
> Do you see yourself? No, by Jove, but Cleisthenes.

Suidas records this and says it applies to those who have smooth, shaven skin. For it was the custom of Cleisthenes to always have his beard shaved so that he might still seem a youth. It is also expressed in this way: **More intemperate than Cleisthenes** <note>original Greek: *Κλισθένους ἀκρατέστερος* (Klisthenous akratesteros)</note>, regarding a lewd man effeminated by luxuries. The opposite of this is: **More temperate than Zeno** <note>original Greek: *Ζήνωνος ἐγκρατέστερος* (Zenonos enkratesteros)</note>.

### Cleocritus.
<margin>XI</margin>
**Cleocritus.** <note>original Greek: *Κλεόκριτος* (Kleokritos)</note>. This name was thrown as an insult against lewd, effeminate men.

# CHILIAD THREE, CENTURY II
Kk 4
<meta>catchword: Ciffa-</meta>

soft and hardly men. For the insults of Old Comedy made this man famous. He was called an effeminate catamite <note>original: *cinædus*</note>, a stranger of obscure and filthy stock, and the "Son of Cybele," because the mysteries of Rhea were performed by those who had been castrated and un-manned. Not even his appearance differed from his character, for his face resembled that of a bird. Suidas specifically records this as a proverb; otherwise, I would not have included it among the adages myself.

->To act like a thrush.<-
->XXIIII<-

**To chirp like a thrush** <note>original Greek: *Κιχλίζειν* (Kichlizein)</note> was a proverb used for those who feasted on fat quails or thrushes, or for those who laughed lasciviously and in an unseemly manner. Consequently, they also call a soft and indecent laugh **thrush-chirping** <note>original Greek: *κιχλισμόν* (kichlismon)</note>. Therefore, it will apply either to gluttons and those addicted to delicacies, or to those playing too wantonly. Starlings will imitate anything, and the thrush is listed by Pliny among the birds that mimic human speech. Indeed, authors apply this term in various ways.

->Cilician destruction.<-
->XXV<-

**Cilician destruction** <note>original Greek: *Κιλίκιος ὄλεθρος* (Kilikios olethros)</note>. This was said of someone cruel and monstrous. For the Cilicians were infamous for their inhumanity and cruelty because of the piracy they practiced and their constant plundering of enemies. For this reason, the Athenians used to call particularly bitter vengeances **Cilician** <note>original Greek: *κιλικίας* (kilikias)</note>. Hesychius mentions this among others. Of a similar form is what we read in the works of the Jurists: **Isaurian**, used to mean a cruel and monstrous bandit.

->Centaur-like.<-
->XXVI<-

**To be done in the manner of a Centaur** <note>original Greek: *Κενταυρικῶς* (Kentaurikōs)</note>. This was said of anything done in a monstrous, ferocious, or uncivilized way, the word being taken from the character of the Centaurs. Aristophanes in *The Frogs* says:
**Who hammered the door so Centaur-like?** <note>original Greek: *Τίς τὴν θύραν ἐστάταξεν ὡς κενταυρικῶς;*</note>
For the Centaurs carried out everything by strength and violence, ignorant of laws and all justice. Although some believe this was said in Aristophanes' play to mock Dionysus <note>Erasmus uses "Bacchus"</note>, who was otherwise soft and un-warlike, for acting with such competitive aggression.

->Cilician commanders.<-
->XXVII<-

**Cilician leaders** <note>original Greek: *Κιλίκιοι στρατηγοί* (Kilikioi strategoi)</note>. This was a term for men who were shaggy and covered in hair. From this, shaggy cloaks woven from hair are called **Cilicia** <note>often translated as "hair-cloth" or "cilice"</note>. The authority for this is Diogenianus. Simply put, **Cilicians** was a name for those who were robust, filthy, and large; hence, those of wicked character are said **to act like Cilicians** <note>original Greek: *κιλικίζεσθαι* (kilikizesthai)</note>. Also, **Cilician words** <note>original Greek: *κιλίκιοι λόγοι* (kilikioi logoi)</note> refers to barbaric voting, because they were accustomed to decide matters by throwing pebbles into a helmet with great force. Mention is made of the **Cilicines**, who, although they were slaves, seized the region after driving out their masters. We have reviewed **Cilician goods** <note>original Greek: *κιλικικῶς ἀγαθὰ* (kilikikōs agatha)</note> elsewhere.

->We are playing "Cities."<-
->XXVIII<-

**We play "Cities"** <note>original Greek: *Πόλεις παίζομεν* (Poleis paizomen)</note>. This is a type of game in which tokens were played in ancient times, which they used to call **cities** <note>original Greek: *πόλεις* (poleis)</note> in the old days. More recent writers began to call them **spaces** or **regions** <note>original Greek: *χώρας* (chōras)</note>. Cratinus used the adage in *The Fugitives*. This is surely the passage, unless I am mistaken, which Julius Pollux cites in his ninth book *On Vocabulary*: **"The Pandionian city of the king, flattering beyond measure. You know the one we mean, both the dog and the city which we play."** He describes the type of game in these words: **"The game played with many tokens is a board having regions marked out in lines. The board itself is called the 'city,' and each of the tokens is called a 'dog.' Since the tokens are divided into two colors, the skill of the game consists in surrounding a token of a different color with two tokens of the same color, and then removing it from the board."** Plato alluded to this proverb in the fourth book of *The Republic*: **"For each of those is many cities, but not 'a city,' as the players are wont to say."** Zenodotus records this, though he does not indicate the same meaning for the adage. Therefore, I leave it to everyone to guess what seems closest to the truth. To me, it seems to fit whenever anyone pursues their own advantage by any path and sets traps in every way for a rival or competitor—a type of "game" that is frequent in the courts of princes and in public offices. From this game, it seems, came the one now commonly called **chess** <note>original: *scacarius*</note>.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<margin>XXI</margin>
**Cissamis of Cos.** <note>original Greek: *Κίσσαμις κῶος*</note>. That is, Cissamis the Coan. They say this man was exceedingly wealthy in herds of cattle. However, an eel used to appear every year, which would snatch away the most beautiful animal of them all. When the eel appeared to him in a dream and warned him to bury it, he neglected to do so; as a result, it happened that both he and his entire family line were utterly destroyed. This account is from Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and literary critic</note>. This proverb also requires "a Delian swimmer" <note>a phrase used for something very difficult to understand or navigate</note>. It appears closely related to what is said elsewhere: "The spirit of Temessa will be present."

<margin>XXII</margin>
**Poems of Carcinus.** <note>original Greek: *Καρκίνου ποιήματα*</note>. This was said of things that seemed obscure and spoken in the manner of a riddle. Carcinus was a certain poet whom we have mentioned elsewhere in this work, and whom Aristophanes mocks in the comedy titled *The Wasps*: 
->He who seemed luckier even than Carcinus's spinning tops.<-
According to Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>, this poet depicted Orestes—driven from Troy—answering in riddles when forced to confess his matricide. Suidas also testifies that the proverb was used by Menander in *The False Hercules*. Stratonicus, as recorded in the eighth book of Athenaeus, once heard someone singing unskillfully and asked whose song it was. When the man replied it was by Carcinus, Stratonicus said, "It is certainly much more like a crab's than a man's." This is because the Greek word *karkinos* <note>original: *κάρκινος*</note> means "crab." Thus, the joke was based on the double meaning of the name.

<margin>XXIII</margin>
**A Carian sacrifice.** <note>original Greek: *Καρικὸν θῦμα*</note>. This was said of a lean sacrifice that was not at all fit for eating. It is derived from the fact that it was the custom of the Carian people to sacrifice a dog. It can be aptly applied to food served that is tasteless and which no one would want to touch. Some people, out of stinginess, deliberately serve their guests rotten and unpalatable food, partly so they can buy it cheaper, and partly so that less is consumed during the banquet. One might elegantly say of such hosts that they are "serving a Carian sacrifice."

<margin>XXIV</margin>
**More numerous than the Callicyrii.** <note>original Greek: *Καλλικυρίων πλέους*</note>. This was said of a very large, but low-class, crowd of people. According to Timaeus, the Callicyrii were the slaves of exiles who practiced agriculture in Syracuse. Because that class of men was a massive multitude, it was accepted as a proverb that if anyone wanted to signify something very numerous, they would call them "Callicyrii." Aristotle, in his *Constitution of the Syracusans*, shows that this crowd of slaves had flowed together into one group from all sorts of peoples. The Callicyrii held the same social position among the Syracusans as the captives <note>Helots</note> did among the Spartans, the Penestae among the Thessalians, the Elarotae <note>Clarotes</note> among the Cretans, and the Hebrews among the Egyptians. This adage is most commonly used whenever people wish to indicate a fearsome multitude which, relying on its numbers, sometimes overthrows its masters. For these slaves were more numerous than their masters, which is why they eventually expelled them. This is roughly what is reported by Suidas.

<margin>XXV</margin>
**More malleable than wax.** <note>original Greek: *Κηροῦ εὐπλαστότερος*</note>. This was said of someone who is extremely teachable, or of a character that is easy, manageable, and following any shape. Horace writes:
->Yielding like wax to be bent toward vice, but harsh to advisors.<-
Persius, in his fifth Satire:
->And he draws a skillful face under your thumb.<-
And Horace again:
->The wet clay will imitate whatever you wish.<-
It is a peculiar quality of wax that it softens when handled by the hands. From this, various shapes of things are typically molded. There was also a type of painting made from colored waxes, just as there are mosaics made from tiles of stone and wood. Although a young age is more similar to clay than wax: at first, it can be molded while it is tender, but once the character has hardened, it is not easily reshaped into another form. As Plato said in the fourth book of *The Republic*: 
->The danger is that in education, toward whatever direction one sets out, those are the things that will follow.<- 
That is to say, there is a danger that whatever a person applies themselves to from childhood, such things will persist in the future.

<margin>XXX</margin>
**The wing of slaughter.** <note>original Greek: *Φόνου πτερόν*</note>. This was commonly said of a sudden death. The meta... <note>text cuts off</note>

...away from winged arrows, which repeatedly bring death. Although Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and the first librarian of Alexandria</note> prefers that we understand the phrase "winged slaughter" <note>original Greek: φόνον πτερόεν</note> as a poetic expression—that is, a circumlocution—for death, as if death herself were winged.

### Celmis in iron. XXXV

**Celmis in iron.** <note>original Greek: Κέλμις ἐν σιδήρῳ</note>. This was commonly said of those who relied excessively on their own strength, as if they were impregnable and invincible to others. Celmis, as Zenodotus writes, was one of the **Idaean Dactyls** <note>mythical male figures associated with the Mother Goddess Rhea and the discovery of iron-working on Mount Ida</note>, who was rejected by his brothers after he violated Rhea, the mother of the gods. Because of this, he was said to forge the hardest iron. Zenodotus mentions that this story is referenced in Sophocles's satyr plays. A commentator on Apollonius, writing about the Idaean Dactyls (among whom was Celmis), records these verses from the author of the *Phoronis* <note>an ancient lost epic poem</note>: 
->There lived the mountain-born Phrygians of Ida, men of the hills, a race famous for their art: Celmis, and the mighty Damnameneus, and the proud Acmon, skilled servants of mountain Adrastea. By them, it is said, the art of the many-skilled Hephaestus <note>god of fire and metalworking, known to the Romans as Vulcan</note> was first discovered in the mountain glens—the dark-colored iron—and they brought it to the fire and demonstrated a magnificent craft.<- **That is:**
> There lived the mountain-born Phrygians of Ida, a race famous for their art, 
> Celmis, and the mighty Damnameneus, and the proud Acmon, 
> the learned servants of mountain Adrastea. 
> By them, it is said, the art of Vulcan was first discovered, 
> and they showed how to forge the dark iron found in the wooded mountain 
> for various uses, and how it shines with wondrous beauty when placed in the fire.

### They have the girdle of Venus. XXXVI

**They have the girdle of Venus.** <note>original Greek: Τὸν κυπρίδος κεστὸν</note>. Those who entice anyone to fall in love with them using new or unusual charms are said to possess this. This expression is taken from Book 14 of Homer’s *Iliad*, in the passage where Juno <note>Hera</note>, intending to sleep with her husband Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, visits Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> and asks to borrow her belt—a reconciler of favors and loves. The poet describes it in this way:
->She spoke, and loosened from her breast the embroidered belt, patterned, where all charms were crafted. In it was affection, and desire, and womanly sweet-talk <note>original: ὀαριστὺς</note>, which indeed steals the wits even of the exceptionally wise, aided by secret tricks. She placed it in Juno's hands, spoke a word, and addressed her by name: "Take this belt now, and fasten it to your bosom, this varied weave in which all things are fashioned; I tell you that you shall not return with your task undone, whatever your heart desires."<- **That is:**
> She spoke, and loosened from her breast the embroidered strap 
> with its patterns, in which she carried all her charms. 
> In it was desire, in it was love, in it was womanly 
> sweet-talk, which indeed deceives and captures even the exceptionally wise, 
> aided by secret deceits. 
> As she placed it in Juno's hands, she spoke thus with her voice: 
> "Take this now, and fasten this varied belt to your bosom, 
> through which I promise that whatever you prepare, 
> you shall never attempt anything in vain."

Theocritus also mentions this in his elegy for Adonis:
**Your girdle perished along with you.** <note>original Greek: Σοὶ δ’ ἅμα κεστὸς ὄλωλε</note>.

The **cestus** <note>a belt or girdle</note> of Venus is, therefore, an effective belt for the allurements of grace and love, with which she is said to have won over Mars. Martial also mentions it:
> Tie pure loves around the boy's neck, 
> the girdle still warm from the bosom of Venus. 

**And elsewhere by the same author:**
> Take the girdle treated with Cytherean nectar.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

> That belt of yours scorched the lover Jove. <note>original Latin: *Ussit amatorem balteus iste Iouem*</note>
> Let Juno herself, and even Venus, seek the girdle from you. <note>original Latin: *A te Iuno petat ceston & ipsa Venus*</note>

->Again, elsewhere,<-

**This adage has a twofold use**: either when we say someone possesses the "girdle of Venus" <note>the *cestus*, a legendary belt that made the wearer irresistible</note> because they inflame everyone with love for them; or when we say there is a need for Venus’s girdle, meaning it would benefit one whose strength and beauty have faded with age, and who seems to have become <unclear>worn out</unclear>. For the bloom of youth inspires love of its own accord, but old age must win favor through gifts or "medicines" <note>here meaning artificial enhancements or charms</note>, although even by these means it can rarely achieve being truly loved.

### A pontifical feast. <margin>XXX</margin>

In ancient times, they used to call sumptuous and magnificent banquets "pontifical." Horace <note>a leading Roman lyric poet</note> alludes to this in his *Odes*:
> A worthier heir will consume the Caesar-brand wine
> preserved behind a hundred keys, and will stain
> the floor with a magnificent vintage,
> better even than the feasts of the high priests <note>original Latin: *Pontificum potiore coenis*</note>.

In this passage, commentators remark that extremely lavish dinners were proverbially called "pontifical." Macrobius <note>a Roman provincial writer and philosopher</note>, in the third book of his *Saturnalia*, describes a very ancient feast of a high priest, prepared with the greatest display and overflowing with every kind of luxury. This clearly arose from the fact that solemn and sacred banquets are usually prepared with the most exquisite delicacies. What Horace wrote is not unlike what people today in Paris call "theological wine" in a common joke—meaning wine that is very strong and not at all watered down.

Nor was a certain man lacking in wit when, asked for the reason for this proverb, he replied that the lawyers occupy the positions called <term>prebends</term> <note>stipends from a cathedral or collegiate church</note>, deaneries, and archdeaconries, leaving nothing for the theologians except the "cures" <note>the actual pastoral care of souls</note>, as they call them. Since it is written of these pastors, "You shall eat the sins of the people," <note>a reference to Hosea 4:8</note> surely a most powerful wine is needed to digest such heavy food! And so, this common saying was born. Plautus <note>a Roman playwright</note>, in his play *The Menaechmi*, used a similar figure of speech when he spoke of "Cerealian feasts" <note>feasts in honor of Ceres, the goddess of agriculture</note>. He says: "He gives Cerealian feasts," describing how he piled the table high: "He heaps up such stacks of dishes. You’d have to stand on the bed if you wanted to reach anything from the top." We also read of "fatty feasts," "rich feasts," and "inaugural feasts." Terence <note>another Roman playwright</note>, in his *Phormio*, used the phrase "a doubtful feast" to mean one so lavish and abundant that a guest is "in doubt" as to which dish to try first.

### To eat or smell onions. <margin>XXXI</margin>

**To eat onions.** <note>original Greek: Κρόμμυα ἐσθίειν</note>. This was said in a proverbial joke about people who seem to be crying. It originated from an <term>apophthegm</term> <note>a pithy saying</note> of Bias <note>one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>. When King Alyattes sent a messenger to him, ordering him to come to him at once, Bias replied in this manner: "I order Alyattes to eat onions." <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ ἀλυάτῃ κελεύω κρόμμυα ἐσθίειν</note>. That is: "I tell him to weep and wail" <note>original Greek: κλαίειν καὶ οἰμώζειν</note>. By these words, he indicated his supreme contempt for the king. The proverb is derived from the fact that the smell of onions, being sharp, is known to force tears from the eyes. Aristophanes <note>the great Greek comic playwright</note> wrote: "He hasn't even eaten an onion yet," implying that the person was going to cry even without the help of onions. Since mustard produces the same effect, nothing prevents the proverb from being derived from that as well. Columella <note>a Roman writer on agriculture</note> wrote in a poem:
> And mustard, which will bring tears to the one who provokes it.

And shortly after, he mentions the onion:
> And the root of the dark vegetable, and the tear-inducing onion.

By a similar figure of speech and with a related meaning, those who were crying were said **to smell of onions.** <note>original Greek: κρομμύων ὀσφραίνεσθαι</note>. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
"Why then are you weeping?" "I’m smelling onions, of course." <note>original Greek: Τί δῆτα κλαίεις; κρομμύων ὀσφραίνομαι</note>
Suidas <note>the author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> records much the same. However, Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> in Book 20, Chapter 5, reports that onions are actually a remedy for watery eyes and blurred vision. This does not contradict what we have said, since it cleanses the eye by drawing out the fluid. Xenophon <note>a Greek historian and philosopher</note>, in his *Symposium*, used the phrase **to smell of onions** <note>original Greek: κρομμύων ὄζειν</note> to describe people who are filthy and unwashed. Akin to this is the term **to garlic-ize** <note>original Greek: σκοροδίζειν</note>, meaning to cause annoyance or to drive one to tears. Aristophanes, in *The Knights*, speaking in the persona of the Athenian people, says: "While claiming to love me, you have 'garlic-ed' me" <note>i.e., treated me harshly or made me cry</note>. However, that word was coined by the comic poet for the sake of humor.

### Blacker than a beetle. <margin>XXXII</margin>

**Blacker than a beetle.** <note>original Greek: Κανθάρε μελάντερος</note>. Said of those who are hideous and intensely dark or swarthy. For the beetle is an animal of a remarkable and foul blackness, about which more will be said below.

<summary>Erasmus explains three main adages: "Pontifical feasts" (referring to luxury), "eating onions" (referring to crying or contempt), and "blacker than a beetle" (referring to appearance).</summary>

->CHILIAD THREE, CENTURY TWO<-

### To Act Like a Chalcidian. XL

*Chalcidissare* and *chalcidissasthai* <note>original Greek: χαλκιδίζειν and χαλκιδίζεσθαι</note> were terms used for those who appeared more rapacious and excessively attentive to profit. The Chalcidians were a people on the island of Euboea, often marked by the insults of Old Comedy for being overly greedy. Hesychius <note>an Alexandrian grammarian</note> indicates that this nation also had a bad reputation for the foul love of boys, and that the proverb arose as an insult toward those prone to a similar vice.

### To Act Like a Phicidian. XLI

*Phicidissare* <note>original Greek: σικυΐζειν</note> was a common term for those devoted to the obscene love of boys. Some prefer to refer it to those who used the letter *r* immoderately and to the point of annoyance. Indeed, that people were accustomed to changing the letter *s* into *r*. The Eretrians are also noted for this vice, as attested by the proverb "to rhotacize" <note>original Greek: ῥωτερίζειν</note>, that is, "the Eretrian rho." Today, there is a common joke among the people regarding the Picards <note>people from Picardy, France</note>; meanwhile, Parisian women, out of a certain linguistic delicacy, turn *r* into *s*, pronouncing "Masia" instead of "Maria." <note>This refers to a 16th-century linguistic trend in Paris called 'lambdacism' or 'sigmatism' where the 'r' was softened to an 's' sound.</note>

### Shrewder than Cantharus. XLII

"Shrewder than Cantharus" <note>original Greek: Κανθάρω σοφώτερος</note>, or more cunning. Zenodotus says there was a certain innkeeper in Athens named Cantharus, whom they sentenced to death because of his crimes, impostures, and betrayals. Consequently, it became a common saying for the crafty and for impostors. To me, however, it seems more likely if it refers to the nature of the insect <note>the *cantharus* or dung beetle</note> and to the Aesopic fable. In that story, it is told how the beetle, though so much weaker in strength than the eagle, nevertheless surpassed the queen of all birds through its ingenuity.

### Like a dog sailing to Delos. XLIII

"Like a dog sailing to Delos" <note>original Greek: Κύων ὥσπερ εἰς Δῆλον πλέων</note>. This was said of a person leading a lazy, idle, secure, and pleasure-seeking life. For the voyage from Athens to Delos was easy and safe. Thus, it happened that those who set sail for that place were carefree during the voyage and would sing, fearing no danger. It was the custom of the Athenians to send a ship to Delos every year with solemn preparation for religious reasons, as Plato indicates in the *Crito*. From this, it is consistent that those carried on this ship were accustomed to chanting certain hymns in praise of Apollo.

### Caunian love. XLIV

"Caunian love" <note>original Greek: Καύνιος ἔρως</note>. This was said of a foul love, or when someone desired things that were neither divine to covet nor possible to achieve. Byblis fell helplessly in love with her brother Caunus; when she was rejected by him, she took her own life. Ovid writes:
> Byblis is an example, that girls should love what is permitted. <note>original Latin: *Byblis in exemplo est, ut ament concessa puellae*</note>
This adage is recorded by Diogenianus and also by Eustathius in his commentary on Dionysius.

### The shadow of a beetle. XLV

"The shadow of a beetle" <note>original Greek: Κανθάρου σκιά</note>. This was said of a vain fear, because this insect, flying suddenly toward nightfall with a horrible humming sound, is sometimes accustomed to terrify those who are not paying attention. It is listed by Diogenianus.

### The fruit of the papyrus does not demand a heavy ear. XLVI

"The fruit of the papyrus does not demand a heavy ear" <note>original Greek: βύβλου δὲ καρπὸς ἐπ' αὐτᾷ μέγαν στάχυν</note>. That is:
> The green papyrus hardly asks for a heavy ear of grain.
Even if the Greek hexameter is corrupted in the word *auta*. In Aeschylus’s *Suppliants*, it is read as:
> The fruit of the papyrus does not sustain a heavy ear. <note>original Greek: βύβλου δὲ καρπὸς οὐ κρατεῖ στάχυν μέγαν</note>
This was commonly said of those who could not enjoy their own goods, because the papyrus, on account of its weak stalks, cannot bear an ear weighed down with grain. Consequently, it does produce ears, but they are empty. Now, the *byblus* is a species of rush which the Latins call *papyrum*. It appears that in the Greek poem *auta* was corrupted for *kratei* <note>meaning "to support" or "to hold"</note>, as the meter itself indicates.

### In the manner of Budorus. XLVII

"In the manner of Budorus" <note>original Greek: Βουδώρω νόμῳ</note>, or as I find elsewhere, *Boudoro nomo*. That is, "by the custom or law of the Budori." Suidas and Zenodotus interpret this as referring to those who are worthy of being skinned like an ox. Diogenianus explains it as referring to things to be wondered at. According to Stephanus, Budorum is a promontory opposite Salamis. Budora is a city in Magnesia, which Homer called Bedorus. The Budori are a people of Scythia, so called because they are carried by oxen, as they are "wagon-dwellers" <note>original Greek: ἁμαξόβιοι</note>—that is, using wagons in place of houses. From this, there seems to be a twofold allusion to the etymology: "to skin an ox" and "the gift of oxen" <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ, βοῦς δέρειν, καὶ τὸ βοῦς δῶρα</note>. Strabo, in his tenth book, points out a river of Euboea...
