# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM ON ADAGES
XLV

...of the Budini. The same author <note>Pliny the Elder</note> indicates a mountain of Salamis looking towards Attica. Again, Pliny in book 4, chapter 12, mentions the Budini between the Geloni and the Agathyrsi. However, I do not see what they make for themselves as a proverb. Hesychius indicates that *Bosboron* <note>original Greek: Βόσβορον</note> is the "bolt" <note>original Greek: μοχλὸν</note> by which oxen are joined. There will be a place for this proverb if someone says that one must deal with a wicked person not with arguments or laws, but by "force of law" <note>original Greek: βίᾳ νόμῳ; used here to mean brute force or extra-legal compulsion</note>, just as Sannio hears in Terence: "For if you are more troublesome, I will seize you inside now, and there you will be covered with lashes even unto death."

### Boeotian ear.

*Boeotian ear* <note>original Greek: Βοιώτιον οὖς</note>. This fits a man of dull or "thick" judgment. The stupidity of the Boeotians <note>a region in Greece north of Attica</note> gave rise to several proverbs. It is very similar to the saying "Batavian ear" <note>A joke Erasmus often applied to his own Dutch countrymen, who were likewise stereotyped as rustic or dull</note>. Diogenianus <note>a Greek grammarian</note> mentions this adage. There are those who write that once Anaxagoras <note>a pre-Socratic philosopher</note>, while reciting at Thebes of the Boeotians, when he saw no one was paying attention, closed his book and said: "You are rightly called Boeotians, for you have the ears of oxen" <note>original Greek: εἰκότως καλεῖσθε βοιωτοὶ, γὰρ ὦτα ἔχετε</note>. He seems to be alluding to the etymology of the name: *bous* <note>original Greek: βοῦς</note> means ox, and *ota* <note>original Greek: ὦτα</note> means ears; from these, the name of the Boeotians seems to be composed. Indeed, Homer in the fifth book of the Iliad calls the Boeotian race "fat":
*But those who held the land nearby were Boeotians, possessing a very fat country.* <note>original Greek: πὰρ δὲ οἱ ἄλλοι Νᾶον βοιωτοὶ μάλα πίονα δῆμον ἔχοντες</note>
Horace also noted the sluggishness of the Boeotians in his epistle to Octavius Augustus:
*But if you called that subtle judgment, so keen in viewing the arts, to books and these gifts of the Muses, you would swear he was born in the thick Boeotian air.*
In this passage, I wonder why none of the commentators have asked why Horace attributes a "fatness of wit" to the Boeotians as if it were peculiar to that nation, since among the Latins there is little or no other evidence for this. Closely related to this is what we have mentioned elsewhere: the "Boeotian song," which can be understood as rustic and poorly modulated, so that a coarse harmony might suit coarse ears. 

However, Eustathius <note>a 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note>, in his commentary on the second book of the Iliad, tells a slightly different story regarding the name. He says there are those who think Boeotia was named after a cow. For when Europa, the daughter of Phoenix, was snatched from Sidon by Jupiter, Cadmus, the brother of the kidnapped girl, was sent by his father to find his sister. When he found her nowhere, he went to Delphi to consult the oracle. The god replied that he should not be anxious or curious about Europa, but should follow a cow as a guide, and build a city wherever the exhausted cow should lie down. Having received this response, he made his way through the region of Phocis. Then, when he came upon a heifer near the pastures of Pelagon, he followed her as she went. When she had wandered through all of Boeotia, she lay down from exhaustion at the place where the city of the Thebans now stands. When Cadmus wished to sacrifice the heifer to Pallas <note>Athena</note>, he sent some of his companions to draw water for the sacrifice from the Aretiade spring. But a dragon, the guardian of the spring, which was believed to be sacred to Mars—for the spring itself took its name from Mars—was stirred by the noise and killed many of those who had been sent. Cadmus, taking this indignity badly, killed the dragon, and at the suggestion of Pallas, sowed the teeth of the slain creature, from which sprang the "earth-born brothers." For this reason, Mars was indignant and prepared to kill Cadmus, but was appeased by Jupiter, who gave Harmonia, the daughter of Mars and Venus, to Cadmus in marriage. This was on the condition that before he could touch his bride, he would serve a year of servitude, and that at the wedding the Muses should sing the marriage song <note>epithalamium</note>, and each of the gods should give a wedding gift to Harmonia. These are the words of Eustathius. 

I personally think this was the original source of the adage, however much it was later twisted to other uses. It is well known, however, that the Thebans were once very fond of music. An argument for this is what is reported of Alcibiades: when people wondered why he neglected the study of the flute <note>tibia</note>, he condemned it in favor of the lyre with this reasoning: that the lyre could imitate the human voice with a plectrum and that it preserved a noble appearance and form, whereas the flute turned a noble look into an ignoble one. He rejected the flute for two reasons: because it so changed a man's face that he could scarcely be recognized by his closest friends, and because it took away a man's own voice and robbed him of the faculty of speech. He soon added: "Let the Thebans play the flute, for they do not know how to speak."

It is used either when some people wish to appear as equals in some business and eventually bring influence to each other, so that neither should yield to the other. Or when we mean...

THIRD CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
LI
<meta>catchword: Add</meta>

...to be a work of your own services; so that it is very similar to what we have related elsewhere, "hand washes hand" <note>original Greek: χὼς χάρα νίπτα; usually *cheir cheira niptei*</note>. Or if we should ever say that each person turns out like those with whom they associate. For constant association has this effect: it makes the vices of neighbors common to one another. As that six-foot verse testifies, which the commentator on Pindar <note>Pindar was a famous Greek lyric poet</note> cites from Aristarchus <note>a celebrated grammarian of Alexandria</note>:
> If you live near a lame man even for one day,
> You yourself will soon learn to walk with a limp.
Although I remember this was cited by us in another place—namely, in the adage, "If near a lame man"—nevertheless, since I happened upon a text somewhat different from the previous one, it pleased me to refer to it again as the occasion arose. The adage is metaphorically drawn from grapes, which, by being placed opposite one another, mutually give and receive ripeness. To this, that line of Juvenal <note>a Roman satirical poet</note> refers:
"And a grape takes on a leaden hue from the sight of another grape."
The adage is recorded by Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>.

### To sacrifice oxen.
<margin>50</margin>
*To sacrifice oxen* <note>original Greek: Βουθυτεῖν</note> was said proverbially of those who engaged in large and magnificent expenditures. For it is the mark of the wealthy, or rather of kings, to sacrifice oxen. Aristophanes <note>the famous Athenian comic playwright</note> in *Plutus*:
> And now indeed the master is sacrificing oxen within.
And they use the term "ox-sacrifice" <note>original Greek: βουθυσίαν</note> to describe a magnificent display.

### Oxen waiting for harvest time.
<margin>51</margin>
*Oxen watching the harvest* <note>original Greek: Βῶς ἄμητον ἐπιτηρῶντες</note>. This was usually said when someone undertook labor in the hope of immense rewards. Some express it thus: *An ox toward the harvest* <note>original Greek: βῶς εἰς ἄμητον</note>, where "looks for" or something similar must be understood. It is derived from the fact that at harvest time, oxen work with greater benefit to themselves, because they graze during the threshing and a more generous supply of fodder is set before them. By contrast, when they plow the field in spring or winter, the labor of plowing is more troublesome because it is not softened by any immediate benefit.

### The Ox of the Homolottians.
<margin>52</margin>
*The Ox of the Homolottians* <note>original Greek: Βῶς ὁμολοττιῶν</note> was said of a matter distracted or, as it were, dissected into very many pieces of business. It can also be applied to a situation where someone divides an argument into such tiny details that they seem to be shredding and tearing it apart rather than dividing it. Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and the first librarian of Alexandria</note> records that the Homolottian people, having cut an ox into the smallest parts, would join in a treaty. Lucian <note>a Syrian-Greek satirist</note> in *Toxaris* testifies that this was a custom among the Scythians.

### The ox at the heap.
<margin>53</margin>
*An ox on the heap* <note>original Greek: Βῶς ἐπὶ σωρῷ</note>. Said of those living splendidly and amply, and who, in a fertile abundance of things, spend more lavishly. Or, as Suidas says, of those who, being situated in the midst of a plenty of things, do not enjoy the good things present. He thinks it is a metaphor from oxen performing the threshing, who, because they have their mouths bound—for some do this—are not allowed to eat the wheat they are shaking out; so that it is similar to the proverb: "Tantalus thirsts in the middle of the waves" <note>Tantalus was a mythological figure punished in the underworld by being unable to reach the food and water surrounding him</note>. Julius Pollux <note>a Greek grammarian and rhetorician</note> relates something similar in his seventh book regarding slaves working in a mill, for whom a round machine was placed around the neck so that they could not move a hand to their mouth. This was done so they would not devour the flour. They called the machine a "gluttony-stopper" <note>original Greek: παυσικάπην or καρδοπάπην</note> because it kept them from devouring. What the Jews did not do to oxen <note>A reference to the Biblical law in Deuteronomy 25:4: "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn"</note>, these people did to men.

### Either everyone must act in tragedies, or be mad.
<margin>54</margin>
> Either one must be mad, or act in tragedies. <note>original Greek: Ἢ χρὴ τραγῳδεῖν πάντας ἢ μελαγχολᾶν</note>
This was usually said of those who are always, as it were, stunned and cold, and can neither rejoice from the soul nor grieve. Furthermore, tragedy consists of the most violent emotions, so that to "act in tragedies" seems to be something very similar to madness. Hence Lucian, in the commentary titled *How one should write history*, relates that a fever broke out publicly among the people of Abdera <note>a city in Thrace whose people were stereotyped as fools</note> while the tragic actor Archelaus was reciting from a tragedy of Euripides; seven days later, it turned into madness, so that everyone shouted out certain verses from Archelaus's *Andromeda*. Nevertheless, Plato attributes a certain sacred frenzy to all poets. And Aristotle in the *Problems* mentions a certain Maracus of Syracuse, who made better poems when his mind was alienated <note>meaning, when he was in a state of madness or trance</note>. To this same point belongs that saying of Horace...

<keywords>proverbs, social influence, mimicry, sacrifice, wealth, harvest, labor, treaties, muzzling oxen, slavery, tragedy, madness, theater, classical authors</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, moving from regional metaphors to specific social behaviors and literary critiques. It finishes a previous entry on finishing what one starts before transitioning into the LV through LX sequence of adages.</meta>

Add poems now—that is, "add oil to the fire" <note>original Latin: *oleum adde camino*; from Horace's *Satires* 2.3.321</note>.
This seems related to that which we have related in another place:
"Either eat the meat of a tortoise or do not eat it" <note>original Greek: ἤ δέ χελώνης κρέα φαγαν ἢ μὴ φαγαν; a proverb suggesting that if one does something, one should do it thoroughly</note>.
Athenaeus <note>a Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> cites this six-foot verse from Terpsion, the teacher of Archestratus. We have mentioned it elsewhere.

---

### Remove the Mothon from the oar. <sig>LV</sig>

"Remove the Mothon from the oar" <note>original Greek: Ἄπαγε τὸν μώθωνα ἀπὸ κώπης</note>. This adage warns that one should not obstruct or rudely disturb those who are otherwise occupied with serious business—for instance, if someone brings music to a person worried by affairs of state, or recites love poetry to one facing a capital trial. The "Mothon" <term>Mothon: a term used for a vulgar dance, a specific class of Spartan slaves, or a person of low character</term> was a foul, slavish, and riotous type of dance. The Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> call household slaves—that is, slaves born in the home—"mothones"; or they use the term for those who educate the sons of free men, whom the Athenians call "oikotribas" <note>household-slaves or those raised in the master's house</note>. From this, it began to be used as an insult against low and sordid men. Others think Mothon was a certain dancer and drunkard. There are those who believe the Athenians were called "Mothones" because they had been tamed and forced into slavish service. The Greek grammarians trifle with these explanations of the Mothon in this manner. Julius Pollux <note>a 2nd-century Greek scholar</note> writes in his fourth book that the mothon is a troublesome and nautical type of dance. And from this I would certainly believe the proverb arose, so that we may take "from the oar" to mean "originating from the oar" <note>implying a common, unrefined sailor</note>.

### With ears pricked. <sig>LVI</sig>

"With ears pricked" <note>original Greek: Ὠσὶν ὀρθοῖς</note>. This is recorded by Diogenianus as a proverb. It applies to those who listen thirstily and greedily to what is said, or who wait for what is to be spoken. The metaphor is drawn from animals, most of whom have the habit of pricking up their ears whenever they hear something from a distance. For nature gave immobile ears to humans alone among animals. Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> records that this is characteristic of stags: when they have raised their ears, nothing is more acute than their hearing; conversely, when they have lowered them, nothing is deafer. Likewise, Aristotle in the ninth book of *On the Nature of Animals* states that stags are by no means unaware of traps whenever their ears are pricked, because then their hearing is sharpest; on the other hand, when they lower their ears, they are easily captured. Terence says in his play *Andria*: "Prick up your ears, Pamphile." And Virgil: "They stand by with ears pricked." Propertius in his third book writes:
> Begin to speak from the very first origin; 
> I shall drink those words in with ears suspended.
->To this, what Horace writes may seem the opposite:<-
"I lower my ears like an ill-tempered donkey, when a heavier load has come upon its back."

### Colophonian gold. <sig>LVII</sig>

"Colophonian gold" <note>original Greek: Χρυσὸς ὁ κολοφώνιος</note>. Zenodotus shows this was commonly said of the most proven gold, because the finest gold used to be produced among the Colophonians <note>residents of Colophon, an ancient city in Ionia</note>. He cites Aristophanes in his comedy *Cocalus* and Herodotus as authorities, who called the most excellent and "purely pure" gold (as the ancients used to say) "Colophonian." It will become more elegant if it is applied further—for instance, toward intensely uncorrupted morals or an exquisite and exceptional talent.

### The deaths of an ass. <sig>LVIII</sig>

"The deaths of an ass" <note>original Greek: ὄνου θανάτους</note>—one must understand the word "tales" or "narrations." It was said of those who told absurd and ridiculous stories, such as if someone were to follow the dangers of an ass in a long narrative, just as Homer described the adventures of Ulysses. Apuleius in his *Metamorphoses* <note>famously known as *The Golden Ass*</note> clearly recounts "the deaths of an ass." The adage is recorded by Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>.

### The ass is rained upon. <sig>LIX</sig>

"The ass is rained upon" <note>original Greek: ὄνος ὑεται</note>. Cephisodorus, quoted in Suidas regarding the Amazons, says: "You mock me, but I am like an ass being rained upon by these words" <note>original Greek: Σκώπτης μ', ἐγὼ δὲ τοῖς λόγοις ὄνος ὕεσθαι</note>. That is:
> You laugh, but like an ass I am drenched by your words.
From this it is clear the saying was used for those who were not moved at all by insults. Just as an ass, due to the toughness of its skin, is so little offended by rain that it barely even feels a club.

### You have sprinkled water. <sig>LX</sig>

A person is said to have "sprinkled water" who, by some saying, has restored someone's spirit and taken away their fear. The metaphor is borrowed from those who, in a fainting fit <note>original Greek: λειποθυμίαν, *leipothymian*</note>, are called back to their senses by water sprinkled on the face. Plautus in the *Bacchides*: "Hurrah! You have sprinkled water." The same in the *Truculentus*: "You have sprinkled water; now my spirit has returned." Which Terence says more simply: "You have restored my spirit."

# THIRD CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY
<sig>Ll 2</sig>

->You ask Arcadia of me.<-
<margin>LXI</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀρκαδίαν μ' αἰτεῖς</note></margin> **You ask Arcadia of me.** <note>original Latin: *Arcadiam me postulas*</note>. Diogenianus <note>a Greek grammarian and proverb collector</note> shows a twofold use for this proverb. It is suitable for someone asking for either a very large thing or a useless thing. He does not indicate the origin, which is typical of this writer. However, Herodotus in his first book sufficiently teaches that it was born from an oracle: <margin><note>original Greek: Ἀρκαδίαν μ' αἰτεῖς, μέγα μ' αἰτεῖς, οὐδέν σ' δώσω</note></margin> which is to say:
*You pray for Arcadia of me; you ask a great thing; I shall give you nothing.*
Cicero notes this proverb in a letter to Atticus in the fourth book: "As for what you commission me regarding a certain person's guidance, it is an 'Arcadia' <note>meaning a difficult or impossible task</note>; nevertheless, I shall omit nothing."

->Imitating the Arcadians.<-
<margin>LXII</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀρκάδας μιμούμενοι</note></margin> **Imitating the Arcadians.** <note>original Latin: *Arcadas imitantes*</note>. Zenodotus indicates this was said against those who labor for others and not for themselves. Plato writes to Pisander that he "imitates the Arcadians" because, out of poverty, he handed over comedies written by himself to be produced by others. The adage is derived from this: that the Arcadians were once the most warlike among the Greeks, yet under their own auspices and their own title, they never overcame any enemy; rather, they very often brought aid to others. Thus it seemed to be their fate to conquer for others, not for themselves.

->To leap from five rocks into the waves.<-
<margin>LXIII</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ πέντε ἀμαθῶν πετρῶν ἐπὶ κῦμα</note></margin> **To leap from five rocks into the waves.** <note>original Latin: *A quinque desilire rupibus in undam*</note>. This is usually used by those who, now impatient with present evils, threaten that they would rather throw themselves headlong into any other evil than endure what they have. It is certainly close to that which we have related elsewhere: "A tree must be chosen for hanging." The Virgilian shepherd alludes to this:
*Headlong from the watch-tower of a towering mountain into the waves*
*I shall be carried; take this as the final gift of a dying man.*

->The water flows through.<-
<margin>LXIV</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ὕδωρ παραῤῥεῖ</note></margin> **The water flows through**, or **The water flows past.** <note>original Latin: *Perfluit aqua*</note>. Zenodotus and Suidas advise that this was often said of one who refused no business and promised he would perform whatever was commanded; indeed, he was so ready to undertake anything that he would not even hesitate to board a leaking ship, despising the influx of water, which is prone to flow in and out.

->The eagle does not catch flies.<-
<margin>LXV</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀετὸς οὐ θηρεύει τὰς μυίας</note></margin> **The eagle does not hunt flies.** <note>original Latin: *Aquila non aucupatur muscas*</note>. Great men ignore certain tiny details. An exalted mind despises humble things. Alternatively, the exceptionally learned sometimes slip in certain very small matters. And those occupied with the greatest business overlook certain petty things. The adage is also expressed without the negation: <note>original Greek: ἀετὸς μυίας θηρεύει</note>, that is, "The eagle hunts flies," whenever great men take care of the smallest things. Not unlike this is what Gregory the Theologian <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus</note> says in a letter to Eudoxius the rhetorician: <note>original Greek: μὴ ἀνάγκη ἀριστεύειν ἐν τοῖς κολοιοῖς ἀετὸς</note>, that is, "you would not endure being the foremost eagle among jackdaws."

->You are "uncaprificated."<-
<margin>LXVI</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀνερίναστος εἶ</note></margin> **You are "uncaprificated."** <note>original Latin: *Incaprificatus es*</note>. Suidas thinks this applies to a soft and unfruitful person. There are those who apply it to those who cannot protect the good they have obtained. Hermippus used the adage in *The Soldiers*. Suidas and Zenodotus give the reasoning for it in this way: they say that in the wild fig, which is the fruit of the "caprifig" <term>Caprifig: a wild fig tree whose fruit is not eaten but is used to help ripen domestic figs</term>, a little worm is born which the Greeks call a *psen*. The farmers collect the force of these and hang them from the branches of the fig tree, so that the fruit does not fall off prematurely and unripe. For the worms immediately creep through the cracks, and in this way the figs ripen. Theophrastus in his second book *On Plants* thinks these "fig-gnats" are born from the seeds of the wild figs, because as soon as they have flown out, no seeds remain. They fly out almost always leaving a wing or a foot in the fruit. But many things regarding the method of **caprification** <term>Caprification: the ancient agricultural practice of hanging wild figs in domestic fig trees so that pollinating wasps (the "worms" described) will mature the crop</term> are found there, if anyone cares to know. He says almost the same in the second book of *The Causes of Plants*, chapter 12. Pliny also mentions it in book fifteen, chapter nineteen. And Aristotle in the fifth book of *The History of Animals*. Therefore, a tree to which this remedy for ripening had not been applied was called "uncaprificated" <note>Greek: *anerinstos*</note>, and from there it was transferred to a useless man from whom no good fruit was to be expected. The word is composed of the privative "a" and "erineos" <note>wild fig</note>, as if you were to say, "un-wild-figged."

->To act like the Parians.<-
<margin>LXVII</margin>
<margin><note>original Greek: Ἀνεπαριάζειν</note></margin> **To act like the Parians.** <note>original Latin: *Repariazare*</note>. This was said of those who regretted a plan and departed from their agreements; it was born from history. When the Parians were once pressed by the Thebans in war, they requested that the Thebans desist from the war, promising they would hand the city over to their power. When the Thebans had desisted on this condition, and in the meantime a hope of help had appeared to the Parians from elsewhere, the Pa-

<meta>This page continues the Second Century of the Third Chiliad of Erasmus’s collection of proverbs. The previous page discussed the Arcadians and the concept of working for others' benefit. This page concludes a historical anecdote about the siege of Paros before moving into several adages concerning redundant efforts, grandiloquent speech, and social behaviors.</meta>

...they voided the [treaty], and renewed the war with the Thebans. From this was fashioned the proverbial term <term>to act like a Parian</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναπαριάζειν</note>, meaning to invalidate agreements, following the example of the Parians. Stephanus mentions the proverb under the entry <term>Paros</term> <note>original Greek: πάρος</note>, citing the author Ephorus, though he varies in the historical details. For when Miltiades <note>an Athenian general</note> was pressing the Parians hard, and they had already begun to treat for the surrender of the city, a certain path near Myconus suddenly began to burn. The Parians, suspecting that Datis <note>the Persian admiral</note> had given them a signal by lighting a fire, tore up the conventions and refused to hand over the city. Aemilius <note>the biographer Cornelius Nepos</note> agrees in his *Life of Miltiades*. Paros is one of the Cyclades <note>a group of Greek islands</note>, as is Myconus.

->Water from a ditch to the sea.<-
<margin>LXVI</margin>

<term>Water from a lake to the sea</term> <note>original Greek: Θαλάττῃ ἐκ χαράδρας ὕδωρ</note>. That is, you are pouring water from a lake into the sea. This is similar to that other saying: <term>A clod to the field</term> <note>original Greek: βῶλον ἀρούρᾳ</note>. Ovid says in his *Love Elegies*:
> Why do you add collected waters to the deep seas?

It is related to the ones we have reviewed elsewhere: "To carry wood to the forest," and "To add oil to the furnace."

->Wagon-sized.<-
<margin>LXVII</margin>

<term>Wagon-sized</term> <note>original Greek: Ἁμαξιαῖα</note>. This proverbial word was used for things that were ample and magnificent; it sounds as if you were to say "cart-like" or "wagon-loads"—that is, things so large they could be seen as a proper load for a wagon. Hence they used to say <term>wagon-sized words</term> <note>original Greek: ἁμαξιαῖα ῥήματα</note> in the same way Horace <note>Flaccus</note> spoke of "words a foot and a half long" <note>original Latin: sesquipedalia uerba</note>. Such are those types in Aristophanes' *Wasps*:
<term>early-rising-sycophantic-lawsuit-enduring-ways</term> <note>original Greek: ὀρθοφοιτοσυκοφαντοδικοταλαιπώρων τρόπων</note>.
In Plautus' *Curculio*, there is a soldier's name, *Therapontigonoplatagidorus*, with which he says he often filled four whole wax tablets while writing it in his accounts. There is also a joke by someone against a certain Hermes, an affecter of such foot-and-a-half-long words:
> Hermes delights in honorificabilitudinitatibus,
> in habitualities, in solicitudes.
<note>The first word is a famous example of an absurdly long word, meaning "the state of being loaded with honors."</note>

Athenaeus in his tenth book relates that the gluttony of the Thessalians was once rebuked; he calls their dinners <term>wagon-sized</term> <note>original Greek: ἁμαξιαίας</note> or <term>cart-loads</term> <note>original Greek: καπανικάς</note>. He cites a poem by Aristophanes in the *Fryers*:
<term>How are the dinners of the Lydians and the Thessalians?</term> And again:
<term>The Thessalian ones are much more wagon-like.</term> That is:
To what end are the Lydian or Thessalian banquets?
The Thessalian ones are much more like wagon-loads.
Furthermore, the Thessalians call vehicles <term>kapanas</term> <note>original Greek: καπάνας</note>. Likewise in the seventh book, he records that among the Sicyonians many <term>man-burdens</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνδραχθεῖς</note> are gathered—that is, things of such magnitude that they burden a porter with a full weight—and some even <term>wagon-sized</term>, that is, a proper load for a vehicle. Even more, <term>angginaia</term> <note>original Greek: ἀγγιναῖα</note> was said of huge things, either from a talent-weight that was larger than others among them, or from the packs of merchants containing various goods, which Hesychius testifies are called *angginaia* by the Greeks. At Sicyon, the word is written with an accent on the third-to-last syllable. Those who trade in these packs are called <term>angginaioi</term>. He adds that a certain huge silver coin is called <term>angginaion</term> by the Greeks.

->To mow the moss.<-
<margin>LXVIII</margin>

<term>To mow the moss</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄμνιον θείρειν</note>. This was usually said when someone still tender and untimely was treated too harshly, or when a profit was taken before it was opportune. It is drawn from those who, as soon as a field begins to be covered with grass, mow it down and do not allow the sprout to grow. For <term>mnion</term> <note>original Greek: μνίον</note> means moss, and with the addition of a letter it becomes <term>amnion</term> <note>original Greek: ἄμνιον</note>, just as <term>asachys</term> is used for <term>stachys</term> <note>an ear of corn</note>.

->It's raining sausages.<-
<margin>LXIX</margin>

<term>It's raining sausages</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀλασιν ὕει</note>. That is, it rains Lucanian sausages. A proverbial expression for a prodigious abundance of things, since this term still persists among the common folk. For <term>allas</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλᾶς</note> is a type of entrail for the Greeks, from which sausages are made by stuffing them with chopped pieces. This kind of food seems to have passed into a comic joke, from which the vile and despised <term>sausage-sellers</term> <note>original Greek: ἀλλαντοπῶλαι</note> are called so in the adage. Related is the phrase <term>the hailing drachma</term> <note>original Greek: δραχμὴ χαλαζῶσα</note>.

->To some a tongue, to others teeth.<-
<margin>LXX</margin>

<term>To some a tongue, to others teeth</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄλλοισι γλῶττ’ ἄλλοισιν εἰσὶ γόμφιοι</note>. That is:
*To these a tongue, but to those in turn there are molars.*
It is usually said of the talkative and the gluttonous. Just as it often happens at banquets, while some are babbling and intent on stories rather than food, others meanwhile are silent and strenuously devouring what has been set before them. It will be more elegant if it is twisted a little further, as if someone were to threaten...

# THIRD CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY

...to do harm to him who has merely offended with words. Poets have a tongue with which they may attack, but princes have molars with which they may crush them.

-> The counsel of the wicked falls into the extreme evil. <-
### LXXIII
<margin>73</margin>
"At length the arrow of evil reaches the extreme point." <note>original Greek: Απλῶς ῆκε κακοῦ βελή πῶς ὑπο' γ' ακρη ἄτλω.</note> That is,
The wicked mind at last falls into the ultimate punishment.
A proverbial heroic verse directed at one who, after sinning with impunity for a long time, finally falls into calamity, so that he pays the penalty for all his crimes at once.

-> The owl sounds one way, the crow another. <-
### LXXIIII
<margin>74</margin>
"The owl utters one sound, the crow another." <note>original Greek: Αλλο γλαὺξ ἄλλο κορώνη φθέγγεται.</note> That is, the owl sounds one way, the crow sounds another. Or, "One is the voice of the owl, another the voice of the crow." This can be applied either to those who contend with people far superior to them, or to those between whom there is no agreement because of a conflict in character and disposition. It can also apply when one person is far more eloquent than another. For just as you can distinguish a bird by its song even if you do not see it, so a different style reveals a person’s <gloss>individual constitution</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἰδιοκρασίαν</note> and <unclear>personal character</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἰδιομαρζίαν</note>. For there is no class of authors where you will not find certain known and counterfeit works mixed in with the <term>genuine ones</term> <note>original Greek: τοῖς γνησίοις</note>. Anyone can attach a false title to a work. However, the diction itself—which is almost never exactly the same between two people—either reveals or rejects the author.

-> To find a crack. <-
### LXXV
<margin>75</margin>
Plautus used this proverbial figure in his play *Curculio*: "You will find some crack." It is used against those who make excuses and evasions, who cannot be bound by any bonds of faith in any case without finding some way to slip out. Similarly, Horace says: "Add a hundred chains, yet this wicked Proteus will escape these bonds." The metaphor is drawn from captured birds or mice.

-> I am kneading white bread for you. <-
### LXXVI
<margin>76</margin>
"I knead or prepare white bread for you." <note>original Greek: λευκὴν μᾶζαν φυρῶ</note>. This was usually said when someone offers great hopes of grand things. For <term>maza</term> <note>a Greek term for a barley-cake or simple bread</note> is a type of bread. Furthermore, Lucian testifies in several places that white bread was a luxury for the Greeks, specifically in his pamphlet *On Salaried Posts*: "Not even in a dream was he ever sated with white bread." <note>original Greek: οὗδ' ὄναρ λευκοῦ ποτε ἄρτου ἐμφορηθείς</note>. And Saint Jerome, in his letter to Nepotian, lists similar luxuries. He asks, "What does it profit to avoid oil and seek out certain troubles and difficulties in food, such as dried figs, pepper, nuts of the palm trees <note>dates</note>, fine flour, honey, and pistachios?" Pliny, in his eighteenth book, chapter eleven, is a witness that there were not even any bakers in Rome until the war with Perseus, more than five hundred and eighty years after the city’s founding; there he shows several methods of bread prepared by art. Furthermore, the first product of wheat flour is whiter; conversely, what is last produced from barley is whiter, as Aristotle indicates in his *Problems*, Section 21, problems 8 and 7, where he gives the reason for this. The Greeks called more elegant breads <term>white</term> <note>original Greek: λευκοὺς</note> and the coarser ones <term>gray</term> <note>original Greek: φαιούς</note>, that is, dusky or black. Thus Alexis says in a fragment preserved by Athenaeus in his third book:
> Eight white loaves, and then an equal number of dark ones.

To this belongs the saying, "They devour black bread with yesterday's broth." In the same place, a rather witty story is told about Diogenes the Cynic: when he was eating a cake, and someone asked what he was eating, he replied that he was eating "well-made bread." It seemed worthwhile to add this so that we might understand that in ancient times there were wonderful delicacies in the preparation of breads. In the fourth book of the same author, an Attic banquet is described in which breads are mentioned that were "whiter than snow." <note>original Greek: λευκότεροι χιόν@</note>.

-> You take a wife of white linen for the sake of profit. <-
### LXXVII
<margin>77</margin>
"You take a wife of white linen for the sake of gain." <note>original Greek: λευκάλινον λίνον κέρδους ἕκατι</note>. This fits a man who, for the sake of a dowry, marries someone either deformed or an old woman. Furthermore, he calls the wife "linen," either because in ancient times only women used linen garments, or because she is bound to the husband in marriage and ceases to be free. For the Greeks sometimes use the word <term>linon</term> <note>linen or thread</note> for a bond or chain. <term>White-armed</term> <note>original Greek: λευκάλινος / λευκώλενος</note> was an epithet for Juno in Homer, referring to her white forearms. This is recorded by Diogenianus.

-> To the wild goats. <-
### LXXVIII
<margin>78</margin>
"Against the wild goats." <note>original Greek: Κατ' αἶγας ἀγρίας</note>. This is the speech of one who feels loathing and prays against evil, turning it away toward the wild goats. It is similar to what is said elsewhere, "to the fire" <note>original Greek: εἶς πύρραν</note>. Also that phrase: "May such feasts happen to our enemies." Athenaeus used this adage in the second book of his *Deipnosophistae*: "For they used to say..."

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the page is the Greek word "ὥσπερ" (hosper), meaning "just as."</meta>

<summary>Erasmus explores several Greek and Latin adages concerning the inevitability of justice for the wicked, the unique "voice" or style of different authors, and social metaphors involving bread and linen to describe luxury and marriage for profit.</summary>
<keywords>divine justice, literary style, white bread, ancient diet, dowry hunters, curses, Pliny, Aristotle, Diogenes the Cynic</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM: ADAGES

...as if sending us off to the wild goats <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ εἰς αἶγας ἡμᾶς ἀγρίας ἀποπέμπων</note> as if we were seekers; for Myrtilius asserted <note>original Latin: Nam Myrtilius asserebat</note> that Hegesandrus of Delphi, in his commentaries, made mention of this expression. He used "To the wild goats" to signify something that is extremely difficult to find, or which exists nowhere at all. For he had cited testimony from an author which Plutarch soon denies can be found in that writer's work. I believe Apuleius alluded to this proverb in *The Golden Ass*, when he imagines Psyche being sent by Venus to the "wild rams."

<margin>70</margin>
->May the blessed gods be present.<-
<note>original Greek: Σὺν δὲ θεοὶ μάκαρσίν</note> That is,
May the happy ones above be present.
This is the speech of one offering a good omen when embarking upon some task. For the rhapsodes <term>Rhapsodes: professional performers of Homeric poetry</term>—that is, the reciters and interpreters of Homeric poems—were accustomed to speak in this way. It was also the custom for cithara players <term>Citharoedis: professional singers who accompanied themselves on the cithara, a type of lyre</term> when about to sing to invoke Apollo with a song so that he might be favorably present, saying: "At length, hail greatly, O King" <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ ἄναξ μάλα χαῖρε</note>. Furthermore, those about to write a will would say a preface for the sake of the omen: "May this be well" <note>original Greek: ὅπερ καλῶς ἔσω</note>. Likewise among the Romans, the dictator, when heading to an assembly, used a similar prayer, that what he was about to say might be happy and favorable for the Republic. This is recorded in Zenodotus.

<margin>71</margin>
->In Aphannae.<-
<note>original Greek: Εἰς ἀφάννας</note> That is, in Aphannae. Stephanus relates that Aphannae is some place in Sicily that is exceedingly obscure and ignoble, from which the name itself appears to be derived <note>The name is related to the Greek word 'aphanes,' meaning 'invisible' or 'hidden'</note>. From this arose the proverb "Or in Aphannae" <note>original Greek: ἢ εἰς ἀφάννας</note>, used for uncertain things and those which are nowhere to be found. Zenodotus says it arose from an incident of this kind: The Sybarites once approached the oracle, praying that victory over the Crotonians be granted to them, and this in the presence of the Crotonians themselves. One of the Crotonians responded in jest after this fashion: "You shall indeed achieve that—in Aphannae." The Sybarite, believing this was a response from the god, wondered what this word "Aphannae" meant. The proverb, he says, fits those who think they are invincible and unbearable. But to me, Stephanus’s interpretation is more approved.

<margin>72</margin>
->For what was necessary.<-
<note>original Greek: Εἰς τὸ δέον</note> That is, "for that which was a requirement." One must understand the word "I spent" or something similar. For they say this comes from a speech by Pericles. They relate that he, by giving money, persuaded Astyanax the king of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, who was already preparing for war, to depart from Attica. Later, when Pericles was rendering the accounts of that money to the people, and was ashamed to speak openly about the purpose for which the money was spent, he signified it covertly, saying: "I spent so many talents for what was necessary" <note>original Greek: ἀνήλωσα τοσαῦτα τάλαντα εἰς τὸ δέον</note>. These things are generally recounted by Zenodotus. Aristophanes also mentions the adage in *The Clouds*:
"Just as Pericles, I lost it on what was required." <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ περικλέης εἰς τὸ δέον ἀπώλεσα</note>
In that passage, the commentator brings forward various stories from which they think the proverb arose; if anyone seeks these, we have shown where they can be found. It can be elegantly twisted as a joke against those who have managed someone else's money in such a way that they cannot give a proper account of it.

<margin>73</margin>
->An induced oath.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἐπακτὸς ὅρκος</note> That is, it was called an "induced" or "imported" oath, either because it was not native but foreign and brought in from elsewhere, as Zenodotus indicates—such as if a Greek were to swear in the Scythian manner: "By the wind and the scimitar" <note>original Greek: νὴ τὸν ἀκινάκην ἢ νὴ τὸν ἄνεμον</note>. For every nation is accustomed to swear by its own gods. Or, it refers to an oath that is not spontaneous but "induced" by force. Or, it is an oath undertaken of one's own accord with no one compelling them, if we believe Suidas and the *Etymologicum*. For there are three kinds of swearing: one which they call *epōmoton* <term>an oath taken to confirm a statement</term>, another *katōmoton* <term>a binding or affirmative oath</term>, and finally the *epakton*. Hesychius, on the other hand, says it is "that to which another person drives you, not something spontaneous." <note>original Greek: ἐφ’ ὃν ἕτερός ἀγεῖ, οὐκ αὐθαίρετος</note> I personally would not have included this among the adages had not Zenodotus first placed it on this list.

<margin>74</margin>
->Rougher than a sloughed skin.<-
<note>original Greek: Κυνηρότερος λεβερίδος</note> That is, harsher than a *leberis*. Used for things that are exceedingly rough and unpleasant. *Leberis* is the Greek name for that cast-off skin <note>slough</note> of either snakes or fish that shed their "old age," which is also called *syphar* <note>original Greek: σύφαρ</note>. It is well known that this is extremely rough, surely on account of its extreme dryness. This is recorded by Suidas.

<summary>This page catalogs several ancient Greek proverbs collected by Erasmus, covering themes of obscurity ("In Aphannae"), political evasion ("For what was necessary"), and the nature of ritual oaths and physical textures.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Pericles, political bribery, Sybarites, ancient oaths, Greek etymology, Aphannae, Plutarch, Aristophanes</keywords>

--- Page 803 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus's compilation of proverbs, moving from general prayers and omens into metaphors for character, business ethics, and geographical wonders. It continues the "Third Thousand, Second Century" of his massive collection of ancient wisdom.</meta>

### 84. May the news stay far from my ears.

<note>original Latin: Procul auribus nuncius ueniat</note>
<note>original Greek: Απ' ὤατ' ἄγγελο' ἔλθοι</note> That is, "May the messenger stay far from the ear."
This is the speech of someone praying to avert an ill-omened messenger. Suidas <term>Suidas: a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia and lexicon, now usually called the Suda</term> cites this from Callimachus. Homer also uses it in the eighteenth book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original Greek: Αἲ γὰρ δή μοι ἀφ' ὤατο' ὧδε γένοιτο</note> That is,
"I would wish those things to be far from my ears."

---

### 85. Pure water flows from a pure source.

<note>original Latin: A puro pura defluit aqua</note>
Theognis <term>Theognis: a Greek elegiac poet of the 6th century BCE</term> says in his moral verses:
<note>original Greek: Εἴ μ' ἐθέλεις πλύνειν, κεφαλῆς ἀμίαντον ἀπ' ἄκρης / Αἰεὶ λευκὸν ὕδωρ ῥεύσεται ἡμετέρης.</note> That is,
"Clear water will flow down again from the very top of my head, if you should perhaps prepare to wash one who is innocent."
We have included this couplet because it seemed to contain a proverb. It will apply to a man who is entirely blameless and innocent; even if someone occasionally brings a charge against him, his reputation is not only untarnished but is rendered even more illustrious. Not without reason do they credit this praise to Cato the Censor <term>Cato the Censor: a Roman statesman known for his rigid morality</term>: though he was accused and summoned to court so many times—forty-four times, to be precise—he was always acquitted by the verdicts of the judges.

---

### 86. From a wolf-hunt.

<note>original Latin: A lupi uenatu</note>
<note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ λύκου θήρας</note> That is, "From a wolf-hunt." It was usually said when someone departs immediately with the business unfinished, or concerning a troublesome and rough piece of work. For it is neither safe to pursue a wolf, nor is it easily captured, whereas the hunting of other wild beasts brings no common pleasure. Suidas mentions this.

---

### 87. From a ship entering harbor.

<note>original Latin: A subeunte portum naui</note>
<note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ καταδυομένης</note> That is, "Taking profit from a [ship] putting in." The adage warns that speed is of the greatest value for gain. This applies especially to a businessman: "Let sleep be absent" <note>original Greek: ὕπνο' ἀπέστω</note>. It is taken from the diligence of merchants who buy merchandise immediately from the sailors themselves as they put into port. For then, goods are bought for less and sold for a greater profit. It can be drawn toward the sentiment that if any opportunity for gain is offered, it must be seized at once. Or, it suggests that one should ask a favor of someone just when fortune has presented them with some fresh advantage. For most of us are then more inclined toward being generous. Persius, in his fifth Satire, varied the metaphor when he said:
> Be the first to take the fresh pepper from the thirsting camel.
<note>original Latin: Tolle recens primus piper ē fitiente camelo</note>

That is, do it immediately, while the camel that brought the goods is still thirsty from the journey. Suidas mentions the proverb.

---

### 88. From twice seven waves.

<note>original Latin: A bis septem undis</note>
<note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ δὶς ἑπτὰ κυμάτων</note> That is, "From twice seven waves." This applies to those who have been purified of some stain, because in ancient times it was the custom for those polluted by homicide to wash their clothes with seven immersions or soakings. Suidas is the witness.

---

### 89. He even demands flour from statues.

<note>original Latin: Exigit & à statuis farinas</note>
<note>original Greek: Αἰτεῖ καὶ σὺν ἀνδριάντας ἄλφιτα</note> That is,
"He truly demands food even from the statues themselves."
This should be said against a man who, pitying no one, tears away whatever he can from anywhere, even from the very statues of the dead. It is very similar to that other saying: "And you collect tribute from a corpse" <note>original Greek: κἀπὸ νεκρῶ φορᾶς</note>. It applies to princes who plunder the common people, squeezing a tax out of everything—even from urine—or to greedy priests, among whom not even a grave is granted for free.

---

### 90. Athos hides the sides of the Lemnian cow.

<note>original Latin: Athos celat latera Lemniæ bouis</note>
<note>original Greek: Ἄθως καλύπτει πλευρὰ λημνίας βοός</note> That is,
"Athos overshadows the sides of the Lemnian cow."
Used when someone gets in the way, or is troublesome, or obscures another's glory, or otherwise stands in opposition. They say there was a huge statue of a cow in Lemnos made of white stone. Mount Athos, although separated by a long distance, nevertheless obscures it with its shadow because of its extreme height. Athos is a massive mountain in Thrace, so large that it casts a shadow for three hundred stadia <term>Stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</term>, according to Stephanus. Apollonius mentions this in the first book of the *Argonautica*:
> As they sailed, the Thracian peak of Athos rose up, which stands as far off from Lemnos as a well-equipped galley could travel by dawn.
<note>original Greek: Ἐν δὲ νιοσομένοισιν ἄθω ἀνέτελλε κολώνη...</note>

<vocab>Suidas, Callimachus, Homer, Theognis, Cato the Censor, Persius, Apollonius of Rhodes, Mount Athos, Lemnos, Adages, Erasmus</vocab>

<summary>This page catalogs proverbs 84 through 90, covering topics such as avoiding bad news, the resilience of an innocent reputation (notably Cato the Censor), business opportunism, and the literal and metaphorical shadows cast by greatness.</summary>
<keywords>innocence, Cato the Censor, greed, taxation, Mount Athos, merchant diligence, purification, Greek poetry, ancient customs</keywords>

680
DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### The highest peak of the shadow, even as far as Myrina.

<note>original Greek: Ἀκροτάτη κορυφῇ σκιᾶς, καὶ ἂν ἄχρι μυρίνης</note> That is:
> At the rising of the sun, for those cutting the false shallows,
> Athos shows itself with its high peak, a Thracian mountain, which,
> Separated from sacred Lemnos by so great a distance
> As a winged ship can cross in a day:
> Yet the shadow of its airy peak touches this place.
> Indeed, it even reaches as far as distant Myrina.

Plutarch mentions this proverb in his *Moralia*, specifically in the commentary he titled *On the Face Which Appears in the Orb of the Moon*, testifying that the shadow stretches for seven hundred stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters; 700 stadia is about 80 miles.</note>. The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts</note> on Theocritus cites this verse from Sophocles:
<note>original Greek: Αἰθὼ σκιὰ ζῆ νῶτα λημνίας ἁλός</note> That is:
"The shadow of Athos grazes the back of the Lemnian sea."

<margin>90</margin> **Milk the one at hand; why do you pursue the one fleeing?**
<note>original Greek: τὴν παροῦσαν ἄμελγε, τί τὸν φεύγοντα διώκεις;</note> That is:
"Milk the present one, why do you follow the one that runs away?"
A proverbial heroic line advising that present profit should not be let go in the hope of advantages that do not seem to be equally at hand. It is taken from Theocritus’s *Cyclops*. The Scholiast cites a verse from Hesiod of similar sentiment:
<note>original Greek: νήπιος ὃς τὰ ἕτοιμα λιπὼν τ' ἀνέτοιμα διώκει</note> That is:
"Foolish is he who, leaving what is ready, pursues what is not."
He considers this to have the same meaning as what we have said elsewhere: <term>τὸν θέλοντα βίῳ ἐλαύνειν</term> <note>original: "to drive one's life as one wishes"—referring to managing one's own affairs practically.</note>.

<margin>90</margin> 
## What has this to do with Mercury?
<note>original Greek: Τί πρὸς τὸν ἑρμῶ;</note> That is: "What to Mercury?" This is the same as that other saying, <term>οὐδὲν πρὸς ἔπος</term> <note>Nothing to the purpose</note>, and "Nothing to Bacchus," meaning "Nothing to the point." For Mercury is the author of speech <note>As the messenger god, Mercury/Hermes presided over eloquence and communication</note>. These apply to those who say things foreign to the business being conducted.

<margin>91</margin> 
## Why do you judge the Achaeans from the tower?
<note>original Greek: Τί οὖν ἀχαιοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ πύργου κείνεται;</note> That is:
"Why do you judge the Greeks from the walls?"
This will be appropriate to say whenever someone pronounces judgment on a matter without sufficiently accurate consideration. Aristides says of Themistocles: <term>τί ταῦτα τοῖς ἀχαιοῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ πύργου κείνομεθα;</term> <note>Why in these matters do we judge the Greeks from the tower?</note> It appears to be taken from the third book of the *Iliad*, in the place where Priam, on the walls of Troy, asks Helen (who had been summoned) who those men were whom he could see far off in the Greek army. He praises Agamemnon’s appearance in this manner:
<note>original Greek: ος τις ὅδ᾿ ἐστιν ἀχαιὸς ἀνὴρ ἠΰς τε μέγας τε; / Η τοι μὲν κεφαλῇ καὶ μέίζονες ἄλλοι ἔασιν, / Καλὸν δ᾿ οὕτω ἐγὼν οὕπω ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσιν, / Οὐδ᾿ οὕτω γεραρόν, βασιλῆϊ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἔοικεν.</note> That is:
> Who is that man, tell me, that Greek man, both great and good?
> There are others, I confess, who surpass him in height by a head.
> But truly, I never remember seeing one so handsome with my eyes,
> Nor so venerable; he seems like a kingly man.

This can also be aptly turned against those who, standing in safety, pass judgment on those who are in the midst of danger. Just as those who, sitting idle on a tower or a rampart, watch and judge those fighting, and find fault in many for a lack of courage or wisdom—though they themselves would by no means stand firm if they were in the same peril. Aristides in *Themistocles* says: "It is not the same thing for someone with his foot in a ship in the middle of the sea to speak of courage, as it is for those sitting far from the storm between walls."

<margin>92</margin> 
## What use is a rotten onion?
<note>original Greek: Τίς χρεία πυθομένης κρομμύης;</note> That is: "What use for a putrefied onion?" Said of rejected things, or even of men who are worthless and of no use anywhere. For although the onion is a plant most useful in itself, as soon as it has rotted, nothing can be more contemptible. This is kin to that line of Plautus: "Not worth a spoiled nut."

<margin>93</margin> 
## Not Philoxenus’s.
<note>original Greek: Τὸ Φιλοξένου</note> That is: "Philoxenus’s no." To be said when someone obstinately either denies or...

<meta>catchword: cu</meta>

<summary>This page explores proverbs regarding physical and metaphorical perspectives, including the famous shadow of Mt. Athos and the folly of judging others' struggles from a position of safety (the "tower"). It emphasizes practical wisdom, such as valuing present gains over uncertain future ones.</summary>
<keywords>Mount Athos, Lemnos, Theocritus, Plutarch, Homer, Iliad, Agamemnon, Priam, Mercury, Aristides, courage, perspective, Philoxenus</keywords>

--- Page 805 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of Greek and Roman adages, moving from political behavior (the poet Philoxenus and the tyrant Dionysius) to metaphors for irrelevant speech, the ease of vice, and the inevitable decay caused by time. It completes the second "century" (group of one hundred) of the third "chiliad" (thousand) of his collection.</meta>

...accuses: or where someone does not know how to yield to another, nor speak anything to please. This kind of person should stay away from the company of princes, in whose presence one must either keep silent or say what is pleasing to the ears. The poet Philoxenus <note>Philoxenus of Cythera (c. 435–380 BCE) was a celebrated Greek dithyrambic poet who was famously imprisoned in the stone quarries by the tyrant Dionysius I of Syracuse for criticizing the ruler's bad poetry.</note>, as we have said elsewhere, was so unable to approve of Dionysius’s poems that he preferred to be taken back to the stone quarries.

### I weave my own clusters.
->XCVI<-

<note>original Greek: τοὺς ἐμοὺς κορύμβους πλέκω</note> That is, *I weave my own curls* <note>The word "corymbos" can refer to clusters of ivy berries or a specific hairstyle where hair is pulled into a top-knot.</note>. This is used when someone gives an answer that has nothing to do with what was asked. It is related in this manner: "Greetings, Hypsipyle." "I am weaving my clusters." "I am not speaking to you about that. Is my husband here?" <note>Erasmus is quoting a lost comedic fragment where a character ignores a greeting to talk about their own task.</note> It appears to be taken from some passage of a comedy in which a character, through feigned ignorance, gives a completely different answer. 

This is the same kind of thing found in Terence’s *Phormio*, when Phaedria, asked where on earth Antipho might be, responds by repeating the greeting and then simply saying he is doing well. There is a similar passage in Plautus’s *The Merchant*: "Now the sword is in my hand. For if I lead you in there... I’ll take the flask and go from here," and so forth. For the passage is too long to be reviewed here without causing boredom. It is close to what we reviewed elsewhere: *He asks for buckets* <note>A proverb for responding with something irrelevant.</note>.

### Wickedness is a shortcut.
->XCVII<-

<note>original Greek: Σύντομος ἡ πονηρία, βραδεῖα ἡ ἀρετή</note> That is, *Wickedness is a shortcut, virtue is a long road.* He who has once surrendered his mind to vices will easily commit any kind of crime. But individual virtues must be acquired with great sweat. And it happens, by some corruption of nature, that we immediately seize upon things that are shameful as if we were "self-taught" <note>original Greek: αὐτοδίδακτα</note>; whereas things that are honorable are scarcely instilled even by long-lasting labors. Plutarch, in his *Sayings of Kings and Commanders*, attributes this quote to Cleomenes <note>Cleomenes III, a reformist King of Sparta.</note>. When a certain pirate had made an incursion into Spartan territory and, once captured, said he had done it because he had nothing with which to feed his soldiers, and therefore turned to those who had a surplus and did not share, Cleomenes said: "Wickedness is a shortcut."

### A shadow instead of the body.
->XCVIII<-

<note>original Greek: Σκιὰ ἀντὶ τοῦ σώματος</note> *A shadow instead of the body.* This is used whenever someone seems to have achieved something great, when in the end they take away nothing but a title or mere hopes. It is borrowed from Aesop's fable about the dog who, while trying to grab the shadow of the meat because it appeared larger, lost the real meat. A certain Gabrias <note>Referring to Babrius, the writer of Aesopic fables in verse.</note> composed this in iambic verse in this way:

> A dog carrying meat near a flowing river,
> Looking into the water, saw another dog like himself.
> Opening his mouth to take the meat below,
> He was deprived of that which he held before.

->that is:<-

> While a dog carries meat next to a flowing stream,
> He catches sight of another as he bows his head in the river,
> Gaping downward so that he might seize those meats,
> He lost also those which he held before.

### You play the Sinopian.
->XCIX<-

<note>original Greek: Σινωπίζεις</note> That is, *You play the Sinopian*, meaning you are licentious or wanton. This comes from Sinope, a certain noble courtesan celebrated for her wantonness, whose name seems to have been given to her because she had "harmful eyes" <note>A play on words suggesting her gaze was dangerous or captivating.</note>. Athenaeus, in his fifteenth book, teaches that she was from Aegina. There was also a Sinope, daughter of Asopus <note>Erasmus writes "Aesopi," but likely means the river god Asopus.</note>, to whom nothing was dearer than her virginity.

### Lengthy time decays even stone.
->C<-

<note>original Greek: Σήπει καὶ πέτρην ὁ πολὺς χρόνος</note> That is,
*Even rocks will the long passage of time cause to rot.*
Nothing in the nature of things is more durable than stone. Yet the length of time consumes even that. This is surely what the poets mean when they imagine that Saturn <note>The Roman god identified with Chronos, or Time.</note>, the god of time, devoured a stone that had been put in the place of Jupiter. Ovid says in the fourth book of *Letters from the Black Sea*:

> The drop hollows the stone, the ring is worn away by use,
> The curved plowshare is rubbed thin by the pressed earth.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
## THIRD THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY

### The Sileni of Alcibiades.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, holding a staff or instrument, surrounded by ornate foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc> The "Sileni of Alcibiades" <note>This refers to a famous passage in Plato's *Symposium* where the character Alcibiades compares Socrates to these statues.</note> have passed into a proverb among the learned; certainly, they are recorded as a proverb in the Greek collections. It is used for anything that appears cheap and, as they say, ridiculous at first glance, but which, upon closer and more internal contemplation, proves to be admirable. It also applies to a person who, in appearance and manner, shows far less than what he hides within his soul. For they say that the "Sileni" were certain small, carved figurines made in such a way that they could be opened up and unfolded. When closed, they had the ridiculous and monstrous appearance of a flute-player; but when opened, they suddenly revealed a deity, so that a humorous trick might make the sculptor's art more pleasing. The theme for these statues was taken from that ridiculous Silenus, the tutor of Bacchus <note>In Greek mythology, Silenus was the fat, drunken, but wise companion and tutor of the wine-god Dionysius/Bacchus.</note>, who was a kind of "divine fool" for the poets. Since even the poets, following the example of our own princes, have their own <term>laughter-makers <note>original Greek: γελωτοποιός (gelōtopoiós)</note></term>.

Accordingly, in the fifth book of Athenaeus, the young man Critobulus, mocking the elderly and deformed Socrates, said that he was <term>uglier than the Sileni <note>original Greek: τοῖς σιληνοῖς ἀρχιω (tois silēnois archiō)</note></term>. This passage is also found in Xenophon’s *Symposium*. Socrates says: <margin><term>For you boast as if you were more beautiful <note>original Greek: ὡς γὰρ κατ’ ὤψ ἦσαν κομπαζής (hōs gar kat’ ōps ēsan kompazēs)</note></term></margin> "As if you are boasting as if you were more beautiful." Critobulus responds: <margin><term>By Jove, I would be the ugliest of all the Sileni in the Satyr plays <note>original Greek: νη Δία, ἢ πάντων σιληνῶν τῶν ἐν τοῖς σατυρικοῖς, αἴχιστος ἂν εἴην (nē Dia, ē pantōn silēnōn tōn en tois satyrikois, aichistos an eiēn)</note></term></margin> "By Jove, I would be the most shameful of all the Sileni who appear in the Satyr plays."

And Alcibiades, in Plato’s *Symposium*, about to deliver a praise of Socrates, makes him similar to those very Sileni, because he was something far different to one looking inside than he appeared to be in his outer habit and appearance. If anyone had judged him by his "outer skin," as the saying goes, he wouldn't have bought him for a penny. His face was rustic, with a bull-like gaze, and his nostrils were snub and full of mucus. You would have called him some dull and stupid clown. His dress was neglected, his speech simple, common, and humble, as he always had wagoners, cobblers, fullers, and blacksmiths on his lips. For it was from these sources that he usually drew his <term>analogies <note>original Greek: εἰκαγωγὰς (eikagōgas)</note></term> with which he pressed his points in debate. His fortune was meager, and his wife was of a sort that not even the most patient charcoal-burner could endure. He liked to admire the beauty of youths; he seemed to love them and be touched by jealousy, yet Alcibiades discovered he was entirely free from those <term>passions which all experience <note>original Greek: οἷς οἷα πασῶν (hois hoia pasōn)</note></term>.

In short, his perpetual joking gave him the appearance of a fool. At that time, while the ambition to profess wisdom raged like madness among fools, and there was no shortage of men like Gorgias <note>A famous Greek sophist who claimed to be able to answer any question.</note> who boasted they knew everything—and while everywhere was crowded with busybodies of this sort—this man alone repeatedly said he knew nothing, except that he knew he knew nothing. He seemed inept for all duties of the state; for instance, having tried one day to address the people, he was laughed off the stage.

But if you had "opened" this ridiculous Silenus, you would indeed have found a deity rather than a man: a soul vast, sublime, and truly philosophical. He was a despiser of all those things for which other mortals run, sail, sweat, litigate, and go to war. He was superior to all injuries, a man over whom fortune had no power at all. He was so fearless that he even despised death, which is dreaded by everyone. He drank the poison with the same expression he usually wore when drinking wine. Even as he was dying—as we see in the *Phaedo*—he reminded his friends to pay a debt, a cock for Asclepius <note>Socrates' famous last words. Asclepius was the god of healing; Socrates suggests that death is a "cure" for the sickness of life.</note>, as if, having received the medicine, he already felt the benefit of health as he was leaving the body, where all diseases of the soul swarm and sprout.

Therefore, not without cause, when everything was full of sophists in that age, this "fool" alone was pronounced wise by the oracle. He was judged to know more because he knew he knew nothing, than those who proclaimed they knew everything. Indeed, for that very reason, he was judged to know the most: because he alone of all men knew he knew nothing.

Antisthenes <note>A pupil of Socrates and founder of the Cynic school.</note> was a Silenus of this kind; with his staff, bag, and cloak, he surpassed the fortunes of the greatest kings. Diogenes <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the most famous Cynic, who lived in a tub.</note> was a Silenus of this kind, commonly considered a "dog." But Alexander the Great, the <term>leader <note>original Greek: κορυφαῖος (koryphaios)</note></term> and "Alpha" of all princes, noticed something divine in this "dog." Marvelling at his greatness of soul, Alexander said that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes—though Diogenes' soul had to endure much more because he *was* Alexander. Epictetus <note>A Stoic philosopher who was born a slave and lived in extreme poverty.</note> was a Silenus of this kind: a slave, poor, and lame (as his epitaph indicates), but at the same time—which is the greatest happiness—dear to the gods above. This is what integrity of life joined with wisdom provides. For this is the nature of truly honorable things: whatever excellence they possess, they hide and bury deep within; what is most contemptible, they carry on the surface, like a treasure hidden in a cheap shell...

# THIRD THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY 653

...they hide, nor do they show them to profane eyes. But the nature of common and superficial things is far different; they charm with a great appearance, and whatever they have that is most beautiful, they immediately display to those they meet. If you look deep within, they are nothing less than what they claimed to be by title and appearance. 

Was Christ not a kind of marvelous Silenus? If it is permitted to speak of him in this way—and indeed, I do not see why all who glory in the name of Christian should not strive to express this to the best of their ability. If you look at the outer face of this Silenus, what is more abject or more contemptible according to popular estimation? Lowly and obscure parents, a humble home; he himself was poor and had few, and very poor, disciples; he did not summon them from the palaces of the great, nor from the chairs of the Pharisees, nor from the schools of the philosophers, but from the tax office and from fishing nets. Then his life, how far removed from all pleasures! Through hunger, through weariness, through insults, through mockery, reaching finally even to the cross. It is in this state that the mystic prophet contemplates him when describing him: "He had no form," he says, "nor beauty. We saw him, and there was no sightly appearance; and we desired him, despised, and the last of men." <note>original: Isaiah 53:2-3. Erasmus quotes the Latin Vulgate here to show how the Messiah’s humble appearance was prophesied.</note> And many other things follow in this same vein. 

Now, if it should happen that this Silenus is seen open and closer—that is, if he himself deigns to show himself to one with cleansed eyes of the mind—immortal God, what an ineffable treasure you will find! In such usefulness, what a pearl! In such humility, what sublimity! In such poverty, what riches! In such weakness, what unthinkable power! In such ignominy, what glory! In such labors, what absolute rest! Finally, in a death so bitter, a perennial fountain of immortality. 

Why do they shrink so from this image, those who nevertheless boast of his title? Surely it was easy for Christ to seize the monarchy of the whole world, and to possess that which the Roman princes once sought in vain: to surpass Xerxes in guards, to exceed Croesus in wealth, to impose silence on all philosophers, and to strip away their empty title of "wise man." But this one form pleased him, which he would propose to his disciples and friends, that is, to Christians. He chose this philosophy above all, far and wide different from the decrees of philosophers and from the logic of the world, but the one that alone excelled all others in achieving what others try to attain by different paths: namely, happiness. 

Of this kind were the prophets of old: exiles, wandering in solitudes, spending their lives with wild beasts, living on cheap vegetables, clothed in the skins of sheep and goats. But he who said that "the world was not worthy of them" <note>original: Hebrews 11:38.</note> had looked inside these Sileni. John the Baptist was a Silenus of this kind, who, covered in camel hair and girded with a leather belt, far surpassed the purple robes and gems of kings; eating locusts, he excelled the delicacies of all princes. Surely he who, encompassing the sum of his praises in that wonderful eulogy, said: "Among those born of women, there has not risen a greater than John the Baptist," <note>original: Matthew 11:11.</note> saw what treasure lay hidden under that rustic cloak. 

The apostles were Sileni of this kind: poor, unrefined, illiterate, ignoble, weak, abject, exposed to all the insults of all men, mocked, useless, accursed, and almost the public object of both the hatred and the mockery of the world. But open the Silenus for me: which of the tyrants can be compared with their power, they who command demons with a word, calm the raging seas with a nod, and restore the dead to life with a word? Which Croesus would not seem poor compared to these men, who bring health to the sick even by their shadow, who impart that heavenly spirit by the touch of a hand alone? Which Aristotle would not seem a fool, unlearned, and a trifler when compared with these men, who speak from the very fountain? Let it be said with the peace of those who consider it a crime and impious to ever pull down the authority of Aristotle. I confess that he was a man of extraordinary learning, but what light is so excellent that it is not obscured when compared to Christ? 

Then indeed the Kingdom of Heaven had the image of a mustard seed, small and contemptible in appearance, but greatest in power—from which, as I said, the logic of this world is entirely and <term>diametrically <note>original Greek: ἐκ διαμέτρου (ek diametrou). A technical term for things that are polar opposites.</note></term>, as they say, at odds. Of this kind was that despised and mocked Bishop Martin. <note>Saint Martin of Tours (c. 316–397), a saint famous for his extreme humility and simple lifestyle despite his high rank.</note> Such were those ancient bishops, sublime in humility, rich in poverty, glorious in their neglect of glory. And today some good Sileni lie hidden, but alas, too few. A good part of men represent a "backward Silenus." <note>Erasmus uses this to describe the "Inverted Silenus": people who look magnificent and holy on the outside but are empty or corrupt within.</note> If anyone looks deep into the force and nature of things, he will find that none are further from true wisdom than those who, with magnificent titles, with wise men's caps, with splendid belts, with jeweled rings, profess absolute wisdom. So much so that not rarely you may find more true and genuine wisdom in some "little fellow"—who according to common opinion is a simple and half-witted idiot—whose mind is enlightened not by the "subtle" Scotus <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a Scholastic philosopher known for his extremely complex and "subtle" logic, which Erasmus often found uselessly over-complicated.</note>, but by the heavenly...

<meta>catchword: ...heavenly (stis)</meta>

He contrasts the hidden power of the Apostles and early Saints with the superficial pomp of contemporary religious and academic leaders.</summary>

# 684 DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
Xxxx
<meta>catchword: citizens</meta>

...that spirit of Christ taught more than in many of those "tragic personas" of theologians, those "thrice-and-four-times" masters of ours, swollen with their Aristotle and stuffed with a crowd of "masterly" definitions, conclusions, and propositions. I would not say this of all, but of alas, too many. Likewise, you might see that in none is there less true nobility than in those braggarts <note>original: "Thrasonibus istis" – referring to Thraso, the boastful soldier from Terence’s Roman comedies.</note> who boast of supreme nobility because of old family trees, gold chains, and splendid surnames; nor are any further from true courage than those who, because of their rashness and ferocious tempers, are judged by the common people to be the bravest and "invincible." None are more abjectly or servilely slaves than those who think themselves closest to the gods, as they say, and masters of all. None are so wretched as those who seem most happy. None are more poorly "poor" than those whom the common crowd adores as rich. None are less bishops than those who hold the primary seats among bishops. 

Again and again I ask you, reader, do not think these things are said to insult anyone. We are noting the reality, not the men. We wish there were none to whom these things apply. And if there are none such now—which may Christ grant—there were such once, and perhaps will be in the future. And would that this too were false: that often those who profess absolute religion by title, dress, and ceremonies are the furthest removed from true religion. To such an extent is it true that whatever is most excellent in every kind of thing is least conspicuous. In trees, the flowers and leaves charm the eyes; the bulk of the tree shows itself broadly. But the seed, in which the power of all things resides, how tiny a thing it is, how hidden, how little it flatters the sight, how little it shows itself off! Gold and gems nature has hidden in the deepest recesses of the earth. In the "elements," as they call them, the more excellent a thing is, the further it is removed from the senses—like air and fire. In the animal kingdom, that which is best and most effective is hidden in their innermost parts. In man, that which is most divine and immortal—the soul—is the only thing that cannot be seen. In any kind of thing, the material (the cheaper part) is most exposed to the senses; the power and benefit of the form is felt through its utility, yet it remains far from the senses. Again, in the temperament of the physical body, while phlegm and blood are familiar and exposed to the senses, that which contributes most to life—namely, the spirit—is least exposed. Finally, in the universe, the things that exist most fully are not seen, such as the "separate substances" <note>This refers to angels or pure spiritual intelligences in medieval philosophy.</note>. And that which is highest among these is furthest removed from the senses: namely, God, so much so that He can neither be fully understood nor even thought of, since He is the unique source of all. 

Indeed, one might also find a certain "Image of the Sileni" in the sacraments of the Church. (Let no offense be taken at my words). You see water, you see salt and oil, you hear a voice, as if seeing the outer face of a Silenus; but the heavenly power you neither hear nor see. If that power were not present, the rest would be mere mockery. Even the secret scriptures have their own Sileni. If you stop at the surface, the matter is sometimes ridiculous; but if you penetrate through to the spiritual meaning <term>anagoge: a method of interpreting the Bible by finding its higher, spiritual or mystical meaning</term>, you would adore the divine wisdom. 

For, to speak of the Old Testament: if you look at nothing but the story and hear of Adam created from mud, a little wife stealthily taken from his sleeping side, a serpent tempting the little woman with the bait of an apple, God walking in the breeze, and a flaming sword <note>original: "romphaea" – a large sword or polearm.</note> presiding over the gates so the exiles could not return, would you not think it a fable produced from Homer’s workshop? If you read of Lot's incest, the whole story of Samson (which Saint Jerome, judging it from the "bark" <note>original: "e cortice" – Erasmus uses the image of tree bark to mean the literal, outer surface of a text.</note>, calls a fable), David's adultery, the young girl sleeping in the lap of a cold old man, or Hosea’s marriage to a prostitute—would not anyone with more modest ears turn away as if from an obscene story? But under these wrappings—immortal God!—how splendid the wisdom that lies hidden! If you judge the parables of the Gospel by their outer shell first, who would not judge them to be the work of an ignorant man? But if you break the nut, you will surely find that hidden, sharp divine wisdom, something clearly very like Christ himself. 

And lest I become too long-winded by pursuing every detail: in both nature and mystical things, you will see that whatever is most excellent is also most hidden and furthest removed from profane eyes. Likewise in knowledge, the genuine truth of things always lies deepest, and it is found neither easily nor by many. The thick-headed common crowd, because it judges perversely, estimating everything from the things that most readily meet the physical senses, constantly slips and errs, and is deluded by false images of good and evil; it admires and looks up to "inverted Sileni." I speak of the bad; I shall not hurt the good—indeed, not even the bad, since a general discussion of vices pertains to no specific person's injury. And would that there were fewer in whom these things fit! When you see a scepter, when you see the insignia, when you see the guards, when you hear the titles "Most Serene," "Most Clement," and "Illustrious," do you not adore the prince as some earthly deity, and think you are looking at something greater than a man? But open the "inverted Silenus," and you will find a tyrant, or sometimes...
