# 685 THIRD CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
Mm
<meta>catchword: marriage</meta>

...an enemy of the citizens, a hater of public peace, an expert in sowing discord, an oppressor of good men, a plague to the laws, a destroyer of cities, a plunderer of the church, a thief, a sacrilegious man, an incestuous person, a gambler—briefly, as it says in the Greek proverbs, an *Iliad of woes* <note>original: "iliada malorum" — a proverb meaning a vast or infinite amount of trouble, referring to the many disasters in Homer's Iliad.</note>. There are those who, by their title and appearance, present themselves as magistrates and as the guard of the state, when in reality they are wolves and plunderers of the city. There are those whose shaved heads you might consider a mark of priesthood; but if you look inside the Silenus <note>referring to the statues of Silenus that were ugly on the outside but contained images of gods inside; here Erasmus means looking at the inner character.</note>, you will find they are more worldly than the laity. Perhaps you might even find some bishops whose solemn consecration you might observe, or inspect their new finery—a miter shining with gems and gold, a staff likewise bejeweled. In short, seeing that whole mystical *suit of armor* <note>original Greek: "panoplian"</note> from *head to toe* <note>original Greek: "ek podos eis kephalēn" – literally "from foot to head."</note>, you might expect some heavenly being, a man greater than human. Turn the Silenus inside out, and you will sometimes find nothing but a warmonger, a merchant, or finally, a tyrant; and then you will judge those magnificent insignias to have been a stage-play. 

There are—and would that they were not so commonly met with—those whom one might judge to be Serapions and Pauls <note>referring to St. Serapion and St. Paul the Hermit, famous for their extreme asceticism in the desert.</note> if one were to judge them by the forest of their beards, their paleness, their hoods, their bowed necks, their belts, their eyebrows, and the sternness of their faces. But if you unfold them, you will find pure jesters, gluttons, imposters, debauchees, indeed plunderers and tyrants—but in another way, and I know not if this is more pestilential for being more hidden, and plainly what the saying calls *charcoal instead of treasure* <note>original Greek: "anthrakes ē thēsauros" – a proverb about finding something worthless where you expected something of value.</note>. Again I warn that no one should be offended by these things, since no one’s name is designated. If anyone is not of this kind, let him think that this does not pertain to him; but if he recognizes his own evil, let him think himself warned. Let the former congratulate himself; let the latter thank me. 

Finally, everywhere in every race of mortals, there are those who, if you contemplate the form of the body, you would call humans and distinguished humans; but if you unfold the Silenus, inside you will perhaps find a pig, or a lion, or a bear, or an ass. And something will happen contrary to what was handed down in the poets' fables about Circe's <note>The sorceress from the Odyssey who turned Odysseus's men into swine.</note> sorceries. For in her case, the beasts had the minds of humans; these men, under a human appearance, hide something more savage than a beast. On the other hand, there are those whom you would scarcely judge to be men by their appearance, as has been said, while they hide an angel in the inner chambers of their soul. 

In this, therefore, is the difference between the worldly man and the Christian: that the former admires and pursues all the coarsest things, which are immediately obvious to the eyes, while those things which are of a different nature, he either completely neglects or certainly puts in the last place. The Christian, on the contrary, pursues only those things which are least seen by the eyes and which have receded farthest from the nature of physical bodies, with the rest either passed over or treated with contempt, drawing every judgment of things from those innermost parts. Among "goods"—for so Aristotle <note>Referring to Aristotle’s classification in the Nicomachean Ethics.</note> calls them—those which do not belong properly to man, the lowest are riches. Yet among the common crowd—indeed among almost everyone—he who possesses these by whatever way is most valued; everyone seeks these through rocks and through fires. The next place is held by the nobility of birth, which, if nothing else is added, is a completely ridiculous and empty name. He is considered a demigod who can trace his lineage back to Codrus of Athens, or to the Trojan Brutus (who I know not if he was ever born), or to the mythical Hercules. And he is obscure who has won fame for himself through letters and virtue. He is "illustrious" whose great-great-grandfather proved himself a vigorous murderer in war; and he is a plebeian and lacks ancestral masks <note>term: "ancestral masks" (imagines) – wax masks of ancestors displayed by Roman nobility to show their status.</note> who has benefited the world with the goods of the mind. In the third class are the comforts of the body: if someone happens to be huge, robust, beautiful, or very strong, they do not indeed remove him from the number of the fortunate, but in such a way that riches nevertheless hold first place, nobility the next, and the care of the soul is the last. 

Now, if you divide man himself according to Paul into three parts—flesh, soul, and spirit, for I will use his words—the crowd mostly embraces the lowest part, which is most in view and which the Apostle utterly condemns. More people approve of the middle part, which he only approves if it has approached the spirit. Furthermore, the spirit, the best part of us, from which all our happiness proceeds as if from a fountain, and by which we are joined to God, they hold in such little value that they do not even inquire whether there is a spirit or what it is, even though Paul insists on it so many times. And from here comes the preposterous judgment of the multitude concerning things, so that those to whom the first honor was owed—for them <margin>the pious.</margin> <note>original Greek: "hōsper tōn megalōn... eiōthōs logos" — as is the custom [to speak] of great things.</note> as is the customary way of speaking—those things which should have been sought with the greatest zeal, they hold among the most contemptible. Hence gold is preferred to letters, ancient lineage to honor, the gifts of the body to the goods of the mind; true piety is postponed to ceremonies, the precepts of Christ to the decrees of men, the persona to the truth, the shadow to the reality, the painted to the natural, the fleeting to the solid, the momentary to the eternal. 

Then, from preposterous opinions come preposterous names for things. What is exalted, they call low; what is bitter, sweet; what is precious, vile; what is life, death. And to taste a few by name in passing: those are said to "love" who either corrupt by indulgence or plot against both modesty and reputation—yet what could be more hostile than this? They call it "justice" when evil is overcome by evil, crime by crime, when an injury received is paid back with much interest. Scarcely fair for marriage...

<summary>Erasmus contrasts the "inverted Sileni" of the world—corrupt leaders and clergy who look grand but are hollow—with the Christian's focus on hidden, spiritual values over material wealth and status.</summary>
<keywords>Sileni Alcibiadis, hypocrisy, bishops, monks, Aristotle's goods, St. Paul, nobility, spiritual vs material, preposterous values</keywords>

# 686 THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...is said of marriage, by those who demand it be kept untainted and as close as possible to virginity, and most distant from brothels. They call that man a "traitor" and an "enemy of the prince" who wishes the prince to allow nothing beyond the laws or contrary to what is fair; that is, one who desires him to truly act as a prince and to stay as far as possible from the image of a tyrant, than which no beast is more foul. On the contrary, that man is called a "counselor," a "friend," and a "supporter" of the prince who corrupts him with a perverse education, who toys with him through foolishly implanted opinions and flattery, who drags him into the hatred of the people through evil advice, and who involves him in civil and insane turmoils. They say the "majesty of the prince has been increased" when some element of tyranny has been added—which is to say, a large portion of the greatest evil. He is called a "thief of public funds" <term>peculator: an embezzler of state money</term> who wishes for something to be trimmed away from the taxes extorted from the people. 

Yet, since the primary goods of a prince are three—by which he who is truly the only King is in some way represented: goodness, wisdom, and power—does it seem that he is a friend to the prince who strips him of the two primary goods, goodness and wisdom, and leaves him only power? And even this power is not only false but not even his own. For power, unless it is joined with wisdom and goodness, is tyranny; it cannot last, since the consent of the people, just as it gave that power, can likewise take it away. Meanwhile, if he were cast down from power, goodness and wisdom would remain with him as his own personal goods. 

It is a capital offense to violate the insignias of a prince, yet there is a reward for those who, by corrupting his mind, render him cruel instead of good, crafty instead of wise, and a tyrant instead of a powerful leader. One death is too little for a man who attempts to infect the prince’s cup with poison; yet he receives a reward who corrupts and poisons the prince's mind with the most pestilential opinions, infecting, as it were, the public fountain of the state—the source of all the world's evils. They call the prince’s duty "dominion," when in truth to act as a prince is nothing other than to administer the common wealth. 

They call the family alliances between kings and the frequent new treaties "the glue of Christian peace," even though we see that almost all wars and the foulest turmoils of human affairs arise from these very sources. They call it a "just war" when princes collude among themselves to exhaust and oppress the state; they call it "peace" when they conspire together for this very purpose. They consider the "empire increased" when the title of one or another small town is added to the prince’s name, bought with such great plundering of the citizens, so much blood, so many widows, and so many orphans. 

In the same way, they call the sacrificers, the bishops, and the supreme pontiffs "the Church," when in reality these are nothing other than the ministers of the Church. For the "Church" is the Christian people, whom Christ himself calls "greater," so that the bishops should serve them as ministers, being lesser in terms of service, but greater in another sense if they represent Christ through the imitation of his life and character as much as they do by the succession of their office. For Christ, although he was in every way the Prince and Lord of all, took up the part of a servant, not a master. 

Every suspicion is twisted against those who are called "enemies of the Church," and almost heretics, if they have defrauded the priestly purse of a few coins. Indeed, I do not support the fraudster—lest anyone misinterpret me—but I ask, if it is helpful to hate the enemy of the Church, can there be an enemy of the Church more destructive or more deadly than an impious Pope? Whenever something is diminished from the estates or the income of priests, there is a cry from every side that "the Christian Church is being oppressed." But when the world is stirred up to war, when the wicked life of priests is out in the open, and when so many thousands of souls are pushed into destruction, no one deplores the state of the Church—even though it is then that the Church is truly afflicted. 

They call the Church "adorned and honored" not when piety flourishes among the people, when vices decrease, when good character increases, or when sacred doctrine thrives, but when the altars shine with gold and gems; or rather, when these are neglected and the priests equal the <note>original: "satrapas" — high-ranking Persian governors, used here to imply oriental luxury and arrogance.</note> satraps in their estates, retinues, luxury, mules, horses, expensive houses (or rather, palace-like structures), and the rest of life’s noise. And these things seem so right that in the very diplomas of the Popes, an endorsement of this kind is inserted: "Since that Cardinal supports so many horses and so many purple-clad servants in his house, he greatly adorns the Church of God; therefore, we grant him a fourth bishopric." And "for the adornment of the Church," bishops, priests, and clerics are ordered to be clothed in purple and silk. O, wonderful dignity of the Church! 

What is left, now that we have even lost the vocabulary for what is honorable? I do not even wish to mention those who squander the wealth of the church on impious uses, to the great scandal of the common people. If their wealth increases, we congratulate them and say the "Church of Christ has been increased"; but the only profit for the Church should be progress in the Christian life. They call it "blasphemy" if someone speaks with too little reverence of Saint Christopher or Saint George, or if one does not equate every single parchment with the Gospel. But Paul calls it "blasphemy" <note>Referring to Romans 2:24, "For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."</note> whenever the wicked behavior of Christians causes the name of Christ to be defamed among the heathens. # 687 THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
## THIRD THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY
### Mm 2

What do you think the enemies of the Christian religion say when they see in the Gospel writings that Christ encourages the contempt of riches, the renunciation of pleasures, and the neglect of glory—yet on the other hand they observe that even the leaders and commanders of the Christian profession live in such a way that they surpass the pagans themselves in their zeal for piling up wealth, in their love of pleasure, in the splendor of their lives, in the ferocity of war, and in almost all other vices? The prudent reader understands what I am keeping silent about here, out of honor for the name "Christian," and what I sigh over in private. 

What mocking laughter do you think those people break into when they see that in the Gospel, Christ did not mark his followers by their dress, nor by ceremonies, nor by food, but wanted Christians to be recognized by this mark: if they are glued together by mutual love—and then they observe that there is so little agreement among us that no pagan nation has ever rioted more shamefully or more destructively. Prince wages war with prince; city fights with city; school does not agree with school, nor "religion" <note>Erasmus uses "religion" here in the sense of a religious order or sect (e.g., Franciscans vs. Dominicans).</note> (as they now call it) with religion. Everything among us is full of brawls, factions, and lawsuits. 

This is finally true blasphemy, and its authors are those who provide the just occasion for it. They call it "heresy" if anyone says or writes something that in some way disagrees with the minor propositions of the master theologians, or even in a matter of grammar. Yet it is not considered heresy when someone treats as a chief part of human happiness that which Christ himself everywhere teaches should be neglected; or when someone introduces a way of life far different from the Gospel precepts and apostolic institutions; or when someone—contrary to the mind of Christ—arms the apostles who are setting out to preach the Gospel with iron weapons to defend themselves against persecution, instead of the "sword of the spirit" (which, by cutting away all earthly affections, alone makes it so that a physical sword is not needed). 

(And there is no doubt that under the name of "sword," he <note>Referring to the corrupt modern interpreter.</note> wishes catapults, cannons, machines, and the rest of the apparatus of war to be included.) Then he loads them with a pouch in which they carry money, obviously so that nothing is ever lacking; and under the name of "pouch," he wants whatever pertains to the provision of this life to be understood. And whoever teaches these things is cited among the great theologians. 

It is an inexpiable sacrilege if someone carries anything away from a temple; yet it is held as a light crime to pillage, defraud, and oppress poor people and widows—the living temple of God—which is done everywhere by princes and nobles, and sometimes by bishops and abbots. He is "profane" who contaminates a sacred building with a fight or a flow of blood; yet do we not curse him who violates, corrupts, and profanes a pure and chaste virgin—the temple of the Holy Spirit—with flatteries, gifts, promises, and pimping? And the one who does these things is commonly called "charming" and "elegant." 

I am not patronizing evil deeds, as I testified before; I am showing that the common crowd of men values much more those things seen with the eyes than those which are truer precisely because they are less visible. You see the consecration of a stone temple; because you do not see the dedication of the soul, you neglect it. You would fight with swords for its ornaments; but to preserve the integrity of morals, no one takes up that Gospel sword which Christ commands to be bought even at the price of selling one's tunic <note>Original: *tunica diuenditæ precio parari*—a reference to Luke 22:36.</note>. 

It is called the "highest piety" if someone takes up arms to defend or increase the domain and money of priests, mixing sacred and profane things in the turmoils of war. And meanwhile, while the money of the priests—a most worthless thing, surely—is being defended, is a huge flood of all piety allowed in through the admission of war? For what evil is there that war does not drag along with it? 

But perhaps the silent thought of the reader will interrupt me, saying: "Where do these tedious points lead? Do you want a prince to be the kind that Plato makes the guardians in his Republic? <note>Plato’s "guardians" were a class of rulers in his ideal city who were forbidden from owning private property to ensure their devotion to the state.</note> Do you call back the priests—stripped of empire, dignity, glory, and riches—to the pouch and staff of the apostles?" Good words! I do not strip them, but I enrich them with these better things; I do not cast them out of possession, but I call them to better things. 

I ask you: which of us thinks more magnificently of the king’s excellence? You, who want him to be allowed to do whatever he pleases—who want him to be a tyrant, not a prince—who fill him with pleasures, who betray him to luxury, who make him a slave and prisoner to all desires, who want him to be no wiser than anyone from the middle of the common people; you load him with these things which even among the pagans it was always magnificent to despise. Or am I the one, who desires the prince to be as similar as possible to God (whose image he bears in a way), to excel others in wisdom (which is the proper praise of kings), and to be far away from all sordid affections and diseases of the mind, by which the thick and low common crowd is <unclear>driven</unclear> and <unclear>lives</unclear>? To admire nothing of the common people, to be superior to wealth; in short, to be in the state what the soul is in the body, what God is in the universe? 

Which of us more truly weighs the dignity of a bishop: you, who load him with earthly riches, involve him in sordid and common cares, and entangle him in the storms of wars; or I, who desire the Vicar of Christ and the guardian of the heavenly bride to be most pure from every earthly contagion, and as far as is permitted...

# 688 THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
## ADAGIORVM

...it is fitting that he be as similar as possible to the one whose place and office he holds. The Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught virtue is the only good and that one should remain indifferent to pleasure and pain.</note> deny that anyone can be a "good man" unless he is free from the diseases of the mind. By "diseases," they mean desires or passions. It is therefore much more the duty of Christians to be free from these, and most of all for a prince. But even more than most, this applies to the prince and father of the Church—that is, the celestial prince of that celestial people. I want the priest to triumph as much as possible, but I say that this worldly dominion is an unworthy burden for a celestial man to be weighed down by. I want the Pope to triumph as much as possible, but not with those bloody triumphs led by the wicked Marius or the impious Julius <note>Refers to Gaius Marius and Julius Caesar, famous Roman generals known for their military triumphs—ceremonial processions celebrating bloody victories.</note>; these were so vain that they were mocked by the "Jests of Saturn." <note>A reference to the *Saturnalia*, a Roman festival where social norms were overturned and mockery was common.</note> If the famous Democritus <note>The "laughing philosopher" of ancient Greece, known for mocking human vanities.</note> had seen such things, I believe he would have died of laughter. 

Instead, let his triumphs be severely magnificent and apostolic, of the kind that Paul—a much more splendid warrior and leader than Alexander the Great—describes and boasts of, as if singing his own song of praise. *In many labors,* he says, *in more abundant imprisonments, in beatings beyond measure, in frequent deaths; from the Jews five times I received forty stripes minus one, three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I was in the depth of the sea; in frequent journeys, in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own race, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers, in labor and hardship, in many sleepless nights, in hunger and thirst, in many fastings, in cold and nakedness; besides those things that are external pressures, my daily concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is led into sin, and I do not burn with indignation?* <note>original: "In laboribus... ego non uror?" This is a translation of 2 Corinthians 11:23-29.</note> 

Again, a little earlier, he says: *In all things let us present ourselves as ministers of God: in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in imprisonments, in seditions, in labors, in watchings, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God; through the armor of justice on the right hand and on the left, through glory and ignominy, through infamy and good fame; as deceivers and yet true, as unknown and yet known, as dying and behold we live, as chastened and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.* <note>original: "In omnibus... omnia possidentes." This is a translation of 2 Corinthians 6:4-10.</note> 

Do you see what the honors of war are, what the victory is, and what constitutes an apostolic triumph? This is that "glory" by which Paul occasionally swears as if it were a sacred thing. These are the outstanding deeds for which he trusts an immortal crown has been set aside for him. Those who claim the place and authority of the apostles for themselves should not be ashamed to walk in the footsteps of the apostles. I desire the Popes to be as rich as possible, but rich in the <term>Evangelical pearl</term> <note>A reference to the "pearl of great price" in the Gospel of Matthew, representing the Kingdom of Heaven.</note> and in celestial wealth; the more they pour this out upon everyone, the more they themselves will abound. There will be no danger that their kindness will perish through being kind. 

I also want them to be extremely well-fortified, but with apostolic weapons—namely, the shield of faith, the breastplate of justice, and the sword of salvation, which is the word of God. I want them to be most warlike, but against those true enemies of the church: <term>simony</term> <note>The practice of selling church offices or spiritual preferences.</note>, pride, lust, ambition, anger, and impiety. These are the "Turks" <note>In Erasmus's time, the Ottoman Turks were seen as the primary external threat to Christendom; here he uses them as a metaphor for internal vices.</note> that Christians must always watch for and always attack. In such wars, let the Bishop be the leader and the one who encourages the troops. 

I want priests to be respected above all others, but not because of tyrannical noise, but because of the excellence of holy doctrine and outstanding virtues. I want them to be revered, but for the integrity and severity of their lives, not merely for their titles or "tragic" <note>In the sense of "theatrical" or "pompous."</note> dress. I want them to be feared, but as fathers, not as tyrants. I want them to be feared only by the wicked; indeed, I want them to be such that the wicked respect them rather than dread or hate them. Finally, I want them to overflow with delights, but with those rare and far sweeter pleasures than the common people know. 

Do you wish to hear the true riches of a High Priest? Hear from the one second only to the Prince of Priests: *Silver and gold I do not have, but what I do have, I give to you: In the name of Jesus, rise and walk.* <note>Acts 3:6, spoken by St. Peter.</note> Do you wish to hear the glory of the apostolic name, which surpasses all titles, all triumphal arches and statues? Hear that truly illustrious Paul: *We are the good odor of Christ to God in every place.* <note>2 Corinthians 2:15.</note> Do you wish to hear of a power greater than that of kings? *I can do all things,* he says, *in him who strengthens me.* <note>Philippians 4:13.</note> Do you wish to hear of his glory? *You are my joy and my crown in the Lord.* <note>Philippians 4:1.</note> Do you wish to hear of titles worthy of a Bishop and the ornaments of a true Pope? The same Paul paints a picture for you: *sober, orderly, prudent, chaste, hospitable, a teacher; not given to wine, not a striker, but modest, not litigious, not greedy for gain, not a neophyte <note>A new convert or someone newly ordained.</note>; one who has a good reputation even among those on the outside, so that he does not fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.* <note>1 Timothy 3:2-7.</note> 

Contemplate the ornaments with which Moses honored Aaron the High Priest: with what wealth he adorned him, with what colors he painted him, with how many stars of various gems he made him shine, and with what brightness of gold he decorated him. If you learn what these things signify from the interpretations of Origen and Jerome <note>Early Church Fathers known for their allegorical and scholarly biblical commentaries.</note>, you will certainly understand...

<summary>Erasmus contrasts the worldly, "bloody" triumphs of secular rulers and corrupt popes with the "apostolic triumph" defined by suffering, virtue, and spiritual wealth as exemplified by St. Paul. He argues that true priestly authority comes from moral integrity and the "arms" of faith rather than political power or outward pomp.</summary>

# 689 THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
### THIRD THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY

What kind of equipment must be prepared for truly great bishops? Is it not better that their lives express the character of a pontiff, rather than having it expressed in **lead** <note>original: "plumbo" — referring to the leaden seals (*bullae*) used to authenticate official papal documents, from which we get the term "Papal Bull."</note>, or representing it through titles, while merely occupying the office? Or is it more fitting for a vicar of Christ to imitate **Julius**, **Alexander**, **Croesus**, and **Xerxes** <note>A list of ancient rulers synonymous with conquest and immense wealth: Julius Caesar, Alexander the Great, the fabulously rich King Croesus of Lydia, and the Persian King Xerxes.</note>—who were nothing other than "great robbers"—rather than Christ himself, the sole leader and commander of the Church? Whom should the successors of the apostles more justly emulate than the Prince of the Apostles? Christ openly denied that his kingdom was of this world; and yet do you think it is appropriate for a successor of Christ not only to accept worldly dominion, but even to pursue it, and for its sake, as the saying goes, to **move every stone**? <note>A proverbial expression meaning to leave no stone unturned or to exert every possible effort.</note>

In this world, there are, as it were, two worlds, fighting against each other in every way: one is coarse and corporeal; the other is celestial, already meditating with all its might on what it will one day become. In the first world, the "greatest" man is the one who is furthest removed from true goods and weighed down by false ones. Like a pagan king, he surpasses everyone in lust, luxury, violence, pride, arrogance, wealth, and greed; he is seen as "first" if the largest portion of this **bilge water** <note>original: "sentinae" — the foul water that collects in the bottom of a ship, used here as a metaphor for moral corruption.</note> flows into him, while having as little as possible of wisdom, temperance, sobriety, justice, and the other things that are truly good. 

Conversely, in the second world, the one who is supreme is the one least defiled by those common and coarse goods, and most abundantly filled with those true and celestial riches. Therefore, why do you want a Christian prince to be that which even pagan philosophers always condemned and despised? Why do you place his majesty in these things, which it is most beautiful to have held in contempt? Why do you burden an **angel of God** (for so a bishop is called in the hidden letters of scripture) with things that are unworthy even of a good man? Why do you measure him by the riches that make robbers wealthy and tyrants formidable? 

A priest is something celestial, something greater than a human being. Nothing is worthy of his sublimity except what is celestial. Why do you dishonor his dignity with common things? Why do you contaminate his purity with the filth of the world? Why do you not allow him to be powerful in his own dominion? Why do you not permit him to be noble in his own glory, revered in his own majesty, and rich in his own wealth? 

The celestial Spirit chose this man from the celestial body, which is the Church, for the highest matters. Why do you drag him away to the furious tumults of **satraps**? <note>Refers to provincial governors of the ancient Persian Empire; Erasmus uses the term here to describe worldly, often tyrannical, political officials.</note> Paul boasts that he was "set apart"; why do you immerse my prelate in the middle of the bilge water of the lowest rabble? Why do you cast him down into the anxieties of moneylenders? Why do you drag a divine man down to business hardly worthy of a human being? Why do you measure the happiness of Christian priests by these things, which **Democritus** laughed at as the height of folly, **Heraclitus** wept over as the height of misery, **Diogenes** spurned as frivolous, **Crates** threw away as a burden, and the saints always fled as a pestilence? <note>Erasmus cites a "Who's Who" of ancient philosophy: Democritus (the laughing philosopher), Heraclitus (the weeping philosopher), Diogenes the Cynic (who lived in a tub), and Crates (who gave away his fortune to live in poverty).</note> 

Why do you value a successor of Peter by the riches that Peter himself boasted he did not possess? Why do you want the apostolic princes to seem great through those ornaments which the apostles became great by **trampling underfoot**? Why do you call that "Peter’s Patrimony" <note>The "Patrimonium Petri" traditionally referred to the land and wealth held by the Papacy.</note> which Peter himself boasted of not having? Why do you think Christ's vicars should be ensnared in riches, which Christ himself called "thorns"? Why do you overwhelm him with wealth—when his proper and chief duty is to sow the seed of the divine word—since the crop is most especially choked by such a burden? Why do you want a teacher and judge of equity to serve the **wicked Mammon**? <note>A biblical term used to personify greed and material wealth.</note> Why do you make a dispenser of celestial sacraments into a manager of the most worthless things? 

The Christian world expects from him the food of sacred doctrine; it expects saving counsel, it expects paternal consolation, it expects a model for living. Why do you thrust someone destined and dedicated to such magnificent things into the **workhouse** <note>original: "ergastulum" — a Roman prison or private dungeon for slaves.</note> of common cares, both stripping the bishop of his dignity and robbing the people of their bishop? 

Christ has his own kingdom, which is too excellent to be polluted by a pagan kingdom—or to speak more truly, by a tyranny. It has its own splendor, its own wealth, its own pleasures. Why do we mix things so contrary to each other? Why do we confound the earthly with the celestial, the lowest with the highest, the pagan with the Christian, the profane with the sacred? So many and so great are the gifts of the Spirit, who is both most rich and most kind: the gift of tongues, the gift of prophecy, the gift of healing, the gift of knowledge, the gift of wisdom, the gift of teaching, the discernment of spirits, exhortation, and consolation. Why do you join the profane gifts of the world with these sacred treasures? (I might even say: why do you extinguish them?) Why do you try to join Christ with Mammon, and Belial <note>A Hebrew term for "worthlessness" or "wickedness," often used as a name for the devil.</note> with the Spirit of Christ? 

What has a **mitre** <note>The ceremonial headdress of a bishop.</note> to do with a **helmet**? What has the sacred **pallium** <note>A circular band of white wool worn by archbishops.</note> to do with a **breastplate of Mars**? <note>Mars was the Roman god of war.</note> What have blessings to do with **bombards** <note>Early types of cannons; Erasmus often lamented how gunpowder had made war more inhuman.</note>? What has the most merciful shepherd to do with armed robbers? What has the priesthood to do with war? Why does he who holds the keys to the kingdom of heaven use siege engines to destroy towns? How is it fitting for the author of war to be the one who greets the people with the omen of peace? With what face will he teach the Christian commoners that riches are to be despised, when the **prow and stern** <note>original: "puppim & proram" — a nautical metaphor meaning from beginning to end, or the entirety of something.</note> of his own affairs is established in money? With what forehead will he teach what Christ both taught and exhibited, which so often...

# 690 THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS
### m m

...as the Apostles teach, we must not resist evil, but rather overcome the wickedness of others with goodness, repay injury with kindness, and overwhelm our enemies with good deeds. Yet, is this the path of one who, for the sake of ruling a small town or collecting a salt tax <note>original: "salinarum uectigal" — salt was a heavily taxed and vital commodity in the Renaissance, often a cause for regional conflict.</note>, throws the whole world into the storms of war? In what way can a man be a leader to the kingdom of heaven—for that is what Christ calls His church—if he is entirely immersed in the kingdom of the world? 

But perhaps you are being exceedingly pious, wishing to adorn the church by adding these very riches. I would approve, if only such a small amount of benefit did not bring such a great deal of evil along with it. When you granted the Church empire, you simultaneously gave it the burden of hoarding money; you gave it tyrannical bodyguards, iron-clad troops, spies, horses, mules, trumpets, war, slaughter, triumphs, riots, treaties, and battles—briefly, everything without which an empire cannot be managed. 

When will there ever be leisure for an inspired mind to perform its apostolic duty, when it is pulled in a thousand different directions by so many cares? When a draft of soldiers is being written, when treaties are being struck or torn up, when those who refuse to obey the rule are being suppressed, when those looking for revolution must be kept loyal, when enemies are being besieged, when fortresses are being fortified, when accounts are being audited, when meaningless <note>original: "amphane" — a term derived from Greek meaning pointless or fruitless diplomatic missions.</note> embassies are being handled, when provincial governors are being received at banquets, when friends are being promoted to honors, when those ordered to make way for more "favored" men are being driven out—when all these other things are being done, which it is unpleasant even to remember, but which nevertheless must be done? 

Does he seem to you to understand the excellence of a Pope or the Cardinals, who thinks they should be dragged down into this filth of worldly affairs? These are men who should be pulled away from the prayer in which they converse with God; away from the sacred contemplation in which they live among the angels; away from the lush meadows of Divine Scripture in which they wander most happily; and away from the apostolic duty of preaching the Gospel, in which they most truly resemble Christ. Does it seem like wishing them well to desire that they be dragged from such a great happiness and tranquility of life into these miseries and these worldly riots? 

For while rule is by its nature subject to infinite labors, it turns out far less happily for priests than for laypeople. This is for two main reasons: partly because the common people more willingly endure a secular ruler than an ecclesiastical one in these matters, and partly because secular rulers, intending to leave their domain to their own children, strive to make it as flourishing as possible. Priests, on the contrary, are usually chosen for rule later in life and are often already old; since they rule for themselves and not for an heir, they pillage the land rather than adorn it, as if it were a prize of war rather than a province. 

Furthermore, where a secular ruler holds power, perhaps there is a struggle for the kingdom only once, and the favorites whom the prince supports are enriched only once. Where it is otherwise <note>meaning: in a priestly state where rulers change frequently by election rather than dynasty</note>, there is a new struggle every so often; those whom the predecessor had raised up must be cast out of their possessions, and again and again, new men must be enriched at the expense of the people. 

There is also the fact that a people much more easily bears the rule of someone they are used to, even if he rules harshly. Even if he dies, he seems to survive in his son and heir; the common people imagine that the prince has not been changed for another, but that the same one has been renewed for them. Children, having been educated by their parents, usually reflect their characters. Conversely, when rule is committed to men dedicated to God, there is usually a sudden change in everything. Add to this that the secular ruler approaches the task having been trained and educated for it from the cradle. In the Church, the supreme power often falls to someone beyond all hope, so that a man whom nature created for the oars of a galley is raised to a kingdom by a game of fortune. 

Finally, it is hardly possible for one man to be equal to two very difficult tasks—just as Hercules could not fight two monsters at once. It is the most difficult thing of all to be a good prince. But it is far more beautiful, and at the same time far more difficult, to act as a good priest. Who, then, can be both? Is it not inevitable that while they take both duties upon themselves, they satisfy neither? 

It is surely because of these things, unless I am mistaken, that while we see the cities of secular kings flourishing more and more in wealth, buildings, and men, the towns of the priests generally grow cold and fall into ruin. Why then was there a need for the addition of these things, which so many disadvantages accompany? Do you fear that Christ will be insufficiently powerful with His own resources unless a secular tyrant imparts some of his power? Do you think the lives of the clergy are insufficiently adorned unless a secular warrior grants them gold, embroidery, white horses <note>original: "candidos mannos" — white horses were a traditional symbol of triumph and high status.</note>, and bodyguards—that is, unless he sprinkles them with some of his own arrogance? 

Does He seem insufficiently splendid unless they are allowed to use those insignia of rank which even the most ambitious Julius <note>original: "Iulius" — referring to Julius Caesar, who famously refused the crown when it was offered to him by Mark Antony to avoid public envy, though Erasmus may also be hinting at the "ambitious" Pope Julius II.</note> refused because of the envy they provoked? Do you judge Christ humble unless He is burdened with worldly empire? If he wields it for himself, he becomes a tyrant; if for the state, he becomes a man overwhelmed by business. Let secular people have secular things; in a bishop, that which is considered the lowest part of his office surpasses the very height of all empire. The more you add of the world's goods, the less of His own goods Christ will bestow. The more he is purified from those things, the more abundantly He will enrich him with these. 

You see, I think, how the whole matter turns into its opposite if you turn the Silenus <note>The "Silenus of Alcibiades" is a metaphor from Plato's *Symposium* describing a statue that is ugly and grotesque on the outside but contains beautiful images of the gods within. Erasmus uses it here to argue that the Church has become the inverse: golden on the outside, but spiritually hollow or "ugly" within.</note> inside out. Those who seemed to favor a Christian prince the most are those who betray...

<meta>catchword: things</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Erasmus argues that the Church's pursuit of temporal power and wealth is a betrayal of its apostolic mission, claiming that spiritual leadership and secular governance are incompatible burdens that distract from the Gospel.</summary>
<keywords>corruption, papacy, secular power, apostolic poverty, Sileni Alcibiadis, church vs state, Renaissance theology, Julius Caesar, salt tax</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Erasmus remains deep in a passionate digression. He has been arguing that when the Church adopts the trappings of worldly empire—armies, taxes, and political intrigue—it abandons its true apostolic mission. He now turns to the irony of how the Church’s original wealth was actually born from a rejection of the world.</meta>

# 691 CHILIAD THREE, CENTURY III
### Mm 4

...the greatest enemies of the prince are discovered: those whom you would have said protect the dignity of the pontiffs <note>original: "pontificum" — here referring to the high-ranking clergy or the Pope</note> are found to be the ones defiling it. I would not say this because I think anything should be snatched away from priests, if they have acquired any power or wealth in whatever manner; for no piously minded person should be pleased by civil unrest. Rather, I want them to be conscious and mindful of their own true greatness, so that they might either voluntarily reject these common—not to say heathen—things and leave them to the lowest of men, or at least possess them with contempt. Following the example of Paul, they should "possess as if they possessed not" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:30–31, where St. Paul advises believers to remain detached from worldly goods.</note>. 

In short, I wish for them to be so adorned with the riches of Christ that whatever worldly splendor is added might be overshadowed by the light of a better glory, or even appear filthy by comparison. Thus it will happen that they will possess what they own more happily because they possess it more securely; for they will not be tormented by the fear that someone might snatch it away, nor will they fight with such great turmoil for humble and fleeting things if some part of it should be lost. Finally, they will not be deprived of their own true goods while they delight in growing rich on the goods of others. They will not lose the evangelical pearl <note>A reference to the "Pearl of Great Price" from the Gospel of Matthew (13:45-46).</note> while they chase after the glass trinkets of the world. 

I will set aside for a moment the fact that these very things we wish to be held in contempt would actually come to us more abundantly if they were despised; they follow those who flee from them more honorably than they are seized by those who pursue them. After all, from where did the wealth of the church arise in the first place, if not from the contempt for wealth? From where did its glory come, if not from the neglect of glory? The laity would give these things more willingly if they saw them being rejected by those whom they believe to be wiser. 

Perhaps sometimes even bad princes must be tolerated, and something must be granted to the memory of those whose place they seem to occupy; something must be given to their title. A remedy should not be attempted which—having been tried unsuccessfully before—might turn into an even more grievous destruction. Yet, how poorly things go for human affairs in the meantime, if those whose entire lives ought to be a miracle are such that the worst people applaud them while the good sigh and groan. Their entire dignity hangs either on the favor of the wicked, the modesty of the average, the ignorance of the simple, or the tolerance of the good. Indeed, they are kept safe only by the discord of the people; nothing makes them great except the disagreements of citizens, and their happiness is nourished by public misfortune. 

If priests judged the matter correctly, the addition of secular power brings so much trouble with it that it ought to be refused even if it were offered voluntarily. They become the slaves of princes and courts; they are attacked by rebellions and entangled in wars in which they sometimes breathe their last. In short, it results in monarchs having a respectable servant-class, but where, in the meantime, are the fathers of the Christian people? Where are the shepherds? 

What kind of thing is it for abbots and bishops to buy titles of this sort from monarchs for huge sums? An abbot does not seem respectable unless he is also a Count. A man thinks his priesthood is adorned if he has purchased the title of Duke. O, what beautifully joined words: abbot and satrap <note>original: "satrapa" — a term for a provincial governor, often implying a luxury-loving official</note>, bishop and warrior! Yet it is much more absurd that while they play the part of "brave men" in these roles, they are mere shadows in the duty that was actually their own. They have hands and swords with which to kill bodies—let this be called "justice" if you like—but they have no tongue with which to heal souls. The abbot knows how to draw up a battle line, but he does not know how to be a leader for religion. The bishop is fully equipped for clashing with arms and cannons <note>original: "bombardis" — early Renaissance artillery</note>, but he is mute when it comes to teaching, exhorting, or consoling. He is armed with javelins and crossbows, but is utterly defenseless when it comes to the Holy Scriptures. 

And yet, meanwhile, they demand from their people every penny of the profit and honor owed to pious abbots and good bishops—indeed, sometimes not just what is owed, but whatever they please. The Lord will crown the tolerance of the people who endure such men for the love of peace, but I fear these leaders will find God a harsher judge. What do these turmoils cry out to us, if not that God is angry with us all? What remains but that all of us, the greatest and the least alike, the sacred and the secular together, flee with humble minds to the mercy of the Lord? How much more sensible this would be than if, while each of us refuses to acknowledge our own fault and casts it upon another, we further exasperate the wrath of the Divine, and instead of healing ourselves, we wound each other more deeply with mutual biting. The people grumble against the princes; the princes spare neither the secular nor the sacred; the common folk mock the priests. Yet it often happens that God, offended by the sins of the people, sends such rulers as they deserve to receive. 

So far, nothing has been gained by complaints, spite, brawls, and riots. The one thing that remains is a common confession by all, so that God’s mercy may be ready for all. 

But where has the course of my speech swept me? Having professed to be a writer of proverbs <note>original: "parœmiographum"</note>, have I begun to be a Preacher <note>original: "Ecclesiastes"</note>? Truly, the drunken Alcibiades has brought his Sileni <note>Erasmus is referencing Plato's *Symposium*, where Alcibiades compares Socrates to "Silenus" statues—unattractive on the outside but containing golden images of gods within. Erasmus uses this to justify his "intoxicated" moral digression within a scholarly book.</note> into this sober discussion. But I shall not very much repent of this error if this material, though it does not pertain to the explanation of proverbs, pertains to the amendment of life; and if what contributes nothing to erudition should lead to piety; and if what seems <unclear>irrelevant</unclear> and <unclear>out of place</unclear> <note>original: "aprosdionyson kai atopon" — Greek idioms for something that doesn't fit the topic.</note> to the plan of the work should be well-suited to the conduct of living.

<meta>catchword: Sarone</meta>

<summary>Erasmus concludes a fierce critique of the "warrior-clergy," arguing that the Church’s true power comes from the rejection of worldly titles and wealth. He apologizes for the long moral digression, noting that while it may be "out of place" in a book of proverbs, it is necessary for the "amendment of life."</summary>

# 692 DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->More of a sailor than Saron.<-

<note>original: "Σάρωνος ναυτικώτερος"</note> That is, more of a sailor than Saron. They say this Saron was a certain god of the sea, from whom the Saronic Gulf <note>A body of water in Greece between the regions of Attica and Argolis.</note> took its name. This proverb is suitable for a rough man with wild manners, the kind of character we see in most sailors. Or, it could refer to a merchant who is constantly flying across every sea. Both Saron and the sea named after him are mentioned by Aristides in his work on Themistocles: "Lest they live in the sea for all time, as they say Glaucus the Anthedonian <note>A mythical fisherman who became a sea-god after eating a magical herb.</note> does, or Saron, for whom the sea is named." Pausanias, in his *Description of Corinth*, also mentions Saron, saying he ruled over the coastal region of Althepia. A contrasting idea is found in Aristophanes’ *Frogs*:

->How shall I,<-
->unskilled, un-sea-faring, un-Salaminian<-
->as I am, then manage to row?<-

->That is:<-

->In what possible way<-
->Can I, being inexperienced and a stranger to the sea,<-
->Lacking any knowledge of Salamis, be so raw at driving a ship?<-

---

->A constant dripping hollows out a stone.<-

<note>original: "ῥανὶς ἐνδελεχοῦσα κοιλαίνει πέτραν"</note> That is, a perpetual dripping hollows out the rock. It suggests that nothing is so hard that it cannot be softened, and nothing so difficult that persistence cannot achieve it. Indeed, a drop of water—surely a thing so thin and light—wears away even the hardest stone, which you could hardly overcome with iron. Pliny records that flint stones are found worn down by the feet of passersby; he considers this a most powerful example of the force of persistence. Menander, as cited by Stobaeus, says:

->For persistence<-
<margin>For persistence is wont to conquer</margin>
->Overcomes any business whatsoever.<-
<margin>Ovid</margin>
> What is harder than stone? What is softer than a wave? 
> Yet hard stones are hollowed out by soft water. <note>From Ovid’s *Epistulae ex Ponto* (Letters from the Black Sea).</note>

Galen, in the third book of *On Temperaments*, relates the same sentiment in a heroic verse: "Indeed, that also seems to have been well said:

The soft little drop of water hollows the stone with its constant strike."

To this, the followers of Homer <note>Erasmus uses "Homeridæ" to refer to scholars or commentators on Homer.</note> add the story that while others could hardly lift a full cup from the table, the aged Nestor lifted it easily and without effort. Even though he was quite old and inferior in physical strength, his long use and practice gave him this ability. For Homer portrays Nestor as a "lover of the cup." Homer’s verse goes like this:

->Another, struggling, could barely move it from the table<-
->When it was full, but the old man Nestor lifted it without effort.<-

This sentiment can be applied not only to persistence but also to the fact that we do easily what we do willingly.

---

->The Salaminian ship.<-

<note>original: "Σαλαμινία ναῦς"</note> That is, the Salaminian ship: a phrase used for things that are exceptionally fast. The naval battle fought against Xerxes <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> at Salamis is especially celebrated; or it refers to the fact that among the Athenians, one of the two ships used for state business was usually called the *Salaminia* and the other the *Paralus*. Aristophanes, in *The Birds*, mentions "the fast ones, the Paralus or the Salaminia." Hence Bacchus, in the passage we just cited, calls himself "un-Salaminian" because he was ignorant of military affairs and rowing. The poet also alluded, I believe, to a proverb we have mentioned elsewhere: "The one who knows how should pull the oar." Plutarch, in the *Life of Pericles*, calls a sturdy ship—in which one’s final hope is placed, as if in the reserve troops—the "Salaminian": "He did not always appear in the crowd, but kept himself like the Salaminian trireme (as Plutarch says) for great occasions." The commentaries on Aristophanes record that there were two ships at Athens destined for public use, of which the Salaminia would carry...

# THE THIRD CENTURY OF THE THIRD CHILIAD

while you were calling them out, the *Paralus* <note>A sacred trireme of the Athenian fleet used for state missions.</note> might carry them away. For the *Theoris* <note>Another sacred ship used for carrying state messengers (Theori) to religious festivals.</note> used to carry those who set out for Delphi or elsewhere for the sake of a vow or religious duty.

->V. Pyrrhander’s device.<-

<note>original: "Πυῤῥάνδρου μηχάνημα"</note> That is, Pyrrhander’s device. It is said of a clever invention. This Pyrrhander was a certain sycophant <note>A professional accuser or trickster in ancient Athens.</note>, remarkably crafty and of known malice. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*: "And by Jove, that too was a device of Pyrrhander’s." That is: "And by Jupiter, that was indeed a Pyrrhandric trick."

->VI. Unenviable wealth.<-

<note>original: "Ἄζηλος πλοῦτος"</note> It was called "unenviable wealth" when someone was ignorant of their own gifts. For instance, if a woman were beautiful, yet she was nonetheless unpleasant and dissatisfied with herself. Or if someone eloquent seemed to themselves to be lacking in speech. Furthermore, no small part of happiness is for each person to know their own blessings. Hence Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> wrote:
"O too fortunate farmers, if they but knew their own blessings."
->Agricolas.<-
I believe it is closely related to "blind wealth" <note>original: "ὁ τυφλὸς πλοῦτος"</note>. For to "envy" or "zealously admire" <note>original: "ζηλοῦν"</note> is sometimes the same as to wonder at and consider someone happy. From this they call what is conspicuous and illustrious "ever-envied" <note>original: "ἀείζηλον"</note>; the opposite of which is "unenviable" <note>original: "ἄζηλον"</note>, which no one admires. Some, however, admire what is hidden and pushed away. Plutarch, in his *Life of Lycurgus*, makes Theophrastus <note>A student of Aristotle and a famous philosopher.</note> the author of this saying; for he praises Lycurgus, who by his institutions brought it about that among the Spartans, wealth was neither liable to thieves and robbers—which he calls "slave-free"—nor admirable—which they call "unenviable"—nor even considered wealth at all, which he calls "wealthless wealth" <note>original: "ἄπλουτον πλοῦτον"</note>, as if you were to say "destitute riches." 

However, I will write down Plutarch's own words, if only to make it clear how much grace is lost by those who prefer to read authors translated into another language rather than hearing them speak in their own tongue: <note>original: "μέγα δ’ ἦν ἐν τοῖς ἴσοις, μᾶλλον δὲ τὸ πλοῦτον ἄσυλον, μᾶλλον δὲ ἄζηλον ὡς φησι θεόφραστος, καὶ μηδὲ ἄπλουτον ἀπεργάσασθαι τῆ κοινότητι τῶν δείπνων."</note> "It was a great thing among equals, or rather, to make wealth safe from plunder, or rather unenviable as Theophrastus says, and to make it even not wealth at all through the community of meals." Plutarch adds there that from these things arose that famous saying: that Plutus <note>The god of wealth.</note>, in the only city under the sun, Sparta, is kept blind <note>original: "τυφλὸν"</note>, that is, hidden away, no different than a lifeless and motionless painting. From these words it is simultaneously gathered that "blind," "wealth," and "unenviable" carry the same force. For a thing is called "blind" not only because it does not see, but also because it lacks light. 

And although this festive proverb is twisted toward the frugality of the Spartans, it fits better those who possess their riches for themselves and hide them away or even bury them. Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen* calls coins hidden in a chest "unseen wealth." For houses and fields cannot be hidden. There is no use for a painting put away, and no greater use for buried riches. For riches are prepared for use. Thus Horace <note>original: "Flaccus"</note> in his *Odes*:
"Silver has no color when hidden in the greedy earth."
->Abdito terris.<-
And Pindar in the first *Nemean Ode*: <note>original: "οὐκ ἔραμαι πολὺν ἐν μεγάρῳ πλοῦτον κατακρύψας ἔχειν, ἀλλ’ ἐόντων εὖ τε παθεῖν, καὶ ἀκοῦσαι φίλοις ἐξαρκέων."</note> That is: "I do not desire to have much wealth hidden away in my halls, but to enjoy well what is present, and to be well-spoken of, sufficing for my friends."

->VII. Say three things from the court.<-

<note>original: "Εἴποις τὰ τρία τὰ ἐξ αὐλῆς"</note> That is: "You may say three things from the court." In ancient times, those who had been condemned to capital punishment by the sentences of judges, before they were led to death, were granted the opportunity to say any three things they pleased, after being filled with wine and food. As soon as they had spoken these things, the sentence having been promulgated, they were led forth to execution. For they once called the place where the condemned were led the "court" <note>original: "αὐλὴν"</note>, which more recent writers call the "noose" <note>original: "ἀγχόνην"</note>. In Suidas it is read as "before the court," in the dative case, that is, "near the court" or "near the enclosure." I have not yet found the use of the adage in any author. I conjecture it was commonly said when someone spoke too petulantly, but to their own great misfortune, or when someone called down destruction upon another. The adage is recorded by Zenodotus.

->VIII. You enjoy the joy of a firefly.<-

<note>original: "Χαίρειν πυραύστου χάραν"</note> That is: "You enjoy the joy of a firefly." Concerning momentary and fleeting pleasure. We have shown elsewhere that the firefly <note>The term "pyrausta" refers to a mythical insect or moth attracted to light.</note>, flying toward the lamps, perishes with its wings burnt; hence also the proverb, "the fate of the firefly" <note>original: "πυραύστου μόρος"</note>, which we mentioned elsewhere.

->IX. You are fluttering.<-

<note>original: "πτερύγίζειν"</note> Someone is said to "flutter" who strives and longs to accomplish something. It is taken from the chicks of birds when they are still fledglings, moving their wings. Lucian uses it for unseemly and scurrilous—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...to gesticulate three times, in the book *On Those Who Serve for Pay*. Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
"And you cannot yet tell me with your foot then, but you talk nonsense and flap your wings." <note>original: "Καὶ σύ γε λέξαι μ' ὄπω δύνασαι ποδὶ τότε, ἀλλὰ φλυαρεῖς, καὶ πτερύγιζεις."</note> That is:
You are not yet able to speak to me on this matter,
But you trifle by gesturing.
And Diphilus in Athenaeus, book six, introduces a parasite speaking in this way:

->You teach old men before you have a beard.<-

<note>original: "πρὸ τῆι μιλλάδος διδάσκεις τοὺς γέροντας"</note> That is: Before the beard you teach the old. Used when a beardless youth teaches someone older. It is a proverbial figure, as Persius says, "Before the hairs." <note>original: "Ante pilos"</note>
"And swift wisdom of things
comes before the hairs; you know what should be said and what should be kept silent."
Apuleius, in his *Second Apology*, shows that this wisdom—which they call <term>precocious</term> <note>meaning "ripened before its time"</note>—was generally considered a not very favorable omen. He writes that this iambic line was noble and famous, by some poet or other (for he does not name him):
"I hate boys of precocious wisdom."
Nor does Quintilian <note>Erasmus refers to him here as "Fabio," using his middle name Marcus Fabius Quintilianus.</note> like a precocious type of talent, which he says does not usually reach full maturity. Pindar, in the *Pythian Odes* <note>hymno quinto</note>, praises someone thus: "He carries a mind and a tongue greater than his age, and a courage like the wide-winged eagle among birds." <note>original: "κρέσσονα μὲν ἁλικίας νόον φέρεται, γλῶσσάν τε, θάρσος δὲ τανύπτερος ἐν ὄρνιξιν αἰετός."</note> That is: He nourishes a mind and tongue more excellent than his age, and indeed a swift audacity like the eagle among birds.

---

->Conon will take care of the war.<-

<note>original: "Πόλεμος κόνωνι μελήσει."</note> That is: Conon will look after the battles.
It is a half-line of Heroic verse, and it is not quite clear from where it was taken. Furthermore, Conon was an Athenian much practiced in the business of war. First defeated in a naval battle by Lysander, the leader of the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note>, he renewed his forces and defeated the same man in a land battle, restoring the freedom of Athens. Therefore, it will be suitable to respond in this way to someone who takes care of business that does not concern them. Likewise, Hector says to his Andromache in the second book of the *Iliad* <note>This line is famously from Book 6, though Erasmus attributes it to Book 2.</note>:
"War will be a care for men." <note>original: "πόλεμος d' ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει."</note> That is:
Future wars are the care of men.
And Turnus in Virgil:
"Let men carry out arms and war, for whom wars must be waged."

---

->Before this, I thought you had horns.<-

<note>original: "πρὸ τούτου σὲ ὤμην κέρατα ἔχειν."</note> That is: Before now, I believed you had horns. Said of those who were held to be brave and vigorous, but later, when the situation demands a man, they appear cowardly. Hence a friend calls a man prepared to defend himself a "horned beast": "You fear a horned beast." And Horace:
"I lift my ready horns."
In the same author, a jester jokes at another jester who, having received an insult, threatens by moving his head because he had an ugly scar on his forehead. "What would you do," he says, "if your horn had not been cut out, when you threaten thus even when mutilated?" <note>A reference to Horace's *Satires* (1.5.60), where the scar is compared to a removed horn.</note> Finally, logicians call a "horned" syllogism a <term>dilemma</term>, which is, as it were, invincible.

---

->You skin it before it is slaughtered.<-

<note>original: "πρὶν ἐκφαχθαι, δέρεις."</note> That is: You skin before you slaughter. This is said whenever something seems to be done <term>preposterously</term> <note>literally "the back part first," or backwards.</note> It can be seen as taken from Homer, in whose works a bull is often skinned before it is killed: a figure that grammarians call <term>prothyron</term> <note>a Greek term for "the gate before the house," used here for a reversal of the natural order.</note>. It is close to what we have reported elsewhere: "To do what is done" <note>original: "Actum agere."</note>. For Marcus Tullius [Cicero] also thinks that adage pertains to the meaning of doing things backwards. For he writes thus in the dialogue *On Friendship*: "For we use backwards counsels, and we do what is already done, which we are forbidden to do by the old proverb."

---

->Before the flour is roasted.<-

<note>original: "πρὶν ὀπῆσαι ἄλευρα."</note> That is: Before you have cooked the flour; one must understand "you sprinkle it," or something similar. Eustathius, in the commentary on the *Odyssey*, book 7, mentions both this and the previous adage. For it is customary for some to sprinkle flour on roasted meats.

->More people worship the rising sun than the setting sun.<-

<note>original: "πλείους προσκυνοῦσι τὸν ἥλιον ἀνατέλλοντα ἢ δύνοντα."</note> That is: More people worship the rising sun than...

<meta>catchword: than</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the adage "To adore the rising sun," explaining that people naturally favor rising power over fading glory. It then moves through several adages regarding bribery, rewards, insignificant critics, and the unchanging nature of character.</meta>

# THIRD CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

...than the setting one. It would cling more to a young man than an old one. Plutarch writes that Pompey threatened Cinna <note>Historical sources usually record Pompey saying this to Sulla, but Erasmus here follows a version mentioning Cinna.</note> with this adage. Pompey perceived that he himself was the rising sun—namely, a young man whose fame was increasing daily—while the other was the setting sun, being of advanced age and someone whose dignity and glory were already growing old. Furthermore, what Pompey was to Cinna, Gaius Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> was later to Pompey. 

Something similar is found in the third book of Athenaeus, from some poet or other: "New things over old, for new things are at once better; young Jupiter reigns." <note>original: "τὰ καινὰ τὰ παλαιὰ, καινὰ γὰρ ἅμα κρείσσω, νέος ὁ Ζεὺς βασιλεύει."</note> That is, I do not sing of ancient things: if there are new things, they are both new and better; Jupiter, who is young, is the one who rules. It was the custom among the ancients to adore the sun, which they considered a god, and it was especially worshipped by the Persians under the name of Mithras. Likewise, it was called Osiris among the Egyptians, Apollo among the Greeks, and by various other names among others. They would salute the sun at its rising for religious reasons. Plato records that Socrates followed this custom. They even say that elephants adore the sun at its rising. The setting sun was also saluted, but by fewer people. Every human life also has its own evening, which, as soon as it arrives, turns the grace of youth into weariness. Thus a certain old man says in the works of Alexis: 
"For already my life leads toward evening." <note>original: "ἤδη γὰρ ὁ βίος ἐμός ἑσπέραν ἄγει."</note> That is: 
Indeed, my life leads into the late evening. 
Moreover, shadows fall toward the setting of the sun; hence Euripides says: 
"What else is an old man but a voice and a shadow?" <note>original: "τί δ' ἄλλο φωνὴ καὶ σκιὰ γέρων ἀνήρ;"</note> That is: 
What else is an old man than a voice and a shadow?

### XVI. When gold speaks, any speech is powerless.

"When gold speaks, every word is ineffective; for how could one not speak if he is born to it?" <note>original: "Χρυσοῦ λαλοῦντος πᾶς ἀπρακτάτω λόος, πόθεν γὰρ εἶδε καὶ πέφυκε μὴ λέγων."</note> That is: 
When gold speaks, any reasoning is useless, 
Since it knows how to persuade, even while saying nothing. 
The proverb indicates that gifts everywhere have by far the greatest power. A common joke says that "tinkling reasons" <note>A metaphor for the sound of coins.</note> have the principal force in persuading—referring to money.

### XVII. A Pellenean cloak.

"A Pellenean tunic." <note>original: "πελλωναῖος χιτών."</note> That is, a Pellenean garment. This concerns ancient dress. Pellene is a very ancient city of Achaia, the homeland of Proteus, in which various forms of clothing used to be made, as Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> bears witness. Julius <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century grammarian.</note> in the seventh book of his *On the Names of Things*, recorded that Pellenean cloaks were once famous, so much so that in the games and contests of Juno, a Pellenean cloak was given as a prize to the victor. Strabo confirms this in the eighth book of his *Geography*. Therefore, this seems different from what we mentioned elsewhere as a "Levidense gift" <note>A term for a slight or thinly-woven gift.</note>; it will be more elegant if used ironically. For example, if a cheap little gift is sent to someone in return for laborious and long-lasting services, we might say a "Pellenean cloak" has fallen to them. Juvenal also indicates that at Rome, the clothes of the elders were customary in military service.

### XVIII. The crow provokes the eagle.

"The crow provokes the eagle." <note>original: "Αἰτὸν κορώνη ἐρεθικελᾶ."</note> They say it is a peculiar trait of crows to annoy the eagle. But the eagle ignores the provocateur, understanding, of course, that it cannot be harmed by it. The adage would therefore be appropriate whenever some insignificant little man, who can neither help nor hinder, barks at great men. Just as Menelaus says about prophets in Euripides’ *Iphigenia in Aulis*: 
"A useless evil, not useful even when present." <note>original: "Κακὸν γ' ἄχρηστον ὀυδὲ χρήσιμον παρόν."</note> That is: 
But it possesses nothing either useful or useless.

### XIX. The wolf changes his hair, not his mind.

"The wolf changes his hair, not his disposition." <note>original: "ὁ λύκος τὴν τρίχα, οὐ τὴν γνώμην ἀλλάζει."</note> Old age brings grayness to the wicked, but it does not likewise take away their malice. For wolves grow gray with age, just as horses and humans do.

### XX. A snare has caught a snare.

"A snare, it seems, has caught a snare once." <note>original: "Ἄπαξ ἡ πάγη ἔοικε λήψεσθαι πάγην."</note> That is: A snare has caught a snare, so it seems. Used when one bad person watches another: such as an adulterer watching an adulterer, a thief a thief, a treacherous person a treacherous person; which sometimes happens in practice, so that while two people are laying traps for each other, each catches the other.

### XXI. You have touched the very threshold of the door.

"You have touched the very threshold of the door itself with your foot." <note>original: "Αὐτὸν κεκρίκας τὸν βατῆρα τῆς θύρας."</note> 
It is said to be common whenever one arrives at the heart of the matter. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES

...life is already setting." <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page.</note> But come, for you have arrived at the very door; know that you have come to the gates themselves. <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἴθ’ ἐπ’ αὐτὴν τὴν θύραν ἀφιγμένοι. id est, Sed noueris uenisse te ipsas ad fores." This indicates being at the very threshold of a matter.</note>

->The rooster leaps in.<-

<margin>XX</margin>
The rooster rings his bell. <note>original: "Ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐπικωδίζει" (Alektryon epikodizei). Erasmus translates the sense as "the rooster leaps in."</note> That is, the rooster leaps to the attack. This is used whenever someone who has been beaten once renews the contest. It is taken from the behavior of fighting cocks, for it is the habit of this creature to incite itself to battle so that it may strike more effectively with its spurs, which were attached to it by nature for this purpose.

->Now wisdom herself lives.<-

<margin>XXI</margin>
Now wisdom herself lives. <note>original: "Αὐτὴ νῦν σοφία ζῇ" (Autē nyn sophia zē).</note> This is the speech of someone applauding and congratulating another, whenever something is seen to be said or done with particular skill and art. It becomes even more witty if it is used ironically against those who handle excellent matters in the most foolish way.

->Now the Muse herself flourishes.<-

<margin>XXII</margin>
Now the Muse herself flourishes. <note>original: "Αὐτὴ νῦν ἀνθεῖ ἡ μοῦσα" (Autē nyn anthei hē mousa).</note> This is very similar to the previous adage. It is used when something is seen to be said or done with erudition, eloquence, and charm, as if the Muses themselves were granting success. Here too, it becomes more charming through irony, when someone thinks they are speaking wonderfully while actually speaking most insipidly.

->The burden of a ship.<-

<margin>XXIII</margin>
The burden of a ship. <note>original: "Ἄχθος νεώς" (Achthos neōs).</note> This is appropriately used for the lazy and useless. <margin>Indeed, a mere burden of the earth.</margin> <margin>Similar to that: A useless burden of the field.</margin> <note>original: "Ἐτώσιον ἄχθος ἀρούρης" (Etōsion achthos arourēs).</note> That is, a useless weight upon the ground. It also fits someone who is both large and troublesome, for ships carry a far greater load than wagons. I have discussed "wagon-sized" things elsewhere.

->Fresh-water speech washes away the salty hearing.<-

<margin>XXIV</margin>
He washed away the salty hearing with a drinkable speech. <note>original: "Ἁλμυρὰν ἀκοὴν ἀπεκλύσατο ποτίμῳ λόῳ" (Halmyran akoēn apeklysato potimō logō).</note> That is, he diluted a bitter conversation with a drinkable discourse; it is used when something that was painful to hear is, as it were, sweetened by a different kind of speech. What applies to taste is here transferred to the ears. For what seawater is to the palate, a grim or insulting speech is to the ears. Likewise, what spring water is to the palate, a calm and kind speech is to the hearing. Plato uses this adage in the *Phaedrus*: <margin>I desire to wash away the salty hearing, as it were, with a drinkable speech.</margin> <note>original: "ἐπιθυμῶ ποτίμῳ λόῳ οἷον ἁλμυρὰν ἀκοὴν ἀποκλύσασθαι."</note> That is, I wish to dilute a bitter speech with one that is potable. Likewise, Athenaeus in the third book of the *Sophists at Dinner*: <margin>After these things were said, Cynulcus asked for a cold drink, saying that bitter words should be washed away with sweet streams.</margin> <note>original: "ἐπὶ τούτοις λεχθεῖσιν ὁ κύνηλκος πιεῖν ᾔτησε ψυχρόν τε, λέγων ἁλμυροὺς λόγους γλυκέσιν ἀποκλύσεσθαι νάμασιν."</note> That is, after these words, Cynulcus asked for a choice drink, saying it was proper to dilute bitter speeches with sweet waters. Cynulcus used a Roman idiom even though he was speaking Greek; indeed, when Ulpian was indignant that he used an unusual and "barbarous" word, Cynulcus replied that he was in the city of Rome and used the native vocabulary of the Roman city. For there, they spoke in this way: "He asked for a cold," or "He asked for a hot," or "a boiled," with the word "water" being understood.

->Arcadian sprout.<-

<margin>XXV</margin>
An Arcadian sprout. <note>original: "Ἀρκάδιον βλάστημα" (Arkadion blastēma).</note> That is, an Arcadian germ, usually said of those who are physically large but lazy. Juvenal says:
> Because in the left part of the breast
> Nothing beats for the Arcadian youth.
<note>Juvenal, *Satires* 7.159-160. This implies the youth has no wit or "heart" for learning.</note>

The Arcadians formerly had a bad reputation for dullness of mind. Athenaeus writes much about their "savagery" in his fourteenth book, noting they were the first who refused to admit any music into their state, nor any liberal disciplines, through the cultivation of which human minds grow mild. Hence, through both the fault of the climate and the neglect of education, they became wild with a total savagery of character. Lucian, in his booklet *On Astrology*, records that the Arcadians were considered stupid for the reason that while everyone else embraced astrology, they alone despised it, claiming they were older than the moon itself. For this reason, they were called "pre-lunar." <note>original: "προσέληνοι" (proselēnoi).</note> The same people are mocked in the jokes of epigrams as "acorn-eaters," <note>original: "βαλανηφάγοι" (balanēphagoi).</note> that is, living on acorns. For this was the food of primitive men before grain was discovered. The epigram goes:
<margin>There are many acorn-eating men in Arcadia.</margin> <note>original: "πολλοὶ ἐν ἀρκαδίᾳ βαλανηφάγοι ἄνδρες ἔασιν."</note> That is:
Many men are in Arcadia, whose nourishment is acorns.
Aristophanes, in *The Birds*, mocks those who boast of their antiquity with various titles:
<margin>And even than Zeus himself</margin>
<margin>You were more ancient, and prior to Cronus and the Titans.</margin> <note>original: "Καὶ τοῦ Διὸς αὐτοῦ / Ἀρχαιότεροι, πρότεροί τε κρόνου, καὶ τιτάνων ἐγένοντο."</note> That is:
You were older than both Cronus and the Titans.

->Here is Rhodes, here is the leap.<-

<margin>XXVI</margin>
Here is Rhodes, here is the leap. <note>original: "Αὐτοῦ ῥόδος, αὐτοῦ πήδημα" (Autou rhodos, autou pēdēma).</note> That is: Here is Rhodes, here is the jump. Commonly tossed at those who...
