He also examines the cultural reputation of the Arcadians as ancient but dull-witted "acorn-eaters."</summary>
<keywords>cockfighting, wisdom, Muses, maritime metaphors, Plato, Athenaeus, Arcadians, Juvenal, astrology, Aristophanes, Rhodes</keywords>

--- Page 821 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Greek adages, beginning with a famous proverb regarding boasting and performance, followed by historical and mythological references to war, grief, and social behavior.</meta>

...they boast too insolently about some business for which no proof exists. It is taken from a fable attributed to Aesop. To a certain young man boasting that while he was at Rhodes he had performed admirable leaps, one of the listeners interrupted his speech and said: <note>original: "ἰδού ῥόδος, ἰδού πήδημα" (Idou Rhodos, idou pēdēma)</note> "Here is Rhodes, here is the leap." <note>This famous retort means "Prove it here and now."</note> This is appropriate whenever someone is commanded to perform on the spot what they boast of having done elsewhere. Ovid says:
> Let Ulysses tell of the deeds
> He performs without a witness.

I believe that what is said in Theocritus in the *Wayfarers* is related to this:
<note>original: "Αὐτόθι μοι ποτὶ ἴσδε, καὶ αὐτόθι βωκολιάσδευ" (Autothi moi poti isde, kai autothi bōkoliasdeu)</note>
> Compete with me right here, and right here graze your bulls.

Some people speak gloriously when it is safe; when danger is present, they turn away. This verse could be sung against them. By a similar figure, the Greeks, when they command that ready money be counted out immediately, say: <note>original: "αὐτοῦ καταβάλλε" (autou kataballe)</note> "Lay it down in this very place." In Athenaeus, book six: "On the condition that you lay down the money itself right here." Then, if you count out ready money—although in the printed books it is written as <note>original: "αὐτοῖς" (autois)</note> "to them," it is an error, unless I am mistaken.

### Archidamian war. <margin>XXIX</margin>

<note>original: "Ἀρχιδάμιος πόλεμος" (Archidāmios polemos)</note> That is, an Archidamian war. This was said of a savage and cruel war, an epithet taken from Archidamus, the leader of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, who made an incursion into Attica with very great forces and harassed it for ten years. He inflicted the most grievous harm upon the Acharnians by cutting down all their trees, as Synesius also testifies in the *Praise of Baldness*. Consequently, when everything is utterly destroyed, it was called an Archidamian war. The interpreter of the speeches of Demosthenes mentions this adage, indicating that it appeared in Lysias. Pausanias also mentions the cruelty of Archidamus in his *Description of Laconia*.

### You anoint a dead man with ointment. <margin>XXX</margin>

<note>original: "Νεκρὸν μυρίζεις" (Nekron myrizeis)</note> That is, you anoint a dead man with ointment. This refers to a superfluous expense, or when something is applied too late. It was a custom among the ancients, especially the Egyptians, to anoint the corpses of the deceased with ointments so they would not rot. This custom still lasts in these times among princes, like many other pagan practices, as a great proof of foolishness.

### The dead man lies farting. <margin>XXXI</margin>

<note>original: "Νεκρὸς κεῖται βδέων" (Nekros keitai bdeōn)</note> That is, the dead man lies farting. It was usually said if a poor man were to feign wealth. I found it in the works of one Apostolius of Byzantium; I do not know whether it should be left to him and the common folk. <note>Erasmus often expresses skepticism toward the reliability of Michael Apostolius's collection of proverbs.</note>

### Exchanged cables and oars for weapons. <margin>XXXII</margin>

<note>original: "Νηΐα καὶ κωπέας ἀνθ’ ὅπλων ἀλλάξαντο" (Nēia kai kōpeas anth’ hoplōn allaxanto)</note> That is:
> They exchanged oars and nautical ropes for arms.

This will be appropriate when someone leaves behind a craft or a customary gain, moved by a desire for glory—as if a sailor were to become a soldier, or a merchant a priest. <term>Nēia</term> are nautical ropes; <term>kōpeas</term> are the pieces of wood from which oars are prepared.

### Niobe’s sorrows. <margin>XXXIII</margin>

<note>original: "Νιόβης πάθη" (Niobes pathē)</note> That is, Niobe’s sufferings. It was said of the greatest and most bitter evils. Niobe was the daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion; she had six sons and as many daughters. Growing insolent at this success, she despised Latona <note>Leto</note>, who was the mother of only two, Apollo and Diana. For the fables tell that after her children were killed, she grew stiff with moderate grief. The commentator on Homer relates that the rock which gave occasion to the fable can be seen on Mount Sipylus in Phrygia, pouring forth fountains of tears. Ovid, in the sixth book of the *Metamorphoses*, telling the story most elegantly, speaks thus of the rock:
> Yet she weeps, and wrapped in a whirlwind of strong wind
> She was snatched to her native land, where fixed on a mountain peak
> She melts, and even now the marble flows with tears.

Those who perish utterly are said by the Greeks <note>original: "πανοικὶ ἀναρπάζειν" (panoiki anarpazein)</note> "to be snatched away with their whole house," as when a pestilence leaves no survivor in a family.

### He shaves even to the skin. <margin>XXXIIII</margin>

<note>original: "Ξυρεῖ ἐν χρῷ" (Xyrei en chrō)</note> That is, he shaves all the way to the skin. Grammarians cite this from Sophocles. It was said of one who seemed to deal too exactly with someone else. It is taken from barbers, some of whom shave through a comb, leaving as it were the stumps of the hairs, while others shave without a comb, right down to the living skin. Plautus in *The Captives*: "But whether I should say he is going to shave me close, or through a comb..."

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### A good sign, or a bad one.
<margin>x</margin>
<note>original: "σύμβολον ἀγαθὸν ἢ καὶ φαῦλον" (sýmbolon agathón ē kai phaūlon)</note> A good sign, or certainly a bad one. Used when someone predicts things that are uncertain. They say a "symbolum" <note>A token or sign</note> refers to an omen taken from seeds, which pertained to the goddess Ceres. They also called the first person one encountered—from which people would anticipate certain outcomes—a "symbolum." Furthermore, this figure of speech was familiar in the past, as evidenced by Homer and Plato. Likewise, in Horace, the prophet Tiresias says:
> Whatever I say will either happen, or it will not.

### Chasing two hares, he catches neither.
<margin>x</margin>
<note>original: "ὁ δύο πτῶκας διώκων, οὐδ' ἕτερον καταλαμβάνει" (ho dyo ptōkas diōkōn, oud' heteron katalambanei)</note> That is: He who hunts two hares catches neither. The meaning of this proverb is: He who seeks a double advantage at the same time fails in both. It is found in the Greek collections even without the metaphorical language: <note>original: "Δυοῖν ἐπιθυμήσας οὐδετέρῳ ἐτυχε" (dyoin epithymēsas oudeterō etyche)</note> "Desiring two things, you achieved neither."

### He who has much pepper even mixes it with vegetables.
<margin>xi</margin>
<note>original: "ὁ πολὺ ἔχων πέπερι, τίθησι κἂν λαχάνοις" (ho poly echōn peperi, tithēsi kan lachanois)</note> That is: He who has a lot of pepper even adds it to the greens. When someone has a lavish supply of a thing, they are permitted to use it profusely. Conversely, that which is scarce must be used sparingly. For example, he who has a great wealth of resources may live sumptuously. That pepper was commonly mixed with vegetables is also testified by the poet Martial:
> So that the bland beets of the workmen may have flavor,
> Oh, how often the cook will seek out the pepper-wines!
I suspect that this saying was drawn from the common people. However, Hermolaus Barbarus uses it in a certain letter to Pico <note>Pico della Mirandola</note>. Similar to this is what we have recorded elsewhere: "The rotten fungus loves oregano."

### A friendly home is the best home.
<margin>xx</margin>
<note>original: "οἶκος φίλος, οἶκος ἄριστος" (oikos philos, oikos aristos)</note> That is:
->A welcome home is always the best home.<-
Nowhere does a man happen to live more comfortably, more freely, or more elegantly than at home. Some jokingly twist this to refer to the tortoise, about whom a fable is told: When Jupiter had invited every kind of living creature to his wedding, and the rest had come, the tortoise alone was missing. Finally, after the banquet was finished, she arrived. Jupiter, wondering what had caused her delay, asked the reason. She replied: <note>original: "οἶκος φίλος, οἶκος ἄριστος"</note> "Home is dear, home is best." Jupiter, angered, commanded that wherever she went, she should carry her home with her. Hence, she is described with humorous obscurity in the second book of Cicero’s *On Divination*:
> The slow-moving creature of the earth, carrying its house, lacking blood.
For I believe one should read "creature of the earth" <note>original: "terrigenam"</note> instead of "earth" <note>original: "terrae"</note>. Furthermore, public laws favor private security. Thus Gaius says in the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, Book 4, title *On Summoning to Court*: "Most have thought that no one should be allowed to be summoned to court from their own house, because the home is the safest refuge and sanctuary for everyone, and he who summons someone from there seems to commit violence." Paulus says similar things in Book 1, title *On the Rules of Law*. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> alluded to this fable in a certain letter to Dolabella: "These places are charming and certainly pleasant, and if you wish to write anything, they are free from observers; but I know not how it is, 'Home is dear.' For my feet carry me back to my villa at Tusculum." To this corresponds another saying we have placed elsewhere: <note>original: "οἴκοι μένειν δεῖ τὸν καλῶς εὐδαίμονα" (oikoi menein dei ton kalōs eudaimona)</note> That is:
->He must stay at home whose fates are prosperous. For to him alone,<-
->Home is dear, home is best.<-
Otherwise, for a man who has a brawling wife at home and nothing to eat, his house is a prison. Plutarch calls this lazy kind of person—who delights in the roof and the shade and always wants to sit idle at home—a "house-watcher" <note>original: "οἰκουρὸς" (oikouros)</note>, as if you were to say, "guardians of the house." And in his booklet *On the Preservation of Health*, he does not approve of this "house-watching and inaction." The same author relates in his *Conjugal Precepts* that the sculptor Pheidias depicted the goddess Venus treading on a tortoise, silently signifying that wives ought to stay at home and keep silent. He also recounts that the Egyptians had a custom that brides should not use sandals, specifically so they would never leave the house. Yet this image by no means fits our modern women, who "fly" through every marketplace, every wine-shop, and finally through every land and sea. To this we should add what Plutarch reports in the life of...

### THE THIRD HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND
Nn 2
<meta>catchword: adds</meta>

...Flamininus. <note>original: "miniũ" refers to Titus Quinctius Flamininus, a Roman general</note> He, when discouraging the Achaeans from claiming the island of Zacynthus for themselves, used to say that <note>original: "κινδυνεύειν αὐτοὺς ὡς χελῶναν ποῤῥωτέρω τὴν κεφαλὴν τῆς πελοποννήσου προτείνωσιν" (kindyneúein autoùs hōs chelōnan porrhōtérō tēn kephalēn tēs peloponnēsou proteínōsin)</note> they were in danger, just like tortoises, if they extended their heads too far from the Peloponnese. Titus Livius writes something similar concerning the Macedonian War in his thirty-sixth book <note>The OCR reads "sexto" (sixth), but this quote appears in Livy's Book 36</note>, where Quinctius speaks thus: "If I thought the possession of that island would be useful to the Achaeans, I would advise the Senate and People of Rome to allow you to have it. However, just as I see a tortoise is safe from all blows when it is pulled into its own shell, but has whatever part it exposes vulnerable and weak when it sticks any part out: not unlike you, Achaeans, whose boundaries are enclosed on all sides by the sea that lies within the Peloponnese, can easily join such places to yourselves and protect them once joined. But if, once seized by the greed of grasping more, you go beyond those bounds, everything you have outside will be naked and exposed to all blows."

->Do not wash a donkey’s head with soap.<-
XXXIX
<note>original: "ὄνου κεφαλὴν μὴ πλύνειν νίτρῳ" (ónou kephalēn mē plýnein nítrō)</note> That is: Do not wash a donkey's head with nitre. <note>Nitre or soda, used as a cleansing agent</note> One should not spend much expense or effort on a cheap and filthy thing. Related to this is: <note>original: "τὴν χοῖραν ποικίλλειν" (tēn choīran poikíllein)</note> To decorate a cooking pot <note>literally "the pig," often used to refer to a common earthenware vessel</note>.

->The jawbone of an ass.<-
XL
<note>original: "ὄνου γνάθος" (ónou gnáthos)</note> That is: The jawbone of an ass. It applies to gluttons, or otherwise to the stupid and lazy. Horace depicts such people:
->We are but a number, born only to consume the fruits of the earth.<-
Hesychius cites this from Eupolis, saying it was used against gluttonous men. He adds that it is also the name of a place. And I wonder if he means the place where Samson found the donkey’s jawbone, which is mentioned in Judges 15.

->He has eyes in the back of his head.<-
XLI
<note>original: "ὄπισθεν κεφαλῆς ὄμματα ἔχει" (ópisthen kephalēs ómmata échei)</note> That is: In the back of the head he has eyes. Said of the shrewd and circumspect, whom it is by no means easy to deceive. Persius calls this kind of man "Januses":
>O Janus, behind whose back no stork-beak mocks. <note>Referring to the Roman god Janus who had two faces, preventing people from making mocking gestures behind his back</note>
And Homer requires a leader to be sharp-eyed <note>original: "πρόσσω καὶ ὀπίσσω" (próssō kai opíssō)</note>, that is: before and behind. Plautus in the *Aulularia* says: "She who has eyes in the back of her head as well."

->Unless the clay is beaten, the pitcher is not made.<-
XLII
<note>original: "ὁ πηλὸς ἢν μὴ δαρῇ, κέραμος οὐ γίνεται" (ho pēlòs ēn mē darē, kéramos ou gínetai)</note> That is: Clay, unless it is beaten, does not become a vessel. Without labor, no one turns out to be a finished man. And this, unless I am mistaken, Apostolicus <note>Likely referring to the scholar Michael Apostolius</note> drew from the dregs of the common folk: a man not as elegant in talent as he was in his palate, as we have heard from those who knew him through domestic habit.

->Men are deceived by oaths, children by dice.<-
XLIII
<note>original: "ὅρκοις ἄνδρας, ἀστραγάλοις δὲ παῖδας ἐξαπατέον" (hórkois ándras, astragálois dè paīdas exapatéon)</note> That is: One ought to deceive men with oaths, but children with knucklebones. <note>An ancient form of dice</note> It teaches that men can be tricked by nothing more quickly than an oath, which no one would believe any man so wicked as to want to violate. This was a saying of Lysander, the leader of the Spartans, according to Plutarch.

->You are looking for birds.<-
XLIIII
<note>original: "ὄρνεις ζητεῖς" (órneis zētēis)</note> That is: You are looking for birds. You are pursuing a wandering thing that is difficult to catch. Persius writes:
>Or do you chase crows everywhere with a shard and mud?
Likewise Aristotle says: <note>original: "τὰ πετώμενα διώκειν" (tà petōmena diōkein)</note> To pursue flying things. And before him, Plato in the *Euthyphro*: <note>original: "τί δ’ ὠκεώμενον τινα διώκεις;" (tí d’ ōkeōmenon tina diōkeis?)</note> "But why do you chase someone who is flying away?"

->Mountain does not mix with mountain.<-
XLV
<note>original: "ὄρος ὄρει οὐ μίγνυται" (óros órei ou mígnytai)</note> That is: Mountain is not mixed with mountain. It is not agreeable between those who are equally lofty or equally powerful. Even though Pliny records that two mountains once collided with a great crash, clashing and recoiling while a great crowd of people watched, and that during the day.

->He who feeds a stranger's dog.<-
XLVI
<note>original: "ὃς κύνα τρέφει ξένον, τούτῳ μόνον λίνον μένει" (hòs kýna tréphei xénon, toútō mónon línon ménei)</note> That is: He who feeds a foreign dog, nothing remains for him but the leash. He who bestows a favor on the ungrateful wastes his effort. For a strange dog, leaving the rope with which it is tied, returns to its original master. This too has a certain common flavor, in my opinion.

->When the Nibas crows.<-
XLVII
<note>original: "ὅτ’ ἂν νίβας κοκκύσῃ" (hót’ àn níbas kokkýsē)</note> That is: When the Nibas crows. Very similar to that saying, "At the Greek Kalends" <note>Meaning 'never'</note>. They say that in Thessaloniki, a city of Macedonia, there is a district named Nibas where the roosters never give voice. Just as cicadas are silent in some places. Furthermore, because in that place...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...he adds to the rooster; art achieves this by adding a collar made of twigs to the neck, if any credit is given to what Pliny <margin>Book 29, chapter 4</margin> recorded. Hesychius adds that crested goats are called *Nibades*, so that from them the word <term>crowing<note>original: "τὸ κοκκύζειν" (to kokkyzein)</note></term> is expressed, which is a characteristic of roosters.

->Fire is not extinguished by fire.<-
<margin>XL</margin>
<note>original: "πυρὶ πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται" (pyri pyr ou sbennytai)</note> That is: Fire is not extinguished by fire. Evil is not removed by evil: anger is not calmed by anger, but ferocity is calmed by gentleness; evil is removed by patience: injury is overcome by kindness. <note>original: "μὴ πῦρ ἐπὶ πῦρ" (mē pyr epi pyr)</note> "Do not add fire to fire," as we have recorded elsewhere from Plato and Plutarch.

->Not even the earth helped.<-
<margin>X</margin>
<note>original: "οὐδ' ἀπὸ γῆς ὤνησεν" (oud' apo gēs ōnēsen)</note> That is: Not even the earth was of use. This means not even in the slightest degree, as if one were to say he did not even grant a clod of dirt: or he did not even deem someone worthy of the hospitality of the land, as in the works of Virgil <note>Erasmus refers to him as "Maro," his cognomen</note>:
>We are barred from the hospitality of the sands:
>They stir up wars, and forbid us to stand on the edge of the land.

->No difficult buyer buys good food.<-
<note>original: "οὐδεὶς δυσώνης χρηστὸν ὀψωνεῖ κρέας" (oudeis dysōnēs chrēston opsōnei kreas)</note> That is:
The difficult buyer does not buy good victuals.
He who is too eager to buy at a bargain always buys defective goods. For it is not possible to buy at a low price and simultaneously buy something of excellent quality. This applies to those who attempt to attain distinguished learning with very little labor—learning which does not happen except through the greatest and most prolonged vigils. Unless I am mistaken, Julius Pollux noted this proverb in his sixth book *On the Names of Things*, when he denies that the word <term>hard-to-please buyer<note>original: "δυσώνης" (dysōnēs)</note></term> was used by classical authors, but is found only in the proverb.

->You cannot love both Thetis and Galatea at the same time.<-
<note>original: "οὐ δύνασαι θετιδός τε καὶ γαλατείας ἐρᾶν" (ou dynasai thetidos te kai galateias eran)</note> That is: You cannot love both Thetis and Galatea simultaneously. This means you cannot pursue different things at once, such as literature and money, pleasure and God, or the world and Christ. For Galatea, being of the river, fits poorly with the waves of the sea. Regarding this, there is a dialogue by Lucian between Galatea and Doris. I suspect this proverb was also drawn from the common dregs of the populace.

->Evil gain is equal to a loss.<-
A celebrated saying of Hesiod:
<note>original: "μὴ κακὰ κέρδαινε, κακὰ κέρδεα ἶσ' ἄτῃσιν" (mē kaka kerdaine, kaka kerdea is' atēsin)</note> That is:
Do not gain evilly; evil gains are equal to losses.
I wish that not only all mortals but especially merchants would inscribe this sentiment on their hearts, and consider that there is no "gain" which costs the loss of a good mind; nor that anything is "useful" which is not likewise "honorable." But to many, that line from Ennius is more pleasing: "No one asks where you got it from, but you must have it."

Sophocles expanded on Hesiod’s sentiment more broadly:
<note>original: "οὐκ ἐξ ἅπαντος δεῖ τὸ κερδαίνειν φιλεῖν. ἐκ τῶν γὰρ αἰσχρῶν λημμάτων πλείονας ἀτωμένους ἴδοις ἂν ἢ σεσωσμένους"</note> That is:
One should not love to seek profit from every source,
For from shameful gains you might see
More people ruined than saved.

Several proverbial iambic verses are carried in the same spirit:
<note>original: "κέρδος πονηρὸν ζημίαν ἀεὶ φέρει" (kerdos ponēron zēmian aei pherei)</note> That is:
A gain sought by fraud always leads to loss. And,
<note>original: "τὰ d' αἰσχρὰ κέρδη συμφορὰς ἐργάζεται" (ta d' aischra kerdē symphoras ergazetai)</note> That is:
But shameful gain brings about misfortune.
To this belongs what we have recorded elsewhere from Pindar’s *Isthmian Odes*: <note>original: "τὸ δὲ πὰρ δίκαν γλυκύ πικροτάτα μένει τελευτά"</note> That is: What is sweet against justice has a most bitter end.

->A friend of Thericles.<-
<note>original: "Θηρίκλειος φíλος" (Thērikleios philos)</note> That is: A friend of Thericles. A saying applied to heavy drinkers. Thericles was the first to devise a certain type of cup, as the author Eubulus is cited. Moreover, the invention was called by the name of the inventor. Indeed, the Greeks call a glass cup a <term>Thericlean<note>original: "θηρίκλειον" (thērikleion)</note></term>, according to Suidas. In the same author is found the saying: <note>original: "θηρικλέους τέκνον κύλιξ"</note> "The cup is the child of Thericles." Athenaeus cites Theopompus in *Nemea* as the author of this saying. Antiphanes calls it a "Thericlean instrument." But Athenaeus wrote more on this matter in his eleventh book, showing that Thericles was a certain Corinthian in the age...

# THIRD CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY

...that <note>original: "Aristophanis"</note> Aristophanes the Comic poet says there was a potter who, by a new art, was the first to fashion a turned cup from terebinth <note>A resinous wood from the turpentine tree</note>, which could not be distinguished from earthenware. Theophrastus mentions this matter in his books *On Plants*. The cup was sufficiently deep, with short handles, so that it could be carried at the hips, fashioned in the likeness of a womb, just as the same Athenaeus reports; it is uncertain whether the name was given to the cup from the man, or to the man from the cup. Others prefer to say it is called "Thericlean" <note>original: "δἰὰ τὸ θηρία ἐν αὐτῷ ἐντετυπῶσθαι"</note> because figures of wild beasts were engraved upon it. Pamphilus of Alexandria prefers the explanation that Bacchus, when making a libation from this cup, was accustomed to drive out wild beasts. But I shall leave the controversy over the name. This much is certain: that thereafter this kind of cup was called "Thericlean," and furthermore, even large mixing bowls were called "Thericlean." Similarly, cups made of wood on the inside but gilded on the outside were nonetheless called Thericlean, which Callimachus called <term>gold-cased<note>original: "χρυσόκασσα" (chrysokassa)</note></term>. Indeed, whatever someone had discovered through a new skill was called "Thericlean." Plutarch mentions this in the *Sayings of Scipio the Younger*, speaking of it as something singular and precious.

### Theagenes’ shrine to Hecate. LIIII

<margin>LIIII</margin>
<note>original: "Θεαγένους ἑκάτειον" (Theagenous hekateion)</note> That is: Theagenes’ shrine to Hecate. This was said against the superstitious and the ridiculously fearful. We read that this Theagenes was so superstitious that he kept a statue of Hecate <note>The goddess of magic and crossroads, often associated with protection or haunting</note> at home, and would never move a foot anywhere unless he had consulted it. From this he was also nicknamed <term>Smoke<note>original: "Καπνός" (Kapnos)</note></term>, because he would make magnificent promises although he was poor. We have mentioned this matter elsewhere.

### Through trust I lost my money. LV

<margin>LV</margin>
It is bandied about even today, and truly said, that most mortals are deceived by trust. It seems, however, to be left over from the proverbs of the ancients, since this little verse is read in Theognis:
> <note>original: "πίστ’ χρήματ’ ὤλεσα, ἀπιστίη δ’ ἐσάωσα"</note>
->id est,<-
> Through trust my wealth perished; through distrust it remained safe.
Accordingly, Epicharmus gives no bad advice: <note>original: "νῆφε καὶ μέμνη’ ἀπιστεῖν"</note> "Be sober, and remember to distrust." Although to trust no one is inhumane, to trust everyone is foolish. The former is more honorable, the latter more secure. This is because, as the same Theognis says:
> <note>original: "Παύροι τοι πολλῶν πιστὸν ἔχουσι νόον"</note>
->id est,<-
> Few among many possess a faithful mind.

### One thing standing, another sitting. LVI

<margin>LVI</margin>
No one would go so far as to deny that the saying of Sallust against Cicero was spoken with a proverbial figure: "He speaks one thing standing, another sitting." We may use this when we mean to signify a person's extreme inconstancy of mind, as if the slightest moment or interval changes the man's opinion. Homer, in the tenth book of the *Iliad*, notes the character of an inconstant man with a verse of this kind:
> <note>original: "ἀλλὰ μετακλίνει, καὶ ἐπ’ ἀμφοτέροις πόδας ἵζει"</note>
->id est,<-
> But he shifts, and wavers on both feet.
Pindar expresses the same sentiment thus in the third *Nemean Ode*: "The man who has escaped six times, breathing now one way, now another, has never descended with a sure foot, but catches a taste of a thousand virtues with an incomplete mind." Pindar prefers nature to training, because he who is good by nature is always like himself, whereas he who strives by learning, though he tries many things, is neither firm nor perfect in anything.

### A friend by the tongue. LVII

<margin>LVII</margin>
<margin>By the tongue.</margin>
<note>original: "Ἀπὸ γλώττης φίλος" (Apo glōttēs philos)</note> That is: A friend by the tongue—one who shows favor in words but does not provide help in reality. Or one who does not love from the heart, but displays goodwill in speech. This is the type of person Candidus is portrayed as in Martial. And in Homer's *Odyssey*, book 14:
> <note>original: "οἷ’ εὖ μὲν βάζουσι, kakῶς δ’ ὄπιθεν φρονέουσι"</note>
->id est,<-
> Those who speak well, but revolve evil thoughts behind one's back.
<margin>Theognis in his *Sentences*,</margin>
> <note>original: "Ἀλλὰ δ’ ὀκ’ μὲν πᾶσιν ἀπὸ γλώσσης φίλος εἴην, Χρῆμα δὲ συμμίξας μηδενὶ μηδ’ ὁτιοῦν"</note>
->id est,<-
> Act so that you seem a friend to all by your tongue,
> But beware of mixing your affairs with anyone in deed.
On the other hand, Sophocles says in *Antigone*:
> <note>original: "λόγοις δ’ ἐγὼ φιλοῦσαν οὐ στέργω φίλην"</note>
->id est,<-
> I do not love a female friend who loves only in words.
Yet the same Theognis, a little later, condemns this kind of friend.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, shifting from physical objects like "Thericlean" cups to moral and intellectual proverbs. It begins with verses on the hypocrisy of false friends before moving into sayings about old age, the necessity of hard work, and the importance of geometric study in Platonic philosophy.</meta>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

"Do not love me with words alone, while your mind and heart are elsewhere." <note>original Greek: "Μή μ' ἔπεσι μλν στέργε, νόον δ' ἔχε καὶ φρένας ἄλλῃ"</note> That is, do not delight in me with words when your mind is in another place.
Again, elsewhere:
"Let no man be a friend to me in tongue, but rather in deed." <note>original Greek: "Μή μοι ἀνὴρ εἴη γλώσσῃ φίλος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔργῳ"</note> That is, let no one be a friend to me in speech, but more so in action.
Very similar to this is what the same author reports elsewhere: "As far as a greeting." <note>original Greek: "μέχρι πλοσγοείας" (mechri prosreseos)</note> That is, only up to the point of saying hello.
"A friend is indeed a thing most difficult, for there are many—indeed, almost everyone—who are friends only as far as a greeting."
<note>Erasmus is quoting verses often attributed to Theognis or similar gnomic poets, emphasizing that true friendship requires more than superficial politeness.</note>

### Saturn's anus.

"Saturn’s buttocks." <note>original Greek: "Κρόνου πυγή" (Kronou pyge)</note> That is, Saturn's behind: used in reference to old meat, already maimed and lacking in sensation. 
For whatever the ancients wished to be understood as already rotten and exhausted, they called "Saturnian." 
Diogenianus mentions this, yet does not explain it. Suidas and Hesychius <note>Ancient Greek lexicographers often cited by Erasmus</note> advise that this was said of someone who is stupid due to old age and devoid of sense, named after the god Saturn, who provided many such proverbs. When applied to the mind, it will have a certain degree of wit.

### He who avoids the mill, avoids the flour.

"He who flees the mill, flees the meal." <note>original Greek: "Ὁ φεύγων μύλον, ἄλφιτα φεύγει"</note> That is, he who avoids the work of the mill, avoids the flour, or:
"Whoever shuns the mill, flees the flour."
For with the article omitted, it appears to be a half-line of heroic verse. He who refuses hard work shall not enjoy the rewards. There are those who are offended by the screeching of the mills, yet without mills it is impossible to live. Similarly, some cannot bear the behavior of wives, even though they desire children. The same is said commonly today: "He who seeks eggs must endure the <term>cackling<note>Erasmus compares the common term "cacalismus" with the more refined Latin "glocitum"</note></term> of the hens." Close to this is: "Where there is honey, there are bees." That is, you get neither the honey nor the bees <note>meaning you cannot have the sweet reward without the sting of the work</note>.

### Let no one ignorant of geometry enter.

"Let no one untrained in geometry enter." <note>original Greek: "Ἀγεωμέτρητος οὐδεὶς εἰσίτω"</note> This warns that an unjust person should not be admitted. For through geometry, men receive a sense of nobility, as found in Aristides’ *Themistocles*: "Where there is need of both equality and geometry." That is, where fairness and proportion are required. The same in *Pericles*: "If geometry is honorable, so too is the equality joined with it." Hence Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> cast out arithmetic from Sparta as being "popular" and turbulent, but introduced geometry as being suited to a modest oligarchy and a lawful kingdom, according to Plutarch. 

But in my opinion, the proverb will have more weight if you use it to mean "with unwashed feet" <note>original Greek: "ἀνίποις ποσίν" (aniptois posin)</note>—that is, rashly and unprepared. For these were the first rudiments of philosophy among the ancients: Music and Geometry. Those who were not initiated into these disciplines were not admitted into the school of Plato, whose inscription is said to have been: "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter." 

The philosopher Taurus speaks in this manner in the works of Aulus Gellius: "But now, for those who suddenly turn aside to philosophers 'with unwashed feet,' it is not enough that they are altogether <term>unreflective, unmusical, and unlearned in geometry<note>original Greek: "ἀθεώρητοι, ἄμουσοι, ἀγεωμέτρητοι"</note></term>." 

Pythagoras was a primary admirer of geometry; they say that upon discovering one specific problem, he sacrificed to the gods. It was of this sort: given two figures, to add a third different from them, which is equal to the one and similar to the other. Then there is Philo, who called geometry the "mother and metropolis" of all disciplines, because it demonstrates the images and traces of intelligible things as if in a highly polished mirror, and gradually leads the purified mind away from the senses. 

Plato is also believed to have said that "God himself always geometrizes," either because the study of geometry leads the mind away from corporeal things toward those which are always the same (for God is the purest of all, free from all matter), or because in the *Timaeus* he divided the principles of the world into three: God, matter, and the Idea. Matter is the substrate of all things, maimed, confused, and disordered; the Idea is the most beautiful of patterns; God is the best of causes. Since he thus founded the world, and always preserves it so that it is equal to the matter and similar to the Idea, he seems to be explaining that Pythagorean problem we just mentioned. 

Hesychius and many others of that kind say similar things. Plutarch, in the second problem of the eighth book of his *Table Talk*, says Plato seems to have emulated the solemn custom of inscribing such a thing upon the doors. There was a certain effeminate eunuch who had inscribed on the door of his house: "Let no evil enter." Diogenes said: "Then how shall the master of the house enter?" 

Socrates, in Plato’s *Theaetetus*, being about to dispute more subtle matters, says: "Look around and see that none of the uninitiated are listening." That is...

...now you will look around, lest any profane person overhear. He imitated Pythagoras, who prefaced his teachings thus: "Forbidden to the uninitiated, let the profane shut the doors." <note>original Greek: "Ἄβατα σωικοῖς, θύρας δ' ἐπίθεθε βέβηλοι"</note> That is:
> I shall sing to the wise, yet shut the doors, O profane one.

Which we have mentioned elsewhere.

### Unless a serpent eats a serpent, it will not become a dragon.
<margin>LXI</margin>
"Unless a serpent eats a serpent, it will not become a dragon." <note>original Greek: "Ὄφις ἢ μὴ φάγῃ ὄφιν, δράκων οὐ γενήσεται"</note> This means that a serpent will not become a dragon unless it devours another of its kind. Powerful men grow through the losses of others, and the fortunes of the elite would not increase so much if there were no ones for them to suck dry. Just as among fish and beasts, the larger live by tearing the smaller. Although, to me at least, this saying seems to smell of the common rabble.

### A contest does not accept excuses.
<margin>LXII</margin>
"A contest admits no excuses." <note>original Greek: "Ἀγὼν δ' ἔχεται σκήψεις"</note> Plato, in the sixth book of *The Laws*: "But they say a contest does not at all admit excuses." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀγῶνα προφάσεις οὐ πάνυ δέχεσθαί φασιν"</note> And: "A contest does not wait for an excuse." <note>original Greek: "ἀγὼν πρόφασιν οὐκ ἀναμένει"</note> When one is in danger, it is not fitting to hesitate or stall. Or, if you prefer: in immediate danger, one should not wait for an opportunity as one might in other matters. For instance, if someone in the grips of a fatal illness were to wait for a famous doctor or for one to be summoned from afar. This very thing killed that divine man, Rodolphus Agricola <note>A preeminent Dutch humanist and teacher whom Erasmus greatly admired</note>. For while the doctor delayed, death arrived first. To this belongs what we read in Quintus Curtius, book seven: "But necessity is before reason, especially in war, which rarely allows time to choose."

### A Phallus for the god.
<margin>LXIII</margin>
"The Phallus for the god." <note>original Greek: "Φαλλὸς τῷ θεῷ"</note> Usually said when things that are not very honorable, but nevertheless appropriate, are given; as if you were to say, "The donkey-driver to the thorn-bush" <note>original Greek: "ὀνηλάτῃ εἰς ἀκίδα"</note> or "To urinate into a chamber pot." Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Love of Wealth*, shows that this was the procession of the ancients in solemn games: first an amphora of wine and a vine-branch (that is, a kind of bean) were led; then someone dragged a goat; then another carried a basket of nuts; and in the last place, the Phallus was carried. That was an image of the obscene male member. Why it was received into the mysteries, Plutarch gives the reason in the book *On Isis and Osiris*. Columella, in verse, calls Priapus himself "Ithyphallus":
> But worship the divinity of the Ithyphallus,
> a trunk of an old tree by chance carved.

And Pompeius <note>Likely referring to Pompeius Festus, the grammarian</note> shows that "Ithyphallus" is the name for the shameful member of a man. From this, even today, the Italians, if they despise someone, mark him by this name. Herodotus mentions several things about Phalli in the second book. We have spoken elsewhere of the Phalli of Bacchus, namely in the proverb "The chickpea Bacchus."

### You disturb me in vain, like a wave.
<margin>LXIV</margin>
"You disturb me in vain, just like a wave." <note>original Greek: "ὀχλεῖς μάτην μὲ, κῦμ' ὅπως"</note> That is:
> You trouble me fruitlessly, as a wave does.

In other words, you are annoying to me to no purpose. This is a fragment of a poem from some poet, a metaphor taken from a wave constantly striking a rock. To which that line of Maro <note>Virgil</note> refers:
> Than if he stood as hard flint or Marpessian rock.

### Labor is the best seasoning for old age.
<margin>LXV</margin>
"Labor is the best seasoning for old age." <note>original Greek: "Ὀψον ἄριστον πόνῳ τῷ γήρᾳ"</note> One must labor in youth so that a means of living more comfortably is available to the old man. Diogenes, when asked what he thought was the most miserable thing, replied: "A destitute old age." However, the adage seems mutilated. Indeed, I think it should be read as "labor" <note>Greek: πόνῳ</note>, so that you understand the weakness of old age must be supported by more exquisite foods; for these to be available to the old man, resources must be prepared in youth.

### All debt is onions, and the fine is garlic.
<margin>LXVI</margin>
"All debt is onions, and the fine is garlic." <note>original Greek: "Πᾶν μοι χρέος κρόμμυα, καὶ ἡ τίμημα σκόροδα"</note> One must understand the word "is" <note>Greek: ἔστι</note>. This is used when someone bound by much debt hopes he can pay off whatever he owes with something of little value. I fear somewhat that Apostolius <note>Michael Apostolius, a 15th-century Greek scholar and collector of proverbs</note> drew this not from ancient authors, but from his own drinking companions.

### It is necessary for all crested larks.
<margin>LXVII</margin>
"It is necessary for all crested larks to have a crest." <note>original Greek: "Πᾶσι κορυδαλοῖσι χρὴ λόφον ἐγγενέσθαι"</note> This is cited from Simonides and used several times by Plutarch, specifically in the *Life of Timoleon*, in this sense: there is no mortal talent in which some vice is not mixed; just as it is natural for a man's nature not to lack vice, so it is natural for a crested lark to have a crest. I will subjoin Plutarch's words: "Since it is a swallow, as it seems, which alone... that a crest should be born in all crested larks..." <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

<margin>LX...</margin>
"Not just according to Simonides, but in every democracy there is a sycophant." <note>original Greek: "μὴ σιμωνίδου, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάσῃ δημοκρατίᾳ συκοφάντων"</note> That is: Just as it is necessary to see that a crest is present on every crested lark, as Simonides said, so too is a sycophant found in every democracy. Aristophanes mentions the *Corydus* <note>the crested lark</note> in *The Birds*, recounting a charming fable from Aesop. He says this bird was the oldest of all creatures, born even before the earth itself; when its father died of a disease and there was no ground to bury him in, the bird buried its father in its own head—which is why its crest stands in place of a burial mound. In that place, the bird established its kingdom. In the same work, Aristophanes indicates that a certain Philoctetes, who had a deformed, cone-shaped head, was nicknamed "Corydus." This matches a saying of Crates, recorded in Diogenes Laertius, that it is nearly impossible to find anyone entirely free of vice; rather, in every pomegranate <note>Erasmus uses the term "Punic apple"</note> there is some rotten seed.

### Having devoured the whole ox, he failed at the tail.
<margin>LX</margin>
"Having chewed through the whole ox, he grew weary at the tail." <note>original Greek: "πάντα ἐκτραγὼν τὸν βοῦν, εἰς τὴν οὐρὰν ἀπεκάμη"</note> That is: after the rest of the business was finished, he became exhausted at the very end. The wording seems a bit rough, perhaps corrupted by time, but it carries the flavor of common folk speech.

### He digs a well next to the river.
<margin>L</margin>
"He digs a well beside the river." <note>original Greek: "παρὰ ποταμὸν φρέαρ ὀρύττει"</note> Said of foolish and useless labor. It is similar to the saying, "He carries wood into the forest." Wells are dug because of a lack of water; to dig one next to a river is redundant.

### More changeable than Erysichthon’s Metra.
<margin>L</margin>
"More changeable than Metra, daughter of Erysichthon." <note>original Greek: "μεταβλητότεροϛ μήτρας τῆϛ ἐρισίχθονοϛ"</note> This applies to someone who is inconsistent, constantly taking on one persona after another. In ancient fables, it is told that the girl Metra was able to transform herself into various shapes. The story goes as follows: Erysichthon, a man of Thessaly, fell into extreme poverty after consuming all his resources. He had a daughter of outstanding beauty named Metra. Whenever he put her up for sale <note>or prostituted her for gain</note>, young men would flock to her, bringing various gifts—one bringing horses, another oxen, another sheep. In those times, gold, silver, and gems were not yet in use. The Thessalians would joke that Erysichthon’s Metra "turned into" all those things which were given to her by her lovers. Hence the proverb. Ovid treats the story of Erysichthon in the eighth book of his *Metamorphoses*.

### A Maltese lapdog.
<margin>L</margin>
"A Maltese little dog." <note>original Greek: "Μελιταῖον κυνίδιον"</note> This is aimed at someone who is kept as a pet, or rather, who is nourished in idleness for pleasure rather than for any use. There are three types of dogs: some are used for hunting, which they call "trackers" <note>original Greek: ἰχνεύταϛ</note>; some are put in charge of guarding the house, called "house-watchers" <note>original Greek: οἰκουροί</note>; and some are fed for the sake of the spirit and for the amusement of women—these they call "Maltese" or "honey-dogs." It is of these that Plato says, "Little dogs imitating their mistresses." <note>original Greek: τὰ κυνίδia μιμούμενα τὰϛ δεσποινάϛ</note> And Gorgo, in Theocritus’s *Syracusan Women*, when she is about to go out, commands her maid to quiet the crying infant and "call the little dog inside." Lucian speaks very mockingly of a bearded Stoic philosopher who, while sitting in a carriage, was entrusted with a lapdog by his mistress; she begged him to care for it by all that is sweetest in life. In the households of the wealthy today, there is a similar class of servants whom they keep at home not for service, but for entertainment.

### Lest avoiding the ash, you fall into the coals.
<margin>LX</margin>
"Lest fleeing the ash, you fall into the charcoal-pan." <note>original Greek: "μὴ τέφραν φεύγων εἰς ἀνθρακιὰν πέσηϛ"</note> This means: do not flee one evil only to run into another much greater one. The text here seems slightly corrupted; it would be clearer if "fall down into" were read instead of "fall."

### Since you are not a Syrian, do not "syrize."
<margin>LX</margin>
"Being no Syrian, do not act like one." <note>original Greek: "μὴ ὢν σύρος μὴ συρίζε"</note> Do not take on a persona that does not suit you, nor wish to seem other than you are. Or: though you were born free, do not behave like a slave or a barbarian. For Syrians had a bad reputation for soft and decadent manners. There is a witty pun here based on the ambiguity of the word *syrizo*, which means both "to act like a Syrian" and "to play the pipe."

### Do not move a straw.
<margin>LX</margin>
"Do not move a straw." <note>original Greek: "μὴ κάρφοϛ κινήϛ"</note> A proverbial phrase for someone who cannot tolerate the slightest noise. You might see some people so cranky that they are offended by whatever you do, even if you only move a bit of chaff.

### While it is tiny, the thorn seems good.
<margin>L</margin>
"From a small size, the thorn appears good." <note>original Greek: "μικρόθεν ἡ ἄκανθα ἀγαθὴ φαίνεται"</note> Childhoo...

<page-num>705</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY</header>

...thoroughly lovely. Just as a thorn too is harmless, and even edible, until it hardens with age. I believe he is speaking of asparagus. There is also a saying tossed about among theologians: "He who is greater in age is greater in iniquity." Such is the condition of human affairs, that all things of their own accord degenerate for the worse. It is quoted from Diphilus <note>A Greek poet of New Comedy, c. 342–291 BCE</note>:
"Old age is a gray-haired craftsman, O stranger;
It delights in reshaping everyone for the worse." <note>original Greek: "Πολιὸς τεχνίτης ἐστὶν ὁ χρόνος ὦ ξένε, Χαίρει μεταπλάττων πάντας ἐπὶ τὰ χείρονα"</note> That is:
Time is a hoary artist, O Jupiter:
For it rejoices in making all things worse.

### Moschus singing in the Boeotian style. LXXVI
"Moschus singing in the Boeotian style." <note>original Greek: "Μόσχος ᾄδων Βοιωτόν"</note> This Moschus was an unskilled lyre-player <term>citharode: a professional performer who sings while playing the lyre</term> who would draw out his voice for a long time without taking a breath. He calls "Boeotian" a type of melody, just like the Phrygian or Dorian modes. It will suit those who talk too much, yet speak foolishly.

### Then there was the thread of contention. LXXVII
"Then there was the thread of contention." <note>original Greek: "Μίτος ἐρίδος τότε ἦν"</note> This was usually said of stubborn people, when both are obstinate and neither yields to the other. It appears several times in the letters of Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century church father known for his Latin translation of the Bible</note> as "to pull the rope of contentions," and I do not recall reading it in any other author except in Tertullian at the beginning of his book *Against the Jews*. It clearly arises from a game where two people hold a rope on opposite sides, and each tries to pull the other toward himself. I believe the saying I have recorded elsewhere also comes from this: "Let us not break the rope by stretching it too much."

### Neither a blind guide, nor a mindless counselor. LXXVIII
"Neither a blind guide, nor a mindless counselor." <note>original Greek: "Μήτε τυφλὸν ὁδηγὸν, μήτε ἀνόητον σύμβουλον"</note> One should understand the instruction: "Do not employ." Learn, but from the learned. Seek advice, but from the consulted. On the other hand, Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet</note> says: "As if a blind man shows the way, yet watch anyway."

### The mouse, not entering the hole, was carrying a gourd. LXXIX
"The mouse, not being able to enter the hole, was carrying a gourd." <note>original Greek: "Μῦς εἰς τρώγλην οὐ χωρῶν, κολοκύντην ἐφόρει"</note> This applies to one who, while unable to look after his own interests, tries to help others. Or to one who attempts things far beyond his strength. It seems to have originated from a fable, an old wives' tale, if I am not mistaken.

### While making new friends, do not forget the old. LXXX
"While making new friends, my good man, do not forget the old." <note>original Greek: "Νέους φίλους ποιῶν, τῶν παλαιῶν μὴ ἐπιλανθάνου"</note> This can also be applied to changing one's studies; it is appropriate to look back sometimes even after you have devoted yourself to a different discipline. For instance, if you were to advise someone who has moved to the study of law to occasionally return to "good letters" <note>the humanities or classical literature</note>. It is used by Hermolaus Barbarus in a certain letter to Pico della Mirandola <note>Two prominent Renaissance humanists</note>.

### He dreams even while sleeping. LXXXI
"He dreams even while sleeping." <note>original Greek: "Ὀνειροπολεῖ καὶ καθεύδων"</note> This is still commonly said today whenever it signifies someone who is devoted and given over to something with his whole heart. Indeed, it usually happens to such people that what they have wanted in their minds during the day, they dream of at night. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*: "For even while sleeping he dreams of horsemanship." <note>original Greek: "ὀνειροπολεῖ γὰρ καὶ καθεύδων ἱππικὴν"</note> This was said of a young man who had consumed his entire family inheritance through his passion for raising horses. Also, a little earlier: "To dream of horses." Someone might say, what is so strange about someone dreaming while they sleep? But the word used here <note>oneiropolein</note> does not mean so much "to dream" as it does to interpret dreams, and from this to conceive or create hope. Furthermore, the poet wants the young man's obsession to be seen as a dream. Thus he dreams the same thing twice, both while awake and while sleeping. Plautus, on the contrary, said: "He dreams while awake." Terence says: "Does he dream of those things which he wanted while awake?" And in Horace, Europa speaks thus: "Do I, awake, weep for a shameful crime committed, or does a vain image play with one free of vice?"

### In place of a string. LXXXII
"As if in place of a string." <note>original Greek: "Ὡς ἀντὶ χορδῆς"</note> This will be appropriate when we indicate that something which seemed diminished in one place has been supplemented from elsewhere. Plutarch in his *Table Talk* seems to have used it as a proverb: "And let these things indeed," you will say, "be added in place of a string to those things which have been discussed by you." It is taken from the story of the Locrian, which we explained in the proverb: "The Locrian cicada." <note>A story where a cicada landed on a lyre to replace a broken string with its song</note>

### To be thrown headlong. LXXXIII
"To be pushed onto the head." <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν ὠθεῖσθαι"</note> That is, to be given a headlong fall; they used to say this of someone who...

<page-num>706</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing an entry about "giving someone the headlong treatment" or throwing them out.</meta>

...be expelled with the greatest insult, or rather, who would utterly destroy. This is found in Lucian's <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist</note> little book *On Salaried Posts*. Terence <note>A Roman playwright</note> used a similar figure of speech: "The authors suggest that I should give her the headlong treatment," <note>original Latin: "Autores sunt ut illā præcipitem darem"</note> that is, that I should throw her out of the house. Plutarch, in his *On the Contradictions of the Stoics*, says: "For Chrysippus, for the sake of profit, pushes the wise man headlong into Panticapaeum and the Scythian desert." <note>original Greek: "ὁ γὰρ χρύσιππος ἕνεκα τοῦ χρηματισμοῦ πρὸς σοφὸν ἐπὶ κεφαλὴν εἰς παντινάπειαν ὠθεῖ σκυθῶν ἐρημίαν"</note> Panticapaeum is a city of Scythia near the Bosporus, according to Stephanus. Indeed, I think this is the same as what Seneca says in the sixth book of *On Benefits*: "I will hold onto some for a longer time, others I will expel and drive out head-first." <note>original Latin: "Alio me tinebo diutius, alia expellam & capite agam"</note> Philo of Colophon noted something of this adage's form in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note>, book twelve, when dealing with King Ninus of the Assyrians, who despised everything in favor of bodily pleasures. His choliambic verses <term>scazons: a "limping" meter used in Greek poetry for satire or character sketches</term> go like this:

->But he was in eating and mixing his cup<-
->Outstanding, but all other things he pushed into the rocks.<- ->that is,<-
->But he was outstanding in eating and mixing his cup,<-
->but all other things he drove away into the rocks.<- ->that is, he utterly despised them.<-

---

->**A war without a truce.**<-
->LXXX<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the ninth book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "I am therefore forced to be a sharer and partner and helper in this war, which is even 'without a truce' <note>original Greek: "ἄσπονδον"</note> among citizens." He calls "without a truce" that which is perpetual, fierce, and irreconcilable. The Suda <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia, here called 'Suidas'</note> shows that "enemies without a truce" <note>original Greek: "ἄσπονδους ἐχθροὺς"</note> are those who cannot be brought back into harmony. It sounds, if we may speak this way for the sake of teaching, as if you were to say "un-covenantable," meaning one will enter into a bitter grudge and disagreement. The divine Chrysostom used this proverb in his forty-seventh homily on Matthew. Likewise, the divine Basil, in a certain letter to Athanasius: "If they are asked what is the cause of this saying of ours, and of the war undertaken without sacred rites, they tell of certain songs and a type of melody which has prevailed among us." <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὴν αἰτίαν ὁρῶσι τὸν ἀκήρυκτον τότε καὶ ἄσπονδον πόλεμον, ψαλμὸς λέγεται τρόπον μελωδίας τῇ παρ’ ἡμῖν κεκρατηκυίας"</note> Aeschines in his oration *On the False Embassy*: "For peace would not become war, but out of peace comes an 'unheralded' war." <note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ δὴ εἰρήνη γένοιτ’ ἂν πόλεμος, ἀλλ’ ἐξ εἰρήνης πόλεμος ἀκήρυκτος"</note> That is, from these things peace would not be made from war, but from peace an "un-notified" war, which is to say, one that is vehement and fierce. The same author in the same work: "But if the causes of wars belong to the orators, and the rewards to the generals, the result will be a war that lacks both sacred rites and formal declarations." <note>original Greek: "εἰ δ’ ἔσονται τῷ πολέμῳ αἱ μὲν λύθυσαι τῶν πρέσβεων, αἱ δὲ δωρεαὶ τῶν στρατηγῶν, ἄσπονδος καὶ ἀκήρυκτος ὢν πόλεμος ἔσεται"</note> For he who declares war, who sends the heralds <term>fetials: Roman priests who acted as diplomatic representatives in declaring war or making treaties</term>, and who performs sacrifices, makes the delay itself milder; and it is likely that these types of delays were invented for this very purpose. Just as in law there is the triple citation and the joinder of issue <term>litis contestatio: the formal beginning of a lawsuit</term>, or in marriage a notice of divorce, so that through mild words like "Keep your things to yourself," while these things are being done, that powerless impulse of anger might subside.

---

->**He traces his lineage from the Eteobutadae.**<-
->LXIX<-

"He traces his lineage from the Eteobutadae." <note>original Greek: "Ἐξ ἐτεοβουταδῶν ἕλκει τὸ γένος"</note> This was usually said of those who are descended from illustrious ancestors and ancient nobility, specifically from a certain Butas, who established priests at Athens. From his descendants, the highest magistrates were later chosen. It will be more elegant if it is taken ironically against an obscure man, or one who makes a show of his nobility and ancestral masks.

---

->**Erginus's gray hairs.**<-
->LXX<-

"Erginus's gray hairs." <note>original Greek: "Ἐργίνου πολιαί"</note> Concerning premature grayness, that is, what happens before the proper time. Erginus was the son of Clymenus and one of the Argonauts <note>The heroes who sailed with Jason to find the Golden Fleece</note>. When Hypsipyle, the daughter of Thoas, king of the Lemnians, had proposed funeral games for her father's spirit, Erginus arrived, already gray beyond the reason of his age, and approached to compete among the others. He was mocked by the Lemnian women for the untimely grayness of his head, and he gave rise to the proverb, especially because he won a most beautiful victory by overcoming all the athletes. It will be more witty if said ironically of old men already gray who nevertheless wish to be considered young, claiming that this grayness happened not from years, but from cares, or occurred prematurely from some other cause. It can also be twisted toward those who are young in age but already act like old men in character and conduct. And to those whose wisdom is precocious, who "come before their hair," as Persius says. Truly, nothing accelerates old age faster than the cares of the mind: love, hate, envy, fear, and sorrow. To this belongs that line from Theocritus in his *Idylls*: "But those who are in love grow old in a single day." <note>original Greek: "οἱ δὲ ποθουντῶν ἐν ἄματι γηράσκουσι"</note> That is:
Truly, those whom love torments, grow old in a single light.
The scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on a text</note> cites a similar verse from the nineteenth book of the *Odyssey*:
"For mortals grow old quickly in misfortune." <note>original Greek: "Αἶψα γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσι"</note>

<meta>This page continues the third "Chiliad" (thousand) of Erasmus’s collection of adages, specifically the third "Century" (hundred) of that book. The text transitions from the effects of stress on aging into various Greek and Latin idiomatic expressions regarding social insults, linguistic superlatives, and moral character.</meta>

<page-num>707</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY</header>

In times of adversity, old age arrives in a hurry. <note>Erasmus is quoting a common sentiment about how stress ages a person.</note>
Pindar <note>A Greek lyric poet from Thebes, known for his odes</note> says the same in the *Olympian Odes*:
"Gray hairs are often born even among young men, even before the time suited to their age." <note>original Greek: "φύονται δὲ καὶ νέοις ἐν ἀνδράσι πολιαὶ θαμὰ καὶ πρὰ τὸν ἡλικίας ἐοικότα χρόνον"</note> that is,
Gray hairs are born even in young men, frequently and beyond the proper time of their age. To those who are waiting or longing, all time feels long. As in the line: "So the year is slow
for wards whom the harsh custody of their mothers oppresses." <note>A quote from Horace, Epistles 1.1.21-22, describing how time drags for those under strict supervision.</note>
Even today, sailors declare that in the immediate danger of shipwreck, gray hair can suddenly appear.

---

->To give the finger. LXXXVII<-

"To be flicked with the finger." <note>original Greek: "Εσκιμαλίχθαι"</note> By this gesture, one signified an insult and the supreme expression of contempt. For among the Greeks, "to flick" <note>original Greek: "ἐκκιμαλίσαι"</note> meant to show the middle finger while the others were tucked in, for the sake of disgrace, or to signify contempt by the snapping of the fingers. This is why Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist</note> says (as we have mentioned elsewhere): "He would bid the noose for him, and show him his middle fingernail." <note>original Latin: "Mandaret laqueum, mediumq́ ostenderet unguem." This refers to telling someone to go hang themselves while gesturing with the "impudent finger."</note>
Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> cites this six-foot verse from Aristophanes <note>The most famous comic playwright of ancient Athens</note>. It appears in his play *Peace*:
"Do you not see how the sickle-maker rejoices,
And how he mocks the spear-maker with his middle finger?" <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ δρεπανουργὸς οὐχ ὁρᾷς ὡς ἥδεται, καὶ τὸν δορυξόον οἷον ἐκκιμαλίσεν;"</note> that is,
Do you not see how the maker of sickles exults,
And shows his middle finger to the spear-maker?
However, as for what the term "to flick" <note>original Greek: "ἐκκιμαλίζειν"</note> properly signifies in its physical detail, he who desires to know would do better to learn it from Suidas than from me. More elegantly and proverbially, it is twisted to refer to fortune, to learning, or to anything else that is utterly despised.

---

->The extreme of extreme evils. LXXXVIII<-

"The extreme of extreme evils has been accomplished." <note>original Greek: "Εσχάτων ἔσχατα κακὰ διαπέπρακται."</note> That is: The most extreme of extreme evils have happened. The logic of the proverb lies in the very grammatical figure, as we advised at the beginning of this work. To this form seems to belong what Hipponax <note>An ancient Greek satirical poet</note> wrote in the 15th book of Athenaeus: "evils of evils," <note>original Greek: "κακῶν κακὰ"</note> meaning the greatest possible evils. Likewise, when someone called Athens "the Greece of Greece," <note>original Greek: "ἑλλάδος ἑλλάδα"</note> as if you were to say the "flower of Greece." Of this kind are also "the goods of goods," "the pain of pains," and "the babbler of babblers." The Greeks seem to have borrowed this style of speech from the Hebrews, who signify intensity and <term>emphasis</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐπίτασιν"</note> by the doubling of the same word. Of this sort is that passage in Jeremiah: "Good, good figs, and bad, bad figs." <note>Jeremiah 24:3</note> When he wants it to be understood as "exceedingly good" and "exceedingly bad."

---

->Someone ran lest he be wet by rain, and was suffocated in a pit. LXXXIX<-

"He flees lest he be wetted, and was drowned in a hole." <note>original Greek: "Εξέχεται μὴ βρεχθείη, καὶ εἰς βόθρον ἀπεπνίγη."</note> Someone ran so that he would not be sprinkled with water, and was suffocated in a pit. This is used when someone, fleeing a lighter evil too incautiously, runs into the greatest one. It seems to have been taken from the common people by Apostolius <note>A 15th-century collector of Greek proverbs</note>, many of which we have omitted on purpose.

---

->You are "Different-Jawed." XC<-

"You are different-jawed." <note>original Greek: "Ετερόγναθος εἶ."</note> This was customarily said of a glutton, who because of his voracity would chew food alternately with both jaws. For he was called "different-jawed" <note>original Greek: "ἑτερόγναθος"</note> because he transfers food now into this jaw, now into that. Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian</note>, however, interprets it as referring to stubborn and ill-mannered people, thinking it was a metaphor taken from horses.

---

->The city-dweller thinks of nothing just. XCI<-
->The city-dweller thinks of nothing just or good.<-

"A man of the city thinks of nothing just." <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν φρονεῖ δίκαιον ἀνὴρ ἀστικός."</note> That is:
It warns that the rustic life is more innocent, as it is the only one that has dealings with the lonely earth. On the other hand, those who live in cities, because of the contagion of business and people, turn out to be more clever—whence "astute" <note>from the Latin *astutus*</note> people are thought to be named after the "city" <note>original Greek: "παρὰ τὸ ἄστυ"</note>. This proverb can also be applied here: that cunning is usually the companion of distinguished social politeness and urban smooth-talking. Conversely, those who are somewhat rustic in their manners usually possess a more reliable loyalty and a more sincere mind. The verse is a six-foot line, but corrupted. And Demea in Terence <note>A character in the play *Adelphoe*</note> says: "In the city, one evil comes out of another."

---

->More stingy than Patroclus. XCII<-

"More parsimonious than Patroclus." <note>original Greek: "Παροκλέος φιδωλότερος."</note> That is: More stingy than Patroclus. Said of a man who is indeed rich, but exceedingly sordid and cheap. For this Patroclus, after he was raised to the greatest wealth—or, as others say, from the time he was born—never used a bath, for the sake of parsimony. He is criticized by Aristophanes in *Plutus*:

<meta>This page continues the third "Chiliad" (thousand) of Erasmus’s collection of adages, specifically the third "Century" (hundred) of that book. It follows a sequence of idiomatic expressions derived from Greek and Roman literature, focusing on social behavior, speech patterns, and historical customs.</meta>

<page-num>708</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

I come from the house of Patroclus. <note>original Greek: "Ἐκ πατροκλέας ἔρχομαι"</note> ->that is,<-
I come from the house of Patroclus.
For he had described Plutus <note>The god of wealth</note> as squalid and full of mold. Eudocia also mentions this proverb.

->Every master is a monosyllable to his servant.<- <margin>X</margin>
Every master is a monosyllable to his servant. <note>original Greek: "πᾶς δεσπότης δούλῳ μονοσύλλαβος"</note> that is, Every master is a monosyllable to his servant. For masters and powerful men need only the shortest little word, whether they nod in agreement or refuse: "Yes," or "No," "I want it," "I command it so," "let my will stand for reason." <note>A reference to Juvenal's Satires 6.223: "hoc volo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione voluntas."</note> But for servants and those with less power, many words are needed to entreat or persuade. It is expressed in full in this way: "Every master is a monosyllable to his servant; but to supplicate is long." <note>original Greek: "πᾶς δεσπότης δούλῳ μονοσύλλαβος, τὸ δὲ ἱκετεύειν, μακρόν"</note> It has been noted by the learned that monosyllabic and disyllabic names suit servants, such as *Mys* <note>meaning "mouse"</note>, which was the name of a servant of Epicurus. Furthermore, Athenaeus in Book 5 cites Herodicus, who mockingly calls grammarians "monosyllables" <margin>One who buzzes in corners, a monosyllable.</margin> because they hide in corners like silkworms <note>or "buzzing things"</note> and because they deal with the minutiae of vocal sounds. In *Lysimachus*, Demosthenes said, if I am not mistaken, that his kingdom differed in no way from a comic stage, where he was exceedingly delighted by ridiculous sayings, because all "disyllables"—that is, actors—departed from him. For he noted Bithen and Paris, who could do anything in his presence. Athenaeus in Book 14 notes that, conversely, the names of great men are made polysyllabic, such as Ariobarzanes, Nebuchadnezzar, and in Plautus, *Polypyrgopolinices* <note>A boastful soldier's name meaning "Frequent-tower-town-conqueror"</note> and *Megalodorus* <note>"Giver of great gifts"</note>.

->To wear a wig / To play the Punic.<- <margin>XC</margin>
"You seem to me to be wearing a wig," <note>original Greek: "πηνικίζειν μοὶ δοκεῖς"</note> is worth the same as saying "to practice deceit," which is also called "to cheat" <note>original Greek: "φενακίζειν"</note>. For to the Greeks, a *penike* <note>πηνίκη</note> signifies hair that is not genuine but attached, which we call a "little cap" or "wig." From this come *penikismata*, meaning tricks or deceptions.

->Full of cicadas.<-
Covered in cicadas. <note>original Greek: "Τεττίγων ἀνάμεσοι"</note> that is, Covered in cicadas. This was once said of boastful and foolish people, or those using obsolete and now-discarded customs. For in ancient times, it was the custom of the Athenians to add golden cicadas to the curls of their hair. From this they were called "cicada-wearers" <note>original Greek: "τεττιγοφόροι"</note>, signifying by this token that they were *autochthonous* <note>original Greek: "αὐτόχθονας"</note>, that is, indigenous; just as cicadas do not migrate from elsewhere like most other creatures, but are born in the same place where they live. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
"These things are indeed ancient and smelling of old age, and full of cicadas,
And of Cecides, and of the Buphonia." <note>original Greek: "Ἀρχαῖά γε καὶ διὰ πολιοδίκου, καὶ τεττίγων ἀνάμεσα, Καὶ κηκείδου, καὶ βουφονίων"</note> ->that is,<-
These things are surely ancient and overgrown with gray hair, and filled with cicadas,
And with Cecides, and the ox-slaying festivals.
Cecides was a very ancient writer of dithyrambs. The *Buphonia* <note>"Ox-slaying"</note> was likewise an ancient festival, long since abandoned due to its antiquity. Indeed, all these things are spoken in a proverbial figure.

->Why do you weave great prologues for tiny matters?<- <margin>XCI</margin>
Why do you weave great prologues about small things? <note>original Greek: "τί μικρῶν πέρι μεγάλα φροιμιάζῃ;"</note> that is, Why do you weave great introductions for minute affairs? Used when someone employs a wordy preface for a matter of no great importance. For in Athens, the herald used to forbid those about to speak in the assembly from using either a preface or emotional appeals; they were to set forth the bare facts, "without prologues and passions." <note>original Greek: "ἄνευ προοιμίων καὶ παθῶν"</note> As Lucian indicates in several places. To which also Terence refers: "He even begins a prologue." And Horace:
"Whither do these so foul things tend?"
Alluding lightly to this, Aelius Spartianus says in *Aelius Verus*: "And since," he says, "very small things must be said, and the prologue ought not to be more enormous than the play, I shall now speak of the man himself." Plutarch, in his *Laconian Apophthegms*, relates of Cleomenes the son of Cleombrotus, that when a certain other man was using a speech more prolix than was necessary, he said: "Why do you weave great prologues for me about small things? For however great the matter is, let the speech you use be of the same size."

->Then the swans will sing, when the jackdaws are silent.<- <margin>XCII</margin>
Then the swans will sing, when the jackdaws have fallen silent. <note>original Greek: "τότ’ ᾄσονται κύκνοι, ὅταν κολοιοὶ σιωπήσωσι"</note> that is, Then the learned will speak, when there is no place for chatterers to speak. Or, among chatterers and clamorous people, there is no place for the learned to speak. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> used the adage in his shorter letters: "Either stop overwhelming us with your nonsense or be silent, or I shall say the proverb—especially if it is most wise—that then the swans will sing when the jackdaws are silent." <note>original Greek: "παύσαι καταφλυαρῶν ἡμῶν ἢ σιωπῆς, ἢ δι προοιμίαν ἐρῶ μάλιστα μὲν ἂν καὶ μάλιστα ᾖ σώφρονα, ὅτι τότε ᾄσοντ’ κύκνοι ὅταν κολοιοὶ σιωπήσωσιν"</note> that is, Either stop...

<summary>This page explores proverbs related to the length and appropriateness of speech, ancient Athenian customs like wearing golden cicadas, and the use of "monosyllables" to describe the brief commands of powerful masters versus the long pleas of servants.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the third "Century" (set of one hundred) and begins the fourth "Century" of the third "Chiliad" (thousand) of Erasmus’s Adages. It transitions from a discussion on the silence of unlearned critics to proverbs regarding justice, scapegoating, and human inconstancy.</meta>

<page-num>709</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Oo</sig>
<meta>catchword: His own</meta>

...swans sing when the jackdaws are silent. <note>This is the conclusion of an adage from the previous page regarding how true talent is often shouted down by the unlearned until the critics are finally silenced by time.</note> Thus now Cicero, Virgil, and Horace speak, while Pero, Philiscus, and Mevius—who used to bark against them while they were alive—are silent, being as much more talkative as they were more unlearned.

### Three evils for the evil. XCVIII

Three evils for the evil. <note>original Greek: "τοῖς κακοῖς τρὶς κακά"</note> That is, "Three evils for the evil." This means that what is deserved happens to those who deserve it. They say this proverb arose from a story of this kind: they tell that the francolins <note>A type of game bird, often called heath-cocks.</note>, when they were first brought from Lydia into Egypt and released into the woods, uttered the voice of a quail. Later, it happened that when the bed of the Nile river dried up, a plague infested the region of the Egyptians and consumed a great force of men. During this, the francolins began to utter a human and articulate voice, somewhat louder than a boy's, saying these words: "Three evils for the evil." <note>original Greek: "τοῖς κακοῖς τρὶς κακά"</note> Athenaeus, in his ninth book, cites Socrates as the author of this story in a work *On Ends*, phrasing the adage thus: "Evils for the evildoers." <note>original Greek: "τοῖς τοις κακούργοις κακά"</note> This verse is also circulated among Greek maxims:

For God also gives good things to a good man. <note>original Greek: "ἐσθλῷ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ ἐσθλὰ καὶ δίδωσι θεός"</note> ->that is,<-
The inhabitants of heaven bestow good things upon a good man.

And these six-foot lines <note>iambic trimeters</note> from some poet or other are recorded in the commentaries *On Listening to Poets*:

For if anyone has destined foul abominations by fate, 
It is necessary for this mortal to reap a foul reward. <note>original Greek: "εἱμαρμένου γὰρ τῷ κακῷ βδελύγματῳ. Κακὰς ἀμοιβὰς δεῖ καρπᾶσθαι βροτοῖς."</note> ->that is,<-
If anyone has intended wicked deeds, 
it is necessary for him to carry away a wicked prize.

### The pig pays for the dog’s sin. XCIX

The pig pays for the dog's trouble. <note>original Greek: "τὸ κυνὸς κακόν, ὑς ἀπέτισεν"</note> That is, "The pig pays for the dog’s sin." This is used whenever one person pays the penalty for the sins committed by another. It is not clear from what event this arose, nor does it matter much, for it smacks of a common folk saying.

### Interrupted music. C

The music has been poured out. <note>original Greek: "Ἐκκέχυτ’ ἡ μουσική"</note> That is, "The music is interrupted." The ancients were accustomed to using learned conversations at banquets. Later, singers, actors, and dances began to be introduced. Therefore, some people, taking it poorly that their conversations were interrupted, would say: "The music is poured out." This expression was turned into a proverb whenever someone intervening interrupted a conversation already begun. I remember reading something similar in Plato, though the specific passage does not occur to me at the moment.

---

-> THE FOURTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD THOUSAND <-

### More changeable than a chameleon. I

<margin>Aristotle, Book 2, *History of Animals*</margin> More changeable than a chameleon. <note>original Greek: "Ἀμιλεόντος εὐμεταβολώτερος"</note> That is, "More changeable than a chameleon." The chameleon is recorded among those animals that change color. Aristotle describes its form carefully in the second book of *The History of Animals*. Regarding the change of color, he records these things: "The change of color happens to it when it is inflated. It becomes black, not far from that of crocodiles, and pale like lizards, or again variegated with black spots, like that of leopards. Such a change happens throughout its whole body; for even the eyes and the tail change along with the rest of the body. Its movement is extremely sluggish, much like that of tortoises. When dying, it becomes pale, and after death, the color remains so." <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ χροιᾶς ἡ μεταβολὴ... ἡ δὲ κίνησις αὐτῷ νωθὴς ἰσχυρῶς ἐστὶ... ἀποθνήσκων δὲ ὠχρὸς γίνεται"</note> Thus far Aristotle. Pliny records nearly the same things in Book 8, Chapter 33, adding this: that this animal reflects with its whole body whatever color it is closest to, except for red and white. Therefore, the adage fits a "turncoat" man, or one who is inconsistent and turns himself into every shape according to the occasion. Plato says in the *Ion*: "But you simply become all sorts of things like Proteus <note>A sea god capable of changing his shape at will</note>, turning yourself up and down." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ’ ἀτεχνῶς ὥσπερ ὁ πρωτεὺς παντοδαπὸς γίγνῃ, στρεφόμενος ἄνω καὶ κάτω"</note> Aristotle, in the first book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, uses the term "chameleon" to express the vice of inconstancy.

<summary>Erasmus concludes the third hundred adages with reflections on justice and social behavior, then begins the fourth hundred by discussing human inconstancy through the metaphor of the chameleon.</summary>
