-> DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, THE ADAGES <-

### His own fart smells sweet to everyone.
<margin>II</margin>

<note>original Greek: "Ἔκαστος αὑτοῦ βδέγμα, μῆλο γλυκύον ἀγαπᾷ"</note> Each man loves his own breaking of wind more than a sweet apple. That is, everyone considers his own fart sweeter than a sweet apple: which means, there is no one to whom his own faults do not seem even the best. Aristotle, in the ninth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, says: <note>original Greek: "τὰ πολλὰ γν' ὅ' γ' ἴου ὑμῶσιν, οἱ ἔχοντες καὶ οἱ βαλόμενοι λαβεῖν. τὰ γν' οἰκεῖα κἢ ἃ διδόασιν ἑκάστοις φαίνετ' πολλῶ ἄξια"</note> For most things are not valued at the same price by those who have them and those who desire to receive them. For one's own things, and what one gives, seem to be of great price. This passage fits more appropriately with the proverb, **"To everyone his own is beautiful,"** but that page had already left my hands <note>Erasmus is noting that he realized this connection too late to include it in the earlier section of his book.</note>. I suspect this proverb about the fart was drawn from the dregs of the common people by Apostolius <note>Michael Apostolius, a 15th-century Greek scholar whose collection of proverbs Erasmus used as a source.</note>. For I have not yet found anyone to whom his own fart smelled sweet. The truth is rather that people are more vehemently disgusted by the excrement and flatulence of others than by their own.

---

### To drink from a perforated cup.
<margin>III</margin>

<note>original Greek: "Ἐκ τετρυμημένης κύλικος πίνειν"</note> That is, to drink from a perforated cup. This is said of those who are leaky and who are not very successful at keeping secrets entrusted to them. This also has the flavor of the common people.

---

### He calls on God at a flea bite.
<margin>IIII</margin>

<note>original Greek: "Ἐπ' ψύλλας δήξε' θεὸν ἐπικαλεῖται"</note> That is, he calls on God at a flea bite. This is said against those who are gravely disturbed by a matter, however slight, just as if it were of the greatest importance. It is drawn from a fable told among those of Aesop: A certain man, offended by the pain of a flea biting his foot, sat down and implored Hercules <term>Alexikakos</term> <note>Meaning "Averter of Evil."</note>. Soon, as the flea jumped away, he spoke ill of Hercules; because the god had not brought help when called upon in such a tiny danger, it did not seem likely that he would be present in more serious matters. Similar to this is what Aristotle reports in the seventh book of the *Nicomachean Ethics* concerning those who are exceedingly timid: <note>original Greek: "οἷος ὁ δείλαια πάντα κἂν ψοφήσῃ μῦς"</note> Like one who fears everything, even if a mouse makes a noise. He calls this kind of timidity <term>theriodes</term>, that is, "brutish" or "ferine."

---

### Adulterated. That is, counterfeit.
<margin>V</margin>

That which is not simple nor sincere, the Greeks call by the common word <term>kibdelon</term>. The word is derived from the fact that they show one thing openly but hide another, from the words for "secretly" and "deceit." Or perhaps because the Athenians, out of their supreme hatred for the Chians, used to engrave the name of Chios on coins if they wished someone ill, adding a letter to curse them as they threw the money to the ground. But properly, they call a plated coin *kibdelon*: and *kibdelia* refers to insincerity or corruption. As Aristophanes says:

> He removed much of life's corruption.
> <note>original Greek: "πολλὴν ἀφάλε' τ' βίω κιβδηλίαν"</note>

And *kibdeloden* means to corrupt with a false dye; and those who are pale are called *kibdeliontas*, because some disease or vice seems to be lurking beneath the surface. Just as in coins, the color sometimes betrays a fake. It will be suitable, therefore, to apply this to an insincere and feigned friendship, or to a man with a flattering face but a poisonous mind: or to one who displays holiness in his dress while his life is impious. For example, Pisides, as cited by Suidas:

> There is one author of two things entirely,
> As they say in common speech: whoever is insincere.
> <note>original Latin: "Rerum duarum prorfus unus autor eft, / Vulgo ut loquuntur, quiſquis inſyncerus eft."</note>

Or to insincere speech, as Plato says in the fifth book of the *Laws*: <note>original Greek: "τὰς δ' αὖ ὑμὰς δ' εῖ σκοπᾷν κἢ ποῖα τίνες ἀληθεῖς, κἢ ὅσαι κιβδηλοι"</note> Again, one ought to consider honors, which of them are true and which are counterfeit. Again in the same book: <note>original Greek: "ὅπως μήτε αὐτὸς κίβδηλος ποτε φανῆται ὁ τῷῤ, ἁπλῶς ἢ κἢ ἀληθὰς ἀεί"</note> So that he himself may never appear counterfeit to anyone, but always simple and truthful. This term, therefore, being transferred from coins, becomes proverbial if applied to various things. But we have made mention of this matter in the proverb **"Of a bad stamp."**

---

### No wicked man shall know this.
<margin>V</margin>

<note>original Greek: "οὐδεὶς κακός ἄσετ'"</note> That is, no wicked man shall know this. We use this whenever we signify something excellent and worthy of being known. Plato in the fifth book of the *Laws*: <note>original Greek: "ὅσῳ γν' δὴ τὸ νῦν ὑπὸ τὰ πομὸν ἀγαθὸν ὂν τυγχάνῃ πάνταις ταῖς πειθομέναις πόλεσιμ, τὼ ἐπομιλίω κατασκδυην προλαβὸν, κἢ τὼ παλαιὰν πῤοιμίαν, οὐδεὶς ἔσεταί ποτε κακὸς ὤν, ἀλλ' ἔμπειρος τε καὶ ἰωφικῆς ἔθεσι γενόμενο"</note> For however much of a good thing that which is now prescribed may happen to be for all states, if only they obey, bringing about order and preparation, no idle or wicked man will ever know it—as the old proverb says—but only he who is skilled and endowed with just character.

<meta>catchword: Hui (Alas/Indeed)</meta>

<meta>This page continues the third "Chiliad," fourth "Century" of Erasmus's *Adages*. It follows the previous page's discussion of Greek proverbs related to human character and wisdom, specifically continuing the theme of how certain truths are not accessible to everyone.</meta>

<page-num>711</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY IV.</header>

Close to this is a saying he [Plato] placed in the *Laches*: <note>original Greek: "οὐ πᾶσιν ὗς ἴσῑν ἄβατον"</note> which means, **"Not every sow knows this path."** It clearly originated from the divine mysteries, which were not permitted to be known by anyone except the initiated and the pure.

---

->Iron walls, not earthen.<-
<margin>VII</margin>
Plato, in the sixth book of *The Laws*: <note>original Greek: "περὶ δὲ τειχῶν ὦ μέγιλλε..."</note> "As for walls, Megillus, I would agree with Sparta: to let the walls lie sleeping in the earth and not raise them up, and for this reason: is it not well said in the poetic tradition that walls ought to be of bronze and iron rather than of earth?" That is to say: Regarding walls, Megillus, I would indeed side with Sparta, that we should let the walls lie on the ground as if sleeping, and not wish to raise them up again for this purpose. Rightly indeed is the poetic saying sung about them: that walls ought to be made of bronze and iron rather than of earth. This seems to have been tossed about as a proverb, and it possesses the quality of a riddle. It suggests that one should not place the defense of a city in its walls, but in its armed men, whose consensus protects the city best in place of impregnable walls. Furthermore, Plato alludes to a Spartan aphorism mentioned by Plutarch. I certainly think Horace also alluded lightly to this when he said:
> Let this be your wall of bronze.
<note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.60. The "wall of bronze" refers to a clear conscience or personal integrity as a defense.</note>

---

### No one is chasing us.
<margin>VIII</margin>
Plato, in the tenth book of *The Laws*: <note>original Greek: "ὡς ἔοικεν ἤδη πρὸν δὲ πειθωμᾶν βραχυλογίαν μᾶλλον ἢ μῆκος, ὡς γὰρ ἡμᾶς τὸ λεγόμενον ἐπείγων διώκῃ"</note> That is: For at present there is no reason why we should prefer brevity to lengthiness. Since no one is pursuing us who might compel us to hurry, as the common saying goes. This proverb remains in common use even today, used when people mean they are free to linger longer on any particular matter. "No one," they say, "is pushing us."

---

->The sea washes away all human evils.<-
<margin>IX</margin>
<note>original Greek: "θάλασσα κλύζει πάντα τ’ ἀνθρώπων κακά"</note> That is: 
The sea washes away all the evils of men.
This is cited by Eustathius in his commentary on the first book of Homer's *Iliad*. It also appears in Euripides' *Iphigenia in Tauris*. It originated from an event of this kind: Diogenes Laertius reports that Euripides was a companion to Plato on his journey when he went to Egypt; there, when Euripides was seized by a disease—the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, if I am not mistaken—the Egyptian priests cured the man by immersion in the sea. From this, he later composed this verse:
"The sea washes away all the evils of men."
He spoke as if seawater were a cure for all diseases. Indeed, even today, people think that those bitten by a rabid dog, if they are submerged nine times in the sea, are freed from the madness.

---

->To sing of Telamon.<-
<margin>X</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Ἄδειν τὰ τελαμῶνος"</note> That is: To sing the song of Telamon. This proverb is spoken regarding a mournful or complaining speech, because Telamon wept excessively when his son Ajax perished at Troy, especially by that kind of death <note>Ajax committed suicide</note>. Eustathius, explaining that Homeric poem in the *Catalogue of Ships*:
<margin>Ajax brought twelve ships from Salamis.</margin>
mentions this proverb: <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὸ ἄδειν τελαμῶνος παροιμιακῶς λεχθὲν..."</note> "And that which is said proverbially, 'to sing of Telamon,' comes from a drinking song whose beginning is: 'Son of Telamon, Ajax the warrior.'" It is very similar to what we have reported elsewhere: **"The song of Admetus"** and **"The song of Harmodius."** <note>These refer to popular Greek 'skolia' or drinking songs often sung at banquets.</note>

---

->Argive calumny.<-
<margin>XI</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Ἀργεῖα φορά"</note> That is: Argive hounding; a saying usually applied to slanderers and informants. For antiquity once marked the Argives as sycophants and people eager for lawsuits. Eustathius is a witness in the *Catalogue of Ships*, citing the adage from Pausanias. Diogenianus also attests to this in his *Collections*.

---

->Confident at the start, timid in action.<-
<margin>XII</margin>
Eustathius, explaining the seventh book of the *Iliad*, records a proverb of this kind: <note>original Greek: "θρασὺς πρὸ ἔργου, ἐκ πολλοῦ κακός"</note> That is: Bold before the business, but generally a coward. He cites the same from Epicharmus: <note>original Greek: "κακὸς θαῤῥεῖ μαλ’ αὐτόθεν, ἔπειτα δ’ φεύγει"</note> That is: The coward is immediately very confident in himself, but later he flees. We see this happen commonly: those who are the boldest and most boastful before danger appears, when the situation demands a man, they are found to have no spirit.

---

<margin>XIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: "γοργὸν βλέπειν"</note> **To look fiercely.** This appears several times in Lucian, meaning to gaze with sharp or piercing eyes. It is taken from the story of Perseus...
<column-break/>
<meta>The catchword "Persei" indicates the next page continues the explanation of the "Gorgon stare" related to Perseus.</meta>

<page-num>712</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

**Of Perseus and the Gorgon.** Some believe the word "Gorgon" <note>original Greek: γοργὸν</note> is derived from the word for "wrath," <note>original Greek: ὀργὴν</note> because those who are angry use sharp, piercing eyes. Likewise, Homer in the eighth book of the *Iliad* says of Hector: 
> With the eyes of a Gorgon and of man-slaying Mars. <note>original Greek: γοργὼ ὄμματ’ ἔχων ἠδὲ βροτολοιγὸ ἄρηθ</note>
In other places, he mentions "looking with a mad expression."

---

->**Lift a finger.**<-

"Lift a finger" <note>original Greek: Αἶρε δάκτυλον</note> means to admit you are defeated. For by this sign, whoever had succumbed in a contest acknowledged his defeat. Persius says in his fifth *Satire*:
> Reason has granted you nothing; stick out your finger, and you do wrong. <note>Persius implies that even the smallest movement or gesture, if not guided by reason, is a fault.</note>
A similar saying used in another context is "To give the grass," <note>original Latin: "Dare herbam," an ancient Roman expression for admitting defeat.</note> which refers to the same idea. To this, if I am not mistaken, Saint Jerome alluded in his dialogue between a Luciferian and an Orthodox Christian when he said: "Lo, I lift my hand, I yield the grass." Athenaeus, in his sixth book, cites these verses from Antiphanes regarding tragic poets:
> Whenever they have nothing left to say,
> And have completely failed in their dramas,
> They lift the 'machine' just like a finger.
<note>Antiphanes compares the "deus ex machina"—a crane used to lower gods onto the stage to solve a plot—to a defeated athlete raising his finger to end a fight.</note>
Marcus Tullius Cicero seems to use it slightly differently in the sixth book of *Against Verres*: "The guardians run up; Uncle Junius lifts a finger." Here it seems to be the gesture of one approving, or declaring himself a buyer or a contractor. Indeed, in old times, votes were cast in this manner, and in auctions, whoever wished to do so declared himself a buyer or contractor by the same sign.

---

->**Seeing me, you will think you are plainly seeing Mars.**<-

"For you will think you are looking directly at Mars" <note>original Greek: Βλέπειν γὰρ ἀντικρὺς δόξεις μ’ ἄρεω</note> means you will clearly seem to see Mars in me. This was said of those who strenuously promised they would bring help and would act like a Veritable Mars [the god of war]. But I do not know where this appears in Aristophanes, for the passage has not yet occurred to me.

---

->**An ox in the city.**<-

"An ox in the city" <note>original Greek: Βοῦς ἐν πόλει</note> is said whenever someone is elevated to new and unexpected honors. For instance, when a bronze image of an ox was placed on the Acropolis in Athens, the matter became a joke among the common people. For the use of oxen belongs in the fields, not in cities. This will also apply to those who are raised to the highest honors beyond their merit—for example, when an unlearned lecher becomes a bishop or an abbot.

---

->**Brasidas was indeed a good man.**<-

"Brasidas was indeed a good man, but Lacedaemon [Sparta] has many who are better." <note>original Greek: Βρασίδας μὲν ἀνὴρ ἀγαθὸς, ἁ δὲ λακεδαίμων πολλοὺς ἔχει κάῤῥονας</note> This is used against those who imagine themselves not only among the best, but the only ones worthy of esteem. It was born from an aphorism, as Plutarch teaches in his *Laconian Sayings* and likewise in the *Life of Lycurgus*. <note>When the Spartan general Brasidas died, his mother told those praising him that while he was noble, Sparta had many superior citizens, reflecting Spartan humility and collective pride.</note> A similar saying is "Many Manlii."

---

->**Ivy after the Anthesteria.**<-

"Ivy after the Anthesteria" <note>original Greek: Κισσὸς μετ’ ἀνθεστήρια</note> is said when something is brought too late. The festival [the Anthesteria] takes its name from the fact that in that month many things bloom from the earth. <note>From the Greek "anthos," meaning flower.</note> It appears it was the custom to be crowned with ivy during this time. Regarding the Anthesteria—that is, the floral festivals—we spoke in the proverb "Carians out the door," <note>original: "Cares foras."</note> for these seem to have been what the Latins call the *Bacchanalia*. Ivy was sacred to Bacchus, which is why those who carried ivy in those games were called *kittophoroi* [ivy-bearers]. This matches what we have recorded elsewhere: "After the feast."

---

->**You come from the Academy.**<-

"You come from the Academy" <note>original Greek: Ἀπ’ ἀκαδημίας ἥκεις</note> is said of someone severe and composed, or learned, as if coming from the school of Plato. However, it can also be twisted ironically against a haughty person who puts on a philosophical face. Indeed, Athenaeus in his twelfth book indicates it was said of those who were elegant and distinguished in dress, because Plato delighted in such cleanliness. Thus Antiphanes, having depicted a philosopher elegantly dressed, says in that same author: "But why is it necessary to say more? I seem to see the Academy itself living in him."

---

->**To set an old man upright.**<-

"It is hard to set upright an old man who fell as a youth." <note>original Greek: Γέροντα δ’ ὀρθοῦν φλαῦρον ὃς νέῳ πέσοι</note> It is not easy for old men to unlearn the vices they learned as boys and which have stuck with them throughout their entire lives.

<summary>This page explores various Greek and Latin proverbs regarding gestures of defeat (lifting a finger), misplaced honors (an ox in the city), and the difficulty of correcting lifelong habits in old age. Erasmus provides historical and literary context for each, ranging from Spartan military history to Athenian theater and Platonic philosophy.</summary>

<page-num>713</page-num>
<header>THIRD THOUSAND, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

And yet, even in old age, we must strive to be free from vices, however much they may have taken hold.

<margin>XXI</margin>
## ->You have it buried in the earth.<-

"You have it buried in the earth" <note>original Greek: τῆ κρύψας ἔχεις</note>. This is said of someone who does not share or bring forth their natural gifts. The expression is taken from misers who bury their treasure in the ground. Plautus depicts the character Euclio doing this <note>Euclio is the protagonist of Plautus's play *Aulularia*, or *The Pot of Gold*</note>. Horace says the same in his *Epodes*:
> I shall not have acquired wealth,
> Only to bury it in the earth like the miser Chremes,
> Or squander it like a dissolute heir.

<margin>XXII</margin>
## ->The ox grows old.<-

"The ox grows old, but the labors of the ox are many" <note>original Greek: Τηρᾶ ὁ βῶς, τὰ δ' ἔργα πολλὰ τῶ βοός</note>. That is, the ox reaches old age, yet much work is still required of it. 
This is used when someone is rendered useless for performing their duties due to the weakness of age. For the common run of wealthy people use their servants no differently than they use horses and dogs—or perhaps even a little more inhumanly. While they are useful, they entice them; when they grow old, they cast them aside. 
Therefore, it is advised that everyone should provide for themselves, so they may more comfortably cherish and nourish their own old age, rather than being forced to depend on the generosity of others at a time when they are despised by everyone. One should remember the aphorism of Diogenes, who, when asked what was the most calamitous thing in this life, replied: "A needy old man" <note>original Greek: γῆρας ἄπορον</note>.

<margin>XXIII</margin>
## ->You pig, you shall pay for the grape-stones.<-

"You wicked pig, you shall pay for the grape-stones" <note>original Greek: Αποτίσεις χοῖρε γίγαρτα</note>. 
You will suffer for what you have committed; you will return what you took, and not without interest. This will apply when a small advantage is paid for with a great evil. It clearly originated from some farmer who threatened his pig with these words while it was feeding on his clusters of grapes.

<margin>XXIIII</margin>
## ->While the North wind ceases.<-

Aristotle, in the twenty-sixth section of his *Problems*, the forty-seventh problem (according to Theodore’s numbering), testifies that this little verse was a celebrated proverb:
"When the South wind begins, and the North wind ends" <note>original Greek: ἀρχομένε τε νότο, καὶ λήγοντος Βορέαο</note>.
By this they signaled the opportune time for a prosperous voyage. For the phrase "to set sail" <note>original Greek: πλῶ πλεῖν</note> is understood, because the South wind arises with less violence, but the North wind, which ends with great force, behaves differently. 
The philosopher provides a very probable reason for this. He says that we are situated more toward the North than the South; the North wind (*Boreas*) blows from the Northern regions, and the South wind (*Notus*) from the South. Thus it happens that the North wind, being closer to its origin, attacks nearby places with immediate violence, later transferring its force to more distant locations. The South wind, conversely, first presses upon those in the South; later, when it has passed by, it reaches us more mildly. 
It is also permissible to twist this proverb further—and not without grace—whenever we wish to indicate that a convenient and fit time for conducting business is at hand, so that it matches the saying found elsewhere: "When it rains, one must grind."

<margin>XXV</margin>
## ->Invulnerable as Caeneus.<-

"You are invulnerable like Caeneus" <note>original Greek: Ἄρωτος ὑπάρχεις ὡς καινεύς</note>. This is said of those who cannot be harmed. It is found in the fables of the poets that Caeneus, by the gift of Neptune, could not be injured by any weapon. 
However, according to historical accounts, they say Caeneus was a certain Thessalian man, highly skilled in military affairs, so much so that although he had been present in many battles, he never received a wound. Finally, while bringing aid to the Lapiths against the Centaurs, he was caught alone and overwhelmed by a multitude of enemies, dying without any physical wound on his body. Therefore, when the Lapiths found his corpse intact, they spread the rumor that Caeneus had been invulnerable throughout his entire life. This will be expressed more elegantly through comparison.

<margin>XXVI</margin>
## ->Rubbed with salt, this man will be helped.<-

"Rubbed with sharp salt, this man will be helped" <note>original Greek: Ἁλοὶν διασμηχθεὶς ὄναιτ' ἂν ὁτοσί</note>. 
This was said of those who were acting deliriously, either because of old age or wine. Some think it was transferred from wineskins, which are made better when washed with salt, as the sharpness of the salt corrects the thickness of the hides. Likewise, it was the custom to rub those suffering from intoxication with salt and oil; they considered this a remedy against drunkenness. Some prefer to think it comes from earthenware vessels, which are seasoned with salt so that they may more reliably hold an unsalted liquid. This proverb is taken from Aristophanes' *Clouds*.

<sig>O o 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: These</meta>

<page-num>714</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

### This is justice.
<margin>XXVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Αὕτη τοι δίκη ἐστὶ θεῶν οἳ ὄλυμπον ἔχουσι</note> That is:
> This is the justice of the gods, whom great Olympus encloses.
This is typically said whenever a wicked person suffers punishment, as if the gods themselves were the avengers. It is taken from the works of Homer.

---

### But there should be no deliberation at the altar.
<margin>XXVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ δεῖ περὶ τοῦ ἐν βωμῷ τὰς ἐπινοίας</note> That is: "But there is no need for thinking once you are next to the altar." One should deliberate before beginning; deliberation is too late once the business is underway. The saying is taken from those performing sacrifices, who prepare everything according to the sacred ritual before they approach the altar. For in the middle of the sacred rites themselves, it was considered dangerous if the priests or the assistants <note>the original refers to *patrimis ac matrimis*, children whose fathers and mothers were still living, required for certain Roman rituals</note> said or did anything that was not strictly according to the rules. Marcus Tullius Cicero explains this in his speech *On the Responses of the Soothsayers*: "If the game stops, or if the flute-player suddenly falls silent, or if that boy with living parents fails to keep his hold on the ground, or lets go of the sacred carriage or the leather strap, or if the official makes a mistake in word or gesture, then the games have not been performed according to the rites."

---

### Mars does not shake his own weapons.
<margin>XXIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἄρης τὰ αὑτ῏ ὅπλα οὐ σαλεύει</note> That is: "Mars does not toss about his own weapons." We carry easily those things to which we have become accustomed and which suit us, even if they are very heavy. We only "toss" or struggle with that which we carry uncomfortably. Hence Juvenal says:
> Nor have they learned to toss the yoke with life as their teacher.
<note>Juvenal, Satires 13.22; meaning they have learned to bear life's burdens through experience.</note>
In the same way, the labor of study which might kill an athlete does not weigh heavily on a scholar.

---

### An emerald dark in the light.
<margin>XXX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀσέληνος σμάραγδος, ἐν τῷ φῶς σκοτεινός</note> That is: "A notable emerald, yet dark in the light." This was usually aimed at those who perversely hide themselves away just when it is most appropriate to display a specimen of their virtue. Pliny, among the varieties of emeralds, mentions those called "blind" because they are of a darker color. This defect is most easily detected in the sun; for a truly great color is one that is pleasantly green and is not changed by sun, nor shade, nor lamps, nor even by being underwater. Pliny teaches this same thing in his thirty-seventh book, chapter six.

---

### A chick of Mars.
<margin>XXXI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἄρεος νεοττός</note> That is: "A chick of Mars." They call someone who is greatly inclined toward war by this name. Aristophanes in *The Birds* says: <note>original Greek: Ἄρεος νεοττός, ὦ νεοττὲ δέσποτα</note>, meaning:
> Chick of the God of War, O chick, ruler and master.
However, he is referring to the rooster, which is sacred to Mars because it is the most pugnacious and warlike of all birds—which is why it is armed with both a crest and spurs. Or it may be because there was once a youth beloved by Mars who used to keep watch while Mars was in bed with Venus, so that none of the gods would interrupt. Later, when the sun arrived while the youth was sleeping and Mars was caught in a shameful position, the angry god changed the young man into a bird; yet traces of his former nature still remain <note>he still crows to announce the sun</note>. Lucian tells this fable in *The Dream, or The Cock*. Diogenes Laertius also mentions the proverb in his *Life of Diogenes the Cynic*.

---

### You are plunging a wineskin full of wind.
<margin>XXXII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀσκὸν βαπτίζεις πνεύματος πλήρη</note> That is: "You are plunging a wineskin full of wind." This applies to someone who struggles in vain, such as one who punishes someone beyond correction; for an inflated wineskin, no matter how much you submerge it, will pop back up. It seems to have arisen from an oracle of the Sibyl which she gave concerning the city of Athens:
<note>original Greek: Ἀσκὸς βαπτίζῃ, δῦναι δέ τοι οὐ θέμις ἐστί</note> That is:
> Like a wineskin you are dipped, but to sink is not your fate.

---

### Hard in speech.
<margin>XXXIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἄτηκτος ἄνθρωπος πᾶσι χρηματίζειν</note> That is: "A man immovable or inflexible in his conversations." The metaphor is drawn from wax, which softens through handling. The term <term>atektos</term> means something that cannot be melted. It applies, therefore, to an inexorable person.

---

### Set out for the Apaturia.
<margin>XXXIV</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀπιὼν εἰς ἀπατούρια ἐπανήκει ὅτε θαργηλιῶνα</note> That is: "Having set out for the Apaturia, he returned in May." This was usually said of those who lingered too long over some business. There was a festival in Athens called the Apaturia, which lasted for three days. They called the first day *Dorpia*, because the members of the clan <note>phratores</note> would gather at nightfall for a banquet; the second day they called *Anarrhysis*, because on that day they performed sacrifices to Zeus Phratrios and Athena; the third day they called *Koureotis*, because on that day young men and girls were enrolled into the clan. Suidas mentions this festival at greater length, though those details do not contribute much to explaining the proverb.

<page-num>715</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Oo 4</sig>

->I speak to you of one thing, you answer about onions.<-
->XXXV<-

I tell you about garlic, you answer about onions <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ σκόροδά σοι λέγω, σὺ δὲ κρόμμυ’ ἀποκρίνῃ</note>. That is: I speak to you of one thing, you answer about onions. It is very similar to the saying, "I asked for other things" <note>original Greek: ἄλλας ἀπῄτουν</note>, used when an answer is given that is different from what you asked, or conversely, when a foolish answer is given to a foolish question. Onions and garlic are related to one another <note>making the non-sequitur even more absurd because the topics are close but the answer is still wrong</note>.

->You thought you would be a goldsmith.<-
->XXXVI<-

You thought you would be a goldsmith <note>original Greek: Χρυσοχόησειν ᾤου</note>. That is, you believed you were about to become a worker of gold. They say this arose from an event of this kind: A rumor once grew strong among the common people of Athens that large fragments of gold were to be seen on Mount Hymettus, guarded by those fierce ants <note>legendary giant ants said to guard gold in ancient lore</note>. Thus, certain gullible people took up arms and went out to conquer them. When they returned to the city unsuccessful, having spent their labor in vain, they were mocked by the rest of the citizens with the taunt: "And you thought you would be a goldsmith" <note>original Greek: σὺ δ’ ᾤου χρυσοχοήσειν</note>; that is, you believed you would soon possess gold. Eubulus mentions this matter in the play titled *Glaucus*:

> We once persuaded the sons of Cecrops <note>the Athenians</note>,
> To take up arms and go out to Mount Hymettus,
> Carrying three days' provisions against the ants,
> As if fragments of molten gold had appeared.

In the second to last line of the Greek, there is either a mistake or a missing word: perhaps instead of "you" <note>Greek: σὺ</note>, we should read "of food" <note>Greek: σίτου</note>. This would certainly make the meter of the verse consistent:

> Carrying three days' provisions of food against the ants.

This also appears in Plato’s fifth book of the *Republic*: "What then? If your friend Thrasymachus, being a goldsmith <note>one who melts gold</note>, had come to those who are here now, would he not rather have come to hear arguments?" <note>Erasmus interprets the Greek *chrysochoos* here as an analogy for someone seeking profit rather than wisdom</note>. Aeschines also writes: "When he withdrew from here, it is clear that he learned how to melt gold, rather than doing or experiencing what was proposed to him." The proverb is suitable when someone has conceived great hopes in their mind but leaves frustrated. This often happens to those who, at their own expense, send people to explore unknown lands, or to those who pour all their wealth into alchemical furnaces <note>Erasmus frequently mocked alchemy as a way to waste money on false hopes of gold</note>.

->The streams of Marah and Siloam are separate.<-
->XXXVII<-

The streams of Marah and Siloam are separate <note>original Greek: Χωρὶς τὰ μεῤῥᾶ καὶ σιλωὰν ῥεύματα</note>.
This refers to things separated by a vast interval, or as if someone were to say there is a world of difference between a friend and a flatterer. It is related to the saying, "The possessions of the Mysians and Phrygians are separate" <note>original Greek: χωρὶς τὰ τῶν μυσῶν καὶ φρυγῶν</note>. It appears to be a more modern proverb, and I suspect it was added by Apostolius from ecclesiastical writings. For Marah <note>Latin: Merrha</note> is the name of the place where Moses turned the pestilential and bitter waters sweet and healthy by throwing in a piece of wood. However, the blind man in the Gospel was sent by Jesus to the waters of Siloam so that he might regain his sight. From this, it is clear that these healing waters were very different from the waters of Marah.

->False Fires.<-
->XXXVIII<-

False fires <note>original Greek: Ψευδύπυρα</note>, such as those used for deception. This refers to empty threats and terrors, or when a danger is artistically displayed when in reality there is no danger. It is borrowed from a military trick, where fires are lit in various places at night to terrify the enemy, making them believe there is a massive army present. These simulated fires are called *pseudypyra*. This will not have the charm of a proverb unless you apply it to those who try to terrify someone with "smoky" words or lure them into a trap. For sailors are also sometimes deceived in this way.

->Phyra brought Bacchus.<-
->XXXIX<-

Phyra brought Bacchus <note>original Greek: Ψύρα τὸν Διόνυσον</note>. That is, Phyra [brought] Bacchus <note>Dionysus/Bacchus was the god of wine</note>. Stephanus and Suidas quote from Cratinus: "Bringing Bacchus into Phyra." Again, in the *Nemesis*: "And you lead Sparta into Phyra." It was also noted by Hermolaus Barbarus. This was a commonly repeated adage used when no one tastes the wine served at a banquet, or regarding a stingy or poor table setting. Phyra is a tiny island not far from Chios where wine is not produced. Strabo also mentions it.

<meta>This page continues the third Chiliad of Erasmus’s Adages. It follows a discussion on obscure terms and misattributed names, transitioning into several well-known proverbs regarding intellect, cruelty, shared responsibility, and intellectual preoccupation.</meta>

<page-num>716</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

Strabo, in Book 14 <note>of his *Geography*</note>, notes that Homer, in the *Odyssey*, calls this <term>psydnē</term><note>original Greek: ψυδνὴν; an obscure word likely meaning "small" or "feeble"</note>. In the commentaries of the Greeks, I have found it written several times as *psydra* (ψυδρᾶ) with a circumflex on the final syllable, but this is an error, if I am not mistaken.

### A head empty of brains.

"Oh, what a head, and yet it has no brain!" <note>original Greek: ὦ οἷα κεφαλή, καὶ ἐγκέφαλον οὐκ ἔχει</note>. This is used against those who are physically outstanding but lack intelligence. It originates from one of the fables attributed to Aesop <note>the fable of the Fox and the Mask, where a fox finds a hollow actor's mask and remarks on its lack of brains despite its beauty</note>. It is also common to say of the foolish and senseless that they are "empty of brain."

### Cruel Bacchus.

"Cruel Bacchus" <note>original Greek: Ωμηστὴς Διόνυσος; literally "Dionysus the Eater of Raw Flesh"</note>. In ancient times, living men were sacrificed to Bacchus. Therefore, the phrase is applicable to cruel people, or perhaps because drunkenness renders men fierce and pitiless.

### Histiaeus sewed this shoe, but Aristagoras put it on.

"Histiaeus indeed sewed the shoe, but Aristagoras put it on" <note>original Greek: τὸν ὑπόδημα ἔρραψε μὲν ἱστιαῖος, ὑπεδύσατο δὲ ἀρισταγόρας</note>. Diogenianus advises that this is said of those who cunningly shift their own misdeeds onto others. The adage arose from the following history: A certain Histiaeus, a Samian by birth and a friend of King Darius, was sent by him into Persia. While staying there, he was seized by a longing to see his homeland again. However, since he could not obtain permission from the king to leave, he wrote to Aristagoras, his nephew (his brother's son), urging him to incite the Ionians to revolt, specifically so that Histiaeus might be sent back to handle the situation. 

He devised a new method for transmitting letters, which Aulus Gellius also mentions in the *Attic Nights*, Book 17, Chapter 9. He took a trusted servant who had long suffered from sore eyes and, under the pretext of medical treatment, shaved all the hair from the man's head. He then tattooed the message onto the smooth scalp. Once he had written what he wished, he kept the man at home until his hair grew back. When the hair had returned, he sent him to Aristagoras. "When you reach him," he said, "tell him that I command him to shave your head just as I did myself recently." The servant did as he was ordered, and Aristagoras, realizing it was not for nothing, shaved the head and read the letters. Learning Histiaeus’s intent, he drew nearly all of Ionia into rebellion. 

When Darius learned of this and summoned the Ionians, he consulted Histiaeus on who should be sent to Asia to settle affairs. Histiaeus persuaded the king to send him, claiming he was the most suitable person to mend the Ionian defection. However, after he arrived in Asia, he fell under the suspicion of the governor of Sardis <note>Artaphernes</note> as being the author of the movement. The governor told him: "The matter stands thus, Histiaeus: you indeed sewed this shoe, but Aristagoras put it on." Herodotus mentions this in his fifth and sixth books, relating it just as I have told it. He meant that Histiaeus was the primary source and author of the plan, while Aristagoras was the administrator. The phrase then, as often happens, became widely known for its novelty and passed into a proverb. It seems most fitting whenever two people assist one another in clever and wicked plans. For giving the plan is like "sewing the shoe," while using and executing the plan is like "putting it on."

### Do not take up what you did not put down.

"Do not lift up what you did not set down" <note>original Greek: ἃ μὴ κατέθου, μὴ ἀνέλῃ</note>. This is cited by Plato in the eleventh book of *The Laws* as being from some poet. Diogenes Laertius records it among the laws of Solon, meaning, I believe, that the boundary markers of fields fixed by ancestors should not be moved. It applies to thieves, to those who demand back what they never entrusted to others, and to those who demand credit for service they did not provide.

### He is looking for bulbs.

<margin>x</margin> "He is looking for bulbs" <note>original Greek: Βολβοὺς ζητεῖ</note>. This is a proverbial phrase used for those who, as Persius puts it, "fix their eyes on the ground with a bowed head." 

Plutarch says in his *Symposiacs*: "For even that man who is laughed at says, and he used a proverb, 'A bulb does not escape me, nor does lightning'; rather, it has a power of resistance, just like the fig tree and the skin of a seal." <note>Erasmus is quoting a passage suggesting bulbs were thought to be safe from lightning, perhaps because they are buried or have some innate property</note>. Furthermore, the "proverbial laughter" mentioned by Plutarch is taken, I believe, from Aristophanes' *The Clouds*. In that play, Strepsiades, entering the school of Socrates, notices the disciples of Socrates looking at the ground with their heads bowed. When someone asks what they are doing, the reply is:

> "These men are seeking things beneath the earth."
> "Then they are looking for bulbs! Do not worry about that now..."

<meta>This page continues the third Chiliad of Erasmus’s Adages, specifically moving into the fourth century of that collection. It maintains the theme of exploring Greek and Roman idiomatic expressions, their literary origins, and their moral applications.</meta>

<page-num>717</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

"...for I know where there are big and beautiful ones" <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ γὰρ οἶδ' ἵν' εἰσὶ μεγάλοι καὶ καλοί</note>. That is: Strepsiades asks what land holds them. They are looking for bulbs <note>likely the edible bulbs of the tassel hyacinth, considered a delicacy and an aphrodisiac in antiquity</note>, of course. "But let no care for that matter trouble you, for I know where there are large and good ones." If someone prefers to relate this to what is found in the same poet’s *Plutus*: "Now you eat thyme" <note>original Greek: τανῦν θύμου φάγητε</note>, which is to say, "You who have eaten the same onions with me," I certainly would not object. It signifies poor friends and those who, as Terence says, "bore heavy poverty together." Persius likewise, in his fourth Satire, writes of a stingy and excessively grasping man:
"May this be well, biting a coated onion with salt, and a pot of porridge while the slaves applaud."
There exists in the same Aristophanes, in *The Assemblywomen*, another joke of this kind about the bulb: "Having devoured a pot of bulbs" <note>original Greek: καταφαγὼν βολβῶν χύτραν</note>. These are the words of an old woman to a young man refusing intercourse, because one man could not be a match for two women. "Fine," she says, "when you have devoured a pot of bulbs." For Martial also testifies that bulbs stimulate Desire <note>Venus</note>:
"You can be full of nothing else but bulbs."
And Columella in his poem:
"Now let the generative seeds of the Megarian bulb come."
There are, however, many species of bulbs, but Dioscorides says in Book 2 that all have a sharp quality and stimulate desire through heat, just like rocket <note>arugula</note>, about which Columella says:
"So that rocket may excite husbands slow to Love."
Suidas refers to two adages about onions: "To eat onions" <note>original Greek: κρόμμυα ἐσθίειν</note> and "To smell onions" <note>original Greek: κρομμύων ὀσφραίνεσθαι</note>, which we have discussed in their proper place.

### Seeking travel-money when the road is finished.
<margin>XLV</margin>
Seneca says in his booklet *On Morals*: "For what is more foolish than, as they say, to seek or increase travel-money <note>Latin: viaticum; funds for a journey</note> when the road is abandoned?" This applies to greedy old men. For that age is usually afflicted by this vice: that the less life remains, the more it is anxious about its livelihood. On the contrary, youth is most negligent in this pursuit. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in *Cato the Elder*: "I truly do not understand what senile greed means. For can anything be more absurd than to seek more travel-money the less of the road remains?"

### To give to the winds.
<margin>XLVI</margin>
"To give to the winds" is used for forgetting and casting something out of the mind. Servius notes that this is a proverbial figure of speech. Virgil in the tenth book of the *Aeneid*:
"Nor does he see the winds carry away his joys."
The same author elsewhere:
"But the breezes tear all away."
Again the same:
"Part he granted in his mind, part he scattered into the flying breezes."
Also Horace in his *Odes*:
"Grief and fears I will give to the boisterous winds to carry into the Cretan sea."
Ovid:
"Did all things go fruitlessly into the sea-winds? Are all things carried submerged in Lethe's <note>the river of forgetfulness</note> waters?"
The same:
"Learn what you must do nonetheless, and do not give my words to be carried by the East winds nor the warm South winds."

### An unbridled mouth.
<margin>XLVII</margin>
"An unbridled mouth" <note>original Greek: Ἀχάλινον στόμα</note>. They call a petulant and slanderous mouth "unbridled." The metaphor is taken from horses not restrained by any bit. So Plato in the third book of the *Laws* calls them "unbridled mouths," imitating Euripides, I believe, who wrote in the *Bacchae*:
"Of unbridled mouths and lawless folly, the end is misfortune,"
as we have mentioned elsewhere. Plutarch, in *On the Education of Children*, said "a mouth without a door" <note>original Greek: ἀθύρωτον στόμα</note>, as if it lacked a gatekeeper. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
"Having a man-eating, unbridled, uncontrolled, un-gated mouth" <note>original Greek: ἀνθρωποφάγον ἔχοντ' ἀχάλινον, ἀκρατὲς, ἀπύλωτον στόμα</note>.
That is, of an impudent mouth, having an unbridled, intemperate, and unworthy mouth of a doorway. Julius Pollux teaches that such men are called "doorless-tongued" <note>original Greek: ἀθυρογλώττους</note>, a word used by Euripides in *Orestes*:
"And after this man stood up a certain doorless-tongued man, strong in boldness, an Argive yet no Argive, forced on, trusting in noise and ignorant outspokenness."

<summary>This page discusses three main proverbs: the use of bulbs (onions) as a metaphor for poverty or aphrodisiacs, the irony of greed in old age (seeking travel-money when the journey is over), and metaphors for lack of self-control in speech (unbridled or doorless mouths).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the third Chiliad of Erasmus’s Adages, moving from the discussion of bulb-eaters and poverty (associated with the previous page) into a critique of foolish oratory and a series of common idioms regarding shared burdens and the revelation of truth.</meta>

<page-num>718</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

...persuasive enough to trip someone up into some evil <note>original Greek: πιθανὸς ἐπ’ αὐτῶν ποδὶ βαλεῖν κακῷ τινί</note>. That is:
> Beneath this crowd there rises a certain man whose mouth 
> Lacked a door, strong in his audacity.
> An Argive yet no Argive, he was driven here,
> Obeying the mob and with unskilled boldness;
> Who with the eloquence of his speech 
> Could involve even the leaders themselves in evil.

So Euripides depicts a foolish orator; but would that this characterization did not apply to many preachers today—not those who preach the Gospel, but those who are sycophants and mere flatterers.

<margin>XL</margin>
->You and I pull the same yoke.<-
I and you draw the same yoke <note>original Greek: Ἐγώ τε καὶ σὺ τὸν αὐτὸν ἕλκομεν ζυγόν</note>. That is:
> You and I equally lead the same yoke.

This is said of those who are liable to similar vices or misfortunes. It is not unlike the phrase, *You are in the same boat*, although that pertains more to a shared danger. Pliny, in his *Epistles*, used the phrase "to pull the yoke from the horse" <note>original Latin: Ex equo iugum ducere</note> to mean sustaining the turns of business equally. The metaphor is transferred from oxen plowing. Horace seems to have alluded to this in the first book of his *Odes*:
> Friends scatter 
> When the casks are drained to the dregs,
> Too treacherous to bear the yoke equally.

<margin>X</margin>
->The matter will show.<-
The thing itself will show <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸ δείξει, with ἔργον ("the work" or "the deed") understood</note>. That is: The matter itself will indicate the truth. We use this when we mean that the truth of a statement is perceived through experience. Plato uses it in the *Theaetetus*. For there, Socrates exhorts his companion to the investigation of a matter, saying: "The man leading the way through the river, O Theaetetus, said, 'the thing itself will show.' And if we continue our search, perhaps the very thing we seek will appear as an obstacle, and there the unclear will be revealed." <note>This refers to a proverb about a guide who, when asked how deep the water is, simply steps in and says "The event will show."</note> It seems to have arisen from an incident: someone about to enter a river to act as a guide for others was asked if the water was deep; he replied, "The thing itself will show." Marsilio Ficino <note>The famous Renaissance translator of Plato</note> translated this as if "the water" <note>Greek: ὕδωρ</note> should be understood, since "the river" preceded it in Plato’s text. But others think "the deed" <note>Greek: ἔργον</note> should be understood—that is, the matter itself. Aristophanes used it in the *Lysistrata*: 
"The deed itself will soon show." <note>original Greek: Τὄργον τάχ’ αὐτὸ δείξει</note>

Pindar says in the *Nemean Odes*: "In the trial, the end shines through, showing in what things one may be more excellent." <note>original Greek: ἐν δὲ πείρᾳ τέλος διαφαίνεται ὧν τις ἐξοχώτερος γένηται</note> Close to this is "The matter itself speaks" <note>original Greek: τὸ πρᾶγμα αὐτὸ βοᾷ</note>, found in Lucian’s *Toxaris*; likewise that line from Aristophanes' *The Wasps*:
"The matter is clear, for it cries out itself." <note>original Greek: Τὸ πρᾶγμα φανερόν ἐστιν, αὐτὸ γὰρ βοᾷ</note>
Marcus Tullius Cicero imitated this in a certain oration when he said that "a man’s whole appearance and his very wickedness seem to cry out."

->Leaving the brace, you chase the foot.<-
Having let go of the brace, you pursue the foot <note>original Greek: Ἀφεὶς τὴν ὑπέραν, τὸν πόδα διώκεις</note>. This is appropriate for someone who, having neglected those things which were more relevant to the matter, cares for trifles. The *hyperae* <note>braces</note> are nautical ropes by which the ends of the yards are moved. They call the lowest part of the sail the "foot" <note>original Latin: pedem</note>. Truly, the greatest use of the braces is in sailing. Suidas cites this adage from Hyperides, who wrote commentaries on Demosthenes, from the first book of *On the Trireme*.

->Beccecelenus.<-
"Bread-Moon-Stupid" <note>original Greek: Βεκκεσέληνος</note>. In the proverb, this was said of someone stupid and delirious, "moon-struck," or very old. In the ancient language of the Phrygians, *Bekos* signifies bread, according to Herodotus in Book 2. *Selene* means the moon. From this, the Arcadians—who wish to be seen as the most ancient of all mortals—are called "Pre-Lunar" <note>original Greek: προσέληνοι</note>, as if they were older than the moon itself. Apollonius notes this in the fourth book of the *Argonautica*:
"The Arcadians, who are said to have existed even before the moon."

King Psammetichus <note>An Egyptian Pharaoh mentioned by Herodotus</note> discovered by this argument that the Phrygians were the most ancient of all peoples: for children who had heard no human voice uttered the sound "Bekos." Suidas notes in this passage that it should not seem surprising if they imitated the voice of goats, as they were raised by a goat. Herodotus asserts this. Plutarch uses the term in his first book, *On the Lives of the Philosophers*...

<summary>Erasmus examines proverbs regarding shared burdens ("pulling the same yoke"), the idea that results speak for themselves ("the matter will show"), and the etymology of "Beccecelenus," a term for ancient or senile foolishness based on Phrygian legends.</summary>
<keywords>oratory, Euripides, shared burdens, Plato, experience vs words, nautical metaphors, Phrygian language, Herodotus, Arcadians, King Psammetichus</keywords>

<page-num>719</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

...the loud-voiced one of words says, "God fashioned the world as a pattern for himself," but that is just "Beccefelene" nonsense <note>original Greek: ὁ μεγαλοφωνος επῶν, ὁ θεὸς επλασε τὸν κὀσμον πῶς ἑαυτῶ ὑποδλγμα, ὁ δὲ ληρος Βεκκεσεληνης</note>, according to the poets of Old Comedy. That is to say: For even the eloquent Plato, when he says God founded the world in his own image, smells of "Beccefelene" delirium, just as the writers of Old Comedy say. The proverb is taken from Aristophanes' *Clouds*: "And how is it, you fool, you who smell of the age of Saturn and Beccefelene?" <note>original Greek: Καὶ πῶς ὦ μωρὲ σὺ καὶ κρονιων ὄζων καὶ βεκκεσεληνε</note>. 

In that passage, many things are reported about this word by the commentator, should anyone happen to seek them out; I have touched upon what I judged would be sufficient for the explanation of the adage. <note>"Beccefelene" is a mock-archaic term combining *bekos* (Phrygian for bread, related to the oldest race of men) and *selene* (the moon), implying someone is an "antediluvian fool" or "older than the moon."</note>

### An ignorant man dressed in trousers shows them to everyone. LII

An ignorant man, having put on fine trousers, displays them to everyone <note>original Greek: Ἀμαθὴς εὐαναξυρίδα περιθέμενος, πᾶσι ταύτην ἐνδείκνυτ</note>. That is: An unskilled man, once dressed in a breech-cloth or trousers, shows them off everywhere. This applies to one who, on account of his lack of sophistication, is puffed up even by the most foolish things. For to those ignorant of the world, whatever is foreign and new seems elegant. Certain learned men think the Greeks used the word *anaxyris* for what the Latins call *brachae* (breeches) or *feminalia* (thigh-wraps), which covered the middle part of the body along with the thighs. Breeches, therefore, were a type of barbarian clothing, but especially of certain Gauls; hence that region was called *Gallia Brachata* (Breeched Gaul). Strabo declares that the *anaxyris* was also in use among the Persians. We have seen even the patrician youths of Venice, whenever they travel abroad, delight in Gallic shirts without an outer garment, which they do not do at home. It will also fit those who think themselves something special because they speak French among Germans, or those who sell themselves using obsolete, obscure, or foreign words. There is a suspicion that this was added by Apostolius from the adages of our own age.

### The vote of Minerva. LIII

Minerva's vote <note>original Greek: Ἡ ἀθηνᾶς ψῆφος</note>. This refers to a precise or decisive judgment. It is the opposite of that other proverb, "The sow has judged" <note>original Latin: sus iudicavit</note>. But it becomes more witty if it is applied through irony to a stupid man of no judgment. <note>In Greek myth, Minerva (Athena) cast the deciding vote to acquit Orestes, establishing the principle of mercy in a tie.</note>

### To speak through a wall. LIIII

To speak through a wall <note>original Greek: Διὰ τοίχε λαλεῖν</note>. This is said of one who does something ridiculous. It is either because, with the wall standing in the way, neither hears the other, or because lovers converse in this manner, as Ovid testifies regarding Pyramus and Thisbe.

### Hunger perishes with an interval, and is best lost. LV

Hunger perishes best by a delay <note>original Greek: Διὰ μεσᾶ ἰὴ λιμὸς ἔρρῤ καὶ κάλλιστ’ ἀπόλλυτ</note>. A delay brings a remedy to many things, and especially to anger. This interpretation is also found: that the meaning is, once the starving man is dead, the hunger must necessarily perish as well.

### You may cool a statue with your throat. LVI

You may cool a statue with your throat <note>original Greek: Ἀνδρίαντα γαργαλίζειν, literally "To tickle a statue"</note>. This is said of a matter that is absurd in the highest degree, and which can in no way be done: as if someone should try in vain to overwhelm a man who is most powerful and invincible; for a statue does not melt. <note>Erasmus translates the Greek for "tickle" with the Latin *colas* (to strain or wash), likely playing on the absurdity of trying to affect an inanimate stone object with one's breath or throat.</note>

### You live an unhoped-for life. LVII

You lead an unhoped-for life <note>original Greek: Ἀνέλπιστον βίου ζῆς</note>. For so the Attics speak; that is, a wonderful life, such as one would not even dare to hope for, or one in which hope does not merely nourish the mind, but the things themselves are present. It appears in Pindar.

### Long and mindless. LVIII

He who is long is mindless <note>original Greek: Ἀνὸς ὁ μακρὸς</note>. This is what they commonly say: that a mind is lacking in those who are very tall, and that those who are small have a surplus of spirit. It seems to be taken from Sophocles, in whose *Ajax the Whip-Bearer* these verses are found:
> For it is not the broad men,
> Nor the wide-shouldered who are the most secure,
> But those who think well.

Homer seems to have been of almost the same opinion, fashioning Tydeus with a small body, but otherwise vigorous. For he says in the fifth book of the *Iliad*:
> Tydeus was small in stature, but a fighter.

The same is held in a certain obscene poem...

<page-num>720</page-num>
<header>DES. ERAS. ROT. ADAGES</header>

More useful was Tydeus, who, if you believe Homer,
Was a fighter in spirit, though small in body.
Greater virtue reigned in his tiny frame.

->And in Statius:<-

### Antiopa’s Lament.

<margin>LIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀντιόπης θρῆνος</note>, that is, Antiopa’s lament. This is commonly said when someone who is undeserving is afflicted by calamities and then later delivered from those evils. The adage arose from the story of Antiopa, who is said to have been the daughter of Nycteus. When she had been violated by a certain citizen, her father, becoming heavily enraged, sent her to his brother Lycus so that he might take punishment upon her. But Lycus, because he saw she was carrying a child in her womb, took pity and spared her. Thus she gave birth to Zethus and Amphion, whom Lycus abandoned on a mountain. Now, Lycus had a wife named Dirce; as soon as she sensed that her husband Lycus had been seized by love for Antiopa, she led the girl away to the mountain and bound her to the necks of a bull, with burning torches hanging from its horns, preparing to kill her by this kind of destruction. However, people rushed to the scene at Antiopa’s outcry—both neighboring rustics and Amphion and Zethus, who, having recognized their mother, rescued her and took vengeance upon Dirce.

### Flee Far from a More Powerful Man.

<margin>L</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἄλευ’ ἀπὸ μείζονος ἀνδρός</note>, that is,
Remember to avoid the one who is stronger than you.
Beware of commerce with the powerful; have your dealings with equals. For indeed, familiarity with the nobility either makes one a shameful slave, or, if you do not know how to flatter, exposes you to dangers. Life is much more pleasant and safer when spent with equals. Pindar in his *Nemean Odes* says: <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἐν ἀκάτῳ. χαλεπὰ δ’ ἔρις ἀνθρώποις ὁμιλεῖν κρεσσόνων</note>, that is, "But in a boat... it is hard for men to engage in strife with those more powerful." This matches what is said elsewhere: "Far from Jove and the lightning bolt," and that other saying, "Kings have long hands." Herodotus in *Urania* writes: <note>original Greek: ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ὑπὲρ ἄνθρωπον ἡ βασιλῆος ἐστὶ καὶ χεὶρ ὑπερμήκης</note>, that is, "For the power of the king is beyond man and his hand is exceedingly long." This was more suited to that other proverb, but when the passage occurred in Herodotus, the printer had already finished the previous sheets.

### Do Not Enter Without a Staff.

<margin>LX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἄνευ ξύλου μὴ βάδιζε</note>, that is, do not enter without a piece of wood. Do not be unarmed. Rather, let there always be something in your hand with which you can drive off anyone who might happen to seek to harm you. They say it originated from a certain Cleomenes, a leader of the Athenians. When he had turned to insanity, because he was held in hatred by everyone, he was accustomed to walk about carrying a staff to beat back those who attacked him.

### He has Put on His Entire Fortune.

<margin>LX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἅπασαν τὴν οὐσίαν ἠμφίασαι</note>, that is, he has clothed himself in his entire substance. Said of a poor man who possesses nothing besides his clothing; otherwise called <note>original Greek: ἀνεσίῳ καὶ ἀνολβίῳ</note> "homeless and luckless." Indeed, even today they say this in a common joke, in this manner: "When I jump, all my assets are moved." That saying of the philosopher Bias is well known: "I carry all my things with me." Plautus in *The Rope*:
> What I am wearing is my total wealth.
> An enemy who is not an enemy.

<margin>LXI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀπόλεμος πόλεμος</note>, that is, an enemy without a war. It is said of someone who, though provoked by no injury, nevertheless does the things that enemies do, or who performs hostile acts under the cover of peace. It will also apply to those who, before they have complained about an injury with a friend, already harm them like an enemy.

### Unlucky Days.

<margin>LXII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀποφράδες ἡμέραι</note>, that is, unlucky or "forbidden" days. Long ago, they were called inauspicious days, and those on which it was not legally permitted to conduct public business. From this, it became accepted to call hated and detestable men <note>original Greek: ἀποφράδες</note>. Lucian is a witness to this in his work against a slanderer of this word. Among the people of Attica, there were seven such days on which funeral sacrifices were performed for the spirits of the dead, and for that reason they were considered inauspicious. To this, the superstition of the ancients persuaded itself that certain days of the moon were of ill omen, such as the fourth, fifth, and second days of the waning moon, which they also called <note>original Greek: ἀποκνάδας</note>. Again, days on which those accused of capital crimes were condemned were called <note>original Greek: ἀποφράδες</note> as being funereal. Finally, days made funereal by some remarkable calamity were called <note>original Greek: ἀποφράδες</note>. Horace says: "He placed you on an unlucky day." Plato mentions these days in the seventh book of *The Laws*, denying that they are <note>original Greek: καθαρούς</note>, that is, pure, but he calls them <note>original Greek: ἀποφράδας</note> as being funereal and sacred for burying the dead. That word was later transferred to men who should be cursed and were of abominable malice, as the little verse testifies:
<note>original Greek: Ἄνθρωπος ἀποφράς, καὶ βλέπων ἀπισίαν</note>, that is,
"An unlucky man, looking with a treacherous face."
The etymology of the Greek word is the same as the Latin, derived from <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ φράζειν</note> "from speaking." Of this kind, it is said...
<margin>Sui</margin>

<header>THE FOURTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND</header>
<sig>Pp</sig>

...Suidas, Hesychius, and the author of the *Etymologicum*. Furthermore, we call detestable men "sacred," as Horace says: "Let him be sacred and detestable" <note>original Latin: *Sacer intestabilis esto*</note>. Virgil even applied this to a state of mind: "The sacred hunger for gold" <note>original Latin: *Auri sacra fames*. Here, "sacred" is used in its archaic sense to mean "accursed" or "devoted to destruction."</note>.

<margin>LXV</margin>
->The old woman drinks like a soldier.<-
<note>original Greek: γραῦς κωθωνιζομένη</note>, that is, "Old women acting like soldiers." This refers to old women who behave with indecent wantonness. For the word *cothon* <note>a Greek drinking vessel used by Lacedaemonian soldiers</note> signifies a drunkard; from this comes the invented verb *cothonizein*, meaning to become intoxicated, and *cothonismos* is the act of drunkenness itself. Hesychius also notes that the Greeks called a drunkard a *cothon*, just as the Latins use the terms "flagon" or "wineskin" for such people. Horace, in his *Odes*, writes regarding the elderly wife of the poor man Ibycus:
>Near the famous Luceria,
>Where the wool is shorn, the lyre does not suit you,
>Nor the purple flower of the rose,
>Nor for an old woman to drink the wine jar to the dregs.
The saying about the dancing old woman was discussed elsewhere.

<margin>LXVI</margin>
->The old woman smells like a goat.<-
<note>original Greek: γραῦς ἀναθύει</note>, that is, "The old woman reeks of the goat." This is said of a lustful old woman, because the odor of the armpits and other parts is stirred up when passion is inflamed. Horace writes of such a woman:
>For I can smell more keenly
>Whether a rank goat lurks in hairy armpits
>Than a sharp hound can tell where a boar lies hidden.

<margin>LXVII</margin>
->With a bare head.<-
<note>original Greek: γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ</note>, that is, "With a bare head." People are said to do things with a bare head when they act openly and without any shame. Those who were doing something shameful had a custom of covering their heads with patchwork cloaks. Plautus says in *The Two Captives*: "They go from the forum to the pimps with such 'open heads' as the guilty are condemned in the tribe with 'open heads.'" It does not matter whether you read "open" or "covered" here as an irony; the sense of both readings is the same. Cyril used this proverb as a title when interpreting the Gospel of John, as did Saint Chrysostom in his *Eulogy for the Martyr Babylas*. Socrates also covers his face in Plato’s *Phaedrus* when he is about to deliver a speech disparaging love.

<margin>LXVIII</margin>
->In a bad situation, if you use a good spirit, it helps.<-
That six-foot verse from Plautus’s *The Two Captives* certainly deserves to be counted among the adages: "In a bad situation, if you use a good spirit, it helps."
An evil that cannot be avoided is conquered by enduring it bravely. He explains the same sentiment slightly differently in *Pseudolus*: "A good spirit in a bad situation is half the evil gone."

<margin>LXIX</margin>
->A woman's eye.<-
<note>original Greek: γυναικὸς ὄμμα τοῖς ἀκμάζουσιν βέλος</note>, that is, "A woman's eye is a dart to youths." And Virgil writes: "The woman burns by looking." Likewise: "How I saw, how I perished, how a wicked error swept me away." We have recorded that other saying elsewhere: <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ ὁρᾷν γίγνεται τὸ ἐρᾷν</note>, that is, "From looking, love is born."

<margin>LXX</margin>
->A ten-foot shadow.<-
<note>original Greek: δεκάπους σκιὰ ἔστι</note>, that is, "It is a ten-foot shadow," meaning it is time for dinner. The ancients marked the hours of the day by the length of shadows. Lucian writes in *The Cock*: "Constantly observing how many feet the line was." In the past, those who invited others to dinner would designate at which shadow on the sundial they wished the guests to be present. Similarly, those who were invited would ask at which line they should arrive so as not to come before the time. Furthermore, a ten-foot shadow was most welcome to "parasites" <note>professional dinner guests</note>, as it gave hope for the meal, just as a large amount of smoke rising from a kitchen would. I see no use for this adage unless someone, wishing to describe a very gluttonous person, says that the ten-foot shadow pleases him greatly. Or that someone does nothing but watch for the ten-foot shadow, as Aristophanes uses it in *The Assemblywomen*:
>But let this be your concern,
>When the shadow has become ten feet long,
>To run sleekly to a lavish dinner.
Ammianus, in Book 23, records that among the Persians there was no prescribed hour for taking food except for the kings; for everyone else, their own stomach was their sundial. And in Plautus, if I remember correctly, a parasite...

...someone is angry with those who invented the use of clocks, because the belly is the best clock. This adage is recorded by Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>.

### The Second Voyage.

**The second voyage** <note>original Greek: Δεύτερος πλοῦς</note>, also called the "secondary course," was the term used when sailors, deprived of wind, had to propel the ship with oars. For a "divine voyage" <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ θείας πλόος πρῶτος</note> was the "first" kind, occurring when one sailed with favorable winds; this is the proper definition of navigation according to Pausanias, whom Eustathius cites in his commentary on the second book of the *Odyssey*, where he also mentions this proverb. 

Aristotle, in the second book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, writes: "Since, therefore, it is extremely difficult to hit the middle exactly, one must, as they say, take the 'second voyage' and choose the least of evils." The Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> means that virtue is located in the middle ground. But since it is sometimes difficult to achieve that, he advises us to deviate as slightly as possible. This relates to the line from Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen*:

->For now we neither sail nor row.<-
-><note>original Greek: νυν͂ μὲν γὰρ οὔτε θείομεν, οὔτε ἐλαύνομεν</note><-

The commentator explains that sailors resort to oars when they are deprived of wind. This is used as a custom whenever the most effective means are unavailable, and one must resort to the next best help. It is similar to what we have recorded elsewhere: "Second thoughts are better." 

John Chrysostom <note>an early Church Father known for his eloquence</note> used this in his first homily on Matthew: "Since we have rejected this grace, come, let us at least embrace the 'second voyage.'" And here, as they say, right in the harbor, the translator Anianus ran aground; for he rendered this passage as: "Because we have shaken off this grace from us, let us hope for 'second riches.'" This is despite the fact that in the common printed editions, "we excuse" <note>Latin: excusamus</note> is read instead of "we shook off" <note>Latin: excussimus</note>, and "we expect" <note>Latin: expectamus</note> instead of "we hope for" <note>Latin: experamus</note>. 

Chrysostom is arguing that the first and best way is to have no need of written laws; but since we have degenerated from that highest state, we must imitate sailors who, when they cannot reach their destination by a straight course, nevertheless try to reach the same place by rowing or by a winding path. However, the translator was deceived by his ignorance of the proverb, and thus turned "from grace" into "riches." I point these things out not to disparage Anianus, to whose industry students owe much, but to warn the readers. 

There exists a poem by Naumachius, a Christian poet I suspect, in which he first praises virginity, then calls marriage a "secondary voyage" compared to it:

>But if a desire for the common life should seize you,
>And you wander with a prudent eye, I will show you how you must complete
>The voyage, as they say—the second one—with a wise soul.
>->that is,<-
>If a common love of life holds you, I will add 
>this which I have learned to use: by what means, as a victor, as they say, 
>this second path must be completed by you with a sagacious mind.

Cicero alludes to this in his *Orator* addressed to Brutus: "But if some force of intellect should perhaps fail, either by its own nature or for lack of exercise, or if one is less instructed in the disciplines of the great arts, let him nevertheless hold whatever course he can. For when one is pursuing the first rank, it is honorable to stand in the second or third." 

Signifying the greatest speed, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> joined both together in his *First Philippic*: "Then indeed, I was set on fire with such a desire for return, that neither oars nor winds were enough to satisfy me."

### Diagoras of Melos.

**Diagoras of Melos** <note>original Greek: Διαγόρας ὁ μήλιος</note>. This is used against a wicked, treaty-breaking, and impious person. After Melos was captured, Diagoras lived in Athens, and he so utterly despised the Athenian sacred mysteries that he turned many away from religion and discouraged others from wanting to be initiated. Furthermore, he profaned those mysteries which it is a sin to reveal to the uninitiated; that impious man published them to the common people, mocking mortals for those theatrical displays. 

For these reasons, he was outlawed by the Athenians, and they posted that proscription on a bronze pillar, adding a reward: one talent for whoever killed the man, and two talents for whoever brought him in alive. Aristophanes mentions this in *The Birds*:

>If any of you kills Diagoras the Melian, 
>he shall receive a talent; and likewise if someone kills 
>any of the dead tyrants. ->that is,<-
>If any of you shall have killed Diagoras of Melos,
>He shall carry off the prize of a talent, and likewise if anyone kills one of those already dead...

<summary>Erasmus explains the proverb "The Second Voyage," referring to using oars (a backup plan) when the wind (the ideal) fails, and discusses the impiety of Diagoras of Melos, who was outlawed for mocking religious mysteries.</summary>

### He exceeded by sixteen feet.
-> LXXIII <-

It is not at all out of place for a proverbial figure of speech to mention what Aristides wrote about Pericles: namely, that the orator Pericles surpassed all other speakers by sixteen feet. He said: <note>original Greek: λέγων, ὡς ἑκκαίδεκα μὲν ποδῶν ὕρε τοὺς ῥήτορας ἐν τοῖς λόγοις, μόνος δ’ ὠθῶν ἐπεκάθιζεν ἐν τοῖς χείλεσιν, πάντας δ’ ἔτι φλυαρεῖαν πρὸς ἐκείνον</note> "Saying that he had outstripped the orators in his speeches by sixteen feet, and that he alone sat upon their lips with a kind of persuasion, while all the rest were mere triflers compared to him." Thus, he used the phrase **sixteen feet** to denote a very great distance. The metaphor is taken from the racetracks where runners compete. This passage regarding Pericles is found in the works of the comic poet Eupolis, in the comedy titled *The Demes*:

> He was the greatest of men at speaking,
> whenever he came forward, just like the good
> runners, he left the orators sixteen feet behind.
> He was swift in speech, and added to that speed,
> Persuasion herself sat upon his lips.

Aristophanes also cites these verses in *The Acharnians* from Eupolis’s *Demes*, adding these two lines:

> He charmed so greatly that, alone among the orators,
> he left a sting behind in the minds of his listeners.

Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his work *Brutus*: "Eupolis wrote that a certain goddess <note>Persuasion</note> sat upon the lips of Pericles." The same poet criticized Pericles’ overwhelming eloquence in that same comedy:

> From there, in his wrath, Olympian Pericles
> flashed lightning, thundered, and threw all Greece into confusion.

Furthermore, regarding "Persuasion," Ennius imitated this in a passage cited by Cicero in *On Old Age*, where he called Marcus Cethegus the "marrow of Persuasion" <note>original Latin: Suadae medulla</note>. The following line from Aristophanes’ *The Clouds* does not differ from the form of this proverb:

> If you say he precedes the race of the Greeks by a hundred stades.
> <note>A "stade" was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>

It will be even more elegant if you substitute "parasangs" <note>a Persian unit of distance</note> for "feet."

### A rolling stone gathers no moss.
-> LXXIIII <-

<note>original Greek: λίθος κυλινδόμενος τὸ φῦκος οὐ ποιεῖ</note>
> A rolling stone is not covered by moss.

This refers to a person who cannot stay in one place; it rarely happens that such a person grows wealthy. Even today, people say almost exactly the same thing. A similar thought is found in Quintilian: "A plant that is moved too often does not take root."

### You are singing the song of Lityerses.
-> LXXV <-

<note>original Greek: Λιτυέρσαν ᾄδεις</note> You are singing the song of Lityerses. Lityerses was the illegitimate son of King Midas. While he lived in Celaenae, he would force those who arrived there to reap grain with him; then, after cutting off their heads, he would wrap the rest of their bodies in the sheaves. He also established the practice of singing a "thericos"—that is, a summer or harvest hymn—in honor of Midas. From this, the proverb arose: those who do not sing from the heart, or who sing under compulsion, are said to **sing the song of Lityerses**. Menander mentions this in *The Chalcedonian*:

> ...singing the Lityerses-song after lunch for a while.

Julius Pollux mentions this story in the fourth book of his *On Vocabulary*, in the chapter "On National Songs." However, he adds a new detail: that Lityerses used to beat those he defeated in reaping with a whip, but when he eventually encountered a reaper stronger than himself, he was slaughtered by him. Some authors, however, claim he perished at the hand of Hercules. Consequently, they say the song was invented to soothe his father’s grief. Theocritus also mentions Lityerses.

<vocab>Pericles (Athenian statesman), Eupolis (Greek comic poet), Aristides (Greek orator), Aristophanes (Greek playwright), Cicero (Roman orator), Ennius (Roman poet), Lityerses (mythological figure), Midas (mythological king), Julius Pollux (Greek grammarian), Theocritus (Greek poet), rhetoric, proverb</vocab>
