# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->**You challenge a Lydian to the plain.**<-

<note>original Greek: Λυδὸν εἰς πεδίον προκαλεῖς</note> i.e., You challenge a Lydian into the open field. This applies to someone who is being urged to do something they have long been inclined and ready to do. The Lydians were noted for being more inclined toward war than was perhaps good for them. Herodotus, in his first book, teaches that the Lydians were particularly strong in their cavalry; hence Croesus wishes that the Ionians would come to attack the Lydians with cavalry <note>implying it would be their downfall</note>. This is very similar to the proverb we have already reviewed: "To the horse in the plain."

->**When the lamp is removed, there is no difference between women.**<-

<note>original Greek: λύχνου ἀρθέντος γυνὴ πᾶσα ἡ αὐτή</note> i.e., Once the lamp is taken away, there is no distinction between women. The proverb suggests that no woman is not unchaste if the opportunity to sin without a witness is granted <note>This reflects a common, if cynical, ancient trope about nighttime and anonymity</note>. This is recorded by the Apostle and used by Plutarch in his *Advice to the Bride and Groom*.

->**A second Lysicrates.**<-

<note>original Greek: Λυσικράτης ἕτερος</note> i.e., Another Lysicrates. A certain Lysicrates became a common laughingstock because he dyed his already gray hair black so that he might still appear to be a young man. Martial writes something similar about a man named Ollus, who dyed his hair because he could not dye his beard.

->**You possess the riches of Lysistratus.**<-

<note>original Greek: Λυσιστράτου πλοῦτον πλουτεῖς</note> i.e., You are wealthy with the riches of Lysistratus. This is a proverbial irony used for a man of very slender means. It is drawn from a certain Lysistratus, a man of extreme poverty.

->**Wait, ox, for the grass eventually.**<-

<note>original Greek: Μένε βοῦς ποτὲ βοτάνην</note> i.e., Wait, ox, for the herb some day. This should be said when something happens too late. For the ox labors in plowing the field, but only much later will it taste the grass that eventually grows there. It is neighbor to that other saying: "And your harvest is still in the blade."

->**Wait, old woman.**<-

<note>original Greek: Μένε γραῦ, ἐμόν σε παῖδα φιλοῦντα</note> i.e., Wait, old woman, for my son to kiss you. That is, before the boy grows up, the old woman will have passed away. This is related to the previous one, used when a hope is shown to be too late.

->**A great dealer in a tiny matter.**<-

<note>original Greek: Μέγας κηληκτὴς ἐν μικρῷ γε πράγματι</note> that is,
->**A mighty dealer in a trivial business.**<-

For if a small conjunction is added, it will form a verse. It fits those who acquire wealth for themselves through an art that is hardly honorable. It arose from an <term>apophthegm</term> <note>a concise, pithy saying</note> of Eudamidas. He was the son of Archidamus and brother of Agis. When a certain musician seemed to have sung quite successfully, someone among those present asked Eudamidas what he thought of him; he replied: "A great charmer in a small matter." He meant that he considered the skill to be laborious but possessing no actual utility. This is recorded by the proverb-collectors. It is also related by Plutarch in his *Sayings of the Spartans*, except that he reads it as "charmer" <note>original: κηληκτὴς</note>, which refers to the way orators soothe and move the emotions. Not dissimilar to this is what Musonius says in Aulus Gellius (Book 5, Chapter 1) regarding those who stir up empty applause from listeners with the modulation of their voice and the enticements of their words: "Know," he says, "that it is not a philosopher speaking there, but a flute-player piping."

->**A deaf man was suing a deaf man.**<-

<note>original Greek: Δύσκωφος δυσκώφῳ ἐκρίνετο, ὁ δὲ κριτὴς ἦν κωφότερος</note> i.e., A deaf man was litigating with a deaf man; the judge, however, was deafer than both. This is used when a matter is conducted between people who are entirely ridiculous and inept. There exists a Greek epigram by Nicarchus on this theme:

> A deaf man was suing a deaf man, and much more
> was the judge deafer than these two.
> Of whom one argued that the other owed him rent
> for five months; the other said he had been grinding at the mill all night.
> The judge, looking at them, said: "Why do you fight?
> She is your mother; both of you must support her!"

Thomas More, when he was a young man, skillfully translated this into Latin in the following manner:

> A lawsuit is underway; the defendant is deaf, the plaintiff was deaf,
> yet the judge himself was deafer than both.
> This one seeks payment for a house, five months having passed;
> That one replies, "I spent the whole night at the mill."
> The judge looks at them and says, "And why do you contend?
> Is there not a mother to you both? Let both of you feed her."

<summary>This page lists several proverbs regarding irony, late-arriving rewards, and the absurdity of poorly matched skill or communication, featuring an epigram translated by Erasmus's friend Thomas More.</summary>

<keywords>Lydians, Lysicrates, Lysistratus, Eudamidas, Thomas More, deafness, irony, Greek epigrams, ancient humor</keywords>

<header>THE THIRD CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

### 84. You have taught the art of diving.

<note>original Greek: Ἐδίδαξάς με κυβιστᾶν, καὶ σὺ βυθίσαι με ζητεῖς</note> i.e., I taught you the art of diving <note>or swimming underwater</note>, and now you seek to drown me. This applies to those who repay good deeds with evil, and turn the benefit they received into the very destruction of the one from whom they received it. It "smells of the dregs" <note>an idiom for something of poor quality or character</note>.

### 85. A bad poet in place of a fine physician.

<note>original Greek: Ἀντὶ χρείηνὸς ἰατροῦ, κακὸς ποιητὴς καλᾶσθαι ἐπιθυμεῖς</note> i.e., You desire to be called a bad poet instead of a charming physician. This was commonly said of someone who, not content with his own professional practice in which he held a respectable position, goes on to profess skills in other areas in which he is not similarly trained, and from which he will not win equal glory. A certain Periander, a physician of no small reputation and highly learned in that art, turned to the study of poetry and began to write rather clumsy little verses. From this, the joke became a popular saying. Plutarch, in his *Laconian Apophthegms*, attributes this saying to Archidamus, the son of Agesilaus.

### 86. From the oar to the tribunal.

<note>original Greek: Ἀπὸ κώπης ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα</note> i.e., From the oar to the judgment seat. This was a common saying used when someone is suddenly promoted from the lowest condition to the administration of an honorable office. I do not know if this ever happened more successfully to anyone than to Pope Julius II. For the story goes that as a young man, he used to row a boat with an oar for a pittance, and yet from the tow-rope he was raised not only to the tribunal but even to that highest peak of human affairs <note>the Papacy</note>. Nor was he content with this height, for he greatly extended the boundaries of the pontifical domain—and would have extended them even further if the cruelty of death had allowed his life to continue. The orator Demades is criticized by Syrianus, the commentator on Hermogenes, because without any knowledge of the legal art, he immediately rushed into arguing cases, "having leaped from the oar to the tribunal with unwashed hands" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς κώπης ἀνιπτοῖς χερσὶν ἐπὶ τὸ βῆμα πηδήσας</note>. That is, he rushed from the oar to the judgment seat with "unwashed hands," as they say <note>an idiom for being unprepared or irreverent</note>.

### 87. You spit at heaven.

<note>original Greek: Εἰς οὐρανὸν πτύεις</note> i.e., You spit at heaven; that is, you do something that falls back upon your own head. Or, you speak ill of those who can easily harm you. Indeed, he who spits at heaven first seems to insult the inhabitants of heaven themselves, and then it often happens that the spit falls back onto his own face. Closely related to this is: "To kick against the pricks" <note>original Greek: πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν; i.e., to struggle against a goad or inevitable force</note>.

### 88. One God, and many friends.

<note>original Greek: Εἷς θεὸς καὶ πολλοὶ φίλοι</note> One God, and many friends. The proverb advises that as many friends as possible should be acquired, because after God, they can be of the greatest help. Although Hesiod does not approve of "having too many friends" <note>polyphilia</note>, neither does he approve of "having no friends" <note>aphilia</note>. I believe this was also borrowed from common speech, rather than from specific authors.

### 89. If I had cheese, I would not want for relish.

<note>original Greek: Εἰ τυρὸν εἶχον, οὐκ ἂν ἐδεσμάτων ὤψα</note> i.e., If I had cheese, I would not lack for a savory dish. This is to be said when someone is content with the smallest and cheapest things. Plutarch relates in his *Laconian Apophthegms* that when a certain Spartan had given a savory dish to an innkeeper to be prepared, and the innkeeper asked for cheese and oil with which to season it, the Spartan said, "I would not have needed the savory dish if I had cheese." If anyone prefers "butter" instead of "cheese" in this context, I will not argue with him; for butter seems to correspond more to oil, even if among the Italians even the driest cheese is used as a condiment.

### 90. You thrust the sting into an unholy hole.

<note>original Greek: Εἰς τριμαλιὰν οὐκ ὁσίαν τὸ κέντρον ὠθεῖς</note> i.e., You thrust the goad into an illicit opening. This was a biting remark by the poet Sotades against Ptolemy Philadelphus, who had married his sister Arsinoe, following the example of Jupiter <note>who was married to his sister Juno</note>. The king, offended by this remark, had the man who said it put to death. Plutarch mentions this in his booklet *On Educating Children*.

### 91. Though you do not say so, it shows from your skin.

<note>original Greek: Εἰ καὶ μὴ λέγεις, ἀπὸ τοῦ δέρματος φαίνῃ</note> i.e., Even if you do not speak, you show it by your skin. The reality itself refutes a liar, as does the expression on his face. Whence that saying of Cicero: "Unless you were faking, you would not speak so." It seems to have originated from a fable.

### 92. The trap has caught the mouse.

<note>original Greek: Εἴληφεν ἡ πάγις τὸν μῦν</note> i.e., The snare has caught the mouse. Said of those caught rightly and deservedly, and who are worthy of misfortune. It is as if you were to say, "the wolf fell into the pit," or "the boar into the nets."

### 93. Comedy and tragedy are composed of the same letters.

<note>original Greek: Ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν τραγῳδία γίνεται καὶ κωμῳδία γραμμάτων</note> i.e., From the same letters both comedy and tragedy are composed. This applies to those who know how to fashion different stories from the same subject matter. Or those who use the same...

different works are possible.

### A cliff in front, wolves behind.

<margin>Note: A choice between two equally dangerous options.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἔμπροσθεν κρημνὸς, ὄπισθεν λύκοι</note> i.e., A cliff in front, wolves behind. This is used when someone is pressed by two great evils from both sides, so that whichever way they fall, they must perish.

### When one yawns, another yawns as well.

<margin>Note: On the infectious nature of habits.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἑνὸς χανόντος μετέχασκεν ἕτερος</note> i.e., When one opens his mouth to yawn, immediately another does the same. This is said whenever someone is provoked to a similar act by the example of a sin or a fault. This happens by a certain force of nature, so that he who sees a yawner is forced to yawn himself. Philosophers even attempt to give an explanation for this phenomenon. In a similar way, certain emotions of the mind are passed along. Socrates, in Plato's *Charmides*, says: "And Critias, hearing these things and seeing me at a loss <note>original Latin: fethæsitantē, likely a typo for 'et hæsitantem'</note>, just as those who see someone yawning in front of them are seized by the same affection, so too he seemed to me to be forced by my hesitation to be seized by hesitation himself." The Latins call yawning <term>oscitantiam</term> <note>sluggishness or negligence</note>. He who lives with the lazy easily becomes like them. For we are all inclined to move from labor to lust, as the comic playwright says. The **torpedo** fish <note>an electric ray</note> by its touch immediately renders one torpid. Plato in the *Meno* says: "And you seem to me to be most like that flat marine torpedo; for it makes anyone who approaches and touches it become numb, and you seem to me now to have done something similar to me, making me numb."

### Among the blind, the cross-eyed man is king.

<note>original Greek: Ἐν τοῖς τόποις τῶν τυφλῶν λάμων βασιλεύει</note> i.e., In the region of the blind, the one-eyed man is king. Among the learned, he who is half-learned is considered most learned. Among beggars, he who has a tiny amount of money is a Croesus <note>a famously wealthy king</note>. It "smells of the dregs of the common people" <note>an idiom for a common or vulgar saying</note>.

### You are hiding on the threshing floor.

<note>original Greek: Ἐν ἅλῳ δρασκάζεις</note> i.e., You are hiding in an open space. Said of someone involved in a business where he cannot help but be conspicuous. Or of one who hides in such a way that he is nevertheless seen by everyone. For on a threshing floor <note>a flat, open area for processing grain</note>, there are no hiding places.

### When you can flee, do not seek a lawsuit.

<margin>Note: Better to avoid conflict than to risk an unfair trial.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἐξὸν φυγεῖν μὴ ζήτει δίκην</note> i.e., When the power to flee is available, do not seek a legal dispute. This arose from an aphorism of Aristotle. When he was summoned from Sicily by the Athenians to answer a charge, he hid himself, saying that one should not litigate if there is any way to escape. There is another story related to this: "Do you not then trust your country to judge you?" "On the contrary," he said, "I wouldn't even trust my mother. For I would fear lest she by mistake should cast the black pebble instead of the white one" <note>In ancient courts, a white pebble signaled innocence and a black one signaled guilt</note>. Alcibiades would subscribe to this opinion, as would anyone who has experienced lawsuits. In Greek, they use a single word, <term>phygodikoi</term>, for those who shrink from a lawsuit.

### He sat on the ox-hide.

<note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ βύρσης ἐκάθεζο</note> i.e., He sat on the hide of an ox; that is, he implores help as a suppliant. This adage comes from a local custom of the Scythians, as Lucian testifies in his *Toxaris*. Among them, if someone happened to be wronged and lacked the means to take revenge, he would slaughter an ox, cut the meat into small pieces and cook it, while he himself sat on the hide spread out on the ground with his hands behind his back. This was considered the greatest form of supplication among them. Anyone who wished to help would approach, taste a portion of the meat, place his right foot on the hide, and promise to be an ally to the best of his strength. This treaty was held most sacred among the Scythians.

### The guest [displaces] the native.

<note>original Greek: Ἔπηλυς τὸν ἐνοικον</note> i.e., The newcomer [expels] the inhabitant—the word "ejected" is understood. It is said when someone of a different profession surpasses another in that person's own craft. For example, if a lover of language <note>a philologist</note> should surpass professional grammarians in the art of grammar. Or if an adopted son should eject a natural son from the family, or if a newly recruited soldier should eject the veteran farmers.

### Sardonic laughter.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within a rectangular frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>
<note>original Greek: Sαρδόνιος γέλως</note> i.e., Sardonic laughter. Said of a fake, or bitter, or even insane laugh. Both the meaning and the origin of this proverb are treated so variously by authors that I fear this Sardonic laughter might not be read without some laughter itself; nevertheless, it is sought out...

### The Sardonian Laugh

...to relate certain things. Zenodotus, in his *Collections*, cites Aeschylus, who reportedly handed down an account of this sort in his work *On Proverbs*: that there is a certain race, a colony of Carthaginians, who inhabit the region of Sardinia. It was their custom to sacrifice those who had passed their seventieth year to Saturn <note>The Roman name for the Greek Titan Cronus, often associated with human sacrifice in ancient accounts of Carthage</note>, laughing meanwhile and embracing one another. For they considered it shameful to utter wailing or to shed tears at a funeral. From this, a simulated laugh began to be called "Sardonian." Timaeus, as cited by the same Zenodotus, says that the Sardinians had a custom where sons would place their elderly parents next to a pit or a precipice in which they were to be buried, and then, beating them with clubs, they would cast them headlong into it. But the parents, meanwhile, would laugh as they perished, believing that such a death was happy and noble because they died through the "piety" <note>Erasmus likely uses "impietate" in the source to mean a subversion of natural filial duty, though the parents viewed it as a ritual service</note> of their children.

There are those who say that a certain herb grows on the island of the Sardinians, nicknamed the "Sardoan" herb, which is similar to wild parsley. They say it tastes sweet, but once tasted, it causes the mouths of men to contract into a grimace of pain, so that they die as if they were laughing. Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman geographer</note> seems to have held this view, as does the grammarian Servius when explaining this passage from Virgil’s *Thyrsis*:

->Nay, let me seem to you more bitter than Sardonian herbs.<-

The interpreter of Lycophron relates almost the same things regarding the Sardonian laugh. Following Servius, Latinus Drepanius says in his *Panegyric*: "Therefore, we put on serene faces, and in the manner of those who, having tasted the juice of Sardinian grasses, are said to laugh in death, we, though grieving, imitated the joyful."

Again, there are those who think the Sardonian laugh is named <gloss>from the baring of the teeth</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ σεσηρέναι τοὺς ὀδόντας</note>, because it opens and exposes the teeth, the kind of laugh usually found in those who do not laugh from the heart. Hence that joke of the parasite in Plautus who complains that the young men had not laughed at his jokes in any way, nor even imitated dogs by showing their teeth. And Apuleius says: "If by chance you laugh with lips drawn back." Homer described this kind of laugh in the fifteenth book of the *Iliad* when speaking of Juno: <gloss>She indeed laughed with her lips, but the brow above her dark eyebrows did not relax.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἡ δ' ἐγέλασσε χείλεσιν, ἠδὲ μέτωπον ἐπ' ὀφρύσι κυανέησιν ἰάνθη.</note> That is:

>She indeed laughed with her lips, but furthermore
>Her clouded brow did not shine at all.

Toward this point, Aristophanes writes in *The Peace*: <gloss>gaping and grinning at one another.</gloss> <note>original Greek: κεχηνότες ἐπ' ἀλλήλοισi καὶ σεσηρότες</note> That is:

>In turn, they were exasperated with one another, drawing back their mouths.

The metaphor is taken from dogs, for whom this is a sign of anger: to bare the teeth. They say this habit is also in horses when they prepare to bite; hence people now commonly call this kind of laugh a **horse laugh** <term>risum equinum</term>.

Furthermore, others claim that it was a custom among the Sardinians to sacrifice the most beautiful and the oldest of their captives who had exceeded seventy years to Saturn, laughing in death because it seemed brave and manly. The author Clearchus is cited, saying it was a solemn custom in Carthage that, in fulfillment of great vows, they would place a boy into the hands of Saturn. The statue of the god was fashioned of bronze with outstretched hands. Under it was a furnace; this was lit, and the boy, contracted and twisted by the heat of the fire, would exhibit the appearance of one laughing.

Finally, Zenodotus also alleges Simonides as the author of a new fable. For he says that a certain bronze man named Talus <note>A giant automaton made of bronze to protect Crete</note>, before he arrived in Crete, came to Sardinia, where he put many mortals to death. When they died, they grimaced <note>original Latin: ringerentur</note>, exhibiting a sort of image of laughter, which gave rise to the proverb. Some add that when he was forbidden to cross from Sardinia to Crete, he leaped into the fire (since he had a bronze body) and then used to kill the Sardinians by clasping them to his chest. They died as if in an embrace, looking like people laughing, surely because their mouths were drawn open by the burning.

A ridiculous story is told about this Talus. They say he was fashioned out of bronze by Vulcan and sent as a gift to Minos for the protection of the island of Crete. He had, however, only a single vein, extending from the top of his neck down to his very ankles. Three times each day he would circle the island, keeping watch. Thus, he even forbade the ship *Argo*, returning from Colchis with Jason, from docking in the Cretan port. But he perished, deceived by Medea—as some say, by a poison that induced madness; or as others prefer, when she promised she would make him immortal, she drew out the nail that was fixed at the end of his vein, and so he died as all the blood and moisture of his body flowed out. Again, others relate that he was killed by Poeas, who struck him in the ankle with a bow. Dioscorides, in his sixth book, placed among poisons a certain species of herb which some call **buttercup** <term>ranunculum</term> in Latin, and the Greeks call <term>batrachion</term>.

### The Sardonian Laugh (Continued)

They call this laughter "Sardoan" or "Sardinian" after the region where it grows most abundantly. When consumed, this herb robs a person of their mind and, by contracting the lips, creates the appearance of a laugh. From this, the proverb of the "Sardonic laugh" emerged as a sinister omen. Pliny mentions this in his 25th book, near the end. Strabo, in the 11th book of his *Geography*, writes that in Cambysena, which borders the Alazonius river, a certain kind of spider is born whose bite forces some to laugh and others to weep with a longing for their loved ones. Some add the story of the *Tarcotella* <note>Likely referring to a tarantula or a similar legendary venomous creature</note>, whose bite is followed by laughter. 

Indeed, even Aristotle, in the 3rd book of *On the Parts of Animals*, says it has been recorded in literature that a blow even piercing the midriff <note>original: "praecordia"</note> in battles has brought about a laugh, and that this happens because of the heat generated by the wound. The painter Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter of the 5th century BCE</note> also died from laughing while he laughed without end at a portrait of an old woman he had painted; so too did Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> upon seeing a donkey eating figs. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the 7th book of his *Letters to Friends* addressed to Fabius, says: "You seem to me to fear that if we have that man, we might laugh a <term>Sardonic laugh</term> <note>original: "γέλωτα" (gelōta)</note>." He meant that if Caesar gained power, many would be forced to smile and applaud things that greatly displeased them.

Lucian, in his work *The Ass*, writes: "they spoke <term>laughing sardonically</term> <note>original: "σαρδάνιον γελῶντες ἔλεγον"</note>," implying a contemptuous and mocking laugh. The same author says elsewhere: "But Damis, <term>sneering with a sardonic laugh, grew even paler</term> <note>original: "ὁ σαρδάνιον ὑπογελῶν ἔτι μᾶλλον ὠχρίωσε"</note>." Plato seems to use it in the same sense in the 1st book of *The Republic*, when he writes that Thrasymachus—whom he depicts everywhere as bitter and arrogant—laughed sardonically: "When he heard these things, <term>he let out a loud and very sardonic laugh, and spoke</term> <note>original: "ἀνεκάγχασέ τε μάλα σαρδάνιον ἡ κήν"</note>." 

Homer also mentions this laugh in several places in the *Odyssey*, recounting how one of the suitors, Ctesippus, took an ox foot from a basket and threw it at Ulysses—who was sitting in the house in the guise and appearance of a beggar—but Ulysses dodged the blow by leaning his body just in time.
<term>He smiled in his heart</term> <note>original: "μείδησε δὲ θυμῷ"</note> <term>a very sardonic smile</term> <note>original: "σαρδάνιον μάλα τοῖον"</note>.

In this passage, the commentator Eustathius <note>A 12th-century archbishop and scholar known for his commentaries on Homer</note> notes that one laughs a "Sardonic laugh" when they laugh with their lips drawn back, while inwardly they are tortured by either anger or distress. For the ancients called it "Sardonic" whenever someone not only laughs in contempt but also in mockery, <term>from the drawing back of the lips</term> <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ σεσηρέναι τὰ χείλη"</note>. This is how those who are planning some mischief against another person usually laugh; just as Ulysses, soon to eliminate the suitors and already deciding it in his mind, laughed a somewhat bitter laugh. A similar laugh is attributed to Jupiter in Hesiod, when he was angry with Prometheus because of the fire stolen by theft. I have translated the verses here, which are found in the first book of the work titled *Works and Days*:

> <term>To him, the cloud-gatherer Jupiter, incensed in spirit, spoke:</term>
> <term>Son of Iapetus, who knows more of craft and guile</term>
> <term>Than all other mortals, you rejoice in having stolen fire and deceived me;</term>
> <term>But a great plague shall come to you and to men of the future,</term>
> <term>For whom I shall give, in exchange for the stolen fire, an evil in which all</term>
> <term>Will delight in their hearts, cherishing their own destruction.</term>
> <term>So he spoke, and the father of men and gods laughed aloud.</term>

They interpret this laugh as "fatal," occurring whenever a destruction destined by the Fates is imminent. Of this kind was the laugh of the suitors, which Homer describes in the same book we just cited and have referred to elsewhere:

<term>Pallas Athena stirred up</term>
<term>Unquenchable laughter in the suitors, and turned their minds astray,</term>
<term>And now they laughed with jaws that were not their own,</term>
<term>And they ate meat drenched in blood; and their eyes</term>
<term>Were filled with tears, and their souls sensed a coming mourning.</term>

> The goddess Tritonia <note>An epithet for Athena</note> stirred up a powerful laughter among the suitors
> That could not be restrained, and she stunned their minds;
> And then they laughed with jaws that were no longer their own,
> Devouring pieces of meat that were raw and bloody.
> Meanwhile, their eyes filled with tears, and their very
> Souls felt the coming grief.
<note>original: Homer, *Odyssey* 20.345-349. Erasmus uses a Latin translation of the Greek here.</note>

I believe this should also be understood as the "Sardonian laugh," which Homer attributed to Ajax in the seventh book of the *Iliad* as he entered into single combat:
> Thus the giant Ajax rose, the bulwark of the Greeks,
> Smiling with a grim and terrifying face.
<note>original: "τοῖος ἄρ’ Αἴας ὦρτο πελώριος... μειδιόων βλοσυροῖσι προσώπασιν."</note>

In some very ancient commentaries on Hesiod, I found an epigram in which the proverb of the Sardonian laugh is explained quite elegantly; it is as follows:

->There is a certain island called Sardo <note>Sardinia</note>, rich in crops,<-
->Where a destructive plant grows from the earth,<-
->Resembling celery, and called "Sardane."<-
->When eaten by those who do not know it, it immediately<-
->Causes a spasm and the appearance of a laugh,<-
->And death soon claims the one who has laughed.<-
->Others say that the Sardanian barbarians,<-
->When their parents have reached the extreme of old age,<-
->Take them to a steep place in the countryside,<-
->And kill them there with clubs and stones,<-
->Then cast the wretched souls down from the rocks,<-
->Laughing recklessly at these "father-killing" games.<-
->Still others prefer the idea that it is the dying themselves<-
->Who laugh, because they see the skillful designs of fate,<-
->And the cycles and turnings of human affairs.<-

I have also, according to my custom, produced a Latin version of this on the spot for those less skilled in Greek, in this manner:

> A certain island is called Sardo, near Iberia,
> In which a deadly herb rises from the soil,
> Named "Sardanæ," bearing the likeness of 
> Wild celery <term>apiastrum</term> <note>Likely *Oenanthe crocata* (Hemlock Water Dropwort) or a similar species found in Sardinia</note>. If eaten by the unwary,
> It soon draws back the lips and displays the 
> Appearance of a laugh; then immediately death takes hold,
> Mimicking a smile. However, there are those who say
> That there is a certain barbarian race of Sardanians,
> Who carry their parents, weary with age, to steep 
> Places, and there deliver the wretched ones to death
> With stones and clubs, and straightway
> Cast them down from the high cliffs.
> Yet in the midst of this, they laugh with impious jokes,
> And play recklessly at parricidal games.
> To others, this interpretation is more pleasing:
> That those who are being killed in this way laugh,
> Because they behold the madness of their own children,
> And the swift and surging changes of human fortune.

Pausanias, in his description of Phocis <note>original: "Phocaicis"</note>, relates that the island of Sardinia produces harmless snakes. Furthermore, he says it is entirely free of poisonous herbs, except for one fatal species resembling celery, which grows near springs but does not infect the water. Those who eat it, he says, die laughing. From this, Homer, and others after Homer, introduced the adage, saying that those who "laugh a Sardonian laugh" are those who laugh a laugh that is "completely unsound" <note>original: "ᾧ τῶν ὀλοῶν ὑγιῆ"</note>, which is to say, entirely insane. Thus, it seems the Sardonian laugh can be appropriately used for a demented laugh, whenever a person is facing imminent...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s deep dive into the "Sardonic laugh" (Risus Sardonius), moving from physical causes to literary usage and etymological variations across Greek and Latin authors. It then transitions to a new adage regarding the appropriate roles for different stages of life.</meta>

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

...one laughs insanely at such evils. Indeed, we read that Gaius Gracchus, while campaigning for office, shouted at his enemies who were laughing insolently at him, saying they were laughing a "Sardonic laugh," as if they were being enveloped by a great darkness arising from their own actions. Plutarch records this in his *Life of the Gracchi*. The same author, in his essay *On Superstition*, writes: "In this case, consider the atheist, who, while drinking, laughs an absurd and Sardonic laugh." <note>original: "Ἐνταῦθα πίνων σκοπεῖ τὸν ἄθεον, γελῶντα μὲν τὸν καὶ τὸν Σαρδάνιον γέλωτα."</note> A certain commentator on Hesiod interprets the Sardonic laugh as a "broad laugh" <note>original Greek: "πλατὺν" (platyn)</note>, that is, a wide one, where the mouth is drawn back violently in a grin. I believe this is the same as what they call a "shaking laugh" <note>original Greek: "γέλωτα συγκρόσιον" (gelota synkrosion)</note>, meaning a laugh that convulses the body. This interpretation is also supported by the etymology of the word itself, which we showed a little earlier comes from "the baring of the teeth." <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ σεσηρέναι τοὺς ὀδόντας" (apo tou seserenai tous odontas)</note> Finally, it will not seem entirely absurd to apply the Sardonic laugh to a mournful and sad laughter, such as Homer attributes to Andromache in the twentieth book of the *Iliad* <note>Erasmus likely means the *Iliad* book 6 or *Odyssey* book 20; here he quotes the famous scene of Andromache's "smiling through tears"</note>, as if it were a sign of a mind foreboding the death of Hector:

> She then received him in her fragrant bosom,
> Laughing through her tears. <note>original: "Ἡ δ’ ἄρα μιν κηώδεϊ δέξατο κόλπῳ / Δακρυόεν γελάσασα."</note>
> That is: She received him in her breathing bosom, mournfully laughing.

Eudemus, in his *Collection of Rhetorical Expressions*, says some prefer it to be understood as a defiant laugh, where one laughs with despite and contempt; a proverb is even told about this: "You laugh at me from a high place." <note>original Greek: "Αὐτὸς κατεγελάς μοι" (Autos kategelas moi)</note> He adds that there is a type of stone called the "Sardonic laugh." Suidas writes that a verb was even formed from this, so that those who laugh a Sardonic laugh are said "to sardaze." <note>original Greek: "σαρδάζειν" (sardazein)</note> But for a long time now I have wanted to depart from the Sardonic laugh, and we shall do so, if we first add that this epithet "Sardonian" is found in various forms among authors. In Lucian and Cicero we read *Sardánion* with an 'a'; in Homer, *Sardánion*; in Virgil, *Sardonium* with an 'o'; in the commentator on Lycophron, "laughter of Sardius"; in Plutarch, *Sardanós*; and in the *Life of the Soul*, "a Sardian laugh of the mind," <note>original: "Ψυχῆς Σαρδανὸς γέλως"</note> meaning if there is a Sardian laugh of the soul. Stephanus indicated that it is also called *Sardōnikón* and *Sardanikón*. However, not all these derive from the same root. For *Sardonius*, *Sardonis*, and *Sardonicus* are derived from "Sardo," the island of Sardinia, which was once named Ichnusa. From "Sardos," a city in Illyria, comes *Sardōos*, which, I believe, changed its vowel to "a" to become *Sardánios*. From "Sardis," the town in Lydia, come *Sardianos* and *Sardianicus*. From these comes a conjecture regarding the Greek epigram we just cited, that perhaps one should not read *ilyotropho* [mud-nourished] but *ilynotropho* [growing in silt]. Salvianus used the adage in his seventh book: "You would think the entire Roman people were saturated with Sardonic herbs: they are dying and yet they laugh."

->Deeds for the young, counsel for those in their prime, prayers for the old.<-

This moral verse is celebrated among the Greeks:
> Deeds of the young, counsels of the middle-aged, and prayers of the old.
<note>original Greek: "Ἔργα νέων, βουλαὶ δὲ μέσων, εὐχαὶ δὲ γερόντων."</note>
> That is: The prayers of the old, the consultations of men, and the deeds of youth.

Aristophanes the grammarian mentions this adage. Hyperides, in his oration against Autocles, cited it as being from Hesiod, for the poem is believed to be his. The meaning is clear in itself: namely, that young men should be employed for carrying out actions, for that age excels in strength. Men of middle age should be brought into counsel, because in them, although the vigor of their strength is somewhat worn down, they nevertheless excel through experience and seasoned prudence. The elderly, being naturally religious, are accustomed to pray for the best things from the gods above; however, they are no longer useful for action, nor are they sufficiently constant in mind due to the defect of their age. Euripides in his *Melanippe*, as cited in Stobaeus, says:
> It is an ancient saying: the deeds belong to the younger,
> But the counsels of the older have the greater power.
<note>original: "Παλαιὸς αἶνος, ἔργα μὲν νεωτέρων, / Βουλαὶ δ’ ἔχουσι τῶν γεραιτέρων κράτος."</note>

Pindar suggests the same when he says:
> For youth, courage in terrible wars is fitting.
<note>original: "Νεότατι μὲν ἀρηγέι θράσος δεινῶν πολέμων."</note>

Likewise, Homer teaches in the nineteenth book of the *Iliad* that strength is required in war, but speech in consultations:
> For the end of war lies in hands, but counsel in words.
> Therefore, one must not increase speech there, but fight.
<note>original: "Ἐν γὰρ χερσὶ τέλος πολέμου, ἐπέων δ’ ἐνὶ βουλῇ. / Τῷ οὔτι χρὴ μῦθον οφέλλειν, ἀλλὰ μάχεσθαι."</note>
> That is: Wars stand by the hand, but consultation by words.
> There one must fight, and sharp words are of no use.

In the same author, Nestor is preeminent in counsel but useless in war. Plutarch, in his commentary...

<header>THIRD THOUSAND, FIFTH HUNDRED</header>

...which is titled, *Whether an Elder Should Engage in Politics.* <note>original Greek: Εἰ πρεσβυτέρῳ πολιτευτέον</note> "And a city is best preserved where there are the counsels of the old and the vigor of the young." <note>original Greek: Καὶ μάλισα σώζεται πόλις, γῆρα βουλαὶ γερόντων, καὶ νέων ἀνδρῶν ἀκμαί</note> That is: And a city is most especially preserved where the wisdom of the elderly and the spears of young men excel. Aeschines, in his oration against Ctesiphon, testifies that this was provided for by the laws of Solon: that in a consultation, the eldest by birth should speak first. And among the Athenians of old, it was the custom that a herald, about to grant the opportunity to speak, would proclaim: "Who among those over fifty years of age wishes to address the assembly?" <note>original Greek: τὶς ἀγορεύειν βούλεται τῶν ὑπὲρ πεντήκοντα ἔτη γεγονότων;</note> That is, who wishes to harangue the people from among those who have exceeded their fiftieth year?

### III. The safe reward of silence.

"The reward of silence is without danger." <note>original Greek: Σιγῆς ἀκίνδυνον γέρας</note> That is, the safe reward of silence. Aristides, in his defense of Pericles, cites this from a certain poet of Ceos <note>This refers to Simonides of Ceos</note>. Plutarch, in his *Apophthegms*, ascribes it to Augustus Caesar, noting that while approving the advice of Athenodorus, he added: "There is also a safe reward for silence." <note>original Greek: ἔσι καὶ σιγῆς ἀκίνδυνον γέρας</note> The complete verse seems to be: 
"For the reward of silence is without danger." <note>original Greek: ἀκίνδυνον γὰρ ἐσὶ τὸ σιγῆς γέρας</note> That is,
->The reward of silence is free from peril.<-
Horace uses this in the third book of his *Odes*: "There is also a certain reward for faithful silence." <note>original Latin: Est & fideli tuta silentio Merces</note>
No one sins by remaining silent, but very often by speaking. That noble sentiment of Simonides has long been a proverb, celebrated even among the Romans as a common saying:
"For it harms no one to have been silent; it harms to have spoken." <note>original Latin: Nam nulli tacuisse nocet, nocet esse locutum</note>
Even so, Valerius Maximus (Book 7, Chapter 2) attributes this sentiment to Xenocrates. "How praiseworthy," he says, "was the response of Xenocrates? When he was present during the malicious talk of certain people in total silence, and one of them asked why he alone held his tongue, he replied: 'Because I have sometimes regretted speaking, but never remaining silent.'"

### IIII. Prosperity has many friends.

"Prosperity has many friends." <note>original Greek: Εὐτυχία πολύφιλος</note> This is very similar to what we have recorded elsewhere:
"Everyone is a relative to the successful." <note>original Greek: τῶν εὐτυχούντων πάντες εἰσὶ συγγενεῖς</note> That is:
Even a stranger is a kinsman to the fortunate.
This sentiment is too well known to require an explanation.
Conversely, in times of adversity, there are either no friends or very few. Pindar says in the tenth Nemean Ode:
"Honor perishes for a man deprived of friends; few mortals are faithful in hard times to share in the labor." <note>original Greek: οἴχεται παρὰ φίλων τατωμένῳ φῶτι, παῦροι δ' ἐν πόνῳ πισοὶ βροτῶν καμάτο μεταλαμβάνειν</note>

### V. Do not give a fool your finger.

"Do not show your finger to a fool, lest he swallow your whole palm." <note>original Greek: Εὐλαθῆ δακτύλου μὴ δείξης, ἵνα μή σοι τὴν παλάμην καταπίῃ</note> That is: Do not show a finger to a fool, so that he does not also devour the palm. Nothing should be permitted to the unwise, no matter how small. For they cause the greatest harm if you entrust them with even the slightest thing. The common people also understand this.

### VI. Wish for your neighbor to have [wealth], but more for your pot.

"Pray for your neighbor to have, but more for your own cooking-pot." <note>original Greek: Εὔχου τῷ πλησίον ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ πλέον ᾖ τῇ χύτρᾳ</note> It is most important to have what is needed at home. Next best is to have a wealthy neighbor from whom you can ask for help. This seems to be drawn from the common rabble.

### VII. Even a fly has a spleen.

"Even the fly has a spleen." <note>original Greek: Ἔχει καὶ ἡ μυῖα σπληνα</note> Very similar to that saying:
"And even boys have the nose of a rhinoceros." <note>original Latin: Et pueri nasum Rhinocerotis habent. This refers to being capable of sharp mockery.</note>
Also this one: "Even in the ant there is bile." <note>original Greek: ἔνεισι καὶ μύρμηκι χολός</note> It smells of the common folk. <note>In antiquity, the spleen and bile were associated with anger or the capacity to feel a grudge; even the smallest creature can be provoked.</note>

### VIII. The camel, desiring horns, lost even its ears.

"The camel, while desiring horns, lost even its ears besides." <note>original Greek: Ἡ κάμηλος ἐπιθυμήσασα κεράτων, καὶ τὰ ὦτα προσαπώλεσεν</note> This applies to those who, while chasing after foreign things, do not even protect their own. It is taken from a fable about camels who, through a spokesperson, asked Jupiter for horns; offended by the foolish request, he cut off their ears as well. This too seems to be from Apostolius.

### IX. Hercules and the ape.

"Hercules and the ape." <note>original Greek: Ἡρακλῆς καὶ πίθηκος</note> Concerning things that are not at all compatible. The ape excels in tricks; Hercules excels in strength. It is related to "The camel and the ant." There is a well-known story about the brothers called "Perperi" <note>The Cercopes, mischievous forest creatures</note>, whom Hercules captured and hung from his club. They say they were turned into apes.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of adages, transitioning from political wisdom for the elderly to various proverbs concerning steadfastness, staying true to one's nature, physical habits, the repetition of sin, and the appropriateness of gifts.</meta>

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

->Either stay and conquer, or die.<-
<note>original Latin: "Aut manenti uincendum, aut moriendum"</note>

"Either to prevail by staying, or to win." <note>original Greek: ἢ μένοντα κρατεῖν, ἢ νικᾶν</note> That is: It is necessary either to conquer while remaining, or to perish. This is said when a firm decision has been made, either to finish a business or to die in the attempt. It is derived from the custom of the Spartans <note>the Lacedaemonians</note>, who entered battle with the mindset that they would either return home as victors or fall in defeat. A famous saying of a certain Spartan woman is celebrated; while handing a shield to her son, she said: "Either this, or upon this." <note>original Greek: ἢ τὰν, ἢ ἐπὶ τᾶς</note> Speaking in the Spartan manner, she meant he must either bring the shield back or be carried home dead upon it.

->Since you belong to the sea, do not wish to become a creature of the land.<-
<note>original Latin: "Maritimus cum sis, ne uelis fieri terrestris"</note>
"Since you are of the sea, never become of the land." <note>original Greek: Θαλάττιος δ' ὢν, μήποτε χερσαῖος γένῃ</note> That is:
If you are a sea-creature, keep away from things of the land.
This warns that one’s condition should not be changed, even for something seemingly better. Indeed, each person should cultivate that way of life for which they seem either suited by nature or into which they have fallen by chance. It is taken from a certain Aesopic fable, which is told as follows: A certain crab, having left the sea, began to feed in a certain field. There, by chance, it was spotted by a fox, and was immediately snatched up and devoured. Thus, as it was about to die, it too late lamented its own foolishness because, though it was of a marine species, it wished to depart into the region of land animals. There is a similar fable about a wolf fishing, who soon lamented as the dogs rushed in that he had turned from a cook into a hunter. Hermolaus Barbarus <note>a prominent 15th-century Italian scholar</note> elegantly inverted the proverb for Pico della Mirandola: "Since you are of the land, do not seek the sea." <note>original Greek: χερσαῖος ὢν ζητεῖς θάλασσαν</note>

->In the manner of a tuna.<-
<note>original Latin: "Thynni more"</note>
"In the manner of a tuna." <note>original Greek: Θύννου δίκην</note> Those who look askance or sideways with one eye or the other are said to see "in the manner of a tuna." Aeschylus, as cited in the seventh book of Athenaeus, says:
"Applying the left eye in the manner of a tuna." <note>original Greek: Τὸ σκαιὸν ὄμμα παραβαλὼν θύννου δίκην</note>
For Aristotle indicates that tuna <note>original Latin: "Thynnos"</note> do not see except with the left eye, as Athenaeus cites in the same place—though a little earlier he had said, from the same author, that they see with the right and are blind in the left. Pliny, in Book 9, Chapter 15, says they are dull-sighted in both, yet see more with the right. This same verse from the same author appears in Plutarch, in his dialogue *On the Comparison of Land and Sea Animals*. He adds that this fish is blind in one eye, and therefore when they migrate into the Black Sea <note>the Pontus</note>, they hug the shore on the right; when they migrate out, they do the opposite. It can also be applied to those who inspect something very diligently. As Persius says:
"Just as if he were directing a plumb-line with one eye."
And Aristotle, in Section 31, problems 3 and 4, rightly thinks this happens because the origins of sight depend on the same source. Whence it happens that when one eye is closed, that power which moved two is concentrated into one, becoming sharper as it is more focused.

->The dog returned to its vomit.<-
<note>original Latin: "Canis reuersus ad uomitum"</note>
"The dog to its own vomit." <note>original Greek: Κύων ἐπὶ τὸ ἴδιον ἐξέραμα</note> This fits those who slide back into the same shameful acts from which they were once cleansed. It is mentioned in the Epistle of Saint Peter in these very words: "For it has happened to them according to the true proverb: The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the sow that was washed to wallowing in the mire." <note>original Greek: Συμβέβηκε γὰρ αὐτοῖς, τὸ τῆς ἀληθοῦς παροιμίας, κύων ἐπιστρέψας ἐπὶ τὸ ἴδιον ἐξέραμα, καὶ ὗς λουσαμένη εἰς κύλισμα βορβόρου</note> The metaphor is obviously taken from dogs that swallow again what they have vomited, and from pigs that go from the river straight back to the mud. That Hebrew proverb-writer <note>referring to Solomon in the Book of Proverbs</note> expressed the same sentiment: "As a dog that returns to his vomit, so is a fool who repeats his folly." For this is the passage, if I am not mistaken, that Peter pointed out.

->You give straw to the dog, and bones to the donkey.<-
<note>original Latin: "Cani das paleas, asino ossa"</note>
"You give straw to the dog, and to the donkey, bones." <note>original Greek: Κυνὶ δίδως ἄχυρα, ὄνῳ δ' ὀστέα</note> This is used when things are distributed preposterously. For example, if someone sends a literary gift to an unlearned man, or trifles to a scholar; a sword or a belt to a scholar, a book to a soldier, or hunting dogs to a bishop. For gifts that are pleasing in themselves are unpleasing when they are not appropriate. Sometimes they are even turned into an insult.

->To disturb the hunt.<-
<note>original Latin: "Præmouere uenatum"</note>
"To drive away the prey prematurely." <note>original Greek: προεξελεῖν τὴν θήραν</note> Aristides, in his work on Pericles, cites from Plato: "As he himself says, he drove the prey away from them prematurely." Thus, in that manner, as he says, to disrupt the hunting. Furthermore, the words of Plato in the *Lysis* go like this: "What kind of person would he seem to be who, thinking himself clever at these things, should frighten the prey while hunting and make the catch more difficult to take?" <note>original Greek: ποῖός τις ἂν εἴη ὁ δοκῶν εἶναι δεινὸς τὰ, εἰ ἀνασοβοῖ θηρεύων καὶ δυσαλωτοτέραν τὴν ἄγραν ποιοῖ</note> That is: What kind of person would he seem to you...

Erasmus also explores the biological observations of ancient authors like Aristotle and Pliny regarding tuna vision as a basis for metaphorical speech.</summary>

<header>THE THIRD CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Qq</sig>

...hunter, if while hunting he rouses the beast and makes the capture more difficult? It appears this was a common saying used when someone does not sufficiently hide what they are working toward. Just as it happens in practice, where a beast, roused by the noise and sensing a trap, withdraws itself.

->To enter the right path.<-
->XVI<-

"To walk the right path." <note>original Greek: τὴν ὀρθὴν βαδίζειν ὁδὸν</note> That is, one who never deflects from what is honorable is said to walk the right way. Aristides <note>A Greek orator of the 2nd century AD</note> in his *Pericles*: "so as to proceed in order, and keep to the right path, according to the proverb." <note>original Greek: ὥς τε βαδίζειν κατὰ γλῶτταν καὶ τὴν ὀρθὴν ὁδὸν σῴζειν κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν</note> Philo <note>A Jewish philosopher from Alexandria</note> in *On Humanity*: "for he had not even learned this public road which leads to equity." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ οἷα λεωφόρον ἄγειν ἐφ' ὁσιότητα ταύτην ἠπίστασο</note> Plautus <note>A Roman comic playwright</note> in *Casina*: "Now by Pollux, I have returned to the right path." Also a little later: "Wisely returning from the road to the path." <note>Plautus plays on the words 'road' (via) and 'path' (semita) to suggest shifting from a main course to a shortcut or a side-scheme.</note> The maidservant in the play, however, is ordering that the person who had carelessly blurted out the truth should return to the deception they had originally planned.

->Drop it right there.<-
->XVII<-

"Drop it right there." <note>original Greek: αὐτόθεν κατάβαλλε</note> That is: set it down in this very place. Aristides in *Pericles*: "Now as for those talkative or fabricated stories, and contests and nonsense, drop them right there, Plato, lest perhaps some other god rouses the Trojans." <note>original Greek: πόθεν δὴ μὴ λάλων ἢ πλάττων καὶ ἀγώνων καὶ φλυάρων αὐτόθεν κατάβαλλε, μή που τις καὶ τρῶας ἐγείρῃσι θεὸς ἄλλο</note> The commentator indicates this is a proverb, taken from victors who forbid the defeated from leaving, but require them to "stretch out the grass" <note>an ancient gesture of surrender and acknowledgment of the victor's land rights</note> right there, acknowledge the victor, and pay the prize of victory. It is used whenever we order something to be produced immediately and without delay, such as a proof of what someone has said, or a promise, or a sample of an art in which someone boasts they excel. It is also used in Plato.

->Shut the door, you profane ones.<-
->XVIII<-

"Place the doors [shut], you profane ones." <note>original Greek: θύρας ἐπίθεσθε βεβήλοι</note> That is: lock the doors, all you who are uninitiated. The allusion is taken from Orpheus, whose poem is cited thus: "I shall speak to those for whom it is lawful; you profane crowd, block the doors." <note>original Greek: φθέγξομαι οἷς θέμις ἐστί, θύρας ἐπίθεσθε βεβήλοι</note> It is commanded that the profane person place a door upon their ears, so that nothing of the secret discourse can enter. Aristides in *Pericles*, says: "Because of these things, I speak to those to whom it is permitted; but for the profane, there is no account of the speech at all." <note>original Greek: λέγων διὰ ταῦτα πρὸς οὓς ἔξεστι, τοῖς δὲ βεβήλοις ὁ λόγος πάντως</note> It is appropriate to use this whenever we signify that we are about to speak of difficult and secret matters. Horace <note>A famous Roman lyric poet</note> looked to this when he wrote in his *Odes*:
>I hate the profane crowd, and keep them away,
>Be silent with your tongues; songs never before
>heard, I, the priest of the Muses,
>sing for maidens and boys.

Ovid <note>Another major Roman poet</note>:
>Let a favoring tongue be present, forgetful of our labors,
>Which I think has now unlearned how to speak good words.
Before a sacrifice, the herald used to cry out to order the people "to favor with their tongues" <term>fauete linguis: a ritual command for silence or the avoidance of unlucky words during a religious ceremony</term>, which is to speak words of good omen: hence "fauetia" is called a good omen. Likewise Seneca, dealing with philosophy: "Revere it as you do the gods, and its professors as high priests; and whenever mention of sacred letters occurs, favor with your tongues." This word, contrary to what many think, is not derived from "honeycomb" <note>Latin: favus</note>, but silence is commanded so that the rite may be properly performed without any bad-omened voice interrupting. But it will have a bit more wit if it is applied through irony, such as if someone about to recite some of the sophistical subtleties of the <term>Scotists: followers of Duns Scotus, medieval theologians often mocked by Renaissance humanists for their dense and complex logic</term> were to preface it by saying: "Shut the doors, you profane ones." Lucian <note>A Greek satirist</note> used it in this manner more than once.

->To the rope, a little cord.<-
->XIX<-

"To the rope, a little cord." <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ σπάρα σχοινίον</note> That is: "to the rope, a cord." One must understand the verb "you add" or "you return." It is used when someone has an abundance of the same things, or repays like with like. Kindred to that is: "You join linen to linen." <note>original Greek: λίνον λίνῳ συνάπτεις</note> That is: you weave a lie onto a lie, a trick onto a trick, a trifle onto a trifle.

->Salt and a bean.<-
->XX<-

"Salt and a bean." <note>original Greek: ἅλα καὶ κύαμον</note> That is: salt and a bean. One must understand: "they set forth," or some other word better suited to the meaning. Diogenianus <note>A Greek grammarian and proverb collector</note> warns that it was usually said of those who pretended to know something they did not, and that the proverb arose because it was once the custom for diviners to set out salt and a bean. Because I was doubting whether it was different...

<meta>This page continues the fifth hundred of the third "Chiliad" (thousand) of Erasmus's collection of adages. It follows a discussion on hunting metaphors and transitions into the behavior of partridges as a symbol for clever escapes.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Whether this was different from the one we recorded in the first Thousand <note>A "Chiliad" or "Thousand" refers to the major sections of Erasmus's massive collection of proverbs.</note> or not, I decided it should be repeated here. For I find it cited just now in ancient Greek manuscripts.

<margin>To escape like a partridge.</margin>
"To escape like a partridge" <note>original Greek: Ἐκπέρδικίσαι</note> is what the Greeks call slipping away and fleeing, using a proverbial metaphor. Aristophanes <note>A famous Athenian comic playwright</note> says in *The Birds*:
"Indeed, with us it is not at all shameful to escape like a partridge." <note>original: ὡς πῦρ' ἡμῖν οὐδὲν αἰσχρόν ἐστιν ἐκπερδικίσαι</note> That is: 
"For among us it is not a disgrace to slip out of the nets."
It is derived from birds that sometimes escape from nets or snares. They say the partridge is especially cunning in order to escape the hands of fowlers. Regarding this matter, I would like to include the words of Aristotle, which are written in the ninth book of *The History of Animals*: "They do not lay eggs and brood in the same place, lest someone notice the spot if they sit there for too long. Furthermore, when someone hunting happens upon the nest, the partridge rolls itself at the feet of the hunter, just as if it were about to be caught, enticing him toward itself as if he could catch it, until in the meantime the chicks have escaped one by one. When this is done, the bird itself flies up and calls the chicks back." Thus far Aristotle. Nor does it bother me to add to this place what Plutarch writes on nearly the same sentiment, in the book he titled, *Whether Land or Sea Animals are Cleverer*: "The partridges display another cleverness combined with love for their offspring toward hunters. For they train those not yet able to fly to lie flat on their backs, holding a clod of earth or some chaff over their bodies so they might hide as if covered; meanwhile, the parents lead the hunters away by another path. They entice them to themselves, flying toward their feet and moving backward, and for so long they offer hope of being caught, until they have led the hunter far away from the chicks." From these words, I think it is clear enough what "to escape like a partridge" means—namely, to slip away with skill and wit. In the meantime, there is an allusion to a certain notably wicked innkeeper named Perdix (Partridge), because he was lame. Aristophanes mentions him in *The Birds*.

<margin>A slight gift.</margin>
"A slight gift" <note>original Latin: Munus leuidense</note> is what Cicero <note>The Roman statesman and orator</note> calls a cheap gift of little duty, the kind that wealthy people are accustomed to send to their common friends. For he writes thus to Dolabella <note>Cicero's son-in-law</note> in the ninth book of his *Letters to Friends*: "The little speech for Deiotarus <note>A king of Galatia defended by Cicero</note> which you were looking for, I had with me, which I had not thought; therefore I have sent it to you. I would wish you to read it as a thin and meager case, not greatly worthy of writing. But for an old host and friend, I wanted to send it, not only as a 'slight gift' of coarse thread <note>original: leuidensae crasso filo</note>, such as his own gifts are wont to be." Here he shows that "Leuidensa" is a type of cheap garment, with a thin and loose weave. Formerly, among humble things, these garments were foremost. Whence also in Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist</note> someone complains of being clothed in "bad, thick wool and a foul color":
> And poorly struck by the comb of a Gallic weaver.
Therefore, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> calls his own speech, which was not very labored or polished, a "slight gift." It will be elegantly applied to a trivial gift or a common favor, not performed very heartily or diligently for some ordinary friend. Similar to this is "a Pellenæan tunic" <note>original Greek: πελλωναῖα χιτὼν</note> and "a Sylofontian cloak" <note>original Greek: συλόσυντος χλαμύς</note>.

<margin>Many students are better than their teachers.</margin>
Marcus Tullius, in the ninth book of his *Letters to Friends*, writing to Varro <note>A great Roman scholar</note>, records a certain verse, surely from some poet. The sentiment of which is considered famous even in modern times. "Dolabella has arrived," he says. "I think he will be the teacher."
"Many students are better than their masters." <note>original Greek: πολλοὶ μαθηταὶ κρείσσονες διδασκάλων</note>

<summary>Erasmus explains the origins of three proverbs: escaping like a partridge (cleverness), the "slight gift" (humility or cheapness in social favors), and the idea of students surpassing their teachers.</summary>
<keywords>Partridge, cleverness, Aristotle, Plutarch, Cicero, gifts, leuidense, Dolabella, education, students and teachers</keywords>

### THE THIRD CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY

**Many disciples surpass their teachers.**

This can be applied to various uses: either in a simple sense—as it frequently happens that a student excels in learning over the one from whom he learned his letters or some art—or as a joke, when we wish to indicate that the one who was the teacher of malice is himself surpassed in wickedness. For instance, if someone were deceived by the very person to whom he had once shown the way and method of cheating; or when someone inferior in rank or condition nevertheless possesses more power than the one who seems to command rather than obey.

->**To the pillars of Hercules.**<-
->XXIIII<-

"The Pillars of Hercules" <note>original Greek: Ἡράκλειαι στῆλαι</note> have long been a proverb, as the commentator on Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet known for his victory odes</note> reminds us. For it is commonly said: "The things beyond Gades are not passable." <note>original: τὰ πόρρω γαδείρων οὐ περατά. Gades is the modern city of Cadiz, Spain.</note> By this, they mean that there is no place to go beyond the Pillars of Hercules. Hercules is said to have fixed these pillars there while he was tracking the cattle of Geryon <note>One of the twelve labors of Hercules was to steal these cattle from a three-bodied giant</note>, marking that spot as the ultimate boundary of the world. Pindar says in the *Nemean Odes*: "Toward the darkness beyond Gades, there is no passage." <note>original: γαδείρων τὸ πρὸς ζόφον οὐ περατόν</note> Also elsewhere:
"But if someone, performing beautiful deeds and matching them with a form to suit,
Has stepped upon the highest peaks of manhood,
The son of Aristophanes <note>referring to a victor in the games</note> finds it no longer easy to cross
The impassable sea beyond the pillars
of Hercules, to the furthest reaches of navigation."

He means that the son of Aristophanes has reached the pinnacle of praise, beyond which it cannot grow, since he has joined illustrious deeds to an excellent physical form. If anyone were to seek any more praise beyond this, it would be as if someone were trying to pass beyond the pillars fixed by Hercules. Again, in the third *Olympian Ode*:
"Now indeed, reaching the furthest limits
By his virtues, Theron <note>The tyrant of Akragas and a victor in the chariot race</note> reaches
The pillars of Hercules from his home. What lies beyond
Is inaccessible to the wise
and the unwise alike."
Which is to say:
Now indeed, reaching the extreme limits by his virtues, Theron reaches the pillars of Hercules from his home. But what is beyond is inaccessible to the wise and the foolish equally. Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop and theologian</note> used the expression in a similar way in his *Monody*, suggesting that Basil had reached such a point of perfection that it was denied to human nature to go any further. Heraclides Ponticus, in his *Allegories of Homer*, thinks that the wicked interpreters of Homer's poems should be driven "beyond the furthest pillars of Hercules and the impassable sea of the Ocean." <note>original: ὑπὲρ ἡρακλέος ἐσχάτας στήλας καὶ τὴν ἄβατον ὠκεανοῦ θάλασσαν</note>

->**To play the seer.**<-
->XXV<-

"To play the seer" <note>original Latin: Ariolari. Derived from "hariolus," a soothsayer or diviner.</note> was a proverbial way of describing someone who brought nothing certain and no immediate benefit, but merely made promises for the future. Thus Dorio, the pimp in Terence’s *Phormio*, responds to the young man Phaedria (who was promising to give him money and asking, "Don't you believe me?") by saying: "You're playing the seer." <note>i.e., "You're just telling fortunes/talking nonsense."</note> Likewise Sannio in the *Adelphoe*: "But I am merely divining these things." It is taken from diviners who predict things to come. However, there is no certain knowledge of future events, as was elegantly stated by Pindar:
"The signs of future things are blinded,
And many things fall out for men contrary to their expectation."
The meaning of these verses is that the knowledge of future things is blind, and many things happen to mortals beyond their hope.

->**A buyer of chickpeas.**<-
->XXVI<-

Indeed, I believe that what Horace says in his *Art of Poetry* should also be counted among the proverbs: "A buyer of chickpeas and nuts." <note>original: Ciceris & nucis emptor</note>
He means a man of the lowest sort, someone from the very dregs of the common people.
"For those who have a horse, a father, and property are offended,
Nor, if the buyer of cracked chickpeas and nuts approves of something,
Do they receive it with calm minds or grant it a crown." <note>Horace is explaining that the upper classes (the knights with horses and the wealthy) have different tastes in theater than the poor who snack on cheap chickpeas.</note>

->**No one forbids anyone from traveling the public road.**<-
->XXVII<-

That line of Plautus from the *Curculio* also has the appearance of a proverb: "No one forbids anyone from traveling the public road." By this, they mean that the use of common things is equal for everyone, and no one should be blamed for doing what public law allows. Plautus twisted the sense toward something a bit shameful—namely, the use of a common prostitute. It seems, however, to be modeled on the imitation of Pythago- <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the next page will likely discuss a "Pythagorean" precept or saying.</note>

<summary>This page explores proverbs regarding the limits of human achievement (The Pillars of Hercules), the uncertainty of the future (playing the seer), and social class distinctions (the buyer of chickpeas). It also begins a discussion on the right to use public resources and common property.</summary>
<keywords>Pillars of Hercules, Gades, Pindar, Horace, Terence, Roman comedy, social class, chickpeas, divination, common law, Greek literature, adages</keywords>

<page-num>736</page-num>
# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Of the Pythagorean symbol that commands one "to walk on the highway" <note>original Greek: τῇ λεωφόρῳ βαδίζειν</note>, that is, to enter upon the public path, or conversely, "not to walk on the highway" <note>original Greek: τῇ λεωφόρῳ μὴ βαδίζειν</note>. Indeed, Horace <note>referred to here by his family name, Flaccus</note> seems to me to have looked toward this in his *Art of Poetry* when he says:
> Public material will become private right, if
> You do not linger around the common and open circuit,
> Nor take care to render word for word.

-> Hinc belli initium. <-
-> XXV <-

Among proverbs that are taken from allusions to authors, I do not think that one should be passed over in silence which Lucian, in his *Pseudomantis*, borrowed from Thucydides <note>Thucydides was a famous Athenian historian; Lucian was a 2nd-century satirist</note>: "And according to Thucydides, from here the war now begins" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡ Θουκυδίδου ἀρχὴ ὁ πόλεμος ἐνθένδε ἤδη</note>. This can be adapted to various uses, whether when we mean we are girding ourselves to start a business, or when we hint at a grudge born from somewhere, or the eruption of a tumult of affairs. There is no doubt that Aristophanes alluded to the same passage of Thucydides in his play *The Acharnians*: "And from here is the beginning of the war" <note>original Greek: Κἀντεῦθεν ἀρχὴ ἡ τοῦ πολέμου</note>. And he repeats that phrase "and from here" more frequently in that passage, which makes it even more likely that he used the allusion for the sake of a joke.

-> Inanium inania consilia. <-
-> XX <-

"Empty plans of empty people" <note>original Greek: Κενοὶ κενὰ βουλεύονται</note>. That is, "Empty thoughts of empty people" <note>original Greek: τὰ κενοὶ κενὰ λογίζονται</note>, used when someone is frustrated in their hope. Akin to this is "A fool speaks foolish things" <note>original Greek: μωρὰ μωρὸς λέγει</note>. They say it was born from an event: for Archias, having bargained with Demetrios for five hundred gold talents to betray Cyprus, was caught in the act; he seized a rope from those used to stretch tents and hanged himself. This is recorded in the Greek collections.

-> Nutricum more male. <-
-> X <-

"You feed poorly, just like nurses" <note>original Greek: Καθ’ ὥσπερ αἱ τίτθαι σιτίζεις κακῶς</note>. I have found this in certain very old collections of proverbs, which some attribute to Plutarch. It appears in Aristophanes' *The Knights*, who explains the reasoning of the metaphor in these words:
"You feed poorly, just like nurses:
For when you chew, you put a little in his mouth,
But you yourself have swallowed three times as much food as him" <note>original Greek: Καθ’ ὥσπερ αἱ τίτθαι γε σιτίζεις κακῶς / μασώμενος γὰρ τῷ μὲν ὀλίγον ἐντιθεῖς / Αὐτὸς δ’ ἐκείνου τριπλάσιον κατέσπακας</note>.
It will therefore be suitable for those who impart only a tiny bit of profit to their partners, or those who manage the resources of others so as to convert the greatest part to their own use—something the common crowd of guardians <note>term: guardians (tutorum), referring here to legal executors or trustees of estates</note> does even today.

-> Amphictyonum consessus. <-
-> X <-

"An assembly of the Amphictyons" <note>original Greek: Ἀμφikτυονικὸν συνέδριον</note>. This refers to a frequent gathering of very serious or important people. It is derived from that once-famous assembly of the Greeks called the Amphictyonic Council, either named after Amphictyon, the son of Deucalion, who is said to have summoned the Greek tribes when he was in power (as cited by the author Theopompus in the eighth book of his *Histories*, and testified by Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* regarding Phocis). Furthermore, the peoples who used to meet in that council are numbered as twelve: the Ionians, Dorians, Perrhaebians, Boeotians, Magnetes, Achaeans, Phthians, Malians <note>original Latin: Molienses</note>, Dolopes, Aenianes, Delphians, and Phocians. Or, the name "Amphictyon" was given because people gathered to that council from everywhere out of all Greece <note>Note: This is a play on the Greek word 'amphi', meaning 'around'</note>, as is favored by Anaximenes and Androtion in their descriptions of Attic affairs, found in Pausanias in the place I just indicated. Indeed, many other things not unworthy of reading are reported on this matter if anyone cares to seek them out; for our explanation of the proverb, we think these details are enough. The adage will be more elegant if it is twisted through irony to refer to a gathering of unlearned people who nevertheless see themselves as Solons <note>Solon was a legendary Athenian lawmaker known for his wisdom</note>.

-> Etiam capillus unus. <-
-> XX <-

A line from a mime by Publilius <note>original Latin: Publianus</note>, if I am not mistaken, is also celebrated with a very proverbial appearance:
"Even a single hair has its own shadow" <note>original Latin: Etiam capillus unus habet umbram suam</note>.

<summary>Erasmus explores several Greek and Latin proverbs, including warnings against greedy trustees, the origins of the famous Greek Amphictyonic Council, and the idea that even the smallest things (like a single hair) have their own significance.</summary>
<keywords>Pythagoras, Thucydides, Aristophanes, Archias, corruption, nurses, Amphictyonic Council, Greek tribes, Publilius Syrus, shadows</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the third "Chiliad" (collection of thousands) of Erasmus’s *Adagia*, specifically the fifth "Century" (hundred) of that group. It follows a sequence of adages focused on literary metaphors, philosophical anecdotes, and historical references.</meta>

<page-num>737</page-num>
# FIFTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD THOUSAND

->However much a very small advantage helps, any small offense harms.<-

### 33. Xenocrates’s little cheese

<note>original Greek: Ξενοκράτης τυρίον</note> That is, "Xenocrates’s little cheese." This is said of food that lasts a very long time before it is consumed. However, nothing prevents it from being applied to other things as well—for instance, to a garment, a book, a small sum of money, or anything similar which someone uses so sparingly and cautiously that it lasts as long as possible. The adage is taken from the remarkable frugality of the philosopher Xenocrates <note>Xenocrates was a student of Plato and head of the Academy, known for his extreme self-discipline</note>. They say he often threw away side-dishes that had already turned rancid, and it not infrequently happened that when he wanted to unseal a jar, he found the wine had already turned to vinegar. Therefore, the proverb will be aptly spoken against certain stingy people whose habit it is to save all their provisions until they have spoiled—just as if it were a sin to enjoy things while they are fresh and whole. This adage is recorded in the *Collectanea* of Stobaeus.

### 34. With an open breast

We say "with an open breast" <note>original: "Aperto pectore"</note> to mean doing something vehemently from the soul and without disguise, as if the inner chambers of the mind were laid bare. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his booklet *On Friendship*: "In which, unless you see an 'open breast,' as they say, and show your own, there is nothing to be trusted." Pliny the Younger writes to Fabatus: "You bid me forget the letters which you wrote to me, as you say, with an 'open breast'; but there are none I remember more gladly." This is an allusion to the saying of Momus <note>Momus was the Greek god of satire and mockery</note>, who is imagined to have wished for windows in the human chest so that one might look in and see what was hidden in those secret hollows. Persius says in his fifth Satire:
> That I may draw out with a pure voice how much of you 
> I have fixed in my winding breast, and that these words 
> May unseal all that lies hidden in my secret heart-strings.

Similarly, in Ovid <note>referred to by his family name, Naso</note>, Phoebus says: ->Look upon my face<-
> Behold my own, and I wish you could 
> Insert your eyes into my breast, and discover a father’s cares within.

### 35. To reach the finish line

"To reach the lime" <note>original: "Ad calcem peruenire"; 'calx' or lime was used to mark the finish line in ancient races</note> means to reach the goal or the end. It takes on a proverbial figure whenever it is turned toward something other than the human body. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his book *On Friendship*: "So that you can live with your equals, with whom—as if released from the starting gates—you might reach the 'finish line,' as they say, with those same people." The same author in *On Old Age*: "Nor indeed would I wish, as if the course were run, to be called back from the finish line to the starting gates." To this form also belong those phrases such as "Until the 'plaudite,'" <note>the request for applause at the end of a Roman play</note> that is, until the very end. Cicero says in the same discourse: "A performer should be approved in whatever act he happens to be. Nor must a wise man live all the way until the 'plaudite.'" Again elsewhere: "Those who have used these things splendidly seem to me to have completed the play of life, and not, like untrained actors, to have collapsed in the final act." And again in the same work: "The final act was neglected as if by a clumsy poet." However, we have made mention of this kind of thing elsewhere.

### 36. War is the father of all

<note>original Greek: ὁ πόλεμος ἁπάντων πατήρ</note> That is, "War is the father of all." Lucian mentions this as a commonly tossed-about proverb in his commentary *On the Way to Write History*: "Rather, Thucydides, Herodotus, and Xenophon are all around us. And so it seems that saying was true: 'War is the father of all things,' since it has produced so many writers with a single blow." The proverb is said because war is the author of renewing all things, so that everything seems to be born from it. Unless one prefers to refer it to the decree of certain philosophers <note>specifically Heraclitus</note> who said that the sum of things is produced from strife.

### 37. Phanias’s door

<note>original Greek: Φανίου θύρα</note> That is, "Phanias’s door." Eustathius, in his commentary on the *Odyssey*, book 24, shows that this is said of those who pretend they have heaps of wealth that exist nowhere. It is drawn from a certain Phanias who provided a false opinion of himself, as if he had a great force of riches built up and hidden away at home. We have spoken elsewhere of "Phanias's door" in the proverb "Phanias's gate"; whether it is the same as this one or not, let the learned decide.

### 38. To escape the nets

<note>original Greek: Εκλινίσαι</note> Eustathius shows this was said as a proverbial figure in his commentary on the third book of the *Iliad*. The metaphor is taken from fish that flee from the nets, or those that slip away from the hook. For *lina* <note>the Greek root 'linon' means flax or linen, from which nets were made</note> are what nets are
<sig>Qq 3</sig> <meta>The catchword "cuntur" indicates the next page begins with "dicuntur" (are called).</meta>

<summary>This page explores several adages related to frugality (Xenocrates's cheese), sincerity (the open breast), reaching the end of a task (the finish line), and the generative power of conflict (war as the father of all).</summary>
<keywords>Xenocrates, sincerity, Momus, Cicero, race metaphors, Heraclitus, Phanias, fishing metaphors, frugality, Roman theater</keywords>
