<meta>This page continues the discussion of metaphors involving nets and snares, transitioning into the fish known for their cleverness in escaping them, before introducing a new adage regarding the perceived trickery of the Egyptians.</meta>

<page-num>738</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>XXX</sig>
<meta>catchword: A</meta>

This is also said by Latin authors, such as Virgil <note>Erasmus refers to him as "Maro," his family name</note>, who wrote: -> They drag the wet nets. <- <note>original: "Humida lina trahunt," from Virgil’s *Georgics*</note>
Indeed, there is a certain natural cleverness in some fish for slipping out of the woven mesh of nets, as Oppian <note>A Greek poet of the 2nd century who wrote the *Halieutica*, a poem about fishing</note> elegantly recounts concerning the grey mullet <term>Cestreus<gloss>A type of mullet known in antiquity for its agility and perceived intelligence</gloss></term> in his third book. But it is better to provide the poem itself, as this author is not yet widely known:
When the mullet is being pulled in the folded arms of the flaxen net, because he did not recognize the circling trap, he leaps high, flicking at the surface of the water, striving straight upward with all his might. With a light jump, he rushes forth, and by his own counsel he has escaped the dark trap. For often by his lunges he easily leaps over the highest ropes of the corks and escapes his doom. But if, having first attempted the leap, he slips back into the snare, he no longer struggles, nor does he jump up in his distress; for having learned of the deception by experience, he ceases his rush. That is:
*While the mullet is dragged through the sea in winding weaves,*
*The art and trickery of how he might escape is not hidden from him.*
*He leaps nimbly into the air, and with a swift jump*
*He strives with all the strength he possesses; he flashes*
*Into the highest waves with his whole body lifted up.*
*Fortune favors his wit, for he often leaps over the corks*
*Which hold up the highest ropes—the restraints of the net—*
*And escaping his black fate, the rogue flees.*
*But if, having tried his first leap, he should fall back*
*And tumble into the nets again, he no longer labors to fight*
*In his anxiety, or strives in vain; taught by the danger,*
*He neither tosses himself about nor ever leaps upward again.*

He recounts in the same manner concerning many other fish, describing the arts by which they slip away when captured. But it would be too long to follow the rest. It is not unpleasant to know what the poet Claudian <note>A Latin poet of the late 4th century</note> tells of the torpedo fish <term>torpedo<gloss>An electric ray; the ancients believed its numbing shock was a form of "poison" or "magic" that could travel through solid objects</gloss></term>: how, when caught on a hook, it sends the force of its poison through the line and the rod all the way to the fisherman’s hand. I will add the poem—for why should I grudge recording something so elegant and so delightful?
*If ever it should swallow the bronze hook more incautiously,*
*When it is covered with bait, and feels itself restrained by the curved barbs,*
*It does not flee, nor does it try to tear away with a vain bite,*
*But craftily it joins itself closely to the dark horse-hair line,*
*And though a captive, it remembers its own power; far through the waves*
*It pours out sluggish breaths from its poisonous veins.*
*The deep force travels through the hair, and leaves the water*
*To bind the man who is standing apart. A terrifying numbness*
*Flashes from the depths of the water, and following the hanging threads,*
*It passes through the nodes of the reed rod with a mysterious chill,*
*And binds the victorious right hand, congealing the blood.*
*The fisherman casts away the harmful burden and the rebellious prey,*
*Returning disarmed, having lost his lead.*

 The commentator on Aristophanes thinks this metaphor was transferred from birds. Persius uses a similar figure in his fifth Satire:
*Lest you wish to tremble and gnaw at the tight nets.*

### Αἰγυπτιάζειν.
<note>original Greek: Aegyptiazein</note>
People were said "to act the Egyptian" when they were being crafty or acting as impostors. This is taken from the character of that nation. Theocritus says in *The Syracusans*:
No criminal
harms anyone now, creeping up in the Egyptian fashion. That is:
*No wicked man now hurts or harms,*
*Sneaking up with Egyptian cunning.*
Aeschylus also testifies to the character of the Egyptians, as we have reported elsewhere.

<vocab>Cestreus, Oppian, Claudian, torpedo, Aegyptiazein, Theocritus, Aeschylus, adagia</vocab>

<summary>Erasmus discusses the natural cunning of fish like the mullet and the electric ray (torpedo) as metaphors for escaping traps, then introduces the adage "to act the Egyptian," meaning to be deceitful.</summary>

<header>THIRD CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Qq 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: But with a nail</meta>

-> The Egyptians are clever at weaving schemes. <- 
<note>original Greek: Δεινοὶ πλέκειν τὰς μηχανὰς αἰγύπτιοι; original Latin: Ægyptij miri struendis artibus</note>

Synesius <note>A 4th-century Greek bishop and philosopher</note> cites this proverb in his *Praise of Baldness*. Although sometimes the verb "to act like an Egyptian" <note>original Greek: αἰγυπτιάζειν</note> is usually taken to mean to scorch or burn, as in this poem:
-> The sun, shining with a flame, will turn your skin into that of an Egyptian. <-
<note>original Greek: Χροὰν δὲ τὴν σὴν ἥλιος λάμπων φλογὶ / Αἰγυπτιάσει</note>
That is:
-> Burning Phoebus <note>A name for the sun god, Apollo</note> with fiery flames will scorch your color. <-

### XL. Not even a morsel left.

-> Not even a bit is left. <- 
<note>original Greek: Οὐδ’ ἔγκαφος λέλειπται</note>
That is, not even a morsel <note>original Latin: bolus</note> remains; in other words, not even a tiny bit. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop of Thessalonica known for his commentaries on Homer</note>, explaining the third book of the *Odyssey*, cites this verse from Eupolis <note>An Athenian poet of Old Comedy</note>:
-> Not even a morsel of my things is left. <-
<note>original Greek: Οὐχὶ λέλειπται τῶν ἐμῶν οὐδ’ ἔγκαφος</note>

For the word *engaphos* <note>original: ἔγκαφος</note> signifies among the Greeks what we call a "morsel" <term>morsellum<gloss>A "little bite" or snack; Erasmus notes this is more of a common or "vulgar" word than pure classical Latin</gloss></term>, derived from the verb *kapto* <note>original: κάπτω</note>, which means "I eat greedily."

### XLI. King or donkey.

-> King or donkey. <- 
<note>original Greek: Βασιλεὺς ἢ ὄνος</note>
That is, either the victor or the vanquished. It is similar to that other saying: "either three sixes or three ones" <note>original: ἢ τρὶς ἕξ ἢ τρεῖς κύβοι; a reference to the best and worst possible rolls in a game of dice</note>. Eustathius, explaining the sixth book of the *Odyssey*, shows that the metaphor is drawn from those who play with a ball <term>sphæra<gloss>A general term for various types of ball games played in antiquity</gloss></term>. Among them, the one who won was called "king," and the one who was defeated was given the name "donkey." Plato says in the *Theaetetus*: "The one who misses will sit down as a 'donkey,' as they say in the ball game; but whoever emerges without missing shall be our 'king.'" 

Julius Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century</note>, in the ninth book of his *On Terms*, records four ways of playing ball. The first is called *episkyros* <note>a team game similar to rugby</note>, the second *phaininda* <note>a game of deception/feinting</note>, the third *aporraxis* <note>bouncing the ball on the ground</note>, and the fourth *ourania* <note>the "sky-ball" game</note>. 

The last of these, as it properly relates to the proverb, he describes in these words: "In the game of *ourania*, one player leans back and throws the ball into the sky. For the others, the competition was to snatch it before it fell to the ground. Homer seems to suggest this among the Phaeacians. Indeed, when they had thrown the ball against a wall, the number of bounces was counted; the one who failed was called the 'donkey' during the play and performed whatever was commanded of him, while the winner was 'king' and gave the orders." Thus far Julius Pollux. Furthermore, the passage he cites from Homer is from the eighth book of the *Odyssey*, in this manner:
-> Another would toss it from a strong hand up toward the shadowy clouds; but the other, leaping high from the earth, would easily catch it before his feet touched the ground again. <-
<note>Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation of the Greek, which describes the skillful ball-play of the Phaeacians before King Alcinous</note>

It seems not unlike the line in Plautus’s *The Little Carthaginian*: "I am a king, if I lure that man to me today." It will be permissible to use this adage when we signify that the "die is being cast" in a way that will make us either the highest or the lowest.

### XLII. To mark the way by the stars.

-> To mark the way by the stars. <- 
<note>original Greek: Ἄστροις σημειοῦσθαι τὴν ὁδόν</note>
Those who investigate a matter that is otherwise difficult to track down by using certain small notes and conjectures are said to "mark their way by the stars." Eustathius, explaining the fifth book of the *Odyssey*, notes that this is appropriate for those who enter upon a long and deserted road. The metaphor is taken from sailors who, in nighttime navigation, guess their path by observing the stars. Just as in Homer, Odysseus in the fifth book of the *Odyssey*:
-> But he steered skillfully with the rudder, sitting there; nor did sleep fall upon his eyelids as he gazed at the Pleiades and late-setting Boötes, and the Bear, which they also call by the name of the Wagon... <-
<note>Odysseus is using the constellations to navigate his raft away from Calypso’s island</note>

<summary>Erasmus explores three adages: one regarding the craftiness of Egyptians, a second on total consumption ("not even a morsel left"), and a third on the "king or donkey" status determined by ancient ball games.</summary>
<keywords>Egyptians, morsel, Eupolis, ball games, King or Donkey, Plato, Julius Pollux, Ourania, navigation, stars, Homer, Odyssey</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial navigation as a metaphor for wisdom. It moves from the steady guidance of the stars to adages about professional mismatch, shared character, and lack of purpose.</meta>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

> But sitting at the helm, he guided the ship with wondrous skill,
> Sleep never seized his drooping eyes;
> Rather, he watches the Pleiades, and Bootes late to set,
> And the Bear, known by another name as the Wagon.
<note>original Latin: At clauo ille sedens, nauim mira arte regebat... These lines are from Cicero’s Latin translation of Aratus’s Phaenomena, a Greek astronomical poem.</note>

Marcus Tullius Cicero alluded elegantly to this in the fourth book of his *Academic Questions*, when he says that it belongs to the wise man not to be led by opinions, but to hold fast to certain truth. He says this is done by the guidance and indication of the Little Bear <note>original Latin: Cynosurae; also known as the Little Dipper</note>, which, because it is carried in a smaller circle as it is closer to the pole, shows the way more certainly, even if it is less conspicuous. However, he who is not yet perfectly wise embraces whatever seems probable at the moment, sometimes wandering, like one following Helice <note>original Latin: Helicen; also known as the Big Dipper or Great Bear</note>. While Helice is brighter and more visible to many, it is not a similarly certain guide because it revolves in a wider circuit, being further from the pole or the world's summit. These are Cicero’s words: "I am not the kind of man who never approves of anything false, who never assents to anything, who never holds an opinion. But we are seeking the wise man. As for me, I am indeed a great opiner, for I am not yet a sage. And I direct my thoughts not to that tiny Cynosura,"

> Which the Phoenicians trust as a guide on the deep sea at night,
<note>original Latin: Qua fidunt duce nocturna Phoenices in alto</note>

as Aratus says—and they steer more directly because they hold to that star,

> Which, in a lower course, turns in a brief circle:
<note>original Latin: Quæ cursu inferiore, breui conuertitur orbe</note>

"but rather toward Helice and the most brilliant seven stars of the North—that is, toward these broader theories, not refined to a point. Thus it happens that I err and wander more widely." I know I have made mention of this proverb elsewhere, but since I have found certain things not unworthy of knowing, it seemed right to repeat them here.

### A harp sooner.
<note>original Latin: Sambucam citius</note>

That verse of Persius <note>A Roman satirist known for his difficult, metaphorical style</note> bears the appearance of an adage:
> You would sooner fit a harp to a tall camp-servant.
<note>original Latin: Sambucam citius caloni aptaueris alto</note>

Its use occurs whenever we wish to indicate that someone is entirely unsuited to learning a discipline or managing an affair. For the <term>sambuca<gloss>A triangular stringed instrument with a piercing tone, or a ship-borne siege engine resembling the instrument</gloss></term> is a musical instrument that would by no means suit a <term>calo<gloss>A low-ranking servant or drudge employed by soldiers to carry wood and equipment</gloss></term>. Although Athenaeus, in his fourteenth book, indicates that a military engine was also called a *sambuca* because it was moved against the enemy walls in the manner of the instrument. *Calones* is the name for those assistants to soldiers who carry stakes and wood. Grammarians think the name is derived from this. Furthermore, since soldiers themselves are unskilled in music, much more so are the camp-servants. Yet it can be understood, not without reason, as referring to the *sambuca* as a military engine which, like a musical instrument, is tightened with certain ropes. Camp-servants are by no means fit to tighten this, as they are dull-witted and for that very reason pushed back into the lowest service, being entirely coarse and unteachable in any discipline. Hence Persius added "tall" not without <term>emphasis<gloss>original Greek: ἔμφασιν; here meaning a deeper hidden meaning</gloss></term>, because exceptionally tall men are noted for their lack of wit even in the proverb: "The tall man is witless."
<note>original Greek: ἄνοος ὁ μακρός (anoos ho makros)</note>

---

### Of our flour.
<note>original Latin: Nostræ farinæ</note>

Those between whom there is an indistinguishable likeness are said to be "of the same flour." For as water is to water when compared, so is flour to flour. Persius says in his fifth Satire:
> Of our flour just a little while ago,
> You still retain the old skin.
<note>original Latin: Nostræ paulo ante farinæ / Pelliculam ueterem retines</note>

It is as if he said, "of our flock," or "of our condition." This belongs to the same class as "of the same wax" and "the same dust," which have been discussed elsewhere. With a similar figure of speech, Seneca said, "of the same mark," in the fourth book of his letters, epistle twenty-four. To these you may also add that it is a mark of the same character—or rather madness—that some men are driven to death by the fear of death itself.

---

### To shoot without a target.
<note>original Latin: Nullo scopo iaculari</note>

<term>To shoot without a target<gloss>original Greek: Ἄσκοπα τοξεύειν (Askopa toxeuein)</gloss></term>. That is, he who has no fixed purpose to follow, and to which he might refer the reasoning of his plans and intentions, is said to shoot without a target. Lucian says in *Toxaris*: "Since we are now shooting without a target, let us choose an arbiter and relate other pairs of friends before him."
<note>original Greek: ἐπειδὴ νῦν ἄσκοπα τοξεύομεν, αὖθις ἑλόμενοι διαιτητὴν, ἄλλως ἐπ’ ἐκείνῳ ἅπτωμεν</note>
Persius says in his third Satire,
> Is there something you aim at, and at which you direct your bow?
> Or do you follow crows everywhere with shards and mud,
> Unconcerned where your feet may carry you?
<note>original Latin: Est aliquid quò tendis... Erasmus uses this to illustrate living without a goal.</note>

### To pluck from the lung.
<note>original Latin: De pulmone reuellere</note>

There is no doubt that this phrase from Persius also belongs to the form of proverbs...

# THIRD CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY

...to pluck from the lungs, which means to remove a foolish and arrogant opinion from the mind. <note>original: "mone reuellere, pro eo quod est, stultam & arrogantem opinionem animo eximere."</note> 
*While I pluck those old grandmothers’ tales from your lungs.* <note>original: "Dum ueteres auías tibi de pulmone reuello." This is from Persius, Satire 5.92.</note>

Ancient writers placed the swelling of the soul and pride in the lungs; hence the Greek expression *to breathe big*, <note>original Greek: "μέγα πνέειν" (mega pnein)</note> meaning to be haughty. Persius says the same thing elsewhere:
*Something grand, which the lung, generous with its breath, may pant out.* <note>original: "Grande aliquid, quod pulmo animæ prælargus anhelet." Satire 1.14.</note>

->**Whom a hundred Egyptians could not carry.**<-
->**XLVII**<-

*Whom even a hundred Egyptians could not lift.* <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἂν ἄραιντ’ ἂν ἔθ’ ἑκατὸν αἰγύπτιοι."</note> That is, whom a hundred Egyptians could not bear.
This was commonly said of annoying people, or those with intolerable manners, or those swollen with pride. It is derived from the fact that most Egyptians used to practice the rather undignified trade of carrying heavy loads for profit; because of this, they were called <term>burden-bearers</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀχθοφόροι" (achthophoroi)</note> and became a proverbial joke. The adage is recorded by Eudemus in his collection of rhetorical terms, and also by Suidas. It appears in Aristophanes’ *The Frogs* in this manner:
*He climbed onto the chariot and took two corpses with him,*
*Whom even a hundred Egyptians could not lift.*
That is:
*Two wagons, and likewise two corpses, he placed,*
*Which even a hundred Egyptians could not carry.*
*Not an Egyptian brick-bearer.* <note>original: "οὐκ αἰγύπτιος πλινθοφόρος." (ouk aigyptios plinthophoros)</note> That is, no Egyptian <term>brick-carrier</term>.

->The same in The Birds:<-

In a similar way, Lucilius says in the works of Nonius:
*Whom bulls born in the Lucanian mountains*
*Could not pull with their strong necks instead of spears.*
*To pull this one's yoke of mules, instead of a spear, a hundred*
*Egyptian brick-carriers.*

->Again, the same elsewhere:<-
->They could not.<-
->**XLVIII**<-

*An Egyptian brick-bearer.* <note>original Greek: "Αἰγύπτιος πλινθοφόρος."</note> That is, an Egyptian carrier of bricks. Suidas specifically records this under the title of a proverb. It appears in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*, where someone asks who had constructed the wooden Horse of Troy on the citadel of Pallas, a hundred cubits high? To which it is answered:
*The birds, and no one else; no Egyptian*
*brick-bearer, nor a stone-mason.* <note>original: "ὄρνιθες, οὐδ’ εἷς ἄλλος, οὐκ αἰγύπτιος / πλινθοφόρος, οὐ λιθουργός."</note>

This seems to fit a person of sordid and the lowest rank, for which use the word <term>Carutilitas</term> <note>likely a reference to a low-status or utilitarian worker</note> was also employed; or for someone weighed down by troublesome business. We just mentioned that Egyptians became the subject of popular tales and laughter because, like donkeys, they made a living by carrying heavy loads on their bodies. I suspect they were more practiced in this labor because, in digging ditches, carrying out mud, and making clay bricks, this kind of work was especially necessary in Egypt due to the silt brought in by the Nile. For I believe the sparrows or swallows there first showed the art of building walls out of mud. The proof is that the Hebrews, when they lived among them, were forced into the slave-labor of carrying mud and bricks for Pharaoh. You will find information about the <term>Mules of Marius</term> elsewhere. <note>A reference to Adage 2.2.14, regarding soldiers carrying their own packs.</note>

->**Teach me how to dine.**<-
->**XLIX**<-

*Teach me how to dine.* <note>original Greek: "Δείπνειν με δίδασκε." (Deipnein me didaske)</note> This is a proverbial figure used by Aristophanes in *The Frogs*. It is used opportunely whenever someone unskilled in the matter being discussed tries to teach, lead, or even refute someone else. They are the words of Bacchus to Hercules, who was judging tragedies, though Hercules was more practiced in devouring bulls than in weighing the poems of authors.

->**The Rhamnusian.**<-
->**L**<-

*The Rhamnusian.* <note>original Greek: "Ῥαμνούσιος." (Rhamnousios)</note> Eudemus, in his rhetorical dictionary, notes that this epithet was once added as a proverb to wise and moderate men. He does not explain the reason for the adage. From this, one can guess that it was either said because of the customs of that people, or because of the <term>Rhamnusian Goddess</term> <note>Nemesis, who had a famous temple at Rhamnus</note>, who teaches that moderation must be applied in every business. We have shown this more extensively elsewhere.

->**Wow, Myxus!**<-
->**LI**<-

*Wow, Myxus!* <note>original Greek: "Βαβαὶ μύξος." (Babai myxos)</note> This was commonly said of boastful and bragging people; for "wow" <note>original Greek: "βαβαὶ"</note> signifies amazement and wonder. Now, Myxus was some priest of Diana, boastful... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, moving from the physical metaphors of the lungs to adages concerning impossibility, deceitful pretexts, and the historical reputation of the Phoenicians for trickery.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...boastful and grandiloquent, who pretended to admire everything. Recorded by Suidas and Zenodotus.

->**You are holding a lentil by the corner.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Φακῆ γωνίας κρατεῖς" (Phakē gōnias krateis)</note>, that is, *You hold a lentil by the corner.* This refers to a task that cannot be done under any circumstances, because this type of legume lacks corners. Recorded by Suidas.

->**Patroclus’s excuse.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Πατροκλέους πρόφασις" (Patrokleous prophasis)</note>, that is, *Patroclus’s excuse*, or pretext. Diogenianus explains that this is usually said of those who, because of fear, do not dare to lament their own calamities directly, but weep for them under the pretext of mourning for someone else. <note>In Homer’s *Iliad*, the captive women are described as weeping for the fallen Patroclus as a socially acceptable way to grieve their own lost lives.</note> Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How one can praise oneself without envy*, says: *And let us not seem to use Patroclus as an excuse, but to praise ourselves through them.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ μὴ δοκῶμὲν πάτροκλου πρόφασιν, σφᾶς δ' αὐτοὺς δ' ἐκείνων ἐπαινεῖν"</note> For this is said of those who slip in their own praises while ostensibly praising others. I believe it is derived from the character of Patroclus, whom Aristophanes jokes about several times.

->**The small price of an obol.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Μικρὸν ὀβολῶ τίμιον" (Mikron obolō timion)</note>, that is, *The tiny value of an obol.* <note>The obol was a small silver coin of low value in ancient Greece.</note> Suidas cites this from Eupolis’s *Maricas*, noting it applies to worthless and good-for-nothing men. However, there is nothing to stop it from being applied to a worn-out thing. Eudemus also mentions it. We have reported many similar things before: *an obol man*, *a three-farthing man*, *a three-obol man*, and *a man hardly worth two pennies.* <note>original: "homo obolo, homo tressis, homo trioboli, homo uix dupondio estimandus."</note> Justinian the Younger wished for those just beginning their study of law to be called <term>dupondii</term> <note>literally "two-penny men," implying they were of the lowest class of students</note>, as if belonging to the lowest rank; while those who had already made progress he called <term>prolytae</term> and <term>lytae</term>, as if they were "released" or "solvers."

->**The path was seen by the feet.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Τῶν ποδῶν ἐώραται ὁδός" (Tōn podōn eōratai hodos)</note>, that is, *The path was seen by the feet.* This refers to a business where you have finally gained experience through trial. It is taken from travelers. Terence says in *Phormio*: *Ah, not so; the trial has been made, and now the path of the feet has been seen.* <note>original: "Ah non ita: Factu periculum, iam pedum uisa est uia."</note>

->**Phoenician contracts.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Φοινίκων συνθῆκαι" (Phoinikōn synthēkai)</note>, that is, *Phoenician agreements.* The Phoenicians who took possession of Carthage, when they first landed in that region, requested from those who inhabited Libya at that time that they be allowed the hospitality of the land for a day and a night. When they had obtained this, and were ordered to leave the territory after that time had passed, they refused, asserting that they had made a pact that it should be lawful for them to stay there for "nights and days"—clearly twisting the ambiguity of the words to their own advantage. From this, they say the proverb was born concerning treacherous and deceptive contracts. The authors are Suidas and Diogenianus. Indeed, all Phoenicians were generally said to be greedy for profit. Hence Pindar, in his second *Pythian Ode*, spoke of <note>original Greek: "φοινίσσαν ἐμπολὰν"</note> *Phoenician negotiation.* And a commentator cites from some comic poet: *Immediately I become a Phoenician.* <note>original Greek: "εὐθὺς φοινίξ γίνομαι"</note> Likewise from Sophocles:
*He went to buy and sell like a Phoenician man.* <note>original: "Phœnix ut uir, cœpit emere ac uendere."</note>
Finally, Plato in the third book of *The Republic*, discussing those who think lying is appropriate for a magistrate, says: *nothing noble, but something Phoenician.* <note>original Greek: "μηδὲν καλὸν, ἀλλὰ φοινικικόν τι"</note>

->**As tiny as Molon.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Μικρὸς ἡλίκος μόλων" (Mikros hēlikos molōn)</note>, that is, *As tiny as Molon.* Used against little men of extremely short stature. Suidas shows there were two Molons, both notable (as I conjecture) for their physical smallness: one was an actor, the other a thief—both honorable professions, of course!

->**Through an ancient day.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Διὰ παλαιᾶς ἡμέρας" (Dia palaias hēmeras)</note>. Used for a very obsolete and ancient thing. It is reported by Diogenianus. This is similar to what is quite cleverly bandied about today in the schools of philosophers: *In the Great Year of Plato.* <note>The "Great Year" refers to the time it takes for all planets to return to the same relative positions, a period of vast antiquity.</note>

->**The good things have perished.**<-

<note>original Greek: "Ἔῤῥei τὰ καλὰ" (Errhei ta kala)</note>, that is, *The honorable things are gone.* Hippocrates was the secretary to the Spartan Mindarus; when Mindarus was killed by the Athenians, Hippocrates wrote this sort of letter to Sparta: *The good things are gone, Mindarus is lost*, signifying that since the leader was killed, the situation was hopeless. Diogenianus lists the adage; Xenophon records the history in the first book of the *Hellenica*. The Greek words form a hexameter: *The honors have perished, Mindarus is gone.*

->**He who hastens too much, finishes later.**<-

Plato in the dialogue titled *The Statesman* <note>original: "De regno"</note>: *For your current state regarding haste has made you...*

<summary>This page explores several adages related to pretexts, worthlessness, and the historical reputation of the Phoenicians for deceitful contracts, as well as the brevity of Spartan military dispatches.</summary>
<keywords>Patroclus, Phoenicians, Carthage, legal education, Justinian, Spartan history, ancient proverbs, Greek idioms, Plato</keywords>

--- Page 867 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on the value of moderation and careful progress, contrasting the dangers of excessive haste with the wisdom of deliberate action, before moving into a series of shorter adages regarding lifespan, frugality, and foolishness.</meta>

...having acted without calmness in order to succeed, they actually finished more slowly. <note>original Greek: "ποιήσαντας οὐχ ἡσύχως εὖ πράξοντας, ἀνύσαναι βραδύτερον"</note> That is: "For he has brought it about that what is said in the proverb has now happened to us as well: namely, that while we distribute our time poorly through leisure, we have finished later than intended." He alluded to the same proverb in the seventh book of the *Republic*: "As the one who, with everything in view, wishing to accomplish everything quickly, is actually more delayed." <note>original Greek: "ὡς ὁ ὑπ’ ὄψιν ἐφ’ ᾧ, ταχὺ πάντα βουλόμενος, μᾶλλον βραδύνει"</note> That is, he says, while I hasten to run through everything quickly, I am slower. He has something similar in the *Cratylus*: "Lest we be at a disadvantage like those who travel by night at night, and while we think we are arriving late, we find that the facts themselves show we have arrived too late." <note>original Greek: "ἵνα μὴ ὄφλωμεν ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν νυκτὶ νύκτωρ ποδεύοντες..."</note> That is: "Lest it happen to us, as it does to those who walk about at night among the Aeginetans and finish their journey later, that we likewise seem to have arrived at the truth of the matter later than was proper." 

There is also that wise observation of Saint Augustine against Petilianus: that it sometimes happens to those who hurry in a state of agitation that they put on their clothes or shoes backwards, a thing which later causes a delay. The same thing happens to those who try to do many things at once and achieve nothing. Plato writes in the third book of the *Republic*: "Because each individual might practice one pursuit well, but not many; or if he should try to grasp many, he would fail in all of them." <note>original Greek: "ὅτι εἷς ἕκαστ@, ἓν μὲν ἂν ἐπιτήδευμα καλῶς ἐπιτηδεύοι..."</note> That is: "Each person should practice one study correctly, and by no means many. Indeed, if he attempts it, having attacked many things, he will be frustrated in all of them." In the tenth book of the same work, he teaches that the same thing happens to those who rush toward honor not through truth, but through deceptions and evil arts: "Do not those clever and unjust men act just like those runners who run well from the lower end of the track, but not from the upper end? At first, they leap away sharply, but at the end of the race they are made ridiculous, departing without a crown and with their ears drooping on their shoulders." <note>original Greek: "οὐχ οἱ μ’ δεινοί τε καὶ ἄδικοι δρῶσιν..."</note> <note>The "ears on shoulders" is a Greek image for a runner who is exhausted and dejected.</note>

This adage warns us that in establishing any matter, we should apply care rather than speed, lest an error made at the start of the work cause a delay later. Some are liable to this proverb who, for the sake of a shortcut, skip Greek literature and leap straight into the study of philosophy; while they foolishly chase a shortcut, they fall into the greatest expense of time. For it happens that while these men suddenly strive to emerge as philosophers, they never actually attain the knowledge of philosophy; and when they believe they have already reached the finish line, they must return again to the starting gates and begin "from the line" once more, as the Greeks say. Likewise, in warfare, the delay of Fabius achieved more than the headlong rashness of Marcus Minutius. Indeed, he alone overcame Hannibal—who had been invincible in many battles—not by strength, but by slowness. Of him, Ennius wrote famously, as cited by Marcus Tullius Cicero in *On Old Age*:

> One man, by delaying, restored the state for us,
> For he did not place rumors before our safety.

---

<margin>LXI</margin>
### Beyond the catalogue.

"He lives beyond the catalogue." <note>original Greek: "ὑπὲρ τὸν κατάλογον ζῆ"</note> This was said of a person who lived to a great age, so that he seemed to have already passed that prescribed number of years. It is found, if I am not mistaken, in Lucian. It is also recorded by Suidas.

<margin>LXII</margin>
### To be wise beyond the pouch.

"To be anxious beyond the pouch." <note>original Greek: "Ὑπὲρ τὴν πήραν φρονεῖν"</note> This was said as a proverbial figure in Lucian’s *Timon*: "For it is necessary for the philosopher to be content with few things and frugal, and not to seek anything beyond his pouch." <note>original Greek: "ὀλιγαρκῆ γὰρ καὶ μέτριον χρὴ εἶναι..."</note> <note>The "pouch" or scrip refers to the small bag carried by wandering Cynic philosophers to hold their meager belongings.</note> This will apply to a poor man, but especially to a Christian, whom Jesus forbids to worry about tomorrow. Close to this is the adage: *A life in a jar.* <note>Erasmus refers to Diogenes the Cynic, who lived in a large storage jar (often translated as a tub).</note>

<margin>LXIII</margin>
### A virgin at first.

"A virgin at first." <note>original Greek: "Παρθένον τὴν πρώτην"</note> This was usually said of those who squandered their paternal inheritance. I suspect it is derived from the fact that virgins, being as yet inexperienced and ignorant of the trade of a courtesan, easily grant access to themselves. Later, so that they might carry off a greater reward, they show themselves to be difficult. Likewise, young men who have recently acquired wealth, before they understand the value of money, pour it out quite lavishly. Even the first part of our life, which is surely the best, is often wasted by us most foolishly.

<margin>LXIIII</margin>
### The man seemed like a ship entreating a rock.

"The man is like a ship entreating a rock." <note>original Greek: "Ἀνηρ ἔοικε ναῦς ἱκετεύων πέτραν"</note> That is:
-> To be a manly man is a ship beseeching a stone. <-
Suidas indicates this is said of stupid and dull-witted people to whom one thing seems to be another, taking the metaphor from a ship that crashes into a reef.

<summary>Erasmus concludes his reflection on the wisdom of "hastening slowly" by citing Plato, Augustine, and the Roman general Fabius, then transitions to shorter adages about longevity, frugality, and the folly of squandering youth or wealth.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->For a hungry man, stealing is necessary.<-
<margin>60</margin>
"To steal is a necessity for one who is hungry." <note>original Greek: πεινῶντι κλέπτειν ἐστ’ ἀναγκαίως ἔχον</note>. That is, a starving man is forced to be a thief. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note> records this as a proverb, noting that it applies to those driven by extreme necessity to do something. For example, if someone confesses to having lied, they might say, "What was I to do? I had to either lie or face total disgrace," or "to steal through lies." <note>original Greek: ψευδῶν κλέπτειν</note>. Or if someone greedy for glory publishes the works of others as his own because he is unable to produce anything remarkable of his own.

->He lived well, while he lived.<-
<margin>61</margin>
"He lived well, while he lived." This appears in Terence’s play *The Mother-in-Law* <note>Latin: Hecyra</note>. Even the old man in the play indicates it was a proverb when he asks if the speaker had brought nothing but a single cliché. It applies to those who live softly and pleasantly, spending their money so as not to leave much for their heir. There is a double meaning <term>amphibologia|a phrase that can be interpreted in two ways</term> in the word "to live"; sometimes it simply means to be alive, and sometimes it means to live "genially" or for pleasure. As in Catullus:
"Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love."

->Do not touch the smoking nose of a bear.<-
<margin>62</margin>
This passage in Martial also has the appearance of a proverb:
"Nor, lost as you are, should you touch 
The smoking nose of a living bear with a raving mouth:
Though he may be calm and lick your fingers and hands,
If pain and bile, if justified anger compels him,
He will be a bear; you will wear out your teeth on an empty hide."
It warns that those who have the power to do harm should not be provoked. In a similar way, Synesius wrote in his *Praise of Baldness*: "To catch a dog by the nostrils," meaning to provoke one who is biting and harmful. Those who handle wild beasts <note>Latin: bestiarii</note> teach that bears are most easily provoked when struck in this part of the body.

->In the manner of mice.<-
<margin>63</margin>
Plautus in *The Captives*: "Like mice, we are always eating someone else's food." This is said of parasites, for whom it is pleasant to live off another's plate. Freedom and another's food do not go well together, nor do they stay in one place—a point elegantly illustrated by Aesop’s fable of the town mouse and the country mouse. Indeed, among the Greeks, there is a proverbial verb "to play the mouse" <note>original Greek: μυοχολεῖν</note>, said of those who wander and prowl about in the manner of mice for the sake of food. Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian</note> noted this.

->One of three evils.<-
<margin>64</margin>
"One of three evils." <note>original Greek: τῶν τριῶν κακῶν ἕν</note>. Suidas indicates that this proverb appeared in Menander. It was taken from Theramenes <note>An Athenian statesman known for his shifting allegiances</note>, who told someone to choose which of three evils they preferred. Hence Aristophanes, cited by the same Suidas in the *Triphales*, says: "For I have feared these three things from Theramenes." <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ γὰρ ἀπὸ Θηραμένους δέδοικα τὰ τρία ταῦτα</note>. As for what those three things are, the proverb refers to "the three things leading to death." <note>original Greek: τὰ τρία τὰ εἰς θάνατον</note>. Alexander used this in the *Aeopolis*. Aristides says that an oracle used to be delivered sealed, and whoever opened it before it was lawful would face one of three evils: the loss of eyes, the loss of a hand, or the loss of the tongue. Some say that those condemned to death were offered three choices: the sword, the noose, or hemlock <note>Latin: aconitum</note>.

->As easily as a fox eats a pear.<-
<margin>65</margin>
Plautus in *The Haunted House* <note>Latin: Mostellaria</note>: "You will win as easily as a fox eats a pear." This refers to something very easy to do, as it is no trouble at all for a sharp-toothed fox to eat a pear.

->To knit the brow, to puff out the cheeks.<-
<margin>66</margin>
"Drawing up the eyebrows and puffing out the cheeks." <note>original Greek: ὀφρῦς ἀνασπῶντες καὶ γνάθους φυσῶντες</note>. Suidas notes this is said of the proud and the puffed up. Indeed, as we have shown elsewhere, the seat of arrogance is in the eyebrows. Horace used "puffed out cheeks" as a sign of anger:
"Lest Jupiter, enraged,
Puff out both his cheeks."
Saint Augustine, in his *Confessions*, wrote: "With cheeks bursting with pride." <note>original Latin: Buccis typho crepantibus</note>. In this passage, some mistakenly read "type" <note>Latin: typo</note> instead of "pride" <note>Latin: typho</note>. It is remarkable that Augustine was so delighted by this Greek-derived word that, although he could have said "pride" <note>Latin: fastum</note>, he preferred to say "typhus," perhaps because it already seemed to have been adopted into Latin use. It is a metaphor taken from frogs, which puff themselves up in anger. Aesop’s fable of the frog that burst from arrogance is well known. Horace says:

<summary>This page features a collection of adages (LX to LXVI) focused on human behavior, ranging from the necessity of survival and the pursuit of pleasure to warnings against provoking danger and the outward physical signs of pride and anger.</summary>
<keywords>necessity, hunger, lifestyle, parasites, danger, punishment, arrogance, Erasmus, Latin proverbs, Greek proverbs</keywords>

--- Page 869 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient proverbs, specifically focusing on social behavior, legal injustice, and the metaphorical use of "stains" and "silence" in rhetoric and law.</meta>

### Inflate the growing bladder with swelling words.
<note>original: "Crescentem tumidis infla sermonibus utrem." This likely concludes the previous adage about empty pride.</note>

->The pig joins the revelry.<-
<margin>72</margin>
"The pig revels" <note>original Greek: ὗς κώμασεν</note>, or: "The pig has danced" or "The pig joins the feast." Diogenianus <note>a Greek proverb collector</note> explains that this was commonly said of those who act in a way that is utterly indecorous, or those who, having stumbled upon success beyond what they deserve, carry themselves with excessive insolence. Suidas and Zenodotus also touch upon this. Among the Greeks, the word for "reveling" <note>original Greek: κωμάζειν</note> refers to the behavior of young lovers who, in a state of wantonness, put on crowns, sing songs, dance, and engage in other youthful trifles, often breaking into the homes of others. Pigs also "break in," as Theocritus writes in his *Syracusan Women*: "The thick crowd pushes like a pack of pigs." That is:
> The huddled crowd rushes in like swine.

Furthermore, for those of a more rustic disposition, it is surprising how much these festive behaviors misbecome them. The proverb applies whenever a naturally cruel or boorish person attempts to appear charming or festive.

->Censure pardons the crows and harasses the doves.<-
<margin>73</margin>
One egg is not so much like another as this saying is like that one found in Juvenal:
"Censure pardons the crows and harasses the doves." <note>Latin: "Dat veniam corvis, vexat censura columbas."</note>
The punishment of the law is exercised against the humble and those from whom some profit can be extracted due to their mild nature. The predatory ones, however, are forgiven. This is taken from an <term>apophthegm|a concise, pointed saying</term> of Anacharsis, who used this remark to mock Solon’s <note>the famous Athenian lawmaker</note> zeal in writing laws. As Plutarch relates in his *Life of Solon*, Anacharsis said that "laws are like spider webs; for if something light and weak falls into them, they hold it fast, but if something larger falls in, it tears through and escapes." <note>original Greek: ὃς τοὺς νόμους τοῖς ἀραχνίοις ὁμοίους ἔφασκεν, αἳ γὰρ ἐκείνους ἐὰν μὲν ἐμπέσῃ τι κοῦφον καὶ ἀσθενές, στέγουσιν, ἐὰν δ' μεῖζον, διακόψαν οἴχεται</note>. Terence expresses the same sentiment in his play *Phormio*:
> Because the net is not spread for the hawk or the kite,
> Who do us harm; it is spread for those who do nothing.
> For in the former there is profit; in the latter, labor is wasted.

->Shoemaker’s ink.<-
<margin>74</margin>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the ninth book of his letters to Paetus, writes: "His father has already been accused by Marcus Antonius; he is thought to have been acquitted by shoemaker’s ink." There seems to be a proverb underlying this. I believe he means the man was acquitted through the corruption of the judges, but not without infamy. For "shoemaker’s ink" <note>Latin: sutorium atramentum</note> is of such a kind that it does not leave a deep black mark, yet it leaves a stain nonetheless. Poets use the symbol of ink to signify infamy, as Horace does:
"This is the juice of the black cuttlefish, this is 
pure malice."
That "juice" is a liquid which Aristotle, in the fourth book of *On the Parts of Animals*, says is found in many soft-bodied fish, especially the cuttlefish. He writes that it is contained in a membranous tunic and released through a certain tube; they pour it out when frightened to darken the water so they cannot be caught. Horace writes again:
> But just as ink, when handled, leaves a mark and a blemish, 
> so writers generally smear 
> illustrious deeds with foul verse.

Furthermore, what the Greeks call *chalcanthum* <note>original Greek: χάλκανθος</note>, Cornelius Celsus usually translates as "shoemaker’s ink." He mentions it frequently in his medical writings, especially in book five. It is collected from copper. Hence the Greek name, which essentially means "flower of copper." From this, I suspect the proverb refers more to a stain that you can hardly wash away. For the ink they call "writer’s ink" is more easily washed off and does not cling to leather. Pliny, in a letter, used a similar figure of speech when he called a certain mark "a Vitellian scar."

->Deaf testimonies.<-
<margin>75</margin>
"Deaf testimonies" <note>original Greek: κωφὰ μαρτυρία</note>. These are said to be testimonies delivered through written tablets, because when questioned, they do not answer back. This is not unlike the expression "Silent teachers" <note>referring to books</note>. Hence, those are proverbially said to "act with deaf testimonies" who cite people who are either far away or deceased, so that their claims cannot be challenged or caught out.

->To lose the fare.<-
<margin>76</margin>
Juvenal in the Satire that begins *What do pedigrees matter?*:
"Look around for a herald for your rags, Chaerippus."

<summary>Erasmus explains various proverbs concerning social impropriety, the tendency of laws to punish the weak while sparing the powerful, and the use of "shoemaker's ink" as a metaphor for lasting infamy. He also touches upon the unreliability of written "deaf" testimonies that cannot be cross-examined.</summary>
<keywords>social decorum, legal injustice, Solon, Anacharsis, shoemaker's ink, infamy, written vs. oral testimony, Horace, Juvenal, Greek proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion on proverbs related to loss and social behavior, specifically concluding the thought from the previous page regarding the futility of legal battles and the loss of one's final resources.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES

### Since Pansa snatches away whatever Nacta left you,
### Be silent now; it is madness to lose your passage money after everything else.

Domitius Calderinus—an author who, for one of the more recent era, is by no means poor—notes that this is a proverb directed at someone who, having already lost a great deal, seems intent on losing the little that remains. The metaphor is drawn from merchants who, when they sail, if they cannot make as much profit as they desire, at least strive to recover from the sale of their goods enough to pay their <term>naulum|the fee paid for sea passage or freight</term>. When Aristippus <note>a Greek philosopher and follower of Socrates</note> was asked by someone if he was everywhere, he replied with a laugh: "There, I am losing my passage money; come, I am everywhere." <note>original Greek: ἐκεῖ, ἔφη, ἀπολλύμι ναῦλον, ἄγε πανταχόσε εἰμί.</note> By this he meant: "I do not lose my passage money if indeed I am at home everywhere." This is recounted by Plutarch in his essay titled *Whether Virtue Can Be Taught*. <note>original Greek: ὅτι διδακτὴ ἡ ἀρετή</note>

---

### To act like a Sicilian.
<margin>75</margin>
"To Siculize" <note>original Greek: Σικελιζειν</note>, or *Siculissare*. Eudemus indicates that this was used in ancient times to describe someone who handles a matter skillfully or with a certain sternness. He notes that the poet Epicharmus used the term in this way. Others, however, prefer to apply it to those who are wicked and crafty. There is little doubt that the expression is derived from the character of the Sicilian people. Yet Athenaeus, in the first book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The Sophists at Dinner</note>, indicates that the adage arose from Andron the Sicilian, who introduced the custom of dancing and gesturing to the accompaniment of the flute.

---

### A sitting dove.
<margin>76</margin>
"A sitting dove" <note>original Greek: Ἥμενη πέλεια</note>. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> mentions this under his list of proverbs, indicating it was commonly said of those who are excessively gentle and simple-minded. For when doves fly away, they deceive others with the swiftness of their flight; but when they are sitting, nothing is milder or more simple. They possess nothing with which to defend themselves against kites and hawks except the speed of their wings. To me, it seems this could also be said of those who feign simplicity in order to better deceive, because it is the custom of bird-catchers to place a blinded dove in a net; as it flutters about, it lures other doves into the trap. Such a bird is called a <term>paleutria|a decoy bird</term> by the Greeks, from the word *paleuein* <note>original Greek: παλεύειν</note>, which means to seduce or entice into a snare. Aristophanes, speaking of doves in *The Birds*:
"And he compels them, bound in the net, to act as decoys." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐπαναγκάζει παλεύειν δεδεμένας ἐν δικτύῳ.</note> <insert>that is,</insert>
->And he forces them to act as decoys, tied in the net.<-
Reader, consider whether we should read the word as "ensnared" <note>original Greek: ἠμένη</note> instead of "sitting" <note>original Greek: ἥμενη</note>, for that is what the bird endures in order to deceive the others.

---

### A bearded or tailed ape.
<margin>77</margin>
"An ape wearing a beard" <note>original Greek: Πίθηκος πώγωνα ἔχων</note>. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*: "O you ape wearing a beard!" A commentator noted that this is an allusion to a line by Archilochus: "Such an ape having a tail." <note>original Greek: πίθη δ' οἴοι τὴν πυγὴν ἔχων</note> It was usually said of ridiculous people. Regulus called a certain rustic a "Stoic's ape" as an insult, as Pliny records in his *Letters*; I suppose because the man acted the part of a Stoic with his beard and cloak rather than through his actual conduct. The same Aristophanes elsewhere calls certain people "people-apes" <note>original Greek: δημοπιθήκους</note>, as if they were the mimics of the common folk. This animal is by nature a "maker of laughter" <note>original Greek: γελοιοποιόν</note>, and seems born for no other use, since it is not good for eating like sheep, nor for guarding a house like dogs, nor for carrying burdens like horses. Athenaeus, in his fourteenth book, tells that the philosopher Anacharsis—a Scythian by birth—was the only one who did not laugh when men trained to provoke laughter were brought into a banquet. Finally, when an ape was brought in, he began to laugh; asked for the reason, he said: "These are funny by nature; those others merely pretend to be."

---

### To sing to oneself.
<margin>78</margin>
"To play the lyre for oneself" <note>original Greek: Ἑαυτῷ ψάλλειν</note>. This is said of someone who does not act according to the judgment of others, but follows his own mind. In Plato’s *Symposium*, they tell the flute-girl to play for herself. And a certain man—Antigenidas, I believe—ordered a student who was not very popular with the public to "sing for me and the Muses." Marcus Tullius Cicero says in *Brutus*: "It is the mark of a great orator to seem a great orator to the people. Therefore, while the flute-player Antigenidas said to a student who was met with coldness by the crowd, 'Sing for me and the Muses,' I would say to Brute here, when he speaks as he usually does before the multitude, 'Sing for me and the people.'" Saint Jerome attributes this to Ismenias, who was, if I am not mistaken, a student of the former. And he was not singing for himself alone, but for a teacher who was capable of judging.

---

### If the lion's skin is not enough, the fox's must be added.
<margin>79</margin>
"If the lion's hide does not reach, attach the fox's" <note>original Greek: Ἂν ἡ λεοντῆ μὴ ἐξικνῆται, τὴν ἀλωπεκείην προσάπτειν</note>. When a thing cannot be obtained by force, guile must be employed. The adage arose from an <term>apophthegm|a concise, pointed saying</term> of Lysander. For he, as Plutarch records in his *Life*, used to mock those who thought that, as descendants of Hercules, war should be waged with open strength and without deceit; he himself held that it was the duty of a good general, where the lion's p

<summary>This page explores several proverbs related to human behavior, including the loss of resources (naulum), the reputation of Sicilians for craftiness, the use of decoys (sitting doves), and the necessity of using guile when force fails (the lion and the fox).</summary>
<keywords>Aristippus, passage money, naulum, Sicilians, Siculissare, decoys, paleutria, apes, Stoic's ape, Antigenidas, Lysander, guile vs force, Aristophanes, Plutarch</keywords>

--- Page 871 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of a proverb concerning the lion's skin and the fox's skin, a metaphor for blending strength with cunning in leadership and war. The catchword "belli-" from the previous page leads into the discussion of warfare.</meta>

...where the [lion's] skin did not reach, one must stretch it by sewing on a fox's skin <note>This refers to a famous saying by the Spartan general Lysander, who said that where the lion's skin is too short, it must be lengthened with that of a fox—meaning where force fails, use cunning.</note>. Indeed, Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note> almost indicates the same when he says:
> Whether deceit or valor, who would ask in an enemy?

This adage is recorded by Zenodotus. Akin to this is what Carbo is remembered to have said in Plutarch's *Life of Sulla*. For when Sulla conducted war not only by open combat but also by trickery, Carbo said: "that in warring with a fox and a lion, both of which inhabited Sulla’s soul, he was more troubled by the fox." <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀλώπεκι κὶ λέοντι πολεμῶν ᾧ τὴ σύλλα ψυχῇ κατοικῶσιν, ὑπὸ δὲ ἀλώπεκος ἀνιῶ δὲ μᾶλλον.</note> In Aristophanes, a certain man is called a "dog-fox" <note>original Greek: κυναλώπηξ</note> because he had joined dog-like impudence with fox-like cunning.

### 82. A Sicilian soldier.
Σικελὸς στρατιώτης. i.e., *Siculus miles*. This was said as a proverbial jest against a foreign and mercenary soldier, because the Sicilians in the time of Hiero <note>Hiero II, King of Syracuse</note> mostly employed foreign troops, according to Zenodotus. It will be suitable for a man who, for the sake of profit, refuses no kind of service. It is related to what was said elsewhere about the Carians <note>referring to the proverb "To risk it on a Carian," meaning to put a mercenary in danger first</note>.

### 83. Clews of yarn instead of good things.
Ἀντ’ ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθίδες. i.e., *Pro bonis glomi*. This was usually said when someone received a benefit they had bestowed upon another with interest and in abundance. For among the Greeks, *agathides* are what are called clews or balls of yarn. However, the beauty of the allusion lies in the Greek word, which cannot be rendered in the Latin tongue <note>The pun relies on the similarity between *agatha* (good things) and *agathides* (balls of yarn)</note>. Suidas mentions this.

### 84. It is not easy to fly without wings.
Even in modern times, that line from Plautus’s *Poenulus* remains commonly celebrated: "It is not easy to fly without wings." The same author says in *Asinaria*: "Should I cheat you? Come now, fly without wings." This has its place when we mean that the supports are missing without which a business cannot be carried out. It is found among suitable authors: "to clip the wings" <note>Latin: accidere alas</note> is used for taking away the material and the faculty of attempting anything. And "to add wings." Horace spoke in a similar form of "clipped wings":
> When first the battle of Philippi sent me away, 
> humbled, with my wings clipped.

And Cicero to Atticus in the fourth book: "Those who had clipped my wings do not want them to grow back." The same man said in the *Academics*: "To cut the sinews," meaning to take away strength. Related to this is what we have recorded elsewhere: "to card the fire" <note>original Greek: εἰς πῦρ ξαίνειν</note>, that is, to divide the fire. This refers to an impossible or vain labor, because fire soon closes back in on itself. Of this kind is that saying in Plato’s *Eryxias*: "When I had learned that such was the man's nature, that to persuade him was nothing else than—as the saying goes—to boil a stone." <note>original Greek: καππαθὼν ᾧ αὐτῷ ἐγὼ ὅτι ἴον εἴη πεῖσαι, ὅπερ ἂν τὸ λεγόμενον λίθον ἑψῆσαι.</note> I confess these things could have been said more opportunely in other places, but not everything occurs to one in every place.

### 85. To act like a Siphonian.
Σιφνιάζειν. i.e., *Siphniare*. Suidas indicates this proverb is usually said for "applying a hand to the backside." It is taken from the customs of the Siphonians, who were accustomed to do this for the sake of lust. Now, Siphnus is a certain island not far from Crete, which once had the name Merope, or was famous for this title, being one of the Cyclades. Pliny also mentions it in book four, chapter 12. Stephanus also notes the proverb.

### 86. Near the probe.
Κατὰ μήλην. i.e., *Iuxta melam*. Suidas shows this is usually said as a proverb when someone pursues uncertainties by conjectures. The metaphor is taken from doctors exploring an internal ulcer by an instrument inserted through the throat. For they call that instrument a *mele* <note>original Greek: μήλην</note>, and "to probe" <note>original Greek: μηλῶσαι</note> is to test in this manner.

### 87. Writing and Leucaeus are not the same.
γραφή τε κὶ λευκαῖος οὐ ταὐτόν. i.e., *Scriptura & Leucæus non sunt idem*, or they do not agree. This is used when someone writes one thing but does or says another. It will be rightly cast at those who refuse to stand by their agreements. For these usually consist of written contracts. Or at those whose lives do not agree with the books they have published. The Greek verse will be complete if you add "he says" <note>original Greek: λεγεῖ</note>. One may guess that Leucaeus was a scribe of bad faith.

### 88. To sound the battle cry. To sound the retreat.
We have elsewhere advised that metaphors taken from war are almost proverbial, such as...

--- Page 872 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Latin and Greek adages, specifically focusing on military metaphors and then transitioning into adages regarding flattery, debt, social balance, and nostalgia. The catchword "bellicū" from the previous page leads into the phrase "bellicum canere" (to sound the war-trumpet).</meta>

...to sound the war-trumpet <note>original: "bellicū canere"</note>, used in place of "to animate and exhort." Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his 7th *Philippic*: "And when they say that I have sounded it." Likewise, one is said to "sound the signal" <note>original: "Canere classicū"</note> who stirs up discord. To "sound the retreat" <note>original: "Receptui canere"</note> means to finish. Cicero in his 12th *Philippic* asks: "For who would hasten to fight when the commander is calling back and sounding the retreat?" Quintilian in Book 12, in the chapter on studies after retirement, says: "Therefore, before he falls into these snares of old age, he will sound the retreat and arrive in port with his ship intact." "The standards signal" <note>original: "Signa canunt"</note> in Martial means "let us now engage"; and in Plautus, "to fight with joined standards" <note>original: "collatis signis depugnare"</note>; and in the same author, "to fight with turned swords" <note>original: "uersis gladijs depugnare"</note>. Indeed, this very phrase "With joined standards" <note>original: "Collatis signis"</note> undoubtedly has the appearance of an adage when we mean a serious and exact discussion of a matter, as Cicero says in his letters to Atticus: "as if with joined standards against Maphrago." In Juvenal, we find: 
"This is the trumpet of the brawl," meaning, this is the beginning of the war.

### 71. A beautiful monkey. <note>The Latin title is "Pithon formosus," using a Latinized version of the Greek word for a small ape.</note>
Πίθων καλὸς <note>original: "Pithon kalos"</note>, that is, *A beautiful monkey*. This will be appropriate when someone praises falsely through flattery. Pindar in his second *Pythian Ode* says: "A monkey is truly beautiful to children, always beautiful." <note>original: "καλός τοι πίθων παρὰ παισὶν ἀεὶ καλός"</note>. The commentator shows that this was taken from children who, in flattery, would repeatedly call a monkey "beautiful." Furthermore, *pithon* seems to be a diminutive of the word *pithekos* <note>the standard Greek word for ape</note>, as if you were to say "little monkey." Pindar obliquely censures a certain person, either because he was raised up in pride by the praise of an unlearned man, or because he himself was flattering Hiero <note>Hiero I, tyrant of Syracuse</note> by praising things that should not be praised. Moreover, "Self-love" <note>term: "Φιλαυτία" (Philautia) — the Greek concept of excessive self-love or vanity</note> is peculiar to this animal, so much so that they are sensitive to praise and delight in mirrors, and they rejoice in having their offspring handled, though they often kill their own young by crushing them in an embrace. Regarding the habit of speaking to please, the ancients used the word *cheiroethein* <note>original: "χειροηθεῖν" — literally "to make tame" or "to handle gently"</note>, a word used by Aeschylus in his *Prometheus*, as Athenaeus teaches in his fourth book. On the same authority, those who made a study of speaking pleasant things rather than true things were called "sweet-tongued" <note>original: "ἡδυγλώσσαι" (hedyglossai)</note>.

### 72. Once red, and ten times pale.
Ἅπαξ πυῤῥὸς καὶ δεκάκις χλωρὸς <note>original: "Hapax pyrrhos kai dekakis chloros"</note>. That is, *Once red, and ten times pale*. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> remarks that this was said of those who take out a loan; it is necessary for them to frequently turn red with shame and then turn pale with fear. They blush while they seek the loan, and they turn pale when they fear they cannot pay it back, lest they be dragged into court or into the "nerve" <note>term: "neruum" — a Roman term for stocks or a type of prison for debtors</note>.

### 73. Always place a young girl with an old man.
Ἀεὶ γέροντι νέαν ἐμβάλλειν κόρην <note>original: "Aei geronti nean emballein koren"</note>. That is,
->Always place a maiden girl under an old man.<-
A proverbial six-foot verse <note>term: "Senarius" — a common meter in Latin and Greek poetry</note> advising that men of advanced age should marry a young girl rather than an old woman, lest if cold is added to cold and Venus <note>The goddess of love, here representing sexual vitality</note> languishes, the marriage remains sterile. This may be quite aptly applied to other uses whenever we wish to indicate that the joining of things should be so tempered that what is lacking in one place is supplied from elsewhere: namely, that a youth be added to an old man, so that the old man's sadness of age may be moderated by the youth's cheerfulness; and conversely, that the old man's severity may temper the youth's exuberance. Likewise, that a talkative person be joined to one more silent, a bold person to a timid one, or a poor person to a rich one. Diogenianus mentions this proverb.

### 74. Last year’s harvest is always better.
Ἀεὶ τὰ πέρυσι βελτίω <note>original: "Aei ta perysi beltio"</note>. That is,
->The previous year is always preferred.<-
When the present things are displeasing and past things are preferred. Diogenianus notes that this was shouted by the Athenians during the Macedonian conflicts. The metaphor is taken from farmers, who are always complaining to their masters about the fruits of the current year. This relates to that line from Horace: "A praiser of time past when he was a boy."

### 75. The sacrifices are nothing.
τὰ θύματα οὐδέν ἐστιν, πλὴν ψύχα καὶ κόραka <note>original: "ta thymata ouden estin, plen psycha kai koraka"</note>. That is, *The sacrifices are nothing but crumbs and crows*. This was said of lean victims. It can be applied not ungracefully to food that is barely edible. It is recorded by Suidas.

### 90. A Scythian wilderness.
Σκυθῶν ἐρημία <note>original: "Skython eremia"</note>. That is, *A Scythian wilderness*, said of the greatest calamities and ruin. As found in Aristophanes’ *The Acharnians*:
"You shall perish, entangled in a Scythian wilderness." <note>original: "Ἐξολεῖσθε συμπλακέντα τῇ σκυθῶν ἐρημίᾳ"</note>
In this passage, the commentator indicates that the proverb was traditionally used for a vast solitude, derived...

thence, because the Scythians use no fixed dwellings, but are carried about wandering in wagons. For that reason, the region is abundant with wild beasts. Quintus Curtius also mentions the adage in the seventh book of his *History of Alexander the Great*, where a Scythian envoy speaks to him in this manner: "I hear that the Scythian solitudes are mocked even in Greek proverbs. We pursue deserts and places void of human culture more than we do cities and rich fields." Plutarch also uses it in his book *On Stoic Contradictions*, just as we mentioned previously regarding the proverb "To be thrown headlong."

<margin>XCV</margin>
->To break the ice.<-
<note>original: "Scindere glaciem"</note>

"To break the ice" is to open a path and to be the first in beginning a business. It is a metaphor taken from sailors, one of whom is sent ahead when the river is frozen to break the ice and open a way for the rest.

<margin>XCVI</margin>
->You will live, even if receiving only an onion.<-
<note>original: "Viuus fueris, uel cepe solum accipiens"</note>

ζώς χρήσῃ, κρομμύου мόνου λαβών <note>original Greek: "zōs chrēsē, krommyou monou labōn"</note>, that is:
*If you take only an onion, you will surely live.*
Zenodotus and Suidas <note>Byzantine lexicographers and collectors of proverbs</note> show that this was typically said against those who achieve a great reputation from some very small thing. It apparently arose from a sick man who, when a doctor offered him an onion, recovered—a plant that is otherwise common and not particularly healthy for the body.

<margin>XCVII</margin>
->Wise are tyrants by the company of the wise.<-
<note>original: "Sapientes tyranni, sapientum congressu"</note>

Σοφοὶ τύραννοι τῶν σοφῶν συνουσίᾳ <note>original Greek: "Sophoi tyrannoi tōn sophōn synousia"</note>, that is:
*A prince is wise through the company of wise men.*
Zenodotus cites this from the play *Ajax the Locrian*, adding that the same little verse was cited by Plato under the name of Euripides. I have certainly found it cited under his name in the eighth book of the *Republic*: *Wise are tyrants by the company of the wise.*
I wonder all the more why Aulus Gellius cites it from Plato's *Theaetetus*, unless perhaps by a scribe's error "Theaetetus" was corrupted from "Theages," for it is indeed recounted in the *Theages*. Aulus Gellius, in his thirteenth book, shows that the same line was found in both authors: in Sophocles, in a play of the same name, and in Euripides. Just as several other verses are found in Euripides which can also be found in Sophocles and Aeschylus. Furthermore, the little verse we just cited is said by Gellius to be of "noted antiquity," so that you may understand it has passed into a proverb. And would that it pleased the princes of our age as much as it is weightily and elegantly written! Toward them, one might rather say:
<margin>Foolish tyrants by the company of flatterers. <note>original Greek: "мιροὶ τύραννοι τῶν κολάκων συνουσίᾳ"</note></margin>

<margin>XCVIII</margin>
->The lion's skin over the saffron robe.<-
<note>original: "Leonis exuuium super crocoton"</note>

λεοντῆ ἐπὶ κροκωτῷ <note>original Greek: "leontē epi krokōtō"</note>, that is: *The lion's skin over the saffron robe.* Used when two things are joined together which do not match at all. It is taken from Bacchus, who descends to the underworld in this attire in the works of Aristophanes <note>in the play "The Frogs"</note>. He was dressed in a delicate, womanly garment <note>the saffron-colored "crocotos"</note>, and over that garment he wore a lion's skin, so that he might appear formidable to those in the underworld by being mistaken for Hercules. Hercules, seeing him adorned in this fashion, laughs at him in *The Frogs*:
*Indeed, I am quite unable to suppress my laughter,*
*Seeing a saffron robe lying beneath a lion's skin.*
This could be aptly said of certain monks or scholars who wear the insignia of their institution on the outside, but inside they imitate a military lifestyle, or those who have a grim face but effeminate morals.

<margin>XCIX</margin>
->What you know, you do not know.<-
<note>original: "Quod scis, nescis"</note>

"What you know, you do not know." Terence in *The Eunuch* says: "By Pollux, if you are wise, you should not know what you know." The same author in *The Self-Tormentor*: "You should not know what you know, if you are wise." Donatus <note>a famous Roman grammarian</note> advises that this is a proverb. It is taken from the games of the logicians, in which certain riddles <note>term: "scyrpi" — difficult or knotty riddles</note> of this kind are usually proposed: "I do, and I do not do," "I am a friend, and I am not a friend," "I hear, and I do not hear." We made mention of this type at the beginning of the work, advising that all figures of this kind which are taken <term>by way of contradiction</term> <note>original Greek: "kat' enantiosin"</note> belong to the family of proverbs. Of this kind is also that line from Plautus: "Where I am, there I am not." At first glance, as they say, this seems to be an enigma. But it is interpreted: "Where I am not, there is my mind." Thus, by this proverb we signify a certain reliability in keeping silent, when someone contains and hides what they know as if they did not know it.

**DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES**

C

->I have neither ears, nor do I touch.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nec aures habeo, nec tango."</note>

"To have neither ears nor a sense of touch" was a proverb used for someone who was rebuked by everyone for obvious faults. Jerome mentions this in the preface of his declamation, *On the Reconciled Mother and Daughter*: (And why should I fear to call it a declamation, since he himself suggests in a certain place that he composed this argument specifically for the sake of exercise?) For he says: "After I was accused of clever crimes, I became a criminal myself; and according to the common proverb used by the common people, with everyone arguing and denying everything, I believe I have neither ears nor do I touch." This means: I must remain silent, and treat what I hear and touch as if I did not know it. This may seem to be taken from Aristophanes' play *Thesmophoriazusae*: "I neither hear nor see." <note>original Greek: "μήτ' ἀκούω μήτ' ὁρῶ" (mēt' akouō mēt' horō)</note>

### THE SIXTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD CHILIAD

->Before you draw lots, you devour the common goods.<-
<note>original Latin: "Priusquam sortiaris, communia deuoras."</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure and floral motifs.</image-desc>

"You devour the common property before the drawing of lots has even occurred." This applies to someone who seizes a thing without waiting for its formal distribution. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> indicates that the metaphor is drawn from banquets, where in ancient times it was the custom for food to be distributed in portions to each person. This can be gathered from several passages in Homer, where the phrase "And an equal feast" <note>original Greek: "Καὶ δαὶς ἐΐσης" (Kai dais eisēs)</note> is quite frequent.

Later, it became accepted among some that, without a formal distribution, food was set out in common for anyone to take as much as they wished. Plautus <note>a Roman comic playwright</note> indicates this when he writes: "He builds up piles of dishes." Plutarch also mentions this in his *Table Talk*, examining which custom seems more commendable. Furthermore, the proverb is taken from Aristophanes' *The Knights*: "When you devour the public goods before you have even drawn lots for them." <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ τὰ κοινὰ πρὶν λαχεῖν κατεσθίεις" (Epi ta koina prin lachein katesthieis)</note>

->The business is being turned in our own market.<-
<note>original Latin: "Res in foro nostro uertitur."</note>

The character Tranio in Plautus’s *The Haunted House* <note>original: "Mostellaria"</note> says: "When I see the business being turned in my own market." This is a proverbial saying used for when I understand that our fortunes are being changed into a state of confusion. It is transferred from the markets, in which the price of goods often changes according to the moment. Or, it certainly comes from the formulas used in courts and for explaining lawsuits, the opposite of which is the saying: "To litigate in someone else's forum." It is related to "To use the market," which is discussed elsewhere.

->Whatever comes into the soil.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quodcunq̃ in solum uenit."</note>

"Whatever comes into the soil," that is, whatever is produced in the nature of things. Marcus Tullius Cicero in the first book of *On the Nature of the Gods* says: "Hence you fashion and produce whatever 'comes into the soil,' as the saying goes." He is mocking the atoms of the Epicureans <note>followers of Epicurus who believed the world was made of random atomic collisions</note>, from which they believe all things are born, whatever is created anywhere in the universe.

->When that cannot be done.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quando id fieri non potest."</note>

Nothing can be said that is more elegant or more moral than that sentiment found in Terence’s *The Girl from Andros* <note>original: "Andria"</note>: "Since what you want cannot be done, you should want what you can do." <note>original Greek: "ἃ δυνάμεθα, ταῦτα λες, θέλης ἃ δύνασαι" (ha dynametha, tauta les, thelēs ha dynasai)</note>. Great beauty is added by that inversion of words. It is like the saying: "One should not live to eat, but eat to live." This adage is very close to that one: "To make the best of the present." <note>original Greek: "τὸ παρὸν εὖ ποιεῖν" (to paron eu poiein)</note>. And Martial <note>a Roman poet</note>, among his counts of a happy life, reminds us: ->That you should wish to be what you are.<- <note>original Latin: "Quod sis, esse uelis."</note>

->As far as a kite does not fly over.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quantum non miluus oberret."</note>

This is a proverbial hyperbole regarding a man who is wealthy beyond measure, who possesses so much land that not even a kite <note>a bird of prey known for long flights</note> could fly across it all. Persius <note>a Roman satirist</note> says:
> A rich man plows at Cures, over as much as a kite does not fly.

Juvenal imitated this in his ninth satire:
> With so many kites, he says, tired out within your pastures.

So too in Plutarch, a certain tragic poet says:
> I sow a field twelve days' journey wide, the Berecynthian land.
> <note>original Greek: "Σπείρω δ' ἄροραν δώδεχ' ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν, Βερέκυντα χῶρον."</note>

Pliny, in his eighteenth book, calls these *latifundia* <note term="latifundia">massive privately owned estates in ancient Rome</note>, which he says brought ruin to Italy; therefore the ancients judged that: "It is better to sow less and plow better."

->We strike, and in turn we offer our legs to the arrows.<-
<note>original Latin: "Cædimus, inq̃ uicem præbemus crura sagittis."</note>

Persius, in his fourth satire:
