# THE SIXTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD CHILIAD

### Rr 4

->We strike, and in turn we offer our legs to the arrows. VI<-
<note>original Latin: "Cædimus, inq́; uicem præbemus crura ſagittis." This is a line from Persius's Satires.</note>

->that is,<-

We criticize and are criticized in turn; we are laughed at and we laugh; we bite and are bitten; we hurt and are hurt. This metaphor is taken from military service. Horace speaks in the same manner:
"We strike, and we wear down the enemy with just as many wounds."
<note>original Latin: "Cædimus, & totidem plagis conſumimus hoſtem."</note>
Plutarch, in his essay *On Progress in Virtue*, brings up a similar metaphor regarding a ball thrown back and forth: "And we are struck by words just as those who toss straps or balls toward one another," <note>original Greek: "καὶ πεπαιώμεθα οἷον λόγος ὥσπερ ἱμάντας ἢ σφαίρας ὠθουμένοι πρὸς ἀλλήλους"</note> as we have mentioned in another place regarding the proverb "To return the ball to one another."

->A Ptolemaic lawsuit. VII<-
<note>original Greek: "πτολεμαϊκὴ δίκη" (ptolemaïkē dikē)</note>
That is, a Ptolemaic lawsuit. Diogenianus <note>a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note> indicates that this was usually said of those greedy for litigation. There was a certain old woman named Ptolemais who, as long as she lived, stirred up lawsuits and was never on holiday from pursuing legal cases.

->He rolls before the kites. VIII<-
<note>original Greek: "προκυλινδεῖται ἰκτίνῳ" (prokylindeitai iktinō)</note>
That is, he worships the kite. At the beginning of spring, kites <note>a type of bird of prey</note> come out; the poor are happy because they have been relieved of the hardships of winter, so they roll on the ground and seemingly worship them. This can be applied to those who exult in a new hope. Suidas records this as a proverb. Likewise, Juvenal writes:
"Endure, and wait for the cicadas."
<note>original Latin: "Durate, atq́; expectate cicadas."</note>
However, it is taken from Aristophanes' *The Birds*: "To roll before the kites." The commentator on that play adds the reason, teaching that the four parts of the year are announced to men by birds. He attributes spring to the kites.

->Prienean justice. IX<-
<note>original Greek: "πριηνέων δίκη" (priēneōn dikē)</note>
That is, Prienean justice. Suidas shows that this is appropriate when we mean that someone excels in judging. It is taken from Bias of Priene <note>one of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>, whose integrity in judging and conducting cases became a proverb, such that it is said: "To judge better than Bias of Priene." <note>original Greek: "δικάζεσθαι Βίαντος τοῦ πριηνέως κρείσσον"</note> This is cited from the iambic writer Hipponax, by Strabo in the fourteenth book of his *Geography*, and in the *Life of Bias* by Diogenes Laertius. Also, a trochaic verse by Demodicus of Leros says:
"If you should happen to be involved in a trial, let it be judged according to Prienean justice."
<note>original Greek: "εἰ τύχοις πινῶν, δικάζου τὴν πριηνήων δίκην."</note>
A Scazon verse of Hipponax puts it thus:
"Conduct your judgment better than Bias of Priene."
<note>original Greek: "δίκην δικάζου Βίαντος τοῦ πριηνέως κρείσσον."</note>
We have spoken elsewhere regarding the judgments of Bocchoris and Rhadamanthus <note>legendary wise judges</note>.

->At first, Mars was praised in his sons. X<-
<note>original Greek: "τὰ πρῶτα ἄρης εἰς τοὺς παῖδας ἐπηνέθη" (ta prōta arēs eis tous paidas epēnethē)</note>
That is, in the beginning, Mars was praised on account of his children. This refers to those who at first show some sign of an excellent nature, but then gradually degenerate into other habits. This happened to the Romans, who were once strenuous and reflected the virtue of Mars, the author of their race, but later fell into degenerate softness, so that Juvenal not without cause exclaimed:
"But from where
Has this stinging nettle touched your grandsons, O Mars?"
<note>original Latin: "Sed unde / Hæc tetigit Gradiue tuos urtica nepotes?" Gradivus is a title for Mars.</note>
The proverb is recorded by Suidas.

->The wrestling of Phrynichus. XI<-
<note>original Greek: "τὸ φρυνίχου πάλαισμα" (to phrynichou palaisma)</note>
That is, Phrynichus’s wrestling match. Diogenianus indicates this was usually said of those who complete a business through cunning and deceit. This Phrynichus was a traitor to the Spartans, whom Old Comedy marked with a "black coal" <note>a metaphor for being disgraced or censored</note>.

->You ask for a pig in exchange for a bad dog. XII<-
<note>original Greek: "ἀντὶ κακῆς κυνὸς σῦν ἀπαιτεῖς" (anti kakēs kynos syn apaiteis)</note>
That is, you ask for a pig in exchange for a bad dog; meaning, something precious for something worthless. For a pig is edible, while a dog is not eaten at all. This is recorded by Diogenianus.

->Wisely, I put my hand into the flame. XIII<-
Saint Jerome uses a proverb of this kind in a certain place: "Wisely, I put my hand into the flame," meaning that I knowingly expose myself to danger and place myself in the way of evils. It seems to be taken from the history of Mucius Scaevola <note>a Roman hero who famously burnt his own hand to prove his resolve</note>. It also appears in Cicero.

->The material is good, if you employ a good craftsman. XIV<-
Said by Plautus in his play *The Little Carthaginian*, not without the appearance of a proverb: "The material is good, if you employ a good craftsman." <note>original Latin: "Proba eſt materia, ſi probum adhibeas fabrum."</note> Indeed, a nature is excellent if it is rightly trained. A talent is fortunate if an appropriate teacher is found. Or, a business is magnificent, provided it is handled skillfully. The metaphor is too well-known to need further explanation.

<keywords>Bias of Priene, Phrynichus, Mucius Scaevola, Juvenal, legal disputes, character development, Roman virtue, ancient metaphors</keywords>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->Looking there, but send back good things here.<-
<note>original Latin: "Illò reſpiciens, ſed hic remitte bona."</note>

Aeschylus, in Aristophanes’s play *The Frogs*, desiring to return to the world above, says:
"I would speak of it there, but here I do not wish to say anything."
<note>original Greek: Ἐκεῖ φράσαιμ' ἄν, ἐνθάδ' οὐδ' οὐ βούλομαι (Ekei phrasaim' an, enthad' oud' ou boulomai)</note>
That is: "I would tell it there, for here I truly do not want to speak out." To which Bacchus responds in this manner:
"Not at all; rather, bring forth good things here."
<note>original Greek: Μὰ δῆτα σὺ γ' ἀλλ' ἐνθάδ' ἄνευ τ' ἀγαθά (Ma dēta sy g' all' enthad' aneu t' agatha)</note>
The commentator reminds us that this is an allusion to the proverb:
"Looking there, but here she sends back her husband’s goods."
<note>original Greek: Ἐκεῖ βλέπουσα δ' ἐνθ' ἀνήρ τ' ἀγαθά (Ekei blepousa d' enth' anēr t' agatha)</note>
That is: "Looking that way, but sending back advantages to this side."

It is appropriate when we pretend one thing but do another, or when we flatter some people while bestowing the actual benefit on others. Some think it was borrowed from the Graces <note>the Charites, goddesses of charm and beauty</note>, one of whom looks back while offering a gift to another, smiling all the while.

---

### Water to a frog.
<note>original Latin: "Ranæ aquam."</note>

"Water to a frog."
<note>original Greek: Βατράχω ὕδωρ (batrachō hydōr)</note>
The phrase "you are serving" is understood. It is used when something is presented to someone which they especially enjoy. For instance, if you were to provide a natural drinker with certain reasons to drink, or provide a talkative man with material and an occasion for storytelling. It is derived from the phrase, "You are pouring wine for a frog." It is rightly applied when something is given to one who already has plenty. For indeed, there is water in abundance. In the writings of Athenaeus, this song about the people of Syracuse is cited:
"They live only in the manner of frogs, drinking without eating."
<note>original Greek: Οἱ πίνουσι μόνον βατράχων τρόπον οὐδὲν ἔδοντες (Hoi pinousi monon batrachōn tropon ouden edontes)</note>
Theocritus, in his *Reapers*:
"O boys, the life of a frog is desirable, O guardian, since he does not fear pouring out a drink, for an abundant supply is available to him."
<note>original Greek: Εὐκτὸς ὁ τῶ βατράχω παιδίσιον βίος, ὦ μελεδαῖνε / Τὸν δὲ πιῖν ἐκχέοντα, πάρεστι γὰρ ἄφθονον αὐτῷ (Euktos ho tō batrachō paidision bios...)</note>
The shepherd is criticizing the stinginess of Ergodotes <note>likely a reference to the character Lityerses or the employer in the Idyll</note>, because he begrudged giving a drink to those who were sweating, even though frogs, living in leisure, are allowed to drink as much as they please. There are also certain men who seem to themselves to be dying of thirst because they do not live inside the wine jars themselves. Similar to this is the proverb "A horse to the plain." On the other hand, a different saying is: "A bag to the plain," <note>original Greek: ἀσκωλιακα εἰς πεδιάδα (askōliaka eis pediada)</note> regarding Coronea. Coronea is a city in Boeotia which does not produce moles; if any are brought in, they die. So says Stephanus, just as Pliny records that the scarab beetle behaves in a certain place in Thrace near Mount Athos.

---

### Help after the war.
<note>original Latin: "Post bellum auxilium."</note>

"The alliance after the war."
<note>original Greek: Μετὰ τὸν πόλεμον ἡ συμμαχία (Meta ton polemon hē symmachia)</note>
That is: "Help after the war." It is used whenever assistance is applied too late. It is recorded by Suidas. It originated, or was certainly used, by Diogenes the Cynic. Diogenes Laertius tells a story of this kind: A certain rather boastful young man, having recently married, inscribed a title of this sort on his house:
"Hercules, the glorious victor, the son of Zeus, lives here; let no evil enter."
<note>original Greek: ὁ τῶ Διὸς παῖς καλλίνικος ἡρακλῆς ἐνθάδε κατοικεῖ, μηδὲν ἀσίτω κακόν (ho tō Dios pais kallinikos hēraklēs enthade katoikei...)</note>
Diogenes wrote underneath it: "The alliance after the war." Meaning, of course, that the evil had already been received into the house when the master himself—a bad man—had moved in. This agrees with that Platonic saying which we have mentioned elsewhere: "You have arrived after the war." Aristus, in a *Letter to the Lycians*, says: "Your machines were brought after the war, as the proverb has it." Likewise, in a letter to Mynadas: "For slowness in war is the same as if nothing had been done at all, because it was done in vain." Quintilian, in his declamation *The Corpse Fed Upon*, has two sentiments not unlike this proverb: "For what is the use of a late medicine for the dead?" and "For no one pours water onto ashes." Thus, it is a remedy for those who are too late. Since the doctor comes too late if the sick man is dead. And water is poured on too late once the house has been reduced to ashes.

---

### A fat belly does not produce a sharp mind.
<note>original Latin: "Pinguis uenter non gignit sensum tenuem."</note>

Saint Jerome, in a certain letter, cites a proverb of this kind which was famous among the Greeks: "A fat belly does not produce a sharp mind." Though it sounds more elegant in Greek than in Latin. The Greek six-foot verse <note>iambic trimeter</note> exists among the Greeks as follows:
"A thick belly does not give birth to a refined intellect."
<note>original Greek: Παχεῖα γαστὴρ λεπτὸν οὐ τίκτει νόον (Pacheia gastēr lepton ou tiktei noon)</note>
That is: "An obese stomach does not produce a subtle heart."

<sig>I</sig>

<vocab>Erasmus (Dutch humanist), Adagia (collection of proverbs), Aristophanes (Greek comic playwright), Theocritus (Greek pastoral poet), Diogenes the Cynic (philosopher known for biting wit), Quintilian (Roman rhetorician), Saint Jerome (theologian known for his Latin Bible translation)</vocab>

# THIRD CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY

Galen also mentions, in his work *Against Thrasybulus*, a saying that was commonly tossed about: <gloss>“For it is sung by almost all men, because it is the truest of all things, that a fat belly does not give birth to a refined mind.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: καὶ γὰρ ἁπάντων σχεδὸν ἀνθρώπων ᾄδειν... (kai gar hapantōn schedon anthrōpōn aidein...)</note> This means that it is sung by nearly everyone as the truest fact: a heavy stomach does not produce a subtle intellect. Among the Spartans <note>Lacedaemonians</note>, it was considered a disgrace if someone’s body became excessively obese. Agatharchides, in the twelfth book of Athenaeus, records that a man named Anclis was brought before the public assembly because he had become immoderately corpulent due to luxury. There, he was severely rebuked by Lysander and came very close to being driven into exile; the Spartans threatened that this would happen unless he began to live more frugally. In the same work, Menander says of a certain fat man: <gloss>“For a fat pig lay upon his mouth.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: παχὺς γὰρ ὗς ἔκειτ’ ἐπὶ στόμα (pachys gar hys ekeit’ epi stoma)</note> This adage warns us that the edge of the mind grows dull through bodily luxury. As Horace also writes:
> For the body, burdened
> By yesterday’s excesses, also weighs down the soul itself,
> And fastens to the ground that fragment of divine breath.
Plutarch, as cited in Gellius, demonstrates that children turn out to have stupider and slower wits if they are overfed.

### XIX
->You teach a fish to swim.<-
<gloss>“You teach a fish to swim.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἰχθὺν νήχεσθαι διδάσκεις (Ichthyn nēchesthai didaskeis)</note> This is the same as saying, "You teach a learned man." It is related to what we have mentioned elsewhere: <gloss>“You teach a dolphin to swim.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: δελφῖνα νήχεσθαι διδάσκεις (delphina nēchesthai didaskeis)</note> This is also expressed in another way: <gloss>“You are advising a dolphin on how it ought to dive.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: τῇ δελφῖνι κολυμβᾷν συμβάλλῃ (tē delphini kolymban symballē)</note> The author is Diogenianus.

### XX
->I am Pitana.<-
<gloss>“I am Pitana.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: Πιτάνη εἰμί (Pitane eimi)</note> Zenodotus indicates this was usually said of those who, having been reduced to extreme calamities, are restored once again to their former happiness. For it is said this once happened to Pitana, a city in Aeolia. Having been reduced to slavery by the Pelasgians, the Erythraeans eventually vindicated them and restored them to their original freedom.

### XXI
->Blunter than a pestle.<-
This is a proverbial hyperbole which Saint Jerome employed in his letters: "Blunter than a pestle," used to mean someone who is not at all sharp or clever. Timon the Misanthrope, on account of the slowness of his wit, calls Cleanthes: <gloss>“A useless pestle or mortar.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὅλμον ἄολμον (holmon aholmon)</note> In the same author, the word "sharpness" is used ironically to describe Chrysippus when he is being stupid. Likewise, a "horned syllogism" <note>a type of logical dilemma or "sophism"</note> is used for a ridiculous and frivolous argument.

### XXII
->A portion, not a choking.<-
<gloss>“A share, not a strangulation.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: Μερίς οὐ πνιξ (Meris ou pnix)</note> In ancient times, when those who were physically stronger would snatch food away from the weaker ones—literally putting their hands on them to choke them—it was devised that the feast should be divided equally by drawing lots. From then on, everyone began to shout: <gloss>“A portion, not a choking.”</gloss> This phrase passed into a proverb. It can be used whenever we wish to signify that there is no place for violence, but that business ought to be handled with legal equity. Plutarch, in his *Collectanea* (if indeed that work is his), cites it with these words: <gloss>“It is a portion, it does not choke.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: μερὶς, οὐ μὴ πνιξ (meris, ou mē pnix)</note> Suidas also notes that the proverb is expressed in this form.

### XXIII
->A whited wall.<-
<gloss>“A whitewashed or plastered wall.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: Τοῖχος κεκονιαμένος (Toichos kekoniamenos)</note> The Apostle Paul, in the *Acts of the Apostles*, calls the priest Ananias—who was a fake and a fraud—a "whited wall," because he was far different on the inside than what he presented through his outward dress and appearance. Similarly, Christ in the Gospels calls the pretenders of holiness "whited sepulchers," which, while they shine on the outside, are filled with the bones of corpses on the inside. Thus it is written in Matthew: <gloss>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, for you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness.”</gloss> <note>original Greek: οὐαὶ ὑμῖν γραμματεῖς καὶ φαρισαῖοι... (ouai hymin grammateis kai pharisaioi...)</note> Lucian, in his work *The Cock*, applies a similar comparison to the colossal statues of Myron and Praxiteles; from the outside they shine with much ivory and glow with much gold, and they please the eye with various colors. Furthermore, they represent the image of Jupiter or Neptune, holding a lightning bolt or a trident in their right hand so that they clearly seem to be some sort of deity. Yet when you look inside, nothing appears except pitch, nails, spiders, mice, and other such filth, which in no way corresponds to that exterior image. And such are the lives of princes...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of how external appearances can be deceiving, specifically concluding a comparison between those who live lives of luxury and the Sileni—figures who are ugly on the outside but divine within. It then moves into a series of short adages regarding deterrence, balanced remedies, resilience, and character types.</meta>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...affirms that their life is such that if you were to inspect the noise and display, nothing would seem happier, nothing more similar to the life of the gods. But if you were to contemplate the cares, suspicions, and hatreds by which they are tortured within, nothing is more calamitous. Seneca wrote that those philosophers who, while teaching honest things, lived basely, were like the small jars <term>pyxidulis; small boxes used by apothecaries</term> of certain doctors, whose labels promised a remedy while hiding poison inside. Conversely, those who are better within than in their speech or that first appearance of life they show on their faces, Plato makes these similar to the **Sileni** <note>Sileni were statues of the tutor of Bacchus that were grotesque on the outside but contained beautiful images of gods inside; Erasmus uses this as a favorite metaphor for Christ and the Apostles.</note>, about whom we have spoken in another place.

->To nourish a pot.<-

<margin>XX</margin>
<gloss>To nourish a pot.</gloss> <note>original Greek: χύτραν τρέφειν (chytran trephein)</note> They were said to "nourish a pot" who displayed fear in order to deter someone. For example, if someone were to have a garrison stationed somewhere so that his neighbors would not attempt a revolution. The expression is taken from a custom of the city of Athens, in which they were accustomed to set out pots on the roofs to scare away owls, of which there was a great multitude there. For every kind of bird dreads the noise of those pots. This adage is recorded by both Suidas and Diogenianus. It is taken from Aristophanes’ comedy titled *The Birds*:
"Indeed, it is necessary to fight and at the same time to take up the pot."
"But what good will the pot do?"
"The owl then will not come near us."
<note>Erasmus explains that the "pot" here is a defensive measure; the clattering or the visual presence of the pots on roofs was a folk remedy to keep unwanted birds away.</note>

->One ought to buy oil and salt.<-

<margin>X</margin>
<gloss>One ought to buy oil and salt.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἔλαιον καὶ τὸν ἅλα δεῖ ὠνεῖσθαι (Elaion kai ton hala deiōneisthai)</note> Aristotle records this adage in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, treating the topics of arguments and enthymemes. He proposes an example of a "reversal" <term>antistrephontis; a rhetorical device where an argument is turned back on the speaker</term> of this kind: A certain priestess was dissuading her son from ever speaking before the people. "For if you persuade them to do unjust things," she said, "you will have the gods angry at you; but if just things, the men will be angry." But the son reciprocated in this way: "On the contrary, it is expedient to give a speech before the people. Since if I say just things, the gods will love me; if unjust things, men will." And Aristotle thinks this kind of argumentation is close to the proverb by which we are ordered to buy oil and salt. <margin><gloss>This is the same as what is said: to buy oil and salt.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὃς ἤδη ταυτὸ τῷ λεγομένῳ τὸ ἔλαιον πρίασθαι καὶ τοὺς ἅλας</note></margin> This signifies that there is sometimes a need for contrary remedies, now sharpness, now leniency. For salt bites and dries, while oil soothes and moistens. So doctors add oil to salt, lest it erode more than is sufficient; and those who are wise soften the sharpness of an admonition with kind words. It is not hidden from me that in the Aldine edition <note>the famous printing house of Aldus Manutius in Venice</note>, "mercy" <note>eleon</note> is held instead of "oil" <note>elaion</note>, as if from that saying both the evil and the remedy for the evil could be gathered; but who is accustomed to "buy" a wound?

->Like a cork.<-

<margin>X</margin>
<gloss>Like a cork.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὡς φελλός (hōs phellos)</note> This is said of those who do not know how to dissemble, or those who do not know how to be submerged by the adverse storms of fortune. It appears in Pindar. It is drawn from the nature of the wood, which not only is not submerged itself, but even when tied to other things, it keeps them from sinking. Hence it is sewn into nets and placed under those who are swimming.

->To thrust a stroke.<-

<margin>XX</margin>
"To thrust a stroke" <term>obtrudere palpum; to use a soft touch or caress to deceive</term> in Plautus means to deceive by artifice and disguise. "I," he says, "learned that from elsewhere; you cannot thrust a stroke upon me." Hence also "to be stroked" <note>palpari</note> means to be flattered, and we call flatterers "strokers" <note>palpo</note> by a similar metaphor. The metaphor is drawn from grooms who, with horses they know, use the clapping of the hand to coax them, as we have shown elsewhere.

->Lest anyone ever be wiser than the Megarians.<-

<margin>XX</margin>
<gloss>Let no one ever be wiser than the Megarians.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Μηδέ ποτε μηδεὶς μεγαρέων γένοιτο σοφώτερος (Mēde pote mēdeis megareōn genoito sophōteros)</note> This is a proverbial taunt usually thrown at stupid people. It is said through irony <term>acyronem; an improper or ironic use of language</term> about the Megarians, according to Diogenianus.

->No use for fair-skinned men.<-

<margin>X</margin>
<gloss>There is no use for fair-skinned men, except for [pleasure].</gloss> <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν λευκῶν ἀνδρῶν ὄφελος... (ouden leukōn andrōn ophelos...)</note> This is said against the soft and effeminate, born as if for pleasures. For that is what it sounds like, I think, regarding the leather-trade, following that line of Martial: "What is it to you / what that man, or that one, does with his own skin?" <note>Erasmus is contrasting pale men who stay indoors (the "soft") with tanned, "hairy" men who are fit for labor.</note> Furthermore, they are useless for carrying out business. On the other hand, those who are dark-skinned and hairy, these are more...

...should be chosen to administer the Republic. This is why they also call Hercules **Melampygos** <note>original: μελάμπυγον (melampygon); literally "black-buttocks." In Greek lore, this referred to a hairy-bottomed, vigorous man, as opposed to a "smooth" or soft, effeminate man.</note>, as one who is strenuous and far removed from softness, just as has been demonstrated elsewhere in the proverb: *Do not fall in with the Black-bottomed one.*

### XXX. A wet night.

<margin>Wet night. <note>original: Νὺξ ὑγρὰ (Nyx hygra)</note></margin>
**A wet night.** According to Diogenianus <note>A Greek grammarian and proverb collector from the 2nd century AD.</note>, this was typically said of encroaching evils. In the same way, we say "light is arising" when speaking of a more joyful fortune. In the same author, there is the phrase **a thick night** <note>original: νὺξ ἀσάκη (nyx asakē)</note>, referring to a winter night. If anyone thinks these should not be included in a collection of adages, let him take it up with Diogenianus, if he likes.

---

### XXXI. What does this have to do with flour?

<margin>What to the flour? <note>original: Τί πρὸς τ' ἄλφιτα (Ti pros t' alphita)</note>; that is, what does this have to do with acquiring resources? It is common for poets to use "flour" <note>original: τὰ ἄλφιτα (ta alphita); barley-meal or flour, representing the basic necessities of life.</note> to mean one's food or family estate. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*: *What use, pray, will these rhythms be to me for getting flour?*</margin>
**What does this have to do with flour?** That is, what does this pertain to in terms of acquiring resources? To use **the flour** to stand for food or one's livelihood is a common habit of poets. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
->What use, pray, will these rhythms be to me for getting flour?<-
->that is,<-
->*Quid me numeri tandem ad farinas iuuerint?*<-
This can be rightly twisted to refer to sterile arts, such as poetry—"what use is it for the flour?"—which people commonly say regarding "earning one's bread," using a speech that is more popular than it is learned.

---

### XXXII. More obscure than Platonic numbers.

This seems to be a proverbial hyperbole, which Marcus Tullius Cicero uses in his *Letters to Atticus*, book seven: *The riddle of the Oppii from Velia, I simply did not understand. For it is more obscure than a Platonic number.* This was said because Plato obscured his philosophy with Pythagorean numbers <note>Pythagoreanism assigned mystical and philosophical meanings to numbers; Plato incorporates this complex numerology into his cosmological dialogues.</note> and cast a kind of fog over it, especially in the *Timaeus*. For Pythagoras reduced almost every system of philosophy to numbers. Macrobius wrote extensively on these in the commentaries he published on *The Dream of Scipio*.

---

### XXXIII. You say nothing from the field.

<margin>You say nothing from the countryside. <note>original: οὐδὲν ἐξ ἀγρὸ λέγεις (ouden ex agro legeis)</note>; that is, nothing humble or trivial. For whatever is insufficiently elegant or unpolished is said to have "come from the field." Conversely, whatever is witty and charming is called "urban" or "civil." Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> mentions this.</margin>
**You say nothing from the field.** That is, nothing humble or trivial. For whatever is insufficiently elegant or unpolished is said to have "come from the field." Conversely, whatever is witty and charming is called "urban" or "civil." Suidas mentions this.

---

### XXXIV. You have suffered nothing grave, unless...

<margin>You have suffered nothing terrible unless you claim it for yourself. <note>original: οὐδὲν πέπονθας δεινὸν εἰ μὴ προσποιεῖς (ouden peponthas deinon ei mē prospoieis)</note></margin>
**You have suffered nothing terrible unless you claim it for yourself.**
->that is,<-
->Nothing heavy happens unless you take it to heart.<-
Diogenianus mentions this. *No one is hurt, except by himself.* No injury is done to anyone if they consider that it does not pertain to them.

---

### XXXV. Not even a thorn will wound the good.

<margin>Not even a thorn will scratch the good. <note>original: Μηδ' ἄκανθα ἀμύξει τοὺς ἀγαθούς (Mēd' akantha amyxei tous agathous)</note>; No one will be a nuisance to the innocent. For a thorn by its nature pricks anyone. But innocence and integrity of life are safe everywhere.</margin>
**Not even a thorn will wound the good.** No one will be a nuisance to the innocent. For a thorn by its nature pricks anyone. But innocence and integrity of life are safe everywhere.

---

### XXXVI. Naera and Charmione.

<margin>Naera and Charmione. <note>original: Ναίερα καὶ Χαρμιόνη</note>; Zenodotus wrote that this was typically said of faithful friends who did not hesitate to accompany their friends even in death. This kind of friendship was praised among the Egyptians, which they called **those who die together** <note>original: συναποθνησκόντων (synapothnēskontōn)</note>. Those who were pleased by this kind of bond were joined by this law: that if something fatal happened to one, the other would voluntarily join as a companion in death. Mark Antony and Cleopatra had clung together by this pact. Horace also indicates something similar regarding Maecenas in his second book, the seventeenth Ode:</margin>
**Naera and Charmione.** Zenodotus wrote that this was typically said of faithful friends who did not hesitate to accompany their friends even in death. This kind of friendship was praised among the Egyptians, which they called **those who die together**. Those who were pleased by this kind of bond were joined by this law: that if something fatal happened to one, the other would voluntarily join as a companion in death. Mark Antony and Cleopatra had clung together by this pact. Horace also indicates something similar regarding Maecenas <note>Maecenas was the great patron of Horace and a close advisor to Augustus; Horace claimed he could not live without him.</note> in his second book, the seventeenth Ode:

> That day shall bring
> Ruin to both; I have not sworn
> A false oath: we shall go, we shall go,
> Whenever you lead the way, prepared
> As companions to take the final journey. ->And again in another place:<-
> What of us? For whom life would be 
> Pleasant while you survive; if otherwise, it would be heavy.

But to return to the proverb: **Naera and Charmione** were two handmaidens of Queen Cleopatra who imitated Cleopatra’s voluntary death. They were found half-alive, replacing the crown that had slipped from the head of their already dead mistress. It is indeed a story especially worthy of being remembered and not unpleasant to know; however, if anyone should happen to seek it out, let him seek...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Greek and Latin adages. The opening paragraph concludes a discussion from the previous page regarding an adage found in Plutarch’s "Life of Antony," where Erasmus expresses his skepticism about the antiquity of certain proverbs found in the collections of Zenodotus.</meta>

<page-num>756</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...it will come from Plutarch in the *Life of Mark Antony* <note>original: "ex Plutarcho in uita M. Antonij"</note>. I would not have even included this adage had I not been afraid that, since it appears once or twice in the printed collections of Zenodotus <note>A Greek grammarian of the 3rd century BC who collected early proverbs.</note>, some poorly educated person might slander me for omitting it. For, if my nose does not deceive me, I have a suspicion that this proverb did not proceed from antiquity, but was born in the workshop of Zenodotus.

<margin>XX</margin>
->**Neither be a friend to none, nor to many.**<-

That verse of Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet, roughly contemporary with Homer.</note>, like many others, has passed into a proverb:
*Let no one call you either a friend to many or a friend to none.* <note>original: "Μὴ δ' πολύξενον, μηδ' ἄξεινον καλέεσθαι" (Mē d' polyxenon, mēd' axeinon kaleesthai)</note>
Aristotle, in the ninth book of his *Ethics* <note>original: "libro Moralium nono"</note>, cites it as a commonly tossed-about proverb and seems to approve of the saying, because to live entirely without the company of any friend seems beastly and unpleasant. Conversely, we cannot love many people intensely at the same time, nor can we accommodate the habits of too many. Furthermore, Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist of the 2nd century AD.</note> relates in his *Toxaris* that among the Scythians, "polyphilia" <note>original: πολυφιλία; the state of having many friends.</note>—that is, the friendship of many—was considered no less shameful than it was among other nations for one woman to have intimacy with many men. However, Marcus Tullius Cicero feels differently in his book *On Friendship*, as does Plutarch in his commentary *On Having Many Friends*.

<margin>XXX</margin>
->**To thrash the clouds.**<-

*To card the clouds.* <note>original: "Νεφέλας ξαίνειν" (Nephēlas xainein)</note> That is, to thrash the clouds; this is said of someone who spends labor in vain, either on a foolish matter or on something that cannot be done. Diogenianus <note>A 2nd-century collector of Greek proverbs.</note> mentions it. Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia and dictionary.</note> suspects it is derived from the fact that someone once said clouds are like spread-out wool, as if they ought to be carded <note>original: "carminari"; the process of untangling wool fibers before spinning.</note> in a similar way.

<margin>XX</margin>
->**A Myconian neighbor.**<-

*A Myconian neighbor.* <note>original: "Μυκόνιος γείτων" (Mykonios geitōn)</note> This is said against a person who arrives at a banquet uninvited. For antiquity marked the Myconians <note>Inhabitants of the island of Mykonos.</note> with this name because they were "lickerish" <note>original: "liguritores"; meaning greedy or fond of delicacies.</note> and seekers of others' tables. Suidas writes in this manner. Zenodotus, however, says it applies to foul and lowly men, because that island was held in contempt for its infertility, and for that reason, the people were somewhat more greedy and more desirous of what belonged to others. Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the "Deipnosophistae" (The Learned Banqueters).</note> confirms this in the first discourse of the *Learned Banqueters*, citing this from a verse of Archilochus in which he criticized a certain Pericles *as one who rushed into banquets uninvited, in the manner of the Myconians.* <note>original: "ὡς ἄκλητον εἰς τὰ συμπόσια μυκονίων δίκην" (hōs aklēton eis ta symposia mykoniōn dikēn)</note> He adds that the Myconians, being poor because they inhabited a sterile island, were notorious for their stinginess and greed. For poverty makes people greedy for the things of others; hence Cratinus <note>An Athenian poet of Old Comedy.</note> called Ischomachus, who was a slave to his gullet, a "Myconian."

->**Seeing the dead.**<-

*If you see the dead, you have a death of your affairs.* <note>original: "Νεκρὸς ὁρῶν, νέκρωσιν ἔχεις πραγμάτων" (Nekros horōn, nekrōsin echeis pragmatōn)</note>
This is reported by Suidas as a common saying regarding divination, which is taken from the superstition of dreams—by far the most vain of all. Yet it was said in this way because death is the end of the evils of this life.

->**Dead men do not bite.**<-

*The dead do not bite.* <note>original: "Οἱ τεθνηκότες οὐ δάκνουσιν" (Hoi tethnēkotes ou dknousin)</note> This is also commonly said in our own time. I believe it arose from an apophthegm <note>A concise saying or maxim.</note> of Theodorus of Chios, who was the teacher of rhetoric to King Ptolemy. For when he was called into council to deliberate whether Pompey should be repelled from Egypt or admitted, he moved that he be received and killed, adding that *a dead man does not bite.* <note>original: "νεκρὸς οὐ δάκνει" (nekros ou daknei)</note> Plutarch records this in the *Life of Pompey*.

->**Summon knowledge at the end.**<-

*Send knowledge to the extreme.* <note>original: "Πέμπε εἰς ἔσχατον τὴν ἐπιστήμην" (Pempe eis eschaton tēn epistēmēn)</note> That is, call upon knowledge at the very last. One should not immediately use the greatest powers of one's talent, but when the final danger presses, then one should flee to the arts.

->**It is most wretched to die of hunger.**<-

This sentiment was also celebrated in the songs of the ancients, according to the testimony of Plato: that the most wretched kind of death is to die of hunger. It is taken from the twelfth book of Homer's *Odyssey*:
*All deaths are indeed hateful to miserable mortals,*
*But to die of hunger and meet one's fate is by far the most piteous thing.* <note>original: "Πάντες μὲν στυγεροὶ θάνατοι δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι, / Λιῷ δ' οἴκτιστον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν" (Pantes men stygeroi thanatoi deiloisi brotoisi, / Limō d' oiktiston thaneein kai potmon epispein)</note>

<page-num>757</page-num>
<header>CENTURY VI OF THE THIRD CHILIAD</header>

Plato, in the third book of the *Republic*, relates this poem as if it were a plague to the morals of the young, since no death is truly wretched when it is sought for the sake of honor. This can be applied to certain stingy people who, in order to save their coins, cheat their own <term>Genius</term> <note>In Roman belief, the 'Genius' was a personal guardian spirit; 'cheating one's genius' meant depriving oneself of life's pleasures and basic needs.</note>, or to those who perish through ignorance of the truth, since the soul of a human is fed by the word of God no differently than the body is fed by food. It is truly most wretched to die from this kind of hunger.

### 44. Go now and hunt the hare; now you hold the Itys.

Plautus, in his play *The Captives*, used a proverbial figure of speech: "Go now and hunt the hare; now you hold the <note>original: "Itym"</note> Itys." That is to say: for the time being, you have this particular dinner, such as it is; go look for another, better one if you can. For the "Itys" is a bird, which they call a pheasant <note>original: "phasianum"</note> after the Phasis, a river in Scythia. Accordingly, when we command someone who has obtained some small advantage to prepare themselves for something else, we shall use this adage quite opportunely. 

However, I personally believe that this passage in Plautus, like many others, has been corrupted. It should be read not as "Itym," as the manuscripts have it, nor as "ichthyn" <note>Greek for 'fish'.</note>, as someone mistakenly changed it—since neither a bird nor a fish has anything to do with hunting a hare—but rather as "ictin." For that is an animal of the <term>mustelid</term> <note>The family of animals including weasels and ferrets.</note> family, which is sent into burrows to draw out the prey; the Latins call it a <term>viverra</term> <note>A ferret.</note>. Suidas shows that the same animal also lies in wait for fish. Aristotle mentions this in the ninth book of his *On the History of Animals*, chapter six, although he does not specify that it hunts hares, but rather birds and beehives. Yet if it is well-established that the "ictin" is a ferret, Pliny indicates in his eighth book that the primary use of ferrets was for hunting hares and rabbits. "They send them," he says, "into the burrows, which have many openings in the earth—whence the animal also gets its name <note>Pliny links 'viverra' to 'vias' (ways/openings).</note>—and thus they capture them as they are driven out from above."

### 45. To challenge with the little finger.

"To challenge with the little finger" means to challenge someone to a contest with contempt. It is taken from the gesture of those who provoke a fight by stretching out their smallest finger. Horace writes in his *Satires*: "Look, Crispinus challenges me with his little finger. 'Take them,' he says, 'if you wish, take your writing tablets now. Let a place be given to us, an hour, and witnesses. Let us see which of us can write more.'" This will be more elegantly turned toward matters of the mind. For example: "This one grammarian challenges all the theologians with his little finger."

### 46. To bound by a smaller boundary, and similar phrases.

Metaphors of this sort nearly always have the character of a proverb: "To bound by a <term>pomerium</term>" <note>The sacred boundary of a city, especially Rome.</note>; "To set a goal-post"; "To circumscribe with railings"; and any others similar to these. Varro writes in his books *On Agriculture*: "Some have done all the better for having bounded the matter with a smaller boundary, excluding those parts which do not pertain to this subject." He says again in the first book of the same work: "Whether it be an art or something else, and from what starting-stalls it runs toward the goal-posts." Cicero, in the first book of *On the Orator*: "You have circumscribed the entire duty of the orator within certain narrow bounds."

### 47. A wandering mind.

<note>original: "Νοῦς θ' ἕξω" (Nous th' exo)</note> That is, a "wandering mind." Those who are deep in thought, and therefore not sufficiently attentive to the things being done in their presence, are said to have a wandering mind. Aristophanes jokes in *The Acharnians* about Euripides, as if he were using dialectical subtleties—a point also indicated by Quintilian in his *Institutes* with these words:
> "He is not inside, yet he is inside, if you have any wit." 
> "How can he be both inside and not inside?" "Correctly, old man. 
> For his mind is outside, gathering little scraps of verse, 
> and is not inside; but he himself is inside, writing a tragedy 
> with his feet up."

He calls the verses "epyllia," a diminutive word from *epos* <note>Meaning 'little epics' or 'verse-scraps'.</note>. The same author says in *The Knights*:
> "You gape constantly at whoever is speaking, but your mind, 
> though present, is traveling abroad." 
In the same sense, Terence says: "To be present and yet absent."

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

### 47. Milder than a dove.

<note>original: πρᾳότερος περιστερᾶς</note> Milder than a dove. Dove-like simplicity and mildness are praised even in the Holy Scriptures. For the dove is among birds what the sheep is among four-legged animals. It plans no harm to any living creature and has no protection against hawks other than its speed in flight. This adage is mentioned by <term>Diogenianus</term> <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD who compiled a collection of proverbs.</note>.

### 48. Lend me three drachmas for a piglet.

<note>original: Εἰς χοιρίδιόν μοι νῦν δάνεισον τρεῖς δραχμάς</note> Lend me three drachmas now for a piglet. This was said by someone who had decided to die, or who wished to be initiated. For those about to be initiated into the <term>mysteries</term> <note>Specifically the Eleusinian Mysteries, where the sacrifice of a young pig was a standard purification ritual.</note> were accustomed to sacrifice a pig. <term>Suidas</term> cites this from <term>Aristophanes</term>. It appears in the play *Peace*:
Lend me three drachmas now for a piglet,
For I must die as a consecrated pig.
That is:
*Lend me three drachmas now to buy a pig,*
*I must be initiated before I meet my death.*

### 49. A woman's buttocks.

<note>original: γυναικὸς πυγή</note> A woman's buttocks. This was said of a lazy and idle person. A woman is a lazy animal, and the less she possesses a mind, the more she is addicted to dishonorable pleasures. She loves leisure, and in the manner of <term>drones</term> <note>A common classical metaphor for those who live off the labor of others.</note>—as <term>Hesiod</term> says—she consumes what has been acquired by the labors of men. This is also indicated by that other proverb: <note>original: ὄνου οὐρά</note> "The tail of an ass." Indeed, France <note>original: "Gallia"</note> has many such women. On the other hand, Holland has countless women who, by their own industry, support idle and pleasure-seeking husbands.

### 50. A woman's mind.

<note>original: γυναικὸς φρήν</note> A woman’s disposition. Diogenianus shows that this was commonly said of a fool. However, it seems to fit better when applied to the weak and inconsistent. This is the source of that line by <term>Ennius</term>:
*For you, young men, carry the spirits of women, while that maiden has the spirit of a man.*
And <term>Terence</term> says:
*I know the nature of women:*
*They won’t when you want them to; when you don’t, they crave it of their own accord.*

### 51. To predict the wind of the day after tomorrow.

<note>original: Τὸν τριταῖον ἄνεμον προγινώσκειν</note> Those who gather by conjecture what will happen much later are said to foresee the wind of the day after tomorrow. The phrase is taken from sailors or merchants. <term>Pindar</term> writes:
<note>original: Σοφοὶ δὲ μέλλοντα τριταῖον ἄνεμον ἔμαθον</note>
*The wise have known the wind of the day after tomorrow.*
For that is truly being wise: not only to see what is before one's feet, but also to look ahead to that which is far off.

### 52. More talkative than a reef.

<note>original: Ραχίας λαλίστερος</note> More talkative than a reef. A proverbial hyperbole used for a man who is immoderately and annoyingly talkative. The metaphor is taken from reefs which, because they are struck by constant waves, resound with a great crashing noise.

### 53. To a hungry hare, even fig-cakes.

<note>original: Λαγῷ πεινῶντι καὶ πλακοῦντες εἰς σύκα</note> To a hungry hare, even fig-cakes.
Suidas records that this was said of those who, driven by necessity, consume even the most precious things. Perhaps it arose from some fable like the one <term>Apuleius</term> tells about himself <note>In his novel 'The Golden Ass'.</note>: that driven by hunger, he learned first to lick the honey-cakes, and then even to eat them.

### 54. Law and region.

<note>original: Νόμος καὶ χώρα</note> Custom (or Law) and Region. This proverb warns—as we have also indicated in passing elsewhere—that one must serve and comply with the customs of the region where you are living. <term>Zenodotus</term> adds that every nation has its own certain laws and institutions for living. For it is the custom of the Persians to consult while drunk during their drinking bouts, and to worship their kings as a deity. Furthermore, those who are equals kiss one another; those who are inferior modestly touch the cheek of the more powerful. They only look upon their newborn sons after four years have passed. At <term>Gordium</term>, they create as king the one who is the most corpulent among them. The <term>Syrraci</term> offer the crown to the one who surpasses the rest in height of body and, as some relate, to the one whose head is the longest. Among the <term>Stymphali</term>, they hold that woman in honor who has [intercourse] with more men... <note>The text ends mid-sentence.</note>

<keywords>doves, initiation rites, gender roles, foresight, talkativeness, cultural customs, Persians, Erasmus, Holland, France</keywords>

<page-num>759</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY</header>

it changed their custom. The mountain-dwelling <term>Massagetae</term> <note>A nomadic people of Central Asia mentioned by Herodotus.</note> have sexual intercourse in public roads. The <term>Sauromatians</term> <note>Sarmatians, a group of Iranian people.</note> sell their daughters while drinking. The Mazusius abstains from the company of women, unless he has captured one in war. The <term>Tibareni</term> <note>A tribe in ancient Pontus known for the practice of "couvade."</note>, after their wives give birth, lie in bed with their heads bound up, just as if they themselves had given birth. Among the Cecertaeans, craftsmen carry loads until someone happens to buy them. The Sidonians devour their parents, except for the head; for this they cover in gold. The Caesia—or according to others, the Heniochi—follow their newborn with tears, but their deceased with joy. The Bachiri, whenever they recover from an illness, throw themselves to the dogs. The Orgenipei have no homes and do not eat any living creature. They are, however, bald—not only the men, but even the women—and they say this happens because of the natural power of the water they drink. The Thysetae sacrifice bones to the gods but eat the meat themselves; and these, in my opinion, are surely the wisest of all. The <term>Tauroscythians</term> <note>The Tauri, a people inhabiting the Crimea, known in myth for sacrificing foreigners to Artemis.</note> sacrifice humans. The inland Byzoni live on buffalo milk and eat no other food besides that. The Iberians raise packs of dogs instead of sheep; the Ethiopians, who are called Colchians, raise hyenas. Indeed, even today there are no fewer differences in temperaments and customs. To adapt oneself to these as much as possible, and to imitate the "polyp" <note>An octopus; a common classical metaphor for adaptability, changing color to match its surroundings.</note> fish, is no small part of prudence.

### 56. The Aegis has come.

<note>original: Αἰγὶς ᾤχετο</note> The Aegis has come. <term>Suidas</term> <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> indicates that this was commonly said as a proverb about those who act petulantly and impudently. He cites from Pherecrates: "Woe is me, the wretched Aegis has come." Now, "Aegis" signifies various things to the Greeks: a leather garment worn by Africans; furthermore, the waves of a swelling sea and the storms of winds, which is why in the Doric dialect <note>original: ἐπαυγίζειν</note> *epaugizein* is found, meaning "to blow violently." Others prefer it to be something woven from crowns, or a net woven from floral wreaths. He says it is used this way in the fourth book of <term>Herodotus</term> and in <term>Lycurgus</term>. There are even those who think it signifies a priestess who was accustomed to carry the sacred Aegis in Athens, and thus to enter the homes of those who had recently taken wives. It appears there was much license in these types of rites, just as among Christians weddings are celebrated with many follies, and at the same time, it is an allusion to a storm.

### 57. You carry a vast forest.

<note>original: λόχμην πολλὴν φορεῖς</note> You carry a vast forest. This was said against <term>Phormio</term> <note>Likely a reference to a stock character or a specific historical soldier known for his unkempt appearance.</note>, a certain soldier who was shaggy and covered in a thick forest of hair, who is mentioned elsewhere. It will fit a boorish and stupid person, which is generally the nature of soldiers. It is recorded by Suidas.

### 58. To see a lion portends battles with enemies.

<note>original: Λέοντας ἰδεῖν, δυσμενῶν δηλοῖ μάχας</note> To see lions indicates a fight with enemies. This is transferred either from the interpretation of dreams or from those who observe omens. Suidas mentions it. I see these kinds of little verses, which indicate what each dream portends, are diligently recorded by Suidas and <term>Hesychius</term> <note>An Alexandrian grammarian who compiled a rich lexicon of Greek words and phrases.</note>, though nothing is more empty. And yet, it is probable that both of them were monks.

### 59. A gull in the marshes.

<note>original: Λάρος ἐν ἕλεσι</note> A gull in the marshes. Suidas writes that this was often said of those who are easy-going in giving. It is derived from the "larus" bird, which they think is the same as the one called the <term>cepphus</term> <note>A booby or similar seabird, proverbial for its stupidity.</note>, although <term>Theodorus Gaza</term> <note>A 15th-century humanist and translator of Aristotle’s works on animals.</note> translates the latter as a coot and the former as a gull. Because it is easily deceived and enticed, it gave rise to the proverb.

### 60. Issa.

<note>original: Ισσα</note> Issa. This was a proverbial exclamation against those from whom the letter <term>theta</term> <note>The Greek letter Θ (theta). In legal contexts, it stood for "thanatos" (death), as it was marked on ballots to condemn a prisoner.</note> happened to fall, and who were in every way unfortunate. This is from Suidas, who cites the proverb from Menander’s *Mesenia*, testifying that it was used elsewhere among authors. One may guess that this letter was ill-omened in ballots. <term>Martianus Capella</term> <note>A Latin author of late antiquity.</note> in *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury* testifies that this letter was hated by Appius Claudius, because it mimics the teeth of a dead man while it is being pronounced.

### 61. From the granary itself.

Whatever is given lavishly and abundantly is said to be given "from the granary itself," just as one might say "from the basket," because things are taken out more fully from a granary than from a small measure. It is similar to that saying: <note>original: ἐκ πίθου ἀντλεῖς</note> "You are drawing from the jar."

### 62. In your own arena.

In your own arena; that is, in your own art or specialty. Taken from gladiators, who were accustomed to fight in the "arena" (the sand). Nor did it matter little to them whether they fought in a known or an unknown arena.

<page-num>760</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

<margin>61</margin>
->To catch two boars in one thicket.<-

**To catch two boars in one thicket.** <note>original: "In saltu uno duos apros capere."</note> This means to seize two things at once in a single action. Plautus writes in his play 
<margin>*Casina*,</margin>
"Now I shall cleverly catch two boars in one thicket."

<margin>62</margin>
->Fire to the torch.<-

**Fire to the torch.** <note>original Greek: "πῦρ ἐπὶ δαλὸν ἐλθόν"</note> That is, fire coming to a firebrand. This is said of a business that is finished quickly and easily, as if fire spontaneously jumps to a torch because the material is so dry. Diogenianus mentions it. A similar expression would be "Fire to naphtha." Naphtha is a type of bitumen <note>A naturally occurring petroleum-like substance.</note> that catches flame even from a distance.

<margin>63</margin>
->I will imitate Hippolytus.<-

**I will imitate Hippolytus.** <note>original Greek: "Ἱππόλυτον μιμήσομαι"</note> Diogenianus, in his collection of proverbs, says this was a common saying about those who had decided to live a pure and chaste life. The story is well known from the plays of either Euripides or Seneca, telling how this young man, out of a hatred for the female sex, devoted himself entirely to the pursuits of the goddess Diana, despising the power of Venus. For so he speaks in Euripides: 
"I bid a long farewell to your Venus." <note>original Greek: "τὴν σὴν δὲ κύπριν πόλλ’ ἐγὼ χαίρειν λέγω." Venus is referred to here by her Greek name, Cypris.</note>

<margin>64</margin>
->To do nothing.<-

<term>Suidas</term> <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> cites this little verse from a play by Cratinus titled *The Hours*: 
"And doing those things, a certain man says he is doing nothing." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ταῦτα πράττων φάσχ’ ἀνὴρ εἶναι ποιῶν."</note> 
He notes that there is an underlying proverb here which applies to those who labor in vain. Among the Latins, they are also said "to do nothing" who take up useless work, as seen in the works of Terence. Furthermore, this "doing nothing" <note>original: "nihil agere"</note> is also celebrated in the saying of Attilius: "It is better to be idle than to do nothing" <note>Meaning it is better to have leisure than to be busy with pointless tasks.</note>.

<margin>65</margin>
->To fit Hercules’s buskins on an infant.<-

**To fit the mask or the <term>buskins</term> of Hercules on a boy** <note>The <term>cothurnus</term> or buskin was a high-soled boot worn by tragic actors to make them look taller and more heroic.</note> is to apply the greatest things to the smallest, which in no way fit or are appropriate—as if someone were to describe a humble matter in the grand style of a tragedy. Quintilian writes in his sixth book, concerning the conclusion of a speech: "For to stir up these tragedies in small lawsuits is like fitting the mask and buskins of Hercules on infants." Plutarch records a certain saying of Agesilaus <note>A king of Sparta.</note> that is not far from this. When a certain <term>sophist</term> <note>A teacher of rhetoric.</note> was praised to him because he could make small things seem great through the art of speaking, Agesilaus denied that a cobbler was good who put a large shoe on a small foot; he meant that a speech ought to fit the subject matter, just as a garment must fit the body.

<margin>66</margin>
->Cranes swallowing a stone.<-

**Cranes swallowing stones.** <note>original Greek: "Αἱ γέρανοι λίθους καταπεπωκυῖαι"</note> Suidas cites this from Aristophanes, showing it was commonly said of those who manage their business with the greatest foresight. This has even passed into common speech because of the habit of cranes: since they fly very high and are carried with great force, and cannot look down, they are said to carry small stones. When they begin to tire during flight, they drop them from on high, so that they can tell from the sound of the falling stones whether they are flying over land or over the sea. If the stone falls into the sea, they continue their way; if on land, they stop to rest. Pliny relates similar things in Book 10, Chapter 23: "When they set out," he says, "they act in concert: they fly high to see far ahead; they choose a leader to follow; at the rear of the line they have those stationed in turns to call out and keep the flock together with their voice. They have sentries during the night who hold a small stone in their foot; if the sentry grows weary and falls asleep, the stone drops and reveals his negligence by the sound. The others sleep with their heads tucked under their wings, standing on alternating feet. The leader keeps watch with his neck erect and gives warnings." And a little later: "It is certain," he says, "that when they are about to fly across the Black Sea, they first head for the narrows between the two promontories of Criumetopum and Carambis, and then stabilize themselves with 'ballast' <note>Using stones to maintain balance in the wind.</note>; when they have crossed the middle, they throw the stones away; when they reach the continent, they even cough up sand from their throats." Thus far Pliny. Furthermore, the passage Suidas cites is in Aristophanes's *The Birds*: 
"From Libya there came about thirty thousand 
cranes who had swallowed foundation-stones." <note>original Greek: "Ἐκ μὲν γε λιβύης ἥκου ὡς τρὶς μυρίαι / γέρανοι θεμελίους καταπεπωκυῖαι λίθους."</note> 
The commentator on this passage says almost the same things as Suidas.

<header>THIRD CHILIAD, SIXTH HUNDRED</header>

### 69. Tidal Fortune.
<note>original: "Fortuna æstuaria."</note>

**Tidal Fortune** <note>original Greek: "τύχη Εὐριπία," meaning Euripean Fortune.</note> That is, fortune like the Euripus <note>The Euripus is a narrow sea channel between the Greek island of Euboea and the mainland, famous in antiquity for its violent and unpredictable tidal currents that change direction many times a day.</note>, or a turning fortune, because it is accustomed to favor now this person, now that one in turn. Regarding this, <term>Boethius</term> <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose "Consolation of Philosophy" was a cornerstone of medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> wrote:
> It is carried in the manner of the seething Euripus.

We have spoken elsewhere of the "Euripus of the sea." Just as the sea has its tidal ebb and flow, so nothing in human affairs is permanent. However, no sea rushes back more frequently or more swiftly than the Euripus. <term>Pindar</term> <note>The most famous of the ancient Greek lyric poets.</note>, in his third Pythian hymn, took a metaphor from the winds:
> When one receives good things from the gods, one must enjoy them. But at different times, different blasts of high-flying winds occur. <note>original Greek: "χρὴ πῶς μακάρων τυγχάνοντ’ εὖ πασχέμεν. ἄλλοτε δ’ ἀλλοῖαι πνοαὶ ὑψιπετᾶν ἀνέμων."</note>

This means: One must enjoy what comes from the gods. However, at various times there are various blasts of wind. The happiness of mortals does not come to stay for long. A commentator cites verses from <term>Euripides</term> <note>A great Athenian tragedian.</note>:
> For calamities also weigh upon mortals,
> And the blasts of the winds do not always hold their strength. <note>original Greek: "Κάμνει γάρ τοι καὶ βροτοῖς αἱ συμφοραί, Καὶ πνεύματ’ ἀνέμων οὐκ ἀεὶ ῥώμην ἔχει."</note>

That is:
> Indeed, even disasters take their toll on men,
> Nor do the gusts of the breeze always keep their vigor.

### 70. To open the doors.
<note>original: "Fores aperire."</note>

**To open the doors.** <note>original Greek: "Ἀνοίγειν τὴν θύραν."</note> This was a proverb used for someone who reveals the entrance or beginning of any matter. My uncle <term>Pliny</term> <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist.</note> in Book 2, Chapter 8, writes: "It is handed down that **Anaximander of Miletus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> understood the obliquity [of the zodiac], which is to say, he opened the doors of things." <term>Plutarch</term> indicated this adage in the second decade of his *Table Talk*: "For I have unwittingly, O Firmus, opened the world to you through silence, instead of the proverbial door." <note>original Greek: "ἔλαθον γὰρ ὦ Φίρμε, τὸν κόσμον ἀντὶ τ’ προοιμιακῆς θύρας διὰ σιωπῆσ ἀνοίξας."</note> That is: "Imprudent Firmus, you have opened the world to yourself, as if it were the proverbial gate." The expression "To open a window" is used in the same sense in the works of <term>Terence</term> <note>A Roman playwright.</note>.

### 71. Your own business is at stake when your neighbor's wall is on fire.
<note>original: "Tua res agitur, cum proximus ardet paries."</note>

Even in these modern times, this is commonly on the lips of the unlearned common folk: that we must be on our guard when a neighbor's house is burning. The proverb warns us to take an example from the misfortune of another and learn to look after our own affairs by observing someone else's danger. It is taken from the *Epistles* of <term>Horace</term>:
> Do you not feel the dangers that will soon come to you?
> For your own business is at stake when the neighbor's wall is on fire.

And <term>Virgil</term> says:
> Now neighbor
> ->Ucalegon burns.<- <note>Ucalegon was a neighbor of Aeneas in Troy; his name became a synonym for a neighbor whose disaster threatens your own safety.</note>

### 72. Boars in the springs, the south wind on the flowers.
<note>original: "Fontibus apros, floribus austrum."</note>

There is no doubt that this belongs to the class of proverbs; it is found in <term>Virgil's</term> <note>Maro refers to Publius Virgilius Maro.</note> pastoral poetry:
> Alas, what have I wished for myself, wretched as I am?
> Ruined, I have let the south wind onto the flowers and boars into the clear springs.

This is used when someone wishes for things that will be harmful; for the wind is most hostile to flowers, especially the south wind <note>The "Auster" or south wind was often associated with heat, storms, and blight.</note>, on account of its violence.

### 73. A pot-god.
<note>original: "Ollaris deus."</note>

**A pot-god.** <note>original Greek: "χυτρεὸς θεός."</note> This was said of a humble man of a contemptible lot. <term>Aristophanes</term> says in *The Clouds*:
> Since we consider you also to be a pot-god. <note>original Greek: "ὅτι καὶ σε χυτρεῦ ὄντα θεὸν ἡγούμεθα."</note>

That is:
> Since I thought you were also a god made of earthenware.

The great gods were sculpted from ivory, gold, and silver. But those common and tiny ones, of the sort like Silenus and Priapus, were molded from any material, sometimes from wood and clay—evidently the same material from which pots are molded. Hence, it will fit quite aptly for someone who strives to be counted among the high-ranking courtiers, but who possesses neither wealth nor authority with the prince. It is related to the saying, "Corcorus among the vegetables" <note>original Greek: "κόρκορος ἐν λαχάνοις." Corcorus was a poor, common herb.</note> or that other one, "Nothing sacred" <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν ἱερὸν."</note>. It is recorded in the collection of <term>Zenodotus</term>.

### 74. The spirit of Oeta.
<note>original: "Oetaeus genius."</note>

**The spirit of Oeta.** <note>original Greek: "οἰταῖος δαίμων."</note> <term>Diogenianus</term> says that ferocity and arrogance were vehemently hated by this spirit, which was not accustomed to leave them unpunished; hence they used to threaten the puffed-up and overly fierce with the "Spirit of Oeta." The common collections of proverbs attribute this to the author <term>Clearchus</term>. Oeta is a mountain bordering Trachis, and there is a city of the Malians by the same name. Therefore, the use of this proverb will be similar to that of: "The Spirit of Temesa will be present." <note>Both refer to local spirits or ghosts known for exacting vengeance.</note>

### 75. Pitiable even to an enemy.
<note>original: "Vel hosti miserandus."</note>

<term>Suidas</term> cites words of this kind from some author: "So as to pity even an enemy, as the proverb says..." <note>original Greek: "ὡς καὶ τὴν τὼ παροιμίαν, κἄν ἐχθρὸν ἐλεεῖν"</note>

<sig>Ss 3</sig>
<meta>The catchword "Cas" refers to the beginning of the next page's text, likely continuing the entry for adage 75.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, specifically the Sixth Century of the Third Chiliad. On the previous page, he was discussing a proverb regarding "tidal fortune" or things that change as rapidly as the sea. This page concludes that thought and moves into legal metaphors, natural history observations on songbirds, and political metaphors regarding "fishing in muddy waters."</meta>

...beholding the procession of those people <note>original Greek: "σαι θεατόμενον τὴν τότε πομπήν των ἀνθρώπων." This fragment likely concludes a quote from the previous page regarding a sight so pathetic even an enemy would be moved.</note>. That is, according to the proverb, even an enemy would feel pity at the man’s current downfall. This is a hyperbole, for an enemy is not easily moved to compassion. Thus, <term>Virgil</term> <note>The Roman epic poet.</note> writes in the twelfth book of the *Aeneid*:

->A band even Priam would pity.<- <note>original Latin: "Vel Priamo miseranda manus." Priam was the King of Troy; Virgil suggests the sight is so sad even a bitter enemy king would weep.</note>

Likewise in the second book:

->Who, in telling such things—<-
->be he Myrmidon or Dolopian, or a soldier of harsh Ulysses—<-
->could refrain from tears?<- <note>original Latin: "Quis talia fando Myrmidonum Dolopúmue, aut duri miles Vlyssi, Temperet à lachrymis?"</note>

Related to this is: "A thing which even **Momus** <note>The Greek god of satire and mockery, known for finding fault in everything.</note> himself would approve."

### Equal Votes
<margin>71</margin>
**Equal votes.** <note>original Greek: "Ἴσαι ψῆφοι." In ancient courts, voters used "calculi" (pebbles) to cast their ballots—white for acquittal, black for condemnation.</note> This is said when someone narrowly escapes being condemned and is instead acquitted; or when the mind wavers and is uncertain which way to turn, with reasons for and against pulling with equal force. As it says in <term>Terence</term> <note>A Roman playwright.</note>: "When the mind is in doubt, it is driven here or there by a small weight." This metaphor is taken from the ancient custom of legal trials, where a defendant was acquitted if the votes were tied, though not without danger. 

<term>Aristotle</term> <note>The famous Greek philosopher.</note> gives many reasons in his *Problems* as to why the ancients thought a defendant should be acquitted rather than condemned when the votes were equal. For many reasons, it seemed appropriate that, all else being equal, the defendant should be favored over the accuser. Perhaps it is because the accuser comes prepared and fortified, while the defendant is forced to respond to many unforeseen charges. Or perhaps because it is natural that the defendant, speaking under greater danger, might omit certain points out of fear, unlike the accuser. Or perhaps because in an uncertain business, one ought to lean toward the side where, if an error is made, the sin is lighter. It is a lesser evil to acquit a guilty man than to condemn an innocent one, especially in capital cases; if a judge errs there, he cannot repair his mistake once the man is dead. Conversely, if a guilty man escapes, he can be punished another time. Furthermore, an accusation is closer to the suspicion of malice than a defense is. Aristotle provides these and other similar arguments. Therefore, just as a man is safely cleared of guilt when acquitted by all the votes, he is seen as having been very close to danger when he escapes by a tie, as if by a stroke of favor.

### The nightingale lacks its song.
<margin>72</margin>
**The nightingale lacks its song.** A proverbial allegory, as if you were to say: "The woman lacks words," "the poet lacks verses," "the orator lacks style," or "the sophist lacks a quibble." For no bird is as songful as the nightingale—even the female—as <term>Pliny</term> <note>Roman author of "Natural History."</note> testifies in his tenth book. It is worth including his own words here: "In nightingales," he says, "for fifteen continuous days and nights, there is a talkative song without pause when the buds of the leaves are thickening—a bird worthy of great wonder. First, such a voice in such a tiny body! Such persistent breath! Then, in this one bird, there is a perfect knowledge of music: the sound is produced with modulation. Now it is drawn out long with a continuous breath, now it is varied with a twist, now distinguished by short notes, now linked with a trill; it is projected, recalled, and suddenly muffled. Sometimes it even murmurs to itself: full, deep, sharp, rapid, extended; vibrating when it chooses, high, middle, or low. In short, everything is found in that tiny throat which human art has devised through the many exquisite tortures of the flutes." <term>Plautus</term> <note>Roman comic playwright.</note> says in his play *Bacchides*:

> By Pollux, I also fear that the little nightingale may have lost her song.

### I have been moved from one good thing to another.
<margin>73</margin>
**I have been moved from one good thing to another.** <note>original Greek: "Ἐγὼ δὲ ἐκ καλῶ εἰς καλὸν μετήνεγκα."</note> The sense indicates this was usually said of those who exchange one good profession for another. It reportedly originated from a man who went from being a good lyre-player to a tragic poet. For the art of poetry is close to the art of music; hence Terence called the art of poetry "music." The adage is taken from **Aristophanes’** *The Frogs*.

### To catch eels.
<margin>74</margin>
**To catch eels.** <note>original Greek: "Ἐγχέλεας θηρᾶσθαι."</note> Those who stir up civil unrest for the sake of private gain are said to "hunt eels." The comparison comes from the fact that those who catch eels catch nothing when the water is still; but when they stir the water up and down and disturb it, only then do they catch them. This applies to those for whom the tranquil state of the Republic offers no profit. Therefore, they rejoice when seditions arise, so they can turn the public misfortune of the state into their own private advantage.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to legal equity (favoring the defendant in a tie), the natural eloquence of the nightingale, and the political metaphor of stirring up trouble ("catching eels") for personal gain.</summary>

# THIRD CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY
Ss 4
<meta>Catchword: Euri-</meta>

A proverb appears in **Aristophanes** <note>The famous Greek comic playwright of Athens.</note> in his play *The Knights*:

*For you have behaved exactly like those who hunt for eels:*
*When the lake is still, they catch nothing,*
*But if they stir the mud up and down,*
*They take them. And so you take your gain, whenever you disturb the city.* <note>original Greek: "ὅπερ γὰρ οἱ τὰς ἐγχέλεις θηρώμενοι πεπόνθας, ὅταν μὲν ἡ λίμνη καταστῇ, λαμβάνουσιν οὐδέν, ἐὰν δ᾽ ἄνω τε καὶ κάτω τὸν βόρβορον κινῶσιν, αἱροῦσι. καὶ σὺ λαμβάνεις, ἢν τὴν πόλιν ταράττῃς."</note>

Alas, certain princes are too skilled in this art; following tyrannical advice, they sow discord between cities or stir up war from somewhere else, so that they may more freely tax the wretched common people and satisfy their own greed with the hunger of the most innocent citizens.

### I shall do everything in the manner of Nicostratus. LXXX
*I shall have done everything in the manner of Nicostratus.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐγὼ ποιήσω πάντα κατὰ Νικόστρατον."</note>
This is used to mean doing something "excellently." For they say this **Nicostratus** was a comic actor of such caliber as **Roscius** <note>Quintus Roscius Gallus, the most famous actor of ancient Rome.</note> is said to have been among the Romans. Thus, because of the fame of his skill, he became a common household name. **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> records this under his list of proverbs.

### Double Kappa. LXXXI
*Double Kappa.* <note>original Greek: "Διπλῆ κάππα."</note> This is like a riddle used to signify some evil. This is because the word for "evils" <note>original Greek: "κακά" (kaka).</note> is written with two of the letter **Kappa**. Using a similar figure of speech, **Plautus** <note>The Roman playwright.</note> called a thief a "man of three letters." <note>original Latin: "trium literarum hominem." The Latin word for thief is F-U-R.</note>

### Three worst Kappas. LXXXII
*Three worst Kappas.* <note>original Greek: "Τρία κάππα κάκιστα."</note>
This was also once bandied about as a riddle, by which the characters of three nations were noted: the **Cappadocians**, the **Cretans**, and the **Cilicians**. **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo.</note> indicates in his grammatical works that this was twisted to refer to the Roman leaders **Cornelius Sulla**, **Cornelius Cinna**, and **Cornelius Lentulus**. It was also believed that in the **Sibylline books** <note>A collection of oracular utterances from ancient Rome.</note> their names were designated by these three letters. It is also the closing line of a heroic poem.

### A sleeping drunk is not to be woken. LXXXIII
This has the appearance of a proverb, as **Theognis** <note>A Greek gnomic poet.</note> warns that a drunk who has fallen asleep should not be roused from his slumber. It is very similar to: *Do not move an evil that is well settled.* <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ κακῷ εὖ κειμένῳ μὴ κινεῖν."</note> One should not scratch at a hatred over which time has already cast forgetfulness. A wound of the mind, which has already begun to form a scar, should not be reopened. The poem of Theognis goes like this:

*Do not wake any of us who are sleeping, Simonides,*
*Whom, being weighed down with wine, soft sleep holds fast.* <note>original Greek: "μηδ᾽ εὕδοντ᾽ ἐπέγειre σιμωνίδη, ὅν τινα ἡμῶν θωρηχθέντ᾽ οἴνῳ μαλθακὸς ὕπνος ἔχει."</note>

### An opinion nodding both ways. LXXXIIII
*Double-limping opinions.* <note>original Greek: "Δίχολοι γνῶμαι."</note> That is, opinions limping on both sides, or a mind turning this way and that. For I believe the word should be read as *dichōlos* <note>original Greek: "δίχωλος"</note> with a "long o" (omega), so that it means "limping on both sides." In common books, I have found it written with a "short o" (omicron). It will therefore suit a man of slippery faith and uncertain loyalties, for whom that line of **Homer** <note>The legendary author of the Iliad and Odyssey.</note> is fitting:

*He limps in his gait, and wavers on both feet.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ σκαλάζει, καὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀμφοτέρους πόδας ἵζει."</note> This is cited by **Zenodotus** <note>A Greek grammarian and the first librarian of Alexandria.</note>.

### Said and done. LXXXV
*Said and done.* <note>original Greek: "Ῥεχθὲν καὶ πραχθέν."</note> This is a proverbial figure by which we signify that nothing was omitted in managing a business. **Terence** <note>The Roman playwright.</note> wrote: "I returned it as soon as it was said and done." **Donatus** <note>A famous 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note>, commenting on the play *Andria*, indicates this is a proverb for speed: "As soon as it was said and done, he found some excuse." Again, in *The Self-Tormentor*: "Said and done, Clitipho went away." Truly, this color of speech is familiar to the Greek poets: *neither word nor deed* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἔπος, ὅτι ἔργον"</note>, meaning by no means or for no reason. Homer, in the first book of the *Iliad*:

*Neither an honest word nor a deed ever came from you.* <note>original Greek: "ἔλδωρ δ᾽ οὔπω εἶπας ἔπος, οὐδ᾽ ἐτέλεσσας."</note>

<summary>This page explores several adages concerning political manipulation, national reputations (the "Three Kappas"), and the ethics of reviving old conflicts. It emphasizes the importance of stability and the characteristic speed or vacillation of human behavior.</summary>
