# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>764</page-num>

**Euripides** <note>The Athenian tragedian (c. 480–406 BC).</note> in his play *Hecuba*:
*And do not stand in our way at all, I say, in word or in deed.* <note>original Greek: "Σὺ δ᾽ ἡμῖν μηδὲν ἐμποδὼν γίνυ Λέγω τε μηδὲ δρῶτα."</note> That is: "Truly, do not oppose me by word or by fact."

In a different sense, those who are vigorous and skilled in every way are said to be powerful in "words and deeds." Thus, according to **Homer**, Phoenix had taught **Achilles**:
*To be a speaker of words and a doer of deeds.* <note>original Greek: "μύθων τε ῥητῆρ᾽ ἔμεναι, πρηκτῆρά τε ἔργων."</note>

Similarly, **Pindar** <note>The greatest of the Greek lyric poets.</note> in his first *Nemean Ode*: "Concerning your character, [consider] both this and that use," that is: "Your character is useful in both cases: for strength acts in deed, but the mind in counsel." <note>original Greek: "σόο δὲ ἀμφὶ τρόπῳ, τὴν τε καὶ τὴν χρῆσιν... πράσσει γὰρ ἔργῳ μὲν σθένος, βουλαῖσι δὲ φρήν."</note>

---

->He is of that flock. LXXXIV<-

"He is of that flock" signifies someone of the same faction or social circle. **Terence** <note>The Roman comic playwright.</note> in his play *The Brothers*: "By Hercules, he is of that flock." The same author in *The Eunuch*: "That you might receive me into your flock." **Marcus Tullius Cicero** to Atticus: "But I wish you had returned to your old flock." The same Cicero in his first *Speech against Verres*: "I do not see whom he will have as a fourth, unless perhaps from that flock of orators who requested the right to prosecute for themselves," etc. In the fourth action of the same case, he said "from that assembly" regarding a certain Turpio, an "agent and scout" of Verres, and "the worst man of all that assembly of professional informers" <note>term: quadruplatorum (professional informers who received a quarter of the fines collected from those they accused).</note>. 

He alluded to what we have said elsewhere: a "gathering of beggars" <note>original Greek: "ἀγυρμαγέλη"</note>. So also **Horace** <note>The Roman lyric poet.</note>:
*Enroll this man as one of your flock, and believe him to be brave and good.*

However, this phrase is frequently used in a positive sense as well. **Saint Jerome** <note>The prominent early Christian scholar and translator of the Bible.</note> in the second book *Against Jovinian*: "They are of your herd," he says, "or rather, they grunt among your citizens." Cicero calls close friends or members of the same club "flock-mates" (*gregales*), as in his speech *On His House* to the pontiffs: "What you used to say about me to Catiline’s flock-mates."

---

->Toothed paper. LXXXV<-

"Toothed" <note>term: dentata (literally "having teeth").</note> is used to describe things that are "biting" or sharp. Cicero to his brother in the second book: "With a tempered pen and ink. The matter will be handled even with toothed paper." And **Seneca** <note>The Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note> does not want "toothed jests" (that is, malicious ones). Conversely, "toothless" (*edentula*) things are those that lack a bite.

---

->Daulian crow. LXXXVI<-

*Daulian crow.* <note>original Greek: "Δαυλίαν κορώνην."</note> That is, the "Daulian crow" is what the poets call the nightingale: either because **Tereus** <note>A king in Greek mythology turned into a hoopoe, while his sisters-in-law became a nightingale and a swallow.</note> lived with her in Daulis, a city of Phocis, or because **Philomela** was changed into a bird there. I do not see what the adage intends, unless perhaps it was said of those who are talkative or musical. I suspect rather that **Zenodotus**, or **Zenobius**, or whoever else it was, invented this proverb to create an opportunity to tell the myth—something I suspect he has done in several other cases.

---

->With the Muses. LXXXVII<-

*With the Muses.* <note>original Greek: "Μετὰ μουσῶν."</note> That is, "With the Muses favoring." This is said of learned people, or those who speak eloquently, or, as **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> points out, it is used ironically when an illiterate person lives among the learned.

---

->He emulates his tragic friends. LXXXVIII<-

*He emulates his tragic friends.* <note>original Greek: "Τοὺς ἑταίρους τραγῳδοὺς ἀγωνᾶται."</note> Suidas cites this from **Didymus**, adding that it was commonly said of those who adapted themselves and took on a severe character in order to emulate others. It is taken from tragic actors who, though they are the most worthless scoundrels <note>term: nebulones (worthless fellows or "empty clouds").</note>, nevertheless, when they play a god or a king in a play, they imitate a certain majesty in their dress, voice, and gesture.

---

->The Aesopic jackdaw. XC<-

*The Aesopic jackdaw.* <note>original Greek: "Αἰσώπειος κολοιός."</note> This is said of one who usurps the property of others and sells himself using the goods of others. **Lucian** <note>A second-century Syrian satirist who wrote in Greek.</note> uses this in *The Ignorant Book-Collector*. Horace says:
*...lest the little crow move us to laughter,*
*Once stripped of his stolen colors.*

The fable exists among others circulated under the name of **Aesop**. Pindar in his third *Nemean Ode*: "It is better for a man to seek from his own house than to bear the desires for the things of others." The poet also rebukes digression and commands that he should praise the person he has undertaken to celebrate for his own virtues rather than for borrowed ones.

<summary>Erasmus explores various Greek and Latin adages concerning social identity (being of the same "flock"), biting literary styles ("toothed paper"), and the pretense of those who borrow others' merits ("the Aesopic jackdaw").</summary>
<keywords>social circles, literary criticism, Aesop's fables, Pindar, Cicero, nightingale myth, intellectual honesty, theater metaphors</keywords>

<header>THE SIXTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD CHILIAD</header>

### A ram wanton with its horns.
-> XCII <-

*A wanton-horned ram.* <note>original Greek: "Κριὸς ἀσελγόκερως"</note> This is also rendered as: *A ram wanton with its horns.* Diogenianus <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD who collected proverbs.</note> shows that this is applicable to those who are powerful and unrestrained. The horns of well-fed rams itch, and the same thing happens to oxen. **Virgil** <note>The Roman epic poet.</note> says: *Now let him seek with his horn, and scatter the sand with his feet,* indicating a wanton young bull. Hesychius <note>An Alexandrian grammarian and lexicographer.</note> points out the origin of the proverb: on the citadel of Pallas <note>The Acropolis of Athens.</note> there was placed a huge bronze ram, which the comic poet Plato called "wanton-horned," not so much because of its playfulness as because of its massive size. It is even compared to the Trojan Horse. Indeed, the ancients used the word "wanton" <note>Greek: "ἀσελγὲς"</note> not only for something playful and untamable, but also for something oversized; for example, Eupolis <note>A writer of Old Attic Comedy.</note> spoke of a "wanton wind" meaning a great wind. These are the "crosses" of the grammarians—thorny problems for scholars—lest that bronze ram be formidable because of its giant horns. Yet what prevents even a wind from being called wanton and immoderate, because it plays according to its own whim wherever it wishes? To me, the adage seems also to suit those who are foolish but have been raised to dignity beyond their merit.

### A dog led through the Phratores.
-> XCIII <-

*A dog led through the members of the phratry.* <note>original Greek: "Ἄγόμενος διὰ φρατόρων ὁ κύων"</note> That is: *A dog led through the Phratores.* This is used when someone has fallen into the hands of those by whom he will be punished. For among these people, a dog is immediately killed. Among the Athenians, the people were divided into tribes, and the third part of each tribe was called a *phratry* <note>A "brotherhood" or social subdivision of a tribe in ancient Athens.</note>, and the head of this was the *phratriarch*. In the assemblies, therefore, if any dog ran through, it was immediately attacked by the people.

### The gifts of a Calabrian host.
-> XCIIII <-

A proverb seems to lie beneath these verses of **Horace**, which he wrote in his *Epistles*:
> Not in the manner that a Calabrian host bids you eat his pears,
> Have you made me rich. "Eat, I pray you."
> "I have had enough." "But take as many as you wish." "You are kind."
> "You will carry no unwelcome little gifts to your small boys."
> "I am as much beholden by the gift as if I were sent away loaded."
> "As you wish; you will leave these to be eaten by the pigs today."

Thus, you might rightly call the "gifts of a Calabrian host" those that are rustic and trivial, and which burden the receiver more than they help him, or those which are given away because they are held in contempt. Indeed, the Calabrians <note>People from the "toe" of Italy, known in antiquity for rural abundance.</note>, because they have an abundance of pears, are accustomed to set them before guests in plenty; then, when the guests are full, they command them to carry them home in place of delicacies. But if you refuse, the same things are thrown to the pigs. And yet that is hardly giving a gift, but rather throwing it away. Only he truly gives who weighs both the price of the gift he bestows and the merit of the one he gives it to. Antiochus, surnamed Epiphanes <note>The Seleucid king (c. 215–164 BC).</note>, was noted in the writings of Athenaeus; he used to pour out whatever money was left rather than truly giving it. Sometimes standing in the public streets, he was accustomed to say: *Let him to whom fortune gives, take it.* <note>original Greek: "τίνι ἡ τύχη δίδωσι λαβέτω"</note> That is, "to whom luck gives, let him take," and having thrown the money away, he would depart.

### Beautiful at the door.
-> XCV <-

*Beautiful at the door.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐπὶ θύρᾳ καλός"</note> This is said of those who are loved and generally held in favor. It is taken from the custom of the ancients, who used to write the names of beautiful people or their lovers on trees, leaves, and walls, saying: *So-and-so is beautiful.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ δεῖνα καλός"</note> Alluding to this, **Aristophanes** says in *The Wasps*:
> And by Jove, if he sees written anywhere
> On a door that "the son of Pyrilampus is beautiful,"
> He runs up and writes next to it "the voting-funnel is beautiful."
> <note>original Greek: "Καὶ νὴ δί' ἂν ἴδῃ γε που γεγραμμένον / Τὸν πυριλάμπους ἐν θύρᾳ δῆμον καλὸν, / ἰὼν παρέγραψε πλησίον κημὸς καλός."</note>

-> The same author in *The Acharnians*: <-
> He was truly a lover [of yours], so much so that
> On the walls the beautiful Athenians wrote.
> <note>original Greek: "Νικᾷ ἐραστὴς ὢν ἀληθῶς, ὥς τε καὶ / Ἐν τοῖσι τοίχοις ἔγραφον ἀθηναῖοι καλοί."</note>

In the second Greek verse there is an extra syllable, even though the Aldine edition <note>The famous printing press of Aldus Manutius in Venice.</note> has it this way; I suspect the order of the words has been inverted. It will be correct if you read it in this way: *for whom the beautiful Athenians wrote on the walls.* Unless it is more pleasing that we read: *for whom beautiful Athens wrote on the walls,* as if, flattering the city, they had written this on its own fortifications. In the sixth book of Athenaeus, it is reported from some author...

<summary>Erasmus explores four adages: the "wanton-horned ram" (representing powerful or oversized things), the "dog led through the phratry" (punishment), the "gifts of a Calabrian host" (useless or burdensome gifts), and being "beautiful at the door" (public popularity).</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of "Adagia" (Proverbs), specifically continuing the commentary on Athenian pride before moving into common behavioral and idiomatic expressions from Roman and Greek literature. It maintains the sequence from page 765.</meta>

<page-num>766</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...because those who governed the Athenian republic used to flatter the people, saying that while everything else was shared in common by the Greeks, this alone was unique to the Athenians: that they knew the way that leads to heaven. Anyone who reads the praise of Anytus and Meno in **Plato** <note>In the dialogue *Meno*, though Erasmus may be thinking of the ironic praise of sophists and politicians.</note> will understand how beautifully they depicted the Athenians, charming them with the art of flattery. The commentator cites this couplet from **Callimachus** <note>A Greek poet and scholar of the Library of Alexandria.</note>:

*But indeed, carry so many letters inscribed upon these leaves, as many as might speak of beautiful Cydippe.* <note>original Greek: "Αλλ’ εἰνὶ δὴ φύλλοισι κεκομμύθα τόσσα φέροιτε γράμματα, Κυδίππῃ ὅσσ’ ἐρέουσι καλῇ."</note>

**Virgil** <note>The Roman poet, often called Maro.</note> imitated this when he said:
*I am determined to carve my loves on the tender trees; as they grow, so will you grow, my loves.*

This proverb can also be turned against those who are falsely praised through flattery, or against the lying titles of certain princes, such as "Father of the Country," "Delight of the World," "Love of the World," "Most Serene," "Illustrious," or "Most Merciful," when in fact they are nothing but plunderers of the republic.

->### To scratch the head, and similar gestures.<-

To scratch the head or gnaw one's nails are the gestures of a man deep in thought, or one struggling with a decision he might regret. From this, they are drawn into proverbial use. **Horace** writes in the tenth Satire of his first book:

->*But he,*<-
*If he had been dropped by fate into this age of ours, would rub out much of his work, would prune everything that was stretched beyond perfection, and in the making of his verse, he would often scratch his head and gnaw his nails to the quick.*

He also says: *You must often turn the stylus* <note>Erasmus refers to the Roman practice of using the flat end of a stylus to erase wax tablet markings; "turning the stylus" means to edit or rewrite.</note> *if you intend to write something worthy of a second reading.* **Persius** <note>A Roman satirist known for his difficult, metaphorical style.</note> imitated this:
*He neither thumps the desk,* he says, *nor does his work taste of bitten nails.*
The same author says elsewhere:
*Chaerestratus, gnawing his raw nail, says this.*
In the first instance, he is criticizing the negligence of poets in their writing; in the second, he describes a young man contemplating a change in his past way of life.

->### A Carian goat.<-

*A Carian goat.* <note>original Greek: "Καριϰὸς τράγος"</note> **Diogenianus** <note>A 2nd-century Greek proverb collector.</note> indicates this was a common saying for things that are cheap and contemptible. **Hesychius** <note>The lexicographer.</note> notes it was used by **Sophocles**. Because the Carian people everywhere offered their labor as cheap mercenaries, as if their lives were of little value, they became a proverb of contempt. For this reason, **Plato** spoke of a "Carian slave-kin" <note>original Greek: "καριϰὸν ἀνδράποδον"</note> meaning someone cheap and worthless, as has been noted in another place. It is also possible that the proverb refers to the fact that Carians are uniquely known for sacrificing dogs, as noted in the proverb *A Carian sacrifice*.

->### Bubbling trifles.<-

Things that are windy and empty are called "bubbling." The metaphor is taken from bubbles <note>original Greek: "πομφολύγων"</note>, from which another proverb arises: *Man is a bubble*. **Persius** says:
*Lest my page should swell with bubbling trifles.*
He calls "bubbling trifles" an empty heap of noisy words in which there is no solid meaning. **Horace** called them "melodious trifles" in his *Art of Poetry*:
*Verses void of substance, and melodious trifles.*

->### A morsel snatched from the jaws.<-

A morsel is said to be snatched from the jaws whenever some advantage, which was already nearly within one's grasp, is suddenly taken away against all expectation. **Terence** <note>The Roman comic playwright.</note> says in *The Self-Tormentor*: *It tortures me that such a great morsel was suddenly snatched from my jaws.* He used the word *bolus* <note>morsel/choice bit</note>, which the Greeks call *blomos* <note>βλωμόν</note>. The metaphor is self-evident.

->### May it go well.<-

*May it go well.* <note>original Greek: "Καλῶς ἔστω"</note> This was a common phrase used when someone was embarking on something new and difficult. In wills and testaments, they would preface it by saying, *as it may go well*. It was also used if some human misfortune occurred, or in public assemblies: *May it be auspicious and happy.* It expresses the hope that the outcome will be good.

<summary>Erasmus examines proverbs related to flattery, the physical habits of deep thought (scratching the head), and metaphors for worthlessness and sudden loss.</summary>

<header>THE SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND</header>

it should be brought out over the brow <note>An idiom for showing an expression on the face.</note> regarding a ridiculous matter of no importance, as if it were of the greatest weight. Just as **Persius** <note>A Roman satirist known for his difficult style.</note> says of a greedy rich man about to unseal a jar: *This is done well.* It is frequent among authors to say, *May it turn out well* or *May it turn out badly.* **Virgil** says in his *Bucolics*:
> We send these kids to him—and may it not turn out well for him!
And: *May the gods turn what you do to good.* **Servius the grammarian** <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil.</note> thinks this figure of speech was borrowed from the story of **Hector** and **Ajax**, to both of whom their own gifts turned out to be their destruction. <note>original: "Hoc bene fit," "Bene uertat," "Male uertat." In the myth, Ajax gave Hector a belt by which he was dragged, and Hector gave Ajax a sword by which he committed suicide.</note>

### THE SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND

#### I. The beetle seeks the eagle.

<image-desc>Decorative drop-cap letter A containing floral and leafy patterns.</image-desc>

*The coal is always mad* <note>original Greek: "Ἄνθραξ ἀεὶ δὴ μαίνεται." Erasmus notes this as a variant or perhaps a corruption of the proverb about the beetle.</note>; that is, **The beetle seeks the eagle.** This is said when a weaker and less powerful person attempts some evil and sets traps for a far more powerful enemy. There is also another reading, and in my judgment a truer one: <margin>that is,</margin> *the beetle always acts as midwife to the eagle.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ κάνθαρος ἀεὶ τὴν μαίεται."</note> The sense is almost the same whether you read "is mad" or "acts as midwife." For it applies to a humble and weak person who, through malicious traps and secret deceits, schemes for the destruction of one who is far superior in strength. **Aristophanes** says in his play *Lysistrata*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
*For I am angry with you beyond measure, you beetle; I will act as midwife to your eagle eggs whenever you lay them.* <note>original Greek: "Μὴ σχολῇ γὰρ, ἀεὶ δὴ τίκτοντα κάνθαρόν σε Maieύομαι."</note>

On this subject, a certain not-inelegant fable is told among the Greeks, which **Lucian** indicates is one of **Aesop's**, when he says in his *Icaromenippus* <note>A satirical dialogue where a man flies to heaven.</note> that Aesop told a story of how once the beetles and the camels climbed up to heaven. Furthermore, as far as the fable of the beetle and the eagle is concerned, it goes like this: There has been, for a long time now, an old and ancient grudge between the race of eagles and the whole nation of beetles, a war of total destruction, or what the Greeks call *a war without truce.* <note>original Greek: "ἄσπονδον πόλεμον."</note> For they disagree with a hatred greater than that of **Vatinius**, <note>A reference to "Vatinian hate," a Roman proverb for extreme loathing, named after a politician hated by Catullus.</note> so much so that not even **Jupiter** himself—*who holds the greatest power* <note>original Greek: "ὅς κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον."</note> and who makes all Olympus tremble with his nod—could settle the matter between them or end the discord, if the fables tell the truth. In short, nothing is more consistent between them than what is consistent today between those "gods of the court" and the humble, obscure common people. 

But perhaps there will be someone unskilled and ignorant <note>original Greek: "ἀσύνετος."</note> of Aesopic fables who wonders what business a beetle could possibly have with an eagle. What kinship, what neighborhood, what affinity could exist between such dissimilar creatures? For it is among those joined by such bonds that disagreements usually arise, especially among princes. Additionally, what could be the causes of such atrocious hatred? Finally, where did the beetle get such courage that he did not hesitate to take up war against the people of the eagles? Conversely, by what insult was the eagle's *holy wrath* <note>original Greek: "θυμὸς ἄγιος." Erasmus likely means "savage wrath" (*agrios*), but the text reads "agios" (holy), perhaps ironically.</note> so greatly offended that he did not despise so humble an enemy, but judged him worthy of his hatred? Clearly, the argument is massive: the injury is long, the details are winding, and the matter is altogether greater than human eloquence can explain. 

But if the **Muses**, who were not burdened by dictating the *Battle of Frogs and Mice* to **Homer** in the past, <note>A mock-epic poem once attributed to Homer.</note> will allow me to leave Mount Helicon for a while, I will endeavor to explain the sum of the matter to the best of my ability. For what can be so difficult that men would not dare it under their guidance? But so that the matter may become clearer to understand, before I come to the camp of the business itself, I will briefly sketch the habits, form, nature, and character of each leader. 

First, therefore, it occurs to me to wonder what was in the minds of the Romans—men otherwise wise—who boast of themselves above all other nations through the symbol of this bird, and consider themselves closest to the gods. Though they reported so many victories and held so many triumphs under its auspices, they are so far from showing gratitude for its service that they treat it with intolerable insult. For this one bird, the most masculine of all and of invincible strength, they emasculate and unman, making it almost a **Tiresias** <note>The blind prophet of Thebes who was transformed into a woman for a time.</note>—they who are not very manly themselves. Indeed, among the Greeks, the "eagle" is clearly masculine, <note>The Greek word "aetos" is a masculine noun.</note> and if I am not mistaken, this fits him much better, to whom that supreme father and king of both gods and men granted kingship over the wandering birds, having found the eagle faithful in the case of golden **Ganymede**. <note>The beautiful youth abducted by Jupiter in the form of an eagle.</note> It fits him who, while the other gods stand far off, alone hands the three-forked lightning bolts to an angry Jupiter, not at all deterred by the proverb: *Far from Jupiter and his lightning.* <note>original Greek: "πόῤῥω Διὸς τε καὶ κεραυνοῦ."</note> Nor do I think it was done without grave reason that among so many nations of birds and so many numerous tribes, the eagle especially seemed fit to hold not only the scepters <note>original Greek: "σκήπτρα."</note> of the birds, but even the Senate...

<meta>The catchword "popu-" indicates the next page begins with "populusque Romanus" (and the Roman people).</meta>

<summary>Erasmus introduces the famous adage "The beetle seeks the eagle," setting the stage for a grand mock-epic commentary on the enmity between the weak (beetle) and the powerful (eagle), while critiquing the Roman use of the eagle symbol.</summary>
<keywords>beetle and eagle, Aesop's fables, political satire, Roman symbolism, Aristophanes, Jupiter, power dynamics, Greek proverbs, mock-epic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s long essay on the adage "The beetle seeks the eagle." In the previous section, he began explaining the origins of this proverb, which illustrates how even the small and seemingly insignificant can challenge the powerful. Here, he shifts into a sharp critique of monarchy, using the eagle as a symbol for the predatory nature of kings.</meta>

<page-num>768</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...and the poetic people, by a unanimous vote, decided upon a monarchy. For as far as their judgment was concerned, most were leaning toward this side: that they should grant the supreme power to the **peacock**. Indeed, it seemed that the kingdom was clearly owed to his beauty, splendor, loftiness, and pride. And they would have proceeded entirely with this opinion, had not certain creatures experienced in the ways of the world—such as the crows and ravens—pointed out a potential problem. They weighed the fact that if they placed such a bird in charge of affairs, it would happen as it has already for many years with certain monarchs: namely, that he would act as king in name and noise alone, while the **eagle**, by the vote of the people or otherwise, would still wield the actual power. 

Furthermore, I believe the poets—those wisest of men—intended this: that the character and life of kings could be depicted by no better image than the eagle. I am speaking of most, not of all. For in every kind of thing, there has always been and always will be a scarcity of good examples. And every age produces only a few. But if you please, let us briefly bring the matter into the heat of the argument from both sides. First, if there is any omen in a name—as there certainly is—then the Greeks aptly call the eagle *aetos* <note>original: ἀετός</note>, derived from the word *aisso* <note>original: ἀΐσσω</note>, which means to be carried away by an impulse and to be driven violently. 

Some birds are gentle and placid; even those that are wild can be tamed and made mild through skill and care. Only the eagle is neither fit for any training nor can it be tamed by any effort; instead, it is carried headlong by the impulse of its nature, and whatever it strongly desires, it demands as its right. Do you wish to see a fledgling with a truly "aquiline" spirit? **Horace** <note>A famous Roman lyric poet.</note> described it graphically:

> Just like the winged servant of the lightning bolt, <note>In mythology, the eagle carried Jupiter's thunderbolts.</note>
> Whom youth and ancestral vigor once 
> Pushed from the nest, ignorant of labor;
> And now, with the spring clouds removed,
> The winds have taught him unaccustomed efforts 
> While he trembled; soon, a vivid impulse 
> Sent him down as an enemy into the sheepfolds; 
> Now, the love of feast and fight 
> Drives him against struggling dragons.

Those regions that have experienced such things understand this riddle better—regions that have learned at their own cost what evils are brought about by the untameable impulses of young princes. It is the role of philosophers to moderate the passions and to follow nothing but the lead of reason in all things. But, as the **Satirist** <note>Juvenal, a Roman poet known for biting social critique.</note> says, "Nothing is more violent than the ear of a tyrant." For that motto is always ready: *As I will, so I command; let my will stand for reason.* <note>original: "Sic uolo, sic iubeo, sit pro ratione uoluntas." A famous line from Juvenal expressing absolute, arbitrary power.</note>

Furthermore, when the various kinds of eagles are recorded, they all agree on one point: they all have a heavily hooked beak and no less hooked claws. From this physical habit alone, you can understand that this is a carnivorous bird, an enemy of peace and quiet, born for fights, rapine, and plunder. And as if it were not enough to be carnivorous, there are even those called **bone-breakers** <note>original: "ossifragae," likely referring to the lammergeier or bearded vulture.</note> and <unclear>---</unclear>. 

But at this point, dear reader, you might quietly say to me: "What does this image have to do with a king, whose chief praise is mercy? A king who, though he has the greatest power, wishes to harm no one; who lacks a sting and spends himself entirely on the convenience of his people?" Indeed, the wise **Niloxenus** <note>A character in Plutarch's *Banquet of the Seven Sages*.</note>, when asked what was the most useful thing, replied: "A King." He indicated that it is the property of a true prince that he cannot be "greatest" in any other way than by being the "best"—that is, the most beneficent to all. 

I certainly praise this model so skillfully depicted by the philosophers, though I do not know if such princes administer the republic anywhere except in **Plato’s City** <note>The *Republic*, Plato's ideal, imaginary state.</note>. Truly, in the annals of history, you will scarcely find one or two whom you would dare to compare with this image. Furthermore, if anyone examines the princes of more recent times, I fear he will find that the foulest insult which **Achilles** hurls at **Agamemnon** in **Homer** applies to them everywhere: *a people-devouring king* <note>original: δημοβόρος βασιλεύς</note>. **Hesiod** calls them *gift-eaters* <note>original: δωροφάγους</note>, though it would be more accurate to call them *all-eaters* <note>original: παμφάγους</note>. 

**Aristotle** distinguished between a king and a tyrant by a most evident mark: the tyrant looks to his private advantage, while the king consults the affairs of the people. Yet to some, the title of "King"—which seemed excessive to those ancient and great Roman leaders and was avoided out of fear of public resentment—is now scarcely enough, unless you add a long crown of most splendid lies:

„ That they be called **Divine**, though they are scarcely human.
„ That they be called **Invincible**, though they never leave a battle without being defeated.
„ That they be called **August**, though everything about them is "narrow" and shrunken. <note>A pun on the Latin *Augustus* (majestic) and *angustus* (narrow/meager).</note>
„ That they be called **Serene**, though they shake the world with the storms of war and civil upheavals.
„ That they be called **Most Illustrious**, though they are clouded by the deepest ignorance of all good things.
„ That they be called **Catholic**, though they look toward anything rather than toward Christ. 

But...

<meta>Catchword: At (But)</meta>

<summary>Erasmus uses the eagle as a metaphor for the predatory nature of monarchs, contrasting the "ideal king" of philosophy with the "people-devouring" reality of historical and contemporary rulers. He concludes with a biting satirical list of the empty, grand titles used by princes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the eagle as a symbol of tyrannical power. Following the previous page’s discussion on the etymology of "eagle" as something driven by violent impulse, Erasmus now describes the behavior and physical appearance of the bird to mirror the vices of bad rulers.</meta>

# THE THIRD THOUSAND ADAGES, SEVENTH CENTURY
<sig>Tt</sig>

to the divine, the illustrious, the triumphant—if they have any leisure from gambling, drinking, hunting, or consorts, they devote it all to truly "royal" contemplations. Their only pursuit is to direct laws, edicts, wars, peace treaties, alliances, councils, judgments, and matters both sacred and profane to one end: to turn the fortunes of everyone into their own treasury. That is, they gather wealth into a "leaky jar" <note>An allusion to the daughters of Danaus in Greek myth, who were punished in the underworld by having to fill a bottomless vessel—symbolizing insatiable greed.</note> and, in the manner of eagles, fatten themselves and their own "chicks" on the entrails of innocent birds.

Consider if some physiognomist—one who is not entirely unskilled—were to carefully contemplate the very face and beak of the eagle: those greedy and wicked eyes, the threatening maw, the fierce cheeks, the grim brow. Finally, consider that feature which so greatly pleased Cyrus, King of the Persians, in a prince: the <term>γρυπὸν</term> <note>original: grypon; a hooked or aquiline nose, historically associated with leadership and power.</note>. Would he not clearly recognize a certain royal image, magnificent and full of majesty? Add to this the very color of the bird: dismal, foul, and ill-omened, blackening with a dark squalor. From this we even call that which is dark and blackish "aquiline." Then there is the voice: unlovely, terrifying, soul-crushing, and that threatening, plaintive clangor which no kind of living creature does not dread. 

He who has experienced danger—or has at least seen it—immediately recognizes this symbol: how formidable are the threats of princes, even those uttered in jest, and how greatly everything trembles whenever an aquiline voice of this sort thunders:

> But if they do not give it, then I myself will come and take 
> your prize, or that of Ajax, or that of Odysseus; 
> I will take it and lead it away, and he to whom I come shall be wroth.
> <note>original: Greek quote from Homer's Iliad, Book 1, lines 137–139. King Agamemnon is threatening to seize the prizes of other heroes.</note>

Or that phrase, which is no less <term>βασιλική</term> <note>original: basilikē; "regal" or "kingly."</note>:

> Lest all the gods who are in Olympus be of no help to you, 
> when I come near and lay my heavy hands upon you.
> <note>original: Greek quote from Homer's Iliad, Book 1, lines 28–29.</note>

At this eagle’s shriek, I say, the common people instantly tremble, the senate shrinks back, the nobility stands in awe, the judges comply, the theologians fall silent, the lawyers flatter, laws give way, and institutions yield. Neither divine law, nor piety, nor equity, nor humanity has any power. And though there are so many birds that are not uneloquent—so many that are tuneful, with such varied voices and melodies that could even move stones—the unpleasant and entirely unmusical shriek of a single eagle has more power than all of them. 

And yet, there is one kind of eagle that greatly pleased Aristotle, perhaps because he desired such a "chick" for his own pupil Alexander: it was hardly less predatory or voracious, but a little more modest, a bit quieter, and possessing a slightly larger measure of humanity, since it actually rears its own young. For the rest of them act as impious parents are wont to do, exposing their offspring, whereas even tigresses raise their cubs. And for that reason they call this type <term>γνήσιον</term> <note>original: gnēsion; "genuine," "legitimate," or "noble."</note>, as if you were to say "authentic" or truly "high-born." Homer, though blind, saw this kind. For he calls it <term>μελάνετον</term> <note>original: melanaeton; "black eagle."</note> and <term>λαγωφόνον</term> <note>original: lagōphonon; "hare-slayer."</note>—that is, having a black back and being a hunter. These epithets fit most aptly those princes such as Nero, Caligula, and far too many others. 

But by Jove, how much more "noble" <note>original: <term>γνησιώτεροι</term> (gnēsiōteroi)</note> are some of these—I might almost say more than aquiline—who, although they are closest to the gods by virtue of their scepters and ancestral portraits, nonetheless occasionally endure the need to flatter even lowly little men? I might almost say they play the part of parasites, provided there is hope for a prey that is not to be despised. 

Furthermore, it has been handed down by authors that the eagle is long-lived. Yet when it reaches extreme old age, it thirsts for nothing but blood, through the sucking of which it prolongs a life hated by all; this is because its upper beak grows so large that it can no longer feed on meat. And from this arose that most famous adage: <term>ἀετοῦ γῆρας</term> <note>original: aetou gēras; "an eagle's old age." Used to describe the elderly who turn to wine or drink because they can no longer eat solid food.</note>, applied to the elderly who are more fond of wine, since otherwise almost this entire genus of birds with hooked talons either does not drink at all or does so very rarely, if we believe Aristotle. And yet if these birds ever do drink, they drink water. The eagle alone thirsts for blood. 

Therefore, with its twisted beak, nature (certainly not always a stepmother) seems to have looked out for the other living creatures in some way, imposing a certain limit on the eagle’s insatiable voracity. Just as she also provided by this means: she does not allow the eagle to lay more than three eggs, nor to rear more than two chicks. Indeed, if we believe the verse of Musaeus, which Aristotle cites as a witness:

> She hatches two, produces three, but rears only one.

And during those very days in which the eagle broods—she sits for about thirty days—the providence of nature denies them food, while their talons are turned inward so that the young of all wild beasts are not snatched away. Thus, during that time, their feathers turn white from hunger. From this comes the hatred they feel toward their own offspring. But one might wish for this trait in the "Roman eagles" <note>A double reference to the Holy Roman Emperors and perhaps the Papacy, both of which used the eagle as a symbol.</note> rather than actually seeing it; for them, there is neither end nor limit to the plundering of the common people. For their thirst for extraction grows with age, and never...

<meta>catchword: all</meta>

they brood even more heavily once the chick has been hatched. Then indeed the people strike with one gift after another. Above all these things, nature has set many enemies against this one bird, of which we are about to speak. And he will cease to wonder at this care of nature who is persuaded that what Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*.</note> wrote is true—indeed, a portentous thing, and I know not whether it is to be believed even on the authority of Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher.</note>—as an argument for insatiable greed; yet Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and moralist.</note>, a particularly weighty author, narrates it as a thing discovered and confessed. Namely, that the feathers of eagles, if they are mixed with the plumage of other birds, devour them, and gradually consume them until they are thinned out. Such is the power of nature’s rapacity. Indeed, I believe the same would happen if the bones of tyrants were mixed with the bones of commoners; even their blood could no more be mixed than that of Aegisthus and Florus <note>original: "Aegithi & Flori"; Erasmus likely refers to the legendary enmity of Eteocles and Polynices, the sons of Oedipus, whose blood (or the flames of their funeral pyre) was said to refuse to mingle even in death.</note>. 

Now, see for me whether this applies sufficiently to certain princes. For I do not speak of the pious and the good, which I wish the reader to remember everywhere once I have said it. A single pair of eagles requires a vast tract of land to pillage, nor do they allow another robber to be in the vicinity; thus they mark out their spaces. Furthermore, for our own "eagles," what domain is not too narrow? How immense is their zeal for propagating the kingdom? How great is the clashing of swords with neighboring eagles, or kites, over the boundaries of the kingdom—that is, over the boundaries of plundering? 

Yet that other point perhaps does not agree as well: that this bird, although so very rapacious, does not prey in its own neighborhood, evidently lest the turn of injuries eventually be twisted back upon its own head; instead, it carries its prey into the nest from afar. Meanwhile, tyrants do not even spare those closest to them, nor do these rapacious ones hold back their claws from their nearest kin and household members; indeed, each person is more liable to danger the closer he is to the prince, as if to Jupiter and his lightning. 

And this innate hunger for seizing, bred into them by their parents, is increased not a little by their education. For they say the eagle pushes its chicks out of the nest as soon as they are barely fledged enough for preying, so that immediately and "from tender claws" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "from earliest childhood."</note> they may become accustomed to plunder and live by their own talons. But in some princes—immortal God!—how many stimuli are added to their rapacity besides the most corrupt education: such a swarm of flatterers, so many foot-soldier officials, so many corrupt counselors, so many foolish familiars, so many wicked companions, who take delight in public misfortunes even for free. Add to these pride, pleasures, luxury, and delicacies, for which no amount of robbery could be enough. Add folly and ignorance, than which nothing is less stable if it is coupled with good fortune. Since these things can corrupt even the most kindly natures, what do you think will happen if they are added to a greedy and wicked nature, like oil to a furnace? 

But the eagle would be poorly equipped "in the royal manner" <note>original: "βασιλικῶς" (basilikōs)</note> if it were armed only with a hooked beak and sharp, curved claws for preying, unless there were also added eyes more sharp than a lynx’s. These do not even blink at the brightest sun; indeed, by this experiment they are said to test their offspring to see if they are legitimate. Thus they spy out from afar the prey they intend to invade. Although the king of birds has only two eyes, one beak, a few claws, and likewise a single stomach, for our "eagles"—good heavens!—how many are the "Corycean ears" <term>Corycean ears</term> <note>A proverb referring to spies and informants; named after the inhabitants of Mount Corycus who eavesdropped on sailors to help pirates.</note>, how many the eyes of spies, how many the claws of officials, how many the beaks of prefects, how many the stomachs of judges and lawyers, with a hunger utterly insatiable! Thus nothing can be enough, and nothing can be safe from them, not even those things which are hidden in the innermost chambers or the most secret cabinets. 

Nevertheless, the eagle would perhaps be somewhat less harmful if the cunning of the mind were not added to the weapons and gifts of the body—that is, if the iron, harmful enough by itself, were not dipped in poison. Whenever it walks, it retracts its claws, lest it dull their sharpness and they be less effective in preying—a trait it shares with lions. Nor does it attack just anyone, but only him whom it believes to be superior in strength. Nor does it suddenly hurl itself to the ground like other birds when it seeks prey, but lets itself down gradually, lest it be injured by the force of the impact. It does not even attack a hare—for it seeks this most of all—unless it sees that it has descended into flat ground. Nor does it go out at just any time, lest someone overwhelm it while fatigued; instead, it flies out to prey from lunch until midday, sitting idle during the remaining hours until the forums are filled with the gathering of men. Even when it has killed, it does not devour the prey immediately on the spot, lest some sudden incursion of enemies catch it unawares while feeding. But having first reconnoitered and then refreshed its strength, it carries the prey into the nest as if into a fortress. 

By what arts it captures a deer, though the deer is more powerful than itself, will be told shortly. But this first must be remembered as a proof of its cleverness: having snatched up a tortoise from on high and spied a suitable place, it drops it onto a rock, so that by breaking the shell in this way, it may feed on the meat. However, in the case of Aeschylus <note>The famous Greek tragic poet.</note>, the eagle's eyes were not sharp enough; for when it dropped the tortoise on his white, bald head, thinking it a rock, it miserably killed him—so that for this reason alone, by the best right, the poet...

### CHILIADS, THIRD THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY
Tt 2

it is agreed by all that she is hated. And indeed, she now does this persistently as if by her own right. Furthermore, she first lured the tortoise with tricks to this end, while persuading her that it would happen that, by the eagle's help, the tortoise might learn the art of flying. And having lifted her high with this hope, she dropped her onto a rock, so that she might turn that creature's calamity into her own delicacies in a tyrannical manner. <note>Erasmus recounts a fable where the eagle offers to teach a tortoise to fly only to drop it and eat the cracked remains—a metaphor for deceptive rulers.</note> But if anyone considers with himself how many varied arts, how many tricks, how many machines, and how many illusions wicked princes are equipped with to pillage the common people—through profitable laws, fines, false titles, simulated wars, informants, and unworthy alliances—he will almost admit that the eagle is unworthy of being granted the name of royalty. It remains for us to explain in a few words which enemies in particular this "noble robber" contends with. For that which is said in proverbs is true: <term>the eagle does not catch flies</term> <note>original: "aquilā nō captare muscas"</note> nor <term>does the asp look at wood-lice</term> <note>original: "nec aspis cere thripas". These proverbs suggest that powerful people do not bother with insignificant targets, though Erasmus notes they often do if there is profit involved.</note>. She ignores any prey that seems unworthy of royal claws, unless they are related to Vespasian <note>A Roman Emperor famous for taxing even the public urinals, famously saying "money does not smell."</note>, to whom the good scent of profit seemed to come from anything at all. For there are also degenerate eagles who live by fishing, and who are not ashamed to scavenge the carcass of another. But those who are more noble, like tyrants, leave certain things to pirates and robbers; from whom, as that noble pirate said to Alexander of Macedon, they differ in nothing, except that they themselves harass a great part of the world with a larger fleet and a larger hand through their own robberies, leaving those tiny scraps of prey to hawks and kestrels. 

They wage war with quadrupeds, and not without danger, nor again without hope of victory, as is worthy of a strenuous leader. And among these, as I have said, the eagle hunts the hare most of all, which is why the surname "hare-catcher" <note>original: "leporarię"</note> was added to one species, just as you might call a general "Africanus" or "Numantinus." <note>Roman honorary titles given to generals for conquering Africa or the city of Numantia.</note> She does not despise a peaceful enemy, but seeks out one that is good to eat, so that even if little glory comes from the victory, no small amount of gain is nonetheless carried away. But it happens sometimes that while she is most intent on catching the hare, she is most caught herself, struck by a feathered arrow; then she might say the proverb which we have received from her: <term>we are caught by our own feathers</term> <note>original: "τοῖς ἰδίοις πτεροῖς ἁλισκόμεθα". This refers to arrows being fletched with eagle feathers.</note>. 

She also dares to fight with the stag, though she would be inferior unless she added the "fox's skin" <note>An ancient idiom for using cunning when strength fails.</note>. For she supplies by craft what is diminished in strength. About to engage with the enemy, she first rolls herself in the dust. Then, sitting upon the stag's horns, she sprinkles the dust collected in her feathers into its eyes, beating its face with her wings until, blinded, she drives it headlong over the cliffs. But she has an even sharper and much more uncertain fight with the dragon <note>Often used in Latin for a large serpent or snake.</note>, even in the air. The dragon, with malicious arts, seeks out the eagle's eggs. She, in turn, seizes the enemy wherever he is seen. 

As for her irreconcilable feud with the fox, no one will wonder at it who knows how "regally" she once treated her. She had entered into a friendship with her neighbor, and when food was lacking for her while she was brooding, she carried the fox's cubs up into her nest. The fox, returning to see the shameful slaughter of her own, did the only thing she could: she called the gods to witness, and among these especially Jupiter <term>of Friendship</term> <note>original: "Φίλιον" (Philios). Zeus/Jupiter was the protector of oaths and guests.</note>, the avenger of violated friendship. And some god seems to have heard those prayers. A few days later, it happened that the eagle inadvertently carried a burning coal, clinging to meat snatched from a sacrifice, back to her nest. While the eagle was away, the fire was gradually fanned by the winds, and the nest began to burn. The terrified chicks, still unable to fly, threw themselves headlong down. The fox caught them as they fell and devoured them in her den. And after that time, nothing at all is agreed upon between the eagle and the fox, although truly this is to the no-small misfortune of the fox's race. 

Yet I do not know whether they should seem worthy of this, they who once denied help to the hares seeking an <term>alliance</term> <note>original: "συμμαχίαν"</note> against the eagle, as is recorded in the annals of the quadrupeds, from which Homer borrowed <term>The Battle of the Frogs and Mice</term> <note>original: "Βατραχομυομαχίαν". A mock-epic poem traditionally attributed to Homer.</note>. Now indeed there is a sharp disagreement also with the vulture, as with a fellow-craftsman and a rival in greed; although on this account the eagle is as much more noble as she is more cruel, because she does not devour any animal unless she has killed it, nor does she lazily settle on the carcasses of others. 

She also rightly hates the "fitta" <note>Likely a reference to a type of woodpecker or similar bird noted in natural histories for destroying eggs.</note>, which studies with strange arts to break the eagle's eggs. She also fights with herons, because this bird, relying on its claws, does not fear to attack her sometimes, fighting so fiercely that it dies in the conflict. And it is no longer a wonder that she gets along poorly with swans, a truly "poetic" bird; it is a wonder that such a pugnacious beast is often defeated by them. 

The poetic race has not usually been very pleasing to monarchs who are conscious of their own evil, being as it is free and talkative, and which sometimes would rather be led back to the <term>Stone Quarries</term> with Philoxenus than keep silent. <note>Philoxenus of Cythera was a poet imprisoned in the quarries (Latumiae) by the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse for refusing to praise the tyrant's bad poetry.</note> For if anything hurts them, they smear it onto black pages and publish the secrets of kings even to posterity. 

Nor does she get along well enough with cranes, I think for the reason that <term>Democracy</term> <note>original: "Democratia"</note> pleases them immensely—a thing vehemently hated by monarchs, by whom they are nevertheless surpassed in ingenuity. For when cranes migrating from Cilicia prepare to cross Mount Taurus, which is full of eagles, they fly across silently at night, having taken large stones into their mouths to keep their voices in check; and thus, having deceived the eagles, they cross safely.

He contrasts the eagle's isolation with the surprising "humanity" found in other predatory animals.</meta>

...they pass over. But a certain peculiar grudge exists against the Trochilus <note>A name used for various small birds, most notably the wren.</note>—for that is the bird's name—for no other reason, as that "great walker" <note>A reference to Aristotle, the "Peripatetic" philosopher, known for observing nature while walking.</note> asserts, than because the name of "king" <term>orchilos</term> <note>original Greek: "ὄρχιλος"; the OCR "ἀκφόρ" is a corruption of the Greek for wren, which was often called "the little king."</note> is attributed to it as well. This is especially the case among the Latins. Consequently, as if pursuing a claimant to the throne, the eagle hunts it with extreme hatred. Although the wren is not an enemy whose strength the eagle fears—being weak and prone to flight—it is nevertheless endowed with such cleverness and wit, hiding itself in thickets and secret places, that it cannot be easily captured even by a more powerful foe. Indeed, once when it had undertaken a flying contest with the eagle, it won more by trickery than by strength. <note>Erasmus refers to the fable where the wren hides in the eagle's feathers and flies out at the last moment to go higher.</note> Finally, she wages a deadly war with the Cybindus <note>A species of nocturnal hawk or owl.</note>, so much so that they are often found caught together in a death-grip. Now, the Cybindus is a starling-hawk.

Nor is any class of men more hated by tyrants than those who, disagreeing far and wide with the opinions of the common people, see too sharply through the darkness. But would I not be exceptionally foolish if I proceeded to enumerate all the eagle's enemies, when there is no creature with whom she does *not* wage war? In the other orders of living creatures, some have war with one another, while others have friendship. The fox has many enemies, yet it has a friend in the crow, whose help it uses against the Merlin <note>original: "Æsalon"</note> when it harasses the fox's cubs. The fox also gets along well with serpents, since they equally enjoy hunting rabbits. The crocodile has the Ichneumon as an enemy, but maintains such familiarity with the Trochilus that the bird is allowed to enter the very jaws of the beast with impunity. <note>A reference to the "crocodile bird" that cleans the reptile's teeth.</note> For the eagle alone, there is absolutely no friendship, no affinity, no alliance, no social bond, no treaty, no truce with any living thing. She is an enemy to all, and has everyone as an enemy. Indeed, she cannot help but be the enemy of everyone, since she lives and grows fat on the misfortune of all.

Conscious of this, she does not nest on level ground, but on rugged and lofty cliffs, and sometimes in trees, but only very tall ones—clearly ruminating on that tyrannical saying: *Let them hate, so long as they fear.* <note>original: "Oderint dum metuant," a famous line attributed to the tragic poet Accius and favored by the Emperor Caligula.</note> Consequently, while storks are sacred to the Egyptians—so much so that killing one is a capital offense—and while geese were sacred among us <note>Referring to the geese of the Capitoline who saved Rome.</note>, and while no one harms kites among the Britons, and while the Jews spare pigs, and while the ancients did not hunt dolphins, nor was it lawful to harm them (if they accidentally harmed one in a hunt, they were punished only with lashes like children)—yet against eagles, everywhere in the world, the law is the same as against wolves and tyrants: there is a reward for whoever kills the common enemy of all.

Therefore, the eagle neither loves anyone nor is loved by any living creature—no more, surely, than those princes who rule for their own benefit to the great misfortune of the State. Perhaps there are some private individuals of that sort. Great satraps <note>High-ranking officials or governors, used here for powerful courtiers.</note> are so far removed from these affections that sometimes, for the sake of profit, they hold even their own children in suspicion and hatred. That a lion, a creature so fierce, returned gratitude to a man who deserved well of him and spared the life of the one from whom he had received healing for his foot, is believed by almost everyone. <note>The story of Androcles and the Lion.</note> Very many believe that a dragon protected its foster-parent and hurried to the sound of his voice. Indeed, Philarchus related—and Demetrius the Physician thought it should be written, and Pliny thought it should be recounted—that even an asp, accustomed to eat daily at a certain person's table, when it realized that its host's son had been killed by one of its own young, killed its own offspring as punishment for the violated hospitality and, out of shame, did not return to the house thereafter.

Likewise, it is said that a panther, on account of its cubs being rescued from a pit, dutifully led a man until he had left the wilderness and returned to the public road. An elephant was even a rival to Aristophanes the Grammarian for the love of a girl from Stephanopolis. Plutarch related this as a thing very well known to all and celebrated in everyone’s speech. Among the people of Aegium, a certain dragon was desperately in love with an Aetolian girl. As for the service of the Dolphin toward humans—saved for Arion, carried to the shore for Hesiod, a Lesbian maiden saved from the sea, and the duty of carrying a boy back and forth—it is almost common knowledge. But that a maiden was loved by an eagle—not even those who believe everything believe that! For the hatred of this creature toward humans is so fatal that you may gather it from the fact that for Prometheus, the most "friend of man" <term>philanthropotatō</term> <note>original Greek: "φιλανθρωποτάτῳ"</note> of the gods, an executioner was stationed on Mount Caucasus <note>Referring to the eagle that eternally ate Prometheus's liver.</note>.

And yet, among so many vices, there is something you might praise. They are very little given to drink and very little deceitful—though they are extremely rapacious. The eagle snatched Ganymede, but she snatched him for Jove, not for herself. Yet you see some of our eagles snatch things for themselves; they carry away not one Ganymede, but virgins and matrons for themselves, so that in this regard they are almost more intolerable than in their robberies, for which they are already most intolerable. Finally, although there are innumerable species of birds, and among these some are adorned with the wealth and colors of feathers, like peacocks; others are distinguished by snowy whiteness, like swans; others, on the contrary, are gleaming with a becoming blackness, like crows; others are pre-eminent for the height of their bodies, like ostriches; others are famous even for physical miracles, like the phoenix; others are commended for their fertility, like pigeons...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### THE SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND

...pleasing to the tables of the wealthy, such as partridges and pheasants; others are pleasant for their talkativeness, like parrots; others are wondrous in their song, like nightingales; others are outstanding for their courage of spirit, like roosters; and others are born for human delight, like little sparrows. Yet out of all these, only the eagle seemed fit to men of such wisdom to represent the image of a king—a bird neither beautiful, nor melodic, nor good to eat, but rather carnivorous, rapacious, predatory, a ravager, a warmonger, solitary, hated by all, a plague to everyone; who, though she has the power to do great harm, wishes she could do even more than she already does.

Nor was it by any different judgment that the kingdom among the four-legged animals was handed to the lion, than which no other beast is either more monstrous or more foul-smelling. Dogs are useful for many things, especially for standing guard over human property. Oxen are for agriculture. Horses and elephants fight in wars. Mules and asses are useful for carrying loads. Monkeys are merely parasites. Even the dragon <note>Often referring to a large serpent in classical natural history.</note> is useful for this reason alone: that it showed how to use fennel <term>marathrum</term> to sharpen the eyesight. But the lion is nothing but a tyrant, an enemy and devourer of all, safe only through his own strength and the fear he inspires—plainly a "royal" animal, just like the eagle. 

This seems to have been understood by those who decorate noble shields with lions, especially those with wide-gaping mouths and claws outstretched for prey. But Pyrrhus <note>The King of Epirus, famous for his costly victories.</note> appears to have seen even more clearly, as he rejoiced to be called "the Eagle," as did Antiochus <note>A Seleucid king.</note>, who delighted in the nickname "the Hawk." Yet it is less surprising that the lion reigns among the beasts, since even among the poetic gods, Jupiter seemed most fit for governing the realm: a god who was impious for banishing and exiling his father, incestuous through marriage to his sister, and adorned with so many rapes, so many adulteries, and so many abductions; and after all this, terrifying the whole world with <note>original Greek: "κυανέοις ὀφρύσι, καὶ φολιδωτῇ κώδωνι"</note> "his dark brows and scaly rattle." 

Indeed, the government of bees, in which the single king <note>Ancient naturalists usually identified the queen bee as a king.</note> is not permitted to carry a sting, although it is praised by many, is imitated by no one—by Hercules, no more than the Republic of Plato! 

But I return to the eagle, to whom, on account of the qualities I mentioned, so <note>original Greek: "βασιλικῶς"</note> "regally," and for such extraordinary merits toward every kind of living creature, the senate and people of the poets decreed with great consensus: first, that she be called king of all, and even <note>original Greek: "ἀετός"</note> "the eagle," which is to say, "divine." <note>Erasmus likely puns on the Greek word's phonetic similarity to words for "eternal" or "divine."</note> Next, they gave her a sufficiently honorable place among the stars and distinguished her with several little constellations. Finally, they assigned her an honorable duty among the celestials: that she alone should provide weapons to an angry Jupiter, with which he shakes the entire world. Because she can do this with impunity, they also granted her this: that she is the only living creature that neither fears the lightning nor is harmed by it, but gazes at the flashing bolt with the same eyes with which she looks directly at the sun. 

To these things those most wise Romans of old <note>Casci: an archaic term for the ancient, "primitive" Italians.</note> added that the eagle should hold the first place on the banners of their legions. She was to be the "standard-bearer" of the standards themselves, even setting aside the wolves (who nursed the Roman race), the Minotaurs, and the boars—beasts of no small greed—and finally even the horses. For standards marked with these four animals once used to follow the eagle. Shortly thereafter, she would not even tolerate them as companions, but leaving them behind in the camps, she alone went forth into battle. 

This bird, I say, they deemed worthy to decorate the scepters, insignias, shields, houses, clothing, vessels, and services of the monarch of the whole world—even though, if I am not mistaken, the Roman empire was founded on the omen <term>augurium</term> of vultures, not eagles. The college of augurs added this: if an eagle settles on someone's house, or if it drops a cap onto someone's head, it portends imperial power. 

You have heard of one of the two leaders; now I shall come to the Beetle. It is an animal, and yet scarcely an animal, since it lacks several of the senses. It belongs to the lowest class of insects, which the Greeks call by the infamous name <note>original Greek: "κάνθαρον"</note> "kantharos" and the Latins call "Scarabeus." It is foul in appearance, fouler in smell, and foulest in sound, with its wings protected by a crust-like shell. Indeed, the whole beetle is nothing but a shell. It is born in excrement—that is, the dung of living creatures—and in that same dung it lives, moves about, finds delight, and takes its pleasure. 

Its chief pursuit is to form balls as large as possible, like little cakes, not made from perfumes, but from dung—most especially goat dung, for to the beetle that smells exactly like marjoram <term>amaracinum</term>. It rolls these balls with marvelous effort while facing backward, using its hind legs (which are longer) to push from above while its head is bowed to the ground. If it ever happens that it must push its load up a hill and the balls slip and roll back down, you would think you were seeing Sisyphus rolling his stone. <note>A mythological figure condemned to eternally push a boulder up a hill in the underworld.</note> They neither tire nor rest; such is the ardor of their labor until they have carried them into their burrow. In these balls, just as they themselves were born, they also raise their offspring and cherish them as they nest against the winter's chill. 

I know well that the Beetle is known to everyone, since it is encountered everywhere, unless there is a place with no dung at all. But not all species are the same. Indeed, there are some whose shells shine with a certain dark green. Most are bristling with a foul blackness. There are some larger ones, armed with very long, two-pronged horns with serrated pincers at the tip; when they see fit, they contract and tighten these for a bite. There are also reddish ones, and very large ones that [inhabit] the dry earth...

<meta>This page continues the essay "The Beetle Searches for the Eagle" (*Scarabeus aquilam quaerit*). Having criticized the eagle's predatory nature, Erasmus now provides a "defense" of the beetle, arguing that its humble life is actually superior to the eagle's "regal" tyranny.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...they dig in dry places and place their nests there. There are some that fly out with a frightening hum and a formidable noise, so as to terrify the unwary in no small measure. There are also other differences in their forms. But this much is common to all: they are born from dung, they feed on dung, and their life and delight are found in dung. 

Now, I suspect there will be someone who, being a great admirer of Roman leaders, will weep for the fate of the eagle, since it must deal with such a lowly and plebeian enemy—or perhaps with one so "royal" that there is no glory in defeating it, yet it is most shameful to be conquered by it; an enemy who gains more than enough praise simply for having fought the eagle, even if it leaves defeated. In the poets, Ajax is ashamed to have Ulysses as an adversary because he is so unwar-like; and is the eagle to be forced to struggle with a Beetle? 

On the other hand, someone else will wonder even more where this most vile insect gets such spirit and such audacity that it did not fear to undertake a war with the most pugnacious of birds. Then, they will wonder where it found the wealth, strength, resources, and allies to be able to carry on a war for so many years. But if one were to open this Silenus <note>A reference to the "Sileni of Alcibiades," figures that appear ugly or grotesque on the outside but contain something divine or precious within.</note> and contemplate this despised little animal more closely, as if in its own home, he would notice so many extraordinary gifts in it that, after weighing everything carefully, he might almost prefer to be a Beetle rather than an eagle. 

Now, let no one cry out against me or disturb me before they have learned the facts. First, the Beetle excels even the eagle in this: it sheds its old age <term>old skin</term> <note>original: "συῆαρ"</note> every year and immediately becomes young again. Now, this in itself is so valuable that I believe even some Roman Popes—though they are permitted to pass straight into heaven since they hold the key to it—would nevertheless, when they reach that unlovely old age which renounces all pleasures, prefer to cast off their old skin with the Beetles than to receive a sevenfold crown in exchange for their triple crown <note>The "triple crown" refers to the Papal Tiara; Erasmus is satirizing the desire for earthly rejuvenation over heavenly reward.</note>. 

Furthermore, in such a tiny body, what strength of soul, what heroic force of mind, what an impulse for attack! Compared to the Beetle, the Homeric fly is nothing <note>Homer describes the fly as a symbol of persistent courage because it keeps returning even when brushed away.</note>. For this reason, if I am not mistaken, some Beetles are even given the name "bulls." Yet even lions do not rashly engage with bulls, far less do eagles. 

Indeed, its intelligence is no common thing—unless one thinks that the Greek proverb "a beetle is wiser" <term>a beetle is wiser</term> <note>original: "κανθάρος σοφώτερος"</note> was born or celebrated everywhere without cause; a proverb by which, clearly, a certain singular and incomparable wisdom is attributed to it. Nor does it matter to me if someone quibbles that it dwells poorly in an ugly house. For as far as the shape of the body is concerned—provided that a vulgar imagination does not seize the judgment—there is nothing in the Beetle to be despised. For if it has been truly handed down by the Philosophers that the figure they call "spherical" is not only the most beautiful but also the best in every way, and that no other shape pleased the Creator more when he fashioned this heaven (the most beautiful of all things), why should the Beetle not be seen as handsome, since it approaches this shape far more closely than the eagle? 

Finally, if a horse is handsome in its own kind, or a dog in its own, why should the Beetle please any less in its own? Unless we measure all forms by our own, so that whatever does not approach the human form is immediately judged deformed. For I think no one will slander the color of the Beetle, as its hue even recommends certain gemstones. 

Furthermore, the fact that it makes use of the excrement of living creatures for its own convenience is a credit to its ingenuity, not a crime. As if physicians do not do the same, who not only smear but even administer the excrements of many animals—and even humans—in potions during illnesses! Nor are the Alchemists ashamed—those clearly divine men—to use manure to extract that "fifth essence" <note>The quintessence, or the purest form of matter sought in alchemy.</note>. Nor were farmers—a class of men than which none was once more honored—ashamed to fatten their fields with dung. There are also peoples for whom dung serves as plaster for coating the walls of their homes. When crushed and dried in the sun, they use it as fuel for fire in place of wood. The Cypriots fatten their oxen with human dung, and not only fatten them but also heal them with it. 

"But," you say, "that rotten stuff smells bad to them." It would be foolish indeed to expect a human nose in a Beetle. Since it is peculiar to man to be offended by the smell of dung, and the same does not happen in any other living creature, the Beetle is therefore happier than us, not filthier. 

Though even humans are not so much offended by the thing itself as by opinion; for to those ancient mortals, the thing itself did not seem as abominable as it does to us, for they called it by the most auspicious name, "manure" <term>enrichment</term> <note>original: "lætamen," derived from "lætus," meaning happy or fertile.</note>. Nor did they hesitate to add the surname "Sterculeus" <note>From "stercus," meaning dung.</note> to the god Saturn, clearly for the sake of honor, if we believe Macrobius. For Pliny recorded that Stercutus, the son of Faunus, gained not only a name but even immortality in Italy from this. Furthermore, in Greece, the same thing brought the highest glory to two kings: to Augeas, who thought of it, and to Hercules, who made it known. Finally, the memory of the royal old man will never be erased, whom Homer describes—as Cicero relates in his work on Cato—fertilizing the fields with his own hands, and not by any other means...

### THE ADAGES OF ERASMUS, CHILIAD 3, CENTURY 7
#### Tt 4

...than that in which the Beetle delights, and has consecrated it for posterity. The Roman Emperor <note>A reference to the Emperor Vespasian, who famously defended a tax on public urinals by saying "Money does not smell" (*pecunia non olet*).</note> was not at all offended by the stench of urine when it was joined with profit; why then should such a slight inconvenience deter the Beetle from such great advantages—if we even grant that it is an inconvenience? Finally, since we see that the Beetle remains clean while in the dung, always with a shiny shell, while the eagle stinks even while in the air, I ask you: which of the two is cleaner? Indeed, I believe its name was given for this reason, so that the <term>beetle</term> <note>original Greek: *kantharos*</note> was named as if it were <term>pure</term> <note>original Greek: *katharos*</note>, unless someone prefers to think it was named "clean" by the Centaurs. For you must not think the Beetle avoids luxuries because of a "filthy" nature; it also delights most dearly in roses and seeks them out above all else, if we are to believe Pliny <note>The Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder, whose *Natural History* is a primary source for Erasmus.</note>.

But if someone should happen to think these qualities are trivial or common, surely no one will fail to admit the magnificence—and the worthiness of a great crest—in the fact that, in ancient times, the Beetle was held among the foremost of sacred images and in the mysteries of the prophets, as the most fitting symbol of an excellent warrior. Indeed, as Plutarch relates in his commentary *On Isis and Osiris*, in the hieroglyphic pictures of the Egyptians, the image of a king was an eye with a scepter added, by which, clearly, vigilance joined with the right and just administration of affairs was signified. For in those times, I believe, there were still kings of that sort, very much unlike the eagle. 

But at Thebes, the same author says, there were certain images stored away that lacked hands; these represented judges, whom it behooves to be as separated as possible from all corruption of gifts. And among these was one also lacking eyes, which shadowed forth the presiding judge, because it is necessary for him to be entirely free from all emotion, to look only at the matter itself, and not to respect the person. There stood—not "the bitter herb among the vegetables" <note>A proverb meaning something out of place or unwelcome.</note> as the proverb says—but the Beetle among the sacred images, engraved upon a seal. And what, finally, did those wisest theologians imply to us by this strange symbol? Something by no means common: namely, an excellent and invincible leader of war. 

For Plutarch indicates this as well, lest anyone think this is something I have made up, in the way unlearned theologians are sometimes accustomed to invent allegories. But some unskilled person might ask: "What does a Beetle have to do with a leader of war?" Quite a lot of things match, truly. To begin with, you see how the Beetle shines all over in armor, and there is no part of its body that is not diligently fortified with shells and plates, so that the <term>Homeric Mars</term> <note>The god of war, often called *Mauors* in Latin.</note> does not seem better armed even when he equips himself in his greatest panoply. 

Add now the military assault, with its terrifying and "Panic" <note>Meaning a sound that causes "Pan-ic" fear, related to the god Pan.</note> hum, and a truly military song. For what is more un-sweet than the sound of battle-trumpets? What is more harsh than the <term>unstrung</term> <note>original Greek: *anakordou*</note> noise of drums? For the voice of trumpets, in which kings now delight so much, the people of Busiris <note>An ancient city in Egypt.</note> once could not endure, because it seemed similar to a braying donkey; and to that people, the donkey was held among abominable things. 

Add to this the beetle's patience in labor while rolling loads, its invincible strength of spirit, and its contempt for life. To these things, they say that no female is found in the race of Beetles, but all are males. I ask you, what can more fitly suit a brave commander? Indeed, this also fits the matter aptly, as Plutarch indicates: that they give birth to, cherish, nourish, and raise their young in those delicate balls of dung mentioned before; and there is no other place for being born than the place of their food. Truly, this mystery is not easy for me to interpret. 

It will be more correctly explained by the soldiers of emperors, who know what it is <term>to dine in a shield</term> <note>original Greek: *en aspidi deipneisthai*</note>, who know about <term>sleeping on the bare ground</term> <note>original Greek: *chameunias*</note>, who in a siege have often endured harsh winters and harsher hunger while naked, who have prolonged a sickly life not even on the roots of herbs but on foul food, and who have spent several months in ships. If anyone weighs the filth of this life, the Beetle will be clean; if anyone weighs the misery, he has reason to envy the Beetle. But this is the fate and condition of the most praised commanders, lest anyone perhaps despise it. 

But I wish to wonder in passing: what has happened to our <term>braggart soldiers</term> <note>original Latin: *pyrgopolynicis*, a term from the Roman playwright Plautus for boastful soldiers who claim to have conquered "towers and cities."</note> that in their heraldry—in which they think their whole nobility is situated—they prefer leopards, or lions, or dogs, or dragons, or wolves, or some other animal that chance threw in their way or they adopted for themselves, when the Beetle is their own proper symbol? And it is not only most fitting, but truly approved and dedicated by antiquity itself, which is the sole parent of nobility. 

Finally, no one will think the Beetle is to be utterly despised if he considers that magi and physicians seek remedies from this living creature for the greatest of human ills. Indeed, the "horns of the Lucani" (for so they call this kind <note>The Stag Beetle.</note>) are not only carried in a purse but even hung from the neck—sometimes even enclosed in gold—as a defense against all diseases of infants. What of the fact that in the most effective and scarcely believable remedies (unless Pliny were the authority), the Beetle will obtain a power equal to the eagle? For <term>that son</term> <note>original Greek: *ho d' huios ekeino*</note>, the Beetle, is engraved upon an emerald gem; for as the proverb says, "Mercury is not carved from just any wood," nor does the Beetle deign to be carved on just any gem...

He mocks modern soldiers for choosing violent beasts for their heraldry while ignoring the beetle's ancient association with endurance, armor, and discipline.</summary>
