### THE ADAGES OF ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
#### Tt 4

...but if it is carved into an emerald, the most brilliant of all gems, and suspended from the neck—as I have mentioned—provided it is tied with the hair of a <term>Cynocephalus</term> <note>A "dog-headed" baboon, sacred to the Egyptian god Thoth (Hermes).</note>, or at least with the feathers of a swallow, it brings an immediate remedy against every kind of poison. Nor is it at all less effective than the <term>moly</term> <note>A mythical herb with a black root and white flower.</note> which Mercury once gave to Odysseus. It is not only powerful against poison, but also offers no common advantage to anyone preparing to approach a king in any manner; such a ring should be worn especially by those who have decided to seek from a king some <insert>lucrative</insert> <note>original: "non ieiunum," literally "not fasting," meaning a wealthy or "fat" position.</note> priesthood, or an archdeaconry, or a <term>bishopric</term> <note>original: "episcopatum," literally an "overseer-ship."</note>—for that is what they call it. The same gem wards off a heavy head and brings no small relief to those suffering from <term>blood-ailments</term> <note>original: "uēni malũ," likely referring to syphilis or gout, common ailments of the era.</note>, particularly for those who drink heavily. In these wonderful remedies, therefore, those wise men of old made no distinction between the eagle and the beetle.

Why, then, should anyone look down on the Beetle itself, when its image carved in small stones possesses such power? The mention of gems reminds me to add this: if the eagle prides itself on the gemstone named after it, the <term>aetite</term> <note>The "eagle-stone," a geode believed to assist in childbirth.</note>, the Beetle does not yield in this comparison. For there is a stone that owes its name to the beetle, called the <term>cantharias</term>, which mirrors the appearance of the entire insect so marvelously that you would not call it a carved image, but a true, living beetle preserved in a gem. Finally, if it is relevant to the matter, that beetle born from dung has been made famous by no fewer authors than the eagle, the king of birds. For if anyone, favoring the eagle, denies that the Beetle is comparable in this regard because the eagle was once held as a deity among the "thick-headed" <note>Erasmus uses "crassos" (thick/stupid) to mock the Thebans' perceived lack of intellect.</note> Thebans, I shall not strongly object—provided he remembers that the eagle shares this honor with crocodiles, long-tailed monkeys, and finally with onions and <insert>the sound of a fart</insert> <note>original: "ventris crepitu," the sound of the belly.</note>, since among the Egyptians all these monstrosities found divine honors. And if it is worth any consideration, in this comparison of empty godhood, there were those who also attributed divinity to the Beetle. We have now compared the two leaders in various ways.

There remains now for us to recount the causes of so terrible a war. Once, on Mount Etna, an eagle was hunting a certain hare; its talons were already drawn and it was hovering over its prey. The animal, nearly dead from fear and naturally timid, fled to the nearby burrow of a Beetle as if to a sanctuary. For in desperate situations and at the final crisis, protection is sought and hoped for from any source. Now, this Beetle was, as Homer says, <insert>great both in size and in boxing</insert> <note>original Greek: *pyx te megas te*. Erasmus is jokingly applying a description of the hero Ajax to a bug.</note>. For in that mountain, the nation of Beetles is said to be of a very fortunate offspring, so much so that the <term>Etnaen Beetle</term> <note>original Greek: *ho aitnaios kantharos*</note> became a famous proverb because of its remarkable body size. The hare, fleeing to this burrow, rolled itself as a suppliant at the Beetle's knees, begging and entreating that the Beetle’s household gods might protect its life against the most cruel of birds. 

At first, the Beetle was somewhat pleased with himself because there existed someone who wished to owe his life to him, and because he believed such a great thing could be provided by him. Finally, it seemed a matter of great pride that his burrow—which all men usually pass by with plugged nostrils, cursing it—should be the place to which one would flee for safety as if to a sacred altar or the statue of a prince. 

The Beetle immediately flew out to meet the eagle and tried to soothe its rage with these words: "The greater your power, the more it becomes you to spare the innocent. Do not stain your feasts with the death of an innocent creature. Thus may your own nest always be free from this kind of calamity. It belongs to a noble and kingly spirit to grant pardon even to the unworthy. Let the reverence for my home—which equity and laws wish to be safe and inviolable for everyone, and which custom approves—benefit this petitioner, if not by my authority, then certainly by my zeal. Do not despise our person or 'beetle-arms.' But hope that the gods remember what is right and what is wrong. If the fate of violated sanctuaries does not move you—though it will one day return upon your own head—at least revere Jupiter the Greatest, whom you will offend three times in this one act. This is my guest, and you will offend <term>Jupiter of Guests</term> <note>original Greek: *xenion* (Zeus Xenios).</note>; he is my suppliant, and you will violate <term>Jupiter of Suppliants</term> <note>original Greek: *hiketesion* (Zeus Hikesios).</note>; finally, as he is a friend to a friend, you will offend <term>Jupiter of Friendship</term> <note>original Greek: *philion* (Zeus Philios).</note>. You know what certain wraths the angered Jupiter is accustomed to conceive, and how severely he punishes when provoked—you, who serve as the weapon-bearer to his fury! He does not permit everything to his own subjects, nor does he forgive all their whims."

But as the Beetle prepared to say more, the eagle struck him with its wings and threw him headlong to the ground. Then, before the very eyes of the Beetle, the eagle most cruelly throttled and tore the hare to pieces despite its pleas, and carried the mangled remains to its pitiless nest. Neither his authority, nor his prayers, nor his threats had any weight with the eagle. Yet she would not have despised him so if her wisdom had been as great as her pride and strength; or if it had come to her mind how once a lion, in the extreme crisis of its life, was saved by a mouse; or how that gift of life, which the tyrant of all four-legged beasts could scarcely give to himself, was given by such a lowly and despised little creature when the opportunity arose. Or <note>catchword: cogitasset</note> if she had <insert>thought</insert> of how an ant, provoked by a kindness, saved the life of a dove by biting a fowler...

Erasmus is narrating the Aesopic fable where an eagle has ignored the beetle's pleas for mercy on behalf of a hare. The beetle, insulted and grieving, now plots a revenge that transcends his small size, illustrating how even the most powerful can be brought low by those they despise.</meta>

### THE THIRD THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY
#### 777

...no one is so humble, or of such lowly fortune, that they cannot, given the opportunity, both benefit a friend and harm an enemy, even the most powerful. But at that time, none of these thoughts occurred to the eagle; she was entirely possessed by her present prey and enjoyed it. That insult sank deeper into the heart of the high-souled Beetle than anyone would have believed. His lofty and <term>titanic</term> <note>referring to the Titans of myth who dared to challenge the gods</note> spirit was spurred on, partly by shame—because in so just a cause, his authority had carried so little weight—and partly by pity, because an innocent and defenseless animal had been so cruelly torn to pieces. Furthermore, there was the pain that he had been so fiercely and with such impunity held in contempt by the eagle, even though he was not a creature to be despised, as she would soon see. For to no one is their own authority a light matter. Now it also occurred to him that the entire race of Beetles would fall into contempt if this deed of the eagle’s was allowed to pass unpunished. And then the Beetle took action. Indeed, it was just as <term>Calchas</term> <note>The seer in Homer's Iliad</note> said of <term>Agamemnon</term> and other kings:

> For even if he swallows his anger for that same day, yet he still keeps resentment in his heart afterward, until he fulfills it in his breast. <note>original Greek: "Εἴπερ γάρ τε χόλον γε καὶ αὐτῆμαρ καταπέψῃ, Ἀλλά γε καὶ μετόπισθεν ἔχει κότον, ὄφρα τελέσσῃ Ἐν στήθεσσιν ἑοῖσι." from Homer, Iliad 1.81-83.</note>

Therefore, he calls all arts and all guiles into his heart. He does not plot a common punishment; he turned over in his mind a total slaughter and absolute <term>panolethria</term> <note>original Greek: πανωλεθρίαν, meaning "total destruction" or "utter ruin."</note>. But since he judged it not safe enough to try the fortune of war against the eagle itself—an enemy so warlike—not only because he was inferior in forces, but also because <term>Mars</term> <note>The Roman god of war</note> is a stupid and senseless god, no less blind than <term>Plutus</term> <note>The god of wealth</note> or <term>Cupid</term>, and often favors the worse cause. But even if he had been perfectly equal in strength, and even if those with the better cause fought more successfully, he still saw a way in which he could torture the eagle more grievously and satisfy his hatred with a fuller vengeance: if he destroyed her offspring, he would kill the eagle while she was still living and feeling, through a long death. In nothing are parents more grievously tortured than in their children. So much so, that those who neglect the torments of their own bodies cannot bear the agony of their children. He had seen donkeys, with a marvelous contempt for life, rush through fires to help their foals; he had seen examples of this spirit in many animals. He reckoned that the eagle was not exempt from these common feelings. Finally, he judged it safer for his own race if he destroyed such a persistent enemy from the very "root," as they say. He had heard, I believe, that celebrated proverb:

> Foolish is he who, having killed the father, leaves the children behind. <note>original Greek: "Νήπιος ὃς πατέρα κτείνας παῖδας καταλείπῃ." A Greek proverb warning against leaving survivors of a defeated enemy.</note>

A certain flattering hope also tickled him: if the deed succeeded, it might happen that with the eagle overthrown, he himself might seize the kingdom. and as pain makes one not only brave and intrepid, but also sagacious, he diligently scouted the place where the enemy had hidden the hope of her future offspring. Having tracked this down, he went to <term>Vulcan</term> <note>Hephaestus, the blacksmith god</note>, with whom he had some familiarity because of the similarity of their color <note>referring to the beetle's dark, metallic appearance, like a smith covered in soot</note>. He begged him to forge armor for him that would not be heavy for flying, yet would protect him against moderate force. Vulcan armed the Beetle from the top of his head to the very tip of his heel with those arms which he still uses today; for before this, he was unarmed, like the flies. The nest was far removed from there, on a high and sheer cliff, built and fortified with a great mass of brushwood and straw. Whether my excellent Beetle flew here or crawled, is not quite clear; certainly, he arrived. There are some who say that when he was being struck by the eagle’s wings, he clung to her secretly and was carried into the nest by the unknowing eagle. And so the Beetle penetrated to a place where not even humans—than whom no animal is more insidious or more ingenious at doing harm—could have reached. He hid himself in ambush among the straw and, having found a suitable time, he pushed the eagle’s eggs out of the nest, one after another, until none were left. As they fell, they were shattered; the chicks themselves, still unformed, were miserably dashed against the rocks and robbed of life before they had even received the sense of living. Nor was the Beetle’s grieving heart content with this atrocious punishment. There is a gem of primary nobility which the Greeks call <term>aëtites</term> <note>from the Greek "aetos" (eagle); the "eagle-stone," a hollow geode with a smaller stone loose inside</note> after the eagle’s name. It is not unlike an egg and is even distinguished by sex; for in the female, you will find an offspring enclosed, almost in the appearance of a chick. It has a marvelous power for inducing birth. For this reason, even today it is applied to women in labor to accelerate the birth. A pair of this kind the eagle is accustomed to place in her nest; otherwise, she would never lay eggs, or certainly would not hatch the chicks. Even this treasure the Beetle cast down from the nest, so that he might strip away the faculty of breeding for the future; the stones, hitting the sharp rocks, shattered into tiny pieces. Even these things did not yet seem enough for the Beetle's wrath. He thought it a light calamity unless he could also enjoy the enemy's grief and lamentations; therefore, he hid himself deep in the straw again. The eagle returned, beheld the new slaughter of her race, and saw her own vitals torn apart piece by piece; she saw the noble gem...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES
## 778

The eagle laments an inestimable loss: she cries out, shrieks, bellows, screeches, wails, and calls the gods to witness. With those eyes of hers, which grief had now sharpened, she scans the horizon for so potent an enemy. To her mind come all sorts of possibilities as she considers the matter, except for that despised Beetle. She prays for dire threats and calamities upon whoever was the author of such great ruin. Meanwhile, how much pleasure do you think the Beetle felt in his soul while he heard all this? What should the wretched bird do? She had to fly off again to the **Fortunate Islands**, for from nowhere else are the *eagle-stones* <note>original: *ἀετίτης* (aetites). These were hollow stones believed to be found in eagles' nests, thought in antiquity to protect the young and aid in labor.</note> brought. Another pair must be found. The nest is moved to a place much more remote and higher up. She lays her eggs again; yet into this very place the unknown enemy penetrates. He lays waste to everything, repeating the entire tragedy of before. Once more the eagle migrates from here to a safer stronghold; she lays other eggs; she employs other eagle-stones. Once more the Beetle is there. There is neither limit nor end to the fleeing and the pursuing, until the bird, exhausted by so many disasters, decided to **weigh her last anchor** <note>A nautical metaphor for a final, desperate resort.</note> and, distrusting her own strength, fled to the protection of the gods. 

She approaches Jupiter and explains the tragedy of her calamity—an enemy so powerful and, what was most grievous, unknown; so that, having suffered so much, even the power to take revenge was snatched away. She adds that this destruction of hers pertains to Jupiter himself: the gift of empire he had bestowed would perish, and his armor-bearer would have to be changed. If the enemy continued as he had begun, he would strike; it was no small thing to use familiar and known servants, even if the novelty in the substituted **Ganymede** <note>The beautiful Trojan prince whom Jupiter, in the form of an eagle, abducted to be his cupbearer on Olympus.</note> had succeeded happily. Jupiter is moved by the danger to his attendant, especially since the service of the recently snatched Ganymede remained fresh in his mind. He orders that, if she wishes, she should lay her eggs in his own lap; there, or nowhere at all, would they be safe. The bird obeys, and in the lap of the highest Jupiter she deposits the last hope of her race, having prayed much—by those most happy eggs which **Leda** <note>In myth, Leda was visited by Jupiter in the form of a swan; she laid eggs from which Helen of Troy and the Dioscuri were hatched.</note> had once borne him—that he might guard her own in good faith. 

What does persistent grief of mind not achieve? I fear lest this seem beyond belief to some. The unconquered Beetle flies up to the very citadel of highest Jupiter, perhaps aided by the favor of some divinity. He prepares a little ball made from dung for this purpose and drops it into Jupiter’s lap. Jupiter, being unaccustomed to filth—since he lives in the purest part of the world and is removed from earthly contagion by a vast distance—is offended by the foul smell. Striving to shake the dung from his lap, he accidentally casts down the eagle’s eggs. Falling from such a height, they perished, naturally, before they even touched the ground. And thus, at last, that many-times clever craftsman was recognized, and this very thing added a heap of pleasure to the Beetle: it pleased him to be known. It moved the eagle, for she learned of the deed from Jupiter himself; it added no small weight of grief that the author of her calamity was so contemptible. Since this is some small consolation in misfortune: if one is overcome by a great enemy. From this point, as if anew, a dire war arose between them. Wherever she sees them, the eagle harasses, snatches, tramples, and destroys the race of Beetles. In turn, the Beetle strains every nerve toward the destruction of the eagle. Thus, there is no delay, no rest, and no end to the preying, the ambushing, and the slaughtering, unless both races were to be utterly and fundamentally wiped out, so that you might call it a **Cadmean victory** <note>A victory that proves as costly or ruinous to the victor as it does to the defeated.</note>; to such a degree, with the spirits of gladiators, did each seek a way against the other. 

The eagle could not be conquered, nor did the Beetle know how to yield. At last, Jupiter thinks he must assist in such great dangers and tries privately to settle the matter between them. The more he tries, the more their hatred grows raw, their anger swells, and their fire seethes. He was, without doubt, more inclined toward the eagle’s side; but on the other hand, a most pernicious example moved him, if anyone were allowed with impunity to hold Jupiter **the Protector of Suppliants**, **the Protector of Friends**, or **the Protector of Guests** <note>original: *ἱκετήσιον, Φíλιον, ξένιον*. These are sacred titles of Jupiter (Zeus) that govern the laws of hospitality and mercy.</note> in contempt. Therefore, he does what is customary in the extreme crisis of affairs: he calls the gods to a council. Having spoken a few introductory words, he proposes the matter as it happened. By the proclamation of Mercury, the power of speaking is given; opinions are read and spoken. It was varied according to their interests. The more lowly gods generally favored the Beetle. From among the greatest, even **Juno** <note>Jupiter's wife, who famously hated the eagle because it had brought Ganymede—her husband's young favorite—to Olympus.</note> fervently supported him, naturally out of hatred for Ganymede and hostile to the eagle’s affairs. At last, they **went with their feet** <note>A reference to the Roman Senate's method of voting by physically moving to one side of the chamber or the other.</note> into this decree of the senate, which Mercury persuaded them of with his eloquent voice and Vulcan engraved in bronze: that the Beetle and the eagle should wage eternal war at their own discretion. Whatever inconvenience happens to either, it shall not be permitted to bring it to court; they shall be treated harshly in war. Whatever anyone snatches, they shall possess by right of war—only the total destruction of either race was not pleasing to the gods. Therefore, for thirty days, during which the eagle broods, they shall stay their hands and a truce shall be kept. Nor shall it be lawful for Beetles to appear in public during that time, so that the eagle, in addition to the labor of warming her eggs in hunger, would not also have to face the weariness of war. Jupiter added this from his own interest, even though some protested: "It is fair," he said, "that out of such immense spaces of the earth, even a small corner, like an asylum, should remain for my attendant where she may be safe from the incursion of Beetles." But now I introduce a new example. There are places that know no wolf; there are those into which no...

<summary>This page recounts the Beetle's clever revenge against the Eagle, involving Jupiter and the eventual establishment of a divine decree regulating their eternal warfare. It serves as a political allegory for how even the smallest players can disrupt the highest powers through persistence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the long commentary on the adage "The Beetle searches for the Eagle." After the beetle's persistent destruction of the eagle's eggs, the conflict has reached the divine court of Jupiter on Olympus.</meta>

<page-num>779</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>

...poisons: there are places where moles do not live. I myself shall mark out a space of several acres in Thrace near Olynthus, in which, if in any way—whether by accident or design, whether willingly or unwillingly—a Beetle sets foot, it shall be a capital offense. Nor shall it be lawful to exit once one has entered, but there he shall twist and turn himself until he dies. To this place they gave the name **Cantharolethrus** <note>original: "Cantharolethrus," from the Greek *kantharos* (beetle) and *olethros* (destruction). It literally means "Beetle-bane."</note>, so that the Beetle, warned by the very name, may know it is all over for him if he dares to break into that place against our decree. The eagle is an exile from Rhodes, lest it seem inhumane for the Beetle to be excluded from Olynthus. Thus he spoke, and shook all Olympus with his nod.

All the assembly of the gods roared their approval. This decree is valid even to this day, and will always be valid. A fatal war persists between Beetles and eagles; during the days when the eagle broods, the children of the Beetles appear nowhere. They avoid that place designated by Jupiter with the greatest care; if anyone carries one in, it immediately expires. If anyone requires proof of this matter, Pliny offers testimony in the eleventh book, chapter 28. And even more weight is given by an even graver authority, Plutarch, in his commentary *On Tranquility of Mind*. 

But I know well enough, excellent reader, what you have been thinking for a while now: "What came into his mind to babble so many trifles about nothing? He is making not just an **elephant out of a fly** <note>A common ancient proverb for making a great deal out of a small matter.</note>, as they say, but a giant out of a Beetle." As if it were not enough effort to unroll thousands of adages, unless he also kills us with such wordy fables. I shall tell you. As every man has his own opinion, there are some to whom I seem poor and meager in explaining adages. For they think it only magnificent if one extends a volume to an immense size. I wished to show those people that I am briefer in other places by choice; that there would be no lack of material to enrich the work if I had preferred to show off my abundance rather than study to help the reader. But to return to the business of proverbs, the comic poet Aristophanes mentions this fable in *Peace*, in these verses:

<margin>
It was found in all those Aesopic tales, / that he alone of winged creatures reached the gods. / You tell an unbelievable story, father, father, / how a foul-smelling creature went to the gods? / He went because of an old grudge against the eagle, / rolling out her eggs and seeking mutual vengeance.
</margin>

->that is,<-

> In Aesop's fables it is found,
> That he alone of birds approached the gods.
> An unbelievable tale you tell, father, father,
> That a filthy and stinking creature went to the gods.
> He arrived once, I say, due to a bitter rivalry,
> Which he had with the eagle, rolling away her eggs,
> And seeking mutual punishment from his enemy.

The fable warns that no enemy should be despised by anyone, however lowly their fortune. For there are certain little men of the lowest lot, yet malicious, no less black than Beetles, no less stinking, and no less abject, who nevertheless, through a certain stubborn malice of character—though they can be of no use to any mortal—frequently cause trouble even for great men. They terrify with their blackness, they clamor with their buzzing, they disturb with their stench; they fly around, cling, and lie in wait, so that it is sometimes better to take up a rivalry with great men than to provoke these Beetles, whom one would be ashamed even to have conquered, and whom you can neither shake off nor struggle against without coming away more contaminated.

# Timid Plutus. 11

<margin>Wealth is cowardly.</margin> That is, Timid **Plutus** <note>The personification of Wealth in Greek mythology.</note>. For Aristophanes introduces Plutus in this manner, and Lucian, imitating him in his *Timon*, depicts him fearing everything and trusting no one. Nor do riches bring a different state of mind to the wealthy, while poverty, by contrast, sleeps soundly **on both ears** <note>A Latin idiom, *in utramvis aurem dormire*, meaning to be free from care or worry.</note>. Aristophanes indicates the commonly discussed timidity of wealth when he says,

<margin>But they say entirely that / Wealth is a most timid thing.</margin>

->that is,<-

> Indeed, everyone keeps saying this,
> That wealth is something most timid.

The commentator notes that the comic poet alluded to that line of Euripides,

<margin>Wealth is a cowardly evil and a lover of its own life.</margin>

->that is,<-

<meta>catchword: Res</meta>

<meta>This page transitions from the long fable of the Beetle and the Eagle into a series of shorter adages concerning the anxieties of wealth, the origins of "panic," and the practicalities of agriculture. <page-num>780</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

Wealth is a thing that clings to life; it is a fearful evil.

This was said because many people lay snares for the wealthy: specifically robbers, legacy-hunters, princes, sycophants <note>Professional informers or "yes-men" in ancient Greece</note>, and sometimes even a wife and children. For this reason Euripides added the phrase <gloss>of a base soul</gloss> <note>original: ψυχου κακου</note>, either because they have more reason to want to live than those of slender means, or because they are often anxious about their lives because of their riches. Juvenal explains this elegantly:

> Though you carry but a few small vessels of pure silver,
> Setting out on a journey by night, you will fear the sword and the spear,
> And you will tremble at the shadow of a reed moving in the moonlight.
> The empty-handed traveler will sing in the face of the robber.

In short, in every business the rich man is more fearful than the poor one. He fortifies his house more carefully for fear of thieves. He fears storms because of the grain he has in the fields and the merchandise he has at sea. He fears his friends, lest he be forced to give them something if they ask. He fears his enemies, lest they do him some harm. He is more timid in his speech for fear of a fine. He does and says everything more circumspectly because of the slander that is usually directed at the wealthy—precisely because they have something that can be taken away. If war looms, the rich man is the first to be tormented. Finally, he is not even free from superstition, fearing that some unfriendly deity might send him a loss.

### A Panic occurrence.

The ancients called a sudden and empty disturbance of the mind <gloss>Panic</gloss> <note>original: Πανικὸν</gloss>. For the ancients believed that the god Pan sent sudden terrors and mental consternations, very similar to those of the "lymphatics" <note>Those possessed by nymphs or driven to madness</note>, which were so powerful that people lost not only their reason but their very minds. This often happens in an army when, for no apparent reason, both men and horses are thrown into confusion. Euripides mentions this in his play *Rhesus*:

<gloss>But surely you are terrified by the trembling lash of Pan, son of Cronus.</gloss> <note>original: Ἀλλ’ ἦ κρονὶς πανὸς τρομερᾷ μάστιγι φοβῇ</note>

These are the words of Hector to the guards who report that a new tumult is rising in the camp; he denies that the movement is a "Panic" one. Pindar writes in his *Nemean Odes* that one should not blame a lack of bravery if men flee in a tumult of this kind:

<gloss>For in divine terrors, even the children of the gods flee.</gloss> <note>original: Ἐν γὰρ δαιμονίοις φόβοις φεύγοντι καὶ παῖδες θεῶν</note>

He calls "Panic" terrors <gloss>divine terrors</gloss>. It is said that this same god was the first to discover the twisted and spiral shell which in Greek is called <gloss>kochlos</gloss> <note>original: κόχλος</note>, that is, a snail or conch. By sounding it, he once turned to flight the Titans against whom he was fighting. Pausanias says in his *Description of Phocis*: <gloss>During the night a Panic fear fell upon them, for they say that terrors arising from no cause are sent by him.</gloss> Angelo Poliziano discusses this matter more copiously in the seventy-eighth note of his *Miscellanea*, using evidence even from the Greek civil gods.

Cicero frequently refers to this adage in his letters to Atticus: "I think there will be a most foul war, unless, as you know, some Panic occurrence happens." And elsewhere: "Regarding Ventidius, I think it is a Panic [event]." Also elsewhere: "They bring a great rumor that while Antony was in Rome, all the grain was being carried off; it is certainly a <gloss>Panic</gloss> [rumor]." And elsewhere: "Meanwhile, for you know that certain things are called <gloss>Panic</gloss>, as well as <gloss>the empty fears of war</gloss> <note>original: τὰ κενὰ τοῦ πολέμου</note>, at the rumor of our arrival, courage came to Cassius who was held at Antioch, and fear was struck into the Parthians." The same to Tiro: "Even though our friend Atticus, who once perceived that I was moved by <gloss>Panics</gloss>, still thinks the same; he does not see with what defenses of philosophy I am hedged in." And by Hercules, because he is timid himself, <gloss>he creates a disturbance</gloss> <note>original: θορυβοποιεῖ</note> and is moved by Panics. I believe Apuleius also alluded to this in his *The Golden Ass*, when he has Psyche meet Pan as she is hurrying to the mountain peak.

### Nothing is less profitable than to cultivate a field perfectly.

Pliny testifies in Book 18, Chapter 6, that this was like an adage among the ancients. "It might seem rash," he says, "to have set down a single saying of the ancients, and they might perhaps find it entirely incredible, that nothing is less profitable than to cultivate a field perfectly." L. Tatius Rufus, born of the lowest rank and having earned the consulship through military industry, was otherwise a man of ancient thriftiness. Having obtained about seventy million sesterces <note>A massive sum of Roman currency</note> through the liberality of the late Augustus, he exhausted his wealth to the point of disinheriting his heir by buying up fields in Picenum and cultivating them for the sake of glory. Do we therefore advocate for destruction and hunger? Far from it! By Hercules, I judge moderation to be the most useful of all things. To cultivate "well" is necessary; to cultivate "superbly" is ruinous. Thus far Pliny. Terence also alluded to this when he says in the *Phormio*: "By our own fault we make it profitable for men to be bad."

# THE THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<page-num>781</page-num>

...we strive too much to be called good and kind. Likewise that line from Horace:
*The flight from a fault leads into a vice, if it lacks skill.* <note>Horace, *Ars Poetica* 31. Erasmus is discussing the "Golden Mean"—the idea that trying too hard to avoid one mistake can lead you directly into the opposite error.</note>
Finally, there is the proverb of the Hebrews warning: *Let no one be too righteous.* <note>Ecclesiastes 7:16</note>

->Faster than asparagus is cooked.<-
<margin>v</margin>
*Faster than asparagus is cooked.* <note>original: "Citius quàm asparagi coquuntur"</note> This is said of a matter handled with extreme haste. There are certain proverbial figures of speech that were particularly pleasing to Augustus Caesar; among these is the one recorded by Tranquillus <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, the Roman historian</note> when he writes that Augustus, to express the speed of a finished task, used to say: *Faster than asparagus is cooked.* He used this repeatedly in his letters. Asparagus is a type of prickly herb, useful in medicine and pleasant as food; its tips, before they harden, are cooked lightly, just enough to remove their rawness. It is called *asparagus* because the finest kinds are not cultivated but grow wild, as Athenaeus said. Some learned men suggest that a similar thing is said of salted fish: *Faster than salted fish is cooked,* because certain fish preserved in salt, or dried by smoke or wind, may even be eaten raw or only very lightly boiled. However, I have not yet found this proverb in the works of Athenaeus where they cite it. Close to this is another saying to be discussed elsewhere: *The small fry to the fire.* <note>original: "ἀφύα ἐπὶ πῦρ" (aphya epi pyr). Small, thin fish like anchovies cook almost instantly.</note>

->The mask of friendship.<-
<margin>vi</margin>
*To strip away the mask of friendship within friendship.* <note>original: "τὸ τῆς φιλίας ἀφελῶν τῆ φιλíᾳ"</note> That is, we say we "strip away the mask of friendship" when we openly act and speak among friends exactly as we feel in our hearts, bringing forth whatever is locked in our breast. For a face that disagrees with the soul is more truly a mask <term>persona|In Latin, "persona" originally meant a theatrical mask worn by actors to represent a character</term> than a face. It was elegantly said by Seneca regarding Caesar, that he preferred the mask to the face—that is, he preferred to *seem* rather than to *be*. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> writes in the fifth book of his *Tusculan Disputations* that Epicurus merely "put on the mask of a philosopher." Martial writes:

> You lie about being young, Lentine, with your dyed hair;
> So suddenly a crow, you who were just a swan.
> You don't deceive everyone; Proserpina <note>Queen of the Underworld</note> knows you are gray,
> She will strip that mask from your head.

Nor does "mask" always sound in a negative sense. For when Marcus Tullius writes in *On Duties*: *For he puts off the mask of a friend when he puts on that of a judge,* he does not mean a fake friend or a fake judge. The metaphor is simply drawn from the masks of stage actors.

->Use your own wagons, and do not care about the donkeys.<-
<margin>vii</margin>
*I assign you to your own wagon; have little care for the donkeys.* <note>original: "ἀπονέμω σὶ σῆς ἁμάξης, τὴν δ' ὄνων ὀλίγ' μέλει"</note>
This is a trochaic tetrameter verse. By this proverb, one was warned to take care of one's own affairs and enjoy them, being negligent and indifferent toward the affairs of others. The metaphor is derived from the fact that those who have a wagon at home have no need to hire donkeys from elsewhere to carry their loads.

->The Libyan beast.<-
<margin>viii</margin>
*The Libyan beast.* <note>original: "Λιβυκὸν θηρίον"</note> This is recorded by Diogenianus. It was once said of a man who was crafty, cunning, a "turn-coat," of varied habits and a double-edged nature. Cicero testifies that Catiline was this sort of portent. The saying arose because in Libya, various species of wild beasts often interbreed; thus new types of monsters are frequently produced there as a spectacle, which were then brought to Rome by provincial governors.

->Libya always brings something evil.<-
<margin>ix</margin>
From the same source flowed this saying: *Libya always brings something evil.* <note>original: "ἀεὶ φέρει τὶ λιβύη κακόν"</note> This was because, as I said, monsters were brought to Rome from there. From this, it can also be twisted to refer to the character and nature of that nation: just as the region is fertile in poisons, so is the nature of the people pestilential. It is particularly suited to oath-breakers and those who alter their agreements.

->Africa always brings something new.<-
<margin>x</margin>
Very similar to this is the line from Pliny, which he records in his *Natural History*, that *Libya always brings something new.* This was said because, in that thirsty region, many species of wild beasts are forced to gather at a single river for the sake of drinking; there, through the varied mixing of "violent Venus" <note>An evocative way of describing mating or cross-breeding</note>, various forms of monsters are born, and new ones appear from time to time. Furthermore, Pliny took this from Aristotle, in whose work it is recorded in the second book of *The Generation of Animals*, chapter five. Anaxilas, in the fourth book of Athenaeus, humorously twisted the matter:
*Adultery, by the gods, is just like Libya...* <note>The text cuts off here, but refers to the constant production of "new monsters" or complications.</note>

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, THE ADAGES</header>

*Always something new, every year she brings forth a beast.* <note>original: "Ἀεὶ καινὸν, καθ' ἐνιαυτὸν τίκτει θηρίον." This is a variation of the famous proverb "Always something new from Africa."</note> That is,
->But music, just like the African land, by the gods,<-
->always produces some new beast every year.<-

I am aware that the Greek verse does not stand up in its latter part, but that is how the Aldine edition <note>The prestigious Venetian press founded by Aldus Manutius, which published Erasmus's works.</note> has it, and I do not quite see how it can be restored, unless perhaps instead of "every year" <note>original: "καθ' ἐνιαυτὸν"</note> we should read "in itself," <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῇ"</note> although even then the meter remains shaky; perhaps the word "beast" <note>original: "θηρίον"</note> should be omitted, and instead of "every year" <note>original: "καθ' ἐνιαυτὸν"</note> we should put "in a year." <note>original: "ἐνιαυτῷ"</note> It will apply to men of slippery faith, who are always eager to innovate or change things.

### African bird.

*Libyan bird.* <note>original: "Λιβυκὸν ὄρνεον"</note> That is, an African bird. It is mentioned by Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient world.</note> regarding very large creatures, because birds of enormous size are brought from there. Horace used it to describe a very luxurious dish:
*No African bird would descend into my stomach*
*more pleasantly than an olive picked from*
*the richest branches of the trees.* <note>Horace, *Epodes* 2.53</note>
For Africa used to send very large chickens, the same ones they call Numidian birds. Acron <note>A Roman commentator on Horace.</note> seems to think he means the ostrich, which is itself a bird of miraculous body mass. In my opinion, it could also be aptly thrown at a man notable for his foreign attire. Even Plautus somewhere calls a Carthaginian a "bird" on account of his long sleeves, which hung down on both sides like wings. The proverb appears in Aristophanes' *The Birds*. The commentator indicates it applies to barbarians and the fearful. For very large men are almost always more timid. Terence says: *This great good-for-nothing.*

## It is the part of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to skin them.

This remains a celebrated saying commonly used today whenever a tax collector is too harsh and persistent. You want the fleece and the skin too: as if it were not enough to be content with the wool. Tiberius Caesar, the author of this sentiment, either discovered or certainly made use of this adage. For when he was urged by his friends to increase the taxes of the provinces, he wrote back: *It is the part of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to skin them.* <note>Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius* 32</note> Now, to "skin" <note>original: "deglubere"</note> means to pull off the hide. It is drawn from the language of rustics, who use the term "to skin" for shaking out a husk or pod, or stripping a grain of its casing; from which Catullus twisted the meaning into an obscene sense when he speaks of a man being "skinned" by a woman. And Apuleius's character Fotis says she is accustomed to "skin" living men. Therefore, they "shear" who despoil in such a way that they leave something behind so that the wealth can grow back. They "skin" who leave nothing remaining. For shorn wool grows back. Once the hide is pulled off, there is nothing left for you to take. Alexander, King of the Macedonians, surnamed the Great, expressed the same sentiment with a different metaphor. For when someone suggested that much more tax could be taken from his subjects, he replied: *I hate the gardener who cuts the herbs out by the roots.* <note>original: "μισῶ τὸν κηπωρὸν τὸν ἐκ ῥιζῶν ἐκτέμνοντα τὰ λάχανα."</note> Finally, this very phrase "from the roots," <note>original: "ῥιζóθεν"</note> and likewise among the Latins "to the roots," "as far as the stalks," "from the stem," "from the lowest stem," and other metaphors of this kind, smack of the nature of a proverb.

## The smell of profit is good from any source.

Witty, but nevertheless a pestilential saying of Vespasian. Being a man shamefully greedy, he had imposed a tax on urine; when he was rebuked for this by his son Titus, because he was making a profit from such a disgusting matter, shortly thereafter Vespasian held the money collected from the tax to his son's nose and asked if it stank. From this, Juvenal wrote:
->The smell of profit is good, from any source whatsoever.<- <note>Juvenal, *Satires* 14.204</note>
Alluding to this, Ammianus said in his twenty-second book: *And profit from every opportunity.* By now, even that little verse of Ennius has passed not only into common speech, but deep into the hearts and lives of men:
> No one cares where you get it from, but you must have it.
Indeed, we seriously follow that which was said ironically by Horace:
->O citizens, citizens, money must be sought first, virtue after the coins.<- <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.53</note>
Cephisodorus, in the third book of Athenaeus, teaches that among famous and wise poets, certain disapproved sentiments can be found, such as that in Archilochus: *To flay or despoil any man you please.* <note>original: "πᾶντ' ἀναδην"</note> Or in that saying of Theodorus: *To have more than is fair, yet to praise what is equal.* <note>original: "ἐν μὲν πλέον ἔχειν, ἐπαινεῖν δὲ τὸ ἴσον"</note> Or in Euripides, when he says *the tongue has sworn* <note>original: "τὴν γλῶτταν ὀμωμοκέναι"</note> (meaning that the mind remains unsworn), which we have discussed elsewhere. Or in Sophocles:
*He says such things, how can he do so by grace and by force...*

<page-num>783</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>

"And I, not even I, like the wise, praise what is just, while I hold fast to profit." <note>original: "κἀγὼ, οὐδ' αὐτὸς ὥσπερ οἱ σοφοὶ τὰ μὲν δίκαι' ἐπαίνω, τῷ δὲ κέρδει'νψ ἔχω." This reflects a common ancient theme of the tension between morality and financial gain.</note> That is,
> I say these things to you to please you, I do not command them,
> But I myself, as wise men are accustomed to do,
> Praise what is just, but otherwise stick to profit.

The same author <note>Athenaeus, a Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note> said elsewhere, "Nothing is bad if it comes with profit." <note>original: "μηδὲν σὺν κέρδει κακόν."</note> In Homer, he depicts Juno plotting against Jupiter and portrays Mars as an adulterer. These examples are from Athenaeus. It is a wonder, moreover, that the people are indignant at poets or actors if they ever recite such things in the theaters, when each person ought rather to be indignant at himself for pursuing in his own life the very things whose mention he could not bear in the theater.

### XIV. Profit is better than shame.

*Profit is better than shame.* <note>original: "Κέρδος αἰσχύνης ἄμεινον."</note> That is, profit takes precedence over a sense of modesty. Plautus says in his play *Pseudolus*: "That which causes shame is borne much more easily than that which causes regret." <note>original: "Nimio illud quod pudet facilius fertur, quam illud quod piget."</note> He expressed the same sentiment differently in *Trinummus*: "By Pollux, it is better to be shamed than to be pained," using almost the same number of letters.

This is a sentiment unworthy of a good man, and for that reason, it is spoken in the first instance by a pimp, and in the second by an old man. But he conveniently seized upon even a less-than-honorable opinion for the sake of persuasion. Otherwise, it is far better to accept a loss of property than a loss of reputation. Terence alluded to this in *Phormio*: "Are you not ashamed of your vanity?" "Not as long as it is for my benefit." Indeed, even today, a common proverb bids modesty "farewell" <note>Meaning to discard or ignore it.</note> when a matter of money is at stake. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Listening to the Poets*, cites these six-foot verses from some unknown poet:
-> "Seek the reputation of being just, <-
-> but in deeds, follow the man who does anything as long as you profit." <-
That is,
> Despise the reputation for being just, and follow
> the man who does anything, whenever there is hope of profit.

He also cites this from Sophocles:
"Profit is sweet, even if it comes from lies." <note>original: "τὸ κέρδος ἡδὺ, κἂν ἀπὸ ψευδῶν ἔη."</note> That is,
Profit is sweet, even when it proceeds from falsehoods.

### XV. A thick coat is good in both winter and summer.

*A thick coat is good in both summer and winter.* <note>original: "Βαίτη κἂν θέρει, κἂν ἐν χειμῶνι ἀγαθόν." The "baeta" or "baite" was a rustic garment made of skins or coarse wool.</note> Suidas, who mentions this adage, describes the *Baeta* as a type of skin garment that seems suitable for both seasons. For in winter it keeps out the winds, and in summer, the sun. Julius Pollux, in the seventh book of his *On Vocabulary*, mentions the *baeta* among leather garments; he says it was a very long tunic that covered the whole body. It is applicable, therefore, to something that will be useful for many purposes: for example, to literature, which adorns the young and the old alike. Or to philosophy, which in prosperous times keeps one from insolence, and in adverse times ensures that we are not broken in spirit.

### XVI. Old wives' tales.

*Old wives' tales.* <note>original: "γραῶν ὕθλος." Literally "the idle talk of old women."</note> This refers to empty nonsense of the kind old women are prone to blurt out, when the vice of their age adds to the natural fault of their sex, doubling the disease of talkativeness. The proverb appears in Plato's *Theaetetus*: "For these things are indeed what is commonly called old wives' nonsense." Similarly, Cicero, in his speech *On His House*, spoke of "old-womanish superstition."

### XVII. Before one’s feet.

Something is said to be "before one’s feet" <note>original: "Ante pedes."</note> when it is obvious, or when it is present and close at hand, or imminent. Terence says:
"That is wisdom: not just to see what is right before your feet,
but also to look forward to those things which are to come."
So Pindar says in his last hymn, "Whatever is before the feet is always a better thing." <note>original: "τὸ δὲ πρὸ ποδὸς ἄρειον ἀεὶ χρῆμα πᾶν."</note> Lucian in *The False Logician*: "And you are ignorant of these common things and those things right at your feet." <note>original: "τὰ τὰ κοινὰ ταῦτα καὶ τὰ ἐν ποσὶν ἀγνοεῖ."</note> Philostratus in *Phoenix*: "Where are you going with your face held high, looking down on all the things that are at your feet?" And it is said to be "before the foot" when it is already pressing and threatening; it is said to be "in front" when it stands in the way, and "out of the way" <note>original: "ekpodon"</note> on the contrary. To be "rolling before the feet" <note>original: "prokylindesthai ton podon"</note> appears several times in Plato; that is, to be rolled before the feet, as if it were exposed. For instance, in the *Republic*, Book IV: "Long ago, my blessed friend, it seems to have been rolling before our feet from the beginning, and we did not see it, but we were most ridiculous, like those who hold something in their hands but sometimes look for what they have."

<summary>This page explores several proverbs regarding the conflict between profit and morality, the versatility of useful things (compared to a thick skin coat), and the importance of noticing what is obvious or immediate.</summary>

<page-num>784</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...even if they already possess something, they still seek what they have. <note>Erasmus is commenting on the redundancy of greed.</note> With a similar figure of speech, Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> said in the *Georgics*:
> In the hands of the lands, not here will I hold you with a long song,
> And through windings and long preambles. <note>original: "In manibus terræ, non hic te carmine longo, / Atq; per ambages & longa exorfa tenebo." This refers to keeping a subject close at hand rather than wandering into digressions.</note>

->They hunt others' goods with a white net.<-

It has the appearance of a proverb, what Plautus says in his play *Persa*: "Lest I should make those men appear anywhere... here they attack others' goods with a white net." <note>original: "Ne iſti faxim uſquã appar... hic albo reti aliena oppugnant bona."</note> He calls the false accusations of "quadruplators" <note>Professional informers in ancient Rome who received a quarter of the fine as a reward.</note> a "net." He calls it "white," alluding to the small tablets, the legal summons, and the written contracts with which a lawsuit is intended and driven. It is not entirely unpleasing to suggest he might have looked to the "album" <note>The white-painted board where the Praetor, a Roman official, posted the laws and legal procedures for the year.</note> of the praetor, on which the laws and legal formulas were set out. For even Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawgiver.</note> said that laws were similar to the webs of spiders.

->It is right for everyone to be shrewd toward their own gain.<-

There is a proverbial sentiment in Plautus, found in both the *Truculentus* and the *Asinaria*:
> It is right for everyone to be shrewd toward their own gain.
> <note>original: "Ad suum quemq; quæstum, æquum est esse callidum."</note>
If this is applied a bit more broadly, it will have a bit more grace. For example, one person is eager for profit, another is studious of fame, another is greedy for pleasures, another is thirsty for literature, and another pursues holiness. Each is watchful toward that which he seeks.

->You would have even found a needle.<-

In the same author [Plautus] in his *Menaechmi*, there is a proverbial hyperbole regarding a thing sought for diligently: "I believe you would have found it if you were looking for a needle." <note>original: "cum credo inueniſſes, ſi acum quæreres."</note> For a needle is most difficult to find, because its smallness easily deceives the eyes of the seeker.

->She brings forth wind-eggs.<-

"She brings forth wind-eggs" <note>original: "ὑπηνέμια τίκτει" (hypenemia tiktei).</note>. This is said of vain and frivolous inventions. It is a metaphor taken from birds that conceive eggs through the imagination of passion, but these eggs are empty—that is, they produce no offspring. Aristophanes in *The Birds* says:
> First of all, black-winged Night brought forth a wind-egg.
> <note>original: "τίκτει πρώτιστον ὑπηνέμιον νὺξ ἡ μελανόπτερος ὠόν."</note>
Aristotle demonstrates in the third book of *On the Generation of Animals* that these conceptions happen most often in those birds that are neither swift nor equipped with hooked claws, such as the partridge and the hen. The cause is that they abound more in excrement [excess matter]; swift and hooked-clawed birds are less fertile because in them the seminal matter is diverted into feathers and talons. These types of offspring are sometimes conceived upon hearing the voice of a male, as happens with partridges; sometimes from the rubbing of dust; and sometimes when females, for lack of a male, mount one another. Pliny is also an authority for this. The Greeks call these eggs *hypenemia* [subventanea] or *zephyria* [zephyr eggs], named after the west wind [Favonius]. From this, things that are vain are called *anemiaia* [windy]. Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "But come now, let us consider together whether it is a fertile birth or a wind-egg." <note>original: "ἀλλὰ φέρε δὴ κοινῇ σκεψώμεθα γόνιμον ἢ ἀνεμιαῖον τυγχάνει."</note> And Homer uses "anemolia" <note>original: "ἀνεμώλια"</note> to signify empty things, similar to the winds. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in his *Letters to Atticus* uses "anemophoreta" <note>original: "ἀνεμοφόρητα"</note>, meaning empty things carried by the wind, in reference to gladiators: "Regarding the other things you write, which are empty as the wind, inform me daily."

->Another Phrynondas.<-

"Another Phrynondas" <note>original: "Φρυνώνδας ἄλλος" (Phrynondas allos).</note>. This refers to a wicked man. Lucian mentions him in *The False Prophet* among famous criminals. Phrynondas, while he was a guest at Athens, lived during the Peloponnesian Wars; he was a crafty man, a mischief-maker, a deceiver, and a supreme master of all affairs, so that the man's name turned into a general term for the deed itself. Indeed, whenever people wanted someone to be understood as remarkably evil and criminal, they called him a Phrynondas. Thus Aristophanes in *Amphiaraus*, as cited by Suidas:
> O you scoundrel, you Phrynondas, you wretch.
> <note>original: "Ω μιαρὲ καὶ φρυνώνδα καὶ πονηρὲ σύ."</note>
Plato also used this in the *Protagoras*. Aeschines mentions these men in his speech against Ctesiphon: "Neither Phrynondas, nor Eurybatus, nor any other of the ancient villains was ever such a sorcerer and impostor." <note>original: "οὔτε φρυνώνδας, οὔτε εὐρύβατος, οὔτε ἄλλος οὐδεὶς πώποτε τῶν πάλαι πονηρῶν γόης καὶ μάγος ἐγένετο."</note>

->A pig through roses.<-

"A pig through roses" <note>original: "Ὗς διὰ ῥόδων" (Hys dia rhodon).</note>. Although in other copies it is written "a pig through pomegranates" <note>original: "ὗς διὰ ῥοίδων" (hys dia rhoidon).</note>. Neither spelling is quite satisfactory to me; rather, I think it should be read: "A pig th..." [text ends mid-sentence]

<page-num>785</page-num>
<header>THIRD THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>

*rhoias* <note>original: "ῥοιάς"</note>, so that it is a diminutive noun. Indeed, "rhoae" is what the Greeks call pomegranates. Eudemus cites the proverb from a play by Crates titled *The Earth-Dwellers* <note>original: "χθόνιοι"</note>, indicating it is usually said of the rustic and the intractable. Just as a pig cannot be easily led by pomegranates. <note>Pomegranates were considered delicacies; the proverb implies that fine things are wasted on the coarse.</note>

### A donkey is a bird. XXIV
*Onos ornis* <note>original: "Ὄνος ὄρνις"</note>. That is, "A donkey is a bird." It is found in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*. It was taken from a certain omen. For someone, being consulted about a man suffering from ill health, by chance saw a donkey rising after a fall, and at the same time heard someone else saying, "Do you see how he rose up?" <note>original: "βλέπεις πῶς ἐν ᾧ ἂν ἀνέστη"</note>. Seizing upon that omen, he immediately replied that the sick man would recover his health. Thus, Aristophanes jokes as if the donkey were a bird <note>Ancient Greeks looked to the flight and behavior of birds for omens, a practice called augury.</note> and possessed some power of prophecy. This proverb did not originate in comedy but was twisted into a joke by the common people and then used by the comic poet. It can be said quite timely whenever we gather some conclusion from a ridiculous piece of evidence.

### The arts of Sisyphus. XXV
*Sisyphou mechanai* <note>original: "Σισύφου μηχαναί"</note>. That is, "The arts of Sisyphus." These were said of crafty and cunning plans. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*:
->Then bring forth the clever tricks of Sisyphus.<-
Furthermore, the reason Sisyphus became a proverb for shrewdness was that verse of Homer's:
"Sisyphus, who was the craftiest of men." <note>original: "Σίσυφος ὃς κέρδιστος γένετ᾽ ἀνδρῶν"</note> That is:
"Sisyphus, than whom no other on earth was more cunning." Again, in the *Iliad*, Book 6:
"There lived Sisyphus, who was the craftiest of men."
From him, Ulysses <note>Also known as Odysseus.</note> traced his lineage, whom Homer everywhere depicts as sly and clever.

### A man like Thales. XXVI
*Anthropos Thales* <note>original: "Ἄνθρωπος Θαλῆς"</note>. That is, "A man like Thales." A proverbial irony used against a fool who strives to be considered wise. Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
->The man is a Thales, a Meton.<- <note>original: "Ἄνθρωπος Θαλῆς μέτωψ." Meton was a famous Athenian astronomer.</note>
The same in *The Clouds*:
->Why then do we look up to that man as a Thales?<-
For Thales was one of the Seven Sages of Greece. It is also found in Plautus: "Greetings, Thales," where it signifies a fool. <note>The joke relies on calling someone a "genius" when they are clearly the opposite.</note>

### Sardanapalus. XXVII
*Sardanapalus* <note>original: "Σαρδανἁπαλος"</note>. This man's name became a proverb because of his remarkable soft living. Aristophanes in *The Birds*: "Who is this Sardanapalus?" Sardanapalus was the son of Anacyndaraxis and the king of the Persian region of Nineveh. On the same day, he gained possession of Tarsus and Anchiale, two cities of Cilicia; however, he was so effeminate in his luxuries that he was accustomed to sit among eunuchs and girls, dressed in girlish attire. Apollodorus, as cited by the commentator on Aristophanes, records that an epitaph was inscribed on his tomb in Assyrian letters to this effect: "Eat, drink, make love, for the rest is worth nothing." <note>original: "ἔσθιε, πῖνε, ὄχευε, ὡς τὰ ἄλλα οὐδενὸς ἄξια"</note> Suidas records it in this form from Callisthenes: "But you, stranger, eat, drink, and play, as other human affairs are not worth this." <note>original: "σὺ δὲ ἔσθιε καὶ πῖνε καὶ παῖζε, ὡς τὰ ἄλλα ἀνθρώπια, οὐκ ὄντα τούτου ἄξια"</note>

### What, finally, might hands not achieve? XXVIII
Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
->What then could feet not accomplish?<-
The commentator shows that this is an allusion to a proverb of this kind:
->What, finally, is there that cannot be achieved by hands?<-
It warns that there is nothing in the world that cannot be accomplished by art and industry. However, what Aristophanes wrote you might aptly twist to mock cowardly soldiers, for whom all protection and hope of safety lies not in their hands, but in their feet. <note>Meaning they prefer running away to fighting.</note>

### Pot smashed against pot. XXIX
A pot is said to be smashed against a pot when two people clash to the harm of both. Aristophanes in *The Peace*:

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion from the previous page, concluding a reflection on the destructive nature of war between rulers before moving into a series of Greek and Latin proverbs regarding preoccupation, treachery, and plundering.</meta>

<page-num>786</page-num>
<header>ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>X</sig>

"And struck by a pot, in anger he kicked the pot back." <note>original: "Καὶ πίθῳ πληγεὶς ὑπ’ ὀργῆς ἀντελάκτισεν πίθῳ"</note> That is:
**And kicking back in anger, one clay pot wounds another.**
Such is generally the struggle of kings waging war against each other: it is like one pot clashing with another. Often both perish. Certainly, neither leaves without the heaviest losses, except for what seems to me a most unfairly balanced arrangement: while it would be right for the hardships of war to fall upon the heads of those who are the authors of the war and whose interest it is to win, the greatest part of the evils falls upon those who undertake the war unwillingly and with loathing—and for whom, even if the battle is fought with the most bitter Mars <note>Mars is the Roman god of war; "bitter Mars" refers to a savage or disastrous conflict.</note>, not even a farthing <note>original: "teruncius"; a tiny Roman coin worth a quarter of an as.</note> will ever return to them.

->Animus est in corijs.<-
->**The mind is in the hides.**<-

Aristophanes in *Peace*:
"We erred in these things, but have forgiveness, for our mind was then in the leathers." <note>original: "ἡμάρτομεν ταῦτ’ ἀλλὰ συγγνώμην ἔχε, ὁ νοῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ἦν τότ’ ἐν τοῖς σκύτεσι"</note> That is:
**In these matters indeed I have slipped, but you will grant pardon: for truly our mind was then in the leathers.**
Although we have mentioned this proverb elsewhere, it is very similar to that phrase from Terence: "The mind is in the dishes." <note>original: "Animus in patinis"; describing someone who is thinking only of their next meal rather than the conversation.</note> Likewise, what we read in Athenaeus in the book *The Deipnosophists*:
"Even if someone speaks, we would by no means learn, for the mind is near the table." <note>original: "οὐδ’ ἂν λέγη τις, οὐδαμῶς μαθοίμεν ἂν, ὁ νοῦς γὰρ ἐστὶ τῇ τραπέζῃ πλησίον"</note> That is:
**Lest anyone speak, we shall never be able to grasp it, for the mind itself clings closest to the table.**
The commentator <note>Referring to an ancient scholiast or editor of the text.</note> warns that this proverb—"he looks toward the leather"—is used for those who already look toward war, as has been shown in another place. It may be used when someone, because of anxiety over a specific matter, is insufficiently attentive to what is currently being done.

->Quibus nec ara, neque fides.<-
->**To whom there is neither altar nor faith.**<-

Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*:
"In whom neither altar, nor faith, nor oath remains." <note>original: "οἷσιν οὔτε βωμὸς οὔτε πίστις, οὔθ’ ὅρκος μένει"</note> That is:
**For whom neither altar, nor faith, nor any treaties endure.**
Used of the exceedingly treacherous. It was said of the Spartans, whose perfidy Euripides censured:
"Inhabitants of Sparta, treacherous councils." <note>original: "Σπάρτης ἔνοικοι δόλια βουλευτήρια"</note> That is:
**Inhabitants of Sparta, deceitful deliberations.**
Now, it fits the men of the court <note>original: "aulicos"</note> not at all badly.

->Ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν.<-
->**To drive and to carry.**<-

A very common but nevertheless proverbial figure among Greek authors is "to drive and to carry" <note>original: "ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν"</note> for that which is to pillage or harass in a hostile manner. <note>In antiquity, this referred to "driving" away livestock and "carrying" away inanimate goods.</note> If this is applied to the mind, it becomes not a little more festive. Just as Aristophanes says in *The Clouds*:
"For by most difficult debts and usurers I am driven, I am carried, and my goods are taken as pledges." <note>original: "ὑπὸ γὰρ τόκων χρησῶν τε δυσκολωτάτων Ἄγομαι, φέρομαι, τὰ χρήματ’ ἐνεχυράζομαι"</note> That is:
**By dreadful interest and most difficult moneylenders, I am snatched away, wretched, and I am carried off, offering my possessions as collateral.**
Lucian used "he drives and carries" <note>original: "ἄγει καὶ φέρει"</note> for one who drags things wherever he wishes at his own discretion. Very similar is Cornelius Tacitus in *On Orators*: "Now the leading men in Caesar's friendship drive and carry all things, and are loved by the prince himself with a certain reverence." <note>original: "agunt ferunt cuncta"</note> Homer in the *Iliad*:
"But what is there for me here, such as the Achaeans might carry off or drive away?" <note>original: "Ἀτὰρ ἔτι μοι ἐνθάδε ποῖον, οἷον κ’ ἠὲ φέροιεν ἀχαιοὶ ἤκεν ἄγοιεν"</note> That is:
**Nor indeed is there anything here for me of such a kind that it could be carried or driven by the Danaans.**
These are the words of Sarpedon, having roused Hector to war for the protection of the fatherland, when he himself thinks: "you have nothing that the Greeks could take away," namely from his Lycian homeland. Likewise, Virgil in the *Aeneid*:
"Others snatch away burning Troy and carry it off." <note>original: "Alii rapiunt incensa, feruntque Pergama"</note>
This stands for: they plunder and devastate. In a very similar way, Livy said, in the eighth book of the *Punic War*: "Then at last their stubbornness was broken, when they saw their property being carried and driven away." <note>original: "ferri agique res suas"</note> In Herodotus, Croesus speaks thus to the victor Cyrus: "For none of these things is mine anymore, but they carry and drive them away." <note>original: "οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐμοὶ ἔτι τούτων μέτα, ἀλλὰ φέρουσί τε καὶ ἄγουσι"</note> That is: **For now none of those things is mine, but they plunder your own things.** It seems to be transferred from the habit...

It picks up mid-discussion on the legalistic origins of phrases describing the looting of property.</meta>

<page-num>787</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Vu 4</sig>

...to be plundered, because in that situation men and beasts are driven off, and bundles are carried away. Plato, in his books *On Laws*, says: <term>ἢ ἀλλοβίῳ μηδένα μηδὲν φέρειν, μηδὲ ἄγειν</term> <note>original: "ē allobiō mēdena mēden pherein, mēde agein"</note>, which is to say: "Let no one carry or drive away any of another's property." Thus, the color of the speech seems to be drawn from legal formulas. Quintus Curtius, in his fourth book, used the phrase <term>προάγειν καὶ φέρειν</term> <note>original: "proagein kai pherein"</note> to mean "to be turned and driven." He used it to mock those who are perhaps persuaded that human affairs are turned and driven by chance and rashness. In the same book, he said "to be carried and driven" <note>original: "ferri agique"</note> when describing soldiers who, still maddened, were "carried and driven" while casting away their weapons. With these words, he illustrated the disordered chaos of the soldiers.

->To lick salt.<-
->XXXIII<-

<term>Ἅλα λείχειν</term> <note>original: "Hala leichein"</note>. That is, **To lick salt**. This is said of those who live on extremely meager rations. For thus Persius writes:
"Contented, you will finish your days, even if you live with Jove, though you bore through your salt-cellar with a finger that has tasted it again and again." <note>This refers to someone so poor they have only a cheap salt-cellar, which they scrape constantly for the last grain.</note>
When Diogenes the Cynic was once invited by the immensely wealthy Craterus <note>A famous general and friend of Alexander the Great.</note> to come to him, to enjoy his hospitality and his generosity, he replied that he would rather lick salt at Athens than enjoy the sumptuous tables at Craterus's house. Similarly, Plautus says in his play *Curculio*: "Today you shall never lick salt at my house."

->To fart incense.<-
->XXXIIII<-

<term>Βδέειν λιβανωτόν</term> <note>original: "Bdeein libanōton"</note>. That is, **To fart incense**. This has the character of a proverb. It is applied to those whose very vices are pleasing, either to themselves or to others who love them excessively. For <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia"</note> causes this: that everyone’s own things please and smile upon them, even if they are most foul. Immoderate love also causes this, as when the polyp on Agna's nose delighted her lover Balbinus, as Horace wrote. Aristophanes says in *Plutus*:
<term>οὐ λιβανωτὸν γὰρ βδέω</term> <note>original: "ou libanōton gar bdeō"</note>. That is,
"For I am not in the habit of farting incense."
It will also suit flatterers who praise the most shameful things as if they were most honorable.

->In place of the blind man, he has been un-eyed.<-
->XXXV<-

All formulas of this kind of wit belong to the nature of adages, where we seem to correct what has been said, but with another word that either has the same power or is even more biting. It is as if someone were to say, "He did not steal it, he snatched it," or "He did not steal it, he plundered it." Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
<term>πῶς δ’ ἐκύκλοφας ἀλλ’ ἥρπακας</term>; <note>original: "pōs d’ ekyclophas all’ hērpakas?"</note> That is,
"Have you not stolen it, but snatched it?"
<term>ἀντὶ γὰρ τυφλοῦ ἐξωμμάτωται</term> <note>original: "anti gar typhlou exōmmatōtai"</note>. The same author in the same play:
For the slave plays with the ambiguous word <term>ἐξωμμάτωται</term> <note>original: "exōmmatōtai"</note>, which can mean both that Plutus <note>The god of wealth, traditionally blind.</note> was "endowed with eyes" and that he was "un-eyed" or "blinded."

->Sooner let the wolf marry the sheep.<-
->XXXVI<-

Aristophanes in *Peace*:
<term>πρίν κεν λύκος οἶν ὑμεναιοῖ</term> <note>original: "prin ken lykos oin hymenaioi"</note>. That is,
**Sooner shall the wolf join the sheep in marriage.**
This is said of those between whom there is an incurable discord. Horace used a similar figure when he said:
"But sooner shall she-goats be joined to Apulian wolves."
Plautus in *Pseudolus*: "As you would rather leave wolves among sheep than leave these men as guards at home." It will be applied more elegantly to a situation; for instance, if you should say that the pursuit of money does not go together with the pursuit of literature, you might adapt the proverb to that sentiment.

->The fleeing spondyla farts most foully.<-
->XXXVII<-

The same author in almost the same place:
<term>ὡς ἡ σφονδύλη φεύγουσα πονηρότατον βδεῖ</term> <note>original: "hōs hē sphondylē pheugousa ponērotaton bdei"</note>. That is,
**As the cat is accustomed to fart foully whenever it flees.**
This will apply to those who depart with no small amount of infamy. The *spondyla* is a type of insect with a most foul odor. Pliny, in his twenty-seventh book, chapter thirteen, mentions the *Spondyle* serpent, which is most harmful to the roots of trees; however, he does not explain what kind it is. There is a species of serpent of this kind, with a small and blackish body, which emits a very heavy odor when dying. Hesychius <note>An ancient Greek lexicographer.</note> teaches that among the Athenians, a cat <note>original: "felem"; likely referring to a polecat or weasel in this context.</note> is called a *spondyle*. In Aristophanes, there is the phrase "bull-belted weasels," referring to acidic flatulence from the stomach.

->You will never make crabs walk straight.<-
->XXXVIII<-

Aristophanes in *Peace*:

<page-num>788</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>V</sig>

> You will never make a crab walk straight,
> nor will you later change what has been done. <note>original Greek: οὔποτε ποιήσεις τὸν καρκίνον ὀρθὰ βαδίζειν, οὐδ' ὣς τῷ πραχθέντι ποιήσεις ὕστερον οὐδέν.</note> 
> that is,
> That the crab may walk straight, you will never achieve,
> Nor will you achieve anything once a thing is already completed. <note>original Latin: Ambulet ut cancer recta, haud effeceris unquam, Nec quicquam efficies, ubi res erit ante peracta.</note>

A witty poet pronounces this as if it were an oracle: what is ingrained by nature can be changed by no effort. For it is natural to crabs to walk sideways. In the second of these verses, there is the same sentiment expressed as the one mentioned earlier: "Do not do what is already done." <note>original Latin: Actum ne agas. This refers to the futility of trying to fix or redo something that is already finished and unchangeable.</note>

### To act like a Corybant.

<term>Κορυβαντιᾶν</term> <note>original: "Korybantian"</note>. Aristophanes used this in *The Wasps* to mean "to be insane":
> Either you are truly mad, or you are acting like a Corybant. <note>original: Ἀλλ' ἢ παραφρονεῖς ἐτὸν ἢ κορυβαντιᾶς.</note>

Lucian frequently uses this word in his works *Timon*, *The Saturnalian Letters*, *Lexiphanes*, and *Hermotimus*. The term is derived from the **Corybantes**, the priests and worshippers of the goddess Cybele, who beat cymbals in a state of sacred frenzy, driving others into a similar madness. Elsewhere, the same state is called "being possessed by an evil spirit," <note>original Greek: κακοδαιμονᾶν (kakodaimonan)</note> as if one were being led by a malicious deity.

### To bite with a pebble.

<term>Ψήφῳ δάκνειν</term> <note>original: "Psēphō daknein"</note>. That is, **To bite with a pebble**: this is said of those who cause harm or take revenge upon a person through their vote. Aristophanes says in *The Acharnians*:
> They look for nothing else but to bite with the ballot. <note>original: βλέπουσιν οὐδ' ἓν ἄλλο πλὴν ψήφῳ δακεῖν.</note>

Indeed, the common people used this method above all others to avenge themselves if they were offended, by voting against their opponents in the assembly when the ballots <note>Greek: <term>psēphos</term>, meaning a small stone or pebble used for voting</note> were cast. Consequently, they "bit" not with a tooth (which was not present in the act), but with the voting pebble.

### Charybdis, the abyss.

These are also proverbial hyperboles, used when we call a person who is exceptionally gluttonous, voracious, predatory, or a spendthrift a "Charybdis" <note>A mythical sea monster that created a whirlpool</note> or a "Barathrum" <note>Latin: "barathrum," meaning a bottomless pit or abyss</note>. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
> Both a tax-collector and an abyss, and a Charybdis of plunder. <note>original: Καὶ τελώνην καὶ φάραγγα, καὶ χάρυβδιν ἁρπαγῆς.</note>

I believe we should also include here what Diogenes said, according to Diogenes Laertius: he called the belly "the Charybdis of one's resources." Horace says of a certain glutton:
> The gluttony, the storm, and the abyss of the market. <note>original Latin: Ingluuies & tempestas barathrumq; macelli.</note>

### The tongue is cut out separately.

Aristophanes in *Peace*:
> The tongue itself is cut separately. <note>original: Ἡ γλῶττα χωρὶς τέμνεται.</note>

The commentator <note>A reference to an ancient scholiast or editor</note> advises that this was a proverbial saying. It is taken from Homer’s *Odyssey*:
> Come now, cut the tongues. <note>original: Ἀλλ' ἄγε τέμνετε μὲν γλώττας.</note>

For this opinion, he cites Callistratus as his source. Again, in Aristophanes' *Plutus*:
> The tongue is usually cut out for these heralds. <note>original: ἡ γλῶττα τῷ κήρυκι τούτῳ τέμνεται.</note>

Callistratus, as cited by the commentator, records that in ancient times the tongue was traditionally cut out of the sacrificial victims for the heralds. Otherwise, there are some who say that the tongue from the victims is owed to the god Mercury <note>Hermes</note>. There is, however, a witty ambiguity <note>Latin: "amphibolia"</note> in Aristophanes' words, because the "tongue" can refer to either the god or the heralds. The commentator notes that this alludes to the proverb: "the tongue to the herald" <note>original Greek: ἡ γλῶττα τῷ κήρυκι</note>. We shall seem to use this correctly when we indicate that some reward is owed to one who, according to his strength, was a help in completing a business matter, or to those bringing good news <note>original Greek: εὐαγγέλια (euangelia)</note>. In Plutarch, Antipater, when the mention of Demades arose, remarked: "It appears the tongue, like a profane limb, is not usually admitted to the sacred rites." And Pittacus sent a tongue from a sacrificial victim to King Amasis, as being the worst limb and yet also the best. Heralds, moreover, have a "tongue for sale," and in sacrifices, they used to warn the people to "favor with their tongues" <note>i.e., keep a ritual silence</note>. Plautus in the prologue of *The Little Carthaginian*: "Exercise your voice, by which you live and thrive; for unless you shout, it will soon creep up on you..."
