<page-num>789</page-num>
<header>THIRD THOUSAND, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>

->He takes no sleep unless he has done this or that.<-
->XLIII<-

There are two proverbial figures of speech by which we signify an immoderate and unrestrained desire for something. The first is found in Aristophanes' *The Wasps*, and goes like this:
> Unless he happens to sit in the first row of the bench, 
> he sees no sleep at night, not even a speck. <note>original Greek: μη' με' ἐπι' τω' πρω'τω καθι'ζης ξυ'λου νη'νεδ' ο'ρᾶ' τι' νυκτο'ς οὐδε' πασσα'λω. Latin translation: Ligno nisi fors primus ille assederit / Somni uidet nil nocte, non uel paspalam.</note>

By "the first wood," he meant the first row of seats <note>the seating in the Athenian courts or theaters was often wooden</note>. The Greeks use the word <term>paspale</term> <note>original: πασσα'λω (paspalo)</note> to refer to the finest dust of flour. Along the same lines, Juvenal wrote:
> For some, a brawl induces sleep. <note>original Latin: Quibusdam Somnum rixa facit.</note>

The other figure is in Virgil’s *Bucolics*:
> But if you had not harmed someone in some way, you would have died. <note>original Latin: Quod si non aliqua nocuisses, mortuus esses. This suggests a person so malicious they cannot survive without causing trouble.</note>

The first sentiment is also found in the Hebrew <term>paroemiographos</term> <note>proverb-writer; specifically referring to King Solomon</note>: "For they do not sleep unless they have done evil, nor is sleep taken from them unless they have caused someone to stumble." <note>original Latin: Non enim dormiunt nisi quū male fecerint, nec capitur somnus ab eis nisi supplantauerint. This is a reference to Proverbs 4:16.</note>

->Counsel is better when the stomach is full.<-
->XLIIII<-

Plutarch, in the seventh book of his *Table Talk*, cites this verse:
> Better is counsel and wisdom when the belly is full. <note>original Greek: γαστρο'ς ἀ'χ' πλει'ης βουλη' και' μη'τις ἀμει'νων.</note>

When hunger interrupts, there is no leisure for deliberation, because counsel requires time and a tranquility of mind, whereas hunger sharpens the "bile" <note>in ancient medicine, hunger was thought to increase yellow bile, leading to anger or irritability</note>. It can also be applied to mean that one should first attend to what is urgent and pressing, and only then deliberate on the future. It also fits those who consult on very serious matters while well-inebriated—a custom which Herodotus, in his first book, relates was practiced by the Persians.
Similarly, Persius says: 
> Behold, amidst their cups the well-fed sons of Romulus ask what divine poems have to say. <note>original Latin: Ecce inter pocula quærunt / Romulidæ saturi quid dia poemata narrent.</note>

->Slender hope.<-
->XLV<-

Poets call a weak and uncertain hope "slender," and commentators—specifically Suidas—have noted this as a proverbial figure. Aristophanes in *The Knights*:
> This is some slender hope on which we ride. <note>original Greek: λεπτη'ς ἐλπι'ς ἐσ' εφ' ἡ'ς ὀχου'μεθα.</note>

Euripides, in *Iphigenia at Aulis*, called it "cold hope":
> A cold hope indeed. <note>original Greek: ψυχρα' ἡ' ἐλπι'ς.</note>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in *Pro Roscio Comoedo*, wrote: "You console yourself with an empty and slender hope." Aristophanes took the metaphor from sailors when he used the word <term>ochoumetha</term> <note>meaning "we are carried" or "we ride"</note>. Hence Cicero said, "He hopes some breeze may blow from here," instead of saying "hope was shown." As in the sixth action of the *Verrines*: "I see what I have done; he pulls himself up, he hopes some breeze might be able to blow for him in this charge." This is a metaphor from sailors who, when they are stuck in a sea that is too calm, divine that there will be a wind from a small cloud or from a distant rippling on the water. Plato, in the third book of *The Laws*, used a similar figure: "slender salvation" <note>original Greek: λεπτη'ν σωτηρι'αν (lepten soterian)</note>. In Athenaeus, book thirteen, a line from Callimachus is cited: "My hopes were so labored that they were called the allies of my enemies." <note>original Greek: ὡ'δε ἐμο'χθουν αἱ ἐλπι'δες, ὡ'σε ἐχθρω'ν συμμαχι'ας καλεῖσθαι. This implies hopes so desperate they are as bad as an enemy's help.</note>

->I am becoming a year older.<-
->XLVI<-

Whenever we signify that something is greatly bothersome to us, we commonly say we are growing old from it. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
> Take care you do not do that; for as for me, whenever I behold 
> any of those clever sophistries, 
> I depart, believe me, older by a year. <note>original Greek: πλει'ον ἐ'νιαυτῷ πρεσβυ'τερο' ἀπε'ρχομαι.</note>

Homer also indicates that old age is brought on by weariness and trouble:
> For mortals grow old quickly in the midst of misfortunes. <note>original Greek: Αἶψα γα'ρ ἐν κακο'τητι βροτοι' καταγηρα'σκουσι.</note>

->To glare like a bull.<-
->XLVII<-

"To look bull-wise" <note>original Greek: βλε'πειν ταυρηδο'ν (blepein taurēdon)</note>, meaning to look grimly or sternly. Aristophanes in *The Frogs*:
> Look then like a bull, with your head lowered. <note>original Greek: βλε'ψον οὐ'ν ταυρηδο'ν ἐγκυ'ψας κα'τω.</note>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

Thus, with a downturned face, he gazes like a bull. <note>original Latin: ore prono contuetur tauricum</note> Plato shows that it was Socrates’ habit to stare with "bull-like eyes" <note>referring to Socrates’ intense, steady gaze even in the face of death</note>. And Virgil calls such a gaze grim:
->**The best form is that of the grim cow.**<- <note>original Latin: Optima toruæ Forma bouis</note>

### It is useful to have many names.
Aristophanes says in *Plutus*:
How good it is to have many surnames. <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀγαθόν ἐστ' ἐπωνυμίας πολλὰς ἔχειν; Latin: Vt expedit, si plura habeas cognomina.</note>
This applies to those who profess many skills at once to make a more abundant profit. They belong to opposing sides—just as the bat in the Fables is sometimes a mouse and sometimes a bird. This was said of Mercury <note>the god Hermes</note>, who is given various titles: for example, **the Turner**, <note>original Greek: στροφαῖος (strophaios)</note> either because he turns business well or because he is crafty and a "turncoat"; **of the Market**, <note>original Greek: ἀγοραῖος (agoraios)</note> because he presides over auctions and trade; **the Leader**, <note>original Greek: ἡγεμόνιος (hegemonios)</note> because he is a guide for the road, as seen when he leads Priam; **the Crafty**, <note>original Greek: δόλιος (dolios)</note> because he is the inventor of deception and tricks; **the Profitable**, <note>original Greek: κερδῷος (kerdoos)</note> because he increases the wealth of merchants; and **of the Contests**, <note>original Greek: ἐναγώνιος (enagonios)</note> because he performs the role of a herald in competitions. He is also the messenger of the gods. Likewise, many titles are attributed to Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>. 

This proverb can also be pointedly twisted against those who have titles and nominations everywhere, like traps set to ensnare church offices <note>specifically "benefices," which provided income to clergy</note>. Or it applies to those who profess many arts to win fortune by any means, just as those in the courts of princes act as priest, servant, steward, pimp, and **jester** <note>original Greek: γελωτοποιόν (gelotopoion)</note> all at once.

### Hungry Dorians.
**Hungry Dorians.** <note>original Greek: Λιμοδωριεῖς (Limodorieis)</note> In the collection of proverbs attributed to Plutarch, I find this story: When the Peloponnese once suffered from a shortage of grain, certain people, driven by hunger, packed their bags and migrated. As they wandered here and there without fixed homes, they were received in the city by the Tripolitans. Tripolis is a city in Rhodes. Thus, they were named the "Hungry Dorians." Hesychius adds, on the authority of Didymus, that those who lived nearby were called this because, due to the sterility of the land, they frequently dealt with famine. In Greek, "Dorians" <note>original Greek: Δωριεῖς (Dorieis)</note> seems to be derived from "gift" <note>doron</note> and "going" <note>ienai</note>. Therefore, they were called Dorians because they were "brought by a gift of hunger" <note>a pun on the etymology</note> while wandering. Otherwise, the Dorians are not in the Peloponnese, but between Locris and Phocis, according to Strabo in his ninth book. The term will fit those who, driven by hunger, migrate elsewhere. And among the common crowd of sailors, almost all guests are called "Hungry Dorians," as if they were compelled by hunger to visit the region. Festus Pompeius notes that people of thin means and meager fortune were once called "Gutter-dwellers" <note>Canalicolas</note> because they loitered around the gutters of the forum.

### In three bites.
Plautus in *The Weevil*: "If you wish, I would like the cloak in three bites." <note>original Latin: Si uis tribus bolis, uelim chlamydē</note> He said "in three bites" as a shorthand, as if to say "in three words." For Terence seems to use the word **bite** <note>bolus</note> for what the Greeks call a **morsel** <note>original Greek: βλωμόν (blomon)</note>. Anything that is devoured instantly is said to be eaten "in three bites."

### To follow like a shadow.
To follow just like a shadow. <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ σκιὰ ἕπεται; Latin: Velut umbra sequi.</note> This is said of someone who is never absent. For a shadow stays close to the body, whether it wants to or not. Plautus in *Casina*: "I am determined to follow him like a shadow wherever he goes." This is why we call inseparable companions "shadows," and those who accompany others uninvited to a banquet, as noted elsewhere under the proverb **Shadows**. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the first book of *Tusculan Disputations*: "For even if glory has nothing in itself to be sought after, yet it follows virtue like a shadow."

### Not even a lead coin.
Using a proverbial hyperbole, they use "a lead coin" to represent the smallest amount of money. Plautus in *Casina*: "To which man today is there not even a lead coin of private savings." The same author in *The Three-Dollar Day*: "For if it becomes a capital matter, I will never trust even a lead coin." Similar to this is what the same author says in *The Two Captives*:
> And they do not value jesters at even a farthing now. <note>original Latin: Necque ridículos iam teruncí faciunt. A 'teruncius' was a tiny Roman coin.</note>
Though this was said in another context.

### Satiety breeds insolence.
Nicolaus Stobaeus, in his collection, cites this sentence under the title of a proverb:
For satiety breeds insolence, but ignorance combined with power breeds madness. <note>original Greek: τίκτει γὰρ κόρος μὲν ὕβριν, ἀπαιδευσία δὲ μετ' ἐξουσίας ἄνοιαν; Latin: Parit satietas ferociā, imperitia uerò cum potestate coniuncta, insaniam.</note>
Wealth lifts the spirits; but if abundance is added to ignorance, the matter proceeds all the way to madness. This harmonizes with that other saying: **He has hay on his horn.** <note>a Latin proverb referring to a dangerous bull, used to describe a hot-tempered or dangerous man</note>

<summary>Erasmus discusses proverbs regarding the strategic use of multiple titles, the origins of the 'Hungry Dorians,' and metaphors for worthlessness and inseparable companionship. He concludes with a moral warning on how wealth joined with ignorance leads to arrogance and madness.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, Aristophanes, Socrates, Dorians, Plautus, Cicero, lead coin, satiety, insolence, Greek etymology, Roman comedy</keywords>

--- Page 915 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, specifically focusing on the relationship between wealth, excess, and human behavior, as well as metaphors for completion and preparation.</meta>

<page-num>791</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>

Pindar, in the *Olympian Odes*, reverses the sentiment, saying that "insolence is the mother of satiety." <note>original Greek: ὑβρις κόρος μητέρα (hybris koros metera). Pindar, Olympian 13.10.</note> That is, ferocity is the mother of being over-filled. But he is criticized by the commentator, who instead approves of Homer’s verse: "Satiety gives birth to insolence, when wealth follows a wicked man." <note>original Greek: τικτει τοι κόρος ὕβριν, ὅταν κακῶ͂ ὄλβος ἕποιτο (tiktei toi koros hybrin...)</note> That is, "Abundance creates pride when a low person acquires riches." However, I do not remember reading this verse in Homer, nor does it seem to be his genuine work; what is certain is that it exists among the maxims of Theognis.

### 54. What has a blind man to do with a mirror?

"What has a blind man to do with a mirror?" <note>original Greek: τί τυφλῶ͂ καὶ κατόπτῳ; (ti typhlo kai katoptro?)</note> This is closely related to another: "A jackdaw has nothing to do with a lute." <note>A phrase used to describe someone attempting to use a tool or art for which they have no capacity.</note> A verse from Epicharmus is cited by Stobaeus: "For what fellowship is there between a mirror and a blind man?" <note>original Greek: τις γὰρ κατόπτῳ καὶ τυφλῶ͂ κοινωνία; (tis gar katoptro kai typhlo koinonia?)</note> That is, "What business is it for one deprived of eyes to have a looking-glass?"
To what purpose are books for the illiterate? To what purpose a kingdom for a foolish youth? To what purpose riches for one who does not know how to use them?

### 55. To reap a miserable harvest.

"To reap a bad harvest" means to pay the penalty for evil deeds. This is not very different from what we have mentioned elsewhere: "As you have sown, so shall you reap." Stobaeus cites this poem from Euripides’ *Ion*:
> And now, O wicked mortals, you attract honors,
> And you acquire wealth, hunting for it from every side,
> Mixing the unjust and the just together;
> Afterwards, you reap the harvest of these things from a burdensome god. <note>original Greek: Καὶ νῦν ἐφείλκετ’ ὦ κακοὶ τιμὰς βροτοί... (Kai nyn epheilket’ o kakoi timas brotoi...)</note> That is:
> But now, O wicked ones, you summon honors to yourselves,
> And you prepare riches, fowling for them everywhere,
> Indiscriminately through right and wrong,
> Afterwards you reap a sad and bitter harvest for those things.

<margin>Aeschylus in *The Persians*,</margin>
> For insolence, having flowered, has borne an ear
> Of ruin, from which it reaps a most tearful harvest. <note>original Greek: ὕβρις γὰρ ἀνθῆσα’ ἐκάρπωσε στάχυν / ἄτης... (hybris gar anthesas’ ekarpose stachyn / ates...)</note> That is:
> For flourishing ferocity has brought forth a spike
> Of harm, from which it reaps an utterly mournful harvest.

Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "What kind of harvest do you think that rhetoric will later reap, which it has sown?" <note>original Greek: ποιόν τίνα οἴει μετὰ ταῦτα τῆν ῥητορικὴν καρπὸν ἂν ἔαν ἔσπει θερίζειν (poion tina oiei...)</note> Aristotle, in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, cites from Gorgias: "You indeed have sown these things shamefully, and you have harvested them wretchedly." <note>original Greek: σὺ δὲ ταῦτα αἰσχρῶς μὲν ἔσπειρας, κακῶς δ’ ἐθέρισας (sy de tauta aischros men espeiras...)</note>

### 56. We have come to the final line.

<margin>Euripides in *Antigone*,</margin>
> We have come to the furthest line of evils. <note>original Greek: Ἐπ’ ἄκραν ἥκομεν γραμμὴν κακῶν (Ep’ akran hekomen grammen kakon)</note> That is:
> We have arrived at the final line of misfortunes. Likewise Horace: "We have come to the summit."

Regarding the "line" <term>linea</term> <note>the finishing line or goal-line in ancient racing</note> of the stadiums and games, it has been discussed in more than one place elsewhere.

### 57. Ballasted.

Plautus, in the *Cistellaria*, spoke in a novel but quite elegant way when he said "ballasted" <note>original Latin: saburratus</note> for being "stuffed with food." The metaphor is taken from ships, which they load with sand <term>saburra</term> or clay so that they are not tossed about and do not wobble in the waves. I certainly would not have included this among the adages, were it not also commonly said everywhere. Plautus’s words are these: "The same fault is in me as in a great part of the women who now make a living by trade. When we are 'ballasted' [stuffed with food and drink], we are immediately talkative." It becomes even more graceful if it is twisted further: for example, if one were to say someone's ears were "ballasted" by much talking. Or, a mind "ballasted" with the precepts of philosophy, lest it be tossed by the tempest of circumstances.

### 58. You speak "by the number."

Plautus in the *Casina* said "you speak by the number" <note>original Latin: Numero dicis</note> instead of "easily and briefly." Festus explains it as "quickly and speedily," citing many other authors as well as this passage from Plautus. But in Festus, the text is so corrupted that it is tiresome to report, except for what is gathered there: that the ancients did not only say "you speak by the number," but also "you do by the number," "to strike out by the number," "to believe by the number," "to come by the number," meaning to come easily and quickly. Nonius Marcellus thinks "by the number" <term>Numero</term> is said for "much," but the examples he brings forward indicate more that it is taken for "quickly and easily," or "immediately." Which he himself admits at the end. The same in the *Amphitryon*: "It came to my mind by the number" [immediately]. It is used in the same author and in several other places.

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

->Groping in the dark.<-

<note>original Greek: ψηλαφᾷν ἐν τῷ σκότῳ (psēlaphān en tō skotō)</note>. That is, to feel one's way with the hand in the darkness. This is said of those who investigate an obscure matter by mere guesswork. Aristophanes says in *The Peace*: <margin>Before this time,</margin>
"Previously we were groping for affairs as if in the dark, 
But now we shall deliberate on everything by the light of the lamp." 
The poet is alluding to the cleverness of Hyperbolus <note>A populist Athenian politician often mocked by comic playwrights.</note>, who rose from being a lamp-maker—that is, a manufacturer of lights—to being a leader of the republic. Plato uses the same proverb in the *Phaedo*. Indeed, even today it is common to use the word "groping" <note>original Greek: ψηλαφᾷ (psēlaphā)</note> when speaking of uncertain conjectures.

->Driving away flies.<-

"Driving away flies" is a joke still commonly used today for someone who performs a lazy and useless task. Aristophanes in *The Wasps* says:
"But to keep guard with hand in readiness, taking care even to drive away the flies."

->You draw it out thinly.<-

<note>original Greek: Λεπτὰ ψήχεις (Lepta psēcheis)</note>. That is, you draw it out or split it thinly. Suidas wrote that this was traditionally said of those who live on very little and in a meager fashion. It appears the metaphor is transferred from women carding wool. For we read "to rub" <note>original: ψήχειν (psēchein)</note>... for in the common manuscripts the word is "you rub" <note>original: ψήχεις (psēcheis)</note>. What that word specifically intends is not entirely clear to me. Furthermore, whether you read one spelling or the other, both signify that zeal people have for diligence in trivial matters, which the Greeks call "pettiness" <term>mikrologia<gloss>A narrow-minded attention to tiny details or stinginess</gloss></term>, to the point that they are proverbially said even to "split a cumin seed." <note>A common ancient expression for a miser or a pedant.</note>

Indeed, among the Latins, "the poor keep a thin watch"; and Terence used the phrase "so thinly" regarding a young lover living without managing much money; sometimes they refer this to exact care and subtlety. As Horace says in the *Satires*:
"As befits thin subjects treated in a thin style." 
Aristophanes likewise in *The Clouds* spoke of "thin thought," "the thinnest nonsense," and "speaking thinly"—that is, "thinly reasoning"—undoubtedly mocking the anxious and overly subtle arguments of the philosophers. Seneca remarked that Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher famous for his logical hair-splitting.</note> possessed such an edge: it could prick, but not penetrate. 

Furthermore, just as appropriate and direct speech brings the most light to a conversation, so that overly curious style—chopped into fragments rather than members—sometimes causes us to understand nothing by trying to understand too much. Hence, those who avoid this excessive subtlety are said to speak "broadly" or "more coarsely" <note>original Greek: παχυμερῶς καὶ παχυμερέστερον (pachumerōs kai pachumeresteron)</note>. Ulpian, in the twentieth book of the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, in the chapter "Regarding Private Property," says: "One need not know every single detail out of necessity, but rather more broadly," and Pomponius leans toward this opinion. For the word is composed of "fat" <note>original: παχὺ (pachy)</note> and "part" <note>original: μέρος (meros)</note>. Conversely, those who shake out every single detail into tiny bits are said to speak "minutely" <note>original Greek: λεπτομερῶς (leptomerōs)</note>. 

Instead of "broadly," Aristotle in the *Nicomachean Ethics* said "roughly and in outline" <note>original Greek: παχυλῶς καὶ τύπῳ (pachulōs kai typō)</note>: "It should be acceptable, then, when speaking of such things and from such premises, to indicate the truth roughly and in outline." He means that the scruples of legal exceptions should be omitted when addressing an unskilled audience, but one should speak of things as they generally are or are commonly held to be. In the second book of the same work: "Every discourse concerning actions ought to be stated in outline and not with exactness." It is also frequent in Greek authors to say "to speak in a figure" <note>original Greek: ὡς τύπῳ εἰπεῖν (hōs typō eipein)</note>; that is, to speak thus when they feel they are not expressing the matter precisely as it is, but signifying it with whatever words available—noting it rather than fully articulating it.

->A painted monkey.<-

<note>original Greek: πίθηκος ἀνάπλεως ψιμυθίου (pithēkos anapleōs psimythiou)</note>. That is, a monkey full of rouge. This refers to an ugly old woman who is nevertheless made up and adorned with the seductive tricks of a prostitute. For "white lead" <note>original: ψιμύθιον (psimythion)</note> is what the Greeks call that pigment with which formerly prostitutes—and now even honorable matrons, if it please the gods—smear their faces to hide old age or flaws in their beauty. Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen* says:
"Is this a monkey full of white lead? 
Or an old woman risen from the dead?"
It can also be applied to a situation where someone adorns a shameful legal case with the ornaments of high rhetoric.

<header>THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>

...so that it might appear honest. To "play the monkey" <note>original Greek: πιθηκίζειν (pithēkizein)</note> is to deceive with false colors or flatteries. From this comes "monkey-tricks" <note>original Greek: πιθηκισμὸς (pithēkismos)</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:
> "Woe is me, wretched man, with what kind of monkey-tricks you drive me around!"
That is:
> "Wretched me, with what sort of monkey-business you spin me about."
"Dusk-diners" <note>original Greek: ζοφοροδερπίδης (zophoroderpidēs)</note>, and similar terms.

### LXIII

Plutarch, in his *Table Talk*, shows that in the old days certain nicknames were tossed about as proverbial jokes against those who arrived too late or too hesitantly to a banquet. They were called "dinner-blockers" <note>original Greek: κωλυσιδείπνοι (kōlysideipnoi)</note>, then "dusk-diners" <note>original Greek: ζοφοροδερπίδας (zophoroderpidas)</note>, and "dinner-runners" <note>original Greek: τρεχέδειπνος (trechedeipnos)</note>. If it is permitted to guess the reasoning behind these names, I think it is this: those who were slow to arrive seemed to be a delay and a hindrance to the others, preventing them from beginning their meal; further, by their slowness, they caused the banquet to be extended far into the night. 

The third nickname appears to have been given by way of irony <note>original: κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν (kat’ antiphrasin)</note>. However, someone in Plutarch’s work denies that Pittacus was called a "Dusk-diner" by Alcaeus because he entered the banquet late, but rather because he delighted in filthy and common drinking parties. In ancient times, it was considered inelegant and poorly mannered if someone invited to a dinner arrived too late. Hence Polycharmus, in the defense speech where he gives an account of his life to the Athenians, included this in his own praise:
> "Athenians, and besides these things, never when called to dinner did I arrive last."
That is: "In addition to this, O Athenians, I never arrived after the appointed time when summoned to a meal."

A certain jester named Battus explained the reason for this opinion quite wittily in the presence of Caesar. For he was accustomed to call those who came late to a feast "dinner-cravers" <note>original Greek: ἐθυμοδείπνοι (ethymodeipnoi)</note>, as if you were to say "greedy for banquets," because those who were busy with business would nonetheless not excuse themselves to those by whom they were invited, due to their desire for the feast. Plutarch says roughly this much. 

But Terence, in *The Self-Tormentor*, indicates that it was considered uncivil for a guest to be present immediately and before the time, when Chremes says that "those people have been ready at my house for a long time," and that he himself is a delay to the guests—certainly indicating that the opposite usually happens. In Aristophanes’ *The Assemblywomen*, he alludes to this several times: "I am going to dinner." In the same play: "I will sing some dinner-song" <note>original Greek: μελοδείπνικον (melodeipnikon)</note>.

### LXIIII

-> He who likes those things, let him not enjoy mine. <-

Aristophanes in *The Clouds*:
> "Therefore, let him for whom those things produce laughter not rejoice in mine."
This has the appearance of a proverb, which one may use when we wish to signify a huge gap or difference between our own methods and those of others. The Greek verse limps by one syllable; it will be complete if you read "laughs" <note>original Greek: γελάᾳ (gela-ā)</note> instead of "laughs" <note>original Greek: γελᾷ (gelā)</note>. The opposite of this is that line from Virgil <note>original: Maronis</note>:
> "He who hates not Bavius, let him love your songs, Maevius."
This refers to those things which are of the same sort <note>original: eiusdem sunt farinae, literally "of the same flour"</note> and equally to be despised.

### LXV

-> Altar-lurker, to play the altar-lurker. <-
<note>original Greek: βωμολόχος, βωμολοχεύεσθαι (bōmolochos, bōmolocheuesthai)</note>

"Altar-lurkers" <note>original Greek: βωμολόχοι (bōmolochoi)</note> was a term used as a proverbial insult for the wicked and the shameful. It seems the name was once given to those who, hanging around the altars, were accustomed to lay snares for the sacrificial meats; or to those who performed a sacred rite for the reason that they might carry off some small profit from the accusations of others. For Jupiter hears the prayers of such mortals in Lucian’s *Icaromenippus*. 

Those are also called "altar-lurkers" who, while a sacred rite is being performed, do not offer prayers to the gods but babble empty nonsense. This custom is especially pleasing to the great nobles today, and they think it quite sophisticated if, during the sacrifice <note>Erasmus refers here to the Mass</note>, they constantly bark <note>original: obganniant</note> something into someone's ear. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*: "And an altar-lurker." In the same play:
> "If any of them played the buffoon, or turned some trick."
Though in this very phrase "to turn a trick" <note>original Greek: καμπήν τινα κάμψαι (kampēn tina kampsai)</note> there is a proverbial color. Again, in *The Knights*: "Now an altar-lurking deed has been devised," meaning the adversary has thought up something exceptionally wicked, which he calls "altar-lurking" <note>original: βωμολόχον</note> as if it were remarkably flattering. 

The word is seen to be derived from *bōmos* <note>altar</note> and *lochos* <note>ambush/lurking</note>, because there are never lacking those who would steal the food there or seek it by begging. From there it was transferred to those who flatter abjectly for the sake of their belly. Whence the terms "altar-scrapings" and "altar-lurking tricks" were used for sordid flatteries. Sometimes the word "altar-lurker" is attributed to soothsayers, diviners, flute-players, and that tribe of men which follows the smell of the altar. Finally...

<margin>LX</margin>
### Before the cock crows a second time.
<note>original Greek: πρίν ἢ τὸ δέυτερον ἀλεκτρυὼν ἐφθέγγετο (prin ē to deuteron alektryōn ephthengeto)</note>

->that is,<-

Before the crest-bearing cock sings a second time.

The Greek verse will be consistent if you read "cock" <note>original: ἀλέκτωρ (alektōr)</note> instead of "rooster" <note>original: ἀλεκτρυὼν (alektryōn)</note>, that is, very early and before dawn. This is taken from an ancient custom where the passage and approach of the night were measured by the cock-crow, as hour-tracking sun-dials <note>term: gnomonibus horarijs (hour-indicators)</note> had not yet been invented. The cock crows at three intervals, announcing the day. Regarding this, Pliny writes in Book 10, Chapter 21: "And these our nocturnal sentinels, whom nature produced for the purpose of waking mortals to their work and breaking their sleep. They mark the periods of the night and distinguish the three-hour intervals of the day with their song. They go to bed with the sun. At the fourth watch, they recall us to our cares and labor. They do not allow the sunrise to creep up on the unwary. They announce the coming day with song, and the song itself with a flapping of their sides." Thus far Pliny. 

As to why this happens to cocks, Democritus (as cited in Marcus Tullius Cicero) thinks that digestion <note>original: concoctionem</note> is the cause, because at that time the food is driven from the chest and distributed throughout the whole body. The poets refer it to a fable, which Lucian mentions in *The Dream, or the Cock*. I am more pleased by the reasoning of Ambrose Leo of Nola, a man whom I would not hesitate to compare with any of the ancient philosophers in investigating the mysteries of nature. In his inquiries, he thinks the song of the cocks proceeds from a certain peculiar lustfulness <note>original: falacitate (likely a variant of salacitate, meaning lustfulness)</note>. For this animal is devoted to its hens above others, even "uxorious" <note>term: uxoriū (devoted to a wife or mate)</note>, and is marvelously solicitous about propagating offspring as much as possible—so much so that one cock is put in charge of many hens, and a single husband satisfies such a great crowd, and then fights most fiercely for his females and chicks. 

Furthermore, the fact that they remain silent before they are mature enough to mate with the hens argues sufficiently that the cock's song proceeds from an impulse of Venus <note>note: Erasmus uses "Venus" to refer to sexual desire or mating</note>. Similarly, among other birds, most produce a sound during mating or out of a desire for mating, such as ducks, sparrows, swallows, and partridges. Moreover, in the bird kingdom, the voice of the male has such power to incite lust that some birds conceive eggs merely by hearing it. In this number are the partridges. Thus, when the food is already sliding through the entrails and sleep is departing—at which time bodies are naturally stirred toward Venus—the cock immediately remembers the hens and provokes them with the allure of his song so that the mating might be more plentiful. The reason he crows repeatedly is that the cock's sleep is interrupted and not at all continuous, especially when he is in the prime of his life; you should understand that this, too, proceeds from lust. 

But to return to the interpretation of the adage: the ancients began the day from the first inclination of midnight. They called the next period "cock-crow" <note>original: gallicinium</note>, when the birds, sensing the light of that time far in advance, begin to sing. The third period was "silence" <note>original: conticinium</note>, when the cocks fall silent and men also rest. The fourth is "dawn" <note>original: diluculum</note>, when the day begins to be recognized. The fifth is "morning" <note>original: mane</note>, when the day is already clear and the sun has risen. Therefore, the second cock-crow comes long before the sunrise. Hence Juvenal says:

> Yet that which he does at the second cock-crow,
> The neighboring tavern-keeper will know before dawn.

Similarly, Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen*:
<note>original Greek: Πόθεν; Οὐ δ' ἐμὰ δία τότ' ἦλθεν, ὅτε τὸ δέυτερον Αλεκτρυὼν ἐφθέγγετο.</note>

->that is,<-

By no means.
Not even if you had arrived at that time,
When the cock was crowing for the second time.

Mention of this matter is also made in the Gospel writings <note>note: A reference to Peter’s denial of Jesus</note>.

<margin>L</margin>
### Not even a head of garlic.
A proverbial hyperbole. <note>original Greek: οὐδέ σκορόδου κεφαλὴν Αλεκτρυών (oude skorodou kephalēn alektryōn)</note>, that is: Not even a head of garlic. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
<note>original Greek: οὐδ'ἂς οὐδὲ σκορόδου κεφαλὴν τοῖς ἐν λυκείω δίδωσι.</note>

->that is,<-

No one adds even a head of garlic to the cooked dishes.
It will be suitable for a person who is stingy and excessively sparing with expense.

<margin>LX</margin>
### To ruminate on a business.
<note>original Greek: Αναμασᾶσθαι τὸ πρᾶγμα (Anamasasthai to pragma)</note>, that is: To ruminate or chew over a business. It is said of one who turns something over in his mind, weighing it again and again. The metaphor is taken from animals that chew again what has been brought back into the mouth, and only then pass it into the second stomach.

<page-num>795</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Xx 2</sig>

...does not happen except to those who have two stomachs. <note>Erasmus is finishing a thought from the previous page regarding rumination or "chewing the cud" as a metaphor for deep thought.</note> Aristophanes says in *The Wasps*:
"He has barely grasped the matter by chewing it over."
That is, the cause is hardly understood until they have ruminated upon it. They also call this "re-calculating" <note>original Greek: ἀναπεμπάζειν (anapempazein), literally to count again on the five fingers</note>. Lucian also employs this adage in a certain passage.

->Biting the lip. LXIX<-
<margin>69</margin>

"To eat the lips" <note>original Greek: Ἐσθίειν τὰ χείλη (esthein ta cheile)</note>. That is, to eat one's lips, or as is commonly said in modern times, it refers to one who is fuming and snarling in his mind, a metaphor taken from the gesture of those who are indignant. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
"Eating his lip <note>The Greek text here uses χελώνην (chelōnēn), meaning 'tortoise-shell' or 'lip-growth,' but Erasmus interprets it as the gesture of biting the lip in anger.</note> out of rage."
So too Homer in the *Odyssey*, Book 20:
"But they all bit firmly into their lips with their teeth."

->To act the Lesbian. LXX<-
<margin>70</margin>

In ancient times, "to act the Lesbian" <note>original Greek: Λεσβιάζειν (lesbiazein)</note> was a term used for a specific type of pollution. Aristophanes in *The Wasps*:
"She has already been trained to act the Lesbian for her fellow-drinkers."
That is, she would now contaminate her drinking companions. They say that this foulness performed by the mouth—what I believe is called *fellatio* or *irrumatio*—first originated with the people of Lesbos, and that a woman among them was the first of all to suffer such a thing. As a witness to this matter, the commentator cites Theopompus in *Odysseus*: "Lest I speak that old and commonly gossiped-about trick performed by our bodies, which they say the children of the Lesbians invented." He also cites Stratis in *Troilus*:
"Never, my son, while you live, should you reach this point, but let the Lesbians enjoy it all and bid them farewell."
These seem to be two iambic verses, though somewhat corrupted. Aristophanes hints at the same thing in *The Assemblywomen*:
"You seem to me to be a 'Lambda' <note>term: λάβδα (labda)</note> after the fashion of the Lesbians."
He is alluding to the common letter which is the first of both "Lesbians" and the obscene verb "to perform lewd acts" <note>original Greek: λαικάζειν (laikazein)</note>. This, if I am not mistaken, means the same thing to the Greeks as *fellare* does to the Latins. For the word still remains, though I believe the practice itself was long ago abolished from our midst. <note>Erasmus often adds these moralizing or hopeful disclaimers when discussing ancient vices.</note>

->Bearing the Pyrrhic dance in his eyes. LXXI<-
<margin>71</margin>

"To look the Pyrrhic" <note>original Greek: πυῤῥίχην βλέπειν (pyrrhichēn blepein)</note>. That is, to display tumult and war in one's countenance. It is called this because the "Pyrrhic" <term>Pyrrhiche</term> is a type of dance performed by armed youths, as Athenaeus testifies in the fourteenth book of the *Sophists at Dinner*, showing that an image of war is represented in it: the force and heat of those attacking, and the speed of those fleeing. Aelius Spartianus says in his life of *Hadrian*: "He frequently exhibited military Pyrrhic dances to the people." Suetonius <note>original: Tanquillus</note> also mentions the Pyrrhic dances: "The children of the princes of Asia and Bithynia danced the Pyrrhic." 

Julius Pollux, in Book 4, Chapter 14, commemorates among the various types of dances the *emmeleia* of the tragic actors, the *kordax* of the comedians, the *sikinnis* of the satyr-players, and the *pyrrhiche* and *plesia*, which he calls *psinoplia* because they danced in armor. From this, he indicates it was called *xiphismos* <note>gloss: sword-play</note> because it was performed with swords, and *podismos* <note>gloss: foot-work</note> because they whirled their bodies with wonderful speed of foot. He also records other types of dances that held the image of war, the *komos* and the *tetrakomos*, which he says was sacred to Hercules. Again, another which they called the *karkiniko*, which was also performed with arms. 

Plato, in the seventh book of *The Laws*, teaches that there were two primary types of dance: one warlike and tumultuous which was called the Pyrrhic, the other more moderate which was the *emmeleia*. He describes the Pyrrhic in these words:
"One would correctly name the Pyrrhic as that which imitates the avoidance of all blows and shots by swerving the body, and every method of yielding, by crouching and leaping upward; and also the opposite gestures, those tending toward active movements, attempting to imitate the release of bows and the throwing of spears and all manner of blows. In these, the upright and vigorous posture of good bodies and souls is preserved whenever there is a straight-moving imitation, for the most part, of the limbs of the body. Such a thing is 'upright,' but the opposite of these we reject as 'not upright.'"
That is, you would rightly call it the Pyrrhic, which imitates the avoidance of all blows and missiles by the bending of the body, and by every method of giving way, by crouching and by jumping high. Conversely, it imitates those gestures which are useful for the movements of the body, preparing it for agility, whether in the shooting of bows or the throwing of spears, or finally in every...

<summary>Erasmus explores metaphors for mental reflection and anger before detailing the "Lesbian" reputation in Greek slang and providing an extensive scholarly history of the Pyrrhic dance—a Greek military exercise used to train soldiers in agility.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of ancient Greek culture through their idioms, specifically focusing on the "Pyrrhic dance" as a metaphor for military agility, followed by adages concerning mercy and the joy of rejuvenation.</meta>

<page-num>796</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

through the striking of blows they strive to imitate the images of battle, and at the same time they cultivate uprightness and strength of both good bodies and minds; for whenever imitation is employed, it contributes much to the firmness of the body’s limbs. This is indeed considered "upright," whereas the contrary is not approved as such. The commentator on Homer’s *Iliad* also mentions this, recording three types of dances: the *Pyrrhiche*, the *Sicinnin* (which pertains to sacred rites), and the *Skordakismos* <note>original Greek: σκόρδακισμος</note>, a most lewd dance that is unbecoming and suited for the profane. The *Pyrrhiche* belonged to the Cretans and was performed in armor. Hence Homer, wishing to describe a man agile in the duties of war, calls him a "dancer" <note>original Greek: ὀρχηστὴν (orchēstēn)</note> even though he is a warrior. This type of combat is elegantly depicted from Xenophon in Athenaeus, Book 1:

"First the Thracians stood up and danced to the flute with their weapons; they leaped high and lightly, using their swords. Finally, one struck the other, so that it seemed to everyone that the man had been hit. He fell down quite artfully, and everyone cried out. Then the one who appeared to have struck him, after stripping the other of his weapons, went out singing the *Sitalcas* <note>A Thracian song or hymn</note>. Meanwhile, the other Thracians carried the 'victim' out as if he were dead, although he had suffered no harm."

Athenaeus mentions other types of dances there as well, if anyone desires to know them. Finally, Homer in the *Iliad* calls a certain Cretan who was strenuous in war a "dancer," because of the *Pyrrhiche* dance mentioned above, which was familiar to the Thracians. Thus the commentator, recording the three types of dances, calls the *Pyrrhiche* warlike, the *Sicinnin* suited to sacred rites, and the *Skordakismos* lewd and profane. Aristophanes in *The Birds* says:

"How a messenger comes to us, looking a 'Pyrrhic' <note>i.e., looking like a war-dance, or fierce</note>."

From this also comes the name of the "Pyrrhic foot" <note>A metrical foot of two short syllables</note> in poetry, because it possesses the momentum of a soldier rushing into battle. It is named after Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, as Pliny seems to believe in Book 7, Chapter 56, writing: "The Curetes taught the armored dance, and Pyrrhus taught the *Pyrrhiche* in Crete." Or, as Athenaeus thinks, it is named after a certain Pyrrhichus of Lacedaemonia; for the Spartans are most warlike, and among them, boys learned this dance from the age of five. They call it "the dance" <note>original Greek: ὠν- [referring to the enoplion or armed dance]</note>, and those who practice this type of exercise are called *Pyrrhichistae*. Or, it may take its name from the power of fire <note>original Greek: πῦρ (pyr), fire</note>. Pollux, in the place I just cited, says that the *Pyrrhiche* is the same as the *Telefias*, and that both names signify this type of contest. Indeed, if someone were to say that a person in a state of tumult or heated with anger was "performing the Pyrrhic" <note>original Greek: πυῤῥιχίζειν (pyrrhichizein)</note>, it would not lack the quality of a proverb. By a similar trope, Timocles in Athenaeus says:

"A man who hates speech, never speaking back to Antiphon, but showing Mars <note>The god of war, signifying a fierce expression</note> in his grim face."

Likewise, the poets say "looking grimly," and the Greeks say "looking from under the brow" <note>original Greek: ὑπόδρα βλέπων (hypodra blepōn)</note>.

---

-> There is no oil in the flask. <-
<note>original Latin: Non est oleum in lecytho; original Greek: Ἔλαιον οὐκ ἔνεσιν ἐν τῇ ληκύθῳ</note>

That is, the liquid of the oil is by no means in the flask. We use this when we mean there is no room for prayers with one who is inexorable. It is referenced in Aristophanes’ *The Birds*. It is a pun on the words, for *elaion* <note>ἔλαιον</note> signifies oil, and *eleon* <note>ἔλεον</note> signifies mercy, and I do not know but that one might be derived from the other.

---

-> He rejoices more than one who has shed his old age. <-
<note>original Latin: Magis gaudet eo qui senectam exuit; original Greek: Γέγηθε μᾶλλον ἢ τὸ γῆρας ἐκδύς</note>

This is said of someone who is immensely cheerful and leaping for joy. Aristophanes in *The Peace* says:

"For I am delighted as I rejoice, and I fart and I laugh, more than one who has shed his old age and escaped the shield <note>Meaning he has escaped the burdens of military service</note>."

This is drawn from snakes and cicadas, which shed their "old age" <note>Referring to the sloughed skin, called *senecta* in Latin</note> at fixed times and are, as it were, reborn.

---

This is the disease of good men.
<note>original Greek: Αὕτη γε χρηστῷ δίκη ἀνθρώπῳ ἡ νόσος</note>

--- Page 921 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Greek and Latin idioms, moving from the physical discipline of the "Pyrrhic dance" to metaphors regarding character flaws, minimal quantities, and speech impediments. It transitions from a discussion on what constitutes a "noble vice" to the technical etymology of stammering.</meta>

But this is indeed the disease of an honest man.
<note>original: "At iſte ſanè morbus eſt probi uiri."</note>
Suidas cites this almost as a proverb. It also appears in Aristophanes’s *Wasps*. It may be used when something is given as a reproach which ought rather to have been considered a point of praise. Similar to this is a line from Euripides’s *Iphigenia at Aulis*:
<note>original Greek: Καλὸν γέ μοι τἀνηδὲς ἀγωνιάσας.</note>
which is to say:
->You have reproached me with what is, in fact, an honorable reproach.<-
Or, in a more "competitive" sense <note>original: "ἀγωνικῶς" (agonikōs)</note>, it refers to certain grim and severe vices which, although they are quite harsh, are nevertheless less subject to infamy because great and respected men labor under them. For who does not curse a thief? Yet adultery is far more foul, though the nobility almost claim it as a point of pride for themselves. To envy, to disparage, to be zealous in amassing wealth is far more wicked than to have a girl with whom you sleep "on account of nighttime fears," as Saint Jerome says. Yet a priest who does the latter is called a "good-for-nothing" and a "dunghill," while those who swell with ambition, waste away with greed, and breathe the poison of envy upon everyone are considered upright and holy—evidently because these are the "diseases of honest men."

### Not even a drop. LXXV
Even today, there remains a very common vulgar expression, "Not even a drop" <note>original: "Ne gutta quidem"; Greek: κολικῶς (proverbially)</note>, used for the smallest possible thing.
Aristophanes, in the *Acharnians*:
<note>original Greek: Σὺ δ᾽ ἀλλά μοι σαλαγμὸν εἰρήνης ἕνα.</note>
which is to say:
->But you, give me at least one little drop of peace.<-
He said the same in the *Wasps* with a similar phrasing:
<note>original Greek: Ὕπνου δ᾽ οὐδὲ πασπάλην.</note>
which is to say:
->Not even a speck of sleep.<-
This was used in place of "not the slightest bit of sleep." For the Greeks call a minute crumb of copper or flour *paspale* <note>original: πασπάλην</note>, as we have also mentioned before. Plautus in the *Pseudolus*: "For whom neither a drop of counsel is ready, nor even of silver." For these expressions have more charm when transferred to matters of the mind, such as: "He has not a drop, nor a crumb, nor a hair of good sense."

### To stammer. LXXVI
<note>original Greek: Βατταρίζειν (Battarizein)</note>
Those who stuttered and whose tongues were hesitant and hindered were commonly said "to battarize," which the Greeks call *traulizein* <note>original: τραυλίζειν</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his letters to Atticus, Book 6: "The advocates of my freedman seemed to me to *battarize* [stammer over] my affairs." Hippocrates teaches that this defect arises from excessive moisture. Galen proves this in his sixth Commentary; hence it happens mostly in children and those who are intoxicated. Although he adds other causes, he indicates it occurs most especially with the letters *t* and *r*, for which they sound *tl*. From this it follows that they can hardly pronounce their own defect: "they lisp" <note>original Greek: τραυλῶσιν (traulōsin)</note>. Aristotle asks why children stammer more than men in his *Problems*, Section 11, Problem 30. The philosopher distinguishes there between *traulotes*, *psellotes*, and *ischnophonia*.
He defines *traulotes* <note>original: τραυλότητα</note> as when someone cannot express a certain letter—not just any letter, but a specific one. Theodorus Gaza translates this as *blesitas* [lisping].
He defines *psellotes* <note>original: ψελλότητα</note> as when a certain letter or syllable is suppressed, as when *tadis* is said for *stadis*; Theodorus translates this as *balbuties* [stammering].
Finally, he defines *ischnophonia* <note>original: ἰσχνοφωνίαν</note> as when they are not strong enough to quickly join one syllable to another in pronunciation; Theodorus translates this as "hesitancy of the tongue." These defects happen more frequently to children, as has been said, and to the elderly and those full of wine, whence Horace <note>referred to as "Flaccus"</note> calls old age "stammering." Aristotle thinks the cause is a weakness of strength, which cannot serve the mind.
Even though Cicero seems to take "battarize" almost for "to blather out." From there it was transferred to those who babble trifles. Whence they call "battarism" <note>original: βατταρισμὸν</note> silliness, borrowing the word from a certain Battus of Thebes, whose voice was thin and whose tongue was poorly articulated. To whom the Pythian oracle said: "Battus, you have come for a voice." The author is Hesychius, adding that to some it seems to be an imitative word [onomatopoeia], such as *phloisbos* [the roaring of the sea] and countless others. They also call "battology" <note>original: Βαττολογίαν</note> "much-speaking" [wordiness], from a certain poet named Battus whose custom it was to repeatedly hammer the same points in his poems. Suidas mentions both.
But these meanings have nothing to do with Cicero's sense. To me, it seems more likely that "to battarize" was said for "to act with evil deceit," because among the people of Cyrene a fox is called a *bassas* <note>original: βάσσας</note>, according to Herodotus, just as the Latins say "to fox around" <note>original: uulpinari</note>. For Battus was the leader for the leading of the colony into Cyrene. We have spoken elsewhere regarding *psellismos* [stuttering].

### From which he might boil out the tallow. LXXVII
Plautus, in *The Two Captives*, used a proverbial hyperbole: "From which the old man might boil out the tallow," signifying the most abundant wealth. Nevertheless, this passage does not seem to be free of error. The reason for the trochaic

the poem warns that it should be read as "best" [optimæ], not "not best" [nō optimæ]. This is a verse from Plautus, just as it is circulated in the common manuscripts:
->What are riches, if they are not the best? From which an old man boils down the tallow.<-
<note>original Latin: "Quid diuitiæ sunt ne optimæ? Vnde excoquat seuum senex."</note>
Now "tallow" [seuum], or as others write it, "suet" [sebum], is the harder fat of cattle, which the Greeks call <term>στέαρ</term> <note>stear: hard fat or suet, often used in sacrifice or candle-making</note>.

### To toss the yoke.
### LXXV

To toss the yoke is to bear the necessity of servitude with discomfort. It is a metaphor taken from oxen who are weary of the yoke they are accustomed to. Juvenal says:
->Nor have they learned to toss the yoke, with life as their teacher.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nec iactare iugum uita didicere magistra."</note>
This is similar to "Kicking against the prick." For misfortune is doubled when you bear it impatiently, but it is lessened by evenness of mind. As Plautus says:
->In a bad situation, if you use a good spirit, it helps.<-

### Like oil-merchants in the Velabrum.
### LXXVI

Like oil-merchants in the Velabrum. A proverbial comparison for those who have conspired together and manage a matter by prior agreement. Plautus in *The Captives*:
->It is one and the same thing;
Everyone acts by agreement, like oil-merchants in the Velabrum.<-
<note>original Latin: "Omnes compacto rem agunt, quasi in Velabro olearij."</note>
According to Varro, the Velabrum was a place in Rome where oil-merchants sold their oil. It is more common for this class of men to conspire among themselves regarding the price, so that they may sell for more.

### Of the lowest bench.
### LXXVII

In the same play, Plautus calls "parasites" men of the lowest bench, because they are admitted to a banquet in such a way that they sit in the lowest place. He says, "The Spartans no longer care for men of the lowest bench."
<note>original Latin: "Nihil... morant̄ iam Lacones, imi subsellij uiros."</note>
In the same author's *Stichus*, a parasite is introduced speaking thus: "I certainly do not demand to lie at the head of the table, but to eat quickly. You know I have long been a man of the lowest bench." Horace also uses the phrase:
->The mocker of the lowest couch,<-
<note>original Latin: "Et imi / Derisor lecti."</note>
meaning a buffoon or scoundrel. It will also apply to poor guests, whom those wealthy men sometimes receive, but in the lowliest place. It will be more elegant if it is transferred further—that is, to those who are in the lowest position among the nobles of the court, or the last among the learned; those whom one might call "below the class," "of the last class," or "of the lowest mark." Of these, the latter seems to be taken from merchandise, to which a mark is added to testify to the level of the price; but the former comes from the census of the ancients. For those who were of the "first class" possessed one hundred and twenty thousand pieces of brass, and these alone were called <term>classici</term> <note>classici: citizens of the highest rank; the origin of our word "classic"</note>; all the others—for there were several classes—were said to be "below the class" [infra classem]. The authority for this is Gellius, Book 7, Chapter 13. Although some manuscripts have 25 instead of 20. And Titus Livius says, "A hundred thousand pieces of brass."

### To play the pick-pocket.
### LXXVIII

Festus Pompeius shows that poets used this word "to play the pick-pocket" [manticulari] to mean "to deceive" or "to act craftily." He cites Pacuvius speaking thus: "He approaches with cunning to play the pick-pocket." He thinks it is derived from *manticulae* [little purses], which thieves are accustomed to handle, searching for them, no doubt. For my part, I think the metaphor is taken from the fact that those who dissemble at a banquet cover their faces with napkins [mantilia], as if wiping them. Whence Horace says in his *Satires*:
->To stifle a laugh with a napkin [mappa].<-
<note>original Latin: "Mappa compescere risum."</note>
Plautus likewise, in *The Captives*, used it for a cloak or a hiding place by which a trick can be covered: "Nowhere is there a napkin for my crafty lies, nor is there any napkin at hand for my deceits and pretenses."
<note>original Latin: "Ne mendacijs subdolis mihi usquam mantellum est meis." Erasmus treats 'mantellum' (cloak) and 'mantile' (napkin) as related metaphors for covering deceit.</note>
Indeed, I do not know if this form relates to what is read in Origen’s fifth homily on Ezekiel: "He who said to his neighbor, 'God forgives us our sins.' Since we also play in such mysteries, promising each other in turn, as if God will send peace [pax], that is, cover our shames, once the napkin is dropped [missa mappa]."
<note>original: "missa mappa." This refers to the dropping of a cloth to start a race, but Erasmus suggests it implies "letting something go" or "covering it up."</note>
But since a copy of the Greek manuscript is not available, it would be better to act the Academic <note>Academic: a reference to the Skeptic philosophers who suspended judgment when proof was lacking</note> on this matter. Learned men who have the passage at hand will examine this after being warned by us. Tertullian uses the same saying in his book against the Valentinians: "But, as they say, the napkin having been dropped."

### He has his sole fastened with gold.
### LXXIX

Plautus used this as a proverbial figure in the *Bacchides*:
->But is that Theotimus wealthy?
Do you even ask? A man who has the soles of his shoes fastened with gold.<-
<note>original Latin: "qui foccis habeat auro suppactum solum."</note>
This is said of an extremely rich man, who has such a force of gold available that he tramples it under his feet. For he used "sole" [solum] for the lowest part of the shoes, or certainly for the pavement.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of adages, moving from Roman agricultural metaphors to diverse Greek and Roman idioms. This section focuses on historical anecdotes and cultural quirks from Samos, Sparta (Laconia), and the works of classical authors like Cicero and Aristophanes.</meta>

<page-num>799</page-num>
<header>THE SEVENTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND</header>
<sig>XX 4</sig>

### To the altars.
### LXXXIII
<note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ βωμὸς; Latin: Ad aras</note> This is recorded in the *Collectanea* <note>A "miscellany" or collection of writings</note> attributed to Plutarch, though it is not fully explained there. I personally believe it means "in the heat of the business," much like a proverb we mentioned in another place, where we are forbidden from "consulting at the altars" <note>This implies making decisions at the last moment or when it is too late to change course, as if one is already at the sacrificial altar</note>.

### The Samian Alley.
### LXXXIIII
<note>original Greek: Σαμίων λαῦρα; Latin: Samiorum laura</note> This was a common saying regarding those addicted to shameful pleasures. Among the people of Samos, a "laura" was a type of narrow street or alley where delicacies and the luxuries of cook-shops were sold by women trained for that purpose. This adage also appears in the commentaries attributed to Plutarch. Athenaeus reports the same thing from Clearchus in his twelfth book, adding that this was an invention of Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos. He suggests that this corruption of the city was modeled after the "cubit of Sardis" <note>A reference to the extreme luxury of the Lydian capital, Sardis</note>, which according to Plato was proverbially called "sweet."

### The Taenarian evil.
### LXXXV
<note>original Greek: Ταινάριον κακόν; Latin: Tænarium malum</note> If any cruelty was practiced too harshly against slaves, they called it a "Taenarian evil." This is because the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> once seized captives who had fled for sanctuary to Taenarus, dragged them away, and put them to death. In this context, Taenarus is a town in Laconia <note>The region around Sparta</note> whose inhabitants are called Taenarians; it is also the name of a promontory in that same region where there is a cave thought to be an entrance to the underworld.

### Lesbian Prylis.
### LXXXVI
<note>original Greek: Ὁ λέσβιος πρύλις; Latin: Lesbius Prylis</note> Plutarch, in his collection of adages (if the title of that work is not misleading), relates that this proverb is used as a comparison. He says that Prylis was a son of Mercury <note>Hermes</note> and was skilled in divination. However, in Greek, the word <term>πρύλις</term> <note>prylis</note> also signifies a foot soldier.

### Drive the donkey.
### LXXXVII
<note>Latin: Agas asellum</note> Since this adage is recorded in a mutilated form, it is not entirely clear what it means. It is cited by Cicero in his second book *On the Orator* in this manner: "Proverbs are cast into this category, like that one of Scipio’s; when a man named Asellus <note>literally "little donkey"</note> was boasting that he had traveled through all the provinces during his military service, Scipio replied: 'Drive the donkey,' and so forth." Thus far Cicero. I do not care to repeat what Omnibonus <note>A 15th-century commentator on Cicero</note>—otherwise a decent interpreter—brings to this passage. Nevertheless, I thought it best to put the adage forward so that I might at least provide the learned with an opportunity for investigation. Perhaps it should read "The groom [drives] the donkey" <note>original Latin: agaso asellum</note>. For the ancients used to elide vowels in the Greek fashion even in writing. In this way, the meaning would be that everyone should do what is worthy of themselves: the grandsons squander, the glutton boils away his wealth, the soldier fights with a sword, the pimp commits perjury, and the lawyer lies. Indeed, the very word for groom, <term>agaso</term>, became a proverbial term of contempt. This is even more playful among the Greeks because of a lack of words: for the Dorians call a donkey not <note>original Greek: ὄνον</note> like everyone else, but <note>original Greek: κίλλου</note>, and a groom not <note>original Greek: ὀνηλάτην</note>, but <note>original Greek: κιλλικῆτα</note>, as Julius Pollux testifies in his seventh book *On Vocabulary*. Perhaps what Horace wrote in his nineteenth Epistle to Lollius pertains to this:
> At the very end, he will be a Thracian, or he will drive the nag for a gardener's wage.

### The long-haired Samian.
### LXXXVIII
<note>original Greek: Τὸν ἐν σάμῳ κομήτην; Latin: Samiū comatum</note> They used to say this about someone who was previously considered lazy but behaved more brilliantly than expected in a piece of business. They say there was a certain boxer among the Samians who, when he was mocked by his opponents for having long hair, engaged with them and won. From this, it became a proverb whenever someone takes up a contest with those whom they unexpectedly find to be superior in strength. This is not unlike the warning given by Sulla: "Beware the ill-girded boy" <note>A reference to the young Julius Caesar, who wore his clothes loosely</note>. This is listed in Plutarch's *Collectanea*.

### I do not carry a slave.
### LXXXIX
<note>original Greek: Δῆλον οὐκ ἄγω, εἰ μὴ νεικωμαχήκηι τὸν περὶ τῶν κρεῶν</note>
that is,
> I do not carry a slave,
> Unless he has first fought for his meat,
> In a naval battle.
This means: I do not admit a slave unless he has been tested by many great trials. This verse is found in Aristophanes’ *The Frogs*, and was cited by us in another place. The commentators point out that there is a double reading: "for the meat" <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν κρεῶν</note> and "for the corpses" <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν νεκρῶν</note>. Those who take it as "for the meat" interpret it as "for life," for they call the body "meat" <note>flesh</note>. Furthermore, when slaves fight, since they have no possessions, they struggle only for their lives. Those who read "corpses" bring up this story: in the naval battle fought at Arginusae <note>An Athenian naval victory in 406 BCE where the generals were later executed for failing to rescue survivors or recover the dead</note>, those who were superior...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s explanations of classical adages, moving from the aftermath of a battle in Athens to various Greek idioms concerning Corinthian reputations, the hardships of Corsica (Cyrnus), and the mythical ferryman Charon.</meta>

<page-num>800</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...the Athenians stood their ground and forbade the bodies of the fallen to be removed, and the battle was fought out even in this way. It is recorded that slaves performed exceptional service in this war, for which they were granted freedom. This proverb is found in Plutarch’s *Collectanea*—

->A third head.<-
<note>original Greek: τρίτη κεφαλὴ, καὶ τρίτῳ ἐγκεφάλῳ; Latin: Tertium caput & tertio cerebro</note> **A third head and a third brain.** This was a saying used for heavy burdens, referring to those who carry loads not only on their shoulders but also on their head. It appears in the same *Collectanea* I cited. It can be aptly applied to people distracted by many different affairs.

->You look like a Corinthian woman.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἁ κορινθία ἔοικας χοιροπωλήσῳ; Latin: Corinthia uideris corpore quæstū factura</note> **You look like a Corinthian woman about to make a profit with her body.** This was said of someone behaving lecherously at an improper time. It refers to the prostitutes of Corinth. The word <term>choiropōlō</term> <note>literally "to sell pigs"</note> is a newly coined term indicating one making a profit with their body, as the word <term>choiros</term> <note>meaning "piglet"</note> was also a slang term for female anatomy. This also appears in the same *Collectanea*.

->A Cyrnian loss.<-
<note>original Greek: Κυρνία ἄτη; Latin: Cyrnium malū</note> **A Cyrnian evil.** This was said of great expenses or heavy punishments. <note>Cyrnus is the ancient Greek name for the island of Corsica.</note> There is an island near Apulia <note>in southern Italy</note> whose inhabitants are said to be long-lived because they mostly feed on honey, being neighbors to the island of Sardinia. 
<margin>p</margin>For there the honey is very bitter, as the geographer Stephanus testifies. This island was once inaccessible to sailors because of the 
<margin>p</margin>frequency of bandits and pirates around it. And from this, the proverb became common among the people. 
<margin>p</margin>Pliny, in Book 4, Chapter 12, names Cyrnus, but distinguishes it from Corsica, though Strabo records that Cyrnus is what the Romans call Corsica—an island difficult to inhabit because of the ruggedness of the terrain. The region is impassable in many places, but especially because the inhabitants hold the mountains and live by banditry, being more savage than wild beasts. If any of them are captured by Roman generals and brought to Rome, it is a wonder to see how they display a certain wild and beast-like nature; they either commit suicide or, if they live, they so weary their masters with their stupidity and mindlessness that the masters regret buying them, no matter how cheap the price. Such was Corsica once; now it is famous for its wines and provides for Roman delicacies. Because of the enormity of the banditry and the savagery of the race, it was called a "Cyrnian evil," just as we speak of "Cilician destruction," as we noted elsewhere. We mentioned this adage above under "Cyrnian land."

->Plunder at the Cotytia.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἁρπαγὰ κοτυτίοις; Latin: Rapina Cotytijs</note> **Plunder at the Cotytia.** The Cotytia was a certain festival among the Sicilians in which, according to custom, certain small cakes and the fruits of trees were tied to branches, and these were set out to be snatched away by the people. It is recorded in Plutarch’s *Collectanea*, but not explained there. However, it is easily clear that it was usually said of goods recklessly squandered or plundered.

->Things from the ancient.<-
<note>original Greek: τὰ ἐκ παλαιᾶς; Latin: Quæ ex antiqua</note> **Things from the ancient**, with "Tyre" being understood. It is equivalent to saying the greatest trouble and the extreme evil. For Alexander the Great, after capturing Tyre—which was nicknamed "the Ancient" <note>Palaetyrus</note> and made into a mainland city by Alexander building a causeway from the island—treated it cruelly and inflicted many hardships upon it. From this comes the proverb "Things from the ancient," by which they signified as much evil as ancient Tyre had endured. It is also listed in Plutarch’s *Collectanea* and by Zenodotus. For the history, see Quintus Curtius.

->Three-headed Mercury.<-
<note>original Greek: τρικέφαλος ἑρμῆς; Latin: Triceps Mercurius</note> **Three-headed Mercury.** It seems to be said of those who are ambiguous and double-tongued, or of those who are exceedingly clever. Mercury <note>the god of messages and crossroads</note> was depicted in this way in ancient times, either because speech has great power, or because the same god is a guide on the road; therefore, at three-way intersections, he had an inscription stating where this road led and where that one went. Proclides was the first to set up a statue of Mercury of this kind, according to Philochorus.

->Danake.<-
<note>original Greek: Δανάκη; Latin: Danace</note> **Danake.** This was the name of that small coin paid to Charon for the crossing of the Stygian marsh <note>the river in the underworld</note>, which Lucian mentions in his *Charon*, and Apuleius likewise in the fable of Psyche. Plutarch records it in the *Collectanea*, but its use is not indicated. It seems it would be used correctly if someone were to tell an old man to "prepare his danake," implying that his departure from life is near. Or if one were to say someone has left so little behind that not even a "danake" remained. Juvenal uses this in his third Satire, where he calls this coin a <term>triens</term> <note>a small Roman coin</note>.

<page-num>801</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD THREE, CENTURY VII</header>

The unhappy man hopes not for the boat of the muddy abyss,
Nor has he a coin to offer from his mouth.
<note>original: "Nec sperat coenosi gurgitis alnum Infelix, nec habet quem porrigat ore trientem." These lines from Virgil’s Aeneid describe the souls of the unburied or the poor who cannot pay Charon's toll to cross the river Styx.</note>

### You stood like Bagas.
<margin>XCVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Βάγας ἕστηκας; Latin: Ut Bagas stabas</note> This was said of a person who was stupid or speechless. Bagas was someone who seemed stunned, dull, and senseless. He is mentioned in Plutarch’s *Collectanea* <note>a collection of short works or essays</note>. I am not sure whether it should be read as *Bagoas* instead of *Bagas*; Bagoas was a famous Eunuch. This class of men is often described as timid and un-warlike.

### You are teaching a crab to walk straight.
<margin>XCVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Καρκίνον ὀρθὰ βαδίζειν διδάσκεις; Latin: Cancrum recte ingredi doces</note> Said of someone who tries to teach the unteachable. This is also recorded in Plutarch’s *Collectanea*. It is very close to, or rather the same as, the proverb we mentioned a little earlier from Aristophanes: *You will never succeed*. It belongs to the category of <term>adynata</term> <note>from the Greek for "impossible things"</note>, like *You are whitewashing an Ethiopian*, and so on. This is because this animal only moves with a sideways body and shifts its step in every direction. Some think the word for crab, *karkinos*, is derived from *kakinos*, referring to the movement of the head. It is also said to give birth through its head.

### You are draining the sea.
<margin>XCIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Θάλασσαν ἀντλεῖς; Latin: Mare exhauris</note> Said of someone who attempts what cannot be accomplished. For while mountains can be tunneled through in various ways, the sea cannot be emptied.

### Timid dogs bark more fiercely.
<margin>C</margin>
Quintus Curtius <note>a Roman historian of Alexander the Great</note> in his seventh book demonstrates that a proverb of this kind was commonly tossed about among the Bactrians: *A timid dog barks more fiercely than it bites*. It is typical of "Thrasos" <note>braggart soldiers, named after a character in Terence’s plays</note> to threaten dire deeds with swollen boasts; yet "Chremes" <note>a character type representing a cautious, practical man</note> is more ready to get the job done. So too we read that the Athenians were better suited for speaking well than for acting vigorously. It was not easy for Ajax to speak, nor for Ulysses to refrain from war. The Spartans <note>Lacedaemonians</note> were very sparing with words but far excelled in courage. In Homer, the Greeks enter battle in silence but breathing strength, while the barbarians ran forward with a monstrous shout. Finally, women wage war with their tongues better than with their strength. Quintus Curtius adds a similar allegory in the same passage: *the deepest rivers flow with the least sound*.

---

### CHILIAD THREE, CENTURY VIII

### Some proverbial verses from Homer.

Antiquity held Homer in such high honor—as Macrobius <note>a Latin writer of late antiquity</note> testifies—that almost every single one of his verses was celebrated as a proverb. We have reviewed some of these scattered throughout this work, especially those we found used in the writings of other authors. Now, therefore, I believe I will be doing something worthwhile if I select certain short verses from the entire body of Homeric poetry that so clearly bear the appearance of a proverb that there should be no doubt they were among those antiquity used as adages. Although there is almost no poem by this poet that cannot be twisted into some proverbial sense, we have preferred to pluck only a few out of many. This is partly so that no one can say we are too painstaking in a matter that seems secondary, and partly because, for some reason, those things that each person adopts for himself are more pleasing in this genre. Therefore, we have been satisfied with a few, showing the way in which they ought to be applied. And in these very cases, although we have indicated a use for the verse that came to mind while we were writing, nothing prevents the same verse from being adopted for various uses. I would not allow the same for other poets, unless one thinks it permissible for Virgil <note>Maro</note>, whom you might rightly call the Latin Homer. But a certain divinity in Homer makes it fitting that whatever you borrow from him in any way is appropriate, even if—as is often done in <term>centos</term> <note>a poem made up of verses or passages from other authors</note>—you twist the words to a far different meaning. Although we know these would lack grace unless used in Greek, nevertheless, lest they not be understood by some, we have translated these as well. But now we shall begin to list them.

### Not approving.
<margin>I</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐκ Ἀτρείδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι ἥνδανε θυμῷ; Latin: At non Atridæ sic est Agamemnoni uiſum</note>
"But it did not please the heart of Agamemnon, son of Atreus."
This is used by Lucian as if proverbially in *The Lapiths*. We shall use it correctly when we admit a thing is honorable to do, but that different things please those whose lust has more power than the logic of equity.
