<meta>This page continues the eighth century of the third Chiliad, where Erasmus compiles various verses from Homer’s epics—the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*—that served as proverbial expressions or apt quotations for specific social situations in the classical world.</meta>

<page-num>802</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...reason. This is used either when someone follows a tyrannical manner, acting not according to what equity dictates but according to their own whim; or when a single individual disagrees with everyone else. It is taken from the first book of Homer's *Iliad*, where this verse is repeated:

> Then all the other Achaeans <note>Achaeans was one of the names Homer used for the Greeks.</note> shouted their approval,
> To respect the priest and accept the splendid ransom.
> But this did not please the heart of Agamemnon, son of Atreus,
> Instead, he dismissed him rudely and added a harsh word.
> <note>original: "Ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες... / At reliquæ Danaum placet hæc sententia turbæ..." *Iliad* 1.22–25.</note>

->For one refuting immoderate praise.<-

> I am no god; why do you liken me to the immortals?
> <note>original: "οὔτι ἐγὼ θεός εἰμι, τί μ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἐΐσκεις." *Odyssey* 16.187.</note>

Plutarch, in the commentary titled *How a man may become aware of his progress*, advises that we should always have this Homeric verse ready as if it were a medicine against the poison of flattery, or for when someone praises us more magnificently <term>than</term> we deserve. See also Lucian in his work *Icaromenippus* <note>A satirical dialogue where the character Menippus flies to heaven.</note>. The verse appears in the sixteenth book of the *Odyssey*, spoken by Ulysses to his son Telemachus.

->For one guarding against secret ambushes.<-

> Lest someone fix a spear in your back as you flee.
> <note>original: "μή τις σε φεύγοντι μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ πήξῃ." *Iliad* 8.95.</note>

Used when we mean that one must act more circumspectly, lest someone harm the person who is unaware. Diogenes <note>The famous Cynic philosopher known for his sharp wit.</note> employed this by changing one little word when addressing a handsome youth who was sleeping unguarded:
> Lest someone fix a spear in your back as you sleep.

These words are found in the eighth book of Homer's *Iliad*, spoken by Diomedes to restrain Ulysses from fleeing the battle. Likewise, in the twenty-second book:

> You shall never fix a spear in my back as I flee,
> But rather drive it through my chest as I rush straight ahead.
> <note>original: "οὐ μὲν μοὶ φεύγοντι... / Nunquam mi à tergo fugienti..." *Iliad* 22.273.</note>

This may be used when someone does not shrink from an open contest.

->For one ordering another to speak openly.<-

If we are advising someone to bring forth the causes of their grief or hatred and not hide them in their soul, we might aptly quote this from the first book of the *Iliad*:

> Speak out, do not hide it in your mind, so that we both may know.
> <note>original: "Ἐξαύδα, μὴ κεῦθε νόῳ, ἵνα εἴδομεν ἄμφω." *Iliad* 1.363.</note>

->For one promising to fulfill promises with deeds.<-

When indicating that the faith of our promises will not be in vain, but that we will fulfill in deed what we have promised in words, we can use these verses from the same book:

> For what I confirm with a nod of my head is not
> To be revoked, nor is it deceptive or unfulfilled.
> <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ἐμὸν παλινάγρετον... / Nec reuocanda, nec irrita..." *Iliad* 1.526–527.</note>

These words are spoken by Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> to the goddess Thetis.

->Against one who has spoken absurdly.<-

When someone seems to have said something absurd, or when a word seems to have escaped through imprudence which would have been better kept silent, there will be a place for this line, which is found in several places in Homer, and specifically in the first book of the *Odyssey*:

> What a word has escaped the barrier of your teeth!
> <note>original: "Ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων." *Odyssey* 1.64.</note>

This verse is praised by Aulus Gellius <note>A Roman author of the 2nd century AD.</note> in *Attic Nights*, book 1, chapter 15. He beautifully warns that one must speak sparingly because nature has enclosed the tongue with a wall and a hedge of teeth, whereas it gave us open ears.

<meta>This page continues the eighth century of the third Chiliad of Erasmus’s *Adagia*. Following the previous page, Erasmus continues to extract useful, proverbial verses from Homer’s *Iliad*, particularly from the second and third books, demonstrating how these epic lines can be applied to everyday speech and moral situations.</meta>

<page-num>803</page-num>
<header>THE THIRD CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY</header>

->For frustrated hope.<-

VII
If we ever wish to indicate that someone has been frustrated in their hope, and that a matter has turned out differently than they expected, we can quite aptly apply that line from the second book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "νήπιος οὐδέ τὰ ἤδη, ἅ ῥά ζεὺς μήδεα ἔργα." *Iliad* 2.38.</note>
"Foolish man, he did not know the deeds Zeus was preparing." That is to say:
"Foolish, for Jupiter <note>Erasmus uses the Roman name Jupiter for the Greek Zeus, a common practice in the Renaissance.</note> was preparing things quite different for him while he remained ignorant."

->Fruitless effort.<-

VIII
When we feel that labor is being spent in vain and that nothing is being gained despite long-lasting efforts, that line from the same book will fit quite well:
<note>original: "ἀπρήκτον πόλεμον πολεμίζειν ἠδέ μάχεσθαι." *Iliad* 2.342.</note>
"To wage a fruitless war and a useless battle." That is:
"To lead a joyless fight and an unprofitable war."

->For one swearing to do something.<-

IX
When we swear that we will do something, provided that life does not fail us, we may adapt a verse from the same book:
<note>original: "μήκ' ἔτ' ἔπειτ' ὀδυσῆϊ κάρη ὤμοισιν ἐπείη." *Iliad* 2.259.</note>
"May the head of Odysseus no longer stand upon his shoulders." That is:
"Let this head no longer press upon the shoulders of Ulysses." Likewise, from the fifth book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "αὐτίκ' ἔπειτ' ἀπ' ἐμοῖο κάρη τάμοι ἀλλότριος φώς." *Iliad* 5.214.</note>
"Then let some stranger immediately cut off this head of mine with a sword." That is:
"Let some barbarian soon cut off this head with his blade."
For the common people even in our own times swear in this manner. These expressions are also well known among the Latins: "May I die," or "May I perish" <note>original: "Emoriar, dispeream."</note>.

->Things that come late, but are magnificent.<-

X
Whenever we want it understood that fame or some reward is indeed arriving quite late, but that it is more excellent and durable for having been delayed—so that it compensates for its slowness with stability and permanence—it will not be out of place to use that Homeric line from the second book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "ὄψιμον ὀψitέλεστον, ὅς κλέος οὔ ποτ' ἀπολεῖται." *Iliad* 2.325.</note>
"Late in appearing, late in being fulfilled, but its glory shall never perish."
Cicero translated this verse thus:
"Tardy and far too late, but with fame and praise everlasting."
These are the words of Calchas <note>The primary seer or prophet for the Greek army during the Trojan War.</note> encouraging the Greeks to persevere; for although the victory of the war would only occur in the tenth year, its fame would nevertheless be immortal.

->To give counsel, and to obey counsel.<-

XI
When we advise someone to turn around and give good counsel to others as well as receive it from them—or to weigh a matter carefully with themselves while also listening to another's opinion with attentive ears—it will not be untimely to use this from the same book:
<note>original: "ἀλλὰ ἄναξ, αὐτός τ' εὖ μήδεο, πείθεό τ' ἄλλῳ." *Iliad* 2.360.</note>
"But O King, take good counsel yourself, and obey another in turn." That is:
"Come now, King, deliberate well yourself, and obey in your turn."

->A hungry man should not be interrupted.<-

XII
Whenever we suggest that there is no leisure for conversation unless we have first quieted the "barking" and angry stomach, as Horace says. Or when we mean that someone, as soon as they have obtained what they were seeking, immediately turns to other things, we might aptly produce this verse from the same book (which appears frequently elsewhere in Homer):
<note>original: "αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο." *Iliad* 1.469, 2.432, etc.</note>
"But after they had put away the desire for drink and food." That is:
"But after the craving for drink and food was removed from these men." Virgil renders it this way:
"After hunger was banished and the love of eating quelled" <note>original: "Postquam exempta fames & amor compressus edendi." *Aeneid* 8.184.</note>.

->A vast multitude of things.<-

XIII
When we wish to indicate an admirable multitude of people, or things, or even evils, this line from the same book (and often elsewhere) will be appropriate:
<note>original: "ὅσσατε φύλλα καὶ ἄνθεα γίγνεται ὥρῃ, ἠΎτε μυιάων ἀδινάων ἔθνεα πολλά." *Iliad* 2.468-469.</note>
"As many as are the leaves and flowers that appear in their season, just like the many swarms of thick-flying flies." That is:
"As many as the foliage and the flowers in the springtime,
Or like the many swarms of flies gathered in a mass."

->Things that happen by divine providence.<-

XIV
Anyone who says that a certain thing does not happen to just anyone who wishes for it, but is given by divine providence—such as talent, beauty, or strength—can use that Homeric line from the third book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "ἑκὼν δ' οὐκ ἄν τις ἕλοιτο." *Iliad* 3.66.</note>
"One could not take them of one's own will." That is:
"Not everyone who wishes it may carry those things away."

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Homer’s *Iliad* as a source for proverbs. Having previously looked at themes of frustration and oaths, he now moves into Book 3 and 4, focusing on themes of divine gifts, the limitations of old age, and the dynamics of interpersonal conflict and affection.</meta>

<page-num>804</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

These words are spoken by Hector to the character of Paris <note>Erasmus uses "Alexander," the alternative name for Paris in the *Iliad*.</note>, who had reproached him for his hair, his beauty, and his un-warlike lyre:
<note>original: "οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃ κίθαρις, τά τε δῶρ’ ἀφροδίτης. ἥτε κόμη, τό τε εἶδος ὅτ’ ἐν κονίῃσι μιγείης." *Iliad* 3.54-55.</note>
"Neither your lyre, nor the gifts of Aphrodite, nor your hair, nor your beauty will help you when you are mingled with the dust." That is to say:
"Nothing will profit you—neither your songs, nor the gifts of Venus <note>Erasmus often substitutes the Roman goddess Venus for the Greek Aphrodite.</note>, nor your hair, nor your fair looks—when you meet your end in the dust." <margin>To this, Paris responds thus:</margin>
<note>original: "μή μοι δῶρ’ ἐρατὰ πρόφερε χρυσῆς ἀφροδίτης. οὔτοι ἀπόβλητ’ ἐστὶ θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα, ὅσσάκεν αὐτοὶ δῶσιν, ἑκὼν δ’ οὐκ ἄν τις ἕλοιτο." *Iliad* 3.64-66.</note>
"Do not cast in my teeth the lovely gifts of golden Aphrodite. Indeed, the glorious gifts of the gods are not to be cast aside—whatever they themselves may give—for no man could take them for himself by his own will." That is:
"Do not reproach me for the desirable gift of Venus. The most beautiful gifts of the gods are by no means to be despised, which they give of their own accord; nor can anyone take them for himself just because he wishes it."
Diogenes Laertius records that the Cynic philosopher Diogenes, when criticized for accepting gifts from Antipater <note>Antipater was a powerful Macedonian general and regent.</note>, replied with the Homeric verse I just cited: "Indeed, they are not to be cast aside..." and so on.

->On a lecherous old man.<-

This is used against those who are now useless for active duty because of their age, yet are strong in speech. For instance, if one wished to criticize a "wether" <note>A castrated ram, used here as a metaphor for an impotent man.</note>—as Plautus says—who is old and speaks foully, but is sluggish in the practice of Venus, one might aptly use this line from the same book:
<note>original: "γήραϊ δὴ πολέμοιο πεπαυμένοι, ἀλλ’ ἀγορηταὶ ἐσθλοί." *Iliad* 3.150.</note>
"Already stopped from war by old age, but excellent speakers." That is:
"Now retired from war because of senility, but outstanding only at talking."
The same is said in the fourth book regarding the son of Tydeus <note>Diomedes.</note>:
<note>original: "χέρεια μάχῃ, ἀγορῇ δέ τ’ ἀμείνων." *Iliad* 4.400.</note>
"Inferior in battle, but superior in the assembly." That is:
"Lesser in the fight, but foremost in speaking."

->To be blamed on the Fates.<-

Whenever we wish to free a person from blame and shift it onto either fate or fortune, it will be permitted to use what Priam says there to Helen:
<note>original: "οὔτι μοι αἰτίη ἐσσί, θεοίνυ μοι αἴτιοί εἰσιν." *Iliad* 3.164.</note>
"You are not the cause in my eyes; the gods are the cause for me." That is:
"I blame you for nothing; rather, I blame the gods themselves."

->Revealing what was long hidden.<-

Of someone who, after having long concealed something, finally speaks it out when provoked, that line said in the same place regarding Ulysses will not be awkwardly applied:
<note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ῥ’ ὅπα τε μεγάλην ἐκ στήθεος ἵει." *Iliad* 3.221.</note>
"But when he finally let out the great voice from his chest." That is:
"But when at last he brings forth that grand voice from his breast."

->Obstinate contention.<-

Whenever we wish to point out a stubborn and womanish contention between equals, where neither wishes to seem inferior to the other, that line which Juno speaks to Jupiter in the fourth book of the *Iliad* will be appropriate:
<note>original: "Καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ θεός εἰμι, γένος δέ μοι ἔνθεν, ὅθεν σοι." *Iliad* 4.58.</note>
"For I too am a god, and my lineage is from the same place as yours." That is:
"I myself am also a goddess; my origin is from the same source as yours."

->When each yields to the other.<-

Conversely, when contention is set aside and each yields to the other, there will be a place for the words that follow immediately in the same passage:
<note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ταῦθ’ ὑποείξομεν ἀλλήλοισιν, Σοὶ μὲν ἐγὼ, σὺ δ’ ἐμοί." *Iliad* 4.62-63.</note>
"But indeed, let us yield these things to one another—I to you, and you to me." That is:
"Rather, let us both yield to the other in these matters: you to me, and I in turn to you."

->To love with devotion.<-

Regarding someone who loves another tenderly, or is so devoted that they will not allow them to be affected by even the slightest discomfort from anyone, you might skillfully apply this from the same book:
<note>original: "ὡς ὅτε μήτηρ παιδὸς ἐέργῃ μυῖαν ὅθ’ ἡδέϊ λέξεται ὕπνῳ." *Iliad* 4.130-131.</note>
"As when a mother brushes a fly from her child when he lies in sweet sleep." That is:
"Not otherwise than a mother, dutifully keeping flies away from her boy as he lies sleeping."
This was said of Pallas <note>Athena.</note> tending to the wound of Menelaus.

# THE EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD THOUSAND
### Yy
<meta>catchword: Rejecting</meta>

<margin>xxi</margin>
->A sarcastic remark of one who is contemptuous.<-
If ever we wish to indicate that we are only lightly moved by a taunt or an insult, and that we do not let it sink deeply into our soul, the following from the fourth book of the *Iliad* will be appropriate:
<note>original: "τὸν δ' οὐ κατέδυ ὀξὺ βέλος, ἀλλὰ πάροιθεν εἰρύσατο ζωστήρ τε παναίολος, ἠδ' ὑπένερθεν, ζῶμά τε καὶ μίτρη, τὴν χαλκῆες κάμον ἄνδρες." *Iliad* 4.137-139.</note>
"The sharp arrow did not sink in, but the gleaming belt held it off, and beneath it the kilt and the metal guard which the smiths had fashioned." That is:
"The weapon, once sent, did not pass through to the vitals, but the belt held it at the surface of the skin, along with the bronze scales that the smith had added."

<margin>xxii</margin>
->Forgetfulness of evils.<-
One who wishes to turn away an unlucky omen, or who commands that the memory of evils be wiped away, will not inappropriately use this line from the same book:
<note>original: "τὰ δὲ πάντα θεοὶ μεταμώνια θεῖεν." *Iliad* 4.363.</note>
"May the gods make all these things as empty as the wind." That is:
"May the gods above hand all these things over to the winds."

<margin>xxiii</margin>
->From the smallest beginnings, the greatest things.<-
To indicate that the greatest feuds sometimes arise from the slightest little injuries—no differently than a massive fire starts from the tiniest spark—this passage from the same book concerning Eris <note>The goddess of Strife or Contention.</note> will be wonderfully fitting:
<note>original: "ἥτ' ὀλίγη μὲν πρῶτα κορύσσεται, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα οὐρανῷ ἐστήριξε κάρη καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ βαίνει." *Iliad* 4.442-443.</note>
"She who at first rises small, but then fixes her head in the heavens while she walks upon the earth." That is:
"She who first rises tiny, but immediately reaches the sky with her head, while planting her footprints on the earth."
Virgil, in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*, adapted this passage to describe Fame <note>Or Rumor (Fama).</note>:
"Small at first through fear, soon she lifts herself into the air, walks upon the ground, and hides her head among the clouds."

<margin>xxiiii</margin>
->Of different parties.<-
One who wishes to hint at a "Mettius" <note>Mettius Fufetius was a legendary dictator of Alba Longa who betrayed the Romans by standing neutral in battle to see who would win.</note>—someone playing both sides—or a deceptive lawyer, or a traitorous general, might elegantly use this from *Iliad* Book 5:
<note>original: "τυδείδην δ' οὐκ ἂν γνοίης, ποτέροισι μετείη, ἠὲ μετὰ τρώεσσιν ὁμιλέοι, ἦ μετ' ἀχαιοῖς." *Iliad* 5.85-86.</note>
"You would not know which side the son of Tydeus <note>Diomedes.</note> belonged to, whether he consorted with the Trojans or with the Achaeans." That is:
"Furthermore, you could by no means distinguish the son of Tydeus, whether he moves among the Trojans or the Achaeans."

<margin>xxv</margin>
->Fierce through another's protection.<-
If you wish to imply that someone is fierce and attempts wicked things not because they rely on their own strength, but because they are bolstered by the protection of someone more powerful who secretly supplies them with both courage and resources—just as the common people among our own countrymen suspect the Duke of Guelders <note>Charles of Egmond, Duke of Guelders, a frequent thorn in the side of the Habsburgs.</note> has for so many years caused trouble for us through the hidden support of the French—you may apply this from the same book:
<note>original: "οὐκ ὅγ' ἄνευθε θεοῦ τάδε μαίνεται, ἀλλά τις ἄγχι ἔστηκ' ἀθανάτων νεφέλῃ εἰλυμένος ὤμους." *Iliad* 5.185-186.</note>
"He does not rage like this without a god; rather, one of the immortals stands near him, his shoulders wrapped in a cloud." That is:
"Indeed, this man dares such things by no means without divine power; truly, one of the gods stands by, his shoulders covered in mist."

<margin>xxvi</margin>
->Fortune entirely adverse.<-
When a matter begun with good counsel nevertheless turns out badly, you might aptly say this from the same book:
<note>original: "θεὸς νύτις ὧδε κοτήεις." *Iliad* 5.177.</note>
"Some god is thus angry." That is: "Some god is hostile." Likewise in Book 6:
<note>original: "ἀλλ' ὅτε δὴ κἀκεῖνος ἀπήχθετο πᾶσι θεοῖσι." *Iliad* 6.200.</note>
"But when even he became hated by all the gods." That is: "When he was now hateful even to all the gods."

<margin>xxvii</margin>
->Seize the care of the business.<-
When admonishing someone to diligently take up a task and approach a matter with vigor, we shall use this verse from the same place, where Aeneas encourages his charioteer:
<note>original: "ἀλλ' ἄγε νῦν μάστιγα καὶ ἡνία σιγαλόεντα δέξαι." *Iliad* 5.226-227.</note>
"But come now, take the whip and the shining reins." That is:
"Come now, seize the whip in your hand and the decorated reins."

ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### Rejecting the one who prompts fear.
<meta>XX</meta>

To someone who is terrifying others and instilling empty fear, it will be permitted to chant this verse, with which Diomedes addresses Sthenelus: 
<note>original: "μήτε φόβον δ᾽ ἀγόρευε" (Iliad 5.249)</note>
"Do not suggest fear to me." That is:
"Do not be the one to prompt me to tremble."

---

### To attack with every effort.
<meta>XXI</meta>

If we wish to indicate that someone is striving with all their might to attack another, that line from the same book is appropriate:
<note>original: "Αἰνείας δ᾽ ἐπόρουσε σὺν ἀσπίδι δουρί τε μακρῷ" (Iliad 5.297)</note>
"Aeneas sprang forward with shield and long spear." That is:
"Aeneas rose up against him, with buckler and spear."

---

### To defend with the greatest force.
<meta>X</meta>

Conversely, if someone protects another with the greatest force, what follows immediately in that same place will fit:
<note>original: "πρόσθε δέ οἱ ἔβην᾽ ἔχε καὶ ἀσπίδα πάντοσ᾽ ἐίσην" (Iliad 5.299)</note>
"He stepped in front of him and held his shield, equal on all sides." That is:
"The spear and the round shield protected him from every side."

---

### An equal contest.
<meta>XI</meta>

When we want to indicate two people who are equally prepared for an argument or a brawl, it will be possible to adapt that poem from the same book:
<note>original: "τὼ μὲν δὴ χεῖράς τε καὶ ἔγχεα ὀξυόεντα, Αντίον ἀλλήλων ἐχέτην μεμαῶτε μαχεσθαι" (Iliad 5.506-507)</note>
"They held their hands and sharp spears against one another, eager to fight." That is:
"They, now preparing to fight amongst themselves, hold out their hands and sharpened javelins alike."

---

### Spurring on the runner.
<meta>XII</meta>

For one who wants to indicate that someone is being urged on to that which they are already inclined to do by their own will, that verse from the same book will be useful (though it occurs elsewhere in the same poet):
<note>original: "μάστιξεν ἵππους, τὼ δ᾽ οὐκ ἄκοντε πετέσθην" (Iliad 5.366)</note>
<margin>Taken from charioteers.</margin>
"He lashed the horses, and they flew along, not unwillingly." That is:
"He strikes the horses with the whip, but they were already flying of their own accord."

---

### Ready for either outcome.
<meta>XIII</meta>

A person prepared for either fortune, equally suited for play or serious matters, who knows how to get along with both the good and the bad, we shall mark with this poem which is in the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "οἶδ᾽ ἐπὶ δεξιὰ οἶδ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἀριστερὰ, νωμῆσαι βῶν" (Iliad 7.238)</note>
"I know how to move the ox-hide <note>Referring to the layers of hide on a shield</note> to the right and to the left." That is:
"I indeed know how to move my shield with the right hand and the left."

---

### No distinction.
<meta>XXI</meta>

Aristotle, in the second book of his *Politics*, records this little verse as commonly famous:
<note>original: "Ἐν δ᾽ ἰῇ τιμῇ ἠ μὲν κακὸς ἠδὲ καὶ ἐσθλός" (Iliad 9.319)</note>
"In the same honor are held both the coward and the brave." That is:
"Equal honor belongs to the lazy man and the man strong in virtue."
This may be used whenever we mean there is no distinction between the learned and the ignorant, between the deserving and the undeserving, or between the upright and the wicked. These are the words of Achilles <note>The great hero of the Greeks</note> when he was angry because he was not given proper consideration by Agamemnon, despite being by far the strongest of all. In this passage, the translator Leonardo Bruni <note>Known as Aretinus (1370–1444), a famous Italian humanist and historian</note> slipped; he was a man both learned and eloquent, but human nonetheless. For he thus translated the Homeric poem: "The same honor falls upon the lazy as upon the good," undoubtedly deceived by the person who brought those books to him. Nor did he notice that *iê* <note>The Greek word ἰῇ</note> was used for *miâ* <note>The more common word for 'one' or 'the same'</note>.

---

### The matter is settled with gifts.
<meta>X</meta>

One who says there is no room for right actions or fair reasons, but that the whole business is carried out through bribery and influence, can adapt this from the ninth book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "Δώροισίν τ᾽ ἀγανοῖσιν, ἔπεσσί τε μειλιχίοισι" (Iliad 9.113)</note>
"With splendid gifts and soothing words."
In this verse, the first place is given to gifts, and not without reason.

---

### A frustrated effort.
<meta>X</meta>

He who, frustrated in his hope, does not achieve what he was striving for—concerning him one will not inappropriately complain with this from the eighth book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: "Βαλέψ ὁ δὲ ἵετο θῦμα. Καὶ τ᾽ ῆν γ᾽ ἀφάμαρτε" (Iliad 8.311)</note>
"The spirit desired to transfix him with the weapon, but he missed." That is:
"The mind desired to pierce him with the javelin,"

CHILIADES, THIRD THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY
<page-num>807</page-num>
Yy 2

But that man, his hand failing, did not touch him. ->Again, in another place:<-
<note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὅγε καὶ τόδ’ ἅμαρτε" (Iliad 8.311)</note>
"But he missed even this one." That is:
"But even then he was deceived."

->Powerful through another’s help. XXXVII<-
For those who rely on the protection of others to achieve some remarkable deed, or who do something under the pretext of another's name, this line will be aptly applied from the same book. It was said there regarding Teucer, the brother of Ajax Telamon. For Teucer, hiding behind his brother’s shield, would shoot arrows at the Trojans:
<note>original: "Στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπ’ Αἴαντος σάκεϊ τελαμωνιάδαο" (Iliad 8.267)</note>
"He stood beneath the shield of Ajax, son of Telamon." That is:
"He stood protected by the sevenfold shield of Ajax."

->Beware of the more powerful. XXXVIII<-
To someone who declares they do not wish to have business with a man far more powerful than themselves, who could greatly harm them, one might correctly apply this from the same book:
<note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ γ’ ἐθέλοιμι Διὶ κρονίωνι μάχεσθαι" (Iliad 8.463)</note>
"For I certainly would not wish to fight with Zeus, son of Cronus." That is:
"With Jupiter I would surely not wish to enter into a contest."

->A sudden remedy for danger. XXXIX<-
When we indicate that a matter has been brought to an extreme crisis, and all would have been lost had not a sudden salvation—as if sent by some god—immediately shone forth, this line from the same book will often be suitable:
<note>original: "Εἰ μὴ ἄρ’ ὀξὺ νόησε πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε" (Iliad 8.132)</note>
"Had not the father of men and gods quickly noticed." That is:
"If the father of the gods and of men had not immediately perceived it."

->Perplexed and dismayed in mind. XL<-
For one who is dismayed in a dangerous business and finds no logic by which to explain himself, this line from the same book will fit:
<note>original: "Νέστορα δ’ ἐκ χειρῶν φύγον ἡνία σιγαλόεντα" (Iliad 8.137)</note>
"The shining reins fled from the hands of Nestor." That is:
"The wondrous reins escaped from the hands of Nestor."

->To start a quarrel. XLI<-
For one who, having already been provoked, proceeds to deal in insults, this line from the tenth book of the *Iliad* will be fitting:
<note>original: "Εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ἀκαχμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ" (Iliad 10.135)</note>
"He snatched up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze." That is:
"He grabbed a robust spear with a sharp point."
The opposite of this is "He threw away the spear," which we have recorded elsewhere from Cicero.

->Regarding the fearful. XLII<-
For a man who is vehemently afraid and dismayed in mind, these verses from the same book will fit:
<note>original: "Ἔμπεδον, ἀλλ’ ἀλαλύκτημαι, κραδίη δέ μοι ἔξω, Στηθέων ἐκθρώσκει, τρομέει δ’ ὑποφαίδιμα γυῖα" (Iliad 10.94-95)</note>
"My mind is not steady, but I am distraught; my heart leaps out of my chest, and my shining limbs tremble." That is:
"My mind is not settled, but wavers, moved; and my heart leaps outside my breast, and the joints of my body also tremble."
These things are said by Agamemnon while the people are in fear.

->To speak more flatteringly. XLIII<-
For someone who addresses another more flatteringly and honorifically, even adding family names <note>In the Roman context, Erasmus suggests names like Quintus or Publius to show how using personal names wins favor.</note>—suppose "Quintus" or "Publius"—plainly so that he may gain some favor with him, this line is correctly applied. It was spoken by Agamemnon in the same book when he commanded Menelaus to flatter the Greek troops:
<note>original: "Πατρόθεν ἐκ γενεῆς ὀνομάζων ἄνδρα ἕκαστον" (Iliad 10.68)</note>
"Naming each man by his father and his lineage." That is:
"Addressing each one by the surname of his father and his clan."

->Inexorable. XLIIII<-
For one who is difficult to persuade and stubborn, and should be left to his own devices; or for one whose assistance we no longer care for, this line will be aptly applied. It was said by Diomedes in the ninth book of the *Iliad* regarding Achilles, who had rejected the ambassadors and the gifts of Agamemnon:
<note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κείνου μὲν ἐάσομεν, ἤκεν ἴῃσιν, Ἤκε μένῃ" (Iliad 9.701)</note>
"But truly, let us leave him be, whether he goes or stays." That is:
"Indeed, let us rather leave this man to his own mind and character, whether he wishes to come or to remain here."

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
Y y
<page-num>808</page-num>

->Listen and weigh carefully.<-

Whenever we wish to indicate that we are about to say something pertinent and certain, this line from the same book <note>The "same book" refers to Book 9 of Homer’s *Iliad*.</note> will be appropriate, although it is often found elsewhere in the same author:
<note>original Greek: "Ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ' ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσι." (Iliad 9.611)</note>
"Another thing I will tell you, and you, lay it to heart." That is:
"Furthermore, I shall say another certain thing; hide it in your mind."

->Decision should not be immediate.<-

For someone who indicates that a delay must be introduced before a decision is made, and that the matter should be deferred to the future, this line from the same book will be fitting. It is the response Achilles gave to Phoenix, who had been sent with the legates by Agamemnon to reconcile with him:
<note>original Greek: "Ἀμ' ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι Φρασσόμεθα." (Iliad 9.618)</note>
"When the tomorrow’s dawn arises,
We shall consult."
From this, it appears that the famous Greek proverb was taken: <note>original: "ἐν νυκτὶ βουλή"</note> "Counsel in the night," which we have discussed in another place.

->No friend is to be forced.<-

When you suggest that someone should not be summoned to a business matter against their will, or that a service should not be bestowed upon one who neither acknowledges nor accepts it gladly, this line spoken by Achilles regarding Phoenix in the same book will be suitable:
<note>original Greek: "μη' ἐθέλωσιν. ἀνάγκῃ δ' οὔτιμιν ἄξω." (Iliad 9.429)</note>
"If he is willing; I will by no means lead him away by force."

->The care of life must come before all things.<-

For one who says that everything must be set aside so that we may look to our life, this line from him will be appropriate:
<note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ ἐμοὶ ψυχῆς ἀντάξιον, οὐδ' ὅσα φασὶν Ἴλιον ἐκτῆσθαι εὐναιόμενον πτολίεθρον, Τὸ πρὶν ἐπ' εἰρήνης." (Iliad 9.401-403)</note>
"Indeed, I compare no price with life, not even all
The riches of Troy, which they say that
Opulent city held in the former time of peace."
And soon the reason is given: that life alone can neither be called back nor repaired once it has left the <term>barrier of the teeth</term> <note>Erasmus uses the Homeric metaphor for the mouth as the "fence" or "barrier" of the teeth.</note>:
<note>original Greek: "Ἀνδρὸς δὲ ψυχὴ, πάλιν ἐλθεῖν οὔτε ληϊστὴ, οὔθ' ἑλετή." (Iliad 9.408)</note>
"But the life of a man, to return again, is neither to be seized by raiding nor captured."

->Bad things happen to the bad.<-

When something happens to a wicked person that everyone was praying for and desiring, there is a place for this line from the same book: <note>original Greek: "Θεοὶ δ' ἐτέλεσσον ἐπαράς." (Iliad 9.456)</note> "The gods fulfilled the curses." These are the words of Phoenix, narrating that all the evils had happened to him which his father had once called down upon him in a curse.

->Not even worthy to look at me.<-

For one who utterly despises someone as a coward and far inferior to himself, he may aptly use this line from the same book, which Achilles said against Agamemnon:
<note>original Greek: "οὐδ' ἂν ἔμοιγε Τετλαίη κύνεός περ ἐὼν, εἰς ὦπα ἰδέσθαι." (Iliad 9.372)</note>
"Nor would he indeed dare,
Though he be as shameless as a dog, to look me in the face."
<note>The Latin text uses "perfricta fronte," literally "with a rubbed forehead," an idiom for someone who has rubbed away their ability to blush and is therefore shameless.</note>
This is still commonly said today. It is a sign of a guilty mind not to dare to look at the face of the one you have harmed. This is why Menelaus, in the play *Iphigenia at Aulis* <note>A tragedy by Euripides.</note>, commands Agamemnon to look at him, evidently intending to gather the first proof of his brother's conduct from his gaze.

->Beware of him who has once deceived.<-

He who declares he wishes to have no dealings with one by whom he has been once deceived, will use this from the same book:
<note>original Greek: "οὐ δέ τι οἱ βουλὰς συμφράσσομαι, οὐδὲ μὲν ἔργον. Ἐκ γὰρ δή μ' ἀπάτησε καὶ ἤλιτεν. οὐ δ' ἂν ἔτ' αὖτις Ἐξαπάφοι ἐπέεσσιν, ἅλις δέ οἱ, ἀλλὰ ἕκηλος Ἔῤῥέτω." (Iliad 9.374-376)</note>
"I will not share counsel with him, nor any deed. For he deceived me and did wrong. Never again could he trick me with words; let it be enough for him; let him go to his ruin in peace."

THIRD CHILIAD, EIGHTH HUNDRED
<page-num>809</page-num>

> I shall attempt no such thing, nor is it ever profitable.
> For once he has frustrated me and deceived me with a trick,
> He shall not give me words again, fool that I am; let it be enough for him
> To have done this once; hereafter let him keep his peace,
->And may he fare well.<-
<note>Erasmus translates a passage from Iliad 9.375-377, where Achilles refuses Agamemnon's embassy.</note>

### Friends ought to advise one another. LII

This appears to be a proverbial sentiment, which we read in *Iliad* Book 11:
<note>original Greek: "ἀγαθὴ δὲ παραιφασίς ἐστιν ἑταίρου"</note>
"The advice of a friend is a good thing." That is:
A friend's counsel is beneficial. ->The Advisor.<-
One may use this whenever we say it is a friend's duty to advise a friend more freely if they are in error.

### One is worth as much as many. LIII

What was said in the same book in praise of a doctor can be turned toward anyone outstanding in virtue. The verse is as follows:
<note>original Greek: "ἰητρὸς γὰρ ἀνὴρ πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων"</note>
"For a man who is a healer is worth as much as many others in honor."
Alcibiades cleverly turns this against Eryximachus <note>A physician character in Plato's Symposium</note>, saying he cannot resist his orders because a medical man is worth as much as many. It will be even more charming if it is transferred to matters of the soul. For example, Plato says in the fourth book of the *Republic*:
<note>original Greek: "ἐὰν τὸ λεγόμενον δὴ μέγα φυλάττωσι"</note>
"If they preserve that one 'great thing' that is spoken of."
He indicates that this "great thing" <note>original Greek: "τὸ μέγα"</note> was proverbial. See the proverb: "The fox knows many things," etc. <note>Refers to the proverb: "The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing."</note> The most elegant Gospel parable also reminds us of this, concerning the "precious pearl" and the "treasure in the field." Therefore, a good mind is "worth as much as all others," and so are erudition and a good reputation—"worth as much as many others."

### Despising an enemy. LIIII

He who denies that he is moved by the insults of some contemptible man will not unskillfully adapt what Diomedes says in the same book:
<note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἀλέγω, ὡς εἴ με γυνὴ βάλοι, ἢ πάϊς ἄφρων, Κωφὸν γὰρ βέλος ἀνδρὸς ἀνάλκιδος οὐτιδανοῖο"</note>
"I care no more than if a woman or some foolish child
Had struck me with a dart; for indeed, the weapon of a weak and worthless man
->Flies in vain.<-"

### Obtaining one's wish. LV

When someone has attained what they were striving for or chasing—for instance, if someone sent a gift to a prince in the hope of a priesthood and obtained that priesthood through the prince’s favor—this line from the same book will fit:
<note>original Greek: "Καὶ βάλεν οὐδ’ ἄρα μιν ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγε χειρός"</note>
"He hit his mark, and the arrow sent from his hand did not escape in vain."

### The wolf in the story. LVI
<note>original Latin: "Lupus in fabula" — the Roman equivalent of "speak of the devil."</note>

When by chance it happens that someone who was just being mentioned arrives in the middle of the conversation, this line from *Iliad* Book 10 will be appropriate:
<note>original Greek: "οὕτω πᾶν εἴρητο ἔπος, ὅτ’ ἄρ’ ἤλυθον αὐτοί"</note>
"And now they were present themselves, before the speech was finished."

### Correcting what was said by another. LVII

When we wish to civilly point out that someone has not spoken according to their true mind, or where something has been said that is not quite honorable, we shall twist this little verse from *Iliad* Book 12, which Plutarch also cited somewhere for this purpose:
<note>original Greek: "οἶδα καὶ ἄλλου μύθου ἀμείνονα τόνδε νοῆσαι"</note>
"You know how to bring forward another speech better than this one."

### One must deal differently with different people. LVIII

He who wishes to signify that one must deal more gently with some and more harshly with others, according to each person's nature, fortune, or dignity, will cite this from the same book:
<note>original Greek: "ἄλλου μειλιχίοις, ἄλλου στερεοῖς ἐπέεσσι Νείκεον"</note>
"They rebuked this one with gentle words,
But that one with harsher ones.
->They shouted.<-"

### As men are now. LIX

If you wish to remark on the customs of your own times—as they are always degenerating into something worse from the virtue of their ancestors—for example, if you say this or that prince should be praised "as princes are in this age," you will apply this from the same book:
<note>original Greek: "οἷοι νῦν βροτοί εἰσιν"</note>
"Such as mortals are now." This half-line indeed appears in several...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...is found in several places in Homer: here concerning Ajax and Hector, easily lifting a huge rock from the ground. In *Iliad* Book 5 <note>original: "ε"</note>, likewise concerning Tydeus lifting a rock.

### An undertaking should not be started rashly.

Against a powerful person, with whom one should not take up a grudge or a lawsuit unless you are supported by a great defense, that passage from the same book will apply:
<margin>Iliad Book 13 <note>original: "ν"</note></margin>
"No one meeting him could hold him back, apart from the gods." <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἂν τις μιν ἐρυκάκοι ἀντιβολήσας, νόσφι θεῶν"</note> That is:
> No one would go to meet this man to fight him,
> Without the help of the gods.
This was said of Hector heading into battle with two spears, after he had cast a massive one.

### Of one desiring vehemently.

When the mind itself strongly goads us to do something, this passage from *Iliad* Book 13 <note>original: "ν"</note> will be suitable:
"And for me myself, the soul within my dear breast
Is even more urged on to war and to fight,
My feet below and hands above are eager." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ δ' ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισι, Μᾶλλον ἐφορμᾶται πολεμίζειν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι, Μαιμώωσι δ' ἔνερθε πόδες, καὶ χεῖρες ὕπερθεν"</note> That is:
> Of its own accord, my swelling spirit within my breast desires
> More and more to wage war by hand, and to clash face to face;
> My feet below and my right hand above are in a hurry.

### Excellent virtue shines forth.

Excellent virtue, even if it is sometimes concealed, nevertheless always stands out among others and is perceived from the expression of the face, and shines forth, as it were, on the brow itself. Likewise, a person's appearance, just like their manners, testifies to true nobility. That Homeric line from the same book will suit this sentiment:
"Even the gods are easily recognized." <note>original Greek: "Ἀρίγνωτοι δὲ θεοίπερ"</note> That is:
> The distinguished powers of the gods.

### Mutual defense.

He noted the mutual concord among several people and their mutual defense quite wittily with these verses from the same book:
"Fencing spear with spear, shield with shield in close array,
Shield pressed against shield, helmet against helmet, and man against man." <note>original Greek: "φράξαντες δόρυ δουρί, σάκος σάκεϊ προθελύμνῳ, Ἀσπὶς ἄρ ἀσπίδ' ἔρειδε, κόρυς κόρυν, ἀνέρα δ' ἀνήρ"</note> That is:
> They thickened spears with spears, and with frequent shield-bosses
> They supported shield with shield, clinging together,
> And in turn helmets covered helmets, and man covered man.
Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist</note> says the same regarding the weak: "But their number defends them, and phalanxes joined by the shield-boss."

### Even small resources are bolstered by concord.

There is a proverbial sentiment in the same place, of this sort:
"The combined strength of even very weak men is effective." <note>original Greek: "Συμφερτὴ δ' ἀρετὴ πέλει ἀνδρῶν καὶ μάλα λυγρῶν"</note> That is:
> Those joined together are powerful, even those who are greatly sluggish.
It will be appropriate to use this whenever we wish to indicate that the friendship and multitude of many people are not to be despised, even if they are otherwise weak and each one could easily be looked down upon individually. For just as Ovid <note>Roman poet</note> says:
> And things which do not help individually, help when there are many,
So things which do not harm individually, do harm when there are many.

### Fierce when outside of danger.

Against a timid man who is only fierce if he is far away from danger—like a "kitchen-detractor" <note>Erasmus likely uses "cularium" or "culinarium" to mean someone who is brave only at the dinner table or home</note> who does not dare to engage face to face—that passage from the same place will apply:
"Standing far off from the enemy men to fight." <note>original Greek: "Ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων ἑκὰς ἱστάμενοι πολεμίζειν"</note> That is:
> Skilled at fighting, but from a distance and far from the foe.
Similar to this is the remark of Demosthenes <note>The famous Greek orator</note> in his oration *On the Crown*: "They received us so familiarly that, while the horses and horsemen were there, they received the army into their houses and within, to their children and wives and those things which are most precious." <note>original Greek translated by Erasmus: "οὕτως οἰκείως ἡμᾶς ἐδέχοντο..."</note> That is: They received us so familiarly that although armed men and cavalry were present, they took the army into their homes and into the city, to their children and wives, and to those things which are most dear. We have previously reviewed "Outside the throw of weapons" <note>original: "Extra telorum iactum"</note>, the contrary of which is "Within the weapons." In the fourth action against Verres <note>Cicero’s famous prosecution of the corrupt governor Verres</note>: "Would I not have come from Vibo in a small boat among the weapons of the fugitives and to your house and your weapons?" This is what the Greeks call "within the range of missiles." <note>original Greek: "ἐντὸς βελῶν"</note>

<meta>catchword: But not</meta>

### **Whoever he may be.**
### **LXVI**

We shall indicate any person at all, without any exception, with this little verse, which is found in the same book:
"Whoever might be mortal, and might eat the grain of Demeter." <note>original Greek: "ὃς θνητός τ’ εἴη, καὶ ἔδοι Δημήτερος ἀκτήν"</note> That is:
> One who is merely mortal, eating the gifts of grain.
<note>Demeter was the goddess of the harvest; "eating her gifts" was a poetic way of saying someone is a human being who requires food to live.</note>
It is as if someone were to say that human laws vary from place to place, but the law of nature is common to all, "whoever is mortal."

### **Youth flourishes in strength.**
### **LXVII**

Age—specifically youth—contributes a great deal of weight to one’s strength. To this effect is that line from the same passage concerning Aeneas:
"And he has the flower of youth, when strength is at its greatest." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ δ’ ἔχ’ ἥβης ἄνθος, ὅτε κράτος ἐστὶ μέγιστον"</note> That is:
> The flower of his age is also present, at which time his power is greatest.

### **Of wavering counsel.**
### **LXVIII**

To signify a person who is perplexed, of a doubtful opinion, and suspended in mind, that line from *Iliad* Book 14 <note>original: "Ξ"</note> will be fitting:
"He hesitated between the earth and the asphodel-filled heaven." <note>original Greek: "μερμήριξε γαῖαν, ἠ’ οὐρανὸν ἀσφόδελτον"</note> That is:
> In the middle of the earth and the starry Olympus at once.
This was said by the poet concerning the horses of Juno flying with a swift course between heaven and earth.

### **Exceedingly wealthy.**
### **LXIX**

We shall signify the exceedingly wealthy with these verses in Books 6, 10, and 11 <note>original: "ζ. κ. & λ."</note> of the *Iliad*:
"Many treasures lie in the house of his wealthy father, bronze and gold and much-labored iron." <note>original Greek: "πολλὰ δ’ ἐν ἀφνειοῦ πατρὸς κειμήλια κειται, Χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε σίδηρος"</note> That is:
> In the roof of his rich father many things are stored away,
> Bronze and gold, and a plenty of manufactured iron.
To the same purpose also serves this from *Iliad* Book 10 <note>original: "κ."</note>:
"Rich in gold, rich in bronze." <note>original Greek: "πολύχρυσος πολύχαλκος"</note> That is:
> Of much gold, and of much bronze.

### **With difficulty indeed, but we do it anyway.**
### **LXX**

When we do something indeed with difficulty, and not without very many inconveniences, but we do it nonetheless, driven by necessity, that line from *Iliad* Book 6 <note>original: "ζ."</note> will be suitable:
"And though very much distressed, for necessity presses." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ μάλα τειρόμενοί περ, ἀναγκαίη γὰρ ἐπείγει"</note> That is:
> Although excessively afflicted, yet fate thus compels.

### **What is diminished in one place is made equal elsewhere.**
### **LXXI**

This applies to a man in whom some virtue is lacking, but whose loss you may compensate for with some other gift. For example, if we wish someone to be understood as being a bit ineloquent, but nevertheless of admirable judgment; or one who is indeed unlearned, but well-moneyed; that line from the same place we just cited from *Iliad* Book 10 <note>original: "κ."</note> will fit:
"Who was indeed ugly in form, but swift of foot." <note>original Greek: "ὃς δέ τοι εἶδος μὲν κακός, ἀλλὰ ποδώκης"</note> That is:
> He who was indeed deformed in face, was yet sharp with his feet.

### **Mutual defense is safest.**
### **LXXII**

He who wishes to signify that those who are in agreement and defend one another can be harmed less—whereas those who disagree in internal factions are liable to the injuries of all—will adapt this from *Iliad* Book 8 <note>original: "θ."</note>:
"But far fewer perished, for they always remembered to ward off steep destruction for one another throughout the throng." <note>original Greek: "παυρότεροι δὲ φθινύθουσι, μέμνωντο γὰρ αἰεὶ, Ἀλλήλοις ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἀλεξέμεναι πόνον αἰπύν"</note> That is:
> A much smaller crowd perished, because in the battle-line they always
> Strove to bring mutual help to themselves, and to ward off evil.

### **Those who attack with contempt for life.**
### **LXXIII**

For those who attack someone with a "gladiatorial spirit," as Terence <note>A Roman playwright often quoted for his insights into human behavior.</note> says, so that they either destroy or perish, this from *Iliad* Book 12 <note>original: "Μ."</note> will be fitting:
"Like wild boars." <note>original Greek: "Ἀγροτέροισι σύεσσι ἐοικότες"</note> That is:
> Similar to rustic boars.
For hunters report that these animals, when provoked, charge straight at the one provoking them, nor do they avoid the spear.

### **Foreseeing for others, not for himself.**
### **LXXIIII**

If it should be pleasing to joke about someone who, having professed the art of divination, has predicted their own misfortunes to others, but was not able to foresee his own misfortune himself, we shall not awkwardly adapt that line from Homer’s "Catalogue of Ships": <note>original: "Bœotia"</note>
"But he did not ward off black death with omens." <note>original Greek: "Ἀλλ’ οὐκ οἰωνοῖσιν ἐρύσατο κῆρα μέλαιναν"</note> That is:
> But not

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES<-

"But he did not avert dark fate from himself with auguries." <note>original Latin: "At non augurijs fatum sibi depulit atrum." This is a quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book 9.</note> Virgil imitated this from the line:
"But he was not strong enough to ward off destruction with auguries." <note>original Latin: "At non augurijs ualuit depellere pestem."</note>
This was said of Eunomus, the leader of the Mysians, who was indeed skilled in auguries <note>the practice of interpreting omens from the flight of birds</note>, but was nonetheless killed by Achilles.

---

<margin>LXVII</margin>
### Public disgrace.
You may quite elegantly indicate a thing that is in every way shameful and ruinous by using the words with which Hector rebukes Paris in the third book of the *Iliad*:
"A great bane to your father, to the city, and to the whole people; a joy to your enemies, but a source of shame to yourself." <note>original Greek: "Πατρί τε σῷ μέγα πῆμα ποληΐ τε παντί τε δήμῳ, Δυσμενέσιν μὲν χάρμα, κατηφείη δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ."</note> That is:
> A huge harm to your city, your people, and your father,
> A joy to the enemy, but a source of reproach and grief to yourself.

<margin>LXVIII</margin>
### Do not fight in another’s business.
When we wish to signify that we do not want to involve ourselves in another person's dispute that has nothing to do with us, but will allow those whose business is at stake to fight it out at their own peril, there will be a suitable place for this line from the same book:
"The sort of men who, for the sake of Helen and all her possessions, fight alone." <note>original Greek: "οἵους ἀμφ’ ἑλένῃ, καὶ κτήμασι πᾶσι μάχεσθε."</note> That is:
> To decide for Helen, and for the whole matter, alone.
This was said concerning Menelaus and Paris when they were about to engage in single combat.

<margin>LXIX</margin>
### Prudence joined with strength.
For a man who knows both how to command others on what must be done and is himself eager to carry out what he commands, that line from the same book will fit aptly:
"Both a good king and a mighty spearman." <note>original Greek: "Ἀμφοτέρω βασιλεύς τ’ ἀγαθὸς κρατερός τ’ αἰχμητής."</note> That is:
> At once a good leader and powerful in combat.
For there are those who know how to act as a general, but do not know how to perform as a soldier.

<margin>LXX</margin>
### Of few words but learned.
For one who speaks few things, but things nonetheless worthy of being heard, this line from the same source will be appropriate; it is said there of Menelaus, in the brief-speaking manner of the Spartans <note>Laconism</note>, yet sweet-spoken and clear:
"Few words, but very clearly, since he was not a man of many words." <note>original Greek: "παῦρα μὲν, ἀλλὰ μάλα λιγέως, ἐπεὶ οὐ πολύμυθος."</note> That is:
> He spoke not many things indeed, but most clear ones, for he was
> A man of few words.

<margin>LXXI</margin>
### To resist two evils is most difficult.
"If indeed war and plague together shall subdue the Achaeans." <note>original Greek: "Εἰ δὴ ὁμοῦ πόλεμός τε δαμᾷ, καὶ λοιμὸς ἀχαιούς."</note> That is:
> Now war and disease alike subdue the Greeks.
We may use this whenever we say that the same man is oppressed by two or many evils. It is found in the first book of Homer’s *Iliad*.

<margin>LXXII</margin>
### From the front and back simultaneously.
When we wish to indicate an admirable knowledge of all things, or a singular prudence—which consists not only of knowledge of the present, but also of the memory of the past and foresight of the future—we shall rightly employ this verse from the same book:
"Who knew the things that are, and the things that shall be, and the things that were before." <note>original Greek: "ὃς ἤδη τά τ’ ἐόντα τά τ’ ἐσσόμενα, πρό τ’ ἐόντα."</note> That is:
> Who knows the past, the present, and the future to come.
Virgil translated it in this manner:
"What things are, what things have been, and what are soon to come."

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
### It has harmed and it will harm.
If ever, having demonstrated the cause of past evils, we threaten that greater ones are to come unless someone returns to their senses, we shall not unseasonably employ this Homeric verse from the same book:
"Therefore the Far-shooter <note>an epithet for Apollo</note> gave woes, and will still give them." <note>original Greek: "Τούνεκ’ ἄρ’ ἄλγε’ ἔδωke ἑκηβόλος, ἠδ’ ἔτι δώσει."</note> That is:
> Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> gave many evils for these things, and shall add more besides.
Just as if a doctor, having shown the danger of a disease, should warn a recovering patient to beware of immoderate lust <note>original Latin: "Venere," referring to Venus/sex</note>, lest the evil return with interest.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
### A vast divide.
Whenever we imply a vast difference between men, or things very distant from one another, or an immense interval between separated things, we shall elegantly adapt that line from the same source:
"Since there are many things in between..."

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Greek and Roman adages, specifically focusing on those derived from the works of Homer. # THE THIRD THOUSAND, EIGHTH HUNDRED
<page-num>813</page-num>

<margin>LXXXII</margin>
->Exhorting one to glory.<-
When we wish to exhort someone to seek immortal glory through noble deeds, we might quite elegantly employ a certain verse that Marcus Tullius <note>The Roman orator Cicero</note> used in several places:
"Be brave, so that even someone from a later generation may speak well of you." <note>original Greek: "Ἄλκιμος ἔσσ᾽ ἵνα τίς σε καὶ ὀψιγόνων εὖ εἴπῃ." original Latin translation: "Strenuus esto, quo te posteritas quoque laudet."</note>
This appears in several places in Homer, most notably in the first book of the *Odyssey*. There, Pallas <note>the goddess Athena</note>, in the guise of Mentor, encourages Telemachus <note>the son of Odysseus</note> to virtue by the example of other illustrious heroes:
"You too, my friend—for I see you are handsome and tall—be brave, so that those born hereafter may praise you." <note>original Greek: "Καὶ σὺ φίλος, μάλα γάρ σ᾽ ὁρόω καλόν τε μέγαν τε, Ἄλκιμος ἔσσ᾽ ἵνα τίς σε καὶ ὀψιγόνων εὖ εἴπῃ." original Latin translation: "Tu quoque age, quando te uideo magnumque, bonumque, Strenuus esto, ut tete & postera prædicet ætas."</note>

<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
->One who is ready to resist.<-
A person who wishes to indicate that they are by no means shrinking from a contest, but have plenty of resources to defend their position, will use this line from the thirteenth book of the *Iliad*:
"For I have spears and bossed shields, and helmets and breastplates shining brightly." <note>original Greek: "Τῷ μοι δούρατά τ᾽ ἔστι καὶ ἀσπίδες ὀμφαλόεσσαι, Καὶ κόρυθες καὶ θώρηκες λαμπρὸν γανόωντες." original Latin translation: "Et mihi sunt hastæ teretes, clypeique rotundi, Tum galeæ, tum thoraces procul igne micantes."</note>

<margin>LXXXIIII</margin>
->In a crisis, the man is revealed.<-
Regarding a dangerous and difficult situation that requires a sensible and vigorous man, that which is said in the same book by Idomeneus, the leader of the Cretans, will be fitting:
"There, both the coward and the brave man are made manifest." <note>original Greek: "Ἔνθ᾽ ὅ τε δειλὸς ἀνὴρ ὅς τ᾽ ἄλκιμος ἐξεφαάνθη." original Latin translation: "Illic qui uir iners, qui strennuus ipsa docet res."</note>
To the same point is what follows in the next verse:
"For the color of the coward’s skin changes from one hue to another." <note>original Greek: "Τοῦ γάρ τε κακοῦ τρέπεται χρὼς ἄλλυδις ἄλλῃ."</note>
I have mentioned this elsewhere.

<margin>LXXXV</margin>
->One must not yield to evils.<-
If you ever advise that one ought not to yield either to adversaries or to the assaults of ill fortune—or that one should not fight with those who are fleeing—you might not unskillfully adapt this line from the same book:
"Let the dart not strike his neck or back as he flees, but let it meet either his chest or his belly." <note>original Greek: "Οὐκ ἂν δὴ αὐχέν᾽ ὄπισθε πέλοι βέλος ᾄξοντι, Ἀλλά κεν ἢ στέρνῳ ἢ νηδύϊ ἀντιάσειε." original Latin translation: "Ne feriat iaculum ceruicem aut terga, sed ipsum Aut uentrem, aut pectus feriat aduersa sagitta."</note>

<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
->He brought destruction upon himself.<-
For one who stubbornly brings misfortune upon himself, as if destined for it by fate, this from the same book will be appropriate:
"An evil fate was leading him to the end of death." <note>original Greek: "Τόν δ᾽ ἄγε μοῖρα κακὴ θανάτοιο τέλος δέ." original Latin translation: "Istum mortis in exitium mala parca trahebat."</note>

<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
->Nothing should be attempted beyond one’s strength.<-
He who says that a task should not be undertaken if the strength to complete it is lacking might fittingly adapt this from the same book:
"No one can fight beyond their power, however much they may be eager." <note>original Greek: "Πὰρ δύναμιν δ᾽ οὐκ ἔστι καὶ ἐσσύμενον πολεμίζειν." original Latin translation: "Vires ultra nemo queat bellare, licet sit Quantumuis animo promptus."</note>
These are the words of Paris to Hector.

<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
->Swifter than a hawk.<-
One may indicate an admirable speed by the proverbial hyperbole found in the same book:
"Swifter than hawks." <note>original Greek: "Θάσσον᾽ ἰρήκων." original Latin translation: "Pernices magis accipitre."</note>
It becomes more elegant if one applies it to fame, or talent, or a messenger, or something of that sort.

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
->Of a wavering mind.<-
A wavering mind and uncertain counsel can be indicated by a short verse in the fourteenth book of the *Iliad*. <note>The text ends here; the catchword suggests the next page begins with a comparison to a wave: "As the great [sea...]"</note>

<summary>Erasmus presents several proverbial expressions drawn from Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, focusing on themes of courage in battle, personal responsibility for one's fate, and the importance of acting within one's own capabilities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Homeric verses that have transitioned into common adages. Having previously discussed courage and preparedness, Erasmus here examines verses related to indecision, the propriety of speech, and the persistence of certain character traits.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>814</page-num>

"As the old man pondered, his heart torn **between two ways**." <note>original Greek: "Ως ὁ γέρων ὥρμαινε δαϊζόμενος κατὰ θυμὸν διχθάδια."</note> This is to say:
Thus the elder, turning it over in his mind, searches in both directions, **wavering.** <note>original Latin: "Sic senior uersans animo disquirit utroq; Nutans."</note>

Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> imitated this in this way:
"And now here, now there, he divides his swift mind." <note>original Latin: "Atq; animum nunc huc celerem, nunc diuidit illuc."</note> And again in the *Iliad*, Book 16:
"My heart is divided in two as I ponder in my mind." <note>original Greek: "Διχθὰ δέ μοι κραδίη μέμονε φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντι."</note> That is:
My mind inclines now here, now there, as I turn things over. <note>original Latin: "Huc animus mihi uerstanti inclinat & illuc."</note>

### A correction of speech.

When a saying is somewhat obscene and should be kept silent by good men, or is absurd to say, we shall mark it with this little flower from the *Iliad*, Book 14:
"A speech which no man should ever let pass through his mouth,
at least one who knows how to speak things that are fitting and sound in his mind." <note>original Greek: "μῦθον, ὃν ἤ κεν ἀνήρ γε διὰ στόμα πάμπαν ἄγοιτο, ὅς τις ἐπίσταιτο ᾗσι φρεσὶν ἄρτια βάζειν."</note> That is:
A speech which no one should ever bring forth from his mouth,
Who has only learned to speak from a wise and healthy heart. <note>original Latin: "Sermonem, quem nemo unquam promat ab ore, Qui modo cognorit cordata & sana profari."</note>

### Against the noisy.

<margin>X</margin> We shall indicate an immense shouting during a lawsuit or a dispute by that verse which Homer wrote in the same book concerning Neptune <note>The god of the sea</note>:
"As loud as nine thousand or ten thousand men shout
in war, when they join the strife of Ares <note>The god of war</note>." <note>original Greek: "Ὅσσον τ’ ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον ἢ δεκάχιλοι Ἀνέρες ἐν πολέμῳ, ἔριδα ξυνάγοντες ἄρηος."</note> That is:
Shouting as much as nine or ten thousand
men are accustomed to cry out when they engage in battle. <note>original Latin: "Tantum uociferans, quantum nouies, decieſue Mille uiri clamare ſolent qui prœlia miſcent."</note>
The same poem is found in the *Iliad*, Book 5, regarding Mars.

### To the best of my ability.

<margin>XC</margin> When we promise that we will provide our labor according to our best ability <term>pro mea uirili: "to the extent of my manly power"</term>, that line of Venus to Juno from the same book will be appropriate:
"If indeed I can fulfill it, and if the thing itself can be done." <note>original Greek: "Εἰ δύναμαι τελέσαι γε καὶ εἰ τετελεσμένον ἔσται."</note> That is:
If I am able to provide it, and the matter itself is able to happen. <note>original Latin: "Si præſtare queam, & fieri res ipſa poteſſit."</note>
The same verse is found in the *Odyssey*, Book 5, and the *Iliad*, Book 18.

Plutarch uses this as a proverb in his book *How to tell a flatterer from a friend*: "For our life is in a safe place, for it is a friend's part to make that promise: 'If indeed I can fulfill it, and if the thing itself can be done.' But the flatterer's part is the opposite: 'Tell me whatever is on your mind.'" <note>original Greek: "ἐν γὰρ ἀρκτῇ βίς πῶ ἡμῶν, Φίλε μὲν ἐκείνῳ εἶν’ τὴν ἐπαγγελίαν, εἰ δύναμαι τελέσαι γε καὶ εἰ τετελεσμένον ἔσται. κόλακος δ’ τἀντίω, αὐδ’ ὅ τι φρονέεις."</note> That is: For it was rightly said to those who love us, that a friend promises thus:
If I am able to provide it, and the matter itself is able to happen.
But the flatterer promises in this manner:
Tell me whatever you have in your breast.

### According to the dignity of each.

<margin>XC</margin> When roles are assigned to each person according to the propriety of their character and according to their dignity. For instance, if an arduous task is committed to a prudent and experienced person, and a lighter one to some youth or unskilled person, that line from the same *Iliad*, Book 14, will fit:
"The excellent man put on excellent armor, and gave the worse to the worse man." <note>original Greek: "Ἐσθλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὸς ἔδυνε χέρεια δὲ χείρονι δῶκεν."</note> That is:
The excellent man enters into excellent arms, and gave worse things to the inferior man. <note>original Latin: "Egregia egregius ſubit arma, ac deteriori Deteriora dedit."</note>

### All things yield to one's desire.

<margin>XCI</margin> For those who are greatly fortunate, for whom both well-conceived and poorly-conceived undertakings turn out happily, that line from the *Iliad*, Book 8, will apply:
"For the weapons of all these strike home, whoever might let them fly,
Whether a coward or a brave man, for Zeus directs them all alike." <note>original Greek: "Τῶν μὲν γὰρ πάντων βέλε’ ἅπτεται, ὅστις ἀφείη, Ἢ κακὸς, ἢ ἀγαθὸς, ζεὺς δ’ ἔμπης πάντ’ ἰθύνει."</note> That is:
All the spears of these men strike, whether an idle man
or a brave man has twisted them, because Jupiter himself directs them. <note>original Latin: "Spicula cuncta horum feriunt, ſeu torſerit illa Ignauus, ſeu uir fortis, quia Iuppiter ipſe Dirigit."</note>

### The persistence of a fly.

<margin>X</margin> For one who is persistent and keeps returning repeatedly, even if shamefully repulsed, that line from the same book <note>Iliad 17</note> will fit:
"And he put into his breast the persistence of a fly,
which, though it be driven away often from a man's skin, yet strives to bite." <note>original Greek: "Καί οἱ μυίης θάρσος ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἐνῆκεν, Ἥ τε καὶ ἐργομένη μάλα περ χροὸς ἀνδρομέοιο. ἰχανάα δ’ ἀκέειν."</note> That is:
And he sent the fly's power into his heart,
Which, although it has often been repelled from the skin of a man,
Still leaps forward to bite. <note>original Latin: "Atq; illi muſcæ uim intra præcordia miſit, Quæ quamuis de pelle uiri ſit ſæpe repulſa, Aſſultat morſura tamen."</note>

<summary>Erasmus compiles various Homeric verses that serve as adages for human behaviors, such as indecision, shouting in disputes, the promise of a friend versus a flatterer, and the annoying persistence of certain individuals likened to flies.</summary>

<page-num>815</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY</header>

### I commit it to God and fortune. XCVI

For someone who has decided to test their luck, leaving the outcome of a business matter to fortune, this line from the same book <note>Homer’s *Iliad*</note> will be fitting:
"And I too; all these things shall be the care of Jove."
<note>original Greek: και γάρ καί εγώ, τά δέ κεν Διί πάντα μελήσει</note>
That is to say:
"I shall go, and let these matters be the concern of Jove."

### A plan to be changed for the better. XCVII

Whenever we advise someone to change their plan—perhaps because it is shameful or foolish—or when we criticize something done rashly, this passage from the same book will be useful:
"Which of the gods has put such a thought into your breast, and taken away your good sense?"
<note>original Greek: τις νυ θεών νόον ώδε βάλεν εν στήθεσσιν έθηκε καί εξείλετο φρένας εσθλάς;</note>
That is to say:
"What god has at last suggested such a useless plan to you, and removed a sound mind from your breast?"

### He urges on in every way. XCVIII

When someone tries to provoke or influence another’s mind by every possible means—now with prayers, now with flattery, now with quarrels, now with threats—one may use this line from the same book spoken of Automedon <note>The charioteer of Achilles</note> and the horses of Achilles:
"Often he reached out with the lash, striking with a shout; often he spoke with gentle words, and often with curses."
<note>original Greek: πολλά μέν άρ μάστιγι βοή επεμαίετο θείνων. πολλά δέ μειλιχίοισι προσηύδα, πολλά δ' αρεθή.</note>
That is to say:
"Much did he urge them to speed with the swift whip, much did he speak with flattery, and much with threats."

### Gaping at the same inheritance. XCIX

It is a bit harsh, yet not without wit, if the line spoken in the same book about the Greeks and Trojans fighting over the corpse of Patroclus is twisted to refer to <term>hæredipetas: inheritance-hunters</term> who crowd around the same old man, as if they were all competing for that same corpse:
"Thus they, on both sides, dragged the body back and forth in a small space."
<note>original Greek: ως οíγ' αμφ' ά νέκυι ολίγω ενί χώρω είλκεον αμφοτέρω.</note>
That is to say:
"So they both, with little distance between them, drag the corpse this way and that."

### Premature death. C

For someone who has departed in premature death, leaving their parents behind, one may apply this line from the same book spoken of Hippothous the Pelasgian, son of Lethus, whom Ajax Telamon had killed because he had tried to drag the body of Patroclus to Troy by the foot:
"Nor did he pay back to his dear parents the cost of his upbringing, for his life was short."
<note>original Greek: ουδέ τοκήσι θρεπτά φίλοις απέδωκε, μινυνθάδιος δέ οí αιών.</note>
That is to say:
"But he did not return the grateful duties of being raised to his parents, but a brief span of life befell him."

## NINTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD CHILIAD

### Some things are given, others denied. 1

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V featuring a classical or biblical landscape scene with figures in the foreground and architecture in the distance.</image-desc>
Whenever one of two gifts of nature is granted and the other is denied—as if, for example, someone possesses beauty of form but lacks the praise of intellect—or when only one of two requested things is obtained, this verse from book 16 of the *Iliad* will fit:
"The father granted him one thing, but the other he refused."
<note>original Greek: Τῷ δ' ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατήρ, ἕτερον δ' ἀνένευσε.</note>
That is to say:
"The father of the gods granted this to him, but denied that."
Pliny uses this little verse in one of his letters. Originally, it was said of Achilles, who in the prayers he made for Patroclus (who was about to enter battle in Achilles' armor) had asked for two things: first, that he might fight with glory, and second, that when the battle was over, he might return the armor and himself remain unharmed. Of these, Jupiter granted one—namely, that he should fight most bravely. However, he did not return Achilles' armor, nor did he return safely. Stratonicus the harper <note>A famous Athenian musician known for his wit</note> humorously misused this poem; when he heard someone playing the harp, he added this verse of Homer:
"The father granted him one thing, but the other he refused."
And soon, when someone else asked why he said that, he replied, "Because he granted him the ability to play the harp poorly, but denied him the ability to sing well." This is recorded in the eighth book of Athenaeus.

<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Homer, Iliad, Pliny, Stratonicus, Athenaeus, Achilles, Patroclus, inheritance-hunters, premature death, divine providence</keywords>

--- Page 940 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Erasmus's commentary on various proverbs and idiomatic expressions drawn primarily from Homer’s Iliad, focusing on themes of justice, character, and divine will.</meta>

<page-num>816</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

->**A victory not without blood.**<-
<note>original: "Victoria non incruenta"</note>

The corruption of judges and the greed of legal advocates often result in both sides of a lawsuit being punished, so to speak; it happens quite frequently that even the person who wins the case ends up regretting it. This situation is well-suited to that line from the 17th book <note>Greek letter rho (ρ) denotes the 17th book of the Iliad</note> of the *Iliad*:
"For they did not fight without blood." <note>original Greek: Οὐ δ' οἳ γὰρ ἀναιμωτί γ' ἐμάχοντο</note>
That is to say:
"Nor did these men engage in battle without bloodshed."

->**A degenerating son.**<-
<note>original: "Filius degenerans"</note>

For a son who falls away from his father’s principles, or one who does not long enjoy the things left to him by his father but is cut off from his ancestors’ wealth, one might aptly apply this line from the same book:
"But the son did not grow old in his father's armor." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' οὐχ υἱὸς ἐν' γίνετο πατρὸς ἐγήρα</note>
That is to say:
"The son did not grow old in the arms of his father."

->**An outcome beyond expectation.**<-
<note>original: "Euentus præter expectationem"</note>

Whenever a matter turns out very differently from how it was planned, or from how it seemed likely to result based on probable conjectures, this line from the same book will be appropriate:
"But the mind of Zeus, who holds the aegis, is always stronger." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' αἰεί τε Διὸς κρείσσων νόος αἰγιόχοιο</note>
That is to say:
"Truly, the will of great Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> always prevails."
Pindar, in the last of his Pythian hymns, says: "For that which is fated cannot be escaped; but there will be a time which, casting one into unexpected despair, will give one thing contrary to judgment, but another not yet." <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ μόρσιμον οὐ πάρφυκτον, ἀλλ' ἔσται χρόνος οὗτος, ὃ τὴν ἀελπτία βαλὼν, ἔμπαλιν γνώμας τὸ μὲν δώσει, τὸ δ' οὔπω</note> That is: For what is in the fates cannot be avoided, but there will be a time when one is struck by desperation beyond expectation; it will grant this thing, but another not at all. Again, in the 16th book <note>Greek letter pi (π) denotes the 16th book of the Iliad</note> of the *Iliad*:
"But the mind of Zeus is always stronger than that of men." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' αἰεί τε Διὸς κρείσσων νόος ἠέπερ ἀνδρῶν</note>
That is to say:
"But the will of Jove always prevails more than that of men."

->**A reproach of one's own thought.**<-
<note>original: "Reprehensio cogitationis"</note>

When we ourselves rebuke the plan of our own mind, or a thought that is insufficiently honorable or useful, there will be a place for this from the 17th book of the *Iliad*:
"But why does my dear heart discuss these things with me?" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ τίη μοι ταῦτα φίλος διελέξατο θυμός;</note>
That is to say:
"But why does my mind turn these things over within my breast?"
The same sentiment is repeated in other places as well.

->**To show oneself a man.**<-
<note>original: "Præbere uiros"</note>

We shall exhort someone to act or endure bravely with this verse from the same 17th book of the *Iliad*, which is also frequently repeated elsewhere:
"Be men, my friends, and remember furious courage." <note>original Greek: Ἀνέρες ἐστὲ φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς</note>
That is to say:
"Come, be men, and bring forth your mighty strength."

->**Help should be given in deeds, not words.**<-
<note>original: "Re opitulandum non uerbis"</note>

When action is needed, words are of no use. For example, if someone needs financial assistance, what good does it do to fill his ears with talk? Again, in consultations and judgments, one must act through reason, not force. To this end, that Homeric line from the 16th book of the *Iliad* is useful:
"For the end of war is in the hands, but words are for council." <note>original Greek: Ἐν γὰρ χερσὶ τέλος πολέμου, ἐπέων δ' ἐνὶ βουλῇ</note>
That is to say:
"Words prevail in council, but strength in the struggle."

->**Corrupt judgments.**<-
<note>original: "Corrupta iudicia"</note>

Against those who judge corruptly, or cast their vote looking not to the benefit of the Republic but to private gain; or those who suppress laws through tyranny, this passage from the same book is fitting:
"Who by force in the assembly judge crooked laws, and drive out justice, not regarding the eye of the gods." <note>original Greek: Οἳ βίῃ ἐν ἀγορῇ σκολιὰς κρίνωσι θέμιστας, Ἐκ δὲ δίκην ἐλάσωσι, θεῶν ὄπιν οὐκ ἀλέγοντες</note>
That is to say:
"Who by force in the gathering of the people pervert the common laws, and attempt to drive away justice, fearing nothing of the voice of the gods."

->**A suitable province.**<-
<note>original: "Apta prouincia" — here 'province' refers to a sphere of duty or office.</note>

For one who undertakes a responsibility suited to his strengths, while abstaining from business for which he is unfit—as if someone were to accept a bishopric but refuse the supreme pontificate <note>The Papacy</note>—this line from the same book will be fitting:
"He took the strong spears which fitted his palm, but did not take the spear of the blameless son of Aeacus <note>Achilles</note>." <note>original Greek: Εἵλετο ἄλκιμα δοῦρα τὰ οἱ παλάμηφιν ἀρήρει, Ἔγχος δ' οὐχ ἕλετ' οἷον ἀμύμονος αἰακίδαο</note>
That is to say:
"He grasps the great spears that fit his hands."

<keywords>Homer, Iliad, Pindar, justice, lawsuits, inheritance, fate, courage, deeds vs words, corruption, moderation in office</keywords>
