<page-num>817</page-num>
<header>THE NINTH HUNDRED OF THE THIRD THOUSAND</header>
<sig>Zz</sig>

### Any weapon, but the spear alone of Achilles he does not take.
<note>original Latin: Quaslibet, ast hastam solam non sumit Achilles</note>
This was said of Patroclus <note>The close companion of Achilles in the Trojan War</note>, who, when he was dressed in the armor of Achilles, nevertheless refrained from taking the spear, because it was too heavy for any of the Greeks to wield except for Achilles alone. Homer invented a similar detail in the *Odyssey* regarding the Bow of Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>.

->**Shame and fear.**<-
<note>original: "Pudor & metus"</note>
->X<-
Whenever someone abstains from a certain action because it seems both dishonorable to do and far from safe, this line from the 15th book <note>Greek letter omicron (ο)</note> of the *Iliad* is applicable:
"For shame and fear are both present." <note>original Greek: αἰδώς γάρ τε θέως, καὶ δεῖμος; original Latin: Nam pudor atq; metus uetuit</note>
This was said of a battle line drawn close together, which did not break apart partly because of shame and partly because of fear. That shame provides a great spur to acting bravely is indicated in the same book when he says:
"More men are saved when they feel shame than are slain." <note>original Greek: αἰδομένων δ' ἀνδρῶν πλεόνες σόοι ἠὲ πέφανται; original Latin: Plures sunt salui atq; cadunt his, quis pudor adsit</note>

->**One who falls silent.**<-
<note>original: "Qui obticescit"</note>
->XI<-
For someone who is silent because they are thunderstruck by fear, or stupefied with wonder, or for someone who has no answer to give, this line from the 17th book <note>Greek letter rho (ρ)</note> of the *Iliad* will fit:
"A long silence took hold of his words, and his tongue failed." <note>original Greek: δὴν δέ μιν ἀμφασίη ἐπέων λάβε; original Latin: Illum corripuit stupor, atq; infantia linguæ</note>

->**Death is common to all.**<-
<note>original: "Mors omnibus communis"</note>
->XII<-
Whoever wishes to say that all must die equally, and that the necessity of fate cannot be held back by any strength, will quote that line from the 18th book <note>Greek letter sigma (σ)</note> of the *Iliad*:
"For not even the strength of Hercules escaped his bitter fate." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ βίη ἡρακλῆος φύγε κῆρα; original Latin: Nec uis Herculea fatum euitauit acerbum</note>

->**One person is more excellent in some things than another.**<-
<note>original: "Alius alijs in rebus præstantior"</note>
->XIII<-
For someone who says that different people excel in different gifts, what was said in the same book about Polydamas and Hector will be suitable:
"But while this one conquered with words, the other was far superior with the spear." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ὁ μὲν ἂρ μύθοισιν, ὁ δ' ἔγχεϊ πολλὸν ἐνίκα; original Latin: Hic dictis, hasta longe præstantior ille</note>
Polydamas explains the same sentiment more fully in the 13th book <note>Greek letter nu (ν)</note> of the *Iliad*, speaking to Hector:
"Hector, you are a difficult man to persuade with spoken words.
Just because God has granted you to excel in the works of war,
Do you therefore wish to be wiser than others in counsel?
But you will not be able to possess all things at once yourself.
For to one man God has given excellence in the works of war,
To another the glory of the dance, to another the lyre and sweet song,
And yet to another, wide-seeing Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> puts a noble mind in his breast."
<note>original Greek: Ἕκτορ ἀμήχανός ἐσσι θεῷ ῥητοῖσι πιθέσθαι. οὕνεκα τοι περὶ δῶκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα, τοὔνεκα τῇ βουλῇ ἐθέλεις περιίδmenai ἄλλων; ἀλλ' οὔπως ἅμα πάντα δυνήσεαι αὐτὸς ἑλέσθαι. ἄλλῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκε θεὸς πολεμήϊα ἔργα, ἄλλῳ δ' ὀρχηστὺν, ἑτέρῳ κίθαριν καὶ ἀοιδήν, ἄλλῳ δ' ἐν στήθεσσι τιθεῖ νόον εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς ἐσθλόν; original Latin: Hector non potis es deflectere pectora dictis. An quia dij donant factis præcellere belli, Vis in concilio reliquos præcedere sensu? At non cuncta potes unus simul omnia ferre. Quippe deus dedit huic uirtute excellere belli, Huic laudem choreæ, citharam illi, & carmina blanda, Rursum alij mentem præclaram in pectore, magnus Iupiter inseruit</note>

->**In a dangerous business, one must not sleep.**<-
<note>original: "In periculoso negocio non est dormitandum"</note>
->XIIII<-
When we advise that one must not cease effort in a difficult matter, what is frequently repeated in Homer’s 16th book <note>Greek letter pi (π)</note> of the *Iliad* will be appropriate:
"The breathing-space in war is brief." <note>original Greek: ὀλίγη δ' ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο; original Latin: Exigua est interspiratio belli</note>
This could be applied either to a legal dispute in court, or to a similar odious business full of labor.

->**A distorted mind.**<-
<note>original: "Mens læua"</note>
->XV<-
Often the minds of men are distorted, and they follow the worst things as if they were the best, and reject the best as if they were the worst. Toward this sentiment points that line from the 18th book <note>Greek letter sigma (σ)</note> of the *Iliad*:
"For they praised Hector when he planned evil things,
But no one praised Polydamas, who offered good counsel."
<note>original Greek: Ἕκτορι μὲν γὰρ ἐπῄνησαν κακὰ μητιόωντι, Πουλυδάμαντι δ' ἄρ' οὔτις, ὃς ἐσθλὴν φράζετο βουλήν</note>

<page-num>515</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>Ss 3</sig>

Everyone used to praise Hector's useless advice,
No one Polydamas's, yet he alone gave what was useful.
<note>Polydamas was a Trojan commander who offered prudent counsel, often ignored by the more impulsive Hector.</note>

->**You fight with words, not with deeds.**<-
<note>original Latin: Verbis pugnas non re.</note>

It is easy to bicker with insults, but winning through action is difficult. To this sentiment belongs that line from the 20th book <note>indicated by the Greek letter upsilon (υ)</note> of the *Iliad*, spoken by Aeneas when he was about to clash with Achilles:

> Since I myself also well know
> How to utter both insults and foolish things.
<note>original Greek: Ἐπεὶ σάφα οἶδα καὶ αὐτὸς, ἢ μὲν κερτομίας ἢ δὲ αἴσυλα μυθήσασθαι; original Latin: Siquidem noui probe & ipse Et petere probris inimicasque dicere dicta.</note>

A little later he repeats the same sentiment more fully:

> For it is easy for both of us to speak many insults,
> A burden which even a hundred-oared ship could not carry.
> The tongue of mortals is versatile, and many are the words within it,
> Of every kind; the range of speech is wide on this side and that.
> Whatever word you speak, such a word you might hear in return.
<note>original Greek: Ἔστι γὰρ ἀμφοτέροισι ὀνείδεα...; original Latin: Ambobus siquidem probra dicere...</note>

->**Lest you be moved by the din of words.**<-
<note>original Latin: Ne quid moueare uerborum strepitu.</note>

One who advises another not to be deterred from carrying out a task by fierce words or threats might apply this line from the same book, spoken by Apollo to Aeneas:

> Rather, carry your bronze straight forward, and let him not at all
> Turn you back with wretched words and threats.
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἰθὺς φέρε χαλκὸν ἀτερφέα...; original Latin: Quin rigido ferro magis obuius ito...</note>

->**Food is necessary for those who must endure labor.**<-
<note>original Latin: Cibo opus duraturis in labore.</note>

Those about to enter battle should not be entirely fasting, lest they be deprived of their strength. This can be applied to the study of literature, the exercise of piety, and many other things. Fitting for this are the words of Homer from the 19th book <note>indicated by the Greek letter tau (τ)</note> of the *Iliad*:

> For a man will not be able to fight face to face all day long
> Until the setting of the sun, being without food.
> For even if he eagerly desires in his heart to wage war,
> Yet his limbs grow heavy unawares, and thirst
> And hunger overtake him, and his knees fail as he goes.
> But the man who is satisfied with wine and food
> And fights the enemy all day long,
> His heart is bold within his breast, nor do his limbs
> Tire before he has driven all from the battle.
<note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἀνὴρ πρόπαν ἦμαρ...; original Latin: Nam quis ad occasum usque ualebit...</note>

->**Destitute of all arms and defenses.**<-
<note>original Latin: Omnibus armis præsidijsque destitutus.</note>

We shall describe a man who is unarmed and deprived of all defenses with this verse:
> Naked, without helmet or shield, nor did he have a spear.
<note>original Greek: γύμνος ἄτερ κόρυθός τε καὶ ἀσπίδος...; original Latin: Et clypeo simul & galea nudatus, & hasta</note>

<summary>This page explores several adages derived from Homer's Iliad, focusing on the contrast between empty words and decisive action, the need for physical sustenance before labor, and the vulnerability of being unarmed.</summary>
<keywords>Homer, Iliad, Aeneas, Achilles, insults vs. deeds, preparation, hunger in battle, unarmed, Greek proverbs</keywords>

<header>THIRD CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Zz 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Now</meta>

<margin>XVI Section</margin>->**He has in vain who does not use.**<-
->XX<-
If you wish to rebuke someone because they do not make use of their talent, wealth, or learning, even though they possess them, this line from the same book of the *Iliad*, book 21 <note>original: $\phi$, the twenty-first letter of the Greek alphabet</note>, will be appropriate:
$\tau\acute{\iota}\nu\upsilon$ $\tau\acute{o}\xi\omicron\upsilon$ $\acute{\epsilon}\chi\epsilon\iota\varsigma$ $\alpha\nu\epsilon\mu\acute{\omega}\lambda\iota\omicron\nu$ $\alpha\acute{\upsilon}\tau\omega\varsigma;$
which means:
"Why do you carry a useless bow thus in vain?"
<note>original Latin: Cur frustra tibi iam gestatur inutilis arcus?</note>

->**On a fugitive.**<-
->XXI<-
Whenever someone is driven toward some matter by an uncontrollable desire of the mind—especially an unhonorable one—or even more so if someone flees disgracefully, it will fit to say:
$\tau\omicron\tilde{\upsilon}\tau\omicron\nu$ $\dot{\eta}$ $\kappa\upsilon\nu\acute{\alpha}\mu\upsilon\iota\alpha$ $\dot{\alpha}\gamma\epsilon\iota$.
which means: "The <term>dog-fly</term> <note>original Greek: cynamya; a stinging, irritating insect used as a metaphor for a persistent nuisance or a driving madness</note> seizes this man."
For thus in the same book, Juno says of Mars as he flees from battle:
$\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\delta' \alpha\tilde{\upsilon}\theta'$ $\dot{\eta}$ $\kappa\upsilon\nu\acute{\alpha}\mu\upsilon\iota\alpha$ $\dot{\alpha}\gamma\epsilon\iota$ $\beta\rho\omicron\tau\omicron\lambda\omicron\iota\gamma\grave{\omicron}\nu$ $\alpha\rho\eta\alpha$.
which means: "The dog-flies are again hounding Mars, the plague of mortals."

->**One must not fight with the gods.**<-
->XXII<-
He who wishes to advise that one should not fight against one's own nature, against the powers above, or against great princes <note>whom even the Hebrew scriptures call 'gods'</note>, will employ this line from the same book:
$\theta\epsilon\omicron\tilde{\iota}$ $\delta\acute{\epsilon}$ $\tau\epsilon$ $\phi\acute{\epsilon}\rho\tau\epsilon\rho\omicron\iota$ $\alpha\nu\delta\tilde{\omega}\nu$.
which means: "Truly, men are inferior to the gods."
<note>Erasmus likely refers to the Hebrew word 'Elohim,' which is used in the Bible to refer to the Almighty but also occasionally to judges or rulers.</note>
We have spoken elsewhere of <term>theomachia</term> <note>the act of fighting against gods</note>. Pindar, in the second hymn of the *Pythian Odes*, expressed this sentiment thus:
$\chi\rho\grave{\eta}$ $\delta' \pi\grave{\rho}\varsigma$ $\theta\epsilon\grave{\omicron}\nu$ $\omicron\dot{\upsilon}\kappa$ $\dot{\epsilon}\rho\acute{\iota}\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$.
"It is necessary not to contend against God."

<margin>XVII From which all things arise,</margin>->**The author and source of all.**<-
->XXIII<-
When we wish to indicate the primary author of all things, from whom everything—both the greatest and the least—proceeds as if from a head: for example, if one were to call pride the parent of all evils, or faith the source of all virtues, or Homer the father of all poetry, this line spoken in the same book concerning the Ocean will be quite elegantly adapted:
$\dot{\epsilon}\xi$ $\omicron\tilde{\tilde{\upsilon}}$ $\pi\epsilon\rho$ $\pi\acute{\alpha}\nu\tau\epsilon\varsigma$ $\pi\omicron\tau\alpha\mu\omicron\grave{\iota}$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\pi\tilde{\alpha}\sigma\alpha$ $\theta\acute{\alpha}\lambda\alpha\sigma\sigma\alpha$
$\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\pi\tilde{\alpha}\sigma\alpha\iota$ $\kappa\rho\tilde{\eta}\nu\alpha\iota$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\phi\rho\acute{\epsilon}\alpha\tau\alpha$ $\mu\alpha\kappa\rho\grave{\alpha}$ $\nu\acute{\alpha}\omicron\upsilon\si\nu$.
which means:
"From that one source all seas and all rivers flow,
And all springs and deep lakes stream forth."

<margin>XVIII It pertains to study toward Homer</margin>->**Altogether unknown.**<-
->XXIIII<-
Regarding a man whom we wish to portray as being remarkably unknown to us, this line from the same book—also frequent elsewhere in Homer, such as the *Odyssey* books 1 and 14—may be jokingly twisted:
$\tau\acute{\iota}\varsigma$ $\pi\acute{\omicron}\theta\epsilon\nu$ $\epsilon\tilde{i}\varsigma$ $\alpha\nu\delta\rho\tilde{\omega}\nu$, $\pi\acute{\omicron}\theta\iota$ $\tau\omicron\iota$ $\pi\acute{\omicron}\lambda\iota\varsigma$ $\dot{\eta}\delta\grave{\epsilon}$ $\tau\omicron\kappa\tilde{\eta}\epsilon\varsigma;$
which means: "Tell me, who and from where among men are you? Where is your city and your parents?"
It is related to that proverb: "Whether you are white or black, I do not know." <note>A Roman idiom meaning 'I don't know the first thing about you.'</note> It can also be applied to a situation: for example, if we say that someone entirely unskilled in all philosophy has stumbled into a philosophical book: "Who and from where are you...?"

->**As long as I shall live.**<-
->XXV<-
Whatever we wish to be understood as lasting for our entire life, we may indicate with a Homeric verse from the 22nd book of the *Iliad* <note>indicated by $\chi$</note>:
$\omicron\phi\rho' \dot{\alpha}\nu$ $\dot{\epsilon}\gamma\omega\gamma\epsilon$
$\zeta\omega\omicron\tilde{\iota}\sigma\iota\nu$ $\mu\epsilon\tau\acute{\epsilon}\omega$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\mu\omicron\iota$ $\phi\acute{\iota}\lambda\alpha$ $\gamma\omicron\acute{\upsilon}\nu\alpha\tau' \dot{\omicron}\rho\acute{\omega}\rho\epsilon\alpha$.
which means: "As long as I am among the living, and while these knees of mine are supported."
Virgil <note>original: Maro, the cognomen of Publius Vergilius Maro</note> imitated this:
"While I am mindful of myself, while breath still governs these limbs."

->**Glorious even among posterity.**<-
->XXVI<-
When we describe a deed whose fame seems destined to be celebrated by posterity, this line from the same book will fit:
$\dot{\alpha}\lambda\lambda\grave{\alpha}$ $\mu\acute{\epsilon}\gamma\alpha$ $\dot{\rho}\acute{\epsilon}\xi\alpha\varsigma$ $\tau\iota$ $\kappa\alpha\grave{\iota}$ $\dot{\epsilon}\sigma\sigma\omicron\mu\acute{\epsilon}\nu\omicron\iota\sigma\iota$ $\pi\upsilon\theta\acute{\epsilon}\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$.
which means: "Rather, he performed a signal deed that even posterity itself might hear of."

<margin>XIX This is from Iliad book 21. In vain</margin>->**Vengeance is slow, but heavy.**<-
->XXVII<-
When someone who has committed many crimes with impunity for a long time is finally brought to ultimate ruin and pays for his previous outrages all at once, this line from the same book will be appropriate:
$\nu\tilde{\upsilon}\nu$ $\delta' \dot{\rho}\theta\rho\acute{\omicron}\alpha$ $\pi\acute{\alpha}\nu\tau' \dot{\alpha}\pi\acute{\epsilon}\tau\iota\sigma\epsilon\varsigma$.
which means: "But now you have paid for everything all at once."

Erasmus uses these classical verses to provide tools for moral rebuke, philosophical observation, and poetic expression.</summary>

<page-num>820</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

Now you shall pay for all [your crimes] at once, heaped together. 
These are the words of Achilles to Hector. <note>original: "Nunc cuncta lues semel adglomerata." From Iliad 22.271</note>

->**The outcome of the matter is uncertain.**<-

When we wish to signify a critical moment of crisis, where it is uncertain which way victory may turn, the following from the same book will be appropriate:
<margin>XXI</margin>
"Then the Father held out the golden scales." <note>original Greek: Καὶ τότε δὴ χρύσεια πατὴρ ἐτίταινε τάλαντα.</note> That is to say:
Then the Father balanced the gilded scales on both sides. <margin>This is from the same place, Iliad 22.</margin> <note>This refers to Zeus weighing the fates of Achilles and Hector.</note>

->**A matter of great importance is at stake.**<-

When we want to indicate a massive struggle, where the rewards sought are neither trivial nor playful, that line from the same book will fit:
<margin>XXII</margin>
"For they were not striving for a sacrificial beast or a bull's hide." <note>original Greek: Ἐπεὶ οὐχ ἱερήϊον οὐδὲ βοείην ἀρνύσθην.</note> That is:
For no sacrificial victim or heifer was being sought by them.
This was said of Achilles and Hector as they fought to the death. Lucian employs this in his *The Eunuch* when he mocks philosophers who are shamefully contending before judges over a salary. The full verse is as follows:
"For they were not striving for a sacrificial beast or a bull's hide,
Which are the prizes for the feet of men in a race,
But they ran for the life of Hector, tamer of horses."
Virgil translated this in the twelfth book of the *Aeneid*:
"For no light or playful prizes are sought,
But they contend for the life and blood of Turnus."

->**Putting aside trifles, let us test the matter.**<-

One who commands that insults be set aside so that a trial can be made of the thing itself—to see who wins or is defeated—might not inopportunely use this line from the same book:
<margin>XXIII</margin>
"It is better to clash in strife as quickly as possible,
That we may see to which of us the Olympian will grant the glory." <note>original Greek: Βέλτερον αὖτ’ ἔριδι ξυνελαυνέμεν ὅττι τάχιστα / Εἴδομεν ὁπποτέρῳ κεν ὀλύμπιος εὖχος ὀρέξῃ.</note> That is:
But it is better to join the fight at close quarters, so that soon
It may become clear to which of the two Jupiter wishes the praise and honor to belong.

->**Fear of disgrace.**<-

When we say that we are moved by the opinion and rumors of people so that we change our plan, this line from the same book (and also from Iliad 6) will be suitable. Marcus Tullius Cicero frequently uses it in his *Letters to Atticus*:
<margin>XXIV</margin>
"I feel shame before the Trojan men and the Trojan women with their trailing robes." <note>original Greek: Αἰδέομαι τρώας καὶ τρωάδας ἑλκεσιπέπλους.</note> That is:
I fear and feel shame before the Trojan men and women.
These are the words of Hector, who, out of shame, is unwilling to retreat into the city, lest someone should attribute the destruction of the Trojans to his own disgrace.

->**Different things befit different ages.**<-

When someone wishes to signify a change in age, noting that the same things do not befit a gray-haired man as once befitted a youth, they may use this from the same book, though it is repeated elsewhere:
<margin>XXV</margin>
"But when the head is gray and the beard is gray." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πολιόν τε κάρη πολιόν τε γένειον.</note> That is:
But when now there is both a gray head and a gray chin.

->**What you find fault with in others, do not do yourself.**<-

What you are likely to condemn in others, do not allow in yourself. To this point, that line from Iliad 23 applies:
<margin>XXVI</margin>
"And you would be indignant with any other who would do such things." <note>original Greek: Καὶ δ’ ἄλλῳ νεμεσᾶτον ὅς τις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέζοι.</note>
Indeed, if anyone else prepared to commit
Such a thing, you would condemn it and mark it as a fault.

->**Either it was you, or someone very like you.**<-

If, through a joke, we indicate that someone was the very person present, even though they deny it—or if you accuse someone of drinking among drunkards and they deny they were there, claiming it was someone else—you might not unskillfully twist this line from the same book, which Homer said regarding the ghost of Patroclus:
<margin>XXVII</margin>
"In all things like him, in stature and beautiful eyes..." <note>original Greek: Πάντ’ αὐτῷ μέγεθός τε καὶ ὄμματα κάλ’ ἐϊκυῖα.</note>

<page-num>821</page-num>
<header>THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD CHILIAD</header>

<note>This opening fragment concludes a discussion from the previous page, likely regarding a ghost or a disguise.</note>
"And a voice like all [others] and he wore garments." <note>original Greek: Καὶ φωνήν τε ἴαν πᾶσι καὶ εἵματα ἕσω.</note> ->that is,<-
In all things like him—the voice, the beautiful eyes, 
the shape of the body—and he wore such clothing.

### Hearing he does not hear. XXXV

There are some people who, if something does not quite please them, pretend not to know of it; for instance, when they deny that letters have been delivered to them reminding them of their duty. They would rather escape the task than perform it. For such people, that line from the 23rd book of the *Iliad* <note>Erasmus cites book "ν" (Nu, book 13), but the event of Antilochus occurs in book 23 (Psi).</note> is fitting:
"Like one who did not hear." <note>original Greek: Ως οὐκ ἀΐοντι ἐοικώς.</note> ->that is,<- Pretending to have heard nothing.
This was said of Antilochus, who heard Menelaus calling him back from the race, yet he acted as if he had not heard and ran even faster:
"But Antilochus drove on even much more, 
Urging with the whip, like one who did not hear." <note>original Greek: Ἀντίλοχος δ' ἔτι καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἔλαυνε, / Κέντρῳ ἐπαινήχων, ὡς οὐκ ἀΐοντι ἐοικώς.</note> ->that is,<-
Indeed, Antilochus accelerated his pace even more,
Urging [the horses] with the lash, and pretended not to hear.

### He shows himself a good man by his appearance. XXXVI

Whoever says that a man seems honest based on the very shape of his face will cite that line from the first book of the *Odyssey*:
"For he did not look like a wicked man in his face." <note>original Greek: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι κακῷ εἷς ὦπα ἔωκε.</note> ->that is,<-
By his appearance he seemed 
to be anything but a villain. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] says in his eighth book against Verres:
"That was Apronius, who, as he demonstrates not only by his life but by his body and face, is some immense abyss or whirlpool of all vices and disgraces."

### Let shouting be absent from conversation or play. XXXVII

Whoever commands that one should refrain from loud shouting at a banquet or in conversation will apply that line from the same book:
"Now let us feast and be joyful, and let no shouting be present." <note>original Greek: νῦν μὲν δαινύμενοι τερπώμεθα, μηδ' ὴ βοητὺς ἔστω.</note> ->that is,<-
Now let us dine cheerfully, and let all clamor be far away.

### Pleasing novelty. XXXVIII

Whenever you say that the very newest things are usually the most pleasing to the common people, it would not be out of place to cite this from the same book:
"For men celebrate that song more, 
which comes newest to the listeners." <note>original Greek: τὴν γὰρ ἀοιδὴν μᾶλλον ἐπικλείουσ' ἄνθρωποι, / ἥ τις ἀκονόντεσσι νεωτάτη ἀμφιπέληται.</note> ->that is,<-
That song is by far the most celebrated among the common folk
and the most pleasing, which has most recently reached their ears. Pindar chimes in with this in his 9th *Olympian Ode*:
"Praise old wine, but the flowers of newer hymns." <note>original Greek: Αἴνει δὲ παλαιὸν μὲν οἶνον, ἄνθεα δ' ὕμνων νεωτέρων.</note> This means that hymns celebrating recent deeds are more skillfully received and more pleasing than those dealing with ancient matters. Novelty commends most things, especially among the unlearned. In contrast, in writing, antiquity wins favor while novelty brings envy, which is why Flaccus <note>The poet Horace.</note> says in his *Epistles*:
"I am indignant that anything is criticized, not because it is thought 
clumsily composed or lacking in wit, but because it is recent."
In almost all other matters, the favor shown to novelty wipes out the appreciation for older things. Thus David, the Bishop of Utrecht <note>David of Burgundy (1427–1496).</note>—born of Philip, Duke of the Burgundians, and the maternal great-grandfather of the man who recently passed away—a learned and sensible man, was urged by some to allow a designated successor bishop to be joined to him because of his increasing age. He said he was moved by the example of Saint Anthony and was unwilling to do it. For Anthony began to be neglected as soon as Saint Roch, a more "recent" saint, succeeded him in popularity. There is a similar distaste in the human mind for things that are right at hand. For we admire exotic things, even when we occasionally have better ones at home. This is especially common with doctors: we look down on our own, however learned they may be, but we gaze up at some "beast" who has arrived from distant barbarism. Likewise, pharmacists buy herbs at great expense brought from afar, when sometimes better ones grow in the neighbor's garden. Alexis noted this elegantly in the third book of Athenaeus:
"We love what is foreign, we overlook our kin." <note>original Greek: ἐρῶμεν ἀλλοτρίων, παρορῶμεν συγγενεῖς.</note> ->that is,<-
We love the stranger, we despise the neighbor.

### A modest woman should never be alone. XXXIX

When we advise that it is not fitting for a modest woman to be alone or to speak with men without witnesses, that phrase frequent in Homer concerning Penelope will be useful:
"Not alone, for together with her two handmaidens followed." <note>original Greek: οὐκ οἴη, ἅμα τῇ γε καὶ ἀμφίπολοι δύ' ἕποντο.</note>

<sig>Zz 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Scarcely [Haud]</meta>

<summary>Erasmus examines proverbs regarding selective hearing, the relationship between physical appearance and character, and the human tendency to favor new or foreign things over the familiar and local. He uses examples ranging from Homeric heroes to 15th-century bishops and local doctors.</summary>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Erasmus’s collection of proverbs derived from classical literature, focusing on themes of fate, mortality, and domestic stability. The previous page ended with a description of someone’s appearance; this page begins by concluding that description.</meta>

<page-num>822</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

"Not alone, but two handmaidens accompanied her." <note>original Latin: "Haud sola, ast illam famulæ binæ comitatæ." This concludes the previous entry regarding a dignified appearance.</note>

->The fated time of life has been completed.<-

This phrase applies to the decrepit, whose age seems already spent. It comes from the same book <note>The *Odyssey*, Book 1.</note>:
"Fools, who ate the cattle of Hyperion the Sun." <note>original Greek: νήπιοι, οἳ κτῆ βῦς ὑπερίονος ἠελίοιο ἤσθιον.</note> ->that is,<-
Fools, who consumed the oxen sacred to you, O Phoebus <note>Phoebus Apollo, often identified with the Sun god Helios/Hyperion.</note>, above all others.
For by the "oxen of the sun," the poet implies, in my opinion, the years allotted by fate.

->Not mourning, but a remedy is needed in times of trouble.<-

In times of misfortune, one should not use lamentations, but rather assistance. To this end, a line from the 24th book of the *Iliad* <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter Ω (Omega) to denote the 24th book.</note> is fitting, which is also repeated in other places:
"For there is no profit in chilling lamentation." <note>original Greek: οὐ γάρ τις πρῆξις πέλεται κρυεροῖο γόοιο.</note> ->that is,<-
Indeed, wretched weeping and laments are of no use.

->Even now, some god watches over us.<-

When we are in circumstances of extreme affliction, yet deny that we have utterly lost heart or say that some hope remains, that which is said by Priam in the same book <note>*Iliad*, Book 24.</note> will be appropriate:
"But still some one of the gods held a hand over me." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἔτι τις καὶ ἐμοὶ θεῶν ὑπερέσχεθε χεῖρα.</note> ->that is,<-
Some divine power still extends a friendly right hand to me.

->Death snatches the best and leaves the worst.<-

The best are snatched away from our midst by death, while the worst are left behind. Consequently, we see certain utterly useless people living to a Tithonian age <note><term>Tithonian age</term>: A reference to Tithonus, who was granted immortality but not eternal youth, eventually shriveling into a cicada. It refers to an excessively long, frail old age.</note>, while very few endowed with excellent talent even reach the threshold of old age. This sentiment is matched by a passage from the same book <note>*Iliad*, Book 24.</note>:
"Mars destroyed those men, but all the disgraces were left behind—the liars, the dancers, those best at leading the choral dances, the local plunderers of lambs and kids." <note>original Greek: τοὺς μὲν ἀπώλετ’ ἄρης, τὰ δ’ ἐλέγχεα πάντα λέλειπται, ψεύσταί τ’ ὀρχησταί τε χοροιτυπίησιν ἄριστοι, ἀρνῶν ἠδ’ ἐρίφων ἐπιδήμιοι ἁρπακτῆρες.</note> ->that is,<-
Mars <note>The Roman god of war, used here to translate the Greek *Ares*.</note> carried those men off, but the remaining evil shames were left: the liars, the dancers, those most vigorous at leading dances and snatching away lambs and kids.

Famous is that line of Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>:
"The best day of life is the first to flee for wretched mortals; diseases creep in, etc." <note>original Latin: "Optima quæq; dies miseris mortalibus æui Prima fugit, subeunt morbi, &c." From Virgil's *Georgics*.</note>
Theocritus also harmonizes with this in his *Epitaph for Bion*:
"It seemed good to the nymphs that the frog should always sing; I would not envy them, for he does not sing a beautiful song." <note>original Greek: ταῖς νύμφαισιν ἔδοξεν ἀεὶ τὸν βάτραχον ᾄδειν, τοῖς δ’ ἐγω οὐ φθονέοιμι, τὸ γὰρ μέλος οὐ καλὸν ᾄδει.</note> ->that is,<-
Thus it seemed to the nymphs: the wicked frog always sings. I do not envy him for this, for he does not sing good songs.

->One should stay at home.<-

It is useless to be away from home for a long time, leaving one's possessions behind. This sentiment is matched by a passage from the third book of the *Odyssey* <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter γ (Gamma) to denote the 3rd book.</note>:
"And you, friend, do not wander long far from home, leaving your property and the men who are in your house." <note>original Greek: Καὶ σὺ φίλος, μὴ δηθὰ δόμων ἄπο τῆλ’ ἀλαλήσο, Κτήματά τε προλιπὼν, ἄνδρας θ’ οἳ ἐν εἵσι δόμοισι.</note> ->that is,<-
You also, friend, beware of being absent from home for a long time, leaving your affairs and the men within your roof.
Likewise, Hesiod says:
"It is better to be at home, since it is harmful to be outdoors." <note>original Greek: οἴκοι βέλτερον εἶν, ἐπεὶ βλαβερὸν τὸ θύρηφι.</note> ->that is,<-
It is better to be at home, because being abroad is damaging.
A verse from Euripides is also cited:
"Blessed is he who, being prosperous, remains at home; for the cargo which is kept on the ground can be entrusted to the sea once again." <note>original Greek: μακάριος ὅς τις εὐτυχῶν οἴκοι μένει, ἔν γη δ’ ὁ φόρτος καὶ πάλιν ναυτίλλεται.</note> ->that is,<-
Happy is he who stays at home in prosperity, for the load that is kept on the soil can again be committed to the salt sea.

->Hands must be kept off sacred things.<-

It is also commonly believed that fate looms over anyone who lays hands on sacred things dedicated to God, or who attacks holy men, or certainly those performing sacred ministries—such as the Roman Pontiff, bishops, and abbots—even if they have been of little pious character. This was expressed long ago by Homer in the 17th book of the *Iliad* <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter P (Rho) to denote the 17th book.</note>:
"Whenever a man wishes to fight against a god-like man whom a god honors, a great calamity quickly rolls upon him." <note>original Greek: ὁππότ’ ἀνὴρ ἐθέλῃ πρὸς δαίμονα φωτὶ μάχεσθαι, ὅν τε θεὸς τιμᾷ τάχα οἱ μέγα πῆμα κυλίσθη.</note> ->that is,<-
When someone desires to strive against a divine man, to whom a god wishes well, a huge evil shortly threatens him.

<summary>Erasmus compiles adages regarding the completion of life's fated time, the necessity of seeking remedies over laments, the survival of the "worst" over the "best," and the importance of domestic stability and respecting sacred persons.</summary>

<margin>XL</margin>
->Shameful boasting.<-
<margin>XLVI</margin>
It is not the mark of a noble mind to boast about things one has done bravely or successfully. On this subject, Menelaus <note>A king of Mycenaean Sparta and a central figure in the Trojan War.</note> speaks thus in the same book:
"It is surely not good to boast excessively." <note>original Greek: οὐ μὲν καλὸν ὑπερβίον εὐχετάασθαι.</note> That is,
It is truly not a beautiful thing to boast of oneself pridefully.

<margin>XLI u. quā-</margin>
->The first to arrive takes it.<-
<margin>XLVII</margin>
When someone has snatched away a profit from another through speed, this line from the 23rd book of the *Iliad* <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter ψ (Psi) for Book 23.</note> will be fitting:
"Lest someone might snatch the glory by throwing, and he should come in second." <note>original Greek: μήτις κῦδος ἄροιτο βαλὼν, ὁ δ' δεύτερος ἔλθοι.</note> That is,
Lest anyone, by throwing his spear, should snatch away the praise and honor,
And thus he himself should come later, already in second place.
This was said of Achilles, who signaled to the rest of the Achaeans <note>The Greeks at Troy.</note> that no one should cast a spear at Hector, so that he might keep all the glory for himself.

<margin>XLII ietum</margin>
->Sacred rites should be finished more quickly.<-
<margin>XLVIII</margin>
In divine matters, it is more appropriate to be attentive than to be long-winded, lest the rites become cheapened by constant repetition—contrary to the habit of certain priests who linger too long over the sacred service and the prayers they call "hourly" <note>A reference to the 'Liturgy of the Hours' or 'Canonical Hours,' which Erasmus suggests were often recited mechanically or at excessive length.</note>. To this point, a line from the 3rd book of the *Odyssey* <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter γ (Gamma) for Book 3.</note> can be applied:
"It is not fitting to sit a long time at a feast of the gods, but to depart." <note>original Greek: οὐ δέ ἔοικε δηθὰ θεῶν ἐν δαιτὶ θαασσέμεν, ἀλλὰ νέεσθαι.</note> That is,
Nor is it right to sit too long at the banquet of the Gods; indeed, 
it is proper to rise early.

<margin>XLIII orfus necię</margin>
->Not even the gods deliver from death.<-
<margin>XLIX</margin>
No one is so dear to the powers above that they might escape death through their favor. The testimony of Homer from the same book <note>*Odyssey*, Book 3.</note> supports this sentiment:
"But truly, even the gods are not able to ward off death, which is common to all, even from a man they love, when the destructive fate of long-sorrowing death seizes him." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ἤτοι θάνατον μὲν ὁμοίϊον οὐδὲ θεοίπερ, Καὶ φίλω ἀνδρὶ δύνανται ἀλαλκέμεν, ὁππότεκεν δὴ Μοῖρ' ὀλοὴ καθέλῃσι τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο.</note> That is,
But indeed, the gods cannot drive away death, which is equally common to all,
From a beloved man, when the mournful day of bitter fate 
Already presses upon him.

<margin>aronis, onis,</margin>
->God helps from anywhere, if only he is favorable.<-
<margin>L</margin>
God is present everywhere to help if he favors us; nor does it matter where in the world you are, provided he is well-disposed. You may adapt this line from the same book to this sentiment:
"A god, if he wishes, could easily save a man even from afar." <note>original Greek: ῥεῖα θεός κ' ἐθέλων καὶ τηλόθεν ἄνδρα σαώσαι.</note> That is,
If it pleases them to save, the divine powers can do so even from a distance.

<margin>XLIIII rabit il</margin>
->On luxuries.<-
<margin>LI</margin>
Regarding very choice foods, this line from the same 3rd book of the *Odyssey* will fit:
"The sort of delicacies that kings nurtured by Zeus eat." <note>original Greek: οἵατε οἷα ἔδουσι διοτρεφέων βασιλήων.</note> That is,
The kind of gourmet dishes that purple-clad kings eat.
It will be even more elegant if applied to a speech that is exceptionally refined, as if it were worthy of the ears of the gods.

<margin>en hoc</margin>
->Concord.<-
<margin>LII</margin>
Concerning perfect harmony and the consensus of all things, this line from the same book will be appropriate:
"Never did we speak differently in the assembly or in the council, but having one soul, we planned with mind and prudent counsel." <note>original Greek: οὐδέ ποτ' εὶν ἀγορῇ δίχ' ἐβάζομεν, οὔτ' ἐνὶ βουλῇ, Ἀλλ' ἕνα θυμὸν ἔχοντε νόῳ καὶ ἐπίφρονι βουλῇ.</note> That is,
Never did the assembly nor the council hear us 
clash in our words, but always with the same mind,
It saw us feel the same things and decree the same things.
These are the words of Nestor <note>The oldest and wisest of the Greek kings at Troy.</note> concerning himself and Ulysses <note>Odysseus.</note>.

<margin>XLV s manus arit: uelu ribus. id</margin>
->Immutable Fate.<-
<margin>LIII</margin>
Divine decrees are not changed; human laws are varied according to the time, just as morals and wills change. To this, a line from the same book is consistent:
"For the mind of the gods, who exist forever, is not quickly turned." <note>original Greek: οὐ γάρ τ' αἶψα θεῶν τρέπεται νόος αἰὲν ἐόντων.</note> That is,
For the mind of the gods who dwell among the stars is not easily changed.

<margin>Tur</margin>
->We have no power without divine help.<-
<margin>LIIII</margin>
All the industry of mortals and every effort is crippled unless divine favor breathes upon it. To...

<page-num>824</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

It will be appropriate to apply that Homeric line from the same book:
"All men have need of the gods." <note>original Greek: πάντες δὲ θεῶν χατέουσ’ ἄνθρωποι.</note> That is,
Every mortal desires the help of the divine.

->God helps the industrious.<-

In undertaking any business, some things are provided for by human reason, while others happen by chance or luck, the convenience of which is supplied by the circumstances themselves. This is found in Homer, appearing several times elsewhere, but most notably in the passage we just cited from the book:
"Telemachus, some things you will think of in your own heart, but others a god will suggest to you." <note>original Greek: Τηλέμαχ’ ἄλλα μὲν αὐτὸς ἐνὶ φρεσὶ σῇσι νοήσεις, ἀλλὰ δὲ καὶ δαίμων ὑποθήσεται.</note> That is,
You will weigh these things partly in your own heart,
And a god will suggest part of them to you.

->A favorable outcome.<-

When we wish to indicate that a matter we have begun will turn out well, as if some god were ensuring it, that line from the second book of the *Odyssey* <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter β (Beta) for Book 2.</note> will fit:
"Take heart, nurse, for this plan is not without the will of a god." <note>original Greek: Θάρσει μαῖ’ ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι ἄνευ θεοῦ ἤδε γε βουλή.</note> That is,
Have faith, nurse; this counsel is not without divine power.

<margin>L</margin>
->We are made wiser by age.<-

If we ever wish to deny that we still approve of the same things as older men which once pleased us in the ignorance of youth, but rather that our prudence has increased through experience, this passage from the same book is fitting:
"I was still a child. But now that I am grown, and I hear the words of others and learn, my spirit grows within me." <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δ’ ἔτι νήπιος ἦα. Νῦν δ’ ὅτε δὴ μέγας εἰμὶ, καὶ ἄλλων μῦθον ἀκούω πυνθάνομαι, καὶ δή μοι ἀέξεται ἔνδοθι θυμός.</note> That is,
I was still a boy, but now that I am
Older, and the speech of others makes me learned,
My own mind grows great within me.
This is spoken to the suitors by Telemachus <note>The son of Odysseus, who is maturing and asserting himself against the men courting his mother.</note>.

<margin>I</margin>
->Be at leisure.<-

<margin>Nor anything else to you</margin>
If we command someone to be of a relaxed mind, to "take care of their own skin" <note>An idiom for personal comfort and self-care.</note> and let business be for others, we may apply this from the same book:
"Let no evil deed or word trouble your heart, but rather eat and drink just as you did before." <note>original Greek: Ἐν στήθεσσι κακὸν μελέτω ἔργον τε ἔπος τε, Ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐσθιέμεν καὶ πινέμεν ὡς τὸ πάρος περ.</note> That is, You yourself take care
That no worry of word or deed torments your heart:
But remain tranquil, and eat and drink just as you used to do.

<margin>I</margin>
->He will not finish it.<-

For one who says that a business someone has started will by no means be completed, it is permitted to say so in Homeric words:
"Truly, he will never complete this journey." <note>original Greek: τελεέσθ’ ἐσθλὸν ἔποτε πάντως.</note> That is,
In truth, he shall never finish this path.

->Yielding to the crowd.<-

For one who advises that a single person should not fight against many, and that one must always comply with the multitude, he may bring forth this from the same book:
"He would soon bring a cruel fate upon himself, if he should fight against many." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλότριον αὐτῷ ἀήκεια πότμον ἐπίσποι, Εἰ πλεόνεσσι μάχοιτο.</note> That is,
He will soon summon a cruel death for himself,
If he wishes to fight against many.

<margin>It is difficult</margin>
The same suitors said a little earlier:
"It is a difficult thing to fight alone against many men at a feast." <note>original Greek: Ἀνδράσι καὶ πλεόνεσσι μαχέσαθαι περὶ δαιτί.</note> That is,
It is an arduous matter to fight
Against many men alone amidst the banquets.

->Vain conjectures.<-

Against those who are accustomed to divine the outcome of a business, this from the same book applies:
"Many birds fly about under the rays of the sun, and not all are omens of fate." <note>original Greek: ὄρνιθες δέ τε πολλοὶ ὑπ’ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο φοιτῶσ’, οὐδέ τε πάντες ἐναίσιμοι.</note> That is,
But a great many birds turn about in the air,
Not all of which are suitable for portending fate.

<sig>C</sig>

### I foresee it for certain. LXII

Anyone who wishes to deny that they are sensing the outcome of a matter based on mere whim, or that they feel badly or otherwise about it without cause, but rather that they have been led by certain arguments and have observed it through many experiences, may apply this line from the same book <note>Odyssey, Book 2</note>:
"For I do not prophesy without experience, but knowing well." <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἀπείρητος μαντεύομαι, ἀλλ’ εὖ εἰδώς.</note> That is:
For I shall not have divined as one unskilled, but as one who is exceedingly clever.

<margin>
56
Auspices
</margin>

### God will avenge. LXIII

When we wish to indicate that we currently lack the ability to repel an injury, but hope that the powers above will eventually punish it, this passage from the same book will be of use:
"I will call upon the everlasting gods, if Zeus might somehow grant that deeds of retribution be performed." <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ θεοὺς ἐπιβώσομαι αἰὲν ἐόντας, Αἴκε ποθι Ζεὺς δῷσι παλίντιτα ἔργα γενέσθαι.</note> That is:
But I indeed shall have implored the immortal gods,
If by chance Jupiter himself might one day grant a turn. <note>Erasmus translates "deeds of retribution" as "vices" (turns/repayment).</note>

<margin>
57
Already observed in the book.
</margin>

### Evil’s punishment must be guarded against in time. LXIIII

Whenever we advise that one should meet an evil long before it overwhelms us, or that one must cease from sinning before divine vengeance strikes, this line from the same book will be useful:
"But long before then, let us consider how we may stop it." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρὶν φραζώμεθ’ ὥσπην κατὰ παύσομεν.</note> That is:
Indeed, long beforehand, let us wish to set a limit and an end.
These are the words of the seer threatening the suitors with the return of Ulysses.

<margin>
58
Is a care
</margin>

### A domestic evil. LXV

To signify a private and domestic misfortune that does not concern others, this line from the same book will be appropriate:
"Rather it is my own need, for an evil has fallen upon my house." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ χρεῖος, ὅμοι κακὸν ἔμπεσεν οἴκῳ.</note> That is:
Furthermore, the evil which has fallen into our house pertains to me alone.
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fifth speech of his *Action against Verres*, calls it a "domestic and homegrown crime" <note>Latin: domesticum ac uernaculum crimen</note> when a deed committed within the walls of a house has not yet reached public rumor.

<margin>
59
In Homer
</margin>

### The prudence of the aged. LXVI

Regarding an old man skilled in the use of many things, and who remembers much performed in previous ages, this from the same book will fit:
"Knowing many things and ancient things." <note>original Greek: παλαιά τε πολλά τε εἰδώς.</note> That is:
Who knew both ancient things and many things.

<margin>
60
To carry out
</margin>

### The opportunity must be pressed. LXVII

Anyone wishing to indicate that one must press on by all means, and that an opportunity once offered should not be let out of one's hands, may apply this from *Odyssey* Book 4 (δ):
"You must hold him firmly and press him even harder." <note>original Greek: ὑμᾶς δ’ ἀστεμφέως ἐχέμεν μᾶλλον τε πιέζειν.</note> That is:
You all press him, and bind the captive more tightly with chains.
This can indeed be twisted to mean that the impulses of the soul <note>Latin: impetus animi</note> must be restrained all the more by the governance of reason the more they boil over and solicit us toward evil.

<margin>
61
</margin>

### With every nerve. LXVIII

When we suggest that in any business all strengths must be brought forth and every nerve strained, this from the same place will be suitable:
"Then afterward, let strength and vigor be your care." <note>original Greek: Καὶ τότ’ ἔπειθ’ ὑμῖν μελέτω κάρτος τε βίη τε.</note> That is:
Thereafter, let strength and vigor be a care to you. In a similar vein, Pindar said in *Olympian X*:
"Who then won the fresh crown with hands, feet, and chariot in the contest?" <note>original Greek: Τίς δὴ ποταίνιον ἔλαχε στέφανον, χείρεσσι ποσί τε καὶ ἅρμασιν ἀγώνιον.</note> That is:
Who at last attained the desirable crown with hands, feet, and chariots? This passage should have been added to the proverb "With hands and feet," <note>Referring to the adage *Manibus pedibusque*, meaning to try with all one's might.</note> but those pages had already left my hands <note>i.e., they had already been sent to the printer.</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero in the fifth book *Against Verres*: "Pay attention, judges, for I must contend with every nerve."

<margin>
Certainly
</margin>

### One must not fight with a prince. LXIX

Whoever wishes to signify that it is an arduous thing for a private citizen to overcome a prince, or most difficult to conquer nature, will use this from the same book:
"For it is a hard thing for a mortal man to subdue a god." <note>original Greek: Ἀργαλέον γάρ τ’ ἐστὶ θεὸς βροτῷ ἀνδρὶ δαμῆναι.</note> That is:
It is a difficult thing for a mortal man to conquer a divine power.

<page-num>826</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>
<meta>catchword: He boasted</meta>

### A vast difference.
<margin>50</margin>
A huge interval—as when someone feels there is a world of difference between the pursuit of money and the pursuit of wisdom—can be signified by this verse from the same book <note>Homer, Odyssey, Book 4, 356–357</note>:
"As much distance as a hollow ship covers in a whole day’s course, when a whistling wind blows from behind." <note>original Greek: Τόσσον ἀνδῶν ὅσσον τε πανημερίη γλαφυρὴ νηῦς / Ἤνυσεν ἣ λιγὺς οὖρος ἐπιπνείησιν ὄπισθεν.</note> That is:
It was as far away as the space a vessel driven on a day’s course
Might complete, when a favorable breeze carries it forward.

### To speak openly and simply.
<margin>51</margin>
When we intend to speak simply and openly, without any ambiguity, we shall signify it with this verse, which is in the same book <note>Odyssey 4, 348</note>: "I would not indeed say other things evasively, nor will I deceive you." <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγε / Ἄλλα παρὲξ εἴποιμι παρακλιδὸν, οὐδ’ ἀπατήσω.</note> That is:
I shall not deceive you by hiding the truth with false pretenses.

### The turning of all things.
<margin>60</margin>
The various turns of fortune: now happy things happen to each person, now sad things. To this sentiment one may apply that passage from the same book <note>Odyssey 4, 236–237</note>:
"But God, now to one and now to another, Zeus gives both good and evil." <note>original Greek: Ἀτὰρ θεὸς ἄλλοτ’ ἐπ’ ἄλλω, / Ζεὺς ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε διδoῖ.</note> That is:
Now to this man, now to that,
Jupiter sends now joyful things, now sad.

### Cheerful conversation.
<margin>61</margin>
When someone introduces a very merry and festive speech at a banquet, which dispels all sadness, this line from the same book is fitting. Homer invented the story of Helen casting a drug <term>pharmacon: a Greek word meaning both medicine and poison</term> into the cups of the guests, which would induce forgetfulness of all past troubles <note>Odyssey 4, 220–221</note>:
"Straightway she cast into the wine from which they were drinking a drug that banishes grief and anger, and brings forgetfulness of all ills." <note>original Greek: Αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ εἰς οἶνον βάλε φάρμακον ἔνθεν ἔπινον / Νηπενθές τ’ ἄχολόν τε κακῶν ἐπίληθον ἁπάντων.</note> That is:
Into the wine she soon cast a drug, from which they drank,
The forgetfulness of grief, of bile, and of every evil.
Pliny mentions this in Book 25: "Famous," he says, "is that drug which brings forgetfulness of sadness and grant of pardon, and which was to be offered by Helen to all mortals." Dioscorides in Book 4 mentions a herb <term>alypon: literally "painless"</term> which, when taken internally, cures black bile <note>In ancient medicine, black bile was thought to cause melancholy</note>. From this, the name seems to have been given because it is "without pain," just as <term>nepenthes</term> <note>grief-banishing</note> and <term>adipsos</term> <note>thirst-quenching</note> are named because they drive away grief and thirst.

### He who can harm can also help.
<margin>62</margin>
This will apply to unskilled doctors, who not infrequently administer poison instead of a remedy; it is from the same book, and was used by Lucian in his work *The False Prophet*, and appears in several places in Homer <note>Odyssey 4, 230</note>:
"Drugs, many good when mixed, and many baneful." <note>original Greek: φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ μεμιγμένα, πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά.</note> That is:
Mixed drugs, many healthy, but many harmful.
The same will apply to a man equipped with both good and evil skills, who can either help if he wishes, or hurt.

### To speak with great assertion.
<margin>50</margin>
When we are about to say something rather boldly and with great assertion, because it nevertheless seems so to us, we shall bring forward that verse from the same book which Helen uses concerning Telemachus <note>Odyssey 4, 140</note>:
"Shall I lie, or speak the truth? My spirit commands me." <note>original Greek: ψεύσομαι, ἢ ἔτυμον ἐρέω, κέλεται δέ με θυμός.</note> That is:
Shall I lie, or shall I speak the truth? Yet my mind itself
Commands that I speak. The same verse appears in the *Iliad*, book 10.

### Seize what is offered.
<margin>60</margin>
This little verse is common and repeated in many places <note>e.g., Odyssey 1, 149</note>:
"And they stretched forth their hands to the good things lying ready before them." <note>original Greek: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.</note> That is:
Each one moved his ready hands <margin>To move the hands.</margin>
To the things set before him, if anything were useful.
This can be twisted to refer to guardians who, having obtained the property of their wards <note>orphans under their care</note>, lay their hands upon it and, having divided it among themselves, claim it for their own. Or to a similar class of men, who invade and swoop down upon the property of others.

### The favor of princes is necessary.
<margin>60</margin>
When someone tries to extricate himself from some evil against the will of the leaders, or from a lawsuit from which he cannot be untangled unless aided by their favor, this saying from the same book concerning Ajax will be appropriate <note>Odyssey 4, 504</note>:
"He said that against the will of the gods he had escaped the great gulf of the sea." <note>original Greek: φῆ ῥ’ ἀέκητι θεῶν φυγέειν μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης.</note> That is:

<note>original Latin: "Iactabat sese spatiosi ex aequoris altis / Emersurum undis, inuito numine diuum." This verse refers to the hubris of Ajax the Lesser, who defied the gods after surviving a shipwreck, only to be destroyed by Poseidon.</note>

## An unsuitable task. 78

For someone who refuses a duty or a province that is not suited to them, or for one who says they do not wish to summon someone to a position for which they do not seem fit, one might use this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 4, 601</note>:
> "I will not take horses to Ithaca." <note>original Greek: ἵππους δ’ εἰς ἰθάκην οὐκ ἄξομαι.</note> That is,
> "Moreover, I shall not lead horses to Ithaca."

These are the words of Telemachus <note>The son of Odysseus</note> refusing the horses that Menelaus offered as a gift, because the island of Ithaca was not suitable for rearing horses; it was very rocky and lacked proper pasture land.

## An appeal to past merits. 79

When we plead based on the memory of old services, this line from the same book will be appropriate, although it appears elsewhere in this poet <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 4, 764–765</note>:
> "If ever he burned for you the fat thigh-pieces of an ox or sheep, remember these things now." <note>original Greek: ἤ βοὸς ἤ ὄϊος ἤδη πίοna μηρί’ ἔκηε, / Νῦν μοι μνῆαι.</note> That is,
> If either the fat limbs of an ox or a sheep were burned for you, 
> Be mindful of them now.

These are the words of Penelope <note>The wife of Odysseus</note> praying to a deity, asking that, being mindful of the sacrifices and the savor of the burnt offerings upon which the god had often been fed, the deity might now help her in return.

## A guest, yet no guest. 80

Regarding someone who sits at a banquet but acts only as a spectator of the things served—for in this way certain "stingily magnificent" <term>sordide magnifici</term> <note>People who want to appear wealthy and generous but are actually quite cheap.</note> treat their guests—that which was said in the same book about Penelope will be applicable:
> "He sat without food, without tasting meat or drink." <note>original Greek: κάτ’ ἄρ’ ἄπτος, ἄπαστος, ἐδητύος, οὐδὲ ποτῆτος.</note> That is,
> Undined and unrefined by drink or food, 
> He sat.

## They seek profit from anywhere. 81

For lawyers, false accusers, and bad doctors who snatch profit from everywhere—if anyone falls into their nets whom they can pillage—this line from the same book is fitting:
> "For always wandering about the island, they would fish with curved hooks, for hunger pinched their bellies." <note>original Greek: Αἰεὶ γὰρ ποδὶ νῆσον ἀλώμενοι ἰχθυάσκον / γναμπτοῖς ἀγκίστροισι, ἔτρει δ’ γαστέρα λιμός.</note> That is,
> Always, as far as the island extends, they lay in wait 
> For fish with a hook; black hunger killed their bellies.

## The ingratitude of the masses. 82

One who wishes to express that ingratitude is painful—because they realize that no account is taken of former services—might not ineptly use this line from *Odyssey* Book 5, which also appears in other places:
> "Let no scepter-bearing king henceforth be kind, gentle, and mild, nor let him know justice in his heart. But let him always be harsh and do wicked things." <note>original Greek: Μήτις ἔτι πρόφρων ἀγανὸς, καὶ ἤπιος ἔσω, / Σκηπτοῦχος βασιλεὺς, μηδὲ φρεσὶν αἴσιμα εἰδώς. / Ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ χαλεπός τ’ εἴη, καὶ αἴσυλα ῥέζοι.</note> That is,
> Hereafter let no scepter-bearing king be calm, nor kind, 
> Nor mild, nor a holder of what is just, 
> But let him always be fierce, and always perform injustices.

## The corruption of gifts. 83

Against one who approaches a matter with gold and gifts, you might not unpleasantly twist this line from the same book spoken about Mercury <note>The messenger god</note> wielding his caduceus <note>Mercury's staff, a symbol of his power over sleep and messages.</note>:
> "He took the wand with which he charms the eyes of men, whom he wills, and others again he wakes from sleep." <note>original Greek: Εἵλετο δὲ ῥάβδον τῇ τ’ ἀνδρῶν ὄμματα θέλγει, / Ἧν ἐθέλει, τοὺς δ’ αὖτε καὶ ὑπνώοντας ἐγείρει.</note> That is,
> He snatched the rod with which he soothes the eyes to sleep, 
> Whomever he wishes; he also releases eyes from sleep.

For this will apply beautifully to gifts (bribes), just as was said of Mercury's wand: by gifts, judges are "awakened" who were previously as if dozing; and again, those who are hostile are pacified so that they might "fall asleep" or "shut their eyes" to the case. Aristophanes, in *The Assemblywomen*, says that the gods are also captured by gifts, and for that reason, they stand with their hands turned upward:
"For when we pray to them to give us good things..."
<note>Erasmus implies that the gods, like corrupt judges, have their hands open to receive "gifts" or sacrifices before they will act.</note>

“He stands stretching out his hand palm upwards,  
Not as one about to give, but as one about to receive.” -> that is, <-  
> For when we pray that they may bestow good things,  
> They stand stretching forth the palm of the hand, as if  
> Not about to give, but rather to receive.  

The commentator <note>scholiast</note> points out that statues of the gods were formerly fashioned with upturned palms. For they represent the posture of those making a request, as if prepared to receive.

### Princes are known to each other.
<margin>70</margin>
If anyone wishes to say that there is a mutual recognition between princes, or between learned men—even if they inhabit regions far apart and widely separated—he may use this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 79–80</note>:  
“For the immortal gods are not unknown to one another,  
Not even if one dwells in a home far away.” -> that is, <-  
> The gods who lack death are not unknown to each other,  
> Although they may dwell in different places far removed.  

This can also be twisted to apply to those "satraps" <note>provincial governors or powerful officials</note> who, although they seem to be at war and clashing in a great upheaval of affairs, nevertheless secretly collude with one another. Their only goal is to drain their own common people and, by diminishing the authority of the state, to firmly establish their own tyranny.

### Do not enter danger rashly.
<margin>71</margin>
No one undertakes a long voyage for the sake of pleasure, but rather because they are driven by some heavy necessity; similarly, no one should take up a long and heavy labor rashly. To this end, that line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 100</note> is fitting:  
“Who would willingly run across such a great expanse of salt water?” -> that is, <-  
> Who would of their own accord run through so much of the briny liquid?  

### Inevitable fate.
<margin>72</margin>
What has been decreed by the fates, no one is permitted to avoid. For this sentiment, this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 103–104</note> will serve:  
“But in no way is it possible for any other god  
To evade or nullify the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus.” -> that is, <-  
> But by no reasoning is it ever right for any of the gods  
> To avoid or deceive the mind of Jupiter <note>the Roman name for Zeus</note>.  

### Driven by the fates.
<margin>73</margin>
For someone who has fallen into a certain way of life not by choice, but by chance, or as if driven by the impelling fates, this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 110</note> is suitable:  
“But him the wind and the wave, carrying him along, brought here.” -> that is, <-  
> But the wind and the wave, carrying him, drove him to this place.  

### Poorly matched.
<margin>74</margin>
For a man who is bound in marriage to a woman whom he does not love in return from his heart, or who is loved by his wife only for the sake of physical pleasure, one may not unskillfully twist this passage from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 154–157, describing Odysseus's time with the nymph Calypso</note>:  
“But indeed, he would spend the nights by necessity  
In the hollow caves, unwilling beside her who was willing,  
But during the days, sitting among the rocks and the shores,  
Tormenting his soul with tears, groaning, and grief.” -> that is, <-  
> But though unwilling, he slept with her at night,  
> Unwilling with a willing woman, hidden in dark caves.  
> But through the day he sat upon the rocks and the shore,  
> Tormenting his mind with tears, cares, and groaning.  

### If God wills it.
<margin>75</margin>
Concerning a future matter, the outcome of which depends on the favor of God; for even the common people say that all things will prosper "If God wills it." The apostle James also teaches us to speak this way <note>James 4:15</note>. You can express this with a Homeric verse when we are joking among the learned <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 169</note>:  
“If the gods indeed so will, who hold the wide heaven.” -> that is, <-  
> If it has seemed so to the gods, whom Olympus carries.  

### I advise what I myself would do.
When we give advice to another which we ourselves would not be reluctant to follow in a similar situation, this line of Calypso’s from the same book will be appropriate:  
“But I am thinking and will plan those things which I myself...” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 188</note>

“I myself would not think of it, when such a need should come upon me.” -> that is, <-  
I feel, and I will advise you of things that I myself would not find burdensome to use, should a similar need ever occur to me. <note>original Greek: "Αὐτὴ μηδοίμην..."; Latin: "Sentio, suadeboq;..." This concludes the adage from the previous page regarding Calypso’s advice to Odysseus.</note>

### Habituation to evils. XCI
He who has become accustomed to evils and has endured very many of them, bears more easily any other misfortune that might occur. To this end, a line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 221–222</note> spoken by Odysseus is fitting:  
“For already I have suffered very much and toiled much,  
amid the waves and in war; let this also be added to those.” -> that is, <-  
> I have already endured much evil before, and much of labor  
> in the waves and in wars; come, let this too be added to them.

### Fortune makes people insolent. XCII
For one who, after a more favorable fortune has shone upon him, similarly lifts his spirits and carries himself a little too confidently, this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 269</note> will apply:  
“Odysseus steered by the breeze, with his sail spread out.” -> that is, <-  
> Rejoicing in the winds, he spread his favorable sails.

### The manager of an affair. XCIII
A verse that follows immediately in the same passage will suit one who, through his own prudence and authority, manages some business or affair:  
“But he guided the rudder skillfully.” -> that is, <-  
> He steered the ship with the tiller, expertly and learnedly.

### To be silently resentful. XCIIII
For one who is indignant within himself, this line from the same book will apply:  
“He hated him even more in his heart.” -> that is, <-  
> His heart is inflamed with anger more and more.  
This was said of Neptune, who bore it indignantly that Odysseus was sailing prosperously.

### One who throws everything into confusion. XCV
For one who stirs up the greatest turmoils from every side, this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 292</note> will be aptly twisted:  
“He stirred up all the blasts of all kinds of winds.” -> that is, <-  
> He rouses all the tempests of every kind of wind.

### He does not lose heart. XCVI
Of one who, even in the most afflicted circumstances, does not cast away hope or a plan of action (just as in Virgil <note>original: "apud Maronem"</note>, Latinus "left the reins of affairs" <note>Aeneid 7.600</note>), but thinks of recovering himself however he can, this line said of Odysseus is aptly stated:  
“But not even so did he forget the raft, distressed though he was.” -> that is, <-  
> And not even thus, though afflicted, did he allow forgetfulness  
> of the vessel to seize him.

### Evils follow upon evils. XCVII
For one who is exercised by various misfortunes of fate—now by disease, now by robberies, now by one evil after another—this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 331–332</note> will be suitable:  
“Sometimes the South wind threw him to the North wind to be carried,  
and sometimes the East wind gave way to the West wind to chase him.” -> that is, <-  
> Sometimes the South wind handed him over to the North wind to be carried,  
> now again the East wind handed him over to be tossed by the West wind.  
Ausonius in an *Epigram* elegantly called these "chained labors" <note>original: *Catenatos labores*</note>, because one business is struck out from another. The opposite of this is what Pindar says in *Olympian 8*: "May he wish to heap good deeds upon good deeds." He prays that Jupiter might be willing to pile benefits upon benefits for him.

### Care must be taken for a guest. XCVIII
One who says that the law of hospitality must be respected will use this line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 5, 447–448</note>:  
“Reverend is he even to the immortal gods,  
whosoever comes wandering, just as I do now.” -> that is, <-  
> For that man is to be revered by the gods and the immortals,  
> whoever has arrived driven by many wanderings, just as I am now.

### Wealth does not always fall to the best people. XCIX
One who says that wealth does not always fall to the most sensible people, but happens to now this one, now that one according to the whim of fortune, will cite this line from *Odyssey*, Book 6 <note>the letter zeta (ζ)</note>.

“Zeus himself distributes wealth from Olympus to men,
to the good and the bad alike, just as he wills to each.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 6, lines 188–189. Erasmus provides both the Greek and a Latin translation: *Iupiter emetitur opes mortalibus ipse...*</note> -> that is, <-
> Jupiter himself measures out riches to mortals,
> Just as it seems best to him, whether to a good or a bad man.

These words are spoken by Nausicaa to Odysseus, who is in the guise of a beggar. She does not hold him in contempt because of his poverty, which is to be blamed on fortune rather than the man himself, provided he is otherwise wise and sensible.

-> A small gift, but a timely one. <-

When we indicate a gift that is very small in price, yet very pleasing to the recipient because of the timing—as if someone were to offer a piece of bread to a person in danger of losing their life—we shall cite this from the same book:
“A gift small but dear.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 6, line 208. Original Greek: Δόσις δ' ὀλίγη τε φίλη τε.</note> -> that is, <-
A tiny gift, yet welcome. <note>This same verse appears in another section of the work.</note>

### THE TENTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD THOUSAND

#### Where have I overstepped? etc.

Among the philosophers, you will find hardly another who instituted the training of youth more religiously than Pythagoras. For this reason, he mixed in a good deal of superstition, because that age—much like the unlearned multitude—cannot be ruled by the bare and open precepts of philosophy. To this end, surely, belonged the prohibition of eating meat, the recommendation of beans, and the five-year <term>echemuthia</term> <note>original: ἐχεμυθία; a vow of silence or "keeping of speech."</note>, and finally the Symbols, which were like enigmas that had to be learned before they could be understood. Those who are now monks in title alone seem to emulate some of his institutions. Indeed, they sin the least who keep a restrained and controlled tongue; however, since it is hardly human to be so careful as to never slip, the next best thing is for everyone to frequently demand an account of their own deeds. If any error has been made, they should correct it; if something was done dutifully, they should persevere in it and improve further.

As a kind of <term>Symbolum</term> <note>A "symbol" or "token" used as a rule for living.</note> for this most healthy practice, he handed down a poem. The author is uncertain—for I do not find it recorded by many—but Plutarch seems to have been delighted by it. Indeed, nothing among the pagan philosophers seems more holy than this. The poem goes like this:
“Where did I overstep? What did I do? What duty did I fail to perform?” <note>Original Greek: Πῆι πρέβην, τί δ' ἔρεξα, τί μοι δέον οὐκ ἐτελέσθη; These are known as the Golden Verses of Pythagoras.</note> -> that is, <-
> Where was the slip? What have I done? Or what duty was omitted?

Now, every slip in human life consists of three things: either we act differently than we should (that is, more or less than is fitting), to which error the part "Where did I overstep?" responds; or we did what should have been omitted, to which "What did I do?" responds; or we omit what should have been done, which pertains to the final part, "What duty did I fail to perform?" 

A man who admonishes a sinning wife more gently than is sufficient, or rebukes her too harshly, will say to himself upon reflection, "Where did I overstep?" He who instructs his son in matters that are hardly honorable will say, "What did I do?" He who ignores a friend's sin when it would have been profitable to warn him will say, "What duty did I fail to perform?" Pythagoras used to advise young men to turn this verse over in their minds whenever they entered their homes. That thought made the youths careful, so that if they had done anything wrong or contracted any vice from the company of men, they might guard against it more diligently in the future. 

Whoever wrote that poem "On the Good Man"—which is found among the appendices of Virgil's works <note>Erasmus refers to a poem now attributed to Ausonius, but often included in the "Appendix Vergiliana" in the Renaissance.</note>—explained this sentiment more broadly and fully:
> Let not sweet sleep fall upon your eyes,
> Until you have reviewed all the acts of the long day.
> Where did I overstep? What was done in time, what was not?
> Why was honor lacking in that deed? Or what was the reason for it?

If those who were strangers to Christ taught these things, what ought Christians to do? Would that at least the priests and monks, when they enter their chambers after long and splendid banquets, would say this to themselves:
“Where did I overstep? What did I do? What duty did I fail to perform?”
By the immortal God, how many things would occur to us that are both shameful and to be repented!

-> Each rejoices in his own pursuit. <-

For one who says that different people are held by different interests, and that each person lives by his own gain, he brings forth this line from the same book: <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 6.</note>

# THE TENTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD THOUSAND

<note>original: "οὐ γὰρ Φαίηκεσσι μέλει βιὸς ἠδὲ φαρέτρη, / Ἀλλ’ ἱστοὶ καὶ ἐρετμὰ νεῶν, καὶ νῆες ἐῖσαι."</note>
“For the Phaeacians do not care for the bow or the quiver, 
But for the masts and the oars of ships, and the well-balanced vessels.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 6, lines 270–271. Erasmus translates this into Latin: *Nam Phæacibus haud cordi iacula, atq; pharetra...*</note>

This is related to the saying: *Craftsmen handle craftsmen's tools.* <note>Latin: *Tractant fabrilia fabri*.</note> Pindar also says in his tenth Pythian hymn: <term>τὴ γὰρ ἑτέροισιν ἑτέρων ἔρως ἔκνιξε φρένας</term> <note>original Greek: "Different people are pricked in their hearts by different loves."</note>, meaning that the love of different things strikes the minds of different men.

-> Lowering oneself to the level of others. <-
-> III <-

This is used when someone intentionally moderates their own powers to match the more modest abilities of others. For example, if a teacher delivers to his students not the full extent of what he is capable of teaching, but only as much as they are able to grasp. This fits a passage from the same book concerning Nausicaa <note>The daughter of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians.</note>, who so moderated the pace of her mules that her handmaidens and Ulysses could follow on foot:
<note>original: "ἡ δὲ μάλ’ ἡνιόχυεν ὅπως ἅμ’ ἑποίατο πεζοὶ, / Ἀμφίπολοί τ’ Ὀδυσύς τε, νόῳ δ’ ἐπέβαλλεν ἱμάσθλω."</note>
“She drove the reins so that the handmaids and Ulysses could follow on foot, 
And she applied the whip with judgment and care.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 6, lines 318–319.</note>
This matter shall be my concern.

-> The whip urges. <-
-> IIII <-

When we advise someone to leave the whole business to us while they remain free of worry—promising that the matter will be our concern—we may use this line from Book 7 of the *Odyssey*:
<note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ἴθι σιγῇ τοῖον, ἐγὼ δ’ ὁδὸν ἡγεμονεύσω."</note>
“Rather, proceed in silence; I myself shall be the leader of this way.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 7, line 30.</note>

-> A resolute mind. <-
-> V <-

Presence of mind is useful everywhere, because timidness seems to arise either from a guilty conscience or from a smallness of spirit. This sentiment is supported by a line from Homer in the same book:
<note>original: "θαρσαλέος γὰρ ἀνὴρ ἐν πᾶσιν ἀμείνων, / ἔργοισι τελέθει, εἰ καί ποθεν ἄλλοθεν ἔλθοι."</note>
“For a bold man is better in all deeds, 
Even if he should come as a stranger from far-off lands.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 7, lines 51–52.</note>

In this manner, Pallas <note>The goddess Athena.</note> encourages Ulysses not to tremble as he enters the house of Alcinous. This agrees with what is said elsewhere: *Fortune favors the brave.* Titus Livius writes in the eighth book of his *History of Rome*: “But the outcome taught that fortune favors the brave.”

-> The income of the wealthy. <-
-> VI <-

For the wealthy, whose various sources of income follow one after another, this passage from the same book regarding the orchards of Alcinous will be fitting:
<note>original: "οὐδὲ θέρους ἐπιλείπει, ἀλλὰ μάλ’ αἰεὶ, / ζεφυρίη πνείουσα, τὰ μὲν φύει, ἄλλα δὲ πέσσει, / ὄχνη ἐπ’ ὄχνῃ γηράσκει, μῆλον δ’ ἐπὶ μήλῳ, / Αὐτὰρ ἐπὶ σταφυλῇ σταφυλὴ, σῦκον δ’ ἐπὶ σύκῳ."</note>
“The harvest does not fail in summer, but always, 
The West Wind, blowing with a constant breath, 
Brings some fruit to life and ripens others; 
Pear grows old upon pear, and apple upon apple, 
Furthermore, grape upon grape, and fig upon fig.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 7, lines 117–121.</note>

-> Inevitable fate. <-
-> VII <-

What has been decreed for a man by the Fates, that shall come to pass. Toward this sentiment, Homer says in the same book:
<note>original: "ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα / Πείσεθ, ὅσσα οἱ αἶσα κατακλῶθές τε βαρεῖαι, / Γινομένῳ νήσαντο λίνῳ, ὅτε μιν τέκε μήτηρ."</note>
“And afterwards, he shall suffer 
All that Fate and the heavy Spinners spun into his thread 
At his birth, when his mother brought him forth.” <note>Homer, *Odyssey*, Book 7, lines 196–198.</note>

However, this passage about the Fates ought to be used only in a joking manner. For instance, if someone is sending their son far away for the sake of his studies and says he will not worry about what the boy does there, but will entrust it to God and to fortune.
