<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of the Third Thousand, Tenth Century, moving into Book 7 and 8 of Homer's Odyssey. It maintains the theme of extracting universal human wisdom and social conduct from the interactions between Ulysses and the Phaeacian court.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<meta>Catchword: Anti</meta>

-> Care for something else. <-

When you mean to say there is no reason for someone to doubt or be anxious—as if removing a <term>scruple</term> <note>A 'scruple' originally referred to a small, sharp stone in one's shoe that causes hesitation or unease; here it means a doubt.</note>—this phrase from the same book will be appropriate: 
“Alcinous, let something else be a care to your heart.” <note>original Greek: Ἀλκίνο’ ἄλλοτι τοι μελέτω φρεσίν; original Latin: *Alcinoe cures aliud*. From *Odyssey*, Book 7, line 307.</note> Similarly, Terence writes: “And yet I have already found it; care for something else.” <note>From Terence's play *Andria*.</note>

-> The stomach is a troublesome interrupter. <-

The "shameless stomach" is a persistent interrupter; it never allows anyone to forget its needs. This can be applied to the torment of poverty, which usually compels mortals both to do and to endure all things. Thus Ulysses says in the same book:
“For there is nothing more shameless than the hateful belly, 
Which commands a man to remember it by necessity, 
Even when he is deeply troubled and has sorrow in his heart.” <note>original Greek: οὐ γάρ τι στυγερῇ ἐπὶ γαστέρι κύντερον ἄλλο... From *Odyssey*, Book 7, lines 216–218. Erasmus provides a Latin verse translation: *Non est improbior res altera uentre molesto...*</note>

-> The suspicious common people. <-

The common people are suspicious and interpret most things in a bad light. Homer says in the same book:
“For we tribes of men on earth are prone to be ill-suspicious.” <note>original Greek: Δύσζηλοι γάρ τ’ εἰμὲν ἐπὶ χθονὶ φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων. From *Odyssey*, Book 7, line 307. Erasmus translates this into Latin as: *Quippe homines plerique sumus male suspiciosi*.</note>

-> No one should be forced for the sake of duty. <-

No guest should be detained against his inclination and will. No one should be forced to accept another’s kindness if he does not wish it. This phrase from the same book fits this sentiment:
“If you wish to stay, you may; but no one shall hold you against your will.” <note>original Greek: Εἴκ’ ἐθέλοιμι μένοις, ἀέκοντα δέ σ’ οὔτις ἐρύξει. From *Odyssey*, Book 7, line 315.</note>
This is spoken to Ulysses by Alcinous, the ruler of the Phaeacians.

-> Evil compensated by good. <-

Whenever nature bestows some exceptional gift, but then balances it with some defect; or when someone spoils their own kindness with some injury, this line from the eighth book of the *Odyssey*—said of the musician Demodocus—will fit:
“The Muse loved him above others, and gave him both good and evil: 
She deprived him of his eyes, but gave him the gift of sweet song.” <note>original Greek: Τὸν πέρι μοῦσ’ ἐφίλησε, δίδου δ’ ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε... From *Odyssey*, Book 8, lines 63–64. Erasmus provides a Latin verse: *Hunc alios ultra dilexit musa, deditque / Atque boni, atque mali quiddam...*</note>

-> In every kind of contest. <-

When we suggest that a conflict has taken place in every possible way—as if one were to say that a point was fiercely debated across every branch of learning—this line from the same book will be suitable:
“In boxing, in wrestling, in jumping, and in the footrace.” <note>original Greek: πύξ τε παλαιμοσύνῃ τε καὶ ἅλμασιν ἠδὲ πόδεσσιν. From *Odyssey*, Book 8, line 103. Latin: *Et pugnis, pedibusque & saltibus, atque palaestra*.</note>
Likewise, when someone shows they are not shrinking from any contest, but are ready for any trial of their wit, this passage from the same book is fitting:
“Come here then, let him try me, since you have provoked me so greatly, 
Whether in boxing or wrestling, or even the footrace; I refuse nothing.” <note>original Greek: Δεῦρ’ ἄγε πειρηθήτω... From *Odyssey*, Book 8, lines 204–206.</note>

-> He won by far. <-

For those who feel that someone excels so greatly that there is no risk of anyone snatching the prize from them, this line from the same book will serve:
“But you, take heart; for in this contest no 
Phaeacian shall either reach your mark or surpass you.” <note>original Greek: Σὺ δὲ θάρσει, τόν δε γ’ ἄεθλον... From *Odyssey*, Book 8, line 197.</note>

<header>THE THIRD THOUSAND, TENTH CENTURY</header>

<margin>XV</margin>
## Veneration is owed to the ancients.

One must not contend with the greatest and most invincible, nor with the ancients, who seem to be placed, as it were, beyond the reach of human chance. Instead, one should voluntarily yield to them. For example, if someone were to say he does not wish to struggle against Marcus Tullius Cicero regarding eloquence, yet does not refuse to compete with those of moderate skill, he will employ what is said in the same place by Ulysses:
“I will not strive with men of former times, nor yet with Hercules, nor with Eurytus of Oechalia.” <note>original Greek: ἀνδράσι δὲ προτέροισιν ἐριζέμεν οὐκ ἐθελήσω, οὐδ’ ἡρακλῆϊ ἔτ’ εὐρύτῳ οἰχαλιῆϊ. From Odyssey, Book 8, lines 223–224. Erasmus equates the "ancients" with masters like Cicero who are beyond criticism.</note> That is:
“I would hardly enter into contests with my elders, nor with the strength of Hercules, nor with Eurytus of Oechalia.”

<margin>XVI</margin>
## The shameful end of wicked deeds.

When a matter undertaken wrongly turns out badly, this line from the same book will be appropriate:
“Ill deeds do not prosper.” <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀρετᾷ κακὰ ἔργα. From Odyssey, Book 8, line 329. In the poem, this refers to the god Mars being caught in the act of adultery with Venus.</note> That is:
“Wicked acts do not succeed well.”
This was said regarding the discovery of Mars' adultery.

<margin>XVII</margin>
## A faithful friend.

A faithful friend is not to be ranked below a brother. Homer says in the same book:
“If there be some friend who knows what is pleasing, a good man, since he is in no way inferior to a brother.” <note>original Greek: ἥτις πού κ’ αὖ ἑταῖρος ἀνὴρ κεχαρισμένα εἰδὼς, ἐσθλὸς, ἐπεὶ οὐ μέν τι κασιγνήτοιο χερείων. From Odyssey, Book 8, lines 585–586.</note> That is:
“If perhaps there be a friend, both pleasing and good, for he is to be thought not inferior even to a brother.”

<margin>XVIII</margin>
## His own country is most pleasant to each.

To every person, his own fatherland is the most pleasant, whichever one fell to his lot. Homer in *Odyssey*, Book 9:
“As nothing is sweeter to any man than his own country and his parents.” <note>original Greek: ὡς οὐδὲν γλύκιον ἧς πατρίδος οὐδὲ τοκήων γίγνεται. From Odyssey, Book 9, lines 34–35.</note> That is:
“As nothing is more one's own, or sweeter to anyone, than fatherland and parents.”

<margin>XIX</margin>
## Flight is safer.

He who says it is safer to conquer lust by flight than by fighting against it will be able to apply what was said of Charybdis in *Odyssey*, Book 12:
“There is no defense; to flee from her is best.” <note>original Greek: οὐ δέ τις ἔστ’ ἀλκὴ, φυγέειν κάρτιστον ἀπ’ αὐτῆς. From Odyssey, Book 12, line 120. Erasmus interprets the physical monster Charybdis as a metaphor for overwhelming desire or lust.</note> That is:
“There is no remedy; it is best to flee far from her.”

<margin>XX</margin>
## Some things to be shared, others to be hidden.

One should not blurt out just anything to anyone at random, nor should every secret be brought forth even to close associates; rather, it is fitting to share some things with friends or wives, while keeping others concealed. To this sentiment fits that line from *Odyssey*, Book 11:
“One thing must be told, and another must be kept hidden.” <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲ φάσθαι, τὰ δὲ κ’ αὖ κεκρυμμένον εἶναι. From Odyssey, Book 11, line 443. This advice is given to Ulysses by the ghost of Agamemnon, who was murdered by his own wife.</note> That is:
“One thing is to be said; on the other hand, another is to be kept silent.”

<margin>XXI</margin>
## Nothing is more pestilential than a woman.

Nothing is more pestilential than a woman. Homer expresses this sentiment in the same book as follows:
“So there is nothing more dreadful and more dog-like than a woman.” <note>original Greek: ὡς οὐκ ἀινότερον καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο γυναικός. From Odyssey, Book 11, line 427. The term "dog-like" or "shameless" was a common Homeric epithet for someone acting without honor.</note> That is:
“To such an extent is there nothing more wicked or worse than a woman.”
Frequently among ancient poets, the female sex has a bad reputation. Indeed, even in modern times, they work strenuously so that the poets do not seem to have been entirely idle talkers. <note>Erasmus adds a cynical contemporary commentary here, suggesting that the "wickedness" of women in his own time confirms the ancient stereotypes.</note>

<margin>XXII</margin>
## Exhausted old age.

What was said in *Odyssey*, Book 11, regarding the dead, may be applied to a man who, because of great age, is already failing in strength, or to one who is terrified in spirit:
“For the flesh and bones no longer have strength.” <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἔτι σάρκας τε καὶ ὀστέα ἲνες ἔχουσιν. From Odyssey, Book 11, line 219. This describes the physical dissolution of shades in the Underworld.</note> That is:
“For now the flesh and bones no longer hold together by sinews.”

<margin>XXIII</margin>
## With difficulty, but it still happened.

For those who achieve what they desire, though only with great difficulty, that line from the same book will be appropriate:
“You might yet arrive, though having suffered many evils.” <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ μὰν γε καὶ ὣς κακάπερ πάσχοντες ἵκοισθε. From Odyssey, Book 11, line 111.</note> That is:
“You shall yet arrive, although having endured very many misfortunes.”
These words are spoken to Ulysses by Tiresias. <note>Tiresias was the blind prophet whom Ulysses consulted in the Underworld.</note>

<margin>XXIIII</margin>
## One should not compete with a friend in rivalry.

With a friend and one who has served you well, a contest should not be undertaken, lest friendship be obscured by rivalry, which is a companion of such contentions. Homer hints at this in—

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

In Book 8 of the Odyssey, when Ulysses declines to compete against Laodamas because he was his host, he says:
“Who would fight with one who loves him?” <note>original Greek: τίς ἂν φιλέοντι μάχοιτο; Odyssey 8.208.</note> That is:
“Who indeed would fight with a kind host?”
This will also find a place when we say that it is the duty of a guest to yield to those with whom he stays, even if he is capable of winning. For in that same passage, a sentiment of this kind is immediately subjoined:
“For that man is truly foolish and worthless who challenges his host to a contest during a competition.” <note>original Greek: Ἄφρων γὰρ κεῖνός γε καὶ οὐτιδανὸς πέλει ἀνήρ, ὅστις ξεινοδόκῳ ἔριδα προφέρηται ἀέθλῳ. Odyssey 8.209–210.</note> That is:
“For that man is senseless, and not worth a single penny,
Whoever calls out to the trial of a contest
The one whose hospitality he enjoys, and by whose roof he is helped.”

### Shifting the blame.

Against one who shifts the cause of his own misfortune elsewhere, as people commonly do, that saying from Book 11 of the Odyssey is aptly twisted; it was spoken by the shade of Elpenor, who had died while intoxicated at Circe's home:
“The evil fate of a god and measureless wine destroyed me.” <note>original Greek: Ἄσέ με δαίμονος αἶσα κακὴ καὶ ἀθέσφατος οἶνος. Odyssey 11.61. Elpenor was a companion of Ulysses who fell off a roof while drunk.</note> That is:
“The evil fates of the gods harmed me, and the power of Bacchus.” <note>Erasmus uses "Lyaeus," a poetic name for the god of wine.</note>
So in another place, Agamemnon retorts that the cause of his discord was *Ate*. <note>Ate is the Greek personification of delusion or folly. Agamemnon blamed her for his argument with Achilles in the Iliad.</note>

### Shameful pleasure.

Against dishonest pleasure, or a prostitute equipped with every art for the ruin of young men, that line from Book 10 of the Odyssey spoken about Circe will fit:
“She sent them all, 
and made them either swine or wolves or lions.” <note>original Greek: Ἥκεν ἅπαντας ἢ σῦς ἠὲ λύκους ποίησεν ἠὲ λέοντας. Odyssey 10.212–213.</note> That is:
“Indeed, she made
All of them either swine, or wolves, or fierce lions.”

### A harsh life, but a healthy one.

Regarding a way of life that is indeed somewhat hard, but nevertheless suitable for the proper instruction of character, that line from Book 9 of the Odyssey spoken about Ithaca will be appropriate:
“Rugged, but a good nurse of youth.” <note>original Greek: Τρηχεῖ’ ἀλλ’ ἀγαθὴ κουροτρόφος. Odyssey 9.27. Ulysses is describing his rocky island home.</note> That is:
“A rough land, but a good nourisher of young men.”

### Strong in counsel as well as deed.

For a man excelling equally in wisdom and in strength, that line from Odyssey Book 11 will be fitting:
“Such a man he was, whether in counsel or in battle.” <note>original Greek: οἷος ἐκεῖνος ἔην βουλήμεν ἠδὲ μάχεσθαι. Odyssey 11.512. Spoken regarding Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles.</note> That is:
“He was such a man, whether in the fight or in deliberation.”

### I cannot help but speak.

When someone denies that they can keep silent about what is on their mind, this will be wittily applied from the same book:
“I will speak a word of boasting, for mad wine urges me.” <note>original Greek: εὐξάμενος τι ἔπος ἐρέω, οἶνος γὰρ ἀνώγει ἠλίος. Odyssey 14.463–464. Though Erasmus says "the same book" (referring to 11), this quote is actually from Book 14.</note> That is:
“I shall indeed say something rather boastful, for mad wine drives me.”
In the same place, Ulysses elegantly shows how much power wine has. For he follows with:
“Which sets even the wise man to singing, 
and to laughing gently, and rouses him to dance, 
and lets slip a word which were better left unsaid.” <note>original Greek: ὅς τ’ ἐφέηκε πολύφρονάπερ μάλ’ ἀεῖσαι, Καί θ’ ἁπαλὸν γελάσαι, καί τ’ ορχήσασθαι ἀνῆκεν, Καί τι ἔπος προέηκεν ὅπερ τ’ ἄῤῥητον ἄμεινον. Odyssey 14.464–466.</note> That is:
“Wine incites even the serious and modest man
To song, and to soft laughter, and compels him 
To lead the dances; sometimes it blurts out from 
The unlocked breast a word that were better kept silent.”

### At a loss.

One who says he is involved in the greatest dangers, and that no help shines forth, will use that line from the same book:
“Nor did any other 
land appear, but only sky and sea.” <note>original Greek: οὐ δέ τις ἄλλη φαίνετο γαιάων, ἀλλ’ οὐρανὸς ἠδὲ θάλασσα. Odyssey 12.403–404.</note> That is:
“No land appeared further, 
but to us there was sky everywhere and sea everywhere.” **The same is found in Book 12.**

### One who shrinks back and loathes.

When we say that we vehemently shrink back from some vice, it will be permitted to use that from the same book:

# THIRD THOUSAND, TENTH CENTURY
<sig>Aaa 4</sig>

“For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of Hades.” <note>original Greek: Ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς ἀΐδαο πύλησι; Odyssey 14.156.</note> That is:
“He is as much an object of loathing to me as the thresholds of dark Dis.” <note>Erasmus uses "Dis," the Roman name for the god of the underworld.</note>
The same verse appears in Book 9 <note>The OCR says "I," but the famous line is Iliad 9.312.</note> of the *Iliad* spoken by Achilles. Here, it is spoken by Ulysses.

### XXXII. Unlike oneself.
This will apply to someone who is inconsistent, taken from Book 13 <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter "N" for 13.</note> of the *Odyssey*, where Ulysses says of the goddess Pallas Athena:
“For you make yourself like everything.” <note>original Greek: Σὲ γὰρ αὐτῷ πάντα ἐΐσκεις; Odyssey 13.312.</note> That is:
“Now with one face, now again with another, you meet me.”
The same idea applies wonderfully to wisdom, which among the ancients is covered in various "wrappings" and presented in one form or another—especially in the Holy Scriptures, which consist almost entirely of allegories. <note>Erasmus refers to "involucris," literally "wrappers," a common Renaissance term for the layers of meaning in a text.</note>

### XXXIII. Nothing to the point.
For someone who says something absurd or irrelevant to the matter at hand, this line from the same book will be fitting (though it is repeated in several other places):
“You are a fool, stranger, or you have come from afar.” <note>original Greek: Νήπιός εις ὦ ξεῖν᾽, ἢ τηλόθεν εἰλήλουθας; Odyssey 13.237.</note> That is:
“Guest, you are a fool, or a traveler from distant shores.”

### XXXIIII. Attend to the present. / Be content with what is at hand.
When one advises that it is necessary to be content with whatever fortune grants, they may use this passage from Book 14 <note>Erasmus uses "Ξ" for 14.</note> of the *Odyssey*:
“Eat, noble guest, and enjoy these things, such as they are. For God will give one thing and withhold another, whatever he wishes in his heart; for he can do all things.” <note>original Greek: Ἔσθιε δαιμόνιε ξείνων καὶ τέρπεο τοῖσδε...; Odyssey 14.443–445.</note> That is:
“Guest, take your food, and nourish your happy spirit with what is provided here; for chance will give some things and deny others, just as the heart desires, for indeed he has power over all.”
With these words, Eumaeus the swineherd <term>subulcus: a swineherd</term> invites Ulysses to be content with whatever cheap and rustic food was available. It is applied to the whole of human life whenever we advise that in whatever state fortune has placed us, we should live in it happily and calmly. In the tenth book of Athenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Greek author known for his "Deipnosophistae" or "Banquet of the Learned."</note>, this six-foot verse is recorded:
“Weave your life according to what is at hand.” <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τοῖς παροῦσι τὸν βίον διάπλεκε.</note> That is:
“In those things which are ready, weave your life.”
Isocrates, in his speech *On the Peace*, says that "to be content with one's present lot" <note>original Greek: στέργειν τοῖς παροῦσι.</note> is very difficult for most men, and this is why they prefer war to peace.

### XXXV. Do not force a favor upon the unwilling.
It is an injury if someone forces a service upon a person who does not want it. On this sentiment, Homer says in Book 15 <note>Erasmus uses "ο" for 15.</note> of the *Odyssey*:
“It is an equal evil to urge a guest to leave when he does not wish to go, and to hold back one who is eager to depart. One should treat a guest kindly while he is present, and send him away when he wishes to leave.” <note>original Greek: Ἴσον τοι κακόν ἐσθ᾽...; Odyssey 15.72–74.</note> That is:
“Each man errs equally: the one who pushes out an unwilling guest, and the one who delays one who wants to go. It is fitting to treat a guest kindly as long as he wishes to be present, but he should be sent on his way when he seeks to depart.”

### XXXVI. A good hope shown.
When some good hope shines out from somewhere that we might finish what we proposed, this line from the same book is fitting:
“Even as he spoke, a lucky bird flew by on the right.” <note>original Greek: Ὡς ἄρα οἱ εἰπόντι ἐπέπτατο δεξιὸς ὄρνις; Odyssey 15.160.</note> That is:
“Thus, by a happy fate, a bird flies by from the right.” <note>In the ancient world, birds flying from the right were considered omens of divine favor.</note>

### XXXVII. Unbearable arrogance.
Against those whose arrogance is intolerable, this line from the same book, spoken by Eumaeus regarding the suitors, will be skillfully twisted:
“Their violence and force reach the iron sky.” <note>original Greek: Τῶν ὕβρις τε βίη τε σιδήρεον οὐρανὸν ἵκει; Odyssey 15.329.</note> That is:
“The violence and fierce spirit of these men touches Olympus.”
The same is said in Book 17 <note>Erasmus uses "ρ" for 17.</note> by Ulysses to Eumaeus.

### XXXVIII. The best home.
It is most unhappy to wander with uncertain dwellings, as those who are "hearthless" <note>original Greek: ἀνέστιοι.</note> and living abroad always do. This is supported in the same book:

The previous page discussed the dangers of wandering and the importance of discretion; this page transitions into the divine nature of authority, the avoidance of temptation, and the social realities of poverty.</meta>

<page-num>836</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

“For there is no evil greater than wandering for mortals.” <note>original Greek: πλαγκτοσύνης δ' οὐκ ἔστι κακώτερον ἄλλο βροτοῖσιν; Odyssey 15.343.</note> That is:
“Nothing is more miserable than to wander without a fixed home.”
This can be applied to those who are tossed about by any opinion that comes along, or those who frequently change friends or their way of life.

<margin>XXXIX</margin>
### It does not happen for everyone.

It is not within every man's power to speak with kings, nor does it happen for everyone to penetrate the mysteries of divine scripture. This sentiment is quite elegantly turned from a line in Book 17 <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter "ρ" for 17.</note> of the *Odyssey*:
“For the gods do not appear visibly to all.” <note>original Greek: οὐ γάρ πω πάντεσσι θεοὶ φαίνοντ' ἐναργεῖς; Odyssey 16.161.</note> That is:
“The divine powers do not appear manifest to just anyone.”

### Divine Authority.

It happens by divine will that the same man is sometimes highly esteemed and at other times despised. To this point, a line from the same book applies:
“It is easy for the gods who hold the wide heaven
either to glorify a mortal man or to bring him low.” <note>original Greek: ῥηΐδιον δὲ θεοῖσι καὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι, / ἠ μὲν κυδῆναι θνητὸν βροτὸν, ἠ δὲ κακῶσαι; Odyssey 16.211–212.</note> That is:
“It is effortless for the gods, whom broad Olympus encloses,
either to make a man despised or to add honor to him.”

<margin>XL</margin>
### The opportunity for evil must be removed.

Whoever argues that the opportunity for evil should be taken away will not absurdly cite this line from the same book:
“Iron itself draws a man on.” <note>original Greek: Αὐτὸς ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος; Odyssey 16.294.</note> That is:
“Indeed, the iron itself entices men.”
In the same way, riches entice one toward luxury, and the company of young women leads toward love. <note>Erasmus is suggesting that the mere presence of a "tool" (like a sword or wealth) creates the temptation to use it wrongly.</note>

<margin>XLI</margin>
### When that which was hidden is known.

When a matter that is being discussed with great interest has been discovered in some way, this line from the same book will fit:
“Either one of the gods told them this, or she herself was the singer.” <note>original Greek: ἡ δέ σφιν τόδ' ἔειπε θεῶν, ἢ ἀοιδὸς αὐτή; Odyssey 16.356.</note> That is:
“Either some god revealed this as an informer to them, or they saw it themselves.”

<margin>XLII</margin>
### Violence against kings must be avoided.

Whoever says that one should not rashly lay a hand upon kings, powerful men, or men who fear the gods, will bring up this line from the same book:
“It is a terrible thing to kill the race of kings.” <note>original Greek: δεινὸν δὲ γένος βασιλήϊόν ἐστι κτανέειν; Odyssey 16.401.</note> That is:
“It is a dire thing and full of danger to have killed the royal race.”

<margin>XLIII</margin>
### Domestic discord.

To express detestation for domestic sedition and mutual discord or plots among housemates, this line from the same book will be suitable:
“It is not right to weave evils for one another.” <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι κακὰ ῥάπτειν ἀλλήλοισιν; Odyssey 16.423.</note> That is:
“It is an impious thing to plot evils among one another.”

<margin>XLIV</margin>
### He who is in need should stay in the crowd.

Even in our own times, a story is commonly told about a blind beggar who ordered his attendant to lead him to where the "storm of men" was greatest, adding a saying famous as a popular joke: that the profit is found where the crowd of people is. Homer says the same in Book 17 <note>Greek "ρ".</note> of the *Odyssey*:
“It is better for a beggar to beg for his dinner
through the city than in the fields.” <note>original Greek: πτωχῷ βέλτιόν ἐστι κατὰ πτόλιν, ἠὲ κατ' ἀγροὺς, / δαῖτα πτωχεύειν; Odyssey 17.18–19.</note> That is:
“It is better for a beggar to beg for his meal
through populous towns than in the countryside.”

<margin>XLV</margin>
### A humbler duty.

When someone refuses a task as being too humble or not worthy of them, they will apply this from the same Book 17 of the *Odyssey*:
“For I am no longer of an age to remain at the farmsteads.” <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ σταθμοῖσι μένειν ἔτι τηλίκος εἰμί; Odyssey 17.20.</note> That is:
“For as for me staying in the stables, my age no longer demands it.”
These are the words of Ulysses to the swineherd. <note>Ulysses is explaining that he is too old to be a mere farmhand and would do better as a beggar in the city.</note>

<margin>XLVI</margin>
### Offenses against the powerful should be avoided.

Whoever says that the offenses of the wealthy and princes are to be feared—because no matter how slightly they are offended, they become heavily indignant and, as Plautus says, they "carry leaden angers"—will apply this line from the same book,

<meta>catchword: Grafted</meta>

“Harsh are the rebukes of kings.” <note>original Greek: Χαλεπαὶ δὲ τ’ ἀνάκτων εἰσὶν ὁμοκλαί; Odyssey 17.189.</note> That is:
“The offenses and threats of kings are to be dreaded.”

### An unworthy leader. XLVIII

A negligent tutor ruins a boy, a bad teacher spoils a student, and in the same way, a wicked king corrupts his people. Toward this sentiment, a line from the same book is relevant:
“But bad shepherds destroy the sheep.” <note>original Greek: Αὐτὰρ μῆλα κακοὶ φθείρουσι νομῆες; Odyssey 17.246.</note> That is:
“A bad shepherd ruins the ewes.” These words are spoken by Eumaeus the swineherd to a goatherd.

### Accustomed to hardships. XLIX

Concerning one who has become used to enduring insults, this line from the same book is fitting:
“For he is not at all ignorant of blows or hits.” <note>original Greek: οὐ γάρ τι πληγέων ἀδαήμων οὐδὲ βολάων; Odyssey 17.283.</note> That is:
“By now, he is not at all unrefined in enduring lashes or being struck.”

### Generous with another’s property. L

We grant things easily when they belong to another, but not so with our own. Antinous expressed this sentiment in the same book:
“Since there is no restraint, nor any pity,
in being generous with things belonging to others.” <note>original Greek: ἐπεὶ οὔτις ἐπίσχεσις, οὐδ’ ἐλεητὺς, Ἀλλοτρίων χαρίσασθαι; Odyssey 17.451-452.</note> That is:
“For nothing forbids, nor does it cause regret,
to give away the property of others.”
Seneca writes in his *Epistles*, Book 2, Letter 16: “There is no reason for you to wonder at my spirit; so far, I am being generous with someone else’s property.” Similarly, Micio says in Terence’s *The Brothers*, when Aeschinus says, “Suppose I promised them,” Micio replies: “You promised? Be a big spender with your own money, boy!” <note>Erasmus is contrasting true generosity with the ease of giving away what does not belong to you.</note>

### Poor, but talented. LI

For a man in humble dress but who possesses an excellent physique, this line from Book 18 <note>Erasmus uses the Greek letter “σ” for 18.</note> of the *Odyssey* will fit:
“What a thigh the old man shows from his rags.” <note>original Greek: οἴην ἐκ ῥακέων ὁ γέρων ἐπιγουνίδα φαίνει; Odyssey 18.74.</note> That is:
“What shoulders the elder displays from his cheap rags.”
This was said of Odysseus when he was about to wrestle with Irus <note>Irus was a beggar in Ithaca who challenged the disguised Odysseus.</note>. Lucian, in his *Hercules of Gaul*, twists this to refer to an old man who excels in talent and eloquence.

### Envy follows boasting. LII

To warn someone not to boast too insolently of the gifts of fortune or the endowments of nature—lest Nemesis <note>The goddess of divine retribution against pride.</note> should hear and take them away—one might appropriately use this line from the same book:
“But let him hold in silence whatever gifts the gods might give.” <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ὅγε σιγῇ δῶρα θεῶν ἔχοι ὅττι διδόιεν; Odyssey 18.142.</note> That is:
“Let him possess in silence whatever gifts of the divine are present.”

### A friend in words only. LIII

Regarding someone who fakes goodwill in speech while preparing something far different in his heart, this line from the same book is fitting:
“He soothed his spirit
with gentle words, but his mind intended other things.” <note>original Greek: θέλγε δὲ θυμὸν μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι, νόον δ’ οἱ ἄλλα μενοίνα; Odyssey 18.282-283.</note> That is:
“He softened that soul with very smooth words, but his mind was preparing something different.”

### Nothing given should be refused. LIIII

If you ever wish to say that no gift offered should be rejected, or that an opportunity for some advantage should be seized whenever it arises, this line from the same book is suitable:
“For it is not good to refuse a gift.” <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ καλὸν ἀνήνασθαι δόσιν ἐστίν; Odyssey 18.287.</note> That is:
“It is by no means fitting to reject a gift.”

### The supports of life. LV

All things that pertain to the convenience of life can be elegantly indicated by this verse from Book 19 <note>Erasmus uses “τ” for 19.</note> of the *Odyssey*:
“By which men live well and are called wealthy.” <note>original Greek: οἷσίν τ’ εὖ ζώουσι καὶ ἀφνειοὶ καλέονται; Odyssey 19.114.</note> That is:
“From which things they live rightly and are called rich.”

### One who is self-sufficient. LVI

For one who denies needing the help of others, claiming to be capable enough to finish a task, this line from Book 20 <note>Erasmus uses “υ” for 20.</note> of the *Odyssey* is appropriate:
“I have eyes and ears and both my feet,
and a mind within my breast that is fashioned not unsuitably.” <note>original Greek: Εἰσί μοι ὀφθαλμοί τε καὶ οὔατα καὶ πόδες ἄμφω, Καὶ νόος ἐν στήθεσσι τετυγμένος οὐδὲν ἀεικής; Odyssey 20.365-366.</note> That is:
“I have eyes, I have ears, and my feet are a pair...”

<page-num>838</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

“A mind is implanted in the breast, neither foolish nor heartless.
It knows both bad and good.” <note>These lines serve as an introductory sentiment for the following adages regarding human understanding and moral choice.</note>

<margin>LVI</margin>
Concerning one who, through age and the experience of affairs, is now able to make a choice between what should be avoided and what should be sought, that line from the same book <note>Homer, *Odyssey* 18.228-229.</note> will be fitting:
“For now I perceive and know each thing, 
both the good and the worse.” <note>original Greek: Δὴ γὰρ νοέω καὶ οἶδα ἕκαστα, Εσθλά τε καὶ τὰ χέρεια.</note> That is:
“For a long while now, I have both known and felt all things
that are good, and that are bad.”
Even today, nothing is more common than this figure of speech.

-> For we are not ignorant. <-
<margin>LVII</margin>
Whenever someone encourages themselves to endure present inconveniences by remembering past evils, they may quite appropriately use this line from the same book:
“Endure now, my heart; you once endured something even more dog-like.” <note>original Greek: Τέτλαθι δὴ κραδίη καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο πότ’ ἔτλης; *Odyssey* 20.18. The word "dog-like" in Greek implies something shameful, fierce, or miserable.</note> That is:
“Harden, O soul; you have borne even heavier things before.” <margin>Virgil, emulating this,</margin>
“O you who have suffered heavier things, God will also give an end to these.
Endure, and preserve yourselves for favorable things.” <note>original Latin: O paſſi grauiora, dabit deus his quoque finem. Durate, & uoſmet rebus ſeruate ſecundis; Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.199-207.</note>
Similarly, Horace in his *Odes*:
“O brave men, who have often suffered worse things with me.” <note>original Latin: O fortes, peioraq; paſſi Mecum ſæpe uiri; Horace, *Odes* 1.7.30.</note>

-> Pardon should be given to one who has slipped. <-
<margin>LIX</margin>
One who says that pardon should sometimes be granted if an error is made through neglect—since it is not in a human's nature to always maintain exact diligence—will use this line from the *Odyssey*, book 20:
“But it is not possible for humans to be always sleepless.” <note>original Greek: Αλλ’ οὐ γὰρ πῶς ἔστιν ἄϋπνος ἔμμεναι αἰεὶ Ανθρώπους; *Odyssey* 20.52-53.</note> That is:
“By no means is it possible for a mortal to remain ever-watchful.”

-> Not everything you wish for will happen. <-
<margin>LX</margin>
One who denies that all things a person has hoped for or conceived in their mind will come to pass, will adapt this from the same book:
“Indeed, dreams are baffling and of confused speech; 
they do not all come true for men.” <note>original Greek: Η τοι μὲν ὄνειροι ἀμήχανοι, ἀκριτόμυθοι, Γίγνοντ’ οὐδέ τε πάντα τελείετ’ ἀνθρώποισι; *Odyssey* 19.560-561.</note> That is:
“To be sure, there exist frivolous and empty
dreams, nor does everything you see turn out just so.”
And in this place, he adds that most beautiful fable of the two gates of dreams, which Virgil recounted in his sixth book. <note>The gates of horn (true dreams) and ivory (false dreams).</note>

-> Joy joined to grief. <-
<margin>LX</margin>
When it happens that we simultaneously rejoice and grieve—the sort of thing that occurs if wealthy parents pass away, where one is partly tormented by the death of kin and partly rejoices at the arrival of an inheritance and the increase of freedom—this line from the same book will be suitable:
“At once joy and pain seized the mind.” <note>original Greek: Τῶ δ’ ἅμα χάρμα καὶ ἄλγος ἕλε φρένα; *Odyssey* 19.471.</note> That is:
“Gladness and sorrow together seized his heart.”

-> Evils accelerate old age. <-
<margin>LXI</margin>
One who says that old age should not be measured in years—because those who rack themselves with many labors and cares grow old before their time—will use this from the same book:
“For quickly in misfortune mortals grow old.” <note>original Greek: Αἶψα γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσι; *Odyssey* 19.360.</note> That is:
“Indeed, men grow old suddenly through cares and evils.”

-> The life of mortals is short. <-
<margin>LXII</margin>
One who advises that we should strive to leave behind a memory of an honorable life for posterity, which may live forever—since this life is circumscribed by narrow limits—will adapt this from the same book:
“For humans are short-lived.” <note>original Greek: Ανθρωποι δὲ μινυνθάδιοι τελέθουσι; *Odyssey* 19.328.</note> That is:
“But the age of man is constrained within short spans.”

-> Lying with the appearance of truth. <-
<margin>LXIII</margin>
Against one who tells a falsehood as if it were the truth, this line from the same book will fit:
“He spoke many falsehoods, making them like truths.” <note>original Greek: Ισκε ψεύδεα πολλὰ λέγων ἐτύμοισιν ὁμοῖα; *Odyssey* 19.203.</note> That is:
“He told many fictions very similar to truths.”
This was said of Ulysses. It is also noted in Plato that Homer introduced Ulysses as a liar, but Achilles, by contrast, as truthful. <note>Erasmus refers here to the *Greater Hippias*, where the characters of Odysseus and Achilles are contrasted regarding honesty.</note>

<summary>Erasmus presents a series of adages from Homer's Odyssey concerning human nature, including the necessity of resilience, the inevitability of unfulfilled dreams, and the tendency of suffering to hasten aging. He also touches on the morality of speech, contrasting the deceptive eloquence of Odysseus with the honesty of Achilles.</summary>

<header>THE THIRD CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>

<margin>LXV</margin>
### He found evil for himself.

This will apply to one who is harmed by his own invention; it is adapted from the *Odyssey*, book 21:
"Who first found destruction for himself, being weighed down by wine." <note>original Greek: οἵτ’ αὐτῷ πρώτῳ κακὸν εὗρε οἰνοβαρείῳ.</note> That is,
> Who, conquered by wine, first discovered his own ruin.
This was said of Eurition, who is said to have first discovered the use of wine and was subsequently killed by the Lapiths. <note>Eurition was a Centaur whose drunken behavior at a wedding sparked a legendary battle with the Lapiths, a mythical Greek people.</note>

---

<margin>LXVI</margin>
### He who keeps a secret.

This applies to one who hides a secret entrusted to him and does not blab it to anyone. It is adapted from the *Odyssey*, book 21:
"The word was wingless to him." <note>original Greek: τὸ δ’ ἄπτηρ ἔπλετο μῦθος.</note> That is,
The words lacked wings for this man. This means they did not fly away any further. <note>In Homeric Greek, "winged words" are those spoken aloud that travel to the listener; "wingless" implies the speech was kept internal or the listener remained silent.</note>

---

<margin>LXVII</margin>
### I attempt a new thing.

Whenever you mean to signify that you are undertaking a difficult and new task, as yet unattempted by others, you may adapt this from the *Odyssey*, book 22:
"Now again I will try another mark which no man has yet hit,
if I might happen to reach it." <note>original Greek: νῦν αὖτε σκοπὸν ἄλλον ὃν οὔπως βάλεν ἀνήρ, εἴσομαι αἴκε τύχοιμι.</note> That is,
> Now I will attempt another goal, to see if I can reach it,
> Which no one has yet touched.
These are the words of Ulysses, as he prepares to kill the suitors.

---

<margin>LXVIII</margin>
### Memory of good deeds.

When something good happens to someone because of the memory of past good deeds, this line from the same book will fit:
"How much better is a good deed than a wicked one." <note>original Greek: ὡς κακοεργίης εὐεργεσίη μέγ’ ἀμείνων.</note> That is,
It is much better to perform one's duty than to do wrong.

---

<margin>LXIX</margin>
### The dead must not be reviled.

One should not insult the conquered, nor should reproaches be heaped upon the dead, even if they were justly killed. Homer supports this in the same book:
"It is not a holy thing to boast over slain men." <note>original Greek: οὐκ ὁσίη κtaμένοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν εὐχετάασθαι.</note> That is,
It is hardly right to boast of yourself over the fallen. Ulysses spoke thus regarding the dead suitors.

---

<margin>LXX</margin>
### A bright hearth in the house.

The primary ornament of a house is that the hearth should shine; therefore, those who move into a new home or enter an inn command a fire to be lit before all else. This seems to be taken from Homer’s 22nd book, where Ulysses says:
"Now first of all let a fire be made for me in the halls." <note>original Greek: πῦρ νῦν μοι πρώτιστον ἐνὶ μεγάроισι γενέσθω.</note> That is,
Now before all things let a fire shine in my house. **Also, this celebrated line:**
"A house is more venerable to behold when the fire is burning." <note>original Greek: αἰθομένω δὲ πυρὸς γεραρώτερος οἶκος ἰδέσθαι.</note> That is,
Certainly, a house is more adorned by an ignited fire.
Plutarch seems to have been exceedingly delighted by this little verse, as he uses it frequently and twists it to various purposes. In his commentary *On Virtue and Vice*, he refers it to wealth, power, and glory, which become more pleasant if the mind is free from distress. Again, in the booklet he titled the *Amatorius* (The Dialogue on Love), he turns it toward the mind of a lover, which becomes far more splendid if the heat of love inflames it.

---

<margin>LXXI</margin>
### Those who perished justly.

For those who perish by their own merit, this line from the same book will be appropriate:
"The fate of the gods and their own cruel deeds overcame these men." <note>original Greek: τούσδε δὲ μοῖр’ ἐδάμασσε θεῶν, καὶ σχέτλια ἔργα.</note> That is,
Fate and their misdeeds gave these men over to death and destruction. **Said of the suitors.**

---

<margin>LXXII</margin>
### Inexorable.

For someone harsh and unyielding, this from the *Odyssey*, book 23, will be suitable:
"But your heart is always harder than stone." <note>original Greek: σοὶ δ’ αἰεὶ κραδίη στερεωτέρη ἐστὶ λίθοιο.</note> That is,
But your heart is perpetually harder than any rock.
Thus Telemachus spoke to his mother <note>Telemachus is addressing Penelope, who is slow to recognize the returned Ulysses.</note>.

---

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
### To recover one's spirit.

When someone is stunned by a sudden event and later recovers themselves, this from the *Odyssey*, book 24, will be fitting:
"But when he breathed again and his spirit was gathered into his mind." <note>original Greek: αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ ρ’ ἄμπνυτο καὶ ἐς φρένα θυμὸς ἀγέρθη.</note> That is,
When he breathed again, and his senses returned to his breast.

<keywords>Odyssey, Eurition, Lapiths, Ulysses, silence, hearth, Plutarch, Telemachus, justice, mercy, proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages. While the previous section (page 839) dealt with personal responsibility and the "wingless" nature of secrets, this page moves into proverbs regarding the qualities of leadership, the certainty of experience over prophecy, and cultural stereotypes of the ancient world.</meta>

<page-num>849</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

### The wisdom of the elderly.

Regarding the elderly—specifically those who, despite their experience, are no longer fit for the physical labor of business—one might aptly quote a line from the same book:
**Even though they are gray, they are necessary warriors.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ πολιοί περ ἐόντες ἀναγκαῖοι πολεμισταί.</note> That is to say:
> A white-haired age indeed, but not unfit for war.

### A good commander, and likewise a sturdy soldier.

Plutarch records in his commentary on the *Fortune of Alexander*—if indeed that is the correct book—that when a question was posed at a banquet as to which of Homer’s verses seemed most excellent, and while others preferred various lines, Alexander gave the prize to this verse from the third book of the *Iliad*:
**Both a good king and a mighty spearman.** <note>original Greek: Ἀμφότερον, βασιλεύς τ’ ἀγαθὸς, κρατερός τ’ αἰχμητής.</note> That is:
> A good leader, and a soldier surpassing in strength as well.
For this line expressed the praise of Agamemnon and prophesied the virtue of Alexander. However, in my own opinion, great physical strength does not carry as much weight in a prince as does counsel and prudence. Accordingly, Timotheus spoke gravely when certain rhetoricians were praising a young man of remarkable physical strength, suggesting he was the sort of leader the Athenians should seek for war. "Not at all," he said, "for I might wish for such a man if I were looking for someone to carry the mattresses and bedding for the army. But I would want a leader who is eyed both in front and in back <note>meaning: circumspect and watchful in all directions</note>, and whom no emotional turmoil prevents from weighing what is useful to do."

### They have seen the heavenly goat rising.

**They beheld the heavenly goat rising.** <note>original Greek: Αἶγα τὴν οὐρανίαν ἀνατέλλουσαν ἐθεάσαντο.</note> This was commonly said of those for whom everything succeeded happily and according to their heart's desire. This is because of a common ancient belief that the goat who nursed Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> was placed among the stars for that reason; therefore, whatever people wished for, they would be able to attain. This is discussed more extensively under the adage "The Horn of Amaltheia." <note>Amaltheia was the foster-mother of Zeus, often depicted as a goat whose horn provided a never-ending supply of food.</note> This is also found in Plutarch’s *Collectanea*. He also mentions in the book *On Listening to the Poets*: "A happy owner of many fields, nursing the heavenly goat that brings wealth." <note>original Greek: οὐδαίμων πολὺαγρος ἐν γα πλουφόρῳ τρέφων.</note> However, in the ninth book of Athenaeus, Antiphanes, I believe, cites the "heavenly goat" among the creatures suitable for the table:
**A mountain-roaming buck, a heavenly goat, a ram.** <note>original Greek: τράγος ὑλιβάτας, αἲξ οὐρανία, κριὸς.</note> That is: A wild goat, a heavenly goat, and a castrated ram.

### A goat to the festival.

**A goat to the feast.** <note>original Greek: Αἲξ εἰς τὴν ἑορτήν.</note> This was a common saying when someone arrived just in time for something. Or, it is used when someone conveniently offers themselves up for their own destruction. For during festivals, especially those of Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note>, they used to sacrifice a goat. This is recorded in the same commentaries.

### Soon we shall know better than the seer.

**Soon we shall be superior to the prophets.** <note>original Greek: Τάχ’ ἐσόμεθα μάντεων ὑπέρτεροι.</note> That is:
> Soon we shall know the matter better than the prophet himself.
This was said by those who did not try to guess a matter through conjectures but sought to understand it through experience. For nothing is more certain than experience. This appears in the same *Collectanea* of Plutarch. It is taken from Sophocles’ *Antigone*. Similarly, Titus Livy, in the second book of the Second Punic War, calls the outcome "the teacher of fools." <note>original Latin: euentum... stultorum magistrum.</note>

### Cyzicene Dye.

**A Cyzicene dye.** <note>original Greek: Βάμμα κυζικηνόν.</note> Among the inhabitants of Attica, this was a name for a disgrace that could not be washed away. It was said of those who, out of fear, did something unseemly. For the people of Cyzicus <note>an ancient Greek city in modern-day Turkey</note> were notoriously marked by names for cowardice and softness. It is reviewed in the same *Collectanea*. Hesychius also mentions it, adding that the Cyzicenes were noted for softness because they were Ionians. The commentator on Aristophanes says much the same. Stephanus adds that they were heavy-handed toward the Tyrrhenian pirates. It appears in Aristophanes’ *Peace*; indeed, these are his words:
> If ever he must fight and wear the scarlet cloak,
> He himself is soon dyed there with a Cyzicene dye.
Famous dyes usually take their name from places. Nor does everyone, everywhere...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on metaphors involving "dyeing" or "tincture" as a representation of a person's character or reputation. The text transitions from the physical process of dyeing to the moral "staining" of a person's life.</meta>

<page-num>841</page-num>
<header>THIRD CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Bbb</sig>

is dyed successfully. In a similar way, people speak of "Syracusean sauce" <note>original Greek: ἔμβαμμα συρακόσιον</note> and "Sardanian dye" <note>original Greek: βάμμα σαρδανινόν</note>. Proverbial wisdom has twisted this to refer to the character of men. For the reputation and rumors that follow a person's life are like a kind of dye. This is why those who are condemned are said to be "marked with charcoal." There is also that well-known line of Ennius found in Aulus Gellius: "Those things which are stained with evils, or what things are called good." <note>original Latin: Quæ tincta malis, aut quæ bona dicto.</note> A commentator on Aristophanes indicates that the Spartans used to wear crimson tunics so that they would not be perceived as wounded by the enemy, due to the similarity of the color to blood. In contrast, the cowardly and weak will turn pale. I will add what is found in the fourth book of Herodotus: when the King of the Ethiopians saw a purple garment sent by the King of the Persians, he asked about the method of dyeing it. When he learned the process from the Fish-eaters, he said, "The man is deceitful, and his clothes are deceitful as well." <note>original Greek: δολερὸς μὲν ἄνθρωπος ἔφη εἶν, δολερὰ δὲ αὐτοῦ τὰ ἵματια</note> That is to say, he meant not only that the men were cunning, but that their very clothes were fraudulent.

->You will watch the ox.<-
<margin>LXXX</margin>
*Boukolēseis* <note>original Greek: Βουκολήσεις</note>, that is, "You will be a cowherd." By this riddle, they used to signify exile. For those who were cast out by ostracism <note>The Athenian practice of temporary banishment by public vote.</note> often went into exile in Argos. In that place, there was a bronze ox of remarkable size. This is recorded in Plutarch’s *Collected Sayings*. Hesychius testifies that this expression appeared in Menander’s play *The Phantom*.

->I am an Embarus.<-
<margin>LXXXI</margin>
*Embaros eimi* <note>original Greek: Ἔμβαρός εἰμι</note>, that is, "I am Embarus." This was once said of someone who was insane or delirious. The proverb refers to a story of this kind: Long ago, Piraeus <note>The famous port of Athens.</note> was an island, which the name itself still indicates—it comes from the word "to cross over" <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ πᾶν</note>. While Munychus held the leadership there, he established a temple to Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis.</note>, to whom the surname Munychia was added. Later, when a certain bear sacred to Diana was found there and killed by the Athenians, a famine broke out. They went to the oracle to seek a remedy for the evil. The god replied that the end of the disaster would only come if someone sacrificed his daughter to the deity. Only one man was found, Embarus, who was so out of his mind that he promised he would sacrifice his daughter, on the condition that the priesthood be passed down to his descendants. Therefore, he sacrificed the girl, adorned in a solemn ritual. <note>Some versions of this myth suggest Embarus actually sacrificed a goat dressed as his daughter to trick the gods, hence the link to "craziness" or trickery.</note> Mention of this is also made in Plutarch’s *Collected Sayings*.

->A Colophonian vote.<-
<margin>LXXXII</margin>
*Kolophōnia psēphos* <note>original Greek: Κολοφωνία ψῆφος</note>, that is, "A Colophonian vote." This is used in one of Plato’s letters to Dionysius. As a proverb, it differs more in wording than in substance from the one we recorded in the second Chiliad: "To put the Colophon on it" <note>original Greek: τὴν κολοφῶνα ἐπιθεῖναι</note>, meaning to add the finishing touch. They explain the origin of the proverb in this way: When the Colophonians were once embroiled in domestic riots among themselves, it happened that some of them moved and settled among the people of Smyrna. Later, it happened that when the Smyrneans were waging war and had been defeated many times, they finally prevailed by enlisting the Colophonians whom they had received into their city. From this, a custom was established: just as the Smyrneans did not win in war except by the addition of the Colophonians, so they would not win in votes unless they added the ballot of those people. Furthermore, when the Ionians ruled twelve cities, of which Smyrna was one, in public councils, if the votes of the Smyrneans were ever equal, the side to which those Colophonians—whose help had won the battle—subscribed would win. Nor do these accounts differ from what the Greek writer Iabenus records: that the twelve cities of Ionia used to meet in a council called the Panionium. If it happened that no decision could be reached because the votes were equal on both sides, the Colophonians were called in, and they would bring victory, or their vote would carry the most weight in any matter. We have made mention of this proverb elsewhere.

->These things shall be my concern, etc.<-
<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
*Emoi melēsei tauta kai leukais korais* <note>original Greek: Ἐμοὶ μελήσει ταῦτα καὶ λευκαῖς κόραις</note>, that is:
> These things shall be my concern, and the white maidens’.

This is a six-act line <term>senarius</term> drawn from an oracle into common speech. When Brennus was attacking Delphi with Gallic forces, the Delphians consulted the oracle on what needed to be done. The response was the verse I just quoted. Shortly thereafter, Apollo was seen with two maidens, Pallas <note>Athena</note> and Diana. For these goddesses also have shrines at Delphi. It is appropriate to use this whenever we wish to indicate that there is no danger, and that the business will be taken care of by those whom it concerns. It is recorded in Plutarch’s *Collected Sayings*. Cicero translated the Greek verse in the first book of *On Divination*:
> I shall provide for that matter, and the white virgins.

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

<margin>80</margin>
### A festival brings many things.

"A festival drags many things along" <note>original Greek: ἑορτὴ πολλὰς ἔλκει</note>. This means a festival brings many—one must understand—troubles or busy-work. It was said against those who pack huge bundles when they are about to set out somewhere. It is more elegantly applied to those who do nothing, however small, without great effort, long hesitation, and wonderful preparation, so that they often exhaust themselves and everyone else with the preparing before they even begin. The saying comes from those who usually attend festivals. For it was the custom to carry a great deal of equipment along with them—vessels, clothes, sacred objects, bread, and many other things—lest anything be lacking for the ceremony. This appears in the same collections of proverbs.

<margin>60</margin>
### Other cities are nothing compared to Croton.

"The rest are vain compared to Croton" <note>original Greek: Μάταια τἄλλα πρὰ Κρότονα τἄλλα</note>.
->that is,<-
->All other towns are frivolous compared to Croton.<-
A commentator on Theocritus mentions this proverb. It can be applied to a thing so excellent that others, when compared to it, seem to be nothing. They say it arose from the excellence of the pugilists from Croton <note>Croton was a Greek city in southern Italy famous for its athletes</note>, among whom was Milo, of whom it was said elsewhere in a proverb: "Healthier than Croton."

<margin>70</margin>
### A dog dreaming of bread.

There are some to whom this line in Theocritus’s <term>The Fishermen</term> seems to be a proverbial figure:
> "For in sleep every dog prophesies bread, and I, fish."
> <note>original Greek: Κὰὶ γὰρ ἐν ὕπνοις πᾶσα κύων ἄρτως μαντεύεται, ἰχθύα κἠγώρ</note>
> ->that is,<-
> If indeed every dog foretells bread in its dreams, then I foretell fish.

The sense is that those things which one intensely desires, or to which one is most devoted, occur to each person in their dreams. Aristotle attributes dreaming not only to humans but also to other animals, though it is most evident in dogs; for we often hear them dreaming of the hunt while sleeping, which is easily detected by the nature of the barking they emit while asleep. Therefore, it seems to me it would fit better if instead of "bread" <note>original Greek: ἄρτως (artous)</note> one read "hunts" or "fields" <note>original Greek: ἄγρως (agrous)</note>. However, we propose this only for the learned to weigh, to be decided when they have obtained a more corrected manuscript. We have not had that luck yet. As for those who would divine the future from dreams, they are not lacking even in our times, although Aristotle does not approve of it.

<margin>70</margin>
### The Dog.

"Holding a flute" <note>original Greek: Αὐλὸν ἔχων (likely corrupted in transcription to Αὐὸς ἔχωψ)</note>, that is, "playing the dog" <note>Erasmus likely interprets this as "finding a dog" or "acting the dog," but the Greek refers to a flute-player</note>, used for someone who trifles, talks nonsense, or speaks in vain. It is a figure of the Attic language, just like "you are playing" or "you are joking." For those who sing/play join in a serious matter, but only to soothe the ears with a pleasure that will soon perish.

<margin>70</margin>
### An Ethiopian does not turn white.

"An Ethiopian does not whiten" <note>original Greek: Αἰθίοψ οὐ λευκαίνεται</note>. This was usually said of those whose character is never going to change. For whatever is innate is not easily altered. There is a fable by Aesop about a certain man who, having bought an Ethiopian, thought that his color was not natural but had occurred through the neglect of his previous master; he tormented the man’s face with constant washing, so that he even caused a disease, but the color was no better than it had been before. There is also an epigram under the name of Lucian:
> "Why do you wash the Indian body in vain? Cease your art."
> "You cannot make the dark night into day."
> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὶ μάτην νίπτεις δέμας ἰνδικόν; ἴσχεο τέχνης. οὐ δύνασαι δ’νοφερὴν νύκτα καθηλιάσαι.</note>
> ->that is,<-
> You wash the Ethiopian in vain; why not stop your craft?
> You will never make it so that black night becomes day.

<margin>60</margin>
### Annas found the oven.

"Annas [found] the oven" <note>original Greek: Ἄννας κλίβανον</note>, understand: "found." It does not escape me that this was given by us in another place, but since it occurs to us so many times in a different form in the heaps of proverbs, I wished to advise that there is a threefold spelling. Elsewhere I read, and indeed in most places, "Annos [the man] found the oven" <note>original Greek: Ἄννος κλίβανον</note>. This reading I consider to be corrupted. It is not obscure how the occasion for corruption arose for those who know Greek letters. Elsewhere it is found as if it were a man. In some places, I find it written as "Annas," as if it were a woman's name, or at least a feminine word. By "oven" <term>clibanus: a small, portable earthenware or metal pot used for slow-baking bread or meat by surrounding it with coals</term>, I do not mean the common large oven—for what would be remarkable or new about that?—but that earthenware one which, with the bread inside, is placed in larger ovens, in which bread, or even fish or meat, are cooked gradually by a slow steam.

<header>THIRD CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Bbb 2</sig>

->You tread on Archilochus.<-
<margin>XC</margin>
"You tread on Archilochus" <note>original Greek: Ἀρχίλοχον πατεῖς</note>. This means you tread on or trample Archilochus; it was a saying used for a slanderer. It is said to "tread" either because the slanderer seems to be constantly unrolling the poems of this poet <note>Archilochus was a Greek poet famous for his biting, aggressive satire</note>, or because he follows in his footsteps. Horace also testifies about Archilochus:
> Rage armed Archilochus with his own Iambic meter. <note>original Latin: Archilochum proprio rabies armauit Iambo</note>
Indeed, I suspect this is the same as that which we have placed elsewhere: "the fatherland of Archilochus," <note>original Greek: ἀρχιλόχου πατρίς</note> with the word "tread" <note>pateis</note> being a corrupted form of "fatherland" <note>patris</note>.

->They strain the gnat.<-
<margin>XCI</margin>
Many expressions in the Gospel writings are taken from the common people. This was not unworthy of Christ; rather, it was most appropriate. Just as He wished to be like one of us by taking on a physical body, so He used the most familiar speech, so that He might raise our humility to His sublimity in every way. However, I did not think it best to record many of these, partly because some who are too addicted to poetic studies think anything that tastes of sacred scripture is ungraceful; and partly because I saw that those sayings were already well enough explained to everyone. But most of all, I feared that some pious person might think I was doing an injustice to divine literature if I mixed it into this work, which contains not only many pagan things but even some things that are not quite "clean." We have recorded these both reluctantly and as discreetly as we could, and even then, not all of them. Yet, I cannot omit this one from the Gospel adages, which was spoken by our teacher Jesus against certain superstitious and perversely meticulous people. These people, either being ignorant or pretending not to know what true Christian piety consists of, now please themselves with trifles, now tremble with fear, yet remain unconcerned about the greatest matters—full of Jewish superstitions but empty of true charity. Against these, Christ, the teacher of true piety, hurls this proverb in Matthew 23: "straining out the gnat, but swallowing the camel" <note>original Greek: τὸν κώνωπα διϋλίζοντες, τὴν δὲ κάμηλον καταπίνοντες</note>. This is not far from what we recorded elsewhere: "To strain a statue through the throat" <note>original Greek: ἀνδριάντα γαργαλίζειν</note>.

->There is no plow-head in him.<-
<margin>XCII</margin>
"A plow-head is not in him" <note>original Greek: γύης οὐκ ἔνεσιν αὐτῷ</note>. This was usually said of someone who was of little use for a certain task. The metaphor is taken from the plow, of which the <term>gyes</term> <note>a Greek term for the curved timber of a plow</note> is a part. Some think this is what the Latins call the <term>dentale</term> <note>the plow-head or share-beam to which the plowshare is attached</note>. Since that part seems to be the most essential, if it is missing, nothing can be accomplished with the plow. Hesiod used it in this sense: "Before the plow-head." However, Homer used it for a measure of land, calling a field a "fifty-gyon," that is, of one hundred acres.

->The arrogance of the Giants.<-
<margin>XCIII</margin>
"The madness of the Giants" <note>original Greek: γιγάντων ἀπόνοια</note>. This was said when someone, relying on his own strength, rashly and without any counsel attempted things that should not be tried. It is drawn from the well-known myth of the Giants <note>who attempted to storm heaven and overthrow the gods</note>. The proverb warns that whatever is undertaken through force, without wisdom, and against the gods, against piety, or against what is just and fair, will end in disaster. Horace says in his *Odes*:
> Force void of counsel falls by its own weight; 
> The gods also promote tempered force.

->Into greater things.<-
Homer likewise, in the 23rd book of the *Iliad*, demonstrates with a most elegant sentiment that in every business, reason and counsel have much more weight than bodily strength:
> By wisdom, truly, is the woodcutter much better than by strength; 
> By wisdom, again, the pilot on the wine-dark sea 
> Guides the swift ship when it is tossed by the winds; 
> By wisdom, the charioteer excels the charioteer.
->that is,<-
By counsel, surely, he stands much higher than by brawn, 
Whoever prepares to cut down the shaggy forest. 
By counsel, again, the pilot on the dark sea 
Directs the wave-wandering ship against the snatching south winds; 
By counsel, the driver beats the driver, both winning and leading.
Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, cites this trochaic verse without naming the author:
> It is fitting for a mortal to think mortal thoughts, not a mortal to think immortal things.
->that is,<-
It is not fitting for one who is mortal to care for immortal things;
But rather, for one who is mortal to think upon mortal things.

->You walk through fire.<-
<margin>XCIIII</margin>
"You have stepped into the fire" <note>original Greek: Ἐν πυρὶ βέβηκας</note>. That is, you are involved in a dangerous business. It is found in Ari... <note>The text cuts off here, likely referring to Aristophanes</note>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, specifically focusing on the metaphors of physical risk, the inevitability of meeting a superior opponent, the nature of posthumous fame, and the various forms of human delusion or "madness."</meta>

<page-num>844</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>ddd</sig>

Aristophanes in *Lysistrata*: <margin>Even if I must through the fire</margin>
I am willing to walk. <note>original Greek: Κἂν μὲ χρὴ διὰ τοῦ πυρὸς Θέλω βαδίζειν</note> That is:
I would be willing to walk even through fire, if there were a need. <margin>Horace in the Odes</margin>
> You are handling a work full of dangerous risk, and you walk through fires placed beneath deceptive ash. <note>original Latin: Periculosae plenum opus aleae / Tractas, & incedis per ignes / Suppositos cineri doloso</note>
They also say this fits one who must finish business quickly. He who walks through fire is less harmed if he hurries with feet barely touching the ground. Related to this is what the orator said in Seneca: "I walk through thorns." <note>original Latin: Per spinas ingredior</note>

### A brave man met another stronger.

Being brave, he met another better and stronger. <note>original Greek: Ἐσθλὸς ἐὼν ἄλλου κρείττονος ἀντέτυχεν</note> That is:
Another more powerful and better man happened upon the brave man.
This is usually said when someone, relying too much on his own strength, eventually finds someone by whom he is conquered. Zenodotus <note>a Greek grammarian and literary critic</note> thinks it was taken from the story of Hyllus, the son of Hercules, and Euchemus of Aegeate. But Suidas <note>the author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> records words of this kind without naming the author: "For there are times when even chance meets the efforts of good men. There are other times when, according to the proverb:
> Being brave, he met another better and stronger."
That is: It happens sometimes that, according to the proverb, the situation itself stands in the way of the efforts of good men. It happens again sometimes that:
> A brave man happens upon one stronger and better.
The sentiment can be seen as drawn from the *Iliad*, Book 22, where Hector encounters Achilles:
> The brave man fled before, but a better man pursued him closely. <note>original Greek: Πρόσθε μὲν ἐσθλὸς ἔφευγε, δίωκε δ’ ἔμ’ ἐγγὺς ἀμείνων</note> That is:
> He fled who was previously fierce, whom now one more fierce hard presses.

### Glory of the future.

Glory for those yet to come. <note>original Greek: Τὸ δέ τοι κλέος ἐσσομένοισι</note> This is a half-line of heroic verse. It is mentioned in the same collections of Plutarch. It reminds us that the fame and praise for right actions happen especially among posterity. Otherwise, as Ovid rightly said:
> Envy feeds on the living; after death, it rests. <note>original Latin: Pascitur in uiuis liuor, post fata quiescit</note>

### Madness is not the same for everyone.

Madness is not the same for all. <note>original Greek: Μανία γ’ οὐ πᾶσιν ὁμοία</note> That is:
Insanity is not the same for everyone.
This is a half-line of heroic verse, just like the one above, and is found in the same collections. The meaning is that there is no mortal who does not act foolishly in some matter. Although one person may suffer from one disease and another from a different one: this man from greed, that one from lust; this one from ambition, that one from envy. The Stoic Damasippus demonstrates this at length in Horace’s *Satires*. And in this human calamity, nature plays with a wonderful variety. Among those who have lost their minds, some seem to themselves to have bull’s horns; others think they are in the lead role of a play; others that they are pottery vessels; some believe themselves to be dead; others seem to themselves to be princes; others the most learned philosophers. I knew a man who believed himself to be far more wicked than anyone who is or ever was; I knew another who believed no one was superior to himself in any matter; I knew one who believed he was Christ, and another who thought he was God. That famous man of Argos used to applaud alone in the theater, believing he was hearing wonderful tragic actors. Athenaeus, in his twelfth book, tells of a certain Athenian who was convinced that all the ships arriving in the Piraeus <note>the main port of Athens</note> were his; he would take account of them, send them out, and bring them in, and he received those arriving with as much joy as if he were the master of all the goods being carried; yet if anything was lost, he did not seek it further; if they arrived safely, he rejoiced, spending his life meanwhile with much pleasure, until his brother Crito, having arrived from Sicily, handed him over to a doctor, by whose work he was freed from his madness. However, when he returned to himself, he used to say that he had never lived more pleasantly.

### The water-snake in the jar.

A water-snake in the wine-jar. <note>original Greek: Ὕδρος ἐν τῷ πίθῳ</note> This proverb, to confess frankly, I have not yet found in any ancient author, neither Greek nor Latin, and I do not know if it was taken from my own work, for I do not wish to believe that an eloquent man, and one not least in letters, invented it out of his own head. For Antonius Sabellicus <note>a Renaissance historian and scholar</note> mentions it in a certain military letter. He also adds a story as the parent of the proverb, of this kind: A certain farmer, when he perceived that the wine stored in his jar was being diminished, wondering what the matter was, began to look around to see if...

<vocab>Aristophanes, Horace, Zenodotus, Suidas, Homer, Ovid, Plutarch, Damasippus, Athenaeus, Antonius Sabellicus, insanity, water-snake</vocab>

It concludes with the beginning of a story about a "water-snake in a jar" used to explain disappearing wine.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the Third Thousand (Chiliad) of Erasmus’s collection and begins the Fourth. It finishes a story about a wine-drinking snake, discusses the reputation of the people of Marseilles and flute-players, and introduces one of Erasmus’s most famous and lengthy essays: "War is sweet to those who have not experienced it."</meta>

<page-num>845</page-num>
<header>TENTH CENTURY OF THE THIRD THOUSAND</header>

...so that the liquid would drip from a crack. When he found nothing of the sort, he began to suspect his neighbors, fearing they were unsealing the jar and drinking the wine while he was away. Therefore, he carefully sealed the jars before going out to work. But upon his return, though the seals were unbroken, he saw that the wine was nonetheless diminished. Then indeed he began to lament the luck of farmers, for whom disaster was at hand not only in the vines, but even in the storage jars. At last, when the jar was drained, a water-snake was found at the bottom—a wine-drinker. This event turned into a common joke. Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman naturalist</note> reminds us in Book 10, Chapter 72, that although snakes require very little drink, they especially crave wine when the opportunity arises. Juvenal <note>Roman satirist</note> says of a wine-loving woman in his sixth Satire:

> As if a long snake had fallen into deep
> jars, she drinks and vomits. <note>original Latin: Tanquam alta in dolia longus / Deciderit serpens, bibit & uomit</note>

The adage itself is by no means inelegant, nor to be despised. If this recent author does not move anyone, it will be permitted to use the phrase whenever someone is pressed by a hidden calamity where the cause and the perpetrator are not apparent. Or, when the cause of a long-standing evil is finally discovered. Furthermore, the snake which the Greeks call *hydros*, the Latins call *natrix* <note>a water-snake</note>, because it lives in the water. From an ulcer caused by its bite, a copious watery and foul-smelling humor flows. So says Dioscorides <note>Greek physician and botanist</note> in Book 6. Pliny, in Book 6, Chapter 23, relates that near certain islands before Persia, sea-snakes twenty cubits long terrified the fleet.

### You have come from Marseilles. XCIX

<note>original Greek: Εκ μασσαλίας ἥκεις</note> That is: *You have come from Marseilles.* Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> says this was usually said of those who wore dress poorly suited to men. This was because the people of Marseilles, ruined by luxury, dressed almost in a womanly fashion, with their hair soaked in ointment and tied back. Akin to this is what Athenaeus <note>Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note> records in the twelfth book of the *Banquet of the Learned*: "Wash yourself toward Marseilles," of which we have made mention elsewhere in the proverb *Sail to Marseilles*, and we explained what we thought about it.

### Flute-players are out of their minds. C

Athenaeus, in the eighth book of the *Banquet of the Learned*, writes that this proverb was tossed about among the ancients: that flute-players have no mind. For there is an ancient saying:
> The gods never implanted a mind in a flute-player,
> But as soon as they blow, the mind flies away. <note>original Greek: Ανδρὶ μὲν αὐλητῆρι θεοὶ νόον οὐκ ἐνέφυσαν, / Αλλ’ ἅμα τῷ φυσᾷν χ’ ὁ νόος ἐκπέταται</note>

->that is,<-

> For it is a very old saying, that
> The gods never inserted a mind into flute-players,
> But as soon as they have blown, the mind flies away instantly.

We have said more about this class of men in the proverb, *You live the life of a flute-player.*

->END OF THE THIRD THOUSAND.<-

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
## THE FIRST CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND OF PROVERBS.

### War is sweet to those who have not experienced it. I

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring a classical face in profile surrounded by ornate leaf and vine motifs.</image-desc>This is an especially elegant adage, celebrated in the writings of many. <note>original Greek: γλυκὺς ἀπείρῳ πόλεμος</note> That is: *War is sweet to the inexperienced.* Vegetius <note>Roman military writer</note> renders it thus in his book *On Military Matters*, Book 3, Chapter 14: "Do not trust it enough if a recruit desires battle, for the fight is sweet to the inexperienced." He cites from Pindar <note>ancient Greek lyric poet</note>: *War is sweet to the inexperienced, but anyone who has experienced it shudders in his heart exceedingly when it approaches.* There are certain things in human affairs which you may not understand—how much danger and evil they contain—unless you have made the trial.

->Cultivating a powerful friend is sweet to the inexperienced;
the one who has tried it, fears it.<-

It seems a beautiful and splendid thing to walk among the leading men of the court, to be involved in royal business; but the old men, who know the matter thoroughly by experience, willingly abstain from that "happiness." It seems sweet to love girls, but only to those who have not yet felt how much bitterness is inherent in love. In the same way, it can be applied to any kind of thing joined with danger and many evils, which no one would want to take up unless they were young and unskilled in affairs. Indeed, Ari-
