# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

->**War is sweet to those who have not experienced it.**<-

Aristotle, in his *Rhetoric*, <note>Aristotle, *Rhetoric* 2.12.9 and 2.13.5</note> provides this reason for why youth is bolder and old age more timid: for the young, a lack of experience in the world produces confidence; for the old, an experience of many evils produces fear and hesitation. Yet, if there is anything in human affairs that ought to be approached with hesitation—or rather, that should be avoided by every possible means, prayed against, and driven away—it is surely war. There is no other thing more impious, more calamitous, more widely destructive, more tenaciously clinging, more foul, or altogether more unworthy of man, let alone a Christian. 

But it is a wonder to say how everywhere today, how rashly, and for what trivial reasons it is undertaken; how cruelly and barbarically it is waged, not only by the heathens, but even by Christians; not only by laypeople, but even by priests and bishops; not only by the young and inexperienced, but even by the old who have seen it all before; not only by the commoners and the naturally fickle masses, but most especially by princes, whose duty it was to settle the rash movements of the foolish multitude through wisdom and reason. 

Nor are there lacking lawyers and theologians who add fuel to these nefarious fires and "pour cold water" on peace, as the saying goes. <note>original: "frigidam... suffundūt." This is an idiom meaning to spoil interest in something or act as a wet blanket—here, discouraging the impulse for peace while fanning the flames of war.</note> Because of these things, war has now become so accepted a practice that men wonder if there is anyone whom it does *not* please. It is so approved that it is considered impious—and I might almost say heretical—to have condemned this one thing which is the most wicked and the most miserable of all. 

Yet, how much more just it would be to wonder what evil genius, what plague, what insanity, or what fury first put into the mind of man a thing so brutish? How could that placid animal, whom Nature created for peace and goodwill, whom she produced alone for the safety of all, rush into mutual destruction with such beastly madness and insane turmoil? 

This is something anyone will marvel at even more if they turn their mind away from the opinions accepted by the masses to perceive the actual force and nature of things—if they contemplate for a moment, with truly philosophical eyes, the image of a human being on one hand and the likeness of war on the other.

First, then, if anyone considers the mere appearance and shape of the human body, will they not immediately understand that Nature (or rather, God) created this animal not for war, but for friendship? Not for destruction, but for safety? Not for injury, but for beneficence? 

For Nature equipped every other living creature with its own weapons. She armed the charge of bulls with horns and the rage of lions with claws. She fixed lightning-fast tusks upon the boars. She protected elephants not only with their skin and mass, but also with a trunk. She fortified the crocodile with scales as if with armor plating. To the dolphins, she gave fins to serve as spears. She defended the porcupine with spines and the ray with stingers. To the roosters, she attached spurs. Some she fortified with shells, others with thick hide, others with bark. For the safety of others, she provided swiftness, as with the doves. To some, again, she gave venom in place of a spear. She added to these a grim and beast-like appearance, fierce eyes, and a screeching voice. She even sowed certain innate discords among them. 

But man alone she produced naked, weak, tender, and unarmed, with the softest flesh and smooth skin. Nothing in his limbs can be seen as intended for fight or violence. I will not even mention how other beasts, as soon as they are born, are sufficient to protect their own lives; man alone comes forth in such a state that for a long time he depends entirely on the help of others. He knows neither how to walk nor how to take food; he implores help only with his wailing. From this alone, one might conclude that this animal alone is born entirely for friendship, which is most especially formed and held together by mutual service. 

Thus, Nature willed that man should owe the gift of life not so much to himself as to the kindness of others, so that he might understand himself to be dedicated to gratitude and social bonds. Then, she gave him an appearance that is not grim or terrifying like the others, but mild and placid, bearing the marks of love and goodwill. She granted him friendly eyes, which are the signals of the soul. She gave him the embrace of arms. She gave him the sense of a kiss, by which souls might be joined and touch one another. To him alone she attributed laughter, the sign of cheerfulness. To him alone, tears, the symbol of clemency and mercy. 

Furthermore, she gave him a voice—not threatening and horrible as with the beasts, but friendly and pleasant. Not content with this, Nature granted the use of speech and reason to him alone, a thing which is most powerful in establishing and nourishing goodwill, so that nothing at all should be done through force among men. She sowed in him a hatred of solitude and a love of companionship. She planted deep within the seeds of benevolence. She made it so that what is most healthy is also most sweet. For what is more pleasant than a friend? Yet, on the other hand, what is equally necessary? 

Therefore, even if it were perfectly possible to lead a comfortable life without mutual trade, nothing could seem pleasant without a companion—unless one has completely cast off his humanity and degenerated into a wild beast. Nature added, moreover, a desire for the liberal arts and a fire for knowledge; just as this most effectively draws the human mind away from all wildness, so it has a singular power in reconciling relationships. Indeed, neither kinship nor ties of blood are bound by tighter or firmer chains of friendship than...

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

### CHILIADS, THIRD CENTURY I.

...unites minds and spirits more than the fellowship of honorable studies. Beyond this, with a wonderful variety, Nature has divided the gifts of both mind and body among mortals, clearly so that individuals might find in others what they either love and admire for its excellence, or seek and embrace for its utility and necessity. Finally, she implanted a small spark of the divine mind, so that even when no reward is offered, it is still inherently pleasing to do good for all. For this is most characteristic and natural to God: to provide for the universal good through His own benevolence. Otherwise, what is that common pleasure we feel in our souls when we realize someone has been saved through our efforts? And for this very reason, man is dear to man: because he is bound by some notable kindness. 

Therefore, God established man in this world as a kind of image of Himself, so that, like an earthly deity, he might look out for the safety of all. Even the brute animals feel this; we see not only gentle creatures, but even leopards, lions, and beasts more cruel than these fleeing to man's help in great danger. This is the final asylum for all, this is the most sacred altar for everyone, this is the "sacred anchor" <note>original: "sacra... ancora" — a Greek and Latin idiom referring to one's last resort or final hope.</note> for every living thing.

We have sketched the image of man as best we could. Now, let us set against it, if you please, the image of war. Imagine now that you see barbarian cohorts, terrifying in their very look and the sound of their voices; iron-clad lines of battle drawn up on either side; the fearsome clatter and flash of arms; the hateful murmur of such a vast multitude; threatening eyes; harsh horns; the terrifying song of the trumpet’s *taratantara*; the thunder of cannons, no less frightening than actual thunder but far more deadly; the insane shouting, the furious clash, the monstrous slaughter, the cruel cycle of the falling and the killing, the piled-up heaps of corpses, fields flooding with gore, and rivers stained with human blood. 

It happens meanwhile sometimes that brother falls upon brother, kinsman upon kinsman, friend upon friend, and with the common madness now raving, he drives the steel into the guts of one from whom he had never been hurt by even a word. Finally, that tragedy holds so many evils that the human heart shrinks even from its mention. I shall not refer, meanwhile, to those things that are common and light by comparison: the crops trampled everywhere, the burned villas, the torched villages, the stolen cattle, the raped virgins, the old men dragged into captivity, the plundered shrines, and everything full of robberies, looting, violence, and confusion. 

And let me say nothing of those things that follow even the most "successful" and "just" war: the common people pillaged, the nobles burdened, so many bereaved old men—who die more miserably in the slaughter of their children than if the enemy had taken their sense of pain along with their life—so many destitute old women killed more cruelly than by the sword, so many widowed matrons, so many orphaned children, so many mourning houses, and so many wealthy people reduced to poverty. 

For what is the point of speaking about the destruction of morals, since no one is unaware that the whole plague of life proceeds once and for all from war? From here comes contempt for piety, the neglect of laws, and a mind ready for any daring crime. From this spring flows the massive crowd of robbers, looters, sacrilegious men, and murderers. And what is gravest of all: this deadly pestilence does not know how to contain itself within its own bounds; born in one corner, it spreads like a contagion through neighboring regions and even drags those far away into the common storm, either for profit or through family ties or alliances. 

Furthermore, war is sown from war; from a feigned war a true one arises, and from a small one a great one grows. It often happens in these matters as it is told in the fables of the Lernean monster <note>The Hydra of Lerna, which grew new heads for every one cut off.</note>. For these reasons, I think, those ancient poets—who saw the force and nature of things most sagaciously and shadowed them with apt fictions—handed down the idea that war is sent from the underworld, by the service of the Furies; and not just any Fury is fit for this task. The most pestilent of all is chosen: *She who has a thousand names, a thousand arts of harming* <note>original: "Cui nomina mille, Mille nocēdi artes." A quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (7.337-338) regarding the Fury Alecto.</note>. Armed with countless snakes, she sounds the hellish trumpet. Pan <note>The god of the wild, associated here with "panic" or "insane tumult."</note> fills everything with insane tumult. Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war.</note> shakes her furious whip. Impious Fury, all bonds broken, flies out horrid with a bloody mouth. 

Nor did the grammarians miss this; some say *bellum* <note>Latin for "war."</note> is named "by antiphrasis" <note>original: "κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν" — a linguistic term for naming something by its opposite quality. Erasmus is explaining the theory that war is called "bellum" (which also means "beautiful/fine") precisely because it is *not* beautiful.</note>, because it has nothing good or "beautiful" (*bellum*) about it; and that war is called "fine" in the same way the Furies are called "The Gracious Ones" <note>original: "Eumenides" — the Greek name for the Furies, used as a euphemism to avoid their wrath.</note>. Others prefer it to be derived from "beast" <note>original: "belua"</note>, because it belongs to beasts, not men, to clash in mutual destruction. 

But to me, fighting with weapons seems more than savage, more than bestial. For first, most brute animals live together harmoniously and socially within their own species; they walk in herds and protect one another with mutual help. Not even all wild beasts fight (for there are harmless ones, like deer and hares); only the most savage do, like lions, wolves, and tigers. Yet not even these wage war among themselves as we do. Dog does not eat dog; the ferocity of lions does not clash with other lions; a dragon [does not fight] with a dragon...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s famous anti-war essay, "War is Sweet to those who have not experienced it" (*Dulce bellum inexpertis*). Having previously described the natural, peaceful physical makeup of human beings, Erasmus now contrasts this with the horrific spectacle of human conflict, eventually personifying Nature to scold the "warrior" who has abandoned his humanity.</meta>

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...there is peace; a harmony exists even among venomous creatures. But to man, no wild beast is more destructive than another man. Furthermore, when beasts fight, they fight with their own natural weapons; we, going against nature, are equipped with tools devised by the skill of demons for the destruction of our fellow men. Nor do beasts rage for just any reason, but only when hunger drives them to madness, or when they feel themselves under attack, or when they fear for their offspring. We, for the sake of immortal fame, stir up such tragedies of war for the most trivial of reasons: for the empty titles of kingdoms, for childish anger, for a woman taken away, or for causes even more ridiculous than these. Add to this that among wild beasts, the battle is one-on-one and very brief; even if it is a bloody fight, one or the other departs once wounded. When has it ever been heard—as humans do—that a hundred thousand beasts have fallen in mutual slaughter? Consider also that while some wild animals have a natural discord with those of a different species, they maintain a firm and natural friendship with their own kind. But for man, there is a fight against man, and between any two individuals; no treaty is firm enough among mortals. To such a degree does anything that departs from its own nature degenerate into a species worse than if that malice were innate to its nature.

Do you wish to know how beastly, how foul, how unworthy of man war is? Have you ever watched a lion joined in combat with a bear? What gaping jaws, what roaring, what growling, what monstrousness, what tearing of flesh! Even the one watching from a safe distance shudders. But how much fouler a spectacle, how much more monstrous, is it to see man clashing with man, equipped with so many arms, so many weapons? Who—who would believe these were men, if the habit of seeing evil had not taken away our wonder? Their eyes burn, their faces are pale, their stride displays fury, their voice grinds, their shouting is insane, the whole man is made of iron, weapons clash, and the cannons thunder <note>original: "bombardæ" — an early term for gunpowder artillery.</note>. It would be milder if man devoured man for the sake of food and drank his blood—though some have even come to this, doing out of hatred what hunger or necessity might more excusably do. But now it is done more cruelly with poisoned weapons and shots from hellish machines <note>original: "tartareis machinis"</note>. Not a trace of humanity remains.

Would you believe that Nature herself would recognize the thing she created here? And if someone were to warn them, would this impious deed not be rightly cursed with words like these? "What new spectacle do I see? What hell has produced this monster for us? There are those who call me a stepmother because, in the vast sum of things, I produced certain poisons—though even these were intended for man’s benefit—and because I created some animals that are not very gentle, though no beast is so savage that it cannot be tamed by skill and attention. By human care, lions become mild, dragons soften, and bears serve. Who then is this person, more than a stepmother, who has fashioned for us this new beast, the plague of the whole world? I created one animal entirely for benevolence: peaceful, friendly, and helpful. What has happened, that he has degenerated into a beast of this kind? I recognize nothing of that man whom I fashioned. What evil spirit has corrupted my work? What witch has enchanted the human mind and cast a spell to turn it into a beast? What Circe <note>In Greek mythology, the enchantress Circe famously turned Odysseus's crew into swine.</note> has transformed his native shape? I would command the unhappy creature to look at himself in a mirror, but what can the eyes see when the mind is gone? Yet, look at yourself if you can, you furious warrior, if there is any way you might happen to return to your senses. From where did you get that menacing crest on your head? From where that yellow helmet? From where those iron horns? From where those feathered elbows? From where those scales? From where those bronze teeth? From where those flame-throwing weapons? From where that voice, more than beastly? From where that face, more than monstrous? From where that thunder and lightning, more terrifying and more harmful than the thunderbolt of Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus, king of the gods.</note> himself? I fashioned an animal called 'man'; what came into your mind, that you should transform yourself into such a monstrous beast, so that no wild animal will henceforth be considered a beast when compared with a man?"

Mother Nature, that architect of things, would say these things and many more like them, I believe. Accordingly, since man was fashioned as has been shown, and since war is such a thing as we feel all too frequently, it seems a matter of no small wonder what god, what accidents, or what mishap first sent into the human heart the desire to plunge lethal iron into the guts of another man. It must have taken many steps to arrive at such a notable madness. For "no one ever became extremely wicked all at once," as the Satiric poet says <note>Erasmus is quoting the Roman poet Juvenal (*Satires* 2.83): *Nemo repente venit turpissimus*. This suggests that the descent from natural peace to organized war was a gradual corruption of the human spirit.</note>. The greatest evils have always crept into the lives of men under the shadow and appearance of good.

Long ago, therefore, when the unrefined and ancient mortals lived naked in the forests without walls or roofs, it happened sometimes that they were attacked by wild animals and beasts. It was against these, then, that man’s first war was undertaken; he was considered a brave man and a leader who had driven away the violence of wild beasts from the human race. Indeed, it seemed most just to kill those who were killing us, to slaughter those who slaughtered, especially since they attacked us of their own accord without being provoked by any injury. Because that action was held in the highest praise, this is how Hercules became a god; courageous youth began to hunt beasts everywhere, displaying the hide as a trophy.

<summary>Erasmus contrasts human nature's design for peace with the "hellish" invention of war, using a personification of Mother Nature to shame soldiers for turning themselves into monsters. He argues that human violence began as a justifiable defense against wild animals (the age of Hercules) before devolving into the slaughter of fellow humans.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of the origins of human violence. Having previously argued that humans are naturally peaceful, he now traces a "slippery slope" of moral decay: beginning with the slaughter of animals for clothing and food, which gradually desensitized humanity until they turned their weapons upon one another.</meta>

# FOURTH THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED

Then, not content with merely slaughtering animals, they draped themselves in their skins to ward off the winter’s bite. These were the first murders; these were the first spoils of war. After this, they ventured further into a practice that Pythagoras <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) famous for his belief in the transmigration of souls and his consequent advocacy for vegetarianism.</note> judged to be profoundly impious. It might have seemed a monstrous thing to us as well, were it not for the power of custom. Custom has such great influence everywhere that among certain nations it has been considered a pious act to push an aged parent into a pit and beat them to death, thus snatching away the life of the very person from whom the gift of life was received. Among others, it was held sacred to feast on the flesh of one's own kinsmen or friends. Some thought it a fine thing for a young woman to offer herself to the public in the temple of Venus. If someone were to recount the many other absurdities more shocking than these today, there is no one who would not find them abominable. Truly, nothing is so wicked, nothing so atrocious, that it does not receive approval if it is recommended by habit. 

So, what crime did they then dare to commit? They did not fear to feast upon the corpses of slain beasts, to tear dead flesh with their teeth, to drink blood, to suck out the gore, and—as Ovid says—"to bury bowels within their own bowels." <note>original: "viscera in viscera condere." From Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, Book XV, where Pythagoras argues against eating meat.</note> Although this deed seemed monstrous to those of a gentler nature, use and convenience eventually made it acceptable. The sight of a corpse even became a source of delight. Meats are "entombed" in pastry crusts and seasoned with spices; an inscription is written over them as if on a grave: "Here lies a boar; here is buried a bear." O, what corpse-like pleasures! 

The process went even further. From the slaughter of harmful wild beasts, they moved to innocent livestock. Cruelty was vented everywhere upon the sheep,

-> A creature without fraud or guile, <-

and cruelty was unleashed upon the hare for no other crime than being delicious to eat. Nor did they spare the domestic ox, who had long nourished an ungrateful family with his own sweat. No kind of bird, no kind of fish was spared; the tyranny of the belly <note>original: "gulae tyrannis," literally the tyranny of the throat or gluttony.</note> proceeded so far that no animal anywhere was safe from human cruelty. Indeed, custom also persuaded men that this was not "cruelty," provided they refrained from the slaughter of other humans. 

But while it may be within our power to refuse entry to vices—just as we might keep the sea out—once they are admitted, it is not in anyone's power to set their limits. Once either vice is received, it is no longer led by our judgment but is carried away by its own momentum. After they had been trained in slaughter by these early lessons, anger persuaded them that man should attack man with a club, a stone, or a fist. For I believe it was with such weapons that they fought in those days; having already learned how to kill cattle, they realized that a human could also be destroyed with very little effort. 

For a long time, however, this cruelty remained limited to <term>monomachias</term> <note>Single combats or duels between two individuals.</note>. The loss of a single person ended the conflict; sometimes both fell, but both were deemed unworthy of life. In those times, there was even some appearance of justice in doing away with an enemy. It even began to be a matter of praise if someone finished off a violent and pestilent man—the sort they say Cacus and Busiris <note>Cacus was a fire-breathing giant and Busiris a tyrannical Egyptian king, both slain by Hercules in Greek mythology.</note> were—and freed the world from such monsters. Indeed, we see these very titles standing among the praises of Hercules. 

Then, people began to gather in larger groups, joined by kinship, neighborhood, or necessity. What we now call "robbery" was then called "war." The business was still conducted with stones and stakes hardened in fire. A passing stream, a cliff, or some similar obstacle was enough to break off a battle. Meanwhile, as ferocity grew through practice, as anger spread, and as ambition burned more brightly, they armed their madness with ingenuity. They devised whatever weapons they could to protect themselves, and they devised missiles to destroy the enemy. Now everywhere, in larger numbers and fully armed, they began to clash. 

Nor did this manifest madness lack its own honor. They gave it the name "War," and they decreed it to be "Virtue" if a man, at the risk of his own head, repelled the force of enemies from his children, his wife, his cattle, and his home. And so, as military skill grew alongside the development of society, city began to declare war on city, region on region, and kingdom on kingdom. Although the practice was inherently most cruel, some traces of former humanity still remained. Property was reclaimed through a <term>fecialis</term> <note>A Roman priest whose duty was to ensure that wars were "justly" declared through specific religious rituals.</note>; the gods above were called as witnesses; and the battle was preceded by skirmishes. Matters were settled with common weapons and through valor, not through trickery. It was considered a sin to strike an enemy unless the signal had been given; it was not permitted to fight once the commander had sounded the retreat. In short, it was a contest of virtue and glory rather than a lust for killing. Nor were arms moved except against foreigners, whom they called "enemies" <note>original: "hostes." Erasmus is noting that the Latin word *hostis* originally meant "stranger" or "guest" before it meant "enemy."</note>.

From this were born empires, not one of which, in any nation, was ever established without the shedding of much human blood. Then followed the constant cycles of wars, as one person after another drove someone from power to claim it for himself. Later, when empires fell into the hands of the most wicked mortals, arms were taken up against anyone at all, moved by mere whim. No longer the "ill-deserving" but the "well-fortunate" began to be most subject to the perils of war. Now the goal of battle was not praise, but sordid profit, or something even more wicked than that. I do not doubt that the most wise Pythagoras foresaw these things when, through a philosophical story, he told the multitude...

He argues that the "custom" of violence desensitizes humans, eventually turning a "creature of peace" into a professional killer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the descent from animal slaughter to human warfare. Having previously argued that the first "murders" were against beasts for food and clothing, he now explores how this desensitization led to the "insanity" of war among Christians, where even religious symbols and scriptures are twisted to justify mutual destruction.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...deterring the unskilled from the butchering of cattle. He saw it would come to pass that someone who, though provoked by no fury, had grown accustomed to shedding the blood of an innocent beast, would—when moved by anger and provoked by injury—not fear to kill a man. Furthermore, what else is war but a common homicide and robbery, all the more wicked for being so widely spread? But these are laughed at as the delusions of scholars by the coarse nobles of our time, who, although they have nothing of a man about them but his shape, yet clearly see themselves as gods. And yet, we see that from these beginnings, we have arrived at such a state of insanity that nothing else is done in an entire lifetime. We wage war; nation clashes with nation, kingdom with kingdom, city with city, prince with prince, people with people, and—what even the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnici"</note> admit is impious—kin against kin, relative against relative, brother against brother, son against father. Finally, what I surely think is more atrocious than all these: a Christian against a man; and I will add, though unwillingly—for it is the most atrocious of all—a Christian against a Christian. And oh, the blindness of the human mind! No one wonders at this, no one detests it. There are those who even applaud it, who carry it with praises, who call a thing more than hellish <note>original: "tartaream"</note> "holy," and who urge on princes who are already raging, as they say, "adding oil to the fire." <note>original: "oleum... addentes camino." A common Latin idiom for making a bad situation worse.</note> One man from the sacred pulpit promises the pardon of all sins committed to those who fight under the standards of his prince. Another cries out: "Most invincible prince, only keep your heart firm in this religious faith, and God will fight for you!" Another promises certain victory, twisting the words of the prophets to this end, interpreting those verses: *You shall not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the demon of the noon-day*; and *A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand*; and *You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon.* <note>Erasmus is referencing Psalm 91 (Psalm 90 in the Vulgate), which he notes was being twisted to justify secular warfare for specific princes.</note> In short, this entire mystical psalm was being distorted to serve profane matters for this or that prince. Nor were such prophets lacking for either side, nor were there lacking those to applaud such prophets. 

We hear such warlike sermons from monks, from theologians, and from bishops. Thus, war is waged by decree, war is waged by priests, war is waged by monks, and Christ is mixed into such a diabolical thing! Battle lines rush together, both sides displaying the sign of the cross, which by itself might have taught how it is fitting for Christians to conquer. From that sacred heavenly rite—where that perfect and inexpressible union of Christians is represented—they run to mutual slaughter, and we make Christ both a spectator and an author of such a wicked thing. Where is the devil's kingdom, if it is not in war? Why do we drag Christ here, with whom even a brothel would more quickly agree than war? The apostle Paul is indignant that there should be any dispute among Christians that requires a judge to settle the suit. What if he were to behold us waging war across the whole world, and for any trivial cause, more fiercely than any Pagans ever fought, more cruelly than any barbarians? And what if he saw that this was done by the authority, the encouragement, and the assistance of those who represent that peaceful High Priest <note>Erasmus likely refers here to the Pope or the high clergy who greet the people with "peace."</note> who glues all things together, and who salute all the people? 

Nor is it a surprise that those "Carians" <note><term>Carians</term>: A reference to ancient mercenaries (from Caria in Asia Minor) known for fighting for pay. Erasmus uses the term for those who profit from public misery.</note> have long been shouting against me—those whose harvest comes from public misfortunes. They say: "We undertake war unwillingly, forced by the wrongdoings of others. We are pursuing our rights. Whatever evil there is in war should be blamed on those who gave cause for the war." But let them be quiet for a little while, and we shall refute their excuses in their proper place, and we shall strip away this disguise <note>original: "fucus," meaning a dye or a deceptive pretense.</note> with which we mask our disease. 

Now, just as we have compared man with war—that is, a gentle animal with a thing that is by far the most monstrous—so that the atrocity of war might become clearer, let us now compare war with peace: a thing most miserable and equally wicked against a thing most happy and simultaneously most honest. Thus it will finally appear how great a madness it is to pursue war with such tumult, such labors, such expense, such danger, and so many calamities, when concord <note><term>concord</term>: Harmony and agreement between people or nations.</note> could be bought for much less. In the first place, what is sweeter or better in the nature of things than friendship? Nothing, surely. And yet, what else is peace but the friendship of many among themselves? Just as war is nothing other than the strife of many. The nature of good things is such that the wider they spread, the more benefit they bring. Therefore, if the bond of one man with another is so sweet and healthy, how immense will the happiness be if kingdom is joined to kingdom and nation to nation by the bond of fellowship? On the contrary, the nature of evil things is such that the further they flow, the more they are worthy of their name. Therefore, if it is a miserable and wicked thing for one man to clash with another with a sword, how much more calamitous and wicked is it for this to be done by so many thousands of men? **Through concord small things grow; through discord great things fall apart.** <note>A famous Latin proverb: "Concordia res parvae crescunt, discordia maximae dilabuntur."</note> Peace is both the parent and the nurse of all good things. War, once it suddenly breaks out, overwhelms, extinguishes, and abolishes whatever is joyful, whatever is beautiful, and...

<summary>Erasmus argues that war is a mass insanity that betrays Christian principles, lamenting how clergy and theologians twist scripture and symbols of peace to justify state-sponsored violence and mutual slaughter.</summary>

### THE FOURTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY

...for [Peace] pours a certain light into the life of mortals. In a time of peace, just as if a new spring has shone upon human affairs, the fields are tilled, the gardens turn green, the flocks graze happily, villas are built, towns are raised up, collapsed structures are restored, completed buildings are adorned and expanded, wealth grows, pleasures are nurtured, laws flourish, the discipline of the commonwealth thrives, religion burns with zeal, equity is strong, humanity prevails, the arts of the craftsmen are warm with activity, the gain of the poor is more abundant, and the opulence of the rich is more splendid. The studies of the most honorable disciplines blossom, the youth are educated, the elderly enjoy a tranquil leisure, virgins marry under good omens, and mothers are praised for children who resemble their parents; the good flourish, and the wicked sin less. 

But as soon as the savage storm of war attacks—immortal God!—what a huge sea of evils occupies, floods, and overwhelms everything! Herds are driven off, crops are trampled, farmers are slaughtered, villas are burned, and the most flourishing cities, built over many centuries, are subverted by a single gale. To such a degree is it easier to do harm than to do good. The wealth of citizens is transferred to cursed robbers and assassins. Homes are in mourning; everything is filled with fear, grief, complaints, and lamentations. The arts of the craftsmen grow cold; the poor must either starve or flee to impious trades. The rich either bewail the loss of their resources or fear for what remains—miserable in both cases. For virgins, there are either no marriages or ones that are sad and funereal. Bereft matrons grow sterile at home. Laws are silent, humanity is laughed at, and equity has no place. Religion is a mockery, and there is no distinction at all between the sacred and the profane. Youth is corrupted by every kind of vice, and mournful old men curse their long lives. There is no honor for the noble study of letters. In short, we feel more evils in war than any speech could encompass, let alone mine. 

Perhaps it could be tolerated if war only made us calamitous, and not also guilty and impious; if peace only made us happier, and not also better. But whoever summons war is impious. There were already too many—alas, far too many—evils by which wretched mortality is constantly vexed, worn down, and swallowed up, whether it wants to be or not. Nearly two thousand years ago, three hundred names for diseases were noted by physicians, besides the various species, and now new ones are born every day; and old age itself is an incurable disease. We read elsewhere of entire cities undermined by earthquakes, in another place consumed by lightning, elsewhere entire regions swallowed by a gaping hole in the earth, and towns collapsed by the digging of tunnels—not to mention how great a multitude of men are consumed by the overflow of seas and rivers, the fall of mountains and buildings, poisons, falls, wild beasts, food, drink, and sleep—accidents now held in contempt because they are so common. One man was choked by a hair in a draft of milk, another by a grape seed, another by a fish bone sticking in his throat. There are those whom sudden joy has killed, for it is less surprising when it comes from intense grief. Add now the fatal plagues, raging far and wide. There is no part of the world from which danger does not hang over human life, which is already fleeting enough on its own. So many evils crowd in from every side that not without cause did Homer <note>Homer, *Iliad* 17.446: "Of all creatures that breathe and move upon the earth, nothing is more bred in misery than man."</note> declare man to be the most miserable of living creatures. 

But these evils, since they can neither be easily avoided nor happen through our own fault, make us only calamitous, not criminal. Why does it please those subject to such innumerable calamities to summon an evil upon themselves voluntarily, as if there were not enough already? And to summon not just any evil, but the foulest evil of all: an evil so destructive that it overcomes all others, so fertile that it contains all others within itself, so pestilential that it makes men no less impious than wretched—rendering them most miserable, yet not to be pitied, except for those who least desire it and feel it most. 

Add now to all this that the benefits of peace spread themselves most widely and pertain to the many. In war, if anything falls out happily (though, oh gods, what can be called happy here?), it pertains to a few, and those unworthy. One man’s safety is another’s destruction; one man’s wealth is another’s spoil; this man’s triumph is that man’s mourning. Thus, the misfortune is bitter, and the success is monstrous and bloody. Yet it often happens that, following a Cadmean victory <note>original: "Cadmeam... victoriam." A Greek proverbial expression for a victory where the "winner" suffers as much damage as the "loser," named after the tragic history of Thebes.</note> as they call it, both sides weep. And I do not know if a war has ever turned out so fortunately that a wise victor did not regret having undertaken it. Therefore, since peace is the best and most pleasant of all things, and war, on the contrary, is the most miserable and most wicked, shall we judge those to be of sound mind who, when they could obtain peace with a little effort, prefer to summon war even at the greatest difficulty? First, how hated is that first rumor of war; then, how much envy must a prince undergo while he plunders his own people with frequent tithes <note>original: "decimationibus." Here referring to heavy taxation or the seizure of resources to fund the military.</note>. How much trouble in joining or retaining allies, how much in summoning barbarian cohorts and mercenary soldiers. How much expense and care at once in preparing fleets, in...

<summary>Erasmus presents a vivid rhetorical contrast between the flourishing prosperity of peace and the total societal collapse caused by war. He argues that since human life is already plagued by unavoidable natural disasters and diseases, it is sheer insanity for humans to voluntarily choose the "pestilence" of war.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s scathing critique of war within the Christian world. On the previous page, he contrasted the flourishing state of a peaceful society with the total devastation wrought by the "savage storm of war." Here, he moves from the economic and social costs to the physical misery of the common soldier and the profound theological hypocrisy of Christians fighting one another.</meta>

### DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...[How much labor is spent] in building or repairing fortresses and garrisons, in equipping tents, in manufacturing and transporting machines, weapons, missiles, baggage, wagons, and provisions! How much toil is exhausted in draining water, in constructing ramparts, in emptying ditches, in digging tunnels, in night watches, in sentry posts, and in drills! I pass over the fears; I pass over the dangers. What is there *not* to be feared in war? Who could possibly count the hardships of life that the most foolish soldiers endure in camps—and they are all the more worthy of these hardships because they endure them of their own free will? 

They endure a diet from which even a Cyprian <note>The people of Cyprus were proverbial in the ancient world for their love of luxury and delicate living; Erasmus suggests even the most pampered person would find soldier’s rations revolting.</note> would shrink in disgust; a bed that a beetle would reject; sleep that is rare and never granted at one's own whim. Their tent is open to the winds on all sides—if indeed they even have a tent. They must sleep under the open sky, lie upon the bare ground, stand in their armor, and endure hunger, cold, heat, dust, and rain. They must serve their commanders and be beaten with rods; indeed, there is no slavery of any bond-servant more undignified than that of soldiers. 

Added to this, at a grim signal, they must march toward death, either to kill monstrously or to fall unhappily. Such a mountain of evils is undertaken so that we may arrive at the greatest evil of all. We afflict ourselves first with such immense sufferings just so that we might have the power to afflict others. If we were to call the matter to a reckoning and weigh it with true calculations, we would certainly find that peace could be obtained for a tenth of the care, labor, trouble, danger, expense, and finally, the blood required to summon a war. 

You lead such a vast crowd of men into danger just to overturn some town; yet by the work of these same men, and without any danger, another much more noble town could have been built. You wish to harm your enemy—that itself is inhuman—but consider whether you can harm him without first harming your own people. It seems the act of a madman to take on so much certain evil when it is uncertain where the dice of war will fall. 

But so be it: let folly, or anger, or ambition, or greed, or ferocity drive the pagans to this madness. Or, as I rather believe, let the Furies be sent from the underworld to drive them. But how does it come into our minds that a Christian should draw the sword against a Christian? It is called "parricide" if a brother kills a brother. Yet a Christian is more closely joined to another Christian than any biological brother is to his sibling—unless the bonds of nature are stronger than the bonds of Christ. 

How absurd it is that those whom the one house of the Church holds, who boast of being members of the same body and of having a common head—namely, Christ—should wage war almost continuously among themselves! They have a common Father in heaven, they are animated by a common Spirit, they were initiated into the same mysteries, redeemed by the same blood, reborn at the same font, nourished by the same sacraments, they serve under the same Commander, eat the same bread, and share the same cup. They have a common enemy, the devil, and finally, all have been called to the same inheritance. 

Where there are so many sacraments <note>Erasmus uses "sacramenta" here in the sense of "sacred oaths" or "binding signs" of perfect harmony.</note> of perfect concord, where are the countless lessons of peace? Christ called only one commandment His own: namely, that of charity <note>In this context, "charity" means "Christian love" (Caritas).</note>. What fights against this more than war? He greets His followers with the happy omen of peace. To His disciples, He grants nothing except peace; He leaves them nothing except peace. In those sacred prayers, He specifically asks the Father that just as He was one with the Father, so His own—that is, the Christians—might be one with Him. Now you hear of something more than peace, more than friendship, more than concord. 

Solomon was a "type" or prefiguration of Christ, for his name in Hebrew means "Peaceful." It was by him that Christ wished the temple to be built. David, though otherwise remarkably distinguished by various virtues, was nonetheless removed from the construction of the temple by this decree: because he was a man of blood. And yet, David carried out his wars at the command of God against the ungodly, and indeed in an age before that "Absolver of the Mosaic Law" <note>This refers to Jesus, who fulfilled and set aside the old laws of retaliation.</note> had yet taught that even enemies must be loved. 

When Christ was born, the angels sang not of war or triumphs, but of peace. Of Him yet unborn, the mystic prophet sang: *And his place was made in peace.* <note>original Latin: "Et factus est in pace locus eius," a reference to Psalm 76:2.</note> Examine His entire teaching, and you will find nothing in it that does not breathe peace, sound of friendship, or taste of charity. And because He understood that peace could not stand unless the things over which this world fights were utterly despised, He commanded that we learn from Him to be gentle. He called those "blessed" who considered riches and their daughter, Pride, as nothing (for these He calls "poor in spirit"). Blessed are those who scorn the pleasures of this world (whom He calls "those who mourn"). Blessed are those who allow themselves to be driven from their possessions, knowing that life here is nothing but an exile, and that the true homeland and possession of the pious is located in heaven. Blessed are those who, while doing good to all, are spoken of with insults and treated with evils. He forbade anyone to resist evil. 

In short, just as His whole doctrine commands tolerance and love, so His whole life teaches nothing else but gentleness. Thus He reigned, thus He campaigned, thus He conquered, thus He triumphed. Nor do the Apostles instill anything else—they who had drunk the pure Spirit of Christ and were happily intoxicated with that new wine.

### CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY I

Ccc
<meta>catchword: lectico</meta>

What do all the letters of Paul proclaim from every side, if not peace, if not gentleness, if not charity? What does John speak of, what does he repeat, if not love? What else does Peter say? What else do all truly Christian writers say? Whence comes such a great tumult of wars among the children of peace? Is it a fable that Christ calls himself the vine and his followers the branches? <note>original: "se uitē appellat, suos palmites" — See John 15:5.</note> Who ever saw a branch fight with a branch? Is it in vain that Paul wrote more than once that the Church is nothing other than one body joined together from various members, clinging to one head, Christ? Who has seen the eye fight with the hand, or the belly with the foot? In this entire universe, among all things so diverse, there is harmony. In the body of a living creature, there is peace between member and member: whatever gift each part has, it does not have for itself alone, but in common for all. If anything happens to any single part, the whole body brings help. Can the connection of nature do more in a perishable body than the bond of the spirit in a mystic and immortal one? Do we pray in vain according to the command of Christ, *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven*? In that city [heaven], there is the highest concord. But Christ wished his church to be nothing else than a kind of heavenly people on earth, living according to that image as far as possible, hastening toward it, and depending upon it.

Come, imagine for me now some new guest, either from those lunar cities which Empedocles inhabits <note>Empedocles was an ancient Greek philosopher; Erasmus refers to the idea of "worlds in the moon" often debated in classical thought.</note>, or from one of those innumerable worlds which Democritus fabricated <note>Democritus proposed that the universe consisted of infinite atoms and multiple worlds.</note>, having come into this world of ours, desiring to know what is going on. When, having been instructed about each detail, he hears that there is one certain animal, a wondrous mixture of a body (which it has in common with the beasts) and a soul (by which it reflects the image of the Divine Mind), and that this creature is so noble that although it is an exile here, it nevertheless rules over all other living things; that because of its heavenly origin, it always strives toward heavenly and immortal things; and that it was so much a care to the eternal Godhead that, since it could reach what it sought neither by the forces of nature nor by the reasons of philosophy, He sent His only Son here to introduce a new kind of teaching. Then, as soon as he has thoroughly learned the whole life and decrees of Christ, let him desire to see from some high watchtower what he has heard. 

When he beholds the other living creatures living properly according to their kind, and led by the laws of nature to desire nothing except what nature dictates, but sees one animal—man—cheating one another, trading, quarreling, warring, would he not suspect any animal rather than man himself to be the one he had heard about? Then, warned by a guide as to who is man, let him look for where that flock of Christians might be, who, following the institutions of that heavenly teacher, might exhibit a likeness of the angelic city. Will he not judge that Christians live anywhere rather than in these regions, in which he would see such great opulence, luxury, lust, pride, tyranny, ambition, fraud, envy, anger, discord, brawls, fights, wars, and tumults—in short, a greater Lerna <note>original: "Lernam" — referring to the Lernean Hydra's swamp, a classical metaphor for a bottomless sink of evils.</note> of all the things Christ condemns than among any Turks or Saracens <note>Erasmus frequently uses the "Turks and Saracens" (Muslims) as a rhetorical mirror to shame Christians, suggesting that "infidels" often behave more peacefully than those who claim to follow Christ.</note>?

From where, then, did this plague creep into the Christian people? Surely this evil too, like most others, was received little by little by the unwary. For every evil either creeps stealthily into the life of men or insinuates itself under the pretext of good. First, then, learning crept in, as a thing suitable for refuting heretics armed with the writings of philosophers, poets, and orators. And in the beginning, these things were not learned by Christians, but those who happened to have known them before knowing Christ turned what was already acquired to pious uses. Eloquence also was at first more concealed than despised, then later even publicly approved. Next, under the pretext of defeating heretics, an ambitious lust for quarreling crept in, which brought no small plague into the church. At last, it progressed to the point that Aristotle was received entirely into the midst of Theology, and so received that his authority is almost more sacred than that of Christ. For if he [Aristotle] said anything poorly suited to our life, it is permitted to twist it by interpretation; but he who dares to even slightly resist the Aristotelian oracles is immediately driven out. 

From him we have learned that the happiness of man is not perfect unless the goods of the body and of fortune are added. From him we have learned that a Republic <note>original: "Remp." or "Respublica" — referring to the state or commonweal.</note> cannot flourish in which all things are held in common. We try to glue all his decrees to the doctrine of Christ—that is, to mix water with flames. We have also received something from the Imperial laws <note>original: "Cæsareis legibus" — Roman Civil Law, which Erasmus argues often contradicts the pacifism of the Gospel.</note>, on account of the equity they show, and to make them agree more, we have twisted the Gospel doctrine to them as far as possible. But these laws permit one to repel force with force and for each to pursue his own right; they approve of commerce, they accept usury (provided it is moderate), and they extol war as a glorious thing, provided it is "just." Moreover, they define "just" as that which is declared by a prince, no matter how much a child or a fool he may be. Finally, the whole doctrine of Christ is now [entangled] by the dialectician...

<summary>Erasmus argues that the pervasive warfare among Christians contradicts the core peaceful teachings of the New Testament and the organic unity of the Church. He blames this corruption on the gradual integration of pagan philosophy (Aristotle) and Roman civil law into Christian theology, which sanitized and even glorified conflict.</summary>

-># THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-

### CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY I

...of dialecticians, sophists, mathematicians, orators, poets, philosophers, and lawyers, and it has been so contaminated by the writings of pagans <note>original: "ethnicorum"</note> that the greatest part of one's life must be consumed before there is time to examine the sacred scriptures. By the time you finally approach them, you must come so infected with worldly opinions that the decrees of Christ either immediately offend you, or they are twisted to fit the dogmas of those pagan thinkers. And this state of affairs is so far from being disapproved that it is considered a sin for anyone to speak on Christian literature who has not filled himself "up to the tips of his ears," as the saying goes, with Aristotelian trifles—or rather, sophistries. As if, indeed, the doctrine of Christ were such that it could be shared with everyone, or could in any way agree with the "wisdom" of the philosophers. 

After this, we accepted a bit of honor, but it was freely offered; then, later, we began to demand it as if it were a debt. This did not seem unjust. Then we accepted wealth, but intended to be distributed as aid for the poor, and afterwards even for our own uses. Why not, since we have learned that this is the "order of charity," that "each should be his own closest neighbor"? <note>Erasmus is satirizing the legalistic distortion of the commandment to "love thy neighbor as thyself."</note> Nor were pretexts lacking for this desire: it is pious to provide for one's children, it is fair to look ahead to a coming old age. Finally, they say, "Why should we reject wealth if it comes to us without fraud?" 

By these steps, we have gradually reached the point where he is considered the best who is the wealthiest; never was greater honor given to riches among the pagans than is given today among Christians. For is there anything at all, whether sacred or profane, that is not carried out according to the judgment of money? It seemed that some degree of imperial power should go along with these ornaments. And there was no lack of someone willing to yield it. This too was accepted, but reluctantly and sparingly. At first, they were content with the title alone, and gladly left the actual work to others. Finally, it has come to the point where a bishop does not seem to himself a bishop unless he has acquired some worldly dominion. An abbot is considered insufficiently respectable if he cannot do what tyrants can do. 

At last, with a hardened face <note>original: "perfricta facie" — a Roman idiom for losing all sense of shame or "blushing."</note>, we have wiped away all shame and broken through all the barriers of modesty. Whatever greed, whatever ambition, whatever luxury, whatever pride, whatever tyranny there ever was among the pagans—we imitate it, we equal it, we surpass it. And to say nothing for now of lesser matters, was there ever war among the pagans as perpetual or as cruel as among Christians? What storms, what tides of war, how many broken treaties, what slaughters have we witnessed in these few years? What nation has not clashed with another by the sword? And afterwards, we curse the Turks, as if any spectacle could be more pleasant to the Turks than the one we provide for them every day with our mutual destruction. 

Xerxes was insane when he led that huge multitude out to invade Greece. Do you think he was of sound mind when he wrote letters of threat to Mount Athos <note>Xerxes famously ordered a canal cut through the peninsula of Mount Athos during his invasion of Greece.</note>, warning it to get out of his way? Or when he ordered lashes to be inflicted upon the Hellespont sea because it was not convenient for his sailing? Alexander the Great was raving—who denies it? That "demigod" wished for more worlds to conquer, so great a fever for glory had besieged his youthful mind. And yet those men, whom Seneca did not hesitate to call "mad robbers," fought with more honor than we do; they fought with greater good faith, and not with such machines or such arts, nor under such beautiful-sounding titles as we Christians use when we go to war. 

If you leaf through the histories of the pagans, how many leaders will you find who avoided war through marvelous arts? Who preferred to win over an enemy with kindness rather than conquer them with arms? Some even preferred to give up their leadership rather than experience the "trials of Mars" <note>i.e., the hazards of war.</note>. We pseudo-Christians seize upon anything as an occasion for war. 

The pagans, when about to go to war, would come to a parley before resorting to arms. Among the Romans, after all lands had been consulted, a Fetial <term>Fetial</term> <note>A type of Roman priest responsible for the rituals of declaring war and ensuring it was "just."</note> was sent with the *Pater Patratus* <note>The "Father Spokesman," the head of the Fetial college.</note>, and ceremonies were performed; certainly, delays were sought to temper the fury of warring. Even after these were finished, it was not permitted to join hands with the enemy unless a signal was given, which was given in such a way that the soldier did not know when it would be given. And even with the signal given, it was not permitted for anyone to provoke or strike the enemy if they were not bound by the military oath, even if they were present in the camp. Thus, Cato the Elder warned his son by letter, as he was idling in the camp, to return to Rome—or if he preferred to stay with the army, to seek permission from the leader so that he might be allowed to engage with the enemy. 

Furthermore, just as the signal for war did not grant the power of fighting except to those bound by oath, so the signal for "the retreat" took away the opportunity for killing from everyone. So much so that a certain soldier was praised by Cyrus because he had been about to kill an enemy with a drawn sword, but as soon as he heard the retreat sounded, he let the enemy go. These customs served to ensure that no one believed it was permitted to kill a human being unless extreme necessity compelled it. Now, among Christians, a man is considered "brave" if he kills any person of that nation with which his own is at war—perhaps someone he meets in a forest, not armed but laden with money, not thinking of war but fleeing somewhere to avoid it—and after killing him, robs him, and after robbing him, buries him.

He contrasts the restraint and ritualized "fairness" of ancient pagan war with the unrestrained violence and hypocrisy of modern Christian Europe.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY I

...those are called "soldiers" who, in the hope of a bit of profit, fly forward of their own accord to the fight. In both armies, like gladiators, Germans fight against fellow Germans <note>Erasmus is likely referring to the Landsknecht mercenaries, famous for serving various European masters, often finding themselves on opposite sides of the same war.</note>, even though they belong to the same prince's domain. And when these men return home from such battles, they recount their deeds as if they were true soldiers; meanwhile, they are not punished as robbers, as traitors to their country, or as deserters of their own prince. We loathe the executioner because he is hired to slaughter the guilty and the condemned by the authority of the laws; and yet, those who leave behind parents, wives, and children to run headlong into war—not even hired, but actively seeking to be hired for this impious butchery <note>original: "lanienam"</note>—are almost more favored when they return home than if they had never left. 

They think that some degree of nobility is added to them by these crimes. A man is considered infamous if he steals a garment; yet a man who, while going to war, while fighting, and while returning from service, has plundered so many innocent people, is counted among the honest citizens. Among soldiers, he who has conducted himself most monstrously is deemed worthy to lead in the next war. Thus, if you contemplate the discipline of ancient warfare, the military service of Christians is almost banditry <note>original: "latrocinium"</note>, not soldiering. 

Indeed, if you compare Christian monarchs with the pagans <note>original: "ethnicis"</note>, how much worse is our cause! Those ancient leaders sought nothing but glory. They rejoiced in making the provinces they conquered through war more flourishing; they polished wild peoples who lived like beasts—without letters and without laws—with the civil arts. They made uncultivated regions famous by building towns. They fortified unsafe places with bridges, harbors, and embankments, aiding human life with a thousand such conveniences, so that it was actually advantageous to have been conquered by them. Moreover, even in the midst of their wars, how many things are recorded of them that were either spoken wisely or done with restraint? 

But the things done in the wars of Christians are both more obscene and more atrocious than can be recounted here. Consequently, we only imitate what was worst in the pagans—or rather, we surpass it. 

But now it will be worth the effort to hear by what means we defend this great insanity of ours. "If," they say, "it were in no way lawful to wage war, God would not have been the author of war for the Jews against their enemies." I hear you, but you must add this: the Jews hardly ever fought among themselves, but rather against foreigners and the impious. We Christians fight with Christians. For them, a different religion and different gods were the cause of disagreement; for us, childish anger, a hunger for money, or a thirst for a bit of glory—often a foul reward—brings us to this point. They fought by divine command; for us, the agitation of the mind puts the sword in our hand. 

Furthermore, if the example of the Jews pleases you so much, why don't we likewise cut off our foreskins? Why don't we sacrifice cattle? Why don't we abstain from pork? Why don't we each marry multiple wives? Since we find these things loathsome, why does only the example of fighting please us? Why, finally, do we follow the "letter that kills" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note> in this matter? War was permitted to the Jews, but only in the same way that divorce was: namely, because of the hardness of their hearts. 

But after Christ commanded the sword to be put away, it is not fitting for Christians to fight, except in that most beautiful battle against the foulest enemies of the church: against the love of money, against anger, against ambition, and against the fear of death. These are our Philistines, these are our Nebuchadnezzars, our Moabites, and our Ammonites, with whom there must be no truce. We must join hands in battle constantly until, after our enemies have been utterly cut down, tranquility may follow. Unless we subdue these, true peace can exist neither for a man within himself, nor with anyone else. This war alone gives birth to true peace. He who conquers here will wish to wage war with no mortal man. 

For it does not move me at all that some interpret the "two swords" <note>Refers to Luke 22:38. Medieval political theory often used the "Two Swords" to represent the Pope's authority over both spiritual and temporal realms.</note> as both powers, the civil and the ecclesiastical, claiming both for the successors of Peter; for Christ allowed Peter to err in this very matter, so that after he was commanded to sheath his sword, no doubt would remain for anyone that war was forbidden, though it previously seemed lawful. "But Peter fought," they say. He fought, but as a Jew still, not yet having received the truly Christian spirit. He fought not for his own titles or estates as we do, nor even for his own life, but for the life of his Master. Finally, he who fought was the one who, a little later, denied Christ. If the example of him fighting pleases you, let the example of him denying Him also please you. And though he fell through a simple affection, he was nonetheless rebuked. Otherwise, if Christ approved of this kind of defense, as some most foolishly interpret, why does His whole life and doctrine preach nothing but endurance? Why did He cast His followers—armed only with a staff and a pouch—before tyrants? 

If that sword, which Christ commands everyone to buy after selling everything else <note>Refers to Luke 22:36.</note>, is a moderate defense against persecutors (as some impiously and ignorantly interpret), why did the martyrs never use it? At this point, those Rabbinical definitions are brought forward: "it is lawful for a mercenary soldier to fight, just as it is lawful for a butcher to prepare his living by his trade." For just as the latter learned to butcher cattle, the former learned to butcher men. "It is also lawful for citizens to fight, but only in a just war." <note>original: "bello iusto"</note> Now, a "just war" is whatever...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the theological justifications for war. He is specifically addressing how contemporary churchmen and "scholastic" theologians have reinterpreted the peaceful teachings of the New Testament to accommodate the violent desires of princes and the practicalities of statecraft.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...however and to whomever a prince of any kind has declared it. Priests and monks are not permitted to wield iron weapons, yet they are allowed to be present at and even preside over a war. It is not considered right to wage war with a spirit of vengeance, but rather with a zeal for justice. Yet to whom does his own cause not seem just? Christ sent out his own followers without protection, but as long as he himself was present, they lacked no defenses. When the time of his departure drew near, he warned them to prepare a pouch and a sword: a pouch against a lack of provisions, and a sword against enemies. Furthermore, those other sayings—"do not be anxious for tomorrow," "do good to those who hate you," and other things of that kind—they claim were only valid until the time of his departure. Moreover, wherever Paul or Peter teach similar things, they are considered "counsels" <note>original: "consilii". In theology, a "counsel of perfection" is an optional recommendation for higher spiritual merit, whereas a "precept" is a mandatory command for all Christians.</note> and not "precepts" <note>original: "praecepti"</note>. 

By such distinguished dogmas as these, we nourish the lusts of princes and offer them the means to flatter themselves. And, just as if there were a danger that the world might one day rest from wars, we assert the necessity of war from the very words of Christ; and just as if we feared that the greed of mortals might slacken in the amassing of wealth, we make Christ the author of gathering riches, twisting his words to this end, as if he had commanded—and not merely permitted—what he had previously forbidden. The world had its own laws before the Gospel arose: it punished, it waged war, and it gathered wealth into treasuries and storehouses. The Lord did not come for the purpose of reminding us what was permitted to us—that is, to what degree we were allowed to deviate from perfection—but rather toward what goal we ought to strive with all our might. 

Today, a man is suspected of heresy if he vehemently discourages war; yet those who, with such commentaries, have diluted the vigor of Gospel doctrine and provide princes with occasions to flatter their own desires, are considered "orthodox" and teachers of Christian piety. A truly Christian teacher never approves of war; perhaps in some cases he permits it, but only unwillingly and with grief. 

But, they say, "natural law" <term>natural law: the concept of a universal set of moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and reason</term> dictates this, and it is approved by all and received by custom, that we should repel force with force and that each of us should protect our life and our money, since money is "like a soul," as Hesiod says in his *Meteorology* <note>The original text notes "Heſiodus, meteor." Erasmus is quoting a Greek proverb often attributed to Hesiod: "Money is life [soul] for wretched mortals." The "meteor." likely refers to a specific commentary or a mis-transcription of a citation.</note>. But the grace of the Gospel, which is more effective than all these things, dictates that we should not return curses for curses; that we should deserve well even of those who deserve poorly of us; that we should yield our entire possession to one who takes a part; and that we should pray even for those who intend our death. 

These things, they say, "pertain only to the Apostles." On the contrary, they pertain to the entire people of Christ—to the whole body, which must be healthy and complete, even if one member is more distinguished than another in its gifts. Let the doctrine of Christ pertain to no one who does not hope for a reward with Christ. Let those men fight with swords for money, estates, and empire who laugh at what Christ said: "Blessed are the poor in spirit"—that is, those who are rich because they desire nothing of the world's wealth or honors. Those who have placed the summit of happiness in these riches fight to protect their lives; but they are the ones who do not understand that this "life" is actually death, and that immortality is prepared for the pious. 

Now they object to us certain Roman pontiffs <note>Erasmus likely refers to "warrior popes" like Julius II, who personally led military campaigns, a practice Erasmus found abhorrent.</note> who were the authors and even the helpers of warfare. They point to the decrees of the Fathers in which war seems to be approved. There are indeed some of this kind, but they are among more recent writers, written when the vigor of Christ was already slackening. Even so, these are very few, while there are innumerable passages in the writers of proven holiness which deter us from war. Why do these few examples come to our minds above all others? Why do we turn our eyes from Christ to men, and prefer to follow uncertain examples rather than the undoubted Author? The Roman pontiffs were, first of all, men. Secondly, it is possible they were ill-persuaded, or insufficiently attentive, or finally, lacking in prudence or piety. Although, even in their writings, you will not find that this kind of war, with which we are constantly afflicted, was ever approved. I could prove this with the clearest arguments, if I did not avoid lingering too long on a digression. 

Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), who wrote in support of the Second Crusade and the Knights Templar.</note> praised warriors, but he praised them in such a way that he condemns all of our modern military service. And yet, why should the writing of Bernard, or the disputation of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, who formulated the "Just War" theory.</note>, move me more than the dogma of Christ? For Christ totally forbade us to resist evil—at least in the manner that the common crowd resists it. 

"But," they say, "it is permitted to punish a single criminal with a death sentence; therefore it is permitted to avenge a city through war." What could be answered here is too long to be unfolded now. I will only say this: the difference is that in a legal judgment, only the one who committed the injury suffers the penalty; in war, both sides treat the other as the guilty party. In law, the evil falls only on the person who did the wrong, and the example reaches everyone; here, the greatest part of the evils falls on those who least deserve them: namely, on the farmers, on the elderly, on matrons, on orphans, and on virgins. 

Furthermore, if any benefit at all can be gathered from this worst of all things, it is entirely diverted to a few most wicked robbers: to the mercenary soldier, to the energetic bandits, and perhaps to a few leaders by whose artifice the war was stirred up for this very purpose, and for whom things never go better than during the total shipwreck of the commonwealth. In that situation, truly...
