<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s influential essay "Dulce bellum inexpertis" (War is sweet to those who have not experienced it). Having previously critiqued theologians for twisting scripture to justify violence, he now turns to a pragmatic and humanitarian argument against the dynastic wars of his time.</meta>

# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY

...mercy is shown so that the safety of everyone is considered. Here, however, so that we might avenge the misfortune of a few, or perhaps just one person, we cruelly afflict so many thousands of men who have done nothing to deserve it. It is better to leave the crime of a few unpunished than to bring certain danger upon our own people, our neighbors, and even "innocent enemies" (for so we call them), while we demand the punishment of one or two. It is better to leave a wound alone if you cannot heal it without grave destruction to the entire body. If someone shouts that it is "unjust" for a sinner to escape punishment, I reply that it is much more unjust to call so many thousands of innocent people into extreme calamity without any merit on their part. 

Furthermore, in these times, we see almost every war born from "titles" <note>original: "titulis". In the 16th century, these were legal claims to land based on complex royal genealogies.</note> of some sort or another, and from the ambitious alliances of princes. While they seek to claim some tiny town for their own jurisdiction, they bring the entire empire into extreme peril. Then, the very thing that was claimed with so much blood is often sold back or given away again. Someone might say: "Do you not wish, then, for princes to pursue their own rights?" I know it is not for someone like me to dispute too boldly regarding the affairs of princes; even if it were safe to do so, it would be too long a discussion to fit this place. I will say only this: if any "title" whatsoever is seen as a sufficient cause for starting a war, then in the great shifts and changes of human affairs, no one will ever lack a title. 

What nation has not, at some point, been driven from its lands or driven others out? How many times have people migrated from one place to another? How many times have empires been transferred here and there, either by chance or by treaty? Should the people of Padua today claim the soil of Troy because their founder, Antenor, was once a Trojan? Should the Romans claim Africa and Spain because those provinces once belonged to the Romans? Furthermore, we call a ruler a "lord," but what he holds is an <term>administration</term> <note>Erasmus argues that kingship is a public service or management, not private ownership of the people.</note>. The law governing men who are free by nature is not the same as the law governing cattle. This very right you hold was given to you by the consent of the people. And it belongs to the same people who gave it to take it away. 

Consider, moreover, how small the matter being contested truly is. The struggle is not to ensure that this or that city obeys a good prince rather than serving a tyrant, but rather whether the city is counted under the title of Ferdinand or Sigismund; whether they pay their taxes to Philip or to Louis. This is the "distinguished right" for which the entire world is thrown into the confusion of war and slaughter. But even so, let this right be worth whatever you like; let there be no difference between a private field and a city; let there be no difference between cattle bought with your own money and men who are not only free-born but also Christians. Even then, it is the mark of a wise man to weigh whether the goal is worth pursuing through such immense evils for your people. 

If you cannot provide the spirit of a prince, at least adopt the mindset of a businessman. A businessman despises a loss only if he sees it cannot be avoided except by a heavier loss, and he counts it as a profit when he settles a misfortune with only a small bit of damage. You should at least imitate that private example in the danger of the state, about which a witty story is commonly told: 

Two relatives could not agree on the division of property. Since neither wanted to yield to the other, the matter reached the point where they were going to court to end the controversy through legal judgment. Lawyers were summoned, indictments were prepared, and the matter was in the hands of the legal experts. The judges were approached, the lawsuit was formally contested, and the case began—which is to say, "war was declared." There, one of them, coming to his senses in time, called his adversary aside privately and spoke these words: "First, it is hardly becoming that those whom nature joined together should be separated by money. Second, the outcome of a lawsuit is as uncertain as the outcome of a war. Starting it is in our hands, but ending it is not. The whole dispute is over a hundred gold coins. Twice that sum will be spent on notaries, promoters, advocates, legal experts, judges, and the friends of judges, if we try the case by law. We will have to serve them, flatter them, and pay them; meanwhile, I say nothing of the worries, the running about, and the labors of canvassing. Finally, even if I win most decisively, there will still be more disadvantage than profit. Why should we not be wise for our own benefit rather than for those robbers? Why not divide between ourselves the money that would be so badly spent on them? Give up half of your claim, and I will give up the same amount of mine. In this way, we will gain our friendship—which would otherwise perish—and we will escape such great trouble. If you refuse to concede anything, I will even leave the whole business to your judgment. I would rather this money be in the hands of a friend than in the hands of those insatiable scavengers." 

The truth of the matter, as well as the relative's wit, moved the adversary. They settled the matter between themselves, to the anger of the advocates and judges, whom they had mocked like "gaping crows" <note>original: "corvos deluserant hiantes". In Latin literature, the "gaping crow" is a metaphor for a greedy person waiting to snatch something away, often used for lawyers or legacy hunters.</note> left with nothing. 

You should strive to imitate the wisdom of these men, especially in a matter so much more dangerous. Do not look only at what you wish to achieve, but look at how great a loss of good things, how many dangers, and how many calamities you will endure to achieve it. If, having weighed the advantages and disadvantages as if in a pair of scales, you find that an unjust peace is much better than a "just" war, why do you prefer the dice of Mars? <note>Mars was the Roman god of war; the "dice of Mars" refers to the unpredictable gamble of battle.</note>

He uses a parable of a legal dispute to show that compromise and peace, even if technically "unjust," are far more profitable and rational than a destructive "just" war.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the justifications for war. He has just argued that dynastic "titles" are often used as excuses for widespread slaughter. He now moves to a famous classical metaphor about risk and reward before addressing the specific contemporary obsession with "holy war" against the Ottoman Turks.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...to try the hazard <note>original: "aleam experiri." To "try the die" or "test the gamble" of war.</note>? For who, unless he is mad, would fish with a golden hook? <note>A classic proverb meaning the potential loss (the gold hook) far outweighs the potential gain ( the fish).</note> If you see much more harm than profit, even if everything falls out luckily, isn't it better to concede something of your own right rather than to buy a little convenience with such innumerable evils? I would rather the title remain with whoever has it, if I must defend it with such a great loss of Christian blood. Whoever he is, he has possessed it for many years now, is accustomed to the reins of power, is recognized by his own subjects, and performs the duties of a prince; and then someone arises who, based on some old title dug up from annals or forgotten monuments, turns a well-settled state of affairs upside down. Especially since I see that in human affairs nothing stays in its place for long, but flows and ebbs by the mockery of fortune, like a tide. Why does it matter to claim with such a tumult that which will soon migrate elsewhere by any chance? Finally, if such trivialities cannot satisfy Christians, what need is there to immediately rush to arms? The world has so many serious and learned bishops, so many venerable abbots, so many elderly nobles wise with long experience, so many councils not established in vain by our ancestors. Why aren't these childish complaints of princes settled by their judgment instead? 

But the position of those who pretend to defend the Church is more "honorable": as if the people were not the Church, or as if the whole dignity of the Church rested in the wealth of priests, or as if the Church were born, increased, and established by wars and slaughters, and not rather by blood, endurance, and contempt for life. To me, it does not even seem right that we are constantly planning war against the Turks <note>original: "Turcas." At this time, the Ottoman Empire was the primary military rival to Christian Europe.</note>. It goes poorly indeed with the Christian religion if its safety depends on such protections. Nor is it fitting for good Christians to be born from such beginnings. What is won with the sword is lost by the sword in turn. 

Do you want to bring the Turks to Christ? Let us not show off riches, nor a hand of soldiers, nor strength. Let them see in us not just a title, but those certain marks of a Christian man: an innocent life, a desire to do good even to enemies, an invincible endurance of all injuries, contempt for money, neglect of glory, and a life held in low esteem <note>meaning a life ready to be sacrificed for faith</note>. Let them hear that holy doctrine, consistent with such a life. With these weapons, the Turks are best subdued. Now, quite often, we bad men fight with other bad men. I will say something else—and I wish it were more daring than true—if you take away the title and the sign of the cross, we Turks are fighting with Turks <note>Erasmus suggests that Christians acting with violence are no different from the "infidels" they claim to oppose.</note>. If religion was established by a number of soldiers, confirmed by the sword, and increased by wars, let us defend it with the same protections. But if all things were accomplished by different means, why do we flee to Turkish-like help as if distrusting Christ's protection? 

"But why should I not slaughter those," they say, "who slaughter us?" Is it so unworthy to you if someone is more wicked than you? Why not rob the robber? Why not curse the curser? Why not hate the hater? Or do you think it a Christian deed if you sacrifice a victim most pleasing to the devil by butchering men—who are indeed impious in our opinion, yet still men for whose salvation Christ died—and delight the enemy twice: once because a man is killed, and again because a Christian kills him? Most people, while wanting to seem very Christian, strive to do as much evil to the Turks as possible; and what they cannot do, they curse and imprecate, which itself proves they are hardly Christian. Likewise, some while wanting to seem vehemently orthodox, devote those they call heretics to dire curses, being perhaps more worthy of the name themselves. He who wants to seem orthodox should strive with gentle reasons so that he who errs may return to his senses. We spit on the Turks, and thus we seem to ourselves to be fine Christians, though we are more abominable before God than the Turks themselves. 

If the ancient heralds of the Gospel had been of the same mind toward us as we are toward the Turks, where would we be now, we who are Christians only because of their endurance? Help the Turks; from impious men, make them pious if you can. If you cannot, pray for them, and recognize the Christian mind. There are so many orders of mendicant monks <note>The "begging" orders, like the Dominicans and Franciscans.</note> in the world who want to seem like pillars of the Church; out of so many thousands, how few would hold their life of little value for the sake of propagating the religion of Christ? "But there is no hope," they say. There would be the greatest hope if they brought the character of their ancestors Dominic and Francis <note>St. Dominic and St. Francis of Assisi, the 13th-century founders of the two largest mendicant orders.</note>, in whom I believe there was the greatest contempt for this world—not to mention the apostolic labors. Not even miracles would fail us, if the glory of Christ required it. Now those who boast that they are vicars and successors of Peter, the prince of the Church, and of the other apostles, usually place all their trust in human protections. Indeed, those professors of a different religion live in wealthy cities, ruined by luxury, where they are more likely to be corrupted themselves than to make others better; and where there is an abundance of shepherds to teach the people and priests to sing praises to God. They spend time in the courts of princes, where...

<summary>Erasmus argues against the "holy war" with the Ottoman Turks, claiming that converting them through Christian character and peaceful means is more effective and scripturally sound than military conquest. He critiques the hypocrisy of Christians who act with the same violence and greed they condemn in others.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s critique of the clergy’s role in inciting conflict. He has just mentioned those who pretend to defend the Church through violence. He now turns his focus to the hypocrisy of the ecclesiastical hierarchy and the proposed "holy wars" against the Ottoman Empire.</meta>

# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, FIRST HUNDRED
->Ccc 4<-

...what they are doing, I will not relate for the present. I only wish it were nothing worse than a "dog in a bath" <note>original: "canis in balneo." An old proverb for someone who is out of place or makes a lot of noise to no purpose.</note>. They gape at inheritances, hunt for profit, and serve the tyranny of princes; and so they do not seem to be doing nothing, they mark out articles of faith as erroneous, suspicious, scandalous, irreverent, heretical, and schismatic. For they would rather rule themselves to the detriment of the Christian people than propagate the kingdom of Christ at their own peril. 

Yet those whom we call Turks <note>The Ottoman Turks, the primary non-Christian power threatening Europe at the time.</note> are for the most part half-Christian, and perhaps closer to true Christianity than many of our own. For how many are there among us who believe neither in the resurrection of the body nor that the soul survives the body? And meanwhile, these men rage against heretics who merely doubt whether the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> has jurisdiction over souls tormented in the fire of Purgatory. Let us first cast the beam out of our own eye, then we shall cast the mote out of our brother's eye. The end of Gospel faith is behavior worthy of Christ. Why do we insist on things that contribute nothing to moral conduct, while neglecting those things which, if removed like pillars, cause the entire faith to collapse at once? 

Finally, who will believe us when we use the Cross and the name of the Gospel as a pretext, if our whole life displays nothing but worldliness on every side? To this, Christ—in whom there was nothing imperfect—nevertheless did not extinguish the smoking flax nor break the bruised reed, according to the prophecy, but cherished and tolerated what was imperfect until it improved. Are we preparing to destroy all of Asia and Africa with the sword, when there are many there who are either Christians or half-Christians? Why do we not rather recognize them, cherish them, and gently correct them? But if we are eager to expand our empire, if we gape at their wealth, why do we use the name of Christ as a pretext for such a profane thing? 

What of the fact that, while we attack them with human resources alone, we bring this very remainder of the world left to us into manifest danger? How small a corner of the world remains to us? How many barbarians do we, so few in number, provoke? But someone will say: "If God is for us, who can be against us?" He might rightly say that <margin>who relies on the protection of God alone.</margin> But to those who rely on different protections, what does our commander Christ Jesus say? "He who strikes with the sword, shall perish by the sword." If we wish to conquer for Christ, let us gird ourselves with the sword of the Gospel word; let us take up the helmet of salvation and the shield of faith, and the rest of the truly apostolic armor <note>A reference to the "Armor of God" in Ephesians 6:11–17.</note>. In this way, it will happen that we conquer most when we are conquered. 

But imagine that the dice of Mars <note>original: "Martis aleam." Mars was the Roman god of war; his "dice" refers to the unpredictable outcome of battle.</note> fall luckily for us: who ever saw anyone made a true Christian through the sword, slaughter, fire, and looting? It is a lesser evil to be an open Turk or Jew than a hypocritical Christian. But they say the force of the enemy must be driven from our heads. Why then do we provoke their force against our own heads by our mutual dissensions? Certainly, if we were in harmony, they would not easily attack us, and they would be converted to the faith more quickly by our kind offices if they were saved than if they were destroyed. I prefer an honest Turk to a fake Christian. It is our job to sow the Gospel seed; Christ will give the increase. The harvest is plentiful, if only there were workers. And yet, so that we may turn a few Turks into poorly-fashioned Christians, how many good Christians shall we make into bad ones, and how many bad ones into worse? For what else does such a great tumult of war produce? 

I would not like to suspect here—what has nevertheless been found true all too often—that rumors of a Turkish war are spread as a pretext so that the Christian people may be plundered under this title; so that, oppressed and broken in every way, they might more slavishly endure the tyranny of princes, both secular and religious. I do not say this because I totally condemn an expedition against the Turks if they attack us of their own accord, but so that we might wage a war for which we claim Christ as the author with Christian minds and with Christ’s protection. Let them feel themselves invited to salvation, not targeted for plunder. Let us bring to them conduct worthy of the Gospel (if we lack their language) with which to engage them. Life itself will have a great eloquence. Let us bring a simple and truly apostolic profession of faith, not one burdened with so many articles added by humans. Let us demand from them primarily those things which are clearly handed down to us in the sacred volumes and the letters of the Apostles. Agreement will be easier on a few points, and harmony will be more easily established, if in most matters everyone is free to abound in his own sense, provided that contention is absent. 

But regarding all these matters, you shall hear somewhat more fully when we publish the book to which we gave the title *Antipolemo* <note>original: "Against War".</note>, which we once wrote while living in Rome to Julius II, the Roman Pontiff, at the time when war against the Venetians was being considered. That situation was more to be deplored than refuted. If anyone examines the matter more closely, he will find that almost all the wars of Christians are born either of folly or of malice. Some young men, inexperienced in affairs, are inflamed to this by the evil examples of their ancestors and by the monuments of history—written by fools about fools. Then, they are spurred on by the encouragements of flatterers, stimulated by lawyers and theologians, with bishops perhaps assenting or winking at it, or even demanding it: more rashly than...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>860</page-num>

...how maliciously they undertake war, and learn to the great misfortune of the whole world that war is a thing to be avoided by every possible remedy. Some are driven to war by hidden hatred, others by ambition, others by a ferocity of spirit. Since indeed our own *Iliad* <note>original: "Ilias." Erasmus refers to Homer’s epic to suggest that all human history is merely a tragedy of "foolish kings and peoples."</note> contains nothing but the boiling passions of foolish kings and peoples. There are those who stir up war for no other reason than to exercise tyranny over their own subjects more easily through this path. For in times of peace, the authority of the senate, the dignity of magistrates, and the strength of the laws stand somewhat in the way of a ruler doing whatever he pleases. But once war is undertaken, the entire management of affairs is surrendered to the whim of a few. Those whom the prince favors are promoted; those he resents are cast down. As much money as he wishes is extracted. In short, only then do they feel they are truly monarchs. Meanwhile, the commanders collude until they have gnawed the unhappy people down to the very root. Since this is who they are, do you think they will be slow to seize any offered occasion for war?

See how we cloak our sickness with honorable titles. I gape at the riches of the Turks and trample them down, calling it the "defense of religion"; I indulge my own hatred and use the "rights of the Church" as a pretext. I serve my ambition or give way to my anger—a fierce and uncontrollable spirit carries me away—and I claim a broken treaty, a violated friendship, or some nonsense about marriage laws or something similar as my excuse. It is truly remarkable how they fail to achieve the very thing they desire; while they foolishly try to avoid this or that evil, they fall into another, or even the same evil, but much more severely.

For if they are led by glory, surely it is much more magnificent to preserve than to destroy; much more beautiful to build a city than to demolish one. Furthermore, even if the campaign is conducted with the most successful "Mars" <note>original: "Marte." A reference to Mars, the Roman god of war, here meaning military fortune or the outcome of battle.</note>, how small a portion of the glory will return to the prince? The people, whose money paid for the feat, claim a large part; the foreign and mercenary soldiers, as usually happens, claim another part; the commanders take some, and Fortune—who has the greatest power in every business, but especially in war—takes the most.

If it is "loftiness of spirit" that spurs you, please see how poorly you consult your own interests in this way. While you refuse to yield to one person—perhaps a fellow prince, perhaps a kinsman, perhaps someone who has deserved well of you in the past—how much more abjectly do you humble yourself as a suppliant while you implore the aid of barbarians? And what is more shameful: you promise rewards to and stroke the egos of the most criminal and contaminated men (if indeed such beasts should even be called men)—incestuous men, murderers, and robbers—for it is through these that war is chiefly waged. And while you strive to be a little fierce against your equal, you submit yourself to the lowest dregs of humanity. While you prepare to drive some neighbor or other from his lands, you must admit a pestilent dregs of scoundrels into your own homes. You do not trust a kinsman, yet you trust yourself to an armed mob? How much safer could concord have made you?

If you are drawn by profit, use your calculations. Let war please you only if you see that the gain is not outweighed by inestimable losses—a gain that is not only far smaller but also uncertain. You say you are looking out for the state? On the contrary, there is no faster or more wretched way for states to perish than through war. Before you even begin, you have already done more harm to your fatherland than you will do good as a victor. You exhaust the wealth of the citizens; you fill homes with mourning and funerals; you fill everything with highwaymen, thieves, and rapists. For these are the "relics" that war leaves behind. And where previously you were free to enjoy all of Italy, you now exclude yourself from many regions. If you truly love your people, why do these thoughts not come to mind: "Why should I expose this flourishing youth to every evil? Why will I rob so many wives of their husbands, so many children of their parents? Why should I assert some title or other, I know not what, with the blood of my own people?"

We have seen war undertaken under the pretext of defending the Church, with priests so pillaged by frequent "decimations" <note>original: "decimationibus." A form of heavy taxation, literally taking a tenth part, often levied by the Church or state to fund military campaigns.</note> that no enemy could have been more hostile. Thus, while we foolishly avoid a pit, we throw ourselves into it of our own accord. While we cannot bear to suffer a slight injury, we inflict the greatest insults upon ourselves. While we wish to appear formidable to a prince, we are made suppliants to the lowest of men. While we shamelessly hunt for "liberty," we entangle ourselves in the heaviest slavery. While we hunt for a tiny bit of profit, we afflict ourselves and our own with infinite losses. It was the part of a wise man to weigh these things; it is the part of a Christian (if indeed he is a Christian) to flee, to pray against, and to drive away a thing so hellish <note>original: "tartaream." Referring to Tartarus, the deepest pit of the underworld in Greek mythology, used here to describe the infernal nature of war.</note>, so foreign to both the life and the teaching of Christ, by every means possible.

But if it cannot be avoided by any means because of the wickedness of many, after you have left nothing untried and have moved every stone in the pursuit of peace, the next best thing is to ensure that a bad business is carried out by bad men, and that it is settled with the least possible shedding of human blood. For if we strive to be in reality what we are called—that is, if we admire nothing and desire nothing that belongs to this world—if we only desire to fly away from here as unencumbered as possible, if we are carried with all our might toward heavenly things, if we place the sum of our happiness in Christ alone, if we believe that whatever is truly good, truly splendid...

<summary>Erasmus argues that rulers often provoke war to consolidate domestic tyranny and bypass the law, while masking their greed and ambition with religious or legal pretexts. He highlights the devastating social and economic consequences of war, which he deems entirely incompatible with Christian doctrine.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>861</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND</header>

...we believe that true pleasure is situated in this one thing: if we are convinced that a pious man can be harmed by no one; if we consider how empty and fleeting are the mockeries of human affairs; if we look deeply at how arduous a task it is for a man to be somehow transformed into God, and here, through a kind of tireless meditation, to be purged of the contagions of this world, so that soon, having cast off the husk of the body, he may pass into the company of the angels. In short, if we exhibit these three things, without which no one deserves the name of Christian: **innocence**, so that we are pure from vices; **charity**, so that we may deserve well of everyone as much as possible; and **patience**, so that we may tolerate evildoers and, if it is permitted, overwhelm injury with benefits. I ask you, what war could exist between us over trifles? If Christ is a fable, why do we not frankly reject Him? Why do we glory in His title? But if He truly is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, why do all our calculations differ so greatly from this pattern? If we acknowledge Christ as our author, who is charity itself, and who taught nothing and handed down nothing except charity and peace—come then, let us express Him not by titles and insignia, but by our deeds and our lives. Let us embrace the pursuit of peace, so that Christ in turn may recognize His own. To this end, let the pontiffs, the princes, and the cities contribute their counsels. Enough Christian blood has been shed already. We have provided enough pleasure to the enemies of the Christian name. 

If the common people cause any tumult in their usual way, let them be restrained by the princes, who ought to be in the commonwealth what the eye is in the body and what reason is in the soul. Conversely, if the princes cause any disturbance, it is surely the duty of the pontiffs to settle the movements of affairs by their wisdom and authority. Or at last, satisfied by wars of such long duration, let us be touched by a desire for peace. Calamity itself draws us here; the world, exhausted by evils, demands it; Christ invites us; and the Supreme Pontiff Leo, the tenth of this name, exhorts us. He truly acts on earth as the representative of the peaceful Solomon, Jesus Christ—a lamb toward doing harm, but a roaring lion against those things which are adverse to piety. All his prayers, all his counsels, and all his efforts tend toward this: that those whom a common faith joins together, a common harmony may also unite. He strives so that the Church may flourish, not by riches or empire, but by its own proper gifts. 

This is surely a most beautiful task, and entirely worthy of such a hero, descended from those most famous Medicis <note>The Medici family of Florence, famous patrons of the arts and Renaissance humanism.</note>, by whose civil wisdom it came to pass that the noble city of the Florentines flourished in long-lasting peace, and whose house was a fortress for all good disciplines. Having himself been granted a calm and mild nature, he was initiated from his "tender fingernails" <note>original: "a teneris unguiculis" — a Latin idiom meaning from earliest childhood.</note> into humane letters and the gentler muses. Educated among the most learned men, and as if in the lap of the muses, he brought to the high pontificate a life and reputation beyond reproach—not even in the very free city of Rome was it ever stained by any spot of sinister rumor. He did not force himself into this office, but expecting nothing less than this, he was summoned as if by a divine voice by name, so that he might succor human affairs exhausted by the long storm of wars. Let the glory of war remain with Julius <note>Pope Julius II (reigned 1503–1513), known as the "Warrior Pope" for his military campaigns, whom Erasmus frequently criticized.</note>; let him keep his victories for himself; let him keep his magnificent triumphs. How much these befit a Christian pontiff is not for someone like me to pronounce. I will say only this: his glory, whatever it was, was joined with the destruction and grief of many. The peace restored to the world will produce far more true glory for our Leo than all the wars throughout the entire world—whether bravely provoked or successfully waged—produced for Julius. But we shall seem to have lingered longer on this digression than is proper for those who prefer to hear about proverbs rather than peace and war.

->II<-
->You see Argives.<-

Ἀργείους ὁρᾷς <note>original Greek: "Argeious horas"</note>. That is, "You see Argives," meaning with staring and astonished eyes. I believe this is taken from Orestes <note>In Greek mythology, Orestes was driven mad by the Furies after killing his mother.</note>, who was driven by the Furies. Hesychius sheds some light, noting that those among the Helots <note>The subjugated labor class of ancient Sparta.</note> who possessed some authority or splendor were accustomed to be called "Argives." For the Helots are in the Peloponnese, and the primary city of the Peloponnese is Argos. It was therefore a matter of ambition that they preferred to be called Argives rather than Helots. It does not escape me that among the Lacedaemonians [Spartans], the slaves were called Helots, because they made slaves for themselves from a conquered race. And perhaps from those whom the master trusted more, they preferred to be called Argives rather than Helots. You might find a similar affectation today in certain people who, though born in a very obscure village, adopt the surname of some famous city. Aristophanes in his play *Plutus* said "to look with dark-blue eyes" <note>original Greek: "kyanopen blepein"</note> in the same sense. It is recorded by Suidas under the name of a proverb.

->III<-
->Argive thieves.<-

Ἀργεῖοι φῶρες <note>original Greek: "Argeioi phores"</note>. That is, "Argive thieves." This refers to those who are openly wicked. For the Argives suffered from an infamy of thievishness in ancient times. This also appears in Suidas. However, it seems to be an allusion to the word itself. For *Argos* signified "idle" and "lazy" <note>A pun on the Greek word "argos" (lazy/idle) and the city name "Argos."</note> to the Greeks. Such people are indeed accustomed to be nourished by thefts. The Latins commonly call thievish men *Laverniones* <note>Derived from Laverna, the Roman goddess of thieves and impostors.</note>—using a word that seems to be jocularly invented—because thieves...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>862</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...they would be under the protection of the goddess Laverna: <note>Laverna was the Roman patron goddess of thieves and cheats.</note> in whose dark and hidden grove they were accustomed to bury their thefts and prey. The author is Festus.

### Mars is king.

<note>original: Ἄρης τύραννος (Arēs tyrannos)</note> **Mars is king.** Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> interprets this as being appropriate for a prince who manages the Republic not by laws, but by whim. Zenodotus thinks the phrase originated from Timotheus, an Athenian commander, who conducted many affairs most successfully against the Persians and Asians, and under whose leadership Athens thrived. From this, it was said: "Mars is king." Hesychius merely lists the proverb. Suidas notes that sometimes among the Greeks, the word *ares* <note>Mars</note> is used for iron itself. Thus, the meaning could be: "Iron is the king of affairs," used whenever a matter is settled by force.

### The Francolin.

<note>original: Ἀτταγᾶς (Attagas)</note> **The Francolin.** <note>A bird similar to a partridge or grouse.</note> Suidas indicates that this name was commonly used as a proverbial joke against runaway slaves who had been branded; this is because the bird has feathers distinguished by various colored markings. Aristophanes in *The Birds* says:
*If any of you happens to be a branded runaway,*
*He shall be called among us a "speckled Francolin."*
For this reason, he calls the same bird "the spotted one" in that same work. In the same way, the Greeks call those who are too brightly dressed and clothed in various colors *peacocks*. We shall say more about the Francolin in the proverb: "Not the Francolin's song."

### A man of Tenedos.

<note>original: Τενέδιος ἄνθρωπος (Tenedios anthrōpos)</note> **A man of Tenedos.** Plutarch, in his collection of adages, says this is used of a man with a grim and formidable appearance. As is often the case, he varies the origin. Suidas says there was a certain king of Tenedos named Tenes, who passed a law—as well as a custom—that someone should stand behind the judge holding an axe, clearly prepared so that if anyone said anything false in judgment (I believe it refers to a lie or false testimony), he would immediately strike him with the axe. This interpretation fits closely with the adage we mentioned previously: "The Tenedian axe."

Others pass down the story in this way, though it does not conflict with the former. Cycnus, the son of Neptune and father of Hemithea and Tenes, brought home a stepmother for his children. It happened that Tenes was accused before his father by the stepmother, claiming he had propositioned her for sex. Since Cycnus believed this, he shut the youth in a chest, along with his sister Hemithea because she desired to share her brother's fate, and threw them into the sea. That chest was carried to Leucophryne, which was later renamed Tenedos after Tenes, the son of Cycnus. 

In the course of time, having obtained the rule of that place, he introduced the custom just mentioned: that one should stand in court holding an axe poised over the head of the accuser. If anyone was convicted of false accusation, he would immediately cleave him alive with the axe. Because that sight appeared formidable, it became a proverb: a "man of Tenedos" was one with a menacing and fierce look. Although Pausanias in his *Description of Greece* <note>Phocicis</note> varies the narrative somewhat, we have discussed this elsewhere in this volume under "The Tenedian axe." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his letters to his brother Quintus, says: "The liberty of the Tenedians was therefore cut off by a Tenedian axe, since no one defended them except me, Bibulus, Calidius, and Favonius." He means that their liberty was taken away rigidly and completely.

### A Tenedian advocate.

<note>original: Τενέδιος συνήγορος (Tenedios synēgoros)</note> **A Tenedian advocate.** This also comes from the same source, used of someone who dispatches a case concisely and cuts the knot of a lawsuit quickly. It is derived from the "Tenedian axe," of which we spoke before. Suidas says that two axes are shown hanging among the Tenedians. Aristotle, cited by the same author, adds that besides what we have reviewed, there is a certain place in the Alpheus river on Tenedos—a small stream—in which there are crab shells shaped like the hulls of ships. They are divided in such a way that they present the appearance of an axe. Stephanus also mentions the proverb in his catalog of places, adding that it was commonly said of a rigid and harsh advocate: because it was not safe to babble just anything in judgment.

### Enkotis Day.

**Enkotis Day.** <note>original: Ἐγκωτις ἡμέρα (Enkōtis hēmera)</note> Plutarch, in his *Collectanea*—if the title is indeed authentic—records that this was commonly said of those who hold or provide a banquet. This arose because it was once the custom among them that those entering a magistracy would provide a feast for the people. If there were several magistrates, they distributed the days among themselves. Thus, when they met each other, they would ask: "Which day?" <note>original: Τίς ἡμέρα; (Tis hēmera?)</note>. That phrase passed into a common joke. However, the word *enkotis* seems...

# CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY I
<page-num>863</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY I</header>
<meta>catchword: brings,</meta>

...works ridiculously cobbled together from these words, <note>original: "οὐ κἀν τις" (ou kan tis)</note> which is "unless someone in Ceos," understand, "in a day."

->**The Versatile Artemon**<-
### IX

<note>original: ὁ περιφόρητος ἀρτέμων (ho periphoretos artemōn)</note> **The Versatile Artemon.** This appears in the same collections. They say it was commonly said of those for whose sake a fierce contest is waged. For there was a certain young man named Artemon who was eagerly loved by women for his remarkable beauty. I suspect he was called *periphoretos* <note>literally "carried around"</note> either because he was constantly on everyone's lips, or because he walked about everywhere as if showing himself off. Others prefer the idea that Artemon was a master engineer, pre-eminent in his craft, roughly in the time of Pericles. Since he was lame, he was carried around everywhere to his machines. Athenaeus, in the twelfth book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>The "Philosophers at Dinner," a collection of ancient lore</note>, citing this proverb, quotes the author Chamaeleon of Pontus, who testifies that the surname "carried-around" was added to Artemon because he was carried in a litter due to his delicacies, or because he later began to lead a luxurious and soft life after previously being poor. From Anacreon <note>A Greek lyric poet</note> he cites these lines about the same man: <note>original Greek: "νιλὸν ἢ ἔχων πέρι πλευρῆσι βοὸς νεόπλατον εἴλυμα κακῆς ἀσπίδος..."</note> which means: "Wearing a thin, fresh ox-hide around his ribs like a wretched shield, keeping company with tavern-keepers and prostitutes, leading a fraudulent life; often putting his neck in the stocks, often on the wheel, and often having the hair of his beard plucked out." From these words, it appears the saying was used against a man who was inconsistent with himself and endowed with uneven habits, such as they say Alcibiades <note>A famous Athenian general and socialite</note> was. As Satyrus reports, Alcibiades lived so luxuriously among the Ionians that he surpassed even them; among the Thebans, he was more Boeotian than any Boeotian in his physical exercises; among the Thessalians, he surpassed them in his zeal for horsemanship; among the Spartans, he was more temperate and enduring than the Spartans themselves; and in Thrace, he surpassed the Thracians in violence. This can even be done with praise. However, the term "chaff" or "rubbing-stone" <note>original: περιτρίμμα (peritrimma)</note> is used reproachfully for one who rolls himself through every kind of business. Pollux indicates this in Book VI. Plutarch indicates there was a certain lame man who was carried about in a vehicle, who was otherwise so fearful and mostly stayed at home that two servants held a bronze shield over his head so that nothing might fall on him from above. If he was ever forced to go out, he used a vehicle, but a low one, for fear of a fall. Plutarch relates something of this sort in the *Life of Pericles*. Hence, it seems to have been said of the soft and the fearful. Furthermore, Pliny in Book 34, Chapter 8, among the works of Polyclitus, mentions an Artemon who was called "carried-around." However, there is an allusion to the nautical *artemon* <note>a foresail or a pulley system</note>, by which sails are moved around and loads are lifted from ships; for today, sailors use the yardarm for both. For *Artemon* in Greek is properly a machine fit for lifting loads, which the Latins, unless I am mistaken, call a *trochlea* <note>a pulley</note>. It is so constructed that it is easily rotated.

->**The Placiadae**<-
### X

<note>original: πλακιάδαι καὶ σέλαχοι (plakiadai kai selachoi)</note> **The Placiadae and the handle.** Plutarch, in the same commentaries, shows that this used to be said of adulterers who were caught and treated shamefully, as they deserved. There is a certain village in the region of Attica whose inhabitants are called Placiadae. Among them, it was the custom that whoever was caught in adultery would suffer ignominious punishments, with radishes—which are said to be of a marvelous size among them—thrust into their private parts. If by chance radishes were not at hand, they used a *stelaeo*, that is, the wooden handle of a hoe. I am aware that this was mentioned by us in another place, but in a mutilated form; therefore, we thought it worthwhile to repeat it here in full.

->**The Eye of Justice**<-
### XI

<note>original: δίκης ὀφθαλμός (dikēs ophthalmos)</note> **The Eye of Justice.** A sincere and incorruptible judge, or even judgment itself, is called "The Eye of Justice." Suidas mentions the adage. It appears to be taken from that description by Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> in Aulus Gellius, Book 14, Chapter 4, in which he attributes to Justice eyes that are sharp, straight, and unmoving; because he who is to judge rightly ought not to turn his eyes here or there away from what is honorable. This proverbial six-foot verse is celebrated:
*There is an eye of equity that sees all things.*

->**Juster than Justice**<-
### XII

<note>original: δίκης δικαιότερος (dikēs dikaioteros)</note> **Juster than Justice.** A proverbial hyperbole for those who are exceedingly upright and incorruptible. For the ancients made Justice a goddess, whose image Chrysippus elegantly depicted, as I just mentioned, in Aulus Gellius.

->**As much as from the Bacchanalia**<-
### XIII

<note>original: ὅσον ἐκ Διονυσίων (hoson ek Dionysiōn)</note> **As much as from the Dionysia or Bacchanalia.** <note>The Dionysia were ancient Greek festivals honoring the god Dionysus.</note> Suidas records this in the place of a proverb...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>864</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...brings, but more confusedly, as is usual. Anciently among the Athenians they were accustomed to number the years from the approaching festival of Dionysus <note>Dionysia</note>, just as they did from the Olympiads. They repeated the festival of Dionysus every third year. For this reason, Virgil calls them "trieteric" <note>original: trieterica; occurring every three years</note>. Suidas reviews the phrase in Greek: <note>original: "ὃς αὐτῷ χεῖρον κόσμου ὅθεν ἐκ Διονυσίων" (hos autō cheiron kosmou hothen ek Dionysion)</note>, which is to say, "from this almost as much as the Bacchanalia." He adds that it is a saying used for things vehemently desired and expected. He mentions what he reports from some unknown author: <note>original: "ὦ Διονύσια, αὐτὰ μὲν ὄζουσ’ ἀμβροσίας καὶ νέκταρος" (ō Dionysia, auta men ozous' ambrosias kai nektaros)</note>, that is, "O Bacchanalia, they themselves indeed smell of ambrosia and nectar."

->**He is a merchant.**<-

<note>original: "ἔμπορός ἐστι σκηπτόμενος" (emporos esti skeptomenos)</note>. That is: He pretends to be a merchant. This should be said against one who, out of laziness or cowardice, devises fictitious reasons so that he is not forced to undergo danger. Suidas cites this from Aristophanes, in whose works—both in *Plutus* and in *Ecclesiazusae* <note>The Assemblywomen</note>—someone is introduced speaking in such a way as to say he feigns being a merchant whenever he is ordered to go to war, since merchants were not forced to serve in the field; it was considered expedient that they be left behind to look after the city's commerce. In the play *Plutus*, the passage goes like this:
"Are you a farmer? Do you think me so mad?
But a merchant? Yes, I pretend to be whenever the need arises." 
The other passage goes:
"But I pretend to be a merchant." 
That is: "I behave as if I were a trader." This is not entirely different from the Gospel parable concerning those who, when invited to the wedding feast, excuse themselves with various justifications <note>A reference to the Parable of the Great Banquet in Luke 14:16–24</note>.

->**Approve whatever gift someone gives.**<-

<note>original: "Δῶρον δ’ ὅτι δῷ τις ἐπαίνει" (Dōron d’ hoti dō tis epainei)</note>. That is:
"Approve whatever the gift."
The proverb warns that a gift, or a service, or advice should be taken in good part when it is offered by a friend. The geographer Strabo indicates its origin in his sixth book. When the Achaeans were seeking an oracle about founding the city of Croton, a certain Myscellus was sent to examine the site of the future city. When he saw that the city of Sybaris was already built and that the location seemed more suitable, he returned to the oracle and consulted the god whether it was lawful to found the latter instead of the former. The god responded in this manner:
"Short-eared Myscellus, seeking something else beyond your own, 
You hunt for scraps, but approve as right whatever one gives."
A translator turned those verses into this manner:
"O short-backed Myscellus, omit those thoughts from your heart,
Seeking other things, you hunt for unjust things in vain.
But whatever right thing is given, you approve with praise."
The same entry exists in my *Collectanea* <note>Erasmus's earlier, shorter collection of proverbs</note> of adages, but in a much more corrupted form. Although from the ruins, as it were, a reading of this kind can be gathered:
"Hunchbacked Myscellus, seeking more than the god grants, 
You hunt for trifles; what is given, consider a fair gift." 
Myscellus is said to have been called "short-eared" <note>Greek: Brachyotes</note> because of his thinness, having ears like a mouse, and "Brachynotus" because of his contracted or hunched back. They say that Croton was a most healthy place, while Sybaris was pestilential. Suidas reports other things about the answers given to Myscellus, but they do not contribute much to the explanation of this proverb.

->**Ithorus.**<-

<note>original: "ἴθορος" (ithoros)</note>. Suidas says this was a proverbial word used against someone who was an instigator or a stirrer-up for others. I believe the term was transferred from sailors, whom the voice of the boatswain animates to work harder at rowing, or from the racing of horses. Plutarch, in the seventh decade of his *Symposiacs* <note>Table Talk</note>, fifth problem, writes that a song for inciting mares was called *hippologos*. He mentions the same in his *Precepts of Marriage*. For *thorein* among the Greeks means to leap forward with force. Whence in Homer, Ares <note>The god of war</note> is called *thoreon* from his swift assault. It appears the Greek word is composed of *ithi* (come! or go!) and *thorein* (to leap or incite).

<page-num>865</page-num>
<header>FOURTH THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED</header>
<sig>Ddd</sig>
<meta>catchword: πάλαι (anciently)</meta>

### Lest you eat garlic and beans.
<margin>XVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἵνα μὴ φάγῃ σύφεδρα, μηδὲ κυάμους (Hina mē phagē syphedra, mēde kyamous)</note>, which means: Do not eat garlic and beans. This appears to be a proverbial riddle, used to mean: "Do not be present at wars or in the courts." For in war, garlic <note>original: "syfedra," a term for wild garlic or onions</note> was included as part of a soldier's provisions. And would that it were so arranged by fate that this most pestilential race of men, who delight in wars, should never have anything to eat except garlic—or if there is anything even worse than that! In the courts, however, they were accustomed to eat beans so that they would not fall asleep. These things indeed are found in Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note>. Although I think it more likely refers to the "bean-ballots" <note>term: calculi fabarii; beans used as voting tokens</note> with which votes were cast in ancient times.

### Dead in your sleep, you will be free from cares.
<margin>XVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Θανὼν καθ’ ὕπνους φροντίδων ἔσῃ δίχα (Thanōn kath’ hypnous phrontidōn esē dicha)</note>, that is:
Dead in your sleep, you will be free from cares. This was a verse commonly tossed about among the Greeks, arising from a superstitious observation of dreams. For they believed that he who dreamed he had died would be freed from cares and troubles. This is because death seems to put an end to pains—and indeed it plainly does put an end for those who depart from here into a better life. Perhaps the saying I recorded elsewhere belongs to the same sentiment: "Seeing a corpse, you have a 'death' <note>a cessation</note> of your troubles."

### A spirit of seven ox-hides.
<margin>XIX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Θυμὸς ἑπταβόειος (Thymos heptaboeios)</note>, that is, a "seven-ox-hide spirit," or a "seven-ox-hide anger." This is said of a brave, great, and unconquerable man. The epithet is taken from the shield of Ajax, which Homer calls <note>original: ἑπταβόειον (heptaboeion)</note> because it was covered with the hides of seven oxen, and for that reason was impenetrable. And Ovid says: "Ajax, the master of the seven-fold shield."
The adage is taken from the *Frogs* of Aristophanes:
"But breathing spears and lances and white-crested plumes,
And helmets and greaves, and a seven-ox-hide spirit."
<note>original Latin: Sed spirantes spicula & hastas, albasq́; in uertice cristas, Adde his galeas, adde his ocreas, animos quoq; septebouinos.</note>

### Always evils for Ilium.
<margin>XX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀεὶ ἰλίῳ κακά (Aei iliō kaka)</note>, that is: Always evils for Ilium <note>Troy</note>. This is said of those who are vehemently calamitous and afflicted. The destruction of the Trojans provided many arguments for the tragedies of the poets, and from this came the proverb. It is mentioned by Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop</note> in his commentary on the fourth book of the *Iliad*. When Stratonicus was asked why he did not wish to live among the people of Ilium, he replied: "Always evils for Ilium." The author is Athenaeus in the eighth book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>The Learned Banqueters</note>, although that passage is not free from error.

### Corcyra is free, poop where you please.
<margin>XXI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἐλευθέρα Κέρκυρα, χέζ’ ὅπου θέλεις (Eleuthera Kerkyra, chez’ hopou theleis)</note>, that is: Corcyra is free, therefore defecate where you wish. This is used when we signify the freedom to do anything whatever. It is cited by Eustathius in his commentary on Dionysius, but it is more fitting when we wish to indicate that there is impunity for wrongdoers. Here, I think, we might not absurdly refer to what Plutarch relates: Certain men of Chios, while they were traveling among the Spartans, not only vomited after dinner but even defiled the seats of the Ephors <note>The high-ranking magistrates of Sparta</note>. At first, a diligent inquiry was made as to who were the authors of such a great crime, who would surely have been punished if they had been citizens. But when it was discovered the deed was done by Chians, the Spartans said that "the Chians are permitted to act without restraint."

### A Thessalian mare will be awarded.
<margin>XXII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἐπικρινεῖται ἵππος θεσσαλική (Epikrineitai hippos thessalikē)</note>, that is: A Thessalian mare will be decided upon. This was said regarding the highest prize, because in ancient times the first praise was given to the mares of Thessaly. This is sufficiently indicated by the oracle given to the people of Aegina. Eustathius cites this in his commentary on the second book of the *Iliad*. Suidas records, though I do not yet know from which author: "Cavalry indeed in Thessaly and Thrace, but archers and lighter armor in India, Crete, and Caria." This is similar to what was said in another place: "A Pellenean tunic." It can also be used more elegantly through irony.

### A dog living on the bread-crumb.
<margin>XXIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κύων ζῶν ἀπὸ μαγδαλίας (Kyōn zōn apo magdalias)</note>, that is: A dog living off the bread-scrap. Eustathius, in the fourth book of the *Iliad*, shows that this was usually said of parasites and those who live on the food of others. He calls the <note>original: magdalia</note> something like bran or the scrapings from one's hands. However, in other authors, I find it written as a single word, as in Hesychius: <note>original: ἀπομαγδαλιή (apomagdaliē)</note>, he says, is the fat or dough with which they wiped their hands at banquets, and having thrown it to the dogs, they consumed it after the meal. Julius Pollux likewise, in his sixth book *On Vocabulary*, chapter fourteen, says: "The ancients..."
<margin>anciently</margin>

<summary>Erasmus compiles and explains seven Greek proverbs concerning diverse topics such as the avoidance of military and legal life, the interpretation of dreams, and the behavior of parasites. He draws on a wide range of classical sources including Homer, Aristophanes, and Plutarch to provide historical and literary context.</summary>
<keywords>garlic and beans, Ajax's shield, Troy (Ilium), Spartan tolerance, Thessalian horses, parasites, bread-scraps (magdalia), Greek dream interpretation</keywords>

--- Page 990 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Greek dietary and social customs from the previous page, specifically focusing on the use of bread-scraps (apomagdalia) as napkins and their role in Spartan voting traditions, before moving to proverbs about figs.</meta>

<page-num>866</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

In ancient times they used what were called *apomagdalia* <note>original Greek: ἀπομαγδαλίαις</note>, which were the soft parts of the bread; after wiping their hands with them, they would throw them to the dogs. For this reason, the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemonians"</note> call the *apomagdalia* "dog-scraps" <note>original Greek: κυνάδα (kynada)</note>. Indeed, the ancients used these scraps—for that is what they called the soft and fatty part into which they would wipe the residue of the meat before casting it to the dogs; hence the Spartans call the crumb "dog-food." Aristophanes in *The Knights*:

"I think I will trip you up with these, or in vain do I gape,
Fed on bread-scraps, having been raised like a dog."
<note>original Greek: ὑποβαλείσθαί σε οἴομαι τούτοισιν, ἢ μάτην χάνω / Απομαγδαλίας σιτεύμενος, κινὸς ἐκτραφείσης</note>

The Sausage-Seller boasts that he will overcome Cleon <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and general</note> through impudence and evil arts, or else it was in vain that he grew so large by feeding on bread-scraps. To which Cleon responds:

"Eating bread-scraps like a dog, you scoundrel? Then how
Could you, fed on dog-food, fight a dog-headed one like me?"
<note>original Greek: Απομαγδαλίας, ὥσπερ κυων, ὦ παμπόνηρε; πῶς ἂν / Κυνὸς βορὰν σιτεύμενος μαλχη σὺ κυνοκεφάλῳ</note>

->that is,<-

Like a dog with scraps, you villain? In what way then can you, living on the food of a dog, resist a "dog-head" <note>term: cynocephalus; literally "dog-head," a term Cleon uses to describe his own fierce, watchdog-like nature</note>? Mention of these scraps also occurs in Plutarch’s *Life of Lycurgus*, though I do not know how a certain translator grasped the sense of the passage, as it is not entirely clear to me. The Greek is as follows:

"They say they were tested to see if they wished to participate in the common meals in this way: each of the members took a piece of bread-crumb <note>original Greek: ψωμὸν</note> in his hand, and as a servant carried a vessel upon his head in silence, each member dropped the crumb into it silently, as if it were a ballot. One who approved did so simply, but one who disapproved squeezed the crumb hard with his hand. For the squeezed crumb had the power of a 'perforated pebble' <note>term: calculus perforatus; in Athenian law, a pebble with a hole through it signified a vote for condemnation</note>. If they found even one such squeezed crumb, they would not admit the candidate, wishing all to be happy in one another's company. They say the one thus rejected has been 'caddisated,' for the vessel into which they throw the scraps is called a *caddos* <note>original Greek: κάδδου</note>."

I shall render the Greek as best I can: Indeed, they say that one who wished to be approved for the banquet was tested in this manner: each of the guests took a scrap of bread <note>original: apomagdalia</note> in his hand and, like a ballot, cast it silently into a vessel which a servant carried on his head. One who simply approved dropped it as it was, but another, judging against him, would press it hard with his hand. For the pressed scrap had the same value as a perforated pebble. If even one such scrap were found, they would not allow him entry, as they desired all to dine together willingly. Furthermore, one who was rejected in this way was called "caddisated," for the vessel into which they cast the scraps is called a *caddus*.

However, Lapus <note>Lapo da Castiglionchio, a 15th-century translator</note> translates it in this manner: "Whoever wished to become part of the company was thus tested: then each taking a scrap in hand, while a servant carried a vessel on his head, they cast it in silence like a ballot—he who rejected it simply, he who approved it, pressing it hard with his hand. For the scrap that was pressed had the force of a perforated pebble. If they found any among them less pressed, they did not admit him, since they wanted everyone to meet pleasantly. He who was thus rejected, they call 'caccidiscated,' for the vessel is called a *caddiscus* in which they place the scraps."

If anyone compares these with what Plutarch wrote, he will realize that the Greek manuscript used by Lapus was different from the one recently given to us by the Aldine press. Furthermore, concerning the scraps which were given before a banquet for wiping the hands, not only does Athenaeus mention this in Book 9, but also in Book 4 he relates that among the Arcadians (if I am not mistaken) it was the custom that they went from dinner not indeed with washed hands, but having wiped them with broth or a piece of bread, and whatever they had used to wipe themselves, they carried away with them. They did this because of "night terrors" which are accustomed to happen at crossroads. So he says. And I certainly think it is a not useless remedy against dogs attacking in the crossroads.

I believe Aristophanes had this in mind in *The Knights* when he reproaches Cleon, because while great men were driven into exile, he himself wiped his hands on the most delicate barley:

"And while that man flees the land, you wipe yourself with Achillean bread."
<note>original Greek: Κἀκεῖνος μὲν φεύγει τὴν γῆν, σὺ δ' ἀχιλλείων ἀπομάττῃ</note>

->that is,<-

And while he indeed left his fatherland, you wipe yourself with Achillean barley.
The commentator adds that a type of barley is called "Achillean" <note>term: Achilleis; a superior variety of barley</note> as being of a more noble kind; thus it is less surprising if an argument is called "Achillean" when it is effective and difficult to refute.

***

->Figs after fish.<-
"A fig after fish, legumes after meat."
<note>original Greek: Σῦκον μετ' ἰχθῦν, ὄσπρεον μετὰ κρέα</note>

->that is,<-

**A fig after fish, legumes after meat.**
Athenaeus mentions this in the third book of the *Deipnosophists*. It will be applicable where some things are suited to others. Just as it is commonly ordered that cheese be served after eating meat, and nuts after eating fish.

***

->Figs are dear to birds.<-
"Figs are dear to birds, but they do not wish to plant them."
<note>original Greek: Σῦκα φίλ' ὀρνίθεσι, φυτεύειν δ' οὐκ ἐθελουσιν</note>

->that is,<-

<meta>This page continues the collection of Greek and Latin adages, specifically moving from the customs of bread-scraps to proverbs concerning gluttony, social behavior, and intellectual pretension. The catchword "Cau-" refers to the beginning of the next page's first word.</meta>

### FOURTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
Ddd 2
<meta>catchword: Cau-</meta>

Figs are pleasing to birds, who refuse to plant them.
<note>original: "Fici gratæ auibus sunt, quæ plantare recusant."</note>

A heroic poem is cited from Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, known for his work *Deipnosophistae* or "The Banquet of the Learned."</note> in the same place we have mentioned. It seems to apply to those who seek pleasure and avoid honest labor, while nonetheless desiring the rewards.

->To walk like the Junonian.<-
<margin>XXVI</margin>
To walk in the entangled sacred procession of Juno. <note>original Greek: Βαδίζειν ἡραῖον ἐμπεπλεγμένον (Badizein heraion empeplegmenon)</note> This also appears in the twelfth book of Athenaeus’s *The Banquet of the Learned*. It clearly refers to the haughty and slow gait of certain people, which Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> also notes in his *Satires*:
> As if he were carrying the sacred objects of Juno.

->Drive the willing ox.<-
<margin>XXVII</margin>
Drive the ox that is willing. <note>original Greek: Τὸν θέλοντα βοῦν ἔλαυνε (Ton thelonta boun elaune)</note> Make use of the labor of those who perform it from the heart. It is folly to lead unwilling dogs to the hunt, as Plautus <note>A Roman playwright known for his comedies.</note> says. This is recorded by a commentator on Theocritus. We have spoken of this in the proverb, "Milk the one that is present."

->He has it.<-
<margin>XXVIII</margin>
"He has it" <note>original: "Habet"</note> is said proverbially when something happens to someone that they sought, or which they deserve. "He has what he loves," or "Lips have lettuce like themselves" <note>An adage meaning like-to-like, often used for things of poor quality.</note>. They say this was taken from fowlers, fishermen, or hunters; when they return, people ask: *Do you have anything?* <note>original Greek: ἔχεις τι; (echeis ti)</note>. It is cited from Aristophanes’s *The Clouds*. The tragic poet Seneca says in *Agamemnon*: "He has it, it is finished." Terence says in *Andria*: "I said to myself immediately, surely he is caught, he has it." Donatus <note>A famous Roman grammarian and teacher of rhetoric.</note> shows that this is properly said of gladiators, whom others see have been struck before they even realize it themselves. The proverb seems to have arisen from a public shout.

->Hercules is being entertained.<-
<margin>XXIX</margin>
Hercules is a guest. <note>original Greek: Ἡρακλῆς ξενίζεται (Herakles xenizetai)</note> This was often said when someone seemed to linger too long at a feast; because those who received Hercules as a guest and host had to wait a long time until he was satisfied. For it was hardly safe to disturb him while he was hungry. Nor was that glutton easily satisfied, so much so that it is read that he devoured entire oxen in a single sitting. For this reason, he was called a "glutton" <note>term: adephagos; literally "eater-to-excess"</note> by the Greeks; and they consecrated the gull to him, calling it the "ox-eater" <note>term: bouphagos</note>. It is also read that he entered a contest with a certain Lepreus to see which of them could finish an ox faster. Athenaeus records these and many other things in his tenth book regarding Hercules' gluttony, adding that a certain athlete from Thasos named Theagenes, as well as Milo of Croton <note>A famous 6th-century BC wrestler known for his extraordinary strength.</note>, could also finish an ox in a single day. May such guests befall our enemies.

->Even in the assembly of the gods.<-
<margin>XXX</margin>
Even in the assembly of the gods, or their gathering. <note>original Greek: Κἂν θεῶν ἀγορᾷ (Kan theon agora)</note> Some interpret this as referring to those who are exceptionally honest and fair; others to those who are vehemently abusive. They add that there is a certain place in Eleusis, near the Anactoron <note>The primary temple or "House of the Lords" at the Eleusinian sanctuary.</note>, called the "Assembly of the Gods," which people did not enter unless they were speaking words of good omen; hence they said of anyone who was excessively foul-mouthed, "Let him be a speaker of ill-omens even in the assembly of the gods." <note>original Greek: ἔστω κἂν θεῶν ἀγορᾷ δυσφημιστής (esto kan theon agora dysphemistes)</note>

->Calliphanes.<-
<margin>XXXI</margin>
Calliphanes. <note>original Greek: Καλλιφάνης</note> The ridiculous ambition of this man gave rise to a proverbial joke. For they say it was the custom of this poet to write down the beginnings of various poems and speeches, for about three or four lines, and then recite and show them off, so that to those ignorant of the trick, he might seem widely read and learned. Athenaeus mentions him in the first book of *The Banquet of the Learned*, saying his nickname was "The Gluttonous." Indeed, there is no lack of such "literary impostors" in our own times, whose practice it is to learn by heart several famous passages—and those not very common—from the highest authors of various professions. Equipped with these, they do not fear to attack anyone, no matter how learned, in social gatherings. And they achieve this by promptly chanting those passages of theirs, so that to the unlearned they appear to be absolute Solons <note>A reference to Solon, the wise lawmaker of Athens.</note>. Yet if you were to engage with these "Solons" for a third or fourth time, immortal God, nothing is more speechless, nothing more uneducated—evidently, those treasures have been poured out once and for all. I can hardly restrain my laughter while writing this, as I recall a certain Calliphanes whom I once knew when I was in the household of the most distinguished father, Henry of Bergen, Bishop of Cambrai <note>Erasmus's early patron who helped fund his studies.</note>. But his name shall be spared out of respect for our shared domestic life. He used to compile and decorate many volumes, but with empty pages, except that on the front one could see certain magnificent titles: such as poems, speeches, or letters. On each was inscribed the man’s triple name, so that those who happened to read the titles would believe him learned and toiling at many great works in literature.

<summary>This page discusses proverbs related to social behavior and pretense, including the gluttony of Hercules and a critique of "Calliphanes," a term for those who fake learning by memorizing only the beginnings of books. Erasmus includes a personal anecdote about a similar fraud he encountered in the service of the Bishop of Cambrai.</summary>

<page-num>868</page-num>
### THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->To wag the tail.<-
<margin>XX</margin>

To wag the tail. <note>original Greek: Κέρκῳ σαίνειν (Kerko sainein)</note> This is said of those who fawn upon someone in the hope of gain. Aristophanes <note>An ancient Greek comic playwright known for his political satire.</note> says in *The Knights*:
"Who, wagging his tail while watching you dine, devours your food from within while you gape elsewhere." <note>original Latin translation: "Qui cauda alludens cum coenam obseruat, amica, Te spectante aliò, tua edulia deuorat ille."</note>
For the same idea, he frequently uses the word <term>aikallein</term> <note>original: ἀικἀλλειν</note>, which refers to the way dogs fawn with their ears, tails, and their whole bodies. In *The Knights*:
"These oracles indeed fawn upon me." <note>original: τὰ μὲν λόγι’ ἀικἀλλει με</note>
The word <term>thopteuein</term> <note>original: θωπτεύειν; to flatter</note> is likewise derived from an animal, if we believe the Greek etymologists. The "Thos" <note>A jackal or a species of wolf-like creature.</note> is a kind of animal among the Greeks. Indeed, certain wolves also fawn in the manner of dogs. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History.</note> mentions the "Thoas" in his twenty-fourth chapter as a species of wolf, but one that is a friend to man. Whether the verb *thopteuein* is actually derived from it, I am uncertain.

---

->A mixing-bowl of lawsuits.<-
<margin>XXX</margin>

A mixing-bowl of evils. <note>original Greek: Κρατὴρ κακῶν (Krater kakon)</note> This refers to a very troublesome matter, or a person who instigates lawsuits. Aristophanes in *The Acharnians*:
"A mixing-bowl of evils, a rubber-down of lawsuits," <note>original Latin: "Crater malorum, sector litium"</note> meaning a slanderer and a <term>quadruplicator</term> <note>original: quadruplatorem; a professional informer or bounty hunter in the Roman legal system who received a fourth of the fine.</note>.

---

->Lampon swears by the goose.<-
<margin>XXX</margin>

Lampon swears by the goose. <note>original Greek: Λάμπων ὄμνυσι τὸν χῆνα</note> People used to say this when someone attempted an oath in haste. Lampon was a certain priest and seer, and an author of oracles. He was accustomed to swear by the goose, as if by a bird of augury. Or perhaps it was because Rhadamanthus <note>In Greek mythology, a judge of the dead known for his strict justice.</note> had long ago decreed that one should not swear by any of the gods, but rather by a dog or a goose—an oath that Socrates <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often depicted by Plato as using "by the dog" as a mild oath.</note> made familiar in the works of Plato. They record that this was done on Lampon’s authority, so that the Athenians might become accustomed to the ways of Sybaris <note>A Greek city in Italy famous for its luxury and soft living.</note>. Aristophanes mentions the adage in *The Birds*: "Lampon even now swears by the goose whenever he deceives anyone in something."

---

->To strike with a pat.<-
<margin>XX</margin>

"To strike with a pat" <note>original: Palpo percutere</note> is said of one who flatters and holds out empty hope through words. Plautus in *The Merchant*: "I will make you a free man in a few months." "You are striking me with a pat." "Would I ever dare to utter a false deed?" Elsewhere the same author says: "You cannot thrust a pat upon me." This is a metaphor taken from grooms, who soothe horses by patting them with their hands. Virgil <note>The great Roman epic poet.</note> writes in the third book of the *Georgics*:
> Then more and more to rejoice in the fawning praises 
> Of his master, and to love the sound of his neck being patted.
And Horace in his *Satires*:
> Who, if you pat him clumsily, kicks back from every side, being on his guard.

---

->To snatch the handle from the hand.<-
<margin>XX</margin>

Plautus used this proverbial figure—"To snatch the handle from the hand"—to describe someone who, while another is preparing to do something, wrests away the ability to complete it. The passage is in *The Pot of Gold* (*Aulularia*): "I take up a club, I slaughter the rooster, that thief caught in the act. I believe, by Pollux, those cooks promised him a reward if he made it public. I have snatched the handle from his hand." The metaphor is taken from a sword already being brandished to strike, when suddenly the hilt is knocked out of the hands.

---

->The gifts of the guest from Alybas.<-
<margin>XX</margin>

The gifts of the guest from Alybas, or the hospitality-gifts of a friend from Alybas. <note>original Greek: Τὰ δῶρα τοῦ ἐξ ἀλύβαντος ξένου...</note> Eustathius, the commentator on Homer, thinks this can rightly be said to children whenever it happens that someone falsely boasts that they have bestowed great things, or offers a benefit in words only, not in reality. For in the final book of Homer’s *Odyssey*, Ulysses <note>Odysseus, the hero of the Odyssey.</note>, appearing in an unknown guise while speaking with his father Laertes, pretends that he is an inhabitant of Alybas, the son of the very wealthy man Apheidas, and that he had welcomed Ulysses with hospitality and sent him away after giving him most magnificent gifts.
"For I am," he says, "from Alybas, where I inhabit a noble house, 
The son of King Apheidas, the son of Polypemon; 
But my name is Eperitus."
<note>Erasmus quotes the Greek then provides a Latin translation: "Sum ex Alybante oriundus, ubi mihi splendida tecta, Regis Aphidantis proles Polypemonidae."</note>

### Mushroom. XXXVIII

<margin>
IIII
decimus
utor
verat
Socrati

for now

XXV
merca-
anything
thou from
</margin>
Plautus, in his play *The Bacchis Sisters*, used "mushroom" <note>original Latin: "fungus"</note> to mean someone who is stupid and excessively gullible. This is either because a mushroom is inherently a tasteless thing, or because it is soft and fragile, or because it pops up suddenly. Plautus's words are these: "Was I such a mushroom as to believe him?" The same author in the same play says: "Whoever there are, wherever they are, who have been, and who shall be hereafter—fools, blockheads, idiots, mushrooms, dullards, boobies, numbskulls—I alone surpass them all in stupidity." <note>Plautus, *Bacchides* 283 and 1087-1090. A "mushroom" here implies someone with the intellectual depth of a fungus.</note>

### Eurycles. XXXIX

Eurycles was a commonly known nickname for someone who prophesied about himself and his own troubles. For there was a certain prophet of this name who was called a <term>ventriloquist</term> <note>original Greek: ἐγγαστρίμυθος (engastrimythos); literally 'belly-myth-speaker'. In antiquity, this referred to a prophet whose voice seemed to come from their stomach, often interpreted as spirit possession.</note>, from this, if I am not mistaken, because he predicted truths from the stars, "from looking into the stars" <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὸ ἐς τἄστρα (para to es tastra)</note>. Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> also mentions him, although in his work it is written as *engastrimythos*, that is, a diviner or belly-speaker. This is recorded in the *Collection of Adages* attributed to Plutarch. It is also used by Plato in *The Sophist*. For when he is rebuking those who display their foolishness through tangled and absurd reasoning, he adds: "They do not need others to refute them, but as the saying goes, they have the enemy and opponent at home, and they always go about carrying that absurd Eurycles whispering within them." That is, they do not need others to argue against them, because they have a contradictory voice in their own house, as the saying goes, and they walk around always carrying that absurd Eurycles murmuring within. <note>Plato, *Sophist* 252c. Plato uses the ventriloquist as a metaphor for people whose own arguments contradict themselves.</note>

</margin>
"If there be any shield <note>original Greek: αἰγίς (aigis); often the aegis of Athena, but here used for a shield.</note> around the city." This was a jibe cast at those who patrolled the city in a scattered and disorganized manner, wandering about. It is mentioned in Plutarch’s *Collection*, but not explained.

### A broken crane. XLI

<margin>
XVII
is ho-
bio of
e pre-
te pa-
since
e,
</margin>
"A broken crane." <note>original Greek: Κράδης ῥαγείσης (Krades rhageises)</note> This was said of those who came forward as if they were about to perform some great feat, but then, contrary to everyone's expectations, behaved disgracefully and unbecomingly in the business. The metaphor is taken from actors in tragedies. When a deity had to be introduced, they were suddenly lifted by certain machines and were accustomed to appear at the top of the stage as if hanging in the air, suspended by a hook attached to a belt behind their back. It sometimes happened to these actors that, by chance, the <term>anchor</term> <note>In this context, the hook or support of the crane.</note> by which they were sustained broke, and they fell down—to the great laughter of the spectators, and to their own injury and disgrace. Furthermore, the word <term>krade</term> <note>original: κράδη</note> in this context does not mean a fig-branch, as it does elsewhere, but that bronze hook by which the actors were held fast in the <term>machine</term> <note>original: machina; the theatrical crane used for the 'deus ex machina'.</note>. Julius Pollux <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and sophist.</note> in Book 4, Chapter 19, teaches that it was customary to call "krade" in comedy what was called "machine" in tragedies. It was likely not unlike a fig-branch, since the Athenians call the fig tree *krade*. Although the branches of any trees are sometimes called *kradae*.
