<page-num>870</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

### Every man remembers his own business.

Plautus says in *The Merchant*: "Every man remembers his own business." <note>original Latin: "Suam quisque homo rem meminit."</note> This proverbial sentiment describes a common human habit: someone who dozes off during another person's affairs stays awake and attentive to his own. On this point, Ennius rightly advises in the works of Aulus Gellius:
> Let this be a proof always ready at hand for you:
> Do not expect friends to do what you can do yourself.
There is a very beautiful fable by Aesop regarding the same sentiment about the little bird called the Crested Lark, who does not believe there is any danger as long as her business is entrusted to the hands of others. Plautus alluded to this proverb in *The Little Carthaginian*: "Are you testing whether we know how to remember our own affairs?" He alluded to it more directly in *Phormio*: "But if he had left a fortune of ten talents," etc. Whatever is dear to our hearts, we remember; and for the most part, negligence is the mother of forgetfulness.

### To sleep on either eye.

Plautus in *Pseudolus*: "As for that matter, rest easy on either eye." <note>original Latin: "De isthac re in utrumuis conquiescito."</note> This has the same meaning as what we recorded above: "To sleep on either ear." <note>Erasmus previously discussed "In utramvis aurem dormire," meaning to be free from worry.</note> A joke was snatched by the comic poet from a variation of words. It follows immediately in the play: "Which eye? In the ear?" And the innovator responds: "But that saying is too common." This notes the general human eagerness for constantly inventing new variations of such sayings.

### Troy bears no grudge against the Corinthians.

<margin>X</margin> <note>original Greek: "Κορινθίοις οὐκ ἐμέμφετο τὸ ἴλιον."</note> That is: 
Troy by no means accuses the Corinthians. 
One might use this line to secretly reproach someone for cowardice—someone who has behaved in such a way that his enemies have no reason to be particularly angry with him. However, it is a poem by Simonides which, according to Aristotle in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, the Corinthians took offense to, as if it were written against their excellence, because they did not seem to have performed any particularly noble deeds in the Trojan War. 

It can also be twisted in another way: for instance, if someone wrote so foolishly against <term>good letters</term> <note>A term Erasmus used for classical literature and humanist studies.</note> that he actually commended them rather than defamed them. Plutarch, in his *Life of Dion*, interprets the verse of the adage differently: "For it leads, just as Simonides says, O Sossius, Troy does not complain against the Corinthians, who marched with the Achaeans, because the descendants of Glaucus, who were originally from Corinth, fought zealously as their allies." From these words of Plutarch, it is clear that the proverb suggests one should refrain from offense if those who once were well-deserving should ever cause harm, but rather forgive the present offense for the sake of previous services.

### Maras.

<note>original Greek: "Μάρας."</note> They say there was a man of this name at Beroea in Syria who was extremely wealthy, yet nonetheless kind and helpful to all citizens and guests. From this, it became a commonly accepted term applied to men who seemed born for the benefit of their fellow men. A rather long story about this is told in the Greek collections; but it seemed enough to me to touch upon it, lest I spend my efforts poorly. For I suspect this proverb may be fraudulent and substituted for another. If anyone is seized by a desire to investigate further, there is a work which Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous Venetian printer of Erasmus's work.</note> printed after my adages were already completed.

### From Nannacus.

<note>original Greek: "Ἀπὸ ναννάκου."</note> This is used when we indicate that something is drawn from the most extreme antiquity. King Nannacus is said to have lived before Deucalion <note>The Greek "Noah" figure who survived the great flood.</note>, and to have predicted the coming deluge. We have mentioned him elsewhere as well. Stephanus mentions this in his dictionary under the entry for "Ino," citing another proverb derived from the same source: "To weep for the things of Nannacus." <note>original Greek: "τῶν ναννάκου κλαύσω."</note> This means to weep over ancient or inevitable calamities. Even if we read "Annacus" instead of "Nannacus" in Stephanus. The Latins use a similar figure of speech, such as "traced back to the age of the Aborigines," etc., or "as if you were speaking with Evander's mother." <note>Both suggest something incredibly old-fashioned or ancient.</note> And related to this is the saying: "Older than Cronus," or "You are speaking of things older than the parchment." <note>original Greek: "πρεσβύτερός κρόνου" and "ἀρχαιότερα τῆς διφθέρας λέγεις."</note>

### An ass at the flute.

<note>original Greek: "ὄνος πρὸς αὐλόν."</note> This should be said when someone does not notice, understand, or praise things that are skillfully said. For there are certain living creatures which nature...

<meta>The catchword "non" (not) indicates the start of the next page's sentence, continuing the description of animals' natural lack of appreciation for music or art.</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Roman proverbs, transitioning from metaphors of indifference—symbolized by the donkey's lack of musical appreciation—to sayings derived from mythology, drama, and social satire. ...a sense of music seems to reside in them: such as in horses, birds, and snakes. But a song does not move a donkey. A kindred saying to this is: **An ass at the lyre.** <note>original Greek: ὄνῳ πρὸς λύραν; Latin: Afinus ad lyram</note>

### To weave a cloak for Orestes. XLVIII
-> **To weave a cloak for Orestes.** <note>original Greek: Ὀρέστῃ χλαῖναν ὑφαίνειν</note> That is, <-
To weave a mantle for Orestes was a saying used for one who prepared a gift for someone likely to misuse it. For Orestes, in his madness, used to tear his clothes to pieces. This is a half-line of heroic verse taken from Aristophanes in *The Birds*: "Next, to weave a cloak for Orestes, so that he doesn't strip people while shivering with cold." <note>original Greek: Εἶτα δ' ὀρέστῃ χλαῖναν ὑφαίνειν, ἵνα μὴ ῥιγῶν λωποδυτῇ</note>
The ancient commentary <term>Scholium: an explanatory note written in the margin of ancient manuscripts</term> warns that Orestes was a certain street-mugger who used to attack people in the darkness by feigning madness, and then strip them of their clothing. Thus, the proverb is appropriately used when someone advises that something should be given to a thieving man so that he does not snatch it away. This adage did not originate with Aristophanes, but was adopted by him. For with this roundabout phrase, he is describing winter.

### Pandeletian sentences. XLIX
-> **Pandeletian sentences.** <note>original Greek: πανδελετείους γνώμας</note> That is, Pandeletian opinion. <-
In his play *The Worse Men*, Cratinus calls a peevish and troublesome opinion "Pandeletian," as they cite. It is named after a certain Pandeletus, a sycophant <term>sycophant: in ancient Athens, a professional informer who brought legal charges for profit</term> of that class who, to make a profit, hurl grand accusations at people—as Phormio says in Terence—and cast their votes with similar zeal.

### More long-lived than a Sibyl. L
The long life of the Sibyl gave rise to a proverb. Propertius says in the second book of his *Elegies*:
"But all the age of the Sibyl shall not change me."
He used "the age of the Sibyl" to mean any length of time, however long. Virgil, in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, calls her the long-lived priestess. And Servius, in his commentary on that passage, adds that Apollo, captured by love for the Sibyl, gave her the choice to ask for whatever she wished; she, picking up a handful of sand, asked for as many years of life. Apollo replied that this could happen if she left the island of Erythraea and never returned to it. She went therefore to Cumae, where, her bodily strength having failed, she retained her life only in her voice. When her fellow citizens learned of this—it is uncertain whether out of envy or pity—they sent a letter to her, sealed with chalk in the ancient manner. Upon seeing the earth of her homeland, she dissolved into death. Thus did Phoebus Apollo deceive his own prophetess.

### To snatch food from the flame. LI
Terence, in *The Eunuch*, said of a parasite that he was of such a character that he would even "snatch food from the flame," <note>original Latin: è flāma cibū peteret</note> which is to say, he would suffer or do anything for the sake of food. Catullus explains the proverb in his *Epigrams*:
"Rufa of Bologna cheats Rufulus, the wife of Menenius, whom you have often seen in the graveyards snatching a meal from the funeral pyre itself, when, chasing bread that rolled down from the fire, she was beaten by the half-shaved undertaker." <note>This refers to the "silicernium," a funeral feast; snatching food from it was a sign of the lowest desperation and social standing.</note>

### He turned him into a Harpocrates. LII
Catullus, in his *Epigrams*, used the expression **He turned him into a Harpocrates** <note>original Latin: Reddidit Harpocratem</note> in a proverbial way to mean "he imposed silence." The poem is as follows:
"Gellius had heard that his uncle used to scold anyone who spoke of or indulged in pleasures. To prevent this happening to himself, he seduced his uncle's own wife, and thus turned his uncle into a Harpocrates. He got what he wanted; for even if he should now insult the uncle himself, the uncle will not say a word."
Harpocrates was a god depicted by the ancients with a finger moved to his mouth to command silence, much like the goddess Angerona among the Romans.

### He who is a good Athenian. LIII
Plato, in the first book of *The Laws*, records a proverb "then spoken by many: that those among the Athenians who are good are remarkably so, and this seems most truly said." <note>original Greek: τότε ὑπὸ πολλῶν λεγόμενον... ueriffime dictū uidetur</note> Plato meant that in a poorly established and ill-mannered Republic, those who are good must be naturally and exceptionally good. For they cannot be thought to be faking virtue among the wicked (where they could have gained favor by being like the rest), nor can they be corrupted by the depraved morals of others and the contagion of vice. The same can be said of the Roman state, in...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Latin and Greek adages. The previous page ended with "Pandeletian sentences," a phrase used for peevish opinions. ...not being corrupted by it is a proof of a certain extraordinary integrity. By a similar argument, Terence infers the honesty of his son. It can be applied to courtly life, a kind of path that invites one to destruction.

### Worthy of cedar.

Things are said to be **worthy of cedar** <note>original Latin: Digna cedro</note> which deserve immortality, and are of such a nature that they ought to be consecrated for posterity. Horace says in *The Art of Poetry*: "We hope that poems can be composed which are worthy of being smeared with cedar oil." <note>original Latin: Speramus carmina fingi / Posse linenda cedro.</note> Persius says likewise: "And having spoken things worthy of cedar." <note>original Latin: Et cedro digna locutus.</note> The metaphor is taken from the nature of the tree; things smeared with its juice do not experience decay. Indeed, Pliny relates in Book 13, chapter 13, that the books of Numa, although they were made of paper, lasted for five hundred and thirty-five years while buried. In Book 16, he also lists cedar among the "eternal" materials. Dioscorides says that the juice of this tree is most highly approved when it is thick, translucent, of a very strong smell, and does not run but thickens and remains in drops. It has a cleansing power; it consumes living bodies but keeps dead ones uncorrupted. For this reason, some report it is called "life of the corpse." <note>original Greek: νεκρῶ ζώω</note> To the same point belongs this: "Poems fearing neither mackerel nor incense." <note>original Latin: Nec scombros metuentia carmina, nec thus. Note: This refers to cheap paper being used as wrapping for fish or spices, the opposite of a preserved book.</note> Also Martial: "Lest, snatched away quickly to the dark kitchen, you cover young tuna with damp papyrus." <note>original Latin: Ne nigram cito raptus in culinam, / Cordylas madida tegas papyro.</note> And Horace: "Either you will flee to Utica, or be sent bound to Ilerda." <note>original Latin: Aut fugies Vticam, aut unctas mitteris Ilerdam. Note: Meaning the book will be sent away to the provinces as scrap paper if it is not successful.</note>

### Telemachus’s pot.

**Telemachus’s pot.** <note>original Greek: τηλεμάχου χύτρα</note> Athenaeus mentions this adage in Book 9. He writes that Telemachus of Acharnae was some person who mostly lived on beans. From this, one may gather that it was customary to use this phrase for stingy or sordid people.

### One thing is a scepter, another a plectrum.

Indeed, I would not altogether contend that this is a proverb, but nonetheless the phrasing and character of the speech are so similar to a proverb that "one fig is hardly more like another." It is what Stratonicus the cithara-player <term>Cithara-player: a professional performer on a large, lyre-like instrument</term> replied to King Ptolemy when the king was disputing somewhat too stubbornly with him about the art of singing: "Because, O King, a scepter is one thing, but a plectrum <term>Plectrum: a small tool used to pluck the strings of an instrument</term> is another." <note>original Greek: ὅτι ὦ Βασιλεῦ σκῆπτρον, ἑτέρου ᾗ πλῆκτρον</note> There will be occasion to use this whenever a rich and powerful man, relying on his fortune, debates as an equal with a learned man—since being rich or fortunate is quite a different thing from being literate.

### The things that hurt are troublesome to touch.

Amphis in *The Vine-Dresser*, cited in Stobaeus: "In whatever places a man has been unfortunate, he takes the least pleasure in approaching those spots." <note>original Greek: Εν οἷς αν ἀτυχήση ἄνθρωπος τόποις, / ἥκιστα τόποις πλησιάζων ἥδεται.</note> That is: "In those places where a man is not particularly happy, it is least pleasant to move one's hand toward them." Everyone is unwilling to hear of their own misfortunes, especially those joined with some disgrace, such as the lowliness of one's family or a physical defect. Therefore, it is a mark of courtesy not to "rub a wound raw" <note>original Latin: refricare uulnus</note> or touch an ulcer.

### Gold tested by fire.

**Gold tested by fire** <note>original Greek: ὁ χρυσὸς τῷ πυρὶ δοκιμαθείς</note> is said of one whose loyalty has been explored and proven by adversity. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> uses this comparison in the ninth book of his *Letters to Friends*. Likewise, Pindar in the fourth *Nemean* hymn: "Refined gold shows all its brightness." <note>original Greek: ὁ χρυσὸς ἑψόμενος αὐγὰς ἁπάσας</note> Again in the *Pythian* hymns: "To the one who puts it to the test, gold shines in the touchstone <term>Touchstone: a dark stone used to test the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves when rubbed</term>, as does an upright mind." <note>original Greek: πειρῶντι δὲ χρυσὸς ἐν βασάνω πρέπει καὶ νόος ὀρθὸς</note> Theognis says: "You will find me in all deeds like refined gold, red to the sight, when rubbed against the touchstone." <note>original Greek: Εὑρήσεις δέ με πᾶσιν ἐπ’ ἔργμασιν, ὥσπερ ἄπεφθον / χρυσὸν, ἐρυθρὸν ἰδεῖν, τριβομενον βασάνω.</note> The same author elsewhere: "When it comes to the whetstone and is compared on the touchstone with lead, if it is refined gold, it will all be excellent." <note>original Greek: Εἰς βάσανον δ’ ἐλθὼν παρατριβομενός τε μολίβδω / χρυσὸς ἄπεφθος ἐὼν, καλὸς ἅπας αν ἔση.</note>

--- Page 997 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on proverbs related to testing character and the permanence of virtue. The previous page concluded with the metaphor of "cedar-worthy" works—things that deserve to endure through the ages. This page begins by linking that concept to the biblical testing of faith, comparing it to the purification of gold.</meta>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY
<meta>catchword: tore.</meta>

The Apostle Saint Peter also makes use of this comparison in his first epistle: <term>much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire</term> <note>original Greek: πολὺ τιμιώτερον χρυσίου τοῦ ἀπολλυμένου διὰ πυρὸς δὲ δοκιμαζομένου</note>. That is: "Much more precious than gold, which perishes, or 'destructive' gold, which is nevertheless tested by fire." It is a peculiar property of gold—not short of a miracle—that it not only fails to deteriorate in fire, but shines more and more brilliantly. In the same way, a person who is truly good, when tossed by the storms of misfortune, illuminates the virtue of their soul rather than losing it. Pliny, in Book 33, writes that gold is preferred above all other metals primarily for this reason: it is the only thing that loses nothing to fire; the material survives safely even in conflagrations. Indeed, the more often it is burned, the more it improves in quality. He adds that it is a proof of "honest gold" <note>original Latin: probi auri</note> if it glows red like fire; such gold they call **refined** <note>original Latin: obrisum; a technical term for gold tested by fire</note>.

->To draw down the moon.<-
->LIX<-

<term>He draws down the moon</term> <note>original Greek: τὴν σελήνην κατασπᾷ</note>. This was commonly said of someone who seemed to be facing extreme adversity. A commentator on the fourth book of Apollonius suggests the phrase comes from Aglaonice, daughter of Hegemon. Because of her expertise in astronomy, she could predict lunar eclipses, and she would boast that she was going to draw the moon down from the sky to the earth. Nemesis <note>the goddess of retribution</note> heard such arrogant speech and soon exacted punishment. This is the origin of the proverb.

->You seek the lion’s tracks.<-
->LX<-

<term>You seek the lion’s tracks</term> <note>original Greek: τοῦ λέοντος ἴχνη ζητεῖς</note>. This is a stinging remark aimed at someone who is fierce in words but a coward in action. It is derived from one of Aesop's fables, which tells of a certain hunter who met a shepherd and asked if he had seen a lion anywhere, so that he might show it to him. The shepherd replied: "I will show you the lion's tracks right now, for they are not far off." At this, the hunter said, "That is enough; I require nothing more." This is similar to a phrase found elsewhere: <term>You seek the tracks while the bear is present</term> <note>original Greek: ἄρκτου παρούσης τὰ ἴχνια ζητεῖς</note>.

->One ship does not carry it.<-
->LXI<-

<term>One ship does not carry it</term> <note>original Greek: οὐ μία ναῦς ἄγει</note>. This phrase acts as a proverb in its own right. It is appropriate to use whenever we signify a multitude of people too large for a single ship to contain. For instance, if one were to say: <term>One ship does not carry all the uneducated</term> <note>original Greek: ὡς ἀπαιδεύτους ἡ μία ναῦς ἄγει</note>. It is also found in the works of Theognis:
> <term>You will not find these men by searching, nor indeed all</term>
> <term>The men whom a single ship does not carry</term>. <note>original Greek: Τοὺς δ’ οὐχ’ εὑρήσεις διζήμενος... This implies a group so numerous or widespread they exceed the capacity of one vessel.</note> That is,
Searching among all people, you will not find
Those whom a single raft certainly does not carry.

->This year's harvest.<-
->LXII<-

Plautus, in his play *The Haunted House* (*Mostellaria*), used the phrase **this year’s harvest** <note>original Latin: horna messis</note> as a proverbial figure of speech for a very large profit, as if to say: "as much gain as is expected to come from the fields this year." These are the words of the comic playwright:
> Castor! Not for a long time has a cold bath washed me more delightfully, 
> Nor do I think I have ever been better 'built up' by Scapha.
These words are spoken by a young woman. Then the old woman (the *lena*), wishing that the girl's beauty might yield as much profit as possible, says:
> May the outcome for everyone be like **this year's harvest**.
The girl, being simple and not quite understanding what she meant, asks: "What does that harvest have to do with my bathing?" Closely related to this figure is another by the same author in *The Weevil* (*Curculio*): "This vintage is not enough for this old woman alone." He means she is so fond of drinking that all the wine produced that year would be too little for her thirst.

->Glaucus lives in the sea after eating the grass.<-
->LXIII<-

<term>Glaucus lives in the sea after eating the grass</term> <note>original Greek: γλαῦκος φαγὼν πόαν οἰκεῖ ἐν θαλάσσῃ</note>. This was apparently said in jest about those who have died but are commonly believed to be alive. Such an opinion occupied the minds of our own people for several years, even to the point of madness, regarding Prince Charles, Duke of the Burgundians <note>Charles the Bold, who died in 1477; many of his subjects refused to believe he had fallen in battle</note>. Even though he had perished in war, there were still those who did not hesitate to assert—at great risk to their own affairs—that he was still among the living. Regarding Glaucus, the Greeks tell a story of this sort: there was a certain Glaucus of Anthedon, a fisherman, who was by far the best of all in his skill at swimming. To make himself seem more like a miracle, he devised a trick: he would swim out of the harbor while the people of Anthedon watched until he was out of sight. Having returned to land in a remote place, he would stay there for several days. Then, when he chose to be seen, he would swim back into the harbor in full view of those standing on the shore.

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning the testing of character through fire, the arrogance of claiming supernatural powers (drawing down the moon), and the disparity between boastful words and cowardly actions. He also notes the historical phenomenon of "lost leaders" who are rumored to be alive after death, comparing the myth of Glaucus to the Burgundian belief in the survival of Charles the Bold.</summary>
<keywords>testing virtue, gold and fire, Aglaonice, Aesop's fables, Plautus, Charles the Bold, Glaucus, Greek mythology, nautical metaphors, delusions of survival</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the story of Glaucus, a legendary fisherman turned sea-god, which began on the previous page. Erasmus is exploring the origins of various Greek and Latin proverbs, moving from the mythological (the story of Glaucus) to social stereotypes (the Roman view of Greek luxury) and finally to idiomatic expressions for worthlessness.</meta>

fisherman: When his friends marveled and asked where on earth he had stayed for so long, he pretended that he had been living in the waves of the sea. He bolstered this miracle with a clever lie. During the winter months, when other fishermen could catch nothing, he would ask the citizens what kind of fish they wanted brought to them. Whatever they ordered, he would bring, making it seem as if they had been prepared for this purpose beforehand and kept enclosed elsewhere. It eventually happened that this imposter was devoured by a sea beast. And that was the end of his "comedy." Furthermore, when he did not return from the sea, a popular rumor spread that Glaucus, having tasted a certain herb, had become immortal and was living in the sea. 

A commentator on the poet Apollonius relates similar things about Glaucus: that he was a fisherman who once, when exhausted by the multitude of fish he had caught, threw his burden down in the middle of a field. There, a thing marvelous to tell occurred: one of the fish, already dying, tasted a certain herb and came back to life. Glaucus, observing this, ate the same herb and was rendered immortal. Eventually, out of weariness with life, he threw himself into the sea. Some say he was turned into a sea god, others into a fish; Athenaeus provides more details on this in his seventh book, where he occasionally cites Alexis in his play <term>The Man Turned into Glaucus</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν ἀπεγλαυκωμένῳ</note>. 

If you wish to know the rest of the trifles the Greeks tell about Glaucus, read the seventh book of Athenaeus, which prattles on—enough to make one sick—about the Glaucus-fish and the Glaucus-demon. I am not permitted to repeat so much nonsense here. I have described this fiction with my mind almost rebelling. For to speak simply what I feel, it smells to me like some Greek writer, whoever he was, invented this proverb just so he could recount this fable. I preferred, however, to waste some effort on the matter rather than give certain unlearned men an excuse for slander, claiming that I passed it over out of ignorance, especially since it is found even in the printed Greek commentaries.

### To play the Greek.
<margin>LX</margin>

If there are proverbs among the Greeks like <term>to act like a Chalcidian</term>, <term>to act like a Lesbian</term>, <term>to act like a Corinthian</term>, and others of that kind, what is to stop us from including the adage used by the Romans? Plautus, in his play *The Haunted House*, used <term>to play the Greek</term> <note>original Latin: Pergraecari</note> to mean leading a life of pleasure. The words of Plautus sufficiently indicate what it means to "play the Greek":
> Drink, he says, day and night; play the Greek.
> Buy mistresses, set them free, feed 
> parasites, and shop for food magnificently.

So much for him. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his third speech against Verres, says: "A conversation began among them, and an invitation followed to drink in the Greek fashion." The Greek nation has a bad reputation throughout the Latin poets and likewise in Cicero, not only as being addicted to pleasures and effeminate through luxuries, but also as being of <term>slippery faith</term> <note>original Latin: lubrica fide; i.e., untrustworthy</note>. This may be because the Romans of old, who were still unrefined and held to that ancient integrity, viewed Greek elegance as mere luxury. Or perhaps a rivalry in studies or an ancient hatred was the cause for writing such insults about the Greeks. Or it might be that truly some Greeks in Italy were exactly as Juvenal depicts them—something that even Lucian does not hesitate to admit in his book *On Salaried Posts*—and from those individuals, the Romans judged the entire race.

### Conos and Artoxya.

<term>Conos and Artoxya</term> <note>original Greek: Κῶνος ἀρτόξυα</note>. This refers to things that are similar and correspond to one another. Some learned men think that a **conos** is a baker’s tool, not unlike an **artoxya**, which seems to signify a kitchen knife. However, from what follows shortly after in the writings of Pollux, it appears that **Conos** were small gifts given to children, suited to their age, such as bracelets. Therefore, consider whether this might apply to those who try to win someone's labor with a cheap and trivial little gift.

### Not even worth a strap.

<term>Not worth a cordula</term> <note>original Greek: Κορδύλης οὐκ ἄξιος</note>, or <term>Not even worth a strap</term>. This was said of a worthless man of no value. This proverb survives even today, commonly tossed about among Latin speakers, although I suspect the cheapness of the **cordula** fish gave rise to the proverb. It is the worst of fish, except that it is smaller, as Pliny testifies in Book 32, Chapter 11. Martial also shows the cheapness of these fish in his eleventh book:
> First, a lettuce will be given to you, useful for moving 
> the bowels, and leeks with their own cut fibers.
> Next, an old **cordula**, larger than a thin arm,
> but which, with sprigs of rue, may cover the eggs.
Presently, the poet mentions expensive things to deceive his companion...

> And the bounty of the yard and the birds of the marshes.
<note>Erasmus quotes the Roman poet Martial (Epigrams 10.37), illustrating how one might exaggerate the luxuries of a country estate to entice a guest.</note>

### By the ship. LXVII

<note>original Greek: Κατὰ ναῦν</note>. That is, "By the ship" is said of things that are arranged in order, and which fit and harmonize, because the equipment of ships is usually stored each in its proper place. For my part, I am uncertain whether the words ascribed to this proverb—<gloss>the sails are prepared according to the ship</gloss> <note>original Greek: κατὰ ναῦν ἀρτύεται</note>—are truly part of it. For not every sail is suitable for every vessel.

### He has advanced by a cubit. LXVIII

<note>original Greek: Κατὰ πῆχυν ἐπέδωκε</note>. That is, "He has advanced by a cubit." This was said of someone who had been promoted to better things: whether when someone progresses through a legitimate order, or when they advance by great additions. For a "cubit" <note>A unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches.</note> signifies both a standard measure, so you understand nothing should be skipped, and a somewhat large measure, so you perceive a significant increase. Indeed, we are accustomed to measuring small things by the width of fingers or the span of palms.

### The assembly is held over your life. LXIX

Plautus used this as a proverbial figure in his play *The Pot of Gold* (*Aulularia*):
-> I shall go inside, where the assembly is being held over my life. <-
For the character was deliberating whether or not he should marry the girl he loved. The phrase is taken from the Roman <term>comitia</term> <note>The public assemblies where the Roman people voted on laws or elected magistrates.</note>, in which new magistrates were created by the votes of the people. Therefore, when a decision is being made about any matter upon which someone's happiness depends, it is rightly said that an "assembly is held over their head."

### Until hoarseness. LXX

Just as the Greeks say <note>original Greek: ἄχρι κόρου</note>, that is, "until satiety," so Plautus spoke even more charmingly, saying "until hoarseness," for that which is done excessively, repeatedly, or loudly, to the point that the voice of the person shouting so often grows hoarse. It appears in *The Pot of Gold* in this manner:
-> Have you thrust me here toward this most stingy old man, <-
-> Where if we ask for anything, we must ask until hoarseness  Before anything is given? <-

### They are sacrificing to Ceres. LXXI

Likewise, just as the Greeks say <note>original Greek: ἑστία θύουσι</note>, that is, "they sacrifice to the Hearth," so Plautus almost indicates that it was common among the Latins to say, "they are sacrificing to Ceres," whenever wine was missing at a banquet. This is because in the sacred rites of this goddess it was a sin to bring in wine, just as it was among the Greeks in the sacrifices of certain goddesses, as we showed in the proverb regarding <term>wineless sacrifices</term> <note>original Greek: νηφάλια θυσíαι</note>. The passage is in *The Pot of Gold*, in these very words:
-> Strobilus, are they going to perform a wedding for Ceres? <-
-> Why? Because I see no wine <note>original: temetum (an archaic Latin word for wine)</note> has been brought. <-

### More useless than a blax. LXXII

<note>original Greek: Βλὰξ ἀχρηστότερος</note>. That is, "more useless than a blax," or more worthless. It was said of a man of no account and no good use. It is taken from a fish that is so useless, tasteless, and foul-smelling that it is even rejected by dogs. It is a fish not unlike the Catfish: if we believe the opinions of Greek etymologies, I think it refers to something sterile, whose name is *Blacia*, from which it is suspected the proverb arose. Hesychius also calls it a Sturgeon, though this fish holds the primary place among fishes. He adds there is a marshy place near Cumae, where he thinks astrologers dwell, because "blaces"—that is, fools—resort to them, seeking oracles from the stars. It is certain that stupid, lazy, soft, and tasteless men are called <note>original Greek: Βλᾶκας</note>, from which comes the verb <note>original Greek: Βλακεύειν</note>, to act softly and lazily, and "blakikos," which means foolishly and insipidly. It appears that from this word the Latins derived *Flaccus* (floppy), *flaccidus* (flaccid), and *flaccescere* (to wither). But "enough of the fool’s foot."

### ALITĒRIOS. LXXIII

<note>original Greek: Ἀλιτήριος</note> was commonly said of one who took the property of others by force. It was born from an event of this kind: during the times of the Aetolian War, such a great shortage of grain fell upon the Athenians that the poor, driven by hunger, snatched away the flour of the captives. From there, the word began to be transferred to a man who was criminal in any way. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Curiosity*, gives a different origin for this name. Namely, when Athens was suffering greatly from hunger, and those who had been ordered to do so did not bring their grain into public, but ground it at home secretly and at night, certain busybodies walking about noticed the noise of the millstones and betrayed them. These people were indeed called *Aliterii* <note>Essentially meaning "those of the mill-sin" or "sinful millers."</note>, as were "sycophants" <note>Originally meaning "informers" or "tale-bearers."</note>. However, different from this explanation is...

# ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<note>This section continues from page 875, discussing the Greek term "Aliterios."</note>
Aristotle mentions this in his *Problems*, suggesting that *Aliterios* <note>original Greek: ἀλιτήριος, meaning a cursed person or an "avenging spirit"</note> is derived from "shunning." For among the Greeks, the word *aleo* <note>original Greek: ἀλεώ</note> means both "I grind" and "I shun." He writes that the term was applied to a person of such wickedness that anyone who managed to shun or escape him was considered fortunate. In his play *The Knights*, Aristophanes calls those who violated the temple of Pallas Athena "Aliterioi." He writes: <gloss>I say that you are one of the Aliterioi</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῶν ἀλιτηρίων σε φημι γεγονέναι</note>, that is: "I say you are of the number of those polluted ones who invaded the citadel of the goddess." The commentator, in reviewing this, also records the following: A certain Cylon occupied the citadel through tyranny and was caught plundering the temple of Minerva. He himself escaped when he found the opportunity, but the Athenians dragged his friends, who had fled to the goddess's altar for sanctuary, away from there and killed them. Thus, those who violated the rights of suppliants were called *Aliterioi*. Indeed, those who had killed the suppliants in the temple were later punished with death. Finally, Ceres is also called *Aliteria*, and Jupiter *Aliterios*, because during a public famine they protected the millers <note>The word play here connects "grinding grain" to the name "Aliterios."</note> so that no one would plunder the flour. They also suggest this: those who are frustrated in their hope and do not achieve what they attempted are called *aliterias*. The ambiguity arises from the fact that *aleo* means two things: "I grind" and "I turn away/shun," from which we also get *alites*, meaning "a wanderer." Furthermore, just as *aliterios* is used for a sacrilegious and impious person, so *aliteriæ* are said to be those who commit sacrilege.

->Fish is no good, unless fresh.<-
<margin>LXX</margin>
"Fish is no good, unless fresh" remains a common saying to this day. It is said particularly of a guest or a common friend who is not unwelcome upon first arrival, but begins to stink before three days have passed. As Plautus says:
> A lover of a procuress is just like a fish: he’s no good, unless fresh.

Someone jokes in a play by Alexis (quoted by Athenaeus) that while some of the more frugal people abstained from things that had a soul <note>Meaning they were vegetarians.</note>, he himself had brought nothing of the sort—namely, having bought "dead" fish. But today, those who sell them mimic the tremors of life with their hands to pretend they are alive, even if they died two days ago.

->Nothing is friendlier to a man than a timely friend.<-
<margin>LXXI</margin>
A favor performed at the right time is most welcome. On the other hand, an untimely favor is usually quite bothersome. Plautus says:
> Nothing is friendlier to a man than a timely friend.

Conversely, untimely benevolence is no different from enmity.

->To push a donkey into the rocks.<-
<margin>LXXII</margin>
This has the flavor of a proverb, as Horace writes in his *Epistles*:
> He who pushed his unyielding donkey into the rocks.

This will apply to those born with a perverse nature, who, although they are not wise themselves, refuse to obey the advice of those who counsel them well. These people should even be pushed toward the goal they are aiming for, so that, taught by misfortune, they might finally recognize their own folly. It originated from a story about a rustic who was leading his donkey through the Alps covered in snow; when the beast would not obey the bridle and kept wandering toward the edge, the man in a rage pushed it into the rocks:
> And rightly so; for who would labor to save the unwilling?

->You seem to me to be a "Lambda."<-
<margin>LXXIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Δοκεῖς δέ μοι καὶ λάβδα κατὰ Λεσβίους</note>. That is: "You seem to me to be a 'Lambda' according to the Lesbians." It indicates, as if by the riddle of the first letter, a vice attributed to that nation, as we have pointed out elsewhere <note>The letter L (Lambda) stood for a specific sexual act (fellatio), which ancient Greeks stereotypically associated with the people of Lesbos.</note>. It is taken from Aristophanes' *Assemblywomen*.

->A mocking face behind the back.<-
<margin>LXXIV</margin>
Persius calls a secret mockery a "posterior grimace" <note>original: "postica fanna." Modern editions usually read "posticae sanna," meaning a grimace made behind one's back.</note> proverbially, referring to those who mock someone from behind:
> Confront the grimace behind your back.
Likewise:
> O Janus, whom no stork-beak mocks from behind,
> Nor has a hand mimicked white moving ears,
> Nor a tongue lolled out as far as a thirsty Apulian dog.

For some people mock others from behind their heads with gestures of this kind <note>Erasmus refers to making a "stork" with the fingers or "donkey ears" with the hands behind someone's head.</note>.

->The raven and the snake.<-
<margin>LXXV</margin>
<note>original Greek: Κόραξ τὸν ὄφιν</note>. That is: "The raven and the snake," used when someone perishes by their own discovery. It is taken from one of Aesop's fables. A hungry raven saw a snake sleeping in a sunny spot and snatched it up, but died from the snake's bite. It is related to what we have reported elsewhere: <gloss>The crow and the scorpion</gloss> <note>original Greek: κορώνη τὸν σκορπίον</note>. One may also twist this to refer to a man endangered by his own gluttony.

This page begins with a brief note on the death of Diogenes the Cynic before detailing adages 80 through 84, which cover mythological hubris, metaphors for effeminacy and stinginess, and the behavior of the youth.</meta>

Diogenes the Cynic died from eating raw octopus. <note>Diogenes (c. 412–323 BCE) was the famous "barrel-dwelling" philosopher who advocated for a life according to nature; various accounts of his death exist, including this one involving indigestion.</note>

### The spear of Caeneus.
-> LXXX <-

**The spear of Caeneus** <note>original Greek: Τὸ καινέως δόρυ</note>, that is, *Cænei hasta*. Caeneus, the son of Elatus and King of the Lapiths, had originally been a beautiful girl. She was transformed from a girl into a man by the grace of Neptune, whom she had admitted to her bed. To him <note>Caeneus</note> it was also granted that he could not be wounded by any blow, nor could he fall by the sword, as Ovid recounts in the twelfth book of his *Metamorphoses*. They say that he even competed with Apollo. Furthermore, it was his custom to command those who came to him to swear by his spear; from this, the proverb was taken, as the commentator on the first book of Apollonius’s *Argonautica* indicates. Eustathius also cites this passage in his commentary on the first book of the *Iliad*. He adds that when Caeneus was the most outstanding man of his age, he fixed a javelin in the middle of the marketplace and commanded the gods to count themselves <note>i.e., to pay him homage as a god</note>. Jupiter, offended by this ferocity, took punishment upon him. For when he was waging war with the Lapiths <note>Erasmus's source here likely means the Centaurs, who were the traditional enemies of the Lapith king Caeneus</note> and was invulnerable, they defeated the man in this way: the Lapiths <note>Centaurs</note> threw oaks and fir trees at him, pinning him down and driving him into the earth.

### Melons.
-> LXXXI <-

**Melons** <note>original Greek: πέπονες</note>, that is, *Pepones*. Men who are soft, effeminate, and hardly masculine are called "melons" as a proverbial insult. Homer says in the second book of the *Iliad*:
**O melons, you disgraceful things, Achaean women, no longer Achaean men.** <note>original Greek: ὦ πέπονες, κακ’ ἐλέγχε’, Ἀχαιΐδες, οὐκ ἔτ’ Ἀχαιοί.</note>
Eustathius, in the seventh book of this work, shows that the metaphor is taken from that fruit which, as soon as it has ripened, is indeed sweet, but is flabby and useless. However, this same word is sometimes used not as an insult, but as a more flattering and friendly way of addressing someone, as in the sixth book of the *Iliad*:
**O dear one, O Menelaus.** <note>original Greek: ὦ πέπον ὦ Μενέλαε. Here, "pepon" implies a "ripe" or "mellow" friend.</note>

### Dirty-knuckled.
-> LXXXII <-

The Greeks use the proverbial insult **dirty-knuckled** <note>original Greek: ῥυποκόνδυλοι</note> to describe those who are filthy and excessively stingy. The nickname is derived from those who have dirt sitting under their fingernails and are unwilling to spend even a tiny amount of money to give a coin to a barber to clean their nails. For the word *rhupos* <note>original Greek: ῥύπος</note> properly signifies that dirt which collects at the tips of the fingernails and toes, and *kondylos* <note>original Greek: κόνδυλος</note> means the knuckle or joint of the finger. Julius Pollux, in Book 6, Chapter 4, calls the same people "living on dregs" <note>original Greek: τρυγόβιος</note>, as if they survive on the lees of wine. Some express the adage thus: **I am annoyed by that man's very filth.** <note>original Greek: ἄχθομαι αὐτῷ τῷ ῥύπῳ.</note> The Latins likewise call immoderate parsimony—that is, the vice contrary to luxury—"filth" (*sordes*), and a man subject to that vice "filthy" (*sordidum*).

### To play the youth.
-> LXXXIII <-

Horace used the word **to play the youth** (*Iuuenari*) in his *Art of Poetry*, both as a new coinage and as a proverb. The Greeks likewise use **to be young**, **to act like a youth**, or **to play the young man** <note>original Greek: νεάζειν, νεανιζεύειν, νεανιεύεσθαι</note> in a similar way, to mean acting in the manner of the young: rather boastfully, inconsiderately, or without counsel, or whatever else seems peculiar to that age. The further this is translated into other contexts, the more elegant it becomes; for instance, if someone were to call a florid and decked-out speech "acting like a youth" <note>original Greek: νεανιεύεσθαι</note>. Of the same form is "to act like a woman" <note>original Greek: γυναικίζειν</note>, meaning to represent a woman in gesture or dress. On account of their ignorance of affairs and their unrestrained passions, that age is more slippery; hence the Greeks say something was done "youthfully" <note>original Greek: νεανικῶς</note> when it was performed with more impulse than judgment. Basil, in a certain epistle, says: **And here it is clear that those who were not yet perfected in the inner man, nor had yet reached the full measure of age, were—as the proverb says—carried about and tossed by the waves.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐνταῦθα δῆλον ὅτι οὐδέπω κατηρτισμένος ἦν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, οὐδὲ εἰς τὸ τέλος ἐφθακότας τῆς ἡλικίας μέτρον, τό γε ποδηφορεῖσθαι τῷ κλύδωνί, ἡ παροιμία φησίν.</note> There is also found the term "to be at one's peak" <note>original Greek: ἀκμάζειν</note>, used for doing youthful things. Hyperides used it this way in his speech *Against Mantitheus*, as did Lysias *Against Nicarchus the Flute-player*. Laberius, as cited by Nonius, used the word *Adolescenturire* for the same thing: "I begin to feel like a teenager, and to do I know not what trifles."

### They praise as boys praise a peacock.
-> LXXXIIII <-

What Juvenal wrote against misers has the appearance of a proverb; they are people who merely praise poems but bestow nothing on the poet:
**The miserly praiser has learned only**
**To admire and to praise the eloquent so much,**
**As boys praise the bird of Juno.** <note>The peacock, sacred to Juno, is beautiful to look at but provides no practical use or sustenance.</note>
The same author says elsewhere:
**Integrity is praised—and left to freeze.** <note>Meaning people praise virtue but do nothing to support or reward it.</note>
The metaphor is too well known to require explanation. Ovid mentions the peacock elsewhere...

<meta>This page continues the collection of adages, specifically focusing on Greek-derived proverbs concerning human temperament, sudden changes in fortune, and historical anecdotes regarding the Samians and the Athenians. It follows the discussion of the "Spear of Caeneus" from the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>878</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

->The bird of Juno shows her praised feathers,<-
->If you watch in silence; if not, she hides her wealth.<-
<note>The "bird of Juno" is the peacock; this couplet suggests that beauty or talent is best displayed when not boastfully pursued.</note>

### White-livered. <margin>LXVII</margin>
**White-livered** <note>original Greek: Λευκηπατίας, *leukepatias*</note> was an epithet once used for the fearful. Clearchus, in his *Lives*—as cited by Zenodotus—says that a certain defect occurs in the livers of some people which makes them timid, and from this, the nickname was tossed about as a proverb. The word appears to be composed from the Greek for "white liver," because those whose livers are diseased are usually pale, a condition also seen in those in love. However, the term is particularly suited to the cowardly. <note>In ancient medicine, the liver was considered the seat of emotions; a "white" or bloodless liver suggested a lack of courage.</note>

### To die of laughter. <margin>LXX</margin>
Proverbial hyperboles include such phrases as **to die of laughter** and **to dissolve in laughter**, used to mean laughing excessively.
Homer writes in the eighteenth book of the *Odyssey*:
> But the noble suitors,
> Lifting their hands, died with laughter. <note>original Greek: γέλῳ ἔκθανον, *gelō ekthanon*</note>
That is:
->Then the splendid crowd of suitors,<-
->Dying of excessive laughter, raised their hands<-
->High toward the stars.<-
Terence also used this in *The Eunuch*: "Everyone was dying of laughter."

### The wall of Hipparchus. <margin>LXXXI</margin>
**The wall of Hipparchus** <note>original Greek: ἱππάρχου τειχίον</note> was a phrase used for anything that cost a great deal of money. This originated because Hipparchus, the son of Pisistratus, surrounded the Academy with a wall, and under the pretext of this project, he extorted a vast sum of money from the Athenians. The source for this is the *Suda*. <note>The Academy was a public grove and gymnasium in Athens, later famous as the site of Plato's school.</note>

### A nobody today, the greatest tomorrow. <margin>LXXXII</margin>
**He who is a nobody today will be the greatest tomorrow.** <note>original Greek: ὃ νῦν μὲν οὐδεὶς, αὔριον δ’ ἔσται μέγας</note>
This is said of someone to whom some immense honor has suddenly come beyond all expectation. In common speech, those who are raised from a miserable condition to high dignity are said to have "emerged from nothing." This appears in Aristophanes’ *The Knights*.

### You fear the evils of the Samians. <margin>LXXV</margin>
**You fear the evils of the Samians** <note>original Greek: τὰ Σαμίων ὑφορᾶσθε</note>. This was a common saying regarding those who feared treachery. They say that the Athenians once treated whatever Samians they captured with great severity; some they killed, and others they subjected to a devised form of legal execution. The Samians, in turn, tortured those Athenians they captured in the same manner. From this came the term **lettered Samians** <note>original Latin: *Samij literati*</note>. For the *Suda* indicates this was commonly said of those who feared immediate calamities. The same source indicates that "Samian" was used to describe a type of calamity, because the Athenians branded captured Samians with infamous marks, and the Samians soon did the same to the Athenians. <note>Historical sources suggest the Athenians branded Samians with an owl, and the Samians branded Athenians with a *samaina*, a type of ship.</note> Duris of Samos, the writer, relates many tragic exaggerations regarding the cruelty of Pericles and the Athenians toward the Samians, which Plutarch believes were largely fabricated to incite hatred against Pericles and Athens. A similar figure of speech is "the evils of the Magnesians."

### To fit the first-fruits of Pygmies to a colossus.
<margin>Fitting the first-fruits of Pygmies to a colossus.</margin> <note>original Greek: Ἀκροθίνια τῶν πυγμαίων κολοσσῷ ἐφαρμόζειν</note>
This was said of those who undertook a vain and foolish task, or who inappropriately matched the smallest things with the largest—for instance, if someone were to follow a trivial and minute matter with the most ample and formal praises. Philostratus says in *Nicetas*: "He did not realize he was fitting Pygmy first-fruits to a colossus." Although the *Suda*, citing this passage, says "of Pygmies" rather than "Pygmy." Eustathius mentions the adage in his commentary on the twenty-first book of the *Odyssey*. **Colossi** <term>Colossus: a statue of vast and prodigious size</term> are statues of enormous magnitude; the word is thought to be used by the Greeks because human sight cannot fully grasp their height. **Pygmies** <term>Pygmy: from the Greek *pygmē*, the length of the forearm from elbow to knuckles</term> are those who, at their tallest, do not exceed two feet and a quarter; hence they think the name was given from this cubit-length stature. They are a people inhabiting the outermost parts of Egypt, devoted to agriculture, and constantly waging war with cranes. This war is celebrated in song because the cranes devour the seeds and bring famine to that region. So says the commentator on Nicander. Their women give birth in the fifth year and become sterile in the eighth. Juvenal mentions the Pygmies in his thirteenth *Satire*, and there are many jokes about them in the Greek *Epigrams*. Furthermore, **first-fruits** <note>original Greek: ἀκροθίνια, *akrothinia*</note> are called so by the Greeks because they are usually taken from the top of the heap. *Akron* means the top, and *thines* are heaps of grain.

<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY</header>
<sig>Eee 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Feathered</meta>

->May the gods give you your own mind.<-
<margin>XCI</margin>
**May the gods give you your own mind** <note>original: *Dij tibi dent tuam mentem*</note> is a phrase suitable for an insane person, or one whose behavior is worthy of their own distorted mind. For what more unhappy thing could we pray for wicked men? Martial writes:
> May the gods give you your mind, Philoenis.
And Horace:
> What would you do there? You would bid the wretch be miserable as he pleases, as long as he does so.
In contrast, Demea in Terence’s play says: “That a better mind be given to you.” <note>Erasmus contrasts wishing someone their "own" mind (a curse of continued madness/wickedness) with wishing them a "better" mind.</note>

->Take care to be what you are heard to be.<-
<margin>XCII</margin>
That line of Horace approaches the form of a proverb:
**Take care to be what you are heard to be.** <note>original: *Cura esse quod audis*</note>
It is applicable to the wealthy, who are truly happy only if they strive to actually become the virtuous person their flatterers describe them as being. Horace’s poem says:
> You live rightly, if you take care to be what you are heard to be.
> For a long time now, all Rome has proclaimed you happy,
> But I fear lest you believe anyone else about yourself more than you believe yourself.

->For the cautious wolf fears, etc.<-
<margin>XCIII</margin>
For those who refrain from wrongdoing not from the heart, but from fear of punishment, these proverbial metaphors from the same author will apply:
> For the cautious wolf fears the pit, and the hawk
> The suspected snares, and the kite the hidden hook.
For different traps are set for different creatures; wolves are caught in pits covered with leaves. Hence, in Plautus, a slave threatens a pimp named Lycus <note>The name Lycus means "wolf" in Greek.</note> that he will dig a pit for him. Similar is the phrase about the rod:
**To change one's manner for fear of the rod.**

->If the crow could feed in silence.<-
<margin>XCIIII</margin>
If a short fable by the author Fabius <note>Likely referring to the fabulist Aesop, though sometimes associated with Quintilian's mention of fables.</note> is a type of proverb, why should we not also number among the proverbs what Horace wrote:
> But if the crow could feed in silence, he would have
> More of the feast, and much less quarreling and envy.
Some think this was borrowed from the Fable which Apuleius relates in his book *On the God of Socrates*, concerning a crow that had found prey, which a fox intercepted by skillfully persuading the crow to begin singing. <note>Refers to the famous fable where the fox flattery induces the crow to drop its food.</note> It applies to those who, if they have obtained some good thing, immediately boast and show it off; in this way, they cause others to interfere, both preventing them from obtaining more such advantages and taking away what they have already found.

->To wrest the club from Hercules.<-
<margin>XCV</margin>
One who tries to claim for himself what someone else, more powerful, has already occupied, is wittily said to want **to wrest the club from Hercules.** This has long been celebrated as a proverb among the learned. It arose from an anecdote about Virgil <note>Maro</note>; when certain critics—followers of Zoilus—reproached him for using not a few of Homer’s verses as his own, he replied that this was a magnificent feat: as difficult as snatching the lightning bolt from Jove or the club from the hand of Hercules. Macrobius, in the fifth book of the *Saturnalia*, writes of Virgil using Homeric material so that he made it his own: because these three things are considered equally impossible—to steal the lightning from Jove, the club from Hercules, or a verse from Homer—and even if it could be done, it would suit no one else to hurl the lightning but Jove, to compete in strength but Hercules, or to sing what Homer sang. Virgil, by opportunely transferring what the earlier poet had said into his own work, made it so that the lines were believed to be his own.

->He is killed twice, who perishes by his own weapons.<-
<margin>XCVI</margin>
This is a proverbial line from a mime, though the author is uncertain. It is often celebrated under the name of Seneca, but falsely: **He is killed twice who perishes by his own weapons.** <note>This line is actually from the *Sententiae* of Publilius Syrus.</note> We grieve more deeply over misfortunes for which we ourselves have provided the occasion. It clearly arose from an Aesopic fable. A certain Gabrias <note>Babrius</note> composed iambic verses on this theme in this manner:
> You see the eagle wounded long ago,
> Grieving thereafter in heart and weeping many tears.
> Seeing the feathered arrow, he said:
> "Alas, from whence does this feathered thing destroy me?"
<note>original Greek: Βλέπεις τὸ σκῦθον αἰετὸς τρωθεὶς πάλαι... Erasmus translates the Greek fable of the eagle shot by an arrow fletched with its own feathers.</note>
That is:
> Once an eagle, struck in the breast, looks upon the wound,
> and stood still, weeping much for the pain.

<keywords>Horace, Martial, Virgil, self-deception, reputation, Hercules' club, Homer, Aesop's fables, Publilius Syrus, self-inflicted harm</keywords>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

But as it perceives the feathered arrow, "O heavens,"
It says, "my own winged feathers have brought me to a heavy doom."
The Greek adage, which is likewise taken from this same fable, we have discussed in another place.

-> Silence adorns a woman. <-

Sophocles in *Ajax the Whip-Bearer*:
<note>original Greek: γυναιξὶ κόσμον ἡ σιγὴ φέρει</note> "To women, silence brings an ornament." That is to say:
Silence adds grace to women always.
This is a proverbial sentiment, which Servius cites from Sophocles in his commentary on the first book of the *Aeneid*. No animal is more naturally talkative <note>Erasmus reflects the common ancient and Renaissance prejudice regarding women and speech</note>, yet nothing brings more honor than silence, especially among men when serious matters are being discussed. It is taken from Homer, in whose works it appears more than once:
<note>original Greek: μῦθος δ' ἀνδρεσσι μελήσει</note> "Speech shall be a concern for men."
Nor does Saint Paul grant the right to women to speak even in the church, but commands them to question their own husbands at home.

-> I will imitate the scorpion. <-

One is said "to imitate the scorpion" <note>original: *nepa*</note> when they move backward. This becomes proverbial if twisted to refer to someone who continually degenerates for the worse, "following the path of Mandrabolus" <note>A Greek proverb for things that shrink or go backward</note>. For *Nepa*, as Festus Pompeius informs us, is the African name for the constellation of the Crab—or, as some think, the Scorpion—which is a creature that moves backward. Nonius Marcellus denies that this word signifies anything other than a scorpion, citing the fifth book of Marcus Tullius Cicero's *On Ends*: "We see small snakes crawl, ducklings swim, vipers roll themselves, oxen use their horns, scorpions <note>original: *nepas*</note> use their stings; in short, each has its own nature as its guiding ruler." He also cites Manilius:
To the stars was carried
Erigone, and the struck scorpion, and the lion with its spoil.
Thus says Nonius. But if the *nepa* is nothing but a scorpion, it is a wonder why Cicero preferred to use the word *nepa*. However, it is also a peculiar trait of the scorpion to move backward if it strikes an obstacle, and the crab travels the same way. Plautus says in *Casina*: "I will yield backward toward the wall. I will imitate the scorpion."

-> What another cook seasoned, I will season differently. <-

Whenever someone renews or disrupts an entire matter, that line from Plautus’s same play *Casina* will be appropriate; it was undoubtedly spoken in a proverbial form:
"I will go inside so that what another cook has seasoned, I may now in turn
season in another fashion—whatever it is—so that what was ready might become unready,
and what was not ready might be ready for him."

-> I hate little boys with precocious wisdom. <-

Apuleius, in his *Second Apology*, cites this verse from some unknown poet as if it were a commonly celebrated saying: "I hate little boys with precocious wisdom."
A popular opinion has gained ground that people believe boys who are wise before their time will either not be long-lived or will become foolish as soon as they reach a mature age. Pliny, in his seventh book, reports that Censorinus handed this down as if from an oracle: that "elderly youth" is a sign of premature death. And in Seneca’s second book of *Controversies*, in the first controversy, Cassius was accustomed to declare regarding the talent of Alfius Flavius that a great talent appearing so early is not lasting. Sophocles calls such a boy a "man-child" <term>andropaida: a child possessing the wisdom of a man</term>. This little verse is also cited by the commentator on Pindar in the second *Pythian Ode*:
<note>original Greek: ὃν ἀνδρόπαιδα δεσπότης ἀπώλεσα</note> "Whom, a man-child, I the master myself have lost."
He calls him a "man-child" because, though a boy in age, he was endowed with the wisdom of a man. This can be adapted to a student who is pleased with himself even while still in the very basics of learning. Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, reports this sentiment from some poet:
<note>original Greek: οὐ χρὴ πόθ' ὅστις ἀρτίφρων πέφυκ' ἀνὴρ, παῖδας περισσῶς ἐκδιδάσκεσθαι σοφούς</note>
"Whoever is wise, it is never necessary,
by teaching boys more than enough, to soon turn them into philosophers."

<summary>This page explores adages regarding the virtue of silence in women, the metaphor of the backward-moving scorpion (nepa) for regression, and the classical anxiety surrounding precocious or "man-child" wisdom in youth.</summary>

<header>THE SECOND HUNDRED OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND</header>

## The Trojan Horse. I

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' depicting a landscape or architectural scene.</image-desc>The **Trojan Horse** <note>original: *Dureus equus*</note>: this was a saying used to describe secret ambushes, or situations where many people suddenly appear who were previously hidden. It is taken from the famous horse of Homer, inside which the Greek leaders were hidden; they suddenly leaped out and captured Troy. Homer calls this the *Durateos* <note>meaning "wooden" or "made of beams"</note> in the *Odyssey*, Book 8, because it was constructed of planks:

> For it was fated that the city should perish when it should
> Enclose the great wooden horse, where all the best 
> Of the Argives sat, bringing slaughter and fate to the Trojans.

Plutarch, in his *Life of Themistocles*, relates that Themistocles once asked for a horse as a gift from a horse-breeder named Philides. When the man refused him, Themistocles threatened that he would soon make a "wooden horse" <note>original Greek: *δουράτειον*</note> out of the man’s house, meaning he would bring the crimes of the breeder and his household into the light of day. 

Nor would it be unskillful if someone were to call the school of a learned man a "Trojan Horse," because in a short time, the highest men emerge from it. Among the learned, it is common to say of praised men who suddenly emerge from somewhere that they have come forth from that house "as if from the Trojan Horse." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his second *Philippic*, applied this to the partnership in a great deed: "I do not refuse to be included in the partnership of this plan, as if in the Trojan Horse, along with the leaders." 

Aristophanes, in his play *The Birds*, twists the proverb to emphasize strength and magnitude: "The size of the horses is where the wooden one comes from." The commentator <note>a reference to the ancient scholia on Aristophanes</note> notes that this alludes to a bronze horse of remarkable size which stood on the Acropolis, dedicated to Pallas Athena by Charidemus, as the inscription itself testified; however, that statue was modeled after the Trojan Horse. 

Cicero, in his sixth speech against Verres, takes the "Trojan Horse" to mean an extreme calamity: "What a crowd do you think gathered in the town? What a cry! What weeping of women, who, seeing the Trojan Horse introduced, said the city was captured," and so on. The gates through which the horse was brought, Homer calls the *Scaean* <note>original: *σκαιὰς*</note> in the *Iliad*, Book 3—that is, the "left-hand" or "unlucky" gates—because the Trojans, with a "left-handed" <note>meaning foolish or perverse</note> mind, brought that horse into the city. 

The same Cicero, in his speech *For Murena*, says the Trojan Horse is inside when he senses the Republic is in danger from civil discord: "Inside, I say, inside is the Trojan Horse, by which you shall never be oppressed while sleeping, as long as I am consul." Again, in *For Caelius*: "Was it the Trojan Horse that carried and hid so many invincible men waging a woman’s war?" <note>A reference to the intrigues of the Roman noblewoman Clodia</note>.

## When a road is present, you seek a path. II

> <note>original Greek: ῾Οδοῦ παρούσης τὴν ἀτραπὸν ζητεῖς.</note>
> That is, when the road is ready at hand, you seek a narrow path.

This is cited by Eustathius <note>a 12th-century Byzantine scholar and commentator on Homer</note> in his commentary on the *Odyssey*, Book 16. A "path" <note>original: *ἀτραπὸς*</note> is a track that is different from a wagon road, which they call the "Royal Road." The adage is suitable for shirkers who, in order to escape the business at hand, go hunting for diversions.

## To judge the ear of grain from the stalk. III

Eustathius, explaining a verse in the *Odyssey*, Book 14, which we have cited in another place: "But nonetheless, I think that looking at the stubble, you can recognize it." He shows that Odysseus was alluding to a proverb which is fully expressed thus: "The harvested ear of grain is evident from the stalk." This means that even in an old man, it is apparent what kind of youth he was. Aristotle mentions this passage in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, indicating that by a metaphor, old age is called "stubble" or "the stalk."

## To build in the depths. IIII

*Byssodomeuein* <note>original: *Βυσσοδομεύειν*</note> is a word used frequently by Homer, with a proverbial character, for the act of laboring at something deep in the breast, and secretly building up plots in the mind. It is a metaphor taken from the foundations of buildings which are laid deep. In the *Odyssey*, Book 17:

> They were speaking well, but in their minds they were building evil in the depths.

And elsewhere:

> Revolving fraud in the depths of his mind.

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

->**A self-inflicted evil.**<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐπισπαστὸν κακόν</note> That is, it is called a "self-inflicted evil" when you yourself have provided the cause for your own misfortune.
Homer, in the *Odyssey*, Book 18 <note>indicated by the Greek letter σ</note>:
"Indeed, soon the wretched Irus will have the evil he seeks for himself." <note>original: *Næ mox perditus Irus habebit, quod sibi quærit Vltro malum.*</note>

->**Eurymnus.**<-

**Eurymnus** <note>original Greek: Εὔρυμνος</note> was once a name used proverbially for one who tried to set friends against each other through slander. For this man, when he attempted to create a rift between Castor and Pollux <note>the famous divine twins of Greek mythology</note> by accusing one to the other, was later caught and suffered the heaviest punishments from both. This is generally what happens to those who, through evil arts, strive to separate those whom nature has joined with an unbreakable bond—such as a wife and husband, a parent and son, or brothers. Eventually, these pairs return to mutual favor and together exact punishment for the past hostility from the instigator. This happened in Athens to Hyperbolus <note>an Athenian politician known for his populist tactics</note>, who tried to set Nicias and Alcibiades <note>two powerful and rival Athenian generals</note> against one another.

->**Sprung from the Furies.**<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐριννύων ἀποῤῥώξ</note> That is, "descended from the Furies." In the past, this was said of someone with a foul, hideous appearance who possessed a <term>manic look <note>original: μανικόν βλέπω</note></term>, as Aristophanes says. It also refers to someone who is harmful and deadly. They say such a person is born of the Furies, just as Ajax says in the tragedy:
"Did not a Fury of the underworld forge this blade?" <note>original: *An non mucronem hunc furia cudit tartari?*</note>

->**They look like the Lacedaemonian captives from Pylos.**<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐοίκασι τοῖς ἐκ πύλου ληφθεῖσι τοῖς λακωνικοῖς</note> That is: "They seem to me like the Spartan captives from Pylos."
This is found in Aristophanes, in *The Clouds*. It was commonly said of those who have a pitiable appearance—specifically those who are pale, filthy, and emaciated. Pylos is a city in Laconia <note>the region of Sparta</note> which soldiers once besieged. Those who survived the slaughter were led away to Athens, thinned out, exhausted, pale, and of hideous appearance. This was a natural result of the long siege, especially on a deserted island which yielded a meager supply of necessities, and because they were kept in chains for many days after the city was taken. From this also comes the saying of Zenodotus regarding Pylos, which we have mentioned elsewhere as a proverb: "Pylos before Pylos."

->**You breathe the spirit of a Gyrgathus.**<-

<note>original Greek: Γυργαθου φυσᾷς</note> That is, "You breathe a Gyrgathus"; this is cast at one who is shouting insanely and in vain. For a **Gyrgathus** is a type of bed or stretcher in which paralytics, the mentally ill, and those who "call upon demons" <note>referring to those suffering from fits or seizures</note> are bound; they toss themselves about, making many threats, but all in vain. It is therefore suitable for those who act fiercely but have no real power. However, Hesychius <note>an ancient Greek grammarian</note> indicates that *Gyrgathos* is also the name for a vessel in which a baker places cooked bread. The Greek word seems to be derived from "to roll."

->**Honor yourself.**<-

<note>original Greek: Κόσμησε σαυτόν</note> That is, "Dignify yourself." This is a proverbial phrase for someone who behaves with less magnificence or dignity than they should. For <term>to adorn <note>original: κοσμεῖν</note></term> means to venerate and to hold in honor.

->**Byzenian freedom of speech.**<-

<note>original Greek: Βυζηνὼ παῤῥησία</note> That is, "Byzeni liberty," used when someone speaks quite boldly and freely. It is named after a certain son of Neptune who was accustomed to using a marvelous freedom in his speaking. Stephanus mentions Byzene as a city in Scythia, from which the "Byzeni" come. It is a peculiar trait of that nation to speak fearlessly.

->**Grief-laughter.**<-

**Achthogelos** <note>original Greek: Ἀχθόγελως</note> was a proverbial and newly compounded word for a trifler, or one who delighted in the misfortunes of others. For "Achthogelos" sounds as if you were describing someone who laughs recklessly or at unseemly times. To others, it is a sign of either foolishness or madness.

->**It is immediately apparent which plants will be fruitful.**<-

<note>original Greek: Αὐτίκα καὶ φυτὰ δῆλα ἃ μέλλει κάρπιμ’ ἔσεσθαι</note> That is: "It is immediately clear which plant is going to give fruit."
Similarly, the natural disposition for future honesty shines forth in boys. The future progress of a student is displayed right away.

->**The sow is lost.**<-

<note>original Greek: Ἀπόλωλεν ὗς καὶ τάλαντον καὶ γάμος</note> That is: "I have lost the sow, the talent of silver, and the wedding."

<summary>This page catalogs several Greek proverbs concerning self-inflicted harm, the danger of slandering friends, and the early signs of character in youth. It highlights Erasmus's interest in how ancient social labels and historical events, like the siege of Pylos, became embedded in everyday language.</summary>
<keywords>self-inflicted evil, Eurymnus, slandering friends, Furies, captives of Pylos, Aristophanes, Gyrgathus, Byzenian freedom, Achthogelos, early education</keywords>

<page-num>883</page-num>
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY</header>
<sig>Eee 4</sig>

It used to be said when someone, having been frustrated, had lost the effort they invested. It originated from a certain man who, after preparing everything for a wedding, did not actually achieve the marriage. It is related to the saying: "I have lost both my oil and my labor." <note>original: *Oleum & operā perdidi*. This refers to the oil burned in a lamp while working late and the work itself; a metaphor for wasted time.</note>

->**Both-blooming love.**<-
<note>original Greek: Αμφιθαλὴς ἔρως</note>
->XV<-

**Both-blooming love.** That is, "Love flowering on both sides." In the past, this was said whenever both parties in a relationship were equally safe and healthy, and responded to one another with mutual love. For we are said to be "halved" whenever a friend is pulled away, as if they were the other half of ourselves. This appears in Aristophanes’ *The Birds* at the end of the play. Phaedria wishes for such a love in Terence's *The Eunuch*: "If only I had an equal share of love with you." This agrees with that line of Pindar in the *Pythian Odes*: "Loving the one who loves, and leading the one who leads, with a willing heart." <note>original Greek: Φιλέων Φιλέοντ’, ἄγων ἄγοντα προφρόνως</note>

->**You have drunk from an *amphithetos*.**<-
<note>original Greek: Αμφιθέτῳ ἔπινες</note>
->XVI<-

**You have drunk from an *amphithetos*.** This was said of someone who drank too purely <note>undiluted wine</note> and too deeply. For an *amphithetos* was a type of cup made in such a way that it would stand upright no matter which side it was placed on, having no fixed base. It is more probable, as Hesychius adds among various definitions, that the *amphithetos* is a cup so large it must be lifted and put back down with both hands. Dutch sailors call such a vessel a *busa*. <note>Erasmus likely refers to a "buis," a large drinking vessel or even a type of ship, though here clearly a large container.</note>

->**The beard of Pronomus.**<-
<note>original Greek: Προνόμου πώγων</note>
->XVII<-

**The beard of Pronomus.** This was said of a very long beard. Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen*:
"For Argyrrhius, wearing the beard of Pronomus, has escaped notice."
Which means:
"Argyrrhius has remained hidden until now by wearing Pronomus’s beard."
Pronomus was a certain flute-player with a thick, flowing beard, a style of dress not particularly suited to his profession—since proverbs often note the perceived soft or effeminate nature of flute-players. Argyrrhius was a certain army commander who was considered effeminate and unmanly, possessing nothing of a man except his beard. In the same passage, the beard of a certain orator named Epicrates is mocked; because of his beard, he was given the nickname "Shield-bearer" <note>original Greek: Σακεσφόρῳ</note> in a common joke, as attested by a line of verse that a commentator on Aristophanes quotes from the comic poet Plato:
"King of the beard, Epicrates the Shield-bearer." <note>original Greek: Αναξ ὑπώνης ἐπικράτης Σακεσφόρος</note>
He calls the beard a "shield" because of its resemblance to one, and elsewhere: "For everyone hates the man who has a shield against his jaws." Aristophanes says regarding the same man:
"And I have a beard much more beautiful than that of Epicrates."
This proverb therefore applies to those who, though otherwise very soft, project a facade of disciplined life through the severity of their facial hair and clothing. This is a frequent joke in Lucian regarding the beards of philosophers. Likewise in Horace:
"...he commanded me to grow a wise man’s beard."
Martial also jokes about someone of this sort.

->**To search by every track.**<-
<note>original Greek: Πᾶσαν ἴχνειν ζητεῖν</note>
->XVIII<-

One is said **to search by every track** when they investigate a matter with the greatest care and the utmost diligence. The metaphor is taken from hunters. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fourth speech of the *Action against Verres*: "Do you really trust that you can escape even from those nets? Since we pursue you not by uncertain opinion, but by your own tracks, which you left fresh in the public records." Again in the same work: "So that all mortals may now see not just the tracks of that man's greed, but the very dens where it hides." Likewise in the sixth speech: "I consider those to have been the accusers who used to pursue the thefts of such men by scent, or by some lightly pressed footprint. For what are we doing in the case of this 'Boar' <note>A pun on Verres's name, which means "boar."</note>, whom we find wallowing in the mud with the tracks of his whole body?" In the *Speech for Cluentio*: "What? Must the Albian money be sniffed out by us through tracks, or can we come to the very den with you as our guides?" And a little later: "No money of Cluentius given to a judge is found by any track." In the *Speech against Piso*: "Or do you really think we have not sufficiently investigated the stains of your command and the ruins of your province? We have pursued these indeed, not by sniffing out your entries through tracks, but by the wallowing of your whole body and your dens."

->**To let boars into the springs.**<-
->XIX<-

Against one who brings upon himself, or wishes for, things that will bring ruin, this line from Virgil fits:
"And I have let boars into the clear springs."
It appears this was not said without the character of a proverb. For boars do not only drink from a spring with their feet pressed in, but they also wallow in them.
