<page-num>884</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

### From a dog’s anus.

<note>original Greek: Ἐκ κυνὸς πρωκτῶ</note> That is, from a dog's backside. This seems to have been said by Lucian to describe something narrow and cramped, because that part is tighter in this animal, which is why it excretes with more effort. For he ends his work *The Ass* with these words: "There I performed a sacrifice and hung up offerings to the savior gods, not—by Zeus—'from a dog's anus,' as the common saying goes, but from the 'toil of an ass,' having finally returned home safe, though with great difficulty and after a very long time." <note>original: *ex asini fatigate* - likely a typo for *fatigitate* or *pericvlo* in the source; Erasmus is contrasting the "narrow escape" (dog's anus) with the "long labor" (the ass's journey).</note> It was also used against Zeno, according to Laertius, because he wrote about the Republic "in a dog’s backside"—either because he did so too anxiously or foolishly. However, we have mentioned this proverb elsewhere.

### A bird is known by its song.

This is also cited by some, even if I have not yet read it in suitable authors: "A bird is known by its song." Otherwise, it is not unworthy of being placed in the order of proverbs. The meaning agrees with that other saying: "As the man is, so is his speech." <note>A common classical sentiment that one's character is revealed by their words.</note> A very similar one is commonly tossed about: that a bird is known by its feathers, and a man’s life and character are seen by his outward appearance.

### A dog venting rage on a stone.

<note>original Greek: Κύων εἰς τὸν λίθον ἀγανακτοῦσα</note> That is, a dog indignant at a stone. This applies to those who blame the cause not on the author himself, but on someone else entirely. For instance, if someone attributed their anger to the wind blowing, rather than to the folly from which it originates. Plato, in the fifth book of the *Republic*, condemning those who strip corpses on the battlefield, says they act just like dogs who vent their rage on the stone that hit them, while ignoring the person who threw it. Pacuvius says in *The Judgment of Arms*, as quoted by Nonius: "For when a dog is roused by a thrown stone, it does not seek the one who threw it as much as it seeks the very stone by which it was struck."

### A deep furrow.

<note>original Greek: Βαθεῖαν αὔλακα</note> That is, a deep furrow. This is also included in the collections of adages, said of those who weigh a matter with deep and inward thoughts. It is taken from the tragedy of Aeschylus titled *Seven Against Thebes*, in which these verses are spoken about Amphiaraus:
> Reaping the fruit from the deep furrow of his mind,
> From which noble counsels sprout.

It is cited in several places in the *Moralia* by Plutarch, and by Plato in the second book of the *Republic*. Marcus Tullius Cicero alludes to this proverb in several places, as in a letter to Atticus, book five: "Lest my <term>depth</term> <note>original Greek: βαθύτης (bathythēs) - meaning intellectual depth or reserve/secrecy</note>, which appeared in my actions, should be more hidden in my writing." Again in another place: "You will marvel at my depth when we have returned safe, so much <term>care</term> <note>original Greek: μελέτη (meletē)</note> is given to this matter." Again in book six, first letter: "For I have been delighted by nothing more than the depth in Appius toward you; I am vehemently glad of the liberality in Brutus." It could also rightly be applied to those who measure themselves not by the opinion of others, but by the inner consciousness of their deeds, whether good or bad.

### Ruptured even unto the throat.

<note>original Greek: ψωλὸς μέχρι τῆς μιρρίνος</note> That is, ruptured <note>having a hernia</note> even to the throat. It applies to one who is violently ruptured. The verse is in Aristophanes’ *The Knights*:
> You must become ruptured even unto the throat.

The commentator on Aristophanes shows that this was also found in the works of Diphilus.

### Kinder than a seductive fox.

<note>original Greek: Ω πλεῖον ἵλαως αἱμύλης ἀλώπεκος</note> That is:
> By how much more charming is the seductive little fox.

Said of one who feigns benevolence for the sake of his own advantage. Plato mentions the "little fox of Archilochus" in the second book of the *Republic*: "Since appearance, as the wise men declare, even overpowers truth and is the master of happiness, one must surely devote oneself entirely to this; one must draw around himself a facade and outward show as a screen, but behind one must pull the 'wise fox of Archilochus'..." <note>The text here breaks off as Erasmus quotes Plato discussing the advantage of appearing virtuous while remaining cunningly self-interested.</note>

<summary>Erasmus compiles several proverbs regarding the identification of character, ranging from Lucian's crude metaphors for narrowness to Aeschylus’s poetic "deep furrow" representing profound thought.</summary>
<keywords>character, animal metaphors, Cicero, Plato, Aeschylus, Lucian, intellectual depth, deception, fox, dog, birdsong</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Greek and Roman proverbs, focusing on literary sources like Aristophanes and Menander. The previous page ended with a discussion of misdirected anger; here, the text transitions into metaphors for cunning, retaliation, and the quality of one's speech or possessions.</meta>

<page-num>885</page-num>
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, SECOND CENTURY</header>

...light and the shadow of virtue, but in such a way that he drags the fox of the most wise Archilochus <note>Archilochus was a Greek lyric poet known for his biting lampoons; the "fox" represents his legendary cunning.</note> behind his back. These are the words of Glaucus there, praising injustice in order to provoke Socrates to a defense of justice. Saint Basil also mentions the "little fox of Archilochus," both elsewhere and in his book *To His Nephews*, as does Philostratus in his *Images*. There are many fables concerning the fox's cunning; it is not entirely clear from these which specific one belongs to Archilochus.

<margin>XXVI</margin>
->Not that I should be the first to harm, but that I might retaliate for the injury.<-
Some cite this iambic verse <note>original: *Senarium* - a line of poetry consisting of six feet.</note> from Menander’s *Olynthian Women*, others from Chaeremon’s *Thersites*:
<note>original Greek: ὡς οὐχ ὑπάρχων, ἀλλὰ τιμωρούμενος</note>—that is, 
"As one who would not wish to provoke with evil first, 
But would retaliate for an evil already given."
This agrees with that line from Terence: "Let him consider this a response, not an attack." <note>From Terence's *Eunuchus*, implying that a harsh word is justified if it is a reply to a previous insult.</note>

<margin>XXVII</margin>
->We are not sailing to the Hippolaitae.<-
<note>original Greek: οὐχ ἱππολαίτας πλοῦς ὁ πλοῦς</note>. Indeed, I find it written this way in the common editions, but I do not see what meaning can be scraped out of these words. I will say, therefore, what seems most likely to me, not because I want others to follow my guesswork immediately, but to provide learned men with some occasion for true conjecture. What if you read it as: "We are not sailing to the Hippolaitae"? This would be the word of someone warning that present resources must be used more sparingly, for we are not sailing to a place where there is such an abundance of things that you can easily repair what you have recklessly squandered. For in the Greek Commentaries, I find only this written: <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῶν βραχέα κεκτημένων</note>—that is, "Regarding those who possess little." <term>Hippola</term> <note>An ancient town in the Mani Peninsula of Greece.</note> was a very ancient city of Laconia, not far from the sea, which it is reasonable to believe once flourished with trade due to the convenience of its harbor. Pausanias mentions this in his *Description of Laconia* in these very words: "And by the sea is a temple of Venus and a standing statue of stone. Thirty stades from there are the gates of Taenarum, and the ruins of the city of Hippola, and in them a shrine to Minerva Hippolaitis." <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῦ θαλάσσης ναὸς ἐστὶν ἀφροδίτης...</note>—that is, "And at the sea is a temple of Venus, and a straight stone statue. Leaving here thirty stades, there are the heights of Taenarum, and the ruins of the city Hippola. And in these is the sanctuary of Minerva Hippolaitis." Stephanus also mentions this city. Lest I overlook any conjecture, reader, consider also whether "Hippobotas" should be read instead of "Hippolaitas." This refers to the people of Chalcis, whom Plutarch mentions in his *Life of Pericles*, once famous for their wealth and glory. For the name itself was given from the fertility of their fields, as if you were to say "horse-nurturing" <note>original: *equorum altricem*</note>; the Athenians occupied their region after driving out the natives and leading a colony there. Herodotus also makes mention of this in his book *Terpsichore*.

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
->Epiphyllides.<-
This iambic verse of Aristophanes is also cited from the comedy titled *The Frogs*, as a proverb:
<note>original Greek: Ἐπιφυλλίδes ταῦτ’ ἐστὶ καὶ στωμύλματα</note>—that is,
"These are but <term>epiphyllides</term> and mere bombast."
They say this is suitable for smooth-talkers, those better equipped with the trappings of words than with remarkable deeds. For <term>epiphyllides</term> <note>Literally "grapes upon the leaves."</note> is what the Greeks call the smaller clusters of grapes that cling to the larger ones. Callistratus writes that all tiny little bunches are called *epiphyllides* because they hide under the vine-leaves. Indeed, the name comes from the fact that they cling to the leaves. This is a sign of a luxuriant tree. Theocritus, in his *Aites*, mentions pustules born on the nose which prove a man a liar. That will be discussed in its proper place.

<margin>XXIX</margin>
->From the nozzles of the bellows.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀπ’ ἀκροφυσίων</note>. They used to say this proverbially for something that has just come out of the workshop, as if it were just produced from the bellows and the copper-smith's furnace. For the metaphor is taken from these. Aristophanes says:
"To show off clever words and the playthings of the bellows. 
All from the nozzles and from the sketches." <note>original Greek: ῥήματά τε κομψὰ καὶ παίγνια...</note>
Furthermore, a <term>cinnabeuma</term> <note>A sketch or a prototype.</note> is what they call a model or an image in imitation of which painters and sculptors fashion and represent a figure. Hence, what has been recently born is said to come "from the sketches" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν κινναβισμάτων</note>.

<margin>XXX</margin>
->All these things are upon you, Lepargus.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀνὰ σὲ τάδε πάντα λέπαργε</note>—that is,
Over

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of adages, moving from metaphors of maritime navigation and social conflict into domestic rituals, the burdens of labor, and the cynical wit surrounding marriage and hospitality in the ancient world.</meta>

<page-num>886</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

**On top of all this, Lepargos.**
<note>original: *Super hæc cuncta Leparge.*</note>
This is a heroic half-line of verse <note>original: *hemistichium heroicum*</note> usually said of someone who is not permitted to rest even after their work is exhausted, but is forced to keep going. The metaphor is taken from oxen: after they have finished the labor of farming, they are forced to carry whatever remains, such as the plow and other tools, back home. It is usually directed at the stronger of a pair. He calls the bull or ox <term>Lepyrgos</term> <note>original: *λέπυργον*—literally "white-skinned" or "peeling-bark," referring to the animal's color.</note> because of the brightness of its hair. Consider whether this refers to the words of the donkey who, collapsing under a burden, spoke to the ox; the ox refused to take a part of the pack when asked, and soon, when the donkey failed, the ox was forced to carry the entire load along with the donkey's own hide.

->The snare seems to be helpful.<-

<margin>χ</margin> <term>The mouse-trap, as it seems, was for good.</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἀμυὼς ὡς ἔοικεν ἡ πάγη*</note> That is to say, the snare was beneficial, as it appears. This was commonly said whenever a misfortune turned into something good for someone. For example, if a Turk were captured in war and found himself among Christians, and by this occasion was initiated into the sacred rites of our religion; or if a rich man was reduced to poverty and, by this occasion, turned from luxury to sobriety, or from impiety to piety. To this pertains that saying of the philosopher Zeno—if I am not mistaken—who said he "had a good voyage" <note>original Greek: *εὐπλοεῖν* (euploëin)—to sail well or have a prosperous journey.</note> after he had suffered a shipwreck. <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, famously lost his fortune in a shipwreck, which led him to Athens and the study of philosophy.</note>

-><term>To drink without drawing breath.</term><-
<note>original Greek: *Ἀμυστί πίνειν* (Amysti pinein)</note>

<margin>χ</margin> **To drink without drawing breath** is said of those who drink greedily and in one gulp, not pausing to catch their breath while drinking, but pouring the drink into their belly just as if into a jar. The word <term>amysti</term> sounds, one might say, like "without sucking." It can be applied to those who accept a speech too greedily without any discernment, or those who overwhelm their natural talent with excessive reading when it would be more profitable to mix their own thought with their reading. A similar style of drinking is called <term>amysis</term> by the Greeks because the lips are not closed while drinking.

->You are performing the Amphidromia.<-

<margin>χ</margin> <term>You are performing the Amphidromia.</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἀμφιδρομίαν ἄγεις*</note> This adage can be adapted to various uses: either for those who show off children and carry them around, or those who hunt for small gifts, or those who are in a hurry. It is taken from an ancient custom in which women who had been present at a birth and had served long in midwifery would wash their hands on the fifth day after, and carry the child in a run around the household hearth <note>original: *laribus*—the Roman household gods, here used to explain the Greek custom of the hearth.</note>. On that day, small gifts were sent by relatives, mostly cuttlefish and octopuses; on the tenth day after the birth, a name was given to the infant. Terence mentions such gifts in the first scene of *Phormio*. And Plautus in the *Truculentus*, in which play the courtesan Phronesium orders Dinarchus—who is reclining at a sacrifice for a borrowed child—to instead do that which is customary on that very day. However, Hesychius writes that the **Amphidromia** <note>A naming ceremony where the child was "run around" the sacred fire to purify it and integrate it into the family.</note> was usually celebrated on the seventh day. Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, calls it <term>ta amphidromia</term> in the neuter gender. Ephippus does the same in the ninth book of Athenaeus’s *The Banquet of the Learned*.

->Singing of the span of life.<-

<margin>χ</margin> <term>Every man singing of the span of life over the dill.</term> <note>original Greek: *Ἄδων τὸν σπιθαμιαῖον τοῦ βίου πᾶς ἄνθρωπος*</note> That is: Singing of the "palm" of life. This is said against one who passes through life with thin and trivial means, yet meanwhile thinks he is living elegantly. Or we see this applies to some who, when they set nothing on the table to be eaten, tell various stories or sing little songs so that the pleasure of the ear might make the guests forget the lack of food.

->He who does not quarrel is a bachelor.<-

Saint Jerome cites this as a common proverb: **He who does not quarrel is a bachelor.** By this, the adage says that every marriage is full of strife, and there is no tranquil life except in celibacy. Juvenal says:
> The bed in which a bride lies always has 
> its quarrels and mutual bickering; there is very little sleep in it.

Several proverbial verses agree with this sentiment:
**A woman in the house is a black storm to a man.** <note>original Greek: *Χειμὼν κατ’ οἶκος ἐστὶν ἀνδράσιν γυνή*</note>
Likewise:
**A woman's jealousy sets the whole house on fire.** <note>original Greek: *Ζῆλος γυναικὸς πάντα πυρπολεῖ δόμον*</note>
Likewise:
**Nothing is worse than a woman, even a good one.** <note>original Greek: *Οὐδὲν γυναικός ἐστι χεῖρον οὐδὲ τῆς καλῆς*</note>
But Hesiod, more modestly and, I believe, more truly, says:
**For a man wins nothing better than a good woman; 
But again, there is nothing more chilling than a bad one.** <note>original Greek: *Οὐ μὲν γάρ τι γυναικὸς ἀνὴρ ληΐζετ’ ἄμεινον / Τῆς ἀγαθῆς. τῆς δ’ αὖτε κακῆς οὐ ῥίγιον ἄλλο*</note>

<summary>This page explores adages related to the burdens of labor, the irony of "beneficial" misfortunes like Zeno's shipwreck, the Greek naming ceremony of Amphidromia, and cynical ancient views on marriage and quarreling.</summary>

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
->**No better luck than a good wife ever befell**<-
->**Any man, and conversely, nothing is worse than a bad one.**<-
->It is better to be liable to one evil than to two.<-
Aristophanes, in the *Assemblywomen*, records this proverbial iambic verse:
<note>original Greek: Ἐνὶ γὰρ συνέχεσθαι κρεῖττον ἢ δυοῖν κακοῖν</note>
"For it is better to be gripped by one than by two evils."
Whenever both evils cannot be avoided, effort must be made to decline one, so that we run into the one that holds less inconvenience.

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
->**Both**<-
The commentator on Apollonius cites this little verse from Callimachus:
<note>original Greek: Ἀμφότερον κέντρῳ τε βοῶν καὶ μέτρῳ ἀρούρης</note>
"It is both a cattle-prod and a measure for the land."
This can be said of any thing that is adaptable to different uses. Just as was shown above concerning the "Delphic sword" <note>An ancient tool mentioned in earlier adages that functioned as both a knife and a hammer.</note>. Callimachus, however, wrote this about a rod which the Greeks call an <term>akaina</term> and the Latins, if I am not mistaken, call a <term>decempeda</term> <note>a ten-foot measuring rod</note>. They say it was invented by the Thessalians, being ten feet in length. Shepherds were also accustomed to use this same rod in place of a staff.

<margin>XXXVIII</margin>
->**A Chian.**<-
<note>original Greek: χῖος καπάτω</note> "A Chian defecating." The commentator on Aristophanes, in the play *Peace*, indicates that this proverb was hurled at those who contaminated or defiled a city. For they were accustomed to use this occasion to frame a slander against the Chians. Thus, it will not be improperly applied to those who, having seized an opportunity, slander someone. Just as the wolf in Aesop's fable accuses the lamb of muddying the water while he was drinking. Aristophanes, in the play I just cited, says:
"The city of the Chians will pay the penalty because of your backside."
It is probable that the adage was born from an event recorded by Plutarch in his *Laconian Apothegms*. When some Chians were traveling among the Spartans, they vomited in the hall of the <term>Ephors</term> <note>high-ranking magistrates in Sparta</note> after dinner—those who held the supreme authority among that people—and they even defecated on the chairs where the Ephors were accustomed to sit. At first, a diligent inquiry was made to find out who had committed this outrage, intending to punish them severely if any citizen had done it. When they realized it had been done by the Chians, they announced through a herald: "The Chians are permitted to behave indecently." <note>This was a biting piece of Spartan irony, suggesting the Chians were so naturally base that they were beneath the law.</note>

<margin>XXXIX</margin>
->**To steal the sands of the shore.**<-
One is said to "steal the sands of the shore" who takes something neglected and unguarded by everyone. Ovid says in his *Loves*:
"He is able to steal the sands from the empty shore,
Whoever is able to love the wife of a fool."
This matches what we have related elsewhere from Aristotle: "The water-jar at the doors." The proverb is more aptly used through negation, such as: "Who would steal the sands of the shore?" <note>Meaning, why bother stealing something of no value or something that is free to everyone?</note>

<margin>XL</margin>
->**To cherish a snake in one's bosom.**<-
<note>original Greek: ὄφιν ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ θάλπειν</note> "To warm a serpent in one's bosom" is said of someone who embraces with love and pursues with zeal an ungrateful person who will eventually do harm when the opportunity arises. It is taken from a certain fable attributed to Aesop. A man named Gabrias expressed it in iambics in this manner:
"A certain farmer warmed a snake in his bosom
During the season of frost. But when it grew warm and crawled,
It struck the one who warmed it, and he died from the wound.
Thus do the wicked treat their benefactors."
There is also another fable about a hen warming the eggs of a serpent, about which a swallow warns her not to nourish them to her own destruction.

<margin>XLI</margin>
->**No one will read it except the Sibyl.**<-
Saint Jerome, mocking the style of Jovinian as being disordered and obscure, writes that the Plautine li- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, "librum" or "literas," continuing to the next page.</note>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...of letters, that saying fits him: **No one will read these except the Sibyl.** This is found in Plautus’s play *Pseudolus*, where a character mocks letters written by a mistress. He ridicules the "badly born" marks—the sort of writing typical of women—saying: "These letters are looking for a vacation; one climbs on top of another." "I believe, by Pollux, no one could read these except a Sibyl; no one else could interpret them." "Tell me, I beg you by Hercules, do chickens have hands too? For a chicken certainly wrote these!" <note>The "Sibyl" refers to the ancient prophetess whose oracles were notoriously difficult to decode; "chicken-scratch" remains a common term for messy handwriting today.</note>

->**The onion will be of no use.**<-

Athenaeus, in the second book of the *Deipnosophistae* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned," an ancient Greek work about food and culture.</note>, cites this six-foot verse as a proverb: 
<note>original Greek: Οὐδέν σ’ ὀνήσει βολβὸς ἂν μὴ νεῦρ’ ἔχῃς</note> 
"The onion will benefit you nothing if you lack the nerves." 
Martial likewise says: 
"You can be nothing other than full with onions." 
The onion, however, is believed to be effective for stimulating sexual desire <note>original Latin: ad irritandam Venerem</note>. One may also apply this to a more modest use: that study is of no use unless the power of natural talent is present.

->**What is given.**<-

Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in the sixth book of his letters to Atticus, writes: <note>original Greek: Ἀπογνῶς ἀλόγως εἰ ἀπεῖπ’ ἐπὶ τῆς Αἰσχρόνδι δ’ ἀργοῦ τε μένειν</note>. And he scolded me with an old proverb: <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν διδόμενα</note> [the things given]. He uses it in another place as well. It is not entirely clear what he means, except that one may guess "the things given" is a verse from some poet; for it is an iambic half-verse. It refers to the idea that whatever is granted by fortune should be accepted as good and borne with a calm mind, because it cannot be otherwise. Plato, in the *Gorgias*, seems to indicate the proverb: 
<note>original Greek: νῦν δὲ ἐν τῷ διδόναι, καὶ ὡς ἔοικεν, κατὰ τὸν παλαιὸν λόγον τὸ παρὸν εὖ ποιεῖν, καὶ τοῦτο δέχεσθαι τὸ διδόμενον</note> 
"But now, having been deceived by a lie, and as it seems, it is necessary for me, according to the old proverb, to make the best of what is present and to accept what is given by you." 
Where it is said: "to him as a gift, such as shall be given." To the same purpose belongs: "We do as we can, since we are not allowed to do as we wish."

->**To add stars to the sky.**<-

To add stars to the sky is used for adding to things that are already in the greatest abundance. It is said in a complimentary way, or it may be seen as a sign of redundancy, as Ovid wove two proverbs together in the second book of his *Amores*: 
"Why do you add leaves to the trees, why stars to the full sky? Why do you add collected waters to the deep seas?"

->**The theft of Pamphilus.**<-

<note>original Greek: Παμφίλου νοσφισμός</note>. That is, the taking by Pamphilus. This Pamphilus was a performer of Old Comedy who was noted for having plundered the treasury. It applies to embezzlers who steal from the public funds.

->**Faster than Pegasus.**<-

<note>original Greek: Πηγάσου ταχύτερος</note>. That is, swifter than Pegasus. A proverbial hyperbole for someone very fast. It refers to the famous story of the winged horse. Thus Pindar, in the ninth Olympian Ode: 
<note>original Greek: καὶ ἀγανόρου ἵππου θᾶσσον ναὸς ὑποπτέρου</note> 
"Swifter than a noble horse and a winged ship."

->**You shall test it by the snap.**<-

<note>original Greek: Πλατάγη δοκιμάσεις</note>. That is, you shall test by the *plataga* [clapping sound]. This is said of those who test another’s feelings toward them in a ridiculous way. It is taken from a common joke among girls, who place a poppy leaf over their thumb and middle fingers and strike it against their palm: if it makes a "snap," it is proof of love; if not, it is a sign of ill will. Suidas <note>An ancient Greek encyclopedia writer.</note> indicates this is usually done with a leaf of a poppy or an anemone, which is called a *plataganon* from *platassein*, meaning to make a noise or a bang. Ammianus, in book 15, alluded to the proverb: "When friendship is spoken of truly and from the heart, love is usually shown by a slight snap." Hence there is a place in the proverb where a person's spirit is judged by a simple sound. Among others, it is called a *platagonion*, meaning an instrument with which we make a noise, and *platagan* means to make a snap.

->**Hunger teaches many things.**<-

<note>original Greek: Πολλῶν ὁ λιμὸς γίνεται διδάσκαλος</note>. That is: 
"Hunger is the teacher of many arts." 
Ovid says: 
"Hardships often stir the intellect." 
Persius says: "The belly, the bestower of talent and a craftsman at following voices that were denied." <note>This refers to the idea that a hungry stomach makes even animals learn to "speak" or perform.</note>

->**He has eaten the acorns of many festivals of Jove.**<-

<note>original Greek: Πολλῶν πανηγύρεων Διὸς βαλάνων ἔφαγεν</note>. That is: "He has eaten the acorns of many festivals of Jove." Said of an old man taught by the long experience of many things; it is the same as saying, "He has seen many Olympiads." The oak tree was sacred to Jove [Jupiter]; hence walnuts were called "Jove's nuts." With a similar joke, we also...

<summary>This page explores several Greek and Latin proverbs, focusing on themes of redundancy ("Adding stars to the sky"), the necessity of talent over supplements ("The onion will be of no use"), and the resourcefulness born of hardship ("Hunger teaches many things"). It also describes ancient folk customs, such as girls testing for love by snapping poppy petals.</summary>

<header>THE SECOND CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND</header>
<sig>Fff</sig>
<meta>catchword: Bos (Ox)</meta>

->**Wiser than Prodicus.**<-
<margin>L</margin>
<note>original Greek: Προδίκου σοφώτερος</note> Wiser than Prodicus. They say that this Prodicus was possessed of the keenest judgment when it came to settling disputes and acting as an arbitrator between friends who disagreed. Aristophanes, in his play *The Centaur*, as cited by Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>, says:
"For if anyone wishes to give a judgment, I want him to give it to Prodicus." 
That is to say:
"For if anyone has acted unfairly, 
I want Prodicus to investigate the matter."
However, there is an underlying wordplay on the name itself: for "Prodicus" sounds like "pre-judger" <note>original Latin: praeiudicatore</note>, one who pronounces a verdict on a lawsuit before it is even brought before the judges. There was also a certain Sophist of this name, whom Plato mentions in several places.

->**To a beggar, not even parents are friends.**<-
<margin>LI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Πτωχῷ φίλοι οὐδ’ οἱ γεννήτορες</note> Even parents are not friends to a beggar. Riches win friends; poverty does not even keep those friends whom nature itself has joined. Such is the power of money in human life—an influence that ought to be of the lightest weight if we measured things by their actual use rather than by our own greedy desires.

->**A bad doorkeeper.**<-
<margin>LII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Πυλωρὸς κακός</note> A bad doorkeeper—that is, a negligent overseer or guard. This arose from a saying by a certain Thericyon. When he saw that the troops of Philip of Macedon had occupied the narrow passes of the Isthmus, he said: "O Corinthians, the Peloponnese has bad doorkeepers." For indeed, the Greeks call narrow mountain passes or straits "pylae," which means "gates." This is recounted by Plutarch in his *Apophthegms* <note>A collection of "Sayings of Kings and Commanders."</note>.

->**Listen to the swallow.**<-
<margin>LIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Πύθα χελιδόνος</note> Listen to the swallow—that is, take care of your business in good time. Some claim this originated from a certain theologian named Chelidon <note>The name "Chelidon" is also the Greek word for "swallow."</note>. They say it was his habit to predict the outcomes of events by observing omens. Mnaseas of Patrae is cited as the authority for this opinion in his book *On Asia*. Others prefer it to refer to the bird, the swallow, either because it is a chirping and mournful bird, or because it announces the arrival of Spring.

->**Someone will take an omen upon seeing you.**<-
<margin>LIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἐξ ὁδοῦ οἰωνίσατ’ ἄν τις ἰδών</note> Anyone who sees you on the road could take an omen from it. This was commonly said of people who were deformed or foul in appearance. The ancients used to take omens from the first person they encountered. To meet a handsome person was considered a lucky omen; to meet a deformed or dark-complexioned person was the opposite. A certain Roman Emperor—Hadrian, I believe—since he was a most diligent observer of all superstitions, interpreted his own death as being foretold by meeting a certain North African jester. When the jester was ordered to leave, he added a remark that was itself ominous: "You have conquered everything, you have made everything; now become a god." For deceased emperors were officially enrolled among the gods through certain solemn ceremonies. Juvenal writes:
"And one whom you would not want to meet in the middle of the night."

->**You do not stir things much.**<-
<margin>LV</margin>
<note>original Greek: Οὐ μάλα κυκᾷς</note> You don't stir the pot much—that is, you don't have much power, either to help or to hinder. Pericles was said to have "stirred up all Greece" with his eloquence because he turned everything to his own will. And in the writings of Marcus Tullius [Cicero], those who disturb the republic with excessive power are said to "stir everything up."

->**An ass's tail.**<-
<margin>LVI</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ὄνου οὐρὰ τηλίαν οὐ ποιεῖ</note> An ass's tail does not make a sieve. This is used when someone is said to be useless for this or that task. A sieve is usually made from horsehair, not from the coarse hair of a donkey’s tail. I suspect this was taken from the "dregs" of this present age by Apostolius <note>Michael Apostolius, a 15th-century Greek scholar whose collection of proverbs Erasmus occasionally criticized for being unclassical.</note>.

->**By the bowl itself.**<-
<margin>LVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Αὐτῷ κρατῆρι γίνῃ κακά</note> May evils happen by the bowl itself. This was a saying used for those who fall victim to the very traps they were laying for others. For he calls the bowl <note>original: "crater," a large vessel used for mixing wine and water.</note> a fountain of evils, hence: "A bowl of evils," about which I have written elsewhere.

->**A drop of wine.**<-
<margin>LVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Σταλαγμὸς οἴνου μυρίοις χοέσιν ὕδατος οὐ μίγνυται</note> A drop of wine is not mixed into ten thousand measures of water. This is said when a tiny amount of good is mixed into an overwhelming force of evil. For it is diluted and disappears if you spoil a tiny bit of wine with a vast amount of water.

<summary>This page explores a series of Greek and Roman proverbs concerning social status, omens, and the character of individuals, ranging from the wisdom of Prodicus to the uselessness of an ass's tail for making sieves.</summary>
<keywords>Prodicus, poverty and friendship, doorkeepers, omens and superstitions, Emperor Hadrian, Pericles, sieves, poetic metaphors, Aristophanes, Plutarch</keywords>

<page-num>890</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

### An ox with its head stretched beyond Taygetus.

<note>original Greek: ταῦρος ὑπερκύψας τὸ Ταΰγετον ἀπὸ τοῦ Εὐρώτα πίῃ</note> That is: "A bull, with its head stretched out beyond Mount Taygetus <note>A mountain range in the Peloponnese, Greece</note>, drinks from the Eurotas <note>The main river of Laconia, flowing through Sparta</note>." This is said of something utterly absurd or impossible. It is very similar to the saying, "What if the sky should fall?" 

This proverb originated from a witty remark by Geradas the Spartan. When asked by a visitor what the punishment for adulterers was among the Spartans, he replied that there were no adulterers in Sparta. But the guest persisted, asking, "What if one did exist? What penalty would he pay?" Geradas answered, "He would have to pay a fine of a bull so large that, stretching its head over Mount Taygetus, it could drink from the Eurotas." When the guest laughed and asked, "Where could such a giant bull be found?" the Spartan retorted, "And where in Sparta would you find an adulterer?" This story is recounted by Plutarch in his *Life of Lycurgus*.

### Spoken to the sieve.

<note>original Greek: Τὰ ἐπὶ κοσκίνου</note> That is: "Things said to a sieve." Those who wanted their statements to be seen as true and verified would use this expression. It is related to the phrase "from the tripod" <note>original Latin: τὰ ἐκ τρίποδος, referring to the seat of the Oracle at Delphi</note>. It is derived from a type of divination performed with a balanced and rotating sieve <note>Known as coscinomancy, where a sieve was used to identify thieves or solve mysteries</note>, as we have mentioned elsewhere regarding the writings of Aristotle and Lucian.

### Jupiter’s hide.

<note>original Greek: Διὸς κώδιον</note> That is: "Jupiter’s hide" (or fleece). This refers to something that is quite filthy or lowly, yet nonetheless kept for some useful purpose. In ancient times, people would keep the skin of a sacrificed animal to be carried in the Eleusinian processions <note>Religious rites for Demeter and Persephone</note>, or to be placed under the feet of those who were held by some religious stain or guilt to aid in their purification <note>original Latin: expiationem</note>.

### Evils are present of their own accord.

A sentiment of this kind is found in the *Collections of Proverbs*: <note>original Greek: Ταὐτόματα τοῖς κακοῖς τὰ ἀγαθὰ οὐ προσγίνεται, τὰ δὲ κακὰ καὶ μὴ ζητοῦσιν</note>. That is: "Good things rarely come to those who seek them; bad things happen even to those who do not seek them." Common, unlearned folk say much the same thing, and yet it is no less true: evils are present of their own accord, even when uninvited. And yet, we constantly summon war, lawsuits, and diseases through our own vices, as if there were not enough evils present by their own nature.

### They take an example from their neighbors.

<note>original Greek: Ἐκ τῶν γειτόνων ἔχεσι τὸ παράδειγμα</note> That is: "They take an example from their neighbors." This applies to those who do something simply because they are provoked by the example of others. For one neighbor rubs his "disease" off onto another, and we are made worse through mutual association. Terence surely alluded to this in his play *Andria*, saying: "Is it any wonder if he takes his example from you?"

### You have drawn the letter Mu by lot.

<note>original Greek: Ἔλαχες τὸ μῦ</note> That is: "The letter 'Mu' has fallen to you by lot." This is a riddle aimed at fools. In Greek, the word for "folly" (*moria*) begins with the letter 'Mu' <note>The letter μ</note>. When the letter 'M' once fell to the tyrant Dionysius <note>Dionysius I of Syracuse</note> during a drawing of lots, someone asked what it meant, saying: "You are speaking foolishly, Dionysius" <note>original Greek: μωρολογεῖς, διονύσι</note>. But Dionysius, twisting the meaning to something else, said: "I shall fight in single combat" <note>original Greek: μονομαχήσω</note>. 

The story is told this way in the Greek *Collections*, but it is flawed, as is clear from Plutarch. Plutarch narrates that Dionysius replied with "We shall be monarchs" <note>original Greek: μοναρχήσωμεν</note>, which translators have rendered as "We shall be monarchs" due to a corruption in the text. It should probably be read as "I shall indeed be monarch" <note>original Latin: μοναρχήσω μενοῦν</note>, so that "indeed" (*menoun*) is a single expression that does not just negate but rather strongly asserts the opposite. For he is correcting the other’s divination and suggesting: "No, rather a monarch!" For who talks like that—"We shall be monarchs"? Finally, if you read it as "he was silent" <note>original Greek: ἔμυ</note> as if Dionysius were stiffening up, what else is Dionysius saying but that he would be a monarch because he was a fool?

### To defecate in the Pythian temple.

<note>original Greek: Ἐν πυθίῳ χέσαι</note> That is: "To defecate in the Pythian temple" was a saying used for someone who did something wicked and regrettable. The tyrant Pisistratus, having built a temple, put up a sign forbidding anyone from emptying their bowels there; when a certain traveler was caught doing so, Pisistratus had him put to death.

### Poor on land.

<note>original Greek: Ἐν γῇ πένεσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ πλουτοῦντα πλεῖν</note>. That is:
"It is better to be in want on the soil, than as a rich man
To furrow the waves."
It is better to have a very little in safety than a great deal with danger. Nor did those men please anyone who hung from ropes <note>Sailors on a ship</note>, having much less control over their lives than the winds. The proverb warns that a certain fortune, even if modest, is to be preferred over uncertain fortunes, however much grander they may be.

### An old man among boys.

<note>original Greek: Ἐν πᾶσι μὲν γέρων, ἐν τοῖς δ' γέρουσι παῖς</note>. That is: "A boy among the old, and yet an old man among boys." This applies to a person of somewhat advanced age, who is too old to be seen as a child, yet too young...

<summary>This page contains a series of ancient Greek proverbs collected and explained by Erasmus, ranging from Spartan wit regarding adultery to warnings about the dangers of seafaring and the inevitability of human misfortune.</summary>
<keywords>Sparta, Plutarch, divination, Eleusinian mysteries, Pisistratus, Dionysius of Syracuse, seafaring, folly, moral lessons</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Thousand, Second Century of Erasmus's *Adagia*. The previous page (890) concluded with a series of proverbs on divination and absurdity. This page begins with the conclusion of a previous entry regarding Hermogenes and proceeds to discuss the honors given to age in Sparta, the proportion of things, and various Greek mythological or regional references.</meta>

...as a man. This was said by rivals against Hermogenes the rhetorician <note>Hermogenes of Tarsus (c. 160–230 AD) was a famous oratorical prodigy who reportedly lost his memory and skill as he grew older; Erasmus suggests this adage fits those who are only "learned" among the ignorant.</note>. It can be adapted to a man who is so educated that among the ignorant he might seem a scholar, but among the learned, he seems unlearned.

->**Only in Sparta is it worth growing old.**<-
<margin>LXVIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἐν σπάρτῃ μόνῃ λυσιτελεῖ γηράσκειν</note> That is: "Only in Sparta is it profitable to grow old." This was said because among the Spartans, the highest honor was once held for the elderly. It can be applied to any people among whom virtue is held in high esteem. Plutarch records this in his *Laconian Apothegms*, though the author is uncertain. It was said by a certain visitor when he saw that the young men among the Lacedæmonians <note>Spartans</note> showed so much honor to their seniors. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>, in his work *On Old Age* <note>original Latin: *Cato Maior de Senectute*</note>, ascribes a similar sentiment to Lysander. He says that Lysander the Spartan used to say that Lacedæmon was the most honorable home for old age, for nowhere else is such tribute given to years, and nowhere is old age more honored. 

There is a well-known story of an old man who, when he entered the theater, was given no place by any of the Athenians; yet only the Lacedæmonian ambassadors, out of reverence for his gray hair, rose in a gesture of respect and yielded the most honorable seat to him. When the Athenian people applauded this act, one of the Lacedæmonians said: "The Athenian people certainly know what is right, but they neglect to do it." This is told by many, specifically by Valerius Maximus in his fourth book, fifth chapter.

->**Let the addition not be larger than the sack.**<-
<margin>LXIX</margin>
Lucian, in his *In Praise of Demosthenes*: <note>original Greek: Εἰ δ’ ἴσως εὐλάβεια τὸ τῆ παροιμίας σκῶμμα ἐπὶ τῆ ἀσυμμετρία ἐπαγγέλεται, μὴ δὴ μεῖζον προσκοιοῖ τὸ ἐπίταγμα τῷ θυλάκω</note>. That is: "But perhaps you fear lest that proverbial taunt about poor proportion be turned against you—namely, that the additional little bundle be larger than the sack itself." For a *thylacus* is a sack or knapsack prepared for carrying loads. I am well aware that in common editions the word is *epigramma* <note>epigram</note>, not *epitagma* <note>addition/command</note>. But unless you change the writing, no sense can be drawn from it. An *epitagma* is derived from *satto* <note>to pack or load</note>, meaning an addition to a load. It is a metaphor taken from mule-drivers, who, besides the legal load, pile on certain small vessels. Therefore, when a digression is longer than the subject itself, one may use this proverb. Basil expressed the same idea in other words in his book *On the Holy Spirit*: <note>original Greek: ἢ ὅτα γε ἂν τὸ ἐποίσθιον πολλαπλάσιον εἴη τοῦ κεφαλαίου</note>. That is: "In this way the addition would be much larger than the principal thing itself."

->**Acarnanian horses.**<-
<margin>LXX</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἀκαρνικοὶ ἵπποι</note> That is: "Acarnanian horses." This was said of very large horses. It is similar to that which Aristotle mentions: <note>original Greek: ἵππος θεσσαλική</note>, a "Thessalian mare." Virgil also, in the *Georgics*, gives the highest praise to horses from Epirus: "Epirus sends the palms of Elian mares." For the Acarnanians are neighbors to Epirus, just as the Thessalians are. This will be suitable to use for any extraordinary thing or an outstanding prize.

->**Once made a tribesman, keep your rank.**<-
<margin>LXXI</margin>
<note>original Greek: γενοκὸς γεγονὼς τήρει τὴν τάξιν</note> <note>Erasmus likely means "γεννήτης," a member of a clan</note>. That is: "Having become a tribesman, preserve your order." That is: after you have been admitted into some order or rank, perform your duty just as the others do. This arose from the tribes of the Athenians. The Athenian people were distributed into twelve tribes, according to the number of months; and again, each tribe was divided into thirty clans <note>Latin: *genera*</note>, as they call them, according to the number of days. From this they were called *gennētai* <note>clansmen</note>, not because they were joined by blood relation, but because they were admitted into the same part of the tribe.

->**A second Glaucus.**<-
<margin>LXXII</margin>
<note>original Greek: γλαῦκος ἄλλος ἱππόβρωτος</note> That is: "A second Glaucus, devoured by his horses." This will fit a man who exhausts his resources by feeding horses. It arose from a myth, similar to the one told about Actaeon <note>who was devoured by his own dogs</note>.

->**Perseus attacks the Gorgon.**<-
<margin>LXXIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Γόργονα πέρσεὺς ἐχαράσατο</note> That is: "Perseus set out against the Gorgon." Used whenever someone begins an illustrious or daring deed. The myth is very well known. I would not have even included this proverb had I not found it in the Greek collections.

->**Tyrrhenian chains.**<-
<margin>LXXIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: Δεσμοὶ τυῤῥηνοί</note> That is: "Tyrrhenian chains." This referred to hateful business by which someone was hindered. It is a metaphor from the chains with which the Tyrrhenians <note>Etruscans</note> used to bind captives, which were heavy and troublesome.

->**Deliberate for a long time.**<-
<margin>LXXV</margin>
<note>original Greek: Δικρὸν βουλεύου</note> That is: "Deliberate long." A business should not be undertaken immediately. There is a complete poem of this kind:

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Thousand, Second Century of Erasmus's *Adagia*. <header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

<margin><note>original Greek: Δηρὸν βουλεύου ἵν’ ἔχῃ τὸ πολὺν ἀμείνον.</note></margin> That is: 
**Deliberate for a long time, so that you may far excel.** 
One should deliberate slowly, but once you have decided, what needs to be done must be done promptly. Those who act too quickly often experience that Platonic saying: by hurrying at the start, they arrive later at the end.

<margin>LX</margin>
### The skin of Epimenides.
<note>original Greek: Ἐπιμενιδείου δέρμα</note> That is: *Epimenidia pellis*. This refers to something stored away and kept as a miracle. I have found it written as "Epimelideum" in some manuscripts, but I believe that is a corruption. It is recorded that his skin was kept hidden away as a sacred relic among the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note>. This expression is clearly drawn from Epimenides of Crete, who is said to have slept in a perpetual sleep for fifty-seven years—or, if we believe Diogenes Laertius, he slept for fifty-seven years and lived for many years after. Thus, it is fitting that his remains were preserved as a monument to such a miracle.

<margin>LXI</margin>
### A winged oath.
<note>original Greek: Ταχυβάμονος ὅρκοι</note>. This was the name given to a void or useless oath, which would "fly away" as soon as it was spoken; such are the oaths of lovers. This interpretation is preferred by Suidas. However, Aristarchus, according to Eudemus, thinks it should be understood through "antiphrasis" <note>a rhetorical device where a word is used to mean its opposite</note>: that an oath ought to be slow and not uttered rashly; for one should not act immediately just because something has been sworn.

<margin>LXII</margin>
### You have been beaten by some rooster.
<note>original Greek: Ἡττήθης τινὸς ἀλεκτρυόνος</note>. That is: *Superatus es a gallo quopiam*. This is a proverbial joke directed at those who follow their masters from behind, behaving in a suppliant and abject manner, much like roosters that have been defeated in a fight. For this bird, when conquered, usually falls silent, but crows if it wins, as Cicero attests in his *On Divination*. They add that a rooster defeated in a fight will voluntarily follow the victor. This is taken from Aristophanes, unless my memory fails me. It is also cited by Eudemus.

<margin>LXIII</margin>
### Batacaras.
<note>original Greek: Βατακάρας</note>. This was said of those who are fat and powerless <note>or dull-witted</note>. Eudemus mentions it, adding that it should be understood "by contraction." What he means by these words is not yet entirely clear, unless he refers to a well-known slowness of mind. Indeed, those who possess a lively wit hold their heads high. A lowered head is usually a sign of a more obtuse and sluggish spirit. For the Greek word <note>original Greek: βάβαξ</note>, as Hesychius indicates, means "prone" or "face-down" among the Tarentines, and <note>original Greek: κάρα</note> means "head." From this, the <margin><note>original Greek: γαξ</note></margin> Thracians call the Bacchantes—those inspired by the divinity of Bacchus—"Bassarides," as the *Etymologicum* says. From this, the word was derived for a prostitute who prostrates herself for anyone. In the fourth book of Athenaeus, those whose heads are heavy from a hangover are called <note>original Greek: καρηβαροῦντες</note>. This will apply to the drunken and the drowsy, just as Saint Basil used it in his *Epistles*.

<margin>LXIV</margin>
### Divide equally.
<note>original Greek: Ἐξίσου δὸς πᾶσιν</note>. That is: *Ex æquo da omnibus*. This is transferred from those who divide a banquet or an inheritance. It will suit a judge or a prince, who ought to show themselves to be just.

<margin>LXV</margin>
### Post-nuptial gifts.
<note>original Greek: Ἐπαύλια δῶρα</note>. This was the name for magnificent gifts. Among the Greeks, this was the term for the things the bride's father brought to the groom and bride on the day after the wedding, in a kind of procession. For a boy would lead the way in a white toga, carrying a burning torch. After him came a girl, and after her a long line of people carrying gold, basins, soaps, litters, side-dishes, beds, alabaster jars, sandals, chests, perfume boxes, and sometimes even the dowry itself. They add that this second day after the wedding is called <note>original Greek: ἐπαυλίαν</note> because the bride is then led into the bedchamber. This adage can be applied to those who boast of their own generosity. I believe these are the things legal scholars call *parapherna* <note>property belonging to a married woman beyond her dowry</note>.

<margin>LXVI</margin>
### He retreats on his feet.
<note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ πόδα ἀναχωρεῖ</note>. That is: *In pedem retrocedit*. This is said of one who, out of fear, gives way to someone more powerful, or retreats to safety. It seems to be taken from athletes or gladiators. This is what the Latins call "to retreat a foot" <note>original Latin: referre pedem</note>. It will also suit those who change their purpose or plan.

<margin>LXVII</margin>
### He behaves affectedly in his armor.
<note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ τοῖς ὅπλοις ἀκκίζεται</note>. That is: *In armis accissat*. This is said of one who is pleased with himself and, in a way, puts on airs in his armor. It applies to anyone foolishly pleased with themselves. It is further recorded...

<header>FOURTH THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY</header>

In the *Etymologicum* <note>a Greek grammatical and etymological encyclopedia</note>, concerning the woman Acco, who foolishly flattered herself in the mirror, the word "accissare" <note>to feign or behave like Acco</note> was discussed elsewhere as a proverb.

---

<margin>LXXXIIII</margin>
### You fight at Lipsydrium.

-><note>original Greek: Ἐπὶ Λιψυδρίῳ μάχῃ.</note> That is: You fight at Lipsydrium.<-

Lipsydrium was a place not far from Parnes, which was surrounded by walls by the tyrants <note>the Pisistratids</note>. Those who had fled from the city, the Alcmaeonidae <note>a powerful noble family of Athens</note>, had first established it. But when these men were besieged and defeated by the forces of Pisistratus, a mournful song <note>or "oblique chant"</note> began to be sung in this manner: <note>original Greek: αἰ αἰ Λιψύδριον προδοσέταιρον οἵους ἄνδρας ἀπώλεσας, μάχεσθ’ ἀγαθός τε κἠ εὐπάτριδας οἳ ποτ’ ἔδειξαν οἵων πατέρων ἔσαν</note>. That is: "Alas, alas, Lipsydrium, betrayer of friends, what great men you have lost—men good in battle and well-born, who showed then from what great ancestors they were descended." This proverb is used for vigorous and warlike men. The place takes its name from a lack of water <note>from the Greek 'leipsos' (lacking) and 'hydor' (water)</note>.

<margin>LXXXV</margin>
### To gaze into the desert.

-><note>original Greek: ἔρημον ἐμβλέπειν.</note> That is: To gaze into the wilderness.<-

This was said of one who stared with fixed and astonished eyes. They borrowed the metaphor from those who silently gaze upon the immense sea or a vast solitude. Many people suffer from this defect of the eyes, such that they cannot see objects clearly when they are moved a bit further away. If such people ever have to speak in a crowd, since they cannot fix their eyes surely on anyone, they seem to be "gazing into the desert." Aristophanes is cited from his play *Polyidus*.

<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
### Be the steward.

-><note>original Greek: ἔσω ταμίας, τἄλλα δ’ ὡς θέλῃ κὑων.</note> That is:<-
->**Be the steward; as for the rest, be a dog if you like.**<-

They say this was used against a person upon whom success had fallen undeservedly, specifically against eunuchs. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> indicates that at Athens there was a magistracy committed to ten men who guarded the money placed on the Acropolis of Athena <note>Palladis</note>, which they called sacred and public funds, along with the very statue of Athena and the other ornaments of the temple. There were also "Stewards of the Triremes" <note>warships</note>, who usually accompanied the captains of the triremes as guardians. This magistracy was sometimes committed to thievish men, even though it was necessary to appoint incorruptible men of perfect faith to the task—as if it mattered nothing what sort of person you take for the province, provided the task is assigned. Through irony, this can be said to someone who invades a position of dignity: you care nothing for the learning or the morals that such a dignity requires; as if you were to say, "Be a Bishop in dignity, but a dog in morals if you please." For kings are accustomed to commit their treasures and their wives to eunuchs.

<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
### The life of an ephemeron.

-><note>original Greek: Ἐφημέρῳ ζῶή.</note> That is: The life of a day-fly.<-

Concerning those who die or perish immediately: taken from the living creatures which are so called because they do not live beyond a single day. Aristotle, in Book 5 of *The History of Animals*, records it in this way: The Hypanis river <note>now the Southern Bug in Ukraine</note>, he says, near the Cimmerian Bosphorus, brings forth at the summer solstice what look like little husks larger than grape seeds, from which four-footed winged creatures break out. This kind of animal lives and flies until the afternoon; then, as the sun declines, it grows thin and weak; and finally, as it sets, it dies, its life having lasted no more than a single day; hence it is called "ephemeron" <note>living for a day</note>. Pliny reported similar things in Book 11, Chapter 36, except he says the animal is called a *hemerobion*. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> cites Aristotle in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, adding that the Hypanis flows from the European side into the Black Sea.

<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
### A dog helping a beggar.

-><note>original Greek: Κύων τῷ πτωχῷ βοηθῶν.</note> That is: A dog helping a beggar.<-

This is used when someone opposes us and favors the opposite side, particularly someone on whose help we were relying. For dogs are hostile to beggars, as if they were rivals in the same trade <note>original Greek: ὁμοτέχνοις</note>, unless they are occasionally bribed with a crust of bread.

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
### Jupiter chose the eagle.

-><note>original Greek: Ζεὺς ἀετὸν εἵλετο.</note> That is: Jupiter chose the eagle.<-

Used when someone selects the most excellent and suitable people for his affairs. The poets imagine the eagle handing the thunderbolt to Jupiter, because this bird flies the highest of all and is not harmed by the strike of lightning. Use was also made of its services in the kidnapping of the boy Ganymede <note>the "catamyto" or cup-bearer</note>.

<margin>XC</margin>
### Either less spirit, or more power.

-><note>original Greek: Ἢ φρονεῖν ἔλασσον ἢ δύνασθαι δεῖ μεῖζον.</note> That is:<-

**One ought either to be less spirited, or to have more power.** It applies to fierce men whose strength does not match their arrogance. Or to those who are not afraid to provoke someone they cannot defeat. The word for "spirit" (*phronein*) can be understood as "wisdom": those of humble fortune must overlook many things, since they cannot forbid what they see being done wrongly, and they cannot bring about what they feel ought to be done. Plutarch, in his *Sayings of the Spartans*, attributes this to Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, when he saw his son fighting too headlong and inconsiderately against the Athenians: <note>original Greek: ἢ τῇ δυνάμει πρόσωθε, ἢ τῷ φρονήματι ὑφίεσο</note>. That is: "Either add to your strength, or take away from your spirit."

<summary>A collection of adages covering military history (Lipsydrium), social metaphors (the steward and the desert gaze), and natural history (the one-day life of the ephemeron). Erasmus uses these classical examples to offer moral and political critiques, notably regarding the fitness of individuals for high office.</summary>
<keywords>Lipsydrium, Alcmaeonidae, stewardship, eunuchs, ephemeron, Aristotle, dogs and beggars, Jupiter's eagle, Archidamus, ambition vs power</keywords>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES</header>

->Success comes from God.<-

<note>original Greek: Θεοῦ δῶρόν ἐστιν εὐτυχεῖν βροτούς</note>. That is: Success is given to mortals as a gift from the gods.
Whether our affairs turn out well is not situated within our own power, but depends upon the judgment of the powers above. While even the smallest effort is ours, the outcome belongs to God.

->The quill of a porcupine.<-

<note>original Greek: Θρὶξ ὑστριχος</note>. That is: "The hair of a porcupine." This could be said of a witty remark sharply twisted against someone. It is taken from the nature of this fierce animal which, when provoked, has a habit of launching the prickly spines that bristle on its back like spears, even from a distance, by stretching its skin. With these, it pierces the mouths of dogs that harass it. Some say the porcupine <term>hystrix: a large rodent known for its defensive quills</term> is of the hedgehog family, except that its quills are longer. Pliny, in Book 8, Chapter 35, states that India and Africa are the primary producers of the porcupine.

->Another Janus.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἰανὸς ἄλλος</note>. That is: "Another Janus." This will apply either to someone who is provident and circumspect, or to someone two-faced, double-dealing, and treacherous. Persius wrote:
"O Janus, behind whose back no stork-like finger-pecking happens." <note>original Latin: O Iane à tergo cui nulla ciconia pinsit. This refers to the fact that because the god Janus had two faces, no one could make mocking gestures behind his back without him seeing.</note>
The proverb is taken from the two-faced Janus, whose myth is too well known to need recounting here.

->You carry fire in your clothing.<-

<note>original Greek: Εἱματίῳ τὸ πῦρ περιφέρεις</note>. That is: "You carry fire in your garment." This is used when something is done in a ridiculous manner. Or it refers to one who fosters his own misfortune, such as by keeping a mistress, a flatterer, or a false friend.

->A Fury from a tragedy.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐριννὺς ἐκ τραγῳδίας</note>. That is: "A Fury out of a tragedy." This is said of foul old women. It is taken from Aristophanes' play *Plutus*, in the passage where he speaks of Poverty:
"Perhaps she is a Fury <note>Erinys: a vengeful deity from Greek myth</note> from a tragedy."
Strabo, in the fourth book of his *Geography*, reports that there are ten islands in the Atlantic Ocean called the Cassiterides <note>The "Tin Islands," likely referring to Britain or nearby islands</note>. He says one is completely wild and inhabited by men in dark clothing, wearing tunics reaching to their ankles, cinched at the breast, carrying staffs in their hands—in short, appearing like the Furies of the stage. From these words, it appears that the phrase "equal to war" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἴσῃ πολέμου</note> was widely known.

->Equality does not breed war.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἴσα πόλεμον οὐ ποιεῖ</note>. That is: "Equality does not produce war." Harmony is maintained by equality; inequality is the mother of discord. This is a saying of Solon, as Plutarch records in his *Life of Solon*, noting that the phrase "equal to war" was a common proverb.

->A fish begins to stink from the head.<-

<note>original Greek: Ἰχθὺς ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὄζειν ἄρχεται</note>. That is: "A fish first begins to rot from the head." This is said of wicked rulers, whose contagion infects the rest of the common people. It appears to be a saying taken from the common folk.

->You would even swallow a Baetylus.<-

<note>original Greek: Καὶ Βαίτυλον ἂν καταπίνοις</note>. That is: "You would even gulp down a Baetylus." This is directed at a glutton or someone who covets everything. For "Baetylus" is the name of that stone wrapped in swaddling clothes which Saturn devoured instead of Jupiter, as Hesychius testifies.

->A bad vessel does not break.<-

<note>original Greek: Κακὸν ἀγγεῖον οὐ κλᾶται</note>. That is: "A bad pot is not broken." One who is of worse character is sometimes long-lived and safer in dangers. Using a similar metaphor, people today commonly say that "a bad weed does not die."

->Even the oak tree joins the revel.<-

<note>original Greek: Καὶ δρῦς μαινὰς ἐγέγετο</note>. That is: "Even the oak became a Maenad." This is said of those who can hardly be soothed. It comes from the myth of Orpheus, whose lyre-playing charmed even the oak trees. For the Maenads are women inspired to a frenzy by Bacchus.

---

### THE THIRD HUNDRED OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND

->A ground life.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring a landscape with a building and foliage.</image-desc><note>original Greek: Ἀληλεσμένος βίος</note>. That is: "A ground life," or, if we may speak thus, a "floury" way of living. This adage is understood in various ways: some use it to refer to the ancient life of men who lived on acorns—perhaps because in those ages the eating of meat and fish was unknown, and they lived more on a meal made solely of acorns. Others use it for those who happen upon a luxurious life without labor, because...

<summary>This page concludes the Second Century of Erasmus's Fourth "Chiliad" (Thousand) of adages and begins the Third. The entries cover a range of topics from the inevitability of divine will and the corruption of leadership to Greek mythological references such as Saturn and Orpheus.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the adage "A life of ground flour" from the previous page, detailing the transition from primitive grain-eating to the convenience of processed flour. It then moves into the Third Century of the Fourth Thousand, beginning with reflections on the importance of timing and magnificent monuments.</meta>

# FOURTH THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY

...how long it was after grain was first discovered before the method of making flour was known. However, flour is more "ready to hand" if someone wishes to eat. Otherwise, the field must be ploughed, the wheat sown, harvested, threshed, milled, and kneaded. There were some who lived a life in great abundance of the things they desired, which is related to what is said in another place: <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἀλευροφαγεῖ</note> "For he does not eat flour," meaning he does not eat the rough husks. Caesar, in the first book of his *Commentaries*, says: "They order each man to carry from home ground rations for three months." Aristophanes seems to allude to this in *The Knights*, when Cleon, flattering the people, speaks thus:
<note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἀλφίτων ἤδη σοι ποριῶ μεμαγμένων</note>, that is:
"But I will now provide you with flour already kneaded." To which the other character responds:
<note>original Greek: ἐγὼ δὲ μαζίσκας γε διαμεμαγμένας</note>, that is:
"And I shall give you little cakes well-soaked,
And cooked fish; do nothing else but eat."
This latter part pertains to the proverb we cited before, "A soaked livelihood." Again, in the same play, when Cleon offered <note>original Greek: μαζίσκας μεμαγμένας</note> "kneaded cakes," the other responds:
<note>original Greek: ἐγὼ δὲ μυστίλας, μεμυστιλημένας</note>, meaning bread already soaked and moistened in broth, and for that reason ready for eating. And soon he offers wine already tempered, so that it can be drunk immediately:
<note>original Greek: ἔχε δὴ πιεῖν κεκραμένον τρία καὶ δύο</note>, that is:
"Take and drink it diluted, three and two."
For in ancient times, wine was not drunk unless diluted with water, a custom which is unfamiliar to the Germans <note>Erasmus often remarks on the heavy drinking habits of his contemporary Germans compared to the ancients</note>. They considered the best mixture to be if two <term>cyathis: a small ladle or measure for liquid</term> of water were added to two of wine. Furthermore, the people declare a little later that things which are prepared are more pleasing. For when one was boasting that he had snatched what he gave at his own peril, and the other that he had cooked it, the people respond:
<note>original Greek: ἀπὸ δ’ γὰρ, ἀλλὰ τοῦ παραθέντος ἡ χάρις</note>. Meaning that thanks are due to the one who served the food ready-to-eat.

---

->A good thing is bad.<-
->II<-

<note>original Greek: Καλὸν τὸ κακὸν, ἤντι μὴ καιρῷ τύχῃ</note>, that is:
A good thing becomes bad, if not given in its own time.
Nothing is pleasing that is untimely. A medicine given at the right time brings health; given otherwise, it brings death. This verse from Timon is cited in Athenaeus, Book 7:
<note>original Greek: ὥρη ἐρᾶν, ὥρη δὲ γαμεῖν, ὥρη δὲ πεπαῦσθαι</note>, that is:
There is a time for loving, a time for having a wife,
And a time when the season warns to finally desist from these things.

---

->A Carian tomb.<-
->III<-

<note>original Greek: Καρικὸς τάφος</note>, that is, a Carian monument. Used for something magnificent and sumptuous. Taken from the tomb of Mausolus, which is among the Carians. Pliny, in Book 36, Chapter 5, shows that this work was recorded among the seven wonders of the world, primarily because of the fame of the craftsmen. It extended sixty-three feet from the south and north. It was shorter on the fronts, four hundred and eleven feet in total circuit. It rose to a height of twenty-five cubits. It was surrounded by forty-six columns. Scopas had carved the eastern side, Bryax the northern, Timotheus the southern, and Leochares the western. Artemisia died before the work was finished. The Latins call monuments of this kind "mausoleums." Martial in his first book:
"Nor mausoleums hanging in the empty air." Likewise Propertius in his third book:
"Nor the rich fortune of a Mausolean tomb."

---

->A bad gift.<-
->IIII<-

<note>original Greek: Κακόν γε δῶρον ἴσον ἐστὶ ζημίᾳ</note>, that is:
A bad gift is just the same as a loss.
He hurts, rather than helps, who bestows harmful things. As if someone were to supply money to a youth, or commit command to a fool, or a priesthood to the unlearned.

---

->He burns with empty hope.<-
->V<-

<note>original Greek: Κεναῖσιν ἐλπίσι θερμαίνεται</note>, that is, he is inflamed by empty hopes. Used against one who vainly promises himself great things. For hope adds spirit to fools, even if the goals are far off. The wise man, even if he hopes, conceals it. This appears to be plucked from Sophocles, in whose work Ajax speaks thus:
<note>original Greek: οὐκ ἂν πριαίμην οὐδενὸς λόγου βροτὸν</note>
"I would not value at any price a mortal [who warms himself with empty hopes]..."

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the convenience of prepared food and introduces several adages regarding the importance of timing (Kairos), the grandeur of the Carian Mausoleum, the danger of ill-suited gifts, and the folly of empty optimism.</summary>
<keywords>prepared food, timing, Mausoleum of Halicarnassus, Carian tomb, harmful gifts, empty hope, Aristophanes, Pliny, Sophocles, ancient drinking habits</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, moving from the physical preparation of food to metaphors of behavior, social standing, and specific cultural terms for luxury. It maintains the sequence of the "Fourth Thousand, Third Century."</meta>

### Whoever warms himself with empty hopes. <note>original Greek: ὃς τις κεναῖσιν ἐλπίσιν θερμαίνεται</note> That is,
->I would not buy a man endowed with no mind,<-
->Whomever empty hopes move and incite.<-
Aeschines, in his speech *Against Timarchus*, says: <note>original Greek: ἐλπίδων κενῶν ἐμπλήσας</note> "after he had filled him with empty hopes."

### The jar is rolled.
<note>original Greek: Κεκύλισθαι ὁ πίθος</note> That is: The jar is rolled back and forth. This is said of someone who is moved to action by the example of another, or someone who is driven to do something foolish. For a jar <note>Erasmus uses "dolium," referring to the large clay storage jars like the one Diogenes lived in</note> is rolled wherever you wish with a gentle push. In contrast, a wise man is like a "four-square" <term>tetragonus; a Pythagorean/Aristotelian term for a perfectly stable and balanced person</term>—always fixed and unmoved. It appears this proverb arose from the story of Diogenes the Cynic. During a public commotion in the city, he began rolling his jar, a story told by Lucian in his book *On How to Write History*.

### You plug your ears with wax.
<note>original Greek: Κηρὸν τοῖς ὠσὶν ἐπαλείψας</note> That is: You smear wax in your ears. This is used against those who refuse to hear anything, whether it be just or unjust. It originated from the wax of Odysseus <note>Ulysses</note>, with which he plugged his own ears and those of his companions in Homer's account to protect them against the songs of the Sirens.

### Crows are more honored than nightingales.
<note>original Greek: Κόρακες ἀηδόνων αἰδεσιμώτεροι</note> That is: Crows are more respected than nightingales. This is used when the unlearned are preferred over the learned, the wicked over the upright, loudmouths over the eloquent, and the greedy and thievish over wise and honest men. Or, when more status is granted to wickedness and audacity than to erudition and wisdom.

### A common shipwreck.
<note>original Greek: Κοινὸν ναυάγιον τοῖς πᾶσι παραμύθιον</note> That is: A common shipwreck is a consolation to all. An evil is much more easily endured when it is shared by everyone, or at least many people. This is the origin of the saying tossed about among the Scholastics today: "It is a wretched consolation to have a companion in calamity."

### The fruit of the cypress.
<note>original Greek: Κυπαρίσσου καρπός</note> That is: Cypress fruit; said of words that are magnificent in sound but otherwise useless. The proverb flows from the nature of the tree, which Pliny writes in Book 16 is difficult to grow, unpleasant in appearance, has grim berries, bitter leaves, a violent odor, and provides no pleasant shade. Such is Pliny's description. And yet, because of its height—for which it is called "lofty" by the comic poets—and its perpetual greenness and the difficulty of its cultivation, it seems to promise something remarkable to the sight. However, Theophrastus writes in the first book of *The Causes of Plants* that the seed of the cypress is so tiny it can scarcely be seen by the eye. For the fruit is not that which resembles a ball, but rather what grows within the cone, which is very thin and meager—similar to the fruit of the larch—which falls out when the pod gapes open and can only be collected by an expert.

### To live sumptuously. <note>original Greek: Ματτυάζειν (Mattyazein)</note>
Athenaeus, in the 14th book of *The Sophists at Dinner*, mentions a type of food first discovered by the Thessalians but which was also a delicacy in Athens when they were under the rule of the Macedonians. In the Macedonian language, it was called <term>mattya</term>, from the Greek word <note>original: μάττω (matto)</note> meaning "to knead" or "to soften." From this comes the word for "barley cake" <note>original: μάζα (maza)</note>, which itself created a proverb: those who lived more luxuriously were said to "eat well-kneaded cakes." Whatever was sumptuous and elegant in food they called *mattya*, whether it was birds, fish, meats, or stuffed dishes; and those who lived delightfully were said to "mattyaze" <note>mattyazein</note>. They cite as evidence these verses from the poet Alexis:

> You are not accustomed to drinking so much,
> You are left behind while you feast on delicacies.
->That is:<-
> Prepare the table and lean into the feast,
> Take your pleasure and feast on dainties.

Furthermore, among the people of Attica, those who indulge intemperately in the pleasures of Venus are said "to be left behind" <note>original: λείπεσθαι (leipesthai)</note>; this corresponds, if I am not mistaken, to the fact that <note>original: λειπίζω (leipizo)</note> sounds like "to skin" or "to peel," a word which the Latins also used in an obscene sense. For to the Greeks, <note>original: λειπῶν (leipon)</note> signifies "skin." Whoever wishes to know more about these delicacies should read the end of the fourteenth book I just cited, and he will be filled to satiety with *mattyas*. Athenaeus shows through many authors what a *mattya* is. The same author in Book 4 records that among the Spartans, certain porridges were called <note>original: ματτύλω (mattylo)</note> which were served after the <note>original: ἄικλον (aiklon)</note>, which was their type of banquet; these were also called "oven-breads." Martial also mentions this food in Book 9: "Only delicacies [*mattyas*] please."

### A seeker of delicacies. <note>original: Matiolœchus</note>
<note>original Greek: Ματτυολείχος (Mattyoleichos)</note> was a common insult for a "licker" or one who is fastidious even in the smallest things. Indeed, Hesychius indicates that anything tiny is called <note>original: ματτίον (mattion)</note> by the Greeks. They say it is a type of—
<meta>catchword: food. [bi genus]</meta>
