# FOURTH THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY
<meta>catchword: This thing</meta>

...measure, or a type of measurement. Accordingly, it applies to those who, through fraud, seek a profit from the smallest things, <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ματίου καὶ λογίζεσθαι</note> "calculating from the *matios*" <note>A *matios* was a small Persian dry measure, used here to denote extreme stinginess</note>, unless you prefer the phrase "to lick." It is used by Aristophanes in *The Clouds*, among many epithets by which he marks a wicked man. The commentator explains it in various ways, though he admits he does not truly know, writing that it is said of one who gives a stingy measure, of a parsimonious and filthy person, or of one who contemplates vanities or happens upon trifles.

<margin>XIII</margin>
->A battle after Marathon.<-
<note>original Greek: μετὰ τὴν μαραθῶνα μάχην</note> That is: A battle after Marathon. This is used when someone, after one disaster, falls into another new one. Marathon is a place in Attica, notable for frequent defeats, and was where a most fierce battle was fought against the Persians. Herodotus reports this in Book 6. Similar to this is the phrase: "An alliance after the war," or "A commotion after the battle."

<margin>XIIII</margin>
->Do not corrupt the music.<-
<note>original Greek: μὴ κακουργεῖ τὴν μουσικήν</note> That is: Do not corrupt the music—in other words, do not speak inconsistently or attempt risky novelties. Plutarch, in his *Sayings of Kings and Commanders*, reports that Emerepes spoke thus while cutting two of the nine strings from the instrument of the singer Phrynis, because he believed seven were sufficient. <note>The Spartans were famously conservative regarding music and art, believing that adding strings to a lyre would corrupt the morals of the youth.</note>

<margin>XV</margin>
->More cunning than a cuckoo.<-
<note>original Greek: μηχανικώτερος κόκκυγος</note> That is: More cunning than a cuckoo. This was said of one who looked out for himself with great cleverness. The proverb is taken from the nature of the bird, which places its eggs in the nests of others—especially those of wood pigeons—about which Pliny and Aristotle have written much.

<margin>XVI</margin>
->The apples of the Hesperides.<-
<note>original Greek: μῆλα ἑσπερίδων δωρήσασθαι</note> That is: They say one "bestows the apples of the Hesperides" when they grant great and splendid things. The myth of the golden apples is well known. Our Virgil <note>Maro</note> seems to have alluded to this in his *Eclogues*:
>I have sent ten golden apples; tomorrow I will send another ten.

<margin>XVII</margin>
->Only Spartan women give birth to men.<-
<note>original Greek: Μόναι λακαιναι ἄνδρας τίκτουσι</note> That is: Only Spartan women give birth to men. Among the Spartans <term>Lacedaemonians; residents of the city-state of Sparta</term>, the bravest men were born, and their mothers raised them with great severity. This proverb arose from a saying of Gorgo, a Spartan woman and the wife of Leonidas. When a certain foreign woman said to her, <note>original Greek: Μόναι τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἄρχετε ὦ λάκαιναι</note> "You Spartan women are the only ones who rule over your men," she replied, <note>original Greek: Μόναι γὰρ τίκτομεν ἄνδρας</note> "That is because we are the only ones who give birth to real men." Plutarch records this in his *Life of Lycurgus*.

<margin>XVIII</margin>
->You seek a myrtle crown.<-
<note>original Greek: μυῤῥίνου</note> That is: One was said to "desire the myrtle" if they were seeking a tyranny or a high magistracy. For in ancient times, princes were crowned with myrtle wreaths, if we are to believe the scholar Suidas.

<margin>XIX</margin>
->God forestalls the casting of the anchor.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἀντέπεισε τὴν ἐπ’ ἄγκυραν θεός</note> That is: But God has forestalled the casting of the anchor. This applies when something happens contrary to all hope. It is a metaphor taken from sailors, to whom it often happens that just as they prepare to drop anchor while approaching a harbor, they are driven back by the winds and called back into the middle of a storm.

<margin>XX</margin>
->Calauria instead of Delos.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀντὶ δήλου τὴν καλαυρίαν</note> That is: Calauria instead of Delos. It is said in the myths that Neptune <note>Poseidon</note> made an exchange with Latona <note>Leto</note>, such that she granted the island of Calauria to Neptune and took possession of Delos, and in exchange for giving up Taenarus, she received Delphi <note>Pytho</note>. Calauria is a tiny island not far from Crete. Pausanias, in his description of Corinth, records that Calauria was once sacred to Apollo, and Delphi to Neptune, and that they swapped these places with one another. Strabo also mentions this in his eighth book: Troezen, he says, is sacred to Neptune, which is why it was once called Poseidonia. It stands out in the sea about fifteen stadia <note>roughly 1.7 miles</note> and is not an obscure city. Overlooking its harbor, called Pogon, is Calauria, a small island with a circumference of thirty stadia. Here there was a sanctuary sacred to Neptune. The story goes that this god, having made an exchange with Latona, received Calauria in place of Delos, and from Apollo, he received Taenarus in exchange for Delphi. Ephorus, moreover, records the oracle itself:
>It matters not to you whether Delos or Calauria be inhabited,
>Nor whether you dwell in holy Delphi or windy Taenarus.

It also explains the mythical origins of sacred geography regarding the islands of Delos and Calauria.</summary>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

This matter turned into a proverb whenever "one hand washes the other" and one favor is repaid by another. <note>original Latin: "manus manum lauat, & officium officio pensatur." This is a famous expression for mutual benefit or "scratching each other's backs."</note>

### Older than Codrus.

<margin>older than Codrus <note>Greek: πρεσβύτερος Κόδρου</note></margin> This is said of things that are ancient and to be admired for their antiquity. Codrus was a very ancient king of Attica (the region of Athens), whom I have mentioned elsewhere. Those who wished to appear of noble birth would trace their lineage back to him.

### A swallow will outstrip whole schoeni.

<margin>a certain swallow will outpace whole schoeni <note>Greek: πρόσω τις χελιδὼν ὅλους σχοίνους πήξεται</note></margin> That is: A certain swallow runs ahead by entire units of distance. This is used when someone wins a contest by an immense interval. Among the Greeks, the *schoenus* <term>schoenus: an ancient unit of distance, originally Egyptian</term> was a type of measurement which, according to Herodotus in Book 2, consists of sixty *stadia* <note>about 7 miles</note>. Hermogenes also teaches this in his booklet titled *On the Method of Forceful Speaking*, showing it to be an Egyptian word just as the *parasang* is Persian. However, Pliny in Book 12, Chapter 14, attributes forty stadia to a *schoenus*, which would make it five miles. Again, in Book 5, Chapter 10, he writes that a *schoenus* covers thirty stadia; it seems this variation arose from the errors of scribes. Nevertheless, I suspect that in this context "Swallow" (Chelidon) might be taken as the name of a man mentioned elsewhere, though I do not know if he excelled in speed and running.

### The broker is worth nothing.

Plautus says in his play *Asinaria*: "It is an old saying: the broker is worth nothing." <note>original Latin: "Vetus est, nihili cocio est."</note> This seems to be said against those who make promises for the future but do not produce the actual item in the present. Laberius, as cited in Gellius, used "broker" (*cocio*) as a common word for what the ancients called a "soothsayer" (*ariolator*). These things are said by a character in the comedy who boasted that his hands "had eyes" and that he would only believe what he could see. There are others who read "compulsion" (*coactionem*), but the meter of the verse does not allow for this unless a vowel is elided. From Festus Pompeius, one might almost conjecture that "haggling" (*coctionem*) should be read. For he says they were called *coctiones* from "delay" (*cunctatio*), because in buying and selling merchandise, one arrives slowly at the final fair price. Accordingly, among the ancients, the first syllable was written with the letter *u* rather than *o*. I believe this is supported by what Annaeus Seneca writes in the tenth book of his *Letters*, arguing that we should not cease from doing good deeds simply because we have occasionally encountered an ungrateful man. "Even after a bad harvest," he says, "one must sow the seed. Often, whatever was lost to the barrenness of a wretched, sterile soil is restored by the fertility of a single year. It is worth the effort to find one grateful person even if it means testing the ungrateful as well. No one has such a steady hand that they are not often deceived. Let them miss the mark, so that they may eventually hit it. After shipwrecks, men still brave the seas. A debt-collector (*coactor*) does not drive the moneylender from the forum. Life will grow numb in sluggish idleness if we must abandon everything that causes offense." Thus far Seneca. Whether "debt-collector" (*coactor*) should be read in that passage or not, I leave for scholars to weigh. According to etymology, one should say *cunctio* or *cuntio*, or with a letter changed, *contio*, were it not for the fact that Festus Pompeius shows *coctio* and *cocio* to be the same. In his entry for "Arulator," he confirms this for Gellius, asserting that a *cotio* is the same as an *arulator*. He says *arulator* is derived from the Greek *aire*, which means "take it," because such a person follows the merchandise so that if anything falls off, he himself can take it.

### You do not sail at night.

<margin>no sailing at night <note>Greek: οὐ νυκτὶ πλοῦς</note></margin> That is: You do not sail by night. This is said of one who has nothing certain to follow, because in the night hours sailors actually navigate more accurately due to the markers of the stars—though this has been said differently elsewhere. Chrysippus, as they cite him, removed the negation, leaving it as "Sailing by night" <note>Greek: νυκτὶ πλοῦς</note>, while keeping, I believe, the same meaning. For why else would it have been worth mentioning if Chrysippus had simply removed the "not," as if the same rule of logic did not apply to any speech? Although sailors follow the signs of the stars at night, navigation is far more certain by day.

### Men’s characters match their region.

<margin>Both the seeds of plants and the lives of men are made to resemble their lands. <note>Greek: Καὶ τῶν φυτῶν τὰ σπέρματα, καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ βίοι ταῖς χώραις συνεξομοιοῦνται.</note></margin> That is: Both the seeds of plants and the characters of men correspond to the nature of their region. This is taken from the Greek collections of proverbs. Otherwise, I would not have included it here. Indeed, I believe it comes from an aphorism mentioned by Plutarch. Just as wheat in some fields changes into another type due to a defect in the soil, so the talents of men vary according to the quality of the region. Britons are generally harsh and unrefined. Coastal dwellers are almost always pirates and cruel. The "Capetae" <note>likely referring to a specific group known for luxury or refinement, such as the people of Capua or a similar Eastern group</note> are soft and civilized. Herodotus, at the very end of his final book, clearly shows that this idea first arose from a response by Cyrus. For when the Persians, having gained power, requested that they be moved from the harsh region they then held to a more comfortable and fertile one, he agreed, but warned them [that soft lands breed soft men].

<summary>Erasmus examines proverbs regarding ancient lineages (Codrus), extreme speed (the swallow), and the role of the "broker" or "haggler" in commerce. He concludes with a discussion on how geographical environment shapes the character and temperament of different peoples.</summary>

<keywords>Codrus, schoenus, measurement, brokerage, navigation, stars, geography and character, Herodotus, Seneca, Plautus</keywords>

--- Page 1023 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Fourth Thousand, Third Century" of Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages. The previous page discussed the proverb "A swallow will outstrip whole schoeni," regarding speed and distance. This page concludes a reflection on how geography shapes human character before moving into a series of shorter, pithy adages regarding loss, self-reflection, and the vanity of worldly pursuits.</meta>

...prepared themselves for servitude, not for command. <note>original Latin: "hac sese pararent ad seruiendum, nō ad imperandū"</note> **For it is common for soft men to be born from soft lands; it is not the property of the same soil to produce both wonderful fruit and men who are excellent in warfare.** <note>Erasmus is quoting a famous sentiment from the end of Herodotus's *Histories* (9.122). Original Greek: Φιλέειν γὰρ ἐκ τῶν μαλακῶν χωρῶν μαλακοὺς γίνεσθαι, οὐ γάρ τοι τῆς αὐτῆς γῆς εἶναι καρπόν τε θαυμαστὸν φύειν, καὶ ἄνδρας ἀγαθοὺς τὰ πολέμια.</note> That is: From soft regions, soft men are usually born. Nor is it the same earth that produces exceptional fruit and men outstanding in the art of war.

### XXVI. With the dog, the leash as well.

**With the dog, the leash too.** <note>original Greek: Σὺν τῷ κυνὶ καὶ τὸν ἱμάντα</note> That is: Along with the dog, the strap as well. This is a fragment of a heroic poem. Eudemus indicates that this is said whenever everything perishes at once, so that nothing at all is left behind—not even the hope of recovering what was lost.

### XXVII. Look at yourself.

->**Look not only at my lineage, but also look at your own.**<- <note>original Greek: Μὴ τὸ ἐμὸν ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ σὸν φῦλος σκόπει</note> That is,
->**Come now, do not look at mine, but look into your own race.**<-

Teucer, in a certain tragedy, retorted with this kind of insult against Agamemnon. When Agamemnon tried to shame him for a defect in his lineage because he was a bastard, Teucer reminded him that Agamemnon himself was descended from the effeminate Clisthenes. <note>Teucer and Agamemnon are characters from the Trojan War; Erasmus likely refers to Sophocles's play *Ajax*.</note> It is foolish to say something against another that can be turned back against yourself. This adage is recorded by Plutarch.

### XXVIII. Do not wipe an empty measure for me.

Theocritus in the *Syracusan Women*:
->**May no one exist, Proserpina, whom we acknowledge as master,**<-
->**except one; I do not care for that, beware you do not wipe an empty measure for me.**<- <note>original Greek: Μή φυὶ μελιτώδης ὃς ἀμῶν καρπὸς ἂν, πλαν ἑνὸς, οὐκ ἀλέχω. Μή μοι κινεᾶν ἀμάξης.</note> That is:
> May no one exist, Proserpina, whom we recognize
> As master, save one: I do not care for that; take care
> That you do not wipe an empty one for me.

A proverb seems to lie beneath the phrase:
->**Do not wipe an empty measure for me:**<- <note>original Greek: Μή μοι κινεᾶν ἀμάξης</note>
One must understand "jaw," "hand," or something similar to be implied. It appears to be the voice of someone threatening or fearing a slap or a punch. However, the meaning of the passage is not yet sufficiently clear. Therefore, we leave it to the learned to examine it more diligently. The word *amaxaden* <note>Greek: ἀμαξάδην</note> is also used for sculptors who smear clay while they mold images. Some people are accustomed to feigning a service, as if they want to wipe some dirt from a person's cheek, but in the meantime, they smear more dirt on the unsuspecting person—just as they represent Bacchus with his face smeared with gypsum and the juice of grapes. Nevertheless, a certain commentator—a man neither particularly learned nor diligent—prefers to understand this as a "measure," perhaps a *choenix* <term>choenix: an ancient Greek dry measure, roughly a daily ration of grain</term>. Whatever is excessive in a measure, one wipes away with a smooth stick <note>The Latin *hostorium* or leveling stick</note>. Thus, a person who wipes a measure that is not yet full is a deceiver, pretending that there was an excess to be removed. The speaker feels she is not his servant and should not be scolded by him. A master, having been offended, had defrauded his servants of their daily allowance <note>original Latin: *dimenso*, the measured ration</note>; this is, unless I am mistaken, what she means when she says: "I am not worried, so do not wipe an empty measure for me."

### XXIX. Since you are a dwarf, give way.

**Since you are a dwarf, yield.** <note>original Greek: Νανὸς ὢν ὕπαγε</note> That is: Since you are a dwarf, go away. This is said of puny people. For "dwarfs" (*nani*) are what we call little men who are below the standard of the human body and of a monstrous shortness. Juvenal says: "We call a dwarf Atlas."
For the Greek word *nanos* <note>Greek: Νανὸς</note> is said as if it were *me ano* <note>Greek: μὴ ἄνω</note>, meaning that which does not grow upward. Theophrastus is cited as having thought that those whose private parts are larger than is proper are called dwarfs, which is plausible to find in this race of men. This will apply to thin "little men" of humble fortune and, as Horace says, "of a two-foot measure," <note>original Latin: *moduli bipedalis*</note> who try to equal the powerful in their spending.

### XXX. Bright at night, useless by day.

->**Bright in the night, but useless in the light.**<- <note>original Greek: Ἐν νυκτὶ λαμπρὸς, ἐν φάει δ’ ἀνωφελής</note> That is:
->**Shining in the night, but in the light, useless.**<-

This is said of backward people who are wise when there is no need; but when there is a need, they are asleep. Otherwise, I myself think it more fittingly applies to a man who seems to be something in literature among the unlearned, but among the erudite knows nothing. Or perhaps the proverb should be inverted:
->**Bright in the light, but useless in the night.**<-
This is taken from a certain gemstone, which we have mentioned elsewhere.

### XXXI. You gather fruit from Tantalus’s garden.

**You gather fruit from Tantalus’s garden.** <note>original Greek: Ταντάλου κῆπον τρυγᾶς</note> That is: You gather fruit from the garden of Tantalus; meaning, you pursue those things which exist nowhere, or which one is not permitted to enjoy. This will be said quite appropriately of those devoted to worldly pleasures. For while they enjoy these things as if intoxicated, they seem to themselves to be exceptionally happy.

<summary>This page covers several adages concerning the loss of all possessions, the importance of self-examination before criticizing others, and the deceptive nature of worldly pleasures compared to Tantalus's unreachable fruit.</summary>
<keywords>Herodotus, character and geography, loss, Agamemnon, Teucer, Theocritus, measurement, dwarves, Horace, Tantalus, vanity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Adages" of Erasmus, specifically within the section detailing proverbs related to character, social standing, and theatrical metaphors. The previous page ended with a discussion on how environment shapes human nature; this page begins mid-sentence, concluding a thought on the clarity that follows a period of madness or delusion.</meta>

...But as soon as they have come to their senses, now as if awakened, they understand that all those things are nothing but the dream of a mind that is not quite sane.

### Poorer than Telenicus.

**Poorer than Telenicus.** <note>original Greek: Τελενίκου πενέστερος</note> This refers to a man named Telenicus who was so famously poor that the people of Seriphos <note>An island in the Aegean Sea.</note> coined a verb from his name, saying "to telenicize" <note>original Greek: τελενικῶσαι</note> instead of "to empty out."

### A Telenician echo.

**A Telenician echo.** <note>original Greek: Τελενίκιος ἠχώ</note> This is a fitting way to describe the speech of a fool. For this is what he calls the rattling of empty vessels. The epithet is taken from the same Telenicus we just mentioned. However, Plutarch, among the witty sayings of Epaminondas, mentions a certain Tellen who was a very low-quality flute-player, to whom Antigenidas was the exact opposite. Let the reader consider, therefore, whether the proverb might better be derived from him. Indeed, we have spoken elsewhere of the "tunes of Tellen."

### More foolish than a terebinth tree.

**More foolish than a terebinth.** <note>original Greek: Τερέβινθος ἀνοητότερος</note> That is, "more senseless than a terebinth tree." This is said of a stupid person who is nonetheless pleased with himself. The comparison arises because that tree spreads its branches wide—which is a sign of those who show themselves off insolently—and furthermore, it has black berries, thick leaves, and a fatty, resinous sap, appearing different at different times. It also produces a growth similar to a grape, but it is a false fruit. <note>The terebinth or turpentine tree was often associated with uselessness or deceptive appearances in ancient botanical lore.</note>

### The walls of Semiramis.

**The walls of Semiramis.** <note>original Greek: Τείχη σεμυράμιδος</note> This was said of walls that were impregnable and exceptionally well-fortified. Ovid writes in the fourth book of the *Metamorphoses*:
> Where Semiramis is said to have girt the high city with walls of baked brick. <note>original Latin: "Vbi dicitur altam Coctilibus muris cinxisse Semyramis urbem." Semiramis was a legendary queen of Babylon.</note>

### To lay on a hand.

**To lay on a hand.** <note>original Greek: Τὴν χεῖρα ἐπιβάλλειν</note> This was said of those who would work their way into a share of some distinguished matter. It is a metaphor taken from sacred rites, in which it sometimes happened that while others were performing a divine service, someone else arriving would place a hand on the victim, and thus become a participant in the sacrifice himself.

### He is his father's son.

**The child is of his father.** <note>original Greek: Τοῦ πατρὸς ὅτι τὸ παιδίον</note> They speak this way when someone imitates the manners of his father. In a general sense, we call anyone the "son" of a person whose character they have expressed, because children usually resemble their parents in character. Varro gave this title to one of his Menippean Satires, as cited by Nonius Marcellus. <note>Varro was an ancient Roman scholar; Menippean Satires were a genre of satirical prose and verse.</note> Varro's titles are almost always proverbial. Philostratus records in his life of Aristides that a sophist used this proverb to mock an Alexander, because he imitated his father’s ambition.

### Meat bought cheaply.

**Dogs eat meat bought cheaply.** <note>original Greek: Τὸ εὔωνον κρέας οἱ κύνες ἐσθίουσιν</note> For some people buy food purely for its low price, so as not to spend a few coins more. Since no one else will touch such food, it is often kept to be eaten by dogs. This also smacks of the common people of these times. <note>Erasmus often adds these small "modern" asides to critique the stinginess or lack of taste in his own 16th-century society.</note>

### He who is rained on at home.

**Even God does not pity the man who is rained on in his own house.** <note>original Greek: Τὸν οἴκοθεν βρεχόμενον οὐδὲ θεὸς οἰκτείρει</note> This was a common saying among the Greeks. The meaning is that a man seems worthy of his misfortune in every way if he is so lazy that he cannot even keep himself safe from the rain within his own home. This is very similar to the proverb mentioned above, unless my nose <note>A metaphor for "discernment" or "intuition."</note> fails me entirely.

### A tragic Theocrines.

**A tragic Theocrines.** <note>original Greek: Τραγικὸς θεοκρίνης</note> Demosthenes used this adage against Aeschines. Theocrines was first an actor of tragedies, and later a slanderer and a trickster. Hence Demosthenes, in his oration *On the Crown*, calls Aeschines a "tragic Theocrines." There is an oration extant against this Theocrines, though some attribute it to Dinarchus. Saint Jerome used this proverb, if I am not mistaken, in his *Letter to Furia on Widowhood*: "Wherever they saw a Christian, immediately they would shout that street-slang: 'A tragic Theocrines!'" They would hurl this insult at a Christian as if at a pretender to holiness, who used "tragic" (grand) words to accuse the lives of others.

### A tragic evil.

**A tragic suffering.** <note>original Greek: Τραγικὸν πάθος</note> An "immense evil" or "tragic suffering" refers to the kind of great misfortunes that are depicted in tragedies. For comedy abstains from such things. Quintilian distinguishes between two types of emotions: because tragedy loves those that are more fierce, while comedy uses those that are more mild. The Greeks call the former *pathe* <note>term: passions/sufferings</note> and the comic ones *ethe* <note>term: characters/manners</note>. A tragedy always has a sad ending.

<summary>This page explores several ancient Greek and Latin adages concerning poverty (Telenicus), stupidity (the terebinth tree), and the distinction between tragedy and comedy, often highlighting historical figures like Demosthenes and St. Jerome.</summary>
<keywords>Telenicus, Semiramis, Theocrines, Demosthenes, Saint Jerome, Quintilian, Greek proverbs, tragedy vs comedy, character, poverty</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad of Erasmus's "Adages," a collection of ancient proverbs. The previous page ended with a discussion of theatrical metaphors and the concept of something being "pleasant" or "comical."</meta>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
<note>Chiliad refers to a group of one thousand; Century refers to a group of one hundred.</note>

...pleasant. Whence Plautus, as cited by Festus Pompeius, used the word "comically" <note>original: *comœdice*</note> to mean "pleasantly": "Away! Hey, you stood there both sweetly and comically."

->**Blind in ears and mind.**<-
->**XLI**<-

**Blind in ears, in mind, and in eyes.** <note>original Greek: τυφλὸς τὰ τ' ὦτα, τόντε νοῦν, τά τ' ὄμματ' εἶ</note> That is: 
*You are blind at once in ear, mind, and eyes.* 
This applies to a person who is plainly stupid. <note>This is a famous line from Sophocles’ play *Oedipus Rex*, spoken by Oedipus to the blind prophet Tiresias.</note>

->**A blind dream.**<-
->**XLII**<-

**A blind dream.** <note>original Greek: τυφλὸν ὄνειρον</note> This refers to a frivolous and vain matter. For some dreams portend something, while others are empty, just as there are "senseless lightning bolts" <note>original: *bruta fulmina*, lightning that strikes without divine purpose or effect.</note>.

->**I do not care for donkeys.**<-
->**XLIII**<-

**But donkeys do not concern me.** <note>original Greek: τῶν δ' ὄνων ὔ μοι μέλει</note> That is, "I do not care at all for donkeys." This suits a person who is content with their own domestic resources and does not seek the property of others. For a person who has their own wagon at home has no need for hired donkeys. We have cited the full poem elsewhere.

->**The vote of the majority wins.**<-
->**XLIIII**<-

**The pebble of the many wins.** <note>original Greek: τῶν πλειόνων ψῆφος νικᾷ</note> That is, "The vote of the majority wins." This is used whenever a council yields to the multitude. Pliny complains in his *Letters* that votes are counted, not weighed. And Livy says: "The larger part defeated the better part." <note>A classic critique of democracy: that the sheer number of voters often outweighs the quality or wisdom of the argument.</note>

->**Over-ripened.**<-
->**XLV**<-

**Over-ripened** <note>original Greek: ὑπερφυσικῶν</note> is said of a woman who is close to giving birth. The metaphor is taken from figs that ripen after being pierced by gall-wasps. We explained what this means in the proverb <term>to caprify</term> <note>original: *erinazein*; the process of using wild figs to help domestic ones ripen.</note>. It can also be applied to a natural talent that is strongly inclined toward one thing or another.

->**You are a substitute.**<-
->**XLVI**<-

**You are a changeling.** <note>original Greek: ὑποβολιμαῖος εἶ</note> That is, "You are a substitute." Those births that are faked are called "substitutes" or "supposititious." From there, the term is transferred to a person who is fake, or who has been deceitfully put forward and suborned by someone else. A similar term is **a counterfeit man** <note>original Greek: κίβδηλος ἄνθρωπος</note>.

->**A yoked man.**<-
->**XLVII**<-

**A beast-like man.** <note>original Greek: ὑποζυγιώδης ἄνθρωπος</note> That is, "A yoked man." One who does nothing by his own judgment, but only by the command of another. The term is transferred from pack animals. To this belong those proverbial metaphors: "To send under the yoke." Horace says:
> Just as it pleases Venus, who likes to send 
> unequal forms and minds under her bronze yokes 
> with a cruel joke.
Likewise: "To cast off the yoke," which Marcus Tullius Cicero wrote in the first *Philippic*; or "To withdraw the neck from the yoke," as Ovid wrote:
> And withdraw your neck from the yoke that will hurt you.
Or "To shake off the yoke."

->**Barer than a pestle.**<-
->**XLVIII**<-

**Barer than a pestle.** <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ γυμνότερος</note> Said of someone who is exceedingly thin or poor. Related to this is **barer than a wooden peg** <note>original Greek: παττάλου γυμνότερος</note>, because the bark is stripped from these.

->**Balder than a pestle.**<-
->**XLIX**<-

**Balder than a pestle.** <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ φαλακρότερος</note> This is likewise a proverbial hyperbole used for those who are very smooth or hairless. For the bottom part of a pestle seems to resemble a bald man's skull. It can be transferred to those who are notably destitute, or simple people who are ignorant of how to hide their thoughts.

->**Copper-lined gold.**<-
->**L**<-

**Coppered gold.** <note>original Greek: ὑπόχαλκον χρυσίον</note> That is, "Gold with copper underneath." This is said of a man who is by no means sincere, but displays one thing on the surface while hiding another within. The image is taken from counterfeit coins.

->**Nothing from the yolk.**<-
->**LI**<-

**You give me nothing from the chick.** <note>original Greek: νεοττῦ οὐδέν μοι δίδως</note> That is, "You gave me nothing from the yolk." This fits those who share the worse parts of something while keeping the better parts for themselves. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of *On Divination*, tells a story of this kind from which it is likely this proverb was borrowed: A certain man dreamed he saw an egg hanging tied to the frame of his bed. When he reported the dream to an interpreter, the answer was that a treasure was indicated; therefore, he should dig in the place where he dreamed he saw the egg. When he dug, he found gold surrounded by silver. He sent a little of the silver to the interpreter, concealing the fact that he had found gold. The interpreter, receiving it, said: "Is there nothing then from the yolk?" <note>In the dream, the silver represented the egg white and the gold the yolk.</note>

->**Complainers in friendship.**<-
->**LII**<-

**Those who are fond of complaining are not well-suited for friendship.** <note>original Greek: οἱ φιλομεμφεῖς εἰς φιλίαν οὐκ εὐφυεῖς</note> That is: Those who are complainers toward their friends are not...

<summary>This page explores several Greek and Latin proverbs collected by Erasmus, covering themes of stupidity, majority rule, insincerity, and the metaphors of the "yoke" and the "pestle." It includes a notable anecdote from Cicero regarding a dream about a hidden treasure within an egg.</summary>
<keywords>blindness, majority rule, Pliny, Livy, metaphors of subjection, Horace, Cicero, Ovid, counterfeiting, friendship, Greek proverbs, ancient wisdom</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's "Adages," following a discussion on the importance of choosing suitable and pleasant companions. The current text explores proverbs related to friendship, empty promises, and the substance of persuasive speech.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...also suitable. To wink at the faults of friends; "this thing both joins and preserves joined friends" <note>original Latin: *Coniuere ad amicorū uitia, haec res & iungit, iunctos & feruat amicos*</note>. This sentiment seems to be taken from the historian Herodotus. However, the trimeter <note>a line of verse consisting of three metrical units</note> will be sound if you read: *Those who are fond of complaining are not well-suited for friendship.* <note>original Greek: οἱ φιλομεμφεῖς εἰς φιλίαν οὐκ εὐφυεῖς</note>. Yet I do not see what "fond of complaining" <note>original Greek: φιλομεμφεῖς</note> is in this context. If we read "the fault-finder" <note>original Greek: φιλομεμφής</note> a conjunction must be added, "But he who is querulous...", so the verse will stand:
> He who is querulous is hardly suited for friendship.

### Cleomenes exceeds the bed.
<margin>Cleomenes exceeds the bed <note>original Greek: ὁ κλεομένης τὴν κοίτην ὑπερέχει</note></margin> That is, Cleomenes exceeds the bed. This is said of one who devotes himself more to superfluous matters than to necessary ones. It appears to be derived from someone whose body was larger than the size of his small bed. Just as the poet Juvenal says:
> Codrus had a bed smaller than Procula. <note>Procula was likely a well-known dwarf or a very short woman in Rome; the joke is that even for her, the bed would be too small.</note>

### Rich in promises.
<margin>The speech indeed is wonderful, but the speaker is untrustworthy <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν λόος θαυμαστός, ὁ δὲ λέγων ἄπιστος</note></margin> That is, a magnificent speech indeed, but trust is not given to the speaker. This applies whenever someone promises grand things which he does not seem likely to perform <note>original Latin: *praestiturus*</note>. Plutarch, in his *Sayings of Kings and Commanders*, attributes this to Eudaemonidas, who had heard some Stoic philosopher, I believe, saying that "only the wise man was a good general."
<margin>The speech indeed is wonderful, but the person speaking has never sounded the trumpet <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν λόγος θαυμαστός, ὁ δὲ λέγων οὐ πώποτε σάλπισεν</note></margin> That is, an admirable speech indeed, but he who says it has never been surrounded by the blare of trumpets <note>meaning he has no actual experience in war</note>. Plutarch relates the same thing more fully in his *Laconic Sayings*:
<margin>The speech is wonderful, but the speaker is untrustworthy, for he has never sounded the trumpet <note>original Greek: λογος θαυμαστος, ὁ δὲ λεγων ἄπιστος, οὐ γὰρ πώποτε σάλπισαι</note></margin>. The same will apply to Theologians teaching certain celestial things when their life does not correspond to their preaching.

### Each is both.
<margin>Each is both, but both are neither <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν ἑκάτερος ἀμφότερος, ὁ δὲ ἀμφότερος οὐδέτερος</note></margin> That is: "Each is both, both are neither." This is a type of riddle mentioned by Plutarch in his *Moralia*, and it exists in the *Greek Epigrams*. It concerns two brothers, one of whom was named *Hecateros* <note>meaning "each"</note>, and the other *Amphoteros* <note>meaning "both"</note>. The former was a man of substance, while the latter was worthless. When King Philip of Macedon had seen these two, he is said to have joked about them in this way. It will fit any two people where the honesty of one compensates for the wickedness of the other.

### A bone is in the speech.
<margin>A bone is in the speech <note>original Greek: ὀστῦν ἔνεσι τῷ λόγῳ</note></margin> That is, there is bone and vigor in the discourse. This is said of a speech that is not empty, but contains solid thoughts. This saying is attributed to the Athenian statesman Themistocles. It seems to be taken from some poet, for it is an iambic dimeter <note>a specific poetic rhythm</note>. The Roman rhetorician Quintilian also calls the "discovery of facts" the "bones" of a speech. The comparison is taken from the bodies of living creatures, which are supported by bones, bound together by nerves, clothed in flesh and skin, held together by the soul, and moved by action.

### The river does not always carry axes.
<margin>The river does not always carry axes <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀεὶ ποταμὸς ἀξίνας φορεῖ</note></margin> That is, not always does the river carry axes. This means you should not immediately hope for the same luck that turned out successfully for others. It arose from an Aesopic fable: As a man was cutting wood, his axe fell from his hands into the water. Mercury, being invoked, returned a silver one. When the man denied it was his, Mercury returned a golden one. When he denied this was his as well, Mercury finally restored the iron one, and gave the others as a gift for his honesty. Another man, hoping for the same outcome, intentionally allowed his axe to slip. When it was lost and Mercury was not implored <note>meaning Mercury did not help him</note>, the first man responded to his complaining in this way: *The river does not always carry axes.* Although this fable is told differently in other commentaries—namely, that Mercury was present and asked with a golden axe if it was the one that was lost; when the man immediately affirmed it was his, Mercury, offended by the man's impudence, did not even return the iron one.

### It is not a Dithyramb if he drinks water.
<margin>It is not a Dithyrambus if he drinks water <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι Διθύραμβος, ἂν ὕδωρ πίνῃ</note></margin> That is,
> It is hardly a Dithyramb if he drinks water.

Joy is not present when wine is missing; the genius of poets languishes unless it is stirred by wine. Whence, according to Horace <note>referred to here by his family name, Flaccus</note>:
> By his praises of wine, wine-loving Homer is proved. And,
> Father Ennius himself never leaped forth to tell of arms unless he had drunk. And,
> No poems can please for long or live which are written by water-drinkers.

Indeed, as Plutarch relates in his *Table Talk*, the playwright Aeschylus wrote his tragedies while drinking; for the heat of wine excites the power of invention, which sometimes grows sluggish in those who are fasting; it moves the imagination, adds impulse, and supplies confidence. He adds that the orator Gorgias was wrong to attribute his tragedy to Mars <note>the god of war</note>, since it should rather be ascribed to Bacchus <note>the god of wine</note>. Dithyrambs were sung in honor of Bacchus...

<summary>This page explores several adages regarding the relationship between character and speech, the nature of luck, and the classical belief that wine inspires poetic genius. Erasmus draws on a wide range of authors, including Plutarch, Aesop, Horace, and Quintilian.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, Cleomenes, promises, hypocrisy, riddles, Philip of Macedon, Themistocles, rhetoric, Aesop's fables, Mercury, Dithyramb, wine and poetry, Horace, Aeschylus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s "Adages," specifically the Third Century of the Fourth Thousand. The previous page concluded with a discussion on Cleomenes and the habit of making empty promises. This page begins mid-sentence, concluding an entry about the "twice-born" Dionysus.</meta>

# THE FOURTH THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY
Ggg 2
<meta>catchword: bus in-</meta>

...chi, who was himself called "Twice-married" <note>original: Δίγαμος (Digamos)</note>, because he was born twice, as if emerging from two doors.

->Wiser after bitter events.<-
<margin>LIX</margin>
Wiser after disasters <note>original Greek: παρὰ τὰ δεινὰ φρονιμώτερος</note>. That is, wiser after misfortunes. Close to that is the saying: "Even a fool knows a thing once it is done" <note>original Greek: ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω</note>. Plato in the *Symposium* says: "And these things I say to you, Agatho, so that you are not deceived by this man, but rather learn from our sufferings to be cautious, and not, according to the proverb, to learn only after suffering like a fool." That is: "I say these things to you, Agatho, so that you are not deceived by him, but being taught by my misfortunes, you may take care; do not be wise only after receiving harm, in the manner of a fool." This is suitable for one who has been made more cautious by his own misfortune.

->Poorer than Pauson.<-
<margin>LX</margin>
Poorer than Pauson <note>original Greek: παύσωνος πτωχότερος</note>. That is, more of a beggar than Pauson. Pauson was a certain painter of remarkable thinness <note>meaning he was so poor he was emaciated</note>, much like Codrus in the works of Juvenal. Aristophanes marks him in the *Plutus*, where, when Poverty has cried out, "O city of Argos, hear what he says!" Chremylus replies, "Call Pauson to be your table-companion" <note>original Greek: παύσωνα κάλει γ’ ξύσσιτον</note>. That is: "Invite Pauson to eat with you."

->Beyond Hyperbolus.<-
<margin>LXI</margin>
It surpasses Hyperbolus <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ τὸν ὑπέρβολον</note>. That is, he beats Hyperbolus. Hyperbolus was a certain man who was wonderfully fond of lawsuits. Thus it applies to those who suffer from a similar disease. Plutarch in his *Life of Alcibiades*, Thucydides in the eighth book of the *Peloponnesian War*, and Aristophanes in the *Knights* show that Hyperbolus was a man wicked in every way, famous or powerful for nothing except the vice of his tongue. Furthermore, Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his book *On Famous Orators*, writes thus of Saturninus: "A man very similar to the Athenian Hyperbolus, whose wickedness the ancient Attic comedies have noted." Aristophanes, among other things, writes this about Hyperbolus: "A wicked man, and a citizen of sour, acid wine, Hyperbolus" <note>original Greek: ἄνδρα μοχθηρὸν, πολιτῶν ὀξίνην ὑπέρβολον</note>. That is:
> A wicked man, and a citizen like stale and sour wine, Hyperbolus.

->A sow in a wallow of mud.<-
<margin>LXII</margin>
A sow, having washed, returned to the wallow of filth <note>original Greek: ὗς λουσαμένη εἰς κύλισμα βορβόρου</note>. That is, the washed sow returned to the wallowing-place of mud. This is said when someone repeats shameful acts that had already been atoned for, as we have indicated elsewhere. It appears in the Epistles of Saint Peter. Related to this is what the Proverbs of Sirach <note>The Book of Sirach or Ecclesiasticus</note> have: "He who washes after touching a dead body, and touches it again, what does his washing profit him?"

->Because of the weaver’s mistake.<-
<margin>LXIII</margin>
By the weaver’s stumble, the *hypetes* was beaten <note>original Greek: ὑφάντου πταίσματος, ὑπήτης ἐτύφθη</note>. That is, because of the weaver's error, the *hypetes* took the blow. This is used when one person sins and another pays the price. What a *hypetes* is, I have not yet found among authors <note>Erasmus is noting a gap in his sources; the term likely refers to a subordinate or a specific garment-worker</note>.

->The lying orache.<-
<margin>LXIIII</margin>
The orache is full of lies <note>original Greek: ψευδῶν πλέα ἀτράφαξις</note>. That is, the orache <term>orache: a leafy green plant, also called atriplex, known for growing very quickly but having little substance</term> is stuffed with lies. Said of those who are puffed up and full of hot air. Orache is a type of vegetable that rises quickly to a great height. It is called *atriplex* by the Latins, related, if I am not mistaken, to the beet family, which also grows large suddenly, though they are otherwise tasteless. Theophrastus indicates this in his *History of Plants*, Book 1, Chapter 5. The same herb is listed by him in Book 7, Chapter 1, among those that come forth quickly—namely, on the eighth day from sowing. It has a larger stalk, but it is soft and fleshy. Suidas notes it was said against Cleon, who was falsely slandering the knights in the assembly; when he seemed to be believed, it was said: "Is the Council not full of lying orache?" <note>original Greek: νουδ’ ἀτράφαξις πλέαν εἶναι τὴν βουλήν;</note>. By this saying, both Cleon’s vanity in slandering and the people’s readiness to believe were noted. For it is characteristic of slander to suddenly stir up a massive tragedy from the slightest evil. This is roughly Suidas's meaning. The adage is taken from Aristophanes’s *Knights*.

->Strike the blow from the plow.<-
<margin>LXV</margin>
Strike the one from the plow <note>original Greek: παῖε τὴν ἀπ’ ἀρότρου</note>. That is: inflict the blow of the plow, or, drive in the plowshare. We use this when we order someone to fight strenuously, even if without skill. They say it was born from a story told by Pausanias in his book on Elis. A certain Glaucus of Carystus, while plowing the earth, happened to have the plowshare fall off. He picked it up and fitted it back into place using his hand as a hammer. When his father, Demylus, saw this, he took the youth to Olympia for the boxing match. But when the boy, unskilled in the art, was nearly failing under the blows, his father shouted: "Strike the blow from the plow!" reminding him to attack his opponent in the same way he used to wound the earth with the plowshare. At this shout, the youth’s spirit returned, and he won. The same man later won twice at the Pythian games, eight times at the Nemean, and likewise eight times at the Isthmian. The author is Pausanias.

->To walk on the tips of the toes.<-
<margin>LXVI</margin>
Those who attempt something secretly or cautiously and "step by step," as they say, on the tips of their feet—

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
904
<meta>catchword: rebus</meta>

...are said to enter into matters. The Greeks express this more pleasantly with the compound adverb *akropoditi* <note>original: ἀκροποδιτί, meaning "on the tips of the feet"</note>. Similar to these are the phrases: "With a suspended step," and "With suspended feet." These are derived from the gesture of those who walk so that no one hears the noise of their feet, or those who, with difficulty and caution, place their footsteps lightly. It is somewhat different in Plato’s *Laches*: <margin>on tip-toe</margin> <margin>walking on the very tip of the foot</margin> "walking on the very tip of the foot" <note>original: τῇ γε ἄκρᾳ ποδὶ βαίνοντες</note>. That is, not even entering with the whole foot; this relates to the expressions "To taste with the tips of the lips," or "To touch with the tips of the fingers" <note>meaning to treat a subject superficially or tentatively</note>.

->To touch the sky with a finger.<-
<margin>LX</margin>

By a proverbial hyperbole, a person is said to "touch the sky with a finger" when they seem to be far above the condition of mortals and closest to the gods. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "But our leading men think they touch the sky with a finger if there are bearded mullets in their fishponds that come to their hand." Related to this is what we have mentioned elsewhere from the same author: "To be in heaven." In a similar fashion, Horace writes:
>But if you insert me among the lyric bards,
>I shall strike the stars with my lofty head.

Ovid says:
>Since you please her, you touch the stars with your head.

And in Theocritus’s *The Wayfarers*: <margin>because at some time now</margin>
"When I won the lamb, I shall go among the stars for you." <margin>that is,</margin>

When Lysimachus had come to Thrace, as if he had occupied the furthest borders of the kingdom, he said: "Now I touch the sky with my spear." This most insolent remark was rebuked by Pasiades of Byzantium, who happened to be present, who said: "Let us depart, lest he pierce the sky with his spear."

->To play the Corinthian.<-
<margin>LX</margin>

"To play the Corinthian" <note>original: Κορινθιάζεσθαι (Korinthiazesthai)</note> was a common joke among the ancients for those who lived a life of debauchery and frequenting brothels, or those who ran such establishments; a trade which today is nowhere more profitable than among our own people. It is taken from the Corinthian prostitutes, of whom we have spoken in the appropriate place. For so much honor was given to prostitutes there that, as Athenaeus teaches from ancient authors, they stood for hire in the temple of Venus, and in solemn prayers it was customary to add a request that the gods might increase the number of prostitutes. Indeed, he even records that when the city was suffering in extreme danger, the prostitutes performed a sacrifice and saved the city by appeasing Venus. Stephanus mentions the proverb in *On Cities*, citing Aristophanes’s *Cocalus*.

->Is glass worth as much as a pearl?<-

Saint Jerome, in a certain letter to the virgin Demetrias, says: "It is the custom of worldly people and Christians who are not of full faith to hand over to virginity <note>i.e., to the convent</note> their deformed daughters or those weak in some limb, for whom they cannot find noble husbands; as the saying goes, is glass worth as much as a pearl?" He uses the same phrase in several other places, and it is also used by Tertullian in his book *To the Martyrs*. By this saying, the greatest inequality of things was signified. Among gems, the highest praise was given to "unions" <note>term: unionibus — large, high-quality pearls</note>, while glass was the cheapest; and yet glass somewhat imitates gems. If you labor so much so that the body may live, how much more effort should be given so that the soul may live? If you do everything to please a human prince, how much more should you strive to please God, the prince of all? If riches that will perish by use or theft are prepared with such great labors, why do we not apply ourselves more to accumulating heavenly riches? In these and similar cases, there will be a place for this proverb.

->He is stuck in the shallows.<-

Saint Ambrose, in the commentaries he published on the Gospel of Luke, used this adage quite appropriately to signify that the genealogy of Christ, which is presented differently by the Evangelists, cannot be easily explained. He says: "We have come to a steep part of the discussion; we are stuck in the shallows." This is certainly a metaphor taken from a ship that, having struck the shallows, is tossed about in vain and cannot hold its intended course—a thing that happens to those who fall into quicksands or rough ground. Marcus Tullius Cicero expresses the proverb in the same way in the fifth book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "He has come to the extreme; he is stuck in the rough ground." Again, elsewhere in the same work: "If he knew how to define, how to divide; if he held the power of speaking, or finally, the custom, he would never have fallen into such rough ground." The same Cicero said: "The water is stuck" <note>original: Aqua hæret</note>. For he writes thus to his brother Quintus: "Here the water is stuck for me," signifying that no progress has been made in the case. I suspect it was commonly said of a case that was delayed. For water is poured in only for the one who is about to speak, and it is not permitted to speak after the water-clocks <note>term: clepsydras — ancient water-clocks used to time speeches in court</note> have run out; thus, when...

### FOURTH THOUSAND, THIRD CENTURY
Ggg 3
<meta>catchword: is and</meta>

...the rest of the water remains, the speaker's discourse is interrupted. Plautus in his *Pseudolus* says: "I’m ruined, now the man is in the middle of the mud <note>original: "in medio luto est"</note>, he doesn’t know the name; this business is stuck."

### To plow in the stalk. LXXI

"To plow in the stalk" <note>original: Ἐπὶ καλάμης ἀρᾷν</note>, or in the stubble, is a phrase used for those who exhaust their mental powers through never-ending labor. It can also refer to those who never cease and never allow for a period of rest, but rather drain all the moisture from the soil through constant cultivation, sowing new seeds immediately after the harvest. Suidas cites this from Lysias.

---

### More silent than the Pythagoreans. LXXII

"You seem more silent than those initiated by Pythagoras" <note>original: Σιωπηλότερος ἔοικας τῶν πυθαγόρα τελειωθέντων</note>. This is typically used for those who are exceedingly quiet. It is taken from the school of Pythagoras, where a five-year silence was imposed upon students; they called this *echemythia* <note>original: ἐχεμυθίαν</note>, from the restraint of speech. Suidas records this under his entry for proverbs, as does Zenodotus in his *Collections*.

---

### The Francolin’s New Moon. LXXIII

"The Francolin’s New Moon" <note>original: Ἀτταγᾶς νουμηνία</note>. This is mentioned by Suidas but not explained, except for what can be easily gathered by conjecture from various sources: that it was said of a crowd of low-born and servile men. Indeed, the *Attagen* <note>the francolin or woodcock, a game bird</note> is a marsh bird marked with many-colored spots on its feathers; for this reason, they used to call a branded slave "an Attagena," whose back was patterned with various marks from the scars of beatings. Furthermore, at the new moon—for so the Greeks call the start of the month, since they do not have "Kalends"—slaves were sold at Athens and the selection of soldiers took place.

---

### A vast interval. LXXIV

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the sixth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, uses these six-foot verses as if they were a proverb:

->But the South Wind rolls many waves<-
->in the space between the wide sea.<-
-><note>original: πολλὰ δὲ ἐν μεταιχμίῳ / νότος κυλινδεῖ κύματ’ εὐρέης ἁλός</note><-

By this, he signifies that the person is far away. One might also twist this to mean that a matter is still far from danger.

---

### Alive and seeing. LXXV

What Terence said in *The Eunuch*—"I perish alive and seeing" <note>original: Viuus, uidensq́; pereo</note>—Marcus Tullius indicates was spoken as a proverbial figure. Thus he writes in his *Speech for Publius Sestius*: "That miserable Cypriot, who was always an ally, always a friend, about whom no harsh suspicion was ever brought to the Senate or our commanders, is, as they say, 'alive and seeing' made public property along with his food and clothing." Saint Jerome also uses it in several places. Indeed, that phrase "with his food and clothing" <note>meaning with all his meager possessions</note> also tastes of a proverb.

---

### Better to have bitter enemies. LXXVI

Marcus Tullius in his dialogue *On Friendship*: "For that proverb of Cato is clever: 'One deserves much better from certain bitter enemies than from those friends who seem sweet.'" While I admit this is a magnificent sentiment, I would deny that it is a proverb. Firstly, because it bears no appearance of a proverb at all; secondly, because proverbs belong to the common people, not to this or that specific person. Therefore, I think it should read: "For that saying of Cato is clever," or "that word of Cato." Nevertheless, we thought it should be added lest anyone think it was omitted through negligence.

---

### To burst the columns. LXXVII

Aelian recorded that there were once animals of vast size in Samos called "Neades," whose voices were so powerful they could crack the earth. From this, a proverb arose for loud and shamelessly talkative people, saying they "burst the posts and columns." Virgil used it against Philistus, a noisy lawyer and critic. Likewise, Juvenal writes:

->Fronto’s plane trees and convulsed marbles cry out.<-
<note>Describing a house shaking from the loud recitations of bad poets.</note>

---

### The life of a hare. LXXVIII

"To live the life of a hare" <note>original: λαγὼ βίον ζῆ</note> is said of those who live in constant anxiety and trepidation. This is because that animal, exposed as prey to everyone, does not even take sleep except with its eyes open. Demosthenes says in his speech against Aeschines: "You lived the life of a hare, fearing and trembling and always expecting to be beaten." It was also used by—

THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
M
<meta>catchword: M</meta>

is also mentioned by Plutarch in his small book <term>On the Love of Wealth <note>original: περὶ φιλοπλουτίας</note></term>, which I translated into Latin some time ago. <margin><term>Unambitious <note>original: ἀφιλότιμοι</note></term></margin> was a term used by Athanasius in his first apology; and in Strabo, one finds "more timid than Phrygian hares," a phrase I have discussed elsewhere as the occasion arose.

->The conquered dare not mutter.<-
<margin>LXIX.</margin>

<term>Conquered men are bound by silence <note>original: νικώμενοι ἄνδρες τῇ ἀγρυφίᾳ δέδενται</note></term>. That is, those who are defeated are bound in silence. Hesychius, in the book titled *How one might benefit from enemies*, cites this from Pindar. It agrees with what I have recorded elsewhere: "What is there for the conquered but grief?" Moreover, <term>silence <note>original: ἀγρυφία</note></term> is a very elegant metaphor for when one does not dare to mutter, derived from the verb <term>to grunt or mutter <note>original: γρύζειν</note></term>, which has been discussed more than once.

->Thersites’ face.<-
<margin>LXX.</margin>

<term>The look of Thersites <note>original: Θερσίτου βλέμμα</note></term>. That is, a Thersitic face. This was commonly said of someone monstrously deformed, because Homer wrote that this man was the foulest of all who came to Troy. And even if he depicts him vividly—"from head to foot," as they say—noting both his physical defects and his mental sicknesses, you would say a most wicked spirit inhabited a dwelling worthy of itself. The passage is in the second book of Homer's *Iliad*, too well known to need repeating here. It will be more charming if applied to the soul; for instance, if you speak of someone beautiful but of wicked character: "If you look at the body, you find Nireus <note>a Greek hero known for his beauty</note>; if you look at the soul, you find more than the <term>look of Thersites</term>." Suidas makes mention of this adage.

->The Magpie-bearer.<-
<margin>LXXI.</margin>

<term>Ivy-bearer <note>original: Κιττοφόρος</note></term>. That is, "Magpie-bearer" <note>Erasmus links the Greek term for ivy-bearer to the Latin for magpie-bearer</note> seems to be a common insult for a man of the lowest and most dejected lot. Indeed, Demosthenes, in his oration *On the Crown*, says that Aeschines was called by this name by old women, just as he was called <term>basket-bearer <note>original: λικνοφόρον</note></term>, because he carried magpies and winnowing-fans on his head. For these were used in the Bacchic mysteries, because that bird is sacred to Bacchus, and the winnowing-fan was employed in all mysteries. Hence Virgil wrote: 
"And the mystic fan of Iacchus <note>another name for Bacchus</note>."

->In ready cash.<-
<margin>LXXII.</margin>

To have something "in ready cash" <note>original: in numerato</note>, if transferred to the qualities of the mind, would have the character of a proverb. For as Seneca reports, Octavius Augustus pronounced this of the orator Vinicius: that he had his talent "in ready cash." This was because in arguing cases he possessed a most ready wit; that which long reflection provided to others, the first intent of his mind gave to him immediately. It is taken from those who have reduced their affairs to a most certain reckoning—that is, to counted money. Quintilian says in his sixth book: "It was said of an advocate who spoke easily off the cuff, that he had his talent in ready cash." See the proverb, "You have spoken by the number."

->As much as one has.<-
<margin>LXXIII.</margin>

As much as each person has, so much is he worth. As Horace wrote in his first satire: 
"Nothing is enough," he says, "because you are worth as much as you possess."
Likewise Juvenal in his third satire: 
"As much money as each man keeps in his chest, 
So much credit he has." 
I would not have included this among the proverbs, lest anyone cry out that I have collected maxims rather than adages, had not St. Augustine, in his book *On Christian Discipline*, specifically cited it under the title of a <term>proverb</term>. For he says of it: "And that proverb says: as much as you have, so great you shall be." Although Horace also indicates well enough that it was a commonly tossed-about sentiment by what preceded it: 
"But a good part of men, deceived by false desire..." 
Apuleius also uses it in his *Apology*: "In truth, you are worth as much as you have." It seems also to have come into common speech from Euripides. Seneca records this verse of his among others: 
"Everywhere, each man was worth as much as he had."

->To erase from the deepest wax.<-
<margin>LXXIV.</margin>

To erase from the deepest wax <note>original: Imis ceris eradere</note> is used for that which is to be utterly destroyed, so that no trace at all of the former memory remains. It is taken from those who write on waxed tablets; it is their custom that if they ever wish to delete something, they turn the stylus and draw it over the surface of the wax. If they do this lightly, some traces of the writing remain; sometimes they erase it fundamentally and completely. St. Jerome writes to Chromatius: "You have so utterly forgotten our intimacy, that you have erased that letter which the Apostle says is written in the hearts of Christians, not with a small smudge, but, as they say, from the deepest wax." This will apply to a deep forgetting, whether of friends, or former fortune, or anything of that kind.

FOURTH CHILIAD, THIRD CENTURY
Ggg 4
<meta>catchword: For thus</meta>

### Pressing a swollen foot with a thin hand.
### LXXXV

Hesiod, in the work he titled *Works and Days*, explained poverty as if through a kind of riddle: <margin>XIX Plutarch in Proverbs</margin> <term>Press a fat foot with a thin hand <note>original: Λεπτῇ δὲ παχυὺν πόδα χειρὶ πιέζοις</note></term>. That is: "You may press a swollen foot with a slender hand." For hands grow slender from hunger, while feet swell up from the cold. The verse goes like this:
> <margin>XXX Hesiod in Works and Days</margin> Lest the evil season of winter and helplessness seize you
> Along with poverty, and you press a swollen foot with a thin hand. That is:
> Lest the bad times of winter catch you in want,
> And a withered hand begins to press a swollen foot.

It will be more elegant if it is applied more broadly to preparing "provisions" for old age, or similar situations.

### It will not always be summer.
### LXXXVI

To almost the same sense belongs that saying from the same book: <margin>XXXI Hesiod in Works and Days</margin> <term>It will not always be summer; build your nests <note>original: οὐκ αἰεὶ θέρος ἐσσῆται. ποιεῖσθε καλιάς</note></term>. 
The prime of life will not always be green; prepare a place for old age to retreat. Or: fortune will not always be prosperous; fortify the mind with the decrees of philosophy, so that it can despise adverse fortune. Cato also warns farmers to think about how long the winter is. Well known is the <term>fable <note>original: apologus</note></term> about the ants reproaching the <term>cicada <note>an insect often translated as a grasshopper in later versions of this fable</note></term>, because it had done nothing all summer but sing in idleness, and therefore was begging in the winter. This saying ought to be inscribed on the caps of young men. For it does not only warn that resources must be prepared for old age, but also learning, virtue, and an honorable reputation, which are the best protections for old age.

### When the boneless one gnaws its own foot.
### LXXXVII

With a similar figure of speech, he indicated extreme want in the same work: <margin>XXII Hesiod in Works and Days</margin> <term>When the boneless one gnaws his own foot <note>original: ὅτ' ἀνόστεος ὃν πόδα τένδει</note></term>. That is: "When he who lacks a bone eats his own feet." 
He calls the <term>polypus <note>an octopus</note></term> "boneless" because it lacks bones. It is believed by some to gnaw its own arms when food is scarce. For it is extremely voracious, although Pliny thinks this happens to it because of crabs; however, he believes that the parts, once cut off, grow back, just as tails do on lizards. Alcaeus, in the seventh book of Athenaeus, says: <margin>XXIII</margin> <term>I eat myself in the manner of a polypus <note>original: Ἔδωδ' ἐμαυτὸν ὡς πολύπους</note></term>.
Hence it is also called <term>self-eating <note>original: αὐτοφάγος</note></term>. But Athenaeus also rejects this opinion.

### A hundred beams for a wagon.
### LXXXVIII

It is as similar to a proverb as one egg is to another—what Hesiod wrote in the same work titled *Works and Days*: <term>A wagon is joined together from a hundred timbers <note>original: Ἑκατὸν δέ τε δούρατ' ἀμάξης</note></term>. 
We shall use this opportunely when we wish to indicate that what is being asked of us costs a great deal. For we easily use the things of others, not weighing how much they cost the person who provides them. Hesiod’s verse goes like this: <margin>XXIIII Hesiod in Works and Days</margin>
> For it is easy to say the word: "Give me a wagon and a pair of oxen."
> But it is easy to refuse: "The oxen have work at hand."
> A man wealthy in his mind thinks to build a wagon,
> Foolish as he is, and does not know this: a wagon requires a hundred timbers. That is:
> For it is easy to say: "Give me a wagon and oxen."
> But easy to say no, for look, labor is pressing the bulls.
> But the foolish man thinks in his mind to build a wagon,
> And hardly knows it must be joined from a hundred pieces of wood.

Therefore, whenever many supports are needed for something someone is undertaking—such as holding a magistracy, writing a book, the duty of preaching, establishing a family, or a long pilgrimage—we shall not ineptly employ Hesiod’s phrase: <term>a hundred beams for a wagon <note>original: ἑκατὸν δέ τε δούρατ' ἀμάξης</note></term>.

### Drive out the spiders.
### LXXXIX

This also has the appearance of a proverb, which is found in the same author in the same work: <margin>XXV Hesiod in Works and Days</margin> <term>Drive the spiders out of the vessels <note>original: ἐκ δ' ἀγγέων ἐλάσας ἀράχνα</note></term>. That is: "You should cast out the webs that the spider weaves in the jars." <note>This implies filling the jars with grain so that spiders have no room to live there, symbolizing plenty and foresight.</note>

THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

For in this way they signify emptiness and poverty even today. In the same manner, Catullus says:

> For the purse of your Catullus
> Is full of cobwebs. <note>original: "Plenus sacculus est aranearum." Catullus, Poem 13.</note>

Nothing is more common among the common people today than this saying. Lucian, in *The False Logician*, says: <margin><unclear>Full of woodworms and spiders</unclear> <note>original: θριψὶ καὶ ἀράχναις μεστά</note></margin>
-> that is, stuffed with decay and spiders. <-

### With walls running around.

<note>original: τῶν τοίχων περιεχόντων</note> That is, with the walls surrounding us. Plutarch, in his *Table Talk* <note>original: Symposiacis</note>, seventh decade, fifth problem, indicates that this was a proverb used by women to signify secrets—namely, that the walls keep out witnesses and judges. But he says that the pleasures and games of good men ought to be of such a kind that they have no need for the protection of walls. We may use this when we want to signify that something strange is being shown to another, and for that reason secrecy is sought.

### Struck by a horn.

<note>original: Κερασβόλα / Kerasbola</note> In the same work, the second problem, he teaches that men who are stubborn, of harsh character, and intractable were commonly called "horn-struck." Someone translated this term into Latin not quite conveniently. The metaphor is taken from farmers, among whom seeds that happen to strike the horn of the oxen before falling into the earth are called <term>kerasbola <note>from the Greek "keras" (horn) and "ballo" (to throw/strike)</note></term>. <note>original: πρὰ δὲ εἰς κέρατα βάλλεσθαι</note> These seeds turn out much harder than the others, which is why they also call them "hard-boiled" <note>original: ἀτοράμονα / atoramona - meaning pulses that do not soften when cooked</note>. The author of the *Etymologicum* indicates that this word was used only once by Plato, and was taken from legumes that do not soften either by fire or water; we see certain things of this kind mixed in with legumes, such as vetch and black peas. The passage is in Plato’s ninth book *On Laws*. In that place, it seems the translator was deceived as to what "horn-struck" meant. For he translated it as legumes hardened by a "touch of lightning," as if the Greek had said <term>keraunobola <note>struck by a thunderbolt</note></term>. Furthermore, as to why it happens that seeds which strike the horns of oxen turn out drier and harder when they grow, Plutarch brings forward this reason: because seeds thrown from a warm hand are immediately received and cherished by the earth, they are more aided by heat, which is friendly to the seed. But those that strike the horns seem more like they were "cast away" than sown, and they gather coldness during the delay. Theophrastus doubts whether what the farmers say about these "horn-struck" seeds is merely a trivial superstition.

### The State teaches the man.

<note>original: Πόλις ἄνδρα διδάσκει</note> That is, the Republic teaches the man. It signifies that no one can be fit for managing affairs unless he is trained by practical experience. Plutarch quotes this from Simonides as a half-line of heroic verse: No matter how long you have lived in the countryside, you will not become fit for administering the state unless you have lived in the forum, in the senate house, and among the crowded people. Socrates, in Plato's works, alluded to this when, invited to pleasant places in the countryside, he responded that he was eager to learn, but that trees teach nothing.

### Since you are a craftsman.

Plutarch, in his *Precepts on Statecraft*, quotes this six-foot verse, which is undoubtedly proverbial, from Euripides:
<note>original: Τέκτων γὰρ ὤν, οὐκ ἔπραξες ξυλευγικά</note>
-> that is, <-
-> Since you are a craftsman, you are hardly doing a craftsman's work. <-

This applies to one who attempts things for which he is not suited, either through lack of skill or a defect of nature—for example, if a child or someone incapable of persuasion should undertake an embassy, or an idle person should manage a household; or if an old or weak man should take up military service; or if someone should hunt but not practice rhetoric like a <term>Scotist <note>A follower of the medieval philosopher John Duns Scotus, often criticized by humanists like Erasmus for overly complex, dry logic.</note></term>. Long ago, that line of Horace also became a proverb, which no one seems to have imitated:
-> Craftsmen handle craftsmen's tools. <note>original: "Tractant fabrilia fabri." Horace, Epistles 2.1.116.</note> <-

### To mix water with fire.

Among the proverbs by which we signify <term>impossibilities <note>original: ἀδύνατα / adunata</note></term>, we must also include this one: <note>original: πῦρ ὕδατι μιγνύναι</note>, that is, to mix fire with water. Plutarch, in the booklet he titled *On the Primary Cold*, uses this proverb as evidence while trying to prove that coldness is the essential property of water, as heat is of fire. For fire fights with water in both qualities: it is hot and dry, while water is moist and cold. He relates in the same place that it was a custom among the Persians that a suppliant would go down into a river carrying fire, threatening that if he did not obtain what he sought, he would throw the fire into the water. In this way, he would indeed obtain what he asked for, but he was punished because he had threatened to do something that was against the nature of things. For water is the enemy of fire and always extinguishes it. That kind of supplication was considered the most powerful among the barbarians, and it was not lawful to refuse what was requested. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his thirteenth *Philippic*: "Sooner shall water be reconciled with flame, as the proverb goes." And again: "Sooner water and flame, as some poet says—sooner, in short, everything, before either the Republic returns to favor with the Antonys, or the Antonys with the Republic."

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning secrecy, the origins of stubbornness (the "horn-struck" metaphor), the necessity of civic life for education, and the folly of attempting tasks outside one's expertise or nature.</summary>
<keywords>poverty, Catullus, Plutarch, secrecy, Kerasbola, stubbornness, Plato, agriculture, civic education, Socrates, professional skill, Euripides, impossibilities, fire and water, Cicero</keywords>

CHILIAS FOUR, CENTURY III

->As if from a watchtower.<-
<margin>XCV</margin>
<note>original: Ὡς ἀπὸ σκοπιᾶς</note> That is, "As if from a watchtower." This is a proverbial comparison used when someone contemplates a matter that is placed before their eyes, viewing the whole thing from all sides. Indeed, all things are most conveniently viewed from a height, because there is nothing to stand in the way or hinder the prospect. Plutarch uses this in his short book titled *On the Fortune of the Romans*.

->As if in a friendship bowl.<-
<margin>XCVI</margin>
<note>original: Ὥσπερ ἐν κρατῆρι φιλοτησίῳ</note> That is, "As if in a friendship bowl." This too is a proverbial comparison, by which we signify that previously turbulent matters are being settled and pacified, and those who were formerly enemies are being restored to favor. A "friendship bowl" <note>the original term "crater" refers to a large vessel used for mixing wine and water</note> is what people pass to one another at banquets as a symbol and pledge of friendship. Just as one who betrothed his daughter to someone would offer the future son-in-law a taste, he would present a "friendship bowl." The Scythians also, who are most steadfast in their friendships, established them with a bowl, as Lucian testifies in his work *Toxaris*. Indeed, Christ himself, the prince of our religion, consecrated that secret friendship with his followers with a cup.

->You have come late.<-
<margin>XCVII</margin>
<note>original: Ὀψὲ ἦλθες</note> That is, "You have come late." This applies to those who undertake a task after the proper time—for instance, if someone already chilled by the defects of age prepares to marry, or an older person begins to learn his letters. It arose from an oracle that the Pythian priestess delivered to someone asking whether he ought to take up the administration of the republic: "You have come late seeking to rule and lead the people, and you knock at the door of military command before the hour" <note>original Greek: Ὀψὲ μ' ἦλθες ἄρχειν καὶ δημαγωγεῖν ζητῶν, καὶ πρὸ ὥραν στρατηγὸς κόπτεις θύραν</note>. Plutarch mentions this in his commentary titled *Whether an Old Man Should Engage in Public Affairs*.

->The antidote before the poison.<-
<margin>XCVIII</margin>
Saint Jerome, responding against Rufinus, says: "How can you accuse the prefaces of books you do not know? Which, by a kind of prophecy, responded to future slander, fulfilling the proverb: The antidote before the poison"—understand: "you apply." It is appropriate to use this whenever someone clears their name before they are even accused. For an antidote is given against poisons, and no one takes one unless the poison has already been tasted. However, there are some who fortify themselves with antidotes beforehand, lest it cause harm if they happen to consume a toxin. We read that Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, famous for building immunity to poisons</note> did exactly this.

->More silent than a statue.<-
<margin>XCIX</margin>
Even in these times, it is a proverb: "More silent than a statue." It refers to a person who is exceedingly speechless and quiet. Horace used this hyperbole in his letter to Julius Florus:

> He goes out more silent than a statue
> For the most part, and moves the people to laughter.

Likewise, Juvenal makes a certain wealthy but speechless and unlearned man similar to a statue of Mercury: "Most like a headless trunk of Hermes." In a similar form, Saint Chrysostom, in the sixth book of *On the Priesthood*, says of a slow and stupid person: "Then that thing which we Greeks are accustomed to say, he will differ in nothing from stone figures" <note>original: ὥσπερ δὴ τὸ ἡμέτερον τῶν λιθίνων οὐδὲν διοίσει</note>, which we have also noted elsewhere. Xenophon says in the *Symposium*: "For you would hear a voice from them no less than from stone statues" <note>original: Ἐκείνων γὰρ μὴ ἂν ἧττον φωνὴν ἀκούσαις, ἢ τῶν λιθίνων</note>. That is, you would hear their voice less than that of stone statues. Statues frequently have the appearance of wise and eloquent men, yet they themselves say nothing.

->I knew this before [Theognis was born].<-
<margin>C</margin>
Plutarch, in the booklet titled *That a Philosopher Ought Especially to Converse with Princes*, mocks those who make a twofold account of philosophy: one situated in the emotions which proceeds from Mercury the Leader (*Hegemone*), and the other situated in public speaking which is bestowed by Mercury the Messenger (*Diactorus*). He says this idea is "stale and obsolete" <note>original: ἕωλόν φησιν ... καὶ ἑωποπισμένον</note>, and should be joined with that saying: "I knew this before Theognis was born" <note>original: τῷ τοδί μὲν ἤδη πρὶν Θέογνιν γεγονέναι</note>. He uses the same phrase for the same sentiment in the booklet titled *Why the Pythia No Longer Delivers Oracles in Verse*, citing it from some comic writer. Aulus Gellius, in book one of *Attic Nights*, chapter three, cites it from Lucilius. Cicero says, "Arms should not be taken up for a friend against one's country." This surely no one was ignorant of, even before Theognis, as Lucilius says, was born. There is no doubt that this line of verse is proverbial, by which they signified a thing was "cold" <note>In classical rhetoric, "cold" or "chilly" means dull, uninspired, or lacking wit</note> and inept. It appears to be taken from Theognis the tragic writer, whom Suidas and (unless my memory fails me) Plato testify was "chilly." For there was another man of this name whose moral maxims still exist.

<summary>This page explores several classical proverbs regarding clarity of vision, timely action, and the "chilly" or dull nature of unoriginal ideas. Notable entries include the "friendship bowl" as a symbol of reconciliation and the "statue" as a metaphor for silence or stupidity.</summary>
<keywords>watchtower, friendship bowl, crater philotesius, reconciliation, timeliness, Pythian oracle, antidote, Mithridates, silence, statue of Mercury, Theognis, chilly wit</keywords>
