# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES
# FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY

### Phocian desperation.

<margin>Φ</margin> "Phocian desperation," <note>original: Φωκέων ἀπόνοια, or φωκικὴ ἀπόνοια</note> also known as Phocic desperation. Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century grammarian</note> reminds us that this is commonly said of foolish and insane plans. However, one may gather from Plutarch of Chaeronea that it was usually said when, in desperate circumstances, one resorted to extreme measures. It arose from an event of this kind: There was an atrocious and irreconcilable enmity—or, to use Plutarch's words, a "truce-less war" <note>original: ἄσπονδος & πόλεμος</note>—between the Thessalians and the Phocians. This was because the Phocians had slaughtered every single one of the Thessalian governors in their cities on the same day, and the Thessalians, in turn, had crucified two hundred and fifty Phocian hostages. Then the Thessalians, having gathered all their forces, burst through the territory of the Locrians, having issued an edict that no one of advanced age should be spared, and that children and women should be led away into slavery. 

Therefore, Daiphantus, who was one of the three men to whom the affairs of the Phocians had been entrusted, persuaded the men to go out to meet the Thessalians to do battle; however, they were to gather the women together with the children from all over Phocis and place them in a single location. Having piled up a huge mass of wood, they were to station guards and command them that as soon as they learned the men had been defeated in battle, they should immediately set the wood on fire and burn the wives and children. When the assembly approved of this, a certain man stood up and said it was not right to do this unless the plan was also approved by the votes of the wives; if it did not please them, they should not be forced. However, when the women learned of the matter, they held their own council and praised Daiphantus for having consulted most rightly for the Phocian cause. Their children felt the same way. Once these things were settled, the Phocians engaged the Thessalians and emerged victorious. The Greeks called that decree the "Phocian desperation," because even though it had turned out successfully, it nevertheless seemed rash and lacking in sense. Plutarch relates something of this sort. Pausanias reports almost the same things in his *Description of Greece*. He also mentions the proverb, which he says was commonly used after this event "concerning all ruthless plans" <note>original: ἐπὶ πάντων βεβουλευμάτων ἀναλγητῶν</note>—that is, regarding all plans that are devoid of grief or pity. Stephanus also mentions it, indicating it was commonly said "of those who have planned unfeeling things." <note>original: ποδὶ τῶν τὰ ἀναλγῆ βεβουλευμένων</note>

### With a suspended hand.

Pliny, in the sixth book of his *Epistles*, used the phrase "with a suspended hand" <note>original: Suspensa manu</note> to mean lightly and with little accuracy. He says: "But you ought not to recommend to me with a suspended hand those whom you think should be protected." This same expression is more elegant if you transfer it from the body to the mind. Quintilian, in his twelfth declamation, uses "with a light hand" <note>original: Leui manu</note> in the same sense, as if it were a proverb. Cicero uses "with a light arm," <note>original: Leui brachio</note> about which I have spoken elsewhere. Likewise, we say "with a suspended foot" <note>original: Suspenso pede</note> for "gradually" and "silently." Ammianus, in his fourteenth book, writes: "and they threw themselves into the skiffs with suspended steps." <note>original: suspensis passibus; this is the origin of the English "on tiptoe" or "walking on eggshells"</note>

### May the itch take the hindmost.

Formerly, children competing in a race used to shout: "May the itch seize the last one!" <note>original: Occupet extremum scabies</note> encouraging each individual to the race with this cry, and calling down a curse upon whoever was the last of all. From this, it was drawn into a proverb used by those who wanted to signify that they wished to win by any means possible, and would not allow themselves to be among the last. Thus, those who increase their wealth through right or wrong so as not to seem among the commoners, those who emerge into magistracies by evil arts, and those who hunt for grand priesthoods by any means, can respond to someone calling them otherwise: "May the itch take the hindmost." 

Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from twisting this into a good sense; for instance, if someone strives furiously with all their might so as not to be surpassed by their peers in learning, or in good deeds, or in duties toward friends, they might say: "May the itch take the hindmost." We see, therefore, that this proverb was received from children, just like that one: "Drive the one near you" <note>original: τὴν περὶ σαυτὸν ἔλα; a racing metaphor</note> and this Gospel phrase from Matthew 11: "We piped to you, and you did not dance." Horace used it in his *Art of Poetry*:
> May the itch seize the last one; it is a disgrace for me to be left behind.

Acron <note>a commentator on Horace</note> indicates its origin.

### Day-sleeper.

In common jest, thieves seem to have been called "day-sleepers" <note>original: ἡμερόκοιτοι</note> because they sleep during the day and stay awake at night. For Hesiod says in *Works and Days*:
> Lest the man who sleeps by day should take away your goods.
> <note>original: Μήποτε σ’ ἡμερόκοιτος ἀνὴρ ἀπὸ χρήμαθ’ ἕληται</note>

This will be aptly twisted to refer to a pilferer and a thief. There is also a fish of the same name, as Suidas <note>The Suda, a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> indicates; I believe it is the seal. <note>Erasmus notes the word "Phoca," which is Latin for seal, punning on the "Phocians" mentioned earlier</note>

<summary>This page explores several adages derived from Greek history and Roman literature, including the "Phocian desperation" (extreme measures in war), "with a suspended hand" (hesitation or lack of care), and "the itch take the hindmost" (ruthless competition).</summary>
<keywords>Phocians, Thessalians, Daiphantus, Plutarch, Pliny the Younger, competition, thieves, Horace, Hesiod, day-sleeper</keywords>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY

### V. Powerful in all things.

This line from Hesiod <note>Hesiod was an ancient Greek poet, often cited alongside Homer as a foundational source for Greek mythology and ethics.</note> will fit those who have the greatest power to either harm or help:
> For among the more powerful <note>original: Ἐν τοῖς γὰρ πλείοσίν</note> there is an equal share of both good and evil things.
> That is:
> For in these is placed equally the sum of both the best and worst things.

While this was indeed said by the poet concerning the gods, it can be applied either to a man of the highest authority, or to a matter of the greatest importance. For example, it could apply to a prince, or someone who is intensely favored, or—jokingly—to money, or—seriously—to literature and the virtues.

---

### VI. Do not put all your resources on one ship.

Furthermore, it seems this also belongs to the class of proverbs, if we interpret it broadly, which is found in the same work <note>Hesiod’s *Works and Days*.</note>:
> Do not place your entire livelihood in hollow ships. <note>original: μὴ δ' ἐνὶ νηυσὶν ἅπαντα βίον κοίλησι τίθεσθαι</note>
> That is:
> Do not commit all your goods to spreading ships at once.

Do not undertake anything in which everything must be risked at once. One should not throw every die at the same time. Maritime business is dangerous, for a shipwreck takes everything away. Commerce with the land is safer. Elsewhere we have recorded the saying of a Spartan <note>original: Laconis</note> who said he did not care for wealth that "hung from ropes" <note>Referring to the rigging of a ship, meaning wealth that is unstable and at the mercy of the sea.</note>.

---

### VII. She burns without a torch.

Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and essayist known for his moral philosophy.</note> frequently uses this verse as a proverb:
> She scorches without a torch and gives him over to a raw old age. <note>original: Εὐὴ ἀτὲρ δαλοῖο καὶ ὠμῷ γήραϊ δώκεν</note>
> That is:
> She burns without a firebrand, and delivers him to a heavy senescence.

This refers, of course, to a wicked wife, who by her behavior brings about a premature old age for her husband. The same may be elegantly transferred to greed, ambition, envy, shameful love, and similar vices of the mind, by which those who are susceptible are tortured and wasted away.

---

### VIII. The sky still turns.

Whenever we want to signify that hope still remains, and that the time which usually brings an opportunity for better fortune has not yet expired, this line from Theocritus <note>A Greek poet from Sicily, famous for inventing pastoral poetry.</note> in his *Graces* will be fitting:
> The sky has not yet grown weary of bringing months and years. <note>original: οὔπω μῆνας ἄγων ἔκαμ' οὐρανός, ἀλλ' ἐνιαυτῶν</note>
> That is:
> The ether has not yet ceased to roll forward
> Months and years.

For what one year denies, another offers of its own accord.

---

### IX. Many wheels will yet turn.

He expressed this proverbially, and it pertains to the same sentiment that follows immediately after:
> Many horses will yet move the wheel of the chariot. <note>original: Πολλοὶ κινήσουσι ἔτι τροχὸν ἅρματος ἵπποι</note>
> That is:
> The wheel, set in motion by many horses, will still roll on.

That is: Much time still remains, and many changes of affairs will occur. Indeed, this adage is even today in common use among our own people <note>Erasmus often points out parallels between classical Greek/Latin proverbs and the Dutch or German vernacular of his own 16th-century world.</note>. For the interpretation some provide regarding the Olympic games is rather dull, as the poet does not deal with those in a pastoral poem.

---

### X. Not even the name.

The following from the same Eclogue is also a proverbial figure of speech:
> And let there no longer be even a name for war. <note>original: Βοᾶς δ' ἔτι μηδ' ὄνομ' εἴη</note>
> That is:
> Further on, there shall not even be a name for war and tumult.

Likewise Paul to the Ephesians: "But let fornication and all uncleanness or covetousness not even be named among you." What then? Is it such a crime to even name greed or lust? I think not; but the Apostle, in order to sternly detest these vices, used a proverbial hyperbole. For even among the pious, both Judas and Pilate are named.

---

### XI. The stag drags the dogs.

Among the adages by which we signify an <term>adynaton</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a physical impossibility is used to highlight the absurdity of a situation (literally: "the impossible").</note>, or something completely backwards, we must include that which is found in Theocritus’s *Thyrsis*:
> The stag drags the dogs. <note>original: τοὺς κύνας ὁ ἔλαφος ἕλκῃ</note>

For it is backwards for a stag to hunt the dogs. The verse of Theocritus goes like this:
> Since Daphnis is dying, let the stag himself drag the hounds. <note>original: δάφνις ἐπεὶ θνῄσκει, καὶ τοὺς κύνας ὡς ἔλαφος ἕλκοι</note>

In a similar form, Virgil <note>The famous Roman poet of the *Aeneid* and the *Eclogues*.</note> says in his *The Sorceress*:
"Now let the wolf flee from the sheep of his own accord."

<meta>The catchword at the bottom of the original page is "Bubo" (The Owl), indicating the topic of the first adage on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page contains a collection of short adages (V through XI) focused on power, risk management, and hope, drawing heavily from the Greek poets Hesiod and Theocritus. It highlights the use of hyperbole and the rhetorical concept of the 'adynaton'—the description of impossible reversals of nature.</summary>
<keywords>Hesiod, Theocritus, risk management, hope, hyperbole, adynaton, St. Paul, Virgil, Greek proverbs, pastoral poetry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad of Erasmus’s *Adages*, specifically exploring metaphors and proverbial expressions found in the pastoral poetry of Theocritus. # THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->The owl sings to the nightingale.<-

The following saying is very similar:
> Let the mountain owl hoot even at the nightingales themselves. <note>original: Κὴξ ὀρέων τοι σκῶπον ἀηδόσι γηρύσαιντο; Latin: Buboq; montanus philomenis occinat ipsis.</note>
This is used when an infant tries to persuade an eloquent speaker, or an unlearned person attempts to teach the most learned.

->He has not even seen oil.<-

The Eclogue titled *The Shepherds* <note>Theocritus, Idyll 5.</note> abounds with proverbial phrases and figures of speech, the first of which is this:
> And when did he ever lay eyes on oil? <note>original: Καὶ πόκα τῆν’ ἔλαιον ᾠν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ὀπώπει?</note>
It is suitable for those who are completely crude and unskilled in some art. For instance, if someone tries to practice medicine without ever having studied any of that art, they might be charmingly mocked with this: "And when did he ever lay eyes on oil?"
For athletes used to be anointed with oil so that their limbs would become more supple and firm; hence, "oil" is used as a metaphor for the training or the contest itself. However, the scholarly commentaries <note>The ancient "scholia" or marginal notes on classical texts.</note> declare that some refer this to the tree, because at the Olympic games, victors were often crowned with wild olive or olive branches.

->And my mother [said], etc.<-

Likewise, this follows in the same poem:
> My mother also said I was better than Pollux. <note>original: Κἤμ’ ἔφαθ’ ἁ μάτηρ πολυδεύκεος ἦμεν ἀμείνω.</note>
This is said when someone is preferred over, or equated to, those with whom they cannot be compared at all. For parents are often blinded by love for their children and think those who are deformed are most beautiful, or those who are most cowardly are the bravest. Furthermore, Pollux <note>In Greek mythology, Pollux (Polydeuces) was a divine twin famed for his skill in boxing.</note> is believed to have been the greatest boxer. As Horace <note>referred to by his family name, Flaccus.</note> testifies:
> Castor delights in horses; he who was born from the same egg <note>Pollux, brother of Castor.</note> delights in boxing.

->Persuade the wolves to go mad.<-

Again in the same work:
> Now, Milo, go and persuade the wolves to go mad. <note>original: πείζει βι μάλων καὶ τὼς λύκως αὐτίκα λυσσῶ.</note>
This is used when someone sets their mind to a most foolish thing, which they would not undertake unless they were insane. Or, it applies when one incites a tyrant to cruelty when he is already savage enough by his own nature, just as wolves are "mad" by their own accord. "Rabies" or madness is properly a condition of dogs, which is why the commentator on Theocritus thinks this is presented as an absurdity <note>suggesting wolves don't get rabies</note>. But while dogs only go mad occasionally, wolves are never *not* "mad" in their ferocity.

->He feeds on dew.<-

For a man of a very thin or slight body, this line from the same Idyll will fit, which is said of a lean heifer:
> Does she not live on dew like the cicada? <note>original: Μὴ πρώκας σιτίζῃ ὥσπερ ὁ τέττιξ?</note>
The Dorians <note>A group of ancient Greeks; Theocritus wrote in the Doric dialect.</note> call dew *prokas* because it falls in the morning <note>proï</note>. Furthermore, Pliny <note>A Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*.</note> testifies in Book 11, Chapter 36, that cicadas lack a mouth but have a prickly pipe-like structure in their chest similar to a tongue. With this, they lick the dew. When they fly up after being disturbed, they discharge a liquid, which is the only evidence that they feed on dew. Nor is there any opening for bodily waste. Hence Virgil <note>referred to as Maro.</note> says:
> While the bees feed on thyme, while the cicadas on dew.
It will be more elegant if transferred to a person's intellect, or to a dry and meager style of writing. Or, through irony, it can be said of a man with a heavily obese body.

->Tread your own ground.<-

When we command someone to keep to their own place and not intrude upon ours, we may use this from the same *Wayfarers*:
> But treading your own ground, keep to the oak-groves. <note>original: τὰν σαυτῶ πατέων ἔχε τὰς δρύας.</note>
This is appropriate when we do not quite trust someone and do not wish to admit them into our domestic intimacy.

->Nothing like it.<-

To signify an unfair or lopsided comparison, this from the same source will be effective:
> The bramble is not comparable [to the rose], nor the anemone to roses. <note>original: Βάκ’ ὀ συμβλητ’ ἐστὶ κυνόσβατος ὀ δ’ ἀνεμώνη πρὸς ῥόδα.</note>

<summary>Erasmus catalogs several proverbs from the poet Theocritus, dealing with themes of misplaced confidence, parental bias, and natural boundaries. He provides philological context, such as the ancient belief that cicadas survive solely on dew.</summary>
<keywords>Theocritus, Greek proverbs, Pollux, cicada, Pliny the Elder, Virgil, Horace, pastoral poetry, metaphors for lack of skill</keywords>

### FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY
Hhh
<meta>catchword: tex</meta>

->Indeed, it is a foolish thing to have compared the sweetbrier or the anemone to roses.<-

*Cynosbatos* <note>original: "Cynosbatos"; a wild rose or sweetbrier</note> in Greek sounds like "dog-brier." It is a type of shrub, but it produces a rose that is held in contempt and has very little pleasant scent. Dioscorides <note>A famous ancient Greek physician and botanist.</note> seems to suggest that the *Anemone* <note>The windflower.</note> is a species of poppy.

<margin>XIX</margin>
->Lest you bewitch.<-
<margin>Lest you bewitch me. <note>original: Ἵνα μὴ βασκαίνης με.</note></margin>
"Lest you bewitch." This was commonly said when someone, having obtained something pleasant, shares a portion of it with those present, so that they do not sadden others by enjoying it alone. Aristotle indicates this in the twenty-fourth problem of his twentieth section. Where someone might take something privately for themselves from a communal table, they would say to a bystander while sharing it, "Lest you bewitch me." <note>This refers to the "evil eye" or "fascination," where envy was thought to physically harm the person enjoying good fortune.</note> Therefore, those about to eat food would first eat rue <note>A bitter herb (*Ruta graveolens*) used in antiquity for medicinal and protective purposes.</note> as a remedy against bewitchment. For they feared the harm of the "evil eye" whenever they ate too greedily, or were gripped by a suspicion of some inconvenience, or held the food they were taking in suspicion. Thus it happened that they would always drink or eat with a certain agitation, while simultaneously swallowing air; if this air is expelled, the food comes out with it; if it is retained, it causes griping pains. Thus, rue eaten beforehand warms both the stomach and the rest of the body, so that the trapped wind can be dissipated and driven away. From this, there is also a certain proverbial saying, "There is need of rue," which we use when we wish to indicate the danger of some upcoming trouble, just as we have said elsewhere regarding wild spikenard and parsley.

<margin>XX</margin>
->Not every land bears all things.<-
Just as that line of Virgil’s, "Not every land bears all things," <note>original: "Non omnis fert omnia tellus"; from Virgil's *Georgics*.</note> will be a proverb if one applies it to different natural talents, or to the idea that one should not seek just anything from anyone. Likewise, that line of Theocritus from the *Cyclops* has the quality of a proverb:
<margin>But some things belong to summer, and others happen in winter. <note>original: Ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν θέρειος, τὰ δὲ γίγνεται ἐν χειμῶνι.</note></margin>
that is:
Some things indeed winter produces, while others summer brings forth.
This is used when we mean that a young man should do one thing, an old man another; and that different customs should be employed at different times. What each land may bear is elegantly described by Virgil in the *Georgics*, and by Hermippus in the first book of Athenaeus.

<margin>XXI</margin>
->While the knees are green.<-
Nor is that lacking the appearance of a proverb which is found in the same author in *Thyonichus*:
<margin>Those whose knees are green ought to do something. <note>original: Ποιεῖν τι δεῖ οἷς γόνυ χλωρόν.</note></margin>
that is:
While the knees are green, then it is right that we do something.
One must study good literature while the intellect is still vigorous. A wife should be taken, but by a young man. Horace speaks in a very similar way:
"And while the knees are green,
And it is fitting, let old age be dismissed from the clouded brow." <note>original: "Dumq; uirent genua..."</note>
And yet this figure itself, "the knee is green," is proverbial whenever we signify youth.

<margin>XXII</margin>
->Neither the worst, nor the first.<-
It will be possible to signify mediocrity in this way:
<margin>Neither the worst, nor the first. <note>original: Οὔτε κάκιστος οὔτε πρῶτος.</note></margin>
that is:
Not the worst, but not the First.
It becomes more charming if it is transferred to the praise of one's intellect. For in Theocritus’s *Thyonichus*, it was said of a soldier who boasts of himself with modesty.

<margin>XXIII</margin>
->He knows how Jupiter married Juno.<-
For busybodies, and those who investigate what everyone does at home, this phrase from the *Syracusan Women* will be suitable:
<margin>Women know everything, and even how Jupiter took Juno to wife. <note>original: Πάντα γυναῖκες ἴσασι καὶ ὡς Ζεὺς ἠγάγεθ' Ἥρην.</note></margin>
that is:
The female race knows all things; it even knows
In what manner Jupiter once married Juno.
The commentator on Theocritus <note>The ancient scholiast.</note> thinks this signifies the secret marriage of Jupiter and Juno, such as Homer describes:
<margin>Entering the marriage bed, they escaped the notice of their dear parents. <note>original: εἰς εὐνὴν φοιτῶντε φίλους ἐλάθοντο τοκῆας.</note></margin>
that is:
They went to the marriage bed while both parents were unaware.
He adds a story, which some Aristotle or other related in the book he wrote *On the Temple of Hermione*. Jupiter laid a trap for his sister's modesty when he happened to see her separated from the rest of the gods—for it is not safe even for virgin goddesses to walk alone—and he turned himself into a cuckoo and perched on a mountain, which was previously called Thronax, but is now called Coccyx <note>The Greek word for "cuckoo".</note>. On that day, Jupiter stirred up a great storm. Juno thus arrived at the mountain alone and sat down in that place where the temple of Juno Telia (that is, "the Perfecter") now stands. The cuckoo, shivering and trembling because of the storm, flew down and settled on Juno's knees. Juno, taking pity on it, covered it with her garment. Here...

...the king of the gods, having suddenly turned from a cuckoo into Jupiter, embraced Juno. And when she refused to mate with him out of respect for her mother <note>original: "matris"; Erasmus is likely referring to a specific version of the myth or a textual variant where Juno's maternal modesty is cited</note>, Jupiter promised he would take her as his wife. They think the proverb was born from this. He adds that a statue of this Juno was placed in a temple represented in this image: sitting on a throne, she held a scepter in her right hand, on the tip of which sat a cuckoo. Indeed, I believe this fable is found among the ancients, but I suspect it was made up by some idle grammarian, as it tastes so much like an old wives' tale. Very similar to this is what Plautus writes in *The Three-Penny Day*: "They know what the king said in the queen’s ear; they know what Juno chatted about with the cow <note>original: "cum ue:"; likely "cum uacca," referring to the goddess Io who was turned into a cow</note>—things that neither will happen nor have happened, yet they know them."

### After you have fed, give orders.
In the same Eclogue <note>Referring to Theocritus</note>, "After ceasing, command." <note>original: Παυσάμενος ἐπίτασσε</note> That is:
*Give orders after you have satisfied yourself with food.*
Women respond in this way to someone scolding them, because once they have become more talkative, they command silence. It is fitting when someone is overbearing toward those from whom they have earned nothing.

### A cock is most powerful on his own dunghill.
What is written in Seneca’s satire <note>The *Apocolocyntosis*, a mock-deification of the Emperor Claudius</note> has the appearance of a proverb. "He understood," he says, "that no one was his equal in Rome, and that there he did not have the same influence. A cock is most powerful in his own domain." He alluded to the Emperor Claudius, who was born in Lyon <note>Erasmus highlights a pun: in Latin, *Gallus* means both "a cock" and "a Gaul" (someone from the region of France). Claudius, being born in Gaul, is the "cock" on his own "dunghill."</note>. Even today, people commonly say that a man is most daring on his own dunghill. In a foreign place, people are more timid; in his own kingdom, everyone is fiercer and more spirited.

### To dig through the Isthmus.
They used to say "to dig through the Isthmus" <note>Referring to the Isthmus of Corinth in Greece</note> of those who undertook a task with great effort but in vain. It is derived from the Isthmus of Corinth, which forced ships to be driven around the peninsula in a long and dangerous circuit. Hence, several attempted to dig through where it was narrowest: namely King Demetrius, Caesar the Dictator, the Prince Gaius <note>The Emperor Caligula</note>, and Domitius Nero, whose failure in the attempt was visible to everyone. The author is Pliny in Book 4, Chapter 4. Tranquillus <note>The historian Suetonius</note> says the same was attempted by Caligula. Philostratus, in the *Life of Apollonius*, denies that Nero stopped because of the difficulty of the work, but because he feared that if the sea were let in, the island of Aegina would be destroyed, or new revolutions would arise in the Roman Empire; for the Egyptians had predicted this. Furthermore, the very ancient writer Herodotus, in the first book of his *History*, related that those who attempted to make the Isthmus an island where the space was narrowest (namely five stades) were struck by rocks in their eyes; the Delphic Apollo, being consulted by them, answered in three-measure verse:

> Neither fortify the Isthmus with towers, nor dig it up.
> For Zeus would have made it an island, if he had wished. <note>original Greek: Ἰσθμον μὴ πυργοῦτε, μηδ᾽ ὀρύσσετε. Ζεὺς γάρ κ᾽ ἔθηκε νῆσον, εἴ κ᾽ ἐβούλετο.</note>

Finally, Nicanor Seleucus attacked the Isthmus that separates the Black and Caspian Seas, but did not finish it, as he was killed by Ptolemy Ceraunus.

### To lick salt.
In olden times, for men of meager fortune, salt served as a side dish <note>original: "pulmentarij"; a relish or side dish eaten with bread</note>, as it does for some today. This matter also passed into a proverb, although it is not quite clear what kind of proverb it was. But it is worth writing down Pliny's own words on this matter from Book 31, Chapter 7. "Varro," he says, "is the authority that the ancients also used it as a side dish. For salt existed even with cheese, as appears from the proverb." Persius says in his fifth Satire:

> Swear, but Jupiter will hear. Alas, alas,
> Content, you will spend your life boring into a salt-cellar
> tasted again with your finger, if you aim to live with Jupiter.

This means you will lead a most impoverished life.

### To act like Selles.
"To act like Selles" <note>original: Σελλίζειν (Sellizein)</note> was said in a proverbial joke of those who are boastful and swollen with pride. Suidas <note>An ancient Greek encyclopedia</note> warns that it is taken from the character of a certain Selles, who, although his wealth was very thin, nevertheless affected a grand manner. It can also be applied to those who boast and market themselves on a reputation for learning, when they have nothing from literature. Hesychius indicates that "to act like Selles" and "to lisp" <note>original: ψελλίζειν (psellizein)</note> mean the same to the Greeks. Plato used this word again in the *Gorgias*, and says he is "lisping" <note>original: ψελλὸς (psellos)</note> who pronounces the letter sigma too thickly, regarding which...

...we touched upon in the proverb regarding "the psenma nations." <note>original: ἡ ψεμμὰ τ’ ἔθνη; likely referring to obscure or foreign groups</note> Hesychius adds that sometimes "to act like a celery-crown wearer" <note>original: σελινίζζειν; likely referring to those who boasted of their victories in games like the Isthmian or Nemean where celery crowns were awarded</note> is the same as "to boast," clearly agreeing with Suidas.

### XXIX. Of Cecides and the Buphonia

*Of Cecides and the Buphonia.* <note>original: τὰ κηκείδου καὶ βουφονίων</note> This refers to something incredibly ancient, which has long since become obsolete and fallen out of use due to its great age. Aristophanes says in his comedy *The Clouds*:
> These things are truly ancient and overgrown with gray hair, full of cicadas, 
> and Cecides, and the Buphonia. 

Indeed, Cecides was a very ancient poet of Dithyrambs <note>choral hymns sung in honor of Dionysus</note>, whose writings already smelled of decay in antiquity, which is why they became a common joke. In the same way, people are rightly laughed at today who, with an excessive and untimely craving for antiquity, seek out their vocabulary from the Twelve Tables <note>the earliest code of Roman law</note> or from the poets Ennius and Lucilius, as if they were speaking with the mother of Evander <note>Carmenta, an ancient prophetic goddess; the phrase implies speaking an archaic language no one understands</note>. Such people think no word is elegant unless it is removed from common use and far from our own century. Likewise, the "Buphonia" <note>literally "the ox-slaughtering"</note> was a certain festival among the Athenians, which had been neglected and discontinued because of its antiquity; it was so named from the killing of oxen. We see games of this sort still lasting among the Italians, especially the Romans. 

We can use this expression when we want to indicate that something is being neglected as being too old-fashioned. For instance, if you wished to criticize popes, bishops, and priests because they now treat the Gospel precepts—on poverty, on enduring injuries, on the contempt for life—or the decrees of the ancient popes—on the sale of church offices, on choosing bishops without corruption, on removing the wicked—as if they were antiquated, you might well say: *These are things of Cecides and the Buphonia.*

### XXX. He brings a cloud over the serenity

One egg is not so much like another as this expression resembles the face of a proverb. It is recorded by Plutarch in his essay *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*: *He brings a cloud over the serenity.* <note>original: συνία γὰρ ἐπάγει τῇ γαλήνῃ</note> This refers to someone who, in the midst of drinks and games, mixes in something poisonous or bitter, which wrinkles the brow and causes the eyebrows to knit, darkening the general cheerfulness. In the same manner, Horace writes in the 15th Ode of his third book, concerning a deformed old woman who was mingling with the dances of young girls:
> And to scatter a cloud over the bright stars.

### XXXI. Monograms (Outline-men)

In olden times, men who were exceedingly thin from wasting away, or who were puny and pale, were called "monograms" <note>original: μονόγραμμοι</note> in a proverbial joke. Lucilius says: "Scarcely a living man, but a monogram." Again, the same author elsewhere: "What piety of a monogram!" Nonius Marcellus <note>a 4th-century grammarian</note> conjectures that the term is derived from painting, which is first sketched as a shadow with only the outline of the body. Marcellus is not wrong; however, the adage will be more elegant if we look back to the painting of the ancients. 

By the agreement of all, painting originally took its beginning from the lines drawn around the shadow of a man; this they call *Delineating*. Then, they began to paint with single colors, and they called those pictures *monochrome* <note>original: μονοχρωμάτους</note>. Soon, the art distinguished itself and discovered light and shadows, so that some parts seemed to stand out and others to be hidden or recessed through the difference in colors. Next, "splendor" <note>luster</note> was added, which they claim is different from light, yet stands between light and shadow; accordingly, they call it *Tonos* <note>Tone</note>. The joining and transition of colors they call *Harmoge* <note>Blending</note>. Pliny records things much like this in the thirty-fifth book, chapter five, of his *Natural History*. 

The term will therefore suit a deformed man with no color or a single uniform color in his face, such as the images of the ancients were. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*: "For they are not composed of veins, nerves, and bones; nor do they eat food or drink, lest they collect humors that are too sharp or too thick. Nor do they have such bodies that they should fear accidents or blows, or dread diseases from the exhaustion of their limbs. These were the 'monogram' gods and 'do-nothings' that Epicurus invented. But the true gods, endowed with the most beautiful form and placed in the purest region of the sky, are carried along and govern their courses in such a way that they seem to have agreed together for the preservation and protection of all things." Cicero calls those things "monograms" which are formless and have no distinct appearance.

### XXXII. A physician to others

This saying remains very famous even in these centuries; it is recorded by Plutarch in his essay *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*, taken from some poet or other:
> He heals others, while he himself is teeming with ulcers.
<note>original: Ἄλλων ἰατρὸς, αὐτὸς ἕλκεσι βρύων; this is the classical equivalent of "Physician, heal thyself"</note>

He also uses it in the commentary he wrote against Colotes. <note>Colotes was an Epicurean philosopher and a contemporary of Epicurus; Plutarch wrote a famous polemic against him.</note> It applies to those who are wise for others but not for themselves; those who are sharp-eyed and cautious for others, but not for themselves; those who know how to console others, while they themselves bear their own misfortunes with an uneven mind. Christ used this same sense in the Gospel of Luke; for when the Jews were opposing his words and deeds and saying, "Is this not the son of Joseph?" <note>original Greek: οὐχ οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱὸς ἰωσήφ</note> He responded in this manner: "You will surely say this proverb to me: 'Physician, heal yourself.' ---

->To live on wild mustard.<-
<margin>XXX</margin>
You might wittily say "to live on wild mustard" <note>original: *lapsana uiuere*; lapsana refers to a type of wild cabbage or charlock</note> of those who live very sparingly and on far too thin a diet. For it is consistent with that military joke that passed into a popular tale, in which Caesar’s soldiers taunted him in alternating verses because they had lived on wild mustard at Dyrrhachium. <note>Dyrrhachium was a key site in the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey.</note> Now, *lapsana* is a wild and common vegetable, growing everywhere, having three leaves, and belonging, if I am not mistaken, to the genus of cabbages. But if anyone should happen to ask, these are Pliny's words in his nineteenth book, eighth chapter: "There is also a wild vegetable with three leaves, celebrated in the songs of the Divine Julius, especially in military jokes. Indeed, they taunted him in alternating verses that they had lived on wild mustard at Dyrrhachium, mocking the stinginess of their rewards. It is, moreover, a wild sprout." Thus far Pliny. The same author, in his twentieth book, says that this sprout is useless and difficult to digest. He interprets "sprout" as the more delicate and tender little stalk of the cabbage, which is also prized in burrs and asparagus. Dioscorides says that *lapsana* is called *napium* by the Romans, the leaves and stalks of which are eaten together after being boiled; he thinks this is more friendly to the stomach than the "sorrel" vegetable <note>original: *olus lapathum*</note> mentioned by Horace when speaking of a frugal dinner: 
> "Or the herb of the sorrel, which loves the meadows, and mallows,
> healthy for the body."

---

->Hardly against the door.<-
<margin>XXXI</margin>
"Not at the door." <note>original Greek: οὐ πρὶ θύρας</note> That is, "hardly against the door," used for something that is not properly to the point or apt. Thus, regarding the subject at hand, it was certainly said with a proverbial figure by Aristotle in the fourth book of his *Physics*: "These men, then, do not encounter the question at the door." <note>original Greek: οὗτοι μὲν οὖν οὐ πρὶ θύρας πῶς τὸ πρόβλημα ἁπαντῶσιν; meaning they are far from the solution.</note> Argyropylus <note>Joannes Argyropylus, a Greek scholar who translated Aristotle into Latin</note> translated "at the door" incorrectly, nor did he even render the meaning. It has the same force as if you were to say, "wide of the mark." Consider this, reader, whether this adage might be related to that one: "Who could miss the door?" <note>original Greek: τίς ἂν θύρας ἁμάρτοι; a phrase used to describe something so obvious it cannot be missed.</note>

---

->Little Ladders.<-
<margin>X</margin>
"Little Ladders." <note>original Greek: Κλιμακίδες</note> Those who submit themselves to the wealthy for any service, even the most sordid, could be called this in jest. Certain Cypriot women, flatterers among the Syrians, were called this by a common insult because they would prostrate themselves for the wives of kings so that the queens might climb into their carriages using them as if they were ladders. Plutarch mentions this in his book *On Discerning a Flatterer from a Friend*. So does Athenaeus in the sixth book of the *Sophists at Dinner*. And Valerius Maximus in the ninth book, first chapter, of *Memorable Deeds and Sayings*.

---

->Farewell to friend and foe alike.<-
<margin>XI</margin>
"Let the friend perish along with the enemy." <note>original Greek: Ἔῤῥέτω φίλος σὺν ἐχθρῷ</note> This fits those who are entirely focused on themselves and have no more regard for a friend than for an enemy; such was Timon the Misanthrope <note>A legendary Athenian recluse famous for his hatred of mankind.</note> said to be. Plutarch, in the commentary we just cited, says: "If that saying should by no means and in no way be pleasing, 'Let the friend perish with the enemy.'" It is, among the Greeks, a half-line of trochaic verse.

---

->Manic deeds.<-
<margin>XII</margin>
"Manic things" <note>original Greek: μανικὰ</note> was a Phrygian proverb used for immense and extraordinary deeds, the word being derived from a certain Manis, an ancient king among them, whom they say was a very powerful man endowed with admirable virtue. The author is Plutarch in his book *On Isis and Osiris*. Indeed, even the Latins call something "insane" <note>original: *insanum*</note> when it is beyond the common measure. "He wishes to be insane." And, "It pleases him to indulge in insane labor."

---

->Dug and cut.<-
<margin>XX</margin>
"Not even in things dug or cut." This was undoubtedly said in a proverbial way by Cicero in the second book of *On the Orator*, meaning "in no part" or "not at all." He says: "But he will say that when you sold the house, you did not reserve for yourself even the things dug or cut, not even your father's bathtub." In this passage, it should be noted in passing that in the common manuscripts of Cicero, the word is incorrectly read as "left behind" instead of "reserved," and that...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal and proverbial expressions found in classical literature, specifically clarifying the legal term "ruta caesa" before moving on to proverbs regarding mountains and social contributions.</meta>

<page-num>917</page-num>
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

This is clear from Nonius Marcellus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian and lexicographer</note>, who, in his entry on "Reserved Property," cites this very passage from Cicero. For in this context, "to receive" is the same as "to except" or "to reserve." Furthermore, what is meant by <term>things dug and things cut</term> <note>original: *Ruta caesa*; a legal term referring to minerals or timber extracted from the land</note>—terms peculiar to legal scholars—is abundantly clear from the nineteenth book of the *Pandects* <note>The *Pandects*, or *Digest*, is a vast collection of Roman legal writings compiled under Justinian</note>, in the eighteenth law. Ulpian says: "If 'things dug and things cut' are reserved in a sale, it is settled that 'dug things' <note>original: *ruta*</note> are those which are extracted from the earth, such as sand and the like; and 'cut things' <note>original: *caesa*</note> are those such as felled trees, charcoal, and similar items." Gallus or Aquilius, whose opinion Mela cites, rightly says it is pointless to include "things dug and cut" in a contract of sale, because if they have not been specifically sold, one can sue for their production. Nor must the seller take more care regarding cut timber, or building materials, or sand, than for other things that are more valuable. Marcus Cicero also mentions "things dug and cut" in his *Topics*. Indeed, lest I pass over anything that might pertain to finding an argument in every mode of reasoning, I have perhaps included more than was strictly required by the matter at hand. I have done what generous sellers often do: when they have sold a house or a farm, having reserved "things dug and cut," they nevertheless grant something to the buyer that seems aptly placed for the sake of ornament. He also mentions this in his *Partitions*. And when we wish to signify that everything is being taken away rather harshly, with nothing left behind, we may elegantly say: **Not even with "things dug and cut" reserved**, speaking in the manner of the legal experts.

## Etna, Athos.
### XXXIX

That the mountains Etna and Athos passed into a proverb for trouble and weariness is attested by Lucilius in Aulus Gellius, book sixteen, chapter nine, even if that passage is considered corrupted. The verses of Lucilius that he cites are these:
> But here there is play, and everything is topsy-turvy, and so they were.
> Topsy-turvy, I say, everything was play and a joke.

That work was hard, as when we reached the borders of Setia, and "the mountains of Etna," as they say, and "all the rugged Athoses" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἄθου</note>. Regarding Etna, the mountain in Sicily, it was said that it crushes a giant under its mass, according to the fables of the poets; or because it was once heavy and destructive to the inhabitants due to frequent eruptions. Hence, Marcus Tullius in *Cato the Elder* said: **a burden heavier than Etna**. Regarding Athos, however, it was said that because of its immense height, it is troublesome due to its shadow, which it casts as far as Lemnos, three hundred stades distant, as we have said elsewhere. Pomponius Mela recorded that its peak is higher than the point from which rain falls; a conjecture for this is gathered from the fact that ash is not washed away from the altars it supports on its summit, but remains in the heap where it was left. It also stands in the way of sailors because its entire long ridge extends into the sea where it joins the mainland. For this reason, it was also tunneled through by Xerxes <note>The Persian King Xerxes I famously dug a canal through the Athos peninsula to avoid the dangerous waters where his fleet had previously been wrecked</note>. Athenaeus, in book 10, mentions a certain Erysichthon of unquenchable greed, who was commonly called an **Athos of gluttony** <note>original Greek: Βορᾶς ἄθωνα</note>.

## To come without a contribution.
### XL

The Latins use the term "un-tributed" <note>original: *immunem*</note> for one whom the Greeks call "without a symbol" <note>original Greek: ἀσύμβολον; meaning someone who does not pay their share of a communal meal</note>, namely, one who contributes nothing to a banquet. Horace says in his *Odes*:
> A small onyx jar of nard will entice a cask.
> I do not intend to soak you in my cups
> without a contribution, as if I were a rich man
> in a well-stocked house.

But it will have a little more grace if it is transferred to matters of the mind, such as learning, verses, or something similar. Aulus Gellius, in book 6, chapter 13, indicates that this expression passed into a proverb. "Lest we should come," as he says, "entirely without contribution and empty-handed, we brought together for our little dinner not delicacies for eating, but subtle questions." Terence says in *Phormio*: "Are you to come empty-handed, anointed and bathed from the baths?" In Athenaeus, Ephiphus spoke elegantly of an **uncontributing hand**:

->Entering to eat another’s food, arriving at dawn,<-
->I stretch out an empty hand for the meal.<-
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλότριον εἰσελθὼν ὄψον ἔωθεν μολῶν, Ἀσύμβολόν τε χεῖρα προϐάλλω Βορᾷ</note>

## Soterichus’s couches.
### XLI

It appears that **Soterichus’s couches** passed into a common joke regarding something cheap, old-fashioned, not at all ambitious, and of crude workmanship. For Seneca, mocking the verses of Ennius regarding Cethegus, says: "Those who love verses of this kind may also be allowed to admire them and Soterichus’s couches." Aulus Gellius—for these things are recounted by him in book twelve, chapter 2—says: "Seneca might indeed seem worthy of reading and study by young men, who compares the dignity and color of ancient speech to Soterichus’s couches."

...seemed to be of very little value, things already abandoned and held in contempt. One may conjecture that Sote- was some craftsman <note>original: *Sote-fabrum*; likely a reference to a specific artisan of antiquity whose work was considered unrefined</note> whose works displayed that ancient and unpolished simplicity. For Pliny testifies in book thirty-three, chapter eleven, that silver <term>dining couches</term> <note>original: *triclinia*; the three-sided couch arrangements used in Roman dining rooms</note> were later in use among the wealthy at Rome. Horace, in his *Satires*, indicates that Fulvius, Rutuba, and Placidianus were among the painters of this sort:

> Or when you stand dazed, you madman, before a painting by Pausias, 
> how are you less at fault than I, when I admire the 
> battles of Fulvius, Rutuba, or Placidianus, painted in 
> red chalk or charcoal, with their hamstrings tensed? <note>Pausias was a famous Greek painter known for technical mastery; Horace contrasts his high art with the crude, "charcoal" sketches of gladiators like Fulvius and Rutuba</note>

-> You will perish if you don't do it. <-

Whenever someone is reduced to such a position that they can neither undertake a matter without great inconvenience nor safely omit it, this saying will be appropriate. It originated from an oracle, and then became popular, as is common in speech: "I will perish if I don't do it; if I do it, I'll get a beating." It is recorded by Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author and grammarian</note> in book three, chapter three, from a comedy by Plautus titled *The Straits* <note>original: *Fretum*</note>. The verses of Plautus are:

> Now it is as the oracle of the Ram-man at the Great Games: 
> I'll perish if I don't do it; if I do, I'll be beaten.

Furthermore, what the history of this delivered oracle might be, Gellius himself admits is not clear to him, and he noted these verses of Plautus so that he might search for the history. However, they are iambic tetrameter catalectic verses. From this, the word "I have removed" is used, added I believe by an interpreter. In the common manuscripts it is written: "It is said at the Great Games."

-> He weaves from himself like a spider. <-

This comparison also seems proverbial: that of a spider weaving webs from itself, and of a man devising lies from his own mind. For thus Plutarch says in his short book titled *On Isis and Osiris*: <margin>The story-writers, just like spiders, generating from themselves baseless beginnings, weave them.</margin> That is: Just as poets and orators, like spiders producing from themselves, weave and bring forth falsehoods suggested by no one. Pliny reports that larger spiders stretch out a small net in the hollows of the earth, while the smallest do not weave at all; a third kind is conspicuous for its skilled operation. He says they begin their webs when the womb is sufficient for the material of such a great work—whether the nature of the belly is corrupted by time, as Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher</note> believes, or whether there is a certain wool-bearing fertility within. With such moderate, thin, and smooth thread, and so equal, the spider draws out the warps, using its own weight. It begins to weave from the middle, connecting the wefts in a circular orb; it entangles the meshes at always equal intervals, widening from the narrow part with an indissoluble node. Nor does Aristotle disagree with this in the ninth book of *On the History of Animals*, adding that spiders, as soon as they are born, can cast threads, not from their interiors like excrement (as Democritus thinks), but from the surface of their body, like a bark, or in the manner that a porcupine shoots spines from its skin. However, they do not weave, nor do they hunt, unless they are females. The male is a companion in enjoyment, not in labor.

-> To hunt a hare with an ox, and similar sayings. <-

<margin>"To hunt a hare with an ox." This is said of those who approach an absurd or preposterous matter.</margin> For example, if someone in the Roman Court <note>The Papal Curia</note> should seek the dignity of a bishop without money. Plutarch, in his commentary *On Tranquility of Mind*: <margin>For neither is he unfortunate who wishes to throw a javelin with a plow and to hunt a hare with an ox. Nor does any evil spirit mock him who fails to catch deer with fishing nets; rather, it is the stupidity and perversity of those who attempt the impossible.</margin> That is: For neither is he unfortunate who wishes to hurl a javelin with a plow, and to hunt a hare with an ox. Nor is any malicious genius involved for the one who does not catch stags with fishing nets, but it is stupidity and perversity that attack things which cannot be done. Not everyone is suited for all things; as if one should entrust war or the administration of the republic to a man born for study and leisure, <margin>"To hunt a hare with an ox."</margin> Or if one should commit legal judgments to a stupid and ignorant man. In the same book he cites verses, if I am not mistaken, of Pindar <note>A famous Greek lyric poet</note>: <margin>The horse in the chariot, the ox at the plow, but the dolphin glides most swiftly past the ship; and for a boar planning death, one must find a dog.</margin> The horse in the chariot, but the ox at the plow; the dolphin outstrips the ship as quickly as possible. As for the boar preparing death, a brave dog must be found. For these also have the appearance of a proverb.

Plutarch in the book *On the Difference Between a Flatterer and a Friend*: <margin>But the flatterer, from one...</margin>

<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>

...is always devoted to what is pleasant, and immediately strikes a chord to find favor. When he knows an action is offensive or a word is painful, he refuses to acknowledge it, but looks only to what his target wishes, always harmonizing and speaking in accord. <note>original: "οἰκεῖος ἀεὶ τὸ ἡδὺ..." / "Adulator autem..."</note> That is, the flatterer always sings along to the same melody, focusing on what is sweet and what charms; he knows neither how to resist an action nor how to cause grief with a word, but only complies with the wishes of another, always singing in harmony and consonance with him. It is clear that the proverb is expressed through the figure of "from a single diagram" <note>original: "ἀφ᾽ ἑνὸς διαγράμματος"</note>. A "diagram" is a drawing or a description used by philosophers to place a matter before the eyes; thus the phrase carries the weight of saying "from the very same formula."

### Not the son of Achilles. XLVI

Among the verses of noble poets which are used by the learned as proverbs, this one also seems worthy of inclusion:
"Not everyone is born of Achilles, but you are Achilles himself." <note>original: "οὐ πᾶς ἀχιλλέως, ἀλλ᾽ ἀχιλλεὺς αὐτὸς εἶ"</note> This seems to be taken from some tragedy or comedy, for it is an iambic trimeter verse. It is used by Plutarch in that same essay he titled *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*. He says the flatterer imitates a friend in every way, so that it might be said of him, "Not everyone is born of Achilles," etc. Likewise, Parmeno in Terence’s play <note>The Roman playwright Terence, in the play *The Eunuch*</note> says of Gnatho, who was subservient to the speech of the braggart Thraso:
-> "My word, you would say this one was born from the other." <-

### Ulysses strips off his rags. XLVII

In the same essay I just mentioned, Plutarch uses this Homeric verse, not without a proverbial quality, from the twenty-second book of the *Odyssey*:
"Then the resourceful Ulysses stripped off his rags." <note>original: "Αὐτὰρ ὁ γυμνώθη ῥακέων πολύμητις ὀδυσσεύς"</note>
This can be applied to those who, having suddenly changed their way of life, emerge as rich men from poverty, clean from squalor, or cheerful from gloom. For as soon as Ulysses had stripped off the rags in which he had acted the beggar among the suitors and was adorned with magnificent clothing, he suddenly appeared to be a different person. Plutarch twists this to apply to the flatterer, who, like a polyp <note>A common ancient metaphor for someone who changes their "color" or character to match their surroundings</note>, adapts himself to the interests of everyone. Thus, a man who a moment ago wore a long beard and a philosopher’s cloak while staying with a friend devoted to philosophy—constantly poring over books and speaking of nothing but the numbers, rectangles, and triangles of Plato—might, if he happens upon a friend addicted to pleasures, immediately change his appearance as if transformed by Circe and become a Sardanapalus <note>A legendary king of Assyria synonymous with extreme luxury and decadence</note>.

### Suddenly another. XLVIII

In a similar way, he also twists that Homeric line from the sixteenth book of the *Odyssey* to describe a man suddenly changed, who appears to have unexpectedly become someone else:
"Stranger, you seem different to me now than you did before." <note>original: "Αλλοῖος μοι ξεῖν᾽ ἐφάνης νέον ἠὲ πάροιθεν"</note>
With this agrees the line from Theocritus:
"Suddenly, by some divine power, I have become another mortal." <note>original: "Αφάτης ἐξαπίνης μὲ θεὸς βροτὸν ἄλλον ἔτευξεν"</note>

### Against the hard and implacable. XLIX

Against a man who is excessively rigid and unyielding, one might rightly hurl this Homeric line from the tenth book of the *Odyssey*:
"But you have an unyielding mind in your breast." <note>original: "Σοὶ δέ τις ἐν στήθεσσι ἀκήλητος νόος ἐστί"</note>
Plutarch, in his essay *On Discerning a Flatterer from a Friend*, says this verse was often thrown at Mark Antony by his sycophants because, although he loved Cleopatra desperately, he did not always respond to her in love as they wished.

### The bath-man's donkey. L

"Like the bath-man's donkey." <note>original: "Ωσπερ ὄνος βαλανέως"</note> This was said of those who received no fruit or benefit from their own labors. Plutarch, in his booklet *On the Love of Wealth*, writes: "Receiving no good from it, like a bath-man’s donkey, which carries down the wood and brushwood, always filled with smoke and ash, yet never partaking in the bath, nor its warmth, nor its cleanliness." He is speaking of the stingy and sordid rich man who, though weighed down by riches, nevertheless does not enjoy them.

### Lamp-livers. LI

It appears that "Lamp-liver" <note>original: "λυχνόβιος"</note> was a proverbial term used jokingly for those who led a life by lamplight...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...it was as if they were of the least grace, and already left behind and despised. One can guess that Sotes was some craftsman whose works showed that ancient and crude simplicity. For Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, Roman natural historian</note> testifies in book thirty-three, chapter eleven, that silver dining couches later came into use for the wealthy at Rome. Horace indicates in his *Satires* <note>original: "Sermonibus"</note> that among painters of this kind <note>meaning crude or amateur</note> were Fulvius, Rutuba, and Placidianus:

> Or when you, madman, are spellbound by a small painting by Pausias,
> How are you less at fault than I, when I admire
> The battles of Fulvius, Rutuba, or Placidianus
> With strained leg, painted in red ochre or charcoal? 
> <note>original: "Vel cum Pausiaca torpes insane tabella..." Horace, Satires 2.7.95-98. Pausias was a master painter, while the others were likely gladiators depicted in crude advertisements.</note>

-> **You will perish if you do not do it.** <-

When someone is reduced to such a point that they cannot attempt a matter without great inconvenience, nor omit it safely, this phrase will be appropriate, having come from an oracle; thereafter it became popular, as a common saying: I shall perish if I do not do it; if I do it, I shall be beaten. It is reported by Aulus Gellius <note>Roman author of *Attic Nights*</note>, in book three, chapter three, from a comedy by Plautus named *Fretum*. The verses of Plautus are:
"Now it is like the response of the Ram at the Great Games:
I shall perish if I do not do it; if I do it, I shall be beaten."
<note>original: "Peribo, si non fecero: si faxo, uapulo."</note>
Furthermore, Gellius himself testifies that the history of the given oracle is not clear to him, and that he noted these little verses of Plautus so that he might seek out the history. However, they are iambic tetrameter catalectic verses <note>A specific meter in classical poetry consisting of four iambic units with the last syllable missing</note>. From this is said the word <note>I think added by the interpreter, we have removed it</note> in the common manuscripts it is written, "It is said at the Great Games."

-> **He weaves from himself like a spider.** <-

This comparison also seems proverbial: the spider weaving webs from itself, and a man inventing lies from his own mind. For so Plutarch says in his booklet titled *On Isis and Osiris*: <margin>Just as the story-writers, like spiders, generating from themselves, weave thin and baseless webs.</margin> <note>original: "οἷα τ κὴ λογογράφοι καθάπερ οἱ ἀράχναι..."</note> That is, just as poets and orators, if there is some "wool-bearing fertility" within, suggested by no one, they weave and produce lies. Pliny relates that larger spiders hang in small webs in the caves of the earth, while the smallest do not weave at all; a third type is conspicuous for its skillful operation. He says the womb is sufficient for the material of the webs and such great work: whether the nature of the belly is corrupted at that time, as Democritus <note>Presocratic Greek philosopher</note> believes, or if there is some "wool-bearing fertility" within: with such moderate, fine, and equal thread, it draws out the warp, using its own weight. It begins to weave from the middle, connecting the cross-threads in a circle; and it entangles the meshes with always equal intervals, but decreasing from a narrow point, with an indissoluble knot. This is not far from what Aristotle relates in the ninth book of his *History of Animals*, adding that spiders, as soon as they are born, send out threads, not from their interiors like excrement—as Democritus thinks—but from the highest part of the body, like a bark, or in the manner of a porcupine throwing spines from its skin. However, none but the females weave or hunt. The male is a companion for enjoyment, not for labor.

-> **To hunt a hare with an ox, and similar things.** <-

<margin>To hunt the hare with the ox.</margin> <note>original: "Τῷ βοὶ τὸν λαγὼ κυνηγετᾶν."</note> That is, they are said to hunt a hare with an ox who attempt something absurd and preposterous. Just as if someone in the Roman Court, without money, should strive for the dignity of a bishop. <note>Erasmus frequently criticized the corruption and bribery in the Church hierarchy.</note> Plutarch in his commentary *On Tranquility of Mind*: <margin>For he who wishes to throw a spear with a plow and to hunt a hare with an ox is unfortunate. Nor does any wicked spirit oppose him who does not catch stags with fishing nets, but it is stupidity and perversity to attempt impossible things.</margin> <note>original: "οὐδὲ γὰρ Τῷ ἀρότρῳ βελόμεθα..."</note> That is, for he who wishes to hurl a javelin with a plow, and hunt a hare with an ox, is not simply unfortunate. Nor is any malicious spirit involved for him who fails to catch deer with fishing nets, but it is folly and perversity to attack what cannot be done. For everything has its proper use, just as if someone should entrust war or the administration of a republic to a man born for studies and leisure, <margin>He hunts the hare with an ox.</margin> Or if one commits judgments to a stupid man. He cites in the same booklet verses, if I am not mistaken, by Pindar: <margin>The horse for the chariot, the ox for the plow, but the dolphin swifter than any ship, and for the boar planning death, a strong dog must be found.</margin> <note>original: "ἐν ἅρμασιν ἵππος..."</note> In chariots the horse, in the plow the ox, but the dolphin outstrips the ship. Just as for the one preparing death for a boar, a strong dog must be found. For these also have the appearance of a proverb.

-> **From the diagram.** <-

Plutarch in the booklet *On the Difference Between a Flatterer and a Friend*: "The flatterer from one..."

# FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY
## Hhh 4

...the flatterer always sticks to what is pleasant, and just as he is accustomed to sounding a note of grace, he knows neither how to resist an action nor how to cause pain with a word, but only complies with what is desired, always singing and sounding in harmony with his patron. <note>original Greek: "μαῖος ἀεὶ τὸ ἡδὺ..."</note> It is clear that the proverb was spoken in the form "from a single diagram." Now, a <term>diagram</term> <note>original: "diagramma"</note> is a drawing or a description used by philosophers to set a matter before the eyes; thus, it is as if you were to say "from the same formula."

### Not the son of Achilles.
->XLVI<-

Among the songs of noble poets which are used by the learned in the place of proverbs, this also seems able to be included: 
"Not the son of Achilles, but Achilles himself." <note>original Greek: "οὐ παῖς ἀχιλλέως, ἀλλ’ ἀχιλλεὺς αὐτὸς."</note> 
It seems to be taken from some tragedy or comedy, for the verse is an iambic trimeter. It is used by Plutarch in the same commentary he titled *How to Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend*. He says there that a flatterer imitates a friend in every way, so much so that it could be said of him: "Not the son of Achilles," etc. Likewise, Parmeno in Terence’s play says of Gnatho, who was subservient to Thraso’s speech:
->You would say this second man was born from the first.<- <note>A reference to Terence's *The Eunuch*, where one character so perfectly mimics another's behavior they seem identical.</note>

### Ulysses strips off his rags.
->XLVII<-

In the same commentary I just mentioned, Plutarch uses this Homeric verse, not without a proverbial quality, from the twenty-second book <note>designated as "χ" in Greek</note> of the *Odyssey*:
"Then the wise Ulysses stripped himself of his rags." <note>original Greek: "αὐτὰρ ὁ γυμνώθη ῥακέων πολύμητις ὀδυσσεύς."</note>
It will be appropriate to apply this to those who, having suddenly changed their way of life, emerge from poverty to wealth, from filth to elegance, or from sadness to joy. For as soon as Ulysses stripped off the rags in which he had played the beggar among the suitors and was adorned with magnificent clothes, he suddenly appeared to be another person. Plutarch twists this to refer to the flatterer, who, in the manner of a polyp <note>A common ancient metaphor for a chameleon-like person who changes color to match their surroundings.</note>, adapts himself to the interests of everyone. Thus, a man who a moment ago wore a long beard and a cloak while staying with a friend devoted to philosophy, constantly busying himself with books and muttering nothing but the numbers, right angles, and triangles of Plato, might by chance run into a friend addicted to pleasures; immediately his shape is changed as if transformed by Circe, and he becomes a Sardanapalus. <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary king of Assyria, famous in antiquity as the ultimate symbol of luxury and decadence.</note>

### Suddenly another.
->XLVIII<-

In a similar way, he also applies that Homeric line from the sixteenth book <note>designated as "π"</note> of the *Odyssey* to a man suddenly changed, who seems to have suddenly become someone else:
"Stranger, you appear different to me now than you did a moment ago." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλοῖός μοι ξεῖν’ ἐφάνης νέον ἠὲ πάροιθεν."</note>
Agreeing with this is that line from Theocritus:
"Suddenly, by some divine power, a god has made me into another mortal." <note>original Greek: "ἀφάνης ἐξαπίνας μὲ θεὸς βροτὸν ἄλλον ἔτευξεν."</note>

### Against the hard and implacable.
->XLIX<-

Against a man who is excessively rigid and implacable, that Homeric line from the tenth book <note>designated as "κ"</note> of the *Odyssey* will be rightly applied:
"But there is in your breast a mind that cannot be charmed." <note>original Greek: "σοὶ δέ τις ἐν στήθεσσι ἀκήλητος νόος ἐστί."</note>
Plutarch, in his commentary *How to Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend*, says that this verse was habitually thrown at Mark Antony by his sycophants because he did not respond with enough passion to Cleopatra, who loved him desperately.

### The bathman's donkey.
->L<-

"Like a bathman's donkey." <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ ὄνος βαλανέως."</note> 
This was said against those who receive no fruit themselves from their own labors. Plutarch, in his little book *On the Love of Wealth*, says: "Experiencing no good, like a bathman’s donkey, which carries down wood and brushwood, always filled with smoke and ashes, but never sharing in the bath, nor the warmth, nor the cleanliness." <note>original Greek: "οὐδὲν εὖ πάσχων..."</note> He is speaking of a stingy and sordid rich man who, although he is burdened with riches, does not enjoy them.

### Lamp-livers.
->LI<-

It appears that those who lead a life by lamplight were called "lamp-livers" <note>original: "λυχνόβιος" (lychnobios)</note> in a proverbial joke, so as to twist—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of adages derived from the behavior of flatterers and those who live disordered lives. It transitions from the previous discussion of "Ulysses stripping off his rags" into descriptions of those who live by the lamp and the origins of several specific Roman and Greek proverbial phrases.</meta>

...can be applied to a night-drinker, or to a man excessively studious, such as what was said of Demosthenes: that he consumes more oil than wine. Or it could apply to a sordid and stingy man living on lamp oil. Seneca, in the 22nd book of his *Epistles*, letter 122, shows this was said of a certain "light-fleer" <note>original: "fugam"; Seneca uses this to describe those who "flee the light" or live backwards</note>, whose whole life was backwards, so much so that whatever the common crowd usually does by day, he did at night. He woke up towards nightfall and went to bed at dawn. Concerning him, Varus, a most witty storyteller, joked that he lived quite frugally, since he consumed nothing but "night." When some called him sordid and greedy, he said, "You should also call him a **lychnobius**" <note>original: "lychnobiũ"; from the Greek, meaning "one who lives by the lamp"</note>. There is a double meaning in the joke: that he was so far from stingy that he even "consumed" the lamps [the night], or that he was so parsimonious that he lived only on lamp oil. Furthermore, this alludes to a man's disordered life, such as Seneca describes in the same epistle regarding a certain Atilius Buta.

->As if they were going to Sutrium.<-

Sutrium is an ancient town in Etruria. It had once defected from the Romans when they sought an alliance. Camillus was chosen by the Senate to force them back to their loyalty. So that time would not be wasted in preparing provisions and so that the people of Sutrium might be overwhelmed by speed itself, he ordered that each soldier carry three days' worth of provisions with him. This afterwards turned into a proverb, which is usually used whenever someone performs a task at their own expense. Festus Pompeius interprets this in certain fragments found in Rome. I believe it is the same history that Titus Livy tells somewhat differently in his book *From the Founding of the City*. Plautus says in *Casina*: "You also see to it that they come, as if they were going to Sutrium." He orders Alcesimus to send his people to him, but supplied with their own food. The poem of Catullus is well known, in which he invites Fabullus to dinner, but on the condition that he brings whatever pertains to a sumptuous meal with him.

->Self-flask-bearers.<-

**Autolecythoi** <note>original Greek: "Αὐτολήκυθοι"</note> was a common word for those who cultivated friendships not from the heart but for the sake of their bellies. The word was coined because they would come of their own accord to the oil-flask <note>lecythus; used at the baths and gymnasia</note> and were ready and uninvited at banquets. Eupolis testifies that these same people were called "table-friends" <note>original Greek: "τραπεζέας"</note> and "friends who appear after lunch" <note>original Greek: "τοὺς γλωσυ ἰγ̄ μετ' ἄρισον φίλους"</note>. Plutarch, in the booklet titled *How to Distinguish a Flatterer from a Friend*, says: "But let us not—as the crowd does with those called **Autolecythoi**, 'table-friends,' and those who only listen after the water is poured on the hands—think of them as flatterers." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ μὴ καθάπερ οἱ πολλοὶ τοὺς αὐτολήκυθους τούτες λεγομένους..."</note> This word is also used by Demosthenes in his oration *Against Conon*. Interpreters explain it in various ways: of those ready to endure anything, or of the poor who possess nothing besides an oil-flask, or of those who are quick to draw out money (because some were said to hide money in little jars), and in other ways, none of which agree with Plutarch's meaning. In Athenaeus, Book 4, they are called "eaters of others' food" <note>original Greek: "ἀλλοτριοφάγοι"</note>, to whom it is sweet to eat from another's plate. He relates something quite witty there: when a dispute arose as to which water was best, with some preferring the Lernaean, others the Pyrenaean, and others another, Carneus spoke the opinion of Philoxenus: "The water on the hands is the sweetest" <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἐπὶ χειρῶν ὕδωρ ἥδιστον"</note>, meaning the water poured over the hands, because it declares that the dinner is ready when the host bids the guests wash. This agrees with what is said elsewhere: "The pot boils, friendship lives."

->Maltese puppy.<-

A **Maltese puppy** <note>original Greek: "Μελιταῖον κυνίδιον"</note> was the name given to one whose labor served no wild or useful purpose, but was raised solely for the sake of pleasure—the kind of which there is no small number in the households of the wealthy. The use of other dogs varies. There are those to whom the guarding of the house is delegated, so that they keep watch against thieves at night; these are called **house-guards** <note>original Greek: "οἰκουροί"</note>. There are those whose labor we use in hunting, who are called **hunters** <note>original Greek: "θηρευτικοί"</note>. There are those for whom there is no use except to play with delicate matrons; it is remarkable how much they are in favor even in our own times. They are called **Maltese** <note>original: "Melitaei"</note>, undoubtedly from the island of Melita, between Black Corcyra and Illyria. The author is Pliny, Book 3, last chapter. Likewise Strabo and Stephanus. Aristotle mentions these in Section 10, Problem 14, indicating that they were small in all their limbs; and they are recommended for this quality. Just as there are those who cannot live without dwarfs and midgets. In Lucian’s *The Lapiths*, the jester calls Alcidamas the Cynic a "Maltese puppy."
