<meta>This page continues the discussion of human behavior and social critiques, moving from the previous page's mention of "going to Sutrium" into a commentary on the misplaced affections of the wealthy. It then transitions into a series of numbered adages (LV through LVIII) concerning natural omens, medical incompetence, and the habits of the stingy or the wasteful.</meta>

<margin>little dog <note>original: κυνίδιον</note></margin> he calls it. Athenæus, in his twelfth book, writes that the Sybarites <note>The inhabitants of Sybaris, famous for their luxury and decadence.</note> were exceedingly fond of Melitean dogs <note>Maltese dogs; a small, ancient breed of lapdog.</note> as pets. These seem to be among the canine race what dwarfs and pygmies are among men. However, Masinissa is rightly praised because, instead of monkeys and puppies, he preferred to raise boys until their third year, at which point he returned them to their parents. But it is even more intolerable that among the Britons, many keep packs of bears for dancing—a gluttonous and harmful animal—while so many of the needy are starving. Yet why do we lament these things, when there are those wandering about who, following an example originating in Italy, carry around a girl or a boy taught to perform foolish gestures? Thus, the misfortune of one girl supports the idleness of four or five robust scoundrels. And Christian men watch these kinds of spectacles with indifferent eyes.

<margin>LV</margin>
### Immediately it will be winter.

Aristotle, in the thirteenth section of his *Problems*, cites this verse without naming an author, but as if it were a common saying:

> If the south wind summons the north, immediately it is winter. ->that is,<-
> <note>original: Εἰ νότος βορέαν προκαλέσεται, αὐτίκα χειμών</note>
> Winter occurs at once when the South wind has summoned the North.

He offers this reason: the South wind, by its own nature, gathers clouds and rain in abundance. Therefore, if the North wind arrives at that moment, everything freezes due to its rigor, and thus it is immediately winter. He adds another poem in the same problem with almost the same sentiment:

> If the north wind seizes soft mud, immediately it is winter. ->that is,<-
> <note>original: Εἰ βοῤῥᾶς πηλὸν καταλείψει, αὐτίκα χειμών</note>
> If the North wind seizes the soft mud, winter occurs at once.

Although this appears to be a simple folk saying, we can adapt it to mean that a great danger is imminent if one evil follows another. For instance, if someone who is already excessively tormented by the labors of study also begins to fall in love; or if someone who was previously unpopular with the prince also falls into the hatred of the common people; or if a very harsh ruler succeeds a king who was exceedingly mild and peaceful, or vice versa. For sudden changes of this kind usually stir up the greatest upheavals in affairs.

<margin>LVI</margin>
### To put the same shoe on every foot.

Galen, in the ninth book of *On the Method of Healing*, says: "Some, when they search, do not even know what they are looking for; rather, according to the proverb, they want to put everyone in the same shoe-last." <note>original: ἑνὶ καλαπόδι πάντας ὑποδήσειν</note> That is: those men neither inquire nor know; rather, they follow the proverb and shoe everyone with the same footwear. He is speaking about certain unskilled doctors who, without taking the nature of the diseases into account, apply the same remedies to everyone, even though different ailments require different cures. This is not unlike what is said in another place: "You know how to mimic a cypress." <note>A reference to an artist who only knew how to paint one thing (a cypress tree) regardless of what the commission required.</note> Jerome refers to this concept in the first preface of his *Commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians*: "Nor, like an unskilled doctor, should one wish to cure the eyes of all with a single eye-salve."

<margin>LVII</margin>
### The life of a snail.

<note>original: Κοχλίου βίος</note> i.e., The life of a snail. Used for those who live sparingly and on very little, or who are withdrawn from business and removed from the light of the marketplace. The animal from which the metaphor is taken is well known. Plutarch, in his booklet *On the Love of Wealth*, says: "But you endure so many troubles, disturbing and twisting yourself, while living the life of a snail because of your small-mindedness." <note>original: κοχλίου βίον ζῶν διὰ τὴν μικρολογίαν</note> Regarding snails which, when it is hot, live off their own moisture, we have related elsewhere from Plautus's *The Two Captives*.

<margin>LVIII</margin>
### Gained in war.

<note>original: Ἐκ πολεμίας</note> i.e., From the enemy's region. Used when someone spends immoderately. For we are accustomed to squander things more quickly and recklessly if they have been snatched from an enemy. Indeed, this adage is heard everywhere today, commonly spoken against gluttons and drunkards. Plutarch, in the booklet he titled *Precepts for Health*, writes: "To fill oneself with the expensive foods of others and to enjoy them just as if they were provisions taken without restraint from an enemy region." <note>original: καθάπερ ἐκ πολεμίας ἀφειδῶς ἐπισιτιζομένους</note> That is, loading oneself amply with food. The same is used in the seventh decade of the *Table Talk*, problem six. Satyrus, in the fourth book of Athenæus, depicts men of this kind with these words: "Overrunning the field, plundering the house, selling off the possessions as if they were spoils of war." <note>original: κατατρέχοντες τὸν ἀγρὸν, διαρπάζοντες τὴν οἰκίαν, λαφυροπωλοῦντες τὰ ὑπάρχοντα</note> For "selling spoils" <note>original: λαφυροπωλεῖν</note> is to sell the plunder taken from enemies under the spear <note>A Roman custom of selling war booty at public auction.</note>. And those things are usually valued less, as if they belonged to someone else. Hence the Greeks call those who squander their family estate through luxury "plunderers" <note>original: λαφυκτὴ</note>, as Athenæus indicates in book eleven, and this kind of profusion is called "gluttony" <note>original: λαφυγμός</note>; and "to plunder" <note>original: λαφύσσειν</note> is to pillage, or to [eat] intemperately...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of adages by Erasmus of Rotterdam, transitioning from natural omens on the previous page to metaphors for social behavior, stinginess, and the psychological role of hope.</meta>

...to pour out or devour threefold, as Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> indicates. For "spoils" <note>original: λάφυρα (laphyra)</note> are the name for things stripped from the living, just as "booty" <note>original: σκῦλα (skyla)</note> refers to things taken from the dead.

->**Stony bread.**<-
<note>original: Panis lapidosus</note>

If anyone denies that this is a proverb, I will not fight him too hard over it, though it is certainly worthy of being adopted into the company of adages through constant use. It is recorded by Seneca in the second book of *On Benefits*: "Stony bread." (This is how Fabius Verrucosus <note>A Roman statesman and general famous for his "delaying" tactics against Hannibal.</note> described a favor given harshly by a stern man.) It is something that a hungry person finds necessary to accept, yet it is bitter to swallow. In this way, some people ruin a favor through hesitation, a grim expression, or harshness of speech—making it so unpleasant that no one would accept it if they could possibly do without it.

->**From the house of Patrocles.**<-
<note>original: ἐκ πατροκλέους (ek patrokleous)</note>

This is said of the filthy or the stingy. It is taken from the habits of Patrocles of Athens, who was quite wealthy but excessively thrifty and dirty. Ancient accounts depict him much like the character Euclio in the plays of Plautus. According to the commentator on Aristophanes, whose words Suidas also records, this is considered a proverb. It appears in Aristophanes’ play *Wealth* <note>original: Plutus</note>. When a character who was unkempt, neglected, and covered in filth was asked where he had come from:
"Tell me then, why do you walk about so filthy?"
<note>original: πόθεν οὖν φράσον αὐχμῶν βαδίζεις;</note>
He replies:
"I come from the house of Patrocles,
Who has not washed once since the day he was born."
<note>original: Ἐκ πατροκλέους ἔρχομαι οἷς οὐκ ἐλούσατ’ ἐξ ὅτουπερ ἐγγένη</note>

->**As easy as falling rain.**<-
<note>original: Tam in procliui quàm imber</note>

This phrase, which appears in Plautus’s play titled *The Captives*, is not without the character of a proverb: "This is as easy for you as rain is when it pours." 
For "downward-sloping" <note>original: procliue</note> is properly said of what hangs from a height toward the ground. It is hard to push things upward, but they roll down of their own accord.

->**One must sow even after a bad harvest.**<-
<note>original: Et post malam segetem ferendum est</note>

I will not argue that this is a proverb, even if it is very much like one. It is a sentiment from Seneca in his eleventh book of *Letters*: "One must sow even after a bad harvest." We may use this whenever a matter has not turned out according to our wishes, to indicate that we must not cease our efforts. Although Seneca is speaking of those who refuse to bestow a favor on any man just because they once encountered someone ungrateful. Of the same kind is the phrase added in that passage: "After a shipwreck, the seas are tried again."

->**Hope saves the afflicted.**<-
<note>original: Spes seruat afflictos</note>

Plutarch, in his short book *On the Method of Living*, indicates that there was a common proverb of this kind, though he does not explain exactly what it was. "Weakness and lack of self-control bring most people together under the proverbial hope, which leads them to return boldly to their usual vices once they have recovered." <note>original: τοὺς πλείονας ἡ μαλακία καὶ ἀκρασία συνήγαγεν εἰς τὴν προοιμίαν ἐλπὶς ἀναπάθει ἣν προσάγειν βαδίζειν ἀνασάντας ἰταμῶς ἐπὶ τὴν συνήθειαν</note> But what that proverb is which people use to excuse their intemperance, he declares in what follows: "As if curing wine with wine, and driving out a hangover with a hangover." <note>original: ὡς οἴνῳ δ’ ἡδὺ οἶνον, καὶ κραιπάλῳ ἐξελόντας καὶ διαφορήσαντας</note> From this, it appears Plutarch was alluding to the proverb "Driving out a nail with a nail" <note>An adage meaning to cure one trouble with another of the same kind; here, the "hair of the dog."</note>. This remains equally celebrated today among heavy drinkers. They jokingly add "the hair of a mad dog," trying a bit of wit that proves fatal to many. However, we should also note in passing a line found in the collected sentiments of the comedies:
"A man in misfortune is saved by his hopes."
<note>original: Ἀνὴρ ἀτυχῶν, σώσεται ταῖς ἐλπίσι</note>
That line by Ovid <note>original: Naso</note> is well known:
"Good hope gives strength, good hope also firms the spirit;
I have seen a man live on hope who was about to die."
<note>original: Spes bona dat uires, animum quoq; spes bona firmat. Viuere spe uidi, qui moriturus erat.</note>
Furthermore, that saying of Pindar has almost passed into a proverb among the learned:
"Hope, the nurse of old age."
<note>original: Ἐλπὶς γηροτρόφος (Elpis gerotrophos)</note>
For so Plutarch says in his book *On Tranquility of Mind*: "And a memory both more pleasant and more firm, which Pindar calls the hope that nurses old age." <note>original: καὶ τὴν μνήμην ἡδίονά τε καὶ βεβαιοτέραν ἣν πινδαρικῶς γηροτρόφον ἐλπίδ’</note>

<summary>This page explores several adages concerning human character and resilience, including the "stony bread" of harsh favors, the "filthy house of Patrocles" representing stinginess, and the vital, yet sometimes misused, role of hope in human life.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Adagia, Seneca, Plutarch, Ovid, Pindar, hope, stinginess, favors, perseverance, Greek proverbs, Latin literature</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's collection of ancient adages, moving from the comforting power of hope in old age to practical advice on health, social etiquette, and metaphors for absurdity and stupidity.</meta>

...with that hope, the nurse of old age. Pindar's passage is cited by Plato in the first book of the *Republic*: <note>original: ὅτι ὃς ἂν δικαίως καὶ ὁσίως τὸν βίον διαγάγοι, γλυκεῖά οἱ καρδίαν ἀγάλλουσα, ἡ γηροτρόφος συναορεῖ ἐλπίς, ἣ μάλιστα θνατῶν πολύστροφον γνώμαν κυβερνᾷ</note> "Whoever has lived a just and holy life, a sweet hope accompanies him, gladdening his heart, the nurse of old age, which most of all governs the fickle mind of mortals." That is to say: Because he who has spent his life justly and piously has a sweet hope as a familiar companion, cheering his heart and nurturing his old age—a hope that especially guides the versatile minds of men.

->**Three most healthy things.**<-
->LXIV<-

In the same work <note>Plato’s *Republic*</note>, since he mentions it without naming an author, it seems this was also tossed about as a proverb. But it is better to transcribe his own words: <note>original: ὅθεν ἀρίσα λέλεκται προφῆς ἀποσχέσθαι, καὶ πόνων ἀσκείσθαι, καὶ σπέρματος ὁσίως συντήρησιν, ὑγεινότατα εἶναι</note> "Whence it is excellently said that to refrain from overeating, to practice labor, and to holily preserve one’s seed, are the healthiest things." That is: From which it is best said, to eat short of satiety, not to flee from work, and to conserve the nature of the seed <note>A reference to sexual continence as a health practice common in ancient medicine.</note>, are most health-giving.

->**With the head moved close.**<-
->LXV<-

Plutarch, in the little book titled *How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend*, uses this verse—which is frequently found in Homer—as if it were a proverb:
<note>original: ἀγχὶ σχὼν κεφαλήν, ἵνα μὴ πευθοίαθ’ οἱ ἄλλοι</note>
"Holding the head close, so that the others might not hear."
In that passage, he advises that if a friend must be rebuked, it should be done first at the right time, then kindly and as a friend rather than harshly, and finally in secret with witnesses removed: "Whence it was best, with the head moved close." For this, Livy, in his *History of Rome* <note>original: ab urbe condita</note>, book 10, used the phrase "To bring heads together" <note>original: conferre capita</note>, as in: "The Consuls, as if deliberating, bring their heads together."

->**Why was it stopped?**<-
->LXVI<-

In the same commentary, he also uses this verse of Homer from the eleventh book of the *Iliad*:
<note>original: Τυδείδη, τί παθόντε λελάσμεθα θούριδος ἀλκῆς</note>
"Son of Tydeus <note>Diomedes, a hero of the Trojan War</note>, tell me what has happened to us, that our martial courage has slipped from our minds?"
It will be permitted to use this whenever we acknowledge a common fault with a friend and indicate that something has gone poorly or ceased.

->**To be thrown far away.**<-
->LXVII<-

When we advise that some vice or otherwise harmful thing should be thrown far away, that Homeric verse (if I am not mistaken) will be appropriate:
<note>original: Εἰς ὄρος, ἢ εἰς κῦμα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης</note>
"Into the mountain, or into the waves of the loud-roaring sea."
So also Horace in the *Odes*, Book 3, Ode 24 <note>Erasmus's text cites Ode 14, but it is actually Ode 24</note>:
"Or let us send into the Capitol,
Where the shout and the crowd of supporters call us,
Or into the nearest sea,
Our gems and stones and useless gold,
The material of the greatest evil,
If we truly repent of our crimes."
On the other hand, Theognis <note>A Greek gnomic poet</note> commands that not wealth, but poverty itself be "thrown into the deep-abyssed sea." Likewise, we say a person who is violently pestilential should be deported to the furthest islands.

->**A horse pursues a tortoise.**<-
->LXVIII<-

Plutarch in the book he wrote *Against the Stoics*: <note>original: πολλῷ δ’ ἔσω σχετλιώτερον ἐστὶ καὶ μᾶλλον ἀπερκταῖον τῶν φλυαριῶν, τὸ μηδὲν ὑπὸ μηδενὸς ποθ’ ἵνα καταλαμβάνεσθαι, μηδ’ εἰ χελώνην, ὡς τὸν λόγον φασί, μετόπισθε διώκοι ἀδράστου ταχὺς ἵππος</note> "It is much more wretched and even further from the realm of nonsense that nothing is ever caught by anyone, even if—as the saying goes—a swift horse of Adrastus <note>Adrastus was a legendary king of Argos; his horse, Arion, was famous for its supernatural speed.</note> follows a tortoise from behind." This will be suitable to use when we signify a matter is being handled preposterously and absurdly. It is related to what we have said elsewhere: "You are comparing a tortoise to Pegasus" and "A tortoise will have overtaken a hare sooner."

->**Stupider than Melitides.**<-
->LXIX<-

<note>original: Μωρότερος μελιτίδου (Moroteros Melitidou)</note> Stupider than Melitides. Melitides is one of those most fortunate fools whom Homer made famous in his poetry. It is read that he came to bring aid to Priam even after Troy had already fallen, as Eustathius mentions when explaining the tenth book of the *Odyssey*. Lucian in his *Loves* says: "Do you think me, by the gods, a Melitides or a Coroebus?" <note>Coroebus was another legendary archetype of stupidity.</note> Zenodotus records the proverb, showing that he was traditionally mocked by comic poets for his stupidity,
<meta>catchword: nor (Latin: nec)</meta>

It emphasizes the importance of private rebuke among friends and illustrates the archetype of the "legendary fool" through the figure of Melitides.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient Greek and Roman proverbs collected by Erasmus, finishing a section on legendary fools before moving into metaphors for clarity, vulnerability, and duplicity.</meta>

<page-num>924</page-num>
->THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-

...and was unable to count beyond five; moreover, after taking a new bride, he did not touch her, lest she should complain about it to his mother. In the same passage, he mentions another man remarkably known for his stupidity, who was in doubt as to which of his two parents he had been born from. Regarding Coroebus, the companion of Melitides, I have mentioned him elsewhere. Pausanias reminds us that Coroebus, along with Butalion and Melitides, were numbered among the fools by Aristophanes. Suidas says the same, citing this verse from Aristophanes:
<note>original: Τέως δ’ ἀβελτερώτατοι κεχηνότες, μαμμάκυθοι, μελιτίδαι καθήλωνται.</note>
"Until now, they sat there like the most worthless fools, gaping like Mamacuthae and Melitidae." <note>Mamacuthae and Melitidae were proverbial names for blockheads in Greek comedy.</note>

### It does not rain, etc.

Plutarch, in his *Natural Causes*, records that this little verse was tossed about as a proverb among children:
<note>original: Μηκέτι νυκτὸς ὕει, μηκ’ ἥκη ἀγροτόφα σῦς.</note>
That is: "Now it no longer rains at night, nor does the wild sow come forth."
He asks why domestic sows give birth more frequently and at uncertain times, whereas wild sows give birth only once a year, and almost on the same days. These days are at the beginning of summer, which is the time of year with the least rain, especially among the Greeks. I see no other use for the proverb unless one wishes to signify that, once spring or autumn has passed, there will be serenity. But if one wishes to twist the meaning further, it may be used jokingly to signify that when this or that has happened—which is likely to happen—there will be an end to our troubles.

### Clearer than amber.

<note>original: Ἠλέκτρου διαφανέστερος.</note> That is: More transparent than amber. <note>The Greek "electrum" can refer to both the golden-colored fossil resin (amber) and a natural alloy of gold and silver.</note> This is said of a thing that is exceedingly clear, or a person of extraordinary brilliance, because amber shines with a wonderful transparency. Hence Virgil calls it "liquid" when he says: **Or like liquid amber.**
Lucian in *The Loves* says: <note>original: Ἠλέκτρου φασὶν, ἢ τῆς Σιδωνίας ὑέλου διαφανέστερος.</note> That is: Clearer than amber or Sidonian glass. He calls it Sidonian glass because that city was once famous for the invention of glass.

### It perishes as easily as the bean at the edge.

Festus Pompeius shows that it was a common proverb to say, "It perishes like the bean at the edge," because beans at the edge of a field are usually either trampled or picked off by passers-by. Therefore, it will apply to a person or a thing exposed to all the injuries of everyone. For example, someone might say that theology perishes like the bean at the edge, because it is everywhere corrupted by being handled by the unskilled. <note>Erasmus often used these classical proverbs to take a satirical jab at the unlearned theologians of his own day.</note>

### Tyrian seas.

"Tyrian seas" was a proverb used for a thing that was greatly tumultuous and full of dangers. Festus Pompeius indicates the adage arose because the Phoenicians, originating from Tyre, were so powerful at sea that navigation was dangerous for all mortals because of them. He cites Afranius, who says of someone that he "stirred up Tyrian seas," which is to say, he excited huge disturbances.

### In one hand he carries water, etc.

<note>original: Τῇ μὲν ὕδωρ φορεῖ, τῇ δ’ ἑτέρᾳ τὸ πῦρ.</note> That is: In one hand he carries water, in the other fire. You may use this against someone who is flattering to your face but secretly harmful. Or against a double-tongued man, who now praises and now disparages, or who feels two different ways. Similar to this is the line from Plautus:
**In one hand he carries a stone, while he shows bread in the other.**
The adage is recorded by Plutarch in his commentary *On the First Cold*: <note>original: τῇ μὲν ὕδωρ δολοφονήσων χέει, τῇ δ’ ἑτέρᾳ τὸ πῦρ.</note> That is: With a treacherous hand he was carrying water, but in the other, fire. He is speaking of a woman equipped with diverse and contrary things. It is marvelous, however, that the same saying is in common use today among the people in exactly the same words.

### Be beaten, Papyria.

"Be beaten, Papyria" <note>Latin: Vapula Papyria</note>—Sisinnius Capito writes that this was a common proverb used whenever they wished to indicate they were ignoring someone’s threats. We find only this much in the fragments of Festus Pompeius. I suspect it originated from Papirius Praetextatus, from whom his mother tried in vain to squeeze out what had been done in the Senate by threatening him with blows. Therefore, we should probably read it as "Papirius," not "Papyria," unless you want to understand "law," as if it were a punishment threatening from the Papirian law. Or, unless it is more pleasing that it be said of Papiria, the wife of Paullus Aemilius, who was divorced by her husband although the cause of the divorce could not be known. For what can you do? One must guess where authors do not help us.

### As if no [hair] for a dog.

This proverb also has a certain flavor, which Scipio Aemilianus said to the people in the same passage...

<page-num>925</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD FOUR, FOURTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Iii</sig>

"...you will be," he says, "a defense for the republic, like a spiked collar <term>millus: a leather dog collar with outward-facing iron spikes</term> for a dog." For a *millus* is a collar for hunting dogs, made of leather and fixed with protruding iron nails to ward off the attack of wolves. In this way, therefore, we signify a certain and firm protection.

<margin>77</margin>
->A shoe does not cure the gout.<-

Plutarch, in his essay *On Contentment of Mind* <note>original: περὶ τῆς εὐθυμίας</note>, records a sentiment of this kind as if it were a common saying, though the phrasing itself carries the mark of a proverb: "Neither does a fancy slipper <note>original: καλπίκιος</note> rid one of gout, nor a costly ring of a hangnail <note>original: παρωνυχίαν, which the Latins call a "reduvia"</note>, nor a diadem of a headache." Plutarch uses it in this manner: If riches and the other gifts of fortune do not remove the diseases of the body, how much less can they heal the evils of the soul? A ring is the insignia of a doctor, but it does not remove mental dullness. A diadem is the insignia of kings, but it does not take away a man’s folly. A purple cap is the insignia of exceptional piety, yet it does not free the mind from impiety.

<margin>78</margin>
->With one little finger.<-

With "one little finger" <note>original: Vno digitulo</note>, they used to signify the greatest ease in handling a matter. Terence says in *The Eunuch*: "You who now luckily open the door for me with one little finger, I shall surely make you kick at it often in vain." Jerome says in his *Dialogue between a Luciferian and an Orthodox*: "This spear, therefore, which you have thrown with all your might and with which you threaten us, I shall repel, as they say, with one little finger." To this also belongs what is said elsewhere: "To challenge with the smallest effort" <term>Minimo provocare</term>, when we signify that we can win with no trouble at all.

<margin>79</margin>
->Marius's mules.<-

"Marius's mules" <note>original: Muli Mariani</note> was a military proverb for soldiers with varicose veins, who, by the ordinance of the general Gaius Marius, became accustomed to carrying their own burdens on a forked stick <note>original: furca</note> with a small board inserted, as Festus Pompeius testifies. But Plutarch, in his *Life of Gaius Marius*, records the origin of the adage in two ways. When Marius as general exercised his soldiers with running, various long marches, and the carrying of burdens, and they—having become accustomed to it—bore these things without complaint and in silence, they were called "Marius's mules" <note>original: ἡμίονοι μαριανοὶ</note> as a camp joke. From there, it was transferred to anyone who easily obeyed orders. Julius Frontinus also mentions the adage in the fourth book of his *Stratagems* in these words: "Gaius Marius, for the sake of reducing the baggage train by which an army’s line of march is most burdened, packed the soldiers' vessels and food into bundles and placed them on forked sticks, under which the load was manageable and rest was easy; hence it was drawn into a proverb, 'Marius's mules,'" clearly on account of their endurance of labor, which Homer repeatedly calls "sturdy-shielded" <note>original: ταλαύρινος; a term for a tireless warrior</note>. There are those who report a different origin for the adage. For when Scipio was besieging Numantia, he decided to inspect not only the soldiers' arms, but also their horses, mules, and chariots, to see how each man kept them trained and prepared; Marius produced a horse most beautifully nourished by himself, and furthermore a mule that far excelled the others in its physical condition, docility, and strength. And so, since the general was delighted by Marius’s pack animals and frequently made mention of them, it eventually happened that, by way of jocular praise, anyone who proved himself diligent, patient, and industrious in his duty was called a "Marius's mule." Plutarch records this second origin of the proverb in the *Life of Marius* which I just cited. Seneca, in that humorous book he wrote against Claudius Caesar <note>The *Apocolocyntosis*</note>, calls them "permanent mules." It will be more witty if it is twisted to refer to a man distracted by immense study or vehement, perpetual business.

<margin>80</margin>
->An Osculan battle.<-

Festus Pompeius indicates that "an Osculan battle" <note>Refers to the Battle of Asculum</note> was commonly used as a proverb whenever the defeated became the victors. This arose because the general Valerius Laevinus, having previously been defeated by Pyrrhus, a little while later utterly conquered the same king. He cites Ticinius, who made mention of this adage. However, this passage in Festus is also mutilated and truncated.

<margin>81</margin>
->To speak Oscan.<-

By an ancient proverb, those who spoke basely and with little modesty were said "to speak Oscan" <note>original: Osce loqui</note>. The allusion is taken from the customs of the Oscans <note>An ancient people of southern Italy</note>, because among them the practice of filthy lusts went unpunished; whence some think that "obscene" things <note>original: obscœna</note> are named—whatever things are shameful to do or say—even if Festus Pompeius disagrees. He cites a certain Ticinius, who wrote as follows: "They chatter in Oscan and Volscian, because they do not know how to speak Latin."

<margin>82</margin>
->The mills of the gods grind late.<-

Plutarch, in his commentary titled *On the Delays of Divine Vengeance* <note>original: περὶ τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεῖου βραδέως τιμωρουμένων</note>...

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad, Fourth Century of Erasmus's collection of adages. <page-num>926</page-num>
<header>ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

"...the mills of the gods grind late, but they grind fine" <note>original: ὀψὲ θεῶν ἀλέουσι μύλοι, ἀλέουσι δὲ λεπτά</note>. That is: "Therefore you do not see what benefit there is in those mills of the gods which are said to grind late." However, from those things which precede in that same passage, one may gather that it was common to say this of those who, though it be late, eventually pay the penalty for their misdeeds to a vengeful God.

->In passing.<-
<margin>81</margin>

Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Education of Children*, says: "But these things I say in passing <note>original: ἐκ παραδρομῆς</note>, as if for the sake of a taste." This metaphor clearly has the flavor of a proverb. Quintilian, in place of this, said "In transit" <note>original: In transitu</note>. Erasmus prefers "In passing" <note>original: In transcursu</note>. "Incidentally" <note>original: Obiter</note> has the same meaning.

->In three words.<-
<margin>82</margin>

To say "in three words" instead of "in very few" is proverbial. Saint Jerome, in his dialogue between a Luciferian and an Orthodox, says: "In three words, as they say, you have untangled this great matter." Likewise, Terentianus <note>likely referring to the character in Terence's play</note> in *Phormio* denies that certain people will "exchange three words." Pindar, in the twelfth Nemean Hymn: "Three words will suffice" <note>original: τρία ἔπεα διαρκέσει</note>. Yet it does not escape the interpreters here to philosophize rather over-scrupulously about these "three words." Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in *Pro Cluentio*: "He accused Scamander, however, in three words: that poison had been discovered, etc." It is a comic figure; we say "six hundred" for many. "Write to me six hundred things." Catullus. One who explains in few words is said to "settle the matter with a word" <note>original: Verbo rem expedire</note>. And "not to touch it even with a syllable" <note>original: Ne syllaba quidem attingere</note> is said of one who remembers nothing at all. Thus Galen against Erasistratus, I believe: "How is he not ashamed that, while he has clearly distinguished the misfortunes of indigestion—both how many they are and that they happen for many reasons—yet concerning the failures of blood-making, he has not spoken even a single syllable, nor even one word, nor even a point?"

->Not even a point.<-
<margin>83</margin>

Saint Jerome, in his Epistles: "And following the footsteps of the apostolic will, let us not depart even a point <note>original: punctum</note>, as they say, or a finger's breadth from his opinions." To mathematicians, a point is the smallest thing in the dimension of a body, so much so that it cannot have parts; when extended in length by the imagination, it creates a line; again, a straight line extended in width creates a surface. In the same way, Terence in *The Girl from Andros*: "Are you at this point for me regarding the truth?" <note>Erasmus's memory of the quote "Tun’ ueris ad hoc mihi punctum est" varies slightly from standard editions of Terence.</note>

->Spur the horse near the turning post.<-
<margin>84</margin>

"Spur the horse near the turning post" <note>original: κέντει τὸν πῶλον περὶ τὴν νύσσαν</note>. That is, "Prick the horse near the line or the goal." It is said when the speaker's discourse wanders from what was intended. It seems to have arisen from that passage in Homer's twenty-third book of the *Iliad*, where Nestor teaches his son Antilochus with many words how he should guide the horses. He adds this also: "Drive the horse close to the turning post" <note>original: ἐγγὺς δὲ τῆς νύσσης ἐλαύνειν τὸν ἵππον</note>. That is: "Let the line of the goal constrain the horse on the left." It is taken from equestrian racing, which was conducted between prescribed goals and lines which it was a sin to cross. To this Fabius <note>Quintilian</note> undoubtedly alluded in the eleventh book of his *Institutes of Oratory*, reporting that Cassius Severus was accustomed to "ask for a line" against those who wandered into others' benches, as if they were stepping outside the prescribed limit. Similar to this is "Outside the olive trees" <note>original: ἐκτὸς τῶν ἐλαιῶν; a reference to the boundaries of the racecourse</note>. Also that one: "To leap beyond the dug-up lines" <note>original: ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα πηδᾶν; referring to the long jump pit</note>. Gregory of Nazianzus used the proverb as a title in his sermon *On the Holy Passover*: "But perhaps some of those who love festivals and are more fervent might say to us: 'Spur the horse near the post,' and philosophize about the feast." He uses the same proverb in his sermon *On the Birth of Jesus Christ*. He varied it somewhat in his sermon against the Eunomians: "Lest, like hot and stumbling horses, after we have thrown off the rider of reason and the religious caution that keeps us beautifully within the enclosures, we run far from the post."

->It is better to be envied, etc.<-
<margin>85</margin>

Nothing is so common in everyday speech as this sentiment: "It is better to be envied than to be pitied." For envy is generally the companion of happiness, and pity the companion of calamity. It is moreover...

<page-num>927</page-num>
<header>THE FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>lii 2</sig>

Herodotus in *Thalia* <note>The third book of Herodotus’s Histories</note>, where Periander speaks thus to his son: "You, however, having learned how much better it is to be envied than to be pitied." <note>original: σὺ δὲ μαθὼν ὅσῳ φθονέεσθαι κρέσσον ἐστὶ ἢ οἰκτείρεσθαι / *Tu uero doctus, quanto satius sit, inuidiosum esse quàm miserandum*</note>. There exists a Greek epigram by Palladas on this sentiment:
"Envy is better than pity, according to Pindar,
For those who are envied lead a brilliant life.
But we pity those who are too unfortunate; yet let no one
be too happy or too pitiable to me.
For the middle ground is best, since the extremes
tend to bring danger, and the lowest state holds misery." <note>Erasmus translates the Greek into Latin verse here, which I have rendered into English</note> that is:
"Pity is worse than envy, Pindar says,
For they are happy whom envy seeks out.
We, on the contrary, pity those whose lot is harsh.
But I do not desire to be given either one,
To be excessively happy, or to be miserable to anyone.
For it is better for a limit to be present in all things.
Since nearby dangers attend a high station,
And the lowest is weighed down, bearing things intolerable."
This is found in Pindar's first Pythian hymn:
"But nevertheless, for envy is better than pity.
Do not let go of honorable things; guide the host with a just rudder." <note>original: ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως, κρέσσων γὰρ οἰκτιρμοῦ φθόνος. μὴ παρίει καλὰ, νώμα δικαίῳ πηδαλίῳ στρατόν / *Veruntamen melior est commiseratione inuidentia. Ne omitte honesta, guberna iusto clauo exercitum*</note>.
Again in the eighth Nemean hymn: "Slander is a choice dish for the envious; it always fastens upon the noble, and does not contend with the base." <note>original: ὄψον δὲ λόγοι φθονοροῖσιν, ἅπτει δὲ ἐσλῶν ἀεὶ, χερόνεσι δ᾽ οὐκ ἐρίζει / *obsoniū est inuidis obtrectatio. Attingit autem honestos, cum deterioribus non contendit*</note>. Again in the eleventh Pythian:
"For prosperity holds no small amount of envy.
But he who breathes low, grumbles in obscurity." <note>original: ἴσχει τε γὰρ ὄλβος οὐ μείονα φθόνον. ὁ δὲ χαμηλὰ πνέων ἄφαντον βρέμει / *Habet enim felicitas haud minimam inuidiam. At qui humilia spirat, in obscuro fremit*</note>.

<margin>88</margin>
->To seek bait from a fish-trap.<-

This was certainly said with a proverbial figure by Plautus, as cited by Festus Pompeius: "By Hercules, I shall never seek bait from that fish-trap today." <note>original: *Nunquam hercle ex ista nassa hodie escam petam*</note>.
And Cicero to Atticus in the last letter of the fifteenth book: "I have decided to leave this fish-trap, not for flight, but for a better hope of death." <note>original: *Ex hac nassa exire constitui nō ad fugam, sed spem mortis meliorem*</note>. A *nassa* <note>a "weel" or wicker trap</note> is a type of fisherman’s vessel from which, after a fish has entered, it cannot exit. From this source, these were also proverbial: "To fall into the fish-trap," and "Escaped from the fish-trap."

<margin>89</margin>
->Neither a woman nor a lap should be trusted.<-

The same Festus indicates that a proverb of this kind was commonly repeated: that it is proper to trust neither a woman nor a lap <note>original: *Nec mulieri nec gremio credi oportere*</note>. This is because the former is of an uncertain and light mind, and it often happens that things placed in the lap fall out when one stands up, having been forgotten. Likewise, things committed to the fold of a garment <note>the *sinus* or pocket-like fold of a toga</note> fall out unless you are belted. Therefore, Marcus Tullius [Cicero], promising silence, says: "It is in the fold of my robe, and I am not unbuckling." <note>original: *In sinu est, nec discingor*</note>.

<margin>90</margin>
->Together with temples and altars.<-

Plutarch in several places in the *Symposiacs* indicates that it was an ancient custom that whenever a divine rite was performed for any single god, vows were made to all of them at once; clearly so that the tragedy of the Calydonians would not be renewed for his own people. <note>In Greek myth, King Oeneus of Calydon forgot to sacrifice to Artemis, who then sent a monstrous boar to ravage the land</note>. Invoking the gods, they added these words as if ceremonial: "Together with temples and altars." <note>original: ἅμα σὺν ναοῖς καὶ βωμοῖς / *Vnà cū phanis et aris*</note>. He does not explicitly state that these ceremonial words were a proverb, yet he seems to use them in such a way that you might guess it was accustomed to be said as a proverb when they wanted to signify that nothing at all was omitted. Just as today people commonly say: "Along with clothes and shoes." And: "They moved out along with packs and baggage."

<margin>91</margin>
->Mercury has arrived.<-

"Mercury has entered." <note>original: ὁ ἑρμῆς ἐπεισελήλυθεν / *Mercurius superuenit*</note>. They were accustomed to speak thus if ever a silence arose in a gathering of many people, signifying that it is not permitted to speak while Mercury is present, who is the author of speech. Even today it is thought to be an omen if, in a meeting or a banquet, a sudden silence of everyone should arise. The adage is recounted by Plutarch in his commen— <note>The text cuts off mid-word "commentary"</note>

<page-num>928</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

commentary, <term>ποῦ δὲ ἀδωλεχίας</term> <note>original: "where is the babbling?"</note>. It is related to that which is said elsewhere, "The wolf in the story" <note>Equivalent to the English "speak of the devil," used when someone being discussed suddenly appears</note>.

-> Sweet is the fruit when the guard is away. <-

<term>γλυκὺ ὀπώρα φύλακος ἐκλελοιπότος</term> <note>original: "sweet is the autumn fruit when the guard has left"</note>. That is:
Where the guardian is lacking, the fruit is surely sweet.
It is a proverbial iambic line <note>Erasmus identifies this as a "senarius," a six-foot verse line common in Latin drama</note>, which we may use when we wish to indicate that the wicked are provoked to sin by the hope of getting away with it. The metaphor is taken from boys and youths who cannot restrain themselves from stealing fruit if they realize the watchman is absent. Plutarch uses this in his booklet titled <term>ὀφωλικὸν</term> <note>Likely referring to a passage in *Moralia* regarding desire</note>, against philosophers who, under the pretext of philosophy, serve their own lusts. <term>πρόφασις δὲν φιλία καὶ ἀρετή. κονιερὴ καὶ ψυχρολοτεῖ καὶ τὰς ὀφρῦς αἴρει, καὶ φιλοσοφεῖν φησίν. ἐννῶν ἔξω διὰ τὸν νόμον, εἶτα νύκτωρ καὶ κατ’ ἡσυχίαν, γλυκεῖ’ ὀπώρα φύλακος ἐκλελοιπότος</term>. That is:
Therefore, the occasion is friendship and virtue. He covers himself in dust, washes in cold water, raises his eyebrows, and proclaims himself a philosopher; he is sober outdoors because of the law, but then by night and in silence:
The fruit is sweet, then, when the guard is away.
This also appears in the proverbs of the Hebrews: "Stolen waters are sweeter" <note>Proverbs 9:17</note>. And Pindar, in his sixth Isthmian hymn: <term>Τὸ δὲ πᾶς δίκαν γλυκὺ πικροτάτα μένει τελευτά</term> <note>original: "That which is sweet against justice and right remains a most bitter end"</note>. That is, that which is beyond right and law is then sweet, but a most bitter end remains.

-> You are healthier than a fish. <-

Juvenal undoubtedly used this proverbially when he said, "You are healthier than a fish." For even today people commonly speak in that way: "You are as healthy as a fish." This is derived from the belief that fish do not feel diseases. However, Aristotle opposes this view in the eighth book of *On the Nature of Animals*, followed by Pliny in his ninth book. Indeed, fishermen conclude that fish do fall ill based on the fact that sometimes, among many very fat ones of the same species, they catch some that are thin, languid, and changed in color. Nevertheless, a plague does not generally strike the race of fish, as frequently happens to humans and other animals, not only domestic ones but also wild beasts.

-> Snatched from Crete. <-

Plutarch in his commentary *On the Education of Children*: <term>καὶ οὐ μὲν ἐνικοίη καὶ οὐκ ἤπιον ἔρωτας, καὶ τὸν ἐκ κρήτης καλεμένην ἁρπαγμόν. οὓς δὲ ἀίθωνσι καὶ οὓς ἐν λακεδαίμονι</term> <note>Erasmus is quoting a passage discussing different regional customs regarding mentorship and relationships</note>. That is: "One ought to flee the loves of the Thebans and the Elians, and that which is called the 'Cretan abduction,' but imitate those of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>." It appears that a noble or high-born love was once signified by these words, because occasionally maidens were carried away from there by their suitors <note>Erasmus is interpreting a complex Greek social custom of ritualized abduction</note>.

-> A fine-bordered man from a comedy. <-

Plutarch spoke with a very proverbial figure in his *Table Talk* <note>Symposiacs</note> of <term>εὐπάρυφον ὑπόκρισιν κωμῳδίας</term> <note>original: "a fine-bordered acting of a comedy"</note>, signifying a man magnificently dressed and dragging a great crowd of servants behind him. For "boastful soldiers" are depicted in this way in comedies. Their distinguishing mark is a purple cloak, as Donatus indicates. So Lucian says of a soldier: <term>ἐγὼ δὲ εὐπάρυφον λέγω τὸν ἐν χλαμύδι</term> <note>original: "I call that man 'fine-bordered' who is in a cloak"</note>. That is: "I call him 'fine-bordered,' that man in the military cloak." Hence the Greeks call the wealthy and those distinguished by splendid dress <term>εὐπαρύφους</term> <note>euparyphous</note>, which itself has a proverbial flavor. For *Paryphis* is a type of garment mentioned by Julius Pollux in book seven. It had a pure border sewn on both sides; in the Ionian tongue, purple stripes woven into a garment are called <term>πάρυφαι</term> <note>paryphai</note>. The same author notes that "fine-bordered" <note>euparyphon</note> is a word from the New Comedy. Conversely, the poor and humble, distinguished by no fine dress, are called "tunic-wearers" <note>tunicati</note>. Cornelius Tacitus in his *Dialogue on Orators*: "Whom the ignorant commoners and this tunic-wearing people more often call by name and point out with a finger as they pass by." Similarly Horace:
"Selling cheap junk to the tunic-wearing commoners."
For the *praetexta* <note>a purple-bordered toga</note> belonged to the nobles, and the *toga* was the mark of citizens. Marcus Tullius Cicero against Rullus: "Now there was your fear of those tunic-wearers." Likewise in *Pro Caelio*: "For us, indeed, formerly one year was established for keeping the arm within the toga, and so that you might practice exercises and games in the field while wearing only the tunic."

-> In a calm sea, anyone is a pilot. <-

Seneca in a certain letter to Lucilius: "Otherwise, a storm does not so much need the pilot’s art as it reveals it. For in a calm sea, as they say, anyone is a pilot." He says this against adverse fortune and difficult circumstances; they not only do not hinder the wise man, but indeed [reveal him]...

<page-num>929</page-num>
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FOURTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Iii 3</sig>

[virtue] brings itself forth most in these matters, which lay hidden in prosperous and peaceful times. It is no great thing to manage the state when all is constant in peace.

### Neither Lydian sauces. XCVII

<term>μήτε λυδῶν κάρυκας, μήτε μασίγων ψόφους</term> <note>original: "mēte lydōn karykas, mēte masigōn psophous"</note>. That is, "Neither Lydian condiments, nor the sound of whips." This will be a trochaic tetrameter catalecticus <note>A specific meter in classical poetry consisting of seven and a half "feet" or beats</note> if you add the article <term>τῶν</term> <note>the</note>. We read <term>κηρύκας</term> <note>heralds/sauces</note> with a double 'kappa' in Hesychius and Athenaeus. Hesychius indicates that <term>καρυκκή</term> <note>karykkē</note> refers to a dish made from blood and various seasonings. Athenaeus cites this little verse:
<term>Εἴωθας εἰς ταυτὸν καρυκκύειν, μέλι, Σεμίδαλιν, ὠά. πάντα γὰρ τἀναντία.</term> <note>original: "Eiōthas eis tauton karykkyein, meli, Semidalin, ōa. panta gar tanantia."</note> That is:
You have been accustomed to mix into one: honey, and with it
Fine flour and eggs. For they are all opposites.
From this comes <term>καρυκκεύειν</term> <note>karykkeuein</note>, used for "mixing various kinds of things," and <term>καρυκκεύματα</term> <note>karykkeumata</note> for foods seasoned in various ways, and <term>καρυκκεία</term> <note>karykkeia</note> for a more exquisite seasoning. But in what things and in what ways this kind of food is prepared, he declares seriously in his twelfth book, saying that this was an invention of Candaules <note>A King of Lydia</note>, who earned a famous name for himself from this. Suidas records the adage but does not explain it. 

One might conjecture that it was commonly said whenever people signified a moderate way or condition of life, which was equally far from the highest luxuries and from extreme evils. For we read that the Lydians were most corrupt in their luxury and delicacies, so much so that they gave their name to stage-players <note>Latin: "ludijs"</note>. Furthermore, it is certain regarding the Tyrrhenians—and I suspect also the Lydians—that they were accustomed to beat their slaves to the tunes of a flute, joining the highest softness with the highest cruelty. 

It will be more elegant if it is transferred to matters of the mind, such as to a speech that is neither entirely rustic nor too laboriously polished. Hence, those are said to "mix sauces" <note>original: "karykkeuein"</note> who not only infect food with various seasonings, but also those who season a speech with the manifold allurements of words and figures, or those who weave together a public address from diverse, poorly-fitting parts. This is the habit of certain show-offs: they explain a few words of scripture, add a "Sorbonnic" question <note>A reference to the complex, often hair-splitting theological debates at the University of Paris, the Sorbonne</note>, sew on something from Imperial law, something from Canon law, then something from Aristotle or the poets. To all these they add a "Colophon" <note>A finishing touch or crowning stroke</note> consisting of an old wives' tale; this is truly "mixing Lydian sauces." However, if I am not mistaken, I have made mention of this adage elsewhere as well.

### As if from a medicine chest. XCVIII

Very similar to a proverb is that phrase of Cicero in his second book *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "as if from a medicine chest" <note>original: "tanquam de narthecio"</note>. It stands for that which is prepared and ready at hand. For I believe he calls a <term>narthecium</term> <note>derived from the Greek 'narthex'</note> the box from which pharmacists take out their medicines. Cicero’s words are: "Now they bring forth those Epicurean remedies for pain, as if from a medicine chest: 'If it is heavy, it is brief; if it is long, it is light.'" <note>A famous Epicurean maxim suggesting that intense pain does not last long, and long-lasting pain is not intense.</note>

### What is not needed is dear at a penny. XCIX

The "Catonian" oracles <note>Wise sayings attributed to Cato the Elder, a Roman statesman known for his austerity</note> seem to have passed into proverbs among the ancients, no differently than those of Apollo, such as "Know thyself" and "Nothing in excess." Among their number is that most aptly spoken phrase which Seneca records in a certain letter to Lucilius: "What is not needed is dear at a penny." 

Cato wishes the diligent father of a family to be fond of selling, not fond of buying, and to buy not what is merely "needed" but what is "necessary." For what is not needed, he says, is "dear at a penny"—that is, no matter how cheaply it is bought, it is still expensive if you have no use for it. He calls "necessary" that which you cannot be without, such as a plow for a plowman; he calls "needed" that which might be of use if one had it, but which is of such a kind that you could do without it. Furthermore, what is not "needed" is entirely superfluous and useless. This can be applied to many situations: for example, if someone were to say that some art can be learned with very little effort, but it will bring no fruit, one could respond: "What is not needed is dear at a penny."

### Now your iron is in the fire. C

They used to say the iron of a man was "in the fire" when his business was currently being handled. For iron is softened by fire so that it may be forged. Thus Seneca says in that playful book he wrote on the death of the Emperor Claudius <note>The *Apocolocyntosis* or "Pumpkinification"</note>: "For Hercules, seeing that his iron was in the fire, began running here and there, saying, 'Do not envy me, my own business is at stake; afterwards, if you want anything, I will do it in turn: hand washes hand.'" <note>Hercules is portrayed as an advocate for Claudius's deification because he himself was a mortal who became a god.</note> He alluded to the fact that Hercules also had been made a god from a man, which was what Claudius was soliciting. Alexander the Great, when asked how he had gained possession of Greece, replied: <term>μηδὲν ἀναβαλλομένος</term> <note>original: "mēden anaballomenos"</note>. That is, "By delaying nothing." The Scholiast on Homer’s *Iliad*, book 2, records this.

<header>FIRST CENTURY OF THE FOURTH CHILIAD</header>

### 1. Not even an ox should perish.

We have already declared through several proverbs how much benefit a good neighbor brings and how much trouble a bad one causes. But because these matters contribute so much to a happy life, it is profitable to hammer them home again and again so they may be more deeply fixed in our minds. For this concern does not only apply to purchasing houses or land, but to almost every aspect of life. Just as **Marcus Porcius Cato** <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BCE), a Roman statesman known for his work *On Agriculture*</note> handed down advice about having a convenient neighbor, it pertains not only to farmers but to every single one of us. Indeed, if anyone now advanced in age were to retrace the entire course of their life, they would find that the greatest part of their successes and misfortunes proceeded from good or bad neighbors. **Columella** <note>A Roman writer on agriculture (4–70 CE)</note> cites a poem of **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet, roughly a contemporary of Homer</note> as if it were a proverb:

> *Not even an ox would be lost if there were not a bad neighbor.* <note>original Greek: μηδ᾽ ἂν βοῦς ἀπόλοιτ᾽ εἰ μὴ γείτων κακὸς εἴη</note>
> That is:
> *Nor would an ox perish, if a wicked neighbor were absent.*

Yet the loss of an ox is slight if compared with those evils received from wicked companions, from false friends, or from wives and servants who are hardly faithful. Some have thought that **Cato’s** opinion should be rejected because it is not within our power what kind of neighbor we have, since death and various other causes frequently change them for us. Nevertheless, while that cannot be denied, Cato wisely instructed that a farmer, as much as lies within him, should see to it that he has a good neighbor—and not just a "good" one, but a "convenient" one. For a man can be good without being convenient to you. For this to happen, two things will help most: diligence in preparing the field, and agreeable manners toward the neighbor. For we frequently have a bad neighbor because we show ourselves to be bad neighbors. Therefore, just as Columella elegantly writes, while it is the mark of a wise man to endure accidental misfortunes with a great spirit, it is the mark of a madman to make his own bad fortune. This is exactly what a person does who buys a worthless neighbor with his own money, even though he might have heard from his very cradle—provided he was born to free parents:

> *Not even an ox would be lost if there were not a bad neighbor.*

This is said not only of an ox, but of every part of our household affairs; indeed, many have preferred to lose their homes and have fled their own hearths because of the injuries of neighbors. We must believe that entire nations sought out a different world and left their ancestral soil—I speak of the **Achaeans** and **Iberians**, the **Albans** also, and no less the **Sicilians**, and to touch upon our own origins, the **Pelasgians**, **Aborigines**, and **Arcadians**—precisely because they could not bear bad neighbors. And lest I speak only of public calamities, history records that private individuals also found neighbors to be detestable both in the regions of Greece and here in **Hesperia** <note>A poetic name for Italy, meaning "the Western Land"</note> itself. Could that famous thief **Autolycus** <note>In Greek myth, a master thief and grandfather of Odysseus</note> be a tolerable neighbor to anyone? Or did **Cacus**, the inhabitant of the **Aventine Hill**, bring any joy to his **Palatine** neighbors? <note>Cacus was a fire-breathing giant who lived on the site of Rome and stole cattle from Hercules; the Palatine and Aventine are two of Rome's seven hills.</note> I prefer to remember those of the past rather than those of the present, lest I name my own neighbor, who allows neither a taller tree to stand in our area, nor a nursery of plants to remain untouched, nor a vine-prop to stay attached to the vineyard, and even refuses to let the flocks graze without harassment. Rightly, therefore, in my opinion, **Marcus Porcius** judged that such a plague should be avoided, and especially warned the future farmer not to come upon it by his own choice. Thus far, Columella has both defended Cato with a certain declamatory eloquence and taught us what a plague a bad neighbor is.

However, Cato does not only consider the neighbor’s character, but also how prosperous his affairs are. *Observe,* he says, *in what manner the neighbors shine.* In a good region, they ought to shine well. For sometimes "shining" <note>Prosperity or the well-kept state of the farm</note> proves the goodness of the soil, while in less fertile soil it declares the industry of the farmer. Furthermore, just as a diligent neighbor stimulates one to the zeal of farming well, so the luxury and laziness of neighbors corrupts a neighbor’s household. Likewise, a very powerful neighbor oppresses a poor propinquity, and neighbors who are excessively thin <note>Impoverished or desperate</note> are always scraping something away, whether by begging or by theft. Finally, with surly and wicked neighbors, there is never a time without a quarrel—now about boundaries, now about damages, now about **dripping eaves**, now about a **path or driveway**, now about a **view or light**. <note>Erasmus lists common Roman legal disputes regarding property rights (*servitutes*).</note> But if fortune has given us such a neighbor and it is not possible to change, what remains is that we, by our own obliging nature, turn him from bad to good; at the very least, let us take care that he does not become more troublesome by being provoked. For it would be most shameful if, by our own behavior, we turned a convenient neighbor into an inconvenient one. Clearly, this is what he instructs...

While the previous page introduced the proverb from Hesiod via Cato, this page transitions from agricultural advice to a deeply personal tribute to Erasmus's greatest patron, William Warham, Archbishop of Canterbury.</meta>

<page-num>931</page-num>
<header>SIXTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH CHILIAD</header>
<sig>Iii 4</sig>
<meta>catchword: habits</meta>

**Cato** says: *Be good to your neighbors.* And lest you should think it enough if you yourself refrain from injuring a neighbor, he adds: *Do not allow your household to do wrong.* Presently he indicates what utility one gains from good neighbors: *If,* he says, *the neighborhood sees you gladly, you will sell your goods more easily, you will lease out your tasks more easily, and you will hire laborers more easily. If you build, they will help with labor, draft animals, and materials. If any need arises regarding your good health, they will kindly defend you.*

Therefore, in the old days, those who advertised a farm for sale would inform the auctioneer of the qualities for which the land was commendable: how healthy the air was, how convenient the location, how fertile the soil, and how well-built the villas were. But **Themistocles** <note>A famous Athenian statesman and general (c. 524–459 BCE)</note>, a man of the sharpest wit, when he was selling a farm, ordered that among such qualities this also be added: *that it had a good neighbor.* This act was first received with laughter and jokes from the crowd, but soon it was understood that this was the most excellent recommendation for the land.

It matters a great deal, therefore, for the convenience of one's whole life, what kind of neighbor each person chooses for himself, and then in what manner he treats the neighbor he happens to have. A Prince who seeks a territory which he cannot protect without great trouble and the highest expense to his ancestral domain adds a "bad neighbor" to himself. On the other hand, he who adopts wise and faithful counselors, and magistrates who are upright and lovers of the republic, adds "good neighbors." Nor is it of little importance what nations he joins together in alliance. He who, for the sake of a dowry or honor, takes a bride with troublesome habits, or one who has insolent relatives, adds "bad neighbors" to himself. He who enters into a treaty of friendship with the wicked invites a "bad neighborhood." He who, led by a love of ease, throws himself into a college or monastery of impious or even superstitious men, prepares a "bad neighborhood" for himself.

The first caution, therefore, should be in choosing; the next in correcting; and the last in fleeing what cannot be corrected. Although even flight should not lack caution. Otherwise, the flight from a fault leads to a vice if it lacks skill; nor is it rare that out of hatred for one evil we throw ourselves headlong into another more serious evil. Rarely has anyone repented of a friendship who chose a friend with judgment. And often it is by our own fault that a friendship is broken, because we do not use good friends well, or because we neither know how to endure nor how to improve friends who are not quite suitable. Nor indeed do those sin less lightly who, when they have fallen among "pestilential" friends, do not know how to withdraw themselves, but either cling to those they secretly hate, or do not gradually drift apart but rather break off violently.

The same thing happens to people like me in choosing and retaining patrons and foster-fathers of our studies. We neglect those offered to us, or we embrace those poorly suited to us; or, if someone suitable has fallen to our lot, we do not strive to nourish his benevolence toward us with mutual services. In the first part, certainly, I sinned most gravely as a youth. For if I had then responded to the favors of the great men who had begun to embrace me, I would have become something in literature; but an immoderate love of liberty caused me to struggle for a long time with perfidious friends and stubborn poverty.

Nor would there have been an end to it, had not that **William Warham**, Archbishop of Canterbury—a man to be revered not so much for the dignity of his title and office as for his outstanding virtues worthy of a supreme prelate—lured me into the "snares" of his friendship as I was, so to speak, fleeing. Having merely tasted his humanity, I betook myself to Italy. There, while I was idling and thinking of nothing less than returning to Britain, he recalled me of his own accord, offering a benefice <note>A church office that provides an income</note>. This too was neglected.

However, when another wind had carried me back to England, he bound me to him—not so much by his generosity, although that too was and is singular in him, but by a certain lovable pleasantness of character and a wonderful constancy in loving (a thing which is truly very rare in leading men)—so that I unwillingly gave him my hands. This was the bait by which he drew me into his jurisdiction. Thus I was captured for my own good, happy on this one account: that this **Maecenas** <note>Gaius Maecenas was the legendary patron of Virgil and Horace; his name became a synonym for a wealthy supporter of the arts</note> fell to my lot; though I would have been far happier if it had happened sooner. Whether he repents of this protégé, I do not know; certainly, in my own mind, I have not yet satisfied him with mutual services, nor does it seem I ever shall.

Therefore, I must ask all who are led by a love of good literature and religion, that if they have gathered any fruit not to be repented of from my late-night labors, they should give thanks to this most holy prelate on my behalf, and even repay him if they can. They will repay him, however, if they do not allow his memory to die out among posterity—he to whose kindness they owe whatever they have drawn from my books, if indeed they have drawn anything at all fruitful.

On every side, complaints resound from those lamenting that they lack "Maecenases" for the cultivation of their studies. And yet Maecenas did not immediately embrace **Virgil** or **Horace**, nor was he a Maecenas to **Bavius** or **Maevius** <note>Inferior poets of the Augustan age often used as examples of bad writers</note>. Let a young man first see to it that he offers some excellent specimen, like a pledge of himself that will not perish, which might be invested in. Nor let him think it enough to have carried off a gift, or rather a prey, by whatever means. Kindness is not to be sought after by the impudence of begging, but by letters and virtue.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discourse on social and professional ethics, moving from the relationship with neighbors to the delicate relationship between a scholar and his patron, as well as the defense of humanistic studies against contemporary critics.</meta>

<page-num>932</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

with habits always progressing toward the better. In this way, a field invites the farmer to a more abundant harvest if it returns what was entrusted to it in good faith and with much interest. Nor should a patron be changed frequently, so that, having exhausted one, you seek another who is fresh, as if shaking acorns from one oak and then moving to another to gather more. Rather, one must serve one or two patrons as if you intend to stay with them forever. For how many scholars do we see who, by their own behavior, fill their studies with hatred and burden their patrons with shame. To be sure, it is a part of gratitude to celebrate the name of one's patron through writings and speeches. But it matters greatly whom and in what manner you praise. Vain praise destroys the credibility even of those who speak the truth; thus, it happens not that the reader thinks better of the one being praised, but worse of the one doing the praising. Immoderate praises stir up envy rather than glory. Furthermore, those who extol things that are condemned by the judgment of good and wise men actually disparage by their praising. First, let what you bring to an Encomium <note>A formal speech or piece of writing that highly praises someone or something.</note> be true; then, let what is true be handled so that it also becomes believable. Let there be no hyperboles of the kind used by some, by which they turn any man they please into a god; these do not paint a holy image of virtue, which should instead win over favor and goodwill—qualities such as loyalty, integrity, modesty, restraint, kindness, and a bright and easy disposition. Nothing is more envious than the human mind, and nothing more peevish than the judgments of men. Accordingly, if one must touch upon those things which the common people admire so much that they envy those who possess them, it must be handled with such skill that the one praised need not fear the "evil eye." No one envies a wealthy man who possesses what he has—whether by divine favor or without fraud—in such a way that he acts as a steward rather than a master. No one ever envies a powerful man who is powerful for the benefit of the state, who, as much as he stands out in dignity, so much does he humble himself in modesty, surpassing even the lowly in his courtesy. No one will envy a beautiful person who has joined modesty and chastity to the gift of nature. No one envies a healthy or vigorous person who lives and thrives for the great good of the many. But if someone lacks the talent or eloquence to handle a subject with the dignity it deserves, let him abstain rather than, like a bad painter, make a beautiful form look worse by his own attempt. Perhaps Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE), who famously decreed that only the artist Apelles should paint his portrait.</note> was somewhat particular in that he wished to be painted by no hand but that of Apelles. Yet no one with a distinguished body would wish to be painted by a Fulvius or a Rutuba <note>References to notoriously bad or low-status painters/gladiators mentioned in the satires of Horace.</note>. What you send out into the public light should be such that it promises to be remembered by posterity. Finally, praise should be so tempered that this service does not appear to be a tribute paid to the ego of the one you praise. For those who most deserve it often least desire or even endure being praised. Let it follow virtue instead, for glory follows even those who are unwilling, but let it serve to kindle others toward similar pursuits. In this way, he who has earned it will be praised usefully, and without the danger of envy or the suspicion of flattery. In the case of the deceased, the power of eloquence should be poured out more abundantly, since envy is then milder and the suspicion of flattery is less. Thus far I have shown how students can be recommended to their patrons. Now I will briefly touch upon the means by which they can win the favor of everyone for their studies themselves. For in many places now, "good tongues" <note>A reference to the study of classical languages: Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.</note> and the restored humanities are burning with great envy. This happens partly through the fault of the elders, who feel their own authority is diminished if any new learning is added to the youth; content with what they learned as boys, they will neither allow other things to be taught nor endure learning them themselves, either because they are lazy or because they are ashamed. It also happens partly through the fault of those who bring in these "new" ancient things. For there are some in this rank of intolerable insolence who, as soon as they have mastered twelve Latin words and a few Greek ones, think themselves Demostheneses and Ciceros <note>Refers to the greatest orators of Athens and Rome, respectively.</note>; they babble out foolish little books, sometimes venomous ones, scorn all liberal disciplines with wondrous arrogance, and rage childishly against the professors of these arts. Nor are there lacking those who abuse good literature for the worst purposes—for factions, for slander, and for shaking, dislocating, and undermining the concord and tranquility of the Christian commonwealth. But those who were once trained in these letters used their eloquence to settle the turmoils of princes; they campaigned against the leaders of heresy; they celebrated the praises of the saints; they sang the praises of Christ in pious verse and prose; they exhorted people to contempt of this world and to the love of heavenly things. Such was Basil, such was Nazianzen, such was Ambrose, such was Prudentius, such was Lactantius <note>Erasmus lists early Christian Church Fathers and poets who combined classical learning with Christian piety.</note>, in whom the knowledge of languages and of more polished literature did not lack envy, because it served piety. But the morals of men are also usually blamed on their studies. There are not a few today who detest the Gospel because of the impure morals of certain people who hawk themselves under the name of the Gospel. But if, as Paul warns, one shrinks from every appearance of evil and glorifies his Gospel, becoming all things to all men to win them all, then the professors of such literature, by the integrity of their morals, their courtesy, and the temperance of their <unclear>life</unclear>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s defense of the "new learning" (the Humanities and ancient languages) against its critics. He argues that what his opponents call "new" is actually the restoration of the ancient, superior way of learning practiced by the Church Fathers and classical authors.</meta>

<page-num>933</page-num>
<header>CHILIADS, FOURTH THOUSAND, FIFTH CENTURY</header>

if they would recommend their profession by their conduct, there would be far more fruit and less envy. On the other hand, if their elders would receive them in a civil and fair-minded way—not as new arrivals, but as old guests returning home by right <note>original: *postliminio*, a legal term for the recovery of rights by a person returning from captivity</note>—they would feel a significant light and no common utility growing from this addition. As it is, they wage an irreconcilable war with old friends just as if they were enemies. They call "new" those things which are the most ancient; they name "old" those things which are new. Among the ancient teachers of the church, a knowledge of the sacred volumes was joined with skill in languages and more humane literature. We see the same in the ancient philosophers, physicians, and lawyers. Where does Aristotle or Hippocrates speak poorly? Are not Plato and Galen eloquent? Among the ancient lawyers, moreover, the fragments preserved for us by the glorious Justinian—even though these very pieces swarm with monstrous errors—declare what their skill was in both languages <note>Greek and Latin</note> and show the purity and majesty of their Roman speech.

It is a *new* thing to hammer "modes of signifying" <term>modi significandi: a complex medieval system of grammar that focused on the logic of language rather than how it was actually used</term> into boys during their grammatical training, or to read out delirious commentaries that teach nothing other than how to speak impurely. It is a *new* thing for a young man to be admitted to the study of philosophy, law, medicine, or theology when, through ignorance of language, he understands nothing in the ancient authors. It is a *new* thing to be excluded from the inner shrines of theology unless one has long wallowed in Averroes <note>An influential medieval Muslim philosopher who commented on Aristotle</note> and Aristotle. It is a *new* thing to hammer sophistical trifles and certain fabricated difficulties—mere tortures for the intellect—into young candidates of philosophy. It is a *new* thing in the public schools for answers to be given according to the "way" of the Thomists or the Scotists, the Nominalists or the Realists <note>These were competing schools of medieval Scholastic thought</note>. It is a *new* thing for arguments drawn from the fountains of the divine volumes to be excluded there, while only those are received which are drawn from Aristotle, from decretal letters, from the decrees of the Scholastics, from the glosses of the professors of pontifical law, or from analogies that are usually cold and twisted out of Imperial law. If we are offended by novelties, these things are truly new. If we approve of what is old, then these things being offered now are the most ancient of all—unless perhaps it is "new" because it proceeds from the age of Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note>, and it is "old" because it arose three hundred years ago and has always progressed toward the worse.

But certain men, even more unjust than these, do not fear to babble privately and publicly—and even in sacred sermons—that these letters <note>The study of Greek, Hebrew, and Classical literature</note> are the sources of all heresies. They do not realize that this blasphemy falls upon Jerome, Ambrose, and Augustine, and many others in whom the Church glories as its teachers. They hammer such incredibly stupid nonsense into the ears of young men in the secrecy of confession: "Beware of the Greeks, lest you become a heretic; flee Hebrew letters, lest you become like the Jews; cast away Cicero, lest you be damned with him." O, what grave admonitions! Nor do they consider that in the future, boys everywhere will blurt these things out to be laughed at by all sensible people. They instill the same things into the ears of parents, acting so that the care of educating the children might be entrusted to them. It is easy to deceive poor women and simple, uneducated folk with the dye of "holiness." But you would no more rightly commit a sheep to a wolf than children to such "bellies" <note>An ancient slur for those who live only for their own appetites</note>.

What is this I hear? Did the Waldensians, the "Poor Men of Lyon," or Wycliffe <note>Groups and individuals labeled as heretics by the medieval Church</note> have mastery of languages and fine literature? Furthermore, was Jerome a heretic because he excelled in languages and every kind of literature? If someone skilled only in the French tongue were to write heretical opinions in his own language, would we immediately warn everyone not to learn French? Recently, they have even begun to persuade the courts of princes that this whole tumult—both of Lutheranism and of the peasant rebellion—was born from languages and more humane letters. These courts have their Midases and their Thrasones <note>Midas represents a foolish judge; Thraso represents a bragging, empty-headed soldier</note>, and the greatest princes are more exposed to the snares of such men the more noble they are and the more vehemently they indulge their own emotions.

If a man who knows Greek and Hebrew is in danger of heresy because Luther is not ignorant of these languages, why is it not rather said that the Church is safe because John Fisher, the Bishop of Rochester, and Girolamo Aleander, the Archbishop of Brindisi, are champions of the tottering Church? For the latter excels in all languages, and the former, now in his declining years, embraces the three languages with no common zeal.

They add another calumny. Perhaps in the secret confessions of sins they hear something of the lustfulness of young men, which is a disease peculiar to that age. They ask which authors the boys are reading; when they hear "Virgil" or "Lucian," they blame the studies for the vice of the age or the person. They immediately disparage both the age and the literature, as if they did not hear much worse things from those who have touched no literature at all. For just as the study of literature does not free one from all vices, so it cannot be denied that it keeps a slippery age away from many. Nothing, however, is so holy that he who is wicked by nature cannot turn it into an occasion for sinning. But if whatever provides an occasion for foulness in any way must be abolished, why is this forced celibacy so highly praised? Do they think...

<meta>catchword: Do they think [tant]</meta>

<summary>Erasmus defends the study of ancient languages and classical literature against Scholastic critics who label these "Humanities" as the source of heresy. He argues that it is the medieval innovations in grammar and theology that are truly "new," while the study of Greek and Hebrew is the "old" way of the Church Fathers.</summary>
<keywords>Humanism, Scholasticism, heresy, Greek, Hebrew, John Fisher, Girolamo Aleander, education, Church Fathers, Erasmus</keywords>
