<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s argument that the humanities and ancient languages should not be seen as enemies to traditional disciplines like Theology, Law, and Medicine, but as their essential supporters.</meta>

<page-num>934</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>
<meta>catchword: mem (referring to the next word in the original sequence)</meta>

...they do not know what a "Lerna of evils" <note>original: *lerna malorum*; a reference to the Lernaean Hydra, meaning a bottomless source of many troubles</note> may spring from this. But what fruit will there be at last, if all honorable disciplines collapse while their professors tear each other apart? We see this already happening to a great extent in several places. Yet without these disciplines, the life of men is not that of men, but of wild beasts. What remains, then, except that languages and good literature—returning home by right <note>original: *postliminio*, a legal term for the restoration of rights to one returning from captivity</note> and sprouting again as if from the root—should civilly and courteously introduce themselves into the fellowship of those disciplines which have reigned in the Universities for so many centuries? They should not attack anyone’s studies, but rather assist the studies of all. Let them yield somewhat to the authority of the professors; let them endure something of long-standing custom that has turned, as it were, into nature; and let them yield something to the age of those who cannot easily be bent to different things. Those whom they see are incurable, let them leave to their own temperament, lest they stir up greater tragedies. Those who are more manageable, let them entice with timely and gentle advice. Let them advise, assist, and correct in such a way that they act like a dutiful handmaid who is nearby to assist and correct her mistress. By right, Theology is the queen of all disciplines, but she will be both more honorable and better equipped if she receives such useful handmaids into her household with the courtesy they deserve. Philosophy is a magnificent thing, but much dignity will be added to her if she recognizes her old friends. Jurisprudence <note>The study and theory of Law</note> is an honorable mistress, but such elegant handmaids will bring no small ornament to her. Medicine is an excellent thing, but without the knowledge of languages and these literatures, it is almost blind. In this manner, if they share their goods with one another in turn, both sides will become richer and more splendid. I would also wish monarchs to be warned not to lend their ears to whisperers of this sort, but rather to consider how much praise and dignity will come to their affairs from this kind of study, as has happened in the past. Finally, the affairs of everyone, both publicly and privately, will be more fortunate if each person acts as a good neighbor to his neighbor. To return to the proverb, it agrees with what has been mentioned elsewhere: "Some evil because of a evil neighbor," which Demosthenes used in his speech against Callicles: <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἦν ἄρα ἀνδρὸς Ἀθηναίου χαλεπώτερον οὐδὲν ἢ γείτονος πονηροῦ καὶ πλεονέκτου</note>, that is: "It turns out, O men of Athens, there was nothing more ruinous than to have encountered a wicked neighbor who is not content with his own."

->The chief point of art is that what you do should be becoming.<-

Quintilian, in the eleventh book of his *Institutes of Oratory*, seems to cite this as a common saying: "The chief point of art is that what you do should be becoming" <note>original: *Caput est artis decere quod facias*; here 'becoming' means appropriate, fitting, or in good taste</note>. I will transcribe his own words: "One thing must be added to these: since appropriateness is especially looked for in performance, one thing often becomes one person, another becomes another. For there is a certain hidden and inexpressible logic in this; and as it has been truly said, 'the chief point of art is that what you do should be becoming,' so this can neither exist without art, nor can it be entirely handed down by art." Thus far Quintilian. It will be permitted to use this not only when something is done with little grace—as if an old man should hum or dance wantonly, or if a youth should lead and rebuke—but also when we deny that just anyone can do just anything becomingly. For we frequently see it happen that while something said or done by one person pleases everyone, if another person attempts the same thing, even if he is more learned or more skilled, no one can bear it. Although we see this happen daily, the reason why it happens cannot be explained.

->A right house.<-

Annaeus Seneca, in the sixteenth book of his *Moral Letters*: "We shall see that it is not expensive, that it is not elaborately built, that it lacks this modern polish. When you have looked around at everything, you will see no empty narrowness. Let there be no variety of marbles, no cutting of waters flowing from tunnels, no 'pauper’s cell,' or whatever else luxury, not content with simple grace, mixes in; it is what is commonly called 'a right house' <note>original: *domus recta*; implies a house that is 'straight' or 'proper' in its functional simplicity</note>." Thus far Seneca. Because the passage is not free from error, it indicates that "a right house" is commonly called one that is not indeed wealthy or ambitious, but which lacks nothing of proper furnishings. In the same way, Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> compares an elaborate tongue to an ambitious prostitute who overflows with much luxury, but the Latin language to an honorable and modest matron who lacks nothing pertaining to honest cleanliness.

->He is not happy, who does not know himself to be so.<-

The same author in the same work <note>Seneca</note> alleges this verse from some comic poet: "He is not happy, who does not know himself to be so." There is no doubt that this was tossed about in popular speech, since he did not add the author's name. The meaning is that it is not enough for happiness to be present, unless you understand your own happiness. Vergil alludes to this:
>O farmers, too fortunate, if only they knew their own blessings.

Martial also refers to the same thing when he counts this among the ingredients of happiness.

<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY</header>

**Be what you are, and wish to be so.**
<note>original: "Quod sis, esse uelis."</note>
For what is happier than liberty? Yet you may see not a few who deplore their lot because they do not find a place in the courts of princes: they think themselves miserable because they are not allowed to serve. But just as a man is not blessed if he does not think himself so, he is twice miserable who, being unhappy due to the evils of his mind, nevertheless seems happy to himself. For just as a person who is healthy but seems to himself to be sick does not enjoy his own good health, so he who is held by a disease, not understanding his own evil, is furthest from health; indeed, he is so far from being healthy that he is even incurable.

->A sure friend is seen in an unsure matter.<-
->V<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his dialogue *On Friendship* <note>original: *Laelius*</note>, cites this six-foot line of verse from the poet Ennius as a proverb:
*A sure friend is seen in an unsure matter.*
<note>original: "Amicus certus, in re incerta cernitur."</note>
By this, it is meant that a friend's loyalty is tested in adverse circumstances. For that which is joined with danger they call "doubtful," for which Ennius used "unsure" <note>original: *incertum*</note>, aiming for <term>opposition <note>original: ἐναντίωσιν (*enantiōsin*)</note></term> and <term>word-play <note>original: παρονομασίαν (*paronomasian*)</note></term>, rhetorical figures in which he took great delight—and not only he, but that whole age up until Cicero. Plautus likewise declares him a friend who helps in a doubtful matter. The proverbs of the Hebrews contain the same sentiment: *A friend loves at all times, and a brother is proven in distress.*

->The miser does nothing right, except when he dies.<-
->VI<-

I see that almost all the maxims of Publilius Syrus <note>original: *Publianas sententias*</note> were celebrated as proverbs, and not without reason. For nothing can be imagined more witty or more pleasant than they are. We ourselves recently edited his *Mimes* and did not hesitate to explain them with very brief scholarly notes. Therefore, it is not my intention to admit all of them into this collection, except for one or two that please me more than the rest, of which this is one: *The miser does nothing right, except when he dies.*
For he who has devoted himself to the pursuit of money is useful to no one while he lives. Death alone brings pleasure and profit to the heir.

->No hour is good for everyone.<-
->VII<-

This one also pleased me: *No hour is good for one man, without being bad for someone else.* Fortune has so tempered the affairs of mortals that what is joyful to one brings grief to another; what is a gain for one brings loss to another. No one grows rich except by another’s misfortune. No one conquers in war except by another’s destruction. Unless you prefer to read "somewhere" <note>original: *alicubi*</note> instead of "for someone" <note>original: *alicui*</note>.

->Self-chosen trouble.<-
->VIII<-

A particularly fine and elegant three-meter verse is celebrated among the Greeks:
<term>The begetting of children is a self-chosen sorrow. <note>original: Αὐθαίρετος λύπη ’στὶν ἡ τέκνων σπορά (*Authairetos lypē 'stin hē teknōn spora*)</note></term>
It cannot be said how great and how troublesome a business it is to raise children, especially when there are so few who live up to the duty they owe their parents. Truly, there is no one they can blame for this trouble, since it is permitted to live as a bachelor. This can be extended further to those who voluntarily bring danger and trouble upon themselves. Indeed, the condition of those raising children and those writing books is almost similar. What you have written must be defended and corrected, and yet there is no one we can accuse, since we were free to stay asleep.

->The wise man carries his goods with him.<-
->IX<-

<term>The wise man carries his substance within himself. <note>original: Ὁ σοφὸς ἐν αὑτῷ περιφέρει τὴν οὐσίαν (*Ho sophos en hautō peripherei tēn ousian*)</note></term> That is, the wise man always has his riches with him; this was born, if I am not mistaken, from an apothegm <note>a concise saying</note> of Bias. When asked why he was carrying away none of his possessions from his burning homeland, he said, "Indeed, I carry all my goods with me," meaning that those things which are truly ours are within us, such as learning and virtue. Conversely, we cannot escape those things which are truly our own evils, no matter how much we change our location.

->I would sooner give it to Telegoras.<-
->X<-

Telegoras was a very wealthy and powerful man among the Naxians. Because many people sought his favor daily, it became a common saying among sellers when people bid too little: <term>I would rather give it to Telegoras. <note>original: μᾶλλον ἐθέλοιμι τῷ Τελεγόρᾳ διδόναι (*mallon etheloimi tō Telegora didonai*)</note></term> This is recorded in the eighth book of the *Deipnosophists* by Athenaeus, citing Aristotle. We have followed this matter further in the proverb "No bad man is a big fish." Nor do I see what the use of this adage could be, unless we say that a duty is more rightly placed for free with the good and the great, than for a price with the wicked and the base.

->Hecate’s supper.<-
->XI<-

The ancients called a very meager and excessively frugal meal "Hecate's supper," because among the...

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

among the dead they live on a very thin diet, and the smallest and cheapest food, according to the accounts of the poets. Indeed, common ghosts live on mallows and leeks, but Hecate <note>The goddess of magic, crossroads, and the underworld, often depicted with three faces.</note> holds the *maenides* <note>original: "maenides" — small, cheap fish often pickled.</note> and red mullets <note>original: "trig-pisces" or *triglae*.</note>—which are most despised among us—as delicacies, sacred to her. Hence it was said at Athens that the red mullet belonged to her, and there was a statue of "Hecate of the Red Mullet" <note>original: *Triglantine*</note> in that city. Others think the red mullet is dedicated to her because of its name, which is derived from the number three <note>original: "ternione" — the Greek *trigla* resembles the word for "three."</note>, since Hecate herself is triple-formed. This appears in Athenaeus in book 7 and he mentions it again in book 8. Lucian also mentions it somewhere. But the learned reader might weigh whether this proverb could be applied to that supper which the wealthy used to set out at crossroads for Hecate every month, which the poor then snatched away. Aristophanes mentions this in his play *Plutus*:

> You can learn this from Hecate, if you wish,
> Whether it is better to be rich or to be hungry. For she says 
> That those who have means and are wealthy should bring a supper every month,
> But the hungry people snatch it before they can set it down.

->that is,<-

> You may learn this from Hecate, if you please,
> Whether it is better to be wealthy or needy. Since she commands 
> Those who have property to set out a generous supper once a month,
> But the needy plunder this before they can even set it down.

In this passage, the commentator writes: In old times they worshipped Hecate at crossroads because she is called by three names: the Moon, Artemis, and Hecate. At the new moon, the wealthy sent a supper in the evening, as a "Supper of Hecate" at the crossroads. But the hungry poor snatched and devoured the things that were set there, saying Hecate had eaten them. Thus, the proverb fits when something is snatched away in a scramble or tumult.

### The mind sees, the mind hears.

The mind sees and the mind hears. <note>original: Νοῦς ὁρᾷ καὶ νοῦς ἀκούει (*Noūs horā kai noūs akouei*).</note> that is, the mind sees, the mind hears. The first part of this line appears to be a <term>trochaic tetrameter catalectic <note>A specific rhythm of ancient verse, common in comedy and early philosophy.</note></term>. It is cited by Aristotle as a common saying in the thirty-third problem of the tenth section, where, having proposed the question of why we hear more keenly at night than during the day, he gives this among other reasons: that during the day the mind is distracted by various affairs, and unless the mind is present, the senses of the body do not perform their duty. Indeed, when the mind is elsewhere, we sometimes do not even feel physical pain. I myself have experienced this during the torture of a toothache or a kidney stone: the sensation of pain is rendered lighter if you can focus the mind on some other thought. "As if on purpose," Aristotle says, "the mind sees and the mind hears." At night, however, because the senses of the eyes are at rest and the thoughts of the mind are more tranquil, and since the passages of the ears are no less open at night than by day, they are no less capable of sounds; rather, they report them more easily to the mind because it is then distracted by no other business and is not called away by the sense of sight as it is in the day. Thus, the sense of hearing becomes sharper. There will be a place for this adage when we command someone to be attentive, just as we say, "Be here," and "I am here." We have spoken elsewhere about the mind "wandering abroad."

### Living on savory.

"Savory-eaters" <note>original: Θυμβροφάγοι (*Thymbrophagoi*).</note> that is, "Living on savory," they were called by this adage—either those who led a safer and freer life, or those whose manners were not very charming, or those who lived cheerfully and without worry, content with very little. This is because *Thymbra* (which they also call *cunila*) is a common herb, which Pliny does not distinguish from savory <note>original: *Satureia*</note>, though Columella seems to distinguish them. 

Columella says: "And savory, bringing the flavor of thyme and savory." <note>original: *Thymbraeque saporem*.</note>
It has a somewhat bitter taste and grows everywhere in the fields; the wild variety is more useful for medicine than the garden variety, according to Dioscorides, as it delights in stony places. The garden variety is better suited for food. Suidas and Hesychius reviewed this proverb. It is said that Epaminondas <note>A famous Theban general known for his frugality and integrity.</note> lived an amazingly frugal life and said of a meager and thin lunch: "Such a lunch does not admit betrayal." <note>original: τὸ δεῖπνον ἄδειπον, οὐ χωρεῖ προδοσίαν (*to deipnon adeipnon, ou chōrei prodosian*).</note> that is, such a lunch does not receive treason. The meaning of the saying is twofold: either because no one plots treachery against those of modest means, or because those who are content with little are not easily corrupted into betraying the state. Amphis says in Athenaeus, book ten:
"Where the meal is frugal, there is no drunken revelry." <note>original: εὐτελὲς γὰρ δεῖπνον οὐ ποιεῖ παροινίαν (*euteles gar deipnon ou poiei paroinian*).</note> ->that is,<-
Where the supper is frugal, there is no debauchery.
The Greek <term>trimeter <note>A line of verse consisting of three measures.</note></term> appears corrupted by the inversion of two words. It should be restored as: "Let the supper be frugal." And he adds from Alexis: that from lavish banquets first arise insults, from which there is usually more pain than pleasure. Hence it becomes a curse. This is retorted...

is turned against the speaker, soon moving from words to blows. Not so for those who live on savory <note>original: "thymbra" — a herb like savory, associated with a simple, calming diet.</note>.

->14. In the manner of a Doryphorema<-

The Greeks call that retinue of guards recruited from the dregs of the barbarians a *doryphorema* <note>original: "δορυφόρημα" — literally "a body of spear-bearers."</note>, which tyrants once employed for the protection of their persons, but which are now maintained by kings more for the sake of pomp than for safety; and not only by kings, but even by the highest pontiffs. In tragedies, therefore, a *doryphorema* was added to the characters of kings in such a way that they merely stood by and said nothing. Hence, those who sit by in silence are said to be present "in the manner of a Doryphorema" <note>original: "δορυφορήματος τρόπον".</note>. Thus Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae* or "Banquet of the Learned."</note> in book five, when Pisistratus <note>A tyrant of ancient Athens.</note> introduced a certain topic of conversation: "For it is not right for this man to be present in the manner of a Doryphorema," that is, silent and contributing nothing to the group. It is used by Lucian <note>A Hellenistic satirist and rhetorician.</note> in his small book *On Writing History*, in these very words: "I am considering, O Philo, lest I be the only mute phantom in such a vocal time, nor walk about gaping in silence like a comic Doryphorema."

->15. Love teaches music<-

Plutarch cites this proverb as well, expressed in a trochaic verse:
*Love teaches music, even if one was unmusical before.* <note>original: "Μουσικὴν ἔρως διδάσκει, κἂν τις ἄμουσος ᾖ τὸ πρίν."</note>
The meaning is that love rouses the mind to industry, and is the best teacher of the arts and of all elegance. Socrates, in Plato's *Symposium*, thinks that the soul, immersed in the body, is awakened as if by the stings of love, and from this takes its first impulses toward honorable things, as if shaking off a lethargy. Hence Plato calls this god "the leader of every song" <note>original: "παντὸς ὠδηγέτην" — or "leader of all music."</note> because there is nothing he does not attempt. Indeed, he makes the silent man talkative, the modest and dull man courteous and charming, and the negligent man diligent. There exists a not-inelegant tale by Boccaccio <note>The Italian author Giovanni Boccaccio; the story is from the *Decameron*, Day 5, Tale 1.</note>, if I am not mistaken, concerning Cymon, who, being touched by love for a girl, polished himself in every kind of literature and manners so that he might not be despised as a rustic. For "Music" here refers to "letters" (liberal arts), which antiquity dedicated to the nine Muses. Bion <note>A Greek bucolic poet.</note> alludes to the proverb in his *Bucolics*, where, after teaching many verses that the Muses are always the companions of love, he adds:
*I am witness that this saying is true for all.* <note>original: "μάρτυς ἐγὼν, ὅτι μῦθον ὅδ' ἔπλετο πᾶσιν ἀληθής."</note>
The proverb can also be twisted to a more modest use, if you say that it is no small step toward learning to have loved the teacher. It can also be used piously, if you say that charity (love) is the mistress of all virtues, which, if it be absent, you shall have done nothing rightly.

->16. Gnawing a Sicyon, wife, weave the cloak<-

Athenaeus in the third book of the *Deipnosophistae* cites this heroic verse as a proverb:
*Gnawing a Sicyon, wife, weave the cloak.* <note>original: "Τὸν σικυὸν τρώγουσα γύναι, τὴν χλαῖναν ὕφαινε."</note>
These appear to be the words of a husband commanding his wife to finish her work while being content with meager food. For a *Sicyon* (or *Sicyos*) is a type of bulb, or perhaps a melon; some think it is a cucumber. This saying almost fits the princes of our time, who strenuously squander what the starving people have produced with the greatest labor. And they think it is their right to enjoy the sweat of others like certain drones. Hermolaus Barbarus <note>An Italian Renaissance scholar.</note>, in his *Corollaries to Dioscorides*, chapter 366, seems to guess something else, writing from Aristotle's opinion that many weaver-women are unchaste; whether the *Sicyos* tempers lust, I do not know.

->17. He touched a stone bitten by a dog<-

Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*.</note> in book 29, chapter 5, dealing with the poison of a rabid dog, says: "So great is the power of the evil that even the urine of a rabid dog, if stepped upon, may do harm, especially to those having an ulcer. The remedy is horse dung, sprinkled with vinegar, warmed in wine and applied." He who considers that "a stone bitten by a dog" has passed into a proverb for discord might wonder at this less. Thus far Pliny. From his words, one may conjecture that it was commonly believed that if anyone touched or stepped on a stone bitten by a dog, he would become more irascible and prone to quarrels. Perhaps they used to say this against a person who was abusive and quarrelsome: "He stepped on a stone bitten by a dog."

->18. Erected<-

Athenaeus in the 5th book of the *Deipnosophistae*: "And the marvel was, that having gone out they were aroused..." <note>original: "Καὶ τὸ θαυμάσιον, ὅτι ἐξελθόντες καρχαροῦντο". The entry breaks off here.</note>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s Fourth Chiliad, Fifth Century. The previous page discussed the concept of a "Doryphorema" (a silent attendant). This page begins mid-explanation of a proverb regarding sudden alertness or focus.</meta>

<page-num>938</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...and because of the intoxication, whenever we caught sight of those things being brought in, we were all roused, and would remain upright, as the saying goes <note>original Greek: "ὑπὸ δὲ μέθης... ὀρθοὶ δὲ διὰ λεγομένων μένοι." This passage refers to guests at a banquet who, despite being heavy with wine, snap to attention when new entertainment or dishes are presented.</note>. That is: And what is marvelous to say, though we were weighed down and our heads were heavy with drunkenness, when we had looked upon any of the things being brought in, we all woke up, rising upright, as the saying goes. This will be suitable when we want to indicate that someone is focused with their "whole heart" on a certain matter. For those who listen or watch eagerly stand up straight and sometimes even stand on the tips of their toes.

->Oxen from the oven.<-

This proverb smacks of what Aristophanes wrote in the *Acharnians*:
"Then he brought out and served us whole <margin>Oxen from the oven.</margin> oxen from the oven" <note>original: "Ἐκ κριβάνου βοῦς". A humorous exaggeration of a lavish feast.</note>.
It should be used whenever we are describing the splendor of a banquet or remarkable gluttony. Otherwise, they called a sacrifice of a hundred oxen a "hecatomb," a term which follows a little later in the same poet: "and a hecatomb of polyps" <note>original: "καὶ πολυπόδων ἑκατόμβω". A "hecatomb" usually refers to cattle, so applying it to polyps (octopuses) is a comedic touch by Aristophanes.</note>.

->The perch follows the cuttlefish.<-

Athenaeus, in book seven, records a proverb of this kind without naming an author: "the perch follows the black-tail" <note>original: "ἕπεται πέρκη μελανούρῳ".</note>. The cuttlefish takes the perch as its companion. In book ten, he cites this from Aristophanes, but does not add the sense in which it is usually employed, except that I conjecture it was said regarding the fellowship of wicked men. In the same author, a little further down, these verses of Numenius are cited, who wrote about fish:
"the wrasse and the red scorpion-fish among the rocks, or the black-tail that leads the perches."

->Strike, boy!<-

Athenaeus, in the fifteenth book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>The "Banquet of the Learned," a massive collection of ancient lore and conversation.</note>, demonstrates that in ancient times it was customary to shout a proverb at a banquet to signify that someone had fulfilled their duty. It is almost the same as when we are accustomed to say to someone who has achieved perfect virtue: "Blessings on your courage, blessings on your merit" <note>original Latin: "Macte animo, macte uirtute."</note>. For when someone had departed from a banquet properly drunk and greatly sleepy, the boy <note>A servant or slave at the banquet.</note> would shout at him: "Io Paean!" <note>original: "ἰὴ παιάν". A ritual cry of triumph or a prayer for help.</note>. Mention of this adage is made by Clearchus in his first book, which he records as being born from an event of this kind: When Latona <note>The mother of Apollo and Diana (Artemis).</note> was carrying Apollo and Diana from the island of Delos, and had already come to the cave of the Python, and the dragon rushed at them, Latona—carrying the girl in her arms and imploring the protection of Apollo—cried out: "Shoot, boy!" <note>original: "ἵε παῖ".</note>. Since he, by chance, held a bow, she meant "Strike, boy!" or as you might say, "Let fly and hit him, son!" Some, with the sounds slightly altered, cry "Io Paean," and this is usually said as a prayer whenever we implore help in afflicted circumstances. Again, others think it is shouted in this way for those who have happily performed their duty and obtained what they sought. However, because of its common use, it does not seem like a proverb, as they used these words solemnly in the sacred rites of Apollo: "Io Paean, Io Paean, Io Paean."

From this, they think the iambic trimeter meter arose, because it has a certain momentum and speed. For if you lengthen the first syllable in "ie," the poem will be a heroic hexameter: "Shoot, boy, shoot, boy" <note>original: "ἵε παῖ, ἵε παῖ".</note>. If you shorten it, it is Iambic. Furthermore, regarding the fact that in Athenaeus the words "ie" and "hie" are sometimes aspirated and sometimes smooth, I do not know if this happened through the negligence of the scribes. Ovid, in the *Art of Love*, seems to use this exclamation to congratulate a victor who has achieved their wish:
"Cry 'Io Paean,' and twice cry 'Io Paean,'
The sought-after prey has fallen into my nets."

->He beautifully deceives the fox.<-

"He beautifully decoys the fox" <note>original: "παλεύει καλῶς τὴν ἀλώπεκα".</note>. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia.</note> merely lists this but does not explain it. It appears to be said of one who captures a cunning person with tricks, or for whom snares would be set in vain. For the word used here <note>original: "παλεύειν" (paleuein).</note> means to entice by artifice. From this, blinded pigeons, which fowlers place in a net so that by hopping about they might entice other deceived birds, are called "decoys" <note>original: "παλεύτριαι" (paleutriae).</note>. And the nets which they stretch out are called "paleuta." But to circumvent a fox with a trick is difficult.

->It smells either of fish, or of the flower.<-

It smells either of fish, or of the *thymallus* <note>The grayling fish.</note>. Ambrose, in the fifth book of the *Hexaemeron* <note>A commentary on the six days of creation by St. Ambrose.</note>, chapter two, testifies that this was said of one who smelled good, because the *thymallus* fish has a most pleasant odor, as fragrant as the flower of its name <note>The fish was thought to smell like thyme.</note>. But it is better to provide Ambrose’s own words: "Nor shall I leave you unhonored in this pursuit, O thymallus, you who took your name from a flower; whether the waters of the Ticino flow over you, or the waters of the pleasant Atelis nourished you, you are a flower. Finally, the speech is more well-attested, because regarding him who [is] pleasant..."

<page-num>939</page-num>
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Kkk 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: to be</meta>

...brings sweetness, it may be said wittily that it smells either of fish or of a flower: thus it was pronounced that the scent of the fish is the same as that of the flower. What is more pleasing than your appearance? What is more delightful than your sweetness? What is more fragrant than your scent? Whatever fragrance honey possesses, you breathe forth from your very body. However, I am not sure whether in the works of Ambrose one should read <term>tithymallus</term> <note>original: "tithymallus"; a type of spurge or milkweed</note> instead of <term>p timalo</term>, of which Pliny recounts various kinds in Book 26, Chapter 8, and which Dioscorides mentions repeatedly in different places.

->**To inspect the teeth of a gifted horse. XXIIII**<-

There are certain sayings bandied about by the common people even today that are not unworthy of being numbered among the ancient adages, such as this one: **One ought not to inspect the teeth of a gifted horse.** This is used when we mean that we should accept something with good will, whatever its quality may be, when it is not purchased but given for free. Indeed, a person about to buy a horse inspects its teeth—where the most certain signs of age are found—lest he be cheated. But it would be uncivil to do the same with a horse received as a gift. Saint Jerome used this proverb in his preface to the *Commentaries* he wrote on Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians. "I am not very eloquent," he says. "What is that to you? Read someone more silver-tongued. I do not translate Greek into Latin worthily? Either read the Greeks themselves, if you have knowledge of that language; or if you are only a Latin speaker, do not sit in judgment of a free gift, and, as the common proverb goes, do not inspect the teeth of a gifted horse." Thus far Jerome. But we ourselves have recently experienced and wondered at this very incivility of men which Jerome accuses. We gave them the New Testament; we either emended or explained innumerable passages, and that with labors that cannot be measured. It is incredible to say how certain theologians and the common mob of monks—to whom this labor of mine brought the greatest assistance—bellowed and protested. The more each one lacked my industry, the more hatefully he protested. They are an ungrateful race of men; if someone provides them with a slightly more lavish lunch, from which they depart stuffed and tipsy, they practically worship the man; yet when someone gives them such great utility for free, costing so much sweat, they even pursue him with insults.

->**Grace in brevity. XXV**<-

<note>original Greek: "χάρισ βαιοῖσιν ἐπηδεῖ"</note> Grace attends small things. This is a half-line of heroic verse, clearly proverbial in nature. For even today the same idea is so common that nothing is more trite. Some things please by their bulk and magnitude. There are others that are pleasing for the very reason that they are minute, such as certain gems and carvings. The same thing happens in letters and books, which are not infrequently rendered more commendable by their very brevity, especially among the fastidious and the busy. Even dwarves are held as delights for no other reason than the remarkable smallness of their bodies.

->**Friendships ought to be immortal. XXVI**<-

Titus Livius, in Book 10 of *The Macedonian and Asiatic War*—a fragment of which we owe to the golden city of Mainz—writes in this manner: "That common saying, because it was true, passed into a proverb: **Friendships ought to be immortal, but enmities mortal.**" For the very tenor of the speech suggests that it must be read this way. The proverb gives right counsel indeed, but the morals of mortals have sunk to the point that grudges are immortal, while friendships are more fragile than glass. A single <term>Ate</term> <note>The personification of mischief, delusion, and blind folly that leads to strife.</note> can do more than a hundred <term>Litae</term> <note>The daughters of Zeus who personify prayers of repentance and follow Ate to heal the wounds of her strife.</note>, and anger grows old the slowest of all things, while benevolence dies at any slight occasion. Even if a friendship is patched up, it never truly heals and is torn open again. I think the cause is that we have learned from those philosophers to serve our own private interests while neglecting the public good. In support of this sentiment, Aristotle in the second book of his *Rhetoric* cites a verse which, if I am not mistaken, we have related elsewhere:
> <note>original Greek: "οὐδεὶσ ἐραστὴσ ἤστισ οὐκ ἀεὶ φιλεῖ"</note> that is,
> **He is no friend who has ceased to love.**
> He cites another verse in the same place:
> <note>original Greek: "ἀθάνατον ὀργὴν μὴ φύλασσε θνητὸσ ὤν"</note> that is,
> **Let not immortal anger remain within you, since you yourself are mortal.**

->**To good fruit. XXVII**<-

Those who return to their senses, having changed their habits for better pursuits, were said by a proverb **to betake themselves to better fruit.** <note>original: "ad bonam frugem"; a metaphor for returning to a productive, virtuous life.</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero uses this in his speech *For Marcus Caelius*: "And he has betaken himself, as he says, to good fruit, and has become a man of weight and distinction." Likewise Plautus in the *Trinummus*: "It is certain that I shall apply my mind to fruit." Lampridius in his life of *Heliogabalus* says: "The soldiers said they would spare him if he would return to good fruit." From this, they use the terms <term>Frugi</term> and <term>Bonę frugi</term> <note>Literally "of fruit," meaning honest, temperate, or useful.</note> for those who perform their duty, especially regarding the servants we maintain for labor. Ulpian, regarding the Aquilian Law, chapter "Next, Neratius": "But if a servant of 'good fruit' <note>Meaning a virtuous or useful slave.</note> should be killed within a year after having changed his ways..." Likewise the title "Regarding what matters should go before the same judge," Chapter "If anyone a servant": Inter-

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on various Latin and Greek adages, specifically concluding a discussion on the term "frugi" (thrifty or worthy) and moving into expressions concerning the passing of objects or traditions by hand, as well as metaphors for over-praising the trivial or grasping the difficult.</meta>

<page-num>940</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<sig>xx</sig>

...to be a usufructuary <note>One who has the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property</note> seems to be the mark of a "good fruit" <note>original: "bonæ frugi"; meaning a thrifty or honest person</note> servant. Again, in the *Digest* <note>A compendium of Roman law</note>, Book 11, under the title "On Corrupted Servants," in the paragraph beginning "What the Praetor says": "But whether it holds only if he urged a 'good fruit' servant to commit a crime." Plautus writes in his play *Casina*: "By Pollux, I believe it is so, if you are of 'good fruit' <note>thrifty/honest</note>." Again in *Pseudolus*: "You desire me to be worthless, yet I shall be of 'good fruit'." For "worthless" <note>original: "nequam"</note> is of no use to anyone. And so we call a person "thrifty" <note>original: "frugi"</note> just as we call them "worthless" <note>original: "nequam"</note>, with both words being indeclinable. Columella writes in *On Agriculture*, Book 1: "A man of the same agility will act more thriftily than one who is worthless." And in the *Declamations*, a "thrifty" son is contrasted with a "luxurious" <note>extravagant</note> one, and is called "frugal." The term seems to be taken from the fields, which are rendered "fruit-bearing" <note>original: "frugiferi"</note> through cultivation.

->**To hand down from hand to hand.**<-

What comes from some people to others through a kind of succession is said to be "passed through the hands" <note>original: "per manus tradere"</note>. This seems to be a metaphor taken from those who unload a ship or a wagon. The same thing frequently happens in war, as in the first book of the *Commentary on the Civil War*: "Steep rocks," it says, "blocked the way in many places, so that weapons were necessarily passed from hand to hand, and the soldiers, being unarmed, were lifted up by others to complete a great part of the journey." Again, in the seventh book of the *Gallic War*: "A certain Gaul, in front of the town gate, was passing lumps of tallow and pitch by hand <note>original: "per manus... traditas"</note> into the fire opposite the tower." In the same book: "Some women were lowered from the walls by hand." Likewise in the eighth book: "They entered upon such a plan for retreat: where the ranks had settled, they placed before the battle line bundles of straw and brushwood—of which there was a great supply in the camp—passed among themselves from hand to hand <note>original: "per manus... traditos"</note>." But in these cases, there is no metaphor. Whenever a metaphor is added, it passes into the form of a proverb, as is frequently encountered among authors. For instance, in Fabius <note>Quintilian</note>, Book 12: "One should know not only those things which are recorded in histories, or passed down as if by hand in conversations and daily affairs, but one should not even neglect those things which are invented by poets." Likewise, Livy in *From the Founding of the City*, Book 5: "Even if no religious rites had been established for us at the same time as the city and passed down by hand." Also in Book 9: "Then military discipline, passed down by hand since the very beginnings of the city, had come into the form of a system organized by perpetual precepts." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] in his speech *On the Consular Provinces*: "For that Gaius Julius, though honored by the Senate with all extraordinary and new things, should hand over this province to one whom you least desire." Indeed, even among the legal experts, "to be passed by hand" is said of that which is given from hand to hand. For instance, Papinian in the *Pandects* <note>another name for the Digest of Roman law</note>, Book 20, under the title "On the Law of Codicils": "That which has been passed by hand cannot be given as an inheritance by codicils," and it follows that reasoning and so forth. Plautus in *Trinummus*: "He himself gave it from his hands into my hands." He is speaking of a letter. However, it becomes more pleasing whenever it is applied to matters of the mind or youth, as when we say that an institution, or an opinion, or a custom, or some discipline has come down to us, "passed down by hand."

->**From hand into hand.**<-

While I do not think this is the same as the previous one, it is not entirely dissimilar; Cicero uses it in the *Letters to Friends*, Book 7: "In short, I hand the whole man over to you from my hand, as they say, into that hand of yours, which excels in both victory and loyalty." For even those who are being recommended are "handed over." Terence says: "He gives this into the hand." Likewise Horace:

> So that I might attempt to praise and hand him over to you.
> If you were willing to hand this man over.

->**Wonders about a lentil.**<-

Rodolphus Agricola <note>A preeminent Dutch humanist (1444–1485) whom Erasmus greatly admired</note>, a man worthy of immortality, testifies in Book 3 of his *Dialectics* that among the Greeks there is a proverb: **Excellent things about a lentil**, used whenever a humble and tiny matter is extolled with magnificent words—just as if you were to adorn a lentil, a small and cheap legume, with splendid encomiums. I believe it is expressed in Greek in this manner: <term>Φακῆν μύρῳ μύρειν</term> <note>original: "Phakēn myrō myrein"; literally "to perfume a lentil with myrrh"</note>.

->**Not to be caught with one hand.**<-

<term>Οὐ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ληπτέον</term> <note>original: "Ou tē hetera lēpteon"</note>, that is, "It is not to be caught with only one hand." This refers to a slippery, shifting, and very difficult matter. For in such cases, we are accustomed to apply both hands. Plato used it in the *Statesman* <note>Erasmus likely refers to the "Sophist"</note> thus: <term>ὁρᾷς δὴ ὡς ἀληθῶς λέγεται τὸ ποικίλον εἶναι ζῶον τὸ θηρίον, καὶ τὸ λεγόμενον, ὅτι τῇ ἑτέρᾳ ληπτέον οὐκ ἔστι</term> <note>original: "horās dē hōs alēthōs legetai to poikilon einai zōon to thērion, kai to legomenon, hoti tē hetera lēpteon ouk esti"</note>. "You see, therefore, it is truly said that this beast is a varied thing, and (as the saying goes) is not to be caught with one hand." It is taken from hunting, in which certain wild beasts frequently slip out of the very hands of the hunters by marvelous tricks; Plato thinks the "Sophist" <note>A type of teacher in ancient Greece often accused of deceptive reasoning</note> is similar to these, being equipped with all manner of deceits. It can also be applied to a rich priesthood, which no one easily attains unless he strives with his greatest might.

<page-num>941</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY FIVE</header>
<sig>Kkk 3</sig>

->**To escape all snares.**<-
->XXXII<-

In the same dialogue <note>referring to Plato's *Sophist*, which follows from the previous page's discussion</note>, Plato introduces an allegory not unlike this one, which is tossed about like a proverb: **To escape all snares.** This is itself a metaphor transferred from hunting, in which the exits are hedged in on all sides so that the wild beast must necessarily fall into some trap. <term>ὀρθὴ γὰρ ἡ παροιμία, τὸ τὰς ἁπάσας μὴ ῥᾴδιον εἶναι διαφυγεῖν</term> <note>original Greek: "orthē gar hē paroimia, to tas hapasas mē rhadion einai diaphygein"</note>, which is to say: "For the proverb holds true, which says it is by no means easy to escape every snare."

->**A domestic enemy.**<-
->XXXIII<-

Again, in the same work, he testifies that it is common to speak proverbially of a **domestic enemy** <note>original: "hostis domesticus"</note> when an evil does not come from elsewhere but is born from within ourselves. For instance, when someone betrays or refutes themselves, or consumes themselves with their own bile or envy. <term>ἐκ ἄλλων δέονται τῶν ἐλεγχόντων, ἀλλὰ τὸ λεγόμενον, οἴκοθεν τὸν πολέμιον καὶ ἐναντιωσόμενον ἔχοντες</term> <note>original Greek: "ek allōn deontai tōn elenchontōn, alla to legomenon, oikothen ton polemion kai enantiōsomenon echontes"</note>, which is to say: "They have no need of others to refute them, but according to the proverb, they have the enemy and the opponent at home." He is speaking, I believe, of the sophist who, because he is so talkative, usually provides from his own mouth the very means by which he is proven wrong.

->**To capture a city.**<-
->XXXIIII<-

Plato, in the same dialogue, indicates that it is a common proverb to say **to take or capture a city** when someone has achieved a difficult task. For a city is not captured at the very first assault. In that passage, the stranger encourages Theaetetus to pursue what he has begun, because anyone who either gets stuck or stops at minor difficulties will never accomplish anything in the main point of the dispute. Plato's words are as follows: <term>θαρρεῖν ὦ θεαίτητε χρὴ τὸν καὶ σμικρόν τι δυνάμενον εἰς τὸ πρόσθεν ἀεὶ προϊέναι. τί γὰρ ἂν ὁ τοιοῦτος δράσειεν ἂν ἐν ἄλλοις, ἢ μηδὲν ἐν ἐκείνοις ἀνύτων, ἢ πάλιν ἐπ' ἐλπίδων ἀπωθεὶς, χαλεπὸν τὸ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν, ὅγε τοιοῦτος ἄν ποτε ἕλοι πόλιν</term> <note>original Greek: "tharrein ō Theaitēte chrē..."</note>, which is to say: "One must take heart, Theaetetus, that he who is able to do even a little something will always move further forward. For what would such a person do in other matters if he lost heart in these? Either achieving nothing in them or being forced to retreat—such a man would never, as the saying goes, 'capture a city'." In war, it is easy to achieve something in skirmishes or the burning of villages, but to capture fortified cities is extremely difficult. It is similar to that other saying: "The timid never erected a trophy."

->**I except divine discourse.**<-
->XXXV<-

Plato, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, demonstrates that it was a common popular proverb: <term>θείου ἐξαίρω λόγον</term> <note>original Greek: "theiou exairō logon"</note>. That is, **I except divine discourse.** This was used, I believe, whenever something particularly glorious was said; for the sake of a good omen, they would except the gods, who can do anything and to whom no one dictates. I will include Plato's words below: <term>οὔ τε γὰρ γίνετ' οὔτε γέγονεν, οὐδ' οὖν μὴ γένηται ἀλλοῖον ἦθος πρὸς ἀρετὴν, παρὰ τὴν τούτων παιδείαν πεπαιδευμένον ἀνθρώπειον, ὦ ἑταῖρε. θεῖον μὲν γὰρ κατὰ τὴν παροιμίαν ἐξαίρω λόγον</term> <note>original Greek: "oute gar ginet' oute gegonen..."</note>, which is to say: "For there is not, nor has there been, nor will there be a human character trained toward virtue differently than through this education, my friend. I speak of human things, for I except the 'divine discourse,' according to the proverb." It appears to be a fragment of an iambic poem:
> **I except the divine discourse,**
> perhaps originating from Homer:
> **But the gods can do all things.** <note>original Greek: "Theoi de te panta dynantai"</note>

This can be applied to the highest princes, such as the pope, or cardinals, or monks <note>Erasmus likely intends this ironically, suggesting these figures are often treated as if they are above human rules</note>.

->**With one pole.**<-
->XXXVI<-

**With one pole** <note>original: "Una pertica"</note> is used to mean "by the same effort" or "in the same way." Pliny the Younger says in Book 8, Letter 2: "For in the whole region, both the novelty of the remission and its form are praised, even by those whom I treated not with 'one pole,' as they say, but distinctly and step by step. The better and more honest a man is, the more he leaves feeling obliged to me, having experienced that with me it is not—**the bad man and the brave are held in the same honor.**" <note>original Greek: "en de iē timē hēmen kakos ēde kai esthlos"</note> It seems to be taken from those who measure fields. He used "pole" <note>pertica</note> for a ten-foot measuring rod <note>original: "decempeda"</note>. For Servius Sulpicius, as Festus Pompeius indicates, said the *pertica* was the line by which fields are divided. The verse is from Homer, *Iliad* Book 9, which we have reviewed and explained elsewhere.

->**In good repair.**<-
->XXXVII<-

**In good repair** <note>original: "Sarta tecta," literally "patched and roofed"</note> is used for things that are finished, properly cared for, and in which nothing has been omitted. It passed into a proverb from the formal language of legal scholars. Plautus writes in *The Three-Dollar Day*: "Lest I should cause you distress, father, I have been diligently sparing. I have kept your instructions 'in good repair' <note>sarta tecta</note> through my modesty." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Letters to Friends*, Book 13: "Grant me this, and bestow it: that you keep Marcus Curius 'in good repair' <note>sartum et tectum</note>, as they say, from every inconvenience, loss, and trouble—undamaged and whole." The same author, in the third speech *Against Verres*: "But regarding how he conducted himself in the matter of 'buildings in good repair,' what need I say?"

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal and architectural metaphors, specifically the phrase "farta tecta" (sound and repaired), before transitioning into a new series of adages concerning laziness, military engagement, and moral character.</meta>

<page-num>942</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

The same author <note>referring to Cicero</note> in a speech to the people before he went into exile said: "If therefore you have at any time looked to these things, whose spirit has performed the duty of religious piety, you ought also to provide for me, who has been consecrated to the power of the gods, **kept sound and repaired** <note>original: "fartum tectum"</note> and preserved from every danger." The same author in the same action against Verres: "Therefore, listen to me regarding the crimes of the praetorship in this way: that you may demand from me both kinds of things—the administration of justice and the requirement of **buildings kept sound and repaired** <note>original: "sartorum tectorum"</note>—which are worthy of me and of such a defendant." And in the same work: "He asked who ought to keep the temple of Castor **sound and repaired**." And in many other places, such as in the fifth action against Verres. 

Ulpian, in the first book of the *Pandects*, under the title *On the Office of the Proconsul and Legate*, in the chapter "If in any," says: "It is the duty of the proconsul to go around the sacred buildings and public works for the sake of inspection, to see whether they are **sound and repaired** <note>original: "sarta tectaque"</note>, or whether they require any repair." Likewise, Celsus in the seventh book of the *Pandects*, under the title *On Usufruct*, in the chapter "Thus far," speaking of repairing buildings: "Thus far, however," he says, "that he should keep them **sound and repaired**; if any parts, however, should fall down through old age, neither party is compelled to rebuild them." And shortly after: "Whence Celsus, concerning the manner of keeping things **sound and repaired**..." and so on. Again, in book 48, under the title *On the Julian Law Concerning Extortion*, in the chapter "The Julian Law": "This also must be guarded against, that a public work to be done, or grain to be given publicly, be entered as received, or that **sound and repaired** things be maintained, before they have been approved, completed, and delivered." 

Festus Pompeius teaches that the ancients used the word *farte* to mean "entirely," which is why those works that are contracted so that they are guaranteed to be "entirely covered" are called *sarta tecta*. For *sarcire* <note>to patch or repair</note> means to make whole. But Festus seems to have read *sarte tecta* as "entirely covered," unless perhaps the reading in earlier texts should be *sarta et integra* <note>repaired and whole</note>.

---

<margin>XXXV</margin>
### The lung would have arrived sooner.

**The lung would have arrived sooner** <note>original: "Pulmo prius uenisset"</note> was a saying used long ago against the sluggish and the loitering. I believe it is because the lung is in perpetual motion, yet it never moves itself from its place. Plautus in *Epidicus*: "Immortal gods! I ordered those feet to be taken away. For the lung, as they say, would have arrived before you did."

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
### To bring the foot together.

**To bring the foot together** <note>original: "Pedem conferre"</note> is a metaphor taken from military service. It is used when one approaches closer to the matter at hand. In the speech *For Plancius*: "I cannot **bring the foot together** any more, as they say, or go any closer." We have mentioned this in passing elsewhere from Quintilian. It seems to be taken from Homer, with whom the phrase "coming near" <note>original Greek: "ἐγγὺς ἰόντες"</note> is frequent, that is, engaging in close combat. 

Vegetius expressed this with a less pleasant figure of speech in *On Military Matters*, book 3, chapter 14: "The first and second lines, when it comes to the **long-swords** <note>original: "spathas"</note> and **javelins** <note>original: "pila"</note>, as the saying goes, sustain the whole weight." Now, they used to call longer swords *spathae*, just as *pila* were short spears of five and a half feet, which were later called *spicula*. The author Modestinus describes this kind of fighting, as does Quintus Curtius in book 3: "Therefore, forced to engage in close combat, they vigorously drew their blades; then indeed much blood was shed, for the two lines were so joined that armor clashed against armor and they directed their points at faces. It was not permitted to the timid or the idle; with **feet brought together** <note>original: "collato pede"</note>, as if they were fighting individually, they stood on the same spot until they could make a place for themselves to advance." And Virgil says: "Foot clings to foot, and man is crowded by man."

### One who has done much harm.

Just as it belongs to the same craftsman to measure excellently and to speak the truth, so it belongs to the same person to be of great use and to do harm. Thucydides testifies in book 6, in the speech of Alcibiades, that this was once tossed about as a proverb: "Just as I might be helped by the words of all, so as an enemy I would have done great harm to those whom I was once able to help." <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ δ᾽ ἂν ὑπὸ πάντων ὠφελοίμην λόγου, ὡς ἐν πολεμίῳ γε ἂν σφόδρα ἔβλαψα ἂν ὧν ἱκανῶς ὠφελήμην</note>. That is to say: That well-known saying used by everyone, that since I was a powerful enemy, I will be able to be a great help even if I am a friend.

### He does not lean on a common anchor.

Demosthenes in the speech *On the Crown*: "He does not ride at the same anchor as the common people" <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐπὶ τῇ αὐτῇ ὁρμεῖ τοῖς πολλοῖς</note>. That is: He relies on the same anchor as the crowd, signifying that he strives with new and by no means common supports. Suidas advises that this is a proverb, and the word "anchor" is to be understood.

### No more than monkeys.

The monkey is a ridiculous animal and commonly held in contempt; it has provided the occasion for more than one proverb. Dio Chrysostom <note>Erasmus likely refers to Dio, though the OCR text "In fenfis" is corrupted</note> in his book *On Troy Not Being Captured* says: "Whom I value no more than monkeys, as the saying goes."

### An asp from a viper.

Tertullian, in his third book *Against Marcion*, records this under the title of a proverb: **An asp from a viper** <note>original: "Aspis a uipera"</note>, meaning a very bad thing takes some evil from another very bad thing. "Let the heretic now cease," he says, "from borrowing poison from the light, as they say, from a viper." It is also recorded among the sayings of Diogenes.

<summary>This page covers various classical adages, beginning with the legal/architectural term for "good repair" (farta tecta) and moving into metaphors for sluggishness (the lung), close combat (foot to foot), and the moral quality of those who swap "poison" or assistance.</summary>

<keywords>farta tecta, Pulmo prius uenisset, Pedem conferre, close combat, Thucydides, Demosthenes, monkeys, Tertullian, asps, legal metaphors, military metaphors</keywords>

<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Kkk 4</sig>

who, upon seeing two women whispering together in secret, quoted a verse taken from some comedy:
*The asp borrows its poison from the viper.* <note>original Greek: "ἀσπὶς παρ’ ἐχίδνης φάρμακον δανείζεται"</note> That is to say, 
the venom of both serpents is incurable and equally harmful, except that the bite of the viper kills with great agony, while the asp brings so little pain that there is even a sense of pleasure involved, if we believe Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman naturalist and author of the *Natural History*</note>. There is also a type of asp which, without biting, kills a person by spitting venom; for this reason, the Greeks call it the *ptyas* <note>from the Greek word for "spitter"</note>. This proverb will be useful whenever someone who is already bad by nature becomes even worse through contact with another evil person.

-> Neither inside, nor outside. XLIIII <-

Irenaeus <note>An early Christian bishop and theologian (c. 130–202 AD)</note> records this proverb in the first book of his work, chapter 9, saying that it applies to certain foolish women. These women, although they realized they had been deceived by the disciples of Valentinus <note>a prominent Gnostic teacher in the early Church</note>, nevertheless did not commit themselves to the Church to recover their place in the community through the remedy of penance. Instead, living between the two, they neither adhered to the Valentinians nor reconciled themselves to the Church. Today, we use a similar figure of speech: **Neither fish nor flesh**, <note>original: "Neq; caro est, neq; piscis"</note> describing a man who lives only for himself and takes no side in a conflict.

-> From the toga to the cloak. XLV <-

This certainly has the appearance of a proverb, which Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD)</note> mentions in his short book *On the Cloak*: "This will surely be an indignity: to go from the toga to the cloak." <note>original: "à toga ad palliū"</note> This has a double use: either when someone has moved to a completely different way of life, or when one moves from a more honorable fortune to a humbler one—for instance, if a courtier becomes a monk, or a prefect becomes a schoolteacher, or a consul becomes a public speaker. The **toga** was the garment of the Romans, while the **cloak** <note>original: "pallium"</note> was the garment of the Greeks. Later, the cloak became the standard attire of philosophers. A related saying is: **From horses to donkeys**.

-> The final line. XLVI <-

Since in ancient times the starting point from which a race began was marked with a drawn line, and the finish was likewise marked with a line, those who repeated a matter from the beginning were said "to start from the line" or "to return to the line." Consequently, they called whatever was the very last thing in any matter the **final line**. Thus, the character Phædria in Terence <note>A Roman playwright</note> says: "In the end, to love at the **final line** is something." And Tertullian, in the book he wrote against Hermogenes, calls him the "**final line** of the ignorant," because he was the last of the heretics—at least, he was still alive when Tertullian was writing those words.

-> The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple. XLVII <-

The second book of Kings, chapter 5, <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 5</note> relates that when David had accepted the kingship of the entire Israelite nation by the consensus of all the tribes, and had decided to establish his royal seat on Mount Sion (which was then the citadel of Jerusalem held by the Jebusites), the Jebusites warned him that he would not enter the city unless he first removed the blind and the lame. Once this was done, it turned into a proverb: **The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple**. There is not much agreement among interpreters as to what "the blind and the lame" means in this passage. Some think it was said in contempt: "You shall not enter here unless you can overcome our wall-defenders, for even our blind and lame are sufficient to protect them." The Hebrews are prone to inventing stories to explain difficult questions. They say that two statues were placed on the city walls, Isaac and Jacob: the former is described as having gone blind in his old age, and the latter as having been lame from his wrestling match with the angel. They say these were placed there as a monument to the covenant they had once struck with Abraham, a matter mentioned in Genesis chapter 21. Thus, when these were removed, the citadel was captured, and the proverb was born, though I do not entirely perceive its sense. For the fact that in Leviticus the blind and the lame are barred from the sacred ministries of the temple does not seem to me to relate to this history. If I may venture a guess: perhaps there were small statues on the very tops of the houses, such as are usually placed on the gables of buildings. The common people called these "the blind and the lame" because, being fixed, they could not walk, nor could they see. Access to the area was therefore not open unless one climbed over the gables of the houses. Furthermore, David promised as a reward that whoever first touched the water-pipes of the house would be the leader of the army. Perhaps there will be a place for this adage whenever someone is excluded from an honor as if they were unworthy. For those who seemed to exclude others are themselves deservedly excluded. Such statues are fixed to the outside of temple roofs, while they themselves never actually enter the temple.

-> For the diligent man. XLVIII <-

**For the diligent man, something always remains.** Chrysostom, <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an important Early Church Father</note> in his 19th homily on John, mentions this saying as a proverb worn thin by common speech: He who is truly diligent in business is never satisfied with himself, and always sees something that can be added to the work he has begun, whereas to the lazy, whatever they have done seems like too much.

Erasmus provides historical context from Church Fathers like Irenaeus and Tertullian, as well as classical authors.</summary>

<page-num>944</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

### Mandron too had a fig-wood ship.

<margin>Mandron too had a fig-wood ship. <note>original Greek: "Ἐγέγετο ἡ μάνδρωνι σικύνη ναῦς"</note></margin> This was commonly said of those who, having been elevated to happiness and wealth beyond their merit, do not remember their former condition, but instead abuse their current success. This is often the habit of the *nouveaux riches* <note>original: "τοῖς νεοπλουτοῖς," those newly wealthy</note>—that is, those who are propelled into new riches from the lowest state of fortune. It is taken from a certain Mandron who, though unworthy and undeserving, rose from being a common boatman to a high commander. The term "fig-wood" <note>original: "sicuinam" or "siculnam"</note> was used as a term of contempt. For the Greeks generally use "fig-wood" to describe anything they wish to signify as weak or contemptible.

### The wolf in the story.

Although this proverb was explained by us with no small care in the first edition published in Paris, it seems to have been omitted in subsequent editions by some accident. It is usually said whenever the person who is the subject of a conversation arrives unexpectedly. Donatus, the commentator on Terence <note>Aelius Donatus was a 4th-century grammarian and teacher of St. Jerome</note>, thinks this comes from the belief that a wolf is said to steal the voice of anyone it sees first; thus, when a person is caught in the very thought they were having, they lose both their voice and their words. There are those who try to provide a philosophical reason for this phenomenon or belief: namely, that the wolf is by nature an enemy to man, and therefore certain spirits and a power proceeding from its eyes by its native force strike the one it sees unexpectedly, numbing their strength—hence the sudden silence. Donatus thinks that the line from Theocritus <note>A Greek bucolic poet</note> belongs here: *You have seen a wolf.* <note>original: "Λύκον εἶδες"</note> Again, there is that line of Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note>: *The wolves saw Moeris first,* used when a shepherd complained that his voice had been lost with age. 

There are some who believe this comes from the nursery tales of nurses, who tell a story of a boy being teased with the terror of a wolf, and then a real wolf came from its den shortly after to the threshold of the bedroom. For there is also a fable where a mother, to quiet a crying child, frequently cried out "Wolf!", saying that unless he stopped crying, he would be taken away to be devoured. At last, the wolf came in hope of prey, but left with his jaws gaping in vain, having learned only this lesson: that one should not put faith in women. This, I think, is what Donatus meant. 

However, the passage in the published books seems to contain an error. Donatus rejects a third opinion, which suggests the proverb arose when, during a play by Naevius <note>Gnaeus Naevius, an early Roman dramatist</note> representing how Romulus and Remus were nursed by a she-wolf, a real wolf suddenly interrupted the action. This caused a sudden silence throughout the whole play because such an unexpected spectator had intervened. Terence used it this way in *The Brothers* <note>original: "Adelphis"</note>, hinting at silence to Ctesipho because Demea, the young man's father (whom he believed to be elsewhere), suddenly appeared beyond expectation. He adds to the proverb, saying, "Look, here is your wolf; he is present in the conversation, hungry for you." He is speaking of the parasite Gelasinus, who suddenly arrives while the brothers are talking about him. He adds charm to the proverb by alluding to the man's greed, just as in the line from Theocritus where the name "Scetas" is added to the phrase: *You have seen a wolf.* Marcus Tullius Cicero also uses it in his *Letters to Atticus*, Book 13: *We were speaking of Varro; the wolf in the story. For he came to me.* It usually happens that whenever the person we are talking about arrives, we fall silent; this is because if we were praising them, it feels shameful to say to their face what is rightly told of them while absent; or if we were criticizing them, we fear giving offense.

### More long-winded than the Iliad.

<margin>Speaking things more long-winded than the Iliad. <note>original Greek: "Μακρότερα τ' ἰλιάδος λαλῶν"</note></margin> Julius Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian and sophist</note> records this in Book 6 of his *On Vocabulary*, chapter 26. He joins it to what we have taught elsewhere, noting it applies to vehemently talkative men: *the bronze of Dodona* <note>a reference to a perpetually clanging cauldron</note> and *the Arabian flute*; for so it is recorded there. Aeschines used it in the same sense against Demosthenes, a passage we have cited elsewhere. Not dissimilar to this is *An Iliad of woes*. But since that phrase applies to immense evils, while the one we record here refers to immoderate talkativeness, it seemed best to separate them due to their different usage. Indeed, the work of Homer is an incredible thing, in which he explains the history of the capture of Troy in twenty-four books, whereas Virgil encompassed it in twelve books, having chosen what seemed best to pluck from both works.

### To complain to a stepmother.

Those who lament their misfortune to people who will offer no help, or who will rather rejoice in the evils of the complainers, are said to *complain to a stepmother*, because stepmothers are generally malevolent toward their stepchildren. As the pimp Ballio says in Plautus's *Pseudolus*:
> For that which you now lament—that you have no money—
> Complain of that to your stepmother.

The pimp substituted "stepmother" for himself. Pseudolus, pretending not to understand the saying, replied:
> Oh? Did you ever marry this man's father?

<page-num>949</page-num>
<header>THE FIFTH HUNDRED OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND</header>

<sig>LIII</sig>

### The soul dwells in the ears.

The ancients assigned the seat of the soul to the eyes, and most to the heart. But Herodotus, in his book *Polymnia* <note>Herodotus was a 5th-century BCE Greek historian; *Polymnia* is the seventh book of his *Histories*</note>, following what seems to be a common folk saying, teaches that the soul dwells in the ears. This is because those who hear good things are filled with pleasure, while those who hear the opposite are provoked to bitterness. I will transcribe Herodotus’s words here: <note>original Greek: "Καὶ νῦν τό γε ἐξεπίστω, ὡς ἐν τοῖσι ὠσὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἰκέει ὁ θυμός; ὃς χρηστὰ μὲν ἀκούσας, τέρψιος ἐμπίπλεα τὸ σῶμα, ὑπεναντία δὲ κλύουσι ἀνοιδέει."</note> *“And now know this for certain: the soul of men dwells in their ears. When it hears good things, it fills the body with delight; but when it hears the contrary, it swells with irritation.”*

I believe the meaning of the adage is this: the soul is most easily calmed or irritated by the things we hear. For this is the primary path to a person's spirit. A kind and flattering word often turns fierce anger into goodwill, while harsh speech provokes deadly enmities. Indeed, some people are "slaughtered" by insults just as surely as by a sword or poison. Consequently, the most pestilent kind of murderers—who reign supreme in this current age—are those who carry the "venom of asps" <note>A biblical reference to Psalm 140, describing slanderers</note> on their tongues, and who accomplish with their speech the same destruction that assassins achieve with steel.

<sig>LIIII</sig>

### Ignorance breeds confidence.

<note>original Greek: "Ἀμαθία μὲν θράσος, λογισμὸς δ' ὄκνον φέρει."</note> That is: *Ignorance indeed brings daring, but careful reasoning brings hesitation.* This is found in the second book of Thucydides’s history of the Peloponnesian War. Saint Jerome, in his *Epistle to Evagrius*, relates it thus: *“Inexperience creates confidence; education creates fear.”* Pliny also mentions it in the fourth book of his *Letters*: *“Just as ignorance brings daring and reasoning brings hesitation, so modesty weakens right-thinking minds, while audacity strengthens perverse ones.”* Lucian also uses it in his work *Nigrinus*, so there is no doubt that this sentiment was once a very common proverb. 

A thorough knowledge of things makes a person more hesitant to rush into a task. This is surely why youth is bolder than old age; and, as Quintilian <note>A famous Roman teacher of rhetoric</note> teaches, those with less skill speak more forcefully, while a wise orator who understands the risks will tremble at the start of a speech. Those who know less have less shame. Those who have not yet learned what it means "to know" claim knowledge of everything. Finally, those who have never experienced what it is to wage war are the ones who desire it most—just as today the world is miserably thrown into turmoil under the rule of young princes <note>A common criticism by Erasmus of the young, aggressive monarchs of his time, such as Henry VIII, Francis I, and Charles V</note>.

<sig>LV</sig>

### The end does not appear immediately.

Herodotus, in *Polymnia*, indicates that this was once a common proverb: *The outcome of a matter does not appear at the same time as the beginning.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὸ παλαιὸν... ἔπος ὡς εὖ εἴρηται, τὸ μὴ ἅμα ἀρχῇ τὸ τέλος καταφαίνεσθαι."</note> *“And the old saying is well put, that the end is not revealed simultaneously with the start.”* 

This applies to those with premature hopes who, having barely begun a business, immediately think they have the matter settled, even though the end often fails to match the beginning. There is a common joke about a certain Dutchman <note>original: "Batauum," referring to the inhabitants of the Netherlands, Erasmus's own people</note> who, when ordered to take a pill, asked the doctor what it would do. When the doctor replied that it would move his bowels, he swallowed it and, before the doctor had even left the room, shouted that he needed the toilet—evidently suspecting the "end" should appear at the exact same time as the "beginning." 

Another person of similar "wisdom," having been sent to France by his parents to learn the French language, stayed there for four days and then complained to his family that he did not yet speak French; he thought the soil itself had such power that anyone who stepped into France would speak French on the spot. There are also people like this who, as soon as their son has spent three days in grammar school, wonder why he does not yet know literature, complaining that both their effort and their money have been wasted. 

This can be applied to serious matters: one must devote oneself strenuously to honest pursuits so that one may eventually reap a rich harvest from great labors. We must always act rightly in this life; rewards will not be lacking in the future, even if they do not happen to fall to us in this world.

<sig>LVI</sig>

### Thinner than Philippides.

Athenaeus, in the twelfth book of the *Deipnosophists* <note>“The Banquet of the Learned,” a vast collection of Greek lore</note>, shows that the comic poet Philippides had such a thin body that people even used the verb *“to be Philippidized”* to mean "to become gaunt." He cites a proverb from Aristophontes: *“Within three days I will show him to be thinner than Philippides.”* And again from Menander:
> When hunger has bitten this pretty boy of yours,
> I will show you a corpse thinner than Philippides.

<meta>catchword: And again-</meta>

<summary>This page explores four classical adages regarding human psychology, the dangers of ignorance, the necessity of patience in learning, and a humorous hyperbole about physical thinness. Erasmus uses these to critique contemporary social issues, such as the recklessness of young rulers and the lack of persistence in students.</summary>

<keywords>Herodotus, Thucydides, Pliny, Quintilian, soul and ears, ignorance vs. knowledge, war and youth, patience in learning, Dutch humor, Philippides, thinness, proverbs</keywords>
