Erasmus here focuses on metaphors of impossibility, social status, and the weight of moral authority.</meta>

<page-num>946</page-num>
<header>ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

Again, from Alexis <note>A Greek comic poet of the 4th century BCE</note> he cites this saying, <term>Λυκτιππίδου Φιλιππίδου λεπτότερον</term> <note>original Greek: Lyktippidou Philippidou leptoteron</note>, that is, "Thinner than the cup of Philippides." This may be applied not without elegance to a meager speech or an argument of idle subtlety.

->She who was once a maid, will never be a mistress.<-

As a commonly tossed-about saying, it is referenced in the Greek Epigrams, Book 1, under the title of Palladas <note>A 4th-century Greek poet known for his cynical epigrams</note>.
<term>Μή ποτε δουλεύσασα γυνὴ δέσποινα γένοιτο</term> <margin>It is a proverb.</margin> <note>original Greek: Esti paroimian</note> that is,
"If any woman was once a maidservant, let her never rule as mistress," <margin>As the proverb has it.</margin>
This seems to be said because those who are raised from a humble fortune to great affairs tend to be more insolent and less tolerable toward others than those who are born into prosperity.

->To burn the sea.<-

We have advised that "impossible things" <term>ἀδύνατα</term> <note>original Greek: adunata</note> almost always belong to the family of proverbs. To this class belongs that which Virgil records in Book 9 of the *Aeneid*:
"To burn the seas before Turnus, / sooner than the sacred pines shall be granted." <note>A reference to the transformation of Trojan ships into sea nymphs to save them from fire</note>
Not dissimilar is what Propertius has:
"You will sooner be able to dry up the marine waves, / and drag down the high stars with a mortal hand."

->Obedience is the mother of happiness.<-

Aeschylus in *Seven Against Thebes*:
<term>Πειθαρχία γάρ ἐστι τῆς εὐπραξίας / Μήτηρ, γυνὴ σωτῆρος, ὧδ’ ἔχει λόγος.</term> <note>original Greek: Peitharchia gar esti tēs eupraxias / Mētēr, gunē sōtēros, hōd’ echei logos</note> that is,
"Obedience is the mother of happiness, / and the wife, as they say, of Savior Jove."
The poet imagines a "Savior Jupiter," by whose favor safety and salvation are granted; his wife is "success" <term>εὐπραξίαν</term> <note>original Greek: eupraxian</note>, that is, happiness. But the governing principle is "obedience" <term>πειθαρχία</term> <note>original Greek: peitharchia</note>. This term denotes obedience, but specifically the kind by which we obey magistrates and princes. Thus, from their marriage is born a daughter named "success," that is, happiness. For it is the prince's duty to consult the safety of the citizens, which he attempts through good and fair laws; it is the people's duty to comply with these if they wish to be happy. But would that there were no "averting" <note>original Greek: ἀλεξεῖοι (alexeioi) — a title of Jupiter as a protector from evil</note> Jupiters, whose wife was "poverty" <note>original Greek: ἀφενία (aphenia)</note>, and daughter "misfortune" <term>δυσπραξία</term> <note>original Greek: duspraxia</note>.

->To take the spring out of the year.<-

<term>Ἐκ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ τὸ ἔαρ ἐξαιρεῖν</term> <note>original Greek: Ek tou eniautou to ear exairein</note>. That is, "To take the spring out of the year" was said of one who would remove that which was most excellent in any given thing. Herodotus mentions this in his book *Polymnia*. When the Spartans and Athenians sent legates to Sicily, they asked Gelon of Syracuse for both an alliance and military aid against Xerxes, who was bringing war to Greece. Gelon did not refuse, provided they appointed him commander of either the naval forces or the land armies. When the legates rejected this condition, he ordered them to depart immediately and report to the Greeks <term>ὅτι τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ τὸ ἔαρ αὐτοῖς ἐξήρηται</term> <note>original Greek: hoti tou eniautou to ear autois exērētai</note>, that is, "that the spring has been taken from their year." He was indicating, of course, that his army was the choice flower and strength of Greece; if it were missing, whatever was most excellent would be lacking to them. For spring is the most excellent part of the year. Aristotle mentions it in the third book of *Rhetoric* among the types of metaphors. Again, in the first book of *Rhetoric*, he shows this was a saying of Pericles in a funeral oration, who said <term>τὴν νεότητα ἐκ τῆς πόλεως ἀνῃρῆσθαι ὥσπερ χρὴ εἴ τις τὸ ἔαρ ἐκ τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ ἐξαιρεθείη</term>, that is, "youth has been taken from the State just as if one were to take the spring out of the year." It can be applied further, so that those who remove the knowledge of languages and good literature from schools are said to take the spring from the year.

->Even if Cato should say so.<-

Plutarch, in his *Life of Cato of Utica*, relates that Cato's credit and authority with the Roman people were so great that concerning unbelievable things it was said as a proverb, <term>τοῦτο μὲν οὐδὲ τῷ Κάτωνι λέγοντι πιθανόν ἐστιν</term> <note>original Greek: touto men oude tō Katōni legonti pithanon estin</note>, that is, "This is incredible, even if Cato says it." And a certain orator, when he hyperbolically said that one witness should not be believed, added, "not even Cato." Marcus Cicero, in the second book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "What of our famous Cato, who to me alone is worth a hundred thousand?" Similar was the authority of Aristides among the Athenians, and of Xenocrates, for whom the people waived the oath, even though otherwise no witness there was admitted without an oath. Akin to this is the phrase: "I wouldn't believe that even if he swore it."

->To one who deceives once.<-

I suspect it is a common saying among the Italians, which Giovanni Campano, a man of... <unclear>fame/letters?</unclear>

<summary>Erasmus explores several classical adages related to social hierarchy, the impossibility of certain tasks, and the vital importance of youth and education (the "spring of the year"). He also notes how the extreme moral integrity of figures like Cato the Younger led to proverbial expressions about credibility.</summary>

<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY</header>

...a man of great and admirable genius, in the second book of his work *On Avoiding Ingratitude*: "To the one who deceives me once, may the gods do evil; and may they do so twice if the same man should deceive me again." <note>original Latin: "Decipienti me semel, dij male faxint: faxintque bis idẽ deceperit."</note> This suggests that being deceived once should be blamed on the treachery of the deceiver; but truly, he who has experienced it once and then trusts the same man again seems to deserve to be cheated. This is consistent with what we reviewed elsewhere: "He wrongly accuses Neptune who suffers shipwreck twice." Since Campanus <note>Johannes Antonius Campanus (1429–1477), an Italian humanist and bishop</note> was a man of varied and hidden reading, it is possible he read this saying cited somewhere. For these lines seem to be two iambic verses <term>senarii</term> <note>A common meter in Roman comedy consisting of six iambic feet</note> with a few small changes:
*May the gods do evil to the one who deceives me once.*
*And may they do well, if the same man deceives me twice.*
For Campanus himself brings this forward under the title of an "ancient proverb," although anything born in our own memory can also be called "old."

->As is the mistress, so are the handmaidens. LXIII<-

Even today it is commonly said—distorted from the Athanasian Creed <note>The "Quicunque Vult," a statement of Christian belief</note>—"As is the father, so is the son." Very similar to this is an ancient adage found in the eleventh letter of the fifth book of Cicero’s *Letters to Atticus*. He says: "If that saying is true, <term>as is the mistress, so are the handmaidens</term>." <note>original Greek: ὁποία ἡ δέσποινα, τοῖαι καὶ θεραπαινίδες</note> Indeed, this is not far from being an iambic verse: "As the mistress, so the maidservant." <margin>Adage 4.</margin> Plato, in the fourth book of *The Republic*, writes: "Does not like always summon like?" <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ ἀεὶ τὸ ὅμοιον τῷ ὁμοίῳ πηακαλᾶ</note>

->To drink mandrake. LXIIII<-

There is a sleep-inducing power in the mandrake <note>A plant in the nightshade family often associated with magic and medicine in antiquity due to its root's resemblance to the human form</note>, so much so that it can even kill if drunk too heavily, if we believe Pliny in the eleventh chapter of the twenty-fifth book of his *Natural History*. Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and pharmacologist</note> indicates that the root is boiled in wine down to a third part, and a small cup <term>cyathus</term> of the strained liquid is taken for insomnia. It is also given to those about to be cut <note>i.e., undergoing surgery</note> against unbearable pain. Furthermore, the herb, when applied as a suppository in the place of an acorn-shaped pill, causes sleep. Pythagoras called this plant "man-formed" <term>anthropomorphon</term> because the root mimics the human shape. Hence Columella, in his poem, calls it "half-human":
*Although the field, pregnant with the insane herb,*
*Produces the flowers of the half-human mandrake.*
He also calls the plant "Circean" <note>Referring to the sorceress Circe from the Odyssey</note>, because its root is believed to be useful for love charms. From this, those who fail in their duty and doze off are said to have "drunk much mandrake." Julian <note>The Roman Emperor Julian 'the Apostate'</note> used it this way in a certain letter to Callixene: "Does he not seem to have drunk quite a lot of mandrake?" <note>original Greek: οὐ φανεῖται πολλὴν πάνυ μανδραγόραν ἐκπεπωκώς</note> Demosthenes also employs it in his *Fourth Philippic*: "But we seem like people who have drunk mandrake, or some other such drug." <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ μανδραγόραν πεπωκόσιν... ἐοίκαμεν ἀνθρώποις</note> Likewise, those who drowse during business are said to "sleep under the mandrake." Lucian, in his *Timon*, says: "Whenever you sleep, you sleep as if under a mandrake." <note>original Greek: ὅπουγε καθεύδεις ὑπὸ μανδραγόρᾳ καθεύδεις</note> This is not unlike that which we recorded elsewhere: "Drink hellebore" <note>A reference to a plant used to treat madness</note>.

->He hasn’t even seen it in a picture. LXV<-

Just as we say of something completely unknown, "I didn't even know he was born," so we say, "He hasn't even seen it in a picture." For we know many cities and things, and even people we have never looked upon, through pictures in some way or another. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the final book of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*: "You say all these things are both good and evil, which indeed those people say who, as the saying goes, have never seen a philosopher even in a picture." Plautus in the *Asinaria*: "For never was it fashioned, or painted, or written in poems, where a procuress acts well." It becomes even more elegant if it is transferred further: "He has not even seen Rhetoric in a picture," or "Virtue, not even in a picture." For these things are also painted <note>Erasmus refers to allegorical paintings of abstract concepts</note>.

->To cast in a pebble. LXVI<-

"Scruples" <term>scrupuli</term> <note>The origin of the modern word 'scruple,' meaning a moral hesitation</note> are tiny little stones which, while walking, jump into a person's shoes and pinch the foot; from this, one is said to "cast in a scruple" who casts anxiety into someone's mind. And one "removes a scruple" who removes anxiety. Terence in *The Brothers*: "He is afraid; I have cast a scruple into the man." Marcus Tullius Cicero, at the end of the discussion in the fourth book of *On the Ends*: "A scruple for you as you depart? But we shall see." This is not unlike what we have recorded elsewhere: "To flee with the javelin fixed in." Again, Terence in *The Woman of Andros*: "But one scruple still remains for me, which keeps me uneasy."

->In a corner. LXVII<-

"In a corner" <note>original Greek: Ἐν γωνίᾳ</note>. Something is said to be done "in a corner" when it is done in secret. This was used in the Gospels by the Lord Jesus Christ, and it is also found in Plato's *Gorgias*: "To spend the rest of life whispering in a corner with three or four youths." <note>original Greek: Τὸν λοιπὸν βίον βιῶναι, μετὰ μειρακίων ἐν γωνίᾳ τριῶν ἢ τεττάρων ψιθυρίζοντα</note> That is, to spend the rest of one's life with young—

<meta>catchword: young— (adoleſcen-)</meta>

<page-num>948</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...whispering to three or four young men in a corner. Likewise, Lucian in *The Assembly of the Gods*: <margin>LX</margin> <note>original Greek: μηκέτι ἐνθεάζετε ὦ θεοί, μηδὲ κατὰ γωνιάς συστρεφόμενοι, πῶς ὃς ἀλλήλοις κοινολογεῖσθε</note> "O gods, do not act as if inspired any longer, nor, huddling together in corners, whisper secrets to one another." That is: Do not mingle whispers hereafter, O gods, nor, turned toward corners, conspire in each other's ears. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the first book of *On the Orator*: "To whom I [spoke] of all these things in corners for the sake of mocking, so that they might differ," etc. So too is that proverbially said in the Gospel writings: "To preach upon the housetop," standing for that which is to preach openly and in public. Whence we also read that the apostles shouted from the roof.

### A hot lie.
<margin>LX</margin>
We have advised elsewhere that a "hot deed" <note>original Greek: θερμὸν ἔργον</note> is said for a bold one. By a similar figure, they called a "hot lie" one that is audacious and impudent, as Plautus teaches in *The Haunted House*:
> By Hercules, I have heard that a hot lie is the best.

Either one must not lie, or one must lie boldly; otherwise, he who lies bashfully is soon caught. Just like Aeschinus in Terence's *The Brothers*: "Not those, as far as I know." <margin>LXI</margin>

### Mute men will speak sooner.

To the class of "impossible things" <term>adynata</term> <note>A rhetorical device listing impossible occurrences to emphasize the impossibility of a situation</note> belongs also this which Plautus has in *The Persian*: "Mute men will speak before I do."
> It was strictly ordered of me, he says,
> Not to tell this to any man, nor to trust any man,
> So that all mute men would speak this sooner than I.

### To lead into the lattice-trap.

He who deceives by a trick "leads into the lattice-trap." Plautus in *The Persian*:
> Today I will lead this man into the lattice-trap with learned deceits.
> And so, snares have been prepared for him; I will approach the man closely.

The expression is taken from bird-catchers, who scatter bait inside lattices <term>transenna</term> <note>A lattice-work cage or window used as a snare for birds</note> while lying in wait for small birds; whence even today, he who is caught by a trick is said to be "within the lattice." Very similar to this are "to lead into the pit" and "into the snare," which we have mentioned elsewhere.

### To seek food from the lattice-trap.

He is said to "seek food from the lattice-trap" who is very close to danger. Plautus in *The Bacchis Sisters*:
> Now this thrush seeks the worm from the lattice-trap.

It is said against an old man reading a letter by which he was meant to be deceived. It is taken from the same metaphor we just mentioned. <margin>L</margin>

### To employ every machine.

Marcus Tullius Cicero in the book of *Letters to Brutus*: "In addition to the rest, this labor has also fallen to me: that I must employ every machine to hold the young man." Likewise, Plato in the seventh book of *The Laws*: <note>original Greek: οὐδεμιᾷ παλαιᾷ μηχανήσει μηχανήν</note> "by no old device of device-making." That is: Therefore we say every machine must be employed. Rufus in the same [context]: <note>original Greek: πᾶσαν μηχανὴν προσφέρειν</note> "bringing every machine to bear." It is taken from those who attack a citadel or a town with the greatest force, bringing every kind of machine to bear and leaving nothing untried. <margin>L</margin>

### A lion bound with a little cord.

Lucian in his booklet *On Salaried Posts in Great Houses*: <note>original Greek: Νῦν δ' ὁ λόγος, λέων κρόκῃ δεθεὶς, κάτω πορεύομαι</note> "But now, as the saying goes, a lion bound with a thread, I am carried up and down." This is said when someone, caught by a meager benefit, is displayed everywhere among courtiers, though he is the sort of man who should be nourishing others. For princes consider it glorious for themselves if they force bishops and learned men to abandon their own affairs and serve courtly pomp. <margin>LX</margin>

### To live on mustard.

Those who are gloomy and stern beyond measure are said to "live on mustard," a phrase that is still commonly used today.
Plautus in *The Truculentus*:
> By Castor, if this man lived on mustard,
> I do not believe he could be so gloomy.

Aristophanes in *The Knights* used a similar figure: "To look mustard,"
<note>original Greek: καὶ βλέπειν νᾶπυ, καὶ τὰ μέτωπ' ἀνέστασε</note> that is,
Glaring grimly, like those who live on mustard,
He contracted his stern brow.

The commentator on Aristophanes notes that *napy* is the seed from which mustard <term>sinapi</term> is made. Its power is sharp...

...tears, and Ennius, quoted in Macrobius, calls them "sad":
> He seeks neither the sad mustard, nor the mournful onion.
<note>original Latin: "Nec triste quaeritat sinapi, neque moestum cepe."</note>

We have spoken of onions elsewhere.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
->Boys and old men<-
At the beginning of these *Chiliads*, we advised that almost all figures of this kind are proverbial when they consist of opposites: the greatest and the least, young and old, gods and men, sacred and profane, right and wrong, things to be spoken and things unspeakable. Horace says: "Let us, small and great, hasten," since he feels everyone must strive toward this. Plato, in the seventh book of *The Laws*: <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ τὸ λεγόμενον πᾶντ’ ἄνδρα καὶ παῖδα, κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν</note> "But as the saying goes, every man and child, according to their strength," etc. That is: Indeed, as is commonly said, every boy and old man to the best of his ability, etc.

<margin>LXXVI</margin>
->With every voice<-
What is asserted with the greatest intensity is said to be proclaimed "with every voice" or "with the whole voice." For a vehement emotion of the soul usually intensifies the voice. Plato, in the tenth book of *The Laws*: <note>original Greek: πᾶσαν δὴ τὸ λεγόμενον φωνὴν ἱέντι</note> "Letting out, as the saying goes, every voice." We speak clearly when we affirm something, and we sound out with as much a cry as we can if something moves us greatly. It can also be adapted to this use: that he is said to "bring forth every voice" who tries to persuade in every way, now flattering, now scolding, now promising, now threatening.

<margin>LXXVII</margin>
->A stretched bow breaks<-
Plutarch, in the short book he titled *Whether an Old Man Should Govern the Republic*: <note>original Greek: τόξου μὲν, ἰσχυρῶς φασιν ἐντεταμένου ῥήγνυσθαι ψυχὴ δὲ ἀνιεμένη</note> "A bow, as they say, is liable to break when it is stretched tight; conversely, the soul [breaks] when it is relaxed." This is also referred to in the epitaph of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note>, who remained vigorous as long as he was at work, but as soon as he relaxed his study, he perished.
> It was not, therefore, in vain that it was said of you,
> That a bow is broken when friendship's tension is relaxed.
> For while Theophrastus labored, he was sound
> In body; but once relaxed, he died with failing limbs.
<note>Erasmus provides this in both Greek and Latin verse; the sense is that for some, like the philosopher Theophrastus, constant mental activity is what keeps them alive, and stopping "breaks" them just as over-stretching breaks a bow.</note>
That is:
> That the bow is broken once you loosen the taut study
> Were truly the words of a truth-telling man.
> For Theophrastus flourished with assiduous work, and likewise,
> Once his study was relaxed, he died with his members loosened.

<margin>LXXVIII</margin>
->Not even Apollo would understand<-
Whatever was exceedingly obscure and very difficult to understand, they used to say that not even Apollo <note>The Greek god of prophecy, known for his wisdom and the oracles at Delphi</note> could understand it. Athenaeus, in the third book of the *Deipnosophists*: <note>original Greek: Τί δὲ ἡ ἐπιστολὴ δηλοῖ, νομίζω ἐγὼ μηδὲ τὸν πύθιον διαγνῶναι</note> "But what the letter means, I personally think not even the Pythian [Apollo] could discern." He cites a line of verse there from Antiphanes:
> Not even Apollo would learn what these things are.
<note>original Greek: ταυτί θ’ ὅτ’ ἐστὶν οὐδ’ ἂν ἀπόλλων μάθοι</note>
That is:
> Nor would Apollo understand what these things wish for themselves.

<margin>LXXIX</margin>
->When the winds fail, take to the oars<-
When a matter does not succeed as we wish, we must flee to other defenses; or when fortune is adverse, then we must labor all the more. Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus, a Renaissance scholar</note> mentions the adage in a certain Greek letter which is mixed in with those of Politian: <note>original Greek: νὴ τὸν πνεύματος ἁμαρτών φασιν, ἐπὶ τὰς κώπας χωρεῖ</note> "By Zeus, missing the wind, as they say, he goes to the oars." That is: And deprived of winds, betake yourself to the oars, as the saying goes.

<margin>LXXX</margin>
->Lions in peace<-
Aristophanes in *Plutus*:
> Lions at home, but in battle, little foxes.
<note>original Greek: οἴκοι λέοντες, ἐν μάχῃ δ’ ἀλώπεκες</note>
The commentator on Aristophanes shows that the proverb was tossed at the Laconians <note>Spartans</note>, who had managed affairs unsuccessfully in Asia:
> Lions at home, but in Ephesus, little foxes.
<note>original Greek: οἴκοι λέοντες, ἐν ἐφέσῳ δ’ ἀλώπεκες</note>
Doubtless, the comic poet alluded to this. Plutarch, in his comparison of Sulla and Lysander, reports this sentiment as one commonly tossed at leaders. For he speaks thus of Lysander's frugality:
> But no one else having escaped that handle,
> Lions at home, but in the open air, little foxes.
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ τις ἄλλ’ ἐκπεφευγὼς τοτὶ τὸ πόριακον, οἴκοι λέοντες, ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ δ’ ἀλώπεκες</note>

<summary>This page explores several proverbs concerning human behavior and effort, including the necessity of using all available resources (oars vs. wind) and the hypocrisy of those who act brave only when safe (lions at home).</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

Indeed, if anyone else escaped that which is commonly circulated:
->Lions at home, but little foxes abroad.<-
<note>original Latin: "Domi leones, sed foris uulpeculæ."</note>
Perhaps in the past, powerful men emerged this way; later, they began to be lions both at home and abroad—for what animal is more violent than a lion? This proverb applies to those who behave in a backwards manner: fierce where there is no need, but fleeing when the situation demands a real man. Or it applies to those who are cruel toward their own people, yet not the same toward their enemies. This is the charge Sallust brings against Cicero: namely, that he was "abusive to his friends, but a suppliant to his enemies." It may also apply to those who arrive at a position of tyranny through a feigned gentleness.

<margin>70</margin>
->The most certain poverty.<-
<note>original Latin: "Certissima paupertas."</note>
Junius Columella records this proverbial sentiment in his book *On Agriculture*, book 12, chapter 2. Once the storage areas have been prepared, it will be necessary to put everything in its proper place, categorized by kind and even by specific type, so that when use requires something, it can be retrieved more easily. For the old proverb says that "the most certain poverty is when you need something and cannot use it," because it is unknown where the desired object lies cast aside. Thus far we have recounted Columella's words. The meaning, unless I am mistaken, is that if someone has something at home which cannot be found when it must be used, they suffer more from the lack of what they actually possess than if they did not own it at all. For he who does not have it, asks to borrow it from elsewhere; but he who has it—when it comes to the critical moment where it must be used—neither has his own (since he does not know where it is), nor has he another's that he might use.

<margin>71</margin>
->Merchant, sail in and unload.<-
<note>original Latin: "Mercator nauiga & expone."</note>
Strabo, in the 14th book of his *Geography*, records a proverb of this kind: <term>ἔμπορε κατάπλευσον, ἐξελοῦ, πάντα πέπραται</term> <note>original Greek: "Merchant, sail in, unload; everything has been sold."</note>. He says this originated from the Cilicians who formerly practiced piracy. Their chief profit came from slaves who, because of the convenience of the location, were easily captured and very quickly sold off, because the island of Delos, which was not far away, provided a market both large and wealthy. In that place, on the same day and for ready cash, many thousands of slaves could be sold and shipped away. From this also came the fact that the Romans became exceedingly wealthy after the destruction of Carthage and Corinth, and therefore began to employ more slaves. If the proverb holds any meaning beyond the memory of history, we can use it whenever we wish to indicate that something is of such low value (or so common) that no amount of supply is enough—especially if the thing being sought is something bad. In the same way, nothing is bought more greedily today than certain trifling and seditious booklets, while good authors are loathed.

<margin>72</margin>
->Unless his legs were broken, etc.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nisi crura fracta, &c."</note>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his 13th *Philippic*, teaches that it was tossed about as a proverb regarding Gaius Plancus: that "he could not perish unless his legs had been broken." This man had set fire to the Senate house, for which crime he had been driven into exile; nevertheless, he later dared to return to the city in arms. The adage is drawn from those who are fastened to a cross for their crimes; the vitality of their malice is so great that they cannot perish even there, unless death is accelerated by breaking their legs. Cicero jokes, however, that Plancus’s "legs were broken" when his legal power to return to the state was taken away. And yet, he lived and thrived. I will add the words of Marcus Tullius: 
> Others of tribunician rank follow, Gaius Plancus foremost among them, who, if he had loved the Senate, would never have burned the Senate house. Condemned for that crime, he returned to that city from which he had departed by law; but this he has in common with many men very unlike himself. However, there is that which is usually said as a proverb about this Plancus: that he could not perish unless his legs were broken. They were broken, and yet he lives. 

This, however, like many other things, is said to be "accepted by the eagle." Thus far we have reviewed the words of Tullius. In the last part, there is a joke about "the eagle," by which he means an armed force. For the primary standards of the Romans featured an eagle. He also mentions this in his speech *For Roscius of Ameria*: 
> But if you act in such a way as to charge that someone killed his father, yet you cannot say why or how, but merely bark without suspicion—no one will indeed "break your legs" <note>a metaphor for stopping a prosecutor from 'running' a false case</note>. But if I know these men well, they will so forcefully fix that letter <note>The letter 'K' for 'Kalumnia' (slander), branded on the forehead</note>, which you hate so much that you hate all letters, to your head, that hereafter you can accuse no one but your own fortunes. 

Some think the letter meant here is <term>θ</term> (theta), because of the proverb about "affixing a theta" <note>Theta stood for *thanatos*, or death, in judicial voting</note>. To me, he seems rather to be thinking of <term>τ</term> (tau), which has the shape of a cross, and it is on the cross that legs are usually broken. By this "letter" (the cross), the matter is indeed finished, but in the meantime, the accuser carried the mark of slander and impudence for having brought a terrible charge which he was unable to prove by any arguments.

<margin>73</margin>
->Cuckoo.<-
<note>original Latin: "Cuculus."</note>
In the past, those who were caught in some dishonest matter were called "Cuckoos" as a common insult...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...was called. This originated from vine-dressers who were late to begin pruning their vines and had not finished the task before that bird was heard, as if it were reproaching the farmers for their idleness. Travelers, imitating the bird's call, would mock the vine-dressers. Thus Pliny writes in Book 18, Chapter 26: "In this interval of fifteen days, the farmer must finish those tasks which he could not complete before the equinox; he should know that the bird's arrival gave rise to those stinging jokes played on the vine-dressers by mimicking the song of that seasonal bird, which he calls the cuckoo <note>original: "cuculus"</note>. For it is considered a disgrace and a deserved reproach to be caught with a pruning hook in the vine by that bird; for this reason, those stinging jokes are played even in early spring." Yet, as an omen, they are considered detestable. To such an extent are even the smallest things in the field drawn from natural arguments. 

Furthermore, what Pliny calls "stinging jokes" can still be recognized today among some nations. For in the spring months, when the cuckoo <note>original: "coccyx," Erasmus notes this is the same as the "cuculus"</note> is heard—if indeed this is the cuckoo, as Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza, a 15th-century translator of Aristotle</note> believes—married men tease one another with mutual jokes, saying, "That bird sings for you," implying that a wife is not being guarded vigilantly enough. Indeed, Plautus in the *Asinaria* depicts a wife shouting at her husband when he is caught with a mistress: "But the cuckoo is still in bed; get up, lover, go home!" And shortly after: "With your white hair, your wife drags you, you cuckoo, out of the brothels." Horace also writes in the first book of his *Satires*, Satire 7:

> Then the man from Praeneste, with insults drawn from the vineyard,
> Retorts against the traveler's many biting words—a tough
> And undefeated vine-dresser, to whom the traveler had often
> Yielded, calling out 'cuckoo' in a loud voice.

These things certainly agree with what Pliny writes: that it was a standard insult to throw at vine-dressers if the cuckoo caught them still pruning the vine. Porphyrio <note>A 3rd-century commentator on Horace</note> explains that passage of Horace thus: "For it is common for the common folk pruning around those trees to be called 'cuckoos' by travelers; when provoked, they pour out such bitterness of words upon them that the travelers yield, content to call them 'cuckoos' again and again." Acron <note>Another ancient commentator on Horace</note> adds this: "We know this from experience, that travelers often drive vine-dressers to insults as they pass by, and the workers respond in such a way that they call the traveler a 'cuckoo,' as if he were a lazy person, and they repeat this to the guards because they are always sitting by." In these words of Porphyrio and Acron, I see several errors in the text. The Plautine phrase "But the cuckoo is still in bed" fits with this, because the girl's companion was reluctant to get up. Indeed, I suspect that in the insult of the "cuckoo," there was an allusion to the word for "lying down" <note>original Latin "cubandi," playing on the phonetic similarity between "cuculus" and "cubat"</note>. Therefore, where Porphyrio’s text has "levia" (light things), perhaps we should read "lenti" (slow/lazy people). Now, as for those who turn "cuculus" (the bird) into "cucullus" (a hood or garment), making a cloak out of a bird, there is no need for it, since the second-to-last syllable is long, as seen in Plautus in the trochaic meter:

-> But the cuckoo is still in bed; get up, lover, go home. And shortly after, <-
-> With your white head, your wife drags you, you cuckoo, out of the brothels. <-

It is trochaic. In the *Pseudolus*, he seems to have used it as a general insult: "Why are you crying, you cuckoo? You shall live." Unless, perhaps, he calls a weeping and sobbing lover a cuckoo because of the sound <note>original Greek: κόκκυγα (kokkyga)</note>. Similarly in the *Mercator*: "I won't trust those things to a son who obeys his father—not to him, for he is a mere cuckoo." Likewise in the *Persa*: "For your sake, you cuckoo, I wouldn't fear death, by Hercules, even if I cut your face off."

### The ploughman, unless he stoops, goes crooked. LXXXV
<note>original Latin: "Arator nisi incuruus præuaricatur."</note>

What Pliny records in Book 18, Chapter 19, has the appearance of a proverb: *The ploughman, unless he stoops, goes crooked.* He instructs that the ploughman should first break the field with straight furrows, and then subdue it with diagonal ones. This can hardly happen unless he leans his whole body into the labor, which is why Virgil called him the "curved ploughman." Furthermore, "to prevaricate" <note>original Latin: "præuaricari"</note> means to deviate from a straight furrow. From this, those who help the opposing side in legal cases are said to "prevaricate." This is clearly what Pliny means when he says: "From there, this crime was transferred to the forum. Let it be avoided there, where it was first discovered." It can be transferred to anyone, such as: "The pimp, unless he is a perjurer, is prevaricating." "The soldier, unless he is impious, is prevaricating." It will apply to any business that cannot be completed without great sweat.

### To measure with the fingers. LXXXVI
<note>original Latin: "Metiri digitis."</note>

One who weighs a matter more accurately than is necessary is said to "measure with the fingers," as if one were to settle accounts with a friend to see which of them had contributed more favors to the other. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his third *Paradox*: "I do not listen to a poet regarding trifles; shall I listen to a citizen in the society of life who measures his sins with his fingers? If they seem smaller, how can they seem lighter? Since whatever sin is committed, it is a sin against the perturbation of reason and order." Cicero alluded here to the fact that poets are accustomed to measure the "feet" of a poem with their fingers; hence Horace says:

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...and we know the legitimate sound by our fingers and our ear. <note>original Latin: "Legitimumque sonum digitis callemus & aure." A quote from Horace’s *Art of Poetry*, line 274.</note>
A man is not seen as the best poet if he does not immediately detect the flaws of a poem by the judgment of his ears.

->To eat salt and cheese.<-
->LXXX.<-

Pliny, in Book 21, Chapter 7, mentions this proverb, though he does not actually record the text itself. Indeed, among the praises of salt, he mentions this point. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> is also an authority for the fact that the ancients used it in place of a side dish <note>term: pulmentarium - a relish or side dish eaten with bread, often used to describe simple, humble fare</note>; for he says they "dined with bread and cheese," as is apparent from the proverb. One may gather that the saying was used as follows: "Nothing was lacking in the way of seasoning; we had salt and cheese." Or: "Do not be anxious about what preparations you should receive me with; I shall require nothing besides salt, bread, and cheese." The matter of Xenocrates’ cheese is discussed elsewhere.

->Goats in a young plantation.<-
->LXXXI.<-

Varro, in *On Agriculture*, Book 1, Chapter 2, brings forward this saying as a kind of agricultural law: "Let the tenant not graze goats in a young plantation" <note>original Latin: "in agro furculario," literally a "forked field," referring to a place where young vines or trees are supported by forked props.</note>. This can be applied to those who, by introducing harmful things or people, corrupt the tender years of youth. For example, if someone were to place lascivious young men among sacred virgins, or add wanton girls to the company of young boys. Or if someone were to mix pleasures that are hostile to study with one's academic pursuits. For the goat is destructive to all plants, not only by wounding them, but even by the "poison" of its teeth <note>Ancient writers often believed a goat's saliva was literally poisonous to plants</note>, especially to the olive and the vine. This is why the goat is sacrificed to Bacchus <note>The god of wine</note> for the sake of revenge; however, nothing of the goat species is sacrificed to Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom</note>, because the former is said to be the discoverer of the vine, while the olive is sacred to the latter.

->The field ought to be weaker.<-
->LXXXII.<-

Columella, in Book 1, Chapter 4, testifies that among African farmers a proverb of this kind was famous: "The field ought to be weaker than the farmer." Virgil explained this enigma in a phrasing no less proverbial:
"Praise large estates, cultivate a small one." <note>original Latin: "Laudato ingentia rura, Exiguum colito."</note>
But it is better to add the words of Columella himself: "A limit and measure must be applied to things, and this should be understood as being said not only for those about to do other things, but also for those about to prepare a field, lest one wish to buy a greater burden than the calculation of one's accounts permits. For the sentiment of our poet pertains to this:
'Praise large estates, cultivate a small one.'
Which most learned man (in my opinion) gave a poetic shape to an ancient precept that had been handed down. For it was appropriate for the Carthaginians, a most sharp-witted people, to have said that the field should be weaker than the farmer, since when one must struggle with it, if the farm prevails, the owner is crushed. Nor is there any doubt that a wide field poorly tilled yields less than a narrow one tilled excellently." This will apply to those who are eager to extend their empire when they cannot even administer what they already have, or to those who undertake a duty for which they are unequal. It agrees with what we have related elsewhere: "You have obtained Sparta, adorn her."

->From the harvest itself.<-

It is not my intention to sweep into this work every single thing that has some appearance of a proverb. It seemed best not to pass over a few that have offered themselves by chance, especially if they seemed more conveniently or wittily said. Of this kind is that phrase in Seneca’s *Letters*, Book 4, Letter 22: "I shall depart from the harvest itself." For he is dealing with those who are detained either by comforts or the hope of comforts from disentangling themselves from business, as if they were about to desert a field just as the harvest is imminent. How many there are in the courts of princes who are weary of that life and tortured by a longing for freedom, but their greed cries out against those aspiring to liberty: "Can I leave such great hopes, before I depart from the harvest itself?"

->To swim out with one's baggage.<-

No less aptly said in the same letter is: "No one swims out with his baggage." That is, no one recovers his freedom unless he has despised the rewards of slavery. For he cannot put away his preoccupations who cannot neglect the "enlistment-pay" of his cares. This agrees with what we related elsewhere from Martial: "I have ransomed my freedom with all my baggage," and again with the fable which Horace brings forward regarding the fox that had fattened itself in a granary.

->The Givers.<-

Plutarch, in the *Life of Aemilius Paullus*, records that King Antigonus, the grandson of Demetrius, because he promised kindly to everyone but did not perform his promises, was called "Doson" by a popular joke—as if you were to say "Dabo" in Latin <note>meaning "I will give"</note>—because he was accustomed to answer "I will give" <note>original Greek: δώσω</note> to anyone making a request. Such are the "gold-talkers" <note>term: chrysologoi - those who speak of gold or riches but do not possess or give them</note> of whom we have spoken elsewhere. Ovid writes:
"Make sure you promise; for what does it hurt to promise?
Anyone can be rich in promises."

### FOURTH CHILIAD, FIFTH CENTURY
Lll 3

The courts of princes abound with "Dosons" of this kind: "Tomorrow," or "Come back soon." <note>original: "Cras, mox redi." Erasmus is mocking those who delay favors indefinitely.</note>

->To support on one's shoulders.<-
<margin>XCIII</margin>
Those whose authority and diligence are most effective in preserving someone's safety are said to **support them on their shoulders**. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *For Flaccus*: "I say nothing of the highest state of the Republic, which you judges, in this trial, support entirely upon your shoulders." <note>original: "vestris inquam humeris iudices sustinetis."</note> Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman soldier and historian.</note> writes in Book 16: "Where, carrying the weight of flooding wars upon his shoulders, as the saying goes, he was split into manifold cares." Akin to this is the phrase "To bring back on one's shoulders." Cicero, in *On His House*: "You said that you would bring me, the guardian of the city, back into the city on your own shoulders." From this metaphor, the leaders of a Republic are called **Atlases of the State**, as they support it on their shoulders; otherwise, it would collapse.

->To make a citadel out of a sewer.<-
<margin>XCIIII</margin>
Those who elevate a worthless thing or person with magnificent praise are said to **make a citadel out of a sewer**. <note>original Latin: "arcem ex cloaca facere." A metaphor for extreme exaggeration or polishing a turd.</note> Cicero, in his speech *For Plancius*: "Now I come to that final point you made: that while I was extolling the merit of Plancius toward me with words, I was making a citadel out of a sewer, and worshipping a stone from a tomb as if it were a god; for you claimed there was no danger of ambush nor of death." So far Cicero. In his words, there is also another phrase with the form of a proverb: **A stone from a tomb**, used for a man of no power or influence.

->Archimedes could not describe it better.<-
<margin>XCV</margin>
Archimedes of Syracuse was a most celebrated mathematician <note>term: geometra - in antiquity, this encompassed both geometry and general mathematics</note>, who was never not intent upon his geometric figures—so much so that he was killed while he was drawing them. <note>Archimedes was famously killed by a Roman soldier during the Siege of Syracuse (212 BCE) while distracted by his diagrams in the sand.</note> From this, it became a kind of proverb, as found in Cicero’s speech *For Cluentius*: "If, as you say, for the sake of winning favor, what is the value of an addition of forty thousand of those coins? If, as we say, forty thousand coins were given to sixteen judges, Archimedes himself could not have described the matter better." For mathematicians are accustomed to drawing their figures in the dust.

->The gate is the longest part of the journey.<-
<margin>XCVI</margin>
Marcus Varro, in *On Agriculture*, Book 1, Chapter 2, suggests it is a common saying that **the gate is the longest part of a journey**. I believe the sense is the same as that other proverb: "He who has begun has half the deed done." Even today, people say a good part of the journey is finished for one who has passed through the gate. For there is always something that delays a person preparing for a trip; even if there is no business to attend to, the affections of friends cause delays. Among our own people, a departure is not believed to be successful unless several days have been devoted to the feasts and drinking bouts of friends. I will subscribe Varro's words here: "Shall we then use the old proverb, 'A Roman wins by sitting,' while he arrives? And at the same time, thinking that the gate is said to be the longest part of the journey, he proceeded to the benches with us following."

->The assembly of the gods.<-
<margin>XCVII</margin>
*Theōn agora*. <note>original Greek: "Θεῶν ἀγορά" - the meeting place or market of the gods.</note> That is, the assembly or court of the gods. Hesychius <note>A Greek grammarian of the 5th or 6th century.</note> indicates this was usually said of those who speak freely and with great authority, as if they were gods speaking to men. He adds that there is a place of this name in Athens. It applies well to the rich or powerful who, though they may speak very foolishly, nevertheless rely on their wealth and power and wish whatever they say to be held as an oracle. Related to this is what we have recorded elsewhere: "Silver fountains speak." <note>A proverb meaning that money makes people listen.</note>

->To speak like Camarina.<-
<margin>XCVIII</margin>
Not dissimilar to this is the phrase found in the same author: *kamarinōs legein*. <note>original Greek: "καμαρίνως λέγειν"</note> That is, to speak like Camarina, meaning to speak boldly, precisely, and severely. It is not entirely clear where this originated, except that Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist.</note> lists the Camarinos among families of ancient nobility:
> "Lest you be," he says, "a Creticus or a Camarinus." <note>original Latin: "Ne tu, inquit, sis Creticus aut Camarinus." Reference to *Satire* 8.38.</note>

Hesychius indicates that soldiers' belts are called *kamaras*. <note>original Greek: "καμάρας"</note> Thus it is possible the proverb took its origin from their ferocity. The same author teaches that certain columns, on which the circuit of Asia was depicted, were called *kamaras*. Perhaps from this display, those who boasted in a barbaric manner were said to **speak like Camarina**. Again, the same author shows that *kamarian* <note>original Greek: "καμαρίαν"</note> refers to a bedchamber in which there are several rooms. In his own bedroom, everyone speaks as he wishes. I could bring forward more guesses, were I not afraid that these itself are already more than enough for the reader.

->Tongue-bellies.<-
<margin>XCVIIII</margin>
Those who have a tongue for sale, speaking only those things which benefit their stomach, were criticized by the wit of the Comic poets and called *glōttogastores* <note>original Greek: "γλωττογάστορες"</note>—a ridiculous word composed of "tongue" and "belly." This will fit bad lawyers, or preachers whose speech tastes of profit, or flatterers. The authority for this is Julius Pollux in his second book *On Vocabulary*. Athenaeus in Book 3 teaches that such men were called by some poets *knisoglōssas* <note>original Greek: "κνισογλώσσας" - literally "grease-tongues" or "smoke-tongues"</note> and *knisolonchos*, because on account of the smell of the kitchen they approach...

...fawn over things and lick up the steam of cooking; a disease called <term>knisoleichia</term> <note>original Greek: κνισολειχίαν; literally "steam-licking," referring to a parasite or professional dinner-guest who hangs around for the smell of food.</note>. As Juvenal says:
> He thinks you are captured by the smell of his kitchen.

->Let friends perish, etc.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *For King Deiotarus*, records this little verse as having become a proverb: **Let friends perish, provided that enemies perish along with them.** <note>original: "Pereant amici, dum unà inimici intereant."</note> 
He says the same sentiment is celebrated in a Greek verse, which I have not yet found. Perhaps it is the fragment we mentioned earlier: **Let a friend go to ruin along with an enemy.** <note>original: ἐῤῥέτω φίλος σὺν ἐχθρῷ.</note> I will transcribe Cicero's words: "Therefore, when it was announced to him that Domitius had perished in a shipwreck, and that you were being besieged in a fortress, he said of Domitius a Greek verse with the same meaning as our Latin one: *Let friends perish, provided that enemies perish along with them.* Even if he were your greatest enemy, he would never have said that; for he himself is mild, and the verse is empty." 

This proverb applies to those who spare neither friends nor enemies, provided they achieve what they intensely desire. However, the verse is not only "empty" <note>original: inanis</note>, but truly **monstrous** <note>original: immanis</note>, since it is the part of humanity even to let enemies go unpunished so as not to harm friends. Indeed, I would not hesitate to argue that Cicero wrote "monstrous" (*immanis*), but a scribe corrupted it into "empty" (*inanis*), since "mild" does not contrast well with "empty," but it does with "monstrous." Nor is there anything "empty" (that is, boastful or frivolous) in this verse; rather, it is a ferocity unworthy of a human being. Although the meter in Cicero's quote is not quite right, it will be correct if you read it as: *Let friends perish, so long as enemies perish at the same time.*
Similar to this is that other verse we cited elsewhere:
->When I am dead, let the earth be mixed with fire.<-

### FOURTH CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY

---

->With full sails.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'P' with stylized foliage and floral patterns inside a square border.</image-desc>**W**ith sails spread and **with full sails** is a phrase used for those who exert themselves with all their might and greatest effort. Thus Marcus Tullius Cicero, in *On His House*, addressed to the Pontiffs: "What if you, in those shadows of the Republic and those dark clouds and storms, had thrown the Senate from the helm, driven the people from the ship, and you yourself, as a Chief Pirate with a most filthy crew of robbers, had **sailed with full sails**—if you could have carried through what you then promulgated, decided, promised, and sold? What place on earth would have been free from Clodius’s extraordinary commands and power?" Thus far Cicero. Philostratus says of Polemon: "After he heard Euphrates the Tyrian, he betook himself **with full sails** toward that man's philosophy." <note>original: πλήρεσιν ἱστίοις</note> We have spoken of similar figures of speech more than once elsewhere.

->Money without a private reserve.<-

It appears there was once a proverb tossed around among farmers: **Money cannot be made without a private reserve.** <note>original: "Pecuniã sine peculio fieri non effe."</note> The *Digest* <note>The Pandects or Digest, a compendium of Roman law.</note> records this in Book 32: "If my immovable goods are given or bequeathed, and the coins stored there are to be given as a loan, they are not part of the legacy, as the private reserve says." But those coins which he kept aside for the sake of protection (as was done in certain civil wars), those are included in the legacy. He adds that he often heard old country folk saying: **Money without a private reserve is fragile.** They called "money" that which was set aside for protection. We have included this proverb because it warns us not to trust our entire substance to a single ship, lest nothing remains if the property is destroyed by fire, war, or theft. If you wish to turn the adage in another direction, it could be applied to someone who does not share all his plans with his friends. Or perhaps to one who does not place the sum of his happiness in external things, but in the goods of the soul, so that if the former are lost by chance, he has a place to flee and does not lose heart. For that which is properly our own is called a **private reserve** <term>peculium</term> <note>In Rome, a *peculium* was a small sum of money or property that a father or master allowed a son or slave to manage as their own, though legally it still belonged to the head of the house.</note>. Only those things are truly ours which Fortune cannot snatch away.

->A frog with a locust.<-

Theocritus expressed an unequal contest with this figure in the *Thalysia*:
**As if a frog were to strive against locusts.** <note>original: Βάτραχός ποτ’ ἀκρίδας ὥς τις ἐρίσδω.</note>
The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on the text.</note> adds that among the Greeks the frog is called *batrachos*, as if it were *boatrachos*, on account of the harshness of its voice.

->Birds of the Muses.<-

**Birds of the Muses** <note>original: Μουσῶν ὄρνιθες</note> is a name given to poets in the same Eclogue, because they constantly modulate their songs.

...And as many birds of the Muses as strive against the Chian singer <note>The "Chian singer" refers to Homer, traditionally said to be from Chios.</note>, they labor in vain with their cuckooing. <note>original Greek: Καὶ μοισᾶν ὄρνιχον ὅθι ποτὶ χῖον ἀοιδὸν, Ἀντία κοκκύζοντες ἐτώσια μοχθίζοντι.</note> That is:
As many birds of the muses as dare to compete with the Chian poet, they attempt a vain task with their cuckooing. <note>original Latin: Quotquot aues musarum, audent certare poetæ Chio, coccyfando, opera conantur inani.</note>

### At the feet, at the head. V

It seems that a phrase by Theocritus in his *Pastorals* <note>The *Idylls* of Theocritus.</note> was spoken with the character of a proverb, concerning abundant and flowing wealth:
**Woe is me, fleeces lie all at my head and all at my feet.** <note>original Greek: Ὤ μοι πᾶς κεφαλᾶ, καὶ πᾶς ποσὶ κώεα κεῖνται.</note> That is:
**At my head and at my feet, the fleeces of which surround me.**
This is the speech of a shepherd boasting of the riches with which he was overflowing on all sides.

### Pustules. VI

Theocritus in *The Beloved*:
**I will not blow up lies upon my slender nose.** <note>original Greek: ψύδρα κινὸς ὕπ’ ῥῖν’ ἀραιᾶς ὐκ ἀναφυσῶ.</note> That is:
**No lies will be born upon my nose.**
The commentator adds that among the Sicilians, those who had white pustules—which they called <term>psydrakia</term>, <term>ionthes</term>, or <term>inthioi</term>—above their noses were commonly considered to be liars. Indeed, even today people commonly say, "Your nose proves to me that you are lying." The same joke exists among the common folk regarding white spots on the fingernails; even the Greeks call these pustules on the nose "whispers" <note>original Greek: ψύσματα (*psysmata*).</note>, as the same commentator indicates. The lover, using this riddle, signifies that he will tell no lies about his mistress. The Ionians call various pustules <term>psydrakas</term>. Hence the diminutive <term>psydrakia</term>, or "skin-blossoms" <note>original Greek: ψυανθήματα (*psyanthēmata*).</note>, because they flower on the surface of the skin. This matter is plainly superstitious, and I think it was mere chance that I once knew a certain man whose not only nose, but almost his entire face was covered in these pustules—yet I never saw any living creature more vainly or impudently a liar.

### To arrive with a sack. VII

This was spoken as a proverbial figure of speech, cited from the jurist Paulus in the forty-sixth book of the *Pandects* <note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* is a massive compendium of Roman law.</note>, under the title "On payments and releases," in the chapter "What we say." He says: "What we say regarding that heir—who must immediately pay the testator's guarantor what was paid by him before the inheritance was entered upon—must be understood with a certain moderation of time; for he ought not **to arrive with a sack**." There you have it. There is no doubt that this was a commonly used expression about anyone who demands that what they seek be handed over instantly. Otherwise, a sack is not necessary for receiving everything—for instance, oil or wine. Among the Greeks, one is said to "act with a pouch" <note>original Greek: θυλακίζειν (*thylakizein*).</note> who follows someone with a bag demanding something, which is the habit of beggars; hence the proverb: "the beggars' pouches are always empty." A <term>thylakos</term> is a vessel for flour. Hesychius indicates that this word was peculiar to the people of Tarentum.

### To obstruct the lights. VIII

One is said **to obstruct the lights** who obscures the glory of another. This figure of speech is taken from the writings of the legal experts, in which provision is made regarding "predial servitudes" <note>Property laws concerning rights over a neighbor's land.</note> so that a neighbor does not obstruct the neighbor's light by raising a building higher. Thus Paulus says in the *Pandects*, book 8, title "On the servitudes of urban estates," chapter 3: "When a servitude of lights is established, it is acquired so that the neighbor may receive our light. However, when a servitude is imposed so that he does not obstruct the lights, we seem to have gained this most of all: that the neighbor does not have the right to build higher against our will, and thus diminish the light of our buildings." Marcus Tullius Cicero elegantly twisted this to another purpose in his *Brutus*: "For just as Theopompus, with the loftiness and height of his oration, **obstructs** the concise and sometimes even insufficiently clear sentences of Philiscus and Thucydides—as Demosthenes did to Lysias—so this later oratory, being as it were built up higher, **blocked the lights** of Cato." The same author, in *For Gaius Rabirius Postumus*, speaking of Julius Caesar, says: "He neither allows a modest friend to fall, nor does he dim the sharpness of that man's mind with the splendor of his own name, nor does the height of his fortune and glory **obstruct the lights**, as it were, of his mind."

### To hand over with a long hand and a short hand. IX

In the forty-sixth book of the *Pandects*, under the title "On payments," it is written in this manner: "You owe me money or another thing; if I should order you to place it in my sight, it follows that you are immediately released and it begins to be mine. For then, because possession of that thing is held physically by no one, it must be considered as acquired by me and in a certain way **handed over by hand**." It was said with a similar figure "to give with a short hand" in the twenty-third book of the *Pandects*, title "On the law of dowries," in the chapter "Although it is customary." However, whenever a third party gives credit to a debtor for the sake of establishing a dowry, if indeed...

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad of Erasmus’s Adages. The opening text concludes a discussion on the legal and metaphorical concepts of "long-hand" and "short-hand" delivery of goods or promises, likely following Adage VII or VIII from the previous section.</meta>

...indeed, if the marriage has not followed, liberation <note>In a legal sense, the release from an obligation.</note> will not follow, unless perhaps it was accepted in such a way that he wished it to be a total gift to the woman. For then it must be believed to have been received by a **short hand** <note>original Latin: "breui manu"; a legal term for transferring possession when the receiver already has the item.</note> and given to the husband. If you pivot this toward a metaphor, it will have more charm: for instance, one who acts on promises shows a great deal and gives with a **long hand** <note>original Latin: "longa manu"; transferring possession by pointing something out from a distance.</note> what you can contemplate in your mind but cannot immediately take away; while he who is present and immediately exhibits what he promises gives with a **short hand**. Boys show a coin to an elephant but do not dare to stretch out their hand. The long hands of kings have been discussed elsewhere.

->**I am drawn by the Iynx.**<-

Those who are drawn toward something by a vehement and powerless desire are said to be **drawn by the Iynx**. Pindar, in the fourth *Nemean Ode*: **I am drawn in my heart by the Iynx.** <note>original Greek: ἴϋγγι ἕλκομαι ἦτορ.</note> To this, the commentator adds a fable of this sort: they say the Iynx was the daughter of Echo, or according to others, of Peitho <note>The personification of Persuasion.</note>, who, when she had incited Jove to a love for Io using charms, was turned by an angry Juno into a bird. Women used this bird in love-potions and sorcery, as Theocritus indicates in *The Sorceress*: **Iynx, I pray, let that man of mine be drawn to my house.** <note>original Greek: ἴυγξ ἕλκε τὺ τήνον ἐμὸν ποτὶ δῶμα τ' ἄνδρα.</note> Some translate <term>Iynx</term> as the "wagtail," because it constantly moves its tail. <note>The bird is usually identified as the Wryneck (*Jynx torquilla*), known for its strange neck movements.</note>

->**The gods can do all things.**<-

A Homeric half-line:
**But the heavenly ones are able to do all things.** <note>original Greek: Θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται.</note>
This will apply to monarchs, for whom it is easy to do whatever pleases their mind, whether by right or by wrong. Pindar in the third *Pythian Ode*: **But God accomplishes every end according to his own desire.** <note>original Greek: θεὸς ἅπαν ἐπὶ ἐλπίδεσσι τέκμαρ ἀνύεται.</note>

->**The mother of a timid man does not weep.**<-

Cornelius Nepos, in the *Life of Thrasybulus*, testifies that this was commonly tossed about like a riddle: that a mother does not weep [for a timid son], because in war, those who despise the enemy and think nothing is to be feared—because they take too little care for themselves—usually perish and bring grief to their mothers through their loss. On the other hand, he who fears everything and despises nothing at all, using safer counsel, rarely falls into danger. For when Thrasybulus had declared war on the thirty tyrants who had oppressed Athens and had occupied the Attic fortress of Phyle, he had no more than thirty comrades with him. This, he says, was the beginning of the salvation of the Athenians, this was the strength of the liberty of a most famous city. Truly, he was not only despised at first by the tyrants, but his plan was as well; which indeed resulted in destruction for those despisers, and safety for the one who was looked down upon. This made the former slow to pursue, and made the latter stronger by giving him time to prepare. Therefore, that precept ought to be in everyone's mind: that nothing in war should be despised, and it is not said without cause that **The mother of a timid man is not accustomed to weep.** Although it is clear enough that this passage is read corruptly, from which I guess it was written thus: "Nor indeed was he only despised at first by the tyrants, but also his **loneliness** (*solitudo*)." Thus, *modo* ("only") was corrupted into *non* ("not"), and *solitudo* into *sollicitudo* ("anxiety"), and one corruption then draws another, **as one handle draws another.** <note>An adage meaning one thing leads to another.</note> For Nepos means that Thrasybulus himself, being a man of moderate nobility and wealth, was an object of contempt to the tyrants. Then, he was even more an object of contempt because he had so few men in his faction. We have mentioned elsewhere the fortitude that "breaks into the sinew."

->**In the manner of cuttlefish.**<-

Themistocles, as Plutarch relates in his *Life*, reproaching a certain Eretrian for cowardice, said: **"Do you indeed have something to say about war, you who, just like cuttlefish, have a sword but do not have a heart?"** <note>original Greek: ἢ γὰρ ἔφη καὶ ὑμῖν περὶ πολέμω τίς ἐστι λόγος, οἳ καθάπερ αἱ τευθίδες μάχαιραν μὲν ἔχετε καρδίαν δ' οὐκ ἔχετε.</note> Some think the <term>teuthidas</term> are what we call <term>sepias</term> (cuttlefish). The cuttlefish is of the "soft" genus <note>Mollusks.</note>, and I believe this genus lacks a heart. <note>The "sword" refers to the internal "cuttlebone" or pen of the squid/cuttlefish.</note>

->**Literate Samians.**<-

Plutarch, in the *Life of Pericles*, cites this verse from Aristophanes the Comic poet:
**The people of the Samians are very literate.** <note>original Greek: Σαμίων ὁ δῆμός ἐστιν ὡς πολυγράμματος.</note>
I believe this was said because when the Samians had branded the Athenian captives with an owl, the Athenians in turn branded the Samian captives with a **Samaina**, which in the collection of proverbs is called a **samyla**. That was a type of ship with a wide belly, appearing from the prow like a swine’s snout. <note>The joke is a pun: "literate" here means "covered in letters" (branded), not "educated."</note>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad of Erasmus’s *Adages*, specifically within the sixth "Century" (group of 100). The text continues a discussion regarding the "Samian ship," a vessel known for its peculiar prow, and its metaphorical application to people who are heavily scarred or branded as punishment.</meta>

...bearing [it], from which this verse was also widely quoted: *A swift Samian ship was mine, and in appearance like a sow.* <note>original Greek: ναῦς με τις ὠκυπόρος σημείᾳ υἱὸς εἶδος ἔχουσα</note> That is, the ship was a swift Samian, and in appearance like a pig. <note>original Latin: "Nauis erat uelox Samia, specieq'ue fuilla."</note> It was called a **Samaena** because it was invented by the inhabitants of Samos. It will therefore apply to those who are scarred and full of **stigmata** <note>marks or brands burned into the skin, usually as a punishment for slaves or criminals</note>. Hesychius and Suidas add that among the poets, this was said of the Babylonians emerging from the grinding-mill, marked with brands. Indeed, Aristotle also demonstrates the origin of this saying: when the Samian people were oppressed by tyrants, they were forced—due to a lack of people to manage the state—to admit some of the slaves into the partnership of governing as magistrates. So says Aristotle. Now, it is the mark of a slave or a criminal to be branded with stigmata. In Plautus’s play *Cassina*, he says: *If this lettered man should let me.* <note>original Latin: "Si hic literatus me finat."</note> He calls him **lettered** <note>A dark joke: a "lettered man" usually means an educated person, but here it refers to a slave whose skin is "written upon" with branding irons.</note> because he is distinguished by burnt-in marks. Pliny, in Book 18, Chapter 3, calls them "inscribed." But now those same fields are worked by "fettered feet, damned hands, and inscribed faces."

We have spoken elsewhere of the **Attagena** <note>The Francolin, a bird with spotted plumage, often compared to branded skin.</note>. Nor are there those lacking who bring forward a different cause: that the twenty-four letters of the alphabet were invented among the Samians by Callistratus. So says Andron in his *Tripod*. The same author records that he handed over the Ionian letters to the Athenians. It is probable, therefore, that from the invention and handing over of the letters, the joke was turned toward **stigmata**. For the Samians were simultaneously receiving and handing over "infamous marks." Nicanor, the Alexandrian grammarian, was called "the branded one" in a popular joke because he wrote with such painstaking care about the marks of punctuation, which the Greeks call **stigmai**.

---

->**Samian manners.**<-
XV
**Samian manners.** <note>original Greek: Σαμιακὸς τρόπος</note> Some refer this to the vice of slandering, because, as was said, the Samians both branded marks onto others and suffered them from others. Others prefer to refer it to the new appearance of the ship which the tyrant Polycrates invented among them. Therefore, it will fit those who have certain customs of their own that differ from the customs of others.

---

->**The pit-rich.**<-
XVI
**The pit-rich.** <note>original Greek: λακκόπλουτοι; "lakkoploutoi"</note> A certain barbarian secretly informed Callias <note>A wealthy Athenian general</note> of a great force of gold that had been cast into a certain pit. Callias both killed the informant, so he would not betray the secret, and took the gold. When the matter became known, it was turned into a joke in comedies, so that those who suddenly became wealthy through evil arts were called **pit-rich**. Plutarch records this in his *Life of Aristides*. Hesychius also touched upon it.

---

->**Abydus, Abydenus.**<-
XVII
The manners of the people of **Abydus** passed into a proverb. For the Abydenes were said to be **sycophants** <note>professional informers or slanderers</note>, or soft and effeminate. Pausanias and Suidas mention the adage; the latter also shows that things of no value and mere trifles are called "Abydus," just as we have reported elsewhere regarding **Tricae** and **Apinae** <note>proverbial names for worthless trifles</note>. I suppose this is because at that time Abydus was "cold" <note>unpopular or out of fashion</note> due to its age. Whence Athenaeus, in Book 13, indicates that the prostitute Sinope was commonly called "Abydus" because, being now an old woman, she was visited by no one. Hesychius indicates that someone in a certain poet was called an **Abydene** because he made a trade of slandering. Suidas, if I am not mistaken, cites this somewhere from Aristophanes. Zenodotus sets forth the proverb thus: **An Abydene dwelling** <note>original Greek: Ἀβυδηνὸν οἴκημα</note>, that is, the city of Abydus. Stephanus indicates the proverb was spoken of the Milesian Abydenes, for the Hellespontine Abydus originated from there. Truly, these things pertain more closely to the proverb we recorded previously: *Do not go to Abydus rashly.*

---

->**To neglect.**<-
XVIII
In Greek, **to be atherized** <note>original Greek: ἀθερίζεσθαι; "atherizesthai"</note> refers to that which is rejected and made into nothing. The metaphor is taken from the topmost spikes of barley, which have something like sharp points; these are of no use but perish during the harvest. The Greeks call these **Atheras**. That divine man Hermolaus Barbarus noted this from Galen. There are some who think that useless and discarded spikes are called **Athericae** because they are neglected by the reapers and threshers.

---

->**To play the hand-man.**<-
XIX
Just as thieves are equipped with many arts, so their pursuit was called by various names: such as **to fly-in** <note>original Latin: "inuolare"</note> and **to pick-pockets** <note>original Latin: "manticulari"</note>. For the same thing, Laberius (citing Nonius Marcellus) used the word **to play the hand-man** <note>original Latin: "manuari"; to steal using the hands</note>. There is no doubt that this word was bandied about in popular jest, just as today—since the word for "stealing" is too hateful—they say in a milder word, "he fingered it," if they want it understood that something was taken by theft, while at the same time avoiding a lawsuit for slander. "What are you saying? Are you calling me a thief?" "Not at all, but a **hand-man**." Obsolete words of this kind are not without grace if they are applied in the right place, and not without **persuasiveness** <note>original Greek: πειθανότητι; "peithanoteti"</note>, as the ancients used to say, or, "to use an old word."

---

->**Even to the coronis.**<-
XX
**Even to the coronis.** <note>original Greek: Μέχρι τῆς κορωνίδος</note> That is, "up to the very end," used when we signify the extreme limit of any matter. Scholars think it was transferred from ships, for which something bearing the appearance of a beak is accustomed...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

is usually added. For among the Greeks, *Corone* <note>original Greek: κορώνη</note> sounds like a crow, and *coronis* <note>original Greek: κορωνίς</note> like a little crow. In Homer, the word *korōne* is used for a ring, or anything else attached to a door. This same term is added to all completed works as a kind of ornament. Hence, Eustathius <note>a 12th-century Greek scholar and archbishop</note> indicates that a "golden coronis" <note>original Greek: χρυσῆν κορωνίδα</note> is a proverb often used to describe a happy ending to affairs. Plutarch, in his book *On the Fortune of Alexander*, relates that Philoxenus was cast into the stone-quarries—which was the name for a most foul prison—by Dionysius because he had marked through a tragedy that had been handed to him to be corrected "from the beginning even to the coronis," <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς μέχρι τῆς κορωνίδος</note> evidently signifying by a line drawn around it that the whole thing should be struck out. The same author says against the Stoics: "from the entrance of the way to the coronis," <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς ὁδοῦ τῆς ἀρχῆς τῇ κορωνίδι</note> that is, from the entrance and the beginning all the way to the finish. 

It will be more pleasant whenever it is applied to the mind—for example, if one were to speak of the "coronis of studies," or advise that a "golden coronis" be added to noble undertakings, or command that a "golden coronis" be imposed on a life spent laudably, meaning a blessed and pious end. Although a *coronis* is sometimes said to be what is added to a finished work, as Martial <note>a Roman poet known for his epigrams</note> says: "Long with much coronis." <note>original Latin: "Multaq; coronide longus."</note> These are like the items at banquets which the Greeks call *epidorpismata* <note>original Greek: ἐπιδόρπισματα</note> and *metadorpia* <note>original Greek: μεταδόρπια</note>, because they are added after the meal. The Latins, if I am not mistaken, call them *bellaria* <note>sweetmeats or dessert</note>. The same grace would apply if this were transferred to matters of the mind, such as an addition made to a proposed question, or something similar. Finally, grammarians use the term *Coronis* whenever the persona of an actor finishes in the same type of meter as they began; they mark it with lines expressing the shape of a bird's beak <note>the *coronis* was a scribal symbol (looks like  =" ) used in papyri to mark the end of a section</note>. We touched upon this proverb in the entry "From head to heel," but only in passing.

->Let him return unharmed.<-

There is a proverbial appearance to what is found in Theocritus <note>a Greek pastoral poet</note> in *The Wayfarers*: 
"Come, say what you have to say, and let the stranger go back to the city alive." <note>original Greek: Εἴα λέγ᾽ εἴτι λέγεις, καὶ τὸ ξένον εἰς πόλιν αὖθις ζῶντ᾽ ἄφες.</note> That is: 
"Come now, if you are saying anything, permit the guest to return alive to the place from whence he set out." 
So today we say to those who are fierce with threatening words and insults: "Come now, let the man live." These are the words of Lacon to Comatas, who had spoken arrogantly about himself and insultingly toward the other. However, the Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator on a text</note> interprets the passage in various ways.

->On the footprint.<-

It is not unknown to the Latins that something is done "on the footprint" (*e uestigio*), which is done without delay and immediately, which the ancients used to call *extemplo* <note>instantly</note>. The same figure is found among the Greeks as "from the foot" (*ek podos*) <note>original Greek: ἐκ ποδὸς</note> for "on the spot," as in Theocritus’s *Spring Journey*:
"Who then immediately built the fountain." <note>original Greek: ὃς ἐκ ποδὸς ἄννε κράναν.</note> 
Regarding *ek podos*, which signifies "from the bottom," as in "from the feet to the head," we have spoken elsewhere.

->Whoever comes late to dinner.<-

The commentator on Theocritus indicates that these six-meter verses were tossed about as a proverb:
"Whoever is called to dinner and arrives late, 
is either lame, or he does not pay his share." <note>original Greek: ὅστις ἐπὶ δεῖπνον ὀψὲ κληθεὶς ἔρχεται, ἢ χωλός ἐστιν, ἢ οὐ δίδωσι συμβολάς.</note> 
That is: 
"Whoever, having been invited, comes late to dinner, 
is either lame, or he does not give his contribution." <margin>Theocritus has it thus,</margin>
"Or do you hurry anywhere as an invited guest to a meal?" <note>original Greek: ἢ μετὰ δαῖτα κλητὸς ἐπάγεται.</note> 
And he adds that those who are invited go more quickly; those who are not invited, more slowly. For he who was invited and promised to come thinks it uncivil if he causes a delay for the host. He who comes uninvited is either slower by nature, or because he was excluded from the hope of another banquet. Likewise, he who has given his "symbol" <note>original Latin: "symbolum" — a contribution or 'buy-in' for a potluck-style meal</note> hurries so that he is not penalized by loss if he arrives after the time. He who has not given anything, being unconcerned about this matter, walks as he pleases.

->A Gargara of goods.<-

The ancients used to call an innumerable force or quantity of things "gargara," <term>Gargara (a heap or abundance)</term> invented, if I am not mistaken, from the noise made by a multitude of gathered people, or a heap of poured-out things. Astomenes in *The Helpers*, cited in Suidas and the commentator on Aristophanes, says:
"For we have gargara within." <note>original Greek: ἔνδον γὰρ ἡμῖν γάργαρα.</note> 
A certain Tragic poet is also cited—Sophron, I believe—who wrote: "A gargara of money." <note>original Greek: χρημάτων τὰ γάργαρα.</note> From this also comes the verb *gargairō* <note>original Greek: γαργαίρω</note>, which means to resound or buzz because of a multitude. As Cratinus says:
"This whole city resounds with the best men." <note>original Greek: Ἀνδρῶν ἀρίστων πᾶσα γαργαίρει πόλις.</note>
