# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SIXTH HUNDRED

Again, from the play titled *The Lakes*, <note>original Greek: λίμναι</note> this little verse is cited: "With many-brought men, every hearth is a gargara." <note>original Greek: Ἀνδρῶν ἐπακτῶν πᾶσα γάργαρ’ ἐστία</note> That is to say: "The whole house resounds with the men who have been brought in." Furthermore, what is found in Homer, "and the earth rang <note>original Greek: κάγκαγε</note> under their feet," <note>original Greek: κάγκαγε δὲ γαῖα πόδεσσι</note> means "the earth also resounded with their feet." With a change of a single letter, the word for "rang" <note>original Greek: κάγκαγε</note> was used instead of "gargara" <note>original Greek: γάργαρε</note>. Finally, they believe that crabs were called *gargaroi* <note>original Greek: γαργαροὺς</note> because of the multitude of their feet. Macrobius, in the fifth book of his *Saturnalia*, teaches that Gargara is a mountain and a town of the same name situated at the foot of the mountain in Mysia, which is apparently very fertile in crops; thus it came about that whoever wished to signify an immense abundance of things would call them "gargara." He cites examples from Alcaeus and Aristomenes, which are missing here due to the ignorance of the scribes. Aristophanes, in *The Acharnians*, joined two words together for the sake of a laugh to signify an immense multitude: "sand-hundred-gargara instead of bought-from-the-threshing-floor." <note>original Greek: ἀνθ’ ἁλωνήτων ψαμμοκοσιογάργαρα</note> Indeed, the Greeks use the term "sand-hundreds" <note>original Greek: ψαμμοκόσια</note> for things that equal the number of grains of sand, following the same form as when they say "three hundred" <note>original Greek: τριακόσια</note> or "six hundred" <note>original Greek: ἑξακόσια</note>. Alexis, in the sixth book of Athenaeus:
"He shouted, calling for his servant,
Though he had but one and one alone, using
Sand-hundreds of names for him." <note>original Greek: ἔβοα καλῶν τὸν οἰκέταν / ἕν’ ὄντα καὶ μόνον, ὀνόμασι δὲ χρώμενος ψαμμοκοσίοις.</note>
This refers to a poor man making a show of wealth, who, though he had only one servant, nevertheless called him by various names outside the door so that guests would believe there were many people in the house. Macrobius also mentions this compound word in the place we just cited.

### Onobatis (The Donkey-Rider). XXV

Among the people of Cuma, a woman caught in adultery was led into the forum so that, standing upon a stone there, she might be visible to everyone. Then, she was placed upon a donkey and led through the whole city, and brought back to the stone to be a spectacle for everyone again. After these things, she was held in infamy for her whole life, and as a mark of disgrace, she was called an "onobatis" <note>original Greek: ὀνοβάτις</note> because she had ridden the donkey. Moreover, the stone on which the woman had stood was considered cursed and detestable. This will apply to any woman of prostituted reputation. The donkey was a proverbial joke among the Cumans, a matter we have discussed elsewhere. It should be noted here how the severity of laws has decreased. Among the Hebrews, the adulteress was stoned. Among the Romans, the Julian law <note>the *lex Iulia de adulteriis coercendis*, which punished adultery with banishment and property confiscation</note> was sometimes enforced. Among the Cumans, the height of disgrace served as the punishment. Now, among Christians, adultery is a game, even though marriage is a sacrament among them. What is left, except for rewards to be decreed for those who have defiled the wives of many? Formerly, unchaste Vestal Virgins were buried alive. Now, to violate a virgin dedicated to Christ is considered "piety." But as far as the proverb is concerned, it is recorded by Plutarch in his *Greek Questions*.

### Monophagi (The Solitary Eaters). XXVI

The term *Monophagi* <note>original Greek: Μονοφάγοι</note> can be applied to the stingy and inhospitable who invite no one to a banquet. Many of the Aeginetans who had gone to the Trojan War perished in battle; even more were swallowed up by a storm. When the few who returned home safely were received by their kinsmen—seeing the rest of the citizens living in grief and sorrow for the loss of their own—they did not think it appropriate to declare their joy openly or to perform a sacrifice to the gods for their safety. Instead, each family received those who had returned safely at home in secret with banquets and congratulations, serving their fathers, kinsmen, brothers, and relatives themselves, admitting no stranger. Imitating this, the Aeginetans, when they sacrifice to Neptune, spend sixteen days holding what they call *Thiasoi* <note>processions or ritual groups</note>, celebrating banquets secretly among themselves, and none of the servants are permitted to be present. Soon after, sacrificing to Venus, they conclude the festival. Therefore, those who sacrificed in this way were called *monophagi* <note>solitary eaters</note>.

### Let us go to Athens. XXVII

"Let us go to Athens." <note>original Greek: Ἴωμεν εἰς ἀθήνας</note> Plutarch, in his *Life of Theseus*, relates that the Athenians, afflicted by the violence of Minos and simultaneously by a scarcity of resources, entered into a treaty with him on these conditions: that they should send seven boys and as many girls to Crete every year (whom some think were usually killed by the Minotaur, though Aristotle disagrees). But since the Cretans were bound by the religious obligation of an ancient vow, they sent those "first-fruits" of humanity to Delphi. As they were setting out for that place, many sons of the Cretans joined them. However, since they could hardly provide a living for themselves there due to the sterility of the land, they came to that part of Italy which was once called Iapygia. From there, having set out for Thrace,

<meta>catchword: set out,</meta>

<summary>Erasmus explores the origins of "Gargara" as a term for abundance, describes the public shaming of adulteresses in Cuma, explains the ritual origin of "solitary eaters" in Aegina, and begins the history of Athenian tributes to Crete.</summary>
<keywords>Gargara, abundance, adultery, Onobatis, Cuma, Monophagi, Aegina, Theseus, Minos, Iapygia, social customs, Greek history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s catalog of proverbs, moving from the origins of the Bottiaean people into adages concerning regional character traits, the inconstancy of the sea, and practical wisdom regarding property and haste.</meta>

...having set out, they were called Bottiaeans. Whence the girls of the Bottiaeans, at a certain sacrifice, are accustomed to say exactly these words: "Let us go to Athens," testifying by these words to a longing for their former homeland. <note>The Bottiaeans were a people of Macedonia who, according to legend, were descended from Athenian youths sent to Crete as tribute to the Minotaur.</note> Aristotle is cited as the author of this opinion in his *Republic of the Bottiaeans*. It will be permissible to use this when we regret having left behind a better fortune.

<margin>xx</margin>
### Abderite mind.

The people of Abdera became a byword in stories for stupidity and madness, which is clear from an epigram of Martial in his tenth book, concerning a man who, having been condemned, represented Mucius Scaevola in the theater and placed his hand in the fire—but he was ordered to do so, and harsher punishments were prepared if he did not:

> If he seems patient, brave, and tough to you,
> You have the heart of the Abderite common folk.
> <note>Latin: "Si patiens fortisq; tibi durusq; uidetur, / Abderitanæ pectora plebis habes." Martial argues that doing something painful because you are forced to isn't brave; believing it is brave is a sign of stupidity.</note>

We have spoken elsewhere of the Boeotians and Batavians. <note>Erasmus often joked about the supposed "thick-headedness" of his own people, the Hollanders/Batavians.</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero indicates in his books *On the Nature of the Gods* that a peculiar stupidity of mind was natural to the Abderites. And Pliny, in Book 25, Chapter 8, teaches that there are pastures near that city where horses, having grazed, are inflamed with madness, just as asses are in Arcadia. It is a city in Thrace, founded and named after Abdera, the sister of Diomedes, and was the homeland of Democritus the physicist, according to Pomponius Mela. Stephanus thinks the city was named after Abderus, the son of Hermes, beloved by Hercules, whom the horses of Diomedes had torn to pieces.

<margin>x</margin>
### Maritime manners.

It is not far from a proverb what Plautus said in his play *The Cistellaria*: "Maritime manners," <note>Latin: "Maritimos mores"</note> meaning varied and inconstant, like those of lovers who, while carried away by uncontrollable desires, are nevertheless not consistent with themselves. A young man in the comedy complains of a mind dragging him into various emotions. "So," he says, "all my temperaments are: what pleased me just now, displeases me immediately. So love mocks me, a slip of the mind. It chases, drives, seeks, snatches, retains, tosses, gives; what it gives, it does not give; it deludes. What it just persuaded, it now dissuades; what it dissuaded, it now displays. It deals with me with maritime manners." Just as the sea never rests and repeatedly changes its face, so they say maritime people somewhat reflect the nature of the sea. We have spoken of the Euripus elsewhere. <note>The Euripus is a strait in Greece famous for its violent and unpredictable currents.</note>

### Money is compensated by the feet.

Among the sayings of Cato that are celebrated as proverbs, that one is also reported: "Money is compensated by the feet," <note>Latin: "Pecuniam pedibus compensari"</note> though I have not yet found it in the books of that man; but it is possible that Marcus Tullius Cicero said it as a joke. It is not unlike the truth that many of Cato's sentences were celebrated which he only spoke, but did not write. The words of Cicero from the speech *For Lucius Flaccus* are: "If the fields of Crassus delighted you, you should have provided for them here somewhere in the Crustuminian or Capenate districts; let it be, it is a saying of Cato's, that money is compensated by the feet, altogether far from the Tiber," etc. I think the meaning of this is: if a farm is further away, it costs the owner more and returns less profit to him. That loss is repaired by the feet of the owner, if he is not reluctant to visit the farm often.

### Do not go into the mountains unshod.

Theocritus in his pastoral poems: <note>Greek: "ἐν νομοῖσι" (en nomoisi)</note>
"Battus, beware of creeping through the mountain with bare feet, for the mountain is thick everywhere with brambles and gorse." <note>Greek: "Εἰς ὄρος ὅκχ' ἕρπῃς μὴ ἀνάλιπος ἔρχεο βάτα, Εὐ γὰρ ὄρῳ ῥάμνοι τε καὶ ἀσπάλαθοι κομόωνti."</note>

> Battus, beware with naked feet to creep upon the mount,
> For thick with thorns and thistles does the mountain greenly sprout.

He who undertakes a way of life should arm himself against the inconveniences that will occur, lest he regret his plan.

<margin>x</margin>
### You are not walking through fire.

"For you have not stepped upon fire." <note>Greek: "οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ πυρὸς βέβηκας"</note> That is: "You are not walking through fire."
Theocritus in *The Wayfarers*: <note>Greek: "in Hodœporis"</note>
"Do not hurry; for you are not being warmed by fire." <note>Greek: "Μὴ σπεῦδ'· οὐ γάρ τοι πυρὶ θάλπεο"</note>

> Do not hasten, nor indeed by fire are you warmed.

The scholiast <note>An ancient commentator on a text.</note> indicates a proverb lies beneath, by which they signified someone hurrying more than enough. The shepherd, as he was, wanted to enter a singing contest immediately. The other, not approving of such haste, calls him to a more convenient place. For those who walk through fire hurry, so that speed makes the element harmless; just as one is not hurt who sends his hand through a flame, or suddenly throws away a glowing coal snatched by hand. He who is engaged in a dangerous matter is also said to walk through fire. Concerning which we have spoken before.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of regional stereotypes and literary allusions. Having previously discussed the "Abderite mind" (stupidity), he now moves to the "pen-shouter," the universal nature of personal injury, and a famous defense of his own homeland’s "Batavian ear."</meta>

### Pen-shouter.
->XXXIII<-

Antipater, since he neither wished nor was able to clash hand-to-hand with Carneades—who used to launch into the Stoics with great vehemence—turned himself to writing. He published many books, both slanderous and foolish, in which he contradicted Carneades at every turn. Because of this, he earned the common nickname <term>kalamoboas</term> <note>Greek: καλαμοβόας, meaning "one who shouts through a pen"</note>, because he did his vociferating not with his tongue, but with a pen. Plutarch mentions this in his short treatise <term>On Loquacity</term> <note>Greek title: περὶ τῆς ἀδολεσχίας (Peri tes adoleschias)</note>.

### Not only the sons of Atreus love their wives.
->XXXIIII<-

Whenever we wish to indicate that everyone feels the pain of their own injury, insult, or loss, and that no one should be harmed with impunity, this Homeric verse from the ninth book of the *Iliad* will be appropriate.
<margin>The sons of Atreus</margin> <note>Original: Ατρείδαις (Atreidais). Referring to Agamemnon and Menelaus, the leaders of the Greeks at Troy.</note>
> Do the sons of Atreus alone among mortal men love their wives?
> <note>Original: Η μοῦνοι Φιλέουσ’ ἀλόχους μερόπων ἀνθρώπων</note>
> that is,
> Is affection and love for wives found only among the sons of Atreus?

Sextus Coelius (as cited by the jurist Ulpian) brings this up as a commonly used saying in the 48th book of the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, under the title *Regarding the Julian Law on Adultery*, in the law beginning *If a wife*. Virgil imitated this in the ninth book of the *Aeneid*:
> Nor does that grief touch
> the sons of Atreus alone.

### The Batavian Ear.
->XXXV<-

Just as the Greeks say "a Boeotian ear" <note>Greek: Βοιώτιον οὖς (Boiotion ous)</note> to mean a thick and dull one, so Martial, in the sixth book of his *Epigrams*, used "Batavian ear" <note>Referring to the inhabitants of the Rhine delta, ancestors of the modern Dutch</note> to mean something rustic, inelegant, and dour.
> Are you then, he says, that famous Martial?
> He whose wicked jokes and jests are known
> To anyone who does not simply have a Batavian ear.

This is how Domitius Calderinus reads the passage, although some have changed "Batavian" (*Batauaum*) to "severe" (*severa*). The Batavians were a people of Germany, part of the Chatti, who were driven out by a domestic rebellion and occupied the empty ends of the Gallic coast, along with an island situated among the shallows, which the Ocean washes in front and the river Rhine surrounds at the back and sides. At that time, they were a nation powerful in war—as they were highly practiced in the Germanic wars—and strong in resources, because they were not drained by Roman military service. Indeed, they had an alliance with the Empire such that they supplied only men and arms, as Cornelius Tacitus describes more copiously in his twentieth book. 

It is agreed among most scholars, nor do conjectures contradict it, that this island mentioned by Tacitus is the one they now call Holland—a land always to be celebrated and revered by me, as I owe the beginning of this life to it. And I only wish that I could be as much an ornament to her in return as she is a source of no regret to me. For as to Martial's charge that the nation is rustic, or Lucan calling them "fierce": either this does not apply to us at all, or I consider both to be matters of praise. After all, what nation was not unrefined at some point? Or when was the Roman nation more praiseworthy than when it knew no arts besides agriculture and warfare? 

If anyone contends that what was once said against the Batavians applies to the character of our own time, what greater praise could be given to my Holland than if he says it recoils from the jokes of Martial, which the poet himself calls "wickednesses"? I wish that all Christians had "Batavian ears," so that they either would not let in the pestilential jokes of that poet, or certainly would not be captivated by them. If anyone wishes to call that "rusticity," we acknowledge the insult quite willingly; it is surely shared with the upright Spartans, with those ancient Sabines, and with the most highly praised Catos. 

As for Lucan calling the Batavians "fierce," I believe he does so in the same way Virgil calls the Roman "sharp." Otherwise, if you look at domestic manners, there is no other nation more inclined toward humanity and kindness, or one in which there is less savagery or ferocity. They have a simple character, free from snares and all deceit, and are not liable to any serious vices, though perhaps a little too devoted to pleasure, especially that of banquets. I believe the cause of this is the wonderful abundance of all things which usually tempts the pursuit of pleasure. This is partly due to the convenience of imports (since the land occupies the mouths of two most noble rivers, the Meuse and the Rhine, and is also washed on a significant part by the Ocean) and partly due to the native fertility of the region, which is flowed through everywhere by navigable and fish-filled rivers and abounds in the richest pastures. To this, the marshes and groves supply an infinite supply of birds. 

Consequently, they say no other region can be found which, in a similar space, contains so many towns of moderate size, but of incredible polish. In the brightness of their domestic furniture, the merchants who have traveled most of the world concede the palm to Holland alone. Nowhere is there a more frequent number of moderately learned people. As for exquisite erudition, especially of the ancient sort, because it is not as... <note>The text breaks off here, continued on the next page.</note>

<summary>Erasmus defends the "Batavian ear" (referring to his native Holland) against ancient stereotypes of rusticity, arguing that their simple, honest nature and clean, prosperous towns are virtues rather than flaws.</summary>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...many reach this state, either because a luxurious lifestyle is the cause, or because among them, distinguished integrity of character is held in higher honor than distinguished learning. For it is established by many proofs that intellect has not been denied to them, although to me it appeared quite mediocre, not to say small, as is the case with most other things.

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
->Fountain-pot-trifler<-

The Greeks called a foolishly trifling man a <term>krenochytroleraios</term> <note>Original Greek: κρενοχυτρολήραιος</note>, a word ridiculously composed of <term>krene</term> <note>κρήνη</note>, which properly means water gushing out with force, <term>chytra</term> <note>χύτρα</note>, a pot, and <term>lerein</term> <note>ληρεῖν</note>, which means to talk nonsense. We also call stupid people "pots." This is cited by Suidas. It appears in Aristophanes’ *The Frogs*, and with this saying, he seems to have noted immoderately trifling men. For <term>leros</term> <note>λῆρος</note> is a certain [trifle] in... <note>Erasmus likely refers here to the play *Thesmophoriazusae* or a similar context</note>. Elsewhere we have cited the proverb, "Sitting on the trifles of nightingales" <note>Original Greek: ἀηδόνων λέγχαις ἐγκαθήμενοι (aedonon lenchais egkathemenoi)</note>. But later I discovered that <term>lenchai</term> <note>λέγχας</note> is sometimes used by the Greeks for certain public seats in which many idle Athenians would sit together, trifling among themselves about any subject whatsoever, much like semicircular benches <note>Original: hemicycla</note>. As evidence, they bring forward this verse from Homer:
> You do not wish to go sleep in the smithy
> or perhaps in the lounge.
> <note>Original Greek: οὐκ ἐθέλεις εὕδειν χαλκήϊον ὃν δόμον ἐλθὼν ἠπέ που λέγχω. From the Odyssey, Book 18.</note>

Cleanthes wrote that these seats were consecrated to Apollo. Some call that god "the god of the lounge."

<margin>XXIX</margin>
->Bean-gnawer<-

A "bean-gnawer" <note>Original Greek: Κυαμοτρώξ (Kyamotrox)</note> was the name given to one who sold his vote in the election of magistrates, and who therefore spent his time busily in the assemblies for the sake of profit. Would that this did not happen today in the election of the highest leaders of the church and the monarch of the world! <note>Erasmus is criticizing corruption in the election of the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor (the "Caesar").</note> Back then, those who favored a candidate for a small office in exchange for money were marked by the common people; now, immense rewards are openly given to those who vote in the creation of the Supreme Pontiff and the Emperor. Indeed, even certain princes simply sell magistracies, and then we wonder why the fortune of our cities collapses. 

Before the use of pebbles was found—which the Greeks call <term>psephoi</term> <note>ψήφους</note>—votes were cast with black and white beans. Hence, those who made a profit from this were said to "live on beans." Suidas cites a verse, but as is usually his habit, without naming the author:
> The Athenian bean-gnawer will not judge these things.
> <note>Original Greek: Κοινὰ ἢ τότος κ’ κυαμοτρὼξ ἀττικός. Erasmus translates this as: Hos iudicabit non fabæ eſor Atticus.</note>

Hesychius also mentions the proverb, indicating it was a custom among the Aetolians that whoever drew a black bean would undertake the magistracy. From this, the act of voting or drawing lots was called <term>kyamobolein</term> <note>κυαμοβολῆσαι</note>, and a judge was called a <term>kyamobolos</term> <note>κυαμοβόλον</note>, for in certain judgments, sentences were carried not by voice but by pebbles. The custom remains to this day that on Epiphany, a "King of the Feast" is designated by a bean. It also appears in Aristophanes’ *The Knights*:
> For we have a master, rustic in temper, a bean-gnawer.
> <note>Original Greek: Νῷν γὰρ ἔστι δεσπότης ἀγροικὸς ὀργὴν, κυαμοτρώξ.</note>

It could also be said of someone poor and frugal. For from this, the metaphor was taken for those who seek after magistracies or hunt for profit from their votes.

<margin>XXX</margin>
->Lame-pouch<-

They say there was a place near Mount Hymettus named <term>Kyllo-pera</term> <note>κυλλῶ πήρα</note>, that is, "the lame pouch." In it, there was a temple and a spring from which sterile women drank and became fertile. Suidas indicates it is also said as a compound word, <term>kylloperan</term>, warning that it is a proverb for those who apply some force to nature. Hesychius shows that Aristophanes, in the *Centaur*, called a brothel <term>Kyllo-pera</term> because the place of this name was sloping and steep. It will apply to those who stir up lust with bulbs or other drugs. Some assist their intellect with hellebore, or their memory with certain medicines.

<margin>XXXI</margin>
->In the arms of the waves<-

Suidas records this verse from Aristophanes:
> And having these things while in the arms of the waves.
> <note>Original Greek: Καὶ ταῦτ’ ἔχοντες κυμάτων ἐν ἀγκάλαις.</note>

Those who were involved in the greatest difficulties were said to be "in the arms of the waves." For the waves of the sea do not toss those they have embraced gently. This is an allusion to nurses who carry children in their arms and move them with a rocking motion to make them more vigorous, which is itself pleasing to infants and brings on sleep. But the tossing of the waves is a different matter entirely.

# CHILIAD FOUR, SIXTH HUNDRED
Mmm 2
<meta>catchword: Quasi-</meta>

<margin>XL</margin>
### A silent wave.
<term>Kyma kophon</term> <note>original Greek: Κῦμα κωφόν</note>. They used to call a "silent wave" one that did not yet make a crashing sound, but was already beginning to swell. For first the sea rises with quiet waves, and then, as the storm grows harsh, it roars and resounds from afar. This can be said of a person’s anger <note>original: bili, literally "bile"</note> which has not yet erupted into insults, but is silently burning hot. For example, if you were to say, "Yield to the **silent wave**," meaning stop contending so that the dispute does not turn into a brawl. Or, "Resist the **silent wave**," meaning restrain the boiling anger.

<margin>XLI</margin>
### Carian wine.
<term>Karikos oinos</term> <note>original Greek: Καρικὸς οἶνος</note>. Suidas indicates that there was a proverb about wine—in my opinion, a thin or weak wine—which did not bring cheerfulness, similar to the "Carian muse," which was discussed elsewhere. For whatever was cheap, mournful, troublesome, or complaining was called "Carian." However, I am not sure if in Suidas "wine" <note>original Greek: οἴνῳ</note> was written instead of "vine" <note>original Greek: οἰνῷ</note>, except that Hesychius mentions something about a "Carian vine" as being uncultivated and messy. For this class of people, being military-minded, neglect agriculture.

<margin>XLII</margin>
### Sheep-wolf.
<term>Oiolykos</term> <note>original Greek: οἰολυκός</note>. Herodotus in *Melpomene* (that is, his fourth book) relates that when a certain Theras was preparing for a long voyage, and his young son refused to be his companion on that journey, Theras said: "Therefore, I shall leave him as a **sheep among wolves**" <note>original Greek: ὡς γὰρ δὴ εἶχεν, αὐτῷ καταλείψειν οἶν ἐν λύκοισι</note>. From this saying, the name **Sheep-wolf** <note>original Greek: οἰόλυκος</note> was given to the youth, a word composed of "sheep" and "wolf." It can be said of a man who is deserted and destitute of help. If anyone denies that this is a proverb, let him allow it to be an appendix to what we have reported elsewhere: "You have committed the sheep to the wolf." For it is probable that the proverb was born from this history.

<margin>XLIII</margin>
### Nakiosorrhuden.
They used the term <term>Nakiosorrhuden</term> <note>original Greek: Νακιοσοῤῥύδην</note> for those who would belittle something on purpose. Others think the term was usually said to one who, while seeming to confess, did not actually confess, hiding a lie with tangled words—which heretics are usually accustomed to doing when brought into danger. The word seems to be composed of <term>naki</term>, which belongs to one affirming, and <term>kiose</term> (pitch), and <term>rheo</term>, which means "to flow," because with a tangled talkativeness they deny what they seem to affirm, and again affirm what they deny. Hesychius mentions it.

<margin>XLIIII</margin>
### He who had no business, walled in Harmene.
Strabo, in the 12th book of his *Geography*, records a proverb of this kind:
> *Whoever had no work to do, built a wall for Harmene.*
<note>original Greek: ὅστις ἔργον οὐδὲν εἶχεν, Ἁρμένην ἐτείχισεν</note>
->that is,<-
> *He who had no business, added a wall to Harmene.*
For it is a trochaic tetrameter verse. He records, moreover, that Harmene is a village of the people of Sinope, having a port. Stephanus also mentions it, indicating its location in Paphlagonia; some call it "Harmelon," but the meter of the verse certainly does not allow for that here. Neither author indicates the origin or the sense of the adage. I might guess that it was a "cold" <note>meaning dull or insignificant</note> village, which someone surrounded with a wall so that it might become a small town, just as "cold" as before. For the author did not say "he founded" <note>original Greek: ἔκτισεν</note>—which the translator who rendered it "constructed" seems to have dreamed—but "he walled" <note>original Greek: ἐτείχισεν</note>, that is, surrounded it with a wall.

<margin>XLV</margin>
### Neither animate nor inanimate.
It is said as a proverbial figure in Plato’s eighth book *Of Laws*: "of all things both **animate and inanimate**" <note>original Greek: πάντων τῶν τε ἐμψύχων καὶ τῶν ἀψύχων</note>, when we mean that absolutely nothing is to be excepted. We use a similar figure when we say, "The most wicked of both **young and old**," or "**of bipeds and quadrupeds**." Also, "It pleases **neither gods nor men**," or "He spares **neither the living nor the dead**." We cited the passage of Plato in full under the proverb "To fight with shadows."

<margin>XLVI</margin>
### To conspire into the same.
<term>Eis tauton symphysai</term> <note>original Greek: Εἰς ταὐτὸν ξυμφῦσαι</note>, that is, "to coalesce into one." Plato, in the fourth book *Of Laws*: "But to conspire and, just like a yoke of horses, for each to **coalesce into the same** <note>original Greek: ξυμφῦσαι</note>, as the saying goes, requires much time and is very difficult." The translator rendered <term>symphysai</term> as "to breathe one and the same," though it seems rather to be derived from <term>phyo</term> (to be born or to grow). Thus, the word "to coalesce" appealed to me more. However, I defer the judgment of this matter to the learned. If you yoke two horses who are unknown to each other, they do not tolerate one another. At last, through long habit, after each has become accustomed to the other's breath, they are in harmony. Therefore, having panted equally under the same yoke creates concord. And Virgil says: "They teach the graft to **grow into** the wet bark" <note>original Latin: Vdoque docent inolescere libro</note>.

<margin>XLVII</margin>
### This one wove the web, that one unraveled it.
In Julius Pollux, book 7, chapter 10, a six-foot verse is recorded without the author's name, unless perhaps it is Nicophanes in *Pandora*:
> *One is busy weaving the web, the other unravelling it.*
<note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν ἐξυφαίνειν ἰσὸς, ὁ δὲ διαλύειν</note>

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
mmm 2
<meta>catchword: GABO</meta>

Although I think it should be read as, "one weaves the web, the other was anointed," <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν ἐξυφαίνεθ’ ἱστὸν, ὁ δ’ ἐπάλειτο</note> or what is more probable, "was weaving the warp." <note>original Greek: διέζετο</note> For the meter itself rejects the word "web." <note>original Greek: ἱστὸς</note> Now, if some Greek weaver were to explain to us what "weaving the warp" <note>original Greek: διέζεσθαι</note> means—which, as Pollux indicates, the Athenians called "to carry forward"—it would not be difficult to explain the sense of the word. For Suidas only has: "I weave the warp thread." <note>original Greek: διάζομαι τὸν σήμονα</note> Hesychius had added a little light, saying *diezeto* means "he was separating," <note>original Greek: διεχώριζε</note> if *diezeto* comes from the root *diazomai*. But if "to weave the warp" means to add to the thread that remains, the sense will be: "One began, the other finished."

<margin>XLVII</margin>
### To fight with a shadow.
<term>Skiamachein</term> <note>original Greek: Σκιαμαχεῖν</note>.

In the old days, those who labored in vain were said to "fight with a shadow," <note>original Greek: σκιαμαχεῖν</note> that is, to fight with a ghost or a reflection. Plato in the eighth book of *Laws* says: "Just as if we were once deprived of all things both animate and inanimate, and were to practice together in solitude, would we not hope that we were truly fighting with a shadow against ourselves?" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ πάντων τῶν τε ἐμψύχων καὶ τῶν ἀψύχων ἀφῃρηκόντες ποτὲ, ἐρημίᾳ συγγυμνασθῶμεν, ἆραγε οὐκ ἐλπίζοιμεν ἂν αὐτοὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς, σκιαμαχεῖν ὄντως;</note> In addition: if ever we were destitute of all things, both animate and inanimate, and had no competitor, will we ourselves endure to carry out a truly shadow-like fight against ourselves? The same author in the *Apology of Socrates*: "But it is absolutely necessary, as if fighting with a shadow, both to defend myself and to refute when no one answers." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἀνάγκη ἀτεχνῶς ὥσπερ σκιαμαχεῖν ἀπολογουμένόν τε, καὶ ἐλέγχειν μηδενὸς ἀποκρινομένου</note> That is: it is entirely necessary that I fight with a shadow, simultaneously defending and accusing, since no one responds. The same author in the seventh book of the *Republic*: "But as in a dream, as many cities are now inhabited by those who fight with shadows against one another and stir up seditions over who should rule." <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἐν ὄναρ ὡς νῦν αἱ πολλαὶ, ὑπὸ σκιαμαχούντων τε πρὸς ἀλλήλους καὶ στασιαζόντων περὶ τοῦ ἄρχειν, οἰκοῦνται</note> That is: Not in a dream, as many states are now, inhabited by those who fight with a shadow and stir up seditions concerning the leadership. To this, perhaps, pertains what Florus writes in his *Epitome of Titus Livy*, book 49: When Scipio was conducting matters in Africa bravely and successfully, Cato said in the Senate regarding the others who were serving in Africa, that they "fought with shadows," while Scipio fought with "vigor." Julius Pollux, in his sixth book, indicates that those who lived softly and luxuriously were usually called "shadow-reared," <note>original Greek: σκιατρόφους</note> as if educated in the shade, and for this reason impatient of dust and sun; and those who are effeminated by pleasures are said to be "reared in the shade." <note>original Greek: σκιατροφεῖσθαι</note> For light and lust are "shunners of the light"; they love darkness and secrecy. Furthermore, the game of shadow-fighting was, even today, not without charm. He who practices this responds for both sides—both for himself and for the shadow. It seemed right to mention this so that what we cited from the *Apology* might be clearer. Lucian also mentions it in *The Sects*. See the proverb "To wrestle with ghosts."

<margin>XLVIII</margin>
### To lead across the river.
<term>Diabibazein dia potamou</term> <note>original Greek: Διαβιβάζειν διὰ ποταμοῦ</note>.

"To transmit through a river" was said of those who explained the difficulty of a matter which the unlearned or the weaker could not explain themselves. It is a metaphor taken from crossings or rivers deeper than what is safe for anyone to cross. And so, those who are stronger and more practiced take the children, women, or otherwise weak persons upon their shoulders and carry them across. Plato in the tenth book of *Laws*: "I will clearly carry you across the river, just as I am now doing through the stream." <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ σαφῶ ὥσπερ νῦν διὰ ῥεύματος διαβιβῶ τὸν ποταμόν</note> These are the words of the Athenian guest, who delivers the disputation to Cleinias and Megillus, promising that he will be present if any difficulty arises.

<margin>XLIX</margin>
### Gangamon.
<term>Gangamon</term> <note>original Greek: Γαγγάμην</note>.

Julius Pollux in book 10, chapter 40, teaches that this is a type of net, winding with many folds and complicated, which is called *gangame* by the Greeks, from the word for "I catch" <note>original Greek: γᾶν</note>, as the *Etymologicus* indicates, thinking it is named because of "delight," <note>original Greek: γάνυμα</note> from which those who fish with this kind of net are called *gangametikos*, and a *gangameus* is the same as a drag-net or very similar to it. Pollux cites Aeschylus, who called a complicated business that is difficult to unfold a "gangamon," <note>original Greek: γαγγάμωνα</note> just as we say a "weel" or "snare." From this, the place of the belly around the navel was called the "gangamon," because a certain winding of nerves appears there. Perhaps the inner belly is so called because the intestines are folded into themselves, lest the dung immediately flow out.

<margin>L</margin>
### Sacred maniple.
<term>Hieros lochos</term> <note>original Greek: Ἱερὸς λόχος</note>.

A "sacred maniple" <note>a "maniple" was a subdivision of a Roman legion, here used to translate a Greek military unit</note> was once a name used just as we say "casting the sacred anchor," or that the matter has "returned to the triarii" <note>a proverb meaning a situation has reached its final line of defense</note>. Athenaeus, in his thirteenth book, declares that among the Thebans there was a part of the army which they called the "sacred band"; <note>original Greek: ἱερὸν λόχον</note> it consisted of lovers and their beloveds, and for that reason the principal strength of the war was placed in them, because love makes men most brave, even encouraging them to a contempt for death. It will be useful if someone says that the Christian state today depends on the monks as if on a "sacred maniple."

<margin>LI</margin>
### To depart by the back door.
<term>Postico discedere</term>.

Galen, in the second book of *On Natural Faculties*: "But if it consists of many parts, we have withdrawn—or failed—by the back door, as they say, to Asclepiades." <note>original Greek: εἰ δ’ ἐκ πολλῶν σύγκειται, τῇ καταίᾳ πρὸς τῇ οἰκίᾳ, πῶς ἀσκληπιάδην ἀπεχωρήσαμεν</note> He is said to "retreat by the back door" who goes away secretly, stealing away without others knowing. So Horace says: "Deceive the client by the back door," which happens not infrequently even today.

<summary>This page explores several classical adages, including the concept of "shadow-fighting" (futile or solitary effort), the metaphor of carrying someone across a river (intellectual guidance), and the "Sacred Band" of Thebes, which Erasmus dryly compares to the role of monks in his own time.</summary>
<keywords>shadow-fighting, Plato, Scipio, Cato, education, metaphors, fishing nets, Sacred Band of Thebes, monks, back door, Galen, Horace, classical philology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Latin and Greek adages. The opening sentence completes a thought from the previous page regarding how people discreetly change their minds or slip away from responsibilities, likely concluding a discussion on "escaping through the garden gate."</meta>

# FOURTH THOUSAND, SIXTH CENTURY
Mmm 3
<meta>catchword: Om-</meta>

...make great men. He said the same thing in another form: "I slip back stealthily into the teachings of Aristippus." <note>Aristippus was a Greek philosopher who founded the Cyrenaic school, emphasizing pleasure and adapting to circumstances.</note> Thomas Linacre, a man of incomparable learning, translates "kepaia" <note>original Greek: κηπαία</note> as "the garden's back door." Houses to which a garden is attached have two doors: a front and a back. The front door faces the public road; the back door leads to the garden. Through this latter door, those who wished to depart secretly would slip away. Some are ashamed "to sing a different tune" <note>original Greek: παλινωδεῖν — to recant or take back what was said</note> openly, so they cross over to another opinion under a disguise; others withdraw themselves from business when the opportunity arises. This proverb fits such people.

->Wineskins and Sacks.<-
<margin>LIII</margin>
"A wineskin and a sack." <note>original Greek: Ἀσκὸς καὶ θύλακος</note> This was said of someone who indulged excessively in food and drink. For a "wineskin" <note>original Greek: ἀσκὸς</note> is a vessel for wine, and a "sack" <note>original Greek: θύλακος</note> is a container for grain. Athenaeus, in his eleventh book, records these verses from the *Hesione* of Alexis, spoken in the character of Hercules:
> He asked for a cup, and once it was given, drinking frequently,
> He pulls and drains it; and as the proverb goes,
> Man is always a good wineskin, always a good sack.
Likewise Horace:
> If it is well with your belly, your side, and your feet, what more
> can royal riches add?
We have spoken elsewhere more than once regarding gluttons and "bellies."

->To give a fire-stone.<-
<margin>LIIII</margin>
Seneca, in the fourth book of *On Benefits*, records this as a common saying: "Lest it cause you pain," he says, "so that you might speak more considerately afterward, as we are accustomed to say, 'I will give you a fire-stone.'" He is referring, unless I am mistaken, to the pyrite stone, which some call "living stone" and others "fire-stone" <note>Latin: ignarium</note> because it contains so much fire that it burns the fingers when rubbed, and it is otherwise very heavy. Therefore, one was said to "give a fire-stone" when suggesting something that, by a certain pain, would call a person back from sinning—just as a stone applied to the finger, by either its weight or its friction, does not allow a person to forget the reason he took it up. Marcus Tullius [Cicero] spoke in a not dissimilar form against Antony in the second *Philippic*: "Are you waiting until I goad you with prods? This speech, if you have any shred of feeling, mangles and bloodies you." Terence says: "Do not poke my side." Persius writes:
> And someone standing nearby nudges him with an elbow.
By these gestures we give warnings, just as we do by "tugging the ear," about which we have spoken previously.

->Let him spend it on a disease.<-
<margin>LV</margin>
Seneca, in the second book of *On Benefits*, says: "Five hundred denarii is that thing which is commonly said: 'let him spend it on a disease.'" Zeno had promised five hundred denarii as a loan to someone; although warned by friends that the man was of bad faith, he lent it anyway, either because he had promised it or because the sum was small. Creditors, therefore, when they realize a debt will not be repaid and do not think it worth the effort to go to law for such a trifle, are accustomed to say: "Let him have it; let him spend it on a disease." This saying has a double meaning. It can be said by a friend who does not want to fail a friend, meaning it should be spent if an illness strikes; or it can be said by an enemy who wishes a disease upon a wicked man.

->Even as far as Megara.<-
<margin>LVI</margin>
The tone of this saying remains even today, when we signify that something is of great value and is vehemently desired by us, saying: "For the sake of this thing, I would travel even as far as India." Or: "The matter is worthy enough that I would sail even as far as Ireland for its sake." Socrates, in Plato's *Phaedrus*, says: "For truly these speeches would be festive and useful to the public. Indeed, I have such a desire to hear them that even if you were to walk on foot as far as Megara, and following Herodicus, having reached the walls you were to turn back again, I would not leave you." <note>original Greek: ἦ γὰρ ἂν ἀστίου καὶ δημοφελεῖς... οὐ μή σου ἀπολειφθῶ</note> The phrase "according to Herodicus" <note>original Greek: πρὸς ἡρόδικον</note> is spoken ambiguously. For it is uncertain whether some Herodicus said this, or if a certain Herodicus became a laughingstock to the people because, after completing such a long journey, he returned from the walls of Megara to Athens—either having forgotten something or having changed his mind—much like Phaedria in Terence's play returns to the city from a bypass. Hence this very phrase, "according to Herodicus," has the appearance of a proverb applied to a man of uncertain counsel, or one who changes his mind too late, when one ought to deliberate before beginning. Similar to that is: "A thing worthy for which one would forfeit his bail."

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
L

### To let out every voice.

<note>original Greek: πᾶσαν φωνὴν ἱέναι</note> People were said "to let out every voice" when they left nothing undone or unsaid in their efforts to persuade. Indeed, a person who is entirely focused on persuading someone now argues, now scolds, now flatters, now promises, now threatens, and "becomes all things" <note>original Greek: καὶ παντοῖος γίνεται</note> in order to bend the listener to their will. Plato writes in the tenth book of *The Laws*: "By no means, O stranger; rather, if there is even the slightest chance of persuasion in such matters, one ought not to grow weary, especially a lawmaker, if he is worth anything at all; instead, as the saying goes, having **let out every voice**, he ought to come to the aid of the ancient law with his words, showing by reason that the gods exist." He says the same in the *Phaedrus*: "For this reason, one must examine everything, turning all arguments upside down." <note>original Greek: τότε δὲ ἡμᾶς χρὴ πάντας τοὺς λόγους ἄνω καὶ κάτω μεταστρέφοντα ἐπισκοπεῖν</note> This seems to be taken from musical instruments, where if gentle sounds do not move the listener, more powerful ones are employed. Plutarch indicates this somewhere, though the specific passage does not come to mind at the moment. It shall be noted when it is found. Consider whether "every voice" might mean "every effort." For legal advocates are accustomed to straining their voices when they argue a case with great zeal. The Apostle Paul, in the fourth chapter of Galatians, seems to have meant something similar when he said: "I wish I were present with you now and could **change my voice**." <note>original Greek: ἤθελον δὲ παρεῖναι πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἄρτι, καὶ ἀλλάξαι τὴν φωνήν με</note> For he who now scolds, now flatters, now praises himself, now humbles himself, now terrifies, now comforts—whatever the needs of those he does not wish to see perish—changes his voice like a skilled enchanter to persuade them by some means.

### To play the Magadis.

<note>original Greek: μαγαδίζειν</note> In ancient times, those who were "double-tongued" <term>bilingues</term><note>literally "two-tongued," meaning hypocritical or inconsistent</note> were said "to play the magadis," praising and blaming with the same mouth, flattering and scolding, or speaking both virtuously and obscenely. Athenaeus discusses the *magadis* at length in his fourteenth book, doubting whether it was a type of lyre or a pipe. Some even think it is related to the <term>sambuca</term><note>a triangular stringed instrument</note>, and some to the <term>pectis</term><note>an ancient lute-like instrument</note>. But this is irrelevant to the proverb, as it is established that the instrument was "double-toned" <note>original Greek: δίφωνον</note>, because it simultaneously emitted two voices, one low and one high—the harmony which is called "through all" <term>diapason</term><note>an octave</note>. This six-foot line is cited from Alexandrides:
->I will chatter like a magadis, small and great at once.<-
-><note>original Greek: μάγαδιν λαλήσω, μικρὸν ἅμα καὶ μεγαν</note><-
He says it is an ancient type of instrument, discovered by the Lydians. The name was given by a certain Thracian named Magdus. Others think it was invented by Sappho. Pindar calls the magadis a "responsive plucking" <note>original Greek: ψαλμὸν ἀντίφθογγον</note>, such as a song where men and young boys sing together. We touched on this subject regarding the proverb: *To blow hot and cold from the same mouth.*

### Brazen-gutted.

<note>original Greek: χαλκέντερος</note> In the past, a person was called "brazen-gutted" if they were remarkably patient in their labors and indefatigable, as if they had intestines made of bronze—much like the fables say of Talos, the guardian of the island of Crete. This nickname was given to Didymus the Grammarian <note>an Alexandrian scholar of the 1st century BC</note> because of the incredible number of books he is said to have written. For the same reason, Origen <note>an early Christian scholar</note> was called <term>Adamantius</term><note>man of diamond/steel</note>.

### To look like oregano.

<note>original Greek: ὀρίγανον βλέπειν</note> This was said of those who displayed strength and a masculine spirit. This line from Aristophanes survives, as I conjecture, though the meter is corrupted:
->I will show myself to be of manly spirit, and looking like oregano.<-
-><note>original Greek: παρέξομ’ αὑτὸν ἀνδρεῖον τὸ λῆμα, καὶ βλέποντα τ’ ὀρίγανον</note><-
This is taken from the sharpness of the herb. It corresponds to other sayings like "To look like mustard" or "To look like cress." Some call the herb <term>cunila</term>, of the kind that Dioscorides calls "Heracleotic." There is another kind called <term>onitis</term>, and a third which they call "Heraclean Panaces." So says Dioscorides. Pliny, in book 20, chapter 14, records that oregano is not unlike wild pennyroyal.

### A Thuringian spirit.

<note>original Greek: θούριον λῆμα</note> They used this to describe a fearless mind prepared for war. For <term>lema</term> <note>original Greek: λῆμα</note> generally signifies to the Greeks a will, a mind, a purpose, or dignity and authority; it is derived from the word meaning "to want" <note>original Greek: λῶ</note>. However, <term>lemma</term> <note>original Greek: λῆμμα</note>, which is written with a double 'm', comes from the word for "to take" <note>original Greek: λαμβάνω</note>, and refers to an argument assumed for proof. "Thurion" refers to anything that is vehement and warlike. Hence Homer calls it "Thurian strength" <note>original Greek: θούριδα ἀλκήν</note>. Even Mars himself was called "Thouros" <note>original Greek: θοῦρος</note>, from the word meaning "to leap" <note>original Greek: θορεῖν</note>. Suidas cites this from Aristophanes. He also found "Thouros"...

<keywords>persuasion, Plato, Magadis, musical instruments, double-tongued, Didymus the Grammarian, Origen, oregano, warlike spirit, etymology, Greek proverbs</keywords>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, SIXTH CENTURY
967
Mmm 4

...for a divinely inspired and vehement speech, when one speaks fearlessly and with authority.

->Not even an elephant would drink it dry.<-
<margin>LXII</margin>
<note>original Greek: οὐδ' ἂν ἐλέφας ἐκπίοι</note> That is: "Not even an elephant would drink it up." This is said of an enormous drinking cup, since an elephant can swallow an immense volume of water with its trunk whenever it wishes. Athenaeus, in his eleventh book, cites Epinicus: "An elephant would fill an elephant-sized basin or a <term>rhytus</term> <note>A drinking horn or vessel often shaped like an animal head.</note> holding two <term>choas</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of volume, roughly 3 liters or 6 pints.</note>, which not even an elephant could drink dry."

That is:
> Holding two choas, such that not even an elephant
> Could drink it dry.

A *rhytus* is a type of cup, shaped like a horn, which seems to have been made of ivory and placed upon the image of an elephant. He adds: "For you are no different from an elephant yourself," so that there would be a fourfold mention of the elephant. We recorded this latter proverb previously, though without citing this specific passage. Furthermore, a *choa* is a type of measure. This saying can be applied to a dull and wordy book, which even the most patient reader could not endure to finish.

->To ladle out cups.<-
<margin>LXIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: κυαθίζειν</note> Those who indulged in drinking were said "to ladle out cups" <note>the Latin *cyathissare* derives from the Greek *kyathos*, a small ladle or cup used for measuring wine.</note>, just like the term *cothonizin* <note>to drink heavily</note>, which we mentioned earlier. Athenaeus also pointed this out. To me, it seems more appropriate for those who drink sparingly—not gulping down <term>sextarii</term> <note>about a pint</note> at once—but who nevertheless get drunk by repeatedly dipping into the cups. For some people are accustomed to set a rule: "Each shall drink only one <term>hemina</term> <note>about half a pint</note> and no more," and it often happens that as their desire gradually warms up, they end up drinking more.

->Holy fish.<-
<margin>LXIIII</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἱερὸς ἰχθύς</note> A "holy fish" was the name given to one that no one would harm, but which was left to its own devices. Suidas indicates this is found in Homer. For whatever the ancients wanted to be considered huge and excellent, they called "holy," just as in Homer: "the holy strength of Alcinous" <note>original Greek: ἱερὸν μένος ἀλκινόοιο</note>. It could be said jokingly of a very large and highly esteemed man who is otherwise stupid and speechless. Athenaeus also mentions this.

->Cork-like.<-
<margin>LXV</margin>
One is called <note>original Greek: φελλίνας</note> *phellinas* meaning light or "cork-like." For *phellos* <note>cork</note> is the bark of a tree that always floats, which the Latins call *Suber*. From this, a rough and stony place is called *phelleus*, being better suited for grazing goats than for bearing crops, because the earth seems to "float" atop the rocks. From this also comes the verb *phellizo*, meaning to float or to have no roots. Indeed, even today in the British language <note>Erasmus likely refers to Breton or a similar Celtic dialect here.</note>, a convenient and not at all difficult man is called *phellea*. The Greeks call this lightness of character *euetheia* <note>original Greek: εὐήθειαν</note>, a word which can imply a fault. Plato says in the third book of *The Republic*: "Therefore, goodness of speech, harmony, grace, and rhythm follow *euetheia*—not that which is actually foolishness but which we call 'good-naturedness' as a flattering term, but rather that which is truly a mind well and beautifully equipped in character." We touched on this somewhat in the proverb "Lighter than cork." Regarding a deep furrow in the soul, the word *aiphas* was used.

->Drunk on the game of cups.<-
<margin>LXVI</margin>
<note>original Greek: μεθυσοκότταβοι</note> As a common insult, those who were well-soaked were called *methysocottaboi*, as if to say "drunk on the <term>cottabus</term>." For the *cottabus* <note>a Greek game where players threw wine dregs at a target</note> involved a type of cup. Athenaeus, in book 15, relates from some author—Aristophanes, if I am not mistaken:
> The sea of the Gorgons was stirred up...
> Young men, drunk on the cottabus, carry her off by stealth.

That is:
> The youth, well-soaked by the cottabus game,
> Stole and carried away the courtesan Simaetha from Megara.

->Equal for equal.<-
<margin>LXVII</margin>
<note>original Greek: ἴσῳ ἴσῳ</note> "Equal for equal" was said when something signified a moderate balance. The expression is drawn from drinkers, who frequently argue about equality, sometimes with fists and swords. But in the old days, "equality" meant that as much water should be added as there was wine. Athenaeus, in book 11, cites from a play of Aristophanes titled *Philonides*:
> Therefore, just now my master
> Because of the excellence of the Thericlian cups <note>A famous type of large pottery</note>
> Gave me one mixed **equal for equal**, 
> Foaming and sumptuous, like a double-layered shield.

That is:
> Accordingly, just lately, my [master...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Greek and Latin idioms related to drinking, sincerity, and character traits. It concludes a previous entry on drinking measures before moving into several adages recorded by Ammianus Marcellinus, Athenaeus, and others.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
M m m

In Thericlean cups <note>original: "In Thericleis"; <term>Thericlean</term> refers to a high-quality style of Greek pottery named after the potter Thericles.</note>, because of the courage I displayed,
My master gave me a beautifully rounded shield as a gift,
Overflowing with foam, delicate, and mixed equal for equal <note>original: "par pari".</note>.
He cites this verse from the comic poet Strato:
> The Hermes-lot <note>original: "Ἑρμῆς"; refers to the first lot drawn, named after the god of luck.</note> which some draw from a small pitcher,
> And others from a small jar <note>original: "Cadisco".</note>, mixed equal for equal. ->that is,<-
> The lot which some draw from a pitcher,
> And others from a jar, tempered equal for equal.
The first line is an imperfect trochaic meter, and I believe it should be read as "from a small pitcher" <note>original: "προχοϊδίου".</note>; both are types of wine vessels. "Hermes," however, is used to mean the lot that is drawn first, as we have explained elsewhere. In the same book, he relates a line from Hermippus:
> How sweet it was to drain it in one breath, mixed equal with equal. ->Draining it in one breath<-
> ->that is,<-
> Which I had exhausted in a single breath,
> Most pleasantly, mixed equal for equal.
Elsewhere we have discussed the phrase "like for like" <note>original: "par pari".</note>, but it is not the same proverb. That one refers to compensation or retaliation, while this one refers to an equal mixture <note>specifically of wine and water.</note>. For example: "If only nature had mixed the life of men 'equal for equal,' but now there is far more evil than good." These words "equal for equal" <note>original: "ἴσῳ ἴσῳ".</note> are used as if they were an absolute phrase, outside the normal rules of grammar, just as we say "through all" <note>original: "διὰ πασῶν"; a musical term for an octave.</note>.

->LXVIII<-
### With a straight heart.
<margin>LXVIII</margin>
Ammianus Marcellinus, book 17: "After these letters had been long weighed, he replied 'with a straight heart' <note>original: "recto pectore".</note>, as the saying goes, and with consideration." "With a straight heart" is said of someone who speaks candidly and without dissimulation, just as the speech of truth is simple. Those who approve what should be approved and condemn what should be condemned speak with a straight heart. Those who either approve everything or condemn everything do not act with a straight heart.

->LXIX<-
### To carouse.
<margin>LXIX</margin>
Those who drank quite liberally were said "to cothonize" <note>original: "Κωθωνίζειν"; derived from <term>cothon</term>, a Spartan drinking vessel used by soldiers.</note>, and a larger potion was called a "cothonism." Mnesitheus the physician, in Athenaeus book 11, thinks this practice contributes to the health of the body. Plato allows it for correcting character, and Seneca for the sake of the intellect; however, they exclude actual drunkenness and permit it only rarely. Those who drank their wine quite pure were said "to drink from the top of the cothon" <note>original: "Ἀκροκωθωνίζειν".</note>, or as the author of the *Etymologicon* wrote, "to drink unmixed from the cothon." Hesychius thinks these people were called "top-armored" <note>original: "ἀκροθώρακας".</note>, for he associates it with drunkenness. However, from Plutarch’s *Symposiacs* and Aristotle’s *Problems*, it appears that those who are not yet completely drunk—their whole bodies soaked, but only their upper chests <note>A play on words: "thorakas" means both chest and breastplate armor.</note>—are called "top-armored." Julius Pollux also indicates this in book 6, citing the author Hyperides; so does Athenaeus, citing the same author in his speech against Demosthenes. Pollux records from the author Critias that "to cothonize" means to drink immoderately. A *cothon* is a type of cup, which we have touched upon elsewhere.

->LXX<-
### Dreg-livers.
<margin>LXX</margin>
A popular joke once called sordid and stingy men "dreg-livers" <note>original: "Τρυγοβίοι"; from *tryx* (dregs) and *bios* (life).</note>, as if they were "dreg-dwellers." Those who are more refined open another vessel when they reach the dregs. But I have known wealthy men who would place nine-year-old dregs on the table for their children and for friends who were no ordinary people. Some are so naturally miserable that they do not allow wine to be drunk until it has either turned sour or gone flat. Pollux noted this adage in book 6, chapter 4. Eustathius shows that the very stingy are called "dreg-livers" because they live anxiously and with groaning. In Aulus Gellius, book 11, chapter 7, a man is mocked for saying of a very frugal person: "This Roman knight eats <term>apluda</term> and drinks <term>flocces</term>." The ancient farmers called the husks of grain *apluda*; they called *floces* the dregs of wine pressed from the skins, just as *fraces* are the dregs of olives.

->LXXI<-
### A loquacious mole.
<margin>LXXI</margin>
A man of no judgment, but who is nonetheless excessively wordy, was called a "loquacious mole" <note>original: "loquax talpa".</note> in a popular insult. This was first said of Julianus Capella after he had fallen into public hatred; for our moles are as mute as they are blind. He was also called "a monkey in purple" <note>original: "πίθηκος ἐν πορφύρᾳ".</note>, which we mentioned elsewhere. Ammianus records this in book 17.

->LXXII<-
### Not with poles or branches.
<margin>LXXII</margin>
The same author in the same book says of a certain Antonius, who was elevated to the honor of the royal table among the Persians and admitted to the right of giving his opinion: "He spoke in the republic 'not with poles or branches' <note>original: "non contis aut ramulis".</note>, as they say"—that is, not with double-talking evasions or obscurely, but with full sails—and in doing so, he incited the king...

<meta>This page continues the transition from discussions on drinking vessels to metaphors for precision, brevity, and mixtures in speech and lifestyle, drawing heavily on Ammianus Marcellinus and Greek lexicographers like Hesychius and Suidas.</meta>

...oar. Although I think "remulo" <note>original: "remulo"; a small oar</note> should be read instead of "ramulo" <note>original: "ramulo"; a small branch</note>: for those who have head winds push the ship with poles and oars. It is more a part of the adage we reviewed elsewhere, "With sails and oars" <note>original: "Velis remisque"; meaning to use every possible effort</note>, than a new adage.

### LXXIII. Beyond the chalk line

The same author <note>Ammianus Marcellinus</note> in Book 21 says: "Lest therefore the discourse, running 'beyond the chalk line' <note>original: "extra calcem"; <term>calx</term> refers to the limestone or chalk line used to mark the finish line in a racecourse. To go "beyond the chalk" means to overstep or talk too long.</note>, bring weariness to the reader," and he speaks of distributing honors as if "by a plumb line" <note>original: "ex perpendiculo"</note>: and under him, no one about to perform something grand was admitted to the court suddenly or unknown.

### LXXIIII. By the plumb line

The same author in the same book used "by the plumb line" <note>original: "ex perpendiculo"</note> to mean that which was of exact judgment. He says: "distributing the Palatine honors as if by a certain plumb line: and under him, no one about to perform something grand was admitted to the court suddenly or unknown." To this form also belong those phrases which appear frequently elsewhere, as in Gellius, Book 2, Chapter 1: "To examine by the rule" <note>original: "Ad amussim exigere"; <term>amussis</term> was a mason's tool used to check level surfaces</note>, and "To weigh by the pound-scale" <note>original: "Librili perpendere"</note>, and "To estimate by equilibrium." And in Pliny, Book 36, Chapter 25: "to examine by rule and level." Furthermore: "To measure by fingers," "to weigh in the balance," "to do to the fingernail" <note>original: "ad unguem facere"; a metaphor for perfect finish, derived from a sculptor running a nail over a joint to check for smoothness</note>, and others, some of which we have indicated in their places; all of these have more charm if transferred to matters of the mind. The metaphor is taken from the builder's plumb line, with which he explores either the levelness of the ground or the straightness of a wall. An *amussis* is a hanging device, having lead attached at the bottom; it is added to the middle of a rule consisting of two pointers <note>original: "gnomonibus"</note>, and with this one explores the levelness of the ground. Marcus Tullius Cicero in the third action against Verres: "You, Verres, have nothing to do here, unless perhaps you wish to examine columns by the plumb line." They tell him there is almost no column that can be exactly by the plumb line. "For by Hercules," he says, "let us act thus, let the columns be examined by the plumb line," etc.

### LXXV. Not even an "acolo"

->Not even an "acolo" to dip the lips.<-
<note>original: "Ακολω τὰ χαλκεουνα βυσαι" (Akolō ta chalkeouna bysai); Latin: "Acolo non sicut immergere labra"</note>. Suidas <note>a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> indicates this was said when prosperous health was promised, or when it was signified that things should be used boldly. For the Greeks call tiny morsels "akolos" <note>original: "ἀκόλος"</note>. Sometimes also fragments of bread, "because they do not stick together" <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ μὴ κολλᾶσθαι"</note>. Hesychius indicates that those eating "akolos" are rendered free of bile and calm, whereas figs inflame the blood. We have seen Italians, if they ever wished to remove bile, take nothing for several days except a few small morsels boiled in water with a little fresh butter. Some add a tiny bit of herbs and roots. The proverb exhorts one to a thin diet.

### LXXVI. FIVE-FOLD

Athenaeus in Book 11 mentions a type of cup that was formerly called "pentaploa" <note>original: "πενταπλοου"; meaning "five-fold"</note>, which was used in public games. Certain young men <note>Ephebi</note> competed in a race to Athens. They ran carrying a vine branch laden with fruit, which was called an "ozos" <note>original: "ὄζος"</note>. The start of the race was from the temple of Bacchus to the temple of Pallas, who has the surname "Skirras." The victor in that contest took the chalice called "pentaploa," and thus danced in a choir. The name was given to the chalice because five kinds of things were mixed in it: wine, honey, cheese, flour, and a little oil. This could be applied to a speech stitched together from various arguments. There was a similar clay vessel which the Greeks call a "kornos" <note>original: "κόρνος"</note>, sacred to Bacchus. In it were several kinds of things, but distinct in small cups connected to each other. Athenaeus specifically lists about sixteen. Just as we call a "farrago" <note>original: "farraginem"</note> a varied thing composed of diverse kinds, so we could say either "pentaploa" or "kornos." We have spoken of the "Horn of Plenty" <note>Cornu Copiae</note> elsewhere. Nor is it very different from what the ancients called "satura" <note>satire, originally meaning a "mixed dish" or medley</note>, which is discussed in its proper place.

### LXXVII. In the Carian manner

->In the Carian manner or figure.<-
<note>original: "Σχηματι καρικω" (Schēmati karikō)</note>. It was said to be done in the Carian manner when something was done filthily and disorganizedly, especially in obscene matters; which nevertheless can be transferred to other things, such as unbecoming and uncivil manners, or to an unpolished speech. We also read of a "Carian ship" <note>original: "πλοιον καρικον"</note>.

### LXXVIII. To rule like a mouse

Those were said to "act like mouse-rulers" <note>original: "Μυσιναρχει" (Mysinarchei)</note> who lived harshly and drily. The word seems to be a compound of "mouse" and "chaff," because a mouse labors greatly over a small matter; unless we prefer it said from "myoso," which is to dry, and "mysis," a choking, as if someone were choked by a stalk. For Hesychius indicates this word should be pronounced thus, as it is said, "without a contest" <note>original: "ἀκωνεὶ"</note>, used by Cratinus in the play titled *The Seasons*. Others think a certain man was called "Mysinarchos" who could bring forth no witty remarks of his own, but nevertheless gladly smiled at the sayings of others. And mention of this name was made...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...made-up, found in the comic poet Apollophanes. It will therefore be twisted to refer to a man who is stingy, sordid, or coldly humorous.

<margin>LXXVI.</margin>
->Mytes.<-

A person who was excessively silent, or more loosely given to lust, was called a *mytes* <note>original: *μύτης*</note>, as if you were to say "mutterer," from the syllable for the mute, about which we have spoken elsewhere. There is a female fish of this name, and at the end of its life, the male does not feed. From this, the term is applied to the lustful or those excessively devoted to their wives, but more correctly to "viscous" <note>sticky or clinging</note> women. Hesychius is the author for this.

<margin>LXXVII.</margin>
->He who spits into a nest of ants, etc.<-

The same author indicates it was a common saying in the vernacular: "As he who spits into a nest of ants has his lips swell" <note>original Greek: *ὡς ὁ πτύσας εἰς μυρμηκιὰν, οἰδεῖ τὰ χείλη*</note>. Whether this truly happens, or the breath's reflection causes some venom to affect the mouth of the spitter, or it is rashly believed, it can be twisted against those who provoke a multitude of weak people who are nevertheless numerous and united. Hesychius cites Dinolochus as the source. He was a writer of comedies and the son of Epicharmus.

<margin>LXXVIII.</margin>
->No one is born for himself.<-

This sentiment of Plato is so celebrated by all the learned that it may be rightly counted among the proverbs. Plato first put it forward in the letter he wrote to Archytas: "But you must also consider this, that each of us is born not for himself alone, but a certain part of our birth our country claims for itself, another part our parents, another our remaining friends, and much is also given to the circumstances that take hold of our life" <note>original Greek: *Ἀλλὰ κἀκεῖνο δεῖ σε ἐνθυμεῖσθαι, ὅτι ἕκαστος ἡμῶν οὐχ αὑτῷ μόνον γέγονεν, ἀλλὰ τῆς γενέσεως ἡμῶν τὸ μὲν τι ἡ πατρὶς μερίζεται, τὸ δέ τι οἱ γεννήσαντες, τὸ δὲ οἱ λοιποὶ φίλοι, πολλὰ δὲ καὶ τοῖς καιροῖς δίδοται τοῖς τὸν βίον ἡμῶν καταλαμβάνουσι*</note>. That is: "Indeed, you should consider that each of us is born not for ourselves alone, but our country claims a part of our origin, our parents a part, and our other friends a part. Many things are also granted to the opportunities that fall into our life." Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> brings up this passage in the first book of *On Duties*. "But since," he says, "as has been excellently written by Plato, we are not born for ourselves alone, and our country claims a part of our origin, our parents a part, and our friends a part." Since Cicero translated this sentiment clearly, conveniently, and elegantly, I wonder why Seneca preferred to say, "No one happened for himself" <note>original: *Nemo sibi contigit*</note>. For he seems to have wanted to express that word "guarantee" <note>original: *ἐγγύη* (engue)</note>; for he writes thus to Lucilius in Book 5, Letter 32: "Do you wish to know what it is that makes men greedy for the future? No one happened for himself." For he wants to attribute this to parents, that we do not immediately seek the best things. For he adds, "Your parents prayed for other things for you, but I, on the contrary, wish for you a contempt for all those things, and an abundance of these. Their vows rob many to enrich you." Quintilian seems to have had the same zeal—to say everything differently than Cicero had said it. For which reason it happens that he is sometimes less elegant and even more obscure.

<margin>LXXIX.</margin>
->Piraeus does not carry empty vessels.<-

Julius Pollux, in Book 6, Chapter 6, reports this from Aristotle. "The dry land <note>or the port</note> does not lead empty vessels" <note>original Greek: *Ξηρὰ δὲ μὴ κεναγγείαν ἄγειν*</note>. Piraeus was the port of Attica <note>the harbor of Athens</note>. Vessels laden with merchandise used to put in here. Young men would gather in the same place to hold a banquet; Antipho indicates this in Terence’s *The Eunuch*: "A few of us youths met in the Piraeus today to discuss the shared contributions for a meal." There is a Corinthian port of the same name, where it is likely there was greater luxury. From this is drawn a taunt against those who always delight in being stuffed with food and drink. If anything is to be read in Pollux as "potteries" <note>original: *κεραμεία* (kerameia)</note> instead of "vessels" <note>original: *κεναγγεία* (kenangeia)</note>, so that it refers to a man, Saint Jerome indicates that the place and the man who was first called Piraeus was later called "Ceramicus" <note>the potters' quarter in Athens</note>.

<margin>LXXX.</margin>
->Fig-leaf eater.<-

The ancients jokingly called a rustic and sordid man a *cradophagus* <note>original: *κραδοφάγον*</note>, as if he were an "eater of fig-shoots." For they call the leaves of the fig tree *cradas* <note>original: *κράδας*</note>. These same people were called *balanophagi* <note>original: *βαλανωφάγοι*</note>, as if they were living in the manner of those eating acorns.

<margin>LXXXI.</margin>
->The wise man divines.<-

Donatus, in his commentary on *The Mother-in-Law* <note>Terence's play *Hecyra*</note>, indicates it is a proverb: "The wise man divines." This is because from other things prudently compared, he gathers the truth, not only concerning the past but even the future. As in the play, Laches, while "divining," is entirely off track. Phidippus, however, approving of his conjecture, says, "He clearly divines here, for that is it." Seek the rest from the proverb: "Will the wise man not conjecture?"

<margin>LXXXII.</margin>
->To iambize.<-

The ancients used "to iambize" <note>original: *ἰαμβίζειν*</note> to mean to revile and speak evil, a word drawn from the woman Iambe, a foul-mouthed maiden. It is more likely drawn from the "iambic foot" <note>a metrical unit in poetry: short-long</note>, which was invented for insults, in which...

# CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY SIX

...expressing one who is rising and uncontrolled. In this, it also agrees with that which starts from a short beginning and ends in a long one, just as an injury emerges from lighter beginnings into a heavy tragedy—a point also indicated by Homer: *ἦτ’ ὀλίγη μὲν τὰ πρῶτα* <note>original: *hēt’ oligē men ta prōta*</note>, that is, "Which at first is small." From this, they also call a man inclined toward insulting *iambizein* <note>original: *ἰαμβίζου* (iambizou), referring to iambic poetry, which was traditionally used for satire and invective</note>. Suidas and Hesychius provide similar information.

<margin>LXXXVI.</margin>
->The Pottery Whip.<-

*Κεραμεικὴ μάστιξ* <note>original: *Kerameikē mastix*</note>, that is, "The Pottery Whip," was the name given to ostracism <note>a democratic procedure in Athens where citizens could be expelled from the city for ten years</note>, about which we have spoken abundantly under the proverb "The Turning of the Potsherd." They called it a "whip" because individuals were driven into exile by it, and "pottery" because these votes were traditionally carried on small earthenware shards.

<margin>LXXXVII.</margin>
->The Ram's Service.<-

*Κριοῦ διακονία* <note>original: *Kriou diakonia*</note>, "The Ram’s Service." Suidas and Zenodotus record this as a saying usually applied to a duty performed for the ungrateful. This is because a ram strikes the person who is feeding it with its horns. Hesychius records it as being applicable to those who serve unworthy people in the hope of some small reward. When we invite boys to perform a service, we promise something, such as knuckle-bones or nuts. Likewise, in a certain fable, I believe the ram said, "Join me, and I will give you knuckle-bones." 

An added asterisk in the Aldine edition <note>the famous Venice publishing house of Aldus Manutius</note> indicates that *κατάλληψιν* <note>original: *katalēpsin*, meaning "seizing"</note> is a substituted word; I believe it should be read as *κατάλειψιν* <note>original: *kataleipsin*, "leaving behind"</note> from *ἀλείφω* <note>original: *aleiphō*, "to smear or anoint"</note>. I made passing mention of this in the proverb, "The ram's reward for nursing." There is another proverb regarding the ungrateful, which I recorded above: 
*Ἀντ’ εὐεργεσίης ἀγαμέμνονα δῆσαν ἀχαιοί* <note>original Greek phrase</note>, that is, 
> For his good deeds, the Greeks bound Agamemnon.

I found this cited without an author's name. Meanwhile, in the Greek scholia <note>ancient commentaries</note>, I found that in the Stoa Poikile <note>the "Painted Porch" in Athens</note>, which was also called the "Royal Stoa," there were several statues of Mercury, some placed by commoners and some by leaders; one of these had this verse inscribed on it in ancient letters. From there, it became a proverb. Whatever the case may be, this should have been added in its own place, but that sheet had already left my hands.

<margin>LXXXVIII.</margin>
->Upon your own head.<-

Whenever an evil is turned back or falls back upon its author, the Greeks say: *Εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ κεφαλὴν* <note>original: *Eis tēn autou kephalēn*</note>. Demosthenes, in his oration *On the False Embassy*, says: "He would not have remained silent about these things—he who is cursed by his country—things which it is now necessary to turn back upon your own heads." So too Ctesippus in Plato’s *Euthydemus*: "If it were not too rude to say, I would say: 'Upon your own head!'" For the sophist had concluded that those who wish a youth to become learned, when he is not yet learned, are seeking his destruction; for that which ceases to be what it was "perishes," and begins to be what it was not. So also Virgil:
> May the gods first turn this omen upon himself.

In Aristophanes’ *Plutus*, the character Penia <note>Poverty personified</note> reasons that if all men became rich, Chremylus himself would be forced to plow, dig, and endure all other labors, so that he would live more miserably as a rich man than he had previously lived as a poor man. Chremylus, mindful of the labors he endured in poverty, abhors this statement and prays it falls on Penia’s head, saying *ἐς κεφαλὴν σοί* <note>original: *es kephalēn soi*</note>, that is, "Upon your head!"—leaving "may it fall back" to be understood. Caelius wrote to Marcus Cicero in Book 8: "But Domitius, when he had placed his hands to his mouth, spread the rumor that you had perished on the ninth day before the Kalends of June—a rumor that should fall on their own heads."

<margin>LXXXIX.</margin>
->More hot-tempered than the Adriatic.<-

He who is of an unaccommodating character and an irritable nature is compared to the Adriatic Sea in a proverb. Thus Horace's mistress, when he had made a separation:
> You, lighter than cork, and more hot-tempered than the cruel Adriatic.

He himself admits he was of a somewhat hot-tempered nature: "Quick to anger, yet so that I was easily appeased." 
Likewise, in the satire that begins, "I have been listening for a long time." Aeschines says of Demosthenes that he was of such harsh and inconstant character that it is easier to have dealings with the Adriatic than with him. This is not because that sea is fiercer than others—on the contrary, there is hardly any milder—but so it seemed to the Italians, who, if they had sailed the British or Danish seas, would admit that the Adriatic is unworthy of the name of "sea."

<margin>XC.</margin>
->The Sea-Ox.<-

*Βοῦς ἐνάλιος* <note>original: *Bous enalios*</note>, that is, "The Sea-Ox." Used of people who are large, dull-witted, and useful for nothing—such as seals, which do nothing but feed and are useful neither for work nor for eating, unlike land-oxen. This is recorded by Suidas. However, I suspect it should be read as *βοῦς ἐν αὐλίῳ* <note>original: *bous en auliō*</note>, so that it is the same as what follows shortly: "The ox sits in the stall," that is, an ox...

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad of Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs.
