...it is, "the ox sits in the stall." <note>original: "bos in stabulo sedes"</note> For so it is recorded in the Collections of Tarrhaeus and Didymus. It is a hemistich <note>a half-line of verse</note> of an iambic trimeter.

## An Ox in the Stall.

*βῶς ἐν αὐλίῳ* <note>original: bōs en auliō</note>. That is, "An ox in the stall." This was said of someone who is useless and living a life of leisure. Hesychius <term>cites this from Cratinus</term> <note>a Greek comic poet</note> from the play titled *Deliades*, although we have mentioned this elsewhere.

## A Dog to Food.

*Κύων ἐπὶ σῖτον* <note>original: Kyōn epi siton</note>. That is, "A dog to food." This is used for those who hasten to their own destruction. Those who wish to kill dogs lure them by showing them food. Hesychius indicates this is similar to those other sayings: "An ox to the slaughter" <note>original: βῶς ἐπὶ σφαγὰ (bōs epi sphaga)</note> and "A pig in chains."

## An Ox on a Silver Platter.

<margin>x</margin>
*Βῶς ἐπὶ πίνακος ἀργυροῦ* <note>original: Bōs epi pinakos argyrou</note>. That is, "An ox on a silver platter." This is aimed at those who maintain a grand persona, offering something that promises to be extraordinary, yet they are of no use to anyone except for pleasure or vanity. It is very similar to what we reported elsewhere as "the seventh ox." In ancient times, people used to serve desserts shaped so they displayed the horns of a new moon, because the moon appears horned when it is rising and waning. Indeed, these sorts of sweets were called *selēnai* <note>original: σελῆναι, meaning "moons"</note>. On this subject, Suidas cites a rather elegant epigram:

> How is it that, being an ox, you do not cut the furrows of the earth,
> But lie back like a drunken peasant?
> Why do you not run off to the pastures like a goat,
> But instead stand here as a silver image?
> I stand here to prove your own laziness.

->that is,<-

> How can it be, that though an ox, you plow no field,
> But like a drunken rustic, lie down and yield?
> Why don't you, goat-like, to the pastures run,
> But stand a silver image, for show alone?
> Here I stand, your idle ways to make known.

Julius Pollux mentions this ox in Book 6, Chapter 11, demonstrating that this kind of food was traditionally offered to Apollo, Diana, Hecate, and the Moon. We also see various species of animals shaped in sweets today. Not dissimilar to this is what the French call a "king of cards" <note>original: regem chartarum</note>, who is a king more by title than by wealth or power.

## Having Taken a Candle.

<margin>x</margin>
Diphilus, quoted in Athenaeus Book 15, in the play titled *Ignorance* <note>original: ἀγνοία (Agnoia)</note>, says: "Having lit the candle, we looked for the candlestick." <note>original: ἅψαντος λύχνου λυχνίον ἐζητοῦμεν (hapsantos lychnou lychnion ezētoumen)</note> This is said when a matter is handled without foresight; for the candlestick ought to have been ready before you touched the candle.

## To Inhabit an Empty House.

*Κενῷ ἐγκατοικεῖν δόμῳ* <note>original: Kenō egkatoikein domō</note>. That is, "To inhabit an empty house." This is said of those who make a great show of things in appearance, while being empty of any actual substance. Plato cites an iambic trimeter, which was undoubtedly a common saying in his time since he does not mention the author's name: "And practice whatever makes you seem wise to others—whether these things should be called nonsense or follies—from which you will eventually inhabit empty houses; do not value men who find fault with these small things, but rather those who possess strength in life, an honest reputation, and many other goods."

> that is, Practice those things from which you will seem wise, 
> putting aside those things done for show,
> whether it is proper to call them delusions or trifles,
> From which you will inhabit empty houses in the end;
> do not highly value the men who challenge these small things, 
> but rather those who have a strong estate, an honorable fame, and many other good things.

We have spoken elsewhere regarding "the empty casket of the Graces."

## To Rail.

*Στωμύσαι* <note>original: Stomysai</note> means to attack another with harsh insults. In Athens, there was a certain festival in which it was the custom to play at mocking and insulting others. From this, they began to use the word *stomysai* for those who raved quite freely against someone. The name of the festival was *Stomia*. For *stomy* <note>original: στωμὺ</note> is properly said of that which is annoying to the ears. So say Hesychius and the *Etymologicum*. It is similar to the saying, "To speak from the wagon."

## I Come from the Sixty Men.

Athenians were wonderfully delighted by those who knew how to provoke laughter by words or deeds. So much so, that sixty such men used to gather in the district of Diomeia, or at the Temple of Hercules; these were known in the city as "The Sixty Men." Just as we speak of *Duumviri*, *Triumviri*, or *Decemviri* <note>official boards of two, three, or ten men</note> holding office, if anything was said ridiculously, the common people would say, "The Sixty Men said this," <note>original: οἱ ἑξήκοντα τοῦτο εἶπον (hoi hexēkonta touto eipon)</note> or "I come from the sixty men." <note>original: ἀπὸ τῶν ἑξήκοντα ἔρχομαι (apo tōn hexēkonta erchomai)</note> Athenaeus records...

FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
Nnn
<meta>catchword: Mer-</meta>

<margin>book 13.</margin> There was a tribe in Athens called the Diomeians <note>original: *Διομειῶν* (Diomeiōn)</note>, named after a certain Diomus, the son of Colyttus, from which the name "Diomeian" <note>original: *διομειεὺς* (diomeieus)</note> is derived, as may be gathered from Hesychius. This could be used ironically to describe an unrefined or rustic joke as: "A saying worthy of the Sixty Men" <note>original: *Dictū sexaginta uiris dignū*</note>. Or, of a foolishly talkative person: "This one comes to us from the Sixty Men." <note>The "Sixty Men" were a famous club of wits in ancient Athens known for their sharp, sometimes crude, humor.</note>

### To carry on one’s head.
### XCVIII

When we love people dearly, we are said "to carry them on our heads." Plato writes in the tenth book of the *Republic*: "and for the sake of this wisdom, they are loved so vehemently that their companions almost carry them around on their heads" <note>original: *καὶ τῷ ταύτῃ τῇ δόξῃ ὅτω σφόδρα φιλεῖν, ὥστε μόνον οὐκ ἐπὶ ταῖς κεφαλαῖς περιφέρειν αὐτὸν οἱ ἑταῖροι*</note>. This metaphor clearly comes from mothers and nurses, who carry infants on their heads while they are placed in cradles. Cicero used a similar figure of speech, "To carry in one’s eyes," meaning to love someone intensely; and we say "We carry in our bosom" those whom we treat with singular affection.

### With drooping ears.
### XCIX

Those who are dejected in spirit are said to have "their ears over their shoulders." So Plato says in the tenth book of the *Republic*: "having their ears upon their shoulders" <note>original: *τὰ ὦτα ἐπὶ τῶν ὤμων ἔχοντες*</note>, meaning with hearts cast down and sick. This is taken from beasts of burden, which demonstrate their state of mind through the movement of their ears, just as humans do through the forehead and eyes. For to man alone, as Pliny says in Book 11, nature gave immobile ears. However, in pack animals and almost all four-legged creatures, the ears are erect when they are listening, limp when they are exhausted, nodding when they are fearful, upright when they are enraged, and dangling when they are sick. From this comes that line by Horace: "I drop my ears like a donkey of sour mind, when a heavier load is placed on its back" <note>original: *Demitto auriculas ut iniquæ mētis asellus, Quū grauius dorsō subijt onus*</note>. Even today, common people say that those frustrated in their hopes "drop their ears" or "have dangling ears."

### Agathodaemonistai.
### C

The "Agathodaemonistai" <note>original: *Ἀγαθοδαιμονισταί* - literally "Good-Spirit-Drinkers"</note> was the name given in old times to those who drank sparingly. Hesychius simply provides the name based on the custom—unless perhaps the work we have is an epitome of what he actually wrote. It is recorded that Socrates was never accustomed to drink from the first bowl, but saved his thirst for the second. However, they called the third bowl the cup "of the Good Spirit" <note>original: *ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος* (agathou daimonos)</note>, as has been explained elsewhere. Therefore, those who saved their thirst for the third bowl were called *Agathodaemonistai*. Italians drink rarely during a banquet, and only on a "stuffed" <note>original: *faburrato* - a technical term from the playwright Plautus meaning well-filled</note> stomach. We [in Northern Europe] begin the banquet with drinking and close it with drinking, while doctors protest in vain.

->FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY<-

---

### To put bread into a cold oven.
### I

<margin>chapter 11. [they are called]</margin> "To put bread into a cold oven" <note>original: *Εἰς ψυχρὸν ἰπνὸν τοὺς ἄρτους ἐμβάλλειν*</note> is a saying used even today for someone who teaches the unteachable, who advises the unwilling, or who otherwise undertakes a useless task. It is referenced in Herodotus, Book 5, titled *Terpsichore*: The ghost of Melissa appearing to those consulting her refused to reveal where a hidden deposit was buried, as she was shivering and naked. She claimed the clothes she had been buried with were of no use because they had not been burned. She proved her identity with this sign: "that Periander had cast his bread into a cold oven" <note>original: *ὅτι εἰς ψυχρὸν τὸν ἰπνὸν περιάνδρῳ τοὺς ἄρτους ἐπέβαλε*</note>. Periander alone understood this riddle when it was reported to him, being conscious that he had committed necrophilia with her corpse. I believe this is sufficient for the sense of the proverb, which we may use in a more chaste and modest manner.

### With Mercury favorable.
### II

Hesychius indicates that the ancients, when casting lots, used to offer a prayer to Mercury for the sake of a good omen, just as at banquets they toasted to the "Good Spirit" and "Jupiter the Savior," which are discussed in their proper places. He also indicates that in drawing lots, the first lot drawn was customarily called "Mercury." One may use this jokingly when starting something new. Those who risk everything are said to "cast every die"; those who try something for the first time can be said to "draw Mercury." Julius Pollux, in Book 6, Chapter 9, indicates that in the *kreonomia* <note>the ritual distribution of meat</note>, the first portion of meat was customarily called "Mercury’s lot" <note>original: *ἑρμοῦ κλῆρον* (hermou klēron)</note>.

### Not even to believe Mercury.
### III

Strabo, in Book 2, says of a story that is hardly probable: "so that one would not even believe Mercury if he told it" <note>original: *ὥστ’ οὐδὲ τῷ ἑρμῇ πιστεύσαι τις λέγοντι*</note>. Although the passage is corrupted, as many are in this first edition, it should undoubtedly be read this way. It applies specifically to those who, having traveled through distant lands, are accustomed to telling tall tales. Mercury, after all, was considered the god of travelers.

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

### A Mercurial find.
### C

The Greeks used the term *Hermeion* <note>original: *Ἑρμαῖον*; a "godsend" or "gift from Hermes"</note> to describe a profit that came unexpectedly. This refers to the "first fruits" or small offerings that people used to place on the roads for Mercury <note>The god Hermes/Mercury was the patron of travelers and luck.</note>, which travelers would then eat. Others prefer the explanation that it comes from the heaps of stones placed along ambiguous paths as sacred markers for Mercury. These are even mentioned in the Hebrew proverbs: "As he who throws a stone into the heap of Mercury, so is he who gives honor to a fool" <note>This is a reference to Proverbs 26:8. In the Latin Vulgate, it refers to a "heap of Mercury" (*aceruum Mercurii*), though modern translations usually refer to a stone in a sling.</note>. However, this passage has been translated variously by the Greeks. Some interpreted it as: "He who binds a stone in a sling is like one who gives glory to a fool" <note>original: *ὃς ἀποδεσμεύει λίθον ἐν σφενδόνῃ, ὅμοιός ἐστι τῷ διδόντι ἄφρονι δόξαν*</note>.

Others translated *Hermeion* as *polyandrion* <note>original: *πολυάνδριον*; a place of burial for many</note>, a location designated for the burial of the masses. These people take "stone" to mean not just any rock, but a precious gem. There is little difference between those who translated it as a public cemetery and those who used "Mercurial heap," for the graves of common people were also covered by a pile of stones. This is the origin of the line by Virgil <note>original: *Maro*</note>:
->Under this mountain of stones, Ballista lies buried.<-
It is a foolish thing to cast a gem into a filthy and deathly place; it does not adorn the site but is instead defiled by it. Truly, if you throw a common stone into a Mercurial heap, there is no favor in it, for it is lost in the crowd of other stones; and if you throw a gem there, you are even more foolish. But the most clever interpretation belongs to those who translated it as a "sling." For in that case, not only is your effort wasted, but it even recoils to your harm—just as if you were to fix a stone into a fool's sling, you have merely given him the means to strike you. 

However, these points are not strictly relevant to our current purpose. The *Suda* <note>original: *Suidas*; a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> cites these words without naming the author: "It was not otherwise that the cubit-high man found a godsend, nor did he think he did any wrong if, willingly, he bought whatever he wanted from willing sellers" <note>original: *οὐκ ἦν οὐδ’ ἄλλως ὁ πήχας τὸ ἑρμαῖον...*</note>. The same source records this sentiment, again with the author’s name suppressed: "Every gain belongs to the wicked, if you are a person of good character and modesty" <note>original: *κέρδος μᾶλλον ἐστὶ τῆς κακοήθων ἅπας ἀπολαύης*</note>. For the gentleness of good people invites the audacity of the wicked. He also records a line from Damascius, it seems: "And he seemed to have stumbled upon a godsend, whoever had stumbled upon me" <note>original: *καὶ ἐδόκει ἑρμαίῳ ἐντετυχηκέναι, ὁ μοὶ ποθεν τυχών*</note>. For a traveler is refreshed when, uncertain of his path, he finds a heap of Mercury. Such a heap is called a "Mercurial mound" <note>original: *λόφος ἑρμαῖος*</note>, that is, a tomb or hill dedicated to Mercury. Philostratus, in his *Lives of the Sophists*, calls a treasure found in a building a *Hermeion*, and elsewhere he uses the term for any significant profit offered by chance.

### You have spun the thread and now need a needle.

This verse has the appearance of a proverb and seems to be in anapestic meter. Julius Pollux, in his tenth book, records it from the *Fates* by Hermippus:
"You have spun the thread, now there is need of a needle" <note>original: *ῥάμμα ἐπέκλωσας, προσδεῖται καὶ ῥαφίδος*</note>.
We use this when we want to signify that it is not enough to have begun something unless you complete it with equal industry. You have learned the theory of an art; now practice remains. You have learned grammar; logic remains. You have studied the sacred scriptures; now a good life remains.

### Since you are bald.

Gregory the Theologian <note>Saint Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, in a certain letter to the sophist Eustochius (whom he had provoked), writes: "Lest perhaps I should not have been taught by the common proverb that, since I am bald, I should not butt a ram head-on, nor provoke a wasps' nest against myself—certainly a tongue readier for speaking ill than for speaking well" <note>original: *μὴ οὐδὲ ἀπὸ τῆς παροιμίας...*</note>. We have spoken elsewhere about not "stirring up the hornets." <note>This proverb warns a person who has a "bald" or vulnerable spot not to engage in a fight where they are easily hurt.</note>

### A silver well.

"A silver well" <note>original: *φρέαρ ἀργυροῦν*</note>. Athenaeus, in his eleventh book, indicates that in ancient times a huge drinking cup was commonly called a "silver well," for ordinary cups <note>original: *cyathi*</note> were very small. Even today there are those who delight in draining deep cups and, as the poet says, "drenching their lips," having this proverb in their mouths: "Much water applied to the mouth properly softens the beard." This comes from the barbers, who soak the beard with warm water before shaving.

### He rides a bad ass.

Those whose affairs are going poorly are said to be "riding on a wretched donkey" <note>original: *ἐπ’ ὄνου πονηρᾶς ὀχούμενοι*</note>. The *Suda* records this as a proverb under the entry for "wretched" (*poneros*). For the fortunate take joy in sitting upon excellent horses so they may reach their destination more quickly. This can also be aptly cast at a man who is unhappily married.

### Garlic in the nets.

"Garlic in the nets" <note>original: *σκόροδον ἐν δικτύοις*</note>. This was said of a sordid or meager supply of provisions. From this, we find <meta>catchword: nanc</meta>

...because the Athenians, whenever they were preparing for a voyage or a military expedition, would purchase garlic and carry it with them in nets. Likewise, during the sieges of cities, garlic was highly valued; hence the expression found without a specific name in Suidas: "I am undone, losing my garlic in the siege" <note>original: "ἀπόλωμαι τὰ σκόροδα πορθέμενος"</note>. The Thracians are particularly fond of garlic because it is "hot" in nature, which suits those living in a cold region. Even today, garlic is a delicacy for sailors and a food not disliked by country folk, though it was famously detested by the poet Horace. This adage can be applied when you are advising someone who is about to embark on the study of philosophy to prepare themselves for a frugal diet, for sleepless nights, and for hard labors—without which true learning is not acquired: **Garlic in nets** <note>original: "σκόροδον ἐν δικτύοις"</note>.

### Sybarite conversations.
->X<-

Sybarite tales <note>original: "Συβαριτικοὶ λόγοι"</note>. The lexicographer Hesychius records that a certain man—I believe a Sybarite—strove with great effort among the Greeks to ensure his style of speaking was as luxurious and opulent as his lifestyle. From this, a proverbial joke arose: when a speech was overly polished and elaborate, it was called "Sybaritic." Such speech usually lacks credibility, for the language of truth is simple and brief; indeed, a man’s speech is usually a reflection of his life. Examples of this are found in Maecenas <note>A Roman counselor and patron of the arts known for his luxurious lifestyle.</note>, who was softened by his indulgences, and Apuleius <note>The author of *The Golden Ass*.</note>, the African writer and magician. The lavishness of the Sybarites is also mentioned in the proverb "A Sybarite table" <note>Referencing the ancient city of Sybaris, famous for its extreme wealth and hedonism.</note>.

### Riper than a mulberry.
->XI<-

Riper than a mulberry <note>original: "Πεπαίτερος μόρος"</note>. Aeschylus, in his play *The Phrygians*, speaks of the hero Hector in this way, as cited by Athenaeus in his second book: 
"But that man was riper than a mulberry" <note>original: "Ἀνὴρ δ’ ἐκεῖνος ἦν πεπαίτερος μόρος"</note>.
This can be said of a person endowed with a mild nature, or one who is soft, or someone who is vehemently inclined toward something—such as a young woman eager to marry. Erasmus adds, citing Nicander, that the fruit of this tree is the very first to appear. There is also a "tweaking" associated with this tree to help it reach maturity. I believe the Greek word for the fruit is written with an *omicron*—*moron* <note>Erasmus is distinguishing between *móron* (mulberry) and *mōrón* (a fool).</note>.

### Flower is ash.
->XII<-

St. Augustine, in the second book of his work against the letters of Petilianus (chapter 66), mocked his opponent for boasting that heaven was filled with the souls of his followers and that the earth "flourished" with the memory of their bodies. Augustine replied: "Indeed, we see the flowers of the earth growing from the bodies of many of them; but as the saying goes, **flower is ash**." The Donatists <note>A schismatic Christian sect in North Africa known for seeking martyrdom.</note> used to count among the number of their martyrs those who had committed suicide or provoked others to kill them; they frequently visited their monuments. It is for this reason Augustine calls those "flowers" mere ash. The phrase seems to have been commonly used to describe the fleeting nature of human life. Today youth blooms; tomorrow it will be in the tomb. As the prophet says: "All flesh is grass."

### A man always contradicting.
->XIII<-

Galen, in the book where he refutes a certain Julian who was slandering the aphorisms of Hippocrates, records this sentiment as one widely celebrated: "Nothing is more prone to wordy contradiction than a human" <note>original: "οὐδὲν ἐστὶν ἀποφαντολογώτερον ἀνθρώπῳ"</note>. The term *apophantologia* <term>apophantologia: a vice where one does not know how to stop babbling or arguing</term> refers to the habit of endless talking. It applies to those who never admit they are defeated. This vice is most prevalent among the stupid and the ignorant.

### To be mad with the mad.
->XIIII<-

"To join in madness with the mad" <note>original: "Τοῖς μαινομένοις συμμανῆναι"</note> was a saying used for someone who adapted themselves to the habits of those around them, no matter who they were. Galen used this in the first book of *On Natural Faculties*: "Since we have trifled enough—not of our own will, but as the proverb says, forced to be mad with the mad—let us return again to the classification of urines."

### Beautiful buttocks.
->XV<-

Those endowed with an elegant form were called *Callipygos* <note>original: "Καλλίπυγοι"; literally "beautiful buttocks"</note>. Athenaeus, in his twelfth book, traces the origin of the proverb to a story like this: Two sisters, the daughters of a certain farmer, were arguing on the public road about which of them had the more excellent form. A young man approached and, marveling at their beauty, showed them to his elderly father. The father, preferring the elder sister, fell in love with her. Upon returning to the city, he took to his bed in sickness. He revealed the cause of his illness to his younger son. The son went to the countryside, saw the girls, and was seized by love for the younger sister. The father of the girls eventually married them to these sons; the citizens called the women "the beautiful-buttocked ones" because of their remarkable beauty. From their wealth, a temple was built to Venus, whom they also called "Venus of the Beautiful Buttocks." Concerning them, Cercidas is quoted in a Scazon verse:
"There was once a pair of the 'Beautiful-Buttocked' in Syracuse" <note>original: "Ἦν καλλιπύγου ζεῦγος ἐν συρακούσαις"</note>.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient proverbs, specifically focusing on those derived from historical anecdotes, physical descriptions, and cultural customs of the Greeks and Romans. # DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

They call the same people "white-rumped" <note>original: "πυγάργους"</note>, as we have said elsewhere regarding the proverb "white-tails" <note>original: "λευκόπυγοι"</note>.

->**What we desire is considered holy.**<-

<margin>X</margin> Saint Augustine, in the fourth book of his work *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, writes: "It is no longer just as the old proverb goes, 'What we want is holy,' but even 'when we want it' and 'for as long as we want it.'" If I am not mistaken, he cites this elsewhere from Tyconius the Donatist. It is a half-line <note>A "hemistich" or half-verse of poetry.</note> of a heroic poem. This type of person reigns in the world today—those who do not measure piety by the rule of Christ, but by their own whims. Whatever they passionately love, they want to be seen as holy, wondrously flattering themselves even in matters that are by nature most wicked. They think it is "holy" to wear a certain kind of belt. Why? Because they desire to be regarded as saints with very little effort. Yet they do not wish to live soberly or chastely, nor to endure injuries. Why so? Because that is hard and difficult.

->**Not worth even the snap of a finger.**<-

<margin>X</margin> Athenaeus, in his twelfth book, speaking of the epitaph of Sardanapalus <note>A legendary king of Assyria known for his decadence.</note>, says: "And the dead man shows by the form of his laughter with his fingers, as if mocking, that the affairs of men are not worth the snap of one’s fingers" <note>original: "καὶ πλατάζας δείκνυσιν ᾧ γελασμαὸς τύπῳ τοῖς δακτύλοις, οἷον καταγελῶν ὅτι τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων πράγματα, οὐκ ἄξια ψόφου δακτύλων"</note>. Soon after, Aristobulus indicates in the same work that a statue was placed on Sardanapalus’s tomb with the fingers of the right hand positioned in the way we usually produce a snap. Both that gesture and the proverb remain among our own people to this day, when they say, "I don't give a snap for this."

->**Leathery assistance.**<-

<margin>X V</margin> "Leathery assistance" <note>original: "Σκυτίνη ἐπικουρία"</note>, or "skin-like help," was a phrase used among the Athenians to describe something weak and feeble. It is recorded in Hesychius. Athenaeus, in his twelfth book, indicates it was said against a certain Sannyrion, who was so thin that he had nothing but skin. In the thirteenth book of the same author, Antiphanes notes the thin philosophers: "By Jove, with those thin, starving, leathery sophists" <note>original: "μετὰ Θεσπῶν νὴ δία λεπτῶν, ἀσιτῶν, σκυτίνων"</note>. Such were the philosophers of old, just as today there are those with gloomy faces who sell their "holiness."

->**The Tanagraean whale.**<-

They used to call something obese or of a massive body "a Tanagraean whale" <note>original: "ταναγραῖον κῆτος"</note>, named after Tanagra, a city in Boeotia. Homer calls it "the old woman" <note>original: "γραῖαν"</note>, and Lycophron calls it "Poemandria." It is a coastal city where a whale of immense size was washed up, giving rise to the proverb. This is recorded by Athenaeus in his ninth book.

->**An ambassador is neither struck nor violated.**<-

The commentator on the fourth book of the *Iliad* records this proverb: "An elder (or ambassador) is not beaten nor insulted" <note>original: "πρέσβυς οὐ τύπτεται οὐδ’ ὑβρίζεται"</note>. An orator is neither struck nor violated. This is because the class of heralds was once considered sacred. It was accepted by the law of nations that ambassadors should come and go in public faith unharmed, even if they brought harsh news—such were the *feciales* <note>Ancient Roman priests who acted as diplomats.</note> and the *patres patrati* <note>The chief of the feciales.</note> in the old days. Now, even in the midst of wars, heralds are spared. This can be applied to someone giving good warnings, offering right counsel, or speaking freely in a meeting. He is an ambassador; he brings the commands of his prince, or he handles public business; it is not lawful to use force against him.

->**Herculean beds.**<-

"Herculean beds" <note>original: "Ἡράκλειοι στρωμναὶ"</note> was a term for beds that were soft and delicate. Athenaeus is the witness for this in his twelfth book. This is a strange saying, since the Cynic philosophers claim Hercules as their own <note>Because of his endurance and strength.</note>, just as today the Carmelites claim the prophet Elijah. But the person speaking in Athenaeus does this to persuade others that Hercules lived a soft and pleasure-seeking life, and that the stories told by poets about his labors are mere fictions. In this way, men flatter their own vices.

->**To shave in the Scythian manner.**<-

<margin>X</margin> Athenaeus, in his second book, relates that when the Scythians were weighed down by many calamities, they shaved the hair of all the peoples they ruled out of laziness and a love of luxury. From this, the act became a cause for disgrace and mockery for others, and they called it "Scythianizing" <note>original: "ἀποσκυθίσαι"</note>. We read something similar in the tenth chapter of the Book of Kings <note>Known today as 2 Samuel 10:4.</note>: Hanun shaved off half the beards of David’s servants and cut off their garments as far as their buttocks, as a cause for disgrace. This event was the cause of a terrible war. This proverb fits those with harsh manners, with whom hardly anyone has dealings without leaving in disgrace.

->**Thinner than Leotrephides.**<-

"Thinner than Leotrephides and Thaumantides" <note>original: "Λεωτρέφου λεπτότερος καὶ θαυμαντίδου"</note>. Leotrephides, with his remarkably thin body, provided material for the wit of comic poets; the verses of Hermippus regarding them are cited in Athenaeus, book twelve.

<summary>This page explores several ancient proverbs related to hypocrisy, worthlessness, and physical traits, often drawing on anecdotes from the scholar Athenaeus. Erasmus uses these classical examples to critique contemporary religious figures and emphasize the historical sanctity of diplomatic ambassadors.</summary>
<keywords>Augustine, Sardanapalus, diplomatic immunity, Hercules, Scythians, physical thinness, hypocrisy, Tanagra whale, Athenaeus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the seventh century of Erasmus's fourth "Chiliad" (collection of a thousand adages). It concludes a discussion on extreme thinness before moving into proverbs regarding useless efforts, frivolous service, and the Stoic philosophy of doing all things—even small ones—with excellence.</meta>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
Page 977
Nnn 3
<meta>catchword: relentem</meta>

They are now sacrificing to Buba <note>original: "θύουσιν ἤδη Βούβᾳ"</note>, thinner than Leotrophides and Thaumantides. <note>original: "Λεωτρεφίδου λεπτότερα καὶ Θαυμαντίδου"</note>. That is:
> They now sacrifice little cheeks,
> Thinner than those of Leotrophides and Thaumantides.

The poet Cinesias was also noted by many for having a body so tall yet so slender that he supposedly wore stays made of linden-wood <note>The inner bark of the lime tree, used for its flexibility.</note> around his waist so that he would not bend or break; for this reason, he was called "linden-man" <note>original: <term>φιλύρινον</term> (philurinon)</note> by Aristophanes. The poet Philetas was also made famous for this; he reportedly attached lead balls to his feet so that he would not be carried away by the winds. Such was the fragility of his little body. This adage is suitable for people who are sickly and very thin. It will be even more pleasing if it is applied to a poverty of talent, or to a style of speaking that is dry, meager, and bloodless.

->**Take nothing, and hold it well.**<-
->XXIIII<-

"Take nothing, and hold it well" <note>original: <term>λάβε μηδὲν, καὶ κράτει καλῶς</term></note>. This seems to be said against those who, while teaching frivolous things, nevertheless command their listeners to remember them. Galen, in the third book of *On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato*, says: "For in this way alone, I think, will she be persuaded by what is said in the proverb, 'Take nothing and hold it well.'" <note>original: <term>ἔστω γὰρ μόνως οἶμαι πεισθήσεσθαι τῇ παροιμίαν λεγομένου ὑπάρχειν αὐτῇ, τὸ λάβε μηδὲν καὶ κράτει καλῶς</term></note>. Indeed, by this one method she will be convinced, because that proverbial saying applies to her: Take nothing, and hold it well. This is applicable to useless and false doctrine.

->**Fly-shooers.**<-
->XXV<-

Even today, the term "fly-shooers" <note>original: <term>μυοσόβαι</term> (myosobai)</note> is commonly used—that is, those who drive away flies—to describe people who serve someone in frivolous or trivial duties. Athenaeus, in his eleventh book, indicates that this originated from the luxuries of the Persians, who employed "fly-shooers" at their banquets, a practice which is now common among the common people in Italy. And to be a "fly-shooer" is to drive away flies, which can also be applied to those who love someone so tenderly that they are offended by even the slightest inconvenience to them. This aligns with what we have reported elsewhere from Homer:
> Just as when a mother
> drives a fly away from her child, when he lies in sweet sleep. <note>original: <term>Ὡς ὅτε μήτηρ παιδὸς ἐέργῃ μυῖαν ὅθ’ ἡδέϊ λέξεται ὕπνῳ</term></note>
That is:
> Not otherwise than a mother
> wards off a fly from her boy, as sleep soothes him while he rests.

->**More wretched than gladiators.**<-
->XXVI<-

It does not lack the quality of a proverb, that which Athenaeus relates from the comic poet Posidippus in his fourth book: "He was more miserable than the gladiators" <note>original: <term>τῶν μονομάχων ἦν ἀθλιώτερος</term></note>. That is, more wretched than those who practice "monomachia" <note>A Greek term for single combat or gladiator fights.</note>. For these men are engaged under the harshest law: that either one or both must perish. The verse goes like this:
> He who has not sailed has seen no evil,
> we are more wretched than the gladiators themselves. <note>original: <term>ὁ μὴ πεπλευκὼς οὐδὲν ἑώρακεν κακὸν, τῶν μονομαχούντων ἐσμὲν ἀθλιώτεροι</term></note>
That is:
> He has seen no evil, who is ignorant of the sea,
> We are more miserable than the gladiators themselves.

The Latins called these men *gladiatores*. Although no spectacle could be more brutal, it was once a delight to the Romans. It will become more witty if you transfer it to a conflict undertaken with a most wicked man, as if you were calling it a "gladiatorial struggle."

->**It is the Zenonian way even to cook a lentil.**<-
->XXVII<-

Timon of Phlius, as cited by Athenaeus in his fourth book, says: "And it is indeed the Zenonian way even to cook a lentil" <note>original: <term>καὶ Ζηνώνειον γὲ φακὴν ἕψειν</term></note>. Zeno was the prince of the Stoics, who taught that the wise man does all things rightly; it does not matter what he does, but that in the smallest things just as in the greatest, the wise man is consistent with himself. From this, it follows that to cook a lentil correctly, one needs the wisdom of Zeno. This arose from an anecdote <note>original: <term>Apophthegmate</term></note> reported by Diogenes Laertius. For when Zeno was arguing that the wise man does all things rightly, someone mockingly objected: "Therefore, he will also cook a lentil rightly." Zeno nodded and approved of the logical conclusion. We may use this seriously when we say that it is the mark of a good man to be consistent even in the most minute matters, or that an excellent craftsman reveals his skill in whatever material he works.

->**Do not eat the olive.**<-
->XXVIII<-

Chrysippus, in his work *On Beauty*, as cited by Athenaeus in book ten, passes down a sentiment of this kind: "Never eat an olive when you have a nettle in the winter season" <note>original: <term>μή ποτε ἐλαίαν ἔδι’ ἀκαλύφῳ ἔχων χεμῶνι ὥρᾳ</term></note>. I believe he is referring to the herb, not the fish. Nor do I see the use of the adage, unless it is to signify extreme parsimony in living, such that no seasoning is added even to a nettle. Soon after, he mentions "bulb-lentils" <note>original: <term>βολβοφακῶν</term></note> as if they were a delicacy—a type of food (as the Greek word indicates) made from bulbs and lentils. "Bulb-lentils, wow, wow!" <note>original: <term>Βολβοφακῶν, βαβαὶ, βαβαί</term></note>. A nettle is warming, but it costs less than oil. He implies, however, that in the summer months neither oil nor nettles are needed. Such a diet was fitting for those who imagine themselves to be like Paul or Anthony <note>Saint Paul the Hermit and Saint Anthony the Great, early Christian ascetics.</note>, yet in their luxury are closer to Sardanapalus.

->**The pot touched the lentil.**<-
->XXIX<-

Epicharmus, in the place we just cited in Athenaeus, says: "But the pot has touched the lentil" <note>original: <term>χύτρα δὲ φακέας ἧψεν</term></note>. This will apply to those who are strongly inclined toward something, as if born for it, so that they turn themselves toward what they desire even when no occasion is given. An earthenware pot seems to love...

It also touches upon Roman gladiatorial combat and the dietary habits of ancient ascetics versus decadents.</summary>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
Page 978

...to the lentil, and as if coming to the lentil of one’s own accord. This is similar to what we reported elsewhere: "The vegetables choose their own pot" <note>original: "Ipsa olera la legit"</note>, and, "A horse to the plain."

<margin>xi.</margin>
->**He who is not jealous.**<-
St. Augustine, in his work *Against Adimantus*, chapter 13, indicates that it was a common saying: "He who is not jealous, does not love." <note>original: "Quí non zelat, non amat"</note> This is indeed still said today, when people deny that love exists where there is no jealousy. It is true that jealousy is born from the intensity of love, but it also sometimes arises from a poverty of the mind. God is called "jealous" in the sacred scriptures because he alone wishes to be loved, and does not suffer anything to be loved except himself, unless it is loved for his sake.

<margin>xi.</margin>
->**A lentil god.**<-
In Athenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note>, book 4, this verse is cited, which appears to be proverbial:
"May a lentil god and a lentil fortune seize you." <note>original: <term>φάκός σε δαίμων, καὶ φακῆ τύχη λάβοι</term></note>
The word *phakos* <note>original: <term>φάκός</term></note> refers to a raw lentil, while *phake* <note>original: <term>φακῆ</term></note> refers to a cooked one, as the *Etymologist* indicates. This adage is suitable whenever the same tedious things are repeated to the point of disgust. To the Greeks, "Daemon" <note>original: <term>Δαέμον</term></note> signifies fortune, which is why the unhappy are called "cacodaemons" <note>literally "evil-spirits" or "ill-fated".</note>. The word *tyche* <note>original: <term>τύχη</term></note> means the same thing; the only difference is that *daemon* is masculine and *tyche* is feminine.

<margin>xx.</margin>
->**A beam in all things.**<-
"A beam is fashioned in all things." <note>original: <term>Δοκὸς ἐν πᾶσι τέτυκται</term></note> This appears to be a half-line of verse from some poet, signifying that nothing is so certain that some small doubt or "scruple" does not stand in the way, forcing us to consider the matter more exactly. The Gospel also mentions a beam in the eye. Furthermore, the Greek word *dokos* <note>original: <term>δοκὸς</term></note> is ambiguous: it can mean a "beam" (though they prefer the sound of *dokeso* for that) and "consideration" or "opinion" (*dokesin*). That saying of Socrates is well known: "Consider anxiously." <note>original: <term>φρόντιζε</term></note> Galen <note>The most famous physician of the Roman Empire.</note> cites this proverb in his third book *On the Differences of Pulses*. It seems to be a metaphor taken from plowing, when a beam or stump frequently encountered in the field makes the furrowing difficult.

<margin>xx.</margin>
->**Pilots from a book.**<-
Galen, in the book he wrote *On His Own Books*, says: "But those who have not learned from a master are, according to the proverb, like pilots from a book." <note>original: <term>τοῖς ἐκ βιβλίων κυβερνήταις</term></note> He seeks out the same type of people in the third book of *On the Composition of Medicines*: "They are like those who are called 'pilots from a book' in the proverb." We have spoken elsewhere regarding "silent masters" <note>books that provide knowledge without active guidance.</note>.

<margin>xx.</margin>
->**With broken ears.**<-
Galen, writing *Against Thrasybulus*, says: "Those whose wonderful writings are now admired by those with broken ears." <note>original: <term>ὑπὸ τῶν κατεαγότων</term></note> If I am not mistaken, he is referring to boxers who, having later become physicians, write books; or rather, he refers to the books of unskilled doctors which are read by boxers. Boxers typically have broken ears according to their custom, as well as bruised eyes and a face marked by swellings from the trade they practice. Indeed, Galen frequently vents his anger against the race of athletes. Plato used this adage in the *Gorgias*, though the sense is not entirely clear. For when Socrates said he heard that Pythagoras had made the Athenians worse—namely, lazy, cowardly, talkative, and greedy—because he was the first to institute mercenary wages, Callicles replied: "You hear these things, Socrates, from those who have broken ears." <note>original: <term>τὰ ὦτα κατεαγότων ἀκούεις</term></note> He means athletes and barbarians, to whom those who are far removed from military ferocity seem "lazy." I wish for this interpretation of mine to hold until something more certain is brought forward. We have spoken elsewhere of "pierced ears." It is suitable for a pugnacious man, and for one who, just as he marks many people, is himself marked by many.

<margin>xi.</margin>
->**A white crow.**<-
Regarding things that are rare to find, Juvenal <note>A Roman satirist.</note> said:
"Rarer even than a white crow." <note>original: "Coruo quoq; rarior albo"</note>
Ammianus says in an epigram:
"One would sooner find white crows or winged tortoises." <note>original: <term>Θᾶττον ἔην λευκοὺς κόρακας πτηvάς τε χελώνας Εὑρεῖν</term></note>
Galen, in the first book of *On Natural Faculties*, criticizing a certain Lycus who neither possessed the severity of Erasistratus nor offered the truth himself, says: "And so Lycus, when he seems to be telling the truth... is like the crow in the proverb, which can neither mix with the crows themselves because of its color, nor with the pigeons because of its size." <note>original: <term>ἔοικε κόρακι, μήτε αὐτοῖς τοῖς κόραξιν ἀναμιχθῆναι δυναμένῳ</term></note> That is, since it is clear that Lycus neither...

It also discusses "broken ears" as a metaphor for the rough, unrefined perspective of athletes or the unlearned.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the seventh century of Erasmus’s fourth "Chiliad" (a collection of a thousand adages). FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
Nnn 4
<meta>catchword: φαλαῖς (phalaîs)</meta>

...nor the same as Erasistratus <note>A famous Greek anatomist and royal physician in the 3rd century BCE</note>, he seems like a **white crow**, who cannot mix with the crows themselves because of his color, nor with the pigeons because of his size. It applies to a man of his own peculiar nature, one who is a stranger to common sense. For there are those who are ashamed to ever agree with anyone, as if nothing were true unless it were different.

->**A story to an ass.** XXXVI<-

Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note>, in *On Natural Faculties*, book 3: "To others, the writing is composed in such a popular style <note>original: <term>πολιτικῶς</term> (politikōs)</note>, as if one were telling a story to an ass." <note>original: <term>τοῖς δ’ ἄλλοις οὕτω γέγραπται τὸ γράμμα πολιτικῶς, ὡς εἰ καὶ μῦθον ὄνῳ τις λέγοι</term></note>. That is: "Indeed, to the rest, the writing would be as useless as if someone were to tell a story to an ass." It appears in the *Greek Collections*: "Someone told a story to an ass, but he just twitched his ears." <note>original: <term>ὄνῳ τις ἔλεγε μῦθον, ὁ δὲ τὰ ὦτα ἐκίνει</term></note>. Galen alluded to this in *On the Difference of Pulses*, book 2: "Of the others, he who does not write has already, like an ass, twitched his ears." <note>original: <term>τῶν ἑτέρων ὁ μὴ γράφων ὥσπερ ὄνῳ ἔσφαγε ἤδη τὰ ὦτα</term></note>. That is: "In response to these things, that old man indeed, like an ass, was shaking his little ears, I suppose, because he did not agree." I think we have said something about these elsewhere.

->**Fruit under another’s tree.** XXXVII<-

Those who enjoy the labors of others are said to "gather fruit from another's tree." Thus Fabius <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus, the Roman general</note> says in Livy’s *History of Rome*, book 10: "Fabius considered it unworthy that another should gather fruit under the tree he himself had planted." It is closely related to: "He reaps another’s harvest."

->**To bore a hole in a millet seed.** XXXVIII<-

"To bore through a millet seed" <note>original: <term>Κέγχρον τρυπᾶν</term></note> is said of those who labor at something difficult but utterly useless. Galen, in *On Prognosis*, criticizing the sophists who think the study of philosophy is extremely useless, speaks thus: "Rather, they have come to believe it is the most useless of all disciplines, just like boring through a millet seed." <note>original: <term>ἀλλ’ ἁπάντων μαθημάτων ἀχρηστότατον εἶναι νενομίκασιν, ὁμοίως τῷ κέγχρον τρυπᾶν</term></note>. For we think it should be read this way, although in the published books it is written as *the millet* <note>original: <term>τὸ κέγχρον</term></note>. That is: a tiny kind of legume, which you could not easily bore through like a gemstone, and even if bored through, there would be no use for it. Similar was the zeal of that man who used to throw millet grains from a distance through the eye of a needle.

->**Wool to the fuller’s shop.** XXXIX<-

Those who do things in the wrong order—as if someone were to entrust a boy to a Theologian to be taught the basic elements of grammar—are said to "bring wool into a fuller’s shop." For the fuller’s art <note>The process of cleaning, thickening, and finishing cloth</note> deals not with raw wool, but with cloth already woven. Galen, in *On the Difference of Pulses*, book 2: "If anyone wishes to follow these things accurately, since you desire it, he must first be trained in the categories; for the saying of Arcesilaus <note>A Greek skeptical philosopher</note> is fine: 'No one brings a fleece to the fuller.' Just as there is an order in working with wool, so there is in teaching disciplines." <note>original: <term>ὡς οὐδεὶς πόκον εἰς γναφείου φέρει. τάξις γάρ ἐστιν ὥσπερ ἐρίων ἐργασίας, οὕτω καὶ μαθημάτων διδασκαλίας</term></note>. Diogenes Laertius records this about him among the Academics: that he was accustomed not to tolerate those who touched upon the liberal arts at the wrong time—for instance, if someone wanted to learn poetry or rhetoric while ignorant of grammar.

->**From the smoke to the flame.** XL<-

Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note>, book 14: "And as usually happens when the Fates lay their hands on us, the senses of men are dulled and blunted; lured by these attractions toward a better expectation, and having departed from Antioch, with Melevus dictating, he was heading straight from the smoke, as the old proverb says, to the flame." It is said of one who has cast himself from uncertain circumstances into immediate destruction. Elsewhere we reported from Plautus: "Flame is very close to smoke."

->**Rowers of cups.** XLI<-

"Rowers of cups" <note>original: <term>Κυλίκων ἐρέται</term></note> was the name given to those who drank constantly, treating wine as their oar. Thus Dionysius, surnamed "the Bronze," <note>A 5th-century BCE Athenian poet and politician</note> in Athenaeus, book 10, in his *Elegies*:
> "And bringing Antian wine in a rowing-song to you, Bacchus,
> The sailors of the symposium and the rowers of cups."
id est,
> If any bring wines in rowing for you, Bacchus,
> Sailors of drinking, the rowing of cups.
A huge cup is like a bay; in this they "row," not with oars, but with the tongue; and not infrequently they suffer shipwreck, with the loss of both money and mind.

->**To begin from the nails.** XLII<-

"To begin from the nails" <note>original: <term>Ἐκ τῶν ὀνύχων ἄρχεσθαι</term></note> is what they say of those who start from the most trivial things that have very little to do with the matter at hand. Thus Basil <note>St. Basil the Great, a 4th-century Greek bishop</note> in a certain letter: "It being ridiculous to begin from the nails, and not from the heads <note>the main points</note> of the matters themselves."

<summary>Erasmus compiles adages regarding wasted or misplaced effort, such as "telling a story to an ass" or "boring a millet seed," and warns against ignoring the proper order of learning. He also explains metaphors for those who fall from bad situations into worse ("from smoke to flame") and chronic drinkers ("rowers of cups").</summary>
<keywords>useless labor, education, grammar, Galen, Arcesilaus, Ammianus Marcellinus, alcoholism, metaphors, Greek proverbs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Greek and Latin adages. The previous page ended mid-discussion of an adage regarding improper starting points or wasted efforts. This page continues that theme before transitioning into proverbs about uninvited guests, unfair punishments, and ritualistic curses.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES
f 4

...**to be ground by whale-bones** <note>original: φαλαῖς ἀλελεῖσθαι. Erasmus interprets the Greek "phalas" as whale-bones or perhaps claws</note>. That is: it is ridiculous to start from the claws rather than speaking with the very "heads" of the matter. The "head" of a thing is said to be its most important part. This will be used whenever we advise that, leaving aside peripheral and frivolous things <note>original: <term>parergis</term></note>, the core case should be dealt with. Or, if someone wishes to reform the state of the republic, they should start with the princes rather than the humble, who do not bring much weight either to the destruction or the salvation of the city.

->**Flies.**<-
<margin>XL</margin>
In the past, those who delighted in another’s table were called "Flies" <note>original: <term>Μῦαι</term> (myai)</note>; the playwright Plautus compares them to mice, who are always eating someone else’s food. In Athenaeus <note>A 2nd-century Greek author who preserved many fragments of lost literature</note>, book six, a certain parasite compares himself to a fly:
"To dine uninvited, a fly." <note>original: <term>Δεῖπνειν ἄκλητος, μυῖα</term></note>. That is,
"Because I love to dine uninvited, I am a fly."
For this insect flies toward someone else's food and can hardly be driven away. In the same author, Hesychander relates that when Alexander said he was being bitten by flies (for so he called his parasites) and tried to drive them away, Cinesias—one of that rank who happened to be present—remarked: "Truly, other more ticklish flies will press upon you once they have tasted your blood." There is an Aesopic fable about a hedgehog who wanted to be a "fly-life" <note>original: <term>μυσόβιος</term> (mysobios), someone living like a parasite</note> to a fox. Plautus, in his play *The Merchant*, applied this to a curious man who flies at everything: "My father is a fly. Nothing can be kept secret from him; there is nothing so sacred or profane that he is not immediately present."

->**Baon, a bad fish.**<-
<margin>XLI</margin>
Athenaeus, book seven, testifies that there was a proverb among the people of Attica: "Not for me Baon, a worthless fish." <note>original: <term>μή μοι Βαὼν, κακὸς ἰχθύς</term></note>.
He does not indicate the specific use of the proverb, only showing that in the works of Epicharmus <note>an early Greek comic poet</note>, a certain fish was called *Baon*. The name seems to have been given because of its smallness. For large fish are usually praised. It could be said of an ungrateful and annoying guest.

->**To dine from a basket.**<-
<margin>XLII</margin>
Athenaeus, book eight. The Greeks said "to dine from a basket" <note>original: <term>ἀπὸ σπυρίδος δειπνεῖν</term></note>. Properly, they called it a "dinner from a basket" whenever someone prepared a meal for themselves and, having placed it in a basket, went to dine at someone else's house. This custom still exists today among frugal people who neither want to be burdened by the expense of hosting, nor want to burden others. It will be more elegant if transferred to someone who approaches a conversation for the sake of learning, such that they themselves bring something in turn to teach, so that an exchange of erudition occurs.

->**The flute-player gets beaten.**<-
<margin>XLIII</margin>
Eubulus, in Athenaeus book nine, says it was a custom that if the cook made a mistake, the flute-player was usually beaten. Philyllius, in the same author, writes:
"Whatever wrong the cook happens to have done, the flute-player receives the blows." <note>original: <term>Ὅτι ἂν τύχῃ Μάγειρος ἀδικήσας, τὸν αὐλητὴν λαβεῖν πληγάς</term></note>.
Hence, a certain cook in the same author says he is telling a story not of old, but one invented by himself, "lest," he says, "the flute-player be beaten" <note>original: <term>ἵνα μὴ ὁ αὐλητὴς πληγὰς λάβῃ</term></note>. For this reason, I suppose—because it is not safe to harm some people—there is a sentiment cited a little later in the same work:
"No man has ever escaped unharmed after hurting a cook." <note>original: <term>Οὐδεὶς μάγειρον ἀδικήσας, ἀθῷος διέφυγε</term></note>.
Though the Greek verse is not free from errors.

->**To sow curses.**<-
<margin>XLIV</margin>
"To sow curses" <note>original: <term>Ἀρὰς κατασπείρειν</term></note>. Those who had cursed someone with dire imprecations were said to "sow" them. This originated from a solemn custom among the Cypriots: whenever they sowed barley, they would add salt and curse those they wished ill upon. This is from Hesychius <note>a Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note>. Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> teaches that certain things are not sown successfully except when accompanied by insults. There is also a type of curse where, when something is buried in the earth and pressed down with the foot, an imprecation is added: "May you never come out." We have spoken elsewhere of the sacred rites of the people of Lindos.

->**May you be turned back into water and earth.**<-
<margin>XLV</margin>
"May you be turned back into water and earth." <note>original: <term>Ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα γένοισθε</term></note>.
This stands for: "may you be reduced to nothing and perish." This half-line of verse is reported by Hesychius as a commonly tossed-about proverb. It is taken, however, from the *Iliad*, book seven. For with these words, Menelaus rebukes the cowardice of the Greeks because no one dared to take up the single combat with Hector when he issued the challenge.

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient adages. # THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<page-num>981</page-num>

"But may you all become water and earth." <note>original: "Ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς μὲν πάντες ὕδωρ καὶ γαῖα γένοισθε." A quote from Homer's *Iliad* (7.99), used as a curse or a reminder of mortality.</note>

Plutarch, in his *Life of Homer*, and Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle</note> in the first book of his *Problems*, number 77, provide a physical explanation for why Homer spoke this way: all things are born from earth and water, and all things are eventually dissolved back into them. This concept is not far removed from a passage by Epicharmus <note>A Greek comic playwright and philosopher</note> cited by Plutarch in his *Consolation to Apollonius*: "They were combined and they were separated, and they went back again from whence they came; earth to earth, but the spirit upward. What is harsh in this? Not a single thing." <note>original: "συνεκρίθη καὶ διεκρίθη, καὶ ἀπῆλθεν ὅθεν ἦλθε πάλιν, γᾶ μὲν εἰς γᾶν, πνεῦμα δὲ ἄνω. τί τῶνδε χαλεπόν; οὐδὲ ἕν."</note> He is speaking here of death, which is the dissolution of the body and the soul. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the third book of his *Tusculan Disputations*, quotes from Euripides:

> Earth must be returned to earth, then life for all
> Must be reaped like crops; so necessity commands.
> <note>original: "Reddenda terræ terra, tum uita omnibus / Metenda ut fruges, sic iubet necessitas."</note>

Antiochus <note>of Ascalon, a philosopher</note> writes that this sentiment was pleasing to Chrysippus <note>a Stoic philosopher</note>, though Carneades <note>a Skeptic philosopher</note> disagreed. The Hebrew author of Ecclesiastes expressed the same sentiment enigmatically <note>referring to Ecclesiastes 12:7, "the dust returns to the ground it came from."</note>. Finally, Aristotle in the second book of his *Rhetoric* hints that those who in ancient times professed their servitude were accustomed to hand over earth and water to their master, as if renouncing their right to all things and transferring it to their lord. "And that," he says, "to give earth and water, is to serve." <note>original: "τὸ ὅτι... διδόναι γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ, δουλεύειν ἐστὶ." This refers to the Persian demand for "earth and water" as a token of submission.</note>

### Mars is shared.
### XLIX

They used this saying—"Mars is shared"—to note the uncertain and variable outcome of war. <note>original: "Ἄρης κοινός" (Ares koinos). Mars (Ares) was the god of war; to say he is "shared" means he does not always side with one party.</note> It is taken from Homer’s *Iliad*, book 18:
"The War-god is shared, and he slays even the one who would slay." <note>original: "ξυνὸς ἐνυάλιος καί τε κτανέοντα κατέκτα."</note>
Aristotle mentions this saying among his proverbial sentences in the second book of his *Rhetoric*.
Again, in the same book:
"Victory shifts between men." <note>original: "νίκη δ’ ἐπαμείβεται ἄνδρας."</note>
Titus Livy, in the tenth book of the *Punic War*: "Consider in your mind both your own strength and the power of fortune, and that the Mars of war is shared; on both sides there was steel and human bodies; nowhere do results correspond less than in war." Again, in his *History of Rome*, book 8: "What would he have done if—as the chances of war and the shared Mars bring about—the battle had gone unfavorably?" And again in the same book: "Our struggles, Romans—not the words of ambassadors, nor any man as arbiter—but the Campanian field where we must clash, and arms, and the shared Mars of war shall decide." And elsewhere in the same: "There in the councils, their general Numitius, by affirming that the Mars of war is truly shared and had laid low both battle lines with equal slaughter, etc." Again, in the seventh book of the *History*: "The Samnite war," he says, "was waged with an uncertain Mars." In the same author, the phrase "They departed with an equal Mars" <note>original: "Æquo Marte discessum est."</note> is frequent whenever victory fell to neither side. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his eleventh *Philippic*: "But even if I grant that the exits of war are uncertain and Mars is shared, nevertheless we must decide with risk to life for the sake of liberty." We touched upon "the shared Mars" somewhat in the proverb *The Vicissitude of All Things*. Furthermore, Mars is called *Enyalios* <note>an epithet of the war god</note> by Homer, from *Enyo* <note>a goddess of war</note>, whom they believe to be the "fortune of war."

### Law in the hands.
### L

"By the law of the hands" <note>original: "Ἐν χερσὶν νόμῳ."</note> is said when a matter is conducted by force rather than by the prescription of laws. Aeschines, in his speech *Against Timarchus*: "But those who favor oligarchy and those who live under an unequal constitution must be on guard against those who would destroy the state by the law of the hands." <note>original: "φυλακτέον δὲ τοῖς μὲν ὀλιγαρχικοῖς... οὓς ἂν χερῶν νόμῳ τὰς πολιτείας καταλύοντας."</note> He calls violence, or the right of war, the "law of the hands." Polybius used it in this sense in the first book of his *Histories*: "Of the enemies, whomever he once conquered, some he destroyed by the law of the hands, while others, having been brought back alive as captives, he threw to the beasts." Again, in book 2: "In this same time it happened that Gaius the consul, while fighting too boldly, ended his life by the law of the hands." <note>Meaning he died in hand-to-hand combat.</note> The phrase "this authority" <note>original: "αὕτη κυρία"</note> has been discussed elsewhere. In Plautus, a certain servant threatens that he will "conduct the lawsuit with his hand" <note>Meaning he will settle the matter with a fistfight.</note>.

### Nothing is emptier than knowing many things.
### LI

In Athenaeus, book 13, Hippon—who was called "the atheist"—is cited as the author of this little verse:

<meta>catchword: Poly- (likely "Polymathia" or "Much learning")</meta>

He also defines the "law of the hands" as a metaphor for raw violence and military force prevailing over civil law.</summary>

<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion of the Hebrew perspective on mortality and the phrase "returning to the earth." This page transitions into critiques of superficial learning and various ancient metaphors for social behavior, diet, and necessity.</meta>

<page-num>982</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

"What is emptier than much learning?" <note>original: "πολυμαθημοσύνης τί δ’ κενεώτερον ἄλλο." A line from the Greek philosopher and satirist Timon of Phlius.</note> That is to say:
Think nothing else more empty than knowing a great deal.
The same line is cited from Timon:
"What is emptier than much learning?"
This will be suitable for those who prefer to learn many things rather than useful things. The Hebrew book of Ecclesiastes does not shrink from this sentiment: "He who adds knowledge, adds sorrow," <note>Ecclesiastes 1:18</note> and in much knowledge there is much indignation. On the other hand, the <term>polymathia</term> <note>meaning "broad learning" or "versatility"</note> of Hippias <note>A famous Greek Sophist known for his wide range of knowledge</note> was highly praised.

->To draw in a circle.<-

When someone uses artifice to lead another person around so that, while they think they have accomplished something, they have actually achieved nothing—or they fall back into the very situation they wished to escape—it is called "to draw in a circle" <note>original: "κύκλω περιέλκειν" (kyklo perielkein)</note>. Thus Plato says in the *Charmides*: "O you rogue, you have been drawing me in a circle for a long time, hiding your meaning from me." <note>original: "ὦ μιαφλω ἐγὼ, πάλαι με περιέλκεις κύκλω ἀποκρυπτόμενος."</note> This occurs in the <term>sophistic art</term>, where a disputant, after being led through various winding paths, eventually denies what they previously affirmed, or vice versa. The metaphor is drawn from those who, having been driven in a circle, are brought back to the very place from which they had previously shrunk away in fear. A similar game is played in Labyrinths. Closely related to this is: "You have fallen into the same handles."

->Jupiter’s milk.<-

The ancients used the phrase "Jupiter’s milk" <note>original: "Iouis lac"</note> to refer to food that was exceptionally refined or luxurious. Euripides, as cited in Athenaeus <note>A Greek author of the 2nd/3rd century AD known for his "Deipnosophistae" or "Banquet of the Learned"</note>, says:
"And there is juicy cheese and Jupiter’s milk." <note>original: "Καὶ τυρὸς ὀπίας ἐστὶ, καὶ διὸς γάλα."</note>
In the same author, "Jupiter’s brain" <note>original: "διὸς ἐγκέφαλος"</note> is frequently mentioned among the delicacies of food, about which we have spoken elsewhere. The Persians, if something was exquisitely refined, called it "the brain of Jupiter and the King," because the King of the Persians used to give an honorary reward if someone discovered a new kind of edible dish. Clearchus, in the same author's twelfth book, records this in many other words. It seems the ancients attributed whatever they saw as extraordinary to Jupiter. Hence that line from the Satires:
"And you save those things for Jupiter’s ears." <note>Persius, Satire 2.7. Suggesting things of the highest quality or most private importance.</note>

->Maesonic witticisms.<-

Jokes thrown about rather petulantly were called "Maesonic witticisms" <note>original: "σκώμματα μαισωνικά"</note> by the ancients, after a certain comic actor from Megara named Maeson. He invented the mask that the Greeks called a "Maeson" after its inventor; specifically, he invented the masks for the servant and the cook. Indeed, the ancient Greeks called a sophisticated city-cook a "Maeson," and a foreign one a "cricket" <note>original: "τέττιγα" (tettiga)</note>. In comedies, cooks are always portrayed as talkative and witty, especially in the plays of Plautus. Philemon testifies to this somewhere:
"I have received into my house not a cook, but a male Sphinx; for by the gods, I simply do not understand anything he says." <note>original: "Σφίγγ’ ἄῤῥην’, οὐ μάγειρον εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν, Εἰληφ’..."</note>
This is consistent with the style of Hipponax <note>A Greek poet known for his biting satire</note>.

->Necessity the teacher.<-

Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia/lexicon</note> cites this proverb from Carchedonius:
"Necessity is the teacher that makes the wise man out of the unrefined." <note>original: "χρεία διδάσκει, κἂν ἄμουσος ᾖ, σοφόν."</note>
Time, the experience of things, and necessity itself rouse the mind to learn the arts. There is a similar Greek sentiment: "I have been allotted a violent poverty." And in Aristophanes, Poverty boasts that she is the inventor of the arts. Persius says the belly is the "master of art and the giver of genius." And as Quintilian says: "Necessity sharpens laziness."

->A thorny life.<-

"A thorny life" <note>original: "Βίος ἀκανθώδης" (Bios akanthodes)</note>, that is, a life that is prickly, rough, hard, and old-fashioned—the kind of life led by those for whom thistles served in place of cakes. Suidas joins this to the Attic proverbs used to describe a troublesome or un-luxurious life, as a kind of contrary. He also indicates that "a life not worth living" <note>original: "βίος ἄβιος" (bios abios)</note> is used in the same sense: a sad and unpleasant life. For in Latin, "vital" is sometimes said not of those who merely breathe, but of those who live jovially. Conversely, the Greeks use "un-vital" <note>original: "ἀβίωτος"</note> for those who lack the protections and comforts of life. Aeschines, in his speech against Timarchus, speaks of "branding such a woman with disgrace and making her life un-vital."

<summary>Erasmus explores several adages concerning the vanity of excessive but useless knowledge, the nature of circular arguments, and the linguistic origins of terms for luxury, wit, and necessity. He emphasizes the classical view that hardship (necessity) is the primary driver of human ingenuity and art.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of adages from the previous page, concluding a discussion on the quality of life and beginning a series of proverbs related to natural recognition and misguided instruction. It then transitions into a significant dedicatory letter from Erasmus to the young Charles Blount, son of his longtime patron Lord Mountjoy.</meta>

...rendering life not worth living. For to live basely is not truly living. It can also be understood as referring to one's resources being cut off. Likewise, in the speech *On the False Embassy*, it is said: "I consider the rest of my life no longer worth living" <note>original: "ἀβίωτον ἔτι μοι τὸν λοιπὸν βίον νομίζω"</note>, that is, I consider the remainder of my life to be unhappy and calamitous.

<margin>57</margin>
Aristotle, in the first book of his *Rhetoric*, lists this among the proverbs of similarity and kinship:
"The beast surely knows the beast" <note>original: "Ἔγνωκε θὴρ θῆρα"</note>. That is,
A wild animal certainly recognizes another wild animal.

It appears to be a fragment of an iambic trimeter verse, though it is somewhat corrupted in Aristotle’s text. To the Greeks, <term>thēr</term> <note>originally meaning a wild animal or beast of prey</note> refers to a beast, but specifically one that is wild or harmful, such as boars, wolves, and vipers. From this, they call a person of savage character and rustic disposition "beastly" <note>original: "θηριώδη" (thēriōdē)</note>. This is used when two equally wicked people get along. It is similar to the saying: "A thief knows a thief, and a wolf knows a wolf."

<margin>58</margin>
->The blind man’s instruction.<-

"An instruction to a blind man" <note>original: "τυφλῷ παρακελεύσης"</note>, that is, the command or exhortation of a blind person, is said to be absurd whenever the very person who prescribes the rules does not understand what he is saying. Socrates, in Plato’s *Theaetetus*, refutes the absurd instruction of Theaetetus—who commanded that one who holds a correct opinion should assent to that correct opinion—by comparing his speech to a rotating thong or a pestle. However, Socrates thinks it would be more accurately called "the blind man's command" <note>original: "τυφλοῦ ἢ παρακέλευσις ἂν καλῶῖτο δικαιότερον. τὸ γὰρ ἃ ἔχομεν ταῦτα προσλαβεῖν κελεύειν, ἵνα μάθωμεν ἃ δοξάζομεν, πάνυ γυμναίως ἔοικεν ἐσκοτωμένῳ"</note>. That is: "But it might more justly be called a blind man’s instruction; for to command us to accept those things which we already have, in order that we might learn those things which we already believe, clearly suits a man who is remarkably in the dark." Elsewhere, we have noted that line from Horace: "As if a blind man were to show the way." Likewise: "Blind speculation."

### TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS YOUTH CHARLES
->BLOUNT, DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-
->SENDS HIS GREETINGS.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring a classical figure or deity within an architectural frame.</image-desc>

Most distinguished young man, your father was so far from being troubled that the dedication of this entire work was shared with you in the last edition, that he rejoiced greatly. He saw it as a spur added to your natural talent, even though you are already running quite vigorously in the fields of the Muses of your own accord. Being a man as wise as he is pious, he interpreted it as a noble gain that you should have a partner and a rival in this kind of honor, which increases rather than diminishes through being shared. He does not believe that anything has been taken away from his own merits; rather, he judges his own happiness to be splendidly doubled if he sees the virtues with which he is himself uncommonly refined propagated in his son. Therefore, it seemed appropriate to dedicate this addition to the work—which is so large that it could be considered a full volume in its own right—specifically to your name. By this, you may run more eagerly, and he may rejoice more intensely. Indeed, out of his singular affection for you and his equal modesty, he enjoys your good qualities more than his own; or rather, he considers those things his own best goods which he sees blossoming in his son, more so than those he recognizes as having matured in himself. For the goods of the mind do not know old age. Be strengthened in that spirit, excellent youth; press on with what you have begun. Proceed daily to increase the joy of your excellent parent and to bring your own happiness to perfection in every way. You will achieve this if you model your studies after the domestic pattern of your father, joining true piety with liberal education, and if neither the fame of your lineage, nor the indulgence of fortune, nor the customs of the court, nor the love of a wife, nor the care of children distracts your mind from the commerce of <term>Philology</term> <note>In the Renaissance sense: the love of learning and the study of classical literature</note>. If anyone should object here that neither human talent nor the brevity of time can hold so many affairs at once, I ask you to calculate how great a part of life perishes for others in games of cards and dice, and with how much less expense, greater pleasure, and finally greater fruit, this time might be spent in the reading of good authors. Therefore, Charles, make sure you express your father to me in every way, with this one exception: that he was accustomed to pore over books almost from dinner until the middle of the night, so that I have often wondered how he managed it without harm to his health. I have written these things groaning and mourning, and utterly displeased with myself, because I had heard for certain that that incomparable hero, William Warham, Archbishop [of Canterbury]...

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on proverbs, but immediately transitions into a personal and poignant letter from Erasmus regarding the death of his great patron, William Warham, the Archbishop of Canterbury. # DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...that the Archbishop of Canterbury <note>William Warham (c. 1450–1532), a central figure in the English church and Erasmus's most generous patron</note> has exchanged life for death—or rather, to put it more accurately, has emigrated from this shadow of life into the land of eternal life. I deplore my own lot, not his. He was to me like a **sacred anchor** <note>original: "sacra ancora"; a Greek and Latin metaphor for a final refuge or last hope</note>. We had entered into a pact of **those who die together** <note>original: "συναποθνησκόντων" (synapothnēskontōn); a reference to friends who pledge to remain together even in death</note>; he had promised a shared tomb, and I did not doubt that he, although fourteen years older, would survive me. Yet certainly, it was neither old age nor disease that took him from us, but an unhappy turn of fate—less so for him than for scholarship, religion, the kingdom, and the church. Such was the man's piety, such his wisdom in counsel, and such his kindness in helping all people. Now that celestial soul, in exchange for the good seed he sowed here, reaps a rich harvest with Christ. Meanwhile, I linger here "half-souled," <note>original: "semi animis"</note> a debtor to a promised faith, which, unless my mind’s foreboding deceives me, I shall soon discharge. The agreement might have seemed a mere gesture of friendship, but reality cries out that it was a serious contract. Since his death, my spirit has collapsed and cannot be raised by any distractions; even with time, which usually heals the sharpest pains, this wound only grows more raw. From many directions, I feel myself being called. It will be a joy to "die together" with this incomparable and irreplaceable patron, provided that through Christ's mercy I may be allowed to live with him there. He was a brilliant star of the church; now he has reached heaven as a more brilliant one. Would that it befalls me to lie like a tiny little star next to my sun. This commemoration was given not only to my grief, but I judged it relevant to you as well, to refresh the memory of a prelate easily the most praised of all, so that you might more zealously fashion your studies and your life after a double model: your father and your father’s friend. Farewell. Given at Freiburg im Breisgau, on the first of October, in the year 1532.

### Ibycus's horse.

**Ibycus's horse** <note>original: "Ἰβύκειος ἵππος" (Ibykeios hippos)</note>. This seems to have passed into a proverbial joke regarding those who, by nature or beyond their age and strength, are driven into a dangerous business. Plato provides the origin of the saying in the *Parmenides*. The poet Ibycus had a horse that was an aging athlete, worn out by many contests. When it was harnessed for a chariot race, it trembled, clearly having experienced the gamble of such games. With the people laughing, Ibycus rose and said: "The horse is like his master; for I too, now an old man, am compelled to fall in love." He was comparing himself to his horse because he was no less unseasonable for love affairs than the old horse was for the contest. For Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> reminds us here that Ibycus was commonly ill-reputed for his love of youths. With this image, Pherenides complains that he, an old man, is driven to the explanation of very difficult matters. Horace seems to have alluded to this in his *Epistles*: "My age is not the same, nor is my mind," and:

> Be wise and release the aging horse in time, lest
> He fail at the end to laughter and strain his flanks.
> <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.8-9</note>

Perhaps while I am occupied in this **treadmill of adages** <note>original: "adagiorum pistrino"; Erasmus frequently complained that compiling the *Adagia* felt like being a slave in a grinding-mill</note>, I will seem to some not much different from Ibycus's horse. Regarding the "cranes of Ibycus," it has been discussed elsewhere.

### Serious matters for tomorrow.

**Serious matters for tomorrow** <note>original: "Εἰς αὔριον τὰ σπουδαῖα" (Eis aurion ta spoudaia)</note>. Plutarch, in the *Life of Pelopidas*, relates that this expression passed into a proverb among the Greeks. The origin was Archias, a wealthy and powerful man, but one of little sobriety. A letter was brought to him during a banquet. The messenger urged him to read it immediately, for it was written concerning serious matters. Then he, soaked with wine, said with a laugh: "Serious matters for tomorrow then," and at the same time placed the received letter under the cushion he was sitting on, continuing the conversation he had begun with Phillidas. Even today, it is considered uncivil to handle serious business at banquets. Among the Dutch, I had heard a story as a youth not foreign to this adage. A certain man was reclining at a banquet too near the fire, so that the bottom of his garment was being scorched. Noticing this, one of the guests said, "I have something to tell you." The other replied, "If it is anything unpleasant, I do not want to hear it at a banquet, where it is fitting for all things to be cheerful and happy." The first replied, "It is not exactly cheerful." Soon the other said, "After the banquet, serious things." When they had dined merrily, he said, "Now, say whatever you wish." He showed him his garment, which was enormously burnt from behind. At this, the man began to get angry because he had not warned him in time. "I wanted to," he replied, "but you forbade it: **serious matters after dinner.**"

### To attack with tunnels.

**To wage war with tunnels** <note>original: "ὑπονόμοις πολεμεῖν" (hyponomois polemein)</note>, or to fight with mines. This is said of one who conducts business not with open force, but with disguised deceits. Conversely, one who acts openly is said to "act with siege engines." When the power of Gaius Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> was already looking toward manifest tyranny, Luctatius Catulus, a man of the highest authority among...
