# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
<column-break/>
...at that dignity, rising in the senate, he said: **Caesar is no longer using tunnels, but now seizes the state with machines**, <note>original: οὐκ ἔτι ὑπονόμοι Cæsar, ἀλλ’ ἤδη μηχαναῖς αἱρεῖ τὴν πολιτείαν</note> that is, Caesar no longer removes the republic through mines, but through engines of war. Tunnelling is done in secret, while machines—such as battering rams, catapults, and ballistae—are moved forward openly. Plutarch records this saying in his *Life of Julius Caesar*. It will have even more charm if one transfers it to matters of the soul: for instance, if one were to say that evil spirits sometimes attack us with "machines," when they terrify or harass us openly, and sometimes with "tunnels," whenever they creep up on the unwary and deceive them with a false appearance of piety.

->No reasoning for destruction.<-
->LXII<-

**No reasoning for destruction.** <note>original: ὄλεθρος οὐδεὶς λόγος</note> Plutarch records this in his *Life of Eumenes*. While Eumenes was busy with his affairs and had entered Upper Phrygia, he spent the winter in Celaenae. There, because he found Alcetas, Polemon, and Docimus fighting against him for the command, he said: **As the saying goes, there is no reasoning for destruction.** I believe the meaning is that when a fatal destruction hangs over a man, God takes away his judgment and reason. It appears to be a half-line of a poem: **There is no reasoning for destruction.** Close to this is what Quintilian says in his fifth book, speaking of conjecture: "Furthermore," he says, "why did he attack in that particular place or in that particular way?" He also most carefully treats the same topic: "Was he led by no reason, but carried away by impulse and acting without judgment?" For it is commonly said that **crimes have no plan.**

->Those who need a lamp, pour in oil.<-
->LXIII<-

Plutarch, in his *Life of Pericles*, records that Anaxagoras was a great help to Pericles in governing the Republic. But when Anaxagoras was burdened by old age and felt neglected by Pericles, who was intent on public business, he decided to end his life by starvation. When Pericles learned of this, he ran to the philosopher's house and tried with prayers and tears to call him back from his resolve, more for his own sake than for Anaxagoras's. But Anaxagoras, already at death's door, said: **O Pericles, even those who have need of a lamp pour in oil.** <note>original: ὦ Περίκλεις, καὶ οἱ λύχνου χρείαν ἔχοντες, ἔλαιον ἐπιχέουσιν</note> He was reproaching him for neglecting a friend from whom he received no common benefit, just as those who need a lamp, for whatever use they have of it, take care of it by cleaning it and pouring in oil. And those who need the fruit, fertilize the field.

->To leap into the stomach.<-
->LXIIII<-

**To leap into the stomach** <note>original: εἰς τὴν γαστέρα ἅλλεσθαι</note> is said of one who focuses all his care on food and drink. Thus Plutarch speaks of Lucullus in his *Life*: **Since Lucullus was no longer making war for show or ostentation, but, as the saying goes, 'leaping into the stomach,' he was doing everything possible to cut off the enemy's food supply.** <note>original: Ἅτε δὴ μὴ θεατρικῶς μηδὲ ἐπιδεικτικῶς ἀσκόλως πολεμοῦντος, ἀλλὰ διὰ τοῦτο τὸ λεγόμενον εἰς τὴν γαστέρα ἐναλλομένου, καὶ ὅπως ὑφαιρήσει τὴν τροφὴν ἅπαντα πραγματευομένου</note> I will not repeat here how Leonardo Giustiniani <note>An Italian humanist and translator (c. 1388–1446)</note> translated this passage: "There are some whom you can conquer by no better means than by attacking their belly." 

A notable example of this strategy was given to us by Hermann von Neuenahr, <note>Hermannus à noua aquila; a German count, scholar, and friend of Erasmus</note> a man no less distinguished for his learning than for the nobility of his lineage. He had been attacked in a short preface by a certain Dominican, as if he stood on the side of Reuchlin <note>Capnio; a reference to Johannes Reuchlin, the Hebrew scholar whose conflict with the Dominicans of Cologne became a cause célèbre for humanists</note> and was degenerating from the customs and piety of his ancestors. Hermann expostulated with the slanderer, threatening all kinds of consequences. The monk only became more fierce. Finally, the Count's friends hit upon this plan: they announced to the college that if they threw out the slanderer, they would consider the rest of the members innocent. If not, they intended to turn their wrath against everyone, since the slanderer had dared his deed with the consent of all. 

When the warning was ignored, someone was sent to cut off their supplies. The prohibition was ignored, so they moved on to the <term>ooptochia</term> and <term>tyrologia</term> <note>From Greek roots meaning "bread-buying" and "cheese-collecting"—essentially the college's food distributions</note>. But after the Count's servants broke in and they narrowly escaped, a sedition arose among the members. The slanderer was forced to accept peace terms and testified in writing that he had always considered, did consider, and would consider the Count to be a learned, noble, and pious man. He confessed he had written those things which were objected to (for it was not possible to deny what had been published by the printers). Yet what he had written against the Count could only apply to a degenerate man and a patron of impiety. Thus, by his own signature, he achieved nothing except adding scurrilous impudence to his slander. Nevertheless, that man of most noble and truly Christian spirit was content with this satisfaction, with my strong approval. I think Terence had this in mind when he said, "Drive your fists into his belly," for parasites can be hurt in no part more than in the stomach.

->O ancient house, how different a master you are ruled by.<-
->LXV<-

It seems that line of Ennius's poetry should also be added to the proverbs, which Marcus Tullius Cicero records in his book *On Duties*: <note>original: O domus antiqua, quam dispari domino dominaris! The page cuts off here.</note>

<summary>This page explores several adages from Plutarch and Cicero, focusing on metaphors of warfare (machines vs. tunnels), the loss of reason during ruin, and the necessity of sustaining those who provide service. It includes a contemporary anecdote about Hermann von Neuenahr using "belly-strategy" to force a slandering monk to recant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s examination of Greek and Latin adages, moving from political observations to metaphors derived from legal, financial, and gaming contexts. It follows the previous page’s discussion on the loss of reason and historical anecdotes about Caesar.</meta>

# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY

...in the first book, **O ancient house, by how different a master you are ruled!** <note>original: "O domus antiqua quàm dispari domino dominaris"</note> This is applicable to a change of authority for the worse, caused by the faults of those who have succeeded to power—be it in a household, a city, an Academy, a monastery, or a college that has degenerated into a worse state. However, I suspect that this Ennian verse <note>Referring to the poet Ennius, the "father" of Roman poetry.</note> has been corrupted in the manuscripts and should be read as: **O house of Antius, by how different a master you are ruled**, so that it marks the successor of Antius. Since the first syllable in "dispari" is naturally long, the "s" must be removed, a practice Ennius often follows; unless perhaps you prefer "Ancus" or "Annius" instead of Antius, the latter of whom Lucilius attacks elsewhere; this would make the syllable short. Thus the meter is restored. A poorly educated scribe, thinking *antiquam* was a single word, changed it to *antiqua*. Another, unwilling to omit what was in most manuscripts, added the word *quàm*. Marcus Tullius Cicero alluded to this in his *Second Philippic*: **O wretched roofs themselves, by how different a master!** although how could that man [Mark Antony] be a master? And yet, by how different a man were they held.

<margin>LX</margin>
->To pay back both the principal and the interest.<-

They say **To pay back both the interest and the principal**, <note>original: "Καὶ τὸν τόκον καὶ τὸ κεφάλαιον ἐκτίνεῖν"</note> of those who are punished late but more severely, or those who delay their vengeance so they may strike more heavily when the opportunity arises. For interest grows through delay. Dio Chrysostom says in his essay *On Distrust*: **Just as wild beasts are often quiet when sleeping or full, they have not lost their true nature; similarly, those men were silent for a time, but then, when an excuse arose, they paid back—as the saying goes—both the interest and the principal of their malice.** Just as harmful beasts often rest, either when they sleep or when they are stuffed with food, they have not meanwhile cast off their nature; likewise, those men did not cause harm for a time, but when the opportunity presented itself, they paid back both the interest, as they say, and the principal sum of their wickedness.

<margin>LXI</margin>
->To the dead-ends.<-

For those pressed by extreme necessity, things were said to have **returned to the dead-ends.** <note>original: "Ad incitas." This refers to the *lineae incitae*, the "unmoved lines" in an ancient board game similar to backgammon or checkers, where a piece cannot be moved further.</note> Plautus says in *The Three-Penny Man*: **Look now, he to whom this field belongs is reduced to the dead-ends,** that is, to extreme poverty. The same author in *The Little Carthaginian*: **Just keep quiet; he will surely reduce the pimp to the dead-ends if he takes those women away; indeed, he would rather die by a stone than move a single piece.** <note>original: "calcem ciuerit." A *calx* was a gaming piece.</note> But I am not sure if it should be read here as "move a single penny" <note>original: "calcum," a small stone used for counting money.</note>. Nonius Marcellus advises that "incita" is a term for want, and he speaks thus, though not without a trope. For in these two places he cited from Plautus, it signifies extreme poverty, yet "incitae" does not always signify want wherever it is placed. Lucilius seems to have used "incita" in the neuter gender: **When it returns to the dead-ends and intervention.** Also: **Chewed up, he ruined it; he drove it to the dead-ends.** But Isidore, in his eighteenth book, uses it in the masculine gender. **Gaming pieces,** he says, **are moved partly in order, partly at random; those which cannot be moved at all are called "inciti."** *Cio* means "I move"; *inciti* means, as it were, "immobile." The Greeks would say *akinētos* [unmoved]. It is clear enough that the proverb is drawn from a game of pieces, in which a piece is reduced to certain lines from which it can no longer be moved. It will also apply to those who, being caught by manifest arguments, have nothing to answer—what the Logicians call the **Goal of Silence.**

<margin>LXII</margin>
->Circumscribed by center and space.<-

Plutarch in his *Precepts of Statecraft*: **If your resources are modest, let them be circumscribed by center and space according to your need.** <note>original: "ἂν ᾖ τὰ τῆς οὐσίας μέτρια, καὶ κέντρῳ καὶ διαστήματι γραφόμενα πρὸς τὴν χρείαν"</note> He means that fortunes are sometimes so narrow that unless they are managed with a fixed dimension, they will not suffice for necessary uses. Much like those who, having calculated their annual income, subtract how much they can spend each month, each week, and each day. If the arrival of a guest or a similar event causes slightly larger expenses, it is repaired by the parsimony of the following days, so that the account remains balanced. The same author in *On Talkativeness* teaches that an answer should be **circumscribed by center and space**, so that one does not answer more than the inquiry requires. For some, when asked about one thing, answer about everything. The metaphor is taken from a circle made by a compass: the center is fixed and immobile in the middle, and from there the space is equal in every direction to the surrounding line. Hence, things are said to be "circumscribed" which are contained within certain limits.

<margin>LXIII</margin>
->A Roscius.<-

The actor Roscius was so talented in performing plays that whoever excelled greatly in any art was called **a Roscius.** Marcus Tullius indicates this in the first book of *On the Orator*: **And so he had long ago achieved this, that in whatever craft anyone excelled, he was called a Roscius in his own genre.**

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs related to sudden shifts in fortune, delayed retribution, reaching a state of helplessness (using a board game metaphor), and the importance of moderation and excellence in one's craft.</summary>
<keywords>Ennius, Cicero, Plautus, board games, financial metaphors, budgeting, Roscius, acting, excellence, center and space</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of famous figures being used as metaphors for specific virtues or vices, specifically concluding the entry on Roscius. It then transitions into a series of adages regarding social customs, music, and natural metaphors.</meta>

<page-num>987</page-num>
<header>THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Ooo 2</sig>

The same author says in the second book of *On the Orator*: "I am often accustomed to wonder at the impudence of those who perform on the stage with the gestures of Roscius. For who can move himself without Roscius seeing his faults?" <note>Quintus Roscius Gallus was the most celebrated comic actor of ancient Rome, known for such technical perfection that his name became a synonym for excellence in any field.</note> Again in *Brutus*: "And let him understand that Roscius is on the stage." This is that Roscius who was a rival of Cicero, whom he honored with this praise: saying that he was a man so good that he alone was unworthy to step onto a stage, yet so excellent an artist that he alone was worthy to be seen there. Therefore, by the same trope <term>trope: a figure of speech where a word is used in a non-literal way</term> by which we call a man who is exceptionally shrewd in council a **Daedalus**; one patient in labors, **Hercules**; one invincible in debate, **Achilles**; one critical in judgment, **Aristarchus**; so it will be permitted to call a patron who is exceptionally skilled in pleading cases a **Roscius**.

<margin>LXX</margin>
### The Loving-Cup.

The **Loving-Cup** <note>original Greek: "Κρατὴρ Φιλοτήσιος" (Krater Philotesios)</note> is spoken of as that by which friendships are forged at banquets. This custom still survives today among the Germans, for whom it is considered most disgraceful to remember old offenses—even capital ones—after accepting the *Philotesius* cup; not even judges would admit a legal action for injuries in such a case. Plutarch, in his commentary *On the Fortune of Alexander*, says that Alexander—who attempted to lead the barbarians by arms and the Greeks by civil institutions toward a more humane and holy way of life—did so "mixing together their lives, customs, marriages, and ways of living, as if in a loving-cup." <note>Erasmus translates the Greek: "ὥσπερ ἐν κρατῆρι Φιλοτησίῳ μίξας τὸν βίον..."</note> In the play *Pseudolus* by Plautus, a drunken slave thinks it is next to the gods to propose a "sweet-bearing" cup of "mildest friendship" with a clean hand. Hesychius indicates that this *Philotesia* was usually offered after dinner, when everyone drinks the same wine from the same vessel as a sign of friendship. This custom has not yet died out among us, but it is becoming rarer due to the fear of the "new leprosy" <note>likely a reference to the contemporary outbreak of syphilis in Europe</note> from which many suffer. Asconius Pedianus, in his commentary on the third action against Verres, thinks this is what Marcus Tullius Cicero means when he accuses Verres of drinking with his companions "in the Greek fashion." For the common people think those who drink "in the Greek fashion" are those who drink more largely and from greater cups. But he himself prefers that we understand it as drinking wine "neat" <note>undiluted with water</note>. The Greeks are accustomed to do this: when they perform a libation <term>libation: a ritual pouring of wine as an offering</term> at a banquet, they first salute the gods, pouring a little from the cup, and then their friends; they drink neat wine as many times as they name their gods or their dear friends. This is roughly what Pedianus says. Some think this cup is also called the cup of the **Good Spirit** <note>original: "ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος"</note>.

<margin>LXXI</margin>
### The Lyre incites to war.

Plutarch, in the second book of *On the Fortune of Alexander*, declares that this little verse was commonly sung among the Spartans:
> For the fine playing of the lyre goes out against the steel. <note>original: "Ἔρποι γὰρ ἄντα τῷ σιδήρῳ τὸ καλῶς κιθαριζέμεν"</note>

By this they signified that certain modes of playing the lyre could calm the movements of the soul, while others could add vigor for battle. When Alexander heard Antigenidas playing the flute in the "Chariot mode" <term>Harmatium: a spirited, warlike style of music</term>, he was so inflamed that, rising up with his weapons, he laid hands on those sitting nearest to him.

<margin>LXXII</margin>
### The Cup of Bathycles.

**The Cup of Bathycles** <note>original: "Βαθυκλέυς κύλιξ"</note> seems to be said against those who enjoy their wealth alone, sharing nothing with anyone. In Plutarch's *Banquet of the Seven Sages*, a certain Ardalus addresses Aesop thus: "You will never pass the cup here to us, since you see those men passing it among themselves like the cup of Bathycles, but sharing it with no one else." To which Aesop responds: "But this cup isn't for the public either; indeed, it has been standing by Solon for a long time." To the Greeks, *Bathycles* sounds like "deep glory"; he seems to have been some wealthy man who lived for himself and drank for himself.

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
### Grapes do not ripen by the rays of the moon.

Plutarch brings forward this verse of Ion as a proverb, pointing out that because the moon has weaker rays than the sun, it can stir up humors <term>humors: the fluids within a plant or body</term> but cannot "cook" or ripen them.
> For by them the black grape is not ripened. <note>original: "Μέλας γὰρ αὐταῖς οὐ πεπαίνεται βότρυς"</note>

It is suitable for those who attempt what they cannot complete due to a lack of strength. He relates the same in his commentary *On the Face in the Moon*. It will gain more charm if, wishing to signify that human disciplines do not provide true happiness, we say: "For by them the black grape is not ripened." In the phrase "by them," we must understand "rays."

<summary>This page explores several adages related to social and cultural archetypes, including the actor Roscius as a symbol of perfection, the 'loving-cup' as a ritual of reconciliation, and the 'Cup of Bathycles' as a metaphor for stinginess. Erasmus also comments on the psychological effects of music and the scientific limitations of moonlight.</summary>

<page-num>988</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

<margin>LXXI</margin>
->Callias’s feathers are falling off.<-

Callias was a certain man among the Greeks who had squandered his inheritance through luxury and lust. A common joke arose concerning him: "Callias is losing his feathers" <note>original Greek: Καλλίας πτεροῤῥυεῖ (Kallias pterorrhuei)</note>. This refers to how birds sometimes lose their feathers, either due to disease or at specific times of the year—much like how certain four-legged animals change their hair or fur. From this, those who have been stripped of their resources are called "plucked" or "shorn." This term, "feather-shedding" <term>feather-shedding: to lose one's plumage; here used to mean losing one's wealth</term>, is frequently used as a joke in Aristophanes' play *The Birds*.

<margin>LXXII</margin>
->Broadly speaking.<-

The Greeks interpret the phrase "Broadly speaking" <note>original Greek: Ἐν πλάτει (En platei)</note> to mean that a small allowance should be granted beyond the strict letter of a rule, especially in matters of human kindness. For example, if someone promised payment by the tenth day of August but returned it the following day. Julianus, in the 46th book of the *Pandects* <term>Pandects: A massive compendium of Roman legal opinions organized under the Emperor Justinian</term>, under the title *On Payments*, writes: "The master ought to ratify the act as soon as he is first informed, but this should be accepted 'broadly' and with a certain span of time." Ulpian cites this passage of Julianus in the same book, and again in the thirteenth book under the title *On the Action for Wheat*. He says: "It is more true, as Servius says, that the time of condemnation must be looked at; if the person has ceased to be among the living, then the time of death. But even this, according to Celsus, must be looked at 'broadly.' For the very shortest moment of life should not be the measure." Again, in the 22nd book under *On Proofs*, he says: "Nor is it asked whether someone remembers on which day or in which month a thing was done, but whether it can be proven in any way when that work was completed. And this the Greeks are accustomed to call 'broadly speaking,'" and so on. Thus far the *Pandects*.

However, the people of Calais <note>original: "Caletii"</note> do not know that "they know the song" <note>Erasmus likely refers to the Greek idiom ᾠδὴν ἴσασι, "they know the tune," suggesting they lack the "harmony" of legal equity</note>. When ordered to close the city gates at the eleventh hour, they shut them immediately at the first stroke of the bell, repelling both those standing outside and those wishing to leave, even those closest to the gate. Conversely, when excommunication <note>original: "anathema"</note> is threatened against those who do not obey by a prescribed day, they are freed from the "lightning bolt" <note>A common metaphor for the strike of excommunication</note> if they fulfill their duty within fourteen days of that date. These matters pertain to the equity of the law.

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
->In a Hodgepodge.<-

The ancients used the term "Satire" <note>original: "Satyra" or "Satura"</note> for a mixture of various things heaped together scattered and in no order. It appears the word was first derived from the lewdness of the Satyrs, who leap here and there at random. From this, the term was applied to a type of food consisting of various forms of herbs; furthermore, to a platter loaded with various kinds of offerings to the gods. This was not unlike that cup which the Greeks called "all-fruit" <note>original Greek: παγκάρπιον (pankarpion)</note> from its fivefold variety of contents, or a "kernon" <note>original Greek: κέρνον (kernon)</note> mixture, which we mentioned above. Festus says "Satura" or "Satire" is named for being seasoned with various kinds of things, or for a law crowded with many other laws. Therefore, it was common to add to the sanction of laws: "Neither shall it be detracted from or repealed *by way of a Satire*" <note>original: "per Satyram"</note>, meaning the law must be kept as a whole. He cites Annius Luscus from a speech he gave against Tiberius Gracchus: "The power which the common people had given *as a hodgepodge* was repealed." He also cites Laelius from his own defense: "The following day, as if by way of a *Satura*, the law was accepted for surrender with refined opinions." They interpret a "Satire law" as one that encompasses many different things at once, just as Jugurtha was accepted for surrender, but with many prescribed conditions: that he give thirty elephants, many cattle and horses, along with a great weight of silver. 

Justinian uses this adage in the preface to the *Pandects*: "At first, indeed, this work was handed to readers not according to the order of the Perpetual Edict, but collected here and there, and as if *in a hodgepodge*, with the useful mixed with the useless, and for the most part assigned to various categories." Likewise Sallust in the *Jugurthine War*: "As if *in a hodgepodge*, with opinions woven together, he is accepted into surrender." Sallust says these things about Jugurtha, but they are not found in anyone's speech, nor was Laelius present there; hence it is necessary that the passage in Festus is mutilated—the words of Laelius have been omitted along with the name of Sallust.

<margin>LXXIV</margin>
->Do not be headlong to swear.<-

To some not uncommonly learned men, it seems this too should be numbered among the adages, as Ulpian says in the 12th book of the *Pandects* near the end: "If anyone," he says, "in a monetary matter, swears by the genius of the Prince <note>A sacred oath by the guardian spirit of the Emperor</note> that he does not owe money, and it is found within a certain time he has perjured himself; or if he swears he will pay within a certain time and does not, our Emperor has decreed with his father that he be dismissed after being beaten with rods, and that this be said to him: [Do not be headlong to swear]."

<summary>Erasmus examines the origins of the term "Satire" as a mixture of things and explores the legal concept of "broadness" (equity) versus strict adherence to rules, citing Roman jurists and contemporary habits in Calais.</summary>
<keywords>Callias, Aristophanes, satire, legal equity, Pandects, Ulpian, Justinian, Calais, swearing oaths, Roman law</keywords>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH HUNDRED
<page-num>989</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD 4, CENTURY 7</header>
<sig>Ooo 3</sig>

"Do not swear rashly," <note>original Greek: πρεπετῶς μὴ ὄμνυε (prepetos me omnye)</note> that is, do not be headstrong in making oaths. This will take on the character of a proverb if someone warns a person who has already suffered a misfortune: "Do not swear rashly."

->To act according to the contract.<-
<margin>LXXVIII</margin>

There are also those formulas drawn from legal experts that have turned into proverbs: "To act according to the contract" <note>original Latin: Ex syngrapha agere</note> and "To act by sealed records" <note>original Latin: obsignatis tabulis agere</note>. These are used to describe someone acting rigidly and with little courtesy, but rather as if bound by a strict obligation. Cicero, in his speech *For Murena*, says: "Are you proceeding to act with the people as if according to a contract?" To the Latins, a *syngrapha* <term>syngrapha: a written agreement or contract signed by both parties</term> sounds like a "joint-writing," because it is usually written by the hands of both parties and delivered to both. In this, *syngraphae* differ from *tabulae* (ledgers), because ledgers were usually kept by only one party. A *syngrapha* also differs from a *chirograph* (handwritten note), ledger, or codicil, because in those only things already done are recorded, whereas in a *syngrapha*, a pact comes into being even against the good faith of the action; money not yet paid, or not paid in full, is usually recorded according to the temporary will of the men. This is roughly the account given by Asconius Pedianus in his commentary on the third speech against Verres.

->Injury dissolves love.<-
<margin>LXXIX</margin>

In the Greek *Epigrams*, this is cited under the title of a proverb: "Outrage dissolves loves" <note>original Greek: ὕβρις ἔρωτας ἔλυσε (hybris erotas elyse)</note>. This means that injury or insult dissolves affection, because love that is treated with contempt usually turns into anger, and anger into hatred. So in the comedy, the character Phædria says: "She shut me out; now she calls me back; should I return? Not even if she begged me." Likewise, Horace writes: "For if there is any manhood in Flaccus <note>Erasmus refers here to Horace himself</note>, he will not endure your giving your nights continually to a preferred rival, nor will his resolve yield to a beauty that has once offended him; in his anger, he will seek a partner, if once a certain grief has entered his heart." In the epigram, a lover complains that this saying is falsely tossed about by the common people; for he himself, having been shut out by his girlfriend not without insult, and having sworn he would not return to her for a whole year, returned to her as a suppliant at dawn the very next day. The poem goes like this:
"That 'outrage dissolves loves' is a tale spread in vain;
The outrage has instead inflamed my love-madness more." <note>original Greek: ὕβρις ἔρωτας ἔλυσε, μάτην ὅδε μῦθος ἀλᾶται, ὕβρις ἐμὴν φλέξα μᾶλλον ἐρωμανίω</note>
In general, however, it is true that goodwill is nourished by mutual kindnesses and extinguished by injuries.

->To dance eloquently.<-
<margin>LXXX</margin>

Cornelius Tacitus, in his *Dialogue on Orators*, indicates that this insult was commonly tossed at the orators of his time. They expressed the rhythms of stage-players through the decadence of their words, the shallowness of their thoughts, and the lawlessness of their composition. Indeed, they even boasted—as if it were a mark of praise, glory, and genius—that their legal commentaries were "danced and sung." They said that orators spoke recklessly, but actors "danced eloquently" <note>original Latin: diferte saltare</note>. The wit of the saying lies in this: the orators were speaking in the manner of stage-actors, which was unbecoming to them, while the actors were adapting themselves to the delivery of orators. Thus it happened that the former spoke worse, while the latter danced better. It is the job of actors to dance and orators to speak; those who do so skillfully are called "eloquent." This joke, however, joined two different things together.

->What is beautiful is also dear.<-
<margin>LXXXI</margin>

"The beautiful is dear" <note>original Greek: Τὸ καλὸν φίλον (To kalon philon)</note>. Among the proverbs concerning the forming of friendships, this is also mentioned in Plato’s *Lysis*: "And it seems, according to the ancient proverb, that what is beautiful is dear." He who loves for the sake of profit does not love truly; but that which is beautiful is loved for its own sake. Hence, when someone asked Aristotle why we more willingly converse with the beautiful than with the ugly, he replied that such a question was for the blind. Nothing, however, is more beautiful than virtue, and therefore nothing is more lovable.

->Even hares insult a dead lion.<-
<margin>LXXXII</margin>

There exists a Greek epigram whose theme is taken from Homer’s *Iliad*, Book 22. There, the Greeks stand around Hector, who has already been killed by Achilles, insulting him in death; nor was there anyone who did not inflict some wound on the lifeless man. For Homer says:
"The other sons of the Achaeans ran up,
Who marveled at the stature and admirable form
Of Hector; yet no one stood by without dealing a wound." <note>original Greek: ἄλλοι δ’ περιέδραμον υἷες ἀχαιῶν, οἳ καὶ θηήσαντο φυὴν καὶ εἶδος ἀγητὸν ἕκτορος, οὐδ’ ἄρα οἵ τις ἀνουτητί γε παρέστη</note>
And a little later:

<summary>This page explores several proverbs regarding human behavior, including the rigidity of legal contracts, the fragile nature of love when met with insult, and the mockery of fallen enemies. Erasmus also critiques the decline of Roman oratory into theatrical performance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on adages derived from Greek literature and philosophy, specifically focusing on the works of Plato and Aristotle. It transitions from the previous page's discussion of legal metaphors and mocking the dead to philosophical concepts of certainty and materialism.</meta>

...as someone once put it, and set them all up. <margin>that is,</margin>
"Someone had said this, and while standing by, dealt the wound." <margin>The epigram goes as follows:</margin>
"Strike my body now after my death, since even
Hares insult the body of a dead lion." <margin>that is,</margin>
"Now seek my corpse with weapons after my fate is sealed,
Even the hare dares to insult the dead lion."
<note>original Greek: ὡς ἄρα τις ἔθηκε... (os ara tis etheke); Βάλλετε νῦν μετὰ πότμον... (Ballete nyn meta potmon). This refers to the cowardice of attacking those who can no longer defend themselves.</note>
This is said elsewhere regarding those who snap at the dead, who wrestle with ghosts, and who fight against shadows.

### The tongue unrefuted.
<margin>LXXIX</margin>

Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "But as it seems, if you go by this road, a childish thing will happen. Our tongue will be unrefuted, but our mind will not be unrefuted." <note>original Greek: Ἀτὰρ ὡς ἔοικεν... (Atar os eoiken). Erasmus interprets this as a distinction between winning a verbal argument and being truly convinced in one's mind.</note> That is: "But as it appears, if you answer that it is possible, something like the case of Euripides will happen to us: our tongue indeed will be unrefuted, but our mind will not be without proof." This fits those who, though conquered by reason, do not yield nonetheless, but resort to evasions, shouting against their own conscience.

### To hold in the fist.
<margin>LXXX</margin>

"To grasp with the hands in a fist." <note>original Greek: ἀπρὶξ ταῖν χεροῖν λαβέσθαι (aprix tain cheroin labesthai)</note> That is: It is said "to squeeze in the fist" because they feel it by the very touch. Plato in the *Theaetetus*: "those who think nothing else exists, except what they can grasp tightly with their hands." This refers to those who do not believe anything exists in the nature of things except corporeal objects exposed to the senses; they believe that actions, generations, and other things of this kind, which are perceived by the intellect rather than the senses, are empty words. 

Such a man, in Plato's view, was Diogenes, who said that he saw cups and tables, but the "cup-ness" and "table-ness" <term>cyatheity and mensality: the abstract "ideal" or essence of a cup or table in Platonic philosophy</term> which Plato mentioned, he did not see. But in turn he heard: "To be sure, you have the eyes with which cups and tables are seen; but the mind, by which 'cup-ness' and 'table-ness' are discerned, you do not have." Plato orders such a thick-headed class of geniuses to be kept away from the mysteries of philosophy, as if they were profane. For those things which are not seen are more true than those which are seen; and we know those things which we gather by reason more certainly than those which we handle with our hands, for the judgment of the senses is deceptive.

### Not solidly.
<margin>LXXXI</margin>

"Not firmly." <note>original Greek: οὐ παγίως (ou pagios)</note> That is: Not steadily. I wonder why Plato in the *Theaetetus* did not include this as a proverb, unless perhaps because of the somewhat long metaphor; he added "as they say" to "solidly." For in that passage Socrates is dealing with those things which are not firm by their own nature, but, adhering to others, are varied by reciprocal movements, so that they either exist or do not exist—such as white and black, the acting and the suffering. 

The passage goes like this: "For just as we whispered about their manner, that nothing exists as itself by itself, which indeed I and you were saying then. But in that communion with each other, all things come to be in the imagination from movement. Since we cannot solidly understand, as they say, either the 'acting' to be something or the 'suffering' itself, as a single thing." <note>Erasmus is translating a complex Platonic argument about the fluidity of sensory perception.</note>

Aristotle in the second book of his *Rhetoric* says that old men, because of their experience of things, always doubt and never affirm anything, but add to all their statements "perhaps" and "maybe." They know how to say nothing "solidly." That which is "compact" is called *pagion* by the Greeks, from *pegnymi*, which means "I fix" or "I fasten." From this, *pagios* is used for "solidly" and "certainly." 

Accidents <term>accidents: in philosophy, non-essential qualities like color or size that can change without changing the essence of the thing</term> are in a way fluid. Substance is solid, and the logic of those things which are said "in relation to something" depends on something else: for the logic of a "father" perishes as a father if the son perishes, even though the substance of the father remains nonetheless. 

Indeed, even among the Latins, "solid things" are called immovable goods; and "solid" is said to come from *solum* (the ground), meaning that which is whole and compact—Quintilian uses this for the "whole." Juvenal says: "Virtue is the only and unique nobility." Saint Jerome uses this word quite elegantly in this way. Hence Sextus Pompeius Festus thinks that "all-iron weapons" <note>original Latin: soliferrea</note> are so called because they are entirely made of iron; and a "skillful" man <note>original Latin: solertem</note> because he is practiced in *all* arts; and "solemn" <note>original Latin: solenne</note> because it happens in *all* years. From the same source we call the earth the "soil" <note>original Latin: solum</note>, because it is fixed and compact, not hanging in the manner of air and water. The opposite of this is what Marcus Tullius [Cicero] has in the second book of *On Ends*: "Which same things could be said of the other virtues, the entire foundation of which you place in pleasure, as if in water." The word seems to be derived from the Greeks, with the smooth breathing turned into an "s"—*solum*.

### Either leave or strip off.
<margin>LXXXII</margin>

Plato in the *Theaetetus* indicates that there was a custom among the Lacedaemonians <note>the Spartans</note> that in pub-

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's exploration of Greek and Latin adages, moving from metaphors of physical combat and gripping to those involving speed, nature, and the ethics of temperance. # THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
Ooo 4
<meta>catchword: pore</meta>

...in their contests they should force no one to join the gathering, but they proclaimed by law <note>original Greek: ἢ ἀπιέναι, ἢ ἐκδύεσθαι (e apienai, e ekduesthai)</note> "either depart or strip," that is, either leave or take off your clothes. Among the Greeks, those who prepare for a contest are said <term>to strip</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκδύεσθαι (ekduesthai)</note>, because in ancient times they wrestled in a loincloth, but otherwise naked. From this, the very word <term>to strip</term> has the force of a proverb whenever it is transferred to matters of the mind, such as for the purpose of debating or resisting the flesh. Saint Chrysostom and Saint Basil use it frequently in this way. There is a similar saying found elsewhere: "Either drink or depart."

### To outrun Crison of Himera. LXXXVII

The prodigious speed of Crison seems to have given rise to this proverb. Thus Socrates in Plato's *Protagoras*, when asked to finish the discussion he had begun with Protagoras, says: <note>original Greek: βουλοίμην ἂν χαρίζεσθαί σοι... (bouloimen an charizesthai soi...)</note> "I would certainly wish to grant your request, if what you ask were within my power. As it is, it is as if you asked me to follow Crison of Himera, the famous runner, in his prime, or to keep pace with and follow one of the long-distance runners or the day-runners." <margin>That is,</margin> "I would indeed wish to follow your custom, if what you seek were in my ability. Now it is just as if you ask me to follow Crison of Himera, the distinguished runner, or some <term>long-distance runner</term> <note>original: dolichodromon</note>, or to follow and equal a <term>day-runner</term> <note>original: hemerodromon</note> in a continuous race." Himera is a city in Sicily, although there is another of the same name in Africa. From there, Crison was called "the Himerian," celebrated for his speed in running, much like the speed Pliny records in his seventh book regarding Philippides and Canistius the Lacedaemonian, and along with these, Philonides, the runner of Alexander the Great. They were called <term>long-distance runners</term> <note>original: Dolichodromi</note> who would run twelve stages (stadia) with a continuous impetus. <term>Day-runners</term> <note>original: Hemerodromi</note> were those who ran the entire day from morning until evening without taking a breath. Pliny writes of a boy nine years old who continued his run from noon until evening. From this, the Greek poets call the sun the <term>day-runner</term> <note>original: ἡμεροδρόμον (hemerodromon)</note>, because it completes its course in a single day, as if indeed it rests at night in the inn of Thetis <note>Thetis was a sea goddess; this poetic image suggests the sun "sleeping" in the ocean</note>.

### Imitating the Charadrius. LXXXVIII

<term>Imitating the Charadrius</term> <note>original Greek: χαραδριὸν μιμούμενος (charadrion mimoumenos)</note>. That is, "imitating the Charadrius bird," a saying usually applied to someone who is dissembling or hiding something useful. Suidas records this six-foot verse in "limping" meter from Hipponax:
<term>And does the seller, I ask, really hide the Charadrius?</term> <note>original Greek: Καὶ μὴν καλύπτει μῶν χαραδριὸν πέρνας; (Kai men kalyptei mon charadrion pernas?)</note>
Likewise Aristophanes in *The Birds*:
<term>Otherwise, as it seems, the hoopoe has entered the thicket</term>
<term>And hidden himself, imitating the Charadrius.</term> <note>original Greek: ἄλλως ἄρ' οὕτω γ' ὡς ἔοικ' εἰς τὴν λοχμίαν / ἐμβὰς ἐπῶζε χαραδριὸν μιμούμενος. (allos ar houto g' hos eoik' eis ten lochmian / embas epoze charadrion mimoumenos.)</note>
In this passage, the commentator, agreeing for the most part with Suidas, explains that this bird possesses a medicinal power, so that those suffering from jaundice (or the "royal disease") are easily cured simply by looking at it. For this reason, those who sell the bird hide it, so that the bidder does not receive the cure before he has paid for it. He adds that the bird changes color to match the likeness of those to whom it is brought near; however, there are some who believe the remedy comes not from the sight of the bird, but from eating it. The word is distinguished by its accent: for if you pronounce it with the acute accent on the last syllable, <term>charadrión</term>, it indicates the bird; if the acute is on the second to last, <term>charadríou</term>, it is a diminutive from <term>charadra</term>, signifying a whirlpool or a gap in the earth, because water falling into this seems to give off a kind of melody. This much could be handed down from the things carelessly gathered by Suidas. The Comic poet <note>Aristophanes</note> mentions this bird elsewhere in the same play: <term>The Charadrii carried water from below into the air.</term> <note>original Greek: ὕδωρ ἐφόρει κάτωθεν εἰς τὸν ἀέρα οἱ χαραδριοί (hydor ephorei katothen eis ton aera hoi charadrioi)</note> The commentator adds that the name was given to the bird because it delights in dwelling in ravines <note>charadrae</note>. Socrates, in Plato's *Gorgias*, when he had lured Callicles into admitting that a blessed life is not situated in an abundance of things but in a perpetual influx (for he who is full, or does not thirst, because he feels neither annoyance nor pleasure, lives like a stone rather than a man), adds this: <term>You are describing the life of a certain Charadrius, but not that of a dead man or a stone.</term> <note>original Greek: χαραδριοῦ τινὰ αὖ σὺ βίον λέγεις, ἀλλ' οὐ νεκροῦ οὐδὲ λίθου (charadriou tina au sy bion legeis, all' ou nekrou oude lithou)</note> Marsilio Ficino translates this as the bird, whereas Socrates seems to mean the ravine, into which water perpetually flows but is never filled; unless perhaps the Charadrius is a bird of the greedy sort, like the seagull, so that it found its name derived from the word for "ravine" <note>charadra</note>.

### As much as your feet allow. LXXXIX

Socrates speaks as follows in Plato's *Gorgias*: <term>One must pursue and practice temperance, but flee from intemperance as fast as each of our feet can carry us.</term> <note>original Greek: σωφροσύνην μὲν διωκτέον καὶ ἀσκητέον, ἀκολασίαν δὲ φευκτέον, ὡς ἔχει ποδῶν ἕκαστος ἡμῶν (sophrosynen men diokteon kai asketeon, akolasian de pheukteon, hos echei podon hekastos emon)</note> The further this is transferred from physical things, the more it approaches a proverb for speed. What in the body...

# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY
992
DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES
C
<meta>catchword: We</meta>

...just as feet are to the body, so are the affections <note>Erasmus uses "affectus" to refer to passions or emotions</note> to the soul, by which we either seek something out or flee from it.

->Like a vessel<-

<note>original Greek: Ἀγγείου δίκην (Angeiou dikēn)</note>. This is said of someone who, because of their ignorance, cannot produce anything from their own mind, but only repeats what they have heard from others. A fountain contains its own liquid, but a vessel is empty unless you pour something into it from elsewhere. People who lack their own learning are filled through their ears. Socrates says in Plato’s *Phaedrus*: "For I am conscious of my own ignorance, but I believe I have been filled through my ears like a vessel from the fountains of others. It remains then to assume that I have gathered these thoughts from elsewhere, for I confess I have not thought of them myself." <note>Erasmus provides two slightly different Latin translations of the same Greek passage from Plato’s Phaedrus 235c, emphasizing the metaphor of being "filled up" by others' wisdom.</note>

->As a wolf loves a sheep<-

<note>original Greek: Ὡς λύκος ἄρνα φιλεῖ (Hōs lykos arna philei)</note>. This refers to someone who feigns love for the sake of their own advantage. For this is commonly called "love," when in truth it is hatred. A young man "hunts" a girl to snatch away her chastity—an incomparable treasure—to trade her honorable reputation for a shameful rumor, and to make her hateful to her parents, friends, and all good people; finally, to take away what is dearest of all, a sound mind. I ask you, what worse could an enemy do to an enemy? Socrates quotes a verse in the *Phaedrus* as if it were a popular saying:
<note>original Greek: Ὡς λύκοι ἄρνα φιλοῦσ’, ὡς παῖδα φιλοῦσιν ἐρασταί (Hōs lykoi arna philous’, hōs paida philousin erastai)</note>.
"As wolves love the lamb, so do obsessed lovers love a boy."
<margin>That is,</margin> Virgil <note>referred to by his cognomen, Maro</note>:
"The grim lioness follows the wolf, the wolf himself the goat,
The playful goat follows the flowering clover."
And Horace:
"I do not pursue you to crush you, like a fierce tiger or a Moroccan lion."

->Raised on ships<-

<note>original Greek: Ἐν νηυσὶν ἐθραμμένος (En nēusin ethrammenos)</note>. This was said of someone who was unrefined and a stranger to liberal manners and common sense. The seafaring race usually indulges in its own rough nature, as it lives removed from the company of civilized men. Thus Plato in the *Phaedrus*: "Do you not think he would imagine he was hearing men who had been raised somewhere on ships?" The playwright Plautus, in his play *The Casket*, calls such rustic behaviors "maritime"—or rather "inconstant"—because the sea swells and recedes with the tides. Plautus's words are: "So love mocks me for my slip of mind: it chases, drives, seeks, drags, holds, tosses, gives freely what it does not give, deludes; now it dissuades what it just persuaded, and shows what it dissuaded; it treats me with maritime manners, and so breaks my loving heart."

->What is useful is honorable<-

<note>original Greek: Τὸ μὲν ὠφέλιμον καλὸν, τὸ δὲ βλαϐερὸν αἰσχρόν (To men ōphelimon kalon, to de blaberon aischron)</note>. That is: what is useful is honorable, and what is harmful is shameful. Plato records this in the fifth book of the *Republic* as a common saying: "For this is and will be most beautifully said: that what is useful is honorable, and what is harmful is shameful." He is discussing there how women should be called to all the same duties as men, provided they are found equally useful to the state. He argues that their bodies should be stripped for exercise before the guardians of the city, and if they seem fit, they should be exercised publicly alongside the men. He vehemently despises those who would laugh at the naked bodies of women, provided it serves the good of the republic. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> wondered whether it was shameful for a good man to dance naked in the forum if such a dance could help the state. However, the common crowd has inverted the sentiment, claiming that "whatever is useful is honorable," whereas for philosophers nothing is truly "useful" unless it is first "honorable."

->More than the sun of Heraclitus<-

Socrates, in Plato's *Republic* (Book 6), says of those who decline without hope of restoration that they are extinguished "more than the sun of Heraclitus itself." <note>original Greek: εἶναι ᾧ ἡρακλειτεῖος ἥλιος ἀποσϐέννυται (einai hō hērakleiteios hēlios aposbennytai)</note>. He is speaking of old men who are not fit for the difficulties of learning philosophy because they were worn out in their youth. The philosopher Heraclitus believed that the sun was shaped like a bowl <term>scapha</term> <note>a small boat or hollow vessel</note>, and that its light was extinguished every time the hollow side turned upward, but became bright again when it flipped back. Xenophanes had a similar "dream" about the sun, thinking it perished at sunset and a brand new sun was created at sunrise. But old men are never renewed to youthful vigor. Horace seems to have alluded to this in his *Odes*: "The swift moons repair their losses in the heavens; but when we fall to where the ancestors are, we are but dust and shadow."

<summary>This page explores several proverbs regarding human character, morality, and the irreversible nature of time, drawing heavily from Plato's dialogues and Roman poets like Virgil and Horace.</summary>
<keywords>vessel metaphor, predatory love, maritime manners, utility vs. honor, Heraclitus, aging, Plato, Socrates, Horace</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of ancient metaphors and proverbs, moving from the "affections of the soul" discussed on the previous page to metaphors for intellectual clarity, political structure, and moral discipline. It draws heavily on the works of Plato.</meta>

# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, SEVENTH CENTURY

### Barbaric mud. XCV

<note>original Greek: βορβόρῳ βαρβαρικῶ (borborō barbarikō)</note>. That is, **Barbaric mud**. This is used in Plato’s seventh book of the *Republic* to describe a state of intense mental stupor. For in that work, he praises Dialectic <note>The art of logical discussion and investigation of truth</note> as the only thing that lifts up the mind when it is immersed in ignorance, raising it from common opinions to a solid knowledge of the truth. "And in truth," he says, "it gently draws and leads upward the eye of the soul, which had been buried in a kind of barbaric mud." <note>original Greek: καὶ τῷ ὄντι, ἐν βορβόρῳ βαρβαρικῶ τινι τὸ τῆς ψυχῆς ὄμμα κατορωρυγμένον ἠρέμα ἕλκει καὶ ἀνάγει ἄνω</note>. It seems that the word "barbarian" was derived from *borboros* <note>the Greek word for mud or filth</note> as a term of contempt.

---

### Not from oak or rock. XCVI

<note>original Greek: Οὐκ ἐκ δρυός ἢ ἐκ πέτρας (Ouk ek dryos ē ek petras)</note>. That is, **Not from oak or rock**. We use this when we want to indicate that something does not consist of external, physical matter, but arises from the virtues of the mind. For example, the common people call a "city" the walls and houses built of stone and wood. They call a "church" a structure piled up from similar materials, when in reality a city consists of the character of its people, and a church consists of the consensus of minds in true religion. Plato says in the eighth book of the *Republic*: "Or do you think that political systems arise from an oak or a rock somewhere, and not rather from the character of those who live in the cities?" <note>original Greek: ἢ οἴει ἐκ δρυός ποθεν ἢ ἐκ πέτρας τὰς πολιτείας γίγνεθαι, ἀλλ᾽ οὐχὶ ἐκ τῶν ἠθῶν τῶν ἐν ταῖς πόλεσιν;</note>.

---

### To put on a curb-chain. XCVII

<note>original Greek: ψάλιον ἐνβαλεῖν (psalion enbalein)</note>. That is, they are said **to put on a curb-chain** who restrain a fierce spirit with some form of control; the metaphor is taken from high-spirited horses. Plato writes in the third book of *The Laws*: "But your third savior, seeing that the government was still swelling with pride and passion, put a curb-chain on it, so to speak—namely, the power of the Ephors." <note>The Ephors were five high-ranking officials in Sparta intended to balance the power of the kings</note>. He is speaking here of the Republic of the Spartans, in which five Ephors were established to temper the royal power. A *psalion* is a ring added to a bridle, which is why it is sometimes used to mean the bridle itself. Unless, perhaps, he was alluding to water buffaloes, which are led around by an iron ring placed in their nostrils—hence the proverb "to lead by the nose," which is discussed elsewhere.

---

### Beginning, middle, end. XCVIII

Plato, in the fourth book of *The Laws*, records this as if it were a common saying: that God encompasses the entirety of all things—that is, the **beginning, the middle, and the end**. For from Him comes the start, the growth, and the completion of everything that exists. "We say to Him regarding human affairs: God indeed, as the ancient saying goes, holding the beginning, the end, and the middle of all beings, completes His straight course, traveling according to nature." <note>original Greek: ὁ μὲν δὴ θεὸς, ὥσπερ ὁ παλαιὸς λόγος, ἀρχήν τε καὶ τελευτὴν καὶ τὰ μέσα τῶν ὄντων ἁπάντων ἔχων, εὐθείᾳ περαίνει, κατὰ φύσιν συμπορευόμενος</note>.

---

### An Orphic life. XCIX

<note>original Greek: Ὀρφικός βίος (Orphikos bios)</note>. That is, an **Orphic life**. Plato, in the sixth book of *The Laws*, used this to describe a harmless life, pure from luxury and blood-stained feasts. For Orpheus seems to have established this way of life so that people would not only refrain from polluting the altars of the gods with the blood of cattle, but would not even endure eating the flesh of any living creature. Instead, they would perform sacrifices with cakes and fruits sprinkled with honey, and eat nothing else themselves. These are Plato’s words: "But certain so-called 'Orphic lives' existed among your ancestors in those days." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ᾽ ὀρφικοί τινες λεγόμενοι βίοι ἐγίγνοντο ὑμῶν τοῖς τότε</note>. It appears Orpheus attempted to establish among the Thracians what Pythagoras tried among the Ionians, and Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome</note> among the Romans.

---

### Bright speech. C

<note>original Greek: Λευκός λόγος (Leukos logos)</note>. To the Greeks, this refers to **clear and transparent speech**, named after the color that possesses the most light. From this, they use the expression "to speak more whitely" <note>original Greek: λευκότορον εἰπεῖν (leukoteron eipein)</note> for those who express what they feel more clearly—that is, more plainly. And a "white voice" <note>original Greek: λευκή φωνή (leukē phōnē)</note> is one that easily penetrates the ears of the listeners. These are metaphors drawn from related things, just as we say those who understand a matter "feel" or "see" it; those who remember "hold" it; those who suspect "scent" it; and those who err are "blind." They are drawn from nearby senses, as when what belongs to the eyes is transferred to the ears, as in this case.

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, THE EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND OF ADAGES

A

### Ambrones.

In the past, the term **Ambrones** was commonly used to describe those who lived by plunder and wicked arts. Festus Pompeius <note>A 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> explains the whole matter, noting that they were originally a tribe from Gaul. When a flooding sea drove them from their own lands, they began to support themselves and their families through robbery and pillaging while wandering through the territories of others. They were a formidable force, not only in number—for they are said to have been thirty thousand—but also in the ferocity of their spirits and their method of fighting. Indeed, they would charge the enemy in a dense mass, following a certain rhythm and chant, repeatedly thundering "Ambrones! Ambrones!" either to call their own men together or to strike terror into the enemy. The Romans, under the leadership of Manlius and Caepio, were once defeated by them; but they were first broken by the Ligurians, then crushed by Gaius Marius, and finally wiped out at Aquae Sextiae <note>A battle in 102 BCE</note> along with the Cimbri and Teutones. This is roughly how Julius Florus records it in his *Epitome of Book 68*, as does Plutarch in his *Life of Gaius Marius*. In a similar way, the name "Cilician" is misused as a reproach for greed and piracy.

### Vinaria angina.

I have already spoken before about **argentaria angina** or "silver quinsy" <note>original Greek: ἀγχονάγχη (anchonanche)</note>, which took away the voice of many besides Demosthenes <note>A joke referring to Demosthenes allegedly accepting a bribe (silver) to remain silent during a debate</note>. But Festus Pompeius indicates that a joke was directed at those who are suffocated by wine, saying they suffer from **vinaria angina** or "wine quinsy," which you might call *oinanche* <note>original Greek: οἰνάγχην</note>. I myself knew a man in Rome, who was exceptionally learned, who died in earnest from this "quinsy." He was called Hermicus, a Portuguese by nationality. He was a man of excessively obese body, and for that reason short of breath, when he was seized by a slight fever. Christopher Fisher, an Englishman, visited him while he was in bed. "Hermicus," he said, "do you want to be cured by doctors who prescribe mere trifles? This evil will be better washed away with good wine," and at once he ordered four-year-old Corsican wine to be brought. He offered a toast to the sick man, telling him to be of good cheer. The man, being persuaded, drank deeply, and soon, his breath being blocked, he began to give up the ghost. Drunkenness makes some people talkative who were once silent; others, on the contrary, it makes as mute as any fish, though without danger to their health. If only this "wine quinsy" were less frequent among the Germans!

### Titiuillitium.

**Titiuillitium** was once a word that signified no certain thing, but like an interjection, it indicated extreme contempt, similar to the Greek word *pittalo* <note>original Greek: πιτταλό</note>. Plautus, as cited by Festus Pompeius, says: "I wouldn't buy that word for a *titiuillitium*" <note>Meaning: it is utterly worthless</note>. The passage is in the play *Casina*. There is a similar word in the same Festus, *Buttubata*, which Naevius used for trifling and worthless things. Nonius, however, thinks that *pipolo* was a word used for a reproach. Plautus says in the *Aulularia*: "So may Laverna <note>Goddess of thieves</note> love me well, if you don't order the dishes returned right now, I'll distract everyone here with a *pipolo* [outcry] in front of the house."

### Nihil potest nec addi nec adimi.

**Nothing can be added or taken away.** Aristotle indicates in the second book of the *Nicomachean Ethics* that this was a common saying regarding perfect works: "Whence they are accustomed to say of works that are well-made, that it is not possible to take anything away, nor to add anything" <note>original Greek: ὅθεν εἰώθασιν ἐπιλέγειν τοῖς εὖ ἔχουσιν ἔργοις, ὅτι οὐκ ἀφελεῖν ἔστιν, οὔτε προσθεῖναι</note>. For in order for something to be "good," moderation is best, whereas excess or defect ruins it. He who adds brings about excess; he who takes away brings about defect. Horace wrote of Lucilius:
> When he flowed muddily, there was something you would want to remove.

It has been said of Demosthenes and Cicero that nothing could be taken from the former, and nothing could be added to the latter.

### Virtus simplex.

One might doubt whether this was a commonly tossed-about verse which Aristotle cited in the second book of the *Ethics* as being very well known to everyone, or whether a hexameter verse slipped out unintentionally. Discussing the opinion of Pythagoras—that error is infinite, while virtue is finite—just as in a forest one wanders from the right path in a thousand ways, while the path itself is unique; and therefore vice is on a downward slope, while virtue is on a steep climb, just as it is easy to miss the target but difficult to hit it; he adds:
> **For men are good in but one way, but bad in all sorts of ways.** 
<note>original Greek: ἐσθλοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἁπλῶς, παντοδαπῶς δὲ κακοί</note>
That is: Virtue is simple, vice is manifold.

### Extra fumum & undam.

Aristotle, in the same book, records a Homeric verse as if it were a common refrain:
> **Keep the ship out of the reach of that smoke and wave.**
<note>original Greek: ὡς τοῦ μὲν καπνοῦ καὶ κύματος ἐκτὸς ἔεργε νῆα</note>
That is, [Aristotle continues...]

# THE EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND

->**VI. Keep the ship away from the smoke as well as from the waves.**<-

Aristotle indicates that these are the words of Calypso <note>A nymph in Homer's *Odyssey*</note> urging Ulysses not to sail too close to the shore by following the smoke, nor to trust himself to the deep sea, but to cut a path through the middle. The danger in the former lies in rocks and shallows; in the latter, from the waves. However, the translator Argyropylus <note>Johannes Argyropoulos, a 15th-century Greek scholar</note> attributes these words to Circe—I am not sure whose authority he followed.

->**VII. Common as Sisapo.**<-

This was undoubtedly said as a proverbial figure of speech. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his *Second Philippic*: "Do I say your house? What place was there on earth where you could set foot on your own land, except for your one estate at Misenum, which you held with your partners just like a **Sisapo**?" Mark Antony felt that he did not hold Misenum as a true possession, but as a "vein" or mine rented for profit. Pliny, in Book 33, Chapter 7, teaches that minium <note>Red lead or cinnabar, used as a pigment</note>, which the Greeks call <term>miltos</term> <note>original Greek: μίλτον</note> and some call cinnabar, was not only held in the highest price among the ancients but was also of great religious significance. For on feast days, the statues of the gods were smeared with minium, as were those celebrating a triumph—though the elderly Galba <note>A Roman Emperor</note> did not allow this to be done to him, as Cornelius Tacitus reports. 

**Sisapo** <note>Modern-day Almadén in Spain</note> is a town in Baetica which was once tributary to the Romans, possessing veins of minium. Indeed, minium was not brought to Rome from elsewhere without careful control. Pliny denies that the Romans maintained a more diligent watch over any other commodity. It was not permitted to refine or smelt the minium there where it was mined; the ore was sealed and sent to Rome—about ten thousand pounds annually—where it was processed. When sold, the law prescribed a price limit so it would not become excessively expensive. However, it was adulterated in many ways, leading Pliny to say it was "plunder for the company." Shortly after, speaking of fake minium, he says: "This, therefore, is adulterated in the workshops of the partners." From these accounts, it is clear that the region was divided among many partners, just as today silver or gold mines are occupied by contractors across certain tracts of land.

->**VIII. So great it can scarcely be contained by heaven.**<-

With this hyperbole, Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Second Philippic*, expressed the celebrity of fame when speaking of those who killed Julius Caesar for affecting a tyranny: especially since they achieved a glory "which seems as though it can scarcely be contained by heaven." Vergil writes:
>He bounds his empire with the earth, but his fame with the stars.

And Maro <note>Vergil</note> describes Daphnis as known even beyond the stars. Horace writes: "I shall strike the stars with my exalted head." In the works of Marcus Tullius, the phrase "to raise to heaven with praise" is frequently encountered.

->**IX. Now in a Greek cloak, now in a Roman toga.**<-

You may elegantly twist this phrase to describe an inconstant man of fickle loyalty who belongs to different parties: for instance, if someone frequently changes his way of life, now wearing a theological <term>cidaris</term> <note>A ceremonial headdress or cap</note>, and now walking about in a military cloak. Marcus Tullius asks in his *Fifth Philippic*: "Will the man presiding over the inquiry accept the excuse of a Greek judge, who appears now in a Greek cloak, now in a Roman toga?" The <term>pallium</term> <note>A rectangular cloak</note> belongs to the Greeks, just as the <term>toga</term> belongs to the Romans; yet both are garments of peace, just as the <term>saga</term> are garments of war.

->**X. To the military cloaks.**<-

The <term>sagum</term> was a short military tunic. Marcus Tullius, using it almost like a proverb, several times says "to go to the military cloaks" <note>original: *Ad saga iri*</note> to mean that war is being prepared and people are rushing to arms. Thus, in the *Sixth Philippic*: "Let them hurry, as I see they will; prepare your military cloaks. For it has been decreed that if he does not obey the authority of the Senate, we shall go to the military cloaks." Again in the same speech: "I said it was my pleasure that a legal holiday be declared and military cloaks be donned." And earlier in the *Fifth*: "I say it is necessary for a legal holiday to be proclaimed and military cloaks to be donned." Later in the *Seventh*: "They demanded arms, military cloaks, and war." Again in the *Eighth*: "Levies have been decreed throughout all Italy; with all exemptions removed, the military cloaks will be donned tomorrow." And again in the same: "Indeed, Members of the Senate, although those who have enjoyed this honor are usually dressed in the toga, when the state is in arms, I have decided that the Roman people should not differ in dress from you and other citizens in such a time of atrocity and confusion." Again in the *Thirteenth Philippic*: "Do you not understand that with the levy held throughout Italy, the consuls sent out, Caesar honored, and finally the military cloaks donned, you have been judged an enemy?" And in the *Fourteenth* he says frequently: "we would have gone to the military cloaks," "tomorrow let us go forth in military cloaks," "to depart to don the military cloaks," "to have gone to the military cloaks," "to have returned to the togas." In the *Third Action against Verres*, he joins similar terms: "When you have forced miserable and ruined men, as if our laws and courts were hopeless, to flee to violence, to hands, and to arms."

->**XI. To threaten with fire and sword.**<-

Those who announce extreme enmity are said to "threaten with fire and sword," a phrase which even today is commonly understood as most grim. Those who wage a more "civilized" war merely drive away plunder but abstain from slaughter and arson. Marcus Tullius, in the *Fourteenth Philippic*: "The ambassadors, I believe, will be under a more sacred law than the two consuls..."

This page explores proverbs regarding fearlessness, sudden changes in social status (symbolized by footwear), and the historical reputation of the Campanian region for arrogance.</meta>

...consuls, against whom he carries arms, than Mutina which he besieges, than the fatherland which he threatens with fire and sword. Again, in the *Twelfth Philippic* <note>A series of speeches by Cicero attacking Mark Antony</note>: "He threatens this city with fire and sword." It will be more elegant whenever the expression is transferred to matters of the soul; for instance, if one were to say that philosophers "threaten desire with fire and sword," rather than simply saying they prepare to write fiercely against it. Similarly, with those with whom we wish to have no shared community, we "interdict them from water and fire" <note>A Roman legal formula for exile, meaning the person was deprived of the basic necessities of life in the community</note>.

### He fears neither earthquakes nor waves.

Aristotle, in the third book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, teaches that those who fear nothing at all—not out of a habit of virtue, but out of a certain natural savagery—should by no means be called brave, but rather **mad** <note>original Greek: μαινομένους</note> or **unfeeling** <note>original Greek: ἀναλγήτους</note>; that is, insane, stupid, and devoid of sense. He says: "A man would be mad or unfeeling if he feared nothing, neither the shaking of the earth nor the waves, just as they say of the Celts." For nothing is more terrifying than a turbulent sea, and an earthquake seems to threaten the destruction of the foundations of the lower world and the upper world alike. Yet, the savagery of certain Gallic and Germanic tribes was so great that they were not terrified even by these things, which are naturally the most horrific. 

Since Aristotle uses the terms "mad" and "unfeeling" as essentially the same, I believe Diogenes the Cynic had this in mind when he was asked what he thought of Socrates. He said, "He is mad" <note>original Greek: μαινομένόν φησιν</note>: evidently because Socrates had hardened himself against all bodily discomfort, although in other respects he was the most tolerant of all injuries. Unless, perhaps, Diogenes attributed this to a stupor rather than to virtue, because Socrates could not be provoked even by blows to flare up in anger even a little bit.

### To change shoes.

Not without the quality of a proverb, Cicero said that a man had "changed his shoes" when he usurped senatorial dignity through no merit of his own. The insignia of a senator was a black shoe with a small moon <note>called a *lunula*, usually made of ivory</note> added around the ankle. Marcus Tullius Cicero’s words are as follows: "There is also a certain Asinius, a voluntary senator, chosen by himself. He saw the senate-house open after Caesar’s death; he changed his shoes, and suddenly became a Conscript Father <note>A formal title for a Roman senator</note>." Just as the golden stud <note>the *laticlavus*, a broad purple stripe fastened with studs</note> on the toga was a sign of senatorial rank, so the black leather tied around the ankles declared the same dignity.

### Campanian pride.

Fierceness is usually the companion of good fortune. Many authors, including Pliny in Book 3, Chapter 5, testify that Campania <note>A region in southern Italy</note> was once the most blessed region of Italy. Pliny says: "From here begins that happy Campania; from this bay start the vine-bearing hills, famous for their noble intoxication, with a juice renowned throughout all lands, and as the ancients said, the greatest contest of Father Liber <note>Bacchus, the god of wine</note> with Ceres <note>the goddess of grain</note>." He continues with descriptions of both the fertility and the pleasantness of Campania. 

It is well known that the city of Capua once vied with Rome for leadership. From this, **Campanian pride** and **Campanian arrogance** became a proverb. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *Against Rullus*, says: "Therefore, our ancestors, by reason and counsel, reduced that Campanian arrogance and intolerable fierceness to the most inactive and sluggish leisure." In this way, they escaped the infamy of cruelty, because they did not destroy the most beautiful city in Italy, but they provided for the future by cutting out its sinews, leaving the city itself weakened and broken. 

A little later in the same work, he calls Capua the "home of pride and the seat of luxury": "Therefore, chosen colonists were placed in the home of pride and the seats of luxury." Likewise, in the speech he delivered in the Senate after his return: "Did you think," he says, "that you were consul in Capua—a city which was once the home of pride—as you were at that time?" Again, in a fragment of a speech against the same man: "A place which, because of the fertility of the fields and the abundance of all things, is said to have bred pride and cruelty." And shortly after: "If luxury corrupted Hannibal himself <note>The Carthaginian general whose army famously wintered in Capua</note>, if pride is said to have been born there from the disdain of the Campanians." 

Titus Livy also writes in the ninth book of his first Decade that the Campanians possess immense pride. To this, Aulus Gellius adds in Book 11, Chapter 23, that the epitaph of the poet Naevius, which speaks of himself rather boastfully, is a specimen of "Campanian pride." I believe Naevius was himself a Campanian. Thus, just as the people used to call any notable treachery "Punic" <note>Carthaginian</note>, they called any fierce arrogance "Campanian." 

But I will say nothing now of the current character of the people; however, when I myself was traveling through Campania, I nowhere found that "juice renowned throughout all lands." I found not a drop of Falernian, Calenian, Massic, Setine, Caecuban, or Surrentine wine <note>Famous ancient Roman luxury wines</note>. In fact, we were very nearly choked by a "wine quinsy" <note>A play on the "silver quinsy" or bribery mentioned on the previous page; here Erasmus jokes that the lack of good wine was suffocating</note> in the very place that is now shown as Capua.

...we filled the whole bowl with crushed sugar; yet the wine won out, being sharper than any vinegar. They generally use boiled-down must <note>original: "defrutis," a thick syrup made by boiling down grape juice</note>, because otherwise it would not last until the next harvest. And where are those elegant wines whose name and homeland antiquity has erased? We have drunk enough of the dust. Thus nature allows nothing in human affairs to be perpetual.

->To shout of oneself.<-
### XV
We have previously mentioned the proverb *he plays the flute for himself* <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς αὑτὸν αὐλεῖ</note>; that is, he is his own flute-player. Very similar to this is what the Greeks express in a single word, *to shout of oneself* <note>original Greek: αὐτοβοᾶν</note>, used if someone praises himself with his own voice—that is, he acts as his own herald. For heralds are accustomed to publicize the skills and qualities of people for sale <note>a reference to the slave markets of antiquity</note> so that they might better entice a buyer. However, it is considered ridiculous for a man to be his own herald. This aligns with what we have said elsewhere: *the witness is from home* <note>original Greek: οἴκοθεν ὁ μάρτυς</note>. This proverb is recorded in the works of Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world</note>. The inhabitants of Attica use a similar figure of speech: *may you perish along with your own words*, and Aristophanes in *The Knights* says: "so that the gods might destroy the Paphlagonian along with his very counsels." And shortly after: "along with his very slanders."

->Do not cultivate a sterile field.<-
### XVI
*Do not sow a sterile field* <note>original Greek: Στεῖραν ἀγρὸν μὴ σπείρειν</note>. This is recorded among the Platonic laws. With this riddle, the law in Plato modestly discourages male-to-male intercourse, if I remember correctly. In the eighth book of the *Laws*, he says those men "sow seeds upon rocks." However, it can be adapted for other uses: do not attempt to teach the unteachable, or do not seek happiness in riches. For these things do not give birth to true blessedness for a man. Plautus says in *Amphitryo*: "For providing a wife for temporary use is just the same as if you were to take a sterile field to be cultivated."

->A beetle will make honey sooner.<-
### XVII
To the class of "impossible things" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἀδυνάτων</note> belong these phrases recorded in an epigram by Palladas: "A beetle will make honey sooner, or a gnat will produce milk."
*A beetle will make honey sooner, or a gnat milk.* <note>Erasmus provides two Latin poetic variations of the Greek line: Θᾶττον ποιήσει μέλι κάνθαρος, ἢ γάλα κώνωψ</note>

->I see land.<-
### XVIII
One who wished to signify that the end of a long and troublesome labor was at hand used to say: *I see land* <note>original Greek: γῆν ὁρῶ</note>. This is taken from sailors. Quintus Curtius writes in his fourth book: "Not otherwise than those who have entered the deep sea search for land with their eyes." Plautus in *The Merchant*: "Indeed, I already thought I was on land." Marcus Tullius Cicero in his speech *In Defense of Lucius Murena* says: "If those who are already being carried into port from the deep are usually eager to warn those setting sail about the nature of storms, pirates, and places—because nature prompts us to favor those entering the same dangers we have just completed—with what mind should I be, who am now seeing land after a great tossing, toward this man who, I see, must undergo the greatest storms of the Republic?" The same author in *Cato the Elder*: "As if I see land," feeling that the end of his life was pressing near. Diogenes, when he had finally reached the point where he could see the end of a long book being read aloud, said: "It is well, friends; *I see land*."

->More effective than any incantation.<-
### XIX
*Colder than any incantation* <note>original Greek: πάσης ἐπῳδῆς ψυχρότερον; Erasmus translates the Greek "colder" as "more effective," perhaps implying it "cools" or settles a matter better than magic</note>. The ancients were persuaded that a prodigious power resided in the voices of enchanters, so much so that even the mystical Psalm mentions the sorcerer charming wisely, and compares the people who do not obey the commands of the divinity to a deaf asp. Plato, in his letter to Hermias, Erastus, and Coriscus, says: "For I think that words proceeding from us here, joined with justice and shame, will—more than any incantation—reconcile you and bind you back together into your former friendship and community."

->The envious eye of a neighbor.<-
### XX
Aliclytus to Eucymon: "For the eye of neighbors is malevolent and envious, as the proverb says" <note>original Greek: δυσμενὴς γὰρ τὸ βάσκανον ὁ τῶν γειτόνων ὀφθαλμός</note>. He was looking, if I am not mistaken, at the saying of Hesiod about the potter, the singer, and the neighbor, which we have recorded elsewhere. Thus Ovid says:
"The harvest is always more fertile in another’s field,
And the neighbor's herd has a larger udder."

->To heal everyone with the same eye-salve.<-
### XXI
Laws, warnings, and rebukes should not be applied to everyone in the same way, but according to...
