<meta>This page continues from page 997, concluding a discussion on adapting speech to one's audience before launching into a series of proverbs regarding total destruction, public notoriety, and uninvited guests. The previous page mentioned the variety of human temperaments; here, Erasmus cites St. Jerome and Galen on the necessity of flexibility.</meta>

...to temper one’s speech to the variety of nations, times, and temperaments. The blessed Jerome, in his commentary on the *Epistle to the Ephesians*, praises this dexterity in the Apostle Paul, who "became all things to all men, so that he might win all" <note>1 Corinthians 9:22</note>. Jerome’s words are cited in the *Decretum* <note>A collection of canon law</note>, distinction 29. "He does not," says Jerome, "like an unskilled physician, wish to cure the eyes of everyone with a single eye-salve." Elsewhere we have related a similar sentiment from Galen: "To put the same shoe on every foot."

->**Utterly, from the roots, etc.**<-

What is lost entirely and beyond hope of restoration is said to be destroyed **utterly** <note>original: *funditus*, literally "from the foundations"</note> and **from the roots** <note>original: *radicitus*</note>. The first of these is taken from a building when it is leveled to the ground; the second from trees, where not only are the branches lopped off, but the stump itself is cut away or torn out along with the roots. Acinetus, reproaching his mistress Phoebiana because he seemed already stripped of everything by her, said: *Thus, when you have overturned me entirely according to the proverb, you have additionally led me into slavery* <note>Erasmus provides the Greek: ὅτως... ἐπυλάγησας, a line likely from a lost comedy</note>. Plautus in the *Trinummus*: "That worthless fellow has **utterly** ruined [funditus pessundedit] his wisdom, my loyalty, and all our secrets." The same author in the *Mostellaria* used the phrase "with the foundation" for the same idea: "Can I not repair my house before the whole thing collapses forever, before it has perished **with the foundation**, and no one can help?" What we call "from the roots" or "from the stump," the Greeks call *ekpremnizein*, as if you were to say "to extirpate." Cicero used this word in his book *On Fate*: "To be extirpated and **utterly removed** [funditus tolli] as he himself was, etc." The same author in *Pro Sexto Roscio Amerino*: "And from that, Titus Roscius did not just turn a little something to his own profit, but **utterly overthrew** [funditus euertit] this man." Also in the *Orations against Verres*, book 4: "For day, voice, and strength would fail me if I wished now to cry out how wretched and unworthy it is that a festival day is held in his name among those who consider themselves to have been **utterly ruined** [funditus euersos] by his deeds." Again in book 5 of the same work: "For the previous year had violently shaken the farmers; the next year indeed had **utterly ruined** them." The same in *Pro domo sua* to the pontiffs: "You would **overthrow** [euerteres] the city." In the same work: "That all memory of him who had begun ruinous plans for the Republic might be **utterly removed** from the eyes and minds of men." Likewise in his *Letters to his brother Quintus*: "But if we comply in all things, we shall allow them to perish **utterly** [funditus]." Again to the same: "We have **utterly lost** the Republic." Item in the same: "Do you see that he has not **uprooted** [radicitus] all your actions?" Much grace will be added if this is applied to the mind: as if someone should say that ambition, greed, and lust must be torn out **utterly and from the roots** from the soul.

->**In the mouth and eyes.**<-

Things that are done openly are said to be done "**in the mouth and eyes** of everyone." Marcus Tullius Cicero in *Against Verres*, book 5: "When you have confessed these things which were done openly in the forum at Syracuse, **in the mouth and eyes** of the province." Again in the *Divination against Caecilius*: "Does it not occur to you what a task it is to sustain a public cause: to explain the whole life of another, and to expose it not only in the minds of the judges, but in the **eyes and sight** of everyone?" Perhaps he said "mouth" here for "sight." Otherwise, people are said to be "in everyone's mouth" when there is a public rumor about them. And we are said to "carry in our eyes" those whom we watch over and care for.

->**In the manner of the Myconians.**<-

**In the manner of the Myconians** <note>original Greek: Μυκονίων δίκην</note> was a phrase used for those who came to a banquet uninvited. Myconus is one of the Cyclades islands; the people themselves, due to their poverty, were forced to push themselves into banquets; hence the proverbial joke. In the works of Athenaeus, Archilochus tears into Pericles because he would rush into feasts uninvited, **in the manner of the Myconians**—a passage we have noted elsewhere. You may see traces of Myconian manners even today among certain Irishmen. Regarding this, that most distinguished man William Mountjoy <note>Erasmus's patron, William Blount, 4th Baron Mountjoy</note> once recited a not-unpleasant story to me—indeed, not a story, but an event he himself witnessed. A certain unknown Irishman, having entered the Prince's hall at dinner time, sat down uninvited at the table of the royal attendants. They, seeing the bold stranger, asked where he was from. He declared his country. They asked if he had any office in the court. "None," he said, "but I desire to have one." They, marvelling at the man's impudence, ordered him to get up and leave. "I will do this," he said, "at my leisure." To be brief: he won by his persistence, nor did the Irishman leave until the meal was finished. Finally, their anger turning to laughter, they asked the man how he, a stranger and an outsider, had such audacity to push himself into the royal household. "Because," he said, "I knew the King was rich enough to give me dinner."

->**To help the sun with torches.**<-

Elsewhere we have recorded the proverb: *You are lending light to the sun*. Very similar to this is what Gratian records...

<meta>This page continues from page 998, where Erasmus was concluding a discussion on the limitations of human perception. Here, he shifts into a series of adages regarding the fallibility of human justice, the nature of inconstancy, and the corruption of the legal system.</meta>

->EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND<-

Pope Anacletus, in Case 6, Question 1 <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of canon law</note>, writes against those who usurp for themselves divine judgment, which no human can escape. For human judgments are uncertain, and they compare to the judgments of God no differently than a torch compares to the sun. "If all things," he says, "were avenged in this age, there would be no place for divine judgments. He labors with useless expense who strives to help the sun with torches," etc. Although in common books, the scribes had corrupted "torches" <note>original: *facibus*</note> into "bundles of rods" <note>original: *fascibus*, a symbol of Roman magisterial power</note>.

## XXVI. The censorial rod
Among the learned, it is a very somber thing to call the authority of judging—especially when done with a haughty brow—the **censorial rod** <note>original: *Censoria uirgula*</note>; the term is taken from the Roman magistracy. This is the same sentiment expressed by the blessed Jerome in his dialogue against the Luciferians: "No one can take the palm of Christ for himself, no one can judge men before the day of judgment." It seems Jerome alluded to the twenty-fifth chapter of Deuteronomy, where a "palm of justice" is mentioned, which was handed by judges to the one who had proven his innocence and won his case. Christ truly holds this palm, and he does not hand it to the unworthy, since he alone is not deceived in judgment, whereas in human judgments there is a great deal of both error and darkness.

## XXVII. In the manner of a top
**In the manner of a top** <note>Erasmus provides the Greek: Βέμβικος δίκην</note>, that is, like a spinning top, is a saying used for those who are fickle and inconstant. For a *bembix* is a top that boys drive around with a whip. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note> cites from Aristophanes: "He turns just like a top." This means one ought not differ at all from a top. The passage is in *The Birds*. Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian</note> thinks the saying applies to someone who, in flight, does not keep to a straight path but is driven around in a circle. 

This once happened to me while I was traveling from Schlettstadt to Basel. By chance, we encountered a certain knight, and while I rode with him as our guide for a long time in a forest, I asked him if he knew the way for certain. He said he did. When there was no end to it, I said, "We must be lost; for we have been wandering for three hours in a forest that we usually cross within one." To make a long story short: it was discovered we were a hair's breadth away from returning to the very place we started. Now, a top moves with great force, but in a circle, so that in fleeing it does not escape. With a similar metaphor, that wise Hebrew, Sirach, notes the inconstancy of fools in chapter thirty-three: "The heart of a fool is like a cartwheel, and his thoughts are like a turning axle" <note>Ecclesiasticus 33:5</note>. In Plautus, someone is occasionally said to be "more turnable than a top or a potter’s wheel."

## XXVIII. Better to provoke a dog than an old woman
This is recorded from Menander: "It is much worse to irritate an old woman than a dog." The Hebrew proverbs say that no anger is more atrocious than a woman's anger. For the female sex is irritable and vindictive, partly due to a lack of reason, and partly due to lowliness of spirit. For it is a mark of true magnanimity to ignore certain injuries and not to deem all men worthy of one’s anger. Furthermore, a woman is a formidable creature when old age is added to the vice of her sex. A provoked dog only barks, and sometimes bites; but old women, besides the poison of their tongues, are sometimes equipped with evil arts, sorceries, and incantations. And so, some have experienced to their great misfortune that what Menander said is very true.

## XXIX. A wealthy man cannot be condemned
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second action against Verres, says it has become a common saying among everyone—not only among Romans but even among foreign nations—that in the courts of those times, no **wealthy man**, however guilty he might be, could be condemned. And in the third speech against the same man: "For the defendant," he says, "is most guilty. If he is condemned, men will stop saying that money is most powerful in these trials. But if he is acquitted, we shall stop refusing to transfer the courts." Akin to this is what is repeated several times in Sallust's *Jugurthine War*: "At Rome, all things are for sale." Now Rome has lost its empire; would that the saying had not stuck.

## XXX. Between the hand and the chin
Festus Pompeius indicates this is a proverb among the Latins, but derived from that Greek one: "Many things happen between the cup and the edge of the lip." He records its origin thus: when Chalcas <note>A mythical Greek seer</note> was planting a vine, a certain neighboring augur passing by said he was mistaken, for it would not be permitted for him to taste the new wine. This much can be gathered from the fragments that the stupidity of certain people allowed to survive from an author who was most learned in every respect. The proverb warns that in human life nothing is certain. For it often happens that just when we believe we hold something most firmly, some unexpected chance in- <meta>catchword: -tervenes (teruer-)</meta>

...turns back. Just as when someone holds a cup in their hand, and there is the smallest space between the hand and the chin, it nevertheless sometimes happens that he dies before he can drink. This proverb is expressed in various ways, and different authors have provided different origins for it; I believe enough has been said about these in the proverb, *Many things fall between the cup and the highest lips* <note>original: "Multa cadunt inter calicem supremaque labra." This is the classic "There's many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip."</note>. I have recorded it here because it is mentioned with different words by Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>, in which there is a certain grace from the wordplay between "Hand and chin" <note>original: "Manum & mentum." Erasmus appreciates the phonetic similarity in Latin.</note>.

->The Colophonian shoe. XXXI<-

**Colophonian shoe** <note>original Greek: Κολοφώνιον ὑπόδημα</note>. That is, the Colophonian shoe was said to be "hollow." For the ancients almost always used sandals, which protected only the bottom part of the feet. I have seen among our own people a type of footwear made from hollowed-out wood, which in the common tongue they call a **hollow trunk** <note>original: "cauum truncum." Erasmus is likely referring to clogs or wooden sabots.</note>. From this, the term will apply to a man who is stupid, clumsy, and rustic. Such a shoe is suitable for those about to walk through mud. Thus, you might charmingly say that one who is about to deal with "filthy" authors <note>meaning authors of poor quality or crude content</note> has need of **Colophonian shoes**. To this, the **Sicyonian shoe** seems to be the opposite; its name was bestowed by the city of Sicyon in the Peloponnese, as Stephanus indicates, and also Sextus Pompeius Festus. Neither, however, indicates the usage of the adage. Marcus Tullius Cicero indicates that Sicyonian shoes were very pretty, but more suitable for women and the effeminate than for men. I will transcribe the words of Cicero: "Indeed, when the eloquent orator Lysias had brought a written speech to Socrates, so that if it seemed good to him he might learn it by heart and use it on his own behalf in court, Socrates read it willingly and said it was well written. But, he said, just as if you had brought me Sicyonian shoes, I would not use them—even though they were comfortable and fit my feet—because they would not be manly; so that speech seemed to him eloquent and oratorical, but did not seem strong and manly."

->Manduces. XXXII<-

**Manduces** <note>A term for gluttons or grotesque masked figures</note> was the name given to those who were extremely hungry, or those who inspired terror with empty threats. Festus Pompeius records that in ancient processions, among other ridiculous and fearsome figures, there used to go an effigy with large jaws, a wide-gaping mouth, and making a huge sound with its teeth. They called this figure a **Manducus**. In Plautus’s play *The Rope* <note>original: "Rudens"</note>, the parasite Charmides speaks thus: "What if I hire myself out somewhere at the games as a *Manducus*? Why? Because, by Pollux, I am clattering my teeth loudly." The parasite had swum away from a shipwreck and was shivering all over from the cold. Whence, a little later, he says he speaks "all a-quiver." Martial seems to be referring to this or a similar effigy when he says:
>I am a potter's plaything, the mask of a red-haired Batavian.
>These features which you mock, a child fears.
The Greeks call this kind of image **mormolykia** <note>original Greek: μορμολύκια; essentially "bugbears" or "bogeymen"</note>, because they would terrify children with a wolf-like appearance so that they would stop crying.

->Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia. XXXIII<-

Plutarch, in his *Roman Questions*, asks from where that custom arose, that those who lead the bride to the groom command her to speak these words: **Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia** <note>original Greek: ὅπου σὺ κάιος, ἐγὼ κάια</note>. He doubts whether the ancients wanted the bride to bargain with the groom with these words, so that all things would be common between them and they would rule the household equally—as if she were saying, "As you are the master and head of the house, so I am the mistress and lady of the house." The form of the speech seems to come from the legal experts, who use the names **C. Seius and L. Titius** for any person at all <note>equivalent to the modern legal "John Doe"</note>, just as philosophers use **Dion and Theon**. Whence also that proverb which we cited elsewhere from Varro: "The same for Accius as for Titius," when it signifies an equal right between two people. Or perhaps she is called "Gaia" for the sake of a good omen, because there was a certain **Caia Cecilia**, a woman of both elegant beauty and most esteemed character (previously called Tanaquil), who married one of the sons of Tarquinius, namely Tarquinius Priscus. To this Caia, the Romans placed a bronze statue in the Temple of Sancus <note>Erasmus notes the Greek: ἐν τῷ Ϝάγκου ἱερῷ, "in the temple of Sancus"</note>. He was a god once worshipped by this name among the Romans, one of the number of the twelve selected gods. In that same place in ancient times, her sandals and distaff <note>a tool for spinning wool</note> were kept; the former testified that she had stayed at home and cared for the family, while the latter signified her industry, because she diligently performed womanly labors, being devoted to wool-working. Thus, the mention of this name warned the bride to be such a woman to her husband as Caia Cecilia had been to hers. Among the ancient wedding ceremonies, this was also observed (since it was considered unlucky) to call either the groom or the bride by their own proper names. Indeed, even to this day, the custom is observed that the bride, leaving behind her family name, passes to the name of her husband, such as "Hector’s Andromache." This proverb, born from marriage...

CHILIAD 4, CENTURY 8
Ppp 3

...should remain, except that it can also be adapted to apply to a sister and a brother.

### Public rumor is not entirely in vain. XXXIV

Aristotle, in the seventh book of the *Nicomachean Ethics* <note>original: "Moralium Nicomach. vij"</note>, cites a very famous poem by Hesiod: 
> The rumor that many people spread does not perish altogether.
<note>original Greek: "φήμη δ' οὔτι πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται, ἥντινα λαοὶ πολλοὶ φημίζωσιν."</note> 
That is to say:
> That rumor which flits through the mouths of many peoples does not perish entirely.

The Philosopher <note>a common title for Aristotle in the Renaissance</note> brings forward this little verse as a probable argument that pleasure is the highest good, because both humans and brute animals seek it.

### A square man. XXXV

In the first book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Aristotle disputes those who define human happiness by external goods—things which are given and taken away at the whim of fortune. He says that, by this logic, a man is made into a kind of **chameleon**, who is happy one moment and unhappy the next as circumstances change, just as a chameleon changes color according to the appearance of the things it approaches. In truth, real happiness is located primarily in the "goods of the soul" <note>virtues and intellectual qualities</note>. From this he concludes that for one who is truly blessed, nothing stands in the way of being happy throughout their whole life. He adds: 
> For he will always, or most of all, act and contemplate according to virtue; and he will bear the accidents of fortune most nobly and in every way harmoniously—he, indeed, who is truly good and **four-square without blame**. 
<note>original Greek: "τὰ γὰρ ἢ μάλιστα πάντως πράξει καὶ θεωρήσει τὰ κατ' ἀρετὴν, καὶ τὰς τύχας οἴσει κάλλιστα καὶ πάντη πάντως ἐμμελῶς, ὅγ' ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὸς καὶ τετράγωνος ἄνευ ψόγου."</note> 

Aristotle mentions this saying again in the third book of his *Rhetoric* among the types of metaphors. This shape <note>the cube or square</note>, into whatever part it is rolled, remains similar to itself. Likewise, the wise man does not change his mind no matter what fortune befalls him. It will be more elegant if we call the mind of a brave man, which cannot be shaken by any accidents of fortune, **four-square** <note>original Greek: "τετράγωνον"</note>.

### Let a reward be fixed. XXXVI

Plutarch, in his *Life of Theseus*, records that there was a certain Pittheus, the maternal grandfather of Theseus, by whom the chaste Hippolytus was educated. He was famous for his *gnomologies* <note>collections of wise sayings or maxims</note>, which at that time were considered the highest form of wisdom. They say this was one of his sayings:
> Let the reward for a friend be fixed and sufficient.
<note>original Greek: "μισθὸς δ' ἀνδρὶ φίλῳ εἰρημένος ἄρκιος ἔσω."</note> 

Aristotle, in the ninth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, tells how Protagoras <note>a famous Sophist and teacher</note> was not accustomed to make a contract with any of his disciples. Instead, when they had learned what they wanted, he ordered them to consider for themselves how much they valued what they had learned, and he accepted whatever was given by them. For those of such a spirit, Aristotle thinks Pittheus's precept is sufficient in this kind of commerce: it orders a just and fair reward to be set for a friend. It would be well if doctors also made no contracts, but accepted what was given once the sick person was relieved. For what Aristotle relates in the same place about certain Sophists—who would not receive anyone into their teaching unless the fee was paid in advance, and then, having taken the money, did not perform what they had promised—we see happening sometimes with untrustworthy surgeons and doctors. Generally, those who demand a huge prize and will not lift a hand unless either the whole sum or the largest part is paid immediately are found to be impostors.

### Learn good things from the good. XXXVII

In the ninth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, Aristotle shows that virtue is best learned through living with good people, because friends correct one another if any mistake is made, and they excite each other to honorable actions. He cites a poem as if it were well known: 
> For from the good [you will learn] good things.
<note>original Greek: "ἐσθλῶν μὲν γὰρ ἀπ' ἐσθλά."</note> 
This is a verse by Theognis, whom Xenophon mentions in his commentary *On the Sayings and Deeds of Socrates*. Socrates used to say that among ointments, no oil smelled better than that which athletes used; "marjoram" and "leaf-ointment" <note>expensive perfumes of the time</note> should be left to women. When asked what scent was becoming for old men, he replied: **probity**. Then, asked where this ointment was sold, he replied with Theognis's half-line:
> From the good, you will learn good things.
<note>original Greek: "ἐσθλῶν μὲν γὰρ ἀπ' ἐσθλὰ διδάξεαι."</note> 

Likewise, our own **writer of maxims** <note>referring to Cato the Elder, author of the *Distichs of Cato*</note> says: *Learn, but from the learned.*

### A donkey prefers straw to gold. XXXVIII

Aristotle, in the tenth book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*, disputing that pleasure is not the same for everyone—since a dog is delighted by certain things, a horse by others, and a man by others—cites Heraclitus who said...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus's exploration of ancient proverbs, moving from the philosophical ethics of Aristotle to the satirical humor of Aristophanes. It examines the human tendency to value vanity over utility and the importance of moderation in play.</meta>

DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES

...as the saying goes, **an ass would choose sweepings rather than gold** <note>original Greek: "ὄνος σύρματ' ἂν ἕλοιτο μᾶλλον ἢ χρυσόν"</note>, or **an ass's fodder is better than gold** <note>original Greek: "ὄνου χοὰς χρυσῶ τροφὴ ὄνοις"</note>, meaning that a donkey’s food is more delightful to it than gold. In this respect, indeed, donkeys are wiser than humans. They value a thing by its utility; we, led by the whims of our minds, set enormous prices on useless and even harmful things. The fable of the cock is well-known—how he looked down upon a gem he found in a dungheap. For the cock prefers a rotten grain of corn to a pearl or a diamond. So too those who are slaves to their bellies prefer a drunken revelry to all the liberal arts <note>the traditional core subjects of a classical education</note>.

<margin>XXX</margin>
## Play so that you may work.
In the same book, he relates the opinion of Anacharsis <note>Erasmus writes "Anacharlidis," referring to the famous Scythian philosopher</note>, who criticized those who treat serious business as a time to play, whereas a joke should only be admitted occasionally so that one may have the leisure to return to serious matters. This is like those who, with great effort, spend their whole lives trying to become good dancers or excellent flute-players. Aristotle’s words are these: *To be serious about a trifle for the sake of play seems foolish and very much like a child; but to play so that you may be serious seems, according to Anacharsis, to be correct.* <note>original Greek: "σπουδάζειν δὲ ἐν πονηρῷ παιδιᾶς χάριν..."</note> That is to say, to study and labor for the sake of a game seems stupid and quite childish. But to play so that you may perform your duties seems, according to the opinion of Anacharsis, to be proper.

## In the manner of the Cyclopes.
In the same book again, he calls a **Cyclopean life** <note>referring to the one-eyed giants of Homer's Odyssey</note> one where people live under no public laws, but each manages affairs according to his own whim: *In most cities, such things are neglected, and each, as he wishes, in the manner of a Cyclops, lays down the law for his children and wife.* <note>original Greek: "ἕκαστος, ὡς βέλεται, κυκλωπικῶς θεμιστεύων..."</note> That is, in other states there is no care taken regarding the education of children, but everyone lives as he likes, in the rite of the Cyclopes, deciding what is right and wrong for his children and wife. For it is said that the Cyclopes lived scattered in the mountains, with no form of civil life, but each did as he pleased in his own cave; they did not even have any religion. We have discussed the **life of a Cyclops** <note>original: "κύκλωπος βίος"</note> elsewhere.

## Among the hares.
**Among the hares** <note>original Greek: "Ἐν λαγῴοις"</note>. Those who lived sumptuously and in luxury were said to live "among leporine meats." For Martial <note>a Roman poet known for his epigrams</note> declares that the meat of the hare was once considered the height of delicacies:
> If any judge compares the birds, the thrush is best;
> Of four-legged beasts, the hare claims first glory.
The proverb also attests to this: *You are a hare yourself, yet you seek the meat of delicacies.* Aristophanes, in the *Wasps*, says: "There are a thousand cities which now pay us tribute. If it were commanded that each of these should support twenty men,"
> Twenty thousand of the common folk would live on hare-meat,
> And all kinds of garlands, and first-milk, and beestings-cake.
<note>original Greek: "Δύο μυριάδες τῶν δημοτικῶν ζῴων..."</note>
->that is,<-
Twenty thousand people would live on every kind of hare-meat, with various garlands, and *pyon* and *pyarite*. The Greeks call the first milk an animal gives after birth *pyon* <note>term: pyon (πύον) — colostrum or "first milk"</note>, and *pyarite* is the dish made from it. The commentator cites a poem from Homer, if I am not mistaken: *Feasting on first-milk, and filling themselves with beestings-cake.*
Again, Aristophanes in *The Knights*, when Cleon and his adversary compete to promise the most exquisite banquets to the people, mentions many types of delicacies, including hare-meat, as if it were the height of refined luxury.

<margin>X</margin>
## Follow your mother, piglets.
**Follow your mother, piglets** <note>original Greek: "Ἐπεσθε μητρὶ χοῖροι"</note>. He repeats this several times in Aristophanes’ *Plutus*. The commentator notes that this is a proverbial joke against the stupid and the unlearned. For the "pig" <note>term: sus — a pig, often used in proverbs to denote ignorance</note> is contrasted with Minerva <note>the goddess of wisdom</note> in the proverb. It is as if one were to say to unlearned students of an unlearned teacher: *Follow your mother, piglets.* It also fits those devoted to gluttony and the belly.

<margin>XI</margin>
## In the manner of Aristyllus.
The same author in the same place says: *But you, like Aristyllus, look on with your mouth gaping.* <note>original Greek: "σὺ δ' ἀρίσυλλος ὑποχάσκων ὁρᾷς"</note>. The commentator notes that Aristyllus was a poet with a deformed face whose mouth was always open. Aristophanes mocks him in passing, and mentions him in the *Assemblywomen* (*Ecclesiazusae*). It is characteristic of tragic actors to speak with a very wide-open mouth. But it seems to me that Aristyllus was mocked rather because he spoke with his mouth only slightly open, so that his voice came out mostly through his nose with a whistling sound, like the sound pigs make—a defect we see in the pronunciation and singing of some people.

<summary>Erasmus compiles several proverbs relating to the contrast between wisdom and animalistic instinct, including the "Cyclopean life" of lawlessness and the luxurious "life among the hares." He uses these Greek and Latin examples to critique human greed and lack of education.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, transitioning from the previous page's discussion on the vanity of choosing trifles over substance to specific proverbial phrases found in the works of Cato, Plautus, Aristophanes, and Aristotle.</meta>

FOURTH THOUSAND, EIGHTH CENTURY

### Citeria.
<margin>XLIIII</margin>
**Citeria** was a taunt once commonly thrown at excessively talkative people. Cato, in his speech against Marcus Caelius, says: *What more should I say? I believe he will eventually be carried in a procession during the games in place of a Citeria, to chatter at the spectators.* <note>original Latin: "Quid ego dicerẽ amplius... pro Citeria"</note> Festus Pompeius <note>a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> reminds us that a **Citeria** was a type of sharp-tongued and talkative effigy that used to be carried in processions for the sake of a laugh, constantly emitting rattling and clattering noises. Nowadays, the Citeria is no longer carried in processions, but many people have "Citerias" at home who are far more noisy than those manufactured ones.

### Clings like an oyster.
<margin>XLV</margin>
**Clings like an oyster** <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ λεπὰς προσέχεται," literally "sticks like a limpet"</note>, or like a shellfish. Aristophanes used this in reference to an old woman who was difficulty to pull away from a young man:
*O King Jupiter, how forcefully this little old woman*
*Clings to the youth, just like a limpet.* <note>original Greek: "ὦ ζεῦ βασιλεῦ τὸ γραΐδιον / ὥσπερ λεπὰς τῷ μειρακίῳ προσέχεται"</note>
There is a species of shellfish that clings together with certain filaments so that it may be safer against the movement of the waves.

### Nothing succeeds today.
<margin>XLVI</margin>
Plautus’s character Amphitryon, in the play of the same name, cites this as an adage: *There is nothing, as the saying goes, that turns out well for me today.* He was alluding to a common superstition where certain days were believed to be auspicious for conducting business, and others unlucky. If one or two things did not turn out as desired, people would judge the whole day by that result and say, **"Nothing will succeed today,"** and they would refrain from all business.

### Neither running nor rowing.
<margin>XLVII</margin>
In the *Assemblywomen* <note>a comedy by Aristophanes where women take over the government of Athens</note>, Aristophanes has the women, who are striving to take over the Republic because they have been excluded from every function and have achieved nothing so far, say:
*For now we neither run nor are we helped by the rower.* <note>original Greek: "νῦν μὲν γὰρ οὔτε θέομεν, οὔτ' ἐλαύνομεν"</note>
The metaphor is taken from sailors and applied to the governing of the State. Sailors are said to "run" when the winds are favorable; they are said to "row" <note>original Greek: "ἐλαύνειν"</note> when, deprived of wind, they propel the ship by oar—which is called a "secondary course" <note>original Greek: "ὁ δεύτερος πλοῦς"</note>. The women feel they are called to no duties, neither in peace nor in war. This can also be aptly applied to those who, despite trying hard, achieve nothing because fortune is against them.

### Like mud-carriers.
<margin>XLVIII</margin>
**Like those carrying mud.** <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ πηλοφοροῦντες"</note> In Aristophanes’s *Assemblywomen*, the women complain that the Athenian people do not gather for the assembly unless each person is given an obol <note>a small coin</note>, whereas previously they consulted on the Republic at their own expense. He used the term **mud-carrying** <note>original Greek: "πηλοφορία"</note> to represent the most sordid of all profit-seeking trades. This is aptly turned against those who abuse honorable offices for low profit: such as those who preach, sacrifice, bury, or administer the sacraments, and will not do so unless something is put into their hand, **just like mud-carriers.** A well-known sacred history tells of the Hebrews serving in Egypt **in mud and brick.** <note>original Greek: "ἐν πηλῷ καὶ πλίνθῳ"</note>

### As many as a wise man.
<margin>XLIX</margin>
In the third book of his *Rhetoric*, Aristotle, advising that an orator should not use enthymemes <note>a type of rhetorical syllogism or logical shortcut</note> too frequently but only intersperse them, adds this verse—from Homer, if I am not mistaken—as a commonly tossed-about saying:
*Since, dear friend, you have spoken as many things*
*As a wise and experienced man would say.* <note>original Greek: "ὦ φίλ' ἐπεὶ τόσα εἶπες, ὅσ' ἂν πεπνυμένος ἀνήρ"</note>
This is suitable for a person who speaks much rather than opportunely. Aristotle says, "**As many** <note>Greek: τόσα</note> but **not such** <note>Greek: τοιαῦτα</note>." For it does not matter so much how many things we say, but how relevant they are to the matter at hand. Just as a certain philosopher said, those should not be considered learned who have learned many things, but those who have learned useful things.

### Even the prophets know this now.
<margin>L</margin>
A little later in the same work, while discussing how much more difficult it is to speak in public consultations than to plead cases in court—because the advisor speaks of the future while the accuser or defender speaks of the past, and moreover, the latter has the law as a foundation, from which it is easy to find a proof—Aristotle adds the opinion of Epimenides the Cretan: **"That man [knew] even what the prophets [know] now."** <note>original Greek: "ὁ δ' ἐκεῖνος ἤδη καὶ μάντες"</note>
that is,

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient adages, moving from the previous page's discussion on omens and the prophet Epimenides into proverbs regarding novelty, ethnic stereotypes, and the moral consequences of malice.</meta>

...that is to say, what has clearly already happened can now be known by divine beings. He adds that Epimenides was accustomed to prophesying not about the future, which cannot be known, but about the past—specifically about things that were hidden. For this is indeed a certain kind of divination. Saint Paul calls Epimenides a prophet. This joke can be aptly applied to a matter that is finally discovered after having long deceived us.

### New coins.

From Plautus, it appears that it is nothing new for the public currency to be minted of poorer quality year after year. For thus he prefaces his play *Casina*:

> Those who drink old wine, I think, are wise,
> And those who gladly watch old plays.
> Since ancient works and words please you,
> It is right that old plays should please you too.
> For the new comedies that come out now,
> Are much more worthless than new coins.

### To act like a Thracian.

We mentioned in previous sections that "to act like a Cretan" <note>original: "κρητίζειν" (kretizein)</note> had passed into a proverb for fraudulence. The same is indicated somewhat more obscurely by the word **to act like a Thracian** <note>original: "θρᾳκίζειν" (thrakizein)</note>, a term which in Greek means to cause a disturbance or to be troublesome. But if you look to the *Thracidae* <note>original: "θρᾳκίδας"</note>, who were Thracian slave girls, it means to deceive and to conquer with Thracian tricks. Theodorus said of Nicon the cithara-player <note>a professional singer who accompanied himself on the lyre</note> that he was "acting like a Thracian." Nicon, however, actually was a Thracian. Unless you know this, the joke loses its charm. Aristotle records this in the third book of his *Rhetoric*. I believe Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Knights*, where Nicias, ordered to speak boldly what he had in mind, replied: "But 'acting like a Thracian' is not in me." <note>original: "ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔνι μοι τὸ θρᾳκίζειν"</note> The interpreter notes that "to Thracianize" is a barbarian term signifying confidence and encouraging boldness, as if one were to say, "Take on the audacity of the Thracians."

### Neither said nor done.

**Neither said nor done.** <note>original Greek: "Μήτε δεδραμένα μήτε εἰρημένα"</note> There is no doubt that through this proverbial figure of speech, we describe something as being done with great intensity: "neither said nor done." It is of the same kind as the phrase "neither written nor painted." For we speak of a true lie made of mixed elements as "things done and not done." Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen* says: "For I think none of these things were ever done or said before." <note>original: "οὐδὲν γὰρ οἶμαι τῶν δεδραμένων μήτ’ εἰρημένων τῶν πρότερον"</note> Come now, finish your speech; things never done or said before. The comic poet jokingly advises the speaker to say everything new, because old things are heard with boredom. Truly, something must be remarkably new if it has been neither said nor done before, since according to the saying of the Hebrew sage <note>Solomon, in Ecclesiastes</note>, "there is nothing new under the sun." Marcus Tullius [Cicero] frequently says in his speeches that something was done in a "new manner," of which no example ever existed before.

### Greetings, daughters of horses.

It appears this was tossed around as a common joke against those who flatter for the sake of profit. Aristotle records it in the third book of his *Rhetoric*. In a mule-racing contest, when the winner offered a meager prize for a poem, Simonides <note>a Greek lyric poet</note> refused, indignant at the idea of celebrating mules in his poetry. But when the victor offered a large enough reward, he wrote a poem like this:

"Greetings, offspring of storm-footed horses." <note>original Greek: "Χαίρετ’ ἀελλοπόδων θυγατέρες ἵππων"</note> That is:
"Greetings, progeny of the swift-footed horses."

For he remained silent about the fact that they were also born from donkeys, and he expressed what was more honorable, calling them "daughters of horses."

### A priest of Mithras, not a torch-bearer.

He who performs base and despised roles in any duty is called a **Mithragyrtes**; he will be denied the title of **daduchus**. This is because Iphicrates called Callias a "Mithragyrtes, not a daduchus" <note>Mithragyrtes: a wandering beggar-priest of Mithras; daduchus: a prestigious torch-bearer in the Eleusinian mysteries</note>. He meant that the man had not been initiated into the sacred mysteries, yet wished to appear so. Among the Persians, Mithras is the name for the sun, whom they judge to be the greatest of gods. From this, it seems they are called **Mithragyrtae** who wander about with fake mysteries and impose upon the unrefined. Apuleius declares in *The Golden Ass* that this kind of person existed long ago, not unlike those today who carry around the relics of Saint Anthony, Saint Cornelius, or Saint John the Baptist for profit rather than for piety.

### He prepares evil for himself, who prepares it for another.

Aristotle, in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, cites this verse under the name of Democritus of Chios:
"A man fashions evil for himself when fashioning evil for another." <note>original Greek: "οἷτ’ αὐτῷ κακὰ τεύχει ἀνὴρ ἄλλῳ κακὰ τεύχων"</note> That is:
"Each man forges evils for himself while forging evils for another."

No one can inflict an injury on another without first hurting himself. He who cheats another commits a sin; he strips himself of a good mind, and thus hurts himself more severely than the other. Therefore, it is most truly said: "He hurts himself, who seeks to hurt another."

# FOURTH CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY

->**Carrying a beam.** LVII<-

Aristotle, in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, when discussing certain words that lack grace unless they are aided by delivery and gesture, says that otherwise, "he becomes the one carrying the beam" <note>original: "γίνετ' ὁ τὰν δοκὸν φέρων"</note>. This occurs in speech, especially with proper names and pronouns, and with words frequently repeated that contain a hidden emphasis—such as "Thersites despises Achilles," or "And *you* call me an ass?" It is similar with asyndeta <term>a rhetorical device where conjunctions like 'and' are omitted</term>, such as "I came, I saw, I conquered." If such things are not commended by the speaker's action, they do not possess the same charm. Of this kind is that line from Terence: "He shut me out; he calls me back. Should I return?" And shortly after: "I, to her? Who, to him? Who, to me, who—no. Just let it be." Again, in the *Adelphoe*: "Storax? Hasn't Aeschinus returned from dinner tonight?" For "Storax" is the voice of someone calling out, and for that reason, it must be pronounced more clearly, while the rest he speaks to himself.

I have no doubt that this was taken from some play. For "the one carrying the beam" is a fragment of an iambic trimeter. A person burdened with a beam is not fit for gesturing; rather, he must adapt himself to the weight. I suspect such a character was brought onto the stage in a comedy for the sake of a laugh. Sometimes "baggage-bearers" <note>original: "σκευοφόροι" (skeuophoroi)</note> are introduced carrying bundles. Such are those to whom it is said in the *Andria*: "Carry these things inside." And in the *Hecyra*: "Sosia." Such characters either say nothing, or their gestures do not match their speech. Consider whether Aristotle might be referring to Atlases <note>architectural supports in the shape of men</note>, who are often placed under beams to support a building. They appear to be toiling, even though they are doing nothing. Delivery is, as it were, the life of a speech, and the sign of life is movement. There was something similar in tragedies called a "property-bearing" <note>original: "σκευοφόρημα" (skeuophorema)</note>, which merely stood by doing nothing. And perhaps, instead of "the one carrying the beam," it was written "the one looking this way" <note>original: "ὁ δευρ' ὁρῶν"</note>, but I make no firm pronouncement. Let the learned investigate.

->**What one does oneself.** LVIII<-

Aristotle, in the second book of his *Rhetoric*, while discussing the emotions, records this saying as a commonly tossed-about phrase: "For what one does oneself, these things he is said not to begrudge his neighbors" <note>original: "ἃ γάρ τις αὐτὸς ποιεῖ, ταῦτα λέγετ' [ται] τοῖς πέλας μὴ νεμεᾶν"</note>. This agrees with that line from Terence: "Nothing is more unjust than an ignorant man, who thinks nothing is right except what he does himself." For there are those who condemn whatever they themselves cannot achieve.

->**Kinship stirs up envy.** LIX<-

In the same book, Aristotle teaches that envy arises toward neighbors and kin; for no one envies those long dead, or those of a different race, or those who are superior or inferior by an immense interval. He brings forward the testimony of this verse:

> For kinship even knows how to envy.
> <note>original: "Τὸ συγγενὲς γὰρ καὶ φθονεῖν ἐπίστατ'."</note>

Hence, those who have advanced to such a height that they have overcome envy through glory are said to be "beyond every cast of the dice" and beyond the reach of envy's arrows.

->**A wise man does not lack.** LX<-

In the same work, among other maxims, he records this poem:

> A man who is born sound-minded never lacks.
> <note>original: "Χρὴ δ' ᾧ ποθ' ὅστις ἀρτίφρων πέφυκ' ἀνήρ."</note>

This is either because having a good mind is a form of great wealth, or because it is easy for a wise man to become rich if he wishes. For instance, Aristippus, after being cast away in a shipwreck, found people who received him kindly. The same man, when Dionysius said to him as he was asking for a talent <term>a large unit of currency in the ancient world</term>, "Did you not say the wise man does not lack?", replied, "Give it to me, and I will answer." The king gave it, and soon demanded the answer. Then Aristippus said, "Was I not telling the truth? A wise man does not lack."

->**Many unbelievable things.** LXI<-

In the same work, he cites this six-foot verse as if it were a proverb:

> Many unbelievable truths happen to mortals.
> <note>original: "Απις' ἀληθῆ πολλὰ συμβαίνει βροτοῖς."</note>

He thinks this sentiment should be used by one who enjoys lying and wants what he invents to be taken for the truth. And a little later, he cites the same sentiment from Agathon:

> Someone might perhaps say this is probable:
> That many improbable things happen to mortals.
> <note>original: "Τάχ' ἄν τις εἰκὸς αὐτὸ τοῦτ' εἶναι λέγοι, βροτοῖσι πολλὰ τυγχάνειν οὐκ εἰκότα."</note>

->**A flask in the cheeks.** LXII<-

"Everyone has a flask in their cheeks" <note>original: "Ἔχει λήκυθον πᾶς ταῖς γνάθοις"</note>. This is a veiled and enigmatic insult directed at old women who hide their wrinkles by smearing on pigments. Such was the courtesan Phryne, now an old woman, yet not retiring from her trade. Aristophanes in *The Assemblywomen*:

<meta>catchword: blisios</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient adages, moving from rhetorical delivery into a series of proverbial expressions concerning absurdity, redundant actions, noble lineage, and the necessity of risk for achieving true virtue.</meta>

... "Phryne carrying an oil-flask next to her cheeks" <note>original: "φρύνω ἔχειν λήκυθον πρὸς ταῖς γνάθοις"</note>.
He calls a *lecythum* a small jar for ointments, from which the face is painted <note>Phryne was a famous 4th-century BCE Greek courtesan known for her beauty and wealth</note>. This same woman used to say that many "drank the dregs for the sake of the wine’s nobility," because lovers would flock to her on account of her famous name as a courtesan, simply so they could boast that they had an affair with Phryne.

->**The fish needs salt.**<-
LXIII

"The fish needs salt" <note>original: "Ἰχθὺς δεῖται ἁλὸς"</note>. This is said of something absurd and incredible. For it is hardly likely that fish living in the sea would have need of salt. This seems to have been a retort by the people to Androclus of Pitana when, in criticizing a certain law, he had said: "Laws need a correcting law" <note>original: "Δέονται οἱ νόμοι νόμων διορθωθῆναι"</note>, adding: "For even fish need salt." Laws are given for this purpose: that human actions may be corrected according to their rule. But if the laws themselves require correction, they are not truly laws. That would be no less absurd than saying sea-fish need salt. Aristotle records this in his *Rhetoric*.

->**Berries need oil.**<-
LXIIII

In the same place, Aristotle soon adds another of the same form: "The olive-pressings need oil" <note>original: "τὰ στέμφυλα δεῖται ἐλαίου"</note>. For it is not believable that the very thing from which oil is born should have need of oil. Indeed, oil is pressed out of the berries of olives. This is related to the one we mentioned before: "The springs themselves are thirsty."

->**A bird from birds.**<-
LXV

"A bird from birds" <note>original: "ὄρνις ἐκ τῶν ὀρνέων"</note>. This was a proverbial form used ironically by Aristophanes for a nobleman, as if to say "a good man born from good men":
"This hoopoe, who is a bird born from birds" <note>original: "τὸν ἔποφ’ ὃς ὄρνις ἐγένετ’ ἐκ τῶν ὀρνέων"</note>.
Those who boast of their nobility trace the lineage of their race back to their grandfathers and great-great-grandfathers <note>Erasmus plays on the Latin word *avis*, which means both "bird" and "grandfather"</note>. For purchased nobility, or that which is recently acquired, is not held in such high esteem.

->**Give a hollow to the stone.**<-
LXVI

The commentator on Aristophanes indicates that boys, whenever they see birds, are accustomed to say: "Give a hollow to the stone, and they will all fall." It is appropriate when someone pursues what they cannot attain, or threatens those they cannot harm. In a comedy, someone says he wants to stir up the birds with a noise; another responds jokingly: "Strike the rock with your leg" <note>original: "τῷ σκέλει θένε τὴν πέτραν"</note>. In doing so, the birds suffer no disadvantage, but rather the hand or foot that strikes the rock; therefore, the other person tells him to strike the stone with his head so that the noise might be doubled.

->**Do not seek to be a god.**<-
LXVII

"Do not seek to become a god" <note>original: "Μὴ ζήτει θεὸς γενέσθαι"</note>. This is said to a man who is happy in every respect in this life. Pindar says in his fifth *Olympian Ode*: "If anyone tends to healthy wealth, being content with his possessions and adding to them an honest reputation, let him not seek from the gods to become a god." Likewise, it is commonly said among our own people: "You are fortunate enough. What more do you want? Do you demand to be a god?"

->**The beginning work must be favored.**<-
LXVIII

It is a most celebrated saying that "Honor nourishes the arts" and "Virtue grows when praised." Thus Pindar says in his sixth *Olympian Ode*: "At the beginning of a deed, one must set a far-shining face" <note>original: "ἀρχομένου δ’ ἔργου πρόσωπον χρὴ θέμεν τηλαυγές"</note>. That is, those who attempt some excellent deed must be favored, both so that courage may be added to them and so that others may be provoked to emulation. But nowadays, most people annoyingly make an uproar if anyone attempts anything extraordinary. This sense can also be taken: he who affects fame ought to begin with some outstanding deed. For it matters a great deal where the beginnings of one’s reputation arise.

->**Neither among men, nor at sea.**<-
LXIX

In the same place, this was also said in a proverbial pattern: "Virtues devoid of danger are held in no price, neither among men nor in hollow ships" <note>original: "ἀκίνδυνοι δ’ ἀρεταὶ οὔτε παρ’ ἀνδράσιν, οὔτ’ ἐν ναυσὶ κοίλαις τίμιαι"</note>. This stands for "nowhere"—as if you were to say, "neither on land nor at sea." This sentiment agrees with that most famous line from Hesiod:
"The gods have decreed that virtue must be won by sweat."
No one has achieved great praise without danger. Therefore, Pindar calls war "dangerous," because it produces an illustrious name for men. There is a proverbial trope in these words: "Neither on land nor at sea," and "The battle is fought on land and sea."

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of ancient adages, following the discussion of "A bird from birds" (No. 65) and other proverbs regarding lineage and reputation. This section focuses on the fit between a person and their praise, the source of true glory, and the metaphors of domesticity versus public bravery.</meta>

# FOURTH CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY
<meta>catchword: Without...</meta>

### He has his foot in this shoe.
<margin>70</margin>
An expression found in the same place <note>likely referring to Pindar, whom Erasmus was quoting on the previous page</note> in the form of an adage: "For he likely has a divine foot in this sandal" <note>original: "ἴσω γὰρ ἐν τούτῳ πεδίλῳ δαιμόνιον πόδ’ ἔχων"</note>. This means he knows himself to have a "fortunate foot" in this shoe; used when a person knows that certain praises truly apply to him. In ancient times, there was a great deal of luxury associated with slippers and shoes. For the Greeks, a *pedilon* <note>term: *pedilon* (πέδιλον); a type of sandal or footwear</note> was a type of colorful and decorated footwear, named "from being applied to the foot" <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ τῷ ποδὶ ποικίλλεσθαι"</note>. Just as not every shoe fits every foot, so too not every praise is suitable for every person.

### Virtue produces glory.
<margin>71</margin>
In the same Encomium <note>A formal speech or piece of writing that praises someone</note>: "Those who honor virtues walk on an open path. Each thing is judged by its result" <note>original: "τιμῶντες δ’ ἀρετὰς, ἐν φανερᾷ ὁδῷ ἔρχοντ’. τεκμαίρεσ’ δὲ χρῆμ’ ἕκαστον"</note>. This means that those who value virtue reach a path of distinction. Each man’s work ennobles him. The point is that true glory is won by good deeds rather than by wealth, and that honorable fame does not happen in just one way, but that each person becomes famous through their own particular virtue. Homer was made famous by poetry, Demosthenes by eloquence, Aristides by his integrity, and Themistocles by his illustrious deeds; likewise, others became famous in other ways.

### It is good to rely on two anchors.
<margin>72</margin>
Again in the same work: "Two anchors are good to be cast from a swift ship in a wintry night" <note>original: "Ἀγαθαὶ δὲ πέλονται ἐν χειμερίᾳ νυκτὶ θοᾶς ἐκ ναὸς ἀπεσκιμφθαι, δύ’ ἄγκυραι"</note>. That is, it is good to rely on a double protection so that if one fails, we may be helped by the other. Just as the victor whom Pindar praises had a double homeland, so that if anything happened to one, he could retreat to the other. We have spoken of this elsewhere as "mooring with two" <note>original: "ἐπὶ δυοῖν ὁρμεῖν"</note>.

### From home to home.
<margin>73</margin>
We encounter this form of speech several times in the works of Pindar and Aristophanes: "from home to home" <note>original: "οἴκοθεν οἴκαδε"</note>, used when they mean that someone, through his own virtues, has brought some extraordinary praise to his own house or fatherland. For example, in the same Encomium: "from home to home from the Stymphalian walls" <note>original: "οἴκοθεν οἴκαδ’ ἀπὸ στυμφαλίων τειχέων"</note>. Virtue is more pleasing and less subject to envy when it has flowed down from grandfathers and great-grandfathers to their descendants.

### What is usually said.
<margin>74</margin>
Plautus <note>A famous Roman comic playwright</note>, in the same play, hints at an obscene matter through a figure of speech. A character there swears by all the gods that he has nothing to do with a girl: that he does not sleep with her, nor walk with her, nor kiss her, nor do "that which is usually said."

### Fighting at home like a rooster.
<margin>75</margin>
"Fighting at home like a rooster" <note>original: "Ἐνδομάχας ἅτ’ ἀλέκτωρ"</note>. This is said of one who always lingers idly at home and does not dare to go out for war or public contests. For this animal is indeed very combative, but only in its own home. However, it contributes nothing to the state, nor are those domestic battles celebrated. So the commentators say, but I doubt whether it should be written *endomachas*, meaning "hidden at home." *Endomachas* is a newly coined word from "inside" and "I fight." It applies to those who are constantly brawling at home while they behave with the most peaceful manners when abroad. It agrees with what we have said elsewhere: "Lions at home" <note>meaning they are fierce in private but cowardly in public</note>.

### Neither god nor man.
<margin>76</margin>
This proverbial pattern is frequently found among the poets: "Against the will of gods and men," or "By the faith of gods and men!" It is used regarding things both divine and human. Horace writes:
> Neither gods, nor men, nor bookstalls have allowed this. <note>original: "Non dij, non homines, non concessere columnæ." Horace is referring to mediocre poets being rejected by everyone.</note>

Pindar in his second Pythian hymn: "Neither god nor mortal deceives him in deeds or in counsels" <note>original: "κλέπτει τέμιν, οὐ θεὸς βροτὸς, ἔργοις οὔτε βουλαῖς"</note>. He is praising Apollo, who, although he knows all things, nevertheless tells no lies.

### To stay with one's mother.
<margin>77</margin>
"To stay with one's mother" <note>original: "Παρὰ ματρὶ μένειν"</note> was a saying used for those who, staying at home out of laziness, dare no noble deed. Pindar in the fourth Pythian Ode: "lest any man, left free from danger, should stay with his mother" <note>original: "μή τινα λειπόμενον τὰν ἀκίνδυνον παρὰ ματρὶ μένειν"</note>. He is speaking, if I am not mistaken, of the Argonauts <note>The heroes who sailed with Jason to find the Golden Fleece</note>, who sought glory through a bold journey under the protection of Juno. Those who were soft and effeminate in the time of Augustus were called *mammothreptoi* <note>original: "μαμμύθρεπτοι"</note>, either because they were raised by grandmothers—who love their little grandsons more tenderly than mothers do—or because the Greeks use *mamme* as a diminutive for "dear mother." Even today, the common people call a delicately raised youth a "mother's son." Such people were also called *Matrissatæ* <note>Those who take after or imitate their mothers</note>.

<keywords>Pindar, Aristophanes, Plautus, Horace, adages, proverbs, virtue, glory, domestic fighting, staying at home, Argonauts, education</keywords>

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES, LXXVIII

### Without dogs and nets.

"Without dogs and nets" <note>original: Ἄνευ κυνῶν τε καὶ λίνων</note>, that is, apart from the aid of hounds and snares. Pindar used this figure of speech in his *Third Nemean Ode* to signify extreme speed. For who could catch stags on foot unless they were slowed down by dogs or entangled in nets? However, the proverb is also suitable for those who capture their prey by secret or clever arts. Pindar’s words are as follows: "killing stags without dogs and deceptive snares" <note>original: κτείνοντ’ ἐλάφους ἄνευ κυνῶν δολίων θ’ ἑρκέων</note>. It is said of those who manage a business not by the protection of others, but by their own "Mars" <note>A common Latin idiom, *proprio Marte*, meaning by one's own strength or initiative</note>.

### I even loathe the son of Scellius. <margin>LXXIX</margin>

It is a human trait that if someone strongly hates a person or a thing, they shrink not only from mentioning it, but even from words that sound like it. Aristophanes expresses this elegantly in *The Birds*. There, a certain character speaks thus:
-> "It is clear you are seeking Aristocracy." <note>original: Ἀριστοκρατίαν δῆλος εἶ ζητῶ</note> <-
-> The other responds: <-
-> "Not at all; I even loathe the son of Scellius himself." <note>original: Ηκιστα, καὶ τὸν σκελίου βδελύττομαι</note> <-
The son of Scellius was named Aristocrates. This name was rightly hated by someone who detested "Aristocracy," because the sound of the name renewed the memory of the thing he found abominable.

### A Larinian word. <margin>LXXX</margin>

A "Larinian word" <note>original: λαρινὸν ἔπος</note> was what they called something huge and extraordinary. The proverb arose because the oxen in Larissa <note>A region in Greece</note> are exceptionally large and fat. Others think "Larinian" is used for the obese and very large because of a certain shepherd named Larinos who was of an unusually large body. These massive oxen were said to graze in Epirus and were the descendants of the cattle of Geryon <note>A mythological giant whose cattle were stolen by Hercules</note>. Aristophanes says in *The Birds*:
-> "But for a long time I have been seeking to tell you a great word," <-
-> "And a Larinian one." <note>original: Μέγα καὶ λαρινὸν ἔπος</note> <-
To this pertains the Greek habit of adding the word "ox" <term>bou-</term> to signify large things, such as an "ox-eater" <note>original: βουφάγος</note> for a glutton. In a similar way, the ancient Latins used the word "Lucanian" <note>original: Luca</note> to mean something huge <note>Erasmus refers to the "Lucanian ox," the early Roman term for an elephant</note>.

### Cuckoo! Ruptured men to the field! <margin>LXXXI</margin>

"Cuckoo! Ruptured men to the field!" <note>original: Κόκκυ, ψωλοὶ πεδίονδε</note>. Aristophanes mentions this as a proverb in *The Birds*: "Then there was truly that saying: Cuckoo! Ruptured men to the field!" The meaning of these words is this: This is truly what the proverb says, "Cuckoo, you ruptured men, come to the field!" (the word "come" is understood). This bird sings just before the harvest, as if provoking the farmers to the labor of reaping. Hence Hesiod says, "when the cuckoo cuckoos." However, when he uses the word "ruptured" <note>original: ψωλοὶ; literally meaning circumcised or having the glans exposed</note> for the farmers, he is passing a slur on the Egyptians, among whom many are castrated or circumcised, and who are all compelled to be in the fields at the voice of the cuckoo. For he imagines that long ago, the cuckoo reigned among the Egyptians before it became a bird. Indeed, today, men who are "less than men" and whose wives are shared with others are commonly called "cuckoos" <note>The origin of the word "cuckold"</note>. Elsewhere we have noted from Horace that travelers used to call those "cuckoos" who only arrived to prune their vines after the cuckoo had been heard. It sings in late spring because it is late to emerge from the nest, which it prepares for itself before winter in hollow trees, shedding its feathers and wrapping itself up with a supply of apples and pears. The commentator on Aristophanes warns that this proverb, "Cuckoo! Ruptured men to the field," is used when the season itself provokes the lazy to industry.

### Playing the Mellonikian. <margin>LXXXII</margin>

Nicias was mocked for being a delayer in military affairs, just as Fabius is remembered among the Romans. Because of this, the Old Comedy invented a humorous word, "Mellonikian" <note>original: μελλονικιῶν</note>, from *mellein* (to delay) and Nicias, who was a general for the Athenians. Aristophanes in *The Birds* says: "It is no time for nodding off or playing the Mellonikian,"
-> "But we must do something as quickly as possible." <-
-> "Furthermore, there is no more time for yawning," <-
-> "Nor does it befit us to delay in the manner of Nicias," <-
-> "But it is necessary to act as swiftly as possible." <-

### Smoke. <margin>LXXXIII</margin>

"Smoke" <note>original: Καπνὸς</note> is the term for magnificent but empty promises. From this comes "to sell smoke" and "to pour smoke over someone." This name was given to a certain Theagenes, who, although he was poor, nevertheless pretended to be an extremely wealthy and magnificent businessman; hence he was commonly called "Smoke." The commentator on Aristophanes cites the comic poet Eupolis as the author of this in the play titled *The Demes*.

# EIGHTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND

->To pull the oar together.<-
->LXXXIIII<-

Those who row together must strike their oars according to certain rhythms so that they move in unison; otherwise, they will achieve nothing. For this reason, Aristophanes says in *The Birds*: "I row in unison" <note>original: ὁμοῤῥοθῶ</note>, meaning "I agree" or "I strive with the same effort as you." The word is composed of "together" <note>original: ὁμοῦ</note> and "to move with a rush" <note>original: ῥοθέω</note>. "To row in unison" <note>original: ὁμοῤῥοθῶ</note> thus means to want the same thing, to breathe together, or to join in praise. The commentator notes that this word is taken from a play by Sophocles titled *The Colts* <note>original: πωλούς</note>.

->For themselves and the Chians.<-
->LXXXV<-

"For themselves and the Chians" <note>original: Αὐτοῖς καὶ χίοις</note>. It is clear that these words were commonly tossed about as a ritual formula whenever someone prayed for good things for themselves and their friends. Indeed, a bird prays this way in Aristophanes: "To give the inhabitants of Cloud-cuckoo-land <note>original: νεφελοκοκκυγιεῦσιν</note> health and safety, for themselves and the Chians." The commentator explains that this figure of speech is derived from the public custom of the Athenians, who, when praying for the welfare of the Republic in solemn supplications and sacrifices, would add "and for the Chians." As a witness to this history, he cites Theopompus in the twelfth book of his *Philippic Histories*. I believe this was because the Athenians derived some significant benefit from the people of Chios. If someone prays well only for themselves, making no mention of friends or those who have served them well, it is wittily added: "and for the Chians."

->To add wings.<-
->LXXXVI<-

People were commonly said "to be given wings" <note>original: Ἀναπτερῶσαι</note> when someone's spirit was encouraged by words or raised into good hope. Aristophanes in *The Birds* writes:
-> Whenever the fathers speak in this way <-
-> To the youths in the barbershops: <-
-> "It is a terrible thing how Diotrephes, by talking, <-
-> Has given wings to my boy to go horse-riding." <-
Has it not been heard by you
What gray-haired fathers say to the youths
In the barbershops everywhere?
"Wonderfully has Diotrephes, by his speaking,
Affixed wings even to my young lad, so that he now
Yearns to ride."
They say that Diotrephes was a very wealthy man who took great delight in breeding horses, which is why he later became a commander of the cavalry <note>term: Hipparchus; a high-ranking cavalry officer in ancient Greece</note>. By his encouragement and example, many young men were fired up with an interest in equestrian matters; however, the fathers hated this pursuit in their sons because it involved excessive expense.

->Goose-fox.<-
->LXXXVII<-

Because Theagenes was talkative and stupid in the manner of geese, yet slippery and crafty in the manner of foxes, he was called a "goose-fox" <note>original: χλωναλώπηξ</note> in a common joke—a word composed of "goose" and "fox." However, Didymus prefers the idea that the name of the goose was added because he was excessively delighted by poultry, especially geese, presumably after the fashion of foxes. In ancient times, the liver of a goose was considered among the highest delicacies. Aristophanes mentions this adage in *The Birds*.

->To sing in concert.<-
->LXXXVIII<-

"To weep in concert" <note>original: Τὴν ξυναυλίαν κλαίειν</note>. This is used for those who complain about things in a similar way. Aristophanes in *The Knights*: "So that we may weep in concert, in the Olympic mode." They call it "concert" <note>original: ξυναυλίαν</note> either when several people play the same song on flutes, or when a flute accompanies a lyre. Olympus was a disciple of Marsyas who wrote on mournful musical modes. Indeed, this very phrase "the modes of Olympus" <note>original: Olympi modos</note> has the character of a proverb for those who are complainers, just like "to sing a dirge" <note>original: ἰαλεμίζειν</note> and "the Carian muse" <note>A term for mournful or funeral music, as Carians were often hired as professional mourners</note>.

->The Republic is nothing to a musician.<-
->LXXXIX<-

Just as this belief once occupied the minds of many, so even now it sticks with many: the belief that learned and upright men are not suited for governing the Republic. Plato abstained from it; Socrates attempted it in vain; for Demosthenes and Cicero, it turned out poorly. Finally, the mother of Nero deterred her son from the study of philosophy because she judged it useless for one who was to hold the principate. To these points, Saint Augustine, in an epistle, refuted certain people who boasted that the philosophy of the Gospel hindered the administration of the Republic. Aristophanes expressed this gracefully in *The Knights*. For there, to someone refusing the leadership because he was unskilled in music, the following response is given:

[For leading the people]
For leading the people is no longer the task of a musical man,
Nor of one of good character. -> that is, <-
But to manage the Republic now is not for a man
Who is cultured, or of proven character.
<note>original Greek: Ἡ δημαγωγία γὰρ οὐ πρὸς μουσικοῦ Ἔτ' ἐστὶν ἀνδρὸς, οὐδὲ χρηστοῦ τοὺς τρόπους.</note>
Under the name of "music" <note>original: Musices</note>, the ancients used to designate all liberal education and refined learning.

### Culinary words.

"Culinary words" <note>original: Ῥήματα μαγειρικά</note>. That is, "the words of cooks," a phrase used charmingly by Aristophanes in the same play <note>Aristophanes' *The Knights*</note> to describe words that are soft, flattering, and sweet. For it is the job of cooks to sweeten, with various seasonings, food that is naturally somewhat bitter. In that play, someone advises that the Athenian people should be soothed with smooth-talking. The verse goes like this:
Sweetening them slightly with culinary words. -> that is, <-
Charming them with the little words of cooks.
<note>original Greek: ὑπογλυκαίνων ῥήμασιν μαγειρικοῖς.</note>
He said "cook-wise" <note>original Greek: μαγειρικῶς</note> instead of "mildly" or "soothingly" <note>original Greek: μειλιχίως</note>; that is, with calm and sweet words. It would be a graceful metaphor if one were to say that the philosophy of Epicurus soothes the minds of the common people with "culinary words," because it proposes that pleasure is the highest good.

### Cakes for Coalemus.

"Offer cakes to Coalemus" <note>original Greek: Σπύδε τῷ κοαλέμῳ</note>. This is applicable to someone whose own wickedness has turned out to be to his advantage. The comic poet invents the name of a demon, Coalemus, to imply wickedness or stupidity. It is just as if someone were to say, "sacrifice to Folly" <note>original: μωρίᾳ</note>, if someone, by playing the fool, were elevated to wealth and dignity. For to the Greeks, "Coalemus" <term>Coalemus: a personification of stupidity or dull-wittedness</term> signifies a fatuous and stupid person, derived from *ko* <note>original: κῶ</note> instead of *no* <note>original: νοῶ</note>, meaning "to understand." For Callimachus said *konousin* <note>original: κόνουσιν</note> for *phonoisin* <note>original: φόνοισιν</note> (murders). From this, by analogy, *kos* <note>original: κῶς</note> is for *nus* <note>original: νῦς</note> (mind), combined with *aleo* <note>original: ἄλεω</note>, meaning the mind wanders. By a similar figure of speech, those who are lucky in making friends are said to "offer libations to the Graces." Drunkards have their god Comus, and thieves have the goddess Laverna. Therefore, to someone enriched by thefts, it might be wittily said: "Cakes for Laverna."

### He breathes the Caecias.

Regarding the Caecias <term>Caecias: the North-East wind, which was proverbially said to attract clouds toward itself rather than blowing them away</term>, a wind that draws clouds toward itself, we have said enough in previous sections. Alluding to the nature of this wind, Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:
As this man already breathes the Caecias and sycophancy. -> that is, <-
As that man now breathes the North-East wind and false accusations.
<note>original Greek: ὡς οὗτος ἤδη καικίας, καὶ συκοφαντίας πνεῖ.</note>
The commentator reminds us that this is a proverb, although in the Aldine edition, *kakias* (wickedness) is corruptly read instead of *kaikias*, even though the meter of the verse does not allow for that word. The poet used "Caecias" to refer to words and quarrels. For Cleon <note>a prominent Athenian statesman and demagogue</note> is noted there as an informer and a slanderer.

### Broad and narrow.

I think it is obscure to no one that this was said as a proverbial figure by Aristophanes in *The Knights*, under the persona of Cleon. When he was accused of having fed the people poorly, in the manner of nurses—who, after chewing the food a little, put a tiny bit into the infant's mouth but swallow the greatest part themselves—he replied:
And by Jove, by my cleverness,
I am able to make the people broad and narrow. -> that is, <-
So, by Jupiter. For by my skill
I am able to make the people thin or ample.
<note>original Greek: Καὶ νὴ Δί' ὑπόγε δεξιότητος τ' ἐμῆς Δύναμαι ποιεῖν τὸν δῆμον εὐρὺν καὶ στενόν.</note>
For children who are poorly fed grow thin, while those who are well-fed become stout. This will be aptly applied to those who teach the youth either rightly or otherwise, or those who harangue the people skillfully or otherwise. Indeed, these things have the greatest influence on the character of the people, either forming them toward honesty or depraving them toward vice.

### You would sooner persuade a beetle.

"You would sooner lead a beetle to a different opinion" <note>original Greek: Θᾶσσον ὁ κάνθαρος ἂν μεταπεισθείη</note>. This is said of those who have become accustomed to evils, from which they cannot be recalled because those very evils seem good enough to them. Lucian says in *The False Sophist*: "For you yourself would never become better through my rebuke, any more than a beetle could be persuaded to no longer roll such things, once the habit has been formed." The beetle raises its young in dung, especially that of goats, feeds on the same, and lives in the same place. Indeed, they shape the excrement into little spheres and roll them into their nests, with their heads turned down toward the earth and their hind legs raised high. No one is easily led away from the vices in which he was born and raised; even things that are inherently foul seem beautiful and sweet through the recommendation of long-standing habit.

<keywords>Aristophanes, Cleon, demagoguery, education, Coalemus, Caecias wind, habits, corruption, Greek comedy, Epicurus</keywords>
