<meta>This page continues from page 1010, following the discussion of the proverb "Offer cakes to Coalemus," which refers to someone benefiting from their own foolishness or a demon of stupidity. We now move into Centuria VIII of the fourth Chiliad, starting with proverb 95.</meta>

### FOURTH CHILIAD, EIGHTH CENTURY 1011

### To use someone else’s sandals. [XCV]

**To use someone else’s sandals.** <note>original Greek: Ἀλλοτρίοις βλαυτίοις χρῆσθαι</note> That is, those who misuse the habits or manners of others for their own profit are said to "use someone else’s sandals." Aristophanes says in *The Knights*:
> No, but just as a man who has been drinking is affected when he needs to relieve his bowels,
> I use your ways just like I use sandals.
<note>original Greek: οὐκ, ἀλλ’ ὅπη πίνων ἀνὴρ πέπονθ’ ὅταν χεσῇ, τοῖσιν τρόποις τοῖς οἷσιν, ὥσπερ βλαυτίοισi χρῶμαι.</note>

With these words, the character denies that he is tricking the Athenian people, but claims he is doing what people usually do at drinking parties: when the urge to go to the bathroom hits, they get up and grab whatever sandals are nearby, either because they are in a hurry or because they are drunk. In this way, he was taking advantage of the habits of the Athenian people, who allowed themselves to be corrupted by food and preferred to hear flattering words rather than helpful ones. It appears that in ancient times the Greeks used to recline at meals without their sandals. When they were about to leave for home, they would call for their sandals. This gave rise to the profit of the <term>Lopodytis</term> <note>a "clothes-stealer" or "cloak-snatcher" who took advantage of people leaving baths or parties</note>. Some people even used to recline at meals naked.

---

### A long introduction to one eager to hear. [XCVI]

A phrase in Plato’s fourth book of *The Republic* has the quality of a proverb: **A long introduction to one eager to hear.** <note>original Greek: μακρὸν τὸ προοίμιον τῷ ἐπιθυμοῦντι ἀκοῦσαι</note> For someone who desires to know the facts themselves, every introduction seems long. This is the source of that line in Terence: "Bah, he’s even starting an introduction for me." And in Athens, the herald who gave the rhetoricians permission to speak would announce, **without introductions or emotional appeals**, <note>original Greek: ἄνευ προοιμίων καὶ παθῶν</note> because these things are outside the core of the case.

---

### Everything you say is excellent. [XCVII]

Socrates, in Plato's *Euthydemus*, acting <term>ironically</term> <note>original Greek: εἰρωνεύων — acting with "eironia," a stance of feigned ignorance</note> in his usual manner because his opponent had gathered some absurd conclusions—namely, that Socrates knew what he didn't know, and again didn't know what he did know—said: **"Well then, O Euthydemus; for as the saying goes, everything you say is indeed excellent."** <note>original Greek: ὦ εὐθύδημε, τὸ γὰρ λεγόμενον, καλὰ δὴ πάντα λέγεις</note> Marsilius <note>the philosopher Marsilio Ficino</note> translates "Well then" as "Behold!" and he seems to have read the Greek not as "he said" <note>original Greek: ἔφη</note>, but as "behold" <note>original Greek: ἔφ’</note> or "let it be" <note>original Greek: εἴη</note>, which sounds like "En" to the Greeks. This would make it the word of someone wondering <term>ironically</term> <note>original Greek: εἰρωνικῶς</note>. I think this was the genuine writing of Plato. For "well then" <note>meaning a concession</note> adds nothing to the present meaning. He concedes nothing, but marvels at the unheard-of thing through mockery—not to mention that "let it be" <note>original Greek: εἴη</note> is more the word of someone wishing for something than someone conceding. Plato cites "You speak beautifully" as a proverb in several other places, which I believe is taken from some poet. For in Theocritus, Praxinoe says: **"Yes, you have spoken beautifully."** <note>original Greek: ναί, καλὸν εἶπας</note>

---

### What has been rightly given. [XCVIII]

Plato, in the *Philebus*, points out a proverb used by children: that it is not right to ask back for what has once been given. **"But we say what the children usually do: that of things rightly given, there is no taking away."** <note>original Greek: ἡμεῖς δ’ ὃ λέγομεν, καθάπερ οἱ παῖδες, ὅτι τῶν ὀρθῶς δοθέντων, ἀφαίρεσις οὐκ ἔστι.</note> He said this because Socrates was accustomed to bringing back into doubt things that had previously been conceded by restarting the debate from the beginning. A similar thing is still tossed around among children today when someone asks back for what they gave. Thus, sayings of this kind have flowed down to us through so many centuries and so many nations.

---

### Bringing the cord to the stone. [XCIX]

**To bring the cord to the stone.** <note>original Greek: Τὴν σπάρτην πρὸς τὸν λίθον ἄγειν</note> This is said of those who apply every care to ensure that nothing is done in the State otherwise than it should be. The Blessed Chrysostom, in his 35th homily on the first epistle to the Corinthians, says: **"Consider how here again he brings the cord to the stone, seeking the building up of the church everywhere."** <note>original Greek: σκόπει πῶς πάλιν ἐνταῦθα πᾶς τὴν σπάρτην τῷ λίθῳ ἄγει τὴν οἰκοδομὴν πανταχοῦ ζητῶν τῆς ἐκκλησίας.</note> It is a metaphor taken from architects, who do not trust their eyes, but examine the evenness of stones with a plumb line. This signifies exact diligence.

---

### This you will tell to me. [C]

In the ninth book of Plato’s *Republic*, when Socrates asks how a tyrannical man would live, Adimantus replies: **"This you will tell to me, as they say in the game."** <note>original Greek: τὸ τῶν παιζόντων τοῦτό συ ἐμοὶ ἐρεῖς</note> This will be useful when a hateful or difficult answer is thrown back at the questioner, or when the one asking is the type of person who ought to know better than the one he wishes to learn from.

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES:
# FOURTH CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY

### To sell for a single coin.

Among legal scholars, "to sell for a single coin" <note>original: *nummo addicere*</note> is a proverbial expression meaning to sell something at the lowest possible price. However, this is often a legal fiction used to circumvent laws that prohibit making large gifts. Ulpian, in the nineteenth book of the *Pandects* under the title "On Hiring," writes: "If someone has leased a property for a single coin, the lease is void, because this effectively constitutes a gift." The same author in the first book, under the title "On Res Judicata," says: "If someone has both leased and requested a <term>precarium</term> <note>a legal grant of possession that can be revoked at will</note> to use a property, and if he leased it for a single coin, there is no doubt that he holds it solely by the right of the *precarium*." But you should consider whether in these examples, instead of "leased" <note>Latin: *conduxit*</note> and "lease" <note>Latin: *conductio*</note>, we should read "agreed" <note>Latin: *condixit*</note> and "agreement" <note>Latin: *condictio*</note>. Suetonius writes in his *Life of Julius Caesar*: "During the Civil War, in addition to other gifts, he knocked down the most extensive estates for a single coin." Valerius Maximus writes in his second book, in the chapter "On Gratitude": "The equipment for funerals was assigned to the undertakers for a single sesterce coin provided by themselves." Likewise, Plautus says in *Pseudolus*: "Now I will be one coin richer than you." He uses "coin" <note>Latin: *nummum*</note> to refer to the cheapest possible price.

### Truer than truth.

Since nothing can be "truer than truth," we nevertheless use the proverbial trope "truer than truth" <note>original: *Vero uerius*</note> for something we want to be regarded as completely beyond doubt. Martial uses this against a certain Gallicus, whose habit it was to frequently repeat the phrase:
> "Tell me the truth, Marcus, tell me, please."
> "Truer than true," he says; "so hear what it is."
> But Gallicus, you do not listen to the truth gladly.

In a similar form, we say "More certain than certain" <note>original: *Certo certius*</note>, even though nothing can strictly be more certain than something else. Ulpian writes in the twenty-third book of the *Pandects*, under the title "On Testamentary Guardianship": "It is more certain than certain that sponsors given by a will are not to be compelled to give security that the property will be safe."

### To live on air.

Even today, it is a very common saying among the common people to say that those who live at no expense "live on air" <note>original: *vento uiuere*</note>. They often add "in the manner of the <term>silurus</term>" <note>a type of catfish or sheatfish</note>, because it was widely believed that this fish was fattened by the breeze, a trait also attributed to the chameleon. The Emperor Alexander, in the fifth book of the *Codex* under the title "On the Maintenance of a Ward," says: "A young man is not to be tolerated who, having been present, educated in studies, and fed, fails to prove he obtained these things through another and seeks to recover expenses, as if he had lived on air, or as if he did not deserve to be imbued with any study befitting a free man."

### Keep your things to yourself.

Gaius the legal scholar, in the forty-fourth book of the *Pandects* under the title "On Divorces," shows that it was the accepted custom for a divorce to be carried out with these words: "Keep your things to yourself; manage your own affairs." <note>original: *Tuas res tibi habeto, tuas res tibi agito*</note> By the first phrase, the husband returns the dowry; by the second, he renounces his role as the guardian over his wife's affairs. This specific form of words was prescribed so that the divorce would not be considered invalid if performed without formal words, nor unlucky and hateful if performed with uncivil language. Likewise, in breaking off friendships, it seemed appropriate to use these words: "I will not make use of your terms" <note>original: *Conditione tua non utar*</note>. These are considered proverbial for when we civilly renounce a friendship. But it is more elegant if they are transferred to matters of the mind, as if someone were to say: "He has professed the life of a monk; he has ordered the world to keep its things to itself, and to manage its own affairs." Similarly, if someone whose company we judge to be useless to us seeks our fellowship, it is aptly said to him: "I will not make use of your terms," in place of "I will not use your familiarity." Plautus uses this elegantly in *Trinummus*, where the young man Lysiteles complains much about the miseries of lovers and wishes to cast desire and love from his mind: "Away with you, Love, keep your things to yourself; may you never be a friend to me." He uses it without a metaphor in *Amphitruo*: "Farewell, keep your things for yourself, and return mine."

### Gamma pursues Beta.

Procopius, in the third book of *The Vandalic War*, records that an ancient proverb used to be tossed about in Carthage: "That Gamma sometimes pursues Beta, and in turn Beta pursues Gamma." I suspect that a children's game was the source of this, as discord frequently arises between neighbors. This childish saying was twisted to fit historical events: Geiseric <note>whose name starts with G, Gamma</note> had expelled Boniface <note>starting with B, Beta</note>; later, Belisarius <note>starting with B, Beta</note> expelled Gelimer <note>starting with G, Gamma</note>. The proverb was not born from the event, but was a riddle of the Carthaginian children, serving as an oracle of what happened later.

### Worthy of a tomb's epitaph.

This would not seem to belong in the class of proverbs, unless specifically named as a proverb...

# THE FOURTH CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY
### 1013
**Qqq 3**

...as recorded by Procopius in the first book of *The Persian War*, in the character of the Empress <note>Theodora, wife of Justinian I</note> speaking thus to her husband Justinian: "Therefore, most excellent Emperor, if you wish to live now, it is certainly no trouble: we have a great amount of money, the sea is available, and ships are many. Consider, however, whether once you are saved, it might be your lot to trade the sweetness of life for the bitterness of death at the end. As for me, the ancient proverb truly pleases: 'How beautiful it is for an Emperor to be inscribed upon his tombstone.'" <note>The original Greek proverb is *Basileia kalon entaphion*, often translated as "Royalty is a fine winding-sheet" or shroud.</note> I have known some who, at the end of their lives, spent great sums to buy a cardinal’s hat, simply so that the title might be inscribed upon their tomb.

->First, the bees must be driven away.<-
->VII<-

Agathius, in the third book of *The Gothic War*: "These words pleased Vlilago, the prefect of the Heruli." For this reason, the proverb was adopted—though it is of barbarian origin and small weight, it is nevertheless useful and carries a certain energy. He would repeatedly proclaim: "First the bees must be driven away, and then the honey must be taken." Buzes <note>A Byzantine general</note> realized that the approaching enemy forces must first be pushed back so that they could take possession of Asia. The metaphor is taken from those who keep bees, who, in order to snatch the honey from the hives, drive the bees away with smoke or by some other means.

->To stretch out the hands.<-
->VIII<-

"To stretch out the hands" <note>original: *Porrigere manus*</note>, meaning to be of assistance, is very common but elegant. Ulpian, in the forty-second book of the *Pandects* <note>The Digest of Roman Law</note>, under the title "On Res Judicata" <note>Matters already judged</note>, says: "But if the buyer, to whom the pledges have been awarded by the judge, does not pay the price, it must be seen whether those same judges who carry out the sentence ought to **stretch out their hands** toward the buyer." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Speech after his Return*: "He who first, when I was afflicted and cast down, offered me his consular faith and **stretched out his right hand**." It will be even more festive when applied to matters of the mind: as if you were to say, "Philosophy stretches out a hand to a dejected soul," or "In the difficulties of Theology, Dialectics <note>the art of logical argument</note> or a mastery of languages often stretches out a hand to one who is struggling."

->Water is indeed best.<-
->IX<-

<margin>"Water is indeed best" <note>original: *Ariston men hydōr*</note> seems to have passed into a proverb whenever something better is preferred over a thing that is already vehemently praised. In the same way, Pindar, beginning his *Olympian Odes*, admits that water is indeed best, but he prefers gold, because it shines like a fire in the night. For these are the two primary elements, water and fire; hence we "interdict from water and fire" <note>a Roman legal phrase for exile</note> those whom we judge unworthy of life. Aristotle, in the third book of his *Rhetoric*, cites it as a commonly tossed-about phrase, saying: "Hence it is said, **Water is best**." For some things are preferred because they are rarer. Otherwise, water is more necessary than gold. Plutarch mentions the adage in his *Commentary*, in which he asks whether water or fire is more useful. To someone excessively extolling philosophy, one who admits that philosophy is indeed a noble thing, but that Theology is superior to it, might wittily chime in with that fragment of Pindar’s poem: **Water is indeed best.**</margin>

->A guest ought not always to be a guest.<-
->X<-

<margin>"A guest is a guest, but not forever" <note>original: *Xenon men hydōr xenon, xenon de aei*</note>. That is, a guest ought not always to be a guest. Those who are ignorant of the place in which they live are called "guests" <note>or "strangers"</note>. But it is a disgrace to live in the same city for a long time and always be a stranger. The iambic trimeter verse appears to be corrupted. It is a disgrace to have been occupied in the same discipline for a long time and to know nothing.</margin>

->One must die before, etc.<-
->XI<-

<margin>In the same place, he records a saying of Alexandrides, as one widely celebrated and praised: "It is honorable to die before you have done anything worthy of death" <note>original: *kalon g’ apothanein prin thanatou drān axion*</note>. The sense is, as Aristotle himself explains: It is fitting to die while one is unworthy of death; or, it is honorable to die when you have committed nothing that deserves death.</margin>

->To lift up the hands.<-
->XII<-

Those who rejoice exceedingly, as if a matter were handled by divine favor according to their heart's desire, are said to "lift up their hands." Marcus Tullius, in the seventh book of his *Letters*: "Balbus and I **lifted up our hands**. Such was the opportunity that it seemed not something fortuitous, but divine." The same author in his *Academics*: "Hortensius, however, greatly admiring what Lucilius had said throughout his speech, even **frequently lifted his hands**." Horace in his fifth *Satire*:
> The annoying man loves to be praised, until—'enough already!'—
> With **hands lifted to heaven**, he says, 'Keep going!'

->In the Roman manner.<-
->XIII<-

In the same letter, Marcus Tullius said, not without the appearance of a proverb, "In the Roman manner" <note>original: *More Romano*</note>, for that which...

# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
### 1014

...is, simply and without artifice rather than eruditely. For such were those ancient Romans, unlike the Greeks. Regarding this man, [Cicero] says: "I guarantee him to you, not with that old word of mine—which you rightly mocked when I wrote to you concerning Milo—but in the **Roman manner**, as honest men speak: that there is no man more upright, no better gentleman, none more prudent." Among the Romans, there was a "rustic truth." He introduces such a character in the second book of *On Moral Ends*: "Indeed, our people argue most excellently: that there is no need for one who is to be a philosopher to know literature. Just as our ancestors brought that famous Cincinnatus from the plow to be dictator, so you may gather from all the Pelasgians <note>A term for Greeks</note> that they are indeed good men, but certainly not always learned." The same author says to Trebatius in his seventh book: "Balbus confirmed to me that you would be a wealthy man; whether he spoke in the **Roman manner**, meaning you would be well-moneyed, or in the way the Stoics say—that all are wealthy who can enjoy heaven and earth—I shall see later." He said it in the **Roman manner**, meaning "for the unlearned and simple." For the Stoics define "wealthy" and "poor" with great subtlety. And shortly after to the same man: "I will commend you to Balbus when he sets out to us, in the **Roman manner**."

<margin>XIII</margin>
->Nothing dries faster than a tear.<-

Marcus Tullius [Cicero], in the first book of *On Invention*, instructing that an orator—after he has moved the judge's mind to mercy—should not linger too long on the matter, cites a saying of Apollonius: <note>original Greek: δάϰρυον ἐνήνεϰται ἀναίσθητον</note> "A tear is brought forth insensibly," that is, **nothing dries faster than a tear**, because a violent emotion easily turns into weariness.

<margin>XIV</margin>
->To have gone out of one's power.<-

One was said to **have gone out of one's power** who had lost their mind, or who, scorning reason, was carried headlong by the whim of their desires. Marcus Tullius in the third book of *Tusculan Disputations* says: "From this it is necessary to understand who are 'sane.' Therefore, nothing is better than what is found in the custom of Latin speech, when we say that those who are carried away unbridled, either by lust or by anger, have **gone out of their power**." And shortly after: "Those who are said to have **gone out of their power** are so called because they are not under the power of the Mind, to which the sovereignty over the whole soul was granted by nature." Thus says Cicero: from this we say people are "masters of their minds" <term>compos mentis</term> or "powerless over their minds" <term>impotes mentis</term>, and those who do not have their soul in their own power but are carried away by the whim of their passions are said to be "powerlessly moved." This formula of speech seems to be twisted from the legal experts, among whom children born of legal marriages are said to be "in the power" <term>in potestate</term> of their parents, unless they are emancipated or the father dies. Conversely, those who are emancipated are said to have **gone out of the power** of their parents.

<margin>XV</margin>
->Gallonius.<-

Even luxury itself has made many famous, such as Aesop <note>Referring to the son of a famous actor, known for his extravagance</note> and Apicius. Marcus Tullius records that **Gallonius** was made famous by Lucilius, and mentions him in several places. In the speech *For Caecina*: "What is it then? Not to the extent, however, that those who preferred to follow the profit and expenditure of Gallonius, abandoning the discipline of good men, should dominate the lives and fortunes of most honorable men." He also mentions Gallonius in *For Publius Quinctius*. Again, in the second book of *On Moral Ends*, he quotes from Lucilius: "O Publius, O glutton, Gallonius, you are a wretched man," he says, "you have never dined well in your life, since you consume everything on that [expensive] shrimp and a sturgeon of the tenth rank." <note>original: "cum omnē in isto cōsumis squilla, acipensere cũ decumano." A 'decuman' sturgeon refers to one of immense size or high tax grade.</note> Lucilius makes Laelius say these things, who was accustomed to dine on sorrel, [mocking] Gallonius the glutton, who measured everything by the delight of the gullet and the belly. Cicero mentions Gallonius again in the second book of *On Moral Ends*: "But as for one who refers everything to pleasure and lives like Gallonius, yet speaks like that frugal man Piso—him I do not listen to."

<margin>XVI</margin>
->Piety is often wounded by a look.<-

Marcus Tullius, in his speech *For Roscius*, incidentally cites a sentiment tossed about by wise men: "For," he says, "if that which is excellently said by wise men is true—that **piety is often wounded by a look**—what punishment will be found sharp enough for one who brought death upon a parent, for whom the laws themselves demanded one should die, and whom all laws divine and human compelled us to protect?" The proverb warns that piety <note>In the Roman sense: duty and devotion to family and gods</note> toward parents must be cultivated so religiously that we should not only avoid offending them with impious words or deeds, but not even with a harsh or stubborn expression. For the eyes, the brow, and the face itself have their own language. The Gospel seeks this even more deeply, namely from the very fountain of the heart in which anger is conceived. This breaks out into a voice of indignation, though an uncertain one; the next step is manifest reproach, and the third is homicide.

<margin>XVII</margin>
->Worthy of the sack, or, Not worthy of just one sack.<-

When we wish to signify an enormously wicked man, we say he is **worthy of the sack**. This was the punishment for parricides—that is, those who had killed a parent. Although among...

# THE FOURTH THOUSAND, NINTH CENTURY
### 1015
**Qqq 4**
<meta>catchword: τὸ μὲν</meta>

Among the ancients, it was called **parricide** <note>Latin: *parricidium*</note> whenever a person killed another human being; that is, an equal killing an equal <note>Latin: *par parem*</note>. This was presumably in that early age when it was considered a cruelty to have killed an ox, a bird, or a rooster. Later, when it began to be common for one human to kill another, the word "parricide" was redirected to signify the ultimate act of impiety <note>Specifically the murder of a parent or close relative</note>. Now, the **leather sack** <note>Latin: *culleus*</note> was a bag made of hide into which the parricide was sewn, along with a viper, a monkey, and a rooster; thus enclosed, he was thrown into a flowing river. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *In Defense of Roscius of Ameria*, wrote: "How much more wisely did our ancestors act! Understanding that nothing is so sacred that audacity will not eventually violate it, they devised a punishment for parricides so that those whom nature itself could not keep to their duty might be deterred from the greatest of crimes by the magnitude of the penalty. They willed that they be sewn alive into a sack and thus cast into the river. O, the singular wisdom of the judges! Do they not seem to have removed this man from the very nature of things and snatched him away, suddenly depriving him of the sky, the sun, the water, and the earth? Thus, he who killed the one from whom he was born would lack all those elements from which all things are said to be born, etc." Following this, Juvenal, exaggerating the impiety of a certain man, says that for him "one snake or one sack is not enough." Suetonius relates that some people placed a sack near a statue of Nero with the inscription: "You deserved it, but what can I do?" <note>Referring to Nero’s murder of his mother, Agrippina</note>

---

->The calculation indeed is clear, etc.<-
->XIX<-

Plautus says in *The Three-Dollar Day*: "Not at all. The calculation of the silver is clear, however." To which Stasinus replies: "By Hercules, the calculation indeed is clear, but the silver **has vanished** <note>original Greek: οἴχεται</note>." For this is the genuine reading of that passage, though others have variously invented faulty versions. Marcus Tullius Cicero used this in his speech *Against Piso*: "If you examine these accounts, you will understand that no one benefited more from literature than I did. For they were written so skillfully and literately that the clerk who returned them to the treasury, having finished the accounts, scratched his head with his left hand and muttered to himself: 'By Hercules, the calculation indeed is clear, but the money **is gone** <note>original Greek: οἴχεται</note>.'" Likewise, Geta in Terence’s *Phormio* says: "It was not the calculation we lacked, but the silver." Marcus Tullius, in the final letter of the second book to his brother Quintus, writes: "These things are harder to do than to say." To the same point belongs the phrase: "You have spoken beautifully."

---

->Everything except the soul.<-
->XX<-

When we wish to signify that nothing has been withheld except life, we say "everything was surrendered except the soul" <note>In this context, *anima* means "life" or "breath"</note>. Marcus Tullius in *In Defense of Roscius of Ameria*: "But if you have no reason why you wish this miserable man to be afflicted with such great calamity—if he has surrendered all his belongings to you except his life, and has reserved nothing of his father's for himself, not even for the sake of a memorial, etc." By a similar figure of speech, those who owe everything are said to "owe their soul." Terence says: "What if he owes his very soul?" And again: "He owes everything except his soul."

---

->He complains about a hangnail.<-
->XXI<-

**He complains about a hangnail while suffering from a greater evil** <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ἀνωνυχίας μέμφεται ὁ τῷ μείζονι ψόχῳ & κακῷ</note>. This refers to when someone, out of a misplaced sense of shame, seeks a remedy for the most trivial ailments while concealing greater ones. Many are affected by this, even hiding their disease from a doctor, especially those suffering from gout. Plutarch relates that a certain man consulted a doctor about a defect in his nails, even though his complexion proved that he was suffering from a diseased liver. But the doctor, perceiving the man’s foolish shame, said: "There is no danger to you from the **hangnail** <note>term: *reduvia* — a fragment of torn skin at the base of a fingernail, or a whitlow</note>, but a more serious evil presses upon you." Marcus Tullius alluded to this in his oration *In Defense of Roscius of Ameria*: "I understand that I am examining these things prematurely and almost erring; while I ought to be healing the head of Sextus Roscius, I am tending to a hangnail."

---

->To owe to the last farthing.<-
->XXII<-

One who owes ready money of the correct weight is said to "owe to the **farthing**" <note>term: *libella* — the smallest Roman silver coin, or a level/scale</note>. For in the old days, money was given by the scale <note>by weight</note>, not by count. From this come those common terms: *expendere* (to weigh out/spend), *expensum ferre* (to enter as paid), *dependere* (to pay down), *rependere* (to pay back), *impendere* (to expend/weigh out for a purpose), used for making an expense, rendering an account of expenses, paying, releasing, and consuming. Marcus Tullius in *In Defense of Roscius of Ameria*: "Unless he makes it plain that fifty-three thousand sesterces are owed to him **to the last farthing** <note>Latin: *ad libellam*</note>, he loses the case."

---

->A townsman or a neighbor reported this.<-
->XXIII<-

Marcus Tullius in the same oration: "You are accustomed, Judges, when you hear something of this sort, to say immediately: 'It must be that some townsman or neighbor told of it.'" For the crimes of neighbors and townsmen are usually betrayed most of all by neighbors and townsmen. This is still commonly said today: that a man's disgrace arises from his fellow countrymen or citizens. For if there is any misfortune of fate, or any stain upon one's life, it is betrayed by them because they know of it.

---

->The goddess devised it.<-
->XXIV<-

# ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES
### 1016
**PPP**

**The thought was the goddess's, but the theft was mine.** <note>original: "τὸ μὲν νόημα τῆς θεοῦ, τὸ δὲ κλέμμ’ ἐμόν."</note> This means: The goddess thought of it, but the stealing was my doing. It was said with a proverbial flair against rhetoricians who boasted to the people that Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note> had placed into their minds what they were advising, and yet they claimed the glory for the successful deeds for themselves. This rhetorical "color" <note>A technical term in rhetoric for the slant or perspective given to an argument.</note> is taken from Homer, where whenever a reason for an action cannot be given, Pallas <note>Another name for Athena/Minerva.</note> is said to have suggested it. Pallas was the protectress of the Athenians. The comic poet <note>Likely Aristophanes.</note>, however, for the sake of a joke, substituted "theft" for "thought," noting the greed of Cleon <note>A prominent and often criticized Athenian statesman during the Peloponnesian War.</note>.

->**Practice is a second nature.**<-

Nothing is more celebrated than this saying: **Habit is another nature** <note>original: "ἔθος ἄλλη φύσις."</note>. Nothing is more effective or powerful than nature. Hence the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Juvenal.</note> says:
*Nature is more powerful than any guardian or care.*
Habit <note>or custom</note> has a power equal to this, or certainly very close to it. Aristotle, in the first book of his *Rhetoric*, discussing pleasant things, teaches that those things are pleasant which are either according to nature or, what is closest to this, customary. For he thinks there is no difference between nature and practice, except the difference between "always" and "usually." For what nature has implanted is perpetual; what practice has attached is frequent. Therefore, he gave most holy counsel who commanded that from our tender years we should immediately choose the best things, which through practice will later become even pleasant.

->**Necessity is troublesome.**<-

Soon in the same place <note>In Aristotle's *Rhetoric*.</note> he cites a sentiment as if it were a common saying, showing that things which are not according to nature are troublesome. For force fights against nature, and therefore all necessity is troublesome. **And it is rightly said,** he says, **for every necessary thing is by nature distressing.** <note>original: "καὶ ὀρθῶς εἴρηται, πᾶν γὰρ ἀναγκαῖον πρᾶγμα ἀνιαρὸν ἔφυ."</note> Truly we grow accustomed to the best things, unless some force is applied at the beginning; but what was first violent, and therefore troublesome, through practice first becomes light, and later even pleasant.

->**The memory of past evils is pleasant.**<-

In the same work he records this proverbial sentiment from some poet:
**But it is truly sweet for one who has been saved to remember his labors.** <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἡδύ τοι σωθέντα μεμνῆσθαι πόνων." This is a line from Euripides.</note> Likewise that other verse:
**For a man takes great delight in remembering his sorrows, once he has suffered much and accomplished much.** <note>original: "Καὶ μέγα γάρ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι τέρπεται ἀνὴρ μνήμεν@, ὅστις πολλὰ πάθοι καὶ πολλὰ ἐόργοι." A quote from Homer's *Odyssey*.</note>
We have mentioned this elsewhere as well.

->**The best judgment.**<-

Aristotle, in the first book of his *Rhetoric*, seems to touch upon this as if it were a standard formula: **By the best judgment.** <note>original: "γνώμη ἀρίστη."</note> Since there are many kinds of proofs which are sought outside the merits of the case—which the Greeks call **inartificial** <note>original: "ἄτεχνοι," referring to evidence like laws or witnesses that the speaker does not "create" through art.</note>, such as laws, witnesses, contracts, evidence under torture, and oaths—the best proof comes from conjectures which they call **probabilities** <note>original: "εἰκότα."</note>. For one who has no witnesses, the strategy was that a judgment must be made from probable signs; and this is what is called **By the best judgment.**

->**As if to an altar.**<-

We have spoken elsewhere regarding the "sacred anchor" <note>A proverb meaning the last resort.</note>. Very similar to that is the phrase **To the altar**, when we wish it to be understood as the ultimate refuge. It is taken from the fact that in ancient times those who were pressed by extreme necessity were accustomed to flee to the altars of the gods, from which it was a religious crime <note>sacrilege</note> to drag anyone away. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his speech *In Defense of Roscius the Actor*: "As also happened recently with Eros the Actor, who after he was driven off the stage not only by hisses but also by insults, fled to this man’s house **as if to an altar**, seeking his teaching, protection, and name." The same author says in the third book of *On the Nature of the Gods*: "Which you, when you are unable to do so, flee to a god **as if to an altar**." The same in the fourth *Against Verres*: "But they bore the injuries of many of our magistrates in such a way that never before this time did they flee to the **altar of the laws** and your protection by a public resolution." Ovid, in the fourth book of his *Letters from the Black Sea*:
*The only altar found for my fortunes.*
Plautus in the *Mostellaria*: "You have fled to the altar."

<summary>Erasmus explores proverbs concerning human nature, habit, and legal concepts, emphasizing that practice becomes "second nature" and discussing the concept of seeking "the altar" as a final refuge.</summary>
<keywords>habit, nature, necessity, memory, legal judgment, sanctuary, Aristotle, Cicero, Pallas, Minerva, Cleon</keywords>

<page-num>1017</page-num>
<header>THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH THOUSAND</header>

### XXX. To flee to a sanctuary.
Related to the previous entry is "to flee to a sanctuary" <note>original: "ad asylum confugere"</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his third *Action against Verres*, says that a quaestor was prevented from dragging away his slave who had fled to the temple of Diana as a sanctuary. These expressions become more elegant and more philosophical <note>original: "δογματικώτερα"</note> if they are applied to matters of the mind.

### XXXI. The Citadel.
The metaphor of a "citadel" <note>original: "arx"</note> is not far removed from this form, used when we wish to signify a very safe and powerful defense. Marcus Tullius, in his sixth *Action against Verres*: "The same man flees to you judges in private; he makes use of this law under which the court is held, the common citadel of our allies." Again, in the same work: "This is therefore the one place for them to flee, this is the harbor, this the citadel, this the altar of the allies." Likewise, in *For Roscius the Comedian*: "This is the law of allies, this is the right of nations; they have this citadel, though it is somewhat less fortified than before, nevertheless," etc. Also in *For Sylla*: "I have ransomed the lives of all, the state of the world, this city—the seat of us all, the citadel of kings and foreign nations, the light of ethnic groups, the home of the empire—by the punishment of five mad and ruined men." The same author, writing to Publius Lentulus in his *Letters to Friends*, calls the most important part of a legal case "The citadel of the case." He says: "He could not have invaded the citadel of that case more effectively." Aristotle, in his preface to the *Rhetoric to Alexander*, writes: "Knowing well that a citadel of safety is the consideration of agreement made through speech" <note>original: "εἰδότας καλῶς ὡς ἀκρόπολις ἔστι σωτηρίας, ἡ διὰ τῆς συμφώνους γινομένη θεωρία"</note>.

### XXXII. Not even a trace.
Whenever we signify a person or a thing that has been utterly abolished, we say "not even a trace" <note>original: "ne uestigium quidem"</note> remains. Marcus Tullius in the third *Action against Verres*: "For if we grieved for another's lot as we do for our own injury, not a trace of that man would be left in the forum." Again, in the fifth: "Care must be taken that no trace of lust appears in one's life." Also, in the speech *Against Rullus*: "Hardly a trace of Corinth was left." In the same work: "So that the very place of those who vied for empire with this city might show the traces of calamity." Also in *For Cluentius*: "While in the meantime you find no trace of the Cluentian money." The same in *For the Manilian Law*: "whose legions came into Asia in such a way that not only the hand of so great an army, but not even a trace of it, seems to have harmed anyone at peace." Also in *For Lucius Flaccus*: "That the ambassadors were cast into chains, and the memory of the Roman people's name, along with the trace of empire, was deleted not only from the houses of the Greeks, but even from their literature." The same in *For Sylla*: "so that he who a little while before had been consul-elect, suddenly retained no trace of his former dignity." The same to Caecina <note>Erasmus likely means Cn. Plancius, as noted in the source text</note> in Book 5: "Not even any trace of dignity is left to us." Again, to Papirius Paetus in Book 9: "But you may think what you please; I am wonderfully captivated by wit, especially our native kind—particularly when I see it being overtaken by Latium, first when foreignness was poured into our city, and now even by trouser-wearing <note>The Romans considered trousers a mark of "barbarian" Transalpine nations.</note> and Transalpine nations, so that no trace of the old charm appears." Instead of "trace," he used "image" in the fifth *Philippic*: "Unless these things are rescinded by the authority of the Senate, since we have entered into the hope of recovering the Republic, no image of a free state will be left." The same in a letter to his brother Quintus: "For you would not have seen your brother—not the one you knew, not the one whom you left weeping as he saw you off—not even a trace of him nor a likeness, but a certain shadow of the living dead." He expressed the same in other words to Atticus in the fourth book, in the letter beginning "In the midst of my occupations": "My dear Pomponius, we have lost not only all the juice and blood <note>A metaphor for vitality or substance.</note>, but even the color and appearance of the former state." Again, in the first letter of the tenth book of *Letters to Friends*: "Nor is there any likeness at all or trace of the state."

### XXXIII. Two-obolers.
Those whom we wish to be understood as being of the lowest price were once called "two-obolers" <note>original: "diobolares"</note>. For an obol was a bronze coin. This was first said of low-class prostitutes who were for sale at the lowest price, and was later turned toward any man or thing that was remarkably cheap and contemptible. Pompeius Festus mentions this. Plautus calls a cheap harlot a "two-obolar slut."

### XXXIIII. Let the skilled horseman not sing.
"One skilled in horsemanship should not sing" <note>original: "ἱππωσύνην δεδαὼς μὴ ἀείδειν"</note>. This is taken from some poet, applied to one who, having professed serious matters, occupies himself with trifles. Horsemanship is a military skill and pertains to war. Musicians are unwarlike and pursuers of pleasures. Gregory the Theologian <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> in a letter to Eudoxus the rhetorician: "Poetry says that one who has learned horsemanship should not sing, nor even mutter, not like a horseman..."

<meta>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "ἱππω-" (hippo-), continuing the Greek quote on the following page.</meta>

<summary>Erasmus discusses metaphors for safety (the sanctuary and the citadel), total destruction (the lack of a trace), and the importance of maintaining professional focus (the horseman who should not sing).</summary>
<keywords>asylum, citadel, Cicero, metaphors, total destruction, obol, Roman character, horsemanship vs music</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of classical adages, moving from the metaphors of "citadels" and "sanctuaries" into specific cultural observations about the Thebans and Spartans, and then into legal and literary metaphors involving the bat.</meta>

<page-num>1018</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM: ADAGES</header>

"If you fail in horsemanship, do not also fail in the flute." <note>original Greek: "ἱππωσύνης ἁμάρτης, μὴ τ᾽ αὐλῶς"</note> That is, one who has learned the art of riding should not wish to sing poetry, lest it happen that he fails at both riding and singing simultaneously. It is not yet clear from which poet this was taken, but it seems to have been said against the Thebans, who primarily studied two arts: riding and playing the flute, even though the one is hardly compatible with the other.

### XXX. Spartan slaves are the most enslaved.
<note>original: "Spartæ serui, maxime serui"</note>

Plutarch, in his *Life of Lycurgus*, mentions it as a common saying: "In Lacedaemon, the free man is the most free, and the slave is the most enslaved." <note>original Greek: "ἐν Λακεδαίμονι τὸν ἐλεύθερον μάλιστα ἐλεύθερον εἶναι, καὶ τὸν δοῦλον μάλιστα δοῦλον"</note> Among the Spartans, it was not permitted for free-born citizens to learn or practice any craft, trade, or agriculture. Instead, they carried out all these tasks through the Helots—a class of slaves who were forbidden from learning or practicing any liberal art. The Spartans treated these Helots very harshly. They were forced to attend banquets and get drunk there, to sing ridiculous songs, and to perform indecent dances, so that by their example, the free-born might learn how indecent and foul a thing drunkenness is. Furthermore, when the Ephors <note>the high magistrates of Sparta</note> entered office, they would customarily declare war on the Helots so that it would be legally permissible to kill them. By these means, they were driven to such extreme servitude that they dared do nothing without the orders of their masters—to the point that when the Thebans, having made an incursion into Laconia, captured some of the Helots and ordered them to sing the songs of Terpander, Alcman, and Spendon the Spartan, they replied that "the master's daughters would not allow it." We have discussed the phrase "More noble than a Spartan" elsewhere.

### XXXI. The Bat.
<note>original: "Vespertilio"</note>

Those who are weighed down by debt and stay at home during the light of day, coming out only at night when creditors might call upon them, are called "bats." Ulpian, in the twenty-first book of the *Pandects* <note>a massive collection of Roman legal opinions</note>, under the title *On Eviction*, says: "If someone should promise a stipulator that a slave is healthy, not a thief, not a bat, etc." This stipulation seems useless to some, because if a person is in this situation, it is impossible for the claim to be accepted; if they are not, the promise is redundant. But I believe it is more true that this stipulation—that a slave is not a thief, is healthy, and is not a "bat"—is useful; for this encompasses what is in a person's interest to be, or not to be. Thus far Ulpian. Although in this passage, some read "vespillo" <note>an undertaker for the poor</note> or "versipellis" <note>a shapeshifter or werewolf</note> instead of "vespertilio" <note>bat</note>. Alciatus, by far the most learned among legal scholars, thinks in his commentaries *On the Meaning of Words* that the "bat" is spoken of in the way we just mentioned: one who hides during the day for fear of creditors and comes out at night. For he notes that the name comes from the fact that it flies in the evening <note>original: "vesperi volet"</note>, as Nonius Marcellus indicates. 

The adage seems to be taken from some fable, either by Aesop or someone imitating him (for it seems worthy of Aesop), which tells how a bat, a cormorant, and a bramble-bush entered into a partnership to conduct business with pooled resources. The bat contributed money borrowed from moneylenders, the cormorant contributed something else, and the bramble contributed clothing. When they all swam ashore naked from a shipwreck, the bat began hiding during the day for fear of creditors and only flying at night; the cormorant began haunting the shores, frequently dipping its neck into the depths to see if it could find its goods, either cast up on the shore or stuck at the bottom; and the bramble began clinging to the clothes of passers-by, hoping to perhaps find its own. 

It might seem poorly suited for a slave to be weighed down by debt—for who would trust one?—unless we read in Terence's plays that Davus had paid back what he owed to Geta. However, it seems to me that the name of "bat" also applies to a runaway slave who has slipped away from his master at night to hide himself where there is a risk of being recognized. For shortly thereafter in the same chapter, Ulpian uses "stray" and "runaway" in place of "bat." He says: "When someone stipulates that a slave is not a thief, not a runaway, not a stray." Nevertheless, the ancients used that word differently: namely, for a person of fickle or doubtful loyalty, who belongs neither to this group nor that, though he sells himself as belonging to both. This is because the bat is such a creature that it is considered neither among the birds nor among the mice. It has wings, but no feathers; it flies, but only toward evening. It has teeth, which no bird has. Varro, in his *Agatho*, as cited by Nonius, says: "Why have I become a complete bat? I am clearly neither among the mice nor among the birds." The insult of being a "bat" can also be twisted against lovers who fly about at night, whom Plautus in the *Trinummus* calls "dwellers in darkness" <note>original: "tenebricolas"</note>. "A plunderer," he says, "a corrupter of those who dwell in dark hiding places."

### XXXII. To offer in a bag.
<note>original: "In folle offerre"</note>

Callistratus, in the thirty-fifth book of the *Pandects*, under the title *On Conditions and Demonstrations*, in the chapter "When a Slave," says: "We think this condition is 'pure' <note>unconditional</note> when it consists in the giving of a thing, and not a pure condition when it consists in an act, but rather that condition which consists of a certain mixture." For...

certainly, if he offered the remainder in a bag, he shall be free: for the testator did not mean this specifically, but rather that he should render his accounts in the manner a slave is accustomed to: that is, first to offer the accounts to be read, and then to be calculated, so that it can be investigated whether the calculations are reported honestly or dishonestly, and whether the receipts and reports are correct or not. It appears that the phrase "in a bag" <note>original: *in folle*</note> was used for that which was unexamined, unexplained, and confused, just as one who offers contracts and money shut up in a small sack.

### XXXVIII
->A bad chorus-flutist makes a good ensemble-player.<-

Saint Augustine, in his letter to Aurelius (also cited in the *Decretals*, Cause 16, Question 1, chapter *Legi epistolam*), mentions that this was a commonly tossed-around saying: "A bad chorus-flutist makes a good ensemble-player" <note>original: *Malus choraules, bonus symphoniacus*</note>. This is used when someone who is despised in his own field is held in high value in a more prominent one; for instance, if an inept poet were to profess medicine and be considered among the distinguished doctors. Augustine’s words are as follows: "The most unworthy injury is done to the clerical order if deserters from monasteries are chosen for the service of the clergy, since from those who remain in the monastery, we are accustomed to assume into the clergy only the most proven and the better men—unless perhaps, as the common folk say, 'a bad chorus-flutist is a good ensemble-player,' so these same commoners will joke about us, saying, 'a bad monk makes a good cleric.'" It appears to be taken from Marcus Tullius Cicero, who speaks thus in his speech *For Murena*: "And so they seem to me to have preferred this at the beginning; after they could not achieve it, they slipped down to that place especially. Just as among Greek artists, those become flute-players who could not become lyre-players, so we see some who could not turn out to be orators, and they descend to the study of law."

### XXXIX
->By a nod and a shake of the head.<-

To whomever we ascribe supreme power, we say that all things are carried out by his nod and his shake of the head <note>original: *nutu ac renutu*</note>. It is a great thing to accomplish what you wish by a word, but it is more to accomplish it by a mere nod or a refusal. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his third speech *Against Verres*: "Unless he was present at your nod, unless he obeyed your lust and your greed." The same in *For Caecina*: "Can anything more certain be objected than that which he to whom it is objected does not even attempt to weaken with a nod?" The same *Against Rullus*: "Yet all the money would be paid to you at your nod." The same in the *Letters to Friends*, book eleven: "For the king having been killed, we uphold all the royal nods." Again in book 13, first letter: "Nor does he doubt that I can obtain this from you with a nod." In the same to Silius the propraetor: "So that with the Greeks most willing, you may obtain what you wish by a nod." Pliny, in the first book of his *Letters* to Octavius Rufus, indicates this is taken from Homer, who imagines Jove approving or rejecting the prayers of men with a single nod. I will add Pliny’s words: "See on what a height you place me, since you give me the same power and the same kingdom that Homer gave to Jupiter, Greatest and Best:
'The Father granted him one thing, but refused the other with a shake of the head.'" <note>original Greek: "τῶ δ᾽ ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατὴρ, ἕτερον δ᾽ ἀνένευσεν"</note>
For I too can respond to your prayer with a similar nod and shake of the head.

### XL
->Not even beasts could bear it.<-

This is a proverbial hyperbole found in Marcus Tullius Cicero’s fifth speech *Against Verres*: "Finally, so that the foulest odor of Apronius’s mouth and body, which, as they say, 'not even beasts could bear,' seemed sweet and pleasant to that one man alone." Close to this is what we have related elsewhere: "The polypus of Agna delights Balbinus" <note>A reference to Horace, meaning someone is blind to a lover's flaws</note>. The same in the fifth invective *Against Catiline*: "For so much pain of those times has been branded into us, that now not only men, but it seems to me not even the cattle will endure those things." He said it slightly differently in a letter to Atticus (the one beginning "You ask of me"), book 1: "And that which all men, and indeed even the cattle, knew had been done."

### XLI
->Cossi.<-

In the past, men who were naturally wrinkled were called "Cossi" <note>term: *Cossi*; wood-boring larvae or grubs</note> as a common insult, from the similarity to the worms that are born in wood. These have wrinkles by nature, so that they may contract and extend themselves. Pliny mentions these in several places, such as book 11, chapter 33; and again in book 30, chapter 13. Indeed, in book 17, chapter 24, he indicates that the larger ones of this kind were used for food and even considered a luxury in ancient times. Jerome also mentions them in the second book *Against Jovinianus*. The Greeks call them "peras" <note>original Greek: πῆρας; meaning 'maimed' or 'deformed'</note>, who, although they are younger, nevertheless show old age in their face. The authority for this is Festus Pompeius.

### XLII
->The Maenian Column.<-

Just as we say "From the crossroads," or "From the stone," signifying a man who is vehemently despised, so Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the first speech *Against Verres*, said "From the Maenian column" <note>The Maenian column was a place in the Roman Forum where the lowest class of people and petty criminals often gathered</note>: "Do I seem to you," he says, "to be in such a lack of friends that a sub-prosecutor should be added to me not from those whom I brought with me, but from the common people? Or do I think there is such a lack of defendants for you, that you try to snatch the case away from me..."

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...certainly, or rather, unless you find some defendants of your own order at the Maenian column? <note>original: "à columna Menia"</note> Asconius Pedianus <note>A 1st-century Roman historian and commentator on Cicero.</note> indicates that at the Maenian column, low-class defendants, such as thieves or worthless slaves, were usually judged by the "capital triumvirs" <note>officials in charge of prisons and executions</note>. The name was bestowed by Maenius, who, when he sold his house to the censors Cato and Flaccus so that a basilica could be built there, reserved the right to one column upon which he could extend a roof. From there, on projecting wooden galleries, he and his descendants could watch the gladiator shows, which were even then held in the Forum. Hence the surname "Maenian." For the types of cases conducted there, low-class pettifoggers were employed.

---

<margin>XL</margin>
### By the cup of Circe. <note>original: "Circeo poculo"</note>

We spoke before about the wand of Circe. Marcus Tullius Cicero used a similar figure, "the cup of Circe," regarding a man suddenly changed into something else, in his first *Action against Verres*. <note>Cicero's famous prosecution of the corrupt governor Verres.</note> He says: "But suddenly, from a king’s officer, as if by some cup of Circe, he was made a *verres* <note>a pun on the name Verres, which means "boar"</note>; he returns to his true self and to his own affairs." In Cicero's words, there is a silent allusion based on the ambiguity of the word. For a *verres* is a male pig, not yet castrated.

---

<margin>XLI</margin>
### From his bosom. <note>original: "Ex sinu illius"</note>

Those whom we wish to be understood as being of the closest intimacy, we say are "from the bosom" <note>original: "è sinu"</note> of this or that person. Marcus Tullius in the third *Action against Verres*: "As soon as Verres touched the province, he immediately sent letters to Messana, summoned Dio, and appointed false accusers from his own bosom to say that his inheritance had been forfeited to Venus Erycina." Again in the fourth *Action*: "Does it seem to you that this 'man of Venus,' who set out for the province from the bosom of Chelidon <note>Chelidon was Verres's mistress</note>, sought a large enough sum of money in the name of Venus?" Also in the second *Invective against Catiline*: "The last class, however, is not only in number but even in its very kind and lifestyle the one proper to Catiline—from his choice followers, or rather, from his very embrace and bosom." Plutarch, in his *Life of Cato the Younger*, used a similar form: "Gabinium Paulum from the bosom of Pompey" <note>original Greek: "γαβίνιον παῦλον ἐκ τῶν πομπηίου κόλπων ἄνθρωπον"</note>. This passage was cited by us previously in the proverb "To rejoice in one's bosom," but with a somewhat different sense. We have also spoken before about "that flock." Marcus Tullius calls some people "flock-mates" <note>original: "gregales"</note> from a flock—meaning companions of the same social club.

---

<margin>XLII</margin>
### Attendants. <note>original: "Circumpedes"</note>

Those who are close at hand and surround someone, ready for service, are called "attendants" <note>literally "those around the feet"</note>. Marcus Tullius in the third *Action against Verres*: "He said that these attendants—handsome, literate men—were his own, and that he had bought them." Thus he called those joined in constant familiarity "attendants," just as we call those who serve our domestic needs "at our hands" or "at our feet."

---

<margin>XLIII</margin>
### Not even a storm could hurt them. <note>original: "Ne tempestas quidem nocere possit"</note>

Regarding men who are remarkably stripped of goods and destitute, Marcus Tullius said—not without a proverbial flair—in the fifth *Action against Verres*: "Do not wait for the rest of the Leontines, whom not only Apronius <note>an agent of Verres</note> in the fields, but not even any storm could hurt." For indeed, they not only suffered no loss, but even in those robberies of Apronius, they were occupied with gain and profit, etc. There is an allusion hidden in the name of Apronius to the "Calydonian Boar" <note>original: "aprum Calydonium"</note>. Those who possess some land are vulnerable either on the fields or at sea; a storm can hurt them. But he whom no storm can hurt possesses nothing in the fields like a farmer, nor in ships like a merchant.

---

<margin>XLIV</margin>
### Ballio.

Certain names have passed into proverbs because of remarkable wickedness; these are sometimes taken from real people and sometimes from fictional characters in comedy. For Marcus Tullius, in his legal actions, repeatedly calls a certain Gaius Fannius Chaerea a "Ballio," as in his speech *For Roscius the Comedian*: "He is always shaved on his head and eyebrows for this reason," he says, "so that he may not be said to have even a single hair of a good man." Roscius used to play this character excellently on stage, so that no equal thanks were returned to him for the favor; for when he plays that most wicked and perjured pimp Ballio, he is playing Chaerea. That filthy, impure, and hated character is expressed in the morals, nature, and life of this man. Again in the same speech: "By my faith, Fannius, you would hardly dare to ask or be able to obtain this from Ballio or someone like him." Plautus introduces Ballio in the play *Pseudolus* as a most impure, greedy, and wicked pimp. The name is constructed from the Greek word "to throw" <note>original: "βάλλω"</note>, because a pimp is always hunting for some prey; or from "to dance" <note>original: "βαλλίζω"</note>, because he is the architect of a lewd dance.

---

<margin>XLV</margin>
### Door-to-door. <note>original: "Ostiatim"</note>

Marcus Tullius said "door-to-door" elegantly and not without a proverbial touch, meaning "one by one," or...

<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, NINTH CENTURY</header>
<sig>Rrr</sig>

...door to door <note>original: "ostiatim"</note>, in the sixth *Action against Verres*: "At this point, do not expect me to pursue this charge **door to door**: that he stole a libation bowl from Aeschylus of Tyndaris, or a small plate from Thrason, likewise of Tyndaris, etc." It will be more pleasant if this is transferred to matters of the mind: as if someone were to seek testimonies or proofs from individual books or chapters of authors, they would be said to seek them "door to door." In almost the same sense, in the second book of his letters to Atticus, he said he received some things <term>in fine detail</term> <note>original: "κατὰ λεπτόν" (kata lepton)</note>: "And lest you by chance ask for **fine detail** regarding individual matters, the whole business has been brought to such a point that there is no hope."

->Noble at home.<-
<margin>XLIX</margin>

One who is famous not only for wealth or power, but is born noble from nobles, Cicero repeatedly calls "noble at home" <note>original: "domi nobilem"</note>. In the third *Action against Verres*: "He ordered a fire to be made from green and damp wood in a narrow place; there he left a free-born man, **noble at home**, an ally and friend of the Roman people, tortured by smoke and half-dead." The same author in the fourth *Action*: "There was a certain Sopater of Halicyae, a man among the most wealthy and honorable **in his own home**." Again, in the fifth *Action*: "And so, since Pillus of Herbita, an eloquent and prudent man, and **noble at home**." Likewise in the speech *For Cluentius*: "Which letter A. Aurius, a brave and experienced man, and **noble at home**." Again, in the second book of his letters to his brother Quintus, he commends M. Orfius, a Roman knight, as "a man splendid **at home**, and influential even outside his home." It will be suitable for one who is great and famous by his own virtues.

->With a twisted neck.<-
<margin>L</margin>

One who is compelled by force is said to be dragged "with a twisted neck" <note>original: "obtorto collo"</note>. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in the sixth *Action against Verres*: "From this those 'Verrean' acts <note>A pun on Verres' name and his 'boar-like' behavior.</note> were born, because he ordered Sextus Cominius to be dragged into the banquet, at whom he attempted to throw a cup from his hand, and whom he ordered to be snatched away from the banquet into chains and darkness **with a twisted throat**." The same in *For Cluentius*: "Nor was anything done sooner than that he should pursue him and lead him back to the benches **with a twisted neck**, so that he might be able to finish his speech." Plautus, in the *Amphitryon*, said "with a bound neck" <note>original: "obstricto collo"</note>: "Because of that unworthy word, I will tear you apart here **with a bound neck**." Likewise in the same play: "Why, I shall drag Amphitryon from here **with a bound neck**." The same in the *Poenulus*: "I hesitate to flee from here to the wretched cross, before I am dragged to the praetor **with a twisted neck**." Again in the *Rudens*: "Choose quickly: do you prefer to be snatched **with a twisted neck**, or dragged?" And in the same place a little later: "Help me, my Charmides, I am being snatched **with a twisted neck**."

->Hunting dogs.<-
<margin>LI</margin>

Those who are possessed by a zeal for hunting have scout-dogs <note>original: "canes emissarios"</note> who, having tracked the wild beasts by the scent of their tracks, betray them with barking when found. We have spoken of the "Corycaeans" <note>An earlier adage referring to spies or eavesdroppers.</note> elsewhere. M. Tullius in the sixth *Action against Verres*: "He sets one of his **dogs** upon him, to say that he wishes to bring a capital charge against Diodorus of Melite." In the same book, somewhat later: "As soon as he had come into any town, those **Cibyrate dogs** were immediately let loose, to track down and peer into everything." He calls the two brothers from Cibyra "dogs" because Verres used their eyes for stealing, but his own hands. However, it is customary for a surname to be given to dogs from their region, such as "Melitean." And earlier in the same work: "After they arrived, you would say they were **hunting dogs** in a marvelous way, so did they sniff out and track everything, etc."

->Mercenary heraldry.<-
<margin>LII</margin>

Praises not granted from the heart, but offered through adulation for the sake of profit, Marcus Tullius calls "mercenary heraldry" <note>original: "mercenarium præconium"</note> in the third *Action against Verres*. "Therefore, when that head of yours had been adorned with so many words by **mercenary heraldry**, was any praetor found afterward who would issue that same edict?" Although it does not escape me that in common manuscripts "prologue" <note>original: "proœmio"</note> is held instead of "heraldry" <note>original: "præconio"</note>; whether correctly, let the learned decide.

->The price of the hand.<-
<margin>LIII</margin>

Marcus Tullius in the third *Action against Verres*: "A certain stone had to be cut and prepared, with his own machine. For no rock, no timber was brought there; there was only as much work in that contract as a few laborers' wages carried off, and the **price of the hand** <note>original: "manus precium," meaning the cost of labor or workmanship.</note> for the machine." He seems to call "the price of the hand" the wages which are owed to the Architect not for the material, but in the name of his art. The same in the speech *Against Piso*: "When indeed, with the Senate not only demanding and compelling it but unwilling and oppressed—not only with no zeal from the Roman people, but with almost no free vote—that province was for you the **price of the hand** for a city not just overturned by you, but destroyed," and so forth. Thus Gaius says in the book *On the Meaning of Words*, in the chapter "On a Woman": "Since there is more in the **price of the hand** than in the thing itself." And a little before this precedes: "Things are seen to be absent, as Sabinus <meta>catchword: Sabinus</meta>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Roman and Greek idioms, specifically focusing on terms derived from law, maritime practice, and ancient folklore. # DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

Sabinus says, and Pedius agrees <note>Massurius Sabinus and Sextus Pedius were influential Roman jurists</note>, that even those things whose physical substance remains are considered to have changed their form; therefore, things that are corrupted or transformed are seen as "absent" or "departed," since, etc. This can be twisted to apply to those who, through education, shape their students toward virtue or corrupt them.

<margin>LII</margin>
### The tenth thing.
<note>original: "Decumanum"</note>

In the past, people spoke of the **tenth egg** and the **tenth wave** <note>original: "decumanum ouum" and "fluctum decumanum"</note> to mean something very large. This was because farmers and sailors observed that every tenth egg laid is larger than the others, and every tenth wave is more powerful than the rest. Hence Ovid wrote:
> The force of the **tenth wave** rushes on. <note>original: "Decimæ ruit impetus undæ"</note>

From this, whatever was huge began to be called "decuman." As Lucilius says: "With a **huge** <note>original: "decumano"</note> sturgeon."

<margin>LIII</margin>
### A prize-winning deed.
<note>original: "Palmarium facinus"</note>

Terence used the phrase **prize-winning deed** for something remarkable and worthy of a triumph in his play *The Eunuch*: "I have this other thing, which I truly think is my **masterpiece** <note>original: "palmarium"</note>." Marcus Tullius Cicero used "palms" <note>original: "Palmas"</note> in the same sense. For instance, in his speech *For Sextus Roscius of Ameria*: "If, as I hear he is prepared to do, he comes forward as a witness, he will then recognize his other **palms** <note>legal victories</note> as well." Again, in the *Eleventh Philippic*: "A sixth **urban palm** <note>a victory in the city</note>, even for a gladiator, is difficult; but this is the fault of the judges, not mine." Plautus, in his play *The Haunted House* <note>original: "Mostellaria"</note>, used "the palm" in a negative sense, speaking of a young man who had degenerated from very restrained habits to very corrupt ones: "He now holds the **palm** in a different direction."

<margin>LIV</margin>
### To stir the sacred objects.
<note>original: "Commouere sacra"</note>

Plautus, in his play *Pseudolus*, used the phrase **to stir the sacred objects** to mean attempting a feat of extreme treachery. This saying clearly arises from the fact that, in desperate situations, people are accustomed to flee to the protection of the gods. For example, today in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiæ"</note>, when the River Seine floods beyond measure, the body of Saint Genevieve is carried from the church on the "Sharp Mountain" <note>the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève</note> to the cathedral sacred to the Virgin Mother. But consider whether "military cloaks" <note>original: "saga"</note> should be read instead of "sacred objects" <note>original: "sacra"</note>, so that you understand it as "taking up arms," which we have discussed elsewhere. For there follows immediately: <quote>"by this agreement, and what great troubles I am accustomed to cause."</quote> Then follow words like those of someone declaring war: <quote>"Now, lest anyone say they weren't told, I say this in the presence of all the youth, in the assembly of all the people, I proclaim it to all my friends and acquaintances: let them beware of me on this day, and not trust me."</quote> The slave himself thereafter speaks in military terms.

<margin>LV</margin>
### As if a trial date had been set.
<note>original: "Quasi dies dicta sit"</note>

In the past, defendants <note>original: "rei"</note> used to be gloomy and disheveled, looking like mourners, so that they might sway the judges to pity. Hence that line of Plautus in *The Ass-Dealer* <note>original: "Asinaria"</note>:
> Whom I see looking just as gloomy **as if a trial date had been set**.

<margin>LVI</margin>
### Bisaltia.
<note>original: "Βισαλτίαν"</note>

Stephanus writes that **Bisaltia** is a city in Thrace, or as Strabo reports, a village. The wicked character of its people passed into a proverb, so that those who spoke nothing sensible were said to be from **Bisaltia**. Indeed, the entire nation of Thrace had a bad reputation for many reasons, but especially for their savage character and treachery. Polymnestor was a Thracian, who followed the winning side in war, murdered Polydorus, and seized his gold by force.

<margin>LVII</margin>
### With the tip of the foot.
<note>original: "Summo pede"</note>

**With the tip of the foot** <note>original: "Ἄκρῳ ποδί" (Akro podi)</note> is an expression used with the same figurative meaning as "with the tip of the finger." One is said not to have touched a discipline even **with the tip of the foot** if they have never entered it or even touched its threshold. This appears in Plato’s *Laches*, a passage I believe I have mentioned elsewhere.

<margin>LVIII</margin>
### Maritime interest.
<note>original: "Vsuræ nauticæ"</note>

Among legal experts, **maritime interest** refers to rates of one percent <note>per month, or 12% annually</note> and other high rates. Those about to conduct business sometimes take out loans. Because those who conduct business by sea commit themselves to the winds and waves, moneylenders demanded higher interest. Sometimes a loan is taken in one city to be repaid in another; for instance, if a merchant took money in Venice to be repaid in Bruges. This kind of business, which involves risk to both parties <note>or "on both voyages"</note>, is called by the Greeks **a voyage both ways** <note>original: "ἀμφοτερόπλοον" (amphoteroploon)</note>. Such a loan was called a **nautical loan** <note>original: "δάνειον ναυτικόν" (daneion nautikon)</note>. Demosthenes used this in his *Oration against Dionysodorus*. It was also called **an outing** <note>original: "ἔκδοσις" (ekdosis)</note>, a word Demosthenes used against Aphobus, because the money was given "abroad." Furthermore, there is a title regarding maritime interest in the *Pandects* <note>the Digest of Roman Law</note>, Book 22. Modestinus calls this money **transported capital** <note>original: "traiectitiam"</note>, but he is not the only one. Paulus calls it **maritime interest**. There is a similar title in the *Code of Justinian*, Book 4. It is enough for a collector of proverbs to point this out. Whoever seeks more precise details should look there.

<summary>Erasmus explains various adages related to size (the "tenth" wave), excellence (the "palm" of victory), and legal or cultural desperation. He also provides a detailed explanation of "maritime interest," noting the high-risk nature of ancient sea-trade loans.</summary>

# FOURTH THOUSAND, NINTH CENTURY
Rrr 2
<meta>Catchword: setting</meta>

### To play the philosopher.
<note>original: "Philosophari"</note>
->LXI<-

For those who utter serious maxims, the Greeks use the word **to philosophize** <note>original: "Φιλοσοφεῖν"</note>, a term that appears several times in the plays of Plautus. From there, it was transferred to describe any intense and fervent study of a subject. Isocrates used it this way in his speech *On the Peace*. And Menander, in his play *Thrasyleon*, says: "This man is **philosophizing** <note>original: "Φιλοσοφεῖ"</note> on how to successfully arrange the marriage," meaning he is focusing all his efforts on completing the wedding arrangements. John Chrysostom frequently uses "to philosophize" to mean restraining one’s passions and remaining unbroken in the face of bitter circumstances; he calls this moderation of the soul "philosophy." It appears that Saint Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus were also fond of these expressions. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his letters *To Atticus*, writes: "But why do I say these things, which I desire to set aside so that I may **philosophize** <note>original: "Φιλοσοφεῖν"</note> with my whole soul and every care?" And elsewhere in the same letters: "But one must **philosophize**," meaning that everything must be endured with a level head. Horace <note>referred to here as "Flaccus"</note> says the same: "And I wrap myself in my virtue." Cicero uses this word in several other places in this manner, such as in book four: "For I can **philosophize** <note>original: "Φιλοσοφῆσαι"</note> with you," which means to rest so securely in your friendship that I can ignore everything else with a brave heart. It occurs several times in Plautus as well, whenever something particularly grave or sententious is said. In *The Captives*: "The matter is safe; he is even **philosophizing** now, no longer just telling lies."

### To speak Doric among Dorians.
<note>original: "Doribus Dorice loqui"</note>
->LXII<-

This has the appearance of a proverb; it is the response Gorgo gives to a stranger in Theocritus’s *Syracusan Women*, when he tells them to stop chattering like turtles:
"I think it is permitted for Dorians to **speak Doric**." <note>original: "Δωρίσδεν δ᾿ ἔξεστι δοκῶ τοῖς Δωριέεσσι"</note>
This would suit people who are naturally talkative. Or, it applies when someone’s speech matches their character and nature—for instance, when a Carthaginian speaks deceitfully, or a pimp says things worthy of a pimp.

### A winter dream.
<note>original: "Somnium hybernum"</note>
->LXIII<-

A **winter dream** <note>original: "Χειμερινὸς ὄνειρος"</note> is a term for a long-winded but foolish story, because winter nights are longer and therefore dreams are longer. Lucian writes in his work *The Dream*: "But while I was saying these things, some Archicles said, 'How long and legalistic this dream is!' Then another interrupted, 'A **winter dream**.'" He called it "legalistic" <note>original: "Dicanicum"</note> either because two characters were arguing with each other, or because court cases are argued over many **water-clocks** <note>term: "clepsydras," ancient devices used to time speeches in court</note>.

### He challenges the other tragedians.
<note>original: "Alios tragœdos prouocat"</note>
->LXIIII<-

"He will compete against the other tragedians" <note>original: "Τοὺς ἑτέρους τραγωδοὺς ἀγωνιεῖται"</note>; that is, he prepares himself against the remaining tragic actors. This is reported from an oration by the sophist Lycurgus against Demades. Didymus shows that this was commonly said of those who prepare and arm themselves against an opposing party. It seems to be a metaphor taken from the festivals sacred to Bacchus, in which the competition between tragic poets was intense.

### To desert one's bail.
<note>original: "Deferere uadimonium"</note>
->LXV<-

In the past, it was both shameful and costly to **desert one's bail** <note>term: "vadium," a legal promise or bond to appear in court</note>, and the person who promised to appear was not excused except for exceptionally grave reasons. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his second speech against Catiline, says: "And so that army, composed of Gallic legions... I greatly despise it, collected as it is from desperate old men, from bankrupts who preferred to **desert their bail** rather than that army." And there is that talkative man in Horace who, being required to answer his summons, hesitates whether he should desert Horace or his bail. We have mentioned elsewhere the phrase "A thing worthy of deserting one's bail" <note>original: "Dignū ob quod uadimonium deseratur"</note> to describe a matter of the greatest importance.

### To parade/To abuse.
<note>original: "Πομπεύειν"</note>
->LXVI<-

The ancients used the word **to parade** <note>original: "πομπεύειν"</note> to mean "to revile" or "to abuse," and **parade-talk** <note>original: "πομπείας"</note> for insults. This arose because during the Bacchic processions <note>original: "pompis"</note>, certain people would hurl insults at others from wagons and were attacked by them in turn. These verses are cited from Menander’s *Perinthia*:
"In the wagons there are certain **parade-insults** <note>original: "πομπεῖαί"</note> that are very bitter."
We have discussed the phrase "to speak from a wagon" elsewhere.

### To strike with an axe.
<note>original: "Securim injicere"</note>
->LXVII<-

Those who harm or wound someone severely are said to **strike with an axe**. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *For Lucius Murena*, says: "But yet, Servius, what an **axe** do you think you have **struck** into your candidacy, when you led the Roman people into such fear?" And a little earlier in the same passage, where he used the word "axe," it was as if...
