# DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES
<page-num>1024</page-num>

...calls a **blow** <note>original: "plaga"</note>. And of all those, that blow was struck against your petition, with me not remaining silent about its greatness. Likewise in the speech *For Plancius*: "what a heavier **axe** <note>original: "securim"</note> could they strike against the Republic?" Also in the *Letters to his brother Quintus*, book 2: "Thus the liberty of the Tenedians was cut off by the **Tenedian axe** <note>original: "securi Tenedia"; a reference to the proverbial sharpness and finality of justice on the island of Tenedos</note>." And Demosthenes used to call Phocion the "axe" of his own arguments. These are frequent in Plautus: "to throw the javelin," "to throw the spear," "to throw the weapon." Cicero said in *On the Consular Provinces*: "All weapons aimed at the fatherland."

->**Nothing is more useful than salt.**<-
<margin>LXVIII</margin>

I find this also recorded by scholars under the title of a proverb: "Nothing is more useful to the human body than **salt and sun** <note>original: "sale & sole"</note>." Even today we mix salt into all foods; formerly, "basking in the sun" <note>original: "apricatio"</note> was vehemently praised by doctors. Among the Hebrews, it was forbidden to sacrifice any victim without salt.

->**Beside the horse and the girl.**<-
<margin>LXIX</margin>

Aeschines, in his speech *Against Timarchus*, reports that there was a certain man in Athens of such great severity that he took his daughter to a deserted place—because she had behaved immodestly and had not preserved her integrity until marriage—and there shut her in together with a horse, where she would undoubtedly perish of hunger. He relates that the ground of that dwelling still survived in his own time, and because of this event, it was called **beside the horse and the girl** <note>original: "παρ᾽ ἵππου καὶ κόρης"</note>. It can be used as an example of immoderate or excessive severity.

->**Eloquent over wine.**<-
<margin>LXX</margin>

Cicero, in his speech *For Marcus Caelius*, calls those **eloquent over wine** <note>original: "ad uinū difertos"</note> who are inept at conducting serious legal cases but chatter a great deal over their cups where there is no need. They will never truly explain themselves if they step into that place [the court], however witty, sharp-tongued, and sometimes even "eloquent over wine" they wish to be at banquets. The atmosphere of the forum is one thing; that of the dining room <note>original: "triclinij"</note> is another. That saying of Horace <note>referred to as "Flaccus"</note> is well known: "Whom have the flowing cups not made eloquent?" Marcus Tullius [Cicero] alluded to the ancient custom where cases were argued according to the **measure of water** <note>original: "aquæ modum," referring to the clepsydra or water-clock used to time legal speeches</note>. This water was divided into three parts: one poured for the accuser, another for the defendant, and a third for the judge. But those who are eloquent over wine are almost mute when it comes to the water <note>meaning they cannot speak under the strict time limits and sobriety of a courtroom</note>.

->**With a dry rush.**<-
<margin>LXXI</margin>

What appears in Aeschines’s speech *On the False Embassy* has the quality of a proverb: **with an unsoaked rush** <note>original: "ὁλοσχοίνῳ ἀβρόχῳ"</note>, that is, with a dry rush or rope. "For now, boasting that he had abundant springs of arguments, and that he would speak such things concerning the right to Amphipolis and the origin of the war, he said that Philip's mouth was bound with a **dry rope**." **Unsoaked** <note>original: "ἀβροχος"</note> can mean either "dry" because it is not moistened, or something that does not have a noose. For rushes delight in moisture, and from these, they sometimes weave ropes. Hesychius indicates that "holoschoino" is the same as "oxyschoino," that is, a sea-rush; in addition to this, "holotrochon," that is, something that can be turned. Finally, "potheiphere lithon," that is, a round and rolling stone. Therefore, let the learned reader consider whether "with an unsoaked rush" signifies a false speech, not moistened by the "sea water" [of truth], but with sharp and piercing arguments. Indeed, in those words "springs of arguments" <note>original: "πηγὰς λόγων"</note>, there lies a proverb used to signify a massive abundance. It is frequent in the works of John Chrysostom.

->**The eyebrow twitches.**<-
<margin>LXXII</margin>

Whenever some good hope tickles our mind, we may say our **eyebrow twitches** <note>original: "salire supercilium"</note>. Thus Pseudolus in Plautus's play of the same name, answering a lover complaining about money, "But where will it come from?" replies: "Where, I do not know; except that it will be so, for thus my eyebrow twitches." This is taken from common superstition, which catches omens of future events from bodily sensations—such as if a limb itches without an evident cause, if the right eye twitches, or if the right ear rings. I am aware that it is read differently in Plautus; but both the sense itself and the logic of the meter teach that it should be read as I have set it down. For these Iambic trimeters <note>original: "senarij Iambici"</note> should be read thus:
> Truly, I will not desert you in your love, do not fear.
> I hope today from somewhere, by my good works or this hand of mine,
> I shall find for you some financial aid.
> But from where will it come? Where, I do not know,
> Except that it will be so, for thus my eyebrow twitches.

->**With the tips of two fingers.**<-
<margin>LXXIII</margin>

What we snatch greedily, we take with the whole hand, or as the proverb says, "with both." On the contrary, those who take sparingly, receive **with the tips of two fingers** <note>original: "duobus digitis primoribus"</note>. Plautus in the *Bacchides*: "Why then, you fool? Because...

# THE NINTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH CHILIAD
<page-num>1025</page-num>
### Rrr 3
<meta>catchword: Salt and</meta>

...since there was an opportunity for that matter, won by my virtue, so that you might take as much as you wanted. This you were taking with your **two primary fingertips** <note>original: "digitulis duob. fumebas primoribus"</note>. He refers, I believe, to the thumb and index finger. Again in the *Poenulus*: "You hold the matter." "Hardly, by Hercules, it is so tiny, with my **fingertips** <note>original: "digitis primoribus"</note>." When transferred to matters of the mind, it has a bit more charm, such as: "The opportunity was not so great that it should be taken with two fingertips, but seized with the whole body."

<margin>LXXIIII</margin>
->**A Drunkard.**<-

In Plautus’s *Pseudolus*, a drunken slave speaks thus: "I now have a **drunk** <note>original: "madusam"</note> well." Pompeius Festus indicates that among the ancients, *madusa* was commonly used to mean a person intoxicated with wine, and he doubts whether it is derived from the Greeks, for whom a drunkard is a **methysos** <term>μέθυσος; a person intoxicated with wine</term>, or from the Latin verb *madere* [to be soaked], because those well-supplied with wine are said to be "soaked." But if *Madusa* signifies a drunk person rather than the state of drunkenness, the phrase "I have a drunk" sounds absurd. Wherefore I think it should be read thus: "I now have my **drunkenness** well, with my food thus cared for." A slave in his drunkenness seems happy to himself, as if released from all fear and cares, and forgetful of all sad things. Someone might say, what does this have to do with proverbs? Indeed, just as foreign words have entered into use as proverbs through the appeal of novelty, so have certain obsolete ones.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
->**To reset the die.**<-

**To reset the game-piece** <term>τὸν πεττὸν ἀναθέσθαι; literally "to put back the pebble," referring to a move in a board game</term>. That is, those who corrected what had turned out poorly by using "second thoughts" (as they say) were said to "place the die again." Antiphon in his speech *On Concord* says: **"It is not possible to reset life like a die."** <term>ἀναθέσθαι δ’ ὥσπερ πεττὸν τὸν βίον οὐκ ἔστιν</term>. That is, it is not permitted to set up one's life anew just like a game-piece. It is not granted to repeat a life once lived. However, according to the saying of Micio in Terence’s play, it is permitted to correct the slips of a former life with better deeds. Once life is lost, there is nothing left for you to correct.

<margin>LXXVI</margin>
->**To harmonize in the Dorian mode.**<-

Those who disagree are said not to harmonize in **Dorian harmony**. This proverb seems to have been tossed against those whose speech differs from their deeds. Plato in the *Laches*: "It seems then, he says, that **you and I, O Laches, have not yet tuned our speech in the Dorian manner; for our deeds do not harmonize with our words.**" <term>οὐκ ἄρα πω φησὶ τὸν σὸν λόγον Δωριστὶ ἡρμόσμεθα...; the Dorian mode was considered the most stable and "manly" of the Greek musical scales</term>. In other words, we in no way harmonize in the Dorian mode according to your speech, I and you, Laches. For our deeds hardly sound in unison with our words. Among the types of music, the Dorian was most approved, as being moderately tempered between the Lydian and Phrygian modes.

<margin>LXXVII</margin>
->**Consulting present circumstances.**<-

Procopius in the first book of the *Gothic War*: "An old saying surely comes to me, which commands that **present circumstances be consulted**." I think it is the same as what we have reported elsewhere from Plato: **"to set well what is before one's feet"** <term>τὰ πρὸ ποδῶν εὖ τίθεσθαι; to focus on immediate problems rather than distant or past ones</term>. What has passed cannot be restored to its original state; various occurrences interrupt consultation about the future; that which is urgent must be cared for first.

<margin>LXXVIII</margin>
->**To change clothes.**<-

**To change clothes** <note>original: "mutare vestem"</note> beyond common usage is frequently used by Marcus Tullius Cicero, meaning that those who were mourning a dead person, or were defendants in court, were said to "change clothes." For defendants also used to walk about in dark or mourning garments, according to an ancient and most foolish custom: for why should they mourn when not yet condemned? And, as often happens, even when they are innocent? Although even the Senate, with clothes changed, sometimes testified to its grief. Cicero in *For Sestius*: "The law had been passed, with the forum devastated and abandoned, and handed over to assassins and slaves—even that law which the Senate, with **changed clothing**, had tried to prevent from being passed." In the same work: "The Senate was therefore in mourning; the city was in a state of squalor by public counsel, with clothing changed." And shortly after: "When suddenly the two consuls proclaimed that the Senators should return to their own [usual] dress." Also shortly after: "Nor should they signify this grief of theirs by a change of clothing, whether that change of clothing was intended for their own mourning or for the purpose of entreaty." The same in the *Letters to his brother Quintus*, book 2: "Cato proposed a law for ending the command of Lentulus. The son **changed his clothes**." Again in the same: "Who would not even defend their clothing," etc. He calls "clothing" those who had not changed their dress. It will be proverbial if you say: "This case is unworthy for anyone to **change clothes** for." That is, it is unworthy of heavy mourning.

<margin>LXXIX</margin>
->**Smoky images.**<-

**Smoky images** <term>Καπνώδεις εἰκόνες; referring to the wax ancestor masks kept in Roman atriums, which would darken over time from the smoke of household fires</term>. This was said against those who boasted of the very ancient nobility of their lineage. Cicero in *Against Piso*: "You crept into honors through the error of men, by the recommendation of **smoky images**, of which you have nothing similar except the color." Juvenal calls them "old waxes," although: "Old waxes adorn the halls on all sides, yet virtue is the one and only nobility." In the same place he most humorously mocks "the Curii now halved [busts], and the smaller nose of Corvinus" <note>referring to ancient family statues that had crumbled or lost limbs and features with age</note>.

<margin>LXXX</margin>
# Salt and table.

We have mentioned elsewhere that among the ancients, the law of hospitality was considered most sacred. This bond was contracted through the sharing of **salt and table** <note>original: "salis & mēsæ consortio"</note>. In the same way, among the Germans, accepting a cup from someone offering a toast removes any right to take legal action for previous injuries. Aeschines, in his oration *On the False Embassy*, says: <note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ τῆς πόλεως ἅλας καὶ τὴν δημοσίαν τράπεζαν περὶ πλείστου φησι ποιεῖσθαι"</note> "For he says he values most highly the salt of the city and the public table." I had not forgotten that this proverb was mentioned previously, but this example commends to us the religious sanctity of public hospitality, and therefore I thought it worth recording. Traces of this public hospitality remain among the Germans even to this day.

<margin>LXXXI</margin>
# Salarian feasts.

Among the Romans, the most ancient class of priests were the **Salii** <term>Salii; from the Latin 'salio' (to leap), they were the "leaping priests" of Mars who carried the sacred shields</term>, so named because they carried the *Ancylia*—the shields believed to have fallen from heaven—while dancing. Because of them, a sumptuous and magnificent banquet is called **Salarian** <note>original: "Saliare"</note>. Horace writes in his *Odes*:

> Now is the time for drinking, now with free foot
> The earth must be beaten; now was the time,
> My comrades, to deck the couch of the gods
> With **Salarian feasts**. <note>original: "faliaribus... dapibus"</note>

I believe, however, that Horace used "Salarian" to mean "pontifical"—that is, using a specific type to represent the whole category of priestly banquets. For in all sacred rites, a splendid and magnificent preparation was employed, a duty delegated to the *Septemviri Epulonum* <term>Epulones; a college of seven men in Rome responsible for organizing public religious banquets</term>. When the philosopher Aristippus was criticized for living luxuriously, he replied that if this were a crime, the gods would not allow it in their own sacred rites. We have spoken elsewhere regarding the "pontifical supper."

<margin>LXXXII</margin>
# A false reproach.

This is a proverbial sentiment found in Aeschines’s speech *On the False Embassy*: <note>original Greek: "οὐ γὰρ ψευδὴς ὄνειδος ὃ περαιτέρω τῆς ἀκοῆς διikνεῖται"</note> "A false reproach does not reach beyond the ears." A person who hears an insult of which they are guilty is deeply wounded in their soul. But one who is splashed with a false reproach is not moved in the same way. It does not descend deeper into the mind of a person with a clear conscience.

<margin>LXXXIII</margin>
# He does not tell the truth even by accident.

A little later he adds a proverbial hyperbole: <note>original Greek: "συμπεπλεγμέναι γὰρ τῇ πολιτείᾳ... ὃς οὐδ’ ἂν ἄκων ἀληθὲς οὐδὲν εἴποι"</note> "I am entangled in the state with a man who is an impostor and a rogue beyond measure, who could not say anything true **even unintentionally** <note>original: "ne insciens quidem"</note>." By this figure of speech, he marks a man as remarkably vain. Otherwise, even those who are liars by nature usually say something true occasionally through a slip of the tongue or through thoughtlessness. Even today, there is a common saying among our own people about a vain man: "He is lucky at telling the truth"—as if he never speaks the truth unless it is by accident. For whatever happens contrary to one's intention is attributed to luck.

<margin>LXXXIIII</margin>
# To drag by the hair.

To **drag by the hair** <note>original: "τῶν τριχῶν ἕλκειν"</note> is said of those who compel someone by force; today we say "to drag by the ears." Aeschines, in the oration I just cited: "I would not have endured the insult, but would have been incensed when one of Philip's friends, appointed to receive guests, welcomed us at a banquet; I would have **dragged him by the hair** and, seizing a strap, would have lashed the captive woman." Plautus, in the *Menaechmi*: "But who is this who drags me from the chariot by the hair?" I believe this is an allusion to the Pallas Athena of Homer, who pulled Achilles back from the fight by his hair. The same author in *The Merchant*: "I'll drag her along the road by her hair, unless he takes her away from here." We have spoken elsewhere of "being dragged by the nose," "with a twisted neck," and "with a twisted throat." The further the metaphor recedes from physical things, the more elegant it will be, such as if one were to say: "wantonness must be dragged by the hair and chastened by fasting and labor."

<margin>LXXXV</margin>
# An evil Scythian.

So great was the barbarity and ferocity of the **Scythian** <term>Scythians; nomadic people of central Eurasia known to the Greeks as the quintessential "barbarians"</term> race that the very name passed into a proverb. In the same way today, we call a cruel man a "Turk," and a monstrous deed "Turkish." Aeschines in the oration *On the False Embassy*: "I beseech you to save me, and not hand me over to that speechwriter and **evil Scythian**."

<margin>LXXXVI</margin>
# An evil beginning, an evil end.

<note>original Greek: "Ἀρχῆς κακῆς τέλος κακόν"</note> That is: "Of an evil beginning, the end is evil." This iambic verse is attributed to the poet of the *Aeolus*.

<meta>catchword: is attributed</meta>

...is referred to. Things established by sound counsel, even if some difficulty arises, eventually attain a happy outcome; conversely, those begun with bad reasoning, even if they succeed at first, have an unhappy end.

<margin>LXXXVII</margin>
### To seek a laurel leaf in spice-cakes.
<note>original: "Laureolam in mustaceijs quærere"</note>

Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his *Letters to Atticus*: "Bibulus began to seek a laurel leaf in a spice-cake." That is, to hunt for a minor or undistinguished reputation from trivial business. A **spice-cake** <term>mustaceum; a type of wedding cake or sweet bread made with grape must (unfermented juice), flour, and spices</term> is a type of sacrificial cake to which a shaving of a laurel branch is added, and it is baked over laurel leaves, as Cato indicates in his book *On Agriculture*. Consequently, Pliny, in Book 15, Chapter 30, thinks the "spice-cake laurel" was named as a third kind of laurel because it was used for that purpose. Ordinarily, the laurel was "triumphal"—the ornament of the palaces of princes and high priests. Those who could not achieve this true laurel sought a tiny laurel leaf in a spice-cake. Marcus Tullius, in the fifth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, in the letter beginning "On the morning of the Saturnalia," says: "Bibulus, I believe, wanted to be our equal by using this empty title." In the same passage, he says of Mount Amanus: "He began to seek a laurel leaf in a spice-cake." Cicero had performed great deeds in his province, while Bibulus’s reputation was cold and stagnant. Similarly, in a letter to Marcus Caelius Rufus (Book 2), he calls a mediocre triumph a "laurel leaf": "For you say you would wish that I only had enough business to suffice for a little laurel leaf."

<margin>LXXXVIII</margin>
### If you are the prow-officer.
<note>original: "Si tu proreta"</note>

One fig is not as like another fig as this is like a proverb found in Plautus’s play *The Rope*:

> If you are the prow-officer for that ship, I shall be the pilot.

This can be used whenever neither person wants to yield to the other in some business. For the **prow** <note>original: "prora"</note> is that part of the ship which strikes the shore when landing, and the **stern** <note>original: "puppis"</note> is the rear part where the man who controls the rudder sits. Sailors have specific duties assigned to each man, the most important of which are the **prow-officers** <term>proretae; the look-out or forward officer</term> and the **pilots** <term>gubernatores; the steersmen or captains</term>. From this comes the proverb "prow and stern" (meaning the whole of a matter). "Prow" is a Greek word; the person who presides over that part is called by them a **proreus** <note>original Greek: "πρωρεύς"</note> or **prorates** <note>original Greek: "πρωράτης"</note>, from which comes the verb **to command the prow** <note>original Greek: "πρωρατεύειν"</note>. I suspect Plautus used the Greek word for the second role as well, so that it would correspond in Greek: **pilot** <note>original Greek: "κυβερνήτης", transliterated as "kybernetes"</note>. For if you read the Latin *gubernator*, the trochaic verse would have a short syllable in the third-to-last place (*gubernator ero*), which the meter of the poem in no way allows. "If you are the prow-officer for that ship, I shall be the **pilot** <note>original Greek: "κυβερνήτης"</note>." However, whatever the case may be, I leave it to the judgment of the learned. The more honorable part of the ship is the stern. Hence Virgil’s Aeneas "stands high on the stern." And Marcus Tullius says to Cornificius in Book 12: "Therefore, my Quintus, climb aboard with us, and indeed toward the stern."

<margin>LXXXIX</margin>
### More playful than ivy.
<note>original: "Hedera lasciuior"</note>

It is said with a proverbial flavor that the nature of ivy is to bind everything in its embrace. Hence Horace, wishing to describe the tightest embrace of a girlfriend, says in his *Odes*:

> More tightly than the tall oak is bound by the ivy,
> Clinging with pliant arms.

And elsewhere: "More ambitious than the playful ivy." But with its embrace, ivy chokes the trees; wanton girls do the same to their lovers. For this reason, in Rome, it was forbidden for the **Priest of Jupiter** <term>Flamen Dialis; the high priest of Jupiter, who was bound by many strange ritual taboos</term> to touch ivy, and indeed it was not even lawful for him to name it. By this riddle, antiquity declared how much purity and chastity befits a priest, and indeed how much freedom. For to love is sheer slavery. Nor was he allowed to wear a solid ring, or to have any knot whatsoever on his person, as Festus Pompeius testifies—I believe because it is necessary for a priest to be free from all anxiety and not to be conscious of any evil in himself.

<margin>XC</margin>
### Theatrical trifles.
<note>original: "Nugæ theatri"</note>

Plautus, in the comedy *Pseudolus*, calls the everyday insults thrown at prostitutes, pimps, and parasites by comic actors **theatrical trifles**. Thus, when Ballio the pimp is asked what someone had said to him, he says: "Theatrical trifles—the words that are usually said to a pimp in comedies, which even boys know; they said I was wicked, a criminal, and a perjurer." So says the pimp. However, no one ought to be offended by these insults, as Socrates used to say—no more, by Hercules, than by the free speech at a great banquet. Indeed, everything that happens in comedies could be called theatrical trifles: such as young men being in love, old men scolding, slaves tricking their masters, female pimps being thirsty, and so on. Marcus Tullius used the phrase somewhat differently, turning the word "theater" to signify ostentation. For instance, in his speech *For Rabirius*: "I have indeed known many great and incredible virtues of Gaius Caesar, but the rest are set forth in larger, as it were, theaters, and almost..."

<meta>catchword: and almost</meta>

<summary>This page discusses proverbs regarding the pursuit of trivial fame (the laurel in the spice-cake), competition for authority (the ship's prow and stern), the suffocating nature of love compared to ivy, and the ritual taboos of Roman priests.</summary>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...and almost popular, "to take a place in the camp," and so on. Hence, those things are called "Theatrical" which court the favor of the multitude.

<margin>XCI</margin>
->**In outline.**<-
<note>original Greek: "Ἐν τύπῳ" (En typo)</note>

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fifth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, in the letter beginning "On the morning of the Saturnalia," writes: "Hold this now as certain, that with this army such great business could not have been conducted. Which you will learn **in outline**." <note>original: "ἐν τύπῳ"</note> For so you allowed me in your last letters. He said "in outline" for that which was "in few words," summarily and concisely, cutting away those things which pertain less to the matter. For from this comes the Greek word <note>original: "ἐντύμψ"</note> meaning "to happen." The opposite of this seems to be what is said elsewhere: **in breadth** <note>original: "ἐν πλάτει" (en platei), meaning in great detail</note>.

<margin>XCII</margin>
->**Equally with the most ignorant.**<-

Not without the appearance of a proverb, the old man Simo in Plautus’s *Pseudolus*, when asked by Ballio, "Do you not yet know what this matter is?", responds: "**Equally with the most ignorant.**" He means that he knows nothing at all, and nothing more than those who are the most ignorant. A similar form of speech is frequent among the ancients regarding a person, such as, "You are as dear to me as he who is the dearest." Regarding time: "Pamphilus was in love, as much as when he was at his peak." Regarding a thing: "That service was as pleasing to me as that which is most pleasing." "I hate drunkenness as much as those things which I hate most."

<margin>XCIII</margin>
->**With a full bushel.**<-
<note>A "bushel" (modius) was a Roman unit of dry measure, roughly 8.7 liters.</note>

We have said before that to do something "with a full hand" means to do it bountifully and not at all stingily. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the sixth book of his *Letters to Atticus*, in the first letter, used a very similar figure: "**With a full bushel**," if those men already have, with a full bushel, the honor of words, frequent invitations, and so on. For he had said before that he had praised the tax-gatherers’ interests "abundantly."

<margin>XCIIII</margin>
->**To tie a dog with lamb’s sweetbreads.**<-
<note>original: "Agninis lactibus alligare canem." "Lactes" refers to the small intestines or delicate innards, often considered a delicacy for animals.</note>

Ballio says in Plautus’s *Pseudolus*: "By Pollux, with the same effort I would trust you, I would also tie a runaway dog with **lamb’s sweetbreads**." He who ties a dog with lamb’s intestines not only loses the dog, but also gives the prey to the runaway. So he who trusts a man of bad faith both loses his property and holds in vain a debt from one who is insolvent. For the "lactes" are what the softer intestines are called.

<margin>XCV</margin>
->**He surpassed the Trojan trick.**<-

In Plautus’s *Pseudolus*, the old man, praising his servant because he had tricked the pimp Ballio with a new art and a prepared ambush through a certain person who had been suborned, speaks thus:
"Pseudolus has **surpassed the Trojan trick** and conquered."
He refers, of course, to the Trojan horse woven from planks, of which we have already spoken quite often. Just as the Greeks tricked the Trojans through the suborned Sinon, so Pseudolus tricked the pimp through Harpagus.

<margin>XCVI</margin>
->**To laryngize.**<-
<note>original Greek: "Λαρυγγίζειν" (Laryngizein)</note>

The Greeks use the term **laryngize** for those who do not speak in a natural way, but pour out a monstrous voice with a dilated throat. In the same way, some people sing. Demosthenes objected to this vice in Aeschines, saying that because he did not speak from the heart, he strained his voice beyond nature. For it is not the part of an orator to move the emotions by shouting, but by arguments and by placing the matter as if before one’s eyes.

<margin>XCVII</margin>
->**With eyes and hands.**<-

What has been discovered by every means is said to be "seized by **eyes and hands**." Marcus Tullius Cicero in *Pro Cluentio*: "When he had clearly discovered the poison which Oppianicus, his mother’s husband, had prepared for him, and the matter was held not by conjecture but by **eyes and hands**, and no doubt could exist in the case, he brought the accusation." Eyes are believed more than ears. Furthermore, some are so **hard to persuade** <note>original Greek: "δυσπειθεῖς" (dyspeitheis)</note> that unless they touch with their hands, they do not believe. Just as the Gospel history tells of Thomas Didymus <note>Saint Thomas the Apostle, famous for needing to touch Christ's wounds to believe in the Resurrection.</note>.

<margin>XCVIII</margin>
->**Like a summer-solstice herb.**<-

In Plautus’s *Pseudolus*, a lover suddenly cast down from hope speaks thus: "I was like a **solstice herb** for a little while; suddenly I sprang up, suddenly I perished." We have spoken elsewhere about the *Ephemerum* creature <note>The mayfly, which lives for a single day.</note>. There are those who wish the solstice herb in this passage to be understood as the Heliotrope. And yet, although the Heliotrope turns around facing the sun, we nowhere read that it is born and dies on the same day. It is nearer to the truth that Plautus is thinking of the herb **Ephemerum**, of which Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD.</note> makes mention in several places, such as in Book 4, Chapter 698, and also in several others. Again in Book 6, Chapter 11, he identifies two kinds: one is the *Colchicum*, because it grows there in abundance, which is called the "bulbous" or "wild" sort, because toward the end of autumn it pours out a whitish flower, not unlike saffron. The other is what they call the "Wild Iris," with leaves like a lily but thinner, with a stalk... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page.</note>

<summary>Erasmus interprets various proverbs from Plautus and Cicero, focusing on metaphors for summary descriptions, futile trust, and the fleeting nature of success or life, often comparing Roman literary references with Greek botanical and medical texts.</summary>
<keywords>Cicero, Plautus, Pseudolus, Greek etymology, Trojan Horse, Demosthenes, Doubting Thomas, Solstice herb, Ephemerum, Dioscorides, botanical metaphors, ancient rhetoric</keywords>

--- Page 1155 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of ancient metaphors and idiomatic expressions. Having just discussed terms for brevity and ignorance on the previous page, Erasmus now moves into botanical metaphors for youth, the concept of being "of no color" (unpredictable), and political stability using the figure of Cato the Younger.</meta>

<page-num>1019</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD 4, CENTURY 10, 1019</header>

...it has a blue flower and is bitter, the description of which Pliny provides in Book 25, Chapter 13. **Colchicon** <note>the Autumn Crocus, *Colchicum autumnale*</note> attracts the ignorant with its resemblance to a bulb and then kills them, just as poisonous mushrooms do. But the immediate remedy is cow's milk. There is no doubt that the playwright Plautus had this herb in mind. For Dioscorides says it appears at the end of autumn—which is, if I am not mistaken, around the winter solstice. For autumn among the Romans and Greeks occurs later than it does for us. And Theophrastus thinks it is called **Ephemeron** <note>original Greek: "Ἐφήμερον", literally 'living for a day'</note> because it does not live beyond a day, predicting the same of the herb as Aristotle does of the insect of the same name <note>the mayfly</note>.

->**In the blade.**<-
<margin>XCIX</margin>

Things are said to be **in the blade** <note>original: "In herbis"</note> when they have not yet matured but merely offer good hope for the future. Marcus Tullius Cicero said this in his oration *For Marcus Caelius*: "But I do not speak of that wisdom which does not belong to this age; I speak of the impulse of the soul, of the desire for winning, of the ardor of the mind for glory—pursuits which in these ages of ours ought now to be more restrained, but in youth, truly, he indicates they are as if **in the blade**, showing what the maturity of virtue and how great the fruits of industry will be." I remember this proverb was mentioned by us elsewhere, but it seemed fit to add this location. If the reader suffers any loss from this repetition, let it be questioned; but if anyone mocks me for trying to pad my count of proverbs, he will weep if he considers the innumerable proverbs mixed in here that are not actually counted toward the total number of the "Chiliads" <note>thousands</note>.

->**Of no color.**<-
<margin>C</margin>

Elsewhere we mentioned that it is common to say of a man who is unknown in every way, "I know not whether he is white or black." Very similar to this is what the character Harpax says in Plautus: "What Pseudolus, what deceits are you telling me about? I have known that man to be **of no color** <note>original: "nullius coloris", meaning shifty or impossible to pin down</note>." This is a more forceful expression than if he had said "white or black." And a little later, instead of the usual phrase "I do not know the man," he says: "I have not known that mortal who is called Pseudolus, nor do I know him." Again, in the same play: "Those who seek back their own, return what belongs to another to **no one born** <note>original: "nato nemini", meaning absolutely no one</note>." Likewise in *The Rope*: "Lest you be in vain for this master, except for me **no one was born**." Again in *The Haunted House*: "It will be cared for, just as if **no one** lived inside the house." Again in the same: "**No one born** was in the house."

### THE TENTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH CHILIAD

->**Both the booty and the prize.**<-
<margin>I</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a profile of a man's head integrated with foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>
Whenever we mean that something is to be taken away entirely, whether by right or by wrong, we shall say that **both the prize and the booty** <note>original: "& praemium & praedam"</note> are to be taken. A "prize" is given for merit; "booty" is taken away by force or by craft. Ballio says in the same play: "That prize which I promised in jest is taken from me." To which the old man responds: "It is fitting that **the prize and the booty** be taken from wicked men." He feels that the wicked should be despoiled in any way possible, for if anything bad happens to the wicked, it is a good deed—just as it is well said that what is spoken badly of those who deserve it is actually a well-spoken thing.

->**To make a death-day out of a birthday.**<-
<margin>II</margin>

In the same play, Ballio the pimp, forced to return money, says: "I am determined to make here a **death-day** out of a **birthday**." He used "death-day" <note>original: "emortualem"</note> for a sad and funereal day, and "birthday" <note>original: "natalem"</note> for a joyful and happy one.

->**We are content with this Cato.**<-
<margin>III</margin>

Among the phrases that Caesar Augustus used to employ in daily speech, Suetonius records this one: whenever Augustus signified that the present state of affairs ought to be accepted with good grace, he would say, "**We are content with this Cato.**" Cato of Utica attempted to protect the existing state of the Republic by excluding tyranny, but he did not succeed; the faction that seemed to pursue tyranny won out. Augustus, however, agreed with Cato in this: he did not want the current state of the Republic to be changed. And so, in a certain way, Augustus was the Cato of his own time. We have recounted from Macrobius among the *apophthegms* <note>pithy sayings</note> that Caesar Augustus once visited the house where Cato had lived. When a man named Strabo, trying to flatter Augustus, attacked Cato's stubbornness for choosing suicide rather than submitting to the victorious Julius Caesar, Augustus responded: "Whoever does not want the present state of the city to be changed is both a good citizen and a good man." By this saying, he both protected the memory of Cato and looked out for his own interests, ensuring no one would attempt a revolution in the future.

->**Gluttonous triremes.**<-
<margin>IIII</margin>

**Gluttonous triremes** <note>original Greek: "Ἀδηφάγοι τριήρεις", *Adephagoi triereis*</note> are so called because they require enormous expenses. The metaphor seems to be taken from excellent horses bred for racing, which must be voracious eaters. This appears in the orator Lysias. Furthermore, Alcaeus, in a comedy-tragedy, called thirsty lamps **gluttonous** <note>original Greek: "ἀδηφάγους"</note> because they consume much oil. These expressions take on the appearance of a proverb if applied to a man...

<meta>This page continues the "Chiliads" of Erasmus, moving from botanical metaphors into social and legal idioms. Page 1030 focuses on Athenian civic customs, the secrecy of high courts, and common insults or terms of endearment found in classical comedy and oratory.</meta>

<page-num>1030</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<meta>catchword: ca</meta>

...is transferred to someone who is prodigal and of immoderate expense, just as the "Devouring chariot," of which we spoke earlier.

->**Worth an obol.**<-
<margin>V</margin>

**Worth an obol** <note>original Greek: "Ἄξιος ὀβολδ͂"</note>—that is, "worthy of a penny"—was a phrase used jokingly of someone who wished to be counted among a certain number or group. It is a metaphor taken from the custom of the Athenian republic. Those who were enrolled by the senate into the rank of citizens were called **dokimoi** <note>original Greek: "δόκιμοι", meaning "approved" or "tested"</note>, and because of this, they were given one obol from the public treasury each day, as Aristotle records in his *Politics*. Others prefer the view that two obols were usually given; it is possible that after some time this small wage was doubled. Lysias mentions this matter in his oration *On the Cripple* <note>original: "περὶ τ͂ ἀδυνάτδ"</note>. I suspect Aristophanes alluded to this in *The Knights*: "A man has become [great] among all the many, yet not even worth [an obol]." Those were called **adunatoi** <note>original Greek: "ἀδυνάτδ", meaning "the powerless" or "disabled"</note> who were physically lame for a period of three months. Similarly, those were called **adokimasoi** who had not yet been enrolled in the number of citizens, nor were yet judged "worthy of an obol."

->**More silent than an Areopagite.**<-
<margin>VI</margin>

**More silent than an Areopagite** <note>original Greek: "Ἀρεοπαγίτδ στεγανώτερ@"</note> was said of one who could best keep a entrusted secret. Alciphron says in a certain letter: "Be to me now more silent than an Areopagite." For a person is called **steganos** <note>original Greek: "στεγανὸς"</note> not because he is silent himself, but because he contains a secret and does not "leak" it anywhere; the metaphor is taken from solid vessels that do not drip from any part. In Athens, capital cases were heard at the **Areopagus** <note>the "Hill of Ares," the high court of Athens</note>, and this was done at night with great attention. Perhaps it was a religious crime for them to blab to the common people about what had been done there. Even today among the Westphalians <note>referring to the Vehmic courts of medieval Germany</note> there remain relics of this kind of judges. They are commonly called "The Certain Ones." Those admitted into this order are driven to silence by a great religious oath. For there is a certain method of detecting crimes which no one understands except those who are sworn in.

->**To 'brother' someone.**<-
<margin>VII</margin>

People are said **to 'brother' someone** <note>original Greek: "Ἀδελφίζειν", from *adelphos* (brother)</note> when they flatter someone with "adoptive" names. This is still very common today among the Italians, who call those they wish to flatter "little brothers" <note>Italian: *fratercuoli*</note>. To **adelphizein** means to call someone a brother, just as we use terms like "to congratulate" or "to beatify." Horace says in his *Satires*: "Add 'brother' or 'father': as each man's age is, so the witty man adopts him." Again elsewhere: "You have heard me call you 'father' to your face, nor was I more sparing with the word when you were absent." An example of this is in Aristophanes' *Knights*. Also in Plautus, among other places, in the *Pseudolus*. Thus a loving master flatters his slave: "Tell me, Pseudolus, shall I greet you as father or mother?"

->**To prophesy old news.**<-
<margin>VIII</margin>

Elsewhere we have recorded the phrase "to speak ancient things" <note>original Greek: "ἀρχαῖα λέγειν"</note>, meaning to speak trifles. Ballio, in Plautus’s *Pseudolus*, responding to the fierce insults with which he is attacked by two men, replies: "You are prophesying old news." This will be suitable for those who bring nothing new, but only what has long been tossed about by the common crowd. For it is the role of prophets either to say something new that has not yet happened, or to bring forth something known to no one. For certain "prognosticators" are accustomed to divine marvelous things about years that have already passed. To a pimp, it is nothing new to hear himself called "wicked," "perjured," or "sacrilegious."

->**To complain of the same things.**<-
<margin>IX</margin>

They are said **to weep in harmony** <note>original Greek: "Ξυναυλίαν κλαίειν", literally "to weep to a flute-duet"</note> who complain at the same time about the same evils. The metaphor is taken from the fact that among the ancients, two flute players sometimes played the same song together. Aristophanes in *The Knights*: "Let us weep a duet, in the style of Olympus," that is: "Let us sing sad things in the modes of Olympus." A certain **Olympus** was a disciple of Marsyas; he wrote about mournful modes to be played on the flute. But things went badly for Marsyas's music <note>referring to Marsyas being flayed after losing a contest to Apollo</note>. Therefore, the disciple sings mournful things to the master.

->**Rush-scented girl.**<-
<margin>X</margin>

Festus Pompeius indicates that in the past, low and cheap prostitutes were called **schoenicolae** <note>from *schoenum*, a common rush</note>, after the very cheap ointment with which they smeared themselves. Plautus in the *Poenulus*: "Wretched, smeared with rush-oil, filthy rush-girls."

->**Muddier than mud.**<-
<margin>XI</margin>

We call those who are greedy and hungry for profit beyond measure "impure" and "filthy." Plautus exaggerates this hyperbolically in the *Poenulus*: "But in the house of that pimp Lycus, there is nothing muddier than the mud itself." Sometimes it describes a man who is wicked and contaminated rather than just "sordid" or cheap. As Cicero says in his oration *On His House* to the priests: "O filth, O portent, O crime!" and if I am not mistaken, he calls Piso "mud" somewhere. For he calls one "mud" in the same way they are frequently called...

### FOURTH CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>
<meta>The catchword from the previous page "ca" or "cat" completes the word "scelerosum" (wicked or criminal).</meta>

...calls him wicked, a blot, and a stain. Likewise, he frequently calls the author of a riot a "torch," a "storm," or a "tempest."

<margin>To test by the bell <note>original Greek: Διακωδωνίζειν</note></margin>
->XII<-

**To test by the bell**, Demosthenes said, means to explore and examine. They think the term is taken from those who go around the night-watch with a hand-bell <note>original: "tintinnabulo"</note> so that no one falls asleep, or to declare by this signal that they are keeping watch. Alternatively, it may come from those who test quails with a bell to see if they are fit for fighting, as Aristarchus used the term. There are also those who prefer it to be derived from the way horses are tested in the same manner to see if they can endure the noise of trumpets and arms. In a similar way, those about to be initiated into the mysteries were once tested with reproaches; a vestige of this custom is still preserved in the schools of the Theologians <note>Erasmus likely refers to the "deposition" or rigorous, often mocking, oral examinations of university students</note>.

->**Iron and flame.**<-
->XIII<-

When we wish to signify a deadly war, we say the matter is carried out with **iron and flame**, or with **iron and fire**. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> says in his oration *For Lucius Flaccus*: "O immortal gods! What is more wretched than this? We, who wring the iron and flame <note>original: "ferrum & flammam"</note> from the hands of Publius Lentulus, now trust in the judgment of an ignorant multitude." Soon after in the same work: "O, that night which brought almost eternal darkness to this city, when the Gauls were called to war, Catiline to the city, and the conspirators to iron and flame." Again, in *For Sulla*: "Whose iron I have recently blunted, and whose flame I have extinguished." In the oration *For His House*, he adds "torches" <note>original: "faxa"</note>: "Then, when he had brought devastation to my home with rocks and fire and iron." Likewise, in *For Plancius*: "Throughout that whole year, you saw their iron in the forum, their flame in the houses, and their violence turned against the whole city."

->**Mountains of grain.**<-
->XIIII<-

We have spoken elsewhere of **mountains of gold**. But just as the word "fly" <note>original: "Musca"</note> is transferred to any small thing when we deny that anything of the sort exists—"I have not even a fly in my house"—so "mountains" is transferred to an overflowing abundance of any thing. Plautus says in *Pseudolus*: "For all of whom there are the greatest mountains and heaps of grain at home." This use of the word "mountains" survives in common speech, except that in popular usage it is added to increase the sense of abundance. Likewise, the word *oppido* <note>a Latin adverb meaning "very much" or "completely"</note> came into use to mean "greatly," because farmers understood such a great abundance of things to be enough even for a whole town <note>Erasmus is playing on the etymological link between "oppidum" (town) and "oppido"</note>. Plautus, in *The Haunted House*, used **mountain of error** to mean a very grave mistake: "Salvation itself could not save us now, even if she wished; I just caught sight of another massive mountain of error at the harbor: the master has returned from abroad, and Tranio is ruined!" If you read "so soon another," the trochaic verse will be consistent. In *The Braggart Soldier*, he spoke of **mountains of silver**: "Then he has mountains of silver, not just lumps."

->**Since humanity began.**<-
->XV<-

Whenever we want all of humanity to be understood, we say **Since humanity began** <note>original: "Post homines natos", literally "After men were born"</note>. Marcus Tullius says in his oration *For His House* to the Pontiffs: "Who gave to that man—the most shameful, wicked, and contaminated human being since humanity began—that rich and fertile Syria? Who gave war to the most peaceful nations? Who gave the money set aside for buying land, snatched by force from Caesar’s acts? Who gave him infinite power?" Again, in the same work: "But that which he turned into a crime was not only not a sin, but was the most beautiful thing since humanity began." Likewise, in *For Cornelius Balbus*: "Indeed, since the birth of the human race, few have been found who, with no rewards offered, would throw their lives before the weapons of the enemy for the sake of their country," etc. Also in *For Milo*: "The one bravest man since humanity began." Also against Antony: "Two of the most foul and filthy heads since humanity began: Dolabella and Antony." Also in *On the Best Kind of Orators*: "By far the best since humanity began." Also in *Brutus*: "By far the most wicked man since humanity began, Gaius Servilius Glaucia."

->**In the memory of man.**<-
->XVI<-

Very similar to this is **In the memory of man** <note>original: "Post hominum memoriam"</note>. Marcus Tullius in the oration to the Pontiffs, *For His House*: "This is a grave and vehement charge, and the most serious since the memory of man and the establishment of trials for the recovery of funds." Likewise, in the oration *On the Response of the Soothsayers*: "But with you reporting it, the bravest and best consuls in the memory of man." Also in *For Plancius*: "The senate was with me, and indeed in changed raiment, which was undertaken by public counsel for the sake of one man alone for the first time in the memory of man." In the same place: "Nothing in the memory of man is more glorious." Also in the same: "The most foul and shameful consuls in the memory of man." Also to Plancus in the *Letters to Friends*, book 10: "I have seen nothing more glorious in the memory of man, nothing more pleasing, nor anything occurring more opportunely in time itself, than your letters, Plancus." Again, to Brutus...

<meta>This page continues the list of expressions used by Marcus Tullius Cicero to denote the greatest or most significant events "within human memory" (post hominum memoriam), concluding a series of examples before moving on to new Greek and Roman adages.</meta>

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...then in book 11: "Therefore, you indeed have no need of an advisor; yet, before that deed of yours, which was the greatest within human memory <note>original: "post hominum memoriam"</note>, you did desire an advisor." Again, in the speech *For Sestius*: "For who can take from all memory anything more illustrious than that, for the sake of me, a single citizen, all good men by private consensus and the entire Senate by public counsel changed their garments?" <note>In ancient Rome, changing into mourning clothes was a sign of public sorrow or protest.</note> Likewise, *Against Catiline*: "In this one war, the greatest and most cruel within human memory." In the same work: "An internal and domestic war, the most cruel and greatest within human memory." Likewise, in *For Rabirius on a Charge of Treason*: "No matter greater within human memory." Likewise, in *For the Manilian Law*: "Things which have been established as new in all men within human memory." Again, *Against Vatinius as a Witness*: "Unheard of in all memory."

### XVII To dance one's way out.

Those who flee, or turn themselves away from the matter at hand to something else, are said by the Greeks "to dance their way out" <note>original Greek: ἐξορχεῖσθαι, *exorcheisthai*</note>. The metaphor is taken from dances, especially sacred ones, where withdrawing oneself was considered ill-omened. This was indicated in the proverb: "All is well, the old man is dancing." A well-known story is told by Herodotus concerning Hippoclides, who, through an unseemly dance, lost his hope of marriage and heard the remark: "You have danced away your marriage" <note>original Greek: ἀπερχήσαόγε τὸν γάμον</note>.

### XVIII Campanian tapestries.

Origen titled a certain work of his, which treated various subjects, *Stromata* <note>meaning "Patchworks" or "Miscellanies"</note>, taking the metaphor from curtains and embroidered blankets, in which the wealthy once took great delight. This can be applied to a person of shifting character <note>original: "versipellem," meaning a turncoat or one who changes skins</note>. Indeed, tapestries, whether unfolded or folded—and folded again and again in different ways—present various forms of things. The pimp in Plautus's *Pseudolus* threatens his servants in this way: "I will make your sides so variegated with lashes that not even Campanian tapestries <note>original: "peristromata... Campanica"</note> will be as vividly painted." When Campania was flourishing in wealth, it indulged in luxury and delicacies beyond measure. To Campanian tapestries, Plautus adds Alexandrian rugs. The term *Attagena* <note>likely referring to "Attalic" or gold-embroidered cloths</note> has been discussed elsewhere.

### XIX Fortune is the mistress of the field.

In the election of magistrates, it was not always the one who was more worthy who won, but the one whom fortune favored. For the entire matter depended on the votes of the people. Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> in his speech *Against Piso*: "But I leave aside how each of us was made [consul]; let Fortune indeed be the mistress of the field <note>original: "Fors domina campi"; refers to the Campus Martius where elections were held</note>; it is more magnificent to speak of how we conducted the consulship."

### XX A bed-prop.

Nonius Marcellus indicates that a certain proverb was frequent in the works of Varro: "They climb the bed-prop" <note>original: "Fulmentum lectum scandunt"</note>. He neither explains what a "fulmentum" <note>a prop or support</note> is, nor the meaning of the proverb. He only indicates that *fulmentum* is used in the neuter gender, while *fulmentas* is used in the feminine.

### XXI The more the Parthians drink.

It was said of the Parthians in an old proverb that the more they drink, the more they thirst. This is a quality of drunkenness: once the palate has become dulled, they desire to gulp down more and more. This will be aptly said of the greedy, or of scholars, for the desire for learning increases with education.

### XXII Scraptae.

"Scraptae" <note>worthless women or hags</note> was a term used in popular insult for trifling, worthless women; it comes from the word *screo*, which means to spit out the foulness of the mouth with a sound. From this, they understood *screa* to mean the most worthless things. Perhaps it will suit old women who are constantly hacking and coughing. So says Festus. Nonius, however, thinks it is an insult directed at deformed prostitutes, citing this verse of Plautus from the *Vidularia*: "Scraptae, scrupedae, strictivellae, sordidae" <note>A string of insults: Scrap-heaps, limpers, tight-pinchers, and filthy ones</note>.

### XXIII From Phelleus.

"To come from Phelleus" <note>original Greek: Ἐκ φελλέως ἐλθεῖν</note> was a saying used for those who had emerged from humble fortune and a harsh life into a position of dignity. For the Greeks call a place suitable for pasturing goats *phelleus*—harsh, stony, and sterile. For goats delight in pastures of this kind. Aristophanes in *The Clouds*: "When you [lead] the goats from Phelleus, just as your father did, wrapped in a leather tunic." There is a place of this name in the mountainous and rocky part of Attica, which Stephanus also mentions, except that he calls the mountain *Phellas*, perhaps due to a faulty transcription. We have touched on these matters somewhat in the proverbs "Lighter than cork" and "Cork-like."

### XXIV Truth in the marketplace.

"To refrain from lying in the marketplace" <note>original Greek: Ἐν ἀγορᾷ ἀψευδεῖν</note>. There was a law among the Athenians...

--- Page 1159 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on ancient regulations regarding honesty in public spaces, specifically the marketplace, before transitioning into several metaphorical expressions found in Roman comedy and classical oratory.</meta>

<header>THE FOURTH THOUSAND, TENTH CENTURY</header>

...so that all vanity and deceit might be absent from the marketplace where goods are sold. Theophrastus, in his books *On Laws*, shows that the Market-Overseers <note>original: "Agoranomis"; these were officials in ancient Greek cities who regulated trade and ensured order in the markets.</note> must primarily take care of two things: first, that everything in the market is conducted in an orderly fashion without tumult; and second, that both buyers and sellers abstain from lies. This is the origin of the story in Diogenes Laertius where Anacharsis <note>A Scythian philosopher famous for his blunt wisdom.</note> said he marveled that the Athenians prohibited lying in the market by law, yet nowhere did they lie more frequently or more shamelessly.

### XXV To knock out an eye.
<margin>25</margin>
By this figure of speech, the common people take away all hope from a petitioner, saying: "If you obtain this, knock out my eye," or "strike out my tooth." The old man in Plautus's *Pseudolus* says: "By Hercules, knock out my eye if I give it to you." He felt that anything else was more likely to happen than him giving money to a servant for his son's mistress. Likewise, Phormio in Terence: "Or even knock out an eye; there is a place where I may take my revenge."

### XXVI Either by land or by sea.
<margin>26</margin>
Plautus in the *Pseudolus* used "either by land or by sea" <note>original: "aut terra aut mari"</note> to mean "by any means possible." It is taken from historians who report deeds performed "by land and by sea," or nations conquered "by land and by sea." Cicero in his speech *For Cluentius*: "Whose great deeds stood out by land and by sea." Likewise, in *For the Manilian Law*: "How many things he achieved successfully at home and at war, by land and by sea." Again in the same work: "So that at last we seemed truly to rule over all tribes and nations by land and by sea." Also in *Against Verres*, book 2: "How many snares were set for me by Verres, by land and by sea." To Atticus in the seventh book: "By what way, either by land or by sea, shall I pursue him, since I do not know where he is?" Demosthenes, at the conclusion of his oration *For Ctesiphon*: "But if they are indeed so incurable, deliver those men, who are worthy of destruction and ruin, to their end by land and by sea" <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἄρα ἔχοιεν ὅπως ἀνιάτως τότες μὲν αὐτὸς καθ’ ἑαυτὸς ἐξώλεις καὶ προώλεις ἐν γῇ καὶ ἐν θαλάσσῃ ποιήσατε</note>. The words of Plautus are these: "Within these three days, I will roll out that money for you from somewhere, either by land or by sea." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fifth book of *On Ends*, adds a third element: "One part concerns logic, the second living, and the third, nature, was investigated by them in such a way that no part of heaven, sea, or land—to speak poetically—was overlooked." He adds "poetically" because the poets refer to only three elements, as Ovid does:
> Before the sea and the lands, and the sky which covers all.
Terence: "O heaven, O earth, O seas of Neptune!" Plautus in the *Amphitryon*: "So it seems to me that everything—sea, land, and sky—is following me."

### XXVII To be leaf-voted out.
<margin>27</margin>
Those who were deprived of the right to cast a vote and were removed from the roll of judges were once said "to be leaf-voted out" <note>original Greek: ἐκφυλλοφορεῖσθαι, *ekphyllophoreisthai*</note>, just as soldiers who were deprived of the right to fight were said to be "discharged" <note>original: "Exauctorari"</note>. In ancient times, votes were not cast with pebbles <note>original: "calculis"</note> but with leaves; thus the term means, as it were, to be excluded from the casting of leaves.

### XXVIII To fill a gap.
<margin>28</margin>
To "fill a gap" <note>original: "Lacunam explere"</note> is used to mean repairing a loss, not without the character of a proverb. Cicero used it in the fourth action *Against Verres*: "The Censors did the same thing that those in our Republic usually do who have obtained magistracies through bribery: they took care to conduct their power in such a way that they might fill that gap in their family estate." He calls the loss of means a "gap" <note>original: "lacunam"</note>. Likewise in the letters to Atticus: "See that there be no gap in the gold," that is, let nothing be missing. Aulus Gellius, in *Attic Nights*, book 1, chapter 3, spoke of a "gap in reputation" for a stain: "And that smallest blemish, and as it were a gap in an imminent reputation, is resolved by the logic of benefits prepared for a friend." Moreover, in books, a "blemish" <note>original: "mendum"</note> is what is corrupted, while a "gap" <note>original: "lacuna"</note> is where something is missing; the former is washed away, the latter is filled.

### XXIX No part of the body.
<margin>29</margin>
Aeschines, in *On the Misconducted Embassy*: "But he, who has no part of his body idle—not even that from which he produces his voice—just as if he were Aristides, who prescribed the taxes for the Greeks and earned the surname 'the Just,' feels indignation and spits upon the acceptance of bribes" <note>original Greek: ὁ δ’ οὐδὲν ἄπρακτον ἔχων μέρος τοῦ σώματος...</note>. Let the prudent reader discern whether "unsold" <note>original: ἄπρατον, *apraton*</note> should be read instead of "idle" <note>original: ἄπρακτον, *aprakton*</note>, so that you may understand that all his members were for sale, even his mouth and voice. However, it can be said that he is "idle" <note>original: ἄπρακτον</note> who exacts nothing. Thus you would understand him to be greedy not only with his hands, but with his whole body.

### XXX Purely pure.
<margin>30</margin>
Plautus in the *Pseudolus* said "purely pure" <note>original: "purum putum"</note> for "entirely" and "truly": "He is his purely pure self, I know him, the master Polymacheroplacides." It is as if you were to say, "he is his very self." The flavor of the speech remains from antiquity...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s discussion of the etymology of "pure" and "clear," specifically how these terms migrated from technical trades like goldsmithing and viticulture into common and legal Latin usage.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM
<page-num>1034</page-num>

...pure: for they <note>The ancient Romans.</note> called "putum" that which was cleansed, from which they also say vines are "pruned" <note>original: "putare"</note>, and the discarded husks of nuts and similar things are called "putamina" <note>shells or parings</note>. The proverb seems to have originated in the workshops of goldsmiths, who used the phrase "Pure and clear" <note>original: "Purum putum"</note> in that form, just as the jurists say "stuffed and covered" <note>original: "farta tecta"; a legal term meaning a building is in a state of good repair.</note>.

<margin>XXXI</margin>
->Under my own auspices.<-

"Under my own auspices" <note>original: "Meis auspicijs"</note> means according to my own judgment or by my own protection. Virgil used it in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*:
"But if the fates permitted me to lead my life
Under my own auspices, and to settle my cares by my own will."
The phrase is borrowed from the Roman commanders, whose custom it was never to engage in battle without first consulting the <term>auspices</term> <note>Divine signs, usually the flight or feeding of birds, interpreted by an official called an augur.</note>. A matter was said to be conducted under the "auspices" of the person who held the highest authority over the operation. Very similar to this is the phrase we have mentioned elsewhere, "By my own Mars" <note>original: "Meo Marte"; meaning by one's own personal valor or effort.</note>. Cicero in his fifth book *Against Verres*: "Especially since you abound in all these things by your own Mars." Something happens "by our own Mars" when it is done without any help sought from elsewhere.

<margin>XXXII</margin>
->To cling to footsteps.<-

One who imitates the examples of their ancestors or elders is said to "cling to their footsteps" <note>original: "Vestigijs inhærere"</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero in his speech *For Sestius*: "Whom it behoved to stand in the footsteps of his ancestors." This is a metaphor taken from travelers who observe the tracks of those going before them so they do not wander off. Similarly, those who fall away from the examples of their ancestors or teachers are said to "recede from their footsteps." And those who produce nothing new themselves but stick only to the inventions of others are said to "walk in another’s footsteps."

<margin>XXXIII</margin>
->Sweet and bitter.<-

Plautus, in his play *Pseudolus*, used "sweet and bitter" <note>original: "dulce & amarū"</note> as a kind of proverb for "joys and sorrows." A young man in love says of a letter from his mistress: "Now you mix sweet and bitter for me at the same time." In the same play: "I have spoken out all things to you, the sweet and the bitter. You know my love, you know my labor, you know my poverty." Also in the *Truculentus*: "Now, afterwards, I know what is sweet and what is bitter regarding money."

<margin>XXXIIII</margin>
->Winter dust, spring mud.<-

Festus Pompeius quotes this from an ancient poem but does not provide the author’s name, from which we can understand it was commonly sung. In it, a father is introduced giving instructions on agriculture to his son in these words: "With winter dust and spring mud, you shall reap great grain, Camillus." By these words, I believe it is meant that if grain is sown in a clear, dry winter and followed by a wet spring, it will grow more abundantly.

<margin>XXXV</margin>
->To behave like an Aixonian.<-
<note>original Greek: "Αἰξωνεύεσθαι" (Aixoneuesthai); the OCR "Αἰσχυνθεσθαι" appears to be a transcription error for this term.</note>

Just as we have recorded many proverbs taken from the character of certain peoples, so in the past those prone to the disease of slandering were said to "behave like Aixonians." This population was criticized by this name in the wit of Old Comedy, as Stephanus indicates when he teaches that "Aixone" is a town in Attica. There is also "Aixone," with the accent on the last syllable, a people of the Cecropid tribe. From either word is derived "Aixonian." They cite Menander as a witness in his play *The Basket-Bearer*. Plato, in his dialogue on Fortitude <note>The *Laches*.</note>: "I will say nothing in response, though I have things I could say, lest you say I am truly an Aixonian." Martial translates this as a slanderer and a false accuser.

<margin>XXXVI</margin>
->One ought to drink oak-gall.<-

Those who indulge their bellies and gullets more than is proper were told, in a proverbial joke, that they "ought to drink oak-gall" <note>original: "gallam bibere"</note>. This is a fruit that grows on trees, especially the oak, toward autumn, looking like a round nut. Pliny, Dioscorides, Galen, and Theophrastus have written much about its nature. It has the power of binding and drying, and for that reason, it is useful for many things. Hence that line of Lucilius, when he bids profligates and gluttons drink oak-gall to "bring wrinkles to the belly," meaning that their stomachs should be shrunk or tightened. Festus Pompeius reports this. It is similar to that line in Horace where he writes that the bellies of gluttons should be "branded with a white-hot iron plate."

<margin>XXXVII</margin>
->A serious cause.<-

The poet Naevius, as cited by Festus, calls a very grave matter a "serious cause" <note>original: "Sonticam causam"</note> in a trochaic verse:
"There must be a serious cause why you would ruin the woman."
This is borrowed from the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law.</note>, which call a disease "sonticum" <note>serious/dangerous</note> if it is not a common ailment but one so troublesome that the accused is not forced to appear before the judges.

<margin>XXXVIII</margin>
->Stain, Blemish.<-

It is frequent in Marcus Tullius Cicero to call an infamous and wicked man a "stain" <note>original: "macula"</note>, a "blemish" <note>original: "labes"</note>, "filth," or "mud." In place of this, Plautus, as cited by Festus, used "dirt."

--- Page 1161 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of idioms found in the works of the Roman playwright Plautus, beginning with the conclusion of a discussion on the word "suasum" (a stain) and moving through several metaphorical expressions for guilt, opportunity, and poverty.</meta>

"Because at your persuasion you stained your little cloak in a shameful way." <note>original: "Quia tibi suaso infecisti propudiosa pallulam."</note> 
Festus <note>A Roman grammarian.</note> thinks that *suasum* refers to a stain on a white garment caused by a smoky drip. This line, a <term>Trochaic</term> <note>A rhythmic meter in poetry consisting of a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one.</note> verse from Plautus, will apply well to those who contaminate a respectable reputation—whether inherited from ancestors or earned through good deeds—with some shameful act.

### To seize the hair.
<margin>XXXIX</margin>
Plautus, in his play *The Haunted House* <note>original: "Mustellaria"</note>, used the phrase "to seize the hair" <note>original: "capere crines"</note> to mean snatching an opportunity when it is offered and holding onto it once caught. (This is taken either from that god whom the Greeks call *Kairos* <note>The personification of Opportunity.</note>, for they depict him with hair on his forehead but bald on the back of his head; or it comes from the human habit of restraining someone they do not want to leave by grabbing their hair.) "If it is certain to you that he will be your only, eternal, and personal lover for life, then I think you should devote yourself to him alone, and 'seize the hair,' as the saying goes, of the man, and thereafter find your money through him alone."

### Nothing is more wretched than a guilty mind.
<margin>XL</margin>
As the proverb goes, "Even a gardener has often spoken a very timely word." In Plautus’s *The Haunted House*, the wicked servant Tranio utters a sentiment worthy of any theologian: "Nothing is more wretched than a man’s guilty mind." <note>original: "Nihil est miserius quàm animus hominis conscius."</note> This agrees with the Hebrew saying, "A secure mind is like a perpetual feast." <note>original: "Secura mens quasi iuge conuiuium"; see Proverbs 15:15.</note> Likewise with that other saying, "Conscience is a thousand witnesses." Horace also judges it a mark of happiness "to be conscious of no guilt, and to turn pale at no crime."

### The furniture of Celeus.
<margin>XLI</margin>
Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> indicates in the first book of the *Georgics* that the "furniture of Celeus" was cheap and rustic: 
"Furthermore, there is the wickerwork and the cheap furniture of Celeus."
Likewise, Ovid in the fourth book of the *Fasti*:
> Every place has its own fortune: what is now called
> The Eleusis of Ceres, was once the fields of old Celeus.
> He carries home acorns and blackberries shaken from the brambles,
> And dry wood for the hearth soon to be lit.
> His little daughter was driving two goats down from the mountain,
> And his young son lay sick in the cradle.

Celeus was the king at Eleusis and the father of Triptolemus; because he had welcomed the goddess Ceres <note>The goddess of agriculture.</note> with hospitality, she taught him the entire system of farming. The words of Plautus are these: "like the furniture of Celio, one stake is next to another stake." It is strange, however, that the first syllable in "Celione" is lengthened by Plautus, since it is shortened by others. There is nothing unusual in saying "Celionem" for "Celio," just as we say both "scorpio" and "scorpionem" <note>Both mean scorpion.</note>.

### Flask-shaped.
<margin>XLII</margin>
In the *Menaechmi*, Plautus seems to use "flask-shaped" <note>original: "ampullaceam"</note> to describe a woman who is magnificently dressed. The verse is recorded thus: "When he keeps you well-gilded and well-clothed, a flask [of] hope." <note>original: "ampula spem"</note> They rightly claim it is better for a woman to adopt a healthy mind. It is certain that the words "ampula spem" are corrupted. Some suggest "ampullosam" <note>puffed up or bombastic</note>, but the meter of the Trochaic verse does not allow this word. "Ampullaceam" fits both the meter and the sense. Pliny, in his fifteenth book, mentions "flask-shaped" <note>original: "ampullacea"</note> among the varieties of pears. However, I do not know if that passage is free of error. Pliny’s words are: "The myrrh-pear, the laurel-pear, and the nard-pear from their scent; the barley-pear from its season; and the flask-pear <note>original: "ampullacea"</note> and Coriolan-pear from the shape of their necks."

### I would not buy it for a ladle.
<margin>XLIII</margin>
Not without the appearance of a proverb, the soldier in Plautus’s *The Carthaginian* <note>original: "Poenulo"</note> says: "By the clouds, I would not buy seven nights of her for a <term>cyathus</term>!" <note>A *cyathus* was a small ladle or measuring cup, roughly 1.5 ounces; here used to mean a pittance.</note> He is speaking of a woman who is haughty but not correspondingly beautiful; the soldier, whose business involved drinking cups, used "cyathus" to mean the smallest price. A *cyathus* was the smallest vessel, while a *crater* was a larger bowl.

### I am a king.
<margin>XLIIII</margin>
Just as people once used to say "I am a God" or "I am in heaven" to signify remarkable happiness, so Plautus says in *The Carthaginian*: "I am a king, if I can lure that man to me today." These are the words of Lycus the pimp, who hopes he will be rich if he can entice a certain well-funded man to his house.

### More frequent than a sieve.
<margin>XLV</margin>
It was cleverly said by Plautus, and not without the form of a proverb, "more frequent than a sieve" <note>A pun on *cribro* (sieve) and *crebrius* (more frequent/thickly set).</note>, <gloss>for</gloss> that which was in many places and all over. "I realize the whole villa must be re-roofed for me. For now it is more 'frequent' than a sieve" <note>Meaning it is full of holes.</note>. The common people say of a person who is leaky or talkative: "He is as solid as a sieve."
