<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s collection of Latin and Greek adages, moving from general moral sentiments to specific idioms found in the works of Plautus, Cicero, and the Greek poet Theocritus.</meta>

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

->To lose both the effort and the net.<-
<margin>XLVI</margin>
Plautus in *The Rope*: "Now he makes a joke of both the effort and the net." <note>original: "Iam nunc & operā ludos facit & retiam."</note> This was spoken literally by an old man who had sent his slave, Grippus, out to fish when a very heavy storm had arisen during the night. It will be more elegant, however, if used as a <term>trope</term> <note>A figurative or metaphorical use of a word or expression.</note> against a "catcher" <note>A "captator," or legacy hunter, who tries to win an inheritance.</note> whose "hunting" did not succeed. Furthermore, Plautus used the archaic form *retiam* for *rete* (a net). This is related to what I have recorded elsewhere: "I have lost both the oil and the effort," and "The effort and the expense have perished."

->With virtue as leader, and fortune as companion.<-
<margin>XLVII</margin>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the tenth book of his *Letters to Friends* <note>original: "Epistulae ad Familiares"</note> to Plancus: "You have achieved all the highest things, with virtue as your leader and fortune as your companion." <note>original: "uirtute duce, comite fortuna."</note> This was spoken with such gravity and suitability that it has been adopted by some as a public motto. Virtue chooses what is best. Even if it does not succeed, in noble matters—as in great ones—to have even willed the attempt is beautiful. But if it does succeed, the primary praise is owed to virtue, as the leader of the distinguished deed, and the next to fortune, which served virtue.

->To add a farthing to the wealth of Croesus.<-
<margin>XLVIII</margin>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fourth book of *On Moral Ends* <note>original: "De finibus"</note>: "Thus, in those things where observation follows because of their smallness, it often happens that we admit it makes no difference to us whether they exist or not; just as in the sun, as you were saying, it makes no difference to bring a lamp, or to add a farthing to the wealth of Croesus." <note>original: "teruncium addere Croesi pecuniae."</note> The <term>teruncius</term> <note>A tiny Roman coin, originally weighing three ounces, worth a quarter of an "as." It denotes something of negligible value.</note> coin’s worthlessness gave rise to the proverb. Croesus, the King of the Lydians, is celebrated among those who were prodigiously wealthy.

->The Bearded Ones.<-
<margin>XLIX</margin>
It appears that among the Romans, it was common to use "the bearded ones" <note>original: "barbati"</note> as a proverbial joke to refer to men of ancient and simple character and rustic honesty. This is because it was only late in their history that they took up the habit of shaving or trimming the beard. Indeed, according to Pliny, P. Ticinius Mena first brought a barber from Sicily in the 454th year from the founding of the city <note>original: "anno ab urbe condita quadringentesimo quinquagesimo quarto."</note>; until then, the Romans were unshaven. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fourth book of *On Moral Ends*: "But that you could not bear this, which those ancient 'bearded ones' (as we are accustomed to say of our own) believed: that the life of one who lives honorably—if he were also healthy, had a good reputation, and was wealthy—would be more desirable, better, and more to be sought than the life of one who was equally a good man, but in many ways like Ennius's Alcmaeon, beset by disease, exile, and poverty."
Therefore, those ancients do not think that more desirable life is so much "sharper" as it is more excellent and more blessed. The Stoics, however, etc. That line of Juvenal's points to the same thing:
"It is easy to impose upon a bearded king." <note>meaning an old-fashioned or naive ruler.</note>

->To set a footstep.<-
<margin>L</margin>
"To set a footstep" <note>original: "vestigium ponere"</note> for "to touch upon" was used by Marcus Tullius Cicero in the fifth book of *On Moral Ends*: "Although in this city it is indeed infinite; for wherever we walk, we set a footstep upon some history." There is a very witty story told about someone—Stratonicus, if I am not mistaken—who entered a certain town on his tiptoes, looking around meanwhile. When people asked what he was doing, he replied that he was afraid lest he should tread on a herald, implying that there was an immoderate crowd of heralds there. Marcus Tullius in the fifth book of the same work: "For where would Wisdom have to set her foot, if all duties were taken away?" <note>Referring to "officia," the moral duties or social obligations that give wisdom a place to act.</note> I know I have mentioned the proverb "He has nowhere to set his foot" elsewhere. But this passage did not occur to me then, and it is unworthy of being passed over, because it shows an elegant use of this metaphor in matters of the mind. For the point is that there is no place for wisdom if the choice of moral duties is removed.

->One must believe the ancients.<-
<margin>LI</margin>
Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his short book *On the Universe* <note>original: "De universitate"</note>: "One must surely believe," he says, "the men of old and the 'ancients,' as they say, who said they were the offspring of the gods." It is uncertain whether Cicero felt that this sentiment was commonly repeated, or if he is noting the word "ancients" (*prisci*), by which we declare men of the most extreme antiquity, whose origin—since it was unknown to posterity—was generally attributed to the gods.

->All are within.<-
<margin>LII</margin>
Theocritus in *The Syracusan Women*:
"It is well, they are all inside, as he who locked out the bride once said." <note>original Greek: "Κάλις, ᾦνδι πᾶσαι, ὁ τὰν νυὸν εἶπ’ ἀποκλάξας."</note>
The <term>Scholiast</term> <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts.</note> advises that this is a proverb born from such an event, as I conjecture. A certain groom shut his bride out of the house; and when she knocked on the door desiring to be let in, the groom repli<insert>ed</insert> <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the story on the next page.</note>

# CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY TEN
<margin>Sss 3</margin>
<meta>catchword: Mæscu-</meta>

...[she] says, "all are inside." <note>original: "ἔνδοι πᾶσαι," (endoi pasai)</note> That is, everyone is indoors. It is possible that when a bride was led to the bridegroom’s house according to custom, he spoke these words after the doors were shut. It can be adapted to a more serious use, such as when someone who is unworthy of friendship seeks to be admitted into a circle of friends, and the answer given is, "all are inside." Or, what is even more likely, it is used when we wish to indicate that everything is in a safe place. Indeed, the word for "shutting out" <note>original: "ἀποκλείω" (apokleio)</note> sounds not only like excluding, but also including something that we want set apart in safety; hence "a barred place" <note>original: "ἀπόκλεισμα" (apokleisma)</note> refers to custody or a guard. Therefore, it may be that the bridegroom, having shut the bride in the chamber, removed the others by saying, "all are inside." One bride is enough for the groom; he excluded the rest as unnecessary. The Sicilians use the word *klax* <note>original: "κλάξ"</note> for a key, from which come the verbs for "to lock" or "to shut out."

->Do not encounter a hungry man.<-
->LIII<-

In the same *Idyll* <note>Referring to the 15th Idyll of Theocritus, a Greek pastoral poet.</note>, the following also has the appearance of a proverb at the end. Gorgo, urging a return home because her husband was irritable, adds:
"May you never come upon a hungry man." <note>original: "πεινῶντί γε μηδ’ ἔποτ’ ἔλθῃς" (peinonti ge med’ epot’ elthes)</note>
For hunger sharpens anger. Hence, in the works of Plautus, someone asks a person speaking quite angrily how long it had been since he last ate. In the same author, it is said:
"Hunger and delay stir up bile in the nostrils." <note>A Roman way of saying someone is "fuming" or losing their temper.</note>

->Work upon work.<-
->LIIII<-

I will add another from the same source: "work upon work," <note>original: "ἔργον ἐπ’ ἔργῳ" (ergon ep’ ergo)</note> by which we signify that there is no end to the labor. These are the words of a woman complaining about her husband because he had bought dirty, raw wool, which would require a vast amount of work from her. Likewise, Maro <note>The poet Virgil.</note> says of the cultivation of the vine:
"For which there is never enough exhausted effort."

->Thirteen cubits tall.<-
->LV<-

Men of remarkably tall stature are mocked by a popular joke even in these times as being lazy and useless. This, like many other things, seems to have flowed down from antiquity. Thus, in the same poem, Praxinoa speaks of her husband as "a man thirteen cubits tall." <note>original: "ἀνὴρ τρισκαιδεκάπηχυς" (aner triskaidekapēchys). A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm; thirteen cubits would be nearly twenty feet tall.</note> She means hyperbolically that he is enormously tall, yet he was so foolish that he brought back salt from the market instead of nitre <note>A mineral used for cleaning, similar to lye or soap.</note>. We have spoken elsewhere regarding the boot of Maximinus. The ancients, for the sake of a joke, used to call very tall men "Long-poles" <note>original: "Longuriones"</note>. Varro, in his *Tripalus*, as cited by Nonius, says: "I am telling nothing; let the man in front of me take care of these things—I know not what long-pole he is."

->To show the sole of the foot.<-
->LVI<-

"To show the sole of the foot." <note>original: "Τὸ πέλμα τοῦ ποδὸς δεῖξαι" (To pelma tou podos deixai)</note> Those who flee in war are said to show the hollow or the sole of the foot; among historians, this is very frequently called "turning one's back." The proverb is recorded by Hesychius. Even today, it is commonly said of those who flee that they "show their heels."

->Done and settled.<-
->LVII<-

Among legal experts, these words are solemn: "Done and settled" <note>original: "Factum transactum"</note>, whenever they feel nothing has been overlooked that pertains to the handling of a business matter. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his third invective against Catiline: "And that which was first to be done, has been done and settled." It is found elsewhere in Terence, and in several other authors of higher repute.

->Meanders.<-
->LVIII<-

When a matter is conducted not simply, but through crafty and indirect plans, we call them "Meanders," a metaphor taken from the river Meander, which flows in a sinuous and winding way. From this, it seems to have taken its name, as if it wanders about seeking the company of men. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech against Piso: "What Meanders did you seek, while you pursued all those solitudes—what diversions and windings?" Prudentius also uses it in a hymn, which I have cited elsewhere under the proverb "Labyrinth." It is a river of Lydia that drenches the land with winding recursions. Pliny writes of it in Book 5, chapter 29: "The Meander, rising from a lake on Mount Aulocrene, flowing past many towns and filled by many rivers, is so sinuous with frequent bends that it is often believed to turn back on itself. It first wanders through the region of Apamea, then Eumenetica, and then the Bargyliotic plains; finally, it reaches Caria, peacefully watering all those fields with very fertile silt; at the tenth stadium from Miletus, it glides gently into the sea." There is also a type of pattern in painting called a "Meander," intertwined with winding intricacies in the manner of labyrinths, which is usually added to the borders of cloaks <note>original: "chlamydum," a type of Greek cloak.</note>. Hence Maro says in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*:
"To the victor, a gold-embroidered cloak, around which
the Meliboean purple ran in a double Meander."

->THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM<-

<margin>LIX</margin>
### Masculine.

Among the ancients, the word "masculine" <note>original: "Masculus"</note> does not always signify biological sex, but sometimes whatever is vigorous, solid, and robust is called "masculine." Nonius Marcellus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note> cites an example from Varro’s satire titled *An Ass at the Lyre* <note>original: "ὄνος λύρας" (onos lyras)</note>: "I am defeated, not being masculine for the task." Grammarians believe that Horace used the term "male yolk" <note>original: "marem vitellum"</note> to mean something solid and firm. In his *Satires*, he speaks of oblong eggs in this way: "For they contain a male yolk within a tough shell." Virgil also calls "male frankincense" <note>original: "mascula tura"</note> that which is white and of better quality. It will be more elegant if applied to incorporeal things: for instance, when we call a lofty and brave soul "masculine."

---

<margin>LX</margin>
### He laughed within his lips.

We have spoken elsewhere of the "Sardonic laugh" <note>A proverbial expression for a bitter or cynical laugh.</note>. Theocritus describes a similar thing in his poem *Thalysia*: "And he spoke to me calmly, grinning with a smiling eye, but the laughter stayed within his lips." <note>original: "καὶ μ᾿ ἀτρέμας εἶπε σεσαρὼς / ὄμματι μειδιόωντι, γέλως δὲ οἱ εἴχετο χείλευς" (kai m' atremas eipe sesaros ommati meidiōnti, gelōs de oi eicheto cheileus)</note> That is, addressing me with his mouth slightly parted and a smiling eye, but the laughter remained inside the lip. Homer called the Sardonic laugh bitter and slow. This passage, however, describes a modest and friendly laugh, which becomes unseemly if it breaks out into a loud guffaw.

---

<margin>LX</margin>
### With a fat measure.

"With a fat measure" <note>original: "πίονι μέτρῳ" (pioni metrō)</note>; he said this in the same poem to mean "abundantly and generously."
"For truly, with a fat measure, the divinity filled the threshing floors of the fields with a rich abundance." <note>original: "Μάλα γάρ σφισι πίονι μέτρῳ / Δαίμων ὑπερίθου ἀνεπλήρωσεν ἀλωάν" (Mala gar sphisi pioni metrō Daimōn hyperithou aneplērōsen aloan)</note>
This is very similar to what we have said before: "With a full hand," and "With both hands."

---

<margin>LXI</margin>
### By the fate of the Metelli.

Asconius Pedianus <note>A Roman scholar known for his commentaries on Cicero.</note>, in his speech for Milo, records a six-foot verse <note>term: "Senarium" — a line of poetry consisting of six iambic feet.</note> tossed about by the poet Naevius, mocking the family of the Metelli because they were being designated as Consuls by the whim of fortune—which is more truly called luck—rather than by their own merits:
"By fate the Metelli become Consuls at Rome." <note>original: "Fato Metelli Romae fiunt Consules."</note>
To this, the then-angry Consul Metellus replied with a verse that had an extra syllable at the end <note>term: "Senario hypercatalectio"</note>, which he said was also called "Saturnian" <note>An archaic Roman poetic meter.</note>:
"The Metelli will give trouble to Naevius the poet." <note>original: "Dabunt malum Metelli Naevio poetae."</note>
Marcus Tullius Cicero alluded to this rightly when he said, "You, not by fate, as the others of our family..."—a remark made wittily and insultingly against the Metelli. It can be twisted against those who are promoted to wealth and dignity beyond their own merit.

---

<margin>LXII</margin>
### He has nothing to sleep on.

Theocritus in the *Wayfarers* <note>original: "Hodoeporis" (referring to Idyll 5).</note>:
"For even Eumares the Laconian had no fleece." <note>original: "οὐδὲ γὰρ Εὐμάρᾳ τῷ Λακῶνι ἦν τι ψύτταλον" (oude gar eumara tō lakōni ēn ti psyttalon)</note> That is, indeed Master Eumares did not even have a fleece to sleep on.
With this figure of speech, the Laconian shepherd marks the extreme poverty of a certain goatherd, who did not even have a goat-skin upon which to take his sleep. For the ancients were accustomed to recline and sleep on the hides of animals. In Homer, the suitors hold their banquets on ox-hides. Today we say, "he has no bed," or "he has no straw to sleep on."

---

<margin>LXIII</margin>
### A donkey to a donkey, and a pig to its own kind, is beautiful.

"A donkey is most beautiful to a donkey" <note>original: "ὄνος ὄνῳ κάλλιστος" (onos onō kallistos)</note>; that is, like is pleased by like. Alcimus, in Diogenes Laertius, among many things he collected from the writings of the philosopher Plato and the comic writer Epicharmus—by which he tries to persuade us that the philosopher stole many things from the comedians—also records these six-foot verses:
"It is no wonder if I speak thus, and they please themselves and seem well-born; for a dog seems most beautiful to a dog, an ox to an ox, a donkey to a donkey, and a pig to a pig." <note>original: "Θαυμαστὸν οὐδὲν ἐστὶ με ταῦθ᾿ οὕτω λέγειν... ὄνος τ᾿ ὄνῳ κάλλιστον, ὑς δ᾿ ὑῒ συΐς" (Thaumaston ouden esti me tauth' houtō legein... onos t' onō kalliston, hys d' hyi syis)</note> That is, it is no wonder if I speak thus...

<meta>catchword: Ip</meta>

He also discusses the proverbial signs of extreme poverty and the psychological tendency for animals (and humans) to find their own kind most beautiful.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s Fourth Chiliad of adages, specifically the tenth century. The previous page discussed various Greek and Latin proverbs about behavior and physical traits. This page begins with the conclusion of a proverb regarding how creatures of the same kind find each other attractive, moving into specific historical and literary anecdotes.</meta>

<page-num>1039</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD FOUR, CENTURY 10</header>
<sig>Sss 4</sig>

> And if we please each other in turn,
> And seem beautifully born; for even to a dog
> A dog seems most beautiful, and an ox to an ox.
> An ass is beautiful to a little ass, and a sow to its own.
<note>Erasmus is quoting a fragment often attributed to the Greek comic playwright Epicharmus.</note>

This proverb is suitable when a similarity of character and purpose creates goodwill among dishonorable people: just as a soldier is pleased by a soldier, a gambler by a gambler, a drinker by a drinker, or a sophist by a sophist. It is a wonder that Epicharmus overlooked the monkey, since no animal takes more pride in itself.

->Plato's Lice. LXV<-

"Plato's lice" <note>original: "οἱ πλάτωνος φθεῖρες" (hoi Platōnos phtheires)</note> passed into a proverb. As Diogenes Laertius <note>A biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> reports in his life of this philosopher, Myronianus testifies in his work titled *On Similarities* that Plato died of this disease <note>Phthiriasis, or "lice disease," a condition where lice were thought to multiply uncontrollably within the flesh.</note>, because they were commonly called "Plato's lice." The Greeks call this condition *phthiriasis*. It is a foul and agonizing disease, of which Lucius Sulla also died, although there are various opinions among writers concerning the nature of his death. Myronianus does not indicate any specific use for the proverb. However, one may suspect it was said against the "sordid" <note>Those who are unwashed or unkempt.</note>, because philosophers indulge very little in external neatness while they are entirely occupied with the cultivation of the mind.

->Let the prophet take the omen with him. LXVI<-

This will be suitable against those who threaten us with dire things or foretell bitter outcomes. It is found in Theocritus’s *Bucoliastae*:

> But Telemus the prophet, who chants all these dire things to me,
> Let him carry those dire things home, so he may save them for his children.
<note>original: "Αὐτὰρ ὁ μάντις ὁ τηλεμος ἐχθρὰ ἀγορεύων / ἐχθρὰ φέροι ποτ’ οἶκον, ὅπως τεκέεσσι φυλάξῃ."</note>

The Cyclops <note>Polyphemus</note> had sworn by his single eye, which saw everything and would always see. But the prophet Telemus had predicted to him that he would be blinded by Ulysses. The Cyclops rejects this omen and casts it back upon the prophet and his children. Likewise, Virgil says: "May the gods first turn this omen against him." And again: "May the gods reserve this for his own head and his race." Similarly, Homer in the *Iliad*, Book 4: "With their own heads and their wives and children." <note>original: "Σὺν σφῇσιν κεφαλῇσι γυναιξί τε καὶ τεκέεσσι"</note> This is similar to the Platonic saying: "Upon your own head."

->To the ends of the earth. LXVII<-

"To the ends of the earth" <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἔσχατα γῆς" (ep’ eschata gēs)</note> is used when we want to describe a place that is extremely remote. Theocritus in his poem *The Syracusans*:

> That foolish man of mine went to the ends of the earth
> And took a cavern, not a dwelling.
<note>original: "Τἀυτ’ ὁ πάραρος ἐμὸς ἐπ’ ἔσχατα γῆς ἔλαβ’ ἐνθὼν ἰλεὸν οὐκ οἴκησιν."</note>

The wife accuses her husband of preparing a home for her in a place too remote, which is more of a hole than a house. The phrase "to the furthest lands" <note>original: "in ultimas terras"</note> is frequent in Cicero. For example, in the sixth speech against Verres: "How did you think the other nations would receive this? How did you think the fame of this deed of yours would reach the kingdoms of others and the furthest lands?" The same author in his speech *For Publius Sulla*: "Now indeed, how incredible, how absurd it is, that he who wished to commit slaughter in Rome and set this city on fire, would send away his most intimate friend and banish him to the ends of the earth?" Likewise in his *13th Philippic*: "How can I pass over Saxa Decidius, a man brought from the furthest nations?" Again in the *Letters to Friends* to Publius Lentulus, Book 1: "For remember from what furthest lands you sent it, nor did you fear this." Also in Book 15 to Marcus Marcellus: "We were indeed far away and sent by you to the furthest peoples." In Saint Jerome, the phrase "a monster to be deported to the ends of the earth" is frequent. Plautus in *The Haunted House*: "But I have even been carried around to lonely lands and the furthest shores."

->War produces such things. LXVIII<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero cites this six-foot verse in his letters to his brother Quintus, Book 2, as if it were a commonly tossed-about saying:

> Wretched war brings about such things.
<note>original: "Τοιαῦθ’ ὁ τλήμων πόλεμος ἐξεργάζεται."</note>

This refers to the understanding that many absurdities arise from the disagreements of those who administer the republic. Cicero’s words are as follows: "There is the greatest leisure in the forum, but it is the leisure of a city growing old rather than one finding rest. Moreover, my opinion in the senate is of such a kind that others agree with us more than we do ourselves. 'Wretched war brings about such things.' This phrase, if transferred to private discord, will have a bit more grace."

<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM, ADAGES</header>

->With an honest face.<-
<margin>LXIX</margin>

Things that are spoken or done from the soul and without "dye" <note>original: "fucum" — meaning artificial coloring or deception</note> are said to be done **with a true forehead** <note>original: "uera fronte" — in Roman culture, the forehead was considered the seat of shame and honesty</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in his speech *For Gaius Rabirius*: "But if they then spoke the truth with a most honest face, they are lying now; if they are lying now, let them show us the truth." Conversely, we say something is done with a **lying face** <note>original: "mendaci fronte"</note> when it is carried out through pretense. Just as Marcus Tullius says to his brother Quintus (if the title does not deceive us): "The forehead, the eyes, and the expression very often lie, but speech most often of all." The forehead and eyes especially reveal the emotions of the mind; for it is not difficult to feign words, but, as Ovid says, "It is very difficult not to betray a crime with one's expression." And in Virgil, Dido: **"She feigns hope in her face, while pressing deep grief in her heart."** Terence, in his play *The Self-Tormentor*, says: "Bah, even that scoundrel feigns his expression." And in the *Phormio*, Geta composes the expression of Antipho for his meeting with his father, though he could not maintain it.

->The Trojan Pig.<-
<margin>LXX</margin>

The ancient architects of gluttony even devised this: that a whole ox or camel would be served, stuffed inside with various kinds of animals. From this also came the **Trojan pig** in the common stories, to which this name was given because it concealed various species of animals in its belly, just as the Durian horse <note>The Trojan Horse, often called the Durian or Wooden Horse</note> concealed armed men. Macrobius, in the third book of the *Saturnalia*, reports that Cincius, in the speech where he advocated for the Fannian Law regarding the regulation of expenses, complained about his own age because they were bringing "Trojan pigs" to the tables. If I were given the choice, I would prefer a Trojan pig to a Trojan horse; it is suitable for sumptuous banquets, or for a man filled with various delicacies.

->A hair in the middle.<-
<margin>LXXI</margin>

To signify the smallest distinction, we say that "a hair lies between," which is even more emphatic if you say "a stalk's width." Theocritus says in *Thyonichus*:
<margin>that is,</margin>
"But at last, madness will seize me in my ignorance. **A hair is scarcely in the middle.**"
These are the words of a lover fearing lest his love finally turn into insanity, from which he is so little removed that there is "scarcely a hair in the middle." With a similar metaphor, Plautus said in *The Haunted House*: "It makes not a feather’s difference <note>original: "Pluma haud interest"</note> whether the patron or the client becomes more honest, for a man who has no boldness in his heart." He said "it does not matter a feather" instead of "it matters nothing at all." Asinius Pollio wrote to Cicero: "I am not about to depart a footstep from you."

->Struck by the Muses.<-
<margin>LXXII</margin>

**Musopatagos** <note>original: "Μυσοπάταγος" (Mousopatagos)</note> is said of one who is stirred and astonished by the fury of the Muses. Thus Virgil in the *Georgics*:
"Struck by whose love,
->I carry the sacred objects.<-"
It is transferred to those who love their own poems just as parents love their children. Marcus Tullius to his brother Quintus, in book two: "By Hercules, no **Musopatagos** <note>one obsessed with the Muses</note> reads his own fresh poems more gladly than I listen to you." Horace says:
"He loves his verses, this is his one pursuit."

->As Phrygius loved Pieria.<-
<margin>LXXIII</margin>

Plutarch, in his book *On the Bravery of Women*, shows that a custom lasted until his own age that wives would pray to be loved by their husbands **as Phrygius loved Pieria** <note>original: "ὡς φρύγιος ἠγάπησε πιείας"</note>. This arose from a history of this sort: Some of the Ionians who had migrated to Miletus, having started a sedition against the sons of Neleus, withdrew to Myus and established their seat there. They suffered many injuries from the Milesians, who waged war with them because of their defection—yet not harshly, nor with all trade excluded, for on certain feast days the women would go from Myus to Miletus. Among those who had withdrawn was a certain man named Pythes, whose wife was called Ipygia and daughter Pieria. When a festival was being celebrated in Miletus to Diana (whom they call Neleis), Pythes sent his wife and daughter there, having prayed that they be allowed to take part in the feast. Now, by far the most powerful of the sons of Neleus was Phrygius. He was captured by love for Pieria and thought of what he could do that would be most pleasing to the girl. When she said that nothing could happen more pleasingly than if he brought it about that she could frequently travel freely to Miletus accompanied by many maidens, Phrygius, understanding from these words that peace and friendship were sought by her for her citizens, settled the war. Hence the name of Pieria began to be wonderfully popular among both the Milesians and the Myuntians, so much so that girls who were marrying were accustomed to pray, for the sake of the omen, "That I may be so loved by my husband as Phrygius loved Pieria."

->A man's life is a pilgrimage.<-
<margin>LXXIIII</margin>

**Life is a kind of pilgrimage** <note>original: "Παρεπιδημία τις ἐστὶν ὁ βίος"</note>. Socrates says in the *Axiochus* <note>A dialogue formerly attributed to Plato</note>:
Plato

<summary>This page explores adages concerning honesty ("with an honest face"), the luxury of the "Trojan pig" dish, and the romantic origins of the peace between Miletus and Myus. Erasmus uses these classical references to illustrate human character, societal excess, and the power of love to resolve conflict.</summary>
<keywords>honesty, Cicero, Trojan Pig, gluttony, Phrygius and Pieria, Miletus, peace-making, Muses, poetic passion, pilgrimage of life</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s Fourth Chiliad of adages, tenth century. It transitions from a discussion on physical appearances and historical anecdotes to the philosophical interpretation of life as a journey and the use of medical metaphors (ulcers/cancers) for social and personal troubles.</meta>

<page-num>1041</page-num>
<header>FOURTH CHILIAD, TENTH CENTURY</header>

He brings forward this opinion of Plato as one commonly recited by everyone. Although that dialogue <note>likely the *Axiochus*, often attributed to Plato in the Renaissance but now considered spurious</note> is categorized among the spurious works, it seems rather to be the work of a Christian man who wished to imitate Plato. For this sentiment frequently occurs in the sacred volumes: that this life is an exile, a temporary residence, and a pilgrimage. Nevertheless, the Platonic Socrates also recounts that the souls of men have fallen from heaven, to which they prepare a return for themselves through the study of philosophy.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
### It is all an ulcer.

In the same dialogue, in response to the praise of agriculture, Socrates replies: <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' οὐχ ὅλον ὡς φασιν ἕλκος, ἀλλὰ λύπης πρόφασιν εὑρισκόμενον</note> "But is it not, as they say, all an ulcer, always producing from itself an occasion for troubles?" The character Vulteius in Horace <note>referring to Vulteius Mena in Horace's *Epistles* 1.7</note> declared this to be true. Furthermore, whatever is vehemently troublesome to us, we are accustomed to call an **Ulcer**, a **Sore**, or a **Cancer**. Just as it has been handed down in literature concerning Caesar Augustus, that he was never accustomed to call his daughter Julia, his granddaughter Julia, and Agrippa (whom he had first adopted and later disowned) anything other than his **three Sores** and **three Cancers**. Indeed, he so detested their lack of frugality and poor character that at every mention of them he was accustomed to exclaim with a verse from Homer:
<note>original Greek: Αἴθ' ὄφελον ἄγαμος τε μένειν, ἄγονός τ' ἀπολέσθαι</note>
->that is,<-
**"O, would that I had remained unmarried, and perished childless!"**
And this verse also deserves to be counted among the proverbs, to be used by those who have married unhappily or have raised children they must regret. It will also suit a man of troublesome character. Theocritus, in his epitaph for Adonis, calls a sharp pain a **"groin-swelling ulcer"**:
<note>original Greek: Ἄγριον ἄγριον ἕλκος ἔχει περὶ μηρὸν Ἄδωνις, / Μείζον δ' ἁ κυθέρεια φέρει ποτικάρδιον ἕλκος</note>
->that is,<-
**"Adonis has a wild, wild wound around his groin: / But Cytherea carries a greater wound beneath her heart."**

<margin>LXXVI</margin>
### From the praetor's cohort.

Those who are ready at every nod and are delegated with authority to execute this or 그게 <note>meaning to perform various tasks</note> are said to be **from the praetor's cohort**. <note>The "cohors praetoria" was the staff or retinue of a Roman magistrate, not just his military guard.</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his first letter to his brother Quintus, says: "But those whom you wished to have with you, either from your domestic circle or from your necessary attendants, who are usually called 'from the praetor’s cohort,' for these we must be responsible not only for their deeds, but even for their words, etc." The ministers of the praetors need no other excuse than to say they did what they did by the order of those men; thus the legal action is then against the praetor, not against the ministers. A similar power exists over those so bound by food and duties that they dare refuse nothing.

<margin>LXXVII</margin>
### You could light a lamp.

Theocritus, in his poem *Thyonichus*, exaggerated vehement anger with this hyperbole:
<note>original Greek: Κἤφατ' ἐπ' ἀλφαρείως καὶ ἀπ' αὐτῆς ὡς λύχνον ἅψαις</note>
->that is,<-
**"And he grew hot with rage, so that you could easily / have lit a lamp from him."**
These are the words of a lover complaining about the insolence of a girl who, when she was silent at a banquet, someone said to her, "You aren't speaking; have you seen a wolf?" <note>A common ancient belief that seeing a wolf first would make a person lose their voice.</note> She flared up vehemently at the name of the wolf. For there was a young man present named **Lupus** <note>Latin for "Wolf"</note> whom she loved. Those who are angry are said to "burn." A similar hyperbole, though somewhat coarser, is still current today among our own people <note>Erasmus's contemporaries in Northern Europe</note> who say: "He flared up so much with anger that **you could boil an egg on his forehead**."

<margin>LXXVIII</margin>
### Always some great man.

**"But always some great man."** <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' αἰεί τινα φῶτα μέγαν</note> Marcus Tullius Cicero cites this half-line as one commonly tossed about in a letter to his brother Quintus, which begins: "Statius has come to me." He says: "As for the fact that he took away the expectation of you and that crowd which would have occurred if he had left together with you and had not been seen before, that seemed to me to have happened not inconveniently. For the talk of men has been exhausted, and many such words have already been sent out, **'but always some great man,'** which I am glad were finished in your absence." Where this half-line was taken from is not yet clear, except that perhaps instead of "but" <note>Greek: ἀλλ' / all'</note> we should read "atta" <note>Greek: ἄττα</note>, meaning "it asks for" or "it requires."

<margin>LXXIX</margin>
### Not even if to the court of Jove.

Those who fear evil flee to a sanctuary, to an altar, to a citadel, to the statues of a prince, or to the shrines of the gods. But there is no escape from death. Sophocles expressed this in these verses:
<note>original Greek: ὅταν γὰρ ὁ καιρὸς τοῦ θανεῖν ἐλθὼν τύχη / οὐ' ἂν πρὸς αὐλὰς ζηνὸς ἐκφύγοι μολών</note>
->that is,<-
**"When the time of death approaches, / not even if one went to the halls of Jove [could he escape]."**

<meta>catchword: If he fled</meta>

<summary>Erasmus explores several adages concerning inescapable troubles and personal retinue. He discusses the metaphor of life as a pilgrimage, Augustus’s harsh description of his family as "cancers," the origin of the "praetor's cohort" as a term for administrative staff, and the inevitability of death.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Fourth Chiliad, tenth century of Erasmus’s collection of proverbs. It picks up mid-discussion on the inescapable nature of fate or consequences, moving into adages concerning certainty, intellectual refinement, notoriety, and legal judgments.</meta>

<page-num>1042</page-num>
<header>ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

**If you have fled, you still cannot escape.**
This is a type of proverb found in those words, **even to the very courtyard of Jove** <note>original: "ad Iouis quidem atrium"</note>; which he positioned as the safest possible refuge. The Eagle had fled here while being pursued by the beetle.

### To speak oracles.
->LXXIX.<-

<note>original Greek: Χρησμὸς λέγειν</note> **To speak oracles** is a saying used for those who speak things that are certain and indubitable. Theocritus says in the *Syracusans*:
**The old woman departed after she had delivered her oracle.** <note>original Greek: Χρησμὸς ὁ πρεσβῦτις ἀπῴχετο θεσπίσασα</note>
That is to say: "This old woman left, having spoken the oracles of the gods."
**Things from the tripod** <note>original Greek: τὰ ἐκ τριποδὸς</note> is said elsewhere, as is the **leaf of the Sibyl**. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in a letter to his brother Quintus beginning "Already written and sealed," says: "Consider these things as if they were uttered from the oracle of Pythian Apollo." The same author in the fifth book of *On Ends* says: "Because when this is magnificently uttered by Zeno as if from an oracle, that virtue is content with itself for living happily."

### Not from Hymettus.
->LXXX.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of his letters to his brother Quintus, calls that coarse and rustic philosophy—which we learn from the company of common people rather than from the commentaries of Zeno or Plato—**philosophy from a Syrian floor.** <note>original: "philofophiam ab area Syra"</note> For he says: "For we are scholars in such a way that we can even live with craftsmen; we have this philosophy **not from Hymettus, but from a Syrian floor.**" Hymettus is a mountain in Attica, from which comes Hymettian honey <note>symbolizing refined, "sweet" Attic speech</note>. To this he opposes the "Syrian floor," indicating a rustic simplicity. For a little before, he had touched upon sharp-witted witticisms. It appears that at that time Cicero was building on a certain estate. However, I am not sure whether this passage is free from error, as it is found variously in different manuscripts. Let the learned reader discern whether instead of **Syrian floor** (*area Syra*) one should read **Syrian pigsty** (*hara Syra*). For he speaks this way in his oration *Against Piso*: "Brought forth from a pigsty, not a school." The Syrians were famous for their barbarity at that time, just as the Athenians were for the charm of their speech.

### The cymbal of the world.
->LXXXI.<-

Pliny the Elder, in the preface to the Emperor Vespasian, records that Apion the grammarian was accustomed to be called **The Cymbal of the World** by Tiberius Caesar, on account of the celebrity of his name, I believe; though Pliny says he "might rather seem to be the **drum of public fame**." This Apion used to say that those to whom he dedicated any of his compositions were gifted with immortality by him. Tiberius, alluding to this, called him the "Cymbal of the World," because he gifted a man with a respectable reputation that would resonate quite pleasantly throughout the entire world. Pliny, however, because of Apion’s arrogance, prefers him to be called the "drum of public fame," because he gave notoriety rather than a truly respectable reputation. For a drum also resonates, but with an unpleasant noise. He seems to have alluded here to the fact that drums are made from donkey skin.

### In a blessed man, all things are blessed.
->LXXXII.<-

By the wealthy, all things are done magnificently; by the poor, frugally. Praxinoe in the *Graces* <note>Erasmus likely means the *Adoniazusae* or *Idyll 15*</note> of Theocritus, praising Ptolemy because he had prepared the festival of Adonis with magnificent expense, said (not without the flavor of a proverb):
**In a prosperous man, all things are prosperous.** <note>original Greek: ἐν ὀλβίῳ ὄλβια πάντα</note>
That is: "In a rich man, all things are rich."
The use for this will be if you say that from a learned man all things are done learnedly, from a pious man piously, and from a king in a kingly manner.

### Where he might extend a finger.
->LXXXIII.<-

In a proverbial figure of speech, Marcus Tullius Cicero said in his defense of Aulus Caecina: **He has no place where he might extend a finger.** He indicates hyperbolically that there is absolutely nothing for the man to say or do. The passage goes like this: "Finally, that excessive power which dominates in the state rests in this one kind of case; let it rest, for he has no way to approach the judge, and finally **has nowhere to extend a finger.**" This is taken from the gestures of orators, which are recorded in various ways by Quintilian. The simplest gesture is to extend a finger, which is the way of commoners and rustics.

### The sad letter.
->LXXXIV.<-

Marcus Tullius Cicero in his defense of Milo: "Unless he had seen that a man who confessed could be acquitted, when we came to confess, he would never have ordered an investigation, nor would you have given this letter, so salutary in judging, rather than that **sad one**." He calls **theta** (θ) the **sad letter**, and **tau** (τ) the **salutary** one; because by the latter a defendant was acquitted, and by the former condemned. We touched on this somewhat in the proverb *To prefix a Theta*. Asconius Pedianus, if the manuscripts are free of error, indicates that **θ** was the mark of condemnation and **τ** of acquittal. **N. L.** stands for *non liquet* <note>"it is not clear," used when a judge required more evidence</note>, a mark of postponement. Livy called it the "sadder mark."

<header>THE TENTH CENTURY OF THE FOURTH CHILIAD</header>

### Seed of Jove.
### LXXXVI

<note>original Greek: ἐκ Διὸς ἔφυ</note> **Born of Zeus**, or **A sprout of Jove**, was a saying applied to someone endowed with remarkable excellence. These are the words of a shepherd addressed to another shepherd who was beautifully skilled in music, to whom he gave a staff as a mark of honor. A staff, moreover, is the gear carried by Hercules, who was the offspring of Jove. It was observed by the ancients that the sons of Jove are always portrayed by poets as civilized and humane, whereas the sons of Neptune are depicted as fierce and harsh. Music, indeed, is the teacher of civility. The poem goes like this:
**Because you are, / Pan, truly a sprout fashioned from Zeus.** <note>original Greek: οὕνεκευ ἐσσὶ Πᾶν ἐπ’ ἀληθείᾳ πεπλασμένον ἐκ Διὸς ἔρνυ.</note>
That is:
**Since you are indeed, / In truth, a seed made and born from Jove himself.**

However, the commentator prefers to refer it to the idea that those who speak the truth are said to be born of Jove, citing the Homeric poem:
**For what I have nodded my head to / shall not be revocable or deceptive.** <note>original Greek: οὐ γὰρ ἐμὸν παλινάγρετον οὐδ’ ἀπατηλόν, ὅτι κεν κεφαλῇ κατανεύσω.</note>
That is:
**For nothing shall be false or able to be called back / Which I have granted with a nod of my head.**
The shepherd is praised for this reason: because he frankly admits that he should not be compared with distinguished musicians. Such a character is also introduced by Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>: **The shepherds also call me a prophet, but I do not believe them.**

### Birds of the Muses.
### LXXXVII

<note>original Greek: Μουσῶν ὄρνιθας</note> **Birds of the Muses**. Not without the appearance of a proverb, Theocritus in the *Thalysia* calls poets by this name because, in the manner of nightingales, they assiduously sing their poems. The scholar warns that all should be careful not to be called "crow-like" birds of the Muses. He implies his displeasure with poets who, in the manner of cuckoos, dare to sing against Homer.

### No day is entirely bad.
### LXXXVIII

Astrologers designate certain days as fortunate or unlucky, but only for this or that specific business. However, on no day should one indulge in idleness, because no day is so inauspicious that it is not favorable for some business, provided one uses the granted time rightly. A day unfavorable for waging war or for sailing might be favorable for managing domestic affairs. Furthermore, there is no day that is not prosperous for preparing a good mind <note>i.e., for philosophical or moral improvement</note>. Hesiod admits this in his <term>Works and Days</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ ἔργων καὶ ἡμερῶν</note>:
**And whenever there is a thoroughly evil day.** <note>original Greek: Καὶ ὅποτε πάγκακον ἦμαρ.</note>
That is:
**A day bad in every respect shall never occur.**

### To sprinkle a drop.
### LXXXIX

When a tiny bit falls to someone from a large profit, we say **a drop is sprinkled.** Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his speech *In Defense of Aulus Cluentius*: "And even the very 'seasoner' of the whole business sprinkles a 'Drop' on this 'Bulb'." Therefore, that man seemed least "bitter" to him who had tasted a little bit of hope from his conversation. By the same figure of speech, we say **a grain of gold**, meaning a very tiny portion. 

But in the words of Marcus Tullius, besides the proverbial metaphor, there lies a very witty allusion to proper names. Stalenus had promised a great sum of money to the judge Bulbus—for that was the judge's name. But Stalenus, who was "seasoning" this whole business (for here he is called a *conditor* <note>Erasmus notes a pun here: *conditor* with a long 'o' means a seasoner or pickler, while with a short 'o' it means a founder or builder</note>), joins to Bulbus another judge whose name was Gutta <note>Gutta means "a drop"</note>. This matter made Bulbus more eager. Now, cooks are accustomed to add seasonings to *bulbi* (that is, a type of onion) so that they might become sweeter. Alluding to this, Cicero says: "Therefore, he seemed least bitter." 

From this, things are also said to be done **drop by drop**. Plautus says in *The Merchant*: "My heart wastes away drop by drop, as if you had put salt into water." And he "gives drop by drop" who gives often, but in tiny amounts.

### You are on the right path.
### XC

**You have touched the matter with a needle** <note>Meaning "you hit the nail on the head"</note>. Very similar to this is what Plautus has in *Asinaria*: "Is it not as I say, Libanus? Libanus: You are on the right path, that is how it is." Just as those who are mistaken are said to "wander from the whole path," so those who guess a matter well are said to "insist on the right path." This figure of speech is wonderfully common even today among the unlettered public. A similar figure is used in *Casina*: "Now, by Pollux, I have finally returned to the right path," meaning "I have grasped the matter itself."

### Aeacidian threats.
### XCI

In the same play, a merchant speaks thus: "Since indeed, by Hercules, he walks filled with Aeacidian threats and spirit. If he touches me in his anger, he will be beaten in his anger." It is said with the appearance of a proverb for fierce and most haughty threats. The verse allows one to read "Aecine" for "Aeacidian." For some...

<margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin>
<margin>Iliad, Book 1</margin>
...divines, but it is more probable that the poet feels this way about Achilles, the grandson of Aeacus, whom Homer everywhere depicts as hot-tempered and threatening. For instance, in the very first book of the *Iliad*, he flares up against Agamemnon so fiercely that he reaches for his sword hilt, ready to move from insults to blows, had not Pallas Athena pulled him back by his hair. Indeed, the entire work takes its beginning from the wrath of Achilles: <note>original Greek: μῆνιν ἄειδε</note> **"Sing, Goddess, the wrath."** As for what some people say regarding Aeacus being a judge of the underworld, I do not see how that fits this context. We also call anything that we wish to be understood as invincible and insuperable **"Achillean."** <note>Erasmus refers to the term <term>Achilleum</term> as a metaphor for an unanswerable argument or an unstoppable force.</note>

->XCI<-
### Brighter than oil.
The luster of oil had become such a common proverb that even the mystical scriptures suggest washing the face with oil <note>A reference to Psalm 104:15, "oil to make his face shine."</note> to hide the gloom of fasting. Plautus says in the *Truculentus*, speaking of a beautifully dressed mistress: **"How fervently she blooms all over, how brightly she shines like oil!"** Oil adds brightness and light to all things.

->XCII<-
### Hercules's profit.
Plautus used the phrase **"Hercules's profit"** to refer to massive expenditures in the *Mostellaria*: **"He makes lavish expenses, he has ruined his father; that one servant there, Tranio, is the most sharp-witted. He is capable of consuming even the profit of Hercules."** It has been mentioned elsewhere that in ancient times, most people were accustomed to vowing a tenth part of their profit to Hercules. They persuaded themselves that by his favor, their wealth would increase. From so many tithes, an immense sum of money must have been amassed. Plautus calls it "profit" jokingly, as if Hercules had sold his favor.

->XCIII<-
### Said too late.
<margin>Asinaria</margin>
**"You teach the learned," "You remind the mindful," "You speak to the knowing,"** and other phrases of that type have been recorded by us previously. Plautus expressed the same sentiment most wittily in the *Asinaria*: when Demaenetus, complaining about his wife's character, said, **"I admit she is troublesome and annoying,"** the servant Libanus replied, **"You said that later than I believed you."** That is: **"I knew it before you said it."** I do not see why Nonius <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian</note> interprets "later" (*posterius*) here as "less." Not even the phrase that follows shortly after is without a proverbial pattern: **"You are the first to perceive it, yet we knew it beforehand."** The Satirist <note>Juvenal, Satire 3</note> says: **"The master will be the last to know the ills of his own house."** And Terence: **"He alone is ignorant of everything."** But although we may be the first to perceive the misfortunes of others, they do not cause us pain; therefore, the *feeling* of the evil first reaches those whom the matter concerns, while the *knowledge* of it reaches others first.

->XCIIII<-
### As if from a watchtower.
<margin>Book 4 of the Letters to Friends, to Sulpicius</margin>
Those who foresee future events long before they happen are said to have seen them **"as if from a watchtower."** Marcus Tullius Cicero to Servius Sulpicius in his fourth book: **"For long before, as if from some watchtower, I foresaw the coming storm,"** etc. For not only towns and citadels have their watchtowers, but ships have them as well; from there, skilled pilots foresee the onset of winds or whirlwinds.

->XCV<-
### To commit perjury with formal words.
In ancient times, when someone was about to swear an oath, a priest or official would lead them in solemn words so that the oath would be more binding. Plautus in the *Asinaria*: **"When you have knowingly and willingly committed perjury with formal words."** The same author in the *Bacchides*: **"I gave an oath with formal words that I would give it to the woman today."** Sometimes the person swearing would hold onto an altar so that the religious obligation of the oath would be greater. Therefore, to indicate the most sacred of oaths, they would say: **"Unless you swear while holding the altar, I will not believe you."** Marcus Tullius Cicero in his speech *For Lucius Flaccus*: **"Therefore, would no one believe a man who swore while holding the altar, yet he will prove whatever he wants through a letter while unsworn?"**

->XCVI<-
### Agones.
<margin>Ovid, Fasti, Book 1</margin>
We have previously noted that King Antigonus, the grandson of Demetrius, was called **"Doson"** <note>Greek for "the one about to give"</note> as a military joke, because he was always promising things to everyone, saying **"I will give,"** but never actually fulfilling his promises. In the same way, those who struck the sacrificial victim among the Romans were called **"Agones,"** because according to custom, before they struck, they would ask the people: <note>original Latin: Agon'</note> **"Shall I act?"** <note>a contraction of *Ago-ne?*</note>. Ovid says in the *Fasti*:
> **"He always asks if he should act, and does not act unless ordered."**
Lactantius, the commentator on Statius, mentions the Agones. This will apply to procrastinators who are always deliberating and never set about doing anything.

->XCVII<-
### A rotten mushroom.
<margin>Bacchides</margin>
Plautus in the *Bacchides* calls a doting and useless old man a **"rotten mushroom."** Mushrooms, although naturally tasteless, were once considered delicacies—and still are among the Italians—but only when they are tender and fresh; nothing is more tasteless than old ones. Plautus’s words are as follows: **"A walking hatred of the earth. Now he tastes nothing, he feels nothing; he is worth as much as a rotten mushroom."** Indeed, even this phrase, **"hatred of the earth,"** has the form of a proverb, like that other one, **"A useless weight of the earth."** <note>original Latin: Telluris inutile pondus, a translation of Homer's phrase in the Iliad.</note> The same author in the *Bacchides* places "mushrooms" among the synonyms for stupidity: **"Fools, blockheads, idiots, mushrooms, dullards, simpletons, windbags."** In the *Mostellaria*...
<meta>The catchword "stoli" indicates the next page begins with "stolidi" (stupid people).</meta>

<header>FIFTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY</header>
<sig>Ttt</sig>

...calls him a "shrub" <note>Latin: *fruticem*</note> as an insult for being stupid. "You speak neither what is likely nor what is true, you shrub." In other trees, there is some image of dignity and wisdom. A shrub grows haphazardly, lacks cultivation, and either produces no fruit at all, or only that which is wild and useless.

->**Know him while he lives.**<-
<margin>XCIX</margin>
We have mentioned before that one ought to remember the living. A little prostitute in Plautus’s *Truculentus* twists this into another meaning, treating a lover as if he were dead because he had ceased to be able to give money. "While he lives," she says, "you should know the man; once he is dead, let him rest. I knew you while you were 'alive'." According to Hesiod, money is the very soul of mortals; once it is lost, the man is breathless and dead.

->**Like a bleary eye.**<-
<margin>100</margin>
I see some people with such characters that you cannot bear them with a calm mind; yet they are so industrious and disposed to service that whenever the occasion offers itself, you cannot help but entrust something to them. A bleary or inflamed eye is hurt by the touch of the hands, and yet it is natural for us to put our hand where it hurts. Plautus says in *Persa*: "I neither serve willingly, nor am I satisfactory to my master according to his wishes. But like a bleary eye, my master cannot keep his hand away from me: he cannot help but command me and prop himself up with my labor." Likewise in *Bacchides*: "That servant is very much like bleary eyes. If he is not there, you would not want him to be, nor would you miss him; if he is there, you cannot keep yourself from touching him."

---

->**THE FIRST CENTURY OF THE FIFTH CHILIAD**<-

->**You in the legion, I in the kitchen.**<-
<margin>1</margin>
In Plautus’s *Truculentus*, a cook responds to a soldier who is making fierce threats. "Be a warrior in the legion if you wish, but I am Ares in the kitchen." The cook escalated the warrior's own language. For Ares <note>The Greek name for the god of war, known to the Romans as Mars.</note> is the god of war. As for his saying "Ares" instead of "Mars," it is not unusual for Plautus to mix Greek words with Latin ones. Although in some copies the word was written as "birds" <note>Latin: *aues*</note> or "rams" <note>Latin: *aries*</note>, these are errors.

->**Faster than ants with a poppy seed.**<-
<margin>2</margin>
This phrase, found in Plautus’s *Trinummus*, has the character of an adage: "It is finished faster than if you threw a poppy seed to the ants." These are the words of the slave Stasimus, describing how forty minae <note>An ancient unit of currency.</note> were consumed within fifteen days—dissipated on feasts, drinking bouts, baths, and scattered among fishmongers, bakers, butchers, cooks, gardeners, perfume-sellers, and bird-catchers—just as if you threw a poppy seed to a column of ants. For the heap is pulled apart instantly as each one snatches up its own little grain.

->**Just like at Acheron.**<-
<margin>3</margin>
In the same play by the same author, a prostitute responds to a lover who is asking back for what he had given. "For just like at Acheron <note>A river in the underworld, used here to represent the land of the dead.</note>, the account of what is received is written here: once it has been taken inside, it can never be carried back out." She means that what has been given into a mistress's house returns to the lover no more than the dead return from the underworld, from whence, according to Catullus, they say no one returns.

->**A mouse does not trust in a single hole.**<-
<margin>4</margin>
Nothing today is more commonly repeated among the public than that a mouse is miserable if it has only one hole. Plautus expressed the same in *Truculentus*:
> "But consider how wise a beast the tiny mouse is,
> Who never commits its life to a single bed.
> For if one is besieged, it seeks protection from another."
There will be an occasion for this adage if we advise someone to acquire many friends, or to study philosophy alongside wealth, so that if fortune snatches away what is hers, there may be protection in literature.

->**Accounting after the matter is devoured.**<-
<margin>5</margin>
Just as it is said of help that comes too late, "allies after the war," so it is said of late thrift, "accounting after the wealth is spent." Stasimus says in Plautus’s *Trinummus*: "Late and foolishly—that which ought to have been guarded before—he calculates the account after I have eaten the wealth." The slave speaks of his master’s son who is calculating the sum of what he received when the whole amount has already been wickedly spent. Truly, this is counting the waves that have passed when one ought to be judging those that are coming.

->**A public dinner.**<-
<margin>6</margin>
Just as Phormio in Terence’s play calls it a "doubtful dinner" <note>The term <term>cena dubia</term> refers to a meal so lavish that the guest 'doubts' which dish to try first.</note>, when it is prepared with various delicacies...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Roman comedy, specifically the works of Plautus, as a source for common proverbs. The previous page ended with metaphors for uselessness and social awkwardness; here, the focus shifts to table manners, the brevity of life, and the use of "royal" as a synonym for "magnificent."</meta>

<page-num>1046</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

Indeed, when you are in doubt about what you should especially choose, Philto—a character in Plautus—calls a magnificent, exceptionally elegant, and even free banquet a "popular" one, the sort typically presented to the common people. Plautus’s words are as follows: "What if you went to a temple for a meal, and by chance a wealthy man arrived who was your match, and a feast were set out—what they call a 'popular' one. If the heap of food were brought by his clients," and so on.

<margin>VII</margin>
->No one ought to be bashful at the table.<-

In the same passage follows another proverb which, handed down from great antiquity, is still on everyone's lips today:
>No one ought to be bashful at the table,
>For there, matters divine and human are decided.
Except that the common people add, "nor in bed." This sentiment belongs not to a philosopher, but to Stasimus, a slave in a comedy, though there is nowhere one should observe modesty more than in bed and at a banquet. However, there are some guests who are bothersome due to a "country bashfulness" <note>Latin: *rustico pudore*</note>, always waiting for someone to serve them and putting back what has been given. Now, this very phrase, "matters divine and human are decided," is proverbial; it was a figure of speech used to signify that the most important affairs were at stake. It is a saying worthy of a slave, who placed the "stern and prow" <note>A metaphor for the beginning and end, or the sum total.</note> of happiness in the filling of his belly.

<margin>VIII</margin>
->A salt-cellar of a soul.<-

In the same scene, Philto calls a man "a little salt-cellar of a soul," <note>original: *Salillum animæ*</note> meaning that a man’s life is very brief—likening it to the tiny portion of salt placed before each person at a banquet. The passage in Plautus reads: "The gods are rich, wealth befits the gods and their factions; we little humans are but a wisp of smoke, a salt-cellar of a soul, which, as soon as we lose it from the temple <note>meaning the body</note>, the beggar is carried out dead to the Underworld <note>Latin: *Acherontem*</note> just the same as the wealthiest man." Although the end of the line is missing two syllables, it likely means: "he is counted as Pelops, or he is counted as Croesus" <note>Pelops and Croesus were legendary figures of immense wealth</note>, or something similar.

<margin>IX</margin>
->A lead coin.<-

Just as the *as*, the *obol*, and the *teruncius* <note>various small Roman coins</note> once did, so too the "lead coin" <note>original: *nummus plumbeus*</note> became a proverb for worthlessness. Plautus says in *The Three-Dollar Day*: "Even if his life were at stake, I would never trust him with a lead coin." The same author says in *Casina*: "A man who today does not have a lead coin to his name." Flanders still knows copper coins today, and England knows lead ones. But Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the fifth book of his letters to Atticus, calls Vatinius a "half-penny man" <note>Latin: *semissē hominem*</note> to mean he is most vile and contemptible: "At the same time, that half-penny man bore arms against me." Elsewhere, a "three-penny groom" <note>Latin: *tressis agaso*</note> is used for someone most contemptible. Plautus in *The Haunted House*: "Be silent, if you please, you smith, who are accustomed to minting lead coins."

<margin>X</margin>
->Royal deeds.<-

We have previously advised that whatever is magnificent is usually called "royal" <term>βασιλικὸν (basilikon)</term>, such as "faring royally" <term>βασιλικῶς (basilikōs)</term>; and they used to call magnificent houses "basilicas." Plautus, in *The Three-Dollar Day*, says of a worthless slave who was speaking somewhat philosophically: "Immortal gods, this fellow is starting to speak of 'royal deeds' <note>original: *basilica facinora*</note>." There is the well-known response of Porus, who, when asked by Alexander the Great (by whom he had been defeated in war) how he wished to be treated, replied: "Royally" <term>βασιλικῶς (basilikōs)</term>. When Alexander asked if he had anything else to say, he replied that everything was included "in the word 'royally'" <term>ἐν τῷ βασιλικῶς (en tō basilikōs)</term>. For nothing humble befits kings. It is a bit unusual what Plautus said in *Epidicus*: "Immortal gods, how 'royally' I have perished!" <note>meaning "I am utterly ruined"</note>

<margin>XI</margin>
->Neither head nor feet.<-

When a business is so disturbed that you do not know how to either settle it or let it go, the ancients used to say it had "neither head nor feet" <note>original: *nec caput, nec pedes*</note>. For so Marcus Tullius Cicero jokes when responding to his friend Curio: "I understand from your letters that Sulpicius’s help was not much needed, because your affairs are so tangled that, as you write, they have 'neither head nor feet.' For my part, I wish they had 'feet,' so that you might one day return." We have previously mentioned the "headless tale" <term>ἀκέφαλος μῦθος (akephalos mythos)</term> from Plato.

<margin>XII</margin>
->He saw no sleep.<-

Since sleep is not something "seen," but rather something that closes the eyes, there is no doubt that it is said as a proverbial figure: "He did not see sleep with his eyes." For by these words they signify the greatest vigilance. Marcus Tullius Cicero says to Curio in the eighth book of his *Letters*: "Know that while Caninius was consul, no one ate lunch. Yet no evil was done during his consulship. For his vigilance was marvelous, seeing as he saw no sleep during his entire consulship." The wit of the saying lies in the fact that he was consul for only a single day. The logic of the proverb lies in the metaphor.

<margin>XIII</margin>
->To put one's hand to one's mouth.<-

By this gesture, we signify that we know something which we nonetheless do not wish to speak out. Caelius to Cicero in the book...

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s exploration of Roman comedic expressions, primarily from Plautus, which have passed into common usage as proverbs. The previous page discussed metaphors for social interactions and the value of hospitality; this page focuses on expressions concerning social hierarchy, meager living, and metaphors for worthlessness.</meta>

<page-num>1047</page-num>
<header>CHILIAD FIVE, CENTURY I</header>

...in book 9. But Domitius, when he placed his hand to his mouth, said that those who loiter under the Rostra <note>The *subrostrarii* were gossips and idlers who hung around the public speaking platforms in the Roman Forum.</note> had spread the word that you had died on the ninth day before the Kalends of June—a curse on their heads! <note>Latin: *quod illorum capiti sit*</note>

<margin>XIIII</margin>
### Buy someone you can order around.

One is allowed to be imperious toward one's own slaves, but not toward those of others or toward free people. Thus Stalino, in Plautus’s play *Trinummus*, speaks to his master who was calling him back rather imperiously (whom he either did not know was his master or pretended not to know). "It is better," he says, "to buy someone you can command." Likewise in the play *Persa*: "You ought to buy someone whom you want to obey you." This relates to that line of Theocritus which we have reviewed elsewhere: "I am not worried that you might wipe me clean" <note>A metaphorical way of saying "I am not your servant."</note>. A woman takes it poorly to be scolded by a man to whom she is neither a maidservant nor a wife. He also adds this: "You give orders to Syracusan women" <note>Greek: *Συρακουσίαις ἐπιτάσσεις*</note>, that is, you are trying to command women of Syracuse—meaning those who are not yours, but are free.

<margin>XV</margin>
### Of all those whom the sun sees.

There are also those proverbial figures of speech, such as: "the worst" or "the best" "of all whom the earth supports" or "whom the sun has seen." Plautus in *Stichus*: "Father, you will easily find a worse woman and one of worse character than she was; a better one you will neither find, nor has the sun seen." The same author in *Bacchides*: "Because, by Pollux, I know for certain that Vulcan, the Moon, the Sun, and the Day—those four gods—have shone upon no other man more wicked."
Virgil writes:
>Sun, who surveys all works with the flames of the earth.
For this reason, the sun is also called the "eye of the world." Similar is the phrase: "Whatever comes to ground" <note>Latin: *Quodcumque in solum venit*</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero in the last letter of the ninth book of his *Letters to Friends*: "I delight in a banquet; there I speak whatever 'comes to ground,' as they say—both groans and laughter." He means that at a banquet he speaks about any subject whatsoever, whether happy or sad. We cited this adage previously from the first book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, but this passage did not occur to us then, which nevertheless seems to support the validity of the proverb. Plautus in *Poenulus*: "The most wretched of as many men as the earth supports."

<margin>XVI</margin>
### With salt and vinegar.

Signifying a meager and thin meal, Grippus the fisherman in *Rudens* says: "But this king is going to dine with vinegar, without a good lung" <note>A "good lung" refers to a cheap animal organ used as a side dish; here it implies the king is so poor he cannot even afford the lowest meat.</note>. For the miserable, salt with vinegar takes the place of side dishes. Cicero, writing to Papirius Paetus in book 9, mentions *tyrotarichus* <note>A dish made of salt-fish and cheese.</note> as if it were a commoner's condiment. It was a sauce made from cheese, which Italians today call *minestra* <note>Erasmus uses the term for a common vegetable or grain soup.</note>. He also mentions the *pompilus*, a very cheap fish, like the gudgeon. "What *pompilus*," he says, "what denarius <note>Erasmus suspects the word *denarium* here is a corrupted text and is unsure of its meaning.</note> are you telling me about, what dish of cheese-and-fish?" There is frequent mention of the *pompilus* fish in Pliny. Vinegar (*acetum*), however, is sometimes used to signify sharpness of wit, as in Plautus: "He has vinegar in his heart," and Persius: "Washed with biting vinegar." Varro, in his *Sesquilyxe* as cited by Nonius: "Carneades <note>A Greek skeptical philosopher.</note> shaped the other path of virtue from vats of sharp vinegar," that is, with great intellectual subtlety.

<margin>XVII</margin>
### For a hollow acorn.

Among the common adages we have also included: "I would not buy it for a hollow nut." Using a very similar metaphor, Plautus in *Rudens* said "a hollow acorn" <note>Latin: *cassa glans*</note>. Someone promising information asks for a price. The other bids three hundred coins. Grippus responds: "Trifles!" <note>Latin: *tricas*</note>. The other says: "Four hundred." Grippus: "Rotten threads!" <note>Latin: *tramas putidas*</note>. "Five hundred." Grippus: "A hollow acorn!" "Six hundred." Grippus: "You are talking about tiny weevils." He said "hollow acorn" to mean a defective acorn or an empty shell.

<margin>XVIII</margin>
### A mutton-headed statue.

Hegio in Plautus’s *The Captives* calls a stupid slave a "mutton-headed statue" <note>Latin: *statua veruecea*, from *vervex*, a wether or castrated ram, a common Roman symbol for stupidity.</note>, as if you were to say a blunt and mute man. "You lot," he says, "go inside; meanwhile, I want to ask this mutton-headed statue what happened to my younger son." Some read "beaten statue" <note>Latin: *verberea*, from *verber*, a lash.</note> instead of "mutton-headed," as if he called a scoundrel accustomed to lashes a "beaten statue" rather than a marble one. Certainly, the meter of the trochaic verse does not easily allow the word *veruecea*, for there is one syllable too many, unless you use a synaeresis <note>A linguistic feature where two vowel sounds are contracted into one.</note> on the *-cea*.

<margin>XIX</margin>
### Do this.

When we command someone to be attentive, we say "be here" or "do this" <note>Latin: *hoc age*. This was also the ritual cry of a priest or executioner before striking, meaning "Focus on the task at hand."</note>. The Emperor Caligula heard "Do this!" from those who had come to kill him. And Plautus in the same play: "Let us do this."

<margin>XX</margin>
### Like comic actors in a tragedy.

When someone is "on someone else's sand" <note>A metaphor for being out of one's element or depth.</note>, they are said to be like comic actors introduced into a tragedy. Tragedy and comedy are of different genres; it is not right to introduce tragic characters into a comedy, nor...

<page-num>1048</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

...nor vice versa. Plautus says in *The Little Carthaginian*: "By Pollux, I am more unlearned <note>original: *indoctior*</note> than the Comic actor in a tragedy." I believe the reading should be "more inducted" <note>original: *inductior*</note>. For Colabiscus was playing upon what Milphio had said: "Just see to it that these men are hired <note>original: *conducti*</note> for this trick." He replied jokingly: "I am more inducted," which is to say, "I am more instructed."

### Not more than a dog.
->XXI<-

The word "dog" is commonly used to express hatred and contempt. Horace says: "He hates him worse than a dog." And Plautus in *Amphitryon*: "Have you been well all this time? Do you arrive a welcome guest?" Sosia replies: "I have never seen anyone more [welcome]." No one greets a "welcome guest" any more than they would a dog. For I believe it should be read this way so that the rhythm of the trochaic tetrameter catalectic verse remains consistent.

### A stilt-walker's or a tortoise's pace.
->XXII<-

Plautus in *Amphitryon*: Blephiso says, "We could not make our steps any grander than they were." Amphitryon replies: "Whether it be a stilt-walker’s pace or a tortoise’s pace, I am certain I will ruin this scoundrel." Likewise in *The Little Carthaginian*: "You would beat a stag in a race, or a stilt-walker in pace." Stilts <note>original: *gralae*</note> are poles upon which some people lean while walking; the ancients called those who used them "stilt-walkers" <note>original: *gralatores*</note>. In Greek they are called *kalobatai* <note>original: καλοβάται</note>, just as tightrope walkers are called *schoenobatae* <note>original: σχοινοβάται</note>. The longer these poles are from the step where the foot rests, the larger the strides. I was able to extract this much from a very corrupt passage in Nonius, especially in the Aldine edition. The same Plautus says in *The Menaechmi*: "And look, here he comes. Move your ant-like step." Ants seem to be running even when they make very little progress. Again in *The Little Carthaginian*: "You have beaten a snail in slowness." In the same play, he calls slow people "thick-stepped" <note>original: *spissigradissimos*</note>, and says they are slower than grain-ships <note>original: *corbitae*</note> in a calm sea. Again, he says the pace of such people is "sifted through a flour-sieve" <note>original: *succretum cribro pollinario*</note>, because fine flour flows through the narrow holes only bit by bit.

### Daedalean oars.
->XXIII<-

To signify great speed, Plautus said in *Amphitryon*: "With Daedalean oars, by flying forth." "I could not have come more swiftly if I had carried myself on Daedalean oars." <note>A reference to the mythical inventor Daedalus, who escaped Crete by crafting wings, which were often metaphorically compared to oars in ancient poetry.</note>

### I took the silver, I sold my authority.
->XXIIII<-

Nothing is more commonly repeated than this sentiment: he who accepts a benefit loses his liberty. Demaenetus expressed this elegantly in *The Comedy of Asses*:
> I took the silver, and with the dowry I sold my authority.

For a poor man had married a woman with a fine dowry, but over whom he could hold no authority. Nausistrata is introduced as a similar character in Terence’s *Phormio*.

### To spit away evil.
->XXV<-

It remains a custom among the common people even today that if they hear something cursed which they do not wish to happen to themselves, they spit as if in abomination. This originated from an ancient superstition; the ancients were convinced that spitting was a remedy against imminent evils, especially against the "assembly disease" <note>epilepsy, or *morbus comitialis*</note>. It was given this name not only because it often occurs in crowds of people, but also because its occurrence required the public assembly <note>the *comitia*</note> to be dismissed; and in applying remedies, spitting was considered healthy. It was also used against incantations, as Pliny reports. By a similar superstition, they used to spit three times into their own laps to ward off the "evil eye" of improper hope. Plautus says: "And here comes that disease that is spit upon." To which the reply is: "Do you say, you scoundrel, that I have that disease for which I need to be spit upon?" Here another responds: "Do not fear, that disease torments many men, for whom being spit upon was life-saving and proved beneficial." Likewise in *Amphitryon*: "I beseech you by Hercules to spit now that you have spoken."

### By use and by possession.
->XXVI<-

Anyone who wished to be considered entirely belonging to someone else would say: "By use and by possession" <note>original Greek: *Chrēsei kai ktēsei* (Χρήσει καὶ κτήσει)</note>, "I am yours." That is, both by the profit of use and by the right of ownership. Indeed, in matters of property, it often happens that ownership <note>original: *dominium*</note> belongs to one person, while the right to use and enjoy the profits <note>the legal concept of *usufruct*</note> belongs to another. Curius wrote to Marcus Tullius Cicero in his eighth book: "If you are well, it is good; for I am yours by use <note>original Greek: *chrēsei*</note>, but our friend Atticus's by possession <note>original Greek: *ktēsei*</note>." Therefore, the fruit is yours, but the legal ownership belongs to him. Curius feels that he is legally bound to Atticus, but nevertheless wishes to be at Cicero's service. Marcus Tullius, as if explaining this, responds: "And unless I had our friend Atticus as a partner in my studies—since you write that you belong to him by formal transfer and legal bond <note>original: *mancipio & nexu*</note>, but to me by use and profit—I am content with that. For that which each person enjoys and uses is truly his own." Marcus Tullius, joking with the legal expert, shows that ownership consists of two parts: formal transfer and legal bond. He does not lack this right, provided he is allowed to use and enjoy it; for as long as the right of use and profit remains, it is just as if the thing were one's own property.
