<header>FIFTH THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED</header>
<sig>Ttt 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: tur, quæ (which...)</meta>

### To strike the forehead.
<margin>XXVII</margin>
Those who are indignant beyond measure or lose control of their emotions are said to "strike the forehead." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in his *Letters to Atticus*, Book 1: "I think you either laughed or groaned at this, so that you strike your forehead; there are those who even think Caesonius, etc." What he had said before, he judged worthy of either laughter or a groan, but regarding Caesonius, he felt it was so unworthy that Atticus ought to strike his forehead. Those who deny that this is a proverb might as well deny that "To rub the forehead" <note>original: *Perfricare frontem*; meaning to cast off shame</note>, "To press the thumb" <note>original: *Premere pollicem*; a sign of favor or silence</note>, and many other expressions derived from bodily gestures are proverbs.

### Unfold every virtue.
<margin>XXVIII</margin>
In the same book, Cicero uses a line from a poem by Homer as if it were a common saying: <term>Remember every kind of excellence</term> <note>original: παντοίης ἀρετῆς μιμνήσκεο</note>. Take care and ensure that we are both praised and loved by all. The line can be rendered thus:
> Let the image of every kind of virtue come to your aid.

That is to say: in this business, deploy all your strength and every nerve of your intellect.

### A merciful gladiator-trainer.
<margin>XXIX</margin>
Previously we mentioned the Greek proverb, <term>a benevolent slaughterer</term> <note>original: εὐνους σφάκτης</note>. Very similar to this is what Marcus Tullius Cicero has in his first book of *Letters to Atticus* (the letter begins, "You ask of me"): <term>a merciful gladiator-trainer</term> <note>original: *lanista clemens*</note>. For just as a rejection of jurors was made amid the greatest shouting—when the accuser, like a censor, rejected good men as if they were the most wicked, and the defendant, like a merciful <term>gladiator-trainer</term> <note>original: *lanista*; a man who bought and trained gladiators, often viewed as a low or brutal profession</note>, chose all the most frugal men—as soon as the judges sat down, the good men began to lose heart.

### Backward.
<margin>XXX</margin>
When we feel that a matter is being handled "backward" <note>original: *præpostere*; literally 'before-after' or topsy-turvy</note>—as when the people command the princes, or a student teaches the master—that phrase of Cicero's from the same letter will be appropriate. He says: "I will answer you <term>last-first in the manner of Homer</term> <note>original: ὕστερον πρότερον ὁμηρικῶς</note>." This is a figure used by grammarians, which they call either <term>prothysteron</term> or <term>hysterologia</term> <note>rhetorical terms for placing the later event first</note>, when that which is prior by nature is mentioned later. For example, if someone were to say: "Cornelia raised and gave birth to the Gracchi." Such a trope is frequently encountered in Homer.

### A gathering in a gambling den.
<margin>XXXI</margin>
Nor does the expression found in the same letter lack the appearance of a proverb: "A gambling gathering" <note>original: *Consessus talarius*</note>, used for an assembly of men who are not very respectable. For a "gathering" or <term>council</term> <note>original: συνέδριον</note> is properly said of the Senate or of judges, who are usually chosen from the most honorable men. In a "gambling gathering," the one who is most wicked holds the first place. Cicero’s words are these: "For never was there a more disgraceful gathering in a gambling house; stained senators, stripped knights, Tribunes not so much 'of the treasury' as they are called 'of brass' <note>original: *aerati*; a pun on *tribuni aerarii* (treasury tribunes). Cicero suggests they were either bribed or 'made of money' through corruption</note>; yet a few good men were among them, etc." Although this is also a proverbial joke, he says they are commonly called "tribunes of brass" instead of "tribunes of the treasury," meaning they are either burdened with debt or certainly well-funded through embezzlement.

### To pull in the sails.
<margin>XXXII</margin>
In the same letter he said "to pull in the sails" <note>original: *contrahere uela*</note> to mean restraining oneself and acting more cautiously. "I pulled in my sails," he says, "perceiving the neediness of the judges, and I said nothing in my testimony except what was so well known and attested that I could not pass it over." Likewise Horace:
> You will wisely pull in
> the sails swollen by a too-favorable wind.

This is taken from sailors, who pull in the sails when the wind blows too fiercely so that they may sail more safely; when the wind is weaker, they spread them out, catching the breeze.

### Tell me now.
<margin>XXXIII</margin>
In the same letter, he most elegantly employs a Homeric verse to continue a narration:
<term>Tell me now, Muses, how it first fell out</term> <note>original: Ἔσπετε νῦν μοι μοῦσαι ὅπως δὴ πρῶτον ἔπεσε</note>, that is:
> Tell me now, Muses, for you have indeed told the things before.

This will have a certain charm in the recounting of ridiculous matters. In the Aldine edition, only the half-line is cited: <term>Tell me now, Muses</term>. Indeed, it appears more than once in Homer, even if the ending is not the same, such as: "Tell me now, Muses, who have your homes on Olympus" (Iliad, Book 2).

### Into the abyss.
<margin>XXXIIII</margin>
When we pray for someone's destruction, we tell them to "go to the bad cross" <note>original: *in malam crucem*; go be crucified</note>, "to the crows," or "to the Cynosarges" <note>a place outside Athens for the lower classes or outcasts</note>. For the same purpose, the ancients said "into the abyss" <note>original: *in dierectum*</note>, because they called those fixed to a cross *dierecti*. Nonius cites from Varro: "Away into the abyss from our house with that insanity." He thinks they are called *dierecti* as if "raised up in the light of day" <note>original: *in die erectos*</note>. Perhaps it was written "raised into the open air" <note>original: *in dium erectos*</note>, because those who are crucified are exposed under the open sky. Especially since he adds "from our house." Those things which...

<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

which are carried out from the home. Marcus Tullius Cicero used the word <term>insanitatem</term> <note>original: *insanitatem*; meaning "unsoundness" or "insanity"</note> instead of <term>insania</term> <note>meaning "madness"</note>, so that no one should suspect a mistake in the text.

### XXXV
-> To let blood. <-

Long ago, if soldiers had committed a rather serious offense, a vein was cut as a mark of disgrace. They called this <term>sanguine mittere</term> <note>original: *sanguine mittere*; literally "to send blood"</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the same letter: "The blood of envy was let without pain." He feels himself freed from some part of the envy directed at him because his own testimony had not carried weight in that trial—and this was "without pain" because he knew that all the judges had been bribed. The same author in Book 6, Letter 1: "Thus Appius, since he managed the province by <term>stripping it</term> <note>original Greek: ἀφαιρέσεως (*aphaireseōs*); meaning a process of taking away or depletion</note>, let its blood, withdrew whatever he could, and handed it over to me exhausted, etc." Indeed, this very phrase "to manage by stripping" is a <term>mousy character</term> <note>original Greek: ἦθος μυῶδες (*ēthos myōdes*); a reference to a thieving or nibbling nature</note> applied to a thieving and greedy man. The metaphor is taken from physicians who empty the body in certain diseases, drawing off the superfluous through fasting or the cutting of veins.

### XXXVI
-> A bean-coin. <-

It has been mentioned elsewhere that votes were once traditionally cast with beans; they think Pythagoras was hinting at this when he forbade the eating of beans. Therefore, Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the same letter, signified corrupted votes with a most witty trope: "But hey you, do you see that consulship of ours, which Curio used to call an <term>apotheosis</term> <note>original Greek: ἀποθέωσιν (*apotheōsin*); a deification or transformation into a god</note>? If this man is elected, it will be a <term>bean-coin</term>." So he says. Where a bean is a coin, there a vote has been bought.

### XXXVII
-> It is nothing, or it is no concern. <-

In the same book, in the letter beginning "When from Pompey's villa," he refers to a little verse of Rhinto as if it were a common saying. "However," he says, "I would wish you to think that I hold this path of the aristocrats after the death of Catulus without any protection or company." For as Rhinto says, I believe:
> Some are worth nothing, and to others nothing matters.
<note>original Greek: οἱ μὲν παρ' οὐδέν εἰσιν, οἷς δ' οὐδὲν μέλει</note>
He feels he is not using the protection of the great men, because some can do nothing, and others are negligent of affairs.

### XXXVIII
-> To watch a shipwreck from land. <-

Elsewhere we have spoken of "the Achaeans judging from the walls," used for those who watch the dangers of others from a place of safety. Marcus Tullius Cicero expressed this more festively with another metaphor in Book 2 of his *Letters to Atticus*, in the section on geography: "But now, since I am forced to leave the ship—not with the rudders thrown away but torn from me—I desire to look upon the shipworks of those men from the land; I desire, as your friend Sophocles says,
> Even under a roof to hear the steady rain with a sleeping heart."
<note>original Greek: κἂν ὑπὸ στέγῃ ἀκούῃ συκύκλος εὐδούσῃ φρενí</note>
Although this little verse was found in various forms in other manuscripts, but equally corrupted, and in others it was omitted. It seems to be a trochaic catalectic verse. For the word <term>sykyklos</term> <note>perhaps meaning "rhythmically falling"</note>, some manuscripts had <term>psakalos</term> <note>meaning "a drop"</note>. What that might be, I do not understand; the word <term>syklōs</term> does not fit the meter of the poem. The sense, however, seems to be this: he wishes to hear the tumult of others from his roof, while he himself is free and quiet in mind.

### XXXIX
-> He who struck first. <-

In the same book of letters, in the section "Suddenly when he had said to me, etc.," he uses a Homeric verse, threatening vengeance upon the one who should first provoke him. "For we indeed," he says, "if your comrade Publius allows it, intend <term>to play the sophist</term> <note>original Greek: σοφιστεύειν (*sophisteuein*); here meaning to live as a scholar or philosopher</note>. If he thinks only of offending us, then, as is proper to this art, <term>I profess</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπαγγέλλομαι (*epangellomai*)</note>:
> To ward off the man, whoever first acts harshly."
<note>original Greek: Ἀνδ' ἀπαμύνεσθαι ὅς τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ</note>
That is: I declare that I will avenge myself on whoever provokes me first.

### XL
-> What is given. <-

Nonius Marcellus cites this little verse from Caecilius's *Plotius*: "You will endure what they give, since they do not give what is desired." <term>Danunt</term> was an ancient way of saying <term>dant</term> <note>they give</note>. This agrees with what we have related elsewhere from Cicero: "The things that are given" <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν διδόμενα (*ta men didomena*)</note>, and things similar to this.

### XLI
-> Chimera. <-

A person who is inconsistent and of varying habits, or a work that does not hold together, Marcus Tullius Cicero wittily designates with that Homeric verse. Regarding what you write about your brother Quintus's letter, he says, it was to me also:
> A lion in front, a dragon behind, and in the middle a Chimera.
<note>original Greek: πρόσθε λέων, ὄπισθεν δὲ δράκων, μέσση δὲ χίμαιρα</note>
What to say, I do not know; for in the first lines he so deplores his stay that he could move anyone; then again he relaxes so much that he asks me to correct and publish his annals. A letter inconsistent with itself, he calls a "Chimera."

<header>FIFTH CHILIAD, FIRST CENTURY</header>
<sig>Ttt 4</sig>

->Nothing is sweeter than to know everything.<-
### XLII
In a letter to Atticus (Book 4), Marcus Tullius Cicero records this iambic line <note>original: *Senarium*; a line of verse consisting of six iambic feet</note> as if it were a common popular saying:
*Nothing is sweeter than to know all things.* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲν γλυκύτερόν ἢ πάντ’ εἰδέναι</note>
That is to say:
*Nothing is sweeter than to know absolutely everything.*
The corrupted verse will be restored if you add the word "is" <note>original Greek: θεῖν (*thein*), likely a typo for ἐστὶν (*estin*)</note>, like this: *Nothing is sweeter than to know all things.* Or simply: *than to know all.* Shortly after, Cicero adds: "Therefore, as if to a curious man, write to me in full detail what happened on the first day, the second day, what the censors did, what Appius is up to, and what that Apuleian law of the people is about." There is also that phrase found several times in the letters of Marcus Tullius: *Everything about everything.* <note>original Greek: πάντα περὶ πάντων (*panta peri panton*)</note>

->To depart from one's status.<-
### XLIII
Just as those who are driven from their purpose are said "to be knocked off their step"—a phrase we have discussed before—so Marcus Tullius says in Book 4 of his letters to Atticus (in the letter beginning *Occupationum mearum*): "I depart from my status." He uses this to mean: "I am withdrawing from my established way of life." He writes: "Let those be burst with envy who grieved that I could achieve anything; they give me much consolation, yet I do not depart from my status; I am returning to that life which is most in accordance with nature." The metaphor seems to be taken either from athletes or from battles, where it was considered a point of honor not to yield one's ground.

->To cover a tumor with double-dyed purple.<-
### XLIIII
Marcus Tullius, writing to Atticus, used the phrase "to cover a tumor with double-dyed purple" to mean "to hide some disgrace with a high-ranking office." He says: "To cover Vatinius’s tumor <note>original: *struma*; a scrofulous swelling or goiter</note> with the double-dyed purple of the priesthood." He calls the <term>dibaphum</term> <note>a Greek word for cloth "twice-dyed" in expensive Tyrian purple, worn by high Roman magistrates</note> the purple that has been dyed twice. A <term>struma</term> is a bodily tumor, like a hunch. Such a deformity is sometimes concealed by the purple robe. He uses the same idea writing to Marcus Caelius (Book 2): "For our friend Curtius is thinking of the double-dyed purple, but the dyer is delaying him." By the name of the "double-dyed purple," he designates the magistracy that had the right to wear it. But he jokes that the matter is not going according to Curtius's wishes because the "dyer" (the one who grants the office) was stalling. This is one way of blotting out infamy: to deter people's insults with the splendor of a high position. For a modest fortune lies open to envy. And perhaps there are some today who strive for the miters and the Cardinal’s hats with this same intention.

->Many things in the middle.<-
### XLV
We have mentioned before the proverb: "Many things fall between the cup and the upper lips." Marcus Tullius expressed the same idea with a different metaphor in Book 6 of his letters to Atticus: "Even if nothing were to happen... Not that you could help me with anything, since the matter is already at hand, while you are far away in distant lands." He then quotes:
*But many things in the space between, as the South wind rolls the waves of the wide sea.* <note>original Greek: πολλὰ δ’ ἐν μεταιχμίω, νότῳ κυλινδ’ κύματ’ εὐρείης ἁλός</note>
Cicero means that many new turns of events will arise before Atticus, who was far away, could bring help. These are iambic verses which you may translate as:
> But meanwhile, in the middle, the South wind
> Rolls many waves of the wide-stretching sea.

->Armed prayers.<-
### XLVI
In the same Book 9 of his letters (the one beginning *Tuas xi. cal.*), Cicero uses the term <term>anankōn</term> <note>Greek for "necessities" or "compulsions"</note> to describe a persuasion joined with necessity and force. Such are the requests of princes, which Ovid elegantly expressed regarding Jove: "To his prayers he adds threats in the manner of a king." I will record Cicero's words: "I do not fear his <term>goēteian</term> <note>Greek for "sorcery" or "deceptive flattery"</note> as much as his <term>anankōn</term>. For the requests of tyrants, as Plato says, I know are mixed with necessities." That is: I do not fear his tricks as much as the necessity of obeying; for the prayers of tyrants, as Plato says, you know are mixed with compulsion.
There is also that less famous line:
*He who asks while being more powerful, compels by his asking.*

->Nothing is more pleasant than a free bed.<-
### XLVII
In Book 14 of the letters to Atticus (beginning *O mi Attice*), speaking of his brother Quintus: "But he is so averse to taking a wife that he says nothing is more pleasant than a free bed," etc. Quintus had experienced marriage; after his wife died, he was also tormented by great worry regarding the repayment of the dowry. He therefore judged the bachelor life to be the sweetest. He calls it a "free bed." Indeed, as Juvenal says: "Very little sleep is had in that bed in which a bride lies."

->To balance faults with good deeds.<-
### XLVIII
In the same book, in the letter beginning *Certior Pylio factus*, he cites this iambic line without naming the author, as if it were common:
*With other noble deeds they push away this reproach.* <note>original Greek: Ἄλλοις ἐν ἐσθλοῖς τἀπ’ ἀπωθένται ψόγον</note>
He is speaking, if I am not mistaken, of Brutus and Cassius, who had killed Caesar. The passage goes: "And so the Ides of March..."

<page-num>1052</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

The letters to Marcia <note>likely referring to the *Epistulae ad familiares* or specifically Cicero's daughter Tullia, though the text mentions 'Martiæ' which may refer to a specific set of correspondence</note> do not console me as much as before. For they contain a great error, and if those young men, *to others indeed good things* <note>original Greek: ἄλλοις μὲν ἐθλοῖς (*allois men ethlois*)</note>, etc. This agrees with that saying: *You speak not badly, but well spoken.* <note>original Greek: οὐ κακῶς εὖ θῶν λέγεις (*ou kakos eu thon legeis*)</note>

### A storm of affairs.
<margin>XLIX</margin>

When we wish to signify a great confusion of things, we may use those Homeric verses which Marcus Tullius employs in Book 3 of his *Letters to his brother Quintus*:
*In the days of autumn, when Zeus pours down the heaviest rain, when he is angered and harsh toward men.* <note>original Greek: Ἤματ’ ὀπωρινῷ...; Homer, Iliad 16.384-385</note>
That is:
*In the months of autumn Jove pours out the violent rain, when, provoked to anger, he looms over mortals.*
Immediately after, he adds two other verses, by which he signifies that evils are sent by the gods above because of the injustice of men:
*Or in the assembly they give crooked judgments by force, and drive out justice, caring nothing for the vengeance of the gods.* <note>original Greek: Ἢ βίῃ εἰν ἀγορῇ...; Iliad 16.387-388</note>
That is:
*Or in the forum the wicked carry violent votes, and they summon vengeance, scorning the commands of the gods.*

### Higher than Oromedon.
<margin>L</margin>

Theocritus in the *Thalysia*:
*How much I loathe the builder who seeks to build a house as high as the peak of Mount Oromedon.* <note>original Greek: Ὡς μοι καὶ τέκτων...; Theocritus, Idyll 7.45-46</note>
That is:
*Thus the builder is greatly hateful to me, who builds on high, striving to surpass the ridge of Oromedon.*
This is a proverbial allegory, deterring one from insolence <term>insolentia: an overbearing pride or arrogance</term>, lest anyone should place themselves above those with whom they cannot in any way be compared. The Scholiast <note>an ancient commentator on a text</note> indicates that Oromedon is a mountain on the island of Kos. I suspect this is an allusion to a poet of Kos. For a little later, he calls Homer the Chian poet.

### To hold the first place.
<margin>LI</margin>

In Book 3 of the *Letters to his brother Quintus*, Marcus Tullius brings forward a verse as if it were proverbial. "Indeed," he says, "that which I had loved since I was a boy:
*Always to be the best and to excel above others,* <note>original Greek: Αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων (*Aien aristeuein kai hypeirochon emmenai allon*); Homer, Iliad 6.208</note>
has entirely perished." For he complains there that, with the Republic oppressed, there is no place either for the exercise of virtue or for the preservation of dignity. I suspect the verse is from Homer, which can be translated thus:
*To always hold the first place, and to excel others in praise.*
He uses the same in Book 13 [of the *Letters to Friends*] to Caesar.

### To bite the ear.
<margin>LII</margin>

Even today, the unlettered common folk, when they signify an impotent enmity and an impatient desire for revenge, say: "I would have gladly bitten off his ear." Marcus Tullius, in Book 3 of the *Letters to his brother Quintus*, says: "He would have returned to his enmities, if Pacideianus were seen compared with Esernius the Samnite; perhaps he would have bitten off his ear; certainly he would have returned to favor with Clodius." Thus says Marcus Tullius. It is more aptly said of a man who, no matter how much he is indignant, desires to harm more than he is able. For it is the way of women and children to seize an ear with their teeth. Concerning Esernius (or Eferninus) and Pacideianus <note>two famous gladiators</note>, we have spoken elsewhere on the authority of Flaccus <note>the poet Horace</note>.

### To put on a face.
<margin>LIII</margin>

Marcus Tullius seems to have been delighted by this word <note>original Greek: φαινοπροσώπειν (*phainoprosōpein*)</note>. He uses it repeatedly in his *Letters*. It means to display cheerfulness and benevolence in one's expression and brow, while you harbor something else in your mind. Hence that line of Maro <note>the poet Virgil</note>:
*He feigns hope on his face, while deep in his heart he suppresses pain.* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 1.209</note>

### Easy births.
<margin>LIIII</margin>

Theocritus in the *Encomium of Ptolemy*:
*Births are easy, and the children always resemble the father.* <note>original Greek: Ῥηΐδιαι δὲ γοναί...; Theocritus, Idyll 17.44</note>
There are easy births, but the offspring born never fails to resemble the father’s face. According to the legal experts, the father is the one whom the marriage designates, but the offspring does not always express the husband's face as the parent. Therefore, according to Flaccus <note>Horace, Odes 4.5.23</note>, *mothers are praised for similar offspring.* Although even here nature plays with variety, just as in almost everything. The offspring does not always resemble the mother or the father, but sometimes the paternal or maternal grandfather, sometimes the grandmother, sometimes an uncle or a great-grandfather.

CHILIAD FIVE, CENTURY I 1053

<margin>LV</margin>
### In the manner of hired mourners.

*Præficæ* was the name given to women hired for the purpose of lamenting at funerals, proclaiming the praises of the deceased, and leading the way for others in the manner of their weeping. They were called *præficæ* as if they were "placed in charge" <note>original Latin: *præfectæ*</note>. From this, a joke is directed at those who feign love or sorrow, when in fact they do whatever they do for the sake of profit. Lucilius, as cited by Nonius <note>Nonius Marcellus was a 4th-century grammarian whose work preserves many fragments of lost early Roman literature</note>:

> The hired mourners who weep for pay at someone else’s funeral,
> Tear their hair and cry out much more.

Horace imitated this:
> As those hired to wail at a funeral, say
> And do almost more than those grieving from the heart.

Plautus in his *Frivolaria*, according to Nonius:
> They surpassed all the hired mourners in their shrillness.

It is also suitable for those who, out of envy, cannot bear to praise anyone unless they have departed from this life. Naevius, as cited by Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century grammarian</note>: "By Hercules, I think this woman is a hired mourner, the way she praises the dead man so." It is common for wives to endlessly praise a deceased husband specifically to spite another person. It will also apply to those who, having nothing of their own worthy of praise, seek to appear significant by praising others. Plautus in the *Truculentus*: "I would consider a talkative citizen without virtue to be a hired mourner for me, one who praises others but cannot praise herself."

<margin>LVI</margin>
### Socrates' cock: or his callus.

Nonius Marcellus cites "Socrates' cock" from Varro to signify baldness. The passage suggests that a man found himself, when he began to sleep, as smooth as "Socrates' cock" <note>original: *Socratis gallus*</note>, only to have become a hedgehog with bristles and a snout. Whoever is speaking there means that when he went to bed, he had a smooth body without any hair on it, but in his sleep, he was transformed into a hedgehog, which is entirely hairy and has a snout like a pig. I know this passage is corrupt, and it does not escape me what the Aldine edition <note>the famous Venetian printing house of Aldus Manutius</note> contains, which reads "bald" <note>*calvum*</note> instead of "cock" <note>*gallo*</note>. The reading would be tolerable if for "bald" we read "callus" <note>*callum*</note>, in this way: "he found himself, when he began to sleep, as smooth as Socrates' callus or callous skin, only to have become a hedgehog, etc." 

Socrates was a man of the greatest physical endurance, who had grown hardened <note>*occalluerat*</note> to every labor; he walked with bare feet and slept on the ground. Hence the joke about "Socrates' callus." I am not unaware of what they tell regarding the plucked cock which Diogenes—if I am not mistaken—sent into Plato's school <note>Diogenes the Cynic famously plucked a chicken and brought it to Plato's Academy to mock Plato's definition of man as a "featherless biped"</note>, but it is more pleasing to read it as "callus." For the transition from the letter 'c' to its relative 'g' is easy. In the parts of the body that have a callus, hair does not grow, such as in the hollow of the feet and the palms of the hands. The unlettered common folk, wanting to signify they have nothing to give, usually show the palm of the hand and say: "Pluck a hair from here." The adage will be suitable for the destitute and the poor.

<margin>LVII</margin>
### As if from his mother’s knapsack.

Nonius Marcellus reports this trochaic tetrameter catalectic verse from Lucilius:

> Just as each of us is brought into the light from our mother's knapsack.

This can refer to nakedness and poverty. It can also refer to the condition of life being equal for all. For birth does not distinguish a Croesus from an Irus <note>Croesus was a legendary wealthy king; Irus was the beggar in Homer's Odyssey</note>, nor a king from a commoner. The cries of a queen in labor and a beggar woman are the same. The same wailing comes from a Caesar emerging and from the lowliest person. Nor is the "hollow" from which the son of a monarch presents himself any cleaner than that from which the offspring of a maidservant comes. Festus indicates the word "knapsack" <note>*bulga*</note> belonged to the Gauls, who once called little bags, purses, or leather sacks—that is, those made from skins—*bulgas*. Lucilius, with the liberty of a satirist, designated the womb or matrix by the name of a leather bag. What the Greeks say, "Naked as if from his mother," we have mentioned elsewhere.

<margin>LVIII</margin>
### To knock the prey from a hungry lion.

Nonius Marcellus cites this verse from Lucilius:

> As if to knock the prey out of the mouth of a hungry lion.

The verse stands if you remove the word "as," or what is closer to the truth, if you read "by force" <note>*vi*</note> instead of "as" <note>*ut*</note>; and if in the word "hungry" <note>*esurienti*</note> the syllable "ti" is shortened, or if you read "hungry" in a different case <note>*esuriente*</note>. The meter is somewhat harsh because it has no caesura, but it is not inconsistent with Lucilius's style of composition. The adage is very similar to the one we reported elsewhere: "To wrest the club from the hand of Hercules," and "To snatch the lamb from the wolf."

<margin>LIX</margin>
### Halopanta.

The ancients called a "Halopanta" one who lies about everything. Plautus in the *Curculio*: "By Pollux, Phaedromus has charmingly encountered this trifler; whether I should call him a *Halopanta* or rather a sycophant, I know not." These are the words of the soldier complaining about Curculio, who had deceived the pimp using the soldier's ring. Nonius Marcellus, citing this passage of Plautus, reports these things: "Halopanta or sycophan-

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "sycophant" (sycophantam) to be continued on the next page.</meta>

--- Page 1180 ---
<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s philological investigation into Roman and Greek adages, focusing on terms used by early Roman poets like Plautus and Lucilius. It follows a discussion of the obscure term "halopanta" or "halophanta" and transitions into proverbs regarding domestic life, deep affection, and military strategy.</meta>

...as a wicked race of men, who are hired for a most wretched wage to protect lies. Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note> explains it in this way: *halopanta* signifies someone who lies about everything. For the Greeks call someone who deceives "sinfully" <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\lambda\iota\tau\acute{\omega}\rho\omega\varsigma$</note> "all-things" <note>original Greek: $\pi\acute{\alpha}\nu\tau\alpha$</note>. However, I do not know how much credit should be given to fragments of this kind, which are no less corrupted than they are shortened. The Aldine edition <note>The famous printing house in Venice</note> had another etymology, but it was even more faulty. For if *halopanta* comes from "to wander" <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\lambda\acute{\epsilon}\omega$</note> or "to sin" <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\lambda\iota\tau\acute{\epsilon}\nu o\mu\alpha\iota$</note>, neither word has an aspirated first syllable [an 'h' sound]; and both have a short first syllable, whereas in Plautus it is long, as the meter of the Trochaic verse requires. Again, if it comes from "salt" <note>original Greek: $\ddot{\alpha}\lambda\omicron\varsigma$</note>, the aspiration fits, but this word also has a short first syllable. Add to this that it is a new form of word-composition from a noun rather than a verb; it would have been smoother as "all-deceiver" <note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\nu\delta\alpha\lambda\acute{\eta}\tau\eta\varsigma$</note>. Since there is a figure of speech called *paronomasia* <note>a pun or play on words</note> in these two words, *halophanta* <note>salt-informer</note> alludes more closely to "sycophant" <note>fig-informer</note> than *halopanta* does. *Halophantes* <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\lambda\omicron\phi\acute{\alpha}\nu\tau\eta\varsigma$</note> seems to be the name for one who informs on those attempting to cheat the tax-collectors <note>term: *telonas*; Greek for tax-farmers</note> out of duties on salt, just as "sycophants" were named for those who informed on people exporting figs from Athens. If we read it as *amophanton* <note>original Greek: $\dot{\alpha}\mu\omicron\phi\acute{\alpha}\nu\tau\omega\nu$</note>, as if speaking of things belonging to others or lying in various ways, the meter fits, but the aspiration of the first vowel must be discarded. Yet the meter will stand if you pronounce it in the Greek way as *halophanten* or *sycophanten*. For then there will be an anapest <note>a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables followed by a long one</note> in the first place instead of a spondee. Plautus, moreover, not infrequently uses Greek forms in his comedy. But I leave this to be discussed by the learned.

<margin>LX</margin>
->One's own crust.<-

Even today it is commonly said that nothing tastes as good as food taken at one's own home. Nonius <note>Nonius Marcellus, a grammarian who preserved many fragments of lost Latin literature</note> cites this half-line from the *Priapeia* of Catullus: "It is my desire to lick from my own." He used "to lick" <note>original Latin: *ligurire*</note> to mean tasting with pleasure. But the Homeric gods prefer to be invited to the smoke of sacrifices rather than to live "from home" <note>original Greek: $\omicron\iota\kappa\acute{\omicron}\theta\epsilon\nu$</note>. He also cites from Plautus's *Persa*: "To gobble up from one's own, if there is anything at home."

<margin>LXI</margin>
->To give chewed food from the mouth.<-

We are said to give "chewed food from the mouth" to those we love dearly, a metaphor taken from mothers and nurses. Lucilius <note>A Roman satirist of the 2nd century BC</note>, as cited by Nonius:
> Hoping that if he could extend his life for an equal age,
> He would give him food chewed from his own mouth.

Although Marcus Tullius [Cicero] and Aulus Gellius used "to pre-chew" <note>original Latin: *præmandere*</note> in a slightly different sense, as we have noted previously.

<margin>LXII</margin>
->From the marrow, Eye.<-

The ancients expressed deep affection in various ways: "from the heart," "from the soul," "with the whole breast" (of which we have spoken), "deeply," "from the innermost parts," "from the marrow" <note>original Latin: *medullitus*</note>, "from the soul" <note>original Latin: *animitus*</note>, "from the eyes" <note>original Latin: *oculitus*</note>. Plautus, in Nonius under *Cornices*: "Who [loves] my maidservant diligently from his eyes." For it is the way of lovers to call a person "eye" <note>original Latin: *oculus*</note> who is uniquely dear. In the play *Mostellaria*: "Hooray, my eye!" Again: "I wish to please my Philolaches, my eye, my protector."

<margin>LXIII</margin>
->Wisdom is the pilot of the ship.<-

It has been said by the wisest men that even in war, plans have more weight than strength. Titinnius <note>A writer of Roman comedy</note> expressed the same thing elegantly, as cited by Nonius:
> But with wisdom the pilot steers the ship, not by brute force.

<margin>LXIV</margin>
->A new sieve on a new peg.<-

It is by no means obscure that this was tossed about as a proverb, which Nonius cites from Varro's *Eumenides*, where it is said that Zeno was the first to hang a new heresy on a new peg. He is noting Zeno, who first introduced the sect of the Stoics at Athens, and did so with new reasoning and paradoxes. The same in *Bimargus*: "Just as a new sieve hangs from a new peg." For so the Aldine edition has it. It will suit those who devise something new.

<margin>LXV</margin>
->A patch-worker [sews] the top of the rag.<-

In the same author, this verse is cited from Lucilius: "It is the mark of a patch-worker to be best at the top of the rag." It seems to be a trochaic tetrameter catalectic verse <note>a specific rhythm in ancient poetry</note>, and it stands by eliding the 's' in *sarcinatoris*. *Sarcinator* [patcher] is named from *sarcina* [bundle or load], not from *sarciendo* [patching or stuffing]. It agrees with what we have reported elsewhere: "It is the mark of a good poet to be at his best in the final act." However, the saying from Lucilius has a more genuine and charming appearance of an adage.

<margin>LXVI</margin>
->Defeated in battle, but not in the war.<-

He is not immediately the victor who has come out on top in one or another action of a business, but he who has won the whole case. For a "battle" <note>original Latin: *prælium*</note> is a military conflict, but the "war" <note>original Latin: *bellum*</note> refers to this entire period, even if there is a lull in battles or if a truce intervenes. Peace alone ends a war; a truce merely breaks off the engagement. Nonius cites these trochaics from Lucilius: "As the Roman people, conquered by force and overcome...

<meta>catchword: overcome</meta>

<summary>Erasmus provides philological analysis of obscure Latin terms and proverbs, drawing on early Roman poets like Plautus and Lucilius to explain metaphors for affection, novelty, and the distinction between a single battle and a whole war.</summary>
<keywords>halopanta, philology, Plautus, Lucilius, Nonius Marcellus, Zeno, Stoicism, Latin proverbs, Greek etymology, Roman comedy</keywords>

--- Page 1181 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on military persistence and transitions into a series of Greek and Roman proverbs. The catchword "Ad pi-" at the end of the previous page suggests a reference to "Ad pignus" (To a pledge) or similar, but the text here concludes a thought on the distinction between losing a battle and losing a war.</meta>

...often defeated in many battles, but never in a war, in which all things are at stake. This agrees with the saying: *A man who flees will also fight again.*

->**Run again.**<-
->**LXVII**<-

<term>Trech’ authis</term> <note>original Greek: Τρέχ’ αὖθις</note>, that is, "Run again." This is cited by Lucian <note>a 2nd-century Syrian satirist who wrote in Greek</note> in the tragedy titled *Ocypus* <note>The name means "Swift-foot"</note>, as if it were a joke born in a barbershop. Although this entire poem is full of errors and lacks even a grain of Lucianic wit, it introduces a young man suffering from <term>podagra</term> <note>gout, a painful inflammation of the joints</note> who nevertheless pretended to be swift-footed. When asked by an old man how his foot came to be in pain, he replied that while running at great speed, he had grazed his ankle, and the agony came from that. To this, the old man replies:

*Run again, as someone said, or while sitting,*
*Pluck your beard under the arms of the barbers.*

If you read the phrase as <term>eipen hos</term> <note>original Greek: εἶπεν ὅς</note>, the sense will be: "Run again, as a certain man said, who while sitting plucks his beard under the elbows of the barbers"—that is, one who is being treated by a barber. People with gout seek remedies from barbers, yet they do not want to appear to have gout; they want it to look like the foot was injured in another way, such as from excessive running. Meanwhile, someone being shorn, sensing the cause is a lie, replies: "Run again." For that is usually the remedy for a similar ailment: after the tendon has warmed up from violent motion, the pain ceases. This can be seen daily in horses, which after a run either do not limp at all or limp more lightly. It is more probable, however, that instead of <term>keireon</term> <note>original Greek: κειρέων, meaning "of the barbers"</note> one should read <term>keirian</term> <note>original Greek: κειριᾶν</note>, a participle from the verb meaning "to be shaggy and in need of a barber." This refers to someone who, sitting in a barbershop, plucks his shaggy beard under his armpits. For such people sit there in idleness and gossip. As Horace <note>the Roman lyric poet</note> says:

*Gently cleaning his own nails with a small knife.*

If my interpretation does not please someone, let them follow whatever seems more attractive; the matter is not of great importance.

->**A nurse’s cloak.**<-
->**LXVIII**<-

Because nurses handle infants, they often have clothes contaminated by <term>bua</term> <note>a Latin nursery word for a drink or spit-up</note>, saliva, urine, and liquid excrement. Hence Plautus <note>a Roman playwright</note> says in his play *The Bacchis Sisters*: "If you had made a mistake in a single syllable, your hide would become as spotted as a nurse's cloak." In the sacred scriptures, there is frequent mention of a "menstruated cloth" <note>likely referring to Isaiah 30:22</note>.

->**With the scrapings.**<-
->**LXIX**<-

By a proverbial metaphor, a person is said to have returned something "with the scrapings" when they have returned the whole thing without any part being cut away. It appears to be taken from blacksmiths, who keep for themselves whatever they have filed off with a tool. Plautus says in *The Bacchis Sisters*: "Because I returned everything to my father, down to the last scraping." The phrase "with the scrapings" is added for the sake of <term>auxesis</term> <note>original Greek: αύξήσεως, meaning emphasis or exaggeration</note>. He interprets it himself by adding "everything entirely," that is, absolutely everything, "with the little dust" and "with the rust," phrases we have discussed elsewhere. Plautus says in *The Rope*: "He will now sweep me all away, along with the little dust."

->**Cheaper than a dead man.**<-
->**LXX**<-

Nothing is more dejected than a corpse. Plautus says in the same play: "Come now, have a good heart." "From where should I have it? A dead man is of more value than I am." And in *The Persian*, one character calls another <term>morticinum</term> <note>carrion or a carcass</note> out of contempt: "By Hercules, even if I cut your face off, I would not fear you, you piece of carrion!"

->**More than Clinia from Demetrius.**<-
->**LXXI**<-

Plautus says in the same play: "You shall hear more evils from me today than Clinia ever heard from Demetrius." Some learned men read "Lamia" in this passage instead of "Clinia." And it is true that a woman named Lamia was loved beyond measure by Demetrius, the King of the Macedonians—for which reason he was indeed spoken ill of by the public—but we nowhere read that she was treated with insults by the king. Furthermore, the name "Lamia" does not fit the meter of the poem. It is more likely that the line is taken from a comedy by Turpilius titled *Demetrius*, or some other play, where a father rebukes his son at great length and quite bitterly. For such a Clinia is introduced in *The Self-Tormentor* <note>a play by Terence</note>, who, having been rebuked too often and too harshly by his father, finally fled into military service. I suspect Plautus might be alluding to this story. For it is possible that Terence named the old man Menedemus instead of Demetrius. The fact that Terence came after Plautus is no obstacle, since the Greek author of the original play <note>Menander</note> was earlier than both.

->**At a full pace.**<-
->**LXXII**<-

Those who have touched upon a matter lightly are said to have entered "with the tip of the foot"; conversely, those who have undertaken something with great zeal are said to have entered "at a full pace." Trebonius says to Cicero in Book 12: "For as I see he is prepared and has entered at a full pace, we shall not cease to encourage him, so that he may proceed further day by day in learning and exercising himself."

<page-num>1065</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

<margin>LXXIII</margin>
### When it comes to the javelins.

<term>Cicero</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator</note> in a small book *On Military Affairs*—if indeed the title is not misleading—says: "The first and second lines, when it comes, as they say, to the javelins, sustain the whole weight of the battle." A <term>pilum</term> <note>original Latin: pilum</note> is a type of Roman spear, but shorter. Therefore, when a matter is handled at close quarters, it is said "to have come to the javelins." I seem to recall recording this adage elsewhere, but at the moment the location does not occur to me.

<margin>LXXIIII</margin>
### To pray with veiled hands.

Those who pray as suppliants are said to "pray with veiled hands." This is taken from an ancient custom of speakers, by which those who came to seek peace would hold out an olive branch. I believe "veiled" was said instead of "bound with ribbons" <note>Erasmus notes a linguistic shift from "velatas" to "vittatis," referring to the woolen ribbons or "vittae" that adorned sacred branches</note>. <term>Plautus</term> <note>a Roman comic playwright</note> in the play *Amphitryon*: "The next day the leading men come to us from the city into the camp weeping; they pray with veiled hands that we might forgive their sin."

<margin>LXXV</margin>
### The cicadas will sing for themselves.

<note>original Greek: οἱ τέττιγες ἑαυτοῖς χαμόθεν ᾄδοντ'</note>, that is, "The cicadas will sing for themselves from the ground." <term>Aristotle</term> <note>the Greek philosopher</note> in his third book <note>of the Rhetoric</note> brings this example from the poet <term>Stesichorus</term> as a figure of speech in which one says what one does not say. He adds nothing else from which you could grasp the meaning of the saying, except that I suspect the poet threatened those by whom he had been harmed with these words; for if he could not avenge himself otherwise, he would certainly deliver them to infamy through his poems. He cites the same thing in the second book of the same work among obscurely stated maxims: <note>original Greek: ὅπερ Στησίχορος ἐν Λοκροῖς εἶπεν, ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ὑβριστὰς εἶναι, ὅπως μὴ οἱ τέττιγες χαμόθεν ᾄδωσιν</note>, "Which indeed Stesichorus said among the Locrians: That one ought not to be insolent, lest the cicadas sing from the ground." 

Cicadas are a symbol for poets; he said "from the ground" because of their poverty and humble condition. Every animal threatens with the weapons with which it has been equipped by nature. Poets have nothing besides verses, with which they nevertheless transmit a man, whether "white or black" <note>meaning good or bad</note>, to posterity. For this reason, <term>Plato</term> is said to have been accustomed to warn his friends not to make any poetic man their enemy. For, as <term>Horace</term> <note>Erasmus uses his surname Flaccus</note> says, the tribe of seers is irritable, and among them are those who "have hay on their horn" <note>a Roman expression for a dangerous or hot-tempered person, referring to a bull whose horns were tied with hay as a warning</note>. 

However, it pleases some learned men that Stesichorus's saying refers to something else. Since cicadas are accustomed, as <term>Virgil</term> <note>Erasmus uses his name Maro</note> attests, to sing in trees, it appears that Stesichorus, in a civil manner, warned the Locrians with this riddle that they should not, through insolence and a lack of restraint in harming their neighbors, finally provoke them to war. For if an army entered their borders and cut down all the orchards in the fields as an enemy, it would happen that the cicadas would then begin to sing to them on the ground, because the trees they used to sit upon had been removed. Perhaps <term>Gregory Nazianzen</term> <note>a 4th-century Archbishop and theologian</note> relates something similar, whose commentaries on this work we have seen in Venice.

<margin>LXXV</margin>
### Fame brings all things to light.

<term>Aeschines</term> <note>the Athenian orator</note> in his speech *Against Timarchus* refers to a sentiment from <term>Euripides</term>:
> <note>original Greek: φήμη τ' ἔσθλον κᾄν μυχῷ δείκνυσι γῆς</note>, that is,
> "Fame reveals a good man even in the hollows of the earth."

He interprets that the poet felt that not only is the virtue of the living made famous by rumor, but also that of the dead. The earth covers the body, but fame does not allow what someone has done well in life to be hidden. In the same place, he cites a verse of <term>Hesiod</term> which we have mentioned before:
> <note>original Greek: φήμη δ' οὔτις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυτ', ἥν τινα λαοὶ / Πολλοὶ φημί ζωσι, θεός νύ τις ἐστὶ καὶ αὐτή</note>
> "No rumor is ever entirely lost which many people talk about; for rumor is also a kind of goddess."

He cites this passage also in his speech *On the False Embassy*.

<margin>LXXVI</margin>
### To act the Boeotian.

Among the insults with which <term>Aeschines</term> stones <term>Demosthenes</term> <note>the famous Athenian statesman</note>, he even threw this: that he shouted immoderately and indecorously in the manner of the <term>Boeotians</term> <note>people from Boeotia, a region of Greece often stereotyped as rustic or dull-witted</note>. <note>original Greek: ταῦτα δέ με μεταξὺ λέγονθ' ἀναβοᾷ παμμέγεθες Δημοσθένης, ὡς ἴασι πάντες οἱ συμπρέσβεις ἡμῶν, ἢ γὰρ πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις κακοῖς βοιωτιά ζει</note>, that is: "While I was saying these things, Demosthenes cried out loudly, as all who were our colleagues in that embassy know. For besides other evils, he even acts the Boeotian." In the "shouting" there is an allusion to the lowing of oxen <note>the name Boeotia was traditionally thought to derive from 'bous', the Greek word for ox</note>. Although "acting the Boeotian" can also be taken to mean favoring the interests of the Boeotians.

<margin>LXXVII</margin>
### A sprout bearing a sprout.

Those who are weak individually nevertheless have much strength when joined in harmony. So <term>Ennius</term> <note>an early Roman poet</note> says in <term>Festus</term> <note>a Roman grammarian</note>: "One branch [surus] bearing another [surum], yet they could defend themselves." For the ancients, as Festus reminds us, said *surus*, from which we say *surculus* <note>the diminutive form, meaning a small sprout or sprig</note>. It does not escape me that the poem is quoted even in the Aldine edition <note>the famous press of Aldus Manutius in Venice</note>; perhaps it should read: "If one branch bore another, even..."

<meta>catchword: to carry down</meta>

<header>FIFTH THOUSAND, FIRST HUNDRED</header>
<sig>Vuu</sig>
<meta>catchword: Virtue</meta>

...could defend himself or themselves. The trunk has strength; the shoots have no power unless they are joined.

### Salacones.
->LXXIX<-

Just as Irus and Codrus <note>Irus was the beggar in the Odyssey; Codrus was a legendary king of Athens who sacrificed himself, but whose name became synonymous with poverty in later satire</note> became staples of common folk tales on account of their destitution, so too did a certain man named Salacon, a man of extreme poverty, bring it about that all those of meager fortune were called "Salacones," and poverty itself was called "Salaconia." Hesychius <note>a 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> mentions this, but he also indicates that the same name was used to mark out the haughty and the arrogant. From this is derived the verb <term>salakonizein</term> <note>original Greek: σαλακωνίζειν</note> and <term>salakoneuesthai</term> <note>original Greek: σαλακωνεύεσθαι</note>, which means to walk with a rhythmic and delicate gait. They add the testimony of Theophrastus <note>a Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note>, who used the word <term>salakon</term> <note>original Greek: σαλάκωνα</note> to describe one who squanders his possessions recklessly and is reduced to poverty through ostentation and luxury. The word itself seems to be derived from the verb <term>salassein</term> <note>original Greek: σαλάσσειν</note>, which means to be shaken or to tend toward ruin.

### Archilochus’s song.
->LXXX<-

<term>Archilochou melos</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀρχιλόχου μέλος</note>, that is, the song of Archilochus, was a name given to a hymn that could be adapted for many people. They say such a song was invented by Archilochus, who lived before Pindar and other lyric poets of that kind, who used to decorate individuals with their own specific praises. Archilochus’s poem was the same for everyone and was sung to the lyre. The lyre-player simply repeated the names of the victors aloud at each interval of the song; for instance, if he were praising Hercules, he would sing: "Hail, King Hercules, the Great Victor" <note>original Greek: Tenella Callinice χαῖρ’ ἄναξ ἡράκλεις</note>. Or he would sing something else if he were celebrating someone else. Not dissimilar to this is what Horace reports regarding the painter who asked a sailor if he wanted anything added to a painting of a cypress tree <note>an allusion to a painter who could only paint one thing regardless of the commission</note>. This fits a primitive and unrefined situation. It is mentioned by the commentators on Aristophanes and Pindar. It is taken from Pindar’s seventh Olympian Ode: "The song of Archilochus, sounding at Olympia, the victory-song" <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν ἀρχιλόχου μέλος φωνᾶεν ὀλυμπίᾳ καλλίνικος</note>. In that passage, the commentator provides various explanations which do not seem necessary to repeat for our present purpose.

### The whole-rush.
->LXXXI<-

We previously mentioned a phrase from the oration of Aeschines <note>an Athenian orator and rival of Demosthenes</note>, <term>concerning the un-moistened whole-rush</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ ὁλοσχοίνου ἀβρόχου</note>, whereas lexicographers have <term>holoschoenos</term> <note>original Greek: ὁλοσχοίνου</note> instead of <term>holoschoenos</term>. A commentator on Demosthenes cites an oration of Aeschines against Demosthenes <term>On the False Embassy</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ παραπρεσβείας</note>, and also Theophrastus in his fourth book. In Aeschines, I found the word <term>holoschoenos</term> <note>original Greek: ὁλόσχοινος</note>. Similarly, Theophrastus, in the fourth book of his *Inquiry into Plants*, among those plants that grow in water, identifies (as the scholiast notes) three kinds of <term>schoinos</term> <note>original Greek: σχοίνου</note>, that is, types of broom or rush. One is sharp, which they call "male," meaning it bears no fruit; the second is fruitful, which they call <term>melankranis</term> <note>original Greek: μελαγκρανίς</note> from its black fruit; the third is called <term>holoschoenos</term> <note>original Greek: ὁλόσχοινος</note>, which surpasses the others in thickness, size, and toughness. He considers this last one more suitable for weaving ropes, as it is softer and fleshier. Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist</note> in his fourth book distinguishes the types slightly differently, but notes that the third, called <term>holoschoenos</term>, is both rougher and tougher than the rest. As for why some wrote <term>fish</term> <note>original Greek: ἰχθύϊ</note> instead of <term>rush</term> <note>original Greek: σχοίνῳ</note>, I suspect the reason was that Theophrastus mentioned "fleshiness," as if it were a novel thing to hear of the "flesh" of an apple or a cherry. However, the land-urchin, which they call a hedgehog, agrees with the "whole-rush" in this respect: it has a roughness; hence its skin, removed with the spines, is useful for scrubbing vessels. Accordingly, the expression seems to be used for a harsh and insolent speech, with which we might, as it were, strike someone's mouth. I did not wish to hide this bit of an appendix from the reader.

### The Tale of Alcinous.
->LXXXII<-

<term>The Tale of Alcinous</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀπόλογος Ἀλκινόου</note> is recorded in the Greek collections, as we have mentioned before. We guessed its origin then from Homer’s *Odyssey*, in which Odysseus told many lies about himself at a banquet; it would not be an absurd interpretation if the "Tale of Alcinous" were called a fictional narrative delivered at Alcinous's court. Aristotle, however, in the third book of the *Rhetoric*, when he mentions this tale in passing, speaks in such a way that he seems to have noted some writer who forged a speech to Penelope, weaving together all the things that could have happened over many years, telling fictional events as if they were true. Perhaps a writer named Alcinous introduced the character of Odysseus recounting many things to Penelope, as if he had truly suffered them either in war or on his journey. The passage in Aristotle reads: "Furthermore, one must relate past events, provided that they bring about pity or indignation if they are not being currently enacted. An example is the tale of Alcinous, where it is made to Penelope in sixty verses" <note>original Greek: ἔτι πεπραγμένα δεῖ λέγειν ὅσα μὴ πραττόμενα ἢ οἶκτον ἢ δείνωσιν φέρει. παράδειγμα ὁ ἀλκινόου ἀπόλογος, ὅτε πρὸς τὴν πηνελόπην ἐν ἑξήκοντα ἔπεσι πεποίηται</note>. Trapezontius <note>George of Trebizond, a 15th-century translator of Aristotle</note> the translator seems to have read: "Furthermore, one must relate events *not* done as if they were done," etc. But even so, the passage does not seem free of errors. Therefore, we will suspend judgment here until we have obtained something more certain, either from Gregory Nazianzen’s commentaries on these books or from elsewhere.

It also investigates the literary origins of the "Tale of Alcinous" as a reference for long-winded or fictional narratives.</summary>

<page-num>1058</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>
<meta>catchword: fallen</meta>

### Eternal virtue. LXXXIII

Pindar <note>a Greek lyric poet from Thebes, famous for his odes celebrating athletic victories</note> in the ninth *Olympian Ode* records a sentiment of this kind: *A man who has performed noble deeds forgets the struggle of Hades.* <note>original Greek: ἀϊδάρι λάθεται ἀγῶνα πραΰας ἀνὴρ</note> That is, a man who has conducted himself in a manner worthy of himself forgets the realm of the dead. Life is short, but the memory of good deeds is immortal. Therefore, those who have performed illustrious actions worthy of eternal memory depart from life with a more peaceful mind; they do not dread death in the same way, because they understand that they will live forever in the glory of their name among posterity.

### Let him teach who has learned. LXXXIIII

The same author in the same *Ode* says: *Furthermore, it is easier for one who has learned to teach.* <note>original Greek: τὸ δ’ ἀδάεδαυ δὲ τοι ἀϊδρῆ παίτερον</note> This is similar to the saying: "Learn, but from those who are learned." <note>A common pedagogical maxim, often attributed to the *Distichs of Cato*</note> No one passes on an art to another more easily than one who understands it precisely. For such a person knows how to condense many things into a summary and knows how to give light to obscure matters. Consequently, the reason why some people lead young students around in so many circles and hold them back in their studies is either for the sake of profit, or out of spite, or due to their own lack of skill.

### Speed is best in times of trouble. LXXXV

Sophocles <note>one of the three great ancient Greek tragedians</note> in *Antigone*:
*For in the face of present evils, the shortest path is best.* <note>original Greek: Βράχισα γὰρ κράτισα τ’ ἐν ποσὶν κακά.</note> ->that is,<-
When evils are pressing, speed is the best course.
These are the words of the Chorus to Creon <note>the king of Thebes in Sophocles' tragedy</note> amidst the various griefs of his house when he desires to be removed from life. For to die quickly when one is weary of life is something of a gain. Nothing is more distressing than to be tortured in spirit for a long time if some evil is imminent that cannot be avoided; it is best to ensure that it lasts as short a time as possible.

### I am nothing. LXXXVI

In the same play:
*Lead me away from here,*
*I who am no more than one who is already nothing.* <note>original Greek: Ἄγετε μ’ ἐκποδὼν Τὸν οὐκ ὄντα μᾶλλον ἢ μηδένα.</note> ->that is,<-
Lead me away from the midst.
I, who am no more than he who is already non-existent.
By this figure of speech, they signified a destruction without hope of recovering one's well-being. I know that I have previously mentioned "We were Trojans" <note>a phrase from Virgil's Aeneid indicating total downfall</note> and "I am nothing," but on account of the renewed form of the expression, I was pleased to add this here.

### The first part of happiness is wisdom. LXXXVII

In the conclusion of the same play:
*By far the first requirement of happiness is wisdom.* <note>original Greek: Πολλῷ τὸ φρονεῖν εὐδαιμονίας πρῶτον ὑπάρχει.</note> ->that is,<-
To be happy, by far the first thing is to be Wise.
This was said of Creon, who, choosing to obey his own spirit rather than right counsel, utterly destroyed both his family and himself. Great fortune is easily turned into great calamity if wisdom is absent. A little earlier, the author expressed the same idea in contrary words when speaking of Haemon <note>Creon's son, who committed suicide</note>, who had taken his own life:
*Showing among men that lack of counsel*
*Is by far the greatest evil attached to a man.* <note>original Greek: Δείξας ἐν ἀνθρώποισι τὴν ἀβουλίαν Ὅσῳ μέγισον ἀνδρὶ πρόσκειται κακόν.</note> ->that is,<-
Showing that ill-advised rashness, when joined
To a man, is by far the greatest of evils.

### He saw justice too late. LXXXVIII

Again in the same work:
*Alas, it seems you see justice too late.* <note>original Greek: οἴ μ’ ἔοικας ὀψὲ τὴν δίκην ἰδεῖν.</note> ->that is,<-
Oh, how you seem to perceive what is just only when it is too late.
This was said of Creon, who at first obeyed neither Tiresias <note>the blind prophet of Thebes</note> nor any of his own people; taught by great disasters, he blames his own folly. The same sentiment is repeated in the conclusion of the tragedy, but in a different phrasing:
*Having paid the penalty of great blows for their boastful words,*
*They teach wisdom in old age.* <note>original Greek: Μεγάλας δὲ πληγὰς τῶν ὑπεραύχων ἀποτίσαντες, γήρᾳ τὸ φρονεῖν ἐδίδαξαν.</note> ->that is,<-
After the gods have exacted terrible punishments for proud words,
They teach how to be wise in the final stage of life.
This agrees with the saying: "The Phrygians learn wisdom too late." <note>An adage referring to those who only become wise after they have been harmed</note>

### Swift vengeance. LXXXIX

Regarding the late vengeance of the divine powers, it has been testified in several proverbs which we have cited above. But what Sophocles says about the prompt vengeance of the gods is more to the point here: that those who have fallen into some...

<summary>This page explores adages derived from Greek tragedy and lyric poetry, emphasizing that true happiness stems from wisdom and that noble deeds grant a form of immortality, while folly and pride lead to swift or late-arriving ruin.</summary>
<keywords>Pindar, Sophocles, Antigone, Creon, wisdom, immortality, death, justice, vengeance, pedagogical methods</keywords>

--- Page 1185 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of adages drawn from Greek tragedy, specifically focusing on Sophocles' *Antigone*. Erasmus moves from general wisdom about acting in time to specific reflections on the relationship between kings, fate, and the divine authority of seers.</meta>

<page-num>1059</page-num>
<header>THE FIRST HUNDRED OF THE FIFTH CHILIAD</header>

Having fallen into misfortune, let us return to our senses in good time. These are the words of the Chorus to Creon: <note>The Chorus in Sophocles' *Antigone* (lines 1103–1104) advises the king to correct his errors before it is too late.</note>
"O King, do this as quickly as you can, for the swift-footed harms of the gods suddenly overtake the wicked by a short-cut." <note>original Greek: ὠκὺ γ' ἄναξ τάχιστα συντέμνουσι γὰρ Θεῶν ποδώκεις καὶ κακόφρονας βλάβαι</note>

This happened to Creon, for whom vengeance arrived almost before the prophecy of Tiresias <note>the blind prophet of Thebes</note> was fulfilled.

->One must not resist fate.<- XC

In the same play, Creon speaks thus:
"But one must not struggle against necessity." <note>original Greek: ἀνάγκη δ' οὐχὶ δυσμαχητέον</note> That is: against the fates, since it is very difficult, one must not struggle.

We have cited the same sentiment elsewhere from various authors. No one can avoid what God sends upon us. Moreover, that which cannot be avoided must be endured, not blamed. For "the fates lead the willing, but drag the unwilling," as the Tragic poet <note>Seneca the Younger, in his *Epistles*</note> says.

->One should not revile a seer.<- XCI

In the same play, Creon speaks to Tiresias—who, in the manner of prophets, was growing heated and attacking the king with quite free speech—as follows:
"I do not wish to speak ill of the seer in return." <note>original Greek: Οὐ βούλομαι σὺ μάντιν ἀντ' εἰπεῖν κακῶς</note>
What Horace says—"The irritable race of bards" <note>original Latin: *Genus irritabile uatum*</note>—applies not only to poets, but much more so to diviners. One must use flattery if you wish to extract anything from them; if you provoke them, they prophesy nothing but evils. This is suitable for use when someone attacks us with an unrestrained insult, as if inspired by some madness, whom we do not wish to revile in turn for the sake of honor, even though there is no lack of things to hurl back; or when we grant that liberty to anger, as if to a kind of madness. For you can no more sanely argue with an angry man using insults than with a madman. This is close to what we recorded before: "Leave the seer alone." <note>Adage 4.9.91</note> Furthermore, that other saying: "Were you not my father," which appears in this same play spoken by Haemon <note>Creon's son, who argues with his father over Antigone's fate</note>.

->The race of seers is greedy.<- XCII

In the same scene, Creon speaks thus to Tiresias:
"For the entire race of seers is fond of money." <note>original Greek: Τὸ μαντικὸν γὰρ πᾶν φιλάργυρον γένος</note>
In olden times, divine augurs and soothsayers had a bad reputation on this account. Today, I only wish that those who handle divine matters did not hear the same, perhaps deservedly. One who speaks to gain favor with men, being corrupted by gifts, cannot always speak the truth.

->To speak of things that should not be moved.<- XCIII

In the same place, Tiresias, now more irritated, thus threatens Creon:
"You provoke me so that I am forced to speak out those things which lie hidden and unmoved in my heart." <note>original Greek: ὄρσεις με τ' ἀκίνητα διὰ φρενῶν φράσαι</note>
This will be useful whenever the wickedness of our adversaries compels us to bring to light what we had decided to keep covered in silence. For Creon had stung him with an insult, saying:
"You are a wise seer, but fond of doing wrong." <note>original Greek: Σοφὸς σὺ μάντις, ἀλλὰ τ' ἀδικεῖν φιλῶν</note>
This itself is applicable to a man who is prudent or learned, but wicked. It is related to that other proverb: "You move things that should not be moved."

->To kill the dead again.<- XCIIII

In the same place are the words of Tiresias to Creon, urging him to allow the body of Polynices <note>Antigone's brother, whom Creon forbade from being buried</note> to be hidden in a tomb:
"Come, yield to the dead, and do not prick the one who has perished; what strength is there in killing the dead again?" <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' εἶκε τῷ θανόντι, μηδ' ὀλωλότα κέντει, τίς ἀλκὴ τὸν θανόντ' ἐπικτανεῖν;</note>
This is related to what we recorded elsewhere: "To cut the throat of the dead."

->No one can harm God.<- XCV

The sentiment is pious, but spoken by Creon with an impious heart:

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Sophocles' tragedy *Antigone*, specifically the dialogue between King Creon and the blind prophet Tiresias. On the previous page, Creon expressed his reluctance to revile the seer; here, Erasmus explores the theological and moral implications of their debate, drawing parallels between classical drama and Christian doctrine.</meta>

<page-num>1060</page-num>
<header>THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM</header>

"No man has the power to pollute the gods." <note>Erasmus's Latin: *Violare, siue polluere diuos, nemo quit mortalium*. This refers to *Antigone* line 1044, where Creon argues that even if eagles carried the flesh of the unburied Polynices to the throne of Zeus, he would not fear the pollution, as gods cannot be defiled by men.</note>

The ancients were persuaded that the gods of the underworld were offended if burial was denied to the dead, and that Zeus, the protector of suppliants, was offended if anyone rejected a suppliant. Yet Creon thought that such matters were of no concern to the gods, because they cannot be harmed by anyone. This verse can be sung against those who think it unworthy of God to have been hidden in the womb of a virgin and to have come forth through a virgin's womb—from which all other men proceed—or against those who think the body of the Lord is polluted because it descends into the unclean stomach of a man. <note>Erasmus frequently uses classical adages to defend Christian mysteries, here comparing the "unpollutable" gods of Sophocles to the purity of Christ in the Incarnation and the Eucharist.</note>

"No man has the power to pollute the gods." <note>original Greek: Θεὸς μιαίνῃ ὅτις ἀνθρώπων ἀγνή</note>

Even the sun is not polluted, though it shines through all manner of sewers and marshes. <note>A common philosophical trope used to explain how the divine can interact with the material world without losing its sanctity.</note>

### XCVI
->One must listen to one who speaks well.<-

Tiresias says in the same discourse:
"Having thought well of you, I speak well. It is most pleasant to learn from one who speaks well, if he speaks of profit." <note>original Greek: Εὖ σοι φρονήσας, εὖ λέγω. ἃ μανθάνειν δ’ ἥδισον εὖ λέγοντος, εἰ κέρδος λέγοι</note> That is:
Being well-disposed toward you, I speak well; it is most sweet to learn from one who speaks well, if he brings gain.

Haemon had spoken the same sentiment earlier:
"And for those who speak well, it is a fine thing to learn." <note>original Greek: Καὶ τῶν λεγόντων εὖ, καλὸν τὸ μανθάνειν</note> That is:
It is right and fitting to listen to one who speaks correctly.

This agrees with that saying, "Listen to what is spoken from the heart." Likewise with Hesiod, by whom he is also approved who obeys one who advises correctly.

### XCVII
->The razor of Fortune.<-

These are the words of the same Tiresias, warning Creon so that he might be wise when placed in the greatest danger.
"Consider that you are standing once more on the razor's edge of Fortune." <note>original Greek: φρόνει βεβὼς αὖ νῦν ἐπὶ ξυρῶ τύχης</note> That is:
Be wise, having been placed again on the razor of Fortune.

Upon the calamity which the strife of Eteocles and Polynices <note>the sons of Oedipus who killed each other</note> had stirred up, there followed this calamity which Creon stirred up by offending the gods. Although this verse was cited by us in passing elsewhere, it is found in the proverb, "On the edge of a razor."

### XCVIII
->A useful example.<-

Creon, threatening evil to his son Haemon who was acting too freely, speaks thus:
"You shall learn wisdom through weeping, being yourself empty of wisdom." <note>original Greek: Κλαίων φρενώσεις, ὢν φρενῶν αὐτὸς κενός</note> That is:
By weeping you shall cause others to have sense, while you yourself are void of sense.

When the wicked pay the penalties for their own folly, although they themselves become no better, they nevertheless serve as an example to others, lest through thoughtlessness they run into similar calamities.

### XCIX
->Stubbornness pays the penalty for folly.<-

In the same tragedy, Tiresias, warning Creon not to persist in his opinion as one headstrong and rigid, speaks thus:
"Stubbornness, indeed, incurs the charge of folly." <note>original Greek: Αὐθαδία γι, σκαιότητ’ ὀφλισκάνει</note> That is:
A headstrong mind pays the penalties of madness.

That intractable ferocity is usually the prelude to some great calamity, just as the proverbs of the Hebrews also indicate: "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall." <note>original Latin: *Contritionem præcedit superbia, & ante ruinam exaltatur spiritus*; see Proverbs 16:18.</note> Haemon expressed this saying of Tiresias elegantly in the same play, using a double metaphor of trees and sailors. The verse goes like this:
"You see how many trees by the winter torrents, by yielding, preserve their branches; but those that resist perish root and branch. In the same way, whoever, in control of a ship, keeps the sheet taut and yields nothing, is eventually overturned and sails with the benches downward." <note>original Greek: Ὁρᾷς παρὰ ῥείθροισι χειμάῤῥοις ὅσα Δένδρων ὑπείκει... σέλμασιν ναυτίλλεται</note> That is:
You see how in the downward rushes of torrents, the tree which gives way saves its shoots. But that which resists, perishes with the very stump. Likewise the pilot who, holding the tiller, [yields] nothing... <note>The text ends here as the page concludes.</note>

<header>SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIFTH CHILIAD</header>
<sig>Vuu 3</sig>

He yields to the breeze and the waves, he is rolled down,
And now, resting on his back, he sails outside the boat.
<note>Erasmus is finishing a thought from the previous page, using a poetic image of someone surrendering to fate or exhaustion, likely continuing the metaphor of the "ship of state" or personal ruin.</note>

->A companion in navigation.<-
<margin>C</margin>
We have mentioned before the saying: *To be in the same boat*, referring to those held by a common danger. Ismene alluded to this in the same play, saying she did not refuse to undergo the same danger that her sister Antigone was facing.
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ἐν κακοῖς τοῖς σοῖσιν οὐκ αἰσχύνομαι, Ξυμπλοῦν ἐμαυτὴν τοῦ πάθους ποιουμένη</note>
"But in your troubles I am not ashamed to make myself a fellow-passenger in your suffering." <note>Sophocles, *Antigone*, lines 540-541. Ismene, who originally refused to help Antigone bury their brother, now wishes to share the blame and punishment.</note>
That is to say:
But in your misfortunes I do not blush
To join your calamity, carried in the same vessel.

---

### SECOND CENTURY OF THE FIFTH CHILIAD

->The messenger is not to be blamed.<-
<margin>I</margin>
It is a common human impulse to be just as indignant toward someone reporting sad news as if they had actually done what they are reporting. Thus, when Creon is angry at the messenger for bringing news that was far from joyful, the messenger responds:
<note>original Greek: Ὁ δρῶν ἀνιᾷ τὰς φρένας, τὰ δ’ ὦτ’ ἐγώ</note>
"The one who did the deed tortures your mind; I only torture your ears." <note>*Antigone*, line 319.</note>
In the same messenger's lines:
<note>original Greek: Στέργει γὰρ οὐδεὶς ἄγγελον κακῶν ἐπῶν</note>
"For no one loves a messenger of evil words." <note>*Antigone*, line 277. This is the origin of the phrase "don't shoot the messenger."</note>
This can be applied to someone who warns another of a lapse; the person who committed the crime should be more angry at themselves than at the one who offers a necessary correction. For correction is briefly bothersome to the ears, but the conscience of a crime continually stabs the mind.

->What cannot be done should not even be started.<-
<margin>II</margin>
We have previously cited the phrase *to hunt the impossible*. Sophocles expressed this in other words in *Antigone*:
<note>original Greek: Ἀρχὴν δὲ θηρᾶν οὐ πρέπει τ’ ἀμήχανα</note>
"It is not fitting even to begin the hunt for things that cannot be achieved." <note>*Antigone*, line 92.</note>
These are the words of Ismene trying to deter Antigone from burying their brother Polynices against the royal edict.

->A hot heart in a cold matter.<-
<margin>III</margin>
The same Ismene, discouraging Antigone from her daring deed, says:
<note>original Greek: Θερμὴν ἐπὶ ψυχροῖσι καρδίαν ἔχεις</note>
"Truly, you have a hot heart for cold things." <note>*Antigone*, line 88.</note>
Elsewhere we have said that a daring and headlong deed is called "hot." Here she calls "cold" those things for which there was very little hope of a happy completion.

->To strive in vain is madness.<-
<margin>IIII</margin>
Again, in the same play, she speaks thus:
<note>original Greek: Τὸ δὲ περισσὰ πράσσειν οὐκ ἔχει νοῦν οὐδένα</note>
"To do what is superfluous is a mark of great madness." <note>*Antigone*, line 68.</note>
It is not only madness to do what is unjust, but also what is unnecessary. From unjust acts there is sometimes some gain; from unnecessary ones, there is none.

->The prince must be obeyed in all things.<-
<margin>V</margin>
It was said with a proverbial structure in the same tragedy, where Creon says:
<note>original Greek: Ἀλλ’ ὃν πόλις στήσειε, τοῦδε χρὴ κλύειν Καὶ σμικρὰ καὶ δίκαια καὶ τ’ ἐναντία</note>
"But whomever the city has appointed to the leadership, him one must hear, whether he commands trivial things, or just things, or even the opposites of these." <note>*Antigone*, lines 666-667.</note>
However, this is the voice of a tyrant, not a prince. For he who prescribes unjust things is no prince. <note>Erasmus often used his commentary on the classics to critique the absolute power of monarchs in his own time, distinguishing between a "prince" (a lawful ruler) and a "tyrant."</note>

->A city that is not a city.<-
<margin>VI</margin>
Haemon touches upon Creon's leaning toward tyranny in this way:
<note>original Greek: Πόλις γὰρ οὐκ ἔσθ’ ἥτις ἀνδρός ἐσθ’ ἑνός</note>
"For that is not a city which belongs to one man alone." <note>*Antigone*, line 737. Haemon, Creon's son, argues that a state belongs to its people, not just its ruler.</note>
