<meta>This page continues the discussion of Sophocles’ *Antigone* from page 1061, specifically the dialogue between King Creon and his son Haemon regarding the nature of governance and the role of the state.</meta>

<page-num>1062</page-num>
<header>DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES</header>

Creon had said that it was his own right, and no one else’s, to command the region. Haemon denies that it is a city where the ultimate power over all things lies with a single man. For the Greek word *Polis* <note>original: "Polis"</note> seems to be named either from "turning" or from "multitude"; the Latins call it a Republic. But it is not a Republic where all things are done and driven by the whim of one person. Therefore, when Creon had replied that the city is considered to belong to the one who commands it, Haemon adds:

<note>original Greek: Καλῶς, ἔρημός γ’ ἂν σὺ γῆς ἄρχοις μόνος.</note>
"Rightly so: you might rule as king alone over a deserted land."
->that is,<-
Rightly, so that you alone might play the king in a deserted field.
It is the mark of a king to rule over free men, and to attempt nothing without the consensus of the citizens.

### VII. Mind, the queen of heaven and earth.

Socrates says in Plato’s *Philebus*: <note>original Greek: πάντες γὰρ συμφωνοῦσιν οἱ σοφοί, ἑαυτῶν ὄντως σεμνύνοντες, ὡς νοῦς ἐστὶ βασιλεὺς ἡμῖν οὐρανοῦ τε καὶ γῆς.</note> "For all the wise agree, truly honoring themselves in this way, that the mind is our king of both heaven and earth." That is to say: For all the wise agree, honoring themselves by this agreement, that the mind is to us the queen of heaven and earth. He means that all things are governed by wisdom rather than by pleasure. For when Philebus had argued that happiness consists of a mixture of wisdom and pleasure, they began to investigate which of the two carried more weight toward achieving the blessed life. Since Plato says that "all" agree on this, he hints that it was a commonly repeated saying. This agrees with what Haemon says in Sophocles:

<note>original Greek: Πατήρ, θεοὶ φύουσιν ἀνθρώποις φρένας, πάντων ὅσ’ ἐστὶ κτημάτων ὑπέρτατον.</note>
"Father, the gods implant reason in mortals, which is the highest of all possessions that exist."
->that is,<-
Father, the gods insert the mind into mortals,
A thing which, above all else, surpasses all wealth.

### VIII. To throw the first spears.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book *On the Orator*, used the phrase "to throw the first spears" to mean "to skirmish" <note>original: "uelitari," referring to the *velites*, light-armed skirmishers in the Roman army</note>. He transfers this to the orator, whose speech at the beginning ought to be gentle and calm, so that the oration may gradually grow more heated. He notes there the orator Philip, who was accustomed to rise to speak in such a way that he did not know what the first word he was going to say would be; but he said that after he had "warmed up his arm," then he would fight. "And yet," Cicero says, "he does not notice that those very men from whom he draws the metaphor handle those first spears so gently that they serve gracefulness above all, and they preserve their remaining strength." It would be <term>prooimiasasthai</term> <note>original Greek: προοιμιάσεσθαι; to perform a prelude or introduction</note> if it were transferred to the beginning of a dispute or a legal contention. The same thing is expressed in a single word as "to skirmish."

### IX. Neglecting the sources to chase the streams.

In the same book, not without the appearance of a proverb, Cicero spoke of "chasing the streams" to describe saying things that are less pertinent to the matter, while neglecting the heart of the business. Jerome seems to have been quite delighted by this metaphor. The words of Marcus Tullius are as follows: "Nevertheless, it is a sign of a slow wit to chase the streams and not to see the sources of things." Also: "It is a mark of our age and our experience to summon what we want from the source, and to see from where all things flow."

### X. Matters of the wrestling floor and oil.

Things that are not applied to serious business, but to play and display, are called matters "of the wrestling floor and oil," since in battle there is need for greater strength. In the <term>palestra</term> <note>a Greek wrestling school</note>, men competed not armed but anointed with oil, both so that a grip would be more difficult and an escape easier, and so that the body would be more shining, for they competed naked. Marcus Tullius in the first book *On the Orator*: "There is a certain type of words that is polished and joyful, but more suited to the wrestling floor and oil than to this civil crowd and the forum." Of this sort is the trite sophistry found in certain schools today, which renders a man invincible for display and playful competition, but useless for serious dealings. Therefore, in the same book, a certain person rightly advises that we should lead speech out from home-based and "shadowy" exercise <note>the *umbratilis* life of the scholar in the shade vs. the soldier in the sun</note> into the middle of the battle-line, into the dust, into the shouting, into the camp, and into the fray of the forum. Similarly, in the second book, speaking of the disciples of Isocrates, he says: "But of those, some wished to be illustrious in the parade, others in the battle-line." In the first book *On the Laws*, he aims at the same point: "Antipater, however, a contemporary of Fannius, blew a bit more vehemently; he had strength, though indeed rustic and rough, without polish or the wrestling floor, but he was nonetheless able to warn the rest to write more carefully." That is what is said there. What he previously called "oil," he here calls "polish" <note>original: "nitorem"</note>. And in his book *On Famous Orators*, he calls that which is more polished "more oily" <note>original: "unctius"</note>. "Already," he says, "there was a certain more oily and more splendid custom of speaking." Again, in the *Orator* addressed to Brutus: "Rhythm, however, was not yet brought forth, nor did it have any necessity or kinship with speech; therefore, having been noted and recognized somewhat later, it brought to oratory a sort of wrestling school and the final finishing touches." He calls "the wrestling school" the gracefulness added to...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of rhetorical and proverbial expressions used by Cicero and other classical authors, transitioning from metaphors of painting to those of labor and law.</meta>

<page-num>1063</page-num>
<header>THE FIFTH THOUSAND, SECOND CENTURY</header>

...ostentation was employed. Furthermore, in these words, it was said not without a touch of the proverbial: **the final outlines** <note>original: "extrema lineamenta"</note> instead of **the finishing touch** <note>original: "extrema manu"</note>, a metaphor taken from the practice of painters.

->**XI. Day-laborers**<-

In the same passage, and not without a proverbial flair, he calls those who plead cases without the knowledge of philosophy **day-laborers** <note>original: "operarios"</note>. An architect, through his art, prescribes the rationale of the work, whereas the day-laborers do not apply their own judgment, but only their physical labor according to what has been prescribed. But one who is skilled in philosophy is prepared of his own accord to speak rightly on any matter. Marcus Tullius Cicero, speaking of Mnesarchus, said that "those whom we call orators are nothing but certain day-laborers with a fast and practiced tongue; but no one is truly an orator unless he is a wise man." Again, in his work *Brutus*: "For I care little that you have scraped together all those day-laborers, so that some seem to have wished to die just so they might be counted among the orators by you." In his book *On Famous Orators*, he calls orators of this sort **vocalists** <note>original: "vocales"</note>. "Let us add here also," he says, "lest we seem to have passed over any vocalist, Gaius Cosconius Calidianus." 

This can be applied to those preachers who, because they are poorly trained in sacred literature, learn by heart from collections of notes things to bellow <note>original: "detonent"</note> before the people with much shouting and much tossing of the body. Or those who sing in churches with a huge lowing sound <note>original: "boatu"</note> without understanding what they sing: they are not preachers, but day-laborers; not singers, but day-laborers.

->**XII. A schoolroom ditty**<-

Plautus, as I have noted before, calls things usually recited in comedies "theatrical trifles." Marcus Tullius Cicero calls a declamatory and youthful speech—one having more ostentation than wisdom—**a schoolroom ditty** <note>original: "e scholis cantilenam"</note>. The passage in the same book goes like this: "You must indulge these young men, Crassus, who do not seek the daily loquacity of some Greek, nor a ditty from the schools, but wisdom from the wisest and most eloquent of men; one who is a leader in counsel and tongue, not in little books, but in the greatest cases and in this home of empire and glory." 

It will be fitting to use this for those who have never been occupied with good authors, nor have drawn solid erudition from the original sources, but only hold onto things droned out in the schools. Of this kind are phrases like: "I would not believe the Gospel, were I not compelled by the authority of the Church," <note>Erasmus refers to a famous quote by St. Augustine, often used as a rote defense of Church power in his day.</note> and "Whatever is offered is ungrateful to the Holy Spirit if that which was owed is omitted," or "The Lord Jesus did many things which are not written," or "A sin is not forgiven unless the stolen property is restored."

->**XIII. Fashioned by a God**<-

Those who are vehemently inclined toward something by nature, we say in proverbial speech are "born, made, and sculpted" for it. Marcus Tullius elegantly expressed a remarkable natural dexterity in the same book. "There are some," he says, "so skillful in these matters by the gifts of nature, so adorned, that they seem not born, but **fashioned by some god** <note>original: "a deo ficti"</note>." He alluded to Pandora, whom Vulcan fashioned while the other gods likewise contributed their own gifts into one person.

->**XIV. From the circle**<-

We call a common and contemptible man "one from the crossroads." Marcus Tullius used **from the circle** <note>original: "è circulo"</note> for this. He calls a "circle" a small gathering of men chatting in the forum or in the squares. Thus Crassus, in the same book I just cited, says: "I have poured out to you everything I felt; perhaps if you had snatched any father of a family from some circle, he would have answered your questions with the same things."

->**XV. To lose the case; To lose by technicality; To join hands by law**<-

Just as the ancient legal experts used to say that someone was **called to join hands by law** <note>original: "ex iure manu consertum vocari"</note> when a lawsuit was intended against them, so one was said **to lose the case** <note>original: "causa cadere"</note> who, by conducting it poorly, lost his right to sue. Both become <term>idiotikon</term> <note>original: "ἰδιωτικὸν"; meaning a common or non-professional expression</note> if a metaphor is added. For instance, if someone were to say: "The theologians do not cease to call Laurentius Valla to join hands by law because he, a man of grammar, has occupied the territory of theology." Both expressions are found in Marcus Tullius in the same book under the persona of Scævola: "But as for what you assumed at the end of your speech as if by your own right—that an orator can move most fluently in every discussion of speech—had we not been in your kingdom, I would not have borne it, and I would be at the head of many who would either contend with you by interdict or call you to join hands by law." And a little later: "When Hypsæus with a very loud voice and many words pleaded before the praetor Marcus Crassus that the one he was defending might be allowed **to lose the case** <note>original: "causa cadere"</note>; while Gnaeus Octavius, a man of consular rank, refused in no less long a speech that his adversary should lose the case." The same is found in *Pro Murena*: "And if you think it a disgrace that, with you as an advocate, the very man you came to oppose should lose his case." Quintilian also mentions this in Book 7, Chapter 4. Among the ancients, it was superstitiously observed that whoever, in initiating an action, failed in even a single word...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal metaphors used as proverbs, specifically focusing on how a minor technical error could cause a litigant to lose their entire case. The text begins mid-word with the conclusion of the previous page's sentence regarding a "slip of a syllable" (syllabo).</meta>

...if he had slipped by a single syllable, he would **lose his case** <note>original: "causa caderet"</note>. Not a few traces of this superstition still remain among the English, who sometimes reject an entire legal instrument if a single letter in a surname has been written incorrectly. Justinian, in the *Institutes of Law*, Book 4, Title "On Actions," in the paragraph "If anyone," says: "If anyone, in making his claim, includes more than belongs to him, he **lost his case** <note>original: "causa cadebat"</note>," that is, he lost the property, nor was he easily **restored to his original state** <note>original: "in integrum restituebat," a legal remedy to undo a loss</note> unless he was under twenty-five years of age, etc. In the next paragraph, he shows that this word "more" is understood in four ways: in matter, time, place, and cause. In **matter**, if someone asks for twenty gold coins instead of ten; in **time**, if someone asks for it before the due date or before a condition is met; in **place**, if someone asks in Rome for what was promised in Ephesus; in **cause**, if someone who had stipulated for either the slave Stichus or twenty gold coins asks for Stichus alone in a simple action, since the choice of which to pay belonged to the promisor. To express the same thing, one may say **to lose the matter** <note>original: "rem amittere"</note>, **to lose the suit** <note>original: "litem perdere"</note>, and **to fail the formula** <note>original: "formula cadere"</note>. Justinian, Book 4, Title "On Exceptions," in the paragraph "It is called," says: "When they rashly brought a matter into court and wasted it, by that reasoning they lost the matter." Horace says in his *Satires*:

> And by chance he now had to answer his bail,
> which if he had not done, he would **lose his suit**.

Quintilian, in Book 3, Chapter 8, writes: "Nor am I unaware that many things are transferred in almost all cases in which someone is said to have **failed the formula**; these are the questions: whether it is permitted to this person, or with this person, or by this law, or before this judge, or at this time." Seneca, in his sixth book of *Epistles*, Letter 49, speaking of philosophers who show off their learning with clever wordplay, says: "For what else are you doing, when you knowingly lead the one you question into a trap, except making it seem that he has **failed the formula**? But just as the praetor restores the former, so philosophy **restores to the original state** <note>original: "in integrum restituit"</note> the latter." Thus says Seneca. Indeed, this very act of "restoring to the original state," if one transfers it from the courtroom to other things, is <term>ἀποκαθιστάναι</term> <note>original Greek: "apokathistanai," meaning to restore or reinstate</note>. The expression could be twisted so that a man might be said to have "lost his case" who has lost the right to scold his son because he provoked him to wickedness by his own example or by his excessive giving. Furthermore, that formula of speech, **to join hands according to the law** <note>original: "ex iure manu consertum"</note>, seems to be taken from the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE</note>, as Aulus Gellius indicates in the *Attic Nights*, Book 20, Chapter 9. In ancient times, those who had a controversy over a field or a similar thing would go to the site in person, and would "join hands" before the praetor for the sake of claiming possession—that is, one would grab the other’s hand. But when the borders of Italy were extended and it became a burden for the praetors to travel far for the sake of these claims, it was established that litigants should not join hands in person before the praetor, but should call for it **according to the law**, that is, one would call the other according to the law to join hands regarding the matter at stake. At the same time, having gone into the field in question, they would carry some of the earth from it, or a single clod of turf, into the city before the praetor, and they would make their claim on that clod as if it were the whole field. Marcus Tullius Cicero, writing to the lawyer Trebatius in Book 7 of his *Epistles*, says: "I only fear that your craft may be of little use to you. For as I hear, in those parts,

> They seek to recover property and strive for kingdoms
> **not by joining hands according to the law, but rather with the sword**,
> and they proceed by solid force."

Marcus Tullius expressed this kind of legal formula most wittily in his speech *In Defense of Lucius Murena*: "And so, being angry because they feared that if the method of their craft became public and known, legal action could be taken without their help, they composed certain signs so that they might be involved in all matters, even though this could be done most simply. 'The Sabine farm is mine.' 'No, mine.' Then the judgment. They wanted it thus: 'The farm,' he says, 'which is in the territory called Sabine.' Wordy enough. I grant you, what next? 'I say that it is mine according to the law.' What then? 'Thence and there I call you **according to the law to join hands**.' The man from whom the claim was made did not have a way to respond to such a talkative litigant. The lawyer steps across, in the manner of a Latin flute-player. 'From whence you called me to join hands according to the law,' he says, 'from thence and there I call you back.'" So far Marcus Tullius. The metaphor is taken from wars, in which those who fight at close quarters are said to "join hands," as Marcus Varro indicates in the second book of *On the Latin Language*.

### To divide an inheritance
### XVI

->Certain words have the status of a proverb for the very reason that they are either obsolete or peculiar to a certain profession. For example, the ancient lawyers used the word **herciscere** <note>an archaic legal term</note> to mean "to divide an inheritance." Hence, among lawyers, there is the **action for dividing the family estate** <note>original: "actio familiae herciscundae"</note>. Furthermore, the word "family" <note>original: "familia"</note> encompasses the entire inheritance and the inherited property. This action originated from the Twelve Tables, whose words are cited in the Code: "Co-heirs wishing to depart from common ownership shall act." If this is transferred to the division of any other thing, it will be proverbial. For instance, if someone should say: "Between Willi-<-

->CHILIAD FIVE, CENTURY II<-

...with Budé <note>original: "Budæum," referring to Guillaume Budé, the famous French humanist and legal scholar</note> and Leonardo Portio <note>original: "Leonardum Portium," an Italian legal expert</note> debating the discovery of the *as* <note>a Roman copper coin and unit of weight</note>, and Janus Lascaris <note>original: "Ianum Lascarem," a prominent Greek scholar in Italy</note> appointed as the arbiter of the glory of **partitioning the estate** <note>original: "herciscundæ," a legal term for dividing an inheritance</note>. Even in this century, some monks have not hesitated to **divide** <note>original: "herciscere"</note> property that was previously held in common among them, and to do so without a judge.

### XVII. To make the stones weep

This is a proverbial hyperbole used for a deeply pitiable situation, suggesting it is so lamentable that even stones are forced to weep. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the same book, says: "But you, even if you were defending a will, would act in such a way that the entire law of all wills would seem to rest on that trial; or if you were pleading a soldier's case, you would, in your usual way, have raised his father from the dead by your speaking; you would have placed him before their eyes, embraced the son, and weeping, commended him to the **hundred-man court** <note>original: "centumviris," a jury for civil cases</note>; you would, by Hercules, have forced all the stones to weep and lament, so that your use of the phrase **'as the tongue has spoken'** <note>original: "uti lingua nuncupasset," a technical legal phrase from the Twelve Tables</note> would seem written not in the **Twelve Tables** <note>the earliest code of Roman law, which Cicero famously admired</note>, which you prefer above all libraries, but in a magic incantation." Thus he spoke. The Lord used a similar hyperbole once or twice, when he replied to the Pharisees that the stones themselves would cry out if men kept silent. Again, when speaking to the Jews boasting of their noble lineage, he says that God could raise up children for Abraham even from stones. But perhaps nothing is hyperbolic for Christ, who can achieve whatever he wishes. However, in Cicero’s words, the mention of a magic incantation alludes to the proverb; for whatever moves the mind intensely is said to be more effective than any spell, as we have noted elsewhere.

### XVIII. Thonged spears

Marcus Tullius Cicero calls weapons prepared for battle **thonged spears** <note>original: "hastas amentatas"</note>. For a **thong** <note>original: "amentum"</note> is a leather strap attached to a spear, into which the hand is inserted to give the missile spear a spin when hurled. This can be metaphorically applied to a saying or a speech supplied to an orator by someone else. The passage in the book I have cited so far reads: "In that law which is disputed among the most expert, it is not difficult for an orator of either side he defends to find some authority from whom he may receive **thonged spears**, which he himself will hurl with the strength and muscles of an orator." Likewise in the *Brutus*, speaking of Titus Accius of Pisaurum: "He replied on behalf of Aulus Cluentius, speaking both accurately and quite copiously; he was, moreover, learned in the precepts of Hermagoras <note>a Greek teacher of rhetoric</note>, by which, even if the ornaments provided are not the best for speaking, yet just as **thonged spears** are easy to use, so certain ready arguments are handed down, fit for each type of case." Again in the *Topica*, discussing legal experts: "For they are often present, are called into counsel, and provide spears to diligent advocates who take refuge in their wisdom." Likewise, Quintilian in Book 12, Chapter 3: "Neither am I ignorant of our custom, nor have I forgotten those who sit, as it were, by the cases and supply weapons to those pleading; nor am I unaware that the Greeks did the same, whence the name **pragmatists** <note>original: "pragmaticorum," legal assistants who provided the raw material of law for orators to deliver</note> was given to them." Therefore, a weapon ready for hurling—where the invention belongs to another, but the delivery is yours—you might rightly call a "thonged spear." This is not unlike what we mentioned before regarding the shoe that one person puts on though it was stitched by another. Such a weapon and such a shoe was the speech of Lysias, which Socrates approved of as very elegant, but denied that it suited him.

### XIX. They prefer to hear the discus than the philosopher

The common crowd is more inclined toward any foolish pleasures than toward fruitful ones, which Marcus Tullius elegantly expressed in the second book of *On the Orator*. "They prefer," he says, "to hear the **discus** than the philosopher." Now, there was a type of public exercise in which a bronze discus was hurled from the ground high into the air with both skill and strength, so that it would fall within a certain space. However, in the same places where these games were performed, called **gymnasia**, philosophers also used to discourse. But when the clatter of the discus called, everyone would suddenly abandon the philosopher. These are the words of Crassus in Cicero: "For gymnasia were invented many centuries before philosophers began to chatter in them; and even now, when philosophers occupy all the gymnasia, their audience still prefers to hear the discus than the philosopher. As soon as it clatters, they all leave the philosopher—even while he is disputing in the middle of a speech about the greatest and gravest matters—for the sake of the **anointing** <note>original: "unctionis," referring to the oil athletes used before exercise</note>. Thus they prefer the lightest delight over what they themselves call the weightiest utility." As a joke, this can be transferred to a **serving platter** <note>original: "discum escarium"</note>, the clatter of which many hear more gladly than the voice of a philosopher.

### XX. To gather shells

It is a sign of extreme leisure to gather shells and **cockles** <note>original: "umbilicos," literally 'navels,' referring to spiral sea shells</note> on the seashore, which is usually a children's game. Although it can be transferred to those who, while doing something else, incidentally also [attend to] certain lighter [occupations] of the mind...

->DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM'S ADAGES<-

...mingle with grace. Crassus the orator, in Cicero’s second book *On the Orator*, speaking of Laelius and Scipio <note>Gaius Laelius and Scipio Aemilianus, famous Roman friends and statesmen often used as models of refined leisure</note>, says: "I do not dare speak of such great men, but Scaevola usually tells the story that they used to collect **sea snails** <note>original: "conchas"</note> and **pebbles** <note>original: "umbilicos," literally "navels," referring here to smooth, rounded sea-stones or shells</note> at Caieta and the Lucrine Lake, and would descend into every kind of relaxation and play of the mind." I believe he calls them "navels" either because they are shells or pebbles imitating the shape of a navel, or perhaps he refers to the herb called **Venus's navel** <note>original: "Veneris umbilicus," likely *Umbilicus rupestris*</note>, as Dioscorides notes. Nature has indeed played with an incredible variety in shells, as Pliny reports in Book 9, Chapter 33. "There are," he says, "so many differences of color and so many shapes: flat, concave, long, crescent-shaped, rounded into a circle, cut into a half-circle, raised in a hump, smooth, wrinkled, tooth-edged, striated, with the top twisted like a murex shell, the margin tapering to a point, spreading outward, or folded inward. Then there are distinctions: striped, blood-red, wandering like tunnels, combed like a scallop, overlapping like roof tiles, wavy, latticed like a net, spreading obliquely or straight, thickened, stretched out, curved, tied with a short knot, joined along the whole side, open for a clap, or curved back like a trumpet, etc." In the subterranean dwelling shown near Cumae in Italy—which the common people falsely claim was the cave of the **Sibyl** <note>The Cumaean Sibyl, a priestess and prophetess of Apollo</note>, though it is more likely it was a cave for robbers and pirates—one can see walls decorated with various patterns of shells imitating mosaic work. Valerius Maximus, in Book 8, Chapter 8, reports the same thing about Scipio and Laelius that Cicero narrates.

### XXI. He is not free who does not sometimes do nothing

Those who lived in the greatest leisure, holidaying from all business, were said to "do nothing." Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the same book, speaking through the persona of Crassus to Scaevola, says: "When, then, will you deal with public business? When with your friends'? When with your own? When, finally, will you **do nothing**?" Then I added this: "For a man does not seem to me to be free, who does not sometimes do nothing." This is what he said. Shortly after, he interprets what he means by "doing nothing." He says: "In which opinion I remain, Catulus, and when I come here, this very 'doing nothing' and being clearly at leisure delights me." For people are said to "be at leisure" <note>original: "cessare"</note> not only when they stop working, but when they are in a state of ease. It is helpful, however, to do nothing at times so that we may do other things correctly. Elsewhere, we have shown that those who engage in useless labor are also said to "do nothing."

### XXII. Luxury in the blade <note>original: "In herba luxuries"</note>

Farmers say that crops which grow more abundantly than is profitable are "luxuriating." They call this premature joy "luxury," which they correct by sending cattle or flocks into the field, a practice they call "grazing it down." Virgil <note>original: "Maro"</note> says:
> He grazes down the luxury of the crops while they are still in the tender blade.
Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the same book I just cited: "If our friend Sulpicius here did that, his speech would be much more concise; for now, as farmers usually say of crops, in its greatest richness there is a certain luxury which must be grazed down by the **stylus** <note>The tool used for writing; Erasmus means the speech needs to be edited and trimmed</note>."

### XXIII. To hold by the hem <note>original: "Lacinia tenere"</note>

Those who hold a matter lightly are said to "hold it by the hem," that is, by the very edge of the garment. The opposite of this is "to be held by the middle" <note>meaning to be held firmly or caught red-handed</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the third book of *On the Orator*: "For they hold that other kind, which is defined by times, places, and things, and even that they hold only by the hem." There is no doubt that Cicero drew this metaphor from common speech; for the same saying survives today among our people, used when someone gives an unenthusiastic invitation. From this comes the phrase "to tear the cloak" <note>original: "scindere penulam," meaning to pull on someone's coat to keep them from leaving</note>. And in Terence, Mysis pulls Geta back by his cloak. Cicero seems to have alluded to that line of Plautus in *The Ass-Dealer*: "Weeping, she holds him by the hem, weeping herself."

### XXIV. To break off a twig <note>original: "Surculum defringere"</note>

In a similar fashion, he said in the same place "to break off a twig" for the act of not mastering an entire discipline, but plucking a tiny bit from it that suits the present business; just as lawyers sometimes use a certain opinion as a formula. And they speak thus far, even using this division of instruction, but in such a way that they do not seem to act by law or judgment—as in, finally, recovering lost possession—but rather to make use of civil law by "breaking off a twig."

### XXV. A useful lie

The rich man in the satirist Juvenal says: "For what is infamy if the money is safe?" and Terence's Dorio is not ashamed of his vanity, as long as it is for profit. But it is closer to honorable behavior what Orestes says in Sophocles' *Electra*:
> I think no word that brings profit is bad. <note>original Greek: "Δοκῶ μὲν οὐδὲν ῥῆμα σὺν κέρδει κακόν"</note>
That is:
I reckon no word which is for gain to be evil.

She feels that hesitation is ruinous when immediate danger presses.

has cast men down and, at the same time, raised them up.
He [Sophocles] suggests that sometimes great errors are born from a few poorly understood words, and even the correction of an error can come from a few words correctly understood. The saying about the gravest punishments following from the lightest matter was discussed elsewhere.

This is related to that other proverb, "Not even Hercules against two." Catullus also alluded to this in his *Marriage Song* <note>original: "Epithalamio"</note>:

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s commentary on Sophocles’ *Electra*, specifically focusing on the interactions between Orestes, Electra, and their mother Clytemnestra. The previous page discussed the tactical rumors used by Orestes; here, Erasmus explores the moral and philosophical implications of their actions and the inevitability of divine justice.</meta>

# DES. ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM’S ADAGES

...and by plotting the death of her son, she had taught the children to hate their mother. A little later, he explains this:
> Deeds find their own words. <note>original: "τὰ δ᾽ ἔργα τοὺς λόγους εὑρίσκεται" (*ta d' erga tous logous heurisketai*)</note>
-> that is, <-
Furthermore, the facts themselves discover their own words.
There is a famous saying of Socrates, that everyone should prove themselves to be such in reality as they would wish to be thought. For fame is born from deeds as if from a fountain—good from good, bad from bad. Therefore, he who has produced an ignominious reputation for himself by shameful deeds should not be angry with those who speak ill of him, for it is he himself who opened the mouths of the people. Nor should he seek vengeance against his detractors, but rather strive to wipe away the foul rumor with good deeds.

### The wrath of the Deity is inevitable. XXXII

In Homer, Jupiter, when threatening his wife, calls his hands "invincible" <note>original: "ἀάπτους" (*aaptous*), literally untouchable or irresistible</note>, because they harm whomever he wishes, while they cannot be harmed by anyone in return. Similar is what the tutor of Orestes says in the same play:
> But when one of the gods
> inflicts harm, not even the strong could flee. <note>original: "ὅταν δέ τις θεῶν, βλάπτῃ, δύναιτ᾽ ἂν οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἰσχύων φυγεῖν"</note>
-> that is, <-
But when any of the gods harms a man,
No one, however powerful, could avoid it.
People are accustomed to blame this or that cause for their calamities, when in fact most evils happen so entirely beyond expectation that it is clear they are sent from the powers above. Against the decree of the deity, human providence has no power.

### Where on earth are you being swept? XXXIII

Those who are not attentive to the matter at hand are said "not to be at home." Those who wander further from the truth are said to be "in another region." Electra, responding to her sister who announced that Orestes (who was said to be dead) was alive, replies:
> I know not to what ground, nor to what thought you are being carried. <note>original: "οὐκ οἶδ᾽ ὅποι γῆς, οὐδ᾽ ὅποι γνώμης φέρῃ"</note>
-> that is, <-
You do not understand to what soil you are being swept,
Nor where your mind carries you.
The proverb is a <term>trope</term> <note>A figurative use of a word or expression</note>. Thus, it is aptly said of one who wanders from the subject: "Where is he rushing off to now?" or "To what region is he being carried away?" It seems to be a metaphor taken from sailors.

### For the well-born, it is shameful to live badly. XXXIV

Some people think that for this very reason they are permitted to live disgracefully—because they were born to honorable ancestors—when, on the contrary, the brightness of one's lineage acts like a torch held up, ensuring that the errors of the noble carry more disgrace than those born of an obscure family. Electra expressed this in the same play:
> To live basely is a base thing for those born well. <note>original: "ζῆν αἰσχρὸν αἰσχρῶς τοῖς καλῶς πεφυκόσι"</note>
-> that is, <-
For those born honorably, it is shameful to live shamefully.
However, Electra considers those to live shamefully not who are of wicked character, but who live in slavery despite being born free; this agrees with that saying: "When you are no longer who you once were, there is no reason why you should wish to live."

### The dead do not feel pain. XXXV

The same woman, in the same play, indicating that she will seek an end to her evils through a voluntary death, says:
> For I do not see the dead suffering. <note>original: "τοὺς γὰρ θανόντας οὐχ ὁρῶ λυπουμένους"</note>
-> that is, <-
For I see no dead person in pain.
For this reason, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and philosopher</note> thinks that no greater benefit has been given to man by the gods than the fact that every person has it in their own hand to exit life when they wish. Socrates speaks better, teaching that it is a crime for the soul to depart the garrison of the body without the command of God the commander.

### Harmful in every way. XXXVI

In the same work, when Orestes asks in what ways Clytemnestra was troublesome—whether by her hands or by poison—Electra replies:
> By hands, and by outrages, and by all evils. <note>original: "Καὶ χερσὶ καὶ λύμαισι καὶ πᾶσιν κακοῖς"</note>
-> that is, <-
By hand and by poisons and, in short, by all evils.
This will apply to a man who is destructive in every way: through deceits, force, words, and deeds.

### To summon from the head; to lead from the source. XXXVII

When a matter is traced back to its primary point, it is said to be "summoned from the head" <note>In Latin, *caput* (head) often means the source or origin</note>. Marcus Tullius Cicero, in the second book of *On the Orator*: "It is also a matter of our age and experience to summon what we want from the head, and to see from where everything flows." Likewise, in the first book of *On the Laws*: "Indeed, brother, you trace the things we seek deeply and, as I believe, from the head." And a little later in the same work: "Do you wish, then, that we trace the origin of Law itself from the source?" What he previously called "from the head," he here calls "from the source." Again, in the *Topics*, when an argument is drawn from the genus...

<meta>catchword: then,</meta>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Latin and Greek idioms, specifically focusing on metaphors related to theater, geometry, physical training, and athletics as used by Marcus Tullius Cicero and other classical authors. The previous page concluded a series of Greek poetic references; this page transitions into Roman rhetorical and legal metaphors.</meta>

...then it will not be necessary to summon it all the way from the head <note>original: "a capite"</note>. In his *Tusculan Disputations*, Cicero says in one place "to lead from the head" <note>original: "A capite ducere"</note>, used in place of repeating something from the very beginning.

->In the manner of a Latin flute-player. XXXVIII<-

In the words of Marcus Tullius Cicero which we cited just a moment ago from his oration *In Defense of Lucius Murena*, a proverb was embedded when he said that a legal expert, once the petitioner is prepared, "shifts to the side of the one being sued in the manner of a Latin flute-player," <note>original: "Latini tibicinis more"</note> and proceeds to instruct that person with the solemn legal formulas. Where this comparison originated is not entirely clear, except for what seems to be a probable conjecture: that it is derived from those ancient Latins who, in rural districts or small towns, acted out plays with only a single flute-player. The actors would match their voices and gestures to the player’s melody; otherwise, due to their lack of skill, they would not be able to keep the rhythm of the verse. Therefore, after that flute-player had played for one actor, he was forced to cross over to the other actor who was to respond, and in turn lead him through the measures of the meter with the sounding of the pipe—and from there, back to the other again. This was because rustic men could not properly perform the movements of verses or Mimes without a flute-player leading them. This conjecture is supported by a passage in Marcus Tullius’s *The Orator*, dedicated to Brutus, where he discusses verses composed in such a way that they might seem like free and loose speech. "Of these," he says, "there are some similar examples even among our own writers, such as those in the play *Thyestes*: 'Who shall I say you are, who in late old age...' and what follows; which, unless a flute-player is added <note>original: "nisi cum tibicen accessit"</note>, are very much like loose prose." That earlier passage from the oration is also cited as a proverb: "To lose one's case" <note>original: "Causa cadere"</note>.

->To bring into a square. XXXIX<-

Earlier, drawing from Aristotle, we taught that a man of steadfast mind is called "square" <note>original: "tetragonos"</note>, because that figure is the same from every side. From this, whatever is fitting and appropriate is said to "square up." Marcus Tullius, in *The Orator*, applied this to a speech that is elegant and composed with fitting rhythms. Thus, he says, after this "rounding off," or "comprehension," or "continuity," or "circuit" <note>original: "ambitus"</note>—if we may call it that—was born, no one of any reputation wrote a speech of the kind intended for pleasure (and removed from the courts and legal combat) without reducing almost all his thoughts into "squareness" <note>original: "in quadrum"</note> and rhythm. This metaphor is drawn from stonemasons. I am mindful that I have placed this elsewhere, but I wanted to show the passage more clearly, for there I had only briefly indicated it.

->Unpracticed in the wrestling school. XL<-

Marcus Tullius, in the same work, testifies that uncoordinated men who lack art are called <term>ἀπάλαισοι</term> (*apalaisoi*) by the Greeks—as if you were to say they are "strangers to the wrestling school" <note>the *palaestra* was the ancient Greek wrestling school where physical grace was developed</note>. Those who are exercised in the wrestling school possess a certain grace even in their other actions. As he indicates in *The Orator*, "It is not as if everything is contained in it, but it helps in such a way as the wrestling school helps an actor." Such is the dancing of the Cyclops and of Silenus. I will add Cicero’s own words: "Therefore, just as the movement of those whom the Greeks call <term>ἀπάλαισοι</term> is, so the speech of those who do not close their sentences with rhythms seems to me." In his book *On the Best Kind of Orator*, he used the phrase "to walk in the manner of the wrestling school" <note>original: "palaestrice spaciari"</note> to mean walking with a becoming and rhythmic gesture. "These things," he says, "were avoided by almost everyone who is either counted among the Attics or speaks in the Attic style; but so long as they wished to be considered merely healthy and austere, they should be allowed to 'walk in the manner of the wrestling school in the Xystus' <note>the *Xystus* was a covered portico for exercise</note>, but not so as to 'seek a crown from Olympia.'" Indeed, this very phrase, "to seek a crown from Olympia," <note>original: "ab Olympiis coronam petere"</note> has the appearance of a proverb, meaning to strive for great and solid praise from difficult matters—that is, to win in serious and weighty cases. Those who argue for pleasure in private within the porticoes are "walking in the Xystus"; those who conduct serious cases in the forum step out into "the sun and the dust," undertaking great danger in the hope of great praise.

->To fall in the race. XLI<-

Marcus Tullius said "to fall in the race" <note>original: "Cadere in cursu"</note> to mean being frustrated of the praise one sought. It is like someone who, while striving for the theological laurel <note>Erasmus compares the classical race to the pursuit of a Doctorate in Theology</note>, dies before he reaches the highest peak of that title. Marcus Tullius, in his book *On Famous Orators*, speaking of Galba: "Our fathers used to praise this man; they even favored him because of the memory of his father, but he 'fell in the race.' For when he spoke on his own behalf regarding the Manilian law and the hatred of the Jugurthine conspiracy, he was overwhelmed." By a similar trope, we are said to "recall from the race" <note>original: "e cursu revocare"</note> those whom we draw away from a purpose to something else. And those who are striving toward something with great zeal are said to be "in the race." The metaphor is taken from public contests of those running on foot or with horses.

->Titius. XLII<-

Those who gestured in a disorganized and loose manner were said "to dance the Titius." For there was a kind of dancing of this sort which took its name from a certain bad orator named Titius. Marcus Tullius, in the work I just cited...

# THE ADAGES OF DESIDERIUS ERASMUS OF ROTTERDAM

...we have noted in that work: Whom Sextus Titius followed, a man truly talkative and sharp enough, but so loose and effeminate in his gestures that a certain dance was born from him, to which the name "Titius" was given. Thus, one must take care lest in acting or speaking you do something the imitation of which might be mocked. Quintilian cites this passage of Cicero in his eleventh book, in the chapter on delivery. Similar to these are "to dance the Cyclops" <note>original: "saltare Cyclopem"</note>. Horace writes: "He asked that he might dance the Cyclops." And "to dance the cordax" <note>A provocative, rhythmic dance associated with Old Comedy</note>, in the manner of Silenus.

<margin>XLIII</margin>
->Like a statue by Phidias.<-

Things which are approved by the consensus of everyone at the very first glance are said "to please like a statue by Phidias" <note>Phidias was the most celebrated sculptor of ancient Greece, famous for the statue of Zeus at Olympia</note>. For certain statues do not smile upon us immediately, but when inspected frequently and more closely, they begin to please us little by little. Marcus Tullius Cicero says in the same book: "For the talent of Quintus Hortensius, even when he was quite a young man, was like a statue by Phidias: it was no sooner seen than it was approved." He first spoke in the Forum during the consulship of Lucius Crassus and Quintus Scaevola; before these very consuls—who surpassed everyone else in intelligence—he departed having been approved by their judgment as well as that of the bystanders. He was nineteen years old at that time. Thus says Cicero. I believe, moreover, that Cicero is thinking of the Olympian Jupiter, which the illustrious Athenian sculptor Phidias fashioned, as Pliny reports in book 34, chapter 8, and book 36, chapter 5.

<margin>XLIIII</margin>
->To count for something.<-

Those who begin to be held in some value are said "to come into the number" <note>original: "In numerum peruenire"</note>; just as those who are held in some esteem are said "to be in some number," and those who are utterly despised are said to be "in no number." Marcus Tullius in the same book says: "For by these things, though born in the lowest station, having attained honors, influence, and money, he had even come to count for something <note>original: "in numerum peruenerat"</note> among the legal patrons, despite having no learning or natural talent." and a little later, speaking of Gaius Sicinius: "Possessing these qualities and coming prepared to his cases, not lacking for words, by that very comparison and training in speaking he had already come to count among the number of patrons."

<margin>XLV</margin>
->To know by a mole.<-

"To know by a mole" <note>original: "E neuo cognoscere"</note> is to judge a man's entire character from some very small thing, just as we say "to recognize the lion by its claws," and as Protogenes recognized Apelles by a single line. Marcus Tullius in his book *On Famous Orators*: "Now, since you seem to want to know me not just by some mole or by birth-tokens, but by my whole body, I shall also embrace some things which might perhaps seem less necessary." The metaphor is taken from those who, when they cast away or abandon infants, add birth-tokens <note>term: crepundia; small tokens or rattles hung around a baby's neck to help identify them later if they were found</note> through which they might be recognized if by chance the opportunity arose; or perhaps the parents note some mole on the body. Bankers sometimes add such a mark to their financial contracts.

<margin>XLVI</margin>
->Be not ashamed of the craft.<-

There was a verse once tossed about in popular speech: "Be not ashamed to speak openly of the craft you practice." <note>original: "Ne pudeat artem proloqui quam facitites"</note> Many are not ashamed to live by a shameful trade, even while they are ashamed to profess the name of that trade. For example, if someone practicing usury would prefer to be called a "businessman." Marcus Tullius cites the verse in the same book: "As for me, if that very well-known verse, which forbids being ashamed to speak of the craft you practice, does not allow me to hide the fact that this work delights me, then your own zeal has squeezed this volume out of me."

<margin>XLVII</margin>
->To act the Dorian.<-

"To act the Dorian" <note>original Greek: Δωριάζειν (*Doriazein*)</note> was a phrase used in the past for those who walked about with their bodies exposed in an unseemly manner. It is derived from the young women in the Peloponnese who were accustomed to be ungirded and without tunics, covered only by a cloak that was open on both sides like a window, through which the naked parts of the body were visible. Among the Spartans, moreover, the young women walked about entirely naked on certain days. Juvenal complains much regarding the transparent, thin garments <note>term: multicia; soft, sheer, or transparent garments considered decadent or effeminate in Rome</note> of the Romans.

<margin>XLVIII</margin>
->The Aetolians.<-

"In the Aetolian way" <note>original Greek: Αἰτωλιστί (*Aetolisti*)</note> was a term used in the past as a proverbial joke for those who, according to the customs of the Aetolians, were grasping and persistent. It is a pun on the word: just as those greedy for gifts were said "to speak Doric," so they seem to be called "Aetolian speakers" because they ask for everything, the name being derived from the Greek "to ask for the whole" <note>original: "para to holon aitein"</note>. Stephanus mentions this.

<margin>XLIX</margin>
->The Charonites.<-

In the past, the nickname "Charonites" <note>original Greek: Χαρωνίται; those belonging to Charon, the ferryman of the dead</note> was given in a popular Roman joke to those who, by using the private papers of a deceased person, protected the illegal things they were doing. It originated from this: When Mark Antony, having delivered a funeral oration and displayed the robe of Julius Caesar, had incited the people against Caesar's killers, he seized Caesar's Commentaries (the records containing his official acts) and wrote into them whatever he pleased. He then pretended to act on the authority of these papers in whatever he did, assigning magistracies to some...

...magistrates, recalling some from exile and freeing others from their chains. Because all these people excused their actions by citing the notebooks of the deceased <note>Julius Caesar</note>, they were called in a common joke <term>Cheironitae</term> <note>original: "χειρωνῖται" — literally "Hand-men." A pun on those who benefitted from the "handwritten" notes Mark Antony claimed to have found in Caesar's papers, which were widely suspected to be forgeries.</note>, as Plutarch records in his *Life of Mark Antony*. Some people misuse wills with a similar trick, to whom the same nickname would equally apply.

<margin>L</margin>
### To carry in one's eyes, and similar phrases.
These are also proverbial: **To carry in one's eyes**, and **To carry in one's bosom**, used when someone loves and cherishes another remarkably well. It is a metaphor taken from mothers who love to hold their children, from whom they do not turn their eyes—anxious lest any trouble befall them—and whom they carry in their bosoms and in their embrace. Examples of both are frequent in Marcus Tullius Cicero. Not dissimilar is the phrase in Plato's *Republic*, book 10: **to carry upon their heads** <note>original: "ἐπὶ ταῖς κεφαλαῖς περιφέρειν"</note>. That is, "And because of this wisdom they are loved so greatly that their followers all but **carry them around on their heads**."

<margin>LI</margin>
### Older than Iapetus.
**Older than Iapetus** <note>original: "Ἰαπέτου ἀρχαιότερος"</note>. In Lucian, Jupiter addresses Cupid, who is making excuses for his childhood: "You are a mere child, O Cupid, you who are **much older than Iapetus**" <note>Iapetus was one of the Titans, the son of Uranus and Gaia, representing the most ancient generation of the Greek gods. To be older than a Titan is to be ancient beyond reckoning.</note>.

### Older than the world.
Hesiod, in his poem the *Theogony*, uses the phrase **older than the world itself** <note>original: "κόσμου πρεσβύτερος"</note>. This is a hyperbolic expression used to describe anything that is extraordinarily ancient.

### The Front Cover

The volume is encased in a <term>blind-tooled pigskin binding<gloss>a method of decorating leather by pressing heated metal stamps or rollers into the surface without using gold or pigments, creating a darkened, recessed design</gloss></term>. The decoration is composed of multiple rectangular borders surrounding a central scene.

The outer borders feature a repeating pattern of stylized leaves. Moving inward, a secondary border contains figures housed in small architectural niches, representing the three theological virtues:
*   **Faith** <note>original: FIDES</note>
*   **Hope** <note>original: SPES</note>
*   **Charity** <note>original: CARITAS</note>

The central focal point is a detailed panel showing the biblical story of Jael and Sisera. In this scene, the heroine Jael is shown inside a tent, using a mallet to drive a tent stake into the head of the sleeping Canaanite general, Sisera. Below this image, the following inscription is carved:

->SO MAY ALL YOUR ENEMIES PERISH<-
->O LORD — JUDGES 5:31<-

<note>original: "SIC • PEREANT • OMNES • INIMICI • TVI • DOMINE • IVDICVM • V • 81" — The carver or binder appears to have made a numbering error, as the quote comes from verse 31 of Judges chapter 5, the "Song of Deborah."</note>
